### Series title page

THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COLLATIONED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH SEVERAL MANUSCRIPTS, VERY CAREFULLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIOUS READINGS; ENLARGED WITH ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE GREAT EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; PROVIDED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; ENLARGED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, AS WELL AS WITH WORKS POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY AND WEIGHT IN RELATION TO ecclesiastical tradition; AND ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: THE FIRST, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH FATHER HAS WRITTEN ON ANY TOPIC MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE SECOND, OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY EASILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHICH PLACES OF THEIR WORKS, HAVE COMMENTED ON THE INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF THE BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, AND EASILY PREFERABLE TO ALL OTHERS IF ONE CONSIDERS THE CLARITY OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE PERFECTION OF THE CORRECTION, THE VARIETY AND NUMBER OF THE REPRINTED WORKS, THE VERY CONVENIENT FORMAT OF THE VOLUMES, CONSTANTLY AND UNIFORMLY MAINTAINED THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE WORK, THE LOW PRICE, AND ABOVE ALL THIS COLLECTION—SINGLE, METHODICAL, AND CHRONOLOGICAL—OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND SHORT WORKS HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT NOW BROUGHT TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS RELATING TO ALL AGES, PLACES, LANGUAGES, AND FORMS.

# [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF SAINT ISIDORE]

[Col. 0009]

## TWO BOOKS OF THE DIFFERENCES OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, OR ON THE PROPER USE OF WORDS

[Note: [Col. 0009A] All notes whose author is not named are by Pantinus; the various readings appearing in the text within square brackets are likewise to be attributed to him. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0009B] The books *On Differences of Words and Things* have been discussed at length in the Isidorian studies, chapter 56. Since there are two forms of the book *On Differences of Words*—one arranged alphabetically, which Grial placed first with the notes of P. Pantinus, and another without that arrangement, which the same Grial took from the Bignaean Edition—we present the first form as genuine and consign the second to the Appendices as doubtful. I have rearranged Pantinus’s notes and various readings, often placed obscurely, into a better order as far as I could. Barthius, in book 39 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 6, produced the preface from one of his own manuscript codices, with some discrepancy in the wording, such as “the poets confused through necessity ... and for you who read.” He adds other conjectures, which will be indicated below in their proper places. In the Vatican manuscript codex 3321, which I shall cite repeatedly, the following various readings occur: “Most often the ancients ... are distinguished by origin ... I myself have extracted very few,” and I have noted them below for the pleasure of readers. AREV.]

(C)

## Preface

[Note: [Col. 0009B] PREFACE.—Servius, on the passage in *Aeneid* 1: “Among leafy groves.”]

### ISIDORE GREETS THE READER

**1.** Many of the ancients endeavored to distinguish differences in speech, investigating more subtly some distinction between one word and another. But the pagan poets, through metrical necessity, confused the proper uses of words. Thus the practice arose of accepting many expressions indiscriminately from authors, although, despite appearing similar, they are distinguished from one another by a certain proper origin. Among the Latins Cato was the first to write about these matters. Following his example, I have both published a very few myself and drawn others from the books of authors, and have set them down below for you, reader, for the pleasure of readers.

# BOOK ONE: ON DIFFERENCES OF WORDS

[Col. 0009]

## 2. On the letter A

[Col. 0009A]

[Note: [Col. 0009B]

**1.** C. Fronto: “*Aptum* is appropriate to a place and to a time; usage has made *utile* mean useful.”

[Col. 0010A] In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has: “and *utile*—what is the difference?” And in each individual difference it adds, “what the difference is.” AREV.]

**1.** Between *aptum* and *utile*. *Aptum* is appropriate to a particular time; *utile* is useful permanently.

**2.** Between *amicus* and *socius*. A friend is constituted by affection, an associate by a matter or undertaking, because an association is constituted by partnership.

[Note: [Col. 0010A]

**3.** *Abrogans*, meaning humble, perhaps is not found in other writers, but it is not inelegant, says Barthius. For it may be observed that many Latin words which admit *ad-* as an addition also admit *ab-* as a subtraction. AREV.]

**3.** Between *arrogantem* and *abrogantem*. The arrogant person is proud; the *abrogans* is humble. The arrogant person assumes confidence for himself; the *abrogans* takes it away—that is, denies it.

[Note: [Col. 0010B]

**4.** *Etymologies*, book 10, letters A and C.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript omits *desiderat* (“desires”). AREV.]

**4.** Between the avaricious person and the covetous person. The avaricious person is one who does not use what is his; the covetous person desires what belongs to another.

[Note: [Col. 0010B]

**5.** See Nonius, under the entry *Cupido* (“Desire”).

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript omits *ubi* (“when”) after the second *illico*. The same manuscript reads “love from wives.” Barthius says that Cato’s words are exceedingly elegant: when desire enters, honest and Socratic love departs. He reads *Philippi* (“of Philip”) and suspects that some invective of Cato against Philip, or a “Philippic,” is meant. In Barthius’s codex the reading was *obscenus in aeternum* (“obscene forever”); although Barthius corrected it to *obscenus meretricum* (“the obscenity of prostitutes”), he nevertheless wondered whether one might read *obscenus in tenerum* (“obscene toward the tender”), as though the subject were love turned away from Venus, as in the distinction between the impure and the shameless. *Pasiphae* would be better. AREV.]

**5.** Between love and desire. “One thing is,” says Cato, “love at a distance, Philip, and another is desire. The one immediately entered when the other withdrew: one is good, the other bad.” Others more correctly said that love may be both good and bad, whereas desire is always bad. Love has a fourfold distinction: it may be just, dutiful, cruel, or obscene. Just love is the love of wives; dutiful love, of children; cruel love is against nature, as in the case of Pasiphae; obscene love belongs to prostitutes.

[Note: [Col. 0010B]

**6.** I would prefer: “What comes of its own accord to one who is beginning ...”

In the same place: *consolantur* (“they console”); variants: *consulantur* (“they are consulted”), *consultantur* (“they deliberate”).]

**6.** Between auspices and auguries. Auspices are signs that are initiated and come of their own accord; auguries are signs that are consulted and follow.

[Col. 0011A]

[Note: [Col. 0011C]

**7.** The Vatican manuscript gives: “argumentation, which in debate establishes and produces confidence in assertions.” AREV.]

**7.** Between an argument and argumentation. An argument briefly discloses the matter at the beginning of a book; argumentation is what establishes confidence in assertions during a debate.

**3**

[Note: [Col. 0011C]

**8.** The Vatican manuscript has “a liberal art” and shortly afterward “consists in the hands.” AREV.]

**8.** Between art and craftsmanship. Art is liberal by nature; craftsmanship, on the other hand, consists in work performed by the hands.

[Note: [Col. 0011C]

**9.** *Arcanum* (“secret”). Servius, on the passage of the *Aeneid*: “I shall disclose hidden things.” Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 20, chapter 9.

—*Arces* (“fortresses”). *Etymologies*, book 15, chapter 2.

—*Arca* (“chest”). Varro, book 4 of *On the Latin Language*, under the entry *Arca*; and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 20, chapter 9.

—*Arceat* (“may ward off”). It seemed appropriate in the *Etymologies*.

—*Arcus* (“bow”). *Etymologies*, book 18, chapter 9.

In the same place, the Vatican codex has “which are stripped off” instead of “which are woven.” AREV.]

**9.** Between hidden and concealed. Something concealed (*absconsum*) is hidden by some artifice; something hidden (*absconditum*) is naturally kept away. It is said to be *conditum* (“stored away”), not *consum*. Hence *consuere* (“to sew together”) is also used, when things that have been torn apart and opened are sewn together. Moreover, *occultum* (“hidden”) is derived from *occulere*, that is, “to close.” *Arcanum* (“secret”) comes from *arca* (“chest”) or from *arcere* (“to ward off”), because everyone is kept away from it—that is, prohibited from it. Hence fortresses are also called *arces*, because enemies are kept away from them. Hence also a chest is called an *arca*, because it wards off a thief. Hence likewise a bow is called an *arcus*, because it wards off an adversary.

**10.** Between *ante* and *antea*. *Ante* signifies place and person; *antea* signifies time alone.

[Note: [Col. 0011C]

**11.** See Acron, ode 27 of book 3 of Horace.

Variant: “Between *accubuit*, *recubuit*, and *decubuit*.” Barthius thinks that the word *dominus* (“master”) should be moved back to *decubuit*, which is not convincing. By *cubitus* (“elbow”) Horace raises himself according to Roman custom: “And remain leaning on your pressed elbow.” In codex 3984 of the old Vatican Library, in which the regulations of the vice-chancellery under John XXII are written in a semi-Gothic script, the following verses are prefixed:

“The healthy man goes to bed; the injured man goes to lie down;

One who reclines sleeps; one who reclines at table takes the dishes;

He lies with another and commits adultery; he prostrates himself and worships the deity;

He dies; the defeated man is said to yield;

He who lies down is lying; the wakeful keeps watch; the bird broods.”

AREV.]

**11.** Between *accubuit* and *recubuit* there is this difference: the dinner guest *accubuit*—reclined in the dining room; the master *recubuit*—reclined in the bedroom; the sick person *decubuit*—lay down. For *accubare* means to recline with the whole body, whereas *accumbere* means to lean on the elbow.

**12.** Between *abscedit* and *discedit*. Something *abscedit* when it withdraws from any part; but what divides away from the middle *discedit*.

[Note: [Col. 0011D]

**13.** *Etymologies*, book 5, chapter 26.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript omits this difference: “Between adultery, etc.” AREV.]

**13.** Between adultery and fornication. Adultery is desiring another man’s wife; fornication is not the adulteration of the marriage covenant, but committing sexual misconduct with other unmarried persons.

[Col. 0011C]

[Note: [Col. 0012C]

**14.** These are Servius’s words, on the passage of *Aeneid* 2, “Tossed upon lands and the deep”: one must nevertheless understand *altum* (“deep”) as signifying both upper and lower height.

—*Sublime*. *Etymologies*, book 10, letters L, T, and S.

—*Arduum*. Servius likewise interprets the passage of *Georgics* 2, “The lofty palm,” as meaning either high or something difficult to reach.]

**14.** Between *altum*, *excelsum*, *sublime*, and *arduum*. *Altum* applies to both the upper and lower direction; *excelsum* only to the upper. *Sublime* is what is elevated with some dignity; *arduum* is what is elevated with some difficulty. Thus one says “a deep well” and “a high wall.” You will see the highest things *in excelsum* (“in the elevated”), and the lowest things *in alto* (“in the deep”).

[Note: [Col. 0012C]

**15.** One manuscript has *adnixum*. Servius, whom Isidore generally follows, nevertheless prefers the other reading, on *Aeneid* 1: “Triton leaning against the sharp ...”

—*Obnixum*. An old glossary: ἀντίσχοντα, “resisting.” Nonius: “struggling against an adversary.”

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “attempting something ... and columns.” AREV.]

**15.** Between *adnisum*, *innixum*, *subnixum*, and *obnixum*. *Adnisum* means striving toward something; *innixum*, leaning upon something, as when someone leans on a staff or a column. *Subnixum* means equipped with some plan or supported on every side; *obnixum* means obstinate or persevering.

[Note: [Col. 0012C]

**16.** From Agraetius.

In the same place, Vulpius, commenting on Catullus, poem 38, observes that *alloqui* is sometimes used in the sense of “to console.” AREV.]

**16.** Between *alloqui*, *obloqui*, and *eloqui*. *Alloqui* belongs to one who urges or commands; *obloqui* to one who disparages; *eloqui* to an orator.

[Note: [Col. 0012C]

**17.** See Nonius, under the entries *amare* and *diligere*.

—To Dolabella, *Letters to Friends*, book 9, letter 24.

—As for *diligere*, *Etymologies*, book 10, letter D.

In the same place, Barthius points to similar words of Cicero from book 9 of the *Letters to Friends*, letter 14, and adds that *diligere*, meaning “to love exceedingly,” has this force in more than one passage of Suetonius. AREV.]

**17.** Cicero thinks that *amare* and *diligere* differ, and often uses them so as to distinguish them: *amare* means “to love ardently,” while *diligere* means “to love more mildly,” as in his letters to Brutus: “Farewell,” he says, “and love us; or, if that is too much, esteem us.” And again: “Thus you will act: either you will love me, or—and this is enough for me—you will esteem me.” Likewise, in a letter to Dolabella: “Who would have thought that anything could be added to the love I had for you? So much has been added that only now do I seem to love you; previously I merely esteemed you.” Others have said that *amare* is naturally implanted in us, whereas *diligere* arises by choice.

[Note: [Col. 0012D]

**18.** Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 6, chapter 4.]

**18.** *Abicere* and *proicere* differ. What is held in contempt and neglected is cast away (*abicitur*); what lies entirely outside safety and is alien to blessedness is cast out (*proicitur*). *Proicere* is as though it meant “to cast away forward.”

[Note: [Col. 0012D]

**19.** From Agraetius, where *compescere* (“to restrain”) is wrongly printed as *compensare*, and the words “sometimes to accuse, sometimes something” are missing, as in the Paris Edition.

—*Causam*. “The cause of a cause” occurs in Agraetius.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “they display causes.” AREV.]

**19.** Between *arguere* and *coarguere*. *Coarguere* means to restrain and check; *arguere* means sometimes to accuse, sometimes to show or disclose something. Virgil, *Aeneid* 4: “Fear exposes their degenerate spirits.” Hence *argumenta* (“arguments”) are also so called, because they display the cause.

[Note: [Col. 0012D]

**20.** The Vatican manuscript has *quisque proxime* (“each one nearest”). Below it has: “Likewise he looks around—perhaps *circumspiciens*, ‘looking around’—and seeks to discern. For ...” AREV.]

**20.** Between *adlidere* and *elidere*. Someone is struck against something nearby (*adliditur*); someone is dashed out or crushed at a distance (*eliditur*).

[Col. 0013A]

[Note: [Col. 0013C]

**21.** From Agraetius, where “we look upward” is wrong; this should be corrected.

—It should be noted. From Servius, on *Aeneid* 1: “Looking down upon the winged sea.”

—“But if.” Variant: “because if.” Servius.

—“Sometimes.” Servius.

—*Inquirere* (“to inquire”). *Inquirens* (“inquiring”), Servius.]

**21.** Between *aspicere*, *respicere*, and so forth. We look before us (*aspicimus*); we look back (*respicimus*); we look upward (*suspicimus*); we look downward (*despicimus*); we look inward (*inspicimus*); we look into the distance (*prospicimus*, variant *perspicimus*); we look all around (*conspicimus*). Likewise, we look at present things with *aspicimus*, at past things with *respicimus*, and toward future things with *prospicimus*. But someone who turns to the right and left *aspectat*—looks at these things—rather than *aspicit*—looks toward them. It should certainly be noted that if we also say *despiciens* (“looking down”), we sometimes mean “inquiring carefully.” Likewise, one who *circum-inspicit*—or *circumspicit*—seeks to see what he cannot discern. For *circum-inspicere*—or *circumspicere*—means “to seek.”

[Note: [Col. 0013C]

**22.** The commentators on Terence, *Eunuchus*, act 3, scene 4: properly speaking, *intendere* means to bring an accusation against an adversary.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “is for a good purpose.” AREV.]

**22.** Between *attendere* and *intendere*. *Attendere* means to look at; *intendere* means to accuse, either with a view to killing or to inflicting injury. Very rarely, however, it is used in a good sense.

**23.** Between *audire* and *exaudire*: both good and evil people are heard (*audiuntur*), but only the good are heard favorably (*exaudiuntur*).

[Note: [Col. 0013C]

**24.** From Agraetius. See also Nonius, under the entry *Adolere* (“to grow”).

[Col. 0013D] Perhaps it may be read, from Servius, on *Aeneid* 6, “To grow in wondrous ways”: *concrescere* (“to grow together”). I nevertheless think it closer to the truth that we should read, from Agraetius, *inolescere coaugmenti* (“*inolescere* belongs to increase”), and add a third member, *exolescere* (“to fade away”), belonging to disappearance.]

**24.** Between *adolescere* and *inolescere*. *Adolescere* belongs to increase; *inolescere* to becoming accustomed.

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**25.** From Agraetius.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “in the present.” AREV.]

**25.** Between “is announced,” “is reported” (variant: “is declared”), and “is proclaimed” (variants: “is proclaimed and reported”). Something is announced concerning the future; it is reported concerning something distant; it is proclaimed concerning the present; it is reported back in the sense of making an excuse or repudiating.

**6**

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**26.** Asconius Pedianus, on *Divination*.

**26.** Between *advocatur*, *invocatur*, and *evocatur*. Someone is called as an advocate when he is going to provide patronage; he is invoked when he is going to provide aid; he is summoned when he is going to offer service.

[Col. 0013C]

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**27.** From Agraetius, where *adducitur* (“is led toward”) appears instead of *abducitur* (“is led away”).]

**27.** Between *abducitur*, *perducitur*, and *deducitur*. Someone is led away (*abducitur*) to a dishonorable matter; he is led (*perducitur*) to scholarly pursuits; he is led down or conducted (*deducitur*) to honor.

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**28.** Agraetius: “We affect someone with honor; we affect someone with injury”; this perhaps should be corrected here.

In the same place, the Vatican codex has “in honor ... in injury.” AREV.]

**28.** Between *adficimur* and *afficimur*. We are affected with honor (*adficimur*, variant *afficimur*); we are affected with injury (*afficimur*, variant *adficimur*).

[Col. 0014A]

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**29.** From Agraetius.]

**29.** Between *adversum te* and *adversus te*. *Adversum te* means “an adversary against you”; *adversus te* means “an imitator of you.”

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**30.** From Agraetius. See Servius, on *Aeneid* 3: “I found one of these”; and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 10, letter A.]

**30.** Between *alterum* and *alium*. *Alter* is said of two; *alius* of many. For *alter* cannot exist without one other.

[Note: [Col. 0013D]

**31.** From Agraetius and Servius, on *Aeneid* 1: “Rare swimmers appear.” See also Festus, under *Apparet* (“appears”).

—“Not ...” These words are absent from Agraetius, and rightly so.

[Col. 0014C] In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “but by discerning.” AREV.]

**31.** Between *apparet* and *paret* (variants: *adparet* and *apparet*). Someone *apparet*—appears—when he is seen; someone *paret*—obeys—when he obeys not because of a rule but for the sake of the understanding that discerns.

[Note: [Col. 0014C]

**32.** He seems to have composed this difference from several passages of Servius, on *Aeneid* 6: “And now the doors of the house stood open.” You also have this in *Etymologies*, book 5, chapter 7.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “doors by which people are shut out.” AREV.]

**32.** Between an entrance and a doorway. An entrance is what admits people; a doorway is what shuts them out.

[Note: [Col. 0014C]

**33.** Varro, book 4 of *On the Latin Language*.]

**33.** Between an arbiter and a judge. An arbiter is appointed by free choice; a judge by law.

[Note: [Col. 0014C]

**34.** From Servius, on *Aeneid* 8: “Then the hands of Ausonia”; and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 10, letter A.]

**34.** Between an immigrant and a settler. Immigrants come from one place; settlers come from different places.

[Note: [Col. 0014C]

**35.** From C. Fronto and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 10, letter C.

—Likewise ... From Servius, on *Georgics* 3: “The color most harmful to white things.” From this, instead of *aurorae* (“of dawn”), read *pallori* (“to pallor”).

[Col. 0014D] Among the Spaniards even today *alba* denotes dawn, and much the same is true among the Italians, as Barthius observed in connection with the words: “But *album* is what is known to be near the dawn.” He also made several observations concerning Apuleius, who praises the white arm of dawn. AREV.]

**35.** Between *album* and *candidum*. *Album* is a quality of nature; *candidum* results from effort or care. Thus we speak of white hair but shining-white wax. Likewise, *candidum* is something suffused with a certain gleaming light, whereas *album* is what is understood to be near the dawn.

**7**

[Note: [Col. 0014D]

**36.** The Vatican manuscript has: “one who is white; one who is beginning to become white.” AREV.]

**36.** Between *albentem* and *albescentem*. We call someone *albens* who has already become white; *albescens* describes one who is beginning to become white.

[Note: [Col. 0014D]

**37.** *Etymologies*, book 11, chapter 1.

—Moreover ... *Etymologies*, book 10, letter A: “*Animosus* means full of spirit and strength.”

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “is changed by emotion.” In Barthius’s manuscript: “these things are always in being”; Barthius corrects this to “these things are always in one being.” He calls the observation contained in this difference elegant. AREV.]

**37.** The difference between *animus* and *anima* is that *animus* belongs to deliberation, while *anima* belongs to life. The latter always remains the same; the former changes according to emotion. The ancients also separated *mens* (“mind”) from *animus” (“spirit”): the mind, so that one may know; the spirit, so that one may wish or be able to learn. Moreover, *animus* is sometimes used to mean strength.

[Note: [Col. 0014D]

**38.** From Servius, on *Aeneid* 2: “And they fill the belly with armed soldiers.” Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 11, chapter 1.

—Sallust. From fragments of uncertain books.]

**38.** Between *alvus*, *venter*, and *uterus*. *Alvus* is the inner receptacle of food, into which waste flows, as in Sallust: “Pretending that his belly was being purged.” *Venter* is the visible exterior of that part, as in Juvenal: “Montanus’s belly is there as well.” *Uterus* properly belongs to a pregnant woman. But poets vary this usage because of metrical necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0015C]

**39.** *Etymologies*, book 18, chapter 5. Another distinction appears in Festus, under *Arma* (“weapons”).

—Servius, on *Aeneid* 9: “To pour forth weapons of every kind.”]

In the Vatican manuscript, after this difference is inserted: “Between *aqua* and *unda*, etc.,” as number 65. AREV.]

**39.** Between arms and missiles. Arms are what we use for defense; missiles are what we throw. Also, *arma* are weapons of war, while *armamenta* are the equipment of ships.

[Note: [Col. 0015D]

**40.** *Etymologies*, book 14, chapter 9.

“Consumption of the riverbanks.” Barthius calls this elegant: the banks are destroyed so that they are no longer seen. The same writer explained “the rivers die” in this way in Petronius Arbiter. In the Vatican codex: “completion.” AREV.]

**40.** Between alluvial deposit and foul accumulation. Alluvium is the wearing away of riverbanks by water; *colluvium* is the gathering of filth caused by abundant flow.

[Note: [Col. 0015D]

**41.** From Agraetius, where *aquaticum* (“watery”) is nevertheless printed as *aquatum*.

—“We say.” F. It should be added from Agraetius: “what has received water from elsewhere,” *aquosum* (“watery”).]

**41.** Between *aquatum* and *aquosum*. We properly speak of an *aquata* drink, and of an *aquosus* place that pours out water from itself. Similarly, we call a drink *meraca* (“undiluted”), but wine *merosum* (“pure”).

**8**

[Note: [Col. 0015D]

**42.** Variant: “It is shaded, as though covered by the sky.”

—“Without a breath of wind.” I think there is an error here, and that *ἄνευ φρίκης* should be written, that is, “without cold”; likewise in Servius it should be read on *Aeneid* 5: “A station most welcome to sun-loving mergansers,” and on *Aeneid* 6: “He sends [them] into sunny places.” See Festus, under *Apricum* (“sunny”). Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 3, chapter 18.

—“Shaded, dense.” Thus Festus, under *Opacum* (“shaded”).

—“Pleasant.” An old glossary likewise interprets *amoenum* (“pleasant”) as **σύσκιον τόπον**, “a shady place.”

—“Pleasant places,” however ... Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 14, chapter 8; Festus, under *Amoena* (“pleasant places”); Servius on *Aeneid* 5, “the pleasant places of the righteous,” and 6, “the pleasant green spaces.”]

**42.** Between sunny and shaded. *Apricum* is the opposite of *opacum*, as though open to the sky or sun without the chill of cold. And *apricum* means, as it were, “without wind and cold.” Hence some think that Africa is likewise so called, as though it were *Aprica*. By contrast, *opacum* is dense and shady, as is also *amoenum*. *Amoena* (“pleasant places”) are so called because they are loved.

[Note: [Col. 0016C]

**43.** From Agraetius; and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 17, chapter 6.

—*Molem* (“mass”). Variant: *mobilem* (“movable”). Agraetius is wrong.]

**43.** Between *acerbum* and *acervum*. *Acervus*, written with two *v*s, means a mass or heap. *Acerbus*, written with *b*, means unripe.

[Note: [Col. 0016C]

**44.** From Agraetius, and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 17, chapter 6.

[Col. 0016D] In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “and fruitful.” AREV.]

**44.** Between *arbos* and *arbor*. *Arbor* may sometimes be without fruit, whereas *arbos* is understood to be fruit-bearing. Likewise, between *silva* and *nemus*: a *silva* may sometimes be fruitful, whereas a *nemus* is understood to consist of shady and fruitless trees.

**45.** Between *acerbum* and *immaturum*. Something *acerbum* is far removed from ripeness; something *immaturum* is near to ripeness.

[Col. 0015C]

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**46.** From Agraetius. 46; and Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, book 20, chapter 16.]

**46.** Between *avena* and *habena*. *Avena*, with the letter *v*, is a plant. *Habena*, with the letter *b*, is a strap or rein. They think that *habenae* derives from *habere* (“to have”), because by means of them we have—or hold—the horses; hence horses are also called *habiles* (“manageable”).

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**47.** “It runs with winged speed.” Variant: “The winged one will be from a four- ...” [incomplete as printed].

In the same place, the Vatican codex omits “with excessive speed ... signifies”; and likewise in numbers 49 and 50 and several others. Barthius’s codex read: “The four-horse chariot runs with a winged, hastening chariot”; he corrected *citata* (“hastened”) to *cita* (“swift”), so that the line would be an anapaest. AREV.]

**47.** Between a bird and a winged creature. We call those birds which fly lightly through the air on wings; but we call not only birds “winged creatures,” but also quadrupeds running with extraordinary speed—provided that the word is accompanied by an adjective, as, for example, “a winged horse” or “a winged tiger.” Thus Pacuvius says: “The four-horse chariot runs with winged speed.” Arrows too are called *volucres* (“winged”), because feathers are attached to them. Without an accompanying word, however, *volucris* merely means “bird.”

**9**

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**48.** From Servius, on the cited passage of *Aeneid* 2, word for word.]

**48.** Between *anguis*, *serpens*, and *draco*. In the sea there are *angues* (“snakes”), on land *serpentes* (“serpents”), and in a temple *dracones* (“dragons”). Thus Virgil says: “Snakes through the tranquil deep”; and shortly afterward: “Each serpent entwined.” Likewise: “Dragons at the highest shrine.”

**49.** Between golden and gilded. Something *aureum* (“golden”) is made of gold; something *auratum* (“gilded”) is made of another material and covered with gold.

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**50.** C. Fronto: “Living beings are made living by spirit; animals possess a soul.”]

**50.** Between *animalia* and *animantia*. *Animalia* are things that possess a soul; *animantia* pertain only to spirits or minds.

**51.** Between *auster* and *ostrum*. *Auster* signifies a wind; *ostrum* signifies purple dye.

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**52.** See Nonius, under the entries *Innuere* and *Annuere*.

Thus old manuscripts explain the words in Terence: “I deny, refuse, withdraw.”]

**52.** Between *annuit* and *abnuit*. *Annuit* means “he consents”; *abnuit* means “he denies.”

**53.** Between *aes* and *es*. *Aes* is the material of metal; *es* is a verb.

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**54.** Nonius Marcellus, under the entries *Animus* and *Anima*.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has: “the soul, the spirit by which we live.” AREV.]

**54.** Between *animus* and *anima*. *Anima* is without variation; *animus* is variable. By the *animus* we understand; by the *anima* we live.

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**55.** *Etymologies*, book 1, chapter 26.]

**55.** Between *ad* and *at*. *Ad* is a preposition; *at* is a conjunction.

**56.** Between *adiuro* and *abiuro*. *Adiuro* means “I ask solemnly”; *abiuro* means “I deny under oath.”

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**57.** See Festus, under *Apud* (“with, at”).]

**57.** Between *apud* and *penes*. I say *apud te* (“with you”) when I mean some part or the whole. *Penes* signifies possession, whereas *apud* refers, as it were, to a body or a book, not to possession. We say, “I have my money with you” (*apud te*), not “in your possession” (*penes te*). Thus I say *apud te habeo* (“I have with you”) of things that are to be returned; of things that are possessed, I say *penes te habeo* (“I have in your possession”).

[Note: [Col. 0016D]

**58.** F. Read: “To burn means to feel fire thoroughly and to the marrow.” For the expressions “to burn with fire” and “to give to fire” belong to what precedes; they had been inserted here incorrectly.

[Col. 0017C] —*Sepelire* (“to bury”). *Etymologies*, book 11, chapter 22.

In the same place, perhaps “from both sides” should be read. AREV.]

**58.** Between *amburere*, *comburere*, *urere*, and *sepelire*. *Comburere* means to give something to fire; *amburere*, to burn it on both sides; *urere*, to burn it thoroughly with fire and feel the fire to the marrow. *Sepelire* means to surround with a tomb, or to cover the body and bones with earth. Hence Virgil, *Aeneid* 10: “Permit the body to be covered with earth”; or, *Aeneid* 9:

“If some chance shall forbid this,

Let him offer funeral gifts to the absent man

And honor him with a tomb.”

**10**

[Note: [Col. 0017C]

**59.** According to Agraetius’s understanding, rashness is without deliberation, while boldness follows deliberation. C. Fronto may perhaps be corrected from this: “The bold person does not fear; the rash person does not foresee.” Otherwise the reading is wrong: “The bold person does not foresee; the rash person does not fear.”]

**59.** Between the bold person and the rash person. The bold person does not fear; the rash person does not assess the danger.

**60.** Between *ad forum ire* (“to go to the forum”) and *in forum ire* (“to go into the forum”). *Ad forum* indicates some place toward which we are going; *in forum* means into the forum itself.

**61.** Between *Afer*, *Africus*, and *Africanus*. We call a citizen an *Afer*, a wind an *Africus*, and a merchant an *Africanus*.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**62.** Servius, on *Aeneid* 8: “I accept and willingly acknowledge.”]

**62.** Between *agnoscere* and *cognoscere*. We recognize people we know; we come to know those whom we do not know.

[Col. 0017B]

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**63.** C. Fronto: “He takes away (*aufert*) what he has given; he removes (*adimit*) a right when compelled by authority; the person who is stronger snatches away (*eripit*).”

—*Jus* (“right”). F. *Jussi* (“I ordered”), as below under the letter R.]

**63.** Between *auferre*, *adimere*, and *eripere*. We take away what we have given; we remove a right; we snatch away what we seize from someone.

**64.** Between conducting a case and pleading. What the advocate conducts, the defendant pleads.

**65.** Between water and a wave. A wave is always in motion, whereas water is stationary. Moreover, rains belong to clouds, and streams to springs. For *latex* properly means the liquid of a spring, and is so called because it lies hidden in the veins of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**66.** From Servius, on *Aeneid* 2: “What seas can wash me away?”

—Nonius, under *Aequor* (“level expanse”).]

**66.** Between level expanses and seas. *Aequora* (“level expanses”) refers not only to waters but also to fields, because of their evenness; *mare* (“sea”) refers only to a gathering of waters.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**67.** Servius, on *Aeneid* 6: “Whom, for you of long life”: “*Aevum* properly belongs to eternity.” Hence someone may perhaps think that in Isidore one should read: “*Aevum* indicates permanence alone.”]

**67.** Between *aevum* and *saeculum*. *Aevum* indicates time alone; *saeculum* indicates both permanence and time. Hence we also say “for ages of ages.”

[Col. 0017C]

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**68.** *Etymologies*, book 10, under *Aequus* (“equal”), letter A.]

**68.** Between the equitable and the just. The just person derives his character from law, as though preserving *ius* (“right”); the equitable person is just according to nature. Indeed, someone is called *justus* from living according to right—that is, from doing what is right.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**69.** From C. Fronto and Agraetius.

—From Servius, on *Aeneid* 1: “Sick with enormous cares.” The commentators on Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 2.]

**69.** Between *aeger* and *aegrotus*. *Aeger* properly means sorrowful in spirit, for one is called *aegrotus* in body. Thus *aeger* can mean sorrowful and in poor health, whereas *aegrotus*, or *aegrotans*, means merely in poor health.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**70.** Variant: “as Cicero does in *Tusculan Disputations* 3.”

In the same place, I do not know what Pantinus’s note is intended to mean. AREV.]

**70.** Between *aegritudo* and *aegrotatio*. Just as *aegrotatio* (“illness”) has its name from the body, so *aegritudo* (“distress”) has its name from the spirit and is not separated from pain. Pain, therefore, is *aegritudo*—that is, the efficient cause producing distress in the spirit, just as illness does in the body.

# On the letter B

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

**71.** The Vatican manuscript adds “and of all.” AREV.]

**71.** Between kindness and goodness. The Stoics define—or distinguish—them as follows: kindness is a virtue prepared to do good, gentle, affable, and sweet in speech, inviting everyone to friendship with all good people. Goodness, however, is ready to do good and to provide what is requested, but does not know how to be pleasant in companionship or to invite everyone by its own sweetness.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]

72. In this sense also Fronto: *Beatus*, which among the Greeks is **μακάριος** (“blessed”).

—“May you be fortunate.” It seems to come from Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “May you be fortunate,” and from *Eclogue* 5: “May you be good and fortunate.”

The Vatican Codex has: “fortunate in succession and in others . . . and happiness is attained.” AREV.]

72. Between *beatus* (“blessed”) and *felix* (“fortunate”). *Beatus* is blessed for himself alone; *felix* is fortunate both for himself and for others [Al., “in succession and for others”], as in Virgil:

“May you be fortunate, and lighten whatever labor is ours” [Al., “whomever’s labor”].

One is called *felix* (“fortunate”) through whom happiness is both given and received, as in “a fortunate time,” “a fortunate place,” and “a fortunate outcome.”

73. Between *beatus*, *honestus*, and *fortunatus*. *Beatus* in spirit, *honestus* in character, *fortunatus* in possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0018D]

74. In the Regio-Vatican Codex 1838, in which the Differences are sometimes fuller than in the printed editions, it is reported thus: “Between *bibere* and *potare*: we *bibimus* (‘drink’) from necessity, we *potamus* (‘drink deeply’) by choice.” Others say: “*Bibere* belongs to nature, *potare* to luxury.” AREV.]

74. Between *bibere* and *potare*. *Bibere* belongs to nature; *potare* to luxury.

75. Between *balineum* and *balneum*. In ordinary prose speech we say *balineum*; in verse, *balneum*.

[Note: [Col. 0018D]

76. From Servius, on *Georgics* III: “And beards and hoary chins.” The passage cited by Isidore, moreover, is from *Aeneid* VI, in which it is established that he read *barbas* (“beards”) instead of *crines* (“hair”).]

76. Between *barba* (“beard”) and *barbae* (“beards”). We speak of the *barba* of human beings, but of the *barbae* of animals or plants. We also speak of the *barbae* of human beings, as in Virgil: “The beards and hoary chins of the Roman king.”

[Note: [Col. 0018D]

77. Barthius thinks that *bucinus* is an adjective and that the text should be emended to *bucineus canor est ipse clangor* (“the trumpet-like sound is itself the blast”). For this sound, *bucinatus* occurs in Papias. The same Barthius observes elsewhere, namely in Book XXXVI, chapter 13, that *bucinum* is used of the sound of a *bucina* (“trumpet”); he infers this from a fragment of Flavius Caper and from this Difference of Isidore. AREV.]

77. Between *bucina* and *bucinus*. *Bucina* is the trumpet by which a signal is given against the enemy [Al., “against an enemy”]; *bucinus* is the resonant blast itself.

[Note: [Col. 0018D]

78. See Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “Who would follow them into war.”

—“In battle.” C. Fronto.

—“The trumpet of battle.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* XI, at “He gives the signal for battle,” and also from his *Etymologies*, Book XVIII, chapters 1 and 4.

—“Battle is a part.” Thus Nonius, under *Bellum* (“war”).

[Col. 0019C] The Vatican omits “that is, the entire conflict.” Barthius says that these remarks deserve to be remembered, whether Isidore derived them from his own observation or, as was his custom, copied them from elsewhere. But since Barthius often attempts to correct the reading of his manuscript by conjecture, he is generally repeating work already done; for nearly all these passages had already been corrected in Grial’s edition, at least by the time Barthius’s *Adversaria* appeared, and it is established that he had at some point seen Grial’s edition. AREV.]

78. Between *bellum* and *praelium*. War (*bellum*) is declared; battle (*praelium*) is fought. For in a war there is not immediately a battle, whereas in a battle there is immediately also a war. Hence among the ancients the trumpet was the signal of battle, and the *bucina* the signal of war. Likewise, *bellum* means the whole affair, that is, the entire conflict, as in the Jugurthine, Civil, and Punic wars. A *pugna* (“fight”) is a single day’s engagement; a *praelium* (“battle”) is a part of a fight, although a fight may sometimes also involve two parties, and may occur without weapons; hence the word is derived from *pugnus* (“fist”).

[Note: [Col. 0019C]

79. From Servius, on *Georgics* III: “And balsams and berries.”]

79. Between *balsamum* and *opobalsamum*. *Balsamum* is the tree itself; *opobalsamum* is the sap collected from the tree. For *opos* means “sap.” The test of balsam, as Pliny says, is this: if it is held toward the sun and has not been adulterated, it burns the hand of the person holding it.

[Note: [Col. 0019C]

80. An old Glossary: *bassus*, εὔχυλος (“rich in sap”).]

80. Between *Bassos* and *bassus*. *Bassos* is a proper name; *bassus* [Al., *Balsos*] is a common noun.

[Note: [Col. 0019D]

81. *Etymologies*, Book I, chapter 32. See Aulus Gellius, Book V, chapter 20.]

81. Between *barbarismus* and *soloecismus*. A *barbarism* occurs in a single word or language-form; a *solecism* in several.

## Of the Letter C

[Note: [Col. 0019D]

82. Varro demonstrates both usages in Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, under *coelum* (“sky”).

—“Certainly . . .” From Servius, on *Aeneid* III: “Nor does the starry sky shine brightly.”]

82. *Coelum* and *aether* are distinguished in this way. Not only that place bearing the stars, but also this air, is called *coelum* (“sky”). *Aether* is the higher part of the sky, in which the stars are set. More precisely, *aether* is the fiery upper air, whereas *aethra* is the light and radiance of the *aether*.

13

83. Between *cras* and *crastinum*. *Cras* (“tomorrow”) pertains to time; *crastinum* (“tomorrow’s”) to the work belonging to that time.

[Note: [Col. 0019D]

84. Another reading: “sexus” (“sex”). First of these; and below: “to despise what you know best.”

In Grial’s edition it is indicated that in some copies the words “The first . . . the second belongs to continence” are missing. Indeed, in the oldest Vatican Codex 3321 the sentence continues as follows: “renunciation of sexual intercourse. Of these, the first belongs to happiness,” etc. Soon afterward the same Codex has: “They understand [continence] in married couples and parents, chastity in virgins.” AREV.]

84. There is this distinction between *castitas* (“chastity”) and *continentia* (“continence”): chastity is bodily incorruption, whereas continence is renunciation of sexual intercourse after corruption.

* The first of these belongs to happiness: not to have anything that you fear; the second belongs to virtue: to overthrow the enemy, lust, by whom you have so often been defeated and cast down. To yield to the first is humility; to yield to the second is patience.

* Of these, the first belongs to happiness: not to know at all the thing from which you will later wish to be freed; the second belongs to virtue: to despise a vice that you know very well. Others understand continence as applying specifically to married couples [Al., “to spouses”], and chastity to virgins. Some likewise take chastity to reside in the mind, but virginity in the body. True chastity, however, is that which is defiled neither in body nor in mind.

85. Between *clamor* and *clangor*. *Clamor* belongs to rational beings; *clangor* to irrational beings, such as geese or trumpets.

[Note: [Col. 0019D]

86. The other verse is cited by Nonius under *gannire* (“to whine”), from the prose of Afranius (Catius, *Rosa*).

Barthius suspects that the reading should be “doing it secretly with suspicion.” In his manuscript he found: “as criminal as the one whom you reproach.” Others have: “as criminal as a viper.” AREV.]

86. The author Orbilius thinks there is this difference between *criminator* and *criminans*: a *criminator* is one who brings a charge against another and does so repeatedly, whereas a *criminans* is one who brings a charge and does so even with suspicion, so that he appears more culpable. Thus Afranius:

“I am not,” he says, “as criminal [Al., *criminosus*, masculine] as you, viper; I have never learned to whine into my master’s ear” [Al., “your lord’s ear”].

[Note: [Col. 0020C]

87. See Donatus on Terence, *Adelphoe*, Act III, scene 3.

—Thus Festus under *versutus* (“cunning”), and also Isidore in *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letters C and R.

—Plautus, in *Epidicus*, the scene beginning “You have already done it.”]

87. Between *callidus* and *versutus*. *Callidus* is sly in argument; *versutus* is one whose mind readily turns to every kind of fraud in the conduct of affairs. Thus we use *callidus* not merely for “crafty,” but for one cleverly instructed; *versutus* derives from the fact that such a person quickly turns his mind. Hence Plautus:

“You are more *versutus*—more crafty—than a potter’s wheel” [Al., “than a potter’s wheel,” with a different inflection].

[Note: [Col. 0020C]

88. Donatus distinguishes them differently, *Phormio*, Act II, scene 4.

—“But care.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “Sick with immense cares,” and IV: “Long wounded by care.”

The Vatican has: “Care, however, is without anxiety.” AREV.]

88. Between *cura* and *sollicitudo*. *Sollicitudo* (“anxiety”) is moderate and capable of restraint, whereas *cura* (“care”) is without moderation. Hence *cura* is so called because it “burns the heart” (*cor urat*).

89. Some distinguish *cognitio* and *agnitio* in this way: *cognitio* concerns things that we previously did not know but are afterward permitted to know; *agnitio* concerns things that, though previously known, we later ceased to know and subsequently remember.

[Note: [Col. 0020D]

90. In one manuscript only this appears: “Between *commentarii* and *commentaria*. *Commentarii* are books; *commentaria* are volumes.”

—“Composed.” F., “arranged,” or “divided into sections.”

In Vatican Manuscript 3321 only this appears: “A *commentarium* is a book; a *commentum* is a volume.” In the printed editions the distinction is not fully explained, since the explanation of the word *comicus* is omitted. It therefore seems that the text should read: “A *commentum* is a volume, that is, compiled from different books; *comicum* from the Old and New Testaments.” *Comicus*, *commicus*, and *comes* designated an ecclesiastical book, also called a Lectionary; see Ducange under *Commes*, at the first entry. AREV.]

90. Between *commentarium*, *commentum*, and *comicum* [F., *commaticum*]. A *commentarium* is a book; a *commentum*, or *commentatum*, is a volume compiled from different books, namely from the Old and New Testaments.

91. Between *coram* and *palam*. *Coram* refers to a person, for we say *coram illo* (“in his presence”); *palam* is not restricted to a person, because it signifies something known to everyone. Thus *coram* refers to a particular person, *palam* to everyone.

[Col. 0021A] 92. Between *cavum* and *cavatum*. *Cavum* (“hollow”) is natural; *cavatum* (“hollowed out”) is made by hand.

[Note: [Col. 0021C]

93. The Vatican Codex has *non circa esse* instead of *non circasse* or *circaisse*, which seems preferable. AREV.]

93. Between *circiter*, *circa*, and *circum*. *Circiter* refers to number; *circa* to place and time; *circum* means “on every side.” Thus we say *circumisse nos orbem* (“that we went around the world”), not *circasse* [Al., *circaisse*].

[Note: [Col. 0021C]

94. From Agraetius, verbatim.]

94. Between *circumpedes* and *antepedes*. *Circumpedes* are the services of slaves; *antepedes* those of friends.

15

[Note: [Col. 0021C]

95. See another distinction in Agraetius.]

95. Between *contingit*, *obtingit*, *evenit*, and *accidit*. *Contingit* (“befalls”) through an outcome; *obtingit* (“falls to one’s lot”) by chance or fortune; *accidit* (“happens”) by accident; *evenit* (“turns out”) either badly or well.

[Note: [Col. 0021C]

96. Another reading: “We chastise when we believe.”]

96. Between *corripere*, *objurgare*, and *castigare*. We *corripimus* (“correct sharply”) with blows; we *objurgamus* (“rebuke”) with words; we *castigamus* (“chastise”) with words, beatings, and blows.

[Col. 0021B] 97. Between *cupere* and *ambire*. *Cupere* is to seek earthly profits, or any desires of the world, vainly; *ambire* is to aspire to the ranks of honors or the offices of power.

[Note: [Col. 0021C]

98. Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “I sing of arms and the man”; and VIII: “He foretold that they were present at the threshold.”]

98. Between *cantare* and *canere*. *Cantare* is merely to produce sound with the voice or with a cry; *canere* is sometimes to sing in musical measure, sometimes to prophesy, that is, to foretell the future.

[Note: [Col. 0021D]

99. All from Agraetius.

—“Of accusation.” —Or “of opportunity.” Agraetius.

—“Of assignment.” —“Of designation,” Manuscript 1 and Agraetius.

—“Of order.” —“Of arrangement,” Manuscript 1 and Agraetius.

In Pantinus’s note was written: “Perhaps *dictionis*,” which I corrected, as I think accords with his meaning, to perhaps *ditionis* (“of dominion”). Barthius’s Codex had the interpolated reading: “To copy out what has been written elsewhere; this is a medical term, *transcribere*.” In place of “this is a medical term,” Barthius substituted “this is an indecorous term,” since it belongs to plagiarists. He also observes that a *dictio* is a declamatory exercise, such as the *dictiones* of Ennodius that have come down to us. AREV.]

99. Between *conscribere*, *exscribere*, and the remaining terms. Placidus says: “*Conscribere* is to write many things together. *Exscribere* is to transfer what has been written elsewhere; *transcribere*, when our right passes to another. *Inscribere* belongs to an accusation; *ascribere* to an assignment. *Describere* belongs to a *dictio* [F., *ditio*], or to an order.”

[Col. 0021C]

[Note: [Col. 0021D]

100. Read *destruere*, unless one prefers, following Agraetius, *exstruere*, “to build upward.”]

100. Between *construere* and *destruere*. *Construere* is to build; *destruere* is to destroy utterly.

[Note: [Col. 0021D]

101. Agraetius, under *commodatum* (“loaned”).

—Nonius, under *accommodat* (“fits or adapts”).]

101. Between *commodare* and *accommodare*. *Commodare* is to provide something; *accommodare* is to adapt or fit it.

102. Between *consuere* and *suere*, or *assuere*. *Consuere* applies to clothing; *suere* to books; *assuere* to leather.

[Note: [Col. 0022C]

103. Agraetius: “We attain (*consequimur*) by effort; we achieve (*assequimur*) by desire.”]

103. Between *consequimur* and *assequimur*. We *consequimur* by our feet; we *assequimur* through study.

[Note: [Col. 0022C]

104. From Agraetius.]

104. Between *consuescimus*, *assuescimus*, and *insuescimus*. We become accustomed (*consuescimus*) to good things, become habituated (*insuescimus*) to bad things, and grow accustomed (*assuescimus*) to both [Al., “to either one”].

105. Between *capio* and *capesso*. *Capio* means “I take” once in a while; *capesso*, frequently.

[Note: [Col. 0022C]

106. See Fronto, under *omnes* (“all”). Festus has nearly the same account as Isidore under *cuncti* (“all”), and Asconius Pedianus in his commentary on the *Divinatio*.

—The reading will be clearer as follows: “Otherwise all are called *omnes*, not *cuncti*.” See Servius on *Aeneid* I: “All the herds follow.”

The Vatican has: “Otherwise all are called *cuncti*.” AREV.]

106. Between *cunctos* and *omnes*. *Cuncti* means all, provided that they are joined together and doing something together. Otherwise they are called *omnes*, not *cuncti*.

107. Between *caeteri* and *alii*. *Caeteri* (“the others”) belong to the same number or group; *alii* (“others”) to another.

108. Between *curulis* and *curialis*. *Curiales* are public officials; *curules* are the chairs in which magistrates sit when administering justice.

[Note: [Col. 0022D]

109. In Barthius’s manuscript: “We call a man’s expression *censorium*.” Barthius conjectured *vultuosum* (“having a severe expression”), since *vultuosus* denotes severity in Sidonius and others. The association with censorial severity is well known. I would rather read: “We properly call a handsome man *censorium*.” AREV.]

109. Between *censor* and *censualis*. *Censores* are called judges [Al., “only judges”]; *censuales* are officials who collect the provincial census. Meanwhile [Al., “sometimes”], we also call a handsome man *censorius* [Al., *censorem*].

110. Between *cognatus*, *affinis*, and *propinquus*. *Cognatus* is a relative of the same kindred; *affinis* is one who enters through marriage; *propinquus* is joined by blood or affinity.

[Note: [Col. 0022D]

111. An old Glossary has *columina*, ἐπιστηρίγματα (“supports”), and *columen*, ἐπίστυλον (“architrave”), under *columnae* (“columns”). Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter C.]

111. Between *columen* and *incolumis*. We use *incolumis* (“safe, unharmed”) of the spirit, and *columis* (“sound, healthy”) of the body. *Columen* means health or a support, because it is made from *columna* (“column”); hence also *culmen* (“summit”) and *culmus* (“stalk”).

112. Between *comptus* and *compositus*. *Comptus* is produced by care; *compositus* by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0022D]

113. From Agraetius, under *crassari* and *grassari*.

—“Of the mind . . .” Agraetius: “Either of the mind or of cruelty.”

The Vatican omits “of excessive cruelty.” AREV.]

113. Between *crassus* and *grassus*. *Crassus* applies to the bodily fatness [Al., “fat”]. For *grassari* applies to excessive cruelty of spirit.

[Col. 0022C] 114. Between *crassus* and *obesus*. *Crassus* means fat; *obesus* means more than fat.

17

[Note: [Col. 0022D]

115. From C. Fronto; the word *natura* has been displaced from its proper position and should be restored. The reading should be: “*Caerulus* is the color of nature.”]

115. Between *caerulus* and *caeruleus*. *Caerulus* is the color of nature; *caeruleus* is something fashioned from that color. For we call the color itself *caerulum*.

[Note: [Col. 0022D]

116. So also in *Etymologies*, Book XI, chapter 1.

—“From lacking.” In *Etymologies*: “From creating.”]

116. Between *corpus* and *caro*. There is a body in every flesh, but flesh is not in every body. Flesh properly consists of bones and blood, though this too is a body. A stone and wood are also bodies, though neither is flesh. *Corpus* (“body”) is said to derive from *corruptio* (“corruption”), and *caro* (“flesh”) from *carere* (“to lack”) or from *cadere* (“to fall”).

[Note: [Col. 0023C]

117. “The hairlike tips of seeds,” Book V.]

117. Between *capilli* and *capillamenta*. *Capilli* are the hair of the head; *capillamenta* are the tips of trees [Al., “of a tree”].

[Note: [Col. 0023C]

118. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “To place upon our neck.” *Etymologies*, Book XI, chapter 1.

—“Break.” In another copy: “To break necks and bend pride,” which should be inserted as a gloss.]

118. Between *collum* and *cervix*. *Collum* always means the neck; *cervix*, when singular, means the neck, but when plural, pride, as Cicero says in *Against Verres*, Book V: “You accuse the praetor? Break his necks.”

[Note: [Col. 0023C]

119. So Acron also explains the line in Horace, *Odes* I.3: “In vain has God severed”: *abscidit* means “he severed” or “separated.”

Barthius’s parchment reads: “Between *cassidem* and *cassidam* there is no difference. A *cassis* is a helmet, which was made of leather.” AREV.]

119. Between *concidit* and *concidit*. *Concidit*, with the medial syllable shortened, means “he fell”; *concidit*, with the medial syllable lengthened, means “he separated.”

120. Between *cassis* and *galea*. A *cassis* is made of metal plate; a *galea* of leather [Al., “a *galea* is made of leather”].

[Col. 0023B]

[Note: [Col. 0023D]

121. *Clypeum*. From Carisius in C. Fronto, incorrectly: “*Clupeum* of weapons, *clypeum* of an image.”

—*Clypeus*. The passage is mutilated; I think it can be supplemented from Carisius as follows: “*Clypeus* is masculine and is what we call a shield, from *clepo*, καλύπτω, that is, ‘I conceal,’ whereas *clupeum* is an image and is named from *clueo*, because it is clear.” So too in Servius, on *Aeneid* VII: “Nor do the courses and shields resound”: “They are so called because they conceal the body, from Greek κλέπτω, ‘I steal.’”]

121. Between *clypeum* and *clupeum*. We call a shield *clypeum*, and an ornament [Al., “ornaments”] *clupeum*. Between *clypeum* and *clupeum*: *Clypeus* is masculine and means what we call a shield; *clupeum*, neuter, means an image, from the fact that it shines, that is, is spoken of and named because it is bright. Thus *inclytus* also means “illustrious” or “very bright.”

18

[Note: [Col. 0023D]

122. Another reading: “By the ordinary use of the thing, made by agreement.”

The Vatican has: “It depends upon justice.” And “we always look to what is right and holy,” instead of “what is right, equitable, and holy.” AREV.]

122. Between *consuetudo* and *ritus*. *Consuetudo* is the customary use of something, established by the agreement of two or many people. *Ritus*, however, pertains to justice, as though it depended upon what is right, from which come what is pious, equitable, and holy [Al., “we look to what is right, holy”].

[Note: [Col. 0023D]

123. Festus, under *cognitor*: “For a present person, a present representative gives a present [representative].”

—Unless the text should read, following another reading: “A present representative is appointed by order of a present presiding magistrate.” No ancient writer has expressed the distinction between *procuratores* and *cognitores* more precisely in their proper sense, as is observed in the note to Brissonius, Book IV, chapter 20, *Select Antiquities*. In the Vatican Manuscript: “A present representative is given by a present person”; it omits the passage beginning “Likewise, a *cognitor* . . . administers everything.” AREV.]

123. Between *cognitor* and *procurator*. A *cognitor* is appointed only by a present person, to a present person, and in the presence of both; a *procurator*, however, may be appointed even while absent against an absent person [Al., “whom an absent person appoints”]. Moreover, a *cognitor* conducts litigation only against the person against whom he has been appointed to act [Al., “to defend”], whereas a *procurator* acts before everyone. Likewise, a *cognitor* is usually appointed only for a lawsuit, that is [Al., “likewise”], for the purpose of conducting a trial; a *procurator*, however, administers all affairs.

[Col. 0024A] 124. Between *cochlearius* and *cochleare*. *Cochlearius* is the person who sells; *cochleare* is the object or type of spoon.

[Note: [Col. 0024C]

125. The Vatican says “animal.” AREV.]

125. Between *coetus* and *cetus*. *Coetus* means a multitude; *cetus* means a beast.

[Note: [Col. 0024C]

126. So also in *Etymologies*, Book I, chapter 6.

The Vatican Codex has: “The common gender belongs to human beings; the epicene to animals.” Epicene nouns differ from common-gender nouns because common nouns have two articles, such as *hic* and *haec sacerdos* (“this male/female priest”), whereas epicene nouns have only one, such as *passer* (“sparrow”), *lepus* (“hare”), and so forth. See Cledonius, *On the Art*, p. 1862, Putsch. AREV.]

126. Between *commune* and *epicaenum*. *Commune* belongs to a gender [Al., “race”]; *epicaenum* to animals.

127. Between *capillatus* and *capillosus*. *Capillatus* means having abundant hair; *capillosus* means hairy and shaggy.

128. Between *cornua* and *corna*. *Cornua* means the horns of animals or the yards of a ship; *corna* means a type of fruit.

129. Between *coepit* and *cepit*. *Cepit* derives from *capere* (“to take”); *coepit* from *incipere* (“to begin”).

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

130. Decalvation is mentioned in the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, chapter 3; in the Council of Mérida, chapter 15; and elsewhere. In the laws of the Visigoths it was a mark of perpetual disgrace.

The punishment of decalvation is discussed at greater length by Ducange under *decalvare* and *decalvatio*. In Isidore, the words “the *decalvator* with a strong hand” may perhaps have been borrowed from another author as an example. AREV.]

130. Between *calvus* and *calvatus*. *Calvus* (“bald”) is natural; *calvatus* (“made bald”) is done by hand. Hence we also say *decalvatus* (“shorn bald”) and *decalvator* (“the one who forcibly shaves bald”).

[Col. 0024B] 19

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

131. In one manuscript: “Between *circa* and *circum*: *circa* concerns some part of a place; *circum*, every side.”]

131. Between *circa*, *circum*, and *circiter*. *Circa* concerns an uncertain place, some part of it; *circum* concerns every side of a definite place; *circiter* concerns a number that is almost indefinite.

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

132. C. Fronto: “A cause teaches what happened; reason resolves what is obscure.”]

132. Between *causa* and *ratio*. A *causa* precedes a matter or an explanation; *ratio* is present in the matter itself. Likewise, a *causa* is that because of which something happens; *ratio* is that by which it happens.

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

133. Acron and Porphyry distinguish them only in this way: *civicum* is said in the older form; *civile* is not.]

133. Between *civile* and *civicum*. *Civile* is what pertains to the state; *civicum* is what the citizens themselves do.

134. Between *cognoscimus* and *agnoscimus*. We *cognoscimus* (“learn”) things whose character we did not know; we *agnoscimus* (“recognize”) things that had slipped from us.

## Of the Letter D

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

135. Another reading: “added,” which makes no sense, instead of “from the day.”]

135. Between *diurna*, *diutina*, and *diuturna*. *Diurna* (“daily”) is formed from *dies* (“day”), as in *diurna merces* (“daily wages”); *diutina* (“long-lasting”) is so called from having lasted a long time; *diuturna* (“lasting for a long period”) is named from permanence, as though it meant eternal.

[Col. 0024C]

[Note: [Col. 0024D]

136. From Agraetius.

—“Disertus.” Read: “*Desertus*, abandoned,” derived from *deserere* (“to abandon”). In Agraetius’s view, neither of the readings found in the manuscripts can be tolerated. Another reading: “*Dissertus* is learned, from *disserere* (‘to discuss’),” etc.]

136. Between *disertus* and *discretus* [Al., *dissertus*]. *Disertus* describes an orator; *discretus* means learned, derived from *discere* (“to learn”).

[Note: [Col. 0025C]

137. Fronto is perhaps more correct: “*Dives* (‘rich’), because he has the ability to distribute.” Varro derives it from *divus* (“divine”).

—“Of places.” Fronto has almost the same distinction, as does Scaurus in his commentary on Terence IX, and Isidore himself in *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter L.

The Vatican has: “As though full of land.” AREV.]

137. Between *dives* and *locuples*. *Dives* is rich in money; *locuples* [Al., “full of places”] in estates, as though full of the riches of lands.

[Col. 0025A]

[Note: [Col. 0025C]

138. So also Fronto: “Vengeance avenges what has happened; retribution, or vindication, prevents what will happen.”]

138. Between *defensor* and *ultor*. A *defensor* takes care that an injustice not occur; an *ultor* ensures that an injustice already committed does not go unpunished.

[Note: [Col. 0025C]

139. Another reading: “the soul.” Another manuscript: “the crime.”]

139. Between *deformis* and *turpis*. *Deformis* refers to the body; *turpis* to the spirit.

20

[Note: [Col. 0025C]

140. Festus, under “one deprived of his mind.” Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter D.

—Nonius, under *delirus* (“deranged”), and also in the *Etymologies*.

—“Furrows.” In the *Etymologies* is added: “into which all the crop runs,” which is wholly untrue; perhaps those words should also be removed there, or the reading from Nonius should be adopted: “into which all the moisture runs.”

The Vatican has: “defective without a mind”; *delirus*, however, “defective in mind because of age.” I have discussed elsewhere the words added in the *Etymologies* after “they direct the furrows.” AREV.]

140. Between *demens* and *delirus*. *Demens* is a mad person of any age, that is, one without a mind; *delirus* is one whose mind has become defective through age. It is so called because he strays from the straight course, like a *lira*. A *lira* is a type of plowing, when farmers, after sowing the seed, lay out the furrows.

[Note: [Col. 0025D]

141. “Indignant”; perhaps “born,” as Festus has it. See Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “What mind is so dreadful?”

Festus, under *atroces* (“dreadful”). 

Pantinus, from the variant reading, indicates *indignatus* (“indignant”), and from conjecture *natus* (“born”). Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXXVIII, chapter 2, read *neque suasibilis* (“not persuadable”) and explained it as “deliberated,” using the term as in Apicius and Phoebadius. AREV.]

141. Between *dirus* and *atrox*. *Dirus* means merciless, as though driven to it by divine anger. *Atrox* means cruel, that is, harsh and not gentle [Al., “not persuasive”].

[Note: [Col. 0025D]

142. So Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II: “Pain is a harsh movement in the body, alien to the senses.”

Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter D, says *dolosus* (“deceitful”).

The Vatican has *adornat* (“adorns”) instead of *adornata* (“adorned”). AREV.]

142. Between *dolus* and *dolor*. *Dolor* is bodily discomfort or distress. *Dolus* is hidden malice adorned with flattering speech.

143. Between *dolus*, *insidiae*, and *fraudes*. *Dolus* is formed in the mind; *insidiae* (“ambushes”) in a place or by means of a weapon; *fraus* concerns mutual trust [Al., “injustice”].

[Note: [Col. 0025D]

144. *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter D.]

144. Between *dementia* and *amentia*. *Dementia* is a temporary defect; *amentia* a permanent one. *Dementia* is so called as though from a diminution of the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0025D]

145. *Etymologies*, Book I, chapter 18.

—“Sense.” Another reading: “of the mind, or of sense.”]

145. Between *distinctio* and *subdistinctio*. *Distinctio* brings a sense to an end; *subdistinctio* suspends it [Al., “suspends the mind”].

[Note: [Col. 0025D]

146. Agraetius, and at length Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 14.

—Nonius, under *divortium* (“separation”).

[Col. 0026C] —“It turns aside.” There are *diverticula*, which derive from this verb: cross paths branching off to the side, military roads, as Servius says on *Aeneid* IX. See the note under *divortia*.

The Vatican Manuscript has: “or turns aside from reason.” AREV.]

146. Between *dimidium* and *dimidiatum*. *Dimidium* is an equal divided part; *dimidiatum* is likewise a part, but not necessarily an equal one.

147. Between *divertit* and *divortit*. *Divortium* is separation, when a woman leaves her husband; *divertit* applies to one who turns aside from a road or from reason.

21

[Note: [Col. 0026C]

148. From Agraetius.

—“Cleanses.” Another reading: “cleanses or washes,” though this is absent from Agraetius.

—Livy. The passage was from Book CII, as is clear from the epitome of Florus.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXXIX, chapter 14, rather agrees with Festus or Paulus, who explain *deluere* as “to release,” from *luere*, not from “to wash.” AREV.]

148. Between *deluit* and *diluit*. *Deluit* means “cleanses”; *diluit* means “dilutes” or “tempers.” Livy, on the death of Mithridates: “When he had diluted it.”

[Note: [Col. 0026C]

149. Agraetius makes the same distinction: *diligi* belongs to affection; *deligi* to judgment.]

149. Between *dilectum* and *delectum*. *Dilectum* derives from *diligere* (“to love”); *delectum* from *deligere* (“to choose”) [Al., *eligere*, “to select”].

[Note: [Col. 0026C]

150. From Agraetius it is clear that the following should be read; the passage is taken from him in substance: “*Derectum*, fitted across.” So also *Etymologies*, Book X, under D: “*Directus*, because it goes in a straight line.”

Barthius calls this an elegant distinction. AREV.]

150. Between *directum* and *derectum*. *Derectum* extends across; *directum* extends lengthwise.

151. Between *discernere* and *secernere*. One *discernit* who divides into two parts; one *secernit* who chooses several things separately out of many.

[Note: [Col. 0026D]

152. Festus, under *memorare* (“to remember”).

The Vatican has “more often.” AREV.]

152. Between *dicere* and *memorare*. One *dicit* (“says”) who utters the same thing once; one *memorat* (“recounts”) not when he says it once, but when he repeats the same thing frequently in order to preserve it in memory.

[Note: [Col. 0026D]

153. Thus Paulus, from Festus: *Derigere* is found in Plautus for “to depart,” but the learned man reads *discindere* (“to tear apart”); “with someone.” Another reading: “toward someone.”]

153. Between *derigere* and *dirigere*. We *derigimus* things that are crooked; we *dirigimus* when we head in a direction.

[Note: [Col. 0026D]

154. Perhaps, following Agraetius’s sense, one should write: “*Deportare*, to carry those things away”; but he himself has it incorrectly as “to put down.” *Apportare* is to bring something; compare the rest.]

—“To lift.” “To lift from a place.” Agraetius.]

154. Between *deportare*, *comportare*, and *exportare*. *Deportare* is to bring something; *comportare* to bring things together into one place; *exportare* to carry away.

155. Between *discedere* and *abscedere*, and the remaining terms. We use *discedere* for separation, *abscedere* for absence, *secedere* for withdrawal into solitude, and *decedere* for death.

[Note: [Col. 0026D]

156. Thus Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “Looking down upon the sea that bears ships”:

—“I lead away, I follow”; *diduco*, “I divide.”

—“Or I divide.” Another reading: “or I place,” that is, “or I arrange.”

—“Horses.” I would prefer “chariots.”

—“To draw away.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “To draw the fleet away.”

—“They lead away.” *Aeneid* III. Another reading: “They divide.”

The Vatican has *deduco* for “leading away in spirit.” AREV.]

156. Between *deduco* [printed *deauco*] and *diduco*. I *deduco* a friend by leading him forward [Al., “by conducting him”]; I *diduco* draw apart or divide. With reference to triumphal horses, if they are horses, they *duxere triumphos* (“draw the triumphs”); if oxen, they *deduxere* [Al., *duxere*]. With reference to ships, we say *subducere* (“draw up”) when bringing them onto land, but *deducere* [Al., *diducere*] when launching them into the sea, as in: “The companions launch the ships.”

22

157. Between *duo* and *ambo* [Al., *duos ambos*]. Whoever says *duo* (“two”) counts; whoever says *ambo* (“both”) joins them together.

158. Between *dispar* and *impar*. *Dispar* means unequal or unlike; *impar* means without an equal.

[Note: [Col. 0027C]

159. From Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “And twin bridles.” See the same author, on *Aeneid* I:

“Brandishing two spears with broad iron in his hand.”

Another reading: Cicero, *Letters to His Son*.

Barthius says that it is utterly trivial to claim that we use *bina* only for things that do not admit a singular number. Isidore follows Servius and other grammarians, although it is otherwise true that *bini* is often used indiscriminately for “two.” AREV.]

159. Between *duo* and *bina*. Cicero, in his letters to his son, says *duas epistolas* (“two letters”), not *binas*; but *binas litteras* (“two letters”), not *duas*. This is because *litterae*, when it means a letter, is a noun used only in the plural. For we say *bina* only of things that do not admit a singular number, such as *bina castra* (“two camps”) and *bina arma* (“two sets of arms”). Things that admit a singular number we call *duo*.

[Col. 0027B]

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

160. From Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “Do not, stranger, do not ask.”

—And Plautus, *Mostellaria*, the scene beginning: “I have Neptune, with great gratitude,” etc.]

160. Between *domus* and *hospitium*. *Domus* pertains to one’s own inhabitants. It is called *hospitium* when we receive someone or are ourselves received by someone; hence both the one who comes and the one to whom someone comes are called *hospes* (“guest” or “host”). Thus Plautus:

“A guest killed the guest whom he had captured with his hand.”

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

161. C. Fronto: “*Decens* (‘becoming’) is shown in gesture and bodily movement; *speciosus* (‘handsome’) [is shown in appearance].” The text is read incorrectly: “*Formosus* is said of excellent appearance; *forma* is a natural good, hence one is also called *formosus*.”]

161. Between *decens*, *speciosus*, and *formosus*. *Decens* is established by bodily movement; *speciosus* by appearance; *formosus* by nature or form.

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

162. *Etymologies*, Book X, under the letter I.]

162. Between *deformis* and *informis*. *Deformis* is one who lacks form [Al., “ugly form”]; *informis* is beyond or outside form.

163. Between *decus* and *decor*. *Decus* refers to the spirit; *decor* to bodily appearance.

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

164. From Agraetius.

The Vatican has “for offering.” AREV.]

164. Between *delator* and *dilator*. A *delator* is one who brings a charge for the purpose of accusation [Al., “of bringing a case”]; a *dilator* is one who postpones something in order to bring it forward later.

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

165. An anonymous poet, praised by John of Genoa: “I call the *tracones* of the earth animals—dragons.” See Ducange under *tracones*. AREV.]

165. Between *draco* and *traco* [Al., *truaco*]. A *draco* is a monstrous beast; *tracones* [Al., *truacones*] are openings or chasms in the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

166. C. Fronto: “For perhaps something happens.”

The Vatican has “and in virtues.” AREV.]

166. Between *dives*, *potens*, *fortunatus*, *locuples*, and *honestus*. *Dives* is rich in power and virtue; *potens* (“powerful”), as though near to God; *locuples* in estates, as though full of lands; *fortunatus* (“fortunate”), made blessed suddenly [F., “in substance”]; *honestus* in character and in the honor he enjoys.

[Note: [Col. 0027D]

167. C. Fronto: “*Cedo* asks for something for himself and is immovable; he who says *do* gives what he does not cause to be finished.”]

167. Between *do* and *cedo*. Whoever says *do* indicates the person to whom something is given; whoever says *cedo* speaks only of himself.

[Note: [Col. 0028C]

168. From Servius, on *Aeneid* V: “Descended from the high blood of the gods.”]

168. Between *deus* and *divus*. *Deus* always exists as a god; *divus* becomes divine or is made a god.

[Note: [Col. 0028C]

169. “Suddenly,” etc. Another reading: “It happens unexpectedly and without our knowledge.”

—“Loss.” Thus Asconius Pedianus, in the third speech against Verres: “*Detrimentum* (‘loss’) may also be said of a single part.”]

169. Between *damnum*, *jactura*, and *detrimentum*. We knowingly and voluntarily suffer *jactura* (“loss”); *damnum* (“damage”) occurs suddenly and without our expecting it; *detrimentum* is slight damage affecting one part.

[Note: [Col. 0028C]

170. Servius, on *Aeneid* V: “And I would build altars with his own gifts”:

“Gifts,” he says, belong to the gods above; “presents” to the gods below. And more clearly, C. Fronto: “A *donum* is what is given to the gods; a *munus*, what friends, clients, or freedmen send on account of duty.” Isidore himself has the same in *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 19.

The Vatican Codex has “a *munus* for everyone.” AREV.]

170. Between *donum* and *munus*. A *donum* is offered to God; a *munus* to human beings.

171. Between *delicta* and *delecta*. *Delicta* are sins; *delecta* are chosen things.

172. Between *delictum* and *injustitia*. Some have thought *delictum* to be a light sin, as something negligently abandoned, whereas *injustitia* is some monstrous and savage offense.

173. Between *dolus* and *dolor*. *Dolus* is evasion; *dolor* is bodily disturbance.

174. Between *dolosus* and *inimicus*. *Dolosus* is one who proceeds by hidden machination; *inimicus* one who does evil more openly.

[Note: [Col. 0028D]

175. The Vatican Manuscript has *distribuo* (“I distribute”) instead of *distraho* (“I draw apart”). AREV.]

175. Between *deduco* and *diduco*. I *deduco* a friend; I *diduco* draw apart.

24

176. Between *directum* and *derectum*. *Directum* [Al., *derectum*] is going in a straight line; *derectum* [Al., *directum*] extends straight across.

177. Between *disco* and *doceo*. One *discit* (“learns”) who does not know; one *docet* (“teaches”) who knows.

## Of the Letter E

[Col. 0028C]

[Note: [Col. 0028D]

178. The Vatican Codex places certain Differences here and elsewhere in a different order, and adds several at this point. Its letter E begins: “Between *aequora* and *maria*,” etc., as in no. 66; “between *aevum* and *saeculum*,” etc., as in no. 67; “between *externum*,” etc., as in this no. 178; and “between *haeresis* and *schisma*,” as in no. 282. This variation arises from a different manner of writing, for in the Middle Ages people wrote *equora*, *evum*, *eresis*, and so forth. AREV.]

178. Between *externum* and *hesternum*. We call *hesternum* “of the previous day,” but *externum* “foreign,” that is, “belonging to another.”

[Note: [Col. 0028D]

179. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV: *loquax* is one who speaks too much; *eloquens* is one who speaks copiously. He himself says this in the *Etymologies*, book X, under the letters C and L.

—Sallust. The same fragment is cited by Agellius, book I, chapter 15. Its source is uncertain.]

179. Between *eloquentem* and *loquacem*. Sincerity of eloquence belongs to the eloquent; overflowing and disorderly recklessness belongs to the talkative. Hence Sallust: “More talkative than eloquent.” And Cicero: “He was considered talkative, never eloquent.”

[Col. 0029A] [Note: [Col. 0029C]

180. From Servius, on *Aeneid* III: “Practised by the Fates.” He himself says this in the *Etymologies*, book X, under the words *expertus* and *expers*.

—“Ignorant.” Of the matter or cause under discussion. This should be rejected as a gloss, and Servius does not acknowledge it.]

180. Between *expertem* and *expertum*. If we say *expertum rerum*, we mean “experienced” or “skilled”; if *expertem*, “ignorant.”

[Note: [Col. 0029C]

181. From the passage of Servius cited above: “*Exercite*,” he says, “means ‘wearied.’ *Exercitatus* means ‘skilled’; *exercitus*, ‘wearied by labours’; *exercitatus*, ‘skilled through study.’”

[Col. 0029D] In the Vatican manuscript: “wearied by labour.” AREV.]

181. Between *exercitatum* and *exercitum*. *Exercitus* means “wearied by labours”; *exercitatus*, “skilled either by practice or by study.”

182. Between *exosum* and *odiosum*. One is called *exosus* who hates someone; *odiosus*, one who is hated.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

183. Cicero indicates the same distinction, *Tusculan Disputations*, book IV.
