In the same place: “Not an undistinguished orator.” Barthius says that Caelius’s words are being noted; he illustrated the whole passage, which was taken from Quintilian, book XIV, chapter 18. Caelius, however, was speaking about Marcus Antonius. AREV.]

183. Between *ebrietatem* and *ebriositatem*. *Ebrietas* is occasional drunkenness; *ebriositas* is frequent intoxication with wine. Of this the Apostle says (1 Corinthians VI): “Nor will drunkards possess the kingdom of God.” A certain not undistinguished orator elegantly described a drunk man awakened from sleep as follows: “Awakened, he could neither sleep, nor, drunk, remain awake.” By this statement he expressed, in a way, that the man was neither dead nor alive.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

184. Nonius, under the word *eventus*, from book I of Lucretius: “Whatever will have been done may be called an *eventum*.”]

184. Between *eventum* and *eventa*. *Eventus* is the thing itself; *eventa* are said of things that proceed from an event.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

185. A Virgilian epithet: “shameful want.”]

185. Between *egestatem* and *paupertatem*. *Egestas* is worse than *paupertas*: poverty can be honourable, whereas want is always shameful.

186. Between *experientiam* and *scientiam*. *Experientia* can be used of an evil, as in “having experienced punishments”; *scientia*, only of a good.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

187. Alternative: “from us to others.”]

187. Between *emittit* and *admittit*. We send others away from us (*emittimus*); we admit others to us (*admittimus*). Thus someone said to a certain virgin: “Build a wall around your sex, which neither lets your own eyes out nor lets in those of others.”

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

188. Nonius, under *arbitrii*.]

188. Between *existimare* and *arbitrari*. *Existimare* is an opinion formed in our mind; *arbitrari* is to pronounce the judgment of the mind.

[Col. 0029C] [Note: [Col. 0029D]

189. Vatican manuscript: “What is the difference between *emere* and *redimere*? He who buys…” AREV.]

189. Between *emere* and *redimere*. The distinction is that one who buys buys what belongs to another, whereas one who redeems buys, properly speaking, what was his own and ceased to be his own.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

190. From Servius, on *Georgics* I: “Long awaited with much labour”; and in the same author *exspectare* is also used for “to approve,” *Georgics* II: “And await the thick backs.”]

190. Between *exspectare* and *spectare*. One awaits someone who is going to come; one observes someone who is seen or approved.

[Note: [Col. 0029D]

191. Agraetius gives the same account, though nothing about the double *ff*: “*Effertur*,” he says, “is used of one who is carried out; and *eferunt*, of those who exalt by praising.”]

191. Between *efferunt* and *eferunt*. Those who carry things out use *efferunt*, with two *f*s. Those who exalt someone worthy of praise use *eferunt*, with one *f*. Cicero: “Perhaps these things exalt him too much.”

[Note: [Col. 0030C]

192. Between *exsequimur*, *persequimur*, and *prosequimur*. We carry out a death sentence, in which there is vengeance; we pursue someone fleeing; we accompany someone when we perform a duty.

[Note: [Col. 0030C]

193. Varro, book VI of *On the Latin Language*: *extemplo* means “immediately.” Alternative: *extemplo*, “suddenly”; *illico*, “at once”; “immediately.”

—Nonius: *illico* means “at once,” “soon.”]

193. Between *extemplo* and *illico*. *Extemplo* means “suddenly,” or “immediately,” or “at once”; *illico*, “soon” or “continuously.”

194. Between *exstinctum* and *restinctum*. We call a light *exstinctum*, as Cicero says: “The lights of the state have been extinguished”; but a fire *restinctum*, as the same Cicero says: “We extinguished the fires that had nearly been applied and the flames that had been set around them.”

[Note: [Col. 0030C]

195. Servius, on *Aeneid* XI: “And with peace set between them”: “A *sequester* is an intermediary between two disputants, with whom something is temporarily deposited.” Festus is generally similar.

—Those two words, “in arms,” are omitted by Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 3, where he discusses cavalry soldiers; and indeed they seem suspect to me. Perhaps he had added that *eques* can also mean the horse itself, citing Virgil, *Georgics* III: “And they taught the horseman, under arms, to leap over the ground.” Nonius, under *equitem* and *equites*.

—“In order.” Alternative: *sequester* is used of one who receives a pledge. F.: one who receives a pledge.]

195. Between *equitem* [alternative: *equum*], *equestrem*, and *sequestrem*. One who intervenes between disputants is called *sequestris*, through whom each side follows an equitable trust [alternative: “is made equal in good faith”]. An *eques* is one who sits on a horse in arms. *Equestris* refers to a place or rank, as when one says, “That man is of equestrian rank.” Likewise: “He serves in the equestrian order.”

[Note: [Col. 0030D]

196. From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “And the lifeless body with gold”; and from the commentators on Terence, *Andria*, act I, scene 4, and elsewhere.]

196. Between *exanimem* and *exanimatum*. *Exanimis* means dead; *exanimatus*, frightened. As in the line:

“Then, terrified, she would drive the following ranks against the walls.”

[Note: [Col. 0030D]

197. From Agraetius.]

197. Between *eu* and *heus*. *Eu* is the interjection of someone in pain; *heus* is the adverb of one calling.

[Note: [Col. 0030D]

198. *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 6.]

198. Between *ensem* and *gladium*. An *ensis* is merely the iron; a *gladius* is the whole weapon. A *mucro*, however, is not only the point of a sword but the sharp point of any weapon. We also use *gladius* generally, *ensis* in battle, and *mucro* in work.

[Note: [Col. 0030D]

199. It seems to derive from Servius, on *Aeneid* XI: “To carry the leaders themselves.”]

199. Between *exuvias* and *spolia*. *Exuviae* are those of leaders; *spolia*, those of private persons.

[Note: [Col. 0030D]

200. *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 27.

—“It should not benefit.” I read: “It may not be possessed.”

In the same place. This distinction between one relegated and one deported seems foreign to this passage; it is absent from the old Vatican Codex 3321. Barthius found it in his own manuscript, where, as Orenius says, it read: “There is a great difference.” He conjectures—“as Herennius says,” that is, the jurist Modestinus—and shortly afterward: “Thus, in the case of one relegated, if no mention is made of his property, it should benefit the man; in the case of one deported, it should harm him.” AREV.]

200. There is a great difference between one who is relegated to an island and one who is deported. First, the property of the relegated follows him unless it has been taken away by sentence; the property of the deported does not follow him unless it has been expressly granted to him. Thus it happens that, for one relegated, mention of his property in the sentence is of no benefit, whereas for one deported it is harmful. They also differ in the quality of the place. In the case of one relegated, the matter is handled more humanely; to those deported, however, islands are usually assigned that are extremely harsh and almost comparable with the highest punishment.

201. Between *eremum* and *desertum*. *Eremus* is a solitude along a road where no one has ever lived; *desertum* is a place that was once inhabited and then abandoned.

[Note: [Col. 0031C]

202. It seems to derive from Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “Altars and unspeakable swords”: “An *exsecratio* is a prayer against evils; an oath is the wishing of prosperity.”]

202. Between *exsecrationem* and *jurationem*. An *exsecratio* is, for example: “If I do not suffer evil”; a *juratio*: “If good happens to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0031D]

203. From C. Fronto: “He has experienced something,” either in a favourable or unfavourable sense; *experrectus*, “awakened from sleep.”]

203. Between *expertum* and *experrectum*. *Expertum* means something recognized or experienced; *experrectum*, awakened from sleep.

204. Between *en* and *em*. *En* is used when you point something out; *em*, when you rebuke.

[Col. 0031B] 205. Between *ebrium* and *ebriosum*. An *ebrius* has drunk a great deal for a time; an *ebriosus* always drinks a great deal.

[Note: [Col. 0031D]

206. The old custom of writing *ecus*, and then *equs*, for *equus* is indicated, just as *qis* was written for *quis*, and so forth. AREV.]

206. Between *aequum* and *equum*. *Equus*, meaning the animal, is to be written with *e* and *u* alone. But what is written for “just” is to be written with the diphthong *ae* and doubled *u*.

## On the Letter F

[Note: [Col. 0031D]

207. From the commentators on Terence, *Phormio*, act I, scene 2.

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has: “He who lacks weakness, *fidus*; he who has faith, *fidelis*.” *Infirmitatem* is an error for *firmitate*; but the accusative instead of the ablative, as in *utor*, might perhaps be tolerated. AREV.]

207. Between *fidelem* and *fidum*. A friend is called *fidus*; a servant, *fidelis*. Likewise, *infidelis* is one who lacks firmness; *infidus*, one who lacks faith.

[Note: [Col. 0032C]

208. See Nonius, under *fama*.]

208. Between *famosum* and *infamem*. *Famosus* is one about whom fame speaks, whether well or ill; *infamis* is one of bad reputation only.

[Note: [Col. 0032C]

209. From C. Fronto.]

209. Between *ferocem* and *ferum*. The spirit is called *ferox*; the lion, *ferus*.

[Col. 0031C] 210. Between *fallacem* and *mendacem*. Every deceitful person acts so that someone may be deceived; but not everyone who lies wishes to deceive. This is the case with mimes, comedies, and many poems, in which falsehood is written for the pleasure of entertainment rather than with the intention of deceiving. Indeed, nearly all who jest [alternative: “almost all who speak”] lie.

[Note: [Col. 0032C]

211. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “Chorebus, with mind driven mad.”

[Col. 0032D] In the same place: “Whoever became so from a cause,” namely because, as Barthius says, the person becomes frenzied when goads are applied to provoke anger. AREV.]

211. Between *furiatum* and *furiosum*. *Furiosus* is one who is carried along like a wild animal, and from whom madness never departs; *furiatus* is one who rages for a specific reason.

[Note: [Col. 0032D]

212. “Angry.” From the commentators on Terence, *Andria*, act I, scene 1, and *Hecyra*, act III, scene 1.]

212. Between *furiosum*, *furentem* [alternative: *furientem*], and *iratum*. One is *furiosus* in heart, *furens* [alternative: *furiens*] because of a cause, and *iratus* for a justified reason.

213. Between *ferocitatem* and *feritatem*. *Ferocitas* is often considered praiseworthy. Thus we speak of the *ferocitas* of soldiers and call youth *ferox*. *Feritas*, however, is a savage disposition of mind.

214. Between *formidinem*, *pavorem*, and *metum*, or *timorem*. *Formido* is directed either at the eyes or at the mind without the exercise of reason, especially in the case of little children. *Pavor* is a sudden occasion that disturbs the mind with fear, but which is dispelled by reason or time and does not remain. *Metus* is a sudden inward movement of the mind, or of the heart, produced by some sad recollection. *Timor* is an external pain that comes upon the mind from some accidental circumstance. *Timiditas*, moreover, is a perpetual defect of the mind. *Timor* lasts only for a time. Thus a brave man may sometimes experience fear, but never timidity. There is also good fear and bad fear. It is bad when someone dreads that temporal goods will be taken away from him [alternative: “fears that they will be withdrawn”]; it is good when, the more ardently someone loves God, the more carefully he fears offending him. For fear is sometimes useful and fitting, according to the character of the times and circumstances.

215. Augustine seems to distinguish *facinus* and *flagitium* as follows. “Whatever,” he says, “untamed desire does to corrupt its own mind and body is called *flagitium*; whatever it does to harm another is called *facinus*. These are the two kinds of all sins” [alternative: “of all human sins”]. “But *flagitia* come first: once they have corrupted the mind, they burst forth into crimes.”

29 [Note: [Col. 0032D]

216. Briefly in Vatican Codex 3321: “What is the difference between *phantasia* and *phantasma*? *Phantasia* is a conjecture about unknown things formed from known things; *phantasma* is an unknowing of known things.” AREV.]

216. Between *phantasiam* and *phantasma*. *Phantasia* is the image of some body that has been seen and later shaped in the mind by thought—for example, the appearance of a grandfather or father whom we once saw; when we recall him in thought, we call this *phantasia*. *Phantasma*, however, is an image formed from a known image that we have seen—for example, the appearance of a grandfather whom we do not remember ever having seen; nevertheless, his appearance is shaped not by memory but by an act of the mind. Thus, when memory gathers appearances of known things, there is *phantasia*; when an appearance of an unknown thing is shaped in the mind, there is *phantasma*. For shaped phantasms are nothing other than forms abstracted by bodily sense from the appearance of a body; and, once received, it is very easy by thought either to divide them, multiply them, contract them, extend them, arrange them, disturb them, or shape them in any way as a product of memory. But when truth is being sought, it is difficult to guard against and avoid such operations. Likewise, *phantasia* is a conjecture about unknown things formed from known things; *phantasma*, the unknowing of known things.

[Note: [Col. 0032D]

217. From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “The confidence of your ancestry.”]

217. Between *fiduciam* and *confidentiam*. *Fiducia* belongs to good things; *confidentia*, to bad things.

[Col. 0033A] 218. Between *famam* and *gloriam*. *Gloria* belongs to virtues, whereas *fama* belongs to vices. Ennius, in *Achilles*: “You will raise up for yourself the highest fame for an evil life, and glory prepared for a good one” [alternative: “glory prepared”] …; the malevolent raise fame, the benevolent glory [alternatives: “those who live badly” and “those who live well”].

[Note: [Col. 0033D]

219. From the thought of Servius, on *Aeneid* IV: “I have completed the course Fortune had given me.”

In the same place. Some ask whether Christians may use the word *fatum*; it is clear that most use it in a Catholic sense. AREV.]

219. The pagans distinguished *fatum* and *fortuna* in this way: whatever came by chance, with no evident cause, they called *fortuna*; *fatum*, whatever had been assigned and fixed for each person. Thus they said that it belonged to fate that we are born and that we die; whatever variety occurs in life belonged to fortune [alternative: “whatever variation may have occurred”].

220. Between *falsitatem* and *mendacium*. To deny what is true is *falsitas*; to fabricate what is not true is *mendacium*. Hence Cato also says: “If, I say, you suppress what is true [alternative: ‘suppress the truth from us’], you are recognized as a falsifier; if you invent falsehoods, you appear [alternative: ‘will be judged’] to be a liar.”

[Note: [Col. 0033D]

221. From the thought of the commentators on Terence, *Eunuchus*, act I, scene 2.]

221. Between *falsum* and *fictum*. *Falsum* belongs to orators, among whom truth is often so manipulated that things which happened are denied; *fictum* belongs to poets, among whom things that did not happen are said to have happened. Thus *falsum* is what is not true; *fictum*, what is merely plausible.

222. Between *fertilem* and *fructuosum*. An *ager*—a field—is *fertilis*; whatever is profitable to someone is *fructuosum*.

[Note: [Col. 0033D]

223. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “Among leafy groves”; hence a previously mutilated passage was restored.

In the same place, Pantinus notes *locus* from a variant reading, which Grialius himself printed in the text. Perhaps Pantinus intended *lucus* rather than *locus* in his note. AREV.]

223. Between *frondeum* and *frondosum*. *Frondeum* is something made entirely of leaves, such as a couch; *frondosus* is a place [alternative: “grove”]. Although it abounds in leaves, it is not made wholly of leaves. The same distinction applies to *gramineum* and *graminosum* [alternative readings: *germinem* and *germinosum*].

[Col. 0033C] 224. Between *flecti* and *deflecti*. *Flecti* means to turn back [alternative: “from the straight path”] and toward what is near; *deflecti*, to turn farther away and onto a deviating path.

225. There is this distinction between *frui* and *uti*. We enjoy (*fruimur*) what we can in no way do without; we use (*utimur*) things that we sometimes have but do not always possess. Consequently, use is temporal, whereas enjoyment is eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0033D]

226. *Etymologies*, book X, under the letter F.

In the same place. It should rather be written *phrenetici*, since it does not derive from *frendeo* but from the Greek *phrenesis*. AREV.]

226. Between *fremere* and *frendere*. *Fremere* is to stir up the fury of the mind to the point of tumultuous shouting; *frendere*, properly, is to press and gnash the teeth. Hence *frena*—bridles—were so called because horses *frendant*, that is, press [alternative: “imprint”] and bite with their teeth. Hence also *phrenetici*, “frenzied people,” were so called because they gnash their teeth.

[Note: [Col. 0033D]

227. Festus, under *plorare*.

[Col. 0034D] —*Plangere*. Thus the old glossary: “with lamentations.”]

227. Between *flere* and *plorare*. *Flere* is to pour forth abundant tears, as though from *fluere*, “to flow”; *plorare* is, as it were, to weep with the voice; *plangere*, to beat one’s breast or face while shedding tears. *Lamentari* is to weep with certain expressions of sorrow. *Moerere* is to grieve in silence. *Lugere* is to grieve with a change of clothing or appearance. Tears are called *lacrimae* from the laceration of the mind. Mourners are called *lugentes*, as though “lacking light”; hence *luctus* [F.: *lucus*] is also so called.

31 228. Between *fodere* and *effodere*. *Fodere* is merely to disturb the earth; *effodere* is, by doing this, to extract or discover something. Its opposite is *infodere*, “to bury.”

229. Between *famulari* and *obsequi*. *Famulari* belongs to what is owed; *obsequi*, properly, to the will.

[Note: [Col. 0034D]

230. Old glossary: *flagitaverit* for “vigorously.”

—“To impute maliciously.” In the manuscripts: *impura res est* for *imputare*.]

230. Between *flagitare* and *flagitiare*. *Flagitare* means the same as “to address insistently”; *flagitiare* means “to defile.”

231. Between *fugiunt* and *diffugiunt*. They *fugiunt* when they flee together; they *diffugiunt* when they flee separately.

[Note: [Col. 0034D]

232. Nonius, under *confiteri*.

—Servius, on *Aeneid* IV: “For I shall confess to Anna.”]

232. Between *fatemur* and *confitemur*. *Confiteri* belongs to one’s own choice; *fateri* is the act of a compelled mind, not of the will [alternative: “to profess, that is …”].

233. There is a distinction in questioning between “Did you do it?” and “Did you not do it?” Where we want the answer to affirm that the commanded act was done, we say: “Did you do it?” Where we want it to be denied, we say: “Did you not do it?”

[Note: [Col. 0034D]

234. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “Flowing with gore and corruption,” takes the opposite view: “*Sanies* belongs to the dead; *tabum* to the living, namely blood.”

In the same place, the Vatican manuscript has “as the age of a human being.” AREV.]

234. Between *fluit* and *defluit*. What flows (*fluit*) runs naturally, such as moisture; what decays (*defluit*) is dissolved by age or antiquity, such as human life or a tree’s leaf. We use *fluere* in three ways: of the moisture of things, of the gore of living beings, and of the corruption of the dead.

[Col. 0034C] 235. Between *funebre*, *funereum*, and *funestum*. *Funebre* means mournful; *funereum*, something composed of or belonging to a funeral; *funestum*, something polluted by a funeral. Thus a servant is called *funestus* if he has been contaminated by some funeral and is therefore unable to perform sacred rites.

[Note: [Col. 0034D]

236. From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “Fragrant honey”; in another manuscript: “For when it signifies flame and fire, which signifies conflagration.” Perhaps it should be read: “For when it signifies flame and conflagration,” following Servius.]

236. Between *fragrat* and *flagrat*. With *r*, *fragrat* refers to smell; with *l*, *flagrat* refers to flame and fire. When it signifies a conflagration, which is nourished by blowing, we use *l*; when it refers to smell, because the scent is stronger when its substance is broken [alternative: “which comes from a broken form”], it is pronounced with *r* [alternative: “it is spoken with *r*”].

[Note: [Col. 0034D]

237. Thus also in the *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 6.

—“From the same …” From the cited book it seems that one should read “from the same mother,” not “father,” and below: “For he is a brother born from the same mother, not proceeding from the same stock.” Otherwise Isidore contradicts himself in these two passages, as does Servius, from whom he took the material, on *Aeneid* V: “This brother Eryx.”

In the Vatican manuscript: “from the same sea and mother.” BREV.]

237. Between *fratrem* and *germanum*. Those who are born from the same father but not from the same mother are called *fratres*, “brothers.” Those who are born from the same father and mother are called *germani* [alternative: “from the same mother and father”]. A *germanus* is one born from the same mother or proceeding from the same stock.

[Note: [Col. 0035C]

238. The commentators on Terence, *Hecyra*, act III, scene 5: “Strong, robust, and fuller in body.”]

238. Between *firmum* and *valentem*. *Firmus* comes from the firmness of nature; *valens* from exceptional strength, as in the case of an athlete.

[Note: [Col. 0035D]

239. C. Fronto: “A figure is the work of art; form is the good of nature.”]

239. Between *figuram* and *formam*. *Figura* belongs to art; *forma* to nature [alternative: “to a human being”].

240. Between *farctum* and *partum*. We call something *farctum* when it has not been born and lies within the womb; *partum*, when it has been born.

[Note: [Col. 0035D]

241. See Servius, book VIII on the *Aeneid*, on “Three times wearied, he sat down in the valley.” *Etymologies*, book X, under the letter F. Verrius gives a different account in Diomedes, book I: “One is *fatigatus* when he has been compelled to labour through another; one is *fessus* when he gives out from labour, as *lassus*.”]

241. Between *fessum*, *fatigatum*, and *lassum*. *Fessus* applies to the mind and care [alternative: “the body”]; *fatigatus*, to the length of a journey; *lassus*, to labour.

[Col. 0035B] [Note: [Col. 0035D]

242. Thus also in the *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter 6.]

242. Between *frameam* and *machaeram*. A *framea* is a sword sharpened on both sides, which people commonly call a *spatha*; a *machaera* is a long sword sharpened on one side.

243. Between *foedus* and *pacem*. A treaty (*foedus*) precedes peace (*pax*). Peace is received afterward; the treaty is made first.

[Note: [Col. 0035D]

244. C. Fronto, in contrast: “A *flumen* both flows and remains; a *fluvius* dries up with the seasons.” Almost the whole passage is from the *Etymologies*, book XIII, chapter 21. From this, the words “a river whose water is a course of water” seem to require alteration.

—Pacuvius … Festus, under *torrens*, cites a passage from *Antiope*; moreover, the word *torret*, both here and in the *Etymologies*, should be changed from *terrae*, and one should read: “The torrid earth will burn the earth’s offspring with fiery vapour.”

—“A spring, moreover.” Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, under *fons*, and Festus derive it from *fundendo*, “pouring forth.”

[Col. 0036C] —“And from it …” Varro and Festus have the better reading: “from going around,” or “from winding around.”

In the *Etymologies* one now reads *fluvius cursus aquae*, not *decursus*, as Pantinus presents it; but below, no. 499, *decursus* is found. BREV.]

244. Between *flumen* and *fluvium*, *flumen*, *torrentem*, and so forth. A *fluvius* is, generally, a perennial course of waters, so called from *fluere*, “to flow.” Properly, a *flumen* is the water itself; a *fluvius*, that which has water. A *torrens* is so called because it grows through rain and dries up in drought, that is, becomes parched. Hence Pacuvius also says: “A torrid stream burns with fiery vapour.” A *rivus* is a stream formed suddenly by rain, which quickly runs down and disappears; a *fons* is the source [alternative: “body”] of newly arising water. An *amnis* is a river crowned with a grove and foliage, and is called *amnis* from this very pleasantness.

[Note: [Col. 0036C]

245. Thus generally in Nonius, under *fulmen*.

In the Vatican manuscript: “sent forth upon the earth.” And shortly afterward: “with three rays.” AREV.]

245. Between *fulgura* and *fulmina*. *Fulgur* is the splendour of a flashing cloud [alternative: “of flashing clouds”]; *fulmen* is a fiery point, sent from the clouds to the earth by the violence of the winds. There are three related terms: *fulgor* [alternative: *fulgus*; F.: *fulgos*], *fulgur*, and *fulmen*. *Fulgor* is what touches; *fulgur*, what sets fire to and burns; *fulmen*, what splits. Hence they are represented with three rays.

246. Between *florida* and *florulenta*. Trees and grass are *florida*; fields or meadows are *florulenta*. Similar expressions are understood in the same way.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

247. Servius disagrees, for on *Aeneid* I, “And the harvested crops,” he confuses *frumenta* and *fruges*, and in *Georgics* I: “With the rattling pod, the legume.”

—“Prominent …” From Servius read: “The part of the throat beneath the chin”; these words are from the *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 3.]

247. Between *frumenta* and *fruges*. *Frumenta* are dry and arid; *fruges* are liquid. The name *frumentum* is derived from *frumen*, that is, the prominent part of the throat.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

248. *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 2.

—“Natural.” From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “And the fat flesh of wild beasts,” and in the *Etymologies*.]

248. Between *feras* and *bestias*. Every *bestia* is *fera*, but not every *fera* is a *bestia*. *Bestiae* are creatures that rage with bites or claws, such as leopards, lions, and tigers; they are so called from *vastare*, “to ravage.” *Ferae* also include those which, although they do not rage by force [alternative: “although they do not rage through violence”], are nevertheless wild. They are called *ferae* because they enjoy natural liberty and are carried along by their own desire.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

249. Festus, under *fasti*, and Servius, on *Aeneid* III: “The pride of Achilles’ stock.”

In the Vatican manuscript: “to which *nefastus* is opposed.” AREV.]

249. Between *fastos* and *fastos* [alternative: *fastus*] as applied to days. *Fasti* is the general term comprehending both good and bad days; *dies fasti* [alternative: *fastus*] are days to which *nefasti* are opposed.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

250. Festus, under “on festival days.” Varro, book V of *On the Latin Language*, under “fast days.”

In the Vatican manuscript: “on which matters are conducted.” AREV.]

250. Between *fasti dies* and *nefasti dies*. *Fasti dies* are days on which legal judgments may be conducted and a case may be pleaded or prosecuted. *Nefasti dies* are so called because on those days it is unlawful (*nefas*) to conduct or plead any matter or to perform a sacred rite. Thus *nefasti* are opposed to festival days.

251. Between *festi dies* and *sollemnes*. Days are called *festi* according to custom; *sollemnes* are those that concern everyone, such as the *Parentalia*. Thus, when someone has fulfilled the duties owed to the dead, he is said to have performed the solemn rites.

252. Between *fulmen*, *fulgorem*, and *fulgur*. *Fulmen* is what strikes; *fulgor*, what appears; *fulgur*, what is hidden, if it falls from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

253. F.: Between *foedum* and *foedus*: *foedum* means shameful; *foedus*, agreeable.]

253. Between *foedum* and *foedus*. *Foedum* means shameful; *foedus*, agreeable.

[Note: [Col. 0036D]

254. Perhaps from Agraetius: *fides* derives from fidelity; *fidis*, from a string.]

254. Between *fides* and *fidis*. *Fides* refers to faith; *fidis*, to a string.

255. Between *fenum* and *fenus*. *Fenum* is hay; *fenus* is profit.

[Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037C]

256. Hence *flagratores*, because they were beaten with whips for pay. Festus, under *flagratores*.]

256. Between *fragrat* and *flagrat*. *Fragrat* means “smells sweet”; *flagrat*, “strikes with blows.”

257. Between *favorem* and *favum*. *Favor* is assistance; a *favum* is honeycomb.

258. Between *furatum* and *furtatum*. *Furatum* refers to a person who commits theft; *furtatum*, to what the thief steals.

259. Between *fatum* and *fatuum*. *Fatuum* means sluggish or foolish; *fatum* is a decree of fortune.

[Note: [Col. 0037C]

260. From Agraetius.]

260. Between *fastos* and *fastus*. *Fastus* refers to pride; *fastos*, to books.

261. Between *feminam* and *femina*. *Feminam* refers to a human female; *femina* means the thighs.

[Note: [Col. 0037C]

262. Servius gives the better account, on *Aeneid* VIII: “And they turn the iron with the tenacious pincers”: “*Forfices* are instruments with which we cut. *Forcipes* are instruments with which we hold something hot, for *forvum* means ‘hot.’” Festus, under *forcipes*.

[Col. 0037D] In the same place: *tisorias*. This is a Hispanic form, *tijeras*, as shortly afterward *tenaces*, “tongs,” is *tenazas*. But *tisoriae* is found neither among the lexicographers of good Latin nor in Ducange, except that in the supplement to Ducange *tissor* means “weaver.” In Vatican Codex 3321 one reads *forcices incesurias*, perhaps *incisorias*. Thus far I have been able to excerpt, from the papers of the distinguished Cajetan Marini, the variant readings of that codex; other material is lacking. AREV.]

262. Between *forfices* and *forcipes*. *Forfices*, that is, scissors; *forcipes*, tongs.

[Note: [Col. 0037D]

263. *Etymologies*, book V, chapter 26.

—“Scriptures …” Ezekiel XVI, in many places; Hosea II, chapter 14, and elsewhere.]

263. Between *fornicationem* and *adulterium*. *Adulterium* is the defilement of the marital bed; *fornicatio* is love released from lawful marriage, wandering and pursuing permission to satisfy lust. Scripture, however, commonly calls every unlawful corruption *fornicatio*, as with idolatry and avarice, from which transgression of the law arises through unlawful desire. *Fornicatio* took its name from certain vaulted buildings that the ancients called *fornices*, in which prostitutes were established and put on display. Prostitutes are called *meretrices* from *mereri*, that is, “to earn” the wages of lust. Hence soldiers too, when they receive their pay, are said to *mereri*, “earn.”

## On the Letter G

264. Between *grates* and *gratias*. Thanks (*grates*) are rendered to God; *gratiae* are rendered to human beings, because they can be repaid [alternative: “cannot be repaid”]. Therefore *grates*, signifying a relation to worship (*latria*) [alternative: “to what is broad”], is especially appropriate to God.

[Note: [Col. 0037D]

265. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV: “When the mind is moved calmly and steadily by reason, that is called joy; but when the mind exults emptily and extravagantly, that may be called an exuberant or excessive gladness, which they define as ‘an elevation of the mind without reason.’”

—“Scriptures …” Isaiah XVIII and LVII, where the Vulgate has: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.”]

265. Between *gaudium* and *laetitiam*. The Stoics distinguish them as follows. They say that *gaudium* is an elevation of the mind rejoicing in things worthy of exultation, whereas *laetitia* is an unrestrained elevation of the mind that knows no limit and rejoices even in things mixed with vice. Hence Scripture also says: “There is no joy [alternative: ‘no rejoicing’] for the wicked, says the Lord.”

[Col. 0038A] [Note: [Col. 0038C]

266. Nonius, under *grave*. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “Burdened with knots.”]

266. Between *gravitatem* and *gravitudinem*. *Gravitas* arises from the weight of the mind and from judgment; *grav itudo* belongs to the body. Between *grave* and *gravidum*. *Grave* is said of nature; *gravidum* of accidental fertility, as a tree pregnant with fruit.

[Note: [Col. 0038C]

267. From Varro’s view; see the book on the Latin Language, where he derives *loqui*, “to speak,” from *locus*, “place,” because words are spoken each in its proper place.

—*Garrit*. Nonius, under *garrire*.

[Col. 0038D] In Grialius’s edition, the text and note read *temperanter*. Pantinus seems to have intended *temperate* for one reading and *temperanter* for the other. In Varro’s words as printed by Grialius, the reading was *suae quoque*. AREV.]

267. Between *garrire* and *loqui*. One *loquitur* who speaks correctly and moderately; one *garrit* who either says many words or speaks crudely.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

268. See Nonius, under the words *ferre* and *gerere*.]

268. Between *gerere* and *ferre*. We *gerimus* our own things and things that are, as it were, part of our nature; we *ferimus* things imposed upon us, as a burden. But Virgil uses the terms interchangeably (*Aeneid* I): “The faithful Achates was carrying the weapons.” He used *gerebat* for *ferre*.

36 269. Between *gravatur* and *ingravatur* [alternative: *ponderatur*]. One is *ingravatur* [alternative: *ponderatur*] by another’s weight; one is *gravatur* by his own.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

270. *Gens*, *nationis*, and *familiae*, Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “A nation hostile to me.”]

270. Between *gentem*, *gentes*, and *genus*. *Gens* refers to a nation, such as Greece or Assyria; hence *gentilitas* is also derived. *Gentes* refers to families, such as the Julii or Claudii. *Genus* refers to a quality, such as the kind of an animal or fruit.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

271. C. Fronto gives almost the same distinction: we call a person a Corinthian (*Corinthium*), a vessel Corinthian (*Corinthiacum*), and a spring Corinthian (*Corinthiensem*).

In the same place. These and similar distinctions, such as *Hispanus*, *Hispanicus*, and *Hispaniensis*, are not regularly observed. AREV.]

271. Between *Graecum*, *Graecanicum*, and *Graecense*. A person is called *Graecus*; a thing, *Graecanica*; something of the sort commonly made in Greece, *Graecense*.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

272. Thus Fronto: *Gallus* by nationality; *Gallicus* from Gaul.

—F. writes: *Gallicanus*, something that brings or derives something.]

272. Between *Gallum*, *Gallicum*, and *Gallicanum*. *Gallus* is one born in Gaul; *Gallicus* is something brought from Gaul; *Gallicanus* is something that brings something from Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

273. Isidore contradicts himself above.]

273. Between *germanam* and *sororem*. A *soror* is from the same stock but not from the same womb; a *germana* proceeds from the stock of both parents.

[Note: [Col. 0038D]

274. Servius nevertheless, on *Aeneid* I: “The father looking out”: “Venerable,” he says, “as Father Tiber”; therefore the name applies both to a real father and to honour.]

274. Between *genitorem* and *patrem*. *Genitor* is a term of nature [Col. 0038C] or origin; *pater* is a name of dignity and honour. Hence we also call holy men and elders “fathers.” Our *genitores* are those from whom we were born.

275. Between *generat* and *parturit*. We say that males *generant*, “beget”; females *parturiunt*, “give birth.” Thus: “He begot; she gave birth.”

276. Between *gubernatorem* and *nautam*. Every *gubernator* can be a sailor, but not every sailor can be a *gubernator*, a helmsman [alternative: “can be called one”].

[Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039D]

277. C. Fronto: “Great in increase; large in extent.”]

277. Between *grande* and *maximum*. *Grande* pertains to the body; *maximum* to the mind.

## On the Letter H

278. Between *hodie* and *hoc die*. *Hodie* is used as though something were happening for the first time; *hoc die* as though we were reporting something that happened at some point.

279. Between *hunc diem* and *hanc diem*. In ancient usage, *dies* of masculine gender indicated a favourable time; of feminine gender, an unfavourable one, as in Job: “Cursed be the day.”

280. Between *habeo* and *ab eo*. *Habeo* means “I retain”; *ab eo* means “from him,” that is, “from that person.”

281. Between *hos* and *os*. If we write *hos* with *h*, we signify persons; without *h*, it signifies the face.

282. Between *haeresim* and *schisma*. *Schisma* is when one thinks the same as the others and worships according to the same rite, but takes pleasure merely in the division of the congregation. *Haeresis* is when one thinks something entirely different from the others and establishes for himself a form of worship based on a perverse doctrine that is different and far removed from theirs. *Haeresis* is called in Greek from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself what seems better. *Secta* is named from division, as though from “cutting.” Hence philosophical and heretical schools are also called *sectae*.

[Note: [Col. 0039D]

283. Alternative: “*honus regionum*”; but the word *regionum* (“of regions”) has intruded from the following article.]

283. Between *honos* and *onus*. *Honos* refers to honour; *onus*, to a burden.

[Note: [Col. 0039D]

284. From Agraetius.]

284. Between *hora* and *ora*. *Hora*, with the letter *h*, refers to the hours of the days; without *h*, *ora* refers to regions or boundaries, or to the mouth, by which speech is expressed.

[Note: [Column 0039D]

285. From Servius, on the passage in Book I of the *Aeneid*: “Burdened with the spoils of the East.”

—Old Glossary: *Honus*, honor. Τιμὴ θεῶν, τιμὴ ἀνθρώπων, “the honor of the gods, the honor of human beings.” Varro likewise, *On the Latin Language*, Book 4: “The words *onus* and *honos* were so called because one sustains the state.”]

285. The difference between *honustus* and *oneratus* is that *oneratus* is one pressed down by a burden of any kind, whereas *honustus* is one for whom the burden itself is an honor, as when someone carries the spoils of the enemy. But *oneratus* has no aspiration because it comes from *onus*, “burden”; *honustus*, however, retains the aspiration because it derives from *honor*, “honor.”

286. Between *hauritur* and *exhauritur*. Water is *hau­ritur*, “drawn up”; a well is *exhauritur*, “emptied.”

[Note: [Column 0039D]

287. This distinction is explained more fully in the book arranged without alphabetical order, no. 134, where I shall add some observations from Goldast. AREV.]

287. Between *herbidum* and *herbosum*. We call a place *herbidum* in which the greenness of the grasses never ceases; 38 *herbosum* refers to a place that readily produces grass and dries out seasonally.

## On the Letter I

[Note: [Column 0039D]

288. Both manuscripts read *inferi infernum*, mistakenly.

—Beginning “Saying …,” Psalm 85: “And you delivered my soul.”]

288. Between *inferum* and *infernum*. The upper part of hell is *inferus*, where the souls of the righteous rested before Christ’s coming. The lower part, however, is *infernum*, into which the souls of the impious who have sinned greatly are thrust [Al., “handed over”]. Concerning this, the Prophet rejoices [Al., “rejoices together with others”] that his soul has been delivered, saying: “For you have delivered my soul from the lowest hell.”

289. Between *initium* and *principium*. *Initium* is the beginning of things, from which something begins—for example, the foundations of a house or the keel of a ship. *Principium*, however, is the beginning of speech.

290. Between *judicium* and *justitia*. Justice is the pursuit of living rightly; judgment is equity in judging rightly. Therefore, whoever serves through good living [Al., “serves the practice of living well”] practices justice; whoever judges rightly among those subject to him observes judgment. Judgment, however, is corrupted by the time or occasion of cunning, not by its dignity. For each person must first be just, provide for uprightness, and only afterward attain equity in judgments. The first of these belongs to virtue, the second to honor. No one can attain honor except through virtue. Justice differs from judgment. Judgment that is unjust is commonly called wrong; justice, however, can never be [Al., “unjust”] or inequitable.

[Note: [Column 0039D]

291. *Etymologies*, Book 8, chapter 9.

[Column 0040D] In the same place Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book 40, chapter 10, found corrupt words in his manuscripts—“and often they compel bodies to rise”—and restored conjecturally: “and who compel bodies to rise,” etc. AREV.]

291. Between *incantator*, *magus*, *aruspex*, and *maleficus*. Enchanters are those who accomplish a matter by words [Al., “by a word”]. Magi are those who philosophize about the stars. Sorcerers are those who use blood and victims and often touch the bodies of the dead. Soothsayers are those who inspect the entrails of animals and foretell the future from them.

[Note: [Column 0040D]

292. From Servius, *Aeneid*: “That race is unteachable.” Al., “incapable of being taught.”

—“He learns”—“He learned,” from Servius.]

292. Between *indoctus* and *indocilis*. *Indocilis* is one who absolutely cannot 39 learn [Al., “teach”; F., “be taught”]. *Indoctus* is one who has not yet learned but nevertheless can learn. Distinguish similar pairs according to this pattern, such as *immotus* and *immobilis*, and others like them.

[Note: [Column 0040D]

293. From Servius, on the passage in Book 10 of the *Aeneid*: “All harmless.”]

293. Between *innoxius* and *innocuus*. *Innocuus* is one who is not harmed; *innoxius* is one who does not know how to harm.

294. Between *impurus* and *impudicus*. *Impudicus* [Al., *impurus*] is one who inflicts the disgrace of an offense; *impurus* [Al., *impudicus*] is one who suffers it.

[Note: [Column 0040D]

295. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “For we are not ignorant of former evils.” Also *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter I.]

295. Between *immemor* and *ignarus*. *Immemor* is one who has forgotten; *ignarus* is one who is unaware. Hence the nose is called *nares*, because through smell it reminds us so that we may recognize and know something [Al., “may recognize”]. Hence the ancients also said *olfecisse* for *scisse*, “to have known” [Al., “to smell out a matter”].

[Note: [Column 0040D]

296. Festus, entry *iners*, although it is from Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “The Tyrians press on, burning.” Also *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter I.

—*Etymologies*, Book 10, letter S.]

296. Between *iners* and *segnis*. *Iners* means “without skill,” and for that reason not useful for any work at all [Al., “not useful even for work”]. *Segnis* is as if “without fire”; similarly, *securus* means “without care,” that is, cold or sluggish, by which we understand someone useless.

297. Between *insanus* and *insaniens*. *Insanus* is one who is continually held by madness of mind; *insaniens* is one suddenly stirred by indignation or anger.

[Note: [Column 0041C]

298. From Ambrose.

In the same place: This is the reason why the most holy Fathers teach that the impious are not to be judged at the final judgment, because they have already been judged, but that those who are intermediate between the pious and the impious are to be judged. See my *Prudentiana*, no. 179. AREV.]

298. The usual distinction between *impius* and *peccator* is that every impious person is a sinner, but not every sinner is to be regarded as impious. For an impious person is anyone who becomes alienated from the piety of faith, whereas a sinner is one who is stained by wrongful action.

[Note: [Column 0041C]

299. In the text Pantinus perhaps read *totque*, or *totidem et*, instead of the variant reading given as *totidemque*. AREV.]

299. Ambrose says that *iniquitas* and *peccatum* differ in this way: iniquity refers to bitterness of mind, whereas sin refers to a fall of the body. Iniquity therefore comes first, and sin follows. Iniquity, however, is more serious, as the material of sins; in comparison with it, sin is lighter. Likewise, *peccatum* is what is committed; *piaculum* is what has been committed and what is expiated after having been committed. There are three distinctions within iniquity: suggestion, delight, and consent. Saint Jerome makes this distinction between iniquities and sins: we call those acts “iniquities” that are committed before faith has been received, whether through ignorance or knowingly. We call those “sins” that are contracted after knowledge of the faith or the grace of baptism; likewise, sins of word, deed, and consent.

[Note: [Column 0041D]

300. *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter I.

In the manuscript of Barthius: “He envies the more fortunate person and harms himself.” *Invidiosus*: one who suffers harm from someone else. Barthius read: “who is harmed by someone else.” Soon afterward, in the same place, *bonis* occurs instead of *bonus*, and Barthius interprets it as “abounding in goods, wealthy.” AREV.]

300. Between *invidus* and *invidiosus*: the envious person envies someone more fortunate, whereas the *invidiosus* is one who suffers envy from another [Al., “suffers harm”]. Nothing honorable, however, is not subject to envy. No one envies the wretched; but who is good and not subject to envy?

[Note: [Column 0041D]

301. The commentators on Terence, Act 4, Scene 6 of the *Heautontimorumenos*: anger arises from a cause, whereas irascibility arises from the vice of one who becomes angry often. Cicero also distinguishes them, *Tusculan Disputations* 4; and Fronto: “An angry person is so because of an offense; an irascible person by nature.”

In the same place: The words are perhaps from Proverbs 15:18, where the Vulgate has, “An irascible man provokes quarrels”; and chapter 26:21, “An irascible man stirs up quarrels.” Near this passage Barthius indicates a distinction between *jactura* and *damnum*, which has already been explained under the letter D. AREV.]

301. Between *ira* and *iracundia*. *Ira* is present and arises from a cause; *iracundia*, however, is a natural and enduring vice. Likewise, an *iratus* person is stirred up temporarily; an *iracundus* person becomes angry frequently [Al., “is frequently angry”] and is moved by the slightest breath of speech, like a leaf by the wind. Scripture says of such people: “An irascible man is dishonorable.” And again: “An irascible man digs up sins.”

[Note: [Column 0041D]

302. From C. Fronto: “Ignominy is imposed by one who has the power to mark someone with punishment; infamy arises from the speech of many.”]

302. Between *ignominia* and *infamia*. Ignominy is placed in someone’s power [Al., “within someone’s power”]; infamy, however, is produced by the consenting speech of many.

[Note: [Column 0042C]

303. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “He reproaches them with such things,” although he nevertheless goes beyond our text.]

303. Between *incusare* and *accusare*. We *incusamus* our superiors; we *accusamus* our equals. Likewise, we *incusamus* by word, but *accusamus* by charge and deed.

304. Between *jubere* and *imperare*. Among the ancients, *jubere* did not mean the same as *imperare*. *Jubere* was used where obedience was voluntary; *imperare*, where each person obeyed a command that was owed [Al., “doubtful”].

[Note: [Column 0042C]

305. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “Tossed over lands and the deep.”

In the same place, Pantinus’s note has *mars* as the variant reading, but Pantinus perhaps intended *mare*. AREV.]

305. Between *jactamur* and *fatigamur*. We are *jactamur*, “tossed about,” on the waves of the sea; we are *fatigamur*, “wearied,” on land.

306. Between *jaceo* and *jacio*. *Jaceo* signifies lying down; *jacio* signifies throwing or sending.

[Note: [Column 0042C]

307. Festus, entry *focus*, and Servius, on the passage in Book 12 of the *Aeneid*: “And the hearths in the middle.”]

307. Between *ignis* and *focus*. *Ignis* is the flame itself; *focus* is the fuel and nourishment of the fire. For Varro says: “*Focus* was so called because it nourishes the fire.” Thus *focus* is named from *fotus*, “nourishment.”

[Note: [Column 0042C]

308. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “The hinge grated on the bronze doors.”

[Column 0042D] —“The gates,” etc. See Servius, on the passage in Book 2 of the *Aeneid*: “And now they were approaching the gates”; and Book 5 of the *Aeneid*, on “He marks out the city with the plow.” Also *Etymologies*, Book 15, chapter 2.

In the same place, Barthius says that this elegant distinction is useful for a better understanding of many passages from antiquity, especially comic texts. He nevertheless wastes effort trying to restore the true reading in the Grialian edition, where it has already been established. AREV.]

308. Between *janua* and *ostium*. *Janua* is the first entrance into a house; *ostium* is an entrance into any part of a house. Likewise, a *janua* is either closed [Al., “with bolts”] or open; *fores* and *valvae* themselves are closed [Al., “are the actual fastenings”], but *fores* are doors that turn outward, while *valvae* open inward and are double, multiple, or folding. *Portae* properly refers to city walls; they are properly called gates of walls; they were so called because in ancient times they were marked out by a plow carried around them [Al., “the wheel of a cart marks them out”]. When the circuit was drawn, the city was marked out [Al., *urbo*].

309. Between *illius similis* and *illi similis*. *Illius similis* refers to character; *illi similis* to appearance.

[Note: [Column 0042D]

310. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*: “And the light of youth.”

—*Decus*. Read *juvenum*, from Servius.

—*Hominum*. Read *deus*, according to the understanding of Servius and Acron on Ode 3 of Book 1 of Horace. This is ἥβη, “youth,” and Agraetius is generally similar. See also Nonius, entry *juventus*.]

310. Between *juventa* and *juventus*. *Juventus* is a multitude of young people; *juventa* [Al., *juventas*] is the age of human beings. *Juventas*, however, is the adornment of youth, although authors have used these terms differently in many passages.

[Note: [Column 0042D]

311. From C. Fronto: “The dyer changes color; the obstructer harms through his office.”]

311. Between *inficere* and *officere*. *Inficere* means to change color; *officere* means to harm someone.

[Note: [Column 0042D]

312. C. Fronto: “We find our own things; we discover things belonging to others.”

In the same place: In Grialius’s edition, from no. 312 there is a progression to no. 314. Therefore I divided no. 12 into two, so that the numbers would proceed in order. AREV.]

312. Between *invenire* and *reperire*. We *invenimus*, “find,” things we have sought; we *reperimus*, “discover,” things that present themselves spontaneously.

[Column 0043A]

313. From C. Fronto.

—*Ignota*. Al.: “Known discipline,” Fronto.]

313. Between *inquirere* and *quaerere*. We *inquirimus* into matters about which we are uncertain; we *quaerimus* things unknown.

314. Between *impendere* and *impendere*. *Impendere*, with the vowel shortened, derives from *impendere*, “to spend”; *impendere*, with the *e* lengthened, means “to threaten” or “to be imminent,” from *impendeo*.

[Note: [Column 0043C]

315. I think the distinction is between *juvat* and *juvat*, as above between *paret* and *paret*: merely the meaning differs under the same written form, as between *nobilis* and *nobilis*, or *notus* and *notus*. But this occurs in only one manuscript.

In the same place, in Pantinus’s note, perhaps one should read *ut tantum sit juvat*, “so that the distinction is merely in *juvat*.” AREV.]

315. Between *juvat* and *jubat*. *Juvat* means “it pleases”; *jubat* means “it helps.”

[Note: [Column 0043D]

316. From Festus, entry *inlex*.]

316. Between *illicem* and *ilicem*. *Illicem*, with two *l*s, signifies an enticer; *ilicem*, with one *l*, denotes a tree.

317. Between *it* and *id*. *Id* is a pronoun; *it* means “he goes.”

[Note: [Column 0043D]

318. The passage is corrupt, and this is also absent from the other manuscript.

In the same place, Grialius’s text had *inquid* and *inquid … ubi inquid*. Understand *inquid* as *in quid*, “into what” or “with what.” AREV.]

318. Between *inquit* and *inquid*, as in the expression “where he said” [*ubi inquit dictum*].

[Column 0043B] [Note: [Column 0043D]

319. From Servius, on the passage in Book 2 of the *Georgics*: “And to bear pears changed by grafting,” but in another book: “But inserted stalks,” or “stories,” so that Servius’s passage requires further consideration.

In the same place, Barthius says: “I do not sufficiently understand why he says *insertas causas* or *fabulas*, unless, as I know, the ancients called inlaid ornaments *inserta*, because they are inserted as decoration into other things, like wooden splinters or gems. The word *inserta* is explained differently by different authors in Macrobius and Gellius, and it is not written in the same way by everyone.” AREV.]

319. Between *insitum* and *insertum*. We call trees *insitae*, “grafted”; but causes [Al., “rocks”] or stories *insertae*, “inserted.”

320. Between *illud* and *illuc*. *Illud* is a pronoun; *illuc* is an adverb.

[Note: [Column 0044C]

321. Agraetius. See Aulus Gellius, Book 6, chapter 16.]

321. Between *imprecari* and *deprecari*. *Imprecari* means to curse; *deprecari* means to excuse oneself and clear oneself.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

322. See *Etymologies*, Book 8, chapter 4; Festus, entry *inquilinus*.]

322. Between *incola* and *inquilinus*. Both an inhabitant and a tenant are signs of a lost homeland; but one is called an *inquilinus* as long as he is living abroad, and an *incola* once he has found a settled home.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

323. From Servius, on the passage in Book 8 of the *Aeneid*: “Then the hands of Ausonia.”]

323. Between *indigena* and *indigens* [Al., *indigetem*]. *Indigentes* [Al., *indigetes*] are needy people; *indigenae* are those born in the place.

## On the Letter L

324. Between *libertas* and *liberalitas*. *Libertas* concerns one’s condition; *liberalitas* concerns kindness and generosity—for example, clothing the naked, ransoming captives, or supplying food to the poor [Al., with the addition “or providing it”].

325. Between *laudabilis* and *laudandus*. *Laudabilis* is one who can be praised; *laudandus* is one who ought to be praised.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

326. See Nonius, entries *luxum* and *luxuria*, and *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter L.

—Festus, entries *prodegeris* and *prodiguae hostiae*.]

326. Between *luxuriosus* and *prodigus*. *Luxuriosus* is as if “released into pleasures”; hence limbs moved out of place are called *luxae*, “dislocated.” *Prodigus*, however, is extravagant, one who does everything excessively and, as it were, throws everything away.

327. Between *lascivus* and *petulans*. *Lascivus* is characterized by indulgence; *petulans* by recklessness. *Petulantia* is called lust, from the fact that it improperly seeks another’s modesty.

328. Between *litigiosus* and *litigator*. *Litigiosus* is something about which a dispute is conducted, like a field; *litigator* is one who litigates.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

329. In both the text and the note, the variant spelling is *exsultationis*. In either place, *exsultatione* seems preferable. AREV.]

329. Between *laetitia* and *exsultatio*. *Laetitia* is joy of the mind; *exsultatio* is expressed in words and bodily members. Again, *exsultatio* is distinguished from *jubilatio*. When words suffice for joy, and the tongue is capable of expressing the mind’s gladness, there is *exsultatio*. But when someone cannot announce the joy conceived within him in words, and the overflowing gladness of his soul bursts into a certain cry of exultation, there is *jubilatio*.

330. Some have attempted to distinguish *lethum* and *mors*, saying: *lethum* comes by itself, whereas *mors* is inflicted.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

331. *Pertinacia*. Nonius, entry *pervicacia*.

In the same place, Pantinus’s note perhaps had *libidinem*, which I changed, as I think in accordance with his intention, to *livedinem*. Barthius, from his corrupt manuscript, emended it to *immundicinam*; but *immunditias* is better. AREV.]

331. Between *libido* and *lividо* [perhaps *livedo*]. *Libido*, with *b*, is desire of the mind; *livido* [perhaps *livedo*], with *v*, is a bodily bruise or discoloration. There are many different kinds of desire: the desire for revenge, which is called anger; the desire to possess money, which is called greed; the desire to win by any means, which is called obstinacy; and the desire for boasting, which is called arrogance. Although there are desires for many things, and the object of the desire is not specified, the mind generally understands by *libido* only that desire by which the obscene parts of the body are aroused to the filthiness of offenses. Yet this desire rightly secured the name for itself among all the others, because it rages more fiercely than the rest in corruptible flesh. It is called *libido* because one desires or seeks another’s modesty, or any other thing.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

332. Al.: “Its very virtue shines forth.” F.: “That in which its virtue shines.”]

332. Between *laus* and *laudatio*. *Laus* belongs to the one who is praised; *laudatio* to the one who praises. Likewise, *laus* is that in which virtue shines forth; *laudatio* is the speech of the one praising [Al., “the praise of speeches”]. *Laus* and joy [Al., “praise and joy”], without the celebration of the voice, consist in the mind’s admiration; *laudatio*, however, is the proclamation of a particular thing, adorned by the assistance of speech.

[Note: [Column 0044D]

333. From Agraetius.]

333. Between *largitas* and *largitio*. *Largitas* is an act of humanity; *largitio* of ambition.

[Column 0045A] [Note: [Column 0045C]

334. From Agraetius.]

334. Between *laetari* and *gratulari*. We rejoice over our own blessings; we offer congratulations over those of friends [Agraetius, “of others”].

[Note: [Column 0045C]

335. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Georgics*: “Read the shore’s edge”; on the passage in Book 3 of the *Aeneid*: “And we traverse the shores of Epirus”; and Book 2 of the *Aeneid*: “The rest reads the sea behind.”]

335. Between *legere* and *lectitare*. *Legere* refers to a single occasion; *lectitare* to frequency. Sometimes *legere* is also a nautical term, because a ship is said to *legere* whatever it passes over.

[Note: [Column 0045D]

336. From Agraetius.

—“There is no [distinction], except that it is curved,” Agraetius.

—“Most foolishly.” From Servius, on the passage in Book 2 of the *Eclogues*: “To have worn the lip smooth with the reed.”]

336. Between *labium* and *labrum*. We call the upper lip *labium*, the lower lip *labrum*. *Rostrum* is used only of birds and refers to something curved. Some people most foolishly attempt to make a distinction by saying that men have *labra* and women *labia* [Al., “say”].

[Note: [Column 0045D]

337. From Servius, on the passage in Book 1 of the *Georgics*: “The milk-filled breasts swell.”

In Barthius’s manuscript, *lactens*, “one who draws milk”; the verb *ducit* is elegant, as Barthius says, and especially suitable to *lactens*. AREV.]

337. Between *lactantem* and *lactentem*: *lactans* is a female who supplies milk, while *lactens* is one to whom milk is supplied.

[Note: [Column 0045D]

338. From Servius, on the words cited by Isidore, which are from Books 1 and 2 of the *Aeneid*.

—Servius, on the cited passage, which is from Book 2 of the *Aeneid*.]

338. Between *leges* and *jura*. *Jus* is spoken; *lex* is written. Hence Virgil also says:

> He gave laws and statutes to the men.

Likewise, human laws are *leges*, while divine laws are *jura*. Therefore *juramentum* is also used, that is, an oath sworn by God [Al., “the Lord”]. Hence Virgil also says:

> It is permitted me to loosen the sacred laws of the Greeks.

[Note: [Column 0045D]

339. So approximately in *Etymologies*, Book 2, chapter 10, and Book 4, chapter 3.]

339. Between *leges* and *mores*. A *lex* is issued in writing; a *mos* is a kind of law of living, bound by no constraint [Al., “bound”], or an unwritten law retained solely through usage.

[Note: [Column 0045D]

340. So Isidore himself, *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter L. Varro: because it has iron around the sides, *latera*. Festus: because it attacks from the side, or from *λατρεία*, “service.”

—Servius, on the passage in Book 3 of the *Georgics*: “The nocturnal thief in the stalls.”]

340. Between *latro* and *fur*. One who steals something belonging to another is a *fur*, a thief; one who steals and kills is a *latro*, a robber. Properly, *latro* is said to derive from *latitare*, “to lie in ambush,” whereas *fur* is called so from *furvus*, “dark,” because he makes use of the night. Plautus aptly says to a certain thief [Al., “about a certain thief”] in the *Aulularia*:

> You man of three letters—

that is, “thief.”

[Note: [Column 0045D]

341. See Festus, entry *religiosus*, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book 3, chapter 3.

—“Only,” etc. F.: *soli sancti*; the following two words may perhaps be a gloss. [Column 0046C]]

341. Between a *religious*, a *sacred*, and a *holy place*. We call that *sacred* which pertains to the upper gods; that *religious* which pertains to the gods below; and that *holy* which is made holy by some sanctity. Thus, in Homer [*Odyssey* 12], there are bulls sacred to the Sun, holy, sacred, and sacrosanct.

[Note: [Column 0046C]

342. Perhaps *lotorem* or *lavatorem*.

In the same place, Pantinus conjectures *lotorem*, which also appears in the text. Perhaps *lutorem* should be read either in the text or in the note. The word *lutor* and *lotor* occur in certain ancient monuments; the word *lavator* is less certain. AREV.]

342. Between *labat* and *lavat*. *Labat* means “wavers”; *lavat* means “is a washer.”

[Column 0046A]

343. Between *laetus* and *lethum*. *Laetus* means “rejoicing”; *lethum* means “death.”

344. Between *labium* and *labrum*. *Labium* refers to the mouth; *labrum* to a vessel, from *rostrum*, “beak,” because it is curved.

[Note: [Column 0046D]

345. Festus also distinguishes them, entry *lympha*.]

345. Between *lympha* and *nympha*. *Lympha* means “water”; *nympha* means “goddess.”

346. Between *lis* and *rixa*. A *lis* arises between two parties and, once begun, is brought to an end; a *rixa* occurs among many and consists in quarrel [Al., “injury”].

347. Between *ligat* and *legat*. One *ligat*, “binds,” with a bond; one *legat*, “bequeaths,” by a will.

[Column 0046A]

348. From Agraetius, who may perhaps have supplemented it from Isidore.]

348. Between *limen* and *limes*. *Limen* is the entrance of a house; *limes* is the boundary of regions or territories.

[Note: [Column 0046D]

349. Much the same in *Etymologies*, Book 6, chapter 16.

In the same place, *mola* is better than *mole*, since *immolo* truly derives from *mola*. AREV.]

349. Between *libat* and *immolat*. The ancients said *immolare* when, placing victims on the *mola* [Al., *mole*] of the altar, they applied fire to the sacrifice. They said *libare* when they poured bowls full of unmixed wine onto the altars. For *libare* properly means “to pour.” Hence Liber is also so called, because he is said to have shown the use of wine in Greece. Thus, according to the distinction between the words, we *immolamus* bread and *libamus* the cup.

## On the Letter M

[Note: [Column 0046D]

350. *Quippe* appears in the other manuscript.

In the same place, Pantinus’s note perhaps should read *Al., miseratio*, so that the variant reading would differ from the text. AREV.]

350. Between *misericordia* and *miseratio*. Wishing someone well belongs to *misericordia*; doing good belongs to *miseratio*. It is called *miseratio* as if it were “an action of mercy.” For *misericordia* is merely the feeling of the heart by which we are impelled to aid the wretched. Therefore mercy knows how to suffer with the wretched even when there is nothing from which assistance can be given; *miseratio*, however, is demonstrated by action.

351. Between *memorare* and *commemorare*. Few things are *memorantur*, “remembered”; many things are *commemorantur*, “recalled.”

[Note: [Column 0046D]

352. Festus, entry *mansuetus*. Nonius, entry *mansuetum*.

—Nonius, entry *modestus*. Also Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book 10.]

352. Between *mansuetus* and *modestus*. *Mansuetus* is one who inflicts injury on no one; *modestus* is one who does not become angry even when injured.

[Note: [Column 0046D]

353. From Book 10 of the *Etymologies*, letter M. It seems preferable to read: “We call one still living *misellus*, and one dead *miser*.”]

353. Between *miser* and *misellus*. We call one still living *miser*, “wretched”; one who is dead, *misellus*, “poor little one.”

[Note: [Column 0046D]

354. *Etymologies*, Book 10, letter M.]

354. Between *miserandus* and *miserabilis*. *Miserabilis* is one toward whom we may show pity; *miserandus* is one toward whom we ought to show pity.

[Note: [Column 0046D]

355. From C. Fronto, who says somewhat more fully: “The *memoriosus* has memory for recalling words and deeds; the *memor* recalls a benefit or an injury.” Hence, in Isidore, I would prefer *offensionis* to *defensionis*.]

355. Between *memoriosus* and *memor*. *Memoriosus* possesses memory; *memor* remembers a benefit or a defense [the printed text; the note prefers “offense”].

356. Between *mora* and *tarditas*. *Mora* is what impedes; *tarditas* is what is impeded. *Mora* concerns a thing; *tarditas* a person.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

357. Carisius distinguishes *mendum* and *menda* approximately as follows: *Mendum* is distinguished in the sense of a falsehood; *menda* in the sense of a fault in a work or in the body.]

357. Between *mendum* and *mendacium*. *Mendum* properly refers to a fault in a book, whence we also say *emendare*, “to correct.” *Mendacium*, however, refers to falsehood in other matters.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

358. So Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* 3: “For malice is a crafty and deceitful means of causing harm.”]

358. Between *malitia* and *malignitas*. A wicked thought of the mind is called *malitia*; the intention or work of malice is called *malignitas*.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

359. From Varro’s understanding, *On the Latin Language* 5: “Much derives from *pecunia*, which was named by the magistrate so that it might be exacted for an offense.”

—*Poena*. Varro, in the same place: “*Poena* comes from punishing, or from regretting, which follows sin.”]

359. Between *multatio*, *poena*, and *supplicium*. *Multatio* may occur without blood, as a monetary penalty. *Supplicium* involves blood; *poena* is pain without blood.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

360. From Fronto and *Etymologies*, Book 6, chapter 19. See above.

—Likewise, *donum*. From Agraetius, word for word.

—*Monendo*. Agraetius has *movendo*, but in my opinion incorrectly.]

360. Between *munus* and *donum*. *Munus* is something owed, as to a patron; *donum* is an honorarium. Likewise, *donum* belongs to the giver, *munus* to the recipient. *Donum* is derived from *dare*, “to give”; *munus* from *munire*, “to provide,” or from *monere*, “to remind.”

[Note: [Column 0047D]

361. The commentators on Terence, Act 2, Scene 2: “He deserved well, helped, benefited.” Its opposite is *commeruit*; hence one might suspect that *commeritus* should be read instead of *immeritus*. Or from the passage in the *Hecyra*, Act 3, Scene 5:

> She, who has never deserved anything from me, father.

There the same commentators say that we use *mereri* for good things and *commereri* for bad things. See Servius, on the passage in Book 4 of the *Aeneid*: “I shall never deny that the queen deserved well.”]

361. Between *meruit* and *promeruit*. *Meruit* is common to both punishment and reward; *promeruit* applies only to reward. One who does good is called *promeritus*, just as one who does evil is called *immeritus*.

362. Between *magnus* and *grandis*. We refer *magnus* to the mind [Al., “it is referred”], *grandis* to the body.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

363. Abbreviated from Agraetius.]

363. Between *mutuum dare* [Al., *mutuare*] and *commodare*. One who gives a loan expects to receive something else in return; one who lends expects the very same thing to be returned to him.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

364. C. Fronto: “He advises because of goodwill; he admonishes in order to reinforce memory.”]

364. Between *monere* and *admonere*. One *monet*, “advises,” who gives an instruction; one *admonet*, “admonishes,” who brings back to memory something that had slipped away.

365. Between *meretur* and *moeret*. One who *meretur* is worthy of some benefit; one who *moeret* is sad.

[Note: [Column 0047D]

366. From Agraetius.]

366. Between *miramur* and *admiramur*. We *admiramur*, “admire,” virtues; we *miramur*, “wonder at,” works.

[Column 0048A] [Note: [Column 0047D]

367. The sense is expressed by Servius, on the passage in Book 2 of the *Aeneid*: “We pity spontaneously.”]

367. Between *miseremur* and *miserescimus*. We *miseremur*, “pity,” as much as necessary; we *miserescimus*, “feel compassion,” more than necessary. Likewise, we *miseremur* when asked, but *miserescimus* spontaneously.

368. Between *monemus*, *admonemus*, and *commonemus*. We *monemus*, “advise,” concerning the future; we *admonemus*, “admonish,” concerning the present; we *commonemus*, “remind,” concerning the past.

[Note: [Column 0048C]

369. Read *numerum* with the inserted word; *turbam* had wrongly entered from the following verse.

—“Placed in a location.” F.: “the placement of a place.” C. Fronto: “A narrow place creates a crowd.”]

369. Between *multitudo* and *numerus*. A multitude is produced by number; a crowd by being placed in a location. For even a few people can make a crowd in a narrow place.

370. Between *mihi* and *mi*. *Mihi* is the dative case; *mi* is the vocative.

[Note: [Column 0048C]

371. *Etymologies*, Book 9, chapter 4.

In the same place, an error seems to have entered Pantinus’s note. After *originales* one should read *originis*, and in place of *locum*, *loco*. AREV.]

371. Between *municeps* and *municipalis*. *Municipes* are the elders of the curial class, so called because they undertake the duties of the treasury; *municipales* are native citizens [Al., “of origin”] who perform an official function in a place [perhaps *loco*, “in the place”].

[Note: [Column 0048C]

372. From *Etymologies*, Book 11, chapter 1.

In the same place, Grialius’s edition had *mammillas*. AREV.]

372. Between *mamillae*, *mammae*, and *ubera*. *Mamillae* are those of men; *mammae* those of women; *ubera* those of animals [Al., “cattle”]. *Papillae* are the upper tips of the breasts, which nursing infants grasp.

[Note: [Column 0048C]

373. Read “Helius Melissus,” from Aulus Gellius, Book 18, chapter 6, where this opinion of his is reported. See also *Etymologies*, Book 9, chapter 18.

—“In whose.” Al.: “in his.” In Aulus Gellius, “in whose” is clearer.

—“Had come.” Aulus Gellius: “had come into the place.”

—“Matrons,” etc. See Servius, on the passage in Book 9 of the *Aeneid*: “Daring from many mothers.”

—The passage is incomplete and comes from Servius, on the passage in Book 11 of the *Aeneid*: “Mothers through the Tyrrhenian towns.” It should be completed as follows: “Mothers of families, however, who entered into marriage by *coemptio*, since …” For otherwise that description applies least of all to matrons, but only to mothers of families. See also Servius, on the passage in Book 7 of the *Aeneid*: “An heir is sought.” Perhaps a third member concerning the mother is also missing; consult *Etymologies*, Book 9, chapter 8. See Festus, entry *mater familias*, and Nonius, entries *matronae* and *matres familias*.

In the same place, Grialius’s text had *Mesius*. On Melissus, see the catalogue of writers praised by Isidore, drawn from Barthius and Fabricius, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 53, no. 2. Chalcidius, Pliny, and Donatus also mention Melissus, whether the same person or another. I corrected *in matri* to *in mariti*. AREV.]

373. Between *matrona* and *mater familias*. The grammarian Melissus thinks that the distinction is this: a woman is called a *matrona* when she is the mother of her first child, and a *mater familias* when she has borne several. Others have said that a woman is called a *matrona* when she has entered into marriage with a man, and that the marriage has thereby been completed [Al., “thus named”]; but that a *mater familias* is one who is under her husband’s authority and ownership, or in whose authority and ownership her husband would be, since she had entered into the family of both her husband and her own heir. Married women and marriageable virgins are also called *matronae*, since they are already capable of becoming mothers. For through a certain legal solemnity they pass into the family of their husband.

374. Between *mortuus* and *emortuus*. A body that has already breathed its last is *mortuus* [Al., “lifeless”]; one near death is *emortuus*.

[Note: [Column 0049D]

375. From Servius, on the passage in Book 6 of the *Aeneid*: “I entered so many seas.”]

375. Between *mare* and *maria*. *Mare* is the whole element; *maria* are parts of the sea. The same applies to lands: there are *terrae*, while *terra* is the element itself.

[Note: [Column 0049D]

376. Varro, from *colere*, “to cultivate,” *On the Latin Language*, Book 4.

In the same place, “as if *colla*,” “necks.” So also *Etymologies*, Book 14, chapter 8, no. 19. AREV.]

376. Between *montes* and *colles*. Mountains are swellings of the earth; hills are the more prominent ridges of mountains, as if their necks.

377. Between *malogranata* and *malogranatum*. *Malogranata*, feminine, is a tree; *malogranatum*, neuter, is the fruit. The same applies to *persicus* and *persicum*: *persicus*, feminine, is the tree; *persicum*, neuter, is the fruit. Likewise *buxus* and *buxum*: *buxum*, neuter, is the wood; *buxus*, feminine, is the tree.

378. Between *magis* and *potius*. *Magis* is to prefer one of two things when a comparison is made; *potius* rejects one of them.

379. Between *mala* and *malas*. *Mala* are apples; *malae* are jawbones.

380. Between *marem* and *mare*. *Marem* means “male”; *mare* is the element of water.

[Note: [Column 0049D]

381. “Things, however,” etc. Al.: “Things, however, deceive, although …”

—“By appearance,” etc. F.: “Appearances also deceive, as …”

—“Of nature,” etc. F.: “Nature acts … appearances.”

In the same place, Pantinus perhaps read *quia autem*, “because, however.” AREV.]

381. Between *mentiens* and *fallens*. We must consider that the person who wishes to seem to be what he is not is lying; but the person who, without intending to, thinks something other than what is actually the case is not lying but is deceived. Every liar therefore has a will to deceive; things, however, have the power to deceive, not a will to lie. A stone deceives, and many bodies deceive through their appearance—for example, oars appear broken in the water while they are intact. Towers also seem to be moving to the eyes of sailors, as though they were running. Yet these things act through the appearance supplied by nature, not through a will to lie.

382. Between *monile* and *munile*. *Monile* is said to mean a hook, from *monere*, “to remind,” because it reminds a woman that she is under her husband’s authority. *Munile* is said to mean a garment, from *munire*, “to protect”; or *munile* is an ornament of gems that usually hangs from a woman’s neck, named from *munus*, “gift.”

[Note: [Column 0050C]

388. According to Sosipater, Donatus, Diomedes, and others: the *nomen* is what declares the origin of the family, such as *Cornelius*. The *praenomen* is placed before the hereditary name, such as *Publius*. The *cognomen* is appended to hereditary names, such as *Scipio*. The *agnomen* is customarily added from outside, acquired for some reason or through some event, such as *Africanus*. Here, however, in both manuscripts the positions of *cognomen* and *agnomen* had been interchanged; nevertheless, we have restored each to its proper place, not only on the authority of the writers I mentioned, but also of Isidore himself, Book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter “On the Name.”

388. Between *nomen*, *praenomen*, *cognomen*, and *agnomen*. A *nomen* [Al.: *praenomen*] is a name of individual designation; a *praenomen* is placed before names on account of the dignity [Al.: *dignity*] of the family, as *Publius Virgilius*. For we cannot say [Al.: *we do not say*] *Virgilius Publius*. A *cognomen* comes from the family lineage, as, for example, *Scipio Cornelius*, descended from the Cornelian family. An *agnomen* is derived from an achievement or a defect, as *Scipio Africanus*, because he conquered Africa, or *Lentulus Sura*, because his ancestors had unusually large calves. Therefore, the *nomen* derives from individual property, the *praenomen* from rank, the *cognomen* from origin, and the *agnomen* from appearance or action.

[Note: [Col. 0050D]

389. From Agraetius.]

389. Between *nascitur* and *enascitur*. *Nascitur* is used of what falls from the womb; *enascitur*, of what rises from earth or water.

[Note: [Col. 0050D]

390. Festus, under the entry *Navita*.]

390. Between *nauta* and *navita*. *Navita* is poetic. For it was derived from *nauta*, but poets added one letter for the sake of the meter.

391. Between *num* and *nunc*. *Num* means “whether?” or “surely not?”; *nunc*, “now.”

392. Between *ne* and *nae*. When placed first, *nae* is an adverb and is pronounced with a high accent; *ne*, when placed second, is a conjunction and is pronounced with a lowered accent.

393. Between *nigro* and *migro*. *Nigro* means “I make black”; *migro* means “I move away,” or “change of place” [Al.: “change from a place”].

394. Between *neutrum* and *neutrale*. *Neutrum* is a noun, pronoun, or participle; *neutrale* is a verb.

395. Between *notus* and *notus* [Al.: *notu*]. *Notus* means “known,” as in “known by judgment”; *Notus* is the south wind.

[Note: [Col. 0050D]

396. From Nonius, under the entry *Nobile*.]

—Thus says Titinnius: “They would ennoble by wicked deeds,” which Nonius explains as meaning “they would make known.”—

396. Between *nobilem* and *nobilem*. *Nobilis* means “noble-born”; *nobilis* means “known to everyone.”

[Note: [Col. 0050D]

397. From Servius, on *Eclogue* IV: “The Parcae, by the stable power of fate.”]

397. Between *nomina* and *numina*. *Nomina* are names; *numina* are powers.

## On the letter O

[Col. 0051A]

[Note: [Col. 0051D]
