398. The commentators on Terence, *Eunuchus*, Act III, Scene 2: *Oscula* are the kisses of courtesy; *basia*, of chaste affection; *suavia*, of lust. Servius, on *Aeneid* I, “He lightly kissed his daughter”: “It should be understood that an *osculum* belongs to religious observance, a *suavium* to pleasure.”

—*Basia*. Al.: “*Basia* for wives, *oscula* d[...].” [The printed reading is corrupt.]”

In the same place. In some manuscripts: “The difference between *basium* and *suavium* is that a *basium* is given to a wife, a *suavium* to a prostitute. Likewise, *basium* belongs to endearments, *suavium* to pleasure. Someone also distinguished these terms in verse:

“Meanwhile a husband’s *basia*, and *oscula* are given to friends;

“*Suavia* are mingled with the pleasant lips of wantonness.”

These verses concerning *basium*, *osculum*, and *suavium* are also found among other grammarians. Their author remains unknown. The distinction, however, is not always observed. See the Isidorian Glossary, under *Savium*. The variant readings of Pantinus appear to have become confused. AREV.]

398. Between *osculum* and *pacem*. We say that a kiss of peace (*pacem*) is given to friends [Al. adds: “to friends or”] and sons; to wives, a *basium*; to a prostitute, a *suavium* [Al.: *savium*]. Likewise, an *osculum* is a sign of charity, a *basium* of endearment [Al.: “an endearment”], and a *suavium* of pleasure. Someone also distinguished them in these verses:

“*Basia* are given to wives, but *oscula* also to friends;

“*Suavia* are mingled with wanton lips.”

399. Between *occasionem* and *opportunitatem*. In literary usage, *occasio arrisit*, “the opportunity smiled”; *opportunitas se praebuit*, “the favorable occasion presented itself,” or *secunda successit*, “a favorable outcome followed.”

[Note: [Col. 0051D]

400. Asconius correctly says, *Against Verres* II: “They sometimes observe, sometimes merely look, and at other times revere.”]

400. Between *observationem* and *observantiam*. *Observatio* belongs to care, learning, and skill; *observantia* to worship and religious observance.

401. Between *opus* and *operationem*. *Opus* denotes the thing itself that is done; *operatio*, the action of the thing itself.

[Note: [Col. 0051D]

402. See Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “All the herds follow.”]

402. Between *omne* and *totum*. *Omne* pertains to plurality and number: [Al. adds: “to number,”] as we say *omnes homines*, “all human beings”; and, with reference to plurality, *omnis familia*, “the whole household,” *omnis exercitus*, “the whole army,” and *omne pecus*, “all the livestock.” *Totum*, however, pertains to magnitude, as *totum corpus*, “the whole body,” *tota terra*, “the whole earth,” and *totum caelum*, “the whole sky.” Thus *totus homo*, “the whole person,” if we refer to the body; *omnis homo*, “every person,” if we speak of everyone. Accordingly, *omne* is used of distinct parts, whereas *totum* should be without parts.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

403. From Servius, on *Aeneid* III: “He entreats the peace of the gods.”]

403. Between *orare* and *exorare*. *Orare* means “to ask”; *exorare*, “to obtain by entreaty.”

404. Between *obesse* and *officere*. One who *obest* does harm; one who *officit* wishes to do harm.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

405. Above, from C. Fronto.]

405. Between *officere* and *inficere*. *Officere* means wishing to harm someone; *inficere*, to change a color.

406. Between *olet* and *redolet*. A thing *olet*, “has an odor,” either bad or good; it *redolet*, “smells fragrant,” only when the odor is good.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

407. *Etymologies* XV, chapter 4.

—See Servius, on *Aeneid* II, “Dragons toward the highest shrines,” and IV, “They approach the shrines.” Also Asconius Pedianus, in Cicero’s *Divinatio*.]

407. Between *oracula* and *delubra*. *Oracula* are temples where prayer is offered and responses are given. *Delubra* are temples containing springs for purifying and washing the faithful. Hence *delubra* is derived from *diluere*, “to wash away.” For this reason these places initially had no altars, so that they were merely *delubra*, not temples.

[Col. 0052A] [Note: [Col. 0052D]

408. See Festus, under the entry *Orba*.]

408. Between *orbem* and *caecum*. An *orbus* is one who loses children; a *caecus* is one who loses his eyes.

409. Between *occidit* and *occidit*. *Occidit*, with the medial vowel shortened, refers to the one who has died; *occidit*, with the medial vowel lengthened, to the one who kills.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

410. See Servius, on *Georgics* II: “But better among the trunks of the olive.”]

410. Authors distinguish *olea* and *oliva* as follows: *olea* is the fruit, while *oliva* is the tree, since a grove is called *olivetum*, just as *quercetum* [Al.: *querquetum*] and *pometum* [Al.: *vinetum*]. Yet poets frequently used both *olea* and *oliva* for the fruit without distinction [Al.: “without the poets’ distinction”]. Custom, however, has established that *oliva* denotes the fruit. Nor does anything prevent the same name from belonging both to the tree and to its fruit [Al.: “nor has anything prevented…”].

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

411. From Servius, on *Aeneid* IV: “The keen-scented force of the hounds”; from this it seems that *odorisequum*, “following scent,” should be read in place of “fragrant.” Fronto, however, makes nearly the same distinction between *lucidum* and *luminosum*.]

411. Between *odorum*, *odorabile*, and *odoriferum*. Whatever emits an odor from itself is *odorum*; *odorabile* [Serv.: *odoratum*] is what receives an odor from elsewhere [Serv.: “from somewhere else”]; *odoriferum* is what follows an odor.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

412. Or rather: *opera* is what one does; *opus* is what is done.]

412. Between *operam* and *opera*. *Operam* is “what it is” [the reading is uncertain]; *opera*, what is done.

413. Between *ostium* and *hostiam*. An *ostium* is something that is opened; a *hostia* is a sacrificial victim.

414. Between *ortus* and *hortos*. *Ortus* means a rising or advance; *hortos* denotes fields [F.: “we say”].

415. Between *oblitum* and *oblitum*. *Oblitum*, with the vowel shortened, means “smeared over”; *oblitum*, with the vowel lengthened, means “forgetful.”

416. Between *offerre* and *inferre*. *Offerre* means to provide voluntarily; *inferre*, to bring in or import.

## On the letter P

54

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

417. Book II of the *Differences*, section 36.]

417. Between *prudentia* and *sapientia*. *Prudentia* is assigned to human affairs, *sapientia* to divine matters [Al.: “is attributed to”].

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

418. Nonius makes approximately this distinction between *castitas* and *pudicitia*, under the entry *Castitas*.]

418. Between *pudor* and *pudicitia*. *Pudor* belongs to the body; *pudicitia* to the mind.

419. Between *pietas* and *affectio*. *Pietas* is shown among those bound by blood; *affectio* among unrelated persons.

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

420. Understand: in Pantinus’s variant reading, Sallust, *The War with Catiline*. AREV.]

420. Between *patientia* and *tolerantia*. *Tolerantia* belongs to the spirit [Al.: “soul”]; *patientia* to the body. Thus Sallust: “A body enduring hunger and cold.”

[Note: [Col. 0052D]

421. Thus Cicero, *On the Republic* VI, says that *prudentia* received its name from *providere*, “to foresee.”

—*Callidus*. The commentators on Terence, *Adelphoe*, Act III, Scene 3: “One is called *callidus* who has developed a callus through the practice of an art.”]

421. Between *peritus*, *prudens*, *callidus*, and *facundus*. *Peritus* is trained through experience; *prudens*, as if “foreseeing,” is an efficient organizer of future affairs; *callidus* is equipped through the practice [Al.: “for the practice”] of an art; *facundus* is one who can speak readily.

422. The difference between *pudens* and *verecundus* is that one who is *pudens* fears both true and false opinion, whereas one who is *verecundus* fears only true opinion [Al.: “the truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0053C]

423. Asconius Pedianus III, on *Against Verres*. Nonius, under *Nefarius*; Isidore himself, *Etymologies* X, letter N.

In the same place. Perhaps “not even to be named.” That is certainly better. AREV.]

423. Between *profanus*, *nefandus*, and *nefarius*. As Varro believes, *nefarius* means “not worthy of spelt,” by which human life was first sustained [Al.: “supported”]. *Nefandus* means “not even to be named.” *Profanus* is one who is not permitted to participate in sacred rites. Concerning this Sallust says: “The profane man will pollute the sacred rites.” Thus *profanus* means *porro*, “far,” from the shrine.

424. Between *peccator* and *immundus*: every sinner is unclean, but not every unclean person is a sinner. A sinner is one who transgresses God’s commandments, and he must also be unclean because he transgresses them. But one is also unclean if he has slept with his wife or touched a corpse, though for that reason he is not a sinner.

425. Between *ploratus*, *planctus*, and *fletus*. *Ploratus* consists only of tears; *planctus* only of cries; *fletus* pertains to both.

426. Between *pigritia* and *torpor*. *Torpor* belongs to one who is asleep; *pigritia* to one who is awake.

[Note: [Col. 0053C]

427. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, at the beginning. Nonius, under *Pervicacia*.]

427. Between *perseverantia* and *pertinacia*. *Perseverantia* belongs to virtue; *pertinacia* to vice.

[Note: [Col. 0053D]

428. C. Fronto: “A *subsidium*, what supports those who are failing; *praesidium* is imposed [or stationed]; *auxilium* is sudden aid. Thus a *subsidium* is prepared for secondary contingencies; a *praesidium* for protection; *auxilium* comes unexpectedly, so that it may help. See Festus.”]

428. Between *praesidium*, *auxilium*, and *subsidium*. *Praesidium* is something stationed in a useful place; *auxilium* is aid supplied by outsiders; *subsidium* is assistance that arrives afterward.

[Note: [Col. 0053D]

429. Al.: *suae*; two manuscripts have *sui* instead.

In the same place. The variant reading produces agreement with Grialius’s text. One might read *facit*, or something similar, in place of *efficit*. AREV.]

429. Between *potentia* and *potentatus*. *Potentia* is the power belonging solely to each individual [Col. 0053C]; *potentatus* is judicial authority [Al.: “is judicial authority”].

430. Between *pestis* and *pestilentia*. *Pestis* is the name of the disease itself [Al.: “word”]; *pestilentia* is what produces it of itself. There are three kinds of pestilence: from earth, from water, or from air.

[Note: [Col. 0053D]

431. In Codex Regiovaticanus 1838 the differences are arranged in alphabetical order, but in some places they are more concise, in others more extensive, and some have been added, for example: Between *pati* and *perpeti*: *pati* is brief, *perpeti* extends over a longer period. Between *passum* and *expertum*: “We suffer voluntarily; we experience through necessity.” I would prefer: “We experience voluntarily; we suffer through necessity.” AREV.]

431. Between *passio* and *propassio*, Jerome distinguishes in his commentary on Matthew, saying that *passio* is counted as guilt; *propassio*, although it involves guilt [Al.: “although it is regarded as guilt”], nevertheless is not held [Al.: “retained”] as a crime. Thus, if someone sees a woman and his soul is titillated, he has been struck by *propassio*. But if he consents and turns the thought into desire—as it is written concerning David, “they passed over into the desire of the heart”—he passes from *propassio* to *passio*. In the latter case, it is not willingness that is lacking, but opportunity.

[Note: [Col. 0053D]

432. He seems to have taken this from the commentators on Terence, *Andria*, Act V, Scene 4; and D. Augustine likewise.

—Or perhaps also *pron.* Al.: “Thus it will be pronounced”; perhaps also *pron.*

In the same place. Pantinus seems to have read in the text *aut et pronuntiabitur*, for which he conjectures *aut etiam*, which is the genuine reading. AREV.]

432. Between *percunctatio* and *interrogatio*, Augustine considers this to be the difference: many answers are customarily given to a *percunctatio*, for example, “What is this?” or “What is that?”—answers that may be diverse or varied. To an *interrogatio*, however, many answers are not given; rather, either “no” or “yes” is pronounced. For example: “Was it done or said?” “Is it true or false?” The answer is either “no” or “yes.”

433. The difference between *perfectum* and *consummatum* is that *perfectum* is something to which nothing further can be added. *Consummatum*, however, is any work brought to its completion.

[Note: [Col. 0054D]

434. From Servius on *Eclogue* I, “Tityrus, beneath the spreading…”

—From Servius on *Aeneid* VI, “And the shining sphere of the moon”; from this it appears that *lucens*, “shining,” should be read rather than *lucidum*, “bright.” Fronto, however, makes nearly the same distinction between *lucidum* and *luminosum*.]

434. Between *patens* and *patulum*. We call something *patulum* when it is naturally and permanently open, such as the nostrils or a tree. *Patens* is what is opened and closed, such as a door or the eyes. Likewise with *lucidum* and *lucibile*: *lucidum* is what is illuminated from elsewhere; *lucibile*, what shines by itself.

[Note: [Col. 0054D]

435. From Servius, *Aeneid* X, on “Our penetrating weapon.”

—*Penetralia*. From Servius, on *Aeneid* VII, “In the deep inner chambers,” and on VI, “The inner chambers of our realms.”]

435. Between *penetrale* and *penetrabile*. What penetrates is called *penetrale*; what is penetrated is *penetrabile*. *Penetralia* are the hidden recesses of houses, so called from *penitus*, “deep within.”

[Note: [Col. 0054D]

436. Festus, under *Pone*, and Servius, on *Aeneid* II, “The wife follows behind.”

—*Tempus*. F.: “The word *tempus* prevails.”]

436. The apparent difference between *post* and *pone* is that we always use *post* chronologically, as when we say, “I will come after a time”; but *pone* means “behind,” as in “behind the back.”

[Col. 0054C] [Note: [Col. 0054D]

437. From Agraetius, who may perhaps be supplemented from this passage.]

437. Between *precari*, *imprecari*, and *deprecari*. *Precari* means “to ask”; *imprecari*, “to wish”; *deprecari*, “to excuse or clear oneself.” Cicero, *Against Verres* II: “What is Hortensius to do?” he asks. “Is he to ward off charges of avarice by praising frugality?”

[Note: [Col. 0054D]

438. Servius, on *Aeneid* IX: “If for you the things I ask…”—differently from Isidore.]

438. Between *poscere* and *exposcere*. *Poscere* is less forceful than *exposcere*. For those who *poscunt* ask simply; those who *exposcunt* express desire.

[Note: [Col. 0054D]

439. From Servius on *Aeneid* I, “They held under their rule,” and “Having promised.”

—*Scriptura*. Al.: “Less.” F.: *minis*, “threats.”

In the same place. This is the first difference encountered in the other, non-alphabetical book, though it is shorter there than here. AREV.]

439. Between *polliceri* and *promittere*. We use *polliceri* of what we promise voluntarily and without being asked; *promittere*, of what is requested. Thus we *promittimus*, “promise,” when asked, but *pollicemur*, “offer,” spontaneously. Likewise, we *pollicemur* in writing, but *promittimus* orally.

[Note: [Col. 0055C]

440. In the speech he delivered concerning his own virtues, Gellius, Book VI, chapter 14. Nonius, under *Festinare*. Festus, under *Properare*. C. Fronto: “One who *properat* appears not to be exhausted; one who *festinat* seems to be fatigued.”

—*Unumquodque*. Al.: “I never passed over anything that I had undertaken.” The manuscript reads *ortus*. Perhaps *orsus*, “begun.”]

440. Between *properare* and *festinare*. Marcus Cato distinguishes them as follows: “One who brings each thing to completion at the proper time *properat*. One who begins many things at once and completes none *festinat*. I brought each thing that I had undertaken to completion.”

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

441. From Agraetius.]

441. Between *primum* and *priorem*. *Primus* is first among many; *prior*, earlier of two; *primarius*, foremost in rank.

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

442. From Agraetius.]

442. Between *plures* and *pluris*. *Pluris* is used of what is assigned a greater sum; *plures* is written of plurality [Al.: “is written”].

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

443. *Inimicissime*. I read *enixissime*, “with the greatest effort,” or *intensissime*, “most intensely.”]

443. Between *petivit* and *expetivit*. *Petivit* is used for asking little [F. adds: “*petivit*”]; *expetivit* for asking sufficiently. [Col. 0055B] “And he strove *inimicissime* (‘most hostilely’; perhaps read *enixissime*, ‘most earnestly,’ or *intensissime*, ‘most intensely’) and vehemently.” For *ex* is used in the sense of “very much.”

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

444. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II, “They erected pyres.” Festus, under *Bustum*.]

444. Between *pyra* and *rogus*. A *pyra* is a construction of wood before fire has been applied. A *rogus* is what it is while burning. *Bustum* is what it is after it has burned.

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

445. Terentius Scaurus likewise, *On Orthography*: “The *populus* is that in which every part of the state and all its orders are contained; the *plebs* is that in which the patrician families of the citizens are not included.”]

445. Between *plebs* and *populus*. The *plebs* differs from the *populus* in that the *populus* is the general community of citizens together with the elders, whereas the *plebs* is the humble and rejected part.

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

446. Festus, under *Pauperies*; from this it may perhaps be necessary to write: “*Paupertas* is the damage caused by a quadruped.”]

446. Between *pauperies* and *paupertas*. *Pauperies* is damage; *paupertas* is the condition itself.

447. Between *proclivus* and *declivus*. *Proclivus* is an ascent; *declivus*, an easy descent.

[Note: [Col. 0055D]

448. *Etymologies* X, letter P. “A *puella* is a little girl, as if *pupilla*; and in Book XI, chapter 1: ‘A *pupilla*, because she is pure and unpolluted, as girls are.’ Thus someone might perhaps judge that *pulla* should be changed to *pupilla*, since among the Greeks too ἡ κόρη (*hē korē*) signifies both ‘pupil’ and ‘girl.’ Yet the reading *pulla* should not be rejected rashly, since Nonius too says, ‘*Pullum*, of tender age,’ from the ancient verb *pullare*, which the old glossary recognizes; and *παραφυάδας βάλλειν* (*paraphyadas ballein*) means ‘to produce shoots,’ while *pulli* are *παραφυάδες* (*paraphyades*), ‘shoots.’ He himself certainly has this same reading in the preceding book.

[Col. 0056D] —*Etymologies* II, chapter 2.]

448. Between *puerpera* and *puella*. A *puella* is called *investis*, “without adult hair,” and is small in age, as if *pulla*, “young.” A *puerpera*, however, is a woman who has given birth to her first child and gives birth while still in her youthful years. Hence Horace, Book IV, Ode 4:

“Women who have borne children are praised for offspring like his.”

[Note: [Col. 0056D]

449. Servius, on *Aeneid* I, “Among leafy groves.”

In the same place. *Pampinosum*. This word is used by Columella and Pliny. AREV.]

449. Between *pampineum* and *pampinosum*. *Pampineum* is something wholly made of vine leaves; *pampinosum*, something full of vine leaves.

450. Between *populum* and *populos*. When we say *populos* in the plural, we mean cities; when we say *populum*, we understand the multitude of a single state.

[Note: [Col. 0056D]

451. *Etymologies* VII, chapter 12.]

451. Between *pontifex* and *vates*. *Pontifex* signifies only the chief priest; *vates* has several meanings: priests, poets, or prophets.

[Note: [Col. 0056D]

452. See Servius, on *Aeneid* I, “An exile, and he came to the Lavinian shores.”]

452. Between *profugus* and *exsul*. A *profugus* is one by choice; an *exsul*, by necessity.

453. Between *patrius* and *paternus*. *Paternus* is what belonged to one’s father, as a paternal estate. *Patrius* is said of what resembles or is devoted to one’s father [Al.: “is disposed toward one’s father”], as a fatherly spirit [Al.: “love”].

454. Between *proprius* and *propius* [Al.: *proprium*]. *Proprius* is a noun; *propius* means “nearer to me.”

455. The difference between *praegnans* and *gravidus* is this: *praegnans* is a woman who has conceived; *gravidus* is one whom the heaviness of the womb shows to be close to giving birth.

[Col. 0056B] [Note: [Col. 0056D]

456. From Agraetius.]

456. Between *pignera* and *pignora*. *Pignera* are pledges consisting of things; *pignora* are children and objects of affection.

[Note: [Col. 0056D]

457. Fronto. Thus: “A *portentum* is something that remains for a long time and signifies that something will occur later; a *monstrum* is contrary to nature, such as the Minotaur. Below, under *monstrum*: in a *monstrum* the proper order of nature is overturned; in a *portentum* the event is merely delayed.” Nonius, under *Monstra*.]

457. Between *portentum* and *monstrum*. A *portentum* is something presented in diverse forms; a *monstrum* is something born outside nature, either excessively large or excessively small.

[Note: [Col. 0056D]

458. *Etymologies* II, chapter 3.

In the same place. Pantinus read, as I think, *parvitate*, “smallness,” in the text, and conjectured *pravitate*, “deformity.” AREV.]

458. Between *portentum* and *portentosum*. A *portentum* is something that, taking on a transformation of nature in every respect, appears to portend something future—for example, a two-headed creature joined to one body, or, as they say, in the palace of Xerxes a vixen was born from a mare; by this it was shown that his kingdom would be dissolved. Things are called *portentosa*, however, when they undergo a transformation in only one part of the body—for example, those born with six fingers or with some deformity [F.: “smallness”] of the limbs.

[Col. 0056C] [Note: [Col. 0056D]

459. C. Fronto, with the same meaning: an *ostentum* is something displayed contrary to custom; and below, under *ostentum*: “rarity produces astonishment” (I read *admirationem*, “astonishment,” rather than *administrationem*).]

459. Between *portentum* and *ostentum*. A *portentum* is born and remains in its own form; an *ostentum* is suddenly presented to the eyes and then withdrawn. Thus *portentum* is derived from *portendere*, “to show forth,” that is, “to show in advance,” just as *prodigium* is so called because it *porro dicat*, “speaks forth,” that is, proclaims things to come from afar. *Monstrum* is properly derived from warning or showing, because by signifying something it shows it immediately. There are five kinds of prodigies, as Varro says: *portentum*, *ostentum*, *prodigium*, *miraculum*, and *monstrum*.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

460. These points are found almost identically in *Etymologies* II, chapter 2, and in Book II of the *Differences*.

—*Pubertas*, however. Festus, under *Pubes*.

—*Pueritia*, however. Book II of the *Differences*.]

460. Between *pueritia* and *pubertas*. *Pueritia* is tender and early youth, so called from *puritas*, “purity.” *Pubertas* is mature age, when one can already beget children; it is named from *pubes*, that is, the body’s private parts, because these places then first grow a downy covering [L.: “put on” one]. *Pueritia* begins at the seventh year, and *pubertas* at the fourteenth.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

461. From Agraetius.

—“Concerning signs.” Two manuscripts: *designat*, “designates.”]

461. Between *percussum* and *perculsum*. We call one *percussum* in the body, but *perculsum* in the mind. Cicero, *On the Signs*: “As though he himself had been struck by that torch” [Agraetius: “that they had been struck.”]

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

462. Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25.

In the same place. *Paricida* and *patricida* are commonly taken as equivalent. See Festus. AREV.]

462. Between *parricida* and *paricida*. We call one a *parricida* who kills a parent; a *paricida*, one who kills a companion or an equal.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

463. From Servius on *Aeneid* I, “And the African wind, frequent with storms,” and from Isidore himself, *Etymologies* XIII, chapter 11.]

463. Between *procella* and *tempestas*. *Procellae* belong not so much to the land as to the sky; *tempestates* are disturbances of the waves.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

464. From Servius on *Georgics* II, “Cutting off plants from the tender body.”]

464. Between *plantae* and *plantaria*. *Plantae* are taken from trees; *plantaria* are those grown from seeds and transplanted with their roots and their own soil.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

465. From Sosipater Charisius.

—*Pomerium*, etc. I think this is a gloss on the words immediately preceding.]

465. Between *pomarium* and *pometum*. A *pomarium* is where fruit is stored [Al.: “transferred”]; a *pometum*, where fruit grows; a *pomerium*, where fruit is found [Al.: “the place of the trees itself”].

466. Between *pyra* and *pyrum*. A *pyra* is a burning funeral pyre [Al.: “burning wood”]; a *pyrum* is a pear.

[Col. 0057C]

467. Between *piscator* and *piscarium*. A *piscator* is one who catches fish; a *piscarius*, one who sells fish.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

468. I read “made from dust.”]

468. Between *pulvereum* and *pulverulentum*. *Pulvereum* is something made from dust; *pulverulentum* is something full of dust.

469. Between *pennae*, *pinnae*, and *pennum*. *Pinnae* are parts of walls; *pennae* are birds’ feathers, from *pendere*, “to hang”; *pennum* is the end of a sharp piece of iron.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

470. C. Fronto: “*Praeda* strips the defeated.”

—*Compendium*. C. Fronto: “*Compendium* properly relates to weight.”]

470. Between *praeda*, *lucrum*, and *compendium*. *Praeda* comes from an enemy; *lucrum* from business; *compendium* properly from weight.

[Note: [Col. 0057D]

471. From C. Fronto.

[Col. 0058D] —*Pompeiana*. Two manuscripts: *Pompeigena*.

—*Domum*. “He passed over into domination”; I read this from Fronto.]

471. Between *Pompeii porticus*, *Pompeia*, and *Pompeiana*. *Pompeii* means “belonging to Pompey himself”; *Pompeia* means “made public” [Col. 0058A]; *Pompeiana*, when it passes over to another house.

472. Between *populus* and *plebs*. The *populus* is the whole community together with the Senate and Roman citizens; the *plebs* is merely the lower class.

473. Between *partem* and *partim*. *Partem* is a noun; *partim* is an adverb.

474. Between *postremum* and *posteriorem*. *Postremus* is last among many; *posterior*, later of two.

475. Between *principium* and *initium*. *Principium* is the first part; *initium* is the beginning undertaken by each thing that starts.

476. Between *pendent* and *pendunt*. *Pendent* means “they hang suspended”; *pendunt*, “they weigh something.”

61

[Note: [Col. 0058D]

477. Festus, under *Penem*.]

477. Between *pene* and *pene*. *Pene* is an adverb; *pene* is the most shameful [Al.: “last”] part of the body.

## On the letter Q

[Col. 0058B] [Note: [Col. 0058D]

478. C. Fronto: *Quatenus*, *quatine*, *quatinus*, *quoniam*. Festus, under *Quatenus*.

In the same place. *Quatenus* and *quatinus* do not properly differ, whatever Festus and others may say. But because among the ancients *e* and *i* were easily interchanged, forms such as *quatenus* and *quatinus*, *protenus* and *protinus*, and similar pairs occur. AREV.]

478. Between *quatenus* and *quatinus*. *Quatenus* is an adverb; *quatinus* is a causal conjunction, as when you say: “Since you do not do this without a beating, here are your beatings.” *Quatenus* is an adverb either of time or of place; of time when we say, “For how long will you carry on this activity?”

479. Between *quoniam* and *quia*. *Quoniam* is placed first and binds the following sense to it, as in: “Since you say it, I speak.” *Quia* is placed afterward and confirms the preceding sense, as in: “Know that I have learned.”

480. Between *quamdudum* and *jamdudum*. *Quamdudum* belongs to one who is asking; *jamdudum* to one who is answering.

[Note: [Col. 0058D]

481. From Agraetius, from which it is clear that the reading should be: “Between *quaeritur* and *queritur*: *queritur* is used in lamentation, *quaeritur* in inquiry,” unless one prefers to change *quiritur* to *quiritatur*.

In the same place. Pantinus’s conjecture that *quiritatur* should be read is confirmed by Varro, *On the Latin Language* V, chapter 7: “He is said to *quiritare* who loudly implores the protection of the Quirites.” AREV.]

481. Between *quaeritur* and *quiritur*. *Quiritur* is used of imploring; *quaeritur*, of inquiring.

[Note: [Col. 0058D]

482. From Agraetius, in whom *lucro* is wrong.]

482. Between *questus* and *quaestus*. *Quaestus* concerns profit; *questus*, tears or lamentation.

[Col. 0058C]

483. Between *quae* and *que*. *Quae* is a pronoun; *que* is a conjunction.

484. Between *quod* and *quot*. If it is written with *d*, *quod*, it is a personal pronoun; if with *t*, *quot*, it denotes number.

## On the letter R

485. Between *recens* and *novum*. *Recens* is born or newly produced; *novum* is made. Hence Virgil:

“Fresh milk does not fail me in summer or in cold weather.”

62

[Note: [Col. 0058D]

486. Cicero, *On Duties*.

[Col. 0059D] —*Superstitio*, however. Nonius, under *Superstitionis*.]

486. Between *religio* and *fides*. *Fides* is the belief by which we confess God; *religio* is the worship that we who believe in him offer. *Fides* is so called from the fact that what has been agreed between two parties is made good. *Religio* is likewise as if “a bond between God and human beings,” because by it human beings are bound by the obligation of serving in the worship of divinity. *Religio* belongs to virtue; *superstitio* to illicit worship.

487. Between *rationale* and *rationabile*. *Rationale* applies to beings such as an angel and a human being; *rationabile* to what is done or said by reason.

488. Between *rusticus* and *rusticanus*. An agricultural laborer may be called *rusticus*; a landowning head of household, *rusticanus*.

489. Between *rusticitas* and *rusticatio*. *Rusticitas* concerns manners; *rusticatio*, work.

490. Between *ratio* and *ratiocinatio*. *Ratio* is the movement of the mind [Al.: “the mind’s movement”] capable of distinguishing or connecting things that are said [Al.: “learned”]. *Ratiocinatio* is a rational and subtle argument, a thought striving to investigate the uncertain from the certain [Al.: “or the certain from the uncertain”].

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

491. From C. Fronto, under *Regium*.]

491. Between *regium* and *regale*. *Regium* is what belongs to the king himself; *regale*, what is worthy of a king. The same applies to *regia* and *regalis*: a *regia domus* is a house in which the king is; a *regalis* house is worthy of a king.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

492. Old Glossary: *robur*, “a kind of wood, black oak” (*εἶδος ξύλου μελάνδρυς*).]

492. Between *rubor*, *robur*, and *robor*. *Rubor* is the color red; *robur*, strength; *robor*, an oak tree.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

493. *Etymologies* XII, chapter 6.]

493. Between *reptilia* and *repentia*. *Reptilia* belong to the waters; *repentia* to the land.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

494. On this distinction, see no. 244. AREV.]

494. Between *rivus*, *fons*, *torrens*, and *flumen*. A *rivus* arises suddenly; a *fons* is a source and a channel into which naturally flowing water runs; a *torrens* is a precipitous flood of rainwater [Al.: “a rainy flood and a precipitous flow”]; a *fluvius* is, generally, a flowing body of water.

## On the letter S

[Col. 0059C] [Note: [Col. 0059D]

495. *Etymologies* III, chapters 59 and 70.

In the same place. In other manuscripts: “which sailors observe.” AREV.]

495. Between *sidera*, *astra*, *stellae*, and *signa*. Those are called *sidera* by which sailors take their bearings and direct their course; *astra* are large stars, such as Orion; *stellae* are groups of stars, such as the Hyades and Pleiades; a *signum* is an image formed of a living creature, such as Taurus, Scorpio, and the like.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

496. Book of Sentences by D. Isidore.]

496. The difference between *sempiternum* and *perpetuum* is that eternity belongs to God, perpetuity to angels or to human souls [Al.: “the human soul”]. The former always existed and never ceases to exist; the latter began to exist but does not cease to exist perpetually.

497. Between *sensus* and *intellectus*. *Sensus* refers to nature; *intellectus* to art.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

498. Servius, on *Aeneid* I, “He decrees honor for the temples,” and on *Aeneid* III, “The accursed hunger for gold.”]

498. Between *sacrum*, *religiosum*, and *sanctum*. We call that *sacrum* which belongs to God; *religiosum*, that which belongs to righteous human beings; *sanctum*, that by which something is sanctioned, and violation of which incurs punishment. What is *sacrum* is also *sanctum*, but what is *sanctum* is not necessarily *sacrum*. Likewise, *sanctum* is used in a favorable sense; *sacrum* has two meanings, good and evil. Good, as in Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “Among known rivers and sacred springs”; evil, as in: “The accursed hunger for gold” (*Aeneid* III); and “The accursed gates are opened” (*Aeneid* II); and “The sacred procurer” (Plautus); and “The sacred goat” (Ovid). Hence a terrible ulcer is also called *ignis sacer*, “sacred fire.” *Alma* is derived from *alere*, “to nourish.” Thus among the pagans Ceres was called *alma*, as the discoverer of nourishment.

499. *Sapiens* and *prudens* are commonly distinguished in this way: one is called *sapiens* who investigates the nature of eternal things, but *prudens* one who investigates matters experienced through the bodily senses.

[Col. 0060B] [Note: [Col. 0059D]

500. *Etymologies* X, letter S; the commentators on Terence, *Eunuchus*, Act V, Scene 9.

—*Stupidus*. Nonius, under *Stupidus*.]

500. Between *stultus*, *fatuus*, and *stupidus*. Some of the ancients consider a person *fatuus* who understands neither what he himself says nor what others say; a *stultus* is duller in heart or mind. Hence Afranius: “I consider myself *stultus*, but I do not think myself *fatuus*”—that is, my senses are indeed dull, but not nonexistent. *Stupidus* is so called as if from “stony,” like *stolidus*, “stolid.”

501. Between *saevus* and *crudelis*. *Saevus* applies to anger; *crudelis* to bloodshed.

[Note: [Col. 0059D]

502. With widows, Nonius, under *Stuprum*.

[Col. 0060D] —*Etymologies* X, letter I.

—*Etymologies* V, chapter 26, and X, letter A.]

502. Between *stuprum*, *incestum*, and *adulterium*. *Stuprum* is committed with a maiden; *incestum* with a relative or a widow; *adulterium* with a married woman. *Incestum* is so called as if *incastum*, “unchaste.”

[Note: [Col. 0060D]

503. Charisius: *Saturitas* is used only of food; in other matters, *satietas*. C. Fronto puts it more briefly: “*Saturitas* of the belly, *satietas* of the mind.”]

503. Between *satietas* and *saturitas*. *Satietas* results from a variety of spectacles; *saturitas* belongs to food.

[Note: [Col. 0060D]

504. C. Fronto: “*Superbia* comes from *superhabere*, ‘to have above’; *arrogantia* can also apply to a poor man.”

—*Super vult*, etc. Al.: “He always wants what is not.”]

504. Between *superbia* and *arrogantia*. *Arrogantia* is empty glory concerning what one is. *Superbia* is an overstepping elevation of the mind concerning what one is not. There are two kinds of *superbia*: one casts down spiritual and eminent men through boasting of their virtues; the other makes the fleshly disobedient toward the authority of their elders. *Superbia* is so called because it wants more than what is.

[Note: [Col. 0060D]

505. To dissemble is skillfully to conceal and hide what one knows, although one does not say that one is unaware. AREV.]

505. Between *sciens* and *sciolus*. *Sciens* is skilled in knowledge and affairs; *sciolus* is a pretender to knowledge and expertise, the opposite of one who truly knows. Whatever another person knows, he himself would like to appear to know; or he is one who professes to know everything, even to foretell the future.

[Note: [Col. 0060D]

506. Nonius, under *Spurcum*.

—*Spurius*, however. *Etymologies* IX, chapter 5.

In the same place. They called it *spurium*. In the *Etymologies*, at the cited passage, they called it *σπόριον* in Greek letters. AREV.]

506. Between *spurcus* and *spurius*. *Spurcus* means not only impure but also savage; *spurius* means born of an uncertain father and a widowed mother, as though merely the son of a woman. For the ancients [the jurists add: “of the female sex”] called the female sex *spurius*. Some also call such persons *favonii*, because certain animals are thought to conceive after inhaling the breath of the west wind.

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

507. Thus the interpreters of Terence, *Eunuchus*, Act IV, Scene 3: *scelerosus* applies to many, *scelestus* even to one; *scelerosus* properly means the author of a crime, *sceleratus* one in whom a crime has been committed or established.]

507. Between *sceleratus*, *scelestus*, and *scelerosus*. Grammarians say that one is *sceleratus* in whom a crime is committed; as Cicero says: “O you criminal, who have been subdued and prostituted.” But one is *scelestus* through whom the crime is committed. Thus Terence: “Wicked woman, you have entrusted a sheep to a wolf.” *Scelerosus* is one who commits the crime; thus the same author: “Against my will, miserable as I was, I endured that criminal.” But authors do not observe these distinctions consistently.

65 [Note: [Col. 0061D]

508. Alternatively: “Age either is preserved or kept in reserve.”]

508. Between *salus* and *salubritas*. *Salus* is bodily integrity; *salubritas* is a condition conducive to health, through which health is either preserved or restored.

[Col. 0061B] [Note: [Col. 0061D]

509. From Agraetius.

—On *super* in certain uses. Servius, commentary on *Aeneid* III: “O sole image of my Astyanax remaining to me.”]

509. Between *super* and *supra* there is this difference: *super* refers to what overhangs [Agraetius: “rises above”]; *supra* to what has something beneath it. Likewise, *super* is sometimes understood as “too much” or “enough.”

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

510. From Agraetius.]

510. Between *subter* and *subtus*. *Subter* refers to what is depressed and trampled beneath something higher; *subtus* to what has been lowered and is not touched from above.

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

511. Festus, under *supremum*. Nonius, under *supremum*.]

511. Between *supremi* and *supprimi*. *Supremi* and *summi* signify both “highest” and “lowest”; *supprimi*, however, means “to be hidden.”

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

512. Thus C. Fronto: “We take what has been set down; we receive what is held out.”

—On *assumimus*, etc. From Fronto, who writes: “He takes away (*aufert*) what he gave; he removes (*adimit*—Isidore reads *adimimus*) under compulsion; he snatches away (*eripit*) who is stronger.”]

512. Between *sumere* and *accipere* [alternatively: *praecipere*, “to prescribe”]. We *sumimus* ourselves; we *accipimus* from another. When we give something, we say, “Receive”; when we permit someone to take it himself [alternatively: “when we prescribe it”], we say, “Take.” Likewise, we take things through our own agency, receive them from willing persons, and remove them from unwilling persons [alternatively: “from reluctant persons”]. Likewise, we take away [the correction is *adimimus*] by right whatever we have given; we *assumimus* by command; we *eripimus* by force.

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

513. From the interpreters of Terence, *Andria*, Act II, Scene 6.

—“I marvel,” Servius, on the cited verse.]

513. Between *sperare* and *exspectare*. We *exspectamus* both good and evil; but we *speramus* only good things. Yet Virgil, in a remarkable way, separates the particular force of this verb from its proper meaning when he says (*Aeneid* IV):

> If I could only hope for so great a grief;

whereas everything that the mind dreads ought more properly to be called “feared” [the alternative adds: “rather than hoped for”]. But the grammarians explain this by saying: “He used *sperare* for *timere*, ‘to fear.’” Lucan likewise distinguishes the terms when he says: “May one who fears be permitted to hope.”

514. Between *scire* and *nosse*. *Scire* means to give an account of what one has come to know [Col. 0062A]; *nosse* means merely to report what one has heard.

[Note: [Col. 0061D]

515. From Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “They conceal themselves and, wrapped in a hollow cloud, watch.” Alternatively: “We conceal what is known; we pretend what is unknown.”

—“For whoever.” C. Fronto: “He who pretends wishes to prove what is not so.”

—“That pretender.” I think Isidore wrote this, citing the passage from the *Bellum Catilinae* and explaining it as follows: “A pretender regarding anything, and one who conceals what is known.” He was a pretender regarding what was uncertain and one who concealed what was certain. Unless, perhaps, the phrase was added as a gloss by another hand.]

515. Between *simulare* and *dissimulare*. We *dissimulamus* what is known; we *simulamus* what is unknown. For one who pretends to know what he does not know is *simulating*; but one who says that he does not know what he knows is *dissimulating*. Hence Sallustius also says: “He was a pretender regarding what was uncertain and one who concealed what was certain.”

[Note: [Col. 0062D]

516. I do not know whether Isidore wrote: “To stand before one person, but to stand in the presence of many.” The remaining material, which was absent from another copy, should be omitted.]

516. Between *sistere*, *consistere*, and *assistere*. *Sistere* sometimes means “to resist” or “to restrain,” that is, to cause something to stand in a place. Thus Virgil: “To make the waters stand in the rivers.” *Assistere* means both to stand before one person and to stand in the presence of many; *consistere* means to be present in the middle.

517. Between *servire* and *inservire*. One *serves* masters alone; one *inserves* the commands of anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0062D]

518. From Agraetius, though this passage may require correction.]

518. Between *spirare* and *exspirare*. *Spirare* means to live [Col. 0062B]; *exspirare* means to die.

519. Between *surgere*, *exsurgere*, and the related forms. One rises (*surgitur*) from a place; one rises up (*exsurgitur*) from sleep; one rises up against someone (*insurgitur*) for revenge; one rises together (*consurgitur*) to provide assistance.

520. Between *subjicitur* and *supponitur*. Something is placed beneath quickly (*subjicitur*); it is placed underneath slowly (*supponitur*).

521. Between *simul* and *semel*. *Semel* belongs to number, as in “once, twice”; *simul* belongs to bringing things together, as in: “The men, gathered together, rush simultaneously to arms.”

[Note: [Col. 0062D]

522. Festus, under *sepulcrum*. Isidore, *Etymologies* XV.11.

—The same. Servius, on *Aeneid* VI: “She left these memorials behind.”

—Isidore, *Etymologies* XV.11.

—Isidore, *Etymologies* XI.2.]

522. Between *sepulcrum* and *monumentum*. A *sepulcrum* is merely a mound for the dead; a *monumentum* is sometimes a tomb and sometimes a record of deeds. It is so called because it reminds the mind either of the deceased or of a written event. Moreover, *tumulus* has two meanings: it denotes both swelling earth and a tomb. *Sepulcrum* is derived from *sepultus*, “buried.” *Sepultus*, in turn, is so called because one is without palpitation or pulse—that is, without movement. *Cadaver*, “corpse,” is derived from *cadere*, “to fall.”

[Note: [Col. 0063C]

523. Isidore, *Etymologies* VI.19.]

523. Between *sacrificium* and *hostia* there was formerly this distinction: a *sacrificium* was a voluntary offering, whereas a *hostia* was what was sacrificed after enemies had been defeated. It was also called a *victima*. Others think that *victima* was so called because it falls when struck by a blow, or because it is led bound to the altars.

[Note: [Col. 0063C]

524. Isidore, *Etymologies* XX.11.

[Col. 0063D] —*Solium*. Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “And, leaning high upon the throne, she sat.”

—“A seat belonging to one person.” Isidore, in the immediately preceding passage.]

524. Between *sedes* and *thronus*. *Sedes* belongs not only to one person but also to many. For *solium* belongs only to one person, and specifically to kings; *sedes* is proper to anyone. *Solium* is derived either from the sitting of one person (*solius*) or from solidity. The Latins say *solium*; the Greeks say *thronos*. *Sedes* is so called because among the ancient Romans reclining at meals was not customary. Hence the expression *considere*, “to sit down together,” is used in the ancient manner. For the ancients dined sitting. Later, as Varro says in *On the Life of the Roman People*, men began to recline and women to sit, because it was considered shameful for a woman to recline.

[Note: [Col. 0063D]

525. Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII.4.]

525. Between *servus* and *famulus*. Slaves are people captured in war, as though “preserved”; similarly, *mancipium* is derived from being captured by hand from the enemy. *Famuli*, however, are born from one’s own households.

[Note: [Col. 0063D]

526. From Sosipater of Carystus.]

526. Between *servitus* and *servitium*. *Servitus* is the condition of serving; *servitium* is the number of those who serve [alternatively: “the number of slaves”].

[Col. 0063B] 527. Between *socer* and *socrus*. We call a man a *socer*, and a woman a *socrus*.

528. Between *similitudo* and *figura*. *Similitudo* occurs when an image is painted or formed according to some visible likeness. *Figura* occurs when an image is impressed from the form of something, as when a seal takes an image in wax, or when a potter impresses a hand or face into clay and, by shaping it, produces a figure.

[Note: [Col. 0063D]

529. Isidore, *Etymologies* XI.1.

—*Cruor*. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “And the warm blood smoked upon the altars.”

—In Grialius’s text it read *cruor victimarum*, “the blood of victims,” but, I think, erroneously in place of *cruorem*. AREV.]

529. Between *sanguis* and *cruor*. *Sanguis* is blood while it remains in the body; once poured out, it becomes *cruor*. *Cruor* is so called from rawness, whence also *crudelitas*, “cruelty,” and *crudus*, “raw.” Others say that *cruor* is used of the blood of victims, and *sanguis* of human beings. Thus Virgil (*Aeneid* II):

> You appeased the winds with blood and with the slaughter of a maiden,

that is, with the blood of the slain maiden.

530. Between *sinus* and *gremium*. *Sinus* is the receptacle formed by a folded garment; *gremium* is the inner part of a shortened [alternatively: “properly fitted”] garment.

68 [Note: [Col. 0063D]

531. Isidore, *Etymologies* XI.2.

—“Thus an old man.” Perhaps, from the cited passage of Isidore, it should be read as “thus an old man”; but *senior* is less old than *senex*.

—“Now older.” See Servius, at the same place, on *Aeneid* VI.

—On the various stages of life I have said more in the prolegomena to Dracontius, p. 21. Grialius’s text read *sic senes*, “thus old men,” instead of *sic senex*, “thus an old man.” AREV.]

531. Between *senium* and *senectus*. *Senectus* is the more serious age that follows youth; *senium* is the final age that comes after maturity. Thus *senex* and *senior*: an older man is still more vigorous. As in Virgil:

> Now older, but the god’s old age is fresh and vigorous.

Terence likewise says: “The right by which I have lived as a younger man”—not necessarily “more adolescent,” but “less so.” Thus *senior* means “less old” than *senex*. *Senecta* is the condition or state associated with old age.

532. Between *sonus* and *sonitus*. *Sonus* [the alternative has *sonitus*] is anything perceptible that is heard; *sonitus* [the alternative has *sonus*] is the confused sound of voices or trumpets.

533. *Spolia* refers to those who strip others; *exuviae* to those who have been stripped.

[Note: [Col. 0063D]

534. From C. Fronto, who nevertheless does not name Palaemon.]

534. Between *stilla* and *gutta*. The grammarian Palaemon distinguishes them as follows: “A *gutta*, a drop, stands; a *stilla*, a falling drop, falls.”

[Note: [Col. 0063D]

535. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “The anchorage is not trustworthy for ships”; and on *Aeneid* X:

“Nor do I refuse to break the ships at such an anchorage.”

—Perhaps the passage should be read elsewhere, from Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV.8.]

535. Between *statio* and *portus*. A *statio* is a place where ships remain for a time; a *portus* is where they winter. For a harbor is a place protected from the approach of winds, where ships customarily prepare for winter.

[Note: [Col. 0064D]

536. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I: “What must be hastened beneath a clear sky”; “And pray for clear winters”; and elsewhere: “Whence the wind drives clear clouds”; and often elsewhere.

—“Calm.” “Calm across the deep,” *Aeneid* II.]

536. Between *serenus* and *tranquillus*. *Serenus* can be referred to the sky, but not to the sea. We speak of a *serenum caelum*, “a clear sky,” but a *tranquillum mare*, “a calm sea.”

537. Between *saxa* and *lapides*. *Saxa* are only extremely hard; *lapis* may refer to both hard and soft stone.

[Note: [Col. 0064D]

538. The old glossary also recognizes this word.]

538. Between *specus* and *antrum*. The Latins say *specus*; the Greeks say *antron*. These are places from which reflected voices return an image of the sound.

[Note: [Col. 0064D]

539. From Servius, on *Aeneid* IV: “They carry them along the narrow path”; and from Isidore, *Etymologies* XV.16.

—*Semis via*, “half a road.” Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV: “As though *semi iter*, ‘half a journey.’” Isidore himself, in the cited book, derives it from *semi-itus*, “half-going.”

—“A path so called.” It should be read: “A road so called,” for a *semita* does not accommodate a vehicle, whereas a *via* does.

—“It is called an *actus*.” Paulus, under Festus, *actus*. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, in two passages. Isidore himself, *Etymologies* XV.15.]

539. Between *semita*, *callis*, and *trames*. A *semita* is a path for human beings; a *callis* is for cattle or wild animals. *Callis* also means a narrow road, so called from *calcare*, “to tread.” *Tramites* are cross-country routes in fields. Properly, therefore, a *callis* is a narrow path hardened by the hoofs of cattle. *Semita* means, as it were, “half a road.” A *semita* is so called because only one vehicle can travel along it. Its double width is called an *actus*, either because it accommodates two vehicles or because vehicles traveling in opposite directions meet there.

[Col. 0064C] 540. *Succipere* means to receive something bodily falling from above; *suscipere* means to undertake a cause immaterially. *Suspicere* means to look upward or to venerate.

541. Between *simulare* and *dissimulare*. One who *simulat* wishes to appear to do what he does not do; one who *dissimulat* does not wish to appear to do what he does.

[Note: [Col. 0064D]

542. From Servius, on *Aeneid* V: “Bringing you gloomy dreams”; yet also: “A *somnium* is what we see while sleeping.”]

542. Between *somnus* and *somnium*. *Somnus* is the sleep by which we sleep; *somnium* is what we see while sleeping.

543. Between *sum* and *suum*. *Sum* is a verb; *suum* is a pronoun.

544. Between *saevit* and *sevit*. *Saevit* means “he rages” or “is angry”; *sevit* means “he sows.”

[Col. 0065A] [Note: [Col. 0065D]

545. See above.]

545. Between *suus* and *sus*. *Suus* is a pronoun; *sus* is an animal.

546. Between *Syra* and *sura*. *Syra* is a woman of the Syrian nation; *sura* is a part of the leg.

[Note: [Col. 0065D]

547. From Nonius, under *sartores*, apparently.

—*Sarcinatorem*. C. Fronto: “A *sarcinatrix* is a woman who preserves bundles.”

—In the same place: *sartor* is understood not only as one who cultivates a field, that is, removes useless plants with a hoe, but also as one who mends clothes. AREV.]

547. Between *sartor* and *sarcinator*. A *sartor* is one who hoes a field; a *sarcinator* is one who mends clothing.

548. Between *similis* and *simulans*. *Similis* means “like” or “such”; *simulans* means “pretending to be such.”

549. Between *strenuus* and *externus*. *Strenuus* means “strong” or “vigorous”; *externus* means “external” or “foreign.”

[Note: [Col. 0065D]

550. The interpreters of Terence, *Eunuchus*, Act III, Scene 5. *Statura* is applied to the body; *status* refers to condition or appearance. Therefore *status* is σχῆμα (*schēma*), “form” or “figure”; *statura* is the length or size of the body. Instead of *pro quaestionem*, I would prefer *pro quaestionis* or *pro quaestionum*. Moreover, the expressions concerning theatrical dress may perhaps be compressed into σχῆμα, and the passage should be read: “the state of the question, or the form”; or “the state of the question, or the form, that is, the costume.” See Asconius Paedianus on the Third Oration against Verres.]

550. Between *status* and *statura*. *Status* means a question or theatrical costume; *statura* means the size of any object.

70 [Note: [Col. 0065D]

551. What if we read: “Between *scriptura* and *scriptio*: *scriptio* belongs to the work, *scriptura* to intention”? See p. [reference unclear].]

551. Between *scriptura* and *lectio*. *Lectio* belongs to a work; *scriptura* to intention or painting.

## On the Letter T

[Col. 0065B]

[Note: [Col. 0065D]

552. Isidore, *Etymologies* IV.5. Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, under *terra*.]

552. Between *terra*, *tellus*, and *humus*. *Terra* is barren and uncultivated; *tellus* is fruitful; *humus* is lower, downward, and moist [the alternative adds: “earth”]. Hence *humati*, “those buried,” and *sepulti*, “those entombed.” In general, *terra* is found everywhere, but *humus* is not everywhere. There is *terra* in walls—that is, in bricks—but there is not *humus*. *Humus* is moist earth and is named from *humor*, “moisture,” just as *terra* and *tellus* are so called because natural dryness scorches the earth and because we take its fruits.

[Note: [Col. 0065D]

553. From Agraetius, who adds: “the tempering of the winds.”]

553. *Temperantia* and *temperatio* are distinguished in this way: *temperantia* belongs to the mind, *temperatio* to things.

[Note: [Col. 0065D]

554. From Servius, on Eclogue 7: “And Aegle came upon the timid ones.”]

554. Between *timens* and *timidus*. *Timidus* is one who is always afraid; *timens* is one who fears temporarily and for a reason. In the same sense, *pavidus* and *pavens*, *providus* and *providens*, *superbus* and *superbiens*, *languidus* and *languens*, *furibundus* and *furens*, and other similar forms are distinguished.

555. Between *tremulus* and *tremens*. *Tremulus* describes what is so by nature; *tremens* what is trembling at a particular time.

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

556. See above.]

556. Between *temeritas* and *audacia*. *Temeritas* is said of action without deliberation; *audacia* follows deliberation.

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

557. Alternatively: *tum* refers to present time; *tunc* to future time.]

557. Between *tum* and *tunc*. *Tum* refers to future time; *tunc* to past time.

558. Between *tribuere* and *attribuere*. We *tribuimus* when we give something; we *attribuimus* when we distribute ranks and duties.

[Col. 0066A] 559. Between *tulit*, *abstulit*, and *sustulit*. *Tulit* is used of one who carries; *abstulit* of one who takes something away from another; *sustulit* of one who carries something upward.

560. Between *tumidus* and *turgidus*. A sick person’s body *swells* (*tumet*); a corpse *bloats* (*turget*).

71 [Note: [Col. 0066D]

561. Thus Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “He says, ‘I call the divine power to witness.’”

—In some manuscripts: “Between *contestari* and *obtestari* there is this difference: we *contestamur* against adversaries, but we *obtestamur* friends.” AREV.]

561. Between *testor*, *contestor*, and *obtestor*. *Testor* very often relates to an oath, as Virgil says, “I call the stars to witness”; *contestor* relates to judges; *obtestor* to adversaries.

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

562. Charisius gives the shorter version: “The back of a human being is called *tergum*; that of an animal, *tergus*.” See Servius on the passage in the *Aeneid*: “They tear away the hides from the ribs.” For the proper meaning of *tumultus*, see Servius on *Aeneid* I: “As the signal of war”; and VIII, and also VII: “He himself summons the battles.”

—On *tumultus* at greater length, see Isidore, *Etymologies* XVIII.1. AREV.]

562. Between *terga* and *tergora*. *Terga* belongs to human beings; in the singular it is *tergum*. *Tergus* belongs to four-footed animals. Hence, in the plural, *tergora* means hides.

563. Between *tumultus* and *bellum*. A *bellum* arises against enemies; a *tumultus* is stirred up within the community. It is also called *seditio*, “sedition.” For *seditio* is the separation [alternative: “disagreement”] of citizens. Because some go apart from others, it is called *seditio*. Others think that *seditio* is so called because of disagreement among minds; the Greeks call this διάστασις (*diastasis*), “separation” or “dissension.”

564. Between *turbidus* and *turbulentus*. *Turbidus* describes what is so by nature; *turbulentus* what becomes so.

565. Between *terrenus*, *terrestris*, and *terrosus*. We call an earthen work *terrenum*; *terrestre* is used in contrast with maritime, as “land” in contrast with “sea”; *terrosum* describes a sandy kind of grain.

566. Between *tuus* and *thus*. *Tuus* is a pronoun; *thus* is a perfume.

Between *tuum* and *tum*. *Tum* is an adverb; *tuum* is a pronoun.

567. Between *tempore* and *tempori*. *Tempore*, in the ablative case, is a noun; *tempori* is an adverb.

568. Between *tristitia* and *maestitia*. *Maestitia* belongs to the heart; *tristitia* to the face. Thus we call someone *maestus*, “sad,” or *moerens*, “mourning,” in spirit, but *tristis*, “sad,” in appearance. *Maestitia* also belongs to a period of time and sometimes arises from pain caused by an event. *Tristitia*, however, is a permanent defect of nature.

## On the Letter V

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

569. C. Fronto writes: “What has passed beyond the memory of our fathers is ancient. What is old bears the mark of many years.”]

569. Between *vetus* and *antiquus*. *Vetus* is reckoned in years; *antiquus* in centuries.

72 570. Between *virtus* and *fortitudo*. *Virtus* lies in strength and disposition of mind; *fortitudo*, “fortitude,” is one part of it. Fortitude is one of the four virtues, although bodily strength is also called *fortitudo*.

[Note: [Col. 0066D]

571. Thus Festus, under *vecors*.

—For words formed with *ve-*, see Gellius V.12 and XXVI.15. AREV.]

571. Between *vecors* and *vesanus*. *Vecors* means “of an evil heart,” just as *vesanus* means “not sound,” or “not properly sane.”

[Col. 0067A] [Note: [Col. 0067C]

572. From Agraetius, who adds: “The speed of feet and bodies; the swiftness of minds and actions.”]

572. Between *velocitas* and *celeritas*. *Velocitas* belongs to the feet; *celeritas* to the mind.

573. Between *vastitas* and *vastitudo*. *Vastitas* belongs to the body; *vastitudo* means solitude or desolation.

[Note: [Col. 0067C]

574. Fronto gives the shorter formulation: “Volition rejoices in the deed; pleasure desires that it be done”—which Isidore has apparently explained.]

574. Between *voluptas* and *voluntas*. *Voluntas* is desire for something not yet obtained; *voluptas* is delight in something obtained, whether good or bad.

[Note: [Col. 0067D]

575. Isidore, *Etymologies* V, final chapter.

—“And so called.” C. From Servius, on *Georgics* II: “Nor aim the lashes at the top.” Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII.5–6.]

575. Between *verbera* and *flagella*. *Verbera* is any kind of whip or blow; *flagella* properly belong to rods, and are so called because they are shaken and make a sound when moved by the wind.

576. Between *valetudo* and *infirmitas*. *Valetudo* may be good or bad; *infirmitas* is always unfavorable.

[Note: [Col. 0067D]

577. Agraetius: “An ulcer is what arises; a wound is what is inflicted by another.” Servius: “An ulcer is a hidden and closed malignancy; a wound is gaping and open.”]

577. Between *vulnus* and *ulcus*. *Vulnus* is applied to the mind; *ulcus* to an injury of the body. Likewise, a recent bodily wound is a *vulnus*, while an old wound is an *ulcus*.

[Col. 0067B] [Note: [Col. 0067D]

578. Isidore, *Etymologies* V.8.]

578. Between *verbum* and *sermo*. According to the grammarians, *verbum* is one part of speech. *Sermo*, however, is an utterance composed of many words. *Sermo* is derived from *serere*, “to join together,” which we express with the preposition in *disserere*, “to discuss.” Hence one speaks of the *sermo* of Saint Hilary and Augustine—that is, the exposition or discourse of Hilary and Augustine.

579. Between *ultra* and *citra*. *Ultra* means “to that place” or “beyond”; *citra* means “to this side,” toward us, within us.

73 [Note: [Col. 0067D]

580. From Fronto, who writes: “Vengeance avenges a deed; punishment or retribution prevents a future deed.”]

580. Between *ulcisci* and *vindicare*. We *ulciscimur* an injury that has been done; we *vindicate* so that it may not be done.

[Note: [Col. 0067D]

581. From Fronto; yet in place of *aspicere* and *aspicimus*, *spectare* and *spectamus* is more correct, since the same author teaches that *aspicere* means to look at something unexpectedly.]

581. Between *videre*, *aspicere*, and *intueri*. We *videmus* by nature; we *aspicimus* by choice; we *intuemur* with care.

582. Between *veneunt* and *vendunt*. Those who sell are *vendunt*; those who are sold are *veneunt*.

583. Between *volo*, *opto*, and *cupio*. *Volo*, “I wish,” is less intense than *opto*, “I hope or desire”; *opto* is less intense than *cupio*, “I long for.”

584. Between *unum* and *unicum*. *Unus* means one among many; *unicus* means alone. Thus *solus* is counted as one, whereas *unicus* is defined within number.

585. Between *unum* and *solum*. *Unus* pertains to number; *solus* is understood as one among many.

[Note: [Col. 0067D]

586. I read *eligo*, “I choose,” for *eligere*, “to choose.”]

586. Between *uter* and *utrum*. When we say, “Which of the two do you want?” (*utrum vis*), it signifies choosing either this or that. *Uter*, however, is used of persons, as in: “Which one wishes to come to me?”—that is, “Which of the two wishes to come?”

[Note: [Col. 0067D]

587. From Servius, on *Aeneid* II: “We cover the festal city with foliage.” See Nonius, under *urbem*. Between *urbs* and *civitas*. Alternatively: *urbs* signifies the walls of a city; *civitas*, the inhabitants of the city.

—On *urbem*, Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “There was an ancient city”; and Donatus, on the passage where the city is marked out with a plow.

[Col. 0068C] —The plow, or part of the plow: not the plow itself, nor the furrow, but that which makes the furrow. Isidore treats the matter more accurately in *Etymologies* XV.2.

[Col. 0068D] —From *orbis*, “circle.” Servius, in the cited passage, derives it from *orbis*, because ancient cities were laid out in a circle.]

587. Cicero distinguishes *urbs* and *civitas* in this way: *urbs* signifies the walls of a city, while *civitas* signifies the inhabitants. Thus he wrote to Dolabella: “You freed the city from danger and the citizens from fear.” Some think that *urbs* is derived from *urbum*, which the ancients called either a plow or a furrow; others derive it from *orbis*, “circle,” because the state contained within itself the form of a circle. Moreover, *oppidum* pertains to those who inhabit it, *civitas* to its laws, and *urbs* to both.

[Note: [Col. 0068D]

588. *Vir* is masculine, not feminine; *homo* is masculine and feminine. The manuscript is erroneous.]

588. Between *vir* and *homo*. *Vir* is a male, not a female; *homo* may be male or female. *Femina* is the natural designation; *mulier* is the general term, while *virgo*, “virgin,” and *nupta*, “married woman,” are specific terms, to which terms of age may also be added.

74 [Note: [Col. 0068D]

589. From the ancient interpreters of Terence, though they have *forma*, “form,” instead of *facies*, “face.” See Nonius under *facies*, especially under *vultus* and *facies*, and Servius on *Aeneid* I: “You, the face of that man.”

—*Vultuosi*. Nonius, under *vultuosus*.

—“The face of the sea.” *Aeneid* V:

> Do you command me to be ignorant of the face of the calm sea  
> and of its quiet waves?

And Servius there.]

589. Between *vultus* and *facies*. *Facies* is the natural, unchanging appearance of the face; *vultus*, however, varies and changes according to circumstances and times [alternatively: “is changeable”], and in accordance with the mind’s affection is now joyful, now sad. Hence those who often change their expression are called *vultuosi*. Lucilius therefore, distinguishing the terms in something like this way, says: “What is the face, what the expression, of the man?” We also speak of the *vultus* of the sky and of the sea, because the sea is frequently altered into different movements by the blowing of the winds, and the expression of the sky changes from light to darkness and from clear weather to cloudiness, just as the expression of human beings changes with their minds.

590. Between *virgo* and *virago*. A *virgo* is a woman who does not know a man; a *virago* is a woman who acts like a man, that is, who performs manly deeds. Not only virgins but also corrupted women who perform manly deeds are properly called *viragines*.

[Note: [Col. 0068D]

591. From Agraetius.]

591. Between *vivus* and *vivens*. We use *vivus* of one who will live; *vivens* of one who is dying.

[Note: [Col. 0068D]

592. Vatican Manuscript. The difference between *-que* and *ve* is that *-que* is a conjunction, whereas *ve* is disjunctive. AREV.]

592. Between *ve* and *-que*. *Ve* separates; *-que* joins.

593. Between *vae* and *ve*. *Ve* without *a* is a conjunctive conjunction. *Vae*, with *a*, is the exclamation of one who grieves.

594. Between *vox* and *sonus*. *Vox* belongs to a human being; *sonus* to a shoe or sandal.

[Note: [Col. 0068D]

595. From Servius, on Eclogue 10:

“Menalcas comes, wet from the winter acorn.”

] 595. Between *uvidus* and *humidus*. Something is *humidum* when it has moisture on the outside [Col. 0069A]; it is *uvidum* when it has moisture within. Hence grapes are called *uvae*.

[Note: [Col. 0069B]

596. Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV.8. Festus, under *convallis*.]

596. Between *valles* and *convalles*. *Valles* are depressed places in plains [alternative: “hollows”]; *convalles* are the intervals between mountains.

[Note: [Col. 0069B]

597. *Etymologies* XIII.20.

—From *lapsus*. Festus, under *latex*.]

597. Between *unda* and *aqua*. An *unda* is always in motion; *aqua* is stationary. Moreover, rain belongs to clouds, and *latices* to springs. For *latex* properly means the liquid of a spring and is so called because it lies hidden in the veins of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0069B]

598. Isidore, *Etymologies* XV.2, under *vicus* and *plateae*.]

598. Between *vicus*, *via*, and *platea*. *Vici* are the dwellings themselves within cities; *viae* are the narrow spaces between the *vici*, whose continuous and broader forms we call *plateae*. For *platea* derives its name, according to the property of the Greek language, from breadth.

599. Between *viridia* and *virentia*. *Viridia* are trees or pieces of wood; *virentia* are fields or meadows [alternative: “of a meadow”].

600. Between *visus* and *visos*. *Visos* are participles; *visus* is a common noun.

601. Between *virum* and *virus*. *Virum* means “a man”; *virus* means “poison.”

602. Between *vivit* and *bibit*. *Vivit* refers to life; *bibit* to drinking.

603. Between *vinctus* and *victus*. *Vinctus* means bound; *victus* means defeated.

604. Between *vis* and *bis*. *Vis* refers to the will; *bis* means twice.

[Col. 0070A] 605. Between *ullam* and *ollam*. *Ullam* means “any”; *ollam* means “a pot.”

606. Between *vallum* and *murus*. The distinction is not that a wall is also a rampart; rather, whatever is a rampart is a wall.

[Note: [Col. 0069B]

607. *Ragit* is probably a gloss. See the poem attributed to Ovid concerning the various sounds of animals.

—For the sounds of birds, see Appendix 17 to the *Etymologies*, from Palatine Manuscript 281. AREV.]

607. Between *vagire*, *mugire*, and the other animal sounds. An infant *vagit*, “wails”; an ox *mugit*, “bellows”; a horse *hinnit*, “neighs”; an ass *ragit* or *rudit*, “brays”; a lion *rugit*, “roars”; an elephant *barrit*, “trumpets”; a pig *grunnit*, “grunts”; a sheep *balat*, “bleats”; a serpent *sibilat*, “hisses”; a frog *coaxat*, “croaks”; a raven *crocitat*, “croaks”; a crane *arsat* [a materially uncertain verb, apparently meaning “cries”]; a kite *jugit* [uncertain, apparently “calls”]; a dog *baubat* or *latrat*, “barks”; a fox *gannit*, “yelps.”

608. Between *vesperescit* and *vesperascit*. *Vesperescit* means “it becomes late”; *vesperascit* means “the sun declines toward the setting.”

609. Between *viperinus* and *vipereus*. *Viperinus* refers to a young viper; *vipereus* means “resembling a serpent.”

## On the Letter Z

[Note: [Col. 0070B]

610. The author of the Greek verse is uncertain.

—“But envy.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III.

—The following is from Accius’s *Menalippus*, but the verse is truncated. In Cicero it reads:

“Who, then, begrudged me my unenslaved flower?” [Col. 0070C] In Nonius, under *invidia*:

“Whence, or what mortal, begrudged me my unenslaved flower?”

In trochaic meter.]

610. Between *zelus* and *invidia*. *Zelus* can sometimes be taken in a good sense, when someone strives to emulate what is better; *invidia*, as has been said, is tormented by another’s happiness and is divided into a twofold passion: either a person does not wish another to be what he himself is, or, seeing another to be better, grieves that he is not similar. Someone, beautifully translating a Greek verse into elegiac meter, made sport of envy by saying:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which immediately  
> gnaws its very author and tortures the mind.

The name *invidia* is derived from looking too intently upon another’s happiness [Cicero: “fortune”], as in the line: “Who, then, begrudged me my flower?”

# BOOK TWO: ON THE DIFFERENCES OF THINGS

[Col. 0069]

## FIRST DIFFERENCE

[Col. 0069C]

77 [Note: [Col. 0069D]

1. “The Son in the Lord.” Augustine indicates where they may have found the occasion for this, *On the Trinity* II.10.

—The following distinctions are sometimes called distinctions of things and sometimes spiritual distinctions, as was explained more fully in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 56. Roland Wicelius appended notes to Grialius’s edition; I shall therefore cite them under Wicelius’s name. I reserve the various readings for the end of the volume. AREV.]

1. Between *Deus* and *Dominus*, some have defined the distinction in such a way that by the title *Deus* they understood the Father and by *Dominus* the Son. Sacred Scripture, however, affirms both of them to be God and Lord.

[Col. 0069D] 2. Nevertheless, these terms are distinguished from one another. The first is a name of nature, pertaining to love; the second is a name of authority, corresponding to fear. Finally, from the name *God*, observe what you should love; from the title *Lord*, recognize what you should fear.

## II

[Note: [Col. 0069D]

3. “Three names indeed.” There is no danger here from Sabellius. He had already said that there is distinction among the persons, and the final words of this chapter are: “It is impious not to distinguish the Trinity among the persons.” In the following chapter, why would he labor so much over the distinction of persons if he agreed with Sabellius? Nothing would have been necessary. These remarks are nevertheless much more extensive than the matter, which is not at all doubtful, requires. They show, however, that the words of Saint Eucherius—unjustly removed by men who were not themselves bad—were sometimes used by the ancient Fathers. They should not have been removed but explained; or one might cite Augustine, who says in Sermon 192: “For we confess not merely the names but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons”; and *City of God* XI.10: “Nor is this merely a Trinity of names, without the subsistence of persons, as the heretics called Sabellians supposed”; or Gregory the Theologian, who, lest he fall into this error, said that it is not the names of the persons but the persons of the names that truly subsist: “We do not,” he says, “receive the word without the thing, as merely a sound of the voice; rather, we believe in three names and three persons of one essence, one majesty, and one power.”

—In the same place: “Three names indeed.” It should be observed that *names* are often used for *persons*. See note a to the *Hymnodia Hispanica*, April 4, p. 274. AREV.]

3. Between *Trinitas* and *unitas* there is this distinction: *unitas* is named on account of the inseparable substance of the Godhead, whereas *trinitas* is named on account of the diversity of the persons. There is distinction among the persons, but no distinction in the Godhead. There is one who begets, one who is begotten, and one who proceeds. Three names indeed, but one substance. For just as fire, brightness, and color are three names but one thing, so it is here.

[Note: [Col. 0071D]

4. Grialius has *apud patres, ex quibus*; other Fathers have *apud alios patres, et ex quibus*, as in the Vulgate. AREV.]

4. In the relation of the persons there is Trinity; in the substance of the nature there is one God: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. That the Father is God is testified by the Apostle when he says, “One God, the Father, from whom are all things”; likewise, that the Son is God, he says elsewhere: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.”

[Note: [Col. 0071D]

5. The Vulgate reads: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; there are divisions of operations, but the same God.” AREV.]

5. Concerning the Holy Spirit, that he is God, the same Apostle who spoke above says likewise: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God.” Behold: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are God; yet one must not believe that this Trinity constitutes a threefold number of gods.

6. For it is written: “I am God, and there is no other God besides me.” And again: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one.” Therefore it is profane to believe in three gods; it is impious not to distinguish the Trinity among the persons.

## III

[Note: [Col. 0071D]

7. Theodulf of Orléans uses these words of Isidore to prove the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, reading them somewhat differently, as I have said in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 33. AREV.]

7. The persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are distinguished in this way: the Father was neither made nor born; the Son was born, not made; the Holy Spirit was neither made nor born, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Father has eternity without birth; the Son has birth together with eternity; the Holy Spirit has procession without birth, together with eternity.

8. The Father derives his beginning from no one; the Son receives his origin from the Father; the Holy Spirit truly proceeds from the Father and the Son. Yet we speak of the Trinity in this way only insofar as human nature can grasp it. For who could be sufficient to contemplate the inner mysteries of the Trinity itself? How are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit three persons but one nature?

9. How is the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither unbegotten nor begotten? How was the Son born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son? How does the Son proceed by being born, while the Holy Spirit, by proceeding, is not born? How was the Father never without the Son, and yet did the Father beget the Son without the Son?

10. How is the Son never without the Holy Spirit, and yet says: “Unless I depart, the Paraclete will not come to you”? How is the Son not from himself but from the Father [Col. 0071D], and yet is not later than the one from whom he is? How does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, and yet is not preceded by those from whom he proceeds?

11. How are the three one, and the one three? How are they three in relation to one another, yet essentially one? Who could contemplate such things? Who could comprehend them? For if we do not grasp the secrets of Christ’s human birth, how shall we grasp the mysteries of the divine nature?

IV.

12. Concerning the distinction between God’s substance and essence, certain people have defined it as follows: substance is that which is not from another but always exists from itself—that is, subsists within itself by its own proper power; essence, however, is so called in God because it always is: it neither begins at some point nor comes to an end, but its proper characteristic is always to be.

V.

[Note: [Col. 0071D]

13. The sense in which the Son is to be understood as being lesser than the Father is not agreed upon by the ancient Fathers. Some taught that the Father was called greater than the Son because the Son was begotten by the Father. But the more common interpretation, especially among the bishops of the West, was that the Father is called greater than the Son because, having assumed humanity, the Son was made lower not only than God but also than the angels. Isidore maintains this interpretation, which is certainly preferable, along with many others whom Petavius reviews in *On the Trinity*, book II, chapter 2. AREV.]

13. Between the Son’s being now equal to, and now lesser than, the Father, there is this distinction: the first concerns eternal substance, the other human nature. For in the form of a servant, because he was made from a woman, the Father is greater than he; but in the form of God, in which he existed before the assumption of flesh, he is coequal with the Father. With reference to the former it was said, “The Father is greater than I”; with reference to the latter, “I and the Father are one.” Thus he is equal to the Father insofar as he is God, but subject insofar as he is human.

VI.

14. What is the difference between Christ being proclaimed now “only-begotten” (*unigenitus*) and now “firstborn” (*primogenitus*)? The first designation pertains to the Father, the second to us. For, according to the excellence of his divinity, he is the Only-begotten from the Father, in accordance with the Gospel, which says: “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

15.
