But according to brotherly fellowship, he is the firstborn of all creation, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “so that he might himself be the firstborn among many brothers.” He is therefore the Only-begotten in the substance of the Godhead, and the firstborn in the assumption of humanity: firstborn in grace, Only-begotten in nature; firstborn, according to the Apostle, among many brothers; Only-begotten solely from God. Hence he is called both Brother and Lord: Brother because he is firstborn, but Lord because he is Only-begotten.

VII. On the distinction of the various names attributed to the Son of God

[Note: [Col. 0072D]

16. “Now, indeed.” Most of this is from Augustine, *On the Trinity*, sermon 2.]

16. Now the differences or significations of the names distinguished in the Son of God are very numerous. Some of these, however, are natural and pertain to the excellence of his divinity, while others are accidental. [Col. 0072D] The natural names are: God, Almighty, Perfect, Son of God, Word, Beginning, Power, Wisdom, Image, Splendor or Form, and Arm.

[Note: [Col. 0072D]

17. The Son of God is also that which the Father is, though he is not himself the Father. This indicates that the Son and the Father have the same nature, but not the same person. See my notes on Sedulius, book I, verse 319. Isidore also discusses such names attributed to the Son of God in book VII, chapter 2, of the *Etymologies*. AREV.]

17. The accidental names are these: Lamb, Priest, Rock, Stone, Man, Lion, Calf, Eagle, and the like. He is called God because he was begotten from God; Almighty from the Almighty; Perfect from the Perfect. He is the Son of God because, while he is himself that which the Father is, he is nevertheless not himself the Father.

18. The Son of God is the Word because he proceeded, properly speaking, from the divine mouth; or because nothing visible or corporeal exists in the substance of his nature; or because the Father created or commanded all things through him; or because he was made known through him. He is the Beginning because the Father is the origin and cause of all things. He is the Right Hand because of the effect of the whole creation, which was formed through him.

19. He is the Arm because all things are held together by him. He is Power because he possesses in himself all the authority of the Father and governs, sustains, and rules every creature of heaven and earth [Col. 0073B]. He is Wisdom because he himself reveals all the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. He is Image because of the truth of the likeness.

20. For the appearance of the Father is undifferentiated, possessing within itself an indistinguishable nature or essence. He is called Splendor because, since the Father himself is light, the Son proceeds from him inseparably, like splendor from light. He is Form because, in receiving the form of a servant, he represented in himself the image and immense greatness of the Father through the likeness of his works and powers.

21. He is Mediator because he stands between man and God, possessing in himself the substance of both natures—that is, the form of human humility and the excellence of divinity. Moreover, he is called Lamb because of the innocence and suffering of the flesh. He is Priest because he offered himself to the Father as a sacrifice for us. He is Rock because he is the firmness of believers, but the offense and ruin of unbelievers. He is the Cornerstone because he joined and united the Old and New Testaments, like two walls meeting from opposite directions, as at a corner, in the unity of faith.

22. He is Man because, according to the flesh, he was born from a Virgin, subject to suffering and mortal. He is Lion because of the kingship and power by which he conquered the Devil in death. He is Calf because he was sacrificed for the salvation of the nations. He is Eagle because, rising again, he returned to the stars of heaven and once more returned to the paternal seat from which he had come.

VIII.

23. The difference between Christ’s birth and ours is that every human being is found to have been conceived under the law of sin, whereas he was born not from the desire of the flesh or from sexual intercourse, but from the Holy Spirit. He assumed the nature of origin, not the guilt of transgression. He took a body from the Virgin but did not take away the virginity of his mother’s flesh. Likewise, we subsist from one generation, whereas he subsists from two: divinity and humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0073D]

24. In fact, he is from three. At the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, under the presidency of Saint Julian, the assertion that there are three substances in Christ was aptly defended: “We have said that there are three substances in Christ, and we have shown that our predecessors also taught this, honoring and following the judgment of that distinguished teacher, the bishop of the see of Hispalis, which he discussed in his books on the difference between Christ’s nature and ours, where he says, etc.” The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt in 794 were less approving of this manner of speaking, as is clear from the booklet of the bishops of Italy against Elipandus, sent by conciliar decree to the bishops of Spain, in Labbe, volume VII, column 1028: “There are also many who assert that from three substances there is one person of the Mediator—of Word, flesh, and soul—although in a matter of faith it does not seem necessary to scatter, with the hand of syllogistic argument, the calculations of secular literature through sophistical disputation.” Yet Saint Julian of Toledo had defended his position vigorously long before and had even commended it to the Roman Pontiff, although some asserted that “three substances in Christ” could be admitted in no sense. See Flórez, *Hispania sacra*, volume V, page 297, and volume II of the *Fathers of Toledo*. AREV.]

24. From the first birth he took his birth; from the second, his creation. He was born through divine generation, but made through human generation. The first was without time; the second occurred in the fullness of time. We subsist from two substances, namely body and soul; but he from three: Word, body, and soul. Hence he is proclaimed perfect God and man, possessing within himself the twofold substance both of his divinity and of our humanity.

IX.

[Col. 0074B] 25. There is likewise this difference between Christ’s death and ours: we incur death because of the merit of transgression, whereas he willingly accepted death for our salvation, according to his own testimony: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down.”

X.

26. The resurrection of Christ differs from ours in this respect: the time of our resurrection is postponed until the end of the age, whereas his took place on the third day; he had no need of anyone in order to rise again, while we rise through his mercy.

XI.

[Note: [Col. 0074D]

27. “Originally, according to the substance of matter.” Taken from Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 9.

Ibid. “All things were created together.” How this is to be understood is explained by Loaisa in his notes on book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 11. AREV.]

27. The difference between the creation of the world and its formation is that, originally and according to the substance of matter, all things were created together, in accordance with the statement: “He who lives forever created all things together.”

28. But according to the distinction of species, they were formed through the alternation of six days. For the origin of the whole creation existed simultaneously, while its species and forms emerged through the increments of time.

29. First, the matter of heaven and earth was made confused and formless, which the Greeks call *chaos* (χάος). From it afterward, individually, the various species and their proper forms emerged. Scripture speaks of this matter: “You who made the world from formless matter.” It was formless because it was still confused and obscure, and had not yet been distinguished through visible species and diverse forms.

30. But matter was made from nothing, whereas the forms of the world were made from formless matter. Therefore, before any day and time, Almighty God created two things: namely, the angelic creation and formless matter. Although the latter was made from nothing, it nevertheless preceded the things made from it not in eternity but only in origin, as sound precedes song.

31. For he who lives forever created all things together. Thus God did not create everything from nothing: some things from something, others from nothing. From nothing he created the world, angels, and souls; from something, human beings and the remaining creatures of the world.

XII. On the twofold paradise

32. There is one earthly paradise, where the life of the first human beings existed bodily; the other is heavenly, where the souls of the blessed are transferred immediately upon leaving the body and, rejoicing in a happiness worthy of them, await the reception of their bodies. Concerning this paradise the Lord said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” Originally, however, the guilt of the first man’s sin expelled us from paradise and cast us into this exile and pilgrimage.

33. Hence we are bound by the guilt of his transgression. Accordingly, and deservedly, we pay the penalty owed for our ancestral transgression. For the first man was created in such a way that, through the progression of the ages, he would pass without an intervening death from the bodily life of earthly paradise to the life of heavenly paradise.

34. But because he was unwilling to be content with this good, he immediately lost it through the merit of his condition and encountered the twofold death of soul and body. He acquired ignorance of the truth and old age, and transmitted the transgression of his sin to the whole human race—not only to those who sin by their own choice, but also to those who are not yet able to become involved in actual sin.

[Note: [Col. 0075D]

35. “My mother bore me”—so in Gregory, book VII on Kings, chapter 53, and book XII, chapter 10.

Ibid. The Vulgate has: “In sins my mother conceived me.” AREV.]

35. Hence the grace of the washing is granted to infants. For although they do not have the sin of their own deed, they nevertheless bear inherently the guilt of ancestral transgression. Therefore the prophet David, lamenting and grieving over the human race in his own person, says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me.”

XIII. On the degrees of things

[Note: [Col. 0075D]

36. Samson, abbot of Córdoba, enumerates five differences among creatures from Augustine in his *Apologeticus*, book II, chapter 23; then he adds: “But the distinguished teacher Isidore also says in the book of the *Differences*: How many are the degrees or differences of things? Six. Which? Non-living, living, sentient, rational, immortal; the last is that which is above all, God.” “The first degree,” etc., with a slight difference in some words. [Col. 0076D] AREV.]

36. There are six degrees or differences among things: non-living, living, irrational, rational, mortal, and immortal; the last is God, who is blessed above all forever. The first degree consists of things that do not grow and lack life and movement, as is the case with stones.

37. The second degree consists of things that grow and have life and movement without sensation, as is the case with herbs and trees. If they did not possess at least insensible life and movement, they certainly could neither sprout nor grow. These things, which have life without sensation, are placed above stones and earth.

38. The third degree consists of things that not only grow and live but also perceive, although they do not understand, as is the case with cattle. The fourth degree consists of things that grow, live, perceive, and understand, yet are mortal, as animals are—such as human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0076D]

39. “Which perceive and understand, and are immortal.” Augustine says similarly in *City of God*, book VIII, chapter 6: “Or even that which does not need nourishment for its support but only contains, perceives, and understands, as is the case with angels.”]

39. The fifth consists of things that perceive, understand, and are immortal, as is the case with angels. The sixth is that which is immutable, infinite, and simple, from which all this nature receives inspiration, movement, governance, and direction: God.

[Note: [Col. 0076D]

40. “Of an airy body.” Augustine, *On Divination of Demons*, chapter 3: “The nature of demons is such that, through the perception of an airy body, they easily surpass the perception of an earthly body.”]

40. But all these things, just as they increase by degrees, so also surpass one another in the quality of their nature. For a tree is superior to a stone, an animal to a tree, a human being to an animal, an angel to a human being, and God is placed above the angels.

XIV.

41. The ancients wrote that there is this difference among angels, demons, and human beings: angels are a spiritual substance, created before every other creature; they were made mutable by nature but made immutable through the contemplation of God; impassible in spirit, rational in mind, eternal in time, perpetual in blessedness, secure in happiness, knowing the future in advance. When commanded, they govern the world; when sent, they assume bodies from an excellent air; they dwell in the heavenly regions.

42. Demons are impure spirits, subtle and wandering; passible in spirit, rational in mind, airy in body, eternal in time; enemies of humanity, eager to cause harm, swollen with pride, cunning in deceit, always devising new frauds. They disturb the senses, fabricate emotions, disrupt life, trouble sleep, inflict diseases, terrify minds, contort limbs, control lots, fabricate oracles through illusions, entice the desire for love, instill the heat of lust, and hide within consecrated images. When invoked, they appear; they measure out things resembling the truth; they change into various shapes and sometimes transform themselves into the appearance of angels. Once they fell from the heavenly seat because of pride, and now dwell in the air.

[Note: [Col. 0076D]

43. “Again, some to glory.” These words are not found in the manuscript books.]

43. Human beings are capable of reason, wise in understanding, eloquent in speech, endowed with greater natural ability than instruction, upright in posture, erect in countenance, alike in general form yet individually unlike one another; immortal in spirit, weak in sensation, fragile in body, fickle in mind, diverse in character, unequal in errors, sluggish toward study, inclined toward pleasures, exhausted by labor, perishable amid riches, anxious in worry, mortal individually, changeable through offspring, querulous in life, swift in time, slow to wisdom, quick to death; bereft of the past, possessing little of the present, uncertain about the future. They are conceived in iniquity, born in sin, live in labor, and die in sorrow; then, some to glory and others to punishment, rising from the ashes, they pay what is owed.

XV. Between angelic and human transgression

44. What is the distinction between the transgression of angels and that of human nature, and why is the latter redeemed while the former is condemned without end? Transgressing angels have no forgiveness because they are burdened by no weakness of carnal frailty. Human beings, however, can return to forgiveness after sin because they have drawn the weight of weakness from their earthy material.

[Note: [Col. 0077D]

45. The same judgment occurs in Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapters 9 and 21.

Ibid. The Vulgate has: “For he himself knows our formation. He remembered that we are dust.” AREV.]

45. The Psalmist proves that, because of the condition of the flesh, the way back to salvation lies open to them; for he says: “He himself knows our formation. Remember, Lord, that we are earth.” And again: “Remember what my substance is.” But the devil, or the evil spirits, can neither obtain forgiveness nor deserve it, as it is written concerning that same apostate, whose heart will be hardened like a stone—namely, so that it will not be softened by the compunction of repentance.

XVI.

[Note: [Col. 0077D]

46. “Add also another … we can confess.” These words are found in only one book.]

46. The distinction between a human being and an animal is this: a human being is a living creature composed of body and soul and formed through spiritual joining, subsisting through reason and the will of free choice, capable of vices and virtues. An animal, by contrast, is an irrational, mortal creature animated by the movement of flesh and blood; hence its soul, after death, is dissolved together with the flesh. (Add also another distinction by which we differ from them. They are prone and turned toward the earth; our countenance is naturally raised toward heaven. They have leisure and abundance; we have been granted reason and speech, through which we can understand and confess God.)

XVII. Between the members of the human body

[Note: [Col. 0077D]

47. These matters are treated more fully in the *Etymologies*, book XI, chapter 1, where the places from which they were taken are indicated; Augustine’s passage on the ventricles of the brain is in book VII of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 18.

Ibid. Some have *plerique* rather than *et plerique*. AREV.]

47. Lactantius, or rather most authors, defined the structure of the human body and the distinction of its individual members as follows: “Human being” (*homo*) is said from *humus*, earth. A human being subsists from different substances, mortal and immortal. His body consists of bones and flesh and is divided into the four elements.

48. For it contains within itself something of fire, air, water, and earth. The nature of earth is in the flesh; of moisture, in the blood; of air, in the breath; of fire, in vital heat. Indeed, the fourfold structure of the human body displays the form of the four elements. The head is related to heaven, and in it are the two eyes, like the two luminaries of the sun and moon.

49. The chest is joined to air because from it the breath of respiration is emitted, just as the spirit of winds arises from air. The belly is likened to the sea because of the gathering of all bodily fluids, like a congregation of waters. Finally, the feet are compared with earth because they are the lowest and driest—or driest—of the members, just as earth is. Now the mind is placed in the citadel of the head, as God is in heaven, so that from above it may observe and govern all things.

50. Human beings were made upright and erect for contemplation of heaven, not prone and inclined toward the earth like animals. The head was placed at the summit of the body, and it was given this name because the senses and nerves take their beginning there. The hair of the head serves either as an adornment of appearance or to ward off the harmful effects of cold or heat.

51. In the head, as Saint Augustine says, “three structures resembling ventricles of the brain have been established: one anterior, toward the face, from which all sensation proceeds; another posterior, toward the neck, from which all movement proceeds; a third between the two, in which memory is shown to operate, so that when movement follows sensation, a person does not fail to connect what must be done if he has forgotten what he did.”

[Note: [Col. 0078D]

52. The difference between *facies* and *vultus* is expressed in nearly the same words in *Differences of Words*, no. 589, where certain observations are recorded. AREV.]

52. *Facies*—the face—is so called because it makes a person known. The difference between *facies* and *vultus* is that the face is the natural and fixed appearance of the mouth, whereas the countenance is changeable according to the disposition of the mind, now joyful, now sad. Hence those who frequently change their expression are called *vultuosi*.

53. How much dignity does the arrangement of the beard contribute to the countenance? The beard is a sign of beauty and an indication of manhood; it also signifies youth and distinguishes the nature of the sexes. The eyes are enclosed in hollow openings in the face, and from this opening the forehead is named. These same eyes, resembling gems, are covered with translucent membranes. Through these membranes, shining as through glass or a mirror, the mind looks through at the things outside.

54. In the middle of these spheres are enclosed sparks of light, which we call pupils; through them the power of sight is contained. And so that the eyes might be better protected from injury, the supreme Maker concealed them beneath coverings. Hence they are said to be called *oculi*, as though “hidden” (*occultati*), that is, protected on every side. Eyelids were placed over them, called *palpebrae* from fluttering (*palpitando*), because, moving together, they refresh the gaze of the eyes, while the hairs standing in orderly rows protect them.

55. The eyebrows, too, are adorned with short hairs, providing the eyes with protection like small ramparts, lest anything fall upon them from above. The name *ears* (*aures*) is derived from drawing in (*hauriendis*) voices. Through a change of letter they were called *aures*, as though *audes*. Through them sound and voice descend, as if through a spiral, because struck air moves in a circular orbit.

56. The cheeks (*genae*) are named from knees (*genua*). For they say that a human being is conceived and formed in the womb in a contracted position, with the knees raised, and that the eyes are formed by them so as to be hollow and recessed. Therefore those who wish to draw someone’s tears touch the knees and plead through them, because the knees formed the eyes in the womb and nourished them. The swelling of the cheeks, gently rising like hills, makes the eyes safe on every side from blows directed against them.

[Note: [Col. 0079D]

57. Perhaps one should read: “to discharge the brain’s waste.” AREV.]

57. The nostrils (*nares*) are so called because through them air, or breath, never ceases to pass. They have three functions: drawing in breath, receiving odors, and allowing the brain’s waste to flow downward. The mouth (*os*) is so called as though it were the entrance of the body. Its function consists in two activities: taking food and speaking with the tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0079D]

58. “From binding.” So also in the *Etymologies*. Others explain it differently. [Col. 0080D] AREV.]

58. The lips (*labia*) are named from licking (*lambendo*). The upper one is called the lip (*labium*), the lower one the lower lip (*labrum*). The tongue’s name derives from binding food. As the interpreter of the soul, it divides the voice into words through its movements—either by striking the palate and teeth or by compressing the lips.

59. The teeth are so called as though they were “dividing food.” They cut and break up nourishment and deliver it more suitably to the throat and stomach. The front teeth, which cut the food, are called opposing teeth; the innermost, which knead food, are molars; the canine teeth appear in the twentieth year of life.

60. The gums (*gingivae*) are named from producing teeth, and they confer great beauty on the mouth by covering the nakedness of the teeth. The throat consists of narrow tubes, like openings (*foces*), through which the vocal breath, leaping forth from the innermost chest, emits the sound of the voice.

61. The jaws (*mandibulae*) are parts of the cheeks with which we chew. The cheek (*maxilla*) is named by diminution, just as *paxillus* is derived from *palus*. The neck is named after a column, for it is rigid and rounded. It contains two tubes: one for food, the other for air. The upper of these is called the *rumen*, through which food and drink are swallowed; hence animals that bring food back up and chew it again are called ruminants. The lower is called the *gurgulio*, composed of bones joined together, connected, and flexible; it extends from the nostrils to the lung for the passage of breath. Its covering is called the *sublinguium*, “little tongue,” which closes and opens its opening, lest air, rushing violently through the joined sections of the tube, damage the internal organs.

62. The hands are so called because they are a service (*munus*) to the whole body and because we eat with them. The palm of the hand is spread out with extended fingers, just as a tree is spread out with extended branches. With the fingers contracted, it is a fist.

63. The number of the fingers is also perfect, and their order most fitting. The first, the ruler and governor of all, is called the thumb (*pollex*) because it is strongest among the others, that is, because it prevails. The second is called the index and the greeting finger, because with it we generally point and greet. The third is the middle or indecent finger; the fourth is the medical finger, because physicians collect crushed eye-salve with it; the fifth is the little or ear finger, because we scratch the ear with it.

64. The human chest (*pectus*) is named from looking (*aspectus*). In speechless animals it is pressed down toward the earth and removed from view; in human beings it is exposed and raised for viewing. For that which is full of reason ought not to be hidden and low.

65. The nipples are the tips of the breasts. The breasts are swellings of the chest that rise gently. They were given to women for nursing offspring, and to men merely as an adornment, so that the chest would not appear deformed. For in women they ought not to be elsewhere than where an intelligent animal receives nourishment from the heart.

66. The navel is an impressed mark that indicates the middle of the belly. It was made so that through it the fetus might be nourished while in the womb. The viscera of the spleen and liver seem to have been formed as though from disturbed blood. According to those who discuss natural philosophy, sexual desire is said to reside in the liver, the emotion of anger in the gall, fear in the heart, and joy in the spleen. Air is contained in the lungs; it is diffused from the heart through veins called arteries, so that by the gradual process of inhaling and exhaling it gives life to the whole body.

67. Fire has its seat in the liver, and from there it appears to rise upward to the elevated place of the brain, as though to the heaven of our body. Hence rays flash forth from the eyes, and from its middle, as from a certain center, delicate tubes lead not only to the eyes but also to the other senses. Indeed, they hold that the liver’s function consists in pleasure and in the process by which food is digested and, through its heating, changed into blood.

68. The structure of the intestines is arranged in long windings, in the manner of circles, so that they may gradually expel the food received and slowly draw from it the moisture contained within. The belly (*alvus*) is so called because all moisture mixed with food flows and returns into it as into a trough (*alveus*), and in an indescribable manner the juice of food fills the whole body, as water irrigates neighboring valleys from the side.

69. The belly (*venter*), abdominal cavity (*alvus*), and womb (*uterus*) differ. The *venter* is what appears externally and extends from the chest to the groin. The *alvus* is the inner part in which food is usually received and cleansed. Only women have a *uterus*, in which they conceive. Authors nevertheless confuse these terms and use *uterus* for the belly of either sex.

70. The genital organs, as the name itself indicates, are named from generation. The flesh of the buttocks is gathered into a mass for the purpose of sitting, so that under the pressure of the body’s weight it would not yield to the bones. The thighs (*femina*) are the parts of the legs with which, when riding, we cling to the backs of horses. Hence horsemen are said to have brought horses into battle between their thighs.

71. The knees (*genua*) are named from the cheeks (*genae*), because in the womb they are joined together and related to the eyes. Hence Ennius says: “The cheek presses the knees tightly.” The shins (*tibiae*) are called as though they were trumpets (*tubae*). The soles (*plantae*) are named from flatness, because they are not rounded, as in four-footed animals, lest a human being be unable to stand, but are formed flat and elongated so as to make the body stable. The heels (*calces*) are named from the callus of the feet.

72. The toes provide both beauty and usefulness. For we could not run unless, pressing our toes into the earth and relying on the ground, we obtained momentum for a leap and a bound. The remaining bones of the body are inserted like columns, supporting the flesh, and are bound together by the ligaments of the nerves so that they may bend with highly suitable movement. Lactantius and the others have written these things concerning the structure of the body.

XVIII.

[Note: [Col. 0080D]

73. This distinction is found in only one manuscript.]

73. Some have distinguished between a man (*vir*) and a human being (*homo*) as follows: a man, possessing both kinds of knowledge, retains eloquence together with wisdom; a human being surpasses beasts only in natural loquacity. They said that *vir* derives from ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς, that is, “from virtue.” Among the ancients, *virtue* was called knowledge of all things. We, however, use *man* and *human being* for one and the same person. The same applies to Christ, who is called both *man* and *human being* in the holy Scriptures.

XIX.

74. The wise have defined infancy, childhood, and the remaining ages as follows. The first age of a human being is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth old age, and the sixth extreme old age. The first two ages end at periods of seven years each, because of the simplicity of life. Infancy ends in the seventh year, childhood in the fourteenth; thereafter adolescence consists of two periods of seven years because of understanding [Col. 0081C] and action. These two faculties are not yet present in children, and this age extends from the fifteenth year to twenty-eight.

75. After this, the succeeding period of youth lasts for three periods of seven years, because of those three things: understanding, action, and bodily strength. This age begins in the twenty-eighth year and ends in the forty-ninth, when childbirth also ceases in women.

76. Old age is completed in four periods of seven years because of the increasing heaviness of mind and body added to those three faculties. This age begins in the fiftieth year and ends in the seventy-seventh. The final stage, extreme old age, is not defined by any fixed span of years but is brought to its conclusion only by nature’s end.

XX.

[Col. 0081D] 77. The difference between old age and extreme old age is that old age is the declining period that moves from youth toward extreme old age, though it is not yet decrepit; extreme old age, however, is the exhausted and final age, panting after the last breath of life.

XXI

[Col. 0082A]

[Note: [Col. 0081D]

78. “From purity.” Nonius: “Childhood, that is, purity.” Varro, *On Divine Matters*, book I: “What childhood is, uncommonly polluted.”

Ibid. “Because the down has not yet appeared.” Festus: “A boy is called only one who has not yet reached puberty.”]

78. Some of the wise distinguished between an infant and a child. They say that an infant is one who cannot yet speak. A child (*puer*), however, is named from purity, as though “pure,” or because the down and bloom of the cheeks has not yet appeared.

[Note: [Col. 0081D]

79. “As though a young creature.” Nonius says: “A young creature is one of tender age.”

Ibid. “By childhood.” Thus the Hispanic Codex. Varro, *On the Education of Children*: “I would, by Hercules, like to hear the formula of childhood through long usage.” Another reading: “at a childish age.”

Ibid. Wicelius’s notes in Grial’s edition are disordered and placed out of their proper sequence. It was easy to restore to their proper place the notes “From purity” and “because the down has not yet appeared.” The notes “by childhood,” thus the Codex, and “at a childish age,” in the other copies, seem to have been placed in substitution for the words “for a childish age.” AREV.]

79. A girl (*puella*) is named from smallness, as though “a young creature.” Hence we call boys and girls “pupils” not according to their condition but according to their childish age. In former times *puer* was used of both male and female, just as *infans* was. Hence common usage calls a woman in childbirth *puerpera*. Properly, however, *puerperae* are those who have first borne children, because girls give birth at a very young age.

80. After leaving childhood, males are called pubescent (*puberes*), because they now acquire the capacity to generate; females are called virgins or *viragines*. *Virago* is so called either because it is derived from *vir*, man, or because it denotes masculine strength. Once they have likewise passed beyond puberty, they are called adolescents. Adolescents are named from growing and increasing. Hence someone speaking about agriculture called ripening fruit “adolescent.”

[Note: [Col. 0082D]

81. In Grial’s edition there was an obvious error, *juventus* for *juvencus*; in the others these words are absent, as is also the phrase “as in oxen,” etc. AREV.]

81. After adolescence they also become young adults. They are called *juvenes* because they begin to be able to help (*juvare*), just as an ox is called a *juvencus* when it leaves the status of a calf.

[Note: [Col. 0082D]

82. “As though softer.” Other copies have, not improperly, “as though softer” (*quasi mollior*). AREV.]

82. Now, properly speaking, a man and a woman belong to middle age. A man (*vir*), therefore, is named, as Lactantius says, because there is greater strength in him than in women, and hence *virtus*, strength or virtue, takes its name. Likewise, a woman (*mulier*) is named from softness, with a letter changed and removed, as though *mollier*, “softer.”

83. But strength was given in greater measure to men so that women might more easily be compelled to endure conjugal relations. A woman is called *mulier* not because of the corruption of her integrity but solely because of the maturity of her age; likewise, a man is called *vir* solely because of his manhood, even if he is kept free from sexual relations with a woman.

84. Those of the final stage of life are called old men and old women. Some think that *senes* (“old men”) derives from *se nesciunt* (“they do not know themselves”), because through excessive age they become delirious and senseless. Hence Plato also says: “In children understanding grows, in young men it is vigorous, and in old men it diminishes.” *Anus* (“old woman”), however, is derived from *multi anni* (“many years”), as though *annosa* (“aged”).

XXII.

[Note: [Col. 0082D]

85. “Rationale is.” These words are from Augustine, *On Order* II, chapter 11.]

85. A certain wise man said that there is this difference between *rationabile* (“reasonable”) and *rationale* (“rational”): “Rational” is that which makes use of rational understanding, as a human being does; “reasonable,” however, is that which is said or done by reason. [Col. 0082D]

XXIII.

86. There is this difference between the mind and reason: the mind is the superior part of the soul, from which understanding proceeds. [Col. 0083A] Reason, however, is a certain movement of the soul that sharpens the mind’s vision and distinguishes the true from the false.

XXIV.

87. There is the following distinction between memory, mind, and thought: memory retains the past, the mind foresees the future, and thought embraces the present.

XXV.

88. There is this difference between sense and memory: sense is the discovery of each particular thing; memory is recollection of the thing discovered. The former devises and finds, while the latter preserves what has been found.

XXVI.

95 [Note: [Col. 0082D]

89. “To be intelligible … are perceived”: these are Augustine’s words, *City of God* VIII, chapter 6.]

89. The ancients distinguished intelligible and sensible things in this way: intelligible things are those perceived by the mind and soul; sensible things, however, are those perceived by bodily sight and touch.

[Col. 0083B] 90. There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. To sight belong form, color, and the size or measure of a thing. To hearing belong voices and sound; to smell, the fragrance of odors and whatever else is perceived in that way; to taste, a bitter or sweet flavor; to touch, hot or cold, rough or soft, or smooth things.

91. These five senses arise from the parts of the elements, but not from all four elements; rather, they are generated from air and earth. Sight, smell, and hearing arise from air; touch and taste arise from earth.

XXVII.

92. The soul and body are distinguished in this way: the soul is an incorporeal, intellectual, rational, invisible, mobile, and immortal substance, whose origin is unknown, yet with nothing mixed or concretely formed in its nature, nothing earthy, nothing moist, nothing airy, and nothing fiery. In contrast, the body is a visible, mobile, and mortal substance, having its seed from corruption and its material from earthly dregs. But because the soul is a spiritual creature, it knows a beginning but does not know an end. Souls are like angels: they have a beginning but no end. The body, however, because it consists of the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—when it has been dissolved by the departing soul, returns again to the place from which it arose. Hence we are partly mortal and partly immortal. For we share the nature of the soul with angels, but the flesh with animals.

XXVIII.

93. A certain wise man distinguished flesh and body by saying: “Flesh is that which is specifically distinguished by blood, nerves, and bones; body, although it too is called flesh, is sometimes also called ‘airy’ (*aereum*), because it is not subject to touch or sight, and is for the most part visible and tangible. A wall is a body, but not flesh; a stone is a body, but not flesh. Thus the Apostle also calls them ‘heavenly bodies’ and ‘earthly bodies.’ The heavenly body consists of the sun, moon, and stars; the earthly of fire, air, water, earth, and the other things reckoned among those elements without a soul.” [Col. 0083D]

XXIX.

[Col. 0084A]

[Note: [Col. 0083D]

94. Compare *Etymologies* XI, chapter 1, no. 13. AREV.]

94. Lactantius thinks that certain philosophers distinguish mind (*animus*) and soul (*anima*) as follows: “Some,” he says, “claim that the soul by which we live is one thing, and the mind by which we sense and understand another, because, while the soul is vigorous in the body, the mind sometimes perishes, as commonly happens to the demented.

95. “They also add that the soul falls asleep in death, while the mind does so in sleep. For this reason they think that the two are divided, since they are separated in the function of activity. Those, however, who understand both terms without distinction argue more truthfully: we can neither live without sensation nor sense without life.

96. “Therefore that which is in no way separated from itself cannot possibly be divided. Rather, the same one thing both possesses the vigor of living and enjoys the faculty of sensation; [Col. 0084B] and although both are one, they have taken different names in accordance with the diversity of their operations. For just as the spirit is a part of the soul through which images of bodily things are impressed, so the *animus* (“mind”) is a part of that same soul by which one senses and has understanding; and the *mens* (“intellect”) is likewise a portion of it through which all reason and understanding are perceived.

[Note: [Col. 0083D]

97. Much of what is said here about the soul is repeated in a certain book on Numbers, which I think has not yet been published; I shall present it among the appendices, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 63, nos. 10 ff. AREV.]

97. “So too there is the will, by which things understood are assented to; and memory, by which things meditated upon are recalled. Although these faculties are designated by many names, they are not divided in substance as they are in name, because the soul is one and the same. When it contemplates, it is spirit; when it senses, it is sense; when it has understanding, it is *animus* (“mind”); when it understands, it is *mens* (“intellect”); when it distinguishes, it is reason; when it assents, [97] it is will; when it remembers, it is memory; and when it gives vitality to the limbs, [Col. 0084C] it is soul. At one moment it understands, at another it is senseless; at one moment, with its cares briefly removed, it rests, soothed by the body’s sleep; then, stirred again and immediately awakened to contemplate the images of things, it returns to its activity.”

XXX.

98. Teachers have said that there is this difference between soul and spirit: the soul itself is the life of a human being, providing sensation and movement to the body; the spirit, however, is a certain force and rational power of that soul, through which, by the law of nature, a human being appears superior to the other animals. Thus the soul is the breath of life, making a human being an animal; but the spirit is the power that tramples down carnal desires and urges mortal humanity toward the immutability of life.

99. The Evangelist most certainly testifies that the spirit is the soul, because he called the soul that Christ assumed in the flesh “spirit.” For when the Lord had said, “I have power to lay down my soul,” he unquestionably laid it down at the moment when, with his head bowed on the cross, he gave up his spirit. Every soul can be a spirit, but not every spirit is a soul. God himself is spirit, yet he is not a soul; angels and winds are also spirits, yet they are not souls.

[Note: [Col. 0084D]

100. Isidore discusses these matters in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12; Loaisa’s notes on that passage should also be consulted, since they apply here as well. AREV.]

100. As for what the soul itself is, what kind it is, where it is, what form it possesses, or what power it has, the wise men of this world have in no way defined with certainty. Some have said that the soul is fire, others that it is blood, and others that it is incorporeal and has no shape at all. Some, with impious boldness, have even believed it to be a part of the divine nature. [Col. 0085A]

101. We, however, say that it is neither fire nor blood, but incorporeal, subject to suffering and change, and without weight, shape, or color. We do not say that the soul is a part of God, but that it is God’s creature; nor was it made from God’s substance or from any underlying material of the elements, but it was created from nothing.

102. For, as someone has said, if God had made it from himself, it would in no way be corruptible, changeable, or miserable. Likewise, if it had been made from the visible elements, it would necessarily possess either solidity from earth, moisture from water, breath from air, or heat from fire. But because it lacks all these things, it is evident that it does not come from them, since it is shown to share nothing with them. [Col. 0085B]

103. Hence some wrongly believe it to be corporeal, although it was made in the image of God so that, even if it were not immutable like God, it would nevertheless be incorporeal as God is. For if we believe the soul to be corporeal, then we also believe God to have the form of a body, since he created the soul in his own image.

104. Some of the ancients said that this soul has three parts: the rational, the irascible, and the concupiscible. The rational part is that by which it beholds invisible things; the irascible is that by which it corrects and disciplines the impulses of its anger; the concupiscible is that by which it restrains the desire of the flesh through spiritual power. [Col. 0085C] Some wished its dwelling to be in the breast, while others said that it lived in the citadel of the head, as though in heaven it were the ruler, so that from the heights it might contemplate all things. Others assigned it no definite location, but said that it is infused throughout all the limbs and courses through them.

105. There are differing opinions concerning its origin. Nevertheless, without presuming to affirm anything, let us report what the discussion of the Fathers has thought about the matter. Among them, the most holy Fulgentius expresses an uncertain judgment on this question, whose words should briefly be set down: “Whether,” he says, “all souls are believed to come from Adam, just as the flesh of those being born does, or whether they are newly made and are in no way propagated from their parents? This question is difficult to settle, because it is undermined by opposing objections.

[Col. 0085D] 106. “For when those who maintain that new souls are given to individual bodies are asked why the soul of an infant, which is not propagated like flesh, is held together with the flesh in the fellowship of original sin, what will they say? Is God unjust, so that he sends a soul into eternal fire together with flesh, although it shares no sin with the flesh? When this is brought against them, they are utterly at a loss. On the other hand, those who assert that souls are propagated along with the bodies themselves can indeed establish God’s just judgment in the case of infants, so that they share original sin, just as they claim that the propagation of both is shared. But when they consider seeds that perish without being conceived, they too fall completely silent.” [Col. 0086A]

99 107. “It is certain that the human soul received [an object omitted in the source] in the very act of its creation. It must therefore receive at the resurrection the body in which it lived here for however brief a time. Who, then, would say that seeds are endowed with souls—whether those that are never conceived or those that are emitted in nocturnal illusion? Every wise person sees how absurd this is and how entirely alien it is to reason. Thus, in these arguments concerning the origin of the soul, the opposing sides defeat one another, because each destroys the other’s position and is itself unable to establish what it proposes.”

[Note: [Col. 0085D]

108. Isidore likewise struggles with Augustine on this matter, in book II of *On Duties*, chapter 24. See the note, and also book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12, where he rightly asserts that the soul is created when the body is created, and appears to be joined to it. AREV.]

108. For this reason the question of its origin must be investigated with greater caution, especially since nothing more certain has been defined by holy men, nor is anything more explicit pronounced by the authority of the sacred Scriptures. Nevertheless, this must be maintained: the souls of infants are bound by the bond of original sin, and unless they receive the sacrament of baptism, they cannot share in the kingdom of heaven; but they will share sin with the flesh and will be condemned by the same judgment to eternal fire.

XXXI.

[Note: [Col. 0086D]

109. See Cassian, *On the Desire of the Flesh and of the Spirit*, chapter 11 and following.]

109. There is this difference between the desire of the flesh and that of the spirit: the desire of the flesh is a shameful movement of the soul toward the fulfillment of sordid pleasure; the desire of the spirit, however, is the mind’s ardent striving toward the desires of holy virtue. The latter sends those who consent to it to the kingdom; the former sends them to everlasting punishment. The former is the law of sin, descending from the condemnation of the first man; the latter is the law of the mind, proceeding from the gift of our Redeemer. These two, according to the disposition of virtues and vices, oppose one another in a daily and deadly struggle. [Col. 0086C]

110. The desire of the flesh first gives birth to the enticements of vices in the thoughts, while the desire of the spirit, in contrast, continually sets holy thoughts against them. The former delights in empty stories and words; the latter in meditation on the Scriptures and their precepts. The former rejoices in spectacles of earthly things; the latter in contemplation of heavenly joys. The former seeks earthly pleasures; the latter draws forth groans and sighs. The former relaxes the body through the sluggishness of sleep and laziness; the latter labors through vigils and appropriate prayers.

[Col. 0086D] 111. The former burns with the allurements of the belly and the desires of the throat through gluttony; the latter torments and disciplines itself with fasts and abstinence. Subject to lust, the former strives to fulfill, through the completion of pleasure, the desires for shameful acts that it pursues with the fixed intention of thought; the latter loves the beauty of chastity and modesty. Kindled by the flame of greed, the former seeks profit and flees losses of temporal possessions; the latter, scorning the world, claims Christ alone for itself. Through envy the former permits no one to be superior or equal to it, but wastes away with inwardly festering resentment at everyone’s progress; the latter rejoices in everyone’s virtues and, through charity, places those lesser than itself ahead of itself. [Col. 0087A]

112. Boiling with anger, the former bears nothing calmly but raises its troubled mind even to an uproar of the voice; the latter is moved by no provocation but patiently endures all things through tranquility and gentleness. The former is tainted by sadness whenever it senses any adversity; the latter is broken by no grief but, even while bearing the troubles of its neighbors, is not moved from its inward joy. The former is infected by ambition for honors and softened by human praise or the allurements of empty glory; the latter loves humility and delights in pleasing its God alone, who examines the mind. Inflated by the arrogance of pride, the former raises up its miserable heart; the latter humbles itself to the lowest depths lest its heart fall from its height.

[Col. 0087B] 113. But why say more? The desire of the flesh plunges those who consent to it into the multitude of all vices, while the desire of the spirit strengthens the fallen mind, so that it does not fail, through hope of future glory. Therefore, even if the former prevails, one must never despair, because, once the battle has been renewed, we can triumph over it even more gloriously. Although the latter may conquer, it is not secure in its victory, because the crafty enemy, even if defeated at times, eventually conquers the victors. Those whom it does not strike down in the first encounter, it strives to deceive at the end.

114. This is also why the desire of the flesh does not cease to fight until the end of this life. But if the desire of the spirit prevails to the end, secure in the peace of victory, it reigns eternally [Col. 0087C] 101 with its victors. Then, when the sting of desire has been brought to completion, neither will the spirit oppose the flesh nor the flesh the spirit. Rather, joined to one another in the harmony of eternal peace, both will cling forever to their Redeemer without opposition.

XXXII.

[Note: [Col. 0087D]

115. In his work *On Free Choice*, among the sayings of the Fathers, Honorius of Autun also makes use of this passage from Isidore for his own purpose. AREV.]

115. There is this difference between the infusion of divine grace and the will of human free choice: free choice is the will of a free power, which by itself and spontaneously can desire either good or evil; grace, however, is the free gift of divine mercy, through which we merit both the beginning of a good will and the accomplishment of a good work. No one can prevail in anything through the power of free choice unless he is supported by the assistance of heavenly grace. For divine grace precedes a person so that he may be good; human free choice does not precede God’s grace, but God’s grace itself precedes the willing person so that he may also will what is good.

[Note: [Col. 0087D]

116. “Free choice … which the first man had lost.” Augustine expresses the same point in *Enchiridion*, chapter 30: “For by using free choice badly, man both lost himself and lost free choice itself.” How these words are to be understood is sufficiently clear from Augustine himself and from Isidore, who adds shortly afterward: “Before the gift of grace, free choice indeed exists in man, but it is not good, because without the help of grace it remains weak.”]

116. For through the weight of the flesh a person is so driven that he is inclined to sin and sluggish to repent. He has within himself the means by which he may fall, but he has no means by which he may rise again, unless the grace of the Creator stretches out a hand to the one lying prostrate, so that he may be raised up. Finally, through God’s grace, free choice is restored to humanity, which the first man had lost. [Col. 0088A] For he possessed free choice to begin the good, although it was to be perfected with God’s help. We, however, receive from God’s grace both the beginning and the perfection of free choice. For we have from him both the beginning and the accomplishment of the good, since from him the gift of grace has been given and free choice has been restored in us.

117. The good that we do is therefore God’s, because of prevenient and subsequent grace. Yet it is ours because of the consenting will of free choice. For if it were not God’s, why would we give him thanks? And if it were not ours, why would we await recompense for good works? Therefore, insofar as we are preceded by grace, the matter belongs to God; insofar as by doing good we follow the grace that precedes us, it belongs to us. No one precedes God by merits, so as to be able to hold him as though he were a debtor. Yet in a wondrous manner the Creator, who is equitable toward all, chooses some beforehand through predestination, while in a just judgment he leaves others to their evil ways. Hence it is entirely true that the gift of grace is not obtained through human power or the merit of free choice, but is bestowed solely through the goodness of divine mercy.

118. Some are saved by the gift of his most gracious prevenient mercy, having become vessels of mercy; others, regarded as reprobate and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having become vessels of wrath. This example is drawn from Esau and Jacob before they were born. Although they had been brought forth from one conception or birth and were bound by an equal bond of original sin, the gratuitous goodness of divine prevenient mercy nevertheless drew one of them to itself, while the other, regarded with hatred through a certain severity of justice, was condemned and left in the mass of perdition. As the same God says through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

119. It follows, therefore, that grace is conferred not because of any preceding merits, but solely through divine calling. Nor is anyone saved or condemned, chosen or rejected, except according to the purpose of the predestining God, who is just toward the rejected and merciful toward the chosen. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

[Note: [Col. 0088D]

120. In other printed editions, after the words “mercy and truth,” the rest is omitted and the following words occur: “But every gift of grace,” etc., as in no. 122. AREV.]

120. Before the gift of grace, free choice indeed exists in man, but it is not good, because without the help of grace it remains weak. For just as an eye cannot see if it lacks the service of light, so the free choice of the human will is powerless if it lacks the light of grace—that light which illuminates every person coming into this world. Free choice is by itself ready for every evil, but it is in no way ready for good except through the gift of grace. The same grace enables a person both to will and to do good, to mourn past evils, and to avoid present sins both in thought and in deed. The Apostle also writes this more clearly, saying: “We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.” Therefore the benefit of grace is not extended to every kind of human being, but only to those who are illuminated through faith; for the hearing of faith has not reached all nations. [Col. 0089A]

121. Hence the Apostle also says: “How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard?” Even the gift of that same grace, when given to some, is not granted equally to all, but is distributed according to the measure corresponding to the merit of those who receive it, in accordance with what is written: “He will repay each person according to his works.”

122. Moreover, the whole gift of grace is not given in its entirety to everyone, but individual gifts are distributed to individuals, so that, like the separate members of a body, they may each have their own functions, and one may need from another what the other does not possess. Thus everything becomes common, since the members become mutually necessary to one another.

XXXIII.

123. There is this difference between the Law and the Gospel: in the Law there is the letter, in the Gospel grace; the former possessed a shadow, the latter an image; the former was given because of transgression, the latter because of justification; the former reveals the sin of ignorance, while the latter helps the sin that has been recognized to be avoided; the former rebukes those devoted to wicked acts, while the latter liberates sinners through its own goodness; the former decreed that retaliation should be rendered, while the latter commanded that one pray even for enemies; the former, granting free rein to marriage, commanded people to increase and beget children, while the latter commended continence.

124. There circumcision of the flesh alone is proclaimed; here, washing in the cleansing of heart and body. There the kingdom of Canaan and promises of temporal things are contained; here eternal life and the kingdom of heaven are promised. There the leisure and rest of the Sabbath are celebrated; here the very rest of the Sabbath is possessed in Christ, who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you, and you will find rest for your souls.” There the eating of unclean animals is prohibited; here, in the body of Christ—that is, in his saints—whatever was represented in human conduct by those unclean animals is not admitted.

[Note: [Col. 0089D]

125. Vulgate: “All things are new.” The sacrifice of the blood and body of Christ is expressed. AREV.]

125. There, after animals had been sacrificed, offerings of flesh and blood were presented; here the sacrifice of Christ’s flesh and blood is offered, which was represented by those animals. [104] There the Passover is celebrated from the flesh of a lamb; here “our Passover, Christ,” has been sacrificed, and he is the true [Col. 0089D] spotless Lamb. There the beginnings of the new moons, that is, of the new moon, are celebrated; here the new creation is received in Christ, as the Apostle Paul says: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new.”

126. Why say more? In the Law, deeds were announced through figures as signs of things to come; in grace, however, the things announced there are fulfilled in evangelical truth. Likewise, commands and promises were written in the Law: the commands instructed people to fulfill or observe the Law, while the promises, concealed under figures of the sacraments, proclaimed the future grace of the Gospel. Thus the commands are retained in the Law, while the promises are completed in the fullness of the Gospel. The Gospels complete the Law, and the fullness of the Testaments completes the meaning of the command. [Col. 0090A]

127. The Law accomplished nothing else except to show sins without removing them; it reduced all who were brought under its terror to the status of slaves, and the Apostle taught that the earlier people had thereby possessed the spirit of servitude. The Gospel, however, when it came, removed the cruelty of the Law. It loosened through the spirit of adoption the sins that the Law punished through the spirit of servitude; it made sons from slaves; it granted everyone the love by which the Law is fulfilled; and if thereafter they committed acts deserving punishment, it forgave them through that same spirit of adoption. It provided a pattern for right action, and infused the assisting Spirit so that people could do what it taught.

[Note: [Col. 0089D]

128. “For the legal commandments,” etc., from Gregory, *Morals* XXVIII, chapter 9.]

128. The legal commandments given to that people are even called “not good” in comparison with better things, because they do not bring about the fulfillment of what they command. The grace of the Gospel, however, helps inwardly to fulfill what it commands outwardly. This is also said in the testimony of Ezekiel: “I gave them commandments that were not good.” This is because certain things of no benefit were permitted to be done by those of weaker understanding, as in the case where God permitted the Israelites’ desire to be satisfied with the spoils of the Egyptians.

129. Because the carnal people exceeded the proper measure of vengeance, the Law permits the carnal to repay evil in kind, whereas the Gospel forbids this to those who are stronger. Therefore they are called “not good,” because, compared with the Gospel, the commandments of the Law are recognized as inferior. [Col. 0090C] Before the coming of our Redeemer, the Gentile people did not obey the Law because it had not yet been understood in a spiritual sense. The Law commanded grave and harsh things according to the letter, and for that reason it was despised. But the grace of the Gospel came, moderated the severity of the Law, and joined the Gentile people to itself.

XXXIV.

[Note: [Col. 0090D]

130. I consign to the appendices an opusculum on the difference between the active and contemplative life, found by me under Isidore’s name in Codex Regiovaticanus 281; I also discussed it in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 85. AREV.]

130. There is the following distinction between the active and contemplative life: the active life is occupied with works of justice and the benefit of one’s neighbor; the contemplative life, free from every business, is fixed upon the love of God alone. One consists in the work of a good way of life, the other in contemplation of unchanging truth; one lives by faith during this pilgrimage, the other brings those who live well all the way to the kingdom.

131. The rewards of the active life are indeed great, but those of the contemplative life are greater. The active life begins with good works; the contemplative reaches what it seeks. The works of the active life end with the body, whereas the joys of the contemplative life increase more fully at the end. The former, although useful and good, will pass away when rest comes; the latter is the reward of a good work that passes away, and the rest that will remain.

132. The contemplative life is represented by Rachel, who was beautiful and barren, because through the leisure of contemplation fewer children of works are born. Leah, who was without eyes but fertile, represented the active life. Action is indeed laborious and considers less lofty things; but because it gives itself more fully to the benefit of one’s neighbor, it is more fertile in works and grows, as it were, through children. So too with Martha and Mary: one exercised her mind in virtue through activity, while the other rested, fixed upon contemplation.

133. Those who strive to come to the leisure of contemplation must first exercise themselves in the arena of the active life, so that, while works of justice drain away the dregs of sins, they may present a pure heart for seeing God. For the mind that still seeks temporal glory or yields to the temptations of carnal desire is undoubtedly barred from contemplation. [Col. 0091B] Hence, when the people were receiving the Law from the mountain—that is, from sublime contemplation—the curiosity of the carnal was, as it were, removed. And in the Gospel, the man healed of the legion wishes to follow the Lord through contemplation; but he is ordered to return home and engage in the activity of the active life.

134. In the actual practice of contemplation and action, there is sometimes a great difference among minds. For contemplation alone benefits some, while for others only the active life is a consolation. For these people, the middle way, composed of both, is more useful for relieving the mind’s distress, which is often nourished by exclusive concentration, so that it may be better balanced from the resources of both. When the Savior shone forth by day in the cities through signs and miracles, he commended the active life to us. But when he spent the night on the mountain in devotion to prayer, he signified the life of contemplation.

135. Therefore God’s servant, following Christ’s example, neither abandons the active life nor fails to practice the contemplative life. To proceed otherwise is to stumble. For just as God must be loved through contemplation, so one’s neighbor must be loved through the active life. Consequently, we cannot be without both lives, just as we can in no way possess love without both.

XXXV.

[Note: [Col. 0091D]

136. “To be of no benefit”: words such as “they can” or “it is clear” must be supplied, as often happens in Isidore’s works, especially in the *Etymologies*. AREV.]

136. There is this difference between faith and works: through faith the possibility of a good work is begun; through works faith itself is perfected. A work is preceded by faith, and faith is brought to completion through works. Works before faith are of no benefit whatsoever, because it is useless for someone who either denies or does not know the author of salvation to turn away from evil and do what pertains to salvation. Likewise, faith without works is of no benefit, because one who despises God in action cannot please God through faith.

137. For this reason faith without works is also dead, according to James; and work apart from faith is empty, according to Paul. One of them praises devotion to faith, the other praises works. Paul proclaims that before faith there can in no way be a good work; James declares that faith is worth nothing without a good work. Accordingly, according to the former, works preceding faith are of no benefit; according to the latter, works that follow faith are of great benefit.

138. James says: “Abraham our father was justified by works.” Paul says: “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” What then? Do the two contradict one another? Certainly not. Rather, both instruct us. According to Paul, Abraham merited justification from faith when he believed God; according to James, he pleased God through works when, having been tested, he did not refuse to sacrifice his son.

XXXVI.

139. There is this difference between faith, hope, and charity: faith is confession of the divinity and the solid foundation of religion; hope is expectation of future goods; charity is perfect love of God and neighbor. The first of these nourishes present belief, the second awaits the promises of future things, and the third embraces eternal love. These three are so joined together during the time of this life that one cannot stand without the others.

140. Indeed, we cannot truly believe unless we hope for the things that have been promised; nor can we sustain the promises unless the belief of faith is firm; nor will the fruit of hope or the stability of faith be present unless there is the perfect charity of Christ, which both helps faith to believe and strengthens hope in its expectation. According to the Apostle, primacy is specially attributed to charity among these virtues, and its practice remains eternal.

141. For faith will cease when the future things that are believed have arrived; and hope will have an end when each good person has received the blessedness for which he waits. Charity alone will endure forever, bringing both faith and hope to Christ; it alone will enjoy everlasting joy.

XXXVII.

142. There is this difference between love (*amor*) and affection or charity (*dilectio*, *caritas*): love and affection are intermediate and ready for either direction, turning sometimes toward good and sometimes toward evil. Charity, however, turns only toward good; its name is exalted to such a degree that God himself is called “Charity.” Perfect charity is that which both patiently endures enemies and kindly comforts them. Whoever does not do these things departs far from charity. These alone are the supreme goods. For those who possess them truly possess them. Other virtues, however, are intermediate goods, which some may possess for benefit, but which may become harmful if they grow arrogant and puffed up because of them.

[Col. 0092D] 143. There are four things to be loved: God, one’s neighbor, our flesh, and our soul. The first is love of God, and the next is love of one’s neighbor. But just as love of one’s neighbor arises through love of God, so love of God is demonstrated through love of one’s neighbor. Love of God is the origin of love of one’s neighbor, and love of one’s neighbor is knowledge of love of God. Moreover, love of God begins from fear, but it does not remain under fear. For love arising from fear is servile, not free, because it does not proceed from love of God but from fear of punishment.

144. The love of God is expressed in these three matters, so that nothing may remain in a person that is not subjected to divine love. When it is said, “You shall love God with all your heart,” this commands that all thoughts be referred to God. When it is said, “with all your soul,” it commands that all the soul’s affections be referred to God. When it adds, “with all your mind,” it indicates that all human reason, by which we understand and distinguish, is to be occupied with divine matters.

145. Two things must likewise be observed concerning love of one’s neighbor: that one provide for others what one wishes to be provided for oneself by others, and that one not inflict on others what one fears may be inflicted upon oneself. From this twofold virtue of love toward one’s neighbor arise all virtues, by which we either rightly desire what ought to be sought or take precautions against what ought to be avoided.

[Col. 0093B] [Note: [Col. 0093D]

146. The words of Tobit in the Vulgate are: “What you hate to have done to you, see that you never do to another.” The meaning is the same. AREV.]

146. For what the Lord says—“Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them”—pertains to providing good to one’s neighbor. Likewise, what is read in the Old Testament—“What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another”—pertains to taking care that no one inflict evil upon his neighbor. Therefore one appropriately loves one’s neighbor through these two principles: by fostering the neighbor through the provision of benefits and by harming no one through any evil.

XXXVIII.

109 147. There is this difference between knowledge and wisdom: knowledge pertains to recognition, while wisdom pertains to contemplation. Knowledge makes good use of temporal things and is occupied with avoiding evils or understanding and seeking good things; wisdom, however, contemplates eternal things alone. Likewise, some men have wished a distinction to be understood between wisdom and prudence, assigning wisdom to divine matters, but prudence or knowledge to human affairs. Perfect knowledge consists in doing many good things and in not seeking earthly praise for those things that God has commanded one to do, and in regarding oneself as an unprofitable servant before the eyes of God.
to consider.

### XXXIX

148. They distinguish wisdom and eloquence as follows: eloquence consists in words. There is no doubt that wisdom is beneficial without eloquence. Eloquence cannot be effective without wisdom. For indiscriminate prudence is better than foolish talkativeness. It is the study of things that is beneficial, not the ornamentation of words. Eloquence, as we have said, is knowledge of words; wisdom, however, is knowledge of things and understanding of causes.

149. Moreover, the ancients called wisdom “philosophy,” that is, knowledge of all human and divine things. They said that this philosophy has three branches: physics, logic, and ethics. Physics is natural; ethics, moral; logic, rational. The first is assigned to nature and the contemplation of things; the second concerns action and the knowledge of right living; the third consists in distinguishing truth from falsehood.

[Column 0094A] [Note: Column 0094D]

150. Isidore discusses arithmetic, geometry, music, and so forth more fully in the books of the *Etymologies*, where appropriate notes are supplied in their places. [AREV.]

150. This threefold branch of philosophy, according to the wise men of the world, is distinguished in its several parts as follows. They say that seven disciplines belong to physics: first arithmetic, second geometry, third music, fourth astronomy, fifth astrology, sixth mechanics, seventh medicine. Their principles, briefly, are these.

110 151. Arithmetic is the definition by which the order or rational structure of all numbers is established. Geometry is the discipline of magnitude, distinguished by the proper signs and lines of figures, or by their forms. It is called geometry from the measurement of the earth, by which the boundaries of each tract are usually drawn. The Egyptians first discovered it out of necessity, because the Nile, at the time of its flooding, used to obliterate the boundaries of the land. [Column 0094B] Music is an art perceived through voice or gesture, possessing within itself a definite measurement of number and sound together with knowledge of perfect modulation. It consists of three elements: sound, words, and numbers.

152. Astronomy is the law of the stars. Astrology is the system that defines the movement of the heavens and the signs, as well as the powers, risings, and settings of the heavenly bodies. Mathematicians pursue it. Mechanics is a certain skill or discipline in which, they say, the construction of all things is brought together with subtle precision. Medicine is the science of cures, discovered for the balancing or health of the body. Of all these disciplines, some are compatible with religion, while others are altogether alien to it.

[Column 0094C] 153. Having arranged the branches, or distinctions, of the physical art, let us now take up the parts of logic. It consists of dialectic and rhetoric. Dialectic is the method or rule of disputation, sharpening the understanding of the mind and distinguishing truth from falsehood. Rhetoric is the method of speaking, the science of those skilled in law, which orators follow. By it, as someone has said, a judgment is armed with eloquence as iron is with poison.

154. Ethics follows logic; it pertains to the formation of character. For it is the teacher of right living, and it is divided into four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Prudence is recognition of the true faith and knowledge of the Scriptures, in which one ought to contemplate that threefold kind of understanding. The first is that by which certain things are received historically, without any figure, as are the Ten Commandments. The second is that by which certain things in Scripture are received in a mixed manner, both according to the outcome of the events narrated and according to their figurative meaning, as in the case of Sarah and Hagar: first, that they truly existed; then, that they figuratively represent the two Testaments.

155. The third kind is that which is understood only spiritually, as in the Song of Songs. If it is understood according to the sound of the words or the performance of the action, it is taken as bodily lust rather than as the virtue of the sacraments.

111 156. Having defined the nature of prudence, let us now set forth the parts of justice. Its first duty is to fear God, venerate religion, render honor to parents, love one’s country, benefit everyone, harm no one, embrace the bonds of fraternal charity, undertake the dangers of others, bring aid to the wretched, repay in kind the good one has received, and preserve equity in judgments.

157. Fortitude is greatness of spirit, the glory of martial virtue, and contempt for possessions and riches. In adversity it either yields patiently or resists bravely. It is softened by no enticements; it is not broken by adversity or elevated by prosperity. It is unconquered in labor and brave in danger; it neglects money, flees greed, prepares its spirit for danger against the wicked, yields to no hardship, and guards against the craving for glory.

158. Temperance is moderation of life in every word and deed. It is the companion of modesty, preserves the rule of humility, maintains tranquility of spirit, embraces continence and chastity, fosters dignity and propriety, restrains desire by reason, suppresses anger, and does not repay insult. Of these virtues, prudence delights in recognition of the truth; justice preserves love of God and neighbor; fortitude possesses the force of virtue and scorns the fear of death; temperance moderates and extinguishes the passions of the flesh. The first believes and understands, the second loves, the third restrains desire, and the fourth imposes moderation.

### XL. On the Distinctions of the Four Vices

[Column 0095C]

[Note: Column 0095D]

159. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 733: “Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice.” The verb *utantur* is used with passive meaning. [AREV.]

159. Philosophers nevertheless say that four vices are set in opposition to these four kinds of virtues: fear, joy, desire, and grief. We, however, call these not perfected vices but intermediate ones, because, on account of the diversity of human dispositions, they are prepared for either side and, according to the will of one’s choice, turn now toward good, now toward evil. Thus certain virtues, when misused, generate vices from themselves: for example, sluggishness may sometimes arise from gentleness, dissolution of discipline from piety, or immoderate vengeance from justice. Thus these four, when used well, are virtues; otherwise they pass from virtues into vices.

[Column 0095D] 160. Accordingly, when someone fears sinning, or desires to be blessed, grieves over sins, and rejoices in good works, these movements, which proceed from love and devotion, are then regarded as virtues. But when someone is held by fear of losing some earthly thing, or is broken by grief over a lost possession; when inflamed by desire for temporal things, or elated by joy at acquiring something, then these are called not virtues but genuine vices. Of these, two belong to the future, before anything happens—fear and desire; the other two belong to the past, after something has happened—joy and grief.
