[Note: Column 0095D]

161. These principal vices are discussed more fully in Book II of the *Sentences*, chapters 38 and following, where the learned and extensive notes of Loaisa may be consulted. [AREV.]

161. There are eight perfected, or principal, vices that disturb the whole human race, from which a multitude of vices arises: gluttonous desire, fornication, greed, envy, sadness, anger, vainglory, and, last of all, pride itself, the leader and root of these. Of all these, two are carnal—fornication and gluttony of the belly—and the rest are spiritual.

162. They are distinguished in their particular forms as follows. Gluttonous desire is divided into five modes. First, when someone desires food before the proper time, as Jonathan broke his fast by tasting honey. Second, when someone seeks more sumptuous foods, as the people, scorning the manna of the wilderness, craved the meats of Egypt. Third, when someone takes greater care in procuring ordinary foods, as the sons of Eli, contrary to custom, took raw meat from those offering it so that they might prepare it more carefully for themselves. Fourth, when someone consumes cheap foods in excessive quantity. Hence the prophet also accuses Sodom of having an excess of bread. Fifth, when someone consumes anything out of desire, as Esau, because of his craving for lentils, lost his birthright.

163. Fornication likewise has three forms. First, when sexual intercourse is completed through the pleasure of lust; second, when the lust of the flesh is aroused through mere touching and uncleanness; third, when someone is defiled by a nocturnal illusion prompted by an impure thought. According to Scripture there is also a fourth kind of fornication: every unlawful corruption of the mind, such as idolatry and greed, through which transgression of the law results from unlawful desire.

164. Greed, moreover, is divided into two punishments: the desire to increase one’s possessions and the fear of losing them. As someone has said: “The thirst of desire is never filled or satisfied.” Not only are those who love their possessions tormented by the wish to increase them; they are also tormented by fear of losing them.

165. Envy itself is afflicted by a twofold flame: either when someone envies a superior for possessing what he himself does not have, or when he grieves that someone like himself is equal to him.

[Column 0096D] 166. Next comes sadness, which has three forms. The first, as Cassian says, is moderate and reasonable, arising from repentance for sins. The second is disturbed and irrational, arising from anxiety of mind or despair over sins. The third proceeds from anger, from an inflicted injury, or from an obstructed desire.

[Note: Column 0096D]

167. “Through swelling.” This is a phrase used by ecclesiastical writers, who call pride “swelling” because the proud are swollen with it. [AREV.]

167. Vainglory has four kinds of boastful display. Some possess gifts but do not acknowledge the giver. Some say that they received their gifts because of preceding merits, not through the grace of the giver. Others, through swelling pride, imagine that they possess what they do not have. Still others, by despising others, think that they alone possess something distinctive. More pernicious, however, is the elevation that arises from the boastfulness of uniqueness.

168. Finally, pride has three forms. The first kind belongs to those who, through transgression and guilt, hold the divine commandments in contempt. The second belongs to those who are lifted up by observing the commandments and by the exaltation of their virtues. The third belongs to those who, through stubbornness of mind, disdain submission to the commands of their elders.

169. These vices are cured, by divine grace and divine assistance, through the opposing virtues. Watchfulness and compunction of heart restrain gluttonous desire. Fornication is extinguished by contrition of heart, bodily affliction, constant prayer, the exercise of labor, fear of hell, and love of the heavenly homeland. Envy is overcome by the love of fraternal affection. Since only those who are united receive the heavenly kingdom, it is fitting to cast away envy and love one’s brother.

[Note: Column 0097B]

170. Some omit the words “who, while he wishes … earned the infernal realm,” and after “the fear of ruin” immediately add: “Here end the Spiritual Distinctions of blessed Isidore.” They are also called by the title *Distinctions of Things*. [AREV.]

170. Patience and a disposition of equanimity temper anger. Almsgiving and hope of eternal recompense subdue greed. Brotherly conversation and the consolation of Scripture subdue sadness. Fear tramples arrogance, lest empty glory exclude from every virtue the soul it has softened, cause it to lose itself through boastfulness, and destroy it. The example of Christ’s humility, together with fear of the devil’s ruin, suppresses pride. While wishing to become what he was not, he lost even what he was and earned the infernal regions of Tartarus.

[Column 0097]

115 **CERTAIN SACRED ALLEGORIES OF HOLY ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE (C)**

### Preface

**ISIDORE TO THE MOST HOLY AND MOST REVEREND BROTHER OROSIUS**

[Note: Column 0097C]

1. I discussed the work of the *Allegories* in *Isidorian Studies*, chapter 60. Among the ancients, Rabanus Maurus also explained allegories in sacred Scripture; among more recent writers, Jerome Lauretus published the *Silva of Allegories of Sacred Scripture*. Concerning it there is this judgment of Saint Charles Borromeo, reported by Possevinus in Book II, chapter 46, of the *Selected Library*: “But Charles Borromeo, cardinal and holy man, wishing to make the use of this *Silva* easier and more fruitful, had decided to place at the beginning the names of the things designated by the allegorical terms and listed first. Perhaps some pious and learned person will undertake this labor and arrange the allegories themselves in a better order, so as to make them useful to the literary republic for the salvation of those who come after.” The notes on the allegories of Saint Isidore in the Grial edition identify Cyprian Suárez, S.J., as their author, and I shall cite them under his name. In that Madrid royal edition and in others the text read: “The names are read in the law”; I have omitted “are read” with the Verona manuscript so that the sense might proceed more clearly; it is also absent from the first Hagenau edition of the *Allegories*. In the allegories that follow, the diligence of Cyprian Suárez, the annotator, will ensure that our fuller annotations are not missed. I therefore intend to insert only a few. [AREV.]

1. I have quickly gathered and briefly extracted certain very well-known names from the Law and the Gospels that are imaginatively concealed beneath allegory and require interpretation, in order to make them plain and open to readers. Since they were unexplained, the short material available for discussion compelled me to annotate them, yet allowed neither the work to be completed in the form of a little book nor the mysteries of the figures to be explained in full. The sense was such, however, that from what has been set down both what precedes and what follows may be understood.

2. We therefore offer these matters to your judgment for examination and approval, so that you may diligently correct whatever is inadequately expressed in the arrangement of the words and meanings. For I shall consider myself excusable, dearest brother, in the criticism of this work, because I have not preserved these things according to my own judgment but have entrusted them to your judgment for correction.

### FROM THE OLD TESTAMENT

[Column 0099]

[Column 0099A] 116 [Note: Column 0099B]

3. Adam bore the figure of Christ. This allegory is that of the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 15. For he says: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.” In Genesis 2 we read that the first man was made a living soul, that is, one actively working, whose bodily members serve and obey his will and power, as blessed Chrysostom explains. And, as Theodoret writes, he did not call the second Adam a living spirit but a life-giving one. For he gives life to all. God created man in such a way that through reason and understanding he would be superior to all animals, which do not possess such a mind, as blessed Augustine writes clearly in Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 23. [SUAR.]

**Ibid.** Thus in the sixth age of the world. Perfection is comprehended in the number six; therefore God perfected the world in six days, as blessed Augustine teaches in Book XI of *The City of God*, chapter 30. The reason why man was created at the end, that is, on the sixth day, was, as Gregory of Nyssa writes elegantly in Book I of *On the Making of Man*, chapter 2, the following: “Since it was fitting that God should prepare for the future king a kind of dwelling place for his kingdom, and then introduce into the world a man endowed with an immortal soul but a mortal body, so that he might be both spectator and lord of the wonders of the world, enjoying God through his more divine nature but using the earthly goods through a sensation resembling the earth.” John of Damascus writes nearly the same in Book II, chapter 11. Eucherius says in his commentary on Genesis 1 that the second Adam, that is, Christ our Lord, was born in the sixth age, which extends from John the Baptist to the setting and destruction of the world. Then, as blessed Jerome says in his commentary on Amos 5, all labors and troubles will rest in the number seven, just as God rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had done, Genesis 2. This rest, the sanctification of the seventh day, and the blessing after his very good works, as Junilius notes, signify that each of us, after the good works God performs in us, moves toward the rest of heavenly life. Since that life is everlasting, it is rightly not said that the same seventh day had an evening. [SUAR.]

3. Adam (Genesis 1) bore the figure of Christ. For just as Adam was formed on the sixth day in the image of God, so in the sixth age of the world the Son of God assumed the form of flesh—that is, he took the form of a servant—in order to restore man to the likeness of God.

[Note: Column 0099D]

4. “Through the mystery of the washing.” The Apostle also taught and made this allegory illustrious. For since Genesis 2 says, “Therefore the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he was fast asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh for it. And the Lord God built the rib which he took from Adam into a woman,” and so forth, he wrote in Ephesians 5 that this is a great sacrament in Christ and the Church. For, as Prosper says splendidly in his book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*: “This is the great sacrament for which Adam hoped as something promised and foresaw as something future, namely, the formation of the Church from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross.” Accordingly, Theophylact, explaining the words of blessed John in chapter 19—“But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out”—says: “These things are not incidental, because through these two things the Church both comes into being and subsists. Through water we are generated; through blood and the body we are nourished.” Blessed Augustine writes about this more fully in Book XII *Against Faustus the Manichaean*. [SUAR.]

4. Eve (ibid.) signifies the Church, made through the mystery of the washing, which flowed from the side of Christ dying upon the cross, just as Eve came from the rib of the sleeping man.

[Note: Column 0100B]

5. “Abel, shepherd of sheep.” In this allegory the manuscript has a fuller reading than the printed book, for it cites the testimony of blessed John, chapter 10, which is highly relevant. That Abel was a shepherd is declared by Genesis 4. He was the first of all mortals distinguished by virginity, martyrdom, and priesthood; through these adornments he represented the Lord, according to blessed Augustine in his book *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*. He is said to be the future ruler of faithful peoples because he will ultimately be the shepherd of one flock, that is, of Jews and Gentiles, as in Romans 11 and John 10. [SUAR.]

5. Abel, shepherd of sheep (Genesis 4), bore the type of Christ, who is the true and good shepherd, as he himself says: “I am the good shepherd, who lay down my life for my sheep,” the future ruler of faithful peoples.

[Note: Column 0100C]

6. “Cain, his brother, older in age.” Although Philo the bishop thinks without reason that the brothers were twins, this is an especially beautiful allegory. Abel, the shepherd of sheep, is killed by his older brother; Christ, the shepherd and head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the older one. Abel is killed in the field, Christ at the place of Calvary; and both are killed after a sacrifice, while the devil kindles the flames of deadly envy in the minds of the murderers. Indeed, the blood of Abel summoned God to just vengeance by its cry; hence Cain was a wanderer and fugitive on the earth, or, **στένων καὶ τρέμων**, that is, “groaning and trembling,” as the Septuagint translated it. But the blood of Christ cries out far more powerfully, for the reasons that blessed Augustine explains splendidly in his work *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, where he expounds this allegory with great eloquence; blessed Ambrose mentions it in Book I *On Cain and Abel*. [SUAR.]

6. Cain, his brother (ibid.), older in age, who killed that same Abel in the field, signifies the earlier people who killed Christ at the place of Calvary.

[Note: Column 0100D]

7. “Enoch”—it is clear that Enoch, not Enos, should be read. Blessed Augustine, in Book XV of *The City of God*, thinks either that Enoch was not Cain’s firstborn—for Judah was also the fourth son of Jacob, yet Judea and the Jews were named from him—or that the city was founded under his name after a long interval of time, once the human race had become sufficiently numerous for a city to be built; a city is nothing other than a multitude of human beings gathered under some form of association. Blessed Chrysostom, since Genesis 4 says that Cain built a city and called its name after his son Enoch, says similarly to blessed Isidore: “See how they gradually become worse. Once human beings had been made mortal, they were concerned to make their memory immortal, partly through the sons they begot and partly through the places to which they gave their sons’ names. All these things could rightly be called monuments of sinners and of the first fall, by which they fell from their former glory.” [SUAR.]

**Ibid.** In our Vulgate it is written “Henoch.” [AREVAL.]

7. Enoch, son of Cain (ibid.), in whose name his father founded a city, signifies the ungodly, who are grounded only in this life.

[Column 0101A] 118 [Note: Column 0101B]

8. Seth, whose name is interpreted as “resurrection.” Sacred Scripture, as blessed Jerome also noted in his *Questions*, gives the etymology of the name Seth in these words: “And he called his name Seth, saying: God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain slew.” Thus Soth is properly called **θέσις** (*thesis*), that is, “placing,” from the verb *seth*, “he placed.” But because Abel was in a certain sense raised up in his brother Seth—who mitigated the grief of his parents and was destined to be such, as Eucherius says, that he would fulfill Abel’s holiness—the Septuagint translated it: **Ἐξανέστησε γάρ μοι ὁ Θεὸς σπέρμα ἔτερον**, that is, “For God has raised up for me another seed.” Therefore blessed Chrysostom says: “Observe the precision of the word: he did not say, ‘God gave me,’ but ‘God raised up for me.’ See how by this word he obscurely shows us here the beginnings of the resurrection.” Following this, blessed Isidore says: “Seth, whose name is interpreted as resurrection.” For he did not look so much to the etymology of the Hebrew word as to its hidden meaning, as did the Septuagint; Rupert later followed them in this. Finally, blessed Augustine illustrated this same allegory in these words in Book XV of *The City of God*: “In those two men, Abel, whose name is interpreted as ‘mourning,’ and his brother Seth, whose name is interpreted as ‘resurrection,’ the death of Christ and his life from the dead are figured.” [SUAR.]

8. Seth (ibid.), whose name is interpreted as “resurrection,” demonstrates Jesus Christ, in whom there is true resurrection and the life of the faithful.

[Note: Column 0101C]

9. “Enos, his son.” The manuscript books read: “Enos, his son, who began to invoke the name of the Lord.” This agrees with our translation from the Hebrew. The printed books, however, have: “Enos, his son, who hoped to invoke the name of the Lord.” This reading agrees with the interpretation of the Septuagint, who translated it as follows: **οὗτος ἤλπισεν ἐπικαλεῖσθαι τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου τοῦ Θεοῦ**, that is: “He hoped to invoke the name of the Lord God.” Accordingly, Greek writers and blessed Augustine, who used this version, handed down the hidden meaning of this passage in a manner similar to blessed Isidore. Gregory of Nazianzus says: “Faith, hope, and charity—these three—are an excellent thing.” He offered Abraham as a testimony to faith, since he was accounted righteous because of faith; and Enos as a testimony to hope, since he was the first to hope to invoke the name of the Lord. More explicitly, blessed Augustine says in Book XV of *The City of God*: “What does ‘he hoped to invoke’ mean except that it is a prophecy that a people would arise who, according to the election of grace, would invoke the name of the Lord God?” Blessed Augustine thinks this is the reason why what was common to all the godly is attributed particularly to this man. Some, nevertheless, think that in his time the worship of God was restored and that the practice of honoring God with ceremonies began, as Lipomanus writes. Certain famous Greek writers, because they did not know the Hebrew language, thought that the etymology of the name Enos was being rendered when it says, “he hoped,” and so forth. Yet Enos, as blessed Jerome noted, means “man” or “male,” just as Adam means “man.” [SUAR.]

**Ibid.** What Enos signifies Isidore already explained in Book VII, chapter 6, of the *Etymologies*, where he discusses people who received their names through a kind of prophetic indication. Much could be brought here from that chapter. [AREV.]

9. Enos, his son (ibid.), who in hope invoked the name of the Lord, declares the Church living in hope until it reaches the blessedness of the promised happiness.

119 [Note: Column 0102B]

10. “Lamech bore the figure of this world.” Many features came together in Lamech, Cain’s grandson—for those who take him to be the son of Methuselah are mistaken—and in his children that would corrupt human life, as blessed Jerome notes admirably. He himself, a bloody and murderous man, was the first to divide one flesh between two wives, and his children discovered things that would inflame human minds either to pleasure or to cruelty. It is not certain whether he killed one man, and that man Cain, or two. It is certain that he told his two wives that vengeance would be exacted from him seventy-sevenfold. Blessed Jerome wrote the hidden meaning of this passage to Damasus as follows: “It is asked what the seventy-seven acts of vengeance are that must be exacted from Lamech. They say that there are seventy-seven generations from Adam to Christ. Read the evangelist Luke, and you will find that this is so.” And shortly afterward: “Lamech’s sin, that is, the sin of the whole world, and the blood that was shed, will be discharged by the coming of Christ, who took away the sins of the world.” Later the same was written by Nicholas, the pontiff, to King Lothair, and Alcuin followed him. [SUAR.]

10. Lamech bore the figure of this world, whose sin Christ expiated through the shedding of his blood after the seventy-seven generations of the world, as the evangelist Luke enumerated them (Luke 3).

[Note: Column 0102C]

11. “Enoch, who was seventh from Adam.” Concerning Enoch it is written in Genesis 5: “And he walked with God, and he appeared no more, because God took him.” The Septuagint translated the last part as **ὅτι μετέθηκεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεός**, that is, “because God transferred him.” Hence the Apostle cited these same words of the Septuagint in Hebrews 11. Blessed Chrysostom and Theodoret think it idle to inquire where God transferred Enoch or whether he remains alive to the present day. But the Holy Spirit teaches both matters in Ecclesiasticus 44, in these words: “Enoch pleased God, and he was transferred into paradise, to give repentance to the nations.” It should be noted that Enoch, Cain’s son, after whom the first city was named, signifies the ungodly who, as Strabo rightly says, fix the root of their hope in the present life. But this Enoch, who was seventh from Adam and who, like the sixth day and the sixth age of the world, is formed in holiness through Christ’s coming, signifies those who in the seventh age will be transferred into immortal life, as the same Isidore says elsewhere. Blessed Augustine also explained this same allegory in Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 19. [SUAR.]

**Ibid.** Enoch, who was seventh from Adam, signifies the seventh rest; Isidore discusses him in his commentaries, namely, in the *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 6. Those commentaries of Isidore also contribute to explaining these allegories; it is enough to have mentioned this once. [AREV.]

11. Henoch (Genesis 5), who was seventh from Adam and was transferred, signifies the seventh rest of the future resurrection, when the saints will be transferred into the life of perpetual immortality.

[Note: Column 0102D]

12. “Noah, whose name is interpreted as rest.” “Rest is interpreted.” Blessed Jerome says: “Accordingly, he was called ‘rest’ because all the works of the past rested through the Flood.” Blessed Chrysostom likewise says that the child was so named so that, from the interpretation of the word, everyone might learn that universal destruction was impending and might, chastened by fear, hold back and embrace virtue. But, as Cajetan rightly writes: “If Lamech’s words, which explain the etymology of the name Noah, are carefully considered, they seem to concern the labor of agriculture; for he says: ‘This one will comfort us from the works of our hands upon the land which the Lord has cursed.’ Yet these words contained a prophecy concerning the Church and Christ.” It is certain that the Holy Spirit, through blessed Peter in the First Epistle, chapter 3, made this allegory notable and illustrious. [SUAR.]

12. Noah, whose name is interpreted as rest, prefigures the Lord, in whose Church all those who are delivered from the destruction of this age rest, as in the ark.

[Column 0103A] 120 [Note: Column 0103B]

It is therefore clear that Noah prophesied, for Abraham and the patriarchs, and finally the salvation and glory of the human race, Jesus Christ, arose from Shem. [SUAR.]

13. Shem bore the type of the prophets and apostles, who were born from his lineage.

[Note: Column 0103C]

For, as blessed Jerome writes: “From Shem the Hebrews arise, and from Japheth the people of the Gentiles.” Because the multitude of believers is broad, it received its name from breadth, which is called Japheth. When he says, “And may he dwell in the tents of Shem,” he prophesies about us, who, after Israel was cast out, dwell in the instruction and knowledge of the Scriptures. And, as blessed Augustine rightly says: “The breadth of the Gentiles dwells in the churches of Christ, and the Gentiles enjoy what had been prepared for the Jews,” as blessed Chrysostom also writes in his commentary on Genesis 9. [Note: Column 0103C]

15. Ham signifies the Jews, who mock Christ incarnate and dead.

16. Canaan, his son, who is condemned to a curse for his father’s offense (Genesis 9), indicates the posterity of the Jews, who received the sentence of condemnation in the Lord’s Passion, when the Jews cried out: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

17. “Nimrod, a giant.” Concerning Nimrod we read in Genesis 10: “Chus begot Nimrod. The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon, which signifies the world that lies wholly in wickedness; therefore in Revelation 18 it is called the habitation of demons. 18. “Heber, in whose household …” The manuscript book has “the unity of faith,” more correctly than the printed books’ “faith of unity.” Blessed Augustine, in the passage mentioned above, thinks that the Hebrews, who preserved the Hebrew language, were named from Heber rather than from Abraham. Among this people the City of God sojourned in the saints, and everything was shadowed forth in sacramental form. 19. “Melchizedek, who from the fruits …” The printed book has “or the priesthood,” but the manuscript’s “and the priesthood” is better, since Melchizedek signified both the priesthood and the kingship of Christ. Concerning him it is written in Genesis 14: “But Melchizedek, king of Salem, bringing forth bread and wine—for he was the priest of the most high God—blessed him,” namely Abram. Although the Jews and certain others think otherwise, those who affirm that Melchizedek offered a sacrifice to God for Abraham’s noble victory are much more correct. The word *proferens*, “bringing forth” or “offering,” is often used in sacrificial contexts. Thus our translator beautifully rendered what follows: “And he himself was the priest of the most high God.” For he was the priest of the most high God. For *et* (“and”) is often used in place of *enim* (“for”). Blessed Jerome reports in the long and learned letter he wrote to Evagrius that the settled opinion of the Hebrews was that Melchizedek was the son of Shem, son of Noah. He adds that Melchizedek dedicated the sacrament of Christ through a pure and simple sacrifice of bread and wine. The Apostle ennobled this allegory in Hebrews 7, as did the passage of Psalm 109: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” [SUAR.]

Ibid. Even if *vel sacerdotium* were retained instead of *et sacerdotium*, the meaning would still be the same as Suarius maintains: for in Isidore and other writers of the same and even earlier periods, *vel* often occurs in place of *et*. AREV.]
