That Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin is established from chapter III of the Epistle to the Philippians. SUAR.

Ibid. In Grialius’s text, *et novissimus* (“and the last”) had been omitted, contrary, it seems, to Suarius’s intention. AREV.]

46. Benjamin presented an image of the Apostle Paul, [Col. 0107B] because he was both the last and the least of all the apostles by his calling, and he descended from that tribe. He is the ravenous wolf: in the morning a persecutor who ravages, in the evening a teacher who feeds.

[Note: [Col. 0108C]

47. Manasseh, of the former people. This allegory is connected with the following one, in which the printed book has the error *praepositus est major* instead of *majori* (“was placed before the greater”). Blessed Cyril briefly gathers these allegories together in these words: “Ephraim is preferred to Manasseh, that is, the Gentiles to the Jews, who acted impiously against the Savior; thus the last become first, and the first last.” Blessed Ambrose also derives an argument from the etymology of the names in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*: “Manasseh” is interpreted in Latin as “from forgetfulness,” because the Jewish people forgot their God, who made them. Ephraim, however, promises “fruitfulness,” according to the interpretation of the name, which is proper to the younger people, who are the body of Christ, increasing the Father and not abandoning their own God. SUAR.]

47. Manasseh bore the figure of the former people.

48. Ephraim, however, represented the Gentiles, who by the patriarch’s blessing were placed before the greater Jewish people.

[Note: [Col. 0108D]

49. Tamar, of the Church. Blessed Augustine wisely teaches in Book XXII *Against Faustus* why certain evil actions of human beings are said in the sacred Scriptures to signify certain future things that are not evil but good. In the same place he also teaches that Tamar bore a type. SUAR.]

49. Tamar (Genesis XXXVIII) bears the image of the Church, which through the ring of faith and the staff of the cross deserved from Christ the conception of holy fruitfulness.

[Col. 0108A] 50. The twin sons in Tamar’s womb (ibid.) represented the two peoples. The one born later, whose hand the elder first extended from the womb, signified the Gentile people, who had previously been shown through the prophets but were revealed afterward. For this reason the midwife tied his right hand with scarlet, because that same people was marked with the sign of the cross through the blood of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0108D]

51. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. Blessed Gregory elegantly explains this allegory in Book III, chapter 30 of *Pastoral Care*, concerning the mind that neglects its own pursuits and concerns itself with the actions of others. SUAR.]

51. Dinah, Jacob’s daughter (Genesis XXXIV), signifies the Synagogue or the soul. Found amid the external concerns of the world, she is violated by Shechem, the ruler of the land—that is, the devil corrupts her through the vice of carnal desire.

52. Bilhah, Jacob’s concubine (Genesis XXXV), whom Reuben defiled by an incestuous crime, signifies the law of the Old Testament, which the people of Israel stained by transgression.

[Col. 0108B] 53. Job, in his deeds and words, expresses the person of the Redeemer.

54. His wife (Job II), who urged him to curse, designates the perversity of the carnal.

55. Job’s three friends bore the type of heretics, who under the appearance of offering consolation pursue the work of seduction.

[Note: [Col. 0108D]

56. Elihu, however. Elihu’s arrogance is vividly placed before our eyes in Job XXXII, as is the way he, swollen with pride and inflamed by anger, inveighed against his friends and against the holy man Job. SUAR.

Ibid. Concerning the allegories relating to the Book of Job, see Pineda, Corderius, and others, just as other interpreters may be consulted concerning other books; they pursue the allegorical meaning of sacred Scripture at length. AREV.]

56. Elihu, however, demonstrates a proud and arrogant teacher who inflicts his harsh rebuke upon the faithful within the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0108D]

57. Pharaoh as a figure. The works of the flesh, of which the Apostle speaks in chapter V of Galatians, are compared with clay and bricks, which are mentioned in Exodus I. Blessed Augustine pursues this allegory extensively in Sermons 84 and 85 *On Time*, and blessed Cyril in his commentary on the aforementioned chapter of Exodus. SUAR.]

57. Pharaoh bore the figure of the devil, who attempted through the captivity of this age to destroy God’s people and weigh them down with earthly works of vice.

58. Pharaoh’s daughter (Exodus II), who took up Moses, exposed on the bank of the river, is the Church of the Gentiles, which found Christ at the river of saving baptism.

59. Moses (Exodus XIII) bore the type of Christ, who rescued God’s people from the yoke of diabolical slavery and condemned the devil himself to eternal punishment.

60. Aaron the priest, who purified the people with the blood of sacrifices, 127 signifies Christ, who washed away the sins of the world through the sacrifice of his blood.

[Note: [Col. 0109C]

61. Mary, Moses’ sister. Theodoret explains in Question 23 on Numbers why, although Aaron was a partner in the sin, Mary alone was afflicted with leprosy. SUAR.]

61. Mary, Moses’ sister (Numbers XII), presented the image of the Synagogue, which became leprous because of its slander and murmuring against Christ.

[Col. 0109B] [Note: [Col. 0109C]

62. Moses’ Ethiopian wife. Blessed Augustine rightly believes in Book *Questions on Numbers*, Question 20, that Moses had only one wife, Zipporah the Midianite, daughter of Jethro; she was nevertheless called Ethiopian because the Midianites are sometimes called Ethiopians in the sacred writings, as in 2 Chronicles XIV, when Jehoshaphat waged war against them. Theodoret writes the same in Question 22 on the same book of Numbers, refuting the opinion—or rather the fable—of Josephus and Apollinarius. The cause of the reproach, then, was that Moses had taken a foreign woman as his wife, whereas Aaron had taken an Israelite woman. Blessed Augustine explains this same allegory excellently in Sermon 86 *On Time*, as does Theodoret in Question 4 on the Book of Exodus. SUAR.]

62. Moses’ Ethiopian wife (Exodus II) represented the Church from the Gentiles joined to Christ. For this reason, the Synagogue, jealous and slandering Christ, was immediately covered with the contagion of leprosy.

[Note: [Col. 0109D]

63. Amalek designates. The event is narrated in Exodus XVII. Amalekite territory lay in the desert south of Judea, beyond the city of Petra, as blessed Jerome writes in *On Hebrew Place-Names*. Amalek, the grandson of Esau, was the founder of this people by name and descent (Genesis XXXVI). Blessed Augustine treats this noble allegory in Sermon 93 *On Time*, where he says that Moses, by the very raising of his hands, displayed the mystery of the cross. And, as Theodoret learnedly says in Question 34 on Exodus, just as Amalek fell when the servant of the Lord stretched out his hands, so, when the Lord stretched out his hands on the cross, the forces of the devil were slaughtered. SUAR.]

63. Amalek designates a figure of the devil, who, confronting God’s people, is overcome through the sign of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0109D]

64. Sihon also. Here too the manuscript copies are more correct, reading as follows: “He is Og, king of Bashan.” The printed book has “he is king of Bashan.” Both allegories, however, arise chiefly from the etymology of the names Sihon and Og. SUAR.]

64. Sihon also, king of the Amorites, whose name is translated into Latin as “temptation of the eyes,” signifies the same devil, who by lying deception transforms himself into an angel of light. He is Og, king of Bashan, whose name is interpreted as “conclusion”; he strives to block the way of our faith by the difficulty of vices, so that passage to the promised kingdom of eternal life may not be open to us.

[Note: [Col. 0109D]

65. The seventy-two elders. In the manuscript book this passage is written as follows: “The seventy-two elders, upon whom the Spirit of God fell, the seventy-two languages of the nations”; in the printed book, *duo* (“two”) is missing in both places. It is clear to anyone reading Numbers XI that there were seventy-two men upon whom the divine Spirit breathed, counting Eldad and Medad. Blessed Augustine carefully teaches in Book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 3, that there were likewise that many nations descended from the three sons of Noah, counting the nations listed in Genesis X. For this reason it is commonly thought that the Lord chose seventy-two disciples in Luke X, signified by the seventy-two palm trees found at Elim in Exodus XV, as Theophylact notes in his commentary on that chapter of Luke.

Ibid. For this allegory, see the Cotelerian edition of the Apostolic Fathers, 1698, page 738, volume I. AREV.]

65. The seventy-two elders upon whom the Spirit of God fell [Col. 0110A] point to the seventy-two languages of the nations spread throughout this world, from which many believers received the grace of the Holy Spirit. 128

[Note: [Col. 0110C]

66. Dathan and Abiram. Korah and Dathan, together with Abiram and On, and another two hundred and fifty leading men of the Synagogue, became leaders of the revolt against Moses and Aaron (Numbers XVI). It may perhaps be less surprising that Korah stirred up the rebellion, since he belonged to the tribe of Levi; but concerning the leaders of the revolt from the other tribes, Theodoret gives this explanation in Question 33 on Numbers: because they descended from Reuben the firstborn, they thought that the priesthood still belonged to them. It should be noted that Theodoret incorrectly has Eliab instead of On his son. SUAR.]

66. Dathan and Abiram, and the others who separated themselves from Moses and Aaron and attempted to usurp the offering (Numbers XVI), designate the perversity of heretics and the destruction of those who divide themselves from Christ’s priests and from the fellowship of the Church and take up profane sacrifices.

[Note: [Col. 0110D]

67. Balaam, who fell. Our Isidore borrowed this excellent allegory from blessed Gregory, whose devoted student he was. Gregory says in Book XXV, chapter 14, in his commentary on Job XXXIV: “Hence it is also written of Balaam, who, falling, had his eyes open: falling in conduct, he nevertheless kept his eyes open in contemplation. Thus these people too, opening their eyes in faith but not seeing in conduct, though placed within the Church in pious appearance, are in impious behavior placed outside the Church.” SUAR.]

67. Balaam, who, when he fell, had his eyes open (Numbers XXII), bore the type of those who through faith possess knowledge of God but fall, darkened by evil works.

68. Phinehas, who killed Zimri and the harlot together while they were engaged in adultery (Numbers XXV), bore the figure of holy teachers who strike the Jews and heretics with a spiritual sword when they join together in the embrace of false doctrine.

69. The man who, gathering wood on the Sabbath, was ordered to be stoned signifies the person whom Christ will find with sin on the day of judgment.

70. The twelve spies bore the image of the scribes and Pharisees, who turned the Israelite people away from trusting that they could attain the grace of the divine promise through Christ.

71. The two bearers who carried a cluster of grapes from the promised land on a pole upon their shoulders (Numbers XIII) expressed the significance of the two peoples. The former, the Jewish people, walking backward, turns its back on Christ; the latter, the Christian people, looks upon and follows Christ whom it carries. [Col. 0111A] 129

[Note: [Col. 0111C]

72. Joshua, son of Nun. Joshua, son of Nun, whom the Septuagint calls “Jesus, son of Nave,” a man of remarkable courage, was both Moses’ living servant and, after Moses’ death, his successor in command. He is first mentioned in Exodus XVII, when he entered the famous battle against Amalek, in which he was also victorious. Hence Origen says excellently at that passage: “Up to this point no mention has yet been made of the blessed name of Jesus; here the splendor of this name first shone forth.” He also explored the promised land with eleven companions and strengthened the Jews, broken and weakened by fear (Numbers XIII). There he is called Hosea, that is, “Savior,” as noted in Question 25 on Numbers. Finally, after the people of God had defeated thirty-one kings and been brought into the promised land, he divided it. Both by his name and by his outstanding deeds, he most clearly expressed the image of Christ Jesus our Savior. SUAR.]

72. Joshua, son of Nun, expressed the image of the Savior, who led us into the land of promise and established us in the kingdom of heavenly glory.

[Note: [Col. 0111D]

73. Rahab. Jericho, that is, “moon,” signifies the world, which lies wholly in the power of the evil one (1 John, final chapter). From its destruction we are freed by the blood of Christ. SUAR.]

73. Rahab the prostitute bore the figure of the Church, which through scarlet—that is, through the sign of the Lord’s Passion—is saved from the destruction of the world.

74. The two spies sent by Joshua into Jericho, whom Rahab received (Joshua II), are understood as the two Testaments sent into the world, which the Church gathered from the Gentiles received.

75. Achan, who coveted something from Jericho that had been devoted to destruction, signifies the wicked and sinful person who, after faith, desires worldly customs or the enticements of the world.

[Col. 0111B] [Note: [Col. 0111D]

76. Gideon. The discussion concerns the Greek letter Tau. Blessed Augustine treats this allegory excellently in these words in Question 37 on the Book of Judges: “Since they were three hundred, the number suggests the sign of the cross because of the Greek letter Τ, by which this number is signified; through them it was also prefigured that the Gentiles would believe more fully in the Crucified One, since the letter is Greek. Hence the Apostle signifies all the nations by the name of Greeks when he says: ‘To the Jew first, and to the Greek’; for Greek is so prominent among the languages of the nations that through it all are appropriately signified.” SUAR.

Ibid. The sacred poet Prudentius expressed this allegory in the preface to the *Psychomachia*, verse 56, a passage I explained at length in chapter 20 of my work on Prudentius. AREV.]

76. Gideon, who went to battle with three hundred men (Judges VII), bore the type of Christ, who through the sign of the cross gained victory over the world. For the number three hundred is contained in the letter Tau, through which the form of the cross is displayed.

77. Sisera was a type of the devil. Jael, however, who pierced his temple with a nail and hammer, expressed the type of the Church, which through the banner of the cross slew the devil’s dominion.

130 78. Deborah herself, also bearing the type of the same Church, after the devil had been defeated in Sisera, proclaims a song of heavenly glory.

[Note: [Col. 0112C]

79. Jephthah. Blessed Jerome says that Jephthah was foolish in making his vow and impious in fulfilling it. Blessed Thomas holds the same opinion. But blessed Augustine says in Question 49 on the Book of Judges that this is a major and extremely difficult question to judge, and he himself discusses it at length and with great learning. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that in the sacred Scriptures some future things that are not evil but good are signified through certain evil actions of human beings; blessed Augustine proves this learnedly in Book XII *Against Faustus*. SUAR.]

79. Jephthah, who sacrificed his daughter for the victory he had obtained (Judges XI), displayed the figure of the Redeemer, who, triumphing from the world, offered his own flesh as a sacrifice. [Col. 0111C]

[Note: [Col. 0112C]

80. Perhaps: “and more, dying.” AREV.]

80. Samson prefigured the death and victory of our Savior, either because he drew the Gentiles from the jaws of the devil, as a honeycomb taken from the mouth of a lion, or because after his death he won more people and destroyed more enemies by dying than he had while alive.

81. Delilah, who shaved Samson’s head (Judges XVI), signifies the Synagogue, which crucified Christ at the place of Calvary.

82. Ruth, a foreign woman who married an Israelite man, displayed the Church coming from the Gentiles to Christ.

83. Boaz, however, expressed Christ, the true bridegroom of the Church.

84. Hannah, who was barren and afterward became fruitful (1 Samuel I), signifies the Church of Christ, which was formerly barren among the Gentiles but now flourishes throughout the whole earth with the abundant fruitfulness of a numerous offspring.

[Col. 0112B] 85. Eli the rejected priest (1 Samuel III) prefigured the rejection of the priesthood of the Old Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0112C]

86. Samuel, however. Many believe that Samuel was not a priest but a Levite; for he was descended from Abiathar, son of Korah (1 Chronicles VI), whereas priests necessarily had to derive their origin from Aaron. Psalm XCVIII seems to indicate this in the words: “Moses and Aaron among his priests”; concerning Samuel it says: “And Samuel among those who call upon his name.” But blessed Augustine in this very passage affirms that Samuel was a priest, indeed a great one. In Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 43, he says that Samuel’s father was not a priest, although he is found among the sons of Aaron. SUAR.]

86. Samuel, however, who succeeded rejected Eli in the priestly ministry (ibid.), foretold the succession of the new priesthood after the old priesthood had been rejected.

87. The two priestly sons of Eli, who were killed when the ark was captured by the Gentiles (1 Samuel IV), signify that the offspring of the former priesthood was extinguished and that the covenant of the law was transferred to the worship of the Gentiles.

131 88. Saul suggests the promise, or the rejection, of the Jewish kingdom, or the rivalry of that same people, who attempted to kill David—that is, Christ—through the unjust hatred of envy.

89. David expressed the image of the Son of God and our Savior, either because he endured unjust persecution at the hands of the Jews, or because Christ assumed flesh from his lineage. [Col. 0112C]

[Note: [Col. 0112D]

90. That Uriah bore the type of the devil and Bathsheba the type of the Church may seem somewhat difficult; but the difficulty is sufficiently dispelled by the explanation of the matter itself, as happens in many other similar allegories. Isidore took this account of Uriah the Hittite from Saint Augustine, whose words he transcribes at length in *Questions on the Books of Kings*, Book II, chapter 2. Meanwhile, it should be observed that a figure need not represent its figurative counterpart in every respect, nor attain the perfection of what it represents. See Appendix 16 to the *Etymologies*, number 10, volume IV, page 522. AREV.]

90. Uriah the Hittite bore the type of the devil, to whose marriage the Church had previously been joined. Christ desired her as she washed herself from the filth of the world and purified herself through the water of the laver. [Col. 0113A]

91. Solomon prefigured Christ, who built a house for God in the heavenly Jerusalem—not from wood and stones, but from all the saints.

92. The Queen of the South, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings X; 2 Chronicles IX), is understood as the Church, which is gathered from the ends of the earth to the word of God.

93. Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, and Jeroboam the servant, between whom Israel was divided into two parts, signify the division made at the Lord’s coming: one part of the believers from the Jews reigns with Christ, who arose from David’s line; the other, having followed the Antichrist, is bound by the error of an impious slavery to his abominable worship. [Col. 0113B]

94. Goliath (1 Samuel XVII) designates the devil, whose pride of exaltation Christ’s humility cast down.

95. Elijah demonstrates Christ, because just as Elijah was carried upward in a fiery chariot, so Christ was taken up into heaven by the ministries of angels.

[Note: [Col. 0113D]

96. The widow to whom Elijah was sent. Blessed Augustine treats these two allegories concerning Elijah and Christ excellently in Sermon 201 *On Time*, which is Sermon 2 on the Third Sunday after Trinity. SUAR.]

96. The widow to whom Elijah was sent to be fed (1 Kings XVII) is the Church, to which Christ is said to have come through faith. Her flour and oil are blessed and do not fail—that is, the grace of Christ’s body and the anointing of chrism, which are supplied daily throughout the whole world and are never diminished. 132

97. Elisha prefigured the same Redeemer, the Lord, who descended from the height of the mountain—that is, from the sublimity of heaven—and humbled himself from the form of God to the form of a human being; he joined his members to dead limbs and healed our mortality by the medicine of his body. [Col. 0113C]

[Note: [Col. 0113D]

98. The boys who mocked Elisha. The manuscript book more correctly reads “who in childish foolishness,” rather than the printed edition’s “who through foolishness.” This is taught by the following words of blessed Augustine, from whom our Isidore borrowed them. In Book XII *Against Faustus* he says: “The boys who mocked Elisha and shouted, ‘Baldhead, baldhead,’ were devoured by beasts; those who in childish foolishness mocked Christ crucified at the place of Calvary, seized by demons, perished.” Blessed Ambrose explains the preceding allegory concerning the same Elisha and the Lord in the final letter of Book IV. SUAR.]

98. The boys who mocked Elisha, shouting, “Go up, baldhead, go up, baldhead,” and were killed after being attacked by a bear (2 Kings II), indicate the Jewish people, who in childish foolishness mocked Christ crucified at the place of Calvary and, captured by two bears—that is, Titus and Vespasian—perished.

99. Elisha’s boy, sent with a staff to revive the woman’s son (2 Kings IV), displayed the type of the ancient law, which, transmitted to the human race, accomplished nothing except to show, through the rod, the sole authority of severity.

[Col. 0113D] 100. The dead son of the Shunammite woman (ibid.) bears the figure of the human race, over which Christ, yawning seven times, spiritually breathes the sevenfold Spirit of grace, through whom it may rise again from the death of sin. [Col. 0114A]

101. The seven thousand men of whom it was said to Elijah that they had not bent the knee before Baal signify the number of the saints who, filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace, renounced the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0114D]

102. Naaman the Syrian. Blessed Augustine explains this allegory in Sermon 108 *On the Season*, where he says admirably: “Naaman heard the little girl and came to Elisha; the people of the nations heard the prophecy and came to Christ. Naaman, coming to Elisha, is healed of leprosy; and the people of the nations, coming to Christ, are cleansed from every leprosy of sins.” SUAR.]

102. Naaman the Syrian signifies the people from the nations, polluted with the stains of transgressions and purified by Christ through the sacrament of baptism.

103. King Uzziah, who, on account of the merit of his crimes, was covered on the forehead with the contagion of leprosy (II Chronicles XXVI), indicates the kingdom of the Jews, who bear on their forehead the disgrace and evil of faithlessness, where they ought to have borne the sign of the cross.

104. King Hezekiah, to whom fifteen years were added to his life for a good work (IV Kings XX; II Chronicles XXXII; Isaiah XXXIX; Ecclesiasticus XLVIII), signifies all the saints, to whom the five books of the Law, together with the ten commandments of the Decalogue, were given for the acquisition of eternal life, so that through the fulfillment of the Law and the commandments they might attain the fullness of the heavenly kingdom.

105. King Josiah, who celebrated the Passover and removed many idols from the temple of the Lord (IV Kings XXIII; II Chronicles XXXV), signifies Christ, who undertook suffering for us and, casting out from the temples of our bodies all the detestable things of the nations, crushed them after burning them in the fire of his power and cast them into the torrent of this age.

106. Zedekiah, whose eyes the king of Babylon tore out at Riblah (IV Kings XXV), signifies the rich and sinners of this world; for Riblah is translated into Latin as “these many things,” and therefore he signifies those who are entangled in the manifold activity and affection of this world and, taken captive by the devil, lose the eyes of understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0114D]

107. Isidore repeats much concerning Isaiah and the other prophets in the book of the *Prologues*. AREV.]

107. Isaiah expressed the form of the evangelists and apostles, who proclaimed all the mysteries of Christ not as future but as present.

108. Jeremiah, in his words and sufferings, prefigured the death and passion of the Lord and Savior.

109. Ezekiel bore the image of Christ, who, placed in earthly exile, urges the people on with saving commandments.

110. Daniel, who maintained a celibate life, resembled by his continence those who are in holy leisure and do not abuse earthly possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0114D]

111. Hosea. Blessed Jerome illustrated this allegory and enriched it with many similar examples in the prologue to Pammachius on the Prophet Hosea. SUAR.]

111. Hosea demonstrates a figure of Christ, who took the Church, from the fornication of the nations, into his own body.

112. Joel, whose name is interpreted as “beginning,” typologically indicates those who are beginning to know the door of faith and the mystery of divine knowledge.

113. Amos, a shepherd and rustic, is a type of Christ, who, transferred from the pastoral office of tending sheep—that is, from the rule of the Hebrews—now feeds other flocks among the nations.

134. 114. Obadiah, who fed a hundred prophets in Samaria (III Kings XVIII), signifies all preachers of the faith, who in this world nourish all believers with the food of the sacred Scriptures.

115. Jonah (Jonah II) figured the death of Christ, who rested for three days and nights in the heart of the earth, as if in the belly of a sea-monster.

[Note: [Col. 0115C]

116. Habakkuk. Blessed Jerome says in the prologue to Joel: “περιλαμβάνων” (*perilambanōn*), that is, “embracing,” or “an embrace,” or “wrestling.” And, as he likewise says in the prologue to Habakkuk, either because he is beloved of the Lord he is called “an embrace,” or because he engages in contest and wrestling—and, so to speak, an embrace—with God, he received the name of one who embraces, that is, wrestles. For no one dared, with such audacious speech, to summon God to a disputation concerning justice. In the same place he notes that among the Greeks and Latins the name Ἁβακούμ (*Habakoum*), that is, *Habacum*, was read corruptly, whereas among the Hebrews he is called *Habacuc*. SUAR.

In the same place. The words of Habakkuk in the Vulgate, chapter III, verse 4: “Horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden.” AREV.]

116. Habakkuk, the strong wrestler, is the faithful people who, established upon the heights, contemplate the Lord on the cross, saying: “Horns are in his hands; there the strength of his glory has been confirmed.”

[Note: [Col. 0115C]

117. Zephaniah. Blessed Jerome says, in chapter I of this same prophet, that some have translated the name Zephaniah as “watchtower,” and others as “the secret of the Lord.” SUAR.]

117. Zephaniah, whose name is interpreted as “watcher” or “the hidden thing of the Lord,” signifies those who through the secret of contemplation arrive at perfection in their merits.

[Note: [Col. 0115D]

118. Haggai and Zechariah. The reason for this allegory was that these two prophets, in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians and son of Hystaspes, when the seventieth year of the temple’s desolation—which Jeremiah had foretold—had been completed, wonderfully urged the Jews to restore the temple. SUAR.]

118. Haggai and Zechariah bore the figure of the saints, who in the life of this exile declare to us the future time of liberation.

119. Malachi, whose name is interpreted as “angel of the Lord,” bore the type of our Savior, who is called “the Angel of the Great Counsel.”

[Col. 0115C] 120. Jesus, the high priest, bore the figure of Christ, through whom the entrance from the exile of this world into the heavenly Jerusalem lies open to us.

[Col. 0116A] 121. Zerubbabel, the priest (II Esdras II and following), is a type of the Lord and Savior, who brought the people back from captivity and built a temple for the Lord out of living stones.

122. Judith and Esther bear the type of the Church; they punish the enemies of the faith and rescue the people of God from destruction.

123. Tobias bore the image of the ancient Law, whose eyes Jewish swallows blind while, by wrongly understanding the mysteries of light, they blind them.

124. Tobias, his son, bore the image of our Lord Jesus Christ, who illuminates by the brightness of his power the Law, hidden and blinded, as it were, by the darkness of the figure.

125. The three boys (Daniel III) prefigured the saints, who offered their bodies to persecution for the name of Christ.

126. Susanna (Daniel XIII) has the figure of the Church, whom false witnesses—the Jews—accuse as an adulteress against the Law.

127. King Nebuchadnezzar (IV Kings XXV) was a type of the devil, who, after conquering the people of heretics by the captivity of error, led them from Jerusalem—that is, from the Church—into Babylon, that is, into the confusion of ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 0116C]

128. The commander of the cooks. This allegory agrees with the Septuagint version. For what is said in Hebrew concerning Nebuzaradan, at the end of IV Kings, *rab tabbahim*, our translator renders “commander of the army”; but the Septuagint has ἀρχιμάγειρος (*archimagēiros*), that is, “commander of the cooks.” Lippomanus explains the reason for this variation learnedly in his *Catena* on Genesis XXXVII. Blessed Jerome says in the *Hebrew Questions*: “In many places Scripture mentions *archimagiros*, that is, ‘commanders of cooks,’ in place of ‘commanders of the army’; for μαγειρεύειν (*mageireuein*) is interpreted in Greek as ‘to kill.’ Blessed Augustine likewise writes in his *Questions on Genesis*: ‘Some do not wish to interpret it as “superintendent of the cooks,” who in Greek is called ἀρχιμάγειρος, but as “superintendent of the army,” to whom the power of killing belonged. For that is what the man whom Nebuchadnezzar sent was called, and in his case the primacy of the army is more properly found.’” SUAR.]

128. The commander of the cooks, who destroyed the walls of Jerusalem, signifies that all who serve the desire of the belly destroy the virtues of the soul.

[Note: [Col. 0116D]

129. The allegory concerning the Maccabees is explained more clearly at the end of the *Mystical Exposition of the Sacraments*, or *Questions*, in the chapter on the Maccabees. In that work many things that Isidore briefly touches upon in the *Allegories of the Old Testament* are explained more fully, as I have already mentioned. AREV.]

129. The seven Maccabees, who endured the most bitter tortures under Antiochus and were crowned most gloriously (II Maccabees VII), signify the sevenfold Church, which suffered a great slaughter of martyrs at the hands of the enemies of Christ and received the crown of heavenly glory.

## FROM THE NEW TESTAMENT

[Col. 0115]

[Col. 0115D] 136

[Note: [Col. 0115D]

130. I have set forth various opinions concerning the four distinctive symbols of the evangelists in my notes on Juvencus, book I, verse 3. Isidore follows the more common opinion in representing the faces of the animals assigned to each evangelist. Sedulius held the same view in his *Paschal Poem*, book I, verse 355. AREV.]

130. The four evangelists figurally express Jesus Christ under the likeness of four animals.

[Col. 0117A] 131. Matthew, announcing the same Redeemer as born and suffering, compares him to the likeness of a man.

132. Mark, beginning from the wilderness, assumes the figure of a lion and proclaims Christ’s unconquered kingdom and power.

133. Luke likewise preaches Christ as sacrificed for us through the mystical face of a calf.

[Note: [Col. 0117D]

134. But John. These first five allegories are taken from Ezekiel I; there blessed Jerome discusses this subject learnedly, treating it more fully in the prologue to his commentaries on Matthew. What blessed John writes concerning the same animals in Revelation IV agrees with Ezekiel’s prophecy. SUAR.]

134. But John, through the figure of an eagle, demonstrates that the same Lord, after the resurrection of the flesh, flew up into heaven.

135. Peter bears the person of the Church, which has the power to forgive sins and to lead people from the underworld back to the heavenly kingdoms (Matthew VI).

136. All the apostles also bear the type of the whole Church, because they too received a similar power in forgiving sins; and they also bear the form of the patriarchs, who through the word of preaching spiritually begot peoples for God throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0117D]

137. The seventy-two. To say that the world is completed in twenty-four hours is equivalent to saying that, through the movement of the first heaven—excluding the Empyrean—the lower celestial spheres are all carried around in twenty-four hours. SUAR.]

137. The seventy-two disciples signify the illumination of the whole world through the Gospel of the Trinity. For the entire world is completed in twenty-four hours, and this number, tripled on account of the same Trinity, is brought to seventy-two. They are sent two by two because they are to preach love of God and of neighbor, or because of the twin Testaments of the mysteries.

137. 138. Joseph typologically bore the likeness of Christ, who was appointed to guard the holy Church, which has neither stain nor wrinkle.

[Col. 0117C] 139. Mary signifies the Church, which, although betrothed to Christ, conceived us as a virgin from the Holy Spirit and also gives birth as a virgin (Matthew I).

140. Zechariah the priest, who became mute at the angel’s command (Luke I), displayed the silence of the Law and the prophets when Christ arrived.

141. John bore the form of the Law: he announced Christ and proclaimed the remission of sins through the grace of the washing.

[Note: [Col. 0117D]

142. I have commented on the Magi and the offering of gifts by which they worshiped Jesus Christ as God in my notes on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 12, verse 69. See also the notes on Juvencus, book I, verse 285, and on Sedulius, book II, verse 96. AREV.]

142. The Magi figured the peoples of the nations, who would come to know the light of faith. Through the gifts of the mysteries they indicated Christ: through frankincense, as God; through myrrh, as a man who suffered and was buried; and through gold, as the king of all ages (Matthew II).

[Col. 0118A] 143. Herod, who inflicted death on the infants (Matthew II), expressed the form of the devil, or of the nations, which, desiring to extinguish the name of Christ from the world, raged in the slaughter of the martyrs.

144. The mute in the Gospel signify those who do not confess the faith of Christ.

145. The blind signify those who in no way understand the faith they believe.

146. The deaf prefigure those who do not display obedience to the commandments.

147. The lame demonstrate those who neglect to fulfill the saving commandments.

148. The prudent man who built his house upon a rock signifies the faithful teacher who established in Christ the foundation of his doctrine and his life.

[Note: [Col. 0117D]

149. But the man who built his house upon sand. Blessed Chrysostom, in his treatment of Matthew VII, discusses this allegory and gives three reasons why wicked people are compared with sand: they are sterile and unfruitful; divided among various opinions, they do not cohere with one another; and they are innumerable, like sand, as in Revelation XX. Blessed Jerome, however, thinks that this applies particularly to heretics. SUAR.]

149. But the man who built his house upon sand designates a heretic, who builds a false doctrine in order to bring about a great ruin.

138

[Note: [Col. 0118D]

150. The leper. Bede appears to have taken this allegory from blessed Isidore; he was especially devoted to him and lived a hundred years later. SUAR.]

150. The leper whom Christ, descending from the mountain, first healed (Matthew VIII) indicates the human race, stained by the contagion of transgression.

151. When the Redeemer descended from the height of heaven, as if from a mountain, he drew this race away from the varied worship of demons and restored it to the unity of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0118D]

152. Blessed Augustine notes that the centurion, since Judea was already held under Roman garrisons, was a gentile; blessed Jerome says that he was a leader of the nations destined to believe. SUAR.]

152. The centurion (in the same place) signifies the faith of the nations, which, asking for the salvation of its son who was sick unto death, humbly said: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, I who persecuted your Church.”

153. The centurion’s servant and the daughter of the Canaanite woman, whom Christ saved without going to them (Matthew XV), display the same nations, whom the Lord did not visit with bodily presence but saved through faith in the word.

154. The Canaanite woman herself (in the same place) bears the figure of the Church from the nations, which, like a dog, sought crumbs from the table of the masters—that is, to be satisfied with the teachings of the apostles and prophets.

155. Peter’s mother-in-law, suffering from fever (Matthew VIII), signifies the Synagogue, inflamed by the heat of carnal desires; her daughter is that portion of believers which was given to Peter to govern.

[Note: [Col. 0118D]

156. The rejected scribe. Blessed Jerome says that the rejected scribe, seeing the greatness of the signs, wanted to follow the Savior in order to seek profit from his miraculous works; he desired the very thing that Simon Magus also wanted to buy from Peter. SUAR.]

156. The rejected scribe, who followed the Lord for the sake of profit (in the same place), signifies those who desire the faith of Christ not for the Lord’s sake but for worldly gain.

157. The demoniac whom the Lord healed from a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes (in the same place) signifies the gentile people subject to the worship of many demons.

158. The swineherds who fled and reported what had happened in the city (in the same place) signify the rulers of the impious, who, while fleeing the faith of Christ, nevertheless marvel at and proclaim his powers in astonishment.

[Note: [Col. 0119C]

159. The paralytic. The manuscript books are more correct, reading “a soul dissolved by vices,” than the printed editions, which have “a soul desolated by vices”; for the phrase alludes to the etymology of the Greek word. A paralytic is so called because he suffers from paralysis, a disease given this name by the Greeks because it loosens and dissolves the nerves, ἀπὸ τοῦ παραλύειν (*para-luein*), “to dissolve.” Thus Tertullian, accurately and elegantly, said in the *Apology* that Christ “restrains paralytics,” meaning “heals” them. SUAR.

In the *Etymologies*, book IV, chapter 7, section 25, paralysis is said to receive its name from the impairment of the body. But the notes observe that it should be read otherwise, so that a loosening or dissolution of the body is understood. AREV.]

159. The paralytic lying on a bed (Matthew IX) is the soul dissolved by vices in its body. When it has been healed by the grace of Christ through the forgiveness of sins, it immediately rises after recovering its former strength and carries the bed of the flesh on which it had previously lain in weakness back to the house of the virtues, so that it may restrain itself within the secrets of its conscience and no longer run loose amid outward pleasures.

[Note: [Col. 0119C]

160. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue. Blessed Chrysostom correctly writes that the woman did not dare approach the Lord openly because, according to the prescription of the Law, she was unclean. The divine miracle was ennobled by another wholly divine miracle, exceedingly worthy of reading, which Eusebius relates in book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14. SUAR.]

160. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, whom the Lord was going to heal, but before he reached her was touched from behind by a woman suffering from an issue of blood (in the same place), bore the figure of the Church coming from the nations. When it believed after the preaching, passion, and ascension of Christ, it touched the Lord, as it were, from behind, and deserved to receive salvation before the Synagogue.

161. The two blind men sitting beside the road (in the same place) signify both peoples, the Jews and the nations, approaching Christ through faith—he who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

[Col. 0119C]

[Note: [Col. 0119D]

162. In Grialius’s text, as also in other printed editions, *idolatria* is written instead of *idololatria*; the latter should be restored. AREV.]

162. The demon-possessed blind and mute man, whom the Savior is said to have healed (in the same place), indicates those who are converted from the idolatry of the nations to the faith of the Lord. After the worship of demons has been expelled from their hearts and they have first received the light of faith, their tongue is subsequently released for praising God, so that they confess the one whom earlier they denied.

163. The man with the withered hand (Matthew XII) signifies the Synagogue, or the soul unfruitful in works of mercy. When it is told, “Stretch out your hand,” it is admonished always to extend alms to the poor.

164. The man from whom the unclean spirit goes out and then occupies him again (in the same place) signifies the Jewish people and the repentant man. Through subsequent negligence, the pleasure of the flesh takes possession of the mind more fiercely, together with seven other spirits of vices: anger, greed, envy, gluttony of the belly, vainglory, fornication, and pride.

165. The master of the household who brings forth new and old things from his treasure (Matthew XIII) is Christ, bringing forth from his impenetrable wisdom the two Testaments: the Old, in which earthly happiness is promised, and the New, through which the kingdom of heaven is hoped for.

166. The man who sowed a mustard seed in his field (Luke XIII) is Christ, who sowed faith in the world, in which the birds of heaven—that is, spiritual souls—find rest.

[Note: [Col. 0119D]

167. The woman who hides the leaven. Hesychius, in book I on Leviticus, chapter 2, says: “She hid it in three measures of flour, signifying the Church, which ferments the mysteries of theology in the word of the Trinity.” In interpreting this allegory, blessed Jerome first stated that parables and the uncertain understanding of riddles never contribute to the authority of dogmas. But perhaps another author is rightly censured who employed this allegory not to shape the mind through piety but to establish the mystery of the Holy Trinity, contrary to the teaching of blessed Augustine in his letter to Vincentius the Donatist. It should be noted in passing that the *satum*, to which the Hebrew name *seach* corresponds—for *satum* is neither a Hebrew nor a Greek but a Syrian term—was a kind of measure containing one third of an ephah. Blessed Jerome sometimes translates *satum* as such, as in Genesis XVIII, where mention is also made of three *sata*. Thus Abraham says to Sarah: “Hasten, mix three sata of fine flour.” At other times he translates it as “bushel,” as in IV Kings VII: “Tomorrow a bushel of fine flour will be sold for one shekel, and two bushels of barley for one.” The Hebrew there has *seach*, that is, *satum*. Someone might therefore wonder why the same Jerome, explaining this parable in Matthew XIII, wrote: “The *satum* is a kind of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, holding one and a half bushels.” Without doubt he took this from Josephus, who says in book IX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 4: “The *satum* contains one Italian bushel and a half.” But lest a mark of error be imposed on so learned a man, it must be said that the bushel was not the same everywhere but varied according to the regions. Jansenius reasonably suspects, in chapter 57 of the distinguished work he called the *Harmony of the Gospels*, that the Lord mentioned three measures of flour in this parable because it may have been customary in Judea to prepare that much bread at one time for the use of the household. This agrees with the passage cited above from Genesis XVII and with several other places in sacred Scripture. If anyone makes the calculation carefully, he will find that an ephah, or three *sata*, holds somewhat more than ten *celemini* in Spain. SUAR.

In the same place. To explain the question Suarius raises concerning the *satum*, Isidore’s teaching should be compared with the notes on book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 26. AREV.]

167. The woman who hides the leaven in three measures (in the same place) signifies the wisdom of spiritual doctrine, fervent in the love of the Trinity.

168. The man who finds a hidden treasure in a field (Matthew XIII) is the one who, after selling everything in this world, acquires Christ and eternal life.

169. The five thousand men who were fed with five loaves and two fish (John VI) are the peoples of the Church, who through the five bodily senses are refreshed by Christ with the nourishment of the spiritual Law and are filled by the two Testaments, as by twin fish.

170. The four thousand men who are fed with seven other loaves (Mark VIII) are the same Church of the nations, which is spread through the four regions of the world and restored by the abundance of sevenfold grace.

171. The one who repeatedly fell, now into fire and now into water (Matthew XVII), signifies the world. Fire demonstrates burning desire, and water the pleasure of the flesh; seized by these, he is continually plunged downward through daily falling.

172. Moses and Elijah, who appeared with the Lord on the mountain (in the same place; Luke IX; Mark IX), are understood as the Law and prophecy, by whose voices the passion, resurrection, and glory of the Lord are declared.

[Note: [Col. 0121D]

173. This allegory concerning Christ as the good shepherd carrying the lost sheep on his shoulders was especially pleasing to the first Christians, as can still be seen in the paintings of ancient monuments that remain. AREV.]

173. The man who had a hundred sheep, who left them and sought the lost sheep and, having found it, carried it back on his shoulders (Luke XV), expressed a figure of Christ. Leaving the thousands of angels in heaven, he sought and found among the nations the sheep that had been lost in Adam and, as the good shepherd, carried it back to paradise on the shoulders of his cross.

174. The woman who found the lost drachma is the Church, which, when it finds through repentance the soul dragged away and lost in the devil’s snares, makes both angels and human beings rejoice.

175. The debtor of ten thousand talents (Matthew XVIII) signifies people who are liable to God through transgression of the ten commandments. But just as the bonds of sin are released for us when we ask the Lord, so let each of us forgive after the example of the Lord, lest, while we do not forgive those who sin against us their small debts, we be compelled to repay our greater debts with the interest of punishments.

176. The rich man who is compared with a camel (Matthew XIX; Mark X) indicates the person of the Jews, who glory in the power of the Law. Yet, because they cultivate earthly things, they do not possess the kingdom of heaven; there the people of the nations, twisted by crimes and burdened with the baggage of sins, enter more easily through the eye of a needle, as through the narrowness of passion, sorrows, and labors.

177. The master of the household who hires laborers for the vineyard and promises a denarius (Matthew XX) is Christ, who calls everyone to the worship of faith, promising them the reward of perfect blessedness.

178. The laborers hired at the first hour are those who obtained the worship of the faith from the beginnings of childhood.

[Col. 0122A] 179. Those hired at the third hour are those who approached the faith from adolescence.

180. Those hired at the sixth hour are those who believed at the age of youth.

181. Those who came at the ninth hour are those who, already declining from youth into old age, received grace.

[Note: [Col. 0121D]

182. At this point the nominative used for an ablative absolute should be noted, in *conservans Christus*—“Christ preserving”—in the former case and *impendens* in the latter, instead of *in illis conservante Christo*—“with Christ preserving them”—and *in istis impendente*—“with him showing mercy to these.” This manner of expression occurs more often in Isidore’s manuscripts than in the printed editions, from which, as I suppose, the editors removed it because they were convinced that it was not Isidore’s. But the matter should be judged otherwise. AREV.]

182. Those who went at the last hour (in the same place) are those who, already decrepit and called at the end of their lives, came to Christ. Yet they receive an equal reward of blessedness with those who came earlier: Christ preserves justice in those who labored from the first hour of their birth, and bestows mercy on those who labored for one hour of life.

183. The two sons sent to work in the vineyard (Matthew XXI) display the type of two peoples. The first sent is called the people of the nations, summoned through the understanding of nature to cultivate the divine work; yet he was initially disobedient and refused to go. When the Lord arrived, obedience, following upon his former disobedience, cleansed him. The second son sent is the Jewish people, who through knowledge of the Law replied, “Everything that the Lord has said we shall do”; but he is condemned because he not only transgressed the Law he professed but also raised murderous hands against the Lord of the vineyard himself.

184. The man who planted a vineyard (Matthew XXI; Luke XX) is God, who established Jerusalem. In it he built a tower and dug a winepress—that is, the temple and the altar—and often surrounded it, that is, fortified it with the defense of angels.

[Col. 0122C] 185. The tenants to whom he leased the vineyard (in the same place) are the people of Israel, who possessed Jerusalem under divine worship.

186. The servants who were sent at the time of the harvest and killed by the tenants (in the same place) are understood as the prophets, whose blood was shed by the Jews when they demanded from them the fruits of justice and of the Law.

187. The son sent last, whom the tenants threw out of the vineyard and killed (in the same place), is Christ, whom the Jews crucified, casting him outside the gates of Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0122D]

188. In these words Isidore perhaps seems to allude to the dispersion of the Jews, which continued in his time, as it does in ours. AREV.]

188. The tenants whom the lord of the vineyard destroys (in the same place) are also understood as the Jewish people, who, as it appears, were once scattered and slain. The farmers to whom the vineyard is commanded to be transferred signify the apostles or the apostles’ successors.

[Note: [Col. 0122D]

189. The king who made a wedding feast. Blessed Gregory treats this allegory explicitly, as he usually does, but thinks it safer to say that the king made the wedding feast for the king’s son when, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he joined the holy Church to him in the Virgin’s womb, as in a bridal chamber. The reason is that a marriage union ordinarily takes place between two persons, whereas it is impious to believe that there are two persons in Christ. SUAR.]

189. The king who made a wedding feast for his son (Matthew XXII) is understood as God the Father, who joined virgin flesh from a virgin to Christ. The servants who were sent to call those invited are the apostles and prophets, who called the Jews through the Law and the Gospel. But the Jews, at one time oppressed by earthly pleasures and at another by the burden of the flesh and the Law, despised the solemnity of the Lord’s coming; thus they showed themselves unworthy of eternal life, while the nations are shown to have entered.

190. The enraged king who sent his armies, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city (in the same place) is God the Father, who raised up Vespasian Caesar of the Romans. He devastated the people with the sword and utterly overthrew the city of Jerusalem together with everything belonging to it, so that it could no longer wage war.

191. The man without a wedding garment at the banquet, who became silent when the king spoke and whom the king ordered the servants to take away and cast into the outer darkness (in the same place), is the one who indeed rests in faith with the others; but if on the day of judgment he is found to have a garment of flesh polluted, he is immediately ordered by the angels to be taken away and plunged into the hell of eternal fire.

192. The two debtors, one of whom owed the moneylender five hundred denarii and the other fifty (Luke VII), signify the two peoples, namely the Jews and the nations. The one who owed fifty denarii bore the type of the Jews; the one who owed five hundred expressed the figure of the nations, who, having always been debtors from the beginning of the world, did not cancel the record of sin through repentance. When Christ arrived, they finally believed and received the more abundant fruit of mercy. Because more was forgiven to them by Christ, they love Christ more, as it is written: “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more.”

193. The seven brothers who married one woman and died without children (Mark XII) are understood as unbelieving people, who through the seven ages of the world spent their entire life on this earth without the fruit of righteousness.

194. The two in one bed (Matthew XXIV) figure those who, withdrawn from the crowds, seem in some way to devote themselves to the leisure of life.

195. The two women grinding (in the same place) are understood as those who are occupied with the business of temporal affairs.

196. The two in the field (in the same place) are those who labor in the ministry of the Church, as in the Lord’s field. When night arrives—that is, the adversity of the world—some of them remain in the faith and are taken up to life, while others depart and are left for punishment.

197. The five wise virgins (Matthew XXV) are understood as all holy souls. Since through the five bodily senses they admit no corruption of the heart, they are therefore counted by the number five.

198. The five foolish virgins, who have no oil in their vessels (in the same place), are those souls who indeed possess bodily integrity but do not preserve within their conscience the testimony of good works, since they glory in their appearance before human beings and not in their hearts before God. Therefore, because they do not carry the brightness of the mind in the vessels of their breasts, when the Lord arrives they are excluded from the joy of his kingdom.

199. The man departing abroad, who entrusted his possessions to his servants (in the same place), is Christ, who, returning to heaven after his resurrection, entrusted evangelical grace to evangelical merchants to put out at interest. The first servant, in the five talents given to him, received the five books of the Law, which he increased through the teaching and practice of the ten commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0123D]

200. In Grialius’s text it read *ea quae* instead of *eaque*, which is correctly printed in the other editions as well; the error seems to have slipped into Grialius’s text. AREV.]

200. Another, with two talents, acquired the two Testaments and doubled them by piously dispensing them in the moral and mystical sense.

201. The third, under the figure of one talent, obscured the gift of grace he had received in earthly pleasures; therefore he was cast into hell, because he produced no fruit from it.

[Note: [Col. 0123D]

202. “Others in the first servant.” This refers to Saint Gregory, to whose work he was especially devoted; Gregory treats the present allegory in this manner. SUAR.]

202. Others understood the senses of the heart and body as received in the first servant, understanding and action in the second, and reason in the third.

203. The young son of the widow whom the Lord raised from the dead outside the gates of the city (Luke VII) signifies one who openly commits some deadly crime. Having sometimes heard the word of God, he rises from the death of sin and begins to live through Christ by repentance; and he is restored to his widowed mother, that is, to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0123D]

204. The man who was descending. To avoid error, the heavenly paradise should be understood as that Jerusalem, the city of peace, from whose blessedness Adam fell, made wretched through sin. He descended into Jericho, that is, into the world, in which everything that arises dies, like the moon, which Jericho signifies. For Adam, who, if he had obeyed the divine command, would also by divine favor have been immortal, having violated it deservedly suffered the misery of death and many other hardships. Blessed Augustine explains this allegory in this way in his book *On Questions of the Gospels*. SUAR.]

204. The man who was descending from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers (Luke X) figures Adam himself in his race. When he descended from the heavenly paradise into the world, he fell among the angels of darkness.

205. The descending Samaritan, who healed his wounds (in the same place), is Christ, our guardian, who descended from heaven and healed the human race of the wounds of sins.

206. The innkeeper (ibid.) signifies the apostles, or their successors, who restore our weakness through evangelical preaching [Col. 0124D].

207. Martha, who received Christ into her house and ministered to him there (ibid.), signifies the Church, which in this life receives Christ into her heart and labors in works of righteousness.

208. Mary, her sister, who sat beside the feet of Christ [Col. 0125A] and listened to the word (ibid.), represents that same Church, which in the age to come will cease from every work and rest in the sole contemplation of Christ’s wisdom.

209. The man who at midnight asked his friend for three loaves (Luke XI) expresses an image of anyone who, amid tribulation, asks the Lord to give him knowledge of the Trinity.

146 [Note: [Col. 0125D]

210. In the Gospel of Saint Luke, chapter 12, verse 20, it now reads as follows: “Fool! This night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared—for whom will they be?” AREV.]

210. The rich man whose field produced abundant crops (Luke XII) signifies a man devoted to luxury and abounding in sins. The Lord rebukes him as he desires to sin still more excessively, saying: “Fool! This night they take your soul away from you; and the things you have prepared—for whom will they be?”

211. The five in one house—that is, the father, mother, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law—of whom two are divided against three and three against two (ibid.), signify the human race separated from one another in faith and religion: partly in the division of schism, represented by the two, and partly in the number of the Trinity, represented by the three. For the son was divided against his father—that is, the people coming from the Gentiles against the devil, with whom it had previously been associated. The daughter was also divided against her mother—that is, the people believing from among the Jews against the impious Synagogue. And the daughter-in-law was divided against her mother-in-law—that is, the Church from the Gentiles against the Synagogue, the mother of her bridegroom, from whom Christ had been begotten according to the flesh. These people are separated from one another, some seeking earthly glory and others heavenly glory.

[Col. 0125C] [Note: [Col. 0125D]

212. The first two Greek letters of the name of Jesus, ι and η, were used by ancient Christians as an abbreviation of the name Jesus. I have listed the writers who recognized the number eighteen in these two letters as having some mystical or allegorical interpretation in *Prudentiana*, no. 194 and following, with notes. For *insinuat*, perhaps read *insinuant*. AREV.]

212. The eighteen Galileans upon whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them (Luke XIII) signify the destruction of the Jewish people. For among the Greeks eighteen is expressed by the letters iota, ι, and eta, η; with these forms the name Jesus is written. Because those people refused to believe in him, they were likewise overthrown by the Romans together with their city.

213. The man who planted a fig tree in his vineyard is Christ, who established the Synagogue among the Jewish people. When the Lord ordered it to be cut down as though useless, the apostles, its cultivators, dug around it a trench of humility and applied dung—that is, confession of sins. Thus, at the end, by believing it will be changed for the better and will produce abundant fruits of righteousness.

[Col. 0126A] 214. The woman who had suffered from an infirmity for eighteen years and was healed by the Lord (Luke XIII) is a type of the Church, which at the end of time attained the salvation of faith. For this world is completed in six ages, [147] though its time has a threefold division: one before the law, another under the law, and a third under grace. Thus six times three makes eighteen; by this number the time of our salvation is signified, when, released from the bonds of Satan by which we had been bent over, we receive the gift of salvation and the hope of heavenly contemplation.

215. The dropsical man whom the Lord healed (Luke XIV) represents those whom the overflowing discharge of carnal pleasures weighs down.

216. The man who had two sons (Luke XV) is God, possessing two peoples. The elder represented the Jews, who remained in the worship of God; the other, the younger, represented the Gentiles, who, having abandoned their Creator, became slaves to idols. When the latter returned in the poverty of faith, God the Father mercifully received him, and for his conversion sacrificed his only Son under the figure of the calf. He also gave him the ring of faith and clothed him in the robe of immortality. Although the Jewish brother was tormented by envious resentment, nevertheless, because of the younger son’s salvation, the chorus of angels sings for joy.

217. The wasteful steward, whom the master ordered removed from his stewardship, and who, defrauding his master, remitted part of what the debtors owed so that he might have something by which to live afterward (Luke XVI), has been proposed as an example for us. For if he deserved to be praised by his master because, defrauding him, he provided for himself in the future from another’s property, how much more can we please Christ if from our own possessions we show mercy to those in need, by whom we may be received into eternal dwellings?

[Note: [Col. 0125D]

218. “The rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen signifies …” Theophylact, a particularly learned writer, did not hesitate to affirm that the account of the rich man and Lazarus was not history but a fictional parable narrated by the Lord. Yet the name Lazarus clearly argues against him. For blessed Chrysostom says admirably, in his homily on Luke, concerning the father and the two sons: “Names should not be given in a parable. For those stories are parables in which an example is presented and the names are omitted.” Origen also says splendidly, in chapter 1 of *Job*: “Moses, who is the author of the book, necessarily mentioned Job by name, lest, if he had spoken only of a man, he should be thought to have fabricated some argument.” The same judgment applies to the rich man and Lazarus, according to Ambrose, Cyril, Damascene, and Euthymius. The latter also says that the rich man’s name was passed over in silence by the Evangelist as though he were worthy of hatred—for it is written in Psalm XV, “I will not take their names upon my lips”—whereas the beggar’s name was handed down to memory as though he were worthy of love. Some say, on the basis of Jewish tradition, that at that time the rich man was called Nineusis, and that this beggar was Lazarus. This is what Euthymius says. If Theophylact had imitated Chrysostom, a man of outstanding learning and holiness, in this matter as in most others, he would certainly never have departed from the common opinion. SUAR.]

218. The rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen (ibid.) signifies the pride of the Jews, once flourishing through the splendor of empire or the excellence of honor.

148 219. The ulcerated beggar (ibid.) represents the Gentile people, humbled through confessions of sins.

220. The rich man’s five brothers, who was being tormented in hell (ibid.), are understood as the Jews, who are placed under the five books.

[Col. 0127A] 221. The ten lepers whom the Lord cleansed (Luke XVII) signify heretics, who in the variety of their colors possess the diversity of schisms. They are therefore sent to the priests so that, every variation of error being wiped away, they may receive the sacrament of unity.

222. The unjust judge, who did not fear the Lord but nevertheless heard the widow who persistently pleaded with him (Luke XVIII), is a likeness demonstrating how great a hope one who continually entreats the Lord ought to have, since the widow’s frequent persistence in pleading prevailed even upon the ears of an unjust judge. The widow herself may signify the Church, which by its perseverance asks vengeance upon its enemies, the devil or heretics.

223. The Pharisee praying in the temple (ibid.) is the Jewish people, which exalts its merits on the basis of the justifications of the law.

224. The tax collector, however (ibid.), is the Gentile people, which, standing far from God, confesses its sins. One, through pride, withdrew and was humbled; the other, by confession, merited to draw near to God and was exalted.

225. The blind man sitting beside the road (ibid.) represents the Gentile people, which through the grace of Christ merited the illumination of faith.

226. Zacchaeus (Luke XIX) is the Gentile people, small in the grace of merits, which nevertheless, lifted up from earthly actions, contemplates the mystery of Christ through the wood of the Lord’s cross.

227. The nobleman who went away to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself (ibid.) is our Redeemer, who reached the ends of the earth to receive a kingdom among the Gentile peoples.

228. The citizens who did not want him to reign over them (ibid.) are understood as the Jews, who rejected Christ as king.

229. The servant who, having received one mina, acquired ten (ibid.) signifies teachers who, having received the grace of the Gospel, used it well in the ten commandments of the Decalogue and, by teaching, acquired many in the faith. Therefore, when the Lord comes, they will be praised because they have gained profit.

230. The one who acquired five from the one (ibid.) represents those who, keeping God’s commandment, attain knowledge of the law written in the five books of Moses, and by teaching it lend it out for the necessary use of salvation.

[Col. 0127D] 231. The one who preserved the mina itself in a handkerchief (ibid.) shows the person who treated the gift of grace entrusted to him delicately, idly, and carelessly. He therefore rightly loses the grace bestowed upon him, because through negligence he scorned to preach, so that what he had labored for might be increased.

232. The widow who cast two small coins into the treasury (Luke XXI) represents the faithful soul of one who keeps in the treasury of his heart the fruit of love for God and neighbor.

233. The bridegroom (John II) is Christ, whose wedding is celebrated with the Church. In their union water is changed into wine, because believers pass through the grace of the washing to the crown of the Passion.

234. The master of the feast (ibid.) is understood as Moses, who marvels that through Jesus a better and holier people has been gathered into the Gospel than the earlier people led out of Egypt. The wine running out shows that the grace of the Holy Spirit has been taken away from the Jews and bestowed through the apostles upon the Gentiles.

235. The Samaritan woman (John IV) is mystically understood as the Synagogue, subjected to the five books of the law as though to five husbands, according to the literal sense. The Lord mercifully urges her to draw living water—that is, to receive the grace of the washing, or the hidden understanding of the law according to the fleshly sense.

236. The adulterous woman whom the Jews bring before the Lord to be stoned (John VIII) is the Church from the Gentiles. Having first abandoned God, she had committed fornication with idols. The Synagogue, in its jealous zeal, wished her killed, but Christ saves her through the remission of sin and does not allow her to perish, for he knows how to grant pardon to sinners.

237. Simon the leper (Matthew XXVI) is the Gentile people, which has been cleansed by the Redeemer.

238. The woman who anointed the Lord’s head with ointment (ibid.) is the Church, which offers the fragrance of the fruit of its work and faith to the praise of God and the glory of Christ.

239. The angel at whose descent the water surrounded by five porticoes was stirred (John V) is Christ. At his coming the Jewish people, enclosed within the five books, was disturbed. For when the angel descended, the water was stirred and the sick man was healed; when Christ descended from heaven, that same people was stirred by his Passion, and the world was healed.

[Note: [Col. 0127D]

240. This man blind from birth, of whom the Gospel speaks, is often represented on ancient Christian monuments, as may be seen in Bottari, *Roma Sotterranea*, vol. I, p. 179. AREV.]

240. The man blind from birth whom the Lord, after anointing his eyes, sent to wash at the pool of Siloam (John IX) signifies the human race, corrupted from birth—that is, from the first man—by the darkness of errors. The Lord smeared his eyes with spittle and clay because the Word became flesh. He commanded him to wash his eyes in the pool so that, baptized in Christ, he might receive the law of faith and believe in the one who appeared in humility in the world.

241. Lazarus, whom the Lord raised from the tomb on the fourth day, stinking (John XI), signifies the world, which had been corrupted by the most grievous habit of sin, yet on the fourth day of death is raised again. The first day is death, the mortality inherited from Adam; the second day of death is the transgression of the natural law; the third is the violation of the law that was given; the fourth day of death is contempt for evangelical preaching. On that day, looking upon his work, the Lord mercifully deigned to raise him.

242. The servant of the high priest, whose right ear was cut off (Matthew XXVI), is the Israelite people, made a servant because of unbelief. It loses its right ear when it passes over to the left through an understanding of the letter. For this people, in those who believe in him, the Lord restores the hearing of faith and makes it obedient to the evangelical commandment.

243. The high priest who tore his garment during the Lord’s Passion (ibid.) indicates the Hebrew people stripped of the priesthood and deprived of the kingdom, which has been torn apart.

244. Barabbas, who was released to the Jews (Matthew XXVII), signifies the Antichrist, whom those who had gone astray deserved to receive in place of Christ.

245. Herod and Pilate, who, although they were at odds, were joined in friendship during the Lord’s Passion (Luke XXIII), indicate that the two peoples—the circumcised and the Gentiles—were formerly divided, but through the Lord’s Passion were brought into agreement in faith.

246. Simon of Cyrene, whom they compelled to carry the cross (ibid.), [151] is understood as the Gentile people, which, a stranger to the law, becomes obedient to the Gospel. He himself became the bearer of Christ’s cross and the carrier of faith.

[Col. 0130A] 247. The two thieves (ibid.) express the peoples of the Jews and the Gentiles. One, unbelieving, blasphemes Christ hanging on the cross; the other, faithful, rebukes the blaspheming Jews.

248. The four soldiers who divided Jesus’ garments into four portions among themselves (Psalm CXVIII, 162) prefigured the four parts of the world, which divided Christ’s sayings among themselves, as it is written: “I will rejoice over your words, as one who finds abundant spoils.”

249. The women who announce the resurrection to the Lord’s apostles signify the law and the prophecy, which, before it was revealed, proclaimed the glory of Christ’s resurrection like forerunners.

[Note: [Col. 0129B]

250. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 94, no. 18, I noted a certain variant reading at the end of the *Allegories* from Vatican Codex 629, which I described there. AREV.]

250. The seven disciples with whom the Lord is described as having dined after his resurrection indicate the seventh rest after the future resurrection. Through it all the saints will be satisfied by Christ with the nourishment of eternal blessedness. May Christ lead us to that fullness. Amen.

[Col. 0129]

# OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, ON THE BIRTH AND DEATH OF THE FATHERS WHO ARE PRAISED IN SCRIPTURE. (C, S)

152 **Preface.**

[Col. 0129] [Note: [Col. 0129C]

CHAPTER I. 1. Concerning these matters, see Jerome, Epiphanius, Dorotheus’ *Synopsis*, and Josephus. FONTIDONIUS.

Ibid. Peter Fontidonius compared the book *On the Birth and Deaths of the Fathers* with eight manuscript books and added certain brief notes. I shall therefore cite them under the name Fontidonius, which I have appended. What should be thought about this book was explained at length in *Isidoriana*, chapter 61. AREV.]

1. The births or deeds of certain holy and most distinguished men, together with their genealogies, are set down in this little book; their dignity, death, and burial are also recorded in concise statements. Although these matters are known to all who read extensively through the Scriptures, they return more easily to memory when read in brief discourse.
