# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0131A]

2. Adam, the first-formed man and cultivator of paradise, prince of the human race and of sin, made in the image of God, set over the universe, who gave names to creatures and received power to rule over them.

3. Established amid the delights of flourishing paradise, among fragrant groves of spices and fields blooming with flowers, he spent the joys of a new life as a dweller in the countryside: there the fertile earth remained green in perpetual spring, and a flowing spring glided along in a fourfold stream.

4. But after, through the serpent’s deceit and also through a woman’s tongue, he was defiled by touching the tree and profaned the blessedness of the place, he was cast out of paradise and, as a laborer groaning, inhabited earth rough with thorns. Having lost immortality, after the passage of nine hundred and thirty years he returned to the dust from which the flesh had taken its origin. From this point onward his descendants lamented that, through the sin of this ancestor, they had been made exiles from paradise and subjected to labor and death.

[Note: [Col. 0131D]

5. The opinion that Adam was buried on Mount Calvary was received and approved by the ancients after Origen; a small shrine was also erected there and consecrated to Adam’s worship and veneration. See Bolland., vol. IV, February, p. 449. Saint Jerome reports rabbinic traditions concerning the tomb at Arbee of Adam, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in his *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. AREV.]

5. He was buried in the place called Arbee, which took its name from the number—that is, four—for three patriarchs are buried there, and Adam is the fourth. This place is not far from Hebron, the metropolitan city of the Philistines, where it is said that the giants once lived and where David was later anointed king. It is a city belonging to the lot of Judah, set apart for the priests, twenty-two miles south of Jerusalem.

# CHAPTER TWO

[Note: [Col. 0131D]

6. It is uncertain by what instrument Abel was killed. Painters commonly portray Cain armed with a jawbone against his brother, but there is absolutely no foundation for this. Prudentius asserts that Abel was killed with a hoe in the preface to the *Hamartigenia*, verse 16; I have indicated more on this matter from interpreters of Sacred Scripture in the note there. AREV.

[Col. 0132D] Ibid. In Grialius it has *substractus* for *subtractus*. AREV.]

6. Abel, the son of Adam and shepherd of sheep, innocent in life, patient in death, not silent after death, first among martyrs, supreme in obedience, pleasing to God in sacrifices, displeasing to his brother in merits: him impious Cain, a new murderer, driven by envy, struck down with iron not yet stained by blood, while the innocent iron still lacked the crime of human bloodshed.

# CHAPTER THREE

7. Enoch, son of Jared, seventh from Adam, pleasing to God, unaware of evil, ignorant of death, who, unable to endure the distress of wicked men, was withdrawn from the world’s destructive associations [variant: contacts] and, while still living, merited to be transferred to the place from which the first-formed man had been expelled. He was taken away at the age of three hundred and sixty-five. He remains in the body to this day; at the consummation of the world, together with Elijah, he will return to the mortal condition of life [variant: restoring it at the end of the age].

155 # CHAPTER FOUR

8. Noah, son of Lamech, tenth from Adam, second father and restorer of the world, distinguished in righteousness, patient in hope, wise in action, the only just man on earth. At God’s command he built the ark; warned, he entered it. He did not dread the turbulent waves of the flood, nor fear the crashes of the winds or the murmurs of heaven. He is carried through the storms but does not sink; he associates with serpents and beasts but is not terrified. Wild creatures submit their necks to him, and birds serve him.

[Note: [Col. 0132D]

9. Marchio Joannes de Serpos, who published or arranged for the publication of several learned books for the cause of the Armenian Catholics, cites in his *Historical Compendium of Armenia*, book I, no. 6, authors who maintain that the remains of Noah’s ark are still preserved on Mount Ararat. AREV.]

9. For he sent out a bird and waited for its return, but was deceived by the crow’s treacherous behavior; through the service of the dove, carrying a branch of the peace-bearing tree in its beak, he received the message. When the doors of the ark had been opened, he allowed the beasts and all living creatures to depart for seven days. He himself afterward went out with his children, praised God, and joyfully offered sacrifices. The ancients testify that his ark came to rest in Armenia upon the mountains of Ararat. He died in his nine-hundred-and-fiftieth year.

# CHAPTER FIVE

[Note: [Col. 0132D]

10. Jerome, letter to Evagrius. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 1. FONT.

Ibid. In Grialius’ edition it is cited from *Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 1, where there is no mention of Melchizedek, although he is discussed in book VII, chapter 6, and book VIII, chapter 5. AREV.]

10. Melchizedek, king of Salem, the first priest of God Most High and the first offerer of the true sacrifice, whose origin is hidden. The Hebrews say that he was Shem, Noah’s firstborn and Abraham’s great-great-grandfather. He is the father of the fathers, the source of the prophets and apostles; he is the one who, by the blessing of paternal affection, merited to be lord of his brother. Walking backward, he covered his father’s nakedness and did not mock the drunken man like a shameless and rejected son, but veiled him like a modest one.

11. Hence it happened that, among the Jews under the law, parents were never seen naked by their sons. He blessed Abraham when he returned after victory; likewise, as a type of the true sacrifice, he first offered bread and wine from the fruits of the earth to God as a sacrificial offering, because priesthood and kingship properly belonged to the firstborn before Aaron exercised the priesthood.

12. He was also the first of all, after the flood, to found the city of Salem, in which he also reigned. It was later called Jebus or Solyma and is now called Jerusalem by a derivative name [Col. 0133A]. He lived six hundred years and endured until the seventieth year of Isaac’s life. He died and was buried in his own city, Jerusalem.

# CHAPTER SIX

[Note: [Col. 0133D]

13. “Parent,” that is, a relative or kinsman, as below, chapter 9. FONT.

Ibid. What Isidore says, “first in faith,” Prudentius explained at the beginning of the *Psychomachia* with this verse: “Abraham, faithful, the first path of belief.” The Florence Codex adds somewhat: “Willing, who saw the Trinity in a type and venerated unity in the mystery; he was obedient,” and so on. AREV.]

13. Abraham, father of the nations, son of Terah, from the line of Shem, a Chaldean by nationality, first in faith, a voluntary exile, obedient in commandments, believing in promises, poor in his homeland, wealthy in his wandering, victorious in battles, and not greedy in victory. He overcame five kings, stripped them of their spoils, and brought back his captive kinsman.

14. He was so elevated that he saw the Trinity in a type and venerated unity in the mystery; so faithful that, in the promised offspring, he believed God against the hope afforded by nature; so righteous and devout that he did not place his affection for his only child above the divine will. Without hesitation, obeying the command, the religious murderer armed his right hand with a sword to sacrifice his son.

15. When he drew the iron, intending to offer his only child as a victim, he neither lost his son nor forfeited the sacrifice. For he offered his son in sacrifice and sacrificed the ram in place of his son. He lived one hundred and seventy-five years and was buried in the field of Ephron, in the double cave. They say that Adam was buried in its inner part and Abraham in the outer. This place, as Josephus reports, is seven stadia from the city of Hebron; there, he says, Abraham and his sons have a tomb magnificently constructed of marble.

[Note: [Col. 0133D]

16. Abraham’s tomb was discussed at no. 5. Concerning the oak of Mamre, which some translate as “terebinth” from the Hebrew word, in addition to Saint Jerome, Eusebius, Josephus, and others write about it; they are cited in Calmet’s biblical dictionary. AREV.]

16. He also asserts that a great terebinth tree had existed there from the foundation of the world. Blessed [Col. 0133C] Jerome writes that it endured until the reign of Constantine. It is the oak of Mamre of the Amorite, who was Abraham’s friend; among the Gentiles it was held in such veneration that they enclosed it within a circuit of walls and honored it with solemn worship.

# CHAPTER SEVEN

[Note: [Col. 0133D]

17. Abimelech, Ochozach, and Phicol repented. Genesis XXVI. FONT.

Ibid. In Grialius’ edition it was *sacrifandum*. In its place I confidently set *sacrificandus*, which is also found in Breulius and others. AREV.]

17. Isaac, Abraham’s son, born by promise in the land of Canaan, called the eternal seed, distinguished by the chastity of married life, prompt to grant favor and ready to forgive. He expelled those who excluded him, not with weapons but by patience; he received the repentant with kindness; and through love of God he showed such honor to his father that he willingly approached the altar to be sacrificed and did not refuse death as a figure of Christ. He died at the age of one hundred and eighty and was buried beside his father.

# CHAPTER EIGHT

[Col. 0134A]

[Note: [Col. 0134D]

18. Variant: “Innocent, dwelling at home.” Variant: “Innocently.” FONT.]

18. Jacob, son of Isaac, born in the land of Canaan, beloved of his mother, supplanter of his brother, also humble, simple, and innocent, dwelling at home. After he had seized the blessing of the firstborn, he obeyed his mother, patiently yielded to his brother’s anger, and, leaving his homeland and parents, became an exile and endured prolonged servitude. He bore the hardship of hunger and cold; he served his father-in-law, tended the flock as a hired shepherd, and awaited his wages not from the division of the flock but from its increase. Having gone abroad, while he lacked human companionship, he merited the company of angels.

19. He wrestled with the Lord and prevailed; he saw God face to face. Driven by the scarcity of famine, he entered Egypt with his illustrious offspring. After completing one hundred and forty-seven years, he paid the debt owed to nature and was buried with his fathers.

158 # CHAPTER NINE

[Note: [Col. 0134D]

20. Isidore seems to follow the opinion of those who place the city of Segor on the southern shore of the Dead Sea, so that it belongs to Arabia. Some relate that the same city was swallowed up when the earth opened immediately after Lot departed from it, but their arguments are not sufficiently firm. The interpreters discuss these matters more fully. AREV.]

20. Lot, son of Haran and Abraham’s kinsman, father of Moab and Ammon, born among the Chaldeans, was a just and hospitable man who lived piously and chastely among the wicked people of Sodom. Because of the sole duty of hospitality, he was even made the host of angels. He escaped the sulfurous destruction and the conflagration of the Sodomites and afterward remained in the city of Segor, which lies beside the Dead Sea, where balsam grows and palm trees produce abundant fruit.

# CHAPTER TEN

21. Joseph, prince of Egypt, son of Jacob by Rachel, born in the land of Canaan, blessed as Israel’s firstborn and receiving Reuben’s primacy, beloved by his father and alone, above the others, heir to his father’s possession.

22. Raised up against him by jealousy, his brothers cast him into a pit; through envy he was sold; humbled even to servitude, patient even to imprisonment, chaste even amid suffering, he became wise in interpretation, prudent in counsel concerning the future, a sharer in kingship, a provident arranger of abundance, a just dispenser during famine, and ready to repay evil with the favor of a good return. He did not repay his brothers for their injury but supplied them with the support necessary to drive away their hunger.

[Note: [Col. 0134D]

23. The Vulgate, Genesis XLVIII, XXII, reads: “I give you one portion beyond your brothers.” In its place the Septuagint has: “I give you Shechem, a distinguished portion above your brothers.” Others read “Sichem.” The Hebrew word is *Sechem* or *Sichem*, which the Vulgate retains elsewhere, as does Isidore here. AREV.]

23. He held the chief position in Egypt for eighty years. When he had completed one hundred and ten years of life, by the favor of a long repose he brought his final day to a close. He was buried in Egypt, [Col. 0134D] and the children of Israel transported his bones to the city of Shechem, the city of his father Jacob [Col. 0135A], which both Latins and Greeks now call Sichima. It is the city now called Neapolis, belonging to the Samaritans, where his tomb can still be seen to this day.

24. Judah, distinguished by the noble lineage of royal succession, to whom military command was entrusted and the kingdom of Israel, who gave the nation its name from his own, exceedingly powerful like a lion in the strength of his kingdom and brilliant in the splendor of his power. The succession of this kingdom did not cease until Christ, like a lion’s cub, arose from his stock and the hope of the nations, proceeding from a virginal womb, miraculously shone forth.

25. Reuben, the firstborn son of Israel, older than his brothers in age but inferior in the number of his descendants, defiled his father’s bed and lost the rank of firstborn dignity.

35. Ephraim, the seed of Joseph and adopted son of Israel, and, among the number [161] of the patriarchs, left to the blessing of the testament; younger than his brother in age but preferred to him by the greater grace of blessing, stronger among all the tribes and an unconquered ruler among his brothers. 36. Manasseh, expanded into thousands, who together with his father Joseph mystically underwent tribute [variant: possessed a tribe]. [Col. 0136B] These are the fathers [variant: branches] of the apostles and the princes of the Jewish people, the tribes of Jacob and the illustrious offspring of Israel. # CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR

[Note: [Col. 0136D]

37. Isidore, together with Ambrose and Augustine, holds that this is the same Job as Joab of Genesis XXXVI; Jerome holds otherwise, in his *Hebrew Questions* and *Questions on Genesis*, question 36.

—Variant: “Moreover, he patiently endured his wife [who endured] his losses.”]

37. Job, son of Zerah of Bozrah, king of the Idumeans, fourth after Esau, successor to Balak son of Beor, a Gentile man, distinguished in faith, supreme in humility, preeminent in hospitality, gentle in discipline, generous in almsgiving, rich in possessions, suddenly made poor, wealthy in children, suddenly bereaved: he was handed over to temptation, but armed against temptation with the breastplate of faith [variant: armed with the breastplate of the faith of religion]. He became glorious in the contest, even-tempered in sorrow, endured the loss of his possessions, grieved the deaths of his children, and patiently received the wounds of his body [variant: accepted them]. Amid his sufferings he always glorified God; he also wisely endured his wife when she gave wicked counsel. He overcame his friends’ arguments by reason. Therefore, for such great virtue of patience, he was raised up at the end by a double reward, receiving, after the loss of his possessions, a manifold splendor of blessings [variant: gifts].

38. For after the night of sorrow he brought forth a day; after the stench of his ulcers, he produced the fragrance of cassia; after his rejection, he earned the horn of royal anointing, and he took up the pipe in the accent of praise. He lived for another one hundred and forty years after the affliction, and all the days of his life were two hundred and forty-eight years. He died [Col. 0136D] 162 and was buried in his own region. The Hebrews assert that he was not of the race of Esau, but descended from the stock of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, and that he lived in the time of the patriarchs. For Nahor begot Hus, from whose stock he is believed to have been born, according to what is noted at the beginning of his book: “There was a man in the land of Hus whose name was Job.”

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0137A]

[Note: [Col. 0137D]

39. Philo, Josephus, and Aben Ezra say that the name is Egyptian.]

39. Moses, son of Amram from the tribe of Levi, leader and prophet of Israel, adopted son of the king’s daughter, friend of God, lord of Pharaoh, was summoned at the flaming bush that burned without being consumed by angelic voices. To strengthen him by this sign, God commanded that his extended hand should become lifeless, and then restored strength, movement, and heat to it when he drew it back [Alternative reading: color]. His face was illumined by the hope [Perhaps: appearance] of future glory. As a certain wise man says, he was humble in refusing the ministry, obedient in accepting it, faithful in preserving it, exceedingly watchful in seeking it, vigilant in governing the people, forceful in correcting, ardent in loving, patient in enduring. On behalf of his subjects he interposed himself before God when he was consulting, and opposed himself to him when he was angry.

[Note: [Col. 0137D]

40. A noteworthy discrepancy occurs in Scripture, which may be seen among the various readings. [Col. 0138D] It seems that one should read “the champion of God’s Israel.” AREV.]

40. For the freedom of the people he exposed his own safety; he feared neither the threats nor the weapons of the most savage king. Indeed, he raised his staff against his dragons, and by the hand of God he struck the power of the attackers of Israel with ten plagues. First he turned the springs and rivers into blood; then he filled the cities with a multitude of frogs and the air with clouds of flies; he ravaged all growing things with locusts; he brought death upon the animals; he struck human beings with sores; he devastated the lands with hail; he covered the sky with darkness; and with overwhelming terror he killed their firstborn.

41. After this he stripped the Egyptians, and, having led out the people, opened a path through the wilderness, with a pillar of fire going before them. Without delay he divided the sea as they crossed, restraining the heaps of water on either side and providing the advancing people with a road on dry ground. Then he overwhelmed the enemies with the waves and, by the touch of wood, changed the bitter waters into sweetness. Moreover, amid these events he provided heavenly food for Israel when they were hungry and filled the camp sites with the food of birds.

42. He also struck the rock, and at once abundant streams flowed from the hard surface of the stones. He climbed to the summit of Mount Sinai to behold the face of the Lord; there he endured a fast of forty days. Descending, he burned the calf, struck down the sacrilegious with the sword, handed over to the people the law he had received from God, and established the rites of religious worship.

43. Amid these events he also waged wars, became renowned for victories, and, holding the staff in his hand, overcame enemies whom he did not touch. He healed the deadly bites of asps by the sight of a bronze serpent. When the bonds of the earth were broken open, he cast Dathan and Abiron alive into the deep chasm. [Col. 0137D] Finally, he climbed Mount Nebo and, with the Lord showing it to him, looked upon the promised land. He died at the Lord’s command on Mount Abarim and was buried by the Lord in the valley of Moab, which is in Arabia.

44. He ruled the people of God in the wilderness for forty years and died at the age of one hundred and twenty. Some, however, affirm that he is still alive because his tomb is not found. And because he appeared with Elijah to the Lord on Mount Tabor, sacred Scripture most certainly testifies that he died, not that he was taken away.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0138A]

45. Aaron, Moses’ brother, a distinguished companion in miracles, and the first priest of the Lord under the Law, whose staff, chosen by lot, blossomed with leaf and bud. Carrying the censer in his right hand, he opposed himself to the raging flame; standing between the living and the dead, he prevented the fire from passing over to the ranks of the living by placing his own body in its way. Through the offering of victims and the sacrifice of blood he foreshadowed the future passion of Christ; through the order of his lineage and succession he transmitted the right and authority of the priesthood.

46. In the fortieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, when he was one hundred and twenty-three years old, he died according to the Lord’s command on Mount Hor, which is near Petra, the distinguished city of Arabia. There also his sister Miriam lies buried; even now the rock is shown there which Moses struck and from which he gave water to the thirsty people. This place is at the extreme boundaries of Idumea.

## CHAPTER XXVII

47. Joshua, son of Nun, born in Egypt from the tribe of Ephraim, Moses’ disciple and successor in authority, and victor in a new war. When it was necessary to complete the victory so that the sun should stand still, he commanded the heavens. He also made the course of the Jordan resist his crossing [Alternative reading: stand still]. By the sound of the blaring trumpets he cast down the impregnable walls of Jericho.

48. He overturned the kingdoms of the Canaanites, destroyed their kings, alone led the people of God into the promised land, and distributed it by lot. He ruled Israel for twenty-seven years. He died at the age of one hundred and ten and was buried in his own city, Tamnathsare, situated on the side of Mount Gaas, toward the north, where his notable monument is displayed even to this day. It is in the tribe of Dan.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

49. Phinehas, priest, son of Eleazar the priest, son of Aaron, zealous for the Lord, struck Zimri, who was engaging in illicit intercourse with the Midianite prostitute, with a weapon. He thereby earned perpetual priestly headbands and the reward of sacrificial offerings among the generations of Israel, because, inflamed with zeal for divine love, he appeased the Lord’s anger by this slaying.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0138D]

50. On this chapter of Isidore, see the Bollandists under 7 September, p. 85. AREV.]

50. Gideon, son of Joash, from the tribe of Manasseh, born in the wilderness, deliverer of the people and father of many sons, strong in hand and energetic in counsel, tested by signs the indications of future victory and the power of God in the fleece. With three hundred men who lapped water with their tongues, carrying not weapons in their right hands but trumpets, and not shields in their left hands but jars, he struck the enemy with terror and bravely triumphed as victor over Amalek. He judged Israel for forty years, died in old age, and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah, of the family of Ezri.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0139A]

[Note: [Col. 0139D]

51. Isidore praises Jephthah because, faithful to his promises, he sacrificed his daughter. This opinion, approved by certain holy Fathers and more recent theologians, may be confirmed by the testimony of Saint Paul, Hebrews 11:32–33. Others adopt different views, which are set forth by Calmet in his learned Dissertation on Jephthah’s Vow. AREV.]

51. Jephthah the Gileadite, successful in battles, faithful to his promises, exceeding the affection of piety through endurance of mind. For he had vowed to God that if, on his return after victory, anything should first meet him, he would sacrifice it. Returning from the enemy as victor over the Ammonites, he fulfilled the promise he had made, lest he should be stained by the guilt of perjury, and sacrificed his daughter, who had come out to meet the victor. He judged Israel for six years and died and was buried in the city of Gilead, which is in the half-tribe of Manasseh.

## CHAPTER XXXI

52. Samson, son of promise, born to Manoah his father from the tribe of Dan, called a Nazirite, deliverer of Israel, and the strongest of all. He killed a roaring lion and took honeycomb from the mouth of the dead animal; he also lifted the bars of the gates onto his shoulders and placed them on the summit of a mountain. He burned the whole region of the Philistines by tying fire to the tails of foxes. Though bound, he broke the ropes, and with the jawbone of a donkey he killed a thousand men. He broke bonds woven from sinews as though they were threads of wool.

[Note: [Col. 0139D]

53. Alternative: between Zorah and Eshtaol. Judges 16. FONT.]

53. After this, deceived by the greed of an alluring woman, he lost the strength of his power when his hair was cut. Without delay, after his eyes had been gouged out, he shook the pillars of the temple and, crushed by its collapse, perished together with his enemies. He judged Israel for twenty years and was placed in his father’s tomb in the city of Eshtaol, which is in the tribe of Judah, ten miles from Eleutheropolis, toward the north, beside the road leading to Nicopolis.

## CHAPTER XXXII

54. Samuel the prophet, son of Elkanah, from Ramah, of the tribe of Ephraim, counted with Moses among the priests of God, consecrated to the Lord from his very cradle, diligent in ministry, a prince among his people, a seer in the temple. At his word the heavens obeyed, clouds appeared, and rains poured forth.

55. Victorious over the enemies, he set up the Stone of Help; he was the first to anoint a ruler in the kingdom. He was buried in his own village, Ramah, which is in Bethlehem. The emperor Arcadius transferred his bones from Judea to Thrace and erected an altar of Christ over his tomb.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

56. David, at once king and prophet, descended from the tribe of Judah, son of Jesse, born in Bethlehem, a boy and the youngest in age among his brothers but superior in virtue, called by the Lord to the kingship and anointed king by the prophet; a warlike young man, exceptional in combat, glorious in triumph, seasoned by victory, patient in adversity, prudent in danger, grieving over his own sin, mourning at another’s death, inclined to repentance, swift to forgiveness, gentle under insult, and ready for mercy.

57. When he could have done so, he not only spared the hostile king who had been delivered into his hands while he was still unharmed, but also avenged him after he had been killed. [Col. 0140A] He killed a lion and a bear without a sword, drove out an unclean spirit by the sweetness of the lyre, and overcame a giant. Thus, in the fortieth year of his reign and the seventieth year of his life, he completed the final day of his life. He was buried in his own city, Bethlehem, which is also called Ephrathah, where our Lord Jesus Christ was likewise born according to the flesh.

58. Rachel also died there when she had given birth to Benjamin. There too the tomb of Jesse, David’s father, is shown. This place is in the tribe of Judah, six miles from Jerusalem toward the south, on the road leading to Hebron.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

59. Solomon, David’s son, born of Bathsheba in Jerusalem, was called the wisest of all even before he was born, and the dedicator of the Lord’s temple; fortunate in rule, unequal to his father’s merits, beloved by God, wise in judgment, just in decision, and peaceful in his kingdom. He asked for wisdom and obtained it, so that he might know the ordering of the world, the powers of the elements, the natures of animals, and the thoughts of human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0140D]

60. Isidore seems to have the Song of Songs in mind when he says that Solomon revealed the mysteries of Christ and the Church. AREV.]

60. He also regulated customs, discovered the natures of things, and revealed the mysteries of Christ and the Church. His beginnings were good, but his final days were evil. For after the glory of many virtues, corrupted by love of women, he both lost the wisdom he had received and was plunged into the lamentable ruin of idolatry. He reigned for forty years and lived to the age of fifty-two. Thereafter he brought his rule and life to an end and was buried in the city of his father, Bethlehem.

## CHAPTER XXXV

61. Elijah the Tishbite, a great priest and prophet, inhabitant of the wilderness, full of faith, supreme in devotion, strong in labors, skillful in diligence, endowed with outstanding intelligence, formed by the discipline of training, constant in holy meditation, and fearless of the fear of death. He struck tyrants, killed sacrilegious persons, and shone forth with many signs of power. For during a drought of three years he shut the heavens against rain. Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and he raised the woman’s dead son.

[Note: [Col. 0140D]

62. “Against him, or the one who is with him”: that is, against him and the one who is with him; for *vel* is used in place of “and.” AREV.]

62. Through his power the jar of flour did not fail, and the vessel of oil flowed as from a perpetual spring. At his word fire descended from heaven upon the sacrifice. He burned two companies of fifty, together with their soldiers, with heavenly fire. Crossing the Jordan, he divided it by striking it with his mantle. Then he was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot. He is announced as coming with the prophet Malachi at the end of the world, preceding Christ and announcing his final coming with great wonders and miraculous signs, so that Antichrist will even wage war on earth against him and the one who will come with him; he will kill them, and their corpses will lie unburied in the streets.

[Note: [Col. 0140D]

63. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapters 35 and 50, concerning Elijah and Enoch: “They are reserved to die so that they may extinguish Antichrist with their blood.” The claim that afterward they will be raised by the Lord so that they may strike the kingdom of Antichrist with a great blow perhaps rests on no other foundation than these words of Tertullian. It is certain, however, that they will rise to immortal glory. AREV.]

63. Afterward, raised by the Lord, they will strike the kingdom of Antichrist with a great blow. [Col. 0141A] After this the Lord will come and kill Antichrist with the sword of his mouth, together with those who worshiped him. And the Lord will reign with all his saints in everlasting glory.

[Note: [Col. 0141D]

64. These words were added in three copies of Isidore, and Epiphanius has them in his *Life of Elijah*.]

64. Likewise. Elijah the Tishbite, from the land of the Arabs and the tribe of Aaron. While he was in the womb of his mother, Galaath, his father Sobac saw a dream: men in white garments were greeting the newborn Elijah, wrapping him in garments of fire [Alternative reading: bands], and supplying him with fire as food for nourishment. His father reported this vision to the prophets in Jerusalem, and received this answer from them: “Do not fear. His nation will be a light, and his word will be established in fixed judgments. For he will judge Israel with sword and fire.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Col. 0141B]

[Note: [Col. 0141D]

65. Abel Meula, 1 Kings 19. Abel Muth, in Epiphanius. Abel Buel, in Dorotheus.

In the Vulgate it is written “Abel-meholah.” In Dorotheus of Tyre there is an error, “the land of Rubim” instead of “from the tribe of Reuben.” The work is entitled *On the Holy Prophets, Apostles, and the Seventy Disciples of Christ* and is falsely believed to have been attributed to Dorotheus. It was published by Albert Fabricius together with books by Isidore and others on a similar subject; he also included another anonymous work on the twelve apostles in his *Ecclesiastical Library*. The prophecy of the prophetic seer that Isidore reports is similarly narrated in that work of Dorotheus. AREV.]

65. Elisha, Elijah’s disciple, from the town of Abel Meula, of the tribe of Reuben. At his birth a golden calf at Gilgal gave a bellow, and its voice resounded in Jerusalem. Then a certain prophetic seer foretold: “Today a prophet has been born in Israel who will destroy all their idols.”

66. Glorified by a double portion of Elijah’s spirit, he shone forth with very many great signs of power. He divided the Jordan as he crossed, turning the restrained waters backward; he made the barren waters of Jericho fertile by submerging a small vessel; by his word he delivered boys who were mocking him to beasts to be suddenly devoured; he caused bloody waters to flow for the destruction of the enemies. Amid these events he made a barren woman conceive by his word and raised her dead son; he moderated the bitterness of food; finally, after the people had been fed from ten loaves, he collected the leftovers.

67. He cleansed Naaman of the marks of leprosy in the washing of the Jordan; he also inflicted leprosy as a curse upon a disciple. He made the iron of an axe, sunk in the Jordan, float upon the water when wood was thrown into it. He struck the Syrian enemies with blindness, foretold death to an unbeliever, drove away the enemy with the thunder of chariots, dispersed a siege, and drove away famine.

[Note: [Col. 0141D]

68. “In Sebastopolis of Samaria,” says Epiphanius.]

68. Finally, after his death, he gave life to a lifeless corpse. His tomb is displayed to this day in the city of Sebastia, worthy of considerable honor and regarded as deserving of veneration.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0142D]

69. The Hebrews assert that Amos, Isaiah’s father, was the brother of Amaziah, king of Judah, concerning whom see 4 Kings 14.]

69. Isaiah, son of Amos—not of the prophet Amos, but of another who was called by a similar name. The latter was one of the shepherds from the town of Tekoa, whereas this man was born in Jerusalem of noble lineage. The Hebrews also say that he was the father-in-law of Manasseh. Such was his sanctity and excellence of life that he is said to have had only one tunic, and that of sackcloth; when he later cast it aside because of the people’s sin, he covered his limbs with a sackcloth garment.

[Note: [Col. 0142D]

70. Whether Isaiah’s nakedness should be understood literally is disputed by interpreters; see Isaiah, chapter 20, verse 2. AREV.]

70. But after finally setting this aside as well, at the Lord’s command he went about in the assembly of the peoples with naked body and naked feet. In this way he endured the heat of summer, the frosts of winter, and storms of rain, both obeying God’s commands and mourning the sins of the people.

[Note: [Col. 0142D]

71. It is an established tradition of the ancients that Isaiah was sawn in two. See Calmet in the Dissertation on the Punishments of the Hebrews under Deuteronomy, and in the Prolegomena to Isaiah. AREV.]

71. He commanded the shadow that had ascended fifteen steps to descend backward. By his oracle King Hezekiah obtained a postponement of death. But Manasseh stretched him out and cut him in two from the top, killing him after he had been tortured by this cruel punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0142D]

72. They relate this. Origen, in *On Isaiah*, and Jerome.

In the same passage he had explained it: “He had blocked it,” says Jerome.

It should also be noted here—as I have often noted elsewhere—that Isidore sometimes uses a nominative in place of an ablative absolute, as in “the Jews, not noticing” (*Judaei pro non animadvertentibus Judaeis*), unless one refers it to “they relate,” which precedes. Concerning Isaiah’s tomb, Dorotheus reports as follows: “He was buried under an oak near the spring of Rogel, beside the passage of the waters that King Hezekiah had blocked with earth.” Others say that the prophet’s body was transferred to Paneas, at the sources of the Jordan, and from there to Constantinople. AREV.]

72. The Hebrews relate that Isaiah was killed for two reasons: first, because he had called them princes of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah; second, because, when the Lord testified to Moses, “You cannot see my face,” he dared to exclaim, “I saw the Lord seated upon a throne, high and exalted.” The Jews, blinded in mind, failed to notice that in what follows the prophet had stated that the Seraphim covered God’s face and feet, and that he had seen only the middle part of him. He lies beneath the oak of Rogel, beside the channels of the waters that Hezekiah, king of Judah, had exposed by constructing an embankment of earth.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

73. Jeremiah, born from a priestly tribe in the village of Anathoth, which is three miles from Jerusalem, appointed priest in Judea and consecrated prophet among the nations, was known before he was formed, sanctified before he came forth, and admonished to remain a virgin. He began to preach while still a boy, rebuking the people for their sins and frequently exhorting them to repentance. But he was often afflicted and bound by the cruelty of the raging faithless populace; he was also cast into prison, thrown into a pit, surrounded with chains, and finally stoned to death by the people at Taphnas in Egypt.

[Col. 0143A]

[Note: [Col. 0143D]

74. “Asps.” Jerome; Epiphanius and Dorotheus say “crocodiles.”

In the same passage, Tertullian also agrees that Jeremiah was buried under a heap of stones by the Jews, *Scorpiace*, chapter 8. AREV.]

74. He was buried in the place where Pharaoh, king of Egypt, had lived. Nevertheless, because by his prayers he drove the serpents from that place and rescued the Egyptians from the deadly bite of asps, those same Egyptians honor him with remarkable veneration and the greatest honor, and to this day revere his tomb with distinguished devotion.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

75. Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi, born in the land of Sarira, is called “son of man” as a type of Christ. Taken captive with Jehoiachin to Babylon, he prophesied to his fellow captives, reproving their offenses and, moved by zeal for God, censuring all their crimes and indecencies. The leader of the people of Israel killed him because he was rebuked by him with priestly severity and authority for the impiety of sacrilege. He was buried by the people in the field of Maurim, in the tomb of Shem and Arphaxad.

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0143D]

76. From the tribe of Judah. See Epiphanius, Jerome, Josephus.

In the same passage, some copies have *praenotescere* instead of *praenoscere*. I think this is an Isidorian word meaning “to foretell,” that is, “to make known beforehand,” since above he has already used *praescius futurorum*, “one who knows future things beforehand.” In the Palatine Codex there is *promeruit* instead of *praenotescere* or *praenoscere*. AREV.]

76. Daniel, born in Upper Bethoron of the tribe of Judah, noble by birth, foremost among all the Chaldeans, and distinguished by royal descent and the nobility of his homeland. Under King Jehoiakim of Judah, after the destruction of Jerusalem, he was taken to Babylon with three boys while still very young and was made chief of the Chaldeans. He was glorious in character and handsome in appearance, humble in mind, chaste in body, perfect in faith, outstanding in works, supreme in virtue, renowned in wonders, terrifying in signs, a knower of heavenly secrets, foreknowing future events, interpreter of visions, and defender of chastity. Through continual fasts and persistent prayer he merited to know beforehand future mysteries.

[Col. 0143C]

[Note: [Col. 0143D]

77. Perhaps: detecting the falsehood. Dorotheus agrees with this. See also Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 10, final chapter. AREV.]

77. Among the other mysteries of his visions, he shone forth through the following deeds and signs of virtue. At the beginning, by exposing the lie of the wicked elders, he revealed the woman’s chastity. He fasted for three weeks of days, praying for the people. By proofs of divine inspiration he shattered the image of Bel. By divine prompting and to the amazement of all, he destroyed the dragon, the Babylonian deity of that people, with a cake made of pitch, fat, and hair. Thrown into the den, he calmed the fury of the beasts; and, strong and fearless in spirit among the roaring animals, he safely ate among the lions.

78. After Darius overthrew the Babylonian empire, he took Daniel with him, holding him in the highest honor, and brought him into Media. Daniel is also said to have given signs on the mountains above Babylon, saying: “When the mountains have smoked from the north wind, the end of Babylon is near; when they are seen blazing with fires, it will be the end of the whole world. Likewise, when the Tigris has flowed back toward the region of the south, it will be the return of the people to Jerusalem.” He lived until the time of Darius, king of the Persians, for one hundred and ten years, and was buried, already an old man, alone in captivity with glory, in a royal cave.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0144D]

79. Epiphanius and Dorotheus also have “Belemoth.”

—“As an oak.” Alternative: “Like an oak, which is in Shiloh, when it divides itself.”]

79. Hosea, of the tribe of Issachar, born in Belemoth. He gave this sign while announcing beforehand: “The Lord will come into his land if the oak that is in Shiloh divides itself into twelve parts and produces the same number of oaks.” Buried in his own land, he slept in peaceful rest.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Note: [Col. 0144D]

80. Of the tribe of Reuben. Jerome and Epiphanius.]

80. Joel was of the tribe of Reuben, born in the field of Bethoron, where he also died in peace and was buried.

## CHAPTER XLIII

81. Amos, a shepherd and rustic, occupied in tending brambles, was a prophet not by lineage but by the calling of grace. He was from the town of Tekoa, which lies six miles to the south, opposite Bethlehem. Beyond it there is no habitation, but only the broad, open desolation of the wilderness, extending as far as the Red Sea and the borders of the Jews [Alternative reading: Indians], known only to shepherds and widely wandering flocks.

82. Amos therefore came from this pastoral region, one of the number of shepherds. The Lord took him from there and sent him to the people of Israel, commanding him to go to Samaria and prophesy there what was to come. King Amaziah frequently afflicted him with blows; finally, his son Uzziah killed him a cruel death by driving a bar through his temples. Afterward, still half alive, he was carried back to his own land. A few days later, in great pain from the wound, he slowly breathed out his soul [Alternative reading: his soul slowly breathed out], and was buried with his fathers.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0144D]

83. Mariana investigates the time when Obadiah prophesied in the notes to the *Book of Prologues*, no. 67. He also explains similar questions concerning the other prophets in the notes to the same book, which we shall reproduce in their proper place. AREV.]

83. Obadiah, from the land of Shechem, born in the field of Bethacaram. He is the one who, under Ahaziah, king of Samaria, fed one hundred prophets. He is that third captain whom Elijah spared, who later, after abandoning the service of King Ahaziah, became Elijah’s disciple and prophesied. He also died a natural death and was buried with his fathers in the city of Sebastia, where the prophet Elisha and John the Baptist also rest in reverence.

## CHAPTER XLV

84. Jonah, “dove” and “grieving,” son of Amathi, who was from Geth, which is in Opher, was sent to proclaim to the nations. Sent, he despises the mission; despising, he flees; fleeing, he sleeps. Because of him the ship was endangered, but the captain of the ship found him hiding; the whale swallowed him when he was thrown overboard and vomited him out when he prayed. Rejected, he preached destruction.

85. But he was saddened by the repentance of the city and begrudged the nations their salvation. He also rejoiced beneath the shade of the green ivy and grieved when it suddenly withered. The Hebrews relate that he was the son of the widow whom Elijah raised from the dead. His tomb is shown in a certain village of the cities of Geth, two miles from Sepphoris on the road leading to Tiberias.

## CHAPTER XLVI

86. Micah was born in Morasthi, of the tribe of Ephraim. Because he frequently rebuked Ahab for sinning, he was thrown from a great precipice under Joram, Ahab’s son, and died. He was buried in his own land near Polyandrum, which is close to Naim.

## CHAPTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0145D]

87. Dorotheus: “And buried in his own land.” AREV.]

87. Nahum, of the tribe of Simeon, born in Helcesi beyond Betharim, died there and lies in his own tomb.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

88. Habakkuk, of the tribe of Simeon, was born in the field of Bethsachar. Two years before the return of the children of Israel from captivity, he died in the field of Sabarith, which is in Keilah.

## CHAPTER XLIX

89. Zephaniah, of the tribe of Simeon, son of Cushi, born in the field of Sarabath and descended from the glorious line of his ancestors, prophesied, then died and was buried in his own field.

## CHAPTER L

90. Haggai, born in Babylonia, came as a young man to Jerusalem, saw part of the building of the temple, and rests buried in glory beside the monuments of the priests.

## CHAPTER LI

[Col. 0145C]

[Note: [Col. 0145D]

91. This chapter is absent from other copies. See below, chapter 97.]

91. Zechariah returned from the region of the Chaldeans to his own land at a very advanced age. There he died and was buried beside Haggai and rests in peace.

## CHAPTER LII

92. Malachi was born in Sophia after the people’s departure. He was a just man and handsome in appearance. The Jews say that he was called Malachi, that is, “angel of the Lord,” because whatever he foretold was immediately confirmed when an angel came from heaven. He died while still quite young and was buried in his own field.

## CHAPTER LIII

93. Nathan the prophet, one of the Gibeonites, taught King David the law of God and exposed the sin that David had committed concerning Bathsheba. He also foretold that David would not build a temple for the Lord. He anointed Solomon and consecrated him as ruler. He died an old man in his own land and was buried with honor.

## CHAPTER LIV

94. Ahijah the Shilonite, from the city of Eli the priest, where the first tabernacle and the ark of God had been, foretold to King Solomon that he would turn away from God’s commandments through foreign women, and he did not conceal the future division of the people among his descendants. [Col. 0146A] Ahijah therefore died and was buried beside the oak at Shiloh.

## CHAPTER LV

[Note: [Col. 0145D]

95. The prophet who was strangled by a lion, concerning whom 1 Kings 13 speaks, is called Joath by Dorotheus; in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book 4, chapter 6, he is called Adonias; Cotelerius should be consulted there. Others call this prophet Shemaiah; others call him Joam. Some suspect that he was Ahijah. It is not easy, nor is it important, to investigate his true name. AREV.]

95. Addo was born in Samaria [Alternative: Sama, Samaria]. He is the one who was sent to Jeroboam when he was sacrificing a calf. He came with the word of the Lord and rebuked him for sacrificing. As he was returning to his own place, a lion strangled him on the road because of his disobedience. Bethel holds buried both him and the prophet who had deceived him.

## CHAPTER LVI

96. Azariah arose in the land of Sabatha; he died and was buried in his own little field.

## CHAPTER LVII

97. Zechariah the prophet and priest, son of Jehoiada the priest, [Col. 0146B] also called Barachiah. When the people had gathered in the court of the house of the Lord, they stoned him to death at the command of King Joash. The priests immediately carried him away and buried him beside his father in Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LVIII

98. Tobias, son of Ananiel, of the tribe of Naphtali, from the city of Cibel, which is in the region of Galilee. He was taken captive by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, to Nineveh. A man supreme in the fear of God, magnificent in action, glorious in mercy, and devoted to the care of funerals, he lost the light of his eyes while burying the dead and feeding the needy; after the darkness, when his eyes were opened, he obtained the light of brightness. He lies buried in peace in the city of Nineveh.

## CHAPTER LIX

99. The three boys, renowned for royal descent, glorious in memory, learned in knowledge, equal in faith, steadfast in devotion, incorrupt in body, sober in mind, judges of provinces and rulers of regions, mindful also of their ancestral laws, and by no means defiled by the food of the Gentiles or by sacrificed things, lived on legumes and vegetables.

100. Through the strength of their virtue they despised death, did not worship the rites of idols, overcame the most savage king by the power of faith, extinguished the fires of the blazing furnace, and amid the dreadful flames, thick with darkness, sang a hymn aloud. They lie together in Babylonia, placed beneath a single cavern and buried with great veneration.

## CHAPTER LX

[Col. 0146D]

[Note: [Col. 0146D]

101. It is also read in the *Prologues*, where Mariana made certain notes, that some believed Malachi to have been Ezra. AREV.]

101. Ezra, priest of God, is called by many Malachi, that is, “angel of God.” He was a writer of sacred history and the second bearer of the law after Moses; after the captivity, he renewed the law that had been consumed among the nations and discovered the elements of the Hebrew letters. He led Israel back and caused Jerusalem to be rebuilt. He died and was buried with his fathers in Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LXI

102. Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, of the tribe of Judah, built the Lord’s temple under King Darius, constructed the walls of Jerusalem, and restored Israel to its former condition. They also restored the practice of religion and the rights of the priests and Levites. They too lie buried in Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LXII

103. Queen Esther, daughter of the brother of Mordecai, of the tribe of Benjamin, was taken captive from Jerusalem and transferred to the city of Susa. Because of her beautiful appearance and the conspicuous excellence of her virginity, she was joined in marriage to the king of the Persians. To free her people from danger, she offered herself to death and persuaded the king that the friend who had wickedly urged him against the people of God should be handed over to the cross. Thus she rescued the free nation from destruction and delivered it from slavery. She lies buried in Susa, the city of the Medes, where she also reigned.

## CHAPTER LXIII

[Col. 0148A]

[Note: [Col. 0147B]

104. Fontidonius indicates a different reading, *Aapali* instead of Bethulia. But I do not understand what *Aapali* is. The Greek and Syriac say that Manasseh was buried in a field between Dothaim and Belmon. Instead of Belmon, others read Belmaim, Belma, Belem, or Baalmeon. Some think the reference is to Abila, Abelina, or Abilina. But these readings do not sufficiently agree with our Vulgate, which should be preferred, Judith 8:3: “Manasseh died in his city Bethulia, and was buried there with his fathers.” And chapter 16:28: “And Judith was buried with her husband in Bethulia.” AREV.]

104. Judith the widow, daughter of Merari, of the tribe of Simeon, great-hearted in glory and superior to men. For the salvation of the people she offered herself to death and did not fear the king’s fury. She killed the commander while he slept and, preserving her modesty, carried home the triumph of victory to her fellow citizens. She lived for one hundred and five years and was buried in the cave of her husband Manasseh in the city of Bethulia, which is in the tribe of Judah between Dothain and Balmon [Alternative: Babylon].

## CHAPTER LXIV

[Note: [Col. 0148B]

105. In the Verona Codex the following is read concerning the Maccabees: “The seven Maccabean brothers, born of one mother named Maccabaea, observing the law and, according to ancestral tradition, not eating pork, were crowned with the glory of martyrdom by the most savage King Antiochus in Antioch, together with their mother, and were buried with great veneration.” AREV.

In six copies only this latter reading is found.]

105. The seven Maccabee brothers, steadfast in faith, strong in hope, most unwavering observers of the divine law, enduring the most bitter tortures, were brutally slain by King Antiochus, together with their mother, for the law of God; they deserved the crowns of martyrdom.

[Col. 0148B] 106. The history of the Maccabees also relates in full what victories they won against the Persian people and against other neighboring nations, and how severely they were punished for their observance of the law.

## CHAPTER LXV

[Col. 0147C]

107. Zechariah and Elizabeth, righteous before God, childless in their youth and fruitful in old age, rest in Jerusalem.

## CHAPTER LXVI

108. John the Baptist, son of Zechariah, born in Jerusalem from the tribe of Levi, conceived at the announcement of an angel, the forerunner of Christ, herald of the Judge, prophet of the Most High, voice of the Word, friend of the Bridegroom, witness of the Lord, lamp of the Light, and end of the prophets. When he was foretold, he took away his father’s voice; when he was born, he released the office of the tongue. Before he had yet been brought forth, he prophesied Christ; he greeted him in the womb, recognized him in the dove, and pointed him out in the desert.

109. His clothing was camel’s fleece, his dwelling the wilderness, and his nourishment honey, with locusts for food. [Col. 0147D] When he forbade Herod to violate his brother’s marriage, he was delivered into the darkness of prison. The king’s daughter demanded his head from her father as the reward for a dance; and he, drunk amid his cups, gave her the severed head to her wicked request.

[Col. 0148C] 110. He was buried in Sebastia, a town of Palestine formerly called Samaria. King Herod of Judaea, son of Antipater, named it Augusta in the Greek language in honor of Caesar Augustus.

## CHAPTER LXVII

111. Mary—whose name is interpreted as “Lady” or “Illuminatrix”—the illustrious offspring of David, the Rod of Jesse, the enclosed Garden, the sealed Fountain, the Mother of the Lord, the Temple of God, the Sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the holy Virgin, the fruitful Virgin, virgin before childbirth and virgin after childbirth, received the angel’s greeting and recognized the mystery of the conception. She inquired about the manner of the birth and did not refuse, contrary to the law of nature, the obedience of faith. The Lord himself, placed upon the cross, entrusted her to the disciple through the blood of the Testament, so that the mother might have as a companion in life the one whom the Son knew to be the guardian of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0147D]

112. “Some.” See Ambrose.

In the same place: This passage of Isidore is quoted under his name by the author of the sermon on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, whom some believe to have been Ambrose Autpertus; I have cited his words in *Isidoriana*, chapter 61, no. 12. [Col. 0148D] What Isidore says, namely, that Mary’s death is nowhere recorded, Autpertus—or whoever the author may be—explains as follows: “Nor is any Latin commentator found to have clearly said anything about her death.” Saint Epiphanius considered it more probable that God had granted the most blessed Virgin the grace of immortality, but the sentiment of the universal Church opposes this, and the only dispute among writers is whether she died at Ephesus or at Jerusalem. Tillemont discusses this at length, volume I of *The Memoirs for the Ecclesiastical History of the First Six Centuries*, in the *Life of the Mother of God* and in the notes. AREV.]

112. Some assert that she departed this life by a cruel death, on the grounds that the righteous Simeon, embracing Christ in his arms, prophesied to his mother, saying: “And a sword will pierce your own soul.” It is uncertain, however, whether he meant a material sword or the powerful and sharper-than-any two-edged sword that is the word of God. No historical account specifically teaches that Mary was killed by the stroke of a sword, since her death is nowhere recorded. Nevertheless, some say that her tomb is found in the Valley of Jehoshaphat.

## CHAPTER LXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0149D]

113. “Head.” As though from the Greek κεφαλή (*kephalē*).

In the same place: What Isidore suggests—that *Cephas* comes from the Greek κεφαλή, “head”—was believed by many other early writers. John XXII, in his bull against Marsilius and John, says: “Cephas is interpreted from Greek into Latin as ‘head.’” In fact, the name *Cephas* is Syriac and means “rock,” as Isidore also seems to acknowledge in book VII, chapter 9, of the *Etymologies*. Which authors wrote generally about the apostles and the seventy disciples, and individually about certain apostles, is listed by Zaccaria in the *Selected Library of Ecclesiastical History*, part II, chapter 8. It is worth noting that, speaking of Saint James the Greater, he says: “The history of Saint Diego of Alcalá by Antonio Rojo will scarcely satisfy critical scholars.” What does Saint James the Greater the apostle have to do with Saint Didacus, or James of Compostela, a lay brother of the Friars Minor of the Observance? AREV.]

113. Simon Peter, son of John and brother of Andrew, was born in the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, which lies beside the lake of Gennesaret. His first calling by the name Bar-Jona signifies a direct lineage of the law. Peter is the foundation of the Church in Christ. Cephas is the principate and head of Christ’s body. Simon, son of John, is the incorruptible regeneration of virginity.

[Col. 0149B] 114. Although he is ranked third according to John, according to Matthew he is chosen first—and not without reason, since he is the prince of the apostles. He was the first confessor of the Son of God, disciple and shepherd of the human flock, Rock of the Church, holder of the keys of the kingdom, lover of the Lord, and also his denier: praised for confessing, exalted through presumption, fallen through denial, purified by tears, proved by confession, and crowned through suffering. His name is given according to his deed, and his title is imposed according to the merit of his authority.

115. He preached the Gospel in Galatia, Pontus, Cappadocia, Bithynia, Asia, and Italy, and shone forth through signs of these virtues. With wavering steps he trod the raging sea; as he passed by, he restored the dead to life through his shadow; to the lame he restored their former function; and to paralytics he restored their weakened limbs to their proper condition.

[Col. 0149C] 116. Among these deeds, he raised a dead widow. He condemned Ananias and Sapphira, guilty of faithlessness, to death. He also struck Simon, who was ascending toward heaven by magical arts, down to the earth. After founding the Church of Antioch, under Caesar Claudius he went to Rome against that same Simon Magus. There, preaching the Gospel for twenty-five years, he held the pontificate of that city.

[Note: [Col. 0150C]

117. After the most learned work of the most eminent Cardinal Borgia, *On the Vatican Confession*, it is unnecessary to say anything about Saint Peter’s tomb in the Vatican. See also Bosio, *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, II, 2, and Bottari, I, 27. It should be noted that the miles began from the Roman Forum and were shorter than Italian miles. It is not sufficiently clear, however, in what sense Saint Peter’s tomb is said to be on the eastern side. AREV.]

117. In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion, he was crucified upside down in the city of Rome by Caesar Nero, as he himself wished. Thus, after the merit of his apostleship, he was also crowned with martyrdom. He was buried at Rome in the Vatican, beside the Triumphal Way, [Col. 0150A] at the third milestone from the city, on the eastern side.

## CHAPTER LXIX

118. Paul, formerly Saul, apostle of the Gentiles and advocate of the Jews, was called by Christ from heaven and cast down upon the earth. He fell seeing and rose blind. From a persecutor he became a chosen vessel, from a wolf a sheep; last among the apostles in calling, but first in preaching. In the law he was a disciple of Gamaliel; in the Gospel, a servant of Christ. His native city was Tarsus, and his lineage was Benjamin.

119. Baptized in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension, he earned the dignity of apostleship. Laboring more than all the others, he sowed the grace of the word far more widely among them and fulfilled evangelical teaching through his preaching.

[Col. 0150B] [Note: [Col. 0150D]

120. Paul’s arrival in Spain is confirmed by the most ancient testimonies of Hippolytus, Epiphanius, Chrysostom, and others; others deny it, and the dispute remains undecided. AREV.]

120. Beginning from Jerusalem, he advanced as far as Illyricum, Italy, and Spain, and made the name of Christ known among the peoples of many nations to whom it had not previously been proclaimed. His miracles are recognized as having been these.

121. He was carried upward and ascended into the third heaven; cast down into the depths, he was in the sea night and day. He condemned the spirit of the Python by ordering it to depart; he restored the life-giving spirit to a dead youth; he struck a magician with blindness; he restored a lame man’s proper gait; he neither felt nor feared the bite of a savage serpent, but gave it to the fire to be burned; and by his prayer he also healed Publius’s father of fevers.

122. For the love of Christ he endured many sufferings and severe bodily torments: above all, Jewish persecutions, the hardships inflicted by the nations, labor, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness; shipwrecks and a thousand dangers; the fury of wild beasts; blows, prison darkness, and the torments of chains; squalor and bonds.

[Note: [Col. 0150D]

123. It is commonly believed that Paul was struck down by the sword in the same year and on the same day as Peter was crucified. Prudentius maintained that Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom on the same day, but not in the same year. See the commentary on hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 5. Paul is said to have been buried on the western side, which is not easily explained. Others give the eastern side. AREV.]

123. In the midst of these things he is bound by the Jews, handed over to the Gentiles, stoned nearly to death, lowered in a basket through a wall, beaten with rods, confined under punishment, and, while bound in prison, released when an earthquake occurred. Finally, Nero struck him down with the sword on the same day on which Peter was crucified. For it was fitting that those who had confessed together should be crowned on one day. He was buried at Rome on the Ostian Way, thirty-six years after the Lord’s Passion, at the third milestone from the city, on the western side.

## CHAPTER LXX

[Col. 0151A]

[Note: [Col. 0151C]

124. The reading found in some manuscripts, “in the city of Patras,” is perhaps correct, as though *Patras* were indeclinable; similar names of cities occasionally occur in this form in Isidore and others. Some report that Andrew suffered martyrdom in Asia. AREV.]

124. Andrew—whose name is interpreted as “handsome”—was Peter’s brother, first according to John and second from the first according to Matthew. In the allotment of preaching he received Scythia and Achaea, and in the city of Patras he was also hanged on a cross and died.

## CHAPTER LXXI

[Note: [Col. 0151D]

125. We agree with those who consider the word *scripsit* (“wrote”) an interpolation. The remainder appears to have been taken from material added by the Greeks to Jerome’s *Catalogue*.

In the same place: Marmarica. Others read Carmarica, or “the Archis of Marmarica,” or Achimarmarica.

In the same place: What might be noted here concerning the preaching of Saint James the Greater in Spain has already been anticipated by us in *Isidoriana*, chapter 61. Among other writers on this subject should be added the elegant and learned Spaniard Juan José Tolrá: *Historical-Critical Justification of the Coming of James the Greater to Spain and of His Tomb at Compostela*. Madrid, 1797, quarto. Instead of *ab Herode tetrarcha* (“by Herod the tetrarch”), one should perhaps read *ab Herode Agrippa* (“by Herod Agrippa”). To what I said in the cited chapter 61, add the *Martyrology of Gellone*, or of Saint William of the Desert, written around the year 804, in volume III of Dacherii, at the beginning: “James, whose name means ‘supplanter,’ son of Zebedee and brother of John. He preached in Spain and in the western regions, and was struck down by the sword under Herod [Col. 0152C] and died; he was buried in Achaia Marmarica, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.” Also add Hildebert of Le Mans, who flourished in the eleventh and twelfth centuries, column 1350 in Beaugendre’s edition, *On Saint James the Greater*:

[Col. 0152D] “And the land of Galicia rejoices that it possesses him as a settler.” In Vatican Codex Regina 532, page 27, there is an anonymous account of the head of James the Greater, said to be present in the Venetian monastery of Saint Felix among the dead; it asserts that the rest of the body is at Compostela. In Codex Ottobonianus 124 and Codex Regina 1222, a hymn in honor of Saint James is preserved, in which his arrival in Spain and his tomb at Compostela are affirmed. AREV.]

125. James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, fourth in order, wrote to the twelve tribes scattered among the nations and preached the Gospel to the peoples of Spain and the western regions, pouring the light of preaching into the setting of the world. He was struck down by the sword under Herod the tetrarch and died. He was buried in Marmarica.

## CHAPTER LXXII

126. John, apostle and evangelist, son of Zebedee and brother of James, was chosen by the Lord as a virgin and loved more than the others. Reclining upon the breast of the Master, he drank the streams of the Gospel from the sacred fountain of the Lord’s breast itself, and, like one of the rivers of paradise, spread the grace of the word of God throughout the whole world. At Christ’s command he succeeded Christ’s place, when the disciple took the Master’s mother into his care and thus became, in a certain sense, another son left in Christ’s place.

127. While preaching Christ’s Gospel in Asia, he was banished by Caesar Domitian to the island of Patmos to work in the mines; while there, he also wrote the Apocalypse. After Domitian was killed by the senate, John was released from exile and withdrew to Ephesus. There, at the urgent request of the bishops of Asia, to refute the cunning of the heretics, he produced the last of the Gospels.

128. Among his other virtues, the greatness of his signs was as follows. He changed wild branches into gold and stones from the shore into gems. He likewise restored fragments of gems to their proper nature, raised a widow at the people’s prayer, and restored a young man’s revived body by calling back his soul. After drinking a deadly potion, he not only escaped danger but restored those struck down by the same poison to life.

[Col. 0152A] 129. In the sixty-seventh year after the Passion of the Lord and Savior, under the emperor Trajan, already worn out by extreme old age, he sensed that the day of his departure was approaching. He is said to have ordered a tomb to be dug for him and, after bidding farewell to the brothers and praying, entered the tomb alive; then, as though it were a bed, he rested in it.

[Note: [Col. 0152D]

130. Some have asked whether Saint John the Evangelist died, or whether, after death, he rose again so that he might preach against the Antichrist at the end of the world. The common opinion of the Church is that he truly died, like other human beings, and neither rose nor will rise again before the day of the final judgment. See Benedict XIV, *On the Beatification of the Servants of God*, book I, chapter 14, and Serarius, who published a learned little work on the Twelve Apostles. AREV.]

130. Hence some assert that he is alive and contend that he lies in the tomb not dead but sleeping, especially because the earth there gradually wells up from below and rises to the surface of the tomb, while the dust, as though stirred by the breath of one at rest, boils upward from below. He rested at Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

[Col. 0152B] [Note: [Col. 0152D]

131. On Saint Philip the apostle, consult the *Apostolic Fathers* with Cotelerius’s notes, volume I, page 334. AREV.]

131. Philip, from the city of Bethsaida, the city of Peter as well, preached Christ to the Gauls and led barbarous peoples, neighbors to darkness and joined to the swelling Ocean, into the light of knowledge and the harbor of faith. Then, crucified in Hierapolis, a city of the province of Phrygia, he died after being stoned; his body was buried upright, and there he rests together with his daughters.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

132. Thomas, Christ’s apostle, called Didymus—“twin” in Latin, and thus Christ’s double and likeness—was unbelieving in hearing but faithful in seeing. He preached the Gospel to the Parthians, Medes, Persians, Hyrcanians, and Bactrians, and to the Indians who occupy the eastern region. Penetrating the innermost parts of the nations, he carried his preaching there even to the title of his Passion; for he died transfixed by spears in the city of Calamina in India, where he was also honorably buried.

## CHAPTER LXXV

133. The apostle Bartholomew, whose name is derived from the Syriac language, received Lycaonia as his allotted field of preaching and translated the Gospel according to Matthew into the language of the Indians. Finally, in the city of Albanum [another reading: Abanum] in Greater Armenia, he was flayed alive by the most savage barbarous peoples, and thus was committed to the earth.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0153C]

134. In the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, this chapter is presented as follows: “Matthew is expressed in Hebrew as ‘gift.’ He is also called Levi, from the tribe from which he arose; in Latin, however, he received the name from his work as a tax collector, because he was chosen from among the tax collectors and transferred into an apostle,” and so forth. AREV.]

134. The apostle and evangelist Matthew, who also took the surname Levi from his tribe, was chosen by Christ from the ranks of tax collectors and transferred from sinfulness. At first he preached the Gospel in Judaea; afterward he preached in Macedonia; he rests in the mountains of the Parthians.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

135. James son of Alphaeus, the first bishop of Jerusalem, surnamed the Just, son of the sister of the Lord’s mother, and therefore called the Lord’s brother, was a man of light and worker of truth. He possessed such holiness that the people eagerly sought to touch the fringe of his garment.

136. While preaching Christ the Son of God in Jerusalem, he was thrown down from the Temple by the Jews, crushed beneath stones, and buried there beside the Temple. Josephus testifies that he was held in such holiness and veneration in Judaea that Jerusalem is believed to have been destroyed because of his killing.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0153C]

137. “Beritho.” So reads Dorotheus; others have Nerito.]

137. Jude, brother of James, preached in Mesopotamia and the inner regions of Pontus. By his teaching he softened wild and untamed peoples, whose nature was like that of beasts, and subjected them to the Lord’s faith. He was buried in Berytus, a city of Armenia.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

138. Matthias, one of the seventy disciples, was chosen by lot and appointed among the Twelve Apostles in place of Judas Iscariot. He alone had no surname. [Col. 0153C] The preaching of the Gospel in Judaea was assigned to him.

## CHAPTER LXXX

[Note: [Col. 0153D]

139. This material was added by the Greeks to Jerome’s *Catalogue*, but it applies not to this Simon, rather to Simeon.

In the same place: That the apostle Simon lay in the Bosporus is uncertain on other grounds. More reliable evidence establishes that he preached in Egypt and was crowned with martyrdom in Persia. AREV.]

139. Simon the Zealot, formerly called the Cananaean, fervent in the Lord’s zeal, equal to Peter in surname and like him in honor, received Egypt as his field and, after James the Just, occupied the see of Jerusalem. After 120 years he was deemed worthy, under Trajan, to endure the suffering of martyrdom on a cross. He lies in the Bosporus.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

[Col. 0154A]

[Note: [Col. 0153D]

140. Dorotheus of Tyre wrote about the seventy or seventy-two disciples and lists them individually. David Blondel added notes and points out Dorotheus’s more substantial blemishes. AREV.]

140. These were Christ’s disciples, preachers of the faith and teachers of the nations. Although all were one, each received his own particular and definite place in the world as his allotted field for preaching.

141. Peter received Rome; Andrew, Achaea; James, Spain; John, Asia; Thomas, India; Matthew, Macedonia; [187] Philip, Gaul; Bartholomew, Lycaonia; Simon the Zealot, Egypt; Matthias, Judaea; James, the Lord’s brother, Jerusalem; and Jude, the brother of James, Mesopotamia.

142. No particular lot was assigned to Paul with the other apostles, because he was chosen as teacher and preacher to all the nations. For just as apostleship to the circumcision was given to Peter and the others, so to Paul was given that of the uncircumcision among the Gentiles. He preached the Gospel to seven churches and three disciples.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

143. Luke of Antioch, evangelist and writer of the apostolic history, was by nationality a Syrian, by profession a physician, and educated in Greek eloquence. Most report that he was a proselyte and did not know Hebrew letters. Nevertheless, he was Paul’s disciple and his inseparable companion on his journeys.

[Note: [Col. 0153D]

144. Dorotheus incorrectly asserts that Luke died at Ephesus. Some report that he died at Patras in Achaea, others at Achaean Thebes. Isidore’s opinion, however, is more credible. It is the common opinion that Saint Luke’s Gospel was written in Greek, as were the Gospels of Saints John and Mark; Isidore likewise holds this view in the *Book of Prologues*, no. 91, where several observations are made in support of it. AREV.

In the same place: Many believe that Saint Luke’s bones were transferred to Constantinople, not under Constantine but under the emperor Constantius. The foundations on which each opinion rests can be seen in Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, under the chapter on Saint Luke by Saint Jerome; there most read *Constantius*, while others restore *Constantine*. In Fabricius’s edition of this book of Saint Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, which he prepared with others on the same subject, it is noted that Saint Jerome, in the preface to his work on Luke, also assigns Saint Luke’s death to the year 74, but in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* says that he lived eighty-four years without a wife. It is credible that these words were added, since they are absent from the ancient manuscripts; the ordinary gloss is thought to have arisen through scribal error. AREV.]

144. He was most chaste from early childhood and devoted himself to the work of evangelical preaching. He died in the seventy-fourth year of his life. He was buried in Bithynia, and his bones were later transferred to Constantinople during the reign of Constantine.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0154D]

145. In the cited edition of Fabricius, this note appears on the phrase “to have cut off,” and so forth: “Distinction 55: ‘If anyone cuts off,’ in the gloss on the word ‘Cleric.’ It is also found in the prologue to the Gospel of Saint Mark himself. But Baronius teaches that this deed is falsely attributed to Mark the Evangelist, since it was done by a certain Mark the anchorite; see volume I of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 45, marginal no. 46.” AREV.]

145. Mark the evangelist, Peter’s disciple and his son in baptism. Some report that Peter dictated his Gospel at Rome. He is said to have cut off his thumb so that he would not be promoted to the priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0154D]

146. On the translation of Saint Mark’s body to Venice, see, among others, Flaminius Cornelius, volume XIII of *The Venetian Churches*. AREV.]

146. He was the first to occupy the see of Alexandria and the first to found the churches of the Egyptians. He flourished in such virtues of teaching and self-restraint that all Christ’s disciples followed his example. He died in Alexandria in Nero’s eighth year and was buried in peaceful repose.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

[Col. 0155A]

[Note: [Col. 0155B]

147. On Saint Barnabas the Apostle and his epistle, see Cotelerius’s edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* and Galland’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, volume I. AREV.]

147. Barnabas, also called Joseph, was by nationality from the city of Cyprus, founded by King Cyrus of the Persians. He received the apostleship among the Gentiles together with Paul. Later, because of John the disciple, also surnamed Mark, he separated from Paul; nevertheless, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

[Note: [Col. 0155B]

148. “Saying,” and so forth. The Alban Codex reads: “Saying: ‘Receiving the remembrance of the faith that is in you without deceit, which first dwelt in your grandmother,’” and so forth. AREV.]

148. Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, was from the city of the Lystraeans. His father was Greek, that is, a Gentile, while his mother was Jewish, as the Apostle reports, saying: “Because faith dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice, and I am certain that it dwells in you also.”

[Note: [Col. 0155B]

149. Dorotheus of Tyre foolishly lists Timothy among Christ’s seventy disciples, since he was taken up by the holy apostle Paul while still a boy. AREV.]

149. He was Paul’s disciple and his spiritual son; Paul took him with him when he was still a boy. He remained chaste and a virgin, and he lies buried with great honor at Ephesus, on the mountain called Phion.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0156B]

150. Titus should not be placed with Dorotheus among Christ’s seventy disciples, since he was rather Paul’s disciple. See Paul’s Epistle to Titus, chapter II, verse 7. After “buried,” the Verona Codex adds: “Concerning the names of the twelve apostles who were sent throughout the whole world to preach. Christ’s disciples were twelve,” and so forth. “He preaches to three disciples,” as above, chapter 81. AREV.]

150. Titus, Paul’s disciple and son in baptism, was a Greek by nationality. He alone among the Gentiles was circumcised by the apostle Paul after the Gospel, and the Apostle left him behind to instruct the churches of Crete. There he died in peace and was buried.

[Col. 0155]

# PROLOGUES OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, TO THE BOOKS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT (C)

## Prologue

[Col. 0155C] [Note: [Col. 0155C]

1. “Which the Catholic Church receives in the canon.” In correcting this book, we used seven copies: three had been added at Seville, two on paper and the third on parchment.
