In the two paper copies one reads: “Which the sacred canon contains.” But the word “sacred” seemed redundant, and Jerome everywhere says simply “in the canon,” as in the *Galeate Prologue*, in these words: “Therefore, Wisdom, which is commonly titled Solomon’s, and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobit, and the Shepherd, are not in the canon.” Augustine, book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8: “The entire canon of Scripture, in which we say that this consideration is to be pursued, is contained in these books.” It had become customary for a canon to be issued in councils, comprising all the divine Scriptures. From that canon the canonical books were named. Conversely, apocryphal books, that is, “hidden” books, were so called because, since their reading was prohibited, people used them only secretly and in concealed places. In the divine books, moreover, the word “hidden” is sometimes taken in the sense of “forbidden,” as in Psalm XVI, verse 14: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things,” that is, “They ate what had been prohibited by the law.” Apollinarius understands the passage in this way in his *Metaphrase of the Psalms*, in these words:

Τῶν κρυφίων ἔπλησαν ἑὴν πολυχάνδεα νηδύν — Πλησθέντες σιάλων.

“They filled their capacious belly with hidden things—having been filled with fat.”

MARIANA.

In the same place: This book was furnished with learned notes in Grialius’s edition, so that you can easily recognize Mariana, whose name will be given explicitly or indicated whenever his observations are presented. I have discussed this work more fully in *Isidoriana*, chapter 62, where I also transcribed the preface prepared by Zaccaria for these books. In the Hagonoian edition, after “Church” there is added “which the elder Isidore expounded,” as though the title of the work extended through the words “this is.” AREVALUS.]

1. The fullness of the New and Old Testament, which the Catholic Church receives in the canon according to the ancient tradition of the earlier generations, is as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0156C]

2. “That is, Genesis,” and so forth. . . . Some copies have *Numerus* instead of *Numeri*. MAR.]

2. First, namely, the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy—that is, a recapitulation of the law and, as it were, a second law.

[Col. 0156C] [Note: [Col. 0156C]

3. This book seems to belong not to the history of Judges, as the Hebrews assert, but rather to the beginning of Kings. Jerome, referring to the Hebrew canon in the *Galeate Prologue*, says: “Next they place *Sophetim*, that is, the Book of Judges, and join Ruth to it, because her history is related as having occurred in the days of the Judges.” The Hebrews are firmly convinced that Abesan, who ruled over the Jewish people after Jephthah, was Boaz, Ruth’s husband. Isidore refutes this Hebrew opinion and follows Augustine’s view, book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8, where he says: “The entire canon of Scripture, in which we say that this consideration is to be pursued, is contained in these books: the five books of Moses, namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy; one book of Joshua son of Nun; one of Judges; and one little book called Ruth, which seems rather to belong to the beginning of Kings.” In this passage I suspect that Augustine’s text is corrupt and should be corrected from this passage of Isidore. Otherwise the comparison would seem to have been made rather awkwardly. Josephus supports Augustine’s opinion in book V, chapter 11, of the *Antiquities*, when he says that Ruth’s history occurred in the time of Eli the priest. Isidore himself later gives only this reason for the statement: that the lineage of King David is recounted in that little book. MAR.]

3. These are followed by the books of Joshua son of Nun, Judges, and the little book whose title is Ruth, which seems to belong not to the history of Judges, as the Hebrews assert, but rather to the beginning of Kings.

[Col. 0157A] [Note: [Col. 0157B]

4. “Because they contain the causes of the same events.” The word “causes” is used in various senses; among other things, it signifies the subject matter. Hence rhetoricians distinguish three kinds of causes. Here it seems to signify the affair, outcome, and course of events—in the manner of the Spaniards, for whom the word *causa*, that is, “thing,” extends very broadly in the vernacular through common usage and natural idiom and signifies every matter. The Greek word αἰτία (*aitia*) is not far removed from this meaning. The emperor Julian certainly used that word in its broadest sense when he urged Proaeresius to write history and promised that, if he undertook it, he would prepare for him a commentary on his own actions: Τὰς αἰτίας εἰ μὲν ἱστορίαν γράφεις ἀκριβέστατα ἀπαγγέλλω σοι—“If you write history, I will set forth the events for you with the greatest accuracy.” Isidore uses the same word below in the same sense when he says: “They call Deuteronomy a repetition of the same books and, as it were, a kind of exercise in the law; and this for the reason that those four contain the particular causes of events, whereas this one contains them all.” The passage is taken from Jerome, unless the author of the ordinary gloss is mistaken, at the beginning of Deuteronomy: “As the book of Deuteronomy,” he says, “is a repetition of the four books of the law, for they contain within themselves the particular causes, while this one repeats everything.” Cassian, book III of *The Institutes of the Monastery*, chapter 5, and Conference 21, chapter 14, used *causa* for a thing or condition. MAR.]

4. These are followed by the four books of Kings. Alongside them are attached the two books of Chronicles, because they contain the causes of the same events that are found in the books of Kings.

[Note: [Col. 0157C]

5. “The two books of Ezra and Maccabees.” I would prefer to read “the two books of Ezra and the two books of Maccabees,” as Augustine, from whom this passage was taken, says in book II of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8: “Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, the two books of Maccabees, and the two of Ezra.” The word “two” must certainly refer to both, otherwise Isidore’s total of forty-five books of the Old Testament will not stand. Nor should one be troubled by the words found in book VI, chapter 2, of the *Etymologies*: “No one should be troubled that Ezra is said to have one book, because the second, third, and fourth are not held among the Hebrews but are counted among the apocrypha.” These words are clearly corrupt. For although the Hebrews comprise the books of Ezra and Nehemiah in a single book—a practice Isidore may have followed in the *Etymologies*—the apocryphal books of Ezra are not three but only two. MAR.

In the same place: In some manuscripts, “two” is absent after “the books of Maccabees.” I have made some observations in its proper place, in book VI, chapter 2, no. 28, concerning the words of the *Etymologies* that Mariana considers corrupt. This beginning of the *Prologues* should be compared with that chapter of Isidore and its notes. On the number and authors of the books of Sacred Scripture, see the interpreters in various places. AREV.]

5. Although there are also other volumes that weave together, in the sequence of different periods, histories such as the book of Job, and of Tobit, Esther, Judith, Ezra, and the two books of Maccabees.

[192] [Note: [Col. 0157D]

6. “But all these, except the book of Job, follow the history of Kings.” Augustine says in the cited passage: “Such are Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, the two books of Maccabees, and the two of Ezra, which seem rather to follow that ordered history brought to its conclusion through Kings or Chronicles.” What Augustine understood concerning the books of Ezra as being attached to the books of Kings and Chronicles, Isidore extends to the books of Tobit, Esther, Judith, Ezra, and Maccabees; hence the passage becomes somewhat obscure. For, leaving aside the other books, I do not know how this can apply especially to Tobit, since it is clear that Tobit lived in Assyria during the reigns of Shalmaneser and Sennacherib his son, before the destruction of Jerusalem. Unless perhaps Isidore believed that all these books follow the history of Kings because the events explained in them occurred after all, or after some, of the kings. Moreover, he means the annals of the Jews, Josephus’s history, and other Hebrew books concerning their own affairs; from these the *Seder Olam*, that is, the Hebrew Chronicle, was compiled more than four hundred years ago. —In the same place: “They pursue.” Others read “they continue.” —“Occurred.” Others read “were added.” MAR.]

6. But all these, except the book of Job, follow the history of Kings and thereafter, each in its own period, pursue the annals of the Jews, relating the sad or joyful events that occurred among the Jewish people after the destruction of Jerusalem.

7. Of these, the Hebrews do not accept Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees [Col. 0158A]. Nevertheless, the Church numbers these among the canonical Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0158C]

8. Although they are said to have been published by Jesus son of Sirach. The Codex of Saint Laurence reads *although they are*, instead of *although they are said to be*. According to either reading—as often happens in Isidore—the particle *dum* is taken for *cum*, a usage also common among the ancients, as in these words of the *Aeneid* I:

> When she came, the queen, already proud in her splendid tapestries,  
> arranged herself upon the golden couch and placed herself in the middle.

Servius says: “It must certainly be understood that *cum* and *dum* were confused by the Romans through a deplorable error.” As for attributing Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus to Jesus son of Sirach, and repeating the same claim below, Isidore derived this from Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II, chapter 8, where he says: “For those two books—the one entitled Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus—are said, because of a certain resemblance, to be Solomon’s. For Jesus son of Sirach is most consistently reported to have written them.” Hence, also from the words of Augustine himself, *City of God* XVII, chapter 20, it is understood that the words immediately following should read “because of a certain similarity of style” [Col. 0158D], not “because of a great similarity of style,” as two paper manuscripts from Seville read.

Isidore, however, did not notice that Augustine, in *Retractions* II, chapter 4, retracted the opinion concerning the book of Wisdom. Jerome likewise says in his preface to the books of Solomon concerning Wisdom: “Some ancient writers assert that this book belongs to Philo”—an opinion which Isidore himself, wiser than himself in this matter, followed in *Etymologies* VI, chapter 2. By Philo, as I suspect, he meant not the Alexandrian but the biblical Philo, frequently mentioned by Eusebius in the books of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. MAR.]

8. Next come the Prophets, among whom there is one book of Psalms, and three books of Solomon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. There are also those two distinguished little books of holy instruction—I mean Wisdom and the other called Ecclesiasticus—which, although they are said to have been published by Jesus son of Sirach, have nevertheless been marked with Solomon’s name because of a certain similarity of style. Yet they are known to possess equal authority in the Church with the other canonical books.

[Note: [Col. 0158D]

9. Of these, four are those who composed the larger volumes. Here Isidore follows the opinion of the Greeks and Latins, who believe that all the books of the Prophets were composed by the prophets whose names they bear, although in *Etymologies* VI, chapter 2, he asserts that the books of Ezekiel and Daniel were written by certain wise men—a view that is the consistent opinion of the Hebrews [Col. 0159C]. Rabbi Isaac Harama, in his preface to the Song of Songs, and Rabbi Moses Kimhi, in his book on the authors of the sacred books, say that the men of the Great Assembly wrote the book of Ezekiel, the Twelve Prophets, Daniel, and Esther. I am therefore all the more surprised that, from this group, the Hebrews place Daniel alone among the *Ketuvim*, that is, the Hagiographa. Jerome, in his prologue to Daniel and in the preface to his commentary on that prophet, says that Porphyry seized upon this as an occasion for attacking our religion: he denied that Daniel’s prophecy had been produced by the prophet himself and maintained that it had been written by someone who lived in Judaea during the time of Antiochus Epiphanes. MAR.]

9. There remain the books of the sixteen Prophets, of whom four composed the larger volumes [Col. 0159A]: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.

[Note: [Col. 0159D]

10. Some manuscripts read “Lamentations” instead of “Laments,” and “separate” instead of “cut off.” MAR.]

10. The remaining twelve are short and contiguous, and for that reason have been compressed into a single volume. Their names are: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. Some, however, separating Jeremiah’s Lamentations, cut them away from his volume, and thus accept forty-five books of the Old Testament.

11. From this point the New Testament follows. Its first books are the four Gospels, namely Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Next come the fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians [Col. 0159B], one to the Philippians, two to the Thessalonians, one to the Colossians, two to Timothy, and one each to Titus, Philemon, and the Hebrews.

12. There are also three Epistles of the apostle John, two of Peter, and one each of Jude and James.

[Col. 0160A] 194

13. There are also the Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse of John. Thus, in the order of both Testaments, the books number seventy-two.

[Note: [Col. 0159D]

14. Matthew XIII, 52; Isaiah VI, 3. “They burst forth with the hymn *Trishagios*.” Thus the Sevillian manuscript on parchment reads. The Septimancian reads: “They burst forth with the hymn *Ter hagios*.” Two paper manuscripts from Seville and one from Tarragona read: “Saying ‘Holy, Holy, Holy,’ they burst forth with a hymn.” The allusion is to the words of Isaiah VI, 3, where, concerning the two Seraphim, he says: “They cried out to one another and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts.” He says *they burst forth with a hymn* instead of *they burst forth into a hymn*, a construction also used by Virgil when, in *Aeneid* III, he says:

> And at times a dark cloud bursts forth toward the heavens.

MAR.]

14. For these are the new and the old things that are brought forth from the Lord’s treasury, from which all the mysteries of the sacraments are revealed. These are the two Seraphim who, continually singing in confession of the Holy Trinity, burst forth with the hymn Τρὶς ἅγιος—“Thrice Holy.”

[Note: [Col. 0160C]

15. These are also the two olive trees. This comparison with the olive trees occurred only in one Laurentian manuscript and in the margin of another Sevillian manuscript, nor did the readings of the two agree. We did not dare to delete the passage altogether; we were content to mark it with an obelus as a reading of doubtful authenticity. MAR.]

15. These [perhaps: “these two”] are also the two olive trees in Zechariah, which stand to the right and left of the lampstand and illuminate the whole world with the clarity of their teaching through the richness and splendor of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

16. Some manuscripts read *to be counted* instead of *to be compared*. MAR.]

16. These are the sacred Scriptures, complete in number and authority: nothing else is to be compared with them. Whatever lies outside them is in no way to be received among these holy and divine writings [Col. 0160B].

17. Having therefore set out the order and number of the books of the Old and New Testaments, let us now append, briefly and rapidly, short introductory accounts of them.

## THE PREFACES BEGIN

[Col. 0159]

### On Genesis

[Col. 0159B]

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

18. *Condition* in the sense of creation, and *cataclysm* in the sense of the Flood, are terms used by ecclesiastical writers; *cataclysm* is also used by Varro and Hyginus. AREV.]

18. Genesis, according to the truth of its history, describes the construction of the world, the creation of humankind, the Flood, and the division of the earth; also the confusion of languages, and the deeds of all the patriarchs, up to Israel’s entry into Egypt.

### On Exodus

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

19. Mariana indicates that in some manuscripts the words “with which they were nourished” are absent, as is “the striking of the rock.” AREV.]

19. Exodus contains the servitude of the Hebrews, the ten plagues of Egypt, the people’s departure, and the cloud that protected them [Col. 0159C]; also the crossing of the Red Sea, Pharaoh’s drowning with his chariots, and the singing of glory; the entry into the wilderness, the manna with which they were nourished, the striking of the rock, and the waters changed into sweetness; the battle with Amalek; the commandments of the Decalogue; the Ark of the Covenant; and the dedication of the tabernacle and the offering.

### On Leviticus

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

20. Another reading is: “and the diversity of sins and the purifications.” MAR.]

20. In Leviticus the law of sacrifices is described, together with the diversity of offerings and victims [Col. 0160B], the garments of the high priests, and the ministries of the Levites. The distinction among foods and the various purifications—or offerings—for sins are also prescribed.

### On Numbers

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

21. Another reading, perhaps, is *of them* instead of *of their*. MAR.]

21. In Numbers the tribes that departed from Egypt are counted, and their protections are recorded; the census of the men of mature age who departed from Egypt is inserted; the prophecy of Balaam is given; and the mysteries of the forty-two encampments through the wilderness are marked out [Col. 0160C].

### On Deuteronomy

[Note: [Col. 0160D]

22. “Spoken to the people.” The Septimancian and Tarragonian manuscripts read “given to the people.” In any case, *to give* can mean *to say*, as in Virgil: “Grant it to us, Tityrus,” and “Grant it; I ask for no undeserved thing.” Conversely, *to receive* is used for *to hear*, as in *Aeneid* I:

[Col. 0161C]

> Now hear our purpose, by which you may accomplish this.

]

22. In Deuteronomy, which is the second law, the matters that occurred between Paran, Tophel, Laban, and Hazeroth, up to Kadesh-barnea, are recounted as having been spoken by Moses to the people: namely, commandments and promises, curses for sins, and promises of blessedness. There Moses sings a song. There he gives a blessing to the children of Israel; and there, after seeing the promised land, he dies and is buried.

[Note: [Col. 0161C]

23. Some Hebrews count only four books as belonging to the Law. Nicholas of Lyra, at the beginning of his commentary on the first chapter of Deuteronomy, reports that there were people who denied that Deuteronomy had been written by Moses, on these grounds: at the beginning of the book it says, “These are the words that Moses spoke,” not “wrote”; it speaks of things said “across the Jordan,” although Moses never crossed that river; and at the end it describes Moses’ death. There is no need to refute these arguments, although I think that this opinion was derived from ancient Hebrews. For the more recent Jews consistently affirm that the five books of the Law, and all of them, were written by Moses. For Deuteronomy XXXI, 9 says: “And Moses wrote this law and delivered it to the priests, the sons of Levi”; and again, verse 24: “When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book, he commanded the Levites,” and so forth. MAR.]

23. Some Hebrews count only four books as belonging to the Law, namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. They say that Deuteronomy is a repetition of those same books, and as it were a kind of exercise in the Law. Their sole reason is that those four contain the particular accounts of events, whereas this book contains them all.

### On Joshua

[Note: [Col. 0161C]

24. Another reading is: “the division of the land into the inheritance allotted to them.” [Col. 0161D] MAR.]

24. In the book of Jesus son of Nun, the children of Israel, under the leadership of Joshua, cross the Jordan and are circumcised a second time. Then, after the nations of the Canaanites have been overthrown, they receive their allotted inheritances by the division of the land.

### On the Book of Judges

[Col. 0161B]

[Note: [Col. 0161D]

25. The words “prosperity and adversity in the wars” are marked as doubtful by Mariana. AREV.]

25. The book of Judges contains the sins and enslavements of Israel, the people’s cries, and God’s mercies. It describes the successes and reverses of the wars.

### On the Book of Ruth

[Note: [Col. 0161D]

26. Another reading is *are commemorated* instead of *commemorates*. MAR.]

26. The book of Ruth unfolds the history of that same Moabite woman, from whose stock David’s family descended. The Hebrews append this little book to the book of Judges, because they say that the events recorded in it occurred during the days of the Judges. The Latins, on the other hand, argue that it more properly belongs to the body of the book of Kings, because it traces the lineage of King David, whose origin came from Ruth the Moabite.

### On the Book of Kings

[Col. 0161C]

[Note: [Col. 0161D]

27. Another reading is *parts* instead of *in parts*.—“The first wrote Samuel,” while another reads “Samuel wrote the first.” [The statement that] the priesthood of Eli was mystically transferred to Samuel is Augustine’s opinion, *City of God* XVII, chapter 4, where he says: “For when Eli the priest was rejected, Samuel was appointed to God’s service, performing at once the offices of priest and judge; and when Saul was rejected, King David was established in the kingdom. They prefigured what I am saying: namely, the change from the Old Testament to the New.” Isidore intended to signify this by the adverb *mystically*. Jerome, in *Against Jovinian* I, from the words of Psalm XCVIII, 6—“Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name”—concludes that Samuel was not a priest but only a Levite. This opinion is more acceptable to learned men. For how could he have been a priest, especially a high priest, since he was not descended from Aaron? Jerome likewise says appropriately, in his letter to Paulinus, which serves as a general preface to the sacred books, that the change of priesthood occurred not from Eli to Samuel but from Abiathar to Zadok, and he asserts that this signifies the transition from the Old to the New. MAR.]

27. Although among the Latins the Book of Kings has been cut into four parts because of its length [Col. 0162A], among the Hebrews it is divided into two volumes. Of these, Samuel writes the first: how the Ark of the Lord passed from the Jews to the Gentiles, how the priesthood of Eli was mystically transferred to Samuel, and how Saul’s royal rule passed to David.

[Note: [Col. 0162C]

28. Another reading is *from error* instead of *because of error*.]

28. *Malachim*, however, arranges in chronological order the deeds of the kings of Judaea and of the Israelite nation. It also narrates how Israel itself, because of the error of idolatry, was carried away into Assyria. Finally, it teaches that Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem, took captive the ruler and the people, and overthrew the city and the Temple.

### On Paralipomenon

[Note: [Col. 0162C]

29. Among the Hebrews, Paralipomenon is contained in a single volume. This has been taken from Jerome’s second preface to the books of Paralipomenon. The author added on his own that it was divided into two parts, changing the grammatical case, as he often did. A little farther below, where we read “have been explained,” two paper manuscripts read “have been completed.” But it is understood that our reading is more correct, both from the testimony of several manuscripts and from that preface of Jerome [Col. 0162D], although the meaning does not differ whichever reading is followed. MAR.]

29. Among the Hebrews, Paralipomenon is contained in a single volume and is called by them *Dibrehaiamin*, that is, “Words of the Days.” Among us, however, because of its length, it has been divided into two parts [Col. 0162B]. It is a history containing the order of generations and times. In it, certainly, there is no small amount of instruction in the sacred Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0162D]

30. “For beginning from the origin of the world,” and so forth. We marked the passage with an obelus, although it is supported by the reading of three manuscripts, which did not agree either in the number of years or in the generations. We are not greatly concerned with the reckoning of years, since in this matter—perhaps more than in any other—writers differ. Eusebius counts 4,610 years from the beginning of the world to the destruction of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. The Hebrews, in the *Seder Olam*, count 3,338. After spending some effort on this matter, we found 3,390 years. So much for the reckoning of years. As for the statement that there were seventy-two generations, or descendants, from the beginning of the world to the destruction of Jerusalem, I suspect that the reading is corrupt and that fifty-two generations should be supplied—namely, as many as are counted in Luke and as are counted by the Hebrews from Adam to that time on the basis of the Old Testament [Col. 0163C]. MAR.]

30. For in the history of the Old Testament, matters that were either wholly omitted in their proper places or perhaps not fully arranged are explained here summarily and briefly. Its sequence proceeds alongside the Law or the Books of Kings, reaching all the way to the time at which the text of Kings ends. Beginning at the origin of the world’s creation, it extends through the orderly succession of events up to the ruin of Jerusalem, in 3,072 years [Col. 0162C], through seventy-two generations.

### On the Book of Job

[Col. 0163A]

31. The book of Job contains the losses, funerals, or scourges of that holy man; the insulting words of his comforters; his laments, in which he mourns the misery of the whole world; also God’s consolations to him from the whirlwind, and his double recompense of blessings at the end. Through his sufferings and words he expressed an image of Christ; his wife, on the other hand, represents the type of carnal people who, although placed within the Church, scandalize the lives of spiritual people by their conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0163C]

32. Another reading is *preferred* instead of *provided*, and *display* instead of *parade*. MAR.

In the same place, the fact that Job’s friends represented a likeness of heretics is also noted in the *Allegories*, number 55. That work has much in common with the *Prefaces*, a point that need only be mentioned once. AREV.]

32. His friends, however, provided the appearance of heretics and the figure of perverse doctrines. Elihu, who presses his accusation against Job with severe reproach, signifies those who preach arrogantly within the holy Church and, through swelling of heart and the vanity of knowledge, parade whatever they utter as examples of pride.

### On the Psalter

[Note: [Col. 0163C]

33. For there are ten prophets who wrote them at different times. This is Jerome’s opinion: that not all the psalms were produced by David, in his letter to Cyprian, his letter to Sophronius, and his first book *Against Rufinus*. All the Hebrews agree with Jerome. Augustine is inconsistent: see the beginning of his commentary on the Psalms and *City of God* XVII, chapter 14. Nearly all the other Greek and Latin commentators maintain that David produced all the psalms. I make no decision on this matter at present.

The names of the prophets whom Isidore says composed the psalms were extremely corrupt in all the copies. We have restored the true reading both by comparing the manuscripts with one another and from 1 Chronicles VI, 22. The number ten of the prophets is completed among the sons of Korah. Isidore appears to count Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah among the authors of the psalms only tentatively; this is suggested both by the wording and by *Etymologies* VI, chapter 2, where, although the same subject is treated, their names are omitted.

Rabbi Isaac Harama, in his preface to the Song of Songs, counts ten authors of the psalms, but in a manner quite different from Isidore: Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, and the three sons of Korah. We leave these matters to Jewish legends. Men of outstanding authority and learning assert not only that Ezra, as Jerome says in his letter to Sophronius, gathered all the psalms into a single volume [Col. 0164C], but also take it as certain that the first psalm was composed by Ezra himself, so that it might serve as a preface to the entire work and summon the reader to the reading of the divine Law. MAR.]

33. Although the Book of Psalms is contained in a single volume, it was not published by one and the same author [199]. For there are ten prophets who wrote them at different times: Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Heman, Ethan, Jeduthun, and the sons of Korah—Assir, Elkanah, Abiasaph—or Ezra. Some are also thought to belong to Haggai and Zechariah.

[Note: [Col. 0164C]

34. Concerning those that lack titles. This is the tradition both of the Hebrews and of Jerome, in his letter to Cyprian, where he argues that Moses is the author of eleven psalms, beginning with Psalm 89, in which his name appears, since the ten following psalms lack titles among the Hebrews. MAR.]

34. Concerning those that lack titles, the tradition of the ancients is as follows: when the superscription identifying an author has preceded, the others that follow without a title are believed to belong to that same author. This book is marked by allegorical and typological mysteries; specifically, the fact that Christ was born, suffered, and rose again resounds through almost the entire instrument of the Psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0164C]

35. Another reading is *gathered* instead of *compelled*. MAR.

In the same place: “He compelled,” and so forth. Others read: “He gathered”; then the seventy elders, through a certain mystery of spiritual understanding, when they translated them from Hebrew into Greek and arranged them in order and number. AREV.]

35. It must be understood that among the Hebrews all the psalms were mixed together and without order. Ezra first compelled them into a single volume, arranged them in order and number, and, through the hidden sacrament of a mystery, placed some before others in sequence, although the later ones appear later in time. For according to the course of history, the third psalm comes after the fiftieth; but because of its mystery it comes earlier in the order [200]. The others are arranged in the same way, because the Holy Spirit preordained them as he willed.

### On the Books of Solomon

[Note: [Col. 0164C]

36. “He composed disciplines of three kinds.” Jerome holds this view at the beginning of his commentaries on Ecclesiastes and in his letter to Paula Urbica, except that where Isidore places *theoretical philosophy*, Jerome puts theology in the first place and logic in the second. Isidore himself seems to have combined both readings in *Etymologies* II, chapter 24, when he says: “For the divine utterances likewise consist in these three kinds of philosophy. They customarily discuss nature, as in Genesis and Ecclesiastes; morals, as in Proverbs and throughout the books generally; or logic, for which our writers claim the name theology, as in the Song of Songs and the Gospels.”—In the same place, one manuscript reads *instruction* and another *imitation*. MAR.]

36. Solomon published three volumes. The first of these is the book of Proverbs; the second is called Ecclesiastes; the third bears the title Song of Songs. In these three books he composed disciplines of three kinds, by which one arrives at knowledge of things. First he set forth ethics, that is, morality; then physics, which encompasses the nature of things; and finally theory, that is, contemplation.

In Proverbs, teaching moral matters, he conveyed a higher understanding through a common manner of speaking, and fitted the preservation of the commandments and the instruction of heavenly doctrine into concise verses and brief maxims.

37. Proverbs are statements that explain or signify one matter through other words, or that are understood differently from how they are spoken; their force lies more in the substance of their meanings than in the sound of their words. The Greeks call them *paroimiai*. In Ecclesiastes, examining the nature of things, he condemns—or perhaps discovers—that everything in the world is fleeting and vain; and, having perceived the fragility of all things [Col. 0164C], he admonishes us to renounce the world.

[Note: [Col. 0164D]

38. Another reading is *to be advanced* instead of *to be promoted*.—“Among the Hebrews this was an established observance.” Jerome says something similar to this, in his letter to Paulinus, concerning Genesis and the beginning and end of Ezekiel; Origen also uses almost the same words in homily 1 on the Song of Songs. Isidore puts it this way: “For they say that among the Hebrews it is also observed that, unless someone has reached a mature and fully developed age, he is not even permitted to hold this little book in his hands. We have also learned from them that the following practice is maintained: it is their custom for teachers and wise men to hand all the Scriptures over to boys, together with those which they call *deuteroseis*. But four are reserved for the end: the beginning of Genesis, in which the creation of the world is described, and the beginning of Ezekiel,” and so forth.

The mature age was thirty years, as Jerome says in the cited passage. The *deuteroseis*, as Jerome himself explains in his letter to Algasia, question 10, and in his commentary on Ezekiel chapter 36, were Jewish traditions and legends. In the first book of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 7, Clement calls the traditions of the elders *deuteroseis*. Epiphanius, *Against the Ptolemaeans*, heresy 33, says that among the Hebrews they were contained in four books [Col. 0165D]. In our own time the Babylonian Talmud is divided into the Mishnah and the Gemara, according to Elijah in the *Tishbi*. Mishnah and *deuterosis*—as the force of both names shows, since both signify repetition—are the same thing; properly speaking, they signify the precepts or interpretations of the Law that were devised by the Hebrews after Moses. For this reason Deuteronomy bears this name among the books of Moses: it is, as it were, a repetition of the preceding books, or a second law, to use Isidore’s own words. MAR.

In the same place: It should also be noted that the Hebrews believed that all the books of sacred Scripture ought not to be handed over indiscriminately for reading by everyone. At the time when books were not so readily available, since they were all written by hand, perhaps there was not so great a danger. But in our time, when, through the benefit of printing, countless copies of books are easily released among the common people, who could deny that the Church most sacredly established that the reading of the sacred books should not be permitted indiscriminately to everyone? AREV.]

38. In the Song of Songs, having surpassed visible things and contemplating what is heavenly [Col. 0165A], or divine, he declares, under the figure of bridegroom and bride, the unity of Christ and the Church. Stirring the soul to love heavenly things, he calls it forward toward participation in God [201]. Nor should this be omitted: our teachers transmit the tradition that among the Hebrews it was customary not to allow anyone to read this book unless he were already a man of mature knowledge and tested faith, lest, through the weakness of childhood and inexperience of faith, its teaching should not so much educate unstable minds as turn them toward bodily desires.

[Note: [Col. 0166C]

39. “All the Scriptures,” and so forth. Others read: “Since it is their custom for teachers and wise men to hand all the Scriptures over to boys, together with those which they call *deuteroseis*, these four alone are reserved for the end.” AREV.]

39. It is customary for all the Scriptures to be handed over by their teachers to boys, including those which they call *deuteroseis*. Only these four are reserved for the end: the beginning of Genesis concerning the creation of the world; the beginning of Ezekiel, in which he wrote about the cherubim; his ending, which contains the description of the Temple; and the Song of Songs.

### On the Book of Wisdom

[Note: [Col. 0166C]

40. “The Book of Wisdom, which is called *Panareton*.” Thus the Tarragonian manuscript reads. In the other manuscripts the word *Panareton* was corrupt, except that they all ended it in *-on*. Isidore took these words from Jerome’s prologue to the works of Solomon through a certain error. Jerome says: “There is also the book of Jesus son of Sirach, *Panaeretos*, and another pseudepigraphal book entitled Solomon’s Wisdom.” Thus what Jerome said concerning Ecclesiasticus, Isidore transferred to the book of Wisdom, though not with precisely the same word. For *Panaeretos*, the word used by Jerome, means “excellent” or “distinguished,” from *haireomai*, whereas *Panareton* comes “from virtue” (*apo tes aretes*), as if it meant “a treasury of all virtues.” Rabanus, in his prologue to Ecclesiasticus, following Isidore’s etymology, says—not in the genitive case, as Isidore does, but in the nominative, and not of the book of Wisdom but of Ecclesiasticus—that because of the excellence of its virtues it is called *Panaretos*, that is, “possessing every virtue.” MAR.

In the same place, Mariana marks the words “He published this book … composed” with an obelus as doubtful. AREV.]

40. The Book of Wisdom, which is called *Panareton*, openly announces Christ’s coming—Christ who is the wisdom of God the Father—and his Passion. Jesus, son of Sirach, published this book, in which he also composed several precepts for living.

### 202 On Ecclesiasticus

41. Ecclesiasticus, for its part, has set down abundantly and at length the discipline of almost all moral conduct and the practice of holy religion. It is called Ecclesiasticus because it was delivered in the midst of the assembly of the people, that is, before the church. Because of the great similarity of its meaning and equality of style [Col. 0165C] it is marked with Solomon’s name [Col. 0166A]. It is established, however, that this book too was published by Jesus son of Sirach and that it has been held in equal veneration with the other books of sacred Scripture.

### On Isaiah

[Note: [Col. 0166D]

42. “They traverse the whole world with the speed of a bird.” This is a Hispanicism meaning “throughout the whole world.” MAR.]

42. The prophet Isaiah, whose name means “the salvation of the Lord,” after a coal sent from the altar purified his lips, was made worthy of the prophecy of the Holy Spirit. He beholds two Seraphim symbolizing the two Testaments, with twelve wings—that is, the apostles—who through their preaching traverse the whole world with the speed of birds. They cover the face and feet of the one seated on the throne of God, that is, they conceal both the things that existed before the beginning of the world and those that will exist after the present form of this world has passed away.

[Col. 0166B]

43. After the vision of Judah and Jerusalem, however, he turns the discourse of his prophecy against the other nations that surround them, and according to the character of their places and the diversity of their lives announces the evils that are to come upon them. After Jerusalem’s captivity he threatens the ruin of Babylon.

[Note: [Col. 0166D]

44. “The destruction of the Valley of Zion.” All the copies consistently read this except one Laurentian manuscript, to which, because it had been recently copied, we did not attach much weight; it read “the destruction of the Valley of the Vision.” Isaiah XXII, 1. Jerome and the Vulgate read “the burden of the Valley of the Vision.” The Septuagint has ῥῆμα τῆς φάραγγος Σιών, that is, “the word of the Valley of Zion.” Here I suspect that the Hebrew reading, as in many other places, was changed in antiquity; and that, instead of the reading now found in the Hebrew manuscripts and in Jerome, the Septuagint read what it did through an easy interchange of letters. The meaning is not dissimilar, since Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi David Kimhi, in their commentaries on that passage, maintain that the prophet was speaking of the Valley of Zion and Jerusalem. MAR.]

44. Next come the slaughter of the Philistines, the devastation of Moab, the destruction of Damascus, the agitation of Egypt, and the desolation of the Desert Sea; also the siege of Edom, the flight and destruction of Arabia, the destruction of the Valley of Zion, and the overthrow of Tyre—or of the four-footed creatures. Figuratively, however, the Synagogue of Judah is cast down in the vision, and the Church is joined to the Lord. In the ruin of Babylon, the confusion and pride of the whole world are condemned, and its end is displayed. In the devastation of Moab, the error of secular knowledge is changed into silence and mourning [Col. 0166C].

[Col. 0167A]

[Note: [Col. 0167D]

45. I have already noted elsewhere that in Grialius’s text *idolatria* is almost always written instead of *idololatria*. AREV.]

45. In the overthrow of Egypt, the idolatries of the whole world are destroyed, and the building of the Lord’s Temple is proclaimed. In the crushing of the Philistines, the mourning of those who reject Christ’s yoke and raise themselves against the knowledge of God is displayed. Through Damascus, the preaching to the Gentiles and the ruin of the Jewish people are shown. Through the burden of the Desert Sea, the temptation of this world is signified, and the things that are to come upon it are revealed.

46. Through Edom, the sun of righteousness rises for the Gentiles, while darkness comes upon the Jewish people. Through Arabia, the water of baptism is preached as something to be offered to those who have fled the errors—or the blasphemies—of the Gentiles. Through the Valley of Zion, the destruction of Jerusalem and of the heretics who have fallen from the height of the Church is proclaimed. Through Tyre, the Gentiles are urged to abandon the error of the world and turn to Christ the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0167D]

47. “He prophesied for approximately seventy years.” It is not easy to determine how many years each prophet prophesied. Unless the passage in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* is corrupt, nearly one hundred years elapsed from the beginning of Isaiah’s prophecy to his death [Col. 0168D]. There is no less difficulty concerning Jeremiah, whom Isidore says prophesied for seventy-two years and three months, and I strongly suspect that the passage is corrupt. For Jerome, in his commentary on chapter I of that prophet, says that he prophesied for forty-one years, apart from the time when he was taken into Egypt. From Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, forty-five years are reckoned from the beginning of Jeremiah’s prophecy to the overthrow of Jerusalem. MAR.]

47. The rest of his prophecy concerns either Christ, or the Church of the Gentiles, or the consummation of the world. He prophesied for approximately seventy years under four kings of Judah, succeeding one another in order and by lineage: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and finally Hezekiah. Under Hezekiah the greater part of his book is woven together, extending to the end of his prophecy.

### On Jeremiah

48. The prophet Jeremiah, whose name means “the exalted one of the Lord,” is simple in speech and easy to understand; in all his words and sufferings he presented an image of our Redeemer. After, in a type of Christ, he had destroyed the kingdoms of the devil and built the dominion of justice or faith, he is commanded to prophesy against all the nations—namely, Egypt and the Philistines, Moab and Ammon, Edom and Damascus, Kedar, the kingdoms of Assyria, and also Elam and Babylon [Col. 0167C].

49. Amid these things he sees the watchful branch of divine correction and power. He also sees a boiling pot, that is, the Jewish people burning with the fire of carnal desires. He beholds two baskets of figs as a prefiguration of the two peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0168D]

50. “The reduction of the former vessel.” He used *reduction* in the sense of *shattering*, in accordance with Terence:

> I shall smash your head today unless you leave.

MAR.]

50. He also goes down to the potter’s house and sees the shattering of the former vessel and the restoration of the new one, signifying the decline of the former people and the succession of the future people. He also takes the cup of punishment and offers it to all the nations. He receives a loincloth as an image of the Jewish people and, after it has rotted, throws it away [Col. 0167D] across the rivers of the nations, signifying dispersion. He also displays Babylon’s golden cup, by which the world has been drunk with the deadly draught of idolatry [Col. 0168A].

51. He is also commanded to throw into the Euphrates the scroll tied to a stone, to demonstrate the destruction of Babylon, or figuratively that of the whole world. He also rebukes transgressors and calls them to conversion.

52. Finally, he laments the ruin of Jerusalem, the destruction of the Temple, and the dispersion of the people—things which he not only foretold but also saw as present realities. He began in the twelfth year of King Josiah of Judah, at the time when the woman Huldah also prophesied, and his prophecy extended through four kings: Josiah, Eliakim, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah, under whom Jerusalem was destroyed. He prophesied for seventy-two years and three months, except for the period during which, after the destruction of Jerusalem, he was in Egypt with the people.

## Concerning Ezekiel

[Col. 0168B]

53. Ezekiel, whose name is translated “strength of God,” figuratively prefiguring Christ, stands beside the river of the age and beholds glorious mysteries.

54. He sees the likeness of the glory of God, and four living creatures in the likeness of the Gospels, and wheels containing one another as a type of the Testaments. He sees also the charioteer—that is, Christ—shining below with the fire of judgment and above with electrum, that is, with the radiance of divinity. He also eats the book of the divine law, in which are written the lament of penitents, the song of the righteous, and the woe of those who, after sinning, have not done penance.

[Note: [Col. 0168D]

55. Alternatively, “a type of death and a figure of the Antichrist.” MAR.]

55. Next he receives a brick on which besieged Jerusalem is depicted, or on which, under the type of Christ, the mysteries of that same Jerusalem—that is, of the whole Church, which was formed from Christ’s side—are represented. This prophet also receives the dream of lying on his left side, as a type of the death of sinners, who, placed on the left, will suffer eternal punishments; finally, he is commanded to sleep from his left side on his right because of the hope of those who, through a change of conduct, will attain the glory of the resurrection. Meanwhile he also sees two rods joined to one another, in the likeness of circumcision and the Gentiles, or an eagle under Nebuchadnezzar, like a figure of the Antichrist, occupying the empires of the whole world with great wings and swift flight.

56. Moreover, under the appearance of the prince of Tyre, he laments the devil’s blessedness, which he lost, and deplores his great ruin with profound lamentation. [Col. 0168D] Finally, carrying a reed or cord, he measures Jerusalem mystically under the figure of the saints.

[Col. 0169A] [Note: [Col. 0169C]

57. Alternatively, “threatens,” instead of “accuses.” MAR.]

57. In the midst of these things he introduces certain moral teachings in mystical form: he accuses false prophets and commands the watchmen not to keep silent about wickedness. He also proclaims to sinners four punishments of vengeance, and prophesies that souls will return to their bodies. He shows also that each person will give an account to the Lord for himself, and that the stain of a father’s offense can no longer be transmitted to his descendants.

[Note: [Col. 0169C]

58. Alternatively, “completed his prophecy.” MAR.]

58. In the midst of these things, under the names Oholah and Oholibah, he rebukes all the depravity of Samaria and Jerusalem, and casts their shameful birth in their teeth. He often calls captive peoples to repentance and, after their transgression, admonishes the people to return in conversion. He prophesied in Chaldaea in the thirty-fifth year of his life and the fifth year of his captivity, while living there in exile; and there he completed his prophecy. [Col. 0169B]

## Concerning Daniel

59. Daniel, whose name is interpreted as “judgment of God,” is also the clearest of all the prophets concerning Christ. Indeed, he not only foretold the one who was to come, as the others did, but also determined the time of his incarnation and passion in sequence by the succession of kings and by the number of years, so that he seems rather not to be predicting the future but, as it were, narrating events already completed. He repeatedly sees visions of four kingdoms and introduces their differences under various images.

[Note: [Col. 0169D]

60. He also presents the tales of Bel and the dragon. Most manuscripts read *fabula* in the singular instead of *fabulas*. Jerome, however, in his prologue to Daniel, from which Isidore borrowed this material, denies that the story of Susanna, the hymn of the three youths, and the tales of Bel and the dragon are in the Hebrew text. He speaks in the same way in the preface to his commentaries on the same prophet. No one should therefore be disturbed by the unusual word and suppose, on the testimony of Jerome and Isidore, that Daniel’s prophecy is accused of falsity in that part. For *fabula*, derived from *fari*, “to speak,” as Varro says in Book V of *On the Latin Language*, is a matter widely reported, whether it is true or false. Thus the word is commonly used in both senses. Origen, *Homily 5 on Genesis*: “Here now that famous tale of Lot is related.” Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.23: “Hear a tale—not a tale, but an event that happened—about John the apostle.” Jerome, *To Philippians* II: “It would be a lengthy task,” he says, “if I wished to apply Samson’s tale to the mystery of Christ.” MAR.

Same note. In Mariana’s note it read *ut sit Varro*; I changed it to *ut ait Varro*, because I think that is how he wrote it. AREV.]

60. He also shows concerning the Antichrist that he is the little horn, that is, one who will reign for a short time; after subjecting ten kings, he alone will reign in the final times. He writes much about the consummation of Jerusalem or of the world, and about the day of judgment and the kingdom of the saints. At the end of his prophetic book he places the story of Susanna and the tales of Bel and the dragon.

61. This book, among the Hebrews, is written in Hebrew letters but in the Chaldaean language. He prophesied in Babylon, at the same time as Ezekiel.

## Concerning Hosea

[Note: [Col. 0170D]

62. Alternatively, *peritior*, “more learned,” instead of *operosior*, “more laborious.” MAR.]

62. The prophet Hosea, whose name is understood as “saving,” is the first among the twelve prophets, deeper than the rest in his statements and more laborious to understand. He speaks to those tribes called Ephraim and Samaria, the house of Joseph and Israel; but by Ephraim he rebukes heretics who, departing from the unity of the Church, have become participants in idolatry.

[Note: [Col. 0170D]

63. Alternatively, *eorum*, “of them,” instead of *eorumdem*, “of those same people.”—Same note: “They pretend that they have kept the commandments, or the law of God. They will believe in Christ at the end of time.” This is an archaism, used instead of “believe in Christ,” as in *Aeneid* II, “Such was he in the presence of Priam, his enemy.” With similar freedom of expression he said above *transmigratum* instead of *transmigrare*, and *invisi sunt* instead of *inviderunt*, along with other examples whose explanation would take too long. MAR.]

63. Through Samaria he also displays the figure of those same heretics, who pretend to be keepers of God’s commandments and, under the pretext of truth, cultivate falsehood. Historically, he declared that the Jews would believe in Christ at the end of time. He also foretold the third day of the Lord’s resurrection. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, or of Jeroboam, king of Israel, at the same time as Isaiah.

## Concerning Joel

64. The prophet Joel, whose name is interpreted as “beginning,” bringing forth a prophecy concerning Judah and Jerusalem alone, at the beginning of his book calls Jerusalem from luxurious banquets to mourning and foretells its destruction. He also proclaims the calling of the Gentiles and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon assembled believers. He prophesied under Joatham, king of Judah, at the same time as Micah.

## Concerning Amos

[Note: [Col. 0170D]

65. Alternatively, “Samaria.” MAR.]

65. Amos, whose name is interpreted as “burden,” prophesied against Samaria and Jerusalem, describing the three and four crimes of the nations under the figure of the whole world. The first crime is that all sinned in Adam. The second is that, forgetful of reason, they did not understand the law implanted in nature. The third is that of those who did not obey the law that had been given. The fourth, unforgivable, is that of those who did not believe in Christ. Because of these crimes the Lord thunders forth fire—that is, a sentence that will bring eternal judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0170D]

66. Alternatively, *formans*, “forming,” instead of *firmans*, “establishing.” “Announcing Christ among human beings.” Thus four more accurate manuscripts; three others read, “announcing his Christ among human beings,” as it appears in the text of the Septuagint translators and as Augustine read it in *The City of God* XVIII.28. The entire passage is drawn from Amos 4:13, where the Vulgate reads: “For behold, he is the one who forms the mountains, creates the wind, and announces his word to man.” Jerome teaches that at that place the Hebrews of his own and our time read [Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text], whereas the Septuagint read [Greek term omitted in the supplied text]; and this was the occasion for the differing interpretation. MAR.

Same note. In one of my copies the Hebrew words in the note begin with [Hebrew text omitted in the supplied text]. AREV.]

66. Here he thus proclaims the coming of Christ in the voice of the Lord: “I am the one who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces Christ among human beings.” The remaining things that he says about Amaziah and Jeroboam, or Israel, are to be referred tropologically to heretics. He prophesied under King Uzziah, at the time of Hosea and Isaiah.

## Concerning Obadiah

[Col. 0171A]

[Note: [Col. 0171C]

67. Alternatively, “created from their stock.” “He prophesied under Josiah.” The passage is extremely difficult. The Hebrews, as Jerome says in his introduction to this same prophet, think that this is the Obadiah who, in the time of Ahab, fed the prophets in caves. Dorotheus, in the *Synopsis*, says that he was the third commander of fifty sent to Elijah. Isidore himself follows both accounts in *On the Life and Death of the Saints*. If these things are true, he did not prophesy in the time of Uzziah but of Jehoshaphat, as the Septimancensis, Laurentianus, and Hispalensis manuscripts on parchment read. According to Jerome, in his commentary on Hosea I, Hosea, Isaiah, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, and Micah were σύγχρονοι—that is, contemporaries. The reading in two paper manuscripts from Hispalis agrees with this view, namely, that he prophesied under Uzziah. Isidore himself makes Obadiah a contemporary of Micah and Micah a contemporary of Zephaniah. Zephaniah prophesied under Josiah, at the same time as Jeremiah. Therefore the Tarraconensis and Parisian manuscripts say that this prophet prophesied under Josiah. We have followed this reading, although a little above, concerning Joel, he says: “He prophesied under Joatham, king of Judah, at the same time as Micah.” Unless perhaps in that passage too *Josiah* should be read for *Joatham*. MAR.

Same note. I think Mariana wrote “*Joatham* should be read” instead of “*Josiah*,” or at least intended this. See the variant readings. AREV.]

67. Obadiah, whose name is interpreted as “servant of the Lord,” is the shortest of all the prophets in number of words, but equal in the grace of his mysteries. Speaking against Idumaea, he mystically rebukes the pride of Edom, namely, the audacity of the former people, because it killed Jacob its brother—that is, Christ, born from the stock of the Hebrews. On Mount Zion, which is Jerusalem, he announces the salvation that is to come and the Holy One, who is Christ; and on Mount Esau, by which the Church of the Gentiles is represented, he proclaims that the Lord’s kingdom is to come. He prophesied under Josiah, king of Judah, at the same time as Micah.

## Concerning Jonah

[Note: [Col. 0171D]

68. Alternatively, *indicat*, “indicates,” instead of *figurat*, “figures.” MAR.]

68. Jonah, whose name is interpreted as “dove,” figures by both his speech and his shipwreck the passion, death, and resurrection of Christ: either because he was thrown from the ship into the sea, as from the cross onto the earth; or because, received into the belly of the whale, he was hidden for three days and nights as in the burial place of the earth; or because, in the figure of Nineveh, he foretold repentance to the world. In what follows he bears the type of the Jews, who not only did not wish the salvation of the Gentiles to arrive but, when it came, were hostile [Al., “envious”]. Nineveh also signifies the figure of the Gentiles, while Jonah in this passage represents the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0171D]

69. “For when it came,” etc. 2 Corinthians 5:17. He prophesied under Uzziah, 2 Kings 4:15. It is established that Jonah lived in the time of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, who was Uzziah’s contemporary. Those who say that Jonah was the boy whom Elijah restored to life in 2 Kings 4 are mistaken, although they rely on the authority of Dorotheus, Jerome, and many other great men. MAR.]

69. For just as the salvation of the Ninevites provoked Jonah to jealousy, so the redemption of the Gentiles became a stumbling block to the Jews. Appropriately, too, he is read to have sat facing the east of the city beneath the shade of an ivy plant, because that same people, separating itself from the salvation of the Church and wasting away in grief, strives to move its tongue against Christ—that is, against the East of the Church—sitting beneath the shadow of the law. This shadow was dried up by a worm, because, when Christ came, the old things passed away, and behold, all things became new. He prophesied under Uzziah, king of Judah, at the time when Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah prophesied.

## Concerning Micah

[Note: [Col. 0172C]

70. Alternatively, “the people of Israel.” “He prophesied under Josiah, at the time of Zephaniah.” Other manuscripts read “under Uzziah.” Neither reading is satisfactory; I would prefer “under Hezekiah,” because of the passage in Jeremiah 26:18: “Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah.” At the beginning of his prophecy he himself says: “The word that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.” Perhaps it extended into the reign of Josiah, when Zephaniah is known to have prophesied; Isidore makes Zephaniah Micah’s contemporary, and Micah the contemporary of Joel and Obadiah. MAR.]

70. The prophet Micah’s name is interpreted as “Who is this?” He threatens Samaria with the Lord’s anger because of its idols and announces the destruction that will come upon the people of Israel. He also points out the place in which Christ would be born. He prophesied under Josiah, at the time of Zephaniah.

## Concerning Nahum

[Note: [Col. 0172C]

71. Nahum, “the comforter.” Thus the Septimancensis; but the Tarraconensis and Hispalensis manuscripts on parchment read “comforted,” a reading not to be despised. Moreover, in the *Seder Olam* the Hebrews assert that Joel, Nahum, and Habakkuk prophesied in the time of Manasseh and, because he was wicked, suppressed his name. Jerome, in his prologue to the twelve prophets, says: “Wherever the time is not given in the title, they prophesied under those kings under whom the prophets who have titles before them also prophesied.” I do not discover where Jerome derived this opinion. Isidore, at any rate, assigned no dates to the prophecies of Nahum and Habakkuk. MAR.

Same note. In two of my copies of the Grial edition, one had *jejunio* (“fasting”), while in the other I correctly find [the reading] in Mariana’s note; I have observed this elsewhere too, so that it may be clear that some corrections were added to the copies intended for printing. AREV.]

71. Nahum, who is the comforter, declares that the idols of the nations are to be exterminated, as well as Jerusalem, the city of blood, after whose destruction the feet of the one announcing peace—that is, the coming of the Savior—proclaim it. [Col. 0172B]

## Concerning Habakkuk

[Note: [Col. 0172D]

72. Alternatively, “declares the coming.” MAR.]

72. Habakkuk, “the embracer,” or “a strong wrestler,” at the beginning of his book describes the devil with his members and his ways; at the end he foretells the coming and passion of the Savior.

## Concerning Zephaniah

73. Zephaniah, the observer of the Lord’s mysteries and the one who hides them, sees the captivity of the city of Jerusalem that is to come at the hands of the Romans, through the voice of a cry from the Fish Gate and through the crushing of the hills—that is, of Mount Zion, which is the hill of Jerusalem. He also proclaims the overthrow of other nations and thunders forth the terror of divine judgment.

[Col. 0172C] 74. He also speaks against Moab and Ammon; but through them, as neighbors of the people of God and close to Catholic mysteries, heretics are rebuked. He foretells the third day of Christ’s resurrection and announces that, at Christ’s coming, the whole world will serve the Lord under one yoke. He prophesied under Josiah, at the same time as Jeremiah.

## Concerning Haggai

75. Haggai, whose name is interpreted as “solemn,” in the text of his prophecy commanded that the Lord’s Temple be restored; he proclaims the contrition of the nations, or foretells the shaking of the whole world, and under the figure of Zerubbabel prophesies the coming of Christ. He prophesied in the seventieth year of the captivity of the people, preceding Zechariah in his prophecy by only two months.

## Concerning Zechariah

[Col. 0173B] [Note: [Col. 0173D]

76. Alternatively, “among the fathers.” MAR.]

76. Zechariah, whose name means “remembrance of the Lord,” after he had already prophesied to the fathers of the Lord, saw a man seated on a red horse, representing the body of Christ, rosy with the blood of his passion, or myrtle trees signifying the people of the nations. He also sees four horns, or smiths, representing the nations that, scattering Judah and Israel, crushed them beneath a heavy burden.

[Note: [Col. 0173D]

77. I think there is no distinction between *torrem* and *titionem*. AREV.]

77. Likewise he observes Jesus, clothed in the filth of the flesh and mortality; when these have been removed, he is clothed in immortality and glory. He sees also the stone, which is Christ, having seven eyes—that is, the fullness of the sevenfold Spirit. In the midst of these things he observes a log, or an extinguished firebrand, that is, the devil. He sees a lampstand in the figure of Christ, with seven lamps, which are the Churches; and also two olive trees placed at the right and left of the lampstand, signifying the type of the two Testaments.

[Note: [Col. 0173D]

78. Alternatively, “the Devil and the mass,” instead of “the diabolical doctrine and the mass.” MAR.]

78. He also takes two rods, of cord and beauty, as a type of the Jews and the Gentiles. Then he sees two women—that is, communities of heretics, or of Jews—lifting an ephah on their wings, that is, a diabolical doctrine, and a mass of lead, which is the heaviest weight of sin; or a flying scroll, in which the sins and punishments of human beings are described.

[Note: [Col. 0173D]

79. Grial’s text had *infixio* instead of *infixam*; I corrected it on the basis of the other witnesses and of the sense itself. AREV.]

79. He also sees four chariots running under one yoke of evangelical preaching. After this he sees horses sent out to preach to the world: the first red, representing the passion of martyrdom; the second black, representing the squalor of repentance; the third white, representing the brightness of baptism; the fourth variegated, representing the exposition and teaching of the faith. He also sees trumpets representing the saints, through which the Lord sings to the world; and he describes a corner in which two peoples facing one another are joined, or a stake, figuratively Christ, fixed in the hearts of the peoples. He also describes a shepherd, the Antichrist, having his work and intention on the left.

80. He also sees a horse representing the community of heretics, and its rider, the devil. He further proclaims a fountain in the house of the true David, open in the laver of regeneration. Whatever else he writes concerns either the coming of the Lord, or his passion, or the end of the age and the judgment. He prophesied in the second year of Darius, king of the Medes, at the same time as Haggai, in the seventieth year of the Temple’s desolation and of the people’s captivity.

## Concerning Malachi

[Note: [Col. 0173D]

81. Alternatively, “angel of God.”—At the end: alternatively, “announces the end”; alternatively, “declares.” MAR.]

81. Malachi, whose name is interpreted as “angel of the Lord,” at the beginning of his prophecy demonstrates, in Esau, the hatred directed toward the Jews, and, in Jacob, the love directed toward the younger people. [Col. 0174B] In what follows he rejects the former sacrifices of the Jews and announces that the sacrifice will be transferred to the Gentiles. Finally, he speaks of the coming of the Lord, the day of judgment, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishments of the impious. He also proclaims that John was sent before the Lord’s first coming, and announces that Elijah is to be sent before his second coming.

[Note: [Col. 0173D]

82. Alternatively, “that they should be good and without blame”; alternatively, “he commands the peoples to return them.” MAR.]

82. In the midst of these things he explains certain moral matters appropriate to discipline. He rebukes the people, or the priests, who despise the name of the Lord and violate his mysteries with polluted offerings and sacrifices. He also warns learned bishops that they must be good and without blemish and instruct peoples in the truth without partiality; he rebukes the quarrelsome and commands the peoples of the Church to return tithes and first fruits to the preachers. [Col. 0174C]

[Note: [Col. 0174D]

83. “They despise their own wives and become entangled through love of others.” Two Hispalensis manuscripts add after these words: “The Hebrews understand this Malachi as Ezra the priest, for many things written in this prophecy are also contained in his book.” Although these words could have been defended by the authority of Jerome, preface to this prophet, and Augustine, *The City of God* XX.25, they seemed ill-fitted to the passage; we moved and rejected them here. MAR.]

83. He also rebukes those who despise their own wives and become entangled through love of others. Likewise he rebukes those who, grieving over their own misery, praise the happiness of those who enjoy the prosperity of this world. He was the last to prophesy in Babylon, at the time of Haggai and Zechariah.

## Concerning Ezra

[Note: [Col. 0174D]

84. Alternatively, “he wrote: the people.” MAR.]

84. Ezra writes that, when the period of captivity had been completed, under Cyrus, king of the Persians, the people returned to Jerusalem; and that under Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest—or under Nehemiah—the walls of Jerusalem, the Temple, and the altar were restored, the rights of the priests reinstated, and the practice of the holy religion richly adorned by the gifts of the wealth of the nations and of the Persian princes.

## Concerning the Maccabees

85. Although the books of the Maccabees are not included in the canon of the Hebrews, they are nevertheless counted by the Church among the histories of the divine books. They recount the battles between the leaders of the Hebrews and the peoples of Persia, the battle on the Sabbaths, the noble triumphs of the Maccabees, the treaty of friendship with the Roman commanders, and the deeds of the embassies.

## Concerning the Four Gospels

[Note: [Col. 0175C]

86. Alternatively, “may it be fourfold.” — “Vigor”: alternatively, “dew”; alternatively, “strength.” MAR.

Same note. Some printed editions place before it the title: “Prefaces to the Books of the New Testament.” Isidore used the comparison of the four rivers of Paradise in *Etymologies* VI.16: “Among the other councils, we know that there are four venerable synods which principally embrace the whole faith, like the four Gospels, or the same number of rivers of Paradise.” See also Sedulius, Book III, line 173. Instead of *virorem*, “freshness,” *vigorem*, “vigor,” may perhaps be preferable. AREV.]

86. Although the preaching of the Gospels is fourfold, it is nevertheless one, because it proceeded from one and the same mouth of the Divinity. These are the four rivers flowing from one fountain of Paradise; they flow in fourfold unity through the whole world, dispensing the streams of heavenly preaching and pouring in the freshness of grace and faith.

[Note: [Col. 0175D]

87. Alternatively, “subdued” or “subjected,” instead of “subjects,” and “described,” instead of “has described.” MAR.]

87. This is that chariot of the Lord in Zechariah, in which he is carried throughout the whole world and subjects to himself the necks of all nations under an easy yoke. These are also the creatures that prophetic vision described under the form of four living beings: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle.

[Note: [Col. 0175D]

88. Alternatively, “the calf,” instead of “the death of the calf.” MAR.

Same note. The emblems of the Evangelists are related in the same way in the *Allegories*, no. 130 and following. AREV.]

88. The first, namely Matthew, as a man, designates the order of human birth. The second, namely Mark, like a roaring lion, immediately thunders at the beginning of his Gospel the strength of divine power. The third, namely Luke, introducing the priest’s victim, suggests, as it were, the death of a calf. The fourth, namely John, gazing heavenward like an eagle, eagerly flies across the earth and penetrates the birth of the Word through the hidden understanding of the mystery. But of these, the three creatures that walk upon the earth, following an active life, pursued only those things that Christ the man did temporally on earth. The fourth creature, with the sharpness of contemplation, looks upon heavenly things and set forth few works but very many mysteries of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0175D]

89. “Matthew, therefore.” These words, up to “and announced that he existed in the beginning,” were found only in two Hispalensis manuscripts and seemed of doubtful authenticity; therefore they were marked for deletion with an obelus, as was the entire passage concerning the Epistles of blessed Peter, beginning “In the First Epistle” and continuing to the end. In addition, several other words throughout the work were marked with an obelus; we did not judge it necessary to mention each one individually and explain its basis. MAR.

Same note. An error entered both of my copies of the Grial edition: *verum* instead of *rerum*. AREV.]

89. Matthew, therefore, following the royal genealogy of Christ at the beginning, but afterward following moral instruction more closely, composed few accounts of signs and many precepts for living. Likewise Mark, Matthew’s abridger, quickly rewove what Peter taught on the journey concerning the ordering of life. He proceeds midway between Luke and Matthew, yet recalls more from Matthew, preserving not only the order of events but also that of the words.

90. Luke, however, adhering more closely to the order of the history, declares the deeds and virtues of Christ more fully than the others. Finally, John, explaining natural things, flew beyond the heavens and the angels, found the Word of God, and announced that he existed in the beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0176C]

91. The others published their works in the eloquence of the Greek language. It is a much more reasonable opinion that all the Evangelists except Matthew wrote in Greek than the recently advanced view that Mark wrote in Latin, which is supported by no sufficiently adequate argument. MAR.

Same note. Some maintain that Mark wrote in Latin because they think the autograph of the holy Gospel of Mark is preserved at Venice. But whatever is said about this autograph is a dream; concerning it, see P. Blanchini’s *Fourfold Evangelistary* and Zaccaria’s *Literary History of Italy*, vol. I, p. 14 and following. The opinion that not only Mark but also the other Evangelists wrote in Latin is even more absurd. AREV.]

91. Of these, the first and the last proclaimed what they had heard from Christ’s mouth, or what they had heard had been done and accomplished by him. The two middle Evangelists recorded only what they had learned from the apostles. Matthew first wrote his Gospel in Judaea, then Mark in Italy, the third, Luke, in Achaea, and the last, John, in Asia. Of these, only Matthew briefly set down the history of his preaching in Hebrew style. The others published their works in the eloquence of the Greek language.

## Concerning the Epistles of Paul

[Note: [Col. 0176D]

92. To the Thessalonians, to the Hebrews. He does not include the Hebrews among the Churches because he writes to those who, as he says a little later, have departed from the faith. “The remaining.” Alternatively, “the remaining four.” MAR.]

92. The apostle Paul expressed the substance of his preaching in fourteen Epistles. Of these he wrote seven to Churches, because of the type of the sevenfold Church, preserving and not exceeding the number of the mystery because of the efficacy of the sevenfold Holy Spirit. He wrote to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, Thessalonians, and Hebrews; the remaining letters he later addressed to individual persons, so that once again he might turn that same number seven toward the mystery of unity.

[Note: [Col. 0176D]

93. Alternatively, *steterunt*, “stood,” instead of *perstiterunt*, “persevered,” and *gratulatur*, “rejoices,” instead of *gloriatur*, “glories.” MAR.]

93. The subjects of these Epistles are as follows. First, he praises the faith of the Roman people. He chastises the Corinthians with a twofold teaching. Among the Galatians, through the grace of faith, he excludes the works of the law. He magnifies the Ephesians for the faith they received. He praises the Colossians because they persevered in the faith. He rejoices that the Philippians kept the Gospel. In the First Epistle, he boasts that the Thessalonians increased in faith and works; in the Second, that they bravely endured persecutions.

94. Through Timothy and Titus he also instructs Churches. He makes request of Philemon on behalf of his reformed servant Onesimus. Finally, he strengthens the Hebrews who believed in Christ but afterward, frightened by Jewish persecutions, departed from the faith, and he recalls them to the grace of the Gospel. [Col. 0177A]

## Concerning the Epistles of Blessed Peter

95. The apostle Peter wrote two Epistles, which are called catholic. He wrote to those who, believing from the circumcision, were dispersed among the nations. These may seem to some rather plain, although they are filled with such profound meanings that those who are able to investigate the sense of divine knowledge may behold great statements and great mysteries revealed to them through them, as through a small receptacle.

[Note: [Col. 0177D]

96. Concerning the words contained in this number and the three following, Mariana wrote earlier, at no. 89. When it is said that the saints are living stones, etc., there is an allusion to the words of Saint Paul: “Beloved by God, called as saints.” AREV.]

96. In the First Epistle he writes of the power of regeneration and of the prophets who foretold the Church’s future endurance in sufferings. He then admonishes the pontiffs to live in chastity and, like little children, to remain without deceit. He also demonstrates that the saints are living stones, a people of possession, and a royal priesthood. In the midst of these teachings he establishes for ordinary people an order of good living: he exhorts women to be subject and not to walk in luxurious adornment, and men to cling to their wives with moderation, to pray frequently, and to live in harmony with all. He further writes of the mystery of the ark, or the sacrament of baptism, through which a person is freed from the works of the world.

97. He commands the faithful to obey the precepts of the divine will alone and no longer to serve the desires of the flesh. He also teaches the clergy and the people to minister to one another in turn, not to fear the sufferings of Christ, and that judgment should begin with the household of God; he teaches that the saints will be crowned and admonishes them to observe mutual gentleness and humility, taking every precaution against the devil’s snares. He adds that every good work begun through God is brought to completion.

[Note: [Col. 0177D]

98. Perhaps, “enticed by the pleasures of sinners.” MAR.]

98. In the Second Epistle he addresses the faithful as though slain in this world and exhorts all to pass from worse things to better. He also writes that the memories of the righteous should be revived, and mentions the false prophets of both Testaments, who are teachers of lies. Then he introduces the example of the Flood to signify the destruction of the impious and of those who, drawn into the pleasures of sins, have become slaves of corruption.

99. He also writes that mockers will abound in the last times, and proclaims that with God a thousand years are as one day. In the midst of these things he speaks of the resurrection of the elements and the renewal of heaven and earth.
