Finally, he speaks about Paul’s Epistles, which certain unlearned people, because they do not understand them, overthrow by interpreting them perversely.

## Concerning the Epistle of Blessed James

[Col. 0178A]

100. James, the brother of the Lord, wrote one Epistle pertaining to the edification of the Church; its statements seem to pour into readers an immeasurable brightness of knowledge.

## Concerning the Epistles of Blessed John

101. The apostle John wrote three Epistles. The first, commending the duty of charity, is wholly concerned with love of God and fraternal affection.

[Note: [Col. 0177D]

102. “The second also, which he wrote to the elect lady.” Hyginus, in his decretal letter, and Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels* II.39, affirm that the First Epistle of John was written to the Parthians. Cassiodorus, in *On Divine Reading* XIV, says: “Peter’s Epistle is to the Gentiles; those of Jude, James, and John are to the Parthians.” MAR.

Same note. In the Haganoensis edition: “the second also, which is written to the elect.” But the inscription is: “To the elect lady and her children.” This holy woman Electa is mentioned somewhere in the Acts of the Martyrs. AREV.]

102. The second, which he wrote to the elect lady, exhorts the pursuit of love; it also marks out deceivers and warns against turning toward heretics.

218 103. He writes the third to Gaius, in which he praises him for his devotion to the truth and his work of mercy. Then he marks the insolence of a certain Diotrephes and bears witness to the truth concerning Demetrius. [Col. 0178B]

## Concerning the Epistle of the Holy Apostle Jude

104. The Epistle of Jude rebukes those who blaspheme Christ and certain immoral persons, using as an example the impious who, through pride and sensuality, have been handed over to everlasting fires. On their account he admonishes the Church to rebuke them and exhort them to repentance.

## Concerning the Acts of the Apostles

105. The history of the apostles describes the faith and work of the nascent Church; its author is shown to be Luke the Evangelist. It contains the things accomplished or done in Judaea and among the nations through the grace of the Holy Spirit, both by Peter and by the other apostles, and especially by Paul.

## Concerning the Apocalypse

[Col. 0178C] [Note: [Col. 0178D]

106. Alternatively, *procidentia*, “falling forward,” instead of *procedentia*, “proceeding.” MAR.]

106. After John is commanded to write to the seven Churches, he sees the Son of Man seated on a throne, the twenty-four elders, and four living creatures proceeding before the throne. In the right hand of the one seated is a book sealed with seven seals, in which are marked war, scarcity, death, the cry of the slain, and also the end of the world and of the age.

107. He then describes twelve thousand servants of God, who are sealed on their foreheads. There seven angels sound trumpets, followed by hail and fire mingled with blood upon the earth. A third part of the earth is burned up, and a third part of the sea becomes blood; and the shining stars themselves lose a third part of their brightness. There locusts of demons are brought forth from the smoke of the pit, receiving power to harm those who are not sealed by the blood of the Lamb. [Col. 0178D]

108. Moreover, the Evangelist ate the book of the Testament: exceedingly sweet in the proclamation of the mouth, but bitter in the difficulty of its execution. He measures the heavenly temple, and describes the words of the twenty-four elders, the Ark of the Testament, and the woman clothed with the sun, as well as Michael’s battle in heaven with the dragon and the dragon’s downfall. [Col. 0179A] He also beholds the figure of Antichrist, possessing seven heads of royal power, horns of authority, and the number of his name.

[Note: [Col. 0179A]

109. Some copies read *phialas* (“bowls”); others *citharas* (“lyres”) instead of *pateras* (“bowls”). MAR.

In the same place, some printed editions add: “Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor, glory, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.” These words are absent from the better manuscripts. AREV.]

109. Among these things he also recounts the song of the New Testament, observes angels carrying bowls, and likewise sees the destruction of the beast and the blessedness of those who have kept the garments of their bodies clean, free from carnal pleasure. [Col. 0180A] He then relates the destruction of the Babylonian harlot, the marriage of the Lamb, the coming of judgment, the destruction of Antichrist, and the everlasting punishment of the devil. Finally, he mentions the resurrection of the dead, the renewal of heaven and earth, and the description of Jerusalem, as well as the pure river of baptism and the tree of life, the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0179]

# BOOK OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, ON THE NUMBERS THAT OCCUR IN THE HOLY SCRIPTURES (C, S)

220 ## CHAPTER I. What Number Is

[Col. 0179B]

[Note: [Col. 0179D]

1. Everything that could most usefully serve to illuminate this book by way of a preface has been carefully set forth by us in *Isidoriana*, chapter 63, where the authors who discuss the allegorical or mystical interpretation of numbers are also identified; those wishing to do so may compare them with our Isidore. Isidore’s statement, “as you wished,” indicates that the work was addressed to someone; but who that person was is entirely uncertain. Since the book is now being published for the first time and has been transcribed from only one manuscript, the Turin copy—for I know of no other copy existing elsewhere—we cannot provide variant readings, and I shall append only a few conjectures in the more obscure passages. Isidore likewise teaches in many places of the sacred Scriptures that numbers possess some mystery (*Etymologies*, book III, chapter 4). Saint Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, question 152, book I: “We most rightly believe that the numbers found in the Scriptures are supremely sacred and filled with mysteries, on the basis of certain numbers that we have been able to learn from them.”]

1. It is not superfluous to attend to the significance of numbers in the Holy Scriptures. For they contain a certain instruction in knowledge and very many mystical sacraments. Therefore, as you wished, I have decided briefly to explain the principles of certain numbers.

2. First, however, what number is must be defined. Number is a collection of units, or a multitude proceeding from one; its totality, indeed, is infinite and cannot be bounded by any multitude.

[Note: [Col. 0180D]

3. “Even,” etc. *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 5.]

3. An even number is one that can be divided into two equal parts; an odd number, however, is one that cannot be divided into two equal parts, because one is left in the middle, or one exceeds the other. An evenly even number is one that can be divided evenly according to an even number until it reaches the indivisible unit, as, for example, sixty-four. For it has as its half thirty-two; thirty-two has sixteen; sixteen has eight; eight has four; four has two; two has one, which is indivisible as a single unit.

# CHAPTER II. On Unity

[Note: [Col. 0180D]

4. I have added “is established,” which is usually absent from Isidore’s works, as I have often observed.]

4. Unity is the smallest part of numbers, which cannot be divided. This one, moreover, is the seed of numbers, not a number. For all the others flow or are produced from it; it alone is established as measure, the cause of increase, and the condition of decrease. For all increases begin from it and again reach as far as its unity.

[Note: [Col. 0180D]

5. Saint Leander, Isidore’s brother, in his homily on the conversion of the Goths, in the Acts of the Third Council of Toledo: “For there is one Christ the Lord, whose Church throughout the whole world is one,” etc. Leander says much there about its fruitfulness.]

5. For even after ten, unless one begins again from one, no further increase of numbers arises. Unity is likewise indivisible and cannot be divided into any parts, because everywhere it is a part, and everywhere it is whole. Following its example, there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. There is also one Paraclete Spirit; there is one Mother Church, rich in successive fruitfulness. To signify the principle of her unity, that angel in Ezekiel measures the threshold of the gate of Jerusalem with one reed.

[Note: [Col. 0180D]

6. One might read, “one … baptism.” But I make no alteration.]

6. Noah’s ark, too, being gathered together above, is narrowed to one cubit; and in the side of the ark there is one door. There is also one baptism in the Church; there is one and the same faith. The world is likewise one and the same. The sun that we see also has one light. The wise men of this world rightly called this unity concord, or devotion and friendship, because it is joined together in such a way that it is not divided into parts.

[Note: [Col. 0180D]

7. I would prefer to omit the dots: “the conjunction produces two.”]

7. Therefore, since unity cannot admit division of itself, whenever something made one flows into anything, although its line is indivisible and is understood without any indication of breadth, nevertheless, when things are joined, it produces two.

222 # CHAPTER III. On the Number Two

[Col. 0181A]

[Note: [Col. 0181D]

8. Much could be brought here from Isidore’s *Allegories* and his other biblical works; but there is no need to linger over these matters throughout, since it is clear that he often repeats himself.]

8. The number two is the first generation of numbers and the first form, the embodiment of evenness, the companion of the first movement, and the sibling of what precedes it; it is also capable of division into halves. For it participates in good and evil through a certain discord by which they oppose one another. It is the first number that can be separated from what is attached to it, as with those pairs of clean animals that are symbolically introduced into the ark: although they consist of evenness, they nevertheless appear mystically divided within themselves.

9. To this category also belong the two in the field who are separated from one another: when the tribulation of the age arrives, some of them adhere to the faith and are gathered again, while others yield to temptations and, being left behind, are released into the depths. Moreover, both agree in a good sense, inasmuch as there are two Testaments, of the Law and of the Gospels; there are also two stone tablets on which the commandments of the Law were written, and likewise two silver trumpets of the Law and of grace, with which the fathers sounded to advance the camps.

[Note: [Col. 0181D]

10. See again the *Preface*, no. 42.]

10. Two Seraphim are also written of, who sit before the throne and continually burst forth in song; and in Zechariah two olive trees are read of, one on the right and one on the left of the lampstand. There are also the two breasts of the bride of the Testaments, that is, of the Church, in the *Song of Songs*; there too two twin fawns are pastured among the lilies of the field.

11. In the Apocalypse, two witnesses are also commanded to prophesy, and in Jeremiah two are taken from the kinship of the nation. [Col. 0181C] In the Gospel, two from among the seventy disciples are sent ahead of Christ, and two fish are distributed to the people in the wilderness. There are also two commandments of charity, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Hence this number signifies fellowship, by which souls are bound together, and charity exists in no lesser relation than between two. The same number also signifies justice, in which one rejoices in things equally weighed.

12. Moreover, there are two things that lead a human being to blessed life: faith and works. Faith is grounded in divinity, while works consist in uprightness of life. Indeed, two lives are also preached to us in the Church: one temporal, in which we live by faith; the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate God with complete understanding of the truth.

# CHAPTER IV. On the Number Three

[Col. 0181D]

[Note: [Col. 0181D]

13. “Because the three are one.” The manuscript had “who are three,” etc. The reference is to the testimony of Saint John, First Epistle, chapter V, verse 7: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the FATHER, the WORD, AND THE HOLY SPIRIT, and these three are one.” The authenticity of this passage is also proved from this place. [Col. 0182D] But interpreters and other learned men have said more than enough about it, defending the authority of these words from the most ancient manuscripts in particular dissertations, such as Natalis Alexander, Calmet, and others.]

13. Three is the first of the odd numbers and a perfect number; for it first possesses beginning, middle, and end, and joins beginning and end to the central midpoint with equal right. Although it truly consists of three, it is nevertheless in some respect one, because the three are one: one in divinity, three in the distinction of persons; one in nature, three in designation.

14. Rightly, therefore, this number signifies the form of the Trinity. For by this same number the most holy Trinity and Divinity are proclaimed throughout the whole world, and by the same number the hymn *Trisagion* is sung by the angels in heaven. The ark of the Flood is also constructed with three compartments, and from the three sons of Noah all nations are restored after the Flood. This number, multiplied tenfold, mystically determines the height of the ark; counted a hundredfold, it produces its length. Examples of this number are abundant in the sacred writings.

[Col. 0182B] 15. Abraham saw three angels under the likeness of the Trinity; Isaac dug three wells; Jacob placed three rods in the water because of the appearance of the flocks; Jonah was carried for three days in the belly of the whale; for three days the people of Nineveh, through repentance, appeased the wrath of God. In the Gospel, the Lord entrusted his property to three servants. The same Lord overcame Lazarus’s death after three days. The woman in the Gospel hid the leaven of love in three measures of flour.

16. Three times God prayed that the cup of his passion might pass from him. Three times Peter denied Christ. Three times, by confessing him, that same Peter loved him. For three days our Lord and Redeemer rested in the tomb. For the third time, after rising from the dead, he showed himself to the disciples. In three things also, the Apostle commends the three on which all prophecy consists: faith, hope, and charity. There are three evangelical fruits: the first, a hundredfold, belongs to martyrs; the second, sixtyfold, to virgins; the third, thirtyfold, to married people.

17. There are also three things that do not apply to God: measure, place, and time. There are three faculties, or movements, of the soul: desire, anger, and reason. The language of the sacred Law is threefold: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. The sense of understanding is likewise threefold: historical, moral, and mystical. Hence the philosophers of the world also said that there are three parts of wisdom: physics, which is natural; logic, which is rational; and ethics, which is moral.

[Note: [Col. 0182D]

18. The scribe may have omitted *in aere* after “unclean spirits.” Saint Jerome, on Ephesians 6:12: “This is the opinion of all learned men, that the air … is full of opposing powers.” Other ancient writers say the same in various places. What is said as “or Libya” is in Isidore’s manner, where *vel* is used for “and.”]

18. Among musicians there are also three kinds of sound: voice, breath, and striking—voice in the throat, breath in pipes, [Col. 0182D] and striking in lyres. There are also three kinds of rational creatures: angels in heaven, human beings on earth, and unclean spirits. Among these there are three periods of the world: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. The world is also considered to have three parts: Asia, Europe, and Libya. The seasons of the year are distinguished by three-month periods, and every legal action is concluded before three witnesses.

# CHAPTER V. On the Number Four

[Note: [Col. 0183D]

19. In the manuscript, *plenum* appeared more likely than *plenam*. Perhaps Isidore wrote “full perfection,” and shortly before “depth and sublimity.” Saint Augustine very frequently commends the perfection of ten, whom Isidore willingly follows in this mystical exposition of numbers.]

19. What shall I say of four, in which number there is a certain perfection of solidity? For the number ten is composed of length, breadth, and depth, and produces fullness; ten is completed by four numbers rising successively. One, two, three, and four make ten. Similarly, one hundred is formed by the quaternary decade added together: ten, twenty, thirty, and forty, which are one hundred. Likewise, four numbers produce one thousand: one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, and four hundred. In this way ten thousand and the remaining numbers are completed by the same increase.

[Col. 0183B] 20. This square number is assigned to the four Evangelists, who were spread into the four parts, or corners, of the world. There are also four rivers of Paradise, which flow around the whole world. Noah’s ark, too, is constructed of squared timber. Finally, the Ark of the Testament was carried by means of four golden rings.

21. The priestly garment under the Law is also woven from four colors—hyacinth, byssus, scarlet, and purple—together with gold. Moreover, in Ezekiel the four winds of the earth blow, so that the dry bones may rise as a figure of the future resurrection; and in Daniel an equal number of winds of heaven, that is, angelic powers, rush upon the great sea of this age in battle. The same Daniel explains the four kingdoms of the world under different figures.

[Note: [Col. 0183D]

22. The manuscript had *differentiae* (“differences”). Perhaps Isidore wrote “different from one another in appearance.” On the subject itself, see the Apocalypse, chapter IV.]

22. Similarly, Zechariah describes four horns of kingdoms and an equal number of craftsmen, as well as four chariots of the Gospel sent to the four quarters of heaven. In John, four living creatures are likewise described, differing from one another in appearance; each has six wings, and together they produce the number twenty-four, the number of the elders. In the creation of the world there are four parts of the earth and four fronts, or quarters, of heaven: East, West, North, and South.

23. There are also four elements of the world, from which everything subsists: fire, air, water, and earth. The year likewise revolves through four seasons: summer, autumn, winter, and spring. Finally, human nature itself is composed of four elements: hot and cold, moist and dry. Four virtues of the soul are also recorded: justice, prudence, fortitude, [Col. 0184A] and temperance; and correspondingly four vices: desire, fear, grief, and joy.

[Note: [Col. 0183D]

24. Perhaps “with a four-colored splendor.” Those who have accurately described the nature of this phenomenon report that the rainbow, or celestial arc, displays the whole family of colors except black and white. Apart from writers on physics and optics, several particular treatises on the subject are also extant. Isidore may be indicating that four are the principal colors appearing in the rainbow, although they vary among themselves.]

24. Mortal things also have four stages of life: beginning, growth, maturity, and decline. There are likewise four kinds of animals in the world: heavenly, winged, aquatic, and terrestrial. The rainbow itself is also varied by a four-colored splendor. The calculation of the leap year is likewise gathered into four quarters.

# CHAPTER VI. 226 On the Number Five

[Note: [Col. 0184D]

25. Saint Augustine explains the number five in his commentary on Psalm 147, no. 10, and elsewhere. I do not know what relevance the statement that the Apostle is pleased to speak five words in the Church has here.]

25. Next comes the number five, which, whether joined with other odd numbers or associated with its own kind, always manifests itself. For five times five make twenty-five; five times three make fifteen; five times seven make thirty-five; and five times nine [Col. 0184B] make forty-five. This number is also attributed to the Law, for the Law is comprised of five books [perhaps, “is contained in five books”]. Hence the Apostle is also pleased to speak five words in the Church.

26. The altar under the Law is also constructed as a square of five cubits; and in Isaiah five cities speak the language of Canaan. There are also five wise virgins in the Gospel and another five foolish ones. Five loaves were distributed to the people. There were also five minas and five talents. According to the philosophers of the world, there are five zones of the earth; among the Latins, too, there are five vowel letters.

27. There are also five bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; and likewise five kinds of inhabitants of the world: human beings, quadrupeds, [Col. 0184C] reptiles, swimmers, and fliers. Moreover, a lustrum is completed in five years, and an Olympiad ends after five years.

# CHAPTER VII. On the Number Six

[Note: [Col. 0184D]

28. Below, no. 48, it is also said: “Eight is the first and perfect number.” It would not be unsuitable here to read: “The number six is the first perfect number.” It would also be preferable to read: “For it contains within itself its sixth part.”]

28. The number six is the first perfect number, and is first completed by its own parts. For it contains within itself a sixth, which is one; a third, which is two; and a half, which is three. These parts, added together—one, two, and three—make six. No number before six is found that is completed by its own parts when divided; its perfection is also made clear by the work of the world itself.

[Note: [Col. 0184D]

29. Isidore also discusses the six ages of the world elsewhere, in the *Etymologies*, the *Chronicle*, and so forth. But this passage may not be complete; nevertheless, its meaning is sufficiently clear.]

29. For in six days God completed his works. On the first day he created light; on the second, the firmament; on the third, the appearance of the sea and the earth; on the fourth, the stars; on the fifth, the fish and birds; on the sixth, the human being and the animals. [Col. 0185A] There are also six days, corresponding to the ages by which the world is completed. The first extends from Adam to Noah; the second from that point to Abraham; the third to David; the fourth to the Transmigration; the fifth to the coming of Christ; and the sixth, which is the present age, to the end of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0185D]

30. I do not understand what “parts of quarters” means. I would read “parts of a quarter.” Pliny sheds light on this when speaking of the days of the year: “To 365 [days] they additionally add the quarters of a day and night.” Accordingly, I believe this should be restored in Isidore. For a quarter itself consists of six hours: a quarter of a day is six hours, and before the Gregorian calendar’s correction, six complete hours were added to the 365 days in order to complete the year.]

30. The year itself is also completed according to the number six. For the number sixty is the sixth part of the days, whose sum, multiplied by six in the first sequence—that is, six times sixty—is 360. Five days remain; when the quarter-parts are added to them, they make the whole number six. For the quarter itself also consists of these parts.

[Note: [Col. 0185D]

31. The manuscript lacked the conjunction *et* after “the ages of human beings.”]

31. The number six itself, joined to the square and solid number four, measures the hours of day and night. [Col. 0185B] For four times six produces twenty-four. Moreover, the perfection of this number is found both in the ages of human beings and in the stages of things. For the course of mortal life is completed in six ages: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and extreme old age. There are also six levels of all things: nonliving things, such as stones; living things, such as trees; sentient things, such as animals; rational things, such as human beings; immortal things, such as angels; and the last and highest level, which is God, who is above all things.

32. There are likewise six natural functions without which nothing can exist: magnitude, eyes, shape, intervals, position, and motion. 228 The motion itself also has six directions. For we move forward, backward, to the right, to the left, upward, and downward. There are also many examples of this number in the sacred writings. On the sixth day the human being was formed in the image of God; in the sixth age of the world the Savior came in the flesh; and for six days the people in the wilderness were commanded to gather manna.

[Note: [Col. 0185D]

33. I have changed *offerri*, which the manuscript had, to *offerre*. See Ezekiel, chapter XLVI, verse 4.]

33. Hence Ezekiel also related that he saw, in the right hand of a man, a reed six cubits long. He likewise wrote that the fronts of the temple were six cubits high. He commanded the prince to offer six lambs in the burnt offerings. In the Gospel, Christ also changed six jars full of water into the taste of wine. Six days before the Passion, when entering Jerusalem, he likewise sat upon a donkey. There are many other examples, but they are omitted to avoid weariness in reading.

# CHAPTER VIII. On the Number Seven

[Col. 0186A]

[Note: [Col. 0185D]

34. Wonderful things are frequently reported about the number seven, sometimes even superstitious ones. Fludd, *On the History of the Microcosm*, treatise I, section I, book I: “I know,” he says, “a most learned man who, by the power of this number seven, with the assistance of a kind of oracle, did not hesitate to resolve doubtful and ambiguous questions, and even promised in some manner to foretell hidden things, both present and future.”]

34. The number seven is born from no number, nor does it generate or become generated. For all numbers placed within ten either generate others or are generated by others. This one neither generates nor is generated. Six and eight alone are generated. Four and two both create and are created. Seven generates nothing and is generated by nothing else.

[Note: [Col. 0186D]

35. Perhaps: “The number seven is rightly legitimate.” Something is missing from the wording, perhaps “when it testifies, as seventy times,” etc. I have soon afterward substituted “through the four kinds of virtues,” since the manuscript had “and four kinds of virtues,” which makes no sense. On the number seven, compare Saint Augustine, sermon 51, chapter 23, and other passages.]

35. This number seven is, in a sense, legitimate: whether when it expresses testimony, as in seventy and seven hundred, or when it is multiplied by itself, seven times a hundred being seven hundred; and according to the wise men of the world it is considered perfect because it consists of the first even and the first odd number. The first odd number is three, [Col. 0186B] the first even number is four, and from these two the number seven is completed. When these parts are multiplied, they produce twelve: three times four and four times three both make twelve. Through three, the mystery of the Trinity is signified; through four, the activity of the virtues is represented. Thus, in these parts, the activity of the virtues is perfected through the form of the Trinity, and through the representation of the virtues one arrives at knowledge of the Trinity. When it rises again to twelve, it shows the twelve apostles perfected by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit; through the four kinds of virtues, their preaching [perhaps, “through their preaching”] causes faith in the Trinity to grow throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0186D]

36. I cannot find where the words “he will receive sevenfold in this age” occur. Perhaps they refer to Genesis, chapter IV, verse 15: “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Saint Augustine, sermon 114, omitted these words and gave the preceding ones: “What, then, is seven times? Always, whenever he sins and repents.” This is the meaning of: “Seven times a day I praise you,” which is expressed in another psalm as: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”]

36. In the Holy Scriptures this number sometimes signifies the whole duration of the present age, sometimes rest, and sometimes the unity of the Church. It is used for the whole, as in the statement: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164), that is, at all times. The same prophet expresses this elsewhere for the whole of time when he says: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33:1). Hence it is said elsewhere: “He will receive sevenfold in this age.” Likewise, eternal rest is signified by the number seven when the seventh day is called sanctified for the Lord’s rest. On that day evening already occurs, because the rest of eternal blessedness will not be confined by any limits of time.

37. For this reason, the seventh day is also commanded in the Law to be a day of rest, so that eternal rest may be signified in it. Hence, after his resurrection, the Lord is described as having dined with seven disciples. Thus, in a third sense, the number seven represents the universality of the holy Church, as one passes from the particular form to the general reality.

38. Hence John also writes to seven churches in the Apocalypse, although only seven are specifically named, there is one Church, perfectly spread throughout the whole world by the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. For it is written: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song of Songs 6:8). Through such extensive meanings this number is more prominent than the others in the Scriptures, since the Lord sanctified it for his rest and in it promised the rest of the future resurrection.

230 [Note: [Col. 0187D]

39. In the Vulgate: “And the Spirit shall rest upon him,” etc.]

39. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit is fittingly signified by the number seven; hence sanctification under the Law also pertains to the seventh day. For God sanctified no day of his work, but sanctified only the seventh, on which he rested from his works. Rightly, therefore, this number bears the image of the sevenfold Spirit, who dwells in Christ through the fullness of divinity, as the prophet Isaiah testifies: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him,” he says, “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:2).

40. Hence Zechariah also writes, under the figure of Christ, of a stone having seven eyes. Examples of this number are therefore abundant in the divine books. Enoch is translated as the seventh from Adam. Lamech is also counted as the seventh, who paid sevenfold vengeance to Cain. On the seventh day after Noah’s entrance, the Flood came, and in the seventh month the resting ark came to rest. Seven animals also entered the ark, and in the Old Law the Passover was commanded to be celebrated for seven days. Moses the lawgiver established in the tabernacle of testimony a lampstand with seven branches.

[Note: [Col. 0187D]

41. What is said about Elisha appears corrupt. In 2 Kings, chapter IV, verses 33 and following, after Elisha had lain twice or three times upon the dead boy, the boy yawned seven times; this is perhaps what Isidore intended to indicate.]

41. The Ark of the Testament, with the trumpets sounding, was also carried around Jericho seven times and overthrew its walls. Elisha likewise raised the dead boy after lying upon him seven times. In Isaiah, seven women also seized one man; and among the Sadducees, an equal number of brothers marry the same woman in succession. Seven loaves are also distributed to the people in the Gospel, and seven baskets remained over.

42. The Apostle Paul also writes to seven churches: the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, [Col. 0187D] Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. And in the Apocalypse John saw Christ standing in the midst of seven lampstands, that is, the churches of Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.

[Note: [Col. 0187D]

43. “By seven, with one from each,” etc. There is certainly an error here, which may be corrected as follows: “By seven, with one added to each because of the mystery of unity, it produces fifty.” Or: “By seven, with one unit added because of,” etc.]

43. Likewise, in the same book, seven stars are read of in the right hand of God; the slain Lamb breaks the seven seals of the book; seven angels sound with trumpets; and seven receive authority over seven plagues. The heavenly Jerusalem is also founded upon a sevenfold wall, and seven Levites are chosen by the apostles. This number, multiplied by seven and with one added because of the mystery of unity, produces fifty; on the day after the Lord’s Ascension, the Holy Spirit promised by the Father descended upon the believers. Again, multiplied by seven times itself over the course of years and with one unit added, it reaches fifty and displays the perpetual rest of the jubilee. Yet there is also something contrary in it, as when we read of the beast having seven heads. There are also seven principal vices of demons. Indeed, examples of this number in the sacred writings are infinite.

[Note: [Col. 0188D]

44. I think the second occurrence of “seventh” should be corrected, followed by “which,” etc.]

44. But let us turn again to other things that assign significance to the number. Among the ancients, seven branches of philosophy are enumerated: first arithmetic, second geometry, third music, fourth astronomy, fifth astrology, sixth mechanics, and seventh medicine. The same number seven also encompasses the phases of the moon, for the moon has seven forms: the first is horned, the second cut, which is called a half-moon; the third is half-full; the fourth is full; the fifth is a half-moon proceeding from the larger phase; the sixth is cut; and the seventh is scarcely visible, like the first, and horned. For, by defining three of the forms mentioned with the same figure, it repeats them. This number also signifies the names of the moon. For one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven make twenty-eight.

[Note: [Col. 0188D]

45. “The seven-day periods of childbirth,” etc. This is obscure and perhaps corrupt.]

45. There are likewise as many circles, planets of heaven, and days of the world, as there are transformations of the elements. For fire becomes air, air becomes water, water becomes earth—that is, an ascent—and earth becomes water, water becomes air, and air becomes fire. Moreover, seven-day periods of gestation leave the human being fully formed and complete. On the seventh day the sick are also in danger. The Greek alphabet is likewise considered to have seven vowels.

[Note: [Col. 0188D]

46. It would be preferable to read: “the sixth decline.”]

46. The human being himself has seven passages in the head prepared for the senses: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and one mouth. In children, teeth also emerge in the seventh month and are replaced in the seventh year. In the second week, that is, in the fourteenth year, the child reaches puberty and acquires the ability to beget children. In the third, he produces down and the first growth of the cheeks. In the fourth, the growth of stature is determined; in the fifth, the full perfection of youthful age is attained; the sixth is decline; the seventh is the beginning of old age.

47. There are likewise seven hidden natural organs of mortal beings: the tongue, heart, lungs, spleen, liver, and two kidneys. There are also seven bodily parts that complete the human being: the head, neck, chest, belly, two hands, two feet, and, at the crown, the axis of heaven.

# CHAPTER IX. On the Number Eight

[Col. 0189A]

[Note: [Col. 0189D]

48. Since many psalms are entitled “For the Eighth,” this provides an occasion for investigating the mystical interpretations of this number, which Isidore generally gathers from Ambrose, Augustine, and others. See Burius’s *Onomasticon* and Macri’s *Hierolexicon*.]

48. Eight is the first and perfect number. For from the first movement—that is, from two multiplied by two—it generates four, and twice produces the perfect octave. This number is holy and is inscribed as a figure of true circumcision. Moreover, it is first in relation to the number seven and derives from seven, just as the same one who was eighth in the creation of the world was present at the beginning; and it is the perfection of unity.

49. But just as the present life revolves within and is signified by the number seven, so through eight the hope of eternal resurrection is shown. For on this day the Lord rose from the dead; counted from the Lord’s Passion, it is the third day. In the order of the world’s creation, as stated above, it is found after the seventh as the eighth, clearly to demonstrate the blessedness of the future resurrection. Scripture appropriately says: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight, because you do not know what evil may come upon the earth”—as though it were saying: “Distribute temporal things carefully, so that you strive to think about eternal things; for you must anticipate through good action, since you are uncertain what evils of the future judgment may again befall you” (Ecclesiastes 11:2). Finally, this number corresponds to the Lord and to his body, as to one and seven.

50. Hence eight souls entered the ark with Noah. In the seven, the sevenfold Church is signified; in the eighth, Noah signifies Christ, who is the head of the Church. To this also pertains what is read in Micah: seven shepherds and, indeed, an eighth, namely Christ with his sevenfold body. In the Gospel it is likewise read concerning this number that after eight days the face of the Lord shone before his three disciples on the mountain.

51. The Savior likewise manifested himself, after eight days, to Didymus, who did not believe. When multiplied threefold because of the Trinity, this number produces the twenty-four elders who cast their crowns before the Lamb. Conversely, in the Apocalypse the devil is written of as the eighth, whom John saw among the seven Roman kings, as though slain—indeed the eighth, but in treachery. Finally, eight principal vices are also described, from which the multitude of all vices arises: envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, lust, vainglory, and pride.

# CHAPTER X. On the Number Nine

[Col. 0190A]

[Note: [Col. 0189D]

52. I have altered certain words here in order to restore the sense, since the manuscript had: “it is said to be more perfect … according to others … for while it holds the end of the first verses … it is in need, as though it were added to a new certain [perfection].”]

52. The number nine is perfect in itself, and is therefore called more perfect, because it is completed by being multiplied according to its form from three perfect numbers. But according to others it is imperfect; for although it holds the end of the first series, it is always lacking one. If that one is added to nine, it completes the fixed rule of perfection and wholeness. In this number nine, therefore, those are understood who are imperfect and in no way attain the ten commandments of the Law.

[Note: [Col. 0189D]

53. The allegory of the number of the nine lepers is explained at greater length by Saint Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, Question 41, no. 4. In the manuscript, instead of *quamvis in eis* (“although in them”), there was *quam in eos* (“which upon them”).]

53. The nine lepers in the Gospel belong to this number: excluded from the fellowship of unity, they failed through pride to give thanks to their purifier. Some also understand the ninety-nine who do not need repentance as belonging to the same number, since they vainly justify themselves, although some understand heavenly figures in them. Moreover [perhaps: “For this reason”], the Hebrews say that there are nine prophetic books, and the gentiles invented nine Muses, in whom perfect knowledge of musical harmonies consists.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Number Ten

[Note: [Col. 0189D]

54. I substituted *primi versus* (“of the first series”) for *primus versus* (“the first series”), which stood in the manuscript. The first series is like the first decade. I also wrote *secundae monadis* (“of the second monad”) for *secundi monadis* (“of the second monad”), which I believe to be a scribal error. As for the statement that ten completes the beginning of the second monad, I understand it to mean that ten completes one decade, which is the unit of the decades, just as one is the first number, or the origin of numbers, and the unit of numbers.]

54. Ten, however, is to be regarded as a number above all others, because it contains within itself all numbers of differing power and perfection. Although it is the end of the first series, it completes the beginning of the second monad and fulfills the pattern of unity. In it the limit of combination becomes so great that number does not proceed beyond it, but returns again to unity; and so, thereafter, it serves for the infinite multitude of numbers.

[Note: [Col. 0190D]

55. The copyist, as we should reasonably believe, omitted the words of Daniel that follow: “And ten thousand times a hundred thousand served him.” For Isidore’s argument turns on this “ten times.”]

55. In the Holy Scriptures it is a legitimate number, as is the number seven, sometimes signifying perfection and sometimes plainly demonstrating totality. Thus Daniel comprehended the whole Church, or the innumerable multitude of angels, by the number ten, saying: “Thousands of thousands served him” (Dan. 7:10). Hence the Psalm also says: “The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice” (Ps. 72:18).

[Note: [Col. 0190D]

56. I altered certain things here in order to produce a suitable sense. The manuscript read as follows: “The law of the Decalogue is ascribed. Ten … From Adam, for the race, the number ten is brought to an end as far as Noah.” See no. 62.]

56. Finally, this number is ascribed to the law of the Decalogue, for the commandments of the Law are famously ten. From Adam the succession of generations is brought to an end at Noah by the number ten. In the figure of this number the prophet David also sang in the Psalter with ten-stringed music; and as its type King Solomon set ten lampstands in the house of God, on the right and on the left.

[Note: [Col. 0191D]

57. The manuscript had *accipiet* (“he will receive”) instead of *accipies* (“you will receive”).]

57. Finally, in Zechariah there are ten men, representing all nations, holding the fringe of Christ. In the Gospel there are also ten virgins, understood through the fivefold number doubled, in the senses of flesh and spirit. Ten lepers are likewise cleansed by the Lord, with nine of them excluded from unity. Moreover, there are ten cities, and if you rule them well, you will in the future receive the senses of heart and body in a doubled number.

[Note: [Col. 0191D]

58. In the manuscript, here and elsewhere, *in Apocalypsin* (“in the Apocalypse”) stood instead of *in Apocalypsi* (“in the Apocalypse”).]

58. On the other hand, in Exodus Egypt was struck by ten plagues; in the Apocalypse ten horns emerge from the sea; and ten days of affliction for the Church are recorded, in which the condition of this life and its duration are indicated. According to Solomon, moreover, an infant is formed in blood over ten months. There are six hundred other examples. But it is enough to have spoken thus far about ten.

[Note: [Col. 0191D]

59. “He has his own genius.” That is, as I suppose, he always reveals himself, as in no. 25.]

59. This is the rule of the first series of numbers, their mysteries, kinds and species, and distinctions of perfection. Let us now treat all the numbers of the first series by recapitulating them under this truth. One is not a number, but is the origin of all numbers. Two is the first part; three is first in order and power. Four consists of two equal parts. Five has its own genius. Six is perfect in the work of the world and is equal by means of odd numbers. Seven is legitimate, and sometimes stands for the whole.

60. Eight is even by means of even numbers. Nine is odd by means of perfect odd numbers. Ten is perfect and final. The limits, or boundaries, of numbers are these: one, ten, one hundred, and one thousand. Up to this point we have discussed the rule of the first series. Now let us treat the second.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Number Eleven

[Note: [Col. 0191D]

61. Perhaps: “which in its parts has no more … than one, as …”

In the same place. The manuscript has *monades* instead of *monas*.

In the same place. From Saint Augustine, Sermon 51, chapter 23, and elsewhere.]

61. The number eleven is the first unit of the second series. Among its odd parts it has no further one except the eleventh itself, just as five has only the fifth and three only the third. In the Scriptures, the number eleven signifies transgression of a commandment, or diminution of holiness. Thus the eleventh Psalm begins: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed.” For just as the perfection of blessedness is written by ten, so the transgression of the Law is written by eleven.

[Col. 0191D] [Note: [Col. 0191D]

62. The generations from Adam to Noah are said to be ten above, in no. 56. Here eleven generations are said to extend to the sons of Noah. Isidore explains the reasoning in chapter 6 of his *On Genesis*, no. 29. I restored *undecimum bestiae cornu* (“the eleventh horn of the beast”) instead of *undecim bestiae cornu* (“eleven horn of the beast”). One might also read *undecim bestiae cornua* (“eleven horns of the beast”). But *the eleventh horn of the beast* seems preferable in view of Daniel 7:20.]

62. Hence the descendants of Adam through Cain are brought to an end at the Flood by the number eleven, signifying the sin produced by the pride of transgression. For the curtains of goats’ hair with which the tabernacle was covered were also commanded to be eleven, so that by the number sin, and by the goats’ hair the prickings and lamentations of sinners, might be signified. In Daniel, too, the beast is taught to have an eleventh horn, demonstrating that the devil is the author of transgression, and his son Antichrist, whose kingdom derives its power from the strength of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0192D]

63. Some of the ancients maintained that the world was created in autumn; but most of the Fathers hold that it was created in spring: Cyril of Jerusalem, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Theodoret, and others. Compare the council convened by Theophilus of Alexandria at the command of Pope Victor, in Appendix 8, volume III, p. 515.]

63. For this reason, when Judas fell, Peter appointed Matthias by lot as the twelfth, so that the sum of the apostles might not remain in the number eleven, fearing that the sum of apostolic truth might stand in the number of transgression. This number is also found inscribed in the reckoning of times. For the world is said to have been made on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. Eleven epacts are also reported, which are added each year to the course of the moon.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Number Twelve

[Note: [Col. 0192D]

64. The manuscript had *nam quaterni* (“for four each”), for which I read *nam quater terni* (“for four times three each”). I wrote *exceditur* (“is exceeded”) instead of *exciditur* (“is cut off”). Perhaps *simul ductis* (“when multiplied together”) should be read, rather than merely *consummatur* (“is completed”).]

64. The number twelve is, among other numbers, legitimate among legitimate numbers. For this reason, the parts of the number seven are multiplied one by another. Four times three, or three times four, produces the same number; but when its parts are multiplied together, this number is not merely completed but exceeded. For it produces from itself a greater number, since its parts reach sixteen. It has these five parts: the twelfth, which is one; the sixth, which is two; the fourth, which is three; the third, which is four; and the half, which is six.

65. Thus one, two, three, four, and six, added together, make sixteen. For this reason it is regarded as more than perfect. As we have said, the number twelve is legitimate in the Scriptures, whether it stands for the whole or is multiplied by itself. It stands for the whole in the twelve thrones and the twelve tribes: through the twelve thrones all who judge are signified, and through the twelve tribes all nations.

66. It stands for itself when, for example, twelve multiplied by twelve produces one hundred forty-four, by which the whole Church is designated. This number occurs more frequently in the Scriptures and is considered more distinguished than all other numbers because of the total number of patriarchs and apostles.

67. Twelve is the number of the apostles and likewise of the patriarchs; there are also the same number of Minor Prophets. There were also twelve stones that the priests wore on their breast. Moreover, twelve apostolic springs are read of in the Law, beside which seventy palm trees grew; for the tribes of Israel are called twelve. Twelve spies are also sent to the Holy Land, and a cluster of grapes is carried on wood by them as a type of Christ.

68. Finally, as a testimony to eternity, twelve stones are taken from the river Jordan and placed where Israel was circumcised a second time. Elijah also built an altar from twelve stones, and in Matthew twelve baskets of fragments remained in the wilderness. Likewise, in the Apocalypse, twelve thousand from each of the tribes of the patriarchs are marked on their foreheads. Over the head of the Lamb also shines a crown of twelve stars; the foundations of Jerusalem are made of twelve precious stones; the city itself is twelve stadia in every direction; and the entrances of that same city number twelve gates.

69. This number twelve, multiplied six times, produces the seventy-two disciples who were sent to preach throughout the whole world, divided into seventy-two languages. Multiplied by itself, it produces one hundred forty-four, which is the measure of the walls of Jerusalem.

238 [Note: [Col. 0193D]

70. The Gospel mentions twelve hours of the day. The night also consisted of four watches, each watch lasting three hours. The hours of day and night, however, were unequal according to the variation of the seasons.]

70. When multiplied by itself, it also produces one hundred forty-four thousand marked ones, that is, the whole company of the saints. Moreover, this number agrees with the divisions of time and of the world. For the visible sun completes the year in twelve months; twelve winds also traverse the whole world. There are likewise twelve hours of the day and an equal number of hours of the night.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Number Thirteen

71. The number thirteen, because of three and ten, signifies the Law and the Lawgiver—namely, the Decalogue and the Trinity. This number is appropriately ascribed to the apostle Paul, who occupies that number’s place in the order of the apostles.

72. For he had first been a teacher of the Law, and afterward became an evangelistic preacher of the divine Trinity among the nations, as though holding ten and three. Hence Benjamin himself, from whose tribe Paul arose, is counted as the thirteenth tribe, with Ephraim and Manasseh counted in Joseph’s place in the order of the patriarchs.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Number Fourteen

[Col. 0193D]

[Note: [Col. 0193D]

73. “Which they used.” This is an Isidorian phrase, as is often evident especially from his manuscript works. But something else seems to need to be restored in place of *gemitum* (“groaning”), something denoting rest; perhaps *geminum* (“twofold”), with “seven” understood.]

73. The number fourteen, because it consists of two sevens, suggests to us a groaning—or perhaps the twofold [number seven]—whether the temporal groaning that the ancients symbolically used in leisure, or the eternal one in which all the saints await rest from their labors. It is also found, according to the Gospel, in the generations of the ages. From Abraham to David fourteen generations are counted. Likewise, from David to the transmigration, the same number of generations is found; and again, to Christ, fourteen generations are counted.

74. In the Law, too, the Passover is commanded to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, from the flesh of an immaculate lamb. In Ezekiel, the ledge of the heavenly altar extends fourteen cubits (Ezek. 43:17). Jacob also served Laban for fourteen years. There were fourteen years of abundance [perhaps: “of barrenness and abundance”] in Egypt under Joseph.

75. The apostle Paul also went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years to preach the Gospel, taking Barnabas and Titus with him. He likewise concluded the discourse of his preaching in fourteen Epistles. Moreover, Job received fourteen thousand sheep at the end as the reward of his endurance. A boy also passes into adolescence after his fourteenth year and acquires the power of begetting in his fourteenth year.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Number Fifteen

[Note: [Col. 0194D]

76. Perhaps *suarum* (“of its own”) should be read instead of *suavem* (“pleasant”).]

76. The number fifteen, according to the pleasant division of its ratios, is imperfect, because it consists of three parts. For it has only the first, third, and fifth. Its first part is one, its fifth is three, and its third is five; these make nine. But this number, mystically divided into two parts, signifies the present time and demonstrates the eternal.

[Col. 0194C] [Note: [Col. 0194D]

77. The manuscript reads: “But seven for faith.” Perhaps the intended wording is “the Lord’s resurrection and the New Testament,” or rather “the New Testament in place of the Lord’s resurrection.”]

77. It consists of seven and eight, which make fifteen. Its seven belongs to the course of time, which is completed by two sevens; but its eight belongs to the reckoning of faith, where there will be rejoicing in eternal peace. For on the eighth day, which is the first after the Sabbath, the Lord rose again; through the mystery of this figure, the eternity of the future resurrection is revealed. Indeed, its seven signifies the Old Testament through observance of the Sabbath. Its eight demonstrates the Lord’s resurrection and the New Testament.

78. Therefore this number rightly signifies the union of the Testaments. Hence the apostle Paul testifies that he stayed fifteen days in Jerusalem with Peter, so that he might confer with him concerning both Testaments: the seven, because of the time of the present life, and the eight, because of the eternal blessedness of the future resurrection. Thus he might discern how to regulate temporal things and eagerly desire eternal things.

79. This number fifteen is also mystically assigned to the Lord’s temple. There were fifteen steps around the temple, on which the priests and Levites stood according to the order of their merits. Following their example, the prophet sang fifteen Songs of Ascents, by which one gradually ascends from earthly things to the heavenly temple of Jerusalem. Yet if this number is calculated by ten, it produces the one hundred fifty psalms sung by the Prophet.

80. Certainly, if it rises gradually by increments from one up to itself, it designates the one hundred twenty faithful upon whom the Holy Spirit was poured. Through the number seven they received the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, and through the number eight they proclaimed to the world the glory of eternal hope.

[Note: [Col. 0195D]

81. The manuscript read as follows: “But in the element, on the fifteenth lunar day of the earth, in the fifteenth year the solar indiction ends.”]

81. There are also many examples of this number in the Scriptures. The Lord’s solemnities begin on the fifteenth day, and the feast of Tabernacles is held on the fifteenth day of the month, when the children of Israel first ate unleavened bread in the wilderness and fixed their tents. When Hezekiah was dying, he also received fifteen years added to his life. The height of the rising Flood likewise reached the mountain peaks by fifteen cubits. The increase is also governed by the fifteenth moon; in the fifteenth year the solar indiction ends.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Number Sixteen

[Note: [Col. 0195D]

82. “The sixteenth.” Understand “part.” Immediately afterward it seems that *qui faciunt quindecim* (“which make fifteen”) should be read.]

82. The number sixteen consists of two perfect numbers, yet it is contained by these parts. It has the sixteenth, which is one; the eighth, which is two; the fourth, which is four; and the half, which is eight; these make sixteen.

83. This number is nevertheless believed to have been assigned mystically to the prophets. Their books are shown to be sixteen in number: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Malachi, Zephaniah, Haggai, and Zechariah. Their figure was borne by those sixteen silver bases on which the gilded boards stood facing the western side.

84. By the bases we understand the prophets, upon whose most splendid foundation of prophecy rests the expansive teaching of the apostles.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Number Eighteen

85. Eighteen is completed from six by ten [perhaps: “by three”]. These are the six ages of the world, whose sixfold sequence is distributed according to a threefold division of time: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. In the third of these the sacrament of faith is revealed, which we receive for the salvation of souls. The mystery of this number was expressed by that woman in the Gospel who, bearing the figure of the Church, was raised up and healed by the Lord after eighteen years.

86. For our Redeemer descended in the sixth age for our salvation. To the forms of this number six that reckoning was added: three times six makes eighteen, and fulfills the typological sacrament of that woman.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Number Nineteen

[Note: [Col. 0196D]

87. The manuscript had *cycli circuli cursu* (“in the course of the circle of the cycle”). I deleted *circuli*, which appears to be a gloss.]

87. The number nineteen more precisely touches upon the reckoning of the lunar cycle. In its course, the paschal fourteenth moons recur without ambiguity in the revolution of every year, the course of the same nineteen-year cycle continually returning upon itself. When it has completed the end of its circuit, it turns again along the same lines on which it began.

242 ## CHAPTER XX. On the Number Twenty

88. The twentieth number, completing the second series, is regarded as more than perfect in its parts. Consisting of a double Decalogue, it designates the twofold knowledge of the Law, as open and hidden, simple and mystical. It pertains to the sacrament of the Lord’s tabernacle.

89. There, on the southern and northern sides, twenty boards stood upon silver bases; and in the temple that Solomon built, the wings of the two cherubim extended over a measure of twenty cubits. This number is also assigned to Israel and Levi: men are chosen for battle at twenty years, and are commanded to serve the tabernacle from the age of twenty.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Number Twenty-Four

90. The sum of twenty-four contains within itself many mysteries of the Scriptures; hence this number is commended as sacred. For there are twenty-four books of the Law and the Prophets. There are also twenty-four Fathers: twelve apostles and the same number of patriarchs. There were also twenty-four classes of priests among the Jewish people from the beginning of the Law; these took turns offering sacrifices in the temple.

91. Each class had its own high priest, and the classes were named after them. In John, too, there are twenty-four seats, and twenty-four elders holding harps and bowls and worshiping the Lamb; indeed, the four living creatures had twenty-four wings. If the number twenty-four of the elders is calculated beginning from one and gradually adding until one reaches twenty-four, three hundred are produced. By these the length of the ark is signified—that is, the faith of the Church, in which the infinite multitude of all the saints is contained.

92. Moreover, the sum of the number twenty-four is completed from two numbers of twelve, through which the Church gathered from both circumcision and the nations is signified. Thus, if the number eight is also reckoned threefold, in which the figure of true and holy circumcision is found, it makes twenty-four. In this number we are taught figuratively that, by cutting away vices, we ought to believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0197D]

93. “You calculate, and four, etc.” The sense is not sufficiently clear, and something, in my opinion, is missing.]

93. The same number also displays the seventy-two disciples whom the Lord sent ahead of him in pairs, with the number three multiplied into itself. Finally, three times twenty-four makes seventy-two. For if you reckon the fourth number six times, and set forth the four elements of the world, in which all things subsist, and which are in the works of this world, in which those very elements subsist.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Number Thirty

94. The number thirty is completed by setting ten in three forms. It has ten three times, because of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and because of the ten commandments of the Law, which were granted to us by the gift of that same Trinity for the preservation of life. Hence the height of the ark was raised to thirty cubits, because the Church is perfected by faith in the Trinity through the commandment of the Decalogue. Examples of this are found in the Scriptures as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0197D]

95. Isidore perhaps wrote *venumdedit* (“sold”) here.]

95. In Zechariah the Lord received thirty pieces of silver as the price of his death, and in the Gospel Judas sold Christ for the same number of pieces of silver. Our Lord and Savior also descended into the Jordan at that same age and preached the Gospel to the world. Likewise, the thirtieth fruit is given to married people because of the struggle of the flesh, lest they be overcome by lust.

[Note: [Col. 0197D]

96. *Momentum* is used for a brief span of time; but I do not know whether the statement that the hours were divided into thirty parts called “moments” is found elsewhere in writing. That the thirty-year objection sets an end in the repetition of things is also expressed in the Second Council of Seville, presided over by Saint Isidore, chapter 2, where this very phrase, “the thirty-year objection,” is used, as may be seen in Appendix 4 to volume II, p. 520.]

96. Months also consist of thirty days, and hours are completed by the same number of moments; moreover, in the repetition of all things and persons, the objection of thirty years sets an end.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Number Forty

[Note: [Col. 0198D]

97. The mystical exposition of the number forty occurs frequently among the holiest Fathers for these and similar reasons: this number was in a certain sense consecrated by Christ through a fast of forty days. One may read: “As though the ages are brought to completion by it.”]

97. The number forty indicates the fullness of times, as though the ages are brought to completion by it. The Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels are shown through the type of this number; for Moses, Elijah, and the Lord fasted for forty days, giving us a sign that, as long as we remain in this age, we should abstain from all allurements of carnal vices, remaining under the protection of the commandments of the Decalogue. These are spread by faith through the four parts of the world, so that ten multiplied by four completes forty days.

[Note: [Col. 0198D]

98. “And forty years.” That is, “they signified.” The manuscript had *et quadraginta annos* (“and forty years”). Job’s words in the Vulgate are: “The life of man upon earth is warfare.”]

98. The forty days of the Flood signified this—namely, the storms and whirlwinds of this age, which the Church suffers. The forty years in the wilderness also signified that our course in this world is laborious, while we hold out toward the promised kingdom of the heavenly homeland. The fact that the Lord was tempted in the wilderness for forty days declares that, as long as we are in this body, we bear temptations. For, as Job says, “Human life upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1).

[Note: [Col. 0198D]

99. The manuscript had *soli* (“of the only one”) instead of *solis* (“of the sun”).]

99. Hence Ezekiel pronounced the sins of Judah for forty days only, because in this world alone it is permitted to attain the fruit of forgiveness through repentance. In the future, confession accomplishes nothing; only the recompense of the holy and devout will exist.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Number Forty-Six

245 [Note: [Col. 0198D]

100. Perhaps one should read “that he would raise it up after three days.”]

100. The reckoning of forty-six numbers is constructed in the Gospel for the temple; it refers to the structure of the Lord’s body, on account of which the temple is mentioned. As a figure of this, he said that the temple destroyed by the Jews would be summoned within three days [perhaps: raised up]. The senary number, when multiplied, displays the conception and birth of the Virgin. For they said to him: “It took forty-six years to build this temple” (John 2:20).

101. Forty-six multiplied by six makes 276, which number completes eight months [perhaps: “nine months”] and six days, the period in which the full term of women’s pregnancy is found. This is not because the birth is completed at the end of this number, but because the same number is found from the conception of the Lord’s body up to the birth. For he is said to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April and proved to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0198C] [Note: [Col. 0198D]

102. In our Vulgate: “And in three days I will raise it up.”]

102. From that day, therefore, to this day there are found 276 days; when these are counted by the number six, forty-six times is completed. By this number both the building of the temple and the perfection of the body are declared, concerning which he had specifically said: “And in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:20). He was speaking of the temple of his body, which, after conquering the suffering of death, would be raised after three days. Just as the labor or limit of this present time is signified by forty, so that eternal blessedness is signified by fifty.

103. When ten is added to forty, the reward is paid to the faithful laboring in this age—the reward received by the first and last laborers in the vineyard—and thus fifty signifies that eternal rest and joy. Hence, in the Law, rest was observed in the fiftieth year of the Jubilee, signifying that after the labor of this world one reaches the rest of the age to come.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Number Fifty

[Col. 0199A]

246 104. This number is sacred in the Holy Scriptures because of the Holy Spirit. On the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt, the tablets of the Law were given on the summit of Mount Sinai; and on the fiftieth day after Christ’s Passion, the Holy Spirit descended upon the 120 faithful. Therefore the fiftieth Psalm concerns pardon and remission.

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

105. In the Vulgate: “The charity of God has been poured out,” and so forth.]

105. Hence in the Gospel fifty denarii are also forgiven to debtors. The fact that in the Flood the height of the ark extended to fifty cubits signified the grace of the same Holy Spirit, enlarged throughout the world, as the Apostle says: “The grace of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Number Sixty

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

106. The manuscript had *illae reginae* (“those queens”). In a small lacuna I supplied *per* (“through”), to produce the sense; perhaps nothing else is missing except *per fidelem* (“through the faithful one”).]

106. The number sixty, whose sum is completed by the perfect six through ten, signifies all the saints who receive the perfection of holiness through observance of the ten commandments. Solomon speaks of Christ in the *Song of Songs*: “Sixty queens,” he says (Song 6:7)—that is, the souls of the saints, joined to Christ by the bond of faith and love. While they are joined to the Savior … through obedience, they are counted, as it were, by the number sixty.

[Col. 0199C] 107. These are those to whom the sixtieth fruit is granted in the Gospel: those who, made perfect by the divine commandments, wage the contest against the desire of the flesh. They receive the sixtieth fruit for this reason: until this age the struggle of lusts exults [perhaps: “rejoices”]. As long as there is combat, therefore, there is a crown. Hence soldiers stationed in military service are also withdrawn from warfare after their sixtieth year and grow old in leisure.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Reckoning of Holy Pentecost

[Col. 0200A]

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

108. *Assei quadraginta, bis deni quadraginta* (“forty by ones, twice ten forty”) appears corrupt. For these words it would be preferable to read only *bis viceni quadraginta* (“twice twenty forty”).]

108. The number forty also generates fifty from itself, when its parts are added—through the parts by which fifty is produced—as follows: one fortieth; two twentieths; four tenths; five eighths; eight fifths; ten fourths; twenty halves; and, when these are added, fifty is produced.

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

109. Perhaps: “who are destined by God for life,” and so forth.]

109. Through these numbers the present life is signified by forty, and the future life by fifty. The number fifty, tripled, produces the number of the perfect, who have been predestined for that eternal life. For multiplied by three it makes 150, with three also added. These display the Gospel passage in which 153 fish were brought ashore; they were large in weight, that is, distinguished in works and life. The number seventeen begins with one and reaches ten and seven, producing the same 153. The three that are added are the periods before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

[Note: [Col. 0199C]

110. The words of the Psalm in the Vulgate begin: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand …” Instead of *caruisse* (“to have been without”), one may read *cavisse* (“to have taken heed”), although *caruerunt* (“they were without”) occurs again.]

110. Therefore it is said in the seventeenth Psalm: “When he delivers him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul,” so that it might be shown that he had already been free from all the temptations of the present life and was among the number of the saints—that is, among those 153 fish separated on the shore. These are those who, having completed this life, were free from all the temptations of this world, which is like the sea, and are now blessed in that eternal state.

[Col. 0200C] [Note: [Col. 0200C]

111. These words are taken almost verbatim from Saint Augustine, on Psalm 49: “Therefore the 153 fish signify not merely the number of the saints,” and so forth. Ten and seven, if you count from one through seventeen, adding all the numbers progressively—adding two to one, three to the result, four to the result so that it becomes ten, five so that it becomes fifteen, and so forth, adding seventeen—produce 153.]

111. The number that is said to be counted from one up to seventeen by multiplication produces 153: add two to one, and it becomes three; add three, and it becomes six; add four, and it becomes ten; add five, and it becomes fifteen; add six, and it becomes twenty-one; add seven, and it becomes twenty-eight; add eight, and it becomes thirty-six; add nine, and it becomes forty-five; add ten, and it becomes fifty-five; add eleven, and it becomes sixty-six; add twelve, and it becomes seventy-eight; add thirteen, and it becomes ninety-one; add fourteen, and it becomes 105; add fifteen, and it becomes 120; add sixteen, and it becomes 136; add seventeen, and it becomes 153.

[Col. 0201]

# QUESTIONS OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS (C, S)*

## QUESTION ONE

[Col. 0201A]

249 [Note: [Col. 0201C]

On no. 1. I have discussed this work extensively, and the arguments persuading one that it is genuinely by Saint Isidore, although it has not yet seen the light of public circulation, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 64. In describing it, I corrected the scribal errors in such a way that I sometimes left obvious faults untouched, so that the writer’s character might be inferred from them. In place of *respondit* (“he answered”), which is in the manuscript, one might restore *respondet* (“he answers”) or *respondetur* (“it is answered”).]

1. Tell me, what is there between the New Testament and the Old? He replied: The Old is Adam’s sin, concerning which the Apostle says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Rom. 5:14), and the rest. The New is Christ, born of the Virgin.

2. Hence the Prophet says: “Sing to the Lord a new song,” because the new man has come; he brought new commandments, that is, the New Testament.

## QUESTION TWO

[Note: [Col. 0201C]

3. The manuscript had *lex Moysi* (“the Law of Moses”). Isidore likewise counts seventy-two books of the Old and New Testaments in the *Prologues*, at the beginning.]

3. Tell me, how many books are understood to be in the New Testament? He replied: Twenty-seven; and in the Old Testament there are forty-five books of the Law of Moses. According to the seventy-two languages, seventy-two books are understood.

4. The Old is when a person takes what belongs to another; the New is when he gives what belongs to himself. The Old is when evil is repaid with evil, as it is said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” and the other things that pertain to vengeance. The New is to love one’s enemies. The Lord said in the Gospel: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5:44).

250 [Note: [Col. 0201C]

**5.** These are the words of Saint Peter: “But we await, according to his promises, new heavens and a new earth.”

**5.** The old way is for sinners to descend into hell; the new way is for the converted to enter the Lord’s kingdom. And the old way will be for all sinners and ungodly people to descend into hell on the day of judgment, where they will remain forever. The new way is for all the righteous to enter the Lord’s kingdom; hence Saint Peter says: “A new man and a new earth” (2 Peter 3:13); and the former things will be new in memory.

[Note: [Col. 0201C]]

**6.** In the manuscript, *for small sins*; thus the nominative repeatedly occurs in place of the ablative: and perhaps it should be read *in the Lord’s kingdom*, unless some word is missing. Numbers 4, 5, and 6 seem to belong before number 3.

**6.** And the old way will be to be cleansed in purgatorial fire for small sins; the new way, when the one who has been cleansed from them will have entered the Lord’s kingdom.

## QUESTION III

[Note: [Col. 0202C]]

**7.** Perhaps from *reading* … *from storing away*, and so forth.

**7.** Tell me, in what ways is a book so called? He replied: In four ways: books are so called in relation to reading, or to setting free. A *codex* is so called in relation to storing away. A *volume* is so called in relation to rolling.

## QUESTION IV

[Col. 0202A]

[Note: [Col. 0202C]]

**8.** The manuscript has *for what* instead of *why*; so also in no. 11. Perhaps *on account of what* should be read.

**8.** Tell me, from what does the first letter *a* take its name? From angels, from *before the ages*, from Adam, from the soul.

## QUESTION V

**9.** Tell me, by what names is *a* called? He replied: By three: *aleph* in Hebrew, *alpha* in Greek, and *a* in Latin.

## QUESTION VI

**10.** Tell me, in whose language is *Evangelium* spoken? In Greek; and in Latin, that is, “good announcement.”

## QUESTION VII

[Note: [Col. 0202C]]

**11.** In the Vulgate: “Go out from your land,” and so forth.

**11.** Tell me, why did the Lord say to Abraham: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Genesis 12:1)? Abraham represented the person of Christ. Just as Abraham left his land, his kindred, and his father’s house and came into a land that he did not know, so Christ also left his own people, that is, the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0202C]]

**12.** Instead of *we despise*, perhaps *we withdraw*, *we consent*, or *we strive to leave* should be read.

**12.** We likewise leave our land when we despise the riches and resources of this world; our kindred, that is, vices; and our father’s house, that is, the memory of this world.

## QUESTION VIII

**13.** Tell me, in whose language is the name *apostles* spoken? He replied: In Greek; in Latin it is translated as “those who have been sent.”

## QUESTION IX

[Col. 0202C] [Note: [Col. 0202C]]

**14.** Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, chapter 19: “Let him understand that he is not a bishop who has desired to preside, not to be useful.” See also the dialogue of the *Questions* attributed to Augustine, the final question.

**14.** Tell me, in whose language is *bishop* spoken? He replied: In Greek; in Latin, “watchers.” *Bishop* is the name of a duty, not of an honor. Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside, not to be useful.

## QUESTION X

**15.** Tell me, in whose language is *clergy* spoken? He replied: [Col. 0203A] In Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “the Lord’s lot.”

## QUESTION XI

**16.** Tell me, in what language is *abba* spoken? In Hebrew; in Greek, “father”; in Latin, “begetter.”

## QUESTION XII

**17.** Tell me, who was the first cleric? He replied: Saint Peter.

## QUESTION XIII

252 [Note: [Col. 0203D]]

**18.** *Lord* may be read instead of *God*; and immediately afterward *angels*; in the manuscript it is *angels and the remaining … creatures*.

**18.** Tell me, how many are the things that almighty God created from nothing? He replied: Four: an angel, the soul, heaven, and earth. All the remaining creatures proceed from these.

## QUESTION XIV

**19.** Tell me, what is understood by heaven? He replied: An angel; and by earth, the holy Church. Heaven is also the righteous soul, and earth is sinners.

## QUESTION XV

[Note: [Col. 0203D]]

**20.** The codex has *it will be believed … the good God*, and so forth; *it is necessary to believe* should be read.

**20.** Tell me, in what ways is God believed in? He replied: Three or four: God must be believed to be good, perfect, almighty, and everlasting, because without these qualities he cannot be called God.

## QUESTION XVI

[Note: [Col. 0203D]]

**21.** It would seem better to read *because he is worshiped*, and so forth. Again and a third time, *who* should be read instead of *which*.

**21.** Tell me, in what ways is God worshiped? He replied: Three: he who is worshiped and does not worship; he who is creator and not a creature; he who is without sin and forgives sins.
