## QUESTION XVII

**22.** Tell me, in what ways does God administer justice with his saints? He replied: In three: he shows, so that they may know; he persuades, so that they may love; he helps, so that they may attain perfection.

## QUESTION XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0203D]]

**23.** Perhaps *that he was the Lord* should be read.

**23.** Tell me, why did Adam receive a commandment? He replied: So that he would not think himself God, but subject to God.

## QUESTION XIX

253 **24.** Tell me, why was Moses’ face terrifying among the people? He replied: Because he was giving the law to sinners.

## QUESTION XX

[Note: [Col. 0203D]]

**25.** The words of the Apocalypse: “Take the book and devour it … and it was in my mouth as sweet honey, and when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter.”

**25.** Tell me, why does it say in the Apocalypse: “Take the book and eat it; it will be sweet in my mouth, like honey, and bitter in my stomach” (Revelation 10:9–10)? He replied: Scripture is honey-sweet in the mouth of the Church, which consists of the wise and faithful; it is bitter among heretics who rage.

## QUESTION XXI

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**26.** Perhaps not everyone ought to be circumcised; earlier it read *all people*.

**26.** Tell me, why was the Lord circumcised, while people ought not to be circumcised? He replied: Because he instituted circumcision to bring the Old Testament to an end, but baptism to begin the New.

## QUESTION XXII

**27.** Tell me, why did the Savior hunger? So that he might deceive Satan.

## QUESTION XXIII

**28.** Tell me, why did Christ fast no more than forty days? He replied: So that he might correspond with Moses and Elijah.

## QUESTION XXIV

**29.** Tell me, how was the father of the Jews a liar? That is: Cain was called the father of the Jews; he said to the Lord, “I do not know where my brother is,” although he had killed him. And the father of Cain—that is, the devil—lied to Adam: “You will not surely die if you transgress the Lord’s commandment.”

## QUESTION XXV

[Col. 0204B]

254 [Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**30.** Perhaps *to be permitted* should be read instead of *he permitted*.

**30.** Tell me, why was it said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth,” and the other things that pertain to vengeance? He replied: So that there would be fear among the people, lest anything be permitted to them that they did not want done to themselves.

## QUESTION XXVI

**31.** Tell me, in how many or what ways is justice spoken of? He replied: Five: the justice of the Old Testament; the justice of the New Testament; justice for judging; justice for mercy; and justice that appears to exist in the eyes of human beings.

## QUESTION XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**32.** In the manuscript, *he read* instead of *it is permitted*, and *he held* instead of *let him hold*.

**32.** Tell me, how many properties does fire contain in itself? Four: it burns, illuminates, warms, and sanctifies. To sanctify, however, does not properly belong to it according to its nature, although it bears the figure of the Holy Spirit, who burns away vices, warms the cold soul, sanctifies the sinner, and illuminates the heart, thereby driving away the darkness of ignorance.

## QUESTION XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**33.** The manuscript has *the old law*. Perhaps *the new and old law* should be read. What these parts, seven and eight, signify was indicated in the book on Numbers, at chapter 9.

**33.** Tell me, what is understood by what is said: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight”? He replied: The Jews did not give the eighth portion, denying the resurrection on the Lord’s Day; but they gave the seventh portion, believing in the Sabbath. You, however, believe in and honor both, that is, the new and the old parts of the law, so that you may be neither a Jew nor a gentile.

## QUESTION XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**34.** The old codex has: “I understood the beginning to be taken.”

**34.** Tell me, why is it called the head? He replied: Because from it the senses and the nerves take their beginning.

## QUESTION XXX

255 [Note: [Col. 0204D]]

**35.** Perhaps: “Because it helps the wretched-hearted person.”

**35.** Tell me, in what language is *almsgiving* spoken, or what is its interpretation? In Greek it is called *eleemosyne*, which in Latin is “the bestowal of my God.” *Mercy* is so called from *wretched heart*; hence the Lord is called merciful, and because he comes to the aid of a person who has a wretched heart.

## QUESTION XXXI

[Col. 0205A]

**36.** Tell me, how many, or what kinds of spirits did almighty God create? He replied: Three: one not covered with flesh, namely, that of angels; another covered with flesh but not destined to die with the flesh, namely, that of human beings; a third covered with flesh and destined to die with the flesh, namely, that of beasts and irrational animals. Thus the human being was created in the middle, so as to be lower than angels and higher than beasts.

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**37.** The codex has *consists* instead of *consist*, and *second, fourth* instead of *secondly, fourthly*.

**37.** Tell me, in how many ways do affection or charity consist? In four. First, in fear or love of God. Second, just as we love ourselves, so let us love God. Third, our neighbors. Fourth, even our enemies.

[Col. 0205B] [Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**38.** In the manuscript, *potemus* instead of *poterimus* (“we shall be able”).

**38.** Therefore we must love God more than ourselves; our neighbor as ourselves; our enemy as our neighbor. And unless we first love God, we will not be able to love ourselves at all.

## QUESTION XXXIII

**39.** Tell me, in what ways is the kingdom of God understood? He replied: Five: Christ, faith, the Gospel, the present Church, or the kingdom of heaven itself. Repentance was not preached before John, because he himself said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2).

## QUESTION XXXIV

256 [Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**40.** It would be preferable to read: “so that he might sanctify the waters of John”; for *i* is easily changed into *e*.

**40.** Tell me, for what reasons did the Lord wish to be baptized by John? He replied: For four: first, because he was born as a human being, so that he might fulfill all righteousness and humility; second, baptism, so that John might confirm his baptism; third, so that John might sanctify the waters; fourth, so that no one might disdain being baptized by his servant, since the Lord himself was baptized by his servant.

## QUESTION XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**41.** Many theologians distinguish seven grades, or orders, but they enumerate them in another way.

**41.** Tell me, how, or when, did Christ fulfill the seven grades? The first grade is lector, when he opened the book of the prophet Isaiah and said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:18).

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**42.** The grade of exorcist was also begun and signified when Jesus Christ touched the ears of the deaf and mute man, saying: *Ephphatha*, which means “Be opened.”

**42.** The second grade is exorcist, when he cast seven demons out of Mary Magdalene.

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**43.** Others say that the subdiaconate was instituted by Christ at the Last Supper.

**43.** The third grade is subdeacon, when he made wine from water at Cana of Galilee.

[Col. 0206A] [Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**44.** According to the opinion of others, Christ instituted the diaconate when, at the Last Supper, he distributed his body and blood to the disciples.

**44.** The fourth grade is deacon, when he washed the feet of his disciples.

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**45.** Perhaps: “and gave it to his disciples.”

**45.** The fifth grade is priest, when he blessed the bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. Christ fulfilled these five grades before his Passion.

[Note: [Col. 0205D]]

**46.** Others judge that Christ instituted the office of doorkeeper before his Passion in an incipient and, as they say, indicative manner, when he drove the buyers and sellers out of the temple; and in a complete manner when, at the Last Supper, he conferred the first priestly authority upon his disciples.

**46.** The sixth grade is doorkeeper, when he said: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates” (Psalm 23:7).

257 [Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**47.** Most recent theologians, together with the canonists, now maintain that the episcopate is a true order distinct from the presbyterate.

## QUESTION XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**48.** Perhaps *and hunchbacked*. Others explain the camel as a rope.

[Col. 0206B] He replied: What is signified by the camel except gentile people? For before Christ came they were twisted and hunchbacked, worshiping or venerating idols.

**49.** What is signified by that opening except the incarnation of Christ in the womb of holy Mary? What is signified by that rich man except the Jews, who hoped to be rich from the letter of the law?

[Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**50.** This seems to belong to another question whose beginning is missing.

**50.** The Lord had three places of refuge: on the mountain, in the desert, and on the sea. This gives us the example of ascending to a higher righteousness as though onto a mountain; pursuing the contemplative life as though in the desert; and fleeing as though onto the sea.

## QUESTION XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**51.** I think *two* should be restored instead of *three*. This question was mutilated at the end, ending with “while it gives strength to the limbs”; I supplied the text from the *Incomplete Work on Numbers*, perhaps by Saint Isidore, in the manuscript Vatican, Regina 199, where these same words occur, and above them is read: “while the soul has understanding,” and so forth.

**51.** Tell me, of what substances does a human being consist? He replied: Of three, namely soul and body. The soul is one, but while it contemplates, it is spirit; while it perceives, it is sense; while it has knowledge, it is soul; while it understands, it is mind; while it distinguishes, it is reason; while it assents, it is will; while it remembers, it is memory; while it gives strength to the limbs, it is soul.

## QUESTION XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0206D]]

**52.** The beginning of this question is missing.

**52.** There are seven modes of preaching: teaching, persuading, rebuking, arguing, frightening, soothing, and promising. That is: teaching disciples; persuading individuals; rebuking the proud; arguing with opponents; frightening the fearful; soothing the angry; promising the wicked and the good—punishments to the wicked and eternal life to the good.

## QUESTION XXXIX

**53.** Tell me, who first prophesied? He replied: Adam, when he said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.”

## QUESTION XL

**54.** Tell me, how many virtues does a little infant possess? He replied: Four: he does not remember having been harmed; he does not persist in anger; he does not take delight in a beautiful woman; he does not think one thing while saying another.

# THE MYSTICAL WORKS OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE

[Note: [Col. 0207C]]

*Mystical works.* Here Arevalus had written *of secrets*; but in other titles of this work, following Grial’s edition, he restored *mystical works*, “although,” he says, “perhaps *of secrets* is more genuine.” We have retained the second reading. Moreover, Arevalus appends the following note to this passage:

“Concerning the Expositions of the Sacraments of the Secrets—or, as Grial published it, of the Mystical Works—what should appropriately be noted here may be taken from the prolegomena, chapter 65, where I discussed this work at length. For now it is enough to indicate that Grial is the author of those notes among which we shall insert our own, though not very many. Nor is the subject of such a nature that it requires a lengthy explanation; and wherever a reasonable meaning can be derived from Isidore’s words, one need not anxiously inquire whether he reproduced precisely the words of the author whom he follows, or even intended to reproduce them.” [Col. 0207D] EDITOR.

## EXPOSITIONS OF THE SACRAMENTS, OR QUESTIONS ON THE OLD TESTAMENT (C, S)

# ON GENESIS

## PREFACE

[Col. 0207B]

259 **1.** The history of the sacred law was enacted and written down not without some foreannouncement of future events. If the manifold shadow of enacted things did not pertain to the mystery of prefiguration, the Apostle would not also say while teaching: “The law has a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things.”

[Note: [Col. 0207D]]

**2.** And they are full of mystical sacraments. From these words, and from those of Saint Ildefonsus that we shall append, we have restored to this work a title that had already entirely disappeared. For Ildefonsus says this in the *Life of Isidore*: “He also collected from various authors what he himself called the Expositions of the Sacraments of the Secrets; once these had been gathered together, the same book is called the *Book of Questions*. More may be found in the preface to Isidore’s works.” GRIAL.

In the same place: “Those who shrink from excessive length of discourse”—thus the Palatine manuscript and two Oxford manuscripts. “Those whom excessive length of discourse displeases,” the Valencian manuscript. “Those whom excessive length of discourse displeases,” the Guadalupe manuscript. “Those whose excessive length of discourse displeases,” the Laurentian and Complutensian manuscripts. Isidore likewise says in the *Rule for Monks*: “Let the contagion of avarice, like a deadly plague, be shunned.” GRIAL.

In the same place: the names of the ancient ecclesiastical writers whose opinions he gathers are listed by Isidore shortly afterward, at no. 5. AREVALUS.

**2.** Accordingly, with the help of heavenly grace, we have woven into this little work certain things that were said or done figuratively in that history and are full of mystical sacraments; and, gathering together the opinions of the ancient ecclesiastical writers, we have placed them at hand like flowers picked from different meadows. Touching briefly on much while saying little, and also adding many things or altering some in part, we offer this work not only to diligent students, [Col. 0207C] 260 but also to fastidious readers who shrink from excessive length of discourse.

[Note: [Col. 0208C]]

**3.** And since long ago, according to the literal sense—Sigebert says of him: “He goes through the entire Old Testament by interpreting it simply.” It is a great loss for us that this is lacking, unless perhaps these are the works called the *Ordinary Gloss*. GRIAL.

**3.** For a concise exposition, compressed into a brief form, does not cause weariness through prolixity. A long and obscure discourse is tedious; a brief and clear one is pleasing. And since long ago we composed the whole discourse according to the literal sense, it is necessary that, with the foundation of the history preceding it, the allegorical sense should follow. For certain things in it are understood figuratively, truly as prophetic signs anticipating future events.

[Note: [Col. 0208D]]

**4.** Certainly not all the words, up to *are connected*, are Augustine’s; they have been adapted from two passages, *The City of God* XV, chapter 2, and *Against Faustus* XXII, chapter 94. GRIAL.

[Col. 0209C] In the same place: “Whatever things are said.” Thus the manuscripts: *whatever things are said*, the way not only Isidore but sometimes even the best Latin authors speak. Those who did not recognize this were not afraid to add *which are covered*, so that it would read: “whatever things are said are connected.” GRIAL.

**4.** Certainly not everything written in the law and the prophets is covered by riddles of mysteries; but, for the sake of those things that signify something, even things that signify nothing are connected. For just as in lyres and similar musical instruments not everything that is touched produces a musical sound, but only the strings, while the rest of the body of the lyre has nevertheless been made so that there may be something to which those strings can be attached and against which they can be stretched, the strings that the musician is about to tune for the sweetness of the song—so in these prophetic narratives, whatever is said either gives some sound in signifying future things, or, if it gives no sound, is inserted so that the things that signify, like things that sound, may have something by which they can be connected.

[Note: [Col. 0209C]]

**5.** *Cassian.* Some books have *Fulgentius* instead of *Cassian*. In others both names appear, and it is clear that Isidore was a very devoted student of both. Yet throughout this entire work, so far as we know, there is not a single word from Fulgentius; several passages from Cassian, which we have indicated, do occur. GRIAL.

In the same place: I explained in the prolegomena, chapter 65, numbers 19 and 20, why Fulgentius’s name should not be omitted, although Grial omitted it. Certainly the authority of John the Deacon, who cited these words of Isidore in the *Life of Saint Gregory* and named Fulgentius after the others, should be of sufficient weight that it not be rejected. AREVALUS.

**5.** Drawing these figures of historical events from the mystical treasures of the wise, as we have said, we have condensed them into a single form for the sake of brevity; in them the reader will read not our words but those of the ancients again. For what I say, they say; and my voice is their language. They have therefore been taken from the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Fulgentius, Cassian, and the notably eloquent Gregory of our own time.

# CHAPTER I  
## The Preliminary Matter of the Work up to the Expulsion of the Human Being from Paradise

[Col. 0209B] [Note: [Col. 0209D]]

**Chapter I, no. 1.** “The creation of heaven and earth.” He imitated the older translator; for what the Vulgate has, “These are the generations of heaven and earth,” he rendered according to the words of the Septuagint: **Αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς**, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth.” GRIAL.

**1.** We read how the creation of heaven and earth was historically established from the beginning of its origin; but let us understand how it is received spiritually in the Church by the teachers.

[Note: [Col. 0209D]]

**2.** “In the beginning he made,” from the Septuagint. The Valencian and Complutensian manuscripts have “he created,” from the Vulgate. GRIAL.

In the same place: “I am the beginning, who also speak.” “Who also speak” belongs to Augustine; these words are from his *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book I, chapter 2, and occur in the same form at the beginning of Ambrose’s work *Hexaemeron*. GRIAL.

[Col. 0210C] In the same place: “Spiritual … carnal.” From Augustine, *Confessions* XIII, chapter 12. GRIAL.

In the same place: “But the earth was empty and void.” Thus all the manuscript and printed books read, including Eucherius and Bede; but the explanation, or allegory, is not applied to these words, but rather to those from the Septuagint: “But the earth was invisible and unformed.” Augustine, in the passage cited immediately above: “For in his Christ God also made heaven and earth among us—the spiritual and carnal members of his Church—and our earth, before it received the form of instruction, was invisible and unformed, and we were covered by the darkness of ignorance,” and so forth. GRIAL.

[Col. 0210D] In the same place: Saint Augustine often says in the same way: “In the beginning he made,” and so forth. In the same Saint Augustine, others read: “The beginning, because I also speak to you.” AREVALUS.

**2.** “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Christ is the Beginning, just as he himself replied in the Gospel when the Jews questioned him: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). In this Beginning, therefore, God made heaven—that is, spiritual people who meditate on and seek heavenly things; in him he also made the carnal, who have not yet put off the earthly human being. “But the earth was empty and void.” The earth of our flesh, that is, was empty and void before it received the form of instruction. “And darkness was over the face of the abyss,” because the blindness of sins and the profound darkness of ignorance covered our hearts.

**3.** “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” The Spirit of God was already borne over our dark and fluid heart, as over the waters; in him we might remain and rest, by his breath we might be given life, and by his wave we might be washed.

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

**4.** “On the first day,” up to “he wished to appear”: Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, chapter 25. GRIAL.

**4.** And God said: “Let there be light”—that is, “Let the illumination of faith appear.” On the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith is first in conversion. Hence this is also the first commandment in God’s commandments: “The Lord your God is one God.” Because of this faith, the Lord himself also wished to appear visibly in the world.

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

**5.** The Apostle: “For you were once,” and so forth. Grial’s text had the error *sons of God and lights*. AREVALUS.

**5.** “And he divided the light from the darkness.” For then, according to the grace of his foreknowledge, God divided the righteous—that is, the sons of God and of light—from sinners, as from darkness; calling the righteous “day,” and the others “night.” For that the righteous are called by the name of light in the Church, hear the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

**6.** “Then on the second day,” up to “the higher and lower”: excerpted from the same Augustine, *Confessions* XIII, chapter 15, and *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, the cited chapter. GRIAL.

In the same place: The Vulgate has: “The heavens will be rolled together like a book.” AREVALUS.

**6.** Then on the second day God establishes the firmament, that is, the foundation of the holy Scriptures; for in the Church the firmament is understood as the divine Scriptures, as it is written: “The heaven will be folded up like a book” (Isaiah 34:4). And above this firmament he separated the waters—that is, the heavenly peoples of the angels, who do not need to gaze upon this firmament so that, by reading, they may hear the word of God.

**7.** For they always see him and love him; but he placed the firmament of his law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that by gazing upward they might learn there how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the waters above and the waters below.

[Note: [Col. 0210D]]

**8.** “After this, on the third day,” up to “with the strong force of righteous judgment,” from the same book of the *Confessions*, chapter 17. GRIAL.

**8.** After this, on the third day, he gathered together the lower, salty waters: that is, unbelieving people, who are shaken by the storm of desires and the waves of carnal temptations, and within themselves contain something like bitterness. He separated the dry land from them, namely, the people thirsting for the fountain of faith; then he fixed the boundaries of the proud and restrained them, lest by the turbulent waves of their iniquities they disturb the dry land—that is, the soul thirsting for God—and lest they prevent it from producing the fruits of good works according to its kind, loving its neighbor by supplying carnal necessities; and let it have seed within itself according to its likeness, so that from its own weakness it may have compassion in order to help those in need.

[Note: [Col. 0211D]]

**9.** “A sheltering shade.” Thus Augustine, and so it is found in Bede. GRIAL.

**9.** Let it also produce a tree strong in power and fruitful—that is, the beneficence by which one who suffers injury is snatched from the hand of the powerful, and the sheltering shade of protection is provided with the strong force of righteous judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0211D]]

**10.** “Then on the fourth day.” From *Confessions* XIII, chapter 18; *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, chapter 25; and Origen, *Homily 1 on Genesis*. GRIAL.

In the same place: “Clinging to the holy Scriptures.” “Let us appear as lights in the world, clinging to the firmament of your Scripture.” Augustine, *Confessions* XIII, chapter 18. Eucherius and Bede have *showing*, whereas Augustine has *ministering*. GRIAL.

In the same place: “The darkness of the little ones.” These are the words of the same Augustine, chapter 19. Most manuscripts, however, have *of the wicked*. GRIAL.

In the same place: “Because the preachers.” The same author, chapter 16: “The preachers of your word pass from this life into another life, but your Scripture extends over the peoples to the end of the age.” GRIAL.

In the Greek note it read “on the fourth day.” AREVALUS.

**10.** Then on the fourth day the lights embedded in the firmament of the law shone forth—that is, the evangelists and teachers, clinging to the holy Scriptures in their exposition and supplying the light of wisdom to all below. He also brought forth the remaining multitude of shining stars—that is, the abundance of various virtues in the Church—which, shining in the darkness of this life as in night, divide within this firmament of Scripture visible things from intelligible things, as between the light of the mature and the darkness of the little ones; and let them serve as signs of virtues and miracles, and also as signs for times and years, because preachers live and pass away at their appointed times, while the word of the Lord remains forever.

**11.** Why did the earth first bring forth plants, and only afterward were the lights made? Is it not because illumination by light comes after good works, for contemplating the appearance of heavenly virtue?

**12.** Among these things, on the fifth day, living creatures that creep were made in the waters: human beings, namely, renewed to life through the sacrament of baptism. Birds were also made, that is, holy souls flying toward heavenly things.

**13.** After this, on the sixth day, the earth brought forth a living soul, when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, gives birth to living shoots of virtue according to its kind—that is, living by imitating the saints, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me.” For we live according to our kind when in good works we imitate holy men as our neighbors. Then the earth brought forth beasts: human beings powerful in worldly affairs, or fierce through pride. Likewise cattle: the faithful living in simplicity of life. Also harmless serpents: holy men, discerning good from evil by the liveliness of their shrewdness and, insofar as is lawful, investigating earthly things by crawling, so that through them they may understand eternal things—not those venomous creatures that place themselves amid the earthly desires of this world.

[Note: [Col. 0212D]]

**14.** “And of cattle, and of wild beasts, and of creeping things.” Thus Bede and the printed books, from the old translation; others have different readings from the Vulgate. GRIAL.

In the same place: Many theologians and sacred interpreters discuss this passage in Genesis, that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God. Pererius collected various opinions on this subject at this passage. See also the edition of the Apostolic Fathers with Cotelerius’s notes, page 60. AREVALUS.

**14.** After this God made the human being in his image: namely, the perfect man, who practices righteousness not by imitating some particular holy man, but by contemplating and beholding truth itself, so that he may understand and follow the truth in whose image he was made. He also received authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, cattle, wild beasts, and creeping things, because everyone who has become spiritual and has been made like God, according to the Apostle, judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one (1 Corinthians 2:15).

[Note: [Col. 0212D]]

**15.** The Vulgate now has: “So that you may know those who labor among you.” AREVALUS.

**15.** As for what follows, “Male and female he made them,” he showed spiritual people in the Church, and those who obey; for just as the woman is subject to the man, so the less perfect person is obedient to the spiritual and perfect man, as the Apostle says: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you and preside over you in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5:12). And it is said to them: “Increase and multiply,” whether in languages or in the spiritual levels of understanding, so that through the understanding of reason they may rule over all carnal disturbances, like irrational animals.

[Note: [Col. 0212D]]

**16.** The Vulgate has: “For if they have become participants in their spiritual things, they ought to minister to them,” and so forth. AREVALUS.

**16.** Every seed-bearing plant and every fruit-bearing tree, which was given to human beings for food, signifies the faithful who share their resources from the offerings of the saints to meet necessities. Hence the Apostle also says: “For if the gentiles have become participants in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Romans 15:27). These are the fruit-bearing trees. In these stages, therefore, as in certain days, evening is the completion of each individual work, and morning is the beginning of what follows.

[Note: [Col. 0212D]]

**17.** “After these,” up to “the human being hopes for rest,” are Augustine’s words, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* I, chapter 25. GRIAL.

In the same place: “By which the blessed life is signified.” From the same author, book II, chapter 9. GRIAL.

[Col. 0213C] In the same place: “Divided into four parts of virtue.” From the same author, chapter 10. GRIAL.

Breulius adds the following after the four virtues: “Virtue is a disposition of the soul, the adornment of nature, the rule of life, devotion in conduct, worship of the Divinity, the honor of the human being, and the merit of eternal blessedness. Its four principal parts, which are signified by the four rivers of paradise, are prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Prudence is knowledge of divine and human matters, insofar as it has been granted to the human being; through it one understands what must be avoided and what must be done. This is what is read in the psalm (118): ‘Wonderful are your testimonies.’ Fortitude is the soul’s patience, endurance, and perseverance in good works, and victory over every kind of vice. Justice is the nobility of the soul, assigning each thing its proper dignity. In it the worship of the Divinity, the rights of humanity, true judgments, and the equity of the whole of life are preserved. Temperance is the measure of life, so that a person neither loves nor hates anything excessively, but moderates all the variations of this life with considered diligence. These are the four rivers. The trees are all useful virtues,” and so forth. Breulius notes that these words are absent from certain manuscripts. In Solomon’s words the Vulgate has “those who grasped it.” AREVALUS.

**17.** After these works, therefore, as though after six days of very good works, the human being hopes for rest of mind, established in the spiritual paradise, by which the blessed life is signified. There is the fountain of wisdom, divided into four parts of virtue; there he may eat the grace of the tree of life; there he may pluck useful disciplines of conduct as the fruits of trees. For paradise is the life of the blessed; the four rivers are the four virtues; its trees are all useful disciplines; the fruits of the trees are the conduct of the devout; the tree of life itself is the mother of all good things, wisdom, of which it is written, as Solomon says: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and whoever holds her is blessed” (Proverbs 3:18). The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is transgression of the commandment.

# CHAPTER II  
## On the Works of the Six Days

[Col. 0213A]

[Note: [Col. 0214C]]

## CHAPTER II. No. 1

**Note:** “Then what they signify as a figure of the age,” and the remainder of this chapter, have been woven together from the same author’s words in Book I *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 23, with only the order changed. GRIAL.

**[Col. 0214D]** “For six days,” up to “has no evening,” are Augustine’s words, *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 8. GRIAL.

On the six ages of the world, see *Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 38, no. 5. AREV.

1. Thus far, the works of the six days have been explained as they are spiritually understood in the Church; next it must be set forth what they signify as a figure of the age. God completed all his works in six days, and rested on the seventh. In six ages the human race, through the succession of times, marks out God’s works in this world. The first of these is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation into Babylon; the fifth thereafter up to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now in progress, up to the end of the world, until the Most High comes to judgment.

**Note:** 2. “Of the saints, namely.” Some add: “Of the saints, not in this life but in the other, where that rich man saw the present rest while he was being tormented in the underworld; namely.” AREV.

2. The seventh, however, is understood as the rest of the saints, which has no evening, because no end will ever close it. Let us therefore proceed briefly through all the ages of the world, reviewing the order of their times and distinguishing their mystical differences.

3. In the first age, therefore, man was made like light, in paradise. In that age God separated the sons of God, under the name of light, from the sons of men, as from darkness; and the evening of this day was the Flood.

**Note:** 4. Grial’s edition erroneously reads “seas amid the rain.” AREV.

4. The second age was made like a firmament between water and water: namely, that ark which floated amid rain and seas. Its evening was the confusion of languages.

**[Col. 0213C]** 5. The third age was made when God separated his people from the nations through Abraham, distinguishing him as dry land from the waters, so that he might bring forth the shoot of grasses and trees—that is, the fruits of the Holy Scriptures. Its evening was the sin and wickedness of the exceedingly evil king Saul.

6. From there the fourth age began with David, when God appointed lights in the firmament of heaven—that is, the splendor of the kingdom, like the excellence of the sun; and, in the likeness of the moon, the Synagogue obeying like the moon; and its rulers as stars. The evening of this age comes in the sins of the kings, on account of which that people deserved to be taken captive.

7. Further, in the fifth age—that is, during the Babylonian deportation—things were made like creatures in the waters and birds of the sky, because at that time the Jews began to live among the nations as in the sea, having no stable place, like flying birds. The evening, as it were, of this day is the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, when they were so blinded that they could not even recognize the Lord Jesus.

**267** 8. Now the sixth age comes with the advent of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as on that sixth day the first man, Adam, was formed from the clay of the earth in the image of God, so in this sixth age of the world the second Adam, that is, Christ, was born in the flesh from the Virgin Mary: the former into a living soul, the latter into a life-giving spirit. And just as on that day a living soul was made, so in this age those desiring eternal life are made.

9. And just as on that sixth day the earth brought forth the kinds of serpents and wild beasts, so in this sixth age of the world the Church brought forth the nations desiring eternal life. The same meaning was also made clear by the vessel shown to Peter (Acts 10). And just as male and female are created on the sixth day, so in this age of the world Christ and the Church are revealed.

**Note:** 10. “With earthly curiosity.” Augustine has “with dark curiosity.” GRIAL.

10. And just as on that day man is set over cattle, serpents, and birds of the sky, so Christ is set over the peoples and nations in this age of the world, so that they may be ruled by him—whether they are devoted to carnal desire, like cattle; darkened by earthly curiosity, like serpents; or lifted up by pride, like birds.

**Note:** 11. “To conceive,” from Augustine. “To desire,” in Eucherius and the manuscripts, erroneously. GRIAL.

In the same place: The reading in Codex Albornoz should not be passed over: “man, for whom Christ is the minister.” This relates to Matthew 20:28: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister.” AREV.

11. And just as on that day man and the animals with him are fed with seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green plants, so in this age of the world the spiritual man, who is a good minister of Jesus Christ, is spiritually fed with the people alongside him by the nourishment of the Holy Scriptures and by divine law, for conceiving the fecundity of thoughts and words, as by seed-bearing plants; partly for the usefulness of moral conduct, as by fruit-bearing trees; and partly for the vigor of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, as by green plants that wither under no heat of tribulation.

**[Col. 0215A]**

**Note:** 12. “But the spiritual,” up to “is able,” has been emended here from Augustine and Bede. GRIAL.

In the Vulgate: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” AREV.

12. But the spiritual person is nourished by these spiritual foods and provisions in such a way that he understands many things. The carnal person, however—that is, the little one in Christ—is fed like God’s sheep, so that he believes many things which he is not yet able to understand; nevertheless, they both have all the same foods. May the evening, as it were, of this age not find us! For it is of this that the Lord says: “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

**Note:** 13. In our Vulgate: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.” AREV.

13. After that evening there will be morning, when the Lord himself will come in glory. Then those will rest with Christ from all their works to whom it was said: “Be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Matthew 5:48). Such people indeed perform works that are very good. After such works, rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

**Note:** 14. Vulgate: “These are the generations … created on the day on which the Lord God made … the shrub of the field, before it sprang up on the earth, and every plant of the region, before it germinated.” AREV.

14. It follows: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field and every plant of the region, before it existed upon the earth.” Above, seven days were counted; now one day is named, on which God made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every plant of the region.

**Note:** 15. “By the name of this day, according to prophecy.” These two words, “according to prophecy,” are not found in Augustine, from whom the rest is taken, Book II *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 3; nevertheless, they are read in all the books and in Eucherius and Bede. GRIAL.

15. By the name of this day, according to prophecy, the whole time of this life is signified, in which heaven and earth were made—that is, in which visible creatures are ordered. But what does it mean that, after naming heaven and earth, he added “the shrub of the field” and “the plant of the region,” while leaving silent the other things that are in heaven and earth, or even in the sea, unless it is because by “the shrub of the field” he indicates that the invisible creature is to be understood, as is the soul?

16. It is called a shrub because of the vigor of life; a plant because of that same life, which never withers. Then, by adding “before it existed upon the earth,” he indicates “before the soul sinned.” For when soiled by earthly desires, it is rightly said to have been born upon the earth, or to be upon the earth.

**Note:** 17. “The cloud of our flesh.” Augustine has “the cloudiness of our flesh”; Bede has “the mist.” GRIAL.

In the Vulgate: “For it had not rained.” AREV.

17. Hence he also added: “For the Lord God had not yet rained upon the earth,” as though he were plainly saying: Before the soul sinned, the Lord had not yet granted the soul the rain of teaching through the clouds of the Scriptures, to water it; nor had our Lord, on account of man, who is earth, yet assumed the cloud of our flesh, through which he poured out the most abundant shower of the holy Gospel.

**[Col. 0215D]**

**[Col. 0216A]**

**Note:** 18. “There was no man,” up to “was signified,” from the same book of Augustine, chapter 24. GRIAL.

18. But when he added: “And there was no man to work the earth,” this means that no man worked upon the virgin from whom Christ was born. He is the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Daniel 2), that is, cut from the virgin womb without intercourse or human seed, as from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh. But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth. The earth is most properly understood as the Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, of whom it is written: “Let the earth open and bring forth the Savior” (Isaiah 45:8). The Holy Spirit watered this earth, being signified in the Gospel by the name of spring and water.

## CHAPTER III. On the Formation of Paradise and of Man

**[Col. 0216B]**

1. Therefore God formed man from the clay of the earth—that is, Christ was made, as the Apostle says, “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1), as from the clay of the earth. And he breathed into his face the breath of life—namely, the infusion of the Holy Spirit, who fashioned the man Christ. And man became a living soul, namely, so that he who was perfect God might also be seen to be perfect man.

**Note:** Chapter III, no. 2. “Paradise is the Church,” from the same book, chapter 14. GRIAL.

2. Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning. Paradise is the Church; for this is how it is read concerning her in the *Song of Songs*: “A garden enclosed is my sister” (Song of Songs 4:12). Paradise is planted “from the beginning,” because the Catholic Church is known to have been founded by Christ, who is the beginning of all things. The river flowing out from paradise bears the image of Christ, flowing from the paternal spring; he waters his Church with the word of preaching and the gift of baptism.

**Note:** 3. The prophet is perhaps Isaiah, chapter 44:3: “For I will pour out waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry land.” Elsewhere Isidore also compares the four Gospels with the four rivers of paradise. AREV.

3. Concerning this the prophet rightly says: “The Lord our God is a glorious river leaping forth upon thirsty land.” The four rivers of paradise are the four Gospels, sent forth for preaching to all nations.

4. The fruit-bearing trees are all the saints; their fruits are their works. The tree of life, however, is the Holy of Holies, namely Christ; if anyone reaches out his hand toward him, he will live forever. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the free choice of the will, which has been placed in the midst of us for discerning good and evil. Whoever, having abandoned God’s grace, tastes from it will die by death.

5. Therefore God took man and placed him in paradise. **[Col. 0217A]** God assumed flesh and became the head of the Church, so that he might work upon and guard it—that is, by the Father’s will, fill the Church from all nations. God also said: “It is not good for man to be alone.” Heretics are refuted who think that Christ was merely man and not also God.

**Note:** 6. Vulgate: “Like himself.” And shortly afterward: “And Adam called … and all the birds of heaven and all the beasts of the earth.” And in Isaiah: “And he will call his servants by another name.” AREV.

6. “Let us make for him a helper like himself,” because in the man he assumed, the Church has been joined to God. Adam called all the animals, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the earth by their names, signifying the nations that would be saved in the Church and would receive through Christ the name of Christianity, which they had not previously possessed, as it is written: “And I will call my servants by another name” (Isaiah 65:15).

**Note:** 7. In Psalm 85, which Breulius identifies and which is entitled “A Prayer of David,” verse 8 says: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.” The sentence from the Apocalypse is expressed with words somewhat altered. AREV.

7. But no helper like Adam was found for him. **[Col. 0217B]** This is because, however faithful or just anyone may be, no one can nevertheless be made equal to Christ. For Moses says: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?” (Psalm 85). David also says: “More beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Psalm 44). No one could free the human race from death and overcome death itself except Christ, as it is also said in the Apocalypse: “No one was found worthy, either in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, to open the book, except the Lion from the tribe of Judah.”

**Note:** 8. The words of the psalm in the Vulgate: “I slept, and was overcome with sleep, and rose, because the Lord received me.” AREV.

8. Therefore the Lord God cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman. Adam sleeps, and a woman is made for him from his side. Christ suffers on the cross; his side is pierced by a lance, and the sacraments of blood flow forth, from which the Church is formed. The Prophet sings of this sleep, saying: “I slept and rested, and rose again, because the Lord raised me up” (Psalm 3:6).

9. It follows: “And he placed flesh in its place.” Thus Christ, by dying, placed his flesh upon the cross for the Church. Adam also said: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” For whether they are spiritual saints and exceedingly strong in temptations, or less perfect, both are one body of Christ and one Church.

**Note:** 10. “Which were to emerge in the Church.” Bede has “which were to be beneficial.” GRIAL.

In the same place: “For this reason he will leave,” up to “we could be one body,” from the same book of Augustine, chapter 44, or from *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 8; the same things are read in both places, and Isidore seems to have had both passages before him. Yet both Augustine and Paul read “because of this,” not “for this reason.” GRIAL.

In his note Grialius reads *possemus* (“we could be”); but in the text he has *possimus* (“we can be”), which others retain. AREV.

10. “She shall be called woman,” because she was taken from man. Thus Christ also gave the Church the name “Christian,” **[Col. 0218A]** since she was taken from his side. Therefore all these things happened in figure, of what was to emerge in the Church. “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Explaining this, the Apostle says: “This is a great mystery, but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

11. Therefore what was fulfilled historically in Adam is signified prophetically in Christ. He left the Father when he said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Philippians 2). He also left his mother—that is, the Synagogue of the Jews, clinging carnally to the Old Testament, which was his mother from the seed of David according to the flesh—and he clung to his wife, that is, to the holy Church, so that through the peace of the New Testament the two might be one flesh. For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh a participant with us, so that we might be the body of that head.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Commandments of God and the Agreement of the Serpent

**272**

**Note:** Chapter IV, no. 1. “From this point the commandment,” up to “you have done to me,” consists of Augustine’s words, Book II *Against the Manichaeans*, chapter 25. What is read before this in most books—“After this Eve is called,” etc.—does not belong here but to chapter six (more precisely, chapter five), where the same words are repeated. GRIAL.

“Of every tree of paradise,” up to “let us experience evil,” is from the same passage of Augustine. But whereas Augustine had said “lest we wish to grow proud of our nature,” Isidore interpreted it as referring to the nature of our free choice, as he had also done above. GRIAL.

In our Vulgate: “As long as you did it for one of these, my least brothers, you did it for me.” AREV.

1. From this point onward, the commandment that Adam received figuratively we have received in Christ, because every Christian not improperly bears the person of Christ, as the Lord himself says: “What you did for one of my least ones, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40). Thus it is said to him: “Eat from every tree of paradise. But you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

**Note:** 2. “But the serpent,” up to “craftiness,” from chapter 24 of the same Book II *Against the Manichaeans*. GRIAL.

In the words of the Apostle, the Vulgate differs somewhat. I do not think that what is added, “as the Apostle says,” refers to what follows, but rather to what precedes. AREV.

2. For we are commanded to enjoy every tree of paradise, by which spiritual delights are signified, concerning which the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Galatians 5). As the Apostle says. And we are not to touch the tree planted in the middle of paradise, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—that is, we must not wish to grow proud of the nature of our free choice, which is in the middle, lest, deceived through knowledge, we experience evil as well. But that serpent, wiser than all the beasts, indicates the devil, who is called a serpent because he moves with twisting cunning.

**Note:** 3. “But what is it that he deceived through the woman,” up to “conscience is held,” from Augustine, chapter 14. GRIAL.

In the same place: “To be led astray into sin.” Augustine has “to be led into consent to sin.” GRIAL.

3. But what is it that he deceived through the woman herself and not through the man? Our reason cannot be led astray into sin unless pleasure first arises in the affection of carnal weakness, which ought to obey reason as a ruling man. For this is enacted secretly and inwardly in every human being, in a certain hidden marriage.

4. We understand the suggestion as the serpent, the woman as the bodily animal sense, and reason as the man. Therefore, when an evil suggestion occurs, the serpent speaks, as it were. But if thought alone takes pleasure in that suggestion and, while reason restrains it, consent to carrying out the act does not follow, the woman alone appears to have eaten what was forbidden.

5. But if the mind itself also decides that the sin should be committed, then the man has already been deceived; the woman already appears to have given food to the man. To consent to the enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree. Then the human being is rightly expelled from blessed life, as from paradise, and sin is imputed to him, even if the result does not follow: for although guilt is not in the deed, the conscience is nevertheless held guilty in its consent. This is according to the anagogical sense.

**Note:** 6. “But according to the metaphor,” up to “to demonstrate,” from chapter 25. GRIAL.

In the same place: “To no one more talkatively and subtly.” Augustine has “more talkatively and boastfully.” GRIAL.

“His own discernment.” Augustine has “that discernment.” GRIAL.

6. But according to the metaphor, this crafty serpent can signify the cunning of heretics. With illicit curiosity about secret things, they promise no one more talkatively and subtly an opening and a knowledge of good and evil; and in the human being himself, as in the tree planted in the middle of paradise, they strive to demonstrate their own discernment.

**Note:** 7. “Against this serpent,” up to “not Christ,” from chapter 26. GRIAL.

In the same place: “Thus the curious desire of heretics.” Valentinus has “cunning”; Augustine, chapter 28, has “proud and curious desire.” GRIAL.

**[Col. 0220D]** In the Vulgate: “But I fear.” AREV.

7. Against this serpent the Apostle cries out when he says: “I fear lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (2 Corinthians 11:3). Our carnal desire is seduced by the words of this serpent, and through it the Christian Adam, not Christ, is deceived. The serpent therefore says to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” Thus the curious desire of heretics, thus wicked preachers, inflame the hearts of carnal hearers to love the deceitfulness of error, saying: “Why do you flee from possessing hidden knowledge? Always seek something new; penetrate the knowledge of good and evil.”

8. Hence in Solomon that woman, bearing the figure of heretics, says: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Proverbs 9:17). Then the same serpent added: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will immediately be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

**274** **[Col. 0219D]**

**[Col. 0220A]**

**Note:** 9. “Thus also all heretics,” up to “is darkened,” from chapter 25. GRIAL.

9. Thus all heretics profess a claim to divine status, deceive by promising knowledge, and criticize those whom they find believing simply. And because they persuade people of entirely carnal things, as though leading them to the opening of carnal eyes, they strive to bring this about so that the inner eye may be darkened.

## CHAPTER V. On the Sin of the First Human Beings, or Their Punishment

**Note:** Chapter V, no. 1. “With leaves of the fig tree,” up to “they lie,” from chapter 15. Augustine has “with leaves of a fig tree”; Ambrose has “with leaves of the fig.” GRIAL.

1. Therefore the woman saw that the tree was good, took of its fruit, and ate. The woman ate first, not the man, because carnal people are more easily persuaded to sin, whereas spiritual people are not so quickly deceived. And she gave it to her husband, and he ate—namely, because after the pleasure of our carnal desire, our reason also submits to sin. When they realized that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together. Those who embrace the harsh world, who are plowed by the itch of carnal pleasure, and who, deceived by heretical perversity and stripped of God’s grace, gather coverings of lies like fig leaves, make themselves girdles of perversity when they lie about the Lord or the Church.

**Note:** 2. “And rightly at the evening breeze.” Who does not see that the allegory better fits reading “toward evening,” following the Septuagint and Augustine, chapter 16? GRIAL.

In the same place: “That more fervent light.” Augustine has “that inner light.” GRIAL.

2. “And when they heard the voice of God walking in paradise at the afternoon breeze.” God walks in them and does not stand, because they do not remain steadfast in his command. And rightly “at the afternoon breeze,” because that more fervent light of truth is already being taken away from them, as the darkness of error approaches. “They hid themselves from the face of God in the middle of the tree of paradise.” For the one who, turned away from the Creator’s command, lives in the pleasures of error and his own free choice hides himself in the middle of the tree.

3. And God called Adam: “Where are you?” Here he shows that, if some people slide from faith or good works into their own lies and desires, God does not despise them, but still calls them to return to repentance, because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11). Therefore there is no reason to despair of any sinners, since even the ungodly are summoned to hope for forgiveness.

**Note:** 4. “By the name of the breast,” up to “he wishes to deceive,” from chapter 17. GRIAL.

4. Then it is said to the serpent: “You shall be cursed among all the animals. Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl.” By the name “breast,” pride of mind is signified; by the name “belly,” desires of the flesh are signified. For by these two things the devil crawls against those whom he wishes to deceive: either by earthly desire and lust, or by the insane downfall of pride.

**Note:** 5. “And you shall eat earth,” up to “the punishment of judgment,” from chapter 18. GRIAL.

In the same place: “The seed of the devil,” up to “resistance is made,” from the same chapter. GRIAL.

Codex Regiovaticanus 293, in the margin, and Florentine 1, after “you have deceived through desire,” add: “But when it was said to the devil, ‘You shall eat earth,’ it was also said to the sinner, ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go.’ Thus the sinner was given as food to the devil. For just as what we eat is converted into our body, so that the food itself, according to the body, becomes what we are, so through wickedness and impiety each person becomes what the devil is—that is, like him—and is subjected to him, just as our body is subject to us; and this is what it means to be eaten by the serpent. But as for what he added,” etc. AREV.

5. “And you shall eat earth”—that is, those whom you have deceived by earthly desire will belong to you. “All the days of your life”—that is, throughout the whole time during which you exercise this power, before the final punishment of judgment. “I will place enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed.” The seed of the devil is perverse suggestion. The seed of the woman is the fruit of good work, by which resistance is made to perverse suggestion.

**Note:** 6. “She herself shall crush his head,” up to “in the end he strives to deceive,” Augustine: “And therefore he watches the woman’s heel, so that, if she should ever slip into illicit pleasure, he may then seize her. She watches his head, so that she may repel him at the beginning of evil persuasion.” GRIAL.

After “was promised,” some add: “As it is written concerning David, ‘From the fruit of your womb I will place upon your throne’” (Psalm 131). AREV.

6. “She herself shall crush his head,” if the mind repels him at the very beginning of the evil suggestion. He lies in wait for her heel because he strives in the end to deceive the mind that he did not deceive by the first suggestion. Some have understood the words “I will place enmity between you and the woman” as referring to the Virgin from whom the Lord was born, because at that time the Lord was promised as one who would be born from her in order to defeat the enemy and destroy death, whose author he was.

**276** 7. For they also understand the following—“She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel”—as referring to the fruit of Mary’s womb, which is Christ: that is, “You will trip him so that he dies.” But he, after conquering you, will rise again and crush your head, which is death. As David also said, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 110).

**Note:** 8. “But concerning the punishment of the woman,” up to “to the man who commands,” from chapter 19. GRIAL.

8. He called the asp death, the basilisk sin, the lion Antichrist, and the dragon the devil. But what does the punishment of the woman signify, when it is said to her: “In pain you shall bear children,” except that the carnal will, when it wishes to overcome some evil habit, suffers pains at the beginning and, through a better habit, gives birth to a good work, as to children?

**Note:** 9. “And your turning.” The Vulgate has another reading. AREV.

9. But when he added: “And your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you,” this signifies that the carnal will, which had struggled with pain in order to form a good habit, now, instructed by those very pains, becomes more cautious; lest it fall, it obeys reason and willingly serves as a wife to a commanding husband.

**Note:** 10. “After this she is called Eve,” up to “father and mother,” from *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 8. The words belong here, and are wrongly read in some manuscripts in chapter four, since they ought to be repeated here; this is shown both by the matter itself and by Augustine, who writes in Book II *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 21: “Who would not be moved by the fact that, after the sin and the sentence of the judge, Adam calls his wife his life, because she is the mother of the living, after she deserved death?” etc. GRIAL.

10. After this she is called Eve, “life,” and “mother of the living,” who was made from the side of her husband. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone does not eat my flesh and drink my blood, he will not have life in himself”; and all the things understood there, treated clearly and minutely, speak beforehand of Christ and the Church, both in good Christians and in bad. For the Apostle did not say without reason: “Adam, who is a form of the one to come” (Romans 5:14), and also: “A man shall leave his father,” and the rest.

**Note:** 11. “She is thereafter called mother of the living,” up to “are signified,” consists of the same author’s words, Book II *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 21. GRIAL.

11. She is thereafter called the mother of the living—that is, of those who act rightly—to whom sins are opposed, which are signified by the name “the dead.” Now, through the sentence imposed upon the man, our reason is reproved: seduced by the desire for sin and removed from the paradise of blessedness, it has the curses of earthly labor and the pains of temporal cares, as thorns and thistles.

**Note:** 12. “Yet he is dismissed in such a way,” up to “is recovered,” from chapter 22. GRIAL.

12. Yet he is dismissed from the paradise of blessedness in such a way that he may work the earth—that is, labor in this body—and lay up for himself the merit of returning to blessed life, which is signified by the name paradise; and so he may at some time stretch out his hand toward the tree of life and live forever. The stretching out of the hand aptly signifies the cross, or the torment of repentance, through which eternal life is recovered. He also receives a tunic of skins by divine judgment, by which name the mortality of the body is signified historically.

**[Col. 0222C]**

**Note:** 13. “Pleasures withdrawn.” Augustine, chapter 27, has “phantasms drawn forth.” GRIAL.

In the same place: “Which follows the one living carnally.” Thus the other books; Augustine has “which follows the one who lies carnally,” because there he interpreted the tunics of skins as the lust of lying; therefore we change nothing. GRIAL.

In the same place: “If he should at some time,” up to “charity,” the entire passage has been composed from the words of chapter 23. GRIAL.

13. In the allegory, however, the pleasures withdrawn from the carnal senses, which follow and cover the one living carnally under divine law, are meant. If he should at some time turn to God through the flaming sword—that is, through temporal tribulations, by recognizing and lamenting his sins—and through the cherubim—that is, through the fullness of knowledge, which is charity—he will reach the tree of life, Christ, and live forever.

14. For “cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The revolving sword, placed to guard the way to the tree of life, signifies temporal punishments. No one can reach the tree of life except through these two things: endurance of troubles and fullness of knowledge—that is, through love of God and neighbor. For “the fullness of the law is charity” (Romans 13:10).

## CHAPTER VI. On Cain and Abel and Their Descendants

**Note:** Chapter VI, no. 1. “The births of the two sons,” up to “paradise was planted,” is all taken from Augustine’s *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 9, and the four chapters that follow; some passages have therefore been emended. GRIAL.

1. Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain. Again she bore his brother Abel. The births of Adam’s two sons bear the likeness of two peoples who were to come to faith at different times, equal in their work but unequal in their love before God. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer.

**[Col. 0223B]** 2. But just as Cain’s sacrifice from the fruits of the earth is rejected, while Abel’s sacrifice from the sheep and their fat is accepted, so the faith of the New Testament, praising God from innocence, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament. God said to Cain: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” This is because, although the Jews formerly did those things rightly, they are nevertheless guilty of unbelief because, when Christ came, they did not distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old Testament.

**Note:** 3. “Grateful from innocence.” Augustine has “from the grace of innocence”; Grial’s printed text. GRIAL.

**[Col. 0223D]** In the same place: “Is preferred.” After these words, certain passages are inserted in the Val. and Compl. codices that do not belong here. This is sufficiently shown by the interrupted passage of Augustine and by the other manuscript and printed books, which lack them; and if anything sound is contained in them, it is repeated shortly afterward. Nevertheless, there is no harm in reporting them here:

“But this son of Cain, who is called Enoch, in whose name the city was founded, is interpreted as ‘dedication’; for the dedication of the impious is founded in this life. Enoch the just, the seventh from Adam, is likewise called ‘dedication.’ But his translation shows that the just, since he himself is the seventh, will depart at the end—that is, in the seventh thousandth year—from this dedication of the earthly city.”

Concerning this opinion, repeated shortly afterward in this same chapter and in the explanations of Exodus, chapter 29, inappropriately, we shall say what we think presently. GRIAL.

Ibid. In the Vulgate: “If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, sin will immediately be present at the door.” Its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.” Concerning the version followed by Isidore, see the commentary on Prudentius, p. 495. Florentine Codex 1 adds the following after “is placed before” [Col. 0224C]:

“But the question is why God accepted Abel’s sacrifice and turned his eyes away from Cain’s sacrifice, unless it was because there was no charity in Cain; and unless there had been charity in Abel, God would not have accepted his sacrifice. For when both offered—one from the fruits of the earth, the other from the fruits of the sheep—no one should think that God rejected the fruits of the earth and chose the offspring of sheep. God did not look to the gift, but saw into the heart; and the sacrifice of the one whom he saw offering with charity he regarded, while from the sacrifice of the one whom he saw offering with envy he turned his eyes away.”

The other material that Grialius adduces here from the Val. and Compl. manuscripts is found in Flor. 1, no. 22, where Enoch is discussed. AREV.]

[Note: [Col. 0224D]

3. To that same sin. “To it, finally,” Augustine; an easy slip. GRIAL.

Ibid. After the word “saying,” some copies add: “The healthy have no need of a physician.” And again: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.” And again: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.” And again: “I did not come.” AREV.]

3. But if Cain had obeyed God, who said: “Be still; your desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it,” he would have turned his sin toward himself, attributing this to himself and confessing it to God. Thus, aided by the grace of forgiveness, he himself would have ruled over his sin, rather than becoming a slave to sin, with sin ruling over him [Col. 0223C]; nor would he have killed his innocent brother.

So also the Jews, in whom these things were enacted figuratively, if they had ceased from their agitation and, recognizing the time of salvation through grace for the remission of sins, had heard Christ saying, “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,” then they would have turned their sin toward themselves in confession, saying to the physician, as it is written in Psalm 40: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5). Thus, as long as they were still in their mortal bodies, they would have ruled freely over that same sin through hope in grace.

4. But now, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, exalted by works of the law rather than humbled by their sins, they did not become still; instead, they stumbled against the stone of stumbling and burned with anger against Christ. When they saw that his works were acceptable to God, they grieved.

5. Thus, after these events, Abel, the younger brother, is killed by his elder brother Cain. Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the Jewish people, the elder people: the one in the field, the other at the place of Calvary.

6. God questions Cain, not as one ignorant of the matter and seeking information from him, but as a judge questioning a guilty man whom he is about to punish. He asks where his brother is. Cain replies that he does not know and that he is not his brother’s keeper.

What do the Jews answer us even now when, with the voice of the holy Scriptures, we question them about Christ? They answer that they do not know Christ. Cain’s deceitful ignorance is the Jews’ false denial.

[Note: [Col. 0224D]

7. When he had received the sacrament. “When he had received it,” Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Amen” is answered. Thus the response was made in communion under both kinds. Ambrose, On the Sacrament, book IV: “The priest says to you: ‘The body of Christ,’ and you say: ‘Amen.’ This is true; may what the tongue confesses be held by the heart.” GRIAL.]

7. They would in some way have been Christ’s keepers if they had been willing to accept and preserve the Christian faith. God said to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.”

Thus the divine voice accuses the Jews in the holy Scriptures. The blood of Christ has a great voice on the earth; for when, after receiving the sacrament, all nations respond “Amen,” this is the clear voice, the voice of the blood, which that blood expresses [Col. 0224C] through the mouths of the faithful redeemed by the same blood.

8. God said to Cain: “And now you shall be cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand.”

The unbelieving Jewish people is cursed by the earth—that is, by the Church—which opened its mouth in confession of sins to receive the blood of Christ, poured out for the remission of all sins from the hand of the persecutor [Col. 0225A], who did not wish to be under grace but under the law. Thus he was cursed by the Church—that is, the Church showed him to be accursed—the Apostle bearing witness: “For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse of the law.”

[Note: [Col. 0225D]

9. Then, when he had said “until it was revealed,” these words are wrongly absent from the old Val. and Compl. books, since they are Augustine’s and are read in the printed editions and the remaining manuscripts. GRIAL.]

9. Then, after he had said: “You are cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand,” he did not say, “because you will work it,” but said, “because you will work the earth, and it will not continue to give you its strength.”

10. Therefore, it is not necessary to understand that Cain works the same earth which opened its mouth to receive his brother’s blood from his hand. Rather, he is understood to be cursed by this earth because he works the earth which will not yet continue to give him its strength.

That is, the Church recognizes and shows the Jewish people to be accursed because, after killing Christ, it still works an earthly circumcision, an earthly Sabbath, an earthly unleavened bread, and an earthly Passover. Every earthly observance contains the hidden power of understanding Christ’s grace, but this power is not given to the Jews who persist in impiety and unbelief, because it has been revealed in the New Testament.

11. “When you work the earth, it will not give you its fruits.” For in that very earth which Christ bore—that is, in his flesh—they worked our salvation by crucifying Christ, who died for our sins. Yet that same earth did not give them its strength, since they were not justified by the power of his resurrection, who rose for our justification. For although he was crucified in the weakness of the flesh [Col. 0225C], he lives by the power of God.

12. This, then, is the power of that earth which he does not show to the impious and unbelieving. Therefore, even when he rose, he did not appear to those by whom he had been crucified, as to Cain working the earth, so that that grain might be sown.

“You shall be wandering and a fugitive”; or, as it is written in the Septuagint, “You shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth.”

281 [Note: [Col. 0225D]

13. “My iniquity is greater than that I should obtain pardon.” It is astonishing that whoever supplied the Vulgate edition did not see that the words which follow do not cohere: “He says this to be the greater cause.” It should therefore be read: “My cause is greater,” from the Septuagint and Augustine. Shortly afterward he joined both interpretations when he says: “Truly from that point he wanders and flees, groaning and trembling,” whereas Augustine reported only the words of the Septuagint: “Truly from that point he groans and trembles, lest also an earthly kingdom, etc.” GRIAL.

Ibid. In this astonishing dispersion and preservation of the Jewish people there is established a most serious argument for demonstrating the truth of the Christian religion. AREV.]

13. Now, surely, who cannot see or recognize throughout the whole earth, wherever that people has been scattered, how it is wandering among the nations and fleeing from Jerusalem? How it groans in mourning over its lost kingdom and trembles in fear under countless Christian peoples?

Therefore Cain answered, saying: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon. Behold, today you drive me from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden; and I shall be wandering and a fugitive on the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.”

14. Truly, from that point he wanders and flees, groaning and trembling lest, having lost his earthly kingdom, he should also be killed by this visible death [Col. 0226A]. He says that this is the greater cause, rather than the fact that our earth does not give its strength, lest he die spiritually.

For he has a carnal understanding, and he hides himself from the face of God—that is, he does not consider it a serious matter to have God angry with him. Instead, he fears that he may be found and killed. He has a carnal understanding, like one working the earth whose strength he does not receive.

[Note: [Col. 0226D]

15. Having lost his kingdom, he groans and fears bodily death. A liar ought to have remembered. Why, then, does he groan and tremble, if he nowhere intended to explain these words? This point, however, was anticipated by Eucherius. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Or, as the Septuagint translated it.” This is correct, for he saw that what follows did not correspond to the words of the Vulgate edition. See Jerome, Letter 125, to Damasus, question 1. GRIAL.]

15. But to have a carnal understanding is death. Because he did not understand this, he groans after losing his kingdom and fears bodily death.

But what did the Lord answer him? “By no means shall this happen; rather, whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold”; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “shall pay seven punishments.” That is, it will not happen as you say: the impious race of carnal Jews will not perish by bodily death [Col. 0226B].

[Note: [Col. 0226D]

16. In the Vulgate: “Do not kill them.” AREV.]

16. Whoever destroys them in this way shall pay seven punishments—that is, he shall remove from them the seven punishments with which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s death. Thus, throughout the whole period which revolves in the number seven of the days, it may become increasingly clear to Christian believers that the Jewish race has not perished, but has deserved only dispersion, in accordance with what Scripture says: “Do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget your law; scatter them by your power and bring them down” (Psalm 58:12).

17. The Lord placed a sign upon Cain so that everyone who found him would not kill him.

This is truly astonishing: all the nations conquered by the Romans passed over to the rites of Roman worship and accepted those sacrileges for observance and celebration. But the Jewish people, whether under pagan kings or under Christian rulers, did not lose the sign of their law and circumcision, by which they are distinguished from the other nations and peoples [Col. 0226C].

[Note: [Col. 0226D]

18. Breulius notes in the margin that neither in the manuscript Codex nor in the printed Cologne edition of 1530 are these words found: “so that he no longer … dwells in the land of Nod.” AREV.]

18. Every emperor or king who finds them in his kingdom finds them with that same sign and does not kill them. That is, he does not cause them to cease being Jews, distinguished from the fellowship of the other nations by a certain distinctive and proper sign of their observance—unless one of them passes over to Christ, so that he is no longer found to be Cain, nor goes out from the face of God, nor dwells in the land of Nod.

19. Therefore he went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Nod, which is interpreted as “agitation,” or “unstable,” “fluctuating,” and “of uncertain dwelling” [Col. 0226D].

Against this evil God is entreated in the psalm: “Do not let my feet be moved” (Psalm 65); and: “Let not the hands of sinners move me” (Psalm 35); and: “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved” (Psalm 12); and: “The Lord is at my right hand; I shall not be moved” (Psalm 15).

But now the Jews, and all who are obstinate in various errors by resisting the truth, go out from the face of God—that is, from the mercy of his love or from participation in his light—and dwell as fugitives in the land of agitation: that is, in carnal disturbance opposed to the joy of God. This is opposed to Eden, which is interpreted as “feasting,” where paradise was planted.

[Note: [Col. 0227C]
