20. “And Cain built a city,” from Augustine, On the City of God XV, chapters 17 and following, and Gregory, Moralia VI, chapter 4, and book XVI, chapter 5. GRIAL.]

20. Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch; and Cain built a city.

What, then, does it mean figuratively that the offspring of the impious built a city at the very beginning of the world, except that you should know that the impious are established in this life, while the saints are guests and pilgrims? Hence Abel, as a pilgrim on earth—that is, the Christian people—did not found a city [Col. 0227B].

For the city of the saints is above, although here it gives birth to citizens among whom it lives as a pilgrim, until the time of its kingdom arrives.

283 [Note: [Col. 0227D]

21. “This son,” through “is hoped for,” are Augustine’s words. GRIAL.

Ibid. Codex Regiovaticanus 293 adds in the margin after “is hoped for”: “This son of Cain, who is called Enoch, is interpreted as DEDICATION. For the dedication of the impious is founded in this city. But Enoch the righteous, the seventh from Adam, is also called DEDICATION. But his translation shows that the righteous, because he is himself the seventh, will depart at the end—that is, on the seventh thousandth day—from this dedication of the heavenly city. AREV.]

21. Peter, too, is criticized for this reason: he thought of having tabernacles made on the mountain, because the saints do not build a tabernacle in this world.

He built the city from the name of his son Enoch. This son, in whose name Enoch was founded—Enoch being the earthly Jerusalem, interpreted as “dedication”—signifies this city, which has both its beginning and its end on earth, where nothing more than what is seen is hoped for.

[Note: [Col. 0227D]

22. “When he is said to have begotten sons and daughters.” These words were absent from all the books but have been restored from Augustine, chapter 17, and Eucherius. GRIAL.

Ibid. “By which it is signified,” through “come forth,” are Augustine’s words, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. Breulius observes that bigamy arose from Cain in the fifth generation [Col. 0228C]. AREV.]

22. Moreover, Enoch begot Irad, and Irad begot Maviahel, and Maviahel begot Mathusael, and Mathusael begot Lamech. He took two wives: the name of one was Ada, and the name of the second was Sella.

It should be noted that in the progeny of Seth, although sons and daughters are said to have been begotten, no woman born there is mentioned by name; only in the progeny of Cain is a woman specifically commemorated. This signifies that the earthly city will possess carnal generations until the end—generations which arise from the union of males and females.

[Note: [Col. 0228D]

23. “Now elsewhere according to the historical sense,” and so forth. Isidore indicates that he also expounded Genesis in its literal sense. Compare the preface. AREV.]

23. Lamech also said to his wives: “Hear my words, and listen to my speech. For I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise; Cain shall be avenged seven times, but Lamech seventy-seven times.”

Elsewhere it has already been said according to the historical sense [Col. 0228A] that from Adam to Christ seventy-seven generations are found, in which the sin of Lamech—that is, that of the whole world—was loosed by the shedding of Christ’s blood.

24. Likewise, among the Jewish people, because of the killing of Christ, seventy-seven punishments were decreed, according to the Gospel passage in which it was said to the Apostle Peter: “Not seven times, but seventy-seven times,” if he repents, forgiveness must be granted to one’s brother (Matthew 18).

That is, the Jew who returns after the seventy-seven punishments decreed is to be received into Christ’s forgiveness.

284 [Note: [Col. 0228D]

25. “His son Enos is interpreted as MAN.” “Enos” is interpreted as “MAN” in such a way that experts in that language affirm that a woman cannot be called by this name, says Augustine, On the City of God XV, chapter 17. GRIAL.]

25. Adam again knew his wife, and she bore a son and called his name Seth. Seth then had a son, whom he called Enos. Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” and he is Christ; his son Enos is interpreted as “man,” who began to invoke the name of the Lord.

26. What is understood by this except that every human being who is a child of resurrection lives in confession as long as he is a pilgrim on earth?

Likewise, through those two men, Abel—whose name is interpreted as “mourning”—and his brother Seth, whose name is interpreted as “resurrection,” the death of Christ and his life from the dead are represented.

[Note: [Col. 0228D]

27. “This Enoch, seventh,” through “is formed,” are the words of the same author, Against Faustus XII, chapter 14. GRIAL.

Ibid. After “is formed,” Regiovaticanus adds: “For six thousand years are assigned to the ages of this world.” AREV.]

27. Therefore, to put it briefly: Abel is mourning, Seth is resurrection, and Enos is man, because after mourning comes resurrection, and from resurrection comes the human being who invokes God.

Likewise, Enos begot Cainan; Cainan begot Malalehel; Malalehel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch.

This Enoch, the seventh from Adam, who pleased God and was translated [Col. 0228C], signifies the seventh rest, to which everyone is translated who, like one formed on the sixth day—that is, in the sixth age of the world—is formed through the coming of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0228D]

28. “For after,” through “of perpetual immortality.” These words are not the same in all the books, and in the Val. and Compl. they are placed twice in this chapter. I do not at all think that they are Isidore’s. For Augustine, although he often discusses these ages, defines none of them by any number of years, especially not the sixth; nor do Gregory or Origen. Nor is it likely that Isidore proceeded farther, since in book I of the Sentences, chapter 31, he writes: “Christ knows the day of judgment, but he did not wish to tell it in the Gospel or make his disciples know it.” Therefore I have never believed that this reckoning of years, inserted inappropriately here and repeated at Exodus XXIX, in the third precept, and in book II Against the Jews, chapter 15, is Isidore’s. There is also strong evidence for this in the fact that nothing of the kind is found in Eucherius or in the Codex Olivetanus.

Ambrose writes as follows on Luke 9: “But Matthew and Mark record that these men were taken up after six days. Concerning this we might say, ‘after six thousand years.’ For a thousand years in God’s sight are like one day. But more than six thousand years are counted. Yet we prefer to understand the six days symbolically, since the works of the world were created in six days, so that through time we may understand works, and through works the world.”

Most elegantly, Saint Augustine writes in On the City of God XVIII, chapter 53: “He loosens the fingers and orders them to rest of all those who calculate concerning this matter, the one who says: ‘It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power.’” And in On Genesis against the Manichaeans I, chapter 24: “Old age, as in us, is not defined by any fixed span of years, but after those five ages, however long someone has lived is assigned to old age. So too in this age of the world the generations do not appear, so that even the final day may remain hidden—the day which the Lord has shown ought usefully to remain concealed.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “But what is signified through Seth,” through “delight,” is from the same author, On the City of God XV, chapter 20. GRIAL.

Ibid. The matters concerning numbers touched on here and there in these commentaries were deliberately expounded by Isidore in a separate book On Numbers, which I published above. AREV.]

28. For after six thousand years, when judgment has taken place and heaven and earth have been renewed, the saints will be transferred into the life of perpetual immortality.

But the fact that through Seth the number ten is intimated from Adam to Noah represents the completion of the commandments in the works of the Church. If Noah’s three sons are added to this number, with the rejected one placed in the middle, the number twelve is completed. This number is notable among the patriarchs and apostles because the parts of seven are multiplied one by the other. For three times four, or four times three, produces it.

[Col. 0229A] 29. But the fact that the progeny from Adam through Cain ends with the number eleven indicates transgression of the commandments, or sin. For when Lamech is found written as the seventh from Adam, three sons and one daughter are added to him, so that the number eleven may be completed; by this sin is demonstrated.

30. The number itself is also closed by a female, from whose sex the beginning of the sin that was committed arose, through which we all die—namely, so that the pleasure of the flesh, which would resist the spirit, might follow.

Thus Lamech’s daughter herself, Noema, is interpreted as “pleasure.” The fact that, according to the Septuagint, years are counted for Methuselah beyond the Flood signifies that, since Christ alone is the one whose life experienced no age, he also seemed not to have experienced the Flood in those greater years.

CHAPTER VII. On Noah’s ark and the Flood of the world.

[Col. 0229B]

1. Noah, in every respect and in all his actions, signifies Christ. Noah is interpreted as “rest,” and the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

Noah alone is found righteous in that generation, for whom seven men are granted because of his righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0230D]

CHAPTER VII, no. 2. “Noah through water,” through “according to the letter” (the following chapter): all these words, except for a few passages which we shall note, are Augustine’s, from book XII Against Faustus, chapters 14 through 24; several passages have been restored from it. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has “is granted” erroneously, as I think, instead of “are granted,” which also appears in other printed editions. AREV.]

2. Christ alone is righteous and perfect, and the seven Churches are granted to him as one Church through the sevenfold Spirit who illumines.

Noah is saved through water and wood; for wood and water designate the cross and baptism. Just as he and his household were saved through wood and water, so the household of Christ is healed through baptism and the passion of the cross.

Noah constructed the ark from incorruptible wood; the Church is built by Christ from human beings who will live forever.

3. For this ark demonstrated the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. The fact that the same ark was commanded to be made from squared timbers signifies the stable life of the saints on every side, prepared for every good work [Col. 0230A]. Whichever way you turn it, a square stands firmly.

[Note: [Col. 0230D]

4. “By the force of great strength …” “By great force,” in Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “So that it may be secured in the joining,” and so forth. I restore the passage from the Bolognese Albornozian manuscript. Grialius, with the other printed editions, has: “So that the endurance of unity may be signified in the joining,” and so forth. AREV.]

4. The fact that the timbers of the ark are joined with pitch on the outside and inside, “so that it may be secured in the joining of unity,” signifies the endurance of charity, lest the fraternal bond yield to scandals assailing the Church, whether from those within or those outside, and the bond of peace be broken.

For pitch is a very hot and very powerful adhesive, signifying the ardor of love, which by the force of great strength tolerates everything in order to maintain spiritual fellowship.

[Note: [Col. 0230D]

5. “In five through prophecy.” Thus in most manuscripts and in Eucherius. “In the fifth,” in Augustine and Bede and in the Val. and Compl. GRIAL.]

5. The fact that the ark is three hundred cubits long, so that six times fifty may be completed, signifies that, just as the whole period of this world extends through six ages, Christ never ceased to be preached in all of them. In five he was foretold through prophecy [Col. 0230B]; in the sixth he was proclaimed through the Gospel.

The three hundred cubits can also signify the sign of the wood of the Passion. For the number of the letter T itself displays the sign of the cross, through which we become companions of Christ’s Passion and, through baptism, receive the length of eternal life.

287 6. The fact that its width is extended to fifty cubits, as the Apostle said, “Our heart has been enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6:11)—from what source, unless from spiritual charity? For this reason he says again: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

On the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ sent the Holy Spirit, through whom he enlarged the hearts of believers.

[Col. 0230C] 7. The fact that its height rises to thirty cubits, a number which its length of three hundred cubits contains ten times, signifies that Christ is our height. At the age of thirty he consecrated evangelical teaching, bearing witness that he had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.

The heart of the law is recognized in the Ten Commandments. Thus the length of the ark is completed by ten times thirty; and for this reason Noah himself is counted as the tenth from Adam.

[Col. 0231A] [Note: [Col. 0231D]

8. “For the length of the body,” through “high from the ground.” These words are not found in Augustine. Nevertheless, they are found in the other books and in Eucherius. GRIAL.]

8. The fact that its length is six times its width and ten times its height displays the likeness of the human body, in which Christ appeared.

The length of the body, from the crown of the head to the feet, is six times the width, which extends from one side to the other; and it is ten times the height, whose measurement is from the back to the belly.

[Note: [Col. 0231D]

9. “Likewise, that the ark, gathered into one cubit,” from chapter 16. GRIAL.]

9. If you measure a man lying on his back or face down, his length from head to feet is six times his width from right to left, or from left to right, and ten times his height from the ground.

Thus the ark was made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. Likewise, the fact that the same ark is brought together and completed above in a single cubit signifies that the Church, the body of Christ, gathered into unity, is exalted and perfected.

[Note: [Col. 0231D]

10. The words of Luke in the Vulgate: “He who does not gather with me scatters.” AREV.]

10. Therefore it is said in the Gospel: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23).

The fact that an entrance is made for it at the side signifies that no one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The fact that the lower parts of the ark are constructed with two and three chambers signifies that the Church gathers from all nations either a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision [Col. 0231B], or a threefold multitude, on account of Noah’s three sons, whose descendants filled the world.

288 11. “Are completed.” “We are completed,” Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “That all kinds of animals are enclosed,” from chapter 15. GRIAL.]

11. For this reason the lower parts of the ark are mentioned, because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations. But above, all are completed into one, and there is no variety, because Christ is all things and in all things, completing us in one cubit above through heavenly unity.

The fact that every kind of animal is enclosed in the ark signifies that an assembly from all peoples and nations is formed in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0231D]

12. “In the Church and in the sacraments.” “In the sacraments of the Church,” Augustine. GRIAL.]

12. The disk shown to Peter (Acts 10), containing clean and unclean animals, signifies that in the Church and in its sacraments the good and the wicked are present.

The fact that the clean animals are seven and the unclean two does not mean that there are fewer wicked people than good people, but that the good preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

The holy Spirit is commended by divine Scripture in a sevenfold operation: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of God.

[Col. 0231D] 13. Therefore the number of fifty days, which pertains to the coming of the Holy Spirit, is completed through seven sevens, which make forty-nine, with one added.

For this reason it is said: “Striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” The wicked, represented by the number two, are shown to be prone to schisms and, in a certain sense, divisible (Ephesians 4:3).

14. The fact that Noah with his companions is counted as the eighth signifies that in Christ our hope of resurrection appeared. He rose on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day, the Sabbath—first from the dead.

That day is the third from the Passion, but in the number of days which revolve through all time it is both the eighth and the first.

[Note: [Col. 0232D]

15. “That after seven,” from chapter 17. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Because in hope of future rest.” Thus Augustine, Eucherius, Bede, Val. and others; “in the appearance,” in the sense. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has “hope” in the text, but “in hope” in the note. AREV.]

15. The fact that the Flood occurred seven days after Noah entered the ark signifies that we are baptized in hope of the future rest, which was signified by the seventh day.

The fact that, apart from the ark, all flesh which the earth supported was destroyed by the Flood signifies that, apart from fellowship with the Church, the water of baptism, although it is the same water, not only does not avail for salvation but rather avails for destruction [Col. 0232B].

[Note: [Col. 0232D]

16. Grialius had “pertained.” Other printed editions have: “that which pertains to the days,” or “that which pertains to the nights,” and so forth. AREV.]

16. The fact that it rained for forty days and forty nights signifies that every guilt of sin is admitted against the Ten Commandments throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts.

For ten multiplied by four makes forty. Whether that guilt pertains to the days, arising from the prosperity of worldly things, or to the nights, arising from adversity, it is washed away by the sacrament of heavenly baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0232D]

17. “That Noah was five hundred,” chapter 18. GRIAL.]

17. Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord spoke to him and commanded him to make an ark, and he was six hundred years old when he entered it. From this it is understood that the ark was built over one hundred years.

What else do these hundred years seem to signify here except the individual ages of the world? Thus this sixth age, signified by the completion of the five hundred years up to six hundred, constructs the Church in the manifestation of the Gospel.

18. Therefore, whoever takes care for his life should be like squared timber, prepared for every good work, and should enter into the holy structure.

For the second month of the six-hundredth year, in which Noah entered the ark, likewise signifies the same sixfold age; for two months are concluded in the number sixty.

19. From the number six come sixty, six hundred, six thousand, sixty thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundred times, and whatever thereafter rises through the same numerical progression into infinite increases in the larger sums.

[Note: [Col. 0232D]

20. “And that the twenty-seventh,” from chapter 19. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Squared.” “And made square,” Augustine. GRIAL.]

20. The fact that the twenty-seventh day of the month is mentioned [Col. 0232D] pertains to the meaning of the same squareness, which has already been expounded in connection with the squared timbers.

But here it is more evident, because the Trinity perfects us, prepared—that is, squared, in a certain sense—for every good work: in memory, by which we remember God; in understanding, by which we know him; and in will, by which we love him [Col. 0233A].

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

21. “The ark sat.” Thus Augustine. “Rested,” Eucherius and Val. “Sat,” Ambrose. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Where the perfected rest.” “There also,” and so forth. This passage of Augustine, which is circulated corruptly, should likewise be read and punctuated in this manner, following the Louvain correction. GRIAL.]

21. Three times three, and this again three times, make twenty-seven, which is the square of the ternary number 290.

The fact that in the seventh month the ark sat—that is, rested—turns back to signify that seventh rest in which the perfected rest. There also the number of that squareness is repeated.

22. For on the twenty-seventh day of the second month this sacrament was commended. Again, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, the same commendation was confirmed when the ark rested.

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

23. Some have “but that very one,” omitting “because.” AREV.]

23. What is promised in hope is exhibited in reality. Moreover, because that seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection—and rest does not end when the body is restored, the rest which receives the saints after this life—but rather receives the whole human being, no longer in hope but already in reality, renewed in every respect with the immortal salvation of perfected spirit and body, into the gift of eternal life.

24. Therefore, because the seventh rest is joined to the eighth resurrection, and this is a deep and profound mystery in the sacrament of our regeneration—that is, in baptism—the water rose fifteen cubits above, exceeding the height of the mountains.

Thus eight and seven make fifteen. But eight signifies resurrection, and seven signifies rest.

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

25. “So that no nation.” “So that no nation at all,” in Bede and Palentinus. GRIAL.]

25. This sacrament of resurrection and rest therefore transcends all the wisdom of the proud, so that no nation can, by the height of its knowledge, indicate the rest of the resurrection [Col. 0233C].

And because seventy is named from seven, and eighty from eight, when the two numbers are joined, the waters were raised for one hundred and fifty days. This commends and confirms for us the same height of baptism, in the sanctification of the new human being, for maintaining faith in rest and resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

26. “That after forty days,” from chapter 20. GRIAL.]

26. The fact that the raven, sent out after forty days, did not return—whether it was intercepted by the waters or enticed by some floating corpse—signifies people who are most foul in the uncleanness of desire and, for this reason, excessively intent upon the things outside in this world.

It signifies either that they are rebaptized or that they are seduced and held by those whom baptism outside the ark—that is, outside the Church—has killed.

27. The fact that the dove, having found no place of rest, returned shows that rest was not promised to the saints in this world through the New Testament [Col. 0233D].

It was sent out after forty days, and this number signifies the life lived in this world. Finally, when it was sent out after seven days, because of that sevenfold spiritual operation, it brought back a fruitful olive branch [Col. 0234A].

[Note: [Col. 0233D]

28. “Is joined to the Church.” Thus Augustine, Bede, and the Codex [Col. 0234D]. Val. has “is satisfied,” erroneously. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has “is joined to the Church” in the note, but “is joined to Church” in the text. AREV.]

28. This was to signify that some who have also been baptized outside the Church may, if they have not lacked the richness of charity, at a later time—so to speak, at evening—be brought, in the dove’s beak, as in the kiss of peace, into fellowship with unity. The fact that, after another seven days had passed, the dove was sent out and did not return signifies the end of the age, when there will be rest for the saints—not yet in the sacrament of hope, through which the Church is joined together in this present time, as long as what flowed from Christ’s side is being drunk, but already in the perfection itself of eternal salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God and the Father, so that in that clear contemplation of unchanging truth we may have need of no bodily ministries.

[Col. 0234B]  
[Note: [Col. 0234D]

29. Why in the six-hundredth. From chapter 21. GRIAL.]

29. Why is the roof of the ark said to have been opened in the six-hundred-and-first year of Noah’s life—that is, after six hundred years had been completed? When the sixth age of the world has ended, the hidden sacrament and promise will be revealed.

[Note: [Col. 0234D]

30. To have dried the earth. So Augustine and most books. “That the earth had dried”: Valerius. GRIAL.]

30. Why is it said that on the twenty-seventh day of the second month the earth had dried, as though the necessity of baptism had ended on the fifty-seventh day? For this is the twenty-seventh day of the second month; that number, arising from the conjunction of spirit and body, contains seven times eight, with one added because of the bond of unity.

31. Why do those who entered separately leave the ark joined together? For it had been said that Noah, his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons entered the ark. Why are the men and women mentioned separately, [Col. 0234C] unless because in this present time the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh? Afterwards, however, Noah and his wife, and the wives of his sons, leave together.

[Note: [Col. 0234D]

32. Why the animals, “up to the filling of the earth,” are absent from Valerius and most copies, though they are found in Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. Why the animals, etc. These words are also absent from the Cologne edition of 1530. AREV.]

32. That is, the males and females are mentioned as leaving together because at the end of the age, and in the resurrection of the righteous, the body will cleave to the spirit in complete and perfect peace, with no necessity of mortality or concupiscence resisting it. Why, although both clean and unclean animals had been in the ark, are only the clean animals offered to God in sacrifice after leaving the ark?

33. What, then, is intended by God’s speaking to Noah, as though beginning again from the beginning? It was necessary that the figure of the Church should be signified in many ways, with the statement that Noah’s offspring was blessed for the filling of the earth. All the animals are given to them for food, just as it is said to Peter in that sheet: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

[Col. 0235A]  
[Note: [Col. 0235D]

34. “Let it have, as it were, an outpouring.” So Augustine. “Let them have,” in some books; this can be accepted as referring to the men themselves, not to life. What if one reads: “But let it have, as it were, an outpouring through confession”? GRIAL.]

34. They are commanded to eat after the blood has been poured out, so that their former life may not remain, as though suffocated, in their conscience, but may have, as it were, an outpouring through confession. The covenant that God established between himself and human beings, and every living soul, so that he would not destroy it by a flood, is the bow that appears in the clouds and never shines except from the sun. For those are not destroyed by the flood who recognize Christ’s glory in the prophets and in all the divine Scriptures, as in God’s clouds, and do not seek their own glory.

## CHAPTER VIII. Noah and the blessings conferred on his greater and lesser sons

[Note: [Col. 0235D]

CHAP. VIII. NOTE 1. “Now indeed that matter.” From chapter 23. GRIAL.]

1. Now, who would not recognize as a figure of Christ the event after the flood, when Noah became drunk from the wine of the vineyard he had planted and was uncovered in [Col. 0235B] his house? He became drunk when he suffered; he was uncovered when he was crucified; he was uncovered in his own house—that is, among his own people and the members of his bloodline, namely, the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0235D]

2. “A stumbling-block to the Jews, up to ‘from whom they were born’”: we preferred to reproduce the passage from Augustine, with the support of the printed books, rather than present the somewhat abridged text from the older copies. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Because what is foolish … from whom they were born.” These words are not found in the cited Cologne edition. In the Vulgate: “Wiser for human beings … stronger for human beings.” AREV.]

2. Then the weakness of his flesh was exposed: a stumbling-block to the Jews, but foolishness to the gentiles; yet to those who are called, both Jews and gentiles, represented by Shem and Japheth, it is the power of God and the wisdom of God, because “what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25).

3. Accordingly, in the two sons, the greater and the lesser, two peoples are represented—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision—carrying from behind one garment of faith, that is, the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, already past. They do not look upon their father’s nakedness, because they do not consent to Christ’s death, and yet they honor it with a covering, as though knowing from whom they were born.

[Note: [Col. 0236D]

4. “Shem and Japheth, up to ‘looks toward the future.’” From *The City of God* XVI, chapter 2. GRIAL.]

4. Ham saw that nakedness—that is, Christ’s passion—and mocked it; and the Jews, seeing Christ’s death, jeered at it. But Shem and Japheth, like the two peoples believing from circumcision and uncircumcision, recognized their father’s nakedness, by which the Savior’s passion was signified. They took a garment, placed it upon their backs, and, looking away, covered their father’s nakedness; they did not see what they had covered out of reverence.

5. In a certain manner we cover Christ’s passion—that is, we honor it through the sacrament—and, understanding the reason for its mystery, we cover the Jews’ disparagement. The garment signifies the sacrament; the back signifies the memory of past things, because the Church celebrates Christ’s passion as having already taken place and does not yet look toward it as future.

[Note: [Col. 0236D]

6. “The middle brother, up to ‘according to the letter.’” From *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 23. GRIAL.]

6. The middle brother, Ham—that is, the impious Jewish people—is called “middle” because it neither held the primacy of the apostles nor was the last to believe among the gentiles. He saw his father’s nakedness because he consented to the death of the Lord and Savior. Afterward he reported it outside to his brothers. Through him what had been secret in prophecy was disclosed and, in a sense, made public. Therefore he becomes the servant of his brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0236D]

7. “After this the two are blessed … prophesy.” From chapter 24. Since all our manuscripts lack this passage, we think that the copyists were misled by the repeated beginning of the blessing. GRIAL.]

7. What else is that people today than a kind of archivist for Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony to the Church’s affirmation, so that we may honor through the sacrament what it announces through the letter? After this, those two who honored their father’s nakedness are blessed. “Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord God of Shem,” although he is also the Lord God of Israel for the gentiles themselves.

[Col. 0236B] 294

8. And how did this happen except through Japheth’s blessing? For among the people of the gentiles the Church occupied the whole world. This was foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.”

9. See how God enlarges Japheth and dwells in the tents of Shem, as Paul says: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2:19). “Blessed,” he says, “is the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.” This Shem, the elder by birth, is the one from whom the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles were born.

10. Japheth, however, is the father of the gentiles, because his name is also interpreted as “enlargement.” The people from the gentiles were enlarged through an immense multitude, and they were to dwell with the prophets and apostles. Indeed, in accordance with the prophetic blessing of Noah, their father, we have seen Japheth’s dwelling pass into the tent of Shem—that is, in the house of the Law and the Prophets, the Church is justified, lesser in time but greater by the law of grace.

[Note: [Col. 0236D]

11. “But Ham … what is their work?” From *The City of God* XVI, chapter 2. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The hearts of heretics burn.” So in Augustine. Our books have “beginnings.” GRIAL.]

11. Ham, moreover, whose name is interpreted as “hot,” the middle son, as though separated from both sides, neither remaining among the first fruits of the Israelites nor in the fullness of the gentiles, signifies not only the Jewish people but also the hot-headed class of heretics—not hot with the spirit of wisdom, but with impatience, by which the hearts of heretics commonly burn and disturb the peace of the saints.

[Col. 0236D]

12. All who boast of the Christian name yet live wickedly also seem to bear his figure. They announce Christ’s passion—which was signified by that man’s nakedness—by their good profession, but dishonor it by their evil conduct. For it is written of such people: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16). Therefore Ham is also cursed in his son, as in his fruit—that is, in his work. Accordingly, his son Canaan is interpreted as “their movement.” For what else is this than their work?

13. Moreover, the fact that Ham’s descendants are condemned when Ham sins signifies that the reprobate commit sin in the present, but receive the sentence of condemnation afterward—that is, in the future. So too the Jewish people, who crucified the Lord, transmitted the punishment of their condemnation even to their children. For they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

[Col. 0237B]  
[Note: [Col. 0237D]

14. “After the two sons had been blessed, up to ‘cursed’: Augustine’s words, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. “From whom seventy-two nations arose.” See the note on chapter 2 of Book IX of the *Etymologies*. GRIAL.]

14. After Noah’s two sons had been blessed and one of them, their middle brother, had been cursed, their descendants are then set out. From them seventy-two nations arose: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem.

## CHAPTER IX. The giant Nimrod and the confusion of languages

[Note: [Col. 0237D]

CHAP. IX. NOTE 1. “The first after the flood, up to ‘confusion’”: Jerome, commentary on Genesis, chapter 10. GRIAL.]

1. After the flood, Nimrod, the son of Cush, was the first among human beings to seize tyranny through a new desire for power. He reigned in Babylonia, which was called Babel after him because languages were confused there; the name is interpreted as “confusion.” The same Nimrod was the author of the tower’s construction. Because he attempted to penetrate the heights of heaven beyond the limits of his nature, he is not inappropriately compared with the devil, who, swelling with the thought of his heart, wished to exalt himself above the stars—that is, above the whole power of the angels—intending to make himself equal to God, while saying: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.”

[Note: [Col. 0237D]

2. “That he is called a hunter, up to ‘pride’: Augustine’s words, *The City of God* XVI, chapter 4. GRIAL.]

2. What is signified by his being called a hunter except the deceiver of earth-born souls, who captures human beings for death? His tower is the pride of this world, or the impious doctrines of heretics. After they have moved away from the East—that is, withdrawn from the true light—and come into the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking of teeth,” they immediately build a tower of their impiety against God and fabricate doctrines of pride with criminal audacity, wishing by illicit curiosity to penetrate the heights of heaven itself.

[Col. 0237D]

3. But just as those people were divided through pride from one language into many, so heretics, separated from the unity of faith by confusion, are also divided among themselves by the diversity of their error, as though by a discordance of language. [Col. 0238A] Those whom the destructive agreement of an exalted conspiracy arms against God are again divided, when discord among their doctrines intervenes and a sudden confusion arises.

[Note: [Col. 0237D]

4. “At that time, up to ‘the language remained’: the same chapter, section 11. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has *solo* in the text; this appears to be an obvious error. AREV.]

4. The Trinity itself condemns them, against which they offend; it itself scatters them when it says: “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages”—namely, in the diversity of error or of schisms. At that time, when the diversity of languages occurred, the language that had existed previously remained only in the house of Heber. Now also we recognize that only in the Church, which is the house of Christ, does the peace of confession and faith remain united, while all the reprobate are divided.

## CHAPTER X. Abraham’s departure from the Chaldeans

[Col. 0238B]  
[Note: [Col. 0238D]

CHAP. X. NOTE 1. “Who else, up to ‘among the gentiles,’ are Augustine’s words, *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 25. GRIAL.]

1. It remains to explain Abraham’s deeds and the things that the Lord had promised him. For the Lord said to him: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house.” Who else went out in Abraham from his land and his kindred, in order to become wealthy among foreigners and to become a great nation, except Christ, who, having left the land and kindred of the Jews, now, as we see, prevails among the gentiles?

[Note: [Col. 0238D]

2. Grialius and other printed editions have *operibusque*; the Albornozian manuscript has the better reading, *opibusque*. AREV.]

2. We too, following Christ’s example, must go out from our land—that is, from the resources of this world and earthly possessions—and from our kindred—that is, from our former way of life, habits, and vices, which, clinging to us from our birth, are joined to us as though by a kind of affinity and blood relationship—and from our father’s house, that is, from every memory of the world, so that, renouncing it, we may be enlarged among God’s people and, when the time comes, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

[Col. 0238C] 297  
[Note: [Col. 0238D]

3. “The two promises, up to ‘the kindreds of the earth’”: the same author, *The City of God* XVI, chapter 16. GRIAL.]

3. Two promises are given to Abraham. The first is that his seed will possess the land of Canaan, when God says: “Go into the land that I will show you, and I will make you a great nation.” The other is far greater: it concerns not carnal but spiritual offspring, through which he is the father not of one Israelite nation but of all the nations that follow the traces of his faith. This began to be promised in the words: “And all the kindreds of the earth will be blessed in you.”

[Col. 0238D]  
[Note: [Col. 0238D]

4. “Abraham’s departure, up to ‘the land itself’”: the same author, *The City of God* XVI, chapter 18. GRIAL.

Ibid. “He built an altar,” up to “blood”: the same author, chapter 19. GRIAL.]

4. Abraham departed from Harran and came to Shechem. After receiving a second oracle concerning the promise of that land, he built an altar. From there he moved on and lived in the wilderness; then, driven out by the scarcity caused by famine, he [Col. 0239A] went down into Egypt, where he said that his wife was his sister—not falsely, since she was related to him by blood.

[Note: [Col. 0239C]

5. “Whom Pharaoh nevertheless, up to ‘restored her’: the same author, *Against Faustus* XXII, chapter 33. GRIAL.

Ibid. The Vatican manuscript Reg. 293 adds after *restored her*, in the margin: “This, therefore … we shall explain”; and adds: “In Sarah the Church of Christ was represented, which the error of unbelief could not violate, because she is without stain or wrinkle. The portents by which Pharaoh was terrified are the power of miracles; when the world beholds them, it is confounded and amazed.” The Florentine manuscript 1 has the same. On Abimelech, see chapter 16. AREV.]

5. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, nevertheless wished to take her. He was terrified by the gravest portents and afflicted with many misfortunes on her account. When he learned by divine revelation that she was Abraham’s wife, he immediately restored her unharmed and with honor. When we begin to speak about Abimelech, we shall explain this.

## CHAPTER XI. Abraham’s victory and Melchizedek

[Note: [Col. 0239D]

CHAP. XI. NOTE 1. “When he returned, they were quarrelling”: the same author, chapter 20. GRIAL.

Ibid. “He remained as far as Mamre.” He stayed in another place in the same land, namely, beside the oak of Mamre. Augustine, chapter 22. GRIAL.]

1. When Abraham had returned from Egypt, from which he had come, Lot, his brother’s son, withdrew from him into the land of Sodom, preserving their affection and avoiding conflict, because they had become wealthy and their shepherds were quarrelling with one another. Abraham remained in the land of Canaan and lived beside the oak of Mamre.

[Col. 0239B] 298  
[Note: [Col. 0239D]

2. “Then from the five kings, up to ‘household servants’: Augustine, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has *vernulas* in the text and *vernaculos* in the note. Likewise immediately afterward, with *T* and with *T*. AREV.]

2. Then he rescued Lot, who had been captured by the five kings who had attacked Sodom, taking with him in battle three hundred and eighteen household servants. But what did Abraham’s victory over the five kings signify? He overcame them as the father of faith by means of a mystery. It signified that our faith, if it has been confirmed in the governing spirit, should subdue by the word of God the same number of bodily senses within us [perhaps, “subdues”]. For just as Abraham was victorious over the kings in close combat, so our faith, victorious through the soul, triumphs over the outward person.

[Note: [Col. 0240C]

3. “Whose figure is expressed by the letter T.” Augustine and Gregory repeat this several times. See below, on Judges 5. GRIAL.

Ibid. Prudentius elegantly developed this allegory. See my *Prudentiana*, p. 166. AREV.]

3. The fact that he defeated the hostile rulers not through a multitude or the strength of legions, but with only three hundred and eighteen companions, was already then imagined in the mystery of the cross, whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter Tau, which represents the number three hundred. It signified that Christ’s passion would free us from the dominion of the five bodily senses, which had previously overcome us by enslaving us through various vices.

4. As Abraham was returning from the slaughter of his enemies, Melchizedek immediately met him, king of Salem and priest of God, born of an unsearchable parentage. He blessed Abraham, offering bread and wine as a sacrifice to God. The apostle Paul, mentioning Melchizedek as without father and without mother, refers him figuratively to Christ (Heb. 7). He alone was born from a father without a mother according to divinity, and from a mother without a father according to humanity.

5. He is also the eternal priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). This is certainly because of the mystery of the sacrament that he commanded Christians to celebrate: not according to Aaron, with the victims of animals, but by offering as a sacrifice the offering of bread and wine—that is, the sacrament of his body and blood.

[Note: [Col. 0240D]

6. “Having uncircumcision”: several manuscripts and printed copies; not without merit. GRIAL.]

6. After the great patriarch had been blessed, he gave Melchizedek the priest a tenth of all his substance, knowing spiritually that a priesthood among the people of the gentiles would be better than the Levitical priesthood that was to arise from him in Israel. It was also to happen that the priesthood of the Church, possessing uncircumcision, would bless in circumcised Abraham the priesthood of the Synagogue. For the one who blesses is greater than the one who is blessed.

[Col. 0240B] 299  
[Note: [Col. 0240D]

7. The name Melchizedek itself means “king of peace” or “king of righteousness.” The word *Melchizedek* signifies only “king of righteousness.” But since he was also king of Salem, and Salem means “peace,” he appropriately joined the two meanings. GRIAL.]

7. Hence the priests born from Abraham’s seed also blessed their brothers—that is, the people of Israel—to whom those brothers gave tithes according to the commandment, truly treating them as their greater and more eminent superiors. The name Melchizedek itself is interpreted as “king of peace” or “king of righteousness,” which is rightly applied to Christ.

8. For he is the king of peace, because through him we are reconciled to God. He is the king of righteousness, because he will come to distinguish the saints from the impious. He is likewise both one priest and king, because he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for the redemption of all, and, as the true king, rules his people in the present age and will judge them in the future.

## CHAPTER XII. Abraham’s sacrifice and God’s promise

[Col. 0240C]

1. After this victory, the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision. He was anxious about his posterity and saw that no son was being born to him, yet he held fast to the promise made concerning his seed. Immediately a twofold promise of his offspring was made to him in a figure: it would become like the sand of the sea or like the multitude of the stars of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0240D]

CHAP. XII. NOTE 2. Among the letters of Paul Alvarus of Córdoba to Auderius Flavius Johannes, bishop of Seville, from the ninth century, published by Flórez in volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, letter 4, p. 114, this passage of Isidore is cited with some difference in wording: “Hear,” says Alvarus, “your Isidore saying: ‘I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven,’ that is, the Christian people … and he said: ‘So I will multiply your seed,’ that is, etc.” AREV.]

2. God brought Abraham outside and showed him the stars of heaven, saying: “So will I make your seed”—that is, the Christian people, whose father you remain in faith—“so will I make it shine with the light of the resurrection.” Then he [Col. 0241A] showed him the sand of the sea and said: “So will your seed be in multitude.” That is, the Jewish people will indeed be a numerous nation, but it will remain sterile and unfruitful, like the sand.

3. After this, when God promised him that he would become the possessor of the promised land, Abraham asked for a sign by which he might know [300] not as one doubting whether it would happen, but asking how it would happen.

4. The Lord offered him this likeness: “Take for me,” he said, “a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, together with a turtledove and a pigeon.” Abraham took all these, divided them down the middle, and placed the two parts opposite each other, but he did not divide the birds.

5. Birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. When the sun had gone down, terror fell upon Abraham, and a great, dark dread invaded him. A smoking furnace appeared, and a fire passed between the divided pieces. Then he was told: “Know by knowing that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own, and will serve and be afflicted,” and so forth. This, then, is the manner of Abraham’s promised seed, and this is its figure.

[Note: [Col. 0241D]

6. “Through the heifer, up to ‘are promised to Abraham’: Augustine, *The City of God* XVI, chapter 24. GRIAL.]

6. The people placed under the yoke of the Law were signified by the heifer. By the she-goat, that same people was signified as destined to become sinful. By the ram, that same people was signified as destined to reign. The animals are called three-year-old because, through the successive periods of time—from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, and from Abraham to David—that people grew to maturity as though passing through a third age.

[Col. 0241C]

7. The turtledove and the pigeon signify the spiritual people within that nation: the undivided sons of the promise and heirs of the future kingdom. Their temporal age is omitted because, meditating upon eternal things, they have gone beyond temporal desires. But what does it mean that those three animals are divided, with their parts set opposite one another, except that the carnal are divided among themselves, both in the ancient people and now?

8. The birds, however, are not divided because spiritual people are undivided. They do not contemplate schism and are not led astray by heretics; peace is always within them. Whether they withdraw from the crowds, like the turtledove, or live among them, like the pigeon, each bird is nevertheless simple and harmless. The birds of prey descending upon the divided bodies signify unclean spirits, seeking a kind of food for themselves in the division of the carnal.

[Note: [Col. 0241D]

9. “Signifies many.” All the manuscripts rightly have this. Augustine: “The fact that Abraham drove away the birds that settled upon them also signifies that, amid those carnal divisions, true believers will persevere to the end of the age.” The printed editions therefore erroneously have “none.” GRIAL.]

9. The fact that Abraham, sitting among them, drove them away signifies that, through the merits of the saints, many carnal people will be freed from distress at the end of the world. The fact that, around sunset, terror fell upon Abraham, together with a great and dark dread, signified the great disturbance that will come upon the saints from the Antichrist near the end of this age. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matt. 24:21).

10. The statement that follows—“When the sun had gone down, a dark gloom arose, and a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire appeared, passing between the divided pieces”—signifies the day of judgment that will come after the end of the world, when the peoples of the saints and of the wicked will be separated by fire. The statement made to Abraham—“Know by knowing that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own; they will reduce them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years”—was plainly prophesied concerning the people of Israel, who would serve in Egypt.

11. This does not mean that they served under the Egyptians for four hundred years, but that this number was completed in that affliction, being counted from the time when these promises were made to Abraham.

## CHAPTER XIII. Hagar and Abraham’s circumcision

[Note: [Col. 0242D]

CHAP. XIII. NOTE 1. On the reason why circumcision was instituted, compare the Apostolic Fathers, volume I, pp. 27 ff., with Cotelerius’s notes. AREV.]

1. Already then, because of the future sojourn, so that his seed would not mingle among the nations, circumcision was given to him as a sign in these words: “Every male among you shall be circumcised. An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you, whether native-born or purchased. But any male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant.”

[Note: [Col. 0242D]

2. “Here it is already declared, up to ‘resound with newness,’ from chapter 26. GRIAL.]

2. “Sarai shall no longer be called Sarai, but Sarah; and I will give you a son from her, and I will bless him, and he will become nations, and kings of nations will come from him.” Here the promise concerning the calling of the gentiles in Isaac, the son of promise, is already declared. Isaac signifies grace, not nature, because he was born from an aged father and a barren mother.

[Col. 0242C] 302

3. Because this was to come about not through the generation represented by Ishmael but through regeneration, circumcision was therefore commanded. The son promised from Sarah was a type of the Church, unlike Ishmael, who bears the type of the Jews. For what else does circumcision signify except nature renewed through baptism after the stripping away of the old person? And what is the eighth day except Christ, who, after the completed week—that is, after the Sabbath—rose again?

4. The command that not only sons but also slaves, native-born servants, and purchased servants should be circumcised testifies that the grace of redemption pertains to all. The names of the parents are changed so that everything may resound with newness. For Abram, as he was previously called, is interpreted as “exalted father.” Abraham, however, means “father of many nations,” by which it was foretold that many nations would follow the traces of his faith.

[Note: [Col. 0242D]

5. “The male who is not circumcised, up to ‘he himself sinned,’ from chapter 27. GRIAL.]

5. What, then, is meant by the statement: “The male who is not circumcised on the eighth day shall perish; that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant”? Why should the soul of an uncircumcised infant perish, when the infant itself has not broken God’s covenant, but those who neglected to circumcise it have done so? It is to signify that infants have destroyed God’s covenant not according to their own deed but according to their origin in the first human being, in whom all sinned.

6. Every person is born sinful—not personally, but originally (see the variant reading). Unless regeneration frees that person, the soul will perish from its people, because it broke God’s covenant when it too sinned originally in Adam.

## CHAPTER XIV. The three men who came to the oak of Mamre

1. Then the Lord appeared to Abraham as he sat in the valley of Mamre at the entrance of his tent. When he lifted his eyes, three men appeared standing near him. When he saw them, he bowed down and said: “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, let your feet be washed, and rest beneath the tree.”

2. Abraham went to Sarah and ordered her to make cakes baked under the ashes from three measures, which he set before them together with the calf that he had prepared, and likewise milk and butter. He himself stood beside them under the tree. When they had eaten, they said to him: “Where is Sarah, your wife?” He replied: “Look, she is in the tent.” He said to him: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, and Sarah your wife will have a son.”

3. When Sarah heard this, she laughed. It should be noted that Abraham bears a threefold figure in himself. First, he represents the Savior, when he left his kindred and came into this world; second, the Father, when he sacrificed his only son; third, in the figure he bears here, the saints who received Christ’s coming with joy.

4. Abraham’s tent was a type of earthly Jerusalem, where in the first age the prophets and apostles lived; where, when the Lord first came, he was received by believers and hung upon the wood by unbelievers.

5. In the three men who came to him, the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ was foretold, accompanied by two angels. Many understand these as Moses and Elijah: one the giver of the ancient Law, who through that same Law indicated the Lord’s coming; the other the one who will come at the end of the world to announce Christ’s second coming and to preach his Gospel to the Jews. Therefore, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, these two—Moses and Elijah—were seen by the apostles with him (Matt. 17).

6. The fact that Abraham, seeing three, worshiped one indicates the Lord and Savior, whose coming he also awaited, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Abraham longed to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56). Then he looked upon the mystery of the future sacrament.

[Col. 0244A]

7. Therefore he washed their feet, to demonstrate the future life-giving washing at the end of the world. For feet signify the last things. He also prepares a feast, namely, a fattened calf. This tender, fattened calf is the body of the Lord Jesus Christ. This is the Lord’s calf, sacrificed for the salvation of believers upon the tree of the cross. This is the calf of the Lord’s body, killed in the Gospel for the sinful son (Luke 15).

8. He also set butter and milk before them together with the calf’s flesh. The Apostle reminds us that milk represents the ancient Law when he says: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are still unable” (1 Cor. 3). He had handed on to them the commandment of the Law, like milk expressed from the breasts of the two tablets—that is, the covenant of faith.

9. For because of the infancy of their understanding they were not yet able to receive the solid and robust food of evangelical teaching. Butter, rich and very fatty, is the testimony of the Gospels, given to the faithful like oil as a sign. Abraham therefore set the calf with milk and butter before them to eat, because neither the Lord’s body, which is the calf, can exist without the milk of the Law, nor the milk of the Law without butter—that is, without the testimony of the Gospel.

10. The three measures from which Sarah made cakes baked under the ashes indicated the image of Noah’s three sons, from whom the whole human race was born. Believing in the divine Trinity, they were to be moistened through the water of baptism by the Church, of which Sarah was an image, and gathered into one bread, the body of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0243D]

CHAP. XIV. NOTE 11. *Languore* in the Complutensian edition and in Eucherius. GRIAL.

Ibid. *Vapore* should be retained instead of *calore*, *ardore*, or *igni*. Consult Prudentius, pp. 917 and 1035. AREV.]

11. These are the three measures that the woman in the Gospel is said to have leavened (Matt. 13; Luke 13). The loaves were unleavened because the unity of believers was to be without the leaven of malice, without the anguish of wickedness, and without the heat of perverse doctrine. They were baked under the ashes so that, through repentance for past sins, they might be cooked by the vapor of the Holy Spirit and become acceptable, like food pleasing to God.

12. Their sitting beneath the tree was a sign of the Lord’s passion, whose preachers they are. The fact that God promises a son to barren Sarah, saying, “At this time I will come,” does not refer to a period of time but to the character of his coming, when through the promised son a faithful people was to be born. For this is the barren Sarah to whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

[Note: [Col. 0243D]

13. Sarah’s laughter is not doubt. But Ambrose, *Letter* 30 of Book IV: “Sarah,” he says, “because she laughed, was convicted of unbelief.” And Augustine, *The City of God* XVI, chapter 31: “Although that laughter was also one of joy, nevertheless it was not the laughter of complete faith.” GRIAL.]

13. Sarah’s laughter is not doubt but prophecy. That laughter has a twofold significance: either that Christ would become laughter for unbelievers, or that he would laugh at all his enemies in his judgment. Therefore the one who was born from Sarah also received the name “laughter.” For Isaac is interpreted from the Hebrew language into Latin as “laughter.”

14. Then Isaac is again promised a future son who will become a great nation: “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.” In these words two things are historically promised to him: the Jewish nation according to the flesh, and all nations according to faith.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning Sodom, Lot, and his daughters

1. After this promise, Sodom is turned to ashes, while Lot and his daughters are delivered. But what does it mean that the Lord said the city would be saved if fifty righteous persons, down to ten, were found in Sodom? He set the number fifty as a sign of repentance, in case they should perhaps be converted and saved.

2. For the number fifty is always referred to repentance. Therefore David also composed a penitential psalm in that number. Accordingly, when God sees the life of sinners unwilling in any way to return to repentance, which the number fifty prefigures, he immediately restrains the ardor of immoderate lust with the fire of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0245D]

**Chapter XV, no. 3.** Others, perhaps more correctly, read “if in any one.” In Florentine Manuscript 1, *concrematuri* occurs instead of *concremandi*; this manner of expression likewise sometimes occurs in manuscript codices of the *Etymologies*, and also in some printed editions. AREV.]

3. But he said that Sodom would not perish if there were as many as ten righteous persons, as though the name of Christ were found in anyone through the observance of the Ten Commandments: that person would not perish. For the figure of the number ten demonstrates the cross of Christ. And the fact that there are five cities consumed by fiery rains signifies—unless I am mistaken—that all who have indulged lustfully in the five senses of their bodies will be burned in that future conflagration.

4. Lot himself, Abraham’s righteous and hospitable brother in Sodom, who deserved to escape safely from that conflagration, which was a likeness of the future judgment, bore the type of the body of Christ. This body now groans in all the saints amid the wicked and impious, does not consent to their deeds, and at the end of the age will be delivered from their company, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

5. His wife, however, represented the kind of people who, having been called by God’s grace, look back and strive to return to what they had left behind. Concerning them the Lord says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Hence she too is forbidden to look back, so that it might be shown that those who, having been regenerated by grace, desire to escape the final judgment must not return to their former life.

[Note: [Col. 0245D]

**6.** The words from “It should be noted, however, that Lot …” to “alien to the joy of eternal salvation” are Gregory’s, *Pastoral Care* III, chapter 28. GRIAL.]

6. But because she looked back and remained, having been changed into salt, she provides an example for seasoning the faithful, so that others may be salted by them. Christ himself did not keep silent about this, saying: “Remember Lot’s wife,” namely, so that he might season us like salt, so that we would not neglect things like fools but prudently take care. She also gave this warning when she was changed into a pillar of salt. It should be noted, however, that Lot, fleeing burning Sodom, came to Segor and did not climb into the mountains.

7. To flee burning Sodom means to avoid the fires of illicit fleshly desire or the desires of the world. The height of the mountains is the contemplation of the perfect. But since there are many righteous people who flee the allurements of the world yet, being engaged in active life, cannot ascend to the summit of contemplation, this is what is meant by Lot’s leaving Sodom but not reaching the mountains. Although a condemnable life has already been abandoned, the height of contemplation has not yet been grasped with subtle understanding.

8. Hence Lot says to the angel: “This city is nearby, to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not a little one, and shall my soul not live in it?” It is therefore called nearby, yet is said to be safe for salvation, because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor entirely alien to the joy of eternal salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0245D]

**9.** In Florentine Manuscript 2, *utor* is twice used with the accusative *eam*, as also happens not rarely in other works of Isidore. In Florentine Codex 2, after *legitime utatur*, this fragment is added: “We can understand pride and vainglory as the daughters of Lot. These two daughters follow those who have abandoned the incitements of the flesh and adhered to good works, because we are often proud of a good work and eagerly seek human praise. We must flee these daughters, because, if we do not flee them, they will make us drunk and cause us to beget sons, that is, evil works.” AREV.]

9. But in the very act of Lot, when his daughters lay with him, something other than what was signified when he was delivered from Sodom was represented. At that time Lot himself appeared to bear the person of the future Law. Certain people begotten from it and placed under the Law, by misunderstanding it, become drunk in a certain sense, and by using it unlawfully produce works of unbelief. “The law is good,” says the Apostle, “if one uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 1:8).

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Abimelech and Sarah

[Note: [Col. 0246D]

**Chapter XVI.** The whole chapter is from Book XXII of *Against Faustus*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “He kept Sarah silent … until her husband”: from chapter 33. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grial and others read *restauravit marito* (“restored to her husband”), but *restituit marito* (“returned her to her husband”), with the Albornoz Manuscript, is better. AREV.]

1. The history of Abimelech follows: Abraham concealed that Sarah was his wife and said that she was his sister, lest, after he was killed, she should be seized and held captive by foreigners. He was certain that God would not permit her to be violated, just as previously he had not permitted her to be violated by Pharaoh. Therefore Abimelech, warned in a dream, did not defile her by intercourse but returned her untouched to her husband.

[Note: [Col. 0246D]

**2.** “Who then … until ‘is fulfilled,’” from chapter 38. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Honor for honor”: Augustine. GRIAL.]

2. Nevertheless, I wish to know who was represented at that time in that man, and whose wife she is who, during this pilgrimage and among foreigners, is not allowed to be polluted and defiled, so that she may be without blemish or wrinkle for her husband. The Church lives rightly for the glory of Christ, so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, just as Abraham was honored among foreigners because of Sarah’s beauty.

[Note: [Col. 0247D]

**3.** The Vulgate has: “O most beautiful among women.” AREV.]

3. To that same one of whom it is said in the Song of Songs, “O beautiful among women” (Song of Songs 1:7), kings offer gifts because of the excellence of that beauty, just as King Abimelech offered gifts to Sarah, admiring in her above all the splendor of a form that he could love but could not violate. For the holy Church is also, in secret, the wife of our Lord Jesus Christ. Secretly, within the hidden spiritual recess, the human soul cleaves to the Word of God, so that “the two may be one flesh”; and the Apostle commends this mystery of the great marriage in Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5).

[Note: [Col. 0247D]

**4.** *Correptam* (“rebuked”). Others read *correctam* (“corrected”). GRIAL.]

4. Therefore the earthly kingdom of this age—which was represented by the kings who were not permitted to violate Sarah—did not experience or find the Church as Christ’s spouse until it attempted to violate her. For, by the divine testimony borne through the faith of the martyrs, it yielded; and in later kings it even honored with gifts the woman whom, in its earlier kings, it had been unable to subject to corruption.

[Note: [Col. 0247D]

**5.** “But when … until ‘who is in heaven,’” from chapter 39. GRIAL.]

5. For what was represented first and later in that same king is fulfilled first and later in this kingdom. When the Church is said to be Christ’s sister by the father, not by the mother, the kinship being commended is not that of earthly generation, which will be abolished, but of heavenly grace, which will remain forever. According to this grace we shall not be a mortal race; having received power, we are called, and are, children of God. For we received this grace not from the Synagogue, the mother of Christ according to the flesh, but from God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0247D]

**6.** “But when the Church … until ‘theirs,’” from chapter 40. GRIAL.

Ibid. The Vulgate has: “And do not call anyone on earth your father.” AREV.]

6. Christ taught us to deny, not acknowledge, this earthly kinship when he called us into another life, where no one dies, saying to the disciples: “Do not call anyone on earth your father, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9). But why it is concealed from foreigners whose wife the Church is, while it is not concealed whose sister she is, is not immediately easy to explain. It is hidden and difficult to understand how the human soul is joined or united to the Word of God—or whatever better and more suitable expression may be used—since the one is God and the other a creature. In this respect Christ and the Church are called bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife.

[Note: [Col. 0248D]

**7.** *Capacius* (“more fully”). Augustine and Bede; others read *cautius* (“more cautiously”). GRIAL.]

7. By what relationship Christ and all the saints are brothers—by divine grace, not earthly blood relationship, that is, from the father and not from the mother—is expressed more fully and heard more comprehensibly. For all the saints are brothers to one another through the same grace, but among their company none of them is the bridegroom.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Isaac and Hagar

[Note: [Col. 0248D]

**Chapter XVII, no. 1.** The Vulgate has: “Cast out this slave woman.” AREV.]

1. Abraham, therefore, when he was a hundred years old, begot from his wife Sarah a son whom he called Isaac. When his mother saw him playing with Ishmael, she said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” It must therefore now be asked why Sarah earlier wished her husband to receive a son from the slave woman, or why she now orders that woman to be expelled from the house with her son. She did not do this because she was inflamed by jealousy, but because she was compelled by the prophetic mystery. For Hagar, as the Apostle says, gave birth to a carnal people in slavery.

2. But Sarah, who was free, gave birth to a people who are not according to the flesh but were called into freedom—the freedom with which Christ freed them. By this mystery it was prefigured that the former people, generated in the slavery of sins in Sarah’s house, that is, in the Church, would not remain forever, nor be heirs or companions of the worshipers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory with the noble son, that is, with the faithful people.

3. When Abraham therefore cast Hagar out of the house, he took bread and a skin of water, gave them to Hagar, placed the child upon her shoulders, and sent her away. As Hagar went out, she wandered in the wilderness; and when she had cast her son beneath a tree because he was dying of thirst, the angel of the Lord appeared to her, showed her a spring of water, and she gave her son drink. What, then, does it signify that, as Hagar went out, she placed the child upon her shoulders? Nothing other than that the sinful and foolish people burdened the neck of their mother, the Synagogue, when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25). The bread indicated that the old priesthood would carry with it the bread of the Presence, as it is written, and that these things would grow old.

4. The skin of water, which runs out, signified that the Jewish purification would fail, or their carnal doctrine, enclosed in a dead skin—that is, in the flesh of the old man condemned by the sentence of transgression—which neither provides refreshment nor satisfies thirst, but causes vomiting in tepid heat. The fact that Hagar wanders in the wilderness with her son signifies that the Synagogue, expelled from its land together with its people, wanders throughout the world without priesthood or sacrifice, wholly ignorant of the way that is Christ. The fact that her son perishes from thirst shows that the people have no spiritual purification.

[Note: [Col. 0248D]

**5.** These are John’s words: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” AREV.]

5. But the fact that she cast her son, dying of thirst, beneath a tree and then, when the angel showed her the spring, saw it, signified that certain people from that nation would seek refuge under the shadow of the wood of the cross. The boy cried out weeping, and God heard him; then, when the angel showed her the spring, she saw it. This is said on behalf of those who are converted from the Jews to Christ: weeping over the errors into which they had been driven, they are heard, and with the eyes of their heart opened they see the spring of living water, that is, Christ the Son of God, who says: “I am the spring of living water; let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 7:37). Hence Ishmael is interpreted as “hearing” or “exaudition.”

6. This angel is a likeness of Elijah, through whom this people will come to faith, as it is said through Malachi: “Behold, I send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.” But the fact that the angel of the Lord immediately called Hagar, saying, “Arise, take the boy, for I will make him into a great nation,” signified either that the numerous Jewish people would reign forever, or that those among them who believed in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0249D]

**7.** “The Son of God.” The same author, Book I *Against the Jews*, chapters 1 and 3. GRIAL.]

7. Since Scripture first foretells that the same angel who speaks to Hagar is an angel and then calls him God, he must be believed to have been the Son of God, who always spoke through the Law and the Prophets. He is called an angel because of his obedience to the Father’s will, but God according to the nature of the Father, because he too is truly God, just as the Father is.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Abraham’s offering of his son

311 [Col. 0249C]

[Note: [Col. 0249D]

**Chapter XVIII, no. 1.** “He carried the wood.” The following words found in printed editions—“Who else is meant in Isaac, who carried the wood for himself to the sacrifice, except Christ Jesus, who himself carried the cross for his passion?”—and shortly afterward, “Who else was the ram to be sacrificed, caught by its horns in the thicket, except the one who was to be offered for us, fastened to the gallows of the cross?”—are indeed Augustine’s words, *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 25, but they are rightly absent from the better manuscripts. They do not belong to this passage; and Isidore will say nearly the same thing about this shortly afterward. GRIAL.]

1. Abraham is then commanded to sacrifice his only son. Obeying God, he fulfilled his vow: he saddled the donkey, laid on the wood, sent the servants far away, and ascended alone with his son; on the third day he reached the place. Before the son arrived at the place of sacrifice, he carried the wood on which he himself was to be sacrificed.

[Note: [Col. 0250D]

**2.** The Vulgate has *arenam*, “sand,” namely, “which is on the shore of the sea.” AREV.]

2. Then Abraham armed himself with a sword, and when he was already almost striking, he was instructed to spare the boy. Yet he did not depart without sacrifice or the shedding of blood. For a ram appeared caught by its horns in a thicket; it was sacrificed, and the sacrifice was completed. After the sacrifice had been completed, Abraham was told: “I will bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea. Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed, because you obeyed my voice.”

[Note: [Col. 0250D]

**3.** “Come now, let us see … until ‘the person of God the Father,’ and other passages,” excerpted from Augustine’s sermon 71 *On the Season*. GRIAL.]

3. Come now, let us see what mystery lies hidden beneath this sacrament. For when Abraham led his only son to be sacrificed, he bore the person of God the Father. But what does it mean that the old man received him? God does not grow old; rather, the very prophecy concerning Christ had already become old, in a certain sense, when Christ was born.

4. It began with Adam, when it was said: “The two shall be one flesh.” That great mystery in Christ and the Church was completed in the sixth age of the world. This age was signified by Abraham’s old age, because the mystery of God had already existed for a long time. Sarah’s old age also signifies the same thing in the people of God, that is, in the multitude of the prophets, because at the end of time Christ was born from that people of holy souls.

5. Her barrenness indicates that in this age we have been saved by hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born. The Church brought forth this birth at the end of time by the marvelous grace of God, not by natural fertility. We must now examine what the sacrament of the following history figuratively foretold. Who, then, as was predicted, was represented in Abraham through that sacrifice, except the exalted Father? Who in Isaac, except Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0250D]

**6.** “And just as Isaac … until the place of sacrifice.” From the same sermon. GRIAL.]

6. For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so God the Father handed over his only Son for us all. And just as Isaac himself carried the wood upon which he was to be placed, so Christ carried upon his shoulders the wood of the cross on which he was to be crucified. The two servants who were dismissed and not brought to the place of sacrifice represented the Jews. Living as slaves and thinking according to the flesh, they did not understand Christ’s humility or Christ’s passion; therefore they did not reach the place of sacrifice.

7. Why two servants, except because that people was to be divided into two parts? This happened when Solomon sinned, when the same people was divided with respect to the kingdom, not through an error of impiety. To them the prophet also frequently says: “Israel is rebellious, and Judah is transgressing” (Jeremiah 3:6–7). The donkey was the senseless foolishness of the Jews. This senseless foolishness carried all the mysteries, yet did not know what it was carrying.

[Note: [Col. 0250D]

**8.** The Vulgate has: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter.” AREV.]

8.
