Now, concerning what was said to them—“Wait here with the donkey; after we have worshiped, we shall return to you”—hear the Apostle saying: “Blindness in part has happened in Israel” (Romans 11:25). What does “Wait here with the donkey” mean? “Until,” he says, “the fullness of the nations should enter”; that is, after we have worshiped, when the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been completed and preached among the nations—this is what it means, “until the fullness of the nations should enter.”

9. What does “We shall return to you” mean? “And thus all Israel would be saved.” The three days in which they came to the place of sacrifice signify three ages of the world: one before the Law, another under the Law, and a third under grace. Before the Law extends from Abraham to Moses; under the Law, from Moses to John; from there onward, to the Lord. Whatever remains is the third day, the day of grace. In this third age, as after three days, the sacrament of Christ’s sacrifice was completed.

10. Then Isaac, with his feet bound, is placed upon the altar, and the Lord is suspended on the wood and fastened to the cross. But what was prefigured in Isaac was transferred to the ram. Why, except because Christ is a sheep? He is himself son and himself lamb: son because he was born, ram because he was sacrificed. But what does it mean that the ram was caught in the thicket? The cross has horns, for two pieces of wood are joined together so that they form the shape of a cross.

[Note: [Col. 0251D]

**11.** “Horns are in his hands.” Thus in the oldest Vatican Codex: *κέρατα ἐν χερσὶν αὐτοῦ ὑπάρχει*—“horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3). GRIAL.]

11. Hence it is written concerning him: “Horns are in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4). The ram caught by its horns therefore signified the crucified Lord. The thicket consists of thorns. Thorns signify the wicked and sinners who hung the Lord on the cross. Thus the Lord was suspended among the thorns—that is, among the sinful Jews—as he says through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.” Others understood this ram, bound by its horns in the thicket, as the same Christ, crowned with thorns by the Jews before he was sacrificed.

[Note: [Col. 0251D]

**12.** “When the sacrifice had been completed … until ‘he will rule the nations’”: words of Augustine, sermon 72 *On the Season*. GRIAL.

Ibid. The Vulgate has: “They will remember and turn to the Lord … all the families of the nations, for the kingdom is the Lord’s,” and so forth. AREV.]

12. After the sacrifice had been completed, Abraham was told: “All the nations shall be blessed in your seed.” For when did this happen, except when that ram says: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm 21:17, 28)? When this happened, the sacrifice in the Psalms took place. Then in that same psalm it was said: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations.”

13. After Abraham had sacrificed the ram in place of his son Isaac, he called the name of that place “The Lord sees,” which means “The Lord caused himself to be seen,” certainly through the Incarnation. Then Sarah died in the hundred and twentieth year of her life, and Abraham bought a field from Ephron and buried her. But what does it mean that Sarah was buried in a double tomb, except that the soul which dies to the world in order to live for God is received into the twofold rest of life, namely, the practice of good works and contemplation of the Divinity?

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Isaac and Rebekah

[Col. 0252A]

1. Abraham was old and advanced in years. He said to his senior servant, who was in charge of all that he had: “Place your hand under my thigh, so that I may bind you by an oath before the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, but that you will go to my land and my kindred and take a wife from there for my son Isaac.”

[Note: [Col. 0251D]

**Chapter XIX, no. 2.** “What does this mean … until ‘God of heaven’”: words of Augustine, *City of God* XVI, chapter 33. GRIAL.]

2. But what does it mean that Abraham, asking his servant to give an oath-bound pledge of faithfulness, said: “Place your hand under my thigh, and I bind you by an oath before the God of heaven”? What does the God of heaven have to do with Abraham’s thigh, except that a mystery is being disclosed? For by the thigh, descent is understood. What, then, was that oath except a sign that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from Abraham’s descendants?

[Note: [Col. 0252D]

**3.** “And there worshiping” instead of “and he worshiped there”; elsewhere also Isidore uses the nominative for an ablative absolute. AREV.]

3. This senior servant bore the image of the Law, through which the Church, Christ’s bride, was betrothed; he is called senior because of his antiquity. The servant therefore went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor, and stood near the spring, seeking a bride for his master’s son. So too the Law, which came after faith, came to the fountain of baptism; and there, worshiping, he encountered the virgin Rebekah, that is, the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0252D]

**4.** “She received,” and so forth. Thus the Albornoz Manuscript. Grial and others read: “She receives the ornaments of faith,” omitting the other words. AREV.]

4. Rebekah saw the servant, that is, the prophetic word; she lowered the water jar from her shoulder, namely, the elevated eloquence of the world, and inclined herself toward the humble prophetic word. From the servant she received a golden earring, that is, she accepted the ornaments of faith or of conduct; she received the golden meanings of Scripture and the clear eloquence of silver. Thus Rebekah followed the servant and came to Isaac. Following the prophetic word, the Church came to Christ.

315 [Note: [Col. 0252D]

**5.** “Yet she is led on the back of a camel … until ‘is confounded’”: words of Gregory, *Morals* I, chapter 7. GRIAL.]

5. Yet she is led on the back of a camel, because the Church, hastening to Christ from among the nations, is found amid the crooked and vicious ways of her former life. When she saw Isaac, she descended, because, once the Gentiles recognized God, they abandoned their vices and, turning away from the exaltation of pride, sought the path of true humility.

[Note: [Col. 0252D]

**6.** “But when he had bowed … until ‘and kingdom’”: from the same author, Book XXXV, chapter 11. GRIAL.

Ibid. Perhaps: “He went out into the field.” AREV.]

6. She also veiled herself modestly with a cloak, because in his presence she was ashamed of the errors of her former life. The fact that Isaac went out into the field when the day was already declining signified that, at the end of this world, as though at the close of the day, Christ would come and go out, as it were, into the field. Although invisible, he showed himself visible in this world to the Church coming from the nations.

7. The Church found him at the well of vision, that is, in the contemplation and understanding of truth, where she might receive a higher understanding, or the bath of water where she might be purified. Thereafter she is joined to her bridegroom Christ, clinging to him in glory, eternity, and kingdom.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Keturah, or Abraham’s death

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**Chapter XX.** The whole chapter is from *City of God* XVI, chapter 34. GRIAL.]

1. What does it mean that Abraham took Keturah as his wife after Sarah’s death? Was it because of incontinence, when he was already advanced in age? Far from it. It was for the procreation of children, since offspring like the stars of heaven had been promised to him through his son Isaac. What, then, does this Keturah mean except that, just as Hagar and Ishmael signified the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons signified heretics, who consider themselves to belong to the New Testament?

[Col. 0253B]

2. But both women are called concubines. Sarah alone is always called a wife, as it is written: “For my dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song of Songs 6:8). Abraham gave everything he possessed to his son Isaac, but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts and separated them from his son Isaac.

3. What does this mean except that certain gifts are given to the sons of the concubines, that is, to the carnal? But neither heretics nor Jews attain the promised kingdom, because they pursue carnal profits. There is no heir except Isaac, certainly because it is not the children of the flesh but the children of the promise who are reckoned as descendants. Then Abraham died at the age of 175 and was buried in a double cave, in the inner part of which Hebrew tradition testifies that Adam had been placed.

## CHAPTER XXI. That Isaac played with Rebekah

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**Chapter XXI.** The whole chapter is from Book XXII of *Against Faustus*, chapter 46. GRIAL.]

1. A famine then arose over the land, and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar, by the command and blessing of the Lord. There, for fear, he pretended that Rebekah his wife was his sister. The foreign king discovered that she was Isaac’s wife when he saw him playing with her.

2. But what does it mean, in the mystery of Christ and the Church, that so great a patriarch played with his wife, and that their marriage became known through this? Anyone who carefully examines this man’s secret in the holy Scriptures—so as not to sin against the Church by going astray in any matter—will surely see that he had for a little while concealed his majesty, by which, in the form of God, he is equal to the Father, in the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be capable of receiving him; and in this way he suitably adapted himself to his bride.

3. For what is absurd—or rather, what is not appropriately adapted to the foretelling of future things—if a prophet of God played at something bodily in order to capture his wife’s affection, since the very Word of God became flesh in order to dwell among us?

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the wells that Isaac dug

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**Chapter XXII, no. 1.** Everything up to “he changed” is from Origen, *Homily 13 on Genesis*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Into this torrent of Gerar.” “Into this land of Gerar.” Printed editions: “Into this valley of Gerar.” Rufinus. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Moses, who dug the well.” Thus the Albornoz Manuscript. Grial reads: “Moses dug the well.” AREV.]

1. After these things Scripture relates that, after the Lord had blessed Isaac and he had become exceedingly great, he undertook a task and began to dig the wells that the servants of his father Abraham had dug. But the Philistines, envying him, stopped them up by filling them with earth. Who is this Isaac except our Savior? When he descended into this torrent of Gerar, he first of all wished to dig those wells that his father’s servants had dug—that is, Moses, who had dug the well of the Law, and David, Solomon, and the Prophets, who wrote the books of the Old Testament—but which the earthly and filthy understanding of the Jews had filled.

[Note: [Col. 0254D]

**2.** “When Isaac wished to cleanse them.” *Quam cum vellet* (“when he wished to cleanse it”), as in Rufinus, so that the reference is to understanding. GRIAL.]

2. When Isaac, that is, our Lord and Savior, wished to cleanse these wells, to show that whatever the Law and the Prophets said, they said about him, the Philistines quarreled with him—that is, the Jews, alienated from the kingdom of God—and he departed from them. He cannot be with those who do not wish to have water in the wells but earth. And he says to them: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate.”

3. Isaac therefore dug a new well—or rather, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Peter, James, Jude, and the apostle Paul. They all dug the well of the New Testament and found living water, which is a spring of water leaping up into eternal life. But those who think in earthly terms still quarrel over these things; they neither allow the new to be established nor permit the old to be purified. They oppose the Gospel wells and resist the apostolic wells. And because they oppose everything and quarrel over everything, it is said to them: “Because you have made yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, from now on we shall go to the nations.”

4. After this Isaac dug a third well and called the name of that place “Broadness,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and caused us to increase over the earth.” Isaac was truly enlarged and filled the whole earth with knowledge of the Trinity, and the Church established breadth throughout the world. Formerly God was known only in Judea, and he was named in Israel (Psalm 75); but now “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

[Col. 0254D]

5. For Isaac’s servants went out through the whole earth, dug wells, and showed living water to everyone, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But what does it mean that Isaac called the wells Abraham had opened by the same names his father had given them, except that Moses among us is still called Moses, and each prophet is called by his own name, so that the names of the wells are not changed? Christ did not change their names but their meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0255D]

**6.** “Isaac among foreign peoples … until ‘they thrust upon him’”: words of Gregory, *Morals* XXXI, chapter 13. GRIAL.

Ibid. “From exhausting the earth of the heart.” Thus Gregory has “to exhaust the inner parts of the heart”; the Vallicellian and Eucherius have “the earthly things of the heart.” Printed edition. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To dig the heart more diligently.” Thus Gregory. Others read “to pierce through”; and instead of *molestas* (“troublesome”), the Vallicellian has *congestas* (“heaped-up”). GRIAL.

Ibid. “They thrust thoughts upon him.” Thus Gregory has “they plunge them in,” Book [uncertain]; and so does Eucherius. GRIAL.]

6. These things are mystical. Morally, however, Isaac is described as digging wells among a foreign people, by which example we learn that, placed in the hardship of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts. Until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry must not grow sluggish in exhausting the earth of the heart. Yet the allophyli—that is, unclean spirits lying in wait—fill these wells, because unclean spirits, when they see us digging into the heart more diligently, thrust troublesome thoughts of temptations upon us.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Esau and Jacob

[Col. 0255B]

1. Isaac therefore pleaded with the Lord on behalf of his wife, who was barren, and the Lord granted what he asked. Twins struggled within her, enclosed in the narrowness of the womb. When she was distressed, she inquired of the Lord and received this answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.” This was fulfilled figuratively, and even the unbelieving Jews know how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and how the Jewish people, greater in time, serves the smaller people of the Christians.

2. Indeed, this can also be said of each of us: there are two nations and two peoples within us, namely, of vices and virtues. One is smaller and the other larger. For there are always more wicked than good people, and vices are more numerous than virtues. Nevertheless, in us also, by God’s grace, one people overcomes the other, and the larger serves the smaller. The flesh serves the spirit, and vices yield to virtues. Esau then emerged first, red and entirely hairy, as though covered with bristles.

3. Afterward his brother Jacob came out, and his hand was grasping Esau’s heel. But why was he entirely red and bristling with hair, except because the former people was stained with the blood of the Prophets and of Christ, and surrounded by the filth of sin and wickedness? His younger brother therefore held his heel because, mystically, the younger people was destined to overcome the elder people.

[Note: [Col. 0256D]

**Chapter XXIII, no. 4.** The birthright itself was the priestly garment, according to Jerome’s Hebrew traditions concerning this passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. The Vulgate has: “The one who produces its fruit.” AREV.]

4. The fact that this Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food, and afterward was deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him, signifies that same Israelite people, which, as the Book of Exodus indicates, was called the firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). Because of the profits of the present age, it not only lost the honor of its primacy but also failed to obtain the reward of the heavenly kingdom prepared for it, as though the Lord reproached it when he said: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matthew 21:43). The birthright itself was the priestly garment, which the elder sons, clothed in it with their father’s blessing, wore when they offered victims to God like high priests.

[Note: [Col. 0256D]

5. Jerome replied; Epistle 125, question 3. He explained it, according to Bede. GRIAL.]

5. By this gift they—the Jews—were deprived of the desire for earthly love together with the glory of the future kingdom. Next follows the blessing itself given to Jacob. What this blessing nevertheless indicated figuratively must be set forth here in the words of the martyr Hippolytus, as Jerome reproduced them because of their outstanding learning and doctrine. Isaac, he says, bears the image of God the Father; Rebekah, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the earlier people and of the devil; Jacob, of the Church or of Christ. Isaac’s growing old indicates the consummation of the world; his eyes becoming dim signifies that faith had perished from the world and that the light of religion had been neglected before him.

6. That the elder son is called indicates the Jews’ reception of the Law. That his father loves his foods and his captures signifies people rescued from error, whom every righteous person hunts through teaching. The utterance of God’s blessing is the promised blessing and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath. Rebekah, full of the Holy Spirit and knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that the elder would serve the younger—more especially represents the form of the Holy Spirit, who knew beforehand what would occur in Christ and first contemplated it in Jacob.

7. She speaks to the younger son: “Go to the flock and bring me from there two kids,” prefiguring the Savior’s coming in the flesh, in which he would especially liberate those held liable to sins. For throughout the Scriptures kids are understood as sinners. That he is ordered to bring two signifies the taking up of two peoples.

8. That they are tender and good signifies teachable and innocent dispositions. Esau’s garment signifies the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, which were first given to them, and with which the people of the Gentiles were afterward clothed. The skins wrapped around his arms signify the sins of both peoples, which Christ fastened with himself to the cross in the extension of his hands.

[Note: [Col. 0256D]

9. “Behold the fragrance” through “he will be saved” are words of Augustine, *City of God* XVI, chapter 37, though some things have been altered. GRIAL.]

9. That Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly expresses amazement at the swift faith of believers. That pleasing foods are offered signifies a sacrifice pleasing to God, the salvation of sinners. That the blessing follows the eating, and that he enjoys its fragrance, openly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the kingdom. For he is blessed in this manner: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.” The fragrance of Christ’s name fills the world like a field; his blessing comes from the dew of heaven, that is, from the rain of divine words.

[Col. 0257A] [Note: [Col. 0257D]

10. “The multitude of grain,” *πλῆθος σίτου καὶ οἴνου* [“the multitude of grain and wine”], in the Septuagint. The Vulgate says “abundance.” But it is remarkable that “abundance” is read in Ambrose, *On Jacob*, although we read “multitude” in Augustine. The two seem to have used the same translation. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Which he gathers,” so Augustine and the printed editions. “Which gathers,” the manuscripts, incorrectly; for the multitude is gathered through communion in the Eucharist.

Ibid. “The sons of his mother,” from the Vulgate. “Of his father,” Augustine, from the Septuagint. GRIAL.]

10. “And from the fatness of the earth,” that is, from the gathering of the peoples. “The multitude of grain and wine,” that is, the multitude that is gathered through grain and wine in the sacrament of his body and blood. The peoples converted to him from all the nations serve him. The tribes adore him, that is, the peoples believing from circumcision. He is the Lord of his brothers, because he rules over the Jewish people. His mother’s sons adore him, because he too was born from her according to the flesh. Whoever curses him will be accursed, and whoever blesses him will be filled with blessings.

[Note: [Col. 0257D]

11. “From the mouth of the people who do not know the Father,” from the printed edition and Augustine. “From the mouth of the Father,” the manuscripts. GRIAL.

[Col. 0258D] Ibid. “When the elder repeated his request,” from Augustine and the printed edition. “When he asked,” the manuscripts. GRIAL.]

11. Christ, I say, our Christ, is blessed from the mouth of the people who do not know the Father, that is, he is truly proclaimed. But another is thought to be blessed by the Jews, the one whom they, in their error, await. When the elder repeated the promised blessing, Isaac was terrified and recognized that he had blessed one person in place of another; yet he was not indignant when the mystery was revealed to him, but confirmed the blessing upon his son, saying: “I have blessed him, and he is blessed.”

[Note: [Col. 0258D]

12. “But the elder also,” through “he will be saved,” are Jerome’s words, in the same place. GRIAL.]

12. This is Isaac’s first blessing, given to the younger people, the Christians. Yet it is not established that the elder son was wholly despised, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” The prophecy of his second blessing is as follows: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be”; and “in the fatness of the earth,” that is, in the fertility of resources and the power of the kingdom that existed among that people; and “in the dew of heaven shall your blessing be,” that is, in the utterances of God.

[Note: [Col. 0258D]

13. “Servant of the younger people”; another reading, “you shall serve the younger people.” GRIAL.]

13. For to them first were entrusted the utterances of God and the covenants of the Law. “You shall live by the sword,” that is, because this people, devoted to bloodshed, inflicted death upon Christ and the prophets. “And you shall serve your brother,” namely, the younger Christian people. A time will come when you will shake off and loosen the yoke from your neck, when, through knowledge of the faith, you have turned to the grace of Christ and laid down the burden of the Law; then you will no longer be the servant of the younger people, but will be called their brother through faith.

[Note: [Col. 0258D]

14. Grial reads, incorrectly, “not only the Lord to the gallows.” AREV.]

14. Accordingly, after his father’s blessing, Esau, stirred by the goads of envy, deceitfully devises the murder of his brother Jacob. The Jewish people likewise premeditated this against Christ: it not only handed the Lord over to the gallows of the cross, but also persecuted those who believed in him even to the shedding of blood. Jacob, fleeing his brother’s treachery, left his homeland and his parents and went to a distant region to take a wife.

15. In the same way Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people of Israel—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem—and all the regions of Judea, went to the Gentiles and took the Church from them, so that what had been said might be fulfilled: “I will call the people that was not my people, my people, and her that was not beloved, beloved. And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the Ladder Jacob Saw in a Vision

1. As Jacob was going to Mesopotamia, he came to the place now called Bethlehem and placed a large stone beneath his head. While sleeping, he saw a ladder set up and resting upon heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending. When he saw this, he awoke and anointed the stone, saying: “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.” After he had said these things, sleep departed.

[Note: [Col. 0258D]

CHAPTER XXIV, no. 2. “This sleep of Jacob” through “announce temperately” comes from Book XII *Against Faustus*, chapter 26, or Sermon 79 *On Time*; the wording is the same in both places. GRIAL.]

2. This sleep of Jacob is the death or passion of Christ. The stone at his head, which is in a certain sense expressly called anointed, signifies Christ; for Christ is the head of a man. Who does not know that Christ is named from anointing? The house of God is so called because Christ was born there, in Bethlehem. The gate of heaven is so called because there he descended to earth and from there ascended again to heaven. The raising up of the stone is the resurrection of Christ.

3. Moreover, the ladder is Christ, who said: “I am the way.” Through it the angels ascend and descend; by these the evangelists and preachers of Christ are signified. They ascend when, in order to understand his supremely exalted divinity, they rise above the whole of creation, so that they may find him in the beginning as the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made.

4. They descend when they find him made from a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law. On that ladder, from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit, those who are carnal become spiritual by making progress, as though ascending; and the spiritual themselves descend in a certain manner to nourish them with milk, when they cannot speak to them as to spiritual people, but only as to carnal people.

5. He is above in his head; he is below in his body, which is the Church. We therefore understand him as the ladder, because he said: “I am the way.” One ascends to him in order that he may be understood in the heights. One descends to him in order that the little one may be nourished in his members. Through him people raise themselves up so that they may look upon him in a lofty manner. Through him they also humble themselves so that they may proclaim him loftily and temperately.

[Note: [Col. 0259D]

6. In the Vulgate, “he will set the sheep.” Some printed editions likewise have this reading. AREV.]

6. After this vision, as Jacob was traveling from that place, he saw sheep, shepherds, a well of living water, and a large stone placed over the well. Figuratively, the peoples of the righteous were signified by the sheep, as in the Gospel saying: “He will set the sheep on his right” (Matthew 25:33).

[Note: [Col. 0259D]

7. In the Alb[orn] manuscript there is *obtectae* [“covered”], so that the Gentiles may be understood as covered. AREV.]

7. The shepherds are the prophets, who, cleansed by the Holy Spirit until the Lord’s coming, governed the people of Israel by preaching instruction. The stone placed over the well prefigured the Lord. The well prefigured the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was to come through Christ’s preaching to the Church from the Gentiles, who were covered because Christ had not yet come and become human.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning Leah, Rachel, and the Two Maidservants

1. Jacob, therefore, going to Mesopotamia, took two wives, the daughters of Laban, Rebekah’s brother. First Leah, and second Rachel. From there he took for himself Leah’s maidservant, named Zilpah, and Rachel’s maidservant, Bilhah. From these four women he fathered twelve sons and one daughter. By Leah he fathered Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. By Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin. By Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, Dan and Naphtali. By Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, Gad and Asher.

324 [Note: [Col. 0259D]

CHAPTER XXV, no. 2. From here through Victorinus’s interpretation, all the discussion of what the four wives of Jacob prefigured is Augustine’s, *Against Faustus* XXII, from chapter 51 through chapter 38. GRIAL.]

2. These are the twelve sons of Israel. Let us now investigate what realities Jacob’s four wives prefigured, two of whom were free women and two maidservants. We see the Apostle understand, in the free woman and the maidservant whom Abraham had, the two Testaments; but there, because there is one of each, what is being said appears more readily. Here, however, there are two and two.

[Col. 0259C] [Note: [Col. 0259D]

3. The interpretation of Leah and Rachel as the two lives is explained at length in the *Book of Differences of Things*, difference 34: “Between the active and contemplative life.” AREV.]

3. Furthermore, there the son of the maidservant is disinherited, whereas here the sons of the maidservants receive the promised land together with the sons of the free women. Hence something else is undoubtedly signified here. For although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to pertain to the New Testament, into whose freedom we have been called, they are not two without reason, unless because two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0259D]

4. In Florentine Codex 1, after “we contemplate” much additional material is found, which in our edition is placed at the end of the questions on Genesis, namely: “Then some ask” through “upon all flesh.” AREV.]

4. One is temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we contemplate the delight of God. Leah is interpreted as “the laboring one,” while Rachel is “the beginning seen,” or “the word.” The activity of this life, in which we live by faith, is laborious in works and uncertain as to the outcome by which it will reach the benefit of those for whom we wish to care.

[Col. 0259D] [Note: [Col. 0259D]

5. Isaiah: “Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be whitened like snow.” *Coccus*, *coccinum*, and *coccineus* designate a purple-red color, which is also called Phoenician; for *phoenix* sometimes signifies red. AREV.]

5. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife, and for that reason she is also said to have had weak eyes. “The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our providence is uncertain.” The hope of eternal contemplation of God, possessing a certain understanding of truth, is Rachel. Hence she is also called “beautiful in face and lovely in appearance” (Isaiah 1:18). Every devout and earnest person loves her and serves the grace of God for her sake. Through that grace, our sins, even if they are like *phoenicium* [scarlet], will be whitened like snow.

[Note: [Col. 0260D]

6. “For no one turns himself.” Thus Augustine. “He submits,” Valerius. GRIAL.]

6. Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Jacob served him for Rachel; for no one turns himself to serve righteousness under the grace of the remission of sins except in order to live peacefully in the Word from whom the Beginning that is God is seen.

7. Therefore one serves for Rachel, not for Leah. For who would ever love the labor of actions and sufferings in works of righteousness? Who would seek that life for its own sake, just as Jacob did not seek Leah? Yet he embraced her when she was substituted for him by night, for the purpose of begetting, and experienced her fertility. The Lord made her bearable first, because she could not be loved for her own sake, so that Rachel might be reached.

[Note: [Col. 0260D]

8. “Loving something else in his way of life.” Thus one manuscript. “In his conversion,” Augustine. GRIAL.]

8. Then he commended her on account of her children. Thus every useful servant of God, established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, loving something else in his way of life, meditates on nothing but the teaching of wisdom. Many think they will obtain it as soon as they have exercised themselves in the seven commandments of the Law, which concern love of one’s neighbor, so that no one is harmed: “Honor your father and your mother”; “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not kill”; “You shall not steal”; “You shall not bear false witness”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.”

[Note: [Col. 0260D]

9. “The night of the world.” “Nights,” Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The unexpected Leah,” Augustine. “Of the unexpected Leah,” in Eucherius and the manuscripts. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Merciful and pure in heart.” Thus Augustine, elegantly. Others have “of a pure heart.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Pure in heart.” Likewise chapter 1 of the book *Against the Jews*: “impious, hard-hearted.” AREV.]

9. When these commandments have been observed, and after, through various temptations—as through the night of this age—the endurance of labor has clung to a person in place of the desired delight of teaching, Leah, as it were the unexpected one, is joined to him in place of Rachel. He endures her in order to reach Rachel, if he loves perseveringly, after receiving the other seven commandments—as though it were said: “Serve another seven years for Rachel,” so that he may be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and a peacemaker.

10. If it were possible, a person would wish to arrive immediately at the delights of beautiful contemplation without any endurance of labor, which must be embraced in acting and suffering. But this cannot happen in the land of the dying. This seems to be signified by what was said to Jacob: “It is not customary in this place for the younger to marry before the elder.”

326 [Note: [Col. 0261D]

11. “Therefore one must aim at the one thing, but for that reason many things must be endured.” Some manuscripts, from Augustine, read: “Therefore, in order to hold to the one thing, many things must be endured.” GRIAL.]

11. For she is not improperly called “elder” who is earlier in time. In human instruction, the labor of good work comes before the rest of contemplation. Therefore one must aim at the one thing, but for that reason many things must be endured. Thus Jacob has two free wives; both are daughters of the remission of sins, that is, of the whitening that is Laban.

12. Nevertheless, one is loved and the other endured. But the one who is endured is herself first and more abundantly made fruitful, so that, if not for her own sake, at least for the sake of her children, she may be loved. For the labors of the righteous bear their greatest fruit in those whom they beget for the kingdom of God by preaching the Gospel amid many temptations and tribulations. They call those for whom they endure greater labors, immeasurable blows, and frequent deaths—and for whom they have battles outside and fears within—their joy and their crown.

13. They are born more readily and abundantly from that word of faith by which they preach Christ crucified. Rachel, however, bright in appearance, rises beyond herself toward God and sees in the Beginning the Word, God with God. She wishes to give birth but cannot, because “who can recount his generation?” Therefore she desires the leisure of contemplation, so that she may behold the ineffable divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0261D]

14. “And of suffering,” from Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Toward that virtue,” from Augustine. Others have “life.” GRIAL.]

14. She wishes to be free from every occupation and is therefore barren, because she does not come to the aid of people amid various pressures. Yet because she too sometimes burns with the desire to beget—for she wishes to teach what she knows—she sees her sister rich in children through the labor of acting and suffering, and she grieves that people run rather toward that virtue by which their necessities are provided for than toward the one from which something divine is learned.

[Note: [Col. 0261D]

15. “In whatever way of thinking,” from Augustine and Eucherius. These two words are absent from some manuscripts. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To receive children.” Augustine has “children.” GRIAL.]

15. This grief appears to be represented in the statement that is written: “And Rachel envied her sister.” Therefore, because the pure spiritual understanding of a spiritual substance cannot be expressed in words formed from flesh, wisdom chooses to insinuate divine things for consideration, however inadequately, through every kind of bodily likeness. Thus Rachel chose to receive children from her husband by means of a maidservant rather than remain entirely without children.

327 16. Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, is interpreted as “aged.” From the old life devoted to carnal senses, bodily images are stirred up, even when something is heard about the spiritual and immutable substance of divinity. Leah also receives children from her maidservant, inflamed by the love of possessing a more numerous offspring.

17. We find that her maidservant Zilpah is interpreted as “open mouth”; therefore this maidservant represents those whose mouths gape in preaching the faith of the Gospel but whose hearts do not gape. Of them it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15). And of them the Apostle says: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Romans 2:21).

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

18. The meaning of Matthew’s and Paul’s words is expressed, although the actual wording differs somewhat. AREV.]

18. Nevertheless, so that through this condition the free wife, the laboring one, might also receive sons as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord says: “Do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3). Hence the Apostle says: “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice” (Philippians 1), as though she too rejoiced when the maidservant gave birth to a more numerous offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

19. “There is also a certain offspring of Leah,” from Augustine. “A certain affection,” the manuscripts. GRIAL.]

19. There is also a certain offspring of Leah produced through the favor of Rachel, when Rachel allowed her husband to sleep with Leah on the appointed night after receiving the mandrakes from Leah’s son. What should be said about the mandrake? I have found that it is a beautiful and sweet-smelling plant but tasteless in flavor. Therefore I understand that a good popular reputation is represented by the mandrake fruit. Hence the Apostle says: “He must also have a good testimony from those outside” (1 Timothy 3).

20. Although they have little taste, they nevertheless often bestow upon the labor of those through whom their welfare is provided both the splendor of praise and the fragrance of good reputation. The first members of the Church do not attain this popular glory unless they are engaged in the dangers and labor of action. Therefore Leah’s son found the mandrakes while going out into the field, that is, while walking honorably toward those who are outside.

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

21. “By acting and persuading.” Eucherius has “by acting and sweating.” GRIAL.]

21. That teaching of wisdom, however, which is furthest removed from the noise of the crowd and is fixed in the contemplation of truth with sweet delight, would not attain even this small measure of popular glory except through those who preside over peoples amid the crowds, acting and persuading—not in order to rule, but in order to benefit. For while these active and occupied people, through whom the welfare of the multitude is administered and whose authority is dear to the peoples, also bear witness to the more secluded life, because of the leisure devoted to seeking and contemplating truth, the mandrakes somehow come through Leah to Rachel; and to Leah herself they come through her firstborn son, that is, through the honor of her fertility, in which lies all the fruit of laborious action that is exposed to danger amid uncertain temptations.

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

22. “They are carried toward the embrace.” Thus Augustine. “They enjoy embraces,” Valerius and Eucherius. GRIAL.]

22. Many people endowed with good ability and burning with zeal, although they may be capable of governing peoples, nevertheless avoid it because of the turbulent occupations involved and are carried with their whole heart into the leisure of teaching, as into the embrace of beautiful Rachel.

[Col. 0263A] 23. But because it is good that this life too, becoming more widely known, should deserve popular glory, whereas it is unjust for it to obtain that glory if it keeps its lover, one suited and capable of administering ecclesiastical responsibilities, in leisure and does not devote him to the governance of the common good, Leah therefore says to her sister: “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband, but you also want to take my son’s mandrakes?”

24. By one husband she signifies all those who, although capable through the virtue of action and worthy to be entrusted with the governance of the Church for the administration of the mystery of faith, nevertheless, inflamed by zeal for teaching and for investigating and contemplating wisdom, remove themselves from all the burdens of action and wish to sit in the leisure of learning and teaching. Thus it is said: “Is it not enough that you have taken my husband, but you also want to take my son’s mandrakes?”—as though it were said: “Is it not enough that the life devoted to study keeps in leisure the people necessary for the labor of public affairs, but it also seeks popular glory?”

25. Therefore, so that she may obtain it justly, Rachel gives her husband to her sister for that night, so that those who are suited by laborious virtue to govern peoples, even if they have chosen to devote themselves to learning, may accept the experience of temptations and the burden of responsibilities for the common good. Otherwise the teaching of wisdom to which they had resolved to devote themselves might be blasphemed and might not gain a good reputation among inexperienced peoples—which is signified by those fruits and is necessary for the encouragement of learners.

[Note: [Col. 0263D]

26. “To avoid dutiful labor,” from Augustine and the printed edition. The manuscripts have “to flee the labor of duty,” less elegantly. GRIAL.]

26. But that they are plainly compelled by force to undertake this responsibility is also sufficiently signified by the fact that, when Jacob came from the field, Leah went out to meet him, detained him, and said: “You shall come in to me, for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes.” As though she were saying: “Do you wish to bestow a good reputation upon the teaching you love? Do not avoid dutiful labor.” Whoever observes that these things occur in the Church sees them, and we experience in examples what we understand in books.

27. Who does not see this happening throughout the whole world? People come from the works of the world and go into the leisure of knowing and contemplating truth, as into Rachel’s embrace; then they are intercepted by ecclesiastical necessity and appointed to labor, as though Leah were saying: “You shall come in to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0263D]

28. “Let them beget sons of faith,” Augustine and the printed edition. The manuscripts have “Let them beget sons of God.” GRIAL.

[Col. 0264D] Ibid. “By the peoples,” Augustine; “by the apostles,” the manuscripts.

Ibid. “For the ministry of governing the people.” Augustine and the printed edition have “for mercy.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “To which they had turned,” Augustine. Others have “to which she had turned.” GRIAL.]

28. While they chastely administer the mystery of God, let them beget sons of faith in the night of this age. Even that life is praised by the peoples, because of love for which they turned away and abandoned hope in the world, and from whose profession they were taken up into the ministry of governing the people. In all their labors they act so that the profession to which they had turned—because it gave such rulers to the peoples—may be glorified more broadly and more clearly, as though Jacob did not refuse Leah’s night, so that Rachel might enjoy fruits sweet-smelling and brightly shining.

29. Sometimes she herself also gives birth, through the mercy of God, by herself; only with difficulty at last, since it is exceedingly rare for “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and whatever is said piously and wisely about this matter, to be grasped even partially, safely, and without the phantom of carnal thought.

30. In another sense also, the martyr Victorinus and others have interpreted Leah and Rachel as representing the Church or the Synagogue. They think Leah, the elder, bears the type of the Synagogue, because she first bore God’s people. Indeed, she is also read as pregnant in her eyes, because the Law given through Moses is covered and sealed.

[Col. 0264B] 330 31. Rachel, however, younger and beautiful, barren at first and afterward fruitful, is a likeness of the Church. Younger, because later in time. Beautiful, because holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are lovely because they were found worthy to look upon the Gospel. She too remained barren for as long as the Synagogue was producing its people.

32. Why did Jacob serve for Rachel, while Leah the elder was substituted for her, unless because the Lord, in order to take the Church to himself, first joined the Synagogue to himself? Jacob’s service for seven years for the two wives therefore signifies the time of the present life, which revolves through seven days, in which the Lord took the form of a servant and became obedient to the Father’s will even unto death. He serves for sheep, and our Lord says: “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve.”

[Note: [Col. 0264D]

33. “Each one” seems preferable for retention, although some printed editions give “whoever”; *quisque* for *quisquis* is sufficiently customary. AREV.]

33. He fed sheep, and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd.” He took for himself, as the profit of his payment, a varied flock; Christ gathered to himself the diversity of the nations. He cut off the bark from three rods and placed them in the watering troughs, so that by looking at them his sheep might multiply. Our Lord likewise set before the faithful people, in the water of baptism, the names of the three Persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that whoever perceives this with a full heart may become a sheep of God.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Jacob’s Flight and Rachel, Who Stole Her Father’s Gods

[Col. 0264D]

1. After the long servitude that Jacob endured with his father-in-law for the sake of his wives, as though in payment, the Lord commanded him to return to his homeland. Then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hurried away with his wives and company. Laban, however, caught up with him on Mount Gilead in anger and searched for the idols that Rachel had stolen from him, but did not find them.

[Col. 0265A] [Note: [Col. 0265D]

CHAPTER XXVI, no. 2. “For Laban” through “it happened to me” are Gregory’s words, *Moralia* XXX, chapter 16. GRIAL.]

2. What this may signify figuratively must now be examined. 331 Although Laban had assumed another role above, here he represents the type of the devil. Laban is interpreted as “whitening.” Yet “whitening” is not inappropriately understood as the devil, who, although dark by merit, transforms himself into an angel of light.

3. Jacob served him—that is, the Jewish people, in part belonging to the reprobate—from whose flesh the incarnate Lord came. Laban may also represent this world, which pursues Jacob in anger, because it attempts to oppress by persecution each of the elect, who are members of our Redeemer. Jacob took away his daughter—that is, either the world’s or the devil’s daughter—when Christ joined the Church from the Gentiles to himself. He also drew her away from her father’s house, because through the prophet he says to her: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Psalm 44:11).

4. What else is represented by the idols except avarice? Hence Paul says: “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3). Therefore, when Laban came to Jacob, he did not find the idols, because, when the treasures of the world had been displayed, the devil found no trace of earthly desire in our Redeemer. But what Jacob did not possess, Rachel covered while sitting.

[Note: [Col. 0265D]

5. “To sit is.” Grial lacks *est* [“is”]. AREV.]

5. Rachel, who is called “sheep,” represents the Church. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance, as it is written: “Rise up after you have sat” (Psalm 126). Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vices of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Of this covering of vices the prophet says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31).

6. We are therefore represented by that Rachel who, by sitting, suppresses idols, if by repenting we condemn the guilt of avarice. This impurity of avarice certainly does not hinder those who run manfully, to whom it is said: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Psalm 26:14). Rather, it especially befalls those who, walking as though with effeminate steps, are weakened by the allurements of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0265D]

7. *Innotuit* [“became known”] is used actively for *notum fecit* [“made known”]. Isidore and some even earlier writers used *innotescere* actively. Although *inientes* [“entering”] can be accepted, as Grial prints it, I preferred to restore *ineuntes* [“entering into”] with Alborn. AREV.]

7. Hence the following words of that same Rachel occur there: “According to the custom of women, it has now happened to me”—that is, she made it known that she had what is like a woman’s condition. But after Laban had pursued Jacob, found him, and they had spoken with one another as they entered into a covenant, Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar, and said to his brothers: “Bring stones.”

[Col. 0266A] 8. They gathered them and made a mound, which Laban called “the mound of the witness,” while Jacob called it “the heap of testimony.” Among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone bears witness in the likeness of Christ, and the heap of stones is the multitude of believers.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning Jacob’s Wrestling with the Angel

[Note: [Col. 0266D]

CHAPTER XXVII, no. 1. “And behold, a man wrestled with him” through “they limped from their paths” comes from *City of God* XVI, chapter 39. See also Sermon 80 *On Time*. GRIAL.]

1. When these things had been completed, Jacob sent messengers to his brother Esau, and also sent gifts. After he had led all his people across the torrent, he himself remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him; Jacob prevailed against him and did not let him go until he had wrested a blessing from him and received the sacred name Israel.

2. In this, above all, the image of the Lord’s mystery was prefigured. For that man most clearly bore the type of Christ. Yet Jacob prevailed over him because he willed it, so that he might represent the mystery of Christ’s passion, in which Jacob, in the type of the Jews, appeared to have prevailed over God through the offspring of his body, and, as it were, to have engaged in wrestling with his flesh as with a weak opponent and grown strong in his passion, as it is written when they said: “Crucify, crucify.”

3. Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from the same angel whom he had overcome as victor. The imposition of his name was itself a blessing. Israel is interpreted as “seeing God,” which will be the final reward of the saints. The same angel then touched the breadth of his thigh and made him lame. Thus Jacob was one and the same person, both blessed and lame.

4. He was blessed in those from the same people who believed in Christ, and lame in the unbelievers. For the sinew or breadth of his thigh is the multitude of his lineage. There are many in his stock who, degenerating from the faith of their fathers and deviating from the commandments of their creator, limp along the paths of their error.

[Note: [Col. 0266D]

5. “After his strength had been taken away,” from the Palatine manuscript. Others have “after his sinews had been touched.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Let him recount.” Thus the old edition. Grial printed “he recounts.” AREV.]

5. Of them it was prophetically said: “And they limped from their paths.” Yet afterward that people, when its strength had been taken away, not only limps but also grows numb, so that it can no longer beget sons. Finally, when the same patriarch added that he had seen God face to face, although above he had said that a man had wrestled with him, this signifies that the same God was to become man, who would wrestle with Jacob’s people.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning Dinah, Rachel’s Childbirth, and Reuben’s Incest

[Col. 0266D] [Note: [Col. 0266D]

CHAPTER XXVIII, no. 1. “But what does it mean” through “also rejoices in sins” are Gregory’s words, *Pastoral Rule* III, admonition 30. GRIAL.]

1. After these events, Shechem, the son of Hamor, violated Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. After having intercourse with her, he wished to join himself to the family of Israel. But Simeon and Levi, her brothers and avengers of their sister’s virginity, killed him deceitfully together with all his people. But what does it mean that it is written: “Dinah went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, the son of Hamor, the prince of that land, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and slept with her, violating the virgin by force; and his soul was joined to her, and he soothed the grieving woman with blandishments”?

2. For Dina goes out to see the women of a foreign region when each mind, neglecting its own pursuits, concerns itself with the affairs of others and wanders outside its proper character and order. Shechem, the prince of the land, oppresses her because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it occupied with external concerns.

> [Note: [Col. 0267D]
>
> 3. “Is humbled,” Gregory. “Is brought to himself”; *f.*, “is subjected.” For he speaks elsewhere in this way, as we showed above in the exposition of Deuteronomy, chapter 19. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. Florence Codex 1: “comes to his senses, is subjected, and is humbled.” Florence 2: “comes to his senses, is subjected—that is, is humbled”; this confirms Grial’s conjecture that in Saint Gregory one should read *addicitur*. AREV.]

3. “And his soul was joined to her,” because he regards it as united to himself through iniquity; and because, when the mind recovers from guilt, it is humbled and tries to lament what it has done, while the corrupter summons empty hopes and false securities before its eyes in order to take away the benefit of sorrow, it is rightly added there: “and he soothed her sadness with flatteries.”

4. At one moment he speaks of the deeds of others as more serious, at another that what was done is nothing; at one moment he speaks of God as merciful, at another promises that there is still time remaining for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led on by these things, it is suspended from the purpose of repentance, so that it receives no good then, although no evils now cause it sorrow; and then it is more completely overwhelmed by punishments, even though now it rejoices in its offenses.

5. After this God speaks to Jacob, telling him to dwell at Bethel. There Rachel died while giving birth to Benjamin. But what does it mean that, while Rachel was giving birth to this same Benjamin, she called his name “son of my sorrow,” unless she was prophetically announcing the future Paul from his tribe, who would afflict the children of the Church during the time of his persecution?

6. Alternatively, through Benjamin earthly Jerusalem was represented, since Jerusalem lies within the tribe of that same Benjamin. Its people caused their mother grievous sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets, and further by shouting impious cries for Christ’s death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25). Meanwhile Reuben, moved by the desire of lust, burst headlong into passion with his father’s concubine; this crime of incest would not have been recorded unless the future perversity of the Israelite people had been foretold.

7. Although the outrage committed by that individual is also to be considered, in Scripture it is nevertheless a prophecy of things to come. For through Reuben, the firstborn, is signified Israel, the firstborn people by circumcision, who polluted the bed of the concubine—that is, repeatedly defiled the law of the Old Testament by transgression.

8. That the law of the Old Testament is placed in the figure of a concubine was taught by the apostle Paul, who said: “Abraham had two sons: one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. These things are the two covenants.” In this figure Hagar, who was a concubine, represents the Old Testament. There is one perfect dove belonging to her mother, who, as a chaste virgin, queen, and bride, is joined through the Gospel to Christ, the King of the Church.

335 **CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning Judah, when he slept with his daughter-in-law.**

> [Note: [Col. 0267D]
>
> CHAPTER XXIX, Note 1. From “Now thereafter” through “will confess,” the words are Augustine’s, *Against Faustus*, Book XXII, chapters 83–87. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. “Then thereafter.” Grial in the note: “from then on.” AREV.]

1. Let us now consider what Judah did thereafter, when he slept with his daughter-in-law, and what future event it signified. In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the Jewish people are understood. Kings from the tribe of Judah were given to her as husbands; appropriately, her name is interpreted as “bitterness.” For she herself gave the Lord the cup of gall.

> [Col. 0268B] [Note: [Col. 0268D]
>
> 2. “Savage before God.” “Wicked,” the Vulgate; *ponēros* (πονηρός), “wicked” or “malignant,” the Septuagint. “Malignant and savage before the Lord,” Augustine. Hebrew [reading unclear]. GRIAL.]

2. For two classes of rulers who did not act rightly among the people were signified by Judah’s two sons: one class consisted of those who harmed, the other of those who benefited no one. One of the sons was savage before God; the other spilled his seed upon the ground so that he would not provide seed for making Tamar fertile.

3. There are no more than two classes of people useless to the human race: those who do harm, and those unwilling to provide benefit, who, if they possess any good in this earthly life, waste it as though spilling it upon the ground. Because the one who harms is worse than the one who does no good, the former is called “malignant,” while the latter, who spilled his seed upon the ground, follows after him.

4. The name of the elder, who was called Er, is also interpreted as “leathery,” referring to the sort of tunics in which the first human beings were clothed when, as punishment for their condemnation, they were expelled from paradise. The name of the younger, who was called Onan, is interpreted as “their sorrow.”

> [Note: [Col. 0268D]
>
> 5. “Which were not assisted,” from Augustine and the printed editions. “Which were not regarded,” manuscripts. GRIAL.]

5. Whose condition is this, except that of those who benefit no one although they have the means to do good, and waste that capacity upon the earth? A life taken away is a greater evil, signified by “leathery,” than a life not assisted, signified by “their sorrow”; nevertheless, God is said to have killed both. Here is represented the fact that He removed the kingdom from people of this kind.

6. The third son of Judah, who was not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which the kings of the Jewish people began no longer to come from the tribe of Judah.

336 7. He was indeed a son of Judah, but Tamar did not receive him as her husband, because he belonged to that same tribe of Judah, although by then no one from it ruled among the people. Hence his name, Shelah, is interpreted as “his dismissal.” Holy and righteous men do not properly belong to this signification: although they lived at that time, they nevertheless belong to the New Testament, for they knowingly served it by prophesying. David was such a man, even though he lived at a time when Judea had already begun to lack kings from the tribe of Judah.

> [Col. 0269A] [Note: [Col. 0269D]
>
> 8. Calmet gives the genealogy of Herod the Great, or Herod the Elder, in his *Biblical Dictionary*. Herod Antipas, his son, was the one who agreed with Pilate during the Lord’s Passion. AREV.]

8. Herod the Great is not to be counted among the kings of Judah, as though he were Tamar’s husband. He was a foreigner, and he was not bound to her by that sacrament of mystical anointing, as by a marital covenant; rather, he ruled as an outsider. He had received that power from the Romans and from Caesar, and so did his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was called Herod after his father and agreed with Pilate during the Lord’s Passion.

> [Note: [Col. 0269D]
>
> 9. “And they flattered him,” from Augustine and the manuscripts. “And they worshiped him,” in Bede. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. “The true Savior, our Lord, had to come,” from Augustine and the printed editions. “It was necessary to come to Christ, the true Savior, our Lord,” manuscripts. GRIAL.]

9. These foreigners were therefore not counted as belonging to that mystical kingdom of the Jews to such an extent that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). This was not true except in the sense of that universal Roman domination. For Caesar was indeed king, not properly of the Jews, but they condemned themselves to such words in order to deny Christ and flatter this ruler. At that time, when the kingdom had already departed from the tribe of Judah, Christ, our true Savior and Lord, had to come—one who would not harm but would greatly benefit.

> [Note: [Col. 0269D]
>
> 10. “For whom it had been reserved.” We have retained the wording of the Septuagint, which Augustine uses and repeats twice below; this was not noticed by the editor who substituted the wording of the Vulgate. GRIAL.]

10. For it had been prophesied thus: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” By that time all the teaching of the Jews had also failed, as had the mystical anointing from which they were called “Christs,” according to Daniel’s prophecy. Then he came for whom it had been reserved (Daniel 9:24), who is the expectation of the nations; and the Holy of Holies was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

> [Col. 0269C] [Note: [Col. 0270D]
>
> 11. “Of the younger Herod.” “Of Herod the tetrarch,” Augustine and the printed editions. GRIAL.]

11. He was born in the time of Herod the Great, but suffered under Herod the Younger, the tetrarch. This Judah therefore represented the figure of the one who was coming to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel, when he went to shear his sheep at Timnah, which is interpreted as “failing.” For the ruler from Judah and all the teaching and anointing of the Jews had already failed, so that the one for whom it had been reserved might come.

12. He came with his shepherd, the Adullamite, whose name was Hiras. “Adullamite” is interpreted as “testimony in water.” The Lord plainly came with this testimony, although he had a greater testimony than John. Nevertheless, because of the weak sheep he used this testimony in water. For Hiras itself, which was the name of that shepherd, is interpreted as “the vision of my brother.”

> [Col. 0269D] 13. John certainly saw his brother: his brother according to the seed of Abraham, according to the kinship of his mother Mary and John’s mother Elizabeth, and the same one who was his Lord and God. For, as John himself says, “From his fullness he received.” He certainly saw him, and therefore “among those born of women no one has arisen greater than he.” For of all who foretold Christ, he saw what many righteous men and prophets desired to see but did not see.

14. He greeted him from the womb and recognized him more perfectly through the dove; therefore, as an Adullamite, he truly bore witness in water. The Lord came to shear the sheep—that is, to relieve them of the burdens of sins—whose teeth, praised in the Song of Songs, were like a flock of shorn sheep (Song of Songs 4).

15. Then Tamar changes her appearance, for her name also means “changing.” Tamar changes her appearance and her name, and from the Synagogue she becomes the Church. Yet the name of bitterness remains completely in her—not the bitterness in which she gave the Lord gall, but that in which Peter wept bitterly; for Judah in Latin means “confession.” Bitterness, therefore, must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be foreshadowed.

> [Note: [Col. 0270D]
>
> 16. “At the gate of Henam,” or “Henaim.” The Septuagint retained the Hebrew word *Henaim*, which means “eyes” or “springs.” The Vulgate rendered it “at the crossroads.” See Jerome, *Hebrew Traditions*, on Genesis 38. GRIAL.]

16. By this repentance the Church, established among all nations, becomes fruitful. For it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. Even the appearance of a prostitute is a confession of sins. Tamar represents the figure of the Church called forth from the nations, sitting in this appearance at the gate of Henam, or Henaim, which is interpreted as “springs.”

17. For she ran like a deer to the springs of water, in order to reach the seed of Abraham. There she is made pregnant by one who does not recognize her, because this was foretold of her: “A people whom I did not know served me.” In secret she received the ring, necklace, and staff, because she is marked by calling, adorned by justification, and exalted by glorification.

18. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8). But these things, as I said, are still hidden, and there the conception of holy fruitfulness also takes place. A promised kid is sent to her as to a prostitute. The kid is the reproach of sin, sent through that same Adullamite as though he were reproving her and saying, “Generation of vipers.” But the reproach of sin did not find her, for the bitterness of confession had changed her.

> [Note: [Col. 0270D]
>
> 19. “After the signs had already been made public.” “Now already public,” Augustine. GRIAL.]

19. After the signs of the ring, necklace, and staff had been made public, she defeated the Jews who judged rashly, for Judah himself was already representing their person. Even today they say that this people does not belong to Christ and that we do not possess the seed of Abraham. But when the most certain proofs of our calling, justification, and glorification are brought forth, they will undoubtedly be confounded and will confess that we have been justified more than they. For the Church has the pledges with her. She is accused by the Jews as though she were an adulteress against the law, but she displays the staff, the sign of the Passion; the necklace, the lawful teaching; and the ring, the pledge of immortality.

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> 20. “Which she displayed.” Thus the manuscripts. “Which she extended,” in Bede. GRIAL.]

20. The fact that Scripture presents Tamar giving birth and having twin sons in her womb—of whom the first, called Zerah, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it; then, when he drew his hand back inside, the other, called Perez, thrust out his hand and was born first—corresponds figuratively to the fact that Israel extended its hand toward the works of the law and, through the prophets and the Savior himself, drew it back polluted with blood. Afterwards the people of the nations burst forth, so that those who were last would become first, and those who were first would become last.

**CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the history of Joseph.**

[Col. 0271B]

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> CHAPTER XXX, Note 1. See Augustine, Sermon 81, *On the Time*. GRIAL.]

1. Next comes the history of Joseph, who was sold by his brothers, brought into Egypt, and elevated there. Joseph, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, whom his father loved more than the other sons, represented Christ the Lord. God the Father preferred him, born according to the flesh, to the other brothers descended from the stock of Abraham. Hence it is said there: “Jacob loved him because he had begotten him in his old age.”

2. For the Son of God, shining upon an aging world, came late through the birth of the virgin Mary, as a son of old age according to the mystery of the body he assumed; according to the substance of his divinity, however, he had always been with the Father. The many-colored tunic that his father made for him signified the diversity of peoples gathered from every nation into the body of Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> 3. “But that dream,” through “we shall worship you,” are Augustine’s words, in the same work. GRIAL.]

3. That dream, by which his brothers’ sheaves worshiped his sheaf, is what was fulfilled in Christ: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him,” offering, of course, through faith the fruit of good works. He is the one whom the sun, moon, and stars worship; concerning the sun it is said: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars.”

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> 4. “The rebuke” through “they despise” are Ambrose’s words, *On Joseph*, chapter 2. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. “Jacob sends” through “to visit,” Augustine, in the same work. GRIAL.]

4. The excellence of the saints worships him under the name of the sun, the splendor of the Church under the image of the moon, and the multitude of all peoples in the figure of the stars. Hence his father rebuked him, saying: “Shall I and your mother and your brothers worship you?” This rebuke by the father signifies the hardness of the people of Israel: although they recognize that Christ was born from them, they refuse to worship him. Jacob sends his son Joseph to inquire after his brothers.

5. God the Father likewise sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. He was sent by that Father of whom it is written: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh,” to see whether the sheep were acting rightly. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> 6. “Joseph therefore found” through “they determined” are by the same author. GRIAL.]

6. Joseph therefore found his brothers at Dothain. Dothain is interpreted as “failure”; truly they were in great failure, since they were considering fratricide. When Joseph’s brothers saw him from a distance, they resolved to kill him. Likewise, when the Jews saw the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus Christ, they all determined with one purpose to crucify him, saying: “Crucify him.” The most savage beast devoured him—that is, the Jewish people killed him. Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves.”

> [Note: [Col. 0271D]
>
> 7. “Joseph’s brothers stripped him” through “the bodily tunic,” by the same author. GRIAL.
>
> [Col. 0272D] Ibid. “The many-colored tunic” through “the diversity of virtues,” Ambrose, *On Joseph*, chapter 3. GRIAL.]

7. Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his many-colored and ankle-length tunic, and the Jews stripped Christ of his bodily tunic through the death of the cross. The many-colored tunic signifies one adorned with the diversity of all virtues. They sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a kid, because, accusing him with false testimonies, they stirred the envy of the people against him who forgave all sins.

> [Note: [Col. 0272D]
>
> 8. “Then he is sent into the cistern” through “he is sold,” Augustine, in the same work. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. Florence 1 relates the passage as follows: “Joseph, lifted from the cistern and sold to the Ishmaelites, sent into the well and brought out of the well—what else does this foreshadow except the Lord’s death and resurrection?” Likewise Codex Regiovaticanus 293 adds in the margin, after “is compared”: “Joseph sent into the well,” etc. The verb *distraho*, “I sell,” which occurs shortly afterward in place of *vendo*, is also used by others. Below, section 17, *distractus*, in the same sense. AREV.]

8. Then he is sent into a cistern—that is, into a pit—and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descends into hell. Joseph, lifted from the cistern, is sold to the Ishmaelites—that is, to the nations; and Christ, after emerging from hell, is purchased by all nations through the commerce of faith. Joseph is sold for thirty pieces of silver at Judah’s instigation, and Christ, through the counsel of Judas Iscariot, is sold for the same number.

341

> [Note: [Col. 0272D]
>
> 9. “Then Jacob” through “to display the kingdom,” Ambrose, chapter 3. GRIAL.]

9. Then Jacob, mourning the loss of his descendants, lamented his lost son like a father and mourned the destruction of the Jews like a prophet. Finally, he tore his garment, as we read that the high priest did during the Lord’s Passion. The veil of the temple was also torn, so that the prophet might show both that his people had been stripped and that the kingdom had been divided. Thus Joseph descended into Egypt, and Christ into the world.

10. A eunuch bought him—that is, the Christian people, chaste in the disciplines of the Gospel. Joseph had a beautiful appearance; so David says of Christ: “You are more beautiful than the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.” But the woman, it says, cast her eyes upon him so that she might commit adultery with him.

11. This woman represented the Synagogue, which, as it is written, often played the harlot after foreign gods. Likewise, she wished to retain Christ in the crime of her adultery, so that he would deny that he was God and observe the commandments of the Pharisees and scribes rather than those of the law, which was like her husband. But Christ, refusing the unlawful doctrine of the adulterous Synagogue, was seized by the hand through the garment of his body; he stripped himself of the flesh and, freed from death, ascended into heaven.

12. When the prostitute could not hold him, she slandered him, saying that he had blasphemed the temple of the Lord and was called a transgressor of the law. But prison did not frighten him, nor did the underworld hold him; even when he had descended there as though to be punished, he freed others from it.

13. Finally, Joseph found two eunuchs from the royal household bound in prison, bearing the figure of two peoples, one believing and the other unbelieving. They were confined under Adam’s sin and held liable to transgression. They are called eunuchs because they had received a rule of discipline that was chaste. “The sayings of the Lord,” it says, “are chaste.”

14. Finally, when the Lord rose from the dead after the third light, revealing the obscure dreams of the law like Joseph, the people of believers were released from sins and freed from the prison of hell, restored to the service of the divine law. But the unbelieving and impious Jewish people, because they did not believe in the tree of conversion, was hanged upon the tree of transgression, as happened to the other eunuch who represented the Jews.

15. Moreover, Pharaoh relates a dream, which Joseph interprets. 342 But what do the seven years, displayed in the seven full ears of grain or in the seven fat cows, signify except the gifts of the seven spiritual charisms, through which the abundance of faith overflows in generous devotion? On the other hand, the seven barren and famished years signified the famine of truth and righteousness in the last times.

16. For seven years Joseph gathered all the abundance of grain—that is, storing the grain of faith in the granaries of the saints—through those seven charisms, as through seven years. Thus, when the seven years of scarcity begin—that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital sins arises under Antichrist, when there is a famine of faith in the Savior—the saints and believers together may possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, so that their faith does not fail, weakened by scarcity of the word.

17. From there Joseph, who had assumed the type of Christ, earned a chariot, and a herald cried out before him; Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. Our Lord too, after he had been sold by Judas as Joseph was sold by his brothers, rose from the prison of hell and mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, concerning which it is said: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold.”

18. He received power from the Father to preach and judge, as the apostle Paul says: “And he gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” He also received a ring, namely the high priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation; and the figure of the eternal King is impressed upon our foreheads and hearts through the sign of the cross.

19. He is clothed in a linen robe—that is, in holy flesh brighter than fine linen, and in the robe of immortality. He also received a golden chain, that is, good understanding. The herald goes before him—that is, John the Baptist, who preceded him on his way and proclaimed: “Prepare the way of the Lord.”

> [Note: [Col. 0273D]
>
> 20. Codex Regiovaticanus, in the margin: “Another herald will be Elijah, who will announce his future coming, or the angel’s trumpet.” Historians and chronologists do not agree on the year of his life in which Christ the Lord suffered. Zaccaria presents various opinions of authors in *Selected Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, article 1, number 5. For the thirty-first year begun, he lists Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and Julius Africanus, and says that Sedulius supports them in his hymn: “The six periods of five years which he has already completed,” etc. [Col. 0274D] But “Sedulius” should be replaced by Venantius Fortunatus, the true author of that hymn. For the thirty-second year begun, he lists Apollinaris of Laodicea, Orosius, Isidore of Seville, Zonaras, and others. AREV.]

20. He will also have another herald, Elijah, who will announce his future coming, or the angel’s trumpet, because he himself said: “He will come with the angel’s trumpet.” Joseph is called “Savior of the world” in the Egyptian language.
