What could be clearer concerning Christ, when the Savior is shown under the figure of Joseph—not merely of one land, Egypt, but of the whole world? Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh the king. Christ too is read to have been the same age when, under the type of Pharaoh, he appeared revealed before Herod.

> [Note: [Col. 0274D]
>
> 21. “After this Joseph” through “their sound,” Augustine, in the same work. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. Grial: “scarcity,” without the letter *a*. AREV.]

21. Therefore he received a wife from the nations, that is, the Church, from whom he begot two sons—that is, two peoples gathered from Jews and nations. After the years of abundance, famine prevailed throughout the whole world. Rightly so, because there was no one who did good. Afterwards Joseph saved Egypt from the scarcity of grain, and Christ freed the world from the famine of the word of God: for Christ opened his granaries throughout the whole world, and by distributing his grain subjected all things.

22. If Joseph’s brothers had not sold him, Egypt would have perished. If the Jews had not crucified Christ, the world would have perished. Joseph is interpreted as “increase” or “expansion.” But in that Joseph, expansion was granted only to Egypt; in our Joseph, the whole world was worthy to receive increase. That Joseph distributed wheat; our Joseph distributed the word of God. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

> [Note: [Col. 0274D]
>
> 23. “Jacob said” through “my son,” Ambrose, chapter 8. GRIAL.]

23. Jacob said to his sons: “There is grain in Egypt.” God the Father says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.” Therefore ten older brothers descended—that is, the Jews, constituted as though under the Decalogue of the law and its number. Joseph himself recognized them, but he was not recognized by them. The Hebrews are also recognized by Christ, but they do not recognize him.

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 24. “Joseph saw” through “that he might be seen by many,” Ambrose, chapter 10. GRIAL.]

24. They did indeed give him money, but Joseph—that is, Christ—gave them grain and returned their silver, because Christ is not bought with money but with grace. Joseph saw his little brother Benjamin; mystically, Jesus also saw Paul when light flashed around him.

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 25. Some printed editions read: “so that he might restore the light lost by him.” Perhaps: “so that he might restore sight and light.” AREV.]

25. He is called little because he had not yet attained mature age in the faith according to the flesh. Hence he is also read to have been a young man when he guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen. Joseph wept, and Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping. He washes his face so that he may restore the lost light; Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus was to be seen by many. Then a silver cup is placed in the sack of the younger brother alone.

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 26. “But what does it mean” through “he preached,” Ambrose, chapter 11. GRIAL.]

26. But what does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except that in Paul’s body the eloquence of heavenly doctrine already shone forth while he was learned in the law? But because he was not yet subject to divine grace, the cup was inside the sack: doctrine was inside the law, a lamp inside a bushel.

27. Nevertheless Ananias was sent and laid on his hand; he untied the purse. Once the purse was untied, the silver shone forth, and when the scales fell away—as though the sack had been loosened from certain bonds—the sack was opened. That is, after the veil of the law had been put aside, he attained the freedom of grace and, with unveiled face, preached the words of the Gospel.

> [Col. 0275C] [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 28. “The five robes” through “is made alive,” Ambrose, chapter 13. GRIAL.]

28. He was given thirty pieces of silver together with five excellent robes. Whoever preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ receives the thirty pieces of silver from Christ. Therefore Paul says: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” He received five robes—that is, the discipline of wisdom and the manifold instruction in the law of all the senses.

29. Paul therefore excels, and his share of merits overflows; nevertheless the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace. They have two robes, namely, so that they may confess Christ to be both God and man, according to what is read in Proverbs: “All her household are clothed with double garments”—that is, with mystical or moral understanding.

30. Gifts are also sent to the father. The Son honors the Father; Christ invites his people through promises and gifts. Donkeys carry these gifts: formerly useless and laboring Gentiles, now useful, carry the gifts in the type of Christ and will carry, in the Gospel, the giver of gifts.

31. Joseph dismissed his brothers, who reported to their father, saying: “Joseph lives, and he is lord over the whole land of Egypt.” Jacob was terrified—that is, the unbelieving people. But after recognizing the deeds of Christ, his spirit revives, and he who seemed dead is made alive through faith in Christ’s resurrection.

345

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 32. “Therefore he is called” through “might be saved,” Ambrose, chapter 14. GRIAL.]

32. Therefore he is called by his sons—that is, Peter, Paul, and John—and the Jewish people are invited to grace. Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession,” meets him, because confession now goes before those whom unbelief had previously possessed. Thus the true Joseph, Christ, meets them, to receive the Jewish people, already grown old, in the last times—not according to their merits, but according to the election of his grace.

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> 33. “He postponed healing,” from Ambrose. Others read “he postponed blindness,” with the same sense. GRIAL.]

33. He places his hand upon his eyes and removes his blindness. He therefore delayed his healing so that he might believe last—the one who had previously thought that Christ should not be believed—and so that he might lose the privilege of the earlier one. Hence the Apostle says: “A partial blindness has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel may be saved.”

34. Afterwards Joseph gave his parents and brothers the excellent land of Goshen, providing them with food, because famine had oppressed the land. Likewise the Lord, choosing an excellent land, gives it to his parents—that is, to the patriarchs and prophets from whom Christ was born according to the flesh—or to all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel: “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father.” To these, therefore, he gives the land of promise, the kingdom of God, concerning which the Prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.”

**CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the blessings of the patriarchs.**

> [Note: [Col. 0275D]
>
> CHAPTER XXXI, Note 1. See Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVI, chapter 42. These interpretations of the blessings are indeed read in the appendices to Augustine’s works. It is astonishing that the Louvain editors did not notice where they came from; still more astonishing is the fact that they attributed them to Jerome. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. The Maurists reject into the appendices of Saint Augustine’s works the little work *On the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob*, and wish its author to be Alcuin, from whose book *Questions on Genesis* it was excerpted. They add that the same exposition exists in the commentaries on Genesis once attributed to Eucherius of Lyon, in a somewhat different order and with several words changed. Evidently the Maurists too failed to notice what Grial had reproached the Louvain editors for: that these blessings were drawn from the Isidorian commentaries. AREV.]

1. Then Joseph, hastening to receive his father’s blessing, presented two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. In them, just as it happened with Esau and Jacob, when the Lord said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” so too it occurred with these two sons of Joseph. For the elder, Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” represented the Jews, who forgot their God, who made them.

2. The younger represented Christians; his name signifies fruitfulness, which is characteristic of the younger people, who are the body of Christ and have been made fruitful in the breadth of the world. When Jacob wished to bless them, Joseph placed Ephraim on his left and positioned Manasseh on his right.

346

> [Col. 0276D]

> [Col. 0277A] [Note: [Col. 0277D]
>
> 3. The Alborn manuscript has this distinctive reading: “The elder was made left from the right through the mystery of the cross, and the younger right from the left, because the Jews are on the left and we are on the right; while they fall away, we have obtained their grace.” AREV.]

3. But Jacob, crossing his hands and prefiguring the mystery of the cross, transferred his right hand to the younger and placed his left figuratively upon the elder. Thus the likeness of the cross marked upon their heads foreshadowed scandal for the Jews and future glory for Christians; through the mystery of the cross, the elder was made left from the right, and the younger right from the left, because, while the Jews fell into our desolate places, we obtained their glory.

4. Through this sacrament the younger people of the nations was placed before the elder people of the Jews. Hence the same patriarch says: “This one shall indeed become a people, but this one shall be exalted.”

> [Note: [Col. 0277D]
>
> 5. “According to the mystical interpretation” through “my firstborn” are Rufinus’s words—or, if you prefer, Origen’s. GRIAL.]

5. When these things were completed, Jacob called his sons to bless them in a mystical order, speaking as one who knew the future. He told them what would happen in the last times, beginning as follows: “Reuben, my firstborn.” According to the mystical understanding, Reuben appears to represent the earlier people. To him also the Lord says through the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn.”

> [Note: [Col. 0277D]
>
> 6. “For indeed, according to what was due to the firstborn.” See above, the note on chapter 23. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. “The beginning of my sorrow”: *kephalē lypēs mou* (Κεφάλαιον λύπης μου), “the beginning of my sorrow,” Aquila and the Vulgate. *Archē teknōn mou* (Ἀρχὴ τέκνων μου), “the beginning of my children,” the Septuagint. GRIAL.
>
> Ibid. “But how he himself is the beginning of sorrows.” What follows—“unless, while he continually inflicts injury upon God the Father,” etc.—are Rufinus’s words, or Origen’s. Yet this does not appear to be an interpretation of “the beginning of sorrows,” but rather of the Septuagint’s words: “Hard to bear, hard and self-willed”: *sklēros pheresthai, kai sklēros authadēs* (σκληρὸς φέρεσθαι, καὶ σκληρὸς αὐθάδης). GRIAL.]

6. For, according to what was due to the firstborn, it belonged to him to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. It is added: “You are my strength,” certainly because from that people came the foundation of faith, and from that people came the power of God, who is Christ. “The beginning of my sorrow.” But how is he himself the beginning of sorrows, unless because he continually inflicts injury upon God the Father, turning his back toward him and not his face? He was first in gifts, because to the first people were given the sayings of God; to them first were given the legislation and the covenant, or the promise. He was greater in rule, certainly because of the magnitude of his strength, since that same people ruled more extensively than the others in this world.

7. But you were poured out like water, by sinning against Christ; like water that cannot be contained in a vessel, you were poured out in the rush of pleasure. And therefore he added: “You shall no longer increase.” For after that people itself had been scattered throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished and reduced.

[Note: [Col. 0278D]]

8. “Not like the Jews.” From Ambrose, *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 2. GRIAL.

8. But why he deserved such things, he explained as follows: “Because you went up onto your father’s bed.” It is not to be understood, as the Jews understand it, as having been said because he slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. For the prophecy foretold future events, not things that had already happened, as the patriarch himself says: “I will announce to you what shall come to pass in the last days.”

9. And therefore what he foretold as future must not be referred to the past. He was foretelling the Lord’s Passion and the audacity of the firstborn people, because it went up onto the bed of God its Father and defiled his couch when it seized and hung upon the cross the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested, and stained it with iron.

[Note: [Col. 0278D]]

10. “Through Simeon and Levi,” up to “my soul,” from Rufinus. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The scribes and priests,” etc. Thus in the *Allegories*. Compare Suarius’s notes, which illuminate the allegorical expositions of these Blessings. AREV.

10. After this he turns to Simeon and Levi, saying: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; their weapons are instruments of iniquity.” Through Simeon and Levi the scribes and priests of the Jewish people are understood. For the scribes were from the tribe of Simeon, while the chief priests were from the tribe of Levi. Of them it is written: “For they took counsel to hand Jesus over to death” (Matthew 26). Of this counsel the patriarch, who already saw God in his mind, says: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel.” And what follows.

348 [Note: [Col. 0278D]]

11. “Speaking against themselves”: nominative for an ablative absolute; unless one reads with Alborn, “because they devised a plan,” etc. AREV.

11. For already at that time this holy patriarch shuddered to see the counsels of such great crimes that the Jews were going to commit in the last times. It follows: “For in their fury they killed a man,” that is, Christ, in accordance with what Isaiah says: “Woe to their soul” (Isaiah 3:9), because their thought was an evil plan, saying against themselves: “Let us bind the righteous man, because he is useless to us”; and in their anguish they pierced the wall, when they wounded with a lance the spiritual and most powerful bulwark that guards Israel.

12. “Cursed be their fury,” because it was obstinate—certainly, in carrying out so great a crime—when, inflamed with fury and anger, they delivered Christ to Pontius Pilate, saying to him: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23), and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19). “And their indignation,” because it was harsh, when they asked for the robber Barabbas to be released and demanded that the Prince of Life be crucified.

13. “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Here two things are mentioned: division and scattering; for this reason, because some of them believed in the Lord, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate themselves from them and come to the faith are called “divided.” Those whose homeland and temple have been overthrown are “scattered,” since their unbelieving race is dispersed throughout the world.

[Note: [Col. 0278D]]

14. “Through this Judah, the true confessor,” from Ambrose, chapter 4. GRIAL.

Ibid. “His brothers praise him,” up to “his coheirs,” from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 42. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Brothers by grace,” up to “the Lord by nature.” Ambrose, in the same place; some words, however, have been changed, such as “bent” for “subjugated.” GRIAL.

14. “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” Through this Judah, the true confessor, Christ is represented, who was born from his tribe according to the flesh. His brothers praise him—that is, the apostles and all his coheirs, who through adoption have been made sons of God the Father, and brothers of Christ by grace, while he himself is their Lord by nature.

15. “Your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies.” For by the same hands and through the same trophy of the cross he both protected his own and bent his enemies and the opposing powers, in accordance with what the Father promises him, saying: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Psalm 109).

349 [Note: [Col. 0279D]]

16. That is, “ascending onto the cross.” Augustine, *City of God*, book 16, chapter 41: “The very kind of death, that is, the exaltation of the cross, is understood in the one word he says: ‘You have ascended.’” GRIAL.

Ibid. Alborn inserts some words: “They have been saved.” For the prophet indicates that this will happen when the Lord says: “And it shall be in the last days: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.” “A lion’s cub,” etc. Others relegate these words to the end of the chapter. Grialius has in the text: “Ascending onto the cross.” AREV.

16. “Your father’s sons shall worship you.” For many of Jacob’s sons worship him, having been saved through the election of grace. “Judah is a lion’s cub.” For in being born he became small, as it is written: “A child has been born for us.” “You have ascended to the prey, my son” (Isaiah 9), that is, ascending onto the cross, you redeemed captive peoples. And those whom that hostile lion had attacked, you rescued by dying. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive (Ephesians 4).

[Note: [Col. 0279D]]

17. “Most clearly,” up to “he handed over [his spirit],” Augustine, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Or when he was in the tomb,” up to “he rested,” Ambrose. GRIAL.

Ibid. “But why as a lion,” up to “I have power,” Augustine, in the same place. GRIAL.

17. “Resting, you reclined like a lion.” Most clearly, Christ reclined in the Passion when, bowing his head, he handed over his spirit; or when, secure in the tomb, he rested as though in a kind of sleep of the body. But why “like a lion,” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he fulfilled this not from necessity but by power, in accordance with what he himself had said: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (John 10).

[Col. 0279C] [Note: [Col. 0280D]]

18. “Physiologists, however,” up to “he rose again,” are the words of Rufinus. GRIAL.

18. But as for what he added, “and like a lion’s cub”—for he died from the same source from which he was born—physiologists write about the lion’s cub that, when it has been born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then, when the place of its den has been shaken, the father is said to awaken the sleeping cub with his growl or roar.

19. This very appropriately applies to Christ’s death in the Passion: lying for three days and three nights in the chamber of the tomb, he fulfilled the sleep of death. Therefore Christ rightly rested like a lion, who not only did not fear the bitterness of death but also, in death itself, conquered death’s dominion. Again, he rightly rested like a lion’s cub, because on the third day he rose again.

[Note: [Col. 0280D]]

20. “Whence it is also added in this way,” up to “I will raise it,” from *City of God*, book 16, chapter 41. GRIAL.

20. Hence this is also added concerning his resurrection: “Who will raise him?” That is, no human being, but he himself, in accordance with what he said about his body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it” (John 2).

350 21. “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until those things come which have been reserved for him, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.” This passage most clearly refers to Judah; for an unbroken succession of kings from his offspring remained among the Jews until Christ was born of the Virgin for the redemption of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0280D]]

22. “Histories prove this,” up to “his colt,” from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 42. GRIAL.

22. The histories of the Jews prove this, showing that the first foreign king among the Jewish people was Herod, at the time when Christ was born. If the Jews think that Christ has not come, then the kingdom of the Jews from the tribe of Judah remains to this day. Therefore, a king from the people of Judah did not fail until the one came for whom it had been reserved.

[Col. 0280B] 23. But because the one who was to be sent benefited not only the Jews, it follows: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations, binding his colt to the vine.” His colt is from the nations: a people upon whom the burden of the law had never yet been imposed. He joined it to the vine of the apostles, who are from the Jews.

24. For “the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5). “And to the vine, O my son, his she-ass.” He himself said: “I am the true vine” (John 15). To this vine he binds his she-ass, upon which he sits, the Church gathered from the nations. Thus he bound her to the vine of his body by the bond of charity and by the tie of evangelical discipline, so that, living in imitation of him, she might become God’s heir and Christ’s coheir.

[Note: [Col. 0280D]]

25. “He shall wash in wine,” up to “garment,” excerpted from Ambrose. GRIAL.

25. Others interpret this she-ass as the Synagogue, namely, slow-footed and weighed down by the heavy burden of the law. “He shall wash his robe in wine,” or his flesh in the blood of the Passion, or the holy Church in that wine which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0280D]]

26. “For Christ cleansed us,” up to “the cluster hanging on the wood,” from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 42. GRIAL.

Ibid. “But water washed us,” up to “redeemed us by blood,” Ambrose, in the same place. GRIAL.

26. “And in the blood of the grape, his cloak.” The cloak is the nations, whom he joined to his body, as it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as with a garment.” Christ cleansed us in the blood of the grape when he hung like a cluster on the wood of the cross. Then blood and water flowed from his side. Water washed us, but blood redeemed us.

351 [Note: [Col. 0280D]]

27. “The eyes of Christ are the apostles,” Rufinus, in the same place. GRIAL.

27. “His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” The eyes of Christ are the apostles and evangelists, who provide the light of knowledge to the whole body of the Church. They are shown to be more beautiful than wine because their teaching surpasses the austerity of old wine, that is, the tradition of the ancient law. For the evangelical commandments are far clearer than the precepts of the Old Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0281D]]

28. “By the name of milk.” This interpretation is shared by Rufinus with Ambrose and Augustine. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Whose indeed,” etc. These words are obscure, and clearer in the Alborn manuscript: “By this milk the teachers have been made whiter.” AREV.

28. “And his teeth are whiter than milk.” The teeth are the holy preachers, who cut people away from errors and, as though grinding them up, transfer them into Christ’s body. By the name of milk the teaching of the law is signified, which nourished the carnal people like little children with a cup of milk. Its teachers, however, have been made whiter than milk because they chew and distribute the strong and solid food of the word.

29. Of these the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Hebrews 5). And he rightly says that his teeth are whiter than milk. For all who are mature, and who, explaining the nourishment of the Scriptures, provide the Church’s body with a subtle and finely divided understanding—an understanding called spiritual food—ought to be white and pure and free from every stain.

[Note: [Col. 0281D]]

30. “Zebulun,” up to “reached,” from Ambrose, chapter 5. GRIAL.

30. “Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships.” Zebulun, whose name means “dwelling of strength,” signifies the Church, most strong for enduring every suffering. She dwells on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that she may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

31. Established against all the storms of the world with immovable and unshaken firmness, she watches the shipwreck of the Jews and the storms of the heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Although she is battered by the waves, she herself breaks the waves and is not broken; she yields to no storms of heresies and, shaken by no wind of schisms, does she succumb.

[Note: [Col. 0281D]]

32. “It is also read in the Gospel,” up to “great light,” from Rufinus. GRIAL.

32. “He extends even to Sidon,” that is, he reaches as far as the nations. It is also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from that region and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light.”

33. “Issachar is a strong ass.” Issachar, whose name means “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is called a strong ass because formerly the Gentile people were like a brute and lustful animal, existing without any rational order. But now it is strong, submitting its neck to the Lord the Redeemer and bearing the yoke of evangelical discipline.

[Col. 0281D] [Note: [Col. 0282D]]

34. “Lying down here,” up to “gladly bears,” are the words of Gregory, *Moral Expositions on Job*, book 1, chapter 7. GRIAL.

34. “Lying down between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent.” To lie down between the boundaries means to rest while awaiting the end of the world and to seek nothing of the things now occurring in between, but to desire the last things. The strong ass sees rest and the excellent land when the simple Gentile people raise themselves to the strength of good works for this reason: because they are journeying toward the homeland of eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0282D]]

35. “Dan,” up to “are intended to be indicated,” are the words of Rufinus. GRIAL.

35. Hence also “he shall place his shoulder under the burden,” because, desiring to reach the promised rest, he gladly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Therefore he has also become one who serves tribute, that is, who offers gifts of faith and offerings of good works to his king and Christ. “Dan shall judge his people, like another tribe in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent on the road and a horned serpent on the path,” etc. Others say that these words foretell that the Antichrist will come from this tribe.

[Note: [Col. 0282D]]

36. “They pronounce.” I prefer this with Alborn to “they foretell,” with Grialius. AREV.

36. Others refer these words to Judah, by whom Christ was betrayed, and wish the rider and the horse to signify the Lord with the flesh he assumed. They interpret “to fall backward” as returning to the earth from which he was taken. But because he rose again on the third day, he says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord,” just as he says through David: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 15). This is how they explain the passage.

[Note: [Col. 0282D]]

37. “From the tribe of Dan,” up to “faithfully recognizing Christ,” are Gregory’s words, *Moral Expositions on Job*, book 31, chapter 10. GRIAL.

37. Others, however, transfer this prophecy to the Antichrist. For they say that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is asserted to be a serpent and one who bites. Accordingly, not without reason, when the Israelite people received the land in the division of the camps, Dan first encamped to the north, signifying the one who had said in his heart: “I will sit on the mountain of the Testament, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14).

[Col. 0282C] 38. Of him it is said through the prophet: “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jeremiah 8). He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. In Greek, *cerata* means “horns,” and this serpent is said to be horned. Through it the coming of the Antichrist is fittingly signified, because he will be armed against the life of the faithful not only with the bite of a deadly preaching but also with the horns of power.

39. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus Dan becomes a serpent on the road because he urges those whom he flatters, as though sparing them, to walk in the breadth of the present life. But he bites on the road because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty. Again, he becomes a *cerastes* on the path because, when he finds people who are faithful and who constrain themselves within the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he not only attacks them with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also presses them with the terror of power. In the weakness of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of power.

40. In this passage the horse signifies the world, which in its arrogance foams along the course of passing times. And because the Antichrist strives to seize the world’s final moments, this *cerastes* is said to bite the horse’s hoof. To bite the horse’s hoof means to strike the world’s end, so that its rider falls backward.

41. The rider of the horse is anyone who is exalted by the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, and not on his face, as Saul is remembered to have fallen. To fall on one’s face means, in this life, for each person to recognize his own sins and lament them in repentance. To fall backward, where one cannot see, means to fall suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led.

42. And because Judea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits the Antichrist instead of Christ, Jacob is rightly changed at this same point into the voice of the elect, saying: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord”—that is, not, like unbelievers, the Antichrist, but the one who will come for our redemption, truly and faithfully believing in Christ.

43. “Gad, girded, shall fight before him.” This Gad, girded, expresses the person of the Lord, who at his first coming, in the humility of his condition, comes to fight before the coming of the Antichrist. Girded with the sword of his word around his thigh with supreme power (Psalm 44), he divided his enemies—that is, son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law—in accordance with what is read in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword” (Matthew 10).

44. But when he says, “He shall be girded behind,” the glory of our Lord in his second reign is shown. For when the Antichrist comes, Christ himself will meet him from behind, that is, advancing swiftly after his tracks, in order to kill him with the sword of his mouth.

45. Hence Gad is also aptly interpreted as “raider,” because afterward—that is, close behind, as though at his feet—he will leap out like a raider, with a swift and unexpected coming, against the Antichrist’s open attack. Hence the evangelist proclaims, saying: “For the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5). Thus Christ is written to fight against the Antichrist both before and behind him.

[Note: [Col. 0283D]]

46. “Moses clearly demonstrates,” etc. These are Ambrose’s words, with some additions, chapter 8, *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*. The passage in Moses is Deuteronomy 33. GRIAL.

46. “Before him he fights in a hidden coming; after him, manifest in the glory of majesty.” Moses clearly demonstrates that this prophecy of the patriarch specifically refers to Christ. For he says: “Blessed,” he says, “is Gad in breadth.”

[Note: [Col. 0283D]]

47. “And he began the arm steadfastly.” This is found in the printed editions; but I prefer “and he seized the arm,” as in the Vulgate, Deuteronomy 33:20. Immediately it continues: “Who will break the crown of the head and the arms,” etc. AREV.

47. “Like a lion he rested, and he seized the arm and the crown, and he saw his dominion.” Let them recognize who rested like a lion, except Christ in his tomb. Who broke the crown and the arms of the powerful, except our Redeemer, who humbled the strength and pride of the exalted? Who saw his dominion, except the one to whom dominion, honor, and kingship were given?

[Note: [Col. 0284D]]

48. “Asher,” up to “will live forever,” from Ambrose. GRIAL.

48. “Asher’s bread is rich, and he shall provide delicacies for kings.” Asher, whose name signifies riches, is likewise Christ, whose is the abundance of riches, wisdom, and knowledge. Although he was rich, he became poor for our sake; his bread became rich—that is, his flesh, which is the food of the saints.

355 49. Whoever eats this will not die forever. He also provides the delicacies of wisdom to kings, that is, to those who govern their own thoughts well, who rule over their vices, who discipline their bodies and bring them into subjection.

50. Naphtali, which means “expanse,” signifies the apostles and holy preachers, whose teaching has been poured out across the breadth of the whole world. For from this tribe came the apostles, who are the leaders and guides of the Churches: “the leaders of Zebulun and the leaders of Naphtali,” which without doubt refers to the person of the apostles.

51. “They are the sons of those who have been shaken out” (Psalm 126), that is, of the prophets, who are placed in the hand of the mighty God and, like a shot arrow, have reached to the ends of the earth. Hence Naphtali is also rightly written here as “a stag let loose,” because the apostles, or preachers of the Gospel, leaping forth with swift bounds, transcend the entanglements of this world like deer. Thus, meditating on lofty and exalted things, they give words of beauty, that is, they preach the teaching of the Lord the Savior to all nations.

[Col. 0284C] 52. “Joseph is a growing son.” After the Lord’s Passion, this prophecy retained the image of the Father’s voice, because the Father addresses Christ as he returns to heaven after his victory, saying: “Joseph is a growing son”—a growing son, certainly, among the nations. For when he had abandoned the people because of the Synagogue’s unbelief, he enlarged for himself an innumerable people of the Church from all the nations.

53. David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Psalm 21). “A growing son, beautiful in appearance.” His beauty surpasses all others, in accordance with what is also sung of him in the Psalms: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44). “The daughters ran upon the wall,” that is, the nations, or the Churches, which believed in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0284D]]

54. “They were rebuked” is used for “they rebuked,” a usage that would not easily be found in other witnesses. Instead of “or inflicted some wound,” Alborn gives: “Or inflicted some injury.” AREV.

54. These, established upon the solidity of faith as upon a wall, inflamed by love of Christ’s beauty, run about so that they may behold the true bridegroom through contemplation, be joined to him by the kiss of charity, and cling to him. But “they rebuked him” when, making accusations through false testimonies, the people of the Synagogue attempted to suppress the Holy One of the Lord. “And they envied him, having arrows.” For no one shot an arrow into Joseph, nor did anyone cast at him any weapon of injury; rather, this happened specifically in Christ.

55. “His bow rests upon the strong one.” For Christ placed his bow and weapons of warfare in God, who is the strong defender, by whose power all the wickedness of the faithless is destroyed. “And the bonds of his arms were loosed,” the bonds with which his brothers led him bound to Pilate, or with which they crucified him, hanging him upon the wood. For they were cut through by the hands of Jacob—that is, by the hand of the omnipotent God of Jacob—from whose mouth the Lord himself, the good shepherd, went forth, the stone and strength of believers in Israel.

56. “The God of your father shall be your helper.” Who helped the Son except the Father alone, who said: “Jacob is my servant; my soul will receive him”? “And the Almighty shall bless you with blessings from heaven above, with blessings from the abyss lying below.” For through the blessing of the heavenly abyss he subjected to him all heavenly things, and through the blessing of what lies below, earthly things, so that he might rule over all angels and human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0285D]]

57. “With the blessings of breasts,” or of the two Testaments, up to “I sanctified you,” from the same Ambrose. GRIAL.

57. “With the blessings of breasts,” whether of the two Testaments, one of which announced him and the other revealed him, or with the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed because that holy virgin gave the Lord the nourishment of milk. Hence that woman says in the Gospel: “Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you suckled” (Luke 11).

[Note: [Col. 0285D]]

58. “With the blessings of breasts and womb.” These words are from Ambrose. But a second member is missing here: for, attributing the breasts to the mother, he interprets the womb, bosom, heart, and some innermost secret of paternal charity and nature, in which the Son always is and from which he proceeds as from a generative womb. GRIAL.

Ibid. “From which birth.” Thus Ambrose. “From which” is printed incorrectly in all the books. GRIAL.

58. “With the blessings of breasts and womb.” Here too the womb of that same mother is blessed, namely, the virginal womb that gave birth to Christ the Lord for us. Of that birth it is said through Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1). “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your brothers.” “The blessings,” he says, “of your heavenly Father, which were given to you from the summit of heaven and of the abyss, have been strengthened”—that is, they have prevailed—over the blessings of your brothers.

59. For the blessing of the omnipotent Father in the Son prevailed beyond the merit of all the saints, patriarchs, and prophets, so that no saint is equal to him. “Until the desire of the eternal hills shall come.” These hills are the saints who, prophesying Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great desire. Of them the Lord also says: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see” (Matthew 13:17). These saints, therefore, are called hills because of the excellence of their holiness.

60. They are also called eternal because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world but are believed to be eternal. “Let all these things be upon the head of Joseph”—that is, all these blessings are placed upon Christ’s head, which he received when he became incarnate—“and upon the crown of the Nazirite,” of whom it is written: “He shall be called a Nazirite” (Matthew 2), that is, the holy one of God among his brothers, because he is the head, exalted above all the saints, whom he also calls his brothers in the Psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0286D]]

61. “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf,” up to “he did not do before,” all from Gregory, *Moral Expositions on Job*, book 18, chapter 11, and Rufinus. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Because he is faithful.” In Grialius’s text it was *qua fidelis* (“as faithful”). AREV.

61. “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils.” By these words the apostle Paul is represented, born from the stock of Benjamin. In the morning he seized the prey—that is, at the beginning he ravaged whatever believers he could. In the evening he divided the spoils, because afterward, having become faithful, he distributed the sacred words with marvelous discernment to those who heard them. We read of one of the teachers referring to Jerusalem the things written about Benjamin. “Benjamin,” he says, “is interpreted as ‘son of sorrow.’”

[Col. 0286B] 62. By lot he received as an inheritance the place in which earthly Jerusalem is situated, which now, because of unbelief, has been cast away and rejected. This is represented in the sons under the person of Benjamin. For just as Benjamin receives the final blessing, so that same people will be saved last, after the fullness of the nations has entered.

63. For it is said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf.” He is a wolf, certainly, because that people shed the blood of the prophets and the righteous. It is called ravenous because of its great greed. For it will come from great hunger and famine for the word of God; it is ravenous because it also violently seized the kingdom of God. “In the morning he eats the prey.” That morning is believed to be the time when we received the law. For then a first illumination of knowledge was given to the world. He eats in the morning because, by the law he received, he still eats and meditates, although, by following the law of righteousness, he has not reached the law of faith.

64. “In the evening he shall divide the spoils.” The evening is that final time when he will be converted. Then he will divide the food, because then he will understand that the letter must be divided from the spirit, and then he will recognize that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” Therefore, since he has already begun, enlightened by the Lord’s grace, to divide and separate the spiritual things of the law from bodily things, it is said: “In the evening he shall divide the food”—something he did not do before, although he had meditated on the law all day.

[Note: [Col. 0286D]]

65. Some omit this number and what follows up to the end of the commentary on Genesis because they had brought forward these same words elsewhere. AREV.

65. But it is asked why Jacob made all those whom he begot from free women and maidservants sons and heirs with equal honor, unless to show that Christ the Lord bestows heavenly rewards upon all the nations who are reconciled to his body through faith, granting all equal honor and glory? There is no distinction whether one is Jew or Greek, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free, because in all things and in everyone Christ is present.

[Col. 0287A] 66. For this reason our Savior and Lord assumed the form of a servant and served for the free person and the slave, so that he might bestow an equal gift of heavenly blessings upon all who believe in him. In his presence the one who is nobler according to the flesh is not preferred. For whoever wins the Lord’s approval through faith is not darkened by any stains of carnal birth. That this would indeed happen is also signified through the Prophet, when the Lord says: “It shall be in the last days: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.”

# INTO EXODUS

[Col. 0287]

359 PREFACE

[Col. 0287A]

1. We have briefly touched upon certain mysteries from the book of Genesis, and upon the more obscure matters of its historical events, which have been concealed beneath allegorical figures, excerpting them from the books of our predecessors.

[Col. 0287B] [Note: [Col. 0287D]]

PREFACE, no. 2. “Typical.” Thus some manuscripts and printed editions. In Grialius, *typicae* is perhaps an error. AREV.

2. We now add, one by one, certain typical and figurative mysteries of the following law, drawn from the writings of holy men, bringing forward only a few passages from their style.

3. For who could investigate all the matters of the law, which are so immense that they cannot easily be explained even according to the text of the history? Therefore we have followed it only as far as we thought sufficient for the adjoining work, lest the little book exceed its proper limits and the reader encounter weariness.

# CHAPTER I. On the Seventy Souls

[Note: [Col. 0287D]]

CHAPTER I, no. 1. “Seventy souls.” Compare Suarius’s note on the *Allegories*, no. 65, where he gives the reason why the Lord is believed to have chosen seventy-two disciples. It should be noted, however, that a perfect or complete number is sometimes used for an imperfect and incomplete one. The discussion will return to this point later. AREV.

1. First of all, seventy souls entered Egypt with Jacob. The seventy disciples are sent into the whole world to preach the word of God.

2. In another sense, these seventy souls who entered Egypt are mystically understood through the number of remission, namely, so that forgiveness of sins might be granted to this age—which was represented by Egypt—after so many sins and sacrileges. For Egypt is shown, through many prophetic utterances, to signify this world figuratively.

# CHAPTER II. On the Death of Joseph

[Note: [Col. 0287D]]

CHAPTER II. “When Joseph had died,” up to “the Church would have brought forth.” Origen, *Homily 1 on Exodus*. But all our books have “would have taken away,” whereas Rufinus has “would have brought forth.” GRIAL.

1. When Joseph and his brothers had died, the sons of Israel increased and became exceedingly strong. So also our true Joseph, after tasting death for all, through which he destroyed the devil who held the power of death, caused the people of the faithful to multiply. For unless, as he himself says, the grain of wheat had fallen into the earth and died (John 12), the Church of the whole world would certainly not have produced this abundant fruit.

# CHAPTER III. On the Affliction of the People

[Col. 0288A]

[Note: [Col. 0288D]]

CHAPTER III. “To close off.” Another reading: “to harden.” GRIAL.

1. Pharaoh afflicts the sons of Israel with mud and brick. Israel is an image of our people. Pharaoh, however, is the devil, who imposed the heaviest yoke of slavery: to work with mud and brick, that is, to be engrossed in earthly and filthy works, with straw also mixed in—that is, with trivial and irrational deeds—so that through these acts of vice he might crush God’s people and close up everyone’s hearts with a wall of unbelief, so that there would be no one who could destroy or conquer his kingdom.

# CHAPTER IV. On the Killing of the Males

1. Pharaoh also orders the males to be killed and the females to live. So too the devil strives to prevent the strength of faith from prevailing: when the virtues have been killed, vices remain. He seeks to kill the strongest and manly powers of the soul, from which we possess knowledge of heavenly and divine things—that is, reason, prudence, steadfastness, innocence, and faith in a human being—and to leave alive in him what is feminine, weak, fragile, and inclined to vices: ambition, drunkenness, lust, anger, cruelty, rage, and other things like them, which are represented under the figure of women.

# CHAPTER V. On the Finding of Moses

1. Then Moses is found exposed on the bank of the river, and the Lord, whose type Moses had assumed, is found by believers at the river of the washing and at the water of baptism. The infant was weeping because Christ the Lord was lamenting the sins of the old man whom he had assumed; hence, when he raised Lazarus, he wept, mourning the faithlessness of the Jews.

2. Pharaoh’s daughter descended to the river’s washing and gathered up the infant. The Church from the nations, desiring the sanctification of the saving washing, received Christ, expelled like an infant from the Synagogue, his carnal mother. For he then appeared small when he was seen in human form.

[Note: [Col. 0288D]]

[Chapter V, Note 3]

**Chapter V, Note 3.** “In a little vessel, *thibi*.” Another manuscript has *thebe*, not improperly. For in Greek it is θίβις, and θήβη, and also θίβη. Concerning this word Augustine writes in his *Expressions*: “What *thibin* means is difficult to know for this reason: neither did the Greek translator render this name from the Hebrew, nor the Latin translator from the Greek, but he translated it as he found it.” Jerome, Rufinus, and the Greek scholiast removed this difficulty; but whether the word was Hebrew *thibath* or rather Egyptian, it is clear that it later came into use among the Greeks, as is attested by Athenaeus. [Grial.]

3. She found Moses enclosed in a little vessel, *thibi*, [Col. 0289A] which is made from many wild reeds. The Church found Christ concealed in the hearts of the saints, who, woven together into unity from the members of many brothers and all made one body in Christ, receive him with religious devotion and guard him.

**362 Chapter VI. On the Egyptian who was killed**

[Chapter VI, Note 1]

**Chapter VI, Note 1.** “Meanwhile Moses.” The whole chapter is taken from *Against Faustus* XXII, chapter 90. [Grial.]

1. Meanwhile Moses, unable to endure that a brother who was a sojourner and was suffering injury from an Egyptian should go unavenged, defended him and killed that same Egyptian. Its meaning is readily apparent: the devil, who inflicts injury during this pilgrimage, was killed by the Lord Christ while we were being defended.

[Chapter VI, Note 2]

**Chapter VI, Note 2.** Codex Albornoz has *morticina praesentia* (“the presence of a dead thing”); another manuscript has *morticinam praesentem* (“the present dead thing”). The adjective is *morticinus*, that is, “dead of itself,” not slaughtered or killed. [Arevalus.]

2. But the fact that he buried the slain man in the sand makes clear that his now-dead presence already lies hidden in those who do not possess a stable foundation. [Col. 0289B] Hence also the Lord builds the Church upon a rock, and compares those who hear his word and do it to a wise man who builds his house upon rock, so that it may not yield to temptations and collapse.

3. But those who hear the word and do not do it he compares to a foolish man building upon sand, whose house, when tested, brings about a great ruin (Matthew 7).

**Chapter VII. On the fire in the bush**

[Chapter VII, Note 1]

**Chapter VII, Note 1.** “Then, while he was tending … until ‘was burned up,’” from Gregory, *Homily* 7 on Ezekiel. [Grial.]

The manuscript of Albornoz has the distinctive reading: “whom he foreknew would be his own.” [Arevalus.]

1. Then, while Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro his father-in-law, he saw a bush burning and not being consumed. The Lord appeared to Moses in the bush, sending him to a people whom he knew would become wicked. There was a flame in the bush—that is, among the thorns—and the bush was not consumed. The bush signifies the thorns of Jewish sins; the flame in the bush signifies the word of God. [Col. 0289C]

2. Thus, the fact that the Law was given to them was the flame in the bush. The fact that their sins were not consumed after the Law had been given was shown by the bush not being burned up beneath the fire. Others understand the Church in the burning bush that does not burn to be inflamed by persecutions and, with the Lord speaking within it, not to perish.

**363** 3. But the fact that the Lord is read to have appeared to Moses in that same bush shows that he appears to believers nowhere other than in the Church. No one can worthily stand in it or see God unless he has laid aside all earthly and mortal vices; this was signified by Moses’ removal of his sandals.

[Chapter VII, Note 4]

**Chapter VII, Note 4.** Ambrose, *On Ruth*, book III of *On the Faith*, chapter 5: “The one who was to come from the Jews—the Jews from whom Christ is according to the flesh—was being signified; he would raise up the seed of his neighbor, that is, of the dead people, through the seed of heavenly teaching. The spiritual things of the prescribed Law brought the bridal sandal by which the Church was to be joined. Moses was not the bridegroom; for it is said to him: ‘Loosen the sandal from your feet,’ so that he might yield to his lord, and so forth.” [Grial.]

4. The command that Moses be barefoot has another meaning as well. It was the ancient custom that, if a bridegroom wished to repudiate his bride, he would remove his sandal, and this would be the sign of repudiation (Deuteronomy 25). Therefore Moses is commanded to remove his sandals, so that he might not approach the Church, which was signified by the bush, as a bridegroom still wearing his sandal.

[Chapter VII, Note 5]

**Chapter VII, Note 5.** “He removed from them the occasion.” Thus in Albornoz and Florence 1. Grial printed *abstulit illas occasioni* (“he removed them for the occasion”), though I do not know where he obtained this reading, since the other printed editions have *abstulit occasionem* (“he removed the occasion”), omitting *illis* (“from them”). [Arevalus.]

5. This was reserved for Christ, who was the true bridegroom. John says of him: “Of whom I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1). This is plainly as was said concerning Joshua and Moses. The Hebrews, however, say that God appeared to Moses in the bush and not in another kind of wood so that the Jews might perhaps not carve an idol from that same wood. For God always removed from them the occasion of idolatry.

**Chapter VIII. On the rod changed into a serpent**

1. Moses is then sent to free the people of Israel. He says to the Lord: “What sign shall I have, so that they may believe me, because you have sent me?” And the Lord says to him: [Col. 0290B] “Throw upon the ground the rod that you carry in your hand.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent. Moses was terrified and fled. The Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it again became a rod.

2. What does this signify? The serpent persuaded the human being to death. Therefore death came from the serpent. Thus the rod in the serpent signifies Christ in death. And yet Moses was terrified and fled. What does Moses’ flight from that serpent mean, unless what is recorded as having happened in the Gospel? Christ died; the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had stood.

3. But what is meant by the command, “Take hold of its tail”? What is the tail except the latter part? This signified: “You shall see my latter things.” At first it became a serpent; but when its tail was seized, it became a rod, because he was first killed and afterward, when everything had been accomplished, returned by rising again to what he had been. Through the restoration of life, with death destroyed, nothing of the serpent appeared in him.

4. The tail of the serpent may also signify the end of the world, because the mortality of the Church rolls along through the slippery course of time: some depart and others come through death, as though through a serpent; for death was sown through the serpent. But at the final end, like the tail of the world, we return to the hand of God; when seized, we shall be restored, and, when the last enemy—death—has been destroyed, rising again in the right hand of God, we shall be the rod of his kingdom.

**Chapter IX. On Moses’ leprous hand**

[Chapter IX, Note 1]

**Chapter IX, Note 1.** Words of the Vulgate: “Why do you turn away your hand, and your right hand, etc., from the middle of your bosom?” [Arevalus.]

1. Another sign is likewise given to Moses: “Put your hand,” he says, “into your bosom.” And he put it in. “Bring it out,” he says. He brought it out, and it was found white—that is, unclean; for whiteness on the skin is leprosy, not brightness. Thus God’s own inheritance, that is, the people sent out from him, became unclean. Concerning it Scripture says: “Why do you turn away your face and your right hand from the middle of your bosom?” (Psalm 73:11). But what does he say to it? “Bring it back into your bosom.” He brought it back, and it returned to its former color.

2. So also the Jewish people are now alienated from God’s bosom and remain unclean outside; but he will bring them back, and they will return to their former color when they recognize the Lord Savior. For now a partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel is saved.

**Chapter X. On the waters changed into blood**

1. Then the waters poured out by Moses upon the earth are changed into blood, that is, the peoples are brought into faith in the blood of Christ. For the Apocalypse says: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations” (Revelation 17).

**365 Chapter XI. On Moses’ entrance to Pharaoh**

[Chapter XI, Note 1]

**Chapter XI, Note 1.** “What is the three days’ journey … up to the sacrifice of praise?” Origen, *On Exodus* IV, Homily 3. [Grial.]

1. After this Moses and Aaron enter before Pharaoh, asking that the people of Israel be allowed to travel a three days’ journey into the wilderness and there sacrifice to the Lord God. What is the three days’ journey that we must make so that, leaving Egypt, we may reach the place where we ought to offer sacrifice? This way is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

[Chapter XI, Note 2]

**Chapter XI, Note 2.** “The abominations of the Egyptians … until ‘they strive to please,’” Gregory, *Moralia* X, chapter 16. [Grial.]

2. What is the three-day journey that we must make? Whoever confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead on the third day will be saved. This, then, is the three-day journey by which one reaches the place where a sacrifice of praise is offered and rendered to the Lord. “We shall sacrifice the abominations of the Egyptians,” they say, “to the Lord our God.”

3. The Egyptians disdain eating sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate the Israelites offer to God, because the simplicity of conscience that the wise men of this age—that is, the citizens of Egypt—regard as foolishness, the righteous offer to God as a sacrifice. They strive to please God by what they see as rejected and contemptible to the age and to the world, in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1).

4. From the time Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, [Col. 0291D] the people of God were afflicted more severely. Once the word of God has been brought into the human soul, the crafty enemy rises up more fiercely and introduces greater vices by which it may be conquered. Before the word that would rebuke vices arrived, they remained in peace. But when the word of God begins to expose the condition of each person, then great turmoil arises.

**Chapter XII. On the rod changed into a dragon**

[Col. 0292A]

1. Moses then threw down his rod before Pharaoh, and, having become a serpent, it devoured the serpents of the Egyptians. This signified that the Word would become flesh and, through the forgiveness and pardon of sins, would empty out the venom of the dreadful serpent. For the rod is the straight, royal word of God, full of power and marked by sovereignty.

2. The rod became a serpent because he who was the Son of God, born from God the Father, became the Son of Man, born from a virgin. Raised up like a serpent upon the cross, he poured medicine into human wounds. Hence the Lord himself says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3).

[Col. 0292B] 3. For Moses’ rod, changed into a dragon, swallowed the rods of the magicians; and Christ, after the dignity of his glory, became obedient even unto death, and through that death of the flesh consumed the sting of death, as the prophet bears witness: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hosea 13).

**Chapter XIII. On Pharaoh’s hardening**

1. The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, namely because, after sin, he so hardened the devil that he would never be softened by the compunction of repentance, as it is written concerning him in Job: “He will be hardened like a stone” (Job 41).

**367 Chapter XIV. On the ten plagues**

[Chapter XIV, Note 1]

**Chapter XIV, Note 1.** “Then the plagues are inflicted.” What is said about the ten plagues, apart from a few details, is taken from Origen’s fourth homily on chapter 7 of Exodus; they are also read in Augustine, *Sermon* 87 *On Time*. [Grial.]

1. Then plagues are inflicted upon Egypt. Although those events took place bodily among the Egyptians, they now take place spiritually in us. Egypt is a figure of the world. The first plague is that in which the waters are first changed into blood. The Egyptian waters are the wandering and slippery teachings of the philosophers.

2. They are rightly changed into blood, because they think carnally about the causes of things. But when the cross of Christ has shown the light of truth to this world, it will rebuke it with such corrections that, from the character of its punishments, it may recognize its own errors.

[Chapter XIV, Note 3]

**Chapter XIV, Note 3.** “Who in vain.” This seems better with Albornoz and Augustine than *quae inani*, as Grial printed it. [Arevalus.]

3. In the second plague, frogs are produced. By these, some figuratively understand the poems of poets, who, with a certain empty and inflated melody, like the sounds and croakings of frogs, have brought stories of deception into this world. For a frog is exceedingly talkative vanity; the animal is useful for nothing else except that it produces the sound of its voice through shameless and importunate cries.

[Chapter XIV, Note 4]

**Chapter XIV, Note 4.** *Cyniphes* is written thus in the *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 8. Grial printed *scyniphes* here. The variations among others in the spelling of this word are remarkable. [Arevalus.]

4. After this, *cyniphes* are produced. This animal is suspended by wings and flies through the air; but it is so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight of the eyes unless they are sharply discerning. It pierces with a most bitter sting the body upon which it settles, so that although no one can see it flying, he immediately feels it stinging.

5. This kind of animal is therefore compared with heretical subtlety, which pierces souls with subtle verbal stings and surrounds them with such cunning that the one deceived neither sees nor understands how he is being deceived. But the fact that, at the third sign, the magicians ceased, saying, “This is the finger of God,” shows that those magicians bore the type and spirit of heretics.

**368 [Chapter XIV, Note 6]**

**Chapter XIV, Note 6.** Grial writes *Jamnes*; the Vulgate has *Jannes*, and immediately afterward “and these also.” [Arevalus.]

6. The Apostle makes this clear, saying: “Just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth—men corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not progress further, for their folly will be evident to all, as theirs also was” (2 Timothy 3:8). These men, who through that corruption of mind were extremely restless, failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them.

7. For the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is placed third. Hence, failing at the third sign, they said: “This is the finger of God.” Just as the Holy Spirit, reconciled and appeased, grants rest to the meek and humble in heart, so, when hostile toward the harsh and proud, he stirs up unrest. That unrest was signified by those very small flies, under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.”

[Chapter XIV, Note 8]

**Chapter XIV, Note 8.** “For a fly is exceedingly insolent … until ‘are struck,’” words of Gregory, *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 25. [Grial.]

8. In the fourth place Egypt is struck by flies. A fly is a very insolent and restless animal. What else is signified by it than the insolent cares of carnal desires? Egypt is therefore struck by flies because the hearts of those who love this age are tormented by the restlessness of their desires.

[Chapter XIV, Note 9]

**Chapter XIV, Note 9.** Isidore discusses the canine eloquence of lawyers in *Sentences* III, chapter 57; Loaisa has an erudite note on that passage. [Arevalus.]

9. Moreover, the Septuagint translators used *cynomyia*, that is, “dog-fly,” by which canine behavior is signified, in which the pleasure and lust of the human mind are exposed as fleshly. This passage can also signify through the dog-fly the forensic eloquence of human beings, by which they tear one another apart like dogs.

10. Then, in the fifth place, Egypt is struck by the death of animals, or cattle. Here the senselessness and folly of mortals is rebuked: like irrational beasts, they have assigned the worship and name of God to images—not only images of human beings but also of cattle—impressed upon wood and stones. They worship Ammon-Jupiter in the form of a ram, Anubis in the form of a dog, and Apis in the form of a bull; and they also worship the other portents of their gods at which Egypt marvels. In those things in which they believed divine worship to have entered, they saw pitiable punishments.

**369** 11. After this, in the sixth plague, ulcers and swollen blisters accompanied by burning fever are produced as a scourge. In the ulcers the deceitful and purulent wickedness of this age is rebuked; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the burning fevers, anger and the madness of rage. Up to this point such punishments are apportioned to the world through figures of its errors.

12. After this, scourges come from above: namely, voices, thunder, hail, and fire running about. In the thunder, rebukes and divine corrections are understood, because God does not scourge in silence; rather, he gives forth voices and sends teaching from heaven, by which the chastised world may recognize its guilt.

13. He also gives hail, by which the still tender growths of vices are laid waste. He gives fire as well, knowing that there are thorns and thistles for that fire to consume. [Col. 0294B] Concerning this the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). Through this fire the incitements of pleasure and lust are consumed.

[Chapter XIV, Note 14]

**Chapter XIV, Note 14.** “In another sense … until ‘locusts,’” Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 27. [Grial.]

In Grial perhaps one should read: “In another sense, up to pleasures.” [Arevalus.]

14. The fact that locusts are mentioned in the eighth place is thought by some to refute through this kind of plague the instability of the human race, which is divided and discordant within itself. In another sense, locusts should be understood as representing the mobility of fickleness, like a wandering and leaping soul amid the pleasures of the world.

15. In the ninth plague, darkness was made, either to expose the blindness of their minds or to make them understand that the reasons of divine dispensation and providence are exceedingly obscure. For God made darkness his hiding place (Psalm 17). Wishing to search these matters out boldly and rashly, and asserting one thing after another, they descended into the dense and palpable darkness of ignorance.

16. Finally, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed—whether the principalities, powers, and rulers of the darkness of this world, or the authors and inventors of the false religions that existed in this world, which the truth of Christ extinguished and destroyed together with their authors.

17. As for what follows, “Among their gods I shall execute judgment,” the Hebrews assert that, on the night when the people departed, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, either by an earthquake or by the striking of lightning. Spiritually, however, we say that, when we depart from the Egypt of errors, the idols of error fall and the whole worship of perverse doctrines is shaken.

**Chapter XV. On Passover**

[Col. 0294D]

1. Meanwhile Passover takes place: in the slaughter of the lamb, Christ is slain, concerning whom the Gospel says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The lamb is sacrificed in the evening; in the evening of the world the Lord suffered. Those who celebrate Passover are forbidden to break the bones; the Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross, as the Evangelist bears witness: “You shall not break his bone” (John 19). The doorposts of the Israelites are smeared with the lamb’s blood, so that the destroying angel may not dare to bring destruction upon them.

2. Faithful peoples are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s Passion as a safeguard of salvation, so that only those may be freed from destruction who have been marked in heart and forehead by the blood of the Lord’s Passion. They also speak through their deeds: “The light of your face, O Lord, has been marked upon us.” Hence the solemnity itself is called *Phase*, which we may call “passage,” because, proceeding from worse things to better, we leave behind dark Egypt.

3. What he says concerning the eating of that lamb—“No foreigner shall eat of it,” and “It shall be eaten in one house,” and “You shall not carry any of its flesh outside”—is properly understood as written concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body, of which that lamb was a figure. His body and blood are commanded to be eaten in one house, that is, in one Church, and not to be carried outside, namely among the communities of heretics, which wander outside the unity of the Catholic Church.

**Chapter XVI. On the treasures of the Egyptians**

1. God then commanded the people through Moses to ask the Egyptians to lend them things which they might carry away. Thus Moses and the departing people, at the command of the Lord God, stripped the Egyptians of gold and silver, although he commands nothing unjustly.

2. What, then, did these things prefigure except that, in the gold, silver, and clothing of the Egyptians, certain teachings are signified, which are learned from the customs of the nations through no useless diligence? But whether this is what it signifies, or whether it signifies that precious souls from the nations themselves, like vessels of gold and silver together with their bodies—for the clothing signifies these—are joined to the people of God, so that together they may be freed from this age as from Egypt—

**Chapter XVII. On unleavened bread**

1. But when Scripture says that, after the removal of the leaven, the children of Israel departed from Egypt, we too must labor in every way, if possible, so that, leaving the allurements of this age, we may not walk in the leaven of the old malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. This is found in the conduct of the new person, once the former person with his vices has been abandoned.

[Col. 0295D] They indeed ate unleavened bread for seven days. But if, simply and purely, we conduct ourselves during these seven days through which this world is completed—days that continually revolve in their appointed order—and if the Lamb is slain for us daily and Passover is celebrated daily, then we have no leaven of malice and wickedness; renewed, we take no pleasure in doing anything from the malice of the former corruption.

3. For what else is leaven except the corruption of nature? It too first departs from its natural sweetness and is corrupted by an adulterated sourness. In this observance we are commanded always to remember our departure from Egypt, to celebrate Passover—that is, our passage from former things to better things—and to consecrate to the Lord the firstborn of our womb, that is, the beginning of all our works and virtues.

**Chapter XVIII. On the pillar of fire and the cloud**

[Chapter XVIII, Note 1]

**Chapter XVIII, Note 1.** Nearly the whole of this chapter is copied by Saint Ildefonsus, *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, chapter 99, with a few changes, such as: “Christ is also the pillar, because he is the uprightness, firmness, and support of our weakness.” [Arevalus.]

1. Then the Lord is seen by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, going before the people and becoming their guide on the journey. This cloud going before them is Christ; he is also the pillar, because he is upright and firm and supports our weakness. Shining by night and not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (John 9:39).

2. It may also suitably be understood in this way: the mystery of Christ was manifested in the flesh as in the day, as in a cloud; but in the judgment it will be as in the terror of night, because then there will be great tribulation in the world like fire, and it will shine for the righteous and burn for the unrighteous.

**Chapter XIX. On the division of the sea**

1. When the Egyptians follow, Moses strikes the waters with his rod, and the children of Israel pass through the middle of the Red Sea. What is the Red Sea except baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ? The enemies who follow with their king and die behind them are past sins, [Col. 0296C] which are wiped away, and the devil, who is drowned in spiritual baptism. The Egyptians press upon them; sins also urge and pursue, but only as far as the water.

**Chapter XX. On the song**

1. After crossing the Red Sea, the people sing a song to God, with the Egyptians and Pharaoh submerged. In the same way the faithful, after they have risen from the washing, with their sins extinguished, raise a hymn in a voice of thanksgiving, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea.”

2. Yet this is said better and more worthily by the one who has a tambourine in his hand, like Miriam—that is, who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians 5) and has put to death his members that are upon the earth (Colossians 3).

3. After the crossing of the sea, the people are then led through the wilderness. The baptized, indeed, pass through the world without yet enjoying the promised homeland; but because they do not see it, they are in the wilderness, hoping and awaiting it through patience, and there are laborious and dangerous temptations lest they return in heart to Egypt. Nor does Christ finally abandon them there, for that pillar also does not depart.

**Chapter XXI. On the bitter waters**

[Chapter XXI, Note 1]

**Chapter XXI, Note 1.** “When the people had gone out.” From Origen, Homily 7 on chapter 15, or from Augustine, *Sermon* 91 *On Time*. [Grial.]

1. When the people had gone out from the Red Sea, a wilderness confronted them. After traveling through it for three days, they had no water and came to the spring of Marah, which received its name from its bitterness. The people murmured when they saw the water and could not bear to drink it. Moses threw a piece of wood into the water, and it became sweet. Understand that the bitter waters signify the killing letter and the Law.

2. If the confession of the cross is cast into them and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion is joined to them, then the water of Marah becomes sweet, and the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding. Hence it is also written: “The Lord appointed for his people a law and judgments, and tested him.”

[Col. 0297B] 3. In another sense, the fact that the waters of Marah become sweet when they receive wood within them was an indication that the bitterness of the nations would one day be changed into sweetness through the wood of Christ’s cross.

4. In accordance with the preceding interpretation, it should be known that Israel was first led to salty and bitter waters; when the wood shown by the Lord had made them sweet, the people afterward came to springs. For the people of Israel are first led to the letter of the Law, and as long as they remain in it they cannot depart from bitterness.

**Chapter XXII. On the twelve springs**

[Chapter XXII, Note 1]

**Chapter XXII, Note 1.** “When, therefore, through the wood … until ‘he recognized it,’” words of Origen, in the same place. [Grial.]

Prudentius discusses this allegory in *Dittochaeon*, no. 14. In my commentary I have noted several things from Saint Ildefonsus and Saint Martin of León, who likewise follow Isidore. There I also explained why Christ’s disciples are sometimes said to number seventy-two. Instead of “preached the faith of Christ,” Codex Regiovat. 693 has “made the faith of Christ known to the world,” which I consider the genuine reading. [Arevalus.]

1. When, therefore, through the wood of life the water had been made sweet, and the Law had begun to be understood spiritually, the people passed from the Old Testament to the New and came to the twelve apostolic springs. There were also trees of seventy palms. For it was not only the twelve apostles who preached the faith of Christ; the other seventy, sent to preach the word of God, are also mentioned, through whom the world might recognize the palms of Christ’s victory.

[Chapter XXII, Note 2]

**Chapter XXII, Note 2.** *Septiforme* (“sevenfold”). Albornoz has *septiformis* (“sevenfold”). Grial, as I believe, printed *septiformem* incorrectly, although the same form, *septiformem*, is also read in Saint Martin of León, who copies Isidore, volume I, page 298. [Arevalus.]

2. Indeed, these twelve springs, watering seventy palm trees, prefigure apostolic grace, watering peoples in a sevenfold number multiplied by ten, so that through the sevenfold gift of the Spirit the Decalogue of the Law may be fulfilled.

**Chapter XXIII. On the food of birds and on manna**

[Chapter XXIII, Note 1]

**Chapter XXIII, Note 1.** “The people murmured … until ‘above honey and the honeycomb,’” a sentence from the same work of Origen; the wording differs. [Grial.]

On *conturnicem*: Albornoz has *coturnices* (“quail”), which seems preferable. [Arevalus.]

1. Meanwhile the people murmured in the wilderness because of hunger, and, turning, looked from afar upon the glory of God in the cloud. In the evening they saw quail, and on the morning of the following day, manna. What is meant by the food of birds except divinely sent preachings? They pass through resounding words, flying through the air like winged creatures, and those who strive to reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom are nourished by them through faith.

2. The food of birds can also signify the sayings of the ancient Law, which fed the carnal people as with flesh through words sent by God, like flying creatures. Hence they are given in the evening, because all the things that were granted to them carnally were destined to have an end.

3. But when the light of faith had been manifested, manna was given to the people. Manna, of course, is Christ, who descended from heaven like living bread and is rained upon the whole world through evangelical clouds. It is no longer given to the murmuring people and testing Synagogue, but to the Church that believes and places its hope in him. This is the unfailing manna; this is the bread of heaven and the true food of angels, by which the word of God feeds corruptible beings incorruptibly. So that a human being might eat it, it became flesh and dwelt among us.

4. Those who feed on it live spiritually. For those who received the ancient figure carnally died. Manna may also suitably signify heavenly sayings. Hence the interpretation of the name has this meaning: *manna* is interpreted as “What is this?” When we hear the Law of God being read in church, we ask the teachers, saying: “What is this?” This manna was small, like coriander seed, and sweet.
