What is smaller than the word of God? What is more subtle? Or what is sweeter and more pleasant than the sayings of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb (Psalm 118)?

[Chapter XXIII, Note 5]

**Chapter XXIII, Note 5.** “But what does it mean that on the sixth … until ‘it becomes a worm,’” from the same passage. [Grial.]

5. But why is a double portion commanded to be gathered on the sixth day, one that would also suffice for the Sabbath? This sixth day is the sixth age of the world, in which we now are. Therefore the one who hears and does the word of God for the hope of eternal life gathers a double portion in this age; the one who lives well and shows mercy to others stores up a double portion in it.

[Chapter XXIII, Note 6]

**Chapter XXIII, Note 6.** Albornoz has: “And because of the reason for the Sabbath they kept it; it boiled over, etc.” *Propter* (“because of”) should be rejected. Grial printed *praeter causas* (“apart from the reasons”). [Arevalus.]

6. What was stored up for the Sabbath was not corrupted. For good works done for the sake of future rest remain in the future age. But when unbelievers stored manna apart from the reason of the Sabbath, worms boiled out of it and it putrefied. So also, in those who store up for the sake of the present life and love of the world, that worm boils out which never dies. These are the worms generated by avarice and the blind greed for riches in those who possess money and, seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts against them.

[Chapter XXIII, Note 7]

**Chapter XXIII, Note 7.** “But also to those who …” Thus in the Codex of Albornoz. Grial, with the other printed editions, has: “But also for the one who sins after receiving the word of God, the word of God itself becomes a worm for him, which continually gnaws at his conscience,” etc. Although this is somewhat involved, it can nevertheless be tolerated. [Arevalus.]

7. But for those who sin after receiving the word of God, the word of God itself becomes a worm that continually digs into their conscience and gnaws at the secrets of their hearts. Yet Christ too is a worm, as he himself says: “But I am a worm and not a human being” (Psalm 21). Just as he is for some a stumbling block and for others a resurrection, so in the manna he becomes for the faithful the sweetness of honey, but for unbelievers a worm.

**Chapter XXIV. On the rock struck with the rod**

[Chapter XXIV, Note 1]

**Chapter XXIV, Note 1.** “After manna … until ‘their thirst,’” from the same work. [Grial.]

At this point Grial has *quaeritur populus* (“the people seeks”); Albornoz has *ejus aperto latere cuncta fluxerunt* (“when its side was opened, everything flowed forth”). [Arevalus.]

1. After the manna, the people complained under the heat because of thirst, and a spring burst forth from the rock. The same rock, which, when struck, spewed out water, bore the figure of Christ. When it was opened, all the waters flowed forth; the wood of the Passion approached it like a rod, so that grace might flow out for believers. When the rock was struck, a spring flowed forth. When Christ was struck on the cross, he poured out upon the thirsty the grace of the washing and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

2. The Apostle proves that this rock bore the figure of Christ when he said: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” But what does it mean that the thirsty people murmured against Moses because of the water, and that for this reason God commanded him to show them the rock from which they should drink, except that, if there is someone who, while reading Moses, murmurs against him and is displeased with the Law as it is written according to the letter, Moses shows him the rock, who is Christ, and brings him to it so that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst?

**Chapter XXV. On the battle with Amalek**

[Chapter XXV, Note 1]

**Chapter XXV, Note 1.** “After this Moses,” from the same work. [Grial.]

1. After this Moses went up onto the mountain, while Joshua fought against Amalek. Moses held the rod, and stretched out his arms in the form of a cross. Thus the enemy—that is, the devil—who attempted to block the way to the life of the heavenly homeland, is overcome by the sign of the Lord’s cross. While Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered them, Amalek prevailed. [377] For when we raise our deeds toward heaven, the rulers of darkness are subjected.

[Chapter XXV, Note 2]

**Chapter XXV, Note 2.** “The stone upon which …” Albornoz has: “The stone, that is, the Church, upon Christ, who …” [Arevalus.]

2. But when we pray with relaxed hands—that is, when we pursue an earthly way of life—the enemy follows as victor. Moses sits upon the stone that in Zechariah had seven eyes (Zechariah 3) and in the book of Samuel is called the Stone of Help (1 Samuel 7), while Aaron and Hur, like two peoples or two Testaments, support both his hands.

**Chapter XXVI. On Moses’ kinsman**

[Chapter XXVI, Note 1]

**Chapter XXVI, Note 1.** “When Amalek had been defeated … until ‘is completed,’” Origen, Homily 11 on chapter 17. [Grial.]

1. When Amalek had been defeated, Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, arrived and brought Zipporah—that is, the Church—and each of the two sons born from the two peoples. He gave Moses the counsel of the seventy elders. Moses listened to him and did everything he said. Here there is a matter of great wonder: Moses was a prophet full of God, who spoke with the Lord face to face, yet he accepted counsel from a gentile and did everything he said to him. This happened so that he might give the leaders of the peoples an example of humility and signify an image of the future mystery.

2. For he knew that one day it would come to pass that, through the people gathered from the Gentiles, the things lacking in the Law would be completed, at his prompting; and that this people would bring to the Law a good and spiritual understanding. He knew also that that same people would hear the Law and do whatever it said, and that the deficiency of the Law would be completed through the prompting of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Moses’ Ascent of the Mountain

[Col. 0300B]

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

CHAP. XXVII. Note 1. “It followed,” through “opens to their senses”: these are the words of Gregory, *Moralia* V, chapter 27. GRIAL.

In the same place: “He descended.” The Albornozian manuscript adds: “He descended.” But what is the moral meaning of Moses’ ascending the mountain and the Lord’s descending to the mountain? “The mountain…” Grial reads *itaque* (“therefore”) rather than *utique* (“certainly”). AREV.]

1. After these events, on the forty-seventh day after their departure from Egypt, the people came to Mount Sinai. There Moses ascended to the Lord, and the Lord descended to him. The mountain is the height of our contemplation, to which we ascend so that we may be lifted up to behold things beyond our weakness. But the Lord descends into it, because, when the saints make great progress, he reveals a little of himself to their understanding.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Thunders and Lightning

1. Then, on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated, the Law was given to Moses. Likewise, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion—which that Passover prefigured—the Holy Spirit, the promised Paraclete, was given. He descended upon the apostles and upon those who were with them, numbering one hundred and twenty, the number associated with the Mosaic age; and, when the tongues of believers had been divided, the whole world was filled with evangelical preaching.

2. It is said there that the Law was written by the finger of God. And the Lord says of the Holy Spirit: “By the finger of God I cast out demons.” There the whole people behold voices, lamps, and the smoking mountain, thunder and lightning, and the resounding blast of a trumpet. In the voices and thunders, therefore, the cry of preachers is understood; in the lamps, the radiance of miracles; and in the sound of the trumpet, the powerful preaching of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

CHAP. XXVIII. Note 3. “But when the Lord was about to give the Law,” through “blinds”: the words are Gregory’s, *Moralia* VI, chapter 17. GRIAL.]

3. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered forth commandments and signs in a variety of languages. Sinai is interpreted as “thornbush,” signifying the Church, in which the Lord also speaks to Moses. But the fact that the Lord, when about to give the Law, descended in fire and smoke signifies that he both enlightens the faithful by displaying his brightness and darkens the eyes of unbelievers through the smoke of error.

4. But what is seen in darkness signifies that the impious, who set their minds on earthly things, did not recognize him descending—that is, being born in humility—in the darkness of wickedness. In another sense, he gave the Law while appearing in darkness, because he spoke to unbelievers who would not follow the truth of his Law as though through darkness: “That seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not hear.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Ten Words

[Note: [Col. 0301D]

CHAP. XXIX. Note 1. “He wrote. And these…” Others have: “He writes”; and therefore he marks on stone tablets that the Jews were stiff-necked. “And these…” AREV.]

1. Thereupon the Lord gave Moses the Law of our innocence and of the knowledge of God. He established it in ten words and wrote it with his finger on tablets of stone. These commandments were distributed in such a way that three pertain to love of the divine Trinity, while seven pertain to brotherly love, through which human society is not harmed.

[Note: [Col. 0301D]

2. “In this commandment,” through “but with him”: these words alone were read in the Valerian and Complutensian editions. We have therefore accepted them because they are Augustine’s words, *Letter* 119 to Januarius, chapter 11. GRIAL.

In the same place: Codex Regiovatensis 293 adds in the margin: “By this commandment the likeness of God in human representations is forbidden to be worshiped—not because God does not have an image, but because no image of him ought to be worshiped except that which is also what he himself is, neither instead of him but with him.” AREV.]

2. The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, when it says: “The Lord your God is one God.” Thus, when you hear these words, you are to worship one God the Father and not pour out your fornication among many fabricated gods. In this commandment, the worship of any likeness of God fashioned by human beings is forbidden—not because God does not have an image, but because no image of him ought to be worshiped except that which is also what he himself is, neither instead of him but with him.

[Note: [Col. 0301D]

3. “For creation,” through “your God”: found only in the Valerian manuscript; these are likewise Augustine’s words. GRIAL.]

3. The second commandment pertains to the Son, when it says: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” For creation is mutable, and therefore it is said: “Every creature has been subjected to vanity.” Thus, lest anyone should think that the Son of God, the Word through whom all things were made, is a creature, it is said: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”—that is, do not consider the Son of God to be a creature, since every creature has been subjected to vanity; rather, believe that he is equal to the Father, God from God, the true Word through whom all things were made.

380

[Note: [Col. 0302D]

[Col. 0302D] 4. “In the third commandment of the Law.” Everything from the cited letter of Augustine to Januarius, chapter 11 and following. GRIAL.]

4. The third commandment of the Law intimates the observance of the Sabbath, which pertains to the Holy Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised to us. Since the Holy Spirit is spoken of as the one in whom eternal rest is promised to us, God therefore sanctified the seventh day. For on the other days the sanctification of works is not mentioned; it is mentioned only on the Sabbath, where it says: “God rested.”

5. This commandment, therefore, pertains to the Holy Spirit both because of the designation of sanctification and because of the eternal rest belonging to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day: six days you shall labor, and do all your work; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the name of your God; you shall do no work.”

[Note: [Col. 0302D]

6. “In the work of six days the labor of six thousand years is contained.” What we should think about these words was stated in the note on Genesis, chapter VII: they are plainly spurious and are found neither in the Olivetan manuscript nor in Augustine, from whom the remaining material derives. GRIAL.]

6. In the work of six days the labor of six thousand years is contained. In the seventh, however, the rest and period of that blessed kingdom are shown—a period in which the Jews sin by understanding and celebrating things carnally. And lest we accommodate ourselves to the faith of a deceiving falsehood, God cries out through the prophet: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isaiah I).

7. How, then, will those Sabbaths be sanctified which God hated? That Sabbath, therefore, is sanctified in which eternal rest is promised to us after the good works of this life. Accordingly, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of the rest of the age to come, we truly observe the Sabbath—not by thinking that we should already rest in this life, but so that all the good we do may have no other aim than eternal rest.

8. After these three commandments, which pertain to God, there follows the number seven of the commandments pertaining to love of neighbor, beginning with the honoring of parents. This, however, is fourth in order: “Honor your father and your mother.” For from their parents human beings open their eyes, and this life takes its beginning from love of them. Hence this commandment is first among the seven, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Honor your father and your mother,” which is “the first commandment” (Matthew XV).

381

[Note: [Col. 0302D]

9. From some manuscripts it is inferred that the reading is “the children are commanded to honor,” etc. AREV.]

9. But how can it be first when it is fourth? Because, as has been said, within the number seven—which pertains to love of neighbor—it is first on the second tablet. For this is why two tablets of the Law were given. In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents and not to be insulting toward them, but to show them the reverence due through dutiful devotion. For anyone who does not know how to honor his parents—whom will he be able to spare? Or how will he be able to love others who hates his own?

[Note: [Col. 0302D]

10. Albornoz: “For not only does the one who commits murder by deed commit it, but also the one who closes his compassion toward his brother whom he sees suffering a need that leads to death is held to be a murderer.” Instead of “against a hungry man,” others have “a hungry man.” AREV.]

10. Fifth: “You shall not kill.” For not only does the one who commits murder by deed commit it, but also the one who encounters a hungry or naked person who may die unless he comes to his aid by offering clothing and food; he too will be held to be a murderer.

11. Sixth: “You shall not commit adultery”—that is, no one is to join himself to women other than his wife outside the marriage covenant in order to satisfy lust. The one who approaches another woman apart from his own wife commits adultery in the proper sense.

12. Seventh: “You shall not steal,” which is the vice of rapacity.

13. Eighth: “You shall not give false testimony,” which is the crime of lying and falsity.

14. Ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For it is one thing to do something of this kind with a woman other than one’s wife, and another not to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

15. Tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the desire for possessions. Thus the first of these forbids superstition, the second error, the third destroys love of the world, the fourth impiety, the fifth cruelty, the sixth strikes down fornication, the seventh rapacity, the eighth destroys falsity, the ninth adulterous thought, and the tenth desire for the world.

[Note: [Col. 0303D]

16. “Among all these,” through “as they sound”: these words alone are read in the Valerian and Complutensian editions. They are nevertheless Augustine’s words, chapter 12 of *Letter* 119 to Januarius. GRIAL.

In the same place: Grial had printed *sol ibi quod* (“only there that”), but this was an error. Instead of “among all these … as they sound,” Flor. 2 has a shorter reading: “Of these ten commandments, three pertain to embracing God; the remaining seven to brotherly love, through which human society is not harmed.” After “let the peoples of God be ruled,” Flor. 2 adds: “and let the demons be killed.” AREV.]

16. Among all these ten commandments, only the one given concerning the Sabbath is prescribed for observance figuratively. We have accepted that figure as something to be understood, not celebrated through bodily leisure. The remaining commandments there, however, are literal commandments, observed without any figurative meaning. They signify nothing mystically, but are understood just as they sound. It should be noted that, just as the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues, so the tablets were inscribed with ten commandments, by which the people of God might be ruled.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Two Tablets

1. Why was the Law written on two tablets, unless either to signify the two Testaments or because of the two commandments concerning love of God and love of neighbor, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend? These were set forth separately on the tablets: on one, three commandments pertaining to love of God; on the other, seven pertaining to the fellowship of neighbor.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Stone Tablets

1. But why were these same tablets made of stone, unless to signify the stony heart of the Jews? Through the insensibility of stone he demonstrated the hard stupidity of their minds, concerning which the prophet says: “I will take away from them their heart of stone, and I will give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel XXXVI).

2. Hence the Apostle says: “Not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Corinthians III). For the fleshly tablets do not mean that we should think carnally; rather, because flesh is capable of sensation in comparison with stone, which is without sensation, the hardness of stone signifies an uncomprehending heart, while the sensitivity of flesh signifies an understanding heart.

383

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Altar of Earth

[Note: [Col. 0304D]

CHAP. XXXII. Note 1. “But what is added,” through “we establish by faith”: Gregory, *Moralia* III, chapter 15. GRIAL.]

1. The Lord also adds there: “You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver and gold; you shall make an altar of earth for me.” To make an altar of earth for God is to hope in the Mediator’s incarnation. For our offering is then accepted by God when, on this altar, our humility—that is, whatever good we do—has been placed upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation. On the altar of earth, therefore, we offer the gift of our offerings if we establish our actions firmly through faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Making It of Uncut Stones

[Note: [Col. 0304D]

CHAP. XXXIII. The title is understood as “On the altar,” etc. It is sufficiently clear that these titles were made not by the author but by copyists. AREV.]

1. Then he added: “But if you make a stone altar for me, you shall not build it of cut stones; for if you raise your knife over it, it will be polluted.” The cut stones are those who divide unity and separate themselves from brotherly fellowship through hatred or schisms. Christ does not receive such people into his body, whose figure that altar’s construction foreshadowed.

2. The uncut stones from which the altar is commanded to be built are those who are made firm by unity of faith and conduct. Of them the Apostle says: “You are living stones, built together into spiritual houses.” No iron has been applied to these stones, because they are incorrupt; they have not received the flaming darts of the evil one. Together they make one altar because they follow unity of faith and harmony of love.

384

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Not Ascending It by Steps

[Note: [Col. 0304D]

CHAP. XXXIV. Note 1. In Codex Alb. the reading is *ascendes* (“you shall ascend”), as in the Vulgate, Exodus XX:26; and this is also indicated in the title of this chapter, “On not ascending.” I have therefore retained it, although Grial, with others, gives *accedes* (“you shall approach”). AREV.]

1. “You shall not ascend by steps to my altar”—that is, you shall not reach me by gradually preferring one to another, nor shall you distinguish an earlier from a later in time, because you will not have the Lord of unity favorable to you if you divide and separate him. This is what the Arians do: they divide the inseparable substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Many further commandments of the Law are then given; passing over these, we must discuss those that are more pertinent.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Hebrew Servant for Six Years

[Col. 0304D]

1. After this, the Law commands that if a Hebrew boy should happen to fall into slavery, he is to serve for six years, but in the seventh year he is to be released as a free man. If he does not wish to leave slavery because of his wife and children, his ear shall be pierced with an awl, and he shall be a slave forever.

2. “Forever” here does not refer to the present age but to the future. For if, while serving sin, we wish to be free, after serving through the six ages of this world we shall be freed on the seventh day—that is, in the eternal Sabbath. But if we do not wish this, our ear will be pierced as a testimony to disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to freedom—that is, with our flesh and its works—we shall remain perpetually slaves of sin forever.

385

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Retaliation

1. What does it mean that in this Law an eye is commanded to be given for an eye? The eye is each teacher, as one who shows the way of life. But if he attempts to extinguish his hearer’s understanding through some destructive teaching, if he injures the eye of the soul and disturbs its understanding, he must be removed from the episcopate of the Church; and his disturbed and savage understanding, which produces a stumbling block to faith, must be cast out.

2. But if someone injures the hearer’s tooth—the tooth by which he was grinding and spiritually dividing the nourishment of Scripture so as to transmit from it a subtle meaning into the soul’s interior—then whoever, by tearing out such a tooth, attempts to cut someone off from the body of Christ must have that tooth removed.

[Note: [Col. 0305D]

CHAP. XXXVI. Note 3. “Provides a stumbling block.” This is the reading of the manuscripts and most printed editions, and it agrees with the sense. The reading *praebent* (“they provide”) in Grial is therefore an error. AREV.]

3. For of such people it is said: “You have crushed the teeth of sinners” (Psalm III). Likewise, hand is demanded for hand, and foot for foot. The hand is the action of one who works; the foot is that by which one walks toward good or evil works. Therefore let the one who causes scandal be cut off, not only in faith but also in actions, which are signified by the hand, or who provides an obstacle, by which the feet are understood.

4. Let the one who has burned also receive burning, the one who has handed over a brother’s soul to Gehenna. Through these signs it is shown that this smiter, mutilated in all his members, is to be cut off from the body of the Church, so that the others may fear when they see it and not act similarly.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Offering Tithes and Firstfruits

[Col. 0305D]

1. Among these commandments, the Israelite people are also ordered to offer the tithes of their crops and the firstfruits of all their possessions to the Lord. Spiritually, the firstfruits of crops or of the firstborn signify the beginnings of good works, or the good will itself, which precedes the work; the Pelagians offend by attributing this to themselves. When God commands us to offer these things to him, he indicates that they belong to his own grace.

2. In offering tithes to the Lord, the number ten signifies perfection, because counting increases up to it. Thus, just as in the firstfruits we are commanded to refer the beginnings of our intentions to God, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer the completion of our works to him, from whom we receive both the beginning of good work and the effect of its perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0305D]

CHAP. XXXVII. Note 3. “But what he said,” through “perpetual death”: Gregory, *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 11. GRIAL.

In the same place: Grial reads *immunditias* (“uncleannesses”). AREV.]

3. But when he said, “You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep,” the donkey signifies uncleanness in this passage, while the sheep signifies innocence. To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life to the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done all those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now produce, by doing them, those things which he may place as clean upon God’s sacrifice. What follows—“If you do not redeem it, it shall be killed”—means that an unclean mind, liable to sins, if it is not changed for the better, will be killed by perpetual death.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Calf Burned with Fire

[Note: [Col. 0306D]

CHAP. XXXVIII. Note 1. Perhaps the reading in Alborn. is preferable: “With the tablets, when he had heard that the people had turned to idols.” AREV.]

1. Moses descended from the mountain with the tablets. When he heard that the people had been consecrated to idols, he judged them unworthy to receive the Law and threw the tablets from his hands. After breaking them, he burned the calf they had fashioned.

2. But what does this calf, which the children of Israel made for themselves in the wilderness, mean? Or what does it signify that Moses burned the calf itself with fire, reduced it to pieces, sprinkled it into water, and gave it to the people to drink? If he broke the tablets that he had received written by the finger of God—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit—because he judged them unworthy for the tablets to be read to them; if, finally, he burned and crushed that calf and scattered it into water and submerged it so that it might be completely destroyed by them, why did he also give this drink to the people?

3. Who would not be stirred by this deed to seek and understand its prophetic meaning? Let attentive minds now grasp that the devil’s body was signified by the calf—that is, human beings among all the nations, for whom the devil is the head, or author, of these sacrileges.

[Note: [Col. 0306D]

4. The Vulgate has: “For when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God,” etc. AREV.]

4. Moreover, it was golden because the rites of idolatry appear to have been instituted by wise men. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.”

5. For, claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents (Romans I:21–22). From this supposed wisdom came this golden calf, such figures as even the leading Egyptians, as though learned men, were accustomed to worship.

6. This calf, therefore, signified the whole body—that is, the entire fellowship—of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry. The Lord Christ burns this sacrilegious fellowship with that fire of which he says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII), so that, since no one can hide from its heat, when the Gentiles believe in him, the devil’s form may be dissolved in them by the fire of his power.

7. Then that entire body is crushed, that is, torn away from the fusion of its evil conspiracy and humbled by the word of truth. It is crushed and thrown into water so that the Israelites—that is, preachers of the Gospel—may transfer them from baptism into their own members, that is, into the Lord’s body. To one of these Israelites, Peter, it was said concerning the Gentiles: “Kill and eat” (Acts X). If “kill and eat,” why not also “cut up and drink”? Thus, through the fire of zeal, the edge of the word, and the water of baptism, this calf was instead swallowed by those whom it had attempted to swallow.

388

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Three Thousand Who Were Killed

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

CHAP. XXXIX. Note 1. “But now,” through “the service of idols”: from *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 92. GRIAL.]

1. We must now inquire what prophetic meaning was also contained in the fact that he ordered many of those who, in his absence, had fashioned an idol for themselves to be killed, without distinction of anyone’s relationship. It is easy to understand that the killing of those people signified the persecution of such vices as had led them to that same idolatry. The Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians III).

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

2. Some printed editions have the number twenty-three thousand. Grial likewise originally printed that number, but later corrected it to three thousand, which is correct. AREV.]

2. To go from gate to gate means to go from vice to vice, through which death enters the mind, while one runs about with the sword of reproof. But the number three thousand who were killed indicates the threefold form of sins. For every sin is committed either by deed, by word, or by thought.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Breaking of the Tablets

1. Moses therefore ascended the mountain again. Once more God gave him the Law on other tablets, cut like the former ones. But what did those same tablets signify which Moses first received from the Lord and immediately broke?

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

CHAP. XL. Note 2. Codex Alborn. has *ostendatur* (“may be shown”) instead of *ostenderentur* (“might be shown”), and the older Codex, derived from Isidore’s original, has *ostenderetur* (“might be shown”). AREV.]

2. Those tablets displayed an image of the ancient Law, which did not long endure because of the people’s sin. But the others, cut again in the likeness of the former, bore the figure of the New Testament. These are not broken, so that the utterances of the New Testament might be shown to endure.

389

3. Hence, appropriately, they are marked to be read in ten words, so that through the same number the figure of the cross might be expressed. For this shape is found in the letter X: one straight stroke is drawn from the topmost point to the lowest; then another, no different, is joined across it to form the transverse arms. Hence he himself says: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew V), namely, through the Passion of the cross, whose image was present in the tablets.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Forty Days Moses Fasted

1. What does it mean that Moses fasted for forty days? The consideration of this number contains a figure of his action; for Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for forty days.

2. The Law and the Prophets, and the Gospel itself—which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets—command us to restrain our appetite for the allurements of the world as though by a fast of self-control. This is to continue as long as the perfection of the Law’s Decalogue is preached throughout the four parts of the same world, that is, throughout the whole earth, so that ten multiplied by four marks the number forty.

## CHAPTER XLII. That the Lord God Said to Moses: “You Shall See My Back Parts”

1. Moses asked to see the Lord’s glory, saying: “If I have found favor with you, show yourself to me plainly.” He received a fitting answer for the present: that he could not see the face of the Lord, for no one could see it and live.

2. What, then, is “You shall not be able to see my face,” unless it means that, although human nature may progress even after the resurrection to angelic likeness and rise indefatigably to contemplate God, it nevertheless cannot fully prevail to see his essence? Not even angelic perfection itself can wholly or completely attain knowledge of it, according to the Apostle, who says: “The peace of God, which surpasses every understanding” (Philippians IV)—with “understanding” including that of the angels.

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

CHAP. XLII. Note 3. “For the Trinity alone is known wholly to itself, and to the assumed humanity, which is the third person in the Trinity.” These are, as we conjecture, the words of some Greek writer. They are repeated with slight alteration, evidently from a different translation, in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 3. There it reads: “The Trinity alone,” he says, “is wholly known to itself, and to the humanity assumed by Christ, which is the third person in the Trinity.” Both formulations amount to the same thing. For the Trinity is wholly known to the assumed humanity because, under the name of the assumed humanity, we understand the very Word who assumed it. Therefore the humanity assumed by Christ cannot be wholly known by another, because that man is God. The communication of properties—which we call *communicatio idiomatum*—is relevant here. For, as he says in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 6: “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not one person in humanity and another in divinity, but the same one person in both natures.”

The word “third” here signifies order no more than when we call two the third part of six, or when a learned poet sang in an epithalamium:

“Your virginity is not wholly yours; it belongs in part to your parents;

A third part is given to your father, a third part given to your mother;

The third alone is yours: do not contend with two.”

Indeed, Isidore himself elsewhere speaks of the Trinity in the same manner. Thus, in Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 4, he says: “The prophet Haggai also disclosed the mystery of this Trinity in the person of the Lord, saying: ‘My Spirit shall be in your midst.’ Behold God, who speaks; behold his Spirit. After this, concerning the third person, that is, the Son, he added: ‘For behold, I will shake heaven and earth, and the Desired One of all nations will come.’” And shortly afterward: “And now the Lord who sent me, and his Spirit.” Behold two persons, the Lord and his Spirit, who send, and the third person of that same Lord, who is sent. Thus twice he called the Son the third person, that is, one of the three.

In this sense it was permissible to say: “In the divine Trinity the Father is the third person, the Son the third, and the Holy Spirit the third.” But although nothing in this Trinity is earlier or later, our ears, as though seeking an order in divine things based on processions, now recoil from the expression. Accordingly, we do not so much employ these ways of speaking as interpret them soberly.

As for the fact that “humanity” appears to some to be made a person, they fail to notice that the relative pronoun *qui, quae, quod* (“who, which”) when placed between two nouns of different genders can normally be adapted not only to the preceding noun but also to the following one, as in Sallust’s well-known example: *Est locus in carcere, quod Tullianum appellatur* (“There is a place in the prison which is called the Tullianum”), where *quod* is adapted to the following *Tullianum*. Isidore himself also sometimes speaks in this way, as in Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 15: *Inimicos Dei persequuntur tenebrae, qui intelliguntur daemones* (“Darknesses, who are understood as demons, pursue the enemies of God”). This is how all the manuscripts read, while the printed editions have it incorrectly as: *quae intelliguntur daemones* (“darknesses, which are understood as demons”).

Therefore, in Book I of the *Sentences*, although he could have said, “The Trinity alone is wholly known to itself, and the humanity assumed by Christ, who is the third person in the Trinity”—which is what he intended—he nevertheless did not wish to refer the pronoun to the preceding “Christ,” but to the following “person.” He did the same here, although by the expression “the assumed humanity” he conceived of the Son himself as the one who assumed it, as we have said.

There is no reason for anyone to doubt the textual truth either here or in Book I of the *Sentences*. For just as here eight manuscripts, so there sixteen manuscript books—written both in Lombard and in our scripts—all agree entirely with the printed editions. GRIAL.

In the same place: Alborn. has *vobis* (“for you”) instead of *verbis* (“in words”); and shortly afterward: “For the form of this is in the letter X.” Grial’s note had *sed quia subsistit*; the sense, however, requires *sed qua subsistit*. [Col. 0310D] AREV.]

3. For the Trinity alone is wholly known to itself, and to the assumed humanity, which is the third person in the Trinity. In the words of God that follow, the mystery of the future Christ and of the Church is then represented in figure. Moses bore the type of the Jewish people, who would afterward believe in Christ. Therefore it was said to him: “When I pass by, you shall see my back parts.”

[Col. 0309A]

[Note: [Col. 0310D]

4. “You shall see my back parts.” In Flor. 1, in the margin, the following is written in the same hand: “To see the back parts is to contemplate the humanity of the glorified Lord.” AREV.]

4. Some say that this meaning was fulfilled in the Gospel when the Lord ascended the mountain and Moses appeared speaking with Jesus. They therefore say that the promise Moses received on Mount Sinai was fulfilled there, when it was said: “You shall see my back parts.” Thus he saw his back parts—that is, he saw the things that happened later and in the final times.

5. When the Lord said to Moses: “There is a place with me; you shall stand upon the rock,” and shortly afterward: “I will remove my hand, and you shall see my back parts,” this means that, since Christ is seen only through the Catholic Church, the Lord testifies that there is with him a place from which he may be seen. Moses is placed upon the rock so that he may contemplate the appearance of God, because unless someone holds the solidity of faith, he does not recognize the divine presence. Concerning this solidity the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Glorification of Moses

1. When Moses descended again with the tablets, his face appeared glorified, yet it was covered by a veil. This signified that the Law is covered and hidden from unbelievers by a mystical veil. The language of the Law possesses the glory of knowledge, but secretly; it also has the horns of the two Testaments, with which it advances armed against the doctrines of falsehood.

2. For when Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts. And when unbelievers, through the excessive stupidity of their hearts, understand the writing of the Law and the Prophets carnally, the whole face of Moses is covered for them by a kind of veil, so that they cannot endure the glory of the Law as it speaks.

3. But if they turn to God, the veil will be removed; the letter that kills will die, and the spirit that gives life will be raised up. For the Lord is Spirit, and the Law is spiritual. Hence David also prayed in the psalm: “Open my eyes, and I will contemplate the wonders of your Law” (Psalm CXVIII).

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Construction of the Ark

[Note: [Col. 0310D]

CHAP. XLIV. Note 1. “The Church of Christ is signified,” or even our mind, according to Origen. Thus he says in Homily 10 on Numbers: “And the golden ark in which the tablets of the covenant are kept, as I suppose, is declared to be nothing other than our mind, in which we ought to have the Law of God written. This mind ought to be golden—that is, pure and precious—in which we may always have the Law of God written, as the Apostle says: written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” Ambrose, however, held that it was the Savior’s flesh, in chapter IX of his Epistle to the Hebrews. See the note on the following chapter. GRIAL.]

1. Let us now examine the ark of the Lord’s covenant, in which the tablets of the Law had been placed. Through this ark, which Moses made from imperishable wood, the Church of Christ is signified, built from all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body, possessing within it also the two tablets of the covenant—that is, observance of the Law and of the Gospel. The ark is gilded within and without; so too the Church, as though radiating gold, ought to shine both inwardly with the splendor of life and outwardly with the brightness of teaching and wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0310D]

## 2. The golden crown around it

Nothing is said here by Gregory about the golden crown; the rest of the material in the *Pastoral* II, 10, derives from him. Indeed, both the Septuagint and its Latin translator rendered this passage quite differently. For in Augustine’s *Questions on Exodus* the following words appear instead: “Golden mouldings twisted around it.” But in this work, composed from various authors, not only allegories but also translations of Holy Scripture are intermingled, although the poles alone sufficiently indicate that Gregory used the Vulgate edition here; that translator rendered them as “carrying-poles” or “supporting-poles.” GRIAL.

2. The golden crown around it and the four golden rings, which are commanded to be attached at its four corners, signify this: because the Church, extended throughout the four regions of the world, is proclaimed as girded by the four books of the holy Gospel. Yet it is enclosed within the circumference of a single crown—that is, within the unity of the same faith.

[Col. 0311A]  
**3.** *Devinciant*, from Bede and the printed editions; *denuntient*, “let them proclaim,” in the manuscripts. The latter, and in Gregory also, is probably erroneous. GRIAL.

In the Albornozian manuscript too *denuntient* occurs, which Grial considers erroneous. AREV.

3. The poles too are made of shittim wood and are inserted into the same rings for carrying it, because strong and steadfast teachers, like imperishable wood, must be sought—teachers who, always adhering to instruction from the sacred books, should bind together the unity of the holy Church and carry the ark as though the rings had been inserted into them. They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that when they resound to others in speech, they themselves may also shine with the splendor of their life.

# CHAPTER XLV  
## The golden urn, the tablets, and the rod

[Col. 0311D]  
**Chapter XLV, note 1.** “We understand the golden urn also as the flesh of Christ,” etc. These words seem to have been taken from Ambrose, except that he declares the ark, whereas our author declares the urn, to be the Savior’s flesh. Thus Ambrose says in the passage cited: “The ark of the Testament: this is the Savior’s flesh, in which there was a golden urn containing the manna of divinity, and Aaron’s rod, which blossomed in Christ’s priesthood, and the tablets of the two Testaments.” GRIAL.

1. In this ark of the Testament there was a golden urn, as well as the tablets and Aaron’s rod. This ark, as was said above, is the Church, possessing two stone tablets—that is, the perpetual firmness of the twofold Testament. We understand the golden urn also as the pure and undefiled flesh of Christ, which preserves within itself the hidden manna of everlasting divinity and bears the perpetual, heavenly sweetness of that angelic bread. It also bears Aaron’s rod—that is, the saving standard of our same supreme and true high priest, Jesus Christ—always green with the unfading foliage of immortal remembrance.

394

# CHAPTER XLVI  
## The mercy seat and the cherubim

[Col. 0311D]  
**Chapter XLVI, note 1.** Christ himself is indicated. Thus Gregory, *Homily 6 on Ezekiel*: “For what is designated by the mercy seat if not the Redeemer of the human race?” Ambrose likewise says: “Appropriately, the mercy seat is said to have been placed upon the ark, because it was granted by God the Father to the Mediator himself, God and man, that he should be the propitiation for our sins,” etc. But why it is placed above the ark, and concerning the entire matter, Augustine speaks most elegantly in *Question 105*: “The law, the manna, and Aaron’s rod were commanded to be placed in the ark. In the law are the commandments; the rod signifies power; the manna, grace, because power to fulfill the commandments does not exist without grace. Yet because the law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone who is making progress, the mercy seat is above it; for this purpose it is necessary that God be merciful, and therefore it is placed above, because mercy triumphs over judgment.” GRIAL.

1. Now, by the mercy seat placed above the ark of the Testament, Christ himself is likewise indicated: he intervenes as mediator and propitiator between God and humanity. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood” (Romans 3:25). The mercy seat is placed above the ark, just as Christ is the head of the Church, at whose right and left [Col. 0311C] two cherubim stand. “Cherubim” is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” The fullness of knowledge is charity—that is, love of God and neighbor—by which the Lord is made manifest. No one can reach God except through charity, for the fullness of the law is love.

[Col. 0312C]  
**2.** Others understand these same two cherubim [in another way]. Gregory, in the homily cited. GRIAL.

In the same place: “As the prophet testifies: ‘You will be known in the midst of the two living creatures.’” Gregory inserted the testimony from Habakkuk into his allegory. He cited it—not from the Vulgate, but from the Septuagint—in the form that suited him. For Jerome translated these words as: “In the midst of the years you will make yourself known.” Not only does the Hebrew text, marked with different vowel points, admit both interpretations, but the Church also uses both in its divine offices. GRIAL.

2. Others understand these same two cherubim as the two Testaments, which, by the knowledge contained in their multitude, overshadow the mercy seat of God—that is, the mysteries of Christ. The prophet testifies: “You will be known in the midst of the two living creatures” (Habakkuk 3:2). They look toward one another with turned faces when they are directed toward the spiritual meaning; then they agree with one another more fully and harmonize more correctly in all things. For they cover the oracle, or mercy seat, from either side, because the Old and New Testaments conceal both the mysteries of Christ and the mysteries of the Church beneath the figures of enigmas.

# CHAPTER XLVII  
## The altar

[Col. 0312B] 1. That altar signified the body of Christ, or all the saints, in whom the divine fire is always burning and the flesh is always being consumed.

# CHAPTER XLVIII  
## The table

[Col. 0312D]  
**Chapter XLVIII, note 1.** “Saying again”—thus the Albornozian manuscript. Grial, with others, omits *again*. The words are from Proverbs: “Wisdom built her house, hewn out her seven pillars; she slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table.” And in verse 5: “Come, eat my bread.” AREV.

1. The table of peace and faith, once set, bore the figure of the Church, in which we are nourished by the food of the Scriptures. To its unity God’s people are gathered from the whole world by apostolic voices, as Solomon says: “Wisdom built her house, prepared her table, and mixed her wine in the bowl” (Proverbs 9:1), and the rest; saying again: “Come, eat of my breads.”

# CHAPTER XLIX  
## The lampstand and the oil

[Col. 0312D]  
**Chapter XLIX, note 1.** “It bore the image of the Holy Spirit.” Ambrose: “The lampstands are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which shine in the Churches for those who understand, through him upon whom rests the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” Jerome, *On Zechariah* 4: “The solid golden lampstand,” he says, “the Hebrews interpret as the law—that is, *nomon* [νόμον]. The lamp, that is, the flame shining and gleaming at the top of the lampstand, is Christ, who is the head of the law and illuminates the whole world. The seven lamps upon the lampstand are the seven graces of the Holy Spirit.” In this passage he professes to be speaking about the interpretation of the Hebrews. He then adds, on the basis of commentaries by ecclesiastical writers: “They understand the golden lampstand of pure gold as the Church, which in the Holy Scriptures seeks the meaning and mind rather than the words.” GRIAL.

In the same place: Isaiah, in the passage cited: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar.” AREV.

1. That seven-branched lampstand bore the image of the Holy Spirit, who with sevenfold grace illumines the whole Church [Col. 0312C] established in the unity of faith. Others understand the same lampstand as Christ, bearing the seven Churches, in which the splendor of the sevenfold Holy Spirit shines forth. For this lampstand snuffers are made, which in Isaiah are called tongs (Isaiah 6:6).

[Col. 0313D]  
**2.** Grial sometimes writes *obpansum*, sometimes *oppansum*, the latter being more customary. AREV.

2. Some have interpreted these as the two Testaments, by which sins are cleansed and which are joined to one another through the union of the Holy Spirit. The lampstand is commanded to burn outside the veil of the testimony, which is spread across it, because without any veil of the Old Testament the truth of the Holy Spirit now shines.

4. The oil, however, which the Lord commands to be taken from olive trees, displays the same grace of the Holy Spirit, containing peace and mercy through the coming of the Savior. From it the light of truth is kindled in our hearts.

# CHAPTER L  
## The tabernacle

1. Now there follows the figure of the tabernacle, which Moses is commanded to construct at the Lord’s command. Allegorically, this tabernacle is the Church established in the wilderness of this life, concerning which the Psalmist says: “For he hid me in his tabernacle in the day of evils” (Psalm 26:5).

2. The tabernacle is therefore furnished with various kinds of materials, some precious and some less valuable. By this it is shown that some are saints and others sinners within the Church. All the faithful are situated within the body of the Church, whereas unbelievers are placed outside its bosom.

# CHAPTER LI  
## The columns and their bases

1. When the tabernacle itself was made as a type of the Church, the Lord commanded that four silver columns be set into its foundations. These four columns are the holy Evangelists, founded upon the firmness of faith. They are called silver [Col. 0313C] because of the brilliance of divine speech.

2. The bases of these columns are the prophets, who by their support bear the structure of the Church. For upon the foundation of the prophets the Evangelists place the Church, and by their authority they confirm the evangelical faith. The golden capital of the columns is he of whom the Apostle says: “Christ is the head of the man.”

# CHAPTER LII  
## The gilded boards

1. Meanwhile he commands gilded boards to be erected and orders silver bases to be cast for them. For what are meant by the boards if not teachers and apostles, extended throughout the world by the breadth of their preaching? And what by the silver bases if not, as was said above, the prophets, who firmly and solidly support the boards placed upon them?

[Col. 0314D]  
**Chapter LII, note 2.** “Hence the joined bases, two beneath each”—from Origen, *Homily 9 on chapter 28*. GRIAL.

2. Because the life of the apostles and teachers, while it is instructed by their preaching, is strengthened by their authority. Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of the Mediator, the preachers who follow build up the Church without doubt. And because they do not disagree among themselves, they establish those who follow them all the more firmly.

[Col. 0314D]  
**3.** The Albornozian manuscript: “For although he says that the bases are silver, he says that the boards are gilded.” This seems more elegant. AREV.

In the same place: “It is not easily broken,” and from the original it is indicated as *derumpitur*, “is torn apart,” instead of which other manuscripts have *disrumpitur*. The words are from Ecclesiastes: “A threefold cord is not easily broken.” Grial: “by which it is supported.” AREV.

3. By saying that the bases are silver and the boards gilded, he shows that the commandments of the apostles are far more resplendent than those of the prophets. The tent-cloths, sewn together with clasps and suspended and fastened with cords in the manner of curtains, extending twenty-eight cubits in length and four cubits in breadth, signify the remaining multitude of believers, who cling to and hang upon the cords of faith. A threefold cord is not broken [Col. 0314B]: this is the faith of the Trinity, upon which the whole Church depends and by which it is supported.

[Col. 0314D]  
**4.** Others read “when it is joined to it.” But most have “which is joined,” so that it is a nominative used in place of an ablative absolute. AREV.

4. The fact that they extend twenty-eight cubits in length, while the four curtains are of one measure in breadth, signifies that the law is joined to the Gospel. For the number seven generally signifies the law because of the many mysteries associated with the number seven. Joined to the four Gospels, it consequently makes four times seven, the number twenty-eight.

# CHAPTER LIII  
## The ten curtains

1. Ten curtains are made so that they may contain the complete number of perfection and signify the Decalogue of the law. Yet they are joined to one another by fifty golden clasps, because all the faithful are united by the bond of faith and charity through the gift of the Holy Spirit. The number fifty belongs to the Holy Spirit. Hence, on the fiftieth day after Easter, the Holy Spirit descended from heaven.

# CHAPTER LIV  
## The eleven curtains of haircloth

[Col. 0314D]  
**Chapter LIV, note 1.** “Which, through to ‘remission,’” are Augustine’s words, *City of God* XV, 20. GRIAL.

1. The command that eleven curtains of haircloth be made indicates sin through the haircloth, because of the goats placed on the left. Since above he had shown, in the ten curtains, the saints who keep the perfection of the law, the number eleven of the haircloth curtains—because it exceeds ten—clearly signifies that transgressors of the law, that is, sinners, will exist in the Church. Yet the haircloth coverings themselves are joined by fifty clasps [Col. 0314D] as a sign of repentance and hope for the remission of sins through indulgence.

[Col. 0315A]  
**2.** “The coarse minds of human beings.” Thus Grial, with the other printed editions. But it may perhaps be better, with the Albornozian manuscript: “the thick minds of human beings.” Instead of *durae sint*, Grial printed *durae sunt*, “are hard.” In the Albornozian manuscript: “they are hard.” Others: “the minds of human beings who … may be hard.” AREV.

2. Hence the fiftieth psalm also concerns pardon and remission. These haircloth coverings too—by which the tabernacle is covered and which withstand rains, winds, and storms—may be understood as coarse human minds, which at times, by the hidden judgment of God, are given prominence in the Church, although they are hard.

399

3. Hence he also fittingly placed ram skins beneath them, so that by the rams he might indicate the leaders and superiors of the Churches. Because they do not fear devoting themselves to temporal concerns, they ought to bear the winds and rains of temptations arising from the adversities of this world, so that those who shine spiritually within the Church, like fine linen, hyacinth, and purple, may shine securely within while their superiors and rulers labor outside against the storms and tempests of the world.

# CHAPTER LV  
## The veil spread across the middle of the tabernacle

[Col. 0315B]

1. The fact that a veil is extended across the middle of the tabernacle and that the outer part is separated from the inner signifies that the peoples of the Church are not now permitted to see the things that have been promised, as though they were covered by a veil, until they are revealed. Thus the Apostle also says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). Therefore, as long as we are in this world, we see the truth as through a mirror, placed, as it were, in the holy place and not yet reaching the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 0315D]  
**Chapter LV, note 2.** Others read: “where there are also the pure in heart.” But *mundicordibus*, “for the pure in heart,” is correct according to what was said in the commentary on Genesis, chapter 25, number 10. AREV.

2. The holy place can signify those things which holy conduct can possess in the present age. The Holy of Holies, into which one enters only once, signifies passage to heaven, where the mercy seat and the cherubim are, and where God will be able to appear to the pure in heart. Yet while we remain in this way of life, we do not stand without the help of the Holy Spirit. From the one fountain of the Holy Spirit we have seven lamps to illuminate the people of the Church—that is, the Lord’s sevenfold grace sent throughout the whole world—which illumines the peoples of the Church with the radiance of the Holy Spirit in the diverse brilliance of its gifts.

3. This veil spread across the tabernacle, which concealed the inner part of the tabernacle so that the things deposited there could not be seen, can indeed signify the period that existed under the law. For the things that the law and the prophets proclaimed were hidden and could not be seen because a veil intervened.

[Col. 0315D] 400  
**Chapter LV, note 4.** The Vulgate: “For the Spirit searches everything, even the deep things of God.” AREV.

4. But after Christ came and, at the time of his Passion, tore that veil from top to bottom, all those things that had previously been hidden were revealed through the Lord’s Passion for our faith. The Apostle says: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the lofty things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10).

# CHAPTER LVI  
## The various offerings for the construction of the tabernacle

[Col. 0316A]

1. Different offerings are presented with a single purpose for the construction of the tabernacle, according to what is written: “Gold, silver, bronze, precious stones.” In addition, fine linen, scarlet, hyacinth, and purple; red-dyed ram skins and hyacinth-colored skins; also imperishable wood and goats’ hair for the construction of the tabernacle.

[Col. 0316D]  
**Chapter LVI, note 2.** “But also whatever was necessary for worship, through ‘irrigated’”—these are Gregory’s words, *Morals* XXX, 6. See also Origen, *Homily 13 on chapter 25*. GRIAL.

2. Moreover, whatever was necessary for worship and for the holy garments was provided by men together with women: bracelets, earrings, rings, and every golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord. Whoever possessed hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, or goats’ hair [gave it].

[Col. 0316B]

3. The earlier tabernacle, therefore, is a type of the Church. These gifts signify the gifts of merits by which the Church is adorned: its faith is compared with gold, the word of preaching with silver. The fact that men together with women provide whatever is necessary for the ornament or construction of the tabernacle signifies that within the Church the virtues of the strong, represented by men, and the modest works of the weak, represented by women, all find a place and are accepted for the uses of holy edification.

4. The offering itself is not made under compulsion but voluntarily, because faith is voluntary. The bracelets, which bind the arms, therefore demonstrate the works of leaders who labor greatly. The earrings express the obedience of subjects. The rings display the seal of secret things.

401  
[Col. 0316D]  
**5.** The Albornozian manuscript: “Moreover, by the bracelets, ornaments of good action, or good works.” AREV.

5. Hence teachers conceal certain matters from those who understand less, hiding them as though under a seal, lest the mysteries of God be entrusted to the unworthy. Therefore the righteous person rejoices and says: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 118:11). Moreover, by the right-hand ornaments, good works and the right hand are signified.

[Col. 0316D]  
**6.** Grial reads *amando sublevatur*, “is lifted up by loving,” as do the other printed editions. But the reading I retain with the Albornozian manuscript, *amanda sublevatur*, “is lifted up by the things that must be loved,” seems genuine. AREV.

6. By the golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord, understanding of divinity is signified. It is separated from love of inferior things to the extent that it is raised toward loving only those things that are eternal. By the hyacinth, hope of heavenly rewards is indicated. By purple, blood and the endurance of sufferings undertaken for love of the everlasting kingdom are declared. By twice-dyed scarlet, charity is demonstrated, which is dyed twice for the sake of its perfection because it is adorned by love of God and neighbor.

7. By fine linen, the undefiled incorruption of the flesh and the most brilliant whiteness of holiness are indicated; for fine linen is white flax. By goats’ hair, from which the roughness of haircloth is woven, the harsh affliction of repentance is signified. Thus, while some vigorously exercise the office of teaching through bracelets and rings, others display devoted obedience in hearing and upright action through earrings and right-hand ornaments; some possess an excellent and more subtle understanding of God through the golden vessel; others, through hyacinth, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for, believe in, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even when they do not yet know them through a more subtle understanding; some offer the incorruption of the flesh through fine linen; others, through goats’ hair, harshly lament what they willingly admitted.

8. From such a great diversity of works a single tabernacle is fashioned, just as from diverse dust a single globe of earth is formed, watered by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The imperishable shittim wood signifies all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body, not perishing with the world but remaining eternal. The precious stones signify confessors, apostles, priests, and all the righteous.

[Col. 0317D]  
**9.** In the Vulgate: “And you yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house.” AREV.

9. The blessed apostle Peter also calls these “living stones”: “That you may be,” he says, “living stones, built together into the temple of God” (1 Peter 2:5). All these things, then, are offered in the tabernacle of God, so that no one may despair of salvation. In addition to these, one offers gold—that is, understanding; another silver—that is, eloquence; another the voice of bronze. Thus many things come to exist in the tabernacle: the table, that is, and the lampstand, the altar, the columns, the bases, the boards, the bowls, the cups, the censers, the basins, the mortars, the snuffers, the pegs, and the tent-cloths. Through these various forms the whole beauty of the tabernacle—that is, of the Church—is distinguished.

[Col. 0317C]

10. For the tabernacle is the Church, in which there is the table—that is, the unity of faith, or certainly Holy Scripture, by which all the faithful are nourished with spiritual food. The lampstand with its seven lamps is Christ with the seven Churches. Its snuffers are the two Testaments. The columns are holy teachers, made solid by the firmness of faith. The bases are the prophets, who by their foundation bear the structure of the Church.

11. There are also the boards, namely the apostles, extended by the breadth of their preaching. Or the tent-cloths, namely the leaders and preachers, who labor outside against the storms of this age. There are also bowls, that is, distributions of gifts. There are pegs, namely the rulers of the Church, from which all kinds of peoples hang, as vessels. There are also cups, the words or meanings of doctrine.

12. There are also censers, namely the virtues of good works, or the prayers of the saints, by which the fragrance of sweetness rises to the Lord. There are also basins, the apostles and teachers full of life-giving waters. There are lilies, the whiteness of virginity; or mortars, the endurance of labors and sufferings, by which the members of penitents are put to death. These forms and distributions of gifts have been divided among the faithful by the Holy Spirit, so that the perfect tabernacle of Christ may be constructed in each distribution, and God may dwell among the saints.

# CHAPTER LVII  
## The ointment with which the tabernacle is anointed

[Col. 0317D]  
**Chapter LVII, number 1.** The Vulgate: “Who always leads us in triumph … the fragrance of his knowledge.” AREV.

1. The ointment with which the tabernacle is anointed is chrism, with which the faithful people are anointed in the Church, in whom divinity dwells as in a tabernacle. This ointment can also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or the fragrance of righteousness diffused far and wide. Concerning it the Apostle says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his righteousness in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:14).

# CHAPTER LVIII  
## The compound incense

[Col. 0317D]  
**Chapter LVIII, note 1.** I have shown in Prudentius, page 129, that *incensum* is a very ancient word for frankincense, or for some mixture made from various kinds of fragrances. AREV.

[Col. 0318D] In this passage *hic*, “here,” is used as an adverb; but others read *haec*, “these things.” AREV.

1. The incense, composed of four very fragrant substances ground to the finest consistency—that is, storax, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense (Prudentius, p. 129)—is shown by the blessed John’s Apocalypse to have been established as a figure of the prayers of the faithful. The twenty-four elders fall before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5).

[Col. 0318D]  
**2.** Grial reads: “but storax with waters.” AREV.

2. Yet the nature of these four fragrances also seems to signify the form of the four elements: frankincense, because it is translucent, may be compared with air; storax with water; galbanum and onycha with earth and fire. Thus through these things the incense pleasing to God becomes the prayer of the creature’s praise for all that is in heaven, below heaven, on earth, and in the waters.

[Col. 0318D]  
**3.** “By which the whole people,” etc. The Albornozian manuscript: “by which the whole body of the tabernacle, that is, the entire people of Christ, is sanctified.” AREV.

3. The blood with which Moses sprinkles and purifies the people, the tabernacle of the Testament, and everything that was in it, saying, “This is the blood, the blood of the Testament,” is wonderfully shown to proclaim the blood of the Lord Jesus. By it the hearts of all believers are cleansed, by it the faith of the Church is marked, by it the whole people of the Church—that is, the entire body of the tabernacle—is sanctified. The Lord says to his disciples: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (Matthew 26), fulfilling in truth what had been shown figuratively through Moses.

404

# CHAPTER LIX  
## The high priest’s garment

1. We must now explain what the high priest’s garments are and what they chiefly signify. The priest Aaron signifies him to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4). The garment of this priest is the Church, concerning which the Apostle says: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

2. The four colors from which his garment is woven signify the diversity of merits that shines within the holy Church, in the body of Christ. We understand the *poderes*, that is, the priestly linen garment, as the incarnation of Christ, which is from the earth and is signified in the feet. Linen arises from the earth. The turban upon his head and the golden plate we understand as the splendor of divinity, so that the one and same person appears adorned, according to his humanity, with the *poderes*, and, according to his divinity, with the turban.

[Col. 0319D]  
**Chapter LIX, note 3.** The Florentine manuscript 1: “The Church of Christ from the beginning of the world to the end,” etc. AREV.

3. The undergarments with which he is clothed show the chastity and integrity of the body of Christ. The belt with which the priestly breast is bound signifies the choir of the saints, or the concord which they embrace in the unity of Christ’s faith. The long tunic, descending from the head to the feet, is likewise the Church of Christ, which will remain until the end of time.

[Col. 0319D]  
**4.** “The pomegranates, through ‘holds fast to merits’”—Gregory, *Pastoral Rule* II, and *Register* I, letter 24. GRIAL.

4. This garment is entirely hyacinth-colored. Hyacinth shines with a sky-blue color, so that the whole Church may set its mind on the things above and rise entirely toward love of heavenly things. The pomegranates placed below declare the unity of that same Church. For just as within a single outer rind of a pomegranate many seeds are enclosed and protected inside, so the unity of faith covers the countless peoples of the holy Church, whom a diversity of merits sustains within.

[Col. 0319C]  
**5.** “These bells, through ‘may never be silent’”—Origen, *Homily 9 on chapter 28*. GRIAL.

In the same place: The Vulgate: “And the rule was placed upon his shoulder.” The Albornozian manuscript has *potestas*, “power”; others have *imperium*, “authority,” instead of *principatus*, “rule.” AREV.

5. The bells, sounding among the pomegranates, are understood as the prophets and holy teachers placed in the midst of the Church. Their tongue, resounding with the knowledge of doctrine, touches both edges of the bell—that is, the parts of the law and of the Gospel. These bells are placed at the lower edge of the garment so that, when discussing the end of the world and the future life, they may never be silent. The shoulder-piece, the Savior’s mantle, indicates power and kingship, as it is written: “His rule is upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 9:6).

[Col. 0320D]  
**6.** The Albornozian manuscript: “That is, the admirable example of life set by the holy apostles.” AREV.

6. The two emerald stones placed on the shoulder-piece, one on the right and one on the left, are the two peoples: the Gentile people on the right, and the Jewish people, which was once on the right, on the left. They bear engraved upon them the names of the twelve patriarchs [Col. 0319D], that is, for the imitation of the examples of life set by the holy apostles.

7. Others have called these same two stones the two Testaments, or the letter and the spirit, in which all the mysteries of the law are contained: the spirit on the right, the letter on the left. The breastpiece placed over the chest, distinguished by four rows of stones, figures the evangelical word, which through its fourfold arrangement sets forth to us the truth of faith and the doctrine of the Trinity.

8. The apostolic word corresponds to it both in power and in number. This breastpiece is twofold because knowledge of evangelical doctrine is both open and hidden, simple and mystical. Likewise, the same priest, Christ, may appropriately be interpreted in his members, and especially in the high priest, who dwells in the saints and offers a victim for the people, producing with his sacred mouth the flesh of the spotless Lamb.

[Col. 0320D]  
**9.** “First, that Aaron, through ‘the unity of faith is signified’”—from Gregory, *Register* I, letter 24. GRIAL.

9. First, the fact that in Aaron’s breast the breastpiece of judgment is impressed by binding bands signifies that the priestly heart must never be possessed by wandering thoughts, but must be constrained by reason alone. In this breastpiece twelve stones are also carefully attached, so that the names of the twelve patriarchs may be inscribed. For he must always bear the holy fathers whose names are written upon his breast, and never cease imitating their examples.

10. The fact that the priest is bound at each shoulder by the covering of the shoulder-piece signifies that he must always be fortified by the adornment of virtues against adversity and prosperity. The shoulder-piece is commanded to be made of gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, demonstrating how brightly the priest must shine with a diversity of virtues. In the priest’s attire gold gleams when he excels in the understanding of wisdom. Hyacinth, because it shines with the color of the sky, is added to it so that everything he undertakes may rise toward love of heavenly things.

11. Royal purple is mixed with it so that he may suppress suggestions [Col. 0320C] of vices, as though by royal authority. Twice-dyed scarlet is also added to the shoulder-piece so that, before the eyes of the inner Judge, all good works of virtue may be adorned by charity.

[Col. 0320D]  
**12.** The Florentine manuscript 1: “Through which, shining with the beauty of purity, bodily chastity is signified. And this, indeed,” etc. AREV.

12. Since this charity depends upon love of God and neighbor, it shines as though from a double dye. Twisted fine linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet; for fine linen arises from the earth in shining form, and by it the bright splendor and purity of bodily chastity are signified. This twisted linen is joined to the beauty of the shoulder-piece because chastity is brought to the perfect radiance of purity when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence.

13. He is also girded with a belt, by which the incitements of the loins and the lusts of desire are restrained. [Col. 0320D] When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is surrounded by a tunic with bells, so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector through silence. The pomegranates are joined to the bells so that through his teaching the unity of faith may be signified.

14. The fact that the priest entered the first part of the tabernacle every day to offer sacrifices prescribes for us daily perseverance, so that we may never depart from this place where God’s people are instructed by heavenly voices, but may offer every day the spiritual sacrifice of confession and praise—that is, the humility of our souls, which are true sacrifices, as it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Psalm 50).

15. The fact that once a year the high priest, leaving the people, entered the Holy of Holies, where the mercy seat was, signifies our Lord Jesus [Col. 0322A] the high priest. While he was placed in the flesh, he remained with the people throughout the year—that year, namely, of which he himself says: “He has sent me to preach good news to the poor, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of propitiation” (Luke 4).

16. Therefore, once a year, on the day of propitiation, he enters the Holy of Holies. That is, when the dispensation had been completed, he penetrated the heavens and entered to the Father, so that he might make him propitious toward the human race and intercede for all who believe in him.

# IN LEVITICUS

[Col. 0321]

# CHAPTER ONE  
## The figures of the sacrifices

[Col. 0321B]  
**Chapter I, note 1.** The Albornozian manuscript: “The various figures of that promised sacrifice.” AREV.

1. The following book, Leviticus, sets forth the various sacrifices, whose type bore the image of Christ’s Passion. For after he himself had been offered, all those sacrifices ceased which had preceded him as his type or shadow, prefiguring that sacrifice which the one true priest, the mediator between God and humanity, offered. Beforehand, it was necessary to celebrate the promised figures of that sacrifice in the victims of animals, for the sake of the future cleansing of flesh and blood. Through that one victim forgiveness would be effected for sins contracted from flesh and blood, which will not inherit the kingdom of God, because that same bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly quality.

[Col. 0321C] [Col. 0321D]

2. Albornus: It clearly demonstrated the gathered Church, which is the body of Christ. AREV.]

2. For he was offered in the calf on account of the power of the cross; in the lamb on account of innocence; in the ram on account of sovereignty; in the goat on account of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that he might condemn sin through sin; and likewise in the turtledove and the dove, on account of God and man, because the Mediator between God and human beings was shown in the union of two substances. Moreover, in the sprinkling of fine flour, he clearly demonstrated the Church, gathered through the water of baptism, which is the body of Christ.

409 [Note: [Col. 0321D]

3. “But as for us, until we walk” are the words of Origen, *Homilies* 2, chapter 1. GRIAL.]

3. Morally, we offer a calf as a gift to God when we conquer the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational impulses and foolish tendencies; a kid when we overcome wantonness; a dove when we preserve simplicity of mind; a turtledove when we maintain chastity of the flesh; and unleavened loaves when we walk not in the leaven of malice, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5).

## CHAPTER II. On the fire of the sacrifice

[Col. 0322B]

[Note: [Col. 0321D]

CHAP. II. Note 1. The entire chapter is taken from Augustine, *Against Faustus* 22.17. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To be gathered.” Thus the manuscripts. “To be assembled,” Bede and the printed edition. “To be consecrated,” Augustine. GRIAL.
