[Col. 0322D] Ibid. “Sanctuary.” From Augustine and Bede. In another copy, “of sacred things,” erroneously. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grial’s note read *ad sacrarium* (“to the sanctuary”), erroneously, as I think; for in the text *sacrarium* correctly stands without *ad*. AREV.]

1. The fire in the sacrifice figuratively signified this, as though swallowing up death in victory. These rites were duly celebrated among that people whose kingdom and priesthood were a prophecy of the coming King and Priest, destined to govern and consecrate the faithful among all nations, and to introduce them into the kingdom of heaven and the sanctuary of the angels, unto eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0321D]

2. “Religious declarations.” From Augustine. In another copy, “religious sacraments.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Imitations of sacrilege.” From Augustine and Bede. In another version: “The pagans imitated.” GRIAL.]

2. Thus, just as the Hebrews celebrated the religious prefigurations of this true sacrifice, so the pagans performed sacrilegious imitations of it, because, as the Apostle says, what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. For the immolation of blood is an ancient, prophetic rite, bearing witness from the beginning of the human race to the future passion of the Mediator. Scripture records that Abel was the first to offer this sacrifice.

## CHAPTER III. That honey is not offered in God’s sacrifice

1. The fact that honey is not offered in God’s sacrifice indicates that nothing pleasurable, nothing sweet in this world, pleases God—nothing, that is, which does not contain some element of biting truth. Hence the Passover too is eaten with bitter herbs (Exod. 12).

## CHAPTER IV. That salt is mixed into all sacrifices

1. Conversely, salt is commanded to be mixed into all sacrifices, namely so that everything we offer in Christ’s honor may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

## CHAPTER V. That oil is offered in the sacrifice

[Col. 0322D]

1. The fact that oil was offered in the sacrifice signifies that whatever we expend in the worship of Christ and in devotion to the saints, we should do wholly and cheerfully, “not,” as the Apostle says, “out of sorrow or compulsion.” For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9). Oil signifies cheerfulness, as it is written: “That he may gladden his face with oil” (Psalm 103).

## CHAPTER VI. On the four kinds of principal offerings

1. At the beginning of Leviticus, four kinds of principal offerings are described, which are commanded to be offered to the Lord as a pleasing fragrance: first, a spotless calf from the herd; second, a lamb from the sheep; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, fine flour kneaded, unleavened, anointed with oil, and baked in an oven. The remaining sacrifices were offered on behalf of the people according to the circumstances of each case.

2. The first sacrifice, therefore—that is, the calf from the herd—signifies Christ, descending from the lineage of the patriarchs. With the plow of his cross he subdued the soil of our flesh and enriched it with the fruit of virtues through the seed of the Holy Spirit. This calf is spotless because he is led to his passion without sin. It is offered not in the tabernacle but at its entrance, because Christ suffered outside the camp. Its blood is offered through the sons of the priest Aaron.

3. This is understood of Annas and Caiaphas, who, after taking counsel together, shed Christ’s blood. The second victim, the lamb offered from the sheep, likewise represents Christ on account of his innocence. For he is the lamb who, according to Isaiah, is led to sacrifice (Isa. 53), and whom John points out to everyone, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). The lamb is therefore rightly offered in sacrifice, so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and passion might be shown. The kid too is rightly offered, because through its death the author of sin, the devil, is recognized as having been slain.

[Note: [Col. 0323D]

CHAP. VI. Note 4. Florence manuscript 1: “The third sacrifice is offered in the person of the Father.” And shortly afterward: “Joined mysteriously to the Holy Spirit in the person of the Father,” etc. AREV.]

4. The third sacrifice is said to be the turtledove and the dove. It is clear that the turtledove is Christ’s flesh, since Solomon says: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove” (Song 1). John the Baptist declares that the dove bears the figure of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove, this is my Son” (John 1:32–33). Accordingly, we understand the turtledove and the dove—that is, Christ’s flesh joined mystically to the Holy Spirit through the passion—as a sacrifice offered to God for a pleasing fragrance. These three sacrifices are offered by one human being, namely Christ Jesus.

5. The soul, however—that is, the Church—offers the fourth sacrifice, from fine flour. Fine flour foretells the figure of the Catholic Church, which, from its harmonious members, is like fine flour gathered from many grains of believers; separated by the millstone of the Law and the Gospels into letter and spirit; united through the water of baptism; anointed with the oil of chrism; solidified by the fire of the Holy Spirit; and, through humility of spirit, made into an offering pleasing to God. These are the four offerings, displaying the fourfold form of Christ and the Church.

## CHAPTER VII. On the sacrifice of one who uttered an oath and passed beyond it through forgetfulness

[Note: [Col. 0323D]

CHAP. VII. Note 1. The entire chapter is from Gregory, *Moralia* 32.4. GRIAL.]

1. Concerning one who uttered an oath to do something either evil or good and then went beyond that oath through forgetfulness, it is said: “Let him offer a ewe-lamb from the flock or a she-goat, and the priest shall pray for him and for his sin. But if he cannot offer livestock, let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering.” To utter an oath, then, is to bind ourselves by a vow of divine service; and when we promise good works, we pledge ourselves to do well.

2. But when we vow abstinence and the mortification of our flesh, we swear that, for the present, we will do something harmful to ourselves. Yet no one in this life is so perfect that, however devoted to God, he does not sin amid even his small pious vows; therefore a ewe-lamb from the flock or a she-goat is prescribed as an offering for sin.

[Note: [Col. 0323D]

3. “Unless the innocence of the active life.” Thus the Albornus Codex, and the sense also requires it. In Grial and the older printed editions, *nisi activae vitae innocentiam* (“unless the innocence of the active life”) appears corrupt. AREV.]

3. What, then, is signified by the ewe-lamb if not the innocence of the active life? What by the she-goat, which often grazes while clinging to the highest and most remote cliffs, if not the contemplative life? Whoever sees that he has not fulfilled these promises and resolutions ought to equip himself more diligently for God’s sacrifice, either with the innocence of good works or with the sublime nourishment of contemplation.

[Col. 0324C] [Note: [Col. 0324D]

4. Albornus: “Two young pigeons, or two turtledoves.” AREV.]

4. The ewe-lamb is rightly ordered to be offered from the flock, whereas the she-goat is not ordered to be offered from the flock, because the active life belongs to many, while the contemplative life belongs to few. When we do what we see many doing and having done, we give, as it were, a ewe-lamb from the flock. But when the strength of the offerer is insufficient for either a ewe-lamb or a she-goat, two young pigeons or two turtledoves are added as a remedy for the penitent.

5. We know that young pigeons and turtledoves have a song of lamentation. What, then, is signified by two young pigeons or two turtledoves if not the double lamentation of our repentance? When we do not rise to offer good works, we should mourn ourselves in two ways, because we have both failed to do what is right and have done what is wrong.

[Col. 0324D] 6. Hence one turtledove is ordered to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is so called because it is wholly consumed by fire. We offer one turtledove for sin when we offer a lament for our fault. We make the other a burnt offering when, because we have neglected good things, we burn ourselves completely in the fire of sorrow.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the sons of Aaron who were destroyed

[Col. 0325A]

1. The sons of Aaron, who placed foreign fire upon the altar and were consumed by divine fire, signified those who, having rejected God’s tradition, desire alien doctrines and introduce the teachings of human invention. The Lord rebukes and reproves them in the Gospel, saying: “You rejected the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition.”

2. Whoever kindles within the sanctuary of his heart the fire of some bodily or worldly desire and dares to approach the Lord’s altars also appears to kindle foreign fire. These altars receive nothing except the kindling of that fire of which the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” May the Lord Jesus always set us aflame with this fire, so that we may be enlightened in our understanding and not burn with vices.

## CHAPTER IX. On the discernment of foods

[Note: [Col. 0325D]

CHAP. IX. Note 1. On the discernment of foods, compare the Apostolic Fathers, Cotelerius’s edition, vol. 1, p. 35, and theologians passim. AREV.]

1. We must now discuss the discernment of foods. Here the Law, speaking of clean and unclean things, permitted certain animals for eating as clean, while forbidding others as unclean. First, it must be understood that everything created by God is clean, purified by the authority of its original institution, and not to be condemned, lest blame be directed back to the Creator.

2. Next, the Law was given to the children of Israel so that through it they might advance and return to the ways they had previously received from their fathers but had violated in Egypt through conformity to the customs of a barbarous nation. Thus, in order to correct human beings, animals were censured, so that people who possessed the same vices might be judged equal to animals.

3. For human character, actions, and desires are portrayed in animals, and from these people themselves become clean or unclean. Thus the Law says that these are clean: “Whatever has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the livestock, you shall eat.” In saying this, it was distinguishing not animals but human character. Ultimately, those people are clean who chew the cud, who always carry divine commandments in their mouths as though they were food.

4. They also divide the hoof, because believers in the two Testaments, of the Law and the Gospels, walk with a firm step in innocence and righteousness. The Jews indeed chew the words of the Law, but they do not divide the hoof; that is, they neither accept the two Testaments nor plant the steps of their faith in the Father and the Son. For this reason they are considered unclean.

5. Heretics likewise divide the hoof, believing in the Father and the Son and accepting the two Testaments; but because they do not chew the doctrine of truth in their mouths, they too are nevertheless unclean. For Scripture adds: “Of all that are produced in the waters, whatever has fins and scales, these you shall eat; but whatever does not have fins and scales shall be an abomination to you.”

[Note: [Col. 0325D]

6. “For among fish those which are …” Albornus: “For among fish, those sprinkled with scales are considered clean; rough, bristly, rigid, and more serious human characters are approved.” At the bottom of the same Albornus Codex appear the following words: “Isidore in the original says this: For among fish, those with scales and fins, which are considered clean, the rough, fierce, and steadfast in faith, serious characters of human beings are approved.” I therefore think that Isidore’s original, with which the Albornus Codex was collated by Cardinal Albornoz himself, as it seems, was nothing other than a remarkably ancient codex, which some perhaps believed to be the original of Saint Isidore. AREV.]

6. For among fish, those with scales and fins are considered clean; they signify rough and bristling people, strong in faith, and human beings of serious character who possess the fins of contemplation. Those without these features are called unclean; in them, light-minded, slippery, faithless, and effeminate ways are rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0326D]

7. For why God forbade the Jews to eat certain animals, and what allegories are drawn from this, see the Apostolic Fathers with Cotelerius’s notes, vol. 1, p. 30. AREV.]

7. What does the Law mean when it says, “You shall not eat the camel,” except that, by the example of the animal, it condemns a malformed life, twisted by crimes? When it forbids the pig as food, it reproves a life that is filthy, muddy, and delighting in the squalor of vices. And when it condemns the hare, it condemns men deformed into women.

8. Who would make the weasel into food? Yet it reproves theft. Who would eat the lizard? Yet it hates the uncertain variability of life. Who, finally, could eat the stellion, so that the Law would prohibit it so emphatically? Yet it detests the spots of the mind. Who eats the hawk, kite, or eagle? Yet it hates robbers who live by violent crime.

[Note: [Col. 0326D]

9. Albornus: “When it forbids the raven, it rejects black or impure desires,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, “fleeing the light of truth,” instead of “fleeing vanities.” AREV.]

9. Who eats the vulture? Yet it curses those who seek prey from another’s death. Likewise, when it forbids the raven, it forbids pleasures or the enormity of vices. When it forbids the sparrow, it censures intemperance. When it mentions the owl, it hates vanities that flee the light. When it mentions the charadrius and the goshawk, it signifies excessive intemperance of speech. When it forbids the swan, it denotes pride of an uplifted neck. When it mentions the bat, it refers to those who seek errors resembling the darkness of night.

10. Thus the Law curses these and similar things in animals—not because they are criminal in them, for they were born with these characteristics, but because they are culpable in human beings, since they have been acquired contrary to nature, not through institution but through error. There was once, in ancient times, a period when these shadows or figures had to be practiced or observed by the people, so that they would abstain from foods which creation had indeed made suitable but the Law had forbidden.

11. But now Christ, the end of the Law, has come, opening what the Law had closed and unlocking what it had obscured. As a distinguished teacher, heavenly doctor, and instructor, he has disclosed in unveiled truth all the mysteries that antiquity had concealed from us under figures. Under him it is said: “Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and conscience are defiled.”

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

12. “And elsewhere,” through the end of the chapter, is absent from Bede, the Palatine manuscript, and most others. GRIAL.]

12. And elsewhere: “Whatever is set before you, eat.” From this it is clear that all these things have now been restored by their blessings, although they had been forbidden to the carnal people on account of their conduct. Yet care must be taken lest anyone think that this permission has been granted so fully that he may also eat what has been sacrificed to idols. As far as God’s creation is concerned, everything is clean; but when things have been sacrificed to demons, they become defiled. Hence the Apostle says: “But if someone says to you, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat it” (1 Cor. 8).

## CHAPTER X. On the uncleanness of childbirth

[Col. 0327B]

1. The question of the uncleanness of childbirth and the contagion of leprosy follows. For it says: “A woman who has conceived seed and borne a male child shall be unclean for seven days and shall be purified on the eighth.”

2. But a woman who has borne a female child is written to remain in uncleanness for twice seven days. There is no doubt that certain mysteries of a hidden secret are contained in such matters. The week may be understood as the period of this present life, since the world was completed in a week of days. As long as we are placed in the flesh, we cannot be perfectly pure in it unless the eighth day has come, which is the time of the age to come.

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

CHAP. X. Note 3. “For the flesh, having been purified,” etc. Albornus manuscript: “For the flesh will receive purification from vices through the resurrection.” AREV.]

3. Yet the one who has acted manfully must be purified in it. His mother immediately becomes clean, the woman who gave birth to him. For in the resurrection he will receive flesh purified from vices. But whoever has had nothing manly in himself against sin and has remained lax and effeminate in his actions will be purified from his uncleanness neither in the week of the present age nor in the age to come.

## CHAPTER XI. On leprosy

1. The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “When a person’s flesh and skin develop a different color, or a pustule, or something resembling a shining spot—that is, the mark of leprosy—he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to any one of his sons. When he sees leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color, it is the mark of leprosy, and he shall be separated at the priest’s discretion.” Leprosy is false doctrine.

[Col. 0327D] 2. Accordingly, lepers are not improperly understood as heretics, who, lacking the unity of true faith, profess various doctrines of error and mix falsehoods with truths, just as leprosy disfigures human bodies by mottling them with true and false patches.

3. In this leprosy, therefore, we find that the lawgiver established six forms on the human body: the first of the head and beard; the second of baldness and receding baldness; the third of flesh and skin; the fourth of skin and body, and of a white scar with redness; the fifth of ulcer and scar; the sixth of burning.

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

4. Albornus: “Who sins in the divinity, or in the head itself.” AREV.]

4. He bears leprosy on his head who sins concerning the Father’s divinity or concerning the head itself, which is Christ. For “the head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11). The Jews, Valentinians, Marcionites, Photinians, Manichaeans, Arians, Sabellians, Macedonians, Anthropomorphites, Priscillianists, Donatists, Nestorians, and Eutychians have this leprosy. They all bear leprosy on the bald scalp because they defend the faithlessness of their error with manifest perversity.

5. Those bear leprosy on the beard who think perversely about the apostles and saints of Christ and falsely claim that they preached something erroneous. Just as the beard is an adornment of a man, so the holy apostles and teachers provide adornment to the body of Christ.

6. Those have leprosy on the baldness who disparage the Church: the Carpocratians, who deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Novatians, who condemn marriage and deny repentance to sinners; the Hieracites, who, among their other errors, do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven; and the Aerianists, who forbid offering sacrifice for the dead.

7. Those bear leprosy on the flesh and skin who try to advocate carnal or external things, such as the Cerinthians, who suppose that the future resurrection consists in the pleasure of the flesh; and the Actians, who say that sins cannot be counted against those who remain in the faith, even if they live carnally.

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

8. “Healed.” Albornus, from Isidore’s original, reads “healthy.” Instead of “there rises … perfidy,” Albornus has “there hides … perfidy.” AREV.]

8. He bears leprosy in the scar of a healed ulcer who, after knowledge of God, healing, and the manifestation of the faith he received from Christ, again displays in that scar some indication of his former error or the faithlessness of his former doctrine.

9. He bears leprosy in living flesh who holds some false opinion about the soul, which is the life of the flesh, such as the Luciferians, who say that the soul was propagated from the substance of the flesh; and the Arabians, who think that the soul dies together with the body.

10. The Manichaeans have leprosy in the scar of a burn. Through the futile torment of abstinence they burn their bodies, and through unbelief they produce from it not purity but leprosy. The Apostle spoke prophetically about such people: “Some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding to marry and commanding abstinence from foods that God created to be received” (1 Tim. 4:1 ff.).

11. He further added the colors of leprosy: pale, red, white, livid, black, and flowering. Thus, when he speaks of pale leprosy, he denotes a weak and fragile faith of the soul, which, having lost the color of complete health, languishes in the weakness of error. When he displays red leprosy, he denotes a mind infected with the blood of murder, and he implies—

12. When he speaks of white leprosy, he refers to those heretics who call themselves clean, or to others who glory in false merit, such as Pelagius and Novatus. When he mentions lean or livid leprosy, he curses the marks of envy and spite. When he indicates black leprosy, he detests a conscience blackened by the smoke of sacrifices and the pyre of idolatry. When he speaks of flowering leprosy over the whole body, covering the entire skin of the body from head to feet, he reveals the crime of avarice, because in the present world a person is thought to be flourishing and happy when he appears prosperous and rich in this age.

13. This plague of avarice stains the entire human race, as though it were the whole body, with the repeated contagion of error. When he speaks of leprosy that has redness mixed with paleness, he denotes a person who, although weak-minded and deceitful, easily bursts into fury and, through fickleness of character, quickly commits perjury; paleness signifies a lying tongue, while redness reveals anger.

14. There is therefore the leprosy of sin, which is cleansed by sacrificial offerings—that is, by a contrite and humbled heart: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50). There is also the leprosy of idolatry, which is washed away by the water of baptism. There is also the leprosy of heretics, which is dealt with by a seven-day purification outside the camp; that is, it is purified through recognition of the sevenfold Spirit.

15. There is also a kind that is removed by the priest’s inspection through doctrine. But the form of leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all belongs to those who sin against the Holy Spirit and deny that penitents can obtain forgiveness. Concerning them Truth says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

[Note: [Col. 0329D]

16. Albornus: “It is concluded that heretics are to be forbidden from the Church … and thus may be converted.” Grial published “he added the leprosy of Scripture.” I have restored *Scripture* from other printed copies and manuscripts. Instead of “let him teach, or speak,” perhaps one should read “let them teach, or speak.” AREV.]

16. The command that lepers leave the camp and sit outside until their leprosy is cleansed is understood to mean that heretics must be expelled from the Church until they are cleansed of their own error and thus return to the Lord. Such people are commanded to sit with their garments torn, their heads uncovered, and their mouths wrapped, while awaiting the cleansing of their leprosy: with their garments torn, that is, with all their secrets disclosed; with their heads uncovered, so that their exposure may be seen by everyone; with their mouths closed, so that they may no longer teach or utter impious things. Scripture further added that leprosy may be found in vessels, on the walls of a house, in clothing, in the warp, and in the woof.

17. Leprosy on the walls of a house denotes the assembly of heretics, which is commanded to be cleansed through the priest. Leprosy in vessels signifies the sins of each person’s own body. Leprosy in the warp or in clothing signifies sins committed outside the body or perpetrated within the body itself.

[Col. 0330A] 18. The warp is understood as the human soul, and the woof as the sensations of the most delicate body. The fact that lepers in the Law are sent to the priest indicates that, for the cleansing of heretics, the Church must first offer sacrifice to the Lord, and that they are thus to be reconciled to the unity of the Church.

## CHAPTER XII. On the high priest and his worship

[Note: [Col. 0330D]

CHAP. XII. Note 1. Albornus: “And he shall not approach any dead person at all,” etc. AREV.]

1. The Lord said to Moses: “The high priest, that is, the greatest priest among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood, and who is clothed in holy garments, shall not uncover his head, tear his garments, or enter at all where there is any dead person.”

2. “He shall not defile himself even for his father or mother, nor go out from the holy places, lest he pollute the sanctuary of his God, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God has been poured upon him. I am the Lord. He shall take a virgin as his wife. He shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, lest he defile his offspring.”

3. This high priest among his brothers is the one of whom it is written, when he had risen from the dead: “Go to my brothers and tell them: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). Upon his head the oil of anointing has been poured, in accordance with what the prophet David says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

[Note: [Col. 0330D]

4. Albornus: “It is not torn, but is preserved to be possessed indivisibly.” AREV.]

4. His hands have been consecrated. He has consecrated hands when he extends them in his passion for the expiation of the whole world. His garment is not torn; that is, he does not allow his Church, which is his proper garment because it clings to him, to be divided into heresies and schisms. The figure of this garment was that seamless tunic of Jesus, woven throughout, which was not torn during the passion but was preserved intact by its possessor.

5. He must not approach a dead person, because he committed no sin; for death is understood through sin, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die.” He shall not be defiled by his father or mother. Christ was not defiled by his mother when, before the ages, he was born from the Father.

[Col. 0330D] 6. Likewise, he was not defiled by his Father when he was born in time from his mother. He alone entered the world pure, proceeding from a virgin’s womb without the contamination of human generation. We all, when we sin, are defiled in the father from whom we were created if we fall into heresy. Likewise, we are defiled in the mother if, while believing in God, we allow the Church to be harmed in any way, or if we disgrace the freedom of our heavenly mother through an unworthy slavery to sin.

[Col. 0331A] 421 7. He shall not depart from the holy places, because through assuming flesh Christ descended into the world in such a way that he never abandoned heaven. He shall not take as wife a widowed, divorced, or prostituted woman, but a virgin. The widow and divorced woman is the Synagogue, concerning which the Lord speaks through Isaiah: “Where is this bill of divorce of your mother, with which I dismissed her?” (Isa. 50). The prostitute is heresy, which lies open to the error or lust of many. Such women are not joined to Christ; only the virgin Church is joined to him, a Church without spot or wrinkle. Concerning her the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

[Note: [Col. 0331D]

8. Albornus: “Desire takes them captive.” Perhaps: “They are taken captive by desire.” AREV.]

8. The soul too is said to be a bride, but only that soul which is proved incorrupt and virgin through the simplicity of faith and purity of actions. There is also a widowed soul that, having departed from the yoke of the Law, does not keep the commandments of the Gospel. There is also a divorced soul, separated from Christ’s body through sin, even if it is not expelled from the Church. And there is a prostitute, which receives lovers into itself—that is, opposing powers and demons—which are seized by desire for its beauty.

9. The soul was created beautiful by God and exceedingly lovely, since it bears the image and likeness of God. Then follows: “He shall take a wife from his own kind”—that is, a soul joined to him by faith. “Nor shall he defile his offspring”—that is, the word of God preached in the Church, as it is written in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them with their feet” (Matt. 7).

[Col. 0331C] 10. Up to this point, what was said mystically about the high priest has referred to Christ. From here onward, these same things are interpreted with reference to his members, especially priests, to whom the spiritual mysteries pertain. We must briefly review the privileges with which they are endowed.

11. For it says of him: “He shall not uncover his head”; that is, he should honor the mysteries of Christ, who is his head, through the veil of mysteries. “He shall not tear his garments,” lest he pass into heresy or schisms. “He shall not approach any soul that is dead”; he must not approach any sin that leads to death. “He shall not be defiled by his father or mother”; that is, he must not indulge his parents with such excessive affection that he offends his Lord and Creator, nor pity his relatives in such a way that he appears guilty before God.

[Col. 0331D] 422 [Note: [Col. 0331D]

12. The following was written in the margin of the Albornus Codex: “How many in monasteries, canonical communities, and episcopal offices have lost their souls while caring for their parents!” AREV.]

12. How many bishops, how many monks, have lost their souls while caring for their parents! He must not leave the holy places, so that he may always remain in holy action and thought. For whoever speaks what is idle and deserving of reproach departs from the holy places and pollutes God’s sanctification, because he does not walk as Christ’s servant. He shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute as wife, but a virgin; that is, he must embrace nothing belonging to the old human being or former pleasure, but possess a life flourishing in complete purity. He shall take a wife from his own kind; that is, he must embrace the life of the saints, to whom he is close through faith.

13. Along with this, the same priests are commanded, while ministering in the temple, not to drink wine or strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by drunkenness, gluttony, and the cares of this life, and lest they have any portion in the earth except God alone, lest, while thinking about earthly things, they forget heavenly things. The neighbor and the hired man are likewise commanded to be separated from this banquet, and only the servants are to be given the leftovers of the food.

[Col. 0332B] [Note: [Col. 0331D]

14. Albornus: “The right shoulder,” instead of “the right arm.” Shortly afterward, “good works and combat,” which also appears in the old edition of 1530. Finally, “to extinguish and restrain the throat”—that is, gluttony. Isidore uses *altariis* for *altaribus*, as elsewhere *altario* for *altari*. AREV.]

14. The neighbor is the heretic, who claims proximity to himself by the title of Christian; the hired man represents the Jew, who seeks the fruit of observance of the Law in a carnal manner. The priest of God must not share the nourishment of the Gospel with these people, nourishment intended for the refreshment of souls, but only with the servants of Christ. From what is offered upon the altars, the priest is given the breast and the right arm: in the breast we receive pure thoughts of the Law and knowledge of doctrine; in the right arm, good works for battle against the devil and an armed hand, so that what the heart has conceived may be fulfilled through the example of works. He is also given the jaw from the private portion, so that he may possess eloquence. From the victims he is also given the belly, so that by its indication he may learn to extinguish lust and restrain gluttony.

423 ## CHAPTER XIII. On priests who do not offer sacrifice

[Col. 0332C]

[Note: [Col. 0332D]

CHAP. XIII. Note 1. The entire chapter is from Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part 1, chapter 11. GRIAL.]

1. Among these commands, the priests themselves are ordered not to bear any conspicuous bodily defect: not to be blind, lame, or to have a small, large, or crooked nose; not to have a broken foot or hand; not to be hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, or have a white film over the eye; not to have a persistent skin disease, an eruption on the body, or to be heavy. All these things refer to a defect of the soul; for it is character, not nature, that is condemned in a human being.

2. A priest is blind because he does not understand the knowledge of Scripture and, through ignorance, does not know where to direct his step in teaching or action. Of such people it is written through Isaiah: “All his watchmen are blind” (Isa. 56:10). A lame person is one who understands what he ought to teach but nevertheless does not fulfill the precepts he teaches. He has a small nose who is not capable of maintaining the proper measure of discernment.

3. He has a large and crooked nose who is furious and threatening, with arrogant pride or immoderate discernment. He has a broken foot or hand who does not strive to walk along the way of God that he teaches. A priest is also hunchbacked when the weight of earthly desire presses him down and he turns his attention only slowly toward heavenly things. He is bleary-eyed whose intellect flashes toward knowledge of the truth but obscures it by living carnally. He has a white film over his eye who is blinded by arrogant claims to wisdom or righteousness.

4. He has a persistent scab who is continually dominated by the wantonness of the flesh. He also has an impetigo on his body who is ravaged in mind by avarice. Unless this is restrained while still small, it unquestionably spreads without measure. But he is burdensome who, although he does not practice disgraceful behavior in deed, is nevertheless weighed down in mind by continual, uncontrolled thoughts of it. Such a man can neither enter the holy place nor possess the title of bishop, because he is burdened by earthly desires and is lacking in knowledge of the truth.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Washing of Aaron and His Sons

[Column 0333B]

1. What, moreover, is meant by the fact that Moses is read to have washed Aaron and his sons according to God’s commands? Even then they were signifying the purification of the world and the holiness of all things through the sacrament of baptism.

[Note: [Column 0333D]

**Chapter XIV, no. 2.** “Nor are they adorned.” Thus Alborn[oz].’s manuscript and the old edition. Grialius has “nor are they ordained,” which is not satisfactory. AREV.]

2. They do not receive the garments until their filth has first been washed away, nor are they adorned for sacred service unless they are reborn as new men in Christ. But the fact that Moses washes them is an indication of the Law. For we must be washed by God’s commands; and when, prepared to put on Christ, we have rightly laid aside the tunics of skins, then we shall be clothed in a linen garment, bearing nothing of death within it but being entirely white. Thus, rising from baptism, we may gird our loins with truth, and all the shamefulness of our former sins may be concealed. [Column 0333C] Hence David also says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31).

## CHAPTER XV. On the Offering for the Priest’s Sin

1. What, then, does the figurative law mean when it commands a calf to be sacrificed for the priest’s sin and the people to be sprinkled seven times with its blood by the priest’s finger? Then it requires two goats to be offered: one, upon which the Lord’s lot falls, is to be killed, and the people are to be sprinkled with its blood, or with blood from the calf, by the priest’s finger; but the other, upon which all the sins and curses of the entire people are to be placed, is to be led to a deserted place and released there?

[Note: [Column 0333D]

**Chapter XV, no. 2.** “He bore in himself.” Alborn[oz] and Flor. 2 read “he marked in himself,” or “he lined in himself” (*liniabat* or *lineabat*), which is not implausible. Others read *limabat* (“he filed in himself”), which I think is corrupt for *liniabat*. AREV.]

2. But it is first necessary to explain the sacrifice of the calf, [Column 0333D] and then also to relate the cause and mysteries of the goats. This calf, therefore, which is commanded to be killed for the purification of the priest and the whole people, bore in itself the figure of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who was sacrificed, with God the Father permitting it, not only for the sins of the priestly people but also for the entire human race and all nations, as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8).

[Column 0334A] 3. It is fitting, too, that in this passage the people are commanded to be sprinkled seven times with the blood of that calf by the priest’s finger, so that it might be shown that our redemption and purification were bestowed through Christ’s blood by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. The two goats plainly demonstrated the figure of two peoples, bearing the form of goats because of the original transgression of sin.

4. Their likeness appears in the Gospel: the kids—that is, sinners—who will be placed on the left (Matthew 25). But those among them who have believed in Christ and wholeheartedly done penance for their sins, having obtained the grace of baptism, receive the figure of the one goat upon which the Lord’s lot falls. Its blood is commanded to be mixed with the blood of the calf, so that, [Column 0334B] having become sharers in Christ’s passion, they may become participants in his glory.

5. But what does it mean for the goat to fall to the Lord’s lot except that the believing people, whose figure that goat bore, should be regarded as the Lord’s companion and coheir in the kingdom, as the Apostle says: “We are heirs of God, and coheirs of Christ”? The other goat, which does not fall to the Lord’s lot, represents unbelievers, who never wished to believe in Christ. These indeed receive the curse of the entire people and all the iniquities of the human race, and they are cast into a deserted place.

6. But what does it mean to receive all the iniquities and curses except that all the sins committed by the human race from Adam to Christ will be received by those alone [Column 0334C] who were unwilling either to believe in Christ or to be cleansed by Christ’s blood? Thus, laden and weighed down with the iniquities and curses of the entire people—that is, of the human race—they will be cast into a deserted place, that is, into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and into the lake of fire, which is Gehenna, where their fire will not be extinguished and their worm will not die.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Animals That Are Not Offered in Sacrifice

1. The diversity of victims, and which are or are not to be offered, is enumerated in this book of Leviticus. But human conduct is demonstrated by comparison with animals. Anyone who offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the Lord, whether fulfilling a vow or offering voluntarily, shall offer an unblemished animal, whether from cattle or sheep, so that it may be acceptable; there shall be no defect in it.

2. If it is blind, broken, scarred, afflicted with a rash, scabbed, or affected with impetigo, you shall not offer it to the Lord, nor shall you burn any of these upon the Lord’s altar. You may voluntarily offer an ox or a sheep whose ears or tails have been cut off, but a vow cannot be made with such animals. Any animal that has been crushed, shorn, cut, or had its testicles removed you shall not offer to the Lord; and you shall not do this at all in your land.

3. You shall not offer bread to your God from the hand of a foreigner, nor anything else that he wishes to give, because all such things are corrupted and defiled; you shall not accept them. First, the spotted or multicolored animal is rejected from the sacrifice—that is, people in whom there is a diversity of sins and who change now into lust and desire, now into various crimes. The blind animal is also rejected: that is, one who neither sees God nor performs his works.

[Note: [Column 0335C]

**Chapter XVI, no. 4.** *Qui in sortem* (“who comes to the lot”). Thus Alborn[oz]’s manuscript. Grialius has *qui in sorte* (“who is in the lot”). Others have *qui in similitudinem* (“who is in the likeness”). But the reading of Albornoz’s manuscript seems more correct, since *in sortem Domini venire* (“to come to the Lord’s lot”) occurs again. AREV.]

4. The broken animal is also rejected—that is, one tormented and battered by carnal vices. The scarred animal is rejected as well: one who does not lament the wounds of his sins with worthy penitential satisfaction, but still bears inwardly the mark of his former disease through desires for pleasure. The animal with its tongue cut out is likewise rejected: one who does not confess the Lord and does not meditate on the divine law.

[Note: [Column 0335C]

**Chapter XVI, no. 5.** Alborn[oz] has *et scabiosus, qui* (“and the scabbed one, who”); the others have *scabiosum qui* (“the scabbed animal, who”), as above: *Caecum animal, id est, qui* (“the blind animal, that is, one who”). Shortly afterward Alborn[oz] likewise has: “They do not obey by doing what is just.” AREV.]

5. The animal with a rash is also rejected: one who seethes with the itching of lust and the heat of desire. Likewise the scabbed animal: one who completes the sin of the flesh through the contagion of his deed. But the animal with impetigo represents the assembly of heretics, which frequently plunges itself into the body of the Church and, like impetigo, produces a livid discoloration. Those with their ears cut off are people who do not obey the word of God by doing what has been commanded.

[Column 0335B] 6. But the one whose tail has been cut off is the person who does not bring the good work he begins to completion with a persevering end. The animal that has been cut or has had its testicles removed indicates those who, although they are men in body, are feminized by the practice of disgraceful conduct. [Column 0335C] Ensnared in these crimes, therefore, they are rejected from the Lord’s sacrifice; they do not become sharers in Christ’s passion, nor participants in heavenly sanctification.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Remaining Ceremonies

[Note: [Column 0335C]

**Chapter XVII, no. 1.** This chapter has appeared incomplete up to the present in all editions, except that in the latest Madrid edition Ulloae’s supplement was relegated to the appendices, volume II, page 64, from the Bologna manuscript. It also exists complete in Vatican Manuscript 627, which I described in *Isidoriana*, chapter 94, where, in section 11, I noted that the Vatican manuscript differs somewhat from Albornoz’s.

I have before me two copies transcribed from the Bologna manuscript, with variant readings noted in that manuscript from the original of Isidore—whether the Bologna manuscript was truly collated with the saint’s own autograph, or with another old manuscript that the collator believed or called Isidore’s original. Ulloae’s edition contains some brief notes on this chapter, perhaps prepared by the most learned Henry Florez; for it is noted that Don Pedro de Castro, an alumnus of the Bologna College, transcribed the fragment from Albornoz’s manuscript. He recently died in extreme old age during the plague at Seville, while serving as a canon of that metropolitan church. The copy was most generously communicated by the Reverend Father Henry Florez. [Column 0336C]

The older editions present only the beginning of the chapter, and not even as far as “the Catholic Church.” In Grialius, *offerantur* occurs instead of *offeruntur*. I have reproduced the reading attributed in Alborn[oz] to Isidore, or to the Original. For the text of the manuscript reads: “But not even foreign bread is offered.” Grialius soon has: “to the Lord, that is, the doctrine of heretics … which is outside the faith.” AREV.]

1. But neither is foreign bread offered to the Lord, nor the doctrine of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature, because these are outside the faith and are considered foreign. Such offerings, therefore, are rejected by the Lord, and this kind of sacrifice is rejected by the Catholic Church.

[Note: [Column 0336C]

**2.** In my two copies from the Alb[ornoz] manuscript: “When Christ did not come to abolish the Law.” In Ulloae’s edition it is noted that what follows, beginning “It is therefore asked,” is taken word for word from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 19, chapter 9. AREV.]

2. Now we must speak about how certain ceremonies are understood spiritually. The Jews also ask about these matters with the greatest scrupulousness, saying: “Why do Christians not strive to observe them, since Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it?” It is therefore asked why a Christian is no longer circumcised in the flesh, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it.

[Note: [Column 0336D]

**3.** “For I answer briefly.” This is what appears in the Alb[ornoz] manuscript; the collator of that manuscript noted from Isidore: “the answer is: Therefore.” In Ulloae’s edition this variant is taken from Saint Augustine: “And what is to occur in our resurrection is commended through the sacrament of baptism.” AREV.]

3. The answer is: A Christian is no longer circumcised because Christ has already fulfilled what was foretold by that circumcision itself. For the stripping away of carnal generation, which was represented in that act, has already been fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection; and what will occur in our resurrection is commended through the sacrament of baptism. For if the Jews were justified by the Lord’s resurrection—which was an eighth day, after the Sabbath, that is, after the seventh—then surely they would be stripped of the carnal veil of mortal desires, and, rejoicing in the circumcision of the heart, would no longer express in the flesh what had been foreshadowed and represented.

[Note: [Column 0336D]

**4.** “Let a Christian not observe.” Thus the Original of Isidore. In the Alb[ornoz] manuscript: “Let Christians not observe.” Instead of “and this,” Ulloae’s edition, following Augustine, gives “indeed this is indicated.” In that edition *respondetur* (“the answer is”) was omitted, although the Alb[ornoz] manuscript has it, or *responderunt* (“they answered”), according to Isidore’s Original. The collator notes that *vos* (“you”) was placed before *reficiam* (“I shall refresh”) in the manuscript between two columns, following the line, but in another hand. Ulloae’s edition represents it as “You at the beginning of the line,” but in another hand. AREV.]

4. When it is asked why a Christian does not observe Sabbath rest, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Indeed, a Christian does not observe this either for the reason that Christ has already fulfilled what was foretold by that figure. For in him we have the Sabbath, who said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28).

[Note: [Column 0336D]

**5.** “When it is asked, etc.” Ulloae’s edition observes that these words belong to Saint Augustine, cited work, book 19 *Against Faustus*, chapter 10. Likewise, in Saint Augustine, instead of *in illius figuris* (“in the figures of that”), one finds *illis figuris* (“in those figures”), with *in* omitted.

From the words “therefore a Christian does not observe it, because what,” and so on, through the words of section 7, the text reads: “the truth was Christ.” “The answer is: Indeed,” in the Alb[ornoz] manuscript is marked between the columns by the hand of an ancient collator: “I did not find this in the Original of Isidore.” That is, he did not find it in the older manuscript—or, if you prefer, in Isidore’s autograph—which I consider less likely. It would have been easy for a copyist of an older manuscript to be misled by the repetition of the words “the answer is: Indeed” and to omit the intervening words. AREV.]

5. We therefore now consider it superfluous to observe the cessation of Sabbaths, since the hope of our eternal rest has been revealed. When it is asked why a Christian does not observe the distinction of foods prescribed in the Law, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Rather, the Christian does not observe it for the reason that Christ fulfilled what was foretold in those figures, admitting nothing into his body—which he predestined in his saints for eternal life—that was signified by those animals in human conduct.

6. When it is asked why a Christian does not offer God a sacrifice of flesh and blood from slaughtered animals, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Rather, for this very reason the Christian ought no longer to offer these things, because Christ fulfilled through the sacrifice of his flesh and blood what they foretold by such figurative things. For who among us does not know that the sacrifices of those same animals were imposed more suitably upon a perverse people than offered to God as something he desired?

[Note: [Column 0337D]

**7.** The text of Albornoz’s manuscript, reproduced by Ulloae’s edition, was corrupt and incomplete as follows: “Our purification and God’s propitiation are nothing without blood. But the truth of those figures was Christ. The answer is: Rather, for this reason …” These words, however, were marked with an obelus in the manuscript, and the reading I have adopted was added in the margin, except that it has *veritatis* (“of the truth”) rather than *veritas* (“the truth”). AREV.]

7. Yet our figures were present in these things, because our purification and God’s propitiation for us are nothing without blood. According to that figure, Christ is the truth, by whose blood we have been redeemed. When it is asked why a Christian does not observe unleavened bread, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Rather, the Christian does not observe these things for this very reason, because Christ fulfilled what was foretold by that figure, demonstrating a new life after the leaven of the old life had been purged. Therefore, not eating unleavened bread for the prescribed seven days was a sin in the time of the Old Testament; but in the time of the New Testament it is not a sin.

[Note: [Column 0338D]

**8.** In the Alb[ornoz] manuscript and the text of Ulloae’s edition: *animam induens justitiam* (“clothing the soul with righteousness”). I supplied *nostram* (“our”) from Isidore’s Original, and read *justitia* (“righteousness”) from the same source; likewise, shortly afterward, the text itself of Scripture, although the manuscript text and the cited edition omit *ipsa* (“itself”). AREV.]

8. But in the hope of the age to come, which we have from Christ, who, clothing our soul with righteousness and our body with immortality, renews us entirely, it is always a sin, as long as these seven days through which time is carried onward continue to revolve, to believe that we shall suffer or do anything out of the necessity and want of the old corruption. But what was then hidden figuratively in the times of the Old Testament was understood by certain holy people; in the time of the New Testament it is revealed openly and proclaimed to the peoples. Hence Scripture itself was then a command, but now it is a testimony.

[Note: [Column 0338D]

**9.** “Why does a Christian not celebrate Passover from the flesh, etc.” Thus from Isidore’s Original. The Alb[ornoz] manuscript has: “Why does a Christian not celebrate Passover from the blood of the lamb?” AREV.]

9. When it is asked why a Christian does not celebrate Passover from the flesh of a lamb, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Rather, the Christian no longer celebrates Passover in this way because Christ, the spotless Lamb, fulfilled through his passion what was foretold by that figure. When it is asked why a Christian does not celebrate the new moons commanded in the Law, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: Rather, the Christian no longer celebrates them for this reason, because Christ fulfilled what they were celebrated to foretell. For the celebration of the new moon foretold the new creation, of which the Apostle says: “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away, and everything has become new.”

10. When it is asked why a Christian does not observe those purifications for each kind of uncleanness that are prescribed in the Law, if Christ came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, the answer is: The Christian does not observe these things rather because they were figures of things to come, which Christ fulfilled. For he came to bury us with himself through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead, so we too might walk in newness of life.

[Note: [Column 0338D]

**11.** “In a certain manner … prophetically … represented … by some reality.” Thus Isidore. The Alb[ornoz] manuscript has: “in a certain manner … prophetic … are represented … of some city.” AREV.]

11. When it is asked why the Feast of Tabernacles is not a Christian solemnity, if the Law was fulfilled by Christ and not abolished, the answer is that the faithful are God’s tabernacle, in whom he deigns to dwell when they are joined and, in a certain manner, compacted together by love. For this reason Christians especially do not observe it, because Christ has already fulfilled in his Church what that figure prophetically promised. At one time not celebrating the Feast of Tabernacles was a sin; now it is not a sin. But failing to be joined together as God’s tabernacle, which is the Church, is always a sin. What was then done under a figurative command is now read in revealed testimony. For what was then made would not be called the tabernacle of testimony unless it bore some correspondence to a reality that was to be made manifest in its own time.

[Note: [Column 0338D]

**12.** The manuscripts write *jobeleum*. In Ulloae’s edition, at the words “For just as the seventh day,” etc., it is noted that these words are from Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, book 35, chapter 8, section 16. AREV.]

12. When it is asked why the seventh year of remission, or jubilee, was not observed—the year in which trumpets were sounded and everyone returned to his former possession—the answer is that the figure of the jubilee signifies the rest of eternal blessedness. For just as the seventh day is commanded to be a day of rest, so that eternal rest may be signified through it, so in the jubilee, which in the course of the years is brought to fifty by repeating the number seven seven times and adding one, the secure rest of perpetual blessedness is proclaimed.

[Note: [Column 0339A]

**13.** I have reproduced the text of Isidore’s Original. In the manuscript and in Ulloae’s edition: “Everyone returns to the ancient possession of the flesh. Then he returns to the ancient … [Column 0340A] expelled by Cain.” After “may possess it forever” appears this rubric: “The book of Leviticus ends. The book of Numbers begins.” AREV.]

13. When, at the voice of the archangel and the last trumpet sounding, all rise, the ancient possession of the flesh returns to everyone, then Adam will return to the ancient earth of his flesh, in which he dwelt. Then Abel will return to his own earth, from which he was expelled by Cain. Then Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also all the souls of mortals, will receive again their bodies, from which they departed, so that they may possess them forever.

# INTO NUMBERS

[Column 0339]

## PREFACE

[Column 0339B]

1. This book is called *Numbers*, one of the five books of Moses, because in it the census and number of the Israelite multitude that went out from Egypt, and of the perfected men, are recorded.

2. In it their journeys and encampments are also numbered, from the borders of Egypt to the place and time at which Moses died. In it, too, the days of the dedication of the tabernacle and the measure of the offerings are counted—not without the mystery and significance of the sacred number.

[Note: [Column 0339D]

**Preface, no. 3.** “The catalogue of the encampments.” Almost everything is from Jerome, Letter 127 to Fabiola, and Ambrose’s book *On the Encampments*. GRIAL.]

3. The catalogue of the encampments of the children of Israel, from the first to the last, numbers forty-two in all. Matthew speaks of these: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations; from David to the deportation to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the deportation to Babylon [Column 0339C] to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matthew 1), that is, forty-two generations altogether.

4. Through these the true Hebrew passes, hastening from earth to heaven and, having abandoned the Egypt of the world, entering the promised land. Nor is it surprising that by the mystery of this number we arrive at the kingdom of heaven, under which the Lord and Savior proceeded from the first patriarch to the Virgin, as to the Jordan, which flowed with a full current and overflowed with the graces of the Holy Spirit.

# CHAPTER I

[Note: [Column 0339D]

**Chapter 1, no. 1.** From Jerome. GRIAL.

In the same place, Alborn[oz]’s manuscript has: “For when we are stirred to the preaching of the evangelical trumpet and awakened by thunder with joy.” AREV.]

1. The first encampment is the city of Rameses, which was at the farthest borders of Egypt. There the people gathered and went out into the desert on the day after Passover, in the sight of the Egyptians. Some have thought that *Rameses* should be interpreted as “commotion” or “thunder,” because when we are stirred by the evangelical trumpet and awakened by the thunder of joy, we go out in the first month, when winter has passed, when spring begins, and when all things are renewed.

[Column 0340B] [Note: [Column 0339D]

**2.** Alborn[oz]: “After eating the spotless lamb, and being shod, as the Apostle says, and girding the loins with chastity, and having staffs prepared in their hands.” In Grialius’s text there was an error: “and staffs in their hands prepared.” AREV.]

2. We go out on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover, in the full light of the month, after eating the spotless lamb, having our feet shod according to the Gospel—or the Apostle—and our loins girded with chastity, and having staffs prepared in our hands (Ephesians 6).

# CHAPTER II

[Note: [Column 0340D]

**Chapter II, no. 1.** From Jerome. GRIAL.

In the same place: “a journey to the holy heavenly land.” Alb[ornoz] has: “a journey to the holy land, heavenly.” Perhaps the old edition is better: “a journey to the holy land, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.” AREV.]

1. The second encampment is Succoth, where they bake unleavened bread and first pitch their tents. Hence the place received its name. For *Succoth* is interpreted as “tabernacles” or “tents.” When, therefore, we have gone out of Egypt—that is, from the world—let us first pitch our tents, knowing that we must proceed farther and hasten our journey to the holy heavenly land.

# CHAPTER III

[Note: [Column 0340D]

**Chapter III, no. 1.** From Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The third encampment is Etham, which lies at the edge of the wilderness, where the Lord is first seen going before the people in a pillar of fire. *Etham* signifies “strength” or “perfection.” Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves, taking on perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear. Let our day also have a protecting cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the land of holy promise.

# CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Column 0340D]

**Chapter IV, no. 1.** From Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The fourth encampment is Pi-hahiroth, which is opposite Baal-zephon. *Pi-hahiroth* is interpreted as “the mouth of nobles.” Therefore, having taken up strength, let us become noble in the Lord, despising Baal-zephon as well, which is interpreted as “lord of the north,” and let us avoid his pride.

[Note: [Column 0340D]

**2.** “Into the desert.” Thus Alborn[oz]. Grialius has “in the desert.” AREV.]

2. Departing from this encampment, the children of Israel passed through the middle of the sea into the desert, and they saw Pharaoh with his army drowned, while Miriam went before them, singing in advance with tambourines.

# CHAPTER V

[Column 0340D] [Note: [Column 0340D]

**Chapter V, no. 1.** From Jerome. GRIAL.

In the same place: “After crossing the Red Sea.” From Ambrose, *Encampments*, seventh. Others have “after traversing.” GRIAL.]

1. The fifth encampment is Marah, to which the children of Israel came after crossing the Red Sea three days earlier. *Marah* is interpreted as “bitterness.” For after the preaching of the Gospel and the encampments of those who migrate, after taking up the strength of faith, and after baptism and victory, one comes again to bitterness, so that pleasure and luxury may be brought to an end by the bitterness of life, and sweetness may again be restored through the wood of the cross, as through suffering.

# CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**Chapter VI, no. 1.** From Ambrose and Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The sixth encampment is Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, representing the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples of the second rank. From their springs we draw the drink of doctrine, and we gather the sweet fruits of victory. Hence Elim is rightly rendered “strong rams”; for they are the robust leaders of the flock, guides of the sheep, and teachers of the nations.

# CHAPTER VII

[Column 0341B]

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**Chapter VII, no. 1.** What is said about baptism is from Ambrose; the remainder is from Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The seventh encampment is again at the Red Sea, which is a type of baptism consecrated by the Lord’s blood. The question arises: How did they come again to the Red Sea after crossing it, after the bitter springs, and after Elim? Unless perhaps, as they proceeded on their journey, a certain inlet of the sea came before them, beside which they set up camp.

2. For crossing the sea is one thing, and pitching tents nearby is another. From this we are warned that after evangelical instruction and the sweetest nourishment of triumphs, the sea sometimes appears to us and former dangers are placed before our eyes.

# CHAPTER VIII

1. The eighth encampment is in the wilderness of Sin, which extends as far as Mount Sinai. *Sin* is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred,” because after we have come to the place of the Church, from which the Lord is to speak to us, we earn the great hatred of the enemy.

# CHAPTER IX

1. The ninth encampment is at Dophkah, which is called “knocking,” in accordance with what the Lord says: “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7). The meaning is clear: after we have come to the place of the Church, we begin to knock at the mysteries.

# CHAPTER X

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**Chapter X, no. 1.** From “after the Decalogue” through “the bread is eaten.” From Ambrose. GRIAL.]

1. The tenth encampment is at Alush, which is interpreted as “leaven,” the leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Matthew 13). In this wilderness the people murmured because of hunger, and in the evening they received quail, and in the morning of the following day manna. Note that manna is given in the tenth encampment—that is, after the perfection of the Decalogue, the bread of angels is eaten.

# CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**Chapter XI, no. 1.** Alb[ornoz] has “water burst forth.” But “he burst forth water” appears to be the Isidorian reading. AREV.]

1. The eleventh encampment is at Rephidim, which is interpreted as “the dissolution of the strong” or “the loosening of hands.” There, for the thirsty people, water burst forth from the rock of Horeb in the likeness of Christ. There Jesus, in the type of the Savior, fights against Amalek, and by the sign of the cross the assaults of demons rising against us are overcome.

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**2.** “When Jethro came.” See Origen, *Homily 11 on Exodus 18*. GRIAL.

In the same place: “suggesting.” Alborn[oz] has “following.” AREV.]

2. When Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, came, giving the counsel of the seventy elders, and as a type of the Church gathered from the nations, the diminution of the Law is completed through the Gospel’s suggestion. Rephidim is beautifully called “the dissolution and healing of the strong,” either because Amalek was scattered or because Israel was healed.

# CHAPTER XII

[Column 0342B]

[Note: [Column 0341D]

**Chapter XII, no. 1.** From Ambrose and Jerome. GRIAL.

In the same place: “And it is interpreted as ‘bush.’” But in Jerome: “Sinai is interpreted as ‘of bushes,’ not one, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many, so that there it is a beginning, here perfection; there a singular number, here a plurality. For it is one thing to possess one grace, another to possess all graces.”

It will be worthwhile to report an addition from the margin. Someone who had read “it is interpreted as red”—misled by the digamma, which in these manuscripts often occurs for *u* and *b*—added: “red, the Church redeemed from the blood of Christ,” as it appears in the book of Valens. GRIAL.

In the same place: “There the tabernacle is made,” etc. Everything through the end of the encampment is from Ambrose. GRIAL.

In the Alborn[oz] and Florentine manuscripts one reads, as in Valens: “red, the Church redeemed from the blood of Christ.” AREV.]

1. The twelfth encampment is in the wilderness of Sinai. Let the apostolic number immediately come to your mind. For *Sinai* is interpreted as “bush,” by which the Church is signified, in which the apostles preach to us. In this encampment Moses ascended to the Lord, and there the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, giving the Law to his people. There the tabernacle is made; there the variety of sacrifices, the diversity of vessels, the garments of the high priest, and the ceremonies of priests and Levites are prescribed.

2. There the number of the peoples and Levites, and the distribution of the people among the individual tribes, are given. The offerings of the leaders are also described in this encampment. Two silver trumpets are likewise commanded to be made there for moving the camps.

[Column 0342C] [Note: [Column 0342D]

**3.** “They dwelt.” Thus Alborn[oz]. Grialius, with the other printed editions, has “they dwell.” AREV.]

3. There the unclean are commanded, as well as those who were unable to attend the Passover in the first month, to assemble in the second month. But what is meant by the fact that those who lived farther away, or who were unclean in soul, were commanded to celebrate Passover in the second month? Clearly, in a typological sense, the peoples of the nations are understood: when they seemed unclean in soul because they had fornicated with all the demons, they are commanded, after being cleansed by a salutary confession, to pass over to a second birth, as it were to a second month.

[Note: [Column 0342D]

**4.** *Obliviscantur sapientiae* (“they forget wisdom”). Alborn[oz] has *obliviscantur sapientiam* (“they forget wisdom,” with the accusative). AREV.]

4. In this encampment the Nazirites are also commanded not to drink wine, strong drink, or anything made from grapes; nor are they to eat raisins or vinegar made from wine. But in Proverbs the powerful, who are prone to anger, are commanded not to drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom (Proverbs 31).

[Note: [Column 0343D]

**5.** “Arises from passion.” Ambrose has “arises from a muck or mass.” GRIAL.

In the same place, Alb[ornoz] has: “For they drink wine and strong drink.” Grialius seems to have wished to insert *passione* (“passion”) in the text, as the others have, instead of *colluvie* (“muck” or “filth”). AREV.]

5. What, then, is signified by the name of Nazirites except the life of those who abstain and practice self-restraint? In their case, luxury is prohibited in wine, and every earthly pleasure in strong drink. For strong drink is prepared from various ingredients, just as pleasure arises from a diverse accumulation of vices. Those who do not drink wine but do drink strong drink are people who pretend, in order to deceive others, to possess certain shadows and images of virtues.

[Note: [Column 0343D]

**6.** In some manuscripts: “They eat raisins,” as *utor* (“I use”) sometimes occurs with the accusative. AREV.]

6. They eat raisins who, for the sake of human eyes, are discolored by the pallor of abstinence, so that they may seek glory from men. Those drink vinegar who, after a holy way of life, fall back into the oldness of their former vices and take pleasure in the corruption of their former wickedness. God therefore commanded that those who have put on the title of holiness should abstain from all these vices and seek no such disturbance as would overturn the state of the mind.

7. In this encampment lepers, those with discharges, and the unclean are cast out of the camp. Lepers are heretics; those with discharges are unclean in thought; the unclean are so in deed. They are separated from the camp of the Church as defiled and diseased, lest they pollute the life of the innocent through the contagion of their conduct.

438 8. There the people who are chosen for battle are counted from the twentieth year onward. But why from the twentieth year, except because from this age the battles against each of the vices arise? Therefore they are chosen for combat, so that they may contend against lust and not be overcome by luxuries.

[Column 0343C] [Note: [Column 0343D]

**9.** “And from the fiftieth year they become keepers of the vessels.” Thus the old edition. Grialius has *fiant* (“let them become”), probably in error. Breulius gives *fiant*, but in such a way that the phrase reads: “from the fiftieth year … let them become.” AREV.]

9. There too the Levites are commanded to serve the tabernacle from the age of twenty-five, and from the fiftieth year they become keepers of the vessels. For what is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth begins to arise, except the very battles against each of the vices? And what is signified by the fiftieth year, in which the rest of the jubilee is also contained, except the inward rest expressed after the battle of the mind has been subdued? And what are signified by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful?

10. Thus the Levites serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, and from their fiftieth year become guardians of the vessels, so that those who still endure the struggles of opposing vices through the consent of pleasure may not presume to undertake the care of others. But when they have subdued the battles of temptations, when they are already secure in themselves concerning inner tranquility, let them receive the guardianship of souls.

[Col. 0344A] [Note: [Col. 0343D]

11. The Vulgate has: “and making me captive in the law of sin.” AREV.]

11. But who can completely subdue these battles, when Paul says: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23)? Yet it is one thing bravely to endure battles, and another to be enfeebled and overcome by battles: in the former, virtue is exercised, so that no one should become exalted; in the latter, it is utterly extinguished, so that it cannot survive.

[Note: [Col. 0343D]

12. “‘Charity all the hairs of the flesh … renders’ are words of Gregory, *Moralia* V, chapter 24; from it we read *fruticantibus* (“sprouting”), not *fructificantibus* (“bearing fruit”), as manuscript o had. Ambrose has *excrescentibus* (“growing out”). GRIAL.]

[Col. 0344D] The same place. In Grial’s note, *levitis* (“for the Levites”) seems to be the correct reading instead of *charitas* (“charity”), and *reddat* (“may render”) instead of *reddit* (“renders”). AREV.]

12. Then the Law commanded the Levites there to shave all the hairs of their flesh, because those who are taken up for divine service ought to appear pure before the eyes of God from every thought of the flesh, lest the mind bring forth unlawful thoughts and render the beautiful appearance of the soul deformed, as though by luxuriant hairs.

[Note: [Col. 0344D]

13. “For the battle-array of faith”—that is, “for the battle of faith.” Ambrose. GRIAL.]

13. After this, they are also commanded to make two trumpets, at whose blast the people would be moved to battle. For thus it is written concerning them to Moses: “Make for yourself two silver trumpets, hammered out.” And shortly afterward: “When the divided blast sounds, the camps shall move.” For the army is led by means of two trumpets, because through the two Testaments—or through the two commandments of charity—the people are summoned to the battle-array of faith.

14. They are commanded to be made of silver for this reason: so that the words of preachers may shine with the splendor of eloquence and not confuse the minds of their hearers through any obscurity of their own. They are hammered out because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations.

[Note: [Col. 0344D]

15. Codex Bononiensis: “When the preaching is treated more subtly and minutely, conflicts—that is, struggles—are aroused more intensely. From this point the children of Israel move forward,” etc. The Vulgate has: “they shall move the camps.” AREV.]

15. It is rightly said: “When the divided blast sounds, the camps shall move,” because, when the preaching is treated more subtly and precisely, the minds of the hearers are stirred more fervently against the struggles of temptation. From this point the children of Israel move forward from Mount Sinai and pass into the graves of desire.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Note: [Col. 0344D]

Chapter XIII is composed entirely from the words of Jerome and Ambrose. GRIAL.

The same place. “Which are of great flesh.” Thus in book o and in Ambrose. Jerome has: “Which are the songs of poets.” GRIAL.

The same place. Codex Albaniensis: “bread, and not the purulent things of the Egyptians, which are,” etc. AREV.]

1. The thirteenth station is at the graves of desire, where the people, weary of the heavenly bread, desired Egyptian flesh. A sudden fire devoured many of them. From this we learn that those who have abandoned worldly conduct and rejected the Egyptian pots—that is, the burning desires of the flesh—must not murmur against the heavenly bread, nor seek the poisonous corruptions of Egypt, which are “of great flesh,” [Col. 0344D] but must seek the simple food of manna, that is, a pure and heavenly life.

[Col. 0345A] [Note: [Col. 0345D]

2. “Otherwise, if after receiving the angelic manna,” etc. Ambrose differs slightly: “Otherwise, if after the commandments, the angelic food, and the manna of heavenly life—or doctrine—we should again desire Egyptian flesh,” etc. GRIAL.

The same place. “We shall swallow nausea.”—Valentinus has “the nausea of the mind”; but Jerome does not have the word “mind.” GRIAL.

Codices Albaniensis and Florentinus 1: “We shall swallow nauseating things, and immediately … we shall turn them into tombs.” AREV.]

2. Otherwise, if after receiving the angelic manna, which is heavenly life—or doctrine—we should again desire Egyptian flesh, which consists in the carnal pleasures of this age, and the desires of our former ways, we shall swallow nausea, and immediately be tormented by the Lord’s fire; and our desire will be turned into tombs, so that we may be whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity.

3. At this station the spirit descended upon seventy chosen men; then the Lord descended in a cloud, took some of the spirit that was upon Moses, and placed it upon the seventy men. For when Christ descended in the cloud of flesh, the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out through faith upon peoples chosen from the seventy languages of the nations, and that gift of heavenly power came upon all which had once been in Moses and the prophets.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0345D]

Chapter XIV, note 1. From the same sources. GRIAL.]

1. The fourteenth station is in the wilderness of Hazeroth. At this place Aaron the priest, encountering an occasion of offense together with his sister Miriam, both of them spoke against their brother because he had taken a foreign wife. Therefore Miriam immediately blossomed with the contagion of leprosy.

2. Here the figure of the mystery was evident: that priestly people of the fathers spoke against Christ the Savior because of the Church gathered from the nations. Therefore it is covered with the filth of leprosy, nor does it return to God’s tabernacle until the appointed time of the fullness of the nations has been completed. Then that same people will be able to recover its former health, when a sevenfold spiritual recognition has assisted it toward pardon.

## CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0345D]

Chapter XV, note 1. From Jerome. GRIAL.

The same place. “Or courts.” This must unquestionably be read in accordance with Jerome, both at station 14 and here. There *hazeroth* is translated as “courts”; here, however, after the graves of desire, it means “vestibules.” Most books therefore mistakenly have *antra* (“caves”). The cave evidently seemed related to a tomb. GRIAL.]

1. The fifteenth station is at Rethma, which is translated as “sound” or “juniper.” This wood is said to preserve fire for a very long time, so that if coals are covered with its ash, they last until the end of the year. From this we learn that after the graves of desire—or the courts—we pass to wood that remains hot for a long time, so that we may be fervent in spirit and preach the Lord’s Gospel with a clear sound and a voice raised on high.
