2. From this station up to the thirty-second, the following histories are contained. Since they are not distributed among the individual stations, we too shall discuss them together.

[Note: [Col. 0346D]

3. “The assault of giants.” Thus Jerome, Valentinus, Complutensis, Palentinus, and Guadalupensis. “The people of giants.” GRIAL.

The same place. Codex Albaniensis: “A cluster is brought back; in this wood the passion of Christ is briefly shown.” AREV.]

3. Twelve spies are sent to the holy land. [Col. 0346A] A cluster is brought back on a piece of wood, and the passion of Christ is displayed. The Jewish people murmur, fearing the assault of giants. They fight against Amalek and the Canaanite against God’s will; when defeated, they understand what sacrifices they ought to practice in the holy land. Dathan, Abiram, and the sons of Korah rise up against Moses and Aaron, and are swallowed by a chasm in the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0346D]

4. “The green branch is preserved after drying.” Thus in Numbers 17 and in Jerome. “Is consecrated” in book o, erroneously. GRIAL.

The same place. “A propitiatory sprinkling.” Thus Jerome. “A distinctive sprinkling” in book o, erroneously. GRIAL.]

4. Between the dead and the living the high priest enters, armed with a censer, and the wrath of God is halted by the priest’s voice as he runs. Aaron’s rod produces a flower and leaves, and the green branch, though dried, is preserved for everlasting remembrance. A red heifer is burned as a burnt offering, and its ashes are a propitiatory sprinkling.

[Note: [Col. 0346D]

5. The twelve spies: from Ambrose and Augustine, *Sermon* 100 on the seasons. GRIAL.]

5. Briefly noting the figures of these events, we shall begin with the twelve spies. The twelve spies sent to explore the fertile land, who terrified the people so that they would not believe they could receive the land promised by the Lord, prefigured the judgment of the scribes and Pharisees.

6. For just as those men were sent by Moses to examine the fertility of the land through careful investigation alone, so these men were commanded through the Law and the prophets to observe the Lord’s coming by searching the Scriptures. In that coming there was the land—that is, holy flesh—in which they could obtain the kingdom of God, an abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life.

442 [Note: [Col. 0346D]

7. Codex Albaniensis: “They would trust … they would believe in Christ.” Others: “They would believe Christ.” Grialius, erroneously: “warding off corruption.” AREV.]

7. But just as those men terrified the people through despair, so that they would not trust in God’s promise, so also those scribes and Pharisees persuaded the Jewish people not to believe in Christ. They desired to return to the Egypt of this age, rejecting the manna of faith, seeking the black pots of sins, the foul onions of blasphemies, and the melons withered by the corruption of vices and lusts.

8. But what does that cluster of grapes signify, which two bearers brought hanging from a piece of wood out of the midst of the promised land? The cluster hanging from the wood is plainly Christ from the wood of the cross, promised as salvation to the nations, poured forth according to the flesh from the earthly lineage of the womb of Mary his mother.

9. The two bearers who walked beneath the burden of that cluster represent both peoples. The first of them, the Jewish people, is blind and turned away, ignorant of the grace that hung there and weighed down by the burden of what was suspended—he will be subjected to the one who judges him. Of them it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their backs” (Psalm 68). But the one who came behind represented the people of the nations, who, believing and having Christ before their eyes, sees him while always carrying him, and follows him like a servant follows his master and a disciple his teacher, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16).

[Note: [Col. 0347D]

10. Codex Albaniensis: “He drenched it with contrition.” In Grial there seems to be an error: “the wine, the blood of his cross,” etc. The Old Edition: “the cluster which, having been poured out for our salvation, shed the wine of his blood through the crushing of the cross.” Shortly afterward Codex Albornianus: “Through the redness of the sacred blood of Christ, flashing with its sign, also possessing within it,” etc. AREV.]

10. This is the cluster which, poured out for our salvation, poured forth the wine of its blood through the crushing of the cross, and, when pressed, offered the cup of its passion to the Church. This is the cluster which the pomegranate followed as a companion in the grace of its gift—namely, our mother the Church, containing within herself, in the number of its seeds, a multitude of peoples; by its redness, flashing with the sign of Christ’s blood; and within, possessing its seeds distinctly, as the Apostle says: “Charisms are diverse, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are distributed by grace” (1 Corinthians 12). Since the unbelieving judged themselves unworthy of all these things, they did not merit to receive the land of Christ’s flesh flowing with milk and honey; the servants of Christ—that is, the Christian people—have obtained it through faith.

[Note: [Col. 0347D]

11. “To have possessed.” Thus Codex Albornianus. Grialius, with other printed editions, has “to have brought.” AREV.]

11. Concerning its teaching, the Church says daily: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118). We are taught through Gospel examples that the fig which they brought from the promised land together with the cluster represented the Law; and likewise it is established that the cluster displays the figure of the Savior, just as the Church says of Christ in the Song of Songs: “My brother is like a cluster of Cyprus,” because Christ cannot exist without the Law, nor the Law without Christ.

12. After this, a certain man gathering wood on the Sabbath is killed by the people. What does it signify that he was so atrociously slaughtered by the entire people at God’s command? Unbelievers readily bring this forward as an objection. Let them understand, therefore, that all these things happened to those men as types. They were written for our correction.

13. That former, carnal man who dared to violate the Sabbath while gathering wood, and was punished for it, represented the one who today, marked with the sign of Christ, is found to be performing a carnal work—that is, gathering wood, hay, and straw suitable as fuel for the eternal fire. If he gathers these things to his own destruction and is discovered, he is expelled by all and immediately killed, when he is judged by spiritual people. Thus everything that happened to those Jews through the Law is to be understood as a type.

[Note: [Col. 0347D]

14. “The destruction follows,” from Ambrose. GRIAL.

The same place. “They paid the penalty”; others: “they suffered the penalty.” GRIAL.]

14. Now follows the destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, [Col. 0347D] who, claiming for themselves the license to offer sacrifices contrary to Moses and Aaron the priest, paid the penalty for their attempts. They signify those who try to create heresies and schisms and deceive many by drawing them along with themselves, despising Christ’s priests and separating themselves from his clergy and the fellowship of his people. They dare to establish churches and another altar, and to make another prayer in illicit words, profaning the reality of the Lord’s sacrifice through false sacrifices.

15. Because these men strive against God’s ordinance, the bonds of the earth are broken open on account of their audacious presumption, and they are swallowed alive in a deep chasm. Not only those who are leaders of error, but also those who, by consenting, have become participants in the same error, will perish in the vengeance prepared for the fire of eternal judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0348D]

16. “Then holy Aaron, seeing the people being dragged into the ruin of death.” These words are read in various ways in ancient books, though with the same meaning; we have followed the Palentinus Codex, which we found more reliable than the others. GRIAL.

The same place. “Seeing the people being dragged into the ruin of death.” Codex Albaniensis: “The ruin of death cast upon the people.” And from the original of Isidore: “The ruin of death began for the people.” Others: “Seeing the people rushing into the ruin of death.” AREV.]

16. Then holy Aaron, seeing the people being dragged into the ruin of death, took a censer and ran to meet the devastation. Standing between the survivors and the slain, he blocked the deadly blow by placing himself before it, like a wall. This priest is the Lord Jesus Christ, the prince of the chief priests. [Col. 0348B] This priest, seeing the ruin of death in the world, came from the highest heaven and ran to meet it, like a giant hastening to run his course.

17. He stood between the living and the dead, because he was born and died. Taking up the censer of his passion and presenting it as a fragrance of sweetness, he suspended the destruction of eternal fire and struck down hostile death.

18. Aaron’s rod, which blossomed after being dry, signifies the flesh of Christ, which, after being cut from the root of Jesse, revives more vigorously after having been put to death. Thus the rod becoming green after its dryness is Christ rising after death. We understand the rod itself and the flower itself, so that in the rod the power of the one who reigns may be shown, and in the flower his beauty. Hence he also says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2).

[Note: [Col. 0348D]

19. Codex Albaniensis: “Christ, who, offering himself willingly, offered himself to the passion, in the bright light of faith,” etc. AREV.]

19. Others think that this rod, which produced a flower without moisture, represents the virgin Mary, who without intercourse gave birth to the Word of God. Of her it is written: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11)—that is, Christ, who, bearing beforehand the type of the future passion, made the flower of virgins purple with the bright light of faith and the blood of his passion, the crown of martyrs, and the grace of the continent.

20. Meanwhile, there remains the red heifer burned as a burnt offering, whose ashes were the expiation of the people. For thus it is said concerning it to Moses and Aaron: “Command the children of Israel to bring you a red cow of full age, in which there is no blemish and which has not borne a yoke. You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest, who shall lead it outside the camp and sacrifice it in the sight of all; and Eleazar shall dip his finger in its blood and sprinkle it seven times toward the entrance of the tabernacle. He shall burn it while all look on; its hide, flesh, blood, and dung alike you shall consign to the flame.”

[Col. 0349A] 21. “The priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice dyed into the flame that consumes the cow. Then, having washed his garments and body, he shall enter the camp, and he shall be unclean until evening. The one who burns it shall also wash his garments and body, and he shall be unclean until evening.”

22. “A clean man shall gather the ashes of the cow and pour them outside the camp in a very clean place, so that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel and used in the water of sprinkling, because the cow was burned for sin. When the man who carried the ashes of the cow has washed his garments, he shall be unclean until evening. The children of Israel and the resident aliens shall possess this as a holy ordinance forever. Whoever touches a dead person and is consequently unclean for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third day and shall be cleansed on the seventh day. If he is not sprinkled on the third or on the seventh day, he cannot be cleansed.”

[Note: [Col. 0349D]

23. “The red heifer is the flesh of the Savior.” See Augustine, Question 32 on Numbers. GRIAL.]

23. The red heifer is the flesh of our Savior, rosy with the blood of his passion, of full age because he accepted the passion at the perfection of his age. The fact that no yoke was placed upon it shows that Christ’s flesh was not subjected to sin, nor conquered by any sin. The fact that the children of Israel seized it and drove it outside the camp, with Eleazar the priest standing by, signifies the Jewish people and the consent of the priests to the Lord’s death, whom they drove outside Jerusalem and crucified.

[Note: [Col. 0349D]

24. Codex Albornianus: “the peoples whom they gathered for the Lord.” AREV.]

24. Therefore, just as those who offer the heifer are unclean, so those who seized and killed the Lord are considered sinners. And just as the one who gathers the ashes of sprinkling is clean, so all are clean who preached Christ’s passion to the nations and sprinkled his teaching throughout the whole world, gathering peoples for the Lord. The wood and hyssop, however, we believe to represent the cross and baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0349D]

25. Codex Bononiensis has *signify* instead of *represent*, and this is supported by Isidore. AREV.]

25. For by a bundle of hyssop the lambs were sprinkled with blood, and those who were accustomed to be cleansed thereby typologically represented the washing of baptism and the cleansing of the eternal fountain. The scarlet twice dyed signifies the figure of the sacred blood by which sinners are washed. It is twice dyed because through it they are cleansed both in body and in heart. These three things pertain to the purification of sinners: first, through the cedar, faith in the wood of the cross; second, through the hyssop, baptism; third, through the scarlet, the sacrament of the Lord’s blood.

26. Just as those people are commanded to be purified on the third day, so every soul is cleansed from all the filth of its offenses if it believes that Christ the Lord rose from the dead on the third day. Such a person will also be clean on the seventh day—that is, in the kingdom of the saints, when the Lord comes—and, blessed and joyful, will possess a share in that heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0350A] [Note: [Col. 0350D]

27. “From the assembly of the saints.” Others: “from the kingdom of the saints.” Others: “from the kingdom of heaven.” The Vulgate: “from the midst of the Church.” The Septuagint: ἐκ μέσου τῆς συναγωγῆς, “from the midst of the assembly.” GRIAL.]

27. But whoever has not been sprinkled—that is, whoever has not been fortified by faith in this grace—shall perish from the assembly of the saints and from the people of the faithful. The tabernacle is commanded to be sprinkled seven times with the blood of this heifer because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are distributed among the peoples of the Church through Christ’s blood, by which they are cleansed from every offense, as the Apostle says: “You have now been washed in the blood of Christ and in his passion” (1 Corinthians 6).

28. The fact that the heifer is burned with its hide and bones, and that the paschal lamb is likewise burned so that its bones are not broken, shows that the legs of the body of the Lord Jesus Christ were not to be broken in his passion, as the Evangelist testifies (John 19). Morally, however, no one can slaughter and offer at the Lord’s altar the red heifer, whose ashes are the expiation of the people, except one who has not performed earthly works, has not taken on the yoke of sin, and has not been bound by the chains of offenses.

29. From this point, after the spies and the cluster, after the destruction of the proud and the priestly censer, and after the flowering rod and the sprinkling of the burned heifer, let us return to the stations.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 0350D]

Chapter XVI, note 1. From Jerome together with all the others. GRIAL.]

1. The sixteenth station is at Ramoth, which in Latin is called “the division of the pomegranate,” signifying the Church. Like many seeds covered by a single rind, it gathers the whole crowd of believers into the unity of faith.

447 ## CHAPTER XVII

[Col. 0350C]

1. The seventeenth station is at Lebna, which in Latin is translated as “brick.” We read of the bricks of the Egyptians, which the people made and for which they groaned. From this we learn that on the journey of this life, as we pass from one state to another, we sometimes grow and sometimes decline, and after the ecclesiastical order often migrate back to bricks—that is, to carnal works.

## CHAPTER XVIII

1. The eighteenth station is at Ressa, which is translated as “bridles.” For if after making progress we descend again to muddy works, we must be bridled, and our wandering and headlong course must be directed by the restraints of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XIX

1. The nineteenth station is at Caalatha, which is interpreted as “Church,” so that the steps of those who run astray may be drawn back by bridles to the Church, and they may hasten to enter again the doors they had previously abandoned.

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 0350D]

Chapter XX, note 1. Codex Bononiensis: “And observe that the bridles which draw us back from vices introduce us.” AREV.]

1. The twentieth station is at Mount Sepher, which is interpreted as “beauty,” that is, Christ. Observe what the bridles accomplish: if they draw us back from vices, they lead us into the choirs of virtues and make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain, [Col. 0351A] concerning which it is written: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isaiah 2).

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 0351D]

Chapter XXI, note 1. Codex Bononiensis: “After the habitation of the Church, to the mountain.” And immediately, from Isidore: “in which, being placed, we marvel at him.” AREV.]

1. The twenty-first station is at Harada, which is translated as “miracle.” Observe how beautiful is the order of virtues. After the bridles, we are brought into the Church; after the habitation, we ascend to the mountain of Christ, where, being placed, we marvel at those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart.”

## CHAPTER XXII

1. The twenty-second station is at Maceloth, which is translated as “assemblies,” that is, “the Church.” For in it the multitude of believers abides, in accordance with what is written: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Psalm 132).

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0351D]

Chapter XXIII, note 1. Codex Bononiensis: “He is the guardian of blessedness, or of humility, so that he does not think highly of himself,” etc. AREV.]

1. The twenty-third station is at Tahath, which is interpreted as “fear,” because when someone comes to the Church and ascends to the most beautiful mountain, Christ, and confesses the greatness of Christ with awe and wonder, he must then add fear, which is the guardian of blessedness, so that he may not be high-minded, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5).

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0351D]

Chapter XXIV, note 1. “The station is at Thare, which some translate as ‘wickedness’ or ‘pasture.’” These are Jerome’s words, but he rejects this interpretation. Since the allegorical words that follow—“whether this refers to the rulers of the Churches,” etc.—also come from the same source, it is evident that the interpretation he approves is missing, namely “driver away” or “repeller.” We have therefore marked the passage with an asterisk, which anyone can easily complete from Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The twenty-fourth station is at Thare, which some translate as “wickedness” or “pasture” *.

2. This refers either to the rulers of the Churches or to the guardianship of the soul, so that each person may be vigilant and fearful, lest the lion, the devil, attempt to enter the sheepfolds—that is, the Churches—through the various openings of vices.

449 ## CHAPTER XXV

1. The twenty-fifth station is at Methca, which is translated as “sweetness.” You have ascended to the heights, marveled at the choirs of virtues, feared a fall, and driven away ambushers; immediately the sweet fruit of your labor follows, so that you may rightly say: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

## CHAPTER XXVI

1. The twenty-sixth station is at Hesmona, which in Latin denotes “haste.” That is, after we have tasted the sweet fruits of labor, we should not be content with rest and leisure; rather, hastening again toward what lies farther ahead, we should forget what is behind and stretch ourselves toward what is to come.

## CHAPTER XXVII

1. The twenty-seventh station is at Moseroth, which is interpreted as “bonds” or “discipline,” so that we may proceed with hurried step to our teachers, frequent their thresholds, and regard the precepts of virtue and the mysteries of Scripture as eternal bonds.

[Note: [Col. 0351D]

Chapter XXVII, note 2. “Noble men shall pass over to you, and they shall be your servants; they shall walk behind you, bound with fetters.” From the Septuagint, with the word “servants” added. But I wonder why the Latin translator of the Septuagint edition rendered χειροπέδαις, “with fetters,” as “with bonds,” while Jerome rendered Moseroth as “handcuffs,” so that the former seems to have considered not the Greek but the Hebrew word, whereas Jerome, contrary to his custom, seems to have followed the Seventy Translators. GRIAL.

The same place. In Codex Albornianus: “of whom it is read in Ecclesiastes, or Isaiah.” And shortly afterward: “with bonds.” Others understand the bonds as those of the devil, which, once broken … Concerning such things the prophet says. The words of Isaiah in the Vulgate are: “Noble men shall pass over to you, and they shall be yours; they shall walk behind you; bound in their hands they shall go.” AREV.]

2. These are Christ’s bonds, concerning which it is read in Isaiah: “Noble men shall pass over to you, and they shall be your servants; they shall walk behind you, bound with bonds” (Isaiah 45:14). There are also other bonds, those of the devil; when Samson broke them, he conquered his enemies. Concerning them the Prophet says: “You broke my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice an offering of praise” (Psalm 115).

450 ## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0352B]

1. The twenty-eighth station is Baneiacam, which by interpretation is translated as “sons of necessity” or “sons of gnashing.” Who these sons of necessity are, the psalm itself teaches us: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28). What necessity is so great that it is imposed upon the unwilling? Once you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and know their laws and testimonies as bonds of truth, by contending with adversaries you will bind them and lead them captive; and from those who were once enemies and captives you will make them free children of God, so that suddenly you may say with Zion: “I was barren and did not give birth; I was exiled and captive; and who raised these children? I was abandoned and alone; and where were these?” (Isaiah 49:21).

[Col. 0352C] 2. Further, what is interpreted as “sons of gnashing” refers to this meaning: through fear of punishment and of that place where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, crowds of believers abandon the devil’s bonds and submit their necks to Christ the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0352D]

Chapter XXIX, note 1. “Or certainly ‘cutting.’” Jerome: “or certainly—and this is what we think more correct—κατακοπή (*katakopē*), that is, ‘cutting.’” GRIAL.

The same place. “To extract.” Others: “to pull away.” Some add: “To extract, so that we may not grow sluggish in snatching Christ’s enemies from the lion’s mouth by gentle, whispered prayer before the final day.” This seems entirely foreign to Isidore. AREV.]

1. The twenty-ninth station is at Mount Gadgad, which is interpreted as “messenger,” or “girding,” or certainly “cutting.” For we cannot otherwise make the teachers of disciples and believers into sons of necessity unless we kill their teachers. Let us be cruel in killing them; let our hand not hesitate to draw a shoulder or the tip of an ear from the lion’s mouth.

[Col. 0353A] 2. Concerning “messenger” and “girding,” this may briefly be said: we shall supply great incentives to virtue for the sons of necessity when we announce to them the rewards of the future and teach those who are girded to enter into battle. Whatever of these three things the teacher does, he stands upon the mountain.

451 ## CHAPTER XXX

1. The thirtieth station is at Ietebatha, which is interpreted as “goodness,” which is Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXI

1. The thirty-first station is at Hebrona, which is interpreted as “passing over,” that is, the world, concerning which the Apostle says: “For the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7). Coming into it, God’s saints desire to pass over to better things. Concerning them the Psalmist sings: “Nor did those who passed by say: The blessing of the Lord be upon you” (Psalm 128:8).

## CHAPTER XXXII

1. The thirty-second station is at Asiongaber, which is translated as “the wood of a man.” These “woods of a man” can represent the multitude of the nations, with all their kinds of groves and trees. Up to this point the wilderness of Paran contains eighteen stations, which, though described in the catalogue, are not included in the preceding journey.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0353D]

Chapter XXXIII, note 1. “But Kadesh is holy.” Erroneously in some books: “But if holy.” See Jerome. GRIAL.]

1. The thirty-third station is in the wilderness of Sin. This is Kadesh. Kadesh, however, is interpreted as “holy” by antiphrasis, just as a grove may be called *lucus* when it gives no light, or a battle may be called *bellum* even though it is dreadful. At this station Miriam dies and is buried.

[Col. 0353C] [Note: [Col. 0353D]

2. Codex Albaniensis: “Nor lead the people of believers out of the wilderness of this world.” AREV.]

2. In Miriam, prophecy appears to have died; in Moses and Aaron, the Law and the Jewish priesthood appear to have reached their end. For neither can they themselves cross over into the promised land, nor lead the believing people out of the wildernesses of this world, except Jesus alone—that is, the true Savior, the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0353D]

3. “At this station, because of the waters, up to ‘wisdom,’ everything is from Augustine, *Against Faustus* XVI, chapters 16 and 17. GRIAL.]

3. At this station Moses offended God because of the waters of contradiction, [452] and was forbidden to cross the Jordan. Troubled by the people’s murmuring, he struck the rock with his rod in doubt, as though God could not make water flow from a rock, although he had already done so. What, then, does Moses’ faith signify here, since he hesitated to bring water forth from the rock? Let us rightly understand that this prophecy concerned Christ.

4. For although Moses bears one person or another in the sacred Scriptures in order to signify different realities, here he bore the person of the Jewish people placed under the Law, and represented it in prophetic foreknowledge. For just as Moses, striking the rock with his rod, doubted God’s power, so that people which was held under the Law given through Moses, fastening Christ to the wood of the cross, did not believe that he was the power of God. But just as water flowed for the thirsty when the rock was struck, so the wound of the Lord’s passion became life for believers.

[Note: [Col. 0354D]

5. Instead of *dicens* (“saying”), Codex Albaniensis has *dicentem* (“the one saying”), and Florentinus 1 has *dicentis* (“of the one saying”), namely the Apostle’s; this is understood as referring to the apostolic voice. Shortly afterward Codex Albaniensis: “God does not free the one who [suffers] death,” etc. AREV.]

5. We have a most illustrious and trustworthy apostolic statement concerning this matter, when he spoke about it, saying: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). Therefore God commands this carnal despair concerning Christ’s divinity to die upon Christ’s own height, when he commands Moses’ fleshly death to take place on the mountain. For just as Christ is the rock, so Christ is also the mountain: the rock is humble strength, the mountain exalted greatness. For just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” so the Lord himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5), declaring himself to be the mountain and his faithful, founded upon the glory of his name, to be the city.

[Col. 0354B] 6. The wisdom of the flesh lives when Christ’s humility, struck like a rock, is despised on the cross. For Christ crucified is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the nations; but the wisdom of the flesh dies when Christ is recognized as exalted like the height of a mountain. For to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

1. The thirty-fourth station is on Mount Hor, at the farthest boundaries of Edom. [453] Aaron ascended it at the Lord’s command and died in the fortieth year after the departure from Egypt, namely in the year when the new people was about to enter the promised land. And although on the mountain he left the priesthood to his son Eleazar, and although the Law leads those who fulfill it to the summit, nevertheless that very elevation does not extend beyond the Jordan’s waters, but remains at the farthest boundaries of earthly works. The people mourned him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. In the Law there is descent to the underworld; in the Gospel, passage to paradise.

2. The Canaanite also heard that Israel had come, and they entered into battle at the place of the spies, where they had once known that the people had been defeated, and they took Israel captive. Again battle is waged at the same place: the victor is defeated, and the defeated prevail. By this we understand that, when enemies attack us after we have been deprived of God’s help and lead us captive, we must not despair of salvation but arm ourselves again for battle. It may happen that we conquer where we were defeated and triumph at the very place where we had previously been captives. [Col. 0354D]

## CHAPTER XXXV

1. The thirty-fifth encampment is at Salmonah.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

1. The thirty-sixth encampment is at Punon. These two encampments are not found in the historical sequence: at them, after Aaron’s death, the Israelite people murmur against God and Moses, grow weary of the manna, and are wounded by serpents. [Col. 0355A]

[Note: [Col. 0354D]

**CHAP. XXXVI. NOTE 2.** “They may behold the image of the Son of God and his passion, and be saved.” From Origen, through Isidore. AREV.]

2. But what does the fact signify that the deadly bites of the serpents were healed when the bronze serpent had been raised up and looked upon, except that now, in the type of the Savior—who triumphed over the ancient and savage serpent on the gallows—the poisons of the devil are overcome? Thus whoever truly and plainly looks upon the image of the Son of God and his passion is saved. This is also signified by the words of the Lord himself: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.” [Col. 0355A]

[Note: [Col. 0355D]

**3. NOTE.** “That it is bronze,” down to “is accustomed to exist,” from Augustine, *Sermon 101 on Time*. GRIAL.

On the same passage: Concerning the bronze serpent, by which Christ was indicated, see Cotelerius’s *Apostolic Fathers*, vol. I, p. 40, with notes, and the more recent interpreters. AREV.]

3. Since the serpent is bronze, Christ himself is indicated, for he was suspended on wood; bronze, after all, is usually more durable than the other metals. And fittingly the bronze serpent was suspended on wood, so that the Lord might be signified as mortal in the serpent and eternal in the bronze—namely, that he was shown to be dead through humility, yet nevertheless was like bronze through divinity. The first encampment, Salmonah, is beautifully interpreted as “little image,” because there the image of the Savior was plainly represented through the bronze serpent, which there hung upon the wood like an image. [Col. 0355B]

4. Likewise, the second encampment, Punon, is beautifully interpreted as “mouth,” because after we recognize the passion of the Son of God, what we believe in the heart we proclaim with the mouth, reading the Apostle’s words: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0355D]

**CHAP. XXXVII. NOTE 1.** *Sirens.* So also some others. The correct form would be *sirenum*. AREV.]

1. The thirty-seventh encampment is at Oboth, which is translated as “magicians,” or “ventriloquists”; from this it is shown that, after the image of God—which is displayed in the reasoning of the heart—and the confession of faith—which is uttered by the mouth—serpents and magical arts rise up and provoke us to battle. But let us surround our heart with a guard, stop up our ears, lest we hear the voices of enchanters, and disregard the songs of the Sirens. [Col. 0355C]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

1. The thirty-eighth encampment is at Iye-abarim, on the borders of Moab, which signifies “heaps of stones of those who cross over,” that is, the saints who hasten through this world toward other encampments.

455 ## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0355D]

**CHAP. XXXIX. NOTE 1.** “In these kings,” down to “all will be confounded,” are words of Augustine, *On Psalm* 134. GRIAL.]

1. The thirty-ninth encampment is at Dibon-gad. Here the battle is fought against Sihon king of the Amorites [Col. 0355D] and Og king of Bashan. Although the historical event involving these kings is known, a spiritual meaning is nevertheless attached through the meanings and qualities of their names. For Sihon is interpreted as “temptation of the eyes.” Through him the devil is represented, for he transforms himself into an angel [Col. 0356A] of light and, through heresy or schism, lies plausibly in order to deceive the unwary.

2. The Amorites—that is, “those who make bitter”—have him as their king. For unless some imitation of truth precedes them, heresies would not make bitter, nor schisms embitter those in the Church. This king is therefore killed in each person when each condemns imitation and loves the truth. Og, however, is interpreted as “conclusion,” while Bashan means “confusion.” For the devil always strives to close the way to the Lord by setting up his idols, so that people may not believe in Christ. “Conclusion” comes first, as the king; “confusion” follows, as the people, because those whom he now shuts off from believing in Christ will all be confounded when Christ appears.

3. This encampment, Dibon-gad, is interpreted as “a temptation understood with strength,” because, if the imitation that was troubling the Church through schism or heresy is overcome, and the conclusion that closes the way of faith through sacrilege is overcome, nevertheless the temptation is understood and then strongly conquered. [Col. 0356B]

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0356D]

**CHAP. XL. NOTE 1.** “Which is translated as contempt of pastry-cakes.” Our books correctly read this; Jerome’s text has *plagarum* (“of blows”) incorrectly. The *palatae* are masses made from fresh figs. See Ambrose at this passage and Jerome, *On the Names in Numbers*. GRIAL.

On the same passage: Instead of “as contempt,” manuscript Alb. has “as reproach.” Florence 1: “And through this we learn to pass by all the sweetnesses and enticements of pleasures in the world,” etc. This reading is not objectionable. AREV.]

1. The fortieth encampment is from Dibon-gad to Almon-diblathaim, which is translated as “contempt of pastry-cakes,” or “of reproaches.” Through this we say that all the sweetnesses and enticements of pleasures passing away in the world are to be despised, and reproaches are to be loved. If they are falsely brought against us, they produce blessedness, as the Savior most fully teaches when he says: “When people reproach you, you will be blessed” (Luke VI). 456

## CHAPTER XLI

[Col. 0356C]

1. The forty-first encampment is in the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo, which is translated as “mountains of those who cross over.” It is opposite Mount Nebo, where Moses dies and is buried, after having viewed the promised land (Deut. XXXIV). Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” in which the law comes to an end and its memory is not found. The grace of the Gospel, however, extends without any end: “Its sound has gone out into all the earth, and its words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII).

2. At the same time, it should be considered that the dwelling of those who cross over is situated in the mountains and still requires progress. For after many mountains we descend to the plains of Moab and the waters of the Jordan, which signifies “descent.” Nothing is more dangerous than the desire for glory, boasting, and a mind swollen with the consciousness of its virtues. [Col. 0356D]

## CHAPTER XLII

1. The forty-second encampment is in the plains of Moab, above the Jordan, near Jericho, where [Col. 0357A] they pitched their tents from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim, in the plain of Moab. In this forty-second encampment, which is the final one, let us recount certain events that took place.

[Note: [Col. 0357D]

**CHAP. XLII. NOTE 2.** Manuscript Alb. has “as he was reaching his destination and pressing toward his purpose.” AREV.]

2. While the people were staying there, they were blessed at God’s command by Balaam, whom Balak had hired for payment, and the curse was changed into praises. But what does it mean that, while this Balaam was striving to reach his purpose, the donkey on which he was riding spoke when it saw the angel?

[Note: [Col. 0357D]

**3. NOTE.** “For what is this donkey,” down to “laid him beneath,” are words of Gregory, *Morals*, book I, chapter 7, which at this point—through the addition of the word “penitence” and the alteration of *renitens* (“resisting”) to *retinens* (“holding back”)—yielded no intelligible sense. GRIAL.

On the same passage: “But this one saw the angel,” down to “burst forth,” from Ambrose, book IX of the commentary on Luke, chapter 19: “Do not despise this donkey as well. Once it saw the angel of God, whom a human being could not see. It both saw him, carried him, and spoke, so that you might recognize that in later times, at the coming of the great Angel, the Gentiles would speak before those asses”—perhaps “would speak to those asses.” GRIAL.

On the same passage: Manuscript copies vary greatly here. Alb. has briefly: “What is the donkey, except one making use of reason, toward whatever he wished,” etc. Some add “of penitence” after *renitens*. AREV.]

3. For what is this donkey except the brutish Gentile world? Once Balaam—that is, the seducer into idolatry—treated it like a brute animal that made no rational resistance, subjecting it to whatever error he wished. But this donkey saw the angel of God, whom a human being could not see; it saw him, carried him, and spoke, so that we might recognize that in later times, at the coming of the great Angel of God, that Gentile people, after the nature of its harshness and stupidity had been changed, would speak with tongues set free for God. Thus the people that had been subjected to unbelief would break forth into the voice of faith and confession, although our flesh too is animal in nature.

[Note: [Col. 0357D]

**4. NOTE.** “For often the flesh,” down to “did not change the mind,” are words of Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 13. [Col. 0358D] GRIAL.

On the same passage, manuscript Alb. has: “Until the Invisible One, who confronts it, becomes known to it.” AREV.]

4. Often, when the flesh is touched by troubles and chastised by the scourge, it points out God to its own mind, whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. Thus it impedes the anxiety of the spirit that desires to advance in this world, as though traveling along a road, until the Invisible One who meets it becomes known to it. Hence Peter also rightly says: “The mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness” (II Pet. II).

[Col. 0357C]

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**5. NOTE.** Alb. has: “which it ought to preserve, is reminded by afflicted flesh.” AREV.]

5. The madman is rebuked by the mute beast of burden when the exalted mind is reminded by afflicted flesh of the good of humility, which it ought to preserve. But Balaam did not obtain the gift of this rebuke because, as he went to curse, he changed his voice, not his mind. For he gave King Balak the advice to place women in a brothel and altars before their doors, so that the sons of Israel, when they came, might first sacrifice to idols and then enter the women, and that from this the sons of Israel might fornicate with the daughters of Midian.

6. But what does it mean that this Balaam correctly concluded by a definite calculation that the people of God could be deceived, giving advice that destructive snares should be laid for them on the side through which he knew the sons of Israel to be vulnerable? He did not doubt that, when an abundance of women was offered, they would immediately collapse into the ruin of fornication, because he knew that the appetitive parts of their souls had been corrupted.

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**7. NOTE.** Grialius incorrectly has *spiritualis* (“spiritual”). AREV.]

7. Thus spiritual wickednesses, represented by Balaam, assail each of us with cunning malice, laying insidious snares especially for those affections of the soul in which they perceive us to be sick, so that, for example, when they see the rational parts of our soul corrupted, they may attempt to deceive us by that very method.

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**8. NOTE.** “But Phinehas,” down to “the people might be reckoned,” from Jerome, with some intervening material. GRIAL.

On the same passage: “Zimri,” etc. Others have: “Zimri, who entered in to the prostitute, seized a dagger and pierced them both.” AREV.]

8. But Phinehas the priest, being zealous to appease the Lord’s anger, pierced Zimri and the Midianite prostitute with a dagger, signifying that through the cross of Christ not only idolatry but also every carnal affection or worldly desire is put to death, and that God is then appeased when the desire of the flesh is extinguished. After this the people are counted again, and the Levites are also counted, so that, after the carnal have first been killed, a new people of God may be reckoned—one that will cross the Jordan through baptism and receive the promise of the inheritance of heaven. [Col. 0358B]

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**9. NOTE.** Alb. has: “Afterward also many thousands of armed men.” AREV.]

9. Moreover, the fact that six hundred thousand armed men are counted as having gone out of Egypt, while of them no more than two entered the promised land, shows figuratively that many pass through baptism to faith, but very few reach the heavenly homeland, according to that figure in the Gospel in which “many are called, but few are found chosen” (Matt. XX, 22).

10. The fact that only two enter is either on account of those who attain the promise of the heavenly kingdom from both peoples, or on account of those who are predestined to eternal blessedness through the two lives, active and contemplative. [Col. 0358C]

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**11. NOTE.** “Nor the people of the law.” Jerome has: “Lest the female sex.” GRIAL.]

11. Then the five daughters of Zelophehad make their appeal and receive an inheritance among their brothers by God’s judgment. Nor is the people of the law excluded from possession of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**12. NOTE.** Alb. has: “He admonishes, and grace is fulfilled.” AREV.]

12. Then Jesus succeeds Moses on the mountain and learns what things in particular ought to be offered in the Church. For the Gospel succeeds the law, and there the law admonishes us concerning the commandments that must be carried out, while grace fulfills them.

[Note: [Col. 0358D]

**13. NOTE.** Alb.: “At the Kalends, because of the invocation of the life of Christ; what on Easter, when we are buried with Christ through baptism from the dead.” Florence 1: “For the renewal of life,” instead of “for the birth of life.” AREV.]

13. First, what ought to be offered each day; then what on the Sabbath, because of the hope of eternal rest; what at the Kalends, for the invocation of life; what at Easter, when we are buried together with Christ [Col. 0359A] through baptism, as though passing from the dead to the birth of life; what at Pentecost, because of the grace of the Holy Spirit and the pardon of the remission of sins; what at the new moon of the seventh month; what at the fast on the tenth day of that month; and what at the Feast of Booths, when the tabernacles are erected on the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month.

[Note: [Col. 0359A]

**14. NOTE.** “The divine Balaam.” In Scripture the word *divinus* (“diviner”) is often used for a soothsayer, augur, or ventriloquist. AREV.]

14. Then war is waged against the Midianites, and the death of the diviner Balaam, whose killing signifies that the error of unbelief is put to death by the wood of the cross. Afterward the spoil of Amalek is divided, and from it an offering of souls is made for the tabernacle of God.

[Col. 0360A]

[Note: [Col. 0359A]

**15. NOTE.** “For those whom the entanglements of the world involve,” down to “desire,” are words of Gregory, *Morals* XXVII, chapter 7. GRIAL.

On the same passage: “On this side of the Jordan.” Alb. has: “Opposite the Jordan.” AREV.]

15. After this the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, possessing very many livestock, receive a possession on this side of the Jordan and do not wish to have an inheritance in the land of promise. They signify that those whom the entanglements of the world occupy have no desire whatsoever for a dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

16. Then the people are admonished to destroy the idols in the holy land and to spare none of the former inhabitants, signifying that, when we enter the land of holy promise through faith, we must extinguish all vices along with idolatry.

## IN DEUTERONOMY

[Col. 0359]

460 ## CHAPTER I. Why Deuteronomy Was Written in Eleven Days

[Col. 0359B]

1. The book of Deuteronomy is a repetition of the preceding four books of the law. For while those books each contain their own particular matters, this one nevertheless repeats them all. It also contains countless mysteries of its own, a few of which I have undertaken to record for the reader’s exercise.

2. Deuteronomy is called the second giving of the law, which signifies the Gospel. At its beginning we must note what is indicated by the fact that Moses wrote this same Deuteronomy in eleven days: it signifies the fall of the Jewish people in the Gospel through transgression of the commandments of the Decalogue.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the Forty Years in the Wilderness and the Garments That Were Not Worn Out

[Col. 0359C]

1. What did those forty years signify, during which the sons of Israel, after laboring through them, crossed into the land of promise? Through these forty years the whole period of the world is signified, in which the Church lives amid labors and perilous temptations, hoping through patience for what it has not seen, until it reaches the promised homeland of eternal happiness (Matt. IV).

461 2. Therefore the Lord also fasted for forty days and forty nights and was tempted in the wilderness. For his body, which is the Church, must endure temptations and labors in this world until that time comes when, after the temptations, it receives consolations.

[Col. 0359D]

[Note: [Col. 0359D]

**CHAP. II. NOTE 3.** “Moreover, the fact that the garment,” down to “lasted.” Furthermore, that the garments or sandals of the sons of Israel remained unworn and intact for so many years in the wilderness and were not consumed by age: this is the reading of Val. and Compl. The others, including Bede, have the text as we have printed it. GRIAL.

On the same passage, Alb., together with Val. and Compl., has “the garments, etc., but *obvoluta* (‘wrapped up’) instead of *absoluta* (‘intact’).” AREV.]

3. Moreover, the fact that Israel’s garment was not corrupted by age for so many years in the wilderness, and that the dead skin of their sandals lasted for so long without blemish, can signify the future incorruptibility of bodies, where the things that are corruptible will remain without any corruption.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Not Planting a Tree Beside the Altar

[Note: [Col. 0359D]

**CHAP. III. NOTE 1.** “You shall not plant,” etc. Codex Bononiensis, after the end of the preceding chapter, in a note at the lower margin [Col. 0360D], from Origen through Isidore, has this: “They will remain.” Among the commandments of this book innumerable things are ordered, and among them it is asked what is signified by the prohibition: “You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord, nor plant a grove in the land.” For it is forbidden that a grove be planted, etc. AREV.]

1. You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of God, nor make a grove in the land. For it is forbidden that a grove be planted in the temple. Groves consist of leafy and fruitless trees, planted solely for the delight of the eyes. Such also are the Gentiles, who arrange their reason with verbal elegance, not so as to turn people away from vices but to delight them, and through this kind of seduction persuade them.

[Col. 0360C]

2. But in accordance with the commandment, we do not plant a grove beside the altar of God if, concerning the faith of the Lord, we compose nothing fruitless in our words and nothing alluring to worldly hearing, but hold to the knowledge of preaching in the single purity of truth. The Apostle avoided planting this grove in the preaching of wisdom when he said: “We speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching and power of the Spirit” (I Cor. II).

462 ## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Removing the Foreskin of Fruit-Bearing Trees

[Note: [Col. 0360D]

**CHAP. IV. NOTE 1.** “When you have entered,” down to “may be eaten,” are all Gregory’s words, *Morals* VIII, chapter 29. GRIAL.]

1. “When you have entered the land and planted in it fruit-bearing trees, you shall remove their foreskins; their fruit shall be unclean for you, and you shall not eat from them” (Lev. XIX, 23). Fruit-bearing trees are works fruitful in virtues. We remove the foreskins of trees when, suspicious of the weakness of our very beginning, we do not approve the first stages of our works. [Col. 0360D]

2. We consider the fruits that sprout to be unclean and do not adapt them to our food, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that this should not feed the spirit of the one performing it, lest, while the praise received is pleasantly enjoyed, the fruit of the work be eaten prematurely.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Not Working with the Firstborn of an Ox

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**CHAP. V. NOTE 1.** “You shall not work,” down to “lie hidden,” likewise the entire chapter is from the same chapter of Gregory. GRIAL.]

1. “You shall not work with the firstborn of an ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep.” To work with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of a good way of life in the exercise of public action. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to strip our incipient good works from the covering of their concealment and expose them to human eyes. [Col. 0361B]

2. We are therefore forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because even if we begin to practice something vigorous, we ought not quickly display it openly. But when our life begins something simple and innocent, it is fitting that it not abandon the veils of its secrecy or show it to human eyes as though its fleece had been removed.

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**3. NOTE.** “So that if anything perhaps,” from Bede; “So that whatever perhaps,” from Gregory and a manuscript. GRIAL.]

3. Let the firstborn of oxen and sheep therefore serve only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever innocent thing we may begin, we may offer it on the altar of the heart to the honor of the inner Judge. There is no doubt that it is accepted by him all the more willingly the more it is concealed from human beings and left unstained by any desire for praise. 463

[Col. 0361C]

4. Often, however, the beginnings of a new way of life are still mingled with carnal life. For this reason they ought not be made known too quickly, lest, when the good things that please are praised, the mind, deceived by its praise, be unable to detect in them the evils that lie hidden.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Not Plowing with an Ox and a Donkey

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**CHAP. VI. NOTE 1.** “You shall not plow,” down to “burdened,” from the same book, *Morals* I, chapter 7. GRIAL.]

1. “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.” Under the name of the ox is understood the people established through circumcision under the yoke of the law; under the donkey, the people of the Gentiles belonging to the Gospel. One plows with an ox and a donkey together when one receives the Gospel in such a way that one does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which had gone before in shadow and image.

[Col. 0361D]

2. Likewise, sometimes the life of those who act well is signified by the ox, and the senseless folly of fools by the donkey. What, then, does “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” mean, except as if it said: Do not join a fool with a wise person in preaching, lest the one who is unable to fulfill the task obstruct even the one who is capable.

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**3. NOTE.** “An ox and a donkey,” down to “makes companions,” are words of Augustine, *Against Faustus* VI, chapter 9. GRIAL.]

3. If necessary, anyone may yoke an ox and a donkey without harm to the work. But no one can make a wise person and a fool companions without scandal—not so that one commands and the other obeys, but so that they announce the word of God together with equal authority. [Col. 0362A]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Not Muzzling the Ox That Treads Out the Grain

[Note: [Col. 0362D]

**CHAP. VII. NOTE 1.** The words of Deuteronomy in the Vulgate are: “You shall not muzzle the ox treading out its grain on the threshing floor.” AREV.]

1. “You shall not muzzle the ox that is threshing” (I Cor. IX, 9; I Tim. V, 18). It has been said that under the name of the ox the life of every worker is expressed. In one place the Apostle Paul says, reproving and lamenting, that no one had shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving (Phil. IV). What is “in the matter of giving and receiving” except what he explained openly elsewhere, saying: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Tim. IX, 11.) This is what is signified by: “You shall not muzzle the ox that is threshing.” [Col. 0362B]

2. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The worker is worthy of his wage” (I Tim. VI). Scripture therefore wishes material things to be supplied to teachers, from whom spiritual things are received, because preachers occupied with teaching cannot provide for their own necessities.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Not Boiling a Kid in Its Mother’s Milk

1. “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” Here the kid is introduced under the figure of the sinner. Therefore one who has sinned gravely must not be boiled in the milk of his mother—that is, he must not be cleansed by the mildest and tenderest disciplines of the Church. Rather, his sins must be boiled out by her more severe commands, since the one who destroyed himself through the blandishments of lust must redeem himself through stronger discipline. [Col. 0362C]

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Not Wearing a Garment of Wool and Linen

[Note: [Col. 0362D]

**CHAP. IX. NOTE 1.** “You shall not wear a garment,” down to “of malice,” are Gregory’s words, *Morals* VIII, chapter 31. GRIAL.]

1. “You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen.” Through wool simplicity is signified, and through linen subtlety. Indeed, a garment made from linen and wool conceals the linen within and displays the wool on the surface. Thus one wears a garment woven from wool and linen who, under the language of innocence, conceals inward subtlety of malice. This is according to the moral sense.

[Note: [Col. 0362D]

**2. NOTE.** “With linen garments,” down to “in conduct,” Augustine’s words, *Against Faustus* VI, chapter 9, from which some material has been restored. GRIAL.]

2. Moreover, according to the allegorical sense, for wool—or purple—to be mixed with linen garments, and to wear a linen-and-wool garment, is to live disorderly and to wish to mix professions of different kinds: for example, for a nun to have the adornments of married women, or for one who married because she could not remain continent to assume the appearance of a virgin. This is entirely sinful, as is anything improperly woven into someone’s life from a different kind or religious state. What was then represented in garments is now revealed in conduct. 465 [Col. 0362D]

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Not Taking the Upper or Lower Millstone as a Pledge

[Col. 0363A]

[Note: [Col. 0363D]

**CHAP. X. NOTE 1.** “You shall not take,” etc. The entire chapter is from Gregory, *Morals* XXXIII, chapter 11, with some words altered but the meaning retained. GRIAL.

On the same passage: “They are called hawks.” The same opinion appears in the *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 7, no. 55, with the Apostle Paul’s words also cited: “You put up with it,” etc. AREV.]

1. “You shall not take the upper or lower millstone as a pledge.” For sometimes we say “take” in the sense of “remove.” Hence those birds that are eager to seize are called *accipitres*, hawks. Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “You put up with it if someone devours you, if someone takes from you” (II Cor. XI)—as if he were saying, “if someone robs you.” A pledge is the debtor’s confession of sin. A pledge is taken from a debtor when confession of sin is already obtained from a sinner. The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear.

2. Hope carries one upward, while fear presses the heart downward. But the upper and lower millstones are so necessarily joined to each other that one is useless without the other. Therefore hope and fear must continually be joined in the sinner’s breast, because repentance hopes in vain for mercy if it does not also fear judgment.

3. One fears judgment in vain if one does not also trust in mercy. Therefore the removal of either the upper or lower millstone as a pledge is forbidden, because the one who preaches to a sinner must arrange his preaching with such discretion that, without abandoning hope, he does not remove fear, nor, by removing hope, leave him in fear alone.

[Note: [Col. 0363D]

**4. NOTE.** “But usefully,” etc. Alb.: “But one is useless without the other; both together are useful … with hope of forgiveness.” AREV.]

4. He removes the upper millstone if he says to a weeping sinner: “You will not receive forgiveness for what you have done.” He removes the lower if he soothes the sinner through deception, saying: [Col. 0363C] “Do evil as much as you wish without fear, for God is merciful and ready to forgive.” But both millstones are then usefully retained if hope is present with fear that brings correction, and fear that brings correction is present with hope. 466

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Not Abominating the Egyptian

[Note: [Col. 0363D]

**CHAP. XI. NOTE 1.** “You shall not abominate,” from Cassian, *Conferences* 5, chapter 19. GRIAL.

At Grialius the title of the chapter is *Concerning Not Abominating Egypt*. I have restored *the Egyptian* from Deuteronomy, although some manuscripts of Isidore have [Col. 0364D] “You shall not abominate Egypt.” AREV.]

1. “You shall not abominate the Egyptian, because you were an inhabitant in his land.” Although, in renouncing the world, we avoid the Egyptian land—that is, our former way of life in the world or its desire—nevertheless, while we remain subject to the necessities of the present world, we do not entirely destroy the Egyptian nation, even though we separate ourselves from it by a certain discernment. We do not think about superfluous things but, according to the Apostle, are content with daily food and clothing. For this alone was specifically commanded in the law: “You shall not abominate the Egyptian.” [Col. 0363D]

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Not Having Different Weights

[Col. 0364A]

[Note: [Col. 0364D]

**CHAP. XII. NOTE 1.** “You shall not have in your bag,” down to “in his sight,” from Cassian, *Conferences* 21, chapter 22. GRIAL.

On the same passage: “A large weight,” down to “will be fettered.” The punctuation should be noted as differing from that followed by the correctors of the edition of the Septuagint. GRIAL.]

1. “You shall not have different weights in your bag, a larger and a smaller; nor shall there be in your house a larger measure and a smaller. You shall have a just and true weight, and the measure shall be equal and true for you, so that you may live a long time upon the land.” The same lawgiver also forbids this in Leviticus (Lev. XIX), and Solomon expresses a similar judgment on the matter: “A large weight and a small one, and double measures, both are unclean before the Lord, and whoever makes them will be fettered in his devices” (Prov. XX).

467 [Note: [Col. 0364D]

**2. NOTE.** “That bodily one.” Others have: “Even that spiritual one for us.” AREV.]

2. Therefore we must strive not only in that bodily way but also in a spiritual way, so that we have neither different weights in our hearts nor double measures in the house of our conscience—that is, so that we do not, while presuming on a more lenient indulgence in matters that soften the rule of strictness for ourselves, burden those to whom we preach the word of God with stricter commands and heavier weights than we ourselves can bear. [Col. 0364B]

3. When we do this, what are we doing except weighing or measuring the reward and fruit of the Lord’s commandments with a different weight and measure? For if we administer them one way to ourselves and another way to our brothers, we are rightly rebuked by the Lord for having different scales or double measures, according to Solomon’s statement: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful scale is not good in his sight” (Prov. XX). [Col. 0364C]

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Witnesses

[Note: [Col. 0364D]

**CHAP. XIII. NOTE 1.** “One witness shall not stand against another.” See Augustine, *Against Faustus* XVI, chapter 13. GRIAL.]

1. “One witness shall not stand against another, but every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Although historically this divine judgment must be observed, nevertheless, when we act against any impious persons or heretics, it is necessary for us also to call the holy Scriptures as witnesses.

[Note: [Col. 0364D]

**2. NOTE.** “And firmness.” Others have: “To affirm the word of my understanding, I employ two witnesses.” AREV.]

2. Our understanding and testimony have no credibility without these witnesses. Therefore, for the proof and firmness of the word of my understanding, it is more fitting that I employ two witnesses, namely the New and Old Testaments; and that I employ three as well—the Gospel, the Prophet, and the Apostle—and thus every word will stand. [Col. 0364D]

468 ## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Taking a Brother’s Wife

[Col. 0365A]

[Note: [Col. 0365D]

**CHAP. XIV. NOTE 1.** “But the fact that a wife,” down to “loses through disgrace,” are words of Augustine, *Against Faustus* XXXII, chapter 20. GRIAL.]

1. But the fact that a brother was commanded to take his brother’s wife for the purpose of raising offspring not for himself but for his brother, and of calling by his brother’s name whatever was born from her—what else does this prefigure symbolically except that every preacher of the Gospel ought to labor in the Church in such a way that, for a dead brother—that is, Christ, who died for us—he may raise up offspring, and that what has been raised up may receive his name?

2. Finally, fulfilling this not carnally in the preceding symbolism but spiritually in its completed truth, the Apostle corrects those whom he recalls having begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, rebuking and reproving them because they wanted to be called Paul’s. “Was Paul,” he says, [Col. 0365B] “crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. I.) As if he were saying: “I begot you for a dead brother. You are called Christians, not Paulians.”

3. But whoever, having been chosen by the Church for the ministry of evangelizing, refuses it is deservedly and rightly despised by the Church. This is what she is commanded to do: spit in his face, not without a sign of this disgrace, so that the sandal of one foot is removed from him, lest he belong to the lot of those to whom the Apostle himself says: “And having your feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). And concerning whom the Prophet says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. LII; Nah. I; Rom. X)!

4. But whoever holds the evangelical faith in such a way that it benefits him and he does not refuse to benefit the Church is rightly understood to be shod on both feet. Whoever thinks that, because he has believed, he has done enough for himself, but avoids the care of winning others, loses, as though in disgrace, the sandal of one foot.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the Fearful and Cowardly

[Note: [Col. 0365D]

**CHAP. XV. NOTE 1.** “A fearful man,” from Cassian, book VII, chapter 15. GRIAL.]

1. “A fearful man and one timid in heart shall not go out to war. Let him go and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, just as he himself has been terrified by fear.” These words teach that those who are still afraid to strip themselves of earthly works cannot undertake the profession of contemplation or the exercise of spiritual warfare.

2. Lest they turn back again through weakness of mind, recall others from evangelical perfection by their example, and weaken them through unbelieving fear, such persons are commanded to withdraw from the battle and return to their house, because they cannot wage the Lord’s wars with a divided heart.

[Col. 0366A]

3. For a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways. Such persons ought not even to undertake the beginning of renunciation. It is better for them to remain in the active life than, while pursuing contemplation in fear, to involve themselves in greater danger. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill.

[Note: [Col. 0365D]

**4. NOTE.** Grialius printed *filorum* (“of threads”), perhaps by mistake. Others have “a vineyard,” or “the branches of sons.” AREV.]

4. Likewise, the man who has taken a wife is prohibited from such military service; so too the man who has planted a vineyard, as though it were a propagation of sons. For a servant of a wife cannot serve in the divine army, according to the Apostle: “He who is with a wife is anxious about how he may please his wife, and he is divided” (1 Cor. 7).

5. Nor can one devote oneself to contemplation while still fixed in the pleasure of the flesh. “No one,” says the Apostle, “who serves as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Destruction of the Seven Nations

[Note: [Col. 0365D]

CHAP. XVI, no. 1. “When the Lord brings you in,” etc. This chapter was collected piecemeal from Cassian, Conference 5, chapter 16 and the following chapters. GRIAL.]

> 1. When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess, and destroys before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger than you, and when the Lord delivers them to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0366D]

Here: “Which you are entering to possess.” Thus Cassian and the Vulgate. And the Septuagint, εἰσπορεύη, “you shall enter.” “You shall enter,” manuscripts O. GRIAL.

Here: This struggle of the virtues against the vices is splendidly described by Prudentius in the *Psychomachia*, where the example of the seven nations whom the Israelites struck down to complete destruction is also employed. AREV.]

2. These seven nations are the seven principal vices, which every spiritual soldier is admonished to overcome through the grace of God and utterly exterminate. The reason they are said to be more numerous is that there are more vices than virtues. Yet they are listed in the catalogue as seven nations, whereas in the account of their conquest they are mentioned without a number, for it says: “And he destroys many nations before you.”

3. For the people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold tinder and root of vices, is more numerous than Israel. From gluttony arise feasting and drunkenness. From fornication arise obscene speech, buffoonery, frivolity, and foolish talk. From avarice arise lying, fraud, theft, perjury, the pursuit of shameful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity. From anger arise murder, shouting, and indignation. From sadness arise resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair.

[Note: [Col. 0366D]

3. “Frivolities.” Thus Cassian’s *Al.*; “mockeries” in another reading. GRIAL.

Here: “Murders.” Singular, “murder,” in Cassian. GRIAL.]

4. From acedia arise idleness, sleepiness, intrusiveness, restlessness, wandering, instability of mind and body, talkativeness, and curiosity. From vainglory arise quarrels, heresies, boasting, and presumption concerning novelties. From pride arise contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other similar things. Although these are much more numerous than the virtues, once those seven principal vices, from whose nature the others proceed, have been conquered, all the rest immediately fall silent and, together with them, are likewise destroyed in perpetual annihilation.

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

4. “And many others.” Cassian, somewhat earlier. GRIAL.

Here: “The seven principal vices”—Cassian has “eight,” but it is quite apparent why Isidore changed it. GRIAL.]

5. That these plagues are stronger, we perceive from the evident assault they make upon nature itself. For the pleasure of carnal passions fights more powerfully in our members than the pursuit of virtues, which are acquired only through the deepest contrition of heart and body. But when we are commanded to possess safely the territories of these destructive nations, the meaning is as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

5. “That these plagues are stronger.” Cassian, somewhat later. GRIAL.

Here: “Of these destructive nations.” Cassian, chapter 23. GRIAL.]

6. Each vice has its own position in our heart. But if, when the vices and the spiritual peoples—that is, the virtues fighting against them—have engaged in battle, the vices are overcome, then the place in our heart which the spirit of lust or fornication had occupied will henceforth be held by chastity. The place which fury had seized will be reclaimed by patience.

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

6. “The spirit held.” Cassian has “held fast.” GRIAL.]

7. The place which sadness, producing death, had occupied will be possessed by a salutary joy full of gladness. The place which acedia was laying waste, fortitude will begin to cultivate. The place which pride was trampling down, humility will dignify. Thus, when each vice has been expelled, their places—that is, their contrary dispositions—will be possessed by the sons of Israel, that is, by souls who see God.

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

7. “Humility will dignify,” from Cassian. “Humility will begin to cultivate,” manuscripts O., erroneously. For he had said above, “Fortitude will begin to cultivate.” GRIAL.

Here: “That is, dispositions.” Cassian has “effects”; manuscript. GRIAL.]

## CHAPTER XVII. Why, When Speaking to Abraham, God Counted Ten Nations Rather Than Seven

[Col. 0367C]

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

CHAP. XVII, no. 1. “But when the Lord spoke to Abraham.” From the same conference, chapter 22. GRIAL.]

1. The fact that, when the Lord spoke to Abraham about future events, he is read as having counted not seven nations but ten, whose land he promised to give to his offspring, is fulfilled most clearly when the idolatry of the nations, the blasphemy of the Jews, and the error of heretics are added.

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

2. “Or the impious multitude of the nations.” Cassian has “of the Gentiles.” GRIAL.

[Col. 0368D] Here Alborn. also agrees with Cassian in reading “of the Gentiles.” AREV.]

2. Before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism, either the impious multitude of the Gentiles or the blasphemous multitude of the Jews is subject to them while they dwell in intellectual Egypt. But if someone renounces it and, having departed from there through the grace of God, reaches the spiritual wilderness, then, freed from the assault of three nations, he will undertake battle against only the seven counted by Moses.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Beautiful Woman Captured in War

[Col. 0367D]

1. “If,” he says, “you go out to war against your enemies and see a woman beautiful in appearance, and desire her, you shall shave all the hair of her head and trim her nails; you shall clothe her in garments of mourning, and she shall sit in the house mourning her father, her mother, and her paternal home; and after thirty days she shall be your wife.”

2. Let the Jews say, then, how this is observed among them, and what reason there is for shaving the woman and cutting her nails. For example, let us suppose that the man who is said to have found her found her with neither hair nor nails: what would she have possessed that, according to the law, could be removed?

[Note: [Col. 0368D]

CHAP. XVIII, no. 3. “And she mourns her father and mother.” I have restored this reading, whereas Grialius has “and she may mourn her father and mother.” The old edition reads, “and she mourns her father and mother.” AREV.]

3. But for us, whose warfare is spiritual and whose weapons are not carnal but powerful through God, if we find a beautiful woman—that is, a soul created beautiful by God—living among the Gentiles, and wish to unite her to the body of Christ, then, having laid aside the worship of idols, she is clothed in the garments of mourning of repentance and mourns her father and mother—that is, every memory of the world and its allurements.

[Note: [Col. 0368D]

4. Grialius reads, “let her be shaved.” AREV.]

4. Then, with the razor of the word of God and its teaching, all the sin of her unbelief, which is dead and empty, is shaved away; for this is what the hair of the woman’s head and her nails signify. Finally, purified by the water of the saving bath, she is joined to the saints of God—namely, when she no longer has anything dead on her head or in her hands among those things said to be dead through unbelief, so that she carries nothing unclean or dead either in her thoughts or in her actions.

5. As for the command that she be taken as a wife after thirty days, women customarily undergo purification from their menstrual blood after a month. After the purification of sins, therefore, the soul, now made clean and purified from its uncleanness, is joined to the Israelite man—that is, to the body of Christ.

473 6. For by the ternary and denary numbers faith and works are signified. Through faith in the Trinity and through the work of the law, therefore, every soul is rightly joined to the Israelite man—that is, to the body of Christ—cleaving to him without stain, in sincerity of faith and purity of actions. Others have thought that this captive woman, beautiful in appearance, signifies some rational discipline, found wisely expressed among the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0368D]

7. “This, therefore, having been discovered by us.” Thus the Albornoz manuscript, with the nominative absolute; this is better than Grialius’s “this, therefore, having been discovered by us.” One could restore: “For this, having been discovered by us, must first,” etc. AREV.]

7. This, therefore, having been discovered by us, must first have all the uncleanness of its superstition removed and cut away, and must then be taken up in the pursuit of truth. For the disciplines of the Gentiles possess nothing clean, since among unbelievers there is no wisdom to which some uncleanness or superstition has not been added.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Axe That Slips from the Hand

[Col. 0369A]

[Note: [Col. 0369D]

CHAP. XIX, no. 1. “But what this signifies.” The entire chapter is from Gregory, *Moral Expositions*, book 10, chapter 5. GRIAL.]

1. What, then, does this signify, which the Lord commanded through Moses, saying: “If someone goes with his friend into the forest simply to cut wood, and the axe slips from his hand, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes and kills his friend, he shall flee to one of the aforementioned cities and live there, lest perhaps the nearest relative of the one whose blood has been shed pursue him, driven by grief, and seize him and strike his life”? We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn our attention to examining the faults of our subjects; and we simply cut wood whenever we cut away the vices of wrongdoers with a pious intention.

2. But the axe slips from the hand when correction draws itself into excessive harshness; and the iron leaps from the handle when speech becomes harsher than correction requires. He strikes and kills his friend who, by an insult uttered, kills his hearer by driving him away from the spirit of love.

[Note: [Col. 0369D]

3. “He condemns more than he ought.” Thus all the Gregorian and Isidorian books read, both here and in Book 2 of the *Sentences*, chapter 4: “Every righteous person shines with hope and fear, because now hope lifts him toward joy, and now the terror of Gehenna condemns him to fear.” And chapter 44: “Immoderate abstinence must not be imposed upon the body, lest, while the flesh is burdened more heavily by the weight of hunger, it subsequently do evil and cease to do good; and lest the thing imposed so that it may abstain from evil cause it also to lose the duty of goodness, when it is weighed down too heavily.” And Book 3, chapter 5: “For we sin there where we turn aside through desire or will. But where we are forcibly condemned, even if there is no crime or disgraceful act, there is nevertheless misery both as though for a disgraceful act and for a crime.” *Addicere* means, according to Festus, “to condemn”; or, as concerns Isidore and Gregory, what we say in ordinary language: “to press hard.” GRIAL.
