Here: “He does not seek the guilt of the offense.” Gregory has: “He does not seek vengeance for the guilt of the offense.” GRIAL.]

3. For the mind of the person corrected suddenly plunges into hatred if immoderate correction condemns him more than it ought. But the one who carelessly strikes the wood and extinguishes his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that, protected in one of them, he may live—as though, turning to the laments of repentance, he were hidden within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, and not held guilty of the murder he committed. When the relative of the slain man finds him, he does not kill him, because when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through participation in our nature—he unquestionably does not demand from him the guilt of the offense whom hope, faith, and charity have hidden beneath the protection of that Judge’s pardon.

## CHAPTER XX. On Nocturnal Pollution in Sleep

[Note: [Col. 0370D]

CHAP. XX, no. 1. “If there should be among you a man,” through “he rejoices at the heat”: all are Gregory’s words, *Moral Expositions*, book 9, chapter 31. GRIAL.]

1. “If there should be among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return before evening, when he has washed with water. After sunset he shall return to the camp.” A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation, by which something shameful is conceived in the heart through a dark thought, although it is not carried out in bodily action.

[Note: [Col. 0370D]

2. “From the estimation of the good.” Gregory’s other reading is “from the assessment.” GRIAL.]

2. But the man polluted by a nocturnal dream is commanded to go outside the camp, because it is fitting that the person polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful. Let him place the merit of his fault before his eyes and despise himself in comparison with the estimation of the good.

[Col. 0370A] 475 [Note: [Col. 0370D]

3. “By comparison.” Another reading: “by estimation.” AREV.]

3. For the polluted man to go outside the camp means that the person struggling with a shameful assault should despise himself in comparison with those who practice continence. He who washes with water at evening does so when, seeing his failing, he turns to the laments of repentance, so that with tears he may wash away everything that accuses his soul of hidden defilement.

[Note: [Col. 0370D]

4. “Toward the fellowship of the good.” Thus Gregory’s other reading: “Toward the good of the fellowship.” GRIAL.

Here: “After the washing with water.” Thus Gregory’s other reading; Grialius has “after the water.” GRIAL.]

4. But let him return to the camp after sunset, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, it is necessary that he again take confidence with regard to the fellowship of the good. After washing with water, when the sun has set, he returns to the camp who, after the laments of repentance, with the flame of unlawful thought cooled, is restored to the presumption of the merits of the faithful, so that he no longer considers himself far removed from the others, rejoicing that he has been made clean through the death of his inner ardor.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Man Who Goes Out with a Peg for His Needs

[Col. 0370B]

[Note: [Col. 0370D]

CHAP. XXI, no. 1. “Moreover, it is commanded,” etc. From Gregory, *Moral Expositions*, book 30, chapter 13. GRIAL.

Here: “Burdened,” etc. Another reading: “Our burdened mind is burdened by a certain excess of thoughts.” AREV.]

1. Moreover, Moses commands the Israelite people that, when a man goes out for the needs of nature, he should carry a peg on his belt and, after digging a hole in the ground, conceal what has been expelled. For our mind, burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, bursts forth with certain superfluities of thought, as with the burdens of the belly.

2. But we must carry a peg under our belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have a sharp goad of compunction near us, which may continually pierce the earth of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceal what bursts forth from us with foulness.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Forty Stripes

[Col. 0370C]

1. The fact that he commanded offenders to be reproved with forty stripes according to the measure of their sin has already been explained: the number forty signifies an image of this present time, in which the Church, spread through the four regions of the world, lives under the Decalogue of the law. We are therefore struck with the number forty if, in this time, we are scourged by the blows of repentance.

2. Every sinner ought, therefore, to be worn down by temporal scourges, so that he may be found purified at the judgment. For blessed is the person who is reproved by God. No punishment in eternity will be able to afflict those whom the discipline of repentance has struck here. If we are beaten here on account of our sins, there we shall be found without sin.

# IN JOSHUA

[Col. 0371]

477 ## CHAPTER I. On the Death of Moses and the Leadership of Joshua

[Col. 0371A]

1. After the death of Moses, the Lord speaks to Joshua, saying: “Moses my servant is dead. Arise and cross the Jordan, you and all the people, into the land which I shall give to the children of Israel.”

[Note: [Col. 0371D]

CHAP. I, no. 2. “He is dead,” through “the law is dead.” Origen, Homily 1. GRIAL.]

2. Moses, therefore, is dead; the law is dead; the legal commandments now cease, and Jesus—that is, Christ the Savior, the Son of God—holds the leadership. He introduces the people into the land of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER II. On the Two Spies and Rahab the Harlot

1. This Joshua, son of Nun, sends two spies to the city of Jericho, and they are received by Rahab the harlot. [Col. 0371B] This Jesus, leader of the people, manifests the Lord Jesus Christ both by his name and by his deed. Jericho, meanwhile, is this world, to which the Lord Jesus Christ sent the two Testaments to examine human conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0371D]

CHAP. II, no. 2. “Rahab, moreover, represents the Church.” Origen frequently, and Ambrose, *On Solomon*, and Augustine in several places. GRIAL.]

2. For, so that he might more fully test the faith of believers or the obstinacy of rebels, before the advent of his judgment he sent, as two spies, the Law and the Gospel. Rahab represents the Church, which has been gathered from foreign and alien nations, and which formerly lived in carnal desires and prostituted itself to idols. Concerning such people the Lord says: “They will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 21).

3. She alone, therefore, received these Testaments of the Lord and faithfully preserved them; she did not hand them over to the enemies at all, preferring to place herself in danger so long as she kept them unharmed and safe. She firmly believed that the world would fall, like that city. For herself and for the salvation of all her people she made a covenant with the Lord’s Testaments. In her house she placed scarlet, that is, the sign of blood. If anyone is found outside her, he will in no way escape the ruin of the age and the conflagration of the world.

## CHAPTER III. On the Crossing of the Ark and the Division of the Jordan

[Note: [Col. 0371D]

CHAP. III, no. 1. “Then the people cross the Jordan.” Origen, Homily 4. GRIAL.]

1. Then the people cross the Jordan with the Ark of the Covenant. But what does it mean that, while the same Ark crosses the Jordan, the multitude is led by priests and Levites, and, while the river’s water stands in a heap, God’s people proceed on an unhindered path? All these things are fulfilled mystically among the peoples of the Church.

2. For when someone comes to the font of baptism and, with the priestly and Levitical order standing present, has been initiated into the mystical sacraments, then through baptism he enters by the ministry of the priests, as though through the streams of the Jordan, and gains the land of the heavenly promise.

[Note: [Col. 0371D]

3. “But part,” etc. Another reading: “But part flowed down into the bitter sea.” Another: “But part converges in the bitter whirlpool of the sea.” [Col. 0372D] AREV.]

3. The fact that part of the river’s waters recoiled backward and remained in sweetness, while another part flowed down into the bitter whirlpool of the sea, represents the diversity among the baptized. For some of those who are baptized preserve the sweetness of heavenly grace that they have received, while others turn toward the bitterness of sins.

4. The fact that the priestly and Levitical order shows the way to God’s people signifies priestly teaching. For they teach the people to leave Egypt—that is, the errors of the world—and to cross the vast wilderness—that is, the temptations of the age. The fact that the priestly and Levitical order assists the Ark of the Covenant, in which the law is carried, plainly indicates that they themselves enlighten the people.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Two and a Half Tribes That Went Ahead

[Note: [Col. 0372D]

CHAP. IV, no. 1. “The two and a half tribes.” Most of the words are Origen’s, Homily 3. GRIAL.

Here: “They obtained the inheritance of the law,” not of evangelical grace. See Origen. GRIAL.

Here: “And hence,” etc. Another reading: “That all were firstborn who were sent across the Jordan.” AREV.]

1. The two and a half tribes that had received land from Moses across the Jordan, leaving their wives and children behind, crossed with their brothers and provided them assistance in battle until they themselves also obtained their inheritance. Those who receive an inheritance across the Jordan through Moses and proceed armed and girded with their brothers are understood here to signify those who first obtained the inheritance of the law through Moses; hence they are all remembered as firstborn.

2. Reuben is Jacob’s firstborn by Leah; Gad is the firstborn of the same man by Zilpah; Manasseh is Joseph’s firstborn, by the Egyptian daughter of the priest Potiphar. In these firstborn, therefore, those from the earlier people are represented figuratively who pleased God through the law and who do not rest, but rise up equipped to help their brothers. When we labor in the contest of this life and struggle against hostile powers, those who were justified through the law before Christ’s coming come to our aid.

3. We see Isaiah and Jeremiah, girded and equipped for our help, wounding the fiercest enemies of our hearts with the arrows of their books. Daniel, too, girds himself for our help when he instructs and warns us concerning Christ’s kingdom and the future deceit of Antichrist.

[Note: [Col. 0372D]

4. “Twelvefold.” Another reading: “twice seven.” AREV.]

4. Ezekiel is also present, marking out heavenly mysteries for us in the fourfold circles of the wheels. Hosea also leads twelve companies of the army, and they go before us, their loins girded with the truth they proclaim, for our assistance. These strong men therefore fight together with us until we attain the homeland of the heavenly promise.

480 ## CHAPTER V. On the Twelve Stones

1. When the children of Israel had crossed the Jordan, they took twelve stones from the middle of the river and placed them as a testimony at the site of the second circumcision, signifying to us that, when we rise from the bath, we must carry with us the firmest examples of apostolic life, always looking upon their testimony as a model for the imitation of virtues.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Second Circumcision

[Col. 0373B]

[Note: [Col. 0373D]

CHAP. VI, no. 1. “After the Jordan.” Origen, Homily 5. GRIAL.

Here: One may ask whether *percontor* or *percunctor* should be written; the meaning is the same. Grialius reads *percontemur* and shortly afterward *percunctatio*. Grialius’s note had *post Jordanem*, “after the Jordan.” AREV.]

1. After crossing the Jordan, Jesus came to Gilgal, and there he was commanded to make stone knives for himself and circumcise the children of Israel a second time. Let us question the Jews: how can anyone be circumcised a second time with a carnal circumcision? For once circumcised, he no longer has anything that can be removed a second time.

2. But for us, whose law is the spiritual law of Christ, these things are appropriately resolved. We say that the first circumcision took place through the law in Egypt. But if someone passes from the law through the baptism of the Jordan to the Gospel, then he receives a second, spiritual circumcision through the rock, which is Christ. Thus, purified by such circumcision, he is rid of Egypt’s reproach—that is, the allurements of bodily vices.

[Col. 0373C] 3. The name of the place, Gilgal, which is interpreted as “revelation,” shows that, while each person has walked through the desert of this life in the foreskin of unbelief, his eyes have been blinded. Let us also consider what follows. Immediately after the circumcision of the Gospel, Passover is celebrated in the place of revelation, and that Lamb who was slain for the salvation of the world is sacrificed. When the manna of the figurative law has ceased, the people first eat the bread of Christ’s body, which the incorruptible land of promise—that is, the virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother—brought forth, whose grain, falling into the earth, produced abundant fruit. And observe the order.

4. For after we have passed under the leadership of Jesus Christ through the waters of the bath and have been marked with spiritual circumcision through faith, then, arriving by these steps, we celebrate Passover—that is, we believe in Christ sacrificed for the salvation of the world—and then, immediately upon believing, we are nourished by that bread of the Lord’s body.

5. Thereafter Christ, the commander of the armies of the heavenly virtues, meets us, holding the sword of the Gospel to cut away the pollution of our flesh. Joshua’s question to the angel—“Are you for us or for our adversaries?”—indicates the discernment of the saints, who distinguish between good and evil by judgment, lest the adversary deceive them under the appearance of good. Hence it is said to Jeremiah: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you will be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Destruction of Jericho and the Salvation of Rahab

[Note: [Col. 0373D]

CHAP. VII, no. 1. “After this Jericho is surrounded.” Origen, Homily 6. GRIAL.]

1. After this Jericho is surrounded and conquered, but no sword is drawn against it, no battering ram is directed against it, and no weapons are brandished. Only the seven priestly trumpets are employed for seven continuous days; then, when the Ark has been carried around it, the walls of Jericho collapse. Jericho is interpreted as “moon.”

2. The moon represents the appearance of this world, because, just as the moon wanes through its monthly cycles, so this world, moving toward the completion of the ages, falls through daily decline. The Ark represents the Church, while the bronze trumpets signify strong preachers.

[Note: [Col. 0373D]

3. “The exaltation of the world,” etc. The Albornoz manuscript has this reading. Grialius has “the exaltation of the world and the proud obstacles of unbelief,” etc. The old edition has “the pride of the exalted world and of unbelief,” etc. AREV.]

3. For seven days the Israelites carry the Ark around this city of Jericho while the bronze trumpets sound, and its walls fall through the presence of the Ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets. For in this time, which revolves through the succession of seven days, while the Ark is carried—that is, while the Church moves around the globe—at the voices of the preachers, as at the sound of trumpets, the walls of Jericho, that is, the exaltation of the world and the proud obstacles of unbelief, collapse, until at the end of time the last enemy, death, is destroyed and the one house of Rahab, like the one Church, is delivered from the destruction of the wicked: cleansed from the shame of fornication through the window of confession and by the blood of remission. For this harlot dwells in Jericho, as in this age.

4. To be saved, she sends scarlet through the window of her house, as through the mouth of her body; that is, she confesses for salvation the sign of Christ’s blood for the remission of sins. Those who were found in her house were saved from the destruction of the city, and all who are found within the Church alone are saved. Outside this house, that is, outside the Church, no one is saved.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Achan’s Theft

[Col. 0374D] [Note: [Col. 0374D]

CHAP. VIII, no. 1. “He steals.” Origen, Homily 7. GRIAL.

Here: “And a golden tongue.” This must be read exactly so from the Septuagint, not “a bar,” from the Vulgate. Otherwise the allegory, which is wholly Origen’s, does not proceed. It is surprising that whoever once altered this for the worse did not see this. GRIAL.

Here: “A golden tongue.” Grialius defends this reading, and not without reason. But it should be observed that in no. 3 “golden bars” occurs. The ancients used one or another version of the Bible at different times. AREV.]

1. Meanwhile Achan steals from the devoted things of the city of Jericho a cloak and a golden tongue, and because of this, when God became angry, certain people from the nation perished by the hand of the enemy. Jericho, as has been said, represents the world. Therefore, the person who defrauds it of its devoted things and hides them in his tent is the one who inserts secular customs into the secrets of the Church; who, while remaining under the worship of God, loves the festivals or spectacles of the world; who consults diviners, haruspices, and augurs, or recommends other rites; all of which were formerly practiced in Jericho, that is, in this world. Because he introduces the practice of secular life after putting on the garment of faith, he takes away, as it were, a cloak from the devoted things.

[Note: [Col. 0375D]

2. “They stole this.” Thus Albornoz, and indeed better than Grialius, who has “they defrauded themselves of this.” AREV.]

2. The person who defrauds Jericho of its devoted things is also the one who introduces the doctrines of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature into the Church. For this is the golden tongue, fitted for eloquent speech. Arius, Marcion, and Basilides stole it.

483 3. For they stole golden bars from Jericho, those who tried to introduce the sect of the philosophers into the Church and defile the whole Church of the Lord, so that many were destroyed by them. Therefore they were cast out by anathema, and, like a heap of stones, they were overwhelmed and killed by the multitude of their sins. Once their error had been destroyed, King Hai—that is, the devil, who through their impiety had overcome certain believers—is again defeated and overcome, and, suspended by the people of God, is killed by the power of the wood of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0375D]

3. “The king of Hai.” Grialius had added a sign here for some note that has been lost. AREV.]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Construction of the Altar

[Note: [Col. 0375D]

CHAP. IX, no. 1. “Therefore, when the enemies had been overcome.” All the words are Origen’s, though they are not placed continuously in Homily 9. GRIAL.

Here the Vulgate reads: “And you yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house.” AREV.]

1. When the enemies had been overcome, Jesus built an altar to the Most High God from whole stones, on which no iron had been used, as Moses had commanded; he offered a sacrifice and wrote the Deuteronomy of Moses’ law on the stones. Let us see, then, who these stones are from which the altar is built. All who believe in Jesus Christ are called living stones, concerning whom the Apostle says: “You are living stones, built into spiritual houses” (1 Pet. 2:5).

2. Iron was not used on these stones, because they are incorrupt and undefiled in flesh and spirit, and have not received the flaming darts of the evil one. These form one altar in the unity of faith and harmony of charity. In these also the Lord Jesus writes Deuteronomy—that is, the second law of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0375D]

3. “This law in their minds,” etc. Albornoz omits this, which is supplied from Isidore’s original with these words: “Therefore Christ writes this new law in the hearts of believers, namely, in their minds.” AREV.]

3. Let us hear him saying: “It was said to the ancients” (Exod. 20), “You shall not kill”; but I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother is a murderer. And again: “You shall not commit adultery”; but I say to you: if anyone looks at a woman in order to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5). This law, therefore, Jesus marks in the hearts of believers; he writes it in the minds of those who are worthy of the construction of the altar.

## CHAPTER X. On Blessings and Curses

[Col. 0376A]

[Note: [Col. 0376D]

CHAP. X, no. 1. From the same homily of Origen. GRIAL.]

1. After this, all the people, together with the elders, leaders, and judges, proceeded on both sides of the Ark. They stood, as Moses had commanded in Deuteronomy: six tribes on Mount Gerizim, to bless the people. These were the more noble tribes, namely Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.

2. But the other six, less noble, stood opposite on Mount Ebal, to curse; among them were Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed, and Zebulun, Leah’s last son, as well as the sons of the maidservants. This is what the events of the ancient history relate. But we must examine what is conveyed in the exposition of the mystical understanding.

3. Who, then, are those who proceed beside Mount Gerizim, and who are those who proceed beside Mount Ebal? Those who proceed here beside Mount Gerizim, chosen for blessing, figuratively indicate those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise. Those others, however, that half who proceed beside Mount Ebal, where the curses were pronounced, indicate those who fulfill what is written in the law not out of love for blessings or promises, but out of fear of future punishments, so that they may attain salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0376D]

4. “By love of eternal blessing.” This is correct in Origen. Valentinus and Compendius have “by love of blessedness.” GRIAL.

Here: *Condiscere*.—Either Rufinus or Jerome wrote *discernere*, “to discern.” The Valentinian manuscript has *conducere*. GRIAL.

A notable judgment, by which we are taught that contrition and sorrow for sins arising from fear of Gehenna can be good and supernatural. AREV.]

4. All proceed around the Ark, because they do not depart from the bosom of the Church. Yet we call those more noble who act from desire for goodness itself and from love of eternal blessing, which is good, than those who pursue good out of fear of evil. Jesus alone, therefore, can come to know the minds and hearts of all these peoples.

485 5. Some were placed on Mount Gerizim to bless, and others on Mount Ebal to curse—not so that they should receive curses, but so that, looking upon the curses written down and the punishments appointed for sinners, they might take care not to incur them and might correct themselves through the punishment of fear.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Gibeonites

[Note: [Col. 0376D]

CHAP. XI, no. 1. From Homily 10. GRIAL.]

1. Meanwhile the Gibeonites, terrified by fear of destruction, came to Joshua with fraud and cunning, dressed in old rags and worn-out sandals, begging to be saved, and immediately received salvation from Joshua. When he discovered their deception, however, he appointed them cutters of wood or carriers of water. In their figure are shown those who come from the world to the Church, have faith in God, bow their heads to priests, and minister to the saints of the Church or are ready for ministry, but remain bound in their own conduct and former way of life, putting on the old man with his deeds and wrapped in ancient vices, just as the Gibeonites were covered with old rags and worn-out sandals.

[Note: [Col. 0377D]

2. Albornoz: “Or they appear devoted to the observances of the Church.” AREV.]

2. And beyond the fact that they believe in God and appear devoted to the worship of the servants of God or of the Church, they possess no amendment or renewal of character. Such people therefore bear within the Church, for a time only, something like a sign of salvation; but among the Israelites—that is, among the saints of God—they by no means attain eternal kingship or freedom.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the battle at Gibeon

[Note: [Col. 0377D]

CHAP. XII, no. 1. From Homily 11. GRIAL.]

1. It is reported that, while Joshua was fighting at Gibeon, the sun and moon stood still until the enemies of Israel were destroyed, as Scripture says: “The sun stood still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Ajalon”; and Scripture adds and says: “For God never so heard a man.”

2. Our Jesus, therefore, caused the sun to stand still—not only at that time, but much more now, at his coming—while we wage war against the nations of our vices and wrestle against principalities and powers, and against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. The Sun of righteousness continually stands by us; he never abandons us and does not hasten to set, because he himself said: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

3. The five kings signify the five bodily senses, which attack the Gibeonites—that is, carnal human beings. They flee to a cave when, placed in the body, they plunge themselves into earthly actions. Yet while Jesus is fighting—that is, while evangelical preaching is at work—they are overcome; and when the word of God enters us, that is, within the cave of our body, they are all slain together.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the nations that were destroyed and the division of the land

1. After the nations had been destroyed or expelled, Joshua divided the promised land among the peoples by lot. Christ likewise, in a certain sense, expelled from the presence of his faithful the nations—that is, the evil spirits of pagan errors—and divided the land among us by lot, with one and the same Spirit accomplishing all things and distributing his own gifts to each person as he wills.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the division of the land

[Col. 0377D] [Note: [Col. 0377D]

CHAP. XIV, no. 1. The whole chapter is from Homilies 3 and 17. GRIAL.]

1. In these divine utterances, a first and a second division of the inheritance is reported to have taken place (Num. 34). The first was through Moses; the second, which is stronger, through Jesus. Moses granted possession beyond the Jordan to only two and a half tribes—namely, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh; all the others, however, receive their possession through Jesus.

[Col. 0378A] 487 [Note: [Col. 0377D]

2. “Recognition of the Trinity.” Another reading: “knowledge of the truth.” AREV.]

2. This indicates that more people would receive the heavenly promises through faith in Jesus Christ than had obtained them through the law. For those two and a half tribes undoubtedly prefigured the earlier people; but they are called two and a half because those who lived under the law attained recognition of the Trinity, but did not possess perfect knowledge of it, as the book of Ecclesiasticus also says: “One did not first bring knowledge of wisdom to completion, and the weaker person did not investigate it” (Sir. 24).

3. These nine and a half tribes, however, which, as was said, receive through Jesus the promise of the holy land, represented the figure of the new people. Through faith and grace, after baptism—as after the crossing of the Jordan—they received from Jesus our Lord the inheritance of the eternal promise. Yet for this reason these tribes are also called nine and a half, which obtain their inheritance under Jesus, and not a complete ten—the number said to be complete and perfect—because even in the Lord’s coming, or in his incarnation, not everything was perfectly announced to us through him alone.

[Note: [Col. 0377D]

4. The Vulgate expresses this sentence somewhat differently: “I still have many things,” etc. AREV.]

4. Hence he himself also said to the disciples: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot hear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father; he will receive from what is mine and announce all things to you” (John 16). The perfection, therefore, and the fullness of all good things reside in the Holy Spirit; otherwise nothing will be considered perfect in one who lacks the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XV. That the Levites did not receive an inheritance

[Col. 0378C] [Note: [Col. 0378D]

CHAP. XV, no. 1. From Homily 21 on Numbers 26 and Homily 17 on Joshua. GRIAL.

In the same place. Codex Alborn.: “For this reason he wished it to be called the inheritance of the clergy.” Then others: “They are ministers and sharers of his altar, on account of which …” AREV.]

1. Why, then, did the Levites not receive an inheritance of land? Clearly, because our Lord Jesus Christ himself is their inheritance, as it is written: “I am their inheritance, and no possession shall be given to them in Israel. For I am their possession.” God wished himself to be called the inheritance and possession of the clergy because they became ministers of his altar, and a portion; for this reason, too, *clerus* is interpreted as “lot.”

2. Therefore he rightly possesses the Lord’s inheritance who, so that he may be able to serve God without hindrance, strives to be poor in spirit, so that he may fittingly say what the Psalmist says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15).

## CHAPTER XVI. That the dwellings of the Levites were assigned throughout all the tribes

[Col. 0378D]

[Note: [Col. 0378D]

CHAP. XVI, no. 1. From the same Homily 17. GRIAL.]

1. The fact that dwellings are assigned to the Levites by Jesus throughout all the tribes signifies that those in the Church of God who devote themselves to knowledge and administer the grace of teaching should in turn receive from all those for whom they distribute divine things the earthly support that they themselves do not possess, so that what the Apostle commanded may be fulfilled when he says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). And rightly are these men said to be divided among all the tribes, because they live by the provision of all.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the Levites received forty-two cities

[Note: [Col. 0379B]

CHAP. XVII, no. 1. “Forty-two cities.” Breulius noted in the margin: “Rather, forty-eight.” Indeed, Joshua 21:39 expresses it in this way: “All the cities of the Levites in the midst of the possession of the children of Israel were forty-eight.” But, as interpreters observe, the number forty-eight includes the six cities of refuge, which had been granted as places of asylum to all the children of Israel and to the foreigners living among them. Immediately afterward, the Alborn. codex reads: “Those possessing the teaching … and in a fourfold manner … have cities.” AREV.]

1. The fact that they receive forty-two cities undoubtedly signifies the preaching of the saints. They possess the teaching that consists of the Decalogue of the law and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though possessing four times ten cities, with two also added to them because everything they preach they announce in both a moral and a mystical sense.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Canaanite people who were not destroyed

[Col. 0379B] [Note: [Col. 0380B]

CHAP. XVIII, no. 1. The words from “But that” through “does not subdue” are entirely Gregory’s words, *Moralia* IV, chapter 22. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Received.” Another reading: “by God’s command.” AREV.]

1. There is also the matter that, when the promised land, once received, was being divided among the Israelite people, the Canaanite gentile population of the tribe of Ephraim is said not to have been killed but made tributary, as it is written in the book of Judges: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim as a tributary” (Judg. 1). What does “tributary”—what does “Canaanite,” namely a gentile people—signify, if not vice? For often we enter the promised land through great virtues, because we are strengthened by an inward hope of eternity. But when, after greater vices have been destroyed, we nevertheless retain certain lesser ones, we permit the Canaanite, as it were, to live in our land.

[Note: [Col. 0380B]

2. “These are the nations.” Cassian also treats this passage most elegantly, *Conferences* 2, chapter 6, and *Conferences* 13, chapter 10. GRIAL.]

2. Yet it is made tributary because we humbly turn that very vice which we cannot subjugate toward the use of our benefit, so that the mind may think poorly of itself even amid its highest achievements, since by its own strength it cannot conquer even the small things it desires. Hence it is again rightly written: “These are the nations whom the Lord left, to instruct Israel through them” (Judg. 3:1).

3. For this reason certain very small vices are retained in us, so that our purpose may continually exercise itself attentively in the struggle and may not become proud of victory, since it sees enemies living within itself whom it still fears to be able to defeat. Israel, therefore, is instructed by the gentiles being left behind, when the exaltation of our virtue is restrained by certain minor vices, and when, through the small things that resist it, it learns that it does not subjugate greater things by its own power.

# BOOK OF JUDGES

[Col. 0379]

490 ## CHAPTER I. Concerning the people’s servitude and liberation

[Col. 0379C]

[Note: [Col. 0379D]

CHAP. I, no. 1. From Origen, Homily 3. GRIAL.]

1. The history of Judges indicates no small sacred mysteries. First, after Joshua come the Judges, just as after Christ come the apostles and the rulers of the Churches, to govern and direct the faithful whom he himself brings to the hope of the eternal promise. Throughout this book are described the offenses of the Jewish people, their servitudes, their cry, and also God’s mercies.

[Note: [Col. 0379D]

2. “Into the hand of the enemy.” Another reading: “Into the hand hostile to them.” And shortly afterward, “demons and the forces of spiritual wickedness,” etc. AREV.]

2. For many years they served many kings because of their many offenses, and then, having turned back, they were liberated. But what does it mean that those who often sin are delivered into the hand of the enemy, except that our sins, whenever we transgress, give strength to our enemies, and that whenever we do evil in the sight of the Lord, our adversaries—namely, the demons, the forces of spiritual wickedness—are then strengthened?

3. But again, when we turn back, the Lord raises up saviors and judges—that is, rulers and teachers—whom God sends to aid those who cry out to him with all their heart. Thus he sent Othniel, who defeated Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia; thus he sent Ehud, who killed Eglon, king of Moab; thus he sent Jael and Deborah, who killed Sisera. Their history should be briefly recalled for the sake of its mysteries.

491 ## CHAPTER II. Concerning Deborah and Jael

[Note: [Col. 0380D]

CHAP. II, no. 1. From Origen’s Homily. GRIAL.]

1. Deborah, the prophetess, wife of Lappidoth, judged the people at that time. She sat beneath a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, and the children of Israel came up to her for every judgment. Deborah, whose name is interpreted as “bee” or “speech,” is to be understood in prophecy and as a figure of the one concerning whom it is written: “How sweet are your utterances to my throat” (Ps. 118)! Let us consider where the place of prophecy is described.

2. “Under a palm tree,” he says. Prophecy has its seat under a palm tree because those whom it instructs by its teachings it brings to the palm of the heavenly calling. Prophecy is said to sit between Ramah and Bethel because Ramah is interpreted as “the exalted,” while Bethel means “the house of God”—plainly because, teaching us to be placed in the house of God, it instructs us to seek not the things that are on earth but those that are in heaven.

3. “She sent and called Barak to herself.” Barak is interpreted as “lightning.” Lightning has light, but not a lasting light; it shines for a short time and then ceases. Barak, therefore, represents the earlier people, who were first called and invited through prophecy to hear the utterances of God. They did shine in the splendor of the law and flashed for a short time, but did not remain for long.

[Note: [Col. 0381D]

4. Another reading: “On the way along which you walk.” AREV.]

4. When Deborah—that is, prophecy speaking to the earlier people—had said to Barak: “The Lord has commanded you, and you shall ascend Mount Tabor, and take with you ten thousand men,” Barak replied to the prophetess on behalf of the earlier people: “I will not go unless you go up with me.” Deborah said to him: “I will go with you, but the primacy will not be yours on the way along which you walk; the Lord will deliver Sisera into the hand of a woman”—clearly showing that primacy does not belong to that people, nor does the palm of victory remain with it, but with Jael the woman, that is, with the Church. For this Jael, a foreigner in whose hand the victory was achieved, represents the Church gathered from the nations.

492 5. Jael is interpreted as “ascent,” because through the Church one ascends to heaven. With a stake she kills Sisera the enemy—that is, by the power of the wood of the cross she destroys the devil—which Barak, that is, the earlier people, could not do through the commandments of the law. She alone, through the wood in which the salvation of believers lies by spiritual mysteries, fastens the enemy of faith; then she covers him with skins, that is, leaves him enclosed in carnal hearts. His deadly works remain hidden only among those who live in the corruption of life and commit mortal sins; for when, by living wickedly, they are separated from the body of Christ, they become members of the devil.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Gideon and his sacrifice

[Col. 0381C]

[Note: [Col. 0381D]

CHAP. III, no. 1. From Origen, Homily 8, and Augustine, Sermon 108 on the Seasons. GRIAL.]

1. The people of Israel were then delivered into the hand of Midian, and for their liberation the angel of the Lord spoke to Gideon. What his deeds signify mystically must now be demonstrated. Gideon, while beating a harvest of wheat with a staff beneath an oak and threshing the grain from the chaff, saw an angel and received from him an oracle that he should lead God’s people from the power of their enemies into freedom. This Gideon bore the figure of Christ, who, established beneath the shadow of the holy cross through the foreordained mystery of the future incarnation, separated the elect of the saints from the chaff of vices, as though by a staff, through the uprightness of judgment.

2. When this Gideon heard from the angel that, when the thousands of the peoples had been reduced, the Lord would free his people from their enemies through one man, he immediately cooked a kid. According to the angel’s command, he placed its flesh together with unleavened bread upon a rock and poured the broth over it. When the angel touched these things with the tip of his staff, fire immediately burst forth from the rock, and thus the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed.

3. By this sign it appears to have been declared that the rock represented the body of Christ, as Paul testifies: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). Already then, in mystery, it was declared that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would remove the sins of the whole world, and would cleanse not only the offenses of deeds but also the desires of souls. The flesh of the kid refers to the guilt of the deed, while the broth refers to the enticements of desires, as it is written: “The people desired an evil desire, and they said, ‘Who will feed us with flesh?’” When the angel stretched out the staff and touched the rock from which fire came forth, this showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human nature.

[Col. 0382B] [Note: [Col. 0381D]

4. “To be brought by the peoples as the worship of our redemption.” —“To be brought as the worship of the people”; Augustine, from whom the two words “of our redemption” appear to be absent. “To be brought reverently by the peoples,” Bede and Valerius; not implausibly. GRIAL.]

4. Hence the Lord also says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12). Thus the learned man, who foresaw future things, perceived the heavenly mysteries. Therefore, in accordance with the oracles, he killed the bull that his father had dedicated to idols, and he himself sacrificed another seven-year-old bull to God. By this deed he most clearly revealed that, after the Lord’s coming, all pagan sacrifices were to be abolished, and that the one sacrifice of the Lord’s passion was to be brought by the peoples to God as the worship of our redemption. For that bull was a type of Christ, in whom, as Isaiah says, the sevenfold fullness of spiritual virtues dwells.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the fleece and the threshing floor

[Note: [Col. 0381D]

CHAP. IV, no. 1. From the same passages, apart from the matters noted. GRIAL.]

1. Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery of victory; yet, although strong and faithful, he sought still fuller indications from the Lord concerning the future victory: that one night a fleece of wool should be placed on the threshing floor, with dew only upon it and dryness over all the land. Then again the fleece was to be placed in the same way, with dew falling over the whole land and dryness remaining on the fleece.

[Note: [Col. 0382D]

2. “He will ask.” So Albornoz. The codex and Grialius have “he asks.” AREV.]

2. Perhaps someone will ask whether he appears to have been incredulous, since he had already been instructed by frequent signs. Far from it. He was not doubtful; rather, he foresaw the mysteries that were to come. As a prudent man, he carefully examined them so that he might believe more fully in the mystery once he had understood the oracle.

[Note: [Col. 0382D]

3. “What, then, does the fleece … until ‘is empty’?” From *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 32. GRIAL.

In the same place. “That one is empty.” —“It has been emptied,” Augustine. GRIAL.]

3. What, then, does the fleece drenched with dew and the dry threshing floor, and afterward the drenched threshing floor with the fleece dry, signify, except that at first one nation of the Hebrews possessed the mystery of grace while the whole world was empty, but now, in the manifestation of Christ, the whole world possesses it, while that nation is empty? For the threshing floor signifies the entire world.

[Note: [Col. 0382D]

4. “With unfruitful worship.” —“With unfruitful heat,” Augustine.

In the same place. “That is, in Judea.” These words were added from Augustine, since they were lacking in the manuscripts. GRIAL.

In the same place. “That rain.” —“And that divine fountain conveyed its channels into the hearts of the nations,” Augustine. GRIAL.

[Col. 0383D] In the same place. “And with all the spiritual gifts.” —“With the gift,” Valerius. “But the Jews lost their prophets and counselors,” Augustine. GRIAL.

In the same place. The words “that is, in Judea” were absent from Grialius’s text, contrary to his intention. AREV.]

4. In the end, when the whole world was dry with the unfruitful worship of pagan superstition, that heavenly dew of visitation was upon the fleece—that is, in Judea. But afterward, when the lost sheep of the house of Israel, represented under the figure of the fleece, denied the fountain of living water, the dew of faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine rain conveyed its grace into the hearts of the nations. Hence the whole world is now wet with the dew of faith, while the Jews have been deprived of prophets and of all spiritual gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0383D]

5. The Vulgate: “And I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” AREV.]

5. Nor is it surprising that those who have been deprived by the Lord of the abundance of prophetic rain should suffer the dryness of unbelief, since he says: “I will command the clouds above not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5). He signified that people by the name of “fleece” either because it was to be stripped of the authority of teaching, as a sheep is stripped of its fleece, or because, being disobedient, it retained that rain which it did not wish to be preached—that is, revealed—to the uncircumcised nations.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Gideon’s battle with the three hundred

[Note: [Col. 0383D]

CHAP. V, no. 1. The whole chapter is from Gregory, *Moralia* XXX, chapter 17. GRIAL.]

1. After this most careful explanation of the mystery, when Gideon was preparing to fight against the Midianites and was leading out the multitude of his army for battle, a divine admonition commanded that, when he came to the river, all whom he saw drinking water on bended knees should be removed from the conflict of battle. And it happened that only three hundred men remained, those who had drawn water with their hands while standing.

[Note: [Col. 0383D]

2. “By the flashing of the lamps.” Others: “by the gleam of the lamps.” Afterward some add: “Concerning this it is said through the prophet: ‘You have broken the yoke of his burden, and the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his taskmaster, as on the day of Midian.’ For in rescuing the gentiles, the Lord overcame the yoke of their burden when, by his coming, he freed them from the slavery of demonic tyranny. He overcame the scepter of their taskmaster when he destroyed in the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that same devil, who, on account of the destructive practice of vices, was accustomed to exact the due tribute of punishments. What is this, etc.” Grialius wished all this to be omitted entirely. AREV.]

2. With these men Gideon goes into battle, armed not with weapons but with trumpets, lamps, and jars. For, as it is written there, they put lighted lamps inside little jars; they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left. Coming close to their enemies, they blew the trumpets and smashed the little jars. The lamps appeared, and the enemy, terrified on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the lamps, turned and fled.

[Note: [Col. 0384D]

3. “What is this?” The words printed before this are indeed Gregory’s words from chapter 16. But they have not been accepted because they interrupt the sense and are absent from the manuscripts; there is no doubt that they were taken from the margin. GRIAL.]

3. Why is such a battle introduced in the prophet in connection with this passage (Isa. 9)? Did the prophet seek to indicate to us that the victory of that battle under Gideon’s leadership signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil? Certainly, events occurred there which, the more they surpass ordinary military practice, the more they do not depart from the mystery of prophecy.

4. Who ever went into battle with jars and lamps? Who, when confronting weapons, abandoned weapons? These things would surely have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrifying to the enemies. But this victory teaches us not to disregard the seemingly small things that occurred. Gideon, therefore, coming into battle, signifies the coming of our Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23).

5. He prophesied this Redeemer of ours not only by deed but also by name. For Gideon is interpreted as “one who encompasses in the womb.” Our Lord, through the power of his majesty, encompasses all things, yet through the grace of his dispensation he entered the Virgin’s womb. What, then, is “one who encompasses in the womb,” except that Christ, almighty God, was within the womb through the substance of weakness, and outside the world through the power of majesty? Midian, however, is interpreted as “from judgment.”

[Note: [Col. 0384D]

6. “Not one who repels on account of vice.” So Gregory, and in Bede; one manuscript reads “not from judgment.” GRIAL.]

6. The fact that his enemies had to be repelled and destroyed was not a matter of the vice of the one repelling them, but of the judgment of the one who judges justly. Therefore those who are called “from judgment” draw the merit of just condemnation even into the meaning of their name because they are alien to the grace of the Redeemer. Against these Gideon goes into battle with three hundred men.

7. The number one hundred is customarily understood to signify the fullness of perfection. What, then, is signified by the number one hundred multiplied by three, except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? With such men our Lord destroys the adversaries of the faith; with such men he descends to the battles of preaching—men who can know divine things and who know how to think perfectly about the Trinity, which is God.

[Note: [Col. 0384D]

8. In the manuscripts this is found sometimes as T, sometimes as the letter T, and sometimes as *tau*. Isidore also taught elsewhere that the number three hundred is contained in Tau. See *Allegories*, no. 76, with notes. AREV.]

8. It should be noted that this number three hundred is contained in the letter T, which has the form of a cross. If that which projects above the transverse line were added to it, it would no longer be the appearance of a cross but the cross itself. Since, therefore, this number three hundred is contained in the letter tau, T, and since the form of the cross is shown through the letter tau, as we have said, it is not without reason that those who are signified by the three hundred men following Gideon are the ones to whom it was said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16; Mark 8).

9. Those who follow the Lord take up the cross more truly the more vigorously they discipline themselves and the more they are pierced by compassion in charity toward their neighbors. Hence it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “Mark a tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve” (Ezek. 9). Or certainly, in the three hundred who are contained in the letter tau, this is expressed: the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross. They were therefore led to the river to drink water, and those who drank the water on bended knees were removed from the intention of battle.

[Note: [Col. 0385D]

10. “They go into battle.” The Codex Albornoz adds: “All are indeed said to have drunk water at that time, but not all are said to have stood with straight knees; those who bent their knees while drinking water were rejected, because, as the Apostle testifies, it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. Since, as we have said, the dissolution of works is signified by the bending of the knees, Paul rightly says again: ‘Raise up the drooping hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet.’ Thus those who, under Christ’s leadership, advance to war are the ones who show by their deeds what they announce with their mouths, who spiritually drink in the streams of teaching and yet are not carnally bent by wicked deeds, because it is written: ‘Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of sinners.’” AREV.]

10. Water signifies the teaching of wisdom, while standing knee-upright signifies right action. Therefore those who are said to have bent their knees while drinking water withdrew, having been prohibited from joining their contest. These are the people who do not take in teaching together with right works. But those who drink in the streams of teaching in such a way that they are in no way carnally bent by wicked deeds go into battle against the enemies of the faith under Christ’s leadership.

11. They go, therefore, with trumpets, lamps, and jars; and this, as we said, was the order of the battle. They blew the trumpets, while the lamps were placed inside the jars. When the jars were broken, the lamps were revealed; and when their light flashed, the enemies were terrified and put to flight. The trumpets therefore signify the proclamation, the lamps the brightness of miracles, and the jars the frailty of bodies.

[Note: [Col. 0385D]

12. “With the swords of the enemies.” So Albornoz. Others: “with hostile swords”; this perhaps is what Grialius intended, who has “with swords for the enemies.” AREV.]

12. Our leader brought such men with him to the battle of preaching. They despise the safety of their bodies and overthrow their enemies by dying; they overcome their swords not with weapons but with patience. Our martyrs came armed into battle under their leader, but with trumpets, jars, and lamps. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they exposed their bodies, to be dissolved in suffering, to the swords of their enemies.

13. They shone with lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed with miracles. Then the enemies were put to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of the dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were shattered by the light of truth and believed what they had opposed. They therefore blew the trumpets so that the jars might be broken. The jars were broken so that the lamps might appear. The lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight.

14. That is, the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine with miracles. They flashed with miracles so that they might overthrow their enemies by the divine light. And it should be noted that the enemies stood before the jars but fled before the lamps, because the persecutors of the holy faith resisted the preachers while the latter were still in the body.

[Note: [Col. 0386D]

15. Some manuscripts: “Terrified by fear, they ceased their persecution of the faithful.” Grialius: “for the right … for the left.” Albornoz: “for the right-hand … for the left-hand.” AREV.]

15. But after the dissolution of the bodies, when miracles appeared, they were put to flight because, crushed by fear, they ceased their persecution. We should also observe what is written there: they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left. We say that whatever we esteem highly is on the right; what we regard as nothing is on the left.

16. It is therefore rightly written there that they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left, because the martyrs of Christ esteem the grace of preaching highly but regard the usefulness of their bodies as of little account. Whoever values the usefulness of the body more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in the left hand and the jar in the right. For if the grace of preaching is attended to first and the usefulness of the body afterward, it is certain that the trumpets are held on the right and the jars on the left.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Abimelech

[Note: [Col. 0386D]

CHAP. VI, no. 1. We think this chapter was taken from a sermon of the blessed Augustine that no longer survives. This is indicated by the recapitulatory section that follows, beginning with the words “he will devour together”—a device he often used. That recapitulation is not found in Bede, and we have ordered it to be omitted, although it occurs in most manuscripts; for it conflicts with the rule of brevity that Isidore prescribed for himself in these commentaries, since the same matter is reported twice in a single chapter. GRIAL.]

1. Gideon died and left seventy sons and one named Abimelech, born of a concubine. He hired wandering men for himself, and they followed him. He entered his father’s house and killed his seventy brothers upon one stone, while Jotham the younger remained, because he was hidden, etc. If this event indicated nothing prophetic, why would it have been carefully stated that Gideon had seventy sons and many wives, but also a concubine from whom he had begotten one son—and an evil one at that?

[Col. 0386C] 499 [Note: [Col. 0386D]

2. “A shameful deed.” Perhaps: “shameful to do.” AREV.]

2. Since this was a shameful deed, it would be still more shameful if such matters appeared to have been written in the divine books as examples for posterity, unless the deeds themselves, through types and figures, displayed the image of some great reality. Gideon, therefore, as was said above, bore the type of the Lord; his many wives are the many nations that have clung to Christ through faith. His seventy sons are the seventy languages spread throughout the world, among which the Lord was to beget sons for himself through faith.

3. In this passage he calls the concubine the Synagogue. It will believe in the Antichrist in the last times, concerning which the apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “Those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2:9). From her, in the last times, the most wicked son—that is, the Antichrist—is to be born. He will be the son of the slave woman, that is, of that sinful Synagogue, because, as he says, “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin.”

4. This man, having gathered impious people to himself, will wickedly usurp the kingdom, as Abimelech did. After killing the noble sons—that is, those who, believing in Christ, have been generated by God from different nations and languages—he will bring in persecution in order to kill almost all the saints. But, it says, above the seventy there was a younger son from a noble marriage, who had hidden himself. This man, it says, went up to the summit of Mount Garizim and cried out in a loud voice to the people of Shechem, composing a parable for them.

5. This younger son, who fled in order to escape the enemy’s sword, represents the remnant of the people of Israel who, when Elijah preaches, will believe in the final times and escape the sword of the Antichrist. “He went up,” it says, “to the summit of Mount Garizim.” But why did he ascend the mountain? Because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of the Antichrist unless he has first ascended the mountain of blessing—that is, the height of faith and virtues. For this is Mount Garizim, which Moses appointed for blessing (Deut. 29).

6. Therefore, when he had ascended, he raised his voice and cried out, saying: “Hear me, men of Shechem.” The trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and they said to the olive tree: “Rule over us.” It replied: “Can I abandon my richness, which gods and human beings use, and go to be promoted among the trees?” Then the trees said to the fig tree: “Come and accept the kingship over us.” It replied: “Can I leave my sweetness and my most delightful fruits and go to be promoted among the other trees?” The trees also spoke to the vine: “Come and rule over us.” It replied: “Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and human beings, and be promoted among the other trees?”

7. When the trees of the forest had been rejected by the olive, the fig, and the vine, they came to the thornbush to make him their king. But first let us see why the olive, the fig, and the vine did not wish to rule over the trees. By the trees of the forest we understand wandering and empty human beings, prepared for eternal fire. For this reason neither the olive, nor the fig, nor the vine rightly wished to rule over them, because they were unworthy. The olive signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit and the anointing of peace. The fig bears the image of the sacred law, as it is written in the Gospel: “A certain householder planted a vineyard, and in his vineyard he planted a fig tree.”

8. Who is the householder except God, who is the father of his household, that is, of all believers? He therefore planted a vineyard, that is, the people, because he brought a vineyard out of Egypt. And certainly he had brought the people, not a vineyard, out of Egypt. In this vineyard he planted a fig tree—that is, in his people he established the Law. This Law cast the primitive people down upon the earth like large, dry, useless figs, and afterward produced other fruits, that is, the Christian people, whom it brought to the maturity proper to evangelical discipline and to the most pleasant richness of Christ, with glory and honor [Col. 0388B].

[Note: [Col. 0387D]

9. “The rejected one came to the bramble.” Alborn.: “is rejected.” He omits “came to the bramble” and what follows up to chapter 9. But an old collator noted this passage: “There is much more in another, eighth book.” Perhaps this is the book which the Collator sometimes calls Isidore’s *Original* or *Originale*. AREV.]

9. But the vine did not wish to reign over them. It is clear that the vine bears a type of our Savior, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine” (John XV). Therefore, since that people was already destined to become, as the Apostle says, a people given over to a reprobate mind (Rom. I), and was going to serve Antichrist—the people whom he calls the trees of the forest—it was necessary that it should believe a lie, that is, Antichrist, because it had refused to believe the truth, Christ. For this reason, rejected from the reign of the vine, that is, of Christ; from the olive, that is, from the grace of the Holy Spirit; and from the fig tree, that is, from the sweetness of the divine Law, it came to the bramble.

501 [Note: [Col. 0387D]

10. After “he will devour,” several additions occur in Florentine Manuscripts 1 and 2, as also in the Madrid edition of Ulloa among the appendices, p. 54, from a codex said to be of the twelfth or thirteenth century, which formerly belonged to the church of Saint Antoninus of Palencia. The fragment is as follows:

“Gideon, therefore, appears to have borne the image of Christ. The seventy sons are the seventy languages, or nations, which, by believing and through a second regeneration, were deemed worthy to be sons of God. Abimelech, the son of the slave woman, appears to have borne the type of Antichrist, who, having gathered the ruined nations, wickedly usurped the kingdom for himself and slaughtered all the saints by force, persecutions, and every cruelty. Joatham, the younger son, was a figure of the saints. For just as Joatham withdrew by flight while the remaining brothers were killed, so no one will be able to escape the persecution of Antichrist except one who withdraws by flight and ascends the mountain of blessing. For this is the mountain which the saints will surround, which holy Moses, as has already been said above, set forth in Deuteronomy among the blessings.”

In the Florentine manuscripts it reads “through a second generation.” I supplied “appears” after “to have borne.” The Palencia codex has: “wickedly usurped his kingdom . . . and by persecution,” and shortly afterward, “Joatham, however, the younger, a figure”; and near the end, “as has already been said above.” See Grial’s judgment in note 1. AREV.]

10. For the bramble is a kind of shrub, commonly called the “bear’s thorn,” exceedingly rough and thorny; through it the type of Antichrist is rightly signified [Col. 0388C], who will ravage the human race with every form of harshness and savagery. “But fire,” he says, “will come out from the bramble,” that is, iniquity from Antichrist, “and it will devour all who trust in him together with him.”

## CHAPTER VII. On Jephthah and His Daughter

[Note: [Col. 0388D]

CHAP. VII. No. 1. See Augustine, *The City of God*, I.21. GRIAL.]

1. Then the children of Israel again added to their service of the Baals and foreign gods, and they were delivered into the hands of the Ammonites. At that time Jephthah the Gileadite, fleeing from the face of his brothers, was appointed commander for the war against the Ammonites. Returning after his victory, he sacrificed his daughter, who had been the first to meet him after his triumph; for he had made this vow: whatever should first meet him on his return, he would sacrifice to the Lord.

2. Who, then, was prefigured in Jephthah except the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, who, departing from the face of his brothers, that is, the Jews, received rule among the nations? He fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation as one bound by an oath and, as though she were his daughter, offered his own flesh to the Lord for the salvation of Israel.

502 3. For we read that the Father swore and the Only-Begotten made a vow, as the Psalmist says: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Psalm CXXXI), namely, that he would fulfill the sacramental mystery of religion through the passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race. These events, therefore, were historically accomplished through Christ in such a way that they appear to have been fulfilled for the sake of the religion that he had sworn to establish. After Jephthah’s death, Israel was delivered into the hands of the Philistines, and Samson was born, who delivered Israel.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Samson

[Col. 0389B]

1. Samson, once the Lord’s Nazirite, contains in his typological history certain things accomplished as a type of Christ. First, his birth is announced by an angel; then he is called a Nazirite, and he himself delivers Israel from its enemies; finally, he overthrows their temple, and many thousands of men who had mocked him perish.

[Note: [Col. 0389D]

CHAP. VIII. No. 2. In the Vulgate: “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found grace with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb . . . and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great,” etc. See Sabatier. AREV.]

2. Samson’s birth, which is announced through an angel, first bears a likeness to the prophets who announced the Lord’s birth according to the flesh; and then to the angel who speaks to Mary, saying: “Mary, you have found grace before the Lord’s presence, and you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Jesus; for he will save his people from their sins” (Luke I, 30).

[Note: [Col. 0389D]

3. In the Vulgate: “For you who fear my name, the sun will rise,” etc. AREV.]

3. Samson, however, is interpreted as “their sun,” namely, the sun of those for whom he shines—not of everyone, as is the sun that rises upon the good and the wicked, but of certain people. Yet because our Redeemer too is called the sun, hear the Lord Jesus himself called by that name through the prophet: “For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing is in his wings” (Malachi IV, 2). For he truly is the sun of righteousness, who illumines the minds of all believers with heavenly light.

[Note: [Col. 0389D]

4. “But who first . . . up to ‘provide defenses,’” Augustine, *Against Faustus*, XII.32. GRIAL.]

4. He is truly the Nazirite and holy one of God, in whose likeness that Nazirite was so named. As he was going to the service of the wedding, a roaring lion met him. But who was the first to meet and kill the lion in Samson’s path, when he was going among foreigners to seek a wife, except Christ, who, intending to call the Church from the nations and conquering the devil, says: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world”?

[Note: [Col. 0389D]

5. “A honeycomb was taken from the mouth of the slain lion.” —“A honeycomb was constructed in the mouth of the slain lion,” Augustine. GRIAL.

[Col. 0390D] Ibid. “In Samson himself, up to ‘struck down,’” Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX.7. GRIAL.]

5. What does the honeycomb taken from the mouth of the slain lion signify except that, as we observe, the kings of earthly kingdoms, who once roared against Christ, now, their ferocity having been destroyed, provide defenses for the preaching of evangelical sweetness? There is also what Samson represented in himself: while he lived, he killed only a few, but when the temple was destroyed, he killed innumerable enemies by his death.

6. For the Lord extinguished a few, while he lived, from the pride of unbelief, but many more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and those lifted up among the nations, whom he endured while living, he struck down all together by dying. Now, as for the rest of his story—how the deceitful woman had his head shaved and handed him over to the Philistines for mockery; how he was captured, blinded, and assigned to the mill—in these matters it is not Christ who is represented, but those who glory in the Christian Church only in name and are continually entangled in evil deeds.

7. For the man signifies the rational faculty in us, while the flesh is received typologically as the woman. If we consent to the woman—that is, to our flesh—when lust or other works flatter it, we are stripped and deprived of the grace of the spirit, which is signified by the Nazirite’s hair, and we are deceived.

[Note: [Col. 0390D]

8. “But what is it that Samson, up to ‘they send him,’” Gregory, *Moralia* VII.13. GRIAL.

Ibid. In Grial’s note it read *amittunt* (“they lose”) instead of *mittunt* (“they send”). AREV.]

8. Thus the devil mocks the proud and sinners when the grace of Christ has been violated, just as Samson’s hair was cut. But what does it mean that, after that Samson was captured by the Philistines and had lost his eyes, he was assigned to the mill? It means, surely, that after evil spirits have pierced the inward eye of contemplation with the goads of temptations, they send a person outwardly in the circuit of labors.

[Col. 0390C] 9. But if that same person should at some time return by practicing repentance, his hair is restored, as it were—that is, when grace flourishes again, he is restored to virtue. Then, when the columns of desire and lust have been overturned, he throws down the victorious enemies, and, the battle being renewed, he will at the end triumph most courageously over the demons.

## CHAPTER IX. On Ruth

1. Let us now consider Ruth also. For she bears a type of the Church. First, she is a foreigner from a gentile people who, having left her homeland and everything that was there, goes into the land of Israel. And when her mother-in-law prevented her from going with her, she persisted, saying: “Wherever you go, I will go; your people will be my people, and your God my God; the land that receives you when you die, in it I will die” [Col. 0390D].

2. This statement undoubtedly reveals that a type of the Church was present in her. For in the same way the Church, summoned from the nations to the Lord, leaves her homeland—which is idolatry—and abandons every earthly manner of life. She professes the Lord to be her God, in whom the saints believed, and says that she will go to the place where Christ’s flesh ascended after the Passion; that for his name’s sake she will suffer in this world even unto death; and that she will be joined to the people of the saints, namely, the patriarchs and prophets. Moses shows in the Song that she would be associated with their company, that is, joined to the saints coming from the stock of Abraham, when he says: “Rejoice, nations, with his people,” that is, “You who from these nations will believe, rejoice with eternal joy together with those who were chosen first.”

3. When Ruth entered the land of Israel with her mother-in-law, she was rewarded for the merit of her service by being destined to be joined to a man descended from Abraham. First, the one whom she herself thought to be the nearer relative declared that he could not marry her. When he withdrew, she was joined to Boaz through the testimony of ten elders [Col. 0391B], and she was blessed by those ten older men.

4. But in the fact that the first relative confesses that he cannot marry her, we believe that the figure of John the Baptist is shown here. When the people of Israel thought that he himself was the Christ and asked who he was, he did not deny his own identity but confessed, saying that he was not the Christ. When those who had been sent continued to question him and ask who he was, he replied: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Isaiah XL; Matthew III; Luke III; John I; III). Finally, he himself confesses concerning the Lord, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” He shows himself to be the friend of the bridegroom when he adds: “But the friend of the bridegroom is the one who stands and hears him and rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

[Col. 0391C] 5. They therefore thought that this man was the Christ, because they did not understand that Christ had come at the time of his visitation as the bridegroom of the Church, who had been promised beforehand through the prophetic voices. But just as that relative refused, and afterward Ruth was joined to Boaz, so Christ, who is truly the bridegroom of the Church and whom the prophecies of all the prophets had celebrated in song, deigned to take the Church to himself and to offer to God the Father, from all the nations throughout the whole world, innumerable peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0390D]

CHAP. IX. No. 6. “But that he removes his sandal.” See above, Exodus VII. GRIAL.

Ibid. In Grial’s note it read: “but that the sandal is removed.” AREV.]

6. As for the fact that this relative removes his sandal, it was the ancient custom that if a woman wished to reject her bridegroom, his sandal was removed, so that this might be a sign of repudiation. Accordingly, he is commanded to be unshod, so that he would not approach the Church like a bridegroom wearing a sandal; this was reserved for Christ, who was the true bridegroom. The blessing of the ten elders demonstrates that in the name of the Lord Jesus all nations would be saved and blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0391]

7. Some have *Jesu summa perscribit* (“writes out the sum of Jesus”); others, *Jesu exprimit* (“expresses Jesus”). For *praecucurrisse*, some have *praecurrisse* (“to have gone before”). The Albornozian Codex ends in this book. AREV.]

7. For among the Greeks, *iota* signifies ten; as the first letter, it writes out the total of the name of the Lord Jesus. As we have said, this fact demonstrates that all nations are to be saved and blessed through him. Let no one, therefore, hesitate to believe these things as they have been stated, since he sees that all events were anticipated from the beginning by preceding figures and have been manifestly fulfilled through the Lord’s coming—and that what remains is to be completed in truth in this manner, with all the voices and figures of the holy Scriptures agreeing. He who promised these things through his Son, Jesus Christ, our Lord, King, and Savior, will fulfill them. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. [Col. 0392C] Amen.

# FIRST BOOK OF KINGS

[Col. 0391]

## CHAPTER I. On the Birth of Samuel

[Col. 0391C]

[Note: [Col. 0391D]

CHAP. I. No. 1. These expositions are found somewhat more fully also in Eucherius; some passages in Bede were corrected from him, although many more readings in both authors could be corrected from our text. GRIAL.]

1. After the Book of Judges comes the Book of Kings. Observe the sequence of the times: first Judges, afterward Kings, just as there will first be judgment and afterward a kingdom. In these books of Kings, the mysteries of Christ and the Church are revealed in many different ways.

[Col. 0391D] [Note: [Col. 0391D]

2. “For from the very beginning, up to ‘the figure proceeds,’” the words are Augustine, *Against Faustus* XII.33. GRIAL.]

2. For from the very beginning, when the priesthood was transferred to Samuel after Eli had been rejected, and the kingdom was transferred to David after Saul had been rejected, the coming of a new priesthood and a new kingdom is proclaimed: the old, which was a shadow of what was to come, being rejected in the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0392D]

3. Grial: *panes propositiones* (“the loaves of the Presence”). AREV.]

3. Did not David himself, when he ate the loaves of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except priests, represent in one person both things that were to come—that is, kingdom and priesthood—in the one Jesus Christ? Accordingly, the succession of Samuel the priest prefigured, as was foretold, the new and everlasting priesthood, which is Jesus Christ, Eli the priest having been rejected, that is, the Jewish priesthood having been cast aside.

[Note: [Col. 0392D]

4. “The mother also, up to ‘in my saving God,’” from the same book, *The City of God* XVII.4. GRIAL.]

4. Samuel’s mother also, who was formerly barren and rejoiced in later fertility—and whose name, Anna, is interpreted as “his grace”—signifies the Christian religion itself and, finally, the grace of God itself, because Christ is born for us. She also signifies the Church, which was formerly barren but now rejoices in the praise of God through her fertility.

5. In her song she appears to prophesy nothing other than the transformation of the Old Testament, or of the priesthood, into the New Testament, or into the priesthood that is Christ—unless perhaps someone should say that Anna prophesied nothing, but merely praised God in exultant proclamation because a son had been granted to her.

[Col. 0393A] [Note: [Col. 0393D]

6. “And fertile in sons.” Many manuscripts have “many in sons,” as do Augustine and Eucherius; and the Septuagint has ἡ πολλὴ ἐν τέκνοις, “the many among children.” GRIAL.]

6. What, then, does this mean: “He has made the bow of the mighty weak, and the weak have been girded with strength; those who were full of bread have diminished, and the hungry have crossed the land, because the barren woman has borne seven, and she who was fertile in sons has become weak”? Had she herself borne seven, although she had been barren? She had one son when she said these things. Nor afterward did she bear seven, or six with Samuel as the seventh, but three males and two females.

[Note: [Col. 0393D]

7. “Let him say, and a little later, let him say,” from Augustine. The book is cited incorrectly. GRIAL.]

7. Furthermore, when no one yet reigned in that people, why did she place at the end: “He gives strength to our kings and exalts the horn of his Christ”? How could she say this if she was not prophesying? Let the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in God’s offspring, say what she recognizes as having been prophesied about herself so long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother: “My heart has been established in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my saving God.” Meanwhile Samuel was ministering in the temple of God, girded with an ephod.

[Note: [Col. 0393D]

8. Most manuscripts have “Woe is me”; Val. has “Woe is him”; Bede, “Most wretched.” GRIAL.]

8. Eli’s sons, however, profaning the divine sacrifices, sinned before the Lord, and through them many mocked God’s sacrifice. Therefore Eli the priest was condemned for their iniquity, because he punished them when they sinned with insufficient severity. “Woe is me!” He did indeed restrain them, and he did indeed rebuke them, but with the gentleness and mildness of a father, not with the authority and severity of a high priest.
