9. From this judgment let priests learn how they themselves are punished for the sins of their sons, that is, for the crimes of the people. And although they may be holy, the guilt of their subjects is nevertheless reckoned to them if they do not restrain them.

508 ## CHAPTER II. On the Prophet Sent to Eli

1. A certain prophet of God came to Eli the priest and said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Was I not openly revealed to the house of your father when it was in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him from all the tribes of Israel for myself as a priest, to ascend my altar, burn incense to me, and wear the ephod before me; and I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the children of Israel?

2. “Why have you spurned my victim with your heel, and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honored your sons more than that you should eat the first portions of every sacrifice of my people Israel? Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: I solemnly declared that your house and the house of your father would minister in my presence forever.

3. “But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me will be held in low esteem. Behold, days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there will be no old man in your house, and you will see your rival, Christ, in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel.” This prophecy concerning the change of the priesthood was not fulfilled in Samuel, but only foreshadowed.

[Note: [Col. 0393D]

CHAP. II. No. 4. “For after Samuel,” up to the end of the chapter, is all from Augustine, in the passage cited immediately above. Eucherius contains a complete exposition of the song, citing Augustine and adding an explanation of why he used the translation of the Septuagint interpreters. GRIAL.]

4. For after the prophet Samuel there were priests from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar during David’s reign, and others afterward, before the time came when these things concerning the changing of the sacrifice were to be accomplished through Christ.

5. For when he said: “I solemnly declared that your house and the house of your father would minister in my presence forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Whoever honors me, I will honor; but those who despise me will be held in low esteem,” behold, these are the days that were foretold; they have now come. For there is no priest according to the order of Aaron. And what follows there—“I will raise up for myself a faithful priest”—is spoken of Christ, the priest of the New Testament.

6. But what is added—“And whoever remains in your house will come, that he may be prayed for”—is not properly said of the house of this Eli, but of that of Aaron, from whom people remained until the coming of Jesus Christ. Even to this day there are not lacking people from that line who come and are converted. Another prophet said concerning them: “The remnant shall be saved” (Isaiah X). Hence the Apostle also says: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. IX). For such remnants it is rightly understood that the statement was made: “Whoever remains in your house will come, that he may be prayed for.” Certainly, whoever believes in Christ will come, just as in the time of the apostles very many came from that very people and believed.

7. Nor are there now lacking those who, although very rare, nevertheless believe, so that what this man of God said may be fulfilled in them. But when he immediately adds: “And he will offer a silver coin and a round loaf of bread,” what is signified by the silver coin except the confession of the mouth, which is made by believers for salvation? Silver commonly stands for speech, as the Psalmist testifies where it is sung: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm XI).

[Col. 0394D] 8. But when the one who comes says: “Let me go, I pray, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread,” he calls the priestly portion the body of Christ, that is, the Church. The priest of this people is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. The Apostle Peter says to this people: “A holy people, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter II); in this priestly portion he asks to eat a morsel of bread.

9. In these words the sacrifice of Christians itself is elegantly expressed. Concerning it the priest himself says: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” For this sacrifice is not according to the order of Aaron, but according to the order of Melchizedek.

510 ## CHAPTER III. On the Capture of the Ark

[Note: [Col. 0394D]

CHAP. III. (continued column). No. 1. “For their protection.” Eucherius and Bede have “for their station.” GRIAL.]

1. After these things had been announced to Eli by that prophet as a figure of the change of the Old Testament, Israel having offended the Lord, the Philistines drew up their battle line against them. The Israelites brought out the ark for their protection. The ark was captured by the enemies; and not only were they themselves defeated and put to flight, but a great slaughter of the slain also took place.

2. This event nevertheless signifies something concerning the future. For prophetically, the capture of that ark by foreigners indicated that God’s Testament would pass to the nations. When it was announced to Eli the priest that the ark of the Lord had been captured, he fell from his seat and died. When the ark of the Lord passed to the nations, the Jewish priesthood perished and came to an end; and Eli’s two sons fell, one of whose wives was widowed and soon died in childbirth because of the same disturbance.

3. By this evident sign it was prefigured that, after the Jewish priesthood had been extinguished, the carnal Synagogue, which clung to it carnally, would perish; and that, when Eli had fallen from the seat of the Jewish high priesthood, his seat would remain empty, and the glory of the priesthood and kingdom would be extinguished. But what does it mean that, when the Philistines had placed the ark of the Lord in the temple of Dagon their god, they entered the temple and found their god fallen and broken, his head shattered and both his hands cut off?

4. Immediately, when the Lord’s Testament reached the nations, the idols that had possessed the deceived world were destroyed, and all the error of images perished, unable to endure the presence of God. The severed hands of Dagon signified that the work of idolatry had been cut off, while the severing of his head signified the cutting off of the devil’s pride, from which sin had its beginning.

5. As for the fact that it was found on the threshold, this was so that they might recognize the definite and predetermined end of their idolatry; for a threshold signifies the end of a journey. This too contributes greatly to edification and meaning: in the ruin and destruction of Dagon their god, they found only his back, all his other limbs having been broken. For the back signifies flight; whoever flees gives his back to those pursuing him.

[Note: [Col. 0394D]

6. “This punishment appears to be a sign.” Another reading: “By this punishment it appears to have been signified.” GRIAL.]

6. Hence it is also written concerning the enemies: “You will make them turn their backs” (Psalm XX). Where are the idols? They have perished. And if some remain hidden by certain people, they have fled. But the fact that those who captured the ark were struck in their hinder parts appears to be a sign of this punishment: if some have received the Testament of God but have loved the things behind them, they will justly be tormented by those very things which, as the Apostle says, they ought to regard as dung.

[Note: [Col. 0394D]

7. “The glory of man is like the flower of hay,” from the old translation. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grial’s note mistakenly had “the glory of human beings is like the flower of hay.” In the Vulgate, Isaiah, at the passage cited: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field . . . The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen. But the word of our Lord remains forever.” AREV.]

7. For those who receive the divine Testament in such a way that, looking backward, they do not strip themselves of their former vanity are like those enemies who placed the captured ark of the Testament beside their idols. And those old things fall even against their will, because “all flesh is grass, and the glory of man is like the flower of hay; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen” (Isaiah XL, 6; 1 Peter I). But the ark of the Lord remains forever: namely, the hidden mystery of the Testament, the kingdom of heaven, where the eternal word of God is.

8. Those cows of the Philistines carrying the ark of God signified the flight of the saints who renounce the world and bear no yoke of wrongdoing. For just as those cows did not turn aside from the straight path because of affection for their young, so the saints who renounce the world ought not, under the pretext of family ties, to be hindered from their good purpose.

[Note: [Col. 0395D]

9. *Famularius.* Others have *familiariter* (“familiarly”). AREV.]

9. For just as our soul is not to be hated by us, but we ought to hate its carnal affections, so neither are our neighbors to be hated by us; rather, we should hate the impediments by which they hinder us from the straight path, as Moses also says: “Those who say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not know their own sons—these have kept your Testament and your commands. Your judgments, Jacob, and your law, Israel” (Deut. XXXIII). For the one who desires to know God familiarly is he who, for love of his devotion to God, desires not to know whatever he knew carnally.

512 ## CHAPTER IV. On Samuel’s Sacrifice and the Stone of Help

[Col. 0396C]

1. After Eli’s death, Samuel ruled Israel. When the whole people had been gathered, he cried out to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. While he was offering a burnt offering, the foreigners approached to fight against the people of God; then the Lord thundered over them, and they were thrown into confusion, stumbled before Israel, and were defeated.

2. Samuel then took a stone and placed it between Mizpah and Shiloh; as the Septuagint translators rendered it, between New Mizpah and Old Mizpah. He called its name “Stone of Help” and said: “Up to this point God has helped us.” Mizpah is interpreted as “attention” or “watchfulness.” That stone of help is the Savior’s mediatorship, through which one must pass from Old Mizpah to New Mizpah—that is, from the expectation that was held in the carnal kingdom, where there was a false, carnal blessedness, to the expectation held through the New Testament in the kingdom of heaven, where there is the truest spiritual blessedness. Since nothing is better than this, God helps us up to this point.

3. This Samuel, having invoked the name of the Lord, was heard, and at harvest time obtained rain. For in the holy Scriptures rain means the words of the Gospel or of the Law, as Moses also says: “Let my speech be expected like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. XXXIII). Christ therefore gave this rain to the world at harvest time, that is, when the nations had to be gathered, so that, just as grain is gathered into barns, the nations might be gathered into the bosom of the Church.

## CHAPTER V. On Saul’s Anointing

1. Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life, and until his time there had been judges and leaders over Israel. But Samuel’s sons turned aside after greed, accepted gifts, and became such unjust judges that the people, unable to endure them, asked for a king like the other nations.

513 2. He therefore gave them Saul as king, and, at the Lord’s command, the prophet anointed him first for kingship. In the fact that he was anointed, he himself also bore an image of Christ. Hence the blessed David, who himself was also called “Christ,” said to the man who falsely claimed to have killed Saul: “How were you not afraid to lay your hand upon the Lord’s Christ?”

[Note: [Col. 0397D]

3. CHAP. V. Grial published *regnum adeptus* (“having obtained the kingdom”), which can be defended; but the passive sense, *regnum adeptum* (“the kingdom having been obtained”), is preferable, as in others. AREV.]

3. Hence Saul was taller than everyone from the shoulders upward, because our head is above us, raised on high, and this is Christ. But in the fact that he was afterward rejected and cast aside, with David succeeding to the kingdom, he bore the figure of the people of Israel, as was foretold. This people, which had obtained the kingdom, was destined to lose it, while Christ our Lord would reign through the New Testament, not carnally but spiritually.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Fast Imposed by Saul

1. As Saul was going to fight against the Philistines, he imposed a fast upon the whole army until they returned from battle. But his son Jonathan, seeing honey upon the face of the field, extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into the honeycomb, and tasted it; his eyes were enlightened—not enlightened for seeing, since he had seen before, but for understanding that he had touched something forbidden. For that fall, like Adam’s, made him attentive and rendered him ashamed.

2. By this event we are all admonished that we ought to despise the enticements of pleasures in the world when we strive to serve God. For one cannot contend with spiritual Philistines—that is, against the rulers of darkness—with the strength of the soul if one still refuses to avoid the sweetness of this world. “For the lips of the adulterous woman drip honey,” which is the delight of carnal pleasure. According to mystical interpretations, Jonathan is thought to have tasted this honey and, being discovered by lot, was scarcely freed through the people’s prayers.

514 ## CHAPTER VII. On Agag the King Who Was Spared

1. Saul again entered battle against Amalek. After killing all the enemies, he spared Agag the king and did not wish to destroy everything according to the Lord’s command; and the Lord became angry with him. Samuel came, took a sword, and cut Agag into pieces. When some read in the Scriptures that the saints spare none of their enemies, they become cruel and thirsty for human blood, saying that the righteous struck their enemies in such a way that none was left alive by them. They do not understand that mysteries are foreshadowed in these words, and that this is rather indicated to us: when we fight against vices, we must leave none of them at all, but destroy them all.

2. For if we spare them, it will be counted as guilt against us, just as it was counted against Saul, who kept King Agag alive. How will anyone remain righteous if he still preserves some sin in himself, as Saul did? But the saints, represented by Samuel, rage against their enemies—that is, against the vices of sinners—in such a way that they do not allow any sin to remain unpunished.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saul’s Seizure by an Evil Spirit

[Note: [Col. 0397D]

CHAP. VIII. No. 1. “The spirit of the Lord was upon him,” etc. Others have: “An evil spirit from the Lord was upon him, and it tormented him.” Here the question is rightly raised: If it is the spirit of the Lord, why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it of the Lord? Grial published “and in the devil an unjust power,” apparently mistakenly. AREV.]

1. When the Lord departed from Saul because of his disobedience, he was seized by an evil spirit from the Lord, and an evil spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. If it is of the Lord, why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it of the Lord? But this statement contains the whole matter in two phrases: in God there is just power, and in the devil there is unjust will.

[Note: [Col. 0398D]

2. Grial: “or for correction”; others: “or toward correction.” AREV.]

2. For the same spirit is evil by its most wicked will, and is the spirit of the Lord by the most just power it has received. Therefore the devil is called the spirit of the Lord because of his ministry, since God makes good use even of evil spirits, either for the condemnation of some, or for correction, or for testing.

[Note: [Col. 0398D]

3. Others have: “A sleep from the Lord had seized them,” omitting *qui* (“which”). AREV.]

3. Although wickedness is not from the Lord, power nevertheless comes from no one except God, as it is also said elsewhere. There was likewise “a sleep from the Lord” which had seized Saul’s soldiers when David took the spear and cup from beside the sleeping man’s head—not because sleep was then in the Lord, so that he himself was sleeping, but because the sleep that had then seized the men had been infused by God’s command, so that David, his servant, would not be perceived as present in that place.

4. Thus the evil spirit of the Lord is spoken of as God’s minister for doing in Saul what the all-powerful Judge judged that he ought to suffer. For the spirit was not God’s in the will by which it was evil; but the creature, insofar as it had been created, and the power which it had received not from itself but from the equity of the Lord of all, belonged to God.

## CHAPTER IX. On David’s Anointing
1. Therefore, when Saul had been rejected because of his disobedience, the Lord sent Samuel to Jesse; and, taking a horn of oil, he anointed David as king. But let us see how this same David prophetically signified Christ. For David means “strong of hand,” or “desirable.” And what is stronger than that lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquered the world? And what is more desirable than the one of whom it is said: “The Desired One of all the nations will come” (Hag. II)?

[Note: [Col. 0398D]

CAP. IX, Note 2. “With chrism.” Grialius printed *charismate*, which I think is an error. AREV.]

2. This David is anointed king, announcing through that anointing the Christ who was to come; for Christ is named from *chrism*. David is transferred from the pastoral office over cattle to the rule of human beings. Now David himself, Jesus, has been taken away from the sheep of the Jewish people and transferred to rule over the nations; for Christ is no longer in the Jewish people—he has been taken away from there—and now he feeds the flocks of the nations.

[Note: [Col. 0399D]

3. “For of various [sounds], etc.” Others: “For the rational and measured harmonies of various sounds we call a concordant variety, joined together and ordered, which signifies the unity of the Church.” AREV.]

3. David was also trained in musical songs. For the rational and measured harmony of various sounds signifies the unity of the Church, joined together in concordant variety and ordered arrangement. She resounds daily in diverse modes and modulates with mystical sweetness.

4. While still a boy, this David, singing sweetly—or rather, powerfully—on the lyre, restrained the evil spirit that was at work in Saul. This was not because the lyre itself possessed such great power, but because the figure of Christ’s cross, mystically represented by the wood and the stretching of the strings, and the very passion that was being sung, were already then crushing the spirit of the demon. David also killed a lion and a bear: the bear signifying the devil, and the lion Antichrist—the one lying secretly in wait for human beings, the other raging most openly in the future.

## CHAPTER X. David’s Contest with Goliath

[Col. 0399C]

1. This David overcame a giant in battle, when foreigners were fighting against the people of God. One challenged one: Goliath challenged David; pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ. Saint David took military arms in order to advance against Goliath. Because of his age and the small stature of his body, he could not carry these weapons; he threw off what weighed him down, took five stones from the river, and placed them in a shepherd’s pouch.

[Note: [Col. 0399D]

CAP. X, Note 2. “Which we do not observe.” Others add: “For how many things in the old law are both lawful and yet not observed by us?” Others: “Because in the old law we both read and do not observe.” These words may have been omitted by scribes through repetition of the word “observe.” Shortly afterward, perhaps one should read, “the river flowed over them.” In some copies, *fluvium* is read. AREV.]

2. Armed with these, he advanced and conquered. This, indeed, was that David. But if we examine the mysteries, Christ is understood in David. Foreseeing the time when the revelation of the New Testament and the commendation of grace would be made known, he laid down the weapons and took five stones. He therefore laid down the bodily sacraments of the law, which were not imposed upon the nations; he laid down those things that we do not observe, although we understand that they were introduced and established for some symbolic meaning.

3. Finally, he laid down these weapons as burdens of the sacraments of the old law and took up the law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He therefore took those five stones from the river—that is, from the world. For the mortal world flows and passes away; everything that comes into the world flows past. The stones were in the river, as it were, in that first people: they were there useless and idle, producing no benefit; they passed over the rivers. But what did David do so that the law itself might become useful? He received grace. For the law cannot be fulfilled without grace: “For love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII; Eph. IV).

[Note: [Col. 0400D]

4. Others: “does not seek to receive,” which is perhaps better. And shortly afterward, “in the pouch.” AREV.]

4. Therefore, since grace causes the law to be fulfilled, grace is signified by milk. For this is something freely given in the flesh, where the mother does not seek to receive but eagerly strives to give; the mother gives this freely and is saddened if there is no one to receive it. How, then, does David show that the law cannot operate without grace, except when he placed those five stones, which signified the law, in the five books that he wished to join to grace, in the shepherd’s pouch in which he was accustomed to milk?

5. Armed with these, he advanced against proud Goliath, who boasted and trusted in himself. He took one stone and struck down the devil; he struck him in the forehead, and he fell from that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ. You may also observe this: he placed five stones, but sent one.

6. Five books have been read, but unity conquered; for, as the Apostle says, love is the fullness of the law: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” Then, after striking and casting him down, he took away his sword and afterward cut off his head.

7. Our David does this as well. He casts down the devil from his own people when his wicked followers, whom he held in his hand and by whom he slaughtered other souls, believe, turn their tongues against the devil, and thus Goliath’s head is cut off with his own sword.

## CHAPTER XI. David’s Marriage to Saul’s Daughter Michal

1. Meanwhile, David’s victory offended the spirit of King Saul, who was indignant that public acclamations of congratulation resounded with the cry that Saul had slain his thousand, but David his ten thousand. Hence came Saul’s envy and the seed of hatred against David. Craftily concealing his purpose, so that he might expose David to danger without his own ambushes, Saul decided to bind him to a marriage with his daughter Michal, if David would bring him one hundred foreskins of the Philistines as a victor.

2. Instead of one hundred, he gave two hundred; and from the very source by which he was thought likely to perish because of the royal demand, he gained a more glorious trophy. So also the Jews, while striving against the will of God to kill Christ, brought about the salvation of the nations through the very means by which they believed they would destroy him. But the fact that David brought the foreskins of foreigners and thereafter became joined in marriage to Saul’s daughter signified that Christ would not first promise himself in marriage to the Synagogue until he had previously become glorious among the nations.

3. For first he cut away the pollution of the flesh among the nations, and afterward he was joined to the Synagogue. “For after the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI). He brought double, that is, two hundred foreskins, either on account of the Jews and the nations acquired, or because the number of the people acquired from the nations is greater than that of the Jews who believe.

## CHAPTER XII. David Driving Away the Spirit with the Lyre

1. Saul’s hatred of David then increased so greatly that the king attempted to pin David, who was playing the psaltery as usual to heal his spirit, with a spear. But what does it mean that, while an adverse spirit was invading Saul, David’s lyre mitigated his madness when David took it up?

[Col. 0401B]

2. Saul signifies the arrogance of the Jews, while David signifies the humility of Christ. Therefore, when Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David sings, because when the understanding of the Jews is turned to frenzy through blasphemy, it is fitting that their minds should be recalled to salvation, as though by the sweetness of a lyre, through the tranquility of evangelical speech.

## CHAPTER XIII. Saul’s Plots against David

1. Saul sent guards to David’s house to watch him and kill him. David departed by night, fled, and was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, they found a statue placed in David’s bed and a hairy goatskin at its head. Let us therefore hear what this means: Saul sent to guard David’s house in order to kill him. This does not refer to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless it pertains to his passion.

2. For Christ was crucified, died, and was buried. That burial was therefore like a house, to guard which the kingdom of the Jews sent guards when guards were stationed at Christ’s tomb. How, then, was the house guarded, if David represented Christ, so that Christ might be killed, when Christ was killed not in the burial but on the cross?

3. This is therefore referred to the body of Christ, because to kill Christ meant to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards had prevailed—those who were bribed to say, “While we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. XXVIII). This, then, is what it means to wish to kill Christ: to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that the lie might be preferred to the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0401D]

CAP. XIII, Note 4. “Thus this too could not,” through “might erase.” Others: “Thus these men too did not prevail to erase the memory of Christ.” AREV.]

4. But just as Saul was unable to kill David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not accomplish this either: it could not erase the memory of Christ. Those, however, who wished to presume against Christ on the strength of Saul—that is, on the strength of the kingdom of the Jews—stumbled against the stone of stumbling, as against a statue; and the kid appeared to them to be a lamb, because they persecuted as a sinner the one in whom they found no sin.

[Col. 0402A]

5. Therefore David, avoiding the blow of the royal hand and evading Saul’s persecution, fled and came to Samuel. Saul sent messengers to seize David. Samuel was among the prophets, and there was a gathering of prophets who were prophesying at that time.

6. The messengers who were sent, after receiving the same spirit, prophesied; when others were sent, the same thing happened, and likewise with a third group. But afterward, when Saul himself had come, the Spirit of God came upon him, and he walked along entering the place and prophesied.

[Col. 0402D] 520

## CHAPTER XIV. The Plotters Prophesying

1. The question arises how those men, when they had been sent to seize a man and lead him to death, deserved to be made such by the spirit; and how Saul himself, who had sent them, when he came seeking to shed innocent blood, also deserved to receive that spirit and prophesy.

2. As far as the literal sense is concerned, it is not surprising that a rejected man prophesied briefly and temporarily, since many similar men are also recorded to have possessed the gift of prophecy (II Pet. II), such as that rejected Balaam, whom Scripture does not fail to say was condemned by divine judgment, yet who possessed prophecy.

3. Those words written in the Gospel also bear strong witness to this view: many will say on that day, “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank, and in your name we prophesied, and in your name performed many mighty works.” Yet he will say to them: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII).

4. Mystically, however, the example of this Saul and his messengers in this passage represents certain heretics who possess something good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as the Testaments of the law and the Gospel, and the sacrament of baptism. When they come to the Catholic Church, what they possess must not in any way be violated or handed over as though they did not possess it. Nevertheless, they must not for that reason trust in salvation, because we do not reject what we believe they have received.

5. Rather, they must recognize unity and the fellowship of the bond of love. Without these, whatever they may have been able to possess—even if it is holy and worthy of reverence—they themselves are nothing. They have become all the less worthy of the reward of eternal life because they have not used well the gifts that they received in this life, which is passing away.

6. Likewise, the example and image of this Saul and his messengers fittingly represents the Jews in this passage. While they desire to oppose Christ, they have the sacraments of the law and the prophets in their mouths as testimony to Christ, and they dispute from the Scriptures with the Church, as though with prophets, just as those men prophesied with the prophets.

## CHAPTER XV. David and Abimelech

[Col. 0403A]

[Note: [Col. 0403D]

CAP. XV, Note 1. “Then David arose.” Grialius, as I think incorrectly, printed “then he arose and David.” AREV.]

1. David therefore arose again and fled that day from Saul’s presence. He came to the priest Abimelech, from whom he took Goliath’s sword and received the bread of the Presence. This event brought death upon the priest and punishment upon the religious city. This, then, is the historical account of what happened.

[Note: [Col. 0403D]

2. “He passed over.” Grialius: “he passes over.” AREV.]

2. But as far as the prophetic mystery is concerned, it was fulfilled in Christ our Lord. When he was placed in the flesh and avoided Jewish persecution, he passed over to the apostles, with whom he also took the food he desired; for he earnestly desired to eat the Passover.

3. From them he took Goliath’s weapons, that is, the weapons of the devil. For he himself plundered the spoils of the strong one. Therefore the devil brought tribulations and death upon those by whom Christ was received. For, as the Apostle says, “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III). And the Lord says: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV).

[Note: [Col. 0403D]

4. It is well known that *diabolus* is often written *zabulus* in manuscripts. AREV.]

4. In Doeg the Edomite, however, the person of the betraying Judas is represented. Through him the devil accomplished these things, so that, after his betrayal had been carried out against Christ, the Church afterward suffered persecution, very many disciples of Christ were killed, and priests endured the gravest persecutions for his name.

## CHAPTER XVI. David and King Achish

1. Meanwhile, while fleeing from Saul, David wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when David’s glory had been proclaimed, he feared that the king to whom he had fled might, through envy, contrive something against him. He therefore pretended madness and, as though seized by frenzy, changed his mouth. His saliva ran down upon his beard; he collapsed in their hands and fell before the doors of the gate.

2. King Achish said: “Why have you brought this man to me? Are there not enough madmen among us?” And so he dismissed him. Achish means “How is it?”—a phrase signifying ignorance, the speech of one who marvels and does not recognize. This was fulfilled among the Jewish people: when they saw Christ, they did not recognize him; before them he changed his mouth and departed. For there were there the carnal precepts of the law; there was a sacrifice according to the order of Aaron; and afterward he himself established a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek.

[Note: [Col. 0403D]

CAP. XVI, Note 3. “He changed his countenance in the priesthood.” In the sacrifice, Pal. GRIAL.

Ibid. “And he fell.” Certain material is inserted before these words in Val. and Compl.; since it is absent from all the other books, as well as from Eucherius and Bede, and does not fit with what precedes or follows, it should not be admitted. GRIAL.

Ibid. “In the priesthood.” I have restored this reading, although Grialius printed *in the sacrifice* in the text; in the note he appears to prefer *in the priesthood*. After “they crucified,” some manuscripts add: “The Lord admonishes and says: ‘Do not touch my anointed ones.’ Thus kings in the people of Israel are called *christs*. For this was the name used for kings, beginning with Saul, whom David succeeded in the kingdom; thereafter the other kings of Israel were anointed through the continuation of the consecrated custom. In that anointing the one true Christ was represented, to whom it was said: ‘The Lord your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.’” For “he fell before the door,” some manuscript copies read “he fell before the doors.” AREV.]

3. Therefore he changed his mouth in the priesthood; he changed it in the commandments, giving another Testament after the carnal observance had been annulled. Then he collapsed in their hands when they seized him and crucified him. And he fell before the door of the gate—that is, he humbled himself. For this is to fall as far as the door of our faith: the door is the beginning of faith, the door of the gate. From there the Church begins and advances to vision, so that, when she believes what she does not see, she may deserve to enjoy it when she begins to see him face to face.

[Note: [Col. 0404D]

4. “The Apostle makes this clear.” Others: “The Apostle made this clear.” AREV.]

4. But the fact that, in that seeming madness, saliva ran down over his beard, the Apostle makes clear by saying: “The Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the nations foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak of God is stronger than human beings.”

[Note: [Col. 0404D]

5. “Let them not pay attention only to the saliva.” From Eucherius and others: “Do not be offended as though by saliva.” Compl.: “Do not regard it as saliva.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Not only the saliva,” etc. Others: “For saliva signifies foolishness; saliva signifies weakness. But what is foolish of God is stronger than human beings. Do not regard it as saliva” (others: “do not be offended by the saliva”), “but observe that it runs down beneath the beard.” After “was covered,” others add: “For what is worse than the wickedest king Saul, who even sinned against God through disobedience? The evil spirit of the Lord also rushed upon him.” AREV.]

5. Do not pay attention only to the saliva; observe rather that it runs down over the beard. For just as weakness is shown in the saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore covered his strength with the body of his weakness; what was outwardly weak appeared as saliva, while inwardly divine power was concealed as though by a beard.

## CHAPTER XVII. David Cutting Saul’s Cloak

[Col. 0404C]

1. Afterward, in the wilderness of Engedi, when Saul sought to pursue David, David entered a cave and hid there. But the king, unexpectedly caught by the ambush, fell into what he had been plotting against an innocent man. For it is written: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will himself fall into it” (Prov. XXVI). David, however, returning good for evil, did not kill his enemy, but took away a piece of the royal cloak as testimony to what had happened, although it would have been easier to destroy an adversary caught in an ambush than to deceive him.

2. What, then, does it mean that this man, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid in a cave? Why did he hide except to be concealed and not found? What is it to be covered by a cave except to be covered by earth? For whoever flees into a cave is covered by earth so that he may not be seen. Jesus was carrying earth—the flesh that he had received from the earth—and was hiding himself in it, so that God might not be found by the Jews. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II).

[Note: [Col. 0405D]

CAP. XVII, Note 3. “Nor could he die,” etc. Others: “Nor could he die except in a human being; nor could he be crucified except in a human being. He opposed,” etc. AREV.]

3. Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had covered himself in a cave—that is, he exposed the weakness of his flesh to their eyes and concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as in the recess of a cave. Therefore, not recognizing God, they persecuted the man. He could not die except in a human being, because he could not be seized except in a human being. Thus he set earth before those who sought him evilly, but preserved life for those who sought him well.

4. He therefore fled according to the flesh into a cave from Saul’s presence, because he suffered, concealing himself to such an extent from the Jews that he died. But why did he wish to be patient even unto death, so that he might flee from Saul’s presence into a cave? For a cave may be understood as the lower part of the earth. And certainly—something manifest and known to everyone—his body was placed in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock. This tomb, therefore, was a cave; there our David fled from Saul’s presence.

5. For the Jews pursued him until he was placed in the cave. But what does it mean that the persecutor entered the cave to relieve himself, except that the Jews emitted, as a foul odor, the malice conceived in their minds against Christ, and displayed through worse deeds the harmful thoughts they had entertained when they killed Christ?

6. Nevertheless, David did not wish to kill Saul. Although he held him in his power while Saul was hidden in a secret cavern, David preferred to spare rather than kill him. So also Christ, while he was in the cave of the flesh, held the persecuting people in his power but did not kill them. For it had been written concerning them through the prophet: “Do not kill them.” Finally, David silently cut off only the upper edge of Saul’s cloak, to show prophetically that Christ did not kill the Jews but merely took away from them the glory of the kingdom, thus leaving them, through their own persecution, bereft of seat or rule.

[Note: [Col. 0405D]

7. In this passage Grialius printed *dirupit*, and in the following note *disrupit*. AREV.]

7. For the cutting of the cloak signifies the severing of the kingdom. Saul himself also showed this elsewhere when he sinned through disobedience. For when he begged pardon and asked Samuel to return with him to appease God, and Samuel refused and turned his face away and departed, Saul seized the edge of his garment and tore it.

[Note: [Col. 0405D]

8. The Vulgate, chapter XV, 28, Book I of Kings: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.” AREV.]

8. Samuel said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today, and he will give it to your neighbor, and Israel will be divided in two.” Therefore this king figuratively bore the person of the people of Israel, the people that was to lose the kingdom while persecuting Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII. David Taking Saul’s Spear

[Note: [Col. 0406D]

CAP. XVIII, Note 1. “He entered,” etc. Others: “He entered the king’s camp; when he found him sleeping, he did not strike him or kill him.” In place of “the top,” *summit* would be better. AREV.]

1. This was demonstrated again afterward, when the same David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, entered the king’s camp. When he found Saul sleeping, he did not strike or kill him, but took only the spear that was at his head and the water jar. Then, while everyone was asleep, he left the camp and crossed over to the summit of the mountain.

2. What does this mean? The Jews were pursuing Christ, but in pursuing him they were sleeping, because they were not watchful in heart. Hardness of heart is a kind of sleep. They sleep in the old life and do not awaken to the new.

3. Christ came; he did not kill them, but took away from them the cup of water—that is, the grace of the law. He also took away the royal scepter, namely, the power of the kingdom, which they regarded as their greatest possession and by which they protected themselves temporarily, and which through unbelief they wielded against God. Then our victorious David, returning from their camp, rose into the height of the heavenly mountain.

## CHAPTER XIX. David’s Battle with the Amalekites

1. Meanwhile, as David was fleeing and traveling with Achish, king of the Philistines, into battle against Israel, the Amalekites rose up and attacked Ziklag. They burned it and took captive everything belonging to David and his servants. David therefore returned to pursue the Amalekites and found an Egyptian servant who was exhausted. The Amalekites had abandoned him sick along the way.

2. When David found him, he restored him with food and made him the guide of his journey. Thus he pursued the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them. What else does the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites becoming exhausted on the journey signify except that the lover of the present world, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left behind by that same world, weak and despised, so that he is entirely unable to run with it but, broken by adversity, grows numb?

3. But David found him because our Redeemer, truly “strong of hand,” sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by the world’s glory. He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with knowledge of the word. He made him the guide of his journey because he also makes him his preacher.

4. The one who could not follow the Amalekite becomes David’s guide, because the man whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives God when he is converted in his mind, but also, by preaching, brings him into the hearts of others. With this man as guide, David finds the Amalekite feasting and destroys him, because Christ, through the preaching of those whom the world disdained to have as companions, destroys the world’s pleasures.

## CHAPTER XX. Saul Consulting the Witch

[Col. 0407A]

[Note: [Col. 0407C]

CAP. XX, Note 1. “Whether some…” Others: “Whether it was produced by some imaginary deception through the deceit of demons.” AREV.]

1. After Samuel’s death, the Philistines gathered against Israel. Saul consulted the Lord, but he did not answer him. Saul then sought a witch who would raise Samuel for him. Immediately, when he had been raised, he said to Saul: “Why have you disturbed me so that I should be raised?” The historical question is therefore whether the witch herself called the prophet from the underworld, or whether it was some imaginary illusion produced by demonic deceit.

[Note: [Col. 0407D]

2. Augustine to Simplicianus, Book II, Question 3, and to Dulcitius, Question 6. GRIAL.

Ibid. “An evil spirit.” “An unclean spirit.” Augustine and Eucherius, although *evil* is used later in the same passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. “By barriers or…” These words are not found in Augustine or Eucherius. GRIAL.]

2. On this question, the blessed Bishop Augustine of revered memory wrote as follows to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan: “You inquire, I say, whether an evil spirit could raise the soul of a righteous person and, as it were, call it forth from the hidden barriers or receptacles of the dead, so that it might appear and speak with Saul.”

[Col. 0407B] 527

[Note: [Col. 0407D]

3. “For in whatever manner he did this, it happened; likewise, the manner in which Samuel was made to be raised remains hidden.” This passage must be read in this way even in Augustine, where it is defective: the Greek expression *τὸ factum est* (“it happened”), which occurred only once but in different places in the two authors, should be repeated in both, so that each text supplies what is lacking in the other. GRIAL.

Ibid. “He may have done,” etc. Others: “he may have done it. It happened that he was raised.” Others: “However he may have done it, it happened, so that Samuel was raised,” which is less satisfactory. In the note, Grialius appears to have intended: “However he may have done this, it happened.” In the text he omitted “this he did,” which certainly is not necessary. AREV.]

3. Is it not more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and set him on the pinnacle of the temple? However he may have done this, it happened. Likewise, the manner in which Samuel was made to be raised also remains hidden, unless someone should say that the devil had an easier permission to take the living Lord wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling place.

[Note: [Col. 0408D]

4. “Does not disturb.” “Does not trouble,” in Augustine and Eucherius. GRIAL.]

4. If the Gospel account does not disturb us because the Lord willed and permitted it, without any diminution of his power or divinity, just as he allowed himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves—although they were perverse and unclean, and were carrying out the works of the devil—it is not unreasonable to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy prophet should show itself to the king’s eyes, not unwillingly or under the domination of magical power, but willingly and in obedience to God’s hidden dispensation, which was unknown to that witch and to Saul; and that the spirit would strike him with the divine sentence.

5. Nevertheless, this event may admit of another, easier interpretation: we may believe that it was not truly Samuel’s spirit, raised from its rest, but some phantom or imaginary illusion produced by demonic contrivances. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel because representations are customarily called by the names of the things whose representations they are. Thus everything that is painted or fashioned is called by the names of the things whose images they are. When a picture of a person is painted, each picture is unhesitatingly given the person’s own name, and one says: “That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,” although they are nothing other than painted images.

[Note: [Col. 0408D]

6. “Those representations also.” Thus in Augustine, in the Questions to Dulcitius. “Those likenesses also,” in the same author’s book to Simplicianus. GRIAL.]

6. Thus also the cherubim, although they are heavenly powers, were fashioned from metal at God’s command over the Ark of the Testament to signify a great reality; nevertheless, those fashioned images too were called “cherubim.” Likewise, when someone sees a dream, he does not say, “I saw an image of Augustine,” but, “I saw Augustine,” even though, at the time when someone saw such a thing, Augustine himself might not know of it.

[Note: [Col. 0408D]

7. “He transforms himself into an angel.” Thus Augustine to Simplicianus. “He transforms himself as an angel,” to Dulcitius. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius printed *in somnis* (“in a dream”) instead of *in somniis* (“in dreams”), and *as an angel*, although in the note he appears to prefer *into an angel*. AREV.]

7. It is therefore perfectly clear that it is not the people themselves who are seen, but their images. Pharaoh also said that he had seen ears of grain in dreams, and cattle—not images of ears of grain or cattle. If it is therefore plainly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the fabricated contrivance of the one who transforms himself into an angel of light and adorns his ministers as ministers of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0408D]

8. “Even through the lowest and underworld spirits, some truth…” In both places, Augustine. “Through weak and higher spirits,” in Eucherius. GRIAL.

Ibid. Others, in Augustine: “weak and underworld spirits.” Others: “lowest and infernal spirits.” AREV.

Ibid. In place of “of mysteries,” the better manuscripts of Augustine have “of ministries,” so that *ministries* may be understood as referring to ministers. AREV.]

8. “Now,” he says, “if it troubles us how true predictions were made to Saul by an evil spirit, it may also seem astonishing how demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize. When God wills that someone should learn certain truths even through the lowest and highest spirits—truths pertaining only to temporal matters and to this mortal life—it is easy and not unfitting that the omnipotent and just God, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold (so that they may suffer in advance through foreknowledge of the evil that threatens them), should, by the hidden arrangement of his mysteries, grant even such spirits some power of divination, and that they should announce to human beings what they hear from the angels.”

9. They hear only as much as the Lord and ruler of all either commands or permits. Thus the spirit of divination in the Acts of the Apostles also bore witness to the Apostle Paul and attempted to act as an evangelist (Acts XVI, 16). Yet these spirits mingle deceptions with their statements, and they pronounce the truth they have been able to know not so much with the purpose of teaching as of deceiving. Perhaps this is why, when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with Samuel—which is certainly false.

[Col. 0409A]

10. For we read in the Gospel that the good are separated from the wicked by a great interval after death, when it testifies that a great chasm had been placed between that proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the one who had lain ulcerated at his gate and was already established in rest (Luke XVI, 26).

[Note: [Col. 0409B]

11. “By more hidden mysteries.” Thus Augustine to Dulcitius; “by commands,” in the letter to Simplicianus; and likewise in Eucherius. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius distinguished the clauses: “he foretold.” According to both readings, therefore, the distinction can be retained if one reads: “Or for this reason, therefore,” etc. In Saint Augustine, *therefore* is absent after “according to both,” and the sense is thus clearer. AREV.]

11. Or if Samuel said to him, “You will be with me,” so that this referred not to equality of blessedness but to a comparable condition of death—that both were human beings, and both could die, and that the dead man foretold death to the living—then, according to either interpretation, I think your prudence sees that this passage has an interpretation that is not contrary to the faith. Unless, perhaps, through deeper investigation it may be discovered conclusively whether a human soul, after departing from this life, can or cannot be summoned by magical incantations and appear to the sight of the living, even bearing the features of a body, so that it might not only be seen but recognized. And if this is possible, whether even the soul of a righteous person might not indeed be compelled by magical rites but might deign to appear in obedience to the hidden mysteries of the supreme law—if it should become clear that this cannot happen, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the exposition of this passage; rather, once that possibility has been excluded, the imaginary likeness of Samuel produced by a demonic rite should be understood.

[Col. 0410A] [Note: [Col. 0409C]

12. “These are the things he wrote then about the witch.” But see what he later adds in writing to Dulcitius at the end of the question. GRIAL.]

12. But since, whether this can happen or cannot happen, the devil’s deceit and his clever activity in fabricating images are nevertheless watchful in many ways to deceive human senses, let us proceed cautiously. We should not prejudge more careful investigations; nevertheless, until we are given the opportunity to think out and explain something further, let us rather suppose that something of this kind was done through the agency of the evil spirit of that witch. These are the things that the most blessed Augustine then wrote about the witch and Samuel.

[Col. 0409C]

## CHAPTER XXI. The Death of Saul and Jonathan
## CHAPTER XXI

### Note on Chapter XXI, no. 1

“Who, when they were powerful.” In the Val. manuscript there are read, among these passages, many words of Gregory from Book IV of the *Moralia*, chapter 4, concerning the cursing of the mountains—words that are rightly absent from the other books and from Bede, for they plainly do not cohere. GRIAL.

**The same passage, “He mourns.”** The Florence quarto manuscript and others add the following, which Grialius wished omitted:

“For what is the meaning of David himself, who did not repay those who returned evil with evil, cursing the mountains of Gilboa when Saul and Jonathan fell in battle and saying: ‘Mountains of Gilboa, may neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor be fields of firstfruits, for there the shield of Saul was cast down, as though he had not been anointed with oil’? What, then, did the mountains of Gilboa do wrong when Saul was dying, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them, and the word of the sentence should dry them up, depriving them of every shoot of greenness? But because *Gilboa* is interpreted as ‘a descent,’ and through Saul, the anointed and dead man, the death of our Mediator is expressed, the proud hearts of the Jews are not improperly signified by the mountains of Gilboa. While these hearts flow downward in the desires of this world, at Christ’s fall—that is, through his death—they all withered. And because the anointed king dies bodily among them, they themselves are dried up from every dew of grace. Of these it is also rightly said: ‘Nor be fields of firstfruits.’ For they cannot be firstfruits, because the pride of the Hebrews . . . does not bear firstfruits; for, remaining for the most part in unbelief at the Redeemer’s coming, they did not wish to follow the beginnings of faith. The holy Church, made fruitful by the multitude of the nations as its firstfruits, scarcely receives at the end of the world those Jews whom it finds, and, gathering the last, places them as the remnants of the harvest. Of these remnants Isaiah says: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved.’ Then again the same prophet mourns Saul and Jonathan, saying: ‘How have the mighty fallen in the midst of battle?’ Although they were mighty and always prevailed over their enemies, once wounded and struck down they fell in the midst of the battle. In this same way the devout Christian race also mourns, etc.”

Instead of “that is, all,” one should perhaps read “that is, defeated,” since “all” is obscure. In the manuscript, between *Hebraeorum* and *primitivos*, there seems to be written *mente*; perhaps, therefore, one should read: “the proud mind of the Hebrews.” These and similar fragments, which occur in certain manuscripts and are sometimes copied and sometimes omitted by Grialius, are not certainly known to be Isidore’s; nor can it be demonstrated that they are not his, since they do not differ from Isidore’s style. AREV.]

1. When battle had broken out, the Philistines struck Israel with a great slaughter, and Saul and Jonathan fell in the battle. The devout prophet mourns them figuratively. Although they were mighty and always prevailed over their enemies, once wounded and struck down they fell in the midst of the battle.

2. “How,” he says, “have the mighty fallen in the midst of battle?” In this same way the devout Christian race mourns those who, not resisting demons, slip in the world, which is slippery; for *Gilboa* is interpreted as “slippery mountains.”

## IN THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS

[Col. 0409]

# 531 CHAPTER I  
## That David Should Not Build the Temple

[Col. 0409D]

### Note on Chapter I, no. 1

The whole chapter is from Gregory, *Moralia*, Book VII, chapter 16. GRIAL.]

1. After Saul’s death David is anointed and reigns; he transfers the Ark of the Covenant to his own city. When he wished to build a temple for the Lord, he was admonished by the Lord through the prophet as follows: “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of bloodshed.”

2. What, then, is the meaning of the fact that David, laboring amid external wars, is forbidden to build God’s house? We are the temple of God, built for true life through his indwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. III).

### Note on Chapter I, no. 3

“Who still lies upon carnal actions.” Thus in the other book. Gregory has *incumbit*, “lies upon.” GRIAL.]

3. A man of bloodshed is forbidden to build a temple for God because whoever still lies upon carnal actions must not presume to instruct the Church spiritually. For an eye burdened by dust can in no way regard a blemish purely in a member, and a hand holding mud cannot wipe away the dirt that has been thrown upon it.

# CHAPTER II  
## David’s Sin with Bathsheba

### Note on Chapter II, no. 1

The whole chapter is from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XXII, chapter 87. GRIAL.]

1. Let us now touch briefly, as far as we can, upon what David’s sin signified prophetically. For the interpreted names sufficiently show what this deed also prefigured. David, as we have said, is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” Bathsheba is interpreted as “well of satiety” or “seventh well.”

### Note on Chapter II, no. 2

“Perhaps, which is the Church there.” AREV.]

2. Whichever of these interpretations of her name we adopt for what we intend to say, it fits well enough. For in the *Song of Songs* the bride, who is the Church, is called “a well of living water” (Song IV). To this well the name of the number seven is joined in the signification of the Holy Spirit, because of the reckoning of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven, came.

### Note on Chapter II, no. 3

“Others: ‘whom whoever drinks.’” Grialius has: “whom whoever possesses.” AREV.]

3. To forty-nine, which is seven times seven, one is added, by which unity is commended. In this reckoning lives that apostolic saying: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV). Thus, through the spiritual gift—that is, the gift of seven—the Church became a well of satiety, because in it there was made “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life,” and “whoever drinks of it shall not thirst forever” (John IV).

### Note on Chapter II, no. 4

“Others: ‘Now whoever has been.’ That Uriah allegorically indicated the devil was also stated in the *Allegories*, no. 90.” AREV.]

4. But Uriah, who was her husband, what else does he signify by the interpretation of his name except the devil? All those whom God’s grace liberates had been bound to him in a most wicked marriage, so that the Church might be joined to her own Savior without spot or wrinkle.

### Note on Chapter II, no. 5

“My light is God.” Others: “light of the world.” AREV.]

5. For *Uriah* is interpreted as “my light is God,” while *Hittite* means “cut off,” either because he did not stand in the truth but, through the merit of pride, was cut off from the heavenly light he had from God, or because, having fallen and lost his true powers, he transforms himself into an angel of light, still daring to say: “My light is God.” Thus this David indeed sinned gravely and wickedly; God also rebuked his crime through the prophet, and he himself washed it away through repentance.

6. Nevertheless, that desirable one for all nations, as though walking on a balcony—for he set his tabernacle in the sun—loved the Church, washing herself upon the roof; that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world, transcending and trampling upon the earthly house through spiritual contemplation.

### Note on Chapter II, no. 7

“David himself.” Others: “that David.” The latter seems better. AREV.]

7. Having begun with her the knowledge of their first union, he later killed the devil, who had been wholly separated from him, and joined her to himself in an everlasting marriage. Let us therefore hate sin, but let us not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love David himself as much as he is to be loved—the one who in mercy freed us from the devil.

8. Let us love this David, who healed in himself so grave a wound of iniquity through repentance and the confession of his humanity. But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is he said to have had many wives and concubines, since Christ both abhors and condemns such things? This happened for the sake of the figure; for David’s many wives signified the image of the many peoples and nations that would be joined through faith to the fellowship of Christ.

9. His concubines signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name. But because they follow Christ for carnal profits, they are called not wives but concubines. Accordingly, if kings now have several wives and concubines, it is a crime, because the figures for which permission was granted concerning wives or concubines have now passed away; and now, because the figures have passed away, no permission is granted.

# CHAPTER III  
## Absalom

### Note on Chapter III, no. 1

“Parricidal son . . . pursuing,” instead of “parricidal son . . . pursuing him,” namely, the nominative used for the ablative, as often elsewhere. AREV.

**The same passage, “who was looking upon the kingdom.”** Others: “because he knew him to be wicked.” AREV.]

1. What, indeed, does it signify that the parricidal son Absalom pursued his father, while at first his father withdrew and fled before him, confident of victory? He saw the kingdom perish; he even mourned him with great grief and lamented the parricide’s end. It is also written that David fled from the face of his son who was waging war against him.

2. Since it is written concerning the people of Jerusalem: “I have nourished and brought up children, but they have despised me” (Isa. I), his wicked son therefore figuratively signifies the Jewish people, who betrayed him. Absalom, as some interpret the name, is understood as “the father’s peace.” This seems strange in the historical account: how can “the father’s peace” be understood of one who pursued his father in war?

### Note on Chapter III, no. 3

“A figure of his body and blood,” that is, “the sacrament of his body and blood.” I think these are the words of some Greek Father. GRIAL.]

3. But those who attend carefully to the allegory observe that Absalom is Jerusalem, which is itself also interpreted as “peace.” From its face Christ fled when, abandoning it by suffering, he succeeded among the Gentiles through faith. Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured with such great and astonishing patience, as though he were good, although he did not ignore his thoughts, when he admitted him to the banquet in which he commended and handed over to the disciples the figure of his body and blood.

### Note on Chapter III, no. 4

“Because the father had the peace which he did not have.” These are Augustine’s words in Psalm II. Gregory, however, in the prologue to Psalm VII, the penitential psalm, says: “Absalom is interpreted as ‘the father’s peace,’ not because he had any peace with his father, but because through his perversity the father showed how great was the peace and patience he possessed.” Jerome and Eucherius, however, interpret it not as “the father’s peace” but as “the father of peace.” The same author, Isidore, in *Etymologies* VII, chapter 6, thinks that “the father’s peace” is said by antiphrasis. GRIAL.]

4. Since, finally, at the very betrayal he received a kiss, it is rightly understood that Christ offered peace to his betrayer, although the latter was ravaged by the inward warfare of so wicked a thought. Therefore Absalom is called “the father’s peace,” because the father had the peace which he did not have.

# CHAPTER IV  
## Why David, Though Thirsty, Refused to Drink the Water from the Cistern of Bethlehem

1. David himself, during the battle with the Philistines, while moving about thirsty in the war and seeking water, said: “Who will give me a drink from the cistern that is in Bethlehem?” An enemy force lay between the cistern and David at the gates, and hostile troops surrounded the camp. Three men cut through the multitude of their opponents, drew water from the cistern that was in Bethlehem, and offered it to the king to drink.

### Note on Chapter IV, no. 2

“In their souls I shall drink.” Greek: **Ἐν ψυχαῖς αὐτῶν πίομαι**—“I shall drink in their souls”—according to the Septuagint. Some other words of this passage also come from there. The Vulgate translator rendered it: “Shall I drink the danger of the men’s souls?” GRIAL.]

2. But the king refused to drink it and poured it out before the Lord, saying: “Far be it from me to do this, to drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives.” Thus he overcame nature: though thirsty, he did not drink, and he offered himself as an example by which the entire army might learn to endure thirst. But if you wish to look more deeply and penetrate the mystery, David was thirsting not for the water that is in Bethlehem, but in spirit he foresaw Christ, born in that same Bethlehem from a Virgin.

### Note on Chapter IV, no. 3

“But the washing, etc.” Others: “but the water of the washing flowing from Christ’s side.” Shortly afterward, “not the nature of flowing waters” should be read instead of “not the natural stream.” AREV.]

3. Therefore he wished to drink not the water of a river, but the washing flowing from Christ’s side; that is, he was not thirsting for the element of water but for the blood of Christ. Hence he did not drink the water offered but poured it out before the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice—not for a natural stream, but for that sacrifice in which there would be forgiveness of sins; he thirsted for that eternal fountain, not one sought through the dangers of others but one that would erase the dangers of others.

# CHAPTER V  
## Psalm XVII

1. It is asked why Psalm XVII alone is found written in the Books of Kings. Not without reason is this psalm alone found in the Books of Kings, because it signifies that kingdom in which we shall have no adversary. For its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

### Note on Chapter V, no. 2

“Whom he slaughtered with his voice.” Thus in some manuscripts. *He struck down with his voice* is Eucherius’s reading, though it is not equally elegant; for what follows is: “And, transferring him into his own body, he in a certain way devoured him.” GRIAL.

**The same passage, “he slaughtered with his voice.”** Thus also the old edition. Grialius retained *he struck down with his voice* in the text, although in the note he preferred *he slaughtered with his voice*. AREV.]

2. For who is represented in David except the one who came according to the flesh from David’s seed, who still suffers enemies in his body, which is the Church? Hence to that persecutor whom he slaughtered with his voice and, transferring him into his own body, in a certain way devoured, there sounded from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” But when will this body be delivered from the hand of all its enemies, unless when that last enemy, death, is destroyed, so that we may attain the kingdom of God?

# 536 CHAPTER VI  
## The Catalogue of the Mighty Men

### Note on Chapter VI, no. 1

“Yet they do not at all reach the excellence of the divine Trinity.” Eucherius has a different allegory. GRIAL.

In Grialius’s edition a note had mistakenly intruded at this point, indicating that nearly the whole chapter had been taken from Saint Augustine. We have rejected that note to the third chapter of the following book, to which it belongs; there the same note had been repeated in part. AREV.]

1. Next is woven the catalogue of the mighty men, as a figure of the saints. Although they advance in the sublimity of virtues, they nevertheless do not reach the excellence of the divine Trinity. Hence it is written there: “He did not reach the three.” For who shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God (Ps. LXXXVIII)?

## IN THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS

[Col. 0413]

# 537 CHAPTER I  
## Solomon

### Note on Chapter I, no. 1

“From ‘in whom indeed’ up to ‘peaceful,’ the words are Augustine’s, *The City of God*, Book XVII, chapter 8. GRIAL.]

1. Solomon then succeeds, in whom a certain image of the future was formed in the fact that he built the temple and possessed peace according to his name. For *Solomon* is interpreted as “peaceful.” Accordingly, that title most truly suits the one through whom, as mediator, we are reconciled to God from being enemies, after receiving forgiveness of sins. For while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through his death.

2. He himself is that peaceful one who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of the enclosure, abolishing hostility in his flesh and nullifying the law of commandments by decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace for those who were far away and peace for those who were near. In the Gospel he says: “My peace I leave you” (John XIV). By these and many other testimonies the Lord Christ is shown to be peaceful.

# CHAPTER II  
## The Building of the Temple

[Col. 0415A]

### Note on Chapter II, no. 1

“For what he built,” up to “which you are,” is from Augustine, in the same place. GRIAL.

**The same passage.** Others: “most excellent.” AREV.]

1. For what he built—the most excellent temple for the Lord—also signifies Christ, who built a house for God in the heavens: not from wood and stones, but from holy human beings, that is, from believers, to whom the Apostle says: “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. III).

### Note on Chapter II, no. 2

“That the same house,” up to “we may come,” consists of words from Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIV, chapter 20. GRIAL.

**“Shaped stones.”** Others: “hewn stones.” AREV.]

2. But the fact that the same house was built of shaped and perfected stones, and that no hammer, axe, or iron tool was heard in the temple of God while it was being built—what else did that house signify, as was said above, except the holy Church, which the Lord inhabits in the heavens? For its building the souls of the elect are brought, like polished stones.

3. When it is built in heaven, no hammer of discipline resounds there, because we are brought there as hewn and perfected stones, to be arranged in places corresponding to our merits. Here we are beaten outside, so that we may come there without reproach. The height of this dominical temple refers to faith, its length to hope, and its breadth to charity. By these three virtues, as though by its lines, the structure of the holy heavenly Church rises.

4. Moreover, the fact that the walls of the temple are covered within with wood was fashioned as a mystery of the Lord’s cross, under whose protection all the saints are sheltered. Through perseverance in undisturbed peace they are strengthened, like living stones, in the structure of the Church by the unity of faith. And rightly the temple is clothed with wood within, because one believes with the heart unto righteousness. But the fact that, at the time of the dedication, the glory of the Lord filled the house signifies Christ as the glory of the Lord, whose faith has filled the whole world.

5. When Moses prayed to the Lord concerning that glory, asking him to spare the sinful people because of the worshiped calf, the Lord answered: “I will be merciful to them; nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, all the earth shall be filled with my glory.” Psalm LXXI also sings: “All the earth shall be filled with his glory” (Ps. LXXI). Hence the angels cried out to the shepherds: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

6. But the fact that a cloud filled the house of God, and that the priests could not minister because of the cloud, indicates the proud Jewish priests and teachers. While they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the ministry owed to their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, in accordance with their own merits, they did not recognize the worship of belief.

7. But the fact that Solomon made twelve bronze oxen in the same temple and set them in the bronze basin, facing in different directions but gathered together in one place at the rear—what else do we believe is signified by the twelve oxen except the twelve apostles? They look toward different regions with their faces, but they are placed in the basin so that they are joined together at the rear. In the present life they are divided for the work of preaching in different parts of the world; but in that life which follows this one, because it will be seen after this life, they come together in the eternal unity of glory.

8. Thus they look toward the diverse world through preaching, but they stand together when they reach the one destination. They are bronze because the sound of their preaching resounded throughout the whole world, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII). By the basin we understand the orb of the earth, whose circumference the apostles traversed, teaching the nations to be baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

# CHAPTER III  
## Solomon’s Wisdom

1. Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand. What else is signified by the three thousand proverbs except the fullness of faith handed down by Christ in the Law and in the Gospels? Since it is expounded in many ways through the meanings of allegories under the mystery of the Trinity, it is called, as it were, three thousand proverbs.

2. His five thousand songs are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever governs them well through various virtues is blessed, and through them sings, as it were, five thousand songs to the Lord. Solomon also discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop. By the cedar is understood the height of glory in the elect, as the Prophet also testifies, saying: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, and shall multiply like a cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. XCI). Hyssop, however, is a lowly plant clinging to a rock, by which Christ’s humility is signified.

3. Our Redeemer discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop, because he came down from the other height of heavenly glory to the humility of the flesh. Indeed, by the cedar is also signified the proud elevation of the wicked, as David says: “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars” (Ps. XXVIII).

4. Therefore Christ discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop, because he himself judges the hearts of the wicked and of the humble. He discoursed upon the wood when he hung upon the cross. For then he bent down the arrogance of the world in the cedar and brought it down even to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and the contemptible faith.

# CHAPTER IV  
## Solomon’s Judgment

### Note on Chapter IV, no. 1

See Augustine, sermon 200, *On the Seasons*. GRIAL.]

1. It is also read that this same wisest man first held judgment between two women contending over affection: in one love burned, while in the other pretense had stolen in. In that judgment, therefore, Solomon was a figure of Christ. The wicked woman—namely, the people of the Synagogue or of the heretics—desired the son of the true mother, that is, of the Church; but she wanted him not to preserve him, rather truly to kill him.

2. But just as, when Solomon’s sword divided the child, the true mother was recognized through the testimony of her own lament, so also, when the Spirit of Jesus Christ teaches, those who have been seduced and captured by the error of heretics may sometimes deserve to recognize the Church, their mother, groaning on their behalf. Thus it appears sufficiently and appropriately that this woman figured the impiety of the heretics or of the Synagogue: they wickedly kill their own by nurturing them, and persuade strangers by enticing them until they destroy them.

# CHAPTER V  
## The Queen of the South

1. The Queen of the South, who, summoned from the farthest regions, came wishing to hear Solomon’s wisdom, already then figured the queen who was to come from the Gentiles, desiring Christ. According to the Prophet, she is “clothed in varied garments, in a robe of gold” (Ps. XLIV). Forgetting her own people and her father’s house, she hastened with a barbarian people, though not barbarian in spirit; outwardly a foreigner, she inwardly desired to become a citizen of the saints.

2. Hence she is considered worthy not only of the heavenly reward of resurrection, but also, by apostolic authority, of judging adulterous Jews through the mouth of the Judge himself. Having marveled at Christ in Solomon, she had fulfilled, in the mystical image, the devotion of the true heavenly queen who foresaw the Church.

# CHAPTER VI  
## Solomon’s Other Works

### Note on Chapter VI, no. 1

“Furthermore.” The whole chapter is from Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XXII, chapter 88. GRIAL.]

1. What, then, shall I say about Solomon’s other works, when Holy Scripture vehemently rebukes and condemns him and makes absolutely no mention of his repentance or of God’s indulgence toward him? Nor does it at all occur to me what good his lamentable fall signifies, even in allegory. Unless perhaps someone might say that the foreign women whose love inflamed him signify the elect churches from the Gentiles.
