2. This might perhaps be understood without absurdity if, because of Solomon, they abandoned their gods and worshiped his God. But when he offended his own God because of them and worshiped their gods, nothing good can be inferred from it.

3. Nevertheless, I think it signifies something—not nothing—but evil, just as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters. In the person of this Solomon there appears a remarkable excellence and a remarkable fall. What therefore existed in him at different times—first good and afterward evil—is shown in the Church in this age both together and at one time.

4. For I think that by his good the good members of the Church are signified, and by his evil the evil members of the Church: as within the unity of that threshing floor, so in that one man, the good are the grain and the evil the chaff; or certainly, within the unity of one crop, the good are the wheat and the evil the weeds.

# 542 CHAPTER VII  
## The Division of the Ten Tribes

### Note on Chapter VII, no. 1

From Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XII, chapter 33. GRIAL.]

1. The fact that after Solomon’s death ten tribes were separated from the temple while two remained clearly indicates what the Apostle says concerning that entire people: “The remnant have been saved through the election of grace.”

# CHAPTER VIII  
## Elijah and His Miracles

1. What did those great and distinguished prophets signify, who also performed many wonders—Elijah and his disciple Elisha? Elijah is fed during a time of famine by ravens bringing bread in the morning and meat in the evening, so that you may understand Christ to be signified there.

2. Sinners in a certain manner confess to him, who hungers for our salvation: now faith, as the firstfruits of the Spirit; but at the end, as though at the evening of the world, the resurrection of the flesh. Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow who wished to gather two pieces of wood before she died. Here the sign of the cross is expressed not only by the name of wood but also by the number of the pieces of wood.

### Note on Chapter VIII, no. 3

“It is said not to have failed.” Others: “it does not fail.” AREV.]

3. Her flour and oil are blessed—the fruit and gladness of charity—which, when it is expended, is said not to have failed: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX). This widow, as I think, signifies the Church, whom Christ fed not with grain but with the bread of the word. Concerning her David says: “Blessing I will bless her widow” (Ps. CXXXI). He means that widow whom the Apostle says, after her husband has died, is free to marry whom she wishes (Rom. VII), because, when the Law to which Christ is the end has ceased, the Church, passing over into the freedom of grace, married Christ as though she were the widow of the Law. In her vessels the oil of grace and the flour of blessing do not now fail, while her fame remains throughout all the foreign nations.

### Note on Chapter VIII, no. 4

“Who would cleanse us from sin.” Others: “who would water souls thirsting through faith.” AREV.]

4. That famine of about three years aptly prefigured the hunger of those nations for the food of life and their famine of faith in the Trinity. But the fact that, during the time of drought, that cloud appeared through Elijah and that the sign of the future rain was shown in the impression of a human foot signified that, when Christ was born at the footprint of a man, rain would descend from heaven to the earth to cleanse us from sin.

## IN THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS

[Col. 0419]

# 544 CHAPTER I  
## The Two Captains of Fifty Consumed by Fire

1. The wicked king sends two captains of fifty with their subordinate soldiers to bring Elijah before him; they are consumed by divine fire. But the third man sent is saved.

### Note on Chapter I, no. 2

“Nor the prince of repentance.” Thus in the other books and in Bede. Eucherius has: “nor the prince and bestower of indulgence,” which appears to be another interpretation of the text. GRIAL.]

2. The number fifty is the confession of repentance, by which the forgiveness of sins is declared. Therefore the Jews, unwilling to believe that Christ is perfect God and the prince of repentance, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John VIII). These are extinguished in the future conflagration of divine fire. But the third captain of fifty, because he turned to faith in the Trinity and recognized the sacraments of repentance, earned pardon.

### Note on Chapter I, no. 3

“But it is asked, etc.” In many manuscripts this entire number is omitted up to the end of the chapter. AREV.]

3. It is asked, however, why the holy Elijah imposed a sentence of cursing upon the captains of fifty in such a way that they perished, when it is written: “Bless, and do not curse.” Holy Elijah therefore did not curse them at all because of any impulse of his own; rather, he foretold prophetically what he had recognized in divine predestination. For in God’s arrangement it had been determined that the captains of fifty would perish at Elijah’s word, and Simon at Peter’s sentence. Hence the saints do not curse from a desire for vengeance, but speak what they know to be in God’s will.

# 545 CHAPTER II  
## Elisha and the Healed Waters

1. The people ask Elisha to heal the barren and harmful waters of Jericho. He took a rough earthen vessel, put salt into it, and submerged it in the river; immediately the waters were healed.

2. By this act the prophet foretold that the Word would become flesh and dwell among us. Therefore, in the likeness of the Word, he put wisdom—salt—into the earthen vessel, namely the human body, and submerged it in the water. This signified that all the peoples who, under the figure of waters, were barren throughout the world would receive fertility and blessing through Christ’s incarnation.

# CHAPTER III  
## The Cursed Children

### Note on Chapter III, no. 1

See Augustine, *Against Faustus*, Book XII, chapter 35, and sermon 204, *On the Seasons*. GRIAL.]

1. Elisha himself also bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, his very name is interpreted as “salvation of God.” But who is the salvation of God except his Son, who is certainly also called Savior? Those children who mocked the salvation of God—that is, Elisha—represented the Jews, because they mocked the cross of the Lord the Savior. They said: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” because Christ was to ascend to the cross at the place of Calvary.

### Note on Chapter III, no. 2

“As Elisha went up.” Others: “as Elisha was going up.” AREV.]

2. But when Elisha turned and cursed them, and two bears came from the forest and killed forty-two boys who were blaspheming, so also Christ, after his passion and resurrection from the dead, after he ascended into heaven, as Elisha ascended to Bethel—that is, the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews. In the forty-second year of his ascension he sent two bears from the forests of the Gentiles, namely Vespasian and Titus, and they struck them down in a cruel slaughter.

# 546 CHAPTER IV  
## The Man Raised from the Dead

### Note on Chapter IV, no. 1

From the same Augustine, *Against Faustus*, and sermon 206. GRIAL.]

1. Elisha sends a staff through his servant upon a dead man, and he does not revive. He comes himself, joins himself to the dead man, fits himself to him, and the man revives. The Word of God sent the Law through his servant, and it did not benefit the human race, dead in sins.

2. He himself came down from the sublimity of the heavens, as though from the height of a mountain. He humbled himself, conformed himself to us, fitted his limbs to our dead limbs, and applied medicine to our mortality from his own body. Finally, over the dead man he yawns seven times and gives the sevenfold Spirit to the human race, through which sin, brought to life, may rise from death.

# CHAPTER V  
## The Iron That Rose from the River

### Note on Chapter V, no. 1

From the same chapter of Augustine and sermon 210. GRIAL.

**The same passage.** Others: “from them” instead of “for them.” And afterward: “Descending into the depth of hell, it rose when the spirit returned.” AREV.]

1. While wood was being cut with axes, the iron sprang from the wood, sank into the depth of the river, and, when Elisha threw a piece of wood over it, returned to the wood. Thus, when Christ’s presence, working through his body, cut down the impious Jews as fruitless trees—for John had said of him: “Behold, the axe is laid to the root of the trees” (Luke III)—the body itself, when the passion intervened, departed from them and descended into the depths of hell. When it had been placed there in burial, it rose again, as though the spirit had returned to the handle.

# CHAPTER VI  
## Hezekiah’s Fifteen Additional Years

### Note on Chapter VI, no. 1

“Lying sick,” etc. This must be read exactly so, from Cassian, whose words these are, *Conferences* XVII, chapter 25; likewise in Book I, chapter 2, when he said the same concerning Ahaziah: “The quality of the garment laid out for the sick king was discovered.” GRIAL.

**“Lying sick.”** Others: “reclining”; others: “while reclining.” Shortly afterward, “Hezekiah, and suffering.” Later, “but he, entreating,” should be taken as an absolute nominative; and “of the one begging for life.” AREV.]

1. The prophet Isaiah approached Hezekiah, who was lying on a bed and suffering from a serious illness, in the person of the Lord, and announced to him that he would die. But when he entreated the Lord at the very appointed limit of death, the Lord immediately heard his voice and extended by fifteen years the life of the one who was begging for it [perhaps: “extended fifteen years to the one begging for life”]. We understand what sacrament and mystery this number of fifteen years contains.

2. For, as the Apostle says: “As a person has acted, so shall he receive” (Rom. II). Therefore, because this king had fulfilled the Decalogue of the Law together with the five books of Moses by complete observance, he received fifteen years added to his life according to the number of the Law that he had kept. Through this we learn figuratively that all who, through the mystery of this number, keep the fullness of the entire Law obtain the reward of eternal salvation and, through the completion of the Law, pass over into the fullness of eternal life.

3. As a sign of the salvation to be bestowed on that king, the sun is said to have turned backward toward the rising—whence it had descended—by ten steps of his house, on which the shadow normally descended. Let us see what mystery this number contains.

4. For these steps are the successive ages of time, through which the shadow of Christ’s figures descended, and through which Christ, the Sun of righteousness, again ascended after the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0421C]

5. Isaiah’s passage in the Vulgate: “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God.” AREV.]

5. The first step of the descent from God was into the angel, because he was the angel of the great counsel (Isa. IX, 6). Accordingly, Jacob also says: “And the angel of God said: I am the God to whom you anointed a pillar and vowed a vow” (Gen. XXXI), so that he might show him to be both angel and God. The second step of the descent was from the angel into the patriarchs, because, as the Apostle says, he himself worked in them all (I Cor. XII).

6. The third was in the giving of the Law, because he himself also spoke in the Law. The fourth step was in Joshua son of Nun, so that he might lead the people into the promised land. The fifth was in the judges, because through them he himself ruled the same people. The sixth was in the kings of the Jews, because in them he himself reigned. The seventh was in the prophets, because through them he was announced. 548 The eighth was in the high priests, because he himself is the Father’s supreme Priest. The ninth was in man. The tenth was in the Passion.

7. Through these ten steps, then, by which Christ descended through the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, again ascended through the same steps into heaven after his resurrection, and illumined that entire shadow with the rays of truth, revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and exposing everything that had been concealed.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Chaldean treasures displayed

[Note: [Col. 0421D]

Chapter VII, no. 1. *Qui dum*: perhaps *qui* should be deleted. AREV.]

1. The fact that Hezekiah revealed his riches to the Chaldeans through boastful display, and therefore heard from the prophet that they would perish, signifies the servant of God who, when he has manifested and exposed his virtues through a desire for vain glory, immediately loses them and makes demons the masters of his works—just as that king, through his desire for ostentation, made his treasures come under the dominion of the Chaldeans.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Israel’s migration to Babylon

[Col. 0422B]

[Note: [Col. 0421D]

Chapter VIII, no. 1. “Now the very migration to Babylon …” Nearly the whole chapter is from *Against Faustus* XII, chapters 34–36. GRIAL.

There: *qui attenderit*. Some copies have *qui attendere valeat*. For *evangelico*, Grial published *Evangelio*. Some manuscripts have *Evangelio*, omitting *sacramento*. AREV.]

1. Now the very migration to Babylon—which the Spirit of God also commands through the prophet Jeremiah, telling them to go and pray for those in whose kingdom they are living as foreigners, because their peace would also be the peace of these exiles, and to build houses, cultivate vineyards, and plant gardens—who would not recognize what this prefigured, if he observed that the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit, migrated through apostolic dispensation, with the mystery of the Gospel, into the kingdom of the Gentiles?

[Note: [Col. 0422D]

2. Vulgate: “I ask, therefore, first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions … be made for kings and for all who are … in piety and chastity. For this is good,” etc. AREV.]

2. Therefore the Apostle, repeating Jeremiah’s words as it were, says to us: “I desire, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and charity. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II).

[Note: [Col. 0422D]

3. *Christianarum*. Grial published *Christianorum*; and below *altipetax* instead of *altipeta*; or, as others have it, *appetita*. For *confugiendo*, some copies have *confitendo*. AREV.]

3. From this, dwellings of peace were also built for those who believed: basilicas of Christian congregations, vineyards newly cultivated by the faithful people, and planted gardens. There too, among all the vegetables, that mustard seed reigns; beneath its far-reaching shade even the lofty pride of the nations, like birds of heaven, takes refuge and rests.

# IN ESDRAS

[Col. 0421]

550 ## CHAPTER ONE. On the seventy years of captivity

[Col. 0421D]

[Note: [Col. 0421D]

Chapter I, no. 1. “For what also … as far as ‘I may be pierced’”: these words are from Augustine, *Against Faustus* XII, chapter 36. GRIAL.

There: Grial placed *jam quod* in the text after *post*, whereas in the note he placed *nam quod etiam* after *post*. Others have *jam quod etiam* after *post*. Some have *Esdrae* instead of *Jeremiae*. AREV.]

1. Now, after seventy years, according to Jeremiah’s prophecy, there is a return from captivity and the Temple is restored. What faithful Christian would not understand that, after the ages have run their course—ages which pass by the recurring number of the seven days—we too, that is, the Church of God, must return from our pilgrimage in this world to that heavenly Jerusalem?

[Note: [Col. 0423C]

2. Others: “Christ, the true priest.” And shortly afterward: “his filthy garment having been removed from him and a garment given.” AREV.]

2. Through whom except Jesus Christ, truly the great Priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of that time, through whom the Temple was built after the captivity? The prophet Zechariah saw him in filthy clothing; after the devil, who stood accusing him, had been conquered, the filthy garment was removed from him and a garment of honor and glory was given to him. So the body of Jesus Christ, which is the Church, after the adversary has been overcome by judgment at the end of time, is taken from the grief of pilgrimage into the glory of eternal salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0423C]

3. Others: “That my glory may sing to you.” AREV.]

3. This is also sung most clearly in the psalm of the dedication of the house: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me; you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Ps. XXIX).

## CHAPTER II. On the vessels of the Lord carried away to Babylon

1. It is read that the Babylonian king once removed from Jerusalem the vessels of the Lord, which had been assigned to sacrifices or to sacred mysteries, carried them away together with the captives, and appropriated them for his own uses. But when God showed mercy, after the captivity had been ended, those vessels were brought back unbroken and again devoted to divine worship. The Babylonian king is the devil, who led the faithful people, bound by the captivity of error, from Jerusalem—that is, the Church—into Babylon, that is, into the confusion of heretical depravity.

[Note: [Col. 0424C]

Chapter II, no. 2. Others: “by which Christians too are certainly called.” AREV.]

2. He also carried away part of the vessels, that is, of the sacraments, together with the captives. For the vessels of the sacraments signify the sacraments themselves, through which the perfection of divine worship is fulfilled. Heretics carried some of them away with them. First, they carried away the very name of Christ, by which they certainly call themselves Christians; they carried away the Law, the Gospel, the Apostle, the Psalter, baptism, “Amen,” and “Alleluia.”

## CHAPTER III. On the people’s return to Jerusalem

[Note: [Col. 0424C]

Chapter III, no. 1. *Relicta*. Some copies have *relictus*, so that “the people left behind” is understood. AREV.]

1. When the people, through God’s regard, hasten to return from the confusion of ignorance to Jerusalem—that is, to the vision of peace, which is the Church of the living God—with the Lord as their guide, carrying these vessels, that is, the sacraments, with them, they do not alter them but bring them back intact. They do not break them as though they needed to be renewed for the better; rather, they restore them to the Temple and adapt them to divine uses.

2. Thus the restored people rejoices that these things were not lost but even preserved among the impious. We do not erase the Gospel, nor obliterate the Apostle; we do not change “Amen” or “Alleluia”; we do not repeat baptism.

# ON THE MACCABEES

[Col. 0423]

[Col. 0423D] 552 [Note: [Col. 0423D]

1. “What shall I say to the brothers?” Others: “What shall we say to the brothers?” AREV.]

1. What shall I say to the brothers about the Maccabees, who under King Antiochus endured dreadful tortures for the sacred laws? When the devout mother was being subjected to various punishments, she not only did not weep but, rejoicing, encouraged them toward the glory of martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0423D]

2. “Who could set forth everything … as figures of our own?” From the same book, chapter 37. GRIAL.]

2. So too the mother Church rejoices and shares the joy of her martyrs, attaining greater glory through the martyrdoms of her children, while she celebrates that they have overcome the devil through the sevenfold Spirit. Who could touch upon, however briefly, all that is announced figuratively concerning those ancient books of the Law and the Prophets? Unless someone perhaps thinks that it is accomplished merely by ingenuity that events which unfolded in their proper order through their respective ages should be transformed by interpretation into mystical meanings. Jews or pagans may say this.

[Note: [Col. 0423D]

3. *Who wish to be Christians*. Others: “who are Christians,” which is clearer. The Florentine folio codex, which I have often used, contains at the end a note asserting that it was copied from sufficiently reliable exemplars belonging to King Matthias of Hungary. This commends its value. AREV.]

3. But apostolic authority presses down the necks of those who wish to be Christians, saying: “All these things happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X); and “all these things were figures of us,” upon whom the end of all the ages has come. Everything has been brought to completion in mysteries through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise, honor, and glory, dominion and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0425]

# APPENDIX TO THE BOOKS OF KINGS

553 **On the unity of faith and charity, which is the fullness of the Law**

[Col. 0425A]

[Note: [Col. 0425C]

1. As I said in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 102, no. 25, this fragment is appended, in the same sequence, to Isidore’s commentary on the Fourth Book of Kings in Vatican Palatine Codex 276. Although its title is *On the Unity of Faith*, etc., in reality it is an exposition of certain passages from the Books of Kings, beginning with the First Book, chapter I, verse 1: “There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from Mount Ephraim,” etc. For *competentes*, perhaps *competenter* should be read, although immediately afterward it is denied that the foolish are one.]

1. What does “one man” mean? Not only is that man called one, but all who are striving are called one. All possessing one wisdom confess the one Christ Jesus; they are filled with one Spirit of God. Hence the Apostle says: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (I Cor. IX, 24).

[Note: [Col. 0425D]

2. In the manuscript: *cum videtur*. Many are called foolish because “the number of fools is infinite”; in this sense some understand the statement, “many speak many things,” because fools are talkative.]

2. Each foolish person is not one but many, because in Scripture the fool changes like the moon. Although the moon appears to be one in substance, through the changes of the days it is always different from itself and varied. So too sinners, who are continually changed in knowledge and desire different things.

[Note: [Col. 0426C]

3. Perhaps, as it is written: “But you …,” etc.]

3. God, however, is called one not numerically, but because he never becomes other than himself. Therefore he never changes, as it is written: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28).

4. “From Mount Ephraim”—that is, not from valleys, nor from plains, nor from hills. “From Mount Ephraim,” which is interpreted as “fruitfulness”; that is, therefore, from a fruitful mountain. The Lord says: “The Lord of the mountains,” not of the valleys.

5. Elkanah is interpreted as “God is possession.” That man had two wives. The first, the nobler Anna, was barren, as Sarah, Abraham’s first and nobler wife, was barren. The second, the Egyptian Hagar, was of lower status. Abraham became a father through the one of lower status, yet afterward he also became a father through the nobler wife.

6. Thus Elkanah, who is “God’s possession,” first becomes a father through the second wife, because God had closed Anna’s womb, just as he had first closed Sarah’s womb. After Peninnah had given birth, God opened Anna’s womb. Peninnah is interpreted as “conversion,” while Anna is interpreted as “grace.”

7. Whoever wishes to become God’s possession should take these two wives and first join to himself the nobler one, grace. For this one is joined through faith first, as the Apostle says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith” (Eph. II, 8). The second is joined to Peninnah, that is, to conversion, because after the grace of belief comes the correction of conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

8. In the manuscript: “Peninnah had sons.”]

8. Peninnah first bears sons for us, because we produce our first fruits. And unless we turn away from evil, we cannot become fathers through Anna. Peninnah has sons, but they do not attend upon God; nevertheless they are not empty-handed, for they eat from the divine sacrifices.

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

9. In the manuscript: *erat vacat*.]

9. Therefore each person who turns from sin produces works of righteousness through conversion. Afterward Anna, stirred up by good zeal, pours out a prayer to the Lord so that she herself may bear sons who attend upon God—that is, sons of grace, who devote themselves to God. The form of this story is shown in the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

10. Instead of *conversationis*, one should perhaps read *conversionis*. *Gratia gemina* appears corrupt.]

10. Martha, for example, is anxious about frequent service: she completes works of conduct and through them, as it were, produces sons of conduct. Mary, sitting beside the feet of the Lord’s word, is said to have chosen the better part, and is understood to produce, as it were, a double grace.

11. Thus Anna bears the son Samuel, who attends upon God. Of him it is said: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. XCVIII, 6). This is interpreted as: “Where he himself is God.” For where the Spirit of grace is, God is said to be there, as Paul says. And falling on his face, he worshiped God, saying: “Truly God is among you.”

12. Unless works of conversion precede, we cannot produce the gifts of the Spirit at Shiloh. Shiloh is the name of the place where sacrifices were offered before the Temple was built in Jerusalem, and where the cleansing of sins took place. Shiloh is interpreted as “tearing out,” or “unshoeing,” that is, the removal of footwear. The place where sins are cleansed is called “tearing out,” because the heart of stone is torn out there; and “unshoeing,” because, until we come to the holy place, we are all shod. But when we reach it, we are commanded to remove our shoes.

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

13. The manuscript has *incederat*. Perhaps *incedebant* should be read. This and the following passages also pertain to chapter II of the First Book of Kings. In the Vulgate, at the cited passage in Exodus: “Remove the shoe from your feet.”]

13. As it is said to Moses: “Untie the strap of your shoe, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5), so that he might cast off the signs of mortality, which are signified by leather shoes. Hence the Savior says: “Nor shoes on your feet,” since they were walking along that way. He says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” For no one walks the way of life bearing the sign of mortality.

14. Shiloh is where Eli is, a man less worthy of praise; for, falling backward on account of his sin, he died. If anyone turns backward from faith and truth, he must fall and immediately die.

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

15. Perhaps: “He does not discipline his son … and is thus made far from correction.”]

15. Eli is interpreted as “outsider.” He is truly an outsider from God because he does not maintain discipline; he does not consider, rebuke, or correct his son, but indulges his vices. Eli’s son Hophni is interpreted as “lofty conversion,” because he is made far from cleansing, which turns him toward the Lord.

[Col. 0426C] [Note: [Col. 0426D]

16. Perhaps: “so that no evil speech may proceed from the priest.”]

16. We know two Phinehases in Scripture: the righteous one, the son of Aaron, 555 and the unrighteous one, the son of Eli. Phinehas signifies “closing the mouth” and “sparing the mouth.” Among priests today there are both kinds. The one who spares his mouth, so that no evil speech proceeds from the priest, is compared with Phinehas, the son of Aaron. Those priests who have their mouths closed through ignorance, vice, or consciousness of sins are compared with Eli’s son.

17. “Until he had removed him from milk.” Samuel is removed from Anna’s rational milk, because one who is offered to God could not previously be offered until he had been removed from milk. As long as he is a child in understanding, Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

18. Perhaps: “He is alien from the speech of righteousness.”]

18. Everyone who first turns from heresy to the faith is nourished on milk. The speech of righteousness is foreign to him, and he lacks the understanding to distinguish good from evil. A little child cannot ascend to the Temple of God or attend upon the ministries of the priests; nor does his mother ascend with him, although she could ascend. For grace is his mother, and she preserves and nourishes him.

19. “And Anna prayed and said.” She is not found praying except through only two expressions. She says: “My heart has rejoiced in your salvation.” And another expression is: “For there is no God besides you.” Yet the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V, 17).

20. Whoever is engaged in divine service counts all his deeds and words as prayer, because the righteous person acts righteously without ceasing. For this reason the righteous person will pray without ceasing. And in the Psalms he says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

21. He lifts up his hands—that is, his deeds. Likewise, when Moses lifted up his hand, Israel prevailed; when he lowered it, Amalek prevailed. As long as the servant lifts his deeds up to the Lord, the people of God prevail; but when he lowers his deeds, Amalek, the enemy of God, prevails.

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

22. Perhaps: “If I rejoice, and do not rejoice in the Lord, I may be pierced.”]

22. Anna says: “My heart has exulted.” She necessarily added: “in the Lord,” as Paul said: “Rejoice in the Lord” (Phil. IV, 4). For someone may rejoice in carnal things. When people praise me, I do not rejoice in the Lord; if I rejoice, I may be pierced.

23. “Because of the word of the Lord, the horns of the righteous.” This may refer to those who say: “In you we shall gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII, 6). In Greek, it is a joyful testimony. Since, therefore, we seek a horn or shall gore with a horn, the horns belong to the righteous because they are bestowed upon the righteous from the points of Christ’s cross.

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

24. Vulgate: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.”]

24. Through these we shall destroy the hostile powers from our soul. Then a vineyard is planted in us. “My mouth has been enlarged”—that is, through meditation on the word of God, let us come to the elevation of the heart, as the Apostle also says: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11). For wisdom is supplied to the mouth from the height of the heart.

25. “For I have been enlarged in your salvation”—that is, if I rejoice in the Lord’s salvation, then my mouth has been enlarged. “There is none holy like God.” He uses a distinction: he did not say, “unless the Lord,” but “there is none like the Lord.” “There is no God besides you”—that is, none of those things which exist by nature. You alone are; your existence was given by no one. For even a shadow, in comparison with a body, is not; and smoke, in comparison with fire, is not.

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

26. In the Vulgate: “Do not multiply lofty words.”]

26. “Do not multiply lofty speech.” As Solomon says: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclus. III, 22). Concerning what is commanded you to understand, “do not multiply speech” except concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that what we say may be made fully manifest. After these three, say nothing.

27. “Let no empty speech proceed from your mouth,” as the Apostle says: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24). Alternatively: “An angel of Satan, who may buffet me” (II Cor. XII, 7). That is, let me not speak great things about myself. “Let no boastful speech proceed from your mouth.” “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins” (Ps. CXL, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

28. Proverbs XVIII: “He who wishes to withdraw from a friend seeks occasions.” And chapter XXII: “The lazy man says: There is a lion outside.” Something may be missing in the manuscript.]

28. Solomon also says: “The lazy man seeks excuses,” and says: “There is a lion outside.” The same man says: “The devil will mock me, as a woman has seduced me” (Prov. XVIII, 1; XXII, 13). The righteous person is first of all his own accuser. The unrighteous person is not his own accuser but accuses others. Until someone sins, he is neither righteous nor his own accuser. For the one who acts does not accuse.

29. “The bow of the mighty has been weakened.” If you are clothed in the armor of God—the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit—the bow of the mighty will be strengthened by such defenses. “The weak are girded with strength,” as it is written: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. XII, 8).

30. The weak people are the Gentiles, who, though alien from God’s covenant, obtained strength, as the Prophet says: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. CXVII, 14)—that is, Christ himself is strength. “Until now our mother was barren,” the Church. And she bore seven—that is, the number seven.

31. And my flesh, possessing many fruits of the flesh: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, idolatry, sorceries, quarrels, rivalries, provocations, and dissensions. “Barren,” that is, the soul, for at one time it bore no fruits of righteousness; nor was it filled through faith in Christ with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and fear of God.

[Col. 0428B] 32. “God puts to death and gives life.” He puts me to death when I was dead to sin, and then gives me life when he makes me live for God. The true David, guarding his father’s sheep, seized the lion and killed it. The title of the psalm is: “For David himself, when his son was persecuting him.”

[Note: [Col. 0427D]

33. Instead of *sustinuisse*, I would prefer *substituisse* or *adhibuisse*. The passage does not fit very well with the exposition of Anna’s Song: “God puts to death,” etc.]

33. We read in the Books of Kings that this man, not unjustly unloved but piously humbled, received discipline from the Lord, endured a remedy rather than retribution for iniquity. That was the praiseworthy David; but another David, mighty in hand, is the Lord Jesus Christ.

34. For those past events were figures of future things. Let us recognize how his own son also persecuted Christ. Christ had sons, concerning whom he said: “The sons of the bridegroom do not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them.” Among them was the persecutor Judas.

## On the union with the wife of a near relative or deceased brother

[Note: [Col. 0428D]

35. These matters pertain to the Book of Ruth, which is, as it were, an appendix to the Book of Judges and a preface to the Books of Kings. The manuscript has *proximi* above instead of *proximo*, and *fratris* instead of *fratri*, as well as *quia reliquerat* and *eamque colligentem*.]

35. According to the Law, union with the wife of a deceased near relative or brother was accorded, so that the offspring of the brother or near relative might be raised up. Hence Ruth, although she herself was a foreigner, because she had had a husband from among the Jews who had left behind a surviving near relative, was gathering the ears of grain from his harvest to support her mother-in-law. Boaz saw her and loved her.

[Note: [Col. 0428D]

36. This was the ancient custom in Israel, concerning which Ruth IV, 7 speaks: whoever yielded his right removed his sandal and gave it to his near relative.]

36. He did not take her as his wife in any other way than by first removing the sandal of the man to whom the wife was owed by law. The history is simple but contains profound mysteries. One thing was being enacted, another was being signified. The future Christ, arising from the Jews, was being represented: he would raise up, through the seed of heavenly teaching, the offspring of his near relative—that is, the dead people.

37. To whom did the spiritual matters of the written Law bring the nuptial sandal for the Church to be joined in marriage? Not to Moses, the bridegroom. For it is said to him: “Remove your sandals,” lest, because of the similarity of the name, he be thought to be the Church’s bridegroom. There was no other bridegroom, but Christ alone, concerning whom John said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John III, 29).

[Note: [Col. 0428D]

38. In the manuscript: *innubatque* and *nobis pascat*.]

38. Therefore his sandal is removed; Christ’s cannot be removed, as John says: “I am not worthy,” he says, “to loosen the strap,” and so forth. Christ alone, then, is the bridegroom. The bride who came from the Gentiles, formerly poor and famished but now enriched by Christ’s harvest, unmarried and fruitful in sheaves, binds in the inner storehouse of her mind the remnants of the word’s fertile grain, so that she may nourish with new food that exhausted widow, the impoverished mother of a people bereaved by the death of her son, not leaving her destitute and seeking new provisions.

39. Christ alone, then, is the bridegroom, who does not begrudge even the synagogue the sheaves of his harvest. Would that it had not excluded itself! It had those whom it could have gathered through itself, because its people had died. Like a native son who had died, it gathered through the Church sheaves by which it might live—sheaves which, coming in exultation, they carried, as it is written: “They shall come indeed, coming,” and the rest.

[Note: [Col. 0429D]

40. These matters should be referred to the First Book of Kings, chapter I.]

40. Elkanah, the venerable father of Samuel, was God’s possession; for *Elkanah* is transferred as “into God’s possession.” Because of the strength of his spirit he is called a man, and not merely a man but “one man.” He was not carried about wandering in different directions, like one changeable and unstable, but, remaining firm and unshaken, he was one man.

558 41. Therefore he dwelt on fruitful Mount Ephraim, that is, in the lofty contemplation of virtues, so that the sublimity of his mind might not be cast down by any thoughts of vices lying beneath or barking around him, nor its unity be split apart.

[Note: [Col. 0429D]

42. The flight of David is treated in I Kings XIX. The manuscript appears corrupt here, and perhaps *prophetae* should be read instead of *prophetam*.]

42. David, fleeing with his companions from Saul’s presence, figured Christ, who, with the apostles, concealed himself from the ruler of the world, except insofar as he was revealed to the priests, to show that priestly food would pass over for the use of the prophet. Or this was because we must all imitate the priestly life, or because all the children of the Church are priests, offering themselves to God as spiritual sacrifices.

43. David therefore entered the priest’s house, and the priest, although the danger of death had been set before him, did not refuse his guest. This was so that, morally, we might willingly take alien dangers upon ourselves for the sake of hospitality; or, mystically, so that priests might not exclude Christ from the hospitality of their minds even when death’s destruction had been presumed.

[Note: [Col. 0429D]

44. In the manuscripts *spoliavit*, or some similar verb, was lacking. Above, *manubias* had been written by the old hand as *manubrias*. I have restored *libris* instead of *libri*, or perhaps *Christi corpus* should be read.]

44. There, when Christ, taking the spoils of spiritual wickedness, had stripped Goliath of his spoils and weapons, David asked for bread. But he received one loaf, because food for the faithful is prepared not from the five books of Moses but from the body of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0429D]

45. What is related here about Doeg—or, as it is written in the manuscripts, Doech—is found in I Kings, chapter XXII. The manuscripts write *Abimelech*.]

45. Doeg, the keeper of an unfruitful herd of camels, represents Judas the betrayer. But in the house of Ahimelech, only Abiathar, chief of the priests, is immune from the persecutor Saul, because no one can harm Christ, the chief of priests.

[Note: [Col. 0430D]

46. Perhaps *cur David?* should be read as a question. The manuscript has *accumberent* instead of *occumberent*.]

46. Why, then? Because David, who did not return evil for evil, curses the mountains of Gilboa when Saul and Jonathan fell in battle, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, may neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits exist, because there the shield of Saul was cast away, as though he had not been anointed with oil.” Why, then, when Saul died, did the mountains sin, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them? Because Gilboa is interpreted as “descent,” and through Saul, the anointed and dead man, the death of the Mediator is expressed. The mountains of Gilboa therefore fittingly signify the proud hearts of the Jews: while they flow downward into the desires of this world, they joined themselves to the death of Christ, that is, of the Anointed One.

[Col. 0429D] [Note: [Col. 0430D]

47. Perhaps: “They were unwilling to follow.”]

47. And because the anointed king dies bodily among them, they themselves are dried up from every dew of grace. Of them it is rightly said that they cannot be fields of firstfruits. For the proud minds of the Hebrews, bearing no first fruits, remained for the most part in unbelief at the Redeemer’s coming and were unwilling to follow the beginnings of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0430D]

48. Vulgate: “For if your people Israel should be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will return from it.”]

48. The holy Church, made fruitful in its firstfruits by the multitude of the Gentiles, scarcely at the end of the world receives the Jews whom it finds, gathering the last remnants and setting them in place like gleanings of grain. Concerning them Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

49. The mountains of Gilboa may therefore be cursed from the prophet’s mouth so that, while no fruit arises because the earth has dried up, their possessors may nevertheless be struck by the penalty of barrenness, in order that they might receive the sentence of the curse, since by their iniquity they had deserved to accept the king’s death among themselves.

50. Thus, very often, any given matter is a virtue in its historical sense but a fault in its signification. Similarly, an event may be a cause of condemnation in what was done, but a prophecy of virtue in what was written. We shall show this more readily if we bring forward David’s deed and use a single testimony to prove both meanings.

[Note: [Col. 0430D]

51. This allegory concerning David and Bathsheba is also expounded in the *Allegories*, no. 90, but there Uriah is a type of the devil.]

51. Who, hearing this, does not detest—not only among the faithful but even among unbelievers—that David, walking on the roof, desired Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife? Yet he urged Uriah, returning from battle, to go into his house and wash his feet. He immediately replied: “The ark of God is under coverings, and shall I rest in my house?”

52. David received him at his own table and handed him letters by which he was to die. Whom does David, walking on the roof, represent except the one of whom it is written: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII, 6)? And what is it to take Bathsheba except to join the law of the letter, united to a carnal people, to oneself through a spiritual understanding?

53. Bathsheba is called “the seventh well,” because through knowledge of the Law, by the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us. Whom does Uriah signify except the Jewish people, whose name is interpreted as “my light is God”? The Jewish people, because it is elevated by the knowledge of the Law it has received, boasts as though it possessed the light of God.

54. But David took Uriah’s wife from him and joined her to himself, because the strong-handed one called David—that is, the Redeemer appearing in the flesh—made it known that the Law spoke spiritually about him. By this very fact, that it was held according to the letter, he showed it to be alien from the Jewish people and joined it to himself, declaring that he was proclaimed through it.

55. David nevertheless urges Uriah to go into his house and wash his feet, because the incarnate Lord, coming among the Jewish people, commanded them to return to their conscience and wipe away the filth of their deeds, so that they might understand the commandments of the Law spiritually and, after such hardness of precepts, finding the fountain of baptism, return to the water after their labor.

56. But Uriah, remembering that the ark of God was under coverings, replied that he could not enter his house. It was as though the Jewish people were saying: “I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to my conscience through spiritual understanding.” For the one who understands God’s commandments only as the performance of carnal sacrifice is, as it were, saying that the ark is under coverings.

560 57. Nevertheless David summons him even though he is unwilling to return to his house. For although the Jewish people disdains returning to its conscience, the coming Redeemer still preaches the spiritual commandments, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V, 46).

58. The Jewish people therefore holds the Law because it speaks of the divinity of the one whom that same people disdains to believe. Hence Uriah is sent to Joab with the letters by which he was to be killed, because that same Jewish people carries the Law, by which it is convicted and condemned to die. While it retains the commandments of the Law and strives to fulfill them, it itself carries the judgment by which it will be condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0431D]

59. The manuscript has: “who applaud themselves.”]

59. Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron will endure different punishments. Gaza is interpreted as “his strength.” Therefore all who applaud themselves in bodily strength and worldly power, and say with the devil, “I will make strength,” will be plundered on the day of the Lord’s wrath and reduced to nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0431D]

60. I supplied *interpretatur*, a verb found in the preceding number. The manuscript had *concremetur*, and above *concrematur*.]

60. Ashkelon, which is interpreted as “weights,” or “the fire of the murderer,” when the day of wrath comes, will feel the measure of its crime and will be crushed by the same weight with which it acted. And because it burned with a desire to shed blood, scandalized many souls, and the words were fulfilled in it, “The Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man,” it will not be plundered like Gaza; instead, reduced to a wilderness, it will be burned in the fires of Gehenna down to the dust.

61. Moreover, Ashdod, which in Hebrew is called *es David* and in our language sounds like “fire of generation,” will bear witness in clear daylight. For it burned with lust and was scattered by the fire of generation; and because all adulterers are like an oven, and their hearts have been wounded by burning arrows, they will be cast—not in darkness or under a hidden judgment, but at midday, that is, when the saints receive their full radiance—into darkness, and will have no share in the company of the saints on the day of judgment.

62. But Ekron also, which is interpreted as “sterility” or “eradication,” because it produced no fruits and by the perversity of its teaching eradicated many, will itself be eradicated. Understand all these variations as referring to the vices and sins of souls. And the fire will test what each person’s work is like. Therefore the weak often judge many things said by the strong, because they do not know that, when the Ark of the Testament had been tilted by the stumbling oxen and the Levite, believing that it was already about to fall, wished to raise it up, he immediately received the sentence of condemnation.

63. For what is the mind of the just man except the Ark of the Testament? It is tilted when carried by stumbling oxen, because sometimes even one who governs well, while being subjected to agitation by the confusion of the peoples, is moved, solely out of love, to condescend to an accommodating administration. But in what is done as an administrative concession, the uninstructed regard this very inclination of strength as a fall. Hence some subjects send forth words of reproach against this hand, but immediately the very merits of their life fail them.

64. Oza is rightly so called, for the name is interpreted as “robust of the Lord.” For if presumptuous people did not believe, with an audacious mind, that they were strong in the Lord, they would by no means judge the deeds or words of their betters to be weak.

[Col. 0431D] [Note: The word *de* before *sola* appears to require deletion. What is said in this and the following sections about rulers—or superiors—and subjects is treated more fully by Isidore in Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 48 and following.]

65. “I will give you kings in my wrath.” If, therefore, when God is angry, we receive rulers according to our merits, we learn from their actions that we must weigh them by estimation alone, although the chosen often lie beneath the reprobate. Thus David endured Saul, because at that time he was worthy to be oppressed by such severity on the part of a ruler.

[Col. 0432A] Thus, according to the merits of subjects, the deeds of rulers are assigned to their persons, so that those who seem good are often changed as soon as they receive authority, as Scripture says: “He who changed the heart along with the dignity.”

66. Hence it is written: “Behold, when you were small in your own eyes, I appointed you head over the tribes of Israel.” Thus the actions of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, on account of a bad flock, the life of an actually good shepherd may offend. That David—the man praised with God as his witness, that prophet David who knew heavenly things—sinned by numbering the people. Yet, when David sinned, the people received the punishment.

[Note: It would seem that one should read *a culpa alienus non fuit* (“he was not free from guilt”), or *a culpa alienos* (“those free from guilt”).]

67. Why is this? Clearly, the order of rulers is arranged according to the merit of the peoples. But the just Judge corrected the fault of the one who sinned by their own punishment, since he had sinned because of them. But because, in his very will, he grew proud and did not remain free from guilt, he too received the punishment for the guilt. For the raging wrath that struck the people bodily also laid low the ruler of the people through the deepest anguish of his heart.

[Note:]

68. These matters are taken from the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter 6.

68. “The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh, going and lowing, and they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left.” What, then, do the cows signify except the faithful within the Church? While they consider the commands of sacred speech, they carry, as though placed upon them, the Ark of the Lord.

[Note:]

69. “Behold, for ‘Baal Beth-shemesh’ ...” appears corrupt. In place of *dicit* (“says”), I would suppose that *dicitur* (“is called”) should be restored. Malachi’s words in the Vulgate are: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of justice shall rise” [Malachi 4:2].

69. The following must also be noted about them: they are said to have been calving, because there are many who, inwardly placed on the way of God, are outwardly bound by carnal affections; yet they do not turn aside from the straight path, since they carry the Ark of the Lord. For “Baal Beth-shemesh” means “house of the sun.” And the Prophet says: “But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of justice shall rise” (Malachi 4:2). If, then, we are striving toward the dwelling-place of the eternal sun, it is certainly fitting that, because of carnal affections, we should not turn aside from the way of God.

70. For it must be weighed with all one’s strength that the cows, placed beneath God’s cart, proceed and groan; they give lowings from their inmost parts, and yet do not turn their steps from the road. So indeed the preachers of God’s word, so the teachers, so all the faithful within the holy Church ought to be: they should sympathize with their neighbors through charity, and yet not deviate from the way of God through compassion.

[Note:]

71. The deed of Benaiah is related in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 23, verses 20 and following. In the manuscript it seems to read *quoniam infrixerunt* (“because they broke”) instead of *quo refrixerunt* (“by which they grew cold”).

71. Snow may therefore be understood now as the brightness of innocence and grace, now as winter and the coldness of charity. When we read in the Books of Kings that a certain Benaiah, one of the mighty men of Israel, descended into a cistern and struck down a lion during a time of snow, I think that snow was placed in those passages without distinction, because both the grace of Christ, which shone forth in this world, and the coldness of the charity of God, by which human beings grew cold, could have been signified by the name “snow” in sacred Scripture.

[Note:]

72. Perhaps “who through him.” In the manuscript: *quia verbum* (“because the word”); I corrected it to *quod verbum* (“which word”).

72. We understand Benaiah figuratively as the Savior, because, according to the force of his name, he is himself “the Lord who builds.” Concerning him the prophet had foretold, saying that the Church would be built through him: “The Lord builds Jerusalem.” Likewise: “He built Zion.” Scripture used this word in its proper sense in the making of Eve, who bore the type of the Church, saying: “And the Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman.” And Paul, seeing that she was being constructed, says: “You are God’s building.”

[Note:]

73. With the order of events and years confused, this fragment ends here, with the rubric added: “Here begin the chapters from the Book of Ezra. Concerning the seventy years of captivity,” etc., as in Isidore. Isidore elsewhere attests to Samuel’s priesthood; others deny it, as stated in the note to the *Book of Allegories*, no. 86.

73. Why is Samuel called three times? Because he was a prophet, a priest, and a leader. David reigned for forty years, first from the tribe of Judah. Rehoboam for ... years; Abijah for ...; Asa, the just, for ...; Jehoram for ...; Ahaziah for ...; Athaliah for ...; Joash for ...; Amaziah for ...; Azariah for ...; Jotham for ...; Ahaz for ...; Hezekiah for ...; Manasseh for ...; Amon for ...; Josiah for ...; Joash for ...; Eliakim for ...; Jehoiakim for ...; Hezekiah for ...; Astraph for fourteen years, three years, forty-one years, seven years, fifty years, four years, forty years, six years, fourteen years, sixteen years, twenty-nine years, and fifty-five years.

**RUBRIC**

Here begin the chapters from the Book of Ezra.

Concerning the seventy years of captivity, etc.

[Col. 0433]

**VARIOUS READINGS**

**TO THE BOOK OF DIFFERENCES**

[Col. 0433A]

No. 1: *ut in Dei* (“as in God”); another reading: *in Dei*, omitting *ut* (“in God”). Likewise, *intelligerent* (“they might understand”); another: *intelligunt* (“they understand”). No. 3: *et color* (“and color”); another: *et calor* (“and heat”). No. 7: *Spiritus sanctus ... procedens* (“the Holy Spirit ... proceeding”); another: “The Spirit, begotten neither from the Father nor from the Son, but proceeding.” No. 9: *nec genitus* (“nor begotten”); others add: “It seems to be neither begotten nor a creature, but uncreated.” No. 11: *relative tria* (“three relational [things]”); another: *relativa tria* (“three relational [things]”). No. 14: *gratiae et veritatis* (“of grace and truth”); another: *gratia et veritate* (“by grace and truth”). No. 30: *facta, praecessit* (“having been made, it preceded”), etc.; another: “Having been made, it proceeded, although the thing made by itself is not eternal.” Likewise, *cantum* (“song”); another: *cantu* (“by song”). No. 32: *receptionem* (“reception”); another: *resurrectionem* (“resurrection”). No. 35: *genus* (“kind”); another: *genus futuri saeculi* (“the kind of the age to come”). No. 36: *De rerum ...* (“Concerning things ...”); another omits the titles *De rerum* here and elsewhere. No. 41: *scripserunt* (“they wrote”); another: *decreverunt* (“they decreed”). No. 43: *singuli animo immortales* (“each individually immortal in mind”); another: *singulari animo mortales* (“mortal in a single mind”). Likewise, *impares* (“unequal”); another: *pares* (“equal”). Likewise, *ad voluptates ... caduci* (“liable to pleasures”); another: *ad voluntatem Dei vita caduci* (“liable in life to the will of God”). Likewise, *queruli* (“complaining”); another: *quasi soli* (“as though alone”). No. 53: *confert decentiam* (“contributes seemliness”); another: *conferat dignoscentiam* (“may contribute discernment”). No. 55: *aggeribus* (“embankments”); another: *custodiarum aggeribus* (“embankments of the guard-posts”). Likewise, *aer ictus* (“struck air”); another: *aer erectus* (“raised air”). No. 57: *defluendi* (“of flowing down”); another: *defluentis* (“of what flows down”). No. 61: *partes sunt* (“are parts”); another: *arces sunt* (“are citadels”). No. 68: *in circulorum ...* (“in [the arrangement] of circles”); another: “They have been arranged in the grouping of circles in this manner.” No. 70: *admisisse* (“to have admitted”); another: *adivisse* (“to have approached”). No. 74: *et actionem* (“and action”); another: “and reason, and the power of the body from the twentieth [year].” No. 75: *quadragesimo* (“fortieth”); another: *quadragesimo nono* (“forty-ninth”). No. 78: *inducunt* (“they bring in”); another: *induunt* (“they clothe”). No. 80: *potestatem* (“power”); another: *possibilitatem* (“possibility”). Likewise, *pubertatem, etc.* (“puberty, etc.”); another: “But, having passed puberty, they immediately become adolescents.” No. 82: *mollier* (“more gently”); another: *mollior* (“gentler”). No. 83: *virilitate* (“manhood”); another: *viriditate* (“greenness”). No. 93: *caro est, quae proprie* (“flesh is that which properly ...”); another: “All flesh is body, but not every body is flesh; rather, flesh is so called because properly ...” Likewise, *non subjaceat* (“does not lie subject”); another omits *non*. No. 95: *sopiri* (“to be lulled to sleep”); another: *separari* (“to be separated”). No. 98: *corporis* (“of the body”); perhaps *corpori* (“to the body”). No. 101: *sive colore* (“or by color”); another: *sine calore* (“without heat”). No. 103: *Deus esset* (“God might be”); another: *Deus non esset* (“God might not be”). No. 104: *dixerunt*, etc. (“they said,” etc.); another: “They said: the rational faculty, by which it desires an invisible thing; the irascible faculty, by which impulses of anger are corrected and amended; the appetitive faculty, by which ...,” etc. No. 107: *non concipiuntur* (“are not conceived”); another omits *non*. Likewise, *alteram propositionem destruit* (“destroys the other proposition”); another: *alienae propositioni deseruit* (“serves a foreign proposition”). No. 109: *procedens* (“proceeding”); another: *descendens* (“descending”). No. 112: *exaltat* (“exalts”); another: *exsultat* (“exults”). No. 113: *lapsam* (“fallen”); another: *lassam* (“weary”). Likewise, *victores ultimo* (“the victors at last”); another: *victores ultimus* (“the last victor”). No. 115: *effectum* (“effect”); another: *affectum* (“affection”). Wisdom”); another: “From words; wisdom from judgments—but wisdom.” Likewise, *indiserta* (“inarticulate”); Grialius has *indiscreta* (“indiscriminate”), which I think is an error. No. 153: *hac*, etc. (“this,” etc.); another: “This, as someone says: just as iron [is] poison, so eloquence arms.” No. 156: *referre* (“to report”); another: *deferre* (“to defer”), which may be better. No. 158: *restinguit* (“extinguishes”); another: *restringit* (“restrains”). No. 160: *studioque* (“and zeal”); another: *studioque boni* (“and zeal for the good”). Likewise, *tenetur* (“is held”); another: *terretur* (“is frightened”). No. 161: *octo sunt* (“there are eight”); another: *septem sunt* (“there are seven”). Likewise, *et harum*, etc. (“and of these,” etc.); another: “And their queen is drunkenness and pride.” No. 165: *dum quemlibet* (“while anyone”); another: *dum quia non libet* (“while, because it is not pleasing”). Superbiam* (“and through greed. Pride”).

**TO THE ALLEGORIES**

No. 1: *obteguntur* (“are covered”); another: *leguntur* (“are read”). Likewise, *annotata* (“noted”); another: *mutata* (“changed”). No. 5: *pastor ovium* (“shepherd of sheep”); another: “shepherd and ruler of the faithful.” No. 6: *aetate* (“in age”); another: *fratre* (“brother”). No. 81: *Dalila*. Grialius mistakenly has *Dalida*. No. 87: *sacerdotes* (“priests”); another: *sacerdotis* (“of the priest”), which is not displeasing.
