Thus the Vulgate, Luke 12:20. No. 211: *humanum ... schismatis* (“human ... of schism”); another: “human faith and religion, separated from one another into the dissension of schism.” No. 213: *humilitatis* (“of humility”); another: *per gratiam humilitatis* (“through the grace of humility”). Likewise, *commutabitur* (“will be changed”); another: *renovabitur* (“will be renewed”). No. 214: *curata* (“healed”); another: *erecta est* (“was raised up”). Likewise, *quibus ... accipimus* (“by which ... we receive”); another: “by which she had been bent, she is raised up, receiving ...” No. 216: *conversione* (“conversion”); another: *confessione* (“confession”). No. 221: *ad sacerdotes* (“to the priests”); another: *ad sacramentum* (“to the sacrament”). Likewise, *varietate* (“variety”); another: *vanitate* (“vanity”). No. 229: *accepta gratia* (“grace having been received”); another: *acceptam gratiam* (“received grace”). I use *utor* with the accusative here, as elsewhere. No. 231: *quod laboravit* (“what labored”); another: *qui inde plus laboravit* (“who labored more from that”). No. 233: *mutatur* (“is changed”); another: *misit* (“sent”). No. 234: *per Jesum deductum* (“led out through Jesus”); another: “led through Jesus in the Gospel before the one brought out of Egypt.” No. 239: *angelo* (“by an angel”); another: *piscina illa* (“by that pool”). No. 240: *vitiatum* (“corrupted”); another: *venumdatum* (“sold”). No. 241: *quatriduanum* (“of four days”); another: *triduanum* (“of three days”). Likewise, *propago mortis* (“offspring of death”); another: *pro plaga mortis* (“for the wound of death”). Likewise, *contemptus* (“contempt”); another: *tempus* (“time”). No. 242: *servus* (“servant”); another: *similis* (“like”). No. 244: *Barabbas*. The Florentine manuscript has *Barrabas*, with this note: “If it is read with two *r*s, it means ‘son of the master,’ because *rabbi* means ‘master’; but if with one *r*, it means ‘son of the father,’ because in Hebrew *barabas* means ‘father.’” No. 246: *peregrinus* (“pilgrim”); another: *ductor* (“leader”). No. 250: *per quam* (“through which”); another: *in qua* (“in which”).

**ON THE BIRTH AND DEATH OF THE FATHERS**

No. 1: *sententiali brevitate* (“with concise statement”); another: *sententia, et libri novitate* (“with the substance of the statement and the novelty of the book”). Likewise, *notata* (“marked”); another: *sociata* (“joined”). Likewise, *leguntur* (“are read”); another: “they are read, those who hold precedence in the praises of Scripture.” No. 2: *dominandi* (“of ruling”); another: *dominatus* (“rule”). No. 3: *florentis* (“flourishing”); another: *fluentis* (“flowing”). Likewise, *fecunda ... vere* (“truly fruitful”); another: “she was continually made fruitful by perpetual greenness.” No. 4: *exsulem*, etc. (“an exile,” etc.); another: “she groaned, having been expelled from the joys of paradise and overcome by the labor of death.” No. 6: *non silens* (“not silent”); another: *nobilis* (“noble”). No. 7: *angustias* (“straits”); another: *insaniam* (“madness”). Likewise, *contractibus* (“by contacts”); another: *contactibus* (“by touches”), which I think genuine in place of “contagions.” Likewise, *expulsus* (“expelled”); another: *exclusus* (“excluded”), namely, into an equal dwelling-place of blessed life. Likewise, *restituet*, etc. (“he will restore,” etc.); another: “he will be restored with Elijah to the condition of mortal life.” I think this is correct, so that *restiturus* (“about to restore”) stands for *restituendus* (“to be restored”) in Isidorian usage. No. 8: *iste jussus* (“this man, ordered”); another: *iste justus* (“this just man”). Likewise, *nec horruit* (“nor did he shudder”); another: “nor did he shudder at the turbulent flood of the deluge.” No. 9: *edocetur* (“is instructed”); another: *educitur* (“is led out”). Likewise, *ac laetus* (“and joyful”); another: *electusque* (“and chosen”); or *electisque* (“and with the chosen”). Perhaps *electasque* (“and the chosen [feminine]”). No. 10: *versis* (“having been turned”); another: *aversis* (“having been turned away”). No. 11: *vere* (“truly”); another: *jure* (“rightly”). No. 12: *Isaac annum* (“the year of Isaac”); another: *Abrahae annum* (“the year of Abraham”). No. 13: *peregrinatione* (“by wandering”); another: *peregrinis* (“by strangers”). Likewise, *victoria* (“victory”); another: *victoriae praeda* (“the spoils of victory”). No. 14: *in mysterio veneraretur* (“might be revered in mystery”); another: *in ministerio demonstraret* (“might be shown in service”). Likewise, *genere* (“by kind”); another: *germine* (“by offspring”). Likewise, *devotus* (“devoted”); another: *dilectus* (“beloved”). No. 15: *septimo* (“seventh”); another: *sexto* (“sixth”). Likewise, *marmore* (“marble”); another: “marble, and of very elegant workmanship.” No. 16: *qui fuit amicus Abrahae* (“who was Abraham’s friend”); another: *quae fuit curia Abrahae* (“which was Abraham’s court”). Likewise, *veneratione* (“by veneration”); another: *consecratione* (“by consecration”), or *sacrutione* (“by sanctification”), or *sacramentis* (“by sacraments”). No. 17: *amorem* (“love”); another: *timorem* (“fear”). No. 18: *et innocentem habitans domum* (“and inhabiting an innocent household”); another: “and rejecting an innocent household; having departed abroad, while he sought the company—perhaps, fled the company—of human beings, he earned the companionship of angels. But this man ...” Another reading: “innocently inhabiting a household, neither shaggy like his brother nor bloodthirsty like Edom. But this man ...” Likewise, *pertulit* (“endured”); another: *praecipuit* (“commanded”). Likewise, *dum consortio* (“while in companionship”); another: *dum consortium* (“while [seeking] companionship”), so that the accusative is used for the ablative. No. 19: *cum patribus suis* (“with his fathers”); another adds: “and he was brought back by his sons into the land of Canaan and buried beside his father.” No. 21: *possessionis* (“of possession”); another: *successionis* (“of succession”). No. 22: *fit ... futuro* (“he becomes ... future”); another: “by interpretation he becomes wise in the future assembly.” Likewise, *ad reddendam*, etc. (“for returning,” etc.); another: “for returning good in place of evil and for repaying grace.” Likewise, *fame depulsa necessitatis* (“necessity driven away by hunger”); another: *famis depulsa necessitate* (“necessity driven away by famine”). No. 23: *centum, et decem annis* (“one hundred and ten years”); another: *CXV annis* (“115 years”). Likewise, *quam nunc*, etc. (“which now,” etc.); another: “which is now called Sicham in both Latin and Greek.” No. 25: *primogenitus* (“firstborn”); another: *primitivus* (“primitive” or “first”). No. 27: *junctus* (“joined”); another: *unctus* (“anointed”). Likewise, *sortibus* (“by lots”); another: *sceptris* (“by scepters”), or *sceptis* (“by staffs”). No. 29: *de benedictionibus*, etc. (“from the blessings,” etc.); another: “giving the fruit of blessings and extending it to kings.” No. 31: *pro fratribus* (“for the brothers”); another: *pro filiis Israel* (“for the sons of Israel”). Likewise, *hostes gentesque* (“enemies and peoples”); another: *hostes gentis* (“enemies of the nation”). No. 32: *replens deliciis principes* (“filling princes with delights”); another: *repletus deliciis principum* (“filled with the delights of princes”). No. 33: *abundans* (“abounding”); another: *abundantior* (“more abundant”). No. 34: *escas principibus* (“food for princes”); another: “by his mystical strength he possesses the tribe, granting [it] to princes.” No. 36: *una cum Joseph*, etc. (“together with Joseph,” etc.); another: “together with his brother, Joseph possessed the tribe.” No. 37: *clarus* (“illustrious”); another: *stabilis* (“steadfast”). Likewise, *extemplo* (“immediately”); another: *exemplo* (“by example”). Likewise, *fidei lorica armatur* (“he is armed with the breastplate of faith”); another: *fidem religionis armans* (“arming religious faith”). Likewise, *doluit* (“he grieved”); another: *non doluit* (“he did not grieve”). Likewise, *inter supplicia* (“amid punishments”); another: *super dira supplicia* (“over dreadful punishments”). Likewise, *male suadentem* (“one giving evil advice”); another: *malesuadam* (“evil-advising”). Likewise, *duplicem claritatem* (“double brightness”); another: *multiplici claritate* (“manifold brightness”). No. 38: *in accentu* (“in accent”); another: *in accinctu* (“in being girded”). Likewise, *quadraginta* (“forty”); another: *septuaginta* (“seventy”); another: *septuaginta octo* (“seventy-eight”). Likewise, *quadraginta octo* (“forty-eight”); another: *sexaginta quatuor* (“sixty-four”). Likewise, *notatur* (“it is noted”); another adds: “noted, saying: ‘Amram’s mother, whose name was Jochebed, was from the tribe ...’” No. 39: *firmaret* (“might strengthen”); another: *formaret* (“might form”). Likewise, *insinuatam* (“introduced”); another: *in sinu*, or *in sinum positam* (“placed in the bosom,” or “placed into the bosom”). Likewise, *caloris* (“of heat”); another: *coloris* (“of color”). Likewise, *exquirendo* (“by seeking out”); another: *exsequendo* (“by carrying out”). Likewise, *interposuit* (“he interposed”); another: “he interposed [himself] before the angry man and the one consulting him, and imposed a limit on anger.” No. 40: *oppugnatores Israel* (“attackers of Israel”); another: *oppugnatum Israel* (“Israel attacked”); or *oppugnatoris* (“of the attacker”). Perhaps *propugnatoris Israel* (“of Israel’s defender”), or *oppugnatoris* without *Israel*. Likewise, *eorumque* (“and of them”); another: *ad ultimum* (“finally”). No. 42: *pertulit* (“endured”); another: *adimplevit* (“fulfilled”). No. 43: *non contigit* (“did not happen”); another omits *non*. Likewise, *superavit* (“overcame”); another: *separavit* (“separated”). Likewise, *Nebo*; another: *Thabor*. No. 45: *Moysi* (“of Moses”); another: *Moysi uterinus* (“Moses’ uterine [brother]”). Likewise, *electa* (“chosen”); another: *ejecta* (“cast out”). No. 46: *qua percussa Moyses* (“Moses, having struck her”); another: *quae percussa a Moyse* (“she who was struck by Moses”). No. 47: *expediret victoriam* (“might secure victory”); another: *expediretur victoria* (“victory might be secured”). Likewise, *resistere* (“to resist”); another: *stare* (“to stand”), or *sistere* (“to make stand”). Likewise, *inexpugnabiles* (“unassailable”); another: *inaestimabiles* (“immeasurable”). No. 49: *percussit* (“struck”); another: *perculit* (“stunned”); or *transfixit* (“pierced through”). Likewise, *praemiumque ... meruit* (“and earned a reward”); another: “he first earned the name of Israel, everlasting in memory.” Likewise, *placavit* (“appeased”); another: *accepit* (“received”). No. 50: *explorans* (“examining”); another: *exploratus* (“examined”). No. 51: *Galaadites* (“Gileadites”); another: *filius meretricis mulieris Galaaditis* (“son of a Gileadite prostitute”); another: *ortus ex tribu Gad* (“born from the tribe of Gad”). Likewise, *exsuperans* (“surpassing”); another: *spernens* (“despising”). No. 52: *rugientem* (“roaring”); another: *fugientem* (“fleeing”). Likewise, *mortui* (“of the dead”); another: *leonis mortui* (“of the dead lion”). Likewise, *vinctis* (“bound”); another: *junctis* (“joined”). Likewise, *rescissis* (“cut off”); another: *rescin­ctis* (“unbelted”). No. 53: *viginti* (“twenty”); another: *XXII* (“twenty-two”). No. 54: *connumeratus Moysi* (“numbered with Moses”); another: *cognominatus cum Moyse* (“named together with Moses”). No. 55: *in Bethlehem* (“in Bethlehem”); another: *secus Bethleem* (“near Bethlehem”). No. 57: *innocuum non tantum* (“not merely harmless”); another: “he did no harm, and not merely ...” Likewise, *quadragesimo* (“fortieth”); another: *quadragesimo, atque tertio* (“forty-third”). No. 58: *in Hebron* (“in Hebron”); another: *contra Hebron* (“opposite Hebron”). No. 59: *dispositionem* (“arrangement”); another: *disputationem* (“discussion”). Likewise, *cogitationes* (“thoughts”); another: “the rages of beasts and thoughts.” No. 61: *Elias* (“Elijah”); another: “Elijah, whose name is interpreted ‘the Lord God.’” Likewise, *disciplinae structus in sancta* (“formed in holy discipline”); another: *districtus in disciplinae sanctae* (“strict in holy discipline”). No. 62: *vel qui cum eo* (“or he who is with him”); another: “and Enoch, who is with him.” Likewise, *jacebunt* (“they will lie”); another: “they will lie for three days and six hours.” No. 63: *suscitati* (“raised up”); another: *suscitata* (“raised up,” feminine), that is, corpses. No. 65: *personavit* (“resounded”); another: *personuit* (“rang out”). No. 66: *vasculo* (“in a little vessel”); another: *solis vasculo* (“in the sun’s vessel”). Likewise, *insultantes sibi* (“mocking him”); another: *insultantes se* (“mocking themselves”). Likewise, *plebe refecta* (“the people restored”); another: *ubertate facta* (“abundance having been produced”). No. 67: *lavacro* (“by washing”); another: *repletum lavacro* (“filled with washing”). Likewise, *misso* (“having been sent”); another: “having been sent, to rebound, and ...” Likewise, *fecit* (“he made”); another: *coepit* (“he began”). Likewise, *praedixit* (“he foretold”); another: *praedicavit* (“he preached”). No. 68: *cadaveri* (“to the corpse”). Thus the manuscripts; Grialius has *cadaveris* (“of the corpse”). Likewise, *satis dignum*, etc. (“sufficiently worthy,” etc.); another: “he died sufficiently worthily, and, having been buried in Samaria, was regarded as worthy of veneration.” No. 69: *ex numero* (“from the number”); another: *ex genere* (“from the kind”). Likewise, *quaque ... abjecta* (“and each ... having been cast away”); another: “each of which he left and ...”; perhaps *abjecit* (“he cast away”), and ... No. 70: *tempestates* (“storms”); another: *potestates* (“powers”). No. 71: *ascendentem* (“ascending”); another: *recedentem* (“receding”), or *redientem* (“returning”), in place of *redeuntem* (“returning”). Likewise, *descendere* (“to descend”); another: *ascendere* (“to ascend”). Likewise, *secuit* (“he cut”); another: *serra secuit* (“he cut with a saw”). The Florentine Codex of Saint Mark presents the sentence as follows: “Finally, he is said to have been killed by Manasseh, his son-in-law, having been cut from the crown of his head through the middle.” No. 72: *non poteris*, etc. (“you will not be able,” etc.); another: “No one can see my face and live.” Likewise, *narraverat* (“he had related”); another: *noverat* (“he had known”). Likewise, *ac media*, etc. (“and the middle,” etc.); another: “and that he had seen only the middle of his appearance,” omitting *propheta scribat* (“let the prophet write”). In place of *mediam* (“middle”), another has *nudam* (“naked”). Likewise, *exposuerat* (“he had exposed”); another: *operuerat* (“he had covered”). No. 74: *colunt*, etc. (“they worship,” etc.); another: *coluerunt* (“they worshiped”), “whose tomb the same Egyptians still honor with distinguished observance.” No. 76: *Chaldaeorum* (“of the Chaldeans”); another: *Chaldaeorum sacerdotum* (“of the Chaldean priests”). Likewise, *Juda post* (“Judah afterward”); another: *Juda filio Josiae post* (“Judah, son of Josiah, afterward”). Likewise, *instantia* (“urgency”); another: *constantia* (“steadfastness”). No. 77: *gestis* (“deeds”); another: *portentis* (“portents”). Likewise, *mendacium* (“falsehood”); another: *judicium* (“judgment”). Likewise, *aspirationis* (“of aspiration”); another: *inspirationis* (“of inspiration”). No. 78: *subvertit* (“he overturned”); another: “he destroyed together with Cyrus.” Likewise, *montes a Borea* (“mountains from the north wind”); another: *montis arbores* (“trees of the mountain”). Likewise, *ad partem*, etc. (“toward the region,” etc.); another: “may not have flowed toward Parthia.” No. 79: *effecerit* (“he may have accomplished”); another: the same, *effecerit*. “And so it happened.” No. 80: *hic fuit*, etc. (“this man was,” etc.); another: “son of Pethuel, of the tribe ...” No. 81: *ruborum mora distringens* (“plucking the delay of brambles”); another: *sycomoros vellicans* (“plucking sycamores”), or *roborum moras distribuens* (“distributing the delays of oaks”). Likewise, *ad Australem plagam* (“toward the southern region”); another: *ab australi plaga* (“from the southern region”). Likewise, *eremi* (“of the desert”); another: *in eremo* (“in the desert”). Likewise, *usque ad mare*, etc. (“up to the sea,” etc.); the Alban Codex has: “up to the Red Sea, and from the Red Sea to the borders of the Indians.” No. 83: *prophetavit* (“he prophesied”); another: “he prophesied for five years.” No. 84: *de Geth, quae est in Opher* (“from Geth, which is in Opher”); another: *de Geth civitate* (“from the city of Geth”). Likewise, *sed magister* (“but a teacher”); another: *sed sors* (“but a lot”). No. 85: *in poenitentia* (“in repentance”); another: *in praesentia* (“in presence”). Likewise, *et saluti* (“and to salvation”); another: *et salutem* (“and salvation”). Likewise, *umbraculo* (“by a shade”); another: *umbram* (“a shadow”). No. 86: *magno projectus* (“thrown greatly”); another: *valde porrecto jactatus* (“tossed by something greatly extended”). No. 92: *egressionem* (“departure”); another: *regressionem* (“return”). Likewise, *praedicebat* (“he foretold”); another: *praedicabat* (“he preached”). No. 93: *esset* (“might be”); another: *gessit* (“he carried out”). Likewise, *praevaricatus* (“having transgressed”); another: *praedicaturus* (“about to preach”). No. 94: *gentium* (“of the nations”); another: *gentium alienigenarum* (“of foreign nations”). No. 95: *sepultumque*, etc. (“and buried,” etc.); another: “and he was buried at Bethel, and that prophet who ...” No. 97: *sacerdotis, qui*, etc. (“of the priest, who,” etc.); another: “of the priest, who, at the age of 130, after gathering the peoples, died.” No. 98: *lumine* (“by light”); another: *caecitatem luminis incurrit* (“he incurred blindness of light”). No. 99: *immolatis* (“sacrificed things”); another: *immolatitiis* (“sacrificial things”). No. 100: *restinxerunt* (“they extinguished”); another: “they also extinguished the furnace of the blazing fire.” No. 101: *fecit Jerusalem* (“he made Jerusalem”); another: *fecit templum in Jerusalem* (“he made the temple in Jerusalem”). No. 102: *jus quoque sacerdotum* (“also the right of the priests”); another: *ejusque sacerdotes* (“and its priests”). No. 103: *Susim*; another: *Susis*, which I think correct, so that *Susis* is indeclinable. Likewise, *cruci tradendum* (“to be handed over to the cross”); another: *trucidandum* (“to be slaughtered”). No. 104: *viris* (“for men”); another: *virorum* (“of men”). This is not displeasing. Likewise, *principem* (“a prince”); another: *principem saevum* (“a savage prince”). No. 108: *vox Verbi* (“the voice of the Word”); another: *dux Verbi* (“the leader of the Word”). No. 109: *Herodi prohiberet* (“he might forbid Herod”); another: *Herodem prohiberet* (“he might forbid Herod”). Likewise, *praemium* (“reward”); another: *promissum* (“promise”). No. 110: *sermone* (“by speech”); another: *nomine* (“by name”). No. 111: *clara stirps* (“illustrious offspring”); another: *clara ex stirpe* (“illustrious from an offspring”). Likewise, *pertransibit* (“will pass through”); another: *pertransiet* (“will pass over”). Likewise, *an pro verbo*, etc. (“or in place of *verbo*,” etc.); another: “or by a strong and sharp word, entirely ...” Likewise, *reperiatur* (“may be found”); another: *nec reperiatur* (“nor may be found”). No. 113: *Petrus* (“Peter”); another: *Petrus obediens, vel agnoscens* (“Peter, obedient or recognizing”). Likewise, *principatus, et caput* (“rule and head”); another: *firmamentum* (“foundation”). No. 115: *harum virtutum signis* (“by the signs of these virtues”); another: *his virtutibus magnus* (“great in these virtues”). Likewise, *mortuos animavit* (“he gave life to the dead”); another: *infirmos sanavit* (“he healed the sick”). Likewise, *reiteravit* (“he repeated”); another: *redintegravit* (“he restored”). No. 116: *viduam* (“widow”); another: *filiam* (“daughter”). No. 117: *sexto* (“sixth”); another: *septimo* (“seventh”). No. 119: *verbi* (“of the word”); another: *verbi Dei* (“of the word of God”). No. 121: *Pythonis*, etc. (“of the Python,” etc.); another: “he ordered the Python to depart and condemned it after it had departed.” No. 222: *nuditatem*, etc. (“nakedness,” etc.); another: “nakedness, shipwrecks by day and night in the deep sea, a thousand dangers from beasts, blows,” etc. No. 123: *sexto* (“sixth”); another: *septimo* (“seventh”). No. 128: *fuit* (“was”); the Patavine Codex has *fecit* (“did” or “made”). Likewise, *littoreaque ... fragmina* (“and fragments on the shore”); another: “and shore-rocks into fragments of gems.” No. 129: *sexagesimo septimo* (“sixty-seventh”); another: *LXVIII*, or *LXXVII* (“sixty-eighth,” or “seventy-seventh”). Likewise, *vetustatis* (“of old age”); another: *vetusto* (“old”); perhaps *vetustus* (“ancient”). No. 131: *Philippus* (“Philip”); another: “Philip, whose name is interpreted ‘mouth.’” Likewise, *unde et Petrus* (“hence also Peter”); another: *Andreae, et Petri* (“of Andrew and Peter”). Likewise, *Gallis* (“to the Gauls”); another: *Galatis*, or *Galliis* (“to the Galatians,” or “to the Gauls”). Likewise, *crucifixus ... obiit* (“crucified ... he died”); another: “he was crucified and died after being stoned.” Likewise, *requiescit* (“he rests”); another adds: “whose feast is on the Kalends of May.” No. 132: *Thomas*, etc. (“Thomas,” etc.); another: “Thomas, whose name is interpreted ‘the abyss of Christ,’ called *Didymus* in Greek.” No. 133: *ex Syra lingua suscipiens* (“receiving [his name] from the Syriac language”); another: “the Syriac language received [it]; it is interpreted ‘son of the one who hangs the waters.’” Likewise, *in sorte* (“in the lot”); another: *in sortem* (“into the lot”). Likewise, *conditur* (“he is buried”); another: “he was buried; his feast is believed to be on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.” No. 134: *Matthaeus* (“Matthew”); another: “Matthew, whose name is interpreted ‘given.’” Likewise, *electus*, etc. (“chosen,” etc.); another: “he was chosen and transferred to the apostleship.” No. 136: *in Jerusalem* (“in Jerusalem”); another adds: “Here he writes an epistle to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion of the nations, while he was in Jerusalem ...” No. 137: *frater* (“brother”); another adds: “whose name is interpreted ‘confessor.’” Likewise, *urbe* (“in the city”); another: “in the city, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.” No. 138: *septuaginta* (“seventy”); another: *septuaginta duobus* (“seventy-two”). No. 149: *spiritualis* (“spiritual”); another: *apostoli* (“of the apostle”). No. 150: *a Paulo apostolo* (“by the apostle Paul”); another: *a populo* (“by the people”). Likewise, *instruendas Cretae Ecclesias* (“to instruct the Churches of Crete”); another: *instituendas Cretae Ecclesias* (“to establish the Churches of Crete”).

**TO THE PREFACES**

[Col. 0438A]

No. 1: *Testamenti*, etc. (“of the Testament,” etc.); another: “of the Testament in the canon of the Catholic Church, both according to the ancient tradition of earlier writers and according to that of later writers.” No. 6: *acciderunt* (“occurred”); another: *accesserunt* (“were added”). No. 7: *enumerat* (“enumerates”); another: *commemorat* (“mentions”). No. 13: *apostolorum* (“of the apostles”); another: “of the apostles written by Luke.” No. 20: *ordinantur* (“are arranged”); another: *ordinantur ducentorum* (“two hundred are arranged”). No. 21: *signantur* (“are marked”); another adds: “their journeys too, up to the place where Moses was buried.” No. 23: *quoddam legis meditatorium* (“a certain meditation on the law”); another: *quemdam legis mediatorem* (“a certain mediator of the law”). Likewise, *omnium* (“of all”); another: “it contains everything, as though by repetition.” No. 26: *commemorant* (“they mention”); another: *memorantur* (“they are mentioned”). No. 29: *ab eis* (“by them”); another: *apud Hebraeos* (“among the Hebrews”). Likewise, *in duabus*, etc. (“in two,” etc.); another: “it was divided into two parts.” No. 30: *textus* (“text”); another: *tempus* (“time”). No. 32: *proferunt* (“they bring forth”); another: *prophetaverunt* (“they prophesied”). No. 33: *existimantur* (“are thought”); another: *existimant* (“they think”). No. 2: *quae media est* (“which is in the middle”); another: *quae in Ecclesia est* (“which is in the Church”). No. 4: *intuentes* (“looking upon”); another: *intrantes* (“entering”). No. 5: *praeteritorum* (“of past things”); another: *peccatorum* (“of sins”). # Complete Works of Saint Isidore

## Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, on the Catholic Faith from the Old and New Testament against the Jews, to Florentina, his sister

### Dedication Letter

Isidore to his holy sister Florentina.

> **Preface.** The title of this work has been taken from two Gothic codices, which are evidently more than six hundred years old. For the five other codices that we obtained for correcting these books differed very considerably. Braulio, speaking of these books in Isidore’s Life, says: “Against the Jews, at the request of his blood sister Florentina, abbess of virgins, he wrote two books, in which he approved everything that the Catholic faith believes from the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets.” Ildefonsus, speaking of the writings of illustrious men, says of Isidore: “He wrote two little books to his sister Florentina against the wickedness of the Jews.” — Mariana.
>
> *Ibid.* Or, “concerning his incorporation.” The major Tarragonese codex reads *corporatione* (“corporation”) instead of *incorporatione* (“incorporation”). We have followed the testimony of the other codices, especially since Hilary, in canon 6 on Matthew, used *incorporationem Verbi Dei* (“the incorporation of the Word of God”).
>
> After the letter prefixed to the work, most codices followed with a list of chapters. Since a similar list was lacking in the second book, we judged that it should also be removed here as superfluous, since it is sufficiently clear that even the chapter summaries prefixed by Isidore were not his, but were added at a later time; moreover, they are entirely absent from the minor Tarragonese codex, on which we chiefly relied. Accordingly, the reader will notice that certain items in them have been altered by us, according to our judgment, into better form. — Mar.
>
> *Ibid.* Since in the Isidorian collection we have brought together everything that can in any way be referred to the individual works of Saint Isidore, it would be superfluous to repeat here what we explained in chapter 66 concerning these two books against the Jews. There is a ridiculous error in the Florentine manuscript in folio—which I shall call the first, to distinguish it from the other, in quarto—in that it gives this heading: “Isidore, bishop of Toledo, to his holy sister Florentina,” although in the very title of the work immediately preceding it Isidore is called Bishop of Seville. The same error occurs in several other manuscripts of this work. We shall place our notes beneath Mariana’s, in our usual manner, together with various readings and certain interspersed fragments. Instead of *secundum divinitatem* (“according to divinity”), some have *secundum deitatem* (“according to deity”). And at the end of the preface, instead of *ut quam consortem perfruor* (“that I may make her with whom I enjoy fellowship”), which accords with Isidore’s style, some read *ut quam consortem*, using *utor* with the accusative. — Arevalus.

1. I have thought it right to set forth, according to the ability of my knowledge, a few of the many things that were foretold at different times in the books of the Old Testament concerning the birth of our Lord and Savior according to his divinity, or concerning his incorporation, and also concerning his passion and death, or his resurrection, kingdom, and judgment, 2 so that the authority of the prophets might strengthen the grace of faith and expose the ignorance of the unbelieving Jews. Therefore, holy sister, at your request I have dedicated these things to you for the cultivation of your devotion, so that, as I enjoy your fellowship in blood, I may make you a coheir of my labor also.

# Book One

## Chapter I. That Christ was begotten by God the Father

> **Note to Chapter I, no. 1.** Another reading: *Duri cordis* (“hard of heart”), or *duri corde* (“hard-hearted”). — Mar.
>
> *Ibid.* *Duricordes* (“hard-hearted”). Isidore used this same word in his Commentary on Genesis, chapter 25, no. 9, and in his Commentary on Exodus, chapter 55, no. 2. Thus anyone can readily see that this word ought to be retained. — Arev.

1. The Jews, denying Christ the Son of God with wicked unbelief—impious, hard-hearted, unbelieving toward the ancient prophets and closed against the new—prefer to remain ignorant of Christ’s coming rather than know it, and to deny rather than believe. They accept that the one who is to come will come, but refuse to acknowledge that he has already come. They read that he will rise again, but do not believe that he has risen.

> **Note to no. 2.** Another reading: *Quo genitor* (“by whom the begetter”), omitting *pater* (“Father”). — Mar.

2. But they pretend not to understand these things because they recognize that they have been fulfilled in their sacrilege. To refute their faithlessness, we have assembled certain testimonies from the Old Testament, by which they may recognize Christ of the nations, with the almighty Father himself bearing witness: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3). Therefore “from the womb” means from that innermost and incomprehensible substance of the Father, or from that divine and immeasurable mystery of the paternal breast, by which the Father, the begetter, brings forth the good Word from his heart.

3. As he himself says elsewhere: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Psalm 44:2). And elsewhere the Father himself says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). 3 This was not said of David, nor of any of the kings who followed him. For it is added: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” This was granted neither to David nor to the Hebrew people, but only to Christ, whose name has been spread among all nations, to whom kings obey and nations serve, as it is written elsewhere concerning him: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:11).

> **Note to no. 4.** “Whom you desire.” This is a passage from Malachi 3:1. In the Vulgate, however, we read: “Whom you wish,” and the Septuagint says: Ὅν ὑμεῖς θέλετε (“whom you desire”). More suitably and significantly, the force of the Hebrew verb is expressed by the word “desire”; and the fathers wanted not merely, but very ardently, yearned for the coming of Christ the Redeemer. The word derived from that verb does not signify will in the absolute sense, but good pleasure, longing, or desire. The Greeks commonly express this with the word τῆς εὐδοκίας (“of good pleasure”). And at Isaiah 58:3, where that noun occurs and we read, “Behold, on the day of your fast your will is found,” the Mozarabes read: “Behold, on the day of your fast your pleasure is found.” — Mar.

4. Likewise Solomon, wishing to acknowledge the name of the Father and the mystery of Christ’s birth according to his deity, thunders forth these words in Proverbs: “Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the boundaries of the earth? What is his name, or what is the name of his son, if you know?” (Proverbs 30:4).

> **Note to no. 5.** After “the Savior,” some manuscripts omit *esse* (“to be”). — Arev.

5. Seeing this Son of God, that impious king in Daniel said: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Daniel 3:92). We firmly believe, without the slightest doubt, that he is the Lord Savior. But it is objected that in Daniel this Son of God is also previously called an angel (Daniel 3:49). I agree. For Christ, too, the Son of God, is called an angel. Thus the prophet says of him: “The ruler whom you seek will come to his holy temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Malachi 3:1).

> **Note to no. 6.** Another reading: *Praeparavi* (“I have prepared”) instead of *paravi* (“I have prepared”); and *Peccaveritis* (“you will have sinned”) instead of *peccaveris* (“you will sin”). — Mar.

6. For Christ is called the Son of God insofar as he was begotten by the Father; but insofar as he is often read to have been sent by the Father to announce him to the patriarchs, he is called an angel. Concerning him the Father also testifies to the lawgiver, saying: “Behold, I send my angel, who will go before you and guard you on the way and bring you into the place that I have prepared. Observe him and heed his voice, and do not think him contemptible, for he will not forgive when you have sinned, and my name is in him” (Exodus 23:20).

7. For he is the Son who, always sent by the Father, appeared visibly to human beings. Isidore clearly holds the view common among the ancient Fathers: whenever, from the beginning of the world, God offered himself to human beings to be seen in human form, it was not the Father or the Holy Spirit who appeared, but the Son of God. Thus think Tertullian, in Book II Against Marcion; Clement of Alexandria, Book I of the *Paedagogue*, chapter 7; Irenaeus, Book IV Against the Heresies of Valentinus, chapter 17; Eusebius, at the beginning of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Hilary, Book XII on the Trinity; and Basil, Book I Against Eunomius. Therefore the Son of God spoke to Adam, as the Jerusalem Targum also indicates when it says at Genesis 3: “That is, the Word of the Lord God called Adam.” He rebuked Cain himself, appeared to Abraham, and wrestled with Jacob. The council of Sirmium, in canon 13, commanded that this be believed in these words: “If anyone says that it was not the Son who wrestled with Jacob as a man, but the unbegotten one, or his Father, let him be anathema.” Moreover, he spoke with Moses from the bush, led the children of Israel out of Egypt, and gave them laws in the desert. Cassianus confirms this with two testimonies in Book IV on the Incarnation: namely, Jude 5: “Knowing this once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe, and the angels, etc.”; and Paul, 1 Corinthians 10:9: “Nor let us test Christ, as some of them tested him, and perished by serpents.” — Mar.

7. Who, then, is this angel to whom God gave both his power and his name? If it is said that there is some other angelic power, it is impious to believe this. For “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88:7). Whoever is not equal in nature cannot be equal in name. For he is the Son who, always sent by the Father, appeared visibly to human beings. Therefore, from this mission, he is rightly called an angel. Isaiah, however, more clearly confirming that the Son was begotten by God, announces as follows: “The voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies” (Isaiah 66:6), namely, to those who do not believe, the Jews: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; and before her labor came, she brought forth a male child” (ibid., 7).

> **Note to no. 8.** Another reading has *uspiam* (“anywhere”) instead of *quidpiam* (“anything”). — Mar.

8. As though he were plainly saying: before the Virgin brought forth Christ in the flesh, the Father generated the Son in divinity; and before the time for the Virgin’s labor arrived, the Father begot him without time. Hence he says below: “Who has ever heard such a thing, or who has seen anything like it?” (Isaiah 66:8). Truly, because nothing of this kind, or anything similar, occurs among human beings, he then adds: “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not give birth myself? says the Lord; and shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren? says the Lord” (Isaiah 66:9). By all these testimonies the unbeliever must be compelled to choose one of two alternatives: either to believe that Christ is the Son of God, or to regard as liars the prophets who sang these things.

## Chapter II. That Christ was ineffably begotten by the Father before the ages

> **Note to Chapter II, no. 1.** *Dum* (“while”); another reading has *cum* (“when”). — Mar.
>
> *Ibid.* “His name endures before the sun, and his throne before the moon.” The passage is taken from Psalm 71:17: the first words according to the Vulgate edition, but the latter words from the Roman Psalter, which Isidore frequently uses. In the time of the Goths that Psalter was used in all the churches of Spain, as the Mozarabic breviary demonstrates, though with not a few alterations, in my opinion made by Isidore himself. For in his Life written by Braulio—in two certainly ancient codices—I find it written that he published a fourth translation of the Psalter, after the three famous ones prepared by Saint Jerome, according to Sigebert. We shall henceforth call this Psalter of Isidore, which the Mozarabes use, the Hispanic Psalter, in comparison with the Roman and Gallican Psalters. Throughout this work Isidore cites testimonies from all these Psalters, according as it was more convenient or as memory more readily supplied them. He also uses Jerome’s version and the ancient Latin Vulgate edition indiscriminately in the other books of divine Scripture, for both were in circulation in his time, as Gregory teaches at the beginning of the *Moralia*, and Isidore himself indicates in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4. Often also, as he did here, he combines a single testimony from various interpretations. — Mar.
>
> *Ibid.* “Eternal by his birth.” I have restored this reading from the Hagano edition, other editions, and manuscripts, since Grialius had *sua nativitate alternus* (“alternating by his birth”), which must be attributed to a typographical error. The words of the psalm in the Vulgate are only these: “His name endures before the sun.” In the ancient versions: “His name shall endure before the sun forever, and his throne before the moon.” I have subjected to examination Mariana’s opinion that Isidore published a fourth translation of the Psalter in *Isidoriana*, chapter 87. — Arev.

1. If it is asked when or how the Father begot the Son, the answer is: Why is the time at which the Son of God was begotten being sought, when he is eternal by his very birth? As it is written concerning him: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2). And again: “His name endures before the sun, and his throne before the moon” (Psalm 71:17).

> **Note to no. 2.** *Quod et* (“which also”); another reading has *sicut* (“as”). — Mar.
>
> *Ibid.* Another reading has *concepta* (“conceived,” feminine) instead of *conceptus* (“conceived,” masculine). — Mar.

Ibid. “Conceived.” Isidorus perhaps used the masculine gender so that it might be understood of the Son of God. Otherwise, *concepta* should be retained, as it appears in our manuscripts and in the older editions. AREV.]

2. But the Father also testifies that he begot him before the morning star—that is, before all times—which the Son of God himself, the Word, Power, and Wisdom, confirms concerning his birth, saying: “The depths did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the springs of the waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet been established with their massive weight; before the hills I was being brought forth. He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the hinges of the world; when he was preparing the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the depths with a fixed law and circle; when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things” (Prov. VIII, 24).

6 [Note: [Col. 0454C]

3. Others read *did he learn*, instead of *he says*. MAR.

Ibid. “That he should be begotten.” Here too Grialius had the error *that he should be the same kind*, which I corrected on the basis of the sense and of the printed editions and manuscripts. AREV.]

3. By such authority, therefore, it is declared that the Son was begotten by the Father before all ages, since all things are known to have been created by the Father through him. Yet the question is raised again: how was he begotten, when neither the Apostle speaks of the mysteries of his sacred birth, nor the prophet discovers them, nor the angel knows them, nor any creature comprehends them? Isaiah testifies to this when he says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8). Therefore, if the prophet could not recount his birth, who will claim to know how the Son could be generated by the Father?

4. Hence comes the statement in the Book of Job: “Wisdom—of God the Father—from where will you find it? For it is hidden from the eyes of human beings and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job XXVIII, 20), that is, it is unknown even to the angels themselves. Likewise there: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed?” (Ecclus. I, 7)—that is, the origin of the Son of God. Therefore, since this surpasses even the understanding and knowledge of the angels, what human being can describe it?

[Col. 0453C] 5. It is clear, however, that only the Father knows how he begot the Son, and the Son knows how he was begotten by the Father. For if the manner of the Son’s begetting is sought, on the grounds that a son is born only from two, let this condition of generation belong, I say, to the perishable origin of mortals; Christ, however, shone forth from the Father as radiance from light, as a word from the mouth, as wisdom from the heart.

CHAPTER III. That Christ is God and Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0454C]

CHAP. III. No. 1. Others read *of direction*, instead of *of righteousness*. MAR.

Ibid. “Therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.” Who, then, is this God anointed by God? You see the force of the argument placed in the repetition of the word *God*, so that in the first occurrence it is vocative and refers to Christ, while in the second it is nominative and refers to the Father. MAR.

Ibid. Mariana rightly criticized Pagninus in his treatise in defense of the Vulgate edition, chap. 25, because he translated this passage in the following way: “Therefore the Lord your God anointed you with the oil of gladness”; and thus weakened the argument by which the most holy Fathers—Ambrose, Athanasius, Jerome, Augustine, Isidore here, and others—confirmed that the Father who anoints is distinct from the Son who is anointed. AREV.]

1. Having established the mystery of Christ’s divine birth, let us next demonstrate, through examples drawn from the sacred Scriptures, that he is also God and Lord. If Christ is not God, to whom is it said in the Psalms: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a rod of righteousness is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 7)?

2. Who, then, is this God anointed by God? Let the Jews answer us. Behold, God is said to have been anointed by God, and plainly Christ is indicated by that anointing, since God is presented as anointed. When you hear “God anointed,” understand Christ; for Christ is named from *chrism*, that is, from anointing.

Through Isaiah, the Father testifies that this Christ, under the persona of Cyrus, king of the Persians, is God and Lord, saying: “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and turn the backs of kings; I will open doors before him, and the gates shall not be closed. I shall go before you, and I shall humble the glorious ones of the earth. I shall break bronze doors and shatter iron bars, and I shall give you hidden treasures and secret things kept in hiding, so that you may know that I am the Lord who calls you by your name, the God of Israel” (Isa. XLV, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0454D]

3. Christ was prophesied in the persona of Cyrus. Isidorus maintains that Isaiah’s words, “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, Cyrus” (Isa. XLV, 1), are not to be understood of Cyrus, but solely of Christ under the name of Cyrus, since it would seem absurd for Cyrus, who served the superstition of the gods, to be called Christ, Lord, and God. For Isidorus himself judged that the words which follow—“I who call you by your name, the God of Israel”—must refer to the one of whom he had just spoken and whom he had called Christ. Moreover, the translation of the Septuagint interpreters does not read, “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, Cyrus,” but, “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, the Lord.” Lactantius cited this testimony in this form in Book IV, chapter 12, of *The Divine Institutes*.

Jerome, however, in his commentary on that passage of Isaiah, considers the reading which Isidorus says was found in the Septuagint to be corrupt. He holds that the Greek should be read as follows: οὕτως λέγει Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Κυρίῳ μοῦ Κύρῳ—“Thus says the Lord God to my Lord Cyrus.” By the addition of a single letter in place of Κύρῳ, that is, *Cyrus*, some read Κυρίῳ, that is, *Lord*. Accordingly, both Jerome and most other commentators think that Isaiah’s prophecy is to be understood only of Cyrus. Indeed, Josephus, in Book XI, chapter 1, of *The Antiquities*, asserts that Cyrus, moved by this prophecy, sent the Jews back to their homeland.

The ancient Hebrew commentators favor Isidorus, judging that this passage should be understood of the true Messiah. I, however, maintain that the passage can be understood of both: of Cyrus according to its historical sense, and of Christ allegorically. MAR.

Ibid. “Which is specifically understood in the person of Christ our Lord.” Perhaps *spiritually* should be read instead of *specifically*, since both adverbs are commonly written with the same abbreviation. In the larger Tarraconensian manuscript the following words appeared: “Let us read Xenophon’s history of the eight books concerning Cyrus the Elder, and we shall see the prophecy fulfilled. For what city was not open to him? What king did he not subject? Etc.” Since these words were absent from the other manuscripts and contrary to Isidore’s purpose, we judged that they had plainly been transferred from Jerome’s commentary on this passage by someone else and ought to be omitted. MAR.

Ibid. In Codex Palatinus 278, *specifically* is clearly read, without ligature; Mariana thought it should be changed to *spiritually*. AREV.]

3. Christ, therefore, was prophesied in the persona of Cyrus, since the nations and kingdoms were subjected to him in faith. Moreover, no Cyrus is named in the kingdom of Israel. But if anyone believes that this was prophesied of Cyrus, king of the Persians, let him recognize that it is absurd and profane [8] that a wicked man devoted to idolatry should be called Christ, God, and Lord. Hence the Septuagint does not have “to my Christ, Cyrus,” but “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, the Lord.” This is understood specifically in the person of Christ our Lord.

4. If Christ is not God, let the Jews tell us to which God God spoke in Genesis when he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” For it follows: “And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him” (Gen. I, 26). Let them therefore ask which God created him, or in whose image he fashioned the man whom he created.

[Note: [Col. 0456C]

5. In whose image man is believed to have been created. Isidorus takes “image” here in a personal sense and understands that man was created according to the model and image that is the Son, following Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chap. 7; Eusebius, Book XI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 12; and Procopius on Genesis II. Augustine, however, undertook to refute this opinion in Book III, chap. 19, of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. Cyril likewise did not hesitate to call it foolish in Book I *Against Julian*.

Perhaps at that time the Arians were abusing this interpretation as a defense of their error and to separate the persons of the Trinity; otherwise there is no danger in it. Certainly, more recent theologians understand man to have been created in the image of the whole Trinity, and they maintain that the word “image” in these words signifies not an image in God but rather one impressed in us, so that “Let us make man in our image” is equivalent to saying: “Let us make one who is our image, formed and conformed according to the model of our essence.”

As for the reading, in the words immediately following, where we printed “unless in the image of him who has one image with God,” three manuscripts read: “whose image is one with God.” The larger Tarraconensian manuscript reads: “whose image is with God.” MAR.]

5. But if they answer, “In the image of the angels,” does an angel have an image equal to God, when the image of a creature is so far removed from the one who created it? Or could an angel have made man together with God? To think so would be the height of folly. To whom, then, is it said, or in whose image is man believed to have been created, unless in the image of him who has one image with God and one name of divinity?

9 [Note: [Col. 0456D]

6. In this interpretation no one doubts that the second person is intended. In the words of Genesis XIX, 24—“The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and sulfur from the Lord”—Isidorus refers the repetition of the word *Lord* to the first and second persons of the Trinity. Before him this had been done by Eusebius, Book I, chap. 1, of *Ecclesiastical History*; Irenaeus, Book III, chap. 6; Basil, Book V *Against Eunomius*; Pope Marcellinus, in his letter to Bishop Solomon; and Jerome, in his commentary on Hosea I. MAR.]

6. Likewise, if Christ is not the Lord, which Lord rained fire upon Sodom from the Lord? For Genesis says: “And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord” (Gen. XIX, 24). In this interpretation no one doubts that the second person is intended. For who is that Lord from the Lord, unless undoubtedly the Son from the Father, who was always accustomed to descend and ascend after being sent by the same Father? By this testimony both the divinity and the distinction between the persons of the Father and the Son are demonstrated more clearly than by daylight.

7. Likewise, if Christ is not the Lord, of whom did David say in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1)? Although that same Christ is, according to the flesh, the son of David, in spirit he is nevertheless his Lord and God.

If Christ is not the Lord, of whom did David say in the Books of Kings: “The man to whom it was revealed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent psalmist of Israel, said: The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was through my tongue” (II Kings XXIII, 1)?

8. Likewise, if Christ is not the Lord, who is that Lord of hosts who is sent by the Lord of hosts, as he himself says through Zechariah: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: After glory he sent me to the nations that have despoiled you. For whoever touches you touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I shall raise my hand against them, and they shall become booty for those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me” (Zech. II, 8)?

[Note: [Col. 0456D]

9. Others read, “Come now, let us see.” MAR.

Ibid. Others read, “became obedient,” instead of “was made obedient.” MAR.]

9. See now whose voice this is, unless it is the Savior’s, since almighty God testifies that he was sent by the almighty Father. He was sent to the nations after the glory of his divinity, which he possessed with the Father, when “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 7).

He also speaks in what follows, saying: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I am coming, and I shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord; and many nations shall join themselves to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people, and I shall dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you” (Zech. II, 10).

[Note: [Col. 0457C]

10. “To show that the same Spirit is God.” After these words, the Hispanic manuscript continued: “But from this these people do not think Christ to be God. And many other things.” Since the passage was interrupted and corrupted by a lacuna, was absent from the other manuscripts, and is repeated almost word for word at the beginning of the next chapter, we moved it from this place as an addition. Nevertheless, we appended the fifth chapter, which appears in the printed manuscripts, to the end of chapter 3, following the Hispanic manuscript, since it seemed to connect more conveniently there; we did so without introducing a new division of the chapter. In the other manuscripts all these passages were entirely absent, and for that reason they might have seemed suspect. MAR.

Ibid. The words which Mariana found in the Hispanic manuscript are also found in Florentine Codex 1, in the Barberinian manuscript dating from approximately the eighth century, and in many other manuscripts; they therefore ought not to be omitted altogether. They are as follows: “[lacuna] would show that he is God. But from this these people do not think Christ to be God, because on Mount Sinai they heard the voice of God thundering: ‘Hear, Israel,’ it says, ‘the Lord your God is one’; and again: ‘I am God, and there is no other besides me.’ And this: ‘I am God, and I do not change, and I shall not give my glory to another.’ When, therefore, they read these things, blinded by the error of their unbelief, they do not believe that Christ is God. Let them therefore recognize that these statements had been proclaimed to them at that time, lest perhaps, departing from the unity of faith, they pass over to many fabricated gods and worship the idols of the nations—which they did when they expressly judged Christ to be God by the testimonies of the prophets.”

For “had been foretold,” others have “had been proclaimed,” and for “specifically,” *spiritually*. These two adverbs are frequently confused in the manuscripts. AREV.]

10. Who, then, is this Lord of hosts sent by the Lord of hosts, unless it is the same Lord Jesus Christ? There remains the question of the Holy Spirit, concerning whose divinity Jacob speaks as follows: “Since the spirit of God is in me, the spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life. Behold, God made me as he made you” (Job. XXXIII, 4). For of the one concerning whom he had said, “The Spirit of the Lord made me,” he added again, “Behold, God made me as he made you,” in order to show that the same Spirit is God.

CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Significance of the Trinity.

[Col. 0457B] [Note: [Col. 0458C]

CHAP. IV. No. 1. Others have “to be one God” twice, instead of “to be God.” MAR.]

1. It is evident from the words of the Old Testament that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are God. But from this these people do not consider the Son and the Holy Spirit to be God, because on Mount Sinai they heard the voice of God thundering: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God, is one” (Deut. VI, 4); not understanding that in the Trinity there is one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—not three gods, but one name of undivided majesty in three persons.

[Note: [Col. 0458D]

2. “In the Second Book of Kings.” In the Hispanic and smaller Tarraconensian manuscripts it read, “also in the First Book of Kings.” This may perhaps be Isidorus’s genuine reading. For, as Junilius teaches in Book *On the Parts of the Divine Law*, chap. 12, and Jerome in the *Galeate Prologue*, the Hebrews count only two Books of Kings: namely, the Book of Samuel, which includes the First and Second Books, and the Book of Kings, which contains the Third and Fourth. Isidorus himself followed this method of counting in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chap. 1.

Since, however, other manuscripts differ, and Isidorus himself speaks of four Books of Kings in the *Book of Prologues*, we judged the differing reading preferable, as more consistent with the Vulgate edition and common usage. MAR.]

2. Let us therefore seek this same Trinity in the Scriptures of the Old Testament. In the Second Book of Kings it is written: “David, son of Jesse, said: The man to whom it was revealed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent psalmist of Israel, said: The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was through my tongue.” He then added who he was: “The God of Israel spoke to me; the strong one of Israel, the ruler of human beings, the just one” (II Kings XXIII, 1).

3. By saying “the Christ of the God of Jacob,” he displayed both the Son and the Father. Likewise, by saying “the Spirit of the Lord spoke through me,” he clearly disclosed the Holy Spirit. The same is found in the Psalms: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6). In the person of the Lord we understand the Father; in the Word we believe the Son; in the spirit of his mouth we understand the Holy Spirit. By this testimony both the number of the Trinity and the fellowship of their cooperation are revealed.

[Note: [Col. 0458D]

4. Others read, “the Spirit of the Lord was borne.” Nevertheless, there. MAR.]

4. Likewise, the same prophet says in what follows: “He will send his word and melt them; his Spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (Ps. CXLVII, 18). Behold the three: the Father who sends, the Word who is sent, and his Spirit who blows.

When Genesis likewise says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. I, 1–2), the Father is understood under the name of God; the Son is recognized in “the beginning,” who says: “In the beginning of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will” (Ps. XXXIX, 8–9). For “God spoke, and God made”; but in the one who was borne over the waters the Holy Spirit is signified.

5. When God says there, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), the plurality of persons is an evident signification of the Trinity. Yet, in order to show the unity of the Godhead, he immediately adds: “God made man in his image and likeness.” And when the same God says, “Behold, Adam has become like one of us,” the very plurality of the persons demonstrates the mystery of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0458D]

6. “Concerning the third person.” That is, one of the three persons. Grialius’s learned note on Exodus XLII, no. 3, explains this manner of speaking. AREV.]

6. The prophet Haggai also disclosed the mystery of this Trinity in the following way, speaking in the person of the Lord: “My Spirit shall be in your midst” (Hag. II, 6, 8). Behold God speaking; behold his Spirit. After this he added the following concerning the third person, that is, the Son: “For behold, I shall shake heaven and earth, and the Desired One of all nations shall come.”

7. In Isaiah also the distinction of the Trinity is shown under the proper person of each, when the same Son says: “I am the first, and I am the last; my hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens” (Isa. XLVIII, 12–13, 16). “I have not spoken from the beginning in secret; from the time before it came to be, I was there.” He then added: “And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.” Behold two persons, the Lord and his Spirit, who send, and the third person, the same Lord, who is sent.

8. Elsewhere the significance of the Trinity is likewise demonstrated through the same prophet. “Behold,” he says, “my servant; I shall receive him, my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased; I have given my Spirit upon him” (Isa. XLII, 1). The Father calls the beloved Son a servant, upon whom he has given his Spirit. Concerning him the Lord Jesus Christ himself testifies in his own voice: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.”

9. In another passage the same Isaiah, comprehending the whole Trinity in the number of fingers, proclaims as follows: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with his span? Who has suspended the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. XL, 12). In the three fingers the prophet, as though on a scale of mystery, weighed the threefold equality of divine omnipotence; and from the equality of power he declared the cooperation of might and the unity of substance, which is one and the same in the Trinity.

10. The same prophet testifies elsewhere that he had recognized the mystery of this Trinity, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne; the Seraphim stood above it, one having six wings and another having six wings; with two they veiled his face, with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew” (Isa. VI, 1). In order to show him threefold in persons and one in divinity, he goes on to say: “And they cried out, one to another, and said: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

[Note: [Col. 0459C]

11. For what does “THRICE HOLY” indicate, unless it shows the glory of the same threefold Omnipotence and signifies the divinity of the three persons? The manuscripts varied greatly at this point. The Hispanic manuscript reads: “Unless the glory of the same threefold Omnipotence, which was manifested in the divinity of the three persons, is the sanctification.” The smaller Tarraconensian manuscript reads: “Unless the glory of the same Threefold Omnipotence is manifested, yet as the signification of the God of the three persons.” Another printed copy reads: “Unless the glory of the same threefold Omnipotence, which was manifested in the divinity of the three persons, is the sanctification.” The reading we printed was taken from the Parisian and larger Tarraconensian manuscripts. I suspect that it should read: “For what does ‘thrice Holy’ indicate, unless the glory of the same threefold Omnipotence is manifested, signified in the divinity of the three persons?” MAR.

Ibid. Florentine Codex 1 and others omit this and the following number—or rather, they place them earlier—and add here: “For in order that the Trinity of persons might be displayed, ‘Holy’ is said three times. But so that it might be evident that the substance of the Trinity is one, it is not called ‘Lord of Sabaoth,’ but ‘Lord.’ David also says: ‘May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.’ Although he had named God three times, in order to show that this one is God, he added: ‘And may all the ends of the earth fear him.’ We have noted these few things concerning the Trinity for the sake of brevity, while very many others are disclosed at length in the books of the Scriptures.” AREV.]

11. Behold, the heavenly host exults in a threefold sanctification under one confession; the Seraphim proclaim the one glory of the Trinity by a threefold repetition. For what does “thrice Holy” indicate, unless the glory of the same threefold Omnipotence is manifested as the signification of the divinity of the three persons? Yet, just as there are three persons, so three gods are not to be believed; rather, one divinity is to be proclaimed in those persons, according to the statement of Moses: “Hear, Israel: God, your God, is one God” (Deut. VI, 4). And again: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. XLV, 21).

12. Against this the destructive unbelief of the Jews objects, saying: “If the Father is God and the Son is God, then there are two gods and not one God.” Let them therefore hear Isaiah speaking for me, who calls both persons one God: “You are God, and in you is God.” In saying “You are God,” he indicates the Father; in adding “In you is God,” he declares the Son.

13. Nevertheless, in order to show that the same Father and Son are one God, he added: “There is no God besides you; truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel.” Elsewhere also the united name of the Father and the Son is confirmed, when the Father himself testifies to the lawgiver Moses: “Pay attention to him, and do not disobey him; for my name is in him.”

14 CHAPTER V. That the Son of God, who is God, became human.

[Note: [Col. 0460D]

CHAP. V. No. 1. Others read *shoulders*, instead of *shoulder*. MAR.]

1. Thus far we have shown the mystery of Christ’s heavenly birth and the significance of the divine Trinity. From this point onward, by the authority of Scripture, let us demonstrate that the same Son of God was born in the flesh, first making clear that the Son of God was incarnate and became human for our salvation. Thus Isaiah proclaims concerning him: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and his principate has been placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His rule shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of his peace” (Isa. IX, 6).

2. Christ is a child because he is human; and he was born for us, not for himself. His becoming human benefited us, and therefore he was born for us. A son, moreover, was given to us—but whose son, if not the Son of God? “His principate is upon his shoulder”: either because he himself carried the cross upon his own shoulders, or because Pilate wrote the title of his kingdom upon his shoulders and head.

[Note: [Col. 0460D]

3. Others read *to call upon*, instead of *to be called*. MAR.

Ibid. “You made him a little lower than the angels.” The larger Tarraconensian manuscript reads: “You made him a little lower than God.” In the Hebrew Psalm VIII, 6, the reading is: “You made him a little lower than *Elohim*.” This term often signifies God, but sometimes also angels, so that both interpretations are possible. The Septuagint said, “You made him a little lower than the angels,” which Paul followed in Hebrews II, 7. Jerome, however, in his translation, said: “You made him a little lower than God.” MAR.

Ibid. Again, indicating his future birth in the flesh, he added: “And as though from the womb, the dew of your youth shall arise for you.” This passage is from Psalm CIX, 3. Here I am surprised that Isidorus, after citing the words “Before the morning star I begot you,” added, as though they were the continuation, “And like dew from the womb the dew of your youth shall arise for you,” since the latter is rather a different translation of the same passage in Jerome’s version. Through the same lapse of memory, below, in chapter 10, he joined the two translations, where he says: “Before the morning star I begot you, and like dew from the womb the dew of your youth shall arise for you.” MAR.]

3. Therefore let the impious Jews be ashamed and acknowledge that Christ, the Son of the living God, was called the one who was born and, through the assumption of a body, became a child. Of him David says: “You made him a little lower than the angels,” because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II, 6). When the Father said to him in the Psalms concerning that eternal birth, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3), he again indicated his future birth in the flesh, adding: “And as though from the womb, the dew of your youth shall arise for you.”

[Note: [Col. 0461D]

4. “But to Zion it shall be said: A man and a man was born in her,” etc. This passage is from Psalm LXXXVI, 5, according to Jerome’s version. The Gothic manuscripts, following the Roman Psalter translation, read: “The mother Zion shall say: A man and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” Perhaps this was Isidorus’s genuine reading. MAR.

Ibid. Others read *the Most High*, instead of *the Highest*, and *peoples*, instead of *to the peoples*. MAR.

Ibid. In Saint Jerome’s version from the Hebrew it reads: “The Lord counted, writing down the peoples: This one was born there for you.” Accordingly, *peoples* could be restored on the basis of many of Isidorus’s manuscripts. AREV.]

4. The Holy Spirit foretold this incorporation of the Son of God in the Psalms as follows: “But to Zion it shall be said: A man and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her.” Behold, the one who is born in Zion, and who in that same city was made most humble, is himself the one who founded it as the Most High. And because he is also the Lord, it follows: “The Lord counted, writing down the peoples: This one was born there.” Who is this one? A man, clearly; and the Most High; and the Lord. A man, because he became human. The Most High, because the heavens and angels receive him above themselves. The Lord, because every creature of heaven and earth serves him.

5. But whenever the enemies of Christ hear all this prophecy of his birth, they are trapped; having nothing to put forward, they argue that Christ has not yet come, of whom all these things were sung beforehand by the prophetic mouths. Let us therefore determine the time of Christ’s birth: has it already arrived, or is he still to be awaited? In Daniel, then, the time of his coming is shown with complete certainty; the years are counted, his manifest signs are proclaimed, and the future destruction of the Jews after his coming and death is there revealed with complete certainty.

[Note: [Col. 0462D]

6. Ecclesiastical writers frequently discuss Daniel’s seventy weeks. See Cotelerius, *Patres apostolici*, vol. I, p. 49. Calmet published a dissertation on this subject before his commentary on Daniel; and in the *Sacred Library*, prefixed to his *Biblical Dictionary*, he identifies the principal ancient and modern authors who have dealt with this question. AREV.]

6. Thus the angel says to him: “Daniel, pay attention to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX, 23). If these seventy weeks are counted from Daniel’s time, there is no doubt that the Holy of Holies, the Lord Jesus Christ, is known to have come long ago.

7. For in the sacred writings a week is completed in seven years, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall count seven weeks of years” (Lev. XXV, 8)—that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine years. Likewise, seven times seventy make four hundred ninety. Therefore it must be believed that this many years elapsed from Daniel to Christ. From the time of Daniel the prophet until the present, therefore, more than one hundred forty weeks are counted. Hence Christ has already come, whom the prophetic word announced.

8. For after the seventy weeks Christ is shown both to have been born and to have suffered; Jerusalem is shown to have been brought to destruction, and sacrifice and anointing to have ceased. The same prophet added: “Christ shall be slain, and the people with the leader who is to come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; its end shall be devastation, and after the end of the war desolation shall be decreed.” After Christ’s Passion, therefore, Titus came, defeated the Jews, destroyed the city and the Temple, and the offerings and sacrifices ceased. They could no longer be celebrated there, so that what had previously been foretold by the prophet might be fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 0462D]

9. Others read “honored with beauty,” instead of “adorned with beauty.” MAR.]

9. But, O hardness of the Jewish heart! Because they themselves killed Christ, they do not believe that he has yet come. We have proved that our Lord Jesus Christ was already born according to the flesh. But the unbeliever asks why he came in the flesh. Hear, then, the reason. When God had made man endowed with supreme blessedness and adorned with the beauty of the divine image, he placed him in paradise, so that he might be subject to God and superior to the other creatures.

[Note: [Col. 0462D]

10. Others read, “he assumed a human body together with a soul.” MAR.]

10. But when man became rebellious, despising the divinity, he violated the forbidden commandment. God did not kill him after casting him out because of his pride, but made him an exile from paradise, awaiting the possibility that he might be restored to pardon through repentance. When he did not return to the way of virtue, God gave the law through Moses, so that by means of it he might at least return to the love of God and the practice of righteousness. But when the stubborn and unbelieving man did not keep even this law, the Son of God finally came and assumed a human body, so that, while he was seen, he might be believed, and so that, once the idols of demons had been abandoned, the world might be reconciled to the grace of its Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0462D]

11. “Beginning.” It refers to *let us follow*. The Hagano edition omits “beginning … to speak.” AREV.]

11. This is the reason for Christ’s birth. Although the Jews admit that he was born, they are nevertheless scandalized that he was crucified and died, not understanding that just as it was fitting for him to be born for the redemption of the world, so it was necessary for him to suffer. In its proper place we shall establish his Passion and death by the testimonies of Scripture. For now, let us follow the proper order: since his human birth after the glory of his divinity has been demonstrated, let his lineage and homeland also be demonstrated, beginning first to speak of his name.

CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Name Jesus.

[Col. 0463A]

[Note: [Col. 0463C]

CHAP. VI. No. 1. Others read *the things foretold*, instead of *the things proclaimed*. MAR.

Ibid. “For a certain Auses, who was called the son of Nave.” The larger Tarraconensian manuscript and the printed editions read: “For a certain Joshua, etc.” Our reading was found in the Hispanic and smaller Tarraconensian manuscripts. At Numbers XIII, 17, where we read, “And Moses called Hosea son of Nun Joshua,” the Septuagint says: Ἐπωνόμασε Μωυσῆς τὸν Αὐσῆ υἱὸν Ναυὴ Ἰησοῦν—“Moses named Auses, son of Nave, Jesus.” Isidorus followed this translation of the Septuagint.

The entire passage, and much of chapter 6, is taken from Tertullian’s book *Against the Jews*, where he says: “When Auses son of Nave was appointed as Moses’ successor, he was certainly transferred from his former name and began to be called Jesus,” etc. From this we infer that a little farther on one should also read, “than which nothing is sweeter,” rather than “than which what is sweeter.” Nevertheless, this reading was found in the smaller Tarraconensian and Hispanic manuscripts. MAR.

Ibid. Others read, “the land of the promised inheritance.” MAR.]

1. For the first designation of the name Jesus is found previously proclaimed in a figure of our Lord Jesus Christ. For a certain Auses, who was called the son of Nave, was surnamed Jesus by Moses (Num. XIII, 17). After Moses’ death he became leader and obtained authority, and distributed the promised land as an inheritance. What did the change of name signify, except that, after Moses had died—that is, after the law had died and the legal commandment had come to an end—the Lord Jesus Christ was destined to be our leader, bringing us, sanctified through the waters of the Jordan—that is, through the grace of baptism—and after every kind of vice had been expelled, or the enemies of the evil angels driven away, into the land of the heavenly promise, flowing with honey and milk: that is, into possession of eternal life, than which nothing is sweeter?

> **Note: [Col. 0463D]**
>
> **2.** “To the saving God,” that is, “to Jesus our Father.” He rendered the Latin expression through the Hebrew one, wishing only to indicate that wherever the Latin version has the word *saving* or *salvation*, the name *Jesus* corresponds to it in Hebrew. Following this same principle in the next testimony, taken from Psalm CXLIX, 4, where we read, “He has exalted the meek unto salvation,” he himself, following Jerome’s translation, said, “And he has exalted the meek in Jesus.” Finally, we added the following testimony from Habakkuk III, 18, “I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus,” because it is especially relevant; but it is marked with an obelus, since we found it only in the Hispalensis manuscript. — MAR.

2. For that man assumed the image of this sacrament in order to be called Jesus, signifying that true Jesus of whom it is written in the Psalms: “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us acclaim God our savior” (Ps. CXLIX, 4), that is, “Jesus our Father.” Here it is shown that Jesus is Lord and God, of whom it is also said elsewhere in the Psalms: “Because the Lord takes pleasure in his people, and he will exalt the meek in Jesus.” For this is how the words stand in Hebrew. Of him Habakkuk thunders more plainly, saying: “I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus” (Hab. III, 18).

# CHAPTER VII. Christ was from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh.

[Col. 0463C]

> **Note: [Col. 0464C]**
>
> **Chapter VII, Note 1.** “Of which seed, through Isaac, the promise had been made to him by the Lord.” Five manuscripts consistently read *Isaiah* instead of *Isaac*. In the Gothic manuscripts there was nothing; only in the Tarraconensis major the name *Isaiah* seemed to have been somewhat obscurely changed to *Isaac*. We followed this reading as the correct one. Yet a little farther on it read, “from this seed and through the same Isaiah,” etc. We judged the expression “the same” to be superfluous and marked it for deletion with an obelus, but did not dare omit it altogether without a manuscript witness. — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Grialius printed “through Isaiah Isaac,” contrary to the intention of the annotator Mariana, who wanted only “through Isaac.” Both expressions cannot be retained: one must read either only “through Isaiah” or “through Isaac.” — AREV.

1. That the Lord Jesus Christ was to come from the seed of Abraham, Genesis shows when Abraham says to his servant: “Place your hand beneath my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven” (Gen. XXIV, 2). By this expression he testified that Christ, the God of heaven, was to come in the flesh from his lineage. For by “thigh” lineage is understood; it signified that the God of heaven was to come in the flesh from the seed of Abraham, concerning which seed the Lord had made him a promise through Isaac: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18), that is, in Christ, of whom the Psalmist says: “And in him all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed; all the nations shall magnify him” (Ps. LXXI, 17).

2. Concerning this seed, and through the same Isaiah, the word of the Lord speaks: “I will bring forth seed from Jacob,” he says, “and from Judah those who possess my mountains” (Isa. LXV, 9).
