Of it the same prophet says elsewhere: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9).

# CHAPTER VIII. Christ arose from the tribe of Judah.

> **Note: [Col. 0464D]**
>
> **Chapter VIII, Note 1.** “Nor a leader from his thighs.” Thus read five manuscripts. Julianus, *Against the Jews*, and Hilary, on Psalm LIX, likewise read it. The Septuagint indeed said, ἐκ τῶν μηρῶν αὐτοῦ, that is, “from his thighs”; we followed this reading. Although the Hispalensis and the Tarraconensis minor, as in our Vulgate, read, “Nor a leader from his thigh.” Tertullian himself, *Against the Jews*, reads “from his thighs.” — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Perhaps *potestati* (“authority”) had intruded. — AREV.

1. And because Christ was to be awaited from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh, the patriarch Jacob signifies this when he says: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent. And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). For it is certain that, until the birth of Christ, princes of the Jewish people from the lineage of Judah did not fail, nor leaders from his thighs, until Herod, a foreign king, who had seized power through ambition for the kingdom.

> **Note: [Col. 0464D]**
>
> **2.** “Lying about some king from the lineage of Judah in the farthest regions of the East.” Julianus, archbishop of Toledo, transferred this passage almost word for word into his work *Against the Jews*, where in Book I he says:
>
> “Or perhaps, still persisting in the shameless obstinacy of your impudent forehead, you bring forward that claim which your ancestors habitually put forth while lying: that even today there is some king from the lineage of Judah who seems to hold a kingdom in the farthest regions of the East.”
>
> And much else in the same vein. Indeed, that Jews are confined in great numbers in the East within the Caspian Mountains is not merely their own story—for there exists a book on this matter in Hebrew called *Baldad the Shuhite*—but it was also Prosper’s belief, in the final part of his book *On Predictions*, chapter 9, where he says: “Here it is shown that Antichrist will come from the Jews, from the tribe of Dan, which is even today in Persia.” Porchetus touches upon this Jewish opinion in the first part of *Victory against the Jews*, chapter 2. — MAR.

2. For as soon as this had happened, and the leader from the seed of Judah had failed, he came who was to be sent, whom the nations and peoples were awaiting. But the Jews, with the obstinacy of an impudent forehead, say that this time has not yet been completed, falsely claiming that some king from the lineage of Judah holds a kingdom in the farthest regions of the East.

[Col. 0465A] 3. And, blinded in mind, they do not notice that the lie of their pretense is exposed, because now, just as the Jews have no temple, no altar, and no sacrifice, so too no king and no priest remain among them. For the prophet Hosea cannot be false when he says: “The children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without altar, without priesthood, without manifestations” (Hos. III, 4). Who does not see that all these things have now been fulfilled in them?

# CHAPTER IX. Christ was born from the stock of David.

> **Note: [Col. 0465D]**
>
> **Chapter IX, Note 1.** Some manuscripts read, “to be future … was foretold.” — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** “The Lord swore.” Psalm CXXXI, 11, in the Gothic manuscripts reads: “The Lord swore to David in truth, and he did not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne,’” as it is read in the Hispanic Psalter. Perhaps Isidore also read it this way. — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Some read *eam* (“her”) instead of *de fructu* (“from the fruit”), and “and it shall remain forever.” — MAR.

1. We are taught from which tribe Christ was to be born. That he was to come from the stock of David according to the flesh was foretold through the Holy Spirit in the Psalms: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne’” (Ps. CXXXI, 11). And again: “Once I swore by my holiness: If I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne like the sun before me, and like the full moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 36 ff.).

2. Likewise in the Book of Chronicles: “And the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: I announce to you that the Lord will build you a house. And when your days are fulfilled, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will make his throne firm forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son, and I will not remove my mercy from him as I removed it from him who was before you. And I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be most firmly established forever” (II Kings VII, 4; I Chronicles XVII, 3).

21

> **Note: [Col. 0466D]**
>
> **3.** Some read “the days of your life.” — MAR.

3. Whoever thinks that all these things were fulfilled in Solomon seems greatly mistaken. For how is it to be understood of Solomon that it was said: “After you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall come from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom”? Was this prophesied of that Solomon? Certainly not. He began to reign while his father was still alive. Here, however, it is said: “When the days of your life are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed.” From this it is understood that another was promised, one who was foretold as to be raised up not before David’s death but after his death.

[Col. 0466A]

> **Note: [Col. 0466D]**
>
> **4.** “Who would build the house of the Lord.” This entire passage was marked with an obelus only in the printed editions; it seemed suspect to us and did not sufficiently cohere. Nevertheless, we left it untouched, except that where it read *qui dum bonus fuisset* (“who, although he had been good”), we removed the relative pronoun *qui*, which had been inserted rashly, so that the grammar would be sound. — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Perhaps *habuit* (“he had”) stood in place of *fuisse* (“he had been”). — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Perhaps one should read *Salomonis quippe … fuisse*, with *constat* (“it is evident”) understood, as often elsewhere. — AREV.

4. He who would build the house of the Lord—not of walls made by human hands, but of living and precious stones, that is, of holy and faithful people. For let anyone attend to and consider also what follows: “His house shall be faithful, and his kingdom forever before me” (II Kings VII, 16). It was not spoken of Solomon. Solomon is known to have had a house full of foreign women worshiping idols; he himself, a king, was seduced by them into idolatry and cast down. Although he had been good at the beginning, he had an evil end.

5. Who, then, is the one whose house is faithful forever and who is promised to be raised up after David’s death? He is certainly the one concerning whom David himself, burning with longing, cries out in the eighty-eighth Psalm: “But you have delayed your Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 39). It is therefore not Solomon; nor was this David delayed as Christ. Behold, the foregoing promises were fulfilled not in Solomon but in Christ our Lord, who arose from David’s lineage.

6. Concerning him the Lord himself says through Jeremiah: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and a king shall reign and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice on the earth. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord is our righteous one’” (Jer. XXIII, 5–6).

7. He is the one who is promised through Nathan from the seed of David (I Chronicles XVII; II Kings VII), and who is also foretold through the prophet Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” he says, “and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI, 1). This rod from the root of Jesse is the virgin Mary, sprung from David’s root, who bore the flower, the Lord and Savior. Of him it further says: “And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

8. Such great gifts of the Spirit are proclaimed concerning him because the Holy Spirit dwells in him not according to measure (John III, 34), as in us, but the whole fullness of divinity and of graces is present in him (Col. II, 9). He is the one who does not judge according to the sight of the eyes or the hearing of the ears, but “justice shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins” (Isa. XI, 3). In his Church the wolf dwells with the lamb: that is, the one who used to seize prey from her, when he is converted to her, dwells among the innocent.

[Col. 0467A]

> **Note: [Col. 0467D]**
>
> **9.** Some read “with sinners” instead of “with the simple.” — MAR.

9. In his fold the leopard lies down with the kid: the deceitful are mingled with the simple. There also the calf from the circumcision, the lion from worldly power, and the sheep from the common people dwell together, because in faith the condition of all is common. The little child who leads them is certainly the one who humbled himself for us as a little child. The ox and the lion shall eat straw there, because rulers and subject peoples share a common teaching.

> **Note: [Col. 0467D]**
>
> **10.** “Little kings,” that is, “basilisks.” — AREV.

10. The infant also delights at the breast over the holes of the asp, when nations that once used to proclaim poisons, having been converted, and even the little ones, delight in hearing the faith of Christ. The den of the basilisk is the hearts of unbelievers, in which that crooked serpent used to rest; the weaned child seized him and dragged him away captive, so that he might not harm anyone on his holy mountain, which is the Church.

> **Note: [Col. 0467D]**
>
> **11.** Some read “was born” instead of “was to be born.” — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** “He impresses the sign of the cross upon their foreheads.” This refers either to the sacrament of confirmation, when children’s foreheads are marked with chrism, or to the custom by which individual believers have been accustomed to fortify their foreheads with the sign of the cross. Concerning this, see Tertullian, *To His Wife*, Book II. Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, Book II, chapter 21, said that in this sign there is salvation for all who are marked on their foreheads. — MAR.

11. The same Isaiah continues to speak of Christ, since he was to be born from the seed of David according to the flesh: “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, shall be entreated by the nations, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI, 10). The root of Jesse stands as a sign for the peoples when Christ impresses the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. “The nations shall entreat him”—and it is already seen that all this has been fulfilled. His tomb is so glorious that, besides the fact that we who are redeemed through his death render glory to him, the place itself, shining with miracles, draws the whole world to itself for the sake of its glory.

[Col. 0467C]

> **Note: [Col. 0467D]**
>
> **12.** The Vulgate adds to “I will place upon Dibon”: “for those who have fled from Moab, a lion, and for the remnant of the land.” — AREV.

12. In Hebrew this passage reads: “And his resting place shall be glorious.” This is certainly because, although his flesh died, it did not see corruption, according to the saying of the Psalm: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. XV, 10). Now, because prophetic speech bears witness to Christ being born from Moab, the same Isaiah testifies: “For I will place upon those who have fled from Moab a lion, and upon the remnant of the land. Send forth the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XV, 9; XVI, 1).

> **Note: [Col. 0467D]**
>
> **13.** “The rock of the desert” signifies Ruth. This passage is taken from Jerome, at the beginning of his commentary on Isaiah XVI, where he says: “‘From the rock of the desert,’ that is, Ruth, who, widowed by her husband’s death, bore Obed from Boaz, and Jesse from Obed, and David from Jesse, and Christ from David.” Isidore said, “Christ from David’s stock.” Because of Jerome’s authority, we preferred this reading to the variant reading. For three manuscripts read: “And Christ was born from David’s lineage.” — MAR.

13. From this people of the Moabites came forth the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who rules over the whole earth. “The rock of the desert” signifies Ruth, who, bereft through her husband’s death, bore Obed from Boaz, and Jesse from Obed, and David from Jesse, and Christ from David’s lineage. By “the mountain of the daughter of Zion” he either means historically the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the allegorical sense, the Church, established on a height—that is, on the sublimity of virtues.

# CHAPTER X. Christ was born from a virgin without intercourse with a man.

1. Thus far we have briefly touched upon the faith of the Old Testament concerning the name, nation, and lineage of our Lord Jesus Christ. From this point let us show his human generation from the Virgin. For Isaiah, filled with the Holy Spirit, thus foretells the mystery of the future incarnation of the Son of God; for he says: “And the Lord continued to speak to Ahaz, saying: Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either from the depths of hell or from above in the height” (Isa. VII, 10). And he added: “Hear, therefore, house of David,” that is, “lineage of David.”

> **Note: [Col. 0468D]**
>
> **Chapter X, Note 2.** Some read *vocabit* (“he will call”) instead of *vocabitur* (“he will be called”). — MAR.

2. For he was rightly speaking to the house of David, that is, to the royal stock, from which stock Mary descended. And he added: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us.” Therefore, since he whom the Virgin conceived in her womb and bore is called “God with us,” God is recognized as having been conceived and born in the Virgin’s womb. Let unbelieving Jews be ashamed, then, and submit their necks to the grace of Christ.

> **Note: [Col. 0468D]**
>
> **3.** “In Hebrew, not ‘virgin’ but ‘young woman,’ etc.” I have not chosen to discuss here the word *halma*, which Isaiah uses in chapter VII, since Jerome may be consulted on that passage, as may *On the Mysteries of Catholic Truth*, Book VII, chapter 15. — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** Grialius had punctuated this incorrectly; for the Lord says: “He will give you a sign.” — AREV.

3. Behold, the one whom the Virgin bore is called “God with us.” At this point the Jews argue that the prophetic utterance in Hebrew does not indicate a virgin but a young woman who is to give birth. To them the answer is that it would not be a sign if a young woman gave birth, since that is a matter of age. But it is a sign because of the novelty of the event if a virgin gives birth, since that is a matter of integrity. For when he says, “The Lord will give you a sign,” he indicates a remarkable miracle—namely, that a virgin will give birth—which plainly would not be a sign unless it were something new. Christ therefore had to be born in the flesh from a virgin because of this remarkable miracle.

> **Note: [Col. 0468D]**
>
> **4.** “It follows, and he says: ‘Before the child knows,’ etc.” Isidore, whether because his memory failed or deliberately, suddenly passed from Isaiah chapter VII to chapter VIII and explains the expression, “Before the child knows,” as “before he causes it to be known that he has God as his father and a virgin as his mother.” This is subtle enough and not contrary to the usage of the divine writings. Jerome, on these words, and Augustine, *On the Season*, sermon 32, readily resolve the matter by explaining: “Before the child knows how to call father and mother,” that is, “before he becomes a human being.” — MAR.

4. It follows concerning him: “He shall eat butter and honey.” Butter is the fruit of the Church coming from the circumcision, like an ox under the yoke—that is, placed under the law. Honey, however, is the Church coming from the nations; Christ is nourished by its sweetness and by the goodness of its works and faith. It follows, and he says: “And before the child knows how to call father or mother.” What he said, “before he knows,” means “before he causes it to be known, by his divinity, that he has God as his father and, by his assumption of flesh, a virgin as his mother,” in accordance with what is written in Genesis, when the Lord says to Abraham: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. XXII, 12), that is, “Now I have caused you to be known as fearing.” For far be it from God that there should be ignorance, so that he would then know what he had previously not known.

5. How great the power of this Emmanuel is, the prophet repeatedly announces, saying: “And the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of the land, O Emmanuel” (Isa. VIII, 8). Since we believe that he was born from a virgin, let us hear the Father speaking in the Psalms. For when the Prophet had said concerning Christ, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” immediately the voice of the Father followed, saying to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you, and like dew from the womb your youth shall arise for you. The Lord swore, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. The Lord at your right hand has shattered kings on the day of his wrath” (Ps. CIX, 1). And again: “Where,” he says, “glory may dwell in our land, mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have embraced one another. Truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked forth from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV, 10 ff.).

> **Note: [Col. 0469D]**
>
> **6.** Some read “our flesh” instead of “for flesh.” — MAR.

6. What is the truth that has sprung from the earth, except Christ born from a woman, the Son of God proceeding from flesh? For flesh is earth. When Christ was born, justice looked forth from heaven. Justification would not be given from heaven unless Christ were born in the flesh. And to show that this truth, having sprung from the earth, was a human being, he added in what follows: “Justice shall go before him, and shall set his steps upon the way.” Likewise the same David says: “The earth shall give its fruit” (Ps. LXVI, 7–8). The earth, Mary, gave its fruit, Christ. But what is this fruit? “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us.”

> **Note: [Col. 0469D]**
>
> **7.** Some read *commistione* (“intercourse”) instead of *commistio* (“union”). — MAR.

7. The prophet Isaiah announces this fruit of the earth more clearly elsewhere, saying: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened and germinate the Savior, and let justice arise together. I, the Lord, have created him” (Isa. XLV, 8). The heavens, which are also the clouds—that is, the prophets—through whom the coming of Christ was foretold; the earth is Mary, who, opened by faith and not by corruption, gave birth to the Savior, because the Lord alone created him, without the intercourse of male seed.

> **Note: [Col. 0469D]**
>
> **8.** “Cut off without hands, filling the whole earth.” The Hispalensis inserts certain words, for it reads as follows: “Cut off without the hands of those who embrace him, that is, born from the Virgin with the Holy Spirit alone cooperating, without the intercourse of male seed, filling the whole earth.” — MAR.

8. Therefore Isaiah also says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. LIII, 8). For no human being was privy to Christ’s conception; the Virgin appeared pregnant through the word of God alone. The prophet Daniel had also foretold this figuratively, saying: “I saw a stone cut from the mountain without the hands of those who cut it, and when it came upon the earth it filled the whole globe of the earth” (Dan. II, 34). This stone is Christ, cut off without hands, filling the whole earth, because his kingdom is among all nations.

> **Note: [Col. 0469D]**
>
> **9.** Some read *ingressurus* (“about to enter”) instead of *ingressus* (“having entered”). — MAR.

9. Concerning this stone God speaks through Isaiah: “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen and angular, and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. XXVIII, 16). Daniel saw this stone cut from the mountain—that is, from the Jewish people—without hands, that is, without the work of a man, born from the virgin Mary. Without any doubt we believe that she was a virgin before giving birth and remained a virgin after giving birth, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies: “I turned toward the way of the gate of the sanctuary outside, which faced east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God has entered through it; and it shall remain closed’” (Ezek. XLIV, 1).

10. By this testimony he confesses that holy Mary conceived as a virgin and remained a virgin. For female genitalia are called “gates,” because they open the barriers of childbirth, as Job says: “Because he did not close the doors of the womb that carried me” (Job III, 10). Our Lord Jesus Christ, born wondrously and by divine power, came forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber (Ps. XVIII, 6), that is, from the Virgin’s womb. We profess that after his birth no man had intercourse with Mary and that no one was born from her womb.

# CHAPTER XI. Christ was born in Bethlehem.

> **Note: [Col. 0470D]**
>
> **Chapter XI, Note 1.** “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are you perhaps little among the thousands of Judah?” Thus read two Gothic manuscripts, and so did Julianus, Book I *Against the Jews*, except that he used the masculine form: “Are you perhaps little?” Jerome, in the Septuagint version itself, has: “You are by no means least, so as to be among the thousands of Judah.” Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, Book II, chapter 11, cites the same passage from Micah as follows: “You are not insignificant, so as to be established among the thousands of Judah.” Isidore himself, Book II, chapter 3, says: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not least among the thousands of Judah.” All the manuscripts agreed on this reading in that passage, while in the passage under discussion most read affirmatively: “You are little,” or “You are little” in the masculine. Only the Tarraconensis minor had: “You are not little.” It is tempting to suspect that the Hebrew manuscripts of Micah were corrupted by the Jews, and that the Septuagint translators of old, as well as the ancient writers, read the passage with the negation, as it stands in Matthew. Nevertheless, some in our own time attempt to reconcile Matthew’s words with the passage in Micah by saying that the Hebrew should be interpreted in this way: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, it is little”—with “for you” understood—“that you should be among the thousands of Judah.” In other words, they prefer to take the Hebrew word *zahir*, which others rendered “little” in the feminine or masculine, as a neuter. If this is accepted, Matthew can easily be reconciled with Micah. We append the Hebrew for those acquainted with that language. — MAR.

1. We have foretold the birth of our Lord from the Virgin; let us also show the place of his origin. For he was born in Bethlehem, concerning which the prophet Micah says: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are you perhaps little among the thousands of Judah? From you one shall come forth for me who is to rule in Israel, and his going forth is from the days of eternity. Therefore he will give them up until the time when she who is in labor shall give birth” (Mic. V, 2).

[Col. 0471A] 2. After he had foretold the place of his origin, he then set forth his future kingdom throughout the whole world, saying: “He shall stand, and shall see, and shall feed his flock in the strength of the Lord; and in the honor of the name of his God they shall be, for now he shall be magnified even to the ends of the earth. And this man shall be peace.”

> **Note: [Col. 0471C]**
>
> **3.** “God shall come from the southwest.” This is a passage from Habakkuk III, 3. Augustine likewise said, in *On the Shepherd*, chapters 15 and 16: “God shall come from the southwest, and the Lord from the shadowy mountain.” This reading was found in all Isidore’s manuscripts except the Hispalensis, which reads, as in the Vulgate edition: “God shall come from the south.” We followed the authority of the other manuscripts. — MAR.

3. Concerning this place of Christ’s birth the prophet Habakkuk also says: “God shall come from the southwest.” For the region of Bethlehem, where Christ was born, looks toward the southern quarter from Jerusalem. Thus he is rightly written to have come from the southwest, because he was foreseen as coming from Bethlehem.

# CHAPTER XII. Christ’s birth is shown by the sign of a star.

> **Note: [Col. 0471D]**
>
> **Chapter XII, Note 1.** “That divine Balaam.” The word “divine” is ambiguous. Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book IV, chapter 6, does not hesitate to place Balaam among the number of great and divine prophets, since God so often spoke to him, through him blessed the Israelites, and through him foretold future events so clearly. The opinion of the ancient Fathers resists this: Justin, Question 2; Chrysostom, Homily 21 on Genesis; Basil, Letter 80; Augustine, Sermon 103. The authority of the divine Scriptures also supports this, since in Joshua XIII, 22 he is called a diviner in Hebrew. — MAR.

1. Because his birth was made known by the sign of a star, that divine Balaam sang in the Book of Numbers as follows: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel.” For the Magi, coming from the regions of the East, were the first to announce Christ’s birth, with the star as their guide, so that, having observed the heavenly sign, they might point out the one whom the ancient master of their art had foretold.

# CHAPTER XIII. The Magi offered gifts.

> **Note: [Col. 0471D]**
>
> **Chapter XIII, Note 1.** “From whom the Magi came.” Remigius, in his commentary on Matthew II, says that there have been various opinions concerning the Magi: some think them Chaldeans, others Persians, and some the descendants of Balaam; some affirm that they came from the farthest ends of the earth. Isidore makes the Magi Persians in this chapter. Those peoples were especially devoted to the knowledge of the stars, which is why astrologers were commonly called Chaldeans, as is clear from Gellius, Book XIV, chapter 1. Magi from Elimaid, the first region of Persia, were called Elimaean. Hence the statement in Acts XIII, 8: “But Elymas the magician resisted them,” for this is how his name is interpreted. Whether these kings were called Magi because of their wisdom, as Origen judges in *Commentary 5 on Matthew* and is criticized for this by Theophilus in Book II of *The Paschal Work*, or because of condemned arts, as Justin *Against Trypho* and Basil *On the Birth of Christ* hold, is a major question and does not suit the brevity intended here. Jerome, on Daniel II, where the text reads “The king ordered the diviners to be summoned,” says that the Magi are those who philosophize about individual matters; he indicates that this word does not always signify condemned arts. What he added—“For the East has also had Magi as kings”—is taken from Tertullian, *Against the Jews* and Book III *Against Marcion*. Cicero, *On Divination* I, says: “No one can be king of the Persians who has not first learned the discipline and knowledge of the Magi.” That the Magi who came to Christ were kings is taught by Cyprian, *Sermon on the Baptism of Christ*; Athanasius, Question 2; Jerome, on Psalm VII; Augustine, Sermon 43, *To the Brothers in the Desert*; and Christianus Druthmar, on Matthew II. — MAR.

1. Because the Magi offered him gifts, the prophets also tell us this. Isaiah says: “At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts by a people scattered and torn apart, by a people terrible, after whom there has been none” (Isa. XVIII, 7). The prophet says this concerning the very powerful nation of the Persians, whose might at that time no people equaled; from them the Magi came and brought gifts to Christ.

> **Note: [Col. 0472D]**
>
> **2.** Some read *personat* or *praecinit* (“proclaims” or “sings beforehand”) instead of *praedicavit* (“proclaimed”). — MAR.

2. And again he himself says: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense, and announcing praise to the Lord.” David also proclaimed these gifts, saying: “And to him shall be given the gold of Arabia” (Ps. LXXI, 11). And again: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabians and of Sheba shall bring presents.” For the East has also had Magi as kings.

# CHAPTER XIV. He was anointed by God the Father.

1. Because Christ was not anointed with this human oil, as were the other kings and priests of the Hebrews, but was anointed by the paternal Spirit, Isaiah sang of him, speaking in the person of Christ himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isa. LXI, 1).

[Col. 0472B]

> **Note: [Col. 0472D]**
>
> **Chapter XIV, Note 2.** Some read *directionis* (“of guidance”) instead of *aequitatis* (“of justice”). — MAR.

2. In the same way the Psalmist, inspired by the divine Spirit, speaks to this same Christ: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the rod of justice is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 7). In this statement the prophet first demonstrates Christ’s divinity and eternity.

> **Note: [Col. 0472D]**
>
> **3.** Some read *imaginarie praecesserant* (“had gone before figuratively”) instead of *praecesserant* (“had gone before”). — MAR.

3. Next, through the rod of justice, he announces the scepter of Christ’s power and his kingdom. Finally, he indicates that this same God was anointed by God—not with ordinary oil, like his other participants, that is, rulers, who had gone before in a figurative way, but with the oil of gladness, by which the Holy Spirit is mystically signified. Through the Spirit’s heavenly infusion and power Christ was consecrated.

# CHAPTER XV. He came poor and despised at his first advent.

[Col. 0472C]

> **Note: [Col. 0472D]**
>
> **Chapter XV, Note 1.** “The holy Isaiah indicates this, saying: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion.’” The words “Say to the daughter of Zion” are indeed in Isaiah, chapter LXII, 11; what follows, “Behold, your king comes to you,” is taken from Zechariah IX, 9. Isidore, however, cited both as though they belonged to Isaiah. This is not surprising, since in Mark I, 2 a testimony is cited under Isaiah’s name whose first part, “Behold, I send my angel before your face,” etc., is taken from Malachi III, 1. Nevertheless, it is impious to acknowledge what Porphyry criticized, as Jerome reports in his commentary on Matthew III, and what certain others have dared to imagine: that the evangelists’ memory failed them. Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, Book II, chapter 28, cites this entire passage as belonging to Zechariah, in these words: “That he is the king who will reign forever is found in Zechariah [supply: ‘in these words’]: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, just and saving, gentle, seated upon a tamed ass.’” Hence I suspected three things: first, that Isidore had written not Isaiah but Zechariah, and that the reference had been altered by the copyists; next, that one should read “just and saving,” where the Hispalensis and Tarraconensis minor, as in our Vulgate, read “just and savior”; finally, that one should read not “an untamed ass” but “a tamed one,” as Cyprian said—namely, ὑποζύγιον, the word used by the Septuagint translators. The ancients called it *subjugale* (“a yoked beast”), unless perhaps Isidore looked to the words that follow, “a new colt,” or “the foal of a she-ass,” and therefore called it an untamed ass. — MAR.
>
> **The same passage.** The name of one prophet sometimes falls out in place of another in other writers as well. — AREV.

1. Because he came at his first advent poor and despised, the holy Isaiah indicates this, saying: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, just and saving, poor, seated upon an untamed ass” (Isaiah LII, 13). Likewise, in the same prophet, speaking in the person of God the Father: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, lifted up, and shall be very high. Just as many were astonished at you, so his appearance shall be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men.”

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

2. Another reading has *ascendit* (“he ascended”) instead of *ascendet* (“he shall ascend”), and *sicut virgultum* (“like a shoot”). *Et consideravimus* (“and we considered”) instead of *et desideravimus* (“and we desired”). MAR.]

2. “He shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him. For those to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who had not heard shall look. Who has believed what we have heard? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah LIII, 1). “And he shall ascend like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has no appearance or beauty; and we saw him, and he had no aspect, and we desired him as despised and last among men; a man of sorrows and acquainted with suffering; and, as one whose face was hidden, he was despised, and therefore we did not esteem him.”

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

3. Another reading has *vulneratus* (“wounded”) instead of *humiliatus* (“humbled”). MAR.]

3. “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses and carried our pains; and we considered him as one afflicted with leprosy, struck by God, and humbled. But he was humbled for our iniquities and crushed for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. All we, like sheep, have gone astray.”

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

4. Another reading has *ducitur* (“he is led”) instead of *ducetur* (“he shall be led”). MAR.]

4. “Each one turned aside into his own way, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth; like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall become silent, and he did not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away; who shall declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living. Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he shall give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was there deceit in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity. If he should offer his life for sin, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.”

5. “Because his soul labored, he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge the righteous one himself shall justify my many servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities. Therefore I shall allot him many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he surrendered his soul to death, was counted among criminals, himself bore the sins of many, and prayed for transgressors.”

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

6. Another reading has *ejus manifestatur* (“his … is revealed”) instead of *monstratur* (“is shown”). MAR.]

6. In this passage not only is Christ shown to have appeared despised, but his heavenly generation is also expressed there; likewise, the weakness of the flesh he assumed is revealed, as well as the disgrace of his passion. The cross, death, and burial are shown there, together with the fact that the innocent is condemned and that, while silent, he suffers.

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

7. Another reading has *carnem pauperis forma* (“the form of poor flesh”). MAR.]

7. For God, assuming in the flesh the form of a poor person, deigned to humble himself; and for our sake, so that salvation might be restored to the lost, he even became obedient unto death. The same Isaiah declared this elsewhere: “He shall not cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets; he shall not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax; but in truth he shall bring forth judgment, until I establish judgment on the earth, and the nations shall hope in his name” (Isaiah XLII, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

8. Another reading has *tibi enim peccavimus* (“for we have sinned against you”). And *potest salvari* (“can be saved”). MAR.]

8. And Jeremiah foretold that God would come in the flesh, despised and humble, in this manner: “Lord, act for the sake of your name, because our apostasies are many. We have sinned against you, O hope of Israel, its savior in the time of tribulation. Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay? Why will you be like a wandering man, and like a strong man who cannot save? Yet you are among us, Lord, and your name has been invoked over us; do not abandon us” (Jeremiah XIV, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

9. Another reading has *salvari* (“to be saved”) instead of *salvare* (“to save”). MAR.]

9. When he says, “We have sinned against you,” he expresses the person of the Jews, who sinned against God when they crucified him as he came in human form. For he presented himself to human sight as a wandering and resident stranger; but they, thinking him to be only what he appeared to be, killed the man as one who could not save.

## CHAPTER XVI. Because he performed signs and miracles

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

CHAPTER XVI, no. 1. Other readings have *patebunt* (“they shall be open”) instead of *audient* (“they shall hear”); *clara* (“clear”) instead of *plana* (“smooth”); *unxit* (“he anointed”) instead of *unxerit* (“he has anointed”); *praedicandum* (“to preach”) instead of *annuntiandum* (“to announce”); and *remissionem* (“forgiveness”) instead of *redemptionem* (“redemption”). MAR.]

1. The kinds and miracles of healings were foretold long beforehand through the prophet Isaiah, who said: “Behold, our God himself shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” (Isaiah XXXV, 4). And again: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to preach redemption to captives, and sight to the blind” (Isaiah LXI, 1; Luke IV, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

2. Another reading has *detegitur* (“is uncovered”) instead of *detergitur* (“is wiped away”). MAR.]

2. All these signs of healing took place at Christ’s advent. For as soon as he was born, the Magi worshiped him, the star having gone before him, and offered gifts. Then his advent displayed various miracles. In the case of the blind, the darkness of profound night was wiped away so that they might recognize God. To the dead, the grace of renewed light was restored, so that their souls might be brought to life.

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

3. Another reading has *abluendis* (“for washing away”) instead of *abolendis* (“for abolishing”). MAR.

Ibid. In the note to the Grial edition there was *abluendas* (“to be washed away”), which I changed in the text to *abluendis*. AREV.]

3. The deaf began to hear so that they might receive the hearing of faith. The lame were strengthened with vigorous steps so that they might run toward God. The mute cried out in clear voices so that they might confess God. Lepers, in order to abolish the contagions of the soul, laid aside their sallow limbs; for by the effect of his majesty he did many things that must be passed over while all are being read.

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

4. Another reading has *obitu* (“at the death”) instead of *obitum* (“the death”). MAR.

Ibid. Others have: “even the elements feared.” AREV.]

4. For by the power of his excellence he trod the swelling waves of the sea with wavering steps, and by his command he calmed the storms of the great sea. But at his death in the passion, the elements also trembled: the sun fled, the earth was shaken, and the rocks, striking against one another, were shattered; indeed, death itself could not hold him.

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

5. At this point Codex Florentinus adds another chapter: “Because he was to be tempted by the devil.” That he was to be tempted by the devil and would conquer the devil, the holy prophet Zechariah says: “I saw Jesus the priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him,” etc. These words are taken from Zechariah III, 1 and following: “And the Lord showed me Jesus the priest,” etc. These words are also brought forward in the *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19, no. 55. But where the Vulgate has *elegit Jerusalem* (“he chose Jerusalem”), Isidore’s manuscript here reports *redemit Israel* (“he redeemed Israel”). AREV.]

5. For, rising on the third day, he flew back to the paternal seat, and through the ministry of angels he was led from earth to heaven. Many other similar things were also accomplished by his omnipotence. But the unbeliever says that the prophets too performed many miracles. It is true; yet none of them rose from the dead and ascended into heaven.

## CHAPTER XVII. He was to be seen in the body

[Note: [Col. 0476D]

CHAPTER XVII, no. 1. Another reading has *occultus* (“hidden”) instead of *occursus* (“coming” or “encounter”). MAR.]

1. That the same God would be seen by human beings in the body, he testifies through Isaiah, saying: “Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am the very one who was speaking; behold, I am here” (Isaiah LII, 6). And David: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Psalm LXXXIII, 8). And again: “Your processions have been seen, O God, the processions of my God and king” (Psalm LXVII, 25)—namely, in the comings by which he came into the world and again ascended into heaven. For then the occurrence of his advent was made manifest and revealed; had the Jews known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians II, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0476D]

2. And Jeremiah, in the book of Baruch. Since Baruch was Jeremiah’s secretary, his prophecy is commonly cited as Jeremiah’s. Thus Augustine, in his *Sermon against the Jews, Pagans, and Arians*, chapter 13, cites the words of Baruch III, 38, “After this he appeared on earth,” under Jeremiah’s name; he does the same in *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 33. So also Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book I, chapter 10; Basil, *Against Eunomius*, book IV; Cassiodorus, on Psalm LXXXI. The Sixth Synod, act 8, likewise cites similar passages from Baruch as Jeremiah’s. I think this is the one reason why, in the catalogues of divine Scripture formerly drawn up by the Fathers and councils, no separate mention of Baruch’s prophecy is found. MAR.]

2. Of this bodily vision the aforesaid Isaiah also announced: “His appearance,” he says, “shall be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. Those to whom nothing was announced concerning him shall see, and those who did not hear shall look.” And Jeremiah, in the book of Baruch: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him who found every way of wisdom and showed it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings.”

3. And Habakkuk says: “Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified. In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known; when the years draw near, you shall become known; when the time arrives, you shall be revealed” (Habakkuk II, 10). Likewise, he himself says: “The nations shall see you, and the peoples shall grieve”—that is, the Jews.

4. Indeed, the aforementioned Isaiah sang of him in this way: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like splendor, and her Savior is kindled like a lamp; and the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your illustrious one.” And again: “The voices of your watchmen have been raised; together they shall praise, because they shall see eye to eye.” And below: “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” (Isaiah LXII, 1; LII, 8, 10).

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Jews were not to recognize him

[Col. 0476C] 1. And because the Jews were not to recognize him, Jeremiah had foretold this in the person of the Lord: “The house of Israel has utterly transgressed against me, and the house of Judah,” says the Lord; “they denied me and said, ‘It is not he’” (Jeremiah V, 11). Even now the Jews say this about Christ: “It is not he,” while awaiting another, who is the Antichrist.

2. And Isaiah: “He has no appearance or beauty; and we saw him, and he had no aspect, and we desired him, despised and last among men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with suffering; and, as one whose face was hidden, he was despised. Therefore we did not esteem him” (Isaiah LIII, 2). By these words he signifies the unbelief of the Jews, to whom Christ appeared to have neither appearance nor beauty, and therefore was not esteemed to be God.

[Col. 0476D]

[Col. 0477A] 3. Yet because they would neither recognize nor receive him, the same Isaiah elsewhere confirms this, saying: “Hear, O heavens, and listen, O earth, because the Lord has spoken: I nourished sons and raised them up, but they despised me. The ox knows its owner, and the ass the manger of its lord; but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood” (Isaiah I, 2). And again: “With hearing you shall hear, and you shall not understand; seeing, you shall see, and you shall not know, for the heart of this people has grown fat” (Isaiah VI, 9; Matthew XIII, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0477C]

CHAPTER XVIII, preceding column, no. 4. Another reading has *dementia* (“madness”) instead of *duritia* (“hardness”). MAR.]

4. Hence Ezekiel also says: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Son of man, you dwell in the midst of a house that provokes me; they have eyes to see and do not see, and ears to hear and do not hear’” (Ezekiel XII, 2). For they were so blinded that they neither recognized nor received the Savior. The one whose day Abraham saw and rejoiced in, and whose advent the prophets awaited with great desire (John VIII, 56), they both saw and did not recognize; moreover, they blasphemed, crying out: “We have no king except Caesar,” and the other things that follow. The hardness of this people does not change, just as neither the Ethiopian can change his skin nor the leopard its markings, as Jeremiah testifies: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his markings?” (Jeremiah XIII, 23).

## CHAPTER XIX. Because, not recognizing him, the Jews gathered against him

1. But because, not recognizing him, the Jews gathered to kill him and gave universal consent to his passion, it is written as follows: “Why did the nations rage”—that is, the Romans—“and the peoples devise vain things”—that is, the Jews? “The kings of the earth stood forth”—namely, Herod and Pilate—“and the princes gathered together”—that is, the chief priests and elders of the Jews—“against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm II, 1).

[Col. 0478A] [Note: [Col. 0477C]

CHAPTER XIX, no. 2. “All blind dogs.” The Hispalensian and the lesser Tarraconensian manuscripts read: “All mute dogs,” as in the Vulgate edition of Isaiah LVI, 10. We followed the former reading because below it says: “But these blind dogs, not seeing their shepherd,” etc. The words attributed here to Hilary are nowhere found, as far as I know, in his works. MAR.]

[Col. 0477D] Ibid. “They became for me a returning arrow.” These words are not found in the sacred books currently used by the Church. Clearly Isidore used a Latin edition different from ours, one of those editions—of which Augustine affirms there were innumerable ones (*On Christian Doctrine*, II, 11). Hence many passages of divine Scripture survive in common usage and in the writings of the ancient Fathers that are not now found in the same words, such as: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” And: “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood.” “The life of man upon earth is a temptation.” “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently.” Ambrose, in *On Duties*, I, 31, also cites from Proverbs XXI, 1 the words: “For you ought to prepare such things,” which are not found in our Vulgate. There are innumerable other examples, most of which are not found even in the Greek manuscripts of the Seventy Interpreters. But, to return to Isidore, I suspect that these words were taken from Hosea VII, 16, where it says: “They turned back to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow.” MAR.

Ibid. In book XVIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 7, no. 7, I noted that a returning arrow was called a *cateia*: according to Servius’s explanation, those who hurled it at the enemy made it return by means of the cords with which they had fastened it. See that note, and the *Isidoriana*, chapter 87, no. 25. But what is transmitted in the *Isidoriana* from Nicolás Antonio concerning the returning arrow should rather be corrected from Servius, so that a returning arrow is understood not as one that strikes the person who drew the bow, but as one that is drawn back toward him by the same person. Again, in chapter 47 of this book, a passage from Hosea occurs. The ancient version presents it thus: “They turned into nothing; they became like a drawn bow.” AREV.]

2. And again, speaking in the person of the same Lord: “Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me” (Psalm XXI, 17). The name of dogs is also applied to them by another prophet. For it is written in Isaiah: “All the dogs are blind, not knowing how to bark.” For it is the custom of dogs, as our Hilary says, to fawn upon the shepherd, know the flock, and pursue beasts lying in wait. But these blind dogs, not seeing their shepherd and not understanding their duty, turned their barking from beasts toward the flock and from thieves toward the Lord. Hence another prophet also says of them: “They became for me a returning arrow.”

1. Because he was valued at and sold for thirty pieces of silver, he himself foretold this through Zechariah: “If it is good in your sight,” he says, “give me my wage”; and they weighed out my wage—thirty pieces of silver. ## CHAPTER XXI. He was betrayed by his disciple

1. Since the Lord also indicated his betrayer to the apostles through the bread he offered, he recalled in the Psalms that this had been fulfilled in him, saying: “He who ate my bread magnified his treachery against me.” And again: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food” (Psalms XL, 10; LIV, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0479C]

CHAPTER XXI, preceding column, no. 2. Another reading has *traditore* (“betrayer”) instead of *proditore* (“traitor”), and *posset* (“could”) instead of *potest* (“can”). MAR.]

2. Concerning Judas the traitor, Jeremiah, who knew beforehand, foretold this long in advance: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus on a diamond point” (Jeremiah XVII, 1). This applies appropriately either to Judas or to the Jews, who sinned against Christ in such a way that their sin is not written in ink, which perhaps can be erased, but with an iron stylus on a diamond point—that is, in a way that cannot be erased because of the hardness of their hearts, unless they believe.

## CHAPTER XXII. He was delivered up by himself

[Note: [Col. 0479D]

CHAPTER XXII, no. 1. Other readings have *morte* (“by death”) instead of *mortem* (“death”), and *manu* (“hand”) instead of *manus* (“hands”). MAR.]

1. Because he himself willingly delivered himself up for us, Isaiah says: “He was offered because he himself willed it.” And below: “Because he surrendered his soul to death, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isaiah LIII, 7). And he himself speaks through the prophet Jeremiah in this way: “I have abandoned my house, I have forsaken my inheritance, I have delivered my beloved soul into the hands of its enemies” (Jeremiah XII, 7)—that is, into the hands of the Jews, who killed him.

## CHAPTER XXIII. He was seized

1. Because he was to be seized, the prophet Jeremiah foretold this long beforehand: “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was seized in our sins” (Lamentations IV, 20). By this prophecy he plainly demonstrated both that Christ is Lord and that he was delivered up for our sins.

[Col. 0479C] 2. Likewise, the Book of Wisdom says: “The wicked said among themselves: ‘Let us seize the Just One, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works; he claims to possess knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God.’” And below: “If he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and free him from the hand of his enemies.” And below: “So that we may know his reverence and test his patience, let us condemn him to a most shameful death”—that is, by crucifixion.

## CHAPTER XXIV. He was judged

1. Because he was to be judged, David cries out under the figure of the people sinning against God: “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you, so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm L, 6). For Christ, coming in the body, constituted himself as though guilty and presented himself to be judged by human beings, the judge of men submitting to human judgment. Thus, gentle and patient while he was judged, he conquered, because the persecuting people found nothing in him worthy of judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0479D]

CHAPTER XXIV, no. 2. Another reading has *servitutis* (“of servitude”) instead of *servientium* (“of those serving”). MAR.]

2. Hence the prophet, announcing the coming of his judgment, threatens the same people in this way: “Hear what the Lord says: ‘Arise and contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Let the mountains hear the judgment of the Lord, and the strong foundations of the earth’” (Micah VI, 1 and following). “For the Lord’s judgment is with his people, and he shall be judged with Israel,” saying: “My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Answer me, for I brought you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of those serving; I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam before you.” There he shows the Lord’s benefits bestowed upon his people, and, in contrast with them, their evils against him. Then he adds what is to come upon that same people: “Hear, O tribe; who will approve it? Is there still fire in the house of the wicked, treasures of iniquity?”

[Note: [Col. 0479D]

2. “A false witness shall not go unpunished, because he sold the Just One for silver.” The first part of this testimony is taken from Proverbs XIX, 5; the second from Amos II, 6. Isidore attributes both to Isaiah, unless all the manuscripts are corrupted—which does not seem likely, since in chapter 20 he reports the same words under the same name of Isaiah. There too the words “If your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord,” etc., which are from Malachi III, 13, are brought forward under the name of Zechariah by mistake. Through a similar lapse of memory, in chapter 29 of this book he cites as Jeremiah’s, as though it were from him, the words: “I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows.” This passage is taken from Isaiah L, 6. For where the Vulgate reads, “I gave my body to those who struck me and my cheeks to those who plucked them,” words that Isidore had already cited, the Septuagint read: “I gave my back to whips and my cheeks to blows.” Cyprian, in *Against the Jews*, II, 12, and Lactantius, in *Divine Institutes*, IV, 18, likewise cite these under the name of Isaiah. Moreover, in chapter 31 of this book Isidore cites as Jeremiah’s the words: “This people surrounded me with the thorns of their sins.” I have nowhere been able to find any trace of them, just as I cannot find the passage that Lactantius cites under the name of the same Jeremiah concerning Christ, in book IV, chapter 8: “Blessed is he who existed before he was born.” Nor can one find, in chapter 12, that passage from Solomon: “The virgin’s womb was weakened and received the strong one; it was burdened, and the virgin mother became greatly compassionate.” MAR.]

2. And Zechariah: “If your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord, and you said, ‘What have we spoken against you?’” And in the Psalms he says: “Unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied against itself” (Psalm XXVI, 12). And Isaiah says concerning Judas: “A false witness shall not go unpunished, because he sold the Just One for silver.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Jews cried out that he should be crucified

1. Because they cried out to Pilate that he should be crucified, Christ had already foretold this through Jeremiah concerning the Synagogue, saying: “I abandoned my house; my inheritance became for me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me” (Jeremiah XII, 7)—blaspheming, namely, and saying: “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke XXIII, 21; John XIX, 6).

2. And elsewhere he himself says: “Against whom have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you loosened your tongues?” (Isaiah LVII, 4). And Isaiah: “Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue is against the Lord” (Isaiah III, 8). Likewise, he himself says: “I expected them to do judgment, but they did iniquity—not justice, but a cry” (Isaiah V, 7).

## CHAPTER XXXII. He was clothed in scarlet

[Col. 0482D]

1. And because the soldiers, mocking him, clothed him in scarlet, the prophet Isaiah foretold this, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra? Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (Isaiah LXIII, 1). He answered: “I have trodden the winepress alone.” He said that he alone had trodden the winepress because he alone accepted the passion for the sin of the world, and alone washed away the offenses of all with his blood.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. While suffering, he was silent

[Note: [Col. 0483C]

CHAPTER XXXIII, no. 1. Another reading has *tondente se, obmutescet* (“before his shearer, he shall become silent”); thus it does not have “he did not open his mouth.” MAR.]

Isaiah says of him: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah LIII, 7). During his passion he said nothing to Pilate when questioned; but through humility his judgment was taken away. At first he was silent so that he might be judged, when, like a lamb before its shearer, he was without a voice, did not open his mouth, and restrained his power.

3. But at the end it is written of him: “God shall come manifestly, our God, and he shall not be silent” (Psalm XLIX, 3). He was silent so that he might be judged when he came hidden; but he shall by no means be silent when he comes manifestly to judge.

[Col. 0483C]
