2. But Christ alone, the King of the ages, raised the glory of his power and majesty upon his shoulders. Isaac too prefigured this: when he was led by his father as a sacrificial victim, he himself carried the wood (Genesis XXII, 6), thereby prefiguring at that time Christ’s extraordinary passion, as he carried the wood of his passion.

## CHAPTER XXXV. He was affixed to the cross

[Note: [Col. 0483D]

# Chapter 35, no. 1. “Let us cast wood into his bread.”

**Chapter 35, Note 1.** “Let us cast the wood into his bread.” This is Jeremiah 11:19, where, to use Jerome’s words, there is the consensus of all the Churches that these words are spoken concerning Christ under Jeremiah’s persona. Cyprian, *Book II Against the Jews*, chapter 14; Lactantius, *Book IV*, chapter 18; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, except that he reads: “Let us cast his bread into the wood.” All certainly refer the passage to Christ, into whose body—which is truly bread and life—the wood was cast when he was affixed to the cross. Justin, *Against Trypho*, asserts that the Jews formerly deleted this passage from their copies out of hatred for Christ. MAR.

In the same place: “the prophet Jeremiah.” The Barberini Codex omits this. AREV.

1. Because he was suspended and fastened to the wood of the cross, the prophet Jeremiah, speaking in the person of Christ, foretold this, saying:

> I was like a gentle lamb being led to the sacrifice, and I did not know that they had devised plots against me, saying: “Let us cast wood into his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living.” [Jer. 11:19]

For the prophet presents those things which the Lord was about to suffer at the hands of the Jews as though they had already happened.

**Note.** 2. Another reading: “of the flesh into the wood.” MAR.

In the same place: “in the evening,” or “before evening,” instead of “at evening.” MAR.

2. For what is the wood cast into the bread except the fastening of Christ’s flesh to the wood? We acknowledge that the bread is his body; our faith recognizes the wood in the bread as the cross in his body, because the bread is the life of his body. For it is written:

> And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear day and night, and you shall not believe in your life. [Deut. 28:66]

But again, in the Psalms, because he extended his hands upon the cross, he says:

> The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice. [Ps. 140:2]

Either because, with the evening of the world approaching, or because the sun was already declining toward evening, the Lord gave up his spirit on the cross, lifting his hands upon that same wood of the cross and offering himself to God as a sacrifice for us, so that through that sacrifice our sins might be erased.

**Chapter 35, Note 3.** “The Lord reigned from the wood.” This is a passage from Psalm 95:10. For where we now read, “Say among the nations that the Lord has reigned,” it was formerly read, “The Lord has reigned from the wood.” The Jews, however, removed this passage, like the preceding one, as Justin says in *Against Trypho*, because it pressed them more than anything else. The passage remains whole in the Roman and Hispanic Psalters in this form:

> Say among the nations that God has reigned from the wood.

Accordingly, Bishop Fortunatus said in his hymn concerning the cross:

> What David sang in faithful song  
> Has now been fulfilled,  
> When he said: “Among the nations  
> God reigned from the wood.”

With similar boldness, the same Justin says that the Jews removed from the sacred books these words:

> “This Passover is our Savior and our refuge. Consider it, and let it rise into your heart, because we must humble him upon the wood. After this we shall hope in him, lest this passage be abandoned forever,” says the Lord God of hosts.

These words are indeed cited by Lactantius, *Book IV*, chapter 18. Yet no trace of them exists in the sacred books, nor are they cited by Isidore anywhere in this whole work. MAR.

In the same place: Grialius’s edition had “and after this we shall overcome” in Justin’s citation, “This Passover,” etc.; these words are said to have been removed from the books of Ezra. See Mariana himself, who discusses these matters more fully, chapter 7, concerning the Vulgate edition. AREV.

3. Isaiah also writes concerning the proclamation of his cross:

> And his principality shall be upon his shoulders. [Isa. 9:6]

That is, the standard of his cross, which he carried before him upon his shoulders, in accordance with the prophecy of the prophet David, who says:

> The Lord reigned from the wood.

The prophet Habakkuk likewise foretold the passion of Christ’s cross, saying:

> Horns are in his hands. [Hab. 3:4]

What else is this except the trophy of the cross? Again, concerning his ascent upon the cross, in which, when exalted, he drew all things to himself, he says:

> Lord, my strength, he established my feet for completion. Upon the heights he will set me, so that I may triumph in his glory. [Hab. 3:19]

# Chapter 36. The nails pierced his hands, and his feet were fastened.

**Chapter 36, Note 1.** “They pierced my hands and my feet,” Psalm 21:18, where the sufferings of Christ the Redeemer are recounted individually. Yet Jewish faithlessness also corrupted this passage. Instead of “They pierced my hands,” they read in Hebrew, “Like a lion, my hands.” Isaac, although Jewish by birth, nevertheless admits in the book in which he argues on behalf of the Hebrew manuscripts that this passage has been corrupted. MAR.

In the same place: another reading is read incorrectly. MAR.

1. Because he was crucified, and his hands and feet were fastened with nails, he himself speaks through David, saying:

> They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon me and saw me. [Ps. 21:18]

By these words he clearly signifies a body stretched out upon the cross, with hands and feet fastened and pierced through by the penetration of nails. David did not suffer this, for he is read to have rested in peace without any bodily suffering.

2. But this was foretold concerning Christ’s passion: he was fastened to the wood by the Jewish people with nails. Hands and feet are pierced only in one who is suspended upon wood. Likewise, in the *Song of Songs*:

> My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the finest myrrh. [Song 5:3]

He said this specifically on account of the nail wounds.

3. And through Malachi, because he was to be crucified, the same Lord first declared concerning himself:

> If a man affixes God, he says—because you affix me, and you have said, “In what have we affixed you?” [Mal. 3:8]

After this God added to them:

> You affix me, the whole nation.

This pertains to the mystery of the Lord’s passion, in which the Jews crucified Christ when they laid their criminal hands upon him.

4. God again recalls this through Zechariah, saying:

> And they shall look upon me whom they pierced, and they shall mourn for him with mourning as for an only son, and they shall grieve over him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn. [Zech. 12:10]

We recognize that this was fulfilled in Jesus, whom the Jews pierced upon the cross and whom they will grieve to have crucified by them on the day of judgment, when they see him reigning in the majesty of the Father and of himself. [Luke 9:26]

# Chapter 37. He was crucified between two thieves.

1. That he was to be crucified between two thieves had been foretold long beforehand through Isaiah:

> And he was reckoned among the transgressors. [Isa. 53:10]

And the prophet Habakkuk says:

> In the midst of two living creatures you will be known. [Hab. 3:2]

That is, in the midst of two thieves.

# Chapter 38. His garments were divided.

**Chapter 38, Note 1.** “For it was a seamless tunic,” that is, woven together on every side. This is John 19:23. In fact, only in the lesser Tarraconensian manuscript was the word “seamless” read; it was absent from all the others. For this reason it was marked with an obelus. In the Vulgate edition we read: “For the tunic was seamless, woven from above throughout”; the Greek likewise reads: Ἦν δὲ ὁ χιτὼν ἄῤῥαφος ἐκ τῶν ἄνωθεν ὑφαντὸς δι’ ὅλον, “And the tunic was seamless, woven from above throughout.” Where the Vulgate says “throughout,” Isidore says “on every side.”

The kind of garment mentioned there is called by Festus Pompeius a *tunica recta*, when he says: “Straight garments are men’s garments which fathers arrange to have made for their children as an auspicious sign; they are so called because they are woven while standing and upward in height.” The Greeks call this an ὀρθοστάδιον χιτῶνα, an “upright tunic.” Nonnus explains its form in that Gospel passage in these two verses:

> Ὅστις ὅλος καὶ ὕπερθεν ὁμοῦ καὶ ἔνερθε φορῆος  
> Ἄῤῥαφος ἦεν ὕφαντος ἀπ’ αὐχένος εἰς σφυρὰ λήγων.

“The garment that was worn whole, alike above and below, was seamless, woven from the neck down to the ankles.”

Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book 19, chapter 22, says: “A garment is called *recta* when they weave it upward while standing.” Thus Isidore and Festus say that the *recta* tunic is woven upward, while the Gospel and Nonnus say that it begins from the upper part, evidently being woven downward. Perhaps this kind of garment was woven in both ways. MAR.

In the same place: *Etymologies*, Book 19, chapter 22, section 18: “A garment is called *recta* when they weave it upward while standing.” Compare the note at that passage. AREV.

1. After the sentence of the cross came the division of the garments and the casting of lots for the robe. The same Lord had foretold this through David, saying:

> They divided my garments among themselves, and for my robe they cast lots. [Ps. 21:19]

The Gospel history relates how this prophecy was fulfilled. For when the soldiers had divided the other garments, concerning the tunic they said:

> Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for whose it shall be. [John 19:24]

For it was a seamless tunic, that is, woven together on every side.

# Chapter 39. He was given gall and vinegar to drink.

**Chapter 39, Note 1.** Psalm 68:22, “my food.” MAR.

In the same place: another reading has “of another” instead of “foreign.” MAR.

Mariana perhaps intended to indicate the variant “my food” instead of “my food” in the accusative. In the Corbie Psalter, as cited by Sabatier, the reading is indeed: “And they gave gall as my food.” AREV.

1. That they gave vinegar mixed with gall to him hanging upon the cross had already been foretold by the Lord in the Psalms:

> They gave gall as my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. [Ps. 68:22]

He also proclaims the same thing elsewhere against Jerusalem, saying:

> I planted you as a choice vine; how have you become a bitter, foreign vine? [Jer. 2:21]

2. God had planted a good vine, that is, the Jewish people; but it was corrupted by its own fault and gave its Creator bitterness to drink. Therefore Moses also says:

> Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitter to them. [Deut. 32:32]

Accordingly, rebuking them above, he says:

> Thus you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people? [Deut. 32:6]

# Chapter 40. They surrounded a sponge full of vinegar with hyssop.

1. That they surrounded a sponge full of vinegar with hyssop had been stated in the Psalms:

> You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed. [Ps. 50:9]

Hence also in the Law, by means of a bundle of hyssop, lambs’ blood was sprinkled upon those who wished to be cleansed. [Exod. 12:22] This signified that through the Lord’s passion the sins of the world would be washed away.

# Chapter 41. The inscription of his cross was not altered.

**Chapter 41, Note 1.** “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title.” The title is Psalm 56, although I find these words neither in the Greek nor in the Vulgate edition, but only in one Hispanic Psalter:

> To the end; do not corrupt David in the inscription of the title.

Augustine, in his commentary on that Psalm, has: “Do not corrupt David in the inscription of the title.” In the commentaries circulated under Jerome’s name: “To David himself, in the inscription of the title, do not destroy,” that is, “do not corrupt the inscription of the title”; these are Isidore’s words.

The Hebrew has:

> Do not corrupt David, *Michtam*,

that is, “Do not corrupt David, Michtam”; some take this word to mean “a little golden object.” The Septuagint and the ancient Fathers thought that it signified an inscription of a title and referred it to Christ’s cross. Pagninus left it untranslated in his version, fearing the variety of opinions. MAR.

In the same place: Sabatier cites a Vatican manuscript Psalter, preserved in Hilary, with “do not destroy”; yet Hilary seems to prefer “do not corrupt.” AREV.

1. Concerning the title of the cross, the Jews said:

> Do not write, “King of the Jews,” but that he himself said, “I am King of the Jews.”

And Pilate replied:

> What I have written, I have written. [John 19:21]

For it had already been prophesied in Psalm 56:

> Do not corrupt the inscription of the title,

in the sequence of which Psalm not only the Lord’s passion and death but also his resurrection and ascension are proclaimed.

# Chapter 42. Hanging upon the cross, he prayed to the Father for his enemies.

1. Because, hanging upon the cross, he prayed to the Father for his enemies, Isaiah says:

> He bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors. [Isa. 53:12]

And in the Psalms:

> In return for my love they opposed me, but I prayed for them. [Ps. 108:4]

**Chapter 42, Note 2.** Another reading: “while he had said.” MAR.

In the same place: “remembering his mercy.” MAR.

2. Likewise, when Habakkuk had said of him:

> In the midst of two living creatures you will be known,

he added:

> When my soul is troubled, you will remember mercy in wrath. [Hab. 3:2]

By this statement the prophet prefigured in himself the person of the Jews, who, stirred by anger, crucified Christ. Yet he, remembering his mercy, said:

> Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. [Luke 23:34]

# Chapter 43. He was crucified for our sins.

**Chapter 43, Note 1.** That is, “a sacrifice for our sins.” These words occurred in only one lesser Tarraconensian manuscript. As for what follows, “But why did he suffer for us?”, I think the adversative has been used in place of an inferential conjunction, a fault common among the Spaniards. MAR.

1. Because he was crucified not for his own sins but for ours, Isaiah says:

> For the iniquities of his people he was led to death; I will give the wicked for his burial. And again: He was wounded because of our iniquities and crushed because of our crimes; by his bruising we were healed. And again: We all went astray like sheep; each turned to his own way, and the Lord placed upon him the iniquities of us all. [Isa. 53:5 ff.]

In accordance with the Apostle, who says:

> Because he knew no sin, he himself was made sin for us, [2 Cor. 5:21]

that is, a sacrifice for our sins. Why, then, did he suffer for us? This is the reason.

# Chapter 44. Because he died.

**Chapter 44, Note 1.** “Our God, God will save us”; “the Lord’s death”; and “the Lord’s exit from death.” From Psalm 67:21, with the word “death” added from the lesser Tarraconensian manuscript, in which alone it occurred. I found the earlier words, “Our God, God will save us,” in one Hispanic Psalter; in the same Psalter the latter words were read in this form: “And the exit from the death of the Lord God.” Perhaps this was how it was to be read in Isidore, but all the manuscripts differed. MAR.

1. After the scourges and the cross, and the drinking of gall and vinegar, his death follows. The Law itself did not keep silent concerning it, saying:

> Lying down, he slept like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who will awaken him? [Gen. 49:9]

Psalm 67 also proclaims this same death:

> Our God, God will save us, and the Lord’s death, and the Lord’s exit from death.

**Note.** 2. Another reading: “and to go forth into life.” MAR.

2. What could be said more plainly? The Lord Jesus, whose name means “Savior,” is himself our God, saving us. Since he had to be born and to depart from life through death, therefore it is added:

> The Lord’s death, and the Lord’s exit.

Likewise, through Isaiah:

> He was led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. For the sins of his people he was led to death. [Isa. 53:7]

**Chapter 44, Note 3.** Another reading: “it is sweet to me” instead of “it is sweet for me.” MAR.

In the same place: after the words “my sleep is sweet to me,” Codex Florentinus 2 contains a fairly long fragment, which I reproduce here:

> “And indeed sleep is sweet, because it proceeds from that intoxication concerning which it is written: ‘Be intoxicated, beloved ones.’ Joseph was intoxicated with his brothers at midday by this intoxication; here, bearing the figure of Christ, he intoxicated the weary soul and satisfied the hungry one, and therefore was awakened from sleep. That sleep is sweet both to him and to us alike, because in John it is written that the Lord, speaking to the disciples, wished his joy to be in them and that they should be filled with joys. This occurs in those who, after Christ’s grace, have rested in the sleep of death and will rise again in glory by that same grace.
>
> “This is to be understood [perhaps supply: ‘joy’] of those whose hearts directed themselves along the right way, in which they walked—those who resolved to proceed in the heavenly way of righteousness according to the teaching of the Scriptures, as they had promised in baptism, and neither to turn aside into the byways [perhaps: ‘nor by the way’] of error nor to deviate through the pleasures of the world, foreseeing from a lofty consideration the struggles with vices that were to come. This is most clearly shown when the mind of the elect places bitterness before the eyes of the heart: even when established in the peace of virtues, seeing the evils lying in wait, it does not consent to rest securely.
>
> “For first he has within himself, established by firm resolution [perhaps: ‘he ought to have’], that he should do no evil. Second, he considers that he should not do good carelessly; and after he has done wrong, he strives to subject even his righteous deeds to himself, lest, if they pass into the rule of the mind and fall into the fault of pride, evils should arise from the very good things through the vice of negligence—arrogance from instruction, cruelty from justice, laxity from piety, anger from zeal, sluggishness from gentleness, and the like.
>
> “Let them also attend to that singular teaching of the prophet, who says: ‘Direct your heart along the right way’—which is indeed the path of God’s commandments, in which one must walk without turning to the left. Thus, awakened by divine revelation from the sleep of weariness and sadness, may we be able to receive the promised sleep of rest and peace, which those consoled by the divine promises will be granted to find. Hence, by experience, what is promised fittingly comes to pass, as those who preceded us also maintain.
>
> “It is written in the sacred Scriptures: ‘If you sleep, you shall not fear; you shall rest, and your sleep shall be sweet.’ In accordance with this, the one who remembers how to live innocently and justly before God sleeps securely here, remains awake, rests, and walks. But when the righteous man sleeps in death, he not only does not fear the powers of the evil spirits; he also rests in peace, sleeps securely, and awaits the day of resurrection. If these things are so sweet to creatures that do them, how much sweeter [perhaps: ‘the sweeter’] are they to him from whom the capacity to do what has been said is granted?”

Thus far Codex Florentinus 2, which nevertheless omits the passage concerning Daniel through the end of the chapter, “let us condemn him.” AREV.

3. The Jews, however, do not expect the Christ whom they hope will come to die. Therefore let them answer: Who is this whom the prophet announces? Likewise, Jeremiah says:

> I have intoxicated the weary soul, and I have satisfied every hungry soul; therefore I awoke as though from sleep, and I looked, and my sleep was sweet to me. [Jer. 31:25]

4. The angel also speaks to Daniel concerning Christ’s slaughter and death, saying:

> Know and understand: from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the ruler, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and after the sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed—that is, after four hundred and ninety years—and his people, who will deny him, shall no longer be his.

Hence the destruction of the Jews follows there, which was later completed:

> The people, together with the coming ruler, will destroy the city and the sanctuary, [Dan. 9:25]

that is, the Roman army together with Vespasian.

5. Likewise, in the *Wisdom of Solomon*, this is read concerning his death:

> Let us question him with insults and torments, so that we may know his reverence and test his endurance; let us condemn him to a most shameful death. [Wis. 2:19]

# Chapter 45. Darkness occurred during his passion.

1. That darkness occurred at midday during his passion and the sun itself withdrew is also declared by the divine books, as the prophet Amos testifies:

> On that day, says the Lord, I will make the sun set at midday, and I will darken the earth in the day of light. [Amos 8:9]

**Chapter 45, Note 2.** “Through Vespasian.” Others have “through Vespasian and Titus.” AREV.

2. And Jeremiah says:

> She who gives birth was terrified—that is, Jerusalem—and her soul was afflicted; her sun set while it was still midday. She was confounded and accursed; I will give their survivors to the sword. [Jer. 15:9]

This was accomplished through Vespasian.

# Chapter 46. They did not break his legs.

1. Moreover, because they did not break his legs, but only those of the thieves, it had already been foretold:

> You shall not break his bone. [Exod. 12:46; Num. 9:12; John 19:36]

For they had been commanded to celebrate the Passover in the likeness of a sheep, in which the shadow of the Lord’s passion had gone before: he was led like a sheep to slaughter. [Isa. 53:7] That figure of the lamb signified Christ’s passion.

# Chapter 47. He was pierced with a lance.

1. Because his side was pierced with a lance, this had been foretold by Job himself:

> He broke me and set me as a target; he surrounded me with his spears; he pierced my loins with wounds; he cut me down with wound upon wound. [Job 16:13]

That is, with the wound of the lance upon the wounds of the nails. Hence also through David it was foretold by him:

> They added to the pain of my wounds. [Ps. 68:27]

**Chapter 47, Note 2.** “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.” Zechariah 12:10, where the Septuagint says: “They shall look toward me because they insulted me.” John the Evangelist, 19:37, says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced.”

In the following words, where we have placed, “Certainly, the man whom they crucified,” both Tarraconensian manuscripts read: “Certainly, the man whom they crucified.” The Hispalensian manuscript has: “Certainly, the man whom they pierced, and not God.” We removed the words “and not God” as an interpolation, because they were absent from the other copies and lest they should appear to favor those who denied the communication of properties, among whom was Theodoret, as is clear from his dialogues. MAR.

2. And through Jeremiah:

> He bent his bow and set me as a mark for the arrow; he sent the daughters of his quiver into my reins. [Lam. 3:12]

And again, concerning that same people, the Lord says through the prophet:

> They became for me a returning arrow. [Hos. 7:16]

And Zechariah:

> They shall look upon him whom they pierced.

Certainly, the man whom they crucified. By this testimony Christ was also promised as coming in the flesh in which he was crucified.

# Chapter 48. Blood and water flowed from his side.

1. Because blood and water flowed from his side, Zechariah says:

> You also, through the blood of your covenant, sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water. [Zech. 9:11]

And again:

> As a man went out from the east, behold, waters flowed from his right side, [Ezek. 47:3]

namely, from Christ’s side.

**Chapter 48, Note 2.** Another reading: “which flows from his side.” MAR.

“Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” In John 7:38 we read:

> Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers shall flow from his belly, etc.

Yet it is not sufficiently clear from which passage of divine Scripture this testimony was taken. Jerome says in his prologues to the Pentateuch and Chronicles that it is found only in the Hebrew, without designating the passage. Some think it was taken from Proverbs 5:16, where it says: “Let your fountains flow forth.” But in that passage the Septuagint manuscripts do not differ from the Hebrew. Chrysostom, commenting on this passage in John, thinks that it occurs nowhere in the Old Testament but is quoted from some book that no longer exists. MAR.

In the same place: another reading has “they shall flow from his side,” or “from his belly.” MAR.

2. Another prophet speaks likewise of this same water flowing from his side:

> Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly, [John 7:38]

namely, the waters of baptism, which give life to believers and are bestowed upon the thirsty, when what is written is fulfilled:

> Wash yourselves; be clean. [Isa. 1:16]

And:

> You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. [Ps. 50:9]

# Chapter 49. He was buried.

**Chapter 49, Note 1.** “They placed me in darkness,” Psalm 142:3. In all the Psalters, however, the singular is read: “He placed me in darkness.” Isidore, I think, seeing these numbers frequently alternate, read the passage in the plural, which better supported his arrangement. MAR.

In the same place: another reading has “he will give the wicked.” MAR.

1. Because he was handed over to burial and buried, it is said in the Psalms:

> They placed me in darkness, like the dead of the ages. [Ps. 142:3]

As though he were saying: “Like human beings”—certainly because he was God himself. Likewise Isaiah:

> And the Lord shall be named as an eternal sign that shall not be removed, and his tomb shall be glorious. [Isa. 55:13; 11:10]

And elsewhere:

> I will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death. [Isa. 53:9]

# Chapter 50. A stone was placed at the entrance of the tomb.

1. Because, after he had been buried, a stone was placed at the entrance of the tomb, the same prophet says through Jeremiah:

> My life slipped into the pit, and they placed a stone over me. [Lam. 3:53]

And again:

> He closed my ways with hewn stones; he built around me so that I could not escape. [Lam. 3:9]

**Chapter 50, Note 1.** Another reading: “he labored in the pit,” Lamentations 3:53. MAR.

In the same place: another reading has “they closed” instead of “he closed,” there, verses 7 and 9. MAR.

After “so that I could not escape,” Codex Florentinus 2 continues as follows:

> “All this occurred in the flesh. While the devil attacked it, because it was exposed, he was caught as by a hook by its divinity, which was hidden. For in the Lord Christ divinity is the hook, etc.” [As in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 14, through “our return to the heavens.”]
>
> “Those crowned with the splendors of glory will not be able to harbor sorrow because of the condemned. In the future the heart of the righteous will not be made miserable by compassion for the condemned, where the joy of the saints in contemplating God will be so great that no entrance will be granted to sadness. Just as white, compared with black, appears more beautiful, so the rest of the saints, compared with the condemnation of the wicked, will be more glorious. Thus justice,” etc.

The Codex continues in this manner, as in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 30, through “we shall ascend.” Since this is clear, I do not pursue it with other testimonies. Thus the same Codex concludes Isidore’s work *On the Lord’s Passion*. AREV.

# Chapter 51. He descended to the underworld.

**Chapter 51, Note 1.** Another reading: “All who hope are illuminated.” MAR.

In the same place: “he made it his own” instead of “he drew near.” MAR.

1. Because he descended into the underworld, the same Lord says in Ecclesiasticus:

> I shall penetrate all the lower parts of the earth, and I shall look upon all who sleep, and I shall illuminate those who hope in God. [Sir. 24:45]

Likewise, in the Psalms:

> My life has drawn near to the underworld; I have been reckoned among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead. [Ps. 87:4–5]

For he descended into the underworld as a man, but alone among the dead he was free, because death could not hold him.

# Chapter 52. Descending from death, he freed whom he wished.

**Chapter 52, Note 1.** Another reading: “he returned to the heavenly seat.” MAR.

1. Because, descending into the underworld, he rescued those who were held captive by the devil and then returned again to the heavenly realms, he had earlier foretold this through Hosea:

> I, even I, will seize and go; I will take away, and there is no one who can rescue. Going away, I shall return to my place—that is, to the heavenly throne.

And below:

> From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O underworld. [Hos. 5:14; 13:14]

# Chapter 53. The body of Christ did not see corruption in the tomb.

**Chapter 53, Note 1.** “For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld,” Psalm 15:10. These words are cited by Peter in Acts 2:31 concerning Christ’s resurrection. MAR.

In the same place:

> I slept, rested, and rose again, because the Lord raised me.

From Psalm 3:6, according to the Hispanic Psalter, which often differs not only from the Gallican but also from the Roman Psalter, as stated above. MAR.

Mariana also observes in his treatise concerning the Vulgate edition, chapter 19, that the Gothic and Roman Psalters differ in certain places. From the Roman Psalter he cites this passage as follows:

> I slept, I was overcome by sleep, and I rose, because the Lord received me.

Compare the *Isidoriana*, chapter 87, sections 15 and 16. AREV.

1. That Christ’s body did not see corruption in the tomb, but, immediately overcoming death and rising again, returned from the underworld, he himself also foretold through the prophet in the Psalms:

> My flesh rests in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. [Ps. 15:9–10]

Concerning this resurrection it is also sung in the third Psalm:

> I slept, rested, and rose, because the Lord raised me. [Ps. 3:6]

**Note.** 2. Another reading: “I shall sleep in the same place.” MAR.

2. What else does the prophet indicate when he says that he slept and rose, except that this sleep was death and the awakening was resurrection? This is shown more clearly in Psalm 40, where he says:

> But you, Lord, have mercy on me, raise me up, and I will repay them. [Ps. 40:11]

And again:

> Will not one who sleeps also rise again? [Ps. 40:9]

Likewise, in Psalm 4:

> In peace I shall sleep and rest, because you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope. [Ps. 4:9]

“Uniquely,” because he alone rested in such a way that he rose immediately after death.

**Note.** 3. Another reading: “I shall be exalted” instead of “I shall be lifted up.” MAR.

3. Again, through Isaiah, he cries out concerning this same resurrection:

> Now I shall arise, says the Lord; now I shall be exalted, and now I shall be lifted up. [Isa. 33:10]

Here the testimony of his resurrection and ascension is openly displayed. Hence there also he adds the zeal of the Jews, saying:

> You will conceive error and give birth to it; your spirit, like fire, will devour you.

# Chapter 54. He rose from the underworld.

1. Because he rose from the underworld on the third day, the prophet Hosea had foretold this, saying:

> Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has seized us and will heal us; he will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight. [Hos. 6:1]

All these things were fulfilled in Christ. For he was handed over on Thursday, suffered on Preparation Day, and rose around dawn on Sunday, returning from the underworld.

**Chapter 54, Note 2.** “He was prepared as at dawn,” Hosea 6:3. Jerome and the Vulgate say “as the dawn.” Isidore, however, changed the grammatical form in order to demonstrate by these words that Christ returned to life in the morning—a view held by many, although others, with considerable numbers and authority, thought that it occurred at midnight. The Hebrew could perhaps support Isidore’s reading, with the Hebrew term [the supplied text is uncertain here] taken adverbially. The Greek word ὄρθρον, “dawn,” does not permit this, since it is distinguished from the adverb πρωΐ, “early.” MAR.

2. Therefore the prophet added:

> His going forth was prepared as at dawn. [Hos. 6:3]

When he said, “We shall rise and live in his sight,” the prophet speaks of himself or of the saints who were in the underworld and rose with him on the third day.

# Chapter 55. The apostles were sent to preach.

1. Because after his resurrection Christ appeared to fishermen and sent them to preach to the nations, Jeremiah had previously mentioned this, saying:

> Behold, I will send many fishermen, says the Lord, and they will fish for them. [Jer. 16:16]

Accordingly, according to Matthew’s Gospel, it is read that Jesus, coming beside the Sea of Galilee, saw Peter and Andrew his brother casting nets into the sea, and said to them:

> Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. [Matt. 4:18–19]

**Chapter 55, Note 2.** Another reading: “spiritually” instead of “specially.” MAR.

2. Similarly, when he saw two other brothers, James son of Zebedee and John his brother, weaving nets in the boat with their father Zebedee, he summoned them and transformed them from fishermen of fish into fishers of men, so that through the net of preaching they might draw all believers out from the depths of this world.

After these fishermen the passage continues:

> And I will send hunters, and they will hunt them from every mountain, from every hill, and from the caves of the rocks. [Jer. 16:16]

This pertains specifically to the conversion of the nations, whom the apostles captured from every direction, having been appointed for the taking of souls.

**Note.** 3. Another reading: “Come,” or “I shall come,” instead of “I come.” And “spiritually” instead of “specially.” MAR.

In the same place: In the Vulgate: “Into Africa and Libya, holding a bow.” The same testimony is repeated in Book II, chapter 1, section 9. AREV.

3. Since after the glory of his resurrection the Lord was to send them to preach among the nations, he also spoke beforehand through Isaiah, saying:

> I am coming to gather all nations and tongues, says he; they shall come and see my glory, and I shall place among them a sign, namely, the cross. And I shall send survivors from them to the nations, to the sea, to Africa and Libya, holding a bow—that is, the swift word of preaching—to Italy and Greece, and to the distant islands, and to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. [Isa. 66:18–19]

In this statement the apostles are specifically prophesied as being sent.

4. The prophets did not remain silent about the fact that they preached the Gospel throughout the whole world. This too had previously been foretold in the Psalms:

> There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. [Ps. 18:4]

# Chapter 56. He ascended into heaven.

1. Now, because after his resurrection Christ ascended in human form into heaven, even to the Father, Daniel says: “I was looking in a night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming in the clouds of heaven, and he came even to the Ancient of Days”—that is, to the Father. After this he added: “And they presented him before him, and he gave him authority, kingship, and every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him; his authority is an everlasting authority that shall not be taken away, and his kingship shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 13).

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]**
>
> **CHAP. LVI, no. 2.** Some copies read *sedem* (“seat”) instead of *dexteram* (“right hand”). MAR.]

2. The Psalmist again indicates his ascension into heaven in this way: “He himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his return reaches even to its summit” (Ps. XVIII, 6). For, coming from heaven, he descended even to the underworld; and, returning, he reclaimed his dwelling, ascending and sitting at the right hand of the Father, from whom alone he had previously gone forth.

[Col. 0494C] 3. The Psalmist shows with what joys his ascent into heaven, or his entrance, is proclaimed. For when the heavenly powers saw Christ’s flesh ascending in the clouds and entering the gates of heaven, they said: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII, 7).

4. David, commemorating his ascent elsewhere also, says: “He ascended upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII, 11). And again: “He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII, 19). For unless he had been on earth, he would not be said to ascend. But what does “he led captivity captive” mean except that, having conquered death, he was leading into heaven, as a captive, the very flesh that he had assumed from the earth?

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]**
>
> 5. Some copies read *Christi* (“of Christ”) instead of *Dei* (“of God”), and *ejus* (“his”) instead of *Christi* (“of Christ”). MAR.
>
> In the same passage: “The same place is in the eastern regions.” Not only is the place from which Christ ascended situated in the eastern regions, but he also ascended into heaven with his face turned toward the East, as the footprints indicate, which are still visibly impressed there to this day. Severus Sulpicius, Book II of his *History*, and Paulinus, Letter 10, write about these; hence the tradition of turning toward the eastern part of heaven when praying and building churches, as Basil teaches, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27. On the contrary, while hanging on the cross, he had his face turned toward the West, as Sedulius bears witness in Book V of his *Carmina*, where he says:
>
> “From there he gathers the four regions of the square world.” MAR.]

5. Therefore, after this the prophet exhorts all the nations, calling them to praise God, and again announcing Christ’s ascent to them in these words: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord; sing praises to God, who ascends above the heavens of heavens toward the East.” He rightly added, “toward the East,” because the same place is in the eastern regions, where Christ rose and from which he ascended into heaven. After this he added: “Your entrances were seen, O God, the entrances of my God and King” (Ps. LXVII, 25). For, while all the apostles and five hundred men were looking on, he thus ascended into heaven.

> **[Note: [Col. 0495D]**
>
> 6. Some copies read *in coelo* or *in coelis* (“in heaven” or “in the heavens”) instead of *in coelum* (“into heaven”), and *puer* (“child”) instead of *servus* (“servant”). MAR.]

6. Solomon also proclaims his ascension in the *Song of Songs*: “Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song II, 8). Amos likewise says: “The Lord built his ascent in heaven and established his promise on earth” (Amos IX, 6). Moreover, the statement that the Lord makes through Isaiah—“Now I shall arise, now I shall be exalted, now I shall be lifted up” (Isa. XXXIII, 10)—declares the resurrection and ascension of Christ, as though he were openly saying: “Now I shall rise from the dead; now I shall be exalted into heaven; now I shall be lifted up in the kingdom.” Hence Isaiah himself says elsewhere: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, lifted up, and shall be very high” (Isa. LII, 13). This certainly pertains to his ascension into heaven and to the glory of his kingdom.

## CHAPTER LVII. He sits at the right hand of the Father.

1. That he sits at the right hand of the Father is written in the Psalms: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX, 1). Let the Jews therefore inquire to whom the Lord said, “Sit at my right hand.” Was it to an archangel? I do not think so; nor to an angel, nor to a prophet. For none of them possesses that glory, but the one whom the invisible God considers worthy of sitting beside him—he sits at the right hand of the Father.

> **[Note: [Col. 0495D]**
>
> **CHAP. LVII, no. 2.** Some copies read *omnium* (“of all”) instead of *omnibus* (“over all”). MAR.]

2. As he is worthy of sitting beside God, so also is he worthy by nature and by name. Concerning him the Psalm likewise says: “The Lord shall reign over all the nations; God has sat upon his holy seat” (Ps. XLVI, 9). And again: “The Lord has prepared his seat in heaven, and his kingdom shall rule over all” (Ps. CII, 19).

## CHAPTER LVIII. Christ’s kingdom will be everlasting.

> **[Note: [Col. 0496D]**
>
> **CHAP. LVIII, no. 1.** The Vulgate reads: “And he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him, and he gave him authority, honor, and kingship,” etc. AREV.]

1. Because his kingdom in heaven and on earth will remain eternal and everlasting, Daniel says: “I saw in a night vision, and behold, one like a son of man was coming in the clouds of heaven, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and he was brought before him; and dominion, honor, and kingship were given to him, and every people, tribe, and tongue shall serve him; his authority is an everlasting authority that shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII, 13).

2. By this testimony it is shown that Christ received dominion and kingship from almighty God in such a way that his authority is eternal and his kingdom remains without any end of corruption. Again the same Daniel says: “In those days the Lord of heaven will raise up a king who shall never be overthrown, and his kingdom shall not be handed over to another people. He shall strike and shatter all kingdoms, and it shall stand forever” (Dan. II, 44).

> **[Note: [Col. 0496D]**
>
> 3. Some copies read “there shall be no end of his peace.” MAR.]

3. The prophet Isaiah likewise says of him: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isa. IX, 7). And in the Psalms it is written: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is lifted up” (Ps. LXXI, 7)—that is, until the consummation of the age.

## CHAPTER LIX. After his ascension Christ sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

1. Because after his ascension he sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, David says: “He ascended on high, he took captivity captive, he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII, 19). For after his ascension he sent the Holy Spirit, in whom there is the fullness of all gifts.

2. Concerning this he also announced through the prophet Joel, saying: “It shall come to pass after these things: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Moreover, upon my servants and my handmaids in those days I will pour out my Spirit” (Joel II, 28). And Zechariah says: “I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and prayers” (Zech. XII, 10).

## CHAPTER LX. The apostles spoke in various languages.

1. Because, filled with the Holy Spirit, the apostles spoke of the mighty works of God in the languages of all nations, this too was foretold earlier by the Psalmist, who says: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 4).

## CHAPTER LXI. He will come to judge.

[Col. 0496D]

> **[Note: [Col. 0496D]**
>
> **CHAP. LXI, no. 1.** Is this not he who raised up the lowly, Ezek. XXI, 26? Except that in all languages it is read in the feminine gender: “Is this not she who raised up the lowly?” Nevertheless Jerome, in his commentary on that passage, explains the words as referring to the last judgment. MAR.]

1. That we expect Christ to come from heaven as judge, and that the Father gave him all judgment, is thus announced through Ezekiel: “Thus says the Lord God: Remove the turban, take off the crown. Is this not he who raised up the lowly and humbled the lofty? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I shall make it so; and this has not taken place until he comes whose is the judgment, and I shall give it to him.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0497D]**
>
> 2. “I shall speak like a wall,” Isa. XLII, 13. The Hispalensian reads “I shall speak as a woman in labour”; the lesser Tarraconensian, “I shall speak as one giving birth.” This is the true reading. But we necessarily retained the corrupt reading, because below, where this testimony is explained, Isidore himself says: “Judging, he will cry out; he will speak like a wall, because suddenly, like a falling wall, he is about to crush his enemies.” MAR.
>
> In the same place, some copies read *judicet* (“may judge”) instead of *judex* (“judge”). MAR.]

2. Of him Isaiah says: “The Lord shall go forth as a strong man, and as a man of war he shall arouse zeal; he shall cry out and shout, and shall prevail over his enemies. I have always been silent; I kept silence; I was patient. Like a wall, I shall speak; I shall lay waste and swallow up at once” (Isa. XLII, 13). This pertains to the second advent, in which he will go forth not lowly, to be judged, but as a strong judge; nor will he keep silence, as he did at his first advent, or be patient, as he was in the passion of the flesh; but, judging, he will cry out and speak like a wall, because suddenly, like a falling wall, he is about to crush his enemies.

[Col. 0497B] 3. This is also taught by the testimony of the Psalmist, where he says: “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not keep silence” (Ps. XLIX, 3). For although in the first advent of his humility he kept silence while being judged, at the second, when he comes manifestly to judge, he will not keep silence, but will cry out, to render to each according to his works.

> **[Note: [Col. 0497D]**
>
> 4. Some copies read *sursum, et terram, ut discerneret populum* (“from above, and the earth, that he might distinguish the people”). MAR.]

4. It follows: “Fire shall burn before him,” because he will consume the works of sinners as wood, hay, and stubble, and will test the deeds of the righteous as gold, silver, and precious stones (I Cor. III, 12). They will say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us into refreshment. He shall call heaven from above and the earth to distinguish his people. Gather to him his saints, who order his covenant above sacrifices, and the heavens shall declare his righteousness, because God is judge” (Ps. LXV, 12; XLIX, 4).

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D]**
>
> 5. Some copies read *lapidibus grandinis* (“hailstones”) instead of *lapide grandinis* (“a hailstone”). MAR.]

5. Isaiah too says: “The Lord shall make the glory of his voice heard, and shall show the terror of his arm in the threat of wrath and the flame of devouring fire. He shall strike in a whirlwind and with a hailstone” (Isa. XXX, 30). For the arm of God is Christ, who will come to judge in flame and the terror of a storm. Of whose judgment the same prophet again says: “Rise up, as in ancient days, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon?” (Isa. LI, 9).

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D]**
>
> 6. Some copies read *principibus, quando* (“at the beginning, when”) instead of *generationibus saeculorum* (“in the generations of ages”). MAR.]

6. This second advent of Christ is proclaimed: he will rise for judgment, for the separation of good and evil, with the power with which he rose in the generations of ages—that is, in the beginning, when he struck the proud one, namely the devil, separating him from the fellowship of the good angels. Of this judgment of Christ the prophet Micah also speaks, saying: “Hear, O mountains, the judgment of the Lord, and you strong foundations of the earth, because the Lord has a judgment with his people, and he will contend with Israel, saying: My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I troubled you? Answer me” (Mic. VI, 1).

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D]**
>
> 7. “For I believe that my Redeemer lives.” This is Job XIX, 25, a passage which Jerome, writing to Pammachius, affirms is the clearest in the Old Testament for proving the future resurrection of bodies. MAR.]

7. Then, according to Zechariah, “They shall look upon him whom they pierced, and mourn for him as for an only son, and grieve over him as men usually grieve at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. XII, 10). For they will grieve over him whom they crucified when they see him judging and reigning in the majesty of the Father and his own majesty. Job also, illustrious before the law for evangelical virtues, declares with prophetic authority that he will be redeemed and raised again, and presented to God the judge, who will come to judge the living and the dead, saying: “For I believe that [Col. 0498B] my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour.” What God, if not he who is to be seen in judgment? As we read: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. XII, 10).

> **[Note: [Col. 0498D]**
>
> 8. Some copies read *elevationem* (“elevation”) instead of *abbreviationem* (“shortening”). MAR.
>
> In the edition of Grialius, *consumatio* and *consumationem* sometimes occur instead of *consummatio* and *consummationem*, which is the correct spelling. AREV.]

8. Some say that he will judge the wicked in the place where he himself was judged, as the prophet Joel testifies: “Let all nations arise and go up into the valley of Jehoshaphat; there I shall sit to judge all the nations round about” (Joel III, 12). For many maintain that the judgment will occur where the Lord suffered, Isaiah furnishing proof: “The Lord God of hosts shall bring about a consummation and a shortening in the midst of the whole earth” (Isa. X, 23).

9. What could this consummation and shortening that is to precede be, except that of the future judgment? But David gives trustworthy testimony concerning the Lord’s passion as to where that midst of the earth is, saying: “But God, our king before the ages, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII, 12). For our salvation is nothing other than the redemption of our Lord, Saviour, and judge, which arose in the midst of the earth.

## CHAPTER LXII. Epilogue of the work.

1. Behold, from the prophets we have shown the judge and king of the New Testament; behold, from the law we have shown Christ to be Lord of all. The books of the Hebrews contain all these things; the Jews read everything, but do not understand. For everything is sealed to them, as the prophet testifies: “The words of this book shall be like the words of a sealed book, which, if someone gives it to a man who does not know letters and says, ‘Read,’ he replies, ‘I do not know letters’; and if he gives it again to another who knows letters and says, ‘Read,’ that man replies, ‘I cannot, for the book is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX, 11).

[Col. 0499A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0499A]**
>
> **CHAP. LXII, no. 2.** Arrests, slaps, scourges, spittings. These were absent from the Hispalensian manuscript and seemed to us to be additions; yet we retained them marked with an obelus, to warn the reader. MAR.
>
> [Col. 0500A] In the same place, some copies read *coelis* (“the heavens”) instead of *coelum* (“heaven”). MAR.
>
> In the same place, this whole chapter is called not an epilogue but a postscript in many manuscripts. AREV.]

2. These are the seals of the Old Testament, which the Son and heir unsealed, enlightening the eyes of our heart, as it is written: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.” For, in order to understand Christ, we have the law as guide and the prophets as witnesses, from whom we have set forth his divinity and name, his nation also and lineage, country, birth, miracles and healings, arrests, slaps, scourges, spittings, the drinking of gall and vinegar, death, the arrow, burial, hell, the incorruption of his body, the resurrection of the flesh, his ascension into heaven, kingdom, and judgment.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0499]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0499B]

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D]**
>
> **PREF., no. 1.** Some copies read *ascensum* (“ascent”) instead of *ascensionem* (“ascension”). MAR.]

1. Since the Breviary of the preceding book has in some measure explained the birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of our Lord and Saviour, the following little work will set forth the prophecy concerning the two peoples, that is, the Jews and the Gentiles. In this work, holy sister, you will be able to observe from a few examples how greatly the voices of the prophets have sung of the rejection of the Jewish people and its ceremonies, and how greatly they have thundered in praise of the people of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER I. The calling of the Gentiles.

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D]**
>
> **CHAP. I, no. 1.** Some copies read *reliqua contineantur* (“the remaining matters may be contained”) instead of *reliqua contueantur* (“the remaining matters may be considered”). MAR.]

1. At the beginning of this little work, then, we must speak of the faith of the Gentiles, so that the remaining matters may more easily be considered once the faith of the Church itself has first been set forth. Accordingly, when Moses prayed to the Lord for the people that he might spare the sinful people on account of the worshipped calf, the Lord replied: “I shall be merciful to them; nevertheless, as I live and as my name lives, all the earth shall be filled with my glory” (Num. XIV, 21).

2. Therefore, because all nations were to be called to the worship of the one true God, the prophet David testifies, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations” (Ps. XXI, 28). And again: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wonders. The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. XCVII, 1).

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D]**
>
> 3. Some copies read *gregem* (“flock”) instead of *regem* (“king”). MAR.]

3. He proclaims that this multitude of nations will be united in worship of the one God thus: “When peoples are gathered together as one, and kingdoms, to serve the Lord” (Ps. CI, 23). “As one,” certainly, that is, under one king: so that kingdoms and many peoples which were called such through the diverse rites of idols, by coming together in one faith, may be called one people of God and one kingdom.

4. This gathering of the people from the Gentiles is the Church itself, to which it is prophetically said in the Psalms: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and the house of your father, because the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. XLIV, 11). For the prophet calls the people of the Gentiles to forget their people, that is, the assembly of unbelievers, and the house of their father, namely Babylon, which is both the house and wife of the devil, and to be joined to Christ in the marriage of faith.

5. To its peoples Isaiah cries, saying: “Gather yourselves and come; draw near together, because you have been saved from the Gentiles. For those who lift up the sign of their graven image and pray to a god that does not save have not known” (Isa. XLV, 20). Who are these saved from the Gentiles, if not those who believed from among the Gentiles? And when he says, “Gather yourselves and hear together,” he shows that the nations ought to be gathered into one faith and communion.

> **[Note: [Col. 0499D]**
>
> 6. Some copies read *omnes* (perhaps *omnis*) *fines terrae* (“all ends of the earth”). MAR.
>
> In the same place, the Hispalensian reads: “Let the Jews be ashamed of certain things concerning God”; the printed editions, “Let the Jews be ashamed, who, while [Col. 0500D] claiming God specially for themselves”; the Tarraconensian, “Let the Jews indeed be ashamed, claiming God specially for themselves.” We have adopted this reading. MAR.]

6. Likewise he says: “Turn to me and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth, because I am God and there is no other. I have sworn by myself; a word shall go out from my mouth and shall not return: every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear by the Lord.” We now see this fulfilled, when the Church of God is spread through all the ends of the earth. By this prophecy let the Jews indeed be ashamed, who claim God specially for themselves, when they hear, “Every tongue shall swear by the Lord,” that is, not only the people of the Hebrews now, but also the whole multitude of the Gentiles.

> **[Note: [Col. 0500D]**
>
> 7. Some copies read “in addition, the same Isaiah.” MAR.
>
> In the same place, Isidore follows the Vulgate: “but [the barren woman] has more [children], she who has a husband.” AREV.]

7. Again the same Isaiah, after setting forth Christ’s humiliation, which he endured in the flesh, proclaimed anew the praise of the Church of the Gentiles, for which he suffered such things, and at the same time disclosed prophetically that it is one throughout the whole world, saying: “Praise, barren woman, who do not bear; sing praise and whinny, you who did not bear; for the children of the deserted woman are now more numerous than of her who had a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare; make your cords long and strengthen your stakes. For you shall spread abroad to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations and inhabit deserted cities” (Isa. LIV, 1).

[Col. 0501A]

> **[Note: [Col. 0501C]**
>
> 8. Some copies read *tuum* (“your”) instead of *meum* (“my”). MAR.
>
> In some manuscripts, as in Florence 1 and in the Lucchese manuscript, after the words “all day to an unbelieving people,” other words are added, namely: “For the nations now sought me, though they had not asked, because the prophets did not come to them; and they found me when Christ was announced to them. But what of the Jewish people, except what follows: ‘I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people’? And again, concerning the same promise to the Gentiles: ‘The open country shall be sheepfolds, and the valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for my people who sought me. But you who have forsaken the Lord I shall number to the sword, and all of you shall fall in slaughter.’ To what people do these promises belong, if not to the Gentiles, who sought the Lord? Of them he said above: ‘They sought me, who had not formerly asked.’ And who are they who forsook God and will fall in slaughter, if not the Jewish people? Of them he said: ‘I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people.’ What follows is also directed against them: ‘Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger,’ because, while the people called from the Gentiles feed on the bread of God’s word, Judaea wastes away in fasting. Likewise he himself says, ‘My house,’ etc. These passages should be compared with the end of chapter 6 of this book; but it should be observed that Isidore repeatedly repeats the same things, both often in this work and in others, so that we should not therefore suppose to be additions all those things which elsewhere Isidore discusses either more fully or more briefly.” AREV.]

8. And again: “I created the fruit of the lips: peace, peace to him who is far off and to him who is near” (Isa. LVII, 19). The Apostle also explains this where, speaking of the Church coming from circumcision and uncircumcision, he says: “He preached peace to those who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Eph. II, 17); and again: “They sought me who had not formerly asked; they found me who did not seek me. I said: Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not call upon my name; I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people” (Isa. LXV, 1).

> **[Note: [Col. 0501D]**
>
> 9. “Into the sea, into Africa, into Libya.” The Hispalensian has “into the sea, into Africa, into Lydia,” a more suitable reading, for the Hebrew, Greek, and Vulgate editions have it thus at Isa. LXVI, 19. But because all the other manuscripts in this place differed, and in Book I, chapter 55, where the same testimony is cited, all manuscripts consistently read “Libya,” we retained that word in the text. MAR.]

9. Likewise Isaiah himself says: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, says the Lord” (Isa. LVI, 7). Finally he says: “I come to gather together all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my glory, and I shall set a sign among them, and from among them I shall send those who have been saved to the nations, to the sea, to Africa, to Libya, those who hold the arrow” (Isa. LXVI, 18). Thus Isaiah.

> **[Note: [Col. 0502C]**
>
> 10. Some copies read *repromissionem* (“promise”) instead of *compromissionem* (“mutual promise”). MAR.
>
> In Mariana’s note was *repromissione*, which I changed to *repromissionem*; for, I think, that is what Mariana intended, and that is what our manuscripts exhibit, which for the most part agree with Mariana’s copies. AREV.]

10. Jeremiah, however, thus shows the promise to the Gentiles: “All nations shall be gathered in the name of the Lord in Jerusalem, and shall not walk after the perversity of their heart” (Jer. III, 17). And shortly afterward: “The Lord has sworn in truth and in judgment, and the nations shall bless him and praise him” (Jer. IV, 2). The same Jeremiah on the calling of the Gentiles says: “O Lord, my strength, nations shall come to you from the ends of the earth, and say: Truly our fathers possessed falsehood” (Jer. XVI, 19). The same Jeremiah says to the Israelite people: “Hear the sound of the trumpet”; and they said, “We will not hear.” “Therefore hear, O nations” (Jer. VI, 17).

> **[Note: [Col. 0502C]**
>
> 11. Some copies read “men shall worship him, each from his own place.” And: “but that every place throughout the world is a place of prayer.” MAR.]

11. Likewise in Hosea: “I shall have mercy on her who was without mercy, and I shall say to that which was not my people: You are my people; and he shall say: You are my God. And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. II, 23). Likewise in Zephaniah: “For then I shall restore to the peoples a chosen lip, that all may call upon the name of the Lord and serve him with one shoulder” (Zeph. III, 9). And after this: “Each man shall worship him from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. II, 11). In this passage too the calling of the Gentiles is prophesied; and it shows that there is no longer one place of prayer in which the carnal people seemed in some way to confine God, but that every place is a place of prayer, when it says: “Each man shall worship him from his own place.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0502D]**
>
> 12. Some copies read *recipiant* (“may receive”) instead of *percipiant* (“may learn”); *prophetabunt* (“shall prophesy”) instead of *properabunt* (“shall hasten”); and *ambulabimus* (“we shall walk”) instead of *ibimus* (“we shall go”). MAR.
>
> In “He shall rebuke strong nations afar off,” the passage is Micah IV, 3. But below, in chapter 19, Isidore cites those words under Isaiah’s name—certainly Isa. II, 4: “He shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples, unto a distance.” By a similar error Julian, imitating Isidore, does the same in Book I *Against the Jews*; for the phrase *usque in longinquum* must not be attached to Isaiah’s words, and in Micah, where the phrase is added, it ought not to have been *usque in longinquo*, but *usque in longinquum*, as in all the versions and as grammatical usage requires. MAR.]

12. Micah too foretells that all nations will be gathered, in order that they may learn the discipline of faith, thus: “And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten and say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we shall walk in his paths, because the law shall go out from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he shall judge many peoples and rebuke strong nations, unto a distance” (Mic. IV, 1).

> **[Note: [Col. 0502D]**
>
> 13. Some copies read “into the nations, with the Jews left behind,” etc. MAR.
>
> In others: “into the nations, while the Jews remain in barrenness.” AREV.]

13. These are the last days in which the faith of the Saviour has shone forth. The mountain prepared above the top of the mountains is Christ, because he is the head of the apostles and prophets. The house of the Lord is the Church of Christ, established upon him, to which the diversity of the Gentiles is gathered. The law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, either that it might come to the nations, the Jews having been left behind because of unbelief, or because Jesus, being among that same people, said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 19).

[Col. 0502C]

> **[Note: [Col. 0502D]**
>
> 14. Some copies read *habitabunt* (“they shall dwell”) instead of *habitabo* (“I shall dwell”); *populus* (“people”) instead of *in populum* (“as a people”); and *ut scias* (“that you may know”) instead of *et scies* (“and you shall know”). MAR.]

14. Likewise Zechariah says of the Church of the Gentiles: “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion, for behold, I come and shall dwell in your midst, says the Lord; and many nations shall be joined to the Lord on that day, and they shall be a people to me, and I shall dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you” (Zech. II, 10). Likewise there: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Until peoples come to dwell in many cities, and inhabitants go, one to another, saying: Let us go and entreat the face of the Lord and seek the God of hosts; I too will go; and many peoples and strong nations shall come to seek the Lord of hosts in Jerusalem” (Zech. VIII, 20).

> **[Note: [Col. 0503D]**
>
> 15. “Let them be ashamed,” etc. Vatican manuscript 278 has: “Let the Jews be ashamed; let us emulate the same things which, conquered, they may recognize and hear, with the Lord proclaiming in Deuteronomy: ‘You shall be nations,’ etc.” AREV.]

15. Therefore, with so many and such great testimonies, let the Jews, emulators of the converted Gentiles, be ashamed; and, at last convicted, let them recognize and hear the Lord proclaiming in Deuteronomy: “You shall be nations at the head, but the unbelieving people at the tail” (Deut. XXVIII, 44).

## CHAPTER II. All nations are commanded to believe in Christ.

[Col. 0503B]

> **[Note: [Col. 0503D]**
>
> **CHAP. II, no. 1.** “By the hearing of the ear he obeyed me,” Ps. XVII, 45. The Hispalensian has “in the hearing of the ear he obeyed me,” as in the Gallican Psalter. We preferred the reading found in the printed editions because it was in the Hispanic Psalter, which Isidore frequently uses throughout this work. MAR.]

1. Because all nations are commanded to believe in Christ the Son of God, Jacob said in the blessings of the patriarchs: “A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). And David, speaking in the Psalms in the person of that same Christ: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II, 7). And again: “You shall make me head of the nations; a people whom I did not know has served me; by the hearing of the ear they obeyed me.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0503D]**
>
> 2. Some copies read *sanctificabunt eum* (“they shall sanctify him”) instead of *servient ei* (“they shall serve him”). MAR.]

2. Likewise, elsewhere, the Psalmist says the same of him: “His name endures before the sun, and his throne before the moon; all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him, all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI, 17–18). Concerning his dominion he had also spoken above (v. 8): “He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the world.”

3. This testimony fits neither Solomon nor David. For it is known within what boundaries Solomon’s kingdom was confined. But we see this fulfilled in Christ, whose name is great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting. He began to rule from the river, where he was baptized by John, and through faith he reached the nations to the ends of the earth.

> **[Note: [Col. 0503D]**
>
> 4. “And after other things: He shall raise a standard among distant nations and whistle.” The preceding words, namely “On that day the root of Jesse shall be,” etc., are read at Isa. XI, 10. The words that follow, “He shall raise a standard among nations,” etc., are taken from chapter V, 26. Isidore, deceived by a lapse of memory and the similarity of the passages, cited what came first as though it came later and followed from it. The Tarraconensian reads *sibilabunt* (“they shall whistle”) for *sibilabit* (“he shall whistle”), but corruptly, as the other manuscripts show, agreeing in this part with the Vulgate and the Septuagint edition. MAR.]

4. Likewise in the same Psalms, concerning his eternal birth and his power among the nations, the Lord says: “Before the morning star I begot you; you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek; he shall judge among the nations, fill the ruins, and shatter heads in the land of many” (Ps. CIX, 3). And Isaiah says: “On that day the root of Jesse shall stand as a sign for the peoples; the nations shall entreat him” (Isa. XI, 10). And after other things: “He shall raise a standard among distant nations and whistle to him from the ends of the earth.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0504D]**
>
> 5. Some copies read *calcantium* (“of those treading”) instead of *calcantibus* (“to those treading”). And: “For we now see this.” MAR.
>
> In Florence 1, “in the prison of ignorance” occurs instead of “in the flesh of ignorance,” which is in the edition of Grialius. But “in the prison” is preferable. AREV.]

5. Likewise Isaiah, concerning Christ our Lord who would reign among the nations: “Thus says the Lord God, creating the heavens and stretching them out, establishing the earth and what springs from it, giving breath to the people who are upon it and spirit to those who tread it: I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness, and have taken hold of your hand and preserved you, and have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, that you may open the eyes of the blind and lead the bound out from confinement, those sitting in darkness out of the prison-house. I am the Lord; this is my name” (Isa. XLII, 5 ff.). We now see this fulfilled through Christ, who became light to the Gentiles set in the prison of ignorance.

6. Of them he also said elsewhere: “And I shall lead the blind in a way which they do not know, and in paths which they have not known I shall make them walk; I shall make darkness before them into light,” so that what had been said through the same prophet might be fulfilled: “The people of the Gentiles who sat in darkness saw a great light; for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, a light arose” (Isa. IX, 2). Again, concerning the calling of the Gentiles, he says: “Attend to me, my people, and hear me, my tribe, because a law shall go out from me, and my judgment shall rest in the light of the peoples; my righteous one is near; my Saviour has gone forth” (Isa. LI, 4).
