Source/review notes: Variant wording and witness readings are retained with their source forms and English glosses where the distinction matters.

7. And after this:

> “Rejoice and praise together, desolate Jerusalem, because the Lord has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (Isa. 52:9).

In addition, through the aforementioned Isaiah, the divine voice thus announces Christ in the flesh as judge of the nations:

> “Behold,” he says, “my servant: I will receive him; my chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased. I have given my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he show partiality, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax. In truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad or troubled, until he establishes judgment on the earth; and the islands will await his law” (Isa. 42:1).

8. The servant, then, but by virtue of his assumption of humanity, is Christ. Since, when he first came to the Jews, he was not received, he brought judgment to the nations. What judgment could this be except that they should be justified by faith? 73 His voice will not be heard outside—that is, among heresies and among the Jews placed outside the Church of God.

Likewise, concerning him Isaiah says:

> “Behold, my servant will understand; he will be exalted, lifted up, and will be very high. Just as many were astonished at you, so his appearance will be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. He will sprinkle many nations; kings will shut their mouths because of him. For those to whom nothing was told about him will see, and those who have not heard will contemplate” (Isa. 52:13).

9. Again, the same prophet says concerning him:

> “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander to the nations. Behold, you will call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you will run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you” (Isa. 55:4).

This entire prophecy clearly concerns the calling of the nations, because they were to believe in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

10. Some copies read *tabulis* (“tablets”) instead of *tabulas* (“tablets”), and *fine* (“end”) instead of *finem* (“the end”). MAR.]

10. Thus Habakkuk says:

> “The Lord speaks: Write the vision clearly, and explain it on tablets, so that the one who reads it may run; for the vision will still appear from afar at the end, and it will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come; it will not be late.”

Concerning the unbelieving Jews he continues:

> “Behold, the unbelieving person: his soul will not be upright within him” (Hab. 2:2, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

11. Some copies read *vestri* (“of you”) instead of *vestrum* (“of you”), and *monebo* (“I will warn”) instead of *commovebo* (“I will shake”). MAR.]

11. Likewise, through Haggai the same Lord prophesied in this way concerning Christ’s reign among the nations:

> “My Spirit will be in your midst; do not fear, because thus says the Lord: Yet a little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the dry land; and I will shake all the nations, and the one desired by all the nations will come” (Hag. 2:6).

But if an unbeliever understands this prophecy as referring to the Antichrist, it is certainly false. The nations do not desire him; only the Jews await him.

## CHAPTER III. The Jews and the nations are called to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

CHAP. III, note 1. Some copies read *Judaea* (“Judaea”) instead of *Judaeis* (“Jews”). MAR.]

1. Since both peoples—the Jews and the nations—are called under Christ’s rule by the prophecies of the prophets, Isaiah says:

> “And it will be in that day: a man will nourish one cow and two sheep, and from the abundance of milk he will eat butter” (Isa. 7:21).

The cow of the cattle is the people of Judaea, coming from the seed of the patriarchs. The two sheep are the Church coming from the nations. They are therefore two sheep and one cow, because the number of the Church from the nations is greater than that from the Jews.

2. The man who will nourish them is Christ himself, who says through Jeremiah:

> “Return, returning children, says the Lord, because I am your husband; and I will take one from a city and two from a family, and I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and instruction” (Jer. 3:14).

For he had said to the proud through Isaiah:

> “A man will nourish one cow and two sheep.”

Now God shows that this man is himself: he will take two from a family and one from a city, because the number of believers from circumcision is smaller than that from uncircumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

3. Some copies read *in terra* (“on the earth”) instead of *super terram* (“over the earth”). MAR.]

3. He calls this city Judaea, or Jerusalem; the family, however, he calls the nations; and the shepherds are the apostles or the teachers of the Church, preaching Christ’s grace.

In another passage the same Jeremiah likewise proclaims that the Jews will serve Christ:

> “And it will be in that day, says the Lord of hosts: I will break my yoke from your neck, and I will tear its bonds apart; foreigners will no longer rule over them, but they will serve the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them” (Jer. 30:8).

Concerning him Jeremiah says:

> “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch; and a king will reign, and he will be wise, and he will execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely; and this is the name by which they will call him: ‘The Lord is our righteous one’” (Jer. 23:5).

[Note: [Col. 0505D]

4. The lemma reads *Commemorabo superbiae, et Babylonis scientium* [Col. 0506D] *me*, “I will commemorate the pride and Babylon among those who know me.” The printed editions read *superbiae Babylonis scientibus me*, “the pride of Babylon among those who know me.” The Tarraconensis reads *superbiae et Babylonis scientibus me*, “the pride and Babylon among those who know me.” We follow the Hispalensis reading found in Jerome’s version, except that Jerome has *commemorabor*, “I will be commemorated,” instead of *commemorabo*, “I will commemorate.” MAR.]

4. The Father’s voice thus announces through the Psalmist the birth of this one for both peoples:

> “I will commemorate the pride and Babylon among those who know me. Behold Palestine, Tyre together with Ethiopia: this one was born there. But to Sion it will be said: ‘A man and a man were born in her,’ and the Most High himself founded her. The Lord will tell it when he registers the peoples: ‘This one was born there.’”

In Babylon, Palestine, Tyre, and Ethiopia the nations are signified. 75 In Sion, however, the people of the Hebrews are signified, because Christ was born for the salvation of both peoples.

5. Ezekiel likewise proclaims that Christ, in the person of David, will reign over both peoples:

> “One king,” he says, “will rule over all, and there will no longer be two nations; they will no longer be divided into two kingdoms; they will no longer defile themselves with their gods, abominations, or any of their iniquities. I will save them from all their dwelling places in which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. They will be my people, and I will be their God; and my servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them” (Ezek. 37:22).

[Col. 0506D] [Note: [Col. 0506D]

6. Some copies read *in visu* (“in a sight”) instead of *in visione* (“in a vision”). MAR.]

6. That Christ is the king of the Jews, Isaiah indicates when he says:

> “Say to the daughter of Sion: Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and saving, poor, riding upon an untamed donkey.”

The prophet Daniel, writing that Christ’s power was given by the Father not only over the nations but also over the Jews, says:

> “I was watching in a vision of the night, and behold, one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven; and he came as far as the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him” (Dan. 7:13).

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

7. In Grial’s text it read: “the Lord your God, Israel.” What follows differs considerably from the Vulgate. AREV.]

7. After saying that he had been taken up into heaven and brought before the Father, he added:

> “And power, honor, and a kingdom were given to him, and all peoples, tribes, and languages will serve him.”

What tribes are meant except the people of the Hebrews? What languages except the nations of the Gentiles?

The prophet Amos likewise summons the Jews from God to Christ’s kingdom, saying:

> “Prepare to meet the Lord your God, O Israel, because behold, I am the one who establishes thunder, creates the spirit, and announces his Christ among human beings” (Amos 4:12).

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

8. Mariana observes in the treatise *On the Revised Vulgate*, chapter 6, that in the Gothic Bibles preserved in the church at Toledo the passage from Micah is read as Isidore reads it in chapter 11 of Book I *Against the Jews*, and almost similarly by Julian of Toledo in Book I *Against the Jews*, namely with a question. On the other hand, with the negation, as Isidore has it here, Jerome, Cyprian, and Origen also read it. Others maintain that the passage of Micah should be read affirmatively. AREV.]

8. So also Isaiah:

> “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord” (Isa. 2:5).

Concerning this David says:

> “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10).

Meanwhile the prophet Micah, when declaring the place of Christ’s origin, added that he would rule over Israel:

> “And you,” he says, “Bethlehem, house of Ephrata, you are not least among the thousands of Judah; from you a ruler will go forth for me in Israel” (Mic. 5:2).

76 9. In this passage he shows that Christ is the Lord of the Jews and that the same people will be subjected to his rule. He also foretold his power throughout the whole world in this way:

> “He will stand and see, and he will feed his flock in the strength of the Lord; and they will be in the honor of the name of their God, because now he will be magnified to the ends of the earth, and this one will be peace.”

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

10. “Say to the cities of Judah: Do not fear.” The printed editions and the Tarraconensis read *nolite timere* (“do not fear,” plural), a reading that was more convenient, except that the order would be awkward. In the Vulgate, Isaiah 40:9 reads: “Do not fear; say to the cities of Judah.” Therefore *noli timere* (“do not fear,” singular) must be referred to the prophet, not to the cities.]

10. Concerning the coming of this one, to be preached to the Jews, the Lord speaks through Isaiah:

> “Go up onto a high mountain, you who evangelize Sion; lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem; say to the cities of Judah: Do not fear. Behold your God. Behold, the Lord God will come in strength, and his arm will rule. Behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him. Like a shepherd he will feed his flock; in his arm he will gather the lambs” (Isa. 40:9).

[Note: [Col. 0507D]

11. Some copies read: “when it had been fulfilled in Christ, the Evangelist bears witness.” MAR.]

11. The prophet Zechariah likewise proclaims Christ’s kingdom among the Jews and the nations:

> “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Sion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king will come to you, righteous and saving, himself poor and riding upon a donkey and upon a colt, the foal of a donkey. His power will extend from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Zech. 9:9).

How this prophecy was fulfilled in Christ, the Gospels themselves bear witness.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the calling of the nations to faith before the Hebrews.

[Col. 0508A]

[Note: [Col. 0508D]

CHAP. IV, note 1. As Isaiah also says: “Until the fullness,” etc. The words “until the fullness of the nations enters” belong to Paul, Romans 11:25. Since the same thought is contained in Isaiah 59:20 in the words “he will come from Sion,” etc., Isidore has substituted Paul’s wording for Isaiah’s. MAR.]

The same passage: “as though he were going to convert at the end,” that is, “as though he were to be converted.” Isidore, following his usual practice, uses active forms for passive ones. For this reason we rejected the reading of the Hispalensis, which had *quasi in novissimo conversus* (“as though converted at the end”), although it seemed more convenient. Again, at the end of chapter 5, where the printed editions and the Hispalensis read *in novissimis conversurus* (“going to convert in the last days”), we, following the Tarraconensis, read *in novissimis convertendus* (“to be converted in the last days”); and shortly afterward, where those same codices read *conversuri sunt* (“they are going to convert”), we have adopted *conversi fuerint* (“they will have been converted”) from the same Tarraconensis, to which we gave greatest credence. We did not wish the reader to be unaware of this variation. MAR.]

1. That the nations could believe in Christ first, and the Jews afterward, David the prophet demonstrates. For he saw that the Lord had come to redeem Judaea, but that the Gentiles would believe first and Judaea would follow afterward, and he says:

> “Ethiopia will stretch out its hands to God” (Ps. 67:32),

that is, before Judaea believes, the Gentile people, blackened by sins, offers itself for salvation to almighty God.

As Isaiah also says:

> “Until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel will be saved”;

and in Deuteronomy:

> “You will be at the head among the nations, but the unbelieving people at the tail” (Deut. 28:44),

as though it were to be converted at the end.

## CHAPTER V. That at the end of the world the Jews will believe in Christ.

[Col. 0508B]

1. After these carnal Jews have passed away, in the last times their sons will believe in Christ, as the prophet Hosea bears witness:

> “For many days the sons of Israel will sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, and without manifestations” (Hos. 3:4–5).

Certainly, just as they now appear to be. Then he adds:

> “Afterward the sons of Israel will return, and they will seek the Lord their God and David their king; they will stand in awe of the Lord and of his goodness, in the last days.”

[Note: [Col. 0508D]

CHAP. V, note 2. Some copies read *venient* (“they will come”) instead of *veniunt* (“they come”). MAR.]

2. This entire prophecy is undoubtedly about Christ, who is signified by the name David. He was born from David’s seed according to the flesh. Concerning him Jeremiah says:

> “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch; and a king will reign, and he will be wise, and he will execute judgment and righteousness on the earth. In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely; and this is the name by which they will call him: ‘The Lord is our righteous one’” (Jer. 23:5).

3. Malachi likewise says that before the end of the world Elijah is to be sent for the conversion of the Jews:

> “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the heart of the fathers toward the children, and the heart of the children toward their fathers” (Mal. 4:5).

Before the coming of judgment, the Lord will send Elijah to turn the heart of the children toward the heart of the patriarchs and prophets, 78 so that their posterity may believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, whom those prophets awaited.

[Note: [Col. 0509D]

4. Some copies read: “that through Elijah he would convert them in the last days.” MAR.]

The same passage: “Make his ears heavy and close his eyes.” In the Tarraconensis the relative *ejus* (“his”) is absent; in the printed editions the words *ejus claude* (“close his”) are not present. This may perhaps be Isidore’s true reading, since in Julian, Book I *Against the Jews*, these two words are likewise lacking. We preferred the reading of the Hispalensis because it was found in the Vulgate. The passage is Isaiah 6:10. MAR.]

The same passage: “May they be converted to me, and …” MAR.]

In Grial’s edition the note reads *quod pro in quo* (“that instead of in which”). Perhaps Mariana intended *quid est quod* (“what is it that”). AREV.]

4. For if the Jews have until now believed rightly, what does the prophet mean when he testifies that Elijah will convert them at the end? At present they are blinded in mind and cannot understand the Savior. They will hear him only at the end of the world, when the consummation of the age has come. For the Lord declares this through the prophet Isaiah:

> “Hear, hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6:9).

[Note: [Col. 0509D]

5. Some copies read *dissolvantur* (“may they be dissolved”) instead of *desolentur* (“may they be desolated”). MAR.]

5. And the prophet said:

> “‘How long, Lord?’ And the Lord said: ‘Until the cities are desolated, without an inhabitant, and the houses without a human being; the land will be left desolate, and the Lord will remove human beings far away. Then it will be converted and will be for a sign, like a terebinth and like an oak that spreads its branches; the holy seed will be what remains in it.’”

Behold, it is evident that they are now alienated from the light of faith and truth. They hear Christ but do not understand; they see but do not recognize him.

[Note: [Col. 0509D]

6. Some copies read *tandiu* (“for so long”) instead of *quandiu* (“how long”). And *salvabuntur* (“they will be saved”) instead of *sanabuntur* (“they will be healed”). MAR.]

In Grial’s text, mistakenly, *crudelitate* (“cruelty”) instead of *credulitate* (“belief”). AREV.]

6. But how long will they remain so? Until the cities are overturned and the land nearly returns to a desert. Then, converted, they will see; they will believe in Christ, and, understanding, they will be healed and will know everything.

In accordance with this Jeremiah also says to them:

> “At the end of days you will understand these things” (Jer. 30:24).

Concerning this final belief of the Jews Zephaniah likewise says:

> “At that time I will save the lame, and I will gather the one who had been expelled; and I will set them for praise and for a name throughout the whole land of their shame, at that time when I bring you and at the time when I gather you. For I will give you for a name and for praise among all the peoples of the earth, when I turn your captivity before your eyes, says the Lord” (Zeph. 3:19).

79 [Note: [Col. 0510D]

7. Some copies read *meum ponam* (“I will place my own”) instead of *novum ponam* (“I will place a new one”), and *novum* (“new”) instead of *carneum* (“fleshly”). MAR.]

7. He called the Jewish people “the lame,” because they now limp away from the paths of faith, as the psalm testifies:

> “They have limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:46).

God declares that he will save this people at the end when he says:

> “I will save the lame.”

And through Ezekiel:

> “After many days,” he says, “you will be visited, and in the last years you will come” (Ezek. 38:8).

A little earlier, because they are to be baptized, he says:

> “I will take you from the nations, and I will gather you from all the lands, and I will bring you into your land. I will pour clean water over you, and you will be cleansed from all your impurities; from all your idols I will cleanse you. I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you. I will take the stony heart from your flesh, and I will give you a fleshly heart, and I will place my Spirit within you. I will make you walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them. You will dwell in the land that I gave to your fathers; you will be my people, and I will be your God, and I will save you from all your impurities” (Ezek. 36:24).

[Note: [Col. 0510D]

8. Some copies read *finem autem* (“but the end”) instead of *vespere autem* (“but the evening”), and *futuris* (“future things”) instead of *futurum* (“future”). MAR.]

8. This is the people who will be converted in the last days. The patriarch Jacob prophesied of them under the figure of Benjamin, “a wolf devouring in the morning and dividing spoils in the evening” (Gen. 49:27).

For at the beginning of the world this same people received the law as though in the morning; but in the evening of the world, when they come to believe, they will divide between the New Testament and the Old.

Concerning those things promised to Israel in the future, the following is said of the same portion—the portion that will believe in Christ when they have been converted in the last times:

> “And it will be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’ And the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel will be gathered together; they will appoint for themselves one head” (Hos. 1:10).

[Note: [Col. 0510D]

9. Some copies read *ponent autem* (“but they will place”) instead of *ponentes* (“placing”). MAR.]

9. This will occur in the last times, when, with Elijah preaching, Judah will be converted to Christ, so that spiritually it may be one with Israel—that is, with the people of the nations, who already see God through faith. They will appoint for themselves one head, which is Christ, and will ascend from the earth—that is, from carnal and earthly hope—to the heavenly promises.

80 ## CHAPTER VI. Many of the Jewish people were not going to believe.

[Note: [Col. 0510D]

CHAP. VI, note 1. Some copies read *non erat ei aspectus* (“there was no appearance in him”) instead of the reading given here. MAR.]

Others read: “Thus Jeremiah foretold that they would suffer destruction.” AREV.]

1. Since many of the Jewish people were not going to believe in Christ, Moses the lawgiver foretold their same unbelief:

> “And your life will hang before your eyes; you will fear day and night, and you will not believe in your life” (Deut. 28:66).

Hence Isaiah also says:

> “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And we saw him, and there was no appearance” (Isa. 53:1).

By these words he signifies the unbelief of the Jews, who saw Christ but did not receive him. Since they could neither believe in nor recognize him, they were immediately destined for destruction.

[Col. 0510D] [Note: [Col. 0510D]

2. Some copies read *non est Domini* (“it is not the Lord’s”) instead of *non sunt Domini* (“they are not the Lord’s”). MAR.]

2. Thus Jeremiah foretold:

> “Go up upon its walls and destroy them; remove its branches, because they are not the Lord’s. The house of Judah has utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord; they denied me and said, ‘It is not he’” (Jer. 5:10).

To this day the Jews say this concerning Christ: “It is not he,” as they await another, who is the Antichrist.

Hence the Lord also says:

> “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5:43).

[Note: [Col. 0511D]

3. Perhaps *illum* (“that one”) instead of *illud* (“it”). The Vulgate has *illud*, because the preceding word is *sermo* (“word,” masculine). AREV.]

3. Likewise, in the same Jeremiah:

> “Behold, the word of the Lord has become a reproach to them, and they do not receive it” (Jer. 6:10).

Furthermore, it is shown in the Psalms that, while the nations would obey Christ, the Jews would not receive him. For when the same Christ had said through the prophet:

> “You will establish me as head of the nations, and a people whom I did not know will serve me,”

he immediately added the Jewish unbelief, saying:

> “The foreign sons have lied to me; the foreign sons have grown old, and they have limped from their paths” (Ps. 17:44).

Who are the foreigners except the Jews? They are rightly called foreigners because, persisting in unbelief, they have been excluded from the rewards of eternal life, which are promised to us according to faith by the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0511D]

4. Some copies read *ambulant* (“they walk”) instead of *ambulabat* (“he walked”). MAR.]

4. This perverse unbelief of the Jews concerning Christ was also recorded through Isaiah, when the Lord said to them:

> “Hear, hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6:9).

And in another passage:

> “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted, who walk in ways that are not good” (Isa. 65:2).

[Note: [Col. 0511D]

5. Some copies read *resonabunt* (“they will resound”) instead of *intumescent* (“they will swell up”). MAR.]

The same passage: Perhaps, “Will you not fear me?” etc. The Vulgate lacks *aut* (“or”). AREV.]

5. To them Jeremiah says:

> “Hear this, foolish and senseless people: they have eyes, and do not see; they have ears, and do not hear. Or will you not fear me, says the Lord, or will you not tremble before my face? I established the sand as the boundary of the sea, an eternal decree that it cannot cross. Its waves are stirred, but they cannot prevail; its billows swell, but they cannot cross it. Yet this people has a disobedient and unbelieving heart” (Jer. 5:21).

[Note: [Col. 0512D]

6. Some copies read *est justitia mea* (“my righteousness is”) instead of *feci justitiam meam* (“I have done my righteousness”). MAR.]

6. And elsewhere the same prophet says:

> “How can you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? Truly, the lying stylus of the scribes has worked falsehood. The wise have been put to shame, terrified, and captured. For they have cast away the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them.”

Concerning them Isaiah says:

> “They made human beings sin in word and turned aside from the righteous for nothing” (Isa. 29:21).

For this reason the same prophet rebukes them, saying:

> “Hear me, hard-hearted, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near; it will not be far away, and my salvation will not delay. I will give salvation in Sion and my glory in Jerusalem.”

7. The same prophet thus announces the faith of the nations and the unbelief of the Jews in Christ:

> “Those who formerly did not ask have sought me; those who did not inquire have found me. I said, ‘Here I am, here I am,’ to a nation that did not call on my name. I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people” (Isa. 65:1–2).

The nations that formerly did not ask have now sought him, because the prophets did not come to them before; and they found him when Christ was announced to them.

8. What, then, was the Jewish people except what follows?

> “I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people.”

And again, concerning the same promise of the nations:

> “And the plains will become sheepfolds, and the valley of Achor a resting place for cattle, for my people who sought me. But you who abandoned God I will number for the sword, and all of you will fall in slaughter” (Isa. 65:10).

[Col. 0512B] [Note: [Col. 0512D]

9. Some copies read *corruent* (“they will fall”) instead of *corruerunt* (“they fell”), and *jejunio* (“with fasting”) instead of *jejuna* (“fasting”). MAR.]

9. To what people, then, do these promises belong except the nations that sought God? Concerning them he said above:

> “Those who formerly did not ask have sought me.”

And who are those who abandoned God and fell in slaughter except the Jewish people? Concerning them he has already said:

> “I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving people.”

Against this people are also the words that follow:

> “Behold, my servants will eat, but you will hunger,”

because, while the people called from the nations feeds on the bread of the word of God, Judaea withers in famine.

## CHAPTER VII. Because of the unbelief of the Jews, Christ was going to pass over to the nations.

[Note: [Col. 0512D]

CHAP. VII, note 1. Some copies read *sicut viator* (“like a traveler”) and *et potest salvare* (“and he is able to save”). MAR.]

1. Because, on account of the unbelief of the Jews, Christ would abandon Judaea and pass over to the nations, the prophet Jeremiah foretold, saying:

> “To you we have sinned, O hope of Israel, its Savior. Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay? Why will you be like a wandering man who cannot be saved?” (Jer. 14:8).

What is understood in this statement except that the prophet saw in the spirit that, when Christ came, he would leave Judaea and go by faith among the nations? Therefore he said:

> “Why will you be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay?”

That is: You came into the land, soon to depart from the Jews.

2. Elsewhere, in the person of the Lord, the same prophet says:

> “Who will give me a travelers’ lodging in the wilderness? I will abandon my people and depart from them, because they are all adulterers, an assembly of transgressors. They stretch out their tongue like a bow of falsehood, and not of truth” (Jer. 9:2).

This is the voice of Christ, who established a travelers’ lodging—that is, the Church—in the wilderness of the nations, where the erring might be converted, while he abandoned the Jewish people.

To them he says through Malachi:

> “I have no further pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations” (Mal. 1:10).

83 [Note: [Col. 0513D]

In Grial’s edition it reads *gentibus profert* (“he brings forth to the nations”), which I consider corrupt. AREV.]

3. God was formerly with them, but after they were rejected on account of their sin, the Redeemer of the world passed over into the people of the nations. The whole of this people now rejoicing throughout the entire world says:

> “The Lord has magnified what he did with them; the Lord has magnified what he did with us; we have become rejoicing” (Ps. 125:3).

Christ first came to the people of Israel, but the prophet did not keep silent about the fact that they would not believe. He says:

> “First he will say to Sion: ‘Behold, I am here’; and I will give Jerusalem an evangelist. I saw, and there was no one among these who would enter into counsel or, when questioned, answer a word” (Isa. 41:27).

But because he passed over to the nations, it follows:

> “Behold, my servant; I will receive him. My chosen one, in whom my soul is well pleased; I have given my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations” (Isa. 42:1).

## CHAPTER VIII. That, after the Jews were rejected, the nations entered.

[Note: [Col. 0513D]

CHAP. VIII, note 1. Some copies read *vos faciet* (“he will make you”) instead of *nos faciet* (“he will make us”). MAR.]

1. It has been shown that the Jews were rejected and scattered on account of the crime by which they sinned against Christ. But because, after their rejection, the nations were to succeed them in their places through faith, the prophets did not remain silent about this either.

Isaiah says:

> “Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears. All the nations have been gathered together and the tribes have assembled. Who among you will announce this? And who will make us hear the first things?” (Isa. 43:8).

Behold, Israel, possessing eyes and ears for earthly promises, is led outside; and the diversity of the nations is gathered together into one, so that where those people were called, these may enter, and the inheritance promised to them may belong to these.

[Note: [Col. 0513D]

Open the gates, and the righteous nation that keeps the truth will enter. The ancient error has passed away. You will preserve peace, because we have hoped in you. He will bend down those who dwell on high; he will humble the lofty city. He will humble it to the ground; he will drag it down to the dust, and the foot of the poor will trample it, the steps of the needy’” (Isa. 26:1).

By this prophecy it is shown that the just and humble people of the nations succeeded to the place that the proud Jewish people had lost.

The one who swears on earth means one who swears in the flesh received from Christ; whoever swears in that flesh truly swears by God.

Is a bird circling around it?” Supply: “different in color,” or “variegated.” Jerome thinks that a peacock is meant, and compares Jerusalem to it because of the notable variety of its feathers. and the rest.

Through Jeremiah the same Son explains that the Jews’ destruction occurred because of his Passion. For he says:

> “My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; it gave its voice against me; therefore I hated it. Is my inheritance for me a bird of different color? Is a bird completely dyed? Come, gather together, all the beasts of the earth; hurry to devour” (Jer. 12:8).

He said, “Gather together,” for the beasts of the field came—that is, the fierce rulers of the nations—and the Jewish people were handed over to them for devouring.

3. Because they raised their voice against the Lord, he therefore adds:

> “Because of me the whole land has been utterly destroyed.”

For this is Christ’s voice. The sons of Israel had previously committed many sins, but they had never before been handed over to such prolonged destruction and captivity. When, however, they had filled up the measure of their fathers and, after killing the prophets, killed Christ, then, piling sin upon sin, they were handed over to a long-lasting destruction.

Therefore it is now said:

> “Because of me the whole land has been utterly destroyed.”

[Note: [Col. 0515D]

4. Because they do not understand this, the prophet Isaiah therefore foretold beforehand that they would be handed over to plunder, saying: “The Lord poured out upon his people the indignation of his anger and the might of war; he burned him all around, yet he did not know it, and he set him on fire, yet he did not understand” (Isa. 42:25). Mournfully lamenting their destruction, the prophet Jeremiah says: “My sons have become lost, because the enemy has prevailed” (Lam. 1:16). And again: “Those whom I raised and nourished, my enemy has consumed” (Lam. 2:22).

## CHAPTER X. On the Ruin of Jerusalem

[Col. 0515C]

1. Because Jerusalem was overthrown on account of the Jews’ denial of Christ, that same Lord proclaims this through Jeremiah, saying: “Climb its walls, and destroy them; remove its branches, for they are not the Lord’s. For the house of Judah has utterly transgressed against me, says the Lord; they denied me and said, ‘He is not the one’” (Jer. 5:10). Isaiah likewise says: “Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their inventions are against the Lord” (Isa. 3:8).

[Note: [Col. 0515D]

CHAPTER X, Note 2. Some copies read *crucify such a man* instead. MAR.]

2. By this testimony it is demonstrated that the city of Jerusalem and the province of Judea alike collapsed. He also shows the cause of their crime: they blasphemed against the Lord, saying, “Take him away, take him away, crucify him. We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15). Indeed, the prophet David, on account of the future passion of Christ and the calamity of the city and the Jews, foretold the following in the person of that same Christ, when they gave him gall and vinegar, as the Gospel relates: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Let their table before them become a snare, and a repayment, and a stumbling-block. Pour out your anger upon them, and let the indignation of your anger seize them. Let their dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one dwelling in their tents” (Ps. 68:22).

3. What had been foretold beforehand was later fulfilled. It happened in this very city of Jerusalem: after they had given Christ a bitter drink, and after they had shouted against the Son of God that he should be killed, vengeance from the Lord followed. The city was conquered, the Jews were defeated, and many thousands were killed; and now no Jew is permitted to approach that place where they had cried out for Christ to be crucified.

87

[Note: [Col. 0515D]

4. Some copies read *the same in Daniel* instead of *likewise in Daniel*. Some read *who is to come* instead of *who was to come*, and *for devastation* instead of *of devastation*, and *which he had planted* instead of *in which he had planted*. MAR.]

4. Likewise, in Daniel, after that angel had foretold the killing of Christ, he immediately announced the subsequent overthrow of Jerusalem, saying: “The people with the leader who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary” (Dan. 9:26)—that is, the Roman army with Vespasian. The prophet Isaiah composed a mournful song about this devastation, in which the same Jerusalem is lamented and its perpetual ruin is sung in prophetic language under the likeness of a vineyard in which God had planted a tower and a winepress—that is, the temple and the altar (Isa. 5:2).

[Note: [Col. 0516D]

5. Some copies read *may they be open* instead of *let it be open*. MAR.]

5. As long as this vineyard bore the richest fruits, therefore, it had God as its guardian, of whom it is written: “He who guards Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120:4). But after it bore thorns for its Creator, God abandoned it, and immediately the boar from the forest ravaged it (Ps. 79:14), and all who passed along the road harvested its grapes. Thus the Lord says: “And now I will show you what I am going to do to my vineyard: I will remove its hedge” (Isa. 5:5)—that is, “I will take away the assistance of the angels,” concerning whom it is written in the Psalms: “The Lord will send his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. 33:8). “It will be plundered by adversaries; I will destroy its walls, so that it may be open to hostile nations, and I will command the clouds above not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5:6).

[Note: [Col. 0516D]

6. Some copies read *they would rain* instead of *they would provide rain*. MAR.]

6. This was not prophesied concerning the earlier captivity. At that time, after the city had been captured, Jeremiah also prophesied, and Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah spoke of things yet to come. But this was foretold concerning the final captivity, because after the Lord’s passion the Jews had neither prophets nor apostles to provide them with the rains of spiritual gifts. Instead, what the Lord promised in Leviticus would happen to sinners befell them: “I will make your heaven bronze and your land iron” (Lev. 26:19).

[Note: [Col. 0516D]

7. Some copies read *where it was shouted* instead of *where they shouted*. MAR.]

7. And in Deuteronomy: “The heaven above you will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron” (Deut. 28:23). And again: “The Lord will give the rain of your land as dust; ashes will descend upon you from heaven, until it destroys you” (ibid., 24). But why did these things happen to them? Because God waited for them to practice righteousness and to receive the giver of such great gifts. They, however, produced thorns with which they crowned Christ, and they raised a cry by which they shouted against the Lord—that is, against Christ—that he should be crucified.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Jews’ Rejection and the Reprobation of the Synagogue

1. Concerning that city the Lord speaks through Isaiah as follows: “Where is this bill of repudiation of your mother, by which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities, and because of your crimes I dismissed your mother” (Isa. 50:1). Likewise through Hosea: “Judge your mother, judge her, because she is not my wife, and I am not her husband” (Hos. 2:2). Concerning the rejection of this people, the Lord also speaks through Jeremiah, saying: “I have abandoned my house; I have dismissed my inheritance. My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; it raised its voice against me. Therefore I hated it” (Jer. 12:7).

[Note: [Col. 0517D]

CHAPTER XI, Note 2. Some copies read *they will devour* instead of *they devour*. After *hostile*, some copies add: “The daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard.” MAR.

2. Isaiah expresses the Jews’ eternal captivity as follows: “Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire; foreigners devour your region in your presence, and it will be desolated like devastation by an enemy” (Isa. 1:7). Although this captivity was partly fulfilled during the time of Babylon, it was fulfilled more completely under Roman captivity, when the Roman army devastated all Judea and the city of Jerusalem was overturned and burned.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Perpetual Ruin of Jerusalem

1. Isaiah says: “It will be desolated like devastation by an enemy, and the daughter of Zion will be left like a shelter in a vineyard” (Isa. 1:7). Thus Jerusalem was overturned and abandoned, once the mysteries of Christian truth had been revealed, just as vineyard shelters are abandoned after the grape harvest has been completed. 89 For just as a shelter is made not for its own sake but for the sake of the harvest, so also the ancient people existed not for their own salvation but for the sake of Christian truth.

[Note: [Col. 0517D]

CHAPTER XII, Note 2. Some copies read *of the world* instead of *of the city*. MAR.

In the same place, the Vulgate reads: “Thorns will rise up … of the joy of the exultant city.” AREV.]

2. The same Isaiah also says: “Upon the soil of my people thorns and briers have risen up” (Isa. 32:13). How much more, then, upon all the houses of joy and the city of rejoicing? “For the house,” he says, “has been abandoned; the multitude of the city has been left; darkness and groping have come upon the caves forever.”

[Note: [Col. 0518D]

3. Some copies read *you covered* instead of *you placed*, *of the proud* instead of *of foreigners*, and *in density* instead of *of clarified wine*. MAR.]

The same Isaiah also proclaims the perpetual ruin of earthly Jerusalem and the calling of the nations as follows: “You are my God, and I will exalt you; I will confess your name, because you have done marvelous things, faithful ancient purposes. Therefore a strong people will praise you; the city of powerful nations will fear you, because you have become a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shelter from the heat. For the breath of the powerful is like a storm driving against a wall; as heat in drought, you will humble the tumult of foreigners; and as heat beneath a pouring cloud, you will cause the branches of the powerful to wither. And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a feast of rich foods, of marrow, of clarified wine” (Isa. 25:1).

By these words he demonstrates the future glory of the Church from the nations, but he turns the oracle’s statement toward earthly Jerusalem, saying: “I will reduce you to nothing, and you will not exist; and though you are sought, you will no longer be found forever.” Concerning the perpetual ruin of this city the Lord also says to Jeremiah: “You will break the flask before the eyes of the men who go with you, and you will say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as a potter’s vessel is broken and cannot be restored again” (Jer. 19:10).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Irreparable Desolation of the Jews

[Col. 0519A]

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

CHAPTER XIII, Note 1. Some copies read *perpetual* instead of *complete*, *worn path* instead of *unworn path*, and *I will scatter* instead of *I will destroy*. MAR.]

1. Because the Jews will never be restored according to their hope, Jeremiah says: “The cities of the South have been closed; all Judea has been carried away in complete exile” (Jer. 13:19)—that is, in irrevocable captivity. The same prophet also says: “Because my people have forgotten me, offering libations in vain and stumbling in their ways and in the paths of Israel, so that they might walk in them on a path not worn, their land will become a desolation and an eternal hissing. Everyone who passes through it will be astonished and will shake his head; like a scorching wind I will scatter them” (Jer. 18:15).

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

2. Some copies read *Jerusalem* instead of *Israel*. MAR.]

2. The same prophet elsewhere also proclaims this eternal desolation of carnal Israel, saying: “Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away” (Jer. 6:30). And shortly afterward: “I will abandon my people and withdraw from them” (Jer. 9:2). And in another place: “I will abandon you and your city, which I gave to you and to your fathers. I will give you over to eternal disgrace and everlasting shame, which will never be erased by oblivion” (Jer. 22:39).

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

3. Some copies read *Jerusalem*, omitting *to them*. MAR.

In the same place, perhaps the reading is *but irreparably*. AREV.]

3. The prophet Amos also speaks most fully concerning them, saying that God has turned away from Israel so completely that he will never again have mercy on them, but that they will remain inseparably in eternal desolation. For he says: “Hear this word, which I raise over you as a lamentation. The house of Israel has fallen; it will not rise again. The virgin Israel has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up” (Amos 5:1). Behold how that people has fallen, so that it will not rise again. By this fall he likewise nullifies the carnal ceremonies of that same people when truth arrives, so that they can never be restored, when he says: “She has been cast upon her land; there is no one to raise her up.”

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

4. Some copies read: “This is understood as the very eternal captivity of the Jews … the wicked will be cast out.” Also: *In the context of this prophecy*, and *I will place tribulation in the midst*. MAR.]

4. This is truly understood concerning the Jews’ earthly hope. The same prophet continues: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not pass through them again. The doorposts of the temple will creak on that day, says the Lord God. Many will die; in every place silence will be cast” (Amos 8:2). In the context of this prophecy he finds, for the third time, that the Lord had so turned away from Israel that, as I have said, he would never again have mercy on them according to their hope. In the first passage he says: “The virgin Israel has fallen; she will not rise again.” In the second he says: “Behold, I will place a mason’s trowel in the midst of my people Israel; I will not pass over him again.” In the third he also says: “The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not pass through them again” (Amos 7:8).

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

5. Some copies read *restorations* instead of *restoration*, and *those who will believe* instead of *those who will be redeemed*. MAR.]

5. All these things concern the kingdom or observance of that people in its carnal form, because these will henceforth be irreparable. For the promises of restoration contained in the speech of those prophets are promised to that part which will believe in God from among the Jews. For not all Jews will be redeemed, nor will all be saved. Rather, after the wicked and sinners have been crushed and consumed, those who have been chosen through faith will be saved. We have spoken about the people and the city; let us say what the prophets have taught concerning the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XIV. That, After the Old Testament Was Abrogated, the New Was to Come

[Col. 0520B]

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

CHAPTER XIV, Note 1. Some copies read *which now* instead of *and now*. MAR.]

1. But because, once that carnal Old Testament had been abrogated, God was going to give a new one, the Lord announces this most clearly through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I am making new things, and now they will arise. Surely you will recognize them: I will make a way in the desert and rivers in the wasteland. The wild beast of the field, dragons, and ostriches will glorify me, because I have given a way in the desert and rivers in the wasteland” (Isa. 43:18, 22).

2. By such prophecies he commends forgetting the law of the Old Testament and makes mention of the new, saying: “Do not remember the former things; behold, I am making new things.” And to demonstrate what the new things would be, he then added: “I will make a way in the desert and rivers in the wasteland.” By this he signified that he had given his teaching among the nations, where the wild beast of the field glorifies him when those who believe in him praise him, and where the kingdoms of the world do so, which he calls a people acquired for himself. But against Israel he adds what follows: “You did not call upon me, Jacob, nor did you labor for me, Israel.”

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

3. Some copies read *they will come* instead of *they have come*. Also *of Christ from his birth* instead of *of the Christian age*. MAR.

In the same place, it is uncertain whether Mariana added the variant *they will come* in place of *they have come*, or in place of *they will arise*. The Vulgate reads *they came* instead of *they have come*. AREV.]

3. Concerning the promise of this New Testament, the same Lord subsequently announces through the same prophet: “The former things—behold, they have come to pass; and I announce new things. Before they arise, I will make them known to you” (Isa. 42:9). By these words he declares that the Old Testament has come and announces the new, which was fulfilled in the Christian age. For the former things are old in relation to the new, in order but not in worth; hence covenants later in time, once the earlier ones have been abrogated, are regarded as greater than the former ones.

[Note: [Col. 0520D]

4. “A new covenant, not according to the covenant,” etc., from Jeremiah 31:31, as Jerome translated it and as it stands in the Vulgate. The Septuagint is much more suitable: “I will establish for the house of Israel and for the house of Judah a New Testament, not according to the testament.” The Hebrew word *berith* signifies this. Thus the ancient Fathers interpreted this passage: Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, book 1, chapter 11; Augustine, *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 33. So also Paul in Hebrews 8:8. Indeed, from the very nature of a testament he infers that Christ, who called it the New Testament, necessarily had to die for it to be valid, in chapter 9:16: “A testament is confirmed over the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the testament is alive.” MAR.]

[Col. 0521D] In the same place, some copies read *when I seized them* instead of *when I took hold of them*. MAR.]

4. Through the prophet Jeremiah also, the Lord promises that he will give a New Testament after abolishing the former one: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant, 93 not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took hold of their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—the covenant which they made void, while I was their master, says the Lord. But this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel, says the Lord: I will give my law within them, and I will write it on their heart.”

[Note: [Col. 0521D]

5. Some copies read *of prophecy* or *of calling* instead of *of prophecies*. Also: *and the covenant that I made with their fathers*, and *and in good hearts of eternal life*, etc. MAR.

In the same place: “And not outwardly on stone diptychs, but inwardly on the tablets of the heart.” All these words were absent from the Hispalensian Codex and, because they seemed suspect, were marked with an obelus. The Greek term *δίπτυχα* properly referred to ecclesiastical tablets on which the names of bishops were written, as is clear from the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book 4, chapter 22, and from Theodore’s *History*, book 5, chapters 34–35. They were double, as the name itself indicates: on one tablet were the names of the living, on the other those of the dead. Traces of this practice remain in the Mozarabic Missal and in Greek liturgies. During the sacred rites, two lists of living and deceased bishops are recited; this is what *δίπτυχα* signifies. Nevertheless, Isidore transferred the word here to signify the commandments of the law, because they too were written on two tablets and handed down by Moses to the ancient people. MAR.

In the same place, Rosweyd discusses the various meanings of *diptych* at greater length in the *Onomasticon* following the *Lives of the Fathers*, where he also cites this passage of Isidore. AREV.]

5. In this passage the prophets’ testimonies concerning the New Testament are recalled. Because it could differ from the Old Testament, he adds: “Not according to the testament that I gave to their fathers.” There is indeed a remarkable difference between the commandments of the two. In the former, apart from the sacraments that were shadows of future things, the other promises are temporal: the Sabbath, circumcision, the manifold practice of sacrifices, the observance of foods, and the ceremonies of days—all of which suit carnal antiquity. By contrast, in the New Testament the goodness of the heart is promised and the blessedness of eternal life is pledged. It is not outwardly on stone diptychs, but inwardly on the tablets of the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0522D]

6. Some copies read *changed by the ancient operation of the flesh*. MAR.]

6. Therefore he continues: “For this is the testament that I will establish with the house of Israel. After those days, says the Lord, I will give my law in their hearts, and I will write it in their minds” (Jer. 31:33). By this he signified that it ought to operate spiritually in our hearts according to the inner person, with the oldness of carnal practice changed. Circumcision is inward—not by cutting the flesh, but by cleansing the heart. The Sabbath is inward—not through abstaining from servile works, but through abstaining from sins.

94 7. The Lord also clearly declares through Isaiah that this law will be revealed to the nations, saying: “A law will go forth from me, and my judgment will rest as a light for the nations” (Isa. 51:4). By this it is shown that the covenant of the New Testament is common to Jews and nations. The prophet Hosea likewise bears witness: “On that day,” says the Lord, “he will call me ‘My husband’; he will no longer call me ‘My Baals.’ I will remove the names of the Baals from his mouth, and he will no longer remember their names. I will establish a covenant with them on that day, with the beasts of the field, with the birds of the sky, and with the reptiles of the earth; I will shatter bow, sword, and war from the land, and I will make them sleep securely. I will betroth you to myself forever; I will betroth you to myself in righteousness, judgment, mercy, and compassion. I will betroth you to myself in faithfulness, and you will know that I am the Lord” (Hos. 2:16).

## CHAPTER XV. On the Cessation of the Sabbath

[Note: [Col. 0522D]

CHAPTER XV, Note 1. Some copies read *would not keep* instead of *would keep*. MAR.

In the same place: “If they knew what the Sabbath was,” etc. Flor. 1 reads: “If they knew why the leisure of the Sabbath had been given, they would not even use the name Sabbath. But they are ignorant of what it means, while they delight in keeping the law carnally,” etc. AREV.]

1. The Jews would rightly keep the Sabbath carnally if they knew what the Sabbath is. They use the name Sabbath, but they are ignorant of what it means. They delight in keeping the law carnally, although the whole law is to be understood spiritually, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak riddles from the beginning of the world” (Ps. 77:2). Therefore, if the law and the prophets consist in parables and riddles, the observance of the Sabbath is not to be accepted except spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 0522D]

2. Some copies read *likewise* instead of *also*. MAR.]

2. For its carnal periods of rest have been dissolved by the Lord and by the Fathers. If it is a crime not to observe the rest of the Sabbath, why does God work on the Sabbath? For it is written in Genesis: “God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made” (Gen. 2:2). Therefore, from the beginning the Sabbath was dissolved, since God worked on it, completing all things on that day and blessing the day itself because he completed everything in it. Likewise, if it is a crime not to observe the rest of the Sabbath, why did Jesus son of Nave, the disciple and successor of Moses, at the Lord’s command lead out the army and weapons for seven consecutive days—including, certainly, the Sabbath—and, while the ark went around and the trumpets sounded, overthrow the walls of Jericho (Josh. 6:15)?

[Col. 0522C] [Note: [Col. 0522D]

3. Some copies read *in my ways* instead of *in my law*, and *purification* instead of *justification*. MAR.]

3. What shall I say also about the Maccabees? It is written of them: “The Jews were unwilling on the Sabbath day to defend themselves against the foreigners” (1 Macc. 2:41). Later, after taking counsel, they fought on the Sabbath and triumphed over their enemies. By these testimonies we are taught that it does not belong to the faith to keep this elemental day, the Sabbath, but another, spiritual one. For this carnal Sabbath was given not for purification but for testing, as the Lord says in the law: “That I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. For six days you will gather manna; on the seventh you will not gather it” (Exod. 16:4, 26).

4. Therefore, when he says, “That I may test them,” it is apparent that the Sabbath was commanded not for justification but for testing. Hence God speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25)—because certain things were permitted to the carnal people to be done carnally, things that nevertheless ceased when the Gospel arrived. Thus he also says through the prophet: “I will cause all her joy and her Sabbaths to cease” (Hos. 2:11). Elsewhere the same Lord says that he hates them: “Your new moons and your Sabbaths my soul has hated” (Isa. 1:13).

[Note: [Col. 0523D]

5. If they are good, why did he hate them? The Hispalensian Codex reads: “Why did God hate them?” The following sentences then appeared: “Likewise, the former things—behold, they have come. Isaiah 42. Likewise, the Sabbath was given only for testing. Exodus 16. Likewise, Elijah walked for forty days, among which he also walked on the Sabbath day.” Some other passages of the same form had undoubtedly migrated from the margin into the text and were therefore rejected. MAR.

In the same place, some copies read *among the living* instead of *serving*. MAR.]

5. Therefore, if Sabbaths are eternal, why did God command them to cease? If they are good, why did he hate them? For the Sabbath that the Israelites received as a gift signified rest of mind, so that no desire for earthly things might weary a person in this life. For “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” But this idle Jewish festival is consumed in luxury, drunkenness, and feasting, with all devoted to lust and to the enjoyment of temporal life, serving belly and sexual desire.

[Note: [Col. 0523D]

6. “The Sabbath of these days is the period of the seventh thousandth year and the rest of the future kingdom and age.” Tarraconensis reads: “The period of the seventh thousandth year, the rest of the future, is the kingdom of the age.” It was the opinion of the Jews, in the book *Sanhedrin*, chapter *Helith*, and in the book *Avodah Zarah*, chapter *Libne*, that the world would last six thousand years and that there would be rest in the seventh. Their arguments were these: the world was created in six days; a thousand years are like one day with God (Ps. 89:4); the letter aleph, which signifies the number one thousand, occurs six times in the first verse of Genesis; and Enoch, the seventh descendant from Adam, was transferred alive. The ancient Fathers followed this opinion: Irenaeus, at the end of book 5; Lactantius, book 7, chapter 14; Tertullian; Victorinus; and Apollinarius. Epiphanius attacks it in heresy 77. Papias, a disciple of the apostle John, introduced this error, affirming that he had received it from the mouths of the Apostles, according to Eusebius, book 3 of the *History*, chapter 39. Who could resist such authority? Isidore might seem here to touch upon and actually follow this view. But the matter is quite different. He is only arguing against the Jews’ argument for introducing observance of the Sabbath on the ground that it was commanded in the Decalogue. Following Augustine’s example (*City of God*, book 22, final chapter), he transfers it to mystical meanings and argues that it signifies the rest of the future age. Julian, for his part, devoted the first book of his work against the Jews to demolishing that opinion. MAR.]

6. But it is asked: If the Sabbath is not to be kept, they say, why was it commanded in the commandments of God: “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and perform all your work, but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it” (Exod. 20:8)? In the work of the six days, the work of six thousand years is indicated. For a thousand years are compared with one day before God, as the prophet testifies: “For a thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Ps. 89:4). The Sabbath of these days is the period of the seventh thousandth year and the rest of the future kingdom and age, where there will no longer be any work of created things, but only the rest of the saints.

7. God hates these temporal Sabbaths, saying: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths.” He rightly said “your,” because these are not the Sabbaths that God commanded, but those that the carnal people chose for themselves. Concerning them he said: “You profaned my Sabbaths” (Ezek. 22:8). Thus it is recognized that the temporal Sabbath is human, while the divine Sabbath is eternal. Concerning the latter Isaiah says: “Month after month, day after day, Sabbath after Sabbath, all flesh will come to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord” (Isa. 66:33).

8. A second question is also raised: Why did Jeremiah say: “Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day, nor bring them through the gates of Jerusalem; do not carry burdens out of your houses on the Sabbath day” (Jer. 17:21)? Hear, therefore, the mystery of his prophecy. The one whom the day of judgment finds with his sin carries burdens on the Sabbath; the one who believes in Christ but does not cease from sin carries burdens on the Sabbath. For he himself is the rest of souls, as he also says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29).

[Note: [Col. 0524D]

9. Perhaps *is proposed* instead of *is placed before*. MAR.]

9. A third question is still raised: Why was the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath day slaughtered by the people so atrociously at God’s command? This is easily put forward by unbelievers. Let them understand, therefore, that all these things happened to them as types, for they were written for our correction. That former and carnal man who dared to violate the Sabbath day by gathering wood—and for this reason was punished—prefigured the one who will be found on the day of judgment engaged in a carnal work, that is, having gathered wood, hay, or straw suitable for the fuel of eternal fire. Gathering these things to his own destruction, when he is judged on the last day, he will be driven away by all the angels and immediately punished with the final death. Thus everything that happened to those Jews through the law is to be understood with fear.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Completion of Circumcision

[Col. 0524C]

[Note: [Col. 0524D]

CHAPTER XVI, Note 1. Some copies read *I have declared* or *I have announced* instead of *I will declare*. MAR.]

1. After the people’s perpetual captivity and the city’s eternal ruin, I will now declare to you the annulment of the Jews’ carnal observances and celebrations. First, therefore, learn the reason for circumcision. Because Christ was to come according to the flesh from the seed of Abraham, in whom the blessing of all nations had been promised, and because many ages were still to pass from Abraham to Christ, God, foreseeing that Abraham’s race might become mingled with the other nations and that his lineage might gradually become uncertain, marked the Jewish people with the sign of circumcision. Thus, while they lived among the Egyptians and Assyrians, among the Babylonians or Chaldeans, they could be distinguished by this sign from those peoples and from the other nations and races.

2. Accordingly, for forty years in the wilderness no one was circumcised, since they alone were living without mingling with another nation. But when the Israelite people crossed the channel of the Jordan and reached the promised land, he provided the sign of circumcision against the error that would arise from intermingling with the nations. We believe that it was reasonably preserved until Christ was born, who had been promised from the seed of Abraham and who would cleanse the hearts of all nations, no longer by circumcision of the flesh but by the cutting away of vices.

[Note: [Col. 0525D]

3. Some copies read *Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem* instead of *Judah*. Also *let it enter* instead of *let it go out*. MAR.

In the same place, in Mariana’s notes on the words “which was not applied to the flesh,” there may perhaps have been a conjecture; but what his conjecture was has fallen out of Grial’s edition, and nothing at all is added after *perhaps*. AREV.]

3. Moses foretold to the children of Israel that this would be not circumcision of the flesh but of the heart, saying: “In the last days the Lord will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring” (Deut. 30:6). Therefore Jeremiah, foreseeing that time as already near, calls the Jews to the New Testament and to circumcision of the heart, not of the body, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the man of Judah and to Jerusalem: Renew your fallow ground, and do not sow upon thorns; circumcise yourselves for your Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest perhaps my indignation go out like fire and be kindled, with no one to extinguish it” (Jer. 4:3).

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

4. Some copies read *Israel from antiquity* instead of *Jerusalem from antiquity*, and *the former things* instead of *of the former things*. MAR.]

4. By these words Jerusalem is admonished to pass from the antiquity of circumcision and the law, which are compared with thorns and briers, to the grace of the New Testament, and through faith in the Gospel to maintain circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, in accordance with what we read from the apostle Peter: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). The Lord likewise announces through Isaiah that this same faith is now to be obtained not through the ancient signs of the flesh and injury to the body, but through the new grace of spiritual washing, saying: “Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I will make new things, which will now arise, and you will recognize them.” And to show what those new things were, he added: “I will make a way in the desert and rivers in the waterless place, to water my chosen race and my people whom I acquired” (Isa. 43:18).

5. What, then, did this indicate except the purification of baptism that was to come? In it no one is now marked by the ancient circumcision of the flesh, but by faith alone is washed through the grace of the sacred water. But because the Hebrews do not accept this circumcision of the heart, Jeremiah foretold, saying: “All the nations have foreskins, but the whole house of Israel is circumcised in heart” (Jer. 9:26).

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

6. Some copies read *was required* instead of *was practiced*. MAR.]

6. For it is also recorded that, under Jesus, the second leader, the people were circumcised, to signify that circumcision had ceased in the wilderness—the circumcision that was practiced in Egypt—and that afterward believers would be cleansed by the Lord Savior through circumcision of the heart. And fittingly the second circumcision is performed with stone knives, because Christ is the rock, through whom believers are purified by spiritual circumcision from all the enticements of sins.

# CHAPTER XVII. On Sacrifices

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

CHAP. XVII, no. 1. Another reading has “rejection” instead of “reprobation”; and “when you stretch out” instead of “when you extend.” MAR.]

1. Now, concerning the rejection of the former sacrifice, because their victims had been cast aside and had become an abomination, the Lord says through Isaiah:

> “Of what use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and of the fat of fattened animals; I do not desire the blood of calves, lambs, or goats. When you come before my presence, who has required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my holy courts? Do not bring sacrifice any longer in vain; incense is an abomination to me. New moons, Sabbaths, and your other festivals I will not endure; your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me. I am weary of enduring them; and when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you. When you multiply your prayer, I will not hear. For your hands are full of blood” (Isaiah I, 11).

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

2. In the Vulgate, “corpses.” AREV.]

2. Again, concerning the sacrifices of the Jews, he himself says: “Their corpses became like dung in the middle of the streets” (Isaiah V, 25). What are these corpses except the sacrifices of the former law, which, since they have now been removed, are regarded as discarded dung? Hence the same prophet elsewhere says concerning their sacrifices:

> “Whoever sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a man; whoever slaughters a sheep is like one who brains a dog; whoever offers an offering is like one who offers swine’s blood; whoever remembers incense is like one who blesses an idol” (Isaiah LXVI, 3).

3. Likewise Jeremiah, concerning the victims and burnt offerings of the Jews rejected by the Lord:

> “Why do you offer me frankincense from Sheba and fragrant calamus from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your victims have not pleased me. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will bring ruin upon this people, and fathers and sons will fall together in it, neighbor and kinsman, and they will perish” (Jeremiah VI, 20).

Observe that their sacrifices are not commended in a carnal sense for their own sake, but because of the obedience of heart and faith alone, which the unbelievers have lost.

4. Hence the same prophet continues:

> “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the flesh, because I did not speak to your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them, saying: Listen to my voice, and I will be your God, and you will be my people; and walk in all that I have commanded you, and it will be well with you. But they did not listen, nor incline their ear; they went after the desires and perversity of their evil heart.”

The meaning to be understood in this statement is: “I did not command them concerning burnt offerings as though I loved those offerings in themselves, but so that I might approve the obedience of their faith” (Jeremiah VII, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0527D]

5. The same author as above. In this book too, through a failure of memory, passages from other books are cited under the names of different books. Thus here the testimony of Hosea VIII, 12 is cited under Jeremiah’s name. Below, at the end of chapter 22, the words “Because you have forgotten me, behold, I will announce your righteousness,” from Isaiah LVII, 12, are likewise introduced under Jeremiah’s name. MAR.]

5. Likewise the same author as above says: “I will write out my many laws for them, which have been counted as something foreign. They will bring victims, sacrifice flesh, and eat it, but the Lord will not receive them.” And afterward, condemning their sacrifices, he says:

> “They will not pour out wine to the Lord, nor will their sacrifices please him; they will be like the bread of mourners. All who eat it will be defiled; they will not enter the house of the Lord” (Hosea IX, 4).

6. And Joel says: “Sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God” (Joel I, 13). Likewise Malachi:

> “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a pure offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord” (Malachi I, 13).

By this testimony it is clear that the sacrifices of the Jews are unclean and rejected, and that the offering of the nations alone is acceptable to the Lord.

# CHAPTER XVIII. On Foods

[Note: [Col. 0527D]

CHAP. XVIII, no. 1. Perhaps the reading is: “It came to pass.” AREV.]

1. In the Book of Kings it says:

> “The word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there. For I have commanded a widow there to feed you. He arose and went to Zarephath of the Sidonians; and when he had come to the gate of the city, a widow appeared to him, and he received food from her and ate” (III Kings XVII, 8).

Then, at God’s command, Elijah filled her vessels, lodged with that foreign woman, and lived on Gentile foods—something that would not have been permitted unless the law had been given spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 0527D]

2. Another reading has “for those predestined to eternal life” instead of “in his saints.” MAR.]

2. For when certain things are condemned as unclean for food under the law, they undoubtedly signify human conduct, since God does not admit into his holy people, who are predestined to eternal life, anything that is represented in human behavior by those unclean animals. For everything that God created at the beginning of the world is declared by the authority of his word to be not merely good but very good. Therefore whatever is signified by the category of unclean animals is more properly applied to human conduct.

# CHAPTER XIX. On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith

[Note: [Col. 0527D]

CHAP. XIX, no. 1. In Codex Florentinus 1 the title of this chapter is worded as follows: “That the Old Testament was given not only because of the Jews but also because of the nations.” Manuscripts often differ in such headings from the printed editions. AREV.]

1. Thus far we have refuted Jewish rites and observances by divine testimonies; from this point let us touch upon the sacraments of our faith, first making clear that the covenant of the law was given not only because of the Jews but also because of all the nations. The prophet David testifies to this, saying:

> “A coming generation will be proclaimed to the Lord, and the heavens will proclaim his righteousness to a people that will be born, whom the Lord has made” (Psalm XXI, 32).

And again he himself says:

> “Until they proclaim your arm to every generation that is to come, your power and your righteousness, O God” (Psalm LXX, 18).

[Col. 0528B] [Note: [Col. 0528D]

2. Another reading has “afterward” instead of “therefore.” MAR.]

2. And Isaiah says:

> “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge the nations and rebuke many peoples, even to the distant regions” (Isaiah II, 3).

David likewise says in the Psalms:

> “Then they will say among the nations: The Lord has done great things for them; the Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful” (Psalm CXXV, 2).

These testimonies make clear that the covenant of the law was first granted to the Jews and afterward to the nations. It was granted to them for this reason: in it they could recognize Christ, whom the Jews, blinded in mind, do not understand at all.

# CHAPTER XX. Scripture Is to Be Understood Not Only Historically but Also Mystically

[Col. 0528C] [Note: [Col. 0528D]

CHAP. XX, no. 1. Another reading has “to be received” instead of “to be understood.” MAR.]

1. That the writing of the law is to be understood not only historically but also in a mystical sense—that is, spiritually—the Lord teaches in the Psalms:

> “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak sayings from the beginning” (Psalm LXXVII, 1).

The prophet confirms this also in another psalm, saying:

> “I will incline my ear to a likeness; I will open my riddles on the lyre” (Psalm XLVIII, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0528D]

2. “Write the law twice and three times in your heart.” Proverbs XXII, 20: “Behold, I have written it for you three times, in thoughts and knowledge.” The Septuagint: “Write it for yourself three times, as counsel and thought.” Unless these words were taken from this passage, I do not know where they could have been drawn from. Evidently Isidore used a different edition. Apart from what has already been said, this is shown by the passage of Habakkuk III, at its final verse, cited by Isidore in the preceding book, chapter 35. For where everyone else reads “like a vine in his song,” or “a victor singing in the psalms,” Isidore reads “like a vine in his splendor.” MAR.]

2. For everything in the law is understood through likeness and enigma. An enigma is an obscure likeness by which a person is urged to sharpen the heart and turn to the understanding of inward things. Thus Wisdom also says through Solomon: “Write the law twice and three times in your heart.” The law is understood twice when it is understood first according to history and then according to the understanding of its sacraments. It is written three times when one is taught not only historically or mystically, but also morally, what one ought to do in each matter.

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

3. Another reading has “was established” instead of “was constructed.” And: “all the mysteries and history of the law.” MAR.]

3. Hence the ark constructed by Noah was commanded to be made with two and three compartments, because within the Church the whole substance of the law and its history has a place, receives mystical meaning, and contains instruction in morals.
