For the law was written in parables and riddles, as were the parables and sayings themselves. This is why everything is veiled and closed to the Jews: unless they believe, they cannot attain its understanding.

# CHAPTER XXI. The Jews Do Not Understand the Covenant of the Law

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

CHAP. XXI, no. 1. Another reading has “seeing a vision” instead of “seeing”; and shortly afterward “you will perceive” instead of “you will know.” MAR.]

1. For they have all these sacraments of Scripture sealed up and do not know what they read. They read everything but do not understand, as the Lord sang concerning them to the prophet:

> “Say,” he says, “to this people: You will hear with hearing and will not understand; and seeing, you will see and will not know, for the heart of this people has become dull” (Isaiah VI, 9).

And again:

> “The Lord will take away from Judah and from Jerusalem the strong and mighty man, the judge and the prophet, the wise architect and the prudent interpreter of mystical speech” (Isaiah III, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

2. Another reading has “indeed,” or “and indeed,” instead of “for all this”; and “to those who know,” or “to those who read,” instead of “to the nations.” MAR.]

2. God has taken all these things away from them and sealed all the sacraments for them according to the hardness of their hearts, lest they should perhaps understand, as the same Isaiah testifies concerning them:

> “And it will be,” he says, “for you a vision like the words of a sealed book. When they give it to one who knows letters, saying, ‘Read this,’ he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isaiah XXIX, 11).

But what did he add concerning the nations?

> “On that day the deaf will hear the words of this book, and from darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see” (ibid., 18).

For the mysteries of the law have been opened.

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

3. Perhaps: “They are closed and sealed,” as in the Vulgate. AREV.]

3. But they are closed to the Jews, as Daniel also says:

> “The words are closed and sealed until the time of consummation, until many learn, the vision is fulfilled, and they understand all these things” (Daniel XII, 9).

For the fact that Moses’ face was also covered with a veil when he descended from the mountain with the tablets signified that, because of the darkness of blindness, the Jewish people could not recognize the law itself. For when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart.

# CHAPTER XXII. The Jews Will Not Understand the Scriptures Unless They Believe in Christ

[Col. 0529D]

[Note: [Col. 0530D]

CHAP. XXII, no. 1. Another reading has “Christo” (“in/with Christ”) instead of “in Christum” (“into Christ”); and “if you do not believe me, you will not understand.” MAR.]

1. For they cannot understand the law and the prophets unless they first believe in Christ, as Isaiah says: “If you do not believe, you will not understand; for the righteous person will live by my faith, says the Lord through the prophet” (Habakkuk II, 4). Hence Abraham also became the father of the nations, because he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Genesis XV, 6). But although these people possess the law and the prophets, they are nevertheless not to be excused, as Jeremiah testifies:

> “And the Lord said to me: Even if Moses and Samuel were standing before me, my soul would not be toward this people. Cast them out from my presence, and let them go forth” (Jeremiah XV, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0530D]

2. Another reading omits “to me.” MAR.]

2. Moses therefore signifies the law, and Samuel the prophets. Although the Jews possess them, they have nevertheless been cast away because of the impiety of their error. For their works and righteousness profit them nothing without faith in Christ, as the Lord testifies through Jeremiah:

> “Because you have forgotten me, behold, I will announce your righteousness, and your works will not profit you” (Isaiah LVII, 12).

# CHAPTER XXIII. The Two Covenants Were Given by God

[Col. 0530B]

[Note: [Col. 0530D]

CHAP. XXIII, no. 1. Another reading has “my beloved” instead of “my brother.” MAR.]

1. But since the two covenants—the New, that is, and the Old—were given by almighty God, Solomon declares in the Song of Songs:

> “At our doors are all kinds of fruits, new and old; my brother, I have stored them for you” (Song of Songs VII, 13).

Concerning these the Lord also said in the Gospel:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matthew XIII, 52).

And elsewhere in Scripture God promises:

> “I will give you the early rain and the late rain”—that is, the Old Testament and the New—“and with both rains I will water you” (Deuteronomy XI, 14).

For rain is understood as the teaching of the covenants. Hence the saying: “Let my word be awaited like rain, and let it pour down upon the earth.”

# CHAPTER XXIV. The Forgiveness of Sins Was to Come through Baptism

[Col. 0530C]

1. That the cleansing of sins was to come through baptism, not through circumcision, which had been a form of baptism, is clearly declared by the voices of Scripture. Isaiah foretold the future mystery of baptism to those who would believe, saying:

> “You will draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior” (Isaiah XII, 3).

By these words the prophet also points to the Savior himself, from whose fountains he proclaims that waters of purification are to be drawn—that is, from the fountains of Jesus. For in the language of the Hebrews this name means “Savior.”

[Note: [Col. 0530D]

CHAP. XXIV, no. 2. Another reading has “milk and honey” instead of “flow”; and “they will flow” instead of “they will go.” MAR.]

2. Hence he himself cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37). To this sacrament of baptism the same Isaiah invites Jews and nations alike, saying:

> “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isaiah LV, 1).

The Holy Spirit foretold these waters and this fountain also through Joel, saying:

> “The mountains will drip sweetness, the hills will flow with milk, and through all the channels of Judah the waters will go; a fountain will go forth from the house of the Lord and water the whole world” (Joel III, 18),

that is, the entire multitude of the nations.

[Col. 0531A] [Note: [Col. 0531D]

3. Another reading: “It goes toward the eastern [sea],” and so forth. MAR.]

3. Concerning this fountain Zechariah also says: “On that day there will be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing away of sin and of menstruation” (Zechariah XIII, 1). Tell me, please: what is this open fountain except that in which we are all reborn, through which the sins of sinners are purified and the stains of menstruation—that is, of unclean souls—are washed away in a saving bath? Concerning its waters the same prophet testifies elsewhere:

> “And on that day,” he says, “living waters will go forth from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the final sea. On that day the Lord will be one, and his name one, and the whole land will return even to the wilderness” (Zechariah XIV, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0531D]

4. Another reading has “by the infusion of the heavenly Spirit”; and “let them give abundantly” instead of “let it give abundantly.” MAR.]

4. What, then, are these living waters except baptism, which gives life to a person through the infusion of the Holy Spirit? But why are they announced as going forth from Jerusalem unless because the Lord, dwelling among that people, said to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew XXVIII, 19)? Half of them goes toward the eastern sea, that is, toward the people of the circumcision; and half toward the western sea, which is the people of the nations, last in faith, so that it may grant [water] to all who thirst, both Jews and nations who believe in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0531D]

5. Another reading has “answered” instead of “looked toward”; and “outside the gate” instead of “out beyond the gate.” MAR.

Ibid. The same prophet. The prophet recently cited was Zechariah, but these words belong to Ezekiel. In the Vulgate, “he turned me” occurs twice instead of “I turned myself.” Perhaps Isidore too should read “he turned me.” It has already been noted several times above that Isidore and other ancient writers sometimes placed the name of one prophet in error for another. AREV.]

5. Concerning these waters it is also said through the same prophet that they go forth from the house of the Lord, grow into a river, and proceed toward the wilderness, or the Dead Sea; and that everything they reach is given life and healed. For the same prophet says:

> “I turned toward the gate of the house of the Lord, and behold, water was coming out from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east. For the front of the house faced east, while the waters descended along the right side of the temple, south of the altar. And I turned toward the road outside the outer gate that faced east, and behold, waters were overflowing from the right side” (Ezekiel XLVII, 1ff.),

that is, from Christ’s side.

[Note: [Col. 0532D]

6. Another reading has “the waters will be healed”; and “and those fishermen” instead of “and fishermen.” MAR.]

6. Then he says:

> “He led me through the waters and said to me: These waters, which go out toward the east and descend to the desert plains—that is, to the nations—will enter the sea and flow out, and the waters will be healed. Every living soul that looks wherever the torrent comes will live, and there will be very many fish,”

that is, regenerated people. And he added:

> “After those waters come, they will be healed, and everything will live wherever the torrent comes. Fishermen will stand beside it,”

that is, apostles and teachers, and there will be many kinds of its fish.

[Note: [Col. 0532D]

7. Another reading has “they will exist on both sides of it.” MAR.

Ibid. “These waters”; perhaps “because the waters,” as in the Vulgate.]

7. He said this to signify the variety of nations coming to the water of the bath. Hence he added:

> “Like the fish of the great sea, in exceedingly great numbers on its banks; on both sides every fruit-bearing tree will grow. Its leaf will not wither, nor will its fruit fail; month by month it will produce firstfruits. For its waters will go forth from the sanctuary, and its fruit will be for food, and its leaves for medicine.”

[Note: [Col. 0532D]

8. Another reading has “will sanctify” instead of “will desire.” MAR.]

8. The prophet Micah likewise reveals the mysteries of the same baptism under the figure of the crossing of the sea, saying:

> “According to the days of your going out from the land of Egypt, I will show them wonders. The nations will see and be confounded in their strength; they will place their hands over their mouths; their ears will be deaf. They will desire the Lord our God and will fear you. What god is like you, who take away iniquity and remove the sin of the remnant of Israel? Because he is merciful, he will turn and have mercy on us; he will cast down our iniquities and hurl all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah VII, 15, 19).

[Note: [Col. 0532D]

9. Another reading has “observe” instead of “will observe.” MAR.]

9. In this statement the reader will see most clearly that the holy mystery of baptism is revealed. “According to the days,” he says, “of your going out from Egypt, I will show them wonders”; then, with the enemies pursuing—that is, our former sins—just as the Egyptians were thrown into the sea, so our sins are declared to be destroyed and extinguished in baptism. He says: “Because he is merciful, he will turn and have mercy on us. He will drown our sins and hurl all our sins into the depths of the sea.”

10. What could be clearer than this testimony? What more evident? Every true Israelite goes out of Egypt through faith when he renounces the world, and enters the Red Sea, that is, baptism marked by the blood of Christ. Then the pursuing enemies perish, because sins immediately die when the souls of those regenerated rise again. We also read that Aaron was washed with water as a prefiguration of baptism, and that his sons, who shared in their father’s priesthood, were likewise purified by the sanctification of water (Exodus XXX, 18; Leviticus VIII, 6). Even then that purification bore the form of baptism; now, through the sacrament of this bath, the whole people of the Church—which is the body of the true and great priest—is washed for the remission of sins, and, once their stains have been cleansed, they are consecrated to divine worship for sanctification.

11. Isaiah the prophet, among other things, shows that the sins of the Jews can in no way be forgiven unless they have been washed in baptism. For through the same prophet the Holy Spirit says:

> “I have grown weary of enduring. If you multiply your prayers, I will not hear; for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah I, 14).

In place of all the victims mentioned by the same prophet, in place of all new moons, Sabbaths, and solemnities, he commanded only the purification of baptism; and in place of all the defilements of sins, only the bath of regeneration, by which alone sins are washed away.

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

12. Another reading has “despise” instead of “reject”; “the Canaanite woman” instead of “Canaan”; “sanctification” instead of “signification”; and “believe in Christ” instead of “turn to Christ.” MAR.

Ibid. In Grialius’s edition: “I entered the pasture.” AREV.]

12. Because the Jews reject this, let them hear the Lord threatening them through the prophet Ezekiel:

> “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make known to Jerusalem her abominations, and say: Thus says the Lord: Your root and your origin are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. And when you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed with water for salvation” (Ezekiel XVI, 1, 3).

Here it is shown that Jerusalem is sunk in grave sins and therefore destined to perish, because she was not washed with water for salvation—which is a complete signification of baptism. But to those who turn to Christ and are baptized, the word of the Lord continues there:

> “I entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord, and I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil,”

signifying by the covenant the New Testament, and by the water and oil baptism and chrism.

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

13. Another reading has “a new spirit” instead of “my spirit.” MAR.]

13. The Holy Spirit promises them through the same prophet that the purification of this baptism will be theirs in the future, saying:

> “I will take you from the nations, gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. I will pour clean water over you, and you will be cleansed from all your impurities.”

And, to indicate that they will receive the New Testament, he continues:

> “I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my spirit within you and cause you to walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them” (Ezekiel XXVI, 24).

# CHAPTER XXV. The Nations Must Be Sanctified with Chrism

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

CHAP. XXV, no. [number omitted]. Another reading has “first myrrh and oil”; “which pertain to the worship of the tabernacle”; and “and all will be most holy.” MAR.]

1. That all the nations would be sanctified with chrism, the Lord speaks to Moses, saying:

> “Take for yourself the finest spices and olive oil, and make an oil of holy anointing, a compounded ointment. With it you shall anoint the tabernacle of testimony, the ark of the covenant, the table with its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altars of incense and of burnt offering, and everything that pertains to their worship. You shall sanctify them all, and they shall be most holy; whoever touches them shall be sanctified. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and sanctify them so that they may serve me as priests. You shall also say to the children of Israel: This holy oil of anointing shall be mine throughout your generations” (Exodus XXX, 23).

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

2. Another reading has “the whole community” instead of “the whole”; and “grace” instead of “glory.” MAR.]

2. The figure of this former tabernacle is applied as a type of the Church, whose entire diversity of peoples is anointed as a testimony of holiness. This was represented by that whole complex of works, so that all, touched with the anointing of sacred chrism, might be sanctified and, once sanctified, prepared for the glory of God.

# CHAPTER XXVI. Believers Would Be Saved through the Sign of the Cross

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

CHAP. XXVI, no. 1. Another reading has “showing” instead of “shown”; “and together” instead of “the old man”; and “the little one” instead of “the child.” MAR.]

1. The figure of the cross, which marks the foreheads of the faithful beforehand for the protection of salvation, is recorded as having been shown through the prophet Ezekiel:

> “And he called,” he says, “the man clothed in linen, who had a writer’s inkwell at his waist, and said to him: Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a Tau on the foreheads of the men who sigh and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst” (Ezekiel IX, 3).

And afterward he added:

> “Go through the city and strike; let your eye not spare, nor show pity to the old man, the young man, the virgin, the child, or the women. Kill them to destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the Tau” (ibid., 5).

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

2. The letter Tau indeed displays the form of a cross. Understand this as referring to the ancient Hebrew characters, for its form is now different. Jerome, commenting on the words that Isidore cites here from Ezekiel IX, says: “And, to come to our own times, in the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans still use today, the final letter Tau has the likeness of a cross, which is painted on the foreheads of Christians,” and so forth. Jerome himself also testifies in the Prologue to the Galeatus that the ancient Hebrew characters were changed by Ezra. MAR.

Ibid. Another reading has “has” instead of “displays”; “are marked beforehand” instead of “have been marked beforehand”; and “the parts” instead of “the doorposts.” MAR.]

2. We must therefore understand this statement. The letter Tau displays the form of a cross, and all who are delivered at their departure from this world have been marked beforehand with its sign. Its type was prefigured in Egypt by the blood of that white and immaculate lamb, with which, figuratively, the doorposts of our bodies are marked, so that we may rightly say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm IV, 7).

[Note: [Col. 0534D]

3. Another reading: “It is shown that, through the lifting up of the cross, the nations come to him, having believed.” MAR.]

3. Concerning this sign Isaiah speaks in the person of the Lord:

> “Behold, I am coming to gather all nations and tongues; they will come and see my glory, and I will place a sign among them” (Isaiah LXVI, 18),

namely, the cross. And elsewhere:

> “The Lord,” he says, “will be named as an everlasting sign, which will not be taken away” (Isaiah LV, 13).

The same prophet also wished elsewhere to signify this concerning Christ, saying:

> “And he will raise up a sign among the nations” (Isaiah V, 26).

Here he shows that, when the sign of the cross was lifted up, the nations would come to him and believe.

[Note: [Col. 0534D]

4. “The Lord reigned from the wood.” After these words, the Hispalensian manuscript continued with: “And elsewhere: Behold, I will place my name among the nations.” We judged these words to have been badly attached and therefore rejected them from this passage. MAR.]

4. The glory of this holy cross was likewise foretold in the Psalms:

> “Say among the nations: The Lord reigned from the wood.”

Concerning this cross of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord speaks through Ezekiel:

> “The sword has been sharpened and polished to slaughter victims. You have been sharpened, you who move the scepter of my Son; you have cut down the wood, and I have given him to be smoothed so that he may be held in the hand” (Ezekiel XXI, 9).

By this testimony both the crucifixion of the Son of God is shown and the sign of his cross is divinely foretold as something to be received by all.

5. The same Ezekiel figuratively marks out the form of this cross, composed of two pieces of wood, saying:

> “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: And you, son of man, take for yourself one piece of wood and write upon it: ‘Judah and the children of Israel associated with him.’ Then take another piece of wood and write upon it: ‘Joseph, the wood of Ephraim, and all the house of Israel and those associated with him.’ Join them, one to the other, into a single piece of wood, and they will become one in your hand” (Ezekiel XXXVII, 16).

[Note: [Col. 0535D]

6. Another reading has “not only by the name of wood.” MAR.]

6. Here it is shown that Judah and Jerusalem must be united and receive the sign of the cross, which was signified by the two pieces of wood. These are the two pieces of wood that the foreign widow to whom Elijah was sent for food wished to gather before she died. Here the sign of the cross is expressed not only by the name of wood but also by the number of pieces of wood.

# CHAPTER XXVII. How the Sacrament of the Eucharist Was Prefigured

[Note: [Col. 0535D]

CHAP. XXVII, no. 1. Another reading has “it would be a burnt offering to God,” and “not a burnt offering”; and “with the priest” instead of “in the priesthood.” MAR.

Ibid. “In the burnt offering.” A similar expression occurs in the Isidorian, or Mozarabic, Breviary on the feast of the apostles Simon and Jude, in the prayer Post pridie: “We set forth the burnt offerings of bread and wine instituted by your only-begotten Son, our Lord.” Lesleus compares this passage with Isidore in his notes on the Mozarabic Breviary. AREV.]

1. That the sacrament of bread and the cup would be pleasing to God as a burnt offering is not passed over in the testimonies of Scripture. The prefiguration of this sacrifice had earlier been expressed in the priesthood of Melchizedek. For this priest of the Most High God, when he blessed Abraham, offered bread and wine in sacrifice to the Lord as a mystery of the future burnt offering. He first expressed this as a type of the Son of God, to whom the Psalmist speaks in the person of the Father:

> “Before the morning star I begot you. You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm CIX, 3).

This is according to the rite of such a sacrifice, which Christ also fulfilled when he completed it in his passion and commanded the apostles to perform it in remembrance of him.

2. Believers therefore no longer offer Jewish victims, such as the priest Aaron offered, but those that the same Melchizedek, king of Salem, sacrificed—that is, bread and wine, which are the truest sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Concerning this the same Lord says:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John IV, 56).

The sacrament of this sacrifice is also shown in Solomon through the offering of bread and wine:

> “Wisdom built herself a house, carved out seven pillars, slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine, set out her table, and sent her servants, saying: If anyone is simple, let him come to me. And she speaks to the foolish: Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you; abandon foolishness and you will live, and walk in the ways of prudence” (Proverbs IX, 1).

3. Christ, the Wisdom of God, therefore established for himself a holy house, the Church, in which he slaughtered the sacrifices of his body, in which he mixed the wine of his blood in the cup of the divine sacrament, and prepared the table—that is, the altar of the Lord—sending his servants, the apostles and teachers, to the foolish, that is, to all nations ignorant of the true God. He says to them:

> “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you”—

that is, “Receive the food of the holy body; and drink the wine I have mixed for you,” that is, “Receive the cup of the sacred blood.”

[Note: [Col. 0536D]

4. Another reading has “of the heart” instead of “of the spirit”; and “he will call his servants by another name, that is, Christian.” MAR.]

4. That the nations receive this grace, while the Jews did not deserve it, the prophet Isaiah declares:

> “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants will eat, but you will hunger; behold, my servants will drink, but you will thirst; behold, my servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame. Behold, my servants will rejoice because of exultation of heart, but you will cry out because of anguish of heart, and because of contrition of spirit you will howl. You will leave your name as a curse for my chosen ones, and the Lord God will kill you and will call his servants”—that is, Christians—“by another name. Whoever is blessed on earth will be blessed in God. Amen” (Isaiah LXV, 13).

[Note: [Col. 0536D]

5. Another reading has “be sent” instead of “be changed”; and “another is given,” namely [Christian]. MAR.]

5. Israel is killed, and a people from the nations succeeds it. The Old Testament is taken from them; the New is given to us. The grace of saving food and the cup of Christ’s blood is granted to us, while they dry up with hunger and thirst. The new people are also given another name, namely Christian; and everything that has taken place resounds with the newness of grace.

113 # CHAPTER XXVIII. Recapitulation of the Work
1. O lamentable madness of the wretched Jews! Behold, they neither understand the coming of the Savior from the authority of the Old Testament, nor accept that he has come. They read of the conversion of the nations, yet are not at all ashamed of their own rejection. They undertake observance of the Sabbath, which they know has been rejected by the testimony of Scripture. They venerate circumcision of the flesh, although they have lost purity of heart.

[Note: [Col. 0536D]

Chapter XXVIII, no. 2. Another reading has *of life* instead of *of rest*. MAR.]

2. But we, placed under grace, already know that all these things and observances—which were signs of things to come—have been fulfilled. For whatever of this kind was foretold in the mystery, Christ has now fulfilled, [Col. 0537A] because he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17). Therefore, when truth arrived, the shadow ceased; and so we are no longer circumcised bodily, because in the type of circumcision we are cleansed through the sacrament of the promised baptism. We regard Sabbath rest as superfluous, because we possess the revealed hope of eternal rest.

[Note: [Col. 0537A]

No. 3. Another reading has *to be insinuated* instead of *insinuated*. “And we walk in the new grace of faith. And the diversity of unclean things was signified.” MAR.]

3. We do not offer the sacrifices of the old law, because through those same sacrifices we recognize either Christ’s passion or the mortification of carnal vices as having been signified. We do not observe unleavened bread, because, once the wickedness of the former life has been purged, we walk in the new grace of faith. We do not maintain distinctions among foods, because we discern spiritually in human conduct all those things that the diversity of unclean animals signified. [Col. 0538A]

[Note: [Col. 0537A]

No. 4. In some manuscripts, the dedication of Isidore to Florentina is placed here after the final chapter, as an epilogue, whereas in the others it more correctly precedes as a prologue. The old editions—the Haganoensis, Bignaeana, and Breuliana—after the words “dwells forever” add further material, entirely omitted in the Grialian edition; we add it here:

“You say that formulas of spiritual understanding should be composed and sent to you; because of my fatherly concern for you, I considered it worthwhile to do so, so that, once they had been received, the mind might readily direct itself toward understanding the meaning throughout all divine Scripture. For since the letter kills but Christ gives life, it is necessary to penetrate, with the life-giving Spirit, into the inner depths of those spiritual discourses.

“Moreover, that the whole of Scripture, both of the Old Instrument and of the New, is to be received allegorically, the following itself admonishes us: what we read in the Old Testament, ‘I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter ancient riddles’; and likewise what is written in the New Testament, ‘Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them.’

“Nor is it surprising that the divine word, spoken through the mouths of the prophets and apostles, departed greatly from that customary manner in which human beings write, since it had easy things readily at hand while containing great things within its interior depths. Indeed, it was fitting that the sacred utterances of God should be distinguished from other writings not only in dignity but also in form, and that the dignity of heavenly mysteries should not lie open indiscriminately to everyone, exposing what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine. Thus the truth is that the middle of the silver-winged dove is such that its hind parts shine with the appearance of gleaming gold. So the first things in divine Scripture should gleam with silver, while the more hidden things should glow with gold.

“Accordingly, it was rightly arranged that the purity of those utterances should be hidden from the common eyes of all and covered, as it were, by a veil of modesty. By this excellent divine dispensation it was provided that the writings themselves should be veiled, overshadowed by heavenly mysteries, just as the Divinity itself was concealed within its secret.

“Therefore, since in the sacred books the eyes of the Lord, the womb of the Lord, the feet, and even the arms of the Lord are found written, and since it is entirely foreign to the Catholic faith of the churches to define God as bodily—for he is invisible, incomprehensible, and infinite—it must be sought how these expressions are disclosed through the Holy Spirit by figurative interpretation. Here, then, the inner chambers of the Lord’s temple are found; here is the holy of holies.

“Thus the body of sacred Scripture, as it is handed down, is in the letter.”

I said that this fragment of Isidore does not seem to occur in the Isidorian materials, chapter 86, no. 11. In the Bignaeana and Haganoensis editions the text read erroneously: “in all divine Scripture, but toward understanding itself, so that the meaning might be directed.” Someone corrected it to: “might readily direct itself toward the spiritual understanding of the meaning.” In place of “the middle of the silver-winged dove,” those same editions had “the manner of the silver-winged dove.” Breulius reshaped the passage as follows: “would expose them, so that, just as the feathers of the silver-winged dove appear, and its hind parts with the appearance of gold, and so forth.” The passage is from Psalm 67. AREV.]

4. We do not celebrate Passover by eating the lamb, because our Passover has already been sacrificed: Christ, who was represented by that lamb, who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and who, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth (1 Cor. 5:7). We do not observe the new moons, because in Christ there is already a new creation: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. We do not observe the Feast of Tabernacles, that is, the festivals of booths, because the saints of God are his tabernacle, in whom he dwells forever.

[Col. 0537]

# The Three Books of Sentences of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville (C)

## Book One

### Chapter One. That God is supreme and unchangeable

[Col. 0537D]

[Note: [Col. 0537D]

Chapter I, no. 1. From this arose the practice whereby this book was called by some *On the Supreme Good*, because they gave the book its title from its first words, following the custom of the Hebrews. Nevertheless, it was entitled by blessed Isidore *The Book of Sentences*, as Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, testifies; all manuscript codices agree, as do Gratian, Ivo of Chartres, and other collectors of decretals.

The Eighth Council of Toledo likewise says: “Isidore, worthy of reverent mention, the outstanding teacher of our age, the final glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him, not inferior in comparison of learning, and—what is greater—most learned at the close of the centuries, in the second book of the *Sentences*.” In this passage Petrus Crabbe and Joverius read *at the end of the centuries* instead of *of the centuries that have ended*. The sentence of Isidore cited there is Book II, chapter 31, on oaths, and is found in Gratian, 22, question 4, chapter *It Must Not Be Observed*. LOAISA.

In the same place, “But creation.” See Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapters 3, 21, and 22, and Augustine, *On the Nature of the Good*, at the beginning. LOAISA.

In the Isidorian materials there are two chapters on this work. The first, chapter 67, is entitled as follows: “The three books of the Sentences of Saint Isidore, or On the Supreme Good. Editions and manuscript codices of this work. The Spanish version. Julian of Toledo, Taio, Peter Lombard, and other writers of Sentences after Isidore. The fourth book of the Sentences—is it falsely attributed to Isidore? The learned observations of Bayer on this book.”

The second, chapter 68, is entitled: “Prefaces to the books of the Sentences of the 1538 edition and of Garcia Loaisa’s edition. Excerpts from the books of the Sentences. Prefaces to the excerpts from the Sentences, namely, to a book entitled *On Converts* and to another entitled *On Prelates*.”

I shall add my notes to those of Loaisa, which are indeed very learned but sometimes more lengthy than they should be. From the annotations of others—such as Vezzosius, who generally agrees with Loaisa in his notes, except that he follows the text of the Breulian edition and indicates some variants from other editions; those of Constantine Cajetan on the fragment *On Converts*; and those of Goldast on the fragment *On Prelates*—I shall collect a summary.

In Taio’s *Sentences*, the first chapter is entitled: “That God exists unchangeable, supreme, and eternal.” AREV.]

1. God is the supreme good, because he is unchangeable [Col. 0538C] and cannot be corrupted in any way. Creation, however, [Col. 0538D] is good but not supreme 116, because it is changeable; and although it is indeed good, it cannot also be supreme.

[Col. 0539A]

[Note: [Col. 0539C]

No. 2. From the divine Gregory, whom Isidore follows above all in these *Sentences*, both because of the admirable teaching concerning morals found in that most holy man—shining remarkably in his writings among his many other great virtues—and because of the affection conceived through the mutual familiarity of Leander and Gregory, as is plainly established from Gregory’s Book I of Letters, indiction 9, his letter to Leander. Hence Isidore honors and venerates Gregory’s writings as supremely authoritative.

Gregory therefore says, *Moralia* XXV, chapter 4: “For what is changeability, if not a kind of death?” and so forth. For an explanation of the whole sentence, see Augustine, Book III *Against Maximinus*, chapter 12. LOAISA.

In the same place, all manuscript codices reject the first conjunction: “For angels and souls”; but it should be retained, as in the printed editions. The passage is found in Gregory, *Moralia* 25, chapter 4. LOAISA.

In the same place, Augustine, in *On Two Souls*, chapter 8, says that the death of the soul is turning away from God; and in Book IV *On the Trinity*, chapter 3: “Just as the soul, when God is absent,” and so forth. LOAISA.

[Col. 0540B] In the same place, others read: “so also the angel is changed from good into evil when, having abandoned God, he has fallen.” AREV.]

2. What is God’s immortality if not his unchangeability? Angels and souls are also immortal, but they are not unchangeable; therefore God alone is called immortal, because he alone is unchangeable. For the soul dies when, with God abandoning it, it is changed from good into evil; so also the angel, when, having abandoned God, he has fallen.

[Note: [Col. 0540B]

No. 3. Augustine, *Commentary on Genesis Literally Explained* VIII, chapters 20 and 22. Every variation and alteration of things originates from matter, because matter contains privation in a compounded form; from privation arises desire, and from desire the impulse toward another form, as Aristotle taught in Book I of the *Physics*. God, however, is alien to all matter, as St. Thomas teaches excellently in Book I *Against the Gentiles*, chapters 16 and 17. LOAISA.

In the same place, “Well and substantially.” Augustine, Book V *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, proves that certain things are properly predicated of God, such as “I am who I am,” and that he is immortal. LOAISA.

In the same place, from Gregory, *Moralia* XVI, chapter 4. This is what Augustine elegantly asserts in Book I *City of God*, chapter 13: “While at rest he knows how to act, and while acting how to rest; and he can apply to a new work a plan that is not new but eternal.” St. Ambrose, Book II *On Duties*, chapter 10, proves that God frequently changes his decision, censuring Herod’s oath and Jephthah’s impious deed. There is a lengthy discussion of this matter in the Eighth Council of Toledo. LOAISA.

In the same place, “We believe.” This is absent from most manuscripts, as we state elsewhere; it is established that such words and similar expressions were added by editors to make the meaning clearer. In any case, Isidore often speaks by means of an infinitive without another expressed verb governing it. The same thing sometimes occurs in the printed editions. AREV.]

3. Whatever has matter from which it exists is changeable, because it passes from the formless to form. Whatever has no matter, however, is unchangeable, as God certainly is. These qualities exist in God well and substantially: incorruption, immortality, and unchangeability. Hence he is rightly placed above every created thing.

4. We believe that in God it is the work, not the plan, that is changed; nor does he vary because at different times he commands different things. Rather, while remaining the same, unchangeable and eternal, what was suitable for each time remained, from all eternity, within the disposition of his plan. [Col. 0539B] 117

[Note: [Col. 0540C]

No. 5. St. Gregory, *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 28; Augustine, Book VI *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, and Book V, chapter 8. LOAISA.]

5. We must not, according to ordinary usage, think of God as one thing, his beauty as another, and his greatness as something else, as a human being is one thing and beauty another, since when beauty ceases, the human being remains. Accordingly, whoever understands God in this way believes him to be corporeal, whereas God himself is his beauty and greatness.

[Note: [Col. 0540C]

No. 6. From Eucherius, *On Formulas*. LOAISA.

In the same place, “To be called,” and so forth. This is found in the *Book of Sentences*, Book I, distinction 3, drawn from Gregory, *Moralia* XVI, chapter 20. LOAISA.

In the same place, “simplicity.” Jerome, in his little book *On Those Things Attributed to God in Scripture*. Isidore himself explains this sentence at length in Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, on God. He took that passage from Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, chapter 6, while interpreting Job’s words: “You have moved me against him.” There he investigates whether there is anger or agitation in God. LOAISA.

In the same place, “for stupidity.” Gregory, Letter 78, to the Emperor Maurice: “By calling me simple, he calls me foolish.” *Simple* is also used to mean “not evil” or “not deceitful.” Matthew 10: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.” And Proverbs 10: “Every simple soul is blessed.” And: “Whoever walks simply walks in confidence.” LOAISA.

In the same place, Vezzosius observes that Isidore explains the same doctrine concerning God’s simplicity in Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, and does so by adding several things that make the matter clearer. In place of “is not,” some copies have “is not in God.” AREV.]

6. Therefore God is called simple, either because he does not lose what he has, or because he himself is not one thing and what is in him another. It is clear that things which are ordered in God are improperly described or associated with vices—for example, simplicity, which is sometimes used to mean stupidity, although it does not mean that here. In God, however, there is supreme simplicity. The other attributes, too, must be assessed according to this rule.

## Chapter II. That God is immeasurable and omnipotent

[Col. 0541A]

[Note: [Col. 0541C]

Chapter II, no. 1. He interprets Jeremiah 25: “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord.” The author of the *Speculum* explains this passage almost word for word in chapters 21 and 22; Gregory does so in Homily 8 on Ezekiel; and Chrysostom in the homily *On the Holy and Adorable Spirit*, volume III. LOAISA.

In the same place, “Nor does he fill things piecemeal.” This is the phrase of the author of the *Speculum*, chapters 2 and 3. See Hilary, Book II *On the Trinity*. LOAISA.

In Taio, the title of this chapter is: “On the immeasurability or omnipotence of God.” AREV.]

1. God does not fill heaven and earth so that they contain him, but rather so that they themselves are contained by him. Nor does God fill all things piecemeal; rather, although he is one and the same, he is wholly present everywhere. We must not suppose that God is in all things in such a way that each thing receives him according to the size of its portion—that the greatest receives more and the smallest less—since he himself is wholly in all things, or all things are in him (Eph. 4:6). 118

[Note: [Col. 0541C]

No. 2. From the author of the *Speculum*, chapter 22. LOAISA.

In the same place, “The majesty of divine omnipotence.” Another reading has “the omnipotence of the majesty of God.” In the same place, “will be able to escape”: another reading has “will escape.” AREV.]

2. The majesty of divine omnipotence encompasses all things within the immeasurability of its power, and no one will be able to find a way of escaping its power, because it constrains everything on every side. For all things are confined within the omnipotence of divine judgment, whether they are to be preserved so that they may remain safe, or cut off so that they may perish. Therefore, we absolutely deny that anyone can escape God. Whoever does not have him as a reconciled Lord certainly cannot escape him when he is angry.

[Note: [Col. 0541C]

No. 3. From the author of the *Speculum*, chapter 23, and *On the Divine Essence*, chapter 1; and from Gregory, *Moralia* II, chapter 16. LOAISA.

In the same place, Petavius, volume I, Book III, chapter 9, no. 7, has similar words: “And therefore you are more inward,” and so forth. He cites the passage from an ancient author of the book *Speculum* among the appendices to Saint Augustine and observes that it was copied by Isidore, Alcuin, and Peter Damian. As usual, Petavius invokes many other Fathers in support of the same interpretation. Loaisa had already identified the author of the *Speculum*. AREV.]

3. The immeasurability of the divine greatness is such that we understand him to be within all things but not enclosed; outside all things but not excluded. Therefore he is inward, so that he may contain all things; outward, so that by the immeasurability of his unbounded greatness he may encompass all things. By being outward he is shown to be the creator; by being inward he is shown to govern all things. And so that created things might not exist without God, God is within all things. Yet so that they might not be outside God, God is outward, so that all things may be encompassed by him.

[Col. 0542A]

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

No. 4. From the author of the *Speculum*, chapter 7. LOAISA.

In the same place, “poverty.” Augustine, in his Commentary on John, tractate 13, expressed this elegantly: “Everything can be said of God, and nothing is said worthily of God; yet nothing is broader than this poverty, which cannot find a suitable name.” LOAISA.]

4. The completion of some deed is called perfection; but God, who was not made, how is he perfect? This expression, however, has been taken from ordinary usage because of human poverty, as have the other expressions, so that what is ineffable may somehow be spoken, since human speech says nothing worthily of God.

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

No. 5. From the book *On the Knowledge of True Life*, cited by Augustine, chapter 29, and from *On the Divine Essence*, chapter 1. Augustine, Letter 28 to Jerome, on the origin of the soul, also shows in what manner God walks in his saints. LOAISA.]

5. Although God is not local, he nevertheless walks locally in his saints, insofar as he is proclaimed by them from place to place. For God, who is moved neither by place nor by time, is nevertheless moved in his servants both by time and by place whenever he is proclaimed by them in different places. 119

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

No. 6. Paul’s passage in Ephesians 3, in the *Speculum*, chapters 13 and 14, and in Letter 112 to Paulinus, chapter 13, and as explained by Gregory, *Moralia* X, chapter 7, just as Isidore explains it. LOAISA.

In the same place, Taio, Book II, chapter 15, expresses this very thing, but has “according to equity” instead of “according to just equity.” Others, also in Isidore, have “in the lower regions according to equity.” AREV.]

6. Although nothing worthy may be said of God according to quantity, quality, position, condition, or motion, there is nevertheless in him, in a certain manner, breadth (Eph. 3:18) of charity, by which he gathers us from error and holds us in the truth. There is also length in him, by which he patiently bears with us until, once corrected, he restores us to the future homeland. There is also height in him, by which he surpasses every understanding through the immeasurability of his knowledge. There is also depth in him, by which, assigning those who are to be condemned to the lower regions according to just equity, he preordains them.

## Chapter III. That God is invisible

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

Chapter III, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 4, where he explains the words: “Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge.”

In the same place, “peace.” The passage is Paul’s, in Philippians 4. Augustine, in the *Enchiridion to Laurence*, chapter 63: “The peace of God,” he says, “which surpasses every understanding,” so that when it says “every,” even the understanding of the holy angels cannot be excepted, but only God’s. LOAISA.

In the same place, “alone,” and so forth. He seems to have had in view either the mystery of the Incarnation or that kind of mission by which the Word is said to be sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit. For this reason Christ is called the third person by Isidore himself, Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 4: “The prophet Haggai also disclosed the mystery of this Trinity in this way, speaking in the person of the Lord: ‘My Spirit will be in your midst.’ Behold God, who speaks; behold his Spirit. After this he added concerning the third person, that is, the Son: ‘And now my Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.’ Behold two persons, the Lord and his Spirit, who send, and the third person of that same Lord, who is sent.”

That the Son is sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, he confirms in this same book, chapter 15, from the same passage in Isaiah: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” Perhaps Isidore wished by this manner of expression to refute the heresies of the Arians and Nestorians: the former impiously denied the second person of the Divinity, while the latter wickedly added a fourth person as well, as Maxentius says against them. LOAISA.

In the same place, Taio has in the title: “On the fact that God is invisible or uncircumscribed” (*de id*, instead of *de eo*). Vezzosius observes that the text does not speak of the Divinity but of the greatness of the Divinity, so that the passage should be understood not of simple vision but of comprehensive vision, as theologians call it, by which a thing is comprehended in its entirety and in the full extent of what it is. Such comprehension of God does not fall within the capacity of a creature.

As for the sense in which the humanity assumed by Christ is called the third person in the Trinity, Grialius explained it fully in his note on Exodus, chapter 42, no. 3: namely, that the Word is one of the three persons of the Trinity. AREV.]

1. When Scripture speaks of God, it often says, “Behold God,” not as though it were displaying someone visible, but signifying that he is present everywhere. By saying “Behold the Lord,” or by saying that no sense—not even an angelic one—can reach the greatness of his divinity, Scripture indicates this. Although after the resurrection human nature may advance to angelic equality and rise indefatigably to contemplate God, it cannot nevertheless see his essence fully; nor can even angelic perfection entirely attain knowledge of it, according to the Apostle, who says: “The peace of God, which surpasses every understanding” (Phil. 4:7), with “even that of the angels” understood.

For the Trinity alone is known completely to itself, together with the humanity assumed by Christ, which is the third person in the Trinity:

[Note: [Col. 0543C]

No. 2. Gregory, *Moralia* V, chapter 20, and *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 2. LOAISA.

In the same place, “work.” From Gregory, *Dialogues* II, chapter 15. LOAISA.

In the same place, “and therefore.” Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, chapter 5, from which Isidore’s passage is taken: “The heavenly judgment,” he says, “although it is not known, should nevertheless not be thought unjust; rather, everything that one suffers should at least be believed just because it is plainly established that one suffers it by God’s authority.” LOAISA.]

2. In an intelligible manner, by a wondrous process, God’s essence can be known insofar as it is believed to exist. His work, however, which certainly cannot be equated with him, and his judgments, are known by no one at all. It is established that God’s hidden judgments cannot be penetrated by understanding, whether angelic or human. Therefore, because they are hidden but just, they must be revered and feared to the same degree, not examined or investigated, according to the Apostle, who says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (1 Cor. 2:16).

## Chapter IV. That the Creator is recognized from the beauty of creation

[Note: [Col. 0543D]

Chapter IV, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXVI, chapter 8. LOAISA.

From this chapter onward Taio preserves a different order of the sentences and treats this subject in chapter 9: “Instead of ‘of creatures . . . is set alongside,’ others have ‘with creation . . . is compared.’” AREV.]

1. The bodily greatness of creatures is often set beside the incorporeal greatness of the Creator, so that great things may be considered from small ones and invisible things judged from visible ones, and so that from the beauty of the works their maker may be recognized—not through equal likeness, but through a certain subordinate and created manifestation of goodness. 121

[Note: [Col. 0543D]

No. 2. A similar sentence occurs in Augustine, Book II *On Free Will*, chapter 7. LOAISA.

In the same place, another reading has: “Just as a work and art . . . so that, because through love,” and so forth. AREV.]

2. Just as art returns praise to the artist, so the Creator of things is praised through his creation; and how much more excellent he is is shown by the very ordering of the work. Through the beauty of bounded creation, God makes his own beauty—which cannot be bounded—understood, so that by those very footprints by which humanity turned away it may return to God. Thus, whoever withdrew from the form of the Creator through love of the beauty of creation may return through the beauty of creation to the beauty of the Creator.

[Col. 0544A]

[Note: [Col. 0543D]

No. 3. From Augustine, on Psalm 148: “They themselves,” he says of irrational things, “do not praise God by their own voice and heart, but they are considered by intelligent beings, and through them God is praised.” LOAISA.

In the same place, another reading has: “because it produces the same praise.” AREV.]

3. By certain steps of understanding, a person advances through creation to understanding God the Creator: rising from insensible things to sensible things; from sensible things to rational things; and from rational things to the Creator. Intelligible things praise God by themselves; irrational and insensible things do not do so by themselves but through us, when, considering them, we praise God. Yet they are said to praise him because the cause that produces their praise also produces theirs.

[Note: [Col. 0543D]

No. 4. He calls “the ancients” the philosophers who wrote and formed various opinions about the nature of God, as Cicero taught in his books *On the Nature of the Gods*. Among other things, Cicero said that God is a mind diffused throughout every part of the world and flowing through all nature, from whom all animals that are born receive life and spirit. Virgil expressed this view remarkably:

“First, heaven and earth, and the watery plains,

and the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,

a spirit nourishes within;

and Mind, infused through all its limbs, moves the mass

and mingles with the great body.”

See Salvian, *On Providence*. LOAISA.]

4. The ancients said that nothing is so dull that it does not possess some sense directed toward God. Hence it is that a spark is struck from hard flint. And if fire is in the stone, then surely there is sensation there where life does not sense itself.

122

## Chapter V. That certain forms are referred to God according to our manner of speaking

[Col. 0544B]

[Note: [Col. 0544D]

Chapter V, no. 1. From St. Gregory, *Moralia* XX, chapter 23, and Augustine, *Questions to Simplicianus*, question 2. St. Jerome wrote a book on the names attributed to God. Augustine also has a book *On the Essence of Divinity*, which is called *On Spiritual Formulas* by Eucherius; Isidore frequently draws sentences from it here. LOAISA.

In the same place, “anger.” Augustine, Book I *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 20: “The anger of God does not possess the heat of a disturbed mind.” From Psalm 77: “Anger and jealousy are not disturbances in God.” Two manuscript codices have: “Sacred reading has called it anger”; one manuscript agrees with the printed edition. In sacred literature I find both *anger* and *wrath* attributed indiscriminately to God. Concerning anger, Job 9: “God, against whose anger no one can prevail”; and Psalm 2: “He will speak to them in his anger.” Paul: “The wrath of God will be revealed”; and: “You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath”; and other passages. Concerning wrath, Isaiah 1 and 30: “You have provoked me to wrath”; and Jeremiah 4 and Revelation 15, where the wrath of God is full. LOAISA.

In the same place, compare Taio, chapter 10, on this same subject. Petavius, volume I, Book III, chapter 3, no. 17 and following, argues against the heretic Vorstius from these sentences of Isidore, which he observes Isidore took from Augustine. Vorstius dared to deny that God is unchangeable in will. In Isidore, some read “or to disturbance there occurs a change.” Immediately afterward they have *wrath* instead of *anger*, to which Loaisa’s note refers. AREV.]

1. In accordance with our manner of speaking, God is said to be jealous or to grieve. There is no disturbance in God arising from these emotions, for in him there is perfect tranquility. We must not hastily form the judgment of our mind and believe that a disturbance of fury or change can arise in God. Rather, sacred reading has called the very equity of justice by which he punishes the guilty “anger,” because what is equitable on the part of the judge is fury and indignation on the part of the sufferer.

2. We must therefore understand the other passions in the same way—those which Scripture transfers from human affection to God—so that he is believed to be unchangeable in himself, while nevertheless, for the sake of the effects of causes and so that he may be more easily understood, he is called by a mode of speech drawn from our mutability.

[Note: [Col. 0545B]

No. 3. “So mercifully does God.” From the author of the *Speculum*, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

3. Does God so mercifully provide for human weakness? [Col. 0544C] Since we cannot know him as he is, he makes himself known to us according to the manner of our speech. Hence he is described as possessing the qualities of our bodily members, and he wished unworthy passions to be spoken of him, so that through what is ours he might draw us toward what is his; and, while he stoops down to us, we might rise up toward him. 123

[Note: [Col. 0545C]

No. 4. I restored the mutilated passage in the printed edition on the basis of all the manuscripts, and from the book *Speculum* cited by Augustine, chapter 13, from which Isidore’s entire sentence is taken: “For in many ways,” he says, “in order to signify you to human beings, you draw forms from lower things toward yourself, although it is established that, according to your own nature, you are invisible, wholly incomprehensible, and uncircumscribed.” LOAISA.

In the same place, Eucherius, *On Spiritual Formulas*, explains the meaning of this word as applied to God in two ways: “God is said to walk,” he says, “not by passing from place to place—for it is impious to believe this—but his walking consists in delighting in the hearts of the saints, as it is written: ‘I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them, and I will be their God.’ Or certainly God’s walking consists in his passing from place to place in his holy preachers.”

Augustine has this same latter interpretation. Isidore recalls it above, in chapter 2, sentence 5: “Although God is not local, he nevertheless walks locally in his saints, insofar as he is proclaimed by them from place to place.” Augustine interprets God’s walking differently in Sermon 3 *On the Words of the Apostle*, concerning the words: “Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” “His majesty,” he says, “walks in us when it finds breadth of charity.” LOAISA.]

4. In many ways God draws forms from lower things toward himself in order to signify himself to human beings, although it is truly established that, according to his own substance, he is invisible and incorporeal. Forms of qualities are often taken from bodies and applied to God; yet they are not in God, because in his proper nature he is incorporeal and uncircumscribed. Rather, because of the effects of causes, forms of things are spoken of him: because he sees everything, he is called an eye; because he hears everything, he is called an ear; because he turns away, he is said to walk; because he waits, he is said to stand.

[Note: [Col. 0545D]

No. 5. The passage occurs in Jerome, in the same work, chapter 51: “The Lord of hosts swore by his soul.” According to Augustine, God’s swearing is the confirmation of a promise. Thus in connection with Psalm 109: “The Lord has sworn,” and in Sermon 17 *On the Lord’s Advent in the Flesh*, and in Book XVI *City of God*, chapter 32. LOAISA.

In the same place, “worm” is found in Psalm 21: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the despised of the people.” Also Hosea 5: “I am like a moth to Ephraim and like rottenness to the house of Jacob.” And Job 25: “Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm.” Augustine explains these passages in his Commentary on John, volume II.

“Worm” signifies one who is despised and rejected, without appearance or beauty, as in Isaiah 33 and Psalm 108. “And not a man” means “not a strong and robust man”; the Chaldean paraphrast expressed this emphasis: “But I am a worm, weak and not strong, bearing the reproaches of men.”

Gregory, *Moralia* XXX, chapter 29, says the following in explaining Job 39: “Who sent the wild ass free?” No one should consider it unfitting that the Lord can be represented by such an animal, since it is established that in sacred Scripture the worm and the beetle are used with a certain signification. As it is written: “But I am a worm and not a man.” And as it is said among the Septuagint interpreters: “The beetle will cry out from the wood.” This is Gregory’s statement.

The passage he suggests is in Habakkuk 2: “The stone from the wall will cry out.” In its place the Septuagint has: “And the beetle will speak these things from the wood” (*Καὶ Κάνθαρος ἐκ ξύλου φθέγξεται ταῦτα*). That is: “The beetle will speak these things from the wood.” Symmachus has a different reading: “The wooden joint of the building will speak these things.” See St. Jerome. LOAISA.]

5. In the same way, in the other similar cases, likeness is transferred from human emotions to God, as when he is said to forget or to remember. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord of hosts swore by his soul” (Jer. 51:14). This does not mean that God has a soul; rather, the prophet speaks in accordance with our manner of feeling. Elsewhere, by a similar figure, he is understood as the worm and the beetle (Ps. 21:7).

[Note: [Col. 0546C]

No. 6. The discussion of the divine names is long and varied. Some names are said of God essentially, such as affirmative names that signify perfection; some are said of God the Father; some of the Holy Spirit by appropriation; some are taken by likeness from the passions and disturbances of creatures; and still others are figurative, such as lamb, lion, and worm.

Dionysius the Areopagite first discussed all these matters obscurely and concisely; afterward Jerome and Eucherius did so; and finally St. Thomas instructed the mind on the subject by method and reasoning. Some modern writers also treat the same subject with learning, although when they depart from Thomas they are helpful neither to themselves nor to others. [Col. 0546D] LOAISA.

In the same place, Loaisa may perhaps have intended Ludovicus Legionensis, whose book *On the Divine Names* is frequently praised highly, though certain things in it are criticized. AREV.

In the same place, the passage was corrupted in some printed editions by a very bad division. In sacred literature it is common for the serpent to be called both death and wisdom. Augustine, Book III *On the Trinity*, chapter 10: “For by the serpent is understood death, which was brought about by the serpent in paradise, in a manner of speech that indicates the effect by means of the agent.” LOAISA.

In the same place, “in the prophet.” From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, chapter 6. LOAISA.

In the same place, “his substance.” Some add: “who is truly established to be invisible and incorporeal according to his own substance,” although this has already appeared above. Loaisa calls this a very bad division. An older codex of the Library of San Marco in Florence inserts more material, namely:

“His substance—not according to knowledge but according to likeness are forms drawn toward God, and not according to the property of substance but according to the effect of causes; hence he is not read to have appeared to human beings except through an assumed form of created things. They are deceived,” and so forth. AREV.]

6. Nor is it surprising that he is represented by lowly figures, since he is known to have descended even to the insults of our passions and flesh. For Christ is also written as a lamb, not on account of his nature but of his innocence; and as a lion, on account of his strength, not his nature; and as a serpent, on account of death and wisdom, not his nature. For in the prophet, too, the likeness of a cart bearing hay is applied to God (Amos II, 13). And all these things [Col. 0546A] are Christ figuratively because none of them corresponds to the proper nature of his substance.

[Note: [Col. 0547C]

7. From the author of the *Speculum*, chapter 13. “They are deceived,” he says, “the followers of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, who, when they read ‘man according to the image,’ etc.” Likewise Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 6. Cassian discusses the origin of this heresy in *Collation* 10; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 14; and Cyril, in his letter to Bishop Calosirius. LOAISA.]

7. Some foolish people are deceived when they read that man was made according to the image of God (Gen. II), supposing that God is corporeal, although it is not the flesh, which is a body, but the soul, which is spirit, that bears the image of God. Let us therefore not believe that there is a bodily form in God, who made man according to his image, because he created the mind, not the flesh, in his likeness. Consider, then, what sort of body truth possesses; and when you find none, that is God.

[Note: [Col. 0547C]

8. This passage occurs in Jerome and Eucherius, *On Formulas*, and in Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIV, chapter 3. He adduces Genesis XXXII: “And after Jacob had spoken with the angel, he said, ‘I have seen the Lord face to face’”—as if he were saying: “I have come to know the Lord because he himself deigned to know me.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “In prayer.” Thus, in the Church’s prayers, these verses are now placed first: “Show us your face, and grant us your salvation,” from Psalm LXXIX. And Augustine, or Eucherius, *On the Essence of Divinity*: “Show us, Lord, your face, and we shall be saved”—that is, he says, “Grant us knowledge of you.” LOAISA.]

8. In the sacred Scriptures, the face of God means not flesh but divine knowledge, in the sense that a person is known by seeing his face. For this is said to God in prayer: “Show us your face” [Col. 0546B]—as though it were said: “Grant us knowledge of you.”

[Note: [Col. 0547D]

9. “The mouth of God,” from Eucherius and Gregory, *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 10. LOAISA.

Ibid. “By which the one who.” Augustine recognizes the use of this figure in *On the Trinity*, book III, chapter 10, explaining the passage in John III: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness,” etc. Thus, he says, “by the serpent is understood the death that occurred in paradise, in a manner of expression that indicates the effect by means of its cause.” Again, in the same book, chapter 11, he explains the passage in Genesis XXII: “Now I know that you fear God.” LOAISA.

Ibid. In some copies, “and thus the mouth of God is put in place of the word.” AREV.]

9. The Only-Begotten Son is his mouth. For just as, in place of words that are produced through the tongue, we often say “this language” or “that language,” so “mouth” is put in place of the word of God, because it is customary for words to be formed by the mouth. And if you wish to express this by that mode of speech in which the one who produces something is named by the thing produced, you rightly put “mouth” for “word,” just as you put “tongue” for words and “hand” for letters.

[Col. 0547A] [Note: [Col. 0547D]

10. He interprets Paul’s passage in 1 Corinthians XIII: [Col. 0548C] “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” as Augustine does in *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapters 8 and 9. Gregory interprets in many ways the traces of God by which we strive toward the heavenly vision, *Moralia*, book X, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

10. The traces of God are those by which God is now known through a mirror. But the Almighty will be found perfectly when, in the future, he is presented face to face to each of the elect, so that they may contemplate that very form whose traces they now strive to grasp; and this is what it means that God will be seen through a mirror (1 Cor. XIII, 12). And so with the rest.

126 CHAPTER VI. That no succession of times is to be ascribed to God.

[Note: [Col. 0548C]

CHAPTER VI, no. 1. From Augustine, in the *Dialogue with Orosius*, and Gregory, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 23. LOAISA.

Ibid. “If always.” Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 6. LOAISA.

Ibid. This statement occurs in Taio, book I, chapter 8. Petavius, volume I, book III, chapter 4, describes, along with our Isidore, several other Greek and Latin Fathers who treat this subject. AREV.]

1. Divine eternity precedes all times, and no past, present, or future is believed to exist in God; rather, all things are said to be present in him because he embraces everything in his eternity. Otherwise God must be believed mutable if successions of times are ascribed to him. If there were always some times with God, it would not be time but eternity; nor would times change, but stand still.

2. Having a present, past, and future belongs to us, not to God. For example, for the present we say, “I hold the book”; for the past, “I held it”; for the future, “I shall hold it.” But God holds the whole universe; and for “he held” and “he will hold,” “he holds” is said.

[Note: [Col. 0548C]

3. From Augustine, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 12. “I find two things,” he says, “which you made,” etc.; there he interprets Genesis I: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” By heaven he understands intellectual nature; by earth, the first unformed matter. For “the earth was formless and empty.” According to Aristotle, *Physics* I, it is indeed first matter, stripped and deprived of every form and appearance. LOAISA.

[Col. 0548D] Ibid. In some copies, “Nor was there a departure of the angels themselves.” AREV.]

3. Nor is there for the angels themselves any coming or passing away of times. For there are two things among creatures to which the alternation of times does not apply: namely, the angels, because they cleave to the immutable Creator; and that unformed matter, before all those things that now roll along in time were formed from it—for time did not apply to it either. Time, therefore, is understood to belong not to those creatures that are above the heavens but to those beneath heaven. Times do not come to or pass from the angels, but to us, who dwell beneath heaven in this lowest world.

127 CHAPTER VII. On times.

[Note: [Col. 0548D]

CHAPTER VII, no. 1. From Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapter 5. Genesis first says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Of the many interpretations of this passage handed down by Basil, Hilary, Jerome, and Ambrose, he embraces the one according to which “in the beginning” signifies that heaven and earth were formed at the beginning of time. LOAISA.]

1. It is clear that there were no times before the beginning of the world, because although time itself is a creature, it must nevertheless be believed to have been made at the beginning of the world. It is therefore called “the beginning” because the beginning of all things began from it.

[Note: [Col. 0548D]

2. From Augustine, *Confessions*, book XI, chapter 12 and following chapters, where he resolves the question that past, future, and present are not an extent in things but are known in the mind: the mind looks toward the future, attends to the present, and remembers the past. Philosophers torment themselves wonderfully over the meaning of Aristotle’s statement in *Physics* IV: “Time does not exist without a soul.” See Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 2. LOAISA.]

2. Times have no bodily extent, because they almost depart before they arrive. Therefore there is no fixed state of times in things, since they are changed by the swift motion of creation. Neither are a hundred years one time; nor is one year one time; nor is one month one time; nor are a day or an hour one time. Since all these approach and withdraw in their several portions, how can that be called one which is not present all at once?

[Note: [Col. 0548D]

3. From Augustine, *Confessions*, book XI, chapter 20. “For these three are to be sought in the soul.” LOAISA.]

3. Whether past or future time exists in the same way as the present—and, if it exists, we must know where it is—but observe that all things, future, past, and present alike, are to be sought rather in the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0548D]

4. From Augustine, at the same place. LOAISA.]

4. It is established that these three—past, present, and future—are found only in the mind: the past by remembering, the present by contemplating, and the future by awaiting. Thus we hope for things that are coming, look upon things that are present, and recall things that are passing away. These things are not so in God, to whom all things are present simultaneously.

128 CHAPTER VIII. On the world.

[Col. 0549A]

[Note: [Col. 0549C]

CHAPTER VIII, no. 1. Taio treats this subject in chapter 16 of book I, where he takes certain material from Isidore. AREV.]

1. The world consists of visible yet investigable things. But man, composed from the totality of things, was created in a certain brief way as another world.

[Note: [Col. 0549C]

2. Hence Paul calls man “the creation of the world,” in Romans I: “The invisible things of God from the creation of the world,” because by his nature he embraces everything. Although Jerome and Theophilus interpret this passage differently: “from the creation of the world,” they say, that is, “from the creation and establishment,” for the Greek word κτίσις (*ktisis*) also signifies this. But the first interpretation is supported by the statement, “That which contains all things has knowledge of speech,” and by Gregory, *Moralia*, book VI, chapter 7, when he interprets the passage in Mark VI, “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” as meaning man, who has something in common with all creatures: being, growing, living through sensation, and understanding. LOAISA.]

2. The structure of the world is to be considered from the example of one man. For just as man moves toward his end through the stages of life, so the world, by being extended through time, declines; because by the same process through which man and the world seem to grow, both are diminished.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

3. Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 6, and *On Genesis*, book V, chapter 5. LOAISA.]

3. It is pointless to say that, after so many ages during which God was supposedly idle, a new thought arose in him to make the world, when the construction of this world remained in his eternal plan; and before the beginning there was not time but eternity. Time began from the establishment of creation, not creation from time.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

4. Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book III, chapter 2. LOAISA.]

4. Some say: “What was God doing before he made the heavens? Why did a new will arise in God to establish the world?” But no new will arose in God, because although the world did not exist in actuality, it always existed in the eternal reason and plan.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

5. Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 2. LOAISA.]

5. Some say: “What suddenly made God wish to create the world, which he had not created before?” They suppose that God’s will changed because at one time he willed what at another time he did not will. They should be answered: God’s will is God, because God himself is not one thing and his will another, but for him to will is identical with what he is; and what he is is certainly eternal and immutable [Col. 0549C]. This, therefore, is his will.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

6. Augustine, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 29, and book I. LOAISA.]

6. The matter from which the world was formed (Gen. I) preceded the things made from it in origin, not in time, as sound precedes song. For sound is prior to song, because the sweetness of a melody belongs to the sound of the voice, not the sound to the sweetness. Thus both exist simultaneously, but the one to which the song belongs is prior, namely sound.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

7. “Not yet from it.” In some copies, “Not yet formed from it.” AREV.]

7. The matter from which heaven and earth were formed was called formless because the things that remained to be formed had not yet been formed; nevertheless, that matter itself had been made from nothing.

8. It is one thing for something to be able to happen, and another for it to be necessary that it happen. That which God has assigned to natures must happen; but that which can happen is what the Creator reserved for himself to do whenever he wished, outside the course imposed upon natures.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

9. From Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 9, and Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

9. Darkness must not be believed to possess substance on the basis of the Lord’s statement through the prophet: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness” (Isa. XLV, 6–7). Rather, the angelic nature that did not rebel is called light, while the nature that rebelled is named darkness. Hence, in the beginning, light is separated from darkness. But because God created both these and those, it is said: “Forming light and creating darkness.” Nevertheless, he not only created the good angels but also formed them; whereas he merely created the wicked angels and did not form them. The same is to be understood of good and wicked human beings.

10. After the creation of heaven and earth has been enumerated, the Holy Spirit is named in Genesis so that, since it was necessary to say that he was borne over them, those things would first be named over which the Holy Spirit, their creator, was said to be borne. The Apostle also indicates this (Eph. III) when he points out the surpassing way of charity.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

11. From Augustine, *Confessions*, book III, chapter 9. LOAISA.]

11. The Holy Spirit is said to be borne over the waters because he is the gift of God in whom we, existing in him, find rest, and because by protecting us he is borne above us.

12. Every nature strives according to its own weight. Fire and oil, however, rightly always seek the higher regions, because through their figure it is shown that the Holy Spirit is borne over the whole of creation.

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

13. Blessed Athanasius asks in the *Questions to Prince Antiochus*, question 1, from what the angels were made. Many of the ancient Fathers judged that the angels were created before the establishment of the world: Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, book 10; the blessed Maximus, in the first *Century of Theological Chapters*; the *Apostolic Constitutions*; Clement, book VIII; Gregory of Nazianzus, in his sermon *On the Nativity of Christ* and in the second sermon *On Easter*; Damascene, book II of the *Orthodox Faith*; and Epiphanius, in his discussion against the heresy of Paul of Samosata and in the synodical letter sent by Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, to the emperor Honorius. This letter was read at the Sixth Synod, session eleven. Augustine examines this question in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapter 2, and concludes that it is a most secret matter, inaccessible to human conjecture.
