All of these agree in affirming that the angels were created before the formation of the world. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Of creatures” occurs in Luke, in place of “of creation.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “It was becoming evening.” This comes from Augustine. For, as the blessed Thomas states in part I, question 58, article 6, what is said about the morning and evening knowledge of the angels was introduced by Augustine, *On Genesis*, book IV, chapter 22; book V, chapter 4; and *City of God*, book XI, chapter 9. John Pico della Mirandola discussed the matter subtly and learnedly in the *Heptaplus*. The blessed Thomas explains Augustine’s view, as does Isidore here: “Just as in a day,” he says, “morning is the beginning of the day and evening its conclusion, so knowledge of the primordial being of things is called morning knowledge. This is according to the way things are in the Word. Knowledge of the being of a created thing, according to the way it exists in its own nature, is called evening knowledge.” LOAISA.]

13. The angels were made as the first day; and, to indicate their unity, it was not called the first day but one day. For this reason that day is continually repeated in the execution of creation. This day—that is, the nature of the angels—was in a certain sense becoming evening when they contemplated creation itself; not by remaining fixed in contemplation of that creation, but by referring its praise to God and seeing it more perfectly in the divine plan, it immediately became morning. But if it had remained, neglecting the Creator, in the contemplation of the creature, it would already have become not evening but night.

[Note: [Col. 0551D]

14. Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 9, and *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV. LOAISA.]

14. Since the creature knows itself better in God than in itself, its knowledge of itself—which is greater in God—is called day and light. But its knowledge of itself in itself, in comparison with that knowledge which is in God, is called evening because it is far inferior. [Col. 0551B] Therefore, after evening there was morning (Gen. I). For when the creature recognized that its knowledge of itself was not sufficient for it, so that it might know itself more fully, it referred its being to God, in whom it would become day by knowing itself better.

131 [Note: [Col. 0551D]

15. Formerly it read “For thus,” but incorrectly, with all the ancient manuscripts agreeing, as well as the following sentence and Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapters 2 and 9, where he treats this matter carefully. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Transitorily.” In its place blessed Augustine says “whether temporally or in the eternity of the Word,” *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapters 2 and 9. LOAISA.]

15. Not in the way that we transiently say, “Let something be made,” did God say, “Let heaven be made in the beginning.” For that was said eternally in the one Word. If God had said “Let it be made” transiently, some creature would already have existed from which such a voice could be produced. But because no creature existed before he said “Let it be made,” that very “Let it be made” was uttered in the eternity of the Word, not in the sound of a voice.

16. The creature was not seen seven times and praised seven times by God, since, before it was made, it was perfectly seen by him. Rather, when we praise each thing as we see it, it is as though he sees and praises through us, just as it is said: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20). Therefore, just as he himself speaks through us, so he sees and praises through us; but through himself he sees perpetually and eternally, whereas through us he sees temporally.

17. Observe that creation as a whole is universally called very good in the beginning, but each individual thing is called merely good, because the members of the body, although each is good individually, together make a greater good when all the individual members form a very good body.

[Note: [Col. 0551D]

18. In some copies: “beautiful to it, which”; in others: “it is beautiful, which.” AREV.]

18. The beauty of all the elements consists in what is beautiful and fitting. But something is beautiful in relation to itself when it is beautiful in itself, as a human being composed of soul and all his members. Something is fitting, however, as clothing and food are fitting. Therefore a human being is said to be beautiful in relation to himself because a human being is not necessary for clothing and food, but these are necessary for the human being; and they are called fitting because they are not beautiful in themselves, like a human being, nor suited to themselves, but accommodated to something else—that is, to the human being—and are not necessary to themselves. The same must be said of the other natures of the elements.

19. All things that exist and have been made are exceedingly marvelous, but through familiarity they have become cheap in our eyes. Therefore examine the works of God in such a way that you always consider them immeasurable.

132 CHAPTER IX. Whence evil.

[Note: [Col. 0551D]

CHAPTER IX, no. 1. In the Gothic Codex the second sentence is: “Heretics believe that the mind was created by God and vices by the devil; hence they suppose that there are two natures, good and evil.” But vice is not a nature; and although it truly comes from the devil, it was not created—not because it exists somewhere or at some time. In fact, this sentence is the fourth below. Augustine, in tractate 2 of his exposition of John, interprets “Without him nothing was made” as referring to sin and evil, which is nothing. And in *On the Nature of the Good*. LOAISA.

Ibid. Taio investigates whence evil comes in chapter 15 of book I, drawing on Isidore. The theologians address the same question with Saint Thomas, part I, question 49. AREV.]

1. Evil was not created by the devil but discovered; and therefore evil is nothing, because “without God nothing was made,” whereas God did not make evil. This is not because evil existed somewhere or at some time from which the devil could become evil, but because, while he was a good angel, he became evil through his own vice by growing proud; and therefore evil is rightly said to have been discovered by him.

[Note: [Col. 0552D]

2. From Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 12, and *On the Nature of the Good*. LOAISA.]

2. It is established that there is no nature of evil, because every nature is either immutable, as God is, or mutable, as creation is. Evil is no nature because, by entering into a good nature, it makes that nature vicious; when evil departs, the nature remains, while the evil that was present is nowhere. From the fact that vice harms nature, it is recognized that vice is not a nature, because nothing that is natural causes harm.

3. When a good nature is condemned on account of an evil will, the evil will itself bears witness to the goodness of the nature, since it testifies so strongly that the nature is good that God does not leave it unpunished for evil.

4. Heretics believe that the mind was created by God and vices by the devil. Hence they also suppose that there are two natures, good and evil. But vice is not a nature; and although it truly comes from the devil, it was not created.

5. For what reason did God permit the condition of evil to arise, except so that the beauty of good nature might stand out from the contrast with evil? This mode is also found in words. In Greek this mode is called ἀντίθετον (*antit­heton*), which in Latin is called *oppositum* or *contrapositum*, “opposed” or “set against”; and speech becomes beautiful when contrary things are immediately set forth. So too evil has been mingled into things so that the goodness of nature might excel by comparison with evil.

133 [Note: [Col. 0553C]

6. “If they use them well.” That is, the creatures; or rather, Isidore uses *utor* in a passive sense by employing it. AREV.]

6. God made all things exceedingly good. Nothing, therefore, is evil by nature, since even those things in creation that appear to be punitive are good when used well, while they harm when used badly. Thus creation is to be judged not good according to our use of it, but exceedingly good according to its nature.

7. If you shave a man’s eyebrow, you remove a small thing but introduce deformity into the whole body; so it is also with the universe of creation. If you call even the smallest worm evil by nature, you do an injury to the whole of creation.

8. Through the sin of the first man, all evils were transferred as punishment to the entire human race. Therefore whatever appears evil attacks us partly by its origin and partly by our fault.

9. Perverse people call many things in creation evil, such as fire because it burns, iron because it kills, and a wild animal because it bites. But a human being, failing to consider their benefits, accuses them of what he ought rather to impute to himself: because of his sin these things became harmful, although before sin they had been entirely subject to him. Through our fault, not by their nature, the things that harm us are evil to us. For light, although good, is harmful to weak eyes; in that case the fault is in the eyes, not in the light. The same applies to the rest.

[Note: [Col. 0553C]

10. “Of creation.” The passage is Wisdom XVI: “Creation, serving you who made it, burns in torment against the unjust,” etc. In place of “burns,” some manuscripts have “glows.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “To exact punishment.” In some copies, “punishment exacts.” The old edition has “with punishment exacting it.” In place of “will fight with him,” my manuscript has “will fight for him.” Then, in place of “milder,” others have “lighter.” AREV.]

10. When man is scourged by the goads of creatures and the adversities of the elements, this exacts the punishment of sin, so that the man who has grown proud against God may suffer adversity from the things beneath him. Hence it is also read in Wisdom concerning God: “The whole world will fight with him against the senseless.” It was therefore rightly done on account of sins that what is naturally prosperous should be changed into adversity for man. Hence Solomon also says: “Creation burns in torment against the unjust, and is milder in doing good to those who trust in God.”

134 11. Flesh will not be subject to the soul, nor vice to reason, unless the mind is subject to the Creator. All things beneath us are rightly subjected to us only if we are subjected to him by whom they have been subjected to us. For even the one who appears to have subjected things to himself, while not subject to God, is rather subjected to those things, because they subjugate his will to the love of what he imagines to be subject to him.

CHAPTER X. On the angels.

[Col. 0554A]

[Note: [Col. 0553C]

CHAPTER X—no. 1. “Name.” From Gregory, *Homily 34 on the Gospels*. LOAISA.

Ibid. Taio discusses the angels in chapters 12, 13, and 14 of book I. In the *Isidoriana*, chapter 72, numbers 20 and following, I observed that this entire chapter is presented in some manuscripts under the title of a sermon of Saint Isidore, with additions from Saint Gregory the Great in certain copies. I reproduced in the cited place the notice that Constantine Cajetan prefixed to this sermon. AREV.]

1. “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; for according to their nature they are called spirits. When they are sent from heaven to announce things to human beings, they are called angels from the announcement itself; by nature they are spirits. They are called angels when they are sent.

[Note: [Col. 0553D]

2. “Mutable.” Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 29, and book XV, chapter 4; and Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 23. L.

Ibid. “Charity.” In some manuscript copies the reading is “eternal brightness”; but “charity,” as in the printed editions, must be read, for Gregory has it this way in *Moralia*, book V, chapter 29. The sentence is taken from him: “Since the angelic nature itself is mutable in itself, it overcame this mutability by being bound by bonds of love to him who is always the same,” etc. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Apostate.” Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 13, interprets the passage in Revelation XX concerning the apostate angel: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss.” And concerning what follows—“When the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released”—he says: “For that apostate angel, who had been created so as to surpass the other legions of angels, fell through pride so completely that he was then placed under the dominion of the angels who stood firm. Thus either he remains bound while they minister for our benefit, or, when they release him for our testing, he is set free and exercises all his strength against us.” LOAISA.]

2. The nature of angels is mutable, because mutability belongs to their nature; but everlasting charity makes them incorruptible. We say that angels are immutable by grace, not by nature. For if they were immutable by nature, the devil would certainly not have fallen. The contemplation of the Creator therefore comes to the aid of their mutable nature; and thus the apostate angel was deprived of his status, when he wished to preserve his strength not from God but from himself.

3. The angels were made before every creature, when it was said, “Let there be light”; for Scripture says of them: “Wisdom was created before all things.” They are called light because they participate in eternal light. They are called wisdom because they cleave to uncreated Wisdom. Although they are mutable by nature, divine contemplation does not permit them to change.

[Note: [Col. 0554C]

4. “Before all.” Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 18. [Col. 0554D] LOAISA.

Ibid. Isaeus, in his notes on Lactantius, *Institutes*, book II, chapter 9, discusses the time of the angels’ creation. He says that Isidore teaches here, along with many others, that it took place many ages before this world, and he notes that certain followers of Saint Thomas’s school wrongly asserted that this was an error against the faith. Certainly the most ancient Fathers, especially the Greeks, teach that the angels were created before heaven and all bodies. Yet Petavius says that Isidore’s meaning appears ambiguous, *On Angels*, book I, chapter 15, number 5. In my judgment, Isidore follows the opinion of Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XXVIII, chapter 14, who says that the angels are called the morning stars because they are believed to have been created first in time, while indicating that they were brought forth before the first day, not together with the light. AREV.]

4. The angels were created before every creation of the world, and the devil was created before every creation of the angels, as it is written: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.” Hence, in comparison with the angels, he was called an archangel. For he was created first by precedence of rank, not by an interval of time.

[Note: [Col. 0554D]

5. “From what confidence he fell.” Perhaps: “from the confidence from which he fell.” Some insert: “Among the angels the devil is established by excellence of precedence; from this confidence,” etc. Theologians inquire by what kind of pride or by what thought the devil became swollen with arrogance. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, verse 169:

“He is puffed up; swelling with greatness, he raises himself higher,

And displays his own fires with more presumptuous boasting.” AREV.]

5. The devil held primacy among the angels, and from this confidence he fell, so that he fell without possibility of restoration. The prophet announces the excellence of his precedence in these words: “The cedars were not taller than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his crown; no tree of paradise was like him”; for God had made him more beautiful.

[Note: [Col. 0555D]

6. “Differs.” From Gregory, at the same place. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Of truth.” The printed editions had “of virtue,” but I have placed “of truth,” with all the manuscripts of class C agreeing. Although the passage is drawn from Gregory, Isidore adds this word to Gregory’s sentence; thus it reads in Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 18: “The more subtle his nature is, the more fully the likeness of God is believed to have been expressed in him.” L.]

6. The condition of an angel differs from the condition of a human being. Man was created according to the likeness of God, but the archangel who fell was called the seal of God’s likeness, as the Lord testifies through Ezekiel: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.” For the more subtle his nature is, the more fully it existed expressed according to the likeness of divine truth.

[Note: [Col. 0556D]

7. “First from heaven.” Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI. L.]

7. It is believed that the devil fell from heaven before man was created. For as soon as he was made, he burst into pride and was cast down from heaven. According to the testimony of truth, he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because as soon as he was made, he fell. [Col. 0555B] He was indeed created in the truth, but because he did not stand, he immediately fell from the truth.

8. In one fall of pride, when they set themselves up against God through arrogance, both man and the devil fell. But man, returning to repentance, recognizes that he is inferior to God. The devil, however, not content merely to have fallen by supposing himself equal to God, even declares himself superior to God, according to the Apostle’s statement concerning the Antichrist: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

9. The devil will no longer seek pardon because he is not moved to repentance; but his members plead hypocritically, although because of their evil conscience they do not deserve to obtain it.

[Note: [Col. 0556D]

10. “Let human misery learn.” From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXII, chapter 5. L.]

10. Let human misery learn that God is more readily moved to grant pardon for this reason: he has compassion on weak humanity, because it has drawn from the lower part an infirmity that makes it liable to sin—that is, from the flesh, by which the enclosed soul is held fast.

[Note: [Col. 0556D]

11. “Remember.” The passage is Psalm CII. In the Vulgate it reads: “He remembered that we are dust.” L.]

11. The apostate angels do not have pardon because they were burdened by no weakness of carnal frailty that might cause them to sin. Human beings, however, return to pardon after sin for this reason: from their clay-like material they have drawn the weight of infirmity. Therefore, on account of the weakness of the flesh’s condition, a return to salvation lies open to man, just as the Psalm also says: “He knows our creation. Remember, Lord, that we are earth.” And again: “Remember,” he says, “what my substance is.”

[Col. 0555D] 12. After the apostate angels fell, the others were strengthened by perseverance in eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven, “Let there be a firmament” is repeated at the beginning, and the firmament was called heaven. Clearly this shows that after the ruin of the angels, those who remained obtained the firmness of eternal perseverance and blessedness, which previously they had received to a lesser degree. Hence it must be understood that the wickedness of the evil serves the benefit of the holy, because where the wicked fall, there the good advance.

13. The number of the good angels, which was diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be completed from the number of elect human beings; that number is known to God alone.

14. There are distinctions of powers among the angels, and ministries have been distributed to them according to the dignity of their ranks. Some are preferred to others both in the height of their power and in knowledge of virtue; therefore some serve under the commands of others and obey their orders. Hence the angel sends one angel to the prophet Zechariah and commands him to announce whatever he must announce.

[Note: [Col. 0556D]

15. “Name.” From Gregory, *Homily 34 on the Gospels*, and *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 18. LOAISA.

Ibid. Vezzosius had noted more about the orders of angels in his notes on chapter 58 of the Augustinian *Enchiridion*, part II, pages 443 and following. AREV.]

15. Sacred Scripture testifies that there are nine distinctions or orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim. The prophet Ezekiel also describes the number of these orders under the same number of names of stones, when he spoke of the primacy of the apostate angel. “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.” By this number of stones the orders of the angels are signified—those whom the apostate angel had before his fall, as though fastened upon the garment of his adornment. When he saw himself more splendid than all of them, he immediately became swollen with pride and raised his heart to arrogance.

16. Angels always rejoice in God, not in themselves. But the devil is evil for this reason: he sought not the things that are God’s, but those that are his own. There is no greater iniquity, however, than for anyone to wish to glory not in God but in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0556D]

17. “Angels.” Augustine, likewise, Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 1. L.]

17. Angels know all things in the Word of God before they come to be in reality; and those things that among human beings are still future, the angels already know because God has revealed them. The transgressing angels, although they lost holiness, nevertheless did not lose the keen perception of the angelic creature. For they possess the acuity of foreknowledge in three ways: through the subtlety of their nature, through experience of times, and through revelation from superior powers.

[Col. 0556D] 18. Whenever God is angered against this world by some scourge, apostate angels are sent to carry out vengeance. Yet they are restrained by divine power, lest they inflict as much harm as they desire. The good angels, however, have been appointed for the service of human salvation, so that they may administer the concerns of the world and govern all things at God’s command, as the Apostle testifies: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

[Note: [Col. 0557C]

19. “Angels.” Augustine, Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23, and *On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture*, Book III; and Gregory, Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 2; Book XVII, chapter 8. LOAISA.]

19. The angels take from the air above the bodies in which they appear to human beings, and put on a solid appearance from the heavenly element, so that through it they may be displayed more clearly to human eyes.

20. Each nation is believed to have angels appointed over it, as is shown by the testimony of the angel speaking to Daniel: “I came,” he says, “to announce it to you, but the prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me.” And later: “There is no one to help me except Michael, your prince.”

[Col. 0557B] [Note: [Col. 0557C]

21. “To have angels.” Augustine, Sermon 68, *To the Brothers in the Desert*; Matthew XVIII. LOAISA.

Ibid. Petavius shows that each nation and all human beings have guardian angels, on the basis of the same passages of Scripture on which Isidore relies, as well as the authority of Isidore himself and of other Fathers. *On the Angels*, Book II, chapter 8. AREV.]

21. It is likewise proved that all human beings have angels, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Hence also, in the *Acts of the Apostles*, when Peter was knocking at the door, the apostles inside said: “It is not Peter, but it is his angel.”

[Note: [Col. 0557D]

22. “If God.” The entire sentence is taken from Gregory, Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 28. LOAISA.]

22. If the angels behold and see God, why did the Apostle Peter say: “Into whom the angels of God desire to look”? Again, if they do not behold or see him, how, according to the Lord’s statement, do their angels always see the face of the Father who is in heaven? But both statements are rightly understood. For we truly believe that the angels both see God and desire to see him, both possess him and hasten to possess him, both love him and strive to love him.

[Col. 0557C] [Note: [Col. 0557D]

23. Saint Julian of Toledo, Book II of the *Antikeimenon*, question 78, resolves this difficulty in the same way. But where Isidore has “necessity,” “this necessity,” and so forth, Julian has “anxiety,” “this anxiety,” and so forth, repeating the word throughout; this is perhaps better. AREV.]

23. For if they desire to see him in such a way that they do not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, this desire entails necessity, and that necessity is penal. But all punishment is far from the blessed angels, since punishment and blessedness never coexist. Again, if we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, satisfaction ordinarily entails weariness; yet we know that they cannot grow weary of the vision of God, which they both desire.

[Col. 0558A] 24. What, then, remains except that we should believe, in a wondrous manner, both things at once: that they desire and are satisfied? They desire without labor, and are satisfied without weariness. So that necessity may not exist in their desire, they are satisfied while desiring. And again, so that weariness may not exist in their satisfaction, they desire to be satisfied. Thus the angels see the face of the Father through satisfaction; but because this satisfaction knows no weariness, the angels desire always to look upon him.

[Note: [Col. 0557D]

25. “Wherever, etc.” Augustine, Book II of *The Trinity*. L.]

25. Wherever in the holy Scriptures an angel is mentioned in place of God, it is not the Father or the Holy Spirit who is meant, but the Son alone, in accordance with the dispensation of the Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0557D]

26. “Before the Lord’s, etc.” Gregory, Book XXVII of the *Moralia*, chapter 8. L.]

26. Before the coming of the Lord’s Incarnation, there was discord between angels and human beings. But when Christ came, he made peace in himself, both with angels and with human beings. For when he was born, the angels cried out: “Peace on earth to people of good will.” Through Christ’s Incarnation, therefore, not only was humanity reconciled to God, but peace between human beings and angels was also restored.

27. That there was discord between human beings and angels before Christ’s coming is recognized above all from the fact that, in the Old Testament, when angels were greeted by human beings, they disdained to be greeted by them. In the New Testament, however, when John did this, the angel not only reverently accepted the greeting but also forbade him to do so.

28. For this reason, in the Old Testament the human being is despised and is not greeted in return by the angel, because humanity had not yet passed into God.

[Note: [Col. 0557D]

29. In the sermon published under Isidore’s name by Cajetan, after the words “and peace restored to the angels,” the following is added, as I observed in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 72, no. 20, drawn from Saint Gregory:

“Sometimes, indeed, God speaks to human hearts through an angel in such a way that the angel himself is also presented to the mind’s eyes. For God speaks words through an angel when nothing is shown in an image, but the words of heavenly speech are heard—as when the Lord says (John X): ‘Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you’; and immediately the reply is made: ‘I have glorified, and I will glorify again.’ For God, who cries out without time through the impulse of his inmost being, did not at that time utter through his substance the voice that he marked off within time by human words. Rather, speaking of heavenly things, he formed his words—those he wished human beings to hear—through the ministry of a rational creature.

“Sometimes God speaks through angels by means of events, when nothing is said in words, but future things are announced through an image taken from the elements. Thus Ezekiel, hearing no words (chapter I), saw the appearance of electrum in the midst of fire, so that, while he looked only upon the appearance, he might perceive what things would come to pass at the end. So the angel Gabriel speaks to Daniel, who says: ‘It happened, when I, Daniel, saw the vision,’ and so forth. [Here many words are quoted from Daniel, chapters VIII, X, and XII.]

“Sometimes God speaks through angels by words and events simultaneously, when he conveys by certain movements what he narrates in words. For after his sin Adam could not see God in the substance of his divinity, but he heard the words of rebuke through an angel.

“Sometimes God speaks through angels by images displayed to the eyes of the heart, as Jacob, while sleeping, saw a ladder resting upon the heavens (Genesis XXVIII), and as Peter, seized in ecstasy, saw a sheet full of reptiles and four-footed animals (Acts X). Unless he had seen these things with incorporeal eyes, he would not have been in ecstasy. Likewise, in a nocturnal vision, a Macedonian man appeared to Paul (Acts XVI) and asked him to cross over to Macedonia.

“Sometimes God speaks through angels by images temporarily taken from the air and set before bodily eyes, as Abraham was able not only to see three men (Genesis XVIII), but also to receive them in an earthly dwelling; and not only to receive them, but also to set food before them for their use. For unless the angels, announcing certain things to us on earth, assumed bodies for a time from the air, they would certainly not appear to our outward eyes, nor would they eat food with Abraham, unless they carried something solid from the heavenly element for our sake. Nor is it surprising that there they are called sometimes angels and sometimes the Lord, since by the name ‘angels’ those who ministered outwardly are expressed, while by the title ‘Lord’ the one who presided over them inwardly is shown—so that through the one name the authority of the presiding one might become clear, and through the other the service of those ministering.

“Sometimes God speaks through angels to heavenly substances, as it is written after the Lord’s baptism (Matthew III, XVII): ‘A voice sounded from the cloud, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’

“Sometimes God speaks through angels to earthly substances, as when he rebuked Balaam (Numbers XXII), forming human words in the mouth of the she-ass.

“Sometimes God speaks through angels simultaneously to earthly and heavenly substances, as to Moses on the mountain (Exodus III), when, giving him the words of his command, he joined fire and a bush, linking what was above with what was below. Yet this occurs only when something is signified by the conjunction itself. For when he addressed Moses through the burning bush, what else did he show except that Moses would become the leader of that people which would receive the flame of the law and yet would by no means escape the punishment of sin? Or that from that people would come one who, by the fire of divinity, would consume the sins of our flesh like the thorns of a bush, while preserving the substance of our humanity unconsumed even within the flame of divinity?

“Sometimes, moreover, God infuses the power of his inspiration into human hearts through angels, by means of their secret presence. Hence Zechariah says (Zechariah I): ‘The angel who spoke in me said to me.’ By saying that the angel spoke to him, yet in him, he clearly shows that the one who had spoken words to him through a bodily appearance was not outside him. Hence shortly afterward he adds: ‘And behold, the angel who spoke in me was going out.’

“For often they do not appear outwardly, but, just as angelic spirits make God’s will known to the minds of the prophets, so they raise them to sublime things and show as present in their original causes whatever is to come to pass in events. For the human heart, weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, does not penetrate inward things because it bears this very corporeality of its own as an obstacle; it lies heavily outward because it does not have within it a hand to raise it. Hence, as has been said, the subtlety of angelic power itself appears to the perceptions of the prophets as it truly is; and their mind, touched by a subtle spirit, is lifted up, no longer lying sluggish and torpid in the lowest places, but, filled with inward breathings, ascending to heavenly things. From there, as from a certain summit of reality, it sees what things below are destined to come to pass.

“Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen. Here ends.” AREV.]

29. Human beings, however, are received by God and reverently greeted by the angel. For we read that the angel Gabriel greeted Mary; and when John greeted the angel, the same angel said to him: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers.” From this it is recognized that through the Lord’s Incarnation peace was restored both to human beings and to angels.

CHAPTER XI. On the Human Being.

[Col. 0559A]

[Note: [Col. 0560B]

CHAPTER XI—No. 1. “Common to all.” Thus the Fathers interpret the saying of Wisdom I: “That which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.” And the saying in Matthew, at the end: “Preach the Gospel to every creature,” so that by “every creature” the human being is understood; especially Gregory, Homily 29, *On the Ascension of the Lord*, and Book VI of the *Moralia*, chapter 7. On this subject, above, chapter 10. LOAISA.

Ibid. “With the rest.” Gregory, Book IX of the *Moralia*, chapter 36, and Augustine, *On Genesis*, in the *Incomplete Work*. LOAISA.

Ibid. Vezzosius notes that the statement of Saint Gregory is famous: that the human being has something in common with all creatures. AREV.]

1. Everything beneath heaven was made for the sake of the human being, but the human being was made for his own sake; hence everything is figuratively referred to his likeness. It is evident that all natural things are common to the human being and to all things that exist, that all things are contained in the human being, and that the nature of all things subsists in him. The human being is a certain great portion of the whole creation; and he is as much superior to the rest as he is nearer to the divine image. How greatly the human being surpasses the other creatures in the dignity of virtue is learned from the very reverence shown in creation: God said of all things, “Let it be,” and they were made, but he willed to create the human being after deliberation according to the counsel of eternity, saying: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.”

2. Since we were created naturally good, by a certain desert of guilt we have become evil against nature.

3. Just as God foreknew that the human being would sin, so he also foreknew how he would restore him through his grace—the one who could have perished by his own free choice.

[Note: [Col. 0560B]

4. “Created together.” This is clear from Genesis I: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.” For “human being” includes both sexes. Hence Eve is called *virago*—a woman derived from man—and “the image of man,” whereas Paul calls the human being “the image and glory of God” (I Corinthians XI). Augustine interprets it this way in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7; and in Genesis V it is said: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. On the day when God created the human being, he made him in the likeness of God; male and female he created them.” And Paul, in I Corinthians XI, when he says, “Just as woman is from man, so also man is through woman,” concludes: “But all things are from God.” Ambrose says there: “Both are one in nature.” Isidore calls this being one originally; specifically, however, the woman was later formed from the man’s side.

Gregory supports this opinion in Book XXXIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 10: “The substance of things,” he says, “was created together, but their form was not formed together,” and so forth. Observe incidentally that Augustine and Gregory disagree about the formation of things: Augustine proves in many places in his writings on Genesis that all things were made together both according to substance and according to form, especially in Book IV of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 34. Gregory, however, says that they were made together according to substance but not according to form. Isidore holds this opinion here and in Book II of the *Differences*, chapter 10: “In the creation and formation of the world, the difference is that originally, according to the substance of matter, all things were created together, but according to the distinction of things they were formed through the alternation of the six days.”

Philo, in Book I of *Allegories of the Law*, says that it belongs to rustic simplicity to think that the world was created in six days, or at least within a definite period of time.

Here Isidore refutes the opinion of those who say that Adam and Eve were created as androgynes—that is, as a human being in whom two bodies, male and female, were joined around the back, so that the human being was double from the beginning, as Plato asserted in the *Symposium*, or *On Love*, and was afterward divided so that the two parts might be joined again opposite one another for the procreation of offspring. For they claim that the woman was formed from the side of the first man, not from a rib, since the Hebrew word *zela* signifies both “side” and “rib.”

Francis Georgius held this opinion. But Saint Augustine attacks the Platonists in Book III of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 22, saying: “Again, lest anyone should think that both sexes were in the human being, as in those whom they call androgynes, it is stated in the plural: ‘Male and female he created them.’” L.

[Col. 0561C] Ibid. There was an error in the note of Grialius’s edition: “On the day which he created,” instead of “On the day when he created.” AREV.]

4. Adam and Eve were created together originally, but specifically the woman was afterward formed from the man’s side. Therefore both were created together according to the order of reason, but not together in the unity of time.

[Note: [Col. 0561C]

5. From Paul, I Corinthians XI: “The man is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man.” The woman is called the man’s glory, as a work derives from its maker. Augustine, in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, explains why the man is especially called the image of God through subjection; hence Acts XVII: “He made from one the whole human race.” LOAISA.]

5. The man was made in the image of God; the woman was formed in the image of the man. Hence by the law of nature she is subject to him.

6. Likewise, the man was made for his own sake; the woman was created to be the man’s helper.

[Note: [Col. 0561C]

7. “You shall eat earth.” Gregory interprets this in the same way in his *Exposition on the Seven Penitential Psalms*, Psalm IV, explaining the words: “And he will have mercy on his land”: “By ‘earth,’” he says, “we understand sinners; hence the Lord said to the serpent: ‘You shall eat earth all the days of your life.’” The same interpretation appears in Book II of the *Moralia*, chapter 30. Likewise Ambrose, Book *On Repentance*, chapter 13, and Augustine, Book *On the Christian Contest*, chapter 1. LOAISA.

Ibid. “The prophet.” Jerome interprets the passage in the same way. LOAISA.]

7. The human being was handed over to the devil on account of sin when he heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go.” At that time it was also said to the devil: “You shall eat earth.” Hence the prophet says: “The serpent’s bread is dust.” For the serpent is the devil; the dust is the ungodly; and they are the devil’s food.

8. Because we fall downward through an evil will, we rightly rise with labor in order to do good. This would not be so if pleasure had not induced the wrongdoing of the first human beings, for whom, in order to live well, willing alone would have sufficed and action would immediately have obeyed without difficulty.

9. Division and conflict in the human soul are the punishment of sin, propagated from the first human being into all his descendants. The one who did not wish to be united with God became divided within himself; and the one who did not wish to be subject to the Lord commanding him became rebellious and opposed to himself. Hence he cannot be brought under his own control unless he has first been subjected to God; and he unwillingly serves himself who did not willingly wish to serve God.

[Note: [Col. 0561C]

10. “Miserable in labor, etc.” Vezzosius calls this a golden passage of Isidore, breathing the genius of Gregory the Great. AREV.]

10. How variously the human race has flowed away through diverse things, since it withdrew from the one stable and ever-abiding solidity of divinity! For whenever it desires some task, it fixes the rest of the mind there, as though it were already in that task. But when this does not satisfy it, changing its aim, it passes on to one action and then another. While it seeks solid rest through diverse things, it neither finds it nor rests; miserable in labor and living amid variety, it remains empty of rest. Although this mutability was not created in humanity along with its nature, but came upon it as the deserved consequence of the first transgression, it has nevertheless become natural, because it passes originally from the first human being into all human beings, just as death does.

144 CHAPTER XII. On the Soul and the Other Faculties of Sense.

[Note: [Col. 0561D]

CHAPTER XII—No. 1. “Life of the body.” From Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Soul*. LOAISA.

Ibid. On this subject, Taio, Book I, chapter 21. AREV.]

1. The soul is the life of the body; God is the life of the soul. And just as the body is dead without the soul, so the soul is dead without God.

[Note: [Col. 0561D]

2. “The soul . . . is not the human being.” Isidore considered the etymology of the word in this statement, so that *homo* (“human being”) is said to derive from *humus* (“earth”), which is the body, and not from the soul. He explains this in Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “Properly, *homo* is said from *humus*, but improperly the whole human being is spoken of as composed of both substances, that is, from the union of soul and body. For properly, *homo* is from *humus*.” Likewise, Book II of the *Differences*, chapter 1; and Saint Gregory, Book XII of the *Moralia*, chapter 16: “For by the word ‘human being,’” he says, “the earthly and infirm being is expressed; the human being is called from *humus*.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*: “God,” he says, “made the human being, raised from the earth, upright and lofty.”

Augustine, however, in Book XIX of *The City of God*, chapter 3, resolves this question according to Varro’s opinion: that a human being is properly said to be composed of both substances, soul and body. In *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 4, he said that it is difficult to judge this controversy; or, if it is easy by reason, it is lengthy in speech. Jerome likewise says so in his letter to Damasus, in his exposition of the Creed; and the Master of the Sentences, in Book III, distinction 2, asserts that those who say that “human being” is derived not from substance but from a property are in error.

Our Isidore, however, is explaining the etymology of the word, not the nature of the human being. He is speaking of the outward human being, of whom Paul says in II Corinthians: “Although our outward human being is being corrupted, yet our inward human being is renewed day by day.” L.

Ibid. “Therefore wrongly.” Saint Augustine, in *On Heresies*, chapter 86, attributes this to Tertullian and refutes it in *On the Quantity of the Soul*. Jerome discusses Tertullian—a presbyter of the province of Africa, at first held in high distinction there, but afterward fallen into the shameful heresy of the impostor Montanus and others—in his letter to Magnus the orator; also Nicephorus, Book IV, chapter 34; Vincent of Lérins; and Hilary, in his commentaries on Matthew. L.

Ibid. “Made from earth.” Vezzosius observes that, although what Isidore teaches here with Saint Gregory is not to be rejected, it nevertheless remains certain that the human being is a subject, or person, composed of two natures, soul and body. Even if the human being was called from *humus*, because Genesis says that he was formed from the clay of the earth, certainly the same human being is said to have been made in the image and likeness of God not because he is from earth, as Isidore himself admits, but because he also consists of a soul, which is not from earth. Loaisa had already answered these points on Isidore’s behalf in his note, if it is properly considered. AREV.]

2. The soul of the human being is not the human being; only the body, which was made from earth, is the human being. But by dwelling in the body, the soul received from its participation in the flesh the name of the human being, just as the Apostle says that the inward human being—the soul, not the flesh—was created in the image of God. Therefore some wrongly believe that the soul of the human being is corporeal, since it was made in the image of God so that, even if it were not unchangeable as God is, it might nevertheless be incorporeal as God is.

145 3. Like the angels, souls have a beginning but no end. For some things in the world are temporal, some perpetual, and some eternal. Temporal things are those that have both a beginning and an end; perpetual things are those that have a beginning but no end; eternal things are those that have neither beginning nor end.

[Note: [Col. 0562D]

4. “Not to be a part.” Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Soul*. Likewise Isidore, Book II of the *Differences*, chapter 27, and the First Council of Braga, canon 5. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Of the philosophers, etc.” That the soul is the form of the body was affirmed by the Council of Vienne under Clement V, and by the Lateran Council, session 8, under Julius II and Leo X. Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 13, and Gregory, Book VII of the *Register of Letters*, chapter 33, to Secundinus. In this statement Isidore has gathered together nearly all the heresies concerning the soul, which modern writers refute at length. LOAISA.]

4. It is evident that the soul is not a part of the divine substance or nature, nor does it exist before it is joined to the body; rather, it is created when the body is created, to which it appears to be joined. The opinions of philosophers say that the soul exists before it is born in the body. But no evidence proves this to be true. For whether we existed beforehand, neither do we ourselves know, nor do we have any human being who says so. It should not, therefore, be sought what becomes more ridiculous the more it is sought.

5. Gentiles and heretics attempt to argue about the soul; but how can they think rightly about it, when they do not know its author, in whose image it was made? And so they have said many things worthy of error.

[Note: [Col. 0563C]

6. “Changeable.” Gregory, Book XXV of the *Moralia*, chapter 3; and Augustine, *On the Knowledge of the True Life*, chapter 5. LOAISA.]

6. The soul is changeable, not locally but temporally, through its affections. The body, however, is changeable both in place and in time, because it changes with time and varies according to place. What the change of places is for the body, the mutability of thoughts is for the soul. This variety of evil movement became attached to the mind when the first human being withdrew from contemplation of eternal things and refused to remain in the one from whom he had wrongly withdrawn; and, justly condemned to inconstancy, he was carried away and flowed through the variety of things.

[Note: [Col. 0563D]

7. Some copies have *quod corrumpitur* (“which is corrupted”) instead of *corruptibile* (“corruptible”), and *habitatio* (“dwelling”) instead of *inhabitatio* (“indwelling”). AREV.]

7. The soul possesses much splendor from its own nature, but it is darkened by its mixture with the flesh, within which it is confined. For through a part of it the soul is turned toward the weakness of sin, as Solomon teaches: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks of many things.”

CHAPTER XIII. On the Senses of the Flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0563D]

CHAPTER XIII—No. 1. The Lucensis Codex, omitting the title, continues the chapter as follows: “Through the senses of the flesh the disease creeps into the mind,” etc., as in Book II, chapter 28. AREV.]

1. It is not by strength or by bodily sensation, but by the reasoning of the mind, that we excel the other animals.

[Note: [Col. 0563D]

2. From Augustine, Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 35. LOAISA.

Ibid. “As they excel.” On the various arrangement of the human senses and their preeminence among one another: Galen, *On the Use of the Parts*; Cicero, in the books *On the Nature of the Gods*; Basil and Ambrose, in the *Hexaemeron*; and Gregory, Book XI of the *Moralia*, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

2. The senses of the flesh suffice for using bodily things, but not for grasping spiritual things. Deluded by their use of bodily things, human beings think that nothing exists otherwise than as they apprehend it through the sense of the flesh. Just as bodily senses excel one another through the diversity of their locations, so they excel one another in the power of perception. For just as the sense of smell is superior to taste in the position of its location and in the distance over which it perceives, so the ear is superior to smell. We hear from farther away than we smell; and so the eyes are superior to the ears, for we see from farther away than we hear.

[Note: [Col. 0563D]

3. “Excels.” Aristotle proves this in Book II of *On the Soul*, at the end: “Sight,” he says, “is especially a sense.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “Hence, etc.” The complete statement is from Augustine, Book of Letters, Letter 112. LOAISA.]

3. The mind, however, surpasses all these senses both in place and in excellence. Established in the citadel of the head, it intellectually beholds what those senses cannot bodily reach. The sense of sight excels the other senses still further, since we use it when speaking of what belongs to the other senses, as when we say: “See how it sounds; see how it tastes,” and so forth.

4. As the eye sees other things but does not see itself, so the mind sees the rest but does not contemplate itself. It perceives the origins, forms, and magnitudes of other things; but it is infected with such great ignorance of the truth concerning itself that it contemplates nothing more uncertain than itself among all these things.

[Col. 0564B] [Note: [Col. 0563D]

5. Augustine, *Confessions* X, chapter 8. LOAISA.

Ibid. “And holding them in the mind, etc.” Some copies read: “and the memory of the mind fixing them there.” Augustine discusses these matters excellently in the cited place, *Confessions*, chapters 8 and 9. AREV.]

5. Human being, you who marvel at the height of the stars and the depth of the sea, enter into the abyss of your own mind and marvel, if you can. We contemplate many things while thinking, without the sense of the flesh and without living images, seeing them only in the mind; and, with the memory fixing them in the mind, we retain them. We also understand many things through a sense that we cannot express fully with the tongue.

6. Infants are innocent in deed but not innocent in thought, because they cannot yet carry out in action the movement that they possess in the mind; thus, in them the age is weak, not the mind. The frailty of the body does not yet obey their will at its command; nor can they do as much harm by action as they are moved to do in thought.

[Note: [Col. 0564C]

7. “Thought” (*cogitatio*) is derived from *cogere* (“to compel”), as Augustine teaches in Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 11. Lactantius, Book VI of *On True Worship*: “Thought is nothing other than the movement of the mind.” Aristotle calls it διάνοια (*dianoia*); in irrational animals it is the estimative faculty, and it is placed among the common senses. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Of all things.” Augustine wrote very acutely about memory in Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 8, from which nearly all these statements are drawn; in the same work, chapter 14, he discusses memory as the stomach of the mind; and in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11, he says that it concerns not only past things but also present things. Isidore says the same in Book II of the *Differences*, chapter 21. Aristotle says that it concerns past things (*On Memory and Recollection*), describing it as the recovery of something apprehended by sense or intellect. L.

Ibid. “And the mind.” Augustine proves this in Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 14. LOAISA.]

7. Thought received its name from its cause. For it is called *cogitatio* because it compels the mind to remember what has been entrusted to memory. Memory is the treasury of all things. It is the guardian of things discovered and of things thought; concerning it, however, it is difficult to discuss anything exhaustively, because its complexity is great—and the mind itself is that memory.

[Note: [Col. 0564D]

8. Aristotle, in Book I of *On Memory and Recollection*, expressing the nature of the image, says: “Just as a painted animal on a panel is both an animal and an image, and although it is one and the same thing, it is both, yet the account by which it is considered as an animal and as an image is different, so we must judge of the phantasm that is in us: it is both something in itself and simultaneously a likeness of something else. For insofar as it is viewed in itself and separately, it is a spectacle and appearance; but insofar as it is referred to something else, it is an image and memorial.” These observations on the nature of the image according to Aristotle are especially useful for understanding this passage, for unraveling the question of the veneration of images against the heresies of our own time, and finally for explaining the true opinion of Saint Thomas. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Blessedness.” The printed editions have *similitudinem* (“likeness”), but the Gothic manuscript has *beatitudinem* (“blessedness”), as do other manuscript codices. I have adopted this reading, led by the authority of Augustine, Book X of the *Confessions*, chapter 21, where he proves that we remember things of which we have never had an image, such as blessedness and joy. Further on, in chapter 25, when asking at what level of memory God is found, he says: “For it is not a bodily image, nor an affection of a living being, such as when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, or forget.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “We remember.” Some copies read *rememoramus* (“we remember again”). The note had *vi beatitudinis*, instead of *ut beatitudinis* (“as blessedness”). AREV.]

8. An image removed from bodily senses leaves in the memory a likeness of its form. But we remember blessedness not through images, as we do other things, but like joy, without an image. When we remember forgetfulness, it is not present through itself. If it were present through itself, we would certainly not be forgetful.

148 [Note: [Col. 0565D]

9. “Common.” Aristotle proves this in *On Memory and Recollection*.]

9. Memory is common to human beings and animals, but no understanding is present in irrational animals; it is found only in the human being endowed with reason. For in the others, in the very quality of their consideration, it is the sense of the flesh, not the intelligence of the mind.

CHAPTER XIV. On Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0565D]

CHAPTER XIV—No. 1. The entire statement is from Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX, chapter 1. On the twofold birth of Christ, however, Lactantius discusses the matter elegantly in Book IV of *On True Wisdom*, chapter 8; and Damascene, Book III of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 7. L.

Ibid. Taio discusses these matters in Book I, chapter 5, and, although in nearly reversed order, pursues substantially the same arguments found in Isidore. AREV.]

1. The perfect birth of the Son of God neither began to be nor ceased to be, lest it be past if it ceased, or imperfect if it is still taking place. Rather, just as it is eternal, so also it is perfect, since in that birth eternity and perfection are both present.

[Col. 0565B] 2. From the Virgin’s womb Christ is said to be less than the Father, namely according to the humanity he assumed, not according to his divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0565D]

3. “And in the form, etc.” Some copies have: “and in the form of a servant, the Lord of human beings.” [Col. 0566C] “Christ in the form of a servant is Lord because of the excellence of his conception,” etc. AREV.]

3. Christ is both a servant in the form of a servant and not a servant in the form of a servant. For in the form of a servant he is the servant of the Lord; in the form of a servant he is Lord of all. Christ in the form of a servant is Lord of all because of the excellence of his conception: although he assumed flesh, he did not assume it through the lustful contagion of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0566C]

4. “Mediator.” From Gregory, Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 27. Augustine, *Meditations*, chapter 16. LOAISA.

Ibid. “But in both natures.” Vezzosius did not wish to omit the words with which Damascene, in the cited passage, explains this Christian dogma, as Loaisa has cited them. They are as follows: “Therefore, even after assuming humanity, we confess that he is one Son of God, and the same Son of Man; one Christ, one Lord, one only-begotten Son, and the Word of God, Jesus our Lord.” AREV.]

4. The man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings, is not one person in his humanity and another in his divinity, but the same one person in both natures. He was not conceived as a mere human being, nor born as a mere human being, nor did he later receive the merit of becoming God. Rather, God the Word, while his unchangeable essence—which he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit and which is coeternal with them—remained unchanged, assumed flesh for the salvation of humanity. In that flesh the impassible could be shown to suffer, the immortal to die, and the eternal before the ages to be temporal.

[Note: [Col. 0566D]

5. “Mediator.” From Gregory, as above. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Nor of the natures.” Some copies have *nec naturae* (“nor of the nature”), and similarly a little later. AREV.]

5. The man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings, although one thing is from the Father and another from the Virgin, is nevertheless not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin. Rather, the same person is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; the same person who made all things is the one who was made; the same person is from the Father without a mother and from the mother without a father; the same person is the temple of the Creator and the Creator of the temple; the same person is the author of the work and the work of the Author. Remaining one person from both sources and in both natures, he is neither confused by the joining of the natures nor divided into two by their distinction.

6. God came in man because he could not be known by human beings through himself. But from the very means by which he came to our aid he suffered contempt, because proud humanity despised the weakness that he assumed for our sake. For this reason he chose the weak and foolish things of the world, so that he might confound the stronger and wiser, through whom he was not known.

[Note: [Col. 0566D]

7. This is found in some manuscripts. This comparison is drawn from Paul, 1 Corinthians 3, Hebrews 5, and 1 Peter 2. LOAISA.

The same place. After this sentence the Luc. manuscript adds: “we shall be satisfied.” The humility of Christ came to the aid of the devil’s pride. But those who imitated the devil despised the humble God. God, however, chose humble and despised things by which to confound the strong, so that, because the proud were not converted through God’s humility, the power of miracles might increase. When the proud saw it, they were astonished, and, confounded, were converted. “The first gifts of God are,” etc. AREV.]

7. Just as a weak infant cannot take strong food unless it is first eaten by its mother and changed into the nourishment of milk, so that what it could not use as food it may drink by suckling milk through the flesh, so also, while we were weak for contemplating the eternity of the Word, the Word itself became flesh. Thus, nourished through the flesh and made stronger, by contemplating the solid food—that is, the word of the Lord, eternal with the Father—we may be satisfied like the angels.

8. [The first gifts of God are those] by which he shows us that we are guilty. While we lay under the guilt of sin, we believed ourselves to be righteous. The physician came, exposed the wound, applied himself as the remedy, and prepared medicine for us from his own death, so that he might be not merely the one who exposed the wound, but also its healer.

9. Christ first came to Israel, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.” He came first to the people of Israel, but the prophet did not remain silent about the fact that they would not believe, saying: “The First One will say to Zion: ‘Here I am,’ and I will give Jerusalem an evangelist. And I looked, and there was no one; nor did anyone arise who would take counsel and, when questioned, give an answer.” But because he passed over to the Gentiles, it follows: “Behold my servant; I will receive him, my chosen one, in whom my soul has been well pleased. I have given my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the Gentiles.”

[Col. 0567A] [Note: [Col. 0567C]

10. From Gregory, *Moralia* 33, chapters 7 and 9. LOAISA.]

10. Although the devil did not know the order of our liberation, he nevertheless knew that Christ had come for the salvation of humanity; but he did not know that Christ would redeem us by his death. Therefore he killed him. For if he had known that Christ would redeem the human race through his death, he certainly would not have slain him.

11. That the devil knew Christ had come for the salvation of the human race is taught by the testimony of the Gospel. When he saw him, he was terrified because he recognized him, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?”

[Note: [Col. 0567C]

12. Gregory, *Moralia* 3, chapter 11. LOAISA.]

12. Just as Christ did not admit sin, which deserves punishment, so he accepted the punishment of our sin, in order by his undeserved punishment to abolish our deserved guilt. Through this the devil lost those whom he held guilty, when he killed one who had committed no sin. Therefore he lost those whom he had held as though justly, because he unjustly killed our Redeemer.

[Note: [Col. 0567C]

13. *Innox.* In the same way below, chapter 27: “The innocent one is consumed by God,” etc.; and shortly afterward: “The innocent one and the impious are consumed.” Also in the *Etymologies*, book 10: *Innox*, “one who does no harm.” And in the Glossary: *innox*, ἀβλαβής, “harmless.” LOAISA.

The same place. *Innox.* Some, unfamiliar with Isidorian style, substituted *innoxius* (“harmless”), as has also happened elsewhere. AREV.]

13. The devil was deceived by the Lord’s death, like a bird. When Christ displayed the mortality of his flesh, which the devil desired to destroy, he concealed his divinity, so that he might ensnare the devil—as an unwary bird—with a cunning trap. For if the innocent Christ had not been killed, the human being delivered over to the devil through transgression would not have been freed.

151 [Note: [Col. 0567C]

14. From Gregory, *Moralia* 33, chapter 7. LOAISA.

The same place. “As with a hook.” Thus it appears in all the manuscripts. I accept this reading, guided by Gregory’s testimony, *Moralia* 33, chapter 10: “Like a hook, it held the throat of the one swallowing; for in him there was both the bait of flesh, which the devourer desired to consume, and the divinity, hidden at the time of the passion, which would harm him.” LOAISA.

The same place. “For there is in Christ.” From the same Gregory, *Moralia* 33, chapter 12, where he expounds the passage from Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” Ezekiel also had foretold this, chapter 32: “I will draw you out with my hook and stretch you over the earth.” And Habakkuk 1: “He lifted everything up with a hook; he dragged it in his net.” LOAISA.]

14. While the devil attacked the human flesh in Christ, which was visible, he himself was caught, like a man, by Christ’s divinity, which was hidden. For in Christ the hook is divinity; the bait is flesh; and the line is the genealogy recited from the Gospel. God the Father holds this line, as the Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God.” Luke, weaving the line of Christ’s generation from the lowest to the highest, begins with Joseph and brings it to completion in God, saying: “Who was of Heli”; and, completing the line of his ancestry, he says: “Who was of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0567D]

15. This refutes the heresy of those who said that the Lord descended into hell and drew out and saved everyone there who confessed him. Gregory rejects this in *Letters* 6, letter 179. LOAISA.

The same place. “Not under punishment.” Isidore explains more clearly in the following sections whom Christ freed when he descended to the lower regions. AREV.]

15. For this reason the Lord descended into hell: to open for those who were being held there without punitive suffering a way of returning to heaven, according to the testimony of Isaiah, who says: “You made the depth of the sea a way, so that the redeemed might cross.” Christ made a way in the depths of the sea when, descending into hell, he showed the saints the path of returning to heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0567D]

16. The entire meaning and sequence of the passage is found in Gregory, *Moralia* 4, chapter 32. LOAISA.

The same place. Concerning the twofold hell, Gregory says in *Moralia* 12, chapter 7: “Yet we do not say that the souls of the righteous descended into hell in such a way that they were held in places of punishment. Rather, it must be believed that some places of hell are higher and others lower, so that the righteous might rest in the higher places and the unrighteous be tormented in the lower. Hence the Psalmist, Psalm 85, because of the grace of God that preceded him, says: ‘You have rescued my soul from the lower hell.’” L.]

16. From the time of Christ’s resurrection, the saints immediately ascend to their heavenly dwelling as soon as they depart from the body—a privilege not granted to the ancient Fathers. For before the Savior’s coming, although the souls of the saints were held without the punishment of suffering, they were held not in heaven but in hell; and the Lord descended into hell to free them.

[Note: [Col. 0568C]

17. “At the completion of the age.” Bignaeus adds other words in parentheses, noting that they are absent from the Vulgate edition but present in manuscript copies. They are as follows: “Here perhaps someone may ask what is meant by what is read: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ How is the ascent into heaven promised to human beings, and especially when he himself says, ‘Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me,’ if he alone ascended into heaven? But if you join the members to the head, Christ is one in himself and in us. Therefore it is rightly said that he alone ascended, because we too are to ascend in him.” These words certainly exist in the ancient Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark, which is older than the eleventh century. AREV.]

17. When ascending into heaven, Christ departed in the flesh, but he remains present in majesty, according to what he said: “Behold, I am with you until the completion of the age.”

[Note: [Col. 0568D]

18. Gregory, *Moralia* 2, chapter 21: “God’s right hand signifies the chosen portion of the angels, while God’s left hand signifies the reprobate portion of the angels.” Isidore says the same in book 2 of *The Ecclesiastical Offices*. LOAISA.

The same place. Fulgentius also discusses the right hand of the Father in divine matters, in Vezzosius, who recorded several observations on this subject on page 265 of volume 4 of the *Theological Institutes*, drawing from Saint Augustine, chapter 7 of *On Faith and the Creed*. AREV.]

18. Christ sits at the right hand of the Father—not because the Father has a bodily right hand, but because the Father’s right hand is blessedness, just as the left hand is misery.

# CHAPTER XV. On the Holy Spirit

[Note: [Col. 0568D]

Chapter 15, note 1. From Saint Augustine, *Letter to Donatus* 106. LOAISA.

The same place. Taio collected sayings on the Holy Spirit in book 1, chapter 6. Theodulf, who frequently cites Isidore’s authority in his work *On the Holy Spirit*, also gives this passage; he reads *inspiraculum* instead of *spiraculum*. AREV.]

1. The Holy Spirit is creator, like the Father and the Word, as the prophet testifies: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life.”

2. The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son. The Father and the Son are therefore one, because the Father has nothing that the Son does not have. For one thing, consubstantial with two, cannot proceed from them and exist in them simultaneously unless those from whom it proceeds are one. The Church received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, so that through him believers might become one body, through whom the Father and the Son are essentially one, as the Savior himself says to the Father: “That they may be one, just as we are one.”

[Note: [Col. 0569C]

3. This passage is found in Isaiah 48. Jerome says of the same passage: “In a brief verse he shows us the mystery of the Trinity.” LOAISA.]

3. Christ testifies that he was sent not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: “Draw near to me and hear this: From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; from the time before it happened, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0569C]

4. Cyprian likewise says in his little work *On the Holy Spirit*: “Be present, Holy Spirit, and descend from heaven upon those awaiting your consolation.” Isidore says the same in *Etymologies* 7, chapter 3. LOAISA.

The same place. One Gothic manuscript has: “When the Holy Spirit reveals.” The other manuscripts agree with the printed edition. LOAISA.]

4. The Holy Spirit is called Paraclete because he is a comforter. For in Latin *paraclesis* means “consolation.” And truly, while distributing the gifts of the sacraments, he provides consolation to the soul. I believe that whoever learns something through the revelation of God’s Spirit experiences great joy.

[Note: [Col. 0569C]

5. From Augustine’s treatises on John, and Gregory, *Moralia* 24, chapter 10. LOAISA.

The same place. John 1: “Full of grace and truth.” The Vulgate edition has *plenum gratiae et veritatis*, “full of grace and truth.” Some read πλήρης, that is, *plenae*—“full of grace and truth,” with *plenae* understood. L.]

5. The gift of the Holy Spirit is distributed individually among the members of the Church, and individual gifts are granted to individuals. Christ, however, possessed the whole fullness of graces, of whom it is written: “Full of grace and truth.” In Christ, therefore, there is the entire fullness of graces. For individual gifts are granted to each of the elect.

[Note: [Col. 0569C]

6. Paul, 1 Corinthians 12, and Galatians. LOAISA.]

6. Every grace of gifts resides in the Holy Spirit. For he distributes the grace of gifts as he wills, giving to some a word of wisdom, to others knowledge, to others faith. Thus, through the power of the Holy Spirit, the distribution of graces is granted to each person, while the same one is possessed in all. For he also teaches ineffable things that human speech cannot express.

[Note: [Col. 0569C]

7. I think this was drawn from Tertullian, *On the Trinity*. “Thus,” he says, “the Spirit is one and the same, who was in the prophets and in the apostles, except that there he was present for a time, while here he is always. In the former case, he was not present in them perpetually; here, he remains always in them. There he was distributed in moderation; here, he was poured out in his entirety.” He then adduces the testimony of the prophet Joel, as Isidore does. LOAISA.

The same place. Joel 2; and it is found in Acts 2, where Peter says: “And it shall be in the last days: I will pour out,” etc. Joel has: “And it shall be, after this, I will pour out.” Jerome, in his Commentary on Joel, citing the passage from Acts 2, reads: “And it shall be after this” (καὶ ἔσται μετὰ ταῦτα), as it is in Joel. Isaiah expressed the same meaning more clearly in chapter 44: “I will pour out water upon the thirsty, and rivers upon the dry ground; I will pour out my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessing upon your offspring, and they shall spring up among the grass like willows beside flowing waters.” This is Isaiah.

But where Joel says, “before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes,” Acts 2 says: “before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes.” Thus the Complutensian Greek reads. The edition of the Bible translates τὴν μεγάλην καὶ ἐπιφανῆ as “great and illustrious.” The translator of Theophylact on the Acts of the Apostles has: “before that great and illustrious day of the Lord comes.” In the Hebrew text it is called “terrible”; in the Septuagint version, “illustrious.” Jerome thinks that this day is either the resurrection or, certainly after many ages, the day of judgment, which will truly be great and terrible. LOAISA.]

7. Before the Lord’s coming, only the prophets and a few righteous people from the whole population were found worthy of the gift of the Holy Spirit. After the Lord’s coming, however, the Holy Spirit was distributed to all believers, according to what the Lord says through the prophet: “And it shall be in the last days: I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” For now the grace of the Holy Spirit has been given to all nations—not to a few, as among the people of Israel, but the grace of the Holy Spirit remains among the entire multitude of believers.

[Note: [Col. 0570C]

8. Thus Tertullian has it in *On the Soul*: “Finally, the Spirit of God afterward changed Saul into another man, that is, into a prophet, when it was said: ‘What has happened to this son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?’ The evil spirit likewise afterward changed him into another man.” This is clearly found in 1 Samuel 10. The causes of Saul’s condemnation are given by Gregory, *Moralia* 34, chapter 15: namely, because he swelled with the arrogance of suspected authority, as is clear from the divine rebuke in 1 Samuel 15. Nor is he truly excused by the Jews through ambiguity of the word, as Sixtus of Siena noted in his *Bibliotheca*, book 3, and as others have noted concerning 1 Samuel. Augustine, in book 17 of *The City of God*, most elegantly interprets the disruption of the kingdom of Israel in the person of Saul. L.

The same place. “And Balaam.” Tertullian, *Against Marcion* 4, and Gregory, *On Ezekiel* 1, homily 10; Origen, *Homilies on Numbers* 13, affirm that Balaam left behind books of his divinations. The Apocalypse, chapter 10, reports his teaching. LOAISA.

The same place. The manuscripts have “they will say to the Lord.” The passage is Matthew 7: “In your name we performed many miracles.” What follows, “I do not know where you are from,” is found in Luke 13: “Wherever you may be.” The manuscripts have the wording as Luke himself does. LOAISA.

In Loaisa’s note one might perhaps read “then the Spirit of God,” with *inquit*—“he says”—removed. AREV.]

8. Sometimes the gifts of the Holy Spirit are granted to those who are unworthy and reprobate, as prophecy was given to Saul and to Balaam. Hence many will say at the end: “Lord, we performed miracles in your name”; and the Lord will say to them: “I do not know where you are from.”

[Note: [Col. 0570D]

9. “As Job.” Gregory proves this in *Moralia* 14, chapter 29, from the words: “For I know that my Redeemer lives.” LOAISA.

The same place. “As Balaam.” Numbers 24: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a staff shall arise from Israel.” Cyprian explains this passage in his work *Against the Jews* and in the little work *On the Star and the Magi*, at the beginning. LOAISA.]

9. The holy prophets who awaited Christ’s coming were not only among the Jewish people; there were also many holy men among the nations who possessed the gift of prophecy. Christ was revealed to them through the Holy Spirit, and they awaited his coming, as did Job and Balaam, who certainly proclaimed Christ’s advent.

155 [Note: [Col. 0570D]

10. As Paul has it in Ephesians 3: “What was not made known to other generations of the children of men has now been revealed: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel.” In Acts 10, concerning the conversion of Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian cohort, it is said that the faithful from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished because the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the nations. And in chapter 11, they said to Peter: “Why did you enter among men having foreskins?” When they heard Peter, they fell silent and glorified God, saying: “Then God has also granted repentance unto life to the Gentiles.” Gregory, *Moralia* 10, chapter 38, proves that the calling of the Gentiles had been hidden from ancient times in God’s plan. On the calling of the Gentiles, see Isidore’s elegant little work. LOAISA.

The words of Habakkuk are reported in a very different way in the Vulgate. Compare chapter 17 of book 1 of *Against the Jews*. AREV.]

10. The conversion of the Gentiles was hidden from the ancient people, but it was nevertheless in God’s plan that it should occur. At that time the coming of Christ was secretly proclaimed by the holy prophets through the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: “When the years have approached, you will be known; when the time has come, you will be revealed.” Now what was then hidden from the carnal is openly revealed, while it was known to the spiritual; yet it was not then stated openly, because the time of manifestation had not arrived.

# CHAPTER XVI. On the Church and Heresies
