[Note: [Col. 0571C]

Chapter 16, note 1. From Saint Gregory, *Moralia* 9, chapter 9. LOAISA.]

1. The Church has a twofold beauty: one that she acquires here by living well; the other by which she will there be glorified through recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0571C]

2. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.]

2. Because of Christ, the Church undergoes a twofold tribulation: either that which she endured from pagans in her martyrs, or that which she endures from heretics in various conflicts. By God’s grace she overcomes both—partly by enduring and partly by resisting.

[Note: [Col. 0571C]

3. It is an error to say that every sinner is outside the Church. See Turrecremata, *On the Church*; Melchior Canus, Bellarmine, and others. AREV.]

3. The holy Catholic Church patiently tolerates within herself those who live badly, but she drives away from herself those who believe wrongly.

[Note: [Col. 0571C]

4. In Gregory, *Moralia* 18, chapters 3 and 19, and chapter 8. L.

The same place. “Now.” These words occur in no manuscript. Nevertheless, I think they should be retained, since they are found in the old printed edition and in Gregory, who says in *Moralia* 18, chapter 1: “The holy Church earnestly strives to possess wisdom and patience; but her wisdom is exercised when she is tested by swords.” He is now speaking of that persecution in which she is attacked not with swords but with false assertions. Thus far Gregory. LOAISA.]

4. The holy Church earnestly strives to oppose wisdom and patience to the obstinacy of pagans and heretics. But her wisdom is exercised when she is tested by words; her patience is exercised when she is tested by swords. For now she is attacked by persecutions, and now she is harassed by false assertions.

[Note: [Col. 0571D]

5. Gregory likewise, *Letters* 7, in his letter to Anastasius, indiction 1. Leander, the most holy bishop of Seville and Isidore’s brother, most elegantly portrayed the growth of the Church while she is harassed by heretics, in a homily delivered at the Third Council of Toledo during the conversion of the Gothic people. I possess it, but it has not yet been printed. LOAISA.

The same place. “More clearly.” Augustine, in his treatise on the harmony of Matthew and Luke: “Heretics,” he says, “are useful for discovering the truth, since by their slander they provoke people toward error; for the truth would be sought less diligently if it did not have lying adversaries.” LOAISA.

The homily of Saint Leander, which Loaisa rightly praises, was published by him in *The Councils of Spain* and was later reprinted in several other collections of councils. AREV.]

5. The Church’s teaching was expanded because of the perversity of heretics; previously it flourished only through simple faith. Thus, on account of heretics, teachers in the faith were multiplied, and through the subtleties of heresies the Church’s teachers increased. For the assertion of truth is manifested more clearly when some disagreement has become evident.

[Note: [Col. 0572B]

6. Pacianus explained what the word “Catholic” means in his first letter to Sempronianus, as did Vincent of Lérins, the Gaul, in that golden little work *Against Heresies*. Clement of Alexandria, in book 7 of the *Stromata*, says that there is one Catholic Church; but the church of the heretics—or rather, their conventicles—is neither one nor Catholic. For heresies divide this unity into multiplicity. Some are named after a person, such as those of Valentinus, Marcion, and Basilides; some after a place, such as the Peratics; some after a people, such as the heresy of the Phrygians; some after a practice, such as that of the Encratites; and some after their distinctive doctrines, such as the Docetists and the Haematites, and so forth. In this passage one may observe vividly the various names of the heresies of our own time, and the uncertain, mutually conflicting sects into which the insane and uneducated crowd is divided. LOAISA.

The same place. Romans 1: “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” Cyprian calls the Roman Church strong in faith because it was founded upon the chair of Peter and in his unity, in his work *On the Unity of the Church*. Augustine taught that the marks of the Catholic Church are found in the Roman Church, in his book *Against the Letter of the Manichaeans*, chapter 4: “There are many things,” he says, “that most justly hold me in the bosom of the Church. The agreement of peoples and nations holds me; the authority begun by miracles, nourished by hope, increased by charity, and strengthened by antiquity holds me; the succession of priests from the very see of the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord, after his resurrection, entrusted his sheep to be fed, down to the present episcopate holds me; finally, the very name ‘Catholic’ holds me, which, not without reason, among so many heresies this one Church alone has retained.” Thus Augustine. LOAISA.]

6. The holy Church is called Catholic because she is spread universally throughout the whole world. The churches of the heretics are confined to particular regions of the world, whereas this Church, spread throughout the entire earth, extends everywhere, as the apostle Paul testifies: “I give thanks,” he says, “to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.” Heresies, however, are found operating in some corner of the world or among a single people. The Catholic Church, just as she extends throughout the whole world, is likewise built from the fellowship of all nations.

[Note: [Col. 0572D]

7. *Heresy* is derived from *election*, as Jerome testifies in his letter on Galatians 5. Clement of Alexandria likewise says in book 7 of the *Stromata*: “Heresy is an election.” Tertullian says the same in *The Prescription Against Heretics*. Cyprian gives an elegant description of heretics in *On the Unity of the Church*. Among other things he says: “These are the people who, of their own accord, appoint themselves over rash assemblies without divine disposition; who establish themselves as leaders without any rule of ordination; who, although no one grants them the episcopate, assume for themselves the name of bishops.” And farther on: “The Lord again designates and brands these same people, saying: ‘They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.’” Augustine, in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, to Honoratus, chapter 1: “A heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—especially empty glory and the desire for pre-eminence—either generates or follows false and novel opinions.” We have a living image of this in these calamitous times. LOAISA.]

7. Who are heretics except those who, abandoning the Church of God, have chosen private associations? Of them the Lord says: “My people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves shattered cisterns that cannot hold water.”

[Note: [Col. 0573C]

8. So Paul says in 1 Corinthians 11: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may also become manifest among you.” Tertullian, *Against Heresies*, at the beginning: “Heresies,” he says, “have been produced for the sickness and destruction of the faith.” LOAISA.

The same place. Clement of Alexandria, in book 7 of the *Stromata*, and Tertullian, in *The Prescription Against Heretics*, teach most elegantly that heresies arose from the obscurity of truth. Augustine gives various accounts of the origin and development of heresies. In *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, he says that heresies arose from pride: “Pride,” he says, “is the mother of all heretics.” In the *Eighty-Three Questions*, he says that they flow from a false understanding of Scripture: “Error could not arise under the cloak of the Christian name unless it arose from Scriptures that were not understood.” See Jerome on Galatians 5; this is also found in *Question* 3, chapter “Heresy.” He calls a heretic one who understands Scripture differently from what the sense of the Spirit demands. Hilary says: “Heresy arises from interpretation, not from Scripture; sense, not wording, creates the crime.” Tertullian, in *The Prescription Against Heretics*, teaches that heresies arose from philosophy: “Indeed,” he says, “heresies are furnished by philosophy.” LOAISA.

The same place. “Nor can they exist,” etc. These words are obscure, and perhaps some words are missing. AREV.]

8. For what reason does heresy arise? For the exercise of faith. The path by which it arises, however, is the obscurity of the divine Scriptures, in which heretics, groping in darkness, understand things differently from the way they are. Nor can they exist, because in the very fact that they exist as heresies, they already do not exist. By thinking wrongly they do not acquire knowledge; they are heading toward nothingness.

158

9. Heretics learn their lies with immense zeal and struggle with great labor, lest they come to the unity of the Church. Concerning them the prophet appropriately says: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies, and they have labored to act wickedly.”

[Note: [Col. 0574C]

10. Innocent III expressed the same idea elegantly: they have different faces, but their tails are tied together, because they agree among themselves in the same matter. This is found in *On Heresy*, book 5, chapter “We Have Excommunicated.” L.

The same place. “They exist as one.” Another reading is “they exist united,” which seems clearer. AREV.]

10. Although heretics tear one another apart when they lead one another into their own sects, they nevertheless clash with one another in such a way that they fight against the Church with an equal spirit of error. Though divided among themselves, they stand united in opposition to the Church. To those who think that heresies possess truth because they appear to be so powerful, one must respond: Diseases are not to be preferred to health merely because they often occupy the world so generally that they leave little room for health.

11. It is clear that heretics cannot obtain forgiveness except through the Catholic Church, just as Job’s friends could not appease God for themselves unless Job had offered sacrifice on their behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0574D]

12. The printed editions read “through Jeremiah,” but I have corrected it to “Isaiah,” in agreement with all the manuscripts and with the truth. The passage is Isaiah 57. From Saint Gregory, *Moralia* 35, chapter 7. LOAISA.

The same place. A similar confusion of names, in which one prophet is substituted for another, is noted more than once in the books *Against the Jews*. This can easily be gathered from Mariana’s annotations. AREV.]

12. The good works that heretics perform, and their righteousness, profit them nothing, as the Lord testifies through Isaiah: “Because you have forgotten me, behold, I will announce your righteousness, and your works will not profit you.”

13. Although heretics fulfill the Law and the Prophets, because they are not Catholics, God is nevertheless not present in their assemblies, as the Lord himself testifies: “Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul would not be toward this people. Cast them out from my presence, and let them depart.” Through Moses, understand the Law, and through Samuel the Prophets. Although heretics strive to fulfill these in their works, because of the impiety of their error they are nevertheless cast away from God’s presence and separated from the assemblies of the righteous.

14. A pagan and a heretic: the former has never been with the people of God; the latter has withdrawn from the people of God. Both, having departed from Christ, belong to the body of the devil.

15. Those who pass from idolatry to Judaism or heresy have, according to the prophet, gone out from evil into evil, and they have not known the Lord, because they have passed from the error of unbelief into another error.

[Note: [Col. 0574D]

16. The righteous have various designations in the divine writings. They are called “sons of God,” as John 8 called those “gods” to whom the word of God came. John 1: “He gave them power to become sons of God.” Romans 5: “Into the hope of the glory of the sons of God”; and chapter 8: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God.” In Genesis 6, those are called “sons of God” who, in faith in the one Most High God and in his worship, virtue, piety, and observance, greatly surpass the other mortals devoted to their bellies, who lead impious and lawless lives and are idolaters. Hence, by excellence, they are called “sons of God.” Our Lord Christ is called the Son of the Most High God by nature, but the righteous are called sons by the grace of adoption.

The righteous are also called by other names: “sons of the resurrection” in Luke 20; “sons of the kingdom” in Mark 13; “sons of the bridechamber” in Mark 2; “sons of the bridegroom” in Luke 5; “sons of peace” in Luke 10; and “sons of light” in Luke 16 and John 20. Justin Martyr, Josephus the Hebrew, Tertullian, and Lactantius Firmianus believe that the angels in Genesis 6 were called “sons of God.” Theodoretus vigorously refutes this opinion in his *Questions on Genesis*, question 47. He interprets the passage about Enos in Genesis 4—“He began to call upon the name of the Lord”—according to Aquila’s version: “Then he first began to be called by the name of the Lord.” These words seem to mean that, through his piety, Enos was the first to acquire the divine name, so that his relatives called him “god”; subsequently, his descendants were called “sons of God,” just as we are called Christians from Christ. Thus Theodoretus. LOAISA.]

16. Everyone is called the son of the one whose teaching he follows. Thus, through the prophet, the Lord calls the Amorite a father and the Hittite a mother of Israel—not by birth, but by imitation. Likewise, in the better sense, those who keep God’s commandments are called sons of God. Therefore we too, not by nature but by adoption, cry out to God, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

17. People can be called someone’s children not only by birth but also by imitation. Thus the Jews are, according to the flesh, children of Abraham, but according to their conduct they are called children of the devil. Consequently, those are the seed of Abraham who imitate his faith, not those who were begotten from his flesh.

18. Both the name and the guilt are derived by some from the author of an error, so that a person is designated by the name of the one whose error he follows. Thus it is said to the church of Pergamum in the Apocalypse: “You have those who hold the teaching of Balaam and of Jezebel.” The church of Thyatira is therefore said to have the teaching of Balaam because of imitation, not because of his bodily presence.

160 # CHAPTER XVII. On the Gentiles

[Col. 0575A]

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

Chapter 17, note 1. Gregory, *Moralia* 25, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

1. The philosophers of the Gentiles, because they did not seek God as they ought, fell in with transgressing angels. The devil became their mediator unto death, just as Christ is ours unto life.

2. The philosophers of the world are greatly praised for their accounts of the dimensions of time, the courses of the stars, and the investigation of the elements. Yet they received this knowledge from God alone. For, flying proudly like birds, they described the air; plunging into the depths like fish, the sea; and walking like animals, the earth. Nevertheless, with their whole mind they refused to understand their Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

3. Romans 1: “They became futile in their thoughts.” L.]

3. Why can they not question brute animals? Because they do not know how to reason. For this reason the Gentiles became like animals: failing to consider such matters and loving the animals themselves even more, they became futile, to the point of worshiping them.

4. Christ is the way; if someone does not walk in it, there is no way for him to come to God. The philosophers of the world certainly knew God, but because Christ’s humility displeased them, they passed along a pathless way rather than on the way. Therefore, becoming futile, they exchanged the glory of God for a lie. Abandoning the straightness of the way, they fell into the winding paths of error.

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

5. “He does not know”—perhaps one should read “let him not know.” AREV.]

5. The first thing for each person is to know what he desires; the second is to obtain what he desires. It is imperfect wisdom to know where you are heading but not to know the road by which it is best to travel. For what benefit is there if, in a time of famine, someone sees a fertile region but does not know the road by which to reach it? Behold, everyone seeks his homeland, but whoever has lost the way walks by wandering rather than by advancing; and the farther he walks, the more he is separated from what he seeks.

6. Whoever abandons the royal way—that is, Christ—even if he sees the truth, sees it from afar, because there is no way to approach it except by the way. But if, walking through the desert, he encounters a lion, he should blame himself when he becomes caught in the devil’s jaws.

# CHAPTER XVIII. On the Law

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the Law

**Chapter XVIII, Note 1.** After this sentence, the Luculian Codex adds: “The way by which one goes to God is the reading of the holy Scriptures. Therefore, whoever wishes to know God should seek the way of Sacred Scripture, through which he may find wisdom. For through it God is understood, through it he is sought, and through it also one arrives at participation in his contemplation.” AREV.]

1. The way by which one goes to Christ is the law; by it those who understand it as they should go to God.

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

2. This occurs in Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXX, chapter 15, where he interprets the passage in Job 39: “He searches out the mountains for his pasture and seeks every green thing.” LOAISA.]

2. The heights of the holy Scriptures are like mountains of pasture (Psalm 6). When each of the righteous climbs them, he rejoices that he has found the refreshment of unfailing pasture.

[Col. 0576B] [Note: [Col. 0576C]

3. This idea is found in Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 103: “The high mountains are for the stags; the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.” Augustine reads: “The rock is a refuge for goats and hares.” The blessed Jerome considers this passage in his commentary on Ezekiel, Book XIII, chapter 43: “The goat,” he says, “is an animal that is always hastening toward high places and suffers no danger on precipices; there it finds a way where other animals find destruction. Hence, in the Greek language, a herd of goats is called the lofty way of life, that is, αἰπόλιον, as though from αἰποπόλιον, since αἰπο signifies ‘high’ and πόλιον ‘way of life.’” [Col. 0576D] The same author writes to Demetrias: “Thus I have set my feet upon the rock, and the rock is a refuge for hares; for this many read ‘hedgehogs,’ a small and timid animal weighed down by the prickles of thorns.” And to Sunia he says that *sephanim* is an animal no larger than a hedgehog, resembling a mouse and a bear, and called in Palestine ἀρκτόμῦν (“bear-mouse”); there is a great abundance of them in that region, and they always live in caves of rocks and hollows in the ground. This is from Jerome. Others read “rabbit.” LOAISA.]

3. In the holy Scriptures, as in lofty mountains, perfect men possess sublime understandings, by which they raise the steps of contemplation like stags; while the simple, like small animals, find modest understandings to which they themselves, in humility, may flee for refuge.

4. Sacred Scripture appears humble in its words to the weak and those of limited understanding, when read according to the historical sense; but with more excellent men it advances more deeply, as it discloses its mysteries to them. Thus it remains common to both: to the simple and to the perfect.

[Note: [Col. 0576D]

5. Gregory, *Morals*, Book I, chapter 21, and Augustine, Book I on the literal interpretation of Genesis, final chapter. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “According to the sense.” Gregory proves this in Homily 10 on Ezekiel, Book I, and in Homily 6: “What else,” he says, “does the wheel signify except Sacred Scripture, which turns on every side toward the minds of its hearers?” LOAISA.

On the same passage, Gregory, Book I on Ezekiel, Homily 6, and Book XXXI of the *Morals*, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

5. Sacred Scripture varies according to the understanding of each reader, like the manna that gave the ancient people different flavors according to each person’s pleasure. The Lord’s discourse corresponds to the capacity of each person’s understanding. Although it is different for each person’s comprehension, it nevertheless remains one in itself.

[Note: [Col. 0576D]

6. Gregory, *Morals*, Book I, chapter 21. LOAISA.

[Col. 0577B] On the same passage, “They provide exercise.” Others read, “They provide desire.” AREV.]

6. For this reason, some things are found obscure and others clear in the sacred books, so that the reader’s understanding and diligence may increase. If everything were exposed, what was immediately understood would quickly become worthless. On the other hand, if everything remained closed, it would promptly produce distrust. Therefore, lest despair arise from obscure things, what is manifest satisfies; and lest weariness arise from what has been understood, what is closed awakens desire. For very many things, the more they remain hidden, the more exercise they provide.

[Note: [Col. 0577B]

7. Gregory discusses the use of the past and future tense in *Morals*, Book XXXIV, chapter 3; Augustine in *On the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 2, in Book IV on Numbers, and in his exposition of Psalm 103; and Tertullian in Book III against Marcion. That this change of tense is frequent in the divine writings, with the future being set for the past, is proved by Psalm 6: “Every night I will wash my bed,” meaning “I washed it”; Psalm 65: “They will pass through the river on foot”; and Isaiah 38: “Like a young swallow, so will I cry out, and I will meditate like a dove,” meaning “I meditated and cried out.” The past is sometimes put for the future, as in Psalm 54: “But I cried to God, and the Lord saved me,” that is, “will save me.” For it follows: “And he will hear my voice.” The future is put for the present in Psalm 144: “They will proclaim the glory of your kingdom, and they will speak of your power.” LOAISA.]

7. In the holy Scriptures, things that are future are often narrated as though they had already happened, as in the passage: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” But why are future things written as though they were past, unless because what is still to be accomplished in action is already accomplished in divine predestination? Thus events occur to us in time that are foreseen by the Creator of all things without time.

[Note: [Col. 0577B]

8. This is frequent in the divine writings, as is clear from Gregory, on Canticle 6; Jerome, on Ezekiel 16; and Augustine, Book XVII of *The City of God*, chapter 3: “The utterances of the prophets,” he says, “are found to be threefold, since some concern earthly Jerusalem, some heavenly Jerusalem, and some both.” Jerome, on Ezekiel 16: “Since Jerusalem is spoken of in four ways, we shall give examples. First, among the Jews, it is that earthly city which Christ mourned over: ‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you’ (Matthew 23). Second, it is the assembly of the saints: ‘Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob’ (Psalm 86). Third, it is the multitude of angels, dominions, powers, and the heavenly paradise: ‘But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all’ (Paul to the Galatians 4); and in Hebrews 12: ‘You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.’ This is also the one described in Revelation 12. Fourth, it signifies the Church militant and triumphant: ‘I saw the holy city, Jerusalem’ (Revelation 21).” Jerome also affirms, in his commentary on Ezekiel 23, that whatever is said of Jerusalem tropically—τροπικῶς, “figuratively”—may be referred to the soul. LOAISA.

On the same passage, Hosea 4: “Ephraim is a partner with idols; let him alone.” And chapter 5: “Ephraim suffers reproach, broken by judgment, because he began to go after filth.” And the passage: “I will be a moth to Ephraim, and rottenness to the house of Jacob.” A moth consumes the whole garment. Job 13: “Like a garment,” he says, “that is consumed by the moth.” Rot does not act in the same way. Thus heresy is the moth of Ephraim, while sin is the rottenness of Jacob. LOAISA.]

8. Therefore prophecy mingles the deeds of future things with present events [Col. 0578A], so that the former may be believed to be future in the same way that the latter are seen to have been completed. In its customary manner it speaks of future things through present ones, as when it speaks in the person of Jerusalem about the Church, and in the person of Ephraim about heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0577D]

9. Psalm 32. To say often signifies a command in the divine writings, as in Paul’s words to the Romans 12: “I say, by the grace that has been given to me, to everyone among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think.” In Greek, λέγω, as Latins say, “I command you to be well,” and “I say health.” And the passage: “Say that these stones become bread,” that is, “Command that the stones become bread,” and so forth. LOAISA.]

9. Words are often put for divine deeds, because God works not by the labor of hands but by the command of speech, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

[Note: [Col. 0578B]

10. Jerome, on Ezekiel 33, observed that the following should be maintained in the sacred Scriptures: where a similarity of meaning seems to occur, the same thing is not said in every respect; rather, something is often subtracted or added, and attention must be paid to each of the differing words in relation to one another. LOAISA.]

10. When the same sentence is repeated twice in the sacred Scriptures, it is either for the sake of confirmation or because of a mystery, as with law and grace, beginning and perfection, good and better.

[Note: [Col. 0578B]

11. “Law” is derived from *deligere*, “to choose,” for it commands what ought to be chosen and done, as Cicero taught in Book I of *On the Laws*. Hence Paul says to the Romans 3: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin.” “Law” is understood as referring to the books of the Old Testament. Isaiah 2: “The law will go forth from Zion.” And Paul says to the Romans 2: “But if you are called a Jew, rest upon the law, glory in God, know his will, and approve what is more excellent, instructed by the law.” And chapter 7: “The law is holy.” The Book of Psalms is also called “law” by Christ our Lord in John 10: “In your law it is written: ‘I said, You are gods,’” as Augustine noted in the same place, Tractate 48. So too Amalarius of Trier, *On the Office of the Mass*. Law is also distinguished from the psalms and the prophets. Matthew 11: “The law and the prophets were until John.” And the passage: “It was necessary that what is written about me in the law, the prophets, and the psalms should be fulfilled” (Matthew 22). LOAISA.

On the same passage, “It is distinguished.” For the divisions of the Old and New Testaments, see Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*; John of Damascus, Book IV of *The Orthodox Faith*; Gregory Nazianzen in his poems; Jerome in the preface to the Books of Kings; and Isidore, Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1. I thought it worth noting in passing that Isidore discusses the parts of the divine law here in the same way as in Book VI of the *Etymologies*. There, after dividing the Old Testament into legal, prophetic, and hagiographical books, he says: “The whole of both Testaments is divided into three parts, namely, history, morals, and allegory.” Thus you may understand the commandments to pertain to morals and the prophets to allegory. For that well-known and widespread division into three kinds, or parts, of exposition—allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—according to the threefold distinction of past, present, and future, was handed down by the ancient Fathers. Allegorical exposition reveals the anticipatory signs and portents of the shadows and figures of past things in the Old Law; hence the prophets belong to the allegorical mode of exposition. Moreover, the allegorical manner of speech is rightly attributed to the prophets because of tropes, verbal enigmas, and metaphors, as Tertullian noted in Book III against Marcion. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “In history.” All manuscript codices read this way. L.

Loaisa praises Amalaricus Tauriensis, who seems to be Amalarius of Trier, to whom many attribute the work *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, while others attribute it to Amalarius of Metz and others to Amalarius of Lyon. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis*, with Mansi’s notes. AREV.]

11. The divine law is distinguished in three parts: in history, 164 in commandments, and in prophecy. History consists in things that have been done; commandments in things that have been ordered; prophecy in things that have been foretold as future.

[Note: [Col. 0579A]

12. Augustine, in his single book on the literal interpretation of Genesis, chapter 2: “Four modes,” he says, “are handed down by certain interpreters of Scripture for explaining the law: according to history, according to allegory, according to analogy, and according to etymology.” History is present when an event is recalled as having taken place either by divine or human agency. Allegory is present when figurative expressions are understood figuratively. Analogy is present when the agreement between the Old and New Testaments is demonstrated. Etymology is present when the causes of words and deeds are supplied. In *On the Usefulness of Belief*, addressed to Honoratus, chapter 3, the same author divides Scripture according to history, etymology, analogy, and allegory. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “Historically.” The historical sense of Scripture, which is the literal sense, is the most powerful and effective of all, and much more illustrious than the others for proving the authority of faith. It is the foundation and basis of all expositions of divine Scripture. Jerome noted its difficulty in the preface to his commentaries on Obadiah, as did Augustine in Book I of the *Retractions*. Yet if it is read as history alone and in a bare manner, without the spirit of the letter, it has little usefulness; Jerome therefore calls it, on Ezekiel 4, “a lesser understanding.” Augustine, in Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 27, asserts that we should agree neither with those who accept only the historical sense without allegorical significance, nor with those who defend only figures while rejecting the truth of history. The useful sense of Scripture—for teaching, reproving, correcting, and instructing in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect—consists of letter and spirit. For the letter alone kills, but the spirit gives life and equips the mind for every good work. Hence Gregory says in Book XVI of the *Morals*, chapter 10: “Sometimes the bare history feeds us; sometimes spiritual allegory, hidden within the text of the letter, refreshes us in our inmost parts.” L.

On the same passage, “Tropologically.” Tropological exposition is the same as moral exposition. Let us give an example from the water in Genesis 1: “The waters were gathered into one place.” Historically this signifies elemental water; tropologically, however, it signifies tribulations, as in Psalm 65: “We passed through water and fire, and you brought us out into refreshment.” And Isaiah 43: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you.” And the passage: “The waters have entered even to my soul.” Tropologically it also signifies wisdom. Proverbs 18: “Deep waters are the words from a man’s mouth, and a flowing stream is a fountain of wisdom.” And the passage: “It will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.” Ecclesiasticus: “The water of saving wisdom will give them drink.” It also signifies heresies. Proverbs 9: “Stolen waters are sweeter.” It signifies human prosperity, as in John 4: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again.” It signifies the infusion of the Holy Spirit, as in John 7: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” The Evangelist interprets this: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive.” It also signifies peoples, as in Revelation 17: “The waters are peoples.” Jerome writes thus about the tropological sense in his commentary on Ezekiel 4: “History and tropology proceed through the same letters, but the former is humbler and the latter more subtle; the former clings to the earth, while the latter raises us to heavenly things.” LOAISA.

On the same passage, “Mystically.” Here Isidore calls the mystical sense spiritual understanding. Jerome, whose division of divine Scripture Isidore follows, writes in his twelfth question on Obadiah: “There is a threefold description and rule of the Scriptures in our heart: first, that we understand them according to history; second, according to tropology; third, according to spiritual understanding. In history, the order of the things written is preserved. In tropology, we rise from the letter to greater things; whatever was done carnally among the former people, we interpret according to the moral sense and turn it to the benefit of our soul. In spiritual θεωρία, ‘contemplation,’ we pass to higher things, leave earthly matters behind, and discuss the blessedness of the future and heavenly things, so that meditation on the present life may be the shadow of future blessedness.” Thus far Jerome. The blessed Eucherius, in his *Book of Spiritual Forms*, sets out four kinds of divine exposition: historical, tropological, allegorical, and anagogical. We have already discussed historical, tropological, and allegorical exposition according to Augustine’s view. Now concerning anagogical exposition, which Eucherius calls the mode that leads to the more sacred secrets of heavenly figures: for example, if we interpret water as eternal blessedness, as in Jeremiah 2: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water”; or as angels, in Psalm 148: “Waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord.” You may place allegorical and anagogical exposition under mystical and spiritual understanding. Thus Eucherius, Jerome, Augustine, and Isidore agree in the manifold and varied division of the Scriptures. LOAISA.]

12. The divine law must be understood in a threefold manner: first historically, 165 second tropologically, and third mystically. Historically, according to the letter; tropologically, according to moral knowledge; mystically, according to spiritual understanding. Therefore faith must be held historically in such a way that we must also interpret it morally and understand it spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 0580C]

13. All manuscript codices read “three and seven, ten commandments,” a reading I strongly approve. This is found in Augustine, *On the Ten Strings*, chapter 5—whence Isidore took the statement—and in Book XV against Faustus, chapter 4. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “On one tablet.” Many Latin saints follow this division of the commandments on the tablets, namely, that three were written on one and seven on the other, including Augustine in the places cited. In *On the Ten Strings*, chapter 5, he proves his opinion from Paul’s statement: “The first commandment with a promise.” Yet he is not consistent on this point, for in the *Book of Questions on the Old Testament*, question 7, he affirms that four words were inscribed on the first tablet [Col. 0580D]. He sets the first as: “You shall have no other gods besides me”; the second: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness”; the third: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”; the fourth: “You shall keep the Sabbath of the Lord your God, and shall do no servile work on it.” The remainder were on the second tablet, so that the first word of the second tablet was: “Honor your father and your mother,” from the Apostle’s words to the Ephesians 6: “Honor your father and mother,” which is “the first commandment with a promise.” “How,” he says, “would it be first unless it began the second tablet?” It is called “with a promise” because the following words are immediately added: “That you may live long upon the earth, and that it may go well with you.” This is the promise made to those who keep the commandments. Josephus, Book III of the *Antiquities*, chapter 6, and Philo, in *Who Is the Heir of Divine Things?*, affirm that five commandments were given on each tablet. Some say that these tablets were found in the temple during the final destruction of Jerusalem under the Roman emperors and were brought to Rome in triumph by Titus Augustus among the other spoils of the captured city.

On the same passage. What Loaisa reports, following the opinion of certain writers—that the tablets of the law were brought by Titus to Rome in triumph—others consider false, since Josephus reports that Titus found nothing in the temple sanctuary. See the commentary on Prudentius, pages 654 and 1234, and Calmet’s dissertation on the ark of the covenant prefixed to the Books of Maccabees. AREV.]

13. There are ten commandments, three and seven; three concern the love of God, and seven concern human beings. Those three that pertain to God were written on one tablet [Col. 0580A], and the remaining seven on the second. On the first tablet of the three commandments, this is the first: “You shall love the Lord your God.” On the second: “Honor your father and your mother.”

14. Hence, when the Savior was asked by a scribe which commandment was first in the law, he said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord; this is the first.” “The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He named one commandment from the first tablet, which concerns love of God, and another from the other tablet, which concerns love of human beings.

## CHAPTER XIX — On the Seven Rules

[Col. 0581A]

[Note: [Col. 0581C]

**Chapter XIX, Note 1.** Ticonius devised these seven rules as keys for opening the hidden meanings of divine Scripture. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book III, chapter 30: “A certain Ticonius,” he says, “who wrote most invincibly against the Donatists, although he himself was a Donatist”; and in Book II against Parmenian’s letter, chapter 28, he calls him a teacher. He valued Ticonius’s laws and formulas for interpreting divine Scripture so highly that he preferred them to Cyprian’s expositions, as is clear from Book II of the *Retractions* and Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 30, where he writes of the usefulness of these rules: “I considered it necessary, before all else, to write a little book of Rules containing what seems to me necessary, and to construct laws of the secrets as keys and lights. For there are certain mixed rules that possess the recesses of the whole law and make the treasures of truth visible to some. If the method of these rules is received without jealousy, as we communicate it, everything closed will be opened and obscure things will be made clear, so that anyone walking through the immense forest of prophecies may be led by these rules, as though by paths of light, and in some manner be guarded from error.” He adds: “It should certainly be read with caution, not only because in certain matters he erred as a human being, but especially because in other matters he speaks as a heretic and Donatist.” Cassiodorus also mentions these rules in the preface to his commentary on the Psalms. Ticonius likewise wrote expositions of the Apocalypse of John, as Gennadius and Bede testify in their commentaries on the Apocalypse. A book of the *Rules* is now extant, published in the *Library of the Saints* compiled by the Parisian theologian Margarino, volume VI. He flourished under Theodosius and his sons, in the year of the Lord 390. LOAISA.

On the same passage. Vezzosius observes that Ticonius the African, the author of these rules, was not only a Donatist but also a Chiliast. Many write *Tichonius*. Loaisa, or Grialius, preferred *Ticonius*, which others also follow; some write *Tychonius*. On him, see Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis*. AREV.]

1. Certain wise men have said that, among other forms of expression in the holy Scriptures, there are seven rules.

167 [Note: [Col. 0582B]

2. The printed edition reads: “What speaks from one to one.” I do not approve this reading. The meaning is that the distinction is made solely by reasoning, when two functions are distinguished within one person by reasoning and thought. Thus it is by reasoning alone that one grasps when the passage moves from the head to the body. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “Isaiah.” This is an example from Isaiah 61, found in Ticonius and Augustine, although the Septuagint uses the following version: “As upon a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament”: Ὡς νυμφίῳ περιέθηκέ μοι μίτραν, καὶ ὡς νύμφην κατεκόσμησέ με κόσμῳ. Isidore always embraces the Vulgate version. LOAISA.]

2. The first rule concerns the Lord and his body: what speaks from one or to one, and in a single person presents now the head, now the body. Thus Isaiah says: “He clothed me with the garment of salvation, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown, and like a bride adorned with her jewels.” In one person, designated by two names, he made manifest the head—that is, the bridegroom—and the Church—that is, the bride.

3. Accordingly, it must be observed in the Scriptures when the head alone is specifically described, when both head and body are described, when the passage moves from either one to either one, or from one to the other. Thus the discerning reader may understand what pertains to the head and what to the body.

[Note: [Col. 0582C]

4. Ticonius spoke of the Lord’s divided body; Augustine corrected this expression, asserting that it ought not to be called that, but rather the Lord’s true and mixed body, or true and fictitious body, or the mingled Church. LOAISA.]

4. The second rule concerns the Lord’s true and mingled body. For it must be considered that certain statements appear to belong to one person although they do not belong to one person, as in the passage: “You are my servant, Israel; behold, I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud and your sins like a mist; turn back to me, and I will redeem you.” This does not apply to one person.

[Col. 0582A] 5. One part is the one whose sins he blotted out and to whom he says, “You are my servant.” The other is the one to whom he says, “Turn back to me, and I will redeem you.” If they turn back, their sins are blotted out. Through this rule Scripture speaks to all in such a way that the good are reproved together with the wicked, and the wicked are praised on account of the good. But the prudent reader will learn to whom each statement belongs.

[Note: [Col. 0582C]

6. Augustine, in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, considers this more a great question than a rule. Ticonius calls it the third rule, concerning promises and the law; Augustine calls it the rule concerning spirit and letter, or concerning grace and commandment. LOAISA.]

6. The third rule concerns letter and spirit, that is, law and grace: law, by which we are admonished to carry out the commandments; grace, by which we are helped to do so. Alternatively, it means that the law must be understood not only historically but also spiritually. For faith must be held historically, and the law must be understood spiritually.

[Note: [Col. 0582C]

7. This entire rule is read corruptly in the printed edition. I restored it from the ancient manuscript Codex Cothonianus. Gregory mentions it in Book III of the *Morals* and in Homily 26 on the Gospels, concerning the passage: “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” LOAISA.

On the same passage, Psalm 44: “The daughters of Tyre shall worship him with gifts; all the rich among the people shall entreat your favor.” Augustine reads the passage in his commentary on the Psalms: “The daughters of Tyre shall worship him,” so that the sentence does not end with “they shall worship him,” as I find it punctuated in many codices. Likewise: “The daughters of Tyre” means “the daughters of the nations”; a part is referred to the whole. Tyre, which was near the place where the prophecy was given, signified the nations that would believe in Christ. Theodoret, in his commentary on the Psalms, reads: “For he himself is the Lord your God, and you shall worship him, and the daughters of Tyre with gifts.” He presents the varying opinions of the interpreters and affirms that by the daughters of Tyre the whole of impiety is signified. “It is the custom,” he says, “of Sacred Scripture to demonstrate the whole by a part.” Thus elsewhere by Lebanon he foretells the cessation of all superstition, for, he says, “Lebanon will fall with its heights.” The blessed Basil says the same; Theodoret largely compiled his scholia on the Psalms from Basil. LOAISA.]

7. The fourth rule concerns species and genus, by which a part is understood for the whole and the whole for a part. Thus, if God speaks to one nation or city, it may nevertheless be understood to concern the entire world, as in the Psalms: “The daughters of Tyre,” he says, “shall worship him with gifts.” “The daughters of Tyre” means “the daughters of the nations,” moving from species to genus; for by Tyre, which was then near the land where the prophecy was given, he signified all the nations that would believe in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0582D]

8. Isaiah, chapter 14, where Jerome writes: “In this passage some think that the prophecy is general, against the whole world. We do not at all contradict them, provided we understand that the entire land of the Assyrians is specifically signified here.” L.

On the same passage, “And Babylon will be.” The passage is found in the same Isaiah, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

8. Hence the following also appropriately continues: “All the rich of the earth shall entreat your favor.” Likewise, when through the prophet Isaiah the Lord threatens Assyria, saying: “That I may crush Assyria in my land and trample him upon my mountains. And that glorious Babylon, renowned among kingdoms, will be as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.” For although through the aforementioned Isaiah the Lord threatens one city, Babylon, nevertheless, while speaking against it, he moves from species to genus and directs his speech generally against the whole world.

9. Certainly, if he were not speaking against the whole world, he would not add below, in general terms: “I will destroy the whole earth, and I will visit evils upon the world,” and the other things that follow and pertain to the destruction of the world. Hence he also adds: “This is the plan that I have conceived over the whole earth, and this is the hand extended over all the nations.”

[Col. 0583B] 10. Likewise, while under the person of Babylon he reproves the whole world, saying: “I will destroy the whole earth, and I will visit evils upon the world,” and the other things that follow and pertain to the destruction of the world, he again returns to the same city, as from genus to species, saying what happened specifically to that city: “Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them.” For while Belshazzar was reigning, Babylon was conquered by the Medes.

11. Likewise, he understands the oracle against Egypt, spoken in the person of Egypt itself, as referring to the whole world, saying: “I will make Egyptians rise against Egyptians, kingdom against kingdom,” although Egypt is recorded to have possessed not many kingdoms but one kingdom.

[Col. 0584A] [Note: [Col. 0583C]

12. Ticonius says that this rule operates in two ways: either through synecdoche or through “legitimate numbers.” He calls those numbers “legitimate” which Scripture commends with particular prominence, such as seven, ten, and twelve. See Ticonius himself and Augustine. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “Concerning the three days.” Augustine discusses this passage extensively in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, Book IV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, and Ticonius in the *Rules*. LOAISA.]

12. The fifth rule concerns times, by which either a greater portion of time is introduced through a smaller portion, or a smaller portion through a greater. Thus it is with the three days of the Lord’s burial: he did not lie in the tomb for three complete days and nights, yet the whole three-day period is understood from a part.

[Note: [Col. 0583C]

13. “The days of a human being shall be 120 years,” although only one hundred years are found between the time when this was established by the Lord and the Flood. Or likewise with the four hundred years, and so forth. The passage is in Genesis 6: “And God said: My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh; their days shall be 120 years.” Lactantius Firmianus, Book II of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 14, interprets this passage by saying that God, in anger, shortened the span of human life and, abolishing the length of life that people had possessed before the Flood, confined it within a period of 120 years. Firmianus derives this from Josephus in Book I of the *Antiquities*. Jerome, however, interprets the passage differently in his *Hebrew Questions*: “This means,” he says, “I will grant 120 years for repentance. Human life was not therefore shortened to 120 years, as many mistakenly think; rather, 120 years were granted to that generation for repentance. But because they refused to repent, God did not wait for the appointed time. He shortened the period by twenty years and brought on the Flood in the hundredth year assigned for repentance.” Chrysostom likewise adopted this interpretation in Homily 22 on Genesis. Gennadius, however, rejects it as absurd and wholly alien to God, since God always proceeds with a slow step toward punishment. See the chain of the Greek Fathers on the Pentateuch. That God, as Jerome judges, shortened twenty years from the appointed time is clear. For Genesis 5 says: “Noah was 500 years old when he begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” Chapter 6 says: “His days shall be 120 years.” Then chapter 7 says: “Noah was 600 years old when the waters of the Flood overflowed the earth.” LOAISA.

On the same passage, “Or likewise.” Genesis 15 says that they would return to the land of promise in the fourth generation, and this was also fulfilled. Jacob was the first to enter Egypt with his sons, while Moses was the fourth from Jacob to lead the people out. On the calculation of these years, see our scholium in Isidore’s *Chronicle*. LOAISA.]

13. Likewise, a part is taken for the whole, as in the passage: “The days of a human being shall be 120 years,” although only one hundred years are found between the time when this was established by the Lord and the Flood; or as in the passage where God foretold that the children of Israel would serve in Egypt for 400 years and then depart. They did not, however, serve for 400 years, since, while Joseph was ruler, they themselves ruled Egypt. Here again a part is added for the whole, because they did not leave Egypt immediately after 400 years, as had been promised, but withdrew from Egypt after 430 years had elapsed.

[Note: [Col. 0584C]

14. The printed editions read: “There is also another figure concerning times, by which certain things that are future are narrated as though they had already happened,” and so forth. I approve the manuscript reading. Everything above in chapter 18, section 7, concerning the law and numbers, is taken from Augustine’s book *On the Words of the Apostle*, and this was noted there. LOAISA.

On the same passage, “In which,” and so forth. Others revise it as follows: “In which future things are spoken of as though they had already happened.” But why are things that still had to be done narrated as already accomplished? Because what is still future for us is already accomplished in God’s eternity. Therefore, when something is announced as still to be done, it is spoken according to us; but when future things are said to have already happened, they must be understood according to God’s eternity, with whom everything that is future is already accomplished. There is great disagreement among manuscript copies in the presentation of all these rules. AREV.]

14. To this rule concerning times also belong those passages in which things still future are narrated as though they had already happened, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones; they divided my garments among themselves,” and similar passages. In these, things that still had to be done are narrated as already accomplished.

[Note: [Col. 0584D]

15. The Gothic manuscript and two other ancient codices read: “In which things that still had to be done are narrated as already accomplished.” But when something is announced as still to be done, it is spoken according to us, and so forth. The remaining words found in the printed editions and other manuscripts are absent from these two. LOAISA.]

15. But when something is announced as still to be done, it is spoken according to us; when future things are said to have already happened, they must be understood according to God’s eternity, because what is still future for us is already accomplished in God’s predestination, with whom everything that is future is already accomplished.

[Col. 0585A] [Note: [Col. 0584D]

16. Augustine writes as follows concerning this rule: “Tichonius calls the sixth rule recapitulation, discovered with sufficient vigilance amid the obscurities of Scripture. For certain things are spoken as though they followed in the order of time, or were narrated in a continuation of events, when the narrative secretly returns to earlier matters that had been passed over; unless this is understood from the present rule, one goes astray.” LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. The Codex Guadal. reads: “As in Isaiah, where, although the prophetic discourse had said much against Babylon—that is, against the body of the devil—the sentence of the oracle again turns back to the head, that is, to the devil, saying: ‘How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn!’ As when Scripture had mentioned the sons of the sons of Noah,” etc. These passages occur in Isaiah XIV. In fact, however, they do not belong to this rule, but to the seventh, concerning the devil and his body, as is clear from Augustine. LOAISA.

16. The sixth rule concerns recapitulation. Recapitulation occurs when Scripture returns to something whose narrative has already passed, as when, after Scripture had mentioned the sons of the sons of Noah, it said that they were arranged according to their languages and nations, and yet afterward, as though this too followed in the order of time, it says: “Now the whole earth had one language, and all had one voice” (Gen. XI, 1). How, then, could they have been arranged according to their nations and languages if everyone had one language, unless the narrative, by recapitulating, had returned to what had already passed?

[Note: [Col. 0585D]

17. None of the manuscript codices that I obtained for the correction of this work contains all these passages. Among them were two extremely ancient parchment codices written in Gothic letters: one belonging to the Church of Toledo, written in the year 953 of the era; the other from the distinguished college of Oviedo at Salamanca, still older, as may be inferred from the letters displaying extraordinary antiquity. I therefore rejected all these passages as foreign to the genuine reading. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “Recapitulation occurs … these things appear to have been accomplished.” Bignaeus says that he found the following in manuscript copies in which the preceding material was lacking: “Recapitulation occurs … the narrative had returned.” The latter passages do occur in the older editions. Loaisa testifies that the other material was absent from his manuscripts; nor does it appear in ours, except that the order of the chapters and matters is so disordered in many manuscripts that it should not seem surprising if these passages occur in one of them. AREV.]

17. Recapitulation occurs when the causes of past events are mingled with future events, as also in Genesis, where, after saying that the human being had been made on the sixth day, Scripture recapitulates by saying of the one already formed: “God formed the human being in his own image” (Gen. II, 7). Likewise, after all the works had been completed, when it says that God rested on the seventh day, it adds by recapitulation:

“These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, on the day when God made heaven and earth, and every plant of the field, before it arose upon the earth. For the Lord God had not yet caused rain upon the earth, and there was no human being to till the ground; but a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.”

All these things, by recapitulation, are joined in the sequence of the narrative to events that are future, although they appear to have been accomplished within the six days.

[Note: [Col. 0586C]

18. The material enclosed in parentheses I found added in the margin only in the Gothic codex of the Church of Toledo. The passage is from Isaiah, chapter XIV, and appears in Saint Augustine among the examples of the seventh rule, as well as in Tichonius. LOAISA.]

18. The seventh rule concerns the devil and his body, because things belonging to the head itself are often said in a way more appropriate to its body; and, conversely, things that appear to be said of its members are often applicable only to the head. Thus in Isaiah, although the prophetic discourse had said much against Babylon—that is, against the body of the devil—the sentence of the oracle again turns to the head, that is, to the devil, saying: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn?” (Isa. XIV, 12).

[Note: [Col. 0586C]

19. The apostate angel is Lucifer, of whom Isaiah XIV says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer?” He is also called “the dragon,” “the ancient serpent,” “the devil,” and “Satan” (Rev. XII). LOAISA.]

19. The head is understood from the name of the body, as in the Gospel concerning the weeds mixed with the wheat, where the Lord says: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 28), calling the devil himself a human being. Conversely, the body is signified by the name of the head, as it is said in the Gospel: “I chose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John VI, 71), indicating Judas, who was part of the devil’s body. The apostate angel is the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are the body of this head. Thus he is one with his members, so that what is said of his body is often referred rather to him; and, again, what is said of him is transferred back to his members.

173. CHAPTER XX. On the Difference between the Testaments.

[Note: [Col. 0586D]

CHAPTER XX, no. 1. “Some.” Another reading: “certain heretics.” Shortly afterward, “with some unknown” instead of “with some great.” AREV.]

1. Some do not accept the Old Testament because one course of action was followed in ancient times and another in the New Testament. They do not understand that God, in a great and fitting distribution, granted to each age what was appropriate to it: thus, in the Law he commands marriage (Deut. XXV), while in the Gospel he commends virginity (Matt. XIX); in the Law, the removal of an eye for an eye (Deut. XIX), while in the Gospel, offering the other cheek to the one who strikes (Matt. V).

2. The former was suitable to a weak people in its own period, the latter to a mature people; yet to each age he supplied what was appropriate to it. Nevertheless, because of this change God must not be thought changeable. Rather, he should be proclaimed all the more wondrous, because, while remaining unchangeable, he granted, with a great ordering, what was beneficial to each age, as we have said.

[Note: [Col. 0586D]

3. “Manifest.” Another reading: “with manifest truth.” AREV.]

3. Under the Old Testament, sins were lesser offenses, because in it not the truth itself but the shadow of the truth was present. For in the New Testament, through higher commandments, we are instructed to abandon certain practices that had served the shadow of the truth among that people. There, fornication and retaliation for injury were permitted and did not cause harm; but in the New Testament they are condemned with severe judgment if they are committed.

CHAPTER XXI. On the Creed and the Prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0586D]

CHAPTER XXI, no. 1. Augustine teaches in the *Enchiridion*, chapters 6 and 7, that the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer contain faith, hope, and charity. That Creed was composed by the Apostles themselves with great care and under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, as is clear from Rufinus in his *Exposition of the Creed*, and from Augustine in his second sermon for Palm Sunday, where he explains what portion each Apostle contributed in the following manner:

“What is called *Symbolum* in Greek is called *Collatio* in Latin. It is called a ‘collection’ because the faith of the whole Catholic law, gathered together into one, is collected in the brevity of the Creed, whose text, God willing, we shall now recite to you.

“Peter said: ‘I believe in one God, the Father almighty.’

“John said: ‘Creator of heaven and earth.’

“James said: ‘And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.’

“Andrew said: ‘Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.’

“Philip said: ‘Suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried.’

“Thomas said: ‘He descended to the underworld; on the third day he rose from the dead.’

“Bartholomew said: ‘He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.’

“Matthew said: ‘From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.’

“James son of Alphaeus said: ‘And in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church.’

“Simon the Zealot said: ‘The communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.’

“Judas son of James said: ‘The resurrection of the flesh.’

“Matthias completed it: ‘Eternal life.’ Amen.”

Ambrose, in sermon 38, on fasts and Lent, also calls the Creed the key of faith, forged through the work of twelve craftsmen. Irenaeus, book I, chapter 2, calls it the unanimous token of faith; so also Leo, in his letter to the Empress Pulcheria. Ambrose, in book III *On Virginity*, calls it the seal of the heart and says that it should be recited daily before dawn. The Apostles’ Creed is meant by “the Creed of faith,” as in the Council of Laodicea, canon 46: “Those who have been baptized ought to recite the Creed of faith,” and canon 47. Likewise in the Council of Agde, canon 9, and in the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, chapter 45. On the Apostles’ Creed, see Jerome’s letter to Pammachius, Augustine’s *Book to the Catechumens*, and Clement of Rome’s letter to James, the brother of the Lord. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “The Lord’s Prayer.” The Fathers call it the daily prayer, as do Cyprian in his exposition, Augustine, book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 27, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 9: both because it is said daily and because it removes minor and daily sins. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “Isaiah,” etc. The passage is found in Isaiah, chapter X, where Jerome says: “In place of all the elaborate ceremonies of the Law he gave the very brief commandment of love and faith.” Cyprian, in his *Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*, interprets the passage as referring to the Creed of faith; so does Augustine in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, response 11, and in *Against Faustus*, book XV, chapter 4, he calls the two commandments of love the Church’s diptych. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. In Grialius’s edition, *capescenda* appeared instead of *capessenda*; and in the note, “published by them,” I supplied “by the Apostles.” AREV.]

1. The Creed of faith and the Lord’s Prayer suffice for the little ones of the Church to attain the kingdom of heaven in place of the whole Law. For the entire breadth of Scripture is contained in the same Lord’s Prayer and in the brevity of the Creed. Hence the prophet Isaiah also says: “I have heard from the Lord God of hosts an abbreviation concerning the whole earth. Attend, and hear my word” (Isa. V, 23).

2. But this abbreviation may mean either what the Lord says—that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon the two commandments of love of God and neighbor—or the brevity itself of the Lord’s Prayer or of the Creed, in which, as stated above, we see the whole breadth of Scripture compressed.

175. CHAPTER XXII. On Baptism and Communion.

[Note: [Col. 0587D]

CHAPTER XXII, no. 1. Isidore does not condemn the baptism of heretics, as Cyprian did together with the bishops of Africa. Jerome speaks of this in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*:

“Cyprian wished to flee from broken cisterns and not drink from another’s water. Therefore, rejecting the baptism of heretics, he sent an African synod on this matter to Stephen, then bishop of the city of Rome, who was the twenty-sixth after blessed Peter; but his effort was in vain.”

Here Isidore is speaking of baptism administered by heretics to adults with invocation of the Most Holy Trinity. Although it is a sacrament and seals a character upon the soul, it nevertheless contributes nothing to their salvation and forgiveness of sins until they are received by the Church. “For it is given to them,” he says, “not for the forgiveness of sins but as a testimony to punishment.” Augustine approves this view in book III *Against the Donatists*, chapter 14, and in *On Baptism*, chapter 12; it is also found in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Then baptism begins to be of value for salvation when pretense has withdrawn from true confession.” Gregory likewise says this to Quiriacus, Letter 61, book IX of the *Register*, as does Pope Nicholas in his response to the Bulgarians, chapter 3.

What Isidore thought about baptism administered by heretics is clear from book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24, where he says:

“If heretics are nevertheless taught to have received baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, they are not to be baptized again, but are to be cleansed only by chrism and the laying on of hands. For baptism is not a merit of the human being but of Christ. Therefore it makes no difference whether a heretic or a believer baptizes: the sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer. The heretic possesses Christ’s baptism; but because he is outside the unity of faith, it benefits him nothing. Once he has entered, however, the baptism that he possessed outside, to his destruction, immediately begins to benefit him for salvation. I approve what is received, but I disapprove because it is received outside; when he comes in, it is not changed but recognized. For it is the character of my King, not sacrilegious error: I correct the deserter; I do not change the character.”

Thus Isidore. Finally, the sacred Council of Trent, session 7, canon 4, says that baptism administered by heretics in the form of the Church is true baptism. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. Loaisa’s note read: “which is given in the canonical form,” etc. AREV.]

1. The prophet Zechariah testifies that only the Catholic Church possesses baptism for salvation: “On that day,” he says, “there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman” (Zech. XIII, 1). The house of David and Jerusalem are the Church of Christ, in which a fountain flows for the washing away of sins. Heretics, however, perform only an imaginary display of this; therefore baptism is given to them not for the forgiveness of sins but as a testimony to punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0588C]

2. Hell is multiple, as the most learned Saint Thomas Aquinas has noted, as he has noted many other things. “Hell,” he says, “is fourfold: that of the damned, that of children, purgatory, and that of the holy Fathers. In the first are three things: the darkness of grace, the darkness of glory, and the punishment of sense. From that eternal punishment, may we be delivered. In the second there are only the first two: the darkness of grace and of glory. In the third there are only the second and third: the darkness of glory and the punishment of sense. In the fourth there is only the second: the darkness of glory; and this is called the bosom of Abraham.” Tertullian discusses this in book IV *Against Marcion*. Saint Gregory, book VII of the *Letters*, letter 53 to Secundinus, discusses the abode of the souls of infants who depart without baptism. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “Therefore,” etc. So the Gothic Codex and other manuscripts read. The passage plainly supports the proposition that the stain of origin is contracted by children from their parents, and that all children are naturally begotten as children of wrath. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. Another reading: “Therefore, because of Adam’s guilt, a newborn infant, if not regenerated, is condemned, because,” etc. Isidore discusses baptism not only in the cited passage of *Ecclesiastical Offices* but also in book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 24. AREV.]

2. Newborn infants suffer punishments in hell solely for original guilt if they have not been renewed through the washing of baptism. Therefore a newborn infant is condemned together with its cause if it is not regenerated, because it is destroyed by the injury of its origin.

3. Why are little children, freed from original sin through baptism and not yet possessing any personal offense, nevertheless torn by wild beasts and subjected to other punishments? This, then, is the reason: baptism frees from eternal punishment, not from the penalties of the present life. For if human beings were freed from present punishment through baptism, they would think that baptism’s reward consisted in this, rather than in the eternal reward. Therefore, although the guilt of sin has been removed, a certain temporal punishment nevertheless remains, so that the life which will be free from every punishment may be sought more ardently.

4. No believer denies that, even after baptism, by which sins are removed, we must turn to God daily as long as we are in this world. Although this must be done every day without interruption, it will never be sufficient to have done it only once.

[Note: [Col. 0589B]

5. This opinion is found in the collections of Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, and in Ivo, part I, chapter 185, and in the Master, book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 6. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. This does not prevent the opinion of certain recent writers from being probable or true: they teach that baptism may be conferred in a case of necessity upon children still in the maternal womb, if baptismal water can reach them. AREV.]

5. Those who are in the maternal womb cannot therefore be baptized together with their mother, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. Nor can regeneration be said to occur in one whose generation has not preceded it.

[Note: [Col. 0589B]

6. Psalm XXXIX. Augustine interprets it in the same way. Basil and Theodoret, however, interpret the passage differently in their scholia on the Psalms. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “Of the predestined.” All manuscript codices and the ancient edition have this reading. I adopted it and removed “in the kingdom of the rejected,” following the exposition of Gregory and Augustine. Gregory therefore adds concerning those who are “above the number”: “For they have been mixed among the faithful through confession, but because of their rejected life they do not deserve to be counted there among the lot of the faithful.” LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. Vezzosius asserts that Loaisa and Breulius observe that one should rather read “in the kingdom of the rejected,” an expression adopted by Bignaeus. But Breulius has nothing apart from Loaisa’s note; and Loaisa clearly teaches that “in the kingdom of the predestined” is to be preferred, which the cited words of Saint Gregory confirm. It is therefore astonishing that Vezzosius should have been mistaken in so evident a matter. AREV.]

6. Those who live within the Church not according to the dignity of the Church, but destroy by their deeds the faith that they hold in word, are spoken of in this passage: “They have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. XXXIX, 6), with the implied phrase, “in the kingdom of the predestined.”

[Note: [Col. 0589C]

7. The whole statement is found in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Those Who Live Wickedly”; a fragment of it is found in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “Those Who Are in the Maternal Womb,” at the end of the chapter. LOAISA.]

7. Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to receive communion, thinking that such communion cleanses them, should learn that it contributes nothing to their purification. The prophet says: “What is my beloved doing in my house, committing many crimes? Will holy flesh take away your wickedness?” (Jer. XI, 15). And the Apostle says: “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the cup” (I Cor. XI, 28).

CHAPTER XXIII. On Martyrdom.

1. A servant of God is not broken by any adversity, but voluntarily offers himself to the struggle in defense of the truth, and never loses confidence in the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0589C]

CHAPTER XXIII, no. 2. In this chapter Isidore gives the name “martyr” not only to those who gloriously suffered the final death for Christ, but also to those whom no cruelty of torture could lead away from confessing the name of Christ. Cyprian, the distinguished praiser of martyrs, does the same everywhere. Tertullian, however, calls the former simply martyrs, while he calls the latter “designated martyrs.” LOAISA.]

2. Often those chosen for martyrdom come from among the disciples; they precede their teachers to the crown, and those who are last in rank sometimes become first in the contest.

[Note: [Col. 0589D]

3. All the old codices without exception read: “A holy man ought voluntarily to offer himself to justice in the arena of combat.” They remove the negation *non* (“not”), but in that form the meaning does not fit what follows: “Yet, seeing the exceedingly abundant fruit of the contest, he ought not to avoid the danger of labor.” I therefore think that the negation, as it appears in the printed editions, should be retained.

Thomas, *Summa*, II–II, question 124, says: “Martyrdom, when offered, ought to be endured patiently, but it ought not to be sought, because one ought not to give occasion for acting unjustly.” Thus he speaks. Hence Cyprian fled martyrdom, as is clear from book I of his *Letters*, and Athanasius, as is evident from the homily on Matthew, chapter X, and from his *Apology for His Flight*, near the middle. Hence Cyprian elegantly says in Letter 83: “The Lord preferred that we confess rather than profess.”

But what shall we say about those virgins who, out of love for chastity and modesty, so that they might not be shamefully violated, brought death upon themselves by water, sword, or noose? The holy Church also numbers them among the holy martyrs, as is clear from Saint Ambrose, book III *On Virgins*, addressed to his sister Marcellina, concerning the death of Pelagia and her daughters; from Eusebius of Caesarea, book VIII of *Ecclesiastical History*, concerning the virgins of Antioch; and from Sophronia, who killed herself so as not to suffer violence from Maxentius.

Jerome, commenting on Jonah, chapter I, on the words “Take me up and cast me into the sea,” says: “It is not for us to seize death, but willingly to accept death inflicted by others. Therefore, during persecutions, it is not permitted to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered; rather, one should submit one’s neck to the one striking.”

Augustine, however, in book I of *The City of God*, proves in many chapters that under no circumstances is it lawful for a person to inflict death upon himself. If one should say that this is permitted so that the integrity of virginity may not be lost, he replies that the sanctity of the body is not lost while the sanctity of the soul remains.

Yet in the same book, as though somewhat relaxing the rigor of his position, he concludes the question in this way:

“But, they say, certain holy women, during the persecution, so that they might escape those pursuing their chastity, threw themselves into a river that would carry them away and kill them, and in this way died; and their martyrdoms are celebrated in the Catholic Church with the greatest veneration. I do not dare to judge rashly concerning them. For whether divine authority persuaded the Church, through trustworthy testimonies, to honor their memory in this way, I do not know. It may indeed be so. What if they did this not because they were deceived by human judgment, but because they were commanded by God—not in error, but in obedience? As in the case of Samson, we are not permitted to believe otherwise. When God commands, and makes it known without any ambiguity that he commands, who would call obedience a crime? Who would accuse an act of pious submission?”

Thus Augustine. From his words one may incidentally note against the heretics of our own time that the Church honors her saints because she has been persuaded by divine authority.

The case of Razias is also usually brought into this question, concerning whom see II Maccabees XIV. Saint Augustine disapproves of it in book II *Against the Second Letter of Gaudentius*, chapter 23, and in Letter 61 to Dulcitius, where he says that Razias is praised not because he killed himself but because he was a vigorous man and a lover of his city and country. Otherwise, it is shameful for a person impatient of spirit to lay hands upon himself, as Aristotle teaches in book III of the *Ethics*, chapter 10. Hence Cicero goes astray in book I of *On Duties*, where, praising Cato’s death, he asserts that it is honorable and lawful for a brave man, when circumstances require it, to destroy himself by violent action. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “Paul,” etc. This is clear from Acts XIX. When Paul wished to go out to the people, his disciples would not permit him. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere.
