Vezzosius does not approve Loaisa’s reasoning that, if the negation is removed, the meaning does not fit what follows, “yet, seeing the fruit of the contest,” etc. Loaisa’s note contained an error: “but nevertheless, if, seeing the fruit of the contest,” perhaps arising from the fact that some printed editions read, “but nevertheless, if he sees the fruit of the contest,” etc. In the same note I corrected *de sententiae suae rigore* to *de sententiae vigore*. In any case, it cannot be denied that the more fitting sense results when the negation is supplied.

Florezius, volume X of *Hispania Sacra*, chapter 10, composed an apology for the martyrs of Córdoba during the Saracen persecution, who voluntarily offered themselves to the struggle in defense of the truth. They were also defended by that most glorious martyr of Christ, Saint Eulogius of Córdoba.

Florezius observes that the words of Saint Thomas cited by Loaisa are not found at that question, II–II, 124, but rather at article 3, reply to objection 1, where he says: “Because of zeal for the faith and fraternal charity, the holy martyrs are often read to have voluntarily offered themselves to martyrdom.” Whether, and when, a voluntary offering of oneself to martyrdom is lawful, Benedict XIV explains with great learning in *On the Beatification of the Saints*, book III, chapter 16. AREV.]

3. A holy man ought not voluntarily to offer himself for righteousness in the struggle of combat; yet, seeing that the fruit of the contest is exceedingly abundant, he ought not to avoid the danger of labor. But if the labor is greater than the gain of souls, the labor should be avoided when only the smallest increase accompanies it. The Apostle did both: he voluntarily exposed himself to dangers where he saw the greatest gain of souls, and wisely withdrew from danger where he perceived that the labor outweighed the gain.

Paul voluntarily exposed himself to danger at Ephesus, because there he saw that gain was preferable to danger. At Damascus, however, he withdrew himself from danger because he judged that the danger itself would produce no fruit.

4. Learn how someone voluntarily offers himself to martyrdom, or how, according to the sentence of God, he is girded by another and led where he does not wish to go: both because, for the sake of future glory, the righteous person rejoices in the contest, and because, on account of the violence of suffering, he recoils from undergoing what causes pain.

5. Receive an example of approaching martyrdom with trembling from the practice of warfare. In battle, a person trained for combat both enters the struggle boldly and is moved by fear to hesitate.

[Note: [Col. 0591D]

6. Others: “concerning the incisions of wounds.” AREV.]

6. Likewise, receive an example of martyrdom from the restoration of the human body to health: each person rejoices in the hope of recovery, yet grieves at the incisions as though they were bitterest cups.

CHAPTER XXIV. On the Miracles of the Saints.

[Note: [Col. 0591D]

CHAPTER XXIV, no. 1. From Gregory, homily 29. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “There was more,” etc. This is established by Luke X: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The venerable and holy Bede also proves this learnedly in his commentary on John I. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “It is better to live well,” etc. Cyprian elegantly proves this in his sermon *On the Unity of the Church*, from Matthew VII: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and in your name perform many mighty works? And then I will say to them: I never knew you; depart from me, you who work iniquity.” Thus Cyprian reads the passage; the Vulgate edition has instead: “Many will say on that day,” etc.; and, “Then I will confess to them that I never knew you. Depart from me.” Saint Ambrose likewise proves the point in his commentary on I Corinthians XII, explaining the words: “And I will show you a still more excellent way.” LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. Loaisa’s note read: “Behold, he gave you,” which I corrected from the Gospel. AREV.]

1. Although the power of signs was given to the Apostles to nourish the faith of the nations, the power of works was nevertheless given to the Church to adorn that same faith. Yet even among the Apostles the power of works was more wondrous than the power of signs. So also now, in the Church, living well is greater than performing signs.

[Note: [Col. 0592C]

2. Augustine also gives reasons why miracles have now ceased in the Church, in book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 13, in *On True Religion*, chapter 25, and Ambrose does so at the end of his commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XII. Saint Gregory, book XXVII of the *Morals*, teaches that the Church once needed the assistance of miracles but no longer does:

“Paul, the distinguished preacher, came to Miletus, a place full of unbelievers. Knowing that Publius’s father was afflicted with dysentery and fevers, he saved him by prayer; yet, when Timothy was ill, he gave him the instruction: ‘Use a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses.’” LOAISA.]

2. The reason why the Church now does not perform the miracles that it performed under the Apostles is that at that time the world had to be brought to faith through miracles, whereas now the world, already believing, must shine through good works. Signs were therefore performed outwardly then so that faith might be strengthened inwardly.

[Note: [Col. 0592D]

3. From Gregory, book XXVII of the *Morals*, chapter 14. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “He medicinally moderates.” Another reading: “he medicinally restores.” AREV.]

3. Whoever now seeks miracles within the faith seeks empty glory, desiring to be praised. For it is written: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers” (I Cor. XIV, 22). Behold, a sign is not necessary for believers who have already believed, but for unbelievers, so that they may be converted. Thus Paul, because of the unbelief of those who did not believe, cured Publius’s father of his fever by miraculous powers (Acts XXVIII, 8), but he treated the faithful Timothy in his illness not by prayer but medicinally, so that you may know that miracles are performed for unbelievers, not for believers.

[Note: [Col. 0592D]

4. From Gregory, book XXXIV of the *Morals*, chapter 2. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “More savage.” The old edition reads “stronger.” AREV.]

4. Before the Antichrist appears, powers and signs will cease from the Church, so that he may persecute it more boldly as though it were more abject. For this purpose miracles and powers will cease from the Church under the Antichrist, so that through this the patience of the saints may shine clearly, the frivolity of the rejected—who will be scandalized—may be displayed, and the audacity of the persecutors may become more savage.

181. CHAPTER XXV. On the Antichrist and His Signs.

[Note: [Col. 0592D]

CHAPTER XXV, no. 1. *Antichrist* is called in Latin “one opposed to Christ,” as Augustine states in tractate 3 on the First Canonical Letter of John, and in the little book *On the Antichrist*, if indeed that work is his, and Gregory, book XXIX of the *Morals*, chapter 6. Tertullian calls him “rebellious against Christ” in *On the Prescription against Heretics*. John I, II calls him a liar: “Who is the liar, except the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the Antichrist.” In Revelation XIII he is called “the Beast.” Paul calls him “the man of sin” and “the son of perdition” in II Thessalonians II. Many other names are attributed to him by transference and allegory in the divine Scriptures. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. On the Antichrist, the work of the very learned Malvenda is well known, to mention no others. AREV.]

1. Everyone who either does not live according to the rule of Christian profession or teaches otherwise is an antichrist.

2. Most people, however, will not see the time of the Antichrist, yet they will be found among the members of the Antichrist.

[Note: [Col. 0593C]

3. The members of the Antichrist are heretics and wicked Christians, who confess Christ with their mouths but deny him by their actions. Augustine says this in tractate 3 on the First Letter of John: “Whoever denies Christ by his actions is an antichrist.” He rightly asserts that all the perjurers, fraudsters, flatterers, drunkards, usurers, and other wicked people of this kind found in the Church are antichrists—that is, adversaries of Christ.

He holds the same concerning heretics, based on the passage from the same place: “The antichrist is the one who denies the Father and the Son. Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the antichrist.” LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. The passage is from Paul, II Thessalonians II: “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work.” On this passage Saint Thomas Aquinas says: “Just as all the good deeds of the saints before Christ were figures of Christ, so in every persecution of the Church there have been tyrants, as it were figures of the Antichrist.” The Greeks understand this passage of Paul as having been spoken about Nero; Saint Ambrose also holds this view in his commentary on the passage. LOAISA.]

3. Before the Antichrist comes, many of his members have preceded him, and by the merit of their wicked actions have anticipated their own head, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement that he already affirms the mystery of iniquity to be at work, even before the Antichrist is revealed (II Thess. II, 7).

4. The magnitude of the signs will cause the elect, if possible, to be led into error under the Antichrist (Matt. XXIV, 24). But if they are elect, how can they be led into error? They will therefore enter briefly into the error of hesitation because of the multitude of prodigies, but they will not be thrown down from their stability by the shock of terror and signs. Hence the phrase “if possible” is used, because the elect cannot perish; rather, quickly recovering their senses, they will restrain the error of their hearts through religion, knowing that the Lord foretold this, so that when the adversaries do these things the saints may not be disturbed.

[Note: [Col. 0593D]

5. Whether the miracles and prodigies of the Antichrist will truly occur, see Augustine, book XX of *The City of God*, chapter 19. LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “A harsher war.” How terrible the future war of the Antichrist will be is clear from Isaiah XIV: “Is this the man who stirred up the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the whole world a desert?” Cyprian reads the passage in this way and interprets it of the Antichrist in book III of his *Testimonies to Quirinus*. The Vulgate edition reads: “Is this the man who troubled the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities?” LOAISA.

Here and elsewhere. “A scruple, which nevertheless.” It would seem better to read: “a scruple which nevertheless.” AREV.]

5. When the Antichrist comes, he will perform signs and prodigies so astonishing that even among the elect a certain scruple will arise in their hearts. Yet reason will quickly prevail among them, by which they will know that the same signs are performed for the deception of the rejected and the testing of the elect. At that time the saints will be glorious through patience, not through miracles, as the earlier martyrs were. For they will have to endure both persecutors and those performing prodigies. Therefore they will endure a harsher war, because they will fight not only against persecutors but also against those who shine forth through miracles.

6. Under the rule of the Antichrist, the Synagogue will rage against the Church more severely than it persecuted Christians at the very coming of the Savior.

[Col. 0593C] [Note: [Col. 0594C]

7. “It will be more cruel,” etc. Another reading: “It will nevertheless be more cruel under the times of the Antichrist,” etc.; “he was able to do while bound—how much,” etc. AREV.]

7. Although the devil, even while bound, will already have exercised great cruelty against the martyrs, he will be more cruel under the times of the Antichrist, when he will also be released. For if he does so much while bound, how much will he do when released?

8. The nearer the devil sees the end of the world, the more cruelly he exercises persecutions, so that, because he sees himself soon to be condemned, he may multiply companions for himself with whom he will be consigned to the fires of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0594C]

9. Thus in the manuscripts and in the old edition. On the time of Antichrist’s coming, see the pious and prudent opinion of Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 93, and Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXIV, chapter 10. LOAISA.

In the same place. Others: “the briefer [time].” My codex: “the devil sees himself reigning.” AREV.]

9. The shorter the time the devil sees remaining to him before he is condemned, the more violently he is stirred by the fury of persecution, by divine justice permitting it, so that the elect may be glorified, the wicked may be made foul, and the severity of the devil’s sentence of condemnation may increase.

## 183 CHAPTER XXVI. On the Resurrection

[Col. 0594D]

[Note: CHAPTER XXVI, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IV, chapters 22 and 23. LOAISA.]

1. The beginning of the saints’ peace is in this life, not its perfection. Then, however, there will be the fullness of peace, when, with the weakness of the flesh absorbed in the contemplation of God, they have grown strong.

[Col. 0594B] [Note: [Col. 0594D]

2. Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapters 14 and 15. LOAISA.

In the same place. Saint Augustine interprets the passage from Paul to the Ephesians and discusses the age at which we shall rise. AREV.]

2. The resurrection of the dead, as the Apostle says, will be “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians IV, 13)—that is, in the age of youth, which has no need of further growth and, without any decline toward decay, is complete and strong in perfection on both sides.

[Note: [Col. 0594D]

3. The faithful are called sons of God by adoption. First Epistle of John III: “Behold,” he says, “what manner of charity the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called, and should be, the sons of God.” And immediately afterward: “Now we are the sons of God” (namely, by grace), “and it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” LOAISA.]

3. Although faithful human beings are now called by the name “sons of God” (Romans VIII, 14), nevertheless, because they still suffer this slavery of corruption and remain subject to the yoke of servitude, they will receive the full freedom of the sons of God, “when this corruptible hath put on incorruption” (I Corinthians XV, 53).

4. Now God is known through a mirror; in the future, however, each of the elect will be presented face to face (I Corinthians XIII, 12), so that he may contemplate that very form which he now strives to see through a mirror.

5. In this life, the Church of God is said to be filled with the number of the elect, who belong on the right, and of the reprobate, who will go to the left; but at the end of the age they will be separated, like weeds from the grain.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Judgment

[Col. 0595A]

[Note: [Col. 0595C]

CHAPTER XXVII, no. 1. “But in the Gospel he did not wish to say that he knew it to the disciples.” Some manuscripts read this way. Otherwise, the Gothic version of Toledo, the most faithful of all, agrees with the printed edition. The passage is Mark XIII, in these words: “But of that day or hour no man knoweth, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father.” And Matthew XXIV: “But of that day and hour no man knoweth, neither the Son of man.” For an interpretation of these passages, see Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 6; Jerome, on Matthew; Ambrose, *On the Faith*, Book V, chapter 8; Theophylact, on Mark, chapter 13; Gregory, *Commentary on 1 Kings*, Book III. All these Fathers say that the Son did not know the day of judgment because he did not wish to disclose it to human beings. Other, more recent teachers say that Christ, insofar as he was man, did not know the day of judgment by natural knowledge. For God alone knows by his natural knowledge the times and moments which the Father has placed in his own power. Hence Matthew, chapter XXIV, adds, “neither the Son of man.” For insofar as he is the Word, he knows it, as does the Father. Basil also seems to follow this interpretation in his letter to Amphilochius, when he interprets these passages of Matthew and Mark. That it is hidden from all the others is confirmed by many testimonies of sacred Scripture. Matthew XXIV: “As in the days of Noe, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.” Luke XVI: “As it came to pass in the days of Lot,” and so forth. And 1 Thessalonians V: “When they shall say, Peace and security, then shall sudden destruction come upon them.” And in the same place: “The day of the Lord shall so come as a thief in the night”; and Luke XII: “At what hour you think not, the Son of man will come.” And elsewhere: “Watch, because you know not the day nor the hour.” Revelation III: “I will come to thee as a thief, and thou shalt not know at what hour I will come to thee.” LOAISA.

In the same place. On the kind of knowledge by which Christ knows the day of judgment, Vezzosius should also be consulted, in his note on chapter 21 of Epiphanius’ *Ancoratus*, part II of the *Institutes of Theology*. AREV.]

1. Christ knows the day of judgment, but in the Gospel he did not wish to tell or to make known this to the disciples. For when the same Lord says through the prophet, “The day of vengeance is in my heart” (Isaiah LXIII, 4), he indicates that he does not fail to know it, but does not wish to disclose it.

[Note: [Col. 0595D]

2. 1 Peter IV: “For the time is come that judgment should begin at the house of God,” where the Greek word for “judgment,” κρῖμα, should be understood as referring to afflictions. LOAISA.]

2. Judgment begins with the house of the Lord, as it is written (1 Peter IV, 17), when the elect—that is, the house of God—are judged here through scourges. But the wicked are to be judged there for condemnation. Hence it continues: “And if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that believe not?”

[Note: [Col. 0596C]

3. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IX, chapters 11 and 12. LOAISA.

In the same place. “So that even it,” and so forth. He has beautifully expressed the difference between the justice by which God and a human being are called just, against the deranged doctrines of the heretics of this age. Concerning this, the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 7, also says: “Finally, the single formal cause is the justice of God, not by which he himself is just, but by which he makes us just; for, being endowed by him, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and are not merely reputed but truly called and are just, receiving justice within us.” LOAISA.]

3. At the strict examination of the judge, not even the justice of the just person is secure, unless through divine mercy even that justice by which each person is just is justified by God justifying him. Otherwise, before God it too is sin. Hence Job says: “He consumeth the innocent and the wicked.” The innocent person is consumed by God when, after innocence itself has been examined more clearly and compared with divine innocence, it amounts to nothing unless the human being is there also justified through the merciful goodness of God. The wicked person is likewise consumed by God when, examined by the subtlety of divine judgment, his wickedness is exposed, judged, and condemned.

4. The innocent and the wicked alike are consumed at the end of the flesh, not by the punishment of condemnation.

5. The learned and the unlearned alike die, but by the death of the flesh, not by the punishment of condemnation. All go to one place, since by bodily death both the just and the wicked return to the earth (Ecclesiastes II, 16; III, 20). Their recompense, however, is unlike, as Solomon himself says: “What hath the wise man more than the fool, except he go to that place where there is life?” (Ecclesiastes VI, 8). Therefore all alike return to the earth; but they do not alike go to the place where there is life.

6. The wicked is punished by a twofold sentence: either here, according to his merits, he is struck with blindness of mind, so that he does not see the truth; or at the end he will be condemned, so that he may pay the penalties he deserves.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

7. “Nor are they judged there.” Thus it is in all the manuscripts; this reading seems to agree with that saying of Paul, 1 Corinthians XI: “If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged.” It also agrees with the saying in Wisdom: “Before judgment prepare justice.” LOAISA.

In the same place. “For purification.” John XV: “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit, he will take away; and every one that beareth fruit, he will purge it.” Gregory: The fruitful branch is said to be purged because, through discipline, it is pruned for more abundant grace. LOAISA.

In the same place. Some printed editions read, “nor are they condemned there,” which is rightly rejected. AREV.]

7. Divine judgment is twofold: one by which human beings are judged both here and in the future; the other by which they are judged here for this purpose, that they may not be judged there. Therefore, for some, temporal punishment is beneficial here for purification; but for others, condemnation begins here, and there perfect destruction is expected.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

8. The Gothic version reads, “they will see in which he was judged”; this is not a bad reading. The statement is found in Augustine, on John, tractate 23, and *On the Trinity*, Book I, chapters 3, 16, and 17. It is also in the *Sentences* of the Master, Book IV, distinction 48. LOAISA.

In the same place. “His divinity.” From Isaiah XXVI: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he see not the glory of God.” LOAISA.]

8. At the judgment the reprobate will see Christ’s humanity, in which he was judged, so that they may grieve; but they will not see his divinity, lest they rejoice. For those to whom divinity is revealed are certainly shown it for joy.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

9. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXV, chapters 5 and 6. The statement is taken from Paul, Romans II: “Their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts between themselves accusing, or also defending one another, in the day when God shall judge the secrets of men.” Ambrose also interprets this passage in the same way. LOAISA.]

9. According to the differing consciences, Christ will appear gentle in judgment to the elect and terrifying to the reprobate. For each person will have the kind of judgment corresponding to the conscience he has brought with him; while Christ remains in his own tranquility, he will appear terrifying only to those whose conscience accuses them of evil.

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

10. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXVI, chapter 24, and the Master, Book IV, distinction 97. LOAISA.

[Col. 0597C] In the same place. “Are not to be judged.” According to John III: “He that believeth not is already judged”; and Paul, Romans II: “For whosoever have sinned without the law shall perish without the law.” LOAISA.

In the same place. Many other Fathers recognize a distinction between the wicked, or unbelievers, and Christian sinners; they say that sinners are to be judged, whereas the wicked have already been judged. See *Prudentiana*, page 153, no. 179. AREV.]

10. There are two differences, or orders, of human beings at the judgment, namely, the elect and the reprobate; yet these are divided into four groups. There is one order of the perfect, which judges with the Lord, and another which is judged; nevertheless, both will reign with Christ. Similarly, the order of the reprobate is divided into two: those who are found within the Church are to be judged and condemned, whereas those who are found outside the Church are not to be judged, but only condemned.

11. The first order, then, of those who are judged and perish is opposed to that order of the good which consists of those who are judged and reign. The second order, of those who are not judged and perish, is opposed to that order of the just in which are those who are not judged and reign. The third order, of those who are judged and reign, is contrary to that order which consists of those who are judged and perish. The fourth order, of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed to that contrary order in which are those who are not judged and perish.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Gehenna

[Col. 0597B]

[Note: [Col. 0597D]

CHAPTER XXVIII, no. 1. Theophylact, commenting on Matthew X on the words, “But rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body into hell,” says: “When he said ‘Gehenna,’ he signified perpetual punishment; for Gehenna is so called from ‘always being born.’ This is that worm of which Isaiah says: ‘Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.’” To this corresponds the passage about Tityus, as it appears in the poets:

> And the huge vulture with its crooked beak,
>
> Beating his immortal liver, and raking
>
> His organs fertile in punishments, and living
>
> Beneath his lofty breast, nor granting rest
>
> To the reborn entrails.

LOAISA.]

1. The punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold: their mind is burned by sorrow, and their body by flame, in correspondence with one another, so that those who conceived in their minds what they would accomplish in the body may be punished both in soul and in body.

[Note: [Col. 0597D]

2. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IX, chapter 39. LOAISA.

In the same place. Petavius, *On Angels*, Book III, chapter 5, proves chiefly from the testimonies of Augustine and Gregory that the fire of hell is corporeal; he adds Isidore as well, but notes that no decree of faith concerning that corporeal fire exists. AREV.]

2. The fire of Gehenna has light in one respect and lacks it in another: it has light for condemnation, so that the wicked may see the source of their grief; and it lacks light for consolation, so that they may not see the source of their joy.

[Note: [Col. 0598C]

3. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.]

3. The furnace of the three boys provides a fitting comparison as an example of the fire of Gehenna. For just as that fire did not burn for the punishment of the three boys, but did burn to consume the bonds with which they were tied, so the fire of Gehenna will shine for the wretched to increase their punishments, so that they may see the source of their grief, but will not shine for consolation, lest they see the source of their joy.

[Note: [Col. 0598C]

4. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IX, chapter 38. LOAISA.]

4. There is a great distinction between the misery of this life and that of future unhappiness. There, there is both misery because of the torment of pains and darkness because of the withdrawal of light. Of these, one—misery—is found in this life, while the other is not; in hell, however, both are found.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Punishments of the Wicked

[Col. 0598A]

[Note: [Col. 0598C]

CHAPTER XXIX, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IX, chapter 39. LOAISA.

[Col. 0598D] In the same place. “Bundles of wood.” See my notes on verse 681 of Book III of Dracontius:

> And, received into the bundle of evils, I shall give thanks.

AREV.]

1. Just as bundles of wood are gathered from similar pieces for burning (Matthew XIII, 30), so on the day of judgment those guilty of similar faults will be joined to their like, so that punishment may bind together equally, as in a bundle, those whom their actions have made alike in evil.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

2. From Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.

In the same place. “Nor will there be lacking,” and so forth. Thus in the Gothic version and other manuscripts; but in one very ancient manuscript it is read: “Nor will the order of condemnation that is to be in the day of punishment be lacking.” LOAISA.]

2. Just as each saint will be glorified in the future judgment according to the measure of his virtues, so each wicked person will be condemned according to the measure of his crimes. Nor will there be lacking an order of condemnation in the future punishment; rather, as the Prophet affirms, there will be a distinction of punishments according to the character of the crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

3. Psalm CVIII: The Vulgate edition reads: “Let his children be continually wandering and begging.” The Hebrew text has: “Let his children wander about.” “Continually wandering” means that they should wander without stability; “begging,” that they should wander about and become vagrants. LOAISA.]

3. Punishment is also added to the dead on account of the sufferings of their dear ones, as the Gospel discourse tells of the rich man in the underworld (Luke XVI, 19); and the Psalm also says, for the increase of Judas’s punishment: “Let his children be moved with continual agitation, and let them beg” (Psalm CVIII, 9).

4. The wicked will therefore be punished more harshly in the judgment by the anguish of mind arising from seeing that the just have deserved the blessedness of glory.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

5. Revelation XX sets out the order of judgment, as does Paul in 1 Corinthians XV. LOAISA.]

5. The devil must be cast down in the sight of all, when, before the eyes of all the good angels and human beings, he is to be sent into the eternal fire together with those who will be on his side.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

6. “Who are to be found in the body.” See Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXIV, chapter 7, and Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, chapter 20, together with Vezzosius’s note, part III of the *Institutes of Theology*, page 283 and following. AREV.]

6. When the devil has been raised up in order to be condemned, many of the elect who are to be found in the body will be shaken with fear when the Lord comes to judgment, seeing that the wicked one has been punished by such a sentence. By this terror they are to be purified, because, if any remnant of sin from the body still remains in them, they will be purified by the very fear with which they behold the devil being condemned. Hence Job says: “When he shall be lifted up, the angels shall fear, and being affrighted shall be purified” (Job XLI, 16).

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

7. The passage is Amos VII: “Behold, the Lord God will call judgment to the fire, and it shall devour the great abyss, and shall consume the portion.” The reading “of the house,” which is found in Isidore, appears in no copy of the Bible, nor in the Septuagint version, whose words are: Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν τὴν δίκην ἐν πυρὶ καὶ κατέφαγεν τὴν μερίδια, “And he called judgment in fire and consumed the portion.” Jerome says: “He consumed the portion,” that is, he reached his saints, who are reckoned among the Lord’s possession and as belonging to his portion. Theodoret, on the same passage, says: “He calls Israel the portion.” For Moses also says: “And the Lord’s portion became his people, Jacob.” LOAISA.]

7. Many of those who now appear to be elect and holy can perish on the day of judgment, as the prophet says: “The Lord will call judgment to the fire, and it shall devour the great abyss and consume the portion of the house.” A portion of the house will indeed be devoured, because hell will also swallow those who now boast that they are among the heavenly commandments. Of them the Lord says: “Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name, and in thy name cast out devils, and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then I will confess to them, I never knew you: depart from me, you that work iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Matthew VII, 22–23).

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Glory of the Saints

[Note: [Col. 0600B]

CHAPTER XXX, no. 1. From Gregory, homily 40. It is found in the Master, Book IV, distinction 50. LOAISA.]

1. In the future, the heart of the just will not be made sorrowful by compassion for the condemned, where the saints’ joy in the contemplation of God will be so great that sorrow will be granted no entrance.

2. Just as, when compared with black, a white color becomes more beautiful, so the saints’ rest will be more glorious when compared with the condemnation of the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 0600B]

3. In the printed edition it was “just as”; but the Gothic version reads: “Thus justice grows through injustice, thus virtue through vice.” Therefore the glory of the saints increases, so that it is the fulfillment of the preceding statement; the same reading is found in nearly all the old codices. LOAISA.

In the same place. Others: “Thus virtue through vice.” Therefore the glory of the saints increases while—. AREV.]

3. Thus justice grows through injustice, and virtue through vice. Therefore the glory of the saints will increase while the wicked are condemned to the punishment they deserve.

4. After the resurrection, ascent to heaven in the flesh has been promised to the saints, Christ saying to the Father: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24). For if we are members of the head, and Christ is one in himself and in us, then wherever he has ascended, we too shall ascend.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0599]

## 190 CHAPTER I. On Wisdom

[Col. 0599B]

1. Everyone who is wise according to God is blessed. The blessed life is knowledge of divinity. Knowledge of divinity is the virtue of good work. The virtue of good work is the fruit of eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0599D]

CHAPTER I, no. 2. Jeremiah X: “Every man is become a fool by his knowledge”; in the Vulgate edition, “his” is absent, as it is also in the Septuagint: Ἐμωράνθη πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ἀπὸ γνώσεως, “Every man became foolish through knowledge.” But in the Hebrew text there is “through his knowledge,” and the holy Jerome translates it so in Jeremiah X, although in chapter 51 he has simply “through knowledge.” LOAISA.]

2. Whoever is wise according to the world is foolish according to God. Hence the prophet says: “Every man is become a fool by his knowledge” (Jeremiah X, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0599D]

3. From the holy Gregory, almost word for word; this sentence and the following one are from *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 25. LOAISA.]

3. The first object of the pursuit of knowledge is to seek God, and next, uprightness of life together with the practice of innocence.

[Note: [Col. 0599D]

4. The passage is Ecclesiasticus XXXVIII, where the Vulgate edition reads: “The wisdom of the scribe is in the time of leisure, and he that is lessened in business shall receive wisdom.” The expression “of the scribe” is not an imperative verb but a genitive, as is clear from the Greek: Σοφία γραμματέος ἐν εὐκαιρίᾳ σχολῆς, “The wisdom of the scribe in a favorable time of leisure.” The Complutensian edition has: “The wisdom of the scribe in a suitable time of leisure,” that is, it consists in or is acquired then. Some read “wisdom,” making “scribe” a nominative, so that the meaning is: scribes—that is, teachers of the law—will receive wisdom at a time when they are free and released from servile and degrading works, devoting themselves entirely to the contemplation of truth. But although this interpretation is approved by learned men, it does not agree with the Greek edition. Isidore took the passage from the holy Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 25: “No one,” he says, “will receive it clearly unless he strives to withdraw himself from every disturbance of carnal actions; hence it is also said elsewhere: ‘The wisdom of the scribe is in the time of leisure, and he who is lessened in activity will himself receive it.’” LOAISA.]

4. No one fully receives the wisdom of God unless he strives to withdraw himself from every concern with activity. Hence it is written: “The wisdom of the scribe is in the time of leisure, and he that is lessened in business shall receive it” (Ecclesiasticus XXXVIII, 25).

5. He has attained no low summit of understanding who knows that he cannot penetrate the secrets of God. God is rightly known precisely when we deny that we can know him perfectly.

[Col. 0600B] 6. Sometimes it is fitting not to know certain things. No one, however, is more culpable than the person who does not know God.

7. Many seek the investigation of truth, but few find it. Things that are above human understanding should not be scrutinized. Whatever is beyond human intellect is not to be sought. Rather, it must be reserved to divine counsel, so that this may be believed to be justice: whatever pleases the divine will. For what pleases the just judge cannot be unjust.

8. All wisdom consists of knowledge and opinion. A judgment arising from knowledge is better than one arising from opinion. The former is true; the latter doubtful.

[Note: [Col. 0600D]

9. He takes the sense from Scripture, not the words. The passage is Luke XII: “But that servant,” and so forth. LOAISA.

In the same place. “It is sin.” Others: “It is sin for him.” AREV.]

9. It adds to the measure of a greater fault for someone to know what he ought to do and not to wish to do what he knows. Hence the Lord says: “The servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it shall deservedly be beaten with many stripes” (Luke XII, 47). And James: “To him therefore who knoweth to do good, and doth it not, to him it is sin” (James IV, 17).

10. Simplicity combined with laziness is called foolishness, whereas simplicity combined with prudence is called wisdom.

11. It is useful to know many things and to live rightly. But if we cannot do both, it is better to pursue the effort to live well than to know many things.

12. Knowledge of things does not contribute to attaining blessedness, nor is the person who knows many things blessed; rather, it is a great thing to live blessedly.

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

13. “To benefit all.” Others: “It benefits a person.” AREV.]

13. It is of no benefit to know every kind of wisdom while remaining ignorant of God, nor does ignorance of the world harm those who know God. He knows perfectly who knows God and these things, not for their own sake, but for God’s sake.

14. It harms no one if, through simplicity, he holds some unworthy opinion about the elements, provided that he makes true assertions about God. For although someone may be unable to discuss incorporeal and corporeal natures, a right life together with faith nevertheless makes him blessed.

## 192 CHAPTER II. On Faith

1. No one can attain true blessedness except through faith. Blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, keeps the right faith.

2. If God is believed in, he is rightly invoked and sought; and therefore he is praised perfectly when he is invoked and believed in.

3. We must not believe only what we discern through the sense of the flesh, but rather what we behold through the understanding of the mind—that is, God. “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI, 6), for “whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Romans XIV, 23).

4. Faith is in no way extorted by force, but is commended by reason and examples. What is imposed violently cannot be maintained in those upon whom it is imposed. It is like, as someone says, a young tree: if someone forcibly bends its top, when it is released it immediately returns to what it was before.

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

CHAPTER II, no. 5. “The truth of faith.” Others: “the firmness of faith.” AREV.]

5. Just as a human being, created with free will, turns away from God of his own accord, so by the mind’s own conversion, through believing, he returns to God, so that both the freedom of the will may be acknowledged through the will itself and the benefit of grace through the truth of faith received.

6. God looks to faith in the heart, where human beings cannot excuse themselves—those who with their mouths pretend to profess the truth while in their hearts they retain the wickedness of error.

[Col. 0601D] [Note: [Col. 0601D]

7. In all printed editions it was “the confession of the mouth,” incorrectly; but in all manuscripts, “by confession of the mouth,” a reading I approve. Thus it is in Paul, Romans X: “With the heart, we believe unto justice; but, with the mouth, confession is made unto salvation.” LOAISA.

In the same place. “May be brought forth.” Others: “may profess.” AREV.]

7. Just as faith that is held in the mouth but not believed in the heart accomplishes nothing, so faith held in the heart will accomplish nothing if it is not brought forth by the mouth. Concerning such faith the prophet rebukes certain people, saying: “Faith hath perished, and is taken away from their mouth” (Jeremiah VII, 28). For the faith that is believed in the heart is brought forth for salvation by confession of the mouth (Romans X, 10).

8. Faith without works is empty, and the person who is not adorned with good works flatters himself in vain about faith alone.

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

9. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book VIII, chapter 26. LOAISA.]

9. Whoever carries the cross must also die to the world. For to bear the cross and die is to put oneself to death; to bear it and not die is hypocrisy’s pretense.

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

10. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXV, chapter 10, word for word. LOAISA.]

10. Those who possess knowledge of God through faith but obscure it by their works follow the example of Balaam, who, although he fell through his conduct, had open eyes through the faith of contemplation.

[Col. 0602B] [Note: [Col. 0601D]

11. John VI. It is also found in Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXIII, chapter 17. LOAISA.

[Col. 0602D] In the same place. “The carnal seek faith.” Others: “It belongs to the carnal to seek faith.” But do not change it, although the latter may seem clearer. AREV.]

11. Carnal people seek faith not as a virtue of the soul, but for temporal advantage. Hence the Lord says: “You seek me, not because you have seen miracles, but because you did eat of the loaves” (John VI, 26).

12. When a bad Christian does not live according to the teaching of the Gospel, he easily loses, when temptation arises, even the faith which he honors in words.

[Note: [Col. 0602D]

13. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXI, chapter 10, and Book XXVII, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

13. Many are Christians in faith alone, but in their conduct dissent from Christian teaching. Many also do not love Christ’s faith from the heart, but pretend through hypocrisy to hold to it because of human fear. Those who cannot be openly wicked are known to be falsely good through fear.

14. Lovers of the world sometimes fight for the faith and indeed benefit others; but they themselves, entangled in earthly love, do not seek heavenly things and defend the faith only in words.

[Note: [Col. 0602D]

15. “With the burden of pride.” My manuscript codex has “with the arrogance of pride,” which is perhaps better. AREV.]

15. Some even persecute heretics on behalf of the faith, but through arrogance they despise those who are within the Church. They refute the adversaries of the faith because of their unbelief, but oppress the faithful with the burden of pride.

## CHAPTER III. On Charity

[Note: [Col. 0602D]

CHAPTER III, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 14; he also adduces Paul’s testimony, 1 Corinthians XIII.

In the same place. “If I deliver up.” Thus all the manuscript codices read, as do Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, and Cassian, *Conferences* 1, *On the Appointment of Monks*, chapter 6. The passage is in Paul, 1 Corinthians XIII. In Greek: ἵνα καυθήσομαι, “that I may be burned.” LOAISA.]

1. Although some appear to share in faith and holy works, nevertheless, because they are deprived of the charity of brotherly love, they make no progress in virtue. For, as the Apostle says: “If I should deliver my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII, 3).

2. Without the love of charity, even if someone believes rightly, he cannot attain blessedness, because the power of charity is so great that even prophecy and martyrdom are believed to be nothing without it.

[Col. 0603A] [Note: [Col. 0603D]

3. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXVIII, chapter 9. LOAISA.]

3. No reward is weighed except by charity. For charity holds the primacy among all virtues. Hence the Apostle calls charity “the bond of perfection” (Colossians III, 14), because all virtues are bound together by its bond.

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

4. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book X, chapter 12; he also cites the words of the Song of Songs VIII: “strong.” LOAISA.]

4. The love of God is compared with death, Solomon saying: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs VIII, 6). This is because, just as death violently separates the soul from the body, so the love of God violently separates a human being from worldly and carnal love.

5. Whoever despises God’s commandments does not love God. For we do not love a king if we hate his laws.

6. Unity of charity must be maintained with holy men; and the more each person separates himself from the world, the more necessary it is that he join the fellowship of the good.

7. Charity consists in love of God and of neighbor. The person who is not separated from love of neighbor preserves love of God within himself. Whoever is separated from brotherly fellowship is deprived of participation in divine charity. Nor can the person who is known to err in love of neighbor love God. Christ is God and man. Therefore, whoever hates the human being does not love the whole Christ.

8. It is characteristic of the discerning good not to hate persons but faults, and not to reject what is rightly said as false, but to test it.

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

9. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XI, chapter 5. LOAISA.

In the same place. Other printed editions and manuscripts: “They often resolve to separate themselves from vices.” AREV.]

9. Those who are imperfect in the love of God often resolve to overcome their vices; but weighed down by the burden of vices, they turn back again to the vices they desire to abandon.

## 195 CHAPTER IV. On Hope

[Col. 0603C]

1. Those who do not cease to do evil seek forgiveness from God’s mercy in a vain hope; they would seek it rightly if they ceased from their evil conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

CHAPTER IV, no. 2. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XX, chapter 7, and Book XXXIII, chapter 11.

In the same place. Some have *adducit* instead of *addicit*; but *addicit* is genuine, as is noted on Deuteronomy XIX, 3. AREV.]

2. We must greatly fear both that, because of the hope of forgiveness which God promises, we may sin persistently, and that, because he justly punishes sins, we may despair of forgiveness. Avoiding both dangers, we should turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from the mercy of God. For every just person shines through hope and fear: now hope raises him up to joy, now the terror of Gehenna assigns him to fear.

## CHAPTER V. On Grace

[Col. 0604A]

1. Sometimes, when we are sinning, God does not withdraw his gifts from us, so that the human mind may rise toward hope of divine reconciliation. For he cannot despise the person who has turned back, whom, while sinning, he summons through his benefits to return to him.

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

CHAPTER V, no. 2. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 23. LOAISA.]

2. A human being’s confession is not the product of human virtue. For if God does not work in us the confession of a good work, why does the prophet say: “Confession and magnificence is his work” (Psalm CX, 3)? All good things are given to us by him, grace going before us. For we have offered no good work by which we might deserve to receive the confession of faith.

3. Human progress is God’s gift. No one can correct himself by his own power, but only by the Lord. A human being has nothing good of his own, for his way is not his own, as the prophet testifies: “I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his; neither is it in a man to walk and to direct his steps” (Jeremiah X, 23).

## 196 [Note: [Col. 0603D]

4. Hosea XIII. The Vulgate edition reads: “Thy destruction is thy own, O Israel; only in me is thy help.” In the Septuagint: “Who will help you in your destruction, O Israel?” The holy Jerome interprets Hosea according to this sense. LOAISA.

In the same place. “To be able to do nothing.” Others: “human beings can do nothing.” Below, the old edition agrees with the Vulgate, except that it has “only” for “merely.” AREV.]

4. Let the defenders of free will know that their own power can accomplish nothing toward the good unless they are supported by the help of divine grace. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Thy destruction is from thyself, O Israel; thy help is only in me” (Hosea XIII, 9). As though he were saying: “That you may perish is by your own merit; that you may be saved is by my help.”

[Note: [Col. 0604D]

5. From the holy Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XVIII, chapter 23, almost word for word. It should be noted that the robber was led to punishment on account of fratricide. LOAISA.

In the same place. The assertion that the robber, who confessed and experienced the Savior on the cross, was guilty of fratricide was, I think, taken from the apocryphal and pseudepigraphal books fabricated in great number during the early centuries of the Church. AREV.]

5. Heavenly grace does not find human merit already present so that it may come; rather, after it has come, it creates merit. Coming to a mind that was unworthy, it makes in that mind the merit which the one who had found only what he might punish may reward. For what did that robber deserve from himself, who climbed from the devil’s jaws to the cross and went from the cross to paradise? He was indeed guilty and came stained with his brother’s blood, but by divine grace he was changed on the cross. It must be understood that our justice is involved in the things we do rightly, and God’s grace in the fact that we deserve it. For this belongs both to God who gives and to the human being who receives. Thus we call it “our bread,” although we ask God to give it to us.

[Note: [Col. 0604D]

6. He is speaking of the grace of perseverance; concerning justifying grace, see the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 17. LOAISA.

In the same place. Isidore seems to understand “the work of faith” as the gift of perseverance. AREV.]

6. Spiritual grace is not distributed to everyone, but is given only to the elect. For faith is not possessed by all; although very many receive it, they do not attain the work of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0604D]

7. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXIV, chapter 6, and Homily 10 on Ezekiel.

In the same place. “For what,” and so forth. Ezekiel I. Gregory interprets it in this way in Homily 3 on Ezekiel. LOAISA.]

7. In the distribution of gifts, different people receive different gifts of God [Col. 0605A]; yet all are not granted to one person, so that, for the sake of cultivating humility, each may admire in another what he himself does not possess. For when, in Ezekiel, the wings of the living creatures strike against one another (Ezek. I), the virtues of the saints are signified: they mutually incite one another through reciprocal affection and instruct one another by alternating example.

8. Some receive these gifts of grace, others those. They are not given to one person in such a way that he has no need of another’s gift.

197

[Note: [Col. 0605C]

9. “They are made.” Perhaps it should read “they may be made.” AREV.]

9. There is no doubt that those whom some surpass in excellence of virtue may, when suddenly anticipated by the grace of God, overtake certain others by a shortened path to holiness; and although they are last in conversion, they suddenly become first in the summit of virtue.

10. When each person receives some gift, let him not desire more than he has deserved, lest, while he attempts to seize the function of another member, he lose what he has deserved. For anyone who, not content with his own function, usurps another’s disturbs the entire order of the body.

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

11. “Because it is not for the praise of God.” Another reading: “because they use them not for the praise of God.” AREV.]

11. The wicked receive gifts for condemnation because they use them not for the praise of God but for their own vanity. They misuse good things who employ for evil purposes what has been bestowed on them by God, such as intelligence and the other gifts of God.

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

12. “That we are wise, that we are rich, that we are powerful.” AREV.]

12. We rejoice in many gifts of God, which we recognize that we have received from him. That we are wise and that we are powerful is due not to another but rather to a divine gift. Let us therefore use God’s benefits in the best possible way, so that God may not regret having given them and so that our having received them may be beneficial to us.

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

13. In Exodus IV, it is said to Moses concerning Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart.” Gregory, *Moralia* XI, chapter 5: “God is said to harden, through justice, when he does not soften a reprobate heart through grace”; and in his exposition of “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Homily 11 on Ezekiel): “The Lord does not harden the heart of the sinner; he is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness.” LOAISA.]

13. God is said to take away some gift from a person that the person did not have—that is, that he did not deserve to receive. Likewise, God is said to harden a person, not by making his hardness, but by not taking away the hardness that he himself has fostered. In the same way God is said to blind certain people, not because he himself creates that blindness in them, but because, on account of the uselessness of their merits, he does not remove their blindness from them.

14. God’s gifts are given to many, but perseverance in the gift is not given. Hence some possess the beginnings of a good conversion but are brought to an end by an evil conclusion. The elect, however, receive both the gift of conversion and perseverance in the gift. That is therefore why some both begin well and end well.

198

CHAPTER VI. On Predestination.

[Col. 0606A]

[Note: [Col. 0605D]

CHAPTER VI, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIII, chapter 20. LOAISA.

On the same passage. “And permit the reprobate always to pursue the lowest and outward things by abandoning them.” Most manuscript copies read: “and permit the reprobate always, by abandoning them, to take delight in the lowest and outward things”; so that it may be questioned whether the expression *infima et exteriora delectari* (“to delight in the lowest and outward things”), instead of *infimis et exterioribus delectari* (“to delight in the lowest and outward things”), is peculiar to Isidore’s period. See Book II of the *Synonyms*, no. 5, with its note; and *Isidoriana*, chapter 43, no. 34, and chapter 94, no. 37, where, from Vatican Codex 657, I noted this variant: “that they may take delight in the lowest and outward things.” Chapter 30 of the *Isidoriana* should also be reread. There the teaching of Saint Isidore on predestination is defended against Hincmar of Reims, who likewise read in Isidore: “that they may take delight in the lowest and outward things.” AREV.]

1. Predestination is twofold: that of the elect to rest and that of the reprobate to death. Both are governed by divine judgment, so that he always makes the elect follow heavenly and inward things, while he permits the reprobate, by abandoning them, to take delight in the lowest and outward things.

2. Just as a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so he knows still less who, before his end, will be anticipated by the light of righteousness, who will remain darkened by the darkness of sins until his end, or who, converted after falling into darkness, will rise again to the light. All these things are open to God but hidden from human beings.

[Col. 0606B]

3. Although the conduct of the righteous in this life is commendable, it nevertheless remains uncertain to human beings to what end they have been predestined; everything is reserved for the future judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0606D]

4. “It is given to the one who wills,” and so forth. The whole sentence is taken from Saint Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX, chapter 18. LOAISA.

On the same passage. Some copies erroneously read: “It is given to him, who wishes to be good, that he is evil.” The reading supplied by others is less objectionable: “This one stands in the good so long as …” AREV.]

4. Wondrous is the arrangement of the heavenly distribution, by which the righteous person is made still more righteous and the impious still more filthy (Rev. XXII); the evil person is sometimes converted to good, and the good person sometimes turns back to evil. One wishes to be good but is unable; another wishes to be evil but is not permitted to perish. It is given to the one who wishes to be good; another neither wishes nor is given the opportunity to be good. One is born in error and dies in it; another perseveres to the end in the good with which he began. This one stands until he falls; that one, after living badly for a long time, is saved at the end, and, having been regarded with favor, is converted.

[Col. 0606C]

199

5. The righteous person wishes to be useful in goodness but does not prevail; the evil person wishes to do harm and succeeds. One wishes to devote himself to God but is hindered by the world; the other desires to become involved in worldly business but does not accomplish it.

6. The evil person rules over the good; the good person is condemned in place of the impious; the impious is honored in place of the righteous. Amid such great obscurity, a human being cannot investigate the divine arrangement or weigh the hidden order of predestination.

CHAPTER VII. On Converts.

[Note: [Col. 0606D]

CHAPTER VII, no. 1. “Converts” is the general name given to all who serve God in the monastic life, as in Pachomius, in the Rule, and in Cassian, Book IV, *On the Institutes of Those Who Renounce the World*, chapter 1. Those who renounce the world are called converts; now, in monastic orders, lay members are called “converts.” LOAISA.

[Col. 0607C] On the same passage. “Not to those who begin,” and so forth. From the older printed editions: “The reward is promised not to those who begin but is given to those who persevere”; all manuscripts read this way. LOAISA.

[Col. 0607D] On the same passage. Some omit *not*; others add *is given* after *to those who persevere*. My manuscript reads: “Rewards are promised not to those who begin but are given to those who persevere.” Loaisa also noted other matters concerning converts in Book III, chapter 15, no. 3. Some people published an excerpt from these chapters under the title *On Converts*, as though it were a separate work of Isidore, as I explained in *Isidoriana*, chapter 68, nos. 7 and following; there I also transcribed the prefaces of Canisius and Constantine Cajetan. Here he added some notes, or variant readings, from his manuscript copy, several of which we shall indicate; it is better to omit the rest, since that copy was extremely corrupt. AREV.]

1. The reward is promised not to those who begin but to those who persevere, as it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22; XXIV, 13).

[Note: [Col. 0607D]

2. Ecclesiastes II. Gregory, Book VI of his exposition of the First Rule, chapter 13, interprets the passage thus: “Those who do not complete the good things they begin lose perseverance.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. “To the one who perseveres,” and so forth. Another reading: “If we do not lose perseverance at the end,” that is, the good work, and so forth. AREV.]

2. Our conversion is pleasing to God when we bring the good work that we begin to completion with a persevering end. For it is written: “Woe to those who have lost perseverance,” that is, who have not completed the good work (Eccles. II, 16).

[Note: [Col. 0608C]

3. Gregory proves this in *Moralia* V, chapter 8, and Book IX, final chapter. LOAISA.]

3. It must be understood where, when, and to whom forgiveness of sins is given. Where, indeed? Unless within the Catholic Church? When, unless before the day of our coming departure? For, behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. VI, 2). To whom, unless to converts, who through humility pass over into imitation of little children? Of these it is said: “For to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 14).

[Col. 0607B]

4. No one can weigh how great is the weight of righteousness, or with how great a radiance righteousness shines, unless he first turns wholly to God with all the striving of his mind, so that by the very light with which he is illuminated he may both recognize his own foulness and understand the light that, with a blind heart, he did not perceive.

5. Divine righteousness, which cannot be reached, can then be understood when someone, having converted, attempts to follow it, because light is not understood unless it is seen.

6. The judgment that lies within human power is the grace of conversion, by which we judge ourselves when, weeping, we punish our evils and cling more firmly to the good that comes to us from God.

7. The progress of each convert is described as threefold: first, correcting evil; second, doing good; third, obtaining the reward of good work. For when the prophet says, “Untie the bundles that oppress” (Isa. LVIII, 6), this refers to the correction of evil. When he adds, “Break your bread for the hungry,” this refers to the performance of good work. When he further says, “Then your morning light will break forth,” this refers to the recompense of good work. Therefore doing good does not advance a person unless evil has first been corrected. No one can advance to the contemplation of God unless he first strives to exercise himself in good works.

8. God terrifies people in many ways, so that they may convert, even if late, and thereafter be more ashamed that they were waited for so long to return. At one time he shakes some by threats, at another by blows, and at another by revelations, so that those who disdain to convert by their own will may be corrected when moved by terrors.

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

9. This is the passage of Psalm XXXI, where it reads: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle.” The Septuagint reads it this way, as do Basil and Theodoret, understanding discipline by “bit and bridle.” Among the Greeks, a *bit* is a kind of bond, κημός (*kēmos*). Some translate “with bit and bridle,” but in Isidore’s Psalter it is “with bridle and bit.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Perhaps Egypt, which …” AREV.]

9. Most people are converted to God through devotion of mind alone; others are converted under compulsion by blows, since they were not converting through devotion, in accordance with the passage of the psalm that says: “Bind their jaws with bridle and bit, who do not draw near to you” (Ps. XXXI, 9).

10. Yet most people, when they are not converted through devotion, are struck by the goads of blows; nevertheless, they do not even feel the lash sufficiently to be corrected, as was the case with Egypt, which both suffered punishments and could not be reformed. Of such people the prophet says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. V, 3).

201

[Col. 0608B]

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

11. Gregory, *Moralia* II, chapter 19, and Book XVIII, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

11. Some secular men, swollen with pride of mind, are later converted to God and follow Christ in religious obedience; those who previously swelled with worldly eminence afterward exchange that very pride for the pursuit of humility.

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

12. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXV, chapters 7 and 10. LOAISA.

On the same passage. “They have risen.” Another reading: “They have corrected themselves.” AREV.]

12. Some have already been converted secretly; because their conversion has not come into public view, in human estimation they are still thought to be what they were. Yet in the eyes of God they have already risen. Likewise, some still appear to stand according to human judgment; yet in the eyes of God they have already fallen.

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

13. “As though of the works of the righteous.” Thus the Gothic manuscript of Toledo. “As though of the souls of the righteous,” Salamanca Gothic manuscript. LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Of the works of the righteous.” Another reading: “the works of the righteous.” AREV.]

13. Many are reprobate among human beings and elect before God; likewise, many are thought elect among human beings but are reprobate before God, as Solomon says: “I saw the wicked buried, who, while they still lived, were in the holy place and were praised in the city as though they were works of the righteous” (Eccles. VIII, 10). Let no one therefore think himself elect, lest perhaps he already be reprobate before God.

CHAPTER VIII. On the Beginnings of Converts.

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

CHAPTER VIII, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 7. LOAISA.]

1. Conversion to God is of three kinds: its beginning with sweetness, its middle with labor, and its perfection with rest. Nevertheless, some generally begin with sweetness, while others begin with the bitterness of temptations.

[Col. 0609A]

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

2. “Clean.” Thus the Salamanca Gothic manuscript. “Cleansed,” Toledo. LOAISA.]

2. Every convert should first begin from fear of sins and then pass over to desire for heavenly things. The vices we have committed must first be cleansed by tears; then, with a clear gaze of mind, let us contemplate what we seek, so that, while the darkness of sin is first wiped away from us by weeping, heavenly things may freely be perceived with the eyes of a cleansed heart.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

3. Gregory, *Moralia* IX, chapter 22. LOAISA.]

3. It is first necessary to be converted to God through fear, so that carnal allurements may be overcome by dread of future punishments. Then, once fear has been cast aside, one must pass over to love of eternal life. For perfect love casts out fear (1 John IV, 18); but the one who fears has punishment and is not perfect. Hence the Apostle also says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption” (Rom. VIII, 15), through which the punishment of sin no longer crushes us as slaves, but the love of righteousness makes us free.

[Col. 0609B]

4. Every convert must, after fear, rise up to love of God as a son and not always lie beneath fear as a slave. We show the love of our conversion when we love as a father the one whom previously, with a slavish mind, we truly feared as Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

5. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 7. LOAISA.]

5. The beginnings of converts must be nurtured by gentle methods, lest, if they begin with harshness, they become terrified and return to their former falls. For one who instructs a convert without gentleness knows how to exasperate rather than correct.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

6. “The desire, the sin.” Another reading: “the desire for sin”; or “the desire and the sin.” AREV.]

6. Each convert must first be corrected in action and afterward in thought, so that he may first restrain the wicked act and then the desire for sin, so that what no longer appears in action may in no way persist in thought.

7. Every new conversion still has an admixture of the former life. Therefore its virtue must by no means advance into public view until the old manner of life has been completely uprooted from the soul.

8. Whoever has begun to become better rather than worse must beware of being elated over the virtues he has received, lest through empty glory he fall more grievously than he previously lay fallen through the collapse of vices.

203

CHAPTER IX. On the Struggle of Converts.

1. If a convert immediately wishes to trample down all the goads of the flesh and strives to ascend to the summit of the virtues, yet still endures some adversity from the troubles of the flesh, he must not be broken, because the dispenser of good things knows how to restrain the adversities of vices by the succession of virtues.

2. Each person recognizes that he is more heavily burdened by the impulse of vices when he has drawn near to knowledge of God, just as the people of Israel were oppressed by a heavier burden by the Egyptians when divine knowledge was disclosed to them through Moses (Exod. V).

3. Before conversion, vices possess something like peace within a person; but when they are expelled, they rise up with more violent force. What formerly smiled favorably upon the sinner becomes hostile to the convert; and what had been hostile to the sinner likewise becomes favorable to the convert.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

CHAPTER IX, no. 4. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 7. LOAISA.]

4. The servant of God has many struggles arising from the recollection of past deeds; and many, even after conversion, endure the movement of lust unwillingly. Yet they do not endure it for condemnation but for testing—namely, so that they may always have an enemy against whom to shake off their inertia and resist, provided that they do not consent. Thus the servants of God should know that they have already been cleansed from sins, although they are still assailed by the intrusion of shameful thoughts.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

5. This entire sentence is taken from Gregory, Homily 2 on the Gospel, Luke XVIII, where he expounds mystically the passage about the blind man who was enlightened: “Those who went before rebuked him, so that he should be silent.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Insolence,” and so forth. Another reading: “Insolence produces in us an intention that often shuts us in through manifold deceit.” AREV.]

5. Before conversion there comes first a crowd of sins; after conversion there follows a crowd of temptations. The former thrust themselves forward lest we convert to God; the latter intrude lest we behold God with the eyes of a free heart. The insolence of the turmoil caused by both produces in us an obstruction and often closes off our intention through manifold deceit.

6. It is useful for God’s servant to be tempted after conversion, so that, through the exercise of the vices that solicit him, he may prepare his soul for virtues and be roused from the torpor of negligence.

204

CHAPTER X. On Negligent Conversion.

[Col. 0610C]

1. A negligent conversion leads many back to their former errors and loosens them during the course of their life. Therefore let every convert avoid their examples, lest, when you begin to emerge from torpor in the fear of God, you again plunge into worldly errors.

2. The lukewarm person in conversion does not recognize idle words and empty thoughts as harmful; but if he awakens from the torpor of his mind, he immediately fears as horrifying and atrocious those things that he had considered trivial.

[Note: [Col. 0610D]

CHAPTER X, no. 3. Gregory discusses sloth and deceit at length in *Moralia* IX, chapter 17; this entire sentence is derived from that passage. LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Whenever,” and so forth. Another reading: “whenever, from his gifts and benefits, we desire our own glory and human praise; and from the good work …” AREV.]

3. Deceit and sloth must be feared in every good work. We deceive God whenever, on account of our good work, we praise ourselves rather than God. We practice sloth whenever, through torpor, we perform God’s works sluggishly.

[Note: [Col. 0610D]

4. “Of divine fear.” Another reading: “of divine love.” On the same passage: “is prepared.” Another reading: “is proclaimed.” AREV.]

4. Every art of this world has energetic lovers who are extremely ready to carry it out; and this happens because it possesses the remuneration for its work in the present. But the art of divine fear has most of its followers sluggish and lukewarm, frozen by the inertia of laziness. This happens because their labor is deferred not for a present but for a future reward. Therefore, since the recompense of their reward does not immediately follow their labor, they grow weak, their hope almost dissolved. Hence great glory is prepared for those who complete the beginnings of a good conversion of life through a more solid increase, and they are prepared to earn recompense in greater splendor in proportion as they both begin and complete the labors of the difficult journey more firmly.

[Note: [Col. 0611C]

5. “Lowest.” Thus the Gothic manuscript of Toledo. “Weak,” Salamanca. LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Seeds.” Another reading: “seeds cast among thorns.” AREV.]

5. Some, at the first heat of conversion, gird themselves for the virtues; but as they progress, when they devote themselves excessively to earthly affairs, they are obscured by the dust of low desires. Hence the Lord says concerning the good seeds: “What fell among thorns—these are those who hear the word of God” (Matt. XIII), “but the anxiety of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.”

[Note: [Col. 0611D]

6. “With external concerns.” Another reading: “with concerns and external matters.” AREV.]

6. Those recently converted should by no means advance into external concerns. For if they become entangled in them, they are immediately shaken and wither together, like a little tree that has been planted but has not yet been fixed by its roots.

[Note: [Col. 0611D]

7. This occurs in Gratian, Distinction 81. In the printed editions and in the Gregorian decree, the reading is “for the salvation of the soul.” In all the Gothic manuscripts, it is “for the salvation of the mind.” LOAISA.]

7. Sometimes a change of place is beneficial to converts for the salvation of the soul. For the affection of the mind is usually changed when the place is changed. It is appropriate also to be physically torn away from the place where one has served one’s allurements; for the place where each person has lived wickedly presents to the mind’s gaze whatever he has always thought or done there.

CHAPTER XI. On the Examples of the Saints.

[Col. 0611C]

[Note: [Col. 0611D]

CHAPTER XI, no. 1. The Gothic codex and many manuscripts read as follows: “For the other examples of the perfect cannot bring the conduct of beginners to completion in good living. But the reprobate do not attend to the instructions of the good,” and so forth. One codex reads: “For certain [examples].” The phrase “unless it is shaped by the examples of perfect fathers” occurs in no manuscript codex. Nevertheless, I retained the reading of the printed codex because the sense is clearer and is supported by Gregory’s authority. In *Moralia* XXV, chapter 7, he has: “For to supply either the examples of the fathers or the Lord’s commandments in the practice of charity is like supplying fuel to a fire.” LOAISA.

[Col. 0612C] On the same passage. “Of the good,” and so forth. Another reading: “of the saints.” “For the other examples of the perfect cannot make the conduct of beginners advance toward good living. But the reprobate,” and so forth. Grial’s text had “complete,” but I restored “advance,” which Loaisa seems to have intended and which Vezzosius found in his first edition. “Complete” will have a place if it is read, as in my manuscript: “For the other … cannot complete,” and so forth. AREV.]

1. The examples of the good greatly aid the conversion or correction of mortals. The conduct of beginners cannot advance toward good living unless it is shaped by the examples of perfect fathers.

2. But the reprobate do not heed the instructions of the good, so that they may imitate them for improvement; instead, they set before themselves examples of evil people, which they use to turn the perversity of their own conduct toward what is worse.

[Note: [Col. 0612D]

3. Gregory, Homily 25 on the Gospels, at the end. LOAISA.]

3. For this purpose the falls and restorations of the saints are written down: to inspire hope of human salvation, so that no one may despair of forgiveness after falling and repenting, when he sees that the saints were restored even after their fall.

4. Those devoted to wickedness should know for what purpose the examples of the saints are set before them: namely, so that they may either have people whom they can imitate for restoration, or at least be punished more severely for disobedience in comparison with them.

[Note: [Col. 0612D]

5. Gregory, *Moralia* IX, chapter 35. LOAISA.]

5. Therefore God set the virtues of the saints before us as an example, so that, to the extent that the rewards of righteousness can be conferred upon us through imitating them, the torments for persevering in evil may be more severe.

6. For if the divine commandments by which we are admonished were lacking as an incentive to goodness, the examples of the saints would suffice for us as a law. But since God both admonishes us through his commandments and sets before us the examples of the saints’ good works, there is now no excuse for guilt: the law of God strikes our ears every day, and the examples of good deeds stir the innermost regions of our hearts.

[Col. 0612B]

7. And if we have often followed the examples of the wicked, why should we not imitate the worthy deeds of the saints that please God? If we have been ready to imitate the unrighteous for evil, why are we sluggish in imitating the righteous for good?

[Note: [Col. 0612D]

8. He alludes to Gregory, *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 6: “The life of the good is a living reading.” LOAISA.]

8. God must be entreated that the virtues he prepared for the saints as a crown may be placed before us for advancement, not for punishment. They will advance us if we wish to imitate so many examples of virtue. But if we reject rather than imitate them, they will be for our condemnation, because, although we read them, we neglected to fulfill them.

[Note: [Col. 0612D]

9. “Of an image.” The Lucerne codex adds: “Just as an image is said to be like a human being, not a human being like an image, because it is not the human being who is formed according to the painting, but the painting according to the appearance of the human being, so the one after whose image another lives is not said to be like him, but the one who takes an example from another’s virtues. For this one lives from a preceding model of virtue; the other is not the image of another’s virtue but its inventor and teacher.” AREV.]

9. Many imitate the life of the saints and take from another’s character the likeness of virtue, as though some image were held up and a painted form were fashioned from its resemblance. Thus the person who lives according to the likeness of an image becomes like the image.

10. Whoever imitates a holy man looks upon him as upon a model and sees himself in him as in a mirror, so that he may add what he recognizes to be lacking in virtue. A person considers himself less clearly by himself; but when he fixes his attention on another, he adds what is lacking in his own light.
