11. It belongs to already perfected men not merely to imitate some saint but, by looking upon the truth itself, according to whose image they were made, to practice righteousness. This is indicated by what is written: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26), because the person who understands imitates the divinity according to whose likeness he was made. Such a person is so great that he does not need a human teacher to demonstrate righteousness; by contemplating righteousness itself, he imitates it.

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

12. Gregory, *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 5. LOAISA.

On the same passage. So that we may imitate these examples of the saints, Isidore composed his book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. AREV.]

12. The examples of the saints, by which a person is built up, lead him to pursue various virtues: humility from Christ, devotion from Peter, charity from John, obedience from Abraham, patience from Isaac, endurance from Jacob, chastity from Joseph, gentleness from Moses, steadfastness from Joshua, kindness from Samuel, mercy from David, and abstinence from Daniel. Thus the holy man observes, in imitation, the other deeds of those who came before: with what labor, restraint, intention, or contrition they were performed.

CHAPTER XII. On Compunction of Heart.

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

CHAPTER XII, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, chapter 13, and Homily 22 on Ezekiel. LOAISA.]

1. Compunction of heart is humility of mind accompanied by tears, arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment.

2. Among converts, the more perfect feeling of compunction is that which drives away from itself every affection for carnal desires and fixes its intention, with the full effort of the mind, upon the contemplation of God.

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

3. Gregory, Homily 22 on Ezekiel, and elsewhere. LOAISA.]

3. There are two kinds of compunction by which the soul of each of the elect is moved on account of God: either when it considers the evils of its deeds or when it sighs with desire for eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

4. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

4. There are four qualities of feeling by which the mind of the righteous is pierced with healthy sorrow: the memory of past crimes, remembrance of future punishments, consideration of one’s pilgrimage during the length of this life, and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as quickly as possible.

[Note: [Col. 0613C]

5. From two psalms: Psalm CIII, “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble”; and Psalm XVII, “The earth was shaken and trembled”; and Psalm LXXVI, “Your flashes shone upon the world of the earth. The earth was shaken and trembled.” In Isidore’s Psalter, the passage in Psalm LXXVI reads: “Your lightnings shone upon the world of the earth; it saw, and the earth was shaken.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Each of the sinners.” Another reading: “each person, when he is among sinners.” But *quisque* can also mean *whoever*. AREV.]

5. Whenever the memory of sins pierces someone and moves him to lamentation, he should know that he is being visited by the presence of God, when inwardly he is ashamed to recall what he remembers having committed and already punishes it by repentance according to his own judgment. For Peter wept when Christ looked upon him (Matt. XXVI, 75). Hence the psalm also says: “He looked, and the earth was shaken and trembled” (Ps. XVII, 8).

6. The steps of God are the inward force in the human heart by which good desires arise so that evil may be trampled down. Whenever these things occur in a person’s heart, it must be understood that God is then present to the human heart through grace. Therefore a person should sharpen himself more intensely for compunction when he feels God working inwardly.

[Col. 0614B]

7. How the mind of the righteous person is carried away by true compunction, and how it returns weakened by the greatness of the light it has tasted, can be known by the one who has already tasted something of it.

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

8. Gregory, *Moralia* XXII, chapter 10, and Book XXIV, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

8. Some do not become their own accusers from true compunction of heart, but merely declare themselves sinners for the purpose of acquiring, through feigned humility, a standing of holiness.

CHAPTER XIII. On the Confession of Sins and Repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

CHAPTER XIII, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia* XXII, chapter 10, and *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 6, near the end. LOAISA.]

1. Each righteous person begins to be righteous from the moment he becomes his own accuser. Many, however, confess themselves sinners while nevertheless not withdrawing themselves from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0613D]

2. The Gothic manuscript and other manuscripts read: “a human being must know himself.” It should incidentally be observed, for understanding divine Scripture and this passage, that the word *human being* (*homo*) is used in the sacred writings in many ways: sometimes for nature, sometimes for guilt, and sometimes for weakness. It is used for human nature in Genesis II: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.” For guilt, Psalm LXXXI: “But you will die like human beings,” that is, like disobedient sinners. Also 1 Corinthians III: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human being?” For weakness, Jeremiah XVII: “Cursed is the human being who places his hope in a human being,” as though he openly said: he relies upon weakness and a fragile foundation. Also Isaiah XXXI: “Egypt is a human being and not God.” A person is also called a human being when he has human concerns, as Gregory noted in *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 6, citing 1 Corinthians III: “Are you not human beings?” The person who is overcome by the allurements of the flesh and the heat of desire is also called a human being, in Ezekiel XXIV: “You are human beings, the flock of my pasture.” Also Isaiah II: “The human being bowed down, and the man was humbled.” Hence carnal people are called beasts of burden, and the affections of animals are attributed to them. Joel I: “The beasts of burden rotted in their dung.” And the passage in Jeremiah: “Each man neighed after his neighbor’s wife,” and Ezekiel XXIII: “Their flesh is like the flesh of donkeys, and their discharge like the discharge of horses.” Thus the saying of David in Psalm XLVIII is expressed: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. In all the printed editions it read “because he is small,” but, with all the manuscript codices agreeing, I inserted “because he is wicked.” LOAISA.

On the same passage. “Because he is wicked.” The sense, says Vezzosius, is that a great part of righteousness consists in a person’s recognizing that he is inclined toward evil. Cajetan published *nosse*, “to know.” What is a human being except ashes?—as follows from this. AREV.]

2. It is already a considerable part of righteousness for a person to know himself, because he is wicked, so that he may submit more humbly to divine virtue once he recognizes his own weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0614D]

3. From Paul’s statement: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.” LOAISA.]

3. The righteous person judges himself well in this life, so that he may not be judged by God with eternal condemnation. Each person then passes judgment upon himself when, through worthy repentance, he condemns his own wicked deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0615D]

4. From Gregory, *Moralia* VIII, chapter 11. LOAISA.]

4. The bitterness of repentance causes the soul both to examine its deeds more subtly and, weeping, to recall the gifts of God that it despised. Nothing is worse than to recognize guilt without weeping over it.

5. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he did not do good, or because through recklessness he committed evil. He failed to do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

6. The person performs repentance worthily who mourns his guilt with legitimate satisfaction—that is, by condemning and bewailing what he has done—lamenting with greater profusion in proportion as he was more inclined to sin.

7. This is found in the *Sentences* of the Master, Book IV, distinction 14, and in Smaragdus, chapter 4 on the Rule of Saint Benedict. It is also recorded in Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 3, chapter 9, as follows: “He performs penance worthily who so mourns the evils he has committed in the past that he does not commit them again in the future; for whoever mourns sin and again admits sin is like someone washing an unbaked brick, because the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.” I possess, in a prominent place, the reading of this canon as examined with great care and painstaking diligence by highly learned men. Nevertheless, I shall set down the readings of other manuscripts, so that the learned reader may understand that I too have applied every care and effort to correcting this book. I have two manuscripts of venerable antiquity: one from the library of the holy and august Church of Toledo, written in the year 953 of the Spanish Era; the other, older, from the distinguished college at Oviedo near Salamanca. Both are written in Lombard letters on parchment, and read as follows: “He performs penance worthily who so mourns the evils of the past that he does not [Col. 0616C] commit them again in the future [another manuscript: admit them again]. For whoever mourns sin, [Col. 0616D] and again commits sin, is like someone washing an unbaked brick, which, the more he washes it, the more mud it makes.” LOAISA.

[Note: In the same place. Others read, “as though he were washing bricks . . . the more he washes it.” See the note on chapter 16, no. 3. AREV.]

7. He performs penance worthily who so mourns the evils of the past that he does not commit them again in the future. For whoever mourns sin and again admits sin is like someone washing an unbaked brick, which, the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.

8. Although someone may be a sinner and impious, if he turns to penance, it is believed that he can obtain forgiveness.

9. No one doubts God’s goodness, but the perversity of those who receive it alone denies that pardon is bestowed upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0616D]

10. The wording is somewhat different in the Vulgate edition, John 9. LOAISA.

In the same place. “Give,” etc. The passage is Jeremiah 13, which Jerome interprets either of the Babylonian captivity or of the final judgment. LOAISA.

In the same place. “Let it grow dark.” So the Vulgate. Others have “let it become dark.” Loaisa’s note indicated chapter 12; I have supplied 13 instead. AREV.]

10. In this life alone is the opportunity for penance open; after death, there is no possibility of correction. Hence the Lord also says: “I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day; but night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9:4). Thus also the prophet says: “Give glory to the Lord your God before it grows dark” (Jeremiah 13:16), that is, before eternal death overtakes you. While you are in this life, glorify God through penance.

11. While they are still in this world and practicing penance, God’s mercy comes to the aid of sinners. In the future life, however, we no longer perform works; we give an account of our works.

12. The wicked are often made worse by the very means through which, by God’s patience, they receive time for correction. They do not use this delay in living for penance, but seize it as an opportunity for the audacity of sinning. Whoever turns the time granted him for penance into freedom for evil conduct proceeds from bad to worse.

13. Each person ought to hasten to God through penance while he can, lest, if he does not wish to do so while he can, he should later wish to do so when he cannot at all. Therefore the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). And where may he be found, unless in this life, in which he is also near to all who call upon him? For then he will already be far away, when he says: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:41). Now he is not seen, yet he is near; then he will be seen, but he will not be near, because he will be able to be seen but will not be able to be found.

[Col. 0616B] 14. Whenever someone repents while he is able to sin and, while living, corrects his life from every crime, there is no doubt that, when he dies, he will pass into eternal rest.

[Note: [Col. 0616D]

15. The remission is uncertain. Vezzosius says that it is uncertain whether someone who repents when the danger of death is imminent truly repents. AREV.]

15. Whoever practices penance while living wickedly, in the danger of death, has a remission as uncertain as his condemnation. Whoever therefore wishes to be certain at death of receiving pardon should repent while in good health and, while in good health, mourn the crimes he has committed.

[Note: [Col. 0616D]

16. The passage is Jeremiah 6, and the whole sentence appears to have been taken from Saint Jerome, in the same place. LOAISA.

In the same place. “They heal.” Others, with the Vulgate, have “they healed.” There others have “there was no peace” instead of “there is no peace.” AREV.]

16. There are people who quickly promise security to penitents, to whom the prophet rightly says: “They heal the wound of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace.” He therefore heals the wound with disgrace who promises security to someone who is sinning and has not performed legitimate penance. Hence it continues: “They were ashamed, because they committed abomination”—that is, they were ashamed, not by repenting, but by suffering punishment.

17. The guilty person is put to shame before the judge in one way when he is punished, and in another the person who blushes at an evil deed is rebuked. The former is ashamed because he has been reproved; the latter because he remembers having done evil.

18. Although through penance there is reconciliation for sins, a person must nevertheless not be without fear, because the satisfaction of penance is weighed only by divine judgment, not by human judgment. Therefore, since God’s mercy is hidden, it is necessary to weep without interruption. The penitent ought never to have security concerning his sins. For security produces negligence, and negligence often leads the unwary person back to the vices he had overcome.

212 [Note: [Col. 0617D]

19. “Of that man.” Others, with the Vulgate, have “of that man.” AREV.]

19. When vices have been expelled from a person through penance, if afterward, through the intervention of security, some fault should creep in, the former delights of the vices immediately invade the mind more eagerly. They assail the person and drag him more violently into his customary deeds, so that his last state is worse than his first.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Despair of Sinners

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

Chapter 14, no. 1. Others read, “but by the progress of deeds or conduct.” Perhaps the reading is “we are drawn away.” AREV.]

1. One departs from God or draws near to him not through distances of place, but through good or evil disposition. For we move away from or approach God not by the steps of our feet, but by the steps of our conduct.

[Col. 0617B] 2. To commit some disgraceful act is the death of the soul; to despise penance and remain in guilt is, after death, to descend into hell. Thus sinning belongs to death, whereas despair means descending into hell. Hence Scripture says: “When the wicked comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3).

3. Often, when the devil sees people turning to penance, he drives them to despair, struck down by the enormity of their crimes. By removing the hope of pardon, he drags into distrust those whom he could not retain permanently in sin. But the penitent ought to anticipate the enemy’s crafty snares against him, and should fear God’s justice in such a way that, even amid great crimes, he nevertheless trusts in God’s mercy.

4. God rejoices more over a soul that had despaired and is later converted than over one that was never lost. So it was with the prodigal son, who had been dead and came to life, had been lost and was found; his return produced great joy in his father (Luke 15).

5. Before God and the angels, there is no greater abundance of joy over someone who is rescued from danger than over someone who has never known the danger of sin. For just as a lost thing causes grief, so, when it is found, it brings greater joy—just as that shepherd in the Gospel rejoices when he finds the lost sheep and joyfully carries it back on his shoulders (Matthew 18:12; Luke 15:5).

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

6. In the printed editions it read “for the innocence of a good end,” instead of “into the innocence of a good end.” I have adopted “into the innocence,” in agreement with all the manuscripts and with Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 27, chapter 11. From that passage this sentence is taken: “To exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep,” he says, “is to transform the beginnings of an unclean life into the simplicity of innocence.” LOAISA.]

6. No one ought to despair of forgiveness, even if he turns to penance near the end of his life. [Col. 0617D] For God judges each person by his end, not by his past life. This too is taught by the testimony of the Law: a person is justified by his final state, when God commanded a sheep to be offered in place of the firstborn of an ass—that is, the uncleanness of an earlier life must be changed into the innocence of a good end. Hence the tail too is commanded to be offered as a sacrifice, that is, the final part of life is to be offered in penance.

7. Many, visited by heavenly grace, return to God through penance at the end of their lives. Whatever evils they had committed, they cleanse with daily tears, and they exchange their evil deeds for good works. They are rightly forgiven everything in which they had offended, because through repentance they acknowledge what they had done wrongly.

8. In a person’s life, the end must be sought, because God does not consider what sort of people we were before, but what sort of people we are near the end of life.

## CHAPTER XV. On Those Who Are Abandoned by God

[Note: [Col. 0618D]

Chapter 15, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 11, chapter 5. LOAISA.]

1. When God abandons someone, no one repents; when God looks upon someone, each person sees and mourns his evils and considers from where he has fallen. For some are so despised by God that they cannot mourn their evils, even if they wish to.

[Note: [Col. 0618D]

2. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 9, chapter 25: “The evil spirits,” he says, “form their plan against the good.” LOAISA.]

2. The plan of unclean spirits is this: since they themselves have been denied the possibility of returning to righteousness after their transgression, they seek to bar human beings from the way of penance, lest human beings themselves return to God. They strive to have as companions in perdition those whom they assail with every kind of deception, so that they may either be abandoned by God or despair under the enormity of the scourge.

3. We must groan continually and, setting security aside, mourn, lest a person be abandoned by God’s secret and just judgment and be left in the power of demons, destined for destruction. For truly, those whom God abandons are taken up by demons.

[Col. 0618C] 214 [Note: [Col. 0618D]

4. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 25, chapter 9. LOAISA.

In the same place. “Which are understood to be demons.” This is correctly read on the authority of the manuscripts. See Grialius’s note on Exodus 42:3. Others foolishly wished to correct *quae* to *qui*. AREV.]

4. Those who despise the Lord’s command, as soon as they turn away from God, are seized by evil spirits, who also persuade them to do evil. Hence comes the prophetic saying: “Darkness pursues the enemies of God” (Nahum 1:8)—by whom demons are understood. Therefore it is also written in the psalm: “The sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77:49).

5. By God’s hidden and most just judgment, some of the reprobate are brought under the power of demons, as Isaiah testifies: “He cast the lot for them, and his hand divided it among them by measure; they shall possess it forever” (Isaiah 34:17).

6. By divine justice, some of the elect are allowed to fall into the error of sin, but through God’s mercy they are brought back and converted again. Concerning such people the Lord speaks through the prophet: “I abandoned him, and I brought him back, and I restored consolation to him” (Isaiah 57:18).

[Note: [Col. 0618D]

7. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 9, chapter 34. LOAISA.]

7. Sometimes, when God returns, he visits again by afflicting the person whom he had abandoned, and cleanses him from sins through lamentation, tears, and the affliction of penance. Job says to God: “Because of pride,” he says, “you will seize me like a lioness, and returning, you torment me wondrously” (Job 10:16). God returns to torment a person when he again visits through chastisement the one whom he had abandoned while sinning.

8. We ought never to provoke heavenly anger further against ourselves by evil deeds; rather, if through repentance we perform deeds worthy of God, we shall change his severity into clemency. For there is no doubt that he who tolerates us while we are wicked mercifully forgives us when we are converted. The fact that time for penance is preserved for us, so that we are not suddenly overwhelmed by a premature death but are given an opportunity for satisfaction, proceeds entirely from God’s clemency: he does not condemn us cruelly, but patiently awaits our repentance.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Those Who Return to Sin after Tears

[Col. 0619B]

[Note: [Col. 0619D]

Chapter 16, no. 1. Taken from Augustine, Homily 41; it is found in Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter 11, and in the Master, Book IV, distinction 14. Nevertheless, in both very ancient Gothic manuscripts the reading is “not to possess the effect of penance and not again to admit what must be mourned.” LOAISA.]

1. He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he regrets; 215 nor does he seem submissively to beseech God, but arrogantly to mock him.

2. A penitent who returns to sin is like a dog returning to its vomit. Many continually pour out tears and do not cease sinning. Some receive tears for penance but do not possess the effect of penance, because through instability of mind they now pour out tears at the recollection of sin, but then, when their former practice revives, they commit again what they had mourned.

[Note: [Col. 0619D]

3. “May be able to mourn.” Others add, “who mourns sin,” etc., as in chapter 13, no. 7; but at the end they read, “the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.” AREV.]

3. Whoever wishes both to mourn past sins and to devote himself to worldly activities does not possess cleansing, since he still does what he is able to mourn through penance.

[Note: [Col. 0619D]

4. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part III, admonition 31. There is also a passage in Isaiah 1. LOAISA.]

4. Isaiah says to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16). Thus the person who mourns the past and does not again commit what must be mourned is washed and is clean. But the person who mourns what he has done, does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats what he had mourned, is washed but is not clean. Thus elsewhere divine discourse rebukes the penitent soul that sins again, saying: “How utterly vile you have become, repeating your ways” (Jeremiah 2:36)! Whoever therefore mourns past faults must observe this rule: he must mourn his sins in such a way that he does not again commit what must be mourned. Woe to me, miserable Isidore, who neglect to repent of past deeds and still commit deeds of which I must repent.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Sin

[Note: [Col. 0620D]

Chapter 17, no. 1. In the Master’s *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 42. LOAISA.]

1. Sin is committed in two ways: either through the force of desire or through fear, when someone wishes to obtain what he desires or fears falling into what he dreads.

[Note: [Col. 0620D]

2. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 4, chapter 25. LOAISA.]

2. Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and is carried out in deed in four ways. In the heart: through the suggestion of demons, the pleasure of the flesh, the consent of the mind, and the defense of pride. In deed: now secretly, now openly, now through habit, and now through despair. By these stages, therefore, one sins in the heart and carries out evil in deed.

[Note: [Col. 0620D]

3. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 25, chapter 11; it is found in the Master’s *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 22. LOAISA.]

3. Sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate intent; but the danger of punishment differs. Eve sinned through ignorance in paradise (Genesis 3), as the Apostle says: “The man was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (1 Timothy 2:14). Eve therefore sinned through ignorance, but Adam deliberately, because he sinned knowingly and consciously, not having been deceived. Whoever is deceived evidently does not know what he is consenting to. Peter, however, sinned through weakness when, out of fear of the maidservant who questioned him, he denied Christ; hence after his sin he wept most bitterly [Col. 0620B] (Matthew 26).

4. It is more serious for someone to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and more serious to sin deliberately than through weakness. The person who sins deliberately does evil with intention and deliberation of mind; the person who sins through weakness falls through accident or rashness. Those who sin deliberately are more wicked when they not only fail to live well but also, if they can, turn those who live well away from the truth.

5. Some sin unknowingly, and some knowingly. There are also people who refuse to know in order to excuse their ignorance and be considered less culpable; yet they do not protect themselves but deceive themselves even more.

[Note: [Col. 0620D]

6. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.

In the same place. “They turn away.” Another reading is “they return.” AREV.]

6. Simply not knowing belongs to ignorance; refusing to know belongs to obstinate pride. For what else is it than wishing to despise the Lord in pride to refuse to know the will of one’s own master? Therefore no one should excuse himself on the ground of ignorance, because God judges not only those who turn themselves away from knowledge of him, but also those who did not know, as the same Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will destroy human beings from the face of the earth, and those who turn away behind the Lord, and those who have not sought the Lord or investigated him” (Zephaniah 1:3, 6). And the psalm says: “Pour out your anger upon the nations that have not known you” (Psalm 68:25).

217 ## CHAPTER XVIII. On Lighter Sins

[Note: [Col. 0620D]

Chapter 18, no. 1. 4. Not only serious sins but also light sins must be avoided. 218 For many light sins produce one great sin, just as immense rivers commonly grow from small and tiny drops. For when many things are gathered into one, they produce an overflowing abundance.

[Col. 0621B] 5. Sins that are light for beginners are counted as serious for perfect persons.

6. A sin is recognized as all the greater in proportion as the person who sins is greater. For the accumulation of guilt increases according to the order of one’s merits, and what is often forgiven to lesser persons is charged against greater ones.

## CHAPTER XIX. On More Serious Sins

[Note: [Col. 0622D]

Chapter 19, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 25, chapter 9. It is also found in the Master’s *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 36. LOAISA.

In the same place. “By experience of lesser sins.” Another reading is “by experience or contempt of lesser sins.” AREV.]

1. Greater sins are committed through the experience of lesser sins, so that those who refused to be corrected by small offenses may be struck more harshly because of great crimes. By divine judgment, those who despise correcting their lesser deeds fall into more grievous guilt.

2. Many fall from one crime into another. Although they know God, they neglect his fear; though they know him in knowledge, they do not venerate him in action. Therefore they are blinded by divine judgment, commit deeds deserving punishment, and, as punishment for the crime they have committed, add a worse crime.

3. Often one sin becomes the cause of another sin, when another sin arises from it like its offspring, as lust commonly arises from excessive indulgence of the belly.

[Col. 0622A] 4. Sin is admitted as the punishment of sin when, in proportion to each person’s sin, and with God abandoning him, he proceeds into another and worse sin, by which the person who commits it becomes more defiled. Thus a preceding sin is the cause of the following sin, while the following sin is the punishment of the preceding offense. Preceding sins are therefore the cause of subsequent crimes, so that the sins that follow are the punishment of those that preceded them.

219 [Note: [Col. 0622D]

5. The passage is in Paul, 2 Thessalonians 2: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so that they might be saved, therefore God sends them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie.” LOAISA.]

5. The punishment of preceding sins is itself called hardening, which proceeds from divine justice. Hence the prophet says: “You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you” (Isaiah 63:17). For God does not drive righteous people to become evil; rather, when they are already evil, they are hardened so that they may become worse, just as the Apostle also says: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth of God so that they might be saved, God sent upon them a spirit of error” (2 Thessalonians 2:10). God therefore causes some people to sin, but only those in whom such sins have already preceded, so that by his just judgment they deserve to proceed into worse things. For such sins fall into a punishment on account of other preceding sins—a punishment which sins deserve.

6. Some sins proceed from God’s anger and are proportionately repaid for other sins. Hence the prophet says: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; we have always remained in them” (Isaiah 64:5), as though he were saying: Because we have always been in sins, you were angry, so that we might sin more gravely.

[Note: [Col. 0622D]

7. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 26, chapter 28. LOAISA.]

7. The prudent reader ought to know what it means to deserve God’s anger and what it means to provoke it. For the anger that is provoked is more serious than the anger that is deserved. We deserve it when we sin through ignorance; we provoke it when we know how to do good but refuse.

8. While we are alive, we can avoid God’s anger. Let us therefore fear lest, when the terror of judgment comes, it can be felt but cannot be avoided.

## CHAPTER XX. On Manifest and Hidden Sins

[Col. 0623A]

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

Chapter 20, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 4, chapter 25, and elsewhere in the *Pastoral Care*. LOAISA.]

1. It is a greater fault to sin openly than secretly. For the person who sins openly is guilty in two ways, because he both acts and teaches. Isaiah speaks of such people: “They proclaimed their sins like Sodom, and did not hide them” (Isaiah 3:9).

2. Many who sin publicly proclaim their crimes without any shame and show no embarrassment about their wickedness.

3. It is already a portion of righteousness for a person to hide his iniquity and to be ashamed within himself of his own sins.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

4. On “clamor,” see Gregory’s exposition of the second penitential psalm, on the words “Because I was silent,” and Psalm 7, and Book III of the *Pastoral Care*, admonition 10, where he says: “He calls the clamor freedom to sin.” LOAISA.]

4. To commit sin is a crime; to proclaim sin is a clamor, concerning which the Apostle also says: “Let all clamor be removed from you, together with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31)—that is, together with the sins themselves.

5. The very fact that someone hides the sin he commits is already an indication of judgment, because a person feels shame only over the guilt of conscience. Therefore, by the very fact that someone is ashamed of his deed, he already becomes his own judge.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Love of Sin

1. It is one thing not to sin out of love for God; it is another not to sin out of fear of punishment. Whoever does not sin out of love of God’s charity abhors every evil, embracing the good of righteousness; sin does not delight him, even if immunity from the crime were promised. But whoever restrains vices within himself only through fear of punishment, although he does not complete the sinful act, nevertheless lives with the will to sin; he grieves that what the law is known to forbid is illicit for him. Therefore the person who acts by loving righteousness receives the reward of a good deed, not the person who unwillingly keeps righteousness merely out of fear of punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

Chapter 21, no. 2. “It is not only.” Others, less appropriately, read, “It is not merely.” AREV.]

2. Some both love sin and commit it; some love it only and do not commit it; most commit it only and do not love it. Some do not commit sin and yet hate righteousness. The person who not only loves sin but also commits it sins more seriously than the person who does not commit it but loves it; and sometimes the person who loves it but does not commit it sins more seriously than the person who commits it but hates it. It is most serious not only to commit sin but also to love it.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

3. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 6, chapter 11. LOAISA.]

3. Some people are immediately ashamed once they have committed a crime, while others not only do not regret having done evil but even glory in the evil deed itself. Thus, by comparison with evil, the situation becomes worse, as they rejoice in their vices and are lifted up into still greater evil. Solomon speaks of such people: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 11:14).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Necessity of Sinning

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

Chapter 22, no. 1. Isidore is speaking of necessity that does not exclude voluntariness, since there are two kinds of sin: absolute sin and conditional sin. The Master, Book II, distinction 36. LOAISA.]

1. Sometimes we are what we are—evil—through necessity rather than through will. But the necessity of evil must be turned toward the will of good. Many sin not willingly but solely from necessity, fearing temporal poverty. While they flee the necessities of the present world, they are deprived of future goods.

2. Again, some commit sin by will, not by necessity. They are not wicked because they have been compelled by any poverty, but simply desire to be evil without cause. For they do not love the thing they seek, but are delighted solely by the wickedness of sin itself.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Habit of Sinning

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

Chapter 23, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 4, chapter 25. LOAISA.]

1. It is better to avoid sin than to correct it. For we resist more easily an enemy by whom we have not yet been conquered than one by whom we already know ourselves to have been overcome and defeated.

2. Every sin is feared more greatly before it is committed. However serious it may be, once it becomes habitual it is considered light and committed without any fear.

[Note: [Col. 0624D]

3. He alludes to the passage about Simon Peter’s mother-in-law suffering from fever, Mark 1: “He approached,” it says, “raised her up, taking her by the hand, and immediately the fever left her.” LOAISA.]

3. Every sin grows through these sources, as though through certain steps. Evil thought produces pleasure, pleasure produces consent, consent produces action, action produces habit, and habit produces necessity. Thus, bound by these chains, a person is held fast by a kind of chain of vices, so that he can in no way be torn away from it unless divine grace takes hold of the hand of the one lying there.

222 [Note: [Col. 0624D]

4. Luke 14: “Which of you, if his ass or ox falls into a pit, will not immediately pull it out on the Sabbath?” See Augustine, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, question 29. LOAISA.]

4. To commit sin is to fall into a pit; to form the habit of sinning is to narrow the mouth of the pit, so that the one who has fallen cannot get out. But sometimes God also frees such people, when he changes their despair into a conversion that brings freedom. Through his mercy sins are forgiven, and through his protection a person is prevented from proceeding into worse things by sinning.

[Note: [Col. 0624D]

5. “Most wicked.” Another reading is “evil.” AREV.]

5. It is most wicked to sin; it is worse to form a habit of sinning. From the former one rises easily; from the latter one rises only with difficulty, while resisting the evil habit.

[Col. 0624D] [Note: [Col. 0624D]

6. The passage is Isaiah 31: “Return, as you had withdrawn into the depths, children of Israel.” Symmachus has: “Repent, you who have withdrawn from the Lord through deep counsel and sin.” From Jerome. LOAISA.]

6. The prophet asserts that the habit of doing evil is a withdrawal into the depths (Isaiah 31:6). Through its use, as though by a kind of law, a person is held fast, so that even when he does not wish to do so, he commits sin. But to rise quickly after a fall is not to go into the depths.

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

7. “In our members.” Another reading is “in his members.” AREV.]

7. The Apostle calls the law of sin “in our members” (Romans 7:23). This law is habit, which we conceive through sinning, and from which we do not depart whenever we wish, because through habit we are already held by the bond of necessity.

8. The love of truth accomplishes much in a person, but the flesh resists under the law of evil habit. The person who boldly rejoices on behalf of a good conscience rejoices well, because he vigorously restrains within himself what insolently attacks him.

9. We must beware of sinning repeatedly. For the fact that God often works salvation for us from our evil is as rare as it is wonderful. Therefore we must fear trusting in being saved in this way, lest, while we await healing from our vices, we multiply the vices and fail to obtain salvation. Let us therefore strive either not to fall or, having quickly turned back, to rise from our fall.

10. Sin must be avoided altogether. If, through human weakness, sin should creep in, what has been wickedly committed must immediately be corrected. A fault that is recognized quickly is corrected quickly; but a wound is healed more slowly when, after a long time, treatment is applied to limbs already putrefying.

223 11. Repeated sin is more serious, just as when illness comes upon illness, or rain upon rain.

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

12. From Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 33, chapter 9. Isaiah 5. LOAISA.

In the same place. Another reading is, “For he draws iniquity with a cord.” AREV.]

12. Delay in sinning makes the crime monstrous. Hence the prophet says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart-rope” (Isaiah 5:18)! Whoever delays turning to God draws iniquity like a cord. To draw iniquity is to delay in iniquity. Hence the psalm also says: “They have prolonged their iniquities; the just Lord will cut off the necks of sinners” (Psalm 128:2, 4).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Remembrance of Sin

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

Chapter 24, no. 1. Others, perhaps better, read “to have one’s own [sins].” AREV.]

1. It is good for a person always to place his own offenses before his eyes, in accordance with the psalm’s statement: “And my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:5). Just as one ought not to dwell emotionally on sin, so it is always necessary for each person to remember his own sin with tears.

2. For the righteous person, remembrance of sin produces weariness of spirit. But those subject to lust and desire, in stubborn pride, even glory in the very act of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

3. From Gregory, in the same place, and Augustine. LOAISA.]

3. The remembrance of sin ought to be so great in God’s servant that he continually confesses what he has done with tears. Hence the psalm says: “I have turned in my misery, while the thorn was fixed in me. I made my sin known to you. I said, ‘I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord’” (Psalm 31:4). Earlier he had said: “Because I was silent”—that is, because I did not confess—“all my bones grew old, while I cried out all day.” What does he regret having kept silent about, then, except the confession of sins? What does he grieve having cried out about, except the defense of evil deeds? Whoever has defended his sins must therefore, through repentance, accuse what he wickedly committed in pride.

224 ## CHAPTER XXV. On Thought

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

Chapter 25, no. 1. Thus Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 10, chapter 11: “Every sin is committed either by thought alone or by thought together with deed. Iniquity, therefore, is in the hand; guilt is in the deed.” LOAISA.]

Job 20: “The tongue of the viper will kill him.” Gregory, *Morals*, book XV, chapter 9, comments on this: When vipers have conceived, their young rage within their mother’s womb. After tearing open their mothers’ sides, they emerge from their wombs; hence the viper is so called because it gives birth violently. Thus the viper is born in such a way [Col. 0626D] that it comes out by force and is produced together with the death of its mother. But that it is false that viper offspring pierce their parent’s entrails Aristotle teaches in book V of *The History of Animals*, chapter 39: “The viper,” he says, “gives birth to young wrapped in membranes, which rupture on the third day, and gives birth to one each day, more than twenty in number. Sometimes those in the womb break through after gnawing through the membranes.” This is Aristotle’s account, which Albert the Great also noted in book XXV, at that place. Pliny, book X of the *Natural History*, chapter 62, says the same, but adds: “Thus the others, unable to endure the delay, burst through the sides, killing their mother.” LOAISA.

[The same passage appears in another copy as “and having conceived within.” AREV.]

1. The cause of sin is divided into two parts, namely, deed and thought. One is called iniquity, because it is carried out in action; the other injustice, because it is committed in thought.

2. Action must first be cut away, and afterward thought; first evil deeds, then desires. Yet actions also proceed from thought, and thought arises from action. Even if someone abstains from an evil deed, he is nevertheless not innocent on account of the wickedness of an evil thought alone. Hence the Lord also says through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isaiah 1:16).

3. We sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts, if we take pleasure in them when they arise unlawfully.

4. Just as the viper is killed after being torn apart by the young placed in its womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us; conceived inwardly, they consume us with viperous poison and destroy our soul with a cruel wound.

[Note: [Col. 0626D]

5. The old edition reads, “to anticipate the thoughts of an evil suggestion,” which is clearer. Shortly afterward, instead of “to arise,” some copies read “to suggest,” which would also be preferable. AREV.]

5. It is not within our power to prevent the suggestions of an evil thought; but to cast a thought into the mind belongs to our will. The former, therefore, is not charged as guilt; the latter is imputed as personal guilt. For the arising of unlawful thoughts belongs to demons [Col. 0627A]; to take pleasure in perverse thoughts belongs to us.

6. It often happens that impure images of bodily things, which we have learned, are set before our minds, and we think of them unwillingly. The more we strive to turn the mind’s gaze away from them, the more they thrust themselves into the soul and creep into us with obscene movements. This happens because of the condition of mortality that the first man merited as punishment for his sin.

[Note: [Col. 0627C]

7. Saint Nicholas the martyr, in the *Sentences*: “Drive away evil thoughts with other, good thoughts.” LOAISA.

In the same passage: “pleasures.” Another reading has “temptations.” AREV.]

7. While each person is anticipated by divine illumination, he is immediately assaulted by the troubles of shameful thoughts. But God’s servant, guided by fear of God, rejects their allurements from himself and drives away shameful thoughts by setting good thoughts against them.

8. Great vigilance must be exercised over the guarding of the heart [Col. 0627B], because the origin of either good or evil is located there. For, as it is written: “From the heart come evil thoughts” (Matthew 15:19). Therefore, if we resist an evil thought at the outset, we do not fall into the deed.

9. We need not fear if good and evil thoughts enter the mind; rather, we should rejoice if the mind distinguishes evil from good by the understanding of reason.

10. It is of no benefit that we distinguish good from evil with more prudent judgment unless, through action, we either avoid the evil we have recognized or do the good we have understood.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Conscience

1. While the human condition troubles the mind with various vices, even before the punishments of Gehenna the soul already suffers the punishments of conscience through an unknown desire.

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

CHAPTER XXVI, note 2. From Gregory, *Morals*, book XXVII, chapter 16. LOAISA.]

2. A person can flee everything except his own heart. No one can withdraw from himself. Wherever he goes, the consciousness of his guilt does not abandon him.

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

3. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.

In the edition of Grialius and Vezzosi, *coelat* and *caelare* are printed; this cannot be accepted. AREV.]

3. Although everyone who acts wickedly escapes human judgments, he cannot escape the judgment of his own conscience. Even if he conceals from others what he has done, he cannot conceal it from himself, since he fully knows that what he did was evil [Col. 0628A]. Thus judgment in him is twofold: here he is punished by the guilt of his conscience, and there he is condemned to everlasting punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

4. Psalm 41, and Augustine’s commentary thereon. LOAISA.]

4. This is what is signified by: “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm 41:8). For “deep calls to deep” means going from the judgment of one’s conscience to the judgment of eternal condemnation; “at the sound of the cataracts” means in the preaching of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Intention of the Mind

[Note: [Col. 0627D]

CHAPTER XXVII, note 1. This alludes to Matthew 6: “If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.” Gregory interprets this passage as concerning the intention of the heart, *Morals*, book XXVIII, chapter 6: “Hence Truth rightly says in the Gospel: ‘The lamp of your body is your eye,’ and so forth. For what is expressed by the eye except the intention of the heart, which precedes its work? Before it exercises itself in action, it already contemplates what it desires. And what is designated by the word ‘body’ except each action, which follows its intention as though it were a seeing eye? The eye is therefore the lamp of the body, because the merits of an action are illuminated by the ray of a good intention. And if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light, because if our intention is right, a good work is produced through the simplicity of thought, even if it may appear less good. And if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark, because when something right is done with a perverse intention, although it may be seen to shine before human beings, it is darkened before the judgment of the inner tribunal.” Chrysostom also interprets it in this way, in homily 2 on Matthew, as does Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, and *Against Lying*, chapter 7. The theologians distinguish between end, will, and intention; see the Master, book II, distinction 39. LOAISA.

In the same passage: “Therefore, if.” Ambrose says the same, though somewhat differently, book I of *Duties*, chapter 30: “Your disposition gives a name to your work.” LOAISA.]

1. A person’s eye is the intention of his work. If his intention is good, the work of his intention is also good. Otherwise, even if a work appears good in its deeds, it is no longer good if the intention is evil, since by its intention it is either approved as good or rejected as unworthy [Col. 0628B]. The intention that is for God is therefore good; the intention that is for earthly profit or empty glory is evil.

227 2. Those who do not perform a good work with a good intention are thereby blinded more through the work by which they could have been enlightened.

3. Let each person perform the good work he does with a good intention, because through an evil intention we often lose the good work we undertake and remain less free from guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0628D]

4. Above, book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 7, no. 13. LOAISA.]

4. What often appears good in human judgment is exposed as blameworthy before the examination of the most diligent and penetrating judge. Therefore every saint fears lest the good he does be rejected in God’s eyes because of some intention of the mind.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Senses of the Flesh

[Col. 0628C]

[Note: [Col. 0628D]

CHAPTER XXVIII, note 1. In the printed editions, *cogitationes* (“thoughts”) appeared; I removed it and restored *cognationes* (“kinships”), from Jeremiah 1: “Behold, I will summon all the kinships of the kingdoms of the north.” Jerome and the other recent interpreters consistently read it in this way. The Septuagint, however, does not have *cognationes*, but only: “Behold, I will summon all the kingdoms from the north”: Ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ συγκαλῶ πάσας τὰς βασιλείας ἀπὸ βορρᾶ — “Behold, I summon all the kingdoms from the north.” LOAISA.]

1. Through the senses of the flesh, sickness creeps into the mind. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: “All the kinships of the earth will come from the north, and each will set up his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 1:15). The kingdoms of the north are vices, which set up their seats at the gates when they bring corruption into the soul through the senses of the flesh; and therefore they reign at the very gates, that is, in the very senses.

[Col. 0629A] [Note: [Col. 0629C]

2. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXI, chapter 2. LOAISA.

In the same passage: “They conquer by enticement.” Perhaps: “They are conquered by enticement.” AREV.]

2. We sin from nowhere else except by seeing, hearing, touching, tasting, and handling. Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Death entered through our windows.” And again: “Strangers entered through its gates and cast lots over Jerusalem.” The strangers are unclean spirits, who enter the soul through the senses of the flesh as through gates and conquer it by enticement.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Speech

[Note: [Col. 0629C]

CHAPTER XXIX, note 1. From Gregory, part III of *Pastoral Care*, admonition 15. LOAISA.]

1. When we do not avoid certain small words of vice, we slip into a great crime of the tongue; and when we freely and fearlessly commit certain deeds that are not serious, we slip into greater crimes through the dreadful habit of sinning.

[Col. 0629B] [Note: [Col. 0629D]

2. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.]

2. Just as the foolishness of those who speak too much is often censured, so the vices of those who are excessively silent are also marked. The former, by loosening the tongue too freely, fall into the vice of frivolity; the latter, by keeping too silent, grow sluggish regarding usefulness.

3. The unskilled, just as they do not know how to speak, likewise cannot keep silent. Uneducated in mind and talkative in mouth, they make a din with words but say nothing in meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0629D]

4. Just as those who are making progress fear the crimes of falsehood, so perfect men avoid idle words. For, as someone has said: “Just as an account is required for an idle word, so punishment is paid for an unjust speech” (Matthew 12:36).

5. Vain speeches ought not to be in the mouth of a Christian. For just as good conversations correct evil morals, so corrupt conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33).

[Col. 0629C] [Note: [Col. 0629D]

6. From Gregory, part III of *Pastoral Care*, admonition 15. LOAISA.]

[Note: [Col. 0629D]

[Note: [Col. 0629D]

8. He who speaks about matters pertaining to God without doing them, although he is useless to himself, nevertheless benefits those who hear.

9. Those who desire to be praised for their wisdom should heed the prophet who says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21).

[Note: [Col. 0629D]

10. This alludes to Wisdom 7: “But God gave me speech according to judgment.” Gregory interprets this passage in *Morals*, book XXIII, chapter 10: “Hence a certain wise man rightly said: ‘May God grant me to speak these things according to judgment,’ for judgment is so called from understanding. [Note: [Col. 0629D]

15. 24. Not everyone who suffers insults is righteous; only the one who suffers innocently for the truth is righteous.

26. He who calmly discloses the insults inflicted upon him opens the pain of his heart and easily expels the poison that seethes [Col. 0631C] within.

231 27. Wounds of the mind quickly exhale when opened; when closed, they fester excessively.

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

28. He who conceals the pain of an injury in a closed breast nourishes an increasingly bitter pain within the more he presses his tongue into silence. Hence one of the pagan poets truly said: “The more the fire is covered, the more fiercely the covered fire burns.” “For blind languor is vehement and excessive,” because a silent wound lives beneath the breast.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Lying

[Col. 0632A]

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

CHAPTER XXX, note 1. A passage from Jerome’s letter to the deacon Julian. There is an old saying: “Liars cause people not to believe even those who speak the truth.” LOAISA.]

1. Liars cause people not to believe even those who speak the truth. For frequent falsehood often makes a person suspect even when he speaks the truth.

2. He who is about to tell falsehoods often begins with truths, so that, once he has first gained credibility, he may make his hearers credulous toward the rest of his lies.

3. Many things that are false seem true to people, and therefore they speak falsehood not from God but from themselves.

4. Sometimes falsehood is joined to truthful speech, and the person who fabricates falsehoods often begins with truth.

5. Poisons often lie hidden beneath honey spread over words; and the deceiver pretends to be telling the truth until, by deceiving, he has deceived.

[Col. 0632B] [Note: [Col. 0631D]

6. *Decretum* 22, question 1; also in the Master, book III, distinction 39; Polycarp, book VI, title 12; Burchard, book XII, chapter 20; Ivo, part XII, chapter 7; Panormitanus, book LXXXVIII. LOAISA.]

6. Sometimes it is worse to meditate a lie than to speak one, for at times an unwary person speaks a lie through rashness; but he cannot meditate one except through deliberate effort. Therefore the person who lies deliberately is considered more seriously at fault than the one who lies from mere rashness.

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

7. Augustine enumerates eight kinds of lies in *On Lying*, chapter 14, and says that the seventh is one that harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if a person lies because he does not wish to hand over someone sought for execution. The Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, also identifies two kinds of lies in which there is no great fault, though they are not entirely without fault: when we joke, or when we lie in order to benefit our neighbors. LOAISA.

In the same passage: “to benefit.” This is indeed how it appears in Gregory and in the Gothic manuscripts, but perhaps the word *vitam* (“life”), absent from the printed editions, is correctly omitted. He often uses *praestare* to mean “to benefit.” LOAISA.

In the same passage: “in what follows,” and so forth. Gregory’s words explain the meaning of this sentence, *Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 4: “For if any fault is usually cleansed by a subsequent pious action, how much more easily is this fault wiped away, when piety, the mother of good action, accompanies it?” LOAISA.

The use of *praestare* for “to benefit” also occurs elsewhere in other authors and in Isidore himself; and in the old edition and my manuscript the word *vitam* is absent. I therefore deleted it, although Loaisa printed *praestare vitam alienae carni* (“to benefit another’s flesh with life”). See the note on Dracontius, *On Satisfaction*, line 64. AREV.]

7. Every lie must be avoided with the utmost care, although sometimes a kind of lie may be a lesser fault if someone lies for the safety of human beings. But because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11), and: “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7), even this kind of lie perfect men avoid with the utmost care, so that no one’s life may be defended through their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while striving to benefit another’s flesh [Col. 0632C]. Nevertheless, we believe that this particular kind of sin is very easily forgiven. For if any fault is cleansed by a subsequent reward, how much more easily is this one wiped away, when the reward itself accompanies it?

8. People tell and fabricate many things for the sake of human praise. Thus it happens that they perish by lying and lead those whom they praise to the ruin of empty glory.

[Note: [Col. 0631D]

9. In Grialius’s edition, a note is indicated for this sentence, but it has been lost. Perhaps this alone is missing: “From Gregory, book IX, letter to Theotistus the Patrician.” AREV.]

9. Just as a person who has a good conscience does not fear the abuse of another’s tongue, so one who is praised by another ought not to heed the error of another’s praise. Rather, each person should seek the testimony of his own conscience, to which he himself is more present than the person praising him.

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

10. This comparison is derived from Paul, Galatians 6: “Let each person test his own work,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.” LOAISA.]

10. “Let each person test his own work,” as the Apostle says. Then each person will have glory only in himself, that is, secretly in his own conscience, not openly in another’s tongue.

11. Perfect people, who are founded on a deep root, may sometimes be bent to some degree by the gust of praise or blame, as though by the force of winds; nevertheless, they are not thrown down completely, but immediately return to themselves through the firmness of their root.

[Col. 0633B] 233 12. A good mind is conquered by evil neither through rewards nor through threats. For the wicked mix threats with flatteries, so that they may either deceive someone by pleasure or break him by terror.

13. One who is praised is admitted into the affection of his hearers; but this is so only if he is praised truthfully and not falsely—that is, if what is said about him is true.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Oaths

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

CHAPTER XXXI, note 1. Although *pejerare* (“to swear falsely”) is said more frequently, *perjurare* is also found in the best authors of Latin. AREV.]

1. Just as someone who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not wish to swear cannot swear falsely. Oaths must therefore be avoided and used only in absolute necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

2. *Decretum* 22, question 1; also in the Master, book III, distinction 39; Polycarp, book VI, title 12; Burchard, book XII, chapter 20; Ivo, part XII, chapter 7; Panormitanus, book LXXXVIII. LOAISA.]

2. To swear is not contrary to God’s commandment; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore let no one swear who fears swearing falsely.

[Note: [Col. 0633D]

3. Augustine interprets this passage from Matthew in this way in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 1: “Although,” he says, “an oath is more than ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’ and is therefore from evil, it is not from your evil but from the weakness or unbelief of those who are not otherwise moved to faith.” LOAISA.]

3. Many people, whenever they speak, always take pleasure in swearing, although only this ought to be in their mouth: “Yes, yes. No, no.” Anything more than “yes” and “no” is from evil (Matthew 5:37).

4. Many swear falsely in order to deceive, using the credibility of an oath to establish the credibility of their words; thus, by swearing falsely and lying, they deceive an unwary person.

5. Sometimes we are deceived even when led astray by false tears, and people are believed while they weep who ought not to have been believed.

6. We often intend to speak without an oath, but because of the unbelief of those who do not believe what we say, we are compelled to swear; and through such necessity we acquire the habit of swearing.

7. Many are slow to believe and are not moved to faith by a person’s word. But those who force people speaking to them to swear commit a serious offense.

234 [Note: [Col. 0633D]

8. *Decretum* 22, question 5; the Master of the *Sentences*, book III, distinction 31. LOAISA.]

8. Whatever verbal art a person may use in swearing, God, who is witness of the conscience, accepts the oath according to the understanding of the person to whom it is sworn. A person becomes guilty in two ways: by taking God’s name in vain and by deceitfully trapping his neighbor.

[Note: [Col. 0634D]

9. *Decretum* 22, question 4; the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2; the Master, book III, distinction 39. LOAISA.

In the same passage, some read: “the oath must not be kept.” But the reading we present is genuine, and it was retained by the Eighth Council of Toledo, where one finds either “what is wickedly and rashly,” or “what is evil rashly,” or “what is evil and rashly.” The council cites, in the same sense, similar words from Saint Isidore’s *Synonyms*. AREV.]

9. An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be kept—for example, if someone promises an adulterous woman that he will remain with her forever. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the crime of sexual immorality.

[Col. 0634B] [Note: [Col. 0634D]

10. The oath of God is that providence by which he has determined not to overturn his decrees. God’s repentance, however, is a change in things; while his not repenting means that he does not revoke his decrees, as in: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Psalm 109:4)—that is, he will not change what he has sworn.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Vices

1. When a person withdraws from God, he is immediately handed over to the power of vices, so that, while suffering hostile vices, he may come to his senses by returning to the place from which he fell.

2. If the saints strive with all their strength to overcome vices and yet do not extinguish them, what do those do who not only do not hate vices but pursue them with all their love?

[Note: [Col. 0634D]

CHAPTER XXXII, note 3. From Gregory, *Morals*, book VII, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

3. He treats himself delicately enough who wishes to overcome vices without labor, although he cannot cut away without painful force the law of sin that he made for himself by serving vices [Col. 0634C].

4. He renounces a vice perfectly who avoids the occasion of committing the sin. For if you merely wish not to sin, but sin when the opportunity is given, you are both defendant and judge to yourself, since you condemn what you have committed and commit what you have condemned. The person who both accuses and perpetrates vices is defendant before his own judgment.

235 [Note: [Col. 0634D]

5. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.]

5. When certain vices are not avoided perfectly, they make their own authors fall back into them. For if one vice is strictly avoided while the others are neglected, the labor is vain. A person cannot persevere firmly in the observance of one virtue when other vices dominate his heart.

[Col. 0634D] [Note: [Col. 0634D]

6. From Gregory, *Morals*, book VI, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

6. Sometimes a person’s own vices persecute him [Col. 0635A], because the one who previously made them his companions by willing them later feels them pricking him even against his will.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

7. Ambrose, book I of *Duties*, chapter 29. The Hebrews call their adversaries *Allophyls*, that is, “foreigners,” in Latin terminology. The Palestinians were called by this name; they are the Philistines, with φ changed into π, according to Saint Jerome. LOAISA.]

7. Some do not fall into the error of vices until they have first lost the eyes of their inner reason. Thus Samson was not bound by the Allophyls to the machinery of error until after the lights of his eyes had been extinguished (Judges 16:21).

8. Some, while the reason of the mind is still vigorous, are overcome by the assault of vices, and afterward lose their resolve to perform good works. Thus the king of Babylon first killed the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and then tore out his eyes; consequently, after the habit of evil deeds and the destruction of good ones, the reason of some people also perishes.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That Vices Arise from Vices and Virtues from Virtues

[Col. 0635B]

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

CHAPTER XXXIII, note 1. From Gregory, *Morals*, book X, chapter 9. LOAISA.

Taio took all the sentences of this chapter from this source, book IV, chapter 12. AREV.]

1. Sins are generated from sin in such a way that, when small sins are not avoided, a person falls into the greatest ones; and when admitted sins are defended and not lamented, one proceeds from crime to pride. Thus it happens that the person who both commits crimes by his will and defends them through the swelling of stubbornness is guilty of a double crime.

2. Vice generates vice just as virtue conceives virtue. For vice is generated from vice, as in David, who, by not avoiding adultery, also committed murder (2 Samuel 11:6).

3. Likewise, virtue conceives virtue, as the apostles merited the virtue of martyrdom through the virtue of evangelical preaching.

[Col. 0635C] [Note: [Col. 0635D]

4. From Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 23, and *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 12. LOAISA.]

4. In the hearts of those who live according to the world, vices succeed one another, so that when one has departed another takes its place, in accordance with the testimony of the prophet Joel, who says: “What the locust left, the consuming locust ate; what the consuming locust left, the caterpillar ate; and what the caterpillar left, the rust ate” (Joel 1:4–5). These things are therefore gathered under the allegory of vices, because what follows is: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep.”

5. Sometimes it is useful to sin in lesser vices, so that greater ones may be avoided more effectively. Read the Apostle Paul permitting lesser sins so that greater ones may not be committed. Vices are truly healed when they are excluded by virtues, not by vices. Certain hidden vices of some people become apparent only when they cease from other vices.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Virtues Used Badly

[Col. 0635D]

1. Sometimes virtues that are used badly themselves generate vices [Col. 0636A]. This happens through the mind’s immoderate desire, which is not satisfied with the gift it has deserved unless it seeks from it either praise or condemnable profits.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

CHAPTER XXXIV, note 2. “For the arrival of a brother,” and so forth. The Rule of the Monks, chapter 10, is relevant here. AREV.]

2. Sometimes virtues generate vices when they are not relaxed at an appropriate time. Thus what is a virtue in a suitable place is judged a vice in an unsuitable one—for example, if the canonical fast is not suspended because of a brother’s arrival.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

3. Acts 15. For Paul forbade the Gentiles who were coming to the freedom of the Gospel to be circumcised, yet, as he passed through Lystra and Iconium, he circumcised Timothy, who had been born of a Gentile father. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXVIII, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

3. Take from the Apostle Paul, therefore, the discernment of virtues: he did for a time what he had altogether forbidden to be done.

[Note: [Col. 0636D]

4. From Gregory, books XXXI and XXXII of the *Morals*, chapters 7 and 17. LOAISA.

In the same passage, others read: “when they do not preserve discernment.” AREV.]

4. Likewise, certain virtues, when they do not serve discernment, pass into vices. For often justice, when it exceeds its proper measure, produces the savagery of cruelty; excessive pity gives birth to the dissolution of discipline; zeal, when it is greater than it ought to be, passes into the vice of anger; and excessive gentleness generates the sluggishness of torpor.

237 5. The discernment of a prudent man carefully takes heed lest he do good intemperately and pass from virtue into vice.

6. Likewise, in some people vice is generated from virtue when someone boasts of the merits of chastity and abstinence. A person who gives alms for the sake of empty glory also turns virtue into vice. So too the person who derives arrogance from wisdom, who seeks a reward for justice, or who turns some gift of God he has deserved toward his own praise or takes it up for evil uses undoubtedly transfers virtue into vice.

7. People nourish the vices by which they perish from their virtues. Again, by a most powerful art God forms virtues from our vice, by which he reforms us from iniquity.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Simulated Virtues

[Note: [Col. 0636D]

CHAPTER XXXV, note 1. From Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXII, chapter 17. LOAISA.]

1. Certain vices assume the appearance of virtues and therefore deceive their followers more perniciously, because they conceal themselves beneath the veil of virtues. For vices that immediately appear contrary to virtues are quickly corrected when they come openly, since their followers are ashamed of such crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0636D]

2. Others do not recognize them because of an insensible blindness of mind. AREV.]

2. Carnal people often do not recognize as culpable the vice that appears worthy of condemnation because of the insensibility of their mind.

[Note: [Col. 0636D]

3. From Gregory, in the same place, and book III, part 3 of *Pastoral Care*, admonition 17. LOAISA.]

3. Likewise, certain vices appear to be virtues, [Col. 0636D] yet are not virtues. For sometimes cruelty is practiced under the pretext of justice, and what is in fact a vice is thought to be a virtue; similarly, lax sluggishness is regarded as gentleness, and what numb negligence does is thought to be the work of merciful indulgence. Sometimes, too, a vice of lavish extravagance imitates the virtue of generosity, and gloomy stinginess imitates the virtue of frugality; the vice of obstinacy is concealed beneath the virtue of steadfastness. Fear, likewise, is hidden under the appearance of obedience, and what is actually the vice of fear is called the virtue of humility. Bold insolence of speech is also taken for freedom in defense of the truth, and the vice of laziness imitates the virtue of repose. Moreover, the vice of restlessness wishes to be called the virtue of diligence; readiness to act rashly is thought to be zeal for good endeavor; and slowness in doing good appears to be deliberative delay—although the former is a vice and the latter a virtue. Thus, by such an example, vices imitate the appearance of virtues; and [Col. 0637B] some people confidently believe themselves just precisely because of what most strongly condemns them.

[Note: [Col. 0637D]

4. Gregory, *Moralia*, book IX, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

4. An apt example of vices may be taken from the likeness of a robber. For just as a robber emerges from ambush and joins travelers on the road, pretending to be their companion until he can deceive the unsuspecting person, and, when he suddenly bursts forth, reveals himself plainly as a robber bent on destruction, so vices sometimes mingle dangerously with virtues until they seize for their own purposes the entire effectiveness of a good work, and the soul that had been pleased with its virtues discovers that it has been deceived and condemned by its vices.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Pursuit of Virtues

1. We rise to virtues with difficulty, but slide into vices without effort. The former are steep, the latter easy. [Col. 0637C] For we endure great exertions in order to be able to climb to heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0637D]

CHAPTER XXXVI, note 2. On the growth of virtues: Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXII, chapter 14. LOAISA.]

2. Just as those who strive toward the summit of virtue do not begin at the highest points but with modest things, so that they may gradually reach what is loftier, so those who slide into vices do not immediately begin with great crimes, but grow accustomed to them through lesser ones, and thus plunge into the greatest.

3. Just as a person gradually plunges from the smallest vices into the greatest, so he advances step by step from modest virtues toward those that are lofty.

4. Whoever tries to acquire virtues in a disorderly manner quickly comes to grief. This is a principle in the natural order: whatever hastens rapidly toward growth undoubtedly comes quickly to an end, like plants, which perish all the sooner the faster they grow. But [Col. 0637D] trees, firmly rooted with deep roots, endure longer because they reach maturity gradually.

5. It is of no benefit to do some good while evil is mixed in; first one must restrain evil, and then practice good. The prophet indicates this when he says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16).

239 6. Vices must first be uprooted from a person, and virtues then planted. Truth cannot cling and be joined to falsehood, modesty to wantonness, [Col. 0638A] faith to treachery, or chastity to lust.

7. Some virtues are supreme, while others are intermediate. Faith, hope, and charity are supreme virtues. For those who possess them possess them truly. Other virtues are intermediate, because they may be possessed either for benefit or for harm if someone becomes arrogantly puffed up by them—for example, learning, fasting, chastity, knowledge, or temporal riches, through which we can act either well or badly.

8. Whoever has begun to become better after having been worse should beware of being exalted by the virtues he has received, lest he fall more grievously through his virtues than previously he had lain fallen through his vices.

9. So that the person whom God justifies may not again exalt himself because of his virtues, God grants him some gifts of virtue and withdraws others, so that when the mind rises up over what it possesses, it may once again be humbled by what it recognizes that it by no means possesses.

10. Whoever, inspired by the gift of heavenly grace, rises toward virtue, if he is perhaps restrained by some adversity through the hand of God who governs him, should not be lifted up by the virtues he has received, nor should he be broken. For it is undoubtedly a great virtue to bear calmly even the very fact that one is humbled by afflictions.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Struggle of Virtues against Vices

[Note: [Col. 0637D]

CHAPTER XXXVII, note 1. Taio, who discusses this struggle of virtues in book IV, chapter 25, reads *concussus* (“shaken”) where the text has *conversus* (“turned”). My manuscript likewise has *concussus*. The older editions read *ab elationis concursu* (“from the assault of elation”). AREV.]

1. Holy men cleanse themselves more truly from the filth of vices when individual virtues are set against individual vices. Sometimes vices struggle with virtues for a useful purpose, so that through the contest itself [Col. 0638C] either the mind may be exercised or the spirit, turned away from elation, may be restrained.

2. The assaults of vices must be fought with opposing virtues. Against lust of the heart, purity must be applied; against hatred, love must be prepared; against anger, patience must be set forth. Against fear, moreover, the virtue of confidence must be applied; against sluggishness, the battle of zeal; against sadness, joy; against acedia, courage; against avarice, generosity; and against pride, humility. Thus each virtue restrains the vice arising against it and extinguishes the movements of temptation through the divine virtue of charity.

3. Abstinence tames lust. For to the extent that the body is weakened by hunger, the mind is recalled from unlawful desire.

[Col. 0638D] 4. Endurance fights against anger; anger, however, destroys itself, while patience wins the victory by enduring.

5. Hope of eternal joy overcomes the sorrow of sadness; and the sweetness of inner tranquility soothes the distress with which a troubled mind is afflicted by external things.

6. Charity should be prepared against envy, and against the fires of anger the tranquility of gentleness should be employed.

7. The proud imitate the pride of the devil, [Col. 0639A] against which the humility of Christ is set, by which the exalted are humbled.

[Note: [Col. 0639D]

8. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXI, chapter 17. LOAISA.]

8. Pride is the queen and mother of the seven principal vices, and those seven principal vices in turn give birth to many vices from themselves. They are joined to one another by a kind of kinship, so that one arises from another.

9. Just as pride, the leader of the seven vices, subjects us to their powers, so Christ, full of sevenfold grace, frees us from the dominion of vices; those whom pride subjects to a sevenfold vice, Christ liberates through the gift of sevenfold grace.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Pride

[Note: [Col. 0639D]

CHAPTER XXXVIII, note 1. John Cassian the hermit discusses pride elegantly in book XII, chapter 1, in these words: “Our eighth and final struggle is against the spirit of pride. Although this disease is last in the conflict of vices and is placed at the end of their order, it is nevertheless first in origin and time: a most savage beast, more monstrous than all those preceding it, especially tempting the perfect and, almost when they have already reached the consummation of virtues, devouring them with a more dreadful bite.” LOAISA.

In the same place: *pensante* (“weighing”); another reading, *dispensante* (“dispensing”). It may be preferable to read *labitur in carnis luxuriam* (“he falls into the lust of the flesh”), or, as in the older edition, *labitur carnis luxuria* (“he falls through the lust of the flesh”). AREV.]

1. Pride is worse than every vice, whether because it is adopted by persons of the highest rank and first importance, or because it arises from a work of justice and virtue and its guilt is less clearly perceived.
