Lust of the flesh, by contrast, is conspicuous to everyone because it is immediately shameful in itself. Yet, when God weighs the matter, pride is the lesser evil. But one who is held by pride and does not perceive it falls into lust of the flesh, so that, humbled by this, he may rise both from shame and from pride.

2. Everyone who sins is proud, because in doing what is forbidden he treats the divine commandments with contempt. Thus pride is rightly called “the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. 10:15), because unless disobedience to God’s commandments has come first, the guilt of transgression does not follow.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

3. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXII, chapter 7. LOAISA.]

3. Every pride lies as low as it raises itself high; and it falls more deeply the higher it elevates itself. For whoever is lifted up by his own pride is brought low by God’s justice.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

4. The ordinary gloss: “The wind will feed him,” that is, empty confidence. In the printed editions the marginal reading is “the proud spirit”; our manuscript copies, however, do not recognize it. LOAISA.]

4. Those who are puffed up with pride feed on wind. Hence the prophet also says: “The wind feeds all your shepherds” (Jer. 22:22), that is, the spirit of pride.

5. Those who are proud of their virtues must be judged by the very works through which they use them as virtues, because they do a good thing without a good intention. For truly, any virtue without humility, and without charity, is counted as a vice.

6. Because of pride the devil deservedly fell from heavenly blessedness. Therefore those who are lifted up by their virtues imitate the devil; and they fall more grievously because they fall from a height.

7. As pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of all virtues. It is first in sin [Col. 0639D] and last in the struggle. For it either lays the mind low through sin at the beginning, or at the end casts it down from its virtues. Hence it is the greatest of all sins, because through both virtues and [Col. 0640A] vices it destroys the human mind.

8. Pride should fall where it was born, so that for the proud one thing may not be the fault and another the punishment, but the fault itself may also be their punishment.

242 9. Arrogance is born from pride, not pride from arrogance. For unless hidden elation of mind has come first, open boasting in praise does not follow. Thus pride precedes arrogance in guilt just as it precedes it in origin.

10. Often, for the correction of elation, God’s providence causes certain people to fall through some accident. Rebuked for this fall, they acquire humble wisdom from themselves and do not seek to be praised for God’s gifts; instead, they praise God, from whom they received what they wish others to praise in them.

11. It is more useful for an arrogant person to fall into any vice and become humble before God after the fall than to grow proud through elation and incur, through pride, the condemnation of a more grievous ruin.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Fornication

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

CHAPTER XXXIX, note 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVI, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

1. From the guilt of pride one usually proceeds to the abominable impurity of the flesh. For one depends upon the other: just as through pride of mind one proceeds into the prostitution of lust, so through humility of mind the chastity of the flesh is preserved. God sometimes casts down hidden pride of mind through the manifest ruin of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

2. Gregory, in the same place. LOAISA.]

2. It is clear that impurity born of lust arises from hidden pride of spirit, following the example of the first human being, who, as soon as he swelled up through pride against God, immediately experienced lust of the flesh and covered his shame. Therefore each person should attribute to his own guilt the fact that he has fallen whenever he is overcome by lust; for unless hidden pride had preceded it, the manifest ruin of lust would not have followed.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

3. Gregory, at the cited place. LOAISA.]

3. Sometimes a Christian is attacked by the devil through a twofold vice: secretly through elation and publicly through lust. Yet while someone avoids lust, he falls into elation. Again, while he carelessly shuns elation, he sluggishly falls into lust. Thus from the hidden vice of elation one proceeds into the open vice of lust, and from the open vice of lust into hidden elation. But God’s servant, weighing both with discernment, avoids lust in such a way that he does not incur elation, and suppresses elation in such a way that he does not relax his mind into lust.

[Col. 0640D] 243 4. Demons are especially helpful to the lustful and the proud. While evil spirits serve other vices, they are joined to these with greater familiarity and serve them more fully according to their desire.

[Col. 0641A] [Note: [Col. 0641D]

5. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 3. LOAISA.

In the same place: *humecta* (“moist places”); another reading, *humentia* (“damp places”). AREV.]

5. The devil chiefly dominates the human race through these two vices: pride of mind and lust of the flesh. Hence the Lord speaks in Job about the devil, saying: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secret places of reeds, in moist places” (Job 40:16). By the reed is signified empty pride, and by the moist places the lust of the flesh. Through these two vices the devil possesses the human race, either by lifting the mind into pride or by corrupting the flesh through lust.

6. Many are subject to lust, and in stubborn pride glory in the very work of lust; they are more exalted by what should have humbled them.

[Note: [Col. 0641D]

7. Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, chapter 25. LOAISA.

In the same place: Others read, “Because he is praised.” AREV.]

7. Evil becomes worse when not only are shameful acts committed, but the perpetrators are also lifted up by the empty praise they receive for those very acts, as it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 9:24). For what is worse than for wretched people to rejoice in the shameful acts over which they ought already to weep more abundantly?

8. Lust is sought more eagerly when it is seen. For, as a certain wise man says: “The first arrows of fornication are the eyes; the second are words.” But one who is not captured by the eyes can resist words. Nature is sufficient while the inclination is still free.

9. Whoever restrains the pleasure of a lustful suggestion does not proceed to consent to lust. For one who does not accommodate himself to the pleasure that tickles him quickly resists the act.

10. The person who is tempted as far as consent, even if not as far as the actual deed, is attacked more harshly than one who is solicited by temptations only through suggestion, according to the condition of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0641D]

11. Paul, 2 Cor. 12: “There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.” There are various opinions among the saints concerning this thorn of Paul. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 11: “After the sublimity of so many revelations, a thorn of the flesh tormented Paul.” And below: “That temptation was not an abyss of vices, but a safeguard of merits.” LOAISA.]

11. The thorns of the flesh that were in Paul, stirred up by the angel of Satan (2 Cor. 12), arose from the law of sin, which necessarily dwells in the members of human beings through lust. As he struggles against this resistance within himself, he is perfected, and from the weakness of lustful titillation he receives the virtue of glorious combat.

12. Many struggles arise for God’s servants from their own flesh. For although their intention in the love of God is unshaken, the mind nevertheless endures inward battles in the flesh that it bears outwardly. But God, who permits these things for testing, does not abandon his own, protected by grace.

13. Therefore the elect sometimes fall through a carnal lapse, [Col. 0641D] so that they may be healed of the vice of pride by which they are puffed up over their virtues; and those who are proud because of their devotion to virtue are humbled by a vice of the flesh, so that they may rise again.

[Note: [Col. 0642D]

14. The passage of Isaiah 32 appears in the Vulgate edition as follows: “Gird your loins; mourn upon your breasts.” The Septuagint has: “Gird yourselves with sackcloth around your loins, and beat your breasts.” That is: “Gird your loins with sackcloth, and mourn upon your breasts.” He shortened this passage in order to adapt it to his purpose. LOAISA.]

14. Before adultery is completed in deed, adultery already exists in thought. For fornications must first be removed from the heart, and then they will not burst forth into action. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isa. 32:11)—that is, cut away lusts in the heart, which pertain to the loins. For the heart is above the breasts, not in the loins.

15. Immoderate license in lust knows no limit. When a vicious mind has relaxed itself in fulfilling fornication, with the flesh indulging in lust, it nevertheless proceeds, at the urging of demons, to other abominable crimes. Once it has immoderately exceeded the bounds of modesty, it adds crime to crime and gradually advances toward worse things.

16. The inexperienced lust of the flesh of lovers—or rather, of madmen—is not as sweet as the experienced kind, nor is fornication as pleasurable when first committed, since repetition produces greater pleasure. When it has become habitual, it becomes so much sweeter to the depraved that it is difficult to overcome. Hence, through the habit of sinning, we are often dragged toward sin like captives, with a kind of violence, and we feel our senses rebelling within us against our right intention.

17. If the pleasure of fornication delights the mind more than the love of chastity, sin still reigns in the person. But if the beauty of inner chastity gives greater delight, sin no longer reigns; justice reigns instead. For sin does not reign in a person only when fornication has been committed; if the person still takes pleasure in it and it holds the mind, sin undoubtedly reigns.

[Col. 0642C] 18. Fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is servitude to idols. There is also spiritual fornication, as the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

[Note: [Col. 0642D]

19. Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 11. LOAISA.]

19. Every impure pollution is called fornication, although each person may prostitute himself to a different pleasure of shamefulness. For from the pleasure of fornication various shameful acts arise, by which the kingdom of God is closed and a person is separated from God.

20. Among the other seven vices, fornication is the gravest crime, because through the impurity of the flesh it violates God’s temple and, taking away the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute.

21. The human race is subjected to the devil more through lust of the flesh [Col. 0642D] than through the other vices. For although the devil tries to corrupt people whom he has enticed by various temptations, he nevertheless suggests the desire for adultery more strongly, because he intends both sexes to be especially diseased by this vice.

[Col. 0643A] 22. Knowing that chastity is the beauty of the soul, and that through it a human being is made equal to the angels in the merits from which the demons fell, the demons, struck by envious spite, inject through the bodily senses the deed and desire of lust, so that they may drag the soul, cast down from heavenly things to earthly ones, and, triumphing over those whom they have conquered, lead them with themselves to Tartarus.

23. When, through the impulse of demons, the mind is driven toward the pleasure of fornication, the fear of divine judgment and the torments of eternal fire should be set before its eyes, because every punishment is overcome by fear of a harsher penalty. For just as one nail drives out another, so recollection of the heat of Gehenna often removes the heat of lust.

24. Some who live lustfully in youth take pleasure in becoming continent in old age, and then choose to serve chastity, when lust scorns to keep them as its slaves.

25. Those who lived lustfully in youth should by no means be called continent in old age. Such people have no reward, because they have not endured the struggle of labor. Glory awaits those in whom there have been arduous struggles.

246 ## CHAPTER XL. On Continence

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

CHAPTER XL, note 1. Others read *appetite* (“ask”) instead of *petite* (“ask”). AREV.]

1. Continence is given by God; but, he says, “Ask, and you shall receive” (Matt. 7:7). It is granted when God is importuned with inward groaning.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

2. Paul, 1 Cor. 7: “Therefore he who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better.” Ambrose, *On Widows*, book I. LOAISA.

In the same place, Paul also says: “Each person has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that.” In Matthew 19, speaking of those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, he says: “Let him accept it who can.” LOAISA.

In the same place: *nuptiis* (“marriage”); another reading, *nuptiarum conjugio* (“marital union”). AREV.]

2. Virginity is to be preferred to marriage. Marriage is good; virginity is best. Marriage has been permitted (1 Cor. 7); virginity has merely been commended, not commanded. It has been commended only because it is exceedingly lofty.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

3. *Amittit* (“loses”); another reading, *adimit* (“takes away”), which may be preferable. AREV.]

3. Virginity is a twofold good, because in this world it loses (*amittit*) worldly anxiety, and in the future receives the eternal reward of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

4. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 29. The passage is Isaiah 56. LOAISA.

In the same place, Grialius indicated Isaiah 36. AREV.]

4. Virgins are more blessed in eternal life, as Isaiah testifies: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: ‘I will give them a place in my house and within my walls, and I will give them a better name than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not perish’” (Isa. 56:4–5). There is no doubt that those who remain chaste, and virgins, are made equal to God’s angels.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

5. There are three kinds of chastity: marital, widowed, and virginal. Ambrose, *On Widows*, book I. In his letter to Syagrius, and especially in his book *On the Patriarchs*, he likewise affirms that chastity ought above all to exist in priests. LOAISA.]

5. The beauty of chastity is to be loved; once tasted, its delight is found to be sweeter than that of the flesh. For chastity is the fruit of sweetness and the inviolate beauty of the saints. Chastity is security of mind and health of body. Hence, we read that some of the pagan gymnasts practiced perpetual abstinence from Venus, lest they break their virtue through lust. For a lustful life quickly weakens the flesh and rapidly brings weakened flesh into old age.

6. Every sin receives healing of its wound through repentance; but if virginity falls, it cannot in any way be restored. For although through repentance it may receive the fruit of forgiveness, it does not in any way regain its former incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

7. Gregory, *Exposition on 1 Kings*, book VI. LOAISA.]

7. A virgin in the flesh but not in the mind has no reward in what is promised. Hence the Savior, coming in judgment, says to the foolish virgins: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). For whenever he finds the mind corrupted while judging, he will undoubtedly condemn the incorruption of the flesh.

8. Bodily incorruption is of no benefit where there is no integrity of mind. Nor is it of any value for someone to be clean in body while polluted in mind.

9. Many among the reprobate are ignorant of the contagion of carnal corruption. Just as they are unproductive in body, so they remain sterile in mind and in the fruitfulness of good works. They would rightly rejoice in virginity if they did not devote themselves to other wicked works.

10. Whoever professes continence but is not withdrawn from other earthly desires, although lust of the flesh does not pollute that person, is nevertheless stained by various activity in worldly conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0644D]

11. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIII, chapter 4, and *Letters*, book IX, letter to Theotista. LOAISA.]

11. Virgins who glory in their merits are compared to hypocrites, who seek publicly the glory of a good work that they ought to possess humbly within their conscience. Such people therefore do not reach the heavenly promises, because through the vice of elation they themselves take away the reward of their virginity. This is what it means in the Gospel for the virgins not to have oil in their vessels: they do not preserve within their conscience the testimony of a good work, but glory in their appearance before human beings, not in their heart before God.

[Note: [Col. 0644D]

12. Augustine expressed this view in book II, chapter 12, *On Adulterous Marriages*, addressed to Pollentius: “When, therefore, he said, ‘I want younger women to marry,’ he was, I say, giving this counsel in order to support the ruin of incontinence.” And in *Against Julian*, book V, final chapter: “We do not say that marriages are shameful, since, lest incontinence fall into damnable disgrace, it must be supported by the respectability of marriage.” And in book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, addressed to Valerius, chapter 16: “Thus,” he says, “the weakness of incontinence, lest it fall into the ruin of disgraceful acts, is received under the respectability of marriage.”

But the meaning of the obscure word *destina* used by Isidore—for that is how it appears in the manuscript copies, especially the Gothic ones, whose antiquity I honor and whose writing and reliability I willingly follow—led copyists of later periods, who did not adequately understand the force of the word *destina*, into error, and caused some to substitute *causam* (“cause”), others *doctrinam matrimonii* (“the teaching of marriage”), others *contemptum* (“contempt”), and still others various incorrect alternatives for *destina*.

*Destina* is a support placed beneath a crumbling wall so that it may not fall. The African poet Corippus uses the word in *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*:

“And Thomas, the support (*destina*) of the wavering Libyan land.”

Arnobius, book II, says: “When did the motion of the stars, or the science of casting horoscopes, begin to be known? Was it not after Atlas—so some relate—the bearer, carrier, flute-player, and support of heaven?” He calls Atlas the support of heaven because, as though by a firm defense, the impending collapse of heaven—so antiquity imagined—was held up by him.

In this sense Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, writes in the *Life of the blessed Isidore* that God, raising him—namely Isidore—in the final times after so many disasters of Spain, “in order, I believe, to restore the monuments of the ancients, lest we grow old entirely through rusticity, placed him there as a kind of support.” Thus the reading must be restored from the old manuscript copy, where it had previously been read incorrectly as *quasi quamdam lucem apposuit destinari* (“as though he had set a kind of light there”).

From this noun *destina* came the verb *destinari*, meaning “to strengthen” and “to support.” Vitruvius, *On Harbors and Structures to Be Made in Water*, book V, chapter 12, says: “Let powder be brought from the regions extending from Cumae to the promontory of Minerva, and let it be mixed so that in the mortar two parts correspond to one. Then, at the place that has been determined, chests enclosed with strong posts and chains must be lowered into the water and supported (*destinandae*).” That is, they must be supported and strengthened with *destinae*. For he immediately adds: “But if, because of waves or the force of the open sea, the supported chests cannot be held in place, then from the land itself, or the embankment, the powder must be laid as firmly as possible.”

Philander says that he read in a manuscript copy: “If the supported chests (*destinae arcae*) cannot be held,” which seems closer to Vitruvius’s meaning at that point. Likewise in the following passage: “But in those places where powder is not found, the work must be done in this way: double chests, joined with boards and chains, must be placed at the spot that has been determined, and between the supports (*destinatas*) chalk must be tamped down with pestles made of marsh rush.” In the manuscript, Philander says that he read *inter destinas* (“between the supports”), which I would prefer.

In another manuscript copy, instead of *destina* one reads *destinatione matrimonii* (“the support of marriage”), with reference to the ancient formula by which wives were said to be “designated” (*destinari*). Ulpian, in the Digest, title “On the Rites of Marriage,” law *Tutor*: “A guardian or curator cannot take an adult woman as wife unless she has been betrothed by her father, or designated in a will with a stated condition, and has entered into the marriage.” And in the Digest, title “On the Julian Law on Adultery,” under “He who [marries] a ward”: “Unless she has been betrothed by her father, or designated in a will with a stated condition, and has entered into the condition of marriage.” This wording is frequently used in the final law, final paragraph, under “On Divorces,” and in law 7, paragraph 1, under “On the Law of Dowry,” as Jacob Cujacius carefully observed in book XVI of his *Observations*, chapter 33. LOAISA.]

In the same place: The learned note of Loaisa on the word *destina* is attributed by Vezzosi to Breulius for no other reason than that Breulius transcribed Loaisa’s notes from Grialius’s edition. See the *Life of Isidore* written by Braulio in *Isidoriana*, [Col. 0646D] chapters 3 and 4. AREV.]

12. The ruin of adultery is shored up by the support of marriage (*destina matrimonii*); and it is better to take a wife than to perish through the heat of lust.

[Col. 0645A] 13. Some are not attracted to the dignity of marriage for the sake of begetting children, but seek it for the turbulent and lustful habit of the flesh, and thus use a good thing badly.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

14. In this place, Grialius’s edition contained a sign for some note that is missing. AREV.]

14. Vices are evil in themselves, whereas marriages and offices of power are good in themselves; but because of the things associated with them they become evil. Marriages are evil insofar as they occasion what the Apostle says: “But he who is with a wife thinks about the things of the world” (1 Cor. 7:33). And: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” (ibid. 7:2). Likewise, offices of power become evil through elation, oppression, and also violation of justice. Riches do harm, and offices of power do harm, but because of what is placed alongside them, not in themselves—like a straight road beside which thorns grow, rising at its side and harming those who walk on the straight road.

## CHAPTER XLI. On Greed

1. No one can undertake spiritual battles unless he has first subdued the desires of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

CHAPTER XLI, note 2. Gregory, *Commentary on 1 Kings*, book I. LOAISA.]

2. The mind cannot be free for contemplating God when it pants after the desires and cravings of this world. For the eye cannot look upon high things when dust obstructs it.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

3. Ecclesiastes 10. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

3. Avarice and love of money are worse than every sin. Hence Solomon says: “There is nothing more wicked than loving money” (Eccl. 10:10). For such a person makes his own soul saleable, because in his lifetime he has cast away his deepest inner things.

[Col. 0646A] 4. Greed is the mother of all crimes. Hence the Apostle says: “The desire for money is the root of all evils; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith” (1 Tim. 6:10). If, therefore, the root of crimes is cut off, the other offspring of sins do not sprout.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

5. “They renounced.” Another reading: “They denied.” AREV.]

5. Many, because of earthly greed, have renounced even the faith itself. Greed sold Christ. In many people the desire for what belongs to others is so great that they do not shrink even from committing murder, as in the case of Ahab, who fulfilled the desire of his greed by shedding blood (1 Kings 21).

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

6. Others read: “May they come to their senses and turn back to God, from whom they have withdrawn in mind.” AREV.]

6. The wicked often obtain the evils they desire, so that they may be punished more severely for the affection of their evil desire. But God does not allow his elect to proceed to the fulfillment of evil desires; rather, he turns their minds toward sorrow for what they wickedly desire in the world, so that through this experience they may come to their senses and return to God, from whom they have withdrawn in mind. Therefore, let the person who is not permitted to accomplish what he temporally desires recognize that God, while favorable toward him, is opposing him. By God’s hidden judgment, it is believed that those perish more harshly whose desire is immediately followed by the accomplishment of their action.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

7. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XV, chapter 12. “The miser is always in need” are the words of Horace, book I of the *Epistles*, letter 2. LOAISA.

In the same place: Vezzosi did not wish Horace’s words to be omitted:

“Despise pleasures; pleasure bought with pain is harmful.

The miser is always in need: set a definite limit to your desire.” AREV.]

7. Greed never knows how to be satisfied. For the miser is always in need; and the more he acquires, the more he seeks. He is tormented not only by the desire to increase his possessions, but also afflicted by fear of losing them.

8. We are born needy in this life, and needy we shall depart from life. If we believe that the goods of this world are destined to perish, why do we desire perishable things with such love?

[Col. 0647A] [Note: [Col. 0647C]

9. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 21. Isaiah 5. LOAISA.]

9. Many powerful people are inflamed by such a furious greed that they exclude the poor from their boundaries and do not permit them to live there. To them the prophet rightly says: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, up to the boundary of the place. Will you alone dwell in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. 5:8, 14). The same prophet subsequently announces that such people are seized by hell—that is, by the devil—and carried off to destruction, saying: “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit, and its strong men, its tall and glorious men, shall descend to it.” Nor is it surprising that those who, while alive, did not extinguish the flame of their greed are assigned, when they die, to the fires of hell.

10. Those who burn with the desire of greed are set ablaze by the breath of diabolical [Col. 0647B] inspiration. Pride kindled Eve’s mind so that she might eat from the forbidden tree. Envy kindled Cain’s mind so that he might kill his brother (Gen. 3:4). It kindled Solomon with the torches of lust so that, through the love of desire, he might worship idols. It kindled Ahab with greed so that he might join murder to avarice (1 Kings 21). Through these inspirations, therefore, the devil secretly corrupts human hearts with evil desires.

251 ## CHAPTER XLII. On Gluttony

1. The first suggestion of desire is bread; if one yields to it not at all, the various desires of gluttony are suppressed. Hence Daniel says: “I did not eat the bread of desire” (Dan. 10:3)—that is, “I did not fulfill its craving.”

[Col. 0647C] [Note: [Col. 0647D]

CHAPTER XLII, note 2. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXX, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

2. The first material of lust is satiety with bread. Hence the prophet accuses Sodom of the satiety of bread, saying: “This was the iniquity of Sodom: pride, satiety of bread, and abundance” (Ezek. 16:49). For the Sodomites, consuming bread immoderately, descended into the shamefulness of sinful acts; and because they did not keep to a proper measure in eating, they deserved, with pride accompanying them, to be burned by heavenly fires.

[Note: [Col. 0647D]

3. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 20. LOAISA.]

3. It is useful to beware of gluttony and the desire for food. For what is so harmful as for the mind to serve the belly and food, which must be destroyed, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13)?

4. Lust is next to the belly, both in position and in vice. For where there is concern for the belly, there also follows concern for the things nearest to the belly. For in the order of the bodily members, the genitals are joined to the belly. And while one of these is excessively nourished, the other is aroused to lust.

[Note: [Col. 0647D]

5. Pope Leo, Sermon 3 on Fasting. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others say: As the philosophers stated, the belly should be fed so that it may sustain the soul, not corrupt it. It would be clearer to say: “For the philosophers explain that foods,” etc. AREV.]

5. Food should be taken neither for lust nor for satiety, but only so that the body may be sustained. For, as the philosophers explain, foods were discovered so that they might sustain the soul, not corrupt it.

[Note: [Col. 0647D]

6. Hence Cato the Elder’s statement, quoted by Cicero in his little book On Old Age: “One should take as much food and drink as will restore one’s strength, not overwhelm it.” Otherwise, as Theognis rightly confirms:

“Far more men has excess destroyed than hunger—men who wished to possess more than their allotted share.”

The general sense of these verses is approximately this: far more people have perished from excessive gorging on food and drink than from hunger. Theopompus likewise speaks well in Book V of his Philippica:

“Eating much and feeding on meats takes away the power of reason and makes the minds slower.”

Accordingly, those Platonic dinners are rightly praised by Athenaeus in Book X and by Cicero in Book V of the Tusculan Disputations, because they were pleasant not so much on the day itself as on the following day. LOAISA.

Ibid. “To vanish.” Hence the passage from Theopompus that I have just cited. Moreover, this passage seems to come from Jerome’s letter to Nepotian, On the Life of Clerics; for he says as follows: “A fine saying is found among the Greeks, and I do not know whether it sounds equally well among us: ‘A fat belly does not produce a refined mind.’” The Greek senarius is as follows:

“An ample belly does not produce a subtle mind.”

Ibid. “To vanish.” Others have “to grow dull.” My codex has “to weaken”; perhaps “to fail.” AREV.]

6. Those who use food excessively dull the mind’s perception all the more as they feed the belly more. For the Greeks said that a subtle understanding cannot arise from a gross belly. Excessive satiety of the throat dulls the mind’s sharpness and causes intelligence to vanish.

[Note: [Col. 0648D]

7. Gregory, Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

7. The fires of lust grow through the fuel of food; but the body weakened by abstinence is not consumed by temptation. Hence, although the three young men abstained from food and were touched by the flame of the Babylonian fire, it did not burn them. For although the fire of carnal desires inflames the minds of those who abstain, it does not burn them through to consent to desire or to the act.

[Note: [Col. 0648D]

8. Gregory, Homily 40 on the Gospels. LOAISA.]

8. Let the rich man’s punishment be kept in mind by anyone who has an abundance of banquets: in hell amid the flames he had as much want as he had abundance of banquets here. For in this world he did not wish to hunger or thirst; therefore there, thirsting amid the flames, he sought a drop of water and did not obtain it.

[Col. 0648C] 9. Consider how severely feasting and lavish banquets are condemned. For through the prophet the Lord threatens that he will not pardon this iniquity in those who eagerly pursue it. He says through Isaiah: “Behold, joy and gladness: killing calves, slaughtering rams, eating meat, and drinking wine. If this iniquity is forgiven you, until you die” (Isa. XXII, 13–14).

[Note: [Col. 0648D]

10. From Gregory, Book III of Pastoral Care, admonition 20. LOAISA.]

10. Just as all carnal desires are cut away by abstinence, so all the virtues of the soul are destroyed by the vice of gluttony. Hence the chief of the cooks overthrew the walls of Jerusalem, because the belly, which is served by cooks, destroys the virtues of the soul. For no one can attain perfection in the virtues unless he has first subdued the greed of the belly.

11. No one can rule over the other vices unless he has first restrained the greed of the belly. Nor can anyone easily expel unclean spirits from himself without abstinence from gluttony. For the enemies outside us are then more powerfully overcome by us when the vices within us have first been extinguished. In vain does one wage war outside who has danger within.

[Note: [Col. 0649C]

12. Gregory, Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

12. It is not the quality of foods but their desire that must be avoided. For carefully prepared foods are often tasted without gluttonous craving, while poor and cheap foods are often taken with a desire to eat. Thus the fault lies not in the quality of the foods, but in the fact that what is tasted with desire is counted as vice.

[Note: [Col. 0649C]

13. The whole substance of this discussion is drawn from Gregory, Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 13. He adds a fifth kind: “It should further be known,” he says, “that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways,” etc. Cassian, in Book V, chapter 23, enumerates only three kinds: “The nature of gastrimargy is threefold: one kind compels a person to anticipate the canonical hour of eating; another rejoices merely in the stuffing and satiety of the belly with any kind of food; the third delights in more elaborate and appetizing banquets.” See the same author at greater length in that place. LOAISA.]

13. There are four kinds of distinctions in the appetite of gluttony, namely: what, when, how much, and how it is desired. “What” concerns the thing itself that is desired. “When” concerns desiring something before the proper time. “How much” refers to excess. “How” is attributed to the impatience of haste.

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

14. Seneca says aptly in his letters: “The belly does not listen to instructions; it demands and pleads. Yet it is not a troublesome creditor: it is dismissed with little, provided that you give it what you owe.” LOAISA.]

14. No exactor is so importunate to a human being as the belly, which satisfies its daily nourishment by the daily demand of hunger. Although we are sometimes born with the other vices, we do not always die with them; but with this one we are born, and with this one we die.

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

15. Here Loaisa’s note is also indicated, although it does not appear. Perhaps it expressed a passage from Saint Augustine, Book X of the Confessions, chapter 31: “It often becomes uncertain whether the necessary care of the body is still seeking assistance, or whether the deceptive illusion of desire is supplying a service.” AREV.]

15. For the most part, the pleasure of eating creeps in under the pretext of necessity, so that while one thinks one is serving necessity, one is serving the desire for pleasure; and it is not easy to discern whether what is taken should be attributed to gluttony or to need.

254 **CHAPTER XLIII. On Drunkenness**

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

CHAPTER XLIII. NO. 1. I understand Augustine’s statement in Book X of the Confessions, chapter 31, in this way: “Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, so that it may not approach your servant. But surfeit sometimes creeps upon your servant; you will have mercy, so that it may be far from me.” Aristotle explicitly testifies in the Problems, section III, text 17, that *crapula* comes from wine. He adds: “For *crapula* is a kind of fever and a subsiding inflammation, which afflicts one more than drunkenness, since the latter shakes and alienates the mind; but *crapula*, while the mind remains itself, causes pain.” LOAISA.]

1. Food produces surfeit; drink produces drunkenness. Drunkenness, however, produces disturbance of the mind, madness of the heart, and the flame of lust.

[Col. 0650A] [Note: [Col. 0650D]

2. Hosea IV: “Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.” LOAISA.

Ibid. The printed editions have: “As Solomon says,” but incorrectly. The Gothic text has: “For fornication, as in Solomon, makes the wise man foolish; drunkenness, as in Lot, seizes the power of reason; hence in Proverbs,” etc. This is an explanation of Hosea’s words: “Fornication and drunkenness take away the heart.” Fornication, namely, as in Solomon; drunkenness, as in Lot. Moreover, this sentence is not found in Proverbs. LOAISA.]

2. Drunkenness so alienates the mind that a person does not know where he is. Hence the evil committed through drunkenness is not even perceived. It is true that the prophet says: “Fornication and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. IV, 11). For fornication, as in Solomon (III Kings XI), makes the wise man foolish. Drunkenness, as in Lot (Gen. XIV), seizes the power of reason. Hence in Proverbs: “Those who are powerful are wrathful; let them not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom” (Prov. XXXI, 4).

3. Many consider it praise to drink much wine and not become drunk. Let them hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to you who are mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isa. V, 22).

[Note: [Col. 0650D]

4. Ecclesiastes X, where the Septuagint has: “Woe to you, city, whose king is young, and whose rulers eat in the morning.” That is: “Woe to you, city, whose king is young, and whose rulers eat at the morning hour.” The Vulgate edition has: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning.” Gregory also follows this version in Book XVI of the Moralia, chapter 13. LOAISA.]

4. Isaiah rebukes those devoted to much wine and living luxuriously, saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine” (Isa. V, 11). Of such people it is also said elsewhere: “Woe to you, city whose king is young and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. X, 16).

5. Many serve drunkenness and the pleasures of gluttony from morning until sunset, and do not understand why they were born; but, held fast by beastlike habit, they devote the whole day only to luxury and banquets.

6. The prophet Joel cries out to those who serve drunkenness, saying: “Awake, you drunkards; weep and howl, all who drink wine with sweetness” (Joel I, 5). In this testimony he does not merely say, “Weep, all who drink wine,” as though drinking were wholly forbidden; rather, he added “with sweetness,” which refers to voluptuous and wasteful indulgence. For the Apostle teaches Timothy to drink as much as necessity requires, saying: “Use a little wine.”

[Note: [Col. 0650D]

7. “Nazirites.” I restored this reading, since Grialius’s edition had “Nazaraeis.” AREV.]

7. People become drunk not only from wine but also from other kinds of drink, which are prepared in various ways. Hence the Nazirites, who consecrated themselves to the Lord, were commanded not to drink wine or strong drink. Both overturn the condition of the mind and make people drunk; both likewise produce carnal lust.

8. Some continent persons, just as they eat bread by weight, also take water in measured amounts, asserting that abstinence from water as well as from food is appropriate for bodily chastity.

**CHAPTER XLIV. On Abstinence**

1. This is perfect and rational fasting: when our outward person fasts, the inward person prays. Through fasting, prayer more easily penetrates heaven. For then, having become spiritual, a person is joined to the angels and is united more freely to God.

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

CHAPTER XLIV. NO. 2. Gregory, Book XXX of the Moralia, chapter 9. LOAISA.]

2. Through fasting, too, hidden mysteries of heaven are revealed and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed. Thus Daniel, when the angel revealed them, was granted knowledge of the mysteries of the sacraments (Dan. X, 3). This virtue displays both manifestations of angels and their announcements.

3. Fastings are powerful weapons against the temptations of demons. For through abstinence they are quickly conquered. Hence our Lord and Savior also teaches us beforehand to overcome their attacks by fastings and prayers, saying: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII, 20). For unclean spirits thrust themselves in especially where they see more food and drink.

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

4. Others: “in the flesh” instead of “and the flesh.” AREV.]

4. As long as the saints dwell in the life of this world, they carry their bodies dry with longing for the heavenly dew. Hence the psalm says: “My soul has thirsted for you, and how greatly my flesh also” (Ps. LXII, 1). The flesh thirsts for God when it abstains through fasting and grows dry. Abstinence both gives life and kills: it gives life to the soul and kills the body.

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

5. Gregory, Book VIII of the Moralia, chapter 26. LOAISA.]

5. Abstinence is often practiced deceptively, and fasts are undertaken hypocritically. Some tear their bodies apart through astonishing hunger, “disfiguring their faces,” as the Gospel says, “so that they may appear to people to be fasting” (Matt. VI, 16). They grow pale in the face, wear down the body, and draw deep sighs from the heart. They even consign themselves to deadly punishments before death; and they pursue such a laborious practice not for the love of God but solely to win human admiration and praise.

6. Some abstain incredibly so that they may appear holy to inquisitive people; but for such persons this good of abstinence should not be counted a virtue but a vice, because they use a good thing wrongly.

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

7. Gregory, Book VIII of the Moralia, chapter 24. LOAISA.]

7. They love fasting and almsgiving to be done in secret, so that God alone, who sees all things, may repay the merit of their good works. For those who perform them with public display are by no means justified by God, since, according to the evangelical saying, they have received their reward from human beings (Matt. VI, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

8. Pope Pius: “It does a person no good to fast and pray and perform other religious acts unless the mind is renewed from iniquity,” On Penance, distinction 3. LOAISA.]

8. Fasts are acceptable to God when accompanied by good works. But those who abstain from food while acting wickedly imitate the demons, who have no food but always have wickedness. A person abstains well from food when he also fasts from deeds of malice and from the ambitions of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0651D]

9. Pope Leo, Sermon 4 on Lent. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Those who, out of zeal for abhorrence,” etc. This was the vice of the Manichaeans, as Vezzosius notes. AREV.]

9. Those who refrain from the food of meat out of a zeal for abhorrence rather than from a resolve to practice abstinence should themselves be detested, because they reject God’s creature, which was granted for human use. For nothing is unclean to the faithful, and nothing is judged impure, as the Apostle Paul testifies: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, because both their mind and conscience are polluted” (Titus I, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0652D]

10. “Let us attend,” Vezzosius said, “to this and the immediately following judgment of the great man.” AREV.]

10. A fast is despised when it is compensated in the evening by filling oneself with food. For abstinence cannot be counted present where satiety of the belly has followed.

[Note: [Col. 0652D]

11. Thus the Gothic text, other manuscripts, and the printed books read it. Jerome, however, has “your will”; and the Septuagint, as the same author reports, has “your wills.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “Your pleasure.” The context of the sentence recommends that this be the reading; it is also read this way in the Mozarabic Breviary, as Mariana noted in Book I Against the Jews, chapter 1, no. 5. AREV.]

11. A fast is despised when it is compensated in the evening with delicacies, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Behold, on the day of your fast your pleasure is found” (Isa. LVIII, 3); “pleasure” means delicacies. For just as the repetition of a debt, lawsuits, contention, and striking are condemned, so delicacies are condemned by the prophet during a fast.

12. A person who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to satisfy his gluttony ruminates on banquets in his thoughts all day long.

[Col. 0652C] [Note: [Col. 0652D]

13. Cassian, Conference 2, On Discernment. LOAISA.]

13. Immoderate abstinence should not be imposed upon the body, lest, while the flesh is burdened more heavily by the weight of hunger, it afterward be unable either to do evil or to begin doing good; and lest that which is subjected to abstinence so that it may avoid the practice of evil should at the same time lose the performance of good by being excessively oppressed. The condition of the flesh must therefore be moderated with careful discernment, so that it is neither completely extinguished nor released without restraint.

14. When bodily weakness prevails excessively, no one can attain perfection. For although a person may possess the love of holiness, he cannot carry out the meritorious work to which he endeavors to devote himself with the intention of his heart.

15. Excessive bodily weakness also breaks the powers of the soul, causes the mind’s intelligence to wither, and through feebleness renders a person unable to complete anything good.

16. Nothing in excess. For whatever is done with measure and moderation is beneficial; whatever is excessive and beyond measure becomes harmful and turns one’s endeavor into its opposite. In every work, therefore, there ought to be measure and moderation. For everything that exceeds the proper limit is dangerous; thus water, if it brings excessively heavy rains, not only provides no benefit but also creates danger.

**BOOK THREE**

[Col. 0653]

258 **CHAPTER ONE. On the Scourges of God**

[Col. 0653A]

[Note: [Col. 0653C]

CHAPTER ONE. NO. 1. From Gregory, Book IX of the Moralia, chapter 12. In confirmation of Jeremiah’s testimony, “I am both witness and judge,” he cites Isaiah XLII: “I have been silent, I have always kept still, I have been patient; like a woman in labor I will speak.” But the words “as judge” are absent from the Gothic text and others. LOAISA.

[Col. 0653D] Ibid. “Of the prophets.” Jeremiah XXIX. In Jeremiah it reads: “I am judge and witness.” And Gregory, Book . . . of the Moralia, chapter 12. A codex of the monastery of La Oliva in the kingdom of Navarre reads: “I am witness and avenger.” The Septuagint has: “And I am a witness, says the Lord.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “Have mercy.” These words are absent from the Gothic Toledo Codex. The codex of the monastery of La Oliva has: “to the unworthy Isidore.” LOAISA.]

1. The subtlety of divine Wisdom, just as inwardly it searches consciences as a witness, so outwardly it inflicts punishments as a judge, so that the prophet’s testimony may be true: “For he himself is both witness and judge” (Jer. XXIX, 23). Have mercy, Lord, on wretched Isidore, doing things unworthy and suffering things deserved, sinning continually and daily enduring your scourges.

[Col. 0653B] [Note: [Col. 0653D]

2. Gregory, Book VII of the Moralia, chapter 8, explaining Job’s statement: “This is my consolation, that, afflicting me with sorrow, he does not spare.” “For this reason,” he says, “he spares some here in order to strike them forever. Let him strike me here by not sparing me, so that he may spare me forever.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “The elect.” Gregory, Book XXVI of the Moralia, chapter 17: “For it is characteristic of the elect to be crushed here, so that they may be instructed for the rewards of the eternal inheritance.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “For more perfect things.” Others: “for perfection.” AREV.]

2. God’s mercy is ordered in such a way that he first corrects a person here from sins through scourges and afterward frees him from eternal punishment. God’s chosen person is worn down by the pains of this life so that he may gain more perfect things in the life to come.

[Note: [Col. 0653D]

3. See Gregory, Book XXVI of the Moralia, chapter 17, where he discusses why some are struck by the Lord here and others are left unpunished. LOAISA.]

3. God by no means spares the offender, since he either strikes the sinner with a temporal scourge for purification, or leaves him to be punished by eternal judgment, or the person himself punishes through repentance what he has committed wrongly; therefore God does not spare the offender.

259 [Note: [Col. 0654C]

4. Gregory, Book VIII of the Moralia, chapter 32, concerning the just: “They rejoice in being despised and do not grieve that they are afflicted by necessities.” The same is found in Augustine, Sermon 105 on the Time, and in Gregory, Book V of the Moralia, chapter 1. LOAISA.]

4. For the just, temporal scourges lead to eternal joys; therefore the just ought to rejoice in punishments, while the wicked ought to fear in prosperity.

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

5. From many passages of Gregory, Book V of the Moralia, chapter 1, and Book XXVI, chapter 18. LOAISA.]

5. God withdraws neither mercy nor justice from the just or the reprobate. For he judges the good here through affliction and rewards them there through mercy; and he rewards the wicked here through temporal clemency and punishes them there through eternal justice.

6. In this life God spares the wicked but does not spare the elect; in that life he will spare the elect but will not spare the wicked.

7. The security of the wicked in this life is dangerous, while the tranquil sorrow of the good is safe. For after death the wicked person is led away to punishment, but the just person, after labor, sleeps securely.

8. This should be understood not only of bodily sufferings but also of spiritual ones, so that each person may hope to be rewarded at the end in proportion to the scourges he endures in body or mind.

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

9. Gregory, Book XXVI of the Moralia, chapter 17, and Books XII and XV. LOAISA.]

9. Often, by the hidden judgment of God, the reprobate in this world remain outside the correction of the scourge; and although they seem to have committed many damnable acts, despised by God they are struck by no blow of correction.

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

10. Gregory, Book VII, Letter 32; Book XVIII of the Moralia, chapters 13, 7, and 12. LOAISA.]

10. The person loved by God is corrected more severely by the scourge if he sins, as the prophet Amos says: “You alone have I known from all the nations of the earth; therefore I will visit all your iniquities upon you.” For “the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

11. “Is reserved.” Others: “is withdrawn.” AREV.]

11. It is very necessary for the just person in this life both to be tempted by vices and to be beaten by the scourge, so that, while he is assaulted by vices, he may not grow proud of his virtues. But while he is worn down by pain of mind or body, he is kept back from love of the world. The just person ought to be tempted, but by the temptation of affliction, not by the temptation of lust.

12. In this life God deals more harshly with his elect, so that, while they are struck by the stronger goads of the scourge, no pleasures of the present life may delight them, but they may ceaselessly desire the heavenly homeland, where certain rest is awaited.

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

13. This is a passage from 1 Peter IV: “The time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God.” Isidore explains this passage above, Book I, chapter 30, sentence 2. Augustine likewise says on Psalm XCIII: “The time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God,” that is, the time has come for those who belong to the house of God to be judged now: if the children of God are scourged, what should the most wicked servants expect? Venerable Bede, on Psalm IX, explains Peter’s passage as referring to the hidden and just judgment that is exercised in the present for purification in the house of God, that is, among unbelievers. Gregory, Book XXVI of the Moralia, chapter 17, interprets the passage as Isidore does. LOAISA.]

13. The elect are tested by the adversity of this life, so that, in accordance with Peter, judgment may begin from the house of God (1 Pet. IV, 17), while in this life God chastises his elect with the scourge of judgment.

**CHAPTER II. On God’s Twofold Striking**

[Col. 0655A]

[Note: [Col. 0655B]

CHAPTER II. NO. 1. “By which we are struck.” Thus all manuscript codices read. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others: “in the flesh . . . in charity.” AREV.]

1. Divine striking is twofold. One is for a good purpose: we are struck in the flesh so that we may be corrected. The other is that by which we are wounded in conscience through charity, so that we may love God more ardently.

[Note: [Col. 0655B]

2. Ambrose, on how God looks upon the just and sinners, in his book on “Blessed are the undefiled,” and in Book I and Book V On the Apology of David. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Peter.” For he looked upon him with the eyes of grace, not of the body, since Matthew and Mark make it clear that Christ was then in the inner courtyard of the house, while Peter was outside below in the courtyard. From Augustine, chapter 6. LOAISA.

Ibid. “About to descend.” Genesis XVIII: “The Lord said: I will descend and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me.” LOAISA.]

2. God looks in two ways, either for pardon or for vengeance: for pardon, as in the case of Peter (Luke XXII, 61); for vengeance, as when he declares that he will descend and see the deeds of the Sodomites (Gen. XVIII, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0655C]

3. Scourges occur in five ways, as Bede testifies in his commentary on Matthew and Augustine in his sermon On Grace: either to the just, so that their merits may increase through patience, as in Job; or for the preservation of virtues, so that pride may not tempt them, as in Paul, 2 Cor. XII; or for the correction of sins, as in Mary’s leprosy, Num. XII; or for the glory of God, as in the case of the man born blind, John 9; or as a judgment of punishment, as in Herod, Acts XII. Isidore gathers all these together here. LOAISA.

Ibid. “For condemnation.” Gregory, Book VII of the Moralia, chapter 10, explaining Ezekiel XI: “I will take from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “For purification.” The same author, Book XXI, chapter 4, where he proves that the just, when scourged temporally, are tested, while the reprobate, who are not among those who suffer human labors, are condemned by eternal anathema; and Book XVI, chapter 16, and Book XI, chapter 21. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Egypt.” Jerome, in his commentary on Nahum, chapter VII, explaining “Affliction shall not rise up a second time,” or “God will not exact vengeance twice for the same thing,” seems to hold that the Egyptians were punished not by the scourge of condemnation but by that of purification. For he says: “If it seems to you cruel, harsh, and bloody that he destroyed the human race in the Flood, rained fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah, drowned the Egyptians in the waves, and cast down the corpses of the Israelites in the wilderness, know that he inflicted punishments for the present so that he might not punish eternally.” The Master of the Sentences, Book IV, distinction 15, considers this passage to be understood not indiscriminately of all, but only of those who repented amid the very scourges. LOAISA.

Ibid. Concerning Job, that he derived his origin from the Idumean nation, Augustine proves this in Book XVIII of The City of God, chapter 47; and concerning the temptation of Abraham, Tobit, and Job, in Book II of Questions on the Old and New Testaments, question 99. Concerning his temptation, Psalm C says: “He received [him] from God to be tempted, not oppressed; to be purified, not overthrown—or perhaps not to be purified but to be tested.” Gregory recalls his praises in Book XXVIII of the Moralia, chapter 1, and, explaining “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips, nor did he speak anything foolish against God,” in Book II, chapter 19. LOAISA.]

3. God strikes whomever he wills in three ways: the reprobate for condemnation, the elect whom he sees to be straying for purification, and the just for the propagation of the glory of their merits. In the first way Egypt was struck for condemnation (Exod. VII, 8). In the second way poor Lazarus was struck for purification (Luke XVI). In the third way Job was struck for testing (Job II).

[Note: [Col. 0656B]

4. 2 Corinthians XII: “And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.” In Greek:

“And because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, so that I might not be exalted, there was given me a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

Here *skolops* (σκόλοψ) means “thorn,” through or in the flesh. Interpreters do not agree on how this thorn should be understood. Some take it as an impulse and movement of lust, as Isidore says in Book II of the Sentences, chapter 39, sentence 11: “The thorns of the flesh that were in Paul, with the angel of Satan arousing them, arose from the law of sin, which by the necessity of lust dwells in human members.” Gregory also seems to hold this view in his treatment of the passage. Others, as Jerome reports in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, understand it as bodily ill health, since Paul was accustomed to be broken and troubled by headaches; Theophylact likewise. Thomas Aquinas holds that he was afflicted with iliac disease. Ambrose calls the thorn the persecution of wicked people and the affliction inflicted by enemies. Theodoret holds this view; but from what follows he proves that the thorn of the flesh was not bodily illness: “Therefore I am pleased with my infirmities, with insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ.” Athanasius, question 139, calls Alexander, a coppersmith, the thorn of the flesh. See the passage. I think that the thorn of the flesh should be understood as the opposition and troubles inflicted by the Jews, who were his relatives according to the flesh, so that the teaching of the Gospel might not advance. Concerning their persecution he says in 1 Thessalonians II: “For you became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they did from the Jews, who both killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, do not please God, and are hostile to all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby filling up their sins forever; for the wrath of God has come upon them to the end.” LOAISA.]

4. A person is often scourged by God before sin, so that he may not become evil, as Paul was, who, with the angel of Satan inciting him, endured thorns in the flesh. But he is also scourged after sin, so that he may be corrected, as the person mentioned by the Apostle was handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved (1 Cor. V).

[Note: [Col. 0656D]

5. Gregory, Book XXXIII of the Moralia, chapter 23. LOAISA.]

5. Even the person who does not know why he is beaten does not justly murmur. For God often scourges the just so that they may not fall by becoming proud of their justice.

[Note: [Col. 0656D]

6. From Gregory, Book XVIII of the Moralia, chapter 13. LOAISA.

Ibid. Gregory, Book XVIII of the Moralia, chapter 12: “The scourge will then wipe away guilt when they have changed their life.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Others: “whom he strikes as enemies and adversaries.” AREV.]

6. In this life God strives all the more to spare a person the more he scourges him while waiting. For by striking he corrects some, but by striking he kills others. He corrects by striking those of whom he says: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. III, 19). By striking he destroys those whom he sees sinning incorrigibly, whom he strikes no longer under discipline, as a father strikes his sons, but with strict condemnation, as an adversary strikes enemies. Of these he says: “With the scourge of an enemy he has struck you with cruel chastisement” (Jer. XXX, 14). And again: “Why do you cry out to me over your brokenness? Your pain is incurable” (ibid., V, 15). Therefore let each person hasten and fear lest his life be struck down together with his guilt. For the scourge wipes away guilt when it changes the life; but when it does not change a person’s conduct, it does not atone for his deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0657C]

7. Some manuscripts have “begin in this life”; “from this life” is better. Thus Gregory has it in the passage cited above: “For these, scourges begin from this life and continue in eternal striking.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Deuteronomy XXXII. Our Latin Vulgate edition reads: “A fire has been kindled in my fury, and it will burn to the depths of hell.” Isidore reads it as Gregory does, Book XVIII, chapter 22: “downward to the underworld.” LOAISA.]

7. Every divine striking is either a purification of the present life or the beginning of punishment to come. For in some people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal striking. Hence through Moses the Lord says: “A fire has been kindled in my anger, and it will burn down to the underworld” (Deut. XXXII, 22).

[Note: [Col. 0657C]

8. From Gregory, verbatim, Book XVIII, chapter 12. LOAISA.

[Col. 0657D] Ibid. Jude, Epistle 1: “For Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.” Gregory explains this passage of Jude in Book X of the Moralia, chapter 33. LOAISA.]

8. Some people are accustomed to say: “God does not judge the same thing twice”; yet they do not pay attention to what is written elsewhere: “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude I, 5). Although one fault is not struck twice, one and the same striking is understood: begun here, it is completed there, so that in those who are not corrected at all, the striking of the preceding scourges becomes the beginning of the subsequent torments.

[Note: [Col. 0657D]

9. Psalm CVIII. The passage is taken verbatim from Gregory, Book IX of the Moralia, chapter 33. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Brokenness upon brokenness.” This is the reading of the Vulgate, which, as Vezzosius observes in his notes, suits Isidore’s purpose well. AREV.]

9. Hence it is written in the psalm: “Let them be clothed with their own confusion as with a double garment” (Ps. CVIII, 29). For *diplois* is a double garment, with which, figuratively, those are clothed who are condemned both to temporal and to eternal punishment. Hence Jeremiah also says: “Brokenness upon brokenness” (Jer. IV, 20), that is, a twofold condemnation, in this world and in the world to come. And elsewhere he says: “With a double brokenness break them” (Jer. XVII, 18), that is, with a twofold punishment, present and future.

10. By the secret judgment of God, some are afflicted here and blessed there, namely, so that, while corrected here, they may be freed from eternal condemnation. Others fare well here and badly there, as happened to the rich man who, conspicuous here for the splendor of his power, was afterward handed over to the fires of Gehenna to be tormented (Luke XVI). Still others fare badly both here and there, because, refusing to be corrected, they begin to be scourged in this life and are condemned by eternal striking.

11. Some are plunged into so deep an abyss of despair that they cannot be corrected even through scourges. Concerning them the Lord rightly says through the prophet: “In vain I struck your sons; they did not accept discipline” (Jer. II, 30).

[Note: [Col. 0657D]

12. From Gregory, Book IX of the Moralia, chapter 24. LOAISA.]

12. Often the just person laments and does not know whether he is suffering the present scourges for all his sins or only for one; nor does he know what that fault is for which he deserved to suffer such punishments, and he is especially grieved by this uncertainty.

[Note: [Col. 0657D]

13. Isaiah XL: “He has received double for all his sins.” And Jeremiah XVII: “With a double brokenness break them.” LOAISA.]

13. Although the present scourges absolve the just person from sins, he is nevertheless disturbed by fear of vengeance, lest the afflictions pressing upon him prove insufficient to purify his offenses. Therefore, while he suffers present things and fears future ones, he receives, in a certain sense, as the prophet says, a double punishment for his sins (Isa. XL, 2).

264 **CHAPTER III. On Bodily Illness**

[Note: [Col. 0657D]

## Chapter III

**Chapter III, no. 1.** Almost all manuscript codices read: “there are some people of this same quality.” One very ancient papyrus codex reads: “there are some people of that quality.” The passage occurs in Gregory, *Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 13. — Loaisa.

1. There are some people of this character who do not know how to be corrected unless they see others being scourged; and so they advance by comparison with the wicked, fearing that what they see happening to others may happen to them and bring about their ruin.

[Column 0657D]

**2.** Theodoret, *Questions on Genesis*, drawing from the words “And therefore I guarded you, lest you should sin against me,” concludes that Abimelech, king of Gerar, was struck with illness by God’s counsel, so that he would not sin against Sarah. — Loaisa.

2. When God sees that some people are unwilling to be corrected by their own choice, he touches them with the goads of adversity. Others, whom he foresees might sin greatly, he scourges for their salvation by bodily illness, lest they sin, so that for them it is more beneficial to be broken by sicknesses for the salvation of the soul than to remain healthy for condemnation.

[Column 0658C]

**3.** Isidore has beautifully gathered together the meaning of “visitation” in the divine writings, for the word is used both in a good and in a bad sense. In the good sense, as in Luke XIX: “He did not recognize the time of his visitation”; and Hosea IV: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication”; and Exodus V: “Visiting, I have visited you, and I have seen your afflictions.” Many other passages occur in the sacred Scriptures in which “to visit” and “visitation” signify God’s care for the human race, his providence, mercy, and benefits bestowed upon human beings.

“Visiting” also signifies God’s granting what he promised, as in Genesis XXI: “The Lord visited Sarah”; and Luke I: “He visited and accomplished redemption for his people.” Sometimes it is also taken in a bad sense, meaning to punish, chastise, or avenge crimes committed against the divine majesty. Thus Exodus XXXI: “But on the day of vengeance I will visit this sin”; and Isaiah: “I will visit the fruit of the greatness of the heart of the king of Assyria”; and XIII: “I will visit evils upon the world”; and Psalm LXXXVIII: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod.” There the words “with a rod” denote an increase of punishment. Likewise Hosea I: “For yet a little while, and I will visit the blood of Jezreel”; and Psalm 18: “The visitations of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts,” denote the justice of visitation. For the Septuagint translated “visitations” as δικαιώματα, “ordinances” or “acts of justice.” — Loaisa.

3. God’s visitation is not always understood in a good sense, nor always in a bad one. It is understood in a good sense, as in the words: “Visit us with your salvation” (Psalm CV, 4). In a bad sense, according to the words: “At the time of their visitation they shall perish” (Jeremiah X, 15).

[Column 0658D]

**4.** As Paul says, I Corinthians XI: “For this reason many are weak and sick, and many sleep.” — Loaisa.

[Column 0659C] In the same place: “By the mercies of God”—namely, by granting, as Vezzosius notes, divine aids by which they may be driven away. — Arevalus.

4. Bodily illnesses arise from three causes: from sin, from temptation, and from the passion of intemperance. Human medicine can assist only the last of these; for the others, only the compassion of divine mercy can help.

[Column 0659C]

**5.** Augustine proves this in his commentary on John, tractate 7. — Loaisa.

[Column 0659D] In the same place: “Lest through vigor”—so in all the manuscripts. — Loaisa.

5. Those who are stronger and healthy benefit from becoming ill and from not sinning, lest, through the vigor of health, they defile themselves with unlawful desires and lustful longings.

[Column 0659D]

**6.** Acts IX. Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 31, interprets this passage in almost the same moral sense. Ambrose, in his book on “Blessed are the undefiled,” says: “At once the eye of the body and of the soul was healed.” — Loaisa.

6. Hardness that weighs upon the mind, yet is not perceived, is beneficially transferred to the flesh, so that it may be felt and, once understood, corrected. For wounds of the flesh are felt more quickly than those of the soul; therefore, through scourges of the flesh, those who go astray are corrected more quickly. This is indicated by the scales of unbelief on Paul’s eyes: when, through reproof, they were changed in the eyes of the flesh, the hardness of his mind was immediately dissolved (Acts IX, 18).

[Column 0659B]

7. There is a harmful health that leads a person to disobedience. There is also a health-giving illness that, through divine correction, breaks the mind’s hardness.

8. Illness of the soul—that is, the harmful illness of sins—is destructive. Concerning it the Apostle also says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (II Corinthians XI, 29). But the same Apostle approves bodily infirmity as beneficial, saying: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Corinthians XII, 10).

## Chapter IV. On Enduring Divine Correction

[Column 0659D]

**Chapter IV, no. 1.** From Gregory, *Morals*, book VI, chapter 17. — Loaisa.

1. A sinful person ought not to murmur against God’s scourges, because it is especially through being corrected that he is amended. Everyone bears what he suffers more lightly if he examines his own evils, for which a just retribution is inflicted upon him.

[Column 0659D]

**2.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXII, chapter 5. — Loaisa.

In the same place: Vezzosius more correctly thinks that the reading is *mala patitur*, “suffers evils,” which others have as *male patitur*, “suffers wrongly.” — Arevalus.

2. Let the person who suffers evil learn not to murmur, even if he does not know why he suffers evil; and let him judge that he suffers justly for this reason: he is judged by one whose judgments are never unjust. Whoever endures scourges and murmurs against God accuses the justice of the judge. But whoever recognizes that he suffers from a just judge, even if he does not know for what he suffers, is already justified by this very recognition; for he accuses himself and praises God’s justice.

[Column 0660A]

3. Since through prosperous circumstances a righteous person offers useful examples to others, it is necessary that he also be touched by adversity, so that his patience may be proved and those who have recognized his moderation in prosperity may once again draw lessons of courage from him.

[Column 0659D]

**4.** This is how the Codex of Toledo and that of the monastery of La Oliva in Navarre read it. The others agree with the printed editions, and I approve that reading. — Loaisa.

In the same place: The Gothic manuscript and another corrected Malacitan papyrus read: “Let him praise God rather, not accuse him.” The other manuscripts agree with the printed editions; that reading is not displeasing. — Loaisa.

4. Let the person who is tormented by the passions of the soul while the adversary lies in wait not therefore believe that he is alienated from Christ because he suffers such things. Rather, let him regard himself as more pleasing to God if, while suffering these things, he praises God rather than accusing him.

[Column 0659D]

**5.** The sense of the entire passage is taken from Gregory, book XXXII, chapter 3. — Loaisa.

In the same place: The Latin Codex of Toledo reads: “if he has considered himself worthy to suffer such things.” Two Malacitan codices agree with it; the others agree with the printed editions. — Loaisa.

5. For great benefit, the mind of the righteous person is disturbed by various temptations of suffering according to divine judgment. If he gives thanks to God for them and attributes them to his own fault, considering himself worthy of such things, then what he endures from the suffering will be reckoned to him as virtue, because he recognizes divine justice and understands his own guilt.

## Chapter V. On the Temptations of the Devil

[Column 0660C]

**Chapter V, no. 1.** As Paul says, Philippians I: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ.” And again: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” And David says: “Alas for me, that my sojourning has been prolonged!” See Gregory, *Morals*, book IX, chapter 17. — Loaisa.

1. In this life the mind of the righteous person is struck by many temptations of calamities; therefore he desires to be wholly removed from this age, so that he may be free from its hardships and find there fixed security.

[Column 0660D]

**2.** Gregory, in the same place. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “For he bears more heavily.” Gregory has: “When he endures scourges outwardly, what he carries inwardly from the adversary’s temptation is more grievous.” — Loaisa.

2. There is a great difference between the punishments that the righteous person suffers in the body and those that he endures in his mind through the devil’s deceit. For he bears more heavily what he mourns inwardly than what he suffers outwardly. The latter he can avoid both in place and in time; the former he can avoid neither in place nor in time.

[Column 0660D]

**3.** Gregory rightly spoke of the devil’s power and his will to harm the elect in *Morals*, book II, chapters 6 and 25: “Satan’s will is always wicked, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself, but his power from the Lord.” Hence Augustine, commenting on John, tractate 7, chapter 1: “The devil tempts only when permitted or sent.” — Loaisa.

In the same place: Others distinguish it thus: “he serves their progress, although unwillingly.” Yet he serves the saints’ benefit, and so forth. — Arevalus.

3. The devil does not tempt the elect beyond what God’s will permits. By tempting them, however, he serves the progress of the saints.

[Column 0660D]

**4.** “He deceives”: the printed books have this incorrectly instead of “he casts down.” — Loaisa.

4. Although unwillingly, the devil nevertheless serves the benefit of the saints when he does not cast them down by his temptations but rather trains them. For the temptations that he arouses for human destruction the Holy Spirit sometimes turns, with salutary benefit, into an exercise of virtue.

[Column 0661A] [Column 0661C]

**5.** “Would restrain.” Thus the Salamanca Gothic manuscript. The Toledo manuscript reads “would repress.” The passage comes from Gregory, *Morals*, book X, chapter 34. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “And therefore every…” This is taken word for word from Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 6. “Will,” not “pleasure,” should be read, as it is in many manuscripts. — Loaisa.

In the same place: Others read, less well, “dispensation” instead of “moderation,” so that it reads: “that it may benefit the pious.” — Arevalus.

5. Although the devil’s snares and cunning spread here and there, seeking someone to devour (I Peter V, 8), they nevertheless do not go beyond divine power, lest they harm anyone as much as they maliciously strive to do. For how could the virtue of the saints endure so much if heavenly providence did not restrain the demons’ wickedness with benevolent moderation? And although the devil always desires to inflict temptation upon the righteous, if he has not received power from God, he can in no way obtain what he wants. Hence the devil’s every will is unjust, yet, with God’s permission, his every power is just. From himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone, but God justly permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted, and in the manner in which they are to be tempted.

6. Hence it is also written in the Books of Kings concerning the devil: “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul” (I Samuel XVI, 14). Here the question is rightly raised: if it is “from the Lord,” why is it evil? If it is evil, why is it “from the Lord”? But two words contain both God’s just power and the devil’s unjust will: the evil spirit is so through its most wicked will, while it is the Lord through the just power it has received.

[Column 0661C]

**7.** It should be read “instigator,” not “originator,” as some manuscript codices have it. Ambrose, in his book on “Blessed are the undefiled,” says of the devil: “He is the instigator, he is the accuser; he himself entered the contest.” The term “introducer” (*immissor*) was used because we embrace vices by our own will. Nor does he introduce them unless a person opens a window to their introduction. Hence Augustine says: “The devil does not harm by forcing, but by persuading; nor does he extort consent from us, but asks for it,” *Homily* 12, volume X. Nor is this contradicted by John XIII: “When the devil had already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, to betray him.” He would not have entered, as Augustine says in his commentary on Psalm CXXXVI, unless a place had been given to him. Accordingly, the passage should be understood of the kind of “sending” that attracts and impels by suggestion, not of the kind that accomplishes something by commanding. The Greek of John is: Τοῦ διαβόλου ἤδη βεβληκότος εἰς τὴν καρδίαν Ἰούδα Σίμωνος Ἰσκαριώτου ἵνα αὐτὸν παραδῷ, “the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, that he should betray him.” Attention must also be paid to the distinction between the words: to send is one thing, and to send into or inspire is another. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “And despised they lie…” This is a verse of Ovid. — Loaisa.

7. The devil is not the introducer (*immissor*) of vices, but rather their instigator (*incentor*). For he kindles the fuel of desire nowhere except where he has first observed the pleasures of wicked thought. If we despise these, he certainly departs in confusion, and the arrows of his desire are immediately broken:
