> And despised, his torches lie there, without their light.

[Column 0661C]

**8.** The Gospel exhortation says: “Simple as doves, prudent as serpents.” And Paul says, Romans XVI: “I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil.” Likewise, I Corinthians XIV: “Do not become children in your understanding; be infants in evil.” — Loaisa.

In the same place: “The prophet”—Hosea VII. Jerome interprets it in Hosea as “a *columba lactata* [reading uncertain], or a foolish and senseless dove.” The Septuagint has ἄνους, “without understanding.” — Loaisa.

8. God’s servant must carefully understand the enemy’s snares and at the same time avoid them. He should be simple in the innocence of his life, yet also prudent in his simplicity. Whoever does not combine prudence with simplicity is, according to the prophet, “a dove seduced, without a heart” (Hosea VII, 11). He is called a dove because he is simple; but he is said to have no heart because he is ignorant of prudence.

[Column 0662C]

**9.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 28. — Loaisa.

9. Satan’s deceit is often revealed to the hearts of the saints when, pretending to be an angel of light under the appearance of goodness, he is exposed and despised while attempting to deceive the elect. Thus God also enables his saints to understand the words of deceptive doctrine, so that inwardly they recognize the devil’s error and carefully avoid it.

[Column 0662C]

**10.** This entire statement, together with its testimonies from Joshua V and Jeremiah XV, has been composed from Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapters 28 and 22. — Loaisa.

10. The discernment of the saints must be such that, endowed with reason, they distinguish between good and evil, lest the devil deceive them under the appearance of goodness. This is the inquiry of Joshua: “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?” (Joshua V, 13). For this reason Jeremiah is also told: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you will be as my mouth” (Jeremiah XV, 19). The saints then judge rightly concerning themselves when God enables them to understand the demons’ deceptive temptations.

[Column 0662D]

**11.** From Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIV, chapter 2, where he interprets the passage from Hosea and affirms that “foreigners” in Scripture signify apostate angels. The Vulgate edition of Hosea VII reads: “and he himself did not know.” — Loaisa.

11. Many are deceived by the devil and do not know that they have been deceived, as the testimony of the prophet Hosea declares: “Foreigners have devoured his strength, and he himself did not know” (Hosea VII, 9). “Foreigners” signifies wicked spirits, who consume the powers of the mind; but the hearts of the negligent do not understand this.

[Column 0662D]

**12.** “Openly.” Most manuscripts read this, and I approve the reading, rather than the printed editions’ “from the open,” together with Gregory, *Morals*, book VI, chapter 5, where the sentence is taken from: “The ancient enemy is conquered as though unarmed when, suggesting open evils to the human mind, he attempts to destroy all good things at once.” — Loaisa.

In the same place: “Those things which…” Thus all the manuscripts read. — Loaisa.

In Grialius’s edition, contrary to Loaisa’s intention, “from the open” was inserted instead of “openly,” without *from*. — Arevalus.

12. The devil is conquered as though unarmed when he tries to corrupt a person through manifest iniquity. But he advances armed when, under the appearance of holiness and virtue, he destroys the things that are holy—when the one who is deceived does not perceive his own losses, but pursues and loves vices as though they were virtues.

[Column 0662C]

**13.** The devil is called *myrmicoleon* by the Septuagint, in place of what is written in Job: “The tiger perished because it had no prey.” Gregory says, *Morals*, book V, chapter 17: “For he is an ant and a lion; to some he is a lion, to others an ant.” See the passage. — Loaisa.

13. In the eyes of the carnal the devil is terrifying; in the eyes of the elect his terror is contemptible. Unbelievers fear him as a lion; those strong in faith despise him as a worm, and repel him as soon as he appears, even for a moment.

[Column 0662D]

**14.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XVII, chapter 20. — Loaisa.

[Column 0663C] In the same place: “The devil…” In the sacred writings he is called a slippery and twisted serpent. Job XXVI: “The crooked serpent was drawn out.” Isaiah XXVII: “Leviathan, the crooked serpent, the bar.” The entire statement occurs in Gregory, *Morals*, book XVII, chapter 20. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “To the head.” He seems to allude to the words of Genesis: “She shall crush your head.” This teaches that the serpent’s head—that is, the devil’s first assault, by which he aims to make the mind surrender—must be driven back. — Loaisa.

14. Whoever does not receive the devil’s suggestions does not fall into his snares. For he is easily repelled in the subsequent act if his first enticements are rejected. The devil is a slippery serpent; if his head—that is, his first suggestion—is not resisted, he slips wholly into the interior of the heart without being perceived.

[Column 0663D]

**15.** Genesis III. Gregory, *Morals*, book I, chapter 38. He interprets the heel as the end of an action, explaining Psalm LV: “They watched my heel,” as well as the passage in Genesis. — Loaisa.

15. The beginnings of diabolical temptations are weak. If they are not guarded against, but pass through use into habit, they grow exceedingly strong at the end, so that they are conquered either never or only with difficulty.

16. Although the devil desires to make a person transgress throughout the whole of life, he nevertheless strives more intensely to deceive him at the end. Hence, at the beginning, it was said to the serpent concerning the first-formed man: “And you shall lie in wait for his heel,” because the devil plans to trip up at the end the person whom he did not deceive during the course of his earlier life. Therefore, even if someone is righteous, he must never be secure in this life; rather, he must always beware humbly and always fear anxiously lest he fall at the end.

[Column 0663D]

**17.** Alexander I, Letter 2. “For just as a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour, so the devil does not cease to go about seeking whom he may destroy among the faithful, especially those whom he finds more ardent in the service of the Savior and more intimate with him.” — Loaisa.

In the same place: It is certainly not surprising that Loaisa sometimes cites letters of the earliest popes that are now considered apocryphal, since in his time many regarded them as genuine. — Arevalus.

17. The devil flatters his supporters, but plots contrary temptations against God’s servants, following the example of the Lord, who allowed himself to be tempted by the devil after his baptism (Matthew IV).

[Column 0664C]

**18.** Gregory, *Morals*, book III, chapter 6, interprets Isaiah XLV: “I am the Lord, forming light and creating darkness.” — Loaisa.

18. The devil does not possess all the saints by holding them, but persecutes them by tempting them. Since he does not reign inwardly in them, he fights against them outwardly. Having lost dominion within, he stirs up war without.

[Column 0664C]

**19.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 18. [Column 0664D] There he explains Job XL: “He tightens his tail like a cedar”—that is, he moves and agitates it as a cedar is shaken by the wind, or he erects the member like a cedar, upright and immense. — Loaisa.

19. The devil rages more fiercely against the one he possesses when he recognizes that he is about to be expelled from him by divine power. Thus the unclean spirit tore the boy in whom it dwelt more violently when it was forced to leave him at Christ’s command (Mark IX). This event also reflects the words in Job, where, at the end, Behemoth “tightens his tail like a cedar” (Job XL, 12).

[Column 0664D]

**20.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXI, chapter 29. — Loaisa.

20. The devil persists with more various temptations against those who can benefit others through their usefulness, so that, while they are hindered, those who are to be taught may not progress.

[Column 0664D]

**21.** Gregory, *Morals*, book VII, chapter 8. — Loaisa.

21. The evil spirits continually attempt to dirty again what we desire to cleanse within us. But the saints foresee their snares with prophetic insight, and whatever earthly thing they perceive within themselves they ceaselessly drain away through holy works, so that they may be found pure in their innermost being.

[Column 0664D]

**22.** Augustine, book II of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, volume I. — Loaisa.

22. People are now deceived by the devil through the same flattery by which the first-formed humans were deceived in paradise. By testing them with many illusions of vice, Satan mocks the minds of the reprobate. At one time he deceives them with promises; at another he entices them with transient things as though they were necessities; at another he even suggests that the punishments of hell are light and temporary, so that he may dissolve the hearts of the wretched into desire and wantonness and lead them with himself to the infernal regions.

[Column 0664D]

**23.** Gregory wonderfully treats this entire statement in *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapters 18, 79, and 20, where he explains the words of Job: “The sinews of his testicles are intertwined.” — Loaisa.

23. The arguments of evil schemes and the seeds of wicked thoughts that the devil scatters in human hearts often entangle the mind, caught on every side, so completely that whoever tries to escape from one direction cannot get out without danger. It is as though one swears that he will do something which, if he does it, is sinful, but if he does not do it, he is guilty of perjury. In such a great danger of evil, in order that a way of escape may be opened, the lesser evils should rather be chosen so that the greater may be avoided.

24. When the devil seeks to deceive someone, he first studies each person’s nature; then he applies himself from the point at which he sees that the person is most suited to sin.

25. The devil tempts people from the point at which he sees that they are easily inclined toward vices through an excess of humors, so that he also applies temptation according to the mixture of the humors (Numbers XXIII). Read the account of Balaam, who, as a figure of the devil, commands destructive snares to be spread before God’s people from the point at which he perceives that they are most likely to fall. For one who diverts water somewhere does not send it by another route, but only where he directs its force.

[Column 0664C]

**26.** Thus also the old edition reads. — Loaisa.

In the same place: Others read, “let no one fail to consider the fault.” — Arevalus.

26. Let no one regard as guilt the condition arising from his own constitution that he suffers; rather, let him fight as much as he can against what he endures. For if one yields to his constitution, he does not resist temptation or vice at all.

[Column 0664D]

**27.** This entire statement is derived from Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 14, where he asks why the devil is called Behemoth, a four-footed beast, and why Leviathan is called a serpent in the waters, which is caught with a hook. Isidore here gives the explanation of these names from Gregory.

Among the devil’s names, which are various and numerous in the divine books, these three—Behemoth, Leviathan, and Bird—are the principal ones. He is also called lion, Baal, north wind, robber, Satan, tail, basilisk, Belial, evil one, tempter, dog, impious one, adversary, foreigner, wolf, exactor, asp, murderer, most wicked one, malignant one, perverse, harsh, Lucifer, furnace, strong one, power of darkness, lion’s cub, prince of power, god of this age, roaring lion, apostate and transgressor, without a yoke, and son of Belial, as Jerome notes on Isaiah XXVIII. He likewise interprets Psalm XVII: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me,” that is, the violent assaults of the demon.

Among the Hebrews, *Behemoth* is plural—an observation I add in passing—and means “beasts.” Although it is one animal, it is assembled from the size and ferocity of many beasts. It is a terrestrial animal, enormous and of extraordinary size. It is said of it in Job XL: “Behemoth, whom I made with you, shall eat grass like an ox.” According to some, it is an elephant. — Loaisa.

[Column 0665D] In the same place: The ancients, according to Jerome, book VI on Isaiah XIV, said that Leviathan was the father of the devil. Jerome himself refutes this opinion and signifies a dragon. Hence Ezekiel XXXII: “He was compared to the lion of the nations and to the dragon that is in the sea.” Jerome’s authority led Aquila to put “Leviathan” for “dragon.” Likewise in Psalm XC, where it says, “You shall trample upon the lion and the dragon,” it is read as “Leviathan.” Here it is called a great sea creature, whose capture by Christ is recounted mystically in Job. Leviathan is therefore a huge sea-fish. Job XL asks: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or bind his tongue with a cord?” The Septuagint there rendered Leviathan as “sea creature” and “dragon.” Likewise in Job III: “Those who are ready to awaken Leviathan,” they render “sea creature”; elsewhere they interpret it as “dragon,” as in Psalm CIII: “That dragon whom you formed to mock.” The creation of Leviathan, and Enoch, are mentioned in IV Esdras VI. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “Bird.” Daniel VII, Isaiah XXXI, and the Gospel’s “birds of the air.” — Loaisa.

[Column 0666C] In the same place: Others read “he fell,” according to the Psalmist, “compared with foolish beasts.” Therefore Leviathan, and so forth. Further below: Behemoth earned the earth because, like a brute animal, he delights in the lowest things; the serpent, because… The book of IV Esdras, cited by Loaisa, must be kept in view as apocryphal. — Arevalus.

27. Therefore in the sacred writings the devil is called Behemoth, that is, an animal, because he fell from heaven to the earth. Therefore he is called Leviathan, that is, a serpent from the waters, because he moves through the shifting sea of this age with crafty cunning. He is called Bird because he is lifted up to the heights through pride. And rightly he is called by these three names, because according to his deserts he earned the air as a bird for his prison, the earth so that he might be a brute animal, and the character of a serpent so that he might be tossed about in irrational agitation in the sea of this age.

[Column 0666C]

**28.** The printed editions have: “from what they have through their members.” Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 22, has the source of this statement: “He is called by the very name of their actions when he is called a beast, dragon, or bird.” — Loaisa.

28. Because the devil works through his members, he acquires names: whatever individuals do at his instigation, he himself is named from it. Whom does the devil not deceive? From the point at which he is an animal—that is, from the point at which he tempts through fleshly lust; from the point at which he is a serpent—that is, through the malice of desire and harm. But when he cannot deceive someone in this way, he lies in wait for him; hence he is a bird, that is, the ruin of pride. For he prepares deceits on every side until he finds a way by which to deceive the unwary.

[Column 0666C]

**29.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 28. — Loaisa.

29. It is one thing for the devil to enter someone’s mind, and another for him to inhabit it. He enters even the hearts of the saints when he insinuates evil suggestions, but he does not dwell in them because he does not lead them over into his own body. Those who are in his body he inhabits, because they are his temple. If the devil slips into the minds of the elect, he does not rest in them as he does in the hearts of the reprobate; for the warmth of faith immediately stirs him to depart from the elect.

30. Some whom the devil had already devoured with his greedy mouth are again snatched from his mouth by the hidden mercy of divine judgment and restored to salvation. For often divine power has drawn from the ancient enemy’s jaws many whom he held submerged in the abyss of lust through repentance.

[Column 0666C]

**31.** A similar question occurs in Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXII, chapter 10, at the end, and in Julian, the most holy archbishop of Toledo, in his book *Anticimenon*, from Job, question 132. — Loaisa.

31. How does the Prophet call the destruction of good people the devil’s chosen food, when it is written elsewhere of him: “He shall eat grass like an ox,” unless those who appear to human beings to be chosen food are, in God’s eyes, grass? Thus those who perish from the number of the good are, among human beings, elect, but before God they are grass.

[Column 0666C]

**32.** Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 17. — Loaisa.

In the same place: “As though in the jaw.” The entire statement comes from Gregory’s interpretation of Job: “You shall pierce his jaw with a hook,” *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapters 40 and 17. — Loaisa.

32. The devil is said already to have swallowed the person whom he appears to have devoured through completed wickedness. But the person whom he has not swallowed through the completion of the act, but whom he bites with the enticements of temptation in order to devour him, he still chews as though in the jaw. Hence Paul has “a thorn of the flesh” by which he may be humbled (II Corinthians XII), but he does not have the completion of sin by which he might be swallowed.

[Column 0666D]

**33.** From Gregory’s explanation of Job XLI: “And flame goes out from his mouth,” *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 41. — Loaisa.

33. The devil’s mouth is his words. His words are hidden inspirations by which, speaking secretly to human hearts, he burns them with concealed desires.

[Column 0666D]

**34.** Paul’s passage, I Corinthians V. Isidore interprets it as bodily handing over, as do Jerome, Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 11, and Anselm, whereas other holy Fathers understand it as separation from Christ’s body and spiritual handing over to Satan’s power.

Both senses affirm the force and authority of ecclesiastical excommunication and show it to be a most severe and greatly to be feared punishment, since it expels a person from the Church, makes him the devil’s slave, and renders him alien to every sacramental power. Hence Pope Pelagius’s statement to the bishops of England: “By the example of apostolic authority we have learned that the spirits of those who err and of those who are wavering in error are to be handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme”; and Pope Urban, canon “Notandum,” 24, question 3.

Cassian, book II, chapter 16, understands Paul’s passage of one who is suspended from prayer. Origen, however, in Homily 2 on chapter II of Judges—which is attributed to Jerome because blessed Jerome translated it into Latin—also explains this passage as referring to ecclesiastical excommunication, showing in two ways that a person entangled in the bonds of excommunication is handed over to Satan. Augustine likewise says in *Sermon 68 on the Words of the Apostle*: “Every Christian, dearly beloved, who is excommunicated by priests is handed over to Satan. How so? Clearly, because outside the Church there is the devil, just as Christ is in the Church; and thus the person removed from ecclesiastical communion is, as it were, handed over to the devil.” — Loaisa.

[Column 0667D] In the same place: “Incorreptible”—others have “incorrigible.” Vezzosius, incorrectly, has “incorruptible.” — Arevalus.

34. Some, because of uncorrectable iniquity and because they do not correct themselves voluntarily, are handed over to be tormented by unclean spirits, so that the demons may have power to seize them bodily; afflicted by their terrors, they may be humbled, repent, and be saved. Thus the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Corinthians V, 5). It is beneficial for some sinners to be bodily handed over to Satan so that they may be saved in soul, in order that through present correction they may fear future judgment and thereafter beware of sinning. Some are handed over to the demons’ power for correction; others, rejected, are handed over only for destruction.

35. The devil is never inactive against a righteous person. Either he intensifies the tribulations of the heart or arouses pains of the body. Hence the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn of the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (II Corinthians XII, 7).

[Column 0667D]

**36.** “Let us accept.” Thus the Gothic, Salamanca, and other manuscripts read. “Let us endure” is found in the Gothic manuscript of Toledo. — Loaisa.

In the same place: Others read: “This person who speaks thus is not separated,” and so forth. — Arevalus.

36. The power of demons often torments the mind of the righteous with various painful afflictions, and therefore sometimes confines him even to the narrow limit of despair. Yet such anguish itself benefits the soul that remains in the love of God. For whether in mind or body the righteous person suffers any adversity through the prompting of unclean spirits, he suffers it by God’s permission. If he humbly refers this very thing to God’s glory and says what Job said concerning bodily suffering—“If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil?” (Job II, 10)—he is not separated from God but joined to him, however cruelly he may be tormented by anguish.

37. The righteous person suffers many adversities in his soul through the instigation of demons, but he cannot perish through such temptations from eternal life, because the merciful Lord does not count toward the condemnation of guilt what a person suffers unwillingly and carries by permission of his divine majesty. We sin where we turn aside through desire or will. Where we are forcibly subjected, even if there is no crime or disgraceful act, there is nevertheless misery in place of crime and disgrace. But whoever praises God for the misery inflicted upon him is undoubtedly free from the crime that was committed.

## Chapter VI. On the Temptations of Dreams

[Column 0668A]

**Chapter VI, no. 1.** Gregory, *Morals*, book VIII, chapter 18, and book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 48, teaches that dreams touch the soul in six ways: first, through fullness of the stomach; second, through emptiness; third, through illusion; fourth, through illusion combined with thought; fifth, through revelation; sixth, through thought combined with revelation. Augustine, in his book *On Divination through Dreams*, conveys much concerning dreams sent by demons. Here our Isidore has gathered together Gregory’s six modes. — Loaisa.

In the same place: *Minitant*, “they threaten.” Thus the Gothic, Salamanca, and other manuscripts read; the Toledo manuscript has *minant*, likewise “they threaten.” — Loaisa.

In the same place: “They strike.” Perhaps he alludes to the blows Jerome received because of his reading of Cicero and the poets. He says that after the dream he had bruised shoulders and felt the wounds, in his letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity* and in his *Apology against Rufinus*. — Loaisa.

In the same place: *Minitant*, “they threaten.” Others have *immittunt*, “they send in,” which Vezzosius considers better. But *minitant* seems correct as an archaic form for *minitantur*, “they threaten,” as in Plautus, Naevius, and others. — Arevalus.

1. Very often demons, appearing at night, disturb human senses through visions, so that they may make people fearful and timid. At times also, having turned the mind toward despair over its sins, they disturb it during sleep and threaten terrible punishments in Gehenna. Sometimes, moreover, raging in open assault, they strike human bodies 276; yet, by God’s permission, this happens to the wicked as punishment and to the just for the glory of endurance.

2. Very often unclean spirits mock those whom they see inclining toward love of the world while asleep, through some empty prosperity of hope. But those whom they perceive to fear certain adversities, they shake while sleeping with groundless terror. Thus, assailing the hearts of the miserable with various illusions, they sometimes soothe them with empty prosperity and sometimes frighten them with vain dread.

[Note: [Col. 0668C]

3. From Gregory, *Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 18, and *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 49. He tells of a certain rich man to whom the devil promised long spans of life in a dream. After he had amassed much money as provision for a longer life, he suddenly died. LOAISA.

On the same passage: “At times.” This is Aristotle’s view in *Ethics*, Book I, at the end: that those endowed with virtue have better contemplations during sleep than the wicked. Hence also, in Ecclesiasticus 34, the Wise Man calls the dreams of evildoers vanity. LOAISA.]

3. Those who are conscious of no sins, or only of rare ones, are either never or only rarely wearied by nocturnal terrors. Resting in tranquil sleep, they sometimes even contemplate and see certain secret and mystical things while asleep. But those who have stained their hearts with graver vices, deceived by the fear of conscience, see terrifying apparitions. For a deceptive image mocks the minds of the miserable with various forms; and those whom it has dragged along while awake in life, it harasses while sleeping, so that it never permits them to rest secure.

[Note: [Col. 0668D]

4. That good dreams are sent by God is beautifully demonstrated in Ecclesiasticus 34: “And just as the heart of a woman in labor suffers fantasies, unless a visitation has been sent from the Most High, do not give your heart to them.” Thus Solomon received divine wisdom from heaven in a dream, 1 Kings 3: “Solomon awoke and understood that it had been a dream.” Some say that this dream was not natural but prophetic, as in Numbers 12: “If there should be among you a prophet of the Lord, I will appear to him in a vision, or I will speak to him in a dream.” Yet in prophetic sleep the power of prophecy is not bound, nor is the exercise of free choice; rather, it remains free. The prophets likewise were instructed by God in sleep and taught about secret and mystical matters, as Joseph was. For while a person sleeps, his intellect can be carried toward God; its function is to perceive and judge. Thus, while he sleeps, he perceives something of what he had previously considered, reasons about it, and unties the knots of arguments. Accordingly Augustine, in *The Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 12, relates that his disciple Eulogius, while interpreting Cicero’s rhetorical books at Carthage, came upon a difficult passage. Unable to understand it, he could scarcely sleep because of his anxiety; yet that night, while dreaming, he seemed to explain to himself what he had not understood. Dreams of sexual matters likewise have this origin: they do not occur unless the mind, while awake, has previously either been tempted by or thought about such matters, as Augustine reports in Book XII of *On Genesis*, chapter 15. Sometimes, however, the intellect is moved in sleep by the illumination of some higher and nobler substance. For instruction and discipline from this source, the resting intellect is more ready and more capable because the senses, thoughts, and fantasies are abundantly at rest; released from these disturbances, it belongs wholly to itself. The Song says: “I sleep, but my heart is awake”; and Job 38: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep usually falls upon human beings and they sleep in their beds, then he opens the ears of men, and, instructing them, teaches them discipline.” Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologica* II–II, question 95, article 6, referred the whole account of dreams to internal causes of soul and body, which arise from divine revelation and heavenly influence, and to external causes, which arise from wakefulness and an abundance of bodily humors. Hippocrates does likewise in *On Dreams*. LOAISA.]

4. Sometimes unclean spirits also try to terrify the minds of the elect with dreadful [Col. 0668C] dream-images 277, and those whom they tempt with vices while awake but do not overcome, they attack fiercely while sleeping.

[Col. 0669A] 5. Although the saints may be shaken for a moment by such visions, nevertheless, as soon as they awaken they despise the emptiness of the illusions and immediately turn their attention toward God.

[Note: [Col. 0669D]

6. Augustine speaks of himself in *Confessions*, Book X, chapter 30: while he was awake, images of things appeared to him, devoid of seductive force, yet in dreams they dragged his soul even to consent. LOAISA.

On the same passage: This statement is also the seventh cause in Gregory, *Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 18, and *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 48. He distinguishes six causes of dreams, as stated above. LOAISA.]

6. Dreams have different qualities. Some occur from fullness, or from emptiness, as is also known by experience. Others arise from one’s own thought; for often we recognize at night what we think about during the day.

[Note: [Col. 0669D]

7. Daytime activities are often represented in dreams, as Hippocrates reports; he also believes that such dreams indicate the body’s health. Similar is the dream of Africanus in Cicero, in which the forms of those matters about which he had spoken the previous day are presented to him in sleep. LOAISA.

On the same passage: Ecclesiasticus 34 reads: “For dreams have led many astray, and those who hoped in them have fallen away.” Gregory, however, in *Morals*, Book VIII, chapter 18, reads it as Isidore does. LOAISA.]

7. Some visions of unclean spirits occur through illusion, as Solomon proves: “Dreams have led many astray, and vain illusions.” Others, however, occur in a proper manner—that is, through the mystery of heavenly revelation—as we read in the Law concerning Joseph, son of Jacob, who is foretold in a dream as destined to be preferred above his brothers [Col. 0669B] (Genesis 37). Or as in the Gospel concerning Joseph, the husband of Mary, who is warned in a dream to flee with the child into Egypt (Matthew 2). Sometimes visions also occur in combination—that is, through thought together with illusion, and likewise through thought together with revelation—as Daniel says: “You, O king, began to think in your bed what would happen after these things, and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come” (Daniel 2:29). Indeed, often the things toward which we direct the sense of our thoughts are revealed through a kind of elevation of the mind while we rest.

[Col. 0670A] 8. Although some dreams are true, it is nevertheless not right to believe them easily, because they arise from different kinds of imaginings, and their origin is rarely considered. One must therefore not put faith in dreams so readily, lest Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light, deceive some unwary person and mislead him through some fraud of error.

[Note: [Col. 0670B]

9. Augustine, in *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 22, discusses the falsity of dreams, the difficulty of distinguishing them, and the way in which they disturb the miserable soul and its senses. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XI, chapter 75, asks whether there are certain foreknowable perceptions of a resting mind and by what method they occur; see also the other matters there. In Book VII, chapter 50, he tells of Publius Cornelius Rufus, who lost his eyesight while asleep, when he dreamed that this was happening to him. Aristotle says that melancholics dream more truly, in *On Sleep and Waking*. Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, Book II, chapter 9, says that true dreams are to be regarded as the thoughts of a sober soul. LOAISA.

On the same passage: In Matthew 23 it reads: “Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not believe it.” The same appears in Mark 13 and Luke 17. LOAISA.]

9. Sometimes demons watch certain curious people through deceptive fraud and mock them in such a way that some dreams come to pass exactly as they are shown. For, although they deceive in many things, they sometimes also announce what is true. But even when this happens, such dreams must be despised, lest they perhaps proceed from illusion, remembering the testimony of Scripture: “If they tell you, and it comes to pass, do not believe” (Matthew 24:23).

[Col. 0670B] [Note: [Col. 0670C]

10. Hippocrates does not reject the art of divination through dreams, in *On Dreams*, conclusions 2 and 3. Aristotle, in *On Sleep and Waking*, reduces dreams to causes, signs, and accidents. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXXVII, chapter 10, says of the stone called *eumetrites* that, when placed beneath the head, it returns nocturnal visions in the manner of an oracle. He likewise makes Amphiction the first author of the interpretation of omens and dreams; in Book VII, chapter 56, he says of laurel placed beneath a pillow that it makes dreams true. The Church condemns interpreters of dreams in the Second Council of Ancyra, canon 23, and in the chapter *Episcopi*, Gratian, *Decretum* 26, question 5. LOAISA.

On the same passage: Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXVIII, chapter 8, writes that Democritus taught that the left foreleg of a chameleon causes dreams one desires, and for those one desires, to be sent. LOAISA.

On the same passage: Some read, “For our minds sometimes …” Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.108:

“… or do lovers themselves fashion dreams for themselves?”

From this I conjecture that Isidore may have read: “For lovers sometimes fashion dreams for themselves.” See also Claudian, *On Dreams*, preface to the Sixth Consulship of Honorius. AREV.]

10. Dreams resemble omens, and those who attend to them are known actually to practice divination. Dreams are not true when a mind, thinking about something, imagines it for itself day and night. For sometimes our minds themselves fashion dreams for themselves.

11. Often, when earlier evils are recalled to the mind through sorrowful memory, we imagine through them the punishment of Gehenna, recalling it within ourselves. Such imaginings of the mind—whether they arise in wakefulness from past offenses or from the memory of future punishment—appear through visions and dreams and shake minds by their thoughts [Col. 0671A] 279. For both occur through the single power of memory, whether we are awake or asleep.

12. By such a movement of the soul we are shaken even in sleep by terrible fear; and in our mind’s sight we contemplate, even in a dream, how grave are the things we have committed and how harsh are the things we fear.

[Note: [Col. 0671B]

13. Gratian: “But then there is sin in the mind.” The sense of this statement is taken from Gregory’s letter to Augustine, bishop of the English, and is found in Distinction 6, chapter *Testamentum*. Ivo, Part IX, chapter 112. LOAISA.]

13. It is not a sin when we are unwillingly deceived by nocturnal images; but it is a sin when, before we are deceived, we are anticipated by the inclinations of our thoughts. For images of lust, which we have entertained in reality, often appear in the mind of those who sleep, but harmlessly if they do not arise with desire.

[Note: [Col. 0671B]

14. Thomas Aquinas discusses nocturnal emissions, their varieties, and their causes most learnedly in his treatises *On Purity of Conscience* and *On the Office of a Priest*. LOAISA.

On the same passage: “Although, even if.” A pleonasm, perhaps introduced by copyists. AREV.]

14. Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal illusion, even if he feels himself defiled without any recollection of shameful thoughts, should nevertheless attribute this to his own fault as a temptation, and immediately cleanse his impurity with tears.

## CHAPTER VII. On Prayer

[Note: [Col. 0671B]

Chapter VII, no. 1. The same is found in Augustine, *On Saving Instructions*, chapter 28. 1 Peter 4: “Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers.” In the manuscripts and old editions, *subdat* is found; the reading is “let him submit,” not “let him turn.” LOAISA.]

1. This is the remedy for one who is seething with temptations to vice: whenever he is touched by any vice, he should submit himself to prayer, because frequent prayer extinguishes the assault of vices.

[Note: [Col. 0671C]

2. Some read *psallendo* (“by singing psalms”) instead of *pulsando* (“by knocking”), and *obstrepunt* (“they obstruct”) instead of *obrepunt* (“they steal upon”). AREV.]

2. We must apply our mind so perseveringly to prayer and knocking that, with the strongest concentration, we overcome the importunate suggestions of carnal desires that steal upon our senses; and we must persist until, by persevering, we conquer. For negligent prayers cannot obtain even from the person himself what they seek.

3. Whenever someone prays, he calls the Holy Spirit to himself. But when the Spirit has come, the demonic temptations that plunge themselves into human minds immediately flee, unable to endure his presence.

[Note: [Col. 0671C]

4. Gregory proves this in *Morals*, Book XXII, chapter 18, when he explains the words of Job: “Who will grant me a hearer, so that the Almighty may hear my desire?” Yet Isidore does not reject vocal prayer here. For since there are two kinds of prayer in the Church, common and private, common prayer is offered in the person of the whole Church and is therefore vocal and spoken aloud. This is proved by the form of prayer prescribed by Christ to the apostles in Matthew 6: “When you pray, do not speak at length, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.” And below: “Therefore you shall pray thus: Our Father”—where he clearly establishes prayer in the voice. Luke 11 likewise shows that the Lord prayed aloud: “And it happened,” says the evangelist, “while he was praying in a certain place, that when he had ceased, one of his disciples said to him: ‘Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.’ And he said to them: ‘When you pray, say: Our Father.’” “When you pray, say,” he says; this is plainly done with the voice.

Hence the Third Council of Toledo, canon 2, prescribes that in all churches the Creed be recited before the Lord’s Prayer is proclaimed in a clear voice, so that the true faith may be manifest and have its testimony, and so that the people, their breasts purified by faith, may approach to partake beforehand of Christ’s body and blood. The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 9, decrees that the Lord’s Prayer be said daily in public or private worship, and proves this by the authority of Cyprian, Hilary, and Augustine. The Council of Girona, canon 10, says that the Lord’s Prayer is to be recited after the morning and evening prayers.

All these things, and many others collected by the most learned men, concern the establishment of public prayer, whose character and nature require that it be vocal. From this arose the Church’s singing, which Paul commends in Ephesians 5: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord,” and likewise in Colossians 3. Acts 16 says the same: “At midnight Paul and Silas, praying, praised God, and those who were in custody heard them.” Besides many testimonies of the saints—Dionysius and Tertullian—and the use and melody of antiphons, responsories, and hymns, Nicephorus attributes this ancient custom of singing in the Church to the apostles, Book XVIII, chapter 51. There are also notable passages in the councils, such as the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapters 14 and 15; the Second Council of Tours under Pelagius I; and the Council of Laodicea under Liberius, chapter 59, where it is determined what is appropriate to sing and read in the Church, while canon 15 prescribes the office of the psalmists.

So much for common, or public, prayer, in cultivating which Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and Isidore labored greatly. Private and individual prayer, however, can be without the voice. The saints speak of this when they praise prayer of the heart, as Cyprian does in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, Augustine on Psalm 118, and Gregory in *Morals*, Book XXII, chapter 18.

Nevertheless, the voice joined to the heart greatly arouses and advances the soul’s inward affection, so that he who dwells within the breast may also be in the voice, and the whole person may serve God in soul and body. As Cyprian says, one should please the divine eyes both by bodily bearing and by the manner of one’s voice, offering to God “the calves of the lips,” as Hosea says, and expressing through the overflow of the voice the affection and love conceived in the mind. Thus Paul says that one believes with the heart and confesses with the mouth. David says in Psalm 15: “My heart rejoiced, and my tongue exulted.” And Job: “Who can restrain the word once conceived?”

Perfect vocal prayer brings many advantages and benefits to the soul. But if the affection and intention of the heart are separated from it, and prayer is merely fluent, wandering, and verbose, prayer made only in the heart is far preferable. Cyprian proves this in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, saying that we ought not indiscriminately scatter our prayers in disorderly sounds, nor toss before God, with tumultuous loquacity, a petition that should be commended to him modestly. For God is a hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Augustine likewise says in *Sermon 18 on the Words of the Lord*: “Let us not be noisy in voice and mute in conduct”; and in *Sermon 2 on Prayer*: “It is better to pray in the heart without the sound of the voice than with words alone, without the mind’s attention.” Jerome says the same; his words are preserved in *Decretum*, Distinction 5, chapter *Non mediocriter*. LOAISA.

[Col. 0673C] On the same passage: “With words alone, without the mind’s attention.” This is vocal prayer, which Isidore criticizes, as Vezzosius observes. The venerable Thomasius, in his Italian work *On the True Norm for Glorifying and Entreating God*, teaches that God can rightly be entreated by heart and voice together; he derives this from Paul’s writing to the Corinthians and from a hymn of Saint Ambrose. AREV.]

4. Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend to the words of the one who supplicates; he looks upon the heart of the one who prays. If the heart prays silently and the voice is quiet, although this may be hidden from human beings, it cannot be hidden from God, who is present to the conscience. It is better to pray in the heart in silence, without the sound of the voice, than with words alone, without the mind’s attention.

[Col. 0673A] [Note: [Col. 0673C]

5. Prayer accompanied by tears has great power with God. Gregory, *Morals*, Book X, chapter 17; Ambrose, in many passages of his work on Psalm 118, and on Psalm 37; and Cyprian, especially in his letter to the clergy and people on entreating God, at the end. LOAISA.]

5. One should never pray without groaning, for remembrance of sins produces sorrow. When we pray, we bring our guilt back to memory and then recognize more clearly that we are guilty. Therefore, when we stand before God, we ought to groan and weep, remembering how grave are the crimes we have committed and how dreadful are the punishments of hell that we fear.

[Note: [Col. 0673C]

6. From Gregory, in the same work. I interpret the passage in Ecclesiasticus 7—“Do not repeat a word in your mouth”—in this sense. LOAISA.]

6. The mind should preserve after prayer the condition in which it presents itself during prayer. For prayer achieves nothing if one again commits the sin for which one must once more seek pardon. Without doubt, the person receives the desired effect of prayer who does not repeat by wrongdoing what he asks to have washed away by prayer.

7. Our mind is heavenly, and it contemplates God well in prayer when it is hindered by no earthly cares or errors. By its nature it is suited to the good; in what is foreign to it, however, it is disturbed.

[Note: [Col. 0673C]

8. Augustine therefore rightly says in *Saving Instructions*, chapter 28: “My brother, strive in your prayer to offer pure prayer to the Lord Christ,” and so forth. LOAISA.

On the same passage: Paul says in 1 Corinthians 14: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray with the mind.” Vigilance is also required in prayer. Hence Mark 13: “Watch, be vigilant, and pray”; and Luke 21: “Therefore keep watch, praying at all times.” Also 1 Thessalonians 5: “Pray without ceasing.” And 1 Timothy 2: “I want men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger or dispute.” Hence also Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus on the manner of life: “Let the understanding be watchful; let the body, open to no wandering thoughts, and the mind alike be directed toward the Lord,” and so forth. LOAISA.

On the same passage: “But very few.” Augustine proves this in his exposition of Psalm 85, explaining the words: “For you, Lord, are sweet and gentle,” and adducing 2 Samuel: “For I have found, O Lord, my heart, so that I might pray to you.” LOAISA.]

8. Prayer is pure when, at its appointed time, worldly cares do not intrude. But the mind is far from God if, during prayer, it is occupied with worldly thoughts. We truly pray, then, when we think of nothing else. Yet very few have prayers of this kind. Even if some do, it is difficult for them to remain so always.

[Note: [Col. 0673D]

9. From Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 8: “The mind is kindled toward compunction, but concerning the things we have done,” and so forth; also *Morals*, Book X, chapter 17. In the Gothic and Salmatic manuscripts it reads *cogitavit* (“he thought”), not *agitavit* (“he stirred”). LOAISA.]

9. When the mind, before prayer, is free from God but occupied with illicit thoughts, as soon as it comes to prayer the images of the things it has recently thought about immediately confront it and block the way of prayer, so that [Col. 0674A] the mind cannot raise itself freely toward heavenly desire.

[Note: [Col. 0673D]

10. Augustine reports this on Psalm 33. For, as Bernard says, prayer has two wings: contempt for the world and afflictions of the flesh, *Sermon 3 on the Epiphany*. [Col. 0674C] LOAISA.]

10. The mind must therefore first be purified and separated from thoughts of temporal things, so that the pure vision of the heart may truly and simply be directed toward God. For we believe that divine gifts are then truly obtained when, as we pray, we stand before God with a simple affection.

11. The focus of prayer is interrupted in many ways when, through carelessness, worldly vanities intrude into the mind of anyone who is praying. The devil especially injects thoughts of worldly cares into human minds when he sees someone praying.

[Note: [Col. 0674C]

12. The sense of this statement is found in Gregory, *Morals*, Book X, chapter 18. Augustine, however, says in *Sermon 2 on Prayer*: “Prayers are impeded in three ways: either when someone asks God for what resists his salvation; or when he prays but does not cease from iniquity; or when he does not forgive another who has sinned against him. When each person has diligently removed this threefold evil from himself, let him devote himself confidently to prayer,” and so forth. Gregory says: “We truly lift up our face without stain when we neither commit forbidden evils ourselves nor retain, out of personal zeal, the evils committed against us by our neighbors. For our mind is weighed down by grave confusion during its prayer if either its own conduct still defiles it or the pain stored up against another’s wickedness accuses it. I therefore think that Isidore drew this statement from Augustine rather than from Gregory.” LOAISA.]

12. Prayer is impeded in two ways, so that a person cannot obtain what he asks: namely, if he continues to commit evil, or if he does not forgive one who has sinned against him. When each person has cleansed himself of this twofold evil, he immediately devotes himself confidently to prayer and freely raises his mind toward the things he desires to obtain through supplication.

[Note: [Col. 0674C]

13. Thus it is written in Matthew 5: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.” The same appears in Luke 6. Therefore everyone is bound, as a matter of obligation, to pray for enemies in the common prayers, and it would be sinful to exclude them. Thomas Aquinas, II–II, question 83, article 8. To pray for them more particularly, however, is an act of perfection. Augustine proves this in Book III of *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 16, when speaking of the usefulness of enemies; and Ambrose on Psalm 38, explaining: “In return for their love of me, they slandered me; but I prayed.” Gregory likewise says in his letter to the bishop of Vercelli, Book X of the *Letters*, letter 82: “The fullness of the Gospel commands us to pray for those who slander and persecute us, so that we may ask forgiveness for their sins,” and so forth. LOAISA.]

13. Whoever is injured should not cease praying for those who injure him; otherwise, according to the Lord’s saying, he sins who does not pray for enemies (Matthew 5:44).

[Note: [Col. 0674D]

14. Gregory says the same in *Morals*, Book X, chapter 17, though in different words: “It is fixed in the mind like a sword, and by its edge the hidden recesses of the very inward parts are pierced. Unless it is first drawn out from the pierced heart, no divine assistance is obtained through prayers.” LOAISA.]

14. Just as no medicine benefits a wound while the iron remains in it, so prayer benefits nothing when pain still remains in the mind or hatred in the heart.

[Note: [Col. 0674D]

15. James 1 says: “Let him ask in faith, doubting nothing; for whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.” LOAISA.]

15. The one who prays should have such affection toward God that he does not despair of the effect of his prayer. We pray in vain if we do not possess confidence of hope. Therefore, as the Apostle says, let each person ask in faith, doubting nothing (James 1:6); for whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and scattered by the wind.

[Note: [Col. 0675B]

16. “Certain.” So in the Gothic and Toletan manuscripts. “Perfect,” in the Gothic and Salmatic manuscripts. LOAISA.]

16. Distrust in obtaining what has been prayed for arises if the mind still feels itself occupied with an inclination toward sinning. For the person who is still sluggish regarding God’s commandments and takes pleasure in the recollection of sin cannot have a sure confidence in prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0675B]

17. The prayer of the sinner is condemned in many passages of Sacred Scripture. Psalm 16: “Give ear to my prayer, not from deceitful lips.” Psalm 65: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.” [Col. 0675C] And Psalm 144: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in power.” Ecclesiasticus 7: “Before prayer, prepare your soul; do not be like one who tempts God.” Ecclesiasticus 3: “Whoever loves God will entreat him for sins and will restrain himself from them, and he will be heard in the prayer of his days.” Proverbs 1: “Then they will call upon me, and I will not hear them,” and chapter 59; and Jeremiah, Lamentations 3: “We have acted wickedly and provoked you to anger; therefore you are inexorable.” Ezekiel 8: “When they cry out in a loud voice into my ears, I will not hear them”; and Hosea 7: “Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they shall be laid waste, because they have transgressed against me.” He adds: “They did not cry to me with their heart, but they howled upon their beds.”

Instructions for prayer are given by our Lord Christ in Matthew 6: “When you pray,” and in chapter 13, and in Luke 1 and 20. Paul says in Philippians 4: “Be anxious about nothing, but in everything, by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” James 4: “You ask, and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your desires.”

Thus Augustine says in many places that the prayer of the sinner is fruitless and unheard, especially in *On True Innocence*, chapter 333, and in his letter to Proba, chapter 13. Ambrose likewise says that the affection of the one who prays must be pure, tranquil, and free from every burden of sin, in his work on Psalm 118 and in Book I of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 9. Cyprian says the same in *On the Lord’s Prayer*.

There is also a serious letter of Gregory the Great to Theodoric, king of the Franks, concerning simoniacal clerics, in which he says: “Therefore a greater calamity must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought into positions of governance—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to appease it through themselves.” The same appears in chapter 6 of his preface to Job, explaining: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to God.” It is found also in the chapter *Gravibus*, Gratian, question 7.

Bernard, in *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 63, explains: “The prayer of the just penetrates the heavens.” If this is so, how is Augustine to be understood in *Tractate 44 on John*, on chapter 9: “We know that God does not hear sinners.” Augustine says: “This is true of the man who is still blind, though anointed—that is, not yet perfectly illuminated. For if God does not hear sinners, the tax collector would have said in vain: ‘Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.’” Chrysostom says the same in homily 18 of the *Opus imperfectum*, explaining: “Everyone who asks receives”: “Whether he is just,” he says, “or a sinner.”

These apparently conflicting passages must therefore be reconciled and interpreted as follows: God does not hear a sinner who has fallen into sin and cries out without any desire to abandon sin; but God does hear a humble sinner who asks out of a good natural desire and prostrates himself before God, as Thomas Aquinas says, II–II, question 83. This does not happen on the basis of justice, since the sinner does not deserve it, but from pure mercy.

Four laws must be observed in the petition of a sinner: first, that he ask for himself; second, that he ask for what is necessary for salvation; third, that he ask piously—that is, for something directed toward piety; fourth, that he ask perseveringly. Then the prayer will be effective in obtaining, though not meritorious. I have set down these observations about the sinner’s prayer because they greatly contribute to understanding the whole chapter. LOAISA.]

17. Whoever turns away from God’s commandments does not deserve to receive what he asks for in prayer; nor does he obtain good from the one whose law he does not obey. For if we do what God commands, we undoubtedly obtain what we ask. As it is written: “Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28:9).

[Note: [Col. 0676C]

18. Literally from Gregory, *Morals*, Book XVIII, chapter 5, except that he has *operatione* (“by action”) instead of *opere* (“by work”). LOAISA.]

18. With God, both are necessarily commended together: action must be supported by prayer, and prayer by action. Hence Jeremiah says: “Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God” (Lamentations 3:41). A person lifts his heart with his hands when he supports prayer with action. For whoever prays and does not act lifts his heart but does not lift his hands. Whoever acts and does not pray lifts his hands but does not lift his heart. But since it is necessary both to act and to pray, the saying is rightly applied to both: “Let us lift our hearts with our hands to God,” lest we be reproached in our hearts for neglecting the commandments while striving to obtain salvation through prayer alone or action alone.

19. After we have performed a good work, let the tears of prayer be poured out, so that the humility of prayer may obtain the merit of the deed.

[Note: [Col. 0676C]

20. A similar example is found in Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; the prayer of the Pharisee is in Luke 18. LOAISA.]

20. A person spreads his hands toward God culpably when, in prayer, he boastfully displays his deeds, as the Pharisee boastfully prayed in the temple and wanted himself, rather than God, to be praised for his righteous works (Luke 18).

[Note: [Col. 0676D]

21. Thus it is written in Psalm 108 concerning the impious person: “Let his prayer become sin.” Jerome says: “Judas’s repentance became a worse sin. How is Judas’s repentance a worse sin? He went away and perished by hanging, and he who had become the Lord’s betrayer became his own murderer. I say this in praise of the Lord’s clemency, because by hanging himself he offended the Lord more than he had by betraying the Lord. His prayer ought to have become repentance, but it was turned into sin. You see a heretic praying; you see a Jew; you see a Manichaean. Although they fast, although they pray, their prayer is nevertheless turned into sin.” These are Jerome’s words, all of which Leo the Great made his own with a few additions and alterations. Gregory does the same in *Homily 27 on the Gospels*. LOAISA.

On the same passage: Others read, “Their prayer does not blot out sin, nor does it contribute to the merit of purification.” AREV.]

21. The prayer of some people is turned into sin, as is written concerning Judas the betrayer (Psalm 108). Whoever prays boastfully, seeking human praise, not only fails to have his prayer blot out sin, but his prayer itself is turned into sin. So it is with Jews and heretics: although they may appear to fast and pray, their prayer does not contribute to their merit of purification; rather, it is changed into sin.

[Note: [Col. 0676D]

22. From Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXVI, chapter 15. LOAISA.

On the same passage: “The three young men.” From Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 68, sermon 2. The story is found in Daniel 3. That the fire was cold is clear from the context of Scripture: “The angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, and drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew; and the fire did not touch them at all, nor trouble them, nor cause them any distress.” It is said below that the heat of the fire did not pass through them. Nicholas of Lyra raises here the question whether that fire was active, and he holds that it had the form and nature of fire, but that its activity and power to burn had been restrained by divine power. LOAISA.]

22. Therefore the prayer of the elect is sometimes delayed in their troubles, so that the perversity of the wicked may increase. Yet when the just are heard in temporal matters, this is done for the salvation of those who afflict them, so that, when temporal relief is granted to the just, the eyes of the wicked may be opened to conversion. Thus the fire of the three young men was cold (Daniel 3), so that Nebuchadnezzar might recognize the true God. As the prophet also says in the Psalms: “Deliver me because of my enemies” (Psalm 68:19).

23. Consequently, the prayers of some are heard only later, so that, when they are delayed, they may be stirred up more powerfully and multiplied by greater rewards. This is like frost and the restraint of harvests: the later the sown seeds emerge, the more abundantly they grow toward fruitfulness.

24. Whenever we who pray are not heard quickly, let us place our deeds before our eyes, so that the delay itself may be attributed to divine justice and to our own guilt.

25. Sometimes it is for our benefit, not our adversity, that we who pray perseveringly are not heard quickly. For God often does not hear many according to their will, so that he may hear them according to their salvation.

26. Many who pray are not heard because God, in his providence, is preparing better things for them than those they ask for—as often happens with little children who pray God that they may not be beaten at school. Yet the fulfillment of their petition is not granted them, because such an answer would hinder their improvement. The same thing happens to certain of the elect. They ask God for some advantages or relief from the adversities of this life, but divine providence does not at that time accommodate their desire, because it promises them better things for eternity.

[Col. 0678A] [Note: [Col. 0677C]

27. He is speaking of private prayer, about which the Lord Christ instructed the apostles. Matthew VI: “But you, when you pray, enter your room, and, with the door closed, pray to your Father in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” Cyprian, in *On the Lord’s Prayer*, gives the reason why Christ prescribed silence and secrecy in prayer: “By his teaching,” he says, “the Lord commands us to pray secretly, in hidden and secluded places, in the very rooms themselves. This is more fitting for our faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears and sees all things, and, in the fullness of his majesty, penetrates even hidden and concealed places.” Thus Cyprian. See also Augustine, on Psalm 141, and Gregory, *Moralia* VIII, chapter 29. LOAISA.]

27. Prayer is more appropriately poured out in private places, and obtains a greater result when it is expressed with God alone as its witness.

[Note: [Col. 0677D]

28. Thus it is written in Matthew VI: “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the street corners, so that they may be seen by people.” LOAISA.]

28. It is characteristic of hypocrites to display themselves in prayer before onlookers; their reward is not to please God, but to acquire glory from human beings (Matthew VI, 7).

29. People are not heard by God because they use many words, as though they were trying to bend him by an abundance of speech. For it is not a multiplicity of words that wins him over, but the pure and sincere intention of prayer.

287 [Note: [Col. 0677D]

30. Hidden and secluded prayer concerns the salvation of the heart; the singing of hymns and psalms concerns the glory and honor of Christ crucified, so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. Therefore those who abolish ecclesiastical song obscure the magnificent glory of Christ, overturn the sweet relief of cares, confuse the hierarchy of ecclesiastical order, and defile the admirable beauty and adornment of Christ’s bride. Finally, they try, as it were, to remove light from the world when they insist that ecclesiastical choirs should be absent from the Church. For just as all things contained in this worldly structure receive splendor, beauty, order, and life from this natural light, so through ecclesiastical choirs all the functions of the Church are illumined, increased, enlarged, and preserved in their proper service. Accordingly, the holy and ancient Fathers labored long and diligently in establishing, composing, and ordering the ecclesiastical offices. See Augustine, on Psalm 148; Jerome, on Psalm 146. LOAISA.]

30. It is good always to pray in the heart, and it is also good to glorify God with the sound of the voice through spiritual hymns. It is worthless to sing with the voice alone, without the intention of the heart; rather, as the Apostle says, “singing in your hearts” [Col. 0678B] (Ephesians V, 19)—that is, singing psalms not only with the voice, but also with the heart. Hence elsewhere also: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing with the mind” (I Corinthians XIV, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0678C]

31. Basil says much in praise of the psalms, in Homily 1 on the Psalms, and Ambrose says still more. Augustine writes: “The one voice of the whole Church—the PSALM—adorns the solemnities; the psalm softens the sadness that is according to God; the psalm also draws tears from a heart of stone; the psalm is the work of angels, the spiritual incense of the heavenly hosts.” I have wished to record these observations, among others, so that you may understand that true wisdom was transmitted from the Fathers of the earlier age to those of the later age, and that all their judgments rest upon them as upon the firmest roots. Basil, Homily 1 on the Psalms: “The PSALM,” he says, “is the voice of the Church. It makes feast days more illustrious and suffuses them with joy; although it ordinarily produces sadness, it produces the sadness that is according to God, and draws tears from a heart of stone. The psalm is the work of angels, the common service set forth in that heavenly commonwealth, spiritual incense,” and so forth. Nearly all that follows Augustine translated word for word. Ambrose, too, most learnedly recalls the praises of the Psalms in his preface to the Psalms; Isidore took these statements about the Psalms from him. LOAISA.]

31. Just as we are governed by prayers, so we take delight in the practice of the psalms. The usefulness of singing psalms consoles sorrowful hearts, makes minds more grateful, delights the bored, rouses the sluggish, and invites sinners to lamentation. For however hard the hearts of carnal people may be, as soon as the sweetness of the psalm resounds, it bends their minds toward the practice of piety.

32. Although a Christian ought to be moved not by vocal modulation but solely by the divine words that are sung, nevertheless, somehow or other, a greater compunction of heart arises from the singer’s melody. Many are found who, moved by the sweetness of the singing, lament their sins, and are more strongly bent toward tears precisely through the most delightful sweetness that has resounded from the psalmist.

33. Prayer is poured out in the present life as a remedy for sins; but the singing of psalms manifests the perpetual praise of God unto eternal glory, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; throughout the ages of ages they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII, 5). Whoever faithfully and attentively performs this ministry is, in a certain way, joined to the angels.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Reading.

[Note: [Col. 0679C]

CHAPTER VIII, no. 1. Paul instructs Timothy: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine.” For frequent reading, Ambrose says (*On the Blessed Man*, book I), “which is interrupted by no interval, performs the office of instruction.” Augustine also discusses the reading of the Scriptures learnedly in Sermon 112 *On the Season*, volume X. LOAISA.

In the same place: “It is better.” Jerome also places prayer before reading, in his letter to Furia. LOAISA.

In the same place, Adhelerus, in his *Admonition to Nosuinda*, chapter 13: “For Isidore says that we are cleansed by prayers and instructed by readings.” AREV.]

1. We are cleansed by prayers and instructed by readings; both are good, if possible. If it is not possible, it is better [Col. 0679B] to pray than to read.

[Note: [Col. 0679C]

2. Taken verbatim from Augustine, Sermon 112 *On the Season*. The fourth sentence occurs in the same place. LOAISA.

In the same place: Thus Gothus’s Codex. “For when we ourselves pray, we speak with God.” Augustine has it likewise. LOAISA.]

2. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought to pray frequently and also to read frequently. For when we pray, we ourselves speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

3. All progress proceeds from reading and meditation. What we do not know, we learn through reading; what we have learned, we preserve through meditation.

4. Reading the holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift: either because it educates the understanding of the mind, or because, having drawn a person away from the vanities of the world, it leads him to the love of God. Often aroused by its message, we are withdrawn from desire for worldly life; and, inflamed with love of wisdom, the vain hope of this mortality becomes so much less valuable to us as, through reading, eternal hope shines more brightly [Col. 0679C].

[Note: [Col. 0679D]

5. Augustine teaches this in book IV, chapter 4, of *On Christian Doctrine*, where he portrays the duty of the teacher of divine Scripture and distinguishes between speaking wisely and speaking eloquently. He applies the three functions of eloquence—to teach, to delight, and to move—to the reading of Scripture. In the same work, chapter 12: “To teach,” he says, “belongs to necessity; to delight, to pleasantness; to move, to victory. Of these three, the first—that is, the necessity of teaching—is established in the things we say; the other two belong to the manner in which, by teaching, we say them.” What Isidore says here about the usefulness and dignity of expression refers, in the case of usefulness, to delight, and in the case of dignity, to victory. LOAISA.]

5. The study of reading is twofold: first, how the Scriptures are to be understood; second, with what usefulness or dignity they are to be expressed [Col. 0680A]. For a person will first become ready to understand what he reads and then capable of expressing what he has learned.

289

[Note: [Col. 0679D]

6. Augustine teaches this repeatedly, especially in his exposition of Psalm XI, and in *On the Work of Monks*, at the end, chapter 17. LOAISA.

In the same place: “To fulfill.” Jerome, commentary on Micah II: “Then Scripture benefits the reader, if what is read is fulfilled in action.” He praises the same quality in the widow Marcella, in her epitaph to Principia [Col. 0680C]. LOAISA.]

6. A vigorous reader will be readiest to fulfill what he reads rather than merely to know it. For it is a lesser punishment not to know what you should desire than not to fulfill what you have learned. Just as by reading we desire to know, so by knowing we ought to fulfill in action the right things we have learned.

7. God’s law contains both a reward and a punishment for those who read it: a reward for those who keep it by living well, but a punishment for those who despise it by living badly.

[Note: [Col. 0680C]

8. Jerome, to Principia, in the epitaph of the widow Marcella: “For even excellent learning blushes when a pious conscience reproves it.” LOAISA.

In the same place, Psalm CXVIII: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I have looked upon all your commandments.” Thus our Latin edition has it. Augustine, in his fourth exposition of this psalm: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I behold all your commandments.” Pagninus renders it: “Then I shall not be made ashamed, when I have looked upon all your precepts.” It is a future tense, “when I have looked upon”—that is, when I understand and comprehend why you commanded those things. For few are granted the ability to grasp the reasons and causes of all God’s commandments and to carry them out carefully. LOAISA.

[Col. 0680D] In the same place: “When I look upon all your commandments.” Sabatier, on Psalm CXVIII, 6, notes that this wording occurs in the Roman and Mozarabic Breviaries. AREV.]

8. Everyone who departs from God’s commandments in action is put to shame in his heart whenever he is able to read or hear those same commandments of God, because he is reminded of what he does not do and is inwardly accused by the testimony of his conscience. Hence the prophet David also prays, saying: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon all your commandments” (Psalm CXVIII, 6). For each person is gravely ashamed when, whether by reading or hearing, he looks upon the commandments of God that he despises in his way of life. He is reproved in his heart when meditation upon the commandments teaches him that he has not fulfilled in action what he learned from the divine command.

290

## CHAPTER IX. On Constancy in Reading.

[Note: [Col. 0680D]

CHAPTER IX, no. 1. Proverbs IV: “Take hold of her, and she will exalt you; you will be glorified by her when you have embraced her.” Earlier he had said: “Love her, and she will preserve you.” Much is handed down by the Fathers concerning the constancy and perseverance with which the holy Scriptures should be read, especially by Cyprian, at the end of *On Spectacles*, and Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 5: “He will be a most diligent investigator of the divine Scriptures.” This is found in distinction 19, and in the remarkable Sermon 38 to the brothers in the desert. Ambrose teaches much about the praise of Scripture and its diligent reading. In his work on “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” he teaches that it must be read constantly: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. But whoever meditates on the law is instructed by the law; and the one whom the law has instructed is instructed by the Lord, who spoke the law.” Also in Letter 3 to Sabinus, concerning his study. Jerome likewise writes to Demetrias at the end: “Love the holy Scriptures, and Wisdom will love you. Love her, and she will preserve you. Honor her, and she will embrace you.” This sentence appears to have been taken from that passage. LOAISA.

In the same place: “When you have embraced her,” etc. This is absent from many manuscript codices. LOAISA.]

1. No one can know the meaning of the holy Scripture except through familiarity with reading, as it is written: “Love her, and she will exalt you; you will be glorified by her when you have embraced her” (Proverbs IV, 8).

[Col. 0681A] [Note: [Col. 0681C]

2. Augustine, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 9, teaches that the precepts for living and the rules for believing must be investigated in the sacred books with the greatest diligence and care. LOAISA.]

2. The more constant a person is in the sacred utterances, the richer an understanding he receives from them—just as the more thoroughly land is cultivated, the more abundantly it bears fruit.

[Note: [Col. 0681C]

3. Exodus XIX and XXXIV. The sentence appears to have been taken from Gregory, *Moralia*, book V, chapters 25 and 26 [Col. 0681D]. LOAISA.]

3. The higher a person climbs toward any art, the more that art itself descends toward him, just as it is written in the Law: “Moses went up into the mountain, and the Lord descended” (Exodus XIX).

[Note: [Col. 0681D]

4. I Corinthians II: “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God,” and below: “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit, but the spiritual person judges all things. But we have the mind of Christ.” Augustine, in his exposition of Psalm CXVIII, explaining: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart.” Gregory also handles the same passage excellently, and I believe the sentence was derived from him, *Moralia*, book XXIII, chapters 20 and 21. LOAISA.

In the same place: “As a blind man.” A similar example occurs in Augustine, Sermon 112. LOAISA.

In the same place: “Fixes.” Gothus’s Codex adds: “The devil fears more the one whom he sees reading constantly.” I find this reading in none of the other thirteen ancient manuscripts that I obtained from all the libraries of Spain for the correction of this work, by order of Philip II, the Catholic and most pious king.

[Col. 0682C] In the same place: “Has withdrawn.” Another reading: “has emptied.” AREV.]

4. This concerns spiritual leisure: only the person who has withdrawn his mind from earthly concerns and clung to the holy Scriptures through diligent familiarity will investigate the secrets of the divine commandments. For just as both a blind man and a sighted man can indeed walk, but not with equal freedom—the blind man, proceeding where he cannot see, stumbles, while the sighted man avoids obstacles and recognizes where he ought to go—so also the person darkened by the cloud of earthly concern cannot investigate the mysteries of God if he attempts to do so, because he does not see through the fog of his cares. Only the person who withdraws himself from the world’s external concerns and fixes himself wholly upon meditation on the Scriptures can accomplish this.

291

[Note: [Col. 0682C]

5. Augustine, in *On the Spirit and the Soul*, chapter 11, defines natural ability (*ingenium*) as a power of the soul, or the concentration by which the soul extends and exercises itself toward knowledge of things unknown. LOAISA.

In the same place: “Taste.” Another reading: “grasp.” AREV.]

5. Some possess intellectual ability but neglect the study of reading; what they could have learned by reading, they contemptuously disregard through negligence. Others have a desire to know but are hindered by slowness of understanding. Yet through constant reading they come to understand what the intellectually gifted do not know because of their idleness.

6. A slower intellect, even if it is not improved by nature, is nevertheless strengthened by constant reading. For although there may be dullness of understanding, frequent reading still increases intelligence [Col. 0681C].

7. Just as the person who is slow to understand nevertheless receives a reward for the earnestness of good study, so the person who neglects the intellectual ability granted to him by God becomes liable to condemnation, because he despises the gift he received and sins through laziness.

[Col. 0682A] 8. Some receive, by God’s judgment, the gift of knowledge that they neglect, so that they may be punished more severely for the truths they have believed. Those who are slower, however, find with difficulty what they desire to know for this reason: so that, for the greatest exertion of labor, they may receive the greatest reward of recompense.

## CHAPTER X. On Learning without Grace.

[Note: [Col. 0682C]

CHAPTER X, no. 1. The divine Hilary, at the beginning of his exposition of Psalm CXXV, teaches most learnedly that the holy Scriptures are not to be received according to our own understanding, as heretics do, but are to be understood through the gift and assistance of the one who said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and opened the hidden and concealed meanings of the Scriptures [Col. 0682D]. The holy Jerome teaches the same in his letter to Paulinus, at the end. Hence Cyprian, in *On the Unity of the Church*, nearly halfway through, calls those people corrupters of the Gospel, while he depicts the character of heretics with great elegance; and, as the holy Jerome says of him in his letter to Paulinus at the end, he proceeds like a most pure fountain, sweet and gentle. LOAISA.

In the same place: “Let it be poured in.” He appears to be explaining Psalm CXVIII: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you.” LOAISA.

In the same place: “The last.” Another reading: “the innermost.” Vezzozi observes that anyone who denied this would at least be a Semi-Pelagian. AREV.]

1. Learning without the grace that assists it, although poured into the ears, never descends into the heart; outwardly it makes a great noise, but inwardly it accomplishes nothing. The word of God poured into the ears reaches the innermost parts of the heart only when God’s grace touches the mind inwardly so that it may understand.

2. For just as God illumines some people with the flame of his love, so that they may possess vital understanding, so he abandons others, cold and sluggish, so that they remain without understanding [Col. 0682B].
