3. Most people are lively in their sharpness of understanding but are constrained by an inability to speak. Others excel in both respects, possessing both an abundance of knowledge and effectiveness in expression.

## CHAPTER XI. On Proud Readers.

[Note: [Col. 0682D]

CHAPTER XI, no. 1. This entire chapter is taken from Gregory, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 11, where he explains the passage from Job: “They gnawed in the wilderness, wretched through calamity and misery.” LOAISA.]

1. Most people use the knowledge they have received from the Scriptures not for the glory of God but for their own praise. They are lifted up by that very knowledge, and they sin precisely where they ought to have cleansed their sins.

[Note: [Col. 0682D]

2. “Always.” Thus Gregory, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 9: “The more they desire, the more they lose.” LOAISA.]

2. The arrogant never attain perfect knowledge through reading. Although they may appear wise on the surface, they do not touch the inner marrow of the mysteries of truth, because they are hindered by the cloud of pride. The proud always read and seek, but never find.

3. The inner chambers of divine law stand open to the humble and to those who rightly approach God, but they are closed to the wicked and proud. For although the divine utterances are open in reading to the arrogant, they are nevertheless closed and hidden in their mystery.

[Note: [Col. 0683B]

4. “Shone,” in the Toledo and Gothic manuscripts, instead of “is light.” LOAISA.

In the same place: “From there,” etc. Augustine, Sermon 30 *On the Season*, says this about the Jews: “Among the Jews the divine writings alone were to remain, by which the nations would be instructed while they themselves would be blinded.” LOAISA.

In the same place: “Is light.” I printed it this way and added in Loaisa’s note “for IS LIGHT.” Otherwise it might seem doubtful whether Loaisa intended *luxit* (“shone”). In Grial’s text it appears joined as *luxsit*. It could be read *lux est* (“is light”) or *lucet* (“shines”), as opposed to *tenebrescit* (“grows dark”) below. AREV.]

4. While the word of God is light to the faithful, it somehow grows dark for the reprobate and proud; and from the same source by which the former are illumined, the latter are blinded.

## CHAPTER XII. On Carnal Readers and Heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0683B]

CHAPTER XII, no. 1. Teachers call the external, carnal understanding of the words of divine law “carnal,” on the basis of what is written by Paul in Colossians II concerning deceivers: “Let no one deceive you, wishing in humility and the worship of angels, intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head.” Hence Augustine frequently speaks of understanding “carnally,” and of earthly and carnal righteousness, especially in his exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter III, and of Psalm X. “To those who understand the law spiritually,” he says, “it is the sacrament of freedom; but to those who perceive it carnally, if they are Jews, it is the yoke of slavery; if pagans or heretics, it is a veil of blindness.” Jerome likewise writes to Algasia, question 10: “The Jew is vainly puffed up and swollen with the sense of his flesh, understanding everything carnally and pursuing the delirious traditions of the Jews, not holding fast to the head.” LOAISA.

In the same place: “The words of the law.” An example is the prohibition issued by Pope Celestine to the priests of Gaul, who ministered in the church wearing cloaks and girding their loins, so that they might fulfill literally the Lord’s command, “Let your loins be girded.” Letter 2 to the bishops of Gaul. “Those who believe,” he says, “that they will complete the faith of Holy Scripture not through the Spirit but through the letter,” and so forth. This was said not only about the divine law but also about civil law. LOAISA.]

1. A person does not understand the law at all if he runs through the words of the law carnally; rather, the law is understood by the one who perceives it through the sense of inner understanding. For those who attend to the letter of the law cannot penetrate its hidden meaning.

[Note: [Col. 0683D]

2. As Augustine reports concerning the Ebionites, in *On Heretics to Quodvultdeus*. LOAISA.]

2. Many, because they did not understand the Scriptures spiritually or perceive them correctly, fell into heresy and slipped into many errors.

[Note: [Col. 0683D]

3. “Bind.” In the printed editions, “sign,” incorrectly; thus Isaiah VIII: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.” Eusebius of Caesarea interprets this passage in book VII, chapter 3, of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*, and Cyprian, book I, chapter 9, *Against the Jews*, concerning the cessation of the Mosaic law, as though he were saying: “Close the law of Moses and open the gentle law delivered by Christ to the apostles and disciples.” LOAISA.

In the same place, John XIII: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another”; this is also how it appears in the Seguntine Codex. LOAISA.]

3. The law has been bound up among the faithful alone, as the Lord testifies through the Prophet: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isaiah VIII, 16), so that neither a Jew nor a heretic may understand it, since he is not a disciple of Christ. For they do not follow the unity of peace that Christ taught, concerning which the same Lord says: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love among yourselves.”

294

[Note: [Col. 0683D]

4. It is characteristic of heretics to corrupt the legitimate and true meaning of Scripture, as Saint Peter says of Paul’s Letters, in his Second Letter, chapter III: “In them are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.” Saint Gregory also noted this, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 9. Augustine likewise writes, on Psalm XLVIII, sermon 1: “All divine utterances are salutary to those who understand them well, but dangerous to those who wish to twist them according to the perversity of their own heart rather than correct their heart according to the truth of those utterances.” Hence Jerome’s statement: “Heresy arises from interpretation, not from Scripture.” The monk Vincent of Lérins says the same in his excellent little book against heresies. Much concerning the transmission and preservation of the true meaning of Scripture was therefore inserted into the *Constitutions of Saint Clement*. The same principle is also established in the sixth Council of Constantinople, chapter 2. It was likewise decreed in the First Lateran Council under Martin I, against Paul of Constantinople: “If anyone does not confess, according to the holy Fathers, properly and truly, everything that has been handed down and preached by the holy and apostolic Church of God through those holy Fathers and the five credible and universal councils, down to the slightest point, in word and in mind, let him be condemned.” And in the other Lateran Council under Julius II and Leo X, session 10, under Leo: “We command all who bear, or shall in the future bear, the burden of preaching, that they preach and explain the evangelical truth and Holy Scripture according to the declaration and interpretation of the teachers whom the Church of God, or long-standing usage, has approved and until now received in reading, and shall receive in the future; and that they add nothing contrary or discordant with them according to their own understanding, but always adhere to those things which, rightly and soundly understood from the words of Holy Scripture themselves and from the interpretations of the aforementioned teachers, do not disagree.” The holy Fathers, inspired by the Holy Spirit, again handed down this rule at the latest universal Council of Trent, session 4, to restrain the reckless minds of the heretics of the present age. Augustine, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 25, explains how that is the sense of Scripture which is the common judgment of all the Church’s teachers, and how their common judgment is the judgment of God. LOAISA.]

4. Heretics do not understand the Scriptures with sound judgment; rather, they drive them toward the error of a perverse interpretation. They do not submit themselves to the meaning of the Scriptures, but perversely drag the Scriptures toward their own error.

5. Teachers of error bind their hearers through deceptive arguments and corrupt persuasions, entangling them as in a labyrinth from which they can scarcely escape.

6. Such is the cunning of heretics that they mix falsehoods with truths and evils with good things, usually inserting the poison of their error into salutary matters, so that they may more easily persuade people of the perversity of their doctrine under the appearance of truth.

[Col. 0684B] [Note: [Col. 0684D]

7. It is characteristic of heretics not only to conceal their deadly poison under the name and authority of the most learned men, but also to serve the cups of their poisonous madness to the ignorant under the title of the apostles, so that they may drink them more sweetly and easily. Hence a Letter is sent to the Thessalonians in Paul’s name, as II Thessalonians suggests: “Nor by a letter as though sent by us.” Hence also those pseudepigraphal works: the Book of Seth, son of Noah; the *Scripture of Ham*; the Gospels of Peter, Thomas, and Matthias. Hence also *Paul’s Rapture*, *Solomon’s Incantations*, and infinitely many others of this kind, as Eusebius reports, book III of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19, and the Second Council of Nicaea. The heretics Priscillian and Dictinius also published writings under the names of prophets, apostles, and patriarchs, as the Council of Braga reports. Nicephorus, too, book XVI of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 28, asserts that writings of the heretic Apollinaris were attributed to Athanasius, Gregory, and Julius. Likewise they falsely foisted Ibas’s letter upon Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, as appears in the Second Council of Nicaea. Articles were also falsely attributed to Augustine, as Prosper records in his response to Vincent, chapter 15. In our own deeply embittered times, a work of Oecolampadius against the sacrament of the Eucharist has been ascribed to the presbyter Bertram, addressed to Charlemagne; Carolostadius’s work against images has been attributed to Charlemagne himself; and a certain book of Calvin’s has been attributed to Alcuin, Charlemagne’s teacher, as Sixtus learnedly noted in his *Bibliotheca*. LOAISA.

In the same place: Thus the writings of Clement, Dionysius, Origen, Athanasius, and other distinguished teachers were corrupted by heretics, as the martyr Pamphilus, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus, Rufinus, and others report. Councils also suffered the same injury, as is clear from the fourteenth act of the Sixth General Council of Constantinople. Whether the books of Origen were in fact corrupted by heretics—I mention this in passing—Pico della Mirandola composed a lengthy discussion. Against those who do not hesitate to commit this crime and dare to impose false books in place of genuine ones, the *Apostolic Constitutions* decree: “If anyone publishes books falsely inscribed as sacred in the church, for the corruption of the people and clergy, let him be deposed.” LOAISA.

In the same place: Loaisa’s note had “Dictivius,” incorrectly, instead of “Dictinius.” Fabricius gathers much additional material on pseudepigraphal books in the work entitled *Codex Pseudepigraphus Novi ac Veteris Testamenti* [*Pseudepigraphal Codex of the New and Old Testament*]. The *Acts of the Academy of Barcelona*, page 268, may also be consulted. I have discussed at length the corrupters of ancient codices in the prolegomena to Sedulius, chapter 7, and added some observations in *Isidoriana*, chapter 70, no. 23 and following, and chapter 108. As for Loaisa’s belief, shared with Sixtus of Siena and other learned men, that heretics of their own time had falsely attributed certain works to Bertram—also called Bertramnus and Ratramnus—and to Alcuin, it has long since been established that this is false. Re-read *Isidoriana*, chapter 30, no. 18, and chapter 67, no. 12. Since Catholics of good faith now acknowledge this, there was certainly no reason for Ittigius, in his work *On the Libraries of the Fathers*, page 167, to revive this controversy with such elaborate apparatus in hatred of Catholics, against whom he also inveighs bitterly against Peter de Marca. Moreover, Acherius maintains, in the preface to volume I of the *Spicilegium*, that Ratramnus asserted nothing in his works contrary to the Catholic doctrine of the Eucharist. AREV.]

7. Heretics very often write their own statements under the name of Catholic teachers so that they may be believed when read without question. Sometimes, too, they insert their blasphemies by hidden deceit into the books of our own writers and corrupt true doctrine by adulterating it—either adding what is impious or removing what is pious.

295

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

8. Thus the Apostle says, I Thessalonians V: “Do not despise prophecies; but test everything.” LOAISA.]

8. What is read must be carefully meditated upon and tested with cautious judgment, so that, in accordance with the apostolic admonition (I Thessalonians V, 20–21), we may retain what is right and reject what is contrary to the truth. In this way we may be instructed in good things while remaining unharmed by evil ones.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Books of the Gentiles.

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

CHAPTER XIII, no. 1. This is cited in Gratian’s *Collections*, distinction 37, chapter “Therefore It Is Prohibited.” The whole of that distinction concerns secular books, based on a decree of the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 16, and on Jerome, Rabanus, Bede, and Clement. LOAISA.

[Col. 0686A] In the same place, Paulinus, Letter 7:

[Col. 0686B]

“Hearts dedicated to Christ refuse the Muses and are not open to Apollo.”

Concerning the reading of bishops and priests, and how, according to the Apostle’s command, they ought to attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine, see Gratian’s *Collections*, distinction 36, chapter “Those Who Are Trained in Ecclesiastical Discipline”; and, if desired, Sozomen, Letter 1 to Hesychius; Origen, Homily 6 on chapter VIII of Leviticus; and Gregory, book IX of the *Register*, Letter 48, where he reproves Bishop Desiderius because he expounded grammar to certain people, since, in one mouth, the praises of Christ cannot be joined with the praises of Jupiter. Nevertheless, not all the fabrications of poets are immediately forbidden to Christians, but only those that arouse the fuel of lust. For, as Ambrose teaches, book III of *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, at the beginning, volume II, poetic figures and comparisons are also found in the divine Scriptures, and poetic verses have been inserted into the divine books. The prophetic sequence of discourse does not shrink from mentioning giants and the valley of the Titans; Isaiah spoke of sirens and the daughters of sparrows, and Jeremiah likewise. Hence Augustine, book II of *The City of God*, chapter 8, condemns the study of tragedies, comedies, and poetic fables, but only those composed with obscene language, and he forbids children to read them. This was taught not only by him and other holy Fathers but also by pagans who set forth laws of virtue, among them Plato in his *Laws*, and others. See Augustine himself, book XIV of *The City of God*. LOAISA.

In the same place: Sedulius, at the beginning of the *Paschal Poem*, etc.

“When the pagan poets strive after their own fictions,” see Cotelerius, *Apostolic Fathers*, volume I, page 204. Before the sentence “Therefore it is forbidden to Christians,” or, as others have it, “A Christian,” some manuscripts place another statement in these words: “Therefore the poets wished to call Venus an immodest goddess and Mars an adulterous god in their books, so that they might persuade people’s minds that evil should be imitated as though it were divine; so that, while they confidently commit their shameful acts through the persuasion of lust, they may appear to imitate not skilled human beings but heavenly gods. Therefore it is forbidden,” and so forth. Thus the old edition. As for Vezzosius’s claim that Loaisa admits this passage is absent from the ancient manuscripts, that does not appear in Grial’s edition. AREV.]

1. A Christian is therefore forbidden to read the fictions of poets, because through the pleasures of empty tales they rouse the mind toward incentives to lust. For a person is sacrificed to demons not only by offering incense to them, but also by willingly absorbing their words.

[Note: [Col. 0686D]

2. “To advance.” Vezzosius printed “to complete,” but admits that “to advance” is perhaps better. AREV.]

2. Some take greater pleasure in meditating on the sayings of the gentiles because of their inflated and ornate style than in reading Holy Scripture because of its humble expression. But what good is it to advance in worldly learning and become empty in divine matters, to pursue perishable fictions and disdain heavenly mysteries? Such books must therefore be avoided and shunned for the love of the holy Scriptures.

[Note: [Col. 0686D]

AREV.]

3. The sayings of the gentiles shine outwardly with the eloquence of words, but inwardly remain empty of the wisdom of virtue; the sacred utterances, however, appear outwardly unadorned in their words [Col. 0687A], but inwardly shine with the wisdom of their mysteries. Hence the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Corinthians IV, 7).

5. Therefore the sacred books were written in simple language, so that people might be led to faith not by the wisdom of speech but by the demonstration of the Spirit (1 Cor. 2:4). For if they had been composed with the subtlety of dialectical acumen or the eloquence of rhetorical art, Christ’s faith would by no means be thought to rest on the power of God, but on the arguments of human eloquence; nor would we believe that anyone was summoned to faith by divine inspiration, but rather seduced by verbal cleverness.

[Col. 0687B] [Note: [Col. 0687C]

[Note: [Col. 0687C]

Ibid. Psalm 70. Here Basil supports Symmachus’s version: “Because I cannot enumerate them, I will enter into the powers of the Lord,” since that wording was more polished: “My mouth will proclaim your righteousness.” This promise, because it exceeds human strength, added: “Because I cannot enumerate them”; for such Scriptures, he says, my nature has not attained. Nevertheless, “I will enter into the powers of the Lord,” so that I may render human weakness capable. Theodoret says the same. Augustine explains what other manuscripts have as “commerce” in relation to the literature of heretics and to commerce: “There are some,” he says, “who interpret this of all literature, sacred as well as profane,” as in Isaiah 29: “I do not know letters”—as though he were saying, “I do not understand the sacred Scriptures sufficiently, nor the mysteries hidden and unknown in their meaning.” He calls the “letters” the law of Moses in its bark and letter; he interprets “to know” as “to approve.” It is as though he said: “I have not approved the killing letter; I have entered into the powers, made life-giving by the Spirit of the Son of God, powers to be recalled and enumerated. 11. Grammarians are better than heretics. For heretics offer people a draught of deadly poison by persuading them to drink it, whereas the teaching of grammarians can also contribute to life when it has been taken up for better uses.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Discussion

[Note: [Col. 0688D]

CHAPTER XIV, no. 1. Augustine, in Book II of the *Soliloquies*, asserts that truth can be sought in no better way than by questioning and answering. And in Book I of the *Academic Questions*, disputation 1, chapter 3: “The search for truth alone is the perfect task of wisdom.” LOAISA.]

1. Reading is useful for instruction, but when discussion is added it provides greater understanding. For discussion is better than reading.

2. Discussion makes a person teachable. For when questions are proposed, hesitation about matters is removed, and hidden truth is often established through objections. What is obscure or doubtful is quickly made clear by discussion.

[Note: [Col. 0688D]

3. Augustine sets out the method of disputation in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, addressed to Honoratus: “Once the trifles of commonplaces have been set aside, let matter contend with matter, cause with cause, reason with reason.” LOAISA.]

3. Comparisons are very useful in discussion. Matters that are less readily perceived in themselves are easily grasped through comparison with other matters. For Scripture often conveys spiritual realities under another appearance; and unless hidden mysteries of the law are displayed in some evident way, they scarcely appear.

[Note: [Col. 0689C]

4. Thus Paul, 2 Timothy 2: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels.” And to Titus, almost the same, chapter 3: “Avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes about the law; for they are useless and vain.” Here, according to Ambrose, he calls many questions unlearned because they arise from contentiousness and provide no benefit for Christian discipline. LOAISA.]

4. Just as discussion usually instructs, so contention destroys. For, abandoning the meaning of truth, it generates quarrels and, fighting with words, even blasphemes against God. Hence arise heresies and schisms, by which faith is overturned, truth corrupted, and charity torn apart (2 Tim. 2:23; Titus 3:9).

5. The zeal of contentious people struggles not for truth but from a desire for praise. Their perversity is so great that they do not know how to yield to truth, and strive to empty out sound doctrine itself.

300 [Note: [Col. 0689C]

6. “Of the faithful.” Another reading is “of the unfaithful,” that is, “against the unfaithful.” AREV.]

6. In the disputation of the faithful, one must beware of the artificial subtlety of propositions, which casts nets through crafty objections. For the disputation of the wicked is so entangled in cunning assertions that they make what they persuade people to accept as perverse appear sound.

7. Reading requires the assistance of memory. If memory is naturally slower, it is nevertheless sharpened by frequent meditation and strengthened by habitual reading.

[Note: [Col. 0689C]

8. “Wears away.” So the Gothic and Toletan manuscripts; the entire sentence is absent from the Salmanticensis, while all the others have “obliterates.” [Col. 0689D] LOAISA.]

8. Lengthy reading often wears away the reader’s memory because of its extent. But if the reading is brief and, after the book has been put aside, the sentence is recalled in the mind, then one reads without effort, and what has been read does not at all slip from memory when it is recollected.

9. Silent reading is more acceptable to the senses than reading aloud. The intellect is more fully instructed when the reader’s voice is still and the tongue moves in silence. For reading aloud both tires the body and dulls the sharpness of the voice.

## CHAPTER XV. On Contemplation and Action

[Col. 0689C]

[Note: [Col. 0689D]

CHAPTER XV, no. 1. Gregory discusses the active and contemplative life in many places, but especially in Book II on Ezekiel, homily 14, and in Book V of his *Exposition on 1 Kings*, chapter 15, in the passage: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit,” from Philippians 3. Augustine depicts the active and contemplative life splendidly, especially in his final treatise on John: “The Church knows two lives divinely proclaimed and commended to it: one in faith, the other in sight; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of dwelling; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation; one turns away from evil and does good, the other has no evil from which to turn away and possesses a great good in which to rejoice.” And in Book II, *On the Words of the Lord*, sermons 26 and 27. Basil says almost the same in the preface to his *Monastic Rules*, where he treats the subject at length. Clement of Alexandria, too, in Book VI of the *Stromata*, divides truth into knowledge and action, and discusses the excellence of the contemplative life in Book VII. Prosper also composed three books *On the Contemplative Life* and established the distinction between the two lives, especially in Book I, chapter 12. LOAISA.]

1. The active life is innocence in good works; the contemplative life is meditation upon heavenly things. The former belongs to many in common, the latter to few.

2. The active life makes good use of worldly things; the contemplative life, renouncing the world, takes delight in living for God alone.

301 [Note: [Col. 0690C]

3. Gregory, Book VI of the *Moralia*, chapter 17. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Although converted.” A *conversus* is one who, renouncing the world, follows Christ in the perfect life. Hence laymen who have renounced the world are called *conversi* in religious life. There is in them a certain conversion, a turning of the heart. The name seems to have been taken from Ezekiel 33, which Augustine cites in *On True and False Repentance* as follows: “At whatever hour the sinner groans and is converted, he shall live.” Augustine adds: “He said ‘converted,’ not merely ‘turned,’ shall live.” I think that one is merely “turned” who grieves over the crime; “converted” is one who grieves over the changeability of his mind which we have described. A person is turned from sin when he already wishes to abandon sin. He is converted when he turns wholly and entirely, when he no longer merely fears punishment but hastens toward the Lord’s good. If such conversion occurs in anyone, even at the end, there is no reason to despair of his forgiveness. But since such a just conversion is scarcely or rarely found, there is reason to fear for the one who repents late. LOAISA.]

3. Whoever first makes progress in the active life ascends properly to contemplation. For the one who is found useful in the former is rightly raised up in the latter. Whoever still seeks temporal glory or carnal desire will be barred from contemplation, so that, placed in the work of the active life, he may be purified. In the active life, all vices must first be drained away through the exercise of good works, so that in the contemplative life each person may pass over to contemplate God with the mind’s vision already purified. And although the convert may immediately wish to ascend to contemplation, reason nevertheless compels him first to engage in the work of the active life.

6. 7. [Note: [Col. 0691D]

10. The right eye that causes scandal, which the Lord commanded to be plucked out (Matt. 5:29), is the contemplative life. 303 ## CHAPTER XVI. On Those Who Despise the World

[Note: [Col. 0691D]

CHAPTER XVI, no. 1. Phanutius, a disciple of Antony, discusses three kinds of vocation—from man, from God, and from necessity—in Cassian, *Conferences* 3, chapter 3; and similarly three modes of renunciation in the same conference, chapter 6, and throughout almost the entire book. Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*, devoutly exhorts everyone to despise the world. LOAISA.]

1. What is dear to lovers of the world, the saints shun as though it were hostile; they rejoice more in the world’s adversities than they take delight in its prosperity.

2. Those to whom this world prospers in every advantage are strangers to God. Everything in this world is contrary to the servants of God, so that, when they experience its adversities, they may be stirred more ardently toward heavenly desire.

3. Great grace shines before God in the person who has been contemptible to this world. For it is truly necessary that the one whom the world hates should be loved by God.

[Note: [Col. 0692D]

4. Paul, Hebrews 11: “Because they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth.” And in 1 Peter: “I beseech you as newcomers and sojourners.” LOAISA.]

4. We read that holy men are strangers and sojourners in this world (Heb. 11:13). Hence Peter is also reproved because he thought of setting up a tent on the mountain (Matt. 17:4), since the saints have no permanent tent in this world; their homeland and house are in heaven.

5. Holy men therefore desire to despise the world and call back the movement of their minds to heavenly things, so that there they may recollect themselves, from where they have flowed away, and withdraw themselves from the place where they have been scattered.

[Col. 0692B] [Note: [Col. 0692D]

6. In this statement Isidore embraces the threefold renunciation which Cassian discusses in *Conference* 3, chapter 6, as I reported above. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Like grass.” An allusion to Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field.” LOAISA.]

6. The righteous, who renounce possessions, honors, and the consolations of life, mortify themselves accordingly with respect to every earthly possession, so that they may live for God. Therefore they trample upon the blandishments of this age, so that, made stronger by the mortification of this life, they may rise toward that life. For all temporal things, like green grasses, wither and pass away. Therefore God’s servant rightly despises these things in favor of eternal realities, which never wither, because he sees no stability in them.

304 7. Whoever, after renouncing the world, longs for the heavenly homeland with holy desires is lifted up and raised above this earthly preoccupation as though on wings. He looks with a groan upon the place where he had fallen and gazes with great joy toward the place to which he has arrived. But whoever, turned back from the repose of contemplation, falls into the cares of this age, immediately groans if he returns to awareness of himself. From the very difficulty of his labor he recognizes how peaceful were the things he lost and how confused are those into which he fell. For what in this life is more laborious than to burn with earthly desires? Or what here is safer than to desire nothing of this world? Those who love this world are disturbed by its turbulent cares and anxieties. But those who hate it and do not follow it, enjoying the tranquility of inner repose, here already begin in some manner to possess the rest of the future peace for which they wait.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Saints Who Separate Themselves from the World’s Fellowship

[Col. 0692D] 1. Holy men, renouncing the world utterly, die to this world in such a way that they take delight in living for God alone. The more they withdraw themselves from the society of this age, the more they contemplate, with the inner vision of the mind, God’s presence and the constant fellowship of the angels.

2. The works of the wicked are so manifestly perverse that those who desire the heavenly homeland flee not only their conduct but also their company. Some even desire to be separated bodily from the wicked, so that they may not become entangled in their crimes. Others, though not departing bodily, nevertheless withdraw spiritually from their way of thinking; though they share their outward society, they are separated from them in heart or conduct. And although God often protects his chosen while they live amid carnal people, it is sufficiently rare for anyone placed among the pleasures of the world to remain undefiled by vices. Even if he is not quickly entangled in them, he is eventually drawn in. For one who has been near danger cannot remain so for long.

3. A way without stumbling: the monk’s life without the hindrance of desire and fear. For when a person is withdrawn from the world’s fellowship, neither desire binds him when he consents, nor does it torture him when he resists.

305 [Note: [Col. 0693D]

CHAPTER XVII, no. 4. Another reading is: “He who is separated from the world both in body and in heart.” This seems more suitable. AREV.]

4. It is good to be physically removed from the world, but it is much better to be removed from it by the will. Both together, however, constitute perfection. Therefore the perfect person is the one who is separated from this world both in body and in heart.

[Note: [Col. 0693D]

5. In Job 39: “He despises,” it says, “the multitude of the city, and he does not hear the cry of the taskmaster.” Gregory interprets this passage in the same way as Isidore, in Book XXX of the *Moralia*, chapter 12, and Cassian, *Conference* 17, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

5. The wild ass, as Job says, despises the city, and the monk despises the common society of worldly citizens. These people desire the adversities of our life and despise its prosperity, so that, while this life is scorned by them, the future life may be found.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Higher Precepts of Monks

[Col. 0693C]

1. One set of precepts is given to the faithful who lead a common life in the world, and another to those who renounce this world. The former are told to manage all that is theirs well; the latter, to abandon all that is theirs well. The former are bound by general precepts; the latter, by living the general precepts more perfectly, transcend them.

[Note: [Col. 0693D]

CHAPTER XVIII, no. 2. Gregory, homily 32 on the Gospel. LOAISA.

Ibid. “To renounce their own wills.” AREV.]

2. To attain perfection, it is not enough to renounce all one’s possessions; each person must also renounce himself. But what is it to renounce oneself except to renounce one’s own pleasures? Let the one who was proud become humble; let the one who was prone to anger strive to become gentle. For if someone renounces everything he possesses but does not renounce his own habits, he is not Christ’s disciple. The one who renounces his possessions renounces what belongs to him; the one who renounces evil habits renounces himself. Hence the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24).

306 ## CHAPTER XIX. On the Monk’s Humility and Work

1. The monk’s highest virtue is humility; his greatest vice is pride. Let each person judge himself to be a monk when he considers himself the least, even after he has performed greater works of virtue.

2. Those who abandon the world yet follow the virtues commanded without humility of heart are like people who fall more heavily from a height, because they are cast down more disastrously by the exaltation of their virtues than they could have slipped through vices.

3. No servant of God should be lifted up by his own merits when he sees that others who were inferior to him can become superior. Every holy person should know that he does not place himself before another person’s holiness. The servant of God’s conscience should always be humble and sorrowful: humble, so that it may not become proud; sorrowful with a useful grief, so that the heart may not dissolve into frivolity.

[Note: [Col. 0693D]

CHAPTER XIX, no. 4. The Vulgate edition, Jeremiah 48: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God deceitfully.” Cassian also reads it in this way in *Conference* 21, on the remission of the fiftieth year, chapter 22. LOAISA.

Ibid. “To have worked.” So the manuscripts, instead of “to have performed.” AREV.]

4. When God’s servant performs some good work, he is uncertain whether what he does will count toward the reward of good, lest perhaps he be judged guilty when the heavenly Judge examines him and it is discovered that he has done something negligently or proudly in matters belonging to God. Therefore, because of this very thing, he becomes sad and sorrowful and is continually troubled, doubtless remembering that it is written: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48:10). For we are truly condemned if, through sluggishness, we do what is good.

[Note: [Col. 0694D]

5. Augustine, *Sermon to the Brothers in the Desert* 17, volume X. LOAISA.]

5. God’s servant ought to read, pray, and work without interruption, lest the spirit of fornication steal upon a mind given over to idleness. Pleasure yields to labor, but it quickly takes possession of an unoccupied mind. Consider Solomon, who through leisure became entangled in many fornications and, through the vice of fornication, fell even into idolatry.

307 ## CHAPTER XX. On the Lukewarmness of Monks

[Note: [Col. 0694D]

CHAPTER XX, no. 1. The Vulgate edition has: “He who adds knowledge adds also labor.” Others nevertheless read “grief,” as our Isidore does, and more correctly. For in Greek it is: Καὶ ὁ προστιθεὶς γνῶσιν, προσθήσει ἄλγημα—“And the one who adds knowledge will add grief.” LOAISA.]

1. Those who pursue the monastic profession without firm resolve, the more carelessly they embrace the purpose of heavenly love, the more readily they are led back to love of the world. For an imperfect profession recalls the desires of the present life. Even if the monk has not yet bound himself to them in action, he already binds himself to them through the love of his thoughts. The mind to which this life is still sweet is far from God. Such a person does not know what to desire among heavenly things or what to flee among earthly things. For as it is written: “Whoever increases knowledge increases grief” (Eccles. 1:18).

[Note: [Col. 0695D]

2. In two manuscripts, the Seguntine and the Toletan, it reads: “Hence the Lord also said to those who are converted on account of this world in order to attain priestly honor: ‘Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep.’” LOAISA.]

2. The more each person is able to know the heavenly things he should desire, the more keenly he ought to grieve over the earthly things to which he clings. For this reason the apostle James also says: “Be miserable, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (James 4:9). Hence the Lord also says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5). And again: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25).

3. Whoever puts forward a religious conversion for the purpose of eventually wishing to preside over others is not a disciple of Christ but a follower of wickedness, because he strives to bear the labor of Christ’s cross not for God but for worldly honor.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Monks Occupied with Worldly Cares

[Col. 0695B]

[Note: [Col. 0695D]

CHAPTER XXI, no. 1. Another reading: “To please both.” AREV.]

1. Those who renounce the world out of fear of God yet become entangled in the cares of household affairs, the more they occupy themselves with the pursuit of such matters, the more they separate themselves from divine love. Those who strive both to obey earthly cares and to engage in divine matters cannot embrace both at once. For two cares cannot exist simultaneously in the human heart, and it is difficult for one who serves two masters to please both.

2. Unless the intrusive multitude of worldly cares is first expelled from the heart’s innermost chambers, the soul lying within will by no means rise again. For while it scatters itself through countless worldly thoughts, it does not gather itself at all for consideration of itself.

[Col. 0695C] 3. The lukewarmness of those people is censured who, wishing to be free for God, renounce the world and scorn their own cares, but, while attending to the interests of their relatives, separate themselves from the love of God.

[Note: [Col. 0695D]

4. Gregory, Book VII of the *Moralia*, chapter 17. LOAISA.

Ibid. Perhaps “the favor of the flesh”; for *praestare* is ordinarily used simply in the sense of “to benefit.” AREV.]

4. A spiritual person ought to benefit his relatives in such a way that, while he strives to extend to them the favor of the flesh, he does not at all deviate from his spiritual purpose. For many monks, through love of their parents, become entangled not only in worldly cares but also in legal disputes, and for the sake of their relatives’ temporal welfare lose their own souls.

[Note: [Col. 0695D]

5. Another reading has “to a parent,” instead of “to a relative,” and “to parents,” instead of “to relatives”; not inappropriately, since *parens* is often taken by writers contemporary with or earlier than Isidore to mean a relative, a kinsman, or an in-law; in Spanish, *pariente*, and in Italian, *parente*. AREV.]

5. Sometimes ordered discernment is required: what is given to a stranger is denied to a relative, so that you may understand that the duty of piety is not prohibited, but the affection of the flesh is denied. What is given to relatives according to the flesh is bestowed upon strangers as an act of piety.

[Col. 0695D] 6. Just as our soul is not to be hated by us, but we ought to hate its carnal affections, so our parents are not to be hated by us; rather, we must hate their impediments, which hinder us from the straight path—provided that the Lord commands us to hate our parents as we hate our own souls.

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

7. Gregory, Book VII of the *Moralia*, chapter 17. LOAISA.]

7. The cows of the Philistines, carrying the ark of God, represented holy men renouncing the world. For just as those cows did not at all turn aside from the straight path because of affection for their calves, so a man who has renounced the world must not, on account of family ties, be hindered from his good purpose.

309 ## CHAPTER XXII. On Those Hindered from God by Love of the World

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

CHAPTER XXII, no. 1. The old edition has: “They fear to lack the pleasures of the world.” AREV.]

1. Many desire to fly toward God’s grace, but they fear being deprived of the world’s pleasures. The love of Christ urges them forward, but worldly desire draws them back. Consequently they forget their vow because they are captured by the allurements of vanity.

[Col. 0696B] [Note: [Col. 0696D]

2. Another reading: “By the storms of the world’s vanities,” and then, “unless you are lifted up by Christ’s cross, he will save.” AREV.]

2. However much your mind may be caught up in the storms of this world, climb upon the wood of the cross, so that you may be freed from the sea—that is, from the storm of this age. For no one will save you from the pit of human death unless Christ rescues you.

3. Whoever has decided to renounce the world is bound by the guilt of transgression if he changes his vow. For those who, after promising in their profession, disdain to fulfill it in practice must be accused severely at the examination of the divine judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

4. This entire statement, previously extremely corrupt in the manuscripts, has been restored through our effort and diligence. LOAISA.]

4. A remarkable comparison is made between a person attempting to return from the pleasures of the world to God while worldly desires hold him back, and someone who tries to rise while drowsy but is weighed down by the sleepiness of slumber. The former knows how to return to the good but is not permitted to do so by the torches of pleasure. The latter chooses better to remain awake but is held by the sluggishness of sleep.

5. Those who have fallen from good into evil become blacker than cold coals, because through the sluggishness of the mind they have been extinguished by the fire of God’s love; deprived, through their desire for the world, of the light of heavenly illumination, they are darkened by the blackness of sins.

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

6. “Cut themselves off.” So the Salmanticensis and Gothic manuscripts. The Toletan has “go beyond.” LOAISA.]

6. Some extinguish their intention to perform good works through fear of poverty and, because of their weakened mind, are not allowed to accomplish what they desire. When they fear lacking what they need in the world, they cut themselves off from heavenly glory.

7. The devil lies in wait for those who had vowed to be content with few and modest things, using many arguments and schemes to persuade them to acquire a great deal. He therefore places before their minds the future poverty of their children and persuades them to possess more, so that they may have enough for themselves and for the needy. In this way he overturns their purpose of good devotion through such blandishments and brings their deceived minds back to earthly profits.

[Note: [Col. 0696D]

8. The Greek *cenodoxia* (κενοδοξία) is “vainglory” in Latin. Cassian frequently uses this word. In Book XI *On the Spirit of Cenodoxia*, he calls it “vainglory,” or “empty glory.” Paul also uses this word in Philippians 2: “Do nothing through contention or through vainglory.” For it is read in Greek as follows: Μηδὲν κατ’ ἐριθείαν, ἢ κενοδοξίαν—“Nothing through selfish ambition or vainglory.” LOAISA.]

8. The devil lies in wait with many schemes for those who renounce the world, so that they may again submit themselves to its love. He strikes most heavily at those whom, after their renunciation, he has brought back to love of the world. Above all, through *cenodoxia*—vainglory—the devil subjects the monk to himself, so that the one whom he could not retain through love of the world he may drag down from the summit of humility and make subject to himself through the swelling of pride.

9. God’s servant must always foresee the snares of the deceiving devil and exercise greater caution in the good works of the heart, lest he lose himself through vainglory and perish, forfeiting all the good things he had obtained by acting rightly.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Self-Display

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

CHAPTER XXIII, no. 1. The Gothic and Toletan manuscripts have: “Self-display must be avoided, yet the ruin by which a person pleases himself more than the Lord and obtains praise from people must be mourned.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Another reading: “He should strive to obtain.” AREV.]

1. Self-display must be avoided in both deeds and words; yet the ruin must be mourned by which a person pleases himself more than God and obtains praise from people.

2. It is vain and full of error to seek reputation and devote one’s efforts to gaining earthly praise. Look closely at yourself, human being, and attribute nothing to yourself except sin. The one who attributes to God, not to himself, the good that he does does not turn to the right; nor does the one who does not presume upon the divine indulgence as permission to sin turn to the left. This is what the Prophet says: “This is the way; walk in it, turning neither to the right nor to the left” (Deut. 17:11).

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

3. Gregory, Book XVI of the *Moralia*, chapter 15. LOAISA.]

3. It is true that nature desires to take delight in praises; but this is right only when each person is praised in God, not in himself [Col. 0697C], as it is written: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Psalm 33:3).

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

4. Augustine, Book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 38. LOAISA.]

4. Often, while despising vainglory, one falls into another kind of exaltation, when someone glories in himself because he despises praise from human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

5. “Tantumdem” [the same amount]. Another reading: “tantum” [only so much]. AREV.]

5. Some are granted to perform an equal measure of good works yet not to possess the fruit of the good work, because they themselves take it away through their pursuit of human self-display.

6. Those who love the applause of vainglory should always look upon their own foulness and grieve that they have lost the good work which they performed for the sake of human ostentation.

[Note: [Col. 0697D]

7. Gregory, Book VIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

7. The lover of vainglory never ceases to act in such a way that he may always be praised, and thereafter a depraved desire continually increases his strength in vanity.

[Note: [Col. 0698D]

8. Thus in the Gothic books and in Gregory, *Moralia* VIII, chapter 35: “Therefore it ought not to become known too quickly among others.” LOAISA.

Ibid. “Coeptio” [beginning]. Another reading: “intentio” [intention]. AREV.]

8. The beginning of a good work ought not quickly to be made public [Col. 0697D] or brought to human attention, lest, when the beginning of the good is disclosed to human eyes, the beginning of holiness become empty of the virtue of perfection [Col. 0698A]. For before the time of maturity, flowering crops quickly perish, and their shoots become useless.

[Note: [Col. 0698D]

9. Gregory, in the same work. LOAISA.]

9. Through the desire for ostentation, the virtues of the saints are subjected to the dominion of unclean demons. Thus King Hezekiah, who ostentatiously revealed his riches to the Chaldeans, heard through the prophet that they would therefore perish. This signified that when God’s servant reveals his virtues through devotion to vainglory, he loses them and immediately makes demons the masters of his works, just as that king, through his ostentation, made the Chaldeans masters of his possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0698D]

10. Gregory, in the same work, chapter 30. LOAISA.]

10. The best discernment is this: our works should be known for the increase of God’s glory and hidden in order to avoid human exaltation. The person who ought to make public the good he does is one established in perfect humility and no longer touched by any exaltation. But whoever understands that he is still being stirred by a love of praise should perform good deeds in secret, lest he lose what he has done.

11. Sometimes holy men, while desiring to correct their own fickleness completely, are touched by the swelling of exaltation when they become conscious of having acted justly; but they are cleansed from the evil of this stealthy intrusion by the remorse of humility.

12. At times holy men instruct those who hear about them, yet they guard themselves with profound vigilance in these matters, lest, while raising others from an earthly preoccupation, they themselves sink into the desire for earthly praise.

13. Some relapse into vices through the incautious display of their virtues [Col. 0698C]; others, while frequently lamenting the impulse of their vices, recover more powerfully from that very weakness through humility.

14. It is often useful for the arrogant to be abandoned by God, so that, becoming conscious of their weakness, they may return to humility and remain humble after their fall.

15. Some imagine themselves perfect through a false opinion born of arrogance, although they are shown not to be so when temptations arise.

16. Each person is nearer to the truth in proportion as he judges himself to be farther from it. For this is humility, which joins a human being to God. Vainglory, however, closes the eyes through which God could have been seen.

17. Just as the ray of the sun, when looked at directly, dulls the sharpness of the eyes, so the person who examines lofty matters without moderation is blunted with respect to the apprehension of truth [Col. 0698D].

[Note: [Col. 0698D]

18. These words are added in two Gothic manuscripts and certain others: “Vainglory closes the eyes through which God could have been seen.” They are found in no printed edition, however, nor in several manuscripts. Nevertheless, they seem to be Gregory’s, *Moralia* XXIV, chapter 28. For he says: “Thus pride is generated in the mind, just as darkness is generated in the eyes.” LOAISA.]

18. Just as an eagle plunges from on high upon its prey, so a human being descends from the height of a good way of life to lower things through carnal desire [Col. 0699A].

# CHAPTER XXIV. On Hypocrisy

[Note: [Col. 0699C]

CHAPTER XXIV, Note 1. This entire chapter is read word for word in the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*. LOAISA.]

1. The hypocrite possesses the words of the saints but not their life. Those whom he has begotten through the speech of his teaching he does not nurture by his example but abandons, because those whom he builds up by his words he destroys by his life and conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0699C]

2. For Latin speakers, *hypocrita* means the same as *simulator* [one who pretends]. Gregory, Book XVIII, chapter 7, on Job 27: “For what is the hope of the hypocrite?” “Hypocrite,” he says, “is called in Latin *simulator*; he does not desire to be just, but to appear so.” Augustine, Book I of *On the Sermon on the Mount*, chapter 3, explains this elegantly and completely: “For hypocrites are pretenders, like performers of other people’s roles, as in theatrical plays.” He calls such a person a “fabricated” or “feigned” person. LOAISA.]

2. Hypocrites are called pretenders: they do not seek to be just, but only desire to appear just. They do evil and profess good. Through ostentation they appear good, but through their actions they are evil.

[Note: [Col. 0699D]

3. From this statement I clearly infer what I have often convinced myself of: these statements were taken not only from Saint Gregory but also from other Fathers, especially Saint Augustine, to whom this entire passage belongs. In the little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* it is written as follows: “All vices can be perpetrated by the simple. Pretence and hypocrisy, however, are committed only by the maliciously clever, who by cunning are able to conceal vices under the appearance of virtues and to display a holiness that is not genuine. The saints not only do not desire glory beyond measure at all, but even avoid appearing to be what they deserve to be,” and so forth. Almost the same things are also said by Gregory, *Moralia* XXVI, chapter 28, where he explains Job 36: “Simulators and the crafty provoke God’s anger.” When he says “simulators,” he appropriately adds “and the crafty,” for unless they are skilled in the art of what they desire to appear, they cannot pretend convincingly. There are some vices that even people of slower understanding easily commit,” and so forth. And at the end: “These things, therefore, scarcely belong to the simple; for if they belong to them, they are no longer simple.” Also, *Moralia* XVIII, chapter 4: “They avoid appearing to be what they are, and before human eyes they clothe themselves in a certain superimposed appearance of innocence.” Hence they are rightly rebuked in the Gospel by the voice of our Redeemer, when he says to them: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you have become like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to people, but within are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear just to people, but inwardly you are full of greed and iniquity.” Thus it is evident that Saint Gregory also received these statements from Saint Augustine, and that our Isidore received them from both. LOAISA.]

3. All vices can be perpetrated by the simple; but pretence and hypocrisy are committed only by the maliciously clever, who through cunning are able to conceal vices under the appearance of virtues and to display a holiness that is not genuine.

4. The saints not only do not desire glory beyond their proper measure at all, but even avoid appearing to be what they have deserved to be. Hypocrites, however, concealing their wickedness before human eyes, clothe themselves in a certain appearance of innocence so that they may be venerated. To them the divine voice says: “Woe to you, hypocrites, because you have become like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly indeed appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead. So you also outwardly appear just to people, but inwardly you are full of greed and iniquity” (Matthew 23:27; Luke 11:44).

[Col. 0699C] 5. Hypocrites are condemned in two ways: either for hidden iniquity or for open pretence [314]. By the former they are condemned because they are wicked; by the latter, because they display what they are not.

6. Hypocrites do not always remain hidden. For although some of them are not exposed at the beginning, before their life ends it is revealed how falsely they have lived. Everything sincere endures; for what is feigned cannot be lasting.

[Col. 0700A] 7. The salvation of those who still have an earthly outlook should not be despaired of, since they can also do in secret what will justify them. They are better than hypocrites because they are evil openly and good secretly. Hypocrites, by contrast, are evil in secret and publicly display themselves as good.

8. A just person is forbidden to rebuke a hypocrite, lest the person rebuked become worse, as Solomon says: “Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you” (Proverbs 9:8).

# CHAPTER XXV. On Envy

[Note: [Col. 0700D]

CHAPTER XXV, Note 1. Gregory, *Moralia* V, chapter 32. LOAISA.

Ibid. Bignaeus notes in the margin: “We have discussed this more fully in our little work which we published *On a Pious Way of Life*, Book III, chapter 7.” AREV.]

1. Envy of another’s good punishes its own author. For from the very thing by which the good person advances, the envious person withers.

[Note: [Col. 0700D]

2. From Gregory, *Moralia* XXIX, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

2. People who live wickedly rejoice over the falls of the good, but they are confounded by their upright deeds and perseverance in goodness (Wisdom 2).

3. The envious person is a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world. So also the proud person is a member of the devil, of whom it is written: “He beholds every lofty thing, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25).

4. There is no virtue that does not have the evil of envy opposing it. Only misery is free from envy, because no one envies the miserable person, against whom envy is not truly directed but only mercy is shown.

5. Many refuse to imitate the good and waste away in the bitterness of envy at the progress of the good. As a result, they are not corrected from their own evil but become worse through envy, attempting, insofar as they can, to corrupt the good from their upright pursuit.

[Col. 0700C] 6. When the good see the wicked prospering, they should not be scandalized; rather, they should think carefully about what end the wicked will have.

7. Every envious person does to the virtues of others what Satan did to blessed Job (Job 1). While he envied Job’s prosperity, he stirred up adversity; but when the devil believed that Job could be overthrown, his merits were thereby increased, and the proofs of his patience thereby shone forth more clearly.

[Col. 0701A] [Note: [Col. 0701D]

8. Gregory, Book VI of the *Moralia*, chapter 13. LOAISA.

Ibid. Another reading: “They saw the walls”; that is, the envious, seeing what was like a wall, did not find the door. AREV.]

8. Thus the envious seek an avenue for evil reputation by which they may stain the life of the good, just as the Sodomites sought a door through which they might enter Lot’s house to harm him. But they, struck by the blindness of error, saw the walls and did not find the door. Likewise, through envy, the envious conceal virtues as though they were a wall, but seek out vices by which they may burn the conscience of the good.

# CHAPTER XXVI. On Pretence

[Note: [Col. 0701D]

CHAPTER XXVI, Note 1. The whole statement alludes to Psalm 10: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.” Augustine reads there, “in the dark moon, at the upright in heart,” and philosophizes about the moon’s light—whether it possesses from itself the fact that one half is luminous and one half dark, just as if one half of a ball were white and the other half black, or whether it is illuminated by the sun. Another passage of the Psalms to which Isidore may seem to have alluded here is Psalm 63: “For they have sharpened their tongues like a sword; they have bent the bow, a bitter thing, to shoot in secret at the blameless.” Augustine has almost the same as Isidore there. LOAISA.]

1. A kind of deceit, like a quiver, subtly conceals the arrows of ambushes, so that it creates a false security and craftily deceives the person against whom it secretly plots.

2. The enemy who is manifest must be guarded against, but still more the one who cannot be seen. For we easily overcome what we see, but what we do not see we drive away from us only with difficulty [Col. 0701B].

3. A person is rarely harmed by outsiders if his own people do not injure him. For we are endangered more by the ambushes of our own people than by those of others.

4. Poisons are often concealed after being coated with the honey of words; and the deceiver pretends goodness for as long as necessary to deceive by his deceit.

# CHAPTER XXVII. On Hatred

[Note: [Col. 0702D]

CHAPTER XXVII, Note 1. “To be held”—that is, it is clear that hatred ought to be directed. Here, as elsewhere, infinitives of this kind, without a governing verb, have been rejected in many copies. For this reason some express the statement as follows: “It is not human beings but their vices that ought to be hated.” See Gratian’s decree, chapter “On Hatred,” where these words are attributed to Saint Gregory. AREV.]

1. It is not the person but the vices that ought to be hated. Those who waste away in hatred of a brother and maintain a destructive ill will against others should, however, be lamented with tears (Psalm 138:21).

2. Those who separate themselves from love thereby separate themselves from the kingdom of God [Col. 0701C].

3. Just as Mother Church is wickedly oppressed by heretical people, yet embraces them with kindly love when they come to her, so each of us must immediately embrace whatever enemies we endure when they return, imitating our mother.

4. Anyone should be forgiven quickly when he asks for pardon.

5. It is not possible for sins to be forgiven the person who does not forgive in himself the debts of those who sin against him. For God has imposed upon us the pattern of forgiveness according to the condition he has established, when he commands us to pray: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). God’s judgment is just, and it shows that as much is forgiven each sinner by God as each person forgives another who has offended him [Col. 0701D].

6. Some, trusting in their own merits, are slow to grant pardon to those who offend against them [Col. 0702A]. But it profits nothing to be free from guilt if one is not prepared to grant forgiveness, since it is rather a great guilt when fraternal offenses are released only slowly.

7. Whoever is slow to reconcile a brother to himself is slow to reconcile God to himself. For in vain does someone seek to have God propitiated toward him if he neglects to be quickly reconciled to his neighbor.

# CHAPTER XXVIII. On Love

1. Two things must be preserved with regard to love of one’s neighbor: first, that one inflict no evil; second, that one provide good [317]. First, one must beware of causing harm; next, one must learn to offer benefit.

2. Friendship is a fellowship of minds. It begins with two people, since love cannot exist among fewer than two [Col. 0702B].

[Note: [Col. 0702D]

CHAPTER XXXVIII, Note 3. Augustine, Book *On Friendship*, chapter 2, volume IV, and Book IV of the *Confessions*, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

3. The ancients said of the fellowship of two people that there is one soul in two bodies, because of the power of love, just as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had one heart and one soul.” This does not mean that many bodies possessed one soul, but that, joined by the bond and fire of charity, they all generally shared one mind without dissension.

4. Friendship makes prosperous circumstances sweeter and, by sharing adversity, moderates and lightens them. When a friend’s consolation is added in tribulation, the spirit is neither broken nor allowed to fall.

5. A friend is loved rightly when he is loved not for himself but for God. Whoever loves a friend for himself embraces him foolishly. The person who loves a mortal human being carnally, more than is fitting, is deeply sunk in earthly things [Col. 0702C]. Whoever loves a friend immoderately loves him more for himself than for God. Therefore, in proportion as the person who loves a brother for God is good, so the person who embraces him for himself is harmful.

[Note: [Col. 0702D]

6. Another reading: “And we love every other such thing.” AREV.]

6. Often a person loves in another what he hates in himself, as in the case of children. We love a certain idleness in them, yet hate it because we do not want to be idle ourselves. So also with stones, horses, and other things: although we love them, we do not wish to be such things ourselves, even if we could.

# CHAPTER XXIX. On Feigned Friendships

1. A deceitful friend is quickly exposed through adversity; in prosperity, however, friendship is uncertain, and it is not known whether the person or the good fortune is being loved.

[Col. 0702D] 2. Often friendship is cultivated through pretence, so that the person who could not deceive openly may deceive fraudulently.

[Col. 0703A] 3. A person becomes more opposed to divine piety and justice when he despises a friend struck by some adversity. In doing so he both removes from himself an opportunity for reward and shows himself cruel toward the affliction of his neighbor, as happened between Lazarus, covered with sores, and the proud rich man. Through adversity and prosperity, therefore, it is proved whether God and one’s neighbor are truly loved; for when adversity comes, the deceitful friend is exposed and immediately despises the person whom he pretended to love.

4. No force excludes a genuine friendship, and no period of time abolishes it. Wherever circumstances may turn, it remains firm.

[Note: [Col. 0703D]

CHAPTER XXIX, Note 5. “Many.” Another reading: “For many.” AREV.]

5. Friends who remain dear to the end are rare. Many are turned away from charity either by the adversity of circumstances or by some dispute in their dealings [Col. 0703B].

6. Often people’s character changes because of honor; and those whom they previously held together in charity they despise as friends after they have reached the summit of honor.

# CHAPTER XXX. On Friendship Arising from a Gift

[Note: [Col. 0703D]

CHAPTER XXX, Note 1. From this arose the celebrated distinction accepted by theologians between love of pure benevolence and love of desire. AREV.]

1. Among true friends, friendship arises from benevolence; among pretended friends, it is joined through a benefit.

2. Those whom a gift, rather than affection, brings together are not faithful in friendship. They quickly abandon the relationship unless they are continually receiving something. For love cemented by a gift dissolves when the gift is suspended. True friendship is that which seeks nothing from a friend’s possessions except benevolence alone—that is, to love the one who loves freely.

[Col. 0703C] 3. Often friendship arises from necessity or want, so that a person may have someone through whom he can obtain what he desires. But the person seeks it genuinely who desires friendship while needing nothing. Friendship arising from poverty is brief and counterfeit; friendship itself is pure and enduring.

# CHAPTER XXXI. On the Concord of the Wicked

1. Friendship should be maintained only in good matters; for those who use it in evil are not friends to one another but enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0703D]

CHAPTER XXXI, Note 2. Acts 23; Exodus 14. LOAISA.]

2. The concord of the wicked is contrary to that of the good. Just as it is desirable that the good should have peace among themselves, so it is desirable that the wicked should be at odds with one another. The apostle Paul demonstrates that the unity of the wicked is contrary to the good: he divided the wicked against one another when he saw that they had agreed upon his death (Acts 23:7). Hence, in the Law, the Red Sea—that is, the concord of wicked people—is divided so that the road of the elect leading toward blessedness may not be obstructed. The journey of the good is obstructed if the sea—that is, the unity of the wicked—is not divided (Exodus 14:21).

# CHAPTER XXXII. On Fraternal Correction

[Col. 0704A]

1. A person who is still subject to the contagion of vices ought not to correct the vices of another. For it is disgraceful to rebuke someone else for what one still reproves in oneself.

[Note: [Col. 0703D]

CHAPTER XXXII, Note 2. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, chapter 8. LOAISA.]

2. Whoever truly wishes to correct a brother and heal his weakness should strive to make himself useful to his brother in such a way that, with a humble heart, he admonishes the person whom he wishes to correct, doing so out of compassion, as though the danger were shared, lest he too should be subjected to temptation.

[Note: [Col. 0704D]

3. “Declinant” [they turn away]. Another reading: “inclinant” [they incline]. AREV.]

3. Just as spiritual men await the correction of another’s sin, so the insolent mock and insult those who are committing offenses and, insofar as they can, consider them incurable. They do not turn their hearts toward the mercy of compassion, but in their pride detest and blaspheme them.

4. Sometimes it happens that a disagreement nourished by some rebuke among friends later gives birth to greater charity—for example, when those things which seem displeasing in a friend are corrected. At first the person admonished receives this not without a certain rivalry, but afterward, once corrected, he gives thanks. On the other hand, many sever the force of charity over a small injury and withdraw themselves permanently from the love of affection [320].

[Note: [Col. 0704D]

5. Gregory, Book X of the *Moralia*, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

5. Many consider correction a duty of charity. Many others, however, turn the very fact that they are corrected out of charity into an insult and an injury [Col. 0704C]. Consequently, they become worse through the very means by which they could have been corrected through obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0704D]

6. Gregory, Book I on Ezekiel, homily 7. LOAISA.]

6. The just receive correction beneficially whenever they are reproved for their offenses. But the humility of those who accuse themselves of acts they did not commit is excessive and useless. Whoever declares his good deeds without arrogance certainly does not sin.

7. Some wicked people make this their perverse defense: when they are reproved for their crimes, they reject the words of the just as a judgment to be avoided, committing themselves to divine judgment, by which they will be punished more severely because they scorn, in this temporal life, to be judged by human beings.

8. Truth is burdensome to the wicked, and the discipline of justice is bitter to them. They take pleasure only in what flatters their weakness: fertile in injustice and barren toward truth; blind when it comes to looking upon the light, yet sharp-sighted in observing the error of darkness [Col. 0704D].

[Note: [Col. 0704D]

9. Another reading: “to consent to evil … to consent to good.” AREV.]

9. The hearts of the reprobate are slippery and yielding when it comes to consenting to evil, but exceedingly hard when it comes to consenting to good.

[Note: [Col. 0704D]

10. Gregory, *Moralia* X, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

10. Solomon proves both the correction of the just person who is corrected and the obstinacy of the fool who is admonished, saying: “Teach the just person, and he will hasten to receive it.” Of the fool he says: “Whoever instructs a scoffer does himself an injury” (Proverbs 9:7, 9) [Col. 0705A].

[Note: [Col. 0705C]

11. The Vulgate Edition has: “For he who turns good things into evil lies in wait, and in the chosen he places a stain.” This is a passage from Sirach 11. LOAISA.

Ibid. “Detrectare” [to disparage]. Another reading: “detrahere famae” [to detract from someone’s reputation]. AREV.]

11. There are some people of such depravity that, while they neglect to be corrected from evil themselves, they disparage the life of those who correct them through false accusation. As a consolation for their own wickedness, they seize upon anything they may discover—even falsely—that they can bring forward to defame the good, as in Solomon’s statement: “The wicked turns good into evil and places a stain upon the chosen” (Sirach 11:34). Woe to the person who refuses to correct his own life and does not cease to disparage the good [321].

12. Many wicked people defend those like themselves in evil and, through their patronage, take up the cause of the perverse against the correction of the good, lest they amend what makes them displeasing. In this way they add the offenses of others to their own, so that they may be punished not only for their own evils but also for the crimes of those whose sins they defend.

# CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Rulers of the Church

[Note: [Col. 0705C]

CHAPTER XXXIII, Note 1. Gregory, Part II of the *Pastoral Care*, chapters 5 and 6, and Book V of the *Moralia*, chapter 2. LOAISA.

[Col. 0705D] Ibid. “The ecclesiastical man,” and so forth. From this chapter a sermon in praise of Saint Aemilianus, attributed to Isidore, has been composed; see *Isidoriana*, chapter 72, sections 3 and following. Regarding the words “though unwilling,” Vezzosius notes that, according to the Church’s consistent teaching, the meaning is this. AREV.]

1. An ecclesiastical man ought both to be crucified to the world through the mortification of his own flesh and, if the administration of ecclesiastical office comes from God’s will, to accept humbly, though unwillingly, the governance of that office.

[Note: [Col. 0705D]

2. This perhaps alludes to Augustine’s letter 81 to Eudoxia, concerning those who, seduced by the charm of idleness, reject the governance of the Church: “Do not,” he says, “place your leisure above the needs of the Church.” He says the same against Faustus, Book XXXII, chapter 10: “Whoever, chosen by the Church, refuses the ministry of preaching the Gospel is rightly and deservedly despised by the Church.” Gregory says the same in Book VI of the *Letters*, in a letter to Bishop Cyriacus: “If one who is able refuses to feed the sheep of almighty God, he shows that he does not love the supreme Shepherd at all.” See also Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, Part I, chapter 5, concerning those who can benefit others by the example of their virtues from the summit of governance but refuse this while pursuing their own quiet [Col. 0706C]. LOAISA.]

2. Satan ensnares by many deceits those who, outstanding in the usefulness of their life and understanding, do not wish to preside over others and benefit them. When governance of souls is imposed upon them, they refuse it, judging it more prudent to lead an idle life than to devote themselves to winning souls. Yet they do this in deception, through the argument of the devil, who misleads them under the appearance of good, so that, by withdrawing them from pastoral office, he prevents those from benefiting who could have been instructed by their words and examples [Col. 0705C].

[Note: [Col. 0706C]

3. Gregory, *Moralia* V, chapter 3. LOAISA.]

3. Holy men do not seek the cares of secular occupations, but they lament those imposed upon them by a hidden ordering. Although they flee these cares through a better intention, they nevertheless bear them through a submissive mind [322]. Whenever possible, they hasten with the greatest eagerness to avoid them; but, fearing God’s hidden dispensation, they accept what they flee and perform what they know they ought to avoid [Col. 0706A]. For they enter into their hearts and there consider what God’s hidden will desires. Recognizing that they must be subject to the highest ordinances, they bow the neck of their hearts beneath the yoke of divine dispensation.

# CHAPTER XXXIV. On Unworthy Rulers

[Note: [Col. 0706C]

CHAPTER XXXIV, Note 1. Gregory interprets 1 Chronicles 17 in this way in his exposition of the fourth penitential Psalm, on the words: “Then you will accept the sacrifice.” LOAISA.]

1. Those who are still subject to vices should not be promoted to govern the Church. Hence David was commanded not to build the visible temple, because he was a man of war and had shed much blood. By this figure those who are still devoted to the corruption of vices are spiritually warned not to build the temple—that is, not to presume to teach the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0706C]

2. The Old Edition adds the following statement after “serve”: [Col. 0706D] “Whoever does not consider himself worthy of the episcopate should not seize in advance the place of one who is worthy. For the name of the priesthood is so holy that it does not permit itself to be stained by any mark of vice. The person who unworthily assumes what he does not deserve will be condemned more severely.” The older manuscript of Saint Mark of Florence immediately adds after “serve”: “For the name of the priesthood is so holy,” and so forth. But Vezzosius’s assertion that Loaisa admits this statement to be absent from all manuscript copies is not found in Grialius’s edition. AREV.]

2. A person who does not know how to lead his subjects along the path of a better life ought not to assume the leadership of an office. No one is appointed for this purpose alone: to correct the faults of his subjects while serving vices himself [Col. 0706B].

[Note: [Col. 0706D]

3. It could be read: “to that to which he is called.” It is easy for copyists to have omitted the second “ad” [to]. AREV.]

3. Whoever eagerly seeks the governance of the priesthood should first examine himself to see whether his life is suited to the honor; and if it is not incompatible with it, he should humbly approach that to which he is called. For a person doubles the guilt of his offense if he aspires to the priestly summit while burdened with guilt. Alas, wretched me, bound by inexplicable knots! If I retain the governance of ecclesiastical office after accepting it, I am shaken by fear as one conscious of guilt; but if I abandon it, I am even more afraid that it is a worse fault to leave the flock entrusted to me. Miserable, I fear on every side, and in so great a crisis I do not know which course to follow.

323 4. Each person’s fall is a greater crime in proportion to the greater virtue he possessed before falling [Col. 0706C]. For the greatness of his preceding virtues increases the accumulation of his subsequent offenses.

[Note: [Col. 0706D]

5. Vezzosius appended this note to the statement: “Would that the things Isidore wrote here were not true, nor applicable to our own age. In Grialius’s edition it incorrectly read *qua gregis* [by which of the flock] instead of *quam gregis* [than of the flock].” AREV.]

5. Most priests desire to preside for the sake of their own advantage rather than that of the flock. They do not wish to become leaders in order to benefit others, but rather to become rich and honored. They assume the summit of rank not for pastoral governance but solely out of ambition for honor; rejecting the work of their dignity, they seek only the dignity of the title [Col. 0707A].

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

6. Gregory, Part I of the *Pastoral Care*, chapter 1; Hosea 8. LOAISA.]

6. Although evil priests do not come into being without God’s knowledge, they are nevertheless said to be unknown to God, as he himself testifies through the prophet: “They have set up princes, but I did not know” (Hosea 8:4). But this “not knowing” of God means his rejection, for God knows everything.

# CHAPTER XXXV. On Unlearned Rulers

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

CHAPTER XXXV, Note 1. Gregory, Part I of the *Pastoral Care*, chapter 1. LOAISA.

Ibid. Perhaps it should read “who themselves,” instead of “which they themselves.” AREV.]
