1. Just as the wicked and sinful are prohibited from attaining the priestly ministry, so the unlearned and inexperienced are held back from such an office. The former corrupt the life of the good by their examples; the latter, through their indolence, do not know how to correct the wicked. What could they teach that they themselves had not learned? Let the person who does not know how to teach cease to assume the place of teacher. The ignorance of rulers is incompatible with the life of their subjects. For if the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit (Matthew 15:14) [Col. 0707B].

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

2. “They did not know.” Thus the Vulgate. Others read “they did not know” in the imperfect, or “they will not know.” AREV.]

2. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord condemns unlearned priests as follows: “They themselves,” he says, “the shepherds, have not understood.” And again: “All the watchmen are blind”—that is, inexperienced bishops—“they did not know,” he says, “all of them; mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10 and following). This means that they are unable, through the word of teaching, to defend the flocks entrusted to them by resisting evils [324].

# CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Teaching and Examples of Rulers

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

CHAPTER XXXVI, Note 1. “A saying worthy of cedar,” says Vezzosius. AREV.]

1. An ecclesiastical teacher ought to be distinguished both in teaching and in life. For teaching without life makes a person arrogant, while life without teaching makes him useless.

[Col. 0707C] 2. A priest’s preaching must be confirmed by his works, so that what he teaches in words he may teach by example. True is the teaching which is followed by a manner of life. For nothing is more shameful than for someone to neglect to fulfill in action the good which he proclaims in speech. Preaching is then delivered beneficially when it is fulfilled effectively.

3. Every teacher ought to devote himself both to good action and to good preaching, for one without the other does not make him perfect. The just person should first act well, so that afterward he may be able to teach well.

[Note: [Col. 0707D]

4. Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, chapter 7; 2 Timothy 4. LOAISA.

Ibid. Another reading: “but toward good action and the authority of life.” AREV.]

4. Every useful teacher ought to conduct himself before the peoples subject to him and devote himself to teaching in such a way that, in proportion as he shines in word, he may also shine in merit [Col. 0707D]. For when the Apostle commands Timothy to teach with all authority (2 Timothy 4), he is not urging the swelling of pride but the authority of a good life—namely, lest Timothy lose the freedom to preach if he taught well but lived badly [Col. 0708A]. Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19). You see that the person who does not do what he teaches lacks the authority of a teacher.

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

5. These words seem to derive from Cassian, *Conferences* I, chapter 20, concerning the trustworthy money-changer. LOAISA.]

5. Just as metal, shape, and weight are examined in a coin, so in every ecclesiastical teacher one must examine what he follows, what he teaches, and how he lives. The quality of the metal signifies teaching; the shape signifies the likeness of the Fathers; the weight signifies humility. Whoever differs from these three will be not metal but earth.

# CHAPTER XXXVII. On Those Who Teach Well but Live Badly

1. Sometimes, because of the teacher’s fault, even true teaching itself becomes worthless; and the person who does not live as he teaches makes the truth he preaches contemptible [Col. 0708B].

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

CHAPTER XXXVII, Note 2. He explains Psalm 77: “They turned back like a crooked bow.” Gregory has this in *Moralia* XXVII, chapter 27: “perverse.” Isidore therefore received both the meaning and the words of this statement from him. LOAISA.

Ibid. This interpretation of the crooked bow seems different from another, explained in Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 19. See the notes. AREV.]

2. The tongue of teachers who teach well and live badly is a crooked bow (Psalm 77:57). Therefore, as though shooting from a crooked bow, they send forth an arrow while piercing their own depraved life with the blow of their own tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

3. Gregory, in the same work, chapter 20. LOAISA.]

3. Those who preach divine things but take little care to live according to the dignity of that preaching—having the word of God in their mouths but not in their works, teaching many good things but doing nothing—imitate Balaam the diviner, who, though he fell in his conduct, had open eyes to behold the light of teaching (Numbers 24:10).

4. Whoever teaches well but lives badly makes a sound for others like bronze or a cymbal, yet remains senseless to himself [Col. 0708C].

5. Whoever teaches well but lives badly: what he teaches well benefits those who live well; but the fact that he lives badly kills himself. Thus, if a priest conducts himself worthily, as befits a priest, his ministry is useful both to himself and to others; but if he lives unworthily, he is useful to others by his speech, while he kills himself by living perversely. Consequently, what is dead in him belongs to him personally; whereas what lives in him—that is, the sacred ministry, which is a source of life—is not his own.

[Note: [Col. 0708D]

6. This is how it stands in most manuscripts. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others read: “and lives badly, he is like a candle, which indeed provides good light, but seems to consume and extinguish itself in its evils.” AREV.]

6. Whoever teaches well but lives badly is like a candle: while explaining what is good, he appears to provide light for others, but he consumes and extinguishes himself in his evils.

7. Whoever teaches well but lives badly appears to join good to evil, to mix light with darkness, and to exchange truth for falsehood.

326 CHAPTER XXXVIII. On examples of wicked priests.

[Col. 0709A]

1. Often the disease of sin creeps in through those by whom righteousness is taught, and death passes over to the peoples—either because they teach evil things or because they do evil things.

2. Many priests and clerics who live wickedly become an example of evil to others, although they ought to have been an example in good things. Without doubt they will have to give an account of all whom they destroy by the example of their evil conduct.

3. The life of subjects generally becomes worse through the example of carnal superiors; and, deservedly by the people, such priests are appointed as destroy the people by a worse example rather than build them up. For bishops are sometimes corrupted because of the people’s merits, so that those who follow may fall more readily.

4. When the head is diseased, the remaining members of the body are infected. Hence it is written: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot even to the crown there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I, 5–6). The sick head is the teacher who commits sin; his evil reaches the body when, whether by sinning or by teaching perversely, the pestilential disease is transferred to the peoples subject to him.

[Note: [Col. 0709D]

CHAP. XXXVIII, no. 5. The passage was corrupted in the printed editions: “without doctrine, without examples.” We have emended it on the authority of the manuscripts. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others read: “they rob us ourselves, since the riches of the righteous are their morals.” AREV.]

5. Those who corrupt the life and morals of good people, whether by doctrine or by example, are worse than those who seize the possessions and estates of others. The latter take away things that are outside us, though nevertheless ours; but corrupters of morals deceive us personally, [Col. 0709C] since people’s riches are their morals. Thus damage to morals differs greatly from damage to temporal goods: the latter are outside us, whereas morals are within us.

CHAPTER XXXIX. On carnal superiors.

[Note: [Col. 0709D]

CHAP. XXXIX, no. 1. This sentence is not easily understood unless one reads Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXV, chapter 16, from which it was taken and reduced to a summary. LOAISA.]

1. By the providence of the divine counsel, superiors who pursue worldly and external matters are often appointed, so that, while they devote themselves entirely to temporal affairs, spiritual persons may practice the contemplative life more securely, since the burdens of episcopal cares are difficult for those who wish to live in quiet. God often provides that those devoted to secular cares assume the burden of government, so that, while these attend to external matters without weariness, spiritual persons may serve interior concerns without the hindrance of earthly affairs.

[Col. 0709D] [Note: [Col. 0709D]

2. Others read *ordinationem* (“ordination”) instead of *ordinem* (“order”). AREV.]

2. Those who condemn bishops because they pursue spiritual matters less and earthly matters more are therefore accusing God’s order, by which they are appointed. For, by the arrangement of the divine tabernacle, bishops devoted to secular cares are appointed to endure the injuries of the world and certain storms, so that those who inwardly desire heavenly things may pursue what they love more freely, with no earthly business standing in the way (Exod. XXVI).

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

3. Gregory, in the passage cited above, chapter 14. LOAISA.]

3. An irregular ruler should not therefore be judged by the people, since the peoples ought rather to know that it was because of their own merits that they received a perverse pontiff as ruler. For God orders the life of rulers according to the merits of peoples, as in the example of David’s sin (II Sam. XXIV), in comparison with rulers who transgress because of the people’s merit.

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

4. Gregory, in the passage cited above, chapter 16. LOAISA.]

4. The sons of Noah, Ham, are condemned by the sentence of Scripture because they publicly expose the faults of their superiors; so Ham did not cover his father’s nakedness, but displayed it for ridicule (Gen. IX, 22). They will have the merit of Shem and Japheth, who reverently cover what they know their fathers have done wrong, provided that they do not love their fathers’ deeds, but merely cover them and do not imitate them. For there are people who judge their superiors perversely when they see them devoted more to earthly pursuits, although they themselves have scarcely given any thought to spiritual things.

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

5. Gregory, in the passage cited above, chapter 14. LOAISA.]

5. Rulers are therefore to be judged by God, but are by no means to be judged by their own subjects. This is exemplified by the Lord, who himself overturned with his own whip the tables of the money-changers and those selling doves, and drove them from the temple (Matt. XXI, 12); or also, as the Psalmist says: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst, however, he distinguishes among the gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

6. Gregory, in the passage cited above. LOAISA.]

6. But if a ruler has departed from the faith, then he is to be reproved by his subjects; whereas for morally reprehensible conduct he is rather to be tolerated, and the people should be more strictly restrained from judging him.

328 CHAPTER XL. On irascible teachers.

[Col. 0710C]

[Note: [Col. 0710D]

CHAP. XL, no. 1. *Crudelitatis* (“of cruelty”). Grialius’s edition, together with others, mistakenly has *credulitatis* (“of credulity”). AREV.]

1. Irascible teachers turn the discipline of correction, through the frenzy of anger, into savage cruelty; and by the very means through which they could correct their subjects, they instead wound them.

2. An irascible superior avenges faults without measure because his heart, dispersed among worldly cares, is not gathered into the love of the one God. For my mind, loosened from the chain of charity among various concerns, is not bound together; rather, being wrongly slackened, it is wrongly moved by every occasion.

CHAPTER XLI. On proud teachers.

[Col. 0710D] [Note: [Col. 0710D]

CHAP. XLI, no. 1. Gregory, XXIV, chapters 19, 21, and 22. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others read: “A good teacher and ruler is also one who is humble.” AREV.]

1. A good teacher is also a ruler who preserves discipline in humility and, through discipline, does not fall into pride.

2. Arrogant shepherds oppress their peoples tyrannically; they do not govern them. They demand from their subjects the glory not of God but of themselves.

[Col. 0711A] 3. There are many who are not humble but arrogant in their teaching, and who announce even the very truths they preach not out of zeal for correction but through the fault of self-exaltation.

4. There are many who teach not deliberately for the sake of building others up, but out of swelling pride; they are not wise in order to benefit others, but strive to teach so that they may appear wise.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

5. “They wish to appear,” etc. Vezzosius notes that this is a truly golden passage. AREV.]

5. There is a perverse imitation among arrogant priests by which they imitate the saints in the strictness of discipline but neglect to follow them in the affection of charity. They wish to appear rigid in severity, yet cannot display the form of humility, so that they may be seen as more terrifying than gentle.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

6. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIV, chapter 9; Proverbs XIV. LOAISA.]

6. Proud teachers know how to wound rather than correct, as Solomon testifies: “In the mouth of the fool is the rod of pride” (Prov. XIV, 3), because they strike harshly when reproving and do not know how to show compassion with humility.

7. A person rightly undertakes to cure another’s sin when he does so out of love of heart and humble awareness. But whoever rebukes an offender with a proud or hostile spirit does not correct him; he strikes him. Whatever a haughty or angry spirit utters is the fury of one who rebukes, not the love of one who corrects.

CHAPTER XLII. On the humility of superiors.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

CHAP. XLII, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVI, chapter 19, and *Pastoral Care*, part II, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

1. Whoever is placed in charge of government must conduct himself toward the discipline of his subjects in such a way that he shines not only through authority but also through humility. Yet his virtue of humility must not dissolve the life of his subjects into vices; and his authority of power must be present in such a way that the severity of immoderation does not arise from swelling of heart. This is true discernment among God’s priests: they are neither proud through freedom nor lax through humility. Hence the saints, with great firmness, rebuked even the faults of rulers. Although they possessed the greatest humility, they nevertheless freely reproved transgressors of justice when necessity required.

2. Sometimes we ought also to be humbler in spirit than our subjects, since their deeds are judged by us, whereas God judges ours.

3. Let a bishop recognize that he is the servant of the people, not their master; yet charity, not legal status, requires this.

CHAPTER XLIII. On discernment in teaching.

[Col. 0711D]

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

CHAP. XLIII, no. 1. Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, in the prologue. LOAISA.]

1. One and the same teaching is not to be applied to everyone; rather, the teachers’ exhortation must vary according to the character of their morals. For harsh rebuke corrects some, while gentle exhortation corrects others.

2. Just as skilled physicians treat different bodily illnesses with different medicines, so that the remedy varies according to the variety of wounds, so the teacher of the Church will apply an appropriate remedy of doctrine to each person and will announce what is suitable to each according to age, sex, and calling.

3. Not everything that is hidden is to be disclosed to everyone. For there are many who cannot comprehend such things; if they are revealed to them indiscriminately, they immediately either disparage them or neglect them.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

4. Others read: “as their faults and morals require them to be taught.” AREV.]

4. The first virtue of prudence is to assess the person whom one ought to teach. To uneducated or carnal peoples one should preach plain and common things, not lofty and difficult ones, lest they be overwhelmed rather than instructed by the magnitude of the teaching. Hence the apostle Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as little ones in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III, 1–2). To carnal minds one should preach neither matters too lofty concerning heavenly things nor earthly things, but should teach them moderately, as their beginnings and their morals require.

[Note: [Col. 0711D]

5. Aristotle, book VI of *The History of Animals*, chapter 5, and Gregory, book XXX of the *Moralia*, chapter 8, where he explains Job XXXV: “Who prepares food for the raven when its young cry out to God, crying as they wander because they have no food?” And also Psalm CXLVI: “Who gives food to their beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.” They affirm that ravens are nourished by divine providence, since, being abnormal and degenerate, they are neglected by their parents because of their whitish feathers. They further relate that they are sustained by the food of flies, which, in God’s provident kindness, thrust themselves into the mouths of the crying young. Chrysostom, Euthymius, and others say the same. LOAISA.

Ibid. “The raven,” etc. See the note on Dracontius, book I, 721. AREV.]

5. When the raven sees that its young are white, it feeds them with no food at all, but merely watches them until they become black with their father’s color; then it restores them with frequent feeding. So the diligent teacher of the Church, unless he sees those whom he teaches becoming black in his likeness through confession of repentance and, having laid aside worldly brightness, putting on the garment of mourning in remembrance of sin, does not open to them the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding while they are still attached to external—that is, carnal—things, lest, unable to comprehend what they hear, they begin to despise the heavenly commandments before they begin to venerate them.

6. One must act differently toward those entrusted to our government when they offend, and differently toward those who have not been entrusted to us. [331] If the latter are righteous, they are to be honored; but if they offend, they are to be corrected, as charity requires and circumstances permit, though not with the severity applied to those entrusted to us for governance.

[Note: [Col. 0712D]

7. Gregory, in the same place; II Timothy II. LOAISA.

Ibid. *Commenda* (“commend”). Another copy has *commendo* (“I commend”). AREV.]

7. The elders of the people should first be taught, so that those beneath them may be taught more easily through them. Hence the Apostle says: “Commend these things to faithful people who are capable of teaching others also” (II Tim. II, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0712D]

8. Gregory, part III of *Pastoral Care*, admonition 18. LOAISA.

[Col. 0713D] Ibid. *Incipientis* (“of one beginning”). Another copy has *incipere* (“to begin”). Vezzosius says that this is a most salutary lesson for those who preside over others. AREV.]

8. It is the mark of a good teacher to begin with praise of those whom he wishes to correct by salutary rebuke, as the Apostle does with the Corinthians: he begins with praise and then tests them with reproofs. Yet there were among the Corinthians people worthy both of praise and of rebuke. The person who speaks indiscreetly is the one who addresses both in the same way to everyone, so that both appear appropriate to everyone.

CHAPTER XLIV. On the silence of teachers.

[Note: [Col. 0713D]

CHAP. XLIV, no. 1. Most manuscripts correctly read this way. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXX, chapter 18. From there this sentence is taken: “Often the word is granted because of the hearer’s merit, and often speech is withdrawn from the teacher because of the hearer’s fault.” LOAISA.]

1. Because of the people’s bad merit, the teaching of preaching is taken away. Because of the hearer’s good merit, speech is granted to the teacher.

[Note: [Col. 0713D]

2. “For useful things,” etc. Thus the Gothic books. Other manuscripts read: “Let it be granted according to the merit of the hearers’ usefulness.” One manuscript of Salamanca has: “For the usefulness of the hearer.” LOAISA.]

2. It lies in God’s power to give or take away the word of teaching from whomever he wishes; and this happens either because of the merit of the speaker or because of that of the hearer. Thus at one time the teacher’s speech is taken away because of the people’s fault, and at another it is granted because of their useful merits. For the good person teaches what is good, the bad person what is bad, the good person what is bad, and the bad person what is good; yet this occurs according to the merit of the peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0713D]

3. Gregory, in the same place; Ecclesiastes III. LOAISA.

Ibid. *Incorrectibilem* (“incorrigible”). So the Gothic books. Others have *incorrigibilem* (“incorrigible”). LOAISA.]

3. Not all times are suitable for teaching, according to Solomon’s saying: “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Eccles. III, 7). Not indeed through fear, but through discernment, the elect must sometimes refrain from teaching because of the incorrigible wickedness of evil people.

332 4. At times the teachers of the Church, burning with the warmth of charity, fall silent from teaching because there is no one to listen, as the prophet testifies: “The cities of the South have been shut, and there is no one to open them” (Jer. XIII, 19).

5. Whoever has received the office of teaching should sometimes remain silent for a time about his neighbor’s deeds, when he does not at once consider them capable of correction. For if he can correct them and pretends not to notice, it is true that he shares in another’s error.

6. Many holy teachers, because of the stubbornness of evil people whom they cannot correct, decide to remain silent toward them; but, unable to endure the heat of the spirit by which they are driven, they again burst forth into rebuking the wicked.

CHAPTER XLV. On the protection priests must provide among the people.

[Note: [Col. 0714D]

CHAP. XLV, no. 1. From Gregory’s letter to John of Constantinople, indiction 9; Isaiah XL. See Gregory, *On Ezekiel*, homily 11. LOAISA.]

1. Those entrusted with the form of teaching incur great danger if they are unwilling to resist those who oppose the truth. The prophet instructs the teacher of the Church to attain the highest degree of righteousness when he says: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” [Col. 0713D] (Isa. XL, 9)—that is, let him rise above others in merit just as he does in rank. Then, lest fear restrain him from teaching, let him hear: “Raise your voice with strength, and do not fear.” Hence the Lord also says to Jeremiah: “Gird your loins and arise; speak to them. Do not be afraid before them, for I will not make you fear their face” (Jer. I, 17). From this it is clear that even not fearing is a gift of God.

[Note: [Col. 0714D]

2. Others read: “he who fears to speak is punished by a graver sentence of guilt.” Another copy has: “of grave guilt.” Shortly afterward: “they conceal, and are held guilty, those who turn away from the good work.” AREV.]

2. Whoever shows partiality to a powerful person and is afraid to speak the truth is punished by a grave sentence of guilt. Many priests conceal the truth through fear of power and are turned away from good work or from preaching justice by fear of some danger or by a power that terrifies them. But alas, sadly, they fear for this reason: either they are entangled by love of worldly things, or they are ashamed because of some criminal deed.

[Note: [Col. 0714D]

3. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIX, chapter 6, and part II of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 4. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others read: “lest they lose the friendship of worldly people.” And shortly afterward: “not fearing that they will have to give an account concerning the truth because of the fact that.” AREV.]

3. Many bishops of the churches, fearing that they may lose friendship and incur the burden of hatred, do not rebuke sinners and are afraid to correct oppressors of the poor. They do not fear the severity of the account they must render because they remain silent about the peoples entrusted to them.

4. When the poor are oppressed by the powerful, good priests bring them the aid of protection to rescue them. They do not fear anyone’s hostility, but openly accuse and rebuke the oppressors of the poor and excommunicate them. They fear their plots to do harm less, even when those plots may succeed, for “the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John X, 11).

5. Just as a watchful shepherd customarily guards sheep against beasts, so God’s priest must be solicitous over Christ’s flock, lest the enemy ravage it, lest the persecutor harass it, and lest the greed of any powerful person disturb the lives of the poor. But wicked shepherds do not care for the sheep; rather, as is read in the Gospel concerning hired servants, they see the wolf coming and flee. They flee when they remain silent before the powerful and fear to resist evil. If they remain silent about such people, they will be condemned for their wickedness.

CHAPTER XLVI. On the discipline of priests toward those who offend.

[Note: [Col. 0714D]

CHAP. XLVI, no. 1. Ezekiel III, and Gregory there, homily 11, and part II of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 6. LOAISA.]

1. Priests are condemned for the people’s wickedness if they either fail to instruct the ignorant or fail to rebuke sinners, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, he will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand” [Col. 0714D] (Ezek. III, 17). Thus the priest Eli was condemned for the wickedness of his sons. Although he admonished them when they offended, he did not rebuke them as he ought to have done (I Sam. II).

[Note: [Col. 0715D]

2. Thus the Gothic, Salamanca, and other better manuscripts read; the reading is supported by the Hebrew truth of Scripture and by the edition of the Septuagint translators. Nevertheless, the Gothic manuscript of Toledo has *robustum*. LOAISA.

Ibid. Others, with the Vulgate, have “the strong one,” “and you will know,” and “you will test their way.” AREV.]

2. Priests ought to investigate the sins of the peoples and test each person with careful diligence, according to the Lord’s testimony addressed to Jeremiah: “I have appointed you as a tester among my strong people, so that you may know how to test their ways” (Jer. VI, 27).

3. Priests ought to scrutinize the deeds of their subjects with the zeal of correction, so that they may win them after they have been reformed. But just as it is appropriate to rebuke the sinner, so it is inappropriate to exasperate the righteous.

4. Priests ought to care for those who are perishing, so that by their rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

[Col. 0715B] 5. Those who deceive sinners are severely rebuked: they not only fail to rebuke them for their sin, but also deceive them through flattery, as the prophet says: “Those who bless this people will be deceiving them, and those who are blessed will be overthrown” (Isa. IX, 16).

6. Again, those who do not receive the sinner but despise and reject him are severely rebuked, since they do not mourn another’s offense as their own. Concerning such people the Lord threatens through Isaiah: “Those who say, ‘Depart from me; do not come near me, for you are unclean’—these shall be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day” (Isa. LXV, 5). Hence the Apostle became all things to all people (I Cor. IX, 22), not by imitating error, but by compassionate mercy: that is, he wept over the vices of others as though he himself were involved in such an error.

[Note: [Col. 0715D]

7. Others read: “not by accusation of what was committed.” AREV.]

7. Good shepherds ought to mourn the offenses of the people and devote themselves entirely to lamentation, imitating the prophet Jeremiah, who says: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the slain of my people?” (Jer. IX, 1). The priest ought therefore to weep over the sins of the people as over his own sins, but with the feeling of compassion, not because he himself committed them.

8. Some bishops of the flock expel certain people from communion because of sin, so that they may repent, but do not visit them with exhortation toward a better way of life, showing them in what condition they ought to live. To them divine speech fittingly issues this rebuking threat: “Shepherds who feed my people, you have scattered my flock, driven them out, and not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your pursuits” (Jer. XXIII, 2).

9. The diligence of good priests investigates even the smallest deeds of the people with great care, so that, by showing themselves most severe in the smallest sins of their subjects, they may make themselves and their subjects cautious and vigilant concerning greater evils.

[Col. 0716A] 335 10. Just as physicians undertake to treat diseases that are already threatening, but, by applying medicine, anticipate future diseases with a certain foreknowledge so that they do not creep in, so good teachers cut away what has been done wrongly in such a way that, with doctrine coming to their aid, they prevent what might be committed from being perpetrated.

11. Whoever is not corrected by a gentle word of chastisement must necessarily be rebuked more sharply. What cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain.

12. Whoever neglects to correct himself after being privately admonished concerning sin must be rebuked publicly, so that a wound which cannot be healed secretly may be openly cured.

[Note: [Col. 0715D]

13. From Gregory, book XII of the letters, to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily. LOAISA.]

13. Manifest sins are not to be cleansed by secret correction. Those who cause public harm must be rebuked publicly, so that, while they are healed by open reproof, those who have sinned by imitating them may be corrected.

14. When one person is rebuked, many are corrected. It is necessary that one be condemned for the salvation of many rather than that many be endangered through one person’s license.

[Note: [Col. 0716D]

15. We have restored the reading of the Gothic books; nevertheless, we think the following is correct: “If it is necessary to apply some salt, that is, to sprinkle it with the word.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Others read: “If it is necessary to sprinkle some harshness of medicine through the words of preaching.” AREV.]

15. Speech should be addressed to an offender according to what the salvation of the person being corrected requires. If it is necessary to apply some medicinal remedy through a word of rebuke, one must nevertheless retain gentleness in one’s heart.

16. Teachers sometimes strike their subjects more harshly with rebukes, yet they do not depart from charity toward those whom they correct.

17. The Church’s discipline often appears to the arrogant to be pride; and what is done piously by the good is thought by the wicked to be done cruelly, because they do not discern with a right eye what the good do with an upright spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0716D]

18. *Remetietur* (“it will be measured back”). Another reads: “it will be measured back in the same measure.” AREV.]

18. Every pontiff must take the greatest care to act toward those entrusted to him with a caution proportionate to the fear with which he dreads being judged by Christ; for, as it is written: “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. VII, 2).

19. Every day we all offend and stumble in many errors.

336 20. Since we are merciful toward our own offenses, we must by no means maintain severity toward another’s sin. Many see the faults of others but do not look at their own. Although they themselves are held liable for the greatest crimes, they do not forgive their brothers’ lesser sins.

21. Hypocrites do not feel the beam standing in their own eye, but stare at the splinter lodged in their brother’s eye.

22. We more readily rebuke the faults of others than our own. Often we fail to recognize that what we judge to be perverse in others is harmful in ourselves; and we are not ashamed to do ourselves what we rebuke in others.

[Col. 0717A] 23. We more readily attend to each person’s faults than to his virtues; we do not acknowledge what good each person has done, but investigate what evil he has done.

CHAPTER XLVII. On subjects.

[Note: [Col. 0717C]

CHAP. XLVII, no. 1. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXI, chapter 11, and Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIX, chapter 15. LOAISA.

Ibid. Augustine’s words on this matter: “The condition … of servitude is rightly understood to have been imposed upon the sinner.” And again: “This name, therefore—servitude—was earned by guilt, not by nature.” AREV.]

1. Because of the sin of the first human being, the penalty of servitude was divinely imposed upon the human race, so that to those whom he sees not to be suited to freedom he mercifully assigns servitude. Although the sin of human origin has been forgiven all the faithful through the grace of baptism, the just God nevertheless ordered human life in this way, establishing some as slaves and others as masters, so that the slaves’ opportunity to do evil might be restrained by the power of those who rule. For if all had existed without fear, who would have prevented anyone from doing evil? Hence rulers and kings were also chosen among the nations, so that by their terror they might restrain peoples from evil and subject them by laws to right living.

[Note: [Col. 0717C]

2. Thus the Gothic, Salamanca, and printed books. Others read *confert consultum* (“he provides counsel”). LOAISA.

Ibid. Goldastus advises that this passage be punctuated as in the first edition of Hadamar’s Council of Aachen, in the note on the following chapter, no. 3. AREV.]

2. As far as reason is concerned, there is no partiality toward persons with God (Col. III, 25). He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh might boast—[337] that is, no carnal power—before him. For there is one Lord, who equally gives counsel to masters and slaves.

3. Subjection in servitude is better than freedom in arrogance. Many are found who serve God freely while placed under wicked masters; although subject to them in body, they are superior to them in mind.

CHAPTER XLVIII. On rulers.

[Col. 0718A]

[Note: [Col. 0717C]

CHAP. XLVIII, no. 1. From Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXIV, chapter 30. Paul says in I Thessalonians II: “Not seeking glory from human beings, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been a burden as apostles of Christ; instead, we became little ones in your midst.” Gregory interprets this passage in the same way in *Moralia*, book XXIV, chapter 30. The Gothic and Salamanca books read *quod decebat* (“what was fitting”); other manuscripts have *quod licebat* (“what was permitted”); the printed editions have the latter. LOAISA.

[Col. 0717D] Ibid. Here begins the little work *On Rulers*, which Goldastus treated in his generally learned, though sometimes unorthodox, notes, as I have already said. I shall select from his notes certain matters that may be relevant. First, he observes that “rulers” here does not mean prefects of churches, but secular princes, as they are called. Thus, in Isidore himself, near the end of the book *On Contempt of the World*, one chapter is entitled *On Rulership*, and in another of the *Synonyms*, *On Rulers and Subjects*. The words *praesul*, *praepositus*, and *praelatus* denote the overseer of anything whatsoever; but usage has now established that they refer to ecclesiastical offices. The first sentence can be illustrated from Isidore’s *Synonyms*, the final chapter, chapters 33 and 42 of book III of this work, the First Council of Aachen, chapters 18 and 21, Tertullian’s book *On Idolatry*, Cicero, and others. In place of *innotescat* (“may become known”), Goldastus read *innotescatur* (“may be made known”) in his manuscript, which truly seems Isidorian. For both Braulio and Isidore use *innotesco* actively. The same manuscript had: “Who neither used the power given to him for what was fitting, but, although he could use what was permitted, refused it.” Goldastus corrected this to: “although he could use what was permitted, he refused it.” Isidore often uses *utor* with the accusative; therefore the sentence could be punctuated: “although he could use what was permitted, he refused”—that is, to use permitted things. AREV.]

1. A just man is either stripped of every secular power or, if he is girded with some power, does not bend beneath it so that he may swell with pride, but subjects it to himself so that he may become known as more humble. This is proved by the apostolic example: although power had been given to him, he did not even use it for what was fitting; although he could have used what was permitted, he refused it, and showed himself as a little one in the midst of those over whom he presided (I Thess. II, 6–7).

[Note: [Col. 0718C]

2. Goldastus’s manuscript has *ad potiendis honoribus*, with a certain appearance of solecism, as in section 3 of the *Institutes* concerning the Aquilian Law, and *ad exercitandis militibus*, from the old books, according to Cujacius. In place of *invenitur* (“is found”), Eglinus corrects it to *invenietur* (“will be found”). Isidore explains the matter in the *Synonyms*, near the end of book II, under the headings *On Rulers and Subjects* and *How One Should Conduct Oneself in Offices*. *In tantoque … quanto* is a Greek construction, with the positive used for the comparative. AREV.]

2. Whoever labors with persistent effort in seeking worldly honors or worldly prosperity is found both here and in the future empty of rest, and is burdened with the loads of sins in proportion as he is alienated from good works.

[Col. 0718B] [Note: [Col. 0718C]

3. This passage occurs in Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 19, and is cited in distinction 13, chapter *Nervi*. There it does not read *supereminet* (“rises above”), but *omne quod hic eminet* (“everything that rises above here”). LOAISA.

Ibid. “The more each person,” etc. See *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 3. A verse by a certain poet is praised:

“If you are ruled in mind, you are a king; if in body, a slave.” AREV.]

3. The more anyone is exalted by the dignity of secular honor, the more heavily he is weighed down by burdens of care; and the more he is subjected in mind and thought to those over whom he is placed by the rank of his eminence. For, as one of the Fathers says: “Everything that rises above is afflicted more by sorrows than it rejoices in honors.”

[Note: [Col. 0718D]

4. Goldastus’s manuscript has: “the more he is oppressed by unhappy vices,” which Goldastus says with great elegance and grace; *unhappy* is used in the sense of making someone unhappy. AREV.]

4. The more anyone is occupied with the greater cares of the world, the more easily he is oppressed by vices. For if the mind can scarcely avoid sins when at rest, how much less when bound by worldly occupation?

[Note: [Col. 0718D]

5. Others read: “when it is given by God the giver,” or “which has been given by God.” Goldastus rightly considers his manuscript’s reading preferable: “not so that he may commit evil through fear.” Nothing is worse than having the freedom to sin through power. He corrects Augustine’s wording in Prosper’s *Sentences*: “nothing is more unhappy than the happiness of sinning,” rather than “the happiness of sinners.” AREV.]

5. Not every mark of power is immediately useful; it is truly useful only when it is exercised well. It is exercised well when it benefits those who are placed beneath the person elevated above them by earthly honor. Power is good when it is given by God the giver so that it may restrain evil through fear, not so that it may rashly commit evil. Nothing is worse than having freedom to sin through power, and nothing is more wretched than the ability to do evil.

[Note: [Col. 0719C]

6. “Whoever rules well within the world,” etc. See Isaiah LX, 3, and Revelation XXI, 24. Saint Bernard illustrates the same sentence in letter 206 to the queen of Jerusalem. Some printed editions had *lapillorumque nitorem* (“the splendor of the little stones”). Goldastus prefers our reading, together with his manuscript, the Council of Paris, book II, chapter 1, and the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious. AREV.]

6. Whoever rules well in temporal matters within this world will reign forever without end, and will pass from the glory of this world to eternal glory. But those who exercise kingship wickedly, after their shining garments and the brilliance of their jewels, descend naked and wretched to be tormented in hell.

[Note: [Col. 0719C]

7. Hence the saying of Peter I, II, and Luke XIX: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.” Gregory also interprets the parables concerning kings as referring almost entirely to just people, in *Moralia*, book XI, chapter 9, explaining Job XII: “He loosens the belt of kings”—those who know how to govern the movements of their members well are not undeservedly called kings. LOAISA.

[Col. 0719D] Ibid. “For rightly.” Augustine piously explains this in Psalm LXXV, on the words “terrible among the kings of the earth.” “Be a king of the earth,” he says, “and God will be terrible to you. How, you ask, shall I be a king of the earth? Rule the earth, and you will be king of the earth. Do not therefore place before your eyes, through a desire to rule, vast provinces over which you may extend your kingdoms; rule the earth that you carry. Hear the Apostle ruling the earth: ‘I do not fight as one striking the air, but I chastise my body and bring it into servitude.’” LOAISA.

Ibid. “From acting rightly.” Goldastus says that this etymology is Stoic and derived from philosophy, not grammar; he assembles many writers who adopted it. The sentence is illustrated by Salvian, book IV of *The Government of God*; Saint Bernard, in the *Sentences*; Pope Nicholas in his letter to the emperor Michael; and others. The Council of Paris, book I, chapter 2, has *noverunt pacificare* (“they knew how to pacify”) instead of *modificare noverunt* (“they knew how to moderate”). Goldastus considers *modificare* preferable, since Cicero used it in the sense of “to moderate” and “to govern.”

AREV.]

7. Kings are so called from acting rightly; therefore the name “king” is retained by doing what is right and lost by sinning. For we also find holy men called kings in sacred writings, because they act rightly, govern their own thoughts well, and regulate with rational discernment the impulses that resist them. Those are rightly called kings who know how to govern and discipline both themselves and their subjects well.

[Note: [Column 0719D]

8. It could be read “through Ecclesiasticus,” since the cited words occur in that book [Column 0720C]. But it is not surprising if Isidore names one book in place of another, especially since Ecclesiasticus and Ecclesiastes are often confused by others as well, because many believe that Solomon was the author of both. In any case, the Fathers of the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, who had Isidore’s works at hand, call it Ecclesiasticus, not Ecclesiastes. AREV.]

8. Some turn the very name of government into a monstrous form of cruelty; and when they have reached the summit of power, they immediately fall into apostasy. They raise themselves up with such an inflation of heart that they despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves and fail to recognize those over whom they have come to preside. To such men Ecclesiastes appropriately says: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclesiasticus XXXII, 1).

[Note: [Column 0720C]

9. “What they bring with them,” etc. Goldastus declares that this passage is plainly corrupt and wastes considerable effort trying to restore it. He does not, in fact, offer a better reading, namely, “that they intend to carry away what they bring with them.” Instead of “if, therefore, they will lack the glory of this age,” others have “if, therefore, they are going to lose the glory of this age.” AREV.]

9. While the kings of the world consider themselves superior to others, let them nevertheless acknowledge that they are mortal. Let them not look to the glory of the kingdom by which they are exalted in this age, but intend the work that they may carry with them to the underworld. 340 If, therefore, they will lack the glory of this age, let them do those things which they may possess without end after the end.

[Note: [Column 0720D]

10. “Of certain authorities.” Others: “of the rule of certain persons.” These are the words of Hosea, but some cite them as “not from me,” while others read “and not through me.” The word “he says” after “he added, ‘I will give’” might seem superfluous. But this kind of expression occurs elsewhere as well, among both Latin and Greek writers, as Goldastus observes. AREV.]

10. Although the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God” (Romans XIII, 1), how does the Lord say through the prophet concerning certain authorities, “They have reigned, but not from me” (Hosea VIII, 4)? It is as though he were saying, “not with me favorable to them, but even supremely angry.” Therefore, farther on, through the same prophet, he added: “I will give you a king,” he says, “in my wrath” (Hosea XIII, 11). From this it becomes clearer that both good and evil authority are ordained by God—but good authority when he is favorable, and evil authority when he is angry.

[Note: [Column 0720D]

11. “Is disposed.” Collectors of canons add “by God,” as Isidore also does above, in chapter 39 of this book, section 3. AREV.]

11. When kings are good, it is God’s gift; but when they are evil, it is the people’s fault. For the life of rulers is disposed according to the merit of their peoples, as Job testifies: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job XXXIV, 30). When God is angry, the people receive such a ruler as they deserve for their sin. Sometimes kings are changed because of the wickedness of the people as well, and those who previously appeared to be good become unjust after receiving the kingdom.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Justice of Rulers

[Note: [Column 0720D]

CHAPTER XLIX, no. 1. II Kings VI. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVII, chapter 26. LOAISA.

Ibid. Many things that Isidore presents in these chapters are repeated in the Councils of Paris, Mainz, and Aachen; Goldastus carefully compares their wording with Isidore’s text. On the clemency of rulers, see Saint Fulgentius, *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, and Isidore himself, in the cited passage of the *Synonyms*. AREV.]

1. He who uses royal power rightly ought to conduct himself toward everyone in such a way that, the more he shines through the height of his honor, the more he humbles himself in mind, setting before himself the example of David’s humility. David did not become swollen with pride over his merits but humbly abased himself and said: “I shall walk in humility, and I shall appear still more humble before God, who chose me” (II Kings VI, 22).

2. He who uses royal power rightly establishes the pattern of justice more by deeds than by words. He is lifted up by no prosperity and troubled by no adversity; he does not rely on his own strength, nor does his heart depart from the Lord. He presides over the height of the kingdom with a humble spirit; iniquity does not delight him, nor does greed inflame him. Without defrauding anyone, he makes the poor rich; and what he could have extorted from the peoples by rightful power, he often bestows through merciful clemency.

[Note: [Column 0721C]

3. Saint Athanasius, in the *Life of Saint Antony*: “Although their dignity is different, nevertheless the condition of being born and dying is the same.” For an explanation of this sentence, Lipsius should be consulted, *Politics*, II, chapter 6. The verb *condescendo* occurs in this sense in Saint Gregory the Great, Lupus, the abbot of Ferrara, and others. “For the protection” appears to be the reading that should be adopted. AREV.]

3. God gave rulers authority for the governance of peoples; he willed them to preside over those with whom they share the same condition of being born and dying. Their rule, therefore, ought to benefit the peoples, not harm them; it ought not to oppress them through domination but to serve them by condescending to them, so that this insignia of power may truly be useful and that they may use God’s gift for the protection of Christ’s members. For the faithful peoples are Christ’s members; when rulers govern them most excellently by the power they have received, they indeed repay a good return to God the giver.

[Note: [Column 0721C]

4. Others: “never to depart from the truth … let him not hesitate to rise again immediately.” AREV.]

4. A good king returns from wrongdoing to justice more readily than he is transferred from justice to wrongdoing, so that you may recognize that here there is a fall, whereas there is purpose there. It ought to be his purpose never to depart from the truth. But if he should happen to stumble through a fall, he should rise again immediately.

[Note: [Column 0721C]

CHAPTER L, no. 1. On the moderation and patience of rulers: Lipsius, *Politics*; Saint Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XIX, chapter 23, and others. Instead of “knows,” others read “ought to.” AREV.]

1. Often a just ruler knows how to overlook even the errors of the wicked—not because he consents to their iniquity, but because he awaits a suitable time for correction, when he may either reform or punish their vices.

[Note: [Column 0721D]

2. “To think evil.” Others: “to plot evil.” AREV.]

2. Many are exposed as guilty of conspiracy against rulers. But God, wishing to demonstrate the rulers’ clemency, permits those men to think evil while he does not abandon these rulers. He brings good to the rulers from the others’ evil, when, with marvelous patience, they forgive the faults those men commit.

[Column 0721C] 342 [Note: [Column 0721D]

3. “But he who adds clemency,” etc. Gratian, distinction 45, chapter 23, question 4; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 75; Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XX, part IV, chapter 6; our Isidore, *Synonyms*, cited passage; and many others. Goldastus interprets *culpatis* as “those who blame,” or “those who commit a fault,” and *offensis* similarly as “those who offend,” just as elsewhere *sacrificatis* is used for “those who sacrifice,” *implicatis* for “those who entangle,” and so forth. AREV.]

3. To return evil for evil is justice’s requital; but he who adds clemency to justice does not return evil for evil to those who have committed faults, but grants good to offenders in return for evil.

[Column 0722A] [Note: [Column 0721D]

4. This passage is discussed by Roderic Sánchez de Arévalo, *Speculum vitae humanae*, book I, chapter 2. Instead of “let them be restrained,” others read “they will have restrained themselves,” or, as Goldastus wishes to preserve in imitation of antiquity, “they will restrain.” AREV.]

4. It is difficult for a ruler to return to what is better if he has become entangled in vices. For sinful peoples fear a judge and are restrained from their evil by laws. Kings, however, unless restrained solely by fear of God and dread of Gehenna, rush freely headlong and, down the precipice of license, fall into every crime of vice.

[Note: [Column 0721D]

5. “The higher each person is,” etc. Augustine, in the *Rule*, or Letter 211, to the Nuns; Isidore, in the cited books *On Contempt of the World* and *On Synonyms*; and others. Goldastus, together with his manuscript and Roderic, prefers “the sinner is greater.” Roderic has “the sin is heavier.” AREV.]

5. The higher the position in which someone has been established, the greater the danger in which he moves; and the higher someone is in the honor of splendor, the greater a sinner he is if he commits wrongdoing. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wisdom VI, 7). For from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more is demanded—even with the interest of punishments.

[Note: [Column 0722C]

which, beyond doubt, was taken from an ancient poet. [Column 0722D] Certainly from Juvencus, as I noted in the notes to his book I, 293. Vezzosi had indicated IV Kings XIII, 4 in the margin. But, as he himself observes, that passage does not concern Jeroboam but Jehoahaz. AREV.]

6. Kings easily build up or overthrow the lives of their subjects by their examples. Therefore a ruler ought not to sin, lest the unpunished license of his sin make a pattern for sinning. For a king who falls into vices quickly shows the way of error, as is read of Jeroboam, who sinned and made Israel sin (Ecclesiasticus XLVII, 29). Whatever is perpetrated by subjects following his example is attributed to him.

AREV.]

7. Just as some follow the deeds of good rulers that are pleasing to God, 343 so many readily follow their evil examples. Most people are wicked under unjust rulers more from necessity than from choice, while they obey their commands. Some, however, are as eager to follow kings into evil as they are sluggish to imitate them in doing good.

[Note: [Column 0722D]

The Fathers of the Eighth Council of Toledo wonderfully clarify this judgment: “We have observed certain kings,” etc. AREV.]

8. Often, from the very things by which evil kings sin, good kings are justified, when they correct the greed and wickedness of their predecessors. For they truly share in their sins if they retain what those others have seized.

9. “To error.” Grialius’ text has *erroris*, incorrectly, as I think. In some manuscripts it is *errore*, an old form found in the Pandects, in place of *errori*. The principle is common among jurists. AREV.]

9. Whoever follows someone’s sin must necessarily follow his punishment. For the one whose error and vice someone shares will not receive an unequal punishment.

## CHAPTER LI. That Rulers Are Bound by Laws

[Note: [Column 0723C]

CHAPTER LI, no. 1. In Gratian, distinction 9, chapter “It is Just.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Goldastus gathers many things in support of this sentence, but it is hardly necessary to repeat them. Instead of “to obey,” some manuscripts and Gratian read “to be bound.” AREV.]

1. It is just for a ruler to obey his own laws. He should then consider his laws to be observed by all, when he himself also shows them reverence.

[Note: [Column 0723C]

2. Thus in Gratian, distinction 9, chapter “It Is Just,” in the recently corrected Gregorian decree: “Nor is it consistent for him to be able to condemn the laws that they establish among their subjects.” [Column 0723D] LOAISA.

Ibid. Instead of “to condemn,” others read “to frustrate.” Goldastus reads and punctuates it as: “they establish; it is just.” For the authority of their words is at issue. I would change nothing. AREV.]

2. Rulers are bound by their own laws and cannot condemn in themselves the laws that they establish among their subjects. Their words have authority only if they do not permit themselves to do what they prohibit the peoples from doing.

[Note: [Column 0723D]

3. Goldastus treats this argument extensively both here and in his note on Valerian. Gratian’s decree, distinction 96, chapter 6, should be consulted. AREV.]

3. The secular powers are subject to the discipline of religion; and although they are endowed with the summit of royal authority, they are nevertheless bound by the bond of faith, so that they may proclaim the faith of Christ through their laws and preserve the proclamation of that faith through good conduct.

[Note: [Column 0723D]

4. In chapter “Rulers,” cause 23, question 5. Council of Paris I, chapter 2, and Aachen, part III, chapter 1. LOAISA.

Ibid. Gratian’s heading reads: “What priests cannot accomplish by teaching, let the power of discipline exact through fear.” Goldastus observes that some editions of Gratian incorrectly read “in the church” instead of “within the Church,” which he confirms from the text of cause 23, question 8, chapter “I Am Summoned,” where Saint Ambrose says: “For the emperor is within the Church.” The whole of this sentence agrees with the Second Council of Mâcon: “It is therefore fitting that, with the force of justice and equity preserved in all things, legal punishment should constrain [Column 0724C] those whom the canonical preaching of priests does not correct,” etc. Instead of “let him command,” some read “let him fulfill”; Goldastus prefers “let him obtain.” AREV.]

4. Secular rulers sometimes hold the summits of the power they have acquired within the Church, so that through that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Indeed, powers within the Church would not be necessary unless the power were to command through the fear of discipline what the priest is unable to accomplish through the word of teaching.

[Note: [Column 0724C]

5. In Gratian, the same chapter “Rulers,” where the corrected decree reads, “and so that he may deserve veneration.” This reading is found in the scholia from the Council of Paris under Louis and Lothair, book II, chapter 2. Very ancient Gothic codices have: “so that he may deserve veneration, let him bestow it by the virtue of power.” LOAISA.

Ibid. Instead of “humility,” Gratian, together with some manuscripts, has “utility.” Shortly afterward there is considerable disagreement among the codices. Some read: “and so that he may deserve reverence, let him bestow virtue upon the powers.” The Council of Paris, book II, chapter 2, has: “and so that he may deserve veneration, let power bestow virtue.” Others: “and so that he may deserve veneration, let it be bestowed by the virtue of power.” AREV.]

5. Often the earthly kingdom advances the heavenly kingdom, so that those within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the severity of rulers; and so that the principal power may impose upon the necks of the proud that discipline which the humility of the Church is unable to exercise, and, so that it may deserve veneration, may bestow it by the virtue of power.

[Note: [Column 0724D]

6. “Let rulers recognize,” etc. See Saint Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 11, chapter 3; Saint Leo, Letter 29 to the Empress Pulcheria; Gratian, cause 23, question 4, chapter 35; and other collectors of canons. Here ends the little work *On Prelates*, which Goldastus undertook to illuminate with his commentary. As for the words Gratian took from Isidore, Berard compared them with Isidore’s works, and I have transcribed them in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 32, especially those concerning the *Books of Sentences*, from section 16 onward. AREV.]

6. Let secular rulers recognize that they must render an account to God concerning the Church, whose protection they undertake from Christ. For whether the peace and discipline of the Church are increased through faithful rulers or dissolved, he will demand an account from them who entrusted his Church to their power.

345 ## CHAPTER LII. On Judges

1. It is counted as a fault of rulers when they set wicked judges over faithful peoples against the will of God. For just as it is the people’s fault when rulers are evil, so it is the ruler’s sin when judges are unjust.

[Note: [Column 0724D]

CHAPTER LII, no. 2. “Who does not weaken.” Others omit “who.” Grialius has *quem* in both of my copies, which I consider an error. AREV.]

2. Just as a good judge does not know how to harm citizens, so he ought to benefit everyone. He offers some the severity of justice and others kindness. He accepts cases without respect of persons—one who does not weaken justice with the flame of greed and does not seek to take from another what he desires for himself.

[Column 0724B] 3. Good judges undertake justice solely to obtain eternal salvation, and do not distribute it in exchange for gifts, so that, by not seeking temporal profits from a just judgment, they may be enriched with an eternal reward.

4. Everyone who judges rightly carries a balance in his hand, bearing justice and mercy in its two pans. Through justice he pronounces the sentence for sin; through mercy he mitigates the sinner’s punishment, so that with a just balance he corrects some things through equity and forgives others through compassion.

5. He who sets God’s judgments before his eyes, always fearful and trembling, is apprehensive in every matter lest, straying from the path of justice, he fall; and lest, by the very means through which he is not justified, he instead be condemned.

6. No fool or wicked person ought to be a judge. The fool, through laziness, is ignorant of justice; the wicked person, through greed, corrupts the very truth he has learned.

7. The poor are torn apart more grievously by wicked judges than by the bloodiest enemies. For no plunderer is as greedy for another’s possessions as an unjust judge is for those of his own people.

[Column 0725A] 8. Robbers, lurking in inaccessible ravines and hidden places, lay ambushes; these men openly rage with the greed of rapacity.

346 9. Enemies seek only the blood of others; judges, like utterly cruel executioners of citizens, extinguish the lives of their subjects through oppression. There are many who destroy, but few who govern peoples by the restraint of laws.

[Note: [Column 0725D]

10. The rapacity of Scylla, to whom that writer—whoever he is—compares rapacious judges, is described by Virgil in *Eclogue* VI in these words:

> “She is said to have harassed the Dulichian ships,  
> her white groin girdled with barking monsters,  
> and, in the deep whirlpool, ah!, to have torn  
> the timid sailors with sea-dogs.”

See Servius on that passage, concerning the two Scyllas, and Virgil himself, *On the Cyrenean [poem] to Messalla*, as well as Fulgentius, *Mythologies* III. LOAISA.

Ibid. Loaisa’s note was corrupt in both of my copies of Grialius: “to whom that rapacious judgment, whoever he is.” AREV.]

10. Often there are good judges, but they have rapacious ministers. Their likeness, as someone says, is painted and described as Scylla: human in appearance, indeed, but girded and surrounded by doglike heads. The same thing happens to certain authorities: their humanity is disturbed by the savagery of unjust associates.

[Column 0725B] [Note: [Column 0725D]

11. Others: “in the examination of cases.” AREV.]

11. Wicked judges often delay or pervert judgments for the sake of greed; nor do they bring the parties’ initiated proceedings to an end until they have drained the purses of those who plead. For when they judge, they consider not the case but the gifts; and just as they are negligent in examining the litigants’ claims, so they are attentive to the litigants’ loss.

[Note: [Column 0725D]

12. The passage is Zephaniah III: “Her judges are wolves; in the evening they leave nothing for the morning.” The manuscripts read it in this way. LOAISA.]

12. Wicked judges, according to the prophet’s word, are like wolves in the evening, leaving nothing for the morning (Zephaniah III, 3); that is, they think only about the advantages of the present life, not about those of the future. This life is understood as evening, whereas the future life is understood as morning. He rightly says “like wolves,” because, after the manner of wolves, they plunder everything and scarcely leave anything for the poor.

[Note: [Column 0726D]

13. “But they assert.” The old edition reads “but they bring forward.” Both are obscure. AREV.]

13. Verbose and arrogant judges, wishing to appear wise, do not examine cases but merely make assertions; and so they disrupt the order of judgment, since, not content with their own office, they presume upon another’s.

14. Some, when they begin to judge, become angry and turn the very sentence of judgment into madness. Concerning them the prophet rightly says: “They turn judgment into fury.” For whoever judges in anger changes judgment into fury and pronounces a sentence before he has understood the case.

15. Fury in a judge is unable to reach an investigation of the truth, because a mind disturbed by anger is alienated from the scrutiny of justice.

347 16. An angry judge is unable to examine the matter of judgment fully, because he cannot see through the darkness of fury. But he who examines after putting anger aside rises more easily, through the serenity of his mind, to behold the truth and reaches an understanding of equity without any disturbance.

## CHAPTER LIII. On Respect of Persons

[Note: [Column 0726D]

CHAPTER LIII, no. 1. Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 30, on the words: “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment,” chapter 7. Leviticus XIX. Deuteronomy I and XIX. Proverbs XXIV. Ecclesiasticus XLII. LOAISA.]

1. A person’s status must not be considered in judgment, but the case; for it is written: “Do not show partiality in judgment” (Leviticus XIX, 15; Deuteronomy I, 17; Proverbs XXIV, 23; Ecclesiasticus XLII, 1). And again: “You shall not show pity to the poor in judgment.” Those who pervert judgment through favor toward relatives or friends, or through hatred of enemies, are without doubt known to sin against Christ, who is truth and justice.

2. Unjust judges err in the truth of their sentence when they focus on the quality of the person, and they often exasperate the just while wickedly defending the unjust. But he who strives to preside rightly knows neither how to flatter one party nor has he learned to restrain himself from justice.

## CHAPTER LIV. On Bribes

1. Whoever judges rightly yet expects a reward for it commits fraud against God, because he sells for money the justice that he ought to have granted freely.

[Note: [Column 0726D]

CHAPTER LIV, no. 2. “Love of reward.” Others: “love of money.” AREV.]

2. Those who judge justly for temporal profit use good things badly. Such men are moved toward the truth not by the defense of justice but by love of reward. If the hope of money is removed from them, they immediately withdraw from the defense of justice.

3. The acceptance of gifts is a betrayal of truth. Hence it is said of the just man: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift, he shall dwell on high” (Isaiah XXXIII, 15–16).

348 [Note: [Column 0726D]

4. Gratian, question 11, distinction 3, and Burchard, book XVI, chapter 28. LOAISA.]

4. The rich quickly corrupt a judge with gifts. But the poor man, since he has nothing to offer, is not only scorned when he seeks a hearing but is also oppressed contrary to the truth.

5. Justice is quickly violated by gold, and the accused fears no guilt that he thinks he can redeem with money. For the love of profit obtains greater power over the censor’s mind than the equity of judgment.

[Note: [Column 0726D]

6. From Gregory, *Homily 4 on the Gospels*. LOAISA.]

6. There are three forms of accepting gifts by which human vanity wages war against justice: the favor of friendship, flattering praise, and the acceptance of a material gift. The mind, however, is more easily perverted by a material gift than by the favor of goodwill and praise.

[Note: [Column 0726D]

7. Others: “to oppose an adversary” and “to benefit” instead of “to provide”; but *praestare* is correct, meaning “to benefit,” as has also been stated elsewhere in the notes to this work. AREV.]

7. Human judgment is perverted in four ways: by fear, greed, hatred, and love. By fear, when through dread of someone’s power we are afraid to speak the truth. By greed, when we are corrupted by the reward of some gift. By hatred, when we strive to oppose anyone. By love, when we attempt to benefit a friend or relatives. For through these four causes equity is often violated and innocence is often harmed.

## CHAPTER LV. On Witnesses

1. If a lie is told without payment, how much more so when it is sought for sale? There will be no shortage of a large gathering of false witnesses if money is merely present.

2. A false witness is liable to three persons. First, to God, whom he despises by perjury; second, to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; finally, to the innocent person whom he harms by false testimony.

[Column 0727B] [Note: [Column 0727D]

CHAPTER LV, no. 3. Vezzosi observes that Margarino and Loaisa do not give this sentence in full here. Grialius does place it here; Margarino places it somewhat later, namely after sentence 5. AREV.]

3. Nearly the same crime is committed by the one who brings forward falsehood and by the one who suppresses truth, because the former wishes to cause harm, while the latter does not wish to provide help. The witness who harms is worse than the one who does not wish to help. For the former is malicious, whereas the latter is useless.

349 4. When false witnesses are joined together, the falsity of their lie is discovered only slowly. But if they are separated, they are quickly exposed by the judge’s examination. For just as the strength of the wicked is great in unity, so their weakness is greater in separation.

5. Falsehood is quickly exposed by fraud, for the testimony of false witnesses does not agree with itself.

[Note: [Column 0727D]

6. Others: “And although he hinders his affairs, he will harm his spirit in no way; indeed, if the attacked man bears it with equanimity, it brings him the greatest profit. But he will be,” etc. AREV.]

6. Although an unjust witness may, through his falsehood, hinder a person’s body and affairs, he will nevertheless bring no harm to his spirit. But before God that person will be condemned who either gives false testimony against an innocent person or believes those who give it. For not only is the person guilty who utters something false about another, but also the one who readily lends an ear to accusations.

7. Whoever conceals the truth through fear of power provokes the anger of that same truth against himself from heaven, because he fears a human being more than he dreads divine indignation. Blessed is the person through whose testimony an innocent man is cleared of the crime alleged against him; impious is the person through whose betrayal even the wicked man is destroyed. For it is not fitting for a Christian to betray someone liable to death or to lend the voice of testimony to the shedding of the unfortunate’s blood. The speech of a just man ought to serve only the ministry of salvation; for [there are] the anger of indignation and tribulation, and sendings through evil angels.

## CHAPTER LVI. On Advocates

[Column 0728A]

1. Those who pursue forensic business ought, for the love of their neighbor, to abandon secular business; or at least, while retaining love of neighbor, they should pursue earthly business. But because it is exceedingly rare for charity to remain among quarrelling parties, the conduct of the case should be postponed so that love may continue.

[Note: [Column 0727D]

CHAPTER LVI, no. 2. Jerome, in his letter to Augustine: “A most difficult time came upon me, when it was better for me to be silent than to speak, so that our studies ceased and, in Appius’ phrase, ‘canine eloquence’ was practiced.” And *Against the Luciferians*: “Recently it happened that a follower of Lucifer, contending with another son of the Church in hateful loquacity, practiced canine eloquence.” And Lactantius, book VI, chapter 18: “But because he himself practiced that canine eloquence (as Sallust reports that it was said by Appius), he also wished the man to live in the manner of a dog, so that he might bite him back.” Two fragments of Sallust also survive in which this saying of Appius concerning canine eloquence is reported. Prudentius likewise writes in the *Hamartigenia*:

> “From there canine eloquence barks in the forum.”

LOAISA.

Ibid. Isidore has already spoken of canine eloquence in *Exodus* XIV, 9. Nonius thinks that abusive speakers are called *rabulae* from canine madness. Becmannus offers more on this subject from ancient writers in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, p. 901, under the word *Rabbi*. AREV.]

2. The ancients called forensic eloquence “canine eloquence,” 350 because advocates, in the contests of lawsuits, abandon the matters with which they are dealing and tear one another apart like dogs, turning the quarrels of cases into personal insults.

## CHAPTER LVII. On Oppressors of the Poor

[Column 0728B] 1. Oppressors of the poor should know that they deserve a more severe sentence when they have prevailed over those whom they wished to harm. For they will be condemned to a punishment all the more atrocious in the future, the more forcefully they have here prevailed against the lives of the wretched.

[Note: [Column 0728D]

2. Others, with the Vulgate: “And you will not know its origin; and it will rush upon you,” etc. AREV.]

2. Let judges and those who rule peoples hear this: because of the temporal hardships they inflict upon the common people, they will be burned in eternal fire, as the Lord testifies through the prophet Isaiah:

> “I was angry with my people,” he says, “and I gave them into your hand. You showed them no mercy, but you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. Descend into the dust; sit; be silent; and enter into darkness. Evil will come upon you, and you will not know it; calamity will rush upon you, which you will be unable to expiate. Misery will suddenly come upon you, which you do not know” (Isaiah XLVII, 5).

[Note: [Column 0728D]

3. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 21. LOAISA.]

3. We ought to grieve more for those who do evil than for those who suffer evil. By doing wicked things, the former advance toward evil; by suffering, the latter are corrected away from evil. Through the evil desires of some, God accomplishes many good things in others.

4. The will of malicious people can never be fulfilled unless God grants them the power. For when people, with God’s permission, accomplish the evil they desire, he who permits it is said to do it. Hence it is written through the prophet: “If there is evil, has the Lord not done it?” Nevertheless, God grants the wicked power to accomplish the evils they seek by their own will through his good will, because from our evil he himself produces many good things.

5. Some, when they resist God’s will, unknowingly carry out God’s plan. From this you may recognize that everything is so subject to God that even those who oppose his disposition fulfill his will.

6. For this reason the good are judged by the wicked in this life, so that in the other life the wicked may be judged by the good; or else so that the good may have temporal affliction here and eternal reward there.

7. The wicked are necessary so that whenever the good sin, they may be scourged by them. Hence the Lord testifies that Assyria is the rod of his anger (Isaiah X, 5, 7). But whenever this happens, it proceeds from God’s indignation, so that God may rage through them against those whom he desires to correct by scourging. He does so with the most just intention, whereas they often act with cruel purpose, as is said by the prophet concerning that same Assyria: “But he does not think so; his heart is set on destruction.”

8. A fierce divine fury will come upon those who are persecutors and violent toward the faithful. Consoling his own through the prophet, God promises that he will judge their adversaries in this way:

> “I will judge,” he says, “those who judged you; I will feed your enemies with their own flesh, and they will become drunk with their own blood as with new wine” (Isaiah XLIX, 25–26).

[Note: [Column 0729D]

9. Thus some manuscripts. Both Gothic manuscripts and the old edition have *moribus*. LOAISA.]

9. The wickedness of the evil has some usefulness: they tear God’s chosen apart with their bites, and consequently the life of the impious is lost to them. The life of the just, however, is not lost but advances, since the wicked train them through the exercise of tribulation to hate the present life and desire the future one.

[Note: [Column 0729D]

10. Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVI, chapter 9. LOAISA.]

10. Sometimes the perversity of the wicked benefits the welfare of the just, since through their own malice they train them and drive them through temporal hardship to seek the kingdoms of heaven. This is proved by the example of the Israelite people, who were treated more harshly in Egypt (Exodus III) precisely when they were to be called by Moses to the promised land, depart from the evils they suffered in Egypt, and hasten toward the promised homeland.

11. When the wicked see the steadfastness of the just amid their persecutions, they waste away in confusion of mind. And while they display adversity without overcoming them, they are finally confounded by the madness of their own perversity.

[Column 0729D] [Note: [Column 0729D]

12. Others: “They always assume the desire to cause harm.” AREV.]

12. Fools always direct their efforts against the good. When prosperity shines upon them, they boast arrogantly of their own merits and disparage the afflictions of the good and just; but when adversity befalls them, they immediately turn in faintheartedness to blasphemy.

13. Some simple-minded people, ignorant of God’s providence, are scandalized by the prosperity of the wicked, saying with the prophet: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why is it well with all who transgress and act unjustly?” (Jeremiah XII, 1). Those who say this should not marvel when they see the temporal and fleeting happiness of wicked people; rather, they should consider their end and how great eternal punishments await them afterward, as the prophet says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and suddenly they descend to the underworld” (Job XXI, 13).

[Column 0730B] [Note: [Column 0729D]

1. Let the just person recognize that he is being tested in adversity, not cast down.
