4. All the tribulations of this life are compared to passing waters; 353 for if any tribulation occurs in this life, it does not remain, but quickly passes away.

[Col. 0730C] 5. Whoever carefully considers the rewards of the future life bears all the evils of the present life with equanimity, because by the sweetness of that life he tempers the bitterness of this one, and by its eternity he scorns the transitory brevity of this one.

6. To be burdened by various temporal evils is beneficial for those who endure the evils of this life, because when they are weighed down by suffering, they do not desire the evils of covetousness, lust, and the other vices.

7. The temptations of the world are more beneficial for salvation than prosperity, as is evident: prosperity leads to deterioration, whereas through the pain of temptation one advances toward what is better.

8. Everyone ought to prepare his mind for temptation (Ecclesiasticus 2:1). For temptation weighs less when it is expected; but it presses harshly if it comes unanticipated.

[Col. 0730D] 9. It is the mark of a wise person to meditate beforehand upon every adversity; no eventuality should arise that his counsels have not anticipated.

1. Lovers of the world are blameworthy not only because they desire lowly things in place of the highest, but are also wretched because they reach the things they desire through grievous hardship.

Those who love transitory things more than they ought inflict upon themselves greater pain from the loss of those things than the love that possession of them had produced. What is held with great love is lost with great pain. We grieve less in lacking what we loved less while possessing it.

[Col. 0731B] 3. Let those who pursue the profits of the age know how vain or harmful are the things they love—things which they do not even acquire in this world without severe anguish, and for which they will pay penalties in future punishment.

But just as it is good to use an evil thing well, so it is better to use a good thing well. And just as it is evil to use a good thing badly, so it is worst to use an evil thing badly.

3. Whoever considers the length of the present life not from its duration but from its end, and weighs how brief and wretched it is, reflects with sufficient usefulness. The present life is also shown to be brief by its very existence, because it does not remain but comes to an end. A woven fabric is completed by its threads, and human life is filled out by each passing day.

4. When someone lives for a long time in this life, it is worth asking whether this should be called an increase, or more rightly a loss. But how can that properly be called an increase which, through the stages of life, moves toward the loss that is death?

# ISIDORE, HOLY BISHOP OF SEVILLE, ON ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES (C)

## Letter of Transmission

363 To my lord and servant of God, Fulgentius the bishop, from Isidore.

You ask me about the origin of the offices by whose instruction we are educated in the churches, so that you may learn briefly by whose authors they were instituted. Therefore, as you requested, I have sent a little book on the origin of the offices, arranged from the very ancient writings of authors and commented upon as the occasion required. In it I have drawn out many things in my own style, but I have also inserted some passages just as they were found in those authors, so that the reading of each matter might more easily retain the authority of faith. If any of these things should nevertheless displease, forgiveness will be more readily granted for my errors, because those matters for which the testimony of authors is adduced should not be charged to the account of my fault.

# BOOK ONE. ON THE ORIGIN OF THE OFFICES

[Col. 0737]

## PREFACE

[Note: [Col. 0739B]

PREF. No. 2. What I discovered concerning the various editions and manuscript copies of this work has already been explained in the *Isidorian Studies*, chapter 69. Grialius added notes, whose name will be given explicitly or by indication whenever they are cited. In the Roman Edition of 1568, Hittorpius, together with other works on the same subject, noted certain differences of reading, of which I shall include the more important ones in my notes.

In the inscription of the letter, Grialius published *Domno*, which I do not think came from Isidore’s hand; other editions and manuscripts have *Domino*. Some immediately afterward have *quorum magisteriis* (“by whose teachings”). Others have *de genere officiorum* (“on the kind of offices”), or *de genere et origine officiorum* (“on the kind and origin of the offices”). Others have *vetustissimorum auctorum* (“of the most ancient authors”). AREV.]

[Col. 0737B]

[Col. 0737C] The things that are celebrated in ecclesiastical offices are found to have been established partly by the authority of the sacred Scriptures, partly by apostolic tradition, and partly by the custom of the universal Church [Col. 0738C]. Retracing their beginnings, let us report from which authors they arose, as we stated above.

## CHAPTER I. On the Church and the Name of Christians

[Col. 0739A]

[Note: [Col. 0739B]

CHAP. I. No. 1. In Vatican Palatine Codex 485 there is a short dialogue *On the Church* under Isidore’s name, which I present here.

“On the Church, by Isidore.

Question. What language does *ecclesia* belong to, and what is its interpretation?

Answer. It is Greek, and it means ‘assembly,’ because it calls everyone to itself.

Question. Why is it called Catholic?

Answer. It is called by a Greek name and means ‘universal’; and it is called universal because it is spread and extended throughout the whole world. The Apostle also confirms this when he says to the Romans: ‘I give thanks always to my God for you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.’

Question. Since the Church is one, why are seven written by John?

Answer. For this reason: although it is one Catholic Church, it is marked as full of the sevenfold Spirit. We also know that Solomon said of the Lord: ‘Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars.’ Yet there is no doubt that these seven are one, since the Apostle says: ‘The Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of truth.’ Hence the universe too is named from the one, because it is gathered into unity. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever does not gather with me scatters.’

Question. Where did the Church begin?

Answer. In the place where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the apostles and others, as they were sitting together in one place.

Question. By how many forms and names is the Church called?

Answer. By two.

Question. By which two?

Answer. Zion and Jerusalem.

Question. Why Zion, and why Jerusalem?

Answer. The Church is called Zion with reference to the present pilgrimage, because, placed at a distance during the length of this pilgrimage, it watches for the promised heavenly things; therefore it received the name Zion, that is, ‘watchtower’ or ‘watching.’ It is called Jerusalem with reference to future peace, for Jerusalem is interpreted as ‘vision of peace.’ There, after every adversity has been swallowed up, it will possess peace, which is Christ, in present vision.

Question. Why is it called Synagogue, and in what language is the word used?

Answer. *Synagogue* is Greek; in Latin it is called *congregatio*, ‘assembly.’

Question. What difference is there between the Church and the Synagogue?

Answer. The people of the Jews retained the name Synagogue; for it is properly their Synagogue, although it has been called a Church. Our apostles, however, never called it Synagogue, but always Church, either for the sake of distinction or because there is some difference between an assembly, from which Synagogue takes its name, and a convocation, from which Church takes its name. Animals are accustomed to be gathered together, and we properly call their groups flocks; being summoned together, however, is more characteristic of beings who use reason, such as human beings.

Question. Why is it called a monastery?

Answer. Among the Greeks *monas* means ‘one,’ and *sterium* means ‘station’; thus it means the dwelling of one living alone.

Question. Why is it called a coenobium?

Answer. It is a compound name from Greek and Latin. For *coenon* is Greek for ‘common’; it is a dwelling place of many.

Question. Why is it called a temple?

Answer. It is called a temple as though it were a broad covered place, and it is also called a temple from contemplation.

Question. How many parts does a temple have?

Answer. Four: the front, the rear toward the west, the left toward the north, and the right toward the south. Hence, when they built a temple, they faced the equinoctial east, so that lines drawn from east to west made the right and left parts of the sky equal [perhaps: ‘so that the right and left parts of the sky were equal’], in order that anyone consulting or praying might look directly toward the east.

Question. Why is it called a basilica?

Answer. Basilicas were formerly called the dwelling places of kings; from this it takes its name.”

I discussed this little work, or fragment, in the *Isidorian Studies*, chapter 85, no. 7. AREV.]

1. The Church was first founded by Saint Peter in Antioch, and there the name “Christians” first arose through his preaching, as the Acts of the Apostles testify (Acts 11:26). They are called Christians, the name being derived from the name of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0740C]

2. “Whose dignity of authority is also a prerogative among the Gentiles and among the Jews.” Both manuscripts read this, and I see that it can stand. Thus Cicero has *praerogativa centuria* (“a prerogative century”) and *praerogativum omen comitiorum* (“a prerogative omen of the assemblies”); and Cyprian, book V, letter 13, has *praerogativa communicatio* (“prerogative fellowship”). But I fear that the word *dignitas* (“dignity”) may be an interpretation and that it does not belong here. Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 24: “This prerogative of authority appears to have been attributed to human beings over the other living creatures, and in the higher parts.” And in *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, chapter 19: “They therefore see in the words a certain prerogative of authority.” Unless one prefers *praerogativa dignitatis et potestatis* (“the prerogative of dignity and authority”), which is somewhat fuller. Nor is the prerogative of dignity limited to priests, says the author of the book *On the Carnal Works of Christ* apud Cyprian. GRIAL.

Here: “But the Church,” and everything through the end of the chapter, is taken from Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 18, in the old translation. GRIAL.]

For just as the Jews drew their name from Judah, from whom the dignity of royal descent became illustrious in that people, so the name of the Christian people has adhered to it from Christ. Whose dignity of authority is also a prerogative among the Gentiles and among the Jews. The Church is properly so called because it calls everyone to itself and gathers them into one.

[Note: [Col. 0740D]

3. From Hittorpius’s notes: one manuscript has *vel quoniam* (“or because”), as in our Edition, which Hittorpius also judges to be the best. Another, as Hittorpius published it, has *vel catholica, quoniam in ea doctrina est* (“or Catholic, because doctrine is found in it”). Immediately afterward, some printed editions have: “for the instruction of all concerning visible things . . . or because it summons every kind of human being to submission to piety, both rulers and those subject to rulers, and the uneducated.” Others have: “Or because it summons every kind of human being to submission to piety, both rulers and those who do not rule, speakers and the uneducated.” Hittorpius conjectured: “Or because it exhorts every kind of human being to submission to piety, both rulers and those subject to rulers,” omitting “the uneducated.” Then perhaps one should distinguish the phrase as follows: “or, more generally, because it takes care of everyone’s sins,” and so forth. AREV.]

It is called Catholic because it has been established throughout the whole world; or because it is Catholic—that is, universal—in its doctrine, for the instruction of human beings concerning visible and invisible things, heavenly and earthly; or because it draws every kind of human being to itself into submission to piety, both rulers and those who rule, speakers and the uneducated; or because it generally takes care of all sins, which are committed through body and soul.

## CHAPTER II. On Temples

66 [Col. 0741A]

[Note: [Col. 0741C]

CHAP. II. No. 1. “Skilled in prudence.” Both manuscripts read this. The printed editions have *prudentiam petiturus* (“seeking prudence”). GRIAL.

Here: “altars.” Others: “courtyards.” GRIAL.]

[Note: Following the Isidorian fragment quoted above from Vatican Codex Palatinus 485, chapter I, another fragment follows in the same codex under this title: “Also, On the Ministry of the Church.” “A church may be established in another place if necessary, and it need not be consecrated again. Only a presbyter ought to sprinkle it with water, and a cross ought to be arranged at the place of the altar. On each altar two Masses may be celebrated in one day. Whoever does not communicate should not approach the bread or the kiss at Mass; and whoever has eaten beforehand is not permitted to receive the kiss. The timber of a church ought not to be put to any other use except for another church; or it may be burned in the fire, or used for the benefit of the monastery, so that the brothers may bake bread with it; but it ought not to be put to secular uses. In a church in which the corpses of unbelievers have been buried, it is not permitted to consecrate an altar. But if the place seems suitable for consecration, after they have been removed and its timbers have been scraped or washed, it should be rebuilt. If it had previously been consecrated, Masses may be celebrated in that place if religious persons have been buried there. But if a pagan has been buried there, it is better to cleanse the place and cast him outside. We ought not to make steps before the altar. The relics of the saints are to be venerated. If it can be done, a candle should burn there every night; but if the poverty of the place does not permit it, this does them no harm. The Lord’s incense should be burned on the feast of the saints in reverence for the day, because they, like lilies, gave forth the fragrance of sweetness and sprinkled the Church of God, just as the church is first sprinkled with incense beside the altar. A layman ought not to recite a reading in churches or say the Alleluia, but he may recite psalms and responsories without the Alleluia. The inhabitants may sprinkle their houses with blessed water whenever they wish; and when you consecrate water, you shall offer a prayer.” AREV.]

1. Moses the lawgiver first constructed the tabernacle for the Lord (Exod. XL). Solomon then, skilled in wisdom, established the temple (III Kings VI). After these, the faith of our own times consecrated Christ’s altars throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER III. On Choirs

[Note: **CHAP. III. Note 1.** “A choir made from the image.” The same appears in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, at the final chapter. But Plato, in Book II of the *Laws*, preferred to say that the choir was led “from joy” (*ἀπὸ τῆς χαρᾶς*). GRIAL.

**Same passage.** Rittorpius, with his manuscripts, reads: “He established them to sing to God in choirs, with the two sexes divided into separate classes, he and his sister leading the singing.” In one manuscript, “with him leading” occurs instead of “he leading.” Some printed editions have “he and his sister leading.” In Grial’s text the reading was *chorum autem*; in the note, correctly, *chorus autem*. Three manuscripts read: “But the choir was made from the image of a crown and was therefore so called,” so that *constat* is supplied, as often happens in the Isidorian works. AREV.]

1. Moses himself was the first to establish choirs after the crossing of the Red Sea (Exod. XV), and, with the two sexes divided into separate classes and with himself and his sister leading, he taught them to sing to the Lord in choirs a song of triumph. But a choir was made from the image of a crown and was therefore so called.

[Note: **2.** Among the Jews, not fewer than ten. Honor is thereby paid to the Decalogue. For this reason they also used a ten-stringed psalterium, whereas Athenaeus says that among other peoples it consisted of only nine strings. More recent Hebrews likewise recognize only ten instruments for the performance of hymns. When he said “not fewer than ten,” he spoke in the same way as in Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, and often elsewhere; nor was this without precedent, as was shown there. GRIAL.]

2. Hence also the Ecclesiastical Book writes: “The priest standing before the altar, and around him the crowns of the brothers” (Ecclus. L, 13). For a choir properly means a multitude of singers; among the Jews it consists of not fewer than ten singers, whereas among us it consists of an uncertain number, whether fewer or more, without any distinction.

## CHAPTER IV. On Songs

[Note: **CHAP. IV. Note 1.** “He was glorified.” Some printed editions add: “The same author wrote in Deuteronomy a song foretelling future events.” AREV.]

1. Moses himself first introduced the song when, after Egypt had been struck by ten plagues and Pharaoh had been drowned with his people, he went out joyfully through the unfamiliar paths of the sea into the desert, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified” (Exod. XV).

[Note: **2.** “A song is the voice of a human being.” Rufinus—or Hilary—in the prologue to the Psalter: “A psalm exists when, the voice ceasing, only the striking of the singing instrument is heard. A song exists when the choir of singers, using its freedom and not constrained to follow the accompaniment of the instrument, exults in a hymn with the melody of the voice alone. A psalm of a song exists when, with the instrument leading, the following voice of the singing choir is heard, answering the instrument and imitating the mode of the psalterium. But a song of a psalm exists when, with the choir singing beforehand, the art of the accompanying instrument is adapted to the hymn of human song, and the voice leading the melody is modulated with equal sweetness by the psalterium. GRIAL.]

2. Then Deborah, a woman of no mean standing, is found to have performed this ministry in the Book of Judges (Judg. V). Afterward, many—not only men but also women—filled with the divine Spirit, are recorded to have sung by God's mystery. A song, however, is the voice of a human being, whereas a psalm is sung to the psalterium.

## CHAPTER V. On Psalms

[Note: **CHAP. V. Note 1.** “Leader of the singers,” according to the Roman edition; “leader of all,” according to the Gothic text. GRIAL.]

1. The Church reveals that the practice of psalm-singing was first handed down after Moses by the prophet David, with great mystery. From childhood he was specially chosen by the Lord for this ministry, and he merited becoming leader of the singers and a treasury of psalms. For this reason his psalterium, with its melody of sweet songs, is frequently used by the Church, so that minds may more easily be bent toward compunction.

[Note: **2.** “More religiously.” The Greek has “for the religious.” AREV.]

2. The primitive Church sang psalms in such a way that it made the singer resound with only a slight inflection of the voice, so that he was nearer to speaking than to singing. The custom of singing was instituted for the sake of the carnal in the Church, not for the spiritual, so that those who are not moved to compunction by words might be moved by the sweetness of the melody. Thus also the most blessed Augustine, in Book X, chapter 33, of his *Confessions*, approves the custom of singing in the Church, saying that “through the delight of the ears the weaker mind may rise toward an affection of piety.” For our minds are moved more religiously and ardently toward the flame of piety by the sacred words themselves when they are sung than when they are not sung. All our affections, through the diversity or novelty of sounds, are aroused more strongly by some hidden familiarity when the song is sung with a sweet and skillful voice.

## CHAPTER VI. On Hymns

[Note: **CHAP. VI. Note 1.** “David himself first composed hymns.” Rufinus says that the Book of Psalms is also called the book of hymns and soliloquies. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** From “in hymns and psalms” through the examples, these words are found in the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 12, and in Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “On Hymns.” GRIAL.

**Same passage.** It should be observed that Isidore wrote these books before the Fourth Council of Toledo, since he sent them to his brother Fulgentius, who died before that council. Therefore the council adopted from Isidore’s books what is taught there about hymns, rather than Isidore adopting it from the council. I published a separate dissertation on hymns in the Salomonian press and prefixed it to the *Hispanic Hymnody*. In it I also explained many matters relating to songs, psalms, antiphons, and responsories. The liturgical works of Cardinal Bona, Thomasius, and others are also relevant here; there is no need to cite them at each individual chapter of these books. AREV.]

1. It is clear that the prophet David himself first composed and sang hymns, and afterward the other prophets as well. Later, the three youths placed in the furnace, summoning all creation, sang a hymn to the Creator of all things and said it (Dan. III). Thus, in singing hymns and psalms, we have the example not only of the prophets but also of the Lord himself and of the apostles, as well as useful instructions on this matter for moving the mind toward piety and kindling the affection of divine love.

[Note: **2.** “Because in his time in the Church of Milan.” Augustine, *Confessions* X, chapters 6 and 7: “Not long before, the Church of Milan had begun to celebrate this kind of consolation and exhortation with great zeal, while the voices and hearts of the brothers sang together. It was evidently a year, or not much more, etc.” GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “But whatever songs are spoken in praise of God.” I would prefer “are sung.” The nature of a hymn absolutely requires this, according to Rufinus and Augustine. Rufinus says: “Hymns are songs containing praise of God. If there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn. If there is praise of God but it is not sung, it is not a hymn. Therefore, for it to be a hymn, it must have these three things: praise, of God, and song.” Augustine says the same in Psalm LXXII, in just as many or even more words. These words are also reported in Book VI of the *Etymologies*. GRIAL.]

2. Some hymns are divine, while others are composed by human talent. Hilary, a Gallic bishop of Poitiers, distinguished for his eloquence, was the first to flourish in the composition of hymns. After him, Ambrose, a bishop of great glory in Christ and a renowned teacher in the Church, is known to have excelled abundantly in this kind of composition. These hymns are called Ambrosian from his name because they first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan in his time; afterward, devotion to this celebration was observed throughout the churches of the entire West. All songs that are spoken in praise of God are called hymns.

## CHAPTER VII. On Antiphons

[Note: **CHAP. VII. Note 1.** “The Greeks first composed antiphons.” See Paulinus, Sigebert, and Rodulf, in Pamelius, Book I of the *Liturgies*. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “Established.” Another reading is “instituted.” GRIAL.]

1. The Greeks first composed antiphons, with two choirs singing alternately, like the two Seraphim and the two Testaments calling out to one another (Isa. VI). Among the Latins, the same most blessed Ambrose was the first to establish antiphons, imitating the example of the Greeks. From then on their use increased throughout all the western regions.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Prayers

[Note: **CHAP. VIII. Note 1.** “From the book of heavenly law.” We have labored to restore the words to their author. For we do not doubt that they are older than Isidore. At times they seem to belong to Tertullian or Cyprian. Now we are more inclined to believe them to be Augustine’s. In Letter 118 to Januarius, chapter 4, he says: “For he will not be about to read these things to me from the book of God. For it seems likely that the Lord Christ is reading from the book of heavenly law.” GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “They might obtain God.” This is certainly the reading of many manuscripts; others have “they might obtain the Lord.” Nevertheless Hittorpius preferred to print “they might obtain from the Lord.” Suárez, vol. XIII, p. 119, treatise 5, Book III, *On Vocal Prayer*, chapter 1, no. 6, uses this chapter of Isidore to show that it is lawful and appropriate to pray to God not only with the words of the Lord’s Prayer but also with other words suited to express a devout disposition of mind. Tertullian teaches the same in *On Prayer*, chapter 9. AREV.]

1. Christ both composed and ordained for us the prayer by which we should beseech the Lord. When the apostles therefore wished to supplicate God and did not know how they should pray, they said to Christ: “Lord, teach us to pray”—that is, “Compose prayers for us.” Immediately the Lord, from the book of heavenly law, taught them how they should pray and how they might obtain God. From this arose the Church’s custom of seeking God through prayers against the illnesses of the soul and of using prayers like those which Christ ordained, and which the first Greeks began to compose, by which they might supplicate the Lord.

## CHAPTER IX. On Responsories

[Note: **CHAP. IX. Note 1.** “Responsories from the Italians.” The same is found in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, except that there he says *responsorios*, as in the *Monastic Rule*, chapter “On the Office.” GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “With the choir sounding together”—that is, responding in the same way. In the *Etymologies* he says that the choir responds to what one singer sings. GRIAL.

Bingham, vol. VI of the *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, part 6, thinks that psalms are meant here, which would be sung by one person in such a way that the choir would answer by singing together. See Ferrari, *Bibliotheca*, under “Cantor,” no. 6, who shows that the rite mentioned by Isidore was practiced at Rome in the ninth century and at Milan in the twelfth. AREV.]

1. Responsories were discovered by the Italians long ago and were called by this name because, when one person sings, the choir answers by singing together. Previously each person performed this alone; now sometimes one, sometimes two or three sing together, with the choir responding in most cases.

## CHAPTER X. On Readings

[Note: **CHAP. X. Note 1.** “When a reading is read, silence having been made.” Ambrose, in the preface to the Psalter: “How much effort is expended in the Church to make silence when the readings are read?” GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “Silence having been made.” The Mozarabic Missal inserts, between the first and second epistle after the verse *Psallendo*, the rubric: “Let the presbyter say: Keep silence.” After “then let him listen,” some add “one,” which is unnecessary. AREV.]

1. The tradition of the Jews teaches that the recitation of readings is an ancient institution. For they too, on appointed and prescribed days, use readings from the Law and the Prophets in the synagogues, preserving this practice from the ancient institution of the fathers. A reading is a considerable edification for those who hear it. Therefore, when psalms are sung, all should sing; when prayer is offered, all should pray; when a reading is read, silence having been made, all alike should listen.

2. Even if someone arrives while the reading is being celebrated, he should merely adore the Lord and, having made the sign on his forehead, attentively lend his ear. The time for prayer is open when we all pray; it is also open whenever you wish to pray privately. Under the pretext of prayer, do not miss the reading, because not everyone can always have it available, whereas the opportunity for prayer is at hand; nor should you think that little benefit arises from hearing the reading.

[Col. 0745B] 3. Indeed, prayer itself becomes richer while the mind, nourished by the recent reading, runs through images of the divine matters that it has just heard. For Mary, the sister of Martha, who sat at Jesus’ feet and, while her sister was neglected, listened more attentively to the word, is confirmed by the Lord’s voice to have chosen the good portion (Luke X). Therefore the deacon also calls for silence in a clear voice, so that whether psalms are being sung or a reading is being recited, unity may be preserved by all, and what is proclaimed to all may be heard equally by all.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Books of the Testaments

[Note: **CHAP. XI. Note 1.** “It is called a testament because it has suitable witnesses.” This is a more modest derivation than deriving *testament* from the monument of the testator or *witnesses* from *testament*, both of which he did in Book V of the *Etymologies*. GRIAL.

The Bignaeus edition is mutilated in this and other chapters. In other editions the order of the chapters is somewhat different. Moreover, nearly all these matters concerning the Old and New Testaments are repeated in the *Prologues* and in Book VI, chapters 1 and 2, of the *Etymologies*, and some also in the *Allegories*. Accordingly, the notes on all these passages mutually assist one another when compared with what is said here. AREV.]

1. In the churches of Christ, readings are recited from the Holy Scriptures. Sacred Scripture consists of the old law and the new. The old law is that which was first given to the Jews through Moses and the prophets and is called the Old Testament. It is called a testament because it was written and sealed by suitable witnesses, namely, the prophets. The new law is the Gospel, which is called the New Testament and which was given through Christ, the very Son of God, and through his apostles.

2. The former law is like a root, while the new is like fruit from the root; for from the Law one comes to the Gospel. Indeed, Christ, who has been manifested here, was previously foretold in the Law. Rather, he himself spoke in the prophets, as it is written: “The one who was speaking said, ‘Behold, I am here.’” He first gave the Law as a pedagogue to children, but he now provides the Gospel as the perfect instruction in life for all who have reached maturity.

3. Therefore, in that former law, the good things of the earth were promised to those who worked; here, however, the heavenly kingdom is granted under grace to those who live by faith. The Gospel means “good news,” and truly good news, so that those who receive it may be called children of God. These, then, are the books of the Old Testament, which the leaders of the churches handed down to be read and received for the love of teaching and piety.

4. First, there are five books of the Law, that is, of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. These are followed by sixteen historical books: Joshua son of Nun, and Judges, one book each; Ruth; four books of Kings; two of Chronicles; two of Ezra; and one each of Tobit, Esther, and Judith; and two of Maccabees. Above these there are sixteen prophetic books: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, one book each; and twelve books, one for each of the twelve prophets. These, indeed, are the prophetic books.

[Note: **5.** “After these, eight books in verse.” Cyril, *Catechesis* 4, lists only the first five and says that Jerome denied finding Wisdom written in Hebrew. But Isidore presents himself here as transmitting not his own material but that of others, now in his own words and now in those of others. A little later he says, on the testimony of a certain wise man, that this book was once received by the Hebrews and later rejected. GRIAL.]

5. After these there are eight books written in verse, which are composed in different meters among the Hebrews: the Book of Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the Book of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah. Thus the books of the Old Testament are completed, numbering forty-five.

6. The first books of the New Testament are the four Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. These are followed by the fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul. To them are added seven catholic epistles: those of James, Peter, John, and Jude. There are also the Acts of the twelve apostles, and the seal of all these books is the Apocalypse of John, which is the revelation of Jesus Christ. It concludes all the books both in time and in order.

[Note: **7.** “Because there were seventy-two languages.” Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, says that Ephorus and other writers reported seventy-five peoples and languages on the basis of Moses’ words: “All the souls of Jacob who went down into Egypt were seventy-five.” But it seems that there were plainly seventy-two languages and dialects, as our Scriptures report. The Hebrews also claim to infer this from the number of families; for just as many are counted in Genesis X. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “Seventy-two languages.” See Suárez’s note on the *Allegories*, no. 65, from which it is clear that the reading here should be: “And for this reason Moses chose seventy-two presbyters who would prophesy.” AREV.]

7. These are the seventy-two canonical books, and for this reason Moses chose presbyters who would prophesy. For this reason also Jesus our Lord commanded seventy-two disciples to preach. And because seventy-two languages were spread throughout this world, the Holy Spirit wisely provided that there should be as many books as there were nations, so that the peoples might be built up to receive the grace of faith.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Writers of the Sacred Books

[Note: **CHAP. XII. Note 1.** “And the first part of Samuel.” Diodorus held the same view. He wishes the words of 1 Samuel IX, “For the seer was formerly called by the people what is now called a prophet,” to be the words not of Samuel himself but of the person who collected Samuel’s writings. It was enough for Isidore to indicate that he was speaking not from his own judgment but from Hebrew opinion and tradition. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “Jeremiah published all of Kings as a whole.” This is no more certain. GRIAL.]

1. According to the tradition of the Hebrews, the following are regarded as the writers of the Old Testament. First, Moses wrote the Pentateuch. Joshua son of Nun published his own book. Samuel composed Judges, Ruth, and the first part of Samuel; David wrote the remainder of Samuel through the end. Jeremiah published all of Kings as a single work, since previously it had been dispersed among the histories of the individual kings. The Hebrews think that Moses wrote the Book of Job, while others attribute it to one of the prophets.

[Note: **2.** “Ten wrote the Psalter.” They are the men whose names are prefixed in the titles of the psalms. One might perhaps persuade someone of this, unless they also assigned psalms to Adam and Melchizedek—to the former Psalm 91, and to the latter Psalm 109. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** “The wise men of the synagogue wrote Ezekiel and Esther.” These are Jewish fables. GRIAL.]

2. Ten prophets wrote the Psalter: namely, Moses, David, Solomon, Asaph, Ethan, Jeduthun, Heman, and the sons of Korah—Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. Some say that Ezra, Haggai, and Zechariah also wrote it. Solomon wrote Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Isaiah wrote his own book, and Jeremiah his own book together with its Lamentations. The wise men of the synagogue wrote Ezekiel, the twelve prophets, Daniel, Chronicles, and Esther. Ezra wrote his own book.

[Note: **3.** Whether Ezra restored books that had been destroyed or burned is an ancient question. Natalis Alexander transcribes the words of the ancient Fathers, most of whom deny it, in his *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, dissertation 4, in the fourth age of the world. Those who affirm it have relied on the anonymous author of the Fourth Book of Ezra, chapter XIX. AREV.]

3. After the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, when the Jews had returned to Jerusalem, the same prophet and scribe Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored all these books; he corrected all the volumes of the prophets that had been corrupted by the nations, and arranged the entire Testament in twenty-two books, so that there would be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

[Note: **4.** “The first after Ezra.” What is related about the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, up to the very wording “they might be found,” is also read in Cyril’s fourth catechesis. Justin, Irenaeus, Augustine, Philo, and others likewise reported it. Jerome laughs at the stories about the cells. Neither he nor they lack the attention of our theologians. They disagree with no less intensity over whether all the books of the Old Testament or only the five books of Moses were translated by them. GRIAL.]

4. After Ezra, the Seventy Interpreters produced the first edition from Hebrew into Greek, under Ptolemy, king of Egypt and successor of Alexander, who was devoted to reading and gathered together the books of all nations. Sending many gifts to the temple, he asked Eleazar, who was high priest, to send him six men from each of the twelve tribes of Israel to translate all the books. So that he might assess the reliability of the translation, he gave each of those who had been appointed a separate cell, assigned all the Scriptures to all of them, and ordered them to translate.

5. When they had completed this task in seventy days, he gathered together all their interpretations, which they had produced separately in different cells, with no one approaching any of the others, and brought them into one place. Thus all the books were found to have been translated through the Holy Spirit, so that they agreed not only in meaning but also in wording. This was the first true and divine translation.

6. The churches of all nations first began to study these books, and the first leaders of the churches handed them down after translating them from Greek into Latin. After this, Aquila produced the second edition, and Theodotion and Symmachus, both Jewish proselytes, the third and fourth. Origen discovered the fifth and sixth editions and compared them with the other editions mentioned above. These, therefore, are the only translators who rendered the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek. They are also counted accordingly.

[Note: **7.** As Saint Augustine mentions in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 11. Jerome says that the same thing happened in the New Testament: in Letter 123 to Damasus, he says that there were almost as many copies as there were manuscripts. GRIAL.]

7. The number of Latin translators who translated from Greek into our language is infinite, as Saint Augustine mentions (*On Christian Doctrine* II, 11). “For,” he says, “when a Greek manuscript came into the hands of someone in the early times of the faith, and he acquired some knowledge of both languages, he immediately dared to translate it. Hence it happened that there arose among the Latins an innumerable number of translators.”

[Note: **8.** “More truthful in meaning and clearer in wording.” According to Augustine’s judgment, this praise applies more appropriately to the Itala, or Old, version than to the Hieronymian, or New, version. Thus Augustine says in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 15, no. 22: “Among the translations themselves, the Itala is to be preferred to the others, for it is more faithful in its words while preserving clarity of meaning.” See Sabatier in the preface, no. 28, and *Isidoriana*, chapter 87, no. 23. Mariana, *On the Edition of the Vulgate*, chapter 18, p. 89, observes that Rabanus repeats Isidore’s words in Book II of the *Institutions of the Clergy*, chapter 54. In that passage Mariana shows that the Latin edition of the Vulgate is the same as Jerome’s. AREV.]

8. Jerome alone translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into the Latin language. All the churches everywhere generally use his edition because it is more truthful in meaning and clearer in wording. Solomon is shown to have written the Book of Wisdom by the testimony of the one who says there: “You chose me,” he says, “as king for your people, and you told me to build a temple in your holy name and in the city of your dwelling” (Wis. IX, 7).

9. The Hebrews, as one of their wise men relates, formerly received this work among the canonical Scriptures. But after they seized Christ and killed him, they recalled the very clear testimonies about Christ in the same book, where it says: “The impious said among themselves, ‘Let us seize the righteous man, because he is useless to us and opposed to our works; he claims to possess knowledge of God, and he calls himself the Son of God.’” And below: “For if he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies.” And afterward: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, so that we may learn his reverence and test his patience” (Wis. II). After comparing these passages, they removed the book from the prophetic volumes and prohibited their people from reading it, lest our people reproach them for so evident a sacrilege.

10. Ecclesiasticus was composed by Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem, the grandson of Jesus the priest, whom Zechariah mentions. Among the Latins this book is prefixed with Solomon’s name because of the similarity of its eloquence. Moreover, it is by no means certain who wrote Judith, Tobit, or the books of Maccabees.

[Note: **11.** “The Epistle to the Hebrews.” From Jerome’s catalogue. But now, after the decrees of the later councils, no room for doubt remains. What is said about the Epistles of Peter, James, and John also comes from the same catalogue. As for the Apocalypse, since it had already been received before Jerome’s time, Isidore seems to have disregarded those who in his own day did not accept it; against such people stands the canon of the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 16. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** Isidore himself does not doubt the Epistle to the Hebrews in the *Prologues*. In Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, no. 45, it is said, on the judgment of several Latins, not to be certainly Paul’s. AREV.]

11. In the New Testament, the four books of the Gospels were written individually by the four evangelists. Matthew alone is said to have written in the Hebrew language; the others wrote in Greek. The apostle Paul wrote his Epistles: nine of them he sent to seven churches, and the remainder he sent to his disciples Timothy, Titus, and Philemon. For most Latins it is uncertain whether the Epistle to the Hebrews is his because of the difference in style. Some suspect that Barnabas composed it; others that it was written by Clement.

12. Peter wrote two Epistles in his own name, which are called catholic. Some do not believe that the second is his because of the difference in style and language. James wrote his Epistle, which some likewise deny to be his and think was dictated under his name by another. John himself published three Epistles. Some assert that only the first is his; the remaining two are thought to belong to a certain presbyter named John, whose second tomb, according to Jerome’s judgment, is shown at Ephesus. Jude published his Epistle. Luke composed the Acts of the Apostles from what he heard or saw. John the evangelist wrote the Apocalypse at the same time as he is said to have been exiled to the island of Patmos because of his preaching of the Gospel.

13. These are the writers of the sacred books, speaking through divine inspiration and dispensing heavenly precepts for our instruction. The author of these Scriptures is believed to be the Holy Spirit. For he himself wrote who dictated to his prophets what they were to write. Now, after the origin of the psalms and hymns, and after the number of the sacred books, I shall set out for you what follows.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Praises

[Note: **CHAP. XIII. Note 1.** “Praises.” Isidore himself explains sufficiently and abundantly what he calls *Praises*, and it can be made even clearer to anyone from the Fourth Council of Toledo. It is therefore astonishing how he could have cast such obvious matters into darkness by laboriously insisting that this material, with the order of several chapters reversed, should be placed after the chapter on morning prayers. There was no way for him to discern what *Praises* or morning prayers meant in Isidore. The matter of morning prayers will be treated in its proper place. Here *Praises* means the Alleluia song. In other regions—as is now done everywhere—it is sung before the reading of the Gospel; in Spain that council prescribes that it be sung after the Gospel, canons 10 and 11. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** In Appendix 9 to the *Etymologies* there is a fragment under Isidore’s name concerning various words for *Alleluia*, etc., which belongs to Book VI, chapter 19, of the *Etymologies*, *On Offices*. Bingham also discusses the Alleluia and the psalms of the Alleluia at length in vol. VI of the *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, pp. 41ff. In the Gothic Mass, immediately after the Gospel reading, the *Lauda* was sung; Isidore calls this *Praises*. Those who are unfamiliar with the Gothic rite easily confuse one part of it with another. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 88, no. 71, I indicated that certain Masses composed by Saint Ildefonsus still lie hidden and that, if they were published, they would shed great light on the order and method of the old Hispanic liturgy. But Pedro Manuel Hernández, prefect of the archiepiscopal library of Toledo and a particularly learned man, replied to my inquiry in a letter dated 10 February 1801 that those Masses of which many had spoken were nothing other than the well-known book of Saint Ildefonsus, *On the Perpetual Virginity of Holy Mary*, divided into seven parts. Perhaps each of these parts was recited by the same Saint Ildefonsus on different feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary during that action of the sacrifice which the Mozarabs called the Mass, from the dismissal of the catechumens. Others who speak of these Masses of Saint Ildefonsus are very far from the truth. AREV.]

1. *Praises*—that is, singing the Alleluia—is a song of the Hebrews. Its explanation consists in interpreting two words: “praise of God.” Concerning its mystery, John reports in the Apocalypse that, through revelation by the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly army of angels, like the voice of many waters and like the voice of mighty thunder, saying “Alleluia.”

2. From this no one ought to doubt that, when this mystery of praise is celebrated with worthy faith and devotion, it is joined to the angels. *Alleluia*, like *Amen*, is not translated from Hebrew into Latin, not because it cannot be interpreted, but because, as the teachers say, its antiquity is preserved for the sake of its more sacred authority.

[Note: **3.** “But in the regions of Africa.” From Augustine, Letter 119 to Januarius, chapters 15 and 17. GRIAL.]

3. In the regions of Africa the Alleluia is not sung at all times but only on Sundays and during the fifty days after the Lord’s resurrection, as a sign of the future resurrection and of joy. Among us, however, according to the ancient tradition of the Spanish churches, it is sung at all times except on days of fasting or during Lent; for it is written: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

[Note: **4.** “Our action will not continue until ‘they will praise you.’” These are Augustine’s words, chapter 15. GRIAL.

**Same passage.** Hittorpius printed “in hope of the future,” although he acknowledged that other copies have “in future hope.” In the edition prepared by Cochlaeus, many passages in this chapter and in most of the others are missing, so that the copy may be regarded in certain places as an epitome of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. AREV.]

4. But the fact that Alleluia is sung at the end after the completion of the recitation or preaching of the psalms or lessons is done by the Church in hope of the future, signifying that after the proclamation of the kingdom of heaven—which is preached to the world in this life through both Testaments—our activity will have no future except in the praise of God, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5). Hence also the book of Psalms concludes with praise, so that the same eternal praise may be displayed after the end of the world.

379 **CHAPTER XIV. On the Offertories**

[Note: [Col. 0751C]

**CHAP. XIV. Note 1.** “The offertories, which are sung in the sacrifices,” etc. The Gentiles too used certain more solemn sounds in libations, which consisted for the most part of spondaic feet; hence the name of this meter, which was also called “pontifical,” is known from the verses of Terentianus:

> “That which, melodious in the temples by the sound of its voice,  
> Offends the ears of the one making the libation, and is pleasing, is spondaic.”

In the absence of singers and instruments, the wheels of bells have fulfilled this function according to an already ancient custom. GRIAL.

In the same place. Many manuscripts read “in the sound of the trumpet.” One has “in voice, preaching, singing.” For *accendimur* (“we are stirred”), two manuscripts have *accendimus* (“we stir”). Hittorpius, with four manuscripts, printed: “We rejoice aloud”; one manuscript added, “in that high place,” and so forth. AREV.]

1. The offertories, which are sung in honor of the sacrifices, are evidence from the Ecclesiasticus that the ancients were accustomed to sing when victims were sacrificed. For it says:

> “The priest,” it says, “extended his hand for the libation, and poured out some of the blood of the grape, and poured forth upon the foundation of the altar a divine fragrance to the Most High Prince. Then the sons of Aaron shouted on their long trumpets, and they sounded them, and made a great voice heard as a memorial before God” (Eccli. L, 16).

Likewise now, through the sound of the trumpet—that is, through vocal proclamation and song—we are stirred, and together, proclaiming praises to the Lord with heart and mouth, we rejoice in that true sacrifice by whose blood the world was saved.

**CHAPTER XV. On the Mass and Prayers**

[Note: [Col. 0751C]

**CHAP. XV. Note 1.** “Whose celebration.” It was handed down by Peter. Some say that, in addition to the words of consecration, he used three prayers at the beginning; others say that he used only the Lord’s Prayer. Later, various prayers and ceremonies were added by different persons, as we see in the liturgies of the Fathers. Augustine also refers Paul’s words, “The rest I will set in order when I come” (1 Cor. XI), to this matter, in Epistle 118, chapter 6. Isidore merely reports the order that, in his own time, had been ordered at the Fourth Council of Toledo to be observed throughout Spain and Gaul. This order, however, is not retained in precisely the same form in the Mozarabic Missal, as James Pamelius also observed. GRIAL.]

1. The order of the Mass and of the prayers by which the sacrifices offered to God are consecrated was first instituted by Saint Peter, and the whole world celebrates it in one and the same manner. The first of these prayers is an admonition directed to the people, so that they may be stirred to entreat God. The second is an invocation addressed to God, asking him mercifully to receive the prayers and offerings of the faithful. The third is poured out for those who offer, or for the faithful departed, so that through the same sacrifice they may obtain forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 0751D]

**2. “Then the fifth illation is introduced.”** Just as the Greeks call payments *eisphoras* (εἰσφοράς), so our people call them *illationes*; this is clear from Cassiodorus, book XII, letter 16. The Council of Toledo VII, canon 4, also used the term *illatio*: “Therefore, let what has evidently been rashly presumed in disorder up to now not happen hereafter; let each of the bishops of the aforesaid province request no more than two solidi annually from each of the basilicas of his diocese, according to the synod of Braga.” The *illatio* seems to lie midway between exaction and offering, or between payment and gift. Just as emperors softened the harsher designation of a payment by calling it an *illatio*, so ecclesiastical men thought they spoke more humbly if they called what they otherwise termed gifts and presents an *illatio*. The same expression is also used in more than one place for a servile obligation. Hence the phrase in the canon: “We offer to your splendid Majesty from your own gifts and donations.” “We offer” would have seemed too bold had it not been followed by “from your own gifts and donations.” But, as I myself think, *illatio* referred both to the bread and wine before they were offered and to the very formula of prayer by which they were brought forward. Thus *illatio* meant both what was brought forward, from which the offering was to be made, and the prayer itself by which it was brought forward, so that the offering might be made from the *illatio*. GRIAL.

In the same place. “That all, reconciled to one another in charity, worthily”—others read *digni* (“worthy”); others, “that all may be worthy toward one another through the charity of reconciliation,” or “that through the charity of reconciliation they may be worthy toward one another.” Hittorpius did not dislike these last two readings, since they refer to the reconciliation prescribed in the Gospel before we offer the gift at the altar. Grial’s note mistakenly had *formula ipsa precationis, quam inferebantur*; I restored *qua*, as shortly afterward: *precatio ipsa qua inferebatur*. In the Mozarabic Missal this first prayer is properly called the “Mass,” although various other prayers precede it in that same Missal. The second prayer, following the prayer called the Mass, has no proper name. The third prayer is called “After the Names,” namely, of those offering and of the departed. The fourth prayer is called “For Peace”; in the Mozarabic Missal this is written incorrectly as “For the Father,” as Lesleus observes in his notes on the Mozarabic Missal, page 1. The fifth is called the *Illation* in that same Missal, as it is by Isidore. The sixth is called “After the Day Before” in the cited Missal, although the reason for this designation is unknown. In the Gallican liturgies it is called “After the Mysteries” or “After the Secrets.” Finally, the seventh is the Lord’s Prayer, as in Isidore. Before this prayer, however, the Constantinopolitan Creed is recited according to the prescription of the Third Council of Toledo; in the following chapter Isidore calls it Nicene, because it was commonly so called. Many matters relating to the Gothic liturgy can be illuminated from the brief exposition of the ancient Gallican liturgy that Martene published, with an erudite preface, in volume V of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, pages 86 and following. AREV.]

2. After this, the fourth is introduced for the kiss of peace, so that all, reconciled to one another in charity, may be joined worthily to the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, because Christ’s indivisible body admits no dissension from anyone. Then the fifth illation is introduced in the sanctification of the offering. In it, the whole assembly of earthly creatures and heavenly powers is summoned to the praise of God, and “Hosanna in the highest” is sung, because, when the Savior was born from the line of David, salvation reached the world even to the heights.

[Note: [Col. 0753D]

**3. “In this prayer there are seven petitions,”** as the Fathers wrote. Each petition receives the response “Amen,” except the fourth, “Give us this day our daily bread,” to which the response is, “Because you are God.” GRIAL.

In the same place. Hittorpius, with his manuscripts, printed: “the confirmation of the sacrament, so that the offering … may be confirmed as the body and blood of Christ.” He does not approve *conformatio* (“conformation”) and *conformetur* (“may be conformed”), because in the books of the Roman Order *confirmare* means to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to others; that distribution may also be understood here. AREV.]

3. There follows, therefore, the sixth, the conformation of the sacrament, so that the offering made to God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, may be conformed to the body and blood of Christ. The last of these is the prayer in which our Lord taught his disciples to pray, saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” In this prayer, as the holy Fathers wrote, seven petitions are contained; but in the first three eternal things are requested, and in the following four temporal things, which nevertheless are requested in order to obtain the eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0753D]

**4. “From the example.”** Older editions read “according to the example.” AREV.]

4. For when we say, “Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth,” these three things indeed begin here, but are hoped for in that life, where the sanctification of God, his will, and his kingdom will remain immortally in his saints. But daily bread, which is attributed either to the soul or to the flesh, is requested here; here also, after the provision of food, forgiveness is sought, following the example of fraternal indulgence; here we ask that we not fall into the temptation of sin. Here, finally, after everything else, we implore God’s help so that we may be delivered from evils. But there none of these things exists.

[Col. 0753C] 5. The Savior therefore taught this prayer, in which both the hope of the faithful and the confession of sins are contained. Concerning it the prophet, foretelling, says: “And it shall be that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II, 32). These, then, are the seven prayers of the sacrifice commended by evangelical and apostolic teaching. The rationale of this number seems to have been established either because of the sevenfold universality of the holy Church or because of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, by whose gift the things introduced are sanctified.

382 **CHAPTER XVI. On the Nicene Creed**

[Note: [Col. 0753D]

**CHAP. XVI. Note 1.** “For all …” Others read: “For he tramples upon all the impieties of error and faithlessness,” or “blasphemies.” For *vel* (“or”), others have *et* (“and”), which amounts to the same thing. AREV.]

1. The Creed, which is proclaimed by the people at the time of the sacrifice, was composed at the Council of Nicaea through the agreement of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers. Its rule of true faith surpasses such great mysteries of the doctrine of faith that it speaks concerning every part of the faith, and there is scarcely any heresy to which it does not respond in its individual words or statements. For it tramples upon all the blasphemies of impiety and faithlessness; therefore, in all the Churches it is proclaimed by the people with the same confession.

**CHAPTER XVII. On Blessings**

[Note: [Col. 0753D]

**CHAP. XVII. Note 1.** “The blessing.” In the Mozarabic Missal, proper blessings are assigned to nearly every Mass. This one is from the seventh Sunday after Pentecost. [Col. 0754D] GRIAL.

In the same place. “May the Lord illuminate his face,” etc. Thus the Gothic codex, following the Septuagint interpretation; in printed books of the Vulgate edition other words have been substituted. GRIAL.

Others read, “and I will bless him.” Shortly afterward: “May he guard you, show his face to you, and have mercy,” etc. AREV.]

1. That a blessing is given to the people by priests is revealed and confirmed by the ancient blessing through Moses, in which priests are commanded to bless the people under the sacrament of the threefold invocation. For the Lord said to Moses:

> “Thus you shall bless my people, and I will bless them: May the Lord bless you and guard you; may the Lord illuminate his face upon you and have mercy on you; may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace” (Num. VI, 24).

**CHAPTER XVIII. On the Sacrifice**

[Note: [Col. 0754D]

**CHAP. XVIII. Note 1.** See Cyprian, Letter 3, book II, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Cup*. GRIAL.

In the same place. *Traderetur* (“was to be handed over”). Others read *pateretur* (“was to suffer”). AREV.]

1. The sacrifice offered to God by Christians was first instituted by Christ our Lord and teacher, when he entrusted his body and blood to the apostles before he was handed over, as is read in the Gospel: “Jesus,” it says, “took bread and the cup, and, blessing, gave them to them” (Matt. XXVI, 26). King Melchizedek of Salem first offered this sacrament figuratively, as a type of the body and blood of Christ, and first expressed imaginatively the mystery of so great a sacrifice, presenting a likeness of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the eternal priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

[Note: [Col. 0754D]

**2. “Which was not from morning until evening of the world.”** These are Cyprian’s words. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Therefore the apostles did not communicate while fasting.” See chapter 54, “Clearly,” in *De consecratione*, distinction 2, GRIAL.

For *imperata*, others have *imperatae*, which is clearer. For “therefore this is done,” others have “therefore this is done today.” AREV.]

2. Christians were therefore commanded to celebrate this sacrifice, with the Jewish victims abandoned and brought to an end—victims whose celebration had been commanded under the servitude of the former people. What we do, then, is what the Lord himself did for us: he offered it not in the morning but after supper, toward evening. Christ therefore had to fulfill it toward evening, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might indicate the evening of the world. The apostles, accordingly, did not communicate while fasting, because it was necessary first to fulfill that typical Passover and then to pass anew to the true sacrament of the Passover.

[Col. 0755A] [Note: [Col. 0755C]

**3.** I defended Isidore’s Catholic teaching concerning the holy Eucharist in *Isidoriana*, chapter 30, sections 15 and following, against Bingham and other heterodox writers. [Col. 0755D] AREV.]

3. For in this sacrament it was then done that the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord while not fasting. But now throughout the universal Church they are always received by those who are fasting. For it pleased the Holy Spirit, through the apostles, that in honor of so great a sacrament the Lord’s body should first enter the mouth of a Christian before any other food; and therefore this custom is observed throughout the world. The bread that we break is the body of Christ (1 Cor. X), who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). The wine, however, is his blood, and this is what is written: “I am the true vine” (John VI). But bread is called Christ’s body because it strengthens the body; wine, because it produces blood in the flesh, is therefore referred to Christ’s blood.

[Col. 0755B] [Note: [Col. 0755D]

**4. “The Lord’s cup” through “joined together”:** all these are Cyprian’s words. GRIAL.

In the same place. The words of Saint Cyprian in Fell’s edition, Letter 63, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Cup*, are not all copied by Isidore. AREV.]

4. Although these things are visible, once sanctified by the Holy Spirit they pass into the sacrament of the divine body. Therefore, as the most holy Cyprian says:

> “The Lord’s cup is offered mixed with wine and water, because we see the people signified by the water, while in the wine the blood of Christ is shown. When water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are joined to Christ, and the people of believers are united and joined to him in whom they have believed. This joining and union of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated from one another, just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ.

5. “Thus, in the sanctifying of the Lord’s cup, water alone cannot be offered, just as wine alone cannot. For if someone offers only wine, the blood of Christ begins to exist without us; but if there is only water, the people begin to exist without Christ. When both are mixed and, through a confused union, joined to one another, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is accomplished. Thus the Lord’s cup is neither water alone nor wine alone unless the two are mixed with one another. Likewise, the body of the Lord cannot be only flour or only water unless both have been united and joined together and solidified by the structure of one bread.

6. “By this very sacrament, our people too are shown to be united, so that, just as many grains gathered, ground, and mixed together make one bread, so in Christ, who is the heavenly bread, we may know ourselves to be one body, joined to him and united as our number.”**

[Note: [Col. 0755D]

**7.** Some say that the Eucharist should be received daily unless some sin intervenes. See chapter 13, *Daily*, in *De consecratione*, distinction 2. GRIAL.

In the same place. “For this is to receive unworthily.” Augustine, Letter 118. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Some say,” etc. See *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 22; Apostolic Canons 8 and 9; Justin, *Apology*, on the Lord’s Day; Basil, Letter 289; and more recent writers who published several works on frequent communion against Arnauld. AREV.]

7. Some say that the Eucharist should be received daily unless some sin intervenes; for we ask that this bread be given to us daily at the Lord’s command, saying: “Give us this day our daily bread.” They speak rightly, provided that they receive it with religion, devotion, and humility, and do not do so presumptuously, trusting in their own righteousness. But if their sins are such as to remove them from the altar like a dead person, they must first perform penance, and only then receive this saving medicine. For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself (1 Cor. XI). [Col. 0756B] This is what it means to receive unworthily: to receive it at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

[Note: [Col. 0755D]

**8.** “But if the sins are not so great.” Words of Hilary or Augustine cited by Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter “If they are not so great.” GRIAL.

[Col. 0756C] In the same place. This passage is commonly cited against those who oppose frequent communion. Petavius, *Dissertationes ecclesiasticae*, book II, chapter 3, volume IV, page 185, observes that Isidore took this from Augustine, Letter 118, chapter 3, to which Isidore prefixed: “But if the sins are such,” etc. Zaccaria, volume XII of *Literary History*, page 451, approves Lesleus’s conjecture that one should read *diu abstinens probetur* (“let one who abstains for a long time be tested”) instead of *diu abstinendus*, or *abstentus prohibetur*, because this is how it is read in the Bolognese Albornozian Codex and because, as Lesleus observes on page 500, the Mozarabic Missal speaks of someone who abstains voluntarily, not of someone prohibited by another. The same Lesleus, page 529, discusses the frequent reception of the holy Eucharist among the ancients. Hittorpius observes that one should read “if the sins are not so great,” and that other copies wrongly omit *non*; for *excommunicandus* (“to be excommunicated”), which he had found in one manuscript, he reads *excommunicatus* (“excommunicated”), and for *abstinendus* (“to be restrained”), *abstentus* (“restrained”), while elsewhere he found *abstinens* (“abstaining”). I do not dislike *prohibetur* (“is prohibited”), that is, by himself. AREV.]

8. But if the sins are not so great that someone should be judged worthy of excommunication, he ought not to separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body, lest perhaps, while he is forbidden as one who must abstain for a long time, he be separated from the body of Christ. For it is manifest that those who touch his body live. Hence it must also be feared that, while someone is separated for a long time from the body of Christ, he may remain alienated from salvation, since he himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). Whoever has now ceased to sin should not cease to communicate.

[Note: [Col. 0756D]

**9.** “Let us reread the books of Kings” through “may approach”: these are Jerome’s words in chapter I of the Epistle to Titus. GRIAL.]

9. Married persons, however, must abstain from intercourse; for many days they ought to devote themselves to prayer, and only then approach the body of Christ. Let us reread the books of Kings, and we shall find that the priest Abimelech was unwilling first to give David and his young men the bread of the Presence unless he had first asked whether the young men were pure from women—not from foreign women, certainly, but from their own wives—and unless he had heard from them that they had abstained from marital relations since yesterday and the day before. He would not have granted the bread he had initially refused unless this were so (1 Sam. XXI).

10. The difference between the bread of the Presence and the body of Christ is as great as that between shadow and body, image and reality, and copies of future things and the things themselves prefigured by those copies. [Col. 0757A] Therefore, several days should be chosen during which a person lives more continently beforehand, so that he may be worthy to approach so great a sacrament.

386 11. We believe that offering sacrifice for the repose of the faithful departed, or praying for them, is a practice handed down by the apostles themselves, since it is observed throughout the whole world. For the Catholic Church maintains this everywhere; unless it believed that sins are forgiven the faithful departed, it would neither make almsgiving for their spirits nor offer sacrifice to God on their behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0757D]

**12.** “The souls of the departed,” through the end of the chapter, are Augustine’s words in the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 110. GRIAL.

In the same place. The same doctrine appears in Augustine’s *City of God*, book XXI, chapter 24, and in *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*. AREV.]

12. For when the Lord also says, “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII), he demonstrates that some sins are to be forgiven there and cleansed by a certain purgatorial fire. Thus Saint Augustine said in a certain passage:

> “There is no doubt that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when sacrifice is offered for them or almsgiving is performed, provided that each person prepared some merit for himself while he was still living in the body, through which these things done on his behalf may benefit him.

13. “For they do not benefit everyone. And why do they not benefit everyone, except because of the difference in the life each person led in the body? For the very good they are expressions of thanksgiving; for those who are not very bad they are acts of propitiation; for the very bad, even if no assistance is afforded the dead, they are at least consolations for the living. But those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be complete remission, or at least so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.”**

**CHAPTER XIX. On the Offices of Tierce, Sext, and None**

[Col. 0757C]

[Note: [Col. 0757D]

**CHAP. XIX. Note 1.** See Cyprian’s book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and Tertullian, *On Fasting*. GRIAL.

For *ratis*, others have *satis*; perhaps it should be *statis*. In some manuscripts: “The Trinity, thrice entreated, was honored,” that is, “invoked.” An old edition had “the determined Trinity.” Grial had *demensionibus*. The reading of Cochleius’s edition should not be omitted: “And likewise, from Tierce to Sext and from there to None, at equal intervals of light, the undivided Trinity was worshiped, thrice invoked each day according to fixed measurements.” On the prayer of Tierce, Sext, and None, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 3, verse 86, and *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19, with the note to section 62; that entire chapter concerns the subject of this work, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. AREV.]

1. Daniel and the three young men devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplication (Dan. VI, 13), so that the three hours extending from sunrise to the time of prayer might declare to us reverence for the Trinity. Likewise, at Tierce, at Sext, and then at None, with the intervals of light bounded by fixed measures, the Trinity was worshiped, invoked three times each day. This too serves as evidence for the venerable Trinity: the Holy Spirit descended to earth at the third hour, that is, in its proper place, number, and time, to fill the grace that Christ promised (Acts II).

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**2.** *Mundialibusque.* Perhaps one should read *dialibusque*, or “daily,” so that it may be contrasted with “nightly.” AREV.

In the same place. “Although,” etc. Others read: “Even if the daytime celebration is calculated through the fourfold number …”; that is, the quaternity is signified, because the world, etc. AREV.]

2. At the sixth hour Christ suffered, and prolonged the torments of the cross until the ninth. Through such a sacrament, at the lawful times for prayer, the perfection of the Trinity is either celebrated with praises or entreated with prayers in intervals of three hours. The daytime celebration may also be calculated by the number four up to the evening office, because by fours the world, divided into four parts, is signified as saved in the Trinity. Likewise, in the night, military watches and vigils are divided into four parts and separated by intervals of three hours, so that even in these nightly and worldly (*mundialibusque*) offices the mystery of the Trinity may be revered.

**CHAPTER XX. On Vespers**

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**CHAP. XX. Note 1.** *Altario.* Isidore, along with others, frequently uses *altarium* and *altarii*. AREV.]

1. The evening office is the end of the daytime office and the setting of the alternating light; its solemn celebration is found in the Old Testament. Indeed, it was customary at this time for the sacrifices of the ancients to be offered and for spices and incense to be burned upon the altar (Exod. XXIX). The hymn-singing king who fulfilled a priestly office bears witness, saying: “Let my prayer rise like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL).

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**2.** “So that the time itself of evening,” through “of the age,” are Cyprian’s words in the cited letter. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Might show the evening of the age.” Others read, “might show the end of the evening of the age.” AREV.]

2. In the New Testament also, at the time when our Lord and Savior first entrusted the mystery of his body and blood to the apostles as they were dining, so that the time itself of the sacrifice might show the evening of the age, it is therefore fitting for us at these times to be present before the sight of God in honor and remembrance of so great mysteries, to resound in his worship, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers and likewise rejoicing in his praises. Vespers is named from the star called Vesper, which rises as the sun declines. Concerning it the prophet says: “And he causes evening to go forth over the children of men” (Job XXXVIII).

**CHAPTER XXI. On Compline**

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**CHAP. XXI. Note 1.** The entire chapter is taken from the letter *On the Observance of Vigils*, 36, in Jerome, volume IX. GRIAL.]

1. Concerning the celebration of Compline, we find the same practice also in the examples of the Fathers, when the prophet David says: “If I enter upon my bed, if I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI). Who would not be astonished at such devotion of spirit in the love of God, that he should entirely deny himself sleep, without which human bodies necessarily fail, until the king and prophet found in his breast a place and temple to be built for the Lord? This ought powerfully to admonish us that, if we wish to be the Lord’s place and desire to be regarded as his dwelling or temple, we should imitate the examples of the saints as far as we can, lest what is written be said of us: “They slept their sleep, and found nothing” (Ps. LXXV), and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXII. On the Antiquity of Vigils**

[Note: [Col. 0759C]

**CHAP. XXII. Note 1.** Most of this material is taken piecemeal from various parts of the same letter. GRIAL.

[Col. 0759D] “For at this time the destroying angel,” from Jerome’s commentary on Matthew XXV. GRIAL.]

1. Devotion to vigils is ancient, a familiar good among all the saints. The prophet Isaiah cried out to the Lord, saying: “At night my spirit watches for you, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI, 9). David also, consecrated with royal and prophetic oil, sings thus: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. CXVIII, 62). For at this time the destroying angel passed through and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exod. XII).

2. Therefore we too must keep watch, lest we be mixed with the danger of the Egyptians. In the Gospel the Savior also affirmed that he would come during these very hours. Hence he rouses his hearers to keep watch, saying: “Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Matt. XXIV). “Whether,” he says, “he comes at the evening hour, or at midnight, or at the crowing of the rooster, and finds them watching, blessed are those servants. Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Luke XII).

[Note: [Col. 0759D]

**3.** “With all the prisoners listening.” The word *cunctis* (“all”) is not found in Jerome or in Acts XVI, and perhaps, through the error of scribes who wrote sometimes *vinctis* (“prisoners”) and sometimes *cunctis*, both eventually became established. GRIAL.

In the same place. “For,” etc. The material from here to the end of the chapter was absent from the old editions; Bignaeus supplied it from the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious, chapter 130, and from Rabanus, book II *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 9. It genuinely appears in Isidore’s manuscript codices. AREV.]

3. He taught vigils not only by words but also confirmed them by example. For the Gospel bears witness: “Jesus was spending the night in prayer to God” (Acts XVI, 25). Paul and Silas are likewise remembered as praying around midnight in the public prison and singing a hymn, with all the prisoners listening.
