Suddenly there was an earthquake, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors opened of their own accord, and everyone’s chains were loosed.

[Note: [Col. 0759D]

**4.** *Nyctages*, or also *Nystages* or *Nystazontes*. *Etymologies*, book VIII, chapter 5. GRIAL.]

4. Therefore, during these hours we ought to practice frequent psalmody and prayer in the holy offices and await our end—or, if it should come during such an activity—with confidence. There is, however, a certain kind of heretics who consider sacred vigils superfluous and unproductive for spiritual work. They say that God’s commands are being rashly violated: he made night for rest, just as he made day for labor. These heretics are called in Greek *Nyctages*, that is, “sleepy ones.”

**CHAPTER XXIII. On Matins**

[Note: [Col. 0759D]

**CHAP. XXIII. Note 1.** The morning prayers mentioned here are what we call Lauds, as is clear from Cassian, book III *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, chapters 3, 4, and 8. After the vigils, a Mass followed after cockcrow; then came what we call Lauds, which Cassian calls the morning solemnity, chapters 4 and 6. Psalm CXLVIII, “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” with the following psalms, was sung during it. The psalms assigned to the “new,” as he calls it, solemnity—that which we call Prime—were Psalm L, “Have mercy on me, O God,” Psalm LXII, “O God, my God, I seek you at dawn,” and Psalm LXXXIX, “Lord, you have been our refuge.” Thus the Lauds of the Western Church seem to contain both of theirs—that is, the ancient morning solemnity and the new one—and something more besides. For other psalms were assigned to the new one, that is, Prime. GRIAL.

In the same place. In several editions and manuscript codices this entire chapter and the following one are missing. In Grial’s edition the text is punctuated as: “was instituted. At first,” etc. AREV.]

1. The same prophet David bears witness to the antiquity and authority of Matins, saying: “In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper”; and elsewhere: “My eyes have anticipated you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your words.” Cassian, however, says that the office of the morning solemnity, although recently instituted, was first established at the monastery of Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born from a virgin for the redemption of the human race. From there, the custom of celebrating it spread throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0760D]

**2.** Grial reads *radianti* (“shining”). AREV.]

2. We pray at dawn, therefore, so that Christ’s resurrection may be celebrated. For at the radiance of the morning light our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld, when the light that had set for sinners at Christ’s death began to rise for the faithful. At the same time, the hope of the future resurrection is believed by all, when the righteous and everyone else, rising from this temporal death as from the sleep of slumber, will awaken.

**CHAPTER XXIV. On the Lord’s Day**

[Note: [Col. 0760D]

**CHAP. XXIV. Note 1.** Almost everything is taken from Augustine’s Letter 119 to Januarius, chapter 10. GRIAL.

In the same place. On “the Lord’s Day,” etc., consult the Apostolic Fathers, with Cotelerius’s notes, volume I, page 47, and *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 18, section 19, with the note. AREV.]

1. The apostles themselves established the Lord’s Day as a religious solemnity, because on it our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is therefore called the Lord’s Day so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and the attractions of the world, we may devote ourselves exclusively to divine worship, giving this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection that we possess in it.

2. For just as our Lord Jesus Christ and our Savior rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too will rise at the end of the world. Hence on the Lord’s Day we pray standing, which is a sign of the future resurrection. The whole Church does this: it exists in the pilgrimage of mortality and awaits until the end of the world what was prefigured in the body of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn from the dead.

**CHAPTER XXV. On the Sabbath**

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

**CHAP. XXV. Note 1.** “The Sabbath was given,” through “is interpreted,” from the same letter, chapter 10. GRIAL.

In the same place. “The Lord’s Day, however,” through “succeeded,” from chapter 13. GRIAL.

“Declared.” Others read “celebrated.” For the matter itself, see again the Apostolic Fathers, the cited edition, volume I, page 43, and Fabricius, *Bibliographia*, page 452, who lists in great number writers discussing the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath. AREV.]

1. The Sabbath was given to the former people to be observed bodily in leisure, so that it might be a figure of rest; hence “Sabbath” is interpreted as “rest.” The Lord’s Day, however, was revealed not to the Jews but to Christians through the Lord’s resurrection, and from that time it began to have its own festival. For it is the first day, which is found after the seventh as the eighth. Hence in Ecclesiastes, to signify the two Testaments, it is said: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. XI).

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

**2.** Others read: “There was none until Christ the Lord, who, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him.” This is better. AREV.]

2. At first the Sabbath alone was commanded to be celebrated, because previously there was only the rest of the dead. [Col. 0761B] But there was no resurrection of anyone who, rising from the dead, would not die again, over whom death would no longer rule (Rom. VI). After such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body, so that it might go before the Church in its Head, which the body of the Church hoped for at the end, the Lord’s Day—that is, the eighth, which is also the first—succeeded it as a festival.

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

**3.** “It is evident,” through “was given,” from the same sermon, 251. GRIAL.]

3. It is evident that this day too is solemn in the sacred Scriptures. For it is the first day of the world; on it the angels were created; on it also Christ rose from the dead; on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles; on the same day manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness. For thus the Lord says: “For six days you shall gather manna, but on the sixth day you shall gather twice as much” (Exod. XVI). For the sixth day is the parasceve, which is placed before the Sabbath.

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

4. “But the Sabbath is the seventh day,” etc., from Sermon 91, which contains the same material as Origen, Homily 7 on Exodus, chapter 15. GRIAL.]

4. The Sabbath, however, is the seventh day, which is followed by the Lord’s Day, 392 on which manna first came from heaven. Hence let the Jews understand that even then our Lord’s Day was placed before the Jewish Sabbath; even then it was indicated that on their Sabbath no grace descended to them from heaven, but on our Lord’s Day, on which the Lord first rained down manna.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0761D]

CHAPTER XXVI, no. 1. In one manuscript, in Hittorp, *gremio* had been substituted for *imperio*, which he himself perhaps thinks is not incorrect. In the Isidorian materials, chapter 95, no. 15, I observed that in Vatican Codex 1267 this chapter 26 is presented as a sermon of Saint Isidore. For more on this, see, if desired, the Isidorian materials, chapter 72, nos. 17 and following, where I also included the preface of Constantine Cajetanus to this sermon. The Regiovat. Codex 125, which also contains this sermon, agrees more closely with our edition than with Cajetanus’s text. AREV.]

1. The day of the Lord’s Nativity was established by the Fathers as a solemn feast of obligation for this reason: on it Christ willed to be born bodily for the redemption of the world, coming forth from the Virgin’s womb, he who was in the Father’s authority. [Col. 0762A] The reason for his assumption of flesh is this. After that first parent, deceived by empty hope through the devil’s envy, fell, he immediately, an exile and ruined, transmitted the root of wickedness and sin throughout his whole race. Every generation of mortals increasingly grew toward evil, crimes having been spread everywhere; and, what was worse, it served the worship of every kind of idol.

[Note: [Col. 0762D]

2. “He should be clothed in flesh.” Cajetanus: “he should assume flesh.” AREV.]

2. Therefore, wishing to put an end to sin, God provided instruction through the Word, the Law, the prophets, signs, afflictions, and miracles. But when the world, even after such admonition, did not recognize its errors, God sent his Son so that he might be clothed in flesh, appear to human beings, and heal sinners. He came in human form because he could not be known by human beings through himself. In order to be seen, the Word became flesh by assuming flesh, not by being changed into flesh. For he assumed humanity but did not lose divinity. Thus the same one is both God and human: in the nature of God, equal to the Father; in the nature of a human being, made mortal among us, for us, and from us, remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, so that he might free what he had made.

3. This, then, is the great solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity; this is the new and glorious festival of this day: the coming of God to human beings. Accordingly, this day is called “Nativity” because Christ was born on it. We customarily observe it with festive solemnity as the yearly cycle returns, so that the day on which Christ was born may be recalled to memory.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Epiphany

[Note: [Col. 0762D]

CHAPTER XXVII, no. 1. “Christ,” etc. Cochleus: “Christ lying in the manger, and they worshiped him, offering him appropriate gifts of the Trinity—gold, incense, and myrrh—to the King, God, and most pure human being.” For *in praesepi*, some have *in praesepe*, which is by no means absurd. See the notes to Sedulius, pp. 104, 203, and 307. AREV.]

1. The apostolic men therefore marked the day of the Epiphany with festive solemnity, because on it the Savior was revealed by a star, when the Magi found Christ lying in the manger and, worshiping him, offered appropriate gifts to the Trinity: gold, incense, and myrrh—to the King, God, and one destined to suffer. They therefore consecrated this day with annual celebration so that the world might acknowledge the Lord whom the heavenly elements revealed.

2. Indeed, on that same day the same Jesus was also baptized in the Jordan’s washing; and when heaven was opened, the testimony of the descending Holy Spirit declared him to be the Son of God (Matt. III). The name of this day derives from the fact that he appeared to the nations, and it is called “Epiphany.” For *epiphany* in Greek means “appearance” or “manifestation” in Latin. This day therefore received that name for three reasons: either because Christ was then manifested to the peoples in his baptism; or because on that day he was revealed to the Magi by the rising of the star; or because he was manifested to many through his first sign, when water was changed into wine.

[Note: [Col. 0763C]

3. Cassian, *Conference* 10. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The letters of the Alexandrian bishop are also sent after that day,” says Cassian. GRIAL.

Ibid. Blanchinus, *Evangeliarium Quadragesimale*, vol. II, p. 553, presents a dissertation, or letter, of Francis de la Torre, in which many matters concerning the rite of announcing Easter on the day of the Epiphany are explained; this rite also flourished in Italy. Benedict XIV should likewise be consulted, *On the Feasts of the Lord*, under the feast of the Epiphany, § 76. AREV.]

3. Cassian reports that among the Egyptians the day of the Nativity and the solemnity of the Epiphany are celebrated not separately, as in the western provinces, but in the festival of a single day. Letters of the Alexandrian bishop are also sent throughout all the churches and monasteries of Egypt, announcing both the beginning of Lent and the day of Easter.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Palm Sunday

[Note: [Col. 0763C]

CHAPTER XXVIII, no. 1. “He is said to have sat upon the colt.” And shortly afterward, “which he came by sitting upon.” Ambrose likewise says: “The colt is sat upon by the she-ass.” GRIAL.]

1. Palm Sunday is celebrated because on it our Lord and Savior, as the prophet sang, is said to have sat upon a colt while making his way toward Jerusalem. Then, as he proceeded with palm branches, a multitude of peoples cried out to meet him: “Hosanna; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (Zech. IX; Matt. XXI; John XII). For the palm branches signified the victory by which the Lord was to overcome death by dying and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0763C]

2. “They call it *Capitilavium*.” Augustine, Letter 118, chapter 7: “But if you ask why the custom of washing also arose, nothing more plausible occurs to me, when I consider the matter, than that the bodies of those to be baptized, soiled through the observance of Lent, would be brought to the font with offense to the senses unless they were washed on some day. This day, which in Spain was apparently Palm Sunday, was in Africa the fifth day, Holy Thursday, as is clear from this passage of Augustine; for he adds: ‘But that day was chosen especially for this purpose, on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated annually,’ etc. This custom had become so established in Africa that they even considered abolishing or at least transferring to another day the washing of the feet, which fell on the same day. Thus Augustine, Letter 119 to Januarius, chapter 18: ‘As for the washing of feet, since the Lord commended this on account of the example of humility—which he had come to teach, as he himself subsequently explained—the question arose at what time such an important matter could most fittingly be taught also by deed; and the time presented itself when that commendation would remain more religiously fixed in the mind. But lest it seem to belong to the very sacrament of baptism, many refused to receive it as a custom. Some did not hesitate to remove it from the custom altogether. Others, in order to commend it at this more sacred time and distinguish it from the sacrament of baptism, chose either the third day of the octave, because the number three is especially prominent in many sacraments, or even the eighth day itself, in order to perform it then.’ GRIAL.

Ibid. *Capitilavium*. In addition to Grial’s learned annotation, see Macri’s *Hierolexicon*, Ducange’s *Glossary*, and the writers on ecclesiastical antiquities. Some write *capitalavium*, but in the *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 18, no. 14, *capitilavium* had already been published. I have made several observations there concerning this most ancient rite, and they are relevant here as well. AREV.]

2. By the colt upon which he came to Jerusalem while sitting, he indicated the simple hearts of the Gentiles, whom, by presiding over and governing them, he was leading to the vision of peace. On this day the Creed is handed over to the competentes, because of the proximity of the solemnity of the Lord’s Easter, so that, since they are already hastening to receive God’s grace, they may recognize the faith they are to profess. The common people therefore call this day *Capitilavium*, because it is then customary to wash the heads of the infants who are to be anointed, lest they should approach the anointing with heads soiled by the observance of Lent.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Lord’s Supper

[Note: [Col. 0764D]

CHAPTER XXIX, no. 1. “To commend the example of humility.” Augustine, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. Others: “which was also fitting for the most powerful.” AREV.]

1. The Lord’s Supper—that is, the fifth day of the final week of Lent—is the day on which our Lord and Savior, after completing that typological Passover and passing over to the true Passover, first handed on the mystery of his body and blood to the apostles (Matt. XXVI); on it, after the heavenly sacraments, the deceitful and treacherous disciple received his price from the Jews and sold Christ’s blood (John XIII). On that day also, rising from the supper, the Savior washed the disciples’ feet in order to commend the example of humility, which he had come to teach, as he himself subsequently explained. This was especially fitting, so that by deed he might teach what he had previously urged the disciples to observe.

[Note: [Col. 0764D]

2. It is so certain that on the fifth day of Holy Week the altars, the walls and pavements of the church were customarily washed that traces of this custom still remain in some churches. Cancellierius, a careful and learned writer, discusses this rite, which is practiced in the Vatican church, in his description of Holy Week, and compares it with similar words of Saint Eligius, *Homily 8 on the Lord’s Supper*: “To commend the example of humility on that day, Christ washed their feet; hence on that same day the altars, the walls of the church, and the vessels are purified.” AREV.]

2. Hence on that day the altars, the walls and pavements of the church are washed, and the vessels consecrated to the Lord are purified. On that day, therefore, the holy chrism is also prepared, because two days before Passover Mary is said to have poured ointment over the Lord’s head and feet. Hence the Lord also said to his disciples: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. XXVI).

## 396 CHAPTER XXX. On the Parasceve

[Note: [Col. 0764D]

CHAPTER XXX, no. 1. “Through the mystery of the wood.” Many manuscripts have “through the wood of the mystery.” Others: “through the mysteries of the wood.” AREV.]

1. The Parasceve—that is, the sixth day of the Sabbath—is held as a solemn feast because on that day Christ accomplished the mystery of the cross, for which he had come into this world: because we had been struck down by wood in Adam, we were to be healed again through the mystery of the wood. For this reason, on account of this triumph, human weakness offers Christ an annual celebration throughout the world, because he deigned by the blood of his passion to redeem the age and, by conquering death through the cross, to absolve the world from sin.

2. The substance of divinity itself did not suffer the injury of that cross, but only the nature of the assumed humanity. The suffering belonged to the body, while divinity remained untouched by injury. The Lord’s passion is shown to have had three reasons. The first reason, then, is that Christ should be given for the redemption of the world from guilt, and that the ancient enemy should be captured, as by the hook of the cross, so that he might vomit out those whom he had swallowed and lose the prey he held—not conquered by power but by justice, not by domination but by reason.

3. The second reason is that he might provide a lesson in life for those who would follow. Christ ascended the cross to offer us an example of passion and resurrection: of passion, to strengthen patience; of resurrection, to arouse hope. Thus he showed us two lives in the flesh, one laborious and the other blessed: the laborious life, which we must endure; and the blessed life, which we must hope for.

4. The third reason for assuming the cross was that the proud and inflated wisdom of the world, humbled by the foolish preaching of the cross, as it is considered, might collapse; so that it might recognize how much wiser the foolishness of God is than human beings, and how much stronger the weakness of God is than all human strength (1 Cor. I).

[Col. 0765C] [Note: [Col. 0765D]

5. “The Apostle teaches,” through “to the depths”: these are the words of Rufinus in the *Symbol*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Whose breadth,” through “is described”: these passages are shared by Rufinus with Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* II, chapter 42, and in *On the Grace of the New and Old Testament*. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius has *docet Apostolus* in the text and *docet autem Apostolus* in the note. AREV.]

5. The apostle Paul teaches (Eph. V) that those who have been enlightened ought to have the eyes of their hearts to understand what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross. Its breadth is the transverse wood on which the hands are extended; its length extends downward from the breadth to the ground; its height extends upward from the breadth to the head; and its depth is what is fixed in the earth and hidden. By this sign of the cross the whole life of the saints is represented.

[Note: [Col. 0765D]

6. “For it is said to a human being,” through the end of the chapter: all these are Augustine’s words from the cited letter to Januarius, chapter 14. GRIAL.]

6. It is said to a human being: “Take up your cross and follow me.” The flesh is crucified when our members upon the earth are put to death—sexual immorality, impurity, lust, and the rest. While the outward person is being corrupted so that the inward person may be renewed from day to day, this is the passion of the cross. Although these are good works, they are still laborious, and their reward is rest. Therefore it is said: “Rejoicing in hope,” so that, while contemplating the rest that is to come, we may work with gladness and labor.

7. This gladness is signified by the breadth of the cross in the transverse wood where the hands are fastened. For the hands signify work, and the breadth signifies the gladness of the worker, because sadness produces narrowness. Moreover, by the breadth of the cross to which the head is joined, expectation of heavenly reward from the height of God’s justice is signified. Thus good works are not to be thought necessary for the sake of earthly and temporal benefits from God, but rather for the sake of what faith, working through love, hopes for from above.

[Note: [Col. 0766D]

8. Another reads as follows. Regiovatican Codex 161 adds: “Finally, he placed the height, because after we hasten by our works toward knowledge of those matters mentioned above, we shall now deserve to ascend to lofty and exalted things.” AREV.]

8. Now by the length, through which the whole body is extended, endurance itself is signified, so that we may remain long-suffering; hence those who endure are called *longanimes*. By the depth, however—that is, the part of the wood fixed in the hidden earth and concealed there, while everything that projects rises from it—the inscrutable judgments of God are indicated. By his hidden will one person is called to participate in so great a grace, and another in another way.

## 398 CHAPTER XXXI. On Holy Saturday

1. The veneration of Holy Saturday is celebrated because on that same day the Lord rested in the tomb. Hence, appropriately, in the Hebrew language *Sabbath* is interpreted as “rest”: either because on that day God rested when the world had been perfected, or because on it our Lord and Redeemer rested in the tomb.

2. This day lies between Christ’s death and resurrection, signifying a kind of rest for souls after death from every labor and every distress. Through this rest there is a passage, by the resurrection of the flesh, to that life which our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to foreshadow by his resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Holy Day of Easter

[Note: [Col. 0766D]

CHAPTER XXXII, no. 1. “Whose paschal resurrection”: everything through the end is taken from Augustine’s cited letter to Januarius. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To be sacrificed.” Others: “to be killed.” More is explained about Easter in the *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17, nos. 10 and following. AREV.]

1. The paschal mystery, which is now celebrated most clearly in the mystery of our Savior, was first enacted figuratively in the Old Testament, when the people of God celebrated the Passover after the lamb had been killed in Egypt (Exod. XII). Its figure was completed in reality in Christ, who was led like a sheep to be sacrificed. When our doorposts were smeared with his blood—that is, when our foreheads were marked with the sign of the cross—we are delivered from the destruction of this age as from Egyptian captivity. We celebrate the mystical day of his paschal resurrection not only because he rose from the dead on it, but also because of the other mysteries signified through it.

2. For since, as the Apostle says, he died for our sins and rose for our justification, a passage from death to life was consecrated in the Lord’s passion and resurrection. Indeed, the very word *pascha* is not Greek but Hebrew; it is not derived from the passion, although “to suffer” is *pathein* (παθεῖν) in Greek, but is called *pascha* from the Hebrew word for “passage.” The Evangelist especially expressed this when the Lord celebrated the Passover with his disciples: “When Jesus saw,” he says, “that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John XIII).

3. The passage, therefore, from this mortal life into another, immortal life—that is, from death to life—is commended in the Lord’s passion and resurrection. This passage is now enacted by us through faith, which is given to us in the remission of sins, when we are buried with Christ through baptism, passing, as it were, from the dead—from worse things to better, from bodily things to spiritual things, from the manner of life of this present age to the hope of the future resurrection and glory.

[Note: [Col. 0767D]

4. Others: “The beginning is given to the new life . . . and, cleansing the old leaven out of the old [man].” AREV.]

4. Therefore, because of the beginning of the new life itself into which we pass, and because of the new person whom we are commanded to put on and to strip off the old, cleansing out the old leaven so that we may be a new lump, since Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, because of this newness of life the first month among the months of the year was assigned to this celebration. For it too is called the month of new things. But because the third period of the whole age of the world has now appeared, the Lord’s resurrection lasts three days.

[Col. 0767C] [Note: [Col. 0767D]

5. Cochleus: “Easter is celebrated in the moon of the third week,” that is, on whichever Sunday occurs from the fifteenth through the twenty-first. AREV.]

5. The first period is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace, in which the mystery that had previously been hidden in prophetic allegory has now been revealed. This is also signified by the lunar number. Since the number seven commonly appears in Scripture as a mystical sign of a certain perfection, Easter is celebrated in the moon of the third week—that is, on whichever day occurs from the fourteenth through the twenty-first.

6. But this is so not only because of the third period, since the third week begins from that point, but also because of the moon’s own turning. For then it turns from lower things toward higher things, and this likeness is taken from the moon for us: we are to pass from visible things to invisible, and from bodily sacraments to spiritual ones, so that we may die more and more to this age and our life may be hidden with Christ, 400 and so that we may turn all the light of our devotion, which had been directed toward lower things, toward higher things—namely, toward the eternal contemplation of unchanging truth (Col. III).

[Note: [Col. 0767D]

7. “Because of the likeness of the whole.” That is, because of the resemblance to the whole. AREV.]

7. Easter is observed through the twenty-first day because of the number seven, by which the meaning of the whole is often signified, and which is also attributed to the Church itself because of its likeness to the whole. Therefore the apostle John also wrote to seven churches in the Apocalypse. The Church, however, while still established in this mortal flesh, is often called by the name of the moon in Scripture because of the moon’s mutability. The reason why the annual day of Easter does not return to the same day of the year, as does the day on which the Lord is believed to have been born, is the Lord’s Day and the moon.

[Note: [Col. 0768D]

8. On the day on which Easter ought to be celebrated, see more extensively the *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17. AREV.]

8. It is evident on which day the Lord was crucified, lay in the tomb, and rose again. The observance of those days was established by the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, and the entire Christian world was persuaded that Easter ought to be celebrated in such a way that we must await not only the paschal moon but also the Lord’s Day on which he rose from the dead. Hence Easter does not return to the same day of the year. For the Jews observe only the month of new things and the moon. Our Fathers, however, judged that the Lord’s Day should be added, so that our festival might also be distinguished from the festival of the Jews.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Ascension of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0768D]

CHAPTER XXXIII, no. 1. Others: “He ascended on high; he led captivity captive.” In some manuscripts: “whose perfection is of the flesh.” Others: “whose flesh indeed.” AREV.]

1. The solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension is celebrated because on that same day, after the victory over the world and the return from hell, Christ is remembered to have ascended into heaven, as it is written: “He ascended on high, he took captivity captive, he gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. LXVII). This festival is celebrated as the cycle of years returns so that the humanity of the assumed flesh of the ascending Lord, placed at the right hand of the Father, may be recalled to memory. We believe that his body is in heaven in the same way as it was when he ascended, as the angelic voice also testifies, saying: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I)—that is, in the same appearance and substance of flesh. His departure granted immortality to the flesh; it did not remove its nature.

2. The right hand of the Father, at which the same Son is believed to sit, is not corporeal, for it is impious to think this of God. The right hand of the Father is everlasting blessedness, which is promised to the saints in the resurrection—that is, to the universal Church, which is Christ’s body. Likewise, his left hand is rightly understood as the misery and everlasting punishment that will be given to the impious.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Pentecost

[Note: [Col. 0768D]

CHAPTER XXXIV, no. 1. Much of this is from the same letter of Augustine to Januarius. GRIAL.]

1. The origin and reason for the festival of Pentecost must indeed be traced somewhat further back. For the day of Pentecost began from the time when the voice of God thundered from above on Mount Sinai and the Law was given to Moses (Exod. XX). In the New Testament, Pentecost began when Christ brought about the coming of the Holy Spirit, which he had promised and which, he said, would not come unless he himself had ascended into heaven.

[Col. 0769A] [Note: [Col. 0769D]

2. Hittorp, together with three manuscripts, printed *in varietate linguarum diffusa* (“spread among a diversity of languages”); in one he found *diffusi* (“spread”). AREV.]

2. Finally, when Christ had entered the gate of heaven, after an interval of ten days the place suddenly trembled while the apostles were praying. When the Holy Spirit descended upon them, they were so inflamed that they spoke of God’s mighty works in the languages of all nations (Acts II). Thus the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the apostles, spread among a diversity of languages, transmitted the solemnity to later generations; and for this reason Pentecost is celebrated, and the day itself is accordingly held in honor.

3. This festival of the Gospel corresponds to the festival of the Law. There, after the lamb had been sacrificed and fifty days had intervened, the Law of Moses, written by the finger of God, was given. Here, after Christ was killed—he who was led like a sheep to be sacrificed—the true Passover is celebrated; and, after fifty days had intervened, the Holy Spirit is given, who is the finger of God, upon the one hundred and twenty disciples, constituted according to the number of the Mosaic age. Indeed, this festival also possesses another mystery.

4. For it consists of a week of weeks (Isa. LIII). The weeks of days produce the same Pentecost, in which the remission of sin occurs through the Holy Spirit; the weeks of years produce the fiftieth year, which among the Hebrews is called the jubilee, in which likewise the land receives release, slaves receive freedom, and properties that had been purchased for a price are restored. For seven multiplied by seven produces the number fifty when the unit is added—the unit which the authority of our predecessors has handed down as anticipated from the figure of the age to come. For it is always both the eighth and the first; indeed, it is always the one, which is the Lord’s Day.

5. The Sabbath-rest of the people of God must necessarily return there and be fulfilled where the portion is given to those who are eight, as someone wisely interpreted the words of Solomon (Eccl. XI). For this reason all the days of the fifty-day period after the Lord’s resurrection are celebrated with abstinence set aside and in joy alone, because of the figure of the future resurrection, where there will no longer be labor but the rest of joy.

[Note: [Col. 0769D]

6. Neither from the Lord’s Resurrection until Pentecost nor on the Lord’s Days is it customary to bend the knees while the antiphons are recited after the lauds or at compline. Isidore, however, speaks generally of not bending the knees in prayer on these days, evidently because the custom derived from apostolic times, when the faithful prayed standing on these days. It is not easy to determine how long this custom lasted, but its memory is still found in the Third Council of Tours, canon 37, in the time of Charlemagne. See Bingham, *Antiquities of the Christian Church*, vol. V, pp. 253 and following. AREV.]

6. Therefore on these days the knees are not bent in prayer, because, as one of the wise men says, the bending of the knees is a sign of penitence and mourning. Hence in every respect we observe in them the same solemnity that we observe on the Lord’s Day, on which our predecessors handed down that neither fasting should be undertaken nor the knees bent, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Festivals of the Martyrs

[Col. 0770A]

[Note: [Col. 0770D]

CHAPTER XXXV, no. 1. The whole chapter is from Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book XX, chapter 21. GRIAL.

Ibid. The title in some manuscripts is: “On the festivals of the apostles, or martyrs.” Grialius printed *ad exercitandam imitationem* (“to exercise imitation”); I do not know whether this was deliberate. Others have *ad excitandam* or *ad excitandum imitationem* (“to arouse imitation”). Instead of *sacrificemus* (“let us sacrifice”), others have *offeramus* (“let us offer”). Grialius: *in memorias* (“at the memorials”). AREV.]

1. The ancient Fathers decreed that the festivals of the apostles, or solemn celebrations in honor of the martyrs, should be observed as a mystery of veneration, either to arouse imitation or so that we might be joined to their merits and aided by their prayers. Yet we sacrifice to God alone, not to any martyr, even though we set up altars at the memorials of the martyrs.

2. For which bishop, standing at an altar in the places where the bodies of the saints lie, has ever said: “We offer to you, Peter,” or “Paul,” or “Cyprian”? Whatever is offered is offered to God, who crowned the martyrs, at the memorials of those whom he crowned. Through the reminder supplied by those places, a greater affection arises to sharpen our love both for those whom we ought to imitate and for him whose help enables us to do so.

3. We therefore honor the martyrs with that worship of love and fellowship by which holy human beings of God are honored in this life—those whose hearts we perceive to have been prepared for such suffering on behalf of evangelical truth. But we honor them with greater devotion because, having overcome their struggles, they are safer, and because we praise them with greater confidence as victors already in the happier life, whereas we are still fighting in this one.

[Note: [Col. 0770D]

4. Others: “of their own divinity.” In some manuscripts: “we command neither any martyr nor any holy soul.” AREV.]

4. But that worship which in Greek is called *latria* cannot be expressed in Latin by a single word, since it is a service owed specifically to the Divinity; we neither practice nor teach that it should be practiced toward anyone except the one God. Since sacrifice belongs to this worship—and hence *idolatry* is named for those who also offer it to idols—we in no way offer anything of this kind, nor command it to be offered, either to any holy soul or to any holy angel. Whoever falls into this error is corrected by sound doctrine, either so that he may be corrected, condemned, or warned against it, while the saints themselves, whether human beings or angels, do not wish what they know is owed to the one God to be offered to them.

5. This appeared in Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians, moved by the miracles performed through them, wished to sacrifice to them as gods. Tearing their garments, confessing and persuading the people that they were not gods, they forbade this to be done to them. It also appeared in the case of the angels, as we read in the Apocalypse of an angel forbidding himself to be worshiped and saying to his worshiper: “I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers; worship God” (Apoc. XXII, 9). Accordingly, Scripture rightly says that the human being was forbidden by the angel to worship him, but was to worship the one God, under whom the angel too was his fellow servant.

[Col. 0771A] 6. Therefore, let us not offer to angels or martyrs that worship which belongs to divine religion, since they are not regarded as beings who seek such honors as God does. For they themselves do not wish to be worshiped in place of God but wish him to be worshiped by us, in whose illumination they rejoice. The martyrs are therefore to be honored for imitation, not worshiped as a matter of religion; honored with love, not with servitude.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Encaenia

[Note: [Col. 0771C]

CHAPTER XXXVI, no. 1. “For *encaenia* is a festival.” From Augustine, *Tractate 48 on John*. GRIAL.

Ibid. It seems that one should read *encaenia vocantur* (“they are called encaenia”), since the Gospel passage precedes: “The encaenia took place.” Saint Augustine, from whom Isidore takes this, has *encaenia vocantur*. Instead of *quia caruerunt* (“because they lacked”), Bignaeus conjectures *quando caruerunt* (“when they lacked”). AREV.]

1. We read in the Gospel that the annual festivals of the dedication of churches are celebrated according to the custom of the ancients, where it says: “The encaenia took place at Jerusalem” (John X, 22). For the *encaenia* was a festival of the dedication of the temple; in Greek, *caenon* means “new.” Whenever something new has been dedicated, it is called *encaenia*. The Jews solemnly celebrated the day on which the temple was dedicated, and that day was observed among them as a festival. Although this practice has died out among them because they lack both worship and a temple, Christians nevertheless preserve that custom of the Fathers, into whom the glory appears to have been transferred.

[Note: [Col. 0771D]

Grialius: *instituta* (“established”). Others: *diversaque . . . tempora . . . instituta* (“established at different times and in different ways”). AREV.]

2. All the festivals were established by prudent men at different times, according to the variety of religious observances and the diverse honor paid to the martyrs, lest perhaps the infrequent gathering of the people should diminish faith in Christ. Therefore certain days were appointed so that all might come together at once, so that through seeing one another both faith might grow and greater joy arise.

## 405 CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Fast of Lent

[Col. 0771C]

[Note: [Col. 0771D]

CHAPTER XXXVII, no. 1. “For the first fast of Lent,” through “to live”: these are Augustine’s words to Januarius, chapter 15. GRIAL.

From this and the following two chapters it is clear that there is a homily on fasting, found in many manuscripts. See the Isidorian materials, chapter 72, nos. 13 and 14. AREV.]

1. According to the holy Scriptures, there are four periods of fasting, in which the Lord must be entreated through abstinence and the lamentation of repentance. Although it is appropriate to pray and abstain on all days, during these periods one ought to devote oneself more fully to fasting and penitence. The first fast is that of Lent, which began, according to the ancient books, from the fast of Moses and Elijah, and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days, demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the prophets.

[Col. 0772A] 2. Moses represents the Law, and Elijah represents the prophets; between them Christ appeared gloriously on the mountain, so that what the Apostle says about him might stand out more clearly: “Having testimony from the Law and the prophets” (Rom. III). In what part of the year, then, could the observance of Lent be established more suitably than adjacent and continuous with the Lord’s passion? For it signifies this laborious life, which also requires self-restraint, so that we may fast from the allurements of the world itself, living on manna alone—that is, on heavenly and spiritual commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0771D]

3. “It is bounded by the four winds.” Both manuscripts read this, as do Augustine and Jerome, vol. IX, Letter 21; for *describitur* (“is described”), which appears in the printed books and in Rabanus, book II *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 20, was doubtless the interpretation of someone who had read *deliniatur*, as it appears in the Roman edition. I interpret *delimatur* as “is purified,” or rather “is carried downward and made oblique,” so that *delimatur* and *erigitur* (“is raised up”) are opposites. For *limus* is transverse and oblique. Thus *delimatur* will be what Virgil said, “sloping downward, is pressed”:

> As the world, steep toward Scythia and the lofty Rhipaean heights...

It rises; sloping down toward Libya’s South Winds, it is pressed. But Maro spoke of the sky, whereas Augustine spoke of the earthly globe. “Declines” might be considered an acceptable reading; thus, in [Col. 0772D] the book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to King Sisebut, chapter 9:

“For just as the world is raised toward the northern region, so it declines toward the southern,”

unless Augustine, whose words these are, stood in the way. GRIAL.

Same passage. Others read: “and the cycle of the year is varied through the four seasons.” A little earlier, *delinitur*, “is smoothed,” instead of *delimatur*, “is bounded/trimmed.” AREV.]

3. This life is therefore represented by the number forty because ten is the perfection of our blessedness, while the creature is represented by seven, which clings to the Creator; in this, the unity of the Trinity, announced temporally [Col. 0772B] throughout the whole world, is declared. And because the world is bounded by the four winds, raised by the four elements, and varied by the four annual changes of the seasons, four times ten is completed in forty. By this number it is shown that at all times one must abstain from pleasure, fast, and live chastely and continently.

[Note: [Col. 0772D]

4. “For by the Mosaic Law, until they should dedicate it”: from Cassian, *Conference* 21, chapter 25. GRIAL.

Same passage. “Thirty-six days.” “Thirty-six and a half.” Cassian. GRIAL.

Same passage. “For after the Sundays have been subtracted from Lent.” If Sundays and Saturdays are subtracted, Cassian reads so. But since, as he himself says, in the cities of the West, and especially in Rome, people fasted on Saturdays, Isidore therefore did not subtract the Saturdays, nor add the half-day, or else he adopted another reckoning; for he did not demand such exactness—*ἀκριβῶς*, “exactly.” GRIAL.]

4. Another mystery of the sacrament is also expressed: the same fasts are observed for forty days. For the Mosaic Law generally commanded the whole people to offer tithes and firstfruits to the Lord God. Thus, while in this statement we are admonished to refer the beginnings of our intentions and the completions of our works to God’s grace, in the reckoning of Lent this total of the legal tithes is nevertheless fulfilled. [Col. 0772C] For the entire period of the year is tithed by the number of thirty-six days: after the Sundays of Lent—on which the fasts are relaxed—have been subtracted, on these days we hasten to the church as though offering tithes for the whole year, and we offer the activity of our deeds to God as a sacrifice of rejoicing.

[Note: [Col. 0772D]

5. “By whose law of Lent, until they should dedicate it”: from the same *Conference*, chapter 29. GRIAL.

[Col. 0773D] Same passage. “As though they should dedicate tithes to the Lord.” Thus Cassian and the Gothic text. The printed books read: “that they should dedicate tithes.” GRIAL.

Same passage. Isidore perhaps calls him “our Cassian” because he often quotes his opinions and words. AREV.]

5. Yet, as our Cassian says, those who are perfect are not bound by the law of Lent, nor are they satisfied with subjection to this small canon. The leaders of the churches established it especially for those who are entangled throughout the whole year in pleasures [Col. 0773A] and secular business, so that, constrained at least by this sort of legal necessity, they might be compelled to devote these days to the Lord, and dedicate to him as tithes the days of their life which they had been about to consume entirely, as though they were fruits.

407 **CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Fast of Pentecost**

[Note: [Col. 0773D]

CHAPTER XXXVIII, note 1. This fast is completed by many, on the authority of the Gospel, after the Lord’s Ascension. Theonas forbids this, in Cassian, *Conference* 21, chapter 20, on the basis of the tradition of apostolic men. GRIAL.

Same passage. On the fast of Pentecost: *The Apostolic Fathers*, Cotelerius’s edition, volume I, page 44, or 27. Instead of *hordearii*, *hordeacei* could be substituted—alternative adjective forms meaning “of barley,” the latter used elsewhere by the Vulgate. The words of Deuteronomy are: “You shall count seven weeks for yourself, beginning from the day on which you put the sickle to the standing grain.” AREV.]

1. The second fast is that which, according to the canons, begins on the next day after Pentecost, in accordance with what Moses also says: “At the beginning of the month of barley you shall make seven weeks for yourselves” (Deut. XVI, 9). Many complete this fast on the authority of the Gospel after the Lord’s Ascension, taking historically that saying of the Lord in which he says: “Can the [Col. 0773B] children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. IX).

2. They say that after the Lord’s resurrection one ought not to fast or mourn during those forty days in which he is afterward read to have lived with the disciples, because we are in gladness. But after the period had been completed in which Christ, flying up to heaven, withdrew his bodily presence, a fast was proclaimed, so that through humility of heart and abstinence of the flesh we might deserve to receive from heaven the promised Holy Spirit (Acts I).

**CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Fast of the Seventh Month**

[Col. 0773C] [Note: [Col. 0773D]

CHAPTER XXXIX, note 1. *Exorationis*, “of supplication.” Others read *expiationis*, “of expiation.” AREV.]

1. The third fast is that which was practiced by the Jews after the solemnity of Tabernacles, which the Church celebrates on the tenth day of the month of September. For this was first instituted in the Law by the Lord, who said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying: The tenth day of the seventh month shall be called the Day of Supplication. It shall be holy for you, and you shall humble your souls in fasting. Every soul that does not humble itself on that day of fasting shall be exterminated from its people, and every soul that performs work on that day shall perish from its people” (Lev. XXIII).

[Note: [Col. 0773D]

2. “Four times by day and four times by night.” These words are absent from the corrected edition of the Septuagint translators; the words “by night” are also absent from the Vulgate and the Hebrew text. GRIAL.

Same passage. Some manuscripts read: “They used this fast,” which is not an inferior reading. Grialius printed: “the children of Israel, and Jerusalem.” Isidore sometimes explains the sense of Sacred Scripture rather than quoting its actual words. AREV.]

2. That the ancients practiced this fast is recorded in the Book of Ezra. “After they had returned,” he says, “the children of Israel to Jerusalem, and had made for themselves a great rejoicing of Tabernacles [Col. 0773D], afterward they assembled in fasting, and in sackcloth, and with earth upon them. They stood [Col. 0774A] confessing their sins and the iniquities of their fathers; and they rose to stand and to read, and they read in the book of the law of the Lord their God. Four times by day and four times by night they confessed and worshiped the Lord their God” (II Esdr. IX).

[Note: [Col. 0774D]

3. “It is restored by the resurrection.” Others read: “It is overcome by the resurrection.” Hittorpius: “It is prepared for the resurrection.” AREV.]

3. In this seventh month the sun also, according to the reckoning, begins to make the day shorter and the night longer—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, when the equinox occurs. Therefore a fast is also kept in this month, because the waning of the sun and the increase of the night show that our life is failing as death approaches; and this death is restored by God’s judgment and by the resurrection.

**CHAPTER XL. On the Fast of the Kalends of November**

[Note: [Col. 0774D]

CHAPTER XL, note 1. In the ancient editions: “The Lord said to him: By sackcloth they provoked the Lord to mercy.” The remainder, to the end of the chapter, was lacking. AREV.]

1. The fourth fast is that of the Kalends of November. [Col. 0774B] That it was either initiated or instituted by divine authority is made clear by the testimony of the prophet Jeremiah, to whom the Lord said: “Take the scroll of the book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel and Judah, and against all the nations, if perhaps each one may turn back from his evil and most wicked way, and I may be merciful toward their iniquities” (Jer. XXXVI). “So the prophet Jeremiah called Baruch, son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the Lord that he had spoken to him in the scroll of the book.

409 2. “And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying: ‘Enter and read from the scroll in which you wrote from my mouth the words of the Lord, while the people listen in the house of the Lord. On the day of fasting you shall read, if perhaps their prayer may fall before the Lord and each one may turn back from his most wicked way, for great is the fury and indignation that the Lord has spoken against this people.’ And Baruch, son of Neriah, did according to all that the prophet Jeremiah had commanded him, reading the words of the Lord from the scroll in the house of God. It came to pass in the ninth month that they proclaimed a fast before the Lord to all the people in Jerusalem.” Therefore, on the authority of this divine Scripture, the Church adopted the practice and celebrates it with universal observance of fasting.

**CHAPTER XLI. On the Fast of the Kalends of January**

[Col. 0774D] [Note: [Col. 0774D]

CHAPTER XLI, note 1. Possidius refers to Augustine’s treatise on the Kalends of January, from which this may perhaps have been taken. The Second Council of Tours, chapter 16, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 10, also mention these Kalends in the same sense. There is also canon 1 of the Council of Auxerre: “It is not permitted on the Kalends of January to play the calf or young stag [printed *Vecolo aut Cervolo*], or to observe devilish New-Year gifts.” See Augustine, Sermon 215 *On the Seasons*, and Appendix, volume IX, treatise 20; Ambrose, *Sermon on the Circumcision*; Peter Chrysologus, *Sermon on the Kalends of January*; Saint Maximus, homily *On the Circumcision*, or *On the Kalends of January*. Alcuin, *Book on the Divine Office*, chapter 4: “These Kalends,” he says, “given the folly of the pagans, should rather be called *cavendae*, ‘days to be avoided,’ than *Kalendae*, ‘Kalends.’” GRIAL.

Same passage. “In religion.” Others read “into religion.” On the fast of the Kalends of January, etc. Fabricius, *Bibliographia*, page 461, lists several authors who discuss the Kalends of January in this connection. Bingham describes the ancient Fathers who inveighed against such observance of the Kalends, volume IX, page 6. In the canon of the Council of Auxerre cited in Grial’s note, one should read *vetula* in the ancient usage for *vitula*, “calf,” as Sirmond and Labbe read, or *vitulo*, “calf,” alongside *cervulo*, “young stag”; that is, disguised men represented the figure of a calf or young stag. Against this custom Saint Pacianus published a work entitled *Cervus*, “The Stag,” from which someone absurdly supposed that Pacianus was attacking a heretic named Cervus. See Flórez, volume XXIX of *España Sagrada*, page 89, who observes that Isidore’s words agree with canon 9 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and with a sermon published under the name of Faustinus. This and the following chapter are missing from the Bignaean edition, although the titles are supplied. Many other passages are also absent from that edition, as Jerome Wullaeus observed in the note before Book II, because they were likewise absent from the earlier Paris and Antwerp editions, and no manuscript codex was available. AREV.]

1. The Church instituted the fast of the Kalends of January because of the error of paganism. Janus was a certain [Col. 0775A] pagan prince, from whom the month of January takes its name. Ignorant people worshiped him as though he were a god and handed down to later generations a religious honor for him; they also dedicated that day itself to theatrical performances and debauchery.

410 2. For then wretched people—and, what is worse, even the faithful—put on monstrous disguises and are transformed into the appearance of beasts. Others, altered by feminine gestures, effeminate their masculine faces. Some are still polluted by various omens of observance from that fanatical custom. Everything resounds with the feet of dancers and the applause of those leaping about; and, what is more shameful, with the sexes joined in intertwined dances, a senseless crowd, raging with wine, mingles together.

[Col. 0775B] 3. Therefore the holy Fathers, considering that a very large part of the human race served such sacrileges and debaucheries on that same day, established throughout the whole world and in all the churches a public fast, by which people might recognize that they were acting so wickedly that it was necessary for all the churches to fast on account of their sins.

**CHAPTER XLII. On the Custom of a Three-Day Fast**

1. Fasting for three days, however, was taken from the example of the Ninevites, who, having condemned their former vices, devoted themselves entirely for three days to fasting and repentance, and, covered with sackcloth, appealed to God for mercy.

**CHAPTER XLIII. On Fasts on Various Days and at Various Times**

[Col. 0775C]

[Note: [Col. 0776D]

CHAPTER XLIII, note 1. Others read: “so that the Jews might not be given occasion to exult in what Christ endured by dying.” It should be noted how much authority was accorded to the custom of the Apostolic See even in Isidore’s time, especially since, he says, “the Apostolic See observes this rule.” See Augustine’s Letter 118, which in recent editions is Letter 54, where, in chapter 2, Saint Augustine discusses the Saturday fast then practiced in some churches but not at Milan. AREV.]

1. Besides these regular periods of fasting, some fast every Friday because of the Lord’s Passion; many also regard Saturday as consecrated to fasting because Christ lay in the tomb on that day—namely, lest, by rejoicing, we concede to the Jews what Christ took away by dying. On Sunday, however, one must always take nourishment, so that we may proclaim Christ’s resurrection and our joy to the nations, [Col. 0776A] especially since the Apostolic See observes this rule.

[Note: [Col. 0776D]

2. “After Easter, however, until Pentecost.” These words are quoted by Gratian, distinction 76, chapter 10. GRIAL.

Same passage. These words are repeated in the *Monastic Rule*, chapter 11, note 2. Sunday is also discussed in the same Rule, chapter 10. AREV.]

2. After Easter until Pentecost, although the tradition of the churches has relaxed the strictness of abstinence by permitting meals, nevertheless, if any monks, clerics, devout women, or religious widows wish to fast, they are not to be forbidden. For Anthony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are also read to have abstained in the desert during these days and not to have broken their fast except on Sunday.

3. Who would not praise frugality or proclaim fasting? Fasting is a holy thing, a heavenly work, the gate of the kingdom, the pattern of the future. Whoever practices it in holiness is joined to God, separated from the world, and made spiritual. Through it vices are overthrown, the flesh humbled, [Col. 0776B] and the temptations of the devil conquered.

**CHAPTER XLIV. On the Various Practices of the Churches**

[Note: [Col. 0776D]

CHAPTER XLIV, note 1. The whole chapter is taken from Augustine’s Letter 118 to Januarius, chapters 1 and 2. GRIAL.

Same passage. On the various practice of the Church, see the *Apostolic Fathers* of Cotelerius, volume I, page 44, or 27. Some have *escarum*, “of foods,” instead of *Ecclesiarum* in the title. AREV.]

1. There are many such things and others like them that are practiced in the Churches of Christ. Of these, some are commended in the canonical Scriptures; others are not written down, but are nevertheless preserved by tradition (*The Apostolic Fathers* I, 44, or 27). Those practices, however, which are observed throughout the whole world are understood to have been established either by the apostles themselves or by the authority of the principal councils—such as the Lord’s Passion and resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit, which are celebrated annually in remembrance—as well as anything else observed by all the churches wherever the Church has spread.

[Col. 0776C] 2. Other practices, however, are observed differently in different places: for example, some fast on Saturday and others do not; some receive Communion daily, others on certain days; some omit no day on which the sacrifice is not offered, while elsewhere it is offered only on Saturday and Sunday, and elsewhere only on Sunday. Whatever else of this kind may be observed, this entire class of practices was instituted as the priests of the Church, or of the religious community over which they presided, saw fit. A serious and prudent Christian has no better rule in such matters than to act in the manner in which he sees the church to which he happens to come act. Whatever is neither contrary to the faith nor contrary to good morals should be followed indifferently and observed for the sake of fellowship with those among whom one lives, lest schisms arise from differing practices.

**CHAPTER XLV. On the Use of Meat and Fish**

[Note: [Col. 0777A]

CHAPTER XLV, note 1. See chapter “From the Beginning,” distinction 35, and Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinianus*. GRIAL.

[Col. 0778A] Same passage. Others read: “was granted to human beings for use.” AREV.]

1. Meat and wine were granted to human beings for use after the Flood. For at the beginning permission had not been given except only for what is written: “I have given you every fruit-bearing tree and seed-bearing plant for food” (Gen. I). Later, through Noah, all animals were given for food, and permission to drink wine was then also granted (Gen. IX). But after Christ, who is the beginning and the end, appeared, he withdrew at the end of time what he had suspended at the beginning, speaking through his Apostle: “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine.” And again: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV).

2. Meat is not forbidden, therefore, because meats are evil, but because feasting on them produces fleshly indulgence. For “food is the fuel and nourishment of all vices”; “food is for the stomach and the stomach for food,” because it is written: “God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI, 13). We may indeed eat fish, because the Lord received it after his resurrection (John XXI). Neither the Savior nor the apostles forbade this.

**BOOK TWO. ON THE ORIGIN OF THE MINISTERS**

[Col. 0777]

413 **PREFACE**

[Col. 0777B]

Since we have explained to some extent the origins and reasons for the offices that are commonly celebrated by the Church, let us now proceed in order to discuss the beginnings of those who devote religious ministries to divine worship.

**CHAPTER I. On Clerics**

[Note: [Col. 0777D]

CHAPTER I, note 1. See Jerome’s Letter to Nepotianus. GRIAL.]

1. All who have been ordained in the ranks of ecclesiastical ministry are generally called clerics. Our teachers say that they are called *cleros*, or clerics, because Matthias was chosen by lot, whom we read was the first ordained by the apostles (Acts I). In the same way, in those times, all whom the leaders of the churches ordained were chosen by lot. For *cleros* is interpreted as “lot”; hence inheritance in Greek is called *cleronomia*, and an heir *cleronomos*.

[Note: [Col. 0777D]

2. Others read: “because they are given to the Lord as his portion.” AREV.]

2. Therefore, they say, they are called clerics because they are assigned to the lot of the Lord’s inheritance, or because the Lord himself is their portion, as it is written concerning them, the Lord saying: “I am their inheritance.” Hence those who possess God as their inheritance ought to strive to serve God without any impediment from the world, and to endeavor to be poor in spirit, so that they may fittingly say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV, 5).

414 **CHAPTER II. On the Rules of Clerics**

[Note: [Col. 0777D]

CHAPTER II, note 1. “By these things, therefore, it is provided by law.” The Council of Mainz enacted canon 10 using the words of this entire chapter. GRIAL.

Same passage. “Occupations of profit” (*occupationes lucrorum*). Thus indeed the Gothic text and the Council of Mainz read, but the reading of another manuscript, *aucupationes lucrorum*, “the pursuits of profit,” is not objectionable. GRIAL.

Same passage. “They should not ascend through ambition.” The same manuscript reads *ad honorum gradus per ambitionem non subvehant*, “they should not raise [others] through ambition to the ranks of honor,” not inelegantly, provided that one reads the passive *subvehantur*, “be raised,” instead of the active *subvehant*, “raise.” For *subvehi* means to be carried from a low place to a high one. Virgil:

“Moreover, to the temple and the lofty citadels of Pallas  
the queen is carried amid a great throng of matrons.” GRIAL.]

1. By the law of the Fathers, therefore, it is provided that, separated from ordinary life, they abstain from the pleasures of the world; that they do not attend spectacles or public processions; that they avoid public banquets, and that at private ones they practice not merely modesty but sobriety. They must not devote themselves to usury, seek disgraceful profit-making occupations or the pursuit of anyone’s fraud, but flee the love of money as the source of every crime; they must reject secular offices and business, and must not rise to positions of honor through ambition.

[Note: [Col. 0778D]

2. “Not with an unbridled tongue” (*non infreni lingua*). The same manuscript reads *effreni*, “unbridled,” an alternative form of the adjective. GRIAL.

Same passage. “Let them walk in bearing” (*gestu incedant*). The printed edition reads *gressu*, “in gait,” instead of *gestu*, “in bearing.” GRIAL.]

2. They must not accept gifts in return for the benefits of God’s healing, but must beware of deceit and conspiracies; they must flee hatred, rivalry, slander, and envy. They must not walk with wandering eyes, an unbridled tongue, or insolent and haughty bearing, but must display modesty and reverence of mind through simple dress and demeanor. [Col. 0778C] They must utterly abhor obscenity of speech as well as of conduct.

3. They must avoid frequent visits to widows and virgins, and must in no way seek to live together with unrelated women. They must also strive continually to preserve the chastity of an undefiled body, or at least be joined by the bond of a single marriage. They must offer due obedience to their elders and not exalt themselves through any desire for self-display. Finally, they must devote themselves to instruction, reading, psalms, hymns, songs, and continual exercise. For those who strive to present themselves as dedicated to divine worship must be such as these, [Col. 0779A] so that, while they apply themselves to knowledge, they may administer the grace of teaching to the peoples.

415 **CHAPTER III. On the Kinds of Clerics**

[Note: [Col. 0779C]

CHAPTER III, note 1. The same synod also used this chapter, enacting a law concerning wandering clerics, chapter 22. [Col. 0779D] GRIAL.

Same passage. Others read: “without a head to follow, a crowd of ignorant people.” AREV.]

1. There are two kinds of clerics: one consists of those living under episcopal rule in ecclesiastical communities; the other consists of acephali, that is, those who do not know what head to follow. Neither the pursuits of secular offices among the laity nor religious devotion among the clerics retains these people; released and wandering, they are embraced only by a shameful and unsettled life.

[Note: [Col. 0779D]

2. “The western region abounds” (*pars occidua pollet*). Thus both manuscripts read. The printed edition has *polluitur*, “is polluted.” GRIAL.

Same passage. “Pleasure” (*voluptatis*). Grialius reads *voluntatis*, “will.” It would seem that one should read “neither horses nor centaurs.” Saint Valerius, the abbot, uses Isidore’s words: “neither horses nor men,” as I have said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 69, note 13. On this passage and other passages of this second book cited in the councils, see *Isidoriana*, chapter 31. Virgil’s words “a mixed race and a two-formed offspring,” in *Aeneid* VI, 25, concern the Minotaur. AREV.]

2. Since, fearing no one, they pursue the freedom to fulfill their pleasure, they are carried along like brute animals by their own liberty and desire. They bear the sign of religion but not the office of religion, resembling Hippocentaurs, “neither horses nor men, but a mixed race and a two-formed offspring,” as the Poet says. Our western region is more than sufficiently rife with such a filthy and infamous multitude.

**CHAPTER IV. On the Tonsure**

[Note: [Col. 0779D]

CHAPTER IV, note 1. The Council of Aachen, in 816, took this entire chapter from Isidore, chapter 1. See also Loaisa in his notes on the Sixth Council of Toledo, chapter 6, and Fabricius, who on page 847 of the *Bibliographia* lists writers who discuss the tonsure of the Nazirite, as well as the note on the *Monastic Rule*, chapter 12, note 4. AREV.]

1. The use of ecclesiastical tonsure arose, unless I am mistaken, from the Nazirites (Num. VI). Having first preserved their hair, afterward, when they had completed a life of great continence with devotion, they shaved their heads and were commanded to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice, so that they might consecrate the perfection of their devotion to the Lord. Following their example, the practice was introduced by the apostles, so that those who are dedicated to divine worship and consecrated to the Lord might, like Nazirites—that is, holy ones of God—be renewed by cutting their hair. [Col. 0779C]

[Note: [Col. 0780C]

2. “Paul.” Others read “Peter,” but “Paul” is also found in the Council of Aachen. AREV.]

2. This is also commanded to the prophet Ezekiel, when the Lord says: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezek. V), because he too served God in the ministry of sanctification as a member of the priestly order. We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that those Nazirites, Priscilla and Aquila, first did this (Acts XVIII), as did the Apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ who were worthy of imitation in this form of observance.

3. Among clerics, the tonsure is a certain sign formed on the body but enacted in the soul: namely, that by this sign vices may be cut away in religious life, and that we may strip off the sins of our flesh as though they were hairs. With our minds renewed, we may shine like fresh locks, stripping off, according to the Apostle, the old person with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God (Eph. IV; Col. III). This renewal must take place in the mind but be displayed on the head, where the mind itself is understood to dwell.

[Note: [Col. 0780D]

4. “But when the upper part of the head has been shaved.” See chapter “There are two kinds,” distinction 12, question 1, from Jerome. GRIAL.

Same passage. “When the upper part of the head has been shaved, a circular crown is left below.” Thus the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 41: “All clerics and readers, like Levites and priests, shall have the entire upper part of the head shaved and leave below only a circular crown—not as readers in the regions of Galicia [others: Gaul] appear hitherto to have done, who, with long hair like laymen, cut a small circle at the crown of the head. For this practice had hitherto belonged to heretics in Spain.” The principal criticism is directed against readers who allowed their hair to grow long like laymen. AREV.]

4. But in the fact that, after the upper part of the head is shaved, a circular crown is left below, I believe the priesthood and kingship of the Church are symbolized in them. Among the ancients, the tiara was placed on the heads of priests. Made of fine linen, it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified by the shaved part of the head. The crown, however, is the width of a golden circle that encircles the heads of kings. Both signs are therefore expressed on the heads of clerics, so that what is written may also be fulfilled through a certain bodily likeness, as the Apostle Peter teaches: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II, 9).

5. It is asked, however, why the hair is not first allowed to grow, as among the ancient Nazirites, and then cut. But those who investigate these matters should consider what difference there is between that prophetic veil and this revelation of the Gospel, of which the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil will be taken away” (II Cor. III, 16). What the veil placed between Moses’ face and the sight of the people of Israel signified, the cutting of the hair as a veil also signified in those times. [Col. 0780C] For the Apostle too says that hair serves as a veil. Therefore the heads of those who are consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be veiled with hair, but only revealed. For what had been hidden prophetically in the sacrament has now been disclosed in the Gospel.

**CHAPTER V. On the Priesthood**

[Note: [Col. 0780D]

CHAPTER V, note 1. Here, as often elsewhere, the term “priests” refers only to bishops. GRIAL.

Same passage. “The beginning of the priesthood, indeed …” From Anacletus’s second letter to the bishops of Italy. GRIAL.]

1. Let us now come to the most sacred orders and explain specifically what constitutes the foundation of the priesthood, or by whose authority the episcopal order grew in the world. The beginning of the priesthood was Aaron. Although Melchizedek had previously offered sacrifice, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, they did so of their own free will, not with priestly authority.

[Note: [Col. 0781C]

2. “Take Aaron,” he says. Exodus XXXIX. GRIAL.

Same passage. In the Vulgate: “And Aaron and his sons you shall bring near,” without “take.” Instead of “priests for me,” as in the Vulgate, some Isidorian books read “my priests.” AREV.]

2. Aaron, however, was the first in the Law to receive the name of priest, and the first, clothed in the pontifical robe, to offer victims, at the Lord’s command, when he spoke to Moses: “Take,” he says, “Aaron and his sons, and bring them to the door of the tabernacle of testimony. When you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments—that is, the linen tunic, the ephod, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with a belt. You shall place the tiara on his head and the holy plate upon the tiara, and pour the oil of anointing upon his head; by this rite he shall be consecrated. You shall also bring his sons near and clothe them in linen tunics; you shall gird Aaron and his sons with a belt, place turbans upon them, and they shall be priests for me by perpetual religious observance” (Exod. XXIX, 4).

3. Here we must understand that Aaron was the high priest, that is, the bishop, while his sons prefigured the presbyters. For Aaron’s sons too were priests, and the Levites ought rightly to have served them, just as they served the high priest. There was also this distinction between the high priest Aaron and his sons, who were themselves priests: Aaron wore over the tunic the long robe (*podere[m]*), the holy robe, the golden crown, the turban, the golden armlet, the golden girdle, the ephod, and the other garments mentioned above. Aaron’s sons, however, stood at God’s sacrifice wearing only linen tunics, girded and turbaned.

[Col. 0781C] 4. But perhaps it will also be asked whom Moses prefigured. If Aaron’s sons represented the presbyters, and Aaron the high priest, that is, the bishop, whom did Moses represent? Without doubt, Christ. Indeed, in every respect he represented Christ, since he was a likeness of the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, who is the true leader of peoples, the true chief of priests, and the lord of bishops. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0781D]

5. “You are Peter,” Matthew XVI. GRIAL.

Same passage. “With an equal partnership of honor,” etc. See canon 2, distinction 22. These words are taken from Saint Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*, pages 107 and following in the edition of John Fell. “The other apostles were certainly what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honor and power, but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church may be shown to be one.” Some printed editions and manuscripts read: “proceeds. The primacy is given to Peter, so that one …” But not only the heterodox Fell but also other Catholic scholars agree that this is an interpolation. Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, Book I, chapter 12, denies that it follows from this that the apostles were equal among themselves, and explains Cyprian through the authority of Saint Leo, who seems in a certain way to have wished to interpret Saint Cyprian’s words, Letter 84: “Among the blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of power in the likeness of honor; and although the election of all was equal, to one alone it was given that he should be preeminent over the others.” Bellarmine gathers many other passages from the same Cyprian elsewhere in defense of Catholic doctrine, and explains Cyprian from Cyprian. The same words of Isidore are cited in the Council of Aachen mentioned above, along with many other passages from Isidore’s books *On Offices* and *Etymologies*. AREV.]

5. Thus far concerning the beginnings of the priesthood in the Old Testament. In the New Testament, however, after Christ, the priestly order began with Peter. For the episcopate in Christ’s Church was first given to him. Thus the Lord says to him: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI, 18). He therefore first received the power of binding and loosing, and was the first to bring a people to the faith by the power of his preaching. Indeed, the other apostles too were made equal sharers with Peter in honor and power, and they preached the Gospel after being scattered throughout the whole world.

[Note: [Col. 0782D]

6. “Thus says the Lord.” I Kings II. GRIAL.]

6. When these men died, bishops succeeded them. They were established throughout the world in the apostolic sees, and are no longer chosen from fleshly and blood descent, as at first according to the order of Aaron, but according to each person’s merit, whatever divine grace has bestowed upon him. Thus the Lord also pronounced to Eli, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I said, Your house and your father’s house shall remain before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be it; rather, I will glorify those who glorify me, and whoever despises me shall be despised” (I Kings II, 30).

[Note: [Col. 0782D]

7. “There are four kinds of apostles.” From Jerome on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Galatians. GRIAL.]

7. There are four kinds of apostles: one comes from God alone, as Moses; another through both a human being and God, as Joshua; a third through a human being alone, as in these times many are appointed to the priesthood through the favor of the people and of the authorities; and the fourth arises from itself, as in the case of false prophets and false apostles. What does the name “apostles” mean? In Latin, apostles are interpreted as “those who are sent,” because Christ sent them to evangelize for the enlightenment [Col. 0782C] of all peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0782D]

8. In the *Questions of Saint Isidore*, published in volume V, page 251: “Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside, not to be of benefit.” See the note. AREV.]

8. As one of the wise men said, “bishop” is the name of a function, not of an honor. For it is Greek, and the term is derived from the fact that the one who is placed over others watches over them, caring for those subject to him; *scopos* indeed means “purpose” or “aim.” Therefore we may call bishops in Latin “overseers,” so that the person who prefers to preside rather than to be of benefit may understand that he is not a bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0782D]

9. “And he led them beyond Bethany” (*et produxit eos trans Bethaniam*). From the older translation. Our version reads: “But he led them out beyond Bethany” (*eduxit autem eos foras trans Bethaniam*). Luke, at the end. GRIAL.

Same passage. “So also the one who more than fulfills the Law” (*sic et superimpletor legis*). Others read: “So also the heavenly fulfiller of the Law” (*sic et supernus impletor legis*). AREV.]
