9. That bishops are ordained by the laying on of hands of their predecessors, the priests of God, is an ancient institution. For the holy patriarch Isaac, placing his hand upon the head of Jacob, blessed him [Col. 0783A] (Gen. 27:28); and Jacob did likewise for his sons. Moses too, placing his hand upon the head of Joshua son of Nun (Num. 27:23), gave him the spirit of power and leadership over the people of Israel. Thus also our Lord Jesus Christ, the fulfiller of the law and the prophets, blessed his apostles by the laying on of hands, as it is written in the Gospel of Luke: “And he led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them; and it came to pass, when he had blessed them, that he departed from them, and they returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24).

[Note: [Col. 0783C]

10. “That one marriage [and] virginity”: see Distinction 3, chapter *Si quis*, and 28, question 3. GRIAL.]

10. And in the Acts of the Apostles, at the command of the Holy Spirit, hands were laid upon Paul and Barnabas by the apostles for the episcopate, and thus they were sent to evangelize (Acts 13). That a priest is made from the age of thirty was taken from the age of Christ, from which Christ himself began to preach. For this age no longer needs the progress proper to children, but is full of the strength and vigor of perfection, and prepared for every exercise of discipline and teaching.

[Note: [Col. 0783C]

11. “Moreover, that a bishop is not [ordained] by one”: *C. Archiepiscopus* and the following, Distinction 66; and Rufinus, *History*, chapter 6, on the canons of the Council of Nicaea. GRIAL.

Ibid. “And therefore he is instituted by all who assemble”: see Distinction 64. GRIAL.

Ibid. “But a digamist, etc.” Some manuscripts read: “But a digamist is said to undertake the priesthood,” from which Hittorp did not conjecture badly: “But a digamist is not said to undertake the priesthood.” In Aeneas of Paris, *Against the Greeks*, chapter 172, it reads: “But the priesthood is taken away from a digamist.” Aeneas of Paris cites several other chapters of this book in support of his position. AREV.]

11. That those chosen for the order of the pontificate should be men of one marriage and virginity was commanded also in the Old Law (Lev. 21), and the Apostle wrote more fully concerning it, saying: “The husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3). The Church seeks a priest who has been ordained either from monogamy or from holy virginity; but a digamist is deprived of the exercise of the priesthood. Moreover, that a bishop is ordained not by one bishop but by all the bishops of the province is recognized as having been instituted because of heresies, so that no tyrannical authority might undertake anything against the faith of the one Church. Therefore he is instituted by all who assemble, or by no fewer than three who are present, while the others consent by written testimony.

[Note: [Col. 0783D]

12. “Let him consider that he has acquired not so much a ministry of humility”: from Jerome, on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The seal of secrets.” Namely, these words are spoken in the handing over of the ring: “Receive the ring of discernment and honor, the sign of faith, so that you may seal what must be sealed and disclose what must be opened.” See Georg Longus, *On Signet Rings*, chapter 3, and the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 1, *Peristephanon*, verse 85. AREV.]

12. At his consecration a staff is given to him, so that by its indication he may either govern or correct the people subject to him, [Col. 0784A] or bear the infirmities of the weak. A ring is also given as a sign of pontifical honor, or as a seal of secrets. For there are many things that priests conceal from the senses of carnal and less discerning people and keep, as it were, under a seal, lest the mysteries of God be opened to the unworthy. Indeed, that secular men are by no means to be admitted to the ministry of the Church, the apostolic authority teaches in the same way, saying: “Lay hands hastily on no one,” and again: “Not a novice” (1 Tim. 5:22; 3), lest, lifted up in pride, he should think that he had obtained not so much a ministry of humility as the administration of secular power, and, condemned for his pride, should be cast down through boastfulness like the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0783D]

13. “But now we often see, even to the dignity”: from the same passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Although Moses could not”: from the same passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To be conferred.” Hittorp likewise printed this, with one manuscript. Others have *defendendum*, “to be defended.” AREV.]

13. For how will a secular man be able to fulfill the teaching of a priest when he has held neither the office nor recognized its discipline? Or what will he be able to teach when he himself has not learned? But now we often see very many arranging ordinations on paper; and they do not choose those who will benefit the Church, but those whom they themselves love, or whose services have softened them, or for whom some person of greater standing has made a request; and, to say what is worse, those who have secured their ordination by gifts. I say nothing of the rest: some make their sons or parents successors, and try to leave the dignity of the episcopate to their descendants. Yet even Moses, the friend of God, could not do this; instead, he chose Joshua from another tribe, so that we might know that leadership among the people is not to be assigned according to blood, but according to the merits of one’s life (Num. 27).

[Note: [Col. 0784C]

14. “Sometimes, moreover”: see chapter *Audaciter*, 8, question 1, from Origen—or rather Jerome. GRIAL.

Ibid. “But that one who, after baptism, has been overtaken by some mortal sin”: that this is the meaning, Gratian says (Distinction 25, chapter *Primum*), so that perpetual infamy results from it. He interprets Jerome’s words in this way in chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus, from which this passage is taken. We shall quote them lest they seem too harsh to anyone: “Accordingly, he is first commanded to be without reproach as a bishop, whom I think is called by another word ‘irreproachable’ to Timothy. [Col. 0784D] Not merely that at the time when he is to be ordained he should be without any fault and should have washed away former stains through a new manner of life, but that from the time when he was reborn in Christ no consciousness of sin should torment him. For how can the ruler of the Church remove evil from one who has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner when, silently, he himself answers that he has committed the same things that he rebukes?” *Corruptus*, “corrupted,” is read in the Gothic manuscript and in the Roman edition, but *correptus*, “overtaken,” seems more likely from Gratian’s meaning. Isidore seems to have softened Jerome’s words, wishing the person to have been overtaken not by just any offense but by a mortal one, and using *correptus* as though he meant “detected.” GRIAL.

Ibid. This harsh opinion of Jerome—that one who has been corrupted by some mortal sin after baptism is not to be advanced to the priesthood—is to be understood as referring to a crime and sin not merely mortal in any sense, but a very grave and enormous sin, which produces not only spiritual death but also canonical death. For among the irregularities that prevented advancement was completed penance. See Petavius, book 2, *On Penance*, chapter 11, no. 13, and book 6, chapter 6, no. 5. AREV.]

14. Sometimes, moreover, persons are chosen as rulers in accordance with the merits of the people; [Col. 0784C] hence let peoples know that they were worthy to receive the government of a corrupt bishop. But that one who, after baptism, has been overtaken by some mortal sin is not to be advanced to the priesthood, the law itself bears witness. For Moses commanded in the Law that priests should not offer any blemished animal upon the altar of God (Lev. 1:21). God later reproached the priests of Israel for offering such things and despising them through Malachi, saying: “To you, O priests, who have polluted my name, and you have said, ‘In what way have we polluted you?’ You offer polluted bread upon my altar. Is it not evil if you offer the blind and the lame?” (Mal. 1:6). Hence also in Numbers the red heifer, whose ashes are the purification of the people, is commanded to be offered upon the altar of the Lord only if it has not performed earthly labor, has not drawn the yoke of sin, and has not been bound by the chains of sins (Num. 19).

[Note: [Col. 0785D]

15. “Therefore, because the law removes sinners,” through “to occupy,” are Jerome’s words in the same passage. GRIAL.]

15. But why should I add more? If one who, already placed in the episcopate or presbyterate, has committed some mortal sin is withdrawn from office, how much more should one found to be a sinner before ordination not be ordained? Therefore, since the law removes sinners from the priesthood, let each person examine himself; and knowing that “the mighty shall be mightily tormented” (Wis. 6:7), let him withdraw from this burden, which is not so much an honor as a load, and not seek to occupy the place of others who are worthy. For he who presides over peoples in instructing and training them in virtue must be holy in all things and considered blameworthy in none. He who rebukes another for sins must himself be free from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0785D]

16. “For with what face,” through “the right things,” belong to the same passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To him also the knowledge of Scripture,” through “to pervert,” from the same passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. The old printed editions have *revincere*, “to overcome,” instead of *repercutere*, “to repel.” [Col. 0786D] AREV.]

16. For with what face will he be able to rebuke his subjects when the person rebuked can immediately say to him: “First teach yourself the things that are right”? Therefore, let him who neglects to do what is right cease teaching what is right. For he who strives to admonish others to live well must first correct himself, so that in all things he may present himself as a model of life [Col. 0785C] and may urge everyone to good work by both teaching and practice. He also needs knowledge of the Scriptures, because if the bishop’s life alone is holy, he can benefit only himself by living in this way. But if he is also learned in teaching and speech, he can instruct and teach others, and repel adversaries who, unless they are refuted and convicted, can easily pervert the hearts of the simple.

[Note: [Col. 0786D]

17. Older editions have *indagari*, “to be investigated,” instead of *judicari*, “to be judged.” AREV.]

17. His speech should be pure, simple, clear, full of gravity and propriety, full of sweetness and grace, treating of the mystery of the law, the doctrine of faith, the virtue of continence, and the discipline of justice; admonishing each person with varied exhortation according to the character of his profession and conduct—that is, so that he may know beforehand what he should say, to whom, when, and how. His special duty above all others is to read the Scriptures, go through the canons, imitate the examples of the saints, devote himself to vigils, fasts, and prayers, [Col. 0786A] maintain peace with the brethren, despise no one among his members, condemn no one unless he has been found guilty, and excommunicate no one unless the matter has been examined. He should display humility and authority together in such a way that, through excessive humility, he neither allows the vices of his subjects to grow strong, nor, through immoderate authority, exercises the power of severity; but he should act toward those entrusted to him with greater caution the more severely he fears being judged by Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0786D]

18. “To display care in all things,” etc. Others read: “to exercise care in all things, and foresight marked by discretion in distribution.” AREV.]

18. He will also possess that preeminent charity above all gifts, without which every virtue is nothing; for charity is the guardian of holiness, while humility is the dwelling-place of this guardian. Among all these things he will also possess the excellence of chastity, so that the mind which is to consecrate the body of Christ may be clean and free from every pollution of the flesh [Col. 0786B]. In all this he must manage the care of the poor with attentive stewardship: feed the hungry, clothe the naked, receive strangers, ransom captives, protect widows and orphans, and display vigilant care in all things, with foresight and judicious distribution.

[Note: [Col. 0786D]

19. “In which hospitality also,” through “inhuman,” Jerome, same passage. GRIAL.]

19. In this respect, too, his hospitality will be so outstanding that he will receive everyone with kindness and charity. For if all the faithful desire to hear that Gospel saying, “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25), how much more should a bishop, whose lodging ought to be the refuge of all? A layman who receives one or two has fulfilled the duty of hospitality; a bishop, unless he receives everyone, is inhuman. In settling secular disputes he must distinguish the case according to merit, not favor; for a bishop must not receive a powerful person in such a way that he saddens the poor person contrary to justice, nor take justice away from the powerful person on behalf of the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0786D]

20. “He will also have, according to the Apostle”: same passage, and *Against Jovinianus*. GRIAL.]

20. He must not defend the wicked, nor think that holy things should be entrusted to the unworthy, nor rebuke or attack anyone whose crime he does not censure. According to the Apostle, he must also possess gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence, or chastity, so that he may abstain not only from an unclean act but even from the casting of the eyes and the wandering of thought; thus, while he permits no vice to rule within him, he may be able to obtain from God forgiveness for the offenses of his subjects. For he who pursues these things will be both a useful minister of God and a representative of perfect priesthood.

## CHAPTER VI. On Chorepiscopi

[Col. 0786D]

[Note: [Col. 0786D]

Chapter 6, note 1. What is said here about chorepiscopi seems to have been taken from the Council of Antioch, chapter 10. See Leo, letter 88, and canon 54 of Nicaea. “Because of their insolence,” says Gratian (chapter *Chorepiscopi*, Distinction 68), “they were prohibited from the Church.” GRIAL.

Ibid. Others read: “appoint readers; they must not dare to ordain subdeacons,” etc. AREV.]

1. Chorepiscopi, that is, vicars of bishops, were instituted, as the canons themselves testify, after the example of the seventy elders, as fellow priests on account of the care of the poor [Col. 0787A]. Established in villages and rural districts, they govern the Churches entrusted to them, having permission to appoint readers, subdeacons, exorcists, and acolytes; but they must not dare to ordain presbyters or deacons without the knowledge of the bishop in whose region they are known to preside. These, however, are ordained only by the bishop of the city to which they are attached.

## CHAPTER VII. On Presbyters

[Note: [Col. 0787C]

Chapter 7, note 1. It took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. Anacletus, letter 2, and Jerome to Nepotianus, letter 2. GRIAL.

Ibid. “For to these, as to bishops,” through “preaching,” is excerpted from the letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, Jerome, volume 9; it seems deliberately to have omitted certain matters, such as the duties of confirmation and blessing. As for seeming to make presbyters equal to bishops, we shall not defend him in any other way than by the argument with which he defends himself: that statements for which the testimony of authorities is cited should not be counted as evidence against him. The words that seem to grant presbyters more than is proper are not Isidore’s but Jerome’s. His purpose and intention seem to have been to restrain and blunt the arrogance and insolence of bishops, not to make presbyters their equals. This is what learned men long ago inferred from comparison with several of his passages, including Franciscus Turrianus, book 8 of the *Constitutions*, chapter 36; Marianus of Reate, on the letter to Evagrius; and Caesar Baronius, *Annals*, volume 1, year 58. For what Isidore thought about the office of bishops is sufficiently clear from chapter *Perlectis*, Distinction 25, and from the final chapter of this work on chrism. GRIAL.

[Col. 0788C] Ibid. For matters belonging individually to presbyters, deacons, and others in their ecclesiastical functions, see Isidore’s Letter to Leudefredus. In section 4 of the final chapter of this book, Isidore very clearly places bishops above presbyters, not only on the basis of ecclesiastical custom but also from a reading of the Acts of the Apostles. Whether Jerome truly thought presbyters equal to bishops was a question vigorously debated among theologians. My friend Raimundus Diosdado treated it most carefully in his learned dissertations, in which he did not show Jerome to be alien from the position of the Catholic Church. AREV.]

1. The order of presbyters took its beginning, as has been said, from the sons of Aaron. Those who were called priests in the Old Testament are those who are now called presbyters; and those who were called chief priests are now called bishops. Presbyters [Col. 0787B] are interpreted as “elders,” because the Greeks call elders in age *presbyteroi*. For to these, as to bishops, the administration of the mysteries of God has been entrusted.

[Note: [Col. 0788D]

2. “For Paul”: from Jerome’s letter to Evagrius and commentary on Titus. GRIAL.

Ibid. *In confectione*, “in the consecration.” Others have *in confractione*, “in the breaking.” For *divini*, “of the divine,” the old printed editions have *divina*, “divine.” AREV.]

2. For they preside over the Churches of Christ, and in the consecration of the divine body and blood they are participants with the bishops; likewise in the instruction of the people and in the duty of preaching. Only, on account of the authority of the high priest, the ordination and consecration of clerics have been reserved to him, lest, if the discipline of the Church were claimed by many, it should dissolve harmony and generate scandals. For the Apostle Paul asserts that these same presbyters, as true priests, are included under the name of bishops, when he says to Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in the cities, as I had arranged for you. If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient. For a bishop must be without blame” (Titus 1). By this statement he shows that presbyters too are designated under the name of bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0788D]

3. “For the second, joined to the first.” Hittorp, with his manuscripts, has: “For the second, and almost joined to the first.” AREV.]

3. Hence, when writing to Timothy about the ordination of a bishop and a deacon (1 Tim. 3), he said nothing at all about presbyters, because he included them under the name of bishops. For the second degree is joined to the first, just as he writes to the Philippians about bishops and deacons (Phil. 1), although one city cannot have several bishops. And in the Acts of the Apostles, as he was about to go to Jerusalem, he summoned the presbyters of the Church, saying among other things: “Take heed to the flock over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Acts 20). Hence the Apostle speaks to Titus, and the canons themselves testify, that such presbyters are to be appointed in the Church just as bishops are.

[Note: [Col. 0788D]

4. “Presbyters are rightly,” through the end, are Jerome’s words in chapter 3 of Isaiah; most of them are also found in Anacletus’s letter 2. GRIAL.

Ibid. I have already noted elsewhere that in the notes to the Gralian edition letters of supreme pontiffs are sometimes cited that are now considered apocryphal, as here and in note 1, Anacletus’s letter 2. AREV.]

4. Presbyters are rightly called so because of merit and wisdom, not because of age; for Moses too was commanded to choose presbyters (Num. 11). Hence it is said in Proverbs: “The glory of old men is gray hair” (Prov. 20). What is this gray hair? Without doubt, wisdom, of which it is written: “The gray hair of human beings is understanding” (Wis. 4). Although we read that human beings lived more than nine hundred years from Adam to Abraham, no one else is called the first presbyter—that is, elder—except Abraham, who is shown to have lived for far fewer years. Therefore they are called presbyters not because of decrepit old age but because of wisdom. If this is so, it is strange that foolish men should be appointed.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Deacons

[Note: [Col. 0788D]

Chapter 8, note 1. Much of this is from the cited letter to Rusticus of Narbonne. GRIAL.]

1. The order of deacons took its beginning from the tribe of Levi. For the Lord commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron the priest and his sons, the tribe of Levi should again be ordained and consecrated to the Lord for all the firstborn in the ministries of divine worship, and should serve for Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle of the Lord, keeping watch in the temple day and night. They themselves were to carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; they were to encamp around the tabernacle; and when the tabernacle was moved, they were to take it down and then set it up again (Num. 3, 8).

[Col. 0789A] [Note: [Col. 0789D]

2. These words are repeated from Isidore in the cited Council of Aachen, chapter 7, and elsewhere. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 49, observes that deacons were so called because servants ministering at tables were generally designated by this Greek term. AREV.]

2. From the age of twenty-five and upward they were commanded to serve in the same way in the tabernacle; the holy Fathers established this rule also in the New Testament. Their beginnings in the Gospel are read in the Acts of the Apostles as follows: “And the twelve apostles, calling together the multitude of the disciples, said: It is not pleasing that we should leave the word of God and minister at tables. What then, brothers? Choose from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint for this task. But we shall devote ourselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. And the statement pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. They set them before the apostles [Col. 0789B], and when they had prayed, they laid hands upon them; and the word of God increased, and the number of believers multiplied” (Acts 6).

[Note: [Col. 0789D]

3. “Nearest to the altar of Christ,” etc. Prudentius, in the hymn of Saint Laurence, p. 892, verse 37:

“He is the first of the seven,

who stand nearest to the altar.”

Saint Laurence was clearly an archdeacon. See Saint Jerome, letter 85, to Evagrius: “In the Church of Rome the presbyters sit, and the deacons stand.” This discipline, as Jerome says, weakened as vices increased. AREV.]

3. From this point the apostles, or the successors of the apostles, decreed that there should be seven deacons in all the Churches, who, in a higher rank and nearest to the altar of Christ above the rest, should stand like pillars of the altar, and this not without some mystery associated with the number seven. For these are the seven angels whom we read of in the Apocalypse singing with trumpets. These are the seven golden lampstands. These are the voices of the thunders. In a clear voice, like a herald, they admonish everyone, whether in prayer, in bending the knees, in psalm-singing, or in listening to the readings. They also cry out, “Let us give ear to the Lord”;  they likewise evangelize. Without them the priest has the name but not the office.

[Note: [Col. 0789D]

4. Others read: “lest they see what they ought not to see and take what they cannot preserve,” etc. But in some manuscripts *qui* is correctly read twice instead of *quae*. The Roman pontiff still preserves the custom of not receiving the chalice—namely, in a solemn Mass—unless it is handed to him by a deacon. Lesleus, in his notes on the Mozarabic Missal, p. 489, illustrates this ancient rite with many collected testimonies of the ancients. AREV.]

4. For just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of the sacrament belongs to the minister: the one is commanded to pray, the other to sing psalms; the one sanctifies the offerings, the other distributes what has been sanctified. Even priests themselves, because of the danger of presumption, are not permitted to take the chalice from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by a deacon. The Levites bring the offerings to the altar; the Levites arrange the Lord’s table; the Levites cover the ark of the Testament. For not everyone sees the lofty mysteries that are covered by the Levites, lest those who ought not see should see, and those who cannot preserve them should take them. For this reason they stand at the altar dressed in white garments, so that they may possess a heavenly life and approach the offerings white and unblemished—that is, clean in body and incorrupt in modesty.

[Col. 0790A] [Note: [Col. 0790D]

5. “Deacons.” Many manuscripts, here and elsewhere, have *diacones*; likewise *diaconibus* instead of *diaconis*. *Diaconibus* also occurs in the following chapter. AREV.]

5. For such ministers ought the Lord to have: men who are corrupted by no contagion of the flesh, but rather shine with the excellence of chastity. The Apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy concerning the kind of men who should be ordained deacons. For after prefacing his discussion with the election of priests, he immediately added: “Deacons likewise must be irreproachable,” that is, without blemish, like bishops; chaste, that is, restrained from lust; not double-tongued, lest they disturb those who are at peace; not devoted to much wine, because where there is drunkenness, lust and rage rule; not pursuing dishonest gain, lest they pursue earthly profit from the heavenly mystery. There is also a shameful desire for gain when one thinks more about present things than future ones. After this he added: “But let these first be tested, and then let them serve, having no crime” (1 Tim. 3). Just as bishops, so these men too must be tested before ordination to see whether they are worthy, and afterward let them serve in this way.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Keepers of Sacred Things

1. The keepers of the sanctuary are Levites. For they were commanded to guard the tabernacle and all the vessels of the temple (Num. 8). For this reason, under the Law, keepers of the vessels are chosen from the age of fifty, so that, after the struggle of the flesh has been subdued, they may now serve God in quiet, pure in body and mind alike, displaying an appearance of gravity, so that they may not be deceived in counsel, abandon the faith, or act with undue excess.

## CHAPTER X. On Subdeacons

[Col. 0790C] [Note: [Col. 0790D]

Chapter 10, note 1. See the cited letter to Rusticus. GRIAL.

Ibid. Grial’s text had *appellaturque*, “and is called.” Others have *divina protectione*, “by divine protection,” instead of *divina proditione*, “by divine betrayal.” AREV.]

1. Subdeacons, who are called *hypodiaconi* among the Greeks, are found in Ezra, where they are called Nathinaeans—that is, those who serve the Lord in humility (1 Esdras 8). From their order was that Nathanael who, in the Gospel of John, having been instructed by divine disclosure (*proditione*), was deemed worthy to confess the Lord and Savior; and who also proved faithful at the first indication of his divinity, when the Lord testified and said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1:47).

[Note: [Col. 0790D]

2. “So that, because,” etc. Others read: “so that, because they have been assigned to the sacred mysteries, they may be free from every carnal impurity.” For *aquaemanili*, others have *aquamanili*, and others *aqua manibus*. See the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 5, and Du Cange. AREV.]

2. Finally, these men receive the offerings in the Lord’s temple from the people; they carry out the duties of the Levites; and they also offer the vessels of Christ’s body and blood to the deacons at the Lord’s altars. Concerning them the Fathers decided that, because they handle the sacred mysteries, they should be chaste and continent with respect to wives and free from every [Col. 0791A] carnal impurity, in accordance with the command given to them through the prophet: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). Therefore, when they are ordained, they do not receive the laying on of hands, as priests and Levites do, but only the paten and chalice from the hand of the bishop; and from the archdeacon they receive the vessel of water, with the ewer and towel.

## CHAPTER XI. On Readers

1. The order of readers received its form and beginning from the prophets. Readers, then, are those who proclaim the word of God, to whom it is said: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58). When these men are ordained, the bishop first speaks to the people about their manner of life. Then, before the congregation, he hands them the Book of the divine writings [Col. 0791B] for proclaiming the word of God.

2. Whoever is advanced to this rank must be instructed in doctrine and books, and richly equipped with knowledge of meanings and words, so that in distinguishing sentences he understands where the connection ends, where the sentence still remains unfinished, and where the final statement is brought to a close. Thus prepared, he will possess the power of delivery, so that he may lead the minds and understanding of everyone toward comprehension, distinguishing the types of delivery and expressing the proper emotions of the sentences: sometimes with the voice of one making a statement, sometimes of one grieving, sometimes of one rebuking, sometimes of one exhorting, or in similar ways according to the kinds of proper delivery.

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

Chapter 11, note 3. “The power of delivery.” Others have: “the practice of delivery.” AREV.]

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

3. Others read: “in which especially that ambiguous character of sentences,” etc. Isidore follows, in the cited passage, the punctuation of the Epistle to the Romans established by Saint Augustine in book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 3, and elsewhere. Sabatier adds several others who hold the same view. In our Vulgate this is expressed as follows: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies? Who is he that condemns?” AREV.]

3. In this matter, above all, knowledge of the ambiguity of sentences must be applied. For there are many passages in Scripture which, unless they are delivered in their proper manner, fall into an opposite meaning, as in: “Who shall bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies” (Rom. 8:33–34). If this is said as though it were an affirmation, without preserving its proper mode of delivery, great perversity results. It must therefore be pronounced as though it said: “Is it God who justifies?”—so that the answer “no” is understood.

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

4. “To have knowledge.” Others read: “to have knowledge of grammatical art.” AREV.]

4. In matters of such importance, therefore, an aptitude for knowledge is necessary, by which each thing may be pronounced properly and suitably. For this reason the reader must also know the force of accents, so that he may know on which syllable the speaker’s voice is extended. Inexperienced readers often err in the accents of words, and those who seem to possess knowledge are accustomed to mock us for our ignorance, criticizing us and swearing that they do not understand at all what we are saying.

[Col. 0792A] [Note: [Col. 0791D]

5. Others read: “so that they could exhaust the tumult.” Others: “so that they could be heard amid the tumult.” AREV.]

5. The reader’s voice should be simple, clear, and adapted to every kind of delivery; full of manly vigor, avoiding an uncultivated and rustic sound; neither low nor excessively high; not broken or delicate; sounding in no way feminine; and accompanied not by bodily movement but only by an appearance of gravity. The reader should attend to the ears and heart, not the eyes, lest he make spectators rather than hearers of those listening. It is an ancient opinion that readers took special care of their voices for the sake of delivery, so that they might be heard amid the tumult. Hence readers were formerly called heralds or proclaimers.

## CHAPTER XII. On Psalmists

1. David or Asaph were the founders and originators of the psalmists, that is, the singers. For after Moses they were the first to compose and sing psalms. After Asaph’s death, his sons were placed in the order by David, and the psalmists continued by hereditary succession, as did the priestly order. They alone sang continually in the temple, dressed in white robes, with a choir responding to the voice of one singer.

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

Chapter 12, note 2. Others read: “so that by the pleasures of sweetness.” [Col. 0792D] A little later they have: “nor does it have the odor of musical gesture or theatrical art.” AREV.]

2. From this ancient custom the Church took the example of supporting psalmists, so that by their songs the minds of hearers might be stirred toward the working of God. A psalmist must be distinguished and outstanding both in voice and in skill, so that he may stir the minds of his listeners through the pleasure of sweetness. His voice should not be harsh, hoarse, or discordant, but musical, pleasing, clear, and high-pitched, possessing a sound [Col. 0792C] and melody suited to holy religion—not one that cries out in tragic fashion, but one that demonstrates Christian simplicity even in its modulation, and that does not smell of musical gesture or theatrical art, but rather produces compunction in the hearers.

[Note: [Col. 0792D]

3. “The ancients, with a plate placed upon the chest.” Pliny reports this of Nero, book 34, chapter 18: “Nero (for so it pleased the gods), the emperor, with a plate placed upon his chest and singing out songs beneath it, demonstrated a method for nourishing the voice.” GRIAL.

Ibid. Others read: “having placed it upon himself to cry out songs, for sustaining the singing voice.” Hittorp, with his manuscripts, printed: “without the knowledge of the bishop.” AREV.]

3. On the day before they were to sing, the ancients abstained from food, yet while singing they regularly used legumes for the sake of the voice. Hence singers among the Gentiles were called *fabarii*, “bean-eaters.” The ancients, placing a plate upon the chest and crying out songs beneath it, demonstrated the method of nourishing the voice. For this office, men are sometimes chosen even without the bishop’s knowledge, by the sole command of the priest, provided that they have been found capable in the art of singing.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Exorcists

[Col. 0792D]

[Note: [Col. 0792D]

Chapter 13, note 1. “Whom Ezra calls administrators of the temple”: What do exorcists have to do with administrators of the temple? I think this is the meaning: our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit. When an evil spirit moves into them, the buildings are then, to use the comedians’ expression, damaged. Sometimes matters reach the point at which the buildings cannot seem to be repaired without collapsing entirely and permanently. An example may be found both in the one whom the apostles could not restore and in the one whom the Lord himself healed and restored, making him mute, deaf, and blind. The duty of exorcists, then, is to repair such buildings and return them sound and whole. There is a passage of a poet, which I indicated, that is extraordinarily elegant for illuminating and expanding this comparison. GRIAL.

Ibid. *Oblationibus*, “offerings.” Others have *actionibus*, “activities.” AREV.]

1. In the order and ministry of the Church, according to the offices that had been established in Solomon’s temple and later distributed by Ezra, we find that those whom Ezra calls administrators of the temple (1 Esdras 2) are now exorcists in the Church of God. Under Ezra, the administrators of the temple were the sons of Solomon’s servants, who had the management of the whole temple under their care, yet did not serve in priestly offices or attend to sacred offerings.

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

2. “For repairing the roof.” Others read: “for the sacred buildings.” AREV.]

2. And although they belonged to the order and ministry of the temple, they were far removed from the office of God’s altar, because neither psalmists, nor doorkeepers, nor servants of the sacred rites were permitted to touch the altar’s offerings—only Levites were. What, then, was their function? The temple overseers had no other responsibility than to repair the structure, so that whatever in the temple building had been damaged or fallen away might be restored and refurbished by those same overseers from the Lord’s treasuries. [Col. 0793B]

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

3. “That he may commit to memory,” etc. Another reading: “and commends the kingdom of God to memory from the testimonies of Scripture, from which he exercises his gift.” AREV.]

3. Therefore the temple overseers are exorcists among the people of God. For just as a prudent and good overseer knows what his master’s property consists of, and the extent of all his substance, and keeps by him the original documents of the entire estate, so the exorcist diligently gathers into his keeping the secrets of the whole kingdom of the Lord, so that he may commit to memory the mysteries of Scripture, from which he exercises the gift granted to him by the Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle’s proclamation.

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

4. From the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 7, Distinction 23, “On Exorcists.” AREV.]

4. The Apostle mentions exorcists when he says: “Do all possess gifts of healing?” (1 Cor. XII). When these men are ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand, as the canon says, a booklet in which the exorcisms are written; and they receive the power to lay hands upon the possessed, whether baptized persons or catechumens.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Acolytes

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

Chapter XIV, no. 1. The same material appears in the seventh book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12. GRIAL.]

1. Acolytes are called in Greek *acolythi* and in Latin *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” from carrying wax candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered. For then they light the lamps and carry them—not to drive away darkness, since the sun is shining brightly at that time, but to display a sign of joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be shown of which it is written in the Gospel: “The true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” [Col. 0794A]

## 434 CHAPTER XV. On Doorkeepers

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

Chapter XV, no. 1. Grialius: “at the gates of Jerusalem.” AREV.]

1. Doorkeepers are those who in the Old Testament were called the gatekeepers of the temple. They presided over the gates of the temple of Jerusalem and, appointed in their respective courses, guarded everything within and outside the temple (1 Chron. XXIII; 2 Chron. XXIII). Finally, distinguishing between what is holy and what is wicked, they admit into the church only those who are faithful. We cannot enter the temple except through them, for they have authority both to admit the good and to reject the unworthy.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Monks

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

Chapter XVI, no. 1. As far as the authority of the ancient sources is concerned, up to “the Jordan.” From Jerome, Letter 13, to Paulinus. [Col. 0794C] GRIAL.

Ibid. “On the different kinds of monks.” Menardus, in chapter 3 of the *Harmony of Rules*, draws from the oldest rules of Basil, Benedict, and others, and, having also produced this chapter of Isidore up to the end of no. 10, is satisfied to the point of nausea. Isidore’s own Rule of Monks should also be consulted. AREV.]

1. From what source did the monks’ devotion to poverty arise, or who was the originator of this way of life, whose habit they imitate? As far as the authority of the ancient Scriptures is concerned, Elijah and his disciple Elisha were the founders of this purpose (2 Kings I, IV), as were the sons of the prophets, who lived in solitude and, abandoning the cities, made huts for themselves near the streams of the Jordan (Jer. XXXV). In the Gospel John the Baptist also became the founder of this way of life: he alone inhabited the wilderness, nourished only by locusts and wild honey (Matt. III). Later there arose the most illustrious founders of this way of life—Paul and Antony, Hilarion, Macarius, and the other Fathers—through whose examples the holy institution of monks grew throughout the world.

[Note: [Col. 0794D]

2. “The remaining kinds, however, are most foul and to be avoided in every way.” Cassian, *Conferences* 18.4: “There are three kinds of monks in Egypt, two of which are excellent, while the third is lukewarm and to be avoided in every way.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “The first kind,” up to “one heart,” from the same Cassian, chapter 5. GRIAL.

Ibid. “In every way.” This is correct and should not be changed to “in all things” or “in every manner,” as some have changed it. For *pro communione vitae*, some read *communi vita* (“a common life”). Menardus reports the passage from Isidore’s works because he did not have Grialius’s edition at hand; in that edition, as in the *Harmony of Rules*, the reading is *communione vitae*. AREV.]

2. There are six kinds of monks: three of them excellent, while the rest are most foul and to be avoided in every way. The first kind is that of the coenobites, that is, those who live in common, like those holy people who, in the time of the apostles, lived at Jerusalem in a holy fellowship of life after selling and distributing all their possessions to those in need. They called nothing their own, but everything was common to them, and they were one soul and one heart directed toward God (Acts II, 4). Monasteries took their beginning from their institution. 435

[Note: [Col. 0794D]

3. “The second kind.” From chapter 6, and from Jerome, Letter 22, to Eustochium. GRIAL.

[Col. 0795B] Ibid. “Which are brought to them at fixed intervals,” etc. In former times the eremites were supplied with food by the coenobitic communities from which they had departed. Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1: “When they have gone out into the desert by order of that abbot, bread and every other kind of food are provided.” MENAR.]

3. The second kind is that of the eremites, who are said to withdraw far from human beings, to seek and inhabit deserted places and vast solitudes, clearly in imitation of Elijah and John the Baptist, who penetrated the retreats of the wilderness. They delight in solitude alone, with an incredible contempt for the world, living only on wild plants, or content with bread alone or water, which is brought to them at fixed intervals. Thus they enjoy complete secrecy, wholly removed from human sight, and converse only with God, whom they serve with pure minds and for whose love they have abandoned not only the world but also human society.

[Note: [Col. 0795B]

4. “The third kind is that of the anchorites.” Here he distinguishes between eremites and anchorites. But anchorites are of three different kinds. First, the term is used for eremites, as may be seen in Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 1. Second, it is used for those monks who, after the coenobitic training-ground, were enclosed in cells; and these were of two sorts. Some were enclosed in cells within the monastery precincts, as is clear from Justinian’s Novella 5: “Unless some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, lead a withdrawn life in a dwelling—those whom they customarily call anchorites, that is, ‘withdrawn,’ and hesychasts, that is, ‘resting,’” etc. Here “dwelling” means a cell, for the discussion concerns those enclosed within monasteries. This is also clear from canon 41 of the Sixth Council, which says that such enclosed persons are to be trained in an ἀναχωρητικὴ παιδοτριβεῖσθαι διαγωγήν—that is, an anchoritic way of life. Others were enclosed outside the monastery precincts; Saint Isidore discusses these in this chapter. Third, anchorites are those who wandered through the wilderness without shelter and settled in no fixed place. Severus Sulpicius speaks of them in *Dialogue* 1: “Most of them live in the desert without any tents; they call them anchorites. They live on the roots of plants and never remain in any fixed place, lest they be visited by human beings.” Cassian suggests this in *Conference* 18.6, when he says: “Also in imitation of Elijah and Elisha, and of those of whom the Apostle says: ‘They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins.’” MENAR.]

4. The third kind is that of the anchorites, who, perfected already through coenobitic life, shut themselves up in little cells, removed far from human sight, admitting no one to them, but living solely in contemplation of God. 436

[Note: [Col. 0795D]

5. “The fourth kind,” up to “how they may be cured,” from chapter 8 of the same *Conference*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The fourth kind,” etc. These statements are taken from Cassian, *Conference* 18.8, whose words are also reproduced. The subject is certain people who flatter themselves with the name of anchorites, but, having grown lukewarm at the beginning of their conversion and no longer able to endure the yoke of their elders, shut themselves in cells, driven to this also by the applause of human praise. As a remedy for their folly, the Seventh Council of Toledo, chapter 5, decreed that no one should be enclosed before having been trained for many years in coenobitic service. The consent of the bishop and abbot was also required, as provided in the Council of Frankfurt, canon 15; and canon 41 of the Sixth Council decrees that those who desire such a life should be tested for four years: first they should enter a monastery and for three years practice this secluded life under the authority of the monastery’s abbot. When that period had passed, they should be examined by the bishop, who would investigate whether their will was firm. After this had been established, they were to leave the cell and remain in the monastery for a full year, so that their purpose might be tested more fully. Once these requirements had been completed, they were enclosed, provided that their will was indeed firm. MENAR.]

5. The fourth kind consists of those who flatter themselves under the appearance of anchorites. As Cassian says, at the beginning they seem, in a brief burst of fervor, to seek the perfection of the coenobium; but they soon grow lukewarm. They disdain to cut away their former habits and vices, are unwilling to endure any longer the yoke of humility and patience, and scorn submission to the authority of their elders. They seek separate cells and desire to sit alone, so that, troubled by no one, they may be thought gentle or humble. Yet once this institution—or rather, this lukewarmness—has infected them, it never permits them to approach perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0796B]

6. Grialius prints: “they are not only not cut off … but recover,” while no one provokes them, “so that.” For *solitarii*, another reading has *solita*. AREV.]

6. In this way their vices are not only not cut off; indeed, they grow still stronger for the worse, like a certain lethal and inward poison which, the longer it is concealed, spreads more deeply and produces an incurable disease in the sick person. Out of respect for the solitary cell, no one dares rebuke the solitary monk’s vices, which he prefers to have ignored rather than cured.

[Note: [Col. 0796B]

7. “The fifth kind is that of the circumcellions.” Augustine says, against Gaudentius, that they were called circumcellions because they went around rural estates for the sake of their food. GRIAL.

Ibid. “The fifth kind is that of the circillions.” This is largely excerpted from Saint Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28. Isidore’s glosses explain what the circillions are: “Circillions, false anchorites”; and likewise: “A circellio, a monk wandering through cells.” Saint Augustine himself says in his commentary on Psalm 132: “What does the name ‘circellions’ mean? But, they say, we are not called circellions. Perhaps we call them by a corrupted pronunciation of the name. For those are called circumcellions who wander around cells.” Papias says of the word: “Circumcellions are those who wander everywhere under a monk’s habit.” The same author says: “Circumcellions are a kind of wandering monks, so called because they wander around cells.” There were also other circumcellions who were heretics and, in order to be regarded as martyrs, killed themselves and also Christians whom they encountered indiscriminately. Saint Augustine discusses them in his commentaries on Psalms 82 and in Letters 48 and 61, as well as in many other places; Philastrius also mentions them in his *Book on Heresies*, as does the *Council of Carthage*.

“Others sell the limbs of martyrs”—if indeed they are martyrs. This was that detestable marketplace of hypocrites, by which those wretched profiteers collected large sums of money. Saint Augustine attributes it to the circellions in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28. A similar trade was practiced by a certain false hermit named Desiderius, who once walked about Paris carrying a sacred cross. In a little bag he carried roots of various herbs, mole teeth, mice’s bones, bears’ claws and fat, which he wanted the approaching common people to venerate as sacred relics. Saint Gregory of Tours reports this in Book VI of his *History*. Rodulfus Glaber, in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 3, tells of a similar wandering charlatan of his own time who deceived superstitious people everywhere by giving various names of prophets, martyrs, and confessors to the bones of the dead that he dug from graves, thereby emptying their purses.

From this arose the superstition of certain people who worshipped false relics and false saints. Such was a woman named Lucilla at Carthage, who was so devoted to the memory of an obscure and as-yet-unvindicated martyr that, before receiving the Holy Eucharist, she venerated his head. Rebuked for this by the archdeacon Caecilianus and inflamed with rage, she withdrew from communion with the Church and, through her own authority and resources, greatly aided the Donatist party, as Optatus of Milevis reports in Book II of *Against Parmenianus*.

The well-known story of Saint Martin is found in Severus Sulpicius’s *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 8. Martin removed the altar of a certain robber who was worshipped as a martyr by an ignorant and inexperienced crowd. Pope Saint Gregory, in Book III of his Letters, letter 30, censures certain Greeks who dug up the bones of the dead at Rome and carried them to their homeland as holy relics.

There was also once a superstition among the Roman common people: they would tear apart the dalmatic in which the dead pope’s body had been wrapped while it was being carried out, and preserve the pieces as relics. Gregory likewise prohibited this practice in Book IV, letter 44. William of Newburgh, in Book V of his *History*, chapters 20 and 21, tells of a certain William of Lund, whom the foolish common people regarded as a martyr. He coveted the money of the rich, stirred up the crowd with seditious sermons, and called himself the savior of the poor. The wandering agitator had already prepared many tools for breaking into the houses of the wealthy when he was captured, condemned by the royal council, dragged by horses, and ordered to hang from the gallows. After his death, a certain priest placed beneath a feverish person the chain with which that thrice-gallows-worthy man and utter rogue had been bound in prison, and publicly spread the shameless lie that the sick person had been healed by it.

Immediately, as is the blind and headlong devotion of the crowd, the gallows on which the impostor had hung was torn from its site and carried away during the night. The very spot where it had been fixed was scraped away on every side by foolish people rushing there to take relics for themselves. Certain nuns of the monastery of Romsey in England began to venerate a recently deceased man as a saint. When Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, learned of this, he prohibited them from such superstition by letter (Book III, letter 151).

In the time of Alexander III, a certain man, drenched and intoxicated with wine and behaving outrageously, was killed and then venerated as a martyr. In former times the foolish populace, deceived by dreams and nocturnal visions, venerated fabricated memorials of martyrs. This was prohibited by the Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 5 (“On the relics and veneration of saints”). Likewise, some more foolish people paid honor to heretical martyrs. This was later forbidden by the Council of Laodicea, canon 34.

“They sell them.” The sale of martyrs’ relics is prohibited in Book III, chapter 1, *On the Most Holy Churches*, etc.: “Let no one sell martyrs; let no one buy them”; and in the chapter *Cum ex eo*, *On Relics and the Veneration of Saints*.

“Others magnify their fringes”—after the manner of the Pharisees and scribes. For fringes are certain woven strips sewn onto the four corners of the garment by the Pharisees and scribes, at the time when they abstained from their wives, as a display of chastity, so that no one would touch those who had been sanctified, as Saint Epiphanius writes in Book I of *On Heresies*, volume I, chapter 15.

“And phylacteries.” Phylacteries are certain purple markings that the scribes and Pharisees attached to their cloaks for display, as Saint Epiphanius reports in the chapter cited. Although he speaks there only of the scribes, in the following chapter he says that the Pharisees were accustomed to use the scribes’ clothing. They were also small tablets or slips of parchment on which the Decalogue was written; the scribes and Pharisees wore them on their foreheads as memorials. Saint Jerome, commenting on Matthew XXIII, says: “They called those little tablets of the Decalogue phylacteries.” The rabbis call them *tephillin*.

Phylacteries are also amulets or protective charms which magicians gave to women to hang around their necks or bind to their arms, either to cure or ward off diseases or to avert some misfortune, as Saint Epiphanius teaches in chapter 15 of the work cited. Ancient glosses give *φυλακτήριον* as “preservative,” “means of relief,” “amulet,” or “preventive.” Isidore’s glosses define phylacteries as “incantations,” that is, magical formulas, in accordance with Virgil’s words in the *Pharmaceutria*:

“By incantations they can even draw down the moon from heaven.” [Col. 0798B]

Bede mentions them as an invention of demons for the seduction of pagans in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 27: “Some, even during the time of the plague, neglecting the sacraments of the faith with which they had been instructed, hastened to wandering idolatrous remedies, as though they could restrain by incantations, phylacteries, or any other secrets of demonic art the plague sent by God the Creator.” The Sixth Council also mentions them in canon 41. Tertullian should be understood in this sense in the *Scorpiace*: “I do not know what magic is being tied around.”

These phylacteries, or bindings, were of various kinds: sinews, bones, and roots enclosed in leather, as Tatian the Assyrian notes in his *Address to the Greeks*, page 172 of the Paris edition. Others led bears around cities and towns, hanging dyed objects from their heads and entire bodies, and distributing some of their hair together with the dyes as phylacteries to ward off diseases and the evil eye, as Theodore Balsamon teaches in his commentary on the canon of the Sixth Council cited above.

He adds that a certain prefect was condemned by synodal judgment because he was found to possess an ἔνδυμα, that is, a garment of a newly born infant, which he had received from a woman to close the mouths of those who might attempt to speak against him. This *ἔνδυμα* was nothing other than a little cap-like membrane of the head with which some people are born. Lawyers once carried it in their bosoms, believing that it contributed to eloquence, as Lampridius reports in his life of Antoninus Diadumenianus: “Boys are sometimes marked by a natural cap, which midwives snatch away and sell to credulous lawyers, since advocates are said to be helped by it.”

Written charms were also phylacteries. Those who carried them on their persons believed that they could not be bound by any means, as may be seen in Bede, Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 22: “Through the recitation of these words what I have mentioned came about, so that no one could bind him.” Meanwhile the count who held him began to marvel and ask why he could not be bound, and whether he had with him those “letters of release” about which stories are told.

The image of Alexander the Great also belongs here. Those who carried it on their persons, whether in rings, bracelets, or every kind of ornament, believed that it helped them in every undertaking, as Trebellius Pollio writes in his life of the emperor Quietus.

Finally, among Christians phylacteries are sacred relics—such as those of the holy cross or of martyrs—concealed in gold, silver, crystal, or any other material. Pope Saint Gregory writes in Book XII, letter 6: “We have arranged to send phylacteries to our most excellent son, King Adulouvaldus: namely, a cross containing wood from the Lord’s cross, and a Gospel reading enclosed in a Persian case.”

Helgaud, a monk of Fleury, writes in the *Life of King Robert*: “Accordingly, wishing to justify his own oath-takers as he justified himself, he had made a phylactery entirely of crystal, ornamented around its circumference with pure gold, without any relic of a saint enclosed within it. The chief men swore upon it, unaware of this pious fraud.”

The *Acts of Saint William of Gellone* say: “He had sent them from Jerusalem, through Zacharias, a priest of great purpose and great testimony, and through two Jerusalemite monks of great devotion and no small authority, that venerable phylactery of the Lord’s cross, to be worshipped by all mortals, most beautifully adorned, as far as human art could achieve, with the brilliance of gems and the purest gold.” MENAR.]

7. The fifth kind is that of the circumcellions, who wander everywhere in the habit of monks, carrying hypocrisy around for sale. They travel through the provinces, sent by no one, fixed nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere. Some fabricate things they have not seen, taking their own opinions for God; others sell the limbs of martyrs—if indeed they are martyrs; others magnify their fringes and phylacteries, seeking glory from human beings; others go about with long hair, so that sanctity with its hair cut may not be considered inferior to sanctity with flowing hair. Thus whoever sees them is supposed to think of those ancients whom we read about—Samuel, Elijah, and the others. 437–439

[Col. 0799A] 8. Others proclaim that they possess honors they have not received. Others falsely claim that they have heard of, seen, or are going to visit their parents or relatives in this or that region. They beg from everyone and demand from everyone either the expense of their profitable poverty or the price of their feigned sanctity. Meanwhile, whenever they are caught in their evil deeds or words, or in any way become known, the monastic profession as a whole is blasphemed under their general name.

[Note: [Col. 0799D]

9. “The sixth kind.” From the same *Conference*, chapters 7 and 10. GRIAL.

Ibid. “As Jerome says of them,” Letter 22, to Eustochium. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Or renuitae.” The word *sive* (“or”) is taken from what has been stated. For *renuitae* is Latin, not Egyptian. Thus Latin authors have explained the name *sarabaitae*. Smaragdus, commenting on chapter 1 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, says: “Sarabaites are interpreted as *renuitae*, because they refuse to follow the examples or virtue of their elders.” Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, in *Conference* 3: “We wretched men are not monks, although we are falsely called so; we are sarabaites, that is, *renuitae*, because we refuse the yoke of regular discipline.” Anonymous glosses: “Sarabaites, in the Egyptian language, are called *renuitae* in Latin—those who refuse to have an abbot.” Hence manuscript glosses on Saint Benedict’s Rule, preserved in Paris in the library of Saint Victor: “Of the sarabaites, who refuse or reject.” MENAR.

Ibid. “Pleasures.” Another reading is “wills.” Following Saint Jerome, Grialius printed *remobothitae*. See Ducange under this word. Menardus has *renuitae*. Grialius has “cells, and these things,” etc. AREV.]

9. The sixth kind of monk is itself most foul and neglected. It sprang up through Ananias and Sapphira at the beginning of the Church and was cut down by the severity of the apostle Peter (Acts V). Because they separate themselves from coenobitic discipline and seek their own free pleasures, they are called in the language of the Egyptians *sarabaitae*, or *remobothitae*. For they build cells for themselves and falsely call them monasteries; freed from the authority of their elders, they live according to their own judgment. They compete eagerly in works, not so that they may distribute to the needy, but so that they may acquire money to store away. As Jerome says of them, “as though the matter were a holy craft and not a way of life, whatever they sell is sold at a higher price.”

10. In reality, as the same author says, they commonly compete in fasts, making a secret victory out of the matter. “Among them,” he says, “everything is contrived: loose sleeves, baggy leggings, coarser clothing, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, disparagement of the clergy; and whenever a feast day arrives, they eat until they vomit.”

11. Cassian distinguishes between a coenobium and a monastery in this way: a monastery may also be called the dwelling of a single monk, whereas a coenobium can mean only the dwelling of many. I shall briefly describe their manner of life, as the institution of the Fathers teaches. As has been said, after first despising and abandoning the attractions of this world, they gather together in the holiest common life. They live in prayer, reading, discussion, vigils, and fasts. Swollen with no pride and darkened by no envy, but modest, reserved, peaceful, and pursuing a life of complete harmony, they reveal their thoughts to one another and mutually examine and correct them.

[Col. 0800A] [Note: [Col. 0800D]

12. “Others never go out.” See the *Rule of Monks*, chapter 5, section 5. AREV.]

12. No one possesses anything earthly as private property. They do not wear costly or brightly colored garments, but the cheapest and plainest. They never use baths for bodily pleasure, but only rarely and because of the necessity of illness. Without consulting the abbot, they go nowhere, nor do they take anything without a sign of the father’s command. They work with their hands at tasks by which the body may be nourished without the mind being distracted. While working with their hands, they sing and console the labor itself, as though with a divine song. 441

[Note: [Col. 0800D]

13. “These Fathers,” etc. Hence the custom arose of calling religious men “Fathers.” “Tolerance,” etc. Another reading: “indicating tolerance and discernment in all things”; another: “distinguished by tolerance and discernment in all things,” etc. AREV.]

13. They hand over their work to those whom they call deans, because each is placed over ten men, so that none of them has to concern himself with the care of his body—not with food or clothing, nor with anything else required either by daily necessity or, as commonly happens, by mutual well-being. The deans hand these matters over to the superior; the superior, arranging everything with great care, makes available whatever their life requires because of bodily weakness. He himself, however, also renders an account to the one whom they call the father. These fathers, distinguished by understanding, tolerance, and discernment and eminent in every respect, care for those whom they call sons without any pride, with great authority on their part in commanding and great willingness on the sons’ part in obeying.

[Note: [Col. 0800D]

14. “With fixed intention of heart.” Grialius printed *intentatione cordis*. Soon afterward, for *in collatione*, some have *in consultatione*, others *in consolatione*. See chapters 7 and 16 of the *Rule of Monks*. AREV.]

14. At a signal, they all frequently assemble by night and by day, hurrying quickly to the prayer of the appointed hours. They celebrate it with fixed intention of heart and persist without weariness until the psalms are completed. Likewise, on alternate days, while they are still fasting, they assemble at the conference to hear the Father. They listen to him with astonishing devotion and profound silence, expressing the movements of their souls—as the speaker’s discourse stirs them—by groaning or weeping. Then, in great silence, they restore their bodies with only as much food as health requires. Each restrains desire and gluttony through frugality, lest the heart be burdened, even by the very things that are provided, which are sparse and of the poorest kind.

15. Accordingly, they abstain not only from meat and wine, as sufficient for subduing lusts, but also from everything that stimulates the appetite of the belly and throat. Whatever remains beyond necessary sustenance from the work of their hands and the restriction of their meals is distributed to the needy with such care that nothing excessive remains. To this purpose of holy service come not only free people but also, for the most part, those of servile condition—men liberated by their masters for this purpose, or rather, men who are to be liberated for this purpose. 442

16. They also come from agricultural life, from the practice of trades, and from the labor of the common people—indeed, all the more blessed because they have been trained with greater hardship. If they are not admitted, it is a grave offense. For many truly great and worthy of imitation have arisen from this number. Therefore God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and chose the base things of the world and things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might glory before God.

[Note: [Col. 0801D]

17. “Likewise, women’s coenobia,” etc. Another reading: “women’s coenobia, that is, monastic virgins, serving God carefully and chastely, who, separated in their dwellings,” etc. AREV.]

17. In the same way there are also coenobia of women who serve God with careful chastity. Separated and removed from men as far as possible in their dwellings, they are joined only by the devout love of holiness and by imitation of virtue. No young man has access to them, nor even the most serious and proven old men, except as far as the vestibule, for the purpose of providing what they need. Each community is governed by women of the greatest seriousness and proven character, skilled and ready not only to train and order conduct but also to instruct minds. They exercise and sustain their bodies through wool-working, and they give the garments themselves to the monks, receiving from them in return whatever is necessary for food. The coenobia of virgins and monks appear to observe these customs, this life, and this institution.

18. Monks, however, are chosen according to humility. For many of them are stained by the disease of vainglory, and many are puffed up by abstinence and exalted by knowledge. They do good deeds, not for eternal life but for fame—that is, either to seek the glory of praise or to reach the height of the honor they desire. Among such people discord frequently arises, and envy is born from the progress of their brothers. Love of temporal things spreads among them, and they pursue earthly desires with greater eagerness the more frequently and shamelessly they do so before human eyes. Such people therefore should not be called monks at all, because they are joined to God by profession alone, not by action.

## 443 CHAPTER XVII. On Penitents

[Col. 0801D]

1. Job first provided an example for penitents. After his bereavements and afflictions, while still reproving himself, he took up the mourning of repentance in sackcloth and ashes, saying: “Therefore I repent in dust and ashes” (Job XLII, 6). After him David offered us instruction in repentance. Having fallen through a grievous wound, when he heard his sin from the prophet, he immediately repented and healed his guilt through a confession of repentance (2 Sam. XII).

[Note: [Col. 0801D]

Chapter XVII, no. 2. “The name repentance,” etc. Another reading: “Repentance, however, is not measured by the passage of months and times, but by the punishment by which the soul is tormented and the flesh is mortified.” Hittorpius likewise found this reading in three of his manuscripts. AREV.]

2. The Ninevites and many others confessed their sins and did penance; they were displeased with what they had been, and they were pleased with what they had become through God (Jonah III). Repentance is the medicine of the wound and the hope of salvation. Through it sinners are saved, and through it God is moved to mercy. It is measured not by time but by the depth of grief and tears. The word “repentance” derives from *poena*, “punishment,” by which the soul is tormented and the flesh mortified.

[Col. 0802B] [Note: [Col. 0801D]

3. It was generally the custom of penitents to cut their hair, but this practice did not prevail universally. For Saint Jerome, Letter 30, says that Fabiola stood among the penitents with her hair loose. See Bingham, volume VIII, pages 122–123. I have explained more than once in my commentary on Prudentius, pages 740, 883, and 1168, that among the Romans accused persons were accustomed to let their hair grow. AREV.]

3. Those who do penance grow out their hair and beard in order to show the abundance of their crimes, by which the sinner’s head is weighed down. Hair is understood as representing vices, as it is written: “Each person is bound by the hairs of his sins” (Prov. V, 22). If a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. XI). Penitents therefore assume that very disgrace in proportion to their sins.

[Note: [Col. 0802D]

4. “Or because dust,” etc. Another reading: “or because they were made from dust—that is, they became impious.” Sozomen describes the rite by which penitents in the Roman Church cast themselves upon the ground in Book VII, chapter 16. AREV.]

4. Their prostration in sackcloth signifies, through the sackcloth, the remembrance of sins, because of the goats destined for the left hand. Therefore we who confess prostrate ourselves in sackcloth, as though saying: “My sin is ever before me.” As for their being sprinkled with ashes, this is either so that they may remember that they are ash and dust, or because they have become dust—that is, impious. Hence those first human transgressors, withdrawing from God and offending the Creator by evil deeds, returned to the dust from which they had originally been taken. It is therefore fitting that the penitent mourn his sin in sackcloth and ashes: in sackcloth there is harshness and the piercing of sins, while in ashes the dust of the dead is displayed. 444

5. For this reason we do penance in both, so that through the piercing of sackcloth we may recognize the vices we have committed through guilt, and through the ashes of the embers we may weigh the sentence of death to which we have come by sinning. The Catholic Church confidently binds the remedy of repentance to the hope of pardon and enjoins its practice. After the one sacrament of baptism—which, commended by a unique tradition, it carefully forbids to be repeated—it substitutes the aid of repentance as a medicinal remedy.

[Note: [Col. 0802D]

6. “With their dignity alone preserved.” This passage has offended some who did not notice that Isidore is speaking here of public penance. These are the words of Felix III, Letter 1, chapter 1. See Gratian, Distinction 50, chapter *Confirmandum*, with what follows. GRIAL.]

Ibid. “With the dignity of these alone preserved.” Hittorpius, together with two manuscripts, reads: “with the dignity of honors alone preserved”; I too would consider this preferable. Petavius, book XII, proves that the public penance of which Isidore speaks here could not coexist with clerical office. For it had been established that no one, after public penance for any crime, might receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, as Saint Augustine reports in Letter 50. AREV.]

### 6

Everyone must acknowledge that he needs this remedy for the daily excesses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life. Yet the dignity of these alone must be preserved, so that it is done by priests and Levites with God alone as witness, but by all others with the priest solemnly standing before God; thus fruitful confession may cover what reckless desire or negligent ignorance is recognized to have brought about. Just as we believe that all iniquities are forgiven in baptism, or that no sins are reckoned against anyone through martyrdom, so through the fruitful contrition of penance let us confess that all sins are erased. For the tears of penitents are reckoned before God in place of baptism. Therefore, however great and serious their offenses may be, one must not despair of God’s mercy in their case.

[Note: [Col. 0803D]

### 7

“As was said above,” namely, section 2. Others give: “as has often been said.” Soon afterward, in the phrase “the more …,” some copies read: “the more ready the mind’s inclination is toward evil, the more devoted it ought to be in doing penance.” Hittorpius conjectures: “the greater the mind’s abrupt rush toward evil, the greater ought to be its intention of devotion, and its affliction in doing penance.” A little later one should read, or understand: “Either when we weep over what we have done wrongly, or when we weep because we have not done what we ought to have done.” That is, penance concerns either sins of commission, as they are called, or sins of omission. AREV.]

### 7

In the practice of repentance, as was said above, the measure of time is not so much to be considered as the measure of sorrow; for God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Nevertheless, as great as the mind’s intention was, when it rushed toward evil in sinning, so great must its devotion be in lamentation. There are two kinds of penitential grief: either when we weep over what we have done wrongly, or when we fail to do what we ought to have done. But he truly does penance who neither neglects penance for past deeds nor commits further deeds requiring penance. Whoever continually pours out tears and nevertheless does not cease sinning has lamentation, but not cleansing.

### 8

Those who are converted to penance through God’s grace ought not to be disturbed if, after their amendment, the abandoned vices again assail their hearts, so long as they cannot harm their good manner of life, provided that such a thought does not break out into consent or action. To endure thoughts of vice without carrying them to completion is not a matter of condemnation but of testing; it is not an occasion for entering into peril, but rather for increasing virtue. Even if someone ceases to be wicked through penance near the end of his life, he ought not for that reason to despair because he is at life’s final limit: God does not regard what we were previously, but what we are near the end of life.

[Note: [Col. 0803D]

### 9

“Conversion,” etc. Others read: “conversion, if uncertain death should overtake him before it comes.” Others: “a hoped-for confession, if uncertain death should overtake him, will in no way help.” AREV.]

### 9

For by his end he either justifies or condemns each person, as it is written: “He himself judges the ends of the earth” (1 Samuel 2:10); and elsewhere: “He himself considers the end of all things” (Job 28:24). Therefore we do not doubt that a person is justified near the end through the contrition of penance. But because this rarely happens, we must fear that, while the hoped-for conversion is postponed until the end, death may come before penance can help. Thus, although conversion at the very end is good, the conversion undertaken long before the end is much better, so that one may pass more securely from this life.

### CHAPTER XVIII  
### On Virgins

[Col. 0804B]

[Note: [Col. 0803D]

Chapter XVIII, section 1. “Of so holy a purpose.” The words that follow are Cassian’s, unless you prefer to regard them as Jerome’s or common to both. GRIAL.

Ibid. In the Isidorian works, chapter 93, section 5, I observed that this chapter appears in Vatican Manuscript 202 under the title *Isidore the Younger, On Virginity*, and agrees with our edition. The word *auctrix* (“originator” or “foundress”), which Isidore uses here, seems to deny that it may properly be used. See the note. Instead of “followers of perpetual continence,” some copies have “followers of perpetual penance.” Immediately afterward: “they sprang up, chastising the desire of lust, and castrating themselves not only …, heavenly, etc.” AREV.]

### 1

Now I shall briefly explain what constitutes the integrity of sacred virginity and from whom the devotion to so holy a purpose arose. As far as the Old Testament is concerned, Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel are known to have been the first to devote themselves to the good of chastity and continence. As far as the New Testament is concerned, Christ is the head of male virgins, and Mary is the head of female virgins. She herself is their foundress, herself the mother of our head, who is the virgin’s son and the bridegroom of virgins. From her arose the ranks of holy men and maidens; from her arose the male and female followers of perpetual continence, chastising themselves and castrating themselves not only in body but also at the very root of desire, meditating upon a heavenly and angelic life amid earthly mortality, and preserving perpetual incorruption in corruptible flesh. To them yields all the fruitfulness of the flesh and all conjugal chastity.

[Note: [Col. 0804C]

### 2

“Since the whole Church itself.” Augustine, Sermon 23, *On the Words of the Lord according to Matthew*: “The whole Church, which consists of virgins, boys, married men, and married women, is called a virgin by one name. How do we prove this?
