Hear the Apostle speaking, not to consecrated women alone, but rather to the whole Church of God: ‘For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.’” And Tertullian, *On Monogamy*: “And they will join you in the virgin Church, the bride of one Christ.” Ambrose likewise, in his exhortation to virginity: “The Church is a virgin whom the Apostle endeavored to present as a chaste virgin to Christ.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Yet let virginity be praised in such a way that marriage is not condemned.” Jerome often repeats this. GRIAL.

Ibid. “For before Christ’s coming, marriages were pleasing.” From Tertullian, from whom Jerome also took the same material. GRIAL.

Ibid. “For did not …,” etc. Others read: “Did not his voice speak in this way: ‘Increase,’ etc.” Immediately afterward some read: “the time has likewise been gathered up,” or “the time in which it was read.” AREV.]

### 2

For since the whole Church itself is a virgin, betrothed to one man, as the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 11), how much more worthy of honor are those members of it who preserve in the flesh itself what the whole Church will preserve at the end? Yet let virginity be praised in such a way that marriage is not condemned. For one must not condemn what is good, but add what is better. Before Christ’s coming, marriages were pleasing to God; after his coming, virginity was pleasing. The first judgment of God commanded, “Increase and beget”; the second urged continence. For there is no longer room for that command: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:28), because another saying has intervened: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing” (Luke 21:23). And also: “The time has now been gathered up. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (1 Corinthians 7).

[Note: [Col. 0805D]

### 3

“And unless I am mistaken, of one and the same God,” through “had permitted,” are words of Tertullian, in his *Exhortation to Chastity*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Having permitted,” etc. Others: “having given rein to the pleasures of marriage.” Others: “having given permission to those wishing to marry.” Below, some copies read: “the matter with a wife is not expedient.” AREV.]

### 3

And, unless I am mistaken, this is the pronouncement of one and the same God. At that time, in the beginning, God sent forth the seed of the human race, giving free rein to marriage until the world should be filled; but now, at the ends of the ages, he has restrained what he sent forth and recalled what he had permitted. Hence Solomon, foreseeing in the Spirit, says: “A time for embracing, and a time to be far from embracing” (Ecclesiastes 3:5). For the old command was that the earth should be filled by procreation, but the new command is that heaven should be filled through continence and virginity. Yet it is clear that virginity is a reward so difficult and exalted that when the apostles said in one place, “If such is the situation of a man with a woman, it is not expedient to marry,” the Lord replied: “Let the one who can receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:10–12).

[Note: [Col. 0805D]

### 4

“And again, if you take a wife,” through “they were struck down,” are words from the commentaries attributed to Jerome on the Epistle to the Corinthians. GRIAL.

[Col. 0806D] Ibid. “He did not sin.” Others: “He did not sin, because it is a matter of free will.” AREV.]

### 4

It is therefore not a commandment imposed upon those who practice continence, but an exhortation; virginity is not enjoined as a necessity, but praised so that it may be a matter of will, as the Apostle testifies: “Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who himself has knowledge of God. For I think this good because of the present necessity, since it is good for a person to be thus” (1 Corinthians 7). But those who cannot endure the temptation of the flesh must seek the harbor of marriage. Hence the same Apostle says: “If he cannot contain himself, let him marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.” And again: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.” And if you do not wish to be greater, be at least lesser, for you are free in your will.

Marriage is therefore not a sin, but because of the world’s cares those who marry can scarcely keep God’s law. He says that those who marry do not sin if they have not previously vowed chastity to God. But whoever has made a promise in his heart and acts otherwise incurs condemnation, because, as the Apostle says, he has made his first faith void. What was lawful by nature he made unlawful for himself by a vow, just as Ananias and Sapphira were permitted to retain nothing from the price of their possession; for this reason they were struck down by sudden death (Acts 5).

[Note: [Col. 0806D]

### 6

“Through the prophet Isaiah he will give.” Basil treats this passage with great elegance in his book *On Virginity*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Much better.” The Vulgate has: “better than sons and daughters.” GRIAL.]

### 6

In the Gospel, various kinds of eunuchs are mentioned, but possession of the kingdom is assigned especially to those who castrated themselves for the love of God—that is, not those whom necessity arising from incapacity compels, but those whom their will has made continent. For it is written, while the Lord was teaching: “There are eunuchs who were born so; there are also eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12). To these he also says through the prophet Isaiah that in his house and within his walls he will give them a named place, much better than that of sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:5).

### 7

For those who are born in this condition, or whose male organ itself has been weakened so that they cannot beget children—as are the eunuchs of powerful men and kings—it is sufficient that they are Christians and keep God’s commandments. Yet their intention is that, if they had been able, they would have had wives. Therefore they are made equal in God’s house to the other married believers, because they were castrated for the sake of the world, not for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; for they do not take wives through spiritual virtue, but fail to take them through the necessity of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0806D]

### 8

“Meetings of women.” Others: “intercourse with women.” A little later: “no one can follow either by hearing,” or “no one can follow or hear.” AREV.]

### 8

How great, then, is the gift of holiness in virgins, since John prescribes that only those who have not been defiled by meetings with women should cling to the Lamb’s footsteps (Revelation 14:4)? They are the twelve times twelve thousand holy harpists, undefiled in virginity of body and inviolate in chastity of heart, who follow the Lamb wherever he goes. No one can follow him wherever he goes, except virginity alone. The other faithful therefore follow the Lamb after losing bodily virginity, but not wherever he goes—only as far as they have been able.

### 9

Therefore, lest so great a gift of holiness be corrupted by pride, one must be on guard. Virginity exalts many, and continence raises them up. I say confidently that humble married people follow the Lamb more easily—even if not wherever he goes, certainly as far as they can—than proud virgins. For how can one follow someone whom one does not wish to approach? Or how can one approach someone who does not come to teach that he is gentle and humble in heart? Let virgins proceed along the road of exaltation, but let them follow Christ with the foot of humility, perseveringly holding what they ardently vowed, so that their confessed and preserved integrity may also be matched by the other virtues, without which virginity unquestionably remains idle and empty. For when good deeds are added to virginity, they display an angelic life to human beings and heavenly conduct upon earth.

[Col. 0807A] ### 10

Those, then, are proved to be virgins who serve continence in such a way that they are weighed down by no crimes and by no burden of earthly concern. For care of the world is produced by the bond of marriage, as Paul teaches when he says: “I want you to be free from anxiety. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but the married man is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Corinthians 7:32–33). From this it is understood that a vow of continence of this kind cannot please God if it is impeded by secular cares. For it is of no benefit to be free from the activity of the flesh if one is bound by worldly concerns. The only result is that such people acquire greater punishments for failing to conquer the world, although they were able to conquer the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0807C]

### 11

“For in ecclesiastical ranks or offices,” through “he may display,” Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Could anything have been more honorably distinguished by some prerogative of a male rank or office?” etc. Most of the remaining words of this chapter come from that passage. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Notable,” or “distinguished.” As usual, he uses disjunction for conjunction. Tertullian wrote “notable and distinguished.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “The honor of the sanctified body.” Tertullian has “the honor of holiness.” GRIAL.]

### 11

It is asked why female virgins are veiled at the blessing. The reason is this: women are in no way assigned ecclesiastical ranks or offices. They are neither permitted to speak or teach in the church, nor to touch or offer, nor to claim for themselves any share in a male function or priestly office. Therefore, since she is a virgin and has purposed to sanctify her flesh, she is granted the allowance of a veil, so that she may enter the church as someone notable or distinguished, display the honor of her sanctified body with freedom of head, and wear upon her head a mitre like a crown of virginal glory.

## CHAPTER XIX  
## On Widows

[Note: [Col. 0807D]

Chapter XIX, section 1. “Anna … who recognized the Lord as an infant.” Tertullian, in *On Fasting against the Psychics*: “Anna, daughter of Phanuel, who both recognized the infant Lord and proclaimed many things about him to those awaiting Israel’s redemption.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Brought back.” Others: “led back.” AREV.]

### 1

There are many examples of widows. The first mentioned in Scripture is Naomi (Ruth 1); then the widow to whom Elijah is said to have been sent (1 Kings 17); and the Shunammite widow, who used to receive Elisha and provide him with food (2 Kings 4). There is also that remarkable widow Judith, who triumphed over Holofernes, commander of the Assyrians, and, after defeating the enemy, brought back her chastity unharmed (Judith 13). In the New Testament, Anna is mentioned as the first widow. She recognized the Lord as an infant and was worthy to recognize the grace of his divinity before she could hear his word (Luke 2).

[Note: [Col. 0807D]

### 2

“Blessed, therefore, is the virgin because she is untouched,” etc. Not Isidore alone but Jerome also drew these words from Tertullian, whose words in Book I *To His Wife* are: “How great is the worth of the widow herself, whose defender the Lord will discuss? I do not think that this has been given only to virgins, although in them a complete and whole integrity will soon see the face of God. Yet a widow has something more laborious, because it is easy not to desire what you do not know, and to reject what you have never desired. More glorious is the continence that knows its own right, that knows what it has seen. The virgin may be considered happier, the widow more laborious: the former always possessed what is good; the latter found what was good for herself. In the former grace is crowned; in the latter virtue is crowned,” etc. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Who, after the bed of one marriage has been interrupted, thereafter renounces,” etc. Both manuscripts have this, very correctly; the editor who did not recognize whose words they were did not dare follow them. They are Tertullian’s, at the beginning of the *Exhortation to Chastity*: “The third degree that remains is monogamy, when, after one marriage has been interrupted, one thereafter renounces sexual relations.” Thus the masculine word had been disgracefully added; it is also found in the Roman edition. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Thereafter renounces sexual relations.” Others: “thereafter renounces the mind.” But the reading established by Grial should be retained. Soon afterward, some manuscripts read: “may lack the name of true widowhood,” taking *careat* with the accusative, as elsewhere *utor* is used, etc. AREV.]

### 2

This state is almost joined to virginity; hence the widow was the first to recognize Christ, whom a virgin bore. Blessed, therefore, is the virgin because she is untouched; stronger is the widow because she has experience. Yet both have a reward before God: the former greater, the latter following. The Apostle calls her a widow who, after the bed of one marriage has been interrupted, thereafter renounces sexual relations. For he says: “Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one man” (1 Timothy 5:9). Consequently, a woman who has been bound to several husbands lacks the name of true widowhood.

[Note: [Col. 0808D]

### 3

“Certainly like Tabitha,” through “of living,” from the commentaries attributed to Jerome on the Epistle to Timothy. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Certainly so that their manner of walking,” through “dignity,” from Jerome’s commentary on Titus 2. GRIAL.]

### 3

The same Apostle expressed what widows ought to be, saying: “If she has a reputation for good works, certainly like Tabitha” (Acts 9:36); if she has brought up children—understood, for God; if she has shown hospitality; if she has washed the feet of the saints; if she has supplied those suffering tribulation—that is, the sick or those in prison; if she has followed every good work—briefly summing up everything so that they may be examples of conduct in all things. And again: “Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior” (Titus 2:3), so that their walking, movements, expression, speech, and silence may present the dignity of sacred continence.

[Note: [Col. 0808D]

### 4

“For they are accustomed,” through “from idleness,” are the words of the same author, in the same place. GRIAL.

Ibid. “At the same time,” through “things that ought not to be said,” from the commentaries cited on the Epistle to Timothy. GRIAL.

Ibid. “For they are accustomed,” etc. Others: “For those ages whose bodies have passed through the luxury of the flesh are accustomed …” AREV.]

### 4

After this he added: “Not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but using little.” For these ages, which have scorched the body with luxury, are accustomed to give themselves over to wine in place of lust. After this is added: “Teachers of what is good,” so that they may teach prudence. He permitted them to teach women, but not in church—privately; for this class of little women tends to be talkative. Hence the same Apostle marks certain widows as curious and wordy, and says that this vice comes from idleness: “At the same time they learn to go about from house to house” (1 Timothy 5:13), namely, while restrained by no fear and subject to no husband’s authority, they roam about not only idle but also inquisitive, saying things they ought not to say.

### 5

The same Apostle declares that widows who, after adopting a purpose of continence, desire to marry have condemnation. “For when they have become wanton against Christ,” he says, “they desire to marry, having condemnation because they have rejected their first faith”—that is, because they did not remain in what they had first vowed. Yet he does not say “they marry,” but “they desire to marry.” For many of them are recalled from marriage not by love of their noble purpose, but by fear of open disgrace.

[Note: [Col. 0809C]

### 6

“Whom they regret,” etc. Others: “whom the form of their profession completely reveals, but whom shame displeases,” etc. And at the end: “serving correction.” AREV.]

### 6

Those, therefore, who desire to marry and for that reason do not marry because they cannot do so with impunity would have done better not to make a vow and to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9)—that is, than to be consumed by the hidden flame of desire. They regret their profession and are ashamed of their disgrace. Unless they correct themselves, direct their hearts, and once again conquer lust through fear of God, they are to be counted among the dead if they live in pleasures. Hence the Apostle says: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Timothy 5:6), whether they live amid hardships and fasts without any correction of heart, serving display more than amendment.

## CHAPTER XX  
## On Married People

[Note: [Col. 0809C]

Chapter XX, section 1. Grialius distinguishes *tenuisset*. After this, etc., others read *tenuisset*. Here, after he had been driven from the blessed dwelling, he knew his wife. AREV.]

### 1

The law of nature concerning married people has existed from the beginning. For God made Adam and gave him Eve as a helper, followed by the command concerning procreation: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). But the woman, once made, was first a comfort before she became a wife, until disobedience expelled from paradise those whom obedience had kept within paradise; and afterward, driven from that blessed dwelling, he recognized the woman as his own, as the Book of Genesis teaches: “And Adam knew his wife, and she conceived and bore a son” (Genesis 4:1).

[Note: [Col. 0809D]

### 2

“Preceded.” Others: “expressed beforehand.” AREV.]

### 2

Therefore marriage preceded the labor that was added, and the unions entered into beforehand by those who were destined to suffer thistles and thorns; then came the wearinesses of procreation. Hence the following decree preceded the woman who was to give birth: “In pain and sorrow you shall bear children” (Genesis 3:16). Those who were thus created would, as we see, be taken away by various misfortunes and griefs. Hence the Apostle, preaching, says: “Such people will have tribulation in the flesh” (1 Corinthians 7:28). Nevertheless, the honorable bed of marriage and the undefiled marriage chamber are not without fruit (Hebrews 13:4). From them comes the offspring of the saints, and what is praised in virginity belongs also to marriage. Therefore we do not call marriage a sin, but neither do we place it on a level with the good of virginal or even widowed continence.

[Note: [Col. 0809D]

### 3

“A man made one female from one of his ribs.” Tertullian, in *On Monogamy*: “God fashioned one female for the male, taking her from one of his ribs, and certainly from among several,” etc. He had said the same in the *Exhortation*, and Jerome adapted the entire passage for his work against Jovinian. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Likewise according to spiritual marriages.” The same author in the *Exhortation*: “But when the Apostle interprets ‘the two shall be one flesh’ as referring to the Church and Christ, according to the spiritual marriage of the Church and Christ—one Christ and one Church of his—we must recognize that the one marriage has been doubled and heightened for us, both according to the foundation of human generation and according to the foundation established by Christ.” GRIAL.]

### 3

Marriage in itself is good; but because of what surrounds it, it becomes bad. It becomes bad through the very things of which the Apostle says: “He who is with a wife considers the things of the world”; and again: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife” (1 Corinthians 7:2). The fact that it is not one man with several women, but one man and one woman who are joined, is itself exemplified by the first union made by God. For when God had fashioned the human being and saw that a partner equal to him was necessary, he took one of his ribs and fashioned one woman for him. Thus Adam and the woman Eve, joined to each other in a single marriage, established for humanity the pattern sanctioned by the authority of its origin and by God’s first will. Likewise, according to spiritual marriage, as there is one Christ and one Church, so there is one husband and one wife, both according to the testimony of human generation and according to the sacrament of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0809D]

### 4

“The number of marriages,” through “may be represented,” are words of Tertullian in the same work and of Jerome, Book I against Jovinian. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Second marriages,” through “it is not a matter of religion but of crime,” are said according to Jerome’s meaning—not that he condemns those who marry twice, or even eight times, to use his own words, but because he wishes celibacy and widowhood to stand far above marriage. Gratian also reported his words, somewhat more freely, in 31, question 1, chapter *Quomodo*. GRIAL.]

### 4

The number of marriages began with a cursed man. Lamech was the first to marry two women and made three into one flesh. But you will say that the patriarchs also had several wives at once; therefore it is permitted for us to marry several. Certainly it will be permitted if any types of a future sacrament still remain, by which several marriages may be represented. The Apostle commands second marriages because of lack of continence (1 Corinthians 7); for it is better to marry one man again than to fornicate with many in order to satisfy lust. The license to marry repeatedly is no longer a matter of religion but of crime.

[Note: [Col. 0810D]

### 5

“But that to virgins legally marrying, a woman who has had one husband,” etc. Tertullian, in the *Exhortation*: “Monogamy is held in the highest honor among the pagans, so that even for virgins legally marrying, women who have had one husband are employed as bridal attendants; although this is the beginning of an auspice, it is nevertheless an auspice of good.” Thus Tertullian’s reasoning must be completed from this passage. I am greatly surprised that those who worked to emend it did not see this, and that they missed nothing in the interrupted and unfinished sentence. GRIAL.

Ibid. “To those marrying,” etc. Others: “to those marrying, a woman who has had one husband must be retained; they are employed for the wedding.” Others: “for those marrying one man, brideswomen are employed … it is an auspice of good.” Instead of this conjecture, the Bignaean edition has: “this is plainly so.” AREV.]

### 5

For the fact that, in the very union, marriages are blessed by a priest was also done by God in the first creation of human beings. For it is written: “God made the human being; in the image of God he made him; male and female he created them, and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:27–28). Thus, by this likeness, what was then done in paradise is now done in the Church. The fact that women who have had one husband are employed as bridal attendants for virgins legally marrying is evidently because of monogamy; although this is done as an auspice, it is nevertheless an auspice of good.

[Note: [Col. 0811C]

### 6

“But that these same women,” through “may arrive.” Almost the entire passage is found in Gratian, 30, question 5, chapter *Feminae*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Hence Rebecca,” through “veiled herself,” from Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*. The same passage also appears at the end of Book I of Ambrose, *On Abraham*. GRIAL.]

### 6

The fact that these same women, when they marry, are veiled is evidently so that they may know that by this they are subject and humble toward their husbands. Hence the veil itself is commonly called *mavortem*, that is, “Mars,” because it bears the sign of marital dignity and authority. “The head of a woman is the man” (1 Corinthians 11:3). They are also veiled, accordingly, when they marry, so that they may recognize the modesty proper to women, because what is shameful follows from this. Hence Rebecca, when she was being led to her bridegroom, as soon as she saw him did not endure greetings or kisses; but immediately, realizing what her future status would be, she veiled her head with a cloak (Genesis 24:65). For *obnubere* means “to cover.” Hence married women are also called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces; and hence clouds are called *nubes*, because they cover the sky.

[Note: [Col. 0811C]

### 7

“Are joined by one bond by a Levite.” This passage is different in Gratian; we have followed our manuscripts. GRIAL.

[Col. 0811D] Ibid. “By a Levite.” Others: “by ribbons.” Others: “bound.” From this passage of Isidore, Ludovicus Dorleans, in *New Reflections on Tacitus*, p. 790, concludes that the flame-colored veil of brides was mixed with white and purple. But according to Pliny and Verrius it was yellow; according to the commentator on Juvenal, Satire 6, blood-colored; according to Festus, white. Perhaps it varied according to times and places. AREV.]

### 7

The fact that those who marry are joined after the blessing by a Levite with one bond is evidently intended to prevent them from breaking the structure of conjugal unity. But the fact that this same ribbon is mixed with white and purple signifies that white is employed for purity of life and purple for the offspring of blood, so that by this sign both are reminded that the law of continence must be observed for a time, but that afterward the marital debt must not be denied. For what the Apostle says to married people—“Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5)—the white color of the ribbon suggests; but what he adds—“and return again to the same”—the purple color demonstrates.

[Note: [Col. 0811D]

### 8

“That the ring is especially …” —“That, especially in business transactions, a ring,” as in Gratian. GRIAL.

Ibid. “In ancient times.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 6: “When gold was known to no one except for the single finger on which the bridegroom had pledged it with a betrothal ring.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “Among Israel, however,” through “maturity,” are Tertullian’s words in *On the Veiling of Virgins*. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Would diminish a single love.” All the manuscripts used by Hittorpius have: “would receive one love.” In one manuscript of his, after “the manifestation of the maturity of the blood.” Brissonius, *On the Rite of Marriage*, p. 290, observes that this was taken from Gellius, Book X, chapter 10, and Macrobius, Book VII of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 13: Isidore reports that the bridegroom’s ring is placed on the fourth finger because a vein in that finger reaches the heart. AREV.]

### 8

The fact that a ring is first given by the bridegroom to the bride is done either as a sign of mutual fidelity or, more particularly, so that their hearts may be joined by this same pledge. Hence the ring is inserted on the fourth finger, because, as is said, a certain vein there carries blood all the way to the heart. In ancient times no more than one ring was given, lest plurality diminish a single love. Among the Israelites, however, it was unlawful to hand a girl over to a man unless the maturity of her blood had first been manifested.

[Note: [Col. 0812C]

### 9

“Among the ancients.” See *Etymologies*, Book IX, chapter 7. GRIAL.

“As a certain wise man says.” Theophrastus, in Jerome, Book I against Jovinian. GRIAL.]

### 9

Among the ancients, four things were considered when husbands were chosen: virtue, family, beauty, and speech; in women, three: whether she was well-born, well-mannered, and beautiful. Now, however, it is not family and character but rather wealth that pleases in wives. It is not asked how chaste a woman is, but rather how beautiful, so that she may nourish the lust of desire and draw after her the sighs of everyone. For a beautiful woman, as a certain wise man says, is quickly loved and difficult to guard, since many love her. Those are true marriages that seek not lust but offspring in marriage. For marriages are not instituted to serve the pleasure of the flesh, but solely to seek the fruit of posterity.

[Note: [Col. 0812D]

### 10

“For the marriage contracts themselves.” Augustine, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*: “Marriage itself, as the marriage contracts proclaim, joins a female and a male for the procreation of children”; and likewise in Sermon 3, on the twenty-second Sunday after Trinity. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Therefore, when anyone lives more luxuriously,” through “defile,” Augustine, in the same place: “But you say: ‘It is indeed a sin, but nevertheless a small one.’ We do not say that it is a capital sin, but if it is practiced too frequently and is not redeemed by fasts or almsgiving, it makes the soul exceedingly unclean.” See Jerome, Book I against Jovinian; Gratian, 23, question 4, chapter *Origo*; and Fulgentius, Letter 1. GRIAL.]

### 10

For the marriage contracts themselves indicate that a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children. Therefore, whenever anyone lives more luxuriously than the necessity of begetting children requires, it is already a sin. Hence those who frequently defile the chastity of the marriage bed through lack of continence must intercede with daily almsgiving and prayers. The goods of marriage are three: offspring, fidelity, and the sacrament. Fidelity requires that no one have intercourse with another man or woman beyond the marital bond; offspring requires that it be received lovingly and raised chastely; the sacrament requires that the marriage not be dissolved and that they not join themselves to another for the sake of offspring.

[Note: [Col. 0812D]

### 11

“Only adultery,” as Jerome says, in his commentary on Matthew 19. These words are cited by Gratian, 32, question 1, chapter *Dixit Dominus*. GRIAL.

“Foolish and impious.” So the Gothic text and Jerome. The Vulgate edition has: “foolish and senseless.” GRIAL.

The statement “wherever there is fornication, and suspicion of fornication, the wife may freely be dismissed” must be explained to mean that divorce may take place, but not that either the husband who dismisses her or the wife who is dismissed may enter another marriage. Maldonatus, in his commentary on Matthew, admirably proves this against the heretics from this passage of Isidore itself. Some more recent theologians also develop the same argument. AREV.]

11. The sacrament is said to exist among married persons for this reason: just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ, so neither can a wife be divided from her husband (Ephesians V). Therefore, what exists in Christ and the Church is, in each individual husband and wife, the inseparable sacrament of their union. Hence the Apostle says: “I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband” (I Corinthians VII). For he forbids her to be dismissed for any reason whatever, lest she join herself to another, according to the custom of the Jews, which the Lord prohibited, saying: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery” (Matthew XIX). Adultery alone, as Jerome says, is capable of overcoming the husband’s affection; indeed, when a wife has divided the one flesh she shared with him and separated herself through fornication, she ought not to be retained by her husband, lest she also bring a curse upon the man, as Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulterous woman is foolish and impious” (Proverbs XVIII). Therefore, wherever fornication exists, or suspicion of fornication exists, the wife may freely be dismissed.

[Note: [Col. 0813D]

12. “What then if she is barren” through “must be regarded [as she is],” from the same passage of Jerome. GRIAL.

Ibid. “As Lactantius says.” Book VI, chapter 23. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Therefore faith must be preserved until he follows Christ,” from Augustine, *On the Ten Strings*, III, cited in Gratian, 32, question 6, chapter “You Shall Not Commit Adultery.” GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius reads *nequam servam* (“a worthless slave-woman”), perhaps for *nequaquam servam* (“by no means a slave-woman”). AREV.]

12. What then if she is barren, if she is deformed, if she is an old woman, if she is foul-smelling, if she is drunk, if she is irascible, if she has bad habits, if she is wanton, if she is foolish, if she is gluttonous, if she is restless, if she is quarrelsome and abusive? She must be kept, [457] whether you wish it or not, and must be regarded as she is, whatever her condition. For when you were free, you voluntarily subjected yourself to servitude. And when a man has a wife, as Lactantius says, he cannot have either a slave-woman or a free woman [in addition], if he is to preserve the fidelity of marriage. For, according to the principle of public law, it is not only the woman who, while she has a husband, is defiled by another man who is an adulteress, while a husband who has another woman is considered free from the charge of adultery. Rather, the divine law has joined the two into one marital body in such a way that whoever tears apart the bodily bond into separate parts is an adulterer. Therefore, each must preserve fidelity toward the other.

[Note: [Col. 0813D]

13. “And without.” Some copies read, “so that without.” AREV.]

13. By the example of continence, the wife should be taught by her husband to conduct herself chastely. For it is unjust to demand what you cannot provide; the husband is the head of the woman. But when a woman lives better than her husband, the household hangs head downward. Therefore the husband ought to go before his wife in every good deed, because he is the head, so that she may imitate her husband and truly follow him, as the body follows its head, just as the Church follows Christ. The Apostle urges spouses to abstain for the sake of prayer and, by mutual consent, to observe periods of sanctification, so that they may devote themselves to prayer without carnal impediment (I Corinthians VII). For in the Old Testament, too, all were first sanctified from women, and thus they were deemed worthy to stand beside God as he descended upon the mountain (Exodus XIX).

[Note: [Col. 0813D]

14. “The same Apostle urges, etc.” through the end: these are the words of Jerome on Titus II. GRIAL.

Ibid. The Vulgate reads: “You shall be under your husband’s authority, and he shall rule over you.” In this passage Isidore follows the older version, along with Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, and others. AREV.]

14. The same Apostle also urges women to be subject to their husbands (Colossians III); for many women, puffed up against simpler men by wealth and nobility, do not remember God’s sentence by which they were subjected to them. For the Lord said to the woman: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis III, 16). Therefore the commands of sacred Scripture must be obeyed, and the husband must be served with a certain free servitude full of love. For man was not created on account of woman, but woman on account of man; and since the man is the woman’s head, while Christ is the man’s head, every wife who is not subject to her husband—that is, to her head—is guilty of the same crime as the husband who is not subject to Christ, his head.

15. The word of the Lord is blasphemed, or God’s first sentence is despised and treated as nothing; or Christ’s Gospel is defamed, when the woman who is Christian and subject according to God’s law desires to rule over the man contrary to the law and faith of nature, even though pagan women also serve their husbands according to the common law of nature. The law of nature is therefore preserved if a woman is subject both to God and to her husband. But if she desires to command her husband, the order of nature is corrupted, and that household will be called wretched and perverse.

# CHAPTER XXI. On catechumens, exorcism, and salt

[Note: [Col. 0814D]

Chapter XXI, note 1. “Various errors.” Another reading is “wicked errors.” On this chapter, see *Isidoriana*, chapter 33, in the description of Vatican Codex 1343, no. 29. AREV.]

1. Let us now pursue the account of the sacraments, or the order of those coming to the faith. Their first degree is that of catechumens, the second that of competentes, and the third that of the baptized. Catechumens are those who first come from paganism, having the will to believe in Christ. Since the first command of exhortation in the law of God is: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy VI), the person to whom God first speaks through the priest, as through Moses, is called a catechumen—that is, a hearer—so that, recognizing the one Lord, he may abandon the various errors of idols.

[Note: [Col. 0814D]

2. Ildefonsus, *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, chapters 23 and 26, transcribes much from this chapter of Isidore. After the words “after it is driven out,” Ildefonsus continues in chapter 24: “The discourse of exorcism is *nonturno verborum*”; it should be read *non torno verborum*, not *nonturno verborum*. Baluzius conjectured *nocturno verborum*. AREV.]

2. I think, moreover, that all those baptized by John for repentance prefigured the catechumens. They are first exorcised, then receive salt, and are anointed. Exorcism is a speech of rebuke made against the unclean spirit in the possessed, or in catechumens, by which the devil’s most wicked power and ingrained malice, or his violent assault, is driven out and expelled from them.

[Note: [Col. 0815D]

3. “Whom he rebuked,” etc. Another reading is: “Jesus, rebuking him, said: ‘Deaf and mute spirit, come out of him.’ And immediately the demon came out of him.” Further on: “Salt was instituted by the Fathers to be given sacramentally to catechumens, so that by its taste they might receive seasoning,” etc. Grialius reads “their taste.” AREV.]

3. This signifies that lunatic whom Jesus rebuked, and from whom the demon departed (Matthew XVII). The devil’s power is exorcised and blown upon them, so that they may renounce him and, rescued from the power of darkness, [459] be transferred into the kingdom of their Lord through the sacrament of baptism. Since little children cannot renounce him on their own, this is accomplished through the hearts and mouths of those who carry them. Salt was instituted by the Fathers to be given as a ministry to catechumens so that, by tasting it, they might receive the seasoning of wisdom and not lose the savor of Christ; nor should they be foolish and look back, like Lot’s wife (Genesis XIX), lest, by giving a bad example, they themselves remain behind while seasoning others.

4. This refers to the woman who, when she was being rescued from Sodom, looked back on the road and there remained as a statue of salt. By this sign those who renounce the world and its actions and desires through faith are seasoned, so that they do not remember their former attachment or return to the enticements of the age, because, according to the Savior’s saying, whoever places his hand upon the plow and looks back cannot be fit for the kingdom of heaven (Luke IX, 62).

# CHAPTER XXII. On the competentes

1. After the catechumens comes the second degree, that of the competentes. The competentes are those who, after instruction in the faith and after a life of continence, hasten to receive the grace of Christ. Therefore they are called *competentes*, that is, “those seeking the grace of Christ”; for catechumens merely listen and do not yet ask. They are like guests and neighbors of the faithful: from outside they hear the mysteries and the grace, but they are not yet called believers.

[Note: [Col. 0815D]

Chapter XXII, note 2. *Commonitorium*. The *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins is well known. The monk Reinerus, about whom see Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume IV, part III, book II, chapter 6, also wrote a *Commonitorium of Piety*. AREV.]

2. The competentes now ask, now receive, and now undergo catechesis—that is, they are imbued with instruction in the sacraments. [460] To these the saving Creed is handed over as a reminder of the faith and a sign of holy confession, so that, instructed by it, they may recognize how they must now present themselves for the grace of Christ.

# CHAPTER XXIII. On the Creed

[Note: [Col. 0816D]

Chapter XXIII, note 1. “For they hand it down in these words” through “a sign”: these words are from Rufinus’s preface to the *Creed*. GRIAL.

Ibid. Saint Ildefonsus, in the work cited, chapters 33 and 34, takes much from this chapter concerning the Creed. AREV.]

1. Our forebears, they say, established the Creed—which the same competentes receive—in the following manner; for they hand it down in these words. After the ascension of our Lord and Savior to the Father, when, through the coming of the Holy Spirit, his disciples, inflamed, spoke in the languages of all nations, so that, by this sign, no foreign nation and no barbarous language appeared inaccessible or impassable to them, the Lord gave them the command to go to each nation to preach the word of God (Matthew XXVIII).

[Note: [Col. 0816D]

2. Another reading is: “All, therefore, placed together in one.” AREV.]

2. As they were about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, lest, as they departed from one another geographically, they should preach anything differing or discordant to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ. Therefore, all placed together in one and filled with the Holy Spirit, they composed for themselves a brief sign of their preaching by bringing together into one what each of them believed; and they determined that this rule should be given to believers.

3. They wished to call this a *symbol* for many and very just reasons. For in Greek, *symbolon* can mean “sign” and “collation,” that is, something that several people bring together into one. The apostles did this in these statements, each bringing together into one what he believed. It is called a sign, or token, because at that time, as the Apostle Paul says and as is reported in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XV), many pretended to be apostles of Christ, indeed naming Christ but not proclaiming him according to the complete lines of the tradition. Therefore they established this sign, by which the person who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules could be recognized.

[Note: [Col. 0816D]

4. Perhaps, “the same institution.” AREV.]

4. Finally, they say that the same practice is observed in civil wars, since the appearance of weapons, the sound of the voice, the custom, and the established methods of warfare are the same. But, so that no deceitful infiltration might occur, [461] each commander gives his soldiers distinctive tokens, which in Latin are called *signa* or *indicia*, so that, if someone should happen to appear about whom there is doubt, he may be questioned and disclose the *symbolum*, revealing whether he is an enemy or an ally. For this reason our Fathers handed down that this should not be written on parchment but retained in the heart, so that it might be certain that no one learned it from reading—which can sometimes reach even unbelievers—but from the tradition of the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0816D]

5. “For it is a brief word of faith,” etc., from the same passage, a little earlier; Cyprian says the same in the *Lord’s Prayer*. GRIAL.]

5. As they were about to depart, therefore, as has been said, to preach, the apostles established this sign of their unanimity and faith. The Creed is that by which God is recognized, and which believers consequently receive so that they may know how to prepare the contests of faith against the devil. It contains few words, but all the sacraments. For these words were collected briefly by the apostles from the whole of Scripture, so that, since many believers do not know letters, or those who do know them cannot read the Scriptures because of the occupations of the world, they may retain these words in their hearts and possess sufficient saving knowledge. It is a brief word of faith, formerly foretold by the prophet: “For the Lord will make a brief word upon the earth” (Isaiah X; Romans IX).

# CHAPTER XXIV. On the rule of faith

[Note: [Col. 0817B]

Chapter XXIV, note 1. “To have assumed a human being.” This is a common expression among the Fathers. Augustine, in his single book *On Genesis Literally*, writes, in the very exposition of the faith: “When the very ineffable and unchangeable Wisdom of God deigned to assume the complete and entire human being.” And in the daily hymn: “You, intending to liberate humanity, did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb.” GRIAL.

Ibid. “To proceed by being born.” Another reading is: “to have been born by being born.” Latinius, in *Bibliotheca selecta*, p. 129, thinks it should be read: “The Son, being born from the Father, does not proceed,” so that it may correspond appropriately to what follows: “but the Holy Spirit, proceeding, is not born.” Rabanus, who has this entire chapter, does not differ from the printed editions. Further, “the perfect Son”; another copy omits “perfect.” AREV.]

1. This, after the Creed of the apostles, is the most certain faith that our teachers handed down: that we confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one invisible God, of one essence, and of the same power and eternity; yet in such a way that, while the distinct properties of the persons are preserved in each, the Trinity must neither be divided substantially nor altogether confused personally. We also confess the Father to be unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. [462] The Son proceeds from the Father by being born, while the Holy Spirit, proceeding, is not born. The Son himself, perfect, assumed from the Virgin a human being without sin, so that the one whom he had created solely by goodness, having fallen of his own will, he might mercifully restore. We confess that he was truly crucified, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven with that same flesh glorified, in which he is awaited as the one who will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0817C]

2. “Divine and human substance.” *Substance* is no less commonly used for *nature*, so that producing testimonies of those who use the term improperly would be a waste of time. GRIAL.

Ibid. “And human substance.” Another reading is “and human nature.” Also, “integrity” instead of “integrity,” and “unity” instead of “unity.” AREV.]

2. And that one Christ, in one person, bore divine and human substance in both respects, because he neither doubled the person through the integrity of the two substances, nor confused the two substances through the unity of the person. In the one case he excluded neither; rather, as one person, he preserved both in inviolate right. The salutary authority of the New and Old Testaments is to be commended: the latter is truthfully fulfilled through prophecy, the former through history. And no opinion is to be held concerning God or any creature of the world together with pagans or heretics in those matters in which they dissent from the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0817C]

3. “And that the origin of the soul is uncertain.” Augustine very often acknowledges his hesitation, as in Letter 157 to Optatus: “I have not yet found anything certain in the canonical Scriptures concerning the origin of the soul.” And in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 1: “For as regards its origin, by which it comes to be in the body—whether it derives from that one soul who was first created when humanity was made a living soul, or whether individual souls are always made individually—I neither knew then nor do I yet know.” Isidore was similarly hesitant, together with Fulgentius, whose words he reports in Book I of the *Differences*, chapter 26, so that neither dared incline decisively in either direction, since nothing had yet been determined. Yet he later expressed sufficiently what he thought in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 14, in these words: “The soul is not a part of the divine substance or nature, nor does it exist before it is joined to the body; rather, it is created when the body is created, and seems to be joined to it.” Gregory says the same in Letter 53 to Secundinus, Book VII. GRIAL.

Ibid. “And therefore incorporeal, because it was created in the image of God.” He used the same reasoning in Book I of the *Sentences*, at the place cited. But although this is the reading of both manuscript codices, the printed books—including, astonishingly, the Roman editions—had made it “corporeal.” It is all the more astonishing because, in the same volume, this very passage, together with the entire rule of faith, has been printed complete and uncorrupted in Rabanus. GRIAL.

[Col. 0818C] Ibid. “And that the origin of the soul is uncertain.” The same reasoning of doubt concerning the soul is used in the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogma*, which is also attributed to Isidore. There is considerable disagreement among the manuscripts in the words “and therefore incorporeal,” etc. Hittorpius published: “And it is clearly shown to be incorporeal. Since, however, it can be grasped and transferred, it is nevertheless shown to be corporeal. It was created in the image of God through uprightness of morals.” Others read the same, but have “by whom, however” instead of “since, therefore.” Others read “it is shown to be,” followed by “which was created in the image,” omitting the rest. Others have “and in the body” instead of “and incorporeal.” Others have “and therefore incorporeal.” Others read: “The soul, without doubt, is shown to be corporeal both to God and to the angels, by whom it can be grasped and transferred, because it was created in the image of God, from the piety of morals.” Vatican Codex 641 reads: “And therefore incorporeal, which I say was created in the image of God according to the grosser substance of our body, from the piety of morals, without which,” etc. Regiovatican Codex 161 reads: “Therefore incorporeal; according to the grosser substance of our body, I say, it is clearly shown to be incorporeal. It was created in the image of God through piety of morals, without which faith,” etc. Some of the most ancient Fathers called the human soul corporeal, either because they mistakenly attributed to it a tenuous and subtle body, or because they called everything corporeal that is defined by a determinate nature and place and has a bounded substance, even if it was in reality spiritual. On this matter, see Petavius, *On Angels*, Book I, chapter 2. In the second sense, I would not strongly object to Isidore’s calling the human soul corporeal. Compare Book I of the *Differences*, no. 101; Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12; Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3; and the *Book on Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapters 11 and 25. AREV.]

3. But we should hold only what the divine utterances testify in both Testaments: that God created neither humanity nor the universe out of necessity, and that no visible or invisible substance exists except either God himself or something created good by the good God; [463] but that God is supremely and unchangeably good, whereas the creature is good in a lower and changeable way. And that the origin of the soul is uncertain. And that the nature of angels and of the soul is not a part of the divine substance, but a creature of God created from nothing, and therefore incorporeal because it was created in the image of God.

[Note: [Col. 0818D]

4. “Through piety of morals.” These words do not appear sufficiently complete. GRIAL.

Ibid. Another reading is: “where consent is not maintained by wills.” Also, “we do not believe,” instead of “it is not believed.” AREV.]

4. Without piety of morals, faith in divine worship grows idle and sluggish; with it, the integrity of divine worship is perfected, so that each person, loving God for God’s sake and his neighbor in God, may advance even to the love of enemies and, advancing, arrive at the goal. Nor can one person be polluted by another’s sin where there is no equal consent of the will. Legitimate marriages are not to be condemned, although offspring born from them is also believed to be subject to original sin, and the integrity of faithful virgins or continent women is taught to be preferred to them.

5. The one baptism of the Trinity must not be repeated—which would be sacrilegious. Nor should it be thought that, because of the diversity of the ministers who administer it, separate baptisms are conferred upon individuals; rather, it is given by God’s single authority. Concerning this we read: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit; [464] and I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I). Nor should we think that we have no need of the remedies of repentance for the daily offenses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life, so that by the fruitful contrition of repentance we confess all sins to be erased, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm XXXI).

[Note: [Col. 0819D]

6. “Nor should anything good be attributed to the free choice of the human will.” These words would produce an absurd statement if read separately, but they must be joined to the following words: “but the entire number of the elect is acquired according to the purpose of God’s will.” The meaning is that our free choice contributes nothing to predestination, but that calling and election are to be assigned solely to the divine will and grace. Thus we easily relieve from fear those whom this passage had troubled when badly understood. GRIAL.

Ibid. “By the free choice of the will.” Another reading is “by the judgment of the will.” Grialius reads “all temporal goods.” AREV.]

6. No one, moreover, is joined to Christ the Head by his own powers, but through divine grace, and is strengthened in the unity of the Church itself by perseverance in unbroken peace. Nor should anything good be attributed to the free choice of the human will; rather, the entire number of the elect is acquired according to the purpose of God’s will. Temporal goods are created by God and are common to good and wicked alike; by his dispensation they are either granted or denied to each individual. In each believer, it is not the possession of these goods but their use that is either to be condemned or approved. But we believe that only the good can attain certain and eternal goods in the future. We believe that the Church, which is now formed by the pledge of those goods, is held in possession of them: here she has the first fruits of the Spirit, in the future perfection; here she is sustained in hope, afterward nourished in reality; here she sees through a mirror in an enigma, but in the future face to face, when she has been brought from faith to vision (I Corinthians XIII).

[Note: [Col. 0819D]

7. “Disposition.” Another reading is “allocation.” Another is “discussion.” AREV.]

7. That, until this is perfected in us, so that we may enjoy the eternal goods of the Most High God, by enjoying temporal things in God we do not harm our neighbors. We also hold this hope of the resurrection: that, in the same order and form in which the Lord himself rose from the dead, we too shall rise in the same body in which we exist or live—not changing our nature or sex, but laying aside only frailty and vices. Satan himself, together with his angels [465] and worshipers, is to be condemned to eternal fire, and is not, according to the sacrilegious opinion of certain people, to be restored to his former—that is, angelic—dignity, from which he fell through his own wickedness (Matthew XXV). This is the true integrity of the faith of catholic tradition; if any one part of it is rejected, the whole belief of faith is lost.

# CHAPTER XXV. On baptism

[Note: [Col. 0820D]

Chapter XXV, note 1. “Moses baptized” through “raise up to heaven.” Everything is from Gregory of Nazianzus’s *Oration on the Holy Lights* (Greek: *eis ta hagia phōta*, “On the Holy Lights”). GRIAL.

Ibid. Grialius had punctuated *pandam* separately from *baptizavit*. The Virgilian words that precede it—“If, returning to the first beginning, I shall unfold”—suspend the sense of the oration. AREV.]

1. If I unfold the sacrament of baptism by returning to its first beginning, Moses baptized in the cloud and in the sea, in type and figure, for so Paul declares (I Corinthians X). The sea therefore represented water, the cloud the Holy Spirit, and the manna the bread of life. There, as the examples of the Fathers teach, the Egyptian was submerged, while God’s people rose again, renewed by the Holy Spirit, who also passed unharmed through the Red Sea. John too baptized (Matthew III), but not wholly in the Jewish manner; for he baptized not only in water, nor yet in the Spirit, but added only this: that he baptized for repentance, as Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance” (Acts XIX, 4). Yet he was given the power to baptize in water for this reason: so that Christ, who was going to baptize in water and the Spirit, might be manifested in Israel through John’s baptism, when, through the descent of the Holy Spirit and the voice of the Father, the Son of God was openly shown to all.

[Note: [Col. 0820D]

2. “A twofold figure of baptism.” Another copy omits “twofold.” AREV.]

2. Perfect baptism therefore began with Jesus; for he first baptized in the Holy Spirit, as John also says: “I indeed baptize in water, but in your midst stands one whom you do not know; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John I). This is the perfection of baptism: it is God who baptizes, so that those who are baptized may become children of God. There are three kinds of baptism. The first is that by which the filth of sins is washed away through the laver of regeneration. The second is that by which someone is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom. [466] Christ too was baptized with this baptism, so that in this, as in other matters, he might give believers an example, as he said to his disciples, the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark X). Thus water and blood are a twofold figure of baptism: one by which we are regenerated through the washing, the other by which we are consecrated through blood.

[Note: [Col. 0820D]

3. “For baptism of water is” through “dwells bodily.” From Jerome’s letter to Rusticus of Narbonne on the seven ecclesiastical grades, volume IX. GRIAL.

Ibid. “Through it.” Another reading is “through him.” AREV.]

3. There is a third baptism of tears, which is accomplished with greater labor, such as that of the person who waters his bed with tears every night (Psalm VI), who imitates Manasseh’s conversion (II Chronicles XXXIII) and the humility of the Ninevites, through which they obtained mercy (Jonah III). He imitates the prayer of the publican who stood far off in the temple and struck his breast, and who did not even dare to raise his eyes toward heaven (Luke XVIII). For the baptism of water is that which flowed from Christ’s side at the time of his Passion. There is no other element that cleanses everything in this world and gives life to all things. Therefore, when we are baptized into Christ, through it we are reborn, so that, purified, we may be given life.

[Note: [Col. 0821D]

4. Instead of “in the solemnity of regeneration,” another copy reads “in the water of regeneration.” Ildefonsus, chapter 110 of *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, repeats this very passage concerning the seven steps of the baptismal font and proceeds to draw much more from Isidore through chapter 121, but explains it more fully. AREV.]

4. The font is the source of all graces, and it has seven steps: three in descent because of the three things we renounce; three others in ascent because of the three things we confess; and the seventh—that is, the one that is also the fourth, like the Son of Man—extinguishes the furnace of fire (Daniel III), is the support of the feet, and is the foundation of the water, in which the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians I). The saving gifts of baptism consist in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore no one is sanctified by the office of baptism unless he is immersed under the sacrament of the Trinity, just as the Lord says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew, last chapter). Accordingly, if baptism is given with any one person of the Trinity omitted, nothing is manifestly accomplished in the solemnity of regeneration unless the whole Trinity is invoked.

[Note: [Col. 0821D]

5. Another reading is: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Further on: “in which we renounce the devil, his pomps, and all his ways of life.” AREV.]

5. For when the Lord was baptized by John, he is also read to have completed that same baptism under the sacrament of the Trinity. For when God said, “This is my Son” (Matthew III), the Father was present in the voice, the Son in the body, [467] and the Holy Spirit was shown in the form of a dove (Luke III). There are two covenants of believers. The first covenant is that in which one renounces the devil, his pomps, and his entire way of life. The second covenant is that in which one professes belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

6. We ought to be washed in Christ only once, because Christ died for us only once. For if there is one God and one faith, there must necessarily also be one baptism (Ephesians IV), because Christ’s death for us is also one. Into its likeness we are plunged through the mystery of the sacred font, so that, dying to this world, we may be buried with Christ (Romans IX), and from the same waters we may emerge in the likeness of his resurrection, never to return to corruption, just as he did not return to death. Even if someone afterward is overtaken by some sin, he is not cleansed again by the benefit of the washing, but by repentance, which, in the likeness of the font, puts sins to death.

[Note: [Col. 0821D]

7. “Little children, with another professing [the faith]” through “let him answer”: cited by Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter 74. GRIAL.

Ibid. “For the abolition.” Another reading is “for the washing away.” AREV.]

7. For adults, we believe that baptism is effective either for the cleansing of original sin or for the abolition of actual sin; for little children, it is effective so that they may be washed from original sin, which they drew from Adam through their first birth. If they depart this life before being regenerated, they are undoubtedly excluded from the kingdom of Christ, as the Savior himself testifies: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God” (John III). These same little children are baptized with another person professing the faith on their behalf, because they do not yet know how to speak or believe; the same is true of the sick, mute, or deaf, on whose behalf another professes, so that he may answer for them while they are baptized.

[Col. 0822B] [Note: [Col. 0821D]

8. “And it remains in them.” Another reading is “it remains in them.” Shortly afterward: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven, and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” AREV.]

8. Although original sin perishes through regeneration, the penalty of death, which entered through the transgression of the commandment, nevertheless remains even in those whom the Savior’s baptism cleanses from the guilt of origin. This is so that a person may know that he receives regeneration in the hope of future blessedness, not so that he may be absolved from the penalty of temporal death. We read in the Gospel that no private persons or clerics may baptize, but only priests; it was permitted solely to the holy apostles, when Jesus said after the resurrection: [468] “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John XX). And when he had said this, he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” And in another place: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew, last chapter).

[Note: [Col. 0822D]

9. “Hence it is established that baptism” through “is summoned.” The same, distinction 4, chapter 19. GRIAL.

Ibid. “They must be cleansed.” Brissonius, in *On the Law Concerning Sunday*, *On Spectacles*, p. 270, observes that this was taken from the author of the *Responses to the Orthodox*, question 14. AREV.]

9. Hence it is established that baptism is to be administered only by priests, and that even deacons are not permitted to perform its ministry without a bishop or presbyter, unless, in their absence, extreme necessity caused by the final illness compels it. This is also often permitted to faithful laypersons, so that no one may be summoned from this world without the saving remedy. Heretics, however, if they have nevertheless been taught to receive baptism with the testimony of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are not to be baptized again, but are to be cleansed by chrism alone and the imposition of hands. For baptism belongs not to humanity but to Christ; therefore it makes no difference whether a heretic or a faithful person administers baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0822D]

10. “For the heretic has baptism.” See Augustine, *Against Parmenianus*, Book II, chapter 3, and, from the same chapter, the passage beginning “although,” in *On Consecration*, distinction 4. GRIAL.]

10. This sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer. A heretic indeed possesses Christ’s baptism, but because he is outside the unity of the faith, it benefits him nothing. Yet once he has entered, the baptism that he possessed outside, to his ruin, immediately begins to benefit him for salvation. What he received I approve; but because he received it outside, I disapprove. When he comes in, it is not changed but recognized; for it is the character of my king. I shall not be sacrilegious if I correct the deserter without changing the character.

# CHAPTER XXVI. On chrism

[Note: [Col. 0823B]

Chapter XXVI, note 1. Another reading is: “The name itself is derived from chrism.” AREV.]

1. Moses first prepared and compounded the ointment of chrism in Exodus, at the Lord’s command; with it Aaron and his sons were first anointed as a testimony to their priesthood and holiness (Exodus XXX). Later, kings too were consecrated with the same chrism, and therefore were called *christs*, as it is written: “Do not touch my christs” (Psalm CIV, 15). At that time the mystical anointing, by which Christ was prefigured, existed only among kings and priests; hence the name itself is said to derive from chrism. [469]

2. But after our Lord, the true King and eternal Priest, had been anointed by God the heavenly Father with the mystical ointment, not only bishops and kings but the entire Church is consecrated through anointing with chrism, because she is a member of the eternal King and Priest. Therefore, because we are a priestly and royal race, we anoint after the washing, so that we may be designated by the name of Christ (I Peter II, 9).

# CHAPTER XXVII. On the imposition of hands, or confirmation

[Note: [Col. 0823D]

### Chapter 27, no. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0823C]

Chapter 27, no. 1. This is the final chapter in most manuscript copies and printed editions. But in Bignaeus and Breulius, after this chapter—which ends with the words “who would give the Holy Spirit to those already baptized”—two further chapters are added, which I append here.

—On the Suffrages of the Church.—“Just as, on account of venial sins, it pertains to the severity of divine justice to punish human beings, so it pertains to the goodness of divine mercy to raise those same people up through suffrages. Suffrages therefore benefit the dead, not toward the merit of eternal life, but toward the remission of punishment, specifically toward the mitigation of punishments or a more rapid liberation.

“There are four general kinds of suffrages, to which all the others are reduced: prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and the sacrament of the altar. Their number is understood in this way: the dead person can be absolved from punishment in two ways, namely, by the way of grace and by the way of justice.

“By the way of grace, in two ways. First, through the public intercession of the head, which occurs in the offering of the holy altar. Second, through the almost private intercession of the members, namely, through the prayers of the righteous.

“Similarly, by the way of justice, in two ways. First, by way of redeeming punishment, namely, through the giving of alms. Second, by way of paying punishment, namely, through the affliction of fasts.

“If it is asked when what someone commanded to be done for himself begins to benefit the deceased, the answer must be that the work of the one who performs it—that is, the merit of the author—continues to affect the condition of the dead through the good works that he commanded to be done for his soul. But not the work performed—that is, the fruit of the work—until those works have been done, because the former benefits by an absolute merit, whereas the latter benefits by a conditional merit.

—Whose Suffrages Benefit Them.—For suffrages to be beneficial, something is required on the part of the agent and something on the part of the deceased recipient. On the part of the agent, it is required that he be in charity and that he direct his intention toward those whom he wishes his works to benefit.

“It must nevertheless be distinguished that suffrages may be performed by an evil person in two ways: either by the author, in which case they do not benefit, except perhaps accidentally—that is, insofar as good poor people are stirred by the almsgiving of an evil person to pray for the dead—or by a minister. This latter occurs in two ways. Either the performer is acting as a public minister of God and the Church, as when an evil priest celebrates Mass or conducts the funeral rites of the dead; such works always benefit, because the minister’s wickedness does not harm the work of the good author, as is evident in the case of a righteous lord giving alms through an evil person.

“If, however, he performs them as the minister of a private person, while nevertheless being in charity, whether the deceased or someone else is concerned, such works benefit, because although the work is dead with respect to the minister, it is not dead with respect to the author. But if an evil minister performs something at the command of one who is not in charity, it does not benefit.

“Something is also required on the part of the recipient, so that the suffrages may benefit him. The first requirement is that he himself be in charity. Hence they do not benefit those who are in hell, because they have been separated from the mystical body of Christ. Therefore no spiritual influence reaches them, just as bodily influence does not benefit members severed from the body.

“The second requirement is need. Nevertheless, suffrages do not benefit the blessed, because they are no longer on the way but at the goal, nor can they ascend to higher things; rather, the suffrages of the blessed benefit us. Both charity and need are present in those who are in purgatory. Thus, just as a person can make satisfaction for another living person who cannot do so for himself, so he can do so for a dead person.

“Note that suffrages benefit the dead, but more or less according to the differing merits of the dead, or according to the quality of the living, who are more solicitous on behalf of some than of others. For those suffrages that are performed spiritually on behalf of certain persons benefit them more than others, although they are in some way communicated to the others as well.

“Suffrages that are commonly performed for a deceased person, although they benefit all according to their measure, benefit more those who, while they were on the way, merited more that the suffrages should benefit them.

“Although, as has been said, suffrages do not benefit those who are in heaven or those who are in hell, they nevertheless benefit them in some way. Hence note that they benefit those in purgatory by way of purification; they benefit those saved in heaven by way of union, because the multiplication of those being saved increases accidental glory. They also benefit the damned in hell by way of diminution: for the more people are saved through the merit of the Church, the fewer will be damned, and thus their punishment will be lessened through the removal of the company of those others.

“They also benefit the impious by way of merit. As for the fact that Masses for the dead are celebrated for deceased children, this is not done for their indulgence, since they immediately fly away to glory, but as an act of thanksgiving.”

The Masses for the dead which, as is asserted here, are said for children are not strictly the Masses that for many centuries have been called Masses for the dead, but psalms and other prayers offered in thanksgiving. Certainly this entire explanation of suffrages is far removed from the age of Isidore. See the note on *The Book on the Order of Creatures*, chapter 14, no. 12, concerning purgatory. AREV.]

1. But because after baptism the Holy Spirit is given through bishops with the laying on of hands, we remember that the apostles did this in the Acts of the Apostles. For it is said:

“It happened, while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, after traveling through the upper regions, 470 came to Ephesus; and when he found certain disciples there, he said to them: ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him: ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ And he said to them: ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They answered: ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul said: ‘John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who would come after him, that is, in Jesus Christ.’ When they heard this, they were baptized 471 in the name of the Lord Jesus; and when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1).

[Col. 0825A]

2. Likewise, in another passage:

“When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, for it had not yet descended upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

3. Innocent writes. To Decentius. See *Manus*, *On Consecration*, distinction 5. GRIAL.]

3. We can receive the Holy Spirit, but we cannot give him; rather, we invoke the Lord that he may be given. As to whom this is chiefly done by, and how, I shall set out what the holy pope Innocent wrote. For he says that it is permitted to be done by no one other than a bishop; for although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate.

[Col. 0826A]

4. That this belongs to bishops alone—that they either mark with the sign or give the Spirit, the Paraclete—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by that earlier passage from the Acts of the Apostles, which asserts that both Peter and John were sent to give the Holy Spirit to those who had already been baptized (Acts 8).

For presbyters, whether outside the presence of a bishop or with a bishop present, may anoint those baptized with chrism when they baptize, but with chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, mark the forehead with the same oil, since this belongs only to bishops when they give the Spirit, the Paraclete.

[Note: [Col. 0826B]

5. “These are a few things.” Many manuscripts: “These are small things.” Thus in Sedulius, book 3, verse 338:

“I speak of small things, if I were to pass through God’s deeds one by one;”

although some also read “a few things” in Sedulius. See the note. In Vatican Codex 641, discussed in *Isidoriana*, chapter 94, nos. 26 and following, the reading is *parva* (“small”), from which manuscript I adopted *percepisse doctrinis* (“to have received teachings”), which seemed better than *praecipisse doctrinas* (“to have prescribed teachings”), found in Grialius and others. In the final words, Isidore commends himself to the prayers of Fulgentius, his brother. AREV.]

5. These are a few things among the many teachings of reputable men that we know we have received, and whose sayings are accordingly known to have been inserted by us in certain places, so that our discourse might be strengthened by the sayings of the fathers. Pray for me.

[Col. 0825]

## The Synonyms of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, on the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul (C, S)*

### Earlier Prologue

472 [Note: [Col. 0825C]

No. 1. *On the Synonyms concerning the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul.* We found various titles prefixed to this work in the ten codices that we used. In one Laurentian manuscript, in the Septimancensis, and in the Navarricus, it is entitled *Soliloquies*. In another Laurentian manuscript, *Dialogue between Reason and Appetite*. The remaining manuscripts have *Synonyms*. Except that some of them read *Synonymam* in the feminine gender, following Saint Ildefonsus in his writings on illustrious men.

In Isidore—unless the reading is corrupt—the work is indeed called *Synonyms* in the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2. So also Braulio in the Life of Saint Isidore. So also Gratian, wherever he has taken fragments from this work, says that he is citing them from the *Synonyms*.

We have added from the Guadalupe and Sevillian manuscripts the words “On the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul,” on the authority of Ildefonsus, who says this about Isidore: “He wrote the Book of Lamentation”—supply “he wrote”—“which he himself called *Synonymam*.” From that time onward, therefore, he preferred both titles: *Lamentation* according to the usage of speakers, but *Synonyms* as the title given by Isidore himself. MARIANA.

Ibid. Others: *convenientia* (“things coming together”) instead of *coeuntia* (“things joining together”). MAR.

Ibid. Others: *miserabili* (“pitiful”) instead of *mirabili* (“marvelous”). MAR.

Ibid. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 70, it is entitled: “The *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*, of Isidore.” Editions; the preface of the 1532 edition; the Italian translation of the *Synonyms*; Breulius’s warning; the heretical corrupter of the *Synonyms*, punished by divine judgment; handwritten codices; and several works derived from the *Synonyms*.

Therefore there is no need to add anything now; I shall only repeat that instead of *Synonyma* in the feminine gender, perhaps *Synonymia* should be read, as may be inferred from the *Etymologies*. In place of “Reason, meeting him in a marvelous encounter,” others have “who, by a pitiable operation.” This prologue is entirely omitted in some manuscripts, and rightly so, unless a certain person’s warning is being presented as Isidore’s work.

We follow the Gralian edition, content with noting what seemed to us worth pointing out.
