In Vatican Codex 628, discussed in chapter 94 of the prolegomena, no. 12, the following prologue appropriately comes after the title of the work: “A certain little book recently came into my hands,” and so forth. Then: “The prologue ends. The argument begins. In this subsequent book, which is called the *Synonyms*,” and so forth.

Constantine Cajetan also noticed this, and published both prefaces in order to correct the editions of Breulius and Grialius. But his contention that Isidore was not the author of the prologue beginning “A certain little book recently came into my hands” is certainly not proved. He advises that the author of both prefaces should be commended for his antiquity and piety, and then adds much to show that nearly all writers of ancient times were accustomed to begin their works with these words: “The book begins,” and so forth.

These two books of the *Synonyms* were once very widely used, as is clear from the cited passage of the prolegomena; and I find it noted in Zaccaria’s papers that the public library at Fulda preserves two books of Isidore of Seville’s *Synonyms*, written in the eighth century. AREV.]

1. In this subsequent book, which is called *Synonyms*, that is, “many words coming together into one meaning,” Isidore, archbishop of Seville, of holy memory, introduces the character of a man lamenting amid the troubles of the present age and mourning himself almost to the point of despair. Reason, meeting him in a marvelous encounter, gently consoles him with mild guidance, restores him from the fall of despair to the hope of pardon, and teaches him marvelously how to avoid the downfall of the deceptive world and grasp the pattern of the spiritual life.

[Col. 0827]

2. Then, advancing him with the greatest effort as far as the ascent of contemplation, it brings him to the citadel of perfection. Finally, when he has been brought to perfection, he gives due thanks to that same Reason.

Whoever strives to proceed through this work with an attentive mind will undoubtedly discover how to guard against vices, how to mourn committed sins, and how, restored through the lamentations of repentance, to approach the fruit of holy action, so that he may not perish with the desires of the world but, rewarded with eternal prizes, may live with Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

### Second Prologue

Isidore to the Reader, Greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0827B]

3. “A certain little book.” That is, a certain booklet, for the word *scheda* is sometimes used in the sense of “book.” In the Guadalupe and Sevillian manuscripts there was read “a certain little book of Cicero,” and indeed there circulates under Cicero’s name a not unserviceable little book in which synonymous words are collected, addressed to Lucius Veturius.

Since that title has been falsely attached to it, and Cicero’s name is absent from all the other manuscripts, we judge that it should be deleted. MAR.

Ibid. “Persuaded my mind.” Others: “persuaded my mind”—that is, “my mind” in the accusative. AREV.]

3. A certain little book recently came into my hands, called *Synonyms*. Its form persuaded me to compose some sort of lamentation for myself, or for the wretched. I imitated, in fact, not the eloquence of that work, but what I myself wished.

474 [Note: [Col. 0827B]

4. In the third Laurentian manuscript, or the quarto manuscript, immediately after this prologue—which is the only one found there—comes the argument of both books of the *Synonyms*, in these words:

“Man sets forth the evils he suffers in the distress of his need and enumerates his desires. He says that justice has perished; he complains that he has been unjustly oppressed; he grieves that he has been consumed by various scourges; he desires that death may come to him sooner.

“Reason admonishes him to have hope. The man asks how this will happen. Reason explains this very thing: that tribulation is useful and that one must not murmur under pressure. Whatever a person suffers is entrusted to God’s just judgment.

“He enumerates the man’s vices and crimes. The man recognizes his evil and mourns it. Reason admonishes him to recognize it more fully. The man affirms this very thing. Reason admonishes him to turn away from vice. The man thinks this difficult to do. Reason admonishes him to resist habit. The destruction of others should draw him back from sin.

“The man asks whether there is hope of pardon. Reason affirms that there is, because confession justifies through amendment. The man turns toward what is better; Reason desires this very thing. The man recognizes his sin and mourns it. Reason, consoling him, asks what the soul fears.

“The man, fearing the day of judgment and the punishment of condemnation, grieves that he was born; he mourns his guilt, enumerates the evils he has committed, and implores the mercy of the Lord. Reason advises the lamenting man and again admonishes him not to sin.

“He advises the man to know himself, to hold the true faith, to live well, to turn away from evil, to resist wicked thought immediately, to resist lust vigorously, to persevere in prayer, to persevere in abstinence, not to gaze with wandering eyes, and always to devote himself to action and reading.

“Humility must be firmly held together with fear, and adversity must be endured courageously. Anger must be restrained; one must not answer an injury; one must forgive the sinner quickly and harbor no hatred. Peace and kindness must always be maintained.

“Vain glory must be avoided; the wicked must be shunned and joined with the good; one must neither hear nor speak evil; one must attend to one’s own faults and not seek out the faults of others. Lies must be avoided in every way; one must abstain from oaths and fulfill whatever one has vowed. One must not speak anything evil in one’s heart or do it secretly.

“Counsel and action must always be turned toward the Lord. Virtues must be concealed and vices made known. One must be watchful in everything, never secure; exercise oneself in good works and devote oneself to wisdom. Words should precede deeds; in every teaching there should be diligence and discernment.

“One must not know superfluous things or display curiosity. Those who are better in knowledge and life must always be venerated. One must not consent to evil in any way. Those subject to one should love one more than fear one. A measure must be maintained in everything.

“What he does not want for himself, he should not do to others. He should begin to judge himself in the way he judges others. Where there is the highest honor, there should be the highest humility, because where there is the highest honor, there is the highest danger.

“One must die to the world. Mercy and alms must be generously given to everyone; nothing should be given grudgingly, and nothing should be taken away.”

The man gives thanks while professing the teaching. The preface ends; the first book begins. AREV.]

4. Whoever you are, then, read this willingly; and when you are touched by the adversities of the world, examine yourself with the judgment of a censor. You will immediately recognize that whatever afflictions you suffer in this age are inflicted upon you as a most just recompense.

Two characters are introduced here: the man who mourns and Reason who admonishes.

## Book One

[Col. 0827C] [Note: [Col. 0827C]

5. Others: *animae* (“of the soul”) instead of *animi* (“of the mind”). Ibid. “I do not comprehend the indications.” Another Laurentian manuscript read: “I do not comprehend the judgments.” We followed the other reading, which is found in all the remaining manuscripts.

Moreover, the words *argumentum* and *indicium* here signify for Isidore a method, form, or means. MAR.

[Col. 0829D] Ibid. “I do not find a means.” Others: “I do not gather means.” And shortly afterward, “I do not find” instead of “I do not gather.” AREV.]

5. My soul is in anguish, my spirit burns, my heart fluctuates; anguish of mind possesses me. Anguish of mind afflicts me; I am surrounded by every evil, hemmed in by hardships, enclosed by adversities, covered with miseries, overwhelmed by misfortune, crushed by distress. Nowhere do I find refuge from such great evil; I find no means of dealing with such great pain; I do not comprehend the indications of escaping calamity; I do not gather arguments for lessening pain; I find no trace of escaping death. Everywhere my misfortune pursues me; at home and abroad my calamity does not abandon me.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

6. “They rage.” Others: “They lie in wait.” AREV.]

6. Wherever I flee, my evils pursue me; wherever I turn, the shadow of my evils accompanies me. Just as I cannot flee from my bodily shadow, so I cannot flee from my evils.

I am that man of unknown name, a man of obscure reputation, a man of the lowest rank, known only by myself and known only to myself. I have never done evil to anyone; I have slandered no one; I have opposed no one; I have harmed no one; I have troubled no one. I lived among people without any complaint.

Yet everyone strives to injure my life; everyone gnashes his teeth against me and rages; with joined hands they bring dangers upon me; they drag me toward destruction; they bring me into danger; they call my safety into question.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

7. Others: “They bring forth from their mouths” instead of “They promise with their mouths.” Ibid. Supply “it is sought” after “safe faith.” MAR.

Ibid. “If justice is not believed.” Others: “if the just person is not believed.” AREV.]

7. No one offers me protection; no one provides defense; no one gives assistance; no one comes to the aid of my evils. I have been abandoned by all people. Whoever looks upon me either flees or perhaps pursues me. They regard me as though I were wretched, and I do not know what things they say to me deceitfully in peaceful words.

They adorn hidden malice with flattering speech; they bring forth one thing with their mouths and turn another over in their hearts. By their deeds they destroy what they promise with their mouths. Under the appearance of piety they walk with poisoned minds.

They veil malice with the cosmetic of goodness; they conceal cunning beneath simplicity; they feign friendship through deceit; they show by their faces what they do not carry in their hearts.

Whom can you trust? In whom can you place faith? Whom can you regard as a neighbor? Where is faith now? Faith has perished; faith has been taken away; nowhere is faith secure.

If nothing is lawful, if there is no truth in judgment, if equity is cast aside, if justice is not believed, if justice is denied to everyone, the laws perish, while avarice judges.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

8. Others: “They have taken away” instead of “They have brought.” MAR.]

8. Avarice has increased; the law has perished through love of greed; laws have no force; rewards and gifts have taken strength away from the laws.

Everywhere money wins; everywhere judgment is for sale. No one fears the laws; no one fears judgment. License to live wickedly remains unpunished; no one contradicts sinners, and no one avenges crime.

Every crime remains unpunished; the unjust go free; the innocent perish; the good are in need; the wicked abound; criminals possess power.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

9. “Are despised.” Others: “Are cast down.” And below: “Instead of the impious.” “The guilty are immune, the innocent…” and so forth. AREV.]

9. The righteous are in want; the unjust are honored; the righteous are despised; the unjust rejoice; the righteous are in sorrow and mourning.

The impious prevails against the righteous; the wicked condemn the good; the unjust is honored in place of the righteous; the righteous is condemned in place of the impious; the innocent perish in place of the guilty, with nothing preventing it.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]

10. Others: “They impose” instead of “They thrust.” Ibid. “Judges do not allow [them] to be enrolled.” What “to enroll judges” means is understood from Asconius Pedianus in the Second *Verrine*, where he says:

“When many judges were to sit in judgment in the council with their praetor, who had been the inquisitor in a public case, it had first been necessary for them to be enrolled from the senatorial curia, when the Senate was judging. Then they had to be placed in an urn, so that the necessary number could be drawn by lot from among the larger number. Third, the accuser and the defendant were allowed to reject from that number those whom they thought would be hostile or inconvenient to them for some reason.

“After the rejection had been carried out, the praetor drew by lot other men to replace those who had been rejected, until the lawful number of judges was completed.”

The meaning of the words, therefore, will be: “They do not allow proceedings to continue according to the accepted custom and established practice of judicial inquiries. They conduct everything in disorder.”

Or perhaps he said, “They do not allow judges to be enrolled,” meaning that they do not permit them to agree among themselves in their judgments. For *συγγράφεσθαι* (*sunggraphesthai*) is sometimes used in the sense of agreeing, as in Theophrastus, book 5 *On Plants*: “Therefore builders also agree to insert the pieces toward the pith, so that they may obtain the densest and softest portion of the wood.”

Or perhaps the reading should be: “They do not cease to restrict the judges.” But all the manuscripts agree on the reading that we have adopted. MAR.]

10. Without any cause, accusation, or malice, they charge me with a crime; they thrust a crime upon me; they tie knots of accusation against me. They turn the place of accusation and suspicion against me. They lead me into accusation and danger; they charge me with a crime of which I have no awareness.

Nothing has been examined; nothing has been exposed; nothing has been investigated; nothing has been discovered. Yet they do not cease fabricating evils against me; they do not cease preparing false testimony; the accusers do not cease bringing charges; they do not allow judges to be enrolled.

477 11. I am judged by the false and cruel sentence of witnesses and judges. By the false sentence of witnesses I, an innocent man, am led to death. The witnesses come from the same council, the judges from the same council, the accusers from the same assembly.

They set wicked judges against me; they bring forward false witnesses, in whose testimony there is confidence. No one dissents from them; no one disagrees; no one rejects their counsel.

To whom shall I speak? Whom shall I believe? To whom shall I talk? To whom shall I go? From whom shall I seek advice? In whom shall I place my mind? Whom above all shall I seek?

12. I am hateful to everyone; I have been abandoned by the affection of all. Everyone casts me away from himself; everyone abhors me with disgust; everyone shudders at me; everyone rejects me; they press for my renunciation.

I want to flee to them, but they threaten me. I desire to entreat at their feet, but they flee, oppose, and hate me. By supplication I want to make them favorable, but they are even more troublesome.

Sometimes they join themselves to me with feigned affection, not for consolation but for temptation. They speak deceitfully, and if they are silent, their silence is not sincere. They seek what they can accuse; they seek what they can hear; they seek what they can betray; they investigate where they can deceive.

[Col. 0831A] [Note: [Col. 0831D]

13. “I withdrew.” I prefer this reading, with Laurentian Codex 1, a Florentine manuscript, or folio manuscript, to *restrinxit* (“he restrained”), found in the Gralian edition. From the same manuscript I substituted *reticere* (“to keep silent”), removing *retinere* (“to retain”), which appeared in that edition, perhaps by error; for the Bignaean edition already had *reticere*. AREV.]

13. But I, with bowed head, humbled face, and lowered countenance, am silent and keep quiet. I persist in the silence I have begun; I have set a guard over my mouth; I have placed a seal upon my lips; I have restrained my voice from speech; I have withdrawn my tongue from speaking.

Even when questioned about something good, I remain silent, for I preferred to keep silent before the wicked rather than answer them.

But they do not cease; they rage more fiercely. They pursue the one who has been struck all the more; they rush upon me more and more; they make an uproar against me with shouts; they recklessly hurl insults at me with voice, appearance, and tumult.

14. They leap upon me; with open voice they hurl abuse and reproach at me. Provoked by another, they all stir themselves against me; they all turn their weapons against me. Everyone rages against me; everyone aims at my destruction; everyone prepares his hands for my death.

In such great fear, such great terror, such great dread, I, miserable man, wasted away; miserable, I grew pale; I became bloodless; my heart withered; I burn with panic; I waste away from fearful dread; fear and trembling have shaken my soul.

[Note: [Col. 0831D]

15. Others: *alimoniam* (“food”) instead of *eleemosynam* (“alms”). MAR.]

15. Thus I have been driven into exile; thus I have been condemned to exile; thus I lament the punishment of exile; thus I groan under the condemnation of exile. I have been assigned to the chain of servitude, weighed down by the burden of my condition, enslaved to servile labor, placed in cold, snow, frost, grim storms, every labor, and every danger.

After the loss of my goods, after the loss of everything, I have become destitute and poor. I am in need; miserable, I beg; publicly I ask for alms. No one extends a hand to the needy; no one comes to the aid of the indigent; I am worthy of pity before no one; I have been abandoned by every mercy; there is no one to have pity.

[Note: [Col. 0831D]

16. Others: “Everyone despises me as a beggar.” MAR.

Ibid. Others: *afflicta* (“afflicted”) instead of *astricta* (“constrained”).

Ibid. “Punishments are not lacking for me.” In another, older Laurentian manuscript: “Punishments are no less lacking.” In the Sevillian and Guadalupe manuscripts: “Punishments no less cease.” In the Parisian: “Punishments are no less.” From the Seguntine, Septimancensian, and Legionensian manuscripts the true reading has been restored. For although these words are absent in them, immediately above they read: “Nor are torments lacking for me.” MAR.]

16. Everyone despises me as a beggar; they do not refresh the hungry man even with their crumbs. No one lets a drop of refreshment fall into the mouth of the thirsty; no one offers me even a little dew of water. For I have become abhorrent to everyone.

Whoever looks at me, they all despise me as though I were covered with sores; they spit me out as though I stank; they shudder to touch me as though I were a leper.

My flesh lies constrained by iron; it lies pressed beneath chains; it lies bound by fetters; it lies shackled in irons. Torments are not lacking; tortures are not lacking; punishments are not lacking for me. Cruelty grows harsher against me every day.

[Note: [Col. 0832D]

17. Others: *putredinem* (“rottenness”) instead of *putredine* (“with rottenness”). And *fluvius* (“river”) instead of *fletus* (“weeping”). MAR.]

17. The executioners of my body tear me apart with new tortures. With an unheard-of kind of punishment they lacerate my entrails and limbs. Whatever cruel thing they can devise against me, they devise.

I am not killed by a bare death; I am wrenched apart by a thousand punishments, subdued by a thousand tortures, torn by a thousand penalties. My flesh, cut by blows, has rotted; my half-burned sides pour out pus; my torn limbs dissolve in corruption; blood flows together with weeping; gore drips together with tears.

Nor is it merely the weeping of tears, but also of wounds.

[Note: [Col. 0832D]

18. Others: *percussa* (“struck”) instead of *praeclusa* (“closed off”). And *perculsus* (“stricken”) instead of *percussus* (“struck”). MAR.]

18. I am consumed by grief, miserable man; in grief both mind and body fail. My mind is already defeated; my soul has been shut in by pain. I have experienced many intolerable things; I have endured many bitter things; I have suffered many grievous things.

Never have I received so grievous and cruel a wound. I have been crushed by an unexpected wound; I have been struck by sudden destruction; an unforeseen calamity has thrown my life into such great evil.

Sudden calamity overwhelmed me while I was unaware; sudden destruction and chance brought me down.

[Note: [Col. 0832D]

19. “May it now be permitted for one desiring to die.” In the old Laurentian manuscript: “It is now permitted for one desiring to die to fall.” In the Guadalupe and Sevillian manuscripts: “It is now pleasing for one desiring to die to fall.” All these words are absent from the other manuscripts.

Because the sense is not sufficiently established by either reading, we have combined what we believe to be the true reading from both, changing only *licet* to *liceat*. We thought it necessary to inform the reader of this, so that he might know how conscientiously we have used these books in correcting the text. MAR.]

19. Why was I born, miserable man? Why was I cast into this wretched life? Why did I, miserable man, see this light? Why did the beginning of this life encounter me in misery?

Would that I might leave the world more quickly than I entered it! By what means might I now depart? But alas, death awaited by the wretched comes slowly.

May it now be permitted for one desiring to die. For I am weary of living; my desire is to die; death alone pleases me.

O death, how sweet you are to the wretched! O death, how pleasant you are to those who live in bitterness! How delightful you are, O death, to the sad and mourning!

[Note: [Col. 0832D]

20. Others: *miseris* (“for the wretched”) instead of *misereri* (“to have pity”). MAR.]

20. Let the great consolation of death therefore approach the great evil of life. Let death be the terminus and end of so many evils. Let the repose of burial bring misery to an end. And if life will not begin to show pity, at least let death begin to do so.

Death puts an end to all evils; death provides a limit to calamity; death removes every calamity.

[Note: [Col. 0832D]

21. Others: *velox* (“swift”) instead of *vel* (“or even”). MAR.]

21. Certainly even death comes to the aid of the wretched. It is better to die well than to live badly; it is better not to exist than to exist unhappily. In comparison with my miseries, the dead are happier than the living.

Spare my pain, I beg you; forgive my sorrow, I beg you. Grant pardon to my anguish; be indulgent toward my pains. In such great pain, do not be stirred against me.

For I mourn my affliction; I lament my calamity; I grieve over the familiar disaster of my misery, for grief supplies more than enough. Miserable, I cannot be consoled; my pain is unendurable; my sorrow is without limit.

My wound is in no way soothed; there is no measure to my tears; there is no end to my pains. There is now no confidence in my spirit; my spirit can no longer bear it; overcome by miseries, my spirit has collapsed.

480 [Note: [Col. 0833D]

22. Others: *confidence in hope* instead of *hope and confidence*. MAR.

Ibid. “Reason.” Others have: “Here Reason answers the man.” Then: “Here the man answers Reason.” AREV.]

22. O man, why do you distrust your spirit so greatly? Why are you so weakened in mind? Why do you lose all hope and confidence? Why are you so cast down in spirit? Why are you thrown down by such faintheartedness? Why are you so broken by adversity?

Put away sadness; cease to be sad; drive sadness away from you. Do not succumb to sorrow; do not give yourself over to sorrow. Drive pain from your heart; exclude pain from your spirit; restrain the assault of pain; do not persist in pain. Conquer the pain of your spirit; overcome the pain of your mind.

23. How? By what means? In what way? How? By what method? By what art? By what counsel? By what ingenuity?

[Col. 0833B] [Note: [Col. 0833D]

24. Others: *temporal* (“of time”) instead of *bodily*. MAR.]

24. By every means, every force, every ingenuity, every virtue, every art, every method, every counsel, and every effort, take up the struggle against bodily troubles. Be firm in every circumstance; endure everything patiently; endure all adversities with an even temper.

Do not attend only to your own condition. Your bitterness is not to be weighed by you alone; your calamity is not to be considered by you alone. Look to the similar circumstances of others; consider the miseries of those to whom something bitter has happened.

While you recall the dangers of others, you bear your own more gently. For the examples of others relieve pain; a person is more easily consoled by the misfortunes of others.

[Note: [Col. 0833D]

25. Others: “of others” instead of “of calamity.” MAR.]

25. Why do you accuse your most bitter decrees? Why do you mourn so greatly the causes of your danger? Your punishments are not new; you have examples of calamity.

How many people have endured such circumstances and such dangers? What has happened to many must be endured patiently by one. The punishment of this life is brief, and both the one who afflicts and the one who is afflicted are mortal. The tribulation of this age has an end.

[Note: [Col. 0833D]

26. Others: “Nothing lasts long, nor is anything so prolonged.” MAR.]

26. Everything in this age passes away and does not remain; nothing that comes can stand. Nothing lasts so long, nothing is so prolonged, that it is not brought to an end shortly. Everything beneath heaven has its end.

It is impossible for you to be human and not taste anguish. Pain and sadness are common to everyone; in this age we all undergo these things with a like fate.

No one is forever free from evil; no one in this age does not suffer; no one placed in this life does not sigh. This life is full of tears; this life begins with weeping. Whoever is born begins to live with a cry; we are cast weeping into this wretched life; the very beginning of what follows is a groan of pain.

[Note: [Col. 0833D]

27. Others: *pertimesces* (“you will fear”) instead of *pertimescis* (“you fear”). And *introire* (“to enter”) instead of *intrare* (“to enter”). MAR.]

Elsewhere. “What is present,” etc. He alludes to Paul, 1 Corinthians IV, 17. The Paris manuscript reads: “For what is presently our tribulation is momentary and light; what is eternal in us is beyond measure, an exceeding weight of glory.” Although this reading did not seem objectionable, we have not followed it, since all the old manuscripts differed. MAR.

In the same place. “Confirms.” Perhaps, “may confirm.” Others omit “the soul confirms reason.” Immediately afterward, instead of “and light tribulations in us,” some read “and the lightness of our tribulation”; others, “in us, which, though light, produces many tribulations.” AREV.]

27. Therefore bring reason to bear upon yourself; take part in reason; let reason prevail over you; govern your spirit by reason; let reason strengthen your soul; let reason restrain the force of such great grief. When your spirit has been strengthened, you will fear no danger. “We must enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations” (Acts XIV, 21). “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII, 18); what is present is momentary, and our tribulations are light; what is eternal is beyond measure, an exceeding weight of glory. Tribulation is useful; the pressures of this life are useful.

28. The perversity of evils does not kill you but instructs you; the hostility of the wicked does not cast you down but raises you up; human temptation reproves you but does not destroy you. For to the extent that we are broken in this age, to that extent we are made firm in the everlasting age; to the extent that we are afflicted in the present, to that extent we shall rejoice in the future. If here we are worn down by scourges, we shall be found purified at the judgment. God always wounds those whom he prepares for everlasting salvation. Gold is tested in the furnace; you, so that you may be free from dross, are purified in the furnace of tribulation; so that you may appear finer, you are melted in the fire of persecution; so that you may be cleansed from the filth of every sin, all these things that you endure are for testing.

29. Therefore do not murmur, do not blaspheme, do not say: “Why do I endure evils? Why am I afflicted? Why do I suffer evil?” Rather say: “I have sinned; I am receiving what I deserved.” I do not experience punishment equal to my sin; I recognize that I have been struck less than I deserved; in proportion to the measure of my crime, the retribution of punishment is less; according to the merit of my sins, the penalty is unequal; the punishments are not as great as the sins have been. For whoever murmurs under scourges irritates God more against himself, provokes God’s fury more greatly, and increases the anger of the offended God against himself.

[Note: [Col. 0834D]

30. Some read “misery” instead of “injury.” And “he recalled” instead of “he was recalling.” MAR.

In the same place. “You will glorify God humbly”; some read, “you will be humbled and glorified by God.” AREV.]

30. But whoever patiently endures adversity appeases God more quickly. For if you wish to be purified, accuse yourself in your punishment and praise God’s justice. It contributes to your purification if you refer what you suffer to God’s justice, if, in place of the injury inflicted, you humbly glorify God. For God corrects you with the scourge of loving chastisement; he disciplines you, and he who, by sparing you, was calling you back to himself, cries out by striking you, so that you may return.

Consider, O human being, every torture of the world; turn your mind to every punishment of this age, every pain of torment, every bitterness of suffering. Compare all this with Gehenna, and everything you suffer is light. If you are afraid, fear those punishments: these are temporal, those eternal; these have an end, those are everlasting; in these, the torments depart with death, but in those, everlasting pain follows death.

[Col. 0835A] 31. For if you have been converted, what you suffer is correction. Scourges free the converted from sins, and afflictions that come upon the converted contribute to purification. Whoever is chastised and corrected here is freed there; but those who are not corrected even under the scourge are condemned both by temporal and eternal punishment, and are judged first in this age and again there in the future. They have a double condemnation, a twofold blow, because here they have the beginning of torments and there the completion of punishments. See that the hand of God has handed you over to punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0835D]

32. Some read “counsel” instead of “counsel.” And “the spirit by the attack” instead of “the spirit of the attack.” MAR.

Elsewhere. In Grialius’s text some letters bearing the indices of the notes are occasionally missing. Therefore, using conjecture and other manuscripts, I have arranged Mariana’s notes. AREV.]

32. Know, O human being, that no one could have opposed you unless God had granted him power; nor would an adversary have had power over you unless God had permitted it. Everything that happens to you comes by God’s will; the power of the wicked over you is granted by God’s permission. All who oppose you act according to God’s counsel; the hand of God has handed you over to punishment; God’s indignation has commanded that you be afflicted. In his anger he himself commanded you to experience every evil: that you are sick, that you are afflicted by diseases of the flesh, that you are broken by bodily weakness, that you are tormented by the goads of illness, that you are shaken by the passions of the spirit, that you are tortured by anguish of mind, that you are driven about by the raging spirit of attack—all this divine justice inflicts upon you for your sin, and for your fault the sentence of divine judgment itself is imposed upon you.

33. For every adversity of circumstances is aroused by the merits of your sins. Your own weapons fight against you; you are pierced by your own arrows and wounded by your own darts. “By the things through which you sinned, by these you are also tormented” (Wisdom XI, 17). You followed the flesh; you are scourged in the flesh. In that very thing in which you sinned, you groan; in that very thing in which you transgressed, you are tormented. That which was the cause of your sin is itself the measure of your punishment. From where you fell into vices, from there you lament your torments.

34. O human being, examine your conscience; direct your mind; scrutinize yourself; let your heart speak to you; consider your deserts. You are rightly reproved, rightly scourged, rightly judged by a just judgment. A just storm crushes you; the punishment of justice weighs upon you. For you do nothing good, nothing upright, nothing fair, nothing just, nothing holy; there is no holiness in you, no modesty, no remembrance of dignity, nothing worthy of God.

[Note: [Col. 0835D]

35. Some read “does not remain” instead of “does not depart.” AREV.]

35. Every day you sin; every day you slip; every day you rush toward what is worse. Your arrogance does not depart; your pride is not laid aside; swelling and boastfulness are not restrained. Fury also carries you away; anger inflames you; shouting excites you; indignation moves you. Always ready for anger, you become angry beyond measure; beyond the proper measure of your spirit, you are stirred by fury. You are accustomed to be zealous against the good, accustomed to envy those who are better; always envious of the virtues of others, always a rival of the prosperity of others.

[Note: [Col. 0835D]

36. Some read “you have overwhelmed,” “you have covered over,” “you have abhorred,” or “you have devoured,” instead of “you have overwhelmed.” And “desires” instead of “desires.” And “to be filled” instead of “to be satisfied.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Others read, “whose life have you not overwhelmed?” perhaps better than “whose,” etc. Then, instead of “you involve yourself daily in new [sins],” others read: “You do not lessen your crimes but increase and enlarge them; you do not extinguish sin in yourself, but rather, as far as you can, give it life; nor are you ever satisfied,” etc. AREV.]

36. Whom have you not torn apart? Whom have you ever not disparaged? Whose life have you not overwhelmed? Upon whom have you not cast infamy? You are deceitful, fickle, faithless, greedy, grasping, barren, inhuman, unfruitful. There is no mercy in you. You have fallen into the desires of the age and have flowed away into the cravings of the world; you burn with earthly love; you heap up things destined to perish; the thirst of your desire does not know how to be satisfied. Every day you entangle yourself in new sins; by new crimes you increase your former ones; you do not wash away your wickedness but prolong it, and you never satisfy the flame of lustful desire.

37. O unhappy you, are you not ashamed to be sprinkled with so many lusts? Corruptor, lustful man, adulterer devoted to pleasure, do you persist in lust in this way? Do you persevere in wickedness in this way? Do you remain in luxury in this way? Do you persist in carnal love in this way? Alas! How long, how much longer will you wander? To what end will unbridled luxury drag you? At last cease sinning; at last desist from wickedness; change your evil ways for the better sometime.

[Note: [Col. 0836D]

38. “Having been beaten, acknowledge it.” Others add: “Correct yourself while there is time. O human being, see that by sinning further you do not go toward what is worse.” AREV.]

38. Why do you remain in the filth of sin? Why do you persist in the will to sin? Do not continue to wander, wretched man; now change from evil to good. Put an end to sin; put an end to the law of wickedness; let guilt have a measure; let iniquity have a limit. Consider the greatness of your offenses; at least, having been beaten, acknowledge your sins.

39. Alas for me! Alas, unhappy me! Alas, wretched me! I did not know that I was struck for my iniquity; I did not know that I was judged according to my deserts. You made clear to me, you indicated to me, you made known to me, through you I learned, that this judgment arose from my injustice. What I did not know, I now know for certain; I now hold it as certain. It is no longer hidden from me; it is quite clear to me; I know it fully; I have considered it sufficiently; it is now established for me; it is no longer concealed or uncertain or hidden from me.

40. From this, O human being, comes all this calamity; from this comes this bitterness, this cross, this punishment, this misery. The causes are known to you. This illness does not arise from some accident, some event, or some chance; this sickness is the result of your own fault; this disease is the result of your own iniquity. Do you think it is otherwise? Do you suppose it otherwise? Do you judge it otherwise? Do you feel it otherwise? Do you see it otherwise? Do you assess it otherwise? Do you reckon it otherwise?

[Note: [Col. 0836D]

41. “Who denies this?” In the Mejorada manuscript and another Laurentian manuscript there was added: “I did not know that, by a just judgment [perhaps, ‘that the judgment was just’], this arose from my injustice; you made it clear to me; through you I learned what I had not previously known.” We judged these words to be additions and rejected them from this passage. MAR.]

41. Certainly nothing—nothing at all, nothing in any respect, nothing whatever—do I have with which to contradict you. I yield to the truth; I cannot deny it; I confess that it is true. Who doubts this? Who questions it? Who denies it?

[Note: [Col. 0837D]

42. “Vice,” from “by vice.” Some read: “Remove vice and crime from yourself; restrain yourself from the evil of vanity; [withdraw] from vice.” AREV.]

42. If this is so, if you think this, if you hold it as certain, if it has been sufficiently considered, if it has been established, then now remove vice from yourself; withdraw from vice and sin. Flee the stain of life; flee the worship of vice; remove crime from yourself; restrain yourself from the evil of vanity. Flee the disgrace of life; hold fast to purity of life; wash away your former stains.

[Note: [Col. 0837D]

43. Some read “it is very difficult.” And “to be washed away” instead of “to be torn away.” MAR.]

43. You speak well, teach well, instruct well, admonish well, persuade well, train well. And I desired to be released from the bond of sin; I longed to be withdrawn from evil custom; I wished to depart from vice and sin; I sought to overcome the most wicked habit. But alas! It is difficult to conquer a perverse habit; a depraved practice is scarcely abolished; constant habit is changed into nature; through continual use, vice is transformed into nature; a mind bound by crimes can scarcely be torn away from them. There are so many vices in me that they can scarcely be uprooted; I scarcely believe that my sins can fade through any passage of time.

[Note: [Col. 0837D]

44. “Thus,” instead of “for himself.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Bignaeus noted that “own judgment” is used for “free will.” AREV.]

44. Previously I corrupted myself voluntarily; long ago I polluted myself by deliberate choice; by my own judgment I first ruined myself; by my own will I stained myself. I was good, but of my own accord I slipped into sin; I was free, but of my own accord I made myself liable to death. Unhappy that I am, I myself first willingly prepared sin for myself; I first embraced the opportunity to sin. Now I am held fast by the practice of sin; evil habit has grievously entangled me in itself; the practice of sin has bound me with the chains of necessity. I want to depart from wrongdoing, but I cannot.

45. Why can I rise from my fall, and yet cannot resist habit? I am drawn by love of the good, but drawn back by the law of evil custom. Long habit has established for itself a right and law in me; long practice of sin has prevailed over me and conquered me. My sins have hardened through habit. I want to do good, but accustomed desires do not permit it. Through the habit of sinning, when I do not know it, I thus transgress; through the practice of sin, when I do not wish it, I fall into it. While carnal habit resists, I cannot accomplish good; I strive to oppose evil practice, but the desire of the flesh weighs me down. Love raises me toward justice, but habit binds me to sin.

486 [Note: [Col. 0837D]

46. Some read “fire” instead of “heat.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Bignaeus remarked in the margin that this is a remedy against desires and pleasures. AREV.]

46. Struggle against evil habit; resist with all your strength the habit of sinning. Conquer carnal practice even with pain; conquer the destructive habit, even with difficulty, even with suffering. Resist the evil practice. Set before yourself, against the present heat of the flesh, the fire of future punishment. Let remembrance of eternal burning overcome the heat of lust; let remembrance of the heat of Gehenna drive out the heat of luxury.

[Note: [Col. 0837D]

47. Some read “foresee” instead of “anticipate.” MAR.]

47. Let fear of the punishment of fornication conquer the lesser pain; let the greater pain surpass the lesser. You will bear lesser things patiently if you remember greater ones. Let the image of the future judgment pass continually before your eyes; foresee what you will afterward suffer. Consider God’s future sentence; fear the future judgments of God against you. Let fear of Gehenna terrify you; let the sentence of the future judgment terrify you; let terror of punishments call you back from guilt.

[Note: [Col. 0838D]

48. Some read “punishments” instead of “darkness.” MAR.]

48. Look daily upon the end of your life; keep death before your eyes at every hour; let the coming of darkness always be before your eyes. Think daily of your death; always consider the end of your life; always recall the uncertain day of death. Be watchful, lest you be suddenly snatched away. Every day the last day draws near; every day the day takes away part of our life; every day we move toward the end; every day we traverse the road of life; every day we hasten toward death; every day we move toward the end of life; as the moments run out, we are led toward the end.

[Note: [Col. 0838D]

49. Some read “of human beings” instead of “of all.” And, “may destruction carry away the unwary.” MAR.

Elsewhere. “Encounter.” Some read “setting” instead. AREV.]

49. We do not know what may happen to us today; we do not know when the final moment of life will arrive. We do not know whether the condition of death will demand our soul this night. Our end is hidden from us; the uncertainty of our coming departure is uncertain to us. The encounter with death is unforeseen; the event and end of all things are uncertain. While we do not know, death suddenly comes; while we do not expect it, we are taken away without warning; while we are unaware, we are suddenly removed. Let us fear lest that day, like a thief, seize us (1 Thessalonians V, 2); lest, while we are unaware, the storm of divine judgment tear us away; lest sudden destruction carry us off; lest calamity suddenly overtake us unawares.

487 [Note: [Col. 0838D]

50. Some read “draws away” instead of “struck down.” MAR.]

50. The spirit that kindles a person to sin often suddenly snatches the sinner away; the spirit that inflames the living suddenly devours the dying; the spirit that bends people toward vices suddenly drags them to torments. How many has unforeseen calamity struck down to the punishment of death? How many has an unexpected departure snatched away? How many suddenly removed have perished? How many, while they did not expect to die, have been carried away? How many are suddenly snatched to death? How many are suddenly led to everlasting punishments? Look, then, at another’s torment and learn what to fear. Look at another’s death and learn what to dread. Avoid the pit into which you see another fall before you; fear for yourself the dangers of others. Make the misfortunes of others your own dangers; let the summons of the dying be your correction; let the ruin of others be your warning.

[Note: [Col. 0838D]

51. Others read: “while there is opportunity. Let it grieve you; hurry while you can.” Instead of “may swallow,” some read “may engulf,” but the former appears genuine. It is clear that many such words compounded with the prefix *ob-* were altered by copyists. See the commentary on Prudentius, p. 623. AREV.]

51. Let the destruction of the impious draw you back from sin. Let the punishment of those who perish withdraw you from guilt; let the end of wrongdoers correct you; let the destruction of the rejected lead you to repentance. Let the punishment of the wicked contribute to your salvation. Correct what you have done badly while you can; while you can, call yourself back from vice and sin; while there is time, cry out; while opportunity is granted, mourn; while there is permission, repent quickly; while you can, weep. While your soul still dwells in the body, while you still live, obtain a remedy for the future—before the day of death overtakes you, before the abyss swallows you, before hell snatches you away, where there is no longer any place for pardon, where no freedom of repentance is open, where no opportunity for correction is granted, where there is no recourse to confession and no return to forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 0839D]

52. Some read “in me” instead of “for me.” And “I desire only to know this.” MAR.

Elsewhere. “You form me.” Thus one customarily says “to form the mind,” and also of the arts by which childhood is accustomed to be formed, etc. AREV.]

52. You speak the truth; you speak truly; you tell me what is timely; you teach me what is more beneficial for me. Nothing is better, nothing more welcome, nothing more acceptable, nothing more pleasant; nothing delights me more, nothing gives me greater satisfaction. This alone I ask. Behold, I know it; I have learned it; I have understood it. This also I ask: I especially want to know whether there is hope in confession, whether there is confidence, remission, pardon, indulgence, whether through repentance there is a way to return to righteousness.

488 [Note: [Col. 0839D]

53. Some read “but toward better things” instead of “if toward better things.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Bignaeus here indicates the fruit of confession. AREV.]

53. There is—plainly there is, certainly there is, entirely there is, without doubt there is, assuredly there is. Confession heals; confession justifies; confession grants forgiveness of sin. All hope rests in confession; in confession there is a place for mercy. Therefore believe this most firmly; do not hesitate in any way; do not doubt at all; do not despair in the least of God’s mercy. Have hope in confession; have confidence. Do not despair of the remedy of healing; do not despair of salvation if you turn toward better things. For whoever despairs of forgiveness for sin condemns himself more by despair than by the crime committed.

[Note: [Col. 0839D]

54. Some read “great” instead of “grave.” MAR.]

54. Despair increases sin; despair is worse than every sin. Therefore correct yourself and hold hope of indulgence. Lay aside injustice and hope for life; lay aside iniquity and hope for salvation. No guilt is so grave that it does not have forgiveness. Although you are a sinner, although criminal, although wicked, although burdened with innumerable and unspeakable crimes, the opportunity for repentance is not denied you. Divine clemency readily comes to the aid of those who repent; through repentance indulgence is granted; through repentance all offenses are wiped away.

[Col. 0839D] [Note: [Col. 0839D]

55. Some read “into this despair” instead of “into despair.” MAR.]

55. Alas, wretched me! I had lost hope; I had lost confidence; I had despaired in spirit; my spirit had been broken; my spirit had almost fallen into despair. Now I have returned to hope; now I have recovered confidence; I now have hope of indulgence; I hope in God’s compassion; I do not doubt God’s goodness. I will dwell in hope. His compassion has raised me to hope; in repentance he has given me hope of life. If God therefore looks upon me, if he comes to my aid, if he helps me accomplish what I desire, this is what I have decided to do; this I have resolved; this is fixed in my mind and cannot be torn from my heart.

[Note: [Col. 0839D]

56. Some read “remove” instead of “wash away.” And “what is lamented” instead of “by lamentation.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Others read: “It is a matter of desire; therefore act while it is permitted, while your lot lingers; pray.” And afterward: “recall by weeping” instead of “wash away by tears.” At the end: “By the lamentation of tears crimes are customarily washed away.” AREV.]

56. May God grant you what you desire; may God favor your vows; may God make you attain what you have vowed; may God bring your will to completion in goodness; may God strengthen your vows; may God support your prayers; may God grant you what you desire; may God enable you to approach the fulfillment of your vows. May you do everything with God’s favor. Therefore act while it is permitted, while death delays.

If it lies close to your heart, if it is your will, if it is your vow, if it is your purpose, if it is your desire, pray, ask, entreat; do not be silent. Break forth in speech; cry out boldly; weep over your iniquities; mourn the evils of your crimes. Wash away with tears what you have wickedly done; cleanse with tears what you have unlawfully committed. Crimes are customarily washed away by lamentation. Recall by weeping the evils you have done. Weep over the pain of your guilt; recognize your punishment through tears. Let the lamentations of repentance wash you; let the wave of your grief water you; let the river of tears compel you to weep.

[Note: [Col. 0840D]

57. Some read “fear” instead of “grief.” MAR.]

57. Alas for me, unhappy soul! Amid so many sins, so many crimes, so many iniquities, what shall I mourn first? What shall I lament first? What shall I grieve over first? What tears shall I take up? Memory does not suffice to recount the deeds of so many crimes. My sins have also taken away my sense of sorrow; through the dullness of my heart my tears have congealed; my spirit has grown stiff and is pricked by no grief.

58. My soul has been turned into stupor; my soul has become senseless. O tears, where have you withdrawn? Where are you, fountains of tears? Where are you, wave of grief? Where are you, lamentations? Return, I beg you, tears. Stir, fountains of tears; sprinkle me with weeping; flow over my face; moisten my cheeks; water my cheeks. Give me bitter lamentation. For among all people I have fallen more grievously; among all I have fallen more disastrously. By my crime I have surpassed the punishments of all the wicked; the Tartarean torments scarcely suffice for my evils.

[Col. 0840D] [Note: [Col. 0840D]

59. “The punishment is lighter than my sin,” etc. Many statements seem to have been adopted from Isidore’s *Synonyms* by Urban VIII in the prayer published by him at the end of the Roman Breviary and inscribed on a tablet near the confession of Saint Peter in the Vatican Basilica: “If we weigh the evil we have done, what we suffer is less, what we deserve is greater. What we have committed is more serious; what we endure is lighter,” etc. AREV.]

59. There is no sin beyond my sin; there is no iniquity beyond my iniquity. I consider myself more wicked than all sinners. In comparison with me, no one is unrighteous. I rightly pay the penalties of deserved misery; I am rightly crushed by such great punishments; from my sin all evils have come upon me. God justly afflicts me; by a just judgment an appropriate recompense is returned for my deeds. Yet less is repaid to me than I myself have done wrong; a lesser recompense is returned for my sins; my wound is found harsher than my guilt; the punishment of my condemnation is lighter than my sin. What I have committed is more serious; what I endure is lighter. The guilt I committed is greater than the vengeance I suffer. I weigh the evil I have done; what I suffer is not so great.

60. My wound is lighter than the weight of my sins. There is something else entirely—something else that afflicts me more, saddens me more, disturbs me more, terrifies me more, something for which no evil is comparable, to which every punishment is unequal, which is preferred to all punishments, which precedes every torment, which surpasses every evil.

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

61. Some read “evil” instead of “much.” MAR.]

61. Alas, soul! What is it that you fear so greatly? What is it that afflicts you more? What is it that drives you more forcefully toward sorrow? What do you fear beyond this? What do you dread beyond this? What do you fear beyond this?

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

62. Some read “after this life, lest,” and “the future punishment more greatly.” MAR.]

62. I fear the day of judgment; I fear the day of darkness, the cloudy day, the bitter day, the harsh day. I do indeed consider the evil I endure, but I fear more what remains. I grieve over what I already suffer in this life, but I fear lest after this I suffer more grievous things. Although I already endure the sentence in punishment, I nevertheless fear the torments of Gehenna because of my guilt. The present punishment now tears me apart, but the future disturbs me more. The things I endure are grievous; those I fear forever are more grievous. I grieve over present punishments, but I groan much more over those to come.

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

63. “Come to my aid,” etc., through the end of no. 74, “the bonds of my sins.” This is the prayer, or confession, of blessed Isidore, published by Constantine Cajetan as a work of Isidore, distinct from the others, as I said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, no. 33, although Cajetan was not unfamiliar with Isidore’s *Synonyms*, as I noted at the beginning of this work. AREV.]

63. Come to my aid, my God, before I die; before death overtakes me; before Tartarus snatches me away; before flame consumes me; before darkness envelops me. Help me before I hasten to torments; before I am devoured by the fires of Gehenna; before I am tortured without end. For I am terrified by fear of your judgment; through dread of sin I fear your anger; because of the enormity of my crime, I tremble in conscience at your examination.

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

64. Some read “all his remembrance” instead of “every remembrance.” MAR.

Elsewhere. Cajetanus reads, “the hour of the dreadful judgment.” AREV.]

64. For if the righteous will scarcely be saved, where shall I, the impious, be? What shall I do when the dread of the judgment arrives? When the examination of judgment comes, what shall I answer (Job XXXI, 14)? What shall I say when I am brought before the tribunal of Christ?

Woe to the day on which I sinned! [Col. 0842A] Woe to the day on which I transgressed! Woe to the day on which I experienced evil! Would that it had not dawned for me! Would that it had not arisen over me! Would that it had not appeared above me! O detestable day! O abominable day! O day that should not be spoken of at all! It brought me into this age; it opened for me the barriers of birth; it unclosed the gates of my coming forth. Let that day be changed from light into darkness; let deep gloom confound it; let eternal blindness overwhelm it; let it lose its place in time; let it be extinguished from every remembrance; let it be remembered by no age.

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

65. Cajetanus’s text differs in places. Here, after “to endure everlasting torments,” he adds: “I desired to be released from the bond of sin; I wished to be withdrawn from evil habit; I longed to depart from vice; but it is difficult to conquer the habit of sinning,” etc. Other passages are similarly taken from numbers 44 and 45, through “habit binds.” “Weep for me, heaven and earth,” etc. AREV.]

65. It would have been better for me not to have arisen, better not to have been born, better not to have been brought forth in this age, than to endure everlasting torments. Weep for me, heaven and earth; mourn for me, all creatures; lament for me, all the elements; groan over me, the whole human race, and with whatever sense of life you possess, pour out lamentation over me. For I have sinned cruelly; I have fallen violently; I have fallen grievously; I have collapsed miserably. No sin is found whose filth has not stained me. There is no disease of vices from which I have not contracted contagion; no cesspool of filth has existed that has not flowed together into wretched me.

[Note: [Col. 0842D]

66. Perhaps, “the foulness of unchastity.” AREV.]

66. Infamous, wicked, overwhelmed by every crime, I practiced the foulness of unchastity beyond measure. I freely promised to live well, but I never kept what I promised. I always returned to my sin; I always repeated my offenses; I constantly joined worse things to my former crimes. I never changed my ways for the better; I never withdrew from evil deeds. I even stained many others, destroying myself; I turned many toward iniquity by my depraved conduct. Through my crime many souls perished; many were overthrown by the example of my life. I became the cause of evil for many; through me the purpose of many was stained; through me the name of holiness was torn apart.

492 [Note: [Col. 0842D]

67. Cajetanus also inserts certain passages here: “My transgressions. Therefore implore for me the mercy of almighty God, all choirs of the blessed. Intercede for me, all multitude of the elect, lest almighty God pour upon me the anger of his indignation because of the multitude of my iniquities. Woe is me! O Lord,” etc. AREV.]

67. Pray to the Lord for me, all holy men; plead for me, all the people of the saints; implore for me, every choir of the righteous. Perhaps God will have mercy on me; perhaps he will receive me; perhaps he will wipe away my sin; perhaps he will remove my iniquity; perhaps he will show me mercy. For he is greatly angry against me; he has completed his fury against me; he has poured out the anger of his indignation upon me because of the multitude of my iniquity, because my apostasies have increased, because my transgressions have multiplied. Woe is me, for I am consumed! Woe is me, for my soul has failed, afflicted by grief, crushed by mourning, weakened by groaning.

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

68. Some read “rushes upon” instead of “has rushed upon.” MAR.

Elsewhere. “All streams of troubles.” Some read, “all masses of troubles.” AREV.]

68. Who will have pity on you, soul? Who will console you? Who will offer lamentation for you? “Great, like the sea, is your contrition” (Lamentations II, 13); your affliction is like a raging sea, your pain like a swelling wave. What storm has not rushed upon you? What tempest has not fallen upon you? All streams of troubles, all most turbulent storms, have thundered over your head. You are full of distress and miseries, full of waves, full of storms, O soul.

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

69. Some read “you open” instead of “you refuse.” MAR.]

69. Where are you, guardian of human beings? Where are you, Redeemer of souls? Where are you, shepherd? Why have you despised me? Why have you turned your face from me? Why have you become far from me, comforter of my soul? Return now, my God. Do not forget me forever; do not abandon me eternally; do not leave me in the power of demons to be destroyed. Although the offense is grave, you are compassionate, you are loving, you are rich in mercy. You abandon no one, despise no one, detest no one, refuse mercy to no one; rather, you freely offer clemency. You wait for sinners to return.

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

70. Some read “sated” instead of “to fatten.” MAR.

Elsewhere. In Grialius’s edition, “for those who mourn” instead of “for those who deserve.” AREV.]

70. How many criminals, how many devoted to luxury, how many fattened on the desires of the age, have reached forgiveness through your goodness? To many who did not deserve it you freely granted forgiveness of sins; show your clemency toward me also; let pardon be open to me; let indulgence be open to me. Do not deny to one what you have lavished upon many.

I do not defend my crimes; I do not excuse my sins; what I have done displeases me; what I have sinned displeases me. I confess the offense; I acknowledge the error; I recognize the fault; I open the voice of confession. Receive, I beg you, the cry of one confessing; attend, Lord, to the voice of one entreating. Hear the voice of a sinner crying out.

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

71. Some read “wipe away” instead of “spare.” And “you will remember” instead of “you have remembered.” MAR.

Elsewhere. The words quoted from Sacred Scripture do not exactly correspond to the Vulgate; Isidore seems to have wished only to express the sense. AREV.]

71. I have sinned, O God; have mercy on me. I have sinned, O God; be propitious to me. Spare my evils; forgive my sins; pardon my crimes; may your grace wipe away my faults. “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Psalm XL, 5). “For if you remember iniquities, who will endure it?” (Psalm CXXIX, 3). At your examination, not even the righteousness of the righteous is secure. For who is righteous enough to dare say that he is without sin? Who would presume to say anything of his righteousness before you? No human being is without sin; no one is clean from offense. Behold, among the saints no one is spotless. Behold, those who served God were not steadfast, and perversity was found among the angels (Job IV, 18). The stars are unclean before you; the heavens are not clean in your sight (Job XV, 15). How much more am I loathsome, corruption, and a son of man, a worm, who gulped down sin like a whirlpool and drank iniquity like water; who dwell in dust (Job VII, 21); who live in a house of clay; who have an earthly foundation.

[Note: [Col. 0844D]

72. Some read “lustful desire.” MAR.]

72. Remember, Lord, what my substance is (Psalm LXXXVIII, 48); remember that I am earth; remember that I am dust and ashes (Genesis XVIII, 27). Extend your right hand to the work of your hands (Job XIV, 15). Care for frail matter; come to the aid of carnal weakness, of my frail condition. Let the return to salvation be open; let my wounds be open to you. My sickness is before you; you see how deeply I have been wounded and weakened. Grant the medicine by which I may be healed; provide the remedy by which I may be cured. Restore what has been infected by vices; reform what has been corrupted by sins. Extinguish in me the flame of desire. Let the fiery darts of the devil penetrate me no further; let them no longer burn within me.

[Note: [Col. 0844D]

73. For “tempests,” Cajetanus and others read “storms.” AREV.]

73. For you know the temptations I bear. You know the waves I suffer. You know the storms I endure; you know where I have fallen, where I have slipped away, where I, unhappy, have been submerged. For, negligent, I fell into ruin. Careless, I fell into the pit of disgrace; I fell into the mud of wickedness; wretched, I descended into the depths of evils. Rescue my captive soul from the underworld; rescue me from the most terrible abyss. Let the deep not enclose me; let it not deny me an exit.

[Note: [Col. 0844D]

Source/review notes: Inflection-only variants are retained with their source forms where English cannot express the distinction.

**74.** Alternatively, *maculam* (“stain”), instead of *vincula* (“bonds”). MAR.

In the same place. In Cajetanus and certain manuscript codices, Isidore’s prayer, or confession, ends as follows: “Loose, before I die, the bonds of my sins, Holy Trinity, who live and reign in the unity of the Godhead forever and ever. Amen.” AREV.]

**74.** Behold, the fearful day already draws near; the final day already approaches; the boundary of life is now at hand. Nothing remains for me except the tomb, nothing remains except the grave (Job XVII, 1). Spare me before I depart; [Col. 0844C] cleanse me from my iniquity before I leave this life. Loose, before I die, the bonds of my sins.

[Note: [Col. 0844D]

**75.** Alternatively, *exigit* (“demands”), instead of *excutit* (“shakes out”). MAR.]

**75.** Moved by your tears, I have been pierced by your weeping; your lamentation has dissolved me; your lamentation demands tears from me. By lamenting, you compelled me to tears; by lamenting, you moved me to weeping. At your lament I poured forth tears; at your mourning I melted into tears. May God grant you pardon; may God forgive your offenses by sparing you. May God suspend your sins from you; may he dismiss your sins by loosening them; may he wash away the stains of your crimes; may he cleanse you from every stain of evil; may he free you from the sin that threatens.

[Note: [Col. 0844D]

**76.** Alternatively, *a quo* (“from which”), instead of *ex quo* (“from which”). MAR.]

**76.** Act now, therefore, as you ought; act as is fitting; [Col. 0844D] act as is worthy; act as is right; act as is just. Resolve that you will sin no further; determine that you will offend no more. Beware of repeating your faults; beware of repeating evil. Do not return to the vice from which you have cut yourself off; do not repeat what [Col. 0845A] you have done wrong; do not repeat past evils. After falling, do not offend again; do not defile yourself after lamentation; after the mourning of repentance, do not return to sin; do not again commit the offenses you have bewailed.

[Note: [Col. 0845A]

**77.** “Vain is the repentance which a subsequent fault defiles,” etc. Gratian, in *De Poenitentia*, distinction 3, chapter [beginning] “Vain,” transferred this passage into his own *Decree*, as though it were Augustine’s, in the book of the *Soliloquies*—for some called this work the *Soliloquies*, as was said at the beginning, and it was customarily attributed to Augustine. [Col. 0846A] Peter of Blois, who was nearly Gratian’s contemporary, likewise demonstrates the same error by citing this very passage under Augustine’s name in his treatise *On Confession*. For *esto* (“be”), some have *ista* (“these things”). MAR.]

**77.** Do not again do what you will once more bewail; do not presume to repeat the fault for which you seek pardon. Vain is the repentance which a subsequent fault defiles; a wound that is reopened is healed more slowly; one who sins and mourns repeatedly scarcely deserves pardon. Lamentations are of no benefit if sins are repeated. It is of no avail to ask pardon for evils and then repeat the evils. Persist, therefore, [Col. 0846A] in confession; stand firmly established in repentance.

[Note: [Col. 0846A]

**78.** Alternatively, *deseras* (“you should abandon”), instead of *desinas* (“you should cease”). And *salus inchoantibus* (“salvation is for those beginning”), instead of *salus perseverantibus* (“salvation is for those persevering”). MAR.]

**78.** Do not cease to maintain the good life which you have begun. Preserve continually your resolve to live well. You will be blessed if you remain; blessed if you persevere. Then your work will be perfect if you endure to the end. Salvation is promised to those who persevere, and a reward is given to those who persevere: “Blessed are those who observe judgment and practice justice at all times” (Psalm CV, 3). Blessed is not the one who does good, but the one who does it without ceasing. “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X, 22).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0845]

[Col. 0845B] 496

**1.** I ask you, soul; I beseech you; I implore you; I entreat you: do not act carelessly in anything any longer; do not conduct yourself thoughtlessly; do not do anything rashly. Let evil not be repeated; let sin not be reborn; let iniquity not return; let wickedness not recur; let depravity not rise again; let injustice not recover its strength.

[Note: [Col. 0845D]

**2.** In Grialius’s edition there was *esto quod factus est* (“be what he was made”), through an error, as can be gathered from the earlier editions, in which *factus es* (“you were made”) is found. AREV.]

**2.** Know yourself, human being; know who you are; know why you have arisen, why you were born, for what purpose you were brought forth, why you were made, under what condition you were produced, or why you were created in this world. Remember your condition; preserve the order of your nature. Be what you were made to be, what God made you, what the Maker formed you, what the Creator established you as.

[Note: [Col. 0845D]

**3.** Alternatively, *incorruptae* (“uncorrupted”), instead of *incorrupta* (“uncorrupted”). And *in fide recta* (“in right faith”), instead of *fidem rectam* (“right faith”). MAR.

In the same place. Perhaps, “whom you invoke in faith.” AREV.]

**3.** Preserve right faith; hold sincere faith; guard undefiled faith; let right faith remain in you. Let the faith of your confession be [Col. 0845C] uncorrupted. Let no foolish doctrine deceive you; let no perverse religion corrupt you; let no depravity turn you away from the solidity of faith. Say nothing rashly about Christ; think nothing perverse or impious about God; by thinking perversely, do not offend against his love. Be righteous in faith; possess right faith and holy conduct. Do not deny by your works what you invoke in faith. Abstain from everything that the law forbids; beware of everything that Scripture prohibits.

**4.** Do not offend in your conduct, since you are perfect in faith. Do not pollute faith by living shamefully; do not corrupt the integrity of faith by depraved morals; do nothing against God’s commandment. Live in goodness, with no evil added; let no evil conduct defile good morals; let left-handed deeds not stain [Col. 0846B] right works. Do not mix vice with virtues; do not add evil to good. Evil mixed with good contaminates many good things. One evil destroys many good things. Know that whoever sins in one matter is subject to all vices (James II, 10).

497 [Note: [Col. 0845D]

**5.** “Toward that which delights the body.” All the codices had *in id quod delectatur corpus* (“toward that in which the body delights”). I judged that one should read *in id quo delectatur corpus* (“toward that by which the body is delighted”), or *in id quod delectat corpus* (“toward that which delights the body”). A little farther below, where he says, “Let a shameful thought not steal away your mind,” I thought one should read *non subrepat* (“let it not creep in”) instead of *non subripiat* (“let it not steal away”), since Isidore himself uses that manner of speaking farther below. But I did not dare change this latter passage without a manuscript witness; as for the former, encouraged by Cassiodorus’s instruction in the book *On Divine Readings*, chapter 15, we changed it, conjecturing that the letter *d*, with which the word *delectatur* (“is delighted”) begins, had been doubled through the scribes’ error. MAR.

In the same place. The Florentine quarto has *in id quod delectet corpus* (“toward that which may delight the body”). I retained *quod delectatur corpus* (“which delights the body”), since this expression is not unusual in Isidore’s manuscript works, and perhaps has the same author, as I noted in Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 6, number 1. AREV.]

**5.** For through one sin many acts of righteousness perish. Through one evil many good things can be overturned. Do not incline your mind toward that which delights the body; do not give consent to carnal pleasure. Do not hand your soul over to the power of the flesh; restrain your mind from its appetite. Examine your heart daily; scrutinize your heart daily; by private examination investigate the hidden recesses of your inner self. Guard your soul from harmful thought; let no shameful thought steal away your mind [Col. 0846C]. Distinguish your thoughts: what you should avoid and what you should do. Cleanse your conscience from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0846D]

**6.** Alternatively, *te tangit* (“touches you”), instead of *titillat* (“tickles you”). And *subjerit* (“will have placed before”), instead of *suggerit* (“suggests”). And *pravam* (“perverse”), instead of *primam* (“first”).]

**6.** Let your spirit be cleansed from every pollution. Let your mind be pure; let no filth remain there. Wipe away vice from yourself in such a way that nothing of it remains in your spirit or within you. Know that you will be judged concerning your thoughts. God judges consciences. God examines not only the flesh but also the mind. God the judge judges the soul even concerning its thoughts. When a perverse thought tickles you, do not consent to it. When it suggests something illicit, do not keep your mind there. Despise the first suggestion of sin; do not allow it to remain in your heart. Whenever it comes, drive it out. [Col. 0847A] When the scorpion appears, crush it. Tread on the serpent’s head; crush the beginning of a perverse suggestion.

[Note: [Col. 0847C]

**7.** Alternatively, *certa* (“certain”), instead of *decerta* (“fight against”). MAR.

In the same place. “For if you wish, it will not be able to overcome you completely.” The codices vary. Some have: “For if you wish, you cannot be overcome at all.” Others: “For if you wish, you cannot be overcome in spirit.” The older Laurentian manuscript, on which we relied greatly in other matters, has: “For if you wish, it will not be able to overcome you at all.” Our reading was taken from the Navarrese manuscript, which was neither less authoritative nor less ancient. Nevertheless, I suspected that the true reading of this passage was: “For if you wish, you cannot be overcome at all.” MAR.

In the same place. “At the very beginning,” etc. Ovid’s well-known verse is relevant here, which Thomas à Kempis also adopted in his little golden book *On Contempt of the World*:

“Resist beginnings: too late is the remedy prepared  
when evils have grown strong through long delays.”

It should be noted in passing that many sentences of synonyms were adopted in the aforementioned book *On Contempt of the World*. The chapter beginning “It cannot” appears in Gratian’s *Decree*, 32, question 5. Instead of *decreta*, Mariana’s note had a variant reading *caetera* (“the remaining things”); but I think *certa* (“certain”) should be read—[Col. 0848C] for this is how it appears in certain manuscripts, and I corrected the note accordingly. Below: “you completely,” etc. Alternatively, “you will not be able to destroy yourself in spirit,” or “you will not be able to be overcome in spirit.” For manuscripts sometimes combine two differing readings in this way. AREV.]

**7.** Correct the fault where it is born; resist the thought at its very beginning, and you will escape the rest. Fight against the beginning of the thought, and you will conquer; exclude the head of the thought, and the rest is overcome. If you drive the thought from your heart, it does not break out into action. If you do not consent to the thought, you will quickly resist the deed; the one whom pleasure does not carry away is not subjected by consent. For the body cannot be corrupted unless the soul has first been corrupted. When the soul slips, the flesh is immediately ready for sin. The soul precedes the flesh in crime, and the flesh can do nothing except what the soul wills. Cleanse your soul, therefore, from thought, and the flesh will not sin. For if you wish, it will not be able to [Col. 0847B] overcome you completely.

**8.** Hear, soul, what I say; listen to what I speak; attend to what I advise. Let no impurity defile you any longer; let no lust stain you. Withdraw yourself from every corruption of the flesh; remove yourself from every defilement of the flesh. Let lust no longer grow strong within you. Let desire no longer overcome you. Guard your body from fornication. Never allow yourself to be polluted by any carnal thought. Consider being defiled by fornication worse than every sin; fornication is greater than all sins.

**9.** Fornication is a grave sin. Fornication precedes every evil. Fornication is more grievous than death. It is better to die than to fornicate; better to die than to be stained by lust; better to pour out the soul than to lose it through lack of self-control. Continence brings a human being [Col. 0847C] near to God; continence makes a human being near to God. Where continence remains, there God also remains.

[Note: [Col. 0848D]

**10.** Alternatively, *castis* (“for the chaste”), instead of *castitati* (“for chastity”). “It makes [the inheritance] available.” Thus the Navarrese manuscript read, except that it added *hominem* (“a person”). Others read *suppetere cupit* (“desires to be available”). The older Laurentian manuscript has *haereditatem coeli suppetere* (“the inheritance of heaven to be available”), without any other verb added. In the second, more recent Laurentian manuscript, the entire phrase “Chastity makes the inheritance of heaven available” was missing. MAR.

In the same place. “Chastity … makes [it available].” Alternatively, “The inheritance of heaven is available to the chaste.” AREV.]

**10.** Chastity joins a human being to heaven; chastity draws a human being toward heaven. The kingdom of heaven is promised to chastity. Chastity makes the inheritance of heaven available. Lust, however, plunges a person into hell; lust sends a person to Tartarus; lust leads a person to the punishments of Tartarus.

[Note: [Col. 0848D]

**11.** Alternatively, *tibi praepone finem* (“set the end before yourself”). MAR.]

**11.** But if you still feel the troubles of the flesh; if you are still touched by the goads of the flesh; if you are still struck by the [Col. 0848A] suggestion of lust; if the memory of fornication still tickles your mind; if the flesh still attacks you; if lust still tempts you; if desire still invites you, set before yourself the memory of death; place the day of your departure before yourself; bring the end of your life before your eyes. Set before yourself the judgment to come; set before yourself the torments to come; set before yourself the punishments to come; set before yourself the perpetual fires of hell; set before yourself the terrible punishments of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0848D]

**12.** Alternatively, *et ora per noctem* (“and pray through the night”), instead of *et ora, pernocta* (“and pray; spend the night in prayer”). MAR.

In the same place. This chapter on prayer appears in the book *On Contempt of the World*, published under Isidore’s name. AREV.]

**12.** Pray continually with tears; pray without ceasing; entreat God by day and by night. Let prayer be without interruption; let prayer be frequent; let the weapons of prayer be constant. Let prayer not fail. Apply yourself frequently to prayer; devote yourself constantly to prayer. Always groan and mourn. Rise at night for prayer; keep watch and pray; spend the night in prayer [Col. 0848B], and in supplication; devote yourself to nocturnal vigils. After closing your eyes for a short while, pray again. Frequent prayer drives away the darts of the devil.

**13.** Continual prayer overcomes the devil’s weapons. This is the first virtue against the assaults of temptations; this is the first weapon against the assaults of enemies.
