The frequency of prayers drives out unclean spirits; the persistence of prayer defeats unclean spirits. Demons are conquered by prayer; by prayer demons are overcome. Prayer prevails over every evil.

[Note: [Col. 0848D]

**14.** Instead of *restringitur* (“is restrained”), it may perhaps be better to read *restinguitur* (“is extinguished”). AREV.]

**14.** Remove from yourself fullness of bread; discipline your body through frugality; devote yourself to fasts and abstinence; wear a pale face; carry an emaciated body. Hunger and thirst; abstain and grow thin. You cannot conquer temptations unless you are trained by fasts. For through food lust grows; fullness of nourishment arouses the wantonness of the flesh; through the vice of gluttony the [Col. 0848C] temptation of the flesh grows. Lust is always joined to fullness; in contrast, through fasting lust is restrained; through fasting wantonness is overcome. When fullness has been removed, wantonness does not rule.

[Note: [Col. 0848D]

**15.** Alternatively, *multum* (“much”), instead of *multo* (“a great deal”). And *generatur* (“is generated”), or *excitatur* (“is aroused”), instead of *pullulat* (“springs up”). MAR.]

**15.** For abstinence overcomes the flesh; abstinence curbs wantonness; abstinence breaks the assault of lust; abstinence dissolves the power of lust. Thirst and hunger kill the wantonness of the flesh; hunger and thirst overcome the flesh’s lasciviousness. The mind is also weighed down by much wine. Wine is poison to the spirit. By wine wantonness is aroused [Col. 0849A]. By wine the fuel of lust is nourished. When the veins are filled with wine, wantonness springs up in the limbs; cups, indeed, are instruments of wantonness. For when fuel is added to fire, the blaze grows greater; when material is added to fire, the flame is increased.

[Note: [Col. 0849D]

**16.** Alternatively, *amor* (“love”), instead of *amoris* (“of love”). MAR.]

**16.** The eyes are also the first weapons of lust; sight is the first desire for a woman, for the mind is captured through the eyes. A gaze shoots the darts of love; a gaze nourishes lustful desire; it entices the mind, tickles the soul, and wounds the heart. Withdraw your gaze, therefore; restrain your eyes from wantonness; do not fix them upon the beauty of the flesh. Look at no woman with a view to desiring her; inspect no one with this intention, that you may desire her. Remove the opportunity for sin; take away the material for wrongdoing.

**17.** If you wish to be safe from fornication, be restrained in body and in [Col. 0849B] sight. By keeping your body apart, you withdraw from the purpose of sin. But you will not remain unharmed for long near a serpent. Standing before fire, even if you are made of iron, you will eventually be melted. One who is near danger will not remain safe for long; through constant exposure a person quickly sins.

[Note: [Col. 0849D]

**18.** Perhaps *voluptas* (“pleasure”), instead of *voluntas* (“will”). And *subrepit* (“creeps upon”), instead of *subripit* (“steals away”). MAR.]

**18.** Familiarity has often ensnared many. Often opportunity for sin creates the will. Often those whom the will could not overcome, persistence overcame. Lust quickly steals upon one devoted to idleness. Lust quickly overtakes one who is unoccupied. Lust burns more severely when it finds someone idle. But lust yields to activity; it yields to work; it yields to diligence and labor. Labor often defeats carnal desire, for a body wearied by work takes less delight in wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0849D]

**19.** Alternatively, *implicetur* (“be entangled”), instead of *infigatur* (“be fixed”). And *quid teneas* (“what you should hold”), instead of *quo tendas* (“toward what you should strive”). MAR.

In the same place. “Even if the other good things are now pleasing.” This was found in all the codices except the Septimancensian and Seguntine manuscripts. Since we did not trust these manuscripts, because many things are also missing in them elsewhere, we were content to mark the passage with an obelus, as not sufficiently coherent either with what precedes or with what follows. MAR.

In the same place. Others punctuate it thus: “What you read, if the other good things are now pleasing,” etc. In this way the passage coheres somewhat less poorly with what precedes. AREV.]

**19.** Therefore guard against idleness; do not love idleness; do not spend your life in idleness. Fatigue your body with labors; [Col. 0849C] exercise yourself in the pursuit of every kind of work; seek useful work to which the mind’s attention may be fastened. While working, devote yourself to reading; devote yourself to the law of God; devote yourself to meditation on the Scriptures. Maintain regularity in the divine books; let constant reading be yours; let reading be frequent; let meditation on the law be daily. Reading removes error from life; reading withdraws one from the vanity of the world; through reading, understanding and intelligence increase. Reading teaches what you should avoid; reading shows toward what you should strive. You make progress in many ways when you read, provided that you do what you read. Even if the other good things are pleasing; if other things too are agreeable; if they are in your will; if they are among your desires; if your mind is intent upon all good things; if your mind is ready for all good things.

**20.** Be humble; be grounded in humility; be [Col. 0849D] the least and the last of all. Make yourself least through humility; put yourself before no one; consider yourself superior to no one. [Col. 0850A] Regard everyone as superior to you; consider yourself the least of all; account yourself lower than everyone. Although you may be the highest, hold to humility. If you hold to humility, you will have glory; for the more humble you have been, the greater the height of glory that will follow you.

[Note: [Col. 0850D]

**21.** Alternatively, *de justitia et virtute* (“concerning justice and virtue”), instead of *de justitiae virtute* (“concerning the virtue of justice”). MAR.]

**21.** Beware of boastfulness; beware of the desire for display. Beware of striving after empty glory. Do not claim things for yourself; do not boast; do not exalt yourself insolently. Do not spread the wings of pride; do not raise the feathers of arrogance. Presume nothing about yourself; attribute no good to yourself. Do not become proud through any elation over the virtue of justice; do not exalt yourself over good deeds; do not glory in good work. Descend, so that you may ascend; humble yourself, so that you may be exalted, lest, once exalted, you be humbled. For whoever raises himself will be humbled; whoever exalts himself will be cast down; whoever is lifted up will be thrown prostrate; whoever is [Col. 0850B] puffed up will be dashed to pieces. The higher the place, the heavier the fall; the greater the height, the greater the ruin. Pride is the beginning of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0850D]

**22.** Alternatively, *ambula in humilitate, sicut* (“walk in humility, just as …”). MAR.]

**22.** Pride brought down an angel; arrogance dissolved kingdoms; exaltation cast down the lofty; haughtiness humbled the eminent. Humility, however, knows no fall; humility knows no collapse; humility never encounters ruin; humility has never suffered a fall. Know, human being, that God came in humility and humbled himself in the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians II, 8). Walk as he also walked; follow his example; imitate his footsteps. Be lowly; be abject; be despised. Displease yourself; be despised in your own eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0850D]

**23.** Alternatively, *semper* (“always”), instead of *quoque* (“also”). And *percusso* (“struck”), instead of *perculso* (“terrified”). And *involuto* (“wrapped”), instead of *involutus* (“wrapped”). And *exhaustum* (“exhausted”), instead of *exustum* (“burned”). MAR.

In the same place. “Proceed with your face lowered,” etc. Alternatively: “Proceed with your face lowered; walk with downcast countenance; with your mouth humbled. Let haircloth and ashes envelop your body; let sackcloth cover your squalid and wasting limbs,” etc. AREV.]

**23.** For whoever is lowly in his own eyes is great before God; whoever displeases himself pleases God. Be small, therefore, in your own [Col. 0850C] eyes, so that you may be great in the eyes of God. For you will be more precious before God to the extent that you are more despised in your own eyes. Also bear shame upon your face from remembrance of your offense; bear embarrassment upon your countenance from memory of the sin committed. In shame over your sin, blush to raise your eyes. Proceed with lowered face, sorrowful mouth, downcast countenance, stricken heart, and mournful clothing, wrapped in sackcloth; let your body be covered with haircloth. Let haircloth and ashes envelop your failing limbs; let sackcloth cover your squalid and wasting members; let mournful dress cover your burned-out body.

[Note: [Col. 0850D]

**24.** Alternatively, *vive* (“live”), instead of *sede* (“sit”). And “let the eyes be drenched with tears.” MAR.]

**24.** Let the earth continually be your bed; lie upon the ground. You are dust: sit in dust. You are ashes: sit always in ashes, mourning always, grieving always, groaning always, and sending forth sighs from your heart. Let there be contrition in your heart; let there be frequent groans in your breast. Let tears frequently pour from your eyes [Col. 0850D]; be ready for tears [Col. 0851A]. Love tears; let tears be sweet to you; let mourning and lamentation always delight you. Always make mourning and contrition your own; never abandon mourning and tears. Be as ready for lamentation as you were inclined toward guilt. As your determination to sin was, so let your devotion to repent be. Return in the same measure as you had withdrawn into the depths. Medicine must be supplied according to the illness; remedies must be applied according to the wound. Grave sins require great lamentation.

[Note: [Col. 0851D]

**25.** Alternatively, *de justitia* (“concerning justice”), instead of *justitiam* (“justice”). MAR.]

**25.** Let nothing make you secure concerning sin; let no deceptive security flatter you; let no security, having deceived you, withdraw you from the purpose of repentance. Let hope and fear continually remain in your heart. Let fear and trust exist equally in you; equally, hope and dread [Col. 0851B]. Hope for mercy in such a way that you fear justice; let hope of forgiveness raise you up in such a way that fear of Gehenna always afflicts you.

**26.** For fear always corrects; fear drives out sin; fear restrains vice; fear makes a person cautious and watchful. But where there is no fear, there is a disordered life; where there is no fear, there is the destruction of death; where there is no fear, there is an abundance of crimes. Do not grieve over your infirmities; give thanks to God in your illnesses. Desire to be strong in spirit more than in body; desire to be sound in mind more than in flesh. Bodily afflictions are remedies for the soul. Illness wounds the flesh but heals the mind; illness burns away vices; illness breaks the strength of lust.

[Col. 0851C] [Note: [Col. 0851D]

**27.** Perhaps *ore* (“by speech”), or *corde* (“in heart”), instead of *jure* (“by right”). And *ad nullam insolentiam* (“toward no insolence”), instead of *nulla insolentia* (“by no insolence”). MAR.]

**27.** If prosperity smiles upon you, do not exalt yourself; if adversity befalls you, do not be cast down. If good fortune shines forth, do not become boastful; if calamity occurs, do not become fainthearted. Maintain moderation in prosperity; maintain patience in adversity. Recognize that you are being tested in suffering, so that you may not be broken. Recognize that you are being tested in prosperity, so that you may not be exalted. Be even-tempered in all things. Change your mind neither through joy nor through grief. Bear everything with equal composure; let no insolence change you.

[Note: [Col. 0851D]

**28.** Alternatively, *tolerabilius* (“more tolerably”), instead of *tolerabiliter* (“tolerably”). And *prospecta* or *perspecta* (“foreseen”), instead of *praeexspectata* (“previously anticipated”). MAR.

In the same place. “It belongs to the wise person to foresee danger,” etc. Alternatively, “It belongs to worldly wisdom to foresee,” etc. AREV.]

**28.** Let no circumstance find you unprepared; let there be no circumstance which your meditation has not anticipated. Set before yourself that there is nothing which cannot happen. Prepare in advance for every chance event; always imagine future misfortunes. In favorable circumstances, consider how you will bear adversity. Always think in your mind [Col. 0851D] lest something adverse occur. It belongs to the wise to foresee the loss caused by danger. Everything contemplated beforehand occurs more lightly; expected evils are endured tolerably. Mishaps yield to counsel; a thing anticipated is not marveled at when it occurs. Meditation breaks the force of approaching events. [Col. 0852A] Forethought lessens future troubles; foresight softens the arrival of evils. Unexpected evil, however, strikes with force.

[Note: [Col. 0851D]

**29.** “Into which we fall” (*in quibus incurrimus*); perhaps, “into which we fall” (*in quae incurrimus*). AREV.]

**29.** Things not previously considered are bitter; the circumstances into which we fall unprepared are serious. Unforeseen evils strike heavily; sudden evil quickly breaks; what has not been foreseen afflicts intensely. A sudden storm at sea arouses terror. An unforeseen enemy causes grave disturbance; an unexpected enemy easily overwhelms. Everything sudden is more serious. Things that occur suddenly are more grievous when they arise. Prepare your heart, therefore, for good things and for evil; bear good and evil as they happen to you; endure adversity and prosperity however they occur. Whatever happens, bear it with a free mind.

[Note: [Col. 0851D]

**30.** Alternatively, *vetare* (“to forbid”), or *vincere* (“to conquer”), instead of *vitare* (“to avoid”). MAR.]

**30.** If anger gets the start, restrain it; if it has [Col. 0852B] taken possession, soothe it. Temper fury; temper indignation; restrain the movement of your spirit; curb the assault of anger. If you cannot avoid anger, at least temper it; if you cannot guard against fury, at least restrain it. Be readier to receive an injury than to inflict one. Learn to endure evils rather than to do them; learn to bear evils rather than to return them. Beware of becoming the avenger of your own injuries.

[Note: [Col. 0852D]

**31.** Alternatively, *opprobria* (“reproaches”), instead of *probra* (“insults”). For *errores* (“errors”), perhaps *irrisiones* (“mockery”). MAR.

In the same place. “By despising mockery.” Alternatively, “by despising the insults of mockery.” AREV.]

**31.** Be patient; be gentle; be mild; be moderate. Preserve patience; preserve moderation; preserve gentleness. Strive for patience and gentleness. Despise the insults of inflicted abuse. By despising mockery, overcome it; by disregarding the faults of detractors, trample them down; by patience, overcome the insults of detractors. Break the arrows of abuse with the shield of patience. [Col. 0852C] Prepare a shield of endurance against harsh words; offer the protection of patience against the sword of the tongue.

[Note: [Col. 0852D]

**32.** Alternatively, *rependas* (“you should repay”), instead of *repetas* (“you should return”). And *vincis* (“you conquer”), instead of *vinces* (“you will conquer”). MAR.]

**32.** No matter who provokes, incites, exasperates, insults, challenges, abuses, accuses, summons you to litigation, summons you to quarrel, speaks an insult, commits an injury, or inflicts abuse upon you: you be silent; you keep quiet; you disregard it; you despise it; you do not speak; you practice silence. When injured, do not answer; do not return abuse; do not repay insult. Hold fast to the patience of silence. By keeping silent, you will conquer more quickly.

[Note: [Col. 0852D]

**33.** Alternatively, *tibi conviciatur* (“abuses you”), instead of *conviciaris* (“you abuse”). MAR.

In the same place. Others have: “Learn mercy and moderation from Christ; learn patience and endurance.” Grialius’s edition: “Do not grieve over injuries.” AREV.]

**33.** Learn moderation from Christ; learn endurance; look to Christ and do not grieve over injuries. For he suffered on our behalf and left us an example (I [Col. 0852D] Peter II, 21). Struck on the cheeks, beaten with whips, mocked with spittle, fastened with nails, crowned with thorns, condemned to the cross, he was always silent. Great is the virtue of not injuring the one by whom you have been injured; great is the strength of forgiving even when injured; great is the glory of sparing someone whom you [Col. 0853A] were able to harm. When you are abused, it happens to you because of your own sins; when you are wronged, your own evils cause it. Whatever adversity has happened to you, consider it to have occurred because of your sin. Temper your pain, therefore, by consideration of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0853D]

**34.** Alternatively, *lenius* (“more gently”), instead of *levius* (“more lightly”). And *grato* (“pleasing”), instead of *gravato* (“burdened”). MAR.

In the same place. “And do not torment yourself.” I restored this in place of *non te excruciat* (“it does not torment you”), which stood in Grialius’s edition. Others have *non te excrucias* (“do not torment yourself”), instead of *non te excrucies* (“do not torment yourself”). At the beginning of this number, instead of *delinire* (“to soothe”), one could read *delini* (“to be soothed”), or *delinire stude* (“strive to soothe”), as in the book *On the Rule of Life*. AREV.]

**34.** You will bear it more lightly if you consider for what reasons it is inflicted. Therefore, when you are disparaged, pray; when you are cursed, bless the one who curses you; set blessing against him; soothe the angry person with patience; dissolve the fury of the raging person with gentleness. Conquer wickedness by mildness; conquer malice by goodness; appease the enemies of peace with complete moderation; bear with a tranquil mind the insults inflicted upon you. Open your pain with a calm heart. The wound of an injury, however serious it may be, evaporates when opened; but an enclosed wound greatly consumes the [Col. 0853B] mind. For the more you cover it, the more you increase it. Open it, therefore, with a burdened mind, and do not torment yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0853D]

**35.** Alternatively, *devotionis* (“of devotion”), instead of *dilectionis* (“of love”). MAR.

In the note to Grialius’s edition there was *repropitia* (“reconciliation”), without indicating the word for which this was a variant reading. But I think one should read *repropitia* for *repropitiare* (“to reconcile”), or *repropitiationem* (“reconciliation”) for *reconciliationem* (“reconciliation”). AREV.]

**35.** If you have saddened your brother in anything, make satisfaction to him. If you have sinned against him, do penance before him. If you have offended anyone, reconcile him by prayer. Go quickly toward reconciliation for your offense; ask pardon promptly. Do not sleep unless you have returned to peace; do not rest unless you have been reconciled to your brother. Call him back with the swiftest affection of love. Call him back to grace through humility; prostrate yourself before him with humble affection; beg pardon with a submissive spirit. Also gladly pardon one who asks forgiveness of you; kindly forgive one who requests pardon. Embrace immediately the one who returns. Receive the returning person at once [Col. 0853C] with gracious love.

[Note: [Col. 0854D]

**36.** Alternatively, *detergitur* (“is cleansed”), instead of *deletur* (“is erased”). MAR.

In the note to Grialius’s edition there was *serves* (“you will preserve”), without indicating the word for which this was a variant reading. In the manuscripts *serves* occurs twice instead of *reserves* (“you will retain”), which, I think, Mariana intended. AREV.]

**36.** Forgive, so that you may be forgiven. Pardon, so that you may be pardoned. Do not repay the one who sins against you according to his guilt, knowing that judgment will also come upon you. For you will not have forgiveness unless you give it. Even if he does not plead, even if he does not ask that he be forgiven, even if he does not undergo the humility of begging, even if a bad conscience does not acknowledge his sin, you must release him from your heart; you must forgive him from your spirit; you must pardon freely; you must grant forgiveness of your own will. Do not retain pain in your heart; do not hold pain in your spirit. Remove your brother’s offense from your heart; do not retain pain over another’s wickedness. For hatred separates a person from the kingdom of God; it removes him from heaven; it casts him out of paradise. Hatred is removed neither by suffering nor [Col. 0853D] expiated by martyrdom nor erased by shed blood.

[Note: [Col. 0854D]

**37.** Alternatively, “envy is like a moth of the spirit.” And *deposcit* (“demands”), instead of *depascit* (“devours”). MAR.

In the same place. Others have, “from the torches of no envy.” AREV.]

**37.** What need is there to speak of the fire of jealousy? Envy burns up every seed of virtue; envy devours every good thing with its pestilential heat. It first harms itself; it first [Col. 0854A] bites itself; it first gnaws at its own author. Envy is a moth of the spirit: it consumes understanding, burns the breast, afflicts the mind, and devours the human heart like a kind of pestilence. Let goodness, therefore, confront jealousy; let love be prepared against envy. Do not grieve over another’s good; do not waste away over another’s progress; do not be torn apart by anyone’s prosperity; do not be tortured by anyone’s happiness; let yourself not be driven by the torches of anyone’s envy.

**38.** Love peace; cherish peace; maintain peace with everyone; embrace everyone in gentleness and love. Prove that you love more than you yourself are loved. Do not be faithless in peace; do not be fickle in friendship. Always preserve the bond of constancy. Invite those who hate to peace; call those who disagree back to harmony; reconcile the hearts of the divided through peace. Possess a forgiving [Col. 0854B] mind; possess kindness of spirit; be ready in affection; courteous in speech; address everyone with a gracious spirit. Let there be no word of quarrels that divides harmony.

**39.** Flee quarrels; avoid disputes; beware of contentions; remove the occasion of litigation. Despise disputes; live always in peace; contend in no matter; strive to fight in no action. Contention demands contradiction; contention gives birth to disputes; contention generates quarrels; contention kindles the torches of hatred. Contention extinguishes peace of heart; contention breaks harmony. If your enemy falls, do not rejoice; do not exalt yourself at the ruin of an adversary. Do not rejoice over the destruction of an enemy, lest similar things come upon you; lest perhaps God turn his anger from him upon you.

[Col. 0854C] [Note: [Col. 0854D]

**40.** One who rejoices at an enemy’s fall will quickly fall into it himself. Let your feeling toward the humbled person be humane; let your gaze upon the fallen person be compassionate. Let it please you to grieve over one who is afflicted. Suffer with others’ calamities; be filled with tears over others’ sorrows. Do not be hard; do not be iron-hearted; do not have a harsh breast. Mourn another’s misery as though it were your own. In another’s tribulation, you too should be sad. Weep with those who mourn; weep with those who weep; join yourself in feeling to those who grieve.

[Note: [Col. 0854D]

**41.** Alternatively, *flagrare* (“to burn”), instead of *fragrare* (“to be fragrant”). And *opprobriis* (“reproaches”), instead of *opinionibus* (“opinions”). MAR.]

**41.** In all your actions, in all your work, in all your conduct, imitate the good; emulate the saints. Keep the examples of the saints before your eyes. Consider the examples of the righteous by imitating them; set the examples of the saints before yourself. Let the examples of the fathers be for you incentives to discipline [Col. 0854D]. Attend to the virtues of the saints in order to act well; attend to the teachings of the righteous in order to live well. Let no infamy in your life scandalize anyone; let no adverse reputation sadden anyone. Learn to be fragrant with a good reputation [Col. 0855A]; possess a good testimony; guard your good name. Let it be obscured by no foulness or torn apart by no adverse reports. For the tearing apart of a good reputation causes loss.

[Note: [Col. 0855D]

**42.** Perhaps *circumlatus* (“carried around”), instead of *circumflatus* (“blown about”). Alternatively, *ad rem* (“to the matter”), instead of *ad te* (“to you”). MAR.]

[Note: In the same place. Much has been taken from here to cobble together the little book *On the Rule of Life*, in Isidore’s name, which may be compared with this work. AREV.]

### 42

But beware popular glory and the admiration of the crowd; stop displaying yourself in the eyes of flatterers; do not be puffed up by the wind of approval. Despise applause; despise the praise of popular favor. Strive to be good rather than to seem good. Do not inquire whether anyone extols or despises you; let neither approval lead you astray nor blame break you. Whoever does not seek praise does not feel insult; if you despise praise, you will easily reject blame as well.

Do not consider yourself good merely because you are proclaimed good. Question your conscience in another’s tongue; judge yourself by your own, not another’s, judgment. Measure yourself not by another’s speech but by your own mind. No one can know better what you are than you, who are conscious of yourself. For what does it profit you, while you are evil, to be proclaimed good? Or what benefit does praise bring you if you are one thing and pretend to be another?

[Note: [Col. 0856D]

43. Another reading has *despise the unknown* for *drive away the cowardly*. MAR.]

### 43

Therefore avoid simulation and pretense; do not feign holiness by means of a darker garment. Be what you wish to be considered. Display your profession both in your dress and in your bearing. Let there be simplicity in your entrance, purity in your movement, gravity in your gesture, and propriety in your walk. Let nothing disgraceful, nothing wanton, nothing impudent, nothing insolent, and nothing frivolous appear in your bearing. For the mind appears in the habit of the body; the gesture of the body is a sign of the mind; by the body’s gesture the mind is revealed, and the disposition of the mind is disclosed. Let your walk therefore bear no image of frivolity; let your bearing offend no one’s eyes.

Do not offer yourself as a spectacle to others; give no one an opportunity to disparage you. Do not join yourself to frivolous people or mix with the vain. Shun the wicked, beware of the unjust, flee the depraved, drive the cowardly away from you. Flee the crowds of people, especially those of an age inclined toward vices.

### 44

Associate yourself with the good; seek the companionship and fellowship of the good. Cleave inseparably to the holy. If you become the companion of their way of life, you will also become a companion of their virtue. Whoever walks with the wise will be wise, but whoever walks with fools will be a fool, for like things are accustomed to join with like.

It is dangerous to lead one’s life with the wicked and destructive to associate with those of perverse will. You nourish disgrace for yourself if you associate with the unworthy. It is better to hate the wicked than to share their company. Just as the common life of the saints possesses many good things, so the society of the wicked brings very many evils. For whoever touches an unclean thing will be defiled by it. Close your ears as well, lest you hear evil.

[Note: [Col. 0856D]

45. Another reading has *steal upon* for *creep in*. MAR.]

### 45

Reject indecent speech; flee dishonorable words. Let no obscenity of speech creep into your ears. A vain word quickly pollutes the mind, and what is willingly heard is easily done.

Let nothing proceed from your mouth that could obstruct; let no sound of your voice burst forth that is not useful. Let what comes from your lips be such as does not pollute the ears of the hearer. Obscenity of words must be avoided; disgraceful speech must be fled. Vain speech is an indication of a vain conscience; the tongue reveals a person’s character. As the speech appears, so the mind is proved to be, for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34).

[Note: [Col. 0856D]

46. Another reading has *increase* for *grow*. Instead of *reject*, perhaps *do not reject*. MAR.]

### 46

Restrain your tongue from idle speech; hold it back from idle words. Beware of the most foolish tales; do not tell old wives’ stories. Do not chatter disgraceful and empty words. Keep silent about a word that does not edify the hearers. Idle speech will not be without judgment. “Everyone will give an account of his words” (Matt. 12:36); each person’s words will stand before his face.

Whoever does not restrain idle words soon passes to harmful ones. Whoever despises the least things easily falls headlong into the greatest; for the lesser fault generates a greater. Vices gradually grow, and while we do not avoid small things, we slide into great ones. Therefore avoid the smallest things, and you will not reach greater ones; reject the little things, and you will not fall into worse.

[Note: [Col. 0856D]

47. Another reading has *you may not be able to recall what you say* [the printed text reads *dciis*]. Flee. MAR.]

### 47

Let what you say be worthy of seriousness and instruction. Let your speech be irreproachable and useful to the expectations of your hearers. Strive to say not what you wish, but what you ought. Distinguish what you should say from what you should keep silent, and be skilled both in speaking and in keeping silent.

Deliberate at length beforehand about what you will say, lest you be unable to retract it. Flee the accidents of the tongue; do not let your tongue destroy you.

### 48

Remove the opportunity from the one lying in wait. Do not let your mouth be exposed to the enemy’s arrows; do not say what your adversary could seize upon. Always keep silence as a friend. Set a guard over your mouth; place a seal upon your lips; oppose the bars of silence to your tongue; surround your tongue with the fortification of watchfulness.

Attend to the proper opportunity for speaking. Seek the time for bringing forth words. Know when to speak; consider when to say something. Speak at the appropriate time, and keep silent at the appropriate time.

### 49

Keep silent until you are questioned. Do not speak unless questioned; do not speak before you have heard. Let questioning open your mouth, and let your words be few.

Remove the verbosity of needless speech; do not exceed the proper measure of speaking, lest through lack of restraint in your tongue you incur danger. Excessive talk does not escape blame; much speaking does not avoid sin. An overflowing river quickly gathers mud; a sea wind beyond measure brings danger; excessive rain raises danger. A talkative person is unskilled; the wise use few words. Knowledge makes speech brief; to speak much is folly, for the voice of the foolish lies in the multiplication of speech.

Let there therefore be measure in your word and a balance in your speech. Always moderate your words; do not pass beyond the proper measure of speaking.

[Note: [Col. 0857C]

50. *Cut off.* Another reading: *cut away*. AREV.]

### 50

Cut off from your tongue as well the vice of slander. Do not tear apart another’s life; do not pollute your mouth with another’s evil. Do not slander the sinner, but sympathize with him. Whatever you slander in another, fear in yourself instead.

Slander is a grave vice; slander is a grave sin; slander is a grave crime; slander is a grave condemnation. Everyone condemns it; everyone reproves it. Nothing is more disgraceful; it is the height of shame.

[Note: [Col. 0857C]

51. Another reading has *tear apart* for *bark*, and *bark against* for *slander*. [Col. 0857D] MAR.

In the same place. *When you slander others.* Thus I restored the reading from the Florentine manuscript, octavo. Grialius has *quando alio*; some manuscripts, *quando alium*; Bignaeus, *quando alii*. AREV.]

### 51

It is the habit of dogs to bark, to thrust out their tongues, and to bite with a deadly tooth; dogs alone know how to slander. When you slander others, examine yourself. When you bite another, rebuke your own sins. If you wish to slander, turn your attention to your own sins. Look not upon another’s faults but your own; attend to your own vices, not another’s.

You will never slander if you have thoroughly examined yourself. Be concerned, then, with your own correction; be attentive to your own salvation and amendment. Do not listen to slanderers; do not lend an ear to whisperers.

### 52

Slanderers and hearers are held guilty in equal measure; the same danger threatens both. The one who listens to the slanderer and the one who slanders are judged equally.

Do not seek what does not concern you. Never desire to learn what people say among themselves. Do not ask what each person says or does. Avoid curiosity; abandon concern for another’s life; abandon concern for what does not pertain to your own case.

Let no curiosity seize your mind; let no desire for detestable curiosity steal upon you. Do not, forgetting your own conduct, investigate that of others. Correct your own vices with as much care as you observe those of others.

[Note: [Col. 0857D]

53. Flee every kind of lie with the utmost care. Gratian took from this passage the chapter beginning “Every kind of lie,” in *Decretum* 22.2. We have therefore corrected the whole passage, since the manuscripts varied greatly: some read *non praestes* (“do not help”) instead of *ut praestes* (“that you may help”); another had *nec per te stes*; and in place of *vitam*, some had *vita* or *vitium*, while some had *vitium* alone. MAR.

In the same place. Codex Regiovat. 254: “Nor should you strive to lie so that you may benefit.” But *that you may profit* should be retained, since it has the same meaning as *that you may benefit*. AREV.]

### 53

Flee every kind of lie with the utmost care. Do not speak falsely either by accident or deliberately. Do not strive to lie even in order to help; do not defend anyone’s life by any deception.

Beware of lying in all things. For by lying faith is removed, error introduced, and truth abolished. There is no just lie; every lie is sin. Everything that disagrees with the truth is wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0857D]

54. Another reading has *kings* for *laws*. Also, *is punished* for *is recorded*, and *of deeds* after *of words*. Also, *will repay* for *will provide*. MAR.]

### 54

The laws of the world condemn forgers, punish liars, and destroy deceivers. If lies are condemned among human beings by law, if deceit is punished by human judgment, if falsehood is registered as a capital offense, how much more severely will it be judged before God, the witness of words? Before him each person will give an account even of an idle word; before him each person will pay the penalty even for idle speech. For “the mouth that lies kills the soul”; and, “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7); and, “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5, 9).

[Note: [Col. 0857D]

55. Another reading has *from a lie* for *a lie …* MAR.]

### 55

Therefore reject deceit and turn aside from lying. Beware of falsehood; speak purely; never lie. Be truthful. Do not deceive anyone by lying; do not lead anyone into error by lying; do not circumvent anyone with words; do not deceive anyone by fraud; do not seduce anyone through the arguments of lying words.

Do not say one thing and do another; do not say one thing while holding another in your heart. Show affection without pretense; display goodness without disguise.

[Note: [Col. 0858C]

56. Another reading has: “Let *yes, yes; no, no* be in your mouth.” MAR.]

### 56

Also prohibit yourself from taking oaths; remove the practice of swearing. For an oath is dangerous: continual swearing creates a habit of perjury. The practice of swearing leads to perjury. Let “it is” be in your mouth, and let “it is not” be in your mouth (Matt. 5:37). Truth does not need an oath. A faithful word takes the place of an oath; let the reliability of your oath also be firm.

[Note: [Col. 0858D]

57. Another reading has *truly* for *of strength*. MAR.

In the same place. “Make no vow.” Another reading: “Presume nothing.” Another: “Make no vow; presume nothing.” AREV.]

### 57

Do the good thing that you have promised. Do not be easy with words and difficult in action. Do not lightly promise anything before God. Without considering your strength, make no vow. Do not promise what you cannot do.

You will be greatly liable before God if you do not fulfill what you have vowed. Those who do not fulfill their vows are displeasing to God.

[Note: [Col. 0858D]

58. “In evil promises, withdraw your pledge.” Gratian, *Decretum* 22.4, chapter “In evil things,” and the Master of the Sentences, book III, distinction 39, chapter 8, read this passage in the form in which we have corrected it, except that where all the manuscripts had *do not do*, they read *lest you do*. The same passage is cited from this book of the *Synonyms* in the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2, and in the printed editions with exactly the words we have adopted.

In two Gothic manuscripts, demonstrably copied more than six hundred years ago, where we read *change the decree in a shameful vow*, there is *in a shameful vow*; the Mejora manuscript and another Laurentian manuscript follow this reading. Perhaps that is Isidore’s genuine reading, although we have not dared to alter the text. MAR.]

### 58

Those who have not fulfilled what they vowed are counted among the faithless. For it is better not to promise than not to discharge the pledge of a promise; it is better not to make a vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill the promise (Eccl. 5:4).

In evil promises, withdraw your pledge; in a shameful vow, change your decision. Do not do what you vowed rashly; a promise that is fulfilled through wickedness is impious.

[Note: [Col. 0858D]

59. Another reading has *hidden away* for *hidden*. Also, *is pressed down* or *is brought forth* for *is deposited*. MAR.]

### 59

Nothing is hidden from God. Do not speak an evil word even in your heart; do not think that a wicked word can be hidden in silence. Every hidden word will be disclosed. What is deposited in secret is brought into the open; consider whatever you do or say within as though it had been placed in public.

For the stones to which we speak as witnesses will not conceal it, and the very walls will not be silent about what they have heard. If human beings are silent, animals will speak. Therefore avoid sins as though you could not conceal them. Sin where you do not know that God is present. Nothing is hidden before God; he who made hidden things sees what is concealed.

[Note: [Col. 0859D]

60. Another reading has *of divine judgment* for *of divine judgments*. MAR.

In the same place. Another reading: *but perhaps*. Another: *you should propose*. MAR.

In the same place. Thomas Gataker, book I of *Adversaria Miscellanea*, chapter 7, quotes from Isidore’s *Soliloquies* this six-line verse: “Do you wish to be continually happy? Live well.” In the index he also cites from the *Soliloquies*: “Do you wish never to be sad? See to it that you live well.” See pages 86 and 212. AREV.]

### 60

For you will be liable to divine judgments, even though you are hidden from human eyes. God is present everywhere; his spirit fills everything. His majesty penetrates all the elements, and his presence, through his power, reaches all things. There is no place outside him.

Nothing is hidden from his knowledge. The power of his might breaks into every secret; it permits no hidden thing to remain concealed from it, and no obstacles prevent it from penetrating. He knows thoughts; he looks into the heart. He sees what is done or hidden within; he comprehends what is planned within. He knows even what a person himself does not know about himself.

### 61

No one can escape even himself. If public opinion does not condemn you, your own conscience condemns you. No punishment is heavier than conscience.

Do you wish never to be sad? Live well. A secure mind endures sadness lightly; a good life always possesses joy. But the conscience of the guilty is always in punishment. A guilty spirit is never secure, for an evil mind is tormented by the goads of its own conscience.

If you remain in goodness, sadness will withdraw from you. If you persevere in righteousness, sadness will not meet you. Neither wound nor death will terrify you if you have lived well and piously.

[Col. 0859C] [Note: [Col. 0859D]

62. “You will not be able to recall it.” Another reading: “You will not be able to be recalled from a bad habit.” AREV.

Another reading has *is obscured* for *is corrupted*. MAR.]

### 62

Always turn your counsel and your work toward the Lord. In every work ask for God’s help. Ascribe everything to divine grace and divine gift. Attribute nothing to your own merits; presume nothing upon your strength; place nothing in your boldness.

Do you wish your virtues to increase? Do not display them. Conceal your virtues lest they produce elation; hide your good deeds lest they produce arrogance. Avoid being seen as what you have deserved to be. What you can lose by revealing, preserve by silence.

But reveal the vices of your heart; immediately disclose your evil thoughts. For a sin that has been exposed is quickly healed, whereas a crime grows through silence, and guilt increases when concealed. If a vice is exposed, what was great becomes small; if it lies hidden, what was small becomes great. If it is covered, it is believed to be worse.

One ought to avoid evil rather than correct it. It is better to avoid vice than to amend it, lest, when you have fallen into it, you be unable to recall yourself from it.

### 63

For habit is conquered with difficulty. The bonds of custom are scarcely broken; what has long become ingrained is corrected more slowly.

Deliberate for a long time about a doubtful decision. Think long before acting; reflect long before beginning a work. Mature your plan so that you can complete it. Examine and test for a long time what you intend to do, and then act. When you have thought for a long time, do what you have approved. Nothing great comes from rashness; delay in deliberation is better.

But in matters that are certain and good, let slowness be removed from you. Eliminate delay; put nothing off until tomorrow. Delay harms good things; in matters that are useful, postponement obstructs. Let sluggish idleness and numbing negligence be absent from good works.

Let the vice of laziness be far from the idle. Vices quickly seize the inactive. Through torpor, strength and intelligence ebb away. Negligence and sluggishness dissolve the mind; idleness corrupts nature; through idleness intelligence grows cold.

[Note: [Col. 0860D]

64. Another reading has *makes more severe* for *surpasses*. Also, *is aroused* for *is known*. Also, *the matter itself proceeds so that you will use it*; and *by will* for *with pleasure*. MAR.]

### 64

For torpor surpasses the senses, and dullness extinguishes the light of knowledge. Skill makes the senses better; negligence makes them worse. Idleness dulls the senses; industry sharpens them. Nature becomes more excellent through instruction; intelligence becomes more ardent when study is applied.

Slower minds are sharpened by study; industry arouses the torpor of nature. Constant practice sharpens sluggishness of perception. The senses advance through exercise; through experience one learns more.

Nature is often changed by character; nature is often overcome by habit, for constant practice forms character. Continual use is turned into nature. Everything yields to use; everything obeys use. The matter itself proceeds according to the way you use it. What you begin with difficulty you will complete with pleasure through practice.

[Note: [Col. 0860D]

65. Another reading has *sloth* for *ignorance*. MAR.]

### 65

Nothing is better than wisdom; nothing sweeter than prudence; nothing more agreeable than knowledge. Nothing is worse than folly; nothing more harmful than foolishness; nothing more disgraceful than ignorance.

Ignorance is the mother of errors and the nurse of vices. Sin prevails more through ignorance, for ignorance does not perceive what deserves blame, nor recognize when it commits an offense. Many sin through inexperience; the foolish sin continually. The uneducated are easily deceived; the fool quickly slips into vices.

The prudent quickly detects snares; the prudent more quickly recognizes errors. We avoid harmful things only through wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0860D]

66. Another reading has *what you hold* for *where you are heading*. MAR.

In the same place. *Not to know where you are heading.* Another reading: *not to know and entirely to be ignorant of what you hold or where you are heading*. AREV.]

### 66

For knowledge abstains from evils, and the wise examine everything prudently. The wise distinguish between good and evil through understanding. The highest good is to know what you must avoid; the greatest misery is not to know where you are heading.

Therefore love wisdom, and it will be revealed to you. Approach it, and it will draw near to you. Be constant in its company, and it will instruct you.

### 67

Learn what you do not know, lest you be found an unhelpful teacher. First be a hearer, afterward a teacher. Receive the name of teacher through discipline. Speak the good that you have heard; teach the good that you have learned. Do not despise the pursuit of learning and teaching.

Pour out through your mouth the knowledge that you conceive with your ear. When you share wisdom with others, you increase it more for yourself. The more widely instruction is given, the more it abounds. Wisdom becomes more generous by giving and smaller by withholding; knowledge is more abundant when it is shared, and the more it is imparted, the more it abounds.

[Note: [Col. 0861D]

68. Another reading has *your words* for *your word*. Also, *you promise* for *you have promised*. Also, *do not despise simple people when speaking*. MAR.

In the same place. *To praise what you say.* I would prefer: *that what you say be praised.* In the manuscripts, *e* and *i* are frequently confused. Later some manuscripts add: “When you teach, after you have been instructed; when you train; when you admonish, do not use words …” AREV.]

### 68

Let works precede the word. Fulfill in action what you promise with your mouth. Show by examples what you teach in words. Be not only a teacher but also an imitator of virtue.

If you teach and act, then you will be regarded as glorious. For it is not enough to praise what you say unless you join deeds to words. In teaching itself, restrain yourself from human praise. Instruct others in such a way that you guard yourself. Teach in such a way that you do not lose the grace of humility. Beware lest, while raising others by teaching them, you yourself be dragged down by the desire for praise.

When you teach, do not use obscure language. Speak so that you may be understood. Do not displease simple people by your speech, nor offend the prudent.

### 69

The teacher’s speech should accord with the understanding of the hearer; instruction should be imparted according to character. Remedies should be applied according to the wound. Different wills require different discipline; each person must be taught according to his profession.

The variety of persons must be examined. Consider how you should instruct each one. Speak what is common to all and what is secret to the more perfect. Proclaim what is open to everyone and what is hidden to the few. Some matters are to be discussed with many, others with few.

### 70

Be ready for instruction at every time. Let no time be empty in which you do not build up; let no hour pass in which you do not contribute something to the pursuit of instruction. Proclaim good words openly and consistently, and do not be ashamed to speak and defend what you know.

What you perceive to be lacking in your knowledge, seek from others. Things concealed become clear through discussion; difficult matters are opened by discussion.

[Note: [Col. 0861D]

71. “In unfamiliar matters he makes one rash.” He used *unfamiliar* for *unknown*, a manner of speaking Isidore often employs. For this reason we preferred this reading, found in several manuscripts, to the reading of the Navarricus manuscript: “In empty matters he makes one rash.” Tacitus frequently uses *known* and *unknown* in the sense of *familiar* and *unfamiliar*. MAR.]

### 71

Let there be no curiosity in you to know hidden things. Beware of investigating what lies beyond human senses. Pass over, as a secret, what you have not learned from the authority of Scripture.

Seek nothing beyond what has been written; investigate nothing more than what divine Scripture proclaims. Do not desire to know what is not permitted to be known. Curiosity is a dangerous presumption; curiosity is a harmful form of knowledge. It provokes heresy, plunges the mind into sacrilegious tales, makes people bold in obscure matters, and makes them rash in unfamiliar matters.

516

### 72

In matters of dispute, remove contention; remove the stubborn defense of victory. Yield quickly to the truth; do not contradict justice; do not strive to empty out what is right.

Contend by right, not by fraud. Do not judge yourself more learned than others; do not prepare yourself for contrary disputes; do not strive against the truth in order to win.

In every disputation, maintain reason. Strive to discuss, not to defeat. Love listening more than speaking; listen more than you talk.

### 73

At the beginning, listen; speak last. The end possesses greater honor. In every matter the conclusion is sought; the final things are examined.

The end is better than the beginning; the last word is better than the first. Revere all who are superior in knowledge and life; revere each person according to the merit of his holiness. Show fitting reverence to the higher rank. Render to each person the honor appropriate to his dignity.

### 74

Do not present yourself as the equal of your superior. Offer obedience to your elders; serve their commands; yield to their authority; comply with their will. Show due obedience to your superiors; obey everyone in good commands.

Obey a human being in such a way that you do not offend the will of God.

[Note: [Col. 0862D]

75. “But even those conscious of the sin are held liable.” We took this reading only from the Septimancensis manuscript, for in the others it read: “But even those conscious of the sin are held or hold liable,” which, if read in that way, produces a defective sentence and requires a word such as *are to be understood* or something similar. MAR.

In the same place. “Equal punishment,” and so forth. See Dracontius, book I, verse 541: “But an equal sentence condemns those whom equal guilt holds, with a mark.” AREV.]

### 75

When ordered to do evil, do not comply; when ordered to do evil, do not consent. Do not consent to evil at the command of anyone, even if punishment compels you, even if penalties threaten, even if tortures confront you.

It is better to suffer death than to fulfill destructive commands. It is better to be slaughtered by a human being than to be condemned by eternal judgment. Not only those who commit the act but also those conscious of the sin are held liable, for the person who obeyed so that it might be done is not free from the crime.

The one who obeys in evil is like the one who does evil; equal punishment binds the perpetrator and the obedient accomplice.

[Note: [Col. 0862D]

76. On rulers, nearly the same material appears in book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 48 and following. AREV.]

### 76

Strive to be revered by your subjects rather than feared. Let those under you respect you more than they fear you; let them cling to you more through the duty of affection than through the necessity of their condition. Make yourself such to your subjects that you are loved more than feared.

For love proceeds from reverence; hatred comes from fear. Fear removes loyalty; affection restores it. Fear does not preserve lasting faith. Where there is fear, boldness follows; where dread is present, despair appears.

[Note: [Col. 0862D]

77. Another reading has *in all your work, in …* MAR.]

### 77

Therefore temper the harshness of your rule. Govern your subjects with the greatest kindness; do not be terrifying to those under you. Dominate them in such a way that they delight in serving you.

Maintain moderation both in discipline and in restraint. Indulge neither too much nor too little; forgive neither too little nor too much. Keep measure in every work; maintain balance in every matter. Do nothing intemperate—neither too little nor too much, neither beyond what is fitting nor below it. Even in good things, excess is not becoming.

[Col. 0863A] [Note: [Col. 0863D]

78. Another reading has *look upon* or *look ahead* for *examine*. MAR.]

### 78

All moderate things are useful; all things are perfect in their proper measure. What is done with moderation is health-giving. Good things become harmful through immoderate use.

Every excess is counted as a vice. Whatever is done with moderation is done beneficially; what is done with moderation is health-giving. Moderate all things prudently, lest good become evil. Examine also what is suitable for whom, for what time, in what place, when, how, and for how long you ought to act.

### 79

Examine the causes of things and the rules of times; recognize the proper discernment of individual works. Carefully distinguish everything you do. Know how to begin a good work and how to carry it through.

Maintain discernment in every action; appear indiscriminate in no matter. Serve each virtue appropriately in its own time. When you have properly distinguished your work, you will be entirely just.

Whatever good you do with discernment is virtue; whatever you do without discernment is vice.

[Note: [Col. 0863D]

80. “Usage must yield to authority.” Gratian transferred this passage into his *Decree*, distinction 11, chapter 1. Moved by his authority, we rejected another reading found in several manuscripts, in which, instead of *usage must yield to authority*, it read: *let custom yield to authority*. Nevertheless, we suspected that both should be read in this order: “Let custom yield to authority; usage must yield to authority,” since it is characteristic of the *Synonyms* to repeat the same thought in several words.

Immediately afterward, where the text reads *Let reason prevail*, the Hispalensis manuscript has *Let reflection prevail*, and the Guadalupe and another Laurentian manuscript have *Let moderation prevail*. We rejected these as corrupt readings. MAR.]

### 80

For undisciplined virtue is counted as vice; virtue without discernment occupies the place of vice. Many things have been corrupted by custom; many have been presumed upon through bad usage; many have been unlawfully appropriated against honorable morals.

Remove custom; preserve the law. Let usage yield to authority; let law and reason overcome bad usage.

518

### 81

What you wish to be done to you, do to another. What you wish another to do to you, do the same to him. Be toward others as you wish others to be toward you.

By your testimony harm no one; do not apply the voice of testimony to anyone’s danger. Let your speech harm neither anyone’s soul nor anyone’s possessions.

What you do not wish to suffer, do not do. What you do not wish done to you, never do to another. Do not inflict evils upon another, lest you suffer similar things.

Maintain modesty in yourself; maintain justice toward others. Uphold equity of law; follow the truth of judgments.

[Note: [Col. 0864D]

82. Another reading has: “When you judge, beware lest you be swayed by affection for the person”; and: “They corrupt the truth of judgments.” MAR.

In Grialius’s edition the punctuation was less satisfactory: “For justice is quickly violated by gold; justice is quickly corrupted.” AREV.]

### 82

Defend no one against the truth. When you judge, do not be turned away from what is true by affection for any person. Whether someone is poor or rich, examine the case, not the person. Preserve truth in everything; let neither ambition nor payment move you.

Despise gifts as well, lest justice be corrupted by them. Gifts always betray the truth. Justice is quickly violated by gold; it is quickly corrupted by a gift. Do not seek temporal profits from a just judgment; seek no worldly reward in exchange for justice. Distribute justice solely for the sake of eternal recompense.

[Col. 0863D]

### 83

For whoever desires present gifts does not hope for future glory. Whoever receives good things here has no further reward to await. When you judge, judge for a future reward; do not seek to have repaid to you what is owed to you in the future.

Shake your hands free of every gift if you wish to dwell on high. In judgment, however, never sit without mercy. Preserve the discernment of justice. Do not be more just than is just (Eccl. 7:17). For everything excessive is a vice.

It is impious justice not to forgive human weakness. Therefore do not love condemning, but rather correcting and reforming.

[Note: [Col. 0864D]

84. Another reading has *punishment* for *of punishment*. MAR.]

### 84

Therefore maintain strictness in examining justice, but mercy in defining the sentence. Let compassion follow the investigation of judgment; let clemency temper the severity of discipline.

Be as merciful toward another’s offenses as toward your own, and judge no one more strictly than yourself. Do not assess yourself one way and others another way. Judge others as you wish to be judged yourself.

When you forgive another’s sin, you show mercy to yourself. By the law with which you have judged another, you will be held. By the law and condition of punishment with which you have judged anyone, you yourself will be judged. Your own law binds you.

519

### 85

The judgment that you impose on others you will yourself bear. For in the matter in which you judge, you yourself are to be condemned; and “with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

First investigate everything, and then define it with justice. Condemn no one before judgment; judge no one on the basis of suspicion. First establish the facts, and then judge. For it is not the accused but the convicted person who is guilty. It is dangerous to judge anyone on suspicion.

[Col. 0864C] [Note: [Col. 0864D]

86. *Brings forth.* Better: *will bring forth*, corresponding to *will illuminate* and *will reveal*. Bignaeus has: *brings forth, illuminates, reveals*. AREV.]

### 86

In uncertain matters, reserve judgment for God. Commit to your own judgment what you know; commit to divine judgment what you do not know. No one whom God has reserved for his judgment can be condemned by human examination.

Let us not judge uncertain things until the Lord comes, “who brings hidden things to light, who will illuminate the things hidden in darkness, who will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:2). Even if things are true, they must not be believed unless they are confirmed by certain indications, unless they are established by manifest examination, unless they are made public through judicial procedure.

[Note: [Col. 0864D]

87. Another reading has: “Although you are exalted in power, restrain your greatness within yourself.” Also, *greater* for *great*. MAR.

In the same place. *A human being.* Some omit this word. AREV.]

### 87

O human being, let your humility be as great as your honor, even though you are in the highest position; hold fast to humility. If you hold fast to humility, you will possess glory. For the more humble you are, the greater height of glory will follow you.

Although the eminence of exalted power is in you, restrain it by humility. Let honor not lift you up; press down the summit of your elevation with humility. Be as much distinguished by greater humility as you are elevated by great dignity.

### 88

Also receive humbly the responsibilities imposed upon you. Fulfill the ministry entrusted to you with a submissive mind. Be obedient to the divine dispensation; do not dare to oppose its will.

Exercise the rights of the power you have acquired with moderation. Administer the rights of authority you have received with an ordered mind. Arrange everything with a tranquil, not a turbulent, heart.

Beware of honors that you cannot hold without guilt. The height of honors is the greatness of crimes; at a higher rank, the punishment is unquestionably greater.

[Note: [Col. 0865D]

89. Compare book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 50. AREV.]

### 89

Whoever is lesser is nearer to forgiveness. “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:7). For “a very strict judgment will be made upon those who rule” (Luke 12:48). From the one to whom much is given, much is required; from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is demanded.

Honors bring dangers with them. Power quickly becomes endangered; it quickly suffers a fall. The greater the honor, the greater the dangers. A tall tree is shaken more violently by the winds, and its branches are broken more quickly in its fall. High towers collapse with a heavier crash. The highest mountains are struck by frequent lightning.

[Note: [Col. 0865D]

90. Another reading has *falls into ambushes* for *is exposed to ambushes*. MAR.]

### 90

Envy quickly falls upon a powerful person; the illustrious person is quickly exposed to ambushes. Glory produces envy, and envy produces dangers.

Even if someone shines with worldly glory, even if he gleams with purple and gold, even if he stands out adorned in costly dress, even if he is fortified by a multitude, even if he is protected by the weapons of guards, even if he is surrounded by countless ranks of attendants, even if he is secured by armies, he is nevertheless always in punishment, always in anguish, always in sorrow, always in danger.

He lies upon silken beds, but troubled; he lies on down, but pale; he lies on golden couches, but disturbed.

91. The happiness of this world is brief; the glory of this age is slight; temporal power is fleeting and fragile. Tell me, where are the kings? Where are the princes? Where are the emperors? Where are the wealthy in possessions? Where are the powerful of this age? Where are the rich of the world? They have passed away like a shadow; they have vanished like a dream. They are sought, but are no more. Riches lead as far as danger; riches draw one onward even to destruction. Many have come to ruin because of their wealth. For many, riches have been deadly; for many, possessions have brought death. [Col. 0865D]

> **Note:** [Col. 0865D]
>
> **92.** Another reading: *secular cares*; another: *the cares of secular affairs*, instead of *the cares of possessions*. MAR.
>
> **On the same passage:** “They agitate the mind.” Some add: “They agitate the mind, entangle and ensnare the mind, afflict and confuse the mind, and plunge it down altogether, with the mind suffocated, even to the depths.” “Power,” etc. AREV.

92. He never has rest of mind who subjects himself to earthly cares; for concern about possessions disturbs the mind, and the cares of possessions agitate the mind. Power is never without the anxieties of solicitude. If, therefore, you wish to be at peace, desire nothing belonging to the age; you will always have rest of mind if you cast the cares of the world away from you. You will always enjoy inward tranquility if you withdraw yourself from the commotion of earthly affairs. [Col. 0866A]

521

> **Note:** [Col. 0866D]
>
> **93.** Another reading: *through love*, instead of *through fear*. “And through love of earthly things.” MAR.

93. If you despise present things, you will undoubtedly find eternal ones; if you trample upon secular and human affairs, you will easily and lightly receive heavenly grace, and you will reign with him who rules the living and the dead. Riches are never acquired without sin; riches are never administered without sin. No one administers earthly possessions without sin. It is very rare that those who possess riches strive for rest; those who entangle themselves in earthly cares separate themselves from the fear of God. Whoever fixes himself upon love of possessions takes no delight at all in God.

94. For the cares of possessions turn one away from devotion to God. No one can embrace the glory of God and of the world at the same time; no one can embrace Christ and the age at the same time. [Col. 0866B] It is difficult to serve heavenly and earthly cares equally; it is difficult to love God and the world at the same time. The two cannot be loved equally together. It is difficult—indeed impossible—for anyone to enjoy both present and future goods, to fill his belly here and his mind there, to pass from one pleasure to another, to be first in both ages, and to appear glorious on earth and in heaven. Renounce everything, therefore, for God; for God suspend yourself from the cares of the age; strive to serve God without the world’s impediment.

95. Let no love of the world separate you from the love of God; let no care withdraw you from the love of God; let no concern for possessions suspend you from devotion to God. Cast away from you whatever can impede your good purpose. With your whole soul both hate and condemn what the world loves; be dead to the world, and let the world be dead to you. Do not look upon the glory of the world as a dead person; as one dead, separate yourself from attachment to this life. Like one buried, have no care for the age. Like one deceased, deprive yourself of every earthly business. While alive, despise what you cannot possess after death. [Col. 0866C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0866D]
>
> **96.** An annotation is indicated in Grial’s edition at the words *of the needy, of want*, but it was omitted. Others read *the need of the needy*, which, in my opinion, Mariana intended to note. AREV.

96. Let what you have be held for mercy; let your virtue assist the needy in their want. If you know anyone placed in necessity, anyone reduced to poverty, anyone emptied by another’s plundering, anyone oppressed, anyone humbled, despise no one, disdain no one, look down upon no one; send no one away empty; let no one depart from you sad, let no one leave you confounded. Share with all, give to all, provide for all. Do not choose whom you will pity, lest you pass over someone who deserves to receive. You are uncertain on whose behalf you may please God more; you do not know for whom a greater fruit of righteousness may be prepared for you. [Col. 0866D]

> **Note:** [Col. 0866D]
>
> **97.** Another reading: *give*, instead of *distribute*. MAR.

97. Whatever you give, distribute with affection; whatever you bestow, bestow with cheerfulness. Show mercy without murmuring; give alms without weariness. Let goodwill be greater than what is given, and gratitude greater than what is expended. Your work will be such as your intention has been; for what is dispensed with a good disposition, that God accepts. But whoever gives with weariness loses his reward; whoever extends his hand with sadness loses the fruit of recompense; whoever bestows with sadness does not receive the fruit of repayment. For there is no mercy where there is no goodwill. [Col. 0867A]

> **Note:** [Col. 0867C]
>
> **98.** Another reading: *from one, in order to give to another* (*uni, ut alteri*), instead of *from another, from which to give to another* (*alteri, unde alteri*). MAR.
>
> **On the same passage:** “But seek what may profit the glory of eternal life.” The word *seek* was found in none of the manuscripts. We added it according to the sense, since something definite was evidently lacking, but with an obelus, so that the reader might recognize it as a suspect reading. MAR.

98. From your just labors provide for the poor; do not take from one person in order to give to another, nor display yourself as merciful through another’s plunder. It does no good if you restore one person from what makes another empty. Such compassion condemns; it does not reconcile. Such mercy does not cleanse sins but increases them. Do the good that you do for the sake of mercy, not for boasting. Seek nothing for praise, nothing for temporal reputation, nothing for fame, but for eternal life. Whatever you do, do it for the future reward; let expectation of eternal recompense hold you more firmly. Do not seek what benefits this life, but what benefits the glory of eternal life. [Col. 0867B]

99. For if praise is sought here, recompense is lost there. The righteous receive their reward not here but in the future. A future reward, not a present one, is promised to the righteous. In heaven, not on earth, reward is promised to the saints; one must not await here what is owed elsewhere.

> **Note:** [Col. 0867C]
>
> **100.** Another reading: *by instruction*. MAR.

100. Behold, you have received admonitions; a rule of life has been given to you. No ignorance now excuses you from sin; you are no longer ignorant of life, imprudent, or uninformed. I have explained the law that you ought to follow; I have described what you ought to be; you possess knowledge of the commandments. [Col. 0867C] You now know what it means to live rightly. See that you do not offend any further; see that henceforth you do not despise the good you know; see that what you respect in reading you do not scorn in living. Retain the gift of knowledge that you have received; fulfill in action what you have learned through teaching. [Col. 0868A]

101. I give thanks, I return thanks, I repay thanks, I discharge acts of thanksgiving. I render and owe you abundant thanks; as many as I can, I celebrate my thanks; as many as I am able according to my strength, I offer thanks. Many things have been granted to me by you, many conferred, many bestowed through special mercy. All please me, all are welcome, all have taken root in my heart, all caress me, all delight me. What satisfaction, then, shall I render? What recompense shall I return? What can I repay for your gifts except to use your commandments, always obey you, submit to you, and obey you when you command? [Col. 0868B]

> **Note:** [Col. 0868C]
>
> **102.** Another reading: *mistress of morals and virtue*. And *to know*, or *to understand*, instead of *to be*. MAR.

102. For you are the guide of life, you are the mistress of virtue. Like a rule, you lead me straight. You are she who never departs from what is right. You are she who never turns away from the truth. You are the discoverer of good things, the teacher of morals, the investigator of virtues, without whom human life can be nothing. Through you, a rule of life is given to all. Through you, people are brought from the perversity of life to a better life.

103. Souls are formed by your commandments. If anything is distorted, you correct it; if anything needs correction, you amend it. Nothing is dearer to me than you, nothing sweeter to me. # RULE OF MONKS BY SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE (C)

524

## PREFACE

[Col. 0867D]

> **Note:** [Col. 0867D]
>
> **Preface, no. 1.** Chapter 71 in the Isidorian materials was inscribed with this title: *Rule of Monks*. The arguments of the very distinguished Peter Emmanuel Hernández are examined; he considers it necessary to deny the work to Isidore. The commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict that Constantine Cajetan falsely attributes to Isidore are fabricated. The Isidorian Rule of Canons. Editions of the Rule of Monks. What is the final chapter of the Rule of Devout Women according to Martène? From this may be taken what ought to be inserted here by way of preface. [Col. 0868D]
>
> In Holstenius’s edition the inscription is: “Isidore to the holy brothers established in the monastery of Honorian.” Concerning this, see more fully the cited chapter 71, nos. 13 and following. In Mabillon, vol. I of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 363, it is called the monastery of Honoriacum; and from a very ancient Lérins manuscript he transcribes the pact made by the monks of that monastery, which is prefixed to Isidore’s Rule in the same manuscript in these words:
>
> “This is the pact that we make, whose names are written below, with you, Father and illustrious abbot. Since ancient monastic tradition teaches us that the monastic life cannot be lived without an abbot, and that it is not profitable for any monk to act according to his own presumption by himself [perhaps: alone], we choose you in the first place as abbot, to whom we entrust our souls and likewise our bodies, so that according to spiritual discipline you may command us in the things that belong to God, and offer our souls, imbued and purified, to God. It will therefore be our duty from this day and time onward to obey your admonitions, keep your precepts, and respect your conduct and conscience; it will be your duty to command us without hesitation whatever you have learned from your elders by reading or hearing. If anyone should attempt to violate this pact—namely, we whose names are affixed below—since he will not do this without the persuasion of the enemy, let him remain guilty and struck with anathema by the assembly of the brothers until, doing penance, he satisfies all the brothers.” [Col. 0869C–D]
>
> A similar pact is read at the end of the Common Rule of Saint Fructuosus. In Grial’s edition there are few notes, which I shall explain under Grial’s name, although Peter Chacón also had some part in collating this work. I shall abridge Menard’s annotations on the *Concordia of Rules*, and, where necessary, I shall give the variant reading that he reports. Likewise, from Peter of Cassino and the notes of Constantine Cajetan, about whom I spoke in the Isidorian materials, chapter 71, nos. 22 and following, I shall select what seems relevant; for it is less necessary to transcribe everything. In Preface no. 1, for *vow*, Menard, p. 33, reads *custom*. AREV.

1. There are many precepts, or institutions of the elders, which are found scattered throughout the writings of the holy Fathers, and which some have handed down to posterity in more extensive or more obscure compositions. Following their example, we have dared to select these few things for you, using ordinary or rustic speech, so that you may understand as easily as possible by what order you are to keep the vow of your profession.

[Col. 0869A] 525

> **Note:** [Col. 0869D]
>
> **2.** Menard notes, from Plautus, that *limitem* means a path or track. He explains *levigato* as easy, level, not rough. He likewise reads: “let him set his step in the discipline of this path”; and for *declinatus* he reads *delicatius*, but advises that *declinatius* should be read. After *sequuntur*, he adds: “Those converted after sin”: “Therefore, O servants of God, these and other things,” which he says are absent from the printed Rule; but in fact these very words occur at the end of the final chapter, as an epilogue. In nearly the same way, the preface and epilogue are joined by Peter of Cassino, chapter 73, where we read: “in the discipline of this threshold.” AREV.

2. Moreover, whoever among you claims to desire the entire discipline of the ancients, let him proceed as far as he wishes and walk along that difficult and narrow path with a smooth course. But whoever is unable to fulfill such extensive commands of his predecessors should set his steps within the limit of this discipline and resolve not to turn aside any further, lest, while seeking to turn downward, he lose both the life and the name of a monk. Therefore, just as those former precepts make a perfect and supreme monk, so these make one at least a monk. Let the perfect keep the former; let those converted after sin follow these.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Monastery

1. First of all, dearest brothers, let your monastery possess remarkable care in its enclosure, so that the fortifications of the cloisters may provide security for its custody. For our enemy, the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about with open mouth, seeking someone among us to devour (I Peter V, 8).

> **Note:** [Col. 0870C–D]
>
> **Chapter I, no. 2.** Justinian, *Constitutions*, Novel 133, chapter 1, at the end:
>
> “Let the monastery be enclosed by a precise wall, so that it have no exit elsewhere except through the small gates.” GRIAL.

2. The monastery’s fortification should have only one entrance from outside, and one rear gate through which one may go to the garden. The estate itself ought to be situated far from the monastery, lest, if placed too near, it bring either the danger of defilement or discredit upon its dignity. Cells for the brothers should be established beside the church, so that they may hurry as quickly as possible to the office.

> **Note:** [Col. 0870D]
>
> **3.** Breulius observes that *coenaculum* here means the refectory. Instead of *praebeatur*, Holstenius reads *praebeat*. AREV.

3. The place for the sick shall be remote from the basilica and from the brothers’ cells, so that they may not be hindered by any disturbance or shouting. The monks’ storeroom ought to be beside the refectory, so that, being situated nearby, the service of the tables may be provided without delay. The garden should be enclosed within the monastery, so that, while the monks work inside, they may not wander outside on any pretext.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Choosing an Abbot

[Col. 0870A]

> **Note:** [Col. 0870D]
>
> **Chapter II, no. 1.** This chapter is the penultimate one in the Gothic Ovetus manuscript. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** Menard, p. 150, says that the reading of the *Concordia of Rules* should be retained: “having passed beyond the age of adolescence, he shall have touched youth or old age,” since, according to Isidore himself, youth begins at twenty-eight, while according to others it begins at thirty-eight. Holstenius likewise reads this way. I would prefer: “having passed beyond the age of adolescence or youth, he shall have touched old age.” Compare the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 3, and the *Code*, law 46, *On Bishops and Clerics*. AREV.

1. In the meantime, an abbot should be chosen who has been hardened by the discipline of a holy life and tested by trials of patience and humility; who, enduring a laborious life through exercise and having passed beyond the age of adolescence, has touched old age in his youth. The elders should not disdain to obey him, obeying him both because of his age and because of the uprightness of his character.

2. He will present himself for imitation in every example of conduct; for no one may command anything that he himself has not done.
