He will encourage individuals by mutual exhortations, addressing all, exhorting them, or building them up in whatever he sees may benefit their lives according to each person’s station.

[Col. 0870B]

> **Note:** [Col. 0870D]
>
> **3.** Menard thinks *compati* may be read, following the Apostle’s mercy. AREV.

3. Toward everyone he will also preserve justice, burning with hatred toward no one, embracing all from the heart, despising no convert, and ready to have compassion in mercy upon the weakness of some, following the Apostle who says: “We became little ones in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her young” (I Thessalonians II, 7).

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Monks

1. Monks must take the greatest care to live by holding to the apostolic life. Just as they are known to have been established as one body, so they should have one heart, claiming nothing as their own and possessing no love, however small, for private property. Rather, following the apostolic example and having everything in common (Acts IV), they should advance by faithfully remaining in Christ’s commandments.

> **Note:** [Col. 0870D]
>
> **Chapter III, no. 2.** Menard, p. 215: “Showing the Father the honor due to him”; from this he concludes that one may read: “Showing the Father due honor.” AREV.

2. Showing the Father the honor due to him, they shall preserve obedience toward their elders, incentives to virtue toward their equals, and the instruction of good example toward their juniors. Let no one judge himself better than the others, but regard himself as inferior to all; let him shine in humility to the same degree that he surpasses the others in the height of virtues. Let the monk also refrain from anger and spare his tongue from slander. [Col. 0871A]

> **Note:** [Col. 0871D]
>
> **3.** “Nor should he walk indecently, etc.” These statements agree with the Rule of Saint Fructuosus of Braga, chapter 8. Menard notably explains *notabiliter* as “proudly and ostentatiously,” but it more likely indicates something unusual. *Philargyria* means avarice, the love of silver. AREV.

3. He should not walk indecently or conspicuously; he should shun the contagion of love of money (*philargyria*) as a deadly plague. He should turn his tongue away from shameful or idle words, and continually present a pure heart and lips. He should also cleanse shameful emotions from the focus of his thoughts; through compunction of heart, he should exercise himself in the arena of holy meditation.

> **Note:** [Col. 0871D]
>
> **4.** From these and other precepts of Isidore, I think, arose a certain little work that exists under Isidore’s name in some manuscripts. I discussed it in the Isidorian materials, chapter 85, no. 9. Its title is: “A certain treatise of Saint Isidore, in which, in brief, everything pertaining to the state of perfection of a certain faithful person is included.” But since this treatise adds nothing distinctive and has been copied in extremely corrupt form, it may be omitted without any loss. AREV.

4. He should flee the torpor of sleep and laziness, and apply himself without interruption to vigils and prayers. He should suppress the desire of the appetite and, through the virtues of abstinence, afflict himself by diligently subduing his lusts, mortifying the flesh by fasts as far as the body’s health permits. He should not waste away through envious resentment at his brothers’ progress, but, tranquil and peaceable through love of fraternal affection, rejoice in the merits of all, rejecting the disturbance of anger and patiently enduring everything. He should be affected by no sadness or temporal grief, but, relying on inward joy against every adversity, should finally cast far from him even the praise of empty glory and strive to please God alone inwardly, with a humble heart, so that, while he shines with these virtues, he may rightly retain the name of his profession.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On Converts

[Col. 0871C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0871D]
>
> **Chapter IV, no. 1.** Holstenius reads: “the conduct of each person in the service of hospitality … ought to be examined.” AREV.

1. Whoever renounces the world and comes to the monastery should not immediately be enrolled among the monks. Each person’s life ought to be examined for three months in the service of hospitality; when these have been completed, he may enter the assembly of the holy congregation. No one should be received inside unless, having first been placed outside, his humility and patience have been proven. Those who, leaving the world, turn to Christ’s service with pious and salutary humility should first either distribute all their possessions to the needy or contribute them to the monastery. For Christ’s servants then offer a free spirit to divine service when they cut away from themselves every bond of hope in the world.

> **Note:** [Col. 0872D]
>
> **2.** “Unless he himself has first, in writing, etc.” Another reading: “unless he has first promised in writing that he will remain there according to his profession.” On recruits who are promoted to secular military service, see Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter 3, nos. 36 and 53, and Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, book I, chapter 8, and book II, chapter 5. From this it is clear that soldiers, after completing their training, were marked by certain punctures in the skin, to which Isidore alludes, and must be marked. AREV.

2. Those who are converted without firm purpose quickly fall under either the disease of pride or the vice of lust. Those who renounce the world must therefore by no means begin with lukewarmness, lest through that very lukewarmness they fall again into love of the age. No convert is to be received into the monastery unless he has first promised in writing that he will remain. For just as those who are promoted to secular military service do not enter the legion unless they have first been enrolled on tablets, so those who are to be marked for the heavenly militia in the spiritual camps cannot pass into the number and fellowship of Christ’s servants unless they are first bound by a profession made by word or in writing.

> **Note:** [Col. 0872D]
>
> **3.** “Whether slave or free,” etc. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Celantia, says among other things to this effect: “The only freedom before God is not to serve sins; the highest nobility before God is to be distinguished by virtues.” AREV.

3. Whoever enters the monastery first shall be first in every rank or order. It should not be asked whether he is rich or poor, slave or free, young or old, rustic or educated. Among monks, neither age nor condition is considered, because before God there is no difference between the soul of a slave and that of a free person. Yet whoever is bound by the yoke of another’s servitude must not be received unless the Lord has broken his bonds. For it is written: “Who has let the wild ass go free? And who has loosed his bonds?” (Job XXXIX, 5). The wild ass released into freedom is the monk who, without domination or impediment from the world, serves and keeps apart from the crowds. Each person then serves God in free servitude when he is not weighed down by any burden of carnal condition. For once Christ’s yoke is sweet and his burden light, it is hard and heavy to bear the service of the world.

4. Those who, possessing something in the world, are converted should not become proud if they have contributed anything from their resources to the monastery; rather, they should fear lest they be lifted up here through pride and perish. It would have been better for them to enjoy their riches in the world with humility than, having now become poor, to be exalted by proud arrogance over their distribution. Those who are converted to the monastery from poverty must not be despised by those who have abandoned the riches of the world, because before God all who turn to Christ are held to belong to one order. It makes no difference whether someone comes to God’s service from a poor or servile condition or from a noble and wealthy life. Many who have risen from plebeian status through outstanding examples of virtue have become superior to nobles and surpassed them in excellence of virtue; those who were lowest in condition have, through the merit of virtue, become first among the wise.

> **Note:** [Col. 0872D]
>
> **5.** “For this reason.” He used the same testimony in *On Duties*, book II, chapter 16. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** This may be connected with what Constantine Cajetan transcribed from Smaragdus, p. 71:
>
> “Hence Isidore says: Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, recites the psalm first, first extends his hand to the table, and receives Communion first in the church; age is not considered among them, but profession. When he says that the boys Samuel and Daniel judged priests, this is understood of Eli and of those who sought to condemn Susanna. Samuel judged the priests when he saw Eli’s sons sinning and judged them in his heart to be transgressors. He likewise reproved and judged Eli because he did not restrain them with strict correction or prevent them from wickedness. Daniel also judged the priests when he reproved and condemned those filled with wicked thoughts who sought falsely to condemn Susanna by their testimony, and foretold that they would be struck down by an angelic sword.” AREV.

5. For this reason God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the base things of the world, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh might glory before him (I Corinthians I, 27). Those who come to the monastery from poverty should not be lifted up in pride because they see themselves there regarded as equals to those who appeared to possess something in the world. For it is not fitting that, where the rich descend to humility after laying aside their worldly prominence, the poor should become proud through mental elation. They ought to lay aside arrogance, think humbly, and always remember their own poverty and want.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Work of Monks

> **Note:** [Col. 0873D]
>
> **Chapter V, no. 1.** *They slip away.* Another reading: *they are torn out*. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** This chapter may be illuminated from volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 52, with Cotelerius’s notes. AREV.

1. A monk should always work with his hands, applying his diligence to every kind of craft and labor, following the Apostle who says: “We did not eat bread free of charge, but worked in labor and weariness night and day”; and again: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (II Thessalonians III, 8–10). Through idleness, lusts and the nourishment of harmful thoughts grow together; through the exercise of labor, vices likewise slip away.

> **Note:** [Col. 0873D]
>
> **2.** “For the patriarchs … to refresh.” Menard notes, p. 820, that this entire period is cited by Haymo of Halberstadt, book II *On Variety*, chapter 2. The pagan philosophers who are listed as tailors and shoemakers include Hippias the Sophist, Simon of Athens, and Menedemus of Eretria. It is the more common opinion that Saint Joseph, the husband of the Virgin Mary, was a carpenter, and Saint Leander, Isidore’s brother, supports this in chapter 14 of *On the Institution of Virgins*. “I do not know,” Breulius says, “where Isidore read that Joseph was an ironsmith, for he is depicted with an adze.” Yet Saint Ambrose and Theophilus of Antioch also mention the bellows and fire in Saint Joseph’s workshop. Some think Saint Joseph was a goldsmith, others a stoneworker. See Calmet, in the *Dictionary*, and especially the learned Mazochi’s supplement on the craft of Saint Joseph and Christ the Lord, appended to the letter *On Dedication under the Adze*. AREV.

2. A monk should by no means disdain to engage in any work necessary for the monastery’s needs. For the patriarchs tended flocks; pagan philosophers were shoemakers and tailors; and the righteous Joseph, to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed, was an ironsmith. Indeed, Peter, chief of the Apostles, practiced the occupation of a fisherman, and all the Apostles performed bodily work by which they sustained the body.

3. If men of such authority devoted themselves to labors and even rustic occupations, how much more should monks, who ought not only to provide with their own hands what is necessary for their own life but also to refresh the need of others through their labors! Those who possess bodily strength and sound health, if they are idle in work, are known to sin doubly, because they not only fail to work but also corrupt others and invite them to imitate themselves. For this reason each person is converted: to serve God and take care for labor, not to be nourished by idleness, inactivity, and laziness.

> **Note:** [Col. 0874C–D]
>
> **4.** “They are to be treated.” In the *Concordia of Rules* and in Holstenius, the following is added:
>
> “Nor should those who have strength for labor murmur against them; rather, concern should be shown for those whom they know to be weak in body. Those who cannot work should acknowledge that those who labor are better and more fortunate than themselves. But whoever is sickly and cannot endure bodily labor should be cared for, and his weakness should be moderated. Those who are healthy, etc.”
>
> Whether this truly belongs to Isidore, or was added to it by someone else, I do not dare determine. AREV.

4. If they wish to devote themselves to reading so that they may not work, they are themselves rebellious toward the reading, because they do not do what they read there. For it is written there: “Let them eat their own bread while working”; and again: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not restless among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without payment, but worked in labor and weariness day and night, so that we might not burden any of you” (II Thessalonians III, 7–8). Those who cannot work because of bodily weakness should be treated more humanely and mercifully. But those who are healthy and deceive others are without doubt to be mourned and lamented, because they are sick not in body but, what is worse, in mind. Although they cannot be convicted by human eyes, they cannot escape God’s notice. Such people should therefore either be tolerated if their illness is hidden, or disciplined if their health is evident.

> **Note:** [Col. 0874D]
>
> **5.** “So that, as a song.” *On Duties*, book II, chapter 16. “While working with their hands, they sing psalms and console the labor itself as though with a divine signal.” GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** Saint Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 17: “Those who work with their hands can easily sing divine songs and console the labor itself with a divine signal.” Saint Augustine adds other material that Isidore also took up, and from Isidore Haymo, in the cited book, chapter 50. AREV.

5. While working, monks should meditate or sing psalms, so that they may console the labor itself with the delight of song and the word of God. For if secular workers do not cease to sing shameful love songs amid their labors, and so entangle their mouths in songs and stories that they do not withdraw their hands from the work, how much more should Christ’s servants work with their hands in such a way that they always have the praise of God in their mouths and devote their tongues to his psalms and hymns! One must labor bodily while keeping the mind fixed upon God; the hands should be occupied in work in such a way that the mind is not turned away from God.

6. A monk should work at appointed times and devote himself at appointed times to prayer and reading. For a monk should have suitable hours assigned to each duty. The portions of the year are likewise assigned in this manner to their respective tasks. In summer, he ought to work from morning until the third hour; from the third until the sixth he should devote himself to reading; thereafter until the ninth he should rest; and after the ninth until evening he should work again. At other times, that is, in autumn and winter or in spring, he should read from morning until the third hour; after the celebration of the third hour until the ninth he should work; after the meal of the ninth hour he ought either to work, read, or meditate aloud upon something.

> **Note:** [Col. 0875B–C]
>
> **7.** “Whatever they work at, etc.” Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 16, from Saint Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book II. In the edition a note marked with the letter *b* is attached to *they slip away*, from the Gothic manuscript; another reading is *they are torn out*. But it has been misplaced and belongs to no. 1 of this chapter. Before this chapter 5, Holstenius prefixes other material from chapter 19. Instead of *he will not spare*, perhaps the reading is *he will not be spared*. AREV.

7. Whatever the monks work at with their hands, they shall hand over to the superior, and the superior to the head of the monks. No work should remain with a brother, lest care for it turn his mind away from the pursuit of contemplation. The brothers should cultivate the vegetables of the garden or prepare food with their own hands; the construction of buildings and cultivation of the fields shall belong to the work of servants. No monk should be bound by love of private work. Rather, all working in common should obey the fathers without murmuring, lest they perish through murmuring, as those who murmured in the desert perished. If those who were still little and inexperienced under the Law were by no means excused, how much less will he spare those who have received the law of perfection if they have acted in such ways. [Col. 0875C]

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Office

[Col. 0875C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0875C]
>
> **Chapter VI, no. 1.** “Hasten with eagerness.” Likewise, book II of *On Duties*, chapter 16: “All frequently come together by night and by day, hastening eagerly to prayer.” GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** “After the completion.” See Cassian, book II, chapter 7. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** “In the offices that are sung”; another reading: “in the office of singing.” AREV.

1. In the offices to be sung, the following order shall be observed: when the signal has been given at the proper times for the canonical hours, all shall hasten eagerly to the choir, and no one may leave before the office has been completed, except one whom the necessity of nature has compelled. While the monks are reciting, after the completion of each psalm all shall prostrate themselves together on the ground in adoration; then, rising quickly, they shall begin the following psalms, and shall do the same in each of the offices.

> **Note:** [Col. 0875D]
>
> **2.** “Two, then praises, that is, Alleluia,” as is clear from book I of *On Duties*, chapter 13. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** “First, the lighting office.” See the notes on Cassian. GRIAL.
>
> **On the same passage:** Others read: “two readings from both Testaments, then praise, a hymn, etc.” In the dissertation on hymns prefixed to the *Hispanic Hymnody*, p. 81, I showed against Martène that mention of hymns occurs in the Rule of Saint Isidore and others. Menard, p. 332, notes that Isidore distinguishes the lighting office from the evening office. At length, on p. 366, in his exposition of the Rule of the Master, he attempts to prove that the nocturnal assembly by lamplight was the same as the evening office, and he explains Saint Isidore’s passage as referring to the prayer said while the lamps were being lit. This is evident from the Mozarabic breviary itself, for first a prayer is made for the light that has been lit and offered, and then the order of Vespers follows. Among others, however, the lighting office and the evening office are commonly used interchangeably. In Grial’s note, the annotations on Cassian seem to refer to the annotations of Peter Chacón. AREV.

2. When the spiritual sacraments of the psalms are celebrated, let the monk flee laughter and stories; but let him meditate in his heart upon what is sung with his mouth. At Terce, Sext, or None, three psalms are to be recited, one responsory, two readings from the Old and New Testaments, then praises, a hymn, and a prayer. At the evening offices, however, first the lucernarium, then two psalms, one responsory, praises, a hymn, and a prayer are to be said.

[Col. 0876B] 3. After the evening office, when the brothers have assembled, they ought either to meditate on something or to discuss questions arising from divine reading, conferring piously and profitably. They should remain at meditation and discussion only until the time of Compline can arrive. Before sleep, after Compline has been completed as usual and the brothers have bid one another farewell, they must rest with all caution and silence until they rise for the vigils.

[Note: [Col. 0876C]

4. Then three Masses. See the annotation on Cassian. GRIAL.]

[Col. 0876D] In the same place. “Masses of psalms.” Menardus understands these to be collects, that is, prayers said at the end of the psalms, especially on the basis of Cassian, *On Nocturnal Prayer*, Book II, chapters 7 and 10. He observes, however, that the practice of saying such collects differed among various nations. Saint Fructuosus of Braga agrees with Isidore in chapter 2 of his Rule. I discussed these prayers, which were attached to the psalms, in *Isidoriana*, chapter 87, no. 20 and following. The prayers that were added not only to psalms but also to canticles are to be understood in what is said in the Roman Breviary about Saint Patrick for March 17: “For they say that he was accustomed daily to recite the entire Psalter together with the canticles and hymns and two hundred prayers.” In Grial’s edition the text is corruptly read: “In the vigils to be recited, he shall be present until the psalming at matins,” which I corrected from Holstenius’s *Concordia regularum*. AREV.]

4. In the daily offices of the vigils, three canonical psalms are first to be recited, then three Masses of psalms, a fourth of canticles, and a fifth of the morning offices. On Sundays and on the festivals of martyrs, for the sake of solemnity, individual Masses are to be added. In the vigils, however, there shall be the practice of recitation; at matins, the custom of singing and chanting, so that in both ways the minds of God’s servants may be exercised by the pleasure of variety and be stirred more abundantly to God’s praise without weariness.

[Note: [Col. 0876D]

5. “They must rest.” Another reading: “they must be refreshed”; the meaning is the same, and this may perhaps be the genuine reading, taken from Cassian, *On Daily Prayer*, Book III, chapters 4 and 8. The following material is taken from Book II, *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 2. AREV.]

5. After the vigils they must rest until matins, or else read something through. After matins they must either do some work or read. Readings from the New or Old Testament are to be recited during the office on weekdays; but on Saturday and Sunday they are to be proclaimed from the New Testament alone. A monk in sound bodily health who is absent from the vigils or the daily offices shall lose communion, if his health is demonstrably sound.

535 **CHAPTER VII. On the Collation**

[Note: [Col. 0877C]

CHAPTER VII, Note 1. “To hear the Father at the collation.” The same wording occurs in Book II *On the Offices*, chapter 16. GRIAL.]

1. Three times a week, after the celebration of Terce and at the giving of the signal, the brothers shall assemble for the collation in order to hear the Father. Let them hear the elder teaching and instructing everyone with salutary precepts; let them hear the Father with the greatest devotion, demonstrating the attentiveness of their minds by sighs and groans. The collation itself shall concern either the correction of vices and the instruction of conduct, or other matters pertaining to the welfare of the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0877D]

2. Grialius reads: “what follows.” AREV.]

2. But if such matters are lacking, the collation is nevertheless by no means to be omitted, for the sake of the customary discipline. On the appointed days, with all assembled together, the regular precepts of the Fathers are to be reviewed, so that those who have not yet learned may receive what they are to follow; while those who have learned may, reminded by frequent recollection, carefully preserve what they know. All shall sit silently at the collation, unless perhaps the authority of the Father orders someone to speak.

**CHAPTER VIII. On Books**

[Note: [Col. 0877D]

CHAPTER VIII, Note 1. “Let them be requested.” The Gothic version has “let them be asked for.” GRIAL.

In the same place. The discussion returns below, chapter 20, section 1, to the custodian of the sacristy. AREV.]

1. Let the custodian of the sacristy have all the books assigned to him. Each brother shall receive his books from him, and, after reading or consulting them carefully, shall always return them after Vespers. The books are to be requested each day at the first hour; but whoever asks later is by no means to receive one.

2. Concerning those questions that are read but perhaps not understood, each brother shall ask the abbot either at the collation or after Vespers, and, after the passage has been read aloud in its place, shall receive an explanation from him, so that while it is being explained to one person, the others may listen.

536 [Note: [Col. 0877D]

3. This precept, by which a monk is forbidden to read books of pagans and volumes of heretics, agrees with what Isidore handed down in *Sentences*, Book III, chapters 12 and 13. AREV.]

3. Let the monk beware of reading the books of pagans or the volumes of heretics. For it is better to remain ignorant of their pernicious doctrines than, through experience, to fall into some snare of error.

**CHAPTER IX. On Meals**

[Note: [Col. 0877D]

CHAPTER IX, Note 1. “Nor let an outsider’s eye.” From the Gothic version. Another reading: “nor let any outsider.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “Let him do penance,” etc. According to the institutions of Saint Pachomius, article 12, as Menardus notes, p. 779. AREV.]

1. At the time when the obligation of refreshment is fulfilled, let the monastery’s gates be closed, and let no outsider presume to be present, lest his presence disturb the brothers’ quiet. At mealtime, when the signal is given, let everyone come together. Whoever comes late to the table shall either do penance or return fasting to his work or bed. No one shall go to eat before the customary signal has sounded to summon everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0877D]

2. “Let speech refresh.” The word “speech” is absent from the Gothic version. GRIAL.

In the Rule of the Master, chapter 29, it is similarly prescribed [Col. 0878C] that the reader ask for a blessing before beginning to read. In the *Concordia regularum*, p. 69, one reads: “so that just as bodily food provides refreshment for the body.” AREV.]

2. There shall likewise be one refectory; ten fellow diners shall sit at each table, while the remaining crowd of boys shall stand nearby. During the meal of the brothers, all shall maintain disciplined silence, obeying the Apostle, who says: “Let them eat their own bread while working in silence” (II Thessalonians 3). One person, however, sitting in the middle, after receiving a blessing, shall read something from the Scriptures; the others shall remain silent while eating, listening most attentively to the reading, so that just as bodily food provides refreshment for their flesh, so spiritual speech may refresh their minds.

[Note: [Col. 0878D]

3. Two notes by Menardus on this passage should not be omitted: “The abbot, except in the necessity of illness. An excellent institution indeed, because regular discipline is preserved and the excessive feasts of abbots, under the pretext of hospitality—and consequently the squandering of the monastery’s resources—are prevented. —Nor more elegantly. An institution no less excellent, which remedies the abbots’ dainty eating.” Menardus treats the same question of the abbot’s table more fully on p. 923. Instead of “the dishes of all the courses,” the *Concordia regularum* and Holstenius have “the dishes of all the tables,” which seems preferable. AREV.]

3. Let no shouting arise at the tables; let concern for whatever the diners need remain solely with the superior. Except in the necessity of illness, the abbot shall take his food in the brothers’ sight together with them. He shall neither have anything different from the others prepared for himself, nor seek anything more delicately prepared than what is provided in common. Thus, while he is present, everything is administered more carefully; and, since the food is common, it is consumed healthfully and charitably. The portions of all the dishes shall indeed be equal, and all the brothers are to be refreshed with similar foods.

[Note: [Col. 0878D]

4. “Pale vegetables.” Book II, *On the Offices*, chapter 12. The ancients abstained from food on the day before they were to sing, taking only pale vegetables for the sake of the voice; hence singers were commonly called “bean-eaters.” GRIAL.

[Col. 0879C] In the same place. “Let them introduce.” Another reading from the Gothic version: “occasionally.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “Pleasure.” Grialius reads “will.” Instead of “let them use,” another reading has “let them have.” In the words “the lightest meats,” Menardus understands quantity rather than quality, which he thinks clear from what follows. To me it does not seem so clear; I rather judge that the quality of meats is prescribed here, while the following words prohibit satiety, whether from vegetables, legumes, or meats. AREV.]

4. Whatever the present meal provides, let everyone receive without murmuring. Let them not desire what the pleasure of eating seeks, but what nature’s necessity requires; for it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13). Throughout the whole week the brothers shall use humble vegetable foods and pale legumes. On holy days they shall introduce the foods of the lightest meats together with several dishes. The body must not be refreshed to satiety, lest the soul perish; for from the fullness of the belly the lust of the flesh is quickly aroused.

[Note: [Col. 0879C]

5. “And strength for service.” Another reading: “and power for service,” with the same meaning. AREV.]

5. Whoever restrains the appetite for gluttony undoubtedly curbs the movements of wantonness. The body must be refreshed with such moderation that neither excessive abstinence weakens it nor superfluous gluttony moves it to wantonness. Temperance must therefore be applied in both respects: so that the vices of the flesh do not prevail and strength for the service of good works remains sufficient. Whoever, sitting at table, wishes to abstain from meat or wine is not to be forbidden; abstinence is not prohibited but rather commended, provided that no one, out of contempt, rejects God’s creature granted for human use.

[Col. 0879B] [Note: [Col. 0879D]

6. “Let no one be defiled by secret contamination.” Cassian, Book IV, chapter 16, counts an extraordinary or secret meal among the offenses of monks. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Eating”: Grialius reads “for eating.” AREV.]

6. Let no eating defile anyone through secret contamination, nor let an impudent or private appetite arise outside the common table. For he shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication who secretly or outside the ordinary table tastes anything. Before mealtime no one may dare to eat except the sick person. Whoever anticipates the time for eating shall be subject to the subsequent penalties of abstinence. A thirsty person or one suffering some deficiency is to be provided for before mealtime by order of the abbot or superior, but not openly, lest this perhaps compel others to thirst or hunger.

[Note: [Col. 0879D]

7. Menardus, p. 642, says that Saint Pachomius establishes the opposite in article 21 of his Rule: “Those who cook the dishes shall themselves eat nothing, but shall serve those who are eating.” But, as I understand it, Saint Isidore merely orders the weekly server to taste the food in order to judge whether it is properly seasoned; Saint Pachomius orders that the cook not eat before serving the others. These two provisions are not contradictory. Grialius has “the superior is different”; Holstenius, “the superior is appointed differently.” AREV.]

7. The weekly server alone may taste the food; no one else may dare to do so, lest under the pretext of tasting he satisfy his appetite or throat. Lay servants shall in no way take part at the monks’ tables, nor can there be a place at the common table for those whose purpose is different. When the monks rise from the table, let them all come together for prayer. Whatever remains from the table shall be carefully preserved and distributed to those in need.

[Note: [Col. 0879D]

8. In the *Concordia regularum*: “he invites … suspends,” with only “he sets out dinner.” The beginning of autumn is the autumnal equinox, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. “Alternate-day midday meals” means meals on Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. During this period they fasted on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, as below, chapter 11. AREV.]

8. At the monks’ meal, from the days of Pentecost [Col. 0880A] until the beginning of autumn, let the entire summer invite alternate-day midday meals; during the rest of the year let it suspend those meals, and let dinner alone be served.

[Note: [Col. 0880C]

9. “In both periods,” namely winter and summer, which include autumn and spring, as Menardus explains, p. 712. In the *Concordia regularum*: “the third shall be fruit … after the fast has been completed, with bread alone or water,” etc. That one should drink three cups is also prescribed by Ausonius in the riddle “Drink three times.” Suetonius reports that Augustus was accustomed to drink three times in the camp at Mutina, chapter 77. In Peter of Cassino, after “fruit,” other material is added from Isidore, apparently: “On feast days, however, the bodies are to be refreshed with three or four dishes, but in such a way that, the more numerous the foods are, the smaller they are in quantity, so that the bodies may be refreshed with necessary food and not ruined by excessive satiety. When food is served at table, no one shall eat before the signal for blessing has sounded; and when they hear the signal, they shall ask for the blessing with one voice, and, once it has been given, they shall eat. We decree this especially: no one may presume either to take from another or to give to another beyond his measure, except the abbot or the superior, to whom the abbot has entrusted this responsibility.” AREV.]

9. In both periods, the meal at table shall consist of three dishes, namely vegetables and legumes, and, if there is a third, fruit. The brothers’ thirst is likewise to be refreshed with three cups. During the observance of Lent, as is customary after the fast has been completed, everyone shall be content with bread alone and water; they shall also abstain from wine and oil.

539 **CHAPTER X. On Days of Reprieve**

1. These are the days of reprieve for monks, on which fasts cease, especially the venerable Sunday, dedicated to the name of Christ. Just as it is solemn because of the mystery of his resurrection, so among all his servants it shall preserve the festivity of a banquet with vowed joy. Likewise, from the first day of Easter until Pentecost—that is, for fifty successive days—the fast has been dissolved by the holy Fathers, on account of Christ’s resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that these days may be celebrated with fasts relaxed, not as a figure of labor, which the period of Lent signifies, but in rest and gladness.

[Note: [Col. 0880D]

CHAPTER X, Note 2. “When each of the brothers has assembled.” Gothic version. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Is converted”: Grialius reads “are converted.” The words of Cassian cited in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, no. 66, in the note, are relevant here. After “the fasts are interrupted,” the *Concordia regularum* adds: “provided that they are not general fasts.” AREV.]

2. The Fathers also decided to make the period from the day of the Lord’s Nativity until the day of the Circumcision solemn, and to grant permission to eat. Likewise, the days of the Epiphany obtained indulgence for refreshment according to the ancient rule, since whenever any brother is converted, or brothers from other monasteries arrive to visit, the fasts are interrupted for the fulfillment of charity.

[Note: [Col. 0880D]

3. “But if any of the monks,” etc. The same passage occurs in Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 43, no. 2. See the note. Other rules of the Fathers also exempted Sunday from the daily fast, in accordance with canon 18 of the Council of Gangra. Compare Cassian, *On Daily Prayer*, Book III, chapter 12. As for the mention of the Circumcision both in this chapter and the preceding one—although this feast does not seem yet to have been instituted in Isidore’s time—there is nothing astonishing in it. For, as I explained more fully in *Isidoriana*, chapter 71, nos. 16 and 17, either such a feast may already have been instituted toward the end of Isidore’s life, or certainly the monks for whom the Rule was being read for observance would, after the institution of the feast of the Circumcision, have added it after the day of the Circumcision instead of the Kalends of January. AREV.]

3. Apart from these periods, let them freely and willingly devote themselves to the observance of fasts. But if any of the monks decide to fast during the times mentioned above, they are by no means to be forbidden. For many of the ancient Fathers are read to have abstained in the desert on those days and never to have broken their fasts, except on Sundays alone, because of Christ’s resurrection.

**CHAPTER XI. On Fasting**

[Note: [Col. 0881D]

CHAPTER XI, Note 1. “Let them abstain.” In Peter of Cassino: “let them abstain”; he also adds: “What they refresh themselves with in the evening, they imitate the example of the Lord himself,” and other material that does not seem to belong to Isidore and certainly does not belong here. AREV.]

1. The ancients chose these days especially for fasting. The first is the daily fast of Lent, during which the monks maintain a stricter observance of abstinence, since they abstain not only from midday meals but also from wine and oil. The second is the alternate-day fast, begun on the day after Pentecost and extending until the autumnal equinox; that is, the fast is observed for three days in each week because of the summer heat of the sun.

[Col. 0881B] 2. The third follows: a daily fast from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the Lord’s Nativity, during which the daily fasts are by no means relaxed. The fourth likewise begins after the day of the Circumcision and continues until the solemnities of Easter.

3. Those who are worn down by old age or constrained by the weakness of tender youth are not to be exercised by daily fasts, lest either old age fail before it dies, or growing youth fall before it advances, and perish before learning to do good.

**CHAPTER XII. On the Monks’ Habit**

[Note: [Col. 0881D]

CHAPTER XII, Note 1. Peter of Cassino, chapter 55, inserts here certain material: “‘He drags along.’ Hence the Lord also says of John: ‘What did you go out into the wilderness to see—a reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see—a man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.’ And Peter”—rather, Paul, I Timothy 2—“‘not in costly clothing.’ Cheap clothing,” etc. AREV.]

1. A monk must put aside conspicuous elegance in clothing and dress. The monk ought to be well equipped, not delicate. But just as a monk’s habit ought not to be conspicuous, so neither ought it to be excessively neglected; for expensive clothing draws the mind toward wantonness, while clothing that is too cheap either produces sorrow of heart or gives rise to the disease of vainglory. Garments are not to be distributed equally to all, but with discretion, according to what each person’s age and rank require. For we read that the apostles did this, as it is written: “All things were common to them, and distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts 4).

[Note: [Col. 0881D]

2. “Birri, planetae.” See the annotation on Cassian. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Foot-cloths and leggings.” Saint Benedict, in his Rule, chapter 55, mentions foot-cloths and leggings as clothing for the feet. Smaragdus. Foot-cloths are now what we call shoes; leggings are not undersocks or socks. GRIAL.

[Col. 0882C] In the same place. Menardus, p. 904, explains “supplement” as abundance. The same Menardus distinguishes two meanings of *orarium*. First, an *orarium* is a linen cloth, or an elongated textile, for catching mucus or wiping away sweat. Second, it is that costly, elongated silk textile used by bishops, priests, and deacons, now called a stole. He thinks Isidore uses *orarium* in this second sense. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verse 86. On *birrus*, *planeta*, and *melote*, see Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24. On leggings, Book XIX, chapter 34. Menardus and Holstenius also discuss these matters extensively; they are now commonly found in dictionaries and glossaries of the Middle Ages. AREV.]

2. Let each brother’s provision or need be examined, so that those who have may be content and those who do not have may receive; for what is given to one who has will not be available for distribution to those in need. Moreover, a monk ought not to be clothed in linen; it is not lawful to use an *orarium*, *birri*, or *planetae*, nor garments or footwear of the kind that the other monasteries generally misuse. Christ’s servants shall be content with three tunics, two cloaks, and one cowl. In addition, they shall have a sheepskin garment, a small towel, sleeves, foot-cloths, and leggings. They shall be content with these alone and presume to have nothing else.

[Note: [Col. 0882D]

3. In the *Concordia regularum*: “They shall use foot-cloths in the monastery.” AREV.]

3. Foot-cloths are to be used in the monastery as long as the severity of winter requires, or while the brothers are traveling on foot or departing for the city. In the monastery the monks shall always cover themselves with cloaks, so that they may walk decently covered and move about ready for the service of their work. If someone happens not to have a cloak, let him place the small towel over his shoulders. No monk should cultivate his appearance in a way that incurs the charge of wantonness and shamelessness; for the mind of the person whose bodily adornment or immodest walk is conspicuous is not chaste.

[Note: [Col. 0882D]

4. “To shear.” Perhaps read “to be shorn,” or understand “to shear the hair or head.” Formerly monks had their entire heads shaved, as Menardus proves. Clerics were tonsured in the form of a crown, while the Greeks were tonsured in the form of a cross; Greek bishops shaved only the middle of the head. The ancient clerical tonsure consisted in shaving the entire head, leaving around the lower circumference a small row of hair, as is clear from Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 57, and Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 4, no. 4. In Grial’s edition, at the end of the chapter, the reading was “a different superior”; I changed this, on the basis of the *Concordia regularum* and Holstenius’s edition, to “a different purpose.” AREV.]

4. No monk ought to grow his hair long. For whoever imitates this, even if he does not do so himself in order to deceive people by an appearance of pretense, nevertheless scandalizes others, placing a stumbling block before the weak and carrying a holy purpose even to blasphemy. He must therefore shear himself when everyone else does—or rather, all together and at the same time. For it is reprehensible to have a different appearance where there is no different purpose.

**CHAPTER XIII. On Bedding**

[Note: [Col. 0883C]

CHAPTER XIII, Note 1. “Also a *galnapis*.” Smaragdus, commenting on chapter 55 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, says: “*Lena* is a kind of garment, which we call a *tonxa*; others call it a *galnapis*.” The word *galnapis* is also read without explanation in Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 26. GRIAL.

In the same place. “When night has joined,” etc. From the Gothic version: “But a lamp shall illuminate the place of those sleeping at night.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “*Storea*”; another reading, *storia*. See Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11. Two woolly skins are also prescribed by Saint Fructuosus of Braga in his Rule. Instead of *galnapis*, some read *galnabis*. Menardus argues, on the basis of the Vindocin manuscript, that *galbanis* should be read. In Martial, Book III, epigram 4, *galbanatus in lecto*—“galbanum-colored on the bed.” In Juvenal, satire 2, *galbana rasa*—“shorn galbana.” AREV.]

1. The abbot ought to live together with the brothers in the community, so that common life may provide both the testimony of a good life and reverence for discipline. It is also fitting, if possible, that all the brothers live in one room. If this is difficult, then certainly at least ten should live together, with one appointed over them as dean, acting as their ruler and guardian. A monk may not possess elegant or varied furnishings. His bed shall consist of a mat, a coverlet, two woolly skins, a *galnapis*, a hand-towel, and a double pillow for the head.

543 [Note: [Col. 0883D]

2. Two men may not lie in one bed. The same matter is indicated shortly afterward concerning individual repose and is again emphasized in chapter 17, no. 3. This same admonition is found among other Fathers: the Master in his Rule, Fructuosus of Braga, Pachomius, the Council of Tours, chapter 15, Saint Benedict, and others. AREV.]

2. Each month the abbot or superior shall inspect everyone’s beds, lest the brothers lack anything or possess anything superfluous. At night, when they go to sleep or after they have lain down, no one shall speak to another. Two men may not lie in one bed. In the darkness of night no one shall speak to a brother whom he meets. When night has fallen, a lamp shall illuminate the place of those sleeping, so that, when the darkness has been dispelled, the evidence of individual repose may be visible.

[Note: [Col. 0883D]

3. One might think that *stratus monachus* should be read, but *monachi* is found in the *Concordia regularum*, p. 463, in Peter of Cassino, and in Holstenius. Instead of *accubans*, some have *accumbens*. The same sentiment occurs in Fructuosus of Braga and Pachomius, as well as in Saint Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book III. Shortly afterward the *Concordia regularum* has: “The flow of the mind thinking shameful things would not be followed in him by a flow of filthy and impure thought.” AREV.]

3. The monk lying in bed shall not be occupied with any shameful thought, but only with contemplation of God. As he lies down, let him have bodily rest and tranquillity of heart, driving evil thoughts away from himself, embracing good ones, and rejecting shameful ones. For the movement of the mind is stirred by its own images, and whatever the thought of the waking person has been, such an image presents itself during sleep. Whoever is polluted by a nocturnal illusion should not delay making it known to the Father of the monastery, and should attribute this to the deserving of his fault, performing penance in secret. He should know that, unless the dissipation of a mind thinking shameful things had preceded in him, filthy and impure pollutions would not have followed; for the person whom illicit thought anticipates is quickly defiled by unclean temptation.

[Note: [Col. 0884D]

4. “Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal,” etc. Menardus says that these provisions are rather severe, although they were formerly practiced by certain saints; other Fathers taught that each person ought in such matters to consult his own conscience. See Saint Thomas, Part III, question 18, article 17, and Saint Gregory the Great in the letter cited by Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book I, chapter 27, where he adds: “But he must be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the sins of his thought with tears.” Instead of *in sacrarium*, as it stood in Grial, I restored *in sacrario* from the *Concordia regularum* and Holstenius. AREV.]

4. Whoever has been deceived by a nocturnal apparition shall stand in the sacristy during the office and shall not dare to enter the church that same day before he has been washed with both water and tears. For in the Law, whoever was polluted by a nocturnal emission was ordered to go outside the camp and not return before washing at evening (Deuteronomy 23). If they acted thus in the carnal people, what ought the spiritual servant of Christ to do? He ought to regard his contamination all the more carefully, fearfully remaining far from the altar in mind and body, and applying tears in the figure of water of repentance, so that he may strive to be cleansed not only with water but also with weeping—whatever unclean contamination may perhaps have polluted him through a hidden fault.

5. Whoever burns with temptations to fornication should pray without ceasing and abstain; he should not be ashamed to confess the heat of lust by which he is consumed, because a revealed vice is quickly cured, whereas the longer a hidden vice remains concealed, the more deeply it spreads. Indeed, whoever neglects to disclose it scarcely desires to be cured.

**CHAPTER XIV. On Those Who Offend**

1. If someone stumbles and goes astray in some light offense, he is to be admonished once and again. If, after the second admonition, he is by no means corrected, he is to be restrained by an appropriate punishment. No one, however, shall conceal a sinner; for after the second admonition, to hide someone who is sinning is complicity in the crime.

**CHAPTER XV. On the One Who Sins Frequently**

1. If someone sees a person sinning frequently, he shall first point this out to one or two brothers, by whose testimony the offender may be convicted. If the one who has offended denies it, a sin committed openly is to be rebuked openly, so that while the manifest sinner is corrected, those who have imitated him in evil may also be corrected. Just as many often perish through the offense of one, so many are generally saved through the correction of one.

545 **CHAPTER XVI. On Granting Pardon for a Fault, or Correcting the One at Fault**

[Note: [Col. 0884D]

CHAPTER XVI, Note 1. “But whoever.” This is more correct than the reading of others, *qui verbo*, as Menardus notes, p. 481. He also explains *inclinatus* as “prostrated on his knees” and defines the collation as an assembly of monks in which the abbot exhorts the monks, faults are corrected, and so forth, on the basis of chapter 7 of Isidore’s Rule and Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 16, no. 14. Instead of *cognoscitur*, Grialius reads *ignoscitur*. AREV.]

1. Whoever has sinned against a brother, if he immediately remembers and bows down to ask pardon, shall receive forgiveness from the one whom he is known to have injured. Whoever does not ask, or does not ask sincerely, shall be brought to the collation and, according to the extent of the injury, shall undergo appropriate discipline. Those who exchange insults with one another, if they quickly forgive one another again by mutual concession, are not to be judged by another, because they hastened to grant one another pardon—provided that they do not presume to exceed against one another more frequently.

[Note: [Col. 0885C]

2. Instead of “for condemnation,” Smaragdus has “for correction.” In some editions *quisque* is printed incorrectly instead of *quousque*. Menardus observes that what Isidore teaches—that someone who can be corrected through prolonged repentance is not to be expelled from the monastery—differs from other Fathers. Yet Isidore too leaves room for those called and shown to be incorrigible to be expelled from the monastery. AREV.]

2. Whoever voluntarily confesses the fault he has committed ought to obtain the pardon he seeks. Let us therefore pray for him, and, if the fault is light, let the forgiveness he has requested be granted to him immediately. Whoever, after being frequently excommunicated for a serious vice, has neglected to be corrected shall remain subject to condemnation until he lays aside his ingrained vices, so that one whom a punishment inflicted once did not restrain may be judged in need of correction by repeated severity. Although someone may be submerged in the abyss of frequent and serious vices, he is nevertheless not to be expelled from the monastery, but is to be restrained according to the character of the offense, lest someone who could have been corrected through prolonged repentance, when expelled, be devoured by the devil’s mouth.

546 **CHAPTER XVII. On Offenses**

[Note: [Col. 0885D]

CHAPTER XVII, Note 1. “Whoever has gone somewhere,” etc. Cassian, Book IV, chapter 16: “If he withdraws anywhere for a moment,” and shortly afterward: “If he attempts to receive anyone’s letter or to reply without his abbot.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “Whoever has answered defiantly,” etc. Cassian, in the same place: “If he has answered superfluously, too harshly, or too defiantly.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “Whoever has prayed with an excommunicated person,” etc. Cassian: “If he has prayed with one who has been suspended from prayer.” GRIAL.

From the cited passage of Cassian, Saint Columbanus also copied much at the end of his *Penitential*. Instead of “has laughed during the hours in the choir,” perhaps read “has laughed during the choir’s hours,” or else *horis* should be omitted, as in the *Concordia regularum*, [Col. 0886C] p. 497. Saint Pachomius also restrains laughter in the choir, and Saint John Chrysostom inveighs against those who laugh in church in Homily 15 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, as does Saint Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book III, against those who occupy themselves with stories in church. AREV.]

1. Offenses are either serious or light. The person guilty of a light fault is one who has preferred to be idle; who has come late to the office, the collation, or the table; who has laughed during the hours in the choir or occupied himself with stories; who, leaving the office or his work, has gone outside without necessity; who has loved sluggishness or sleep; who has sworn repeatedly; who has been excessively talkative; [Col. 0885C] who has undertaken an assigned work without a blessing, or, after completing it, has failed to ask for a blessing; who has completed an assigned task negligently or late; who has broken something accidentally; who has caused damage to a small object; who has used a book negligently; who has withdrawn somewhere for a moment; who has secretly received letters or any gift from someone; who, having received a letter, has replied without the abbot’s consent; who has either seen or spoken with any of his relatives or secular persons without the order of the elder; who has been disobedient to an elder; who has answered an elder defiantly; who has not restrained his tongue toward an elder; who has been wanton in speech [Col. 0886A]; who has walked indecently; who has joked; who has laughed excessively; who has spoken, prayed, or eaten with an excommunicated person; who has not disclosed a nocturnal illusion to the Father. These and similar offenses are to be corrected by a three-day excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 0886D]

2. “Whoever is affected by money,” etc. Cassian: “affected by the contagion of avarice and the possession of superfluous things.” GRIAL.]

2. A person is liable to a more serious fault if he is drunk; if he is quarrelsome; if he is foul-mouthed; if he is familiar with women; if he sows discord; if he is hot-tempered; if he is stiff-necked and unyielding; if he is puffed up in mind or immoderate in his swaggering walk; if he is a detractor, a whisperer, or envious; if he presumes to possess private property; if he is entangled in the contagion of money; if he possesses something superfluous beyond the regular allowance; if he is a defrauder of property entrusted or assigned to him, or of property assigned in lesser measure.

[Col. 0886B] 3. Among these matters, if he has taken away anything from the possessions brought with him, or has murmured about them through disobedience; if he has told a lie; if he has loved disputes or quarrels; if he has openly insulted a brother; if he has stained an innocent person with a false accusation; if, with a stubborn disposition, he has despised his superior; if he has harbored resentment against a brother; if he has not granted forgiveness to one who sinned against him and afterward begged pardon; if he has played, laughed, or kissed little children; if he has lain in the same bed with another; if he has caused damage to an important possession; if he has stolen; if he has sworn falsely; if, outside the common table, he has privately or secretly taken something; if, departing somewhere without consulting the prior or abbot, he has stayed away at midday or longer; if, in order to remain idle, he has pretended a false illness [Col. 0886C]. These and similar offenses are to be cleansed by prolonged excommunication according to the Father’s judgment and corrected with scourging, so that those known to have sinned more grievously may be restrained with harsher severity, while due consideration is nevertheless given to the persons involved—who are humble and who are proud.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Excommunication

[Note: [Col. 0886D]

CHAP. XVIII. Note 1. “He lies prostrate on the ground outside the choir.” From the Gothic. Cassian, Book IV, chapter 16: “When all the brothers have assembled in the synaxis, he shall remain prostrate on the ground and ask forgiveness until the solemnity of the prayers has been completed, obtaining it when he has been ordered, by the abbot’s judgment, to rise from the ground.” GRIAL.

In the same place. From Saint Pachomius, Bishop Fructuosus, and another Fructuosus, it is clear that this was the custom: monks who asked forgiveness, or were publicly rebuked, would loosen their belts. In the Concordia regularum, p. 534: “And entering the choir, let him pray. After this prayer has been offered,” etc. AREV.]

1. This is the satisfaction of those who have offended: when the brothers have taken their places for the office, after the period of penance has been completed, the one who has been excommunicated is summoned; he shall immediately loosen his belt and lie prostrate on the ground outside the choir, doing penance until the service has been completed. When he has been ordered by the abbot to rise from the ground, he shall enter the choir [Col. 0887A]; after the abbot has offered a prayer for him and all have answered “Amen,” he shall rise and ask forgiveness from everyone for his negligence, obtaining pardon after the judgment of this corrective satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 0887B]

2. Smaragdus, chapter 26: “Hence Isidore says: No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person; no one at all may eat with an excommunicated person—not even the one who supplies him with food for his sustenance.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “But those of lesser age,” etc. This admonition occurs not only in the Rule of Saint Benedict but also in the rule called the Rule of the Master. See Menard, pp. 582 ff. In Gratian’s Decree, causa 11, question 3, chapter 18, the following words are cited: “No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person, except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication, nor may anyone eat with him.” In the same way, in Burchard and in Ivo’s Decree, Isidore is given these additional words: “except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication.” Berard should also be consulted on this passage, in Isidoriana, chapter 32, no. 15. In Peter of Casinum, chapter 30, after “let him restrain,” the following is added: “But those brothers, after the age of fifteen, shall be beaten if they have committed a sufficiently serious offense, or the offense of fleeing after theft, or any criminal offense.” AREV.]

2. Those who are of lesser age are not to be restrained by a sentence of excommunication; rather, according to the character of their negligence, they are to be chastised with appropriate blows, so that those whom the weakness of age does not turn away from fault may be restrained by the discipline of the rod. Those who have been excommunicated shall be forbidden to leave the places in which they have been assigned until the period of penance has been completed. No one may enter to visit an excommunicated person without the superior’s command. No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person—not even the one who provides him with food for his sustenance.

[Col. 0887B] [Note: [Col. 0887C]

3. “Their bed is the ground.” Smaragdus: “Their bed is either bare ground or at least a mat, that is, a rush mat laid upon the ground.” [Col. 0887D] GRIAL.

In the same place. “If the excommunication … food.” In the Concordia regularum: “If an excommunication lasting two or three days has been imposed, the only food to be taken in the evening shall be bread and water.” “A shorn covering,” Book XIX of the Etymologies, chapter 22, no. 23, is a *ralla* garment, commonly called *rasilis*; according to Nonius, a *ralla* garment is so called from its loose or open texture, while *rasilis* or “shorn” may perhaps have received its name for another reason. A hair shirt (*cilicium*) is a garment woven from hair, taking its name from the people of Cilicia. Concerning *spartum*, Pliny, Book IX, chapter 2, says: “From it come footwear and the garment of shepherds.” Isidore defines *soleae* in Book XIX of the Etymologies, chapter 24, no. 11, and Gellius agrees with him in Book XIII, chapter 20. AREV.]

3. If the excommunication is to last two days, no food is to be provided to the excommunicated person; but if a suspension from communion lasting several days has been imposed, the only food to be taken in the evening shall be bread and water. Except during the severity of winter, the bed of the excommunicated shall be the ground, with a covering or mat; his garment shall be a shorn covering or at least a hair shirt; his footwear shall be either made of rushes or some other kind of sandal.

549 [Note: [Col. 0887D]

4. “Into the collection.” That is, into the common gathering, concerning which see chapter 7. Certain words copied in the Concordia regularum, p. 568, from the rule of Saint Isidore, bishop, chapter 14, § 4, may be referred to this passage; but they do not occur in the published rule, nor did Menard annotate them in any way [Col. 0888B]:

“If any excommunicated person appears querulous or murmuring at the first interrogation, and arrogantly or importunately defends his own opinions, and the superior recognizes that this is manifest, let him remain excommunicated until the third day, so that no one may speak with him. But if, when questioned on the third day, he is found persisting in the pride of which we have spoken, let him remain confined in the prison until he denies all the arrogance of his pride. But if he persists and continues in evil, and is unwilling to do penance with a willing—perhaps, a perverse—disposition, and repeatedly stands defiantly before the superiors or brothers, and prefers to defend himself with his relatives, let him be brought into the common gathering, stripped of the monastery’s clothing, clothed in the secular garments he formerly wore, and expelled from the monastery with the mark of shame, so that the others may be corrected, while perhaps that offender alone may be corrected by such chastisement.”

If these words belong to Isidore, they can be reconciled with what he said in chapter 16, no. 2: there he denies that those should be expelled from the monastery concerning whom some hope remains that they can be recalled to good conduct, whereas here he orders those expelled who are judged [Col. 0888D] incorrigible. AREV.]

4. The Father of the monastery or the prior shall have the power to excommunicate; the other offenses of the monks, however, shall be reported at the common gathering to the abbot or prior, so that the person recognized to have committed the offense may be restrained with appropriate severity.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Community Life

[Col. 0888A]

[Note: [Col. 0888D]

CHAP. XIX. Note 1. “Nor may they possess anything in their cells,” etc. Pachomius, Teridius, and others likewise prescribe this in their monastic rules. What follows shortly afterward—“If anything is given by parents,” etc.—is expressed in the Concordia regularum as follows: “If anything has been bestowed upon any monk by parents or outsiders, it shall not be held under the authority of private property, but shall be reduced to common ownership under the abbot’s authority and provided when necessary.” The principle that whatever a monk acquires, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery, has been adopted in many places in canon law, such as chapter *Statutum* 1, causa 18, question 1; chapter *Abbates*, 16, causa 18, question 2; chapter *Quia ingredientibus*, 7, causa 19, question 3; and elsewhere. AREV.]

1. Monks living in common shall not presume to make anything private for themselves, nor shall they presume to possess in their cells, without the abbot’s regular dispensation, anything pertaining to food, clothing, or any other matter. At Pentecost, however, which is the day of remission, all the brothers shall bind themselves under a divine profession to have nothing private within their conscience. If a gift has been sent to any monk by parents or outsiders, it shall be converted to the common use of the brothers, so that it may be given to whoever needs it. For whatever a monk acquires, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery.

550 [Note: [Col. 0888D]

2. “For the support of seclusion.” From the Gothic. Another reading: “for the practice of seclusion.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “He incurs vainglory.” In the Gothic, one additional word occurs. GRIAL.]

2. No one shall privately seek for himself a separate cell in which he may live apart from the community, except one who, perhaps worn down by illness or age, has earned this privilege with the monastery Father’s approval. The others, who are afflicted neither by illness nor old age, shall preserve a common life and way of living in holy fellowship. No one shall seek for himself, withdrawn from the community, a separate cell in which he may serve the needs of seclusion, persistent idleness, or concealed vice—and especially vainglory or the reputation and esteem of the world.

3. For many wish to remain hidden in seclusion precisely so that they may become known: those who were insignificant or unknown when placed outside now wish to be recognized and honored when enclosed. Indeed, everyone who withdraws from the crowds for the sake of a quiet life becomes less hidden the more he is separated from public view. Such persons ought therefore to remain in holy fellowship and pass their lives under public testimony, so that, if there are vices in them, they may be treated because they are not concealed; and, if there are virtues, they may benefit others as examples to imitate, while others are instructed by observing their examples of humility.

[Note: [Col. 0889C]

4. “To the needy,” etc. That is, unless necessity presses. See Saint Thomas, II-II, question 32, article 8, and the gloss on 16, question 1, chapter 5. Saint Pachomius and Saint Basil likewise prohibited exchanging anything with another. [Col. 0889D] Even an abbot is forbidden to make a slave free in the Council of Agde, canon 59, and in the Council of Epaon, canon 8. Menard, p. 188, distinguishes two kinds of freedom, or manumission: one royal, which was carried out with the owner’s consent before the king by the striking of a coin; the other ecclesiastical, which was carried out in church before the horn of the altar, in the presence of priests and the people, by both laymen and clergy. AREV.]

4. No one may presume, without the abbot’s knowledge, to give to the needy or to anyone else anything that the monk is known to possess by regular dispensation; nor may anyone exchange anything with another brother unless the abbot or prior has ordered him to do so. No one shall possess any monastery property beyond what has been granted by the monastery’s common rule. Neither the abbot nor a monk of the monastery may make a slave free; for one who possesses nothing of his own ought not to grant freedom over another’s property. For just as the laws of the world have decreed that possession cannot be alienated except by its rightful owner, so everything that enters the monastery in money must be received under the testimony of the superiors.

[Note: [Col. 0889D]

5. “More refined.” Another reading: “for refinements,” from the Gothic. Above, chapter 9: “Nor more refined than those things which are held in common.” Neither reading, however, seems entirely satisfactory here. GRIAL.

In the same place. “Necessity.” From the Gothic. Another reading: “necessaries.” GRIAL.

The keeper of the sacristy is mentioned again in the following chapter, no. 1. Menard, in the cited passage, says that the keeper of the sacristy is the person whom we now call the sacristan, and he discusses the word *sacristy* at length. AREV.]

5. The same money is to be divided into three parts. One shall be for the sick and the elderly, and for purchasing on holy days more refined food for the brothers; another shall be for the needy; the third shall be for the clothing of the brothers and boys, and for purchasing whatever is needed by the monastery. The keeper of the sacristy shall receive these three portions and, at the abbot’s command, shall spend from each portion for its necessary purposes, under the testimony of the prior or the superiors.

## CHAPTER XX. What Pertains to Each Person

[Col. 0889C]

[Note: [Col. 0889D]

CHAP. XX. Note 1. In the Concordia regularum, p. 430, *ratio agrorum*—“the management of the fields”—is given, less correctly, for *satio agrorum*—“the sowing of the fields.” From the same Concordia and from Holstenius I restored *diligentia gregum*, “care of the flocks,” and *vespertinis nocturnisque officiis*, “evening and night offices.” In Grial’s edition: *diligentia legum*, “care of the laws,” and *vespertinis nocturnis officiis*, “evening night offices.” The keeper of the sacristy is called *secretarius* by Lanfranc, Constitutions, chapter 6; by the Greeks, *cimiliarcha*; and in certain churches of Spain, *thesaurarius*, “treasurer.” Here *instrumenta* means documents of contracts, foundations, and so forth. Grial reads *in usum sacrarii*, “for the use of the sacristy,” and *ceram ad luminaria*, “wax for lights.” In the Concordia regularum, instead of *iste a vestiario*, etc., the reading is: “who shall receive the monastery’s clothing and shall also take charge of various threads for sewing”—it should read, “also needles and threads”—“and so forth.” Menard considers this reading better. In the same Concordia, *facta infectaque* occurs instead of *fracta*, and *cerariorum* instead of *calceariorum*. AREV.]

1. The care of the monks, the conduct of legal matters, the management of possessions, the sowing of fields, the planting and cultivation of vineyards, the care of flocks, the construction of buildings, and the work of carpenters or smiths belong to the prior. The care or custody of the church belongs to the keeper of the sacristy, as does giving the signal for the evening and night offices, sewing garments, and caring for the sacred vessels, books, and all documents, as well as oil for the uses of the sanctuary, wax, and lights. He shall receive needles from the monastery’s wardrobe and shall also have various threads for sewing the brothers’ clothing, and shall distribute everything as necessary. To him also belong the gold and silver, and the other broken metals of bronze and iron, as well as the arrangement of the linen-workers, fullers, shoemakers, and tailors.

[Note: [Col. 0890D]

2. “Courtyard.” From the Gothic. Another reading: “from the chest.” GRIAL.

In the same place. “Of outsiders.” In the Concordia regularum, p. 411, *exterorum*, “of outsiders,” occurs, less correctly. In the same Concordia, p. 591, “whatever remains shall be for expenditure,” and shortly afterward, “flax, aviaries, care of food to be supplied to the bakers.” From this Menard thinks it should be read: “flax, aviaries; the care of supplying food to the bakers.” Aviaries are buildings suitable for raising birds. AREV.]

2. The care of the guests, the announcement of those arriving, and the custody of the outer cloisters shall belong to the doorkeeper. The care of what is in the storeroom shall belong to the one placed over the pantry. He shall provide the weekly servers with whatever is necessary for the food of the monks, guests, and sick; in his presence, the things to be taken to the tables shall be distributed; he shall also preserve whatever remains for the use of the poor. After the week has been completed, the weekly server shall present to him the vessels entrusted to him, so that it may be inspected whether they have been kept negligently, and they shall be handed over to the succeeding weekly server in his presence. To him also belong the granaries, flocks of sheep and pigs, wool and flax, the care of the courtyard, the provision of food for the bakers, beasts of burden, oxen, and birds, as well as the making of footwear and the care of shepherds or fishermen.

[Note: [Col. 0890D]

3. “According to custom.” Thus the Gothic and Smaragdus. Another reading: “from the heap.” GRIAL.]

3. The care of the dishes, the management of the tables, and giving the signal for the daytime offices, whether at the conference or at the common gathering after sunset, belong to the weekly server. The protection and custody of the gardens, the bee-hives, the care of various seeds, and announcing what ought to be sown or planted in the gardens, and when, shall also belong to the gardener. The baking craft, however, shall belong to laymen; they shall clean the wheat and, according to custom, grind it. The monks shall only prepare the dough and make their own bread with their own hands. For guests and the sick, the laymen shall make the bread.

4. The custody of tools and implements shall belong to one man whom the Father of the monks has chosen; he shall distribute them to those working and guard what has been returned. [Col. 0891A] Although all these duties remain specially assigned to individuals, everything nevertheless, as ordered by the Father, shall belong to the care of the prior. For guarding the house in the city, one senior and highly respected monk, together with two young monks, shall be appointed; if he is free from fault, it is fitting that he remain there permanently.

[Note: [Col. 0891C]

5. “Studies of letters.” From this Menard concludes that boy-monks ought to be instructed in letters. Saint Caesarius did not wish to receive into the monastery boys who were unable to learn their letters. See Mabillon, On Monastic Studies. In the Concordia regularum, p. 991, certain words from the rule of Saint Isidore are reported which do not occur in the printed rule and may be referred to this passage:

“Whoever has been entrusted to the monastery by his own parents should know that he will remain there perpetually. For Hannah, out of the devotion with which she had vowed it, offered Samuel, once born and weaned, to God; and he remained in the service of the temple in which he had been placed by his mother and served where he had been established.”

The same words are reported in causa 20, question 1, chapter *Quicunque*, without any citation of book or chapter. Smaragdus took them from the Concordia regularum. In the cited cause the reading is “offered with devotion,” and *deputatus*, “appointed,” occurs instead of *functus*, “served.” Berard should be consulted again on this matter, in Isidoriana, chapter 32, no. 46. AREV.]

5. The care of raising the boys shall belong to a man whom the Father chooses, a holy, wise, and mature man, who shall instruct the boys not only in literary studies but also through the teaching and discipline of virtues. The care of travelers and alms for the poor shall belong to the one entrusted with the authority of administration. He shall give and share what he has, as far as he can, not grudgingly or under compulsion: for God loves a cheerful giver (II Cor. 9).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Sick

[Col. 0891B]

[Note: [Col. 0891D]

CHAP. XXI. Note 1. “Concerning expenses,” etc. This is more clearly understood from Saint Fructuosus, chapter 10: “They shall neither defraud them of what remains for them nor secretly pollute themselves there with unlawful eating.” AREV.]

1. The care of the sick is to be entrusted to a man of sound and holy conduct who can bear responsibility for them and provide with great diligence whatever their weakness requires. He shall serve the sick in such a way that he does not presume to eat from their provisions. More delicate foods are to be provided to the sick until they recover. After they have regained their health, they shall return to their former usage.

[Note: [Col. 0891D]

2. In Peter of Casinum, chapter 36, after “let them not doubt,” the following is added:

“Those who are healthy in body ought to be healthy also in mind. Therefore it is fitting that the healthy bear the sick, rather than that they be borne by the sick. For it is necessary that we patiently bear the sick, so that in turn the sick may patiently be borne by the healthy. During the time of their illness, let us by providing for them obtain from them an abundant reward, so that during the time of our illness they may likewise obtain an abundant reward from us by serving us. Hence the Apostle says (Gal. 6): ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.’” AREV.]

2. The stronger brethren, however, must by no means be scandalized by this; those who are healthy ought to tolerate the sick, while those who are sick should not hesitate to place the healthy and those who labor before themselves. No one ought either to conceal a genuine bodily illness or to pretend a false one. Those who are able should give thanks to God and work; those who are unable should make their illnesses known and be treated more humanely.

[Note: [Col. 0892C]

3. In the Concordia regularum, p. 665: “Only insofar as the illness requires.” “Nor is it to be deferred,” etc. Some copies read: “Nor should one murmur if it happens, because it is done,” etc. In Peter of Casinum, after the words “for the remedy of health,” the following is added: “For the care of healing, baths should be used with the greatest diligence; but to the healthy, and especially to the young, they should be granted more slowly.” AREV.]

3. Nothing private is to be possessed under the pretext of illness, lest the desire for indulgence lie concealed under the appearance of sickness. No monk may go to the baths for the sake of washing his body, except solely because of the necessity of illness or nocturnal pollution.
