Nor is it to be deferred when it is beneficial for a cure; nor should anyone murmur, since it is not done out of a desire for pleasure but solely as a remedy for health.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Guests

1. Guests who arrive are to be received promptly and cheerfully, knowing that for this they will receive their reward at the end. For, as the Lord says: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me; whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and whoever gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water only in my name, truly I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matt. 10).

[Note: [Col. 0892D]

CHAP. XXII. Note 2. “A more abundant honor is to be shown to monks,” etc. That is, also according to the prescriptions of Pachomius, Macarius, the Master, and others, as in the Concordia regularum, p. 869. AREV.]

2. Although the good of hospitality ought to be extended graciously to everyone, a more abundant honor of hospitality is nevertheless to be shown to monks. Lodgings are to be provided for them, their feet washed, so that the Lord’s command may be fulfilled; suitable expenses are also to be provided for them as an act of kindness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Departures

[Note: [Col. 0892D]

CHAP. XXIII. Note 1. “Presume.” That is, “do.” It is confirmed in the Concordia regularum, pp. 622 and 874, that letters are neither to be written nor received by monks and religious persons without the superior’s permission. AREV.]

1. No monk shall dare to go anywhere without consulting the abbot, nor presume to do anything without his command or that of the prior. Whenever the abbot or prior goes somewhere, the brother who is second in rank shall take responsibility for the brothers. No one may see a relative or outsider, guest or monk, friend or family member, without the superior’s command; nor may anyone presume, without the abbot’s order, to receive or give a letter to anyone.

[Note: [Col. 0892D]

2. In the Concordia regularum, p. 1061, and in Holstenius, the following is read: “When the brothers depart or return from outside, after all have been assembled together in the church, they shall receive a blessing. The same shall be done for the weekly servers and for administrators of any kind of property, both when they are appointed and when they withdraw. For some necessity of the monastery, two brothers of spiritual character and thoroughly approved shall be chosen and sent to the city or to a possession—that is, an estate, farm, or manor. But young men,” etc. Menard strongly praises these institutions or rules. AREV.]

2. When the brothers depart, or return [Col. 0893A], they shall receive a blessing after all have been assembled together in the church. The same shall be done for the weekly server or any administrator of property; but when they are sent out for some necessity of the monastery, two spiritual and thoroughly approved brothers shall be chosen. Young men and recent converts are to be removed from such service, lest either immature age be polluted by carnal desire or an inexperienced way of life return to longing for the world.

3. When a monk is sent to visit some monastery, for as long as he remains with those to whom he has been sent, he ought to live there in the same way as he sees the rest of the holy community living, for the sake, namely, of avoiding scandal and disturbing the weak.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Dead

[Col. 0893B] 1. When brothers pass from this light, before they are buried, a sacrifice is to be offered to the Lord for the remission of their sins [Col. 0894A]. The bodies of the brothers are to be buried in one place, so that those whom the unity of charity held together while alive may be embraced by one place in death.

556 [Note: [Col. 0893B]

CHAP. XXIV. Note 2. On the ancient custom of offering sacrifice for the dead, or on the purgatorial fire according to Isidore’s view, see Isidoriana, chapter 23, nos. 17 and 18, and the note on the Book on the Order of Creatures, chapter 11, no. 13. Menard, p. 217, gathers much in support of this opinion from Saint Augustine, Cassian, the Councils of Braga, Orléans, Vaison I and II, and others. He lists other authors who, in addition to the funeral rites, mention the third, seventh, ninth, thirtieth, and fortieth days. Moreover, as noted in the Concordia regularum at the cited place, Blessed Aegil, abbot of Fulda, instituted that anniversary prayers and Masses for deceased brothers should be celebrated every year on the day of Saint Ignatius the Martyr [Col. 0893C]. Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, decreed that the same should be done on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost. Others appointed another day. AREV.]

2. On the day after Pentecost, a sacrifice is to be offered to the Lord for the spirits of the dead, so that, having become participants in blessed life, they may receive their bodies more purified on the day of resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0893C]

3. “And in all things let the greater precepts of the Fathers be observed.” The Gothic reading does not agree with the preface. GRIAL.

In the same place. In the Concordia regularum: “the precepts of the greater Fathers,” which also displeased Menard. After this final chapter, certain manuscripts add another chapter, “On the Rule of the Devoted Women,” which I discussed in Isidoriana, chapter 71, nos. 28 ff. It reads as follows:

“Let no one go to visit them except one who has a mother, sister, daughter, female relatives, or cousins there, or the mother of his children. But if there is a necessity for them to see these women, as when paternal authority is owed to them before they renounced the world and entered the monastery, or some evident reason exists, they shall send with them a man of approved age and conduct; they shall see them and return together. Let no one go to them except those whom we have mentioned above. If they wish to see them, they shall first have the monastery’s Father notified, and he shall send for the superiors who have been assigned to the service of the virgins. These men shall meet them and, with them, see whichever women they need to see, with all discipline and fear of God. When they have seen them, they shall not speak to them about worldly matters. Whoever transgresses any of these commands shall perform public penance, without any evasion, for his negligence and contempt, so that we may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.”

Perhaps the final phrase should read: “so that he may be able to possess the kingdoms of heaven.” In Isidoriana, at the cited place, I also said that in certain manuscripts, after the chapter of the rule of the devoted women, the constitution of the Eleventh Council of Hispalis, presided over by Isidore, is added. It concerns monasteries of virgins, so that they may be protected by monks, and can be read in the council itself, printed in Appendix 4 to Isidoriana, p. 525; for this reason it is omitted here. AREV.]

3. These things, therefore, O servants of God and soldiers of Christ, despisers of the world, we wish you to observe in such a way that you rather obey the greater precepts. Receive this admonition of ours among those precepts, therefore, guarding with humble hearts what we say and willingly accepting what we administer, so that glory from the fruit of your work may come to you, and forgiveness requested for this admonition may come to us. May almighty God guard you [Col. 0894B] in all good things, and, as he began, so also confirm his grace in you. Amen.

[Col. 0893]

## LETTERS OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF HISPALIS (C, G, S)*

## FIRST LETTER. ISIDORE TO BISHOP LEUDEFREDUS

[Col. 0893D]

557 Isidore, to my lord Leudefredus, bishop and servant of God.

[Note: [Col. 0893D]

LETTER I. Note 1. Cited by Gratian, distinction 25. Another reading: “for fraternal,” instead of “for paternal.” PEREZ.

In the same place. Much that may help explain this letter has already been discussed in Isidoriana, chapter 73, no. 5 ff., where I also set out the suspicions of certain persons who doubted whether this letter is genuinely Isidore’s [Col. 0894D]. The books of Saint Isidore’s Offices, which treat the same subject, should also be consulted. The letters, as they appear in the edition of Grial, which we follow, were collected and supplied with several notes by the especially learned John Baptist Perez. AREV.]

1. Having read through the letters of Your Holiness, I rejoiced because through their report I learned of your desired good health. Concerning the matters that the message of your eloquence subsequently sought to convey, I give thanks to God that you devote yourself to the concern of pastoral office and inquire how ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered. Although everything is known to your prudence, nevertheless, since you consult me with fraternal affection, I shall explain what I can and speak of all the ranks of the Church, and of what pertains to each.

2. The keys of the church belong to the doorkeeper, so that he may close and open the temple of God; he is also to guard everything that is inside and outside, receive the faithful, and reject the excommunicated and unbelievers.

3. The preparation of the lights in the sacristy belongs to the acolyte; he carries the candle, prepares the stands, and prepares the chalice for the subdeacons for the Eucharist.

4. The exorcist is responsible for memorizing the exorcisms and laying hands upon the possessed and the catechumens to be exorcised.

5. The psalmist is responsible for the ministry of singing, reciting blessings, psalms, praises, and the responsories of the sacrifice, and for everything pertaining to skill in singing.

558 6. The reader is responsible for proclaiming the readings and preaching to the people what the prophets announced.

7. The subdeacon is responsible for carrying the chalice and paten to the altar of Christ, handing them to the Levites, and assisting them; he is also to hold the jug, basin, and towel, and to provide water to the bishop, priests, and Levites for washing their hands before the altar.

8. The deacon is responsible for assisting the priests and ministering in everything performed in Christ’s sacraments—namely, in baptism, chrism, the paten, and the chalice; bringing the offerings and arranging them on the altar; setting the Lord’s table and clothing it; carrying the cross; and preaching the Gospel and the Apostle. For just as the Old Testament has been entrusted to readers, so the New Testament has been commanded to be preached by deacons. The ministry of prayers and the recitation of names also belong to him; he admonishes the ears to attend to the Lord, urges the people with a cry, and announces the peace.

[Note: [Col. 0895C]

9. In Vatican Codex 3788, as I indicated in Isidoriana, at the cited place, no. 10, certain passages from the sayings of blessed Isidore to Bishop Laudefredus are presented. It is preferable to copy them here rather than relegate them to the appendices:

“Priests are responsible for confecting the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, for saying the prayer, and for blessing God’s gifts. Therefore they shall remain unfailingly in the holy church throughout all the canonical hours, so that the work of God may be worthily and sincerely performed by the one to whom it is entrusted, fearing the sentence of that Wise One where it is said: ‘Cursed is the one who performs God’s work negligently.’ Obeying the commands of their bishop, they must not grow sluggish through any idleness or buffoonery, but must remember that ‘the lips of the priest guard knowledge.’ They must also stand constantly in the church and take care that the Eucharist of Christ is not lacking on account of the sick. They must also care for the sick, lest they perhaps die without confession or without receiving the confirmation of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. They must receive the confessions of sinners with the greatest reverence, and thereafter, at the command of the bishop, great concern must be shown for them. Everything in the church concerning Christians and children to be baptized, and concerning assistance to be given, is also to be carried out by the priests.”

As I said in Isidoriana, these words have been added to Isidore, no less than those concerning the archdeacons which Perez copied at no. 12. AREV.]

9. The priest is responsible for confecting the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon the Lord’s altar, saying prayers, and blessing the people.

10. The consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, and the preparation of chrism belong to the bishop. He establishes the offices and ecclesiastical orders mentioned above; he blesses sacred virgins; and although each person presides in his own office, he presides in all of them. These are the orders and ministries of the clergy, which are nevertheless divided by pontifical authority among the care of the archdeacon and the supervision of the first officer and treasurer.

[Note: [Col. 0896D]

11. Another reading: “reports,” instead of “brings.” PEREZ.]

11. The archdeacon commands the subdeacons and Levites, and the following ministries belong to him: arranging the dressing of the altar by the Levites; care of the incense; bringing the sacrifice to the altar; care of the subdeacons in presenting at the altar the things necessary for the sacrifice; and responsibility for determining which of the Levites is to read the Apostle and the Gospel, which is to recite the prayers or the responsory on Sundays or feast days. The care, ordering, and disputes of the parish communities belong to him. He makes representations to the bishop concerning the repair of diocesan basilicas; he inspects the parishes by the bishop’s command; and he reports to the bishop the furnishings or property of the parish basilicas and the records of ecclesiastical liberties.

[Note: [Col. 0896D]

12. In one Complutum manuscript, after the office of the archdeacon and before the first officer, the following is read:

“The archpriest should know that he is under the archdeacon and must obey his commands as those of his bishop; and, in particular, it belongs to his ministry to care for all the priests appointed in the order, to remain constantly in the church, and, whenever the absence of his bishop occurs, to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in his place and recite the collects, or appoint someone to whom he himself has entrusted this duty.”

These words do not occur in the other manuscripts; nor are they from Isidore, but others cite them from the Council of Toledo. See the notes on Gratian and the fragments of the Council of Toledo. PEREZ.]

12. He himself receives the money collected from the communion offering, brings it himself to the bishop, and distributes to the clergy their respective portions. The excesses of the deacons are reported to the bishop by the archdeacon; he himself announces to the priest in the sacristy the days of fasts and solemnities, and they are proclaimed publicly in the church by him. When the archdeacon is absent, the next-ranking deacon fulfills his duties in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0896D]

13. Another reading: *cantandi* (“of singing”), instead of *meditandi* (“of practicing”). PEREZ.]

13. The acolytes, exorcists, [Col. 0896C] psalmists, and lectors belong to the *primicerius*, as does giving the signal for the clerical offices, concern for the integrity of life, and responsibility for practicing and carrying out the duties. Who among the clergy is to deliver the lessons, blessings, psalm, praises, offertory, and responsories; likewise, the order and manner of psalmody in the choir according to the solemnity and season; the arrangement for carrying the lights; and, if anything is needed for the repair of the basilicas located in the city, he himself reports it to the priest. He sends the bishop’s letters concerning the days of fasting in the parishes through the doorkeepers; the clergy whom he knows to be offending he disciplines; but those whom he cannot correct, he reports [Col. 0897A] to the bishop for his knowledge. 560 He himself appoints the basilicarians and arranges the registers. When the *primicerius* is absent, the duties stated above are performed by the person who is either nearest to him in rank or devoted to carrying them out by reason of his training.

[Note: [Col. 0897C]

14. Another reading: *in eadem basilica* (“in the same basilica”), instead of *in eamdem basilicam* (“into the same basilica”). AREV.]

14. The arrangement of the basilicarians and doorkeepers, the care of the incense, the preparation of the chrism, the ordering of the baptistery, and the preparation of the sacrifice from the things to be offered belong to the treasurer. People will come to him from the parishes for chrism. He himself receives the candles and altar offerings from the people; he himself gathers candles throughout the churches on feast days. The furnishings and vestments of the altar belong to him; whatever is used in the temple is under his direction. He guards the veils and furnishings of the basilicas [Col. 0897B] in the city that do not have a priest. As for the daily candles and small lamps, whatever remains in the basilicas the basilicarian brings to him each month. From these the treasurer gives one quarter to the basilicarian; he divides the remaining three quarters equally among himself, the *primicerius*, and the priest who celebrates Mass in the same basilica.

15. The repair and construction of the basilicas, the church’s legal actions, whether in bringing a case or responding to one, the collection of taxes, and the accounting of what is brought in belong to the steward. Also belonging to him are the care of the fields and cultivation of the vineyards, property cases, and the stipends of the clergy, widows, and devoted poor; the distribution of clothing and food for the household servants, the clergy, the other servants, and the [Col. 0897C] craftsmen. All these duties he fulfills by the command and discretion of his bishop.

16. These are the matters that have either been distributed by our predecessors according to the ranks of the offices or preserved by the custom of the churches for each individual office. Do not attribute anything among these matters to our own judgment, except what reason has taught or the antiquity of tradition has established.

[Note: [Col. 0897C]

17. The election of the abbot of a monastery is discussed in the *Rule for Monks*, chapter 2. AREV.]

17. As for the father of the monastery, of whom you have informed us, the one whom holy conduct and upright morals commend ought to be preferred—one in whom, while he was subject to authority, there was no deceit. Grace is rightly heaped upon such a man, as the Lord says: “Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matthew 25:21). But whoever, while still under authority, lived wickedly and did not shrink from defrauding his brothers, once he sees himself in a position of power and freedom will freely and without restraint commit greater and worse offenses.

18. For concerning such men the Apostle says: “But you do wrong, and this to your brothers. Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” (1 Corinthians 6:8). But let it suffice for us to say this to you: fulfill what you judge worthy of God. After this, I do not cease to pray that you may stand as my intercessor before the Lord, so that, because I have fallen through my own fault, I may obtain forgiveness of sins through you.

## LETTER II. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO, ARCHDEACON

[Col. 0898B] To Braulio, most dear and beloved son in Christ, archdeacon, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0897D]

LETTER II, no. 1. “A quaternion of rules.” He means, I think—and I said so in *Isidoriana*, chapter 71, no. 1—the rule that Isidore wrote for monks. In Riscu’s edition of Isidore’s letters to Braulio this is second in order. Riscu appends the following note:

“By Maurentius the *primicerius*. Thus read the printed editions that I have seen; yet I read *primiclerus*, or *primicerius*. The dignity of the *primicerius* is mentioned in the Council of Mérida, chapters 10 and 14, and in the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, in the subscriptions, and in the Council of Compostela, chapter 1. His office was to distribute offerings to the clergy according to each person’s rank and merit. Concerning the *primiceriatus*, see Isidore’s letter to Laudefredus, bishop of Córdoba.”

In this letter, no. 13, he is called *primicerius*; others use *primiclerus*, others *primiclerius*, and others *primicerius*. The first origin of the name appears to be *primicerius*; for that was what the first person of each class was called, as though the first entered upon wax or a tablet. Ducange has more on this subject. AREV.]

1. When you receive a friend’s letter, dearest son, do not delay to embrace it as a friend. For this is the second consolation among absent friends: when the one who is loved is not present, letters may embrace him in his place. We have sent you a ring as a token of our affection and a cloak as a covering for our friendship; from this, antiquity derived the word. Pray, therefore, for me, that the Lord may inspire you so that I may yet deserve to see you in this life. You whom your departure made sorrowful, may you one day again make joyful by presenting yourself. We have sent you a quaternion of rules through Maurentius the *primicerius*. For the rest, I always desire to learn of your well-being, my most beloved lord and dearest son.

## LETTER III. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO, ARCHDEACON

[Col. 0898C]

562 To Braulio, his most dear and beloved brother in Christ, archdeacon, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0898D]

LETTER III, no. 1. “The sixth decade.” The Bollandists, volume II of March, page 638, say that it is impossible to determine with certainty which little works of Saint Augustine were contained in this decade, since the memory of such a division has been lost. But Riscus rightly maintains that there is no doubt that the sixth decade was a definite part of Augustine’s exposition of the Psalms, namely, the part extending from Psalm 51 to Psalm 60. For both Cassiodorus, in his prologue to the Psalms, bears witness that Augustine’s entire commentary was once divided into decades, and several manuscript codices show this, as is clear from the Maurist preface to volume VI of Augustine’s works. Certainly, several codices still exist in the Vatican Library in which Saint Augustine’s exposition is distributed by decades of psalms; and in a privilege of Ordoño II, in Flórez, volume XIV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 370, mention is made of a decade of psalms. Felix also, in the *Life of Julian*, mentions a decade or decades of Saint Augustine’s psalms.

Riscus asserts that the words “in whatever way you may make me known to him” are foreign to Isidore’s meaning and entirely inappropriate. For how could Braulio make Isidore known to Augustine, who had been dead for nearly two centuries? He therefore thinks the text should be restored as: “in whatever way you may make it—the decade—known to me.” I would rather read: “make me acquainted with it,” namely, with that decade; for *cognitus* was used in Isidore’s age for one who was knowledgeable and experienced, just as *ignotus* was used for one who was ignorant. Thus, in Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, no. 3: “Only those KNOWLEDGEABLE IN THIS ART can skillfully solve their figures.” And Braulio, in the *Life of Saint Isidore*: “He will not be UNKNOWN in merit for his knowledge of divine and human sciences.” See *Isidoriana*, chapter 3, no. 16. Yet *make me known to him* may also be retained, as in the book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 34: “to whom we are unknown.” In Grial’s edition the reading is *decadam* instead of *decadem*; but this may have occurred contrary to the editor’s intention. AREV.]

1. Since I cannot enjoy your presence with the eyes of the flesh, let me at least enjoy your conversation, so that the consolation of a friend may be this: to learn through letters that the one whom I long to see is safe. Both would be good, if it were permitted; but if I cannot refresh myself with bodily sight, let me at least be refreshed in mind by you. When we were together, I asked you to send me the sixth decade of Saint Augustine; I now ask you to make me known to him in whatever way you can.

[Col. 0899A] [Note: [Col. 0899D]

2. Another reading: *pro eo quod* (“because of the fact that”), instead of *pro id quod*. AREV.]

2. We have sent you the little book of the *Synonyms*, not because it is of any particular usefulness, but because you had wished for it. I commend this boy, and I also commend myself, that you may pray for me, wretched as I am, because I am greatly weakened both by bodily illnesses and by the guilt of my mind. In both matters I seek your protection, since I deserve nothing by myself. For the rest, ask that, when the opportunity for the bearer to return to us with life as his companion presents itself, you may order us to be made joyful by your words.

## LETTER IV. ISIDORE TO MASSONA, BISHOP

563 To the holy and meritoriously blessed lord Massona, bishop, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0899D]

LETTER IV, no. 1. Concerning Massona: this letter is cited by Gratian, distinction 50, chapter “Domino sancto,” and distinction 33, question 2, chapter “Hoc ipsum.” Massona—also called Massana, Masson, Massanus, or Massenus—was bishop of Mérida and was the first to subscribe the Third Council of Toledo. For *Nicetio*, another reading has *Vincentio*. For *perpatuit*, other readings are *praepatuit* or *apparuit*. PEREZ.

[Col. 0900C] In the same place. I prepared a discussion and defense of the teaching of this letter to Massona in *Isidoriana*, chapter 73, nos. 11 and following. The manuscripts differ considerably at the beginning. Some conform more closely to grammatical rules: “Your religious servant Nicetius, coming to us … brought.” Yet the reading found in the oldest manuscripts may be retained: “With your servant coming,” and so forth, on the basis of what I said concerning Sedulius, Book IV, verse 8:

“For whatever nature denies, in its own judgment, it grants.”

For *vice inquisitionis*, and so forth, others read *inquisitioni vestrae studuit respondere, poscentes* (“he took pains to answer your inquiry, asking”). AREV.]

[Col. 0899B]

1. When your servant, the religious man Nicetius, came to us, he brought us a letter from Your Honor, in which knowledge of your well-being was also especially made manifest through the bearer himself, whose tongue was a living letter. Therefore, having rendered thanks to our God for your welfare, as far as our mediocrity was able, we asked, in place of a personal inquiry, that you be commended to the divine sight through the support of your merits.

[Note: [Col. 0900D]

2. *In lapsu corporali* (“in bodily falling”). The words that are read before this in certain books—“The same is inserted in canon 19 of the Council of Ancyra”—have been added from the margin; for they are found neither in Rabanus nor in other codices of better quality. PEREZ.

In the same place. *Innotuit* (“he made known”) is used instead of *notum fecit* (“he made known”), as has already been noted elsewhere. AREV.]

2. But regarding what Your Venerable Brotherhood subsequently made known in your letters, no diversity of decrees is to be understood in such judgments: in one place it is read that, after penance, the rank of honor is to be restored following bodily falling; elsewhere, that after such a crime the dignity of the former order is by no means to be restored.

3. This difference is distinguished in the following way: the canon commands those [Col. 0899C] to return to their former grades of office who have been preceded by the satisfaction of penance or by a worthy confession of sins. But those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption and who, with a certain superstitious recklessness, even try to defend the very carnal offense they commit receive neither a rank of honor nor the grace of communion.

[Note: [Col. 0900D]

4. Others read *adeptae* (“of the acquired”) instead of *ademptae* (“of the removed”), and *confirmatur* (“is confirmed”) instead of *confirmetur* (“may be confirmed”). AREV.]

4. Therefore the two judgments must be reconciled in such a way that [Col. 0900A] those who have merited reconciliation through penance must be restored to their place of honor. Such people do not undeservedly regain the status of the dignity that was removed, since they are known to have received the remedy of life through the amendment of penance. So that this may not remain more ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the judgment of divine authority.

5. For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of Jerusalem as an unfaithful woman, shows that after the satisfaction of penance the former honor can be restored. “Be ashamed, O Judah,” he says, “and bear your disgrace.” And shortly afterward: “You and your daughters shall return to your former state” (Ezekiel 16:52). By saying “be ashamed,” he shows that after the confusion—that is, after the deed of sin—everyone ought to blush and, for the crimes [Col. 0900B] committed, lower a shamefaced brow to the ground, because he has perpetrated a deed deserving of confusion.

[Note: [Col. 0900D]

6. “Then he commands,” and so forth. This passage is read in different ways, though with the same meaning. “Do your former deeds” is absent from Rabanus but is found in an old codex and in Ambrose. PEREZ.

In the same place. Another reading: *suae lugens cum humilitate* (“mourning his own [state] with humility”). AREV.]

6. Then he commands her to bear her disgrace—that is, the dishonor of her name or dignity—and to return to her former state. Therefore, when someone is ashamed after the deeds that brought him confusion and has humbly borne the disgrace of his deposition, he may, according to the prophet, be recalled to his former condition. Likewise, the evangelist John writes something similar, among other things, to the angel of the church at Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and do your former deeds; otherwise I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place” (Revelation 2:5).

7. By “the angel of the church” he certainly indicates the one placed over the church—that is, [Col. 0900C] the priest—in accordance with Malachi, who says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and the law is sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). Therefore, the superior who has fallen into vice is admonished through the evangelist to remember from where he has fallen, to do penance, and to perform his former deeds, so that his lampstand may not be removed.

[Col. 0901A] [Note: [Col. 0901D]

8. Others read: “for the lampstand of the angel is doctrine,” and so forth. Also, *mentisque* (“and of the mind”), instead of *meritorumque* (“and of merits”). The Vulgate reads: “His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see,” and “before the lamp of God was extinguished,” and so forth. AREV.]

8. For the lampstand is understood as the priestly teaching or the honor of the authority that he bears, in accordance with what is written concerning the condemnation of Eli in Samuel: “His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished” (1 Samuel 3:2). The lamp of God had been that man who, possessing priestly dignity, shone with the brightness of righteousness; the prophet declares that it was extinguished when, because of the crimes of his sons, he lost the authority of the priesthood and the light of his merits. Therefore, according to John, the lampstand or lamp of the priest—which signifies the gifts of honor—is completely extinguished or removed when, after the fall into sin, the admitted crimes are not mourned because penance has been neglected.

9. For he does not say, “Because you have fallen, I will move your lampstand,” but, “Unless you repent, I will move your lampstand.” Therefore, for every sinful superior, if repentance for the offense comes first, [Col. 0901B] forgiveness and restoration of merit necessarily follow. And it is written in Proverbs: “Whoever conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

10. Moreover, the very rule by which the judgment of the canons commands a penitent to return to his former state after seven years was established by the holy Fathers not according to their own choice or discretion, but rather on the basis of the judgment of divine justice. For we read that when Mary, the sister of Moses the prophetess, incurred the sin of speaking against Moses, she was immediately covered with the mark of leprosy. When Moses asked that she be cleansed, God commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, [Col. 0901C] after her correction, to be admitted into the camp again (Numbers 12).

11. Mary, therefore, the sister of Aaron, is understood as the flesh of the priest. When it gives itself over to pride and is stained by the foulest contagions of corruption, it is cast outside the camp for seven days—that is, outside the fellowship of Holy Church for seven years—and after the cleansing of its vices it receives again the merit of its place or former dignity.

12. Behold, insofar as I have been able, I have clearly explained through sacred testimonies the ancient and fully authoritative judgment of the Council of Ancyra. I have shown that the person who knows how to mourn his own offenses through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his proper honor; but the person who neither grieves over what he has done, but commits what ought to be mourned without any religious shame or fear of divine judgment, [Col. 0901D] cannot in any way be restored to his former rank.

13. At the end of this letter I thought it should be added that whenever a conflicting judgment is found in the acts of councils, the judgment of that council should be followed which possesses the more ancient or more authoritative [Col. 0902A] standing. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our most glorious lord, King Witteric.

## LETTER V. ISIDORE TO HELLADIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS

566 To my lords and servants of God, Helladius and the other bishops who are assembled with him, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0901D]

LETTER V, no. 1. The word *Hispalensem* (“of Seville”) may be redundant. PEREZ.

In the same place. Some strongly doubt whether this letter is genuine. The arguments supporting its genuineness may be seen in *Isidoriana*, chapter 74, no. 1 and following; these may also assist in explaining the letter. AREV.]

1. We are moved by tears and pierced by the goads of our sins when we recognize the ruin of a brother, because just as salvation brings joy, so danger to the soul brings groaning. For we have learned that the bishop of the church of Córdoba, a man of Seville, has fallen through carnal defilement from the summit of the episcopate and has been plunged from the height of honor into the mournful depths of shameful deeds. Since pastoral concern rests upon you and divine judgment has ordained that the errors of offenders be examined by your decision, [Col. 0902B] saying, “The priests shall stand in my judgments, and they shall judge between the holy and the polluted” (Ezekiel 44:24), therefore, recognizing this word of the Lord, with an outpouring of tears we beseech Your Holiness that, once this fallen man has been presented to your holy assembly and his confession has been acknowledged by you, he be deposed from the rank of the priesthood by synodal judgment.

2. It is better for him to be judged by you temporarily than to be condemned by eternal judgment. The disgrace of the present time is lighter for him than the future torments of Gehenna. For he should know that he has lost the name and office of priest because he has lost the merit of holiness. Therefore, by the decree of your judgment, let him lament the crimes he has committed with perpetual mourning in penance; let him mourn the dignity of the priesthood, which he lost by living badly; let him grieve [Col. 0902C] the condition of his soul, which he has defiled with so great a mire of corruption. Perhaps the Holy Spirit will at some time extend a hand to him, so that through worthy satisfaction he may deserve forgiveness of sins. For me also, most holy priests, I beg you to pray that you may deign to entreat divine mercy, so that, forgetful of my evils, by which I too have fallen, God may release me from the bonds of the sins with which I have remained bound until now and grant me the fruit of pardon through your merits.

## LETTER VI. ISIDORE TO CLAUDIUS, DUKE

567 To Claudius, beloved son in Christ, duke, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0902D]

LETTER VI, no. 1. Gregory writes to this Claudius in Book VII of the *Register*, letter 124. PEREZ.

In the same place. Most people, especially the heterodox, assert that Isidore’s letter to Claudius is not genuine. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 74, no. 9 and following, I have presented arguments by which this letter is attributed to Isidore, and I have also explained many matters by which the same letter can be illuminated. AREV.]

1. Receiving the notes of your Catholic zeal, we praise exceedingly the omnipotence of our Lord Jesus Christ, who [Col. 0902D] in the present graciously grants His holy Church to triumph over its enemies through the prosperity of your successes and victories. Since your earnest petitions urge me to answer your inquiries, I rejoice in the Lord, because you diligently investigate matters concerning the Catholic faith. To your first objection, therefore, setting aside many arguments, we respond to you reasonably and simply.

2. This is how we understand that we ought to preside over the Church of Christ: we acknowledge that, above all the other prelates of the Church, we owe and must render complete obedience to the Roman pontiff, reverently, humbly, and devoutly, as to the vicar of God. We decree that anyone who insolently acts against this is altogether [Col. 0903A] excluded from the fellowship of the faithful as a heretic. We hold this firmly, and believe it to be established and ratified, not by our own choice or discretion, but rather by the authority of the Holy Spirit.

3. But if someone—God forbid—is secretly unfaithful, our obedience is harmed in no respect unless he commands something contrary to the faith. Moreover, the Lord commands obedience to wicked prelates in their good commands, when He says: “Do what they say,” while He orders their wicked deeds to be avoided by adding: “But do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3). In doubtful commands also, obedience is owed to wicked prelates as long as the Church tolerates them, unless, from the prelate’s manifest ill repute, suspicion of heresy may justly arise in the command. The same seems to apply to similar entanglements. Manifestly evil commands are not to be obeyed under any circumstances, even when issued by good prelates, because sometimes God conceals from the greater what He reveals to the lesser.

[Note: [Col. 0903D]

4. “The objection of certain Greeks,” and so forth. From this an argument is drawn that Isidore was not the author of this letter, but someone much later. In the cited passage I have attempted to answer this difficulty satisfactorily. AREV.]

4. You also took care to inform us of the objection of certain Greeks: it is read that the Council of Nicaea or Constantinople prohibited under anathema [Col. 0903C] any diminution or addition in the Creed and in that statement of Saint Athanasius concerning the Catholic faith. For this reason, some Greeks insolently attempt to criticize the Latins, because in the profession of holy faith they sing with heart and mouth to God: “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son,” whereas in the aforesaid councils it was written, “who proceeds from the Father,” and the holy Roman Church approves and believes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

5. If the prohibition mentioned above is examined carefully and correctly, every ambiguity is removed. For when it prohibited adding or diminishing, it understood this as referring to a contrary matter; to this judgment the Apostle’s statement corresponds: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received from us, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9). The Apostle John [Col. 0903D] also says: “If anyone comes to you and brings another doctrine, do not receive him, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him” (2 John 10). By saying “another doctrine,” he wished, without ambiguity, to indicate that the matter concerned the opposition of doctrine, warning against heresy.

6. The apostles, martyrs, and orthodox teachers of the Church preached many other things; but because these were not contrary, the apostolic prohibition is not understood to oppose them, since they tend toward the one [Col. 0904A] end of truth. Since, therefore, the same judgment is clearly established concerning similar matters, it is beyond doubt that the prohibitions of the aforesaid judgments must be understood as referring to the opposition of heresies.

7. Let us demonstrate more clearly through the testimonies of Holy Scripture that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son, and is sent by the Father and by the Son, and proceeds from both. These are the Apostle’s words: “If the Spirit of Him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you,” and so forth (Colossians 2:12). And elsewhere: “God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts” (Galatians 4:6). It is manifest from the apostolic words that the Holy Spirit belongs to God the Father who raises from the dead and to God the Son who is raised. He is not to be believed in and worshiped as three gods, but as one, just as Moses testifies: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

8. That the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father, the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send [Col. 0904B] in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). And that He is sent by the Son, the Truth itself says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26). These passages therefore fully declare that the mission of the Holy Spirit is from the Father and from the Son. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is shown when it is said: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26); and from the Son, when after His resurrection He breathed upon His disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

9. Isaiah also says in the person of the Father: “The Spirit will go forth from my face.” The word or face of God the Father is His Only-Begotten Son, for a human being is recognized by us through the face, and God the Father became known to the world through the [Col. 0904C] Son. Hence the Son says: “Father, I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me” (Isaiah 57:16). And: “I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known” (John 17:6, 26). We could introduce many more passages to prove this at greater length; but perhaps much will not benefit the person to whom these things are insufficient for, since the merely natural man does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), judging what is said to be foolishness. And because this certainly arises from contempt born of ignorance, the ignorant person will remain unknown.

10. When we distinguish the persons of the Holy Trinity in speech, let us take the greatest care not to appear to divide the undivided [Col. 0904D] and utterly simple essence of the one God. But as for what it means for the Father to generate in an ineffable manner, for the Son to be born, generated, or go forth in an immeasurable manner, and for the Holy Spirit to be sent or proceed from the Father and the Son in an incomprehensible manner, along with the other things of this kind that are said concerning the distinction of the persons: if we do not grasp them with the mind, let us grasp them by faith, so that we may deserve to be saved forever.

11. Behold, in the brevity I have been able to achieve, I have answered your inquiries. But concerning what you added—that you have heretics with whom you dispute continually and whom you strive to recall to the Catholic faith—we praise your zeal but condemn your boldness. For divine Scripture says: [Col. 0905A] “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclesiasticus 13:1). Therefore, dearest son, take care: because God has made you victorious through the valor of your arms, having struck down your enemies with triumphal trophies, do not, to your disgrace, be defeated and succumb to the persuasions of heretics. While you labor to rescue them from the error of death, they themselves are watchful to plunge you into the precipice of error. Under threat of divine judgment, we command every Christian to abstain from their conversation or companionship as from deadly poison, unless they have been proved by the experience of their deeds in the divine commandments and instructed in the sacred Scriptures.

12. Therefore, before God, we testify, admonish, and command with all the exhortation we can offer that, as quickly as possible, exercising zeal for the law of God, you drive them away from you unless they profess the Catholic [Col. 0905B] truth. Do not delay to send us in writing their statements and objections. With God as our witness, we embrace your brotherly affection more dearly in the depths of Jesus Christ; and, as God grants us ability, we shall determine each matter for the salvation of your soul and the honor of your body, supporting our judgments with sacred authorities, so that falsehood may yield to truth, the glory of Christ’s Church may be strengthened, and it may increase. Remember our common teacher Leander, and imitate his faith and teaching to the best of your ability, so that in the present you may enjoy good things and in the future be able to attain a share in heavenly goods. Amen. Pray for me; may the Lord grant that, with the integrity of your soul, body, faith, and honor preserved, I may henceforth deserve to see you, my lord and dearest son.

## LETTER VII. ISIDORE TO REDEMPTUS, ARCHDEACON

[Col. 0905C]

To Redemptus, beloved son in Christ, archdeacon, Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0905D]

LETTER VII. This letter to Redemptus appears much more suspect to most people. In *Isidoriana*, at the passage cited above, I have set forth everything relevant to its elucidation and have proposed arguments by which it may be attributed to Isidore. AREV.]

1. Encumbered by many affairs—not only ecclesiastical but also those of this perishing kingdom—we are presently unable to answer the questions of Your Charity as we desire. Yet, because charity makes us debtors to everyone, insofar as I am able I comply with your affection, prepared to respond briefly to what you have asked. You have made known to us that you are troubled by a scruple: the Eastern Church is accustomed to celebrate the sacrament of the most sacred Body using leavened bread, while the Western Church uses [Col. 0905D] unleavened bread; and because the Easterners do not hesitate to criticize the Latins on this matter, this too has taken root in your mind: they provide silk cloths, whereas we provide linen cloths, which we call corporals, as adornments for so great a sacrifice.

2. Know, then, that we in no way oppose these customs by an obstacle of criticism, so long as the Roman Church has judged that they should be tolerated, especially since they do not belong to the essence or substance of the sacrament. The substance of the sacrament consists in the words of God spoken by the priest in the sacred ministry—namely, “This is my body”—and in bread made from wheat and wine, to which [Col. 0906A] water is customarily added, because blood and water, that is, both, flowed from Christ’s side. The other matters pertain to the dignity of the sacrament, to an example of things to come, to our humiliation and theirs, and to the exercise of praise of God. Once the consecration of the aforesaid elements has taken place, it is not the case, as some unlearned people think, that under the appearance of bread alone the flesh of Christ is received, and in the chalice only His blood; rather, in both is received God and man, the whole and complete Christ in His glorified body—the whole Christ in the chalice, the living bread that descended from heaven, wholly present in both.

3. He is the bread that refreshes and does not diminish; the bread that is received whole by each person and is diminished in none of its parts; visible to the angels, yet believed by us with unwavering faith to be wholly present, miraculously and invisibly, in each communicant. In the fullness of His essence He always reigns visibly in heaven. But because the Easterners, by shamelessly disparaging and criticizing the customs of the Romans—that is, our [Col. 0906B] customs—strive to assail them through the destructive force of reproach, we shall take up the weapons of the divine oracle and, insofar as we can, rise to defend those customs with truth going before us.

4. For when our Lord Jesus Christ entrusted His disciples with the mystery of His body to be performed, He is not read to have taken either leavened or unleavened bread; rather, He took bread and gave it to His disciples, saying: “This is my body; do this whenever you receive it in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Yet we read that the Lord commanded Moses that the Passover should be eaten with unleavened bread and wild lettuce, and that anyone among the Hebrews in whose possession leavened bread was found during the seven days of Passover should be put to death [Col. 0906C] (Exodus 12). Therefore, our Lord celebrated the Passover according to the law, and at the supper He gave His body to His disciples to eat under the appearance of bread and wine, and He granted them the power to consecrate the same, and offered unleavened bread, with which the Passover was celebrated.

5. Likewise, His most sacred body is not read to have been wrapped in silk or woolen cloths, but in clean linen cloths at His burial. Therefore, those who daily offer on the altar the mystery of His passion and burial cannot deviate from the right path when they strive to celebrate, according to the custom of the Roman Church, the most holy sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood with unleavened bread, wine and water, together with clean and holy linen cloths. The Lord also appears to favor us in Exodus, saying: [Col. 0906D] “You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice over leaven”—

6. The same issue concerns the wooden, earthenware, or metal vessel in which the sacrifice is offered. Since none of the evangelists explicitly shows what kind it was, it seems preferable to have recourse to the authority of the law, because in the ministry of the tabernacle or the house of God no vessels anointed with the oil of sacred unction are read to have been [Col. 0907A] wooden or earthenware; rather, they were made of metal. The Lord also commanded that the better things be offered to Him and ordered the tabernacle of testimony to be adorned with the utmost care and with the marvelous beauty of gold and silver. What of Solomon’s temple? In truth, the same applies. If God wished those ceremonial things—which were shadows of the future truth, in which the flesh or blood of animals was sacrificed—to enjoy such splendor, how much more ought the sacred altar and holy vessel, in which the Truth itself, namely the Only-Begotten God, is offered daily to God the Father, to be adorned with diligence and care, with what honor, reverence, glory, and beauty!

7. It is plainly evident that to offer so immeasurable a sacrifice in an earthen or wooden vessel, unless pressing necessity or compelling poverty requires it, is shameful, base, presumptuous, and reckless—something that may rightly be rejected after examination. But perhaps you object that silk cloth is more precious than linen and therefore more suitable for divine uses. To this we reply, from both Testaments, that the whiteness of garments is especially approved, because purity of mind is required in it; and this is plainly more pleasing to God than all other virtues. To your charity, which desires to attain it, we shall make this clearer by the testimonies of sacred Scripture.

8. For Scripture says: “Let your garments be white at all times,” and the priests of the Lord wore the linen ephod above their other garments as a mark of excellence. The Gospel also plainly testifies, in the account of the Lord’s Transfiguration, that the Lord’s garments appeared like snow. In the Apocalypse, those who stood in the presence of the Lamb and those who follow him wherever he goes are said to be clothed in white robes, along with very many other examples. What cloth is clean like linen, whose whiteness is increased by frequent washing, whereas silk seems rather to be darkened by the same treatment? Yet do not understand purity of mind to exist wherever unbelief flourishes; for “there is no fellowship between Christ and Belial.”

9. As for the grammatical incongruity of the expression found in the Old or New Testament, we reply that the words of the heavenly oracle are not subject to the rules of Priscian or Donatus. Although analogy must be understood, usage is above all to be followed. Provided that the meaning does not depart from the truth, one must in no way withdraw from the footsteps of the holy Fathers. You see clearly, dearest son, toward which side you ought to incline the understanding of your mind, and you should entirely lay aside your scruple on this matter. Examine everything carefully, and you will find that the customs of the holy Roman Church deviate in no respect whatsoever from divine authorities. Please deign to pray for me to the Lord.

## LETTER VIII. ISIDORE TO EUGENIUS, BISHOP

[Col. 0908A]

To Eugenius, a most beloved and illustrious bishop in virtues: Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0907D]

LETTER VIII, no. 1. This Eugenius was the second successor of Justus. PEREZ.

I said in the work *Isidoriana*, chapter cited, §74, no. 32, that there is less reason to doubt this letter than the preceding one to Redemptus, but with this qualification: I ultimately concluded that the four letters mentioned above—to Claudius, Helladius, Redemptus, and Eugenius—are at least doubtful. To obtain a suitable meaning, perhaps one should read *jure mediante cassetur* (“let it be annulled by due process”), followed by “the orthodox Fathers,” etc. AREV.]

1. On receiving the letters of your holiness through the messenger Verecundus, we gave thanks to the Creator of all things, who deigns to preserve the health of your mind and body for his holy Church. We also beg, being prepared to answer as far as our ability permits the matters you have asked about, that through the support of your prayers the Lord may raise us up from the afflictions that oppress us. Yet because your venerable fraternity compelled me to respond to certain questions—although we do not fail to recognize your learning—the entanglement of a higher judgment cannot at all be disentangled by a lower one except by an act of dispensation; rather, what has been put forward by an inferior is rightly annulled by a superior through due process. The orthodox Fathers, with the authority of the Holy Spirit preceding them, enacted this; but if anyone asserts otherwise, as your prudence well knows, a perverse thing will arise: “the axe boasting against the one who cuts with it” (Isaiah 10:15).

2. As for the equality of the apostles, Peter takes precedence over the others, because he deserved to hear from the Lord: “You shall be called Cephas; you are Peter” (John 1:42), and so forth. He was the first to receive the honor of the pontificate in the Church of Christ, not from anyone else but from the Son of God and the Virgin himself. After the Son of God’s resurrection, the same Lord also said to him: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:15), designating the prelates of the churches by the name of lambs. Although the dignity of his power has been transferred to all Catholic bishops, it remains more specially, by a singular privilege, with the Roman bishop, as with the head, forever higher than the other members.

3. Therefore, whoever does not reverently render him the obedience due to him, separated from the head, makes himself liable to the schism of the Acephali. Just as the holy Church approves and guards that statement of Saint Athanasius concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity as though it were an article of the Catholic faith—“unless each person believes this faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved”—so too I have briefly set these matters before your most sweet charity, mindful of the philosopher’s saying that little is sufficient for the wise.

## LETTER IX. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO, BISHOP

[Col. 0908D]

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio the bishop: Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0908D]

LETTER IX, no. 1. No one would deny that Isidore’s letters to Braulio, and Braulio’s to him, are genuine. AREV.]

1. With every desire I have desired to see your face now; would that God might at some time fulfill my wish before I die. For the present, however, I beg you to commend me to God in your prayers, that he may fulfill my hope in this life and grant me a share in your blessedness in the life to come. And in his own hand: Pray for us, most blessed lord and brother.

## LETTER X. BRAULIO, BISHOP, TO ISIDORE

To my lord and truly lord, the elect of Christ, Isidore, supreme among bishops: Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

[Note: [Col. 0909D]

LETTER X, no. 1. It should be noted that Isidore is called “supreme among bishops” in the heading of the letter. Some copies have *exigentibus* (“demanding circumstances”) instead of *ingruentibus* (“pressing upon me”) and add: “and also pestilence, the plague of mortality,” etc. On this letter, see *Isidoriana*, chapters 21 and 48. AREV.]

1. O pious lord and most distinguished of men, my inquiry has come late, and the opportunity to write has been granted me tardily, because, with my sins pressing upon me, I have been hindered by a terrible assault—not only by the evil of barrenness or poverty, but also by pestilence and hostility—from making inquiry.

[Note: [Col. 0909D]

2. *Gravedine*. Another reading: *gravitudine*. AREV.]

2. Now, although worn down by a thousand necessities and a thousand cares, after a long period of misery, as though awakened—so to speak—from the heaviness of an evil sleep, I presume to offer the service of greeting through the words of this petition. Prostrate in humility of heart and body, I beseech the exalted power of your blessedness to order that you continue to hold as commended to you, until the end, your particular servant, whom you have always received with that pious gaze of sacred condescension.

[Note: [Col. 0909D]

3. Others have: “such as the books of the *Etymologies*, which we hear have been completed,” etc. AREV.]

3. For I too—Christ knows it—am tortured by grievous sorrow because, after so long a period has passed, I still do not deserve to see your presence. But I hope in him who does not forget to show mercy and does not reject forever, because he will hear the prayer of the poor and will present me, miserable as I am, to your sight. I earnestly petition and beg with every kind of supplication that, mindful of your promise, you order the book of the *Etymologies*, which we have now heard has been completed, with the Lord’s favor, to be sent to your servant. For, as I am conscious, you have labored greatly there at the request of your servant. Therefore be generous first toward me; so may you be considered blessed and foremost among the assemblies of the saints.

4. I also beg that the acts of the synod, in which Sintharius, though not purified by the fire of your examination, is nevertheless found to have been boiled down, be sent to us quickly, at your prompting, by your son, our lord the king. For our petition also sought his glory in this matter, since much is needed in the council for the investigation of the truth. For the rest, I implore the mercy of the Most High Creator, that he order the crown of your blessedness to be preserved for a long time for the integrity of the faith and the condition of his Church; and that the most sacred Trinity, through your intercession, make me secure amid the various and countless dangers of the present world, and, hidden in the bosom of your memory, keep me safe from every storm of sin through your prayer. And in his own hand: I, Braulio, servant of the Lord, to Isidore: May I enjoy you in the Lord, burning and unfading lamp!

## LETTER XI. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO, BISHOP

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio the bishop: Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0909D]

LETTER XI, no. 1. *Pittacium*. In the Isidorian Glosses, *pictatium*: a short and modest letter. *Pictatiuncula*: a small piece of parchment. For the word *pittacium*, Riscus cites Saint Augustine, Sermon 178, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 7; Ducange cites others. Perhaps one would not be far wrong in saying that the Spanish word *pedazo*, “fragment” or “part of something,” derives from *pittacium*. AREV.]

1. Because I learned that you were safe, I gave thanks to Christ; and would that I might behold and see the one whose well-being I learned of in this body! But what has happened to me because of my sins I shall explain. I was not worthy to read through your words as soon as I received your little note. A royal boy came to me; I gave that note to my chamberlain; and immediately I went to the prince, intending to read it afterward and write back.

2. When I returned from the royal palace, I found not only that your writing was missing, but also that whatever else had been on the papers had perished. And therefore, the Lord knows, I lamented my misfortune, because I did not read through your message. But I beg you: whenever an opportunity arises, write back to me. Do not take away the grace of your word, so that what I lost through my own fault I may receive again through your favor. And in his own hand: Pray for us, most blessed lord.

## LETTER XII. BRAULIO, BISHOP, TO ISIDORE

To my lord and truly lord, the elect of Christ, Isidore, supreme among bishops: Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.

[Note: [Col. 0910D]

LETTER XII, no. 1. In the heading of the letter, some copies have *Christoque* (“and Christ’s”) here and elsewhere instead of *Christique*. For *portaque*, as the manuscript copies display it, Grialius printed *portuque* (“and harbor”), perhaps by mistake. AREV.]

1. The inner and spiritual person is usually filled with joy when he conducts an inquiry on behalf of one whom he loves. Therefore, my most reverend lord, this is my desire, unless the wall of my sins obstructs it: that you kindly receive my inquiry and patiently accept the accusation contained in my complaints. I am doing both things—fulfilling the duty of inquiry and directing to you, against you, the necessities of my case. I beg your apostolic eminence to admit this most kindly to your hearing; at the entrance of this composition and gate, prostrate, I ask it. And although an accusation may falter where the mediation of tears is present—for tears are not signs of accusation—still I wish there to be both tearful accusations and accusatory tears. But both are offered through the bold presumption permitted by love, not through the recklessness of arrogance. Now I shall begin my case.

2. The seasons, if I am not mistaken, have completed their seventh year since I remember asking you for the books you composed, the *Origins*. In various and differing ways you have frustrated me when I was present, while when absent you have written nothing in reply. By subtle delay, sometimes saying that they were not yet finished, sometimes that they had not yet been written, sometimes that my letters had gone astray, and offering many other excuses, we have reached this day, and remain without the result of our request. Because of this I too shall turn my prayers into a complaint, so that what I could not obtain by supplication I may perhaps gain by provoking an accusation. For a beggar’s shouting often proves useful.

[Note: [Col. 0911D]

3. *Calumniantem* (“making an accusation”), from the Ovetus Gothic text; *clamitantem* (“shouting”), in the Roman manuscript. PEREZ.]

3. Therefore, I ask you, my lord, why do you not grant what you are asked for? Know this: I shall not give up, as though pretending that I do not want what has been denied. I shall seek, and seek persistently, until I receive or elicit it, at the command of the most merciful Redeemer: “Seek, and you shall find,” and, in addition, “Knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Luke 11:9). I have sought, and I seek; I also knock. Hence I shout, so that you may open. For I am consoled by the discovery of this argument: you who have disregarded the one asking may perhaps hear the one making an accusation.

[Note: [Col. 0911D]

4. From the Ovetus Gothic text; only the word *stulti* (“of a fool”) has been changed in the style. PEREZ.

In the same place, others have: “nor by foolish boasting.” And *famulis* (“servants”) instead of *familiis* (“households”). For *famis* (“hunger”), perhaps *fame* (“by hunger”). AREV.]

4. Thus I too press upon your knowledge, yet I do not foolishly presume, through boastfulness of style, to suggest anything new to one who is perfect. Yet I am not ashamed, though unlearned, to speak to the most eloquent, remembering the apostolic command by which you are instructed willingly to bear with the foolish. Therefore, receive the cries of my accusation. Why do you continue to withhold the distribution of the talents and the dispensing of the provisions entrusted to you? Now open your hand; share them with your households, lest they perish from want and hunger. You know what the creditor will demand from you when he comes. Whatever you give us will not be diminished for you. Remember the multitude fed with a few loaves, and the fragments left over, greater in quantity than the loaves.

5. Do you think that the gift bestowed upon you was given for you alone? It belongs to you and to us; it is common, not private. Who, unless insane, would dare say that you should enjoy as private what you know may be enjoyed blamelessly only as common? Since God has permitted you to hold the stewardship of his treasure and of the riches of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge, why do you not pour out with a generous hand what is not diminished by being given? When, among the members of the heavenly Head, each person possesses in another what he himself has not received, so that he knows that what he has is to be possessed by another, are you perhaps sparing toward us because you find nothing that you can receive back from us in return?

[Note: [Col. 0912D]

6. Others have: “in one joint.” AREV.]

6. But if you give to one who has, you receive the fruit of only a very small reward. If, however, you give to one who does not have, you fulfill the evangelical commands, so that it may be repaid to you in the recompense of the righteous. Therefore I too am stung in conscience, because I find no good in myself that can be shared, since we are commanded through charity to serve one another, and each person is to administer to another the grace he has received, “as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Peter 4:10). Each person, according to the measure of faith God has allotted, ought to communicate it to the other parts in one united structure of members, because all these things are performed by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (Romans 12:3).

7. But I return to the one particular remedy I mentioned earlier: namely, friendly persistence toward those deprived of friendship and adorned with none of the grace of honorable members. Therefore hear my voice across all the lands that lie between us. Give back, give back what you owe. For you are a servant, a servant of Christ and of Christians, so that you may be greater there than all of us; and because the grace of the present has been bestowed upon you for our sake, may you not disdain to distribute it to minds that thirst and are tormented by hunger for knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0912D]

8. *Nec te me non egerere*. The Codex Caesenas has *nec te me non egere*. Either way, the wording appears corrupt. AREV.]

8. At least I am not a foot, able to run about at commands and, by the activity of obedience, serve the belly of the Church—that is, the judge of the members—or please the command of the head by obeying it. Yet even if I know that I am one of the more dishonorable members, let it suffice that what you plainly received from the head should worthily be discharged through me; and do not fail to discharge it through me, although I am very small, yet redeemed by the blood of Christ. For the head does not say to the feet, “You are not necessary to me,” since those members of the body that seem weaker are more necessary, and those thought to be less honorable we surround with greater honor, while our less honorable members possess greater dignity.

9. Thus our Creator and steward arranges all things: when the divine gifts that one person does not perceive in himself are entrusted to another for possession, charity is increased. Indeed, manifold grace is then well dispensed when the gift received is entrusted also to those who do not possess it, when it is considered to have been given for the sake of the one to whom it is imparted. Your charity’s prudence well knows that this entire passage of the Apostle, which we have cited in part above, applies perfectly to this matter; and none of what I have touched upon in summary is hidden from you, who surely know it better.

10. Thus only this remains, and this I earnestly ask: grant what is requested, if not for my sake, at least for the sake of charity itself, which has been bestowed by God. For through it we are commanded both to know and to perform all things, and without it all things are nothing. But if I have poured out anything superfluous, anything carelessly, anything less humbly, or rather uselessly than I ought to have spoken, I beg you kindly to receive everything, forgive everything, and pray for everything, so that God may forgive. I therefore also make this known: the books of the *Etymologies*, which I ask of you, my lord, are already possessed by many, though mutilated and gnawed away.

[Note: [Col. 0912D]

11. Perhaps *dicantur* (“are said”) should be read instead of *dicuntur* (“are said”).]

11. Therefore I ask you to deign to send me complete copies of them, corrected and properly joined together, lest, seized by eagerness, I be forced to take faults for virtues from others. For my part, although you need nothing, I desire that your benevolence command us to do what we can and are able to do—for it is said that voluntary services become putrid—so long as you make use of our service, or rather enjoy the charity that is God.

[Note: [Col. 0912D]

12. *Reseras*. That is, “you open.” AREV.]

12. When these matters have been completed, I shall have questions about the sacred and divine books, whose interpretation the light of your heart would disclose to me, if you would also order it to shine upon us and open the obscurities of divine law. Nor, if I obtain what I ask for here, shall I remain silent about those matters; rather, you open the way for the confidence I need to acquire. Since at this first stage you have not pierced me with the goads of shame and my own sluggishness, and have given room for pardon, you have not ordered the one whom you loved, however undeserving, to be rejected—for it seems exceedingly shameful and base if someone, not yet satisfied with charity, is found to withdraw from the one he loved.

13. In return for the service of my servitude I pay the obligations of greeting, and I ask the mercy of your most holy power that you deign to pray for me, so that through your intercession you may daily win for yourself my soul, tossed about amid evils, and lead it to the harbor of eternal tranquility, rescued from miseries and scandals. It was sweet for me to speak to you at length, as though I were present and saw the face of your countenance. Therefore I did not avoid verbosity, and perhaps I incurred recklessness. But I had to do this or something else, so long as what you were unwilling to grant through humility you might at least grant through my tumultuous persistence.

[Note: [Col. 0913C]

14. The old manuscripts have *de curam*, by abbreviation, instead of *misericordiae curam* (“care of mercy”). PEREZ.]

14. Behold how much boldness the grace of your benevolence has given me. Therefore, if anything in this has displeased you, let it blame itself, since it loves so greatly that it removes fear. “Perfect charity casts out fear.” Relying also on this special grace, I address my special lord, in whom the strength of the holy Church resides: since our metropolitan Eusebius has died, take care of mercy. Also make this request to your son, our lord, so that he may appoint to that place a useful man whose learning and holiness may be an example of life to the others. I commend this son, who is present, in every respect to your most blessed power, and may we deserve through him to be enlightened by your words both concerning what we have suggested here and concerning what we have complained of above.

## LETTER XIII. ISIDORE TO BRAULIO, BISHOP

To my lord and servant of God, Braulio the bishop: Isidore.

1. The letter of your holiness found me in the city of Toledo. For I had been summoned because of a council. But although the prince’s order, while I was on the road, had instructed me to return, I nevertheless preferred not to interrupt the course of my journey, because I was nearer to his presence than to the point of returning. I came into the presence of the prince and found your deacon there. Through him I received your message, embraced it, and read it, and I gave thanks to God for your well-being. With every desire I long to see you; although weak and weary, I nevertheless have confidence through Christ of seeing you in this life, because hope does not disappoint through the charity that has been poured into our hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0913C]

LETTER XIII, no. 2. Others have *prae valitudine* (“because of illness”) and *studueram* (“I had endeavored”) instead of *statueram* (“I had determined”). Compare *Isidoriana*, chapter 48, nos. 7 and following, where I conjectured that one should read: “if you had reached the appointed place of the council.” Isidore, it seems, had been summoned to some council of Toledo that was not held for some reason. Perhaps this would be the place to add a note about the medical letter falsely attributed to our Isidore, which I discussed in *Isidoriana*, chapter 75, no. 3; but since it certainly does not belong to our Isidore and is so corruptly copied in the Vatican manuscript cited there, it seems not worth the effort to reproduce it. AREV.]

2. I sent the codex of the *Etymologies*, together with other codices, from the road. Although it was uncorrected because of my illness, I had nevertheless intended to offer it to you for correction, if I had reached the appointed place of the council. As for the appointment of a bishop for Tarragona, I did not understand the king’s judgment to be what you requested; yet he himself is still uncertain where he should turn his mind with greater assurance. I ask you to deign to become an intercessor for my sins before the Lord, so that through your obtaining it my sins may be erased and my crimes forgiven. Also in his own hand: Pray for us, most blessed lord and distinguished brother.

[Col. 0913]

# THE BOOK OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE, ON THE ORDER OF CREATURES (C, S)*

582 ## CHAPTER ONE. On Faith in the Trinity

[Col. 0913D]

[Note: [Col. 0913D]

CHAPTER I, no. 1. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 23, I showed by many arguments that this work appears to be Isidore’s, and, I believe, adequately dealt with the contrary difficulties. As for my former assertion that I had not found the testimony of Aeneas of Paris, who attributes this work to Isidore, I can no longer make that claim; for afterward I observed that in chapter 94 of Aeneas of Paris’s work *Against the Greeks*, certain words from the book *On the Order of Creatures* are cited under Isidore’s name. In *Isidoriana*, chapter 83, no. 9, I also transcribed Dacher’s, or Acher’s, preface to this book. That preface differs somewhat in the Paris edition of 1655; for example: “We publish and make public for the first time a codex written not far from the author’s age, brought forth from the noble archisterium of our Saint Remigius of Rheims.” In the preface that I published in *Isidoriana*, it reads: “drawn from the monastery,” instead of “brought forth from the archisterium.” In every other respect the two editions agree. In the title of the work I omitted “to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome,” that is, of Zaragoza, being moved by the reasons I explained in *Isidoriana*. All these matters are absent from the Florentine codex. I shall append its variant readings with the diligence and fidelity appropriate, collected by two French priests whom I wish to name in honor and gratitude: Thomas Dendrade and Peter Franc. In the edition of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, prepared by Baluze and Martène, there are some notes, a summary of which I shall not omit. First, these notes observe that Zaragoza could have been called Rome, just as Hericus of Autun said in the *Life of Saint Germanus*:

“Celtic Rome thereafter wished and began to be called.”

But what our judgment is concerning this entire matter remains explained in *Isidoriana*, at the place cited. Now the discrepancy in the reading of the Florentine codex I mentioned is as follows, no. 1: “Let us posit, so as to make equal.” Perhaps: “so as to be made equal.”]

1. The arrangement of the universe must be understood in a twofold manner: in God, namely, and in things—that is, in the Creator and in creatures. This does not mean that we place God as a part of this division or that a creature can be compared with the Creator, but because everything that exists is understood either as made or unmade, either as powerful or subject, either as eternal or temporal. What is made, subject, and temporal is the creature itself. What is unmade, powerful, and eternal is God himself.

[Col. 0915A] 583

[Note: [Col. 0915D]

2. Manuscript: “In every respect inseparable, one divinity in substance, and in the subsistences of the persons an unjoined Trinity … nothing remains future, but all things are present.” Isidore repeats a similar profession concerning the Trinity and the divine attributes elsewhere: for example, at the beginning of Book I of *The Book of Differences of Things*, Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 4; Book I of the *Sentences*, chapters 1, 2, 14, 15, etc.; in the books *On Offices*, and elsewhere.]

2. The Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is in every respect inseparable in substance, that is, one divinity, and an unjoined Trinity in the subsistence of the persons.
