In it nothing inferior, nothing superior, nothing earlier, nothing later in the nature of divinity is to be believed; nothing servile, nothing subject, nothing encompassed by place, nothing temporal, nothing weak, nothing growing, nothing pertaining to sex or bodily appearance, nothing corporeal may rightly be conceived. Rather, it is one God without beginning, eternal without place, wholly everywhere, ordering all mutable things in creatures without changing himself; seeing past, present, and future times equally. For him nothing is past and nothing remains to come, but all things are present. Nothing good displeases him; nothing evil pleases him. No naturally evil thing was created by him, since evil in itself is nothing other than a defect of created good. He is therefore good without quality, great without quantity, eternal without time, preeminent without position. He is infused into all creatures, although no place belongs to him; no creature contains him, and no understanding comprehends him.

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

3. Aeneas of Paris, at the place cited, transcribes this and the following section.]

3. One God Almighty: the Holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. God the Father Almighty derives his origin from nothing, and he himself is the origin of divinity. From him God the Son Almighty is begotten without time—not created, for he is God. Apart from the fact that he is Son, everything in divinity is common to him with the Father: eternity, will, power, and wisdom. Likewise, apart from the fact that he is Father, everything is common to the Father with the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

4. “But from the Father,” etc. Another reading: “but he proceeded from the Father and the Son, to whom,” etc. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is plainly asserted by the Fathers of the Gothic Church and by Isidore in more than one place.]

4. The Holy Spirit is God Almighty. He is not begotten, because he is not the Son; nor created, because he is not a creature, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. Apart from the fact that he is the Holy Spirit, everything is common to him with the Father and the Son. For the person who is the Father is not here the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor is the person who is the Son here the Father or the Holy Spirit; nor is the person who is the Holy Spirit here the Father or the Son. But in essence, what the Father is, the Son and the Holy Spirit are as one; what the Son is, the Father and the Holy Spirit are; and what the Holy Spirit is, the Father and the Son are. Yet the Trinity does not contain a threefold number of gods; for, while the persons remain distinct, the whole of divinity is common.

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

5. “He took flesh,” etc. Manuscript: “He assumed human flesh, which is free from every fault.” Immediately afterward, *excepta divinam naturam* (“except the divine nature”) should be retained instead of *excepta divina natura*. For *in humanitate* (“in humanity”), another reading has *in humana natura* (“in human nature”). Shortly afterward, “he is to be believed, but by power and work.”]

5. In time the Son assumed human flesh, which is free from fault. He possessed human nature, having a rational, intellectual, wise soul, while excepting the divine nature, so that humanity might be complete. Therefore the Son, who is the Son of God the Father without time, assumed it so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might be the Son of man in humanity. In this humanity he was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-Virgin—not because he should be believed to be the Son of the Holy Spirit in the same way as he is the Son of Mary, but because he was conceived through the power and working of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

6. The manuscript has *surrexit* (“rose”) instead of *resurrexit* (“rose again”); shortly afterward, “except that which is not subject to corruption.”]

6. He endured the passion of the cross in the flesh, not in divinity. He suffered death for our redemption and salvation. Buried in a tomb for the space of three days, he rose again in the same flesh by divine power. After instructing the one, holy, catholic Church by his word, strengthening it by his example, establishing it by grace, and fortifying it by peace, he returned to the Father, taking up the whole of human nature except that which is subject to corruption. He had never been absent from the Father, but now he sits at the Father’s right hand. From there he will come in the glory of the Father for the judgment of all human beings who rise again, repaying the impious with eternal punishments and the righteous with eternal rewards.

7. This is the Catholic faith. To believe and confess it is more profitable than to examine it. Neither secular prudence nor worldly philosophy could recognize it, since worldly philosophy follows images of things rather than understanding of the truth. But apostolic faith handed it down, and ecclesiastical vigilance guards it.

## CHAPTER TWO. On Spiritual Creation

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

CHAPTER II, no. 1. “But because creation”; manuscript: “but because spiritual creation.” Further on, “it is evident that they are enclosed below.” In Dacher’s text, in my edition, there is *cluduntur* for *clauduntur*. For “the spirits above,” the manuscript has “the citizens above,” omitting *ministeriorum* (“of ministries”) afterward. For *comprehenduntur* (“are comprehended”), the manuscript has *deprehenduntur* (“are discerned”).]

1. Having said this little about the immensity of the Creator, let us look briefly at the order of creatures. In doing so, we follow not an invention of our own intention, which has no independent existence, but the traces of sacred Scripture and of the explanations handed down by our predecessors, even if only in a slight account. Every creature, then, is either spiritual or bodily. But since creation consists in intellectual spirits, who are not held by flesh, and in the souls of human beings, which are enclosed in flesh, we must first speak of the distinct ranks of the spirits above. Scripture comprehends nine orders of their graces or different ministries: namely, seraphim, cherubim, thrones, dominations, principalities, powers, virtues, archangels, and angels.

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

2. The manuscript has *depicti erant* (“had been depicted”). Dacher has, incorrectly, *depincti*. Below, the manuscript reads: “to have seen the chariot of the cherubim … joins it mystically with wheels … mentioning it, saying, whether thrones or whether …”]

2. Isaiah saw the seraphim standing above the lofty throne of the Lord, and heard them singing; and when one of them was sent to him, he deserved to be cleansed from the pollution of his mouth. The cherubim, fashioned as figures in the sanctuary of the testimony, covered both the mercy seat and the ark; and in the temple of the Lord they had been represented by Solomon together with oxen and lions. Ezekiel also describes himself as having seen in the visions of God a chariot, which he mystically connects with the four symbolic signs of the Scriptures of both Testaments. Writing to the Colossians, the apostle Paul mentions thrones, dominations, principalities, and powers: “whether thrones, or dominations, or principalities, or powers” (Colossians 1:16). He also recounts the virtues in his letter to the Ephesians, saying: “above every principality, and power, and virtue, and domination” (Ephesians 1:21). The fields of the divine books are filled with manifestations and names of archangels and angels.

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

3. Manuscript: “the stones in Ezekiel … the angel of the prophet’s speech is addressed with lamentation; where …” In the printed edition, *quibus* (“with which”) was missing after *ordinibus* (“orders”); I supplied it from the manuscript.]

3. Ezekiel also reveals the significance of these nine orders of citizens above through nine precious stones. There, in the person of the prince of Tyre, the prophet’s words direct a lament over that supreme angel who fell. It is said: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, emerald” (Ezekiel 28:13). He is said to have been covered with these nine stones because he was adorned with the nine orders of spiritual offices over which he presided.

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

4. Manuscript: “every rational creature.” The printed text had *fiant* (“may they become”) instead of *sint* (“are”).]

4. As we have spoken of the number, so let us also disclose something about the distinct ranks of the offices. The seraphim, therefore, are called “burning” or “kindling,” because through a special generosity of the divine gift they burn with the love of God more than every rational creature. And the more they excel all creatures, the more they draw near to the Creator through the privilege of divine charity. They stand exalted in such a height of honor that between themselves and the Lord there are no other spirits.

5. In the second order the cherubim are also counted among the citizens above. The name of this order is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Since their understanding is refreshed by clinging closely to the contemplation of God, it is expanded, through the multitude of knowledge, beyond all intellectual creatures subject to them. For when they gaze more penetratingly upon the mirror of divine brightness, how could the hidden secrets of creatures remain concealed from them?

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

6. “They are interpreted.” Manuscript: “they are called.” And “above these,” instead of “through them.” The manuscript lacks: “And in the revelation … he will defend them.”]

6. In the third order, too, the ranks of the intellectual spirits called thrones have been established; they are interpreted as “seats.” For in them, while the Lord sits by a special gift, through them he exercises his judgments over all creatures in a fearful and wondrous manner. Hence the Psalmist says [Col. 0918B]: “You have sat upon the throne, who judge righteousness” (Ps. 9:5). And in the Revelation of John the angel says: “And he who sits upon the throne will protect them.”

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

7. The manuscript reads: “excel in lofty dominion.”]

7. In the fourth rank of the heavenly offices stand the dominions, which surpass in high dignity the ministries of the five ranks that will be listed below; and in proportion as they are set above the others in greatness of power, so the subjection of the others is rendered to them through obedience. 586

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

8. It omits *Dehinc post illas* (“then after them”). For *ad explenda Dei mysteria* (“to fulfill God’s mysteries”), as it stood in the printed edition, I substituted *ad explenda Dei ministeria* (“to fulfill God’s ministries”).]

8. Then, after them, in the fifth order, the principalities are called the leaders of the heavenly citizens. Since the leadership of the good spirits is now entrusted to them, they preside over the fulfillment of the ministries of God that those subject to them ought to perform.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

9. The manuscript reads: “are ordered, who have received the power to rule over opposing powers … so that they may not exercise savagery more than they are permitted.”]

9. In the sixth rank, the powers are ordered among the good spirits; they have received, by the Lord’s gift, authority to rule over diverse powers. Through this authority they restrain the wickedness of evil spirits, lest, if they are permitted more than is fitting, they dare to exercise their savagery or cling to human senses.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

10. *Ministrationum* (“ministrations”). The manuscript has *dominationum* (“dominions”). And *fiunt* (“are performed”), instead of *factitantur* (“are often performed”).]

10. The virtues are called the seventh rank of spiritual ministrations; through them spiritual powers, signs, and wonders are often performed among human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

11. Perhaps: “there are archangels, who are also called the highest messengers.”]

11. The eighth order consists of archangels—that is, those called the highest messengers—through whom greater matters are announced to human beings. And in proportion as they surpass the angels in the eminence of their order, so, by the Lord’s command, they convey more exalted things to human knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

12. “And common.” The manuscript omits this.]

12. The angels are named as the ninth order of the heavenly ministers. They announce and recommend to human beings, by God’s will, whatever is lesser and common.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

13. The manuscript reads: “it should be understood that whenever … they come, they are said to assume names, because those …” Later the edition has: “Because at the end of the age Antichrist will be sent against him who …” I corrected this from the manuscript, as well as the wording that followed in the edition: “So that he might accomplish what human nature denied would happen.” *Humana* (“human”) seemed superfluous, and this word is absent from the manuscript.]

13. Moreover, it should be understood that whenever these beings are named, they have taken their names from the particular nature of their offices, when they come to human beings; for that supreme fellowship of the heavenly citizens has no need of proper names. Hence Michael is called “Who is like God?” because he is destined to be sent at the end of the age against him who will rise up against God. And Gabriel, that is, “the strength of God,” is recorded as having been sent to Zechariah and to the virgin Mary, so that he who foretold what nature denied would happen might be called “the strength of God.”

[Note: [Col. 0919C]

14. *Divina virtute* (“by divine power”). The manuscript has *divina natura* (“by divine nature”), less appropriately. For *nuncupatur* (“is named”), which I took from the manuscript, the printed book had *nuncuparetur* (“would be named”). The printed edition likewise has “and that which is in the angels individually,” but *angelis* (“in the angels”) should be omitted with the manuscript. Below, for *vicinitate* (“proximity”), the manuscript has *vicinia* (“nearness”).]

14. Raphael, too, is sent to Tobit—that is, “the medicine of God.” Indeed, since he brought healing by divine power, he is not inappropriately called “the medicine of God.” And what can be said of individuals can also be said of the ranks: when one performs the office of another, he may also be regarded under that other’s name, as it is said: “You make your angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4)—that is, “when you will, you make all these spirits angels,” that is, messengers. And sometimes, because of the proximity of other ranks, some ranks assume the offices of others. Thus, because of the proximity of the thrones, the Scriptures also say that the Lord sits above the cherubim; as it is written in the psalm: “You who sit above the cherubim, reveal yourself before Ephraim” (Ps. 79:2). 587

[Note: [Col. 0919D]

15. The printed edition has *sed illa* (“but that”), omitting *in* (“in”). The manuscript reads *in aliquo videt* (“he sees in another”). It also has *et* (“and”), without changing it.]

15. But in that heavenly fellowship, what is possessed individually in a special way is possessed by all in common, because what each one sees in another refreshes him no less than what he possesses in himself. And when they are sent, God, from whom they are refreshed, is never absent from their contemplation—not because those spirits who are sent are able to be everywhere at once, but because the Lord, who is everywhere, is always seen in every place by those who range abroad, without any change in himself. Hence it is written: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10).

[Note: [Col. 0919D]

16. The printed edition corruptly reads “and they are sent to minister.” From the manuscript I also corrected what follows, “as subjects by themselves,” and so forth. I would nevertheless prefer *per se* (“by themselves”) to *pro se*. In the edition these words had been corrupted as follows: “as subjects by themselves for the office of announcing, just as in Daniel … the message, as a saying of a superior,” and so forth.]

16. For the heavenly powers do both things equally: they minister when they are sent, and they stand before him when they contemplate. Sometimes the angels who are sent announce matters themselves to the human beings to whom they come; sometimes they send others, as subjects under their own authority, to announce them. Thus it is written in Daniel: “Gabriel, make this man understand the message” (Dan. 8:16)—words that are unquestionably spoken by someone as if by a superior.

# CHAPTER III. On the waters that are above the firmament

[Col. 0920A]

[Note: [Col. 0919D]

Chapter III, note 1. *Tuae propositionis* (“of your proposition”). From this it would be sufficiently clear that Isidore composed a book *On the Order of Creatures* in order to accommodate someone’s request; this is expressed even more clearly at the end of the published work. However, the Florence manuscript, which lacks that concluding passage, constructs the sentence here in a very different way, namely: “After the spiritual creature, about which we have discoursed briefly, we have attempted to bring forward what the intention of authors has been able to devise concerning the waters that are above the firmament.” I attribute *tentavimus* (“we have attempted”) rather than *tentabimus* (“we shall attempt”) to the error of copyists, since elsewhere *b* was frequently changed into *v*, and conversely *v* into *b*. The edition had *fuisse lux* (“light had been”), instead of *fuisset lux* (“light had been made”). Shortly afterward it had: “the firmament, which divides what is above the firmament and the waters.” I corrected this from the manuscript. By conjecture I restored *locali spatio esse omni creatura corporali superiores* (“to be superior in spatial location to every corporeal creature”), for the edition had *locali spatio ex omni creatura corporali superiores* (“superior in spatial location from every corporeal creature”), while the manuscript reads *locali spatio omni ex corporali creatura esse superiores*. In addition, Isidore discusses the waters that are above the heavens in chapter 14 of his book *On the Nature of Things*, drawing from Saint Ambrose. Likewise, many other matters mentioned in this work are explained partly in *On the Nature of Things* and partly in the *Etymologies*.]

1. But since we have undertaken to speak about the order of creatures, as the contents of your proposition had required, after the spiritual creature, about which we have discoursed briefly, we shall attempt to bring forward what the intention of authors has been able to devise concerning the waters that are above the firmament. For Scripture testifies that, since in the beginning, on the first day, light had been made—and this is recognized as the spiritual creature—on the second day the firmament was made, dividing between the waters that are above the firmament and the waters that are beneath the firmament. From this it is understood that those waters which are above the firmament are, in spatial location, superior to every corporeal creature. 588

[Col. 0920B]

[Note: [Col. 0920D]

2. The manuscript has *inveniantur* (“are found”), whereas the edition has *inveniuntur* (“are discovered”).]

2. For although in the hundred and forty-eighth psalm, after the firmament, the sun, the moon, and the stars, those waters which are above the heavens are found to be placed, nevertheless, in order to show that they are higher than all corporeal creatures, the Psalmist, once again enumerating the abodes of the exalted powers, places the heavens before them, saying: “Praise him, heavens of heavens; and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4).

[Note: [Col. 0920D]

3. *Ut diximus* (“as we said”). The manuscript has *de quibus diximus* (“about which we spoke”). Below, instead of *diceret* (“he might say”), the Prophet has *posuit* (“he placed”); for afterward it continues: “Praise the Lord from the earth.” “Behold these waters,” says the Psalmist, and so forth.]

3. Hence it is shown that after those spiritual regions, whatever they may be, where the spiritual orders dwell, which the prophet calls “the heavens of heavens,” those waters were established before this visible heaven, as if the beginning of corporeal things. Yet, lest anyone should join them to the spiritual creature, he placed them after the heavens of heavens and before speaking of the earth, adding shortly afterward: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses” (ibid., 7).

[Note: [Col. 0920D]

4. The edition has *dixit* (“said”), the manuscript *dicit* (“says”). The manuscript reads: “higher than the corporeal heavens,” which must be said to be prior to the corporeal creatures.]

4. Behold, the Psalmist says that these waters are placed above the heavens, and yet he places the heavens of heavens before them. By this it is demonstrated that they are located between the two kinds of heavens—that is, lower than the spiritual heavens and higher than the corporeal heavens. Nevertheless, they must be said to belong to corporeal creatures, since they were made in the work of the second day and stand above this corporeal firmament.

[Note: [Col. 0921C]

5. The manuscript omits *ibi utilitatis* (“what usefulness there”). For *abolitionem* (“destruction”), the manuscript has *ablutionem* (“washing”), which may perhaps be correct. The same manuscript omits *sicut Geneseos historia narrat* (“as the history of Genesis relates”). Shortly afterward it reads: “all things are conceived from the air of the heavens.” The edition punctuates the passage as: “The heavens will give rain. And the earth will give its fruit.” The manuscript has: “And the heavens will give rain, and the earth will give its fruit.” The psalm cited has only: “The earth gave its fruit.” It is not apparent from where the preceding words have been taken. Jeremiah 14:22 reads: “Are there any among the idols of the nations who give rain? Or can the heavens give showers?” At the end of this section the manuscript has *aestate* (“in summer”) instead of *aestu* (“with heat”), which is not as satisfactory.]

5. But what usefulness they serve in the uses of corporeal things is investigated according to two lines of interpretation by the teachers. Some say that God’s foreknowledge reserved them for the destruction of the earth in the flood that occurred under Noah, as the history of Genesis relates, just as Scripture says: “And the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell for forty days and forty nights” (Gen. 7:11). But since the clouds—from which the showers of rain water the fertility of the earthly soil—and even the air, in which all the hemispheres and breezes are contained, are also often designated by the name “heavens” in the divine Scriptures, as it is said: “He rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven” (Ps. 77:24); and in another place: “The heavens will also give rain, and the earth will give its fruit” (Ps. 66:7), some teachers hold that such an abundance of water was poured out from that lower heaven of clouds that, according to the usual process by which it operates throughout the whole of time, the clouds then too poured forth a great quantity of rain. Yet Scripture mentions that the floodgates were opened because the outpouring of water had been sent in greater measure than usual. Others, however, assert that these same waters were placed above the firmament in order to temper the fire that burns in the luminaries and stars, lest it scorch the regions below with more heat than is sufficient.

# CHAPTER IV. On the firmament of heaven

[Col. 0921C]

[Note: [Col. 0921D]

Chapter IV, note 1. *Dividit* (“divides”). The edition apparently has the erroneous reading *dividi* (“to be divided”). Isidore treats briefly of the firmament in book 13, chapter 4, of the *Etymologies*, and in chapter 13 of *On the Nature of Things*.]

1. After those waters, the firmament appears to occupy the second place in the order of corporeal creatures. It was made on the second day, as we said above, and divides the two groups of waters. Concerning its structure, some theorists have proposed both possibilities: whether, like a disk, it covers the earth from above, or whether, like the shell of an egg, it surrounds the entire enclosed creation on every side.

[Note: [Col. 0921D]

2. The manuscript has *pellem* (“skin”), and “not contrary to both interpretations.” It also has: “and it is not doubted that it can cover the vault.”]

2. For what the Psalmist also mentions concerning it, when he says, “You stretch out the heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103:22), does not conflict with either assertion. For when the skin of an animal covers the flesh of whatever creature it belongs to, it surrounds all its members equally on every side; but when it is cut away from the flesh and stretched out separately, there is no doubt that it can form either a straight or a curved vault.

[Note: [Col. 0921D]

3. The printed edition has *firmamenti cingat* (“surround the firmament”), which makes no sense.]

3. Therefore, whether the firmament covers the earth from above like a tent made of stretched skin, or whether, just as the limbs of an animal are covered by hide, the firmament surrounds the mass of the world on every side, either assertion can be supported without difficulty.

[Note: [Col. 0922D]

4. The edition has *solidum, an firmum* (“solid or firm”) and *deducatur* (“is led”), instead of *deducat* (“leads”). It subsequently omits *ponere* (“to set forth”), along with the following words: “For those among them who prefer the firmament to be empty and penetrable,” without which the sentence would not be complete.]

4. Concerning the position of this firmament also, various authors have put forward their opinions as to whether it is empty and penetrable or solid and firm, as though each were drawing its argument toward these alternatives. I shall set forth their opinions rather than their names, since that is more useful. For those who prefer the firmament to be empty and penetrable bring forward the natures of all the elements in support of their position.

[Note: [Col. 0922D]

5. *Seipsam sufferre* (“to support itself”). So the manuscript, correctly. The printed text has *seipsa sufferri* (“to be supported by itself”). Afterward: *vi aquis subductis fuerit, statim vadit* (“if it has been withdrawn by force from the waters, it immediately goes away”). Perhaps it should be *aquis subductus fuerit* (“if it has been withdrawn from the waters”).]

5. They show no less than they assert that earth is the heaviest of all corporeal creatures. They say that it therefore occupies the lowest place among creatures, because no nature is able to support itself except by itself. Water, however, though we see it as lighter than earth, we find to be heavier than air. For air cannot subsist by itself beneath water; but if, through some force of necessity, it has been withdrawn from its proper regions in some place, it immediately escapes.

[Note: [Col. 0922D]

6. The edition has *deprehenditur* (“is found”), and also “in the matter of the earth,” with the corrupt form *tetrae* (“of the foul earth”). Shortly afterward it has: “if it has been fire, it is directed upward … but … like water, which naturally descends, is shown to be heavier.” It omits *aeris* (“of air”) after *crassioris* (“thicker”) and *cito* (“quickly”) before *evanescit* (“vanishes”). I restored the passage from the manuscript, except that it has *fieri gravior* (“become heavier”) instead of *esse gravior* (“be heavier”).]

6. Fire, too, is found by nature to be above air. This is easily demonstrated even in that fire which burns in earthly matter. For as soon as it has been kindled, it directs its flame upward toward the regions above the air, where its abundance and proper place are; but when extinguished by the surrounding thicker air, it quickly vanishes into the soft air, so that it cannot reach the place proper to its nature. Nevertheless, this shows that the nature of fire, which rises, is lighter than air, just as the nature of water, which descends, is shown to be heavier.

[Note: [Col. 0922D]

7. The manuscript has *supra igneum est* (“is above the fiery region”). Below, *penetrabilibus* (“penetrable”) instead of *penetralius* (“more penetrable”), and *vaporality* instead of *corporeality*; and *fieri* (“to become”) instead of *ibi* (“there”).]

7. For this reason, they also think that the region of the firmament which is above the fire is lighter and thinner, since it is established higher than all the natures we have mentioned. In this region they likewise judge that the light of the shining stars appears unequal because, in that vast space, some of them travel farther away and others nearer. But those who hold this opinion in lower esteem say that above it there is a region more subtle, emptier, and more penetrable than air and fire, and that waters cannot exist there—unless, as those whom we mentioned assert, waters thinner and more subtle than every corporeal substance are located there.

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

8. The manuscript arranges the passage as follows: “What vaporous substance, although the thinnest vaporous substance of waters, could be lighter than the firmament, which would be more subtle and lighter than fire, which is lighter than air, and would become penetrable?” Because of this, therefore, those others [argue] that the firmament is … The edition has *illi aliis* (“to those others”), while the manuscript omits *facilius* (“more easily”) before *putant* (“think”) and *arbitror* (“I think”) before *mittimus* (“we send”).]

8. Others respond to these arguments as follows: “What vaporous substance of waters, however thin, could ever be lighter than the firmament?” Therefore those others more readily think that the firmament consists as something solid and firm, as if cast from the most solid air. They consequently believe that it is called the firmament because it encloses within itself all the regions we have described—solid and empty, light and heavy—and supports the waters placed above it, whatever their nature may be. But since there has been disagreement among so many men concerning such a great and difficult matter, we do not judge that one person’s opinion should be preferred to another’s; rather, we send the reader to the judgment of both sides.

# CHAPTER V. On the sun and moon

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

Chapter V, note 1. The manuscript reads: “in the beginning of Genesis, indeed divine Scripture declares … let Catholic inquiry believe according to sound reason.” Isidore discusses the sun and moon in chapter 15 and following of *On the Nature of Things*, and in book 13, chapter 3 and following, of the *Etymologies*.]

1. Since, in the firmament of heaven, after the appearance of the sea and the earth, two great luminaries were formed, as the Mosaic Law—or rather, divine Scripture—declares at the beginning of Genesis, it is not inappropriate for our discourse, descending from the higher things, to describe the sun and moon immediately after the firmament in the spatial order of creatures. Yet, in the order of their creation, the mind should place these two luminaries and the stars after the earth and sea, in accordance with the words of Scripture, although the Catholic faith believes with sound reasoning that all the elements were made without any lapse of time. 591

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

2. *Instituta* (“established”). Another reading has *constituta* (“appointed”); likewise *statutum* (“appointed”) instead of *constitutum* (“established”).]

2. Therefore the sun and moon are two luminaries established in the firmament of heaven. The one, which is greater, was appointed to rule the day; the second, which is lesser, was established to rule the night. Yet throughout the whole period of their service in the succession of days and nights they do not preserve the same light of their splendor that they possessed when they were created in the beginning.

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

3. The manuscript reads: “while they had been created under the law … they continued … they first shone brightly, after the transgression.” The printed text had *rotulabant* (“they rolled”), but the edition of Baluze added a note that *rutilabant* (“they shone brightly”) should be read by conjecture.]

3. For while these luminaries, having been appointed by God the Creator to serve human purposes, were ministering when human beings lived blamelessly and remained under the law of their Creator by which they had been created, they too ministered adorned with the fullness of their light. But when the human beings with whom they had originally shared their ministry, and alongside whom they first shone, were cast down because of transgression and lost the blessedness of paradise, the luminaries themselves, although through no fault of their own, suffered a diminution of their light, not without sorrow of their own, as the apostle Paul testifies, saying: “For the whole creation groans together and suffers pain until now” (Rom. 8:22).

[Note: [Col. 0924C]

4. *Antiquum* (“former”). This word is absent from the manuscript. The printed edition has a different reading: “when the towers have fallen,” and shortly afterward “of the days,” “on the day when he binds.” The manuscript reads: “it will be changed sevenfold into the light of seven days.”]

4. But because, through the coming of the Redeemer, restoration to the former blessedness in a better state is promised to the human race, there is no doubt that creation too will receive its ancient beauty. Hence the prophet Isaiah, speaking especially of the sun and moon, enlightened by spiritual understanding, says: “And it shall be on that day, when the tower has fallen, the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, when the Lord has bound up the wound of his people and healed the bruise of its blow” (Isa. 30:25 ff.). 592

[Note: [Col. 0924D]

5. *Resurrectorum* (“of those who will rise”). This is better in the manuscript than *resurrecturorum* (“of those who will be raised”) in the editions. From the same manuscript I restored: “and the light of the sun will be restored into the light …,” for nothing is restored unless it has been lost or corrupted. In the edition *restaurabitur* (“will be restored”) is absent after *lux solis* (“the light of the sun”), and *restauratur* (“is restored”) is printed instead of *restaurabitur*.]

5. When the new heaven and the new earth have come to be (Rev. 21:1), and the former things that are subject to corruption are no longer remembered (Isa. 65:17), and the Lord has healed in the bodies of those who will rise the wound of sin and the bruise of the blow of death (Isa. 30:6), and the proud spirits have been removed from the authority they had seized, then the light of the moon will be changed into the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be restored into the light of the seven days in which it had been created—that is, it will be restored to seven times its own light. For nothing is restored except what has been lost or corrupted; therefore whatever the sun and moon have lost, they will receive again.

[Note: [Col. 0924D]

6. The manuscript has *resument* (“they will resume”), followed by “as Habakkuk says: ‘The sun will be raised,’” and “it will suffer no further diminution.” Perhaps the passage of Habakkuk 3:11 is intended, where the Vulgate reads: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling.” The Old Latin version has: “The sun was raised, and the moon stood in its order.” Gregory the Great and many others cited by Sabatier also read it this way.]

6. From this it appears that the luminaries now retain a seventh part of their light, which they will resume sevenfold when, through Habakkuk, the Holy Spirit, speaking of future things in the past tense, says: “The sun will be raised at its rising, and the moon will stand in its order.” For when the mutability of the human condition, which they serve, ceases, the mutability of their course will also cease. When he says, “The sun at its rising,” this indicates that it will never decline toward its setting. And when it is said, “The moon will stand in its order,” this signifies that it will no longer suffer the changes of its waxing and waning, but will always stand in its own order.

[Note: [Col. 0924D]

7. “And they will shine like the sun of righteousness, whose health is everlasting.” The manuscript omits all these words.]

7. This will happen when, as the Apostle says, creation itself is freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. 8:21). For when the saints have been transformed as the reward of their labor, by which they served God, and have shone like the sun of righteousness, whose health is everlasting, then the radiance of this corporeal sun also will be restored sevenfold as the reward of its ministry, by which it has been subjected to slavery under corruption.

[Note: [Col. 0925C]

8. *Agit* (“undergoes”). The manuscript has *sustinet* (“sustains”). The edition had *putandum* (“to be thought”), instead of *putatum* (“it has been thought”), which I restored from the manuscript; likewise, afterward I added *tenebrosa* (“dark”), which was absent from the same printed text.]

8. In the meantime, however, through the daily movements of its ministry, whenever the moon follows the sun, it increases the growth of its light; but whenever it precedes the sun, it undergoes a diminution of its splendor. Concerning the moon’s condition, various opinions have been held: whether its sphere is black and dark in one half and bright and shining in the other, and whether its waxing and waning occur in such a way that, as its bright portion is gradually revealed, the dark portion is concealed in the same measure; and likewise, as the bright portion turns away, the dark portion is revealed again.

[Note: [Col. 0925C]

9. *Rotunda* (“round”). The edition has *rota* (“wheel”). Shortly afterward the manuscript reads: “As if smaller than the ray … appears, its light gradually becoming greater and greater.”]

9. Or whether it is round and illuminated by the sun’s rays, so that whenever it approaches the sun, either before or after it, it shines as if at the edge of a ray of light; but when it appears to withdraw farther and farther away, it gradually increases its light more and more through the sun’s splendor, so that when, with its orb made equal in fullness, it stands face to face opposite the sun, it can then fully possess the sun’s image within itself.

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

10. *Loci* (“of the place”). The manuscript has *brevitatis* (“of brevity”).]

10. But to discuss the courses of the sun and moon belongs neither to the subject of time nor, indeed, to this place. I therefore treat the matter somewhat briefly in this little work, both because its concise brevity does not permit a fuller treatment and because these matters have been turned almost entirely to the use of readers for calculating the days of festivals.

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

11. This chapter ends in the manuscript as follows: “Some think that these instruments of light are insensible creatures. But what we have said is more commonly accepted by Catholic writers.” It seems clear that *sensibiles* (“sensible”) should be read instead of *insensibiles* (“insensible”), that is, creatures possessing awareness of good or evil, as explained in Baluze’s edition. Isidore, in chapter 27 of *On the Nature of Things*, raises this question from Saint Augustine: whether the stars have souls. This was the opinion of certain ancients, but it is now entirely rejected. Moreover, the additions in the old printed text were very corrupt and have been partly repaired in the aforementioned edition of Baluze, whose corrections we follow.]

11. Some think that these instruments of light are sensible creatures, 593 but among these ambiguous judgments and opinions, what we have said is more commonly found among Catholic authorities. Attention must be given to the view that receives the greater support from the authority of the holy Scriptures; yet it must also be examined what the majority of Catholics have accepted into the faith. But the diverse opinions that have likewise been asserted by Catholics, and against which the statements of the sacred canon do not conflict on either side, should be left unresolved to readers as judges, so that they may incline equally toward both.

# CHAPTER VI. On the upper region and the heavenly paradise

[Col. 0926A]

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

Chapter VI, note 1. *Sermone … dicto* (“the discourse … having been spoken”). The manuscript omits this. The printed text has *a coelo firmamento* (“from the firmament of heaven”); the manuscript has *a coelo firmamenti* (“from the heaven of the firmament”), and also omits *fieri* (“to be made”).]

1. After the discourse concerning the firmament and the luminaries, there follows a long empty region extending from the firmament of heaven down to the earth. Some writers explain that it is divided into two regions: the upper region is said to belong to heaven, while the lower is unquestionably joined to the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

2. The manuscript has “nor any changes of the air.” The printed text had *frangores* (“crashes”): “and it … the bodies of birds, and … the spirit of the air.” In Baluze’s edition it is conjectured that *corpora tuetur* (“protects bodies”) should be read instead of *corporatur* (“is embodied”), and *aerii spiritus* (“of the aerial spirit”) instead of *aeri spiritus* (“the spirit of the air”). The latter conjecture is confirmed by the manuscript, which has only *corpora* instead of *corporatur*, and the sense proceeds accordingly. [Col. 0926D] The same manuscript has *spissionem*, but *spissiorem* (“thicker”) should be retained; it would be better to read “a mass thicker than the air itself.” On the subject itself, compare what is said in book 13, chapter 7, of the *Etymologies*.]

2. For the lofty region that we have said belongs to heaven is utterly pure and exceedingly subtle. It has neither the swelling of clouds, nor the inflation of winds, nor the damp formations of rain or showers, nor the icy coagulations of snow or hail, nor changes of the air, nor the crashes of storms and thunder; nor, indeed, does it contain the air itself, which could support the bodies of flying birds and the denser mass of the clouds themselves, and which could refresh the lives of various animals through the alternating inflation of aerial breath and animate them by respiration. It has absolutely none of the disturbances of the various hemispheres.

[Note: [Col. 0926D]

3. The printed text has: “As once the highest [part] of Mount Phrygia”; but it is noted that the codex has *phy* for *Phrygiae*, which was introduced by conjecture. Our manuscript gives the true reading: “like the mountain of Olympus.” The same manuscript omits *aceto* (“with vinegar”) and adds *ori* (“to the mouth”), which is lacking in the edition; it has *aerii spiritus* (“of the aerial breath”) instead of the edition’s *aeri spiritus* (“the breath of the air”). Later the manuscript has *rotas* (“wheels”) instead of *notas* (“marks”), and *conscendentes* (“climbing”) instead of *ascendentes* (“ascending”). Isidore discusses Mount Olympus in books 14, chapters 4 and 8, of the *Etymologies*, and in chapter 30 of *On the Nature of Things*.]

3. This is demonstrated by the highest ridges of Mount Olympus, which are unknown to the rest of humanity because of their height, as reported by those who climb them. They place vinegar-moistened sponges around their mouths and nostrils to preserve the inflation and respiration of the aerial breath, and climb there annually according to a customary practice, though I do not know what superstition leads them to do so. They affirm that there they saw neither any bird, nor a cloud, nor rain, nor any wind; and after completing the rites of the sacrifices for which they go there, they return after impressing certain signs and marks in the sands. When they climb again after a year, they find those marks there intact and untouched. 594

[Note: [Col. 0926D]

4. The manuscript has: “nothing of herbs that belongs to greenness, or of shrubs, can be found or seen.” But *queat* (“can”) should be restored instead of *nequeat* (“cannot”). In the same manuscript, *permutari* (“be changed”) appears instead of *commorari* (“dwell”).]

4. From this it is clearly demonstrated that no disturbed air exists there, especially since in that same place nothing belonging to the greenness of grasses or shrubs can be found or seen. Nevertheless, it should not be thought that this is the very region of which we spoke above, that utterly pure and subtle upper region to which no part of the earth can belong or approach. Rather, this place lies at the outermost limits of the lower region, near the boundary of the upper one. Yet in this place the life of those who are clothed in flesh can by no means dwell.

[Note: [Col. 0927D]

5. The manuscript has “of mortal and corporeal things … because they think that no one has fallen from the heavenly angels, while the subcelestial ones, as long as …”]

5. Hence it is clear that the uppermost, purest, and most tranquil region of which we spoke a little earlier was not prepared as a habitation for those who are carnal, nor for the uses of mortal things. Therefore many Catholic authorities assert that this region was originally destined as a habitation for the angels who fell with their prince, because they think that none of the angels above the heavens fell, whereas the subcelestial angels, while they were in angelic blessedness, had not remained there for any period of time.

[Note: [Col. 0927D]

6. In the edition, after “you were in the paradise of God,” these words are repeated improperly, although they have already preceded this passage: “they think that he received this place of habitation by lot.”]

6. Since, as Scripture says, the devil himself is a liar from the beginning (John 8:44) and did not stand in the truth (1 John 3:8), they think that he received this place of habitation by lot. Scripture declares it to be the heavenly paradise, when, speaking under the persona of the prince of Cyrus to that supreme apostate angel, it says: “You were perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:13).

[Note: [Col. 0927D]

7. “Who [are] in the aerial [region].” The manuscript has: “who [are] also in the upper, purer region of the air itself.” Shortly afterward I restored from the same manuscript “into the lower [region],” and so forth. In the printed text the passage had been corrupted as follows: “having been thrust down into the lower [region], they miserably and unhappily fell from the upper and pure air and from their most fortunate and happy dignity,” and so forth. Concerning “aerial” or “air-like bodies,” the manuscript notes: “The demons have aerial bodies.” Indeed, the most ancient theologians and Fathers assigned bodies either to all angels or at least to demons; their words are reported by Petavius, *On the Angels*, book 1, chapter 2, and book 3, chapter 1.]

7. Just as human beings, after their sin, were cast down from the blessedness of the earthly paradise and thrust into a habitation on the afflicted earth subject to the curse, so that, having sinned on earth, they might afterward live under punishment in a worse dwelling-place of earth, so they think that the angels who are believed to have sinned in the air, or rather in the purer region of the air itself, were driven down into a lower place, darker and more turbulent even than this air. They were miserably and unhappily expelled from the seat of the upper and pure air and from their most blessed dignity, to live in expectation of the future judgment, at which they will be condemned more harshly. Thus, since they have aerial bodies and now dwell in the air, it is not unfitting to suppose that they previously possessed their first seat of blessedness in the air as well, though in a purer and subtler region. 595

[Note: [Col. 0927D]

8. The edition has *dum coelo* (“while belonging to heaven”); another reading has *dum de coelo* (“while falling from heaven”). Shortly afterward the manuscript reads: “the unhappy [inhabitant] of this cloudy region of air.” The printed text lacked *nobis* (“for us”), which I restored from the manuscript, as well as *tenebrarum harum* (“of these darknesses”), whereas the edition had *harum tenebrarum* (“of these darknesses”). The word *brumosus* (“wintry,” “foggy”), which I have retained, can also be written *bromosus*; from the Greek idiom it means “foul-smelling” or “heavy” in Caelius Aurelianus.]

8. Yet since this place belongs to the firmament of heaven, as I said, it is reckoned under the name of heaven, just as the Lord himself bears witness, saying: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). For having been cast down, by the merit of his sin, from the clear and pure blessedness of that place, he was assigned an unhappy and wretched habitation in the lower region—that is, in the cloudy and foggy air. The apostle Paul testifies to this when he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this air, against the world-rulers of these darknesses” (Eph. 6:12). Paul likewise declares that Christ himself triumphed over these spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

[Note: [Col. 0927D]

9. The manuscript reads *id putatores* (“those who hold this view”); the edition, less well, has *id est putatores* (“that is, those who hold this view”). Later the manuscript has “tomorrow you will be with me,” instead of “today you will be with me.” But the reading of the Vulgate must be retained; the Old Latin version does not differ from it, nor do many other Fathers who used those words. Interpreters readily explain how they are to be understood.]

9. Therefore, after the wicked spirits, together with their prince the devil, had been cast down from that clearest dwelling-place of the regions beneath heaven which we mentioned above, and after the human race had subsequently been redeemed from Adam’s fault and from each person’s own transgression through the coming of the Mediator, those who hold this opinion suppose that the same place is meanwhile the resting-place of holy souls as they await the future resurrection. They also assert that it is called the heavenly paradise, concerning which the Lord had answered the thief confessing on the cross: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

[Note: [Col. 0928D]

10. “Pre-eminent.” Another reading has “powerful.”]

10. Indeed, in that paradise planted with trees and possessing a shining, pre-eminent spring, souls stripped of their bodies have no need of such things. Rather, the spiritual person, freed from the carnal use of the body of death, does not possess it, nor does he need to be restored by the fruit-bearing trees of an earthly paradise; for the eternal does not make use of temporal things, but contemplates what is eternal and spiritual.

[Note: [Col. 0928D]

11. “We have touched upon.” At this point the manuscript ends this chapter. Perhaps the reading should be “let us not attribute.” In the Baluze edition, by conjecture, the words “labors” and “estimations” are added, though they are lacking in the older edition. The word “consapientium” is also suspect.]

11. We have touched upon these matters not as assertions but as the judgments of those who estimate such things, especially since we do not attribute to ourselves even the discernment required for estimating matters of this kind. When necessity demands it, we shall be able to bring forward the authors of all these reckonings, to whom either belief or doubt may be assigned. We labor by reporting rather than defending their opinions; for we are ready to submit to the agreement of another, perhaps better, assertion, if one exists, to which either the examples of Scripture or the judgments of fellow-wise men give greater support. But, having explained the preceding region as best we could, let us hasten to what follows.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the lower region and the various hemispheres

[Note: [Col. 0928D]

CHAP. VII, no. 1. “Moves about.” I would suppose that *vescitur* (“feeds”) should be restored. Below, the manuscript reads “which pertain to the higher heaven.” For “which make” the old edition marks in the margin the variant “which do.”]

1. Next, the lower region is called air. We have said that it is joined to the earth, and we recognize that the life of all flesh, which moves about on earth and in the air, is aided and sustained by it; this we recognize in ourselves and through ourselves. In Scripture it is sometimes also called by the name “earth.” Thus the Psalmist speaks when all creation is summoned in due order to praise the Lord the Creator, and when, after those things belonging to the higher order of the heavens have been completed, the discourse reaches these regions of the air and continues as follows: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses; fire, hail, snow, ice, and stormy wind, which perform his word” (Psalm 148:7).

[Note: [Col. 0929D]

2. The manuscript reads: “This air of the earth … and those which, like fish, are almost aquatic, and nearly all water-dwellers.” In the printed edition *aeria* is lacking before “regions”; I restored it from the manuscript.]

2. Up to this point the discourse concerns the air, which is called by the name “earth.” Afterwards, however, Scripture’s words command concerning the soil and the nature of the lower earth: “Mountains and all hills; fruitful trees and all cedars” (Psalm 148:9). The air often receives the name “earth” because, by the density and apparent solidity that it possesses within itself, it supports the bodies of flying birds, even the largest. Just as fish penetrate by swimming the hidden depths of the sea’s waves, so birds pass through the regions of the air by flying.

[Note: [Col. 0929D]

3. “Dwell, etc.” Another reading has: “dwell in the process of inhaling and exhaling.” Soon afterward: “flying things, as I have said … are supported by the same terrestrial density which it possesses within itself … by the mass of clouds … the solidity which the density of the air produces … thus it is formed.”]

3. For everything that water provides to preserve life for aquatic creatures, the air provides for flying creatures. Just as the life of birds and of all things that live in air and on earth is nourished and preserved by the reciprocal breathing in and out, so the vital movement of those that dwell in the waters is renewed through their process of inhaling and exhaling in the water.

4. Hence, when they are drawn into the air, because they do not possess a watery means of breathing, they quickly fail; likewise, things that live in the air cannot continue living when the air is excluded from them. Just as, as I have said, the bodies of flying creatures are supported by the solidity of the air, so the same terrestrial density that the air possesses—and because of which it often receives the name “earth”—supports the swollen mass of clouds. Through that solidity, the density of the air, under the force of cold, produces snow, hail, and ice, when it is formed in this way.

[Note: [Col. 0929D]

5. “Appearance.” The manuscript has “surface.” Shortly afterward: “raising it from the earth, as long as they remain in very small [drops].” For “gathered together,” the edition has “not globular,” which conflicts with the sense and is rejected on the basis of the manuscript.]

5. For this region of the air has implanted in its nature the capacity to draw together and collect, with smoky lightness, the vapors of water from the earth and sea in the form of mist. Raising them upward, as long as they remain in very small drops, the air itself suspends them by gathering them into clouds. But when, under the disturbance of the wind, those little drops come together into larger drops, the nature of the air can no longer support them, and they fall to the earth as rain.

[Col. 0930A] [Note: [Col. 0929D]

6. The manuscript reads: “the drops I mentioned … when it seizes them, it constricts them, coagulated into hailstones by the violence of the cold.” The printed edition had “by the force and violence of the cold.”]

6. But if frost seizes the drops mentioned above after the wind has gathered them into somewhat larger masses, before they rain downward, it constricts them, coagulated into hailstones by the violence of the cold. If, however, frost overtakes the somewhat less compact vapors before they have thickened into drops, a great force of cold transforms them into the form of snow. What the cloud, suspended higher in itself, thus nourishes, the air cannot support; and when the wind scatters it, it releases it to the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0930D]

7. The manuscript reads: “snow like wool … its crystal like … resolved only into waters.”]

7. Referring to this same matter, the Psalmist says of the Lord: “He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes. He sends his crystal like morsels; who can stand before his cold?” (Psalm 147:5). And to show that snow, whether on earth or in the clouds, is accustomed to dissolve again into water, he adds shortly afterward: “He will send his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow” (ibid., 7).

[Note: [Col. 0930D]

8. In the edition, the variant “binds” is marked in the margin instead of “suspends.” The same edition omits “waters” after “the air” and reads “releases.” Later the manuscript reads: “just as when [water is] salty from the depth of the sea.”]

8. To make it clear that the waters themselves are suspended in the clouds in this manner, it appears to be written in the book of holy Job: “He suspends the waters in his clouds, so that they do not burst forth all at once downward” (Job 26:8). Yet the air sends those waters down to the earth and sea which it previously raised from those lower regions. And although the rain-bearing formation has drawn them from the broad salt expanse of the sea, they become sweetened through the air. Just as, when a salty sea wave drawn from the depths is poured through the earth’s soil—as is a common practice among sailors—it immediately changes into the taste of fresh water. Through the changing of the air, and through a more violent agitation, the Creator likewise produces winds, and even fires and thunder, by hidden commands through the angels, by whom the visible world is governed, just as are all other things.

[Note: [Col. 0930D]

9. The manuscript reads: “below, yet the air, heat-wise, from above.” It omits “contrary.” In the margin of the printed edition it is noted that *caumaliter* derives from *cauma* (“heat”). Isidore teaches that *caminus* (“furnace”) is derived from *cauma* or *caumate* in the *Etymologies*, book XIX, chapter 6, no. 6.]

9. Some understand this to concern the effect of thunder: since around the air there are regions belonging to two elements, namely fire and water—one above, as we have said, and one below—and since the nature of the air draws both into itself, water vaporously from below and fire heat-wise from above, those two elements, contrary to one another, clash.

[Note: [Col. 0930D]

10. “Fruit-bearing.” The manuscript has “fruitful.”]

10. For it is impossible for thunder to move without moist clouds and flashes of lightning, as is plainly evident to the eyes of observers. In this conflict, confused sounds and terrifying crashes are produced by the mingling of fire and water. If fire proves victorious, it causes no small harm to the fruits of the earth and trees; but if water prevails, it does not lose its fruit-bearing power, both in trees and in those things that grow in various kinds of vegetables.

[Note: [Col. 0930D]

11. “Are.” The edition has “are made.” For “decrease,” the manuscript has “injuries.”]

11. Thunder sounds especially at the time when the fruits of trees and of the earth are still in the process of appearing, before they begin to ripen. For through the creatures, the increases and decreases of other creatures are governed by the command of the Lord and Creator.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the devil and the nature of demons

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

CHAP. VIII, no. 1. The manuscript has “we mentioned” instead of “we said,” and “are called” instead of “are named.” It also reads: “through Scripture, either by the ancient name, or because …”]

1. In this turbulent and cloudy dwelling-place of the air, the angels who were expelled from the sublime happiness, as we have said, dwell together with their prince. But that prince is called Satan and the devil; the remaining spirits of that prince, his ministers, who had previously been angels, are now called demons. For just as they changed their merits, so they changed their names and places. Nevertheless, even now they are often called angels in Scripture by their ancient name, because they are messengers of wickedness, just as good spirits are messengers of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

2. In the edition, a different reading is supplied in the margin: “which he prepared” instead of “whom my Father prepared,” etc. It also has “they believe” instead of “they fear.” The manuscript reads “they inhabit this place,” omitting “of the air,” and “they cried out” instead of “they shouted.”]

2. Thus it is written in the Gospel: “Which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). And the Apostle says: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (2 Corinthians 12:7). Yet they possess these dwelling-places until the time of judgment, awaiting the Lord’s terrifying coming, not without fear and trembling, although fruitlessly, as the apostolic words testify, which say: “For even the demons fear and tremble” (James 2:19). And to make it clear that unclean spirits inhabit this region of the air while awaiting the time when they will be judged—or rather destroyed—more harshly, they cried out in the presence of the Savior: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here to destroy us before the time?” (Luke 4:34).

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

3. From the manuscript I restored “of the eternal judge,” which is lacking in the edition. Shortly afterward the manuscript reads: “your will, as in heaven and on earth, and into darkness.” The printed edition has: “just as he expelled them from heaven, so he expels them from the earth,” with other differences.]

3. At the coming of the eternal Judge, when the common prayer of all the saints must be fulfilled—“Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10)—the useless servants will be cast into the outer darkness. The Lord will drive his adversaries from heaven just as he expelled them from the earth. For them the punishment of eternal fire, as the Lord himself testifies, has been irreversibly prepared by the Father (Matthew 25:41).

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

4. “They deserve.” The manuscript has: “they deserve, nor could they,” and instead of the variant “nor do they ask,” it has “nor do they seek.” In the same manuscript the variant is “only” instead of “again”; and “they would be recalled” instead of “they would be called,” and “therefore” instead of “for which reason.” From the manuscript I wrote “to which they might again be called” instead of “into what again,” which the edition displayed.]

4. For this reason they deserve to receive neither remission nor redemption, because they fell from the most exalted status of their order. Consequently, having abandoned sin, they had nothing else to which they might again be called, since they polluted all the happiness in which they had been established through the transgression of the natural good that they were and of the Lord’s law in which they had been created. Therefore they neither desire to repent nor, even if they had repented, could they receive forgiveness at all.

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

5. “Because, etc.” The manuscript reads: “But the human race, etc.” [Col. 0932D] I omitted *in*, which the printed edition places between “change” and “better.”]

5. The human race therefore deserved to receive redemption from its Creator because it fell from the lower rank of its order. For while it was still placed in the earthly paradise, assigned to the duty of generation and devoted to the eating of food, it would have received a better, higher, spiritual life without death, if, so long as it remained in this condition, the human being had continued in observance of the commandment.

[Note: [Col. 0932D]

6. The manuscript reads: “to the state which, by sinning, he had reached.” The sense requires something else, although shortly afterward the same manuscript reads “had fallen,” or “to another,” which agrees with the opening words. The same manuscript reads: “the restoration will take place, with him saying … into that immortality … they could not, but …”]

6. Therefore, through the Lord’s passion, the Creator’s mercy recalls humanity to the state which the sinner had not yet reached. If he had fallen from that state, like an angel, he would never again have been recalled. Restoration will take place not to that rank or order from which the first human being had fallen, but to another and higher one, which he hoped for, as the Lord says: “They will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30; Mark 12:25). That is, they will not be like human beings in paradise. For although redeemed, human beings will not return to that mortality which, for a time, was assigned to the begetting of offspring and the eating of food. Rather, after rising from the dead with spiritual bodies, they will share the angels’ happiness, neither increasing, nor growing old, nor dying.

[Note: [Col. 0932D]

7. The manuscript has: “if it is sought, before every time.” Below it reads: “nothing was not made simultaneously in all things.” Whether Isidore believed that the creation of the angels greatly preceded the creation of other creatures, see the note to book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 10, no. 3, where much concerning good and evil angels is discussed.]

7. If the time of the devil’s transgression is sought, the devil’s sin is found to have originally preceded the time of visible things. For Scripture teaches that everything that was made was made simultaneously and without time; it says: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Sirach 18:1). Among all these things there is no doubt that the infernal eternal fire too, of which the Lord says, “Go into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41), was made simultaneously. In saying “he created all things together,” Scripture left nothing among all creatures that was not made.

[Note: [Col. 0932D]

8. “Prepared.” The manuscript has “ready.” Shortly afterward: “he made the one who foresaw that he would sin, and together with his sin he made the punishment of his condemnation, by which the servant would be tormented.”]

8. Therefore, if a prison was prepared for him in that original creation of creatures, his sin originally preceded the creatures themselves. The Lord would certainly not have prepared punishment for one who was still innocent if his offense had not preceded the punishment prepared for him. Yet even this he did without time: he created the punishment of his condemnation, by which the fugitive servant would be tormented.

9. When this angel departed from the Creator’s blessedness, he entirely lost all the good of his nature which he had possessed in his creation. Yet, evil to himself, he always remains good to God, since he obediently obeys the Lord’s command—not willingly, but nevertheless because of God’s power. For of all the natural good that he possessed, he now has only this: that he obeys God the Creator in everything commanded.

[Note: [Col. 0933D]

10. The manuscript reads: “and the Lord said, ‘Go.’”]

10. But this good is not good in the devil and his ministers, who obey for this reason: because they cannot fail to obey. Their obedience, however, is good in God, whose good will the devil’s unwillingly evil will cannot resist when it is commanded to perform a good work. Yet it often happens that, when something is commanded according to God’s good will, the devil’s evil will is nourished by that very work. Thus, when the Lord sent him to deceive Ahab, the most impious king—an idolater and persecutor of the prophets—and asked him by what means he would deceive him, he not only willingly offered himself for this task but also revealed the plan by which he would accomplish it, saying: “I will go, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord says: “Go and do so, and you will deceive Ahab” (2 Chronicles 18:21).

[Note: [Col. 0933D]

11. “He had given, etc.” Thus the manuscript. The edition reads: “he had given, he would perish, seduced by the false speech of the prophets and deceived.” The manuscript has “demon” instead of “devil”; the printed edition has “was able” instead of “could have.”]

11. For it was entirely fitting that the one who had handed over the true prophets of the Lord to death should perish, seduced and deceived by the false speech of false prophets. Behold, the devil, with his evil will most readily and quickly, offered himself for this work of deceiving the impious man. But unless the Lord had permitted him, he could not have done it. In this matter, God’s good will exercised just vengeance on behalf of the holy prophets, while the evil minister nourished his own evil will through the destruction of the impious sinner.

[Note: [Col. 0933D]

12. The edition reads: “but not even in those things subject to human beings.” For “just as … it is reported,” the manuscript has “as the Evangelist says.”]

12. Yet he is unable to do anything either among human beings or among the things subject to human beings without God’s permission, as the Gospel truth testifies, reporting: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matthew 8:31). For just as he could no longer remain among the people from whom he was being expelled, against the Lord’s command, so he showed that he could not enter the pigs without his permission.

[Col. 0933D] [Note: [Col. 0933D]

13. The manuscript reads: “nothing is shown to be … did you not hedge him around, and his house, and all …” It omits “when he learned the losses of his possessions” (the printed edition has “had learned”); and “blessed be the name of the Lord.” For “wickedness,” I have written “his wickedness.”]

13. The same is manifested in blessed Job and in the possessions that he had and lost. It is shown that the enemy’s wickedness accomplished nothing concerning these things without the Creator’s permission, as it is said: “Have you not hedged him around, his house, and all his possessions?” (Job 1:10). And when the Lord permitted his possessions to the power of the wicked enemy, it continues: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand; nevertheless, do not extend your hand against him” (Job 1:12). Knowing this, when Job learned of the losses of his possessions, he replied: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As the Lord willed, so he has done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

[Note: [Col. 0933D]

14. The edition has: “Job did not say.” Below, the manuscript has “recognized” instead of “knew,” and “in that same ministry, in the affairs of the adversary.” For “by the administration of probation,” the printed edition has, erroneously, “by the administration of probation or of Job.” In the Baluze edition [Col. 0934D] there was a note that the reading should be “as in Job.” Our manuscript settles the issue; from it I likewise restored “through acts of vengeance,” where the edition reads “after acts of vengeance.”]

14. He did not say: “The Lord gave, the devil took away,” for he knew with absolute certainty that the adversary could do nothing at all concerning possessions or human beings without God’s permission. But, as I have said, in the same ministry the adversary’s perverse will is often nourished by itself, while the Lord’s benevolence, or his just vengeance, or the administration of fruitful testing, is carried out. Under this twofold distribution of good and evil will, they slay the wicked through acts of vengeance and test the good through trials.

[Note: [Col. 0934D]

15. “So that the wicked.” The printed editions have “so that even the reprobate.” They also had “of impurity” instead of “of punishment,” and “of them” instead of “of these concerning them.”]

15. For this reason their punishment is deferred by the Lord until the time of the final judgment, as long as they still fly freely through this air, so that the wicked among human beings may appear to be their companions both in crime and in punishment, while the good, tested through the tribulations inflicted upon them by these spirits, may be shown to be good.

[Note: [Col. 0934D]

16. I follow the conjecture of the Baluze edition, “the minds of human beings” instead of “the minds of men,” which the older edition presents; our manuscript gives no other indication. It has “distraction” instead of “distortion,” and from it I restore “their lot” instead of “they are accustomed,” as was formerly printed, with the marginal conjecture: perhaps “things alone.” In the Baluze edition this conjecture is rejected because our affairs are certainly not governed by demons, and by demons alone; but nothing is proposed by which the corrupt passage might be healed.]

16. But wicked and impure spirits, wandering and subtle, are susceptible in mind and clothed in aerial bodies. They never grow old. Waging hostilities against human beings, they swell with pride. Deceitful and skilled in fraud, they agitate human minds; bringing terror upon mortals, they disturb life through the disorders of dreams, diseases, and distortion of the limbs. They fabricate apparitions and oracles, govern the lot, and infuse into human hearts a desire for illicit love and other cravings. While uttering plausible falsehoods, they even transform themselves into the appearance and light of good angels.

602 [Note: [Col. 0934D]

17. The manuscript reads: “and so they differ in the degrees of their power.”]

17. Just as they differ in wickedness, so they differ in degrees of power. And just as good spirits—that is, perfect angels—now penetrate the air without susceptibility to suffering, so these spirits, if they had not sinned, would have possessed as their subjects, while living happily and blessedly, the same places which they now occupy in a state subject to suffering.

[Col. 0935A] [Note: [Col. 0935C]

18. The manuscript reads: “just as, when the adversary was questioned by the Lord about his name, he said, ‘Legion,’ etc.”]

18. And whenever they disclose their names, they assume titles from the functions and powers of their wickedness. Thus, when the adversary was questioned by the Lord about his name in the region of the Gerasenes, he replied: “My name is Legion, because we are many” (Mark 5:9). Hence it is clear that he uttered not the name of a proper individual—which he did not possess—but the designation of his rank and power rather than a proper name, which he did not possess. When the Lord questioned him, since he could not speak otherwise, he indicated concerning himself what he truly was.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the nature of the waters and the course of the Ocean

[Note: [Col. 0935C]

CHAP. IX, no. 1. “Uses.” The printed edition had “use,” which I corrected by conjecture. In the manuscript, however, this sentence proceeds in a substantially different manner: “Now concerning the water which is situated between the air and the earth, whose gathering is called the sea; hence in Genesis: ‘And he called the gatherings of the waters seas.’ That part of them which is spread among the lands through springs and rivers possesses sweetness, so that it might provide drink for animals and might more fruitfully irrigate the earth for nourishing its produce.”]

1. After traversing the regions of the air and their inhabitants, attention is now directed to the element of water, which is situated between the air and the earth. Its gathering, as the text of Genesis declares, is called the sea, when it says: “And he called the gatherings of the waters seas” (Genesis 1:10). Of these waters, that part which is distributed among the lands through springs, rivers, and ponds has sweetness, so that it might provide drink for thirsty animals and the comforts of other uses, and might more fruitfully irrigate the earth for nourishing its produce.

[Note: [Col. 0935D]

2. “And the rains which [come] from the clouds.” Thus the manuscript. The edition corruptly reads “because of which indeed from the clouds”; in the margin, perhaps “indeed” instead of “from which.” For “fruit-bearing,” the manuscript has “fruitful.” The edition leaves unchanged “the gathering of waters which spreads through great …”; the manuscript omits “gathering.” In the Baluze edition, instead of “unchanged,” *indigitata* (“designated”) or *nominata* (“named”) is conjectured, and instead of “the boundaries of the water itself,” which seems obscure, “from which the boundaries of it”—namely, of the earth. The manuscript reads: “and the boundary of the water itself is concealed.” The word “itself” does not seem to refer to the earth; for the earth has not previously been mentioned, but rather the regions of the lands. Nor are the boundaries of the earth concealed by water. There is no reason to change *immutata*, which means the same as *mutata*, just as *immuto* and *muto* have the same meaning. Later, “can be omitted,” as in our manuscript, suitably, through “nourished.”]

2. For this reason the rains, which are sifted from the clouds and descend through the air, become flavored, so that, as I said earlier, they may more suitably support fruit-bearing and the quenching of thirst. But that altered portion of the waters which spreads over great expanses of land, and whose boundaries are concealed, naturally retains the saltiness and sharper taste implanted in it, so that it may more usefully nourish, for human purposes, the produce which a stream of flavored liquid would not possess.

603 [Note: [Col. 0935D]

3. The manuscript reads: “natural taste, whether all waters have it equally, God has seen, although … spread through the earth it becomes sweet … while each can be poured back into the other.” I restored “difficult” instead of “more difficult.”]

3. But whether water naturally possesses a sweet or a salty taste, or both equally, God alone certainly knows. Nevertheless, many think that saltiness is the natural taste of water, while they judge that sweetness is imparted by the nature of the earth or air. Yet just as salt water becomes sweet when poured through the earth, so fresh water immediately becomes salty when infused through the ashes of sea plants. Hence it is not difficult to believe that each taste is natural in its own way, since either can be poured back into the other.

[Note: [Col. 0935D]

4. “In straits.” *Fretis* is more usual.
