The manuscript, less appropriately, has “by waves,” and shortly afterward “of fruits” instead of “of waves.” For “inundation,” perhaps “in undulation” should be written, except that the following number again uses *inundationis*. In the manuscript it reads *in cessione*—obscurely written—and *recursu*, which is clear. The manuscript continues: “that the Ocean has, as is plainly evident to those who observe, who daily divide it into corresponding alternations of *ledo* and *malina*.” In the old edition, “the ebbing of the sea” is marked beside *ledo*; beside *malina*, “the rising of the Ocean, the tide.” The note in our manuscript reads: “Papias [perhaps Papias]: *ledona*, when it is more greatly decreasing. Papias: *malina*, that is, the more greatly increasing tide.” *Ledo, ledonis* in medieval authors means the ebbing of the sea; *malina, malinae*, the approach of the sea, just as *liduna* means the withdrawal. See the work *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*, among the appendices to Augustine, book I, chapter 7, where this entire doctrine is explained using the words *ledo* and *malina*, and Marcellus Empiricus, chapter 36, from the middle onward. Isidore’s Glossary has *ledo*, but not *malina*. Du Cange provides much concerning both names and gathers testimonies from every quarter.]

4. The sea’s straits frequently divide the lands, both to establish boundaries between peoples and to enrich all provinces of different nations through the munificence of its waves, and to provide among all countries, through their mutual exchange, all necessary commerce. How great a harmony the Ocean has with the moon’s course in its flooding and ebbing is plainly evident to those who observe carefully. It appears to come to the land and withdraw from it twice each day, continuously over twenty-four hours; its course is divided with complete regularity into alternating periods of *ledo* and *malina*.

[Note: [Col. 0936D]

5. For *assisa* the manuscript has “twice,” with a note that it is *fisa*, from *fido, fidis*, and *fidens*. Du Cange, under *assisa*, has almost nothing that can be applied to this passage. It seems, however, that *assisa* is being used for inundation and flow.]

5. The *assisa* of the *ledo* always completes six hours of its increase according to its unchanging custom, and for an equal number of hours uncovers the very spaces that it had covered. The *assisa* of the *malina*, however, carries out five hours of its flooding and, during seven hours of its ebb, leaves empty the shores that it had filled. It appears to have such harmony with the moon that the moon is always born in its middle, and seems, upon careful investigation, to continue for seven days, twelve hours, and a quarter of a day.

[Col. 0936C] [Note: [Col. 0936D]

6. “To approach the beginnings at any time.” Thus the manuscript. The edition reads corruptly: “the beginnings, into which to approach.” For “are counted,” the manuscript has “are found.” That the Ocean’s reciprocal tide derives its origin from the moon’s increase and decrease Isidore teaches from the opinion of Saint Ambrose in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 40.]

6. Thus it happens that, when the full moon again diminishes, the *malina* also becomes dark and is halved again. In the intervening periods the *ledo* is discerned; it is never seen to approach either the full moon or the beginnings of the rising moon. Through this alternation it comes about that in every ordinary year twenty-four *malinae* and an equal number of *ledones* are counted. In an intercalary year, however, twenty-six *malinae* and the same number of *ledones* are found, because the sea follows the course of the moon inseparably in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

7. “The equinoctial *malinae*, and the other two.” I restored this from the manuscript; the printed edition, without any intelligible sense, has “equinoctial, two *malinae*.” The manuscript then reads: “it may be proved that they are higher by this overflowing,” and “to encircle” instead of “to uncover.” The edition had: “so that it may be asked whether the *assisa* there is an ebb and whether the ebb there is an *assisa*.” The manuscript has “twice, our *ad sisa*.”]

7. Four of these—that is, those at the four midpoints of the seasons—namely, two equinoctial *malinae* and two others, when either day or night brings their increase and decrease to an end, appear to become stronger than usual, as can be proved with the eyes: they become higher in their flooding and are seen to uncover larger stretches of shore. And since it is impossible that the sea does not abandon certain regions, even if they are unknown to us, when it overflows across the ground of our lands, just as, when it withdraws from us, it fills those same places, so that our *assisa* is an ebb elsewhere and our ebb is an *assisa* elsewhere, we are compelled to admit that we are ignorant of half the sea’s function.

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

8. The manuscript reads: “nothing else of our … he arranged in number, measure, and weight.”]

8. But in this and many similar matters, nothing is granted to our knowledge except to proclaim the power and immensity of the Creator, who arranged all things in number, weight, and measure (Wisdom 11:21). Meanwhile, let us say with the renowned teacher of the nations: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect has come, then I shall know, even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:9).

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

9. Concerning the number of the 153 kinds of fish and the mysteries which Augustine and others derive from it, see our Isidore’s book *On Numbers*, which I previously published, before it was printed, in volume V, p. 247.]

9. The text of Genesis declares that from this watery element the various kinds of fish and birds—that is, all aquatic and flying creatures—were made. But philosophers who reason about the nature of things enumerate 153 kinds of fish, that is, of all living creatures in the waters. The apostolic net, gathering together something from every kind of fish, as it were, had drawn together this number.

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

10. The manuscript has: “of living, or flying, or swimming.” It omits “always.” The printed edition has “plains” instead of “fields,” and “may raise” and “may penetrate”; these two readings can be retained if *degunt* is changed to *degant*.]

10. Whether birds themselves also possess this number of kinds, or a greater or smaller number, there are some who estimate that they do. Yet because they cannot support this with sufficiently weighty authority, they should neither be followed nor rejected. Since the origin of all birds proceeded from the water, where did such diverse habits of dwelling, living, or swimming arise among them, so that some always float upon salt waves and find their food there, while others dwell in ponds and rivers of fresh water? Others live on the earth without any habit of swimming: some in fields, some in forests, some in mountains, and some, as is customary, in marshy places. In some, the wing does not lift them for flight; others penetrate such lofty and distant regions of the air by flying that, in summer, they even bring down snow on their wings from the highest clouds.

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

11. “Unless perhaps.” The manuscript omits these two words [Col. 0938D] and reads “produces” instead of “causes.” The edition has “of marshes” and “of aerial vapor.” Later the manuscript reads: “which belonged to the origin of its condition … from which it first had its being.”]

11. Unless perhaps the diversity of their condition produces, in all birds, these very different habits of origin, although they arose from water, so that some were formed from salt water, others from fresh water, others from the dew of herbs, others from the dripping of trees, others from the moisture of marshes, others from the runoff of mountains, others from the vapor of the air, and others from the fluid confluence of the highest clouds. Each bird then naturally acquired the habit belonging to the origin of its condition, so that each bird would live there and from that source from which it had first received its being.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning paradise

[Note: [Col. 0938D]

CHAP. X, no. 1. The manuscript title is: “Concerning paradise, where the first dwelling-place of human beings was.” The edition had “afterward,” instead of “after the waters.” Our manuscript reads: “And since, after the waters, the earth was established, first the discourse must be placed concerning paradise, where the dwelling-place of the first human beings had existed; concerning which …” The printed edition has “the life with which they were endowed before human sin.” It also has “for those living so comfortably and innocently.”]

1. And since, in the order of the elements, the earth was established after the waters, we shall speak first of paradise, where the habitation of the first human beings had existed; although, since this is a matter that must be mentioned, the discussion must be presented concerning a subject on which many differing opinions have been advanced: whether that very immortal life with which human beings were endowed before sin was called by the name “paradise,” or whether this entire earthly globe had been arranged so conveniently for those living innocently that it was called paradise—insofar as, so long as its occupants lived blamelessly and without any fault, the habitation of the earth itself supplied everything happily to them without any labor—and whether afterward, when they sinned and were changed for the worse, their world too was changed and darkened on account of their fault and by the sentence of punishment (as we said concerning the sun and moon), and had lost its beauty and fruit-bearing power, though not entirely, yet for the greater part, so that the things which had assisted the blessedness and happiness of those living well would increase the punishments of those living badly.

[Note: [Col. 0938D]

2. The manuscript copy reads: “or perhaps, specifically”—perhaps better than “spiritually”—“some place full of this earthly happiness had been arranged for human beings who were to preserve the merit of their creation . . . in which he had placed the human being . . . when paradise is mentioned, [it has] sovereignty over the world.”]

2. Or had some place, spiritually, full of the blessedness of this happiness, been arranged for human beings who were to preserve the merit of their creation, a place in which nothing was present that could harm bodily blessedness so long as obedience to the commandment was maintained? The authority of the Scripture of Genesis gives no slight support to this opinion, saying: “Now the Lord God had planted a paradise from the beginning, in which he placed the human being whom he had formed” (Gen. II, 8). For paradise is said to have been planted “from the beginning,” since this place in particular appears to have held sovereignty over the world, and there is no doubt that the first human being was placed there immediately after his creation.

[Note: [Col. 0939D]

3. The manuscript reads: “whom they inhabit, might take its beginning. Of which . . . he recounts, when it is said, ‘From every tree.’”]

3. For it was entirely fitting that the head and beginning of the human race should be placed at the head and beginning of the world, so that from there the human race might take the increase of its members from which the earthly globe, which it inhabits, received its beginning. When the same Scripture enumerates the condition of this paradise, it describes it as planted with fruit-bearing trees and adorned with a great spring by which the surface of the whole earth is watered. Concerning the human being placed there it speaks in this way: “Eat from every tree of paradise” (Gen. II, 16). And the woman says: “We eat from the fruit of the trees that are in paradise” (Gen. III, 2). And a little earlier it states: “And a spring rose from the earth, watering the entire surface of the earth” (Gen. II, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0939D]

4. The manuscript reads: “we believe the human being himself historically,” with the other words omitted.]

4. What, then, would prevent the truth of Scripture itself from being preserved historically, without any allegories, in these matters, just as the authority that contains everything concerning the beginning of the entire visible creation also plainly shines forth in a bodily sense? For we believe historically, without any allegories, that the firmament, the sea, the earth, the luminaries, and the stars were made, as well as the creatures of the waters, the terrestrial animals, and the human being himself, just as the Scripture of Genesis investigates them.

[Note: [Col. 0939D]

5. The printed edition had “the place of paradise”; I have substituted “the place of paradise” [apparently correcting the form].

In the same place: “fruit-bearing.” The manuscript reads “fructiferis,” “fruit-bearing,” instead of “frugiferis,” “productive of crops.” And immediately afterward: “unless it is understood allegorically, that is, according to the historical narrative and in accordance with the moral explanation.”]

5. Should we accept this only as an allegory, when it mentions the place of paradise planted with fruit-bearing trees and illuminated by a great spring? But it can be understood in both ways: both according to the historical narrative of events and according to tropology, that is, according to the moral explanation.

[Note: [Col. 0939D]

6. Jerome, Letter 150, question 12, near the end; and Commentary on Ezekiel, book V, chapter 16.

In the same place: “they appear.” So the manuscript. The edition has “it appears.” Below, the manuscript omits “and of the Gospel . . . they speak of one thing and do another.”]

6. For sacred Scripture is understood in a threefold manner. The first mode of understanding is when it is known solely according to the letter, without any figurative intention, as Saint Jerome says: “The Acts of the Apostles appear to me to sound forth a simple history.” The second mode is when it is investigated according to a figurative understanding, without regard to any events—as in the first and final parts of Ezekiel, the Song of Songs, and the exposition of certain parables of the Gospel, which speak of one thing and accomplish another.

[Col. 0939D] [Note: [Col. 0940D]

7. “Historical.” So the manuscript. The printed edition has “of historical things.” In place of “according to a method,” the manuscript reads “narrative.”]

7. The third mode is when, while preserving the historical narrative of events, it is understood according to a mystical meaning. Thus Noah’s ark, the tabernacle, and the temple were made historically, and intellectually they signify through these things the mysteries of the Church. In the same way, the place of paradise belonging to the first Adam, who had existed as a form of the future [607], prefigured the mysteries of the future Church, which is the earth of the succeeding Adam.

[Note: [Col. 0940D]

8. The manuscript reads: “would not fear that anything among the creatures might harm him.”]

8. But while the human being lived there immortally and blessedly, would not the subjection of the entire world also have been subject to him? For what would have prevented him from entering the world, since among created things he feared nothing that could harm him—since fire would not burn him, water would not drown him, the strength of beasts would not kill him, thorns or the spikes of anything whatsoever would not wound him, the absence of air would not suffocate him, and nothing that harms mortals would hinder him?

[Note: [Col. 0940D]

9. “Forbade.” So the Baluzian edition, whereas the earlier reading was “commanded.”]

9. For, so long as he did not offend the Creator through disobedience, an immortal, invulnerable, unharmed body would have encountered among all creatures nothing that could inflict death, a wound, or injury. What, then, prevented the inhabitant of paradise from surveying everything that had been subjected to him, since the Lord not only did not forbid him to do this but commanded him, saying: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky” (Gen. I, 28)?

[Note: [Col. 0940D]

10. The manuscript reads: “to move through the creation whenever he wished, without his own labor . . . free from weariness and distaste.”]

10. For just as angels are free to move from the seat of heaven through those things that are subject to them, and yet have their dwelling in heaven, what would have prevented human beings established in paradise from moving through all the creation subject to them without labor? For just as they possessed bodies immune from pain, old age, and death, so too they possessed bodies free from every labor and weariness.

11. But when the inhabitant of paradise had committed sin in the place of his earthly happiness, he was thrust down into the habitation of the accursed earth. Immediately he partly lost all those things that he had previously possessed and partly preserved them only with labor. Once he had been excluded from the seat of blessedness, the possibility of returning was likewise shut off. Thus it happened that, just as the apostate angel, cast down with his companions from the supreme serenity of his paradise, received the darkened region of this air, so the human being was thrust from the earthly blessedness of his paradise into the habitation of this accursed earth.

[Note: [Col. 0940D]

12. The manuscript reads: “from the paradise of delight, and he cast him out . . . a cherub having a flaming sword . . . that the cherubim are said to guard.”]

12. For it is written: “And the Lord God cast him out of paradise and threw him onto the earth from which he had been taken. And he placed before paradise cherubim, having a flaming and revolving sword, to guard the way to the tree of life” (Gen. III, 23). This demonstrates that, although the cherub is said to guard the way to the tree of life so that human beings could not return, they were also commanded to defend the whole of paradise, since Scripture indicates that the flaming sword had been placed not merely before the tree of life but before the entire paradise.

[Note: [Col. 0941D]

13. The manuscript reads: “covered his nakedness with the leaves of a fig tree . . . a little before he was to suffer death, he cursed it . . . had infected the earth, before.”]

13. It is not sufficiently clear from which particular tree Adam ate. But it is clear that immediately after his sin he covered his nakedness with the leaves of the fig tree. To this tree alone, during the time of his flesh, the Lord Jesus—shortly before he was to undergo death for Adam’s offense—pronounced a curse, and it quickly withered when he said: “May fruit never grow from you forever” (Matt. XXI, 19); that is, fruit by which it could thereafter harm human beings, as the devil had done above. Behold, Christ took upon this tree—that is, the fig tree—the curse of Adam’s offense, which had infected the whole earth, before he cleansed it with the dew of his blood.

[Col. 0941B] [Note: [Col. 0941D]

14. “Those using it.” The manuscript has “twice, those eating,” omitting “that tree” after the second occurrence of “those eating,” and also omitting “by which the commandment caused death.”]

14. Whether, however, the human being first incurred guilt from this tree or from another, God certainly knows. Nevertheless, whatever that tree now is, which was then called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, we must not suppose that it can now harm those who use it as much as it could then harm those established in paradise, so that even now it could bring death to those who use that tree. For we should not believe that anything deadly existed in the nature of the tree, or that it was capable of producing the knowledge of good and evil; rather, it was the transgression of the Lord’s commandment—by which it was ordered that he should not eat from this tree—that caused death.

[Note: [Col. 0941D]

15. The edition read: “apart from the original obedience, nothing harmful exists in the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”; I corrected this from the manuscript.]

15. If he had obeyed it, this was what it meant to know good; when he disobeyed, this was what it meant to know evil. Yet the human being could not understand the difference between them except through transgression. For when he possessed good alone, he did not know what evil was or how it could harm him. But to make it clear that in this tree, whatever its nature, there was nothing harmful apart from the original disobedience, behold, it is not the way to this tree but the way to the tree of life that is excluded; and in this exclusion the merciful remission of the earlier offense is prepared.

[Note: [Col. 0941D]

16. “To be erased.” This word is missing from the printed edition. In place of “would die,” the manuscript reads “would be erased.” It omits “of the body,” as well as “and a dwelling in heaven,” and also “which was prepared for us in the beginning.” In place of “prepared for you,” the same manuscript reads “prepared for you” in a different form.]

16. For if, after that sin, the human being had eaten from the fruit of the tree of life, he would not have been able to remove the stain of his offense completely, miserably and unhappily, by dying eternally in a body subject to old age and pains. For the Lord prepared no other way for this crime of sin to be erased except death. He foresaw and predestined that this would occur later through the coming of his Son Jesus Christ in the flesh: through his death our guilt would die; through his resurrection the law of our death would be nullified; through the ascent of his body and his dwelling in heaven, immortality would be granted to our humanity; and the fellowship of angelic and spiritual life, which had been prepared for us in the beginning, would be granted to us. Thus, at the final summons of the future judgment, it is certainly declared by the Lord to those placed at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

**609 CHAPTER XI. On the situation of the earthly globe inhabited by the human race**

[Note: [Col. 0941D]

Chapter XI, note 1. The manuscript has in its title: “On the situation of the earthly globe, which . . .” It omits “moreover.” Immediately afterward it reads: “which it inhabits . . . we shall not be shaken . . . the abyss is its garment.” From this it is understood . . . “unless the earth has been founded upon its own power.” In the printed edition there was “and it itself,” instead of “and it”; and “established,” instead of “substituted.” The manuscript immediately continues: “whether it has been substituted, God knows. Therefore, in that part, etc.”]

1. Moreover, concerning the situation of the earthly globe inhabited by the human race, the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be shaken forever and ever. The abyss, like a garment, is its covering; upon the mountains the waters shall stand” (Ps. CIII, 6). From this it is understood that the earth was founded not upon the solidity of another element, but upon its own stability and firmness. Whether, however, one thing has been substituted for another—just as the earth was substituted for the waters, the waters for the air, the air for the space above, that space for the firmament, and the firmament for the waters above—he himself knows, who observes everything everywhere and on every side.

[Note: [Col. 0942D]

2. “The world was established in four divisions.” So the manuscript. In the edition: “the state of the world exists in four divisions,” which does not cohere. The Greek terms for the four regions of the world correspond in Latin as follows: Anatole is the East, Dysis the West, Arctus the North or Aquilo, and Mesimbria the South or Auster. The printed text has “Disis” and “Misimbria.” Others write “Mesenbria.” Compare Du Cange, who cites several verses on this subject.]

2. In that part, then, which was given to human beings for habitation, many authorities have reported that the world was established in four divisions. Learned men understand that the four names of these divisions begin with the four letters of the name of the first earth-born human being, Adam. They are Anatole, Dysis, Arctus, and Mesimbria—that is, East, North, South, and West. For it was fitting that the one who would fill the entire earth through his descendants should gather, in his own name, the names of the four divisions of the square-shaped world.

[Note: [Col. 0942D]

3. “Instituted.” The manuscript reads “established.” And below it omits the other words in “maturescit hieme arescit,” “it ripens in autumn and dries up in winter.”]

3. It is also distinguished by the four seasons in their annual order, and when the year’s span has been completed, the administration of the earthly globe is continually and without cessation brought back into a circle. In springtime, the season in which the world had been instituted, it is ever verdant; in summer it blossoms and bears fruit; in autumn it ripens and supplies mortals with the suitable use of its fruits; but in winter it falls away and dries up.

[Note: [Col. 0942D]

4. The manuscript reads: “and the habit of its decline.” It omits “indeed, of the Lord through Isaiah.”]

4. But it suffers this regular increase and decrease so long as it remains subject to the slavery of corruption and is bound to the service of mortals. For when the condition of being born and dying has ceased among human beings, then the earth itself will no longer possess increases and losses of its greenness and dryness, when the prophecy of Isaiah—or rather, the Lord’s prophecy through Isaiah—has been fulfilled: “Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered, but you shall rejoice and exult in the things that I create.”

**610** [Note: [Col. 0943D]

5. The manuscript reads “will live” instead of “live.”]

5. Since, when their bodies have been changed, human beings will live spiritually, they must inhabit places of habitation changed for the better—that is, spiritual places. “This body,” as Paul says, “is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown an animal body; it shall rise a spiritual body. It is sown in dishonor; it shall rise in glory. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (I Cor. XV, 42ff.). For when corruption and mortality have ceased to exist in bodies, the human being will no longer need to use mortal and corruptible things.

[Note: [Col. 0943D]

6. “After his resurrection in the tomb.” So the manuscript. The edition has “after his resurrection and in the tomb.” In place of “wondering,” the manuscript reads “marveling.”]

6. The holy Gospels confirm that this was also demonstrated in the resurrection of the Lord’s body, when they report that the linen cloths in which it had been wrapped were found lying alone in the tomb after his resurrection, just as it is said of Peter: “And he saw the linen cloths lying alone, and he went away, wondering within himself at what had happened” (John XX, 5). Therefore, for new bodies that will not need the things required by the use of corruptible life, a new earth with a new heaven will be created for habitation. That is, the nature and surface of this earth will be restored to a spiritual condition suited to spiritual beings, without any mutability.

[Note: [Col. 0943D]

7. In the manuscript this chapter ends as follows: “will be restored. But this will happen when Jerusalem has been created on earth.” In the printed edition there was incorrectly “but when this will happen?” In the Baluzian edition it is corruptly written “to be, instead of the spirit of mourning,” and “nor to please, instead of the sackcloth of mourning.” “The mantle of praise instead of the sackcloth of lamentation” and “a song of joy instead of the spirit of mourning” have been conjectured. The text also does not seem entirely sound at “and they will be called mighty in righteousness.”]

7. But when will this happen? When Jerusalem has been created as praise on earth, when its people are joy and exultation, and when the saints rejoice in the things that the Lord creates; when their sun shall not set and their moon shall not diminish; when those redeemed by the Lord shall come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; when they shall obtain joy and gladness, and pain and groaning shall flee away; when the days of their mourning shall be completed; when those who mourn shall be comforted; when God shall wipe away every tear from the face of the saints; when he shall remove the reproach of his people; when the mourning of all who mourn in Zion shall be laid aside; when they shall receive a crown instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, a mantle of praise instead of a spirit of mourning; when they shall be called mighty in righteousness; when the blessed shall come to the right hand and shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

**CHAPTER XII. On the nature of human beings after sin**

[Col. 0943D]

[Note: Chapter XII, note 1. “Which in its creation.” So the manuscript. The edition omits “in.”]

1. But, for the present, although human beings were assigned after original sin to inhabit this world, they did not lose all the natural good that they had possessed in their creation [611]. Rather, what had first been corrupted by the parent’s offense they further corrupted through depraved customs. Thus it happens that, just as they obtain the fruits of the accursed earth with labor, so they cannot preserve the natural good that they possess within themselves without diligent care and toil.

[Note: [Col. 0944D]

2. The manuscript reads: “And how, in Adam’s transgression, they had fallen threefold.” The same manuscript omits “good” and “apart from unjust mammon.”]

2. And just as, through the serpent, the woman, and the consenting man, they had fallen threefold in the transgression of the first parent, so all his descendants, afflicted with three wounds, fail through pain, old age, and death. They scarcely preserve, with great vigilance of mind, whatever good they received naturally implanted in them by the Creator and have discovered through deliberate labor; and whatever good they find through diligence as a gift from God, they leave nothing to their heirs except unjust mammon. All the arts that they individually acquire in life they likewise lose at the failure of this life, when the spirit is poured out.

[Note: [Col. 0944D]

3. “Are afflicted.” The edition has “are constricted.” Immediately after “they fail through death,” the manuscript ends this chapter.]

3. The poor and kings, fools and wise people, are afflicted by the same condition of weakness. For all alike need sleep, must be restored by food, and must be clothed with garments. They are either burdened or corrupted by the sufferings of carnal vices; they are distressed by movements of the mind—that is, anger and love, desire and fear. They fail through pain, old age, and death. They are quickly stripped of the past; they make moderate use of the present; and they await everything concerning the future in uncertainty.

[Note: [Col. 0944D]

4. “But also for these.” I restored this conjecturally. The printed edition has “but from these”; and afterward “or of Scripture.” In the Baluzian edition I conjecturally added “through.” I would prefer, with the editors of this edition, “good defenses,” unless perhaps “a good defense” is preferable.]

4. In the same way they sense and live through hearing, sight, touch, taste, and smell. They are also bound by the same bond of original sin; by the same gift of the Redeemer they are enriched, washed by the waters of baptism and the Holy Spirit. But for these human beings also—those who neglect either faith in redemption or the works of faith—eternal punishment is owed equally with that of the transgressing angels and their prince, the devil. For those who preserve the rights of their first creation, whether through the teachings of Scripture or through the defenses supplied by natural goodness, future life has been prepared through the gift of the Redeemer.

**CHAPTER XIII. On the diversity of sinners and the place of punishments**

[Note: [Col. 0944D]

Chapter XIII, note 1. “To be punished.” The manuscript has “to be included.” Immediately afterward: “they will undergo the punishment of condemnation, just as.” In place of “preceding,” the Vulgate has “going before.” In place of “some,” the manuscript has “of certain persons.”]

1. But since the condition of sins is diverse, there are certain crimes that can be purged through the fire of judgment; others, however, must be punished by the penalty of eternal fire. Among these, some become worthy of eternal punishment, some do not reach judgment, and some, after the examination of judgment, undergo the lot of perpetual damnation, as the Apostle Paul says: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but some they also follow afterward” (I Tim. V, 24).

[Note: [Col. 0945C]

2. The manuscript reads: “The Lord says: Whoever does not believe in the Son has already been judged” [Col. 0945D]. From this it is understood that . . . judgment; hence the Evangelist: “Amen, I say to you, unless . . . can enter the kingdom of God.” Hence the Psalmist: “Therefore they do not rise.” The Vulgate reads: “Therefore the impious shall not rise,” etc.]

2. Concerning those who are without judgment, the Lord himself testifies and says: “Whoever does not believe in the Son has already been judged” (John III, 18). From this it is understood that those who are not deemed worthy to undergo the lot of faith and do not receive the grace of baptism will not proceed to the future judgment, but will leave this life already examined by the word of the Gospel, in which it is written: “Amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 3). The words of the Psalmist also agree with this, for he says: “The impious shall not rise in judgment” (Ps. I, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0945D]

3. The manuscript reads: “They are burdened, some before they leave this life . . . neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor drunkards . . . commit such capital sins until death without repentance.” The opinion asserted here concerns the distinction between unbelievers and Christian sinners. Some are weighed down by capital crimes until death, while others are indeed oppressed by mortal sins, but by common and less serious ones. From this it is inferred that unbelievers and Christian sinners burdened by capital crimes leave this life already judged, whereas other sinners are reserved for the final examination of divine judgment. This, I say, was the opinion of many of the ancient Fathers, as I indicated in the Isidorian Studies, chapter 23, sections 17 and 18. See also the distinction between the impious person and the sinner in Book I of the Differences, section 298, and Book I of the Sentences, chapter 27.]

3. Those, however, who after the washing of baptism are weighed down by a multitude of sins are themselves divided into two groups. Some of them are judged, before they leave this life, by the words of sacred Scripture. Concerning them the Apostle Paul says: “Do not err: neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor those who serve idols, nor the greedy, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9). For those who commit these and similar capital crimes without a remedy until death will depart from this life already judged and go to everlasting punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

4. The manuscript reads: “concerning whom John says: There is a sin unto death . . . who until the very end of life.” This may perhaps be the genuine reading.]

4. Concerning their guilt, John, the guest at the breast of the Lord, says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (I John V, 16). Sin leads to death when a person, even at the end of life, neglects to repent of his former crimes. It must also be noted, according to the Apostle James, that whoever offends in one of these matters becomes guilty of all. For the one who said, “You shall not commit adultery,” also said, “You shall not kill.” If you do not commit adultery but do kill, you have become a transgressor of the law (Jas. II, 10).

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

5. “Will be enveloped.” The printed edition has “will be enveloped” in the subjunctive form.]

5. Others, who will not be enveloped in these capital crimes, are reserved for the judgment of the final divine examination. They depart from this age and nevertheless, by the sentence of the heavenly Judge, will undergo the lot of eternal damnation. They have despised works of mercy and do not refresh Christ in the poor with food or drink, do not clothe him, do not receive him in hospitality, and do not bring the comfort of visitation to him when he is sick, bound in the mines, or confined in prisons. For this reason they will hear from him: “Go, accursed, into the eternal fire prepared by my Father for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

6. The manuscript reads: “good works, as Isaiah says: Cease . . . to do good. And the Psalmist: Turn away . . . of the sentence we have mentioned.”]

6. For it is not enough, in order to seek the kingdoms of heaven, merely not to do evil, if one has not taken care to do good. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord likewise commands: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I, 16). Through the Psalmist the same Spirit of the Lord also composes these same words, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27). And to show that, after the terror of this exceedingly dreadful sentence that we have mentioned, the Judge would not be moved by any repentance, at the end of the entire discussion it is added: “Then these shall go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV, 46).

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

7. That is, “in the prison of hell.” The manuscript omits “that is.” The same manuscript reads “to be tormented” instead of “having been tormented.” The edition had “will be subject”; I changed it to “may be subject” from the manuscript. The manuscript continues: “As the Lord says, ‘Send the useless servant into darkness . . . where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.’ Concerning this passage someone also says: ‘Just as the earth,’ etc.,” omitting the rest.]

7. Concerning the place of that eternal fire—that is, the prison of hell—many have said that it is a corporeal place where the bodies of sinners will be tormented. For unless that fire and that place were corporeal, how could it hold tormented bodies of the resurrected, in which the reality of corporeality will be so capable of suffering that they will be subject to the gnashing of teeth and tearful weeping, as the words of the Lord and Judge himself make clear when he says: “But throw the useless servant into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXV, 30). “Their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24; Mark IX, 45).

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

8. “It is evident.” The manuscript reads “it is said.” And “is called,” instead of “is loudly called.”]

8. In this place the Prophet says to the king of Babylon: “Beneath you the moth shall be spread, and worms shall be your covering” (Isa. XIV, 11). Concerning this place someone else has also said: “Just as the earth is in the depth of the waters, so the lower regions are in the depth of the earth.” Hence that passage appears to have been written concerning it: “No one was found in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, who could open the book and break its seals” (Rev. V, 2). Thus it is plainly evident that this place, whatever its nature, is beneath the earth; it is called the lower hell and the land of oblivion.

[Note: [Col. 0946D]

9. The manuscript reads: “it is said concerning the sons of the eternal resurrection.”]

9. But since this fire is said to have been prepared for the devil and his angels, what sort of corporeality must it be thought to have, if it can torment angels? The soul of the rich man, stripped of its body, is also described as having been tormented by that infernal fire, when it says: “For I am tormented exceedingly in this flame” (Luke XVI, 24). Unless perhaps that fire and place possess the power to torment and retain angels, souls, and bodies in the same way. Or perhaps, since it is said concerning the children of resurrection and eternal blessedness: “And they will be like angels in heaven” (Mark XII, 25),

[Note: [Col. 0947D]

10. The manuscript reads: “when they resume bodies for the punishment of eternal fire . . . the children of the good resurrection . . . undergo the fellowship of Satan’s angels.” The manuscript omits the remainder of this chapter. The edition lacked “to” before “increase.” Concerning the teaching expressed in this chapter, compare Book I of the Sentences, chapters 28 and 29.]

10. Clearly, the children of eternal damnation too, when they have resumed their bodies for the punishment of eternal fire, will themselves be like demons in hell. Thus the children of the good resurrection, since they are children of God, will enter into the fellowship of the good angels; and the children of eternal death, since they are children of the devil, will enter into the fellowship of Satan’s angels. Concerning them it is said: “They shall be gathered together with the gathering of a single bundle into the pit; they shall be shut up there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited” (Isa. XXIV, 22). Whether this will be for the increase or the lessening of their punishments, we do not know.

**CHAPTER XIV. On purgatorial fire**

[Col. 0947B]

[Note: Chapter XIV, note 1. The manuscript reads: “the kingdom of heaven is promised, when it is said: Blessed.”]

1. But those who will receive the consolations of eternal life will also obtain the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven in two ways through the gift of generosity. For to some of these, while they are still on earth and are made poor for Christ, the kingdom of heaven is not merely promised; although they remain in labor and weariness for the time being, it is granted to them already in their absence, when it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 3).

[Note: [Col. 0947D]

2. In place of “for righteousness,” the manuscript has “on account of righteousness.” Immediately afterward: “loosed in heaven.” As if he were saying: “From this it is understood.”]

2. Likewise, those who endure persecutions from human beings on account of righteousness rejoice in the same recompense of reward, when it is added: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 10). He did not say, “for theirs will be,” so that they might await a future calling; rather, when they depart from their bodies, they will receive by themselves what, while dwelling in their bodies, they possess meanwhile through the gift of the giver. Therefore it is also said to those who are still on earth: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

3. “From sins.” The edition omits “from”; the manuscript has “will possess.” “Therefore the Lord commanded these.”]

3. As if he were saying: This is understood to mean that the kingdom of heaven is yours even while you remain on earth: whoever you release from sins, so that he may be able to possess it, will possess it; and whoever you exclude, destined for the mass of perdition, will be excluded from that same kingdom. Therefore the Lord commanded these people: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Matt. V, 12). It is as though it were said: Since your names have been erased and cast out from participation in the earthly inheritance for the sake of the heavenly kingdom, it is necessary that you meanwhile be enrolled as heirs of the eternal homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

4. “Providing.” That is, “with them providing.”]

4. Those, therefore, who receive all pressures and evils in this life will enter eternal refreshment without any examination, without tribulation, and, so to speak, without a summons. On their account some others also, after purification, will be called and will possess consolation without end. After the examination it will be said to them: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom” (Matt. XXV, 34). They will deserve to possess it because of their consoling care for the poor—or rather, for Christ in the poor—when they provided food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, a home to the wanderer, and visitation to Christ in the sick and imprisoned, administering these services to his least brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

5. “From every or even the slightest.” The printed edition has “from all slight” [a corrupt form].]

5. In their summons it appears clear that, although they have been placed at the right hand, they are still now at some considerable distance from Christ, since afterward the supreme Judge says to them: “Come, blessed” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying: Until now, during the examination of purification, so long as you possessed some impurity that had to be purged by the fire of judgment, you were at some distance from salvation; now, having been completely examined and cleansed from every, even the slightest, stain of guilt, draw near and come.

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

6. The manuscript reads: “when he says . . . he does not have remission of sins, neither.”]

6. The Lord himself does not deny that certain faults are remitted in the future, when it is said: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no redemption, neither in this age nor in the age to come, but will be guilty of an eternal offense” (Mark III, 29). From this it is understood that there are certain sins which, even if they are not remitted in this age, can nevertheless be erased in the future judgment through fire. If this were not so, the Lord would never have made this distinction.

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

7. The manuscript reads: “Concerning this fire John the Baptist says: ‘He comes after me,’ etc.” The edition has “he will baptize.”]

7. Concerning this fire, John the Baptist, the forerunner of the Lord’s coming, speaks to the Jews: “He who comes after me, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry, will baptize you [Col. 0948C] in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11). This means: He will cleanse or release you, through the Holy Spirit and the baptism of water, from your preceding sins, and will remit through purifying fire certain of those crimes that will follow afterward. For concerning that fire which is kindled not to cleanse the impious who are judged, but to destroy the condemned, the same John adds shortly afterward: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor, and will gather his wheat into the granary; but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. 3:12; Luke 3:17).

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

8. The manuscript reads: “The Lord says: Whoever says...”]

8. For it is one thing to be baptized with fire, and another to be burned with unquenchable fire. Concerning this fire the same John also says: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10). But concerning the fire of purification the Lord himself speaks in the Gospel: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22). He did not say “eternal fire,” evidently because this offense should be believed to be punished by purifying fire rather than by everlasting flame.

[Col. 0949A] [Note: [Col. 0949C]

9. The manuscript reads: “The Apostle Paul says: If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss...”]

9. The Apostle Paul also explains this distinction between those whom the future fire will not touch with injury and those who will attain salvation after suffering loss through the fire, saying: “For no one can lay any other foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. One person, however, builds upon it gold, silver, and precious stones; another, indeed, wood, hay, and straw. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward; 616 if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:12ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0949D]

10. The manuscript reads: “Works are signified. Hence it is understood...” In this manuscript many things are often omitted that in fact are not necessary.]

10. By these two buildings, therefore—that is, by the gold, silver, and precious stones, and by the wood, hay, and straw—works built upon faith in Christ are signified, some perfect and others less perfect. Yet those [Col. 0949B] signified by the wood, hay, and straw, although fragile, are not shown to be polluted.

[Note: [Col. 0949D]

11. The manuscript reads: “which stain, but these things that do not do much harm can be signified by them ... to eat abundantly, and so far ... to delight ... negligence in prayer, which the appropriate observance of the hours requires, or to rise later ... to raise one’s voice immoderately ... to speak; to think that something is not in fact so; the good that ought to be done ... should be believed capable of being saved.” I restored from the manuscript “but to conceal the truth,” whereas the printed text had “to retain a word”; and “to speak idle things” (*otiosa loqui*), whereas the printed text had “to speak idly” (*otiose loqui*). What follows in the edition is also obscure, and it may perhaps be preferable to correct it according to the manuscript.]

11. Hence it is understood that these do not signify principal crimes, which stain a person—for Paul excluded those who commit them from the kingdom of God—but rather those things that do not do much harm, although they build less: that is, to use lawful marriage more than suffices; to consume an abundance of food immoderately; to rejoice in anything whatsoever; to be moved to anger even to intemperate speech; to take more delight than necessary in one’s own possessions; to devote oneself to prayer less diligently than the proper observance of the hours requires; or to rise later than is fitting; to raise one’s voice immoderately in laughter; to indulge the body in sleep beyond what necessity demands; to conceal the truth; to speak idly; to think something true that is not so in fact; to approve [Col. 0949C] what one has judged false in matters that do not pertain to faith; to forget negligently the good that ought to be done; and to maintain an undisciplined manner of life. It must not be denied that these and similar sins can be purged through fire, and their perpetrator, if he is not burdened by greater sins, should nevertheless be thought to be saved as through fire.

[Note: [Col. 0949D]

12. “May they be erased.” Thus the manuscript reads, instead of “they will be erased” in the edition. Below, the manuscript reads: “the impious person from his evil way, all his iniquities which ... every torment that can be conceived in the present,” etc. In the Isidorian materials, chapter 23, nos. 17 and 18 [Col. 0950C], I showed that the doctrine of purgatorial fire transmitted by Isidore in this chapter agrees most closely with Catholic dogma [Col. 0950D] and with what Isidore taught elsewhere. Add the final chapter of the Rule of the Monks, concerning the dead. The text of Ezekiel is cited from chapters 33:12 and 19; in these places the wording differs somewhat in the Vulgate, namely, in verse 12: “The impiety of the impious will not harm him on whatever day he turns from his iniquity”; and in verse 19: “And when the impious person turns away from his impiety and does justice and righteousness, he will live by them.” The meaning comes to the same point. On this, see Petavius, book VII, *On Penance*, chapter 15, against Arnauld.]

12. But whether those who repent at the final point of their present life receive here a complete remission of sins, or whether their offenses are erased by purgatorial fire, is known by him who, examining the kidneys and hearts, considers the worth of repentance. To the thief on the cross, who had almost no time or opportunity left for repentance, he replied: [Col. 0950A] “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). And to Ezekiel he says: “On whatever day the impious person turns from his impiety, I will not remember any of the iniquities he has committed” (Ezek. 33:12). But concerning that purgatorial fire, this must be observed: it is both longer and more severe than every kind of torment that a person can presently imagine.

617

# CHAPTER XV. Concerning the future life

[Note: [Col. 0950D]

Chapter 15, no. 1. The manuscript reads “in heaven.” Elsewhere: “Then the righteous.” The printed text later reads “the sun of righteousness, and for those who fear,” which I corrected from the manuscript.]

1. Holy Scripture explains that true blessedness of the future life in this way: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). Concerning them the Lord says: “They will be like angels in heaven” (Mark 12:25). And the same Lord’s speech announces something higher concerning them [Col. 0950B]: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43)—namely, the sun of righteousness will rise for those who fear the name of the Lord, in whose wings there is healing; he who on the mountain, before the apostles, caused the face of Moses together with Elijah to shine; and while the saints share in his suffering, they will likewise share in his glory.

[Note: [Col. 0950D]

2. “They will neither desire to sin nor be able to.” Thus the manuscript. In the printed text “to sin” is lacking.]

2. In what he had previously said—“They will be like angels in heaven” (Mark 12:25)—we must observe that, just as the angels, formerly made mutable by nature, as was proved in those who fell, are now made immutable through the contemplation of God, so that they neither fear sinning nor can sin, so human beings, likewise mutable by nature, as was demonstrated in Adam and his offspring, will be made immutable after the resurrection through contemplation of the Creator. They will [Col. 0950C] neither desire to sin nor be able to; for every rational creature that is restored through the contemplation of God cannot sin.

[Note: [Col. 0950D]

3. The manuscript reads: “they admit no offense.”]

3. This does not mean that angels and human beings, being free from defect, lack the choice of free will. For in that life they do whatever they will; but they can in no way will anything that is not good. Therefore, since they never will evil, they commit no offense whatsoever.

[Note: [Col. 0950D]

4. “Creator.” The manuscript reads “judge”; and “to sin” instead of “to transgress.”]

4. But this perfect good will is perfected through contemplation of the heavenly Creator, when what the creature could not possess by itself is bestowed through the gift of the giver himself. Hence it is plainly understood that the angels or [Col. 0951A] human beings who sinned either in heaven or in paradise did not see God; for if they had seen him, they could afterward in no way have transgressed.

5. But someone might perhaps respond against this: Why, then, after the vision of glory—which caused the face of Moses to shine in the wilderness—did he offend at the waters of contradiction? And why did Peter, after the glory of the Only-Begotten had been shown on the mountain together with Moses and Elijah, deny the Lord in the courtyard of the priests? The answer to this proposition is readily given: Moses saw the hinder parts of the glory through an angel or some other creature. 618 Peter and the other disciples perceived Christ’s divinity shining through his human body; for if they had perceived the divinity in itself, they could in no way afterward have continued to live in the flesh.

[Col. 0951B] [Note: [Col. 0951D]

6. “They will see,” etc. The manuscript reads: “They will see, as Paul says: ‘Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle. But when ... I shall know, because I have been known.’ Thus John says: ‘We shall see him ... nor will the splendor of the moon illuminate you.’”]

6. For the Lord himself replied to Moses: “No one shall see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20). Therefore, after the resurrection the saints will see the Lord not through figures and riddles, as the distinguished Teacher of the nations declares concerning this very matter: “For now we see through a mirror in a riddle; but when what is perfect has come, then I shall know just as I have been known” (1 Cor. 13:12). In the same way John, the guest who rested upon the Lord’s breast, says: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Then will be fulfilled what is promised to the Church through the prophet Isaiah: “The sun will no longer be your light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory” (Isa. 60:19).

[Col. 0951C] [Note: [Col. 0951D]

7. The manuscript reads: “but through the majesty of the Lord himself the Church ... [Col. 0951D] the absence of beloved ones, or by defection, nor will any ... be brought to an end; and beyond these there will also be that which neither the thought nor any human reasoning, while still on earth, can ...”]

7. From this it is understood that the Church will be illuminated not by created beings but by the majesty of the Lord himself, when, secure in the serenity of perpetual happiness, she is permitted to enter into fellowship with angelic dignity. In that serenity she will possess every prosperity without oppressive correction: light will not be brought to an end by darkness, life by death, health by pain, joy by sadness, youth by old age, love by the absence of beloved ones, nor beauty by decay or any baseness, strength by weakness, or justice by sin. [Col. 0952A] Beyond these there will also be those things that no thought or human reasoning, while still on earth, can apprehend.

[Note: [Col. 0951D]

8. “Created.” The manuscript reads “made.”]

8. Of all these creatures whose order we have briefly surveyed, the Creator created some from nothing and some from something. He fashioned heaven and earth, the sea, and the things made from them, from unformed matter; but he made unformed matter itself, the orders of angels of which we have spoken above, and the human soul, from nothing. For God did not establish the soul as made either from himself or from some underlying matter of bodily creatures; we believe that it is not a part of God but a creature of God. For if God had made it from himself, it would in no way be subject to suffering, mutable, or miserable.

[Col. 0952B] [Note: [Col. 0951D]

9. “Something corporeal,” etc. The edition reads less correctly: “and would have something corporeal in its nature, or would never have heat from fiery matter, or breath from airy matter, or moisture from watery matter, or thickness and solidity from earthy matter.” In the same edition, “both eternity and mutability” appears, perhaps in the margin as “immutability.” Concerning this conjecture, the Baluze edition adds: “let others judge.” Our manuscript reads: “both eternity and mutability.” Hence “mutability” may be retained, since the soul’s mutability is further declared through the power of free choice. The manuscript continues: “It is recognized. This [soul] possesses the image of God in eternity, and likeness in the free exercise of choice.” This seems clearer in the printed text.]

9. Moreover, if he had created it from bodily creatures, it would have something corporeal in its nature: it would possess either heat from fire, breath from air, moisture from water, or thickness and solidity from earth. But since it lacks all these things, it is fitting to understand that it was created incorporeal; and through this incorporeality, eternity, mutability, and the power of free choice, it is recognized as sharing the same substance and origin of creation with the angels. 619 Yet this image of God freely possesses likeness not in eternity but in free choice. Concerning this likeness of the image of God impressed upon us, the Prophet recalls it, saying: “The light of your face has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:7).

[Note: [Col. 0952C]

10. “Are sent individually by God.” Thus the manuscript. The edition reads “are admitted individually.” In place of “to be discussed,” I would prefer “discussed.” Later, “or what benefit is there for us,” etc., I took from the manuscript; the printed text had confusedly: “Or what benefit to us are these things, in which the parties defeat one another,” etc. The manuscript concludes the entire work as follows: “What has been called insoluble [Col. 0952D] [or: ‘of an insoluble nature’] by many readers, let us reserve for the knowledge of the Creator. The book of Isidore, *On the Order of Creatures*, ends.” Although it is now certain to all Catholics, and must be held as a matter of faith, that souls are sent individually by God into individual bodies, and do not come from Adam by transmission, as the bodies of those who are born do, nevertheless formerly some Fathers, including Saint Augustine, hesitated over this question. Isidore, who generally copies their words, indicates the same uncertainty not only in this work but also in others—for example, in the book of *Differences of Things*, no. 103 and following, where in similar words and opinions he presents the same controversy from Fulgentius: “Whether,” he says, “just as the flesh of those being born, all souls are believed to come from Adam, or whether they are newly made, etc.” In these propositions concerning the origin of the soul, therefore, the opposing sides defeat one another. For each destroys the other’s proposition and is itself unable to establish what it proposes. See the note at that passage.]

10. But whether souls are sent individually [Col. 0952C] by God into individual bodies, or whether they should be thought to come from Adam and from their parents, as the bodies of those being born do, has been discussed by many learned men; yet they have left nothing on this question to which greater credence could be given. What advantage is there, then, for us to attempt anything concerning so great and dangerous a matter? Or what benefit can we derive from bringing forward these arguments, in which the opposing sides defeat one another when they cannot establish their own interpretations?

[Col. 0953A] 11. And therefore, lest we seek something beyond our reach, let us reserve this question—which many writers have declared insoluble—for the knowledge of the Creator. For whatever satiety a person eating the flesh of the paschal lamb cannot consume, the devouring flame consumes with no little care on the following day. By this it is understood that all the things in sacred Scripture that escape the knowledge of our investigation are illuminated and brought to completion by the fire of the Lord’s wisdom.

12. But even those things that, as through a small window of our sense and wisdom, we have touched through some prior illumination of his grace, we are not able to know perfectly in every respect, as we ought. For as long as we are in this world, we know only in part; but if we reach that immeasurable light [Col. 0953B] of the Father of lights, then we shall know as we have been known.

[Note: [Col. 0953B]

13. I noted that this entire epilogue is wholly absent from our manuscript. In the Isidorian materials, chapter 23, no. 16, one might seem to read “a recompense through your prayers.” But I would not dare alter anything. Instead of “for indeed in the treasury,” which the Baluze edition asserts should be read by conjecture, the old edition had “that all things are in the treasury.”]

13. Behold, venerable Father, in response to your request concerning the order of creatures, I have 620 answered you summarily in a concise discourse, according to the measure of my small talent. I shall repay, with your prayers, the reward for this little offering—not because the service of my insignificance can contribute anything worthy to [Col. 0954A] your veneration and authority in obedience, but because the effort of obedience fulfills what it cannot itself attain. For in the treasury of the temple the poor widow’s small offering of bronze is preferred to the abundant gold of many rich people; and in the gilded tabernacle, where gifts of silver and precious gems, linen, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet are presented, even the diligence of those who bring goats’ skins is not despised.

[Note: [Col. 0953B]

14. “And against those who chatter.” Thus it is correctly emended in the Baluze [Col. 0954B] edition, in place of “those who chatter across.” In place of “fear” I substituted “helm,” and for “little complaints,” or “complaints,” as the edition has it, simply “complaints.” I would also prefer “armed” and “to hasten to the harbor,” etc., as I indicated in the Isidorian materials at the cited passage, where I also observed some variation in the reading from the Escorial manuscript, which it is not necessary to repeat.]

14. Therefore do not disdain this obedience of my smallness; in a similar way, receive it in the calm harbor of your heart, and do not be unwilling to steer the little boat of this present work against the unstable waves of those who chatter, by the helm of your authority. For, agreeing with good and Catholic readers, I do not care about the complaints of the envious, who, crawling upon the earth without wings, mock the nests of birds with the flight of frogs. Protected against them by the shield of your reason and armed by the support of the Lord, I shall take care to hasten safely toward my homeland, secure on both sides. For we who seek to please God do not fear human threats at all. Thanks be to God. Amen.

[Col. 0953]

[The Complete Works of St. Isidore]

[Col. 0961]

To the most excellent and most eminent Prince, and most distinguished Lord, Lord Louis Bourbon, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church, titular of Saint Mary of Scala, archbishop of Toledo, greater chancellor of Castile, administrator of the archbishopric of Seville, count of Chinchón, grandee of Spain of the first class, decorated with the Grand Cross of the illustrious Royal Spanish Order of Charles III and with the insignia of the Orders of Saint Januarius and Saint Ferdinand, etc.—Faustinus Arevalus.

I did not doubt, most eminent Prince, that the work whose publication was begun six years ago under the patronage and generosity of my lord Francis Lorenzana, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and which has now at last, after so many and such great vicissitudes, been brought to completion, would be welcome and pleasing to you if it were offered by me. Yet I was prevented from daring to do this both by a certain frank modesty and by consciousness of my own insignificance, and especially by contemplation of your eminence—how great it is, and how highly it ought to be esteemed by all, I could not fail to understand. Indeed, I confess that I should altogether have refrained from offering it to you and have wholly abandoned this thought, had not the Francis Lorenzana whom I have just named intervened with his weightiest authority. By persuasion and exhortation, and almost by command and compulsion, he impelled one who was doubtful and reluctant to do what you now see me doing—timidly and modestly indeed, yet most obediently, as is fitting, and most humbly.

And truly, how could I fail to comply with his wish? Nor, although the occasion seems to require it of me, shall I touch here upon any other praises of that man; for this is least necessary before you, who have known and understood him fully from your earliest childhood, and who continue to honor and love him no otherwise than a son does a father.

But let us come to Isidore. He is indeed the common teacher and father of us all who have been born Spaniards. Yet, besides these common bonds, each of you has certain particular connections with the other which make it fitting that, now that the edition of his works has been completed, he should come to you and you in turn should receive him as he comes. He governed the Church of Seville—with what approval, not to say envy, of the other sees! He also presided over the most celebrated of all the Fourth Councils of Toledo and composed its most distinguished canons. You see, therefore, most eminent Prince, how directly this work concerns you, since, following the example of your most excellent father, the Most Serene Infante of Spain Louis of Bourbon, you govern both the see of Toledo and that of Seville with singular prudence and shape them by your most holy character.

There also occurred to me what John Grialius long ago suggested to Philip III, Catholic King of Spain, when he dedicated to him the royal Madrid edition of Isidore’s works: “You yourself,” he says, “derive your lineage from the stock of that Isidore.” Yet perhaps it will be more agreeable and pleasing to you that Notker Balbulus, in the ninth century, warned Solomon, afterwards bishop of Constance, when he commended to him several writers on ecclesiastical matters: “The books of Isidore, bishop of Seville, entitled *Etymologies*, make you complete in every kind of knowledge. Likewise, there is his most useful book of *Sentences*. Likewise another on ecclesiastical offices and orders. These are especially necessary for you, who by God’s grace will soon be a priest; in them you will find the whole system and the names of the individual festivals and fasts, so that, as God’s herald, you may be able to announce to the people the observances that are to come.” Since you yourself, most eminent Prince and most exalted Prelate, have been trained in these teachings from childhood, being exercised in the most rigorous discipline, I shall never cease to join my prayers to the wishes of all good people that you may, in health, discharge this great office for as long as possible, for the advancement of the Catholic religion and the glory of Spain.

From Rome, the day before the Ides of March, 1803.

[Col. 0963]

## The Book of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, on the Nature of Things, to King Sisebut

[Note: **Title.**—*On the Nature of Things.* From the Gothic and Oviedo Codices, from Braulio and Sigebert in Isidore’s Life, and also from Bede, who, following Isidore’s example, entitled his own books *On the Nature of Things*, although elsewhere this book is entitled *On Astronomy*, *On the World*, or *On the Natures of Things.* (C)]

### Preface. Isidore to His Lord and Son Sisebut

#### 1

[Note: **Preface, no. 1.** “You demand from me things to be supplied to you.” That is, things to be completed, as in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 10, concerning angels: “The contemplation of the Creator supplies mutability to them in their nature.” That is, it fills out and compensates for the weak condition of mutability and serves as support for their frail nature. *Gloss:* *suffrago*, “I support.” Likewise Greek βοηθῶ (*boēthō*), “I help, support, assist, aid.”

**Ibid.** “I do not delay, having traversed the monuments of earlier writers, to satisfy your zeal and mind.” That is: “I do not spare the labor of examining the monuments of earlier writers, in order to satisfy your zeal and mind from their own works.”

**Ibid.** In the Isidorian manuscripts, chapter 76 is prefaced by this title: “The Book of Isidore on the Nature of Things to King Sisebut.” Editions, manuscript codices, and excerpts preserve a chapter of this book that has not yet been published. An astrological poem has been added to this book, perhaps by Isidore; a metrical summary of the same book, not yet published, perhaps by Saint Eugenius of Toledo. Grialius illustrated this book with his notes, which are therefore cited under his name. For *decursa priorum monumenta*, others read *decursis priorum monumentis*. AREV.]

I am not unaware that you are outstanding in talent and eloquence and distinguished by the varied brilliance of your learning; nevertheless, you devote even greater care to the matter and demand from me that certain things concerning the nature or causes of things be supplied to you. For my part, I do not delay in satisfying your zeal and mind by examining the monuments of earlier writers, setting forth, in some measure, an account of days and months, the limits of the year and the changing succession of times, the nature of the elements, finally the courses of the sun and moon, and the causes of certain stars, namely, the signs of storms and the winds, as well as the position of the earth and the alternating tides of the sea.

[Note: **No. 2.** Some copies read: “We have learned from men, and especially …”]

#### 2

We have set all these matters down in a brief outline, presenting them according to what was written by men of old, and especially as it is recorded in the writings of Catholic men. For it is not superstitious learning to know the nature of these things, provided that they are considered only according to sound and sober teaching. Indeed, if such matters were entirely remote from the investigation of truth, that wise king would by no means have said: “He himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of heaven, the powers of the elements, the changes of revolutions, the divisions of times, the courses of years, and the arrangements of the stars.”

#### 3

Therefore, beginning with the day whose first creation appears among the ordered works of visible things, we shall proceed to the other matters about which we know that certain pagan and ecclesiastical writers have expressed opinions, setting forth in some cases both their ideas and their words, so that the authority of their statements may establish their credibility.

## Chapter One: On Days

[Note: **Chapter I, no. 1.** “On days.” From the Oviedo manuscript and Book V of the *Etymologies*. Some copies read, “On the day.”

**Ibid.** “The day is … the last part.” These same words occur somewhat more fully in the *Etymologies*.]

#### 1

A day is the presence of the rising sun until it reaches its setting. “Day” is customarily used in two senses: properly, from the rising of the sun until it rises again; improperly, from sunrise until it reaches sunset. The divisions of the day are two, daytime and nighttime; a day consists of twenty-four hours, while the daytime portion consists of twelve hours.

[Note: **No. 2.** The Chaldeans reckon the day from sunrise. According to the Persians, it is from sunrise; in the *Etymologies*, according to the Babylonians, from the rising of the sun, as in Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 2, and Macrobius, from whom most of this chapter is taken, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 3.

**Ibid.** The Egyptians reckon it from the beginning of night. According to the Egyptians, from sunset, as in the *Etymologies*, from Servius on Book V of the *Aeneid*.

**Ibid.** “Improperly”; some copies have “abusive” or “improperly understood.”

**Ibid.** I do not know whether “the span of a day” in the sense of half a day is found in other writers. The Hebrews derive the beginning of the day from sunset, a practice some Italians still follow. Petavius and others who have written carefully about the work of the six days teach that the first day of the world was composed of the evening preceding and the morning following, and that the other days proceeded in the same manner. AREV.]

#### 2

The improperly divided day has three parts: morning, midday, and evening. Some think that the beginning of the day is at sunrise, others at sunset, [Col. 0964A] and others at midnight. The Chaldeans begin the day at sunrise, calling the entire interval one day. The Egyptians, however, derive the beginning of the following day from the beginning of night. The Romans wish the day to begin at midnight and to end at midnight.

[Note: **No. 3.** “To make the light shine from darkness.” Thus the Gothic manuscript and Ambrose, *Exposition of the Gospel of Luke*, Book I, chapter 7; the Vulgate has “to shine forth,” in chapter 4 of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.

**Ibid.** “As it is written”; some copies have “as it is written in the Apostle.” After “he reaches knowledge,” or, as some copies read, “he reaches knowledge,” a considerable fragment is inserted in many manuscript copies, as follows:

“On the mystical level, too, the day bears the image of the Law. For just as the brightness of day illuminates the darkness of shadows, so the Law, showing the way of life, dispels the darkness of errors, reveals the light of virtues, and, reproving the sins of the wicked, leads the good toward better things.

“In the old Law the following are the feast days. The Day of Unleavened Bread, or Passover, is the fourteenth day of the first month, when, after the leaven had been removed, the lamb was sacrificed under the full moon. The Day of Pentecost is the day when the Law was given to Moses on the summit of Mount Sinai; on it, loaves of the first fruits were offered from the harvest. The Day of Sabbaths is the day on which rest is celebrated according to the Law and on which it was not permitted to gather manna in the desert. The Day of New Moons is the celebration of the new moon; for the Jews always celebrated a feast at the beginning of the months, that is, at the first moon. They did this at the beginning of the months because, when the moon wanes, time comes to an end, and when the moon is born again, it begins anew.

“The Day of Trumpets is at the beginning of the seventh month, when the Jews, celebrating the solemnity, sounded the trumpet more extensively and offered more sacrifices than in the individual months. The Day of Booths is on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, in which the ancients celebrated the solemnity of tabernacles. *Scenopegia* means ‘tabernacles.’

“The Day of the Fast of the Fourth Month is on the seventeenth day of the month of July, when Moses, descending from the mountain, broke the tablets of the Law. On that same day Nebuchadnezzar first destroyed the walls of the city of Jerusalem.

“The Day of the Fast of the Fifth Month is in August, when a rebellion arose in the camp because of the scouts returning from the holy land; consequently, they wandered laboriously through the desert for forty years, and all perished in the wilderness. In that same month the temple was overturned and burned by Nebuchadnezzar and, much later, by the emperor Titus; as a reproach for the destroyed nation, it was inscribed … [lacuna]

“The Day of the Fast of the Seventh Month is in the seventh month, which is called October; in it Godolias was killed, together with the others who were in Jerusalem, as Jeremiah relates.

“The Day of the Fast of the Tenth Month is in the tenth month, which we call December. At that time all the captives in Babylon learned that the temple had been destroyed in the fifth month, and they lamented and fasted.
