“These things were written by the most blessed Jerome in his commentaries on Zechariah.”

Some variant readings occur in the manuscripts, such as: “The Day of the Fast of the Fourth Month is in July, on the fourteenth day of that month.” Later, some copies read: “which we call January, when they learned that the temple had been destroyed in the fourth month,” and so forth.

The passage from Hosea is given in the Vulgate as follows: “At night I caused your mother to be silent. My people was silent because it had no knowledge.” The Old Latin version in Sabatier reads: “I made your mother like the night. And my people became like one without knowledge.” AREV.]

#### 3

At the beginning of God’s works, the day had its origin in light, signifying the fall of humanity. Now, however, it proceeds from darkness to light, so that day is not darkened into night, but night shines into day, as it is written, “to make the light shine from darkness,” because, freed from the darkness of sins, humanity reaches the light of faith and knowledge.

Prophetically, the day signifies knowledge of the divine Law, while night signifies the blindness of ignorance, according to the prophet Hosea, who says: “I made your mother like the night; my people became like one without knowledge.” Sometimes, moreover, day signifies the prosperity of the world, while night signifies adversity.

[Note: **No. 4.** *Fasti* are days on which the law may be spoken. Macrobius, Book I, chapter 16: “The *fasti* are those days on which it is permitted for the praetor to pronounce the three solemn words: ‘I grant,’ ‘I declare,’ ‘I adjudge.’” Their opposites are the *nefasti*. Ovid’s well-known verses are:

> That day will be *nefastus* on which the three words are silent;  
> It will be *fastus* on which legal action may be taken.

**Ibid.** “Black days,” which are also called “common.” Macrobius, in the same passage: “Our ancestors considered the days following festivals to be avoided in every respect; they condemned them under the ominous name ‘black,’ although some, to correct the name, called those same days ‘common.’” Ovid, *Fasti* I:

> Juno’s care claims the Roman Kalends;  
> On the Ides a great white ewe falls to Jupiter;  
> The protection of the Nones is lacking for the god—  
> Beware, lest you be deceived: the next day will be black.  
> The omen comes from what occurred, for on those days  
> Rome suffered grievous losses beneath hostile Mars.

**Ibid.** “Just … military.” Macrobius, chapter 17: “I would not separate the military days from the just days. For the just days are thirty consecutive days during which, after the army has been levied, a red-colored standard is placed on the citadel. Military days, however, are all those on which it is lawful to pursue the enemy or provoke him to battle.”

Festus: “Just days were called thirty days when the army had been levied and the standard had been placed on the citadel.”

A different kind of thirty just days is reported by Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 1: “Thirty days were granted to those who had confessed a debt or had been condemned for debt, for the purpose of collecting the money with which they were to pay it. The decemvirs called these days ‘just,’ as though they constituted a kind of *justitium*, that is, a suspension or cessation of legal proceedings among them, during which nothing could lawfully be done against such persons.” Afterwards, if they did not pay, and so forth.

**Ibid.** “They are excluded.” Some copies read: “They are excluded on the fifteenth day of January and on the fifteenth day of February.” AREV.]

#### 4

The *fasti* are days on which the law is spoken, that is, declared; the *nefasti* are those on which it is not declared. *Feriati* are days on which a religious rite is performed and on which people ought to refrain from lawsuits. *Profesti*, opposed to festival days, are days without religious observance; festival days are wholly devoted to rest and religion. Black days are also called common days. *Sidereal* days are those on which the stars move and from which people are excluded from navigation. *Just* days are thirty consecutive days. *Military* days are those on which it is lawful to provoke the enemy to war, concerning which the Book of Kings bears witness, saying: “At the time when kings usually go forth to war.”

[Note: **No. 5.** Intercalary days are five, which, according to the Egyptians … Macrobius, chapter 15: “Then Horus said: ‘This intercalary day, which must be inserted before the fifth year begins, agrees with the Egyptian mother of the arts.’” Yet in explaining their months, all of which consist of thirty days, the matter seems laborious. Once the twelve months—that is, 360 complete days—have elapsed, they restore the remaining five days to their year between August and September, adding every fourth year an intercalary day, which is made up from the quarters.

**Ibid.** “And they begin on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.” This seems to conflict with the words of Macrobius just quoted. Horus said that after 360 days had elapsed the remaining five were restored to their year, whereas Isidore says that they are inserted before the final month has been completed, by the same method through which we insert one leap day into February.

**Ibid.** “The solstitial days are.” By the name “solstice” he also includes the winter solstice according to his usual practice; thus below, chapter 8: “There are two solstices.”

**Ibid.** “Five, etc.” Here is the calendar system that Gaul adopted not many years ago. As for Grialius’s opinion that Isidore inserts the five intercalary days before the final month has been completed, this does not seem correct to me. According to Isidore’s view, the final day of the twelfth Egyptian month is the tenth day before the Kalends of September. Five days are added to it—or six in a leap year—and the year ends on the fifth day before the Kalends of September; the first day of the first month of the following year begins on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. In the recent Gallican calendar, the year begins on the tenth day before the Kalends of October. AREV.

**Ibid.** “The sun stands, as it increases.” Some copies read: “The sun stands at a greater latitude than it can have while increasing.” AREV.]

#### 5

Intercalary days are five, which, according to the Egyptians, remain after the twelve months; they begin on the ninth day before the Kalends of September and end on the fifth day before those Kalends. The days of the epacts are eleven, which are added each year to the lunar course. For while the twelve lunar months contain 354 days, eleven days remain in relation to the solar year; the Egyptians called these epacts because they are added throughout the year in order to determine the moon.

[Col. 0967A] The solstitial days are those on which the sun stands still as the span of the days or nights increases. The equinoctial days are those on which day and night pass through equal intervals of hours.

## Chapter Two: On Night

[Note: **Chapter II, no. 1.** “The shadow of the earth.” Ambrose, *Hexameron* IV, chapter 3: “Night is, as the more learned have demonstrated—those who have preceded us in age or office—the shadow of the earth.” Shortly afterward: “Thus it is clear that the shadow of the earth produces night.” He is referring to Basil.

**Ibid.** “Which was given for the body’s rest.” Ambrose, Book I, chapter 10: “For we know that night was given for the body’s rest, not for the performance of any duty or work.”

**Ibid.** “Night, from harming.” As in the *Etymologies*, from Atteius Capito and others.]

#### 1

Night is the absence of the sun, for as long as it moves from sunset back to sunrise. We believe that night is produced by the shadow of the earth, which was given for the body’s rest, not for the performance of any work. In Scripture, night is understood in two ways: either as the tribulation of persecution or as the darkness of a blinded heart. It is called *night* from *harming*, because it harms the eyes.

[Note: **No. 2.** The divisions of night. See Book V of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** *Crepusculum.* Properly, *crepera res* means “a doubtful thing.” Hence *crepusculum* means doubtful light.

**Ibid.** “When the star rises.” Some copies read: “from the star that rises at night.” AREV.]

#### 2

The divisions of night are seven: twilight, evening, the time of silence, the deep night, cockcrow, morning twilight, and dawn. *Crepusculum* is so called from *creperum*, which we call “doubtful”; that is, the interval between light and darkness. *Vesperum* is when the star rises, the star to which this name belongs.

[Note: **No. 3.** *Conticere.* Some copies read *conticescere*, “to become silent.” AREV.]

#### 3

The time of silence is when everyone is quiet; *conticere* means “to be silent.” The deep night is the “inopportune” time, when nothing can be done and everything is at rest. Cockcrow is so called because roosters announce the light. Morning twilight is the interval between the departure of night and the arrival of day.

## Chapter Three: On the Week

[Note: **Chapter III, no. 1.** “Among the Hebrews there are seven years.” Not because they also have a week of days, as in Leviticus 12: “But if she gives birth to a female child, she shall be unclean for two weeks.”

**Ibid.** “From speaking.” Some copies read “from striking,” and shortly afterward *fieri* instead of *fari*. Perhaps it should be “from being made,” alluding to *fiat*, “let it be.” The practice of calling Sunday the first weekday (*prima feria*) because it is the first after the day of rest—that is, the Sabbath—and then Monday the second weekday, and so forth, is peculiar to Isidore; Mazochius confirms it in volume III of the *Spicilegium* on Acts, chapter 19. AREV.]

#### 1

Among the Greeks and Romans, the week is completed through the course of seven days. Among the Hebrews, however, there are seven years. Daniel makes this clear in speaking of the seventy weeks. A week consists of seven weekdays. *Feria* is also said to derive from *fari*, “to speak,” as though from *fari*, because in the creation of the world God said on each day, “Let it be.”

Likewise, because the day of the Sabbath has been regarded as a day of rest from the beginning, Sunday is now called the first weekday, because it is the first after the day of rest. Monday is similarly called the second weekday, because it is the second after the day of rest, that is, the Sabbath, which is a day of rest. The remaining days likewise took their names from this numbering.

[Note: **No. 2.** “Which is next to the sun in size.” To those who observe it, it appears so because of its proximity, although otherwise it is the smallest of all the stars. Cicero, *Dream of Scipio*: “There were those stars which we have never seen from this place, and sizes of all kinds such as we had never suspected. Among them was the smallest, which, being nearest to heaven and closest to the earth, shone with borrowed light.”

**Ibid.** “From the star of Mars, which is Pyrois.” In all books, *Vesper* appears through an error, with the letters reversed, instead of *Pyrois*. The same occurs in Book III of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** “Borrows.” Some copies read “borrows for itself.” Immediately afterward comes the third, and so in succession the fourth, etc. AREV.]

#### 2

Among the Romans, these days received their names from the planets, that is, from the wandering stars. They called the first day after the sun, which is chief among all the stars, just as that day is the head of all days. The second was named after the moon, which is nearest to the sun both in brilliance and in size and borrows its light from it. The third was named after the star of Mars, which is called Pyrois.

[Note: **No. 3.** “Which some call the bright circle.” Rather, *Stilbon*. See the note on Book V, chapter 28, of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** “From the star of Saturn, which is placed in the seventh heaven.” In the erroneous form found in Book …, “the sixth heaven,” as also in many copies of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** “The seventh heaven.” Thus some of our manuscripts. AREV.]

#### 3

The fourth was named after the star of Mercury, which some call the bright circle. The fifth was named after the star of Jupiter, which they call Phaethon. The sixth was named after the star of Venus, which they identify as Lucifer, who has more light than all the stars. The seventh was named after the star of Saturn, which is placed in the seventh heaven and is said to complete its course in thirty years.

[Note: **No. 4.** “From Mercury, speech and wisdom.” In the *Etymologies*, “intellect and speech,” from Servius.

**Ibid.** “From Mars, heat; from Mars, blood.” The same source.

**Ibid.** “They gave.” Some copies read “they bestowed.”

Afterward: “from the sun, fire; from the air, spirit.” AREV.]

#### 4

Accordingly, the pagans gave the days their names from these seven stars, because they believed that something was produced for them through them, saying that they received spirit from the sun, body from the moon, speech and wisdom from Mercury, pleasure from Venus, heat from Mars, temperance from Jupiter, and sluggishness from Saturn. Such was the folly of the pagans, who invented for themselves such ridiculous fictions.

## Chapter Four: On Months

[Note: **Chapter IV, no. 1.** “Either the course from new moon to new moon.” The word *course* had been omitted by scribes who were misled by the similarity of the following word, “whose.” We have restored it from the *Etymologies*. There, in chapter 31, the text reads: “Hence among the Hebrews the proper months are counted not from the solar cycle but from the course of the moon, which is from new moon to new moon.”

**Ibid.** “The ancients defined it: As long as the moon is carried through the zodiacal circle.” These are the words of Hyginus at the end of Book IV.

**Ibid.** “Renewal.” Some copies read “return.” AREV.]

#### 1

A month is the circuit and renewal of lunar light, either the course from new moon to new moon. Its figure is often understood as the course of this life, which proceeds through its increases like a month and ends in very certain diminutions. The ancients defined a month as follows: “As long as the moon is carried through the zodiacal circle.”

[Note: **No. 2.** “The ancient pagans gave the months certain names from their gods … from the sacred rites of the Luperci.” The entire passage is taken from Augustine, Book XVIII against Faustus, chapter 5, with a few changes in order. See also Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 12. [Throughout this book, the notes to which no name is attached are to be attributed to Grialius. EDIT.]]

#### 2

The ancient pagans assigned certain names to the months from their gods, certain names from causes, and others from number, beginning with March, because they followed from it the order of the beginning year. They called this month March in honor of Romulus, because they believed him to be the son of Mars. April, however, they named not after any of their gods but from its own character, as though it were called “the opening month,” because at that time a great abundance of budding growth opens into flower.

[Note: **No. 3.** “Sister or wife,” that is, “sister and wife.” AREV.]

#### 3

They then named May after Maia, the mother of Mercury, whom they decreed to be a goddess because of their ancestors. Next came June, from Juno, whom they testify to have been the sister or wife of Jupiter. Others, however, said that just as May was named for the elders, so June was named for the younger people.

They also called July after Julius Caesar and August after Augustus Octavian. Previously July had been called Quintilis and August Sextilis. Their names, however, were changed by the Caesars Julius and Augustus.

[Note: **No. 4.** “October, November, December, from the number of rains and from spring.” Nothing of this kind occurs in Augustine; there the names derive from numbers or from the order of numbers. Shall we therefore suppose that Isidore was playing with etymology, or rather that this material was added to him together with P. Chacon? For the same reason one may suspect the words: “But January is specifically called so because it is the gate and beginning of the year.” Neither Augustine nor Macrobius mentions this etymology.

**Ibid.** “From the februa, etc.” Others have: “They named them in two ways, by reference to the idol and by reference to the thing itself: from the sacred februa of the Luperci, because in this month alone they washed away all the impurities of their bodies and became feverish in cold water. It is said with reference to the thing because many creatures customarily come together in it. Therefore, etc.” AREV.]

#### 4

September was so called because it is the seventh month from March, which is the beginning of spring. In the same order, October, November, and December received their names from the number of rains and from spring. They called January after Janus, but it is specifically called January because it is the gate and beginning of the year. February they called after the *Februa*, the sacred rites of the Luperci.

Thus, among the ancient Latins, the course of the year was reckoned in ten months. But the Romans added January, and Numa Pompilius added February, dividing the year into twelve months.

[Note: **No. 5.** “Most say that Ancus, king of the Sabines …” Numa, who was a Sabine, was the grandson through his daughter. Catullus alluded to this in his hymn to Diana:

> Be, by whatever name  
> You wish to be called,  
> Holy one, and protect  
> The race of Romulus and Ancus  
> As you are accustomed to do,  
> With your benevolent power.

It is surprising that this was not noticed by so learned a man, who restored the true reading from ancient books. Catullus did not merely wish to indicate the Romans when he said “of Romulus and of Ancus”; he meant the Romans whose paternal ancestry they traced to Romulus and whose maternal ancestry they traced to Ancus—that is, to the Sabines.

**[Col. 0970B] Ibid.** “That there were twelve months in the year even before the Flood.” Nothing prevents this from being true, although the passage cited from Genesis does not sufficiently prove it, especially since it mentions only the tenth month, not—as it appears in the Isidorian books—the eleventh. This occurred because, where the Greek translators now read ἐν τῷ δεκάτῳ μηνὶ (“in the tenth month”), other copies read ἑνδεκάτῳ μηνὶ (“in the eleventh month”).

**Ibid.** Some copies read: “Until the tenth month … the tops of the mountains appeared.” For that is how the months were then counted. AREV.]

#### 5

Most authorities, however, assert that Ancus, king of the Sabines, first divided the year into months and established the Ides, Kalends, and intercalary days. The books of Holy Scripture show that there were twelve months in the year even before the Flood. For there we read: “The waters were diminishing until the eleventh month. In the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains appeared.” Thus the month was then counted just as it is now—not according to the Kalends, but according to the interval enclosed by the beginning and ending of the moon.

[Note: **No. 6.** “The Kalends were named from *colere*, to celebrate.” In the *Etymologies* this is not asserted as Isidore’s own opinion but as the opinion of others. It is established, however, that they were named from *calare*, “to call.” See Macrobius.

**Ibid.** “Or from the Idule”; some copies read *Edulium*. *Idule* is preferable. Festus says in *Sacred Way* that the sacrifice made to Jupiter on each Ides, a ewe lamb, was called *Idulium*. “Rather,” you will say, “the ewe was called *Idulis*, and *Idulium* was derived from the Ides themselves.” As though it were surprising or novel for Isidore to derive earlier things from later ones, when the latter are more clearly known. Thus, in his writings, *quadratus* is derived from *four*, *testis* from *testamentum*, *jejunium* from the empty intestine, and hundreds of similar examples. But Macrobius’s other very elegant explanations of the Ides should be consulted.

**Ibid.** “The Nones from the market days.” The Nones have nothing to do with the market days. Rather, Macrobius says that because market days sometimes fell on the Nones, it was stipulated how the market days should not coincide with the Nones.]

#### 6

The Kalends were named from *colere*, “to celebrate,” because among the ancients the beginnings of the months were always celebrated. The Ides were likewise named either from “days” or from *Idulium*, and the Nones from the market days. Among the Latins, all months take their beginnings from the Kalends. Among the Hebrews, they take their beginnings from the return of the rising moon.

[Note: **No. 7.** “Among the Egyptians the beginnings of the months, etc.” The reason for this will be clear from the words of Macrobius cited in chapter 1.

**Ibid.** “Four or five days, etc.” Some copies state: “Four, or five, or six, or seven, or eight days.” The indicated diagram, together with others belonging to chapter 37, is presented elsewhere. AREV.]

#### 7

Among the Egyptians, the beginnings of the months are announced four or five days before the Kalends, as the accompanying formula explains. (See the following page.) [Col. 0971A] You then return to the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and by this method the 360 days of the twelve Egyptian months are completed. Five days remain, which they called ἐπαγόμενοι (*epagomenoi*), or intercalary or additional days. They have been mentioned above.

## Chapter Five: On the Agreement of the Months

[Note: **Chapter V, no. 1.** See Palladius, *Horologium*.]

#### 1

January agrees with December in the measure of its hours. February consumes a span equal to that of November. March corresponds to October. April equals September. May answers to August. June is equal to July.

## Chapter Six: On Years

[Note: **Chapter VI, no. 1.** “A year is the circuit and return of the sun.” Macrobius, Book I on the *Dream*, chapter 6: “Calling the circuit and return of the sun a year: ‘circuit’ because of the extent of the zodiac; ‘return’ because year after year it measures the same signs according to a fixed law.”

**Ibid.** The Vulgate reads: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God.” AREV.]

#### 1

A year is the circuit and return of the sun through twelve months. Its name figuratively signifies the whole period of this life, as it is said through Isaiah: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” For it was not only the year in which the Lord preached that was acceptable, but the entire period, according to the Apostle’s words: “Behold, now is the acceptable time.” Finally, he joined the end of this year to the day of judgment, saying: “To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.”

[Note: **No. 2.** Some begin it from the spring equinox, as the Hebrews do. This applies after Moses, since previously they reckoned it from autumn.

**Ibid.** Some begin it from the solstice, as the Greeks do. He does not say from which solstice; yet it is established that the Greeks had two beginnings of the year, derived from the two solstices. One was natural, from the winter solstice, to which Terence is thought to have referred in the *Phormio*:

> The seer forbade beginning anything new  
> Before the winter solstice.

The other was civil, in the sense in which Plato, in Book VI of the *Laws*, calls the period after the summer turning “the new year.” This was because of the Olympic contest, which was celebrated at the first full moon after the summer solstice. I think Isidore was speaking of this latter beginning, for the ancients called only this one “the solstice.”]

#### 2

Some think that the year is called *annus* as if from *anulus*, “a ring,” that is, a circle. Hence *annuli*, “rings,” are also a diminutive form. Some consider the beginning of the year to be from the winter solstice, as among the Roman peoples; others from the spring equinox, as among the Hebrews; others from the solstice, as among the Greeks; and others from autumn, as among the Egyptians.

The wise men of this world said that the year is partly civil, partly natural, and partly great. The civil year is the one that ends with the return of one star through twelve months.

[Col. 0972B]

[Note: **No. 3.** “But by a certain Milesian philosopher.” Diogenes Laertius, in his Life of Thales, and Plutarch, Book II *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*. But who called this a natural year? Should “lunar” therefore be read? That solution, too, is not entirely satisfactory.]

Ibid. “Which year [the ancients said was completed] in the six-hundredth year.” Why we have printed it thus, despite all the books disagreeing, must be explained. For in the printed editions and older manuscripts—for example, Ovet., Goth., and the twentieth [year]—and in another very old manuscript, the twentieth year is read. Those who could not resolve this calculation made it the nineteenth, as in two other more recent manuscripts, Valent. and Malacitan., thereby confusing the great year with the nineteen-year lunar cycle, without either precedent or reason. For no one has spoken in this way, nor do all the heavenly bodies return to their proper order in that lunar cycle, but the moon alone does so.

“Yet,” you will say, “that may be so; but what has the twentieth or nineteenth year to do with the six-hundredth? Or why should the six-hundredth be regarded as the correct reading?” Bede, who transferred much of this book into his own works *On the Nature of Things* and *On the Reckoning of Time*, writes as follows in chapter 9 of the first edition of *On the Reckoning of Time*:

> The great year is the period in which all the stars, after completing their appointed courses, return to their own places; Josephus says that it is completed in six hundred solar years.

Likewise, in chapter 35 of the later edition of *On the Nature of Things*:

> The great year is when all the wandering stars together return to the several places which they had occupied together.

Josephus, in the first book of the *Antiquities*, mentions it in this way when describing the longevity of the first human beings:

> But let no one, comparing their lives with the present human lifespan and the brevity of the years in which we now live, suppose that the things said about them are false, or, because life is not now prolonged for so long a period, believe that they did not attain that length of life. For they, being religious and created by God himself, and having provisions more suitable for a longer period prepared for them, properly lived through such vast spans of years. Then, because of the virtues and glorious advantages that they continually investigated—that is, astronomy and geometry—God granted them a longer span of life. They could not now have learned these subjects unless they lived six hundred years; for the great year is completed in so many years.

This variation was produced by a script that is ambiguous to the reader: **VIC o.**, from which it is easy for anyone to derive either *vicesimo* (“twentieth”) or *sexcentesimo* (“six-hundredth”). The year in question, however, is not truly the Platonic great year that completes its revolution, about which Cicero speaks in the *Dream of Scipio*. In that year all the stars whatsoever return; in this one, only the wandering stars return together to the places from which they set out. Isidore also defines this year as the great year in book V of the *Etymologies*:

> It occurs when all the planets return to the same place after many solar years.

And Balbus, in Cicero’s second book *On the Nature of the Gods*, says:

> From whose unequal motions mathematicians have named the great year. It is completed when, after all their courses have been fulfilled, the sun, moon, and five wandering stars have returned to the same relation to one another.

That Isidore understood only Josephus by “the ancients” was characteristic of his usual practice. But, not to digress too far, in the preceding chapter 4 he likewise said of Hyginus:

> The ancients defined a month as the time during which the moon traverses the zodiacal circle.

Ibid. Some say that the year which the ancients called the great year was completed or fulfilled in the twentieth year. Others: “the year which the ancients said was completed or fulfilled in the five-hundred-and-thirty-second year, the nineteenth year.” AREV.]

3. The natural year is when the moon places itself beneath the sun and, being positioned between the sun’s orb and our eyes, causes darkness throughout the sun; this is called an eclipse. The explanation of it was obscure for a long time, but it was expounded by a certain Milesian philosopher. The great year is said to be the period in which all the stars, after their appointed times and measured revolutions have been completed, return to their proper place or order. The ancients said that this year was completed or fulfilled in the six-hundredth year.

[Note: [Col. 0974C]

4. The solstitial year. These are the words of Ambrose, book IV, chapter 5.

Ibid. The jubilee year. Concerning it, see Leviticus 25.

Ibid. Others: “According to the law, the trumpets were sounded.” AREV.]

4. The solstitial year is when the sun, having completed its circuit through all the signs, returns to the point from which it began its course. It is itself the solar year, or civil year, which is completed in 365 days. The common lunar year is the year that runs through twelve lunar months, that is, 354 days. The embolismic year is said to contain thirteen moons and 384 days; in this year the date of Easter is extended farther. The leap year is the year in which the total of one day is accumulated over four years from the quarter-day fraction. The jubilee year is the year of remission, formed by seven weeks of years—that is, forty-nine years—in which, according to the law, trumpets were sounded and the ancient possession returned to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0974D]

5. The Olympiad. The Olympiad was held after the fourth year had been completed and the fifth begun; the lustrum was established after the fifth year had been completed. It is therefore not surprising to find among authors Olympiads of five years and lustra of five years. See book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 37.]

5. Among the Greeks, an Olympiad is a four-year period, named from the Olympic contest, which occurs after four years have elapsed. In it the period of the contest reaches its conclusion, because of the sun’s four-year cycle and because, through the yearly accumulation of three hours, one complete day is added over four years. At this time they sent messengers around the cities to urge that people should assemble not only from every region, but also from every class, every age, and both sexes.

[Note: [Col. 0974D]

6. The Romans invented the indictions. Others who wrote about the correction of time have related their beginnings and causes.

Ibid. A fragment concerning the indiction survives from the Albanian Codex in Appendix 6 to book V, chapter 36 of the *Etymologies*. AREV.]

6. A lustrum is a five-year period among the Romans. It was called a *lustrum* because the census was conducted in the republic every five years. Then, after the census had been completed and a sacrifice performed, the city of Rome was purified. The Romans invented the indictions, which proceed year by year up to the fifteenth and then roll back again to the beginning of the first year.

[Note: [Col. 0974D]

7. It was called the era. The same passage occurs in book V of the *Etymologies*.]

7. The era too was established in the time of Caesar Augustus. It was called the era from the time when the world professed to return bronze to the Roman people. The era increases from the day of the January Kalends. The leap day, however, is inserted in the course of the moon from the sixth day before the Kalends of March up to the day before the Kalends. The Egyptian year without a leap day begins on the fourth day before the Kalends of September; with a leap day, it begins on the third day before the aforementioned Kalends.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Seasons

[Note: [Col. 0974D]

CHAP. VII.—No. 1. “As Ambrose says.” Most of this chapter is his; book IV, chapter 5.

Ibid. “According to the Hebrews, a complete year.” So indeed in Daniel at the cited passage. Elsewhere, for the Hebrews it signifies the same period as for the other nations.

[Col. 0975C] Ibid. “Spread out.” Others: “undivided.” AREV.]

1. As Ambrose says, the seasons are cycles of changes in which the sun, by the definite measure of its course, distinguishes the circuit of the year through a dispersed variety. The seasons are movements of the heavenly bodies. Hence, when God established these things, he said: “Let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years”—that is, in some changing motion, in which one thing passes before and another afterward, since they cannot exist simultaneously. According to the Hebrews, a season is a complete year, in accordance with the passage in Daniel: “A time, and times, and half a time.” By “time” he signifies one year, by “times” two, and by “half” six months.

[Note: [Col. 0975C]

2. Others: “it stiffens, freezes, and contracts.” AREV.]

2. Among the Latins, four seasons are assigned to one year: winter, spring, summer, and autumn. Winter is when the sun remains in the southern regions. For then the sun is farther away, the earth stiffens and contracts under the frost, and the spans of night are longer than those of day. Hence it happens that during the winter winds an excessive force of snow and rain is poured down. Spring is when the sun, withdrawing from the southern regions, returns above the earth, makes the periods of night and day equal, and restores a temperate atmosphere. Fostering all things, it compels them to produce offspring again, so that the earth may germinate, the seeds loosened in the furrows may revive, and the succession of yearly offspring of every kind found on land or in the waters may be propagated.

3. Summer is when the sun raises itself toward the north, lengthens the daylight hours, and narrows and contracts the nights. Thus, the more it is joined and mingled with this air through continual contact, the more it heats the air itself; and, when its moisture has been dried up, the earth cracks into dust. It makes the seeds grow and compels the fruits of the forests, as though their green juices, to ripen. Then, because the sun burns with the heat of summer, it makes shorter shadows at midday, since from on high it illuminates that place. Autumn is when the sun, descending again from the highest part of the sky, breaks the strength of the heat and, with its warmth gradually relaxed and diminished, provides temperateness, followed by a season of winds, the whirl of storms, and the force of lightning and sounding thunderclaps.

4. Since we have briefly treated the alternating changes of the seasons according to the preceding definitions and their established distinctions, let us now explain how these same seasons are mutually joined to one another through natural cycles. Spring consists of moisture and fire, summer of fire and dryness, autumn of dryness and cold, and winter of cold and moisture. Hence the seasons are also called periods of the disturbance of the temperament; the figure of this combination is as follows.

[Col. 0975C] [Note: [Col. 0975C]

5. These are the beginnings of the seasons. The common people assign three months to each season of the year. Astrologers begin summer and winter from the solstice, and spring and autumn from the equinoxes, taking their starting points from the signs of the zodiac. Physicians, considering only the principle of temperateness, make winter and summer almost twice as long as spring and autumn. For them, spring begins at the equinox and ends near the end of April; autumn begins before August has ended and generally ends at the beginning of November. Isidore preferred another system. For, placing one month before each equinox, solstice, and winter solstice, he divides the seasons of the year; yet this system was not approved by Bede in book *On the Nature of Things*, second edition, chapter 34.

Ibid. “The eighth day before the Kalends.” Others: “the seventh day before the Kalends.” AREV.]

5. These are the beginnings of the seasons: spring arises on the eighth day before the Kalends of March and lasts 91 days. Summer begins on the ninth day before the Kalends of June and lasts 91 days. Autumn takes its beginning on the tenth day before the Kalends of September and lasts 93 days. Winter begins on the seventh day before the Kalends of December and lasts 90 days. Thus the days of the year total 365. This, then, is according to the natural distinction of the seasons.

[Note: [Col. 0976C]

6. “By the dryness of unbelief.” Others, less well: “by the dryness of faith.” AREV.]

6. In allegorical interpretation, however, temporal winter is understood as tribulation, when the storms and tempests of the world bear down upon us. Summer is the persecution of faith, when doctrine is dried up by the dryness of unbelief. Spring is the renewal of faith, or peace, when, after the tribulation of winter, tranquility is restored to the Church; when the month of new things—that is, Easter, the feast of the Lamb—is celebrated; when the earth, that is, the Church, is adorned with flowers, namely, gatherings of the saints.

7. Thus the year is unfolded through the circuit of the sun and the months. The seasons unfold through cycles of change. The month is completed through the moon’s increase and waning. The week ends with the number seven of its days. Day and night are renewed through the alternating cycles of returning light and darkness. The hour is completed through certain movements and moments.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Solstice and Equinox

[Note: [Col. 0977C]

CHAP. VIII.—No. 1. “The winter solstice, the eighth day before the Kalends of January.” Now, according to the Gregorian calendar, the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

Ibid. “At which the sun stands.” Not that the sun ever actually stands still, but that it brings its course to a halt by descending no farther and turning back. The same is to be understood of the summer solstice—which the ancients alone called “the solstice.” For the sun does not rise any farther either.

Ibid. “The other, the summer solstice, the eighth day before the Kalends of July.” Now the eleventh day before the Kalends of July.

Ibid. “The spring equinox, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.” Now the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. The autumnal equinox is on the Kalends of October.

Ibid. “At which the sun stands.” That is, it appears to stand while it descends and turns back. AREV.]

1. There are two solstices: the first, the winter solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, at which the sun stands still and the days grow longer. The second is the summer solstice, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, at which the sun stands still and the nights grow longer. Opposed to these are two equinoxes: one in spring, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the days grow longer; the other in autumn, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, when the days diminish.

[Note: [Col. 0977D]

2. Others: “because from that day onward the sun’s lamp pours over the day with greater brightness and receives the excessive heat of the approaching summer.” AREV.]

2. The solstice is so called, as though it were the sun’s station. The equinox is so called because at that time day and night return to an equality of twelve hours, their periods having been made equal. The summer solstice is therefore called a lamp, because from that day onward the sun’s lamp receives greater brightness and pours forth excessive heat with the arrival of summer.

## CHAPTER IX. On the World

[Col. 0977C] [Note: [Col. 0977D]

CHAP. IX.—No. 1. “For just as that one is composed of four elements.” He developed this more fully in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 11.

Ibid. “Composed.” Others: “created.” AREV.]

1. The world is the totality of all things, which consists of heaven and earth. Concerning it the apostle Paul says: “For the form of this world is passing away.” In the mystical sense, however, the world is appropriately understood as the human being, because just as the former is composed of four elements, so the latter consists of four humors mingled in one temperament.

[Col. 0978A] 2. Hence the ancients also placed the human being in communion with the structure of the world. For in Greek the world is called *kosmos* (κόσμος), while the human being is called *mikrokosmos* (μικρόκοσμος), that is, “the lesser world.” Scripture sometimes also indicates sinners by “the world,” concerning whom it is said: “And the world did not know him.”

[Note: [Col. 0977D]

3. “For just as the world rises.” Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> As the world rises steeply toward Scythia and the Rhipaean heights,  
> so it sinks down toward Libya and the southern winds.

Ibid. “The northern region.” Others: “the western region.” [Col. 0978C] For an explanation of the four parts of the world as set out here, see *Etymologies* book III, chapters 30 and 41. AREV.]

3. The formation of the world is demonstrated as follows. For just as the world rises toward the northern quarter, so it declines toward the south. Its head, and as it were its face, is the eastern region; its farthest part is the northern region. Its parts are four: the first part of the world is the East, the second the South, the third the West, and the last and most remote the North. Concerning it Lucan says:

> Thus lies the lowest part of the world, which the snowy zone  
> and perpetual winters press upon.

## CHAPTER X. On the Five Circles

[Note: [Col. 0978C]

CHAP. X.—No. 1. “Which the Greeks call zones.” All the books read: “which the Greeks call parallels, that is, zones.” This is erroneous, as appears from *Etymologies* III, chapter 43, and XIII, chapter 6. Although the same material is repeated twice there, the two words “parallels, that is,” are not found. Whoever added them thought *zona* a not-very-Greek word, and had read in Pliny, book VI, chapter 33: “There are several divisions of the world, which our people have called circles, [and] the Greeks *parallēlous* (παραλλήλους).”

Ibid. Virgil, on the five zones, *Georgics* I, 322. AREV.]

1. In defining the world, philosophers say that there are five circles, which the Greeks call zones, into which the globe of the earth is divided. Virgil shows these in the *Georgics*, saying: “Five zones occupy the heavens.” Let us imagine them in the shape of our right hand, so that the thumb is the Arctic Circle, uninhabitable because of the cold; the second circle is the summer circle, temperate and habitable; the middle circle is the equinoctial circle, torrid and uninhabitable; the fourth circle is the winter circle, temperate and habitable; and the fifth circle is the Antarctic Circle, cold and uninhabitable.

[Note: [Col. 0978D]

2. “Where the sun’s powerful wheel never burns with fire.” From those who published fragments of the poets. We shall nevertheless report the readings of the old books, in case someone may make a better conjecture: “Quam solis valido nunquam ut aufferra a igne.” Ovet. “Quam solis valido nunquam aut auffera igne.” Toletan., Malacitan., and Valent. “Quam solis valido nunquam vis auxerat igne.” Printed editions. From this someone might perhaps make: “Quas solis valido nunquam vis usserit igne.” Or: “Qua solis validos nunquam vis afferat ignes.” For we think that *auxerat* was produced from *afferat*, written with two digammas; or again: “Quas solis valido nunquam vis afflet ab igni.”]

2. Of these, the first is northern, the second solstitial, the third equinoctial, the fourth winter, and the fifth southern. Concerning them Varro said:

> But the ethereal sphere is girded by five zones,  
> and the lowest regions are laid waste by winters, the middle by heat;  
> thus the outer regions of the earth and the middle one are inhabited,  
> where the sun’s powerful wheel never burns with fire.

The divisions of these circles are distinguished by the following figure. (See the following page.)

[Col. 0979A] [Note: [Col. 0979B]

3. “But the equinoctial circle is uninhabitable.” Avicenna was the first to say that it is most suitable for habitation, as has in fact been discovered.

Ibid. “But, on the contrary, the northern and southern circles are joined to one another.” “To one another” means joined to and near the equinoctial circle. Otherwise they are very far apart.]

3. The equinoctial circle is uninhabitable because the sun, running through the middle of the sky, produces excessive heat in those regions, so that neither crops grow there because of the scorched earth nor human beings are permitted to live there because of the excessive heat. Conversely, the northern and southern circles are not inhabited because they lie far from the sun’s course and waste away under the excessive rigor of the sky and the icy blasts of the winds.

4. The solstitial circle, which in the East is positioned between the northern and summer circles, and the one which in the West lies between the summer and southern circles, are temperate because they receive cold from one circle and heat from the other. Concerning them Virgil says:

> Between these, and in the middle, two zones were granted  
> to suffering mortals by the gift of the gods.

But those who are closest to the summer circle are the Ethiopians, scorched by excessive heat.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Parts of the World

1. The parts of the world are four: fire, air, water, and earth. Their nature is as follows: fire is fine, sharp, and mobile; air is mobile, sharp, and dense; water is dense, blunt, and mobile; earth is dense, blunt, and immobile. These also mingle with one another in the following way. Earth, being dense, blunt, and immobile, is joined to water through water’s density and bluntness. Then water is joined to air through density and mobility. Again, air is joined to fire through the shared qualities of sharpness and mobility. Earth and fire are separated from each other, but they are joined by the two middle elements, water and air. So that these matters may not be understood obscurely, I have expressed them in the diagram below.

[Col. 0980B] [Note: [Col. 0980B]

CHAP. XI.—No. 2. “Moreover, Saint Ambrose.” Book III, chapter 4.

Ibid. “Joinable qualities.” Ovet. reads this way. The others, and Ambrose, read “joint qualities.”]

2. Moreover, Saint Ambrose distinguishes the same elements according to the qualities through which, by a certain communion of nature, they mingle with one another, in these words: “Earth,” he says, “is dry and cold; water is cold and moist; air is warm and moist; fire is warm and dry. Through these joinable qualities the individual elements are so mingled with one another. Earth, being dry and cold, is joined to water through kinship of the cold quality. Again, water is joined to air through moisture, because air is moist. Water, as though with two arms—cold and moisture—seems to embrace earth with one and air with the other: earth with cold, air with moisture.”

[Note: [Col. 0981B]

3. “Through a kind of chorus they come together in harmonious fellowship.” Ambrose: “through a kind of chorus of harmony and fellowship.”

Ibid. “Hence in Greek they are called *stoicheia* (στοιχεῖα).” All the books erroneously read *koina* (κοινά). For, apart from the fact that Ambrose and Basil have *stoicheia*, *Etymologies* XIII, chapter 3, also says: “The Greeks call the elements *stoicheia*, because they come together through harmony of fellowship and a certain communion.”]

3. Air itself, situated by nature between two opposing elements—that is, between water and fire—reconciles both elements to itself, since it is joined to water by moisture and to fire by heat. Fire too, being hot and dry, is attached to air by heat and associated with earth through dryness. Thus, through this circuit, they come together with one another in harmonious fellowship, as through a kind of chorus. Hence in Greek they are called *stoicheia* (στοιχεῖα), which in Latin are called elements, because they come together and harmonize with one another. The following circular figure shows their distinct communion.

## CHAPTER XII. On Heaven

[Col. 0981B]

[Note: [Col. 0981B]

CHAP. XII.—No. 1. “By virtues.” Others: “by examples and virtues.” This is the place for a short work, or fragment, on heaven; see *Isidoriana*, chapter 86, no. 5:

> It is asked whether there is one heaven or several. They are spoken of in the plural, although in this book heaven is spoken of in the singular, the heaven that is divided between water and water. We read in the Psalm in the plural: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord.”
>
> For if we understand “heavens of heavens” correctly, we take the stellar heavens as the higher heavens and the aerial heavens as the lower ones, as it is said: “Praise him, heavens of heavens.” It is sufficiently clear that this aerial region is called not only “heaven” but also “heavens,” just as “lands” are spoken of in the plural; it signifies nothing other than what is called “earth” in the singular when we say “the globe of the lands” and “the globe of the earth.”
>
> The names of the heavens are these: air, ether, Olympus, the fiery expanse, the firmament, the heaven of angels, and the heaven of the Trinity.
>
> It is asked what form and shape heaven is to be believed to have, since in the Holy Scriptures we find it represented both as a skin and as a vaulted chamber. For what is more different and opposed to itself than the extension of a skin and the joining of a vaulted chamber? And does heaven enclose the earth on every side, like a sphere, with the earth balanced in the middle mass of the world, covering it on one side like a disk, as the philosophers thought?
>
> **Response.** These two testimonies found in Scripture agree with each other, and the opinion of the philosophers concerning a spherical form agrees with them as well. For the likeness of a vaulted chamber is also compatible with a sphere, according to that part of the sphere which is above. Therefore, if it is not a sphere, heaven covers the earth on one side. But if it is a sphere, it is a vaulted chamber on every side.
>
> Thus a disk too is represented both as a vaulted chamber and as a sphere. But let us explain how what is said about a skin can be reconciled with this. Since a vaulted chamber is rightly said to be not only curved but also flat, a skin too is extended not only into a flat surface but also into a rounded cavity. For a wineskin and a bladder are skins.
>
> It is asked how heaven is called the firmament when it is known to move. If it moves, how is it called the firmament? But if it stands still, how are the stars fixed in it believed to travel from east to west and then back again to the east?
>
> **Response.** Heaven was not called the firmament because of standing still, but because of its firmness and its impassable boundary between the waters above and below, since it remains firm in its own circle and securely and impassably contains the waters held above it.
>
> It is asked whether the heaven that exceeds all the regions of the air and every height, where the luminaries and stars were also established on the fourth day, is now being formed, or whether the air itself is called the firmament. The question is reasonable, since many assert that the nature of water cannot exist above the starry heaven, because its weight is so ordered that it either floats above the earth or is carried vaporously through the air near the earth.
>
> They also say that heaven is fiery, that the nature of water cannot be reconciled with it, and that heaven is round, revolving, and burning, so that water cannot remain in that revolving circuit. **Response.** Let those who think this cease their madness and, in confusion, acknowledge what Truth says.
>
> We too shall assert the faith of Scripture to them from visible natures themselves, so that they may recognize what uncertainty they had concerning invisible things. For it is customary in Scripture to call this air “heaven” not only by name but also in its own right; and since birds fly in the air, they are called “the birds of heaven,” while we speak of a clear or cloudy heaven when we mean the air.
>
> Indeed, when the Lord himself was speaking about the clouds, he said: “You can discern the face of heaven.” Thus the air, which lies between the moist vapors from which clouds gather above and the waters spread below, is shown to be heaven between water and water.
>
> The weights of the elements are therefore no obstacle. For if water can be reduced to such tiny drops, as we see, that it may be carried vaporously above this air, which by nature is lighter, or whatever it may be, why cannot water above that lighter heaven be dispersed in smaller drops and lighter vapors?
>
> They assert that the star which they call Saturn is cold, and that it completes its circuit in thirty years because it travels in the higher circle, whereas the sun does so in a year and the moon in a month, and that these are shorter because they occupy a lower position. Why, then, is that star cold, when it ought to be hotter in proportion as it is carried above the heavens and travels more swiftly day by day, unless the nature of the waters above that highest heaven makes it cold?
>
> Let them understand this, then, and cease their madness, because he who could create all things from nothing could also establish those waters in heaven with icy solidity. For when it is said of him, “You who roll the sphere resplendent with burning stars,” did divine providence not necessarily arrange that waters should overflow within and above the sphere of heaven, to temper the fires of that burning axis, lest the conflagration above ignite the elements below?
>
> We, however, do not know what those waters are like or of what kind they may be; we have no doubt that they exist above that highest heaven. For the authority of his Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human mind. AREV.]

1. Spiritually, heaven is the Church, which in the night of this life shines with the virtues of the saints, as with the brightness of stars. In the plural, by the name “heavens” all the saints or angels are understood. Indeed, by “heavens” we should also understand the prophets and apostles. Concerning them it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God”—because they themselves announced to the world Christ’s coming and death, and likewise his resurrection and glory.

[Note: [Col. 0984B]

2. “Ambrose in the books . . . . is called embossed.” Book II, chapter 4.

Ibid. “For its nature is subtle . . . . like smoke.” Book I, chapter 6. These are Isaiah’s words, chapter 51, from the Septuagint: “For heaven was made firm like smoke” (ὅτι οὐρανὸς ὡς καπνὸς ἐστερεώθη).]

2. Concerning the name “heaven,” Saint Ambrose says the following in the books he wrote on the creation of the world: “Heaven is called *ouranos* (οὐρανός) in the Greek language; among the Latins it is called *caelum* because, having the lights of the stars impressed upon it like signs, it is said to be like embossed work, just as silver decorated with projecting figures is called embossed. Scripture also demonstrates that its nature is subtle, saying that he made heaven firm like smoke.”

[Note: [Col. 0984B]

3. *Cous*, or *covus*, or *chous*. Varro, book IV: “Beneath the middle of the yoke, the *covum*, which is closed by the addition of the end of the plow-beam, is called *covum* from *covus*.” Festus: “*Cohum*, the strap by which the plow-pole of the plow is tied to the yoke, is so called from *cohibere*, ‘to hold together.’ Poets called *cohum* heaven, from *Chaos*, from which they thought heaven had been formed. I think, however, that it too was derived from *cohibere*, ‘to contain.’ This is also what Isidore seems to have intended when he says: “*Cohum*, because it contains heaven.”

Ibid. “The poles are the peaks of the celestial circles . . . . is called.” Hyginus, book I: “The peaks of this axis, speaking of the axis, on which the sphere rests most firmly, are called poles. The one looking toward the north is called the Boreal pole; the other, placed toward the south, is called the Notian pole.” Nothing has nevertheless been changed in Isidore. For it is established that this pole is called southern, Notian, Austronotus, or Austronotius. Isidore said that it is opposite the earth because, by the obstruction of the earth, as the commentator on Aratus says, it is not visible to us. See books III and XIII of the *Etymologies*.

Ibid. “The stars. *Chous*, which contains heaven.” Others: “hemispheres. *Chous*, by which heaven is contained.” AREV.]

3. Its parts are *chous*, axis, pivots, convex surfaces, poles, and stars. *Chous* is that which contains heaven. Hence Ennius: “Scarcely able to fill the *chous* with the terrors of heaven.” [Col. 0983B] The axis is the straight line that extends through the middle of the sphere’s ball. The pivots are the extreme parts of the axis. The convex surfaces are the outermost parts of heaven. The poles are the peaks of the celestial circles on which the sphere rests most firmly. One, facing toward the north, is called the Boreal pole; the other, opposite the earth, is called the Austronotian pole.

[Col. 0984A] [Note: [Col. 0984C]

4. “And they said that it was burning.” Plato was also among these; he wrote that heaven and the stars are fiery. But, as Galen interprets him, he did not mean this fire, which has the power to burn, but another fire that shares only in light. Aristotle refuted the reasoning of the ancients, though he was unable to establish his own view against Basil and Ambrose, whom our author follows here.

Ibid. “May they temper its burning.” The following chapter, from Ambrose.

Ibid. “They confirm that it is a sphere.” Hyginus, book I, at the beginning.

Ibid. “But heaven, etc.” Others: “There are two hemispheres, one above the earth and the other beneath the earth. But heaven, etc.” AREV.]

4. The wise believe that heaven turns from east to west once in a day and night. They said that it is round, revolving, and burning. They thought that its sphere was above the waters, so that it might revolve within them and they might temper its burning. They confirm that the sphere has neither beginning nor end, because, on account of its roundness, like a circle, it is not easily understood where it begins or ends. It is said to be equally gathered together from every side, to face everything alike, and to be separated by equal distances from the center of the earth. Through its own equality it is so stable that the equality gathered together on every side does not allow it to decline in any direction, and, supported by no prop, it remains sustained.

[Note: [Col. 0984D]

5. “That it lacks any indication of angles.” Thus the old books read. Perhaps: “that it lacks incisions of angles.” Cicero: “Nothing cut into by angles.”

Ibid. “That it contains within itself the remaining.” The old books erroneously read: “the stars within itself.”]

5. Treating the perfection of the sphere or circle through many arguments, Plato reasonably sets forth the work of the world’s Maker. First, because it consists of one line. Second, because it is without beginning and without end. Third, because it is produced from a point. Again, because it possesses motion from itself. Then, because it lacks any indication of angles, because it contains within itself all other figures, and because it has an undeviating motion, since the other six motions are wandering: forward, backward, right, left, upward, and downward. Finally, because necessity causes this line to be unable to extend beyond the circle.

[Note: [Col. 0985B]

6. “The pole, moreover, with such speed, etc.” The same passage occurs in book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 34.]

6. There are, as we said, two poles on which heaven revolves: the Boreal pole, which we call the Aquilonian pole. Here are the Bears, that is, the northern constellations, which are always visible to us. Opposite it is the Notian pole, which is called southern. This is the pole which, as Cicero says, is hidden by the earth and is called ἀφανής (“invisible”) by the Greeks. The pole is said to move with such speed that, unless the stars move against its precipitous course, they would bring about the ruin of the world. For its headlong revolution is said to be tempered by the course of the stars. Hence Lucan:

> The stars, which alone regulate the flight of heaven,  
> meet the pole; a different power, the first law  
> of the world, has been assigned to them.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Seven Planets of Heaven and Their Revolutions

[Note: [Col. 0985B]

CHAP. XIII.—No. 1. Ambrose, in book II of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 2.

Ibid. Isidore’s short work on harmony and heavenly music, which I reviewed in *Isidoriana*, chapter 86, no. 3, can be referred to this chapter and the following ones. It is as follows:

> The moon is the first of the planets and the smallest of the stars, but it appears larger than the others because it is carried in a circle nearer to the earth and to us. Its body is spherical and fiery by nature, but mixed with water. Hence it does not possess its own light, but is illuminated like a mirror; and therefore the moon is called *luna*, as though *lucina*, that is, “born from light.”
>
> The cloudlike appearance seen on it is believed to arise from the nature of water. For it is said that, if water had not been mixed with it, it would illuminate or enlighten the earth like the sun—or rather, because of its nearness, it would devastate it with enormous heat. Its sphere is much larger than the earth, although, because of the height of its orbit, it appears scarcely larger than a bushel measure at its base.
>
> The moon shines on the side that faces the sun; the side turned away from the sun is dark. When it is farther removed from the sun, it shines in its entirety. For it neither grows nor diminishes, but, because the earth stands in the way, it is illuminated by the light that it receives from the sun.

“Although it is carried daily by the force of the firmament from east to west, nevertheless, pressing against the universe, it traverses all the signs of the zodiac in twenty-seven days. It is said to complete its own circuit in eighteen years.

[Col. 0985D] “When the moon is four days old, if it is red like gold, it indicates winds; if it grows black with spots on its upper horn, the beginning of a rainy month; if [it is dark] in the middle of its full light, fair weather.

“On Mercury.—The second planet is Mercury, also called Stilbon. Its globe is fiery by nature, surpasses the moon in size, receives its light from the sun, and traverses the zodiac in 229 days.

“On Venus.—The third planet is Venus, also called Vesperus, Lucifer, and Vesper: round, fiery, pressing against the universe like Mercury, it traverses the zodiac in 348 days.

“On the Sun.—The fourth planet is the sun, so called because it alone shines while the other stars are obscured, or because it shines above all things. It is spherical in form and fiery by nature; surpassing the earth eightfold in size, it provides light for all the stars.

“It is carried from east to west by the force of the firmament; but, pressing against the universe, it travels through the entire zodiac [Col. 0986B] in 365 days. It is said to complete its circuit in twenty-eight years.

“Its presence produces day, its absence night. For just as it shines above the earth throughout the day, so it shines beneath the earth throughout the night. Traversing the northern region of the sky, it gives us long days and summer; traversing the southern region, it brings us short days and winter.

“When the sun is spotted at its rising, or lies hidden beneath a cloud, it foretells a rainy day; if it is red, clear weather; if pale, stormy weather. If it appears hollow, so that, [Col. 0986C] shining in the middle, it sends rays toward the south, it presages wet and windy weather; if, pale, it sets into black clouds, a north wind.

“On Mars.—The fifth planet is Mars, called Efevona: a globe burning with fire, it traverses the zodiac in two years.

“On Jupiter.—The sixth planet is Jupiter, called Epheton: round and temperate, it traverses the zodiac in twelve years.

“On Saturn.—The seventh planet is Saturn, called Ephetonta: a cold spirit, moving against the universe like the planets above, it traverses the zodiac in thirty years. At Saturn’s rising, after thirty years, whoever cast an image from bronze would prove that it spoke with a human being. All of them, however, complete their circuits after 532 years.

“The apsides of the planets—that is, their circles—are at their greatest heights from the center of the earth: Saturn’s in Scorpio, Jupiter’s in Virgo, Mars’s in Leo, the Sun’s in Gemini, Venus’s in Sagittarius, and Mercury’s in Capricorn. The moon’s is in Aries, [Col. 0986D] in the middle parts of the ram, and, conversely, their lowest points are nearest the center of the earth. Each has its own color: Saturn is white, Jupiter bright, Mars fiery, Lucifer glowing, Vesper radiant, Mercury shining, the moon gentle, and the sun burning.

“Yet their colors are changed by the nature of the neighboring circles: what is colder becomes pale, what is hotter red, what is windy dreadful, and [what is changed by neighboring circles becomes] dark. The zodiac, that is, the circle of the twelve signs, is divided laterally into twelve parts. Beneath these travel the seven planets. The sun occupies only the two middle parts. The moon occupies the entire breadth. Venus extends beyond the two parts, with two in the middle, four above two on earth. Mars is beneath the four middle parts. Jupiter is beneath the middle one and above it by two. Saturn is beneath the two middle parts, like the sun.

“These seven spheres revolve with sweet harmony, and their circling produces the most delightful concords. This sound does not reach our ears because it is produced beyond the range of hearing, and its magnitude exceeds our narrow capacity for hearing; for no sound is perceived by us unless it is produced in this air.

“From earth to the firmament, the music of heaven is measured. Our own musical system is said to have been devised according to its model. On earth is placed Γ, gamma; on the moon, A; on Mercury, B; on Venus, C; on the sun, D; on Mars, E; on Jupiter, F; and on Saturn, G. Thus the measure of the musical art is clearly found.

“Accordingly, from earth to the firmament there are found seven tones: from earth to the moon is a tone; from the moon to Mercury, a semitone; from Mercury to Venus, a semitone; thence to the sun, three semitones; from the sun to Mars, a tone; thence to Jupiter, a semitone; thence to Saturn, a semitone; and thence to Saturn, three semitones, which, joined together, produce seven tones.

[Col. 0987D] “A tone contains 15,625 miles, whereas a semitone contains 7,812 and a half. Hence the philosophers also imagined nine Muses, because they detected nine consonances from earth to heaven and found them naturally implanted in human beings.

“On the human being, who is musical.—Just as this universe is distinguished by seven tones, and our music by seven notes, and just as the bodily structure, from which the body is formed, is joined together in seven ways—when the body is united from four elements and the soul from three powers, which are naturally reconciled through the art of music—so the human being is called a microcosm, that is, a smaller universe, since he is known to participate in the music of heaven through such a harmonious number.

“From earth to the moon there are 126 stadia, which are 40,625 miles. From the moon to Mercury, 7,812 and a half miles; thence to Venus, the same distance. Thence to the sun, 23,436 miles. Thence to Mars, 15,625 miles. Thence to Jupiter, 7,812 and a half miles. Thence to Saturn, the same distance. Thence to the firmament, 23,436 miles.

“Thus from earth to heaven there are 100,000 miles, and 9,000 miles, and 375 miles. We have passed beyond the fire through the globes of the planets; now let us penetrate the celestial regions.”

I have written certain planetary names as they occur in the manuscript and as they are found in some medieval writers. What is said about the image at Saturn’s rising has the character of judicial astrology. AREV.]

1. Saint Ambrose speaks as follows in his book *Hexaemeron*: “We read in David: ‘Praise him, heavens of heavens.’ Whether there is one heaven or several is disputed, since some assert that there are many [24], while others deny that there are any besides the one. The philosophers, however, introduced seven heavens of the universe, that is, the spheres of the planets, moving in harmonious motion. They maintain that everything is joined to their spheres, believing that the bodies attached to and, as it were, inserted into them revolve backward and are carried with a motion contrary to that of the others. Indeed, in the ecclesiastical books both ‘heavens of heavens’ are mentioned, and the apostle Paul understands himself to have been caught up to the third heaven. [25] But concerning their number, let no human presumption make a claim. [Col. 0986A] God made them neither shapeless nor confused, but distinguished them by a certain rational order according to their proper arrangement. For he showed that the heaven of the higher circle was separated by its own boundary and gathered together with equal spaces on every side, and in it he established the powers of spiritual creatures. God, the craftsman of the universe, tempered the nature of this heaven with waters, lest the conflagration of the upper fire ignite the lower elements. Then he solidified the circle of the lower [Col. 0987A] heaven, not with a uniform but with a manifold motion, naming it the firmament because it supports the waters above.”

[Note: [Col. 0988C]

2. “God tempered the nature of this heaven with waters.” The same work, chapter 3.

There: “Others say, ‘for the solidified support of the waters above.’ This opinion of the ancients—that God tempered heaven with waters—is explained in the treatise referred to at chapter 12, no. 1. See also the note on Dracontius, book I, lines 25 and 137. AREV.]

26 **CHAPTER XIV. On the waters that are above the heavens**

[Note: [Col. 0988C]

CHAPTER XIV.—No. 1. This is Ambrose’s opinion. Book II, chapter 3. [Col. 0988D]]

1. This is Ambrose’s opinion: “The wise men of this world say that there cannot be waters above the heavens, arguing that heaven is fiery and that the nature of water cannot be reconciled with it. They add that the sphere of heaven is round, revolving, and burning, and that in such a revolving circuit the waters cannot possibly remain. For they must flow downward and run off when that sphere is twisted from the upper regions toward the lower; consequently, they say, the waters cannot remain there, since the axis of heaven, twisting itself with rapid motion, would spill them as it whirled them.” [Col. 0987B]

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

2. “Between the sphere of heaven and above the sphere,” Ambrose adds.

There: Grialius reads, “but at last.” AREV.]

2. “But let these men at last cease their madness and, recovering from their confusion, acknowledge that he who was able to create all things from nothing was also able to stabilize that watery nature in heaven with icy solidity. Since they themselves say that the sphere gleaming with burning stars revolves, did divine Providence not necessarily provide that waters should overflow between the sphere of heaven, to temper the fires of that blazing axis?”

**CHAPTER XV. On the nature of the sun**

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

CHAPTER XV.—No. 1. These are the words of Ambrose, or words derived from another source. Book II, chapter 3.]

1. These are Ambrose’s words in *Hexaemeron*: “The philosophers deny that the sun is of a hot nature because it is white, not reddish or ruddy [Col. 0987C] in the appearance of fire, and therefore because it is not fiery by nature. If it has any heat, they say that this results from the excessive motion of its revolution. They think this must be said so that it may appear to consume no moisture, since it does not possess naturally the heat by which moisture is diminished or often completely dried up. But they accomplish nothing by proposing this, because it makes no difference whether one has heat by nature, or from an affliction, or from some other cause.” [Col. 0988A]

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

2. “But we believe that, just as it possesses the power . . . it consumes.” From the same author, book IV, chapter 3.

There: “For the sun is fiery . . . dewy.” The interpreter of Aratus: “Meanwhile, although the sun is fiery, it grows hotter through the excessive motion of its revolution. Philosophers say that its fire is nourished by water and that from the contrary element it receives the power both of light and of heat; hence we often see it wet and dewy.”

There: “In which it gives clear evidence . . . it has taken.” These are Ambrose’s words at the cited passage.]

2. But we believe that, just as it possesses the power to illuminate, 27 so also it possesses the power to vaporize. For the sun is fiery; and fire both illuminates and consumes. Some say that the sun’s fire is nourished by water and that from the contrary element it receives the power of light and vapor; hence we often see the sun wet and dewy. In this it gives clear evidence that it has taken the watery element into itself for the sake of tempering its nature.

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

3. “In obscure weather.” Others read, “in obscure slumber.” AREV.]

3. This concerns its nature. But according to spiritual interpretation, the sun is Christ, as it is written in Malachi: “But for you who believe, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in his wings.” Christ is rightly understood as the sun, because at his rising he set according to the flesh, and according to the spirit he rose again from his setting. The sun also illuminates and consumes, and in obscure weather it warms the healthy, but burns those suffering from fever with the blaze of doubled heat. So Christ illuminates believers through the life-giving spirit of faith, but those who deny him he will scorch with the heat of eternal fire.

**CHAPTER XVI. On the size of the sun and moon**

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

CHAPTER XVI.—No. 1. Again, the same teacher in the same work. Book IV, chapter 6.

There: “At the same moment it is seen by both.” These and similar opinions of the ancients are now commonly rejected. AREV.]

1. Again, the same Doctor bears witness in the same work: “The sun’s ray is nearer to no one and farther from no one. [Col. 0988C] Likewise, the globe of the moon is equally distant from all. The sun is the same for Indians and Britons; it is seen by both at the same moment when it rises, nor does it appear smaller to the peoples of the East when it declines toward the West; nor does it seem lower to Westerners when it rises than it is judged by Easterners. As great as the distance,” he says, “from East to West, so great is the distance between them. But the sun is distant from no one; it is nearer to no one and farther from no one.” [Col. 0989A]

[Note: [Col. 0989D]

2. “But this is larger than the earth.” Macrobius says that it is eight times larger than the earth, book I of *The Dream of Scipio*, chapter 20. See Plutarch, book II of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*.]

2. Nor should anyone be disturbed that it appears about a cubit in size in its own sphere when it rises. One must consider how great the space is between the sun and the earth, which the weakness and a certain infirmity of our sight can scarcely span. The wise describe it as larger than the earth by several parts.

[Note: [Col. 0989D]

3. “They say that the moon is smaller . . . it will become larger.” These are the words of Hyginus, book IV, chapter “On the Moon.” But Hyginus should be corrected from Isidore.

There: Hyginus, book 4, chapter 14, “On the Moon,” in Munker's edition: “Things that are near us must be larger”—one should read “appear larger”—“than things that we see with a great intervening distance . . . than the sun. It is also necessary that, when the sun is far from the moon and appears larger to us, if it should approach nearer, it will become much larger”—namely, to our sight. AREV.]

3. They say that the moon is smaller than the sun; for everything near us appears larger, while the sight grows weak because of distance. We therefore see the moon as near to us, and it does not appear larger to our sight than the sun. Thus, although the sun is much higher than the moon, it appears larger to us; yet if it approached near us, it would become much larger.

**CHAPTER XVII. On the course of the sun**

[Note: [Col. 0989D]

CHAPTER XVII.—No. 1. The ancients, Aratus and Hyginus, say this. The interpreter of Aratus, in the final chapter, and Hyginus, book IV, chapter “On the Sun.” All these words belong to them, from “The sun moves by itself” to “it does not revolve fixed by itself, but moves by itself.” The things they state without hesitation, however, Isidore presents with a kind of hesitation while attributing them to them.]

1. The ancients, Aratus and Hyginus, say that the sun moves by itself, not revolving with the universe while remaining in one place. For if it remained fixed, it would necessarily set and rise in the same place from which it had risen the day before, just as the other constellations rise and set. Moreover, if this were so, it would follow that all days and nights would be equal, and that however long the present day was, every day would always be equally long.

[Note: [Col. 0990D]

2. “After he has dipped his burning wheel into Ocean.” Surely these are Lucretius’s words.

There: “Tomorrow he will set.” Others read, “tomorrow he will rise.” AREV.]

2. Night too would always remain equal for the same reason, [Col. 0989C] but since we observe unequal days, and see that tomorrow the sun will set in one place while yesterday it set in another, philosophers therefore think that the sun, which sets and rises in different places, does not revolve fixed together with the universe, but moves by itself. After he has dipped his burning wheel into Ocean, he returns by ways unknown to us to the place from which he emerged; and, when the circuit of night has been completed, he quickly bursts forth again from his place. For he travels along an oblique and broken line from the south toward the north, and thus returns to the east. In winter he runs through the southern region; in summer he is near the north. But when he travels through the south, he is nearer to the earth; when he is near the north, he rises aloft.

[Col. 0990A] [Note: [Col. 0990D]

3. “For this reason God assigned him . . . would consume it.” Translated from Ambrose, book II, chapter 3.

There: “But, as Clement says, he follows different courses . . . the year is brought about.” These are Clement’s words, book VIII of the *Recognitions*.]
