3. For this reason God assigned him different places and times for his courses, lest, while always remaining in the same places, he consume them daily with his vapor. But, as Clement says, he follows different courses by which the tempering of the air is distributed according to the seasons, and the order of alternations and changes is preserved. For when he has ascended to the higher regions, he tempers spring; when he has reached the highest heaven, he kindles the heat of summer. Descending again, he restores the mildness of autumn; but when he has returned to the lower circle, he leaves us the rigor of winter’s cold from the icy structure of heaven.

4. From him come the hours; from him the day when he rises, and from him also the night when he sets; from him the months and years are counted; from him the changes of the seasons occur. Although he is a good servant, created to regulate the changes of the seasons, nevertheless, when correction is inflicted upon mortals according to the will of God, he grows more fiercely hot, burns the world with more violent flames, disturbs the air, sends a plague upon human beings, brings corruption upon the lands, disease upon living creatures, and introduces a pestilential year for mortals everywhere. [Col. 0990B]

[Note: [Col. 0990D]

5. These are the words of Malachi: “And for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in his wings.” AREV.]

5. The fact that the rising sun travels through the south, that is, the meridian, and, having passed through the southern region, goes invisibly to its place as it returns, shows that this world was fashioned in the likeness of the Church. In it the Lord Jesus Christ, the eternal sun, traverses his own region, which is why it is called the meridian. He does not rise for the north, that is, for the opposing region, just as those people will say when he comes in judgment: “The light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise for us.” [Col. 0990C] But for those who fear the Lord, the sun of righteousness rises, and healing is in his wings, as it is written. For the wicked it is night at midday, as it is written: “While they await the light, darkness came upon them; while they await brightness, they walked in dark night.”

**CHAPTER XVIII. On the light of the moon**

[Note: [Col. 0990D]

CHAPTER XVIII.—No. 1. Augustine, on Psalm 10, and book III of *On Genesis*, chapter 15.]

1. Saint Augustine says in his exposition of the tenth Psalm: “The question is,” he says, “where the moon gets its light. Only two opinions are handed down, but it is said that no one can know with certainty which of them is true.” Some say that it possesses its own light, that one part of its globe is luminous and another dark, and that as it moves in its circle, it gradually turns toward the earth the same part by which it shines, so that it can be seen by us; therefore at first it shines with a light shaped like horns. [Col. 0991A]

2. For if you make a ball white on one half and dark on the other, and hold the dark part before your eyes, you will see no brightness. When you begin gradually to turn the white part toward your eyes, you will first see something like horns of brightness; then it will slowly increase until the entire shining part is presented to your eyes and none of the darkness of the other part is visible. If you then turn it gradually again, darkness begins to appear and brightness diminishes until it once more returns to horns; thus all the brightness is turned away from your eyes, and only the dark part can again be seen. [Col. 0991B] They say this occurs when the moon’s light appears to grow until the fifteenth day, then diminish again until the thirtieth, returning to horns until no light at all appears in it.

3. Others, on the contrary, say that the moon does not shine with its own light but receives its light from the sun. The sun is higher than it. Hence, when the moon is beneath it, its upper part shines, while its lower part, which it presents to the earth, is dark. But when it begins to move away from the sun, it is illuminated on the side that it presents to the earth, beginning at the horns. Thus, as it moves farther from the sun, its entire lower part is gradually illuminated until it becomes a full moon. After half a month, when it begins to approach the sun from the other semicircle, the more its upper part is illuminated, the more on the side turned away from the earth it is unable to receive the rays of the sun; and for this reason it appears to wane. [Col. 0991C]

[Note: [Col. 0991D]

4. “For if it used its own light . . . become slender.” These are the words of Hyginus, chapter “On the Moon.”]

4. This much is certainly clear and easily understood by anyone who pays attention: the moon does not grow before our eyes except by moving away from the sun, nor diminish except by approaching the sun on the other side. It therefore receives its light from the sun; and when it is beneath the sun, it is always small, but when it has moved farther away, it becomes broad and full in its circuit. For if it used its own light, it would necessarily always remain equal and would not become slender on the thirtieth day; and if it used its own light, it would never undergo an eclipse.

5. As for mystical interpretation, the moon represents the appearance of this world, because just as the moon wanes monthly, so the world, moving toward the conflagration of the ages, declines through daily failures. Through the variation of its element, the moon ceases in its different courses in order to grow, and grows in order to cease. But it represents the alternation of the heavenly body in successive changes so that it may teach human beings that they will die through rising and live through dying. Therefore, when it grows old, it reveals the death of bodies; when it increases, it indicates the eternity of souls.

[Note: [Col. 0991D]

6. “For just as the moon wanes . . . is crowned.” These are Ambrose’s words, book IV, chapter 8.

There: “Abundant with dew.” Ambrose, book IV, chapter 7.

There: “All fruits increase.” Perhaps, “all waters increase.” Dracontius, page 213, book I, lines 733 and following:

“Who commands that the waters increase with the growing globe of the moon,

that the rivers increase with added waves, increase with their springs.”

See the note. AREV.]

6. Sometimes the same moon is also understood as the Church, because just as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church is illuminated by Christ. For just as the moon wanes and grows, so the Church has times of decline and rising. Often it has grown through its own periods of decline and deserved to be enlarged, being diminished by persecutions and crowned by the martyrdom of confessors. Likewise, just as the moon is rich in dew and a guide of moist substances, so is the Church rich in baptism and preaching. And just as all fruits increase when the moon grows and diminish when it wanes, so we understand the Church: we prosper as it increases. But when it suffers persecution and is diminished, we suffer and are diminished with it. [Col. 0992B]

[Note: [Col. 0991D]

7. “Likewise, just as the moon has seven forms.” The same author, book III of the *Etymologies*, assigns the same number of lunar forms, as does Clement, book VI of the *Stromata*, from Seleucus the mathematician. From this source, and according to Isidore’s own thought, we have revised these forms both here and in the *Etymologies*. We call the form *sectilis*, not *sextilis*, following the ancient books: a half or semicircle.

There: In Grialius’s text it was, “a third half from the greater.” AREV.]

7. Likewise, just as the moon has seven forms, so the Church has as many graces of merits. It has the first form, horned; the second, *sectilis*; the third, half of the greater; the fourth, full; the fifth, again half of the greater; the sixth, again *sectilis*; and the seventh, horned. The distribution of the gifts of grace, which are bestowed by the Holy Spirit upon the whole Church, is likewise established according to this number. The seventh half and the twenty-second half are in the middle of their orbit. The others are proportional.

**CHAPTER XIX. On the course of the moon**

[Col. 0992C]

[Note: [Col. 0992D]

CHAPTER XIX.—No. 1. “The moon, through successive risings . . . rather than remain still.” All these words belong to Hyginus, although they do not occur continuously in his work.

There: “The moon, being near the earth . . . traverses.” These are the words of the interpreter of Aratus, with only the number of the moon’s days changed.]

1. Hyginus says that the moon must move through successive risings and settings, not remain still; this is more easily understood than in the case of the sun’s light. Since it receives its light from the sun and thus appears to shine for us, there is no doubt that it moves rather than remains still. Being near the earth, the moon revolves in a shorter orbit, and traverses in thirty days the path that the sun completes in 365 days. Hence the ancients reckoned months by the moon and years by the sun.

[Note: [Col. 0992D]

2. “Thus the moon, completing its course twelve times in thirty-day periods . . . having celebrated.” These are Ambrose’s words, book IV, chapter 5.

[Col. 0993D] There: “The sea urchin, oysters, and so forth.” Dracontius, cited above:

“May every kind possessing a brain enclosed in its head increase,

and may the flowing waters diminish as the moon diminishes.”

I have said more about these matters in the note. AREV.]

2. Thus the moon, completing its course twelve times in periods of thirty days, completes the year according to the Hebrews, with some days added; according to the Romans, the leap year is observed once every four years by the addition of one day. Through its increases and decreases, by a marvelous art of Providence, everything that is generated is nourished and grows. For the elements also sympathize with its decline, and as it advances, whatever has been emptied is replenished; thus the brains of sea creatures—indeed, sea urchins and oysters are said to be found fuller during the moon’s increase. [Col. 0993A]

33 **CHAPTER XX. On the eclipse of the sun**

[Note: [Col. 0993D]

CHAPTER XX.—No. 1. “The wise say that the sun . . . transmits.” The whole passage comes from Hyginus, book IV, chapter “On the Moon.”

There: In some manuscripts *provehitur* occurs; twice *utitur* is found, and perhaps *vertitur* should be read. AREV.]

1. The wise say that the sun travels higher, while the moon is nearer to the earth. Therefore, when the moon, moving downward, comes to the same sign or line along which the sun travels, it places itself before the sun and produces darkness throughout the entire world. This happens only at the new moon. For then the moon is in the same part of the sign through which the sun travels, and so it becomes close to it; because it stands opposite the sun, its light appears to be obscured from our eyes. It is like someone holding an outspread hand before his eyes: the closer he holds it, the less the sun can be seen; the farther away he moves it, the more everything can appear to him.

[Col. 0993B] [Note: [Col. 0993D]

2. “If the opening of the air,” and so forth. This was the opinion of Anaximander. Plutarch, book II of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, chapters 20 and 24.]

2. In the same way, when the moon reaches the sun’s place or line, it then appears to be nearest to the sun and so obscures its rays before our eyes that they cannot cast their light. But when the moon has moved away from that place, the sun casts out its light and transmits it to our eyes. Thus the moon is placed before the sun just as the earth is placed before the moon; and when neither of these lights reaches the earth, they are said to have suffered an eclipse. Others say that an eclipse of the sun occurs when the opening in the air through which the sun pours its rays is constricted or blocked by some current of air. This is what the natural philosophers and wise men of the world say.

3. Our teachers, however, have said mystically that the mystery of this eclipse was fulfilled in Christ, when, [Col. 0993C] with the course of the eternal covenant interrupted in an unprecedented way, the elements were thrown into confusion and lost their proper order. When this sacrilegious act of conspiracy had taken place, the true sun, appalled, briefly hid itself in death, as darkness from errors was introduced among the Jewish people; and, after being taken down from the cross, it concealed and obscured itself in the tomb until, on the third day, it displayed to this world—that is, to the nations—the power of its glory, greater than usual; and, like the sun shining in its strength, illuminated the darkness of the hidden age.

34 **CHAPTER XXI. On the eclipse of the moon**

[Note: [Col. 0993D]

CHAPTER XXI.—No. 1. Much of this comes from the same chapter of Hyginus, “On the Moon.” [Col. 0994D]]

1. The moon does not diminish, but is overshadowed; it does not suffer any reduction of its body, but its light undergoes an eclipse because the earth, standing before it, casts a shadow. Philosophers maintain that the moon does not have its own light but is illuminated by the sun; and because it is situated at such a distance from the sun that, if anything straight were projected through the middle of the earth, it could reach the sun beneath the earth while the moon remained above the earth; and because the earth’s shadow extends as far as the lunar circle, it sometimes happens that the sun’s rays do not reach the moon because the mass or shadow of the earth intervenes. [Col. 0993D–0994A]

[Note: [Col. 0994D]

2. “For the Stoics say.” All manuscripts read this; the printed historical text of Hyginus reads: “Although some have said that it happens during the sun’s course that, when it reaches the place where it is said to set, the sun’s light is turned away from us by the size of the mountains, and thus night appears. If this happens, we should surely call it an eclipse of the sun rather than night.”]

2. The moon suffers this on the fifteenth day, until it emerges from the center and shadow of the obstructing earth and sees the sun, or is seen by the sun. It is therefore established that the moon receives its light from the sun’s rays, and that when it cannot see the sun because the earth intervenes, it loses its light. For the Stoics say that the entire earth is enclosed by mountains, whose shadow causes the moon suddenly to disappear. Hence Lucan:

“Now, when Phoebe was returning the whole orb to her brother,

she grew pale, struck by the sudden shadow of the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0994D]

3. “Figuratively, however.” From Augustine, on Psalm 10.]

3. Figuratively, the persecutions of the Church are understood through the eclipse of the moon, when, through the slaughter of martyrs and the shedding of blood, the moon seems to display a bloody face, as though in that eclipse and obscuration, so that the weak may be terrified by the Christian name. But just as the moon, after its eclipse, grows bright with clear illumination, so that it seems to have suffered no harm, so the Church, after shedding its blood for Christ through the confession of martyrs, shines with a greater brightness of faith and, adorned with more distinguished light, spreads itself more widely throughout the whole world. [Col. 0994B]

35 **CHAPTER XXII. On the course of the stars**

[Note: [Col. 0994D]

CHAPTER XXII.—No. 1. “The stars indeed revolve with the universe.” Hyginus proves this in the same place. See book III of the *Etymologies*, from chapter 60 through chapter 70.]

1. The stars indeed revolve with the universe; they do not move as wandering stars while the universe stands still, except for those called planets, that is, the wandering stars, which move in wandering arrangements. The others, called *aplanes*, fixed in one place, revolve with the universe. [Col. 0994C] They are called planets, that is, wandering stars, because they run through the whole universe with varied motion.

2. The heavenly bodies move in different regions relative to one another. Some travel above, others below. Hence those nearer to the earth appear larger to us than those that revolve around the sky. For the sight grows weak because of distance. Thus, because the circles are separated from one another by great intervals, some stars return more quickly and others more slowly to the beginning of their course.

3. Some stars, rising more quickly, are thought to set later; others, rising later than the rest, reach the setting sooner. Some rise together but do not set at the same time. All, however, return at their appointed time to their proper course. When impeded by the sun’s rays, the stars become anomalous, retrograde, or stationary. The poet alludes to this when he says:

“. . . The sun divides the seasons of time,

changes day into night, and with its powerful rays

forbids the stars to go, and by standing still restrains their wandering courses.”

**CHAPTER XXIII. On the position of the seven wandering stars**

[Col. 0995A]

[Note: [Col. 0995C]

CHAPTER XXIII.—No. 1. Venus was so called by the Gentiles. Venus was not called this because it has more light, but Lucifer. Thus the *Etymologies*: “Because among all the heavenly bodies it carries more light.”

There: “Thus this star too casts a shadow.” Pliny, book II, chapter 8, on Venus: “Its brightness is indeed so great that the rays of this one star cast shadows.”]

1. Within the circuit of the seven heavenly spheres, the moon was placed first, in the circle of the lower sphere. It was placed near the earth so that it might more readily provide us with light at night. [Col. 0995B] Then, in the second [36] circle, the star of Mercury was placed, equal to the sun in speed but, as the philosophers say, contrary to it in a certain respect. In the third circle is the revolution of Lucifer, which the Gentiles therefore called Venus, because among the five stars it has the greatest amount of light. For, as we said above, just as the sun and moon cast shadows, so does this star also.

[Note: [Col. 0995C]

2. “In the fourth circle, the sun.” He follows Cicero. Plato placed it in the second circle. See Macrobius, book I of *The Dream of Scipio*, chapter 19.

There: “Moreover, in the fifth circle, Pyrois.” All the books have mistakenly read Vesper here also instead of Pyrois. [Col. 0996C]]

2. The course of the sun is placed in the fourth circle. Since it is brighter than everything else, it was placed in the middle so that it might provide light both to the higher and to the lower spheres. It was established in this way by divine reason, because all distinguished things ought to be in the middle. Moreover, the star called Pyrois, which they assign to Mars, is placed in the fifth circle. In the sixth is the star of Phaethon, which they call Jupiter. At the summit of heaven, that is, at the crown of the universe, is the star of Saturn. [Col. 0996A] Although it occupies the highest heaven and is higher than all the others, its nature is nevertheless said to be cold, as Virgil confirms:

“Where the cold star of Saturn withdraws itself.”

[Note: [Col. 0996C]

3. “Not because they themselves wander.” Cicero, book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*: they are called wandering stars although they wander least of all.

There: “For everyone knows the rising and setting of the sun and moon. Therefore Isidore does not regard them as wandering, nor does Aratus, who counts only five:

‘The five stars are accustomed to glide

through the orbit of the twice-six signs.’

]

[Note: [Col. 0996C]

3. “They move retrograde.” Others read *retrograduntur*. *Retrogradiuntur* would be better. Compare the note on book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 67, no. 1. AR.]

3. These heavenly bodies are called wandering stars, not because they themselves wander, but because they make us wander; in Greek these stars are called *planets*. Everyone knows the rising and setting of the sun and moon, and therefore the sun and moon travel in a direct course. These others, however, move retrograde or become anomalous—that is, when they add and subtract portions. When they only subtract, they are called retrograde; they become stationary when they stand still.

[Note: [Col. 0996C]

4. “For the moon, in eight years.” All manuscripts read this, including book III of the *Etymologies*, except the Malacitanus, in which “in nineteen years” appears to have been inserted here by a later hand. This may perhaps refer to that eight-year period mentioned by Plutarch at the end of book II of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*.]

4. Now the periods of the individual stars are as follows, as contained in the sphere shown below. When these periods have been completed, they return to the beginning of their circuit at the same signs and degrees [Col. 0996B]. For the moon is said to complete its circuit in eight years, Mercury in twenty-three years, Lucifer in nine years, the Sun in nineteen years, Pyrois in fifteen years, Phaethon in twelve years, and Saturn in thirty years. The accompanying figure demonstrates the position of their orbits and stars.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Light of the Stars

[Col. 0997A]

[Note: [Col. 0997D]

**CHAP. XXIV.—Note 1. The assertion that not all stars possess light.** Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 19, says that the moon alone shines with borrowed light, while all the other stars shine with their own.

**Ibid.** *Celari* (“to be hidden”). Some manuscripts read *celare dicimus* (“we say ‘to hide’”). AREV.]

1. They say that the stars do not possess their own light but are illuminated by the sun, and that they never descend from heaven, but are hidden when the sun arrives. For all the heavenly bodies are obscured when the sun rises; they do not fall. Once the sun has sent ahead the signs of its rising, the fires of all the stars vanish beneath the brilliance of its light, so that no radiance of any heavenly body is visible except the sun’s fire. Hence the sun has also been called *sol* (“the sole one”), because it alone appears when all the other heavenly bodies have been obscured. Nor is this surprising in the case of the sun, since even when the moon is full and shines throughout the night, many stars do not shine.

That stars are also in the sky during the day is proved by a solar eclipse: when the sun has been obscured by the intervening disk of the moon, the stars appear brighter in the sky [Col. 0997B].

2. In the mystical sense, the stars are understood as holy men. Of them it is said: “He numbers the multitude of the stars.” For just as all the stars are illuminated by the sun, so the saints are glorified by Christ with the glory of the heavenly kingdom. And just as the stars are blunted by the sun’s brilliance and the immense power of its light, so all the splendor of the saints is, in comparison with Christ’s glory, in a certain sense obscured. And just as the stars differ from one another in brightness, so the just differ according to the distinction of their merits.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Falling of the Stars

[Note: [Col. 0997D]

**CHAP. XXV.—Note 1. “A false opinion.”** From Servius, commentary on *Georgics* I, at verse 365:

> Often also, when a wind is threatening, you will see  
> Stars plunge headlong and slide from heaven.

] 1. It is a false and popular belief that stars fall at night, although we know that little flames, having slipped from the ether, travel through the sky, are carried by the winds, and imitate the wandering light of a heavenly body; but the stars themselves remain motionless and fixed in heaven [Col. 0997C].

[Note: [Col. 0997D]

**2.** The three verses beginning “Often also” are Virgil’s; the remaining verses, beginning “Fallen through the heights,” etc., are neither Virgil’s nor apparently complete. At present I cannot recall whose they are. AREV.]

2. For what the poet says is:

> Often also, when a wind is threatening, you will see  
> Stars plunge headlong and slide from heaven, and through the shadows  
> Of night leave long, whitening trails of flames behind them.

And again:

> … Fallen through the heights,  
> Through scattered air, to draw gleaming furrows—  
> Stars, and even those heavenly bodies fixed  
> In the highest poles.

But these poets deliberately accommodated themselves to popular belief. Philosophers, however, whose concern is to seek the explanation of the world, assert what has been stated above.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Names of the Stars

[Col. 0998A]

[Note: [Col. 0997D]

**CHAP. XXVI. Note 1. “The ravings.”** Some editions read “the ravings [Col. 0998D] of the poets.” AREV.]

1. It is written in Job, with the Lord saying: “Can you join the shining stars of the Pleiades, and can you scatter the circle of Arcturus? Can you bring forth Lucifer at its proper time, and cause the evening star to rise over the children of the earth?” And again elsewhere: “He makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades.”

When we read these names of stars in Scripture, let us not assent to the empty ravings of those who, through false opinions, imposed these names upon the stars from the names of human beings or from the names of other creatures. For the wise men of the Gentiles gave names to certain stars, just as they did to the days.

2. The fact that sacred Scripture uses these same names does not therefore mean that it approves their empty fables. Rather, by making visible things figures of invisible realities, it employs as designations those names that are widely known, so that whatever is unknown may more easily be made known to human understanding through what is known [Col. 0998B].

[Note: [Col. 0998D]

**3.** Arcturus is the constellation that the Latins call the Septentrion. These matters are discussed somewhat more suitably in book III of the *Etymologies*, under “The Bear.” Here, however, he has confused the Arctos, Boötes—or Arctophylax—and Arcturus, which are near one another, as he himself admits shortly afterward.]

3. Arcturus is what the Latins call the Septentrion. Shining with the rays of seven stars, it turns around upon itself and revolves; for this reason it is called the Wagon, because it rolls like a vehicle, sometimes raising three of its stars to the heights, and sometimes lowering four [39]. Established on the axis of heaven, it is always turning and never sets. Yet while it revolves upon itself, the night comes to an end.

4. By this Arcturus, that is, the Septentrion, we understand the Church, shining with the sevenfold power. For just as Arcturus on the axis of heaven is continually lowered and raised again, so the Church is humbled by various adversities but soon rises again and is lifted up by hope and virtues. And just as the Septentrion is formed from three stars and four, so the Church is perfected by faith in the Trinity and by the works of the four principal virtues. For a person is justified by faith and works [Col. 0998C].

[Note: [Col. 0998D]

**5.** Sailors especially observe this constellation. Mariners use either Bear without danger, because each is close to the Pole and describes a small circle. Thus Ovid:

> There are two Bears, one of which is called Cynosura  
> By the Sidonians; the Greek keel marks Helice.

**Ibid.** “It quickly sets.” Some add: “On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October.” The Hyades are five stars arranged in the shape of the letter V on the forehead of Taurus. The Pleiades, etc. AREV.]

5. Boötes is the star that follows the Wagon, that is, the Septentrion. It was also called Arctophylax by the ancients, or the Lesser Bear. Hence some also called it the Septentrion. Sailors especially observe it. Lucan writes of it:

> … When swift Boötes rises by night;  
> Once it has risen, it quickly sets.

[Note: [Col. 0998D]

**6.** Pleiades. The same is found in book III of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** “Many closely joined”; perhaps *multijuges* (“many in a connected group”). AREV.]

6. The Pleiades are many closely joined stars, which we also call a cluster because of the multitude of stars. They too are said to number seven, but no one can see more than six. They rise in the east, and as the brightness of day approaches, their arrangement becomes spread out. They are called Pleiades from their plurality, because the Greeks call plurality *πλειότης* (*pleiotēs*). The Latins called them the Vergiliae because they rise in spring. They are praised above the other constellations especially because their rising signifies summer and their setting indicates winter—something that has not been assigned to the other signs.

[Note: [Col. 0999C]

**7. “Because they are seven.”** Clement, *Stromata* VI, seriously affirms that they are seven, and Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah III, says that seven appear, although they are small and clustered. Ovid, *Fasti* IV:

> Though they are usually said to be seven, they are nevertheless six.

Cicero, from Aratus:

> These seven stars are commonly proclaimed according to ancient custom,  
> Yet six small ones are seen everywhere.  
> It is not fitting, however, to suppose that one has perished,  
> But that the common people rashly and without reason  
> Call them seven, as the ancient poets decreed,  
> Honoring all by the everlasting name:  
> Alcyone, Merope, and Celaeno, Taygete,  
> Electra and Sterope, together with holy Maia.

] 7. These stars, because they are seven and shine brilliantly, signify all the saints, radiant with the power of the sevenfold Spirit. Because they draw near to one another without touching, they also represent the preachers of God, close in charity yet divided in time [40].

[Note: [Col. 0999D]

**8.** Orion is a star [lacuna]. We have marked with an asterisk a place that could easily be filled from book III of the *Etymologies* or from the commentator on Aratus, from whom Isidore borrowed this material. He writes as follows: “Orion, also called the Inhabitant, shines before the tracks of Taurus, and is called Orion from *urine*, that is, from an inundation of waters. For it rises in winter, when it disturbs the sea and lands with storms. The Romans call it *Jugula* (“the Collarbone”), because it is armed like a sword and terrifying through the light of its stars,” etc.

[Col. 1000D] **Ibid.** “This Orion is the sword.” So the printed edition reads. All the manuscripts are much worse: “This Orion, however, is said to have been named from the sword.”

**Ibid.** In Grialius’s note, perhaps *jugula* should be read instead of *incola*. AREV.]

8. Orion is a star [lacuna]. This Orion, however, is called the sword [Col. 0999B]. Hence the Latins also call it *Jugula* (“the Collarbone”), a constellation apparently armed and terrifying by the light of its stars. It is exceedingly difficult to overlook, so that even untrained eyes are drawn toward it by the brilliance of its radiance. These Orions rise precisely in the season of winter; by their rising they stir up rains and storms and disturb seas and lands.

9. The Orions signify the martyrs. For just as these stars arise in heaven during winter, so martyrs appear in the Church during persecution. When the Orions appear, the sea and land are disturbed; when martyrs arise, the hearts of earthly and unbelieving people are shaken by the storm.

[Note: [Col. 1000D]

**10.** “Lucifer, a shining star.” Several passages are read here in certain books, brought in from book III of the *Etymologies*; they are not found in the older manuscripts.]

10. Lucifer is a shining star, which appears to be the largest and brightest of all. For, like the sun and moon, it casts a shadow [Col. 0999C]. It precedes the rising sun and, announcing morning, scatters the darkness of night with the light of its radiance. Its figure is Christ, who, like Lucifer, is brought forth through the mystery of the Incarnation; through him the light of faith is displayed, like the day that is to follow.

11. Lucifer, however, is twofold. One part is holy, as the Lord says of himself and the Church in the Apocalypse: “I am the offspring and root of David, the bright and morning star.” Again: “To the one who conquers I will give the morning star.” The other part of Lucifer is recognized as the devil. Of him it is written: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose at dawn,” and he also says that he will set his throne above the stars of God in heaven; but, falling from heaven, he is shattered [Col. 1000A].

12. Vesperus is the western star that ushers in the night. It follows the setting sun and precedes the darkness that comes after it. It expresses the type of Antichrist, who rises like evening, as Job says, “over the children of the earth,” in order to darken the hearts of the fleshly through the succession of blind night. This happens by God’s judgment because, on account of their prior unbelief, by which they refused to believe in Christ, they deserved to receive Antichrist.

[Note: [Col. 1000D]

**13.** Comet. Nearly the same material is found in book III of the *Etymologies*.

**Ibid.** *Intercidit* (“passes across” or “falls between”). I have restored this reading from Prudentius. Grialius reads *intercedit* (“intervenes”); some manuscripts read *incedit* (“advances”). AREV.]

13. A comet is a star that pours from itself something like a mane of light. When it appears, it is said to portend either a change of kingdom, wars, or the rise of pestilences. Prudentius writes of it: “The grim comet intervenes.” Lucan writes:

> … And the comet threatening kingdoms to the lands.

And Virgil:

> … Nor did grim comets so often blaze.

Astrologers say that all wandering stars become comets at certain times, and that, according to the movement of each, they portend favorable or unfavorable events.

[Note: [Col. 1000D]

**14.** “Sirius is so called because of the brightness of its flame.” Quite correctly, so that no suspicion remains concerning the emendation of the passage in book III of the *Etymologies*. The commentator on Aratus says: “They think the star is called Sirius because of the brightness of its flame.”

**Ibid.** “The season of summer.” Some editions add: “The season of summer: fifteen days of July and twenty of August.” AREV.]

14. Sirius is the star commonly called the Dog. It is called Sirius because of the brightness of its flame, which is such that it appears to shine more brightly than the others. When it rises, it sets the world ablaze with excessive heat and, through its burning, scorches the fruits. At times it also afflicts bodies with disease, corrupting the air through the intensity of its fire. The Dog Days are named after this star, since during them the heat burns more fiercely than during the whole period of summer.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Whether the Stars Have a Soul

[Col. 1000C]

[Note: [Col. 1000D]

**CHAP. XXVII.—Note 1. “As Saint Augustine says.”** At the end of book II of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*.]

1. As Saint Augustine says, it is often asked whether the sun, the moon, and the other stars are bodies alone, or whether they have certain spirits ruling them. And if they have such spirits, whether they are also given life by them, just as dogs are animated by the souls of animals, or whether they are present alone, without any admixture. Since the movement of a body cannot exist without a soul, it is not easy to comprehend whether the stars, which move with such order and such rationality that their course is never impeded in any respect, are living beings and appear to possess reason.

[Col. 1001A] [Note: [Col. 1001C]

**2.** “It must be asked what they will become in the resurrection.” This is found in the manuscripts O., and appears to have been taken from book X of *The City of God*, chapter 29.

**Ibid.** In the Vulgate: “It turns toward the south and bends toward the north; circling everything, the wind proceeds and returns to its circuits.” The first of the Virgilian verses occurs in *Aeneid* II, 384; the others in VI, 724. The words “Therefore, etc.” are absent from the old edition. Compare chapter 5 of the book *On the Order of Created Things*. AREV.]

2. When Solomon said of the sun, “The spirit, turning, goes round and round, and returns to its circuits,” he showed that the sun itself is a spirit, that it is an animal, breathes, lives, and completes its annual circuits in its course, just as the poet says:

> Meanwhile the sun revolves through the great year.

And elsewhere:

> The shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars  
> Are nourished by a spirit within.

Therefore, if the bodies of the stars have souls, it must be asked what they will become in the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Night

[Note: [Col. 1001C]

**CHAP. XVIII. Note 1.** Ambrose, in book IV, chapter 3, of the *Hexaemeron*. [Col. 1001D]]

1. I have read Ambrose in his book *Hexaemeron* saying:

> “It is asked how the shadow of the earth occupies the expanse of air and produces night for us, when the sun withdraws from us and covers the day, while it illuminates the lower regions of the northern axis. Every body produces a shadow, and naturally the shadow clings to the body, so much so that painters also strive to represent the shadows of the bodies they have painted, and assert that it belongs to their art not to interrupt the power of nature.

[Note: [Col. 1001D]

**2.** “It reaches the place where it is said to set; there it is separated from us by the mass of the mountains.” These words are not Ambrose’s but Hyginus’s, quoted by us above in chapter 21.

**Ibid.** “And thus, because the earth intervenes, the air is overshadowed from the northern side.” Isidore added the words “from the northern side,” which would be more suitably placed as follows: “The air is overshadowed from the northern side, lest the earth appear to intervene from the northern side.”]

2. Therefore, just as during the day, when some body—a person or a tree—comes between us and the sun, a shadow remains on the side from which the light is reflected, so, when the sun withdraws at the end of day and reaches the place where it is said to set, it is separated from us by the mass of the mountains. Thus, because the earth intervenes, the air is overshadowed from the northern side, so that this very shadow of the earth produces night for us [43].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Thunder

[Col. 1001C]

[Note: [Col. 1001D]

**CHAP. XXIX.—Note 1. “Thunder.”** Ambrose, book II, chapter 4: “For this firmament cannot be broken or penetrated without some crashing sound. Hence, concerning thunder—which, when the breath conceived within the hollow of the clouds violently forces its way out, resounds with a great noise—Scripture says: ‘He makes the thunder firm.’ I suspect that the words of Isidore, ‘And in the manner of chariots leaping from their stalls, the sound of its crash is sent to our ears,’ are missing from Ambrose and should be restored from this passage. Before the words ‘Scripture says,’ they should be enclosed in parentheses, and the whole passage should read:

> “For this firmament cannot be broken or penetrated without some crashing sound. Therefore it is also called firmament because it is neither weak nor slack. Hence, concerning thunder—which, when the breath conceived within the hollow of the clouds violently forces its way out, resounds with a great noise, and, in the manner of chariots leaping from their stalls, the sound of its crash is sent to our ears—Scripture says …”]

1. Thunder is produced by the crashing of clouds. For the breaths of winds, once conceived within the hollow of the clouds, move about there. When they have violently forced themselves out and, through the mobility of their power, burst forth in any direction, they resound with a great roar; and, like the sound of chariots leaping from their stalls, the crash is conveyed to our ears [Col. 1002A].

2. In another sense, thunder is the heavenly rebuke of the divine voice, or the clear preaching of the saints, which resounds with a mighty cry throughout the whole world in the ears of the faithful, so that the world, when admonished, may recognize its sin.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Lightning

[Note: [Col. 1002C]

**CHAP. XXX.—Note 1. “The investigators of natural causes say … until the sound reaches us.”** This has been assembled from these verses of Lucretius, book VI:

> The cloud likewise flashes when many seeds of fire  
> Have been shaken out by their collision, as when a stone  
> Strikes a stone, or iron; for then too a light  
> Leaps forth, and the fire scatters bright sparks.  
>   
> Thus thunder comes, so that we hear it afterward  
> Than our eyes see the flash, because things that move  
> Always arrive at the ears more slowly than at the sight.  
>   
> This can also be learned from the following: if you see someone  
> Far off cutting a tree with a double-edged axe,  
> You see the blow before the stroke sends its sound  
> To your ears. So also we see the flash before  
> We hear the thunder, which is sent forth together  
> With the fire and arises from a similar cause and collision.

**Ibid.** *Compulseris* (“you have forced together”). Some editions read *expulseris* (“you have driven out”). Perhaps *compuleris* (“you will have forced together”). AREV.]

1. Investigators of natural causes say that lightning is generated by the collision and friction of clouds, like harder flints which, when you force them together, release fire between them; or as when one rubs wood against wood and produces fire. Hence Papinius:

> And whenever lightning flashes from storms rubbed together.

By this process, then, when clouds collide with one another, lightning bolts are immediately sent forth.

[Note: [Col. 1002D]

**2.** Hence Virgil also says: “Never otherwise, etc.” Servius comments on these words: “It is an omen,” he says, “both because lightning has been sent from a clear sky and because several flashes have been sent.”

**Ibid.** Grialius reads “they are slower.” AREV.

The Virgilian verse is from *Georgics* I, verse 487. AREV.]

2. Thunder follows. Although it is slower in sound than the preceding brilliance of the disturbed light, it is nevertheless emitted together with the lightning. Its sound reaches the ears more slowly than the brilliance of the lightning reaches the eyes, as when an axe cuts a tree at a distance: one sees the blow before its sound reaches the ears. Lightning, therefore, is born from the friction of clouds. For lightning never flashes in a clear sky. Hence Virgil:

> Never otherwise did more lightning fall from a clear sky.

[Note: [Col. 1002D]

**3.** “After the casting of the lightning.” From the same passage of Lucretius [Col. 1003B].

**Ibid.** Some read: “the violence bursts forth.” AREV.]

3. Lightning is formed from cloud, rain, and wind. When the wind is violently stirred within the clouds, it becomes so hot that it catches fire. Then, as has been stated, lightning and thunder are emitted together. But the former appears more quickly because it is bright, while the latter reaches the ears more slowly. After the lightning has been hurled, the violence of the winds bursts forth [Col. 1003A]; emerging from the clouds, they send down to the earth the fury of the storm that, while confined within the clouds, they had been driving [45].

[Note: [Col. 1003B]

**4.** Lucretius says, in book II, in these words:

> It is now very easy for us to resolve by rational thought  
> Why the fire of lightning flows much more penetratingly  
> Than our own fire, which arises from earthly matter.  
> You may say that the heavenly fire of lightning  
> Is more subtle, consisting of smaller shapes,  
> And therefore passes through openings that our fire,  
> Born from wood and produced by a torch, cannot pass through.

**Ibid.** The Virgilian verse is from *Aeneid* II, verse 698. AREV.]

4. Lucretius says that lightning bolts consist of tiny particles and are therefore able to penetrate. Wherever lightning has struck, it gives off the smell of sulfur. Virgil writes:

> And far around, the places smoke with sulfur.

And Lucan:

> And the iron, made deadly by heavenly sulfur, will smoke.

[Note: [Col. 1003C]

**5.** “Lightning strikes the mountains.” All the books read this, as do certain manuscripts of Horace.]

5. In the lightning of the saints, miracles are understood—flashing with the brilliance of signs and virtues and reaching the innermost parts of the heart. Sublime places are said to feel the violence of winds or lightning more strongly than low-lying earth. Hence Horace:

> And they strike the highest  
> … mountains with lightning.

Yet exceedingly lofty places are safe from storms, such as Olympus, which, because of its height, feels neither the violence of the winds nor the blows of lightning, since it rises above the clouds.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Rainbow

[Note: [Col. 1003C]

**CHAP. XXXI.—Note 1. “Clement of Rome … its form is produced.”** These words are found in book VIII of the *Recognitions*, but it appears that Isidore used another interpretation, and it may be questioned whether the version circulated is Rufinus’s.]

1. Clement, bishop and martyr of Rome, writes as follows:

> “For the rainbow is formed in the air from the image of the sun in this way. When the sun shines from the opposite side through thinning clouds, and moisture, receiving its rays in a straight line and transmitting them into the cloud, impresses them upon it, a reflection of its brilliance occurs in the clouds. From these clouds a gleaming radiance forms the appearance of a rainbow. Just as wax, when impressed, reproduces the image of a ring, so the clouds, receiving from the roundness of the sun a corresponding shape, form a circle and fashion the likeness of a rainbow.
>
> “It does not always appear, but only when the clouds of heaven grow thin. When the clouds again come together and become dense, the form of the rainbow immediately dissolves. For in the density of the clouds the rainbow encloses the air in a complete circle. Finally, a rainbow never appears without the sun and clouds, because its appearance is formed from the pattern of the sun’s rays” [Col. 1004A].

[Note: [Col. 1003C]

**2.** “For it has four colors.” Aristotle holds that it has three colors. Bede followed Isidore.

**Ibid.** After the end of this chapter, some manuscripts add a largely allegorical fragment, which is not inconsistent with Isidore’s style and usage:

> “The rainbow that appears in the clouds God placed as a covenant between himself and us. When Noah had come out of the ark after the Flood, God said to him: ‘I will place my rainbow in the clouds, and it shall be a covenant between me and you; and when my rainbow appears, I will remember my covenant and will no longer bring the water of the Flood upon the earth.’
>
> “The rainbow has four colors: fiery, purple, white, and black. It draws the fiery color from heaven, the purple from water, the white from air, and the black from earth; it draws these four colors from all the elements of the world. The rainbow visibly has three colors: purple, sulfur-colored, and fiery. Through these three colors it signifies three judgments: two that have already passed, and a third that is still to come. By the purple color it signifies the Flood; by the sulfur-colored color, the fire that came upon Sodom; by the fiery color, the fire that will come on the day of judgment.
>
> “The rainbow that appears in the clouds, when a cloud shines before the sun, is painted by the greatness of the sun. The rainbow that is reflected from the sun in the clouds signifies the glory of Christ shining forth in the prophets and teachers. These three colors also have their meanings: by the fiery color the Holy Spirit is signified, as the Gospel says, ‘I have come to cast fire upon the earth, so that it may burn’; by the white color chastity is signified; by the fiery color persecution of the flesh is signified.
>
> “The rainbow that appears in the clouds will not be seen for forty years before the day of judgment. Whoever lives in sin is dead to God and lives for the devil. But if he hears the Gospel of Christ and turns to God, he rises again and lives with Christ. Those who die in their sin go to punishment; they rise to death. Many perish here while thinking that they will live for a long time, and therefore they do not correct themselves. Their hope deceives them: a person does not live as long as he thinks or as long as he hopes.
>
> “Hear where it is said: ‘Do not delay turning to God.’ We have evil days as long as we live among evil people, as the Apostle testifies: ‘See carefully how you walk, not as fools but as wise, making the most of the time, because the days are evil.’ Remove evil people, and there will be no evil days. Those who desire what belongs to others, adulterers, perjurers, slanderers, and oppressors—through evil people the days are evil. We therefore have evil days as long as we live among evil people.
>
> “Those who overcame the world by their manner of life are Elijah and Enoch. On the sixth day God made the human being according to his image. We find that in the sixth age our Lord Jesus Christ came, so that humanity might be restored according to the image of God. The first age, like the first day, was from Adam to Noah; the second age, like the second day, from Noah to Abraham; the third age, like the third day, from Abraham to David; the fourth age, like the fourth day, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth age, like the fifth day, from the Babylonian captivity to the preaching of John; the sixth age, like the sixth day, is the age now in progress until the end.
>
> “If the sixth day is in progress, see what the title contains in the psalm for the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded. Let us now hear the psalm itself and question it: how was the earth founded? We do not read of this in Genesis in this way. When, then, was the earth founded, unless it is when (sic) what has just been read in the Apostle is said: ‘Thus nevertheless stand firm, steadfast in the faith, so that all who believe may be throughout the whole earth’? Then the human being is made according to the image of God. This signifies the sixth day in Genesis: how God made him and how the earth was founded.
>
> “Christ came so that the earth might be founded; for no one can lay a foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. Of him the psalm sings: ‘The Lord reigns; he is clothed with beauty,’ etc.”

The words beginning “Whoever lives in sin,” and continuing to the end, appear to belong to another passage and are not sufficiently complete. AREV.]

2. For it has four colors and draws into itself appearances from all the elements. From heaven it takes the fiery color, from the waters the purple, from the air the white, and from the earth it gathers the black. Since this rainbow shines back from the sun into the clouds, it signifies the glory of Christ shining forth in the prophets and teachers. Others have said that its two colors—the watery and the fiery—signify two judgments: one through which the impious once perished in the Flood, and the other through which sinners will later be burned in hell [Col. 1004B].

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Clouds

[Col. 1005A]

[Note: [Col. 1005D]

**CHAP. XXXII.—Note 1.** See book XIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 7.

**Ibid.** In Job: “It will be gathered into clouds”; perhaps this should be restored here. The Virgilian verse is from *Aeneid* V, verse 20. AREV.]

1. It should be noted from the book of Job that this visible air is compressed so that it gathers into a mass; once gathered, it is transformed into clouds. Job himself says: “Suddenly the air is compressed into clouds, and a passing wind will drive them away” (Job 37:21). Virgil writes:

> The winds rise, and the air is compressed into a cloud.

The clouds are understood as the holy preachers who pour out the rain of the divine word upon believers.

2. This empty and thin air signifies the empty and wandering minds of human beings. Yet, when it is condensed, it becomes clouds, because minds gathered from emptiness are made firm by faith. And just as rain clouds arise from empty air, so holy preachers are gathered to the faith from the vanity of the world. Clouds are so called because they cover the ether; hence brides are also called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces. Hence Neptune is so called because he covers the earth with cloud and sea [Col. 1005B].

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Rains

[Note: [Col. 1005D]

**CHAP. XXXIII.—Note 1.** “Like a medicinal gourd.” From Ambrose, book II, chapter 3.]

1. It is written in the prophet Amos: “He calls the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth” (Amos 9:6). For the exceedingly bitter waters of the sea are suspended by subtle vapor through the heat of the air, like a medicinal gourd, which draws moisture and blood upward through the heat of the upper sphere. In this way, then, the waters of the sea, suspended in the air through extremely fine vapors, gradually thicken; there, boiled by the fire of the sun, they are transformed into the sweet taste of rain.

[Col. 1005C] 2. Then, as the cloud grows heavy, they are scattered over the face of the earth, sometimes forced out by the power of the winds, sometimes dissolved by the sun’s heat. Thus the waters of the sea are snatched up by the clouds and are again returned by them to the earth. But, as we said, so that they may be sweet in the rain, they are boiled by the fire of the sun.

Others say that clouds do not thicken only from the waters of the sea, but also from vapors exhaled by the earth; from these vapors mists grow, and when they have been condensed and compressed, the clouds rise higher. When these same clouds descend, they pour out rain.

[Note: [Col. 1005D]

**3.** Instead of *sententialiter* (“in sentences”), some printed editions read *sensualiter* (“sensibly”). AREV.]

3. The clouds, as we have said, signify the apostles and teachers. The rains of the clouds, therefore, are the sayings of the apostles, which come, as it were, drop by drop—that is, in sentences—but pour forth the fruitfulness of teaching in greater abundance.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Snow

[Col. 1005D] [Note: [Col. 1005D]

**CHAP. XXXIV.—Note 1.** “Ambrose says … snow is poured out.” Book II, chapter 4.

**Ibid.** Some read: “snow is poured over the face of the earth.” Snow signifies the blandishments of the just on the day of judgment, as in the saying: “And his garments were white like snow.” AREV.]

1. Ambrose says that often waters made rigid by the icy blasts of the winds are solidified into snow, and that, when the air is broken open, snow is poured out [Col. 1006A].

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Hail

1. Hail is also formed by a similar process of coagulation. The waters of the clouds are compressed into ice by the rigor of the winds and become hard. Then the ice itself is partly broken into fragments by the crashing of the winds and partly dissolved by the sun’s vapor; in pieces it falls down to the earth. Its round appearance is produced by the sun’s heat and by the delay caused by the resisting air, as it travels over a long distance from the clouds to the earth.

2. Figuratively, hail is the hardness of unbelief, cold through the torpor of wickedness. Snow signifies unbelieving people, extremely cold and sluggish, depressed into the lowest depths by the torpor of their minds [Col. 1006B]. In another interpretation, snow signifies people who are cold in love. Although they may be white through the purity of baptism, they do not burn with the Spirit of charity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Winds

[Note: [Col. 1006D]

**CHAP. XXXVI.—Note 1.** “With Lucretius’s approval: ‘Wind is … when the air is stirred by motion.’” The verse is from book VI. The same view was held by Anaximander and the Stoics, whom Aristotle criticizes.]

1. Wind is air that has been moved and stirred, as Lucretius confirms:

> Wind is made wherever air is violently stirred by movement.

This can also be demonstrated in a perfectly calm place, quiet from every wind, with a small fan, by which we stir the air while driving away flies and feel the breeze. When this occurs through some more hidden movement of heavenly or earthly bodies over the great expanse of the world, it is called wind and receives different names from the different regions of the sky.

[Col. 1006C] [Note: [Col. 1006D]

**2.** “Clement, because the mountains … have grown hot.” These are Clement’s words.]

2. Some say that air is born from water, and winds from air. Clement says:

> “Because lofty mountains are situated in certain places, air, as though compressed and constricted by them, is forced and squeezed out by God’s arrangement into winds. Through their breath the seed of fruits conceives, and the heat of summer receives moderation, when the fiery Pleiades have grown hot under the sun’s burning.”

3. The winds are sometimes understood as the spirits of angels, who are sent from the hidden places of God throughout the world for the salvation of the human race. At other times the winds are understood as spirits that incite, because through the breath of evil suggestion they inflame the hearts of the wicked toward earthly desires, according to what is written: “A burning wind will carry him away” (Job 27:21).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Names of the Winds

[Col. 1006D] [Note: [Col. 1006D]

**CHAP. XXXVII.—Note 1.** “The first of the cardinal winds.” The four that he calls cardinal here he calls principal in book XIII of the *Etymologies*. There he names only two as cardinal winds, the Septentrion and the Auster, and there he begins not from the Septentrion but from the East. See Pliny, book II, chapter 27.]

1. The first of the cardinal winds is the Septentrion, cold and snowy. It blows straight from the axis and produces dry cold and dry clouds. It is also called Aparctias. Circius, also called Thrascias, thunders from the right of the Septentrion and produces snow and the coagulation of hail. The wind Aquilo, also called Boreas, blows from above, cold and dry and without rain. It does not scatter the clouds but compresses them. Hence it not unjustly assumes the form of the devil, who constricts the hearts of the Gentiles with the cold of wickedness.

2. The second of the cardinal winds is the Subsolanus, also called Apeliotes. It thunders from the rising of the sun and is temperate. Vulturnus, also called Caecias, is the right-hand wind of the Subsolanus. It dissolves and dries everything. Eurus, coming from the left side of the Subsolanus, moistens the East with clouds.

[Col. 1007B] [Note: [Col. 1007C]

**3.** *Libonotus.* The books O., and also Bede’s, incorrectly read *Euronotus*. For Euronotus is the same as Euroauster.]

3. The third of the cardinal winds is Auster, the cardinal wind of the southern region [Col. 1008A], also called Notus. Blowing from low altitude, it is moist, warm, and lightning-bearing; it produces heavy clouds and most welcome rains, and also causes flowers to open. Euroauster, a warm wind, thunders on Auster’s right. Libonotus, or the Afric wind, is a moderate wind, warm, blowing from Auster’s left.

51 4. The fourth is the cardinal wind Zephyrus, also called Favonius, blowing from the inner West. It relieves winter’s severity with a most welcome change and produces flowers. Africus, called Lips, thunders from Zephyrus’ right side: it produces storms and rains, causes collisions of clouds, the sounds of thunder, the appearance of frequent flashes, and the strikes of lightning. Corus, also called Argestes, blowing from Favonius’ left, brings clouds when it blows in the East, while in India the sky is clear. [Col. 1008B]

[Col. 1007C] [Note: [Col. 1007C]

5. In the Propontis, *Thracidas*. Thus the O manuscript; the printed edition has *Siracidas*, unless perhaps the reading should be *Thrascias*, mentioned above together with Circius.

In the same passage, concerning *aura* and *altanus*, see Servius and Pliny, Book II, chapter 14. The verses concerning these winds, which are transmitted in extremely corrupt form in the printed books, are absent from the manuscripts; in the Ovetus Gothic manuscript they are found separately from this work, almost intact. Since they are not entirely inelegant and seemed older than Isidore, we thought they ought to be presented. They are as follows:

Four winds rise from the fourfold boundary.

Around these, paired winds are joined on the right and left,

and thus, with twelvefold breath, they surround the world.

First is Aparctias, who breathes from the high axis:

our language fixed for him the name Septentrio.

Circius, his right-hand neighbor, thunders around him

in a frozen cavern.

The Greeks called him *Thrascias* (the Thracian wind)

in their own language.

On his left, Boreas roars in an icy whirlwind:

in our lands this cold wind is called Aquilo.

But Subsolanus blows straight from the rising of the sun;

the Greek name Apeliotes aptly designates him.

To his right rises Vulturnus,

whom the Attic shores call *Graecias* in Greek speech.

With cloud-bearing breath he waters the smooth airs;

the Doric tongue designates him by a similar name.

But Notus sends his breezes from the middle course of the sun:

they rightly call him Auster, because he draws in the clouds with his blasts.

On his right is Euronotus, whom,

with a mixed name, the Latins called Euroauster

in Latin speech.

Libonotus touches the left with warm breezes;

burning with immense heats, he is the Afric wind.

From the setting of the sun, the flower-bearing trumpet of Zephyrus keeps watch;

the Italian language fixed for him the name Favonius.

His right side is touched by the one called Lips

in the language of Attica;

coming from his own region, he is called Africus.

But you, Corus, roar from Zephyrus’ left side:

the Muses called you Argestes

in Greek speech.

In the same passage, Grialius has *Thracidas* in the text and *Iracidas* in the note. What should be thought about the verses on the winds that Grialius presents in his note, I explained in *Isidoriana*, chapter 76, numbers 20 and 21. I shall now provide variant readings from Vatican Codex Ottobonianus 6, page 25, where the heading is “Verses on the Winds,” and from the Albanian manuscript. Verse 1 has *limine* for *limite*. Verse 4 has *altus* for *alto*. Verse 5 reads: “Our language fixed the name Septentrio for him”; in the Bignaean edition it has *finxit* (“fashioned”) instead of *fixit* (“fixed”), and some manuscripts likewise have that reading. Verse 6 has *hunc dextro* or *huic dextra* instead of *huic dexter*. Verse 10 has *medio flat rectus* instead of *flat rectus solis*. Verse 13 has *littera signat* instead of *littora signant*. Verse 14 reads:

“With cloud-bearing breath Eurus waters the joyful region.” [Col. 1009D]

Verse 20 has *adnominat* instead of *adtaminat*. Verse 23 has *huic dextra mugit* instead of *huic dextram tangit*. AREV.]

5. Certain local winds, however, Tranquillus calls by particular names according to their places. Among these are: the Syrus in Syria, the Carbasus in Cilicia, the Thracidas in the Propontis, the Sciron in Attica, the Circius in Gallaecia, and the Sucronensis in Spain. There are also innumerable others named after rivers, lakes, or regions. There are nevertheless two forces, found everywhere beyond these, which are more properly breaths than winds: *aura* and *altanus*.

52 **CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the signs of storm or fair weather**

[Col. 1009A]

[Note: [Col. 1009D]

CHAPTER XXXVIII—Note 1. Tranquillus says this way in *Prata*; other copies have *tranquillis in portis*; others, *tranquillis in pratis*; others, *Tranquillus in partes*. I would read *Tranquillo in portu*—“Thus you will learn in the harbor”—unless Tranquillus had been mentioned in the chapter on the winds, and Pliny had said in his preface that some Greeks entitled their books λειμῶνες, that is, “meadows.”] 

1. A storm is a whirlwind of divine judgment, as the prophet says: “God is in the storm, and his way is in the whirlwind” (Nahum 1:3). Fair weather, however, is the joy of eternal light. Tranquillus, in *Prata*, gives sailors the following signs of storms:

“One should expect a change of weather for the worse when, during nighttime navigation, the water sparkles at the oars and at the steering oars. A change of wind toward the South is indicated when squid (*lulligines*) or swallows fly, or when dolphins display themselves entirely in leaps and strike the water with their tails. For the wind always arises from the direction in which they are carried. It is no wonder that mute animals foresee what lies beneath the waves. The waters are always inclined by the movement of the breeze that is beginning; the first inhabitants of the sea feel this change. Therefore they struggle against the force, either from fear that they may be carried onto the shores, or by nature, lest the wave hurl forward the necks of those turned away. What then? Do only dolphins fear this injury? No, the other fish do as well. But only the dolphins are visible, because they leap out.”

[Note: [Col. 1009D]

2. “When it lightens from the region of Aquilo.” Virgil:

“But when it thunders from the quarter of savage Boreas,

and when the house of Eurus and Zephyrus thunders,

all the fields swim with full ditches.”

[Col. 1010C] In the same passage, “Nigidius also … will be lacking.” These are the words of the translator of Aratus, from whom many passages have been restored, since they were exceedingly corrupt in all the books. But Maro expresses the same thought much more elegantly:

“When the moon first gathers her returning fires,

if dark beneath the obscure …”

In the same passage, “If its horns have been covered by a cloud.” Thus the O manuscript; the translator of Aratus has *tetra fuerint* (“have been foul”). 

In the same passage, “There will be a future storm.” Some copies add: “and when the south wind, Auster, has blown, there will be heat”; others give this at the end of the chapter. AREV.]

2. Varro likewise says that it is a sign of a storm when it flashes from the region of Aquilo and when it thunders from the region of Eurus. Nigidius also says:

“If the moon has black spots on the tip of her horn during the first days of the month, there will be rain; if they are in the middle, then, when her horns are full, there will be fair weather. Certainly, if she is red, like gold, she indicates winds. Wind arises from the density of the air; when the air is thickly overcast, the sun and moon become red.”

Likewise, if her horns have been covered by a cloud, there will be a storm.

53 [Note: [Col. 1010C]

3. If the moon’s northern horn is more upright, this indicates that Aquilo is impending. Likewise, if the southern horn is erect. Thus all the books consistently read, as does the translator of Aratus. Why the moon may appear either erect or inclined, see Bede, chapter 24 of *On the Nature of Things*, second edition.

In the same passage, Virgil’s verses are from *Georgics* I, verses 432 and following. AREV.]

3. Aratus says that if the moon’s northern horn is more upright, Aquilo is impending. Likewise, if the southern horn is more erect, Notus is impending. The fourth day of the moon is considered the surest indication of coming winds. Hence Virgil says:

“If at the fourth rising—for that is the surest sign—

she does not pass through the heavens with blunt horns,

that whole day, and those that will be born from it,

will be free from rain and winds until the month is complete.”

[Note: [Col. 1010D]

4. “If the sun at its rising is spotted …” signifies a storm. These are the words of the same translator.]

4. The same Virgil likewise says: If the sun at its rising is spotted and lies hidden beneath a cloud, or if it appears only in part, rain is to be expected. Varro likewise says:

“If, on rising, it appears hollow, so that it shines in the middle and sends rays partly toward the South and partly toward the North, it indicates a wet and windy storm.”

[Note: [Col. 1010D]

5. “Be red at sunset.” The words *in occasu* (“at sunset”) were missing from all our books.

In the same passage, “almost clear.” The word *fere* (“almost”) is absent from the translator of Aratus, but is read in all our books.]

5. The same author likewise says: “If the sun is red at sunset, the day will be almost clear; if it is pale, it signifies storms.” Nigidius also says: “If the pale sun sets into black clouds, it signifies the north wind, Aquilo.” Likewise, the Lord says in the Gospel: “If in the evening the sky is red, the morning will be fair. If in the morning the sky is red and gloomy, there will be a storm, and when the south wind, Auster, has blown, there will be heat.”

**CHAPTER XXXIX. On pestilence**

[Note: [Col. 1010D]

CHAPTER XXXIX—Note 1. “Some have said.” This refers to Clement, Book VIII of the *Recognitions*, whose words are these: “When, on account of human sins, … and the other animals.”

In the same passage, *quaeque*, that is, “whatever,” as in other authors and elsewhere in Isidore. Some copies have *pene omnia quae* (“almost everything which”), others only *quae*. Virgil’s verses are from *Aeneid* III, verses 138 and following. AREV.]

1. Pestilence is a disease spreading widely and polluting by its contagion whatever it touches. This illness has no interval of time in which either life may be hoped for or death expected; rather, sudden weakness arrives together with death. Some have said that the cause of this pestilence is as follows:

“When, on account of human sins, a plague and chastisement are inflicted upon the earth, then, for some reason—that is, through drought, the force of heat, or excessive rains—the air is corrupted. Thus, when the balance of the natural order has been disturbed, the elements are infected, corruption of the air takes place, and a pestilential breeze arises. Destruction and the fault of corruption come upon human beings and the other animals.”

Hence Virgil:

“Through a corrupted region of the sky, a pitiable plague comes,

upon trees and crops.”

[Col. 1011A] [Note: [Col. 1011C]

2. “Others likewise say that pestilential seeds of things …” It is worthwhile examining from which words of Lucretius the surviving portion of this chapter was composed. He writes in Book VI:

“I have shown above that first there are seeds of many things

which are vital for us,

and, on the other hand, those which necessarily bring disease and death.

Many of these, when they have arisen by chance,

fly about and disturb the sky; the air becomes diseased.

The whole force of diseases and pestilence

either comes from outside, like clouds and mists from above,

through the sky, or often arises of itself

and rises from the earth, when it has encountered decay

struck by unseasonable rains and sunlight.

Do you not also see that, because of a change in the sky and waters,

all who arrive far from their homeland and dwelling

are attacked, because the air is greatly different?”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, when the sky, which happens to be foreign to us,

is stirred and hostile air begins to creep,

as mist and cloud gradually creep along, disturbing everything

wherever it proceeds and forcing it to change,

it also happens that, when at last it comes into our sky,

it corrupts it and makes it like itself, though foreign.

Thus this sudden new disaster and pestilence

falls upon the waters or attacks the crops themselves,

or the other foods of human beings and the nourishment of cattle,

or even remains suspended in the air itself.

And when, breathing, we draw in mixed breezes from here,

we must likewise absorb that force into our bodies.”

In the same passage, *spirantes* (“breathing”). It seems that *spiramus* (“we breathe”) ought to be restored; alternatively, in accordance with the quoted verses of Lucretius, *cum spirantes ducimus auras* (“when, breathing, we draw in the breezes”). AREV.]

2. Others likewise say that many pestilential seeds of things are carried through the air and suspended there, and are transported by winds or clouds into distant regions of the sky. Then, wherever they are carried or fall, they corrupt all places and living growths to the destruction of animals; or they remain suspended in the air, and when we breathe in the breezes, we absorb them together into our bodies. From this, the body, weakened by disease, is either destroyed by hideous ulcers or deprived of life by a sudden stroke. For just as bodies accustomed to arrive from a different sky or from different waters are often attacked, so that they contract disease, in the same way corrupted air coming from other regions of the sky corrupts the body with sudden destruction and abruptly extinguishes life.

55 **CHAPTER XL. On the Ocean**

[Col. 1011B] [Note: [Col. 1011D]

CHAPTER XL—Note 1. “Some say that in the depths of the Ocean there are certain passages.” Plato, in the *Phaedo*.

In the same passage, “The seas flow out, now drawing back, they return.” F has: “the seas flow out, now drawing back, they are returned.” For shortly afterward he will say that they are drawn backward and poured back again, unless you prefer to refer the phrase to the nostrils.

In the same passage, “Some, however, wish it to be poured back with the moon’s increase.” These are the words of Ambrose, Book IV, at the end of chapter 7.

In the same passage, “Some, etc.” Others read: “Some philosophers say that the world, as Solinus reports, is a kind of animal composed from the four elements and moved by a certain spirit; and just as in our bodies there is an exchange of breathing, so in the depths of the Ocean there are certain passages filled with the spirit of the winds, like the nostrils of the world, etc.” After *wish*, some copies add: “as Ambrose says.” AREV.]

1. Concerning why the Ocean returns upon itself in alternating tides, some say that in the depths of the Ocean there are certain spirits of the winds, like the nostrils of the world, through which breaths are either emitted or drawn back in, alternately advancing and retreating. Thus, when the spirit evaporates, the seas flow outward; when it draws back, they are drawn back in return.

Others, however, wish the Ocean to grow with the moon’s increase and to be drawn backward, as though by certain breaths of the moon, and then, again through the same impulse and withdrawal, to be poured back into its proper measure.

[Note: [Col. 1012C]

2. Others have said that the stars are nourished by the waves of the Ocean. See above, chapter 15.] 

2. Others likewise say that the stars are nourished by the waves of the Ocean, and that the sun draws water from the Ocean with its fires and pours it around all the stars to temper them, since they are fiery. Hence they say that when the sun draws up the waves, it raises the Ocean. But whether the waters are raised by the spirit of the winds, increase through the moon’s course, or diminish because the sun draws them upward—this is known to God alone. The world is his work, and the entire order of the world is known to him alone.

[Col. 1012A] [Note: [Col. 1012D]

3. That Clement, the disciple of the apostles, was the author of the books of the *Recognitions* was long ago denied by Saint Athanasius, Eusebius, and others. Nevertheless, some, such as Saint Epiphanius and Rufinus, believed that the work was written by Saint Clement but corrupted by heretics. Lucan’s verses are Book V, verses 623 and following. Grialius, incorrectly, has *tenere* instead of *teneri*. AREV.]

3. The Ocean’s size is said to be incomparable, and its breadth impossible to cross. Clement, the disciple of the apostles, also appears to have indicated this when he says: “The Ocean is uncrossable, and those who are beyond it are worlds.” The philosophers, however, say that beyond the Ocean there is no land, but that the sea is contained only by the dense air of the clouds, just as the earth is contained below; hence Lucan:

“When the sea folded nations together, when Tethys

would not allow any shores to remain contained beneath the sky,

then too such a mass of evils would have grown toward the stars,

had not the ruler of heaven pressed the waters down with clouds.”

**CHAPTER XLI. Why the sea does not increase**

[Note: [Col. 1012D]

CHAPTER XLI—Note 1. “Bishop Clement says.” Book VIII of the *Recognitions*.

In the same passage, “Add also that the winds carry away.” Lucretius:

“Moreover, the sun removes a large portion by its heat.”

And shortly afterward:

“Then, furthermore, the winds too can carry off

a large portion of moisture …”

In the same passage, “Lakes and many pools.” He seems to have played upon Lucretius’ words: “Many lakes and many pools.”]

1. Concerning why the sea does not become larger and why it does not increase despite such an abundance of rivers, Bishop Clement says that naturally salt water consumes the sweet stream received into it. Thus the salty element of the sea, however great the quantities of water it receives, nevertheless drains them away. Add also that the winds carry them off and that the sun’s vapor and heat absorb them. Finally, we see lakes and many pools consumed in a short moment by blasts of wind and the sun’s heat. Solomon says: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return” (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

2. From this it is understood that the sea does not increase because, through certain hidden passages in the depths, the waters flow back to their sources and return along their usual course through their channels. The sea, moreover, was made to receive the courses of all rivers. Although its depth varies, the evenness of its surface is undifferentiated. Hence it is believed to have been called *aequor*, because its surface is level; physicists, however, say that the sea is deeper than the lands.

**CHAPTER XLII. Why the sea has salt water**

[Col. 1013A]

[Note: [Col. 1013C]

CHAPTER XLII—Note 1. “Again Ambrose the teacher … that it is undrinkable.” Book II, chapter 3.

In the same passage, “And by the blasts of the winds.” These words are not Ambrose’s but seem to have been repeated from the preceding chapter.

In the same passage, “This also is said to happen through the sun’s reasoning.” That is, through its skill, judgment, and a certain power of discernment. Thus Ambrose says: “This is said to happen through a certain discrimination by the sun.”]

1. Again the teacher Ambrose taught, saying: The ancients say that the sea has salt and bitter waters because what flows into it from different rivers is consumed by the heat of the sun and by the blasts of the winds. As much is consumed by the vapor of the day as is carried into it each day from all the courses of the rivers. This too is said to happen through the sun’s discernment: it draws to itself what is pure and light, but leaves behind what is heavy and earthy, which is also bitter and undrinkable.

**CHAPTER XLIII. On the Nile**

[Note: [Col. 1013C]

CHAPTER XLIII—Note 1. The substance of the whole chapter is taken from Lucretius’ elegant verses on the same subject in Book VI: “The Nile rises in summer,” etc. But he seems deliberately to have avoided Lucretius’ words here, although he often uses them.]

1. Egypt always has heat in its air and perpetual sun; it never receives rains or clouds. The Nile River floods its regions during the summer, and they use it in place of rain. The river rises between the South and the East. The Etesian winds blow from the region of Zephyrus—that is, from the West—and have a fixed season. They arise in the month of May; their blowing is weak at first but increases day by day.

2. For they blow from the sixth hour until the tenth.
