Since their blowing resists the waters, and since heaps of sand are also placed before the mouths through which the river flows into the sea, the waves of the Nile swell and are forced to turn back. Thus the bursting waters are driven toward the South. When these waters have accumulated, the Nile bursts into Egypt. When the Etesian winds also cease and the sandbanks are broken through, the river returns once more to its channel.

**CHAPTER XLIV. On the names of the sea and rivers**

[Col. 1013C]

[Note: [Col. 1013C]

CHAPTER XLIV—Note 1. Concerning this chapter, which now appears for the first time, I made several observations in *Isidoriana*, chapter 76, number 11. After comparing many different manuscripts, I selected the reading that seemed best. Instead of *in Pratis*, some copies have *in the annalistic books of the Fathers*. See the note to chapter 38, number 1. Fabricius, *Latin Bibliography*, Book II, chapter 24, number 6, thinks that *in Variis* should be read, since Servius and Charisius cite Suetonius Tranquillus’ work *On Miscellaneous Matters*; but he does not reject the view that Suetonius entitled his books *Prata*, “Meadows,” as Grialius believes. He is less persuaded by the readings supplied by others, *in Parergis* or *in Arateis*. Instead of *externum*, some copies have *extremum*. Instead of *superum* and *inferum*, others have *supernum* and *infernum*. AREV.]

1. In *Prata*, Tranquillus asserts the following: “The outer sea is the Ocean; the inner sea, which flows out from the Ocean, is the upper and lower sea, by which Italy is washed. Of these, the upper sea is called the Adriatic, and the lower the Tuscan.”

[Note: [Col. 1013D]

2. Festus: “Estuaries are all places through which the sea …” By conjecture I have restored *vada* (“shallows”), since the manuscripts had *vaga* or *vuaga*. Seneca, in *Agamemnon*, verse 372:

“These shallows of the impoverished wave break them apart.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 115: “Into shallows and sandbanks.” AREV.]

2. A strait is a narrow passage, as if a boiling sea, such as the Sicilian and Gaditanian straits. Estuaries are all places through which the sea alternately advances and retreats. *Altum* properly means the deep sea. *Vada* are places in the sea where one can stand; Virgil calls them *brevia*, “shallows,” which the Greeks likewise call βραχέα (*brachya*).

[Note: [Col. 1013D]

3. Paestanian. I conclude that this is the form that should be printed from Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book XVI, Letter 6: “There were two bays that had to be crossed, the Paestanian and the Vibonian.” The manuscripts had *Pertanus*. Paestum was formerly a city and is now a village of Lucania. In some manuscripts there was *Amyclanus fluctuantes*. I omitted *fluctuantes* because the word is absent from Vatican Palatine 1448. Otherwise one might conjecture *Amyclanus*, or *Fundanus*. In the Albanian Codex: *Amyclanus*, with the rest essentially identical. Concerning the Amyclanian Bay, also called the Fundanian, see Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 16. That *angulus* (“corner”) can mean a bay of the sea is clear from Cato in Charisius, Book II, page 185, Putsch: “You would see the sea blossoming with sails beyond the Gallic corner.” Concerning *flustrum* or *flustra*, see Festus and Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 2. Festus says that *flustra* are formed when the waves do not move in the sea. Instead of *flustra*, some manuscripts of Isidore have *flustrum*, and *stabunt* instead of *stabant*. The Albanian Codex has: “The cargo ships, laden and freighted, stood,” etc. AREV.]

3. Larger bays are called recesses of the sea, such as the Caspian, Arabian, and Indian bays. Smaller ones are called corners, such as the Paestanian, Amyclanian, and others like them. *Flustra* are the movement of the sea when it fluctuates without a storm. Naevius says in *The Punic War*: “The cargo ships, heavily laden, stood in the *flustra*,” as if he had said, “in the open sea.”

[Col. 1014B] [Note: [Col. 1014C]

4. Others read *sub laeta mole abstrusas*; perhaps it should be *sub lata* (“beneath the broad mass”). From this meaning of *moles* seems to have arisen the Spanish word *muelle*, from the masses constructed in harbors to restrain the waves. I do not know what *sinus* means here. I would readily read *obtrusas in sinu* or *obrutas sinu* (“thrust into” or “buried in the bay”). “Blind wave,” etc. Others have likewise recalled *caeci fluctus* in this same sense: Sisenna in Nonius, chapter 6, number 7, and Livy in Seneca, *Suasoria* 7. AREV.]

4. *Moles* are structures that rise up and project into the sea. Concerning them Pacuvius says: “All the hiding places thrust beneath the raised mass.” A blind bay is a swollen wave that has not yet become white with foam. Concerning this, Atta says in his *Togatae*: “They make blind waves for the people through their discord.” And, he says, Augustus said: “We came to Naples amid a truly blind wave.”

[Note: [Col. 1014C]

5. *Alluit* (“washes”). Some have *alluitur* (“is washed”). Pacuvius’ words should be understood and emended from what was said in the note to Book XIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 21, number 2. The manuscripts had *torret* instead of *terrae*. Instead of *tollae*, some have *tolli*, others *tolles*. *Tolles*, *toles*, *tolae*, and *tolia* are customarily used for a swelling in the throat. I therefore think that the meaning was extended from there to steep falls of water, since the waters swell in such places. But what if one should read *tholi*? AREV.]

5. A shore (*litus*) is whatever water washes. A river is any water that flows, even slightly. A torrent is a river that grows through rain and dries up through drought; concerning it Pacuvius says: “The earth, scorched by fiery heat.” The mouths of rivers are their outlets into the sea. *Tollae* are steep falls of water, such as those found especially in the Anio River.

**CHAPTER XLV. On the position of the earth**

[Col. 1014C] [Note: [Col. 1014D]

CHAPTER XLV—Note 1. Thus Ambrose says. Book I, chapter 6.]

1. Concerning how the earth is believed to stand, founded upon the air and balanced by weights, Ambrose says:

“Concerning the nature or position of the earth, it is sufficient, according to Scripture, to know from the Book of Job that ‘he hangs the earth upon nothing.’”

The philosophers likewise believe that the earth is supported by dense air and hangs motionless by its own mass like a sponge. Thus, through equal movement here and there, as though supported by the oars of wings, it hangs balanced on every side, and cannot incline toward one side rather than another.

2. Nevertheless, whether it is supported by the density of the air or hangs above water—for it is written that he “founded the earth upon the waters” (Psalm 135:6)—or how soft air can support so immense a weight of earth; or, if so immense a weight rests upon water, how it is not submerged; or how it maintains the balance of equality so that, leaning toward one side, it does not come to rest upon it—no mortal is permitted to know. Nor is it lawful for anyone to investigate or scrutinize such excellence of divine craftsmanship, since it is established that by the law of God’s majesty it remains stable either above the waters or above the clouds. For who, as Solomon says, is sufficient to recount his works, or who can investigate his great deeds? Therefore, what is a secret from mortal nature must be left to divine power.

60 **CHAPTER XLVI. On earthquakes**

[Note: [Col. 1015D]

CHAPTER XLVI—Note 1. The substance of this chapter too is taken from Lucretius’ Book VI.

In the same passage, “Seeking a way of escape by force.” The copyists had omitted the first *vi*, deceived by the similarity of the following syllable *vi*. The familiar saying is: “By force a way is made.”]

1. The wise say that the earth is shaped like a sponge, and that wind gathered within it twists and travels through caverns. When it has traveled as far as the earth cannot contain it, the wind sends roars and murmurs here and there. Then, seeking a way of escape by force, when the earth can no longer contain it, it either trembles or splits open so that it may expel the wind. Thus an earthquake occurs, when the imprisoned wind shakes everything.

[Note: [Col. 1015D]

2. Hence Sallustius also says: “Winds, driven through the hollow places of the earth, broke apart certain mountains, and then the hills settled.” The same words are cited at the beginning of Book XIV of the *Etymologies*, and by Servius in his note on *Georgics* II, at the verse “Whence the trembling of the earth.”

In the same passage, “And by the movement of the wave.” Lucretius:

“It also happens when an enormous clod of earth

rolls forward from ancient age into great pools of water,

so that the water is tossed about and the earth too trembles with the wave.”

In the same passage, *praecipitati*; perhaps *praecipitari* (“to be driven headlong”), as shortly afterward *sedere* (“to settle”). AREV.]

2. Hence Sallustius also says: “Winds, driven through the hollow places of the earth, broke apart certain mountains, and then the hills settled.” Therefore, as we have said, the trembling of the earth arises either from the breath of wind through the earth’s hollows, from the collapse of its lower regions, or from the movement of the wave. Thus Lucan also says:

“And when the earth split open,

the Alps trembled with unaccustomed movements.”

3. An earthquake occurs continually wherever there are hollow places in the earth into which winds enter and produce earthquakes. For where the earth is sandy or solid, no earthquake occurs. The movement of the earth pertains to judgment, when sinners and earthly people, shaken by the breath of God’s mouth, will be moved. Likewise, the shaking of the earth is the conversion of earthly people to faith. Hence it is written: “His feet stood, and the earth was moved”—namely, toward belief.

**CHAPTER XLVII. On Mount Etna**

[Col. 1016A]

[Note: [Col. 1016D]

CHAPTER XLVII—Note 1. Justinus. At the beginning of Book IV; all this material continues up to the allegorical interpretation.]

1. Concerning Mount Etna, Justinus writes in his *History* as follows:

“The soil of Sicily is thin and fragile, and so penetrable by certain caverns and channels that it is almost entirely open to the blasts of the winds. The substance of the soil itself is naturally suited to producing and nourishing fires, since it is said to be laid internally upon sulfur and bitumen. This causes it, when the spirit struggles inwardly with the fire, frequently and in many places to belch forth now vapor, now smoke.”

2. Hence the fire of Mount Etna has endured for so many centuries. Whenever a more violent wind settles upon the openings of its caverns, it ejects masses of sand. Added to this are the perpetual sources of fuel in the Aeolian islands, as though the fire were nourished by the islands’ own waters. For such a great fire could not have endured for so many centuries within such narrow boundaries unless it were also fed by the nourishment of moisture.

3. Hence the fables of Scylla and Charybdis arose. Hence the barking was heard; hence the monsters; hence the returning images. When sailors, terrified by the great whirlpools of the divided sea, think that the waves are barking, the churning vortex of the swallowing tide strikes them together. The same cause also produces the perpetual fires of Mount Etna. For the gathering of the waters drags the spirit it has seized down into the deepest depths and holds it there, suffocated, until, diffused through the earth’s openings, it ignites the fuel of the fire.

[Note: [Col. 1016D]

4. “That fire.” Some copies have “that eternal fire,” or “that fire of Gehenna.” AREV.]

4. It is understood as an example of Gehenna, whose perpetual fires will blaze to punish sinners, who will be tormented forever and ever. [Col. 1016C] For just as these mountains have continued until now, burning with raging flames through such a long duration of time, so that they can never be extinguished, so that fire will never have an end in tormenting the bodies of the condemned.

**CHAPTER XLVIII. On the regions of the earth**

[Note: [Col. 1016D]

CHAPTER XLVIII—Note 1. This chapter was omitted from Grialius’ edition through the negligence of a copyist or printer, as I believe, and as I stated in *Isidoriana*, chapter 76, number 6. From the manuscripts and printed editions I have assembled the preferable reading. Bignaeus has *definiamus … interfusum*. “From this point let us explain the order.” He omits *coeli* after *partibus* and *siderum* before *signa*. Some copies have *ablu[it]* instead of *allu[it]*. Munckerus also reads *alluit* in his edition of Hyginus, page 353; he says that this chapter should be compared with chapter 8 of Hyginus’ *Astronomica Poetica*, Book I, and emended. Hyginus’ words are: “The earth occupies the center of the sphere of the world … The axis divides this middle point along the dimension of the whole earth. The Ocean, however, in the region of the circuit … is believed to fall into it.” AREV.]

1. Now let us define the position of the earth and explain in order in what regions the sea appears to be interposed. As Hyginus testifies, the earth, situated in the middle region of the world, occupies the center, being separated from all parts of the sky by an equal interval. The Ocean, poured out around the circuit of the sphere, washes nearly the boundaries of the entire world. Hence the signs of the stars, when they set, are believed to fall into it.

[Note: [Col. 1017A]

2. Bignaeus has: “It separates the mouth of the Nile River, which is Canopic.” Hyginus has *Canopicon*. Soon afterward he has *Thanus* instead of *Tanais*, and *Eothis* instead of *Maeotis*. Similar errors occur frequently in Bignaeus. AREV.]

2. The region of the earth is divided into three parts, one of which is called Europe, another Asia, and the third Africa. The sea divides Europe from Africa from the outermost boundaries of the Ocean and from the Pillars of Hercules. It separates Asia and Libya together with Egypt by the mouth of the Nile River, which is called the Canopic mouth. The Tanais divides Asia from Europe in two, flowing into the marsh called Maeotis. Asia, as the most blessed Augustine says, extends from the South through the East as far as the North. Europe, however, extends from the North to the West, and from there Africa extends from the West to the South.

[Col. 1018A] [Note: [Col. 1018A]

3. “The Great Sea.” Isidore often calls the Mediterranean Sea this. See *Etymologies* XIII, chapter 16, number 1. Instead of *influit*, the more recent Madrid edition, in its additions, page 51, has *interluit*. After *aestimaverunt*, some copies add: “300 in length and 200 in breadth”; this will be said in the *Catholic Histories*. AREV.]

3. Hence Europe and Africa together appear to occupy half the world, while Asia alone occupies the other half. But those two parts were made because between them, from the Ocean, whatever waters flow over the lands enters and forms for us the Great Sea. Geometers have estimated the measure of the whole earth at 180,000 stades.

[Col. 1017]

**THE CHRONICLE OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE** [Note: [Col. 1017] The notes without an attached name should be attributed to Loaisa. Published.]. (C)

**Preface**

[Col. 1017] 63 [Note: [Col. 1017C]

PREFACE—Note 1. Besides others, Eusebius mentions Julius Africanus, the historian of times, in the *Chronicle* under the year 224 of the redemption of the world and elsewhere; Augustine, in *Against Faustus*; Jerome, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* and the preface to Daniel; Suidas, under the entries Ἀφρικανός (“Africanus”) and κεστός (“embroidered [work]”); Eustathius, in his elegant work *The Hexaemeron*, which has nowhere yet been published and is in my possession; and most fully of all Photius, in the *Bibliotheca*, which he composed concerning the books he had read. Since this author himself has until now lain hidden in darkness, not without the greatest loss to the public good, I think it worthwhile to set down his words. They are thirty-four in number, as follows:

“An historical work of Africanus was read. This is the author who also composed fourteen books of the so-called *Cesti*. It is concise, indeed, but omits nothing necessary to be recounted. It begins from the Mosaic creation of the world and comes down to the appearance of Christ. It also treats briefly of the events from Christ to the reign of Macrinus, emperor of the Romans, at which time, as he says, this composition too was completed. It comprised 5,723 years and was divided into five volumes. This author also writes to Origen concerning the account of Susanna, saying that he had not read it in the Hebrew writings and that it does not accord with Hebrew etymology—neither the derivation of πρίνος from πρίσαι nor that of σχῖνος from σχίσαι—which Origen, resolving these points, answered him. Africanus also writes to Aristides, in which work he clearly showed that the supposed disagreement in Matthew and Luke concerning the genealogy of our Savior is in complete agreement and harmonious in every respect.”

We read, he says, Africanus’ *History*. This is the man who also composed fourteen books of the *Cesti*—for that is their title. Although it is extremely brief and concise, it nevertheless omits nothing worthy of knowledge. He begins from the creation of the world as set down by Moses and proceeds to the coming of Christ. He also summarizes the events from the time of Christ until the reign of Macrinus, emperor of the Romans, at which time, as he testifies concerning himself, this work was completed. Altogether it contains 5,723 years and is divided into five volumes. The same author writes to Origen concerning what is narrated about Susanna: that he himself had never read anything of the kind in the records of the Hebrews, and that nothing at all in the name agrees with Hebrew etymology—neither τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ πρίνου πρίσαι (“to cut from the holm-oak”) nor τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ σχίνου σχίσαι (“to split from the mastic tree”), all of which Origen, refuting them, answered him. Africanus also writes to Aristides, clearly showing that the disagreement which some suppose to exist in Matthew and Luke concerning the genealogy of our Savior is wholly harmonious and agrees with itself in every respect. These are the words of Photius.

Ibid. In the Isidorian materials there are two chapters concerning Isidore’s Chronicle. The first is chapter 77, with this title: “Our Isidore of Seville, the true author of the Chronicle, which is different from the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja. A summary of the Chronicle inserted by Isidore himself into the Etymologies.” The second is chapter 78, entitled as follows: “Isidore’s interpolated Chronicle, which Lucas of Tuy included among his own Chronicles.” Mellitus’s Chronicle is the same as the Isidorian one, but interpolated in a different manner and more frequently mutilated and abridged. Editions of the Isidorian Chronicle: Loaisa’s prologue; an Italian version that was published; another Spanish manuscript version; manuscript copies of the same Chronicle. There is no need to add anything else at present. AREV.]

### 1

Julius Africanus, the first among our writers, extracted a brief chronological sequence arranged by generations and reigns, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, in a plain historical style. Thereafter Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and Jerome the presbyter, of holy memory, published a more extensive history in the form of chronological canons, arranged simultaneously according to reigns and periods.

[Note: [Col. 1018D]

2. “Tunnensis.” Correctly so here; elsewhere incorrectly “Turonensis.” Victor was in fact bishop of the Church of Tunnuna in Africa, as is clear from Isidore’s book On Illustrious Men. Correct this word also at the beginning of Ado of Vienne’s Chronicle.

Ibid. Another reading: “he explained that of the lesser [one],” instead of “he explained that of the younger [one].”

Ibid. “Of Heraclius and Sisebut.” But in book V of the Etymologies, “of the emperor Heraclius and Suinthila.” Isidore flourished under these rulers, as is evident from Saint Ildefonsus’s addition to the Illustrious Men concerning Isidore, and from Braulio of Zaragoza, about whom more will be said in the final note of this book.

Ibid. Possevinus, vol. II of the Select Bibliotheca, p. 356, book XVI, chapter 13, apparently understands this to be that Victor when, in his list of Spanish writers on Spanish affairs, he mentions Victor, bishop of Toledo. [Col. 1019C] AREV.]

### 2

After these came various others, among whom Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna, was especially prominent. Having reviewed the histories mentioned above, he completed an account of the deeds of succeeding ages down to the consulship of Justin the Younger. We have recorded a summary of these periods, from the beginning of the world down to the reign of the emperor Heraclius Augustus and Sisebut, king of the Goths, with as much brevity as we could, adding alongside it a descending line of chronological figures, by which the sum of the preceding age may be known.

## The First Age of the World

[Col. 1019A]

[Note: [Col. 1019C]

1. Another version: “The first human being, whom he called Adam.”

Ibid. After the words “the man Adam,” Codex Regiovaticanus 1852 inserts much material beginning, “Adam knew his wife,” and so forth, which seems to have been taken from Ado or other sources. Similar additions occur throughout, so that the Chronicle must be regarded as different from the Isidorian one. AREV.]

### 1

God formed all the creatures of the universe in six days. On the first day he created light; on the second, the firmament of heaven; on the third, the appearance of the sea and the earth; on the fourth, the stars; on the fifth, the fish and birds; on the sixth, the beasts and cattle; and finally, in his own likeness, the first human being, Adam.

[Note: [Col. 1019C]

2. According to Josephus, book I, chapter 2 of the Antiquities, “Adam” means “red,” because he was formed from red earth. Zonaras likewise derives it from the same source, volume I. Augustine, however, on Psalm 95, says that Adam signifies the inhabited world, because he was scattered throughout the whole world; so too Cyprian, in his treatise On Sinai and Zion. Observe, however, that in his computation of years Isidore follows the Septuagint—the Seventy Interpreters—as do Julius Africanus, Origen, Eusebius, and other ancient Fathers, whereas others reject this reckoning. Augustine, book XV of The City of God, chapter 13, believes that the corruption of the years found in the manuscripts arose through the fault of the person who first undertook to copy the Septuagint translation from the Library of Ptolemy. [Col. 1019D] Our edition reads: “Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot a son in his own image and likeness, and called his name Seth.” Philo and the Hebrew Chronicle also follow this method of reckoning, in accordance with the Hebrew truth of the divine Scriptures. Saint Jerome, Questions on Genesis: “It must be known,” he says, “that up to the Flood, where in our manuscripts someone is said to have begotten a son at two hundred and more years, the Hebrew has one hundred years and the remaining years that follow.”

Ibid. “Enos.” Genesis 5; and Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, book I, chapter 3. Cedrenus also mentions him immediately at the beginning. Ado of Vienne likewise derives the same material from Isidore, as he does most of the rest.

Ibid. Another reading: “which is interpreted as ‘of the sons of God.’” Mellitus has “which is the stock (*stips*) of the sons of God,” from which Florezius conjectures *stirpes* (“stocks” or “roots”) or *stipes* (“stock”), but *stirps* (“root” or “stock”) should rather be read. This is the nominative singular, and it is so read in the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, which, like our other manuscripts, agrees for the most part with the Chronicle called Mellitus’s. The Modena Codex has *stirpes* (“stocks” or “roots”). AREV.]

### 2

[230 from the creation of the world] Adam, at the age of 230, begot Seth, who was born in place of Abel. His name is interpreted as “resurrection,” because in him the righteous seed, which is the seed of the sons of God, was raised again.

[435] Seth, at the age of 205, begot Enos, who first began to invoke the name of the Lord.

[625] Enos, at the age of 190, begot Kenan, whose name is interpreted as “the nature of God.” At this time Cain was the first before the Flood to found a city, which he filled solely with the multitude of his descendants.

[Note: [Col. 1020B]

3. The apostle Jude takes his testimony from the Book of Enoch: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning these people, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord comes,’” and so forth. That book, however, is rejected from the Canon. Augustine, book XVIII of The City of God, chapter 38, asserts that it was not written by Enoch; Jerome, in his book On Illustrious Men, while discussing the apostle Jude, considers it one of the apocryphal books. Tertullian, on the contrary, in his book On the Dress of Women, asserts that it was written by Enoch and says that, although it was not admitted into the Jewish library, it should nevertheless not be rejected by Christians. He therefore cites entire sections from it, especially in his books On Idolatry, On Modesty, and On the Veiling of Virgins. Origen does the same, in Homily 28 and in book IV of On First Principles. Peter Martínez, an eminent doctor of our Spain, discusses Enoch and the book written by him most learnedly in his commentary on the Epistle of Jude, in the twentieth section, On Prophecy.

Ibid. Another reading: “is interpreted as ‘departing’ or ‘carrying.’” Another: “surpassing” or “strengthening.” Immediately afterward, “but on account of antiquity,” instead of “but because of antiquity.” AREV.]

### 3

[795] Kenan, at the age of 170, begot Mahalalel, whose name is said to mean “plantation of God.”

[Col. 1020A] [960] Mahalalel, at the age of 165, begot Jared, whose name is interpreted as “descending” or “strengthening.”

[1122] Jared, at the age of 162, begot Enoch, who was taken up by God. He is also said to have written certain things, but because of their antiquity they were rejected by the Fathers as of doubtful authenticity.

[Note: [Col. 1020C]

4. “After the Flood.” Jerome discusses at length this question, debated in the books of many writers, in his commentary on Genesis. Augustine does so as well in his Questions on Genesis, question 2, and in The City of God, book XV, chapters 10 and 11. Ado treats it in his Breviary; finally, Bede in his brief work On the Six Ages.

Ibid. “But is not found … they suppose.” These words are absent from some manuscripts.

Ibid. “167 years.” Saint Augustine takes this position in The City of God, book XV, chapters 10 and 11; so does Saint Jerome in his Questions on Genesis and the Venerable Bede in his Chronicle. The Complutensian and Royal editions of the Bible, however, differ from this number by two years, which they contain fewer. Others hold different opinions on the matter, among them Nicephorus, who asserts in his Chronology that Methuselah, at the age of 187, begot Lamech. Ado also follows this view, as does the Aldine and German edition of the Bible. In this diversity of chronological reckoning, I embrace the opinion of Jerome, Augustine, and Isidore all the more willingly because I observe that the Septuagint, whom our author follows as authorities throughout nearly this entire little work, held the same view, as Luke the deacon testifies in a certain preface placed before Isidore’s Chronicle.]

### 4

[1287] Enoch, at the age of 165, begot Methuselah, who, according to the sequence of the years, is found to have lived fourteen years after the Flood. But he is not found to have been in the ark; for this reason some, on a false supposition, believe that he remained for a little while with his father Enoch, who had been taken up, until the Flood had passed. In this generation the sons of God desired the daughters of men.

[1404] Methuselah, at the age of 167, begot Lamech. In this generation giants were born. In this age as well, Jubal, from the line of Cain, discovered the art of music; his brother Tubal-cain was the inventor of the arts of bronze and iron.

[Col. 1021A] [Note: [Col. 1021B]

5. “Who by divine …” Another reading: “to whom, by a divine oracle, the ark was commanded to be built … were destined to perish, among whom … memory, which they had wisely discovered.” AREV.]

### 5

[1642] Lamech, at the age of 190, begot Noah, who by divine command was ordered to build the ark in the five-hundredth year of his life. At this time, as Josephus reports, those men, knowing that they might perish either by fire or by water, wrote down their studies on two pillars, one made of brick and the other of stone, so that the memory of what they had wisely discovered would not be destroyed. The stone pillar is said to have survived the Flood and to remain in Syria to this day.

[Note: [Col. 1021B]

6. The word that is said to be used by Moses, “tabae,” signifies not so much an ark as any vessel suitable for navigation, as the Greek πλοῖον, “ship.” The passage is found in Josephus, Antiquities, book I, chapter 5.

Ibid. “Ararat.” These are mountains in Upper Armenia, near the Persians, which the Greeks call Taurus and which divide Armenia. Berossus calls the mountain Cordyaeus, as Josephus reports, Antiquities, book I, chapter 4; Damascenus calls it Baris. See Jerome, On Hebrew Place-Names.

Ibid. “Seventy.” Augustine, The City of God, book XV, chapter 3, arrives at seventy-three: namely, fifteen from Japheth, thirty-one from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem, although in chapter 11 of the same book he proves that only seventy-two languages and as many nations arose from Noah.

Ibid. “For the years.” In these ten generations of men, Eusebius, Jerome, Zonaras, Isidore in book VI, chapter 39 of the Etymologies, and others follow the same number of years from Adam to the Flood. According to the Hebrew view, however, there are only 1,656 years from the creation of the world to the Flood, as is clear from Genesis 4 and 5 and from Hebrew chronologies. I also possess an anonymous Greek manuscript Chronicle in which 2,262 years are recorded, with these words: Ἐν τῷ ἑκατοστῷ ἔτει τοῦ Σὴμ ἑξακοσιαστῷ καὶ τοῦ Νῶε καὶ ἔτει γενέσεως τοῦ κοσμοῦ β . σ. ξ. β. ἐγένετο ὁ κατακλυσμὸς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς.

“In the one-hundredth year of Shem, but the six-hundredth of Noah, and in the 2,262nd year from the creation of the world, the Flood took place upon the earth.”

Antonius Contius judged that this number should be restored in the notes to Nicephorus’s Chronology. Josephus, however, Antiquities, book I, chapter 4, follows a computation different from both the Hebrew truth and the Septuagint translators. He says that 2,656 years elapsed from Adam to the universal Flood. So various and divergent are opinions concerning the age of the world that I believe this results from corruption in the manuscripts, for it is easy to make mistakes in numerical notation. Hence there are almost as many opinions about the years of the world as there are writers.

Ibid. “In the mountains.” This is how some of our manuscripts and Mellitus read. Grialius’s edition has “into the mountains.” AREV.]

### 6

[2242] It is read that the Flood occurred in Noah’s six-hundredth year. Josephus reports that his ark came to rest upon the mountains of Armenia called Ararat. Noah had three sons, from whom seventy-two nations arose: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem.

[Col. 1022A] The first age ends after 2,242 years.

## The Second Age of the World

[Note: [Col. 1021D]

7. Josephus, Antiquities, book I, chapter 14, believes that Shem was Noah’s third son and Japheth the eldest. Although Genesis 5 says, “Noah begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth,” and although Shem is listed first elsewhere, some Hebrews nevertheless assert that this was done solely because of his dignity, since Christ derived his lineage from him and he was the youngest. They support this by arguing that in genealogies and prophecies concerning the Savior the younger generally occupies the chief place, as with Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Manasseh, David, and Solomon. Augustine, The City of God, book XVI, chapter 2, interprets the history of Shem, Ham, and Japheth as concerning the life and death of the Savior.

Ibid. “Melchizedek.” Jerome says the same in his Questions on Genesis, and in his letter to Evagrius he asserts that until the priesthood of Aaron all the firstborn from the line of Noah, whose succession is described in this second age, were priests and sacrificed victims to God. These are the birthright privileges that Esau sold to his brother Jacob, Genesis 25.

Ibid. “Salem.” Jerome, in his letter to Dardanus and in the one addressed to Evagrius, says: “First Jebus, then Salem, third Jerusalem, now Aelia.” Josephus, Antiquities, book VII, chapter 3, says that some claimed that the poet Homer also called this city Jerusalem; the name was first assigned to it by David after he expelled the Jebusites from the citadel. Yet this city afterward experienced, deservedly, the same shifting and changeable fortune in its names as in its circumstances. On all these matters see what the most illustrious Inicus de Mendoza, whom I mention out of respect, has learnedly collected in his memorial book.]

### 7

[2244] In the second year after the Flood, when he was one hundred years old, Shem begot Arphaxad. From him the Chaldean nation arose. Shem is said to have been Melchizedek, who after the Flood was the first to found the city of Salem, now called Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 1022C]

8. In the edition of the Septuagint translators, Arphaxad is said to have begotten Cainan, and Cainan Sala. The Hebrews reject this, counting only ten generations from Noah to Abraham, just as from Adam to Noah. Blessed Luke, however, in chapter 3, counts eleven, inserting Cainan into this genealogical sequence. In doing so he followed the copies used by the Greeks to whom he was writing, for the Septuagint edition was at that time the most widely received and virtually the only one known to them. Saint Jerome, almost overwhelmed by the difficulty of this question, frankly admits that, because of the slowness of his intellect, he cannot untie this knot. Bede says the same in his preface to the Acts of the Apostles; Augustine, book II Against the Letter of Parmenianus; and more recent writers have also struggled seriously with the question, especially Lipomanus in his Catena on Genesis; Sixtus of Siena, book V of the Bibliotheca, annotation 88, and book VII, heresy 7; and Hermannus Contractus in his brief work On the Six Ages.

Ibid. “Salamites.” If I am not mistaken, I have correctly restored this passage from Lucas of Tuy, where previously “Samaritans” or “Medes” was read. It is clear from Josephus, Antiquities, book VIII, chapter 12, that the Samaritans derived their name from a certain Samarus.

Ibid. In most manuscripts: “Samaritans” or “Indians.” AREV.]

### 8

[2379] Arphaxad, at the age of 135, begot Sala, from whom the ancient Salamites, or Medes, descended.

[2509] Sala, at the age of 130, begot Eber, from whom the Hebrews were named.

[Note: [Col. 1022D]

9. From the Flood to the division of languages, according to the Hebrew reckoning, 272 years elapsed; and from the one Hebrew language, as the Hebrews believe, seventy-two languages were formed. They infer this from the heads of families, as Augustine testifies in The City of God, book XVI, chapter 11.

Ibid. “Four thousand.” This passage is mutilated in some copies, but it has easily been restored in full from Saint Jerome, from whom it is taken word for word. In his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 14, on the words “I will destroy the name of Babylon,” he says: “Its citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, is a tower which, built after the Flood, is said to reach a height of four thousand paces. It gradually narrows from a broad base into a narrower summit, so that the overhanging weight may be more easily supported by the broader lower parts. They describe there marble temples, golden statues, streets gleaming with stones and gold, and many other things that appear incredible.” Josephus, Antiquities, book I, chapter 9, says that the height and breadth of this tower were astonishing. Strabo records the city’s location in book XVI of his Geography; Herodotus reports that the circuit of its walls was 480 stadia. Much else is related about this matter by other writers of Greek and Latin histories.

[Col. 1023C] Ibid. “Nimrod.” Josephus, Antiquities, book I, chapter 9, says that Nimrod was Noah’s grandson through Ham, and calls the tower by the name of Babylon, from the confusion of languages. Genesis 10, however, says that Ham begot Cush, and Cush begot Nimrod; the same is found in 1 Chronicles 1. Incidentally, note that what is written about him in Genesis 10—“And he was a mighty hunter before the Lord”—Augustine, The City of God, book XVI, chapter 4, read as “against the Lord.” “That giant hunter,” he says, “must therefore be understood as a hunter against the Lord. What is signified by the name ‘hunter’ except a deceiver, oppressor, and destroyer of earthly animals?” Others hold that “before the Lord” is a hyperbole, meaning that no one under heaven equaled him in power; hence it is translated “mighty in hunting before the Lord.”

Ibid. Florezius, following Mellitus, gives 2,643, whereas Grialius’s edition has 2,647. The manuscript copies vary: some have 2,609, others 2,573, and others different numbers. AREV.]

### 9

[2643] Eber, at the age of 134, begot Peleg, in whose time the tower of Babel was built and the division of languages took place. The height of this tower is said to have been four thousand paces, gradually narrowing from its broader lower parts into a narrower summit, so that the overhanging weight might be more easily supported. They describe there temples decorated with marble, precious stones, and gold, and many other things that seem incredible. Nimrod the giant built this tower; after the confusion of languages he migrated from there to the Persians and taught them to worship fire.

[Note: [Col. 1023C]

10. From this arose idolatry. For when Belus died, Ninus his son, to console his grief, dedicated a statue to his father and paid it honors and sacrifices. The authorities are Jerome, on Hosea 2; Hegesippus, On the Origin of Idols; Fulgentius, book I of the Mythologies; and Cyril, book III Against Julian.

Ibid. “Of the Scythians.” Four kingdoms arose at nearly the same time: that of the Assyrians in the east, that of the Sicyonians in the west, that of the Scythians in the north, and that of the Egyptians in the south. Eusebius is the authority. The Assyrians, however, were much more powerful and elevated than the others, as Augustine relates in The City of God, book XVI, chapter 17.

Ibid. “Thanaus.” Others write “Taurus.” See Hermannus Contractus.

Ibid. “Loes.” According to Herodotus and Josephus, Antiquities, book VIII, chapter 6, he was called Mincus.]

### 10

[2773] Peleg, at the age of 130, begot Reu. In these times temples were first constructed, and certain leaders of nations began to be worshiped as gods.

[2905] Reu, at the age of 132, begot Serug. Under him the kingdom of the Scythians arose, whose first king was Tanaus.

[3035] Serug, at the age of 130, begot Nahor. The kingdom of the Egyptians began at this time, whose first king was Zoes.

[Note: [Col. 1023D]

11. “Seventy-nine.” Thus Nicephorus; but in Genesis 11, according to the Hebrew truth, twenty-nine; according to the Septuagint, 179.

Ibid. “Belus.” Thus Eusebius in his Chronicle: “In the twenty-eighth year of Terah, Belus, the first king of the Assyrians, died. The Assyrians called him a god, while others call him Saturn; and they handed the kingdom over to his son, who was called Ninus.” At the beginning of the Assyrian kingdom he likewise says: “Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia, except the Indians, for fifty-two years.” I found this passage reading as follows in an ancient manuscript of Eusebius: “Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to rule all Asia, except the Indians.” I accept this reading on the authority of Augustine, The City of God, book XVII, and of Eusebius himself, book X of the Preparation for the Gospel.

Ibid. “Saturn.” Cicero, book I of On the Nature of the Gods, says that the physical interpretation contained in the story of Saturn is not inelegant, and that Saturn is so called because he is “sated with years.”

Ibid. “Aegialeus.” Eusebius writes: “In the forty-ninth year of Terah, Europs ruled in Greece, among the Sicyonians, after the death of Aegialeus, who was the first king of the Sicyonians; from him the territory of the Peloponnesians was called Aegialea.” See Pausanias, Corinthiaca, and Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book I.]

### 11

[3114] Nahor, at the age of seventy-nine, begot Terah. Under him the kingdoms of the Assyrians and Sicyonians arose. The first king among the Assyrians was Belus, whom some consider to have been Saturn; and the first among the Sicyonians was Aegialeus, after whom Aegialea was named, the region that is still called the Peloponnese.

[Note: [Col. 1024C]

12. See Eusebius, Augustine, The City of God, book XXI, chapter 14, and Justin, at the beginning of his History. After the words “instruments of warfare,” one manuscript contained the following: “His wife Semiramis restored the walls of Babylon. Ninus also defeated Ham in war, who was still alive and reigning at Bactra; he was called Zoroaster, that is, the inventor of magical art. He also wrote the seven liberal arts on fourteen columns, seven of bronze and seven of brick.”

Ibid. Another reading: “begot Abraham, under whom Zoroaster, the inventor of magical art, was killed by King Ninus, and the walls of Babylon were built by Semiramis,” and so forth. AREV.]

### 12

[3184] Terah, at the age of seventy, begot Abraham. At this time Ninus, king of the Assyrians, reigned. He was the first to establish warfare and to invent weapons of war. In this age the art of magic was discovered in Persia by Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians. He was killed by King Ninus. The walls of Babylon were also built by Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians.

From the Flood to the birth of Abraham: 942 years.

The second age ends after 3,184 years.

## The Third Age

[Note: [Col. 1024D]

13. The peoples of Arabia were later called Saracens by Muhammad, the scourge of God. For, boastfully and falsely proclaiming himself a prophet of God, he stirred many peoples of Asia and Africa to defect from the Christian faith. Instructing them in a false religion, he claimed that they were called Saracens by God’s command, as legitimate heirs of the divine promise through Sarah, Abraham’s lawful wife. From this the kingdom of the Saracens took its beginning, under the emperor Heraclius.]

### 13

[3284] Abraham, at the age of one hundred, begot Isaac from Sarah, the free woman. For he had first begotten Ishmael from the slave woman Hagar; from Ishmael came the nation of the Ishmaelites, who were later called Hagarenes and finally Saracens.

[Note: [Col. 1024D]

14. Thus Esau is called the father of the Idumeans in Genesis 36 and in Eusebius’s Chronicle. Strabo, book VI, says that they were peoples situated between India and Arabia, near Mount Casius, and descended from the Nabataeans.

Ibid. “Inachus.” Eusebius writes in his Chronicle: “We shall next follow Castor the chronographer in what he says concerning the kingdom of the Argives: the kings of the Argives from Inachus to Sthenelus, son of Crotopus.” Correct this passage from an old manuscript as follows: “Castor speaks as follows concerning the kingdom of the Argives: we shall next follow the kings of the Argives from Inachus to Sthenelas,” and so forth. Pausanias also, in book II of his Corinthiaca, makes Sthenelas the son of Crotopus. Augustine says of him in The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 8: “Phoroneus was the sixth king of the Argives; Jasus, the son of Triopas, was the seventh king; and Sthenelas, or Stheneleus, or Sthenelus, was the ninth king,” for he is found under various forms in different authors. Thus Augustine.]

### 14

[3344] Isaac, at the age of sixty, begot twins. The first was Esau, from whom came the Idumeans; the second was Jacob, who was surnamed Israel, from whom the Israelites were also named. At this time the Greek kingdom began; its first king was Inachus.

[Note: [Col. 1025B]

15. Another manuscript reads: “Jacob was sixty years old,” but this is erroneous, as can be plainly inferred from a calculation based on the sacred writings. Joseph, when he was brought out of prison to interpret the dreams for Pharaoh the king of all Egypt, was thirty years old and was appointed ruler over all Egypt, Genesis 41. When he ordered his brothers to bring his father, he was thirty-nine years old: seven years had passed since the dream announcing the famine, and the second year of abundance was already nearly complete when Jacob came to Egypt, Genesis 45. Before Pharaoh Jacob replied that he was 130 years old, Genesis 47. If, therefore, we subtract thirty-nine years from 130, ninety-one years remain—the age Jacob had reached when he begot Joseph in his old age.

Ibid. “Serapis.” Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book I, writes: “Apis, king of the Argives, built Memphis, as Aristippus says in the first book of his Arcadica. Aristeas the Argive says that he was called Serapis and that he was the one whom the Egyptians worship. But Nymphodorus of Amphipolis, in the third book of his On the Laws of Asia, says that only after Apis had died and been placed in a coffin, called in Greek σορός, ‘tomb,’ and deposited in the temple of the deity who was worshiped there, was he called Sorapis, and later, through the custom of those who lived there, Sarapis. Apis was the third king after Inachus.” This passage is found word for word in Eusebius, book X of the Preparation for the Gospel. See Augustine, drawing on Varro, The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 5; Tacitus, book XX; and Julius Firmicus, in his learned little work On the Errors and Mysteries of Profane Religions.

In Loaisa’s note the reading was “the dream of the famine … the second year of abundance.” AREV.]

### 15

[3435] Jacob, at the age of ninety-one, begot Joseph. At this time Serapis, son of Jupiter and king of the Egyptians, died and was transferred among the gods, and the city of Memphis was founded in Egypt. At that time Minerva appeared in virgin form beside Lake Tritonis; she is said to have excelled in many arts. She is said to have invented the craft of making things; she discovered the shield and bow, and taught the weaving of cloth and the coloring of wool. In this age Phoroneus, son of King Inachus, also flourished; he was the first in Greece to establish laws and judicial proceedings.

[Note: [Col. 1025D]

16. Argus was the fourth king of the Argives, son of Apis. Eusebius’s Chronicle.

Ibid. “Of slavery.” Egyptian slavery is usually reckoned in three ways, according to three different starting points in time. The first begins with the memorable promise made to Abraham in Genesis 12: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I will show you.” From Abraham’s departure from Haran into the land of Canaan to the departure of the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s oppression and harsh slavery there were 430 years. Paul counts them in this way in Galatians 3: “The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed,” and shortly afterward: “This is what I mean: the law, which was made 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant confirmed beforehand by God.” Exodus 12 likewise says: “The dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years; and when the 430 years were completed, on that very day the whole army went out.” It should be observed, however, that after the words “during which they dwelt in Egypt,” the Greek manuscripts contain the additional words καὶ ἐν γῇ Χαναάν, “and in the land of Canaan.” Augustine noted this when examining the passage in his Questions on Exodus, understanding the entire pilgrimage, both in the land of Canaan and in Egypt, to have lasted 430 years. Cyril and Rupertus agree. The second reckoning begins when Jacob descended into Egypt with his sons; according to it, 215 years are counted. The third and final reckoning begins with Joseph’s death. After he had been removed, the true and laborious slavery began, in which the Hebrew nation was worn down by exactions, injuries, persecutions, and every kind of hardship, until by divine favor, under Moses as leader, it was restored to freedom. This lasted 144 years, as Eusebius counts in his Chronicle, as does Augustine in The City of God, book XVI, chapter 43, and in his Questions on Exodus.

Ibid. “Prometheus.” Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book I: “In the time of Piropas there were Prometheus, Atlas, and Epimetheus.” Eusebius says that it was believed that human beings were made by Prometheus because, being wise, he transformed their savagery and extreme ignorance into humanity and knowledge. Augustine says the same in The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 8.

Ibid. “Proclytus.” Other manuscripts have “Procellus,” “Trochilus,” and even “Arogilus.”

Ibid. “At this time Prometheus,” and so forth. See Raderus on Martial, p. 38. AREV.]

### 16

[3545] Joseph lived 110 years. From this time, when Argo was reigning, Greece began to have grain crops, seed having been brought from elsewhere.

[3689] The years of the Hebrews’ slavery in Egypt after Joseph’s death are found to number 144. At this time Prometheus is said to have lived; the myths represent him as having fashioned human beings from clay. Then his brother Atlas also discovered astrology and was the first to consider the movement of the heavens and its system. Mercury, Atlas’s grandson, also lived at this time and was skilled in many arts. For this reason he was transferred among the gods after his death. In this age, too, Proclytus was the first to yoke a chariot. At the same time Cecrops founded Athens and, after the name of Minerva, called the people of Attica Athenians. He also sacrificed an ox and was the first to command that Jupiter be worshiped in a pagan ritual. At this time Corinth was founded in Greece, and the art of painting was discovered there by Cleanthes. Then the Curetes and Corybantes were the first to invent rhythmic dancing in armor and harmonious music. At this time, too, a Flood is said to have occurred in Thessaly under Deucalion, as well as the fabulous conflagration of Phaethon.

[Col. 1026B] [Note: [Col. 1026D]

17. The first inventor of letters is said to have been Taautus, according to Eusebius, book I, chapter 7 of the Preparation for the Gospel. Yet in book X he proves that the invention and dissemination of letters originated with the Hebrews. Isidore says the same in book I, chapter 3 of the Etymologies; Jerome in his preface to the Books of Kings; and Theodoret, commenting on Genesis 5, on the words “And he walked with God, and was not found,” says of Enoch that he was the first to learn letters and the first to record the signs of heaven.

Ibid. Mellitus and other manuscripts read: “the temple at Delphi is built, Lacedaemon is believed,” and “the vine,” and so forth. AREV.]

### 17

[3729] Moses ruled for forty years in the wilderness the people liberated from Egyptian slavery. At this time the Jews, through Moses, began to possess letters together with the Law. At that time the temple at Delphi was established; the vine was discovered in Greece.

[Col. 1027A] 73 [Note: [Col. 1027B]

18. Virgil, Georgics 3:

“Erichthonius was the first to dare to yoke a chariot and four horses.”]

### 18

[3756] Joshua, Moses’ successor, ruled the people for twenty-seven years. In these times Erichthonius, first among the leaders of the Athenians, was the first in Greece to yoke a four-horse chariot.

[Note: [Col. 1027B]

19. “Othniel.” Concerning him, see Judges 3. Isidore omits the judgeship of Ehud either because he ruled the people for only a short time or because he was not a judge but merely a military leader, as in Judges 1. Josephus, Antiquities, book V, chapter 7, calls Othniel “Cenez.”

Ibid. “Cadmus.” Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book I: “Cadmus was a Phoenician who became the inventor of letters for the Greeks, as Ephorus says.” Hence Herodotus also writes that the letters were called Phoenician. Others, however, say that the Phoenicians and Syrians were the first to devise letters. Thus Clement.

Ibid. “Cinus.” Eusebius, year 3780: “Linus and Thebes”; and in a manuscript, “Linus the Theban.”

Ibid. Concerning the Idaean Dactyls, Eusebius says in his Chronicles: “The Idaean Dactyls lived at this time; they discovered iron.” Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book I, relates that the Idaean Dactyls were wise men, inventors of letters and of musical numbers: “For this reason,” he says, “those among musicians are called dactyls.” The Idaean Dactyls were Phrygians and barbarians. Shortly afterward he says: “Celmis and Damnameneus, Idaean Dactyls, first discovered iron in Cyprus. Another Idaean discovered the tempering of iron. The Idaean Dactyls were sons of Minerva and the Sun, or, as others hold, of Saturn and Alciope. They are also called Corybantes by another name.” See Stephanus, On Cities; the scholia on Apollonius; and the Suda, under the entry Ἰδαῖοι δάκτυλοι, “Idaean Dactyls.”]

### 19

[3796] Othniel, forty years. Cadmus reigned at Thebes; he was the first to invent the Greek letters. At the same time Linus and Amphion first became famous among the Greeks for their skill in music; and at that same time the Idaean Dactyls discovered iron metal in Greece.

[Note: [Col. 1027D]

20. Eusebius has it differently in his Chronicle: “Triptolemus, coming to Eleusis in a long ship, distributed grain there.” Augustine, The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 13, agrees with Isidore: “At this time myths were fabricated about Triptolemus, who, at Ceres’ command, carried grain through the air on winged serpents and distributed it to lands in need.”

Ibid. “His sister.” In one manuscript the following is added: “That they flew through the air mounted on a ram.”]

[3876] Ehud, eighty years. ### 43. 34 years

Eusebius gives 36 years. So do Herodotus, Nicephorus, and others. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, counts forty-six years, reckoning the periods of the Persian kings as follows: Cyrus reigned thirty years, Cambyses nineteen, Darius forty-six, Xerxes twenty-six, Artaxerxes forty-one, Darius eight, Artaxerxes forty-two, and Ochus or Arses three, making 235 years in all. Alexander of Macedon extinguished the Persian king Darius, and from that point the kingdom of the Macedonians arose. This is Clement’s account. I therefore think that there is an error in his figures, since he extends the Persian empire to 235 years, a total that does not agree with the years of the kings.

Observe also at this point that Eusebius lists other kings who are rejected by Clement, Isidore, and others because they reigned only a few months: Artabanus for seven months, Xerxes II for two months, and Sogdianus for eight months. For the same reason Otho, Galba, and Vitellius are omitted by many, as Plutarch noted in his *Life of Galba*. Concerning the Persian kings, see Herodotus, Thucydides, and Megasthenes. These writers do not place Cambyses’ reign before Darius’ reign; against them stand Plato, *Laws*, Clement, Josephus, Orosius, and Nicephorus in his *Chronology*. Their view agrees with the sacred writings, specifically 1 Esdras, chapter II. There are also differing and varied opinions in the reckoning of the years, as is clear from Tertullian’s work *Against the Jews*.

Same place. “In the second year.” So Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Josephus, book XI, chapters 2 and 3.]

### 51.

So Josephus, and Isidore himself in book V of the *Etymologies*. Tertullian gives ten years. Nicephorus, in the *Chronicle*, says that after Darius was removed Alexander reigned six years and had possessed power for twelve years before Darius’ death; he died in Babylon at the age of thirty-five, or, according to others, thirty-six. Thus, according to Anastasius’ opinion, he held the kingdom for eighteen years. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, says the same and lists the Macedonian kings as follows: Alexander reigned eighteen years; Ptolemy, son of Lagus, forty; Ptolemy Philadelphus twenty-seven; Euergetes twenty-five; Philopator seventeen; Epiphanes twenty-four; Philometor thirty-five; Physcon twenty-nine; Lathyrus thirty-six; Dionysius twenty-nine; Cleopatra twenty-two. After this came the kingdom of Cappadocia, lasting eighteen days. Thus the Macedonian period totals 312 years and eighteen days. This is Clement’s account. Tertullian, in his work *Against the Jews*, differs.]

Same place. I would like incidentally to correct the passage concerning Ennius, which is corrupt in Eusebius. It now reads: “The poet Ennius, more than seventy years old, died of joint disease and was buried in the monument of Scipio on the Appian Way, within the first mile from the City.” Some assert that his bones were transferred from the Janiculum to Rhodes. I substitute *Rudia* for *Rhodiam*, supported also by the testimony of a written manuscript and compelled by the truth of the matter: Ennius’ homeland was Rudiae, an ancient town of Apulia, as Mela testifies in book II. “After Bari,” he says, “come Egnatia and Rudiae, famous for Ennius; it is plausible that his bones were transferred there.”

[Col. 1036D] Same place. The tomb of the Scipios, in which Ennius’ likeness stood in marble, was located near the Porta San Sebastiano. On this, see Eschinardus in his description of Rome, Vasius, and others. AREV.]

### 62. [5148] Ptolemy Dionysius reigned 30 years

After capturing Jerusalem, Pompey made the Jews tributary to the Romans. At the same time Cato the philosopher became famous. Virgil was born at Mantua, Horace at Venusia. Apollodorus, the teacher of Augustus, was also held in high honor, and Cicero was celebrated for his oratorical distinction.

[Note: [Col. 1037B]

63. Eusebius gives twenty-two years, as do Plutarch in *Antony*, Nicephorus, and others. Epiphanius gives thirty-two [Col. 1037C]; Isidore gives only two. For Julius Caesar, in the third year of Cleopatra’s reign, alone after Pompey had been killed by the eunuchs of the Alexandrian king, obtained whatever was subject to Roman power. From that point the Alexandrian kingdom passed into Roman control, as he himself states below. The same reading is found in the Tudense, in a manuscript codex; and therefore it seemed best to retain this number of years, which the manuscript codices of the *Etymologies* also contain. This is also required by the passage concerning Tiberius, where it is said that Christ suffered after 5,229 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world; Eusebius himself differs from this calculation by only two years. Concerning Cleopatra, Xiphilinus says approximately the following, drawing from Dio, in his account of Julius Caesar: “Cleopatra,” he says, “was extraordinarily beautiful, and at that time in the flower of her age; she surpassed everyone in eloquence, and was agreeable to all with whom she associated.” A little later, speaking of Caesar, he says: “He reduced Egypt to his own power and authority, and handed it over to Cleopatra, on whose account he had waged war.”

In the same place. “Mellitus: Cleopatra, two years. In her third year Julius Caesar assumed power. At the same time a Sicilian writer of Greek history was regarded as celebrated. ‘Gaius Julius Caesar reigns,’ etc.” AREV.]

63. [5150] Cleopatra reigns for two years. She was the daughter of Ptolemy, king of the Egyptians, and became the sister and wife of her brother Ptolemy. When she wished to deprive him of his kingdom during the civil war, she met Caesar at Alexandria while he was besieging the city; and through her beauty and sexual relationship she secured from Julius both the kingdom for herself and Ptolemy’s death. Thus, in the third year of Cleopatra’s reign, the kingdom of Alexandria passed through Julius Caesar into Roman control.

[Note: [Col. 1037D]

64. “He previously … were called”; others read: “He was the first of the Romans to obtain sole rule, from whom the Caesars were also named. From this point the emperors follow.” AREV.]

64. [5155] Gaius Julius Caesar reigns for five years. Previously created consul, he obtained Gaul; he celebrated a triumph over Britain; and finally, after engaging in civil war against Pompey, he obtained the monarchy of the entire empire. From his name the emperors who followed were called Caesars.

65. From the Babylonian captivity to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ: 587 years.

The fifth age ends after 5,155 years.

The sixth age of the world.

[Note: [Col. 1037D]

66. Suetonius says in his *Augustus* that the name “Augustus” was taken from the fact that sacred places, and places in which something is consecrated through augury, are called *augusta*, from an act of consecration or from the movement or taste of birds. Dio likewise says in his account of the monarchy that Augustus was so called as one who surpassed human nature, because things that are sacred and held in the highest honor are called *augusta*. For this reason, he says, the Greeks called him σεβαστός (*sebastos*), that is, one most worthy of worship and honor. The designation of this name, like that of “emperor,” was extended to the others who succeeded him because of their supreme and extensive power [Col. 1038B].

In the same place. “Years: 56.” Thus Eusebius, Victor, and others. Nicephorus and Cassiodorus add six months. Clement, *Stromata* I: forty-six years, four months, one day. Dio says: “He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, on which day he had first become consul; he lived seventy-five years, ten months, and twenty-six days. For he had been born on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. After gaining victory at Actium, he reigned forty-four years, excepting thirteen days.” But Eusebius and Isidore [Col. 1038C] reckon his rule from the death of Julius Caesar.

In the same place. “Seventy weeks.” Others read, “seventy-nine.” See Daniel, chapter 9.

In the same place. This is the famous passage of Daniel 9, which Tertullian interprets very differently from the other chroniclers. For he says as follows:

“We must reckon from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision. Let us therefore see how the years are fulfilled up to the coming of Christ. For Darius reigned nineteen years. Artaxerxes reigned forty years. Then King Ochus, who was also called Cyrus, reigned twenty-four years. Argus, one year. Another Darius, who was also called Melas, twenty-two years. Alexander the Macedonian, twelve years. Then, after Alexander—who had ruled over both the Medes and the Persians, whom he had reconquered, and had established his kingdom in Alexandria, which he also named after himself—Soter reigned there in Alexandria for thirty-five years. After him Philadelphus reigned thirty-eight years. He was succeeded by Euergetes, who reigned twenty-five years. Then Philopator, seventeen years. After him Epiphanes, twenty-four years. Then another Euergetes, twenty-nine years. Soter, thirty-eight years [Col. 1038D]. Ptolemy, thirty-eight years. Cleopatra, twenty years and six months. Another Cleopatra also reigned jointly under Augustus for thirteen years. After Cleopatra, Augustus reigned another forty-three years. For all the years of Augustus’s rule amounted to fifty-six years.

“We see, then, that in the forty-first year of Augustus’s reign—the year in which he ruled after Cleopatra’s death—Christ was born. Augustus survived from the time of Christ’s birth for fifteen years. The remaining periods of years up to the day of Christ’s birth, and up to the forty-first year of Augustus after Cleopatra’s death, amount to 437 years and six months. Thus the sixty-two and a half weeks are fulfilled, amounting to 437 years and six months, up to the day of Christ’s birth. Then eternal righteousness was brought to light, and the Holy of Holies was anointed—that is, Christ—and the vision and the prophecy were sealed, and sins were forgiven, sins which through faith in the name of Christ are forgiven to all who believe in him.

“And further on: ‘Thus, having shown both the number of years and the time of the fulfillment of the sixty-two and a half weeks, and having shown that Christ then came—that is, was born—let us see in what action the other seven and a half weeks, which are divided off by the cutting away of the preceding weeks, were fulfilled. For after Augustus, who survived fifteen years after Christ’s birth, Tiberius Caesar succeeded him and held power for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days. In the fifteenth year of his reign Christ suffered, being about thirty years old when he suffered.

“‘Then came Gaius Caesar, also called Caligula, for three years, eight months, and thirteen days; Nero Caesar, nine years, nine months, and thirteen days; Galba, seven months and six days; Otho, three months and five days; Vitellius, eight months and ten days. In the first year of his reign Vespasian subdued the Jews, making forty-two years and six months. For he reigned nine years; and thus, up to the day of their conquest, the Jews completed the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.

“‘Accordingly, when these periods too had been completed and the Jews had been subdued, the offerings and sacrifices there ceased, since from then onward they could not be celebrated there. For the anointing was also abolished there after Christ’s passion. It had indeed been foretold that the anointing would be abolished there, as it is in the Psalms of the prophets: “They have abolished my hands and feet.” This passion, by which the anointing was abolished, was completed within the period of the seventy weeks under Tiberius Caesar, when Rubellius Geminus and Rufius Geminus were consuls, in the month of March, at the time of Passover, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the first day of Unleavened Bread, on which Moses had commanded that they should kill the lamb in the evening. Thus the entire synagogue of the children of Israel killed him, saying to Pilate, when he wished to release him: “His blood be upon us and upon our children”; and, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend”—so that everything written about him might be fulfilled.’”

This is Tertullian’s account. Clement of Alexandria, however, in *Stromata* I, believes that our Lord was born in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus, when Augustus first ordered a census and registration; and he counts Daniel’s weeks approximately as Tertullian does, also placing Christ’s suffering in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, when Christ was thirty years old, although there is a difference between them in their calculation of the years. Eusebius disagrees with both and believes that Daniel’s prophecy was fulfilled in the tenth year of Augustus’s reign, with Hyrcanus, the last Jewish priest, and that the weeks amount to 483 years. Thus there is nothing consistent or certain in the reckoning of the years. On this subject see also Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 34; Cedrenus, in the *Compendium*; and among our modern writers, Fino, Galatinus, and the Spanish Burgensis in his very learned *Scrutiny of the Scriptures*.

In the same place. Fabricius, p. 262 of *Bibliographia antiqua*, reports that Sigebertus and, on the authority of Ricciolius, Philo the Jew agree with Isidore concerning the year in which Christ was born, and he lists countless other mutually divergent opinions. AREV.]

66. [5211] Octavius Augustus reigns for fifty-six years. After the Sicilian war, during his reign, he celebrated three triumphs [Col. 1038B]: the Dalmatian, the Asiatic, and finally the Alexandrian against Antony, followed by the Spanish. Then, after peace had been established throughout the world by land and sea, he closed the gates of Janus. Under his rule the seventy weeks written of in Daniel were completed; and, when the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews had ceased, the Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judah from a virgin, in the forty-second year of Augustus’s reign.

[Col. 1039A] 67. [Note: [Col. 1039D]

67. “Son.” Understand this as referring to adoption. For he was the son of Livia, Augustus’s wife [Col. 1040A], and of Gaius Drusus Nero.

[Col. 1040B] In the same place. “Twenty-two years.” Thus Eusebius; or twenty-one, he says, as some report. Nicephorus, Orosius, Victor, Cedrenus, and Tertullian, in *Against the Jews*, assign him only twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days. Dio of Nicaea gives twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty days. So also Zonaras, except that he gives seven days.

In the same place. “Kings,” etc. Eusebius says concerning this in the *Chronicle*: “Tiberius never sent back the many kings whom he had enticed to come to him by flattering promises; among them was Archelaus the Cappadocian, whose kingdom having been converted into a province, he ordered its most famous city Mazaca to be called Caesarea.” But read from the manuscripts: “With his kingdom having been converted into a province,” etc. Tacitus and Dio write about this in their accounts of Tiberius.

In the same place. “In his tenth year.” Concerning the day and year of Christ’s death, there are various opinions among the saints in Tertullian’s *Against the Jews*, Clement, Eusebius, and the other ancient Fathers. Onuphrius Panvinius, an Augustinian, collected all of them together in an elegant published commentary, book II of his *Commentary on the Fasti*.

In the same place. “Twenty-nine”; others read “twenty-eight.” AREV.]

67. [5234] Tiberius, the son of Augustus, reigns for twenty-two years. Because, through greed, he did not send back the kings who came to him, many peoples withdrew from the Roman Empire. In the eighteenth year of his reign the Lord was crucified, after 5,229 years had elapsed from the beginning of the world.

[Note: [Col. 1040B]

68. Dio writes that Caligula’s cognomen was given to him because, having been raised for the most part in the army, he used military boots instead of civilian footwear. Dio also testifies, in his account of Augustus, that Augustus Caesar was mockingly called “Caliga” by the soldiers because of his use of military boots.

In the same place. “Four years.” Eusebius, Clement, Nicephorus, and Cassiodorus give three years and ten months. Josephus, book II of the *Jewish War*, chapter 10, gives three years and six months. Elsewhere, book XIX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 2, he says: “He died in the fourth year of his reign, four months short of it.” Tertullian, in *Against the Jews*, gives three years, eight months, and thirteen days.

In the same place. It is commonly asked whether Matthew wrote in Greek or in Hebrew. Jerome says in his *Catalogue*: “His Hebrew Gospel is still preserved today in the Caesarean Library.” The same is stated in book III *Against the Pelagians*. Likewise Eusebius, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18, and book IV, the final chapter. Gregory of Nazianzus, Irenaeus, and Nicephorus, book II, chapter 45, also testify that he wrote his Gospel in his native language.]

68. [5238] Gaius Caligula reigns for four years. He was savage in avarice, cruelty, and luxury; and, exalting himself among the gods, he ordered a statue of Jupiter Olympius to be placed in the temple of Jerusalem under his own name. At this time the apostle Matthew was the first to write a Gospel in Judaea.

[Note: [Col. 1040C]

69. “Years: fourteen.” Nicephorus acknowledges only thirteen years and one month [Col. 1040D]. Epiphanius gives the same number of years and two months. Josephus, book XX, chapter 10 of the *Antiquities*, writes that he ruled thirteen years, eight months, and twenty days, as do Dio and Zonaras. Suetonius simply says that he died in the fourteenth year of his reign. Eusebius and Cassiodorus reckon thirteen years, nine months, and twenty-eight days. Tertullian gives thirteen years, seven months, and twenty days.

In the same place. “Marcus,” etc. Eusebius, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 5 and 16. Nicephorus, book II, chapters 15 and 16.]

69. [5252] Claudius reigns for fourteen years. During his reign [Col. 1040A], the apostle Peter went to Rome against Simon Magus. The evangelist Mark also wrote a Gospel at Alexandria while preaching Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1040D]

70. “Fourteen years.” Thus Eutropius, Suetonius, the Greek Chronicle, Ado, and others. Eusebius gives fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. Epiphanius gives thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days. Nicephorus gives thirteen years and one month. Dio of Nicaea says that he lived thirty years and reigned thirteen years, eight months, less two days. Paul Orosius, book VII, says: “Having obtained the principate, he remained in it for fourteen incomplete years.” Against the opinion of all the others, Tertullian gives only eleven years, nine months, and thirteen days; Cassiodorus gives thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days.

In the same place. “Mother.” Dio, in his biography of him, believes that he did not have intercourse with his mother Agrippina, but with another woman resembling her; referring to her, he used to say that he had intercourse with his mother. Dio and Suetonius give a detailed account of his mother’s death.

In the same place. “Sister … Simon Magus.” Thus Nicephorus, book II, chapter 36; and Chrysostom, book I *Against the Detractors of the Monastic Life*. Linus of Tuscany wrote an account of Peter’s deeds with Simon Magus.

In the same place. “Seneca.” Dio, in his account of Nero, describes Seneca’s character and death as follows—I do not know whether accurately—and says that both were especially unbecoming to a philosophical man: “Although,” he says, “he disapproved of tyranny, he was the tyrant’s teacher; although he mocked those who associated with rulers, he himself never left the palace. He detested flatterers, while himself honoring queens and freedmen. He criticized the rich, although his own fortune amounted to 30,000,000 gold pieces. And although he condemned the luxury of others, he possessed five hundred tripods made of cedarwood, with ivory feet, all alike and matching, on which he dined. Finally, he died in a manner unworthy of a philosopher, with a dejected and feeble spirit.”]

70. [5266] Nero reigns for fourteen years. Devoted to injustice, cruelty, and luxury, he fished with golden nets. He prostituted and murdered his mother and sister; he destroyed a great number of senators; he lost many provinces and cities of the state; and he also burned the city of Rome so that he might watch an image of the destruction of Troy. During his reign, Simon Magus, after proposing a contest with the apostles Peter and Paul and saying that he was some great power of God, promised at midday to fly through the air to heaven. He was carried through the air by demons; but when Peter adjured them by God and Paul prayed, they released him, and he fell with a crash. Because of his death, Nero crucified Peter and struck Paul with the sword. At this time the poet Persius died. Lucan and Seneca were also killed at Nero’s command.

[Note: [Col. 1041C]

71. Before Vespasian, Galba, Otho, and Vitellius ruled for one year and nine months, according to Eusebius; perhaps for this reason they are omitted by Isidore and Orosius, because Plutarch, in his account of Galba, writes that these men were emperors not so much of the Roman Empire as of some kind of comedy. According to Dio, Galba ruled nine months and thirteen days; Otho, ninety days; Vitellius, one year less ten days. According to Clement, however, Galba ruled seven months and six days; Otho, five months and one day; Vitellius, seven months and one day.

In the same place. “Years: ten.” Eusebius, Nicephorus, the Greek Chronicle [Col. 1041D], and Cassiodorus give nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. Epiphanius gives nine years, seven months, and twelve days. Dio gives ten years less six days; so also Zonaras. Orosius writes that he died from dysentery in the ninth year of his principate. Tertullian says that he reigned eleven years. Cedrenus gives ten years and eight days.

In the same place. “Eleven times,” etc. Thus Eusebius: “After Judaea had been captured and Jerusalem overthrown, Titus killed six hundred thousand men”; Josephus, however, writes that 1,100,000 died from hunger and the sword, and another 100,000 captives were publicly sold. This is Eusebius’s account.

In the same place. After Nero and before Vespasian, some manuscripts insert: “After Nero, Galba reigned four months. He was killed in the Forum. In Rome Otho reigned 205 days. He lived thirty-seven years. He killed himself in Italy at Ebraicum [sic]. Vitellius reigned eight months. He lived fifty-seven years. He was killed by Vespasian’s commanders.” AREV.]

71. [5276] Vespasian reigns for ten years. Skilled in military discipline [Col. 1041D], he restored to the state through warfare many provinces that Nero had lost. He was forgetful of offenses and bore insults directed against him lightly. In his second year Titus captured and destroyed Jerusalem, where 1,100,000 Jews perished from hunger and the sword. In addition to these, another 100,000 were publicly sold.

[Note: [Col. 1041D]

72. “Two years.” According to Suetonius and Dio, he reigned two years, two months, and twenty days. Eusebius gives two years and eight months [Col. 1042B]. Eutropius gives two years, eight months, and twenty days. Nicephorus, Cassiodorus, Bede, and others give two years and two months. Epiphanius, together with Isidore and Orosius in book VII, gives two years, two months, and two days. Zonaras gives two years less six days. Cedrenus gives three years.

In the same place. “Twelve.” Dio, in his biography of Titus, says: “Titus not only ordered no senator to be killed for as long as he held the principate, but under his rule no one at all was put to death. He never investigated a charge of impiety and did not allow others to investigate one. For, he said, no one can wrong or pursue me with insult, because I do nothing deserving of blame. Whatever is falsely said about me I completely disregard.”

In the same place. “To have lost a day.” Suetonius says that he uttered a memorable and deservedly praised expression: “Friends, I have lost a day.”

In the text of Grialius, after the words “twelve defenders,” there was an indication of a note, which perhaps has been lost. Mellitus reads: “that he had lost the day on which he had done nothing beneficial to anyone.” Others add: “He lived forty years. To the great grief of all, he was consumed by illness in the same villa as his father.” Thus some interpolated codices give the years of each emperor’s life and the place where he died; but it can be inferred from the ancient copies that these details do not belong to Isidore. AREV.]

72. [5278] Titus reigns for eleven years.
