He was so eloquent in both languages that he pleaded cases in Latin and composed poems and tragedies in Greek; and he was so outstanding in warfare that, while serving under his father during the siege of Jerusalem, he pierced twelve defenders with twelve arrow-shots. In his rule he was of such great goodness that he punished no one at all, but released those convicted of conspiring against him and retained them in the same intimacy in which he had formerly held them. Among his other sayings, this celebrated one is also attributed to him: “I have lost the day on which I did nothing good.”

90 [Note: [Col. 1042C]

73. “Sixteen years.” Eusebius gives fifteen years and five months. So also Epiphanius, Cassiodorus, and Nicephorus. Suetonius simply asserts that he died in the fifteenth year of his reign, as does Orosius. Dio of Nicaea says: “He reigned fifteen years and five days.” Zonaras gives fifteen years and ten months.

[Col. 1042D] In the same place. “God.” Eusebius: “Domitian was the first to order that he be called Lord and God.” Dio says the same. Suetonius writes: “With equal arrogance, when dictating a formal letter in the name of his procurators, he began it as follows: ‘Our Lord and God commands as follows.’ From that point it was established that no one should address him otherwise, even in writing or speech.”

In the same place. “Christians.” This was the second persecution of the Church; the first was under Nero. Concerning it, see Eusebius, book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, chapter 52; Paul Orosius, book VII; and the monk Alexander’s little work *εἰς εὕρεσιν τοῦ σωοποιοῦ σταυροῦ* (“On the Discovery of the Life-giving Cross”), which is in my library and has not yet been published.]

73. [5294] Domitian, the brother of Titus, reigns for sixteen years. The second after Nero, and accursed for his pride, he ordered himself to be called God and instituted the persecution of Christians by the pagans. Under him the apostle John was banished to the island of Patmos, where he wrote the *Apocalypse*. He sent many senators into exile and put them to death; he also ordered all who were descended from David to be killed, so that no one of royal descent would remain among the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 1042D]

74. “One year.” Eusebius gives one year and four months. So also Nicephorus, Cassiodorus, Epiphanius, Clement, and Zonaras. Dio, Eutropius, Bede, Ado, and others add nine days.

In the same place. Others give one year and four months. In his first edict he recalled all the exiles. Hence the evangelist John returned from exile, etc. AREV.]

74. [5295] Nerva reigns for one year. A man moderate in his rule [Col. 1042B], he showed himself equal and accessible to everyone. In his time the apostle John returned from exile to Ephesus and, urged by the bishops of Asia, published the Gospel as the last of the evangelists.

[Note: [Col. 1042D]

75. Trajan. Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, elegantly depicts his character [Col. 1043B]: “He forbade golden or silver statues of himself to be made, and restored all goods still found in the palace to those from whom Domitian had unjustly taken them. To Roman citizens who were in extreme poverty he gave land worth 600,000 gold pieces; certain men of senatorial rank were ordered to purchase and distribute that land. When he lacked money, he sold a great quantity of clothing, many silver and gold vessels, and the rest of his furnishings—not only his private possessions but also imperial property—as well as many estates and houses—in short, everything except what was necessary. He was not miserly in setting prices for these things; rather, in this very matter he was generous and liberal toward many.” This is Dio’s account; he adds other details that demonstrate the extraordinary moderation of this man [Col. 1043C].

In the same place. “Nineteen years.” Thus Epiphanius, the Greek Chronicle, Orosius, and others. Eusebius gives nineteen years and six months, as do Nicephorus and Zonaras. Clement gives nineteen years, seven months, and fifteen days. Dio, Eutropius, Bede, Cedrenus, and Ado give nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days, as does Cassiodorus.

In the same place. “Babylonia.” Another manuscript read: “He captured Asia, Babylonia, and Arabia.” Eusebius says: “After defeating King Decebalus, Trajan made Dacia a province. He received the Iberians, Sarmatians, Osroenians [read: Adiabenes], Arabs, Bosporans, and Colchians into submission; he occupied Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Babylon.” The correction from “Osroenians” to “Adiabenes” is supported by Dio in Xiphilinus, who says that Trajan brought all Adiabene, the part of Assyria extending to Nineveh, under his power. According to Xiphilinus, Trajan was made Caesar and emperor by Nerva, although Nerva had no shortage of close relatives. For Nerva did not put blood relationship before the public good; nor was he deterred by the fact that Trajan was a Spaniard, not an Italian or of Italian origin, and that before him no one of another nation had held the Roman imperial power. Among the ancients, besides others, the following wrote about Trajan: Dio, Sextus Aurelius, Eutropius, Sextus Rufus, Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, Pliny in the *Panegyricus* and book I of the *Letters*.

In the same place. “I established.” “After he came to Rome,” Dio says, “he did much to improve and correct the condition of the state, and to please the good, for whom he took special care; he gave much to the cities of Italy for the education of children, toward whom he showed great generosity.” Shortly afterward he says: “Trajan envied no one and destroyed no one. He honored all good men with offices and increased their dignities; consequently he neither feared nor hated anyone. He placed no trust in accusers, was controlled by no anger, and abstained from another’s money no less than from unjust killings. He incurred great expense and, in times of war and peace, built many things, all of them especially necessary.” Read more in the same author concerning the character and life of this man.]

75. [5314] Trajan reigns for nineteen years. With extraordinary courage [Col. 1043A], he extended the Roman Empire far and wide, as far as the East. He captured Babylonia and Arabia, and, after Alexander, advanced as far as the borders of India; he was generous to all and peaceable. Among his other sayings, this outstanding one is reported: when asked why he was excessively accessible to everyone, he replied that he was such an emperor to private citizens as, while a private citizen, he would have wished an emperor to be toward him. Simon Cleophas, bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified during his reign, and the apostle John died.

[Note: [Col. 1044B]

76. Spartianus writes of him as follows: “The emperor Hadrian’s earlier origin was from the Piceni, and his later origin from the Spaniards. Hadrian himself records in his books of his life that his ancestors, having originated at Hadria, settled at Italica in the time of the Scipios. Hadrian’s father was Aelius Hadrianus, surnamed Afer, a cousin of the emperor Trajan; his mother, Domitia Paulina, was born at Gades.” Dio says that Hadrian was a fellow townsman of Trajan.

In the same place. “Twenty-one years.” Thus Eusebius, Orosius, Nicephorus, and others. Dio and Zonaras give twenty years and nine months. Eutropius gives twenty-one years, ten months, and twenty days; Cassiodorus agrees, except that he omits the days. The little book *On the Lives of the Emperors* gives twenty-one years and two months, as does Spartianus. Cedrenus gives twenty-four years [Col. 1044C].

In the same place. Dio says: “He called it Aelia Capitolina and established a colony there; and where the temple of God had been, he arranged for another temple to Jupiter to be built, to the great distress of the Jews, because foreign peoples were living in their city and foreign rites were being performed there.”

In the same place. Concerning Basilides the heretic, see Eusebius, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7; Irenaeus, book I, chapter 27; Augustine, *On Heresies*; and Nicephorus in various places.]

76. [5335] Hadrian reigns for twenty-one years. Envious of Trajan’s glory, he restored the eastern provinces to the Persians and made the Euphrates River the boundary of the Roman Empire. He also subdued the Jews, who had rebelled for the second time, and restored the city of Jerusalem [Col. 1043B], calling it Aelia after his own name. At this time Aquila of Pontus, the second translator after the Septuagint, arose; and Basilides was recognized as a heresiarch.

[Note: [Col. 1044C]

77. “Twenty-two years.” Thus Epiphanius. Eusebius gives twenty-three years and three months; Orosius and, following him, Ado of Vienne report that he ruled twenty years and less than three additional years; Eutropius acknowledges twenty-three full years, as does the Greek Chronicle. Nicephorus gives only twenty-two years and three months. The recently published *Book of the Lives of the Emperors*, issued at Antwerp under the name of Aurelius Victor, acknowledges only twenty years; by contrast, Xiphilinus, drawing from Dio, gives twenty-four, and Cedrenus agrees with him.

In the same place. It may be necessary to read this on the authority of Eusebius and Paul Orosius, book VII, chapter 9: “Valentinus, and Cerdo, the teacher of Marcion.” Nevertheless, it is clear from the same Eusebius, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10, that Marcion and Cerdon disseminated their perverse doctrines at Rome at the same time.]

77. [5357] Antoninus Pius reigns for twenty-two years [Col. 1044A]. He received this surname because of his clemency: throughout the Roman realm, after the bonds had been burned, he released everyone’s debts; hence he was also called “father of his country.” He was the first to divide the rule of the Roman world with Antoninus the Younger, with their powers made equal. During his reign, the heresiarchs Valentinus and Marcion came to prominence, and Galen, the physician born at Pergamum, became famous at Rome.

[Note: [Col. 1044D]

78. Antoninus. He was surnamed “the Philosopher” and was a good man, as Dio says, since there was nothing artificial or pretended in him. Orosius assigns him only fourteen years of rule. Eusebius, Bede, and Ado give nineteen years and one month. Nicephorus gives nineteen years and two months. Zonaras gives nineteen years and two days. Cedrenus omits the days.

In the same place. “Of the Encratites.” On this heresy see Eusebius, book IV, chapter 27 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and Irenaeus, book I *Against Heresies*, chapter 9. They are called Encratites, as if “the self-controlled”; later they were called Severians, after Severus, the successor of Tatianus. Concerning them see also Nicephorus, book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 4 and 11.]

78. [5375] Antoninus the Younger reigns for eighteen years. He went to the Parthians, captured Seleucia, a city of Assyria, with 400,000 people, and triumphed over the Parthians and Persians. During his reign Montanus, founder of the Cataphrygians, and Tatian arose; from Tatian came the heresy of the Encratites.

[Col. 1044B] [Note: [Col. 1044D]

79. “Thirteen years.” Thus Eusebius, Orosius, Herodian, Bede, Nicephorus, and others; Eutropius, however, gives twelve years and eight months. Dio gives twelve years, nine months, and fourteen days, as do Clement and Zonaras. Cedrenus omits the fourteen days.]

79. [5388] Commodus reigns for thirteen years. He was greatly devoted to luxury. During his reign Theodotion of Ephesus, the third translator, appeared; and Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, was regarded as eminent for his learning.

[Col. 1045A] [Note: [Col. 1045B]

80. “One year.” Eusebius, Epiphanius, Nicephorus, and others give only six months; Eutropius gives eighty-one days. Dio gives fifty-seven days, as do Zonaras and Cedrenus.

In the same place. “He, when the senate entreated,” etc. Thus Eusebius; but Capitolinus gives a different account: “Pertinax,” he says, “neither accepted the title of Augusta for his wife, and concerning his son said: ‘When he has deserved it.’”]

80. [5389] Aelius Pertinax reigns for one year. When the senate entreated him to make his wife Augusta and his son Caesar [Col. 1045B], he refused, saying that it ought to be enough for him that he himself ruled unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 1045B]

81. Before Severus, Didius Salvius Julianus ought to be placed after Pertinax. According to Dio, he ruled sixty-six days; according to Eutropius and Orosius, seven months.

In the same place. “Eighteen years.” Thus Eusebius, Epiphanius, Nicephorus, and almost all the others. Eutropius gives eighteen years and ten months. Dio gives seventeen years and three days. Zonaras, in his account of Dio, reads sixteen years, while otherwise agreeing with him in the days and months. Cedrenus gives seventeen years and eight months.

In the same place. “Britain.” In the time of Titus, Gnaeus Julius Agricola was the first of the Romans to learn that Britain was surrounded on every side by the sea. Dio, in his account of Titus.

In the same place. Concerning Symmachus, see Eusebius, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13, where Narcissus and Origen are mentioned prominently.]

81. [5407] Severus Pertinax reigns for eighteen years. He waged many wars successfully: he defeated the Parthians, obtained Arabia, recovered Britain through warfare, and possessed knowledge of literature and philosophy. During his reign Symmachus, the fourth translator, was recognized; Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, was celebrated for many virtues; Tertullian the African was regarded as illustrious in the Church; and Origen was educated through his studies at Alexandria.

[Note: [Col. 1045C]

82. Antoninus was called Caracalla, as Dio writes, because he invented a distinctive type of garment shaped like a *paenula*. It was a barbarian garment, cut apart and sewn together from many pieces, and he always wore it; hence he was surnamed Caracalla. He also ordered the soldiers to wear garments of the same kind. See Eutropius and others. According to Eusebius, Dio, and others, his stepmother was named Julia.

In the same place. “Seven years.” Thus Epiphanius, Nicephorus, and others. Spartianus and Cedrenus give six years, as does Eusebius; Orosius says that he remained in power for less than seven years. Dio gives six years, two months, and a few days.]

82. [5414] Antoninus Caracalla, the son of Severus, reigns for seven years. He was incapable of controlling his lust and married his stepmother. He accomplished nothing memorable. During his reign the fifth edition of the divine Scriptures was discovered at Jericho [Col. 1045B], though its author is unknown.

[Note: [Col. 1045D]

83. “One year.” Thus Eusebius, Nicephorus, Orosius, and others. Dio and Zonaras give one year, two months, less three days; Eutropius gives one year and two months; Cedrenus, most inaccurately, gives eight years.

In the same place. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*: “Macrinus was killed at Archelais”; Herodian says, “at Chalcedon, a city of Bithynia.” Dio, however, gives the following account of his death: “He sailed to Chalcedon and remained there. Soldiers sent by Pseudo-Antoninus came there, seized him, and led him away to Cappadocia. When he learned that his son had been captured, he threw himself from the vehicle—for he was not bound—and broke his shoulder; not long afterward he was killed.”

In the same place. Mellitus: “He reigned one year. The amphitheater at Rome burned. Abgarus, a holy man, reigned at Edessa.” The Pseudo-Antoninus mentioned by Dio is Aurelius Antoninus Heliogabalus, discussed in the following entry. AREV.]

83. [5415] Macrinus reigns for one year. He and his son, ruling together, accomplished nothing memorable because of the brevity of their time in power. After one year they were both killed in a military revolt.

94 [Note: [Col. 1045D]

84. “Six years.” Thus Eusebius, Nicephorus, Orosius, and others. Eutropius gives two years and eight months. Dio gives three years, nine months, and four days [Col. 1046B]. Herodian gives six years. Zonaras and Cedrenus give three years, nine months, and four days.

In the same place. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*: “Antoninus was killed at Rome in a military disturbance together with his mother Semasyra.” Lampridius has “Semiamira”; Herodian, “Soenida”; Eutropius, “Semea.”]

84. [5419] Aurelius Antoninus reigns for four years [Col. 1046A]. While living in the most obscene manner, he himself was also killed in a military disturbance. During his reign the sixth edition was discovered at Nicopolis; and Sabellius the heresiarch arose.

[Note: [Col. 1046B]

85. “Thirteen years.” Thus almost all the authorities; Herodian alone gives fourteen years. Eutropius gives thirteen years and eight days; Cedrenus, thirteen years and eight months; Zonaras gives only ten years.

In the same place. Eusebius in the *Alexandrian Chronicle*: “He gloriously defeated Xerxes, king of the Persians.” Here, on the basis of Lampridius and Herodian, Artaxerxes appears to be the reading, as also in Orosius and Cassiodorus.

[Col. 1046C] In the same place. Grialius: “of this period.” AREV.]

85. [5432] Alexander reigns for thirteen years. He defeated the Persians with great glory and was favorable toward the citizens. In his time Origen flourished at Alexandria, and at Rome Ulpian was a distinguished jurist.

[Note: [Col. 1046C]

86. Three years. So Eusebius, Nicephorus, the Greek Chronicle, and others. Eutropius gives three years and a few days. Zonaras and Cedrenus, somehow, give six years.

Ibid. In another copy it read “with a military cohort”; but I judged that it should read “from the military body,” on the authority of Eusebius: for he says, “the first from the military body,” as do certain other manuscripts.

Ibid. “He persecutes.” Besides others, Aymo writes about this persecution in book VI, chapter 7, and Alexander the Monk, *On the Discovery of the Cross*.]

86. [5435] Maximinus reigns for three years. He was the first to be made emperor from the military body, without a decree of the Senate, and he persecutes the Christians.

[Note: [Col. 1046C]

87. Six years. So Eusebius, Nicephorus, Paulus, the interpolator of Eutropius, Orosius, and practically all the others.

Ibid. “Zephyrinus.” In another manuscript it is “Flavianus,” but I read this as having happened to Zephyrinus, according to Eusebius, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21, and Nicephorus, book V, chapter 26. Aymo likewise reports that it happened to Fabianus, in book VI, chapter 10. In the manuscript, too, where “Flavianus” is read after the word “is ordained,” the following is added: “Although some affirm that this is more correctly said of Zephyrinus.”

Ibid. Many manuscripts report it as follows: “In his time Flavianus”—which should be read as Fabianus—“is ordained on the testimony ... although some affirm that this is more correctly said of Zephyrinus.” “Mellitus” is corrupt, reading “Severinus” instead of Zephyrinus. Loaisa asserts that this is reported of Zephyrinus by Eusebius; others, on the contrary, read “Fabianus” instead of Zephyrinus in Eusebius, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22, or 29. See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, third century, chapter 2, and Pagius, *Lives of the Pontiffs*. AREV.]

87. [5441] Gordian reigns for six years. He afflicted the rebelling Parthians and Persians. Returning victorious from Persia, he perished through the treachery of his own men. In his time Zephyrinus was ordained bishop of Rome, on the testimony of the Holy Spirit descending in the form of a dove upon his head.

[Col. 1046B] [Note: [Col. 1046D]

88. Seven years. So Eusebius, Nicephorus, Orosius, Cedrenus, and almost all the others. Zonaras says that some report that he ruled for five years, others for six years and the same number of months.]

88. [5448] Philip reigns for seven years. He was the first among the emperors to believe in Christ. It is also taught that in his first year the thousandth year of the city of Rome was completed.

[Note: [Col. 1046D]

89. One year. So the Greek manuscript Chronicle. Eusebius, however, Nicephorus, Ado, and others assign him one year and three months. Eutropius reports that he ruled together with his son for two years, Orosius for three years, and Cassiodorus for two years and four months.

Ibid. “Mellitus, having arisen.” “The amphitheater at Rome was burned.” He omits the rest. AREV.]

89. [5449] Decius reigns for one year. In his time the holy monk Antony is said to have arisen in Egypt; from him monasteries were first founded.

[Note: [Col. 1047B]

90. Two years. Bede and nearly all the others add four months. For I do not think that what is read in Nicephorus—that he ruled for only one year and four months—is free from error, as is clear from the enumeration of the consuls in Cassiodorus.

Ibid. Eusebius writes about Novatus the heretic in book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 33; Pacianus, in his third letter to Symphorinus; and Socrates, book IV, chapter 23. He was condemned in the Roman council, as is established from Eusebius, book VI, chapter 39; Theodoret, book III; and Cyprian, book II, letter 1, and book IV, letter 2.]

90. [5451] Gallus and his son Volusian reign for two years. Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian the bishop, came to Rome and founded the Novatian heresy.

91. [5466] Valerian and Gallienus reign for fifteen years. Cyprian, first a rhetorician and then a bishop, is crowned with martyrdom. The Goths also ravage Greece, Macedonia, Asia, and Pontus. Valerian, after initiating a persecution against the Christians, was captured by the Persian king Sapor and grew old there in a dishonorable condition.

[Note: [Col. 1047C]

92. Two years. Zonaras likewise testifies that this should be written in Eusebius, instead of the one year and nine months now read under Claudius, as in Nicephorus. Eutropius says that he died of illness within two years.

Ibid. On Paul of Samosata, see Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25; Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 69. He was also convicted in the Council of Antioch: Aymo, book VII, chapters 7 and 10; Nicephorus, book VI, chapters 26 and 29.]

92. [5468] Claudius reigns for two years. He overcame the Goths, who were laying waste to Illyricum and Macedonia. Paul of Samosata is recognized as a heresiarch.

[Note: [Col. 1047C]

93. Six years. So Cedrenus; but Eusebius, Nicephorus, Orosius, Eutropius, and Zonaras report that he held the imperial power for six years, except for a few months.

[Col. 1047D] Ibid. Eusebius has the following in his *Chronicle*: “When Aurelian had initiated a persecution against us, lightning struck near him and his companions; and not long afterward he was killed on the old road between Constantinople and Heraclea, at Caenophorium.” Flavius Vopiscus says: “While he was traveling, he was killed through the treachery of a secretary at the station called Caenophorium, which lies between Heraclea and Byzantium.” See also, concerning his death, Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 26; Aymo, book VII, chapter 2; and Nicephorus, book VI, chapter 19. Ado, Bede, and all the rest write that he perished at the hands of his own men.]

93. [5474] Aurelian reigns for six years. By warfare he brought the Roman Empire almost back to its former boundaries; but, after instituting a persecution against the Christians, he was struck by lightning and immediately died.

96 [Note: [Col. 1047D]

94. Others assign him six months; Cedrenus, two years.

Ibid. Others say: Tacitus reigned for one year; after he was killed in Pontus, Florianus held the imperial power for eighty-nine days. AREV.]

94. [5475] Tacitus reigns for one year. The brevity of his life records nothing worthy of history concerning his deeds.

[Note: [Col. 1047D]

95. Eusebius, Nicephorus, Eutropius, Orosius, and others add four months. Zonaras writes that he ruled for fewer than six complete years.

[Col. 1048B] Ibid. Eusebius writes about the heresy of the Manichaeans, which arose from Mani the Persian, in book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VI; Cyril, *Catechetical Lecture* VI; and Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 66.]

95. [5481] Probus reigns for six years. Vigorous in military affairs and distinguished for his civil conduct, he restored to the Romans by warfare the Gallic territories occupied by the barbarians. In his time the Manichaean heresy arose.

[Note: [Col. 1048B]

96. Eusebius has the following in the *Chronicle*: “Carinus, defeated in battle at Murgum, is killed”; Vopiscus has “at Murtium.”]

96. [5483] Carus reigns for two years with his sons Carinus and Numerianus. After triumphing over the Persians, Carus set up camp as victor near the Tigris and fell dead from a stroke of lightning.

[Note: [Col. 1048C]

97. Twenty years. So Eusebius, Nicephorus, Orosius, and others. Cedrenus gives twenty-two; Aurelius Victor, twenty-five—not without error, as is clear from the reckoning of the consuls in Cassiodorus.]

97. [5503] Diocletian and Maximian ruled for twenty years. After burning the divine books, Diocletian persecuted the Christians throughout the world. He was the first to order gems to be set into clothing and footwear, whereas formerly the emperors had used only purple. These emperors waged various wars, defeating the Persians and recovering Mesopotamia. Later, after jointly relinquishing the height of imperial power, they lived as private citizens.

[Note: [Col. 1048C]

98. In the *Chronicle*, Eusebius says: “Galerius held the imperial power as Augustus for two years, and afterward, together with another, for six years.”]

98. [5505] Galerius reigns for two years. The brevity of his reign contributed nothing worthy of history.

[Note: [Col. 1048C]

99. Thirty years. Eusebius, Bede, and Ado add ten months. Nicephorus gives thirty-one years; the Greek manuscript Chronicle, thirty years and one month. Thirty-two years may be inferred from Aurelius Victor. Cedrenus writes that he died in the thirty-third year of his reign. Aurelius Victor also places after Galerius two other Galeriuses, Armentarius and Galerius Maximinus, and Alexander.

Ibid. “Christian.” Besides Eusebius and Zonaras, Cedrenus wrote at length about Constantine’s baptism at the beginning of volume III, in his *Life*. Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 41, reports that he was baptized by the most holy Sylvester, pope of Rome, in the seventh year of his reign, and was freed from leprosy. Ambrose, in *On the Death of Theodosius*, affirms that he obtained the grace of baptism at the end of his life. Alexander the Monk likewise attests this in his book *On the Discovery of the Saving Cross*: he says that Constantine died at Nicomedia, having opportunely attained what he had ardently desired, namely, to be baptized in the Jordan. Hermes, Socrates, and Theodoret also approve this view, according to Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 54; Rufinus, Orosius, Cassiodorus, and others agree with them.

Ibid. “The Cross,” etc. Whether the cross on which the author of our salvation and life hung had four arms, and whether the body of our Lord was pierced by four nails, is discussed piously and elegantly by Lucas, bishop of Tuy in Spain, against the Albigensians; I have a manuscript of his work in my library. On its discovery, there is an unpublished work by Alexander the Monk, which I possess in a Greek manuscript.

Ibid. “The Inorian doctrine.” Cedrenus learnedly refutes this opinion in the *Historical Compendium*, in the *Life of Constantine*.

Ibid. Much and more than enough has been discussed by others concerning Constantine’s baptism. In the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, instead of “But Constantine, at the end ... in an evil conclusion,” the following is substituted: “And while he was preparing war against the Persians, in a public villa arranged near Nicomedia, having properly handed over the state to his sons, he died.” The Alban Codex omits all of this, including “But Constantine ... in an evil conclusion.” The most ancient Caesenas Codex of the *Etymologies* likewise omits it; in that manuscript this *Chronicle* is inserted in place of the shorter one presented by most of the other *Etymologies* codices. Perhaps it was added to Isidore by someone else. In Grialius’s edition it is written “Arrius, Arrianus”; but the more common spelling is “Arius, Arianus,” and this is observed in the *History of the Goths* in the same edition. AREV.]

99. [5535] Constantine reigns for thirty years. He prepared for war against the Persians; at his approach they were so terrified that they came to meet him as suppliants, promising to carry out his commands. Having also become a Christian, he granted Christians permission to assemble freely and to build ninety-seven basilicas in honor of Christ. In these times the Arian heresy arose. The Council of Nicaea was also convened by Constantine for the condemnation of Arius. At that time the schism of the Donatists likewise arose. During the same period the cross of Christ was found at Jerusalem by Helena, Constantine’s mother. At the end of his life Constantine was baptized by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and converted to the Arian doctrine: alas, what grief! He made a good beginning and an evil end.

[Note: [Col. 1049C]

100. Twenty-four years. Orosius, Nicephorus, Cedrenus, and the Greek Chronicle agree. Jerome, in his *Chronicle* addressed to Eusebius, adds five months and twelve days. Ado gives eighteen years, five months, and fourteen days.

Ibid. “Turning aside.” On the death of Arius, see Rufinus, book X of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13. Cedrenus, together with Epiphanius, book II *Against the Heresies*, says: “At night Arius proceeded to the privy to relieve himself, and burst apart, just as Judas once did.” Theodoret says the same in book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14.

[Col. 1049D] Ibid. “Donatus.” Jerome calls Donatus his teacher in many places, especially in his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*, chapter 1, on the words “What is that which has been?”; in the *Apology against Rufinus*; and he says that Donatus wrote commentaries on Virgil.

Ibid. “Bones.” Later the bones of Andrew the apostle were transferred to Amalfi—not Melphin, correct it to Amalfi. His head was brought to Rome by Pius II and placed in the Basilica of Saint Peter.

Ibid. Others: “The monk Antony, at the age of one hundred, dies in the desert.” AREV.]

100. [5559] Constantius and Constans ruled for twenty-four years. Constantius, terrifying in the cruelty of his character, suffered much at the hands of the Persians. Having then become an Arian, he persecuted the Catholics throughout the world. With Constantius’s support Arius, while going to the church at Constantinople to dispute against our people concerning the faith, turned aside through the Forum of Constantine for a necessary bodily function, and suddenly his entrails poured out together with his life. During the same period Athanasius and Hilary became celebrated for their teaching and confession of the faith. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites arose in Syria, Macedonia, and Constantinople. Donatus, a writer of grammatical works and Jerome’s teacher, was renowned at Rome. The monk Antony died. The bones of the apostles Andrew and Luke were transferred to Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 1049D]

101. Two years. Nicephorus and the Greek Chronicle agree. Jerome says that some report that he reigned for one year and seven months, others for two years and eight months. Orosius gives one year and eight months of imperial rule. Paul the Deacon asserts that he died in the third year of his reign.

Ibid. There are various opinions about Julian’s death, as found in Nicephorus, book X, chapter 24; Jerome’s additions to the *Chronicle of Eusebius*; Zonaras, book III; Cedrenus; and Aymo, *On the Memory of Christian Affairs*, book IX. Paulus Orosius writes as follows in book VII, chapter 30: “Therefore, after he had moved the camp away from Ctesiphon, he was led into the deserts through the treachery of a certain deserter. As the army was perishing, exhausted by the force of thirst, the heat of the sun, and, in addition, the labor of crossing the sands, the emperor, anxious amid such a perilous situation, while wandering heedlessly through the wastes of the desert, was struck by a spear by a certain enemy horseman whom he encountered, and died.”

Ibid. Some have “aliqui” instead of “alii,” and “eorum” instead of “cunctorum.” AREV.]

101. [5561] Julian reigns for two years. Having become emperor from a cleric and then a pagan, he turned to the worship of idols and inflicted martyrdoms upon Christians. He forbade Christians to teach or study the liberal arts. After allowing the Jews to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem out of hatred for Christ, and after Jews gathered from every province and laid new foundations for the temple, an earthquake suddenly arose during the night; stones were torn from the bottom of the foundations and scattered far and wide. A fiery globe also emerged from the inner sanctuary of the temple and struck many of them down with its flames. Terrified by this, the survivors confessed Christ against their will. And, lest they think that this had happened by chance, the sign of the cross appeared on the garments of all of them the following night. Julian, advancing against the Persians, engaged them in battle and died after being struck by a javelin.

[Note: [Col. 1050C]

102. One year. Jerome gives eight months and Orosius nine; Nicephorus and Cedrenus give more than fifteen days. The Greek Chronicle gives ten months and fifteen days.

Ibid. “Who by law.” Cedrenus says that he issued an edict throughout the entire Roman Empire; Nicephorus says the same, book X, chapter 39. Ammianus Marcellinus asserts that he was devoted to the Christian law.]

102. [5562] Jovianus reigns for one year. When he saw that the army had chosen him emperor, and, affirming that he was a Christian, he declared that he could not rule over pagans, the entire army said: “We too, who through Julian cast aside the name of Christ, wish to be Christians with you.” Having heard this, he accepted the scepter of empire, made peace with the Persians, and returned. He then issued a law restoring privileges to the Christians and ordered the temples of the idols to be closed.

[Note: [Col. 1050C]

103. Fourteen years. So also the Greek Chronicle: “The same most divine Valentinian ruled over the Romans for fourteen years” (*Ἐβασίλευσε ... Ῥωμαίων ... Οὐαλεντινιανὸς ἔτη ιδʹ*). Nicephorus gives ten years and nine months. Orosius, book VII, chapter 32, says that he remained in power for eleven years. Cedrenus writes that Valentinian ruled for eleven years and Valens afterward for three years.

Ibid. In another manuscript it read: “But Fridigern, after Alaric had overcome him”; but this is corrupt, as is clear from Eutropius’s account of Valens, which states that Athalaric was defeated by Fridigern with the assistance of Valens.

Ibid. Eutropius, book XII, in his account of Valens, says that Ulfila, an Arian bishop who had lived under Constantius, was with the Arians Eudoxius and Aetius. Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 48, calls him Ulfilas; Roderic of Toledo, in his *History*, book II, chapter 1, calls him Gudila; Ado calls him Ulfilas. Some have Gulfias and Gulfilas.

Ibid. “Photinus.” A council was convened against him at Sirmium: Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 3; Socrates, book I, chapter 29; Sozomen, book IV, chapters 5 and 6. He was condemned by Damasus: Nicephorus, book XII, chapters 17 and 18.

Ibid. “Eunomius.” See Rufinus, book X, chapter 25; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 54; Jerome, on Hosea 4. Basil wrote against him, and the first Council of Constantinople was held against him under Damasus, Supreme Pontiff. Augustine, *On Heresies*, 55, and Theodoret, book V, chapter 10, discuss the heresy of Apollinaris.

Ibid. “Gilfulas.” The genuine name appears to be Wulfilas, hence Gulfilas in some authors. Among northern peoples, *Wu* is pronounced *gu*, as I observed in the prolegomena to Dracontius, chapter IX, no. 93. See again the discussion of Wulfila in the *History of the Goths*, no. 8. After the words “at the same time they are recognized,” some manuscripts add: “Thus far Eusebius and Jerome.” AREV.]

103. [5576] Valentinian and his brother Valens reign for fourteen years. The Goths, at the Danube, were divided between two kings, Fridigern and Athalaric. Fridigern, however, overcoming Athalaric with the help of Valens, the Arian emperor, and at Valens’s urging, became an Arian from the Catholic faith, together with the entire Gothic people, in gratitude for this favor, and followed Valens’s error. At that time Gilfulas, bishop of the Goths, devised letters for the Goths after the model of the Greek alphabet, and translated both Testaments into their own language. The heresiarchs Photinus, Eunomius, and Apollinaris also became known at that time.

[Col. 1051A] [Note: [Col. 1051C]

104. Six years. Orosius, Prosper, Paul the Deacon, Zonaras, and others agree; Ado gives seven.

Ibid. On Priscillian, see Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, 7; Jerome, *To Ctesiphon* and in his *Catalogue*; Pope Leo, letter 93; Sulpicius Severus, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*; the First Council of Toledo; and the Council of Braga, where his errors and impiety are recorded.]

104. [5582] Gratian reigns for six years with his brother Valentinian. Ambrose, bishop of Milan, became renowned for Catholic doctrine. Priscillian introduced into Spain the unspeakable heresy named after himself. Martin, bishop of the Gallic city of Tours, shone forth through many signs of miracles.

100 [Note: [Col. 1051D]

105. Eight years. In another copy, nine; but I think eight should be written, on the basis of the reckoning of the consuls listed by Cassiodorus. Prosper gives only seven. In the manuscript codices of the *Etymologies*, sometimes six, sometimes seven, and occasionally eight or nine are found.]

105. [5590] Valentinian reigns with Theodosius for eight years. A synod of 150 holy Fathers is assembled at Constantinople by Theodosius, in which all heresies are condemned. The presbyter Jerome is regarded as renowned throughout the world at Bethlehem. Priscillian, accused by Itacius, is struck down by the sword by the tyrant Maximus. During the same period the head of John the Baptist was brought to Constantinople and buried at the city’s seventh milestone. At the same time, by order of Theodosius, the temples of the pagans throughout the world were also overturned, for until then they had remained inviolate.

[Note: [Col. 1051D]

106. Three years. Prosper agrees, as does he himself in the *Etymologies*. Eutropius, book XIII, says: “He remained in power for eleven years, since he had already ruled in the eastern regions for six years, with Gratian granting him power and reigning jointly with him.” Paul Orosius says the same, book VII, chapter 35. So also Paul the Deacon, book XIII, at the beginning.

Ibid. On this Eugenius, a grammarian and teacher of literature who later became a soldier, see Paul, book XIII, at the beginning. John the anchorite is notably mentioned by Rufinus, book XI, chapters 32 and 19, and by Prosper, together with Zonaras and Paul the Deacon, book XIII.]

106. [5593] Theodosius reigns for three years with Arcadius and Honorius. During the same period John the anchorite was regarded as distinguished for miracles of virtue; when Theodosius consulted him, he foretold victory for him over the tyrant Eugenius.

[Note: [Col. 1052C]

107. Thirteen years. So Prosper, Cassiodorus, Sigebertus, and the bishop of Tuy. Nicephorus adds three months; Cedrenus and the Greek Chronicle give fourteen years. The manuscript *Epitome of the Chronicles of Severus, surnamed Sulpicius*, which I possess, recognizes only twelve. Paul Orosius, book VII, chapter 36, asserts that he reigned twelve years after his father’s death.

Ibid. From Sozomen, book VII, chapter 25, it is clear that Saint Donatus was bishop of Eurea in Epirus; Nicephorus, book XII, chapter 45, likewise says that he was bishop of Eurea in Epirus.

Ibid. “Spitting,” etc. Others have: “spitting into his mouth, he killed him,” whom, etc. AREV.]

107. [5606] Arcadius reigns for thirteen years with his brother Honorius. In his time Augustine, bishop, was regarded as distinguished for his knowledge of doctrine. John of Constantinople and Theophilus of Alexandria were also celebrated as illustrious bishops. During the same period Donatus, bishop of Epirus, was regarded as distinguished for his virtues. By spitting into the mouth of an enormous dragon, he killed it; eight yoke of oxen could scarcely drag it to the place of burning, lest its decay pollute the air. During the same period the bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by divine revelation. The Goths ravaged Italy. The Vandals and Alans attacked Gaul.

101 [Note: [Col. 1052C]

108. Fifteen years. So Cassiodorus, the bishop of Tuy, Ado, and he himself in the *Etymologies*. Sigebertus subtracts one year; Prosper adds one.]

108. [5621] Honorius reigns for fifteen years with Theodosius the Younger, his brother’s son. Under these emperors the Goths captured Rome, while the Vandals, Alans, and Suebi occupied Spain. At this time Pelagius proclaimed the doctrines of his error against the grace of Christ; for his condemnation a council of 214 bishops was assembled at Carthage. At this time Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, was held in distinction.

[Note: [Col. 1052D]

109. Twenty-seven years. So Cassiodorus, Paul the Deacon, the bishop of Tuy, and others. Sigebertus reports that he alone ruled both realms for three years, and afterward associated with himself Valentinian, the son of his paternal aunt Placidia and Constantius, ruling with him for another twenty-four years. Taken together, these years complete our number. Prosper gives thirty years; Bede twenty-six; Martin of Poland twenty-seven, as here.

Ibid. “Reigns,” etc. Others have: “reigns for twenty-six years. The race of the Vandals crosses from Spain to Africa. There ...” AREV.]

109. [5648] Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigns for twenty-seven years. The Vandals cross from Spain to Africa. There they overthrow the Catholic faith through Arian impiety. During the same period Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, contrived the error of his perfidy; against him the Council of Ephesus was assembled and condemned his impious doctrine. At this time the devil, appearing to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses, promised to lead them across the sea on dry ground to the promised land. After killing many of them, the survivors immediately converted to the grace of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1052D]

110. Six years. Paul the Deacon, Sigebertus, the bishop of Tuy, and others agree. Cassiodorus and Cedrenus give seven. Ado of Vienne says: “The emperor Martian died in the sixth year of his reign, after the completion of six months.”

Ibid. “Theodoric.” In another manuscript: “Theuderic”; Augustine and Sigebertus have “Theodoric”; likewise Ado of Vienne; Roderic of Toledo, book II, chapter 8, has “Theuderic.”]

110. [5654] Martian reigns for six years. At the beginning of his reign the Council of Chalcedon was held, where Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, were condemned. In the sixth year of his reign, Theodoric, king of the Goths, entered Spain with a vast army.

[Note: [Col. 1052D]

111. Sixteen years. So Nicephorus, Cassiodorus, Paul [Col. 1053C] the Deacon, Sigebertus, Palmerius, and others. Bede and Cedrenus give seventeen; Zonaras eighteen.

Ibid. “Acephali.” Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 45. He makes Severus of Antioch the leader of this heresy and adds that the Acephali were so called because they were not under bishops.]

111. [5670] Leo the Elder reigns for sixteen years with Leo the Younger. Alexandria and Egypt, rejecting the Council of Chalcedon and languishing in the error of the heretic Dioscorus, filled with an unclean spirit, bark with canine madness. During the same period the heresy of the Acephali appeared, attacking the Council of Chalcedon. They are therefore called Acephali—“headless”—because it cannot be discovered who first introduced this heresy; many among the eastern peoples still languish from the plague of this heresy.

[Note: [Col. 1053C]

112. Seventeen years. So Nicephorus, Cassiodorus, Ado, and others. In Sigebertus’s *Chronicle* it is written that he reigned for nineteen years. Some say seventeen years and six months. Consult the Chronicle of Mercator and the chronological tables of Onuphrius. Our Greek annals agree with Isidore: “Zeno Augustus reigned seventeen years” (*ἐβασίλευσε Ζένων αὔγουστος ἔτη ιζʹ*).

Ibid. “Zete Zeno.” Godfrey, a careful historian and prefect of Conrad III’s sacred archives, expressed this in verse in part XVI of his *Pantheon*:

“Zeno, father of his country, holds his father’s realm;

His illustrious son Leo was his only heir,

Strong in military affairs, often waging battles.

He is falsely accused of having sought his father’s death.

Zeno, the father, whose commands are plain, orders him to die,

His mother skillfully averts it by means of substitutes ...”

[Col. 1053D] Ibid. Cedrenus says: “At that time the relics of the blessed apostle Barnabas were found. His body lay in Cyprus beneath a cherry tree, bearing on its breast the Gospel composed by Saint Matthew and written in Barnabas’s own hand.”

Ibid. “This Zeno, seeking ...,” etc. This is an absolute nominative used for an ablative, as has been noted in many other places. AREV.]

112. [5687] Zeno reigns for seventeen years. He defends the heresy of the Acephali and rejects the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon. Seeking to kill his son Leo Augustus, Zeno offered another person of similar appearance in his place; he secretly made Leo a cleric, and Leo lived in the clerical state until the time of Justinian. During the same period the body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of Matthew, written in Barnabas’s own hand, were found through divine revelation.

[Col. 1053B] [Note: [Col. 1053D]

113. Twenty-seven years. So he himself in the *Etymologies*, the bishop of Tuy, and Ado, together with Paul the Deacon. Nicephorus and Cedrenus add four months; Zonaras, three. Evagrius, book III of the *History*, chapter 44, reports that he died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign, after an additional three months and days. Consult Onuphrius. Godfrey writes that he was struck by lightning and died in the twenty-eighth year of his reign. Pomponius Laetus gives twenty-four years, two months, and twenty-nine days.

Ibid. “It should be read,” contrary to the reading of all the copies, compelled by the truth of history: “Barbas too, a certain Arian bishop, while baptizing contrary to the rule of faith, said: ‘I baptize you, Barbas,’ etc.” This is taken from Paul the Deacon, book XV. He says: “Moreover, Deuterius, bishop of the Arians at Byzantium, while baptizing a certain man named Barbas, said contrary to the rule of faith,” etc. Cedrenus says the same.

Ibid. “Sends ... a certain Olympus.” Others have: “Sends. Fulgentius also flourished in confession of the faith and knowledge. A certain Olympius.” AREV.]

113. [5714] Anastasius reigns for twenty-seven years. Defending the error of the Acephali, he condemns into exile the bishops who defended the Council of Chalcedon. He also criticizes and emends the Gospels, as though they had been composed by ignorant evangelists. At that time Bishop Fulgentius became renowned for his confession of God and his learning. Trasamund, king of the Vandals, closes the Catholic churches in Africa, sends 120 bishops to Sardinia, and rages against the Catholics. During the same period, at Carthage, a certain Olympus, an Arian, blaspheming the Holy Trinity in the baths, was visibly burned by three fiery darts sent by an angel. A certain Arian bishop named Barbas, while baptizing a man contrary to the rule of faith, said: “Barbas baptizes you, in the name of the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately the water of that font, which had been brought for the baptism, disappeared completely. Seeing this, the man who was to be baptized immediately went to the Catholic Church and, according to the custom of the evangelical faith, received the baptism of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1054C]

114. Nine years. So Bede, Cedrenus, the Greek Chronicle, Palmerius, and others. Nicephorus adds three months. Zonaras gives twenty days; Marcellinus, Theodorus Lector, and Evagrius, book IV of the *History*, chapter 9, give nine years and twenty-three days; Sigebertus, ten years; Paul the Deacon, eleven.

Ibid. “From a captive woman.” From Eudoxia, daughter of the emperor Valentinian, who married Trasamund and bore Childeric to him.]

114. [5723] Justin the Elder reigns for nine years. As a lover of the Council of Chalcedon, he rejects the heresy of the Acephali. In his time, after Trasamund, Childeric, born of the captive daughter of the emperor Valentinian, assumed the kingdom among the Vandals. Bound by an oath to Trasamund not to favor the Catholics in his kingdom, before taking up the kingship he ordered the bishops to return from exile and instructed them to restore their own churches.

[Note: [Col. 1054C]

115. Thirty-nine years. The bishop of Tuy, Ado, and he himself in the *Etymologies* agree. Sigebertus gives only thirty years; Nicephorus adds seven days. Zonaras and Cedrenus give thirty-eight years, seven months, and thirteen days. Paul the Deacon gives thirty-eight years, omitting the months and days, in book XVI.

Ibid. “The Three Chapters.” Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*, in his account of Justinian, writes concerning the Council of Chalcedon: “He attempted to condemn the Three Chapters, that is, the statements of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; the writings of Theodoret; and the letter called the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa.”

Ibid. “Narses.” Narses the Eunuch, Justinian’s chamberlain, was made exarch of Italy. Paul, book XVI, and Ado.]

115. [5762] Justinian reigns for thirty-nine years. Accepting the heresy of the Acephali, he compels all the bishops in his kingdom to condemn the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. The Theodosian and Gaian heresies arise in Alexandria. Roman soldiers enter Spain under the tyrant Athanagild. The patrician Belisarius triumphs wonderfully over the Persians. Later, sent by Justinian to Africa, he destroyed the Vandal nation. In Italy as well, Totila, king of the Ostrogoths, was defeated by Narses, the Roman patrician. During the same period the body of the holy monk Antony was found by divine revelation, brought to Alexandria, and buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

104 [Note: [Col. 1054D]

116. Eleven years. Justin the Younger ruled for twelve years according to Sigebertus; according to Nicephorus, twelve years, two months, and twenty days; according to Zonaras and Cedrenus, thirteen years.

Ibid. In Justin’s time, under Pope Vigilius, the Council of Constantinople was convened. But this cannot be understood except of the first Council of Constantinople, consisting of 150 Fathers, held under the elder Theodosius, at which the form of the creed was established; the entire confession of the Greeks and Latins proclaims it in the churches. See Walafrid, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 22, and the Fourth Council of Toledo.]

116. [5773] Justin the Younger reigns for eleven years. He destroyed the measures that had been enacted against the Council of Chalcedon and ordered the creed of the 150 Fathers to be sung by the people during the celebration of the sacrifice. At that time the Armenians first accepted the faith of Christ. The Gepids were destroyed by the Lombards. During the same period Martin, bishop of Braga, was regarded throughout Gallaecia as distinguished for prudence and Catholic doctrine. Narses the patrician, after defeating Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy under Justinian Augustus, was terrified by the threats of Sophia Augusta, Justin’s wife, and invited the Lombards from Pannonia, bringing them into Italy. At this time Leovigild, king of the Goths, brought certain regions of Spain that had rebelled against him back under the authority of his kingdom by conquest.

[Note: [Col. 1055B]

117. Seven years. Bede, Ado, and he himself in the *Etymologies* agree; Cedrenus and the Greek Annals give four years; Zonaras gives four years, ten months, and eight days; Nicephorus, five years; Sigebertus and the bishop of Tuy, six years. Contius discusses the variation in the years of Tiberius in his notes on the *Chronology of Nicephorus*.

Ibid. In the Urbino-Vatican Codex, about which Schelstratius writes, volume I, page 593, after “are ravaged by slaughter,” the words “and he himself is crowned with martyrdom” are added. AREV.]

117. [5780] Tiberius reigns for seven years. The Lombards, having driven out the Romans, enter Italy; the Goths, divided into two factions through Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild, are ravaged by mutual slaughter.

[Note: [Col. 1055C]

118. Twenty-one years. Sigebertus, Ado, and Bede agree. Nicephorus gives twenty years and four months; Cedrenus, twenty years, three months, and two days; Palmerius, twenty years; Zonaras and Nicephorus himself in the *Ecclesiastical History* give the same; Pomponius Laetus likewise agrees.

Ibid. “Leander.” Saint Isidore describes Leander’s life in his little book *On Illustrious Men*.

Ibid. “Mellitus.” The Goths return to the Catholic faith under King Reccared’s leadership. At that time Gregory was celebrated as an illustrious bishop at Rome; and then the Avars, etc. Others, instead of “from the Huns ... he flourished,” present the following: “At this time Saint Gregory, bishop of Rome, was regarded as illustrious.” AREV.]

118. [5801] Maurice reigns for twenty-one years. The Suebi, conquered by King Leovigild, are subjected to the Goths; the Goths themselves, urged on by the most religious prince Reccared, convert to the Catholic faith. The Avars, fighting against the Romans, are driven off more by gold than by iron. Thrace is occupied by the Huns. At this time Leander, bishop in Spain, became renowned for the conversion of the Gothic people through his teaching of the faith and the sciences.

[Col. 1056A] 105 [Note: [Col. 1055C]

119. Eight years. So Nicephorus, Zonaras, Cedrenus, Ado, the bishop of Tuy, and others. Onuphrius gives eight years, four months, and nine days.]

Ibid. According to Cassiodorus, the four ancient factions of charioteers were named from their colors: the blue, green, white, and rose factions. As Suetonius writes, Domitian added two others, one of golden and the other of purple cloth. Thus this class of seditious men received its names from colors. Xiphilinus, in his account of Caligula, relates that this emperor especially delighted in a certain charioteer called “the Green” from the green color of his clothing.

119. [5809] Phocas reigns for eight years. Having been made emperor through a military revolt, he killed the Augustus Maurice and many nobles. During his reign the Greens and Blues wage civil war throughout the East and Egypt, and overthrow one another in mutual slaughter. Extremely serious wars are also stirred up by the Persians against the Roman state; the Romans, vigorously defeated by them, lost many provinces as far as the river Euphrates and, as they say, Jerusalem itself.

[Note: [Col. 1055D]

120. Sisebut, an excellent king and a most religious and vigorous defender and cultivator of the Catholic faith, successor of King Gundemar, convened the Fourth Council of Toledo, which is called the Great Synod. There, in chapter 55, it is said that in the time of the most religious prince Sisebut the Jews were compelled to adopt the Christian faith. Isidore wrote his book *On the Nature of Things* for him.

Ibid. In certain manuscripts apparently written in Gaul, or copied from manuscripts written there, the passage is arranged as follows: “Heraclius reigned for twenty-six years. In the fifth year of his reign, while he was holding office, Sisebut, king of the Goths, converted … except those who, having escaped by flight, secretly migrated to the Franks. During the reign of this emperor, up to the fourteenth year of his reign and the fortieth year of the reign of the most glorious prince Lothar, many losses were inflicted almost everywhere upon the Roman state by various peoples. In his time the Persians reached as far as Chalcedon. Breaking through the long wall and approaching the walls of Constantinople, they converse with the aforementioned emperor, who was standing upon the wall; after receiving a price for peace, they withdraw from him. The remaining period of the sixth age is uncertain to human inquiry,” etc. AREV.]

120. [5814] Heraclius is now entering the fifth year of his reign. At its beginning the Slavs took Greece from the Romans; the Persians took Syria, Egypt, and very many provinces. In Spain also Sisebut, king of the Goths, captured certain cities belonging to the Roman military, and converted the Jews subject to his kingdom to faith in Christ.

[Col. 1056B] [Note: [Col. 1056C]

121. “And fourth.” In another manuscript it read “fifth,” but incorrectly, since Isidore himself makes clear in his *History of the Goths* that Sisebut was elevated to public administration in the second year of Heraclius. Observe, however, that some believe Isidore published his *Chronicle* twice: first up to the fifth year of Heraclius and the fifth year of Sisebut—that is, up to the year 5814 from the creation of the world—and then, after adding thirteen years, up to the eighteenth year of Heraclius and the seventh year of Suinthila—that is, up to the year 5827 from the creation of the world. In many copies I find the first conclusion of this *Chronicle*. In the Soria copy, however, which is the oldest of all, a double conclusion is read: the earlier is the one we have printed, while the later is as follows:

“Heraclius is now in the eighteenth year of his reign, at the beginning of which the Slavs … Thus, from the beginning of the world up to the present era, 665—that is, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Heraclius and the seventh of the religious prince Suinthila—there are 5,826 years. The remaining period of the age …,” as above.

Vasaeus, in book I, chapter 4 of his *Spanish Annals*, states that he found Isidore’s *Chronicle* extending to the fifth year of Suinthila, which was the year of the Lord 626. I also possess a manuscript *Chronicle of Isidore* with a conclusion different from all the others. But concerning this opinion about two editions, I shall state what I think. I believe that this *Chronicle* of Saint Isidore was published by him only once, since in the preface he says—as it is read in the oldest and most carefully corrected copies—that he is writing up to the time of Sisebut. A few years later, however, he composed the book of the *Etymologies*, in whose fifth book, chapter 37, he proceeds to the fifth (elsewhere seventh) year of Suinthila and the eighteenth of Heraclius.

For it is certain that Isidore wrote the book of the *Etymologies* last, at the request of Braulio of Zaragoza, as Saint Ildefonsus testifies in his supplement to *On Illustrious Men*: “Finally, at the request of Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, he wrote the book of the *Etymologies*. Although he strove for many years to complete it, he seems to have closed his final day with the work unfinished.” Braulio himself confirms this in Isidore’s *Life*, saying that the work had been left divided into headings rather than books, which he later arranged.

I therefore think that the conclusion found in the *Etymologies* was transferred by someone into the *Chronicle*, and conversely that of the *Chronicle* into the *Etymologies*: in the *Chronicle* one should read “up to the fifth year of Sisebut,” and in the *Etymologies* “up to the seventh year of Suinthila.” This is what occurs to me; I do not reject the conjecture of anyone who thinks otherwise.]

121. Thus, from the beginning of the world up to the present era, 654—that is, in the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius and the fourth of the most glorious prince Sisebut—there are 5,814 years.

122. The remaining period of the age is uncertain to human inquiry, for our Lord Jesus Christ removed every question concerning this matter when he said: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power.” And elsewhere he says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven, except the Father alone.” Therefore let each person consider his own departure, as Holy Scripture says: “In all your works remember your last things.” For when each person departs from the age, then for that person the consummation of the age has come.

[Col. 1057]

107. THE HISTORY OF THE GOTHIC, VANDAL, AND SUEVIC KINGS BY SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE. (C)

### Prologue

[Note: [Col. 1057B]

Preface, no. 1. This eulogy of Spain, or preface to the *History of the Goths*, is absent from the ancient editions of the works of Saint Isidore, as I observed in my *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, where I gave it the title: “The *History of the Kings of the Goths, Vandals, and Sueves* Vindicated for Isidore against Pellizerius.” Manuscripts and editions differ among themselves concerning the *Chronicle of the Visigoths*, called Wulsa’s: whether it belongs to Isidore. Notice concerning this *Chronicle* from the edition of the Fathers of Toledo. An interpolated copy of the *History* among the *Chronicles of Tudela*. Another appears mutilated from Isidore’s time, and why? Isidore’s words concerning Saint Hermenegild’s war against his father explained. The remarkable silence of Isidore and other Fathers of the Gothic Church concerning the glorious martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild. The compliance of the bishops of the Gothic Church in certain difficult actions of the kings.

The more extensive treatment I devoted in my *Isidoriana* to elucidating the more difficult passages of Saint Isidore’s works, the less labor was now required in preparing notes for this and his other works. Indeed, I could have been much briefer in the *Isidoriana* if I had wished to be more expansive in the annotations appended to it. I shall now indicate the varying wording of the preface.

“Quaeque.” Labbe correctly has this for *quaecunque*, since *quisque* is used for *quicunque*; others read *quae*. Ibid., “and flourishes abundantly”; others, “and would flourish greatly.” AREV.]

1. Of all lands that lie from the West as far as the Indians, you are the most beautiful, O sacred Spain, ever blessed with princes, mother of peoples. Rightly are you now queen of all provinces, from whom not only the West but also the East borrows its light. You are the glory and ornament of the world, the more illustrious portion of the earth, in which the glorious fruitfulness of the Gothic people rejoices greatly and flourishes abundantly.

108 [Note: [Col. 1058B]

2. “Joyful.” Others, “broad.” Ibid. “Leafy.” The Codex Legionensis has “leaf-covered.” Ibid. “Flocks.” This should be retained with Labbe; there was no reason for Florez and the Madrid editor of the recent edition of Saint Isidore to prefer “of Greeks,” with Grotius. AREV.]

2. Nature has rightly endowed you with a more generous abundance than all lands that produce. You are rich in berries, full of flowing strength, joyful in your harvests; you are clothed with grain, shaded by olive trees, bordered by vines. You are flower-filled in your fields, leafy in your mountains, rich in fish along your shores. Situated beneath the most gracious region of the sky, you are neither scorched by the summer heat of the sun nor weakened by icy cold, but, girded by a temperate zone of heaven, you are nourished by blessed west winds. For you produce whatever the fields bear that is fertile, whatever the mines bear that is precious, and whatever living creatures bear that is beautiful and useful. Nor should you be placed below those rivers whose fame for splendid flocks makes them renowned.

[Note: [Col. 1058B]

3. “Will yield.” I would prefer “yields”; and in manuscripts *e* frequently occurs in place of *i*. Ibid. “Olympian.” Grotius reads “once at Pisa,” which is corrupt. Ibid. “You will envy”; others, “you have envied.” Labbe omits this sentence: “Nor will you envy Etruria.” What is called “more abundant in pasture” should be understood as “more abundant in pastures,” much as shortly afterward “full of palms.” AREV.]

3. The Alpheus will yield to you in horses, the Clitumnus in cattle, although sacred Alpheus exercises swift quadrigae over the courses beneath Olympic palms, and Clitumnus once supplied enormous young bulls for sacrifice at the Capitol. You neither seek the pasturelands of Etruria, richer in fodder, nor marvel at the groves of Molorchus, full of palms, nor envy the Eleian chariots in the speed of your horses. You are fertile in rivers pouring over you; you are golden in streams flowing with gold. For you is the fountain, father of horses. For you fleeces dyed with native purple-shells burn with Tyrian red. For you the flashing stone amid the darkness of deep mountains is kindled by a neighboring sun, with a radiance close to its own.

[Note: [Col. 1058B]

4. “Romulean.” Others, “Romulan.” Ibid. “Victorious.” So the Codex Legionensis; others have *victus* (“vanquished,” masculine) or *victam* (“vanquished,” feminine). Ibid. “Promised himself”; others, “betrothed” or “possessed.” “Royal fillets”; others, “kingdoms” or “islands.” John Baptist Perez also illustrated the *Chronicle* itself, which follows, with several notes. AREV.]

4. Rich in foster-children, jewels, and purple, and equally fertile in governors and in the resources of empire, you are so prosperous in adorning princes that you are blessed in producing them. Therefore golden Rome, head of the nations, long ago rightly desired you; and although the same Romulean power, victorious at first, had promised you to itself, afterward the most flourishing nation of the Goths, after many victories throughout the world, seized and loved you in rivalry, and to this day enjoys, amid royal fillets and abundant flocks, the secure happiness of empire.

## HERE BEGINS THE HISTORY

[Col. 1059]

[Col. 1059A] 109 [Note: [Col. 1059C]

1. Jerome, in *Hebrew Questions*, Genesis 10: “And certainly learned men of earlier times were accustomed to call all the Goths Getae rather than Gog and Magog.”

Ibid. “Of the Goths,” etc. Others: “that the kingdom of the Goths is most ancient.” Ibid. “Earlier learning … was accustomed”; others: “Roman writers … were accustomed.” Ibid. “A very brave nation … is described.” This is omitted, along with much else, in the Labbe Codex. Fabricius, in his *Bibliography*, p. 48, praises Fabian Torner, who wrote on the excellence of the ancient Gothic language, and Stirnhilm, who wrote on the origin of the Gothic language. AREV.

Ibid. “Translated into our language as *tecti*, by which”; others: “called in our language *dicti*, because.” Alvarus of Córdoba took certain material from this passage of Isidore. See below, note on no. 67. AREV.]

1. It is certain that the Goths are a most ancient people. Some suppose that their origin is derived from Magog, the son of Japheth, on the basis of the similarity of the final syllable, and they infer this especially from the prophet Ezekiel. Earlier learning, however, was accustomed to call them Getae rather than Gog and Magog. They are also described as a most warlike people, destined to devastate the land of Judea.

2. The interpretation of their name in our language is *tecti*, signifying strength; and in truth no people in the world so exhausted the Roman Empire as they did. These are the people whom even Alexander declared should be avoided, whom Pyrrhus feared, and whom Caesar dreaded. (From Orosius.) For many ages in the past they were led by commanders, and afterward by kings. Their periods must be briefly set out in order, and from histories we must reconstruct under what name and by what deeds they ruled.

[Note: [Col. 1059D]

3. Others have “that one,” for “Julius,” and “to him,” for “to Caesar”; and “he contemplated,” for “having contemplated.” AREV.]

3. In the twelfth year before the beginning of the era, when Gnaeus Pompey and Gaius Julius Caesar had taken up civil arms in their struggle to seize control of the state, the Goths came to Thessaly to aid Pompey and fight against Caesar. There, while Ethiopians, Indians, Persians, Medes, Greeks, Armenians, Scythians, and the other peoples of the East, summoned into Pompey’s army, fought against Julius, these Goths resisted Caesar more bravely than the rest. Caesar, disturbed by their numbers and valor, is said to have contemplated flight, had night not brought the battle to an end. Then Caesar said that Pompey did not know how to win, and that Caesar could not be defeated. For if Pompey had known how to win, he would have overcome Caesar today, with such fierce men at his side.

[Col. 1059C] [Note: [Col. 1059D]

4. Era 294; others incorrectly have era 214. Ibid. “First.” So Labbe, and Florez with him; in Grial’s edition, less correctly, “second.” Lindebrog says that one should read era 293, year 3. The Alps were the name given to any high mountains. See *Etymologies*, book 14, chapter 8, no. 18. AREV.

Ibid. Era 369. This should be retained; others give different numbers. For year 26, Grial incorrectly has 16. AREV.]

4. Era 294. In the first year of the reign of Valerian and Gallienus, the Goths descended from the Alpine mountains where they lived and devastated Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, Asia, and Illyricum. They held Illyricum and Macedonia for about fifteen years. Then, defeated by the emperor Claudius, they returned to their own settlements. The Romans, honoring Claudius Augustus with exceptional glory because he had removed so brave a people from the borders of the Roman state, placed a golden shield for him in the Forum and a golden statue in the Capitol.

5. Era 369, in the twenty-sixth year of Constantine’s reign, the Goths attacked the territory of the Sarmatians and fell upon the Romans in extremely numerous forces, laying everything waste with fierce valor, sword, and plunder. Constantine himself drew up a battle line against them and, after a mighty struggle, scarcely overcame them and drove them beyond the Danube. Thus he became renowned not only for the glory of his valor against various peoples, but even more gloriously for his victory over the Goths. The Romans, with the Senate acclaiming him, pursued him with public praise because he had conquered so great a people and restored his native Roman state.

[Note: [Col. 1060D]

6. Era 407. Perez printed 408, with the note “others have 407”; but 407 is correct, as Florez demonstrates from the Fasti of Hydatius and other records. For “while afflicted,” others have “while suffering”; and afterward, “to migrate into the Roman provinces.” AREV.]

6. Era 407, in the fifth year of the reign of Valens, Athanaric first assumed the administration of the Gothic people, reigning for thirteen years. When a most savage persecution had been stirred up against the faith, he wished to exercise it against those among his people who were known to be Christians. He made many of them martyrs because they would not consent to sacrifice to idols; and although he was horrified to kill the rest because of their great number, he subjected them to many persecutions and gave them permission—or rather compelled them—to leave his kingdom and migrate into the provinces of Roman territory.

[Note: [Col. 1060D]

7. Others have “beyond the Ister … devastating”; Grial’s edition has “into the Istrian territory.” AREV.]

7. Era 415, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Valens, the Goths, divided against one another under Athanaric and Fridigern in the Ister, ravaged one another in alternating massacres. But Athanaric overcame Fridigern through the support of the emperor Valens. For this reason he sent envoys with gifts to the same emperor and requested teachers to receive the rule of the Christian faith. Valens, however, deviating from the truth of the Catholic faith and held fast by the perversity of the Arian heresy, sent heretical priests. Through their wicked persuasion he attached the Goths to the doctrine of his error, and infused the poison of a pestilential seed into so distinguished a people. Thus they retained and preserved for a long time the error which their recent credulity had absorbed.

[Note: [Col. 1060D]

8. “Nor to be the substance.” Labbe has “nor from the substance.” On Gulfila, or Wulfila, see the note to *Chronicle*, no. 103. Fabricius, p. 48 of his *Bibliography*, lists Georg Friedrich Heupel’s dissertation on Ulphila, or the Gothic translation of the four Evangelists. AREV.]

8. Then their Gothic bishop, Gulfilas, devised Gothic letters and translated the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments into the same language. As soon as the Goths began to possess letters and a law, they built churches for their doctrine, holding concerning the divinity such teachings, in accordance with the same Arius, that they believed the Son to be inferior to the Father in majesty and later than the Father in eternity. They held that the Holy Spirit was neither God nor the substance of the Father, but had been created through the Son, devoted to the service of both and subject to the obedience of both. They also asserted a different person and nature of the Father, another of the Son, and another finally of the Holy Spirit, so that no longer, according to the tradition of Holy Scripture, was one God and Lord worshiped, but, in accordance with the superstition of idolatry, three gods were venerated. They held to this evil of blasphemy for 213 years, through the passage of time and the succession of kings. At last, remembering their salvation, they renounced their ingrained faithlessness and, through the grace of Christ, reached the unity of the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 1061D]

9. In Grial’s edition, incorrectly, the forty-fifth year of Valens is given instead of the fourteenth. For “from their land,” others have “from their settlements.” Perez wrote “Ugnis,” and, for the alternative reading, “Huns,” which is more common. For “and having destroyed,” which others present, Grial’s edition has “and having cast down.” Perez perhaps intended “and having scattered.” For “they burned,” etc., others have “they burn,” as he rightly says, “while he was still alive.” AREV.]

9. Era 416, in the fourteenth year of the reign of Valens, the Goths, who had first expelled the Christians from their land, were themselves again expelled by the Huns together with their king Athanaric. After crossing the Danube, and unable to withstand the force of the emperor Valens, they surrendered without laying down their arms and received Thrace for habitation. But when they saw themselves oppressed by the Romans contrary to the custom of their own freedom, they were compelled to revolt. They ravaged Thrace with sword and fire; after destroying the Roman army, they wounded Valens himself with a spear and burned him while he was fleeing in a certain village. Thus, deservedly, he was burned alive by them in a temporal fire, since he had delivered such beautiful souls to eternal fires.

[Note: [Col. 1061D]

10. Others. See Eutropius.]

10. In that battle the Goths found the earlier Gothic confessors whom they had once expelled from their land on account of the faith, and they wished to join them to themselves in sharing the spoils. When these men refused, some of them were killed. Others, occupying mountainous places and constructing whatever refuges they could, not only persevered as Catholic Christians but also remained in concord with the Romans, by whom they had formerly been received.

[Note: [Col. 1061D]

11. “Perished”; others, “died.” AREV.]

11. Era 419, in the third year of the reign of Theodosius the Spaniard, Athanaric established a right of friendship and an alliance with Theodosius. He soon proceeded to Constantinople and died there on the fifteenth day after he had been honorably received by Theodosius. The Goths, with their own king dead, observing the kindness of the emperor Theodosius, entered into a treaty, surrendered themselves to the Roman Empire, and remained with the Romans for twenty-eight years.

12. Era 420, in the fourth year of the reign of Theodosius, the Goths, refusing the protection of the Roman alliance, appointed Alaric as their king. They judged it unworthy to be subject to Roman power and to follow those whose laws and empire they had long before rejected, and whose association they had abandoned in triumph after defeating them in battle.

[Note: [Col. 1061D]

13. “Fifth.” Florez corrected it thus, although others have “fourth,” as also in the following number. He printed 11 instead of 10 because in this way the years of the era agree better with the years of the emperors, and the same method of counting is maintained in the three following eras. For “to plunder whatever regions,” others have “to attack every region.” AREV.]

13. Era 437, in the fifth year of the reign of Honorius and Arcadius, the Goths, divided between Alaric and Radagaisus, while they tore one another apart in two portions of the kingdom through various massacres, became united by the destruction of the Romans. They formed a common plan and, with equal purpose, divided among themselves the various regions of Italy for plundering.

[Note: [Col. 1062D]

14. For year 11, others give 10, as recently stated. Grotius has “with two hundred thousand armed Sarmatians”; Labbe follows the edition of Grial. AREV.]

14. Era 443, in the eleventh year of Honorius and Arcadius, Radagaisus, king of the Goths, a Scythian by origin and devoted to the worship of idolatry, exceedingly savage in barbarian brutality, invaded parts of Italy with a violent devastation, promising, in contempt of Christ, to offer Roman blood as a libation to his gods if he won. His army was surrounded by the Roman commander Stilicho in the mountainous regions of Tuscany and was consumed by hunger rather than by the sword. Finally the king himself was captured and killed.

[Note: [Col. 1062D]

15. Era 447. See Procopius, Jordanes, Marcellinus, and Paul the Deacon.

Ibid. In Grial’s edition: “in the year of the reign of Arcadius.” Perhaps the editor intended “in the year of the reign of Honorius and Arcadius,” as others have. Florez, however, proves that one should read “in the year of the reign of Honorius,” with the name of Arcadius deleted both in this era and in the two following ones, 448 and 454, since Arcadius had already died and had reigned with Honorius for only thirteen years, as is clear from Isidore’s *Chronicle*. As is reasonable to believe, scribes joined the name of Arcadius to that of Honorius from the preceding eras. For “with assault, fire, and swords,” Labbe less suitably has “with a violent assault of great destruction”; for “of the Romans,” others have “of the Christians.” AREV.]

15. Era 447, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Arcadius, after Radagaisus had been destroyed, Alaric, his partner in kingship, a Christian in name but a heretic in profession, grieved that so great a multitude of Goths had been destroyed by the Romans and waged war against Rome to avenge the blood of his people.
