He assaulted the city under siege with violence, fire, and swords, and thus the City victorious over all nations was conquered and brought low by Gothic triumphs, captured, subjected, and made to serve them.

The Goths nevertheless showed such mercy there that they had previously made a vow that, if they entered the City, no Roman found in the places of Christ would be handed over to the devastation of the City. After making this vow, they attacked the City, and mercy was granted both life and freedom to all who fled to the thresholds of the saints. Even those who were outside the martyrs’ shrines, but invoked the name of Christ and of the saints, were spared by the same mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1062D]

16. “The sacred host.” Labbe has “the sacred enemy,” which may perhaps be better. AREV.]

16. As for the rest, although they were exposed to the enemy’s plunder, the savagery of striking them was nevertheless restrained. While the Goths were rushing through the City amid that devastation, a certain powerful man found an elderly consecrated virgin and honorably urged her to bring forth whatever gold or silver she might have. With a faithful conscience she brought out what she had. When he admired the form and beauty of the vessels, relics of the ancient Roman wealth, the virgin said: “These vessels were deposited with me from the treasury of the apostle Peter. Take them, if you dare. I do not dare to give you the sacred host.” That Goth, greatly terrified at the name of the apostle, reported this to the king through a messenger. The king immediately ordered everything to be carried back by that virgin to the treasury of Saint Peter with the greatest reverence, saying: “I have waged war with the Romans, not with the apostles of God.”

[Note: [Col. 1063D]

17. “Carrying back, with weapons drawn,” etc. Grial’s edition has “carrying back.” “Armies from every side, at the king’s command, gather with armed guards for protection.” “From every side, at the voices,” etc. Labbe soon afterward has “bands of pagans who, while pretending to be Christians,” etc. AREV.]

17. The virgin therefore returned, honored with the most reverent services, and with her returned all who had joined themselves to her. They carried those golden and silver vessels above their heads with hymns and songs, while armed guards, drawn from every side by the king’s command, protected them. From their hiding places, bands of Christians hasten from every side to the voices of the singers. Pagans also hasten there, and, mingled among them while pretending to be servants of Christ, they too escaped the destruction of the calamity.

[Note: [Col. 1063D]

18. “Placidia.” Others, “Placidam.”]

18. At this time the Goths captured in Rome Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius and sister of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, together with a vast treasure of gold and silver. After acquiring much Roman wealth, they departed on the third day, after setting fire to and overthrowing the parts of the City. Then, boarding ships and intending to cross to Sicily, which is separated from Italy by a narrow strait, they were endangered by a hostile sea and lost much of their army. Their glory in possessing the Roman city was so great that, in comparison with it, they considered themselves to have suffered no misfortune from that storm, balancing the losses of the shipwreck against the outcome of their victory. Alaric’s death immediately followed; he died in Italy in the twenty-eighth year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 1063D]

19. Grial’s edition gives era 449, the seventeenth year of Honorius, and the sixth year of the younger Theodosius. Florez, from other editions and from Isidore himself elsewhere, restored era 448, the sixteenth year of Honorius, and the first year of the younger Theodosius; but he entirely omits the year of this Theodosius, as do other editions, since Isidore does not specify it elsewhere when he names the years of Honorius. In Lindebrog’s edition the name of Honorius is omitted, and the first year of the younger Theodosius is given. “According to Isidore,” says Lindebrog, “Arcadius died in the year of Christ 410, era 448.” Florez, with Labbe, prefers *in quo* (“in which”) to *in qua*. Grial’s edition has *quibus ait* (“to whom he says”) for *qui ait* (“who says”). AREV.]

19. Era 448, in the seventeenth year of the reign of Honorius and the first of the younger Theodosius, after Alaric had died following the capture of the City, Athaulf was placed by the Goths over the kingdom of Italy for six years. In the fifth year of his reign he withdrew from Italy and went to Gaul. He took as his wife Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius, whom the Goths had captured in Rome. Some believe that in her the prophecy of Daniel was fulfilled, in which he says that the daughter of the king of the South is to be joined to the king of the North, although no offspring of her line was to remain. As the same prophet adds in what follows, saying: “Nor shall his seed stand.” For no child was born from her womb to succeed its father in the kingdom. But while Athaulf, after leaving Gaul, was making for Spain, one of his own men stabbed him at Barcelona during familiar conversation.

20. Era 454, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Honorius, after the death of Athaulf, Sigeric was elected leader by the Goths. Although he was most eager for peace with the Romans, he was soon killed by his own people.

[Note: [Col. 1064D]

21. John Frederick Muldener, in his *Specimen of Ancient Numismatics*, presents a coin of Wallia with an obscure inscription. AREV.]

21. In the same era and year as above, Wallia succeeded Sigeric and held the kingdom for three years. The Goths made him their leader for the sake of war, but divine providence ordained him for peace. As soon as he began to reign, he concluded a treaty with the emperor Honorius and honorably returned to him his sister Placidia, who had been captured by the Goths in Rome, promising the emperor that he would undertake every struggle for the Roman state. Accordingly, summoned to Spain by the patrician Constantius, he inflicted great slaughter upon the barbarians for the sake of the Roman name.

[Note: [Col. 1064D]

22. “The Vandal Selingui.” Some distinguish between the Vandals and the Selingui, as though they were two nations. But they should be read together, and it is shown in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, p. 73, that the Selingui were the same as the Vandals. For “had survived,” others have “survived”; Grial’s edition incorrectly has “had survived.” Labbe has “was preparing to cross Africa in battle formation.” AREV.]

22. He destroyed all the Vandal Selingui in Baetica in war. He so cut down the Alans, who dominated the Vandals and Sueves, that after their king Atax had been killed, the few who survived, having forgotten the name of their kingdom, subjected themselves to the rule of Gunderic, king of the Vandals, who had settled in Gallaecia.

When Wallia had completed the war in Spain and was preparing to cross to Africa with his fleet drawn up for battle, he was shattered in the Strait of the Gaditanian Sea by the violence of a very severe storm. Remembering also the shipwreck under Alaric, he abandoned the danger of the voyage, left Spain, and returned to Gaul. In recognition of his victory the emperor granted him second Aquitania, together with certain cities of the neighboring provinces as far as the Ocean.

[Note: [Col. 1064D]

23. In the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Honorius. Florez takes this from Labbe; Grial’s edition has “in the ninth year of the reign of the younger Theodosius,” omitting the name of Honorius. Florez proves that the name of the younger Theodosius should instead be omitted, and that it was not his ninth year but his tenth, which fell in era 457. For “Theuderedus,” others write “Theodoricus.” Lindebrog gave era 467 and the twentieth year of the younger Theodosius, and consequently assigned only twenty-three years to Theuderedus. AREV.]

23. Era 457, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Honorius, after King Wallia had died, Theuderedus succeeded to the kingdom and reigned for thirty-three years. Not content with the kingdom of Aquitania, he rejected the treaty of Roman peace, occupied most of the Roman municipalities neighboring his settlements, and attacked Arelate, the most distinguished city of Gaul, after laying siege to it with great force. When the military power of Aetius, commander of the Roman army, threatened him, he withdrew from the siege without escaping punishment.

24. After Aetius had been removed from military authority by order of the emperor Valentinian, while Theuderedus was harassing the city of Narbonne with a long siege and famine, he was again driven away by Litorius, commander of the Roman army, with the Huns providing assistance. Although Litorius had at first conducted the campaign successfully against the Goths, he was afterward deceived by the signs of demons and the responses of soothsayers. He rashly undertook war against the Goths; after losing the Roman army, he was miserably defeated and died. He thereby made clear how useful that multitude, which perished with him, could have been if he had preferred to rely on faith rather than on the deceptive displays of demons.

[Note: [Col. 1065D]

25. “By devastation.” Others, “by depopulation.” AREV.]

25. After Litorius had been destroyed, Theuderedus then made peace with the Romans. But when the Huns were ravaging the provinces of Gaul with savage devastation and overthrowing many cities, he engaged them in open battle on the Catalaunian Plains, with Aetius, the Roman commander, assisting him, and died there while fighting as the victor. The Goths, however, while Thurismund, son of King Theuderedus, was fighting, engaged so courageously that between the first and final battle nearly three hundred thousand men were laid low in that conflict.

[Note: [Col. 1065D]

26. Grial has “was brought about.” Ibid. “Of such great extent.” Florez, with Labbe, has “in so great a …” AREV.]

26. At the same time many signs in heaven and on earth preceded the event, whose prodigies indicated such a savage war. For after continual earthquakes, the moon was darkened in the eastern region; at sunset a comet appeared and shone for some time with immense brilliance. In the northern quarter the sky became red, as though made of fire or blood, with brighter lines mingled through the fiery redness and fashioned into the appearance of gleaming spears. It is not surprising that, with so great a slaughter of the fallen, so many signs should have been divinely displayed.

[Note: [Col. 1065D]

27. “Having broken through.” Labbe has “having interrupted.” AREV.]

27. The Huns, however, having been slaughtered almost to annihilation, abandoned Gaul with their king Attila and fled to Italy, after breaking into several cities. There too some died from hunger and others from heavenly blows. Moreover, an army sent by the emperor Marcian struck them with a mighty blow. They were severely afflicted and greatly reduced, and returned to their own settlements. Their king Attila died soon after he had returned.

28. After his death the nation of the Huns further devastated itself by its own destruction. Immediately great conflicts arose among his sons over possession of the kingdom. Thus the Huns, who had previously been diminished by so many disasters, again cut one another down with mutual swords. In their case this is remarkable: although every battle brings loss to peoples, these men, conversely, advance by falling. But this is because they have been set for the chastisement of the faithful, as is the Persian people.

29. For they are the rod of God’s wrath, and whenever his indignation advances against the faithful, they are scourged through these peoples, so that, corrected by their afflictions, they may restrain themselves from the desire for the world and from sin, and possess the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. This nation is so savage that, when it has suffered hunger in war, it touches the vein of a horse and thus drives hunger away by drinking its blood.

[Note: [Col. 1065D]

30. All copies agree on era 490 and the first year of Marcian; this appears to have been written in accordance with Isidore’s intention, as is clear from the following eras and from the interpolated *Chronicle of Hydatius*, to which this method of calculation corresponds. Others, however, follow a different chronology; according to their view Marcian began to reign in the year 450, to which era 488 corresponds. Grial has “son of Theuderedus.” AREV.]

30. In the Era 490, in the first year of the reign of Marcian, Turismund, son of Theuderic, was advanced to the kingship and reigned for one year. While at the very beginning of his reign he was inspiring savage and harmful hostility and acting with excessive arrogance, he was killed by his brothers Theuderic and Frigdaric.

[Note: [Col. 1066D]

31. Portucale. Other copies have *Portumcalem*, *Portucalem*, or *Portalem*. AREV.]

31. In the Era 491, in the second year of the reign of Marcian, Theuderic, succeeding to the kingship after the murder of his brother, ruled for thirteen years. Because he had provided the emperor Avitus with assistance from the Gauls in assuming the imperial dignity, he entered Spain from Aquitania with a huge army and with the permission of that same emperor Avitus, in the fifth year of his reign. King Rechiarius of the Suebi met him with a large force twelve miles from the city of Asturica, at the river called the Urbicus. Battle was immediately joined, and Rechiarius was defeated: 118 Suebi units were slaughtered, some were captured, and very many were put to flight. Finally the king himself, wounded by a weapon, fled; deprived of his followers’ protection, he was captured at the place called Portucale and brought alive before King Theuderic.

[Note: [Col. 1066D]

32. *Eulaliae.* Florez, in volume VI of *Hispania sacra*, appendix 7, published a *Chronicle of Martyrs* by a very ancient author, in which mention is made of Saint Eulalia of Mérida, not of Barcelona. See the commentary on Prudentius, p. 941. For *Maldram*, and in the following number *Maldrae*, Grial’s edition has *Masdram* and *Masdrae*, but *Maldram*, etc., seems preferable, in agreement with Florez; this is also how the name is written in the *History of the Suebi*, no. 88. AREV.]

32. After he had been killed, many of those who had survived the earlier battle surrendered themselves, while nevertheless a considerable number were slaughtered; thus the kingdom was almost destroyed, and the kingdom of the Suebi came to an end. The remaining Suebi who stayed in the farthest part of Galicia made Masila’s son, named Maldra, their king; the kingdom of the Suebi was restored. After Rechiarius had been killed, Theuderic, advancing victoriously from Galicia into Lusitania, was preparing to plunder the city of Mérida when he was terrified by apparitions of the holy martyr Eulalia. He immediately withdrew with his entire army and returned to Gaul.

33. Soon afterward he sent one part of his army, under the command of Ceurila, to the province of Baetica, and directed another part, under the commanders Singeric and Nepotian, toward Galicia; they devastated the Suebi near Lugo with savage plundering. In Gaul, Agrippinus, a count and citizen who was a rival of the Roman count Aegidius, handed Narbonne over to Theuderic in order to obtain the assistance of the Goths. Later, envoys sent by Remismund, king of the Suebi and son of Masdra, came to Theuderic, requesting peace and friendship. Theuderic likewise sent a reply to Remismund, accompanied by arms and gifts, and also sent him a wife whom he had. Theuderic again sent the envoy Sallane to Remismund. When Sallane returned to Gaul, he found that Theuderic had been killed by his brother Euric.

[Note: [Col. 1067C]

34. *(Previous column.)* *Partes.* Other copies have *partem*. In the same place: *Nobilitatem, quae ei repugnaverat*; other copies have *civitates quae ei repugnaverant*. In the same place: *Evertit*; other copies have *peremit*. *In potestatem submittit*; other copies have *in potestate sua mittit*; and *utramque* for *utrasque*. AREV.]

34. In the Era 504, in the eighth year of the reign of Leo, Euric succeeded to the kingship after his brother with the same criminal conduct, and ruled for seventeen years. Once advanced to this position and this crime, he immediately sent envoys to the emperor Leo. Without delay he ravaged the regions of Lusitania with a great assault. From there he sent another army, which captured Pamplona and Zaragoza after sending out its forces, and also brought Upper Spain under its power. The nobility of the province of Tarraconensis, which had resisted him, was overthrown by an incursion of the army. Returning to Gaul, he gained the cities of Arles and Marseille by warfare and added both to his kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1067C]

35. *Under this king, etc.* I discussed the origin of Gothic law in *Isidoriana*, chapter 92, nos. 8 and following, where I observed that some Gothic laws seem to have existed before Euric, although Euric was the first to gather them, together with others, into a single body. AREV.]

35. One day, when the Goths had been assembled for a conference, he observed that the weapons all of them held in their hands had for some time changed their natural iron appearance: on the blade or edge, some were green, some rose-colored, some saffron-colored, and some black. Under this king the Goths began to have the provisions of their laws in written form, for previously they had been governed only by custom and tradition. King Euric died at Arles, dying a natural death.

[Note: [Col. 1067D]

36. *Fludujus.* Other copies have *Fluduildus*. Aimunus calls him *Clodovaeus*. PEREZ.

In the same place: Era 521, year 10. This is found in most Isidorian manuscripts and agrees with the chronology of Isidore. Some editions assign Era 522, and Pagius places Euric’s death in Era 523, which also pleases Florez more. For *Fludvius*, Labbe reads *Hluduvicus*. For *generi*, Florez, with Grotius, has *generis sui*; Labbe has *generi sui*. AREV.]

36. In the Era 521, in the tenth year of the reign of Zeno, after Euric’s death, his son Alaric was established as ruler of the Goths at the city of Toulouse; he reigned for twenty-three years. Against him Fludujus, prince of the Franks, aspiring to the kingdom of Gaul, made war with the Burgundians assisting him. After routing the Gothic forces, he finally defeated and killed the king himself near Poitiers. Theuderic, king of Italy, when he learned of the death of his son-in-law, immediately set out from Italy, crushed the Franks, recovered the part of the kingdom that the hands of the enemy had occupied, and restored it to Gothic rule.

[Note: [Col. 1067D]

37. Era 545. Grial’s edition has Era 544, which appears to be an error, as Florez infers from the years of the emperors and from other passages of Isidore. AREV.]

37. In the Era 545, in the seventeenth year of the reign of Anastasius, Gisaleic, the son of the preceding king, born of a concubine, was made ruler at Narbonne. He reigned for four years; as low-born in origin as he was, so outstanding was he in misfortune and cowardice. Finally, when that city had been plundered by Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, Gisaleic withdrew to Barcelona amid great disgrace for himself and great slaughter of his people. He remained there until Theuderic deprived him even of the insignia of kingship through the disgrace of flight.

[Note: [Col. 1067D]

38. Some copies read: “and by Ebbane, commander of King Theuderic.” Masdeu, in volume X of *Historia de España*, p. 311, cites a *Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings* and reports that Gisaleic reigned for three years and spent one year in hiding. Others say that he reigned for fifteen years, perhaps because they join his reign to that of the succeeding Theuderic. AREV.]

38. From there he set out for Africa and sought the support of the Vandals, so that he might be restored to the kingship. When he did not obtain their assistance, he soon returned from Africa; out of fear of Theuderic he made for Aquitania, and after hiding there for one year, he returned to Spain. Twelve miles from the city of Barcelona, he was defeated in battle by a commander of King Theuderic and put to flight. He was captured beyond the river Druentius in Gaul and died there; thus he first lost his honor and afterward his life.

[Note: [Col. 1068C]

39. *Odovacro*; other copies have *Odoacre* or *Odoacro*; shortly afterward: “had reigned victoriously in Italy.” For *superstes*, which Florez retained with Grotius and the old editions, Grial’s edition and Labbe have *superstiti*. For *urbi Romae*, other copies have *Urbis regia* or *regiae urbi*. Theuderic was in Spain for eleven years; afterward, returning to Italy, he reigned jointly with Amalaric, who ruled alone for five years after Theuderic’s death, as is said below. AREV.]

39. In the Era 549, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Anastasius, Theuderic the Younger, who had long before been created consul and king at Rome by the emperor Zeno, killed King Odovacar, defeated his brother Honoulf and drove him in flight beyond the Danube frontier, and reigned in Italy for forty-nine years. After King Gisaleic had likewise been killed, he held the kingdom of Spain for fifteen years and left it to his grandson Amalaric when he died. Returning thereafter to Italy, he reigned for some time with complete prosperity; through him, too, considerable dignity was restored to the city of Rome. He rebuilt its walls and, for this service, deserved a gilded statue from the Senate.

[Note: [Col. 1068D]

40. Isidore connects Era 564 with Justinian’s first year, as can also be inferred from other passages of his work. Others assign Justinian’s first year to Era 564. Some editions less correctly read Era 566, “the first year of the reign of Justinian.” Grial’s judgment concerning Era 564 and Justinian’s first year can be found in *Isidoriana*, chapter 36, no. 15. Baronius, under the year 531, no. 12, and Pagius, at that passage, discuss the Council of Toledo held under Bishop Montanus in Amalaric’s fifth year. For *Childeberto*, other copies have *Ildeberto*. For *Narbonae*, I would prefer *Narbone*: this is certainly better, and it occurs below. AREV.]

40. In the Era 564, in the first year of the reign of Justinian I, after Theuderic had returned to Italy and died there, his grandson Amalaric reigned for five years. When he was defeated in battle near Narbonne by Childebert, king of the Franks, he fled in panic to Barcelona. Having become contemptible to everyone, he was stabbed to death by the army in the forum at Narbonne.

[Note: [Col. 1068D]

41. *Exstitissent.* This is Labbe’s reading. Grial’s edition has *exstiterunt*. Shortly afterward, *oblata, viam*; other copies have *objecta, vicem*. Bignaeus says that there were five Frankish kings; but Conrad Samuel Schurzfleisch, in *Disputatio historica civilis*, Leipzig, 1609, vol. I, dissertation 3, no. 18, observes that the passage was interpolated, for at that time there were only four Frankish kings. Compare Baronius, vol. VII, under the year 542. AREV.]

41. In the Era 569, in the sixth year of the reign of Justinian, after Amalaric, Theudis was established in Spain and reigned for seventeen years and five months. Although he was a heretic, he nevertheless granted peace to the Church, to such an extent that he allowed the Catholic bishops to assemble at Toledo and to arrange freely and without hindrance whatever matters were necessary for Church discipline. During his reign, when the Frankish kings had entered Spain with countless forces and were devastating the province of Tarraconensis by war, the Goths, under the command of Theudisclus, blocked the passes of Spain and, to everyone’s amazement, overthrew the Frankish army in a great victory. The same commander, after receiving a plea and a large sum of money, granted the remaining enemy a route for flight over the space of one day and one night. The rest of the wretched crowd, which did not reach the crossing within the allotted time, fell beneath the swords of the Goths.

42. After the success of this exceedingly fortunate victory, the Goths behaved imprudently in the crossing. For when they had crossed the straits of the Ocean against the soldiers who, after driving out the Goths, had invaded the fortress of Septem, and when they had stormed that same fortification with great force in battle, Sunday arrived. They laid down their arms so as not to defile the sacred day with battle. Taking advantage of this opportunity, the soldiers attacked them in a sudden assault and so utterly destroyed the army, which was enclosed on every side by sea and land and was inactive and unarmed, that not a single survivor remained to escape the ruin of so great a disaster.

[Note: [Col. 1069D]

43. *Mors debita*; other copies have *mors deinde*. The added phrase *indignantem animam* appears to have been taken from the final verse of the *Aeneid*:

“and life, with a groan, fled indignantly beneath the shades.” AREV.]

43. Without delay, the appointed death overtook the ruler. He was wounded in the palace by a certain man who had long before pretended to be insane in order to deceive the king. He artfully feigned madness and pierced the ruler; struck down by the wound, the king died, breathing out his indignant soul by the force of the sword. [Col. 1069C] It is said that, amid the shedding of his blood, he swore that no one should kill his assailant, saying that he had received a fitting requital for his deserts, since he himself, while still a private citizen, had killed his own commander after being instigated.

[Note: [Col. 1069D]

44. I have assigned Justinian’s twenty-third year with Labbe and Florez; in Grial’s edition the twenty-second year is assigned, apparently by mistake. For “three months,” the *Chronicle of the Visigoths* has “six months, thirteen days”; in Labbe it is printed in a different type as “seven months.” AREV.]

44. In the Era 586, in the twenty-third year of the reign of Justinian, after Theudis had been killed, Theudisclus, the commander of the preceding ruler, was placed over the Goths. He reigned for one year and three months. Because he had defiled the marriages of many powerful men through public prostitution and, on account of this, was preparing his mind for the death of many, he was forestalled by the hand of conspirators and stabbed at Seville during a banquet; pierced with a sword, he was killed.

[Note: [Col. 1069D]

45. Here too Grial’s edition, through the error mentioned above under the preceding era, gives year 23 instead of year 24, which is indicated in the note as the variant reading. There was also a variant reading for the era; but the same number, 587, was expressed both in the text and in the note. Since I did not know which reading Perez preferred, I removed that note, which contained nothing except the number of the era already appearing in the text. In Grial’s edition, *corpori* is missing after *Asciscli*. Other copies have *inferret, ossiumque, ac jumentorum horrore sacrum*, etc. AREV.]

45. In the Era 587, in the twenty-fourth year of Justinian’s reign, after Theudisclus had been killed, Agila was established as king and reigned for five years. When he made war against the city of Córdoba, he insulted the most blessed martyr Acisclus in contempt of the Catholic religion and, as a profaner, polluted the holy place of his tomb with the blood of enemies and animals. When battle was joined against the citizens of Córdoba, he deserved to suffer fitting punishment at the hands of the saints. For, struck by the vengeance of the present war, he lost both his son, who was killed there together with a large part of the army, and his entire treasury with its considerable wealth.

[Note: [Col. 1070D]

46. *Hispalim.* This is Florez’s reading with Labbe. Grial’s edition and others have *Hispali*. AREV.]

46. Defeated and driven into flight by miserable fear, he withdrew to Mérida. After some time had passed, Athanagild, seizing the tyranny in his desire to rule, defeated by military valor the army that Agila had sent against him at Seville. When the Goths saw that they were being overthrown by their own destruction and feared even more that the Roman soldiers might invade Spain under the pretext of providing assistance, they killed Agila at Mérida and surrendered themselves to Athanagild’s rule.

[Note: [Col. 1070D]

47. *Fracti atque finiti.* Florez, with others, adds: “He secretly maintained the Catholic faith and was very well disposed toward Christians.” AREV.]

47. In the Era 592, in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of Justinian, after Agila had been killed, Athanagild held the kingdom that he had seized for fourteen years. When he had earlier assumed the tyranny and was attempting to deprive Agila of the kingdom, he had requested military assistance from the emperor Justinian. Later he was unable to drive those troops from the borders of his kingdom. Conflict has continued against them up to the present: previously they were cut down in frequent battles, but now they have been broken and destroyed by many disasters. Athanagild died a natural death at Toledo, while the kingdom remained vacant for five months.

[Note: [Col. 1070D]

48. “Era 605, in the second year of the reign,” etc. Florez shows that this should be retained with Grial’s edition, although other editions assign different numbers. From Isidore it can be inferred that Liuva reigned for only three years, whereas John of Biclaro counts five years of his reign. The words “of King Liuva,” which are absent from other editions, are later judged by Florez to be superfluous. I believe that *hinc autem* should be read here; the sense then proceeds correctly. AREV.]

48. In the Era 605, in the second year of the reign of Justin the Younger, after Athanagild, Liuva was placed over the Goths at Narbonne and reigned for three years. In the second year after he had assumed the principate, he appointed his brother Leovigild not only as his successor but also as his partner in the kingship, and placed him in charge of the administration of Spain, while he himself was content with the kingdom of Gaul. Thus the kingdom came to have two rulers, although no power tolerates a partner. In the chronological reckoning, only one year is assigned to King Liuva; the remaining years are counted for his brother Leovigild.

[Note: [Col. 1070D]

49. Era 606. Labbe has Era 607, which does not agree with the chronological calculation. Grotius and Labbe have *adepto Hispaniae principatu*, omitting *Galliae*. For *praeclare sortitus est*, Labbe has *praeda resortitus est*. For *Sabaria*, other historians have *Sabaudia*. Florez, with Grotius, has: “He also routed, in a different battle, the soldiers of Justin whom Athanagild had summoned to his aid, and he captured certain fortifications,” etc. Concerning the war and martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild, see, if desired, what was said in *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, no. 25 and following. AREV.]

49. In the Era 606, in the third year of the reign of Justin the Younger, Leovigild, having obtained authority over Spain and Gaul, resolved to enlarge his kingdom by war and increase his wealth. Through his zeal, and with the army’s unanimous support, he achieved many splendid victories. He conquered the Cantabrians; he captured Aregia; all Sabaria was defeated by him; and many rebellious cities of Spain yielded to his arms. He also routed the soldiers in a separate battle and recovered by fighting certain fortifications that they had occupied. Then he overcame his son Hermenegild, who was rebelling against his authority, after besieging him. Finally he made war upon the Suebi and, with remarkable speed, transferred their kingdom to the rights of his own people. He gained possession of most of Spain. Previously the Gothic people had been confined within narrow boundaries, but the error of impiety darkened the glory of such great valor in him.

50. Finally, filled with the madness of Arian perfidy, he stirred up a persecution against the Catholics and banished many bishops into exile. He took away the revenues and privileges of the churches, and by threats drove many into the Arian plague. He deceived many others, without persecution, by enticing them with gold and possessions. Among the other contagions of his heresy, he even dared to rebaptize Catholics, not only members of the common people but also men of priestly rank, such as Vincent of Zaragoza, who was made an apostate from the episcopate and, as it were, hurled from heaven into hell.

[Note: [Col. 1071D]

51. *Exstitit*, etc. The subject is Leovigild, as is clear. Risco, in volume XXX of *Hispania sacra*, p. 130, rightly censures Ambrosio de Morales and Francisco de Padilla, who had attributed this to Vincent of Zaragoza. AREV.]

51. He was also harmful to some of his own people. For whenever he saw men of the highest nobility and power, he either beheaded them or, after confiscating their wealth, proscribed them and sent the proscribed into exile. He was the first to enrich the treasury and the first to enlarge the royal fisc with the spoils of citizens and the booty of enemies. He was also the first among his people to sit upon a throne clothed in royal garments. Before him, both dress and the manner of sitting were shared equally by the people and the kings. He also founded a city in Celtiberia and named it Recopolis after his son. In the laws, too, he corrected what seemed to have been disorderly provisions established by Euric, adding many laws that had been omitted and removing many that were superfluous. He reigned for eighteen years and died a natural death at Toledo.

[Note: [Col. 1071D]

52. “In the fourth year.” Florez corrected this from John of Biclaro and other passages of this chronicle, since Grial’s edition read “in the third year.” For *gentis imperium*, other copies have *gentem imperio*. For *detersa*, Florez, with Grial’s edition, has *deserta*. Grotius, Labbe, and the author of the *Life of Saint Isidore* in the Bollandists have *detersa*. See the note to no. 13 of this *Life* in *Isidoriana*, appendix 2, vol. II. AREV.]

52. In the Era 624, in the third year of the reign of Maurice, after Leovigild’s death, his son Recared was crowned king. He was endowed with religious devotion and was very unlike his father in character. The former was irreligious and exceedingly ready for war; this one was devout in faith and distinguished by peace. The former enlarged the dominion of his people by the arts of war; this one gloriously exalted that same people by the trophy of faith. At the very beginning of his reign he embraced the Catholic faith and recalled the peoples of the entire Gothic nation, having abandoned the stain of their long-standing error, to the worship of the true faith.

[Col. 1072A] [Note: [Col. 1072D]

53. Florez, with Grotius, has: “the unity in God, the Son.” Labbe has: “the unity, God the Son.” AREV.]

53. He then assembled a synod of bishops from various provinces of Spain and Gaul for the condemnation of the Arian heresy. The same most religious ruler attended that council and confirmed its proceedings by his presence and signature. Together with all his people, he renounced the perfidy that the Gothic nation had hitherto learned from the teaching of Arius, and proclaimed the unity of the three persons in God; that the Son was begotten consubstantially from the Father; that the Holy Spirit proceeded inseparably from the Father and the Son; and that the Spirit of both was one, whence they too are one.

[Note: [Col. 1072D]

54. Other copies have *fidei susceptae auxilio*. For *movit*, other copies likewise have *movit*. The phrase appears to have been taken from Florus’s use of *movere lacertos* at the end of the preface: “The empire … flexes its muscles under the emperor Trajan.” For *certaminis*, Labbe has *utilitatis*. AREV.]

54. He also waged war gloriously against hostile peoples with the aid of the faith he had embraced. When the Franks invaded Gaul with a force of nearly sixty thousand armed men, he sent the commander Claudius against them and triumphed with glorious success. No Gothic victory in Spain was ever greater in war or equal to it. Many thousands of the enemy were overthrown and captured; the remaining part of the army, contrary to expectation, took flight, and while the Goths pursued them from behind, they were slaughtered all the way to the borders of their own kingdom. He often also flexed his muscles against Roman insolence and Vascon incursions. Hence he seems to have practiced not so much warfare as the training of his people, as though in a gymnasium for combat.

[Note: [Col. 1072D]

55. Florez added several things, which Labbe printed in a different type: “He ruled. Many who desired to seize tyranny against him were also exposed and could not carry out the plan of their plotting. He was,” etc. AREV.]

55. The provinces that his father had conquered by war, he preserved through peace, arranged with equity, and governed with moderation. He was gentle, mild, and of outstanding goodness. He possessed such grace in his face and carried such benevolence in his spirit that, flowing into the minds of all, he drew even the wicked toward affection for him. He was so generous that he restored to their rightful owners the wealth of private persons and the estates of churches that his father’s stain had attached to the fisc. He was so merciful that he often relaxed the people’s taxes through generous acts of clemency.

56. He also enriched many with possessions and raised very many to positions of honor. Storing his wealth among the wretched and his treasures among the needy, he knew that the kingdom had been granted to him for this purpose: that he might use it beneficially. Having begun well, he achieved a good end. For he finally crowned with a public confession of repentance the faith of true glory that he had received at the beginning of his reign. He passed away peacefully at Toledo after reigning for fifteen years.

[Note: [Col. 1073C]

57. *(Previous column.)* Florez, with Grial’s edition and John of Biclaro, assigns the nineteenth year of Maurice; others give different years, less correctly. See the note to no. 52. AREV.]

57. In the Era 639, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Maurice, after King Recared, his son Liuva reigned for two years. He was born of an ignoble mother but marked by virtue in his character. In the first bloom of youth, Wicteric, having seized the tyranny, deprived him of the kingdom while he was innocent and killed him after cutting off his right hand, in the twentieth year of his life and the second of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 1073D]

58. In Grial’s edition there is a numerical error, namely DCLXI instead of DCXLI, as Florez noted; but he apparently did not notice that Grial had corrected the error in the errata. Florez, with Labbe, has *Segontiae*; Grial’s edition has *Sagontia*, and others *Segontia*. AREV.]

58. In the Era 641, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Maurice, after Liuva had been killed, Wicteric claimed the kingdom that he had invaded while Liuva was alive and reigned for seven years. He was indeed a vigorous man in the art of war, but nevertheless without victory. For although he often attempted battle against the Roman army, he accomplished nothing sufficiently glorious except that, through his commanders, he captured some soldiers at Segontia. During his life he committed many unlawful acts; in death, because he had operated by the sword, he perished by the sword. The death of the innocent did not remain unavenged in him: he was killed during a meal by a conspiracy of certain men, and his body was carried out and buried in disgrace.

[Note: [Col. 1073D]

59. We restore Phocas’s eighth year with Labbe and Florez, since Grial’s edition and others give the sixth year, through the carelessness of copyists or the negligence of editors. Moreover, when Florez notes that Grial’s edition incorrectly placed Era 548 after 648, he does not notice that this error too had been observed and corrected in the errata. Others have the sixteenth year of his life. AREV.]

59. In the Era 648, in the eighth year of the reign of Phocas, Gundemar reigned after Wicteric for two years. In one expedition he devastated the Vascones; in another he besieged the Roman army. He died a natural death at Toledo.

[Note: [Col. 1073D]

60. *Permovens*; other copies have *promovens*. Florez, with Labbe, has: “Christ is proclaimed through the truth; in this I rejoice, and I will rejoice.” *Fuit autem*, etc. AREV.]

60. In the Era 650, in the second year of the reign of Heraclius, the most Christian Sisebut was called to the royal dignity after Gundemar. He reigned for eight years and six months. At the beginning of his reign, when he moved the Jews toward the Christian faith, he did indeed display zeal, but not according to knowledge; for by force he compelled those whom he ought to have invited by reason of faith. Yet, as it is written, whether by pretext or by truth, so long as Christ is proclaimed. He was polished in speech, learned in judgment, and to a considerable degree trained in literary knowledge. In judgments he was vigorous and outstanding in justice and piety, benevolent in mind, distinguished in the splendor of his reign, and renowned also for his military achievements and victories.

[Note: [Col. 1073D]

61. After *reduced*, Labbe adds in italic type [Col. 1074C] “through his commander Rechila,” which Florez followed. Labbe and Grotius omit *alii veneno*. For *habetur*, Florez, with Labbe, has *abiit*; but in Labbe I think *obiit* should be read. AREV.]

61. He sent an army and brought the rebellious Asturians back under his authority. Through his commanders he defeated the Ruccones, who were hemmed in on every side by steep mountains. He also twice triumphed successfully in person over the Romans and, by storming certain of their cities, subjected them to himself; he emptied all the remaining ones between the straits, and afterward the Gothic nation easily brought them under its authority. He was so merciful after victory that he freed, upon payment of a price, many captives whom his army had reduced to slavery as war booty; his treasury became the ransom of the captives. Some say that he was killed by a natural illness, others by an excessive draught of medicine, and others by poison. His death was mourned not only by the devout but also by the best of the laity. He left behind his young son Recared, who after his father’s death is regarded as having been ruler for only a few days, since death intervened.

[Note: [Col. 1074D]

62. *In Hispaniis.* This is Labbe’s reading, and I think *in Hispanis* in Grial’s edition is an error, which Florez also printed. For *patriciorum*, other copies have *praefectorum*. AREV.]

62. In the Era 659, in the tenth year of the reign of Heraclius, the most glorious Suintila, by divine favor, took up the scepters of the kingdom. Having obtained the office of commander under King Sisebut, he subdued the Roman camps and defeated the Ruccones. After ascending to the summit of royal power, he gained by battle the remaining cities in Spain that were held by Roman hands, and carried away, with marvelous good fortune, a triumphal glory greater than that of the other kings. He was the first to possess the monarchy of the whole of Spain within the straits of the Ocean, a distinction granted to none of the rulers before him. His virtuous renown in that war was increased by the capture of two patricians: through his prudence he made one his own, and through the valor of battle he subjected the other to himself.

[Note: [Col. 1074D]

63. *Ologitin*; other copies have *Ologicus* or *Ologitum*. The manuscripts vary greatly in these proper names, as in *Roccones* for *Ruccones* and *Riccimirus* for *Racimirus*. AREV.]

63. At the beginning of his reign he also undertook an expedition against the incursions of the Vascones, who were troubling the province of Tarraconensis. There the mountain-dwelling peoples were so terrified by fear of his arrival that immediately, as though recognizing the rights due to him, they laid down their weapons, stretched out their hands ready for supplication, humbly submitted their necks to him, gave hostages, and built the city of Ologitin at their own expense and through their own labor for the Goths, promising to obey his kingdom and authority and to carry out whatever was commanded.

[Col. 1074C] [Note: [Col. 1074D]

64. This was written while Suintila was alive. Yet he was condemned at the Fourth Council of Toledo, at which Isidore subscribed. PEBEZ.

In the same place: I explained in *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, nos. 20 and following, the difficulty raised by Perez: why Isidore praises Suintila so highly here but condemns him at the Fourth Council of Toledo. AREV.]

64. Besides these praises of military glory, he possessed many virtues of royal majesty: faith, prudence, industry, careful judgment in judicial matters, and vigorous concern in governing the kingdom. He was exceptionally generous toward all and very ready to show mercy to the needy and destitute. Thus he deserved to be called not only ruler of the peoples but also father of the poor.

[Note: [Col. 1074D]

65. *Concessu patrio*; other copies have *consessu patrio*; and *ascensione* for *successione*, and *comparatis* or *comportatis* for *computatis*. AREV.]

65. His son Racimirus was taken into partnership in the kingdom and rejoiced with his father upon the same throne. In his infancy the splendor of his sacred character shone out so brightly that in him, both in merits and in countenance, the likeness of his father’s virtues was already foreshadowed. For his sake the ruler of heaven and of the human race should be entreated that, just as he now exists as his father’s partner by paternal appointment, so after his parent’s long reign he may also be worthy to succeed to the kingdom. Thus, when the times of the Gothic kings are reckoned from the beginning of King Athanaric to the fifth year of the most glorious ruler Suintila, the kingdom of the Goths is found, by God’s favor, to have extended over 256 years.

*The same Isidore’s recapitulation in praise of the Goths.*

[Note: [Col. 1075C]

66. In the title, some copies have *capitulatio* instead of *recapitulatio*. And immediately afterward: “The Goths, sprung from Magog, son of Japheth, are also shown to have been born of one origin together with the Scythians.” Hence, etc. For *Septentrionis*, one copy has *Occidentis*; and *Danubium transeuntes* instead of *transgressoque Danubio*; and *arma sumunt* instead of *regem sibi ex sua turba legunt*. AREV.]

66. The most ancient origin of the Goths was from Magog, son of Japheth; from him also arose the race of the Scythians. For these same Goths are shown to have been born of Scythian origin. Hence they do not differ greatly even in name. For when a letter was changed and removed, they were called Getae, as though they were Scythians. Thus, dwelling in the icy ridges of the North around the Scythian kingdoms, they possessed, together with the other peoples, whatever mountain strongholds there were. Driven from those settlements by the onslaught of the Hunnic nation, and having crossed the Danube, they surrendered themselves to the Romans. But when they could not endure the Romans’ injuries, they became indignant, chose a king for themselves from their own people, invaded Thrace, ravaged Italy, captured the besieged City, attacked Gaul, and, once the Pyrenees had been opened, reached as far as Spain. There they established their seat of life and their imperial power.

[Note: [Col. 1075D]

67. *Tam extollens*; other copies have *tam excellens*. Alvarus of Córdoba alludes to this passage of Isidore in letter 20, addressed “To the Transgressor”: “But so that you may know who I am and avoid me more completely by keeping silent, listen to Virgil:

‘They despise death, the Getae, with a praised wound.’

And also: ‘The Getes, he says, toward which horse does he proceed?’ Hence the poet’s line also exists: ‘On one side let the Dacian press, on the other let the Getae attack.’ I am he, I am he, whom Alexander thought should be avoided, whom Pyrrhus feared, whom Caesar dreaded. Of us also our Jerome says: ‘He has a horn on his forehead; flee far away.’” Florez, from a marginal note in *Bibliotheca veterum Hispaniae*, vol. I, p. 349 of the first edition, observes that those verses are falsely attributed to Virgil. Isidore indeed does not name Virgil. AREV.]

67. The people are swift by nature, lively in intelligence, confident in the strength of their courage, strong in bodily vigor, tall and lofty in stature, distinguished in bearing and appearance, ready with their hands, and hardened against wounds, as the poet says of them:

[Col. 1075C] “They despise death, the Getae, with a praised wound.”

Their greatness in war and the excellence of their glorious victories were so immense that Rome herself, conqueror of all peoples, was subjected to the yoke of captivity and became an addition to the Getic triumphs; mistress of all nations, she served them as a handmaid.

[Note: [Col. 1076C]

68. *Hos*, etc. Other copies have: “These peoples wore down all the nations of Europe”; and *quantum opinione* instead of *quam opinione*. AREV.]

68. All the peoples of Europe trembled before them, and the barriers of the Alps yielded to them. Even the Vandal barbarism, often considered so formidable, was terrified not merely by their presence but driven to flight by their reputation. Through the strength of the Goths the Alans were destroyed. The Suebi, too, confined until now within the inaccessible corners of Spain, experienced the danger of defeat even from their arms and lost, with still greater disgrace, the kingdom that they had held in slothful torpor, although it is indeed astonishing that they have retained it so long without having tested the need for defense.

[Note: [Col. 1076D]

69. *Quo pergit*; other copies have *quod pergit*. AREV.]

69. But who could describe the magnitude of the Gothic nation’s strength, since, whereas many peoples have scarcely been permitted to rule for the sake of prayers and gifts, liberty came to these men more through armed encounter than through requested peace; and whenever the necessity of war confronted them, they employed strength rather than entreaties? Moreover, they are sufficiently distinguished in the arts of warfare, and they fight on horseback not only with spears but also with javelins. They advance not merely in cavalry battle but also on foot. Nevertheless, they rely more heavily on the swift charge of their horsemen; hence the poet says: “The Getan, he says, travels on horseback.”

[Col. 1076B] [Note: [Col. 1076D]

70. “And he sees Spain itself.” So Grialius’s edition reads, and I understand it thus: “the Roman soldier sees all these peoples serving the Goths, and Spain itself.” Florezius, together with Labbe and Grotius, reads: “and Spain itself saw”; I consider this less correct. AREV.]

70. For they especially delight in training with weapons and practicing preliminary engagements. They conduct contests of play in daily exercise. Until now they lacked only this experience of arms: they did not undertake naval warfare at sea. But after the prince Sisebut, by heavenly grace, assumed the scepters of the kingdom, they advanced through his efforts to such a height of fortunate prowess that they approached not only lands but the very seas with their weapons; and the Roman soldier serves those whom he sees so many peoples—and Spain itself—serving.

## History of the Vandals

[Note: [Col. 1076D]

71. “Era 444” is correctly printed in Grialius’s edition; in the others the numbers diverge enormously. The words “two years before the invasion of the Roman city” are those of Orosius, *Book VII, chapter 40*; and perhaps Orosius means the first invasion, during the lifetime of Radagaisus, about which he speaks in *Book VII, chapter 37*. Perezius noted that in an old manuscript the work is entitled *Chronicle of the Vandals*, not *History*. In place of *Veranianum*, some have *Verimianum* or *Verunianum*. AREV.]

71. Era 444: two years before the invasion of the Roman city, when Stilicho stirred up the Alans, Suevi, and Vandals, these peoples, having crossed the Rhine River, invaded Gaul, overthrew the Franks, and, advancing directly, reached as far as the Pyrenees. The passes of the Pyrenees were occupied by Didymus and Veranianus, most noble and powerful Roman brothers; and, being kept out of Spain for three years, they wandered through the neighboring provinces of Gaul. But after those same brothers—who had guarded the passes of the Pyrenees with a private force—were killed by Caesar Constantius on suspicion of tyranny, though innocent and guilty of no offense, in era 446 the aforementioned peoples invaded the provinces of Spain.

[Note: [Col. 1076D]

72. In Grialius’s text the era is given as 456, while the note gives the variant reading 446, which must certainly be preferred with Labbe, although Florezius, on grounds not without merit, argues that era 447 should be substituted. In place of *discursionibus*, some have *discursibus*. AREV.]

72. Era 446: when the Vandals, Alans, and Suevi occupied Spain, they inflicted slaughter and devastation through bloody raids, burned cities, and exhausted the plundered wealth, so that human flesh was devoured by peoples driven by the force of hunger. Mothers ate their children; beasts, accustomed to the corpses of those dying by the sword, hunger, and plague, were also driven into the destruction of the living. Thus, while the four scourges raged throughout all Spain, the prediction once foretold in writing by the prophets of divine wrath was fulfilled.

[Note: [Col. 1077C]

73. In Grialius’s edition era 459 is incorrectly printed instead of 449. Gunderic, successor of his father Godigisel, is said to have reigned in Gallaecia for eighteen years, counting the year 411, when the Vandals obtained the kingdom of Gallaecia, and the year 428, when he died, although he had already withdrawn to Baetica in 420. I have discussed this Gunderic more fully in the prolegomena to Dracontius, no. 96, p. 72, and again no. 115, p. 89. The Erbas Mountains mentioned here seem to be the mountains now called the Arbas, between Oviedo and León. Some call them the Erbasian Mountains, others the Nervasian or Nervosian Mountains. See Florezius, *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XV, p. 61. The same Florezius, vol. IX, pp. 100 ff., observes from Hydatius and others that the Basilica of Saint Vincent was formerly the principal church of Hispalis, although it was distinct from the church now dedicated to Saint Vincent, which stood on the site where the cathedral church now is. AREV.]

73. Era 459: after the terrible destruction inflicted by the scourges with which Spain was struck, the Barbarians at last, through God’s mercy, turned toward making peace and divided the provinces among themselves by lot for possession. The Vandals and Suevi occupied Gallaecia; the Alans, Lusitania and the province of Carthaginia; while the Vandals called Silingui, leaving Gallaecia and, after devastating the islands of the province of Tarraconensis, returned and drew Baetica by lot. The Spaniards, afflicted by the scourges, submitted themselves to the servitude of the dominant Barbarians in the remaining cities and fortified places.

The first king of the Vandals to succeed in Spain was Gunderic, who reigned for eighteen years in the regions of Gallaecia. While he was besieging the Suevic nation in the Erbas Mountains after breaking the peace treaty, he abandoned the siege of the Suevi and plundered the Balearic Islands of the province of Tarraconensis. Then, after destroying Carthago Spartaria, he crossed into Baetica with all the Vandals, demolished Hispalis, and, after perpetrating a massacre, handed it over to plunder. When, with the authority of royal power, he irreverently stretched out his hands against the Basilica of the martyr Vincent in that city, he was immediately seized by a demon at the temple doors through God’s judgment and died.

[Note: [Col. 1077D]

74. I restore era 466 from Florezius; Grialius’s edition gives era 468, and Labbe’s 467. In place of *Gisericus*, some have *Gessericus*, *Gaisericus*, or, as is now more usual, *Gensericus*. In place of *possiderent*, some have *possederant*. I have noted several things about Genseric in the prolegomena to Dracontius, no. 112, p. 87 ff. AREV.]

74. Era 466. Giseric, Gunderic’s brother, succeeded to the kingdom and reigned for forty years. Having become an apostate from Catholicism, he is said to have been the first to pass over to the Arian faithlessness. From the coast of the province of Baetica he crossed over to Mauretania and Africa with all the Vandals and their families, leaving Spain behind. Unable to resist him, Valentinian the Younger, emperor of the West, sent an offer of peace and granted him, as though peacefully, that part of Africa which the Vandals occupied, after receiving from him an oath under the condition that he would invade nothing further.

[Note: [Col. 1078D]

75. “Nothing.” Some have “nothing now,” which Florezius followed. AREV.]

75. But he, whose friendship had seemed beyond all doubt, violated the sanctity of his oath and, under the pretext of peace, invaded Carthage by treachery. After subjecting its citizens to various kinds of torture, he converted all its wealth to his own possession. Then he ravaged Sicily, besieged Panormus, introduced the Arian pestilence throughout all Africa, expelled priests from the churches, made very many martyrs, and, in accordance with the prophecy of Daniel, by altering the sacred rites, handed the churches of the saints over to the enemies of Christ. He ordered that they should no longer be places of divine worship but dwellings for his own people.

[Note: [Col. 1078D]

76. “And the Illyrians.” So the manuscripts and printed editions read. Florezius has “and the Illyricians.” In Grialius’s edition: “into the province of Carthaginia.” The reading “in the province of Carthaginia” is preferable, with Labbe and others. In place of *dispositione*, some have *intentione*, others *dispensatione*. AREV.]

76. Against him Theodosius the Younger, emperor of the East, prepared a war that did not come to fruition. For while the Huns were devastating Thrace and Illyricum, the army sent against the Vandals was recalled from Sicily to defend the Thracians and Illyrians. The emperor Majorian, coming from Italy to Spain, had prepared several ships for himself in the province of Carthaginia to cross against the Vandals. But, informed by traitors, the Vandals seized them from the coast of Carthaginia. Thus Majorian, frustrated in his plan, returned to Italy and was killed after being treacherously ensnared by Ricchimir the patrician.

[Note: [Col. 1078D]

77. “Ginsericus” occurs in an old manuscript instead of “Gisericus.” PEREZ.

Ibid. Some have: “the wife of Valentinian, after leaving the City.” AREV.]

77. When this became known, Giseric, not content with ravaging Africa alone, arrived by ship and entered Rome. After plundering the wealth of the Romans for fourteen days, he took with him Valentinian’s widow, his daughters, and many thousands of captives. Soon he returned to Carthage; and, when peace had been requested through ambassadors from the emperor, he sent Valentinian’s widow back to Constantinople. He united one of her daughters to his own son Hugneric in lawful marriage. Thus, after the disasters suffered by many provinces and the plunder and slaughter of Christians, he died in the fortieth year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 1078D]

78. In Grialius’s edition the era is given as 508; in others, 501. Florezius maintains that it was era 506, based on Hydatius and other considerations. In place of “Giseric’s son,” some have “Gunderic’s son”; and below, “and all the clergy of the sacred order.” AREV.]

78. Era 506. After Giseric, Ugneric, Giseric’s son, reigned for seven years and five months. He had in marriage Valentinian’s daughter, whom his father had brought captive from Rome together with her mother. He too, inflamed by Arian fury, persecuted the Catholics throughout Africa more savagely than his father, removed the churches, and sent priests and clergy of every order into exile. He also banished approximately four thousand monks and laypeople to harsher exiles, made them martyrs, and cut out the tongues of confessors; yet, with their tongues cut out, they continued to speak perfectly to the end.

[Col. 1079A] [Note: [Col. 1079C]

79. Labbe: “the bishop whom the stain of the contagion could not defile with Arian poisons.” “Ugneric,” etc. AREV.]

79. Then Laetus, bishop of the city of Neptis, was gloriously crowned with martyrdom. When he could not be defiled by the stain of the Arian contagion through various punishments, he suddenly gained heaven as a victor. But Ugneric, amid the countless massacres arising from his impieties, which he had inflicted upon the Catholics, miserably ended his life in the eighth year of his reign, with all his inner organs spilling out, like his father Arius.

[Note: [Col. 1079C]

80. Florezius, together with Labbe, adopts era 514. Grialius’s edition has 515. AREV.]

80. Era 514. Guntamund succeeded Ugneric and reigned for twelve years. Immediately restoring peace to the Church, he recalled the Catholics from exile.

[Note: [Col. 1079D]

81. Trasemund is called by others Transimund, Transemund, Trasimund, or Trasamund. AREV.]

81. Era 526. After Guntamund’s death, Trasemund reigned for twenty-seven years and four months. Full of Arian madness, he persecuted the Catholics, closed the churches, and sent 120 bishops from the whole African Church into exile in Sardinia. He died at Carthage. In his time Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, became renowned for our doctrine.

[Note: [Col. 1079D]

82. Grialius’s edition gives era 554, with the variant reading 553 in the note; we prefer the latter with Florezius, on the basis of what was said under no. 78. Grotius, incorrectly, has “after Guntamund” instead of “after Trasemund.” In place of *restauraret*, some have *restitueret*. AREV.]

82. Era 553. After Trasemund, Ilderic, Ugneric’s son, born from the daughter of the emperor Valentinian, reigned for seven years and three months. Bound by an oath imposed by his predecessor Trasemund—not to open churches to Catholics or restore their privileges in his kingdom—he nevertheless ordered, before he became king, lest he violate the religion of the oath, that the Catholic priests be brought back from exile and the churches opened. Gilimer, having assumed tyrannical power, deprived him of the kingdom and consigned him and his sons to prison custody.

[Note: [Col. 1079D]

83. Grialius’s edition gives era 561; Florezius, together with Labbe, gives era 560. In place of *visitatione*, some have *incitatione*, others *visitatione nocturna*; I prefer *visione nocturna*. In place of *Guntemirum*, some have *Gunthimerum*; in place of *versum*, Labbe translates “turned,” while Florezius, with Grotius, has “turning.” Florezius notes and proves at length either that Saint Isidore followed a copy of the Chronicle of Tunnensis in which the years of the Vandal kings had been incorrectly arranged, or that some copyist adapted the eras to the regnal years in which an error in the numbers had occurred; for the eras correspond to the regnal years while preserving the same numerical relation. But the true chronology of the Vandal kings is this: Gunderic took Carthage in the year 439 and died in 477; Hunneric died in 484; Guntamund in 496; Trasemund in 523; Hilderic in 530; and Gilimer in 533. AREV.]

83. Era 560. Gilimer seized the kingdom through tyranny, cruelly destroying many nobles of the African province and confiscating the property of many others. Against him the emperor Justinian sent an army under the command of Belisarius, master of the soldiers, at the instigation of Bishop Laetus, who had been made a martyr by Ugneric, king of the Vandals. When battle was joined, Belisarius first defeated and killed Guntemir and Gebamund, the king’s brothers, in the initial engagement; then he put Gilimer himself to flight. He captured Africa in the ninety-seventh year after the Vandals’ entry.

[Note: [Col. 1080D]

84. In an old manuscript, era 563 occurs instead of 564. PEREZ.]

84. At Belisarius’s very approach, before the battle took place, the tyrant Gilimer killed King Ilderic together with certain relatives of his family. Belisarius, however, captured the tyrant Gilimer and brought him to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople, together with the wealth acquired through the plunder of the provinces and Africa. Thus the kingdom of the Vandals, together with its people and lineage, was destroyed in era 564. It had lasted 113 years, from King Gunderic to the death of Gilimer.

## History of the Suevi

[Note: [Col. 1080D]

85. “Singilium.” Some have “Singilim” instead of “Singilium.” PEREZ.

Ibid. Florezius restored era 447 from the Chronicle of Hydatius and other records. Grialius’s edition, together with Labbe, establishes era 446. AREV.]

85. Era 447. The Suevi, under their prince Hermeric, entered Spain together with the Alans and Vandals and occupied all Gallaecia with the Vandals. When the Vandals crossed over to Africa, the Suevi alone received Gallaecia by lot. Hermeric ruled them in Spain for thirty-two years. The Gallaecians, however, maintained their own kingdom in part of the province. Hermeric repeatedly plundered them through continual devastation, but at last, overcome by illness, made peace with them and appointed his son Recchila as his successor in the kingdom. Recchila, sent with a large part of the army, engaged Andevotus, commander of the Roman forces, in battle at the river Singilius in the province of Baetica, defeated him, and seized his great stores of gold and silver. From there he entered Emerita, which he had besieged, and added the city he had captured to his own kingdom. His father Hermeric, afflicted by a prolonged illness for seven years, died.

[Note: [Col. 1080D]

86. Grialius’s edition gives era 478; Florezius, 479. Florezius counts eight years of Recchila’s reign, but in such a way that the first year is included in this number. Grialius’s edition has seven years, and the note has eight, from an old manuscript. In place of *Emeritae*, which others report, Grialius’s edition has *Emeritam*. AREV.]

86. Era 479. After Hermeric’s death, his son Recchila reigned for eight years. After his father’s death, having captured Hispalis, he brought the provinces of Baetica and Carthaginia under his power; then he ended his life at Emerita, reportedly while still practicing the religion of the Gentiles.

[Col. 1080C] [Note: [Col. 1080D]

87. All the best editions agree on era 486. In place of *Theuderedi*, some write *Theuderici*, others *Theodorici*. It is the same king who is shortly afterward called Theuderic. In place of *initio regni*, some have *initia regni*. Florezius, together with Labbe, reads “he invades, and after treacherously breaking into the city of Ilerda, he carried out a great captivity there.” “The Carthaginians,” etc. This seems to have been taken from Hydatius.

Ibid. “Nine years.” An old manuscript has “eight years.” AREV.]

87. Era 486. Recchiarius, son of Recchila, having become a Catholic, succeeded to the kingdom and reigned for nine years. He married the daughter of Theuderic, king of the Goths. At the beginning of his reign he auspiciously began by plundering the Vascones; soon afterward he went to his father-in-law Theuderic and, returning through the region of Caesaraugusta, devastated it with Gothic assistance. He invaded the province of Tarraconensis, which was subject to the Roman Empire. He delivered the regions of Carthaginia, which his father Recchila had restored to the Romans, over to plunder. Finally, when Theuderic, king of the Goths, entered Spain, Recchiarius engaged him in battle, was first put to flight, and then captured and killed.

[Note: [Col. 1081B]

88. “Without delay.” I consider this genuine, with Labbe and others. Grialius’s edition has “and soon.” AREV.]

88. Era 495. After Recchiarius had been destroyed, the Suevi who remained in the farthest part of Gallaecia appointed Maldra, son of Massila, as their king. Soon they divided into two parts: one called Frantane king, the other Maldra. Without delay, after Frantane died, the Suevi who had been with him followed Recchimundus; and, after making peace with Maldra, they jointly plundered parts of Lusitania. Maldra, however, was strangled by his own men in the third year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 1081B]

89. “Remismundus.” Others have “Reccimundus,” “Recchimundus,” or “Rechimundus.” In place of *Auregensium*, which Florezius says should be preferred, others have *Auriensium* or *Arigensium*. AREV.]

89. Era 498. After Maldra was killed, disagreement over royal power arose between Frumarius and Remismundus. Frumarius, however, with the band of Suevi he commanded, devastated the district of the city of Flavia with severe destruction. Remismundus, meanwhile, ravaged the neighboring coastal districts of the Auregensian and Lucensian districts.

[Note: [Col. 1081C]

90. “From there to Lusitania.” It is cited in the letter of Innocent III to Peter of Compostela. Isidore, in the *Chronicles*, places it under the heading “On the Suevi.”

Ibid. “Having recalled.” Florezius, together with Labbe, has “having summoned.” AREV.]

90. Era 502. After Frumarius died, Remismundus, having recalled all the Suevi under his dominion by royal right, restored peace with the Gallaecians and sent ambassadors of alliance to Theuderic, king of the Goths. From him he also received, through ambassadors, arms and a wife. From there he crossed into Lusitania. He plundered Conimbriga, which had been deceived by the peace agreement. Olyssipona too was occupied by him, after Lusidius, its own citizen who governed it, surrendered it to him.

In his time Ajax, a Galatian by birth who had become an Arian apostate, emerged among the Suevi, with the support of their king, as an enemy of the Catholic faith and of the divine Trinity. He brought this poisonous virus from the Gothic region of Gaul and infected the whole nation of the Suevi with the stain of deadly faithlessness. After many Suevic kings continued in the Arian heresy, Theudemir at last assumed royal power.

[Note: [Col. 1082B]

91. “Miro began in era 609,” from the Second Council of Braga. PEREZ.

Ibid. Labbe has “against the Romans, the Roccones.” In Perezius’s note, “Ruccones” occurs in an old manuscript; this same form appears in the text, and perhaps “Roccones” should therefore be read in the note. See John of Biclaro, under the year 572, below. Labbe: “He came against his rebellious son to besiege Hispalis and brought his life to an end.” AREV.

“Ruccones” in an old manuscript.]

91. He immediately destroyed the error of Arian impiety and restored the Suevi to the Catholic faith, with the support of Martin, bishop of the monastery of Dumium, distinguished for faith and learning. Through his efforts the peace of the Church was enlarged, and many institutions concerning ecclesiastical discipline were established in the regions of Gallaecia. After Theudemir, Miro became prince of the Suevi and reigned for thirteen years. In the second year of his reign he made war against the Ruccones. Then he went to assist Leovigild, king of the Goths, against his rebellious son, to capture Hispalis, and there brought his life to an end.

[Note: [Col. 1082C]

92. “Audeca” occurs in an old manuscript instead of “Andeca.”

Ibid. “Of the presbyterate.” Others have “of a presbyter”; and *congruenti* instead of *congrua*. AREV.]

92. His son Heboricus succeeded him in the kingdom. Andeca, however, seizing tyrannical power, deprived him of the kingdom and condemned him to become a monk in a monastery; for this sentence was not long delayed. For Leovigild, king of the Goths, soon made war upon the Suevi, took possession of the same kingdom, overthrew Andeca, and, after shaving his head, assigned him to the office of the presbyterate, following his royal dignity. For it was fitting that he should suffer again, by an appropriate reversal of fortune, what he himself had done to his king. The kingdom of the Suevi was destroyed and transferred to the Goths; it is said to have lasted 177 years.

[Col. 1081]

# BOOK OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF HISPALIS, ON ILLUSTRIOUS MEN (C)

## Preface

[Note: [Col. 1081D]

1. “Above,” that is, in Jerome and Gennadius. PEREZ.

Ibid. In the Isidorian material I entitled chapter 80 as follows: *Isidore’s Book on Illustrious Men*. Editions of this book and manuscript copies. Zaccaria’s preface. Harduin’s ravings against most of the ancient writings are briefly treated. I shall present the notes of John Baptist Perezius, with his name explicitly given. I shall collect the substance of the other notes, citing the names of their authors: Miraeus, Schottus, Fabricius, Aguirre, Florezius, the editor of the works of the Toletan Fathers, and Zaccaria. The last of these, as I observed in the Isidorian material, had furnished annotations only for this book among all Isidore’s works, because he was hastening to print Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, which contains this book of Isidore, although he did not even complete that task.

In the index of illustrious men prefixed by Perezius, no. 17, there appeared: “Paulinus, presbyter of Milan, later bishop of Nola.” I omitted the final phrase. Compare the note on chapter 17, no. 21. What Isidore says—“although above”—Perezius correctly explained as referring to books on the same subject written by Jerome and Gennadius. Nevertheless, Miraeus, who saw this brief preface prefixed to an appendix on twelve ecclesiastical writers, inferred from this that these twelve chapters were not Isidore’s. Zaccaria too retained some doubt, since Honorius of Autun had obtained an Isidorian copy beginning with Hosius. But I have already discussed this difference among copies in the Isidorian material, at the place cited.

Although Isidore says that he is recording the memory of those writers whose works he remembered having read, this should not be understood to mean that he read all the writers whom he names; it is enough that he examined most of them or some works of each. AREV.]

2. Xystus, bishop and martyr of the city of Rome, composed, after the pattern of Solomon, a book of Proverbs in such concise language that a separate saying is explained in each individual verse. Heretics inserted certain passages contrary to the Church’s faith into this little work, so that, under the name of so great a martyr, the assertion of perverse doctrines might more easily be accepted. But let the person who remembers himself to be Catholic read it discerningly and accept whatever is not contrary to the truth. Some, however, think that the same book was dictated by heretics, not by Xystus. The blessed Augustine refutes this opinion, for in one of his works he acknowledges that this work was composed by the same martyr.

3. The deacon Macrobius, following the zeal and intelligence of Saint Cyprian, brought together from both Testaments appropriate chapters against the cunning of heretics—namely, concerning the majesty of God the Father; the coming of the Son of God; his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; and likewise concerning the election of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews. He then added other matters relevant to the usefulness of life and the discipline of religion, arranging all these in one hundred distinct chapters.
