4. Philastrius, bishop of Brixia. Long before the blessed Augustine, he published a book on heresies, identifying each one individually—whether those that existed among the Jewish people before the incarnation of Christ, which he enumerates as twenty-eight, or those that arose after the coming of the Lord and Savior against the Catholic faith, which he describes as numbering 128. The same man of great glory and most distinguished teacher, Augustine, mentions this about him.

## CHAPTER FOUR

[Col. 1085A]

[Note: [Col. 1085B]

5. Theodorus. He is also praised by Theodoret, Sozomen, and Evagrius, but condemned by the Fifth Synod of Constantinople and by Gregory, *Book VI, Letter 195*. In several places Isidore—namely, when discussing Theodorus, the emperor Justinian, Facundus, and Victor of Tunnuna, as well as in *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 5, and in the *Chronicle*, when speaking about Justinian—may appear to some not to have been sufficiently fair to the Fifth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople.

The whole matter happened as follows. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, whose many learned works we possess, and Ibas, bishop of Edessa, were condemned in their absence in the year of Christ 448 at the second, heretical Council of Ephesus, through the faction of Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who was a Eutychianist heretic, and were expelled from their churches. See Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 10. The stated reason was that Theodoret had written against Cyril’s twelve anathemas, while Ibas had sent the Persian Maris a letter that was not Catholic. Then, in the year 451, at the general Council of Chalcedon under Pope Leo of Rome, that second Council of Ephesus was annulled, and the bishops Theodoret and Ibas were restored to their churches. See Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 4, and Book II, final chapter.

From this arose great tragedies, as provinces and even emperors held differing views about accepting the Council of Chalcedon—matters that you will read about in Evagrius himself, Liberatus of Carthage, and Paul the Deacon. Finally, at the Fifth General Council held at Constantinople under Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian in 553, Theodoret’s writings against Cyril, the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Maris, and the works of Theodorus, bishop of Mopsuestia, which were highly praised in that letter, were condemned. Many received this gravely, as though the authority of the Council of Chalcedon were thereby being rejected. See Evagrius, Book IV, chapter 37. For when they read that those men had been restored to their churches at the Council of Chalcedon, they thought that their works had simultaneously been approved. It was, however, necessary to distinguish the authors from their works, as the emperor Justinian teaches in his profession of faith and Proclus of Constantinople in the letter read at that Constantinopolitan council.

Thereafter prolonged disputes continued in the Church concerning acceptance of this Council of Constantinople. Its defenders were falsely called by the opposing party Acephali heretics and enemies of the three chapters of the Council of Chalcedon. Thus Egypt and Africa, as Liberatus and Victor of Tunnuna, not yet published, testify, and Illyricum as well, according to Paul the Deacon of Aquileia, *Book XVIII*, for some time resisted the Roman pontiffs who approved this Council of Constantinople.

These two African authors, Liberatus of Carthage and Victor of Tunnuna, even dared to accuse Pope Vigilius of having been a defender of those three chapters through the agency of the empress Theodora. This calumny is easily refuted by the three letters of Vigilius read at the Fifth Council, and by what the Fathers at the Sixth Council complain had been falsely fabricated about Vigilius.

I suspect that Spain at one time shared the Africans’ opinion, because so many of Isidore’s words incline toward defending the three chapters. Unless perhaps Isidore drew these words from the Chronicle of his own Victor of Tunnuna, an author he willingly uses; or perhaps approval of the Constantinopolitan Council, especially from the Roman pontiffs Vigilius, Pelagius, and Gregory, reached Isidore and the Spaniards only later. This is particularly plausible since Spain could for some time have been unaware of that council’s authority, having heard that Pope Vigilius of Rome had refused to attend it.

For this reason, I think, Isidore did not mention the already long-concluded Fifth Council of Constantinople after the four general councils in *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 16, although Pope Gregory, his contemporary, declared it equal in authority to the preceding four. You will read more about the defenders of the three chapters in Gregory himself: *Book II of the Register*, letter 36; *Indiction 11*, letter 10; and *Book III*, letter 4. For Gregory says that the copy of the Council of Chalcedon had been corrupted by the Constantinopolitans: *Book V of the Register*, letter 14, and *Book VII*, letter 52, Indiction 2. PEREZ.

Ibid. “The elder Leo.” Year of Christ 457. But Theodoret says that it occurred under Theodosius the Younger. PEREZ.

Ibid. You will find Grialius’s judgment on the controversy of the three chapters as narrated by Isidore in the Isidorian material, chapter 36, no. 26. Miraeus discusses the same matter in his note on Saint Isidore, chapter 33. There is an excellent theological dissertation by John Gisbert, or defense of the Church in the affair of the three chapters, prefaced by the words of Saint Gregory the Great: “Only something concerning persons, not concerning the faith, was done.” Sirmondus too, in his preface to the works of Facundus, discussed in chapter 32, no. 42, deals with the same argument: “Nor,” he says, “can the cause of the three chapters, which Facundus defended, be held against him; for, if one wishes to speak truthfully, it would have been more honorable to fall with Vigilius than to conquer with Justinian.” He concludes: “Out of zeal for that very peace, the successors of Vigilius, when they saw that only a few still resisted, so that there might be one mind and voice of all in the Church, finally assented both to the synod and to the Constantinopolitan council, whose authority had until then been uncertain, and by their confirmation bestowed upon it the force and name of a general council.” Certainly it had not come to Isidore’s knowledge that the Roman pontiffs had already asserted definite authority for the Council of Constantinople when he praised writers who defended the three chapters together with the Council of Chalcedon. AREV.]

5. Theodore, bishop of the city of Mopsuestia, is reported to have shone so brightly and abundantly with learned knowledge that it was said—if it is permissible to repeat it—that he composed in Greek a total of a thousand volumes against the errors of all heretics. At the instigation of the emperor Justinian, the bishops of the Acephali judged that he should be condemned after his death, together with the bishops Ibas and Theodoret, to the prejudice of the Council of Chalcedon. Yet the testimonies of illustrious men make clear that he had been a most distinguished teacher of the Church. He lived until the reign of the elder Leo.

Michael Joseph Maceda wrote most carefully about Hosius in a work entitled *Hosius truly Hosius*, that is, “Hosius truly innocent, truly holy.” Two dissertations: I. On the fictitious lapse of Hosius. II. On the holiness and legitimate veneration of the same. Bologna, 1790, quarto. 6. Hosius, bishop of the church of the city of Córdoba in Spain, trained in the powers of eloquence. He wrote to his sister a letter on the praise of virginity, adorned with beautiful and eloquent expression; and he also composed another work on the interpretation of the priestly garments that are mentioned in the Old Testament, crafted with truly excellent sense and ingenuity. At the Council of Sardica he himself also issued very many judgments.

7. But after a long old age, that is, after his one hundred and first year, when he was already on the very threshold of life, he collapsed from the boundaries of the faith, struck by the serpent’s dart. For, summoned by the emperor Constantius and terrified by threats, fearing that, as an old and wealthy man, he might suffer loss of his property or exile, he immediately assented to Arian impiety. Seized by the madness of impiety, he condemned the term *homoousion*—“of the same substance”—which he had handed down, together with the other holy Fathers, as something to be followed by the Churches. His cruel end promptly terminated his life, as he deserved.

In the year of Christ 552, a certain Verecundus, bishop of Junca in the African province of Byzacena and defender of the Three Chapters, died in exile at Chalcedon, a year before the Council of Constantinople—the fifth general council—was held by order of the emperor Justinian. ## CHAPTER IX

[Note: [Col. 1088B]

11. In the year of Christ 481. Isidore lists two Idacii, or Itacii. Since many, including some of our own countrymen, falsely confuse them into one, I shall seem to be doing something useful if I distinguish all the Idacii. For I find five Spaniards bearing this name, who appear reducible to three. See the note on the three Idacii.

The first is Itacius—for this is how he is written in all the old manuscripts—surnamed Clarus, bishop of Ossonoba, exiled because of the killing of Priscillian together with Ursacius, around the year of Christ 390. Sulpicius Severus, Jerome, and Isidore speak of him. Isidore says that he wrote against Priscillian, but the work is not extant.

The second Idacius was bishop of Mérida, living at the same time as the preceding man, and likewise a persecutor of Priscillian, according to the same Sulpicius Severus. Both of them subscribed to the Council of Zaragoza.

The third Idacius, or Itacius—for I find it written both ways—was bishop of Lamecum in Galicia and the author of an as-yet unpublished chronicle, which I possess in manuscript. He says that he was converted in the year of Christ 417, but Isidore says that he wrote up to the eighth year of Leo, namely the year 481. Sigebert says that he wrote up to the year 490. Trithemius confuses the first with the third.

A fourth Idacius Clarus might also appear to exist, whose work against the Arian Varidadus is extant. But he is, I think, the same as the first, the exile from Ossonoba. While traveling abroad, he could have seen Varidadus’s work at Naples, a city of Campania, as he himself relates.

Someone might add a fourth—or fifth—Idacius: the bishop who held a council with Turibius of Astorga against the Priscillianists by order of Pope Leo in the year 447, as appears in Leo’s letter to Turibius and in another letter from Turibius himself to Idacius and Ceponius, which I possess in manuscript. But, judging from the time and the province of Galicia, this Idacius could have been the same as that third, Galician chronicler of Lamecum. PEREZ.

Ibid. Florez published a very carefully corrected edition of the *Chronicle of Idacius* in vol. IV of *Hispania sacra*. He discusses the Idacii at greater length and, contrary to the common opinion, proves that the author of the *Chronicle* was not Idacius, bishop of Lamecum, but appears rather to have been bishop of Aquae Flaviae in Galicia. Quesnellius did indeed assert that Idacius, the accuser of Priscillian, was bishop of Lamecum, but Florez also shows that this is uncertain. Idacius’s *Chronicle* and *Fasti* may be found in the cited *Bibliotheca* of Galland, vol. X, p. 323. AREV.]

11. Itacius, a bishop of the province of Galicia, following the chronicle of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, or of Jerome the presbyter—which is declared to have been published down to the reign of Valens Augustus—then follows the history appended from the first year of Theodosius Augustus up to the eighth year of the reign of Leo. In it he chiefly recounts the cruel wars of the barbarian peoples that oppressed Spain. He died under the emperor Leo, already almost in the last stage of old age, as the evidence of his own preface also shows.

12. Eusebius, bishop of the city of Dorylaeum. At the assembly of the Council of Chalcedon he presented a book against Dioscorus, the heretical bishop of the city of Alexandria, and read before the present synod all the errors and blasphemies of Dioscorus. Dioscorus had deposed him and Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, by a sentence of excommunication at the Second Council of Ephesus, because they resisted the heresy in defense of the orthodox faith. Therefore, at the Council of Chalcedon, Eusebius later exposed the countless crimes and blasphemies of Dioscorus and invoked the sentence of condemnation against him from the holy council, namely, that what Dioscorus had justly inflicted upon others should justly be turned back upon him.

Ibid. The deacon Ferrandus flourished in the year 507. His works are extant in print: the *Paraeneticus* addressed to Count Reginus, letters, an abridgment of the canons, and so forth. Some attribute to him also the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, bishop of Ruspe. AREV.]

14. Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage, is said to have flourished greatly in the sacred Scriptures, and is reported to have exchanged many propositions with blessed Fulgentius in alternating letters. When the Roman deacons Pelagius and Anatolius consulted him as to whether anyone might be condemned after death, he issued a rescript in which, among other things, he spoke as follows:

“What does it profit to disturb the Church for the sake of those who sleep? If someone accused and condemned while still in this body of death was taken from the Church before he deserved to be absolved, he cannot be absolved by human judgment. If someone accused and acquitted passed in the peace of the Catholic Church to God, he cannot afterward be condemned by human judgment. If someone accused before the day of the sacred examination was overtaken by a sudden summons, he is to be understood as being reserved for divine judgment, established within the bosom of Mother Church; and no human being can pronounce a manifest sentence concerning him. If God has granted him pardon, our severity does him no harm; but if God has prepared punishment for him, our kindness does him no good.”

## CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 1090C]

16. Marcellinus. Gennadius mentions him under Faustinus the presbyter. Ibid. “They assembled.” In the year 559. PEREZ.

Ibid. Marcellinus’s history of the death of Hosius of Córdoba, in the same words but somewhat fuller, is found in a Gothic codex of the library of Complutense, at the end of Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, without the name of Marcellinus as author. Hosius, formerly a most noble confessor and a most learned man, praised by Augustine and Athanasius and personally known by letter to the emperor Constantine—as appears in the Theodosian Code, title *On the Most Sacred Churches*—had been a defender of the Catholics, to his great credit, at the Councils of Elvira, Nicaea, and Sardica. At last, delirious in his old age, he defected to the Arians at the Council of Sirmium. On this matter see also Hilary, *On the Synods*; Athanasius, *On the Unity of the Trinity*; the history of Sulpicius Severus; and Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. PEREZ.

Ibid. *Homoousion*. In some copies, *homousii*. On Saint Gregory of Elvira, see the Roman Martyrology, April 24. In the edition of the Toledan Fathers, an erudite note is appended here, demonstrating that Marcellinus’s account of the end of Hosius is fictitious. Natalis Alexander, Florez, and others have treated this subject. AREV.]

16. Marcellinus, a presbyter of Italy, wrote to the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Arcadius a single little work in which he unraveled the deeds of the bishops who had assembled at Rimini to destroy the *homoousion*, and who so disturbed the whole world by the treachery of their impious doctrine that scarcely a few bishops remained who persevered in the inviolable worship of the faith. He also relates concerning Arius how, while he was going to the council to dispute with Alexander, he turned aside on the road for a necessary purpose and how his bowels were poured out.

Concerning the end of Hosius, bishop of the city of Córdoba, who, out of fear of the emperor, betrayed the faith and became an advocate and agent of treachery and impiety, he speaks as follows:

“For after the impious betrayal of Hosius, when Saint Gregory, bishop of Elvira, had been brought to the city of Córdoba in accordance with the imperial decree and was entirely unwilling to communicate with him, Hosius, angered, said to Clementinus, the vicarious prefect of Constantius, that he should send him into exile. But he replied: ‘I do not dare to send a bishop into exile unless you first depose him from the episcopate.’”

17. When Saint Gregory saw that Hosius wished to pronounce sentence, he appealed to Christ with all the depth of his faith and cried out:

“Christ God, who will come to judge the living and the dead, do not permit a human sentence to be pronounced today against me, the least of your servants, who, standing as though guilty on account of faith in your name, have been made a spectacle. Rather, judge your own cause today; deign yourself to pronounce sentence through vengeance. I do not wish to flee as though I feared exile, since no punishment is burdensome to me for your name’s sake, but I ask this so that many may be freed from the error of betrayal when they see the present vengeance.”

After he had said these things, behold, suddenly Hosius, sitting in the pride of an almost royal power and attempting to pronounce sentence, turned his mouth and twisted his neck at the same time. He was hurled from his seat onto the ground and immediately expired.

[Note: [Col. 1091C]

18. *Vindicantium*. “He vindicates the martyrs” in Optatus, book I. PEREZ.]

18. Then, while everyone was astonished, even that pagan Clementinus was terrified. Although he was the judge, he feared that he might himself be judged with a similar punishment, and so he threw himself at the feet of the holy man, begging him to spare him, since he had sinned against him through ignorance of the divine law, and not so much by his own will as by the command of the one who had issued the order. Hence Gregory alone, among those who vindicated the faith, remained unshaken; he neither fled nor suffered exile, for everyone thereafter feared to pass judgment on him.

## CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 1091C]

19. Priscillian. See Epiphanius, book I, chapter 34, and Irenaeus, book I, chapters 8 and 9. Ibid. Concerning Mani, Cyril, *Catecheses*, 60, and Epiphanius, book II, chapter 66. PEREZ.

Ibid. Florez shows in vol. XV of *Hispania sacra*, p. 13, from Sulpicius and Saint Jerome, that this Marcus withdrew from Gaul to Spain, where he seduced the noble woman Agape and the rhetorician Helpidius. From this arose the heresy of Priscillian. The same Florez discusses Itacius in vol. XIII, p. 150, and vol. XIV, p. 215. AREV.]

19. Itacius, a bishop of Spain distinguished both by his surname and by his eloquence, wrote a certain book in the form of an *Apologeticus*, in which he exposes the detestable doctrines of Priscillian, the arts of his sorcery, and the disgrace of his lusts. He shows that a certain Memphite Marcus, highly skilled in magical arts, was a disciple of Mani and the teacher of Priscillian. Itacius was deprived of communion with the Church together with the bishop Ursacius because of the killing of that same Priscillian, whose accusers they had been; he was condemned to exile and there died on his final day, while Theodosius the Great and Valentinian were reigning.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Note: [Col. 1091C]

20. Siricius. In the year 385. On the decretal, etc. Letters are extant. Eumerius. In the old manuscripts he is always called Eumerius, not Himerius. “And another.” Concerning it, see Ambrose, letters 8 and 81. PEREZ.

[Col. 1091D] Ibid. Schottus advises that *Siricius* should be read, not *Siricus*. Zaccaria had noted a remarkable disagreement among chronologists concerning the beginning of the pontificate assumed by Siricius; on this matter one may consult Papebrochius, both Pagis, Blanchinius, and others. Siricius’s letters, like the other genuine letters of the other pontiffs, were accurately printed by Constant. After him, Gallandius reprinted Siricius’s letters and decrees in vol. VII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 533. Instead of *Eumerius*, some prefer *Himerius*, notwithstanding the authority of the manuscript cited by Perez. The inscriptions of the basilica of Saint Paul at Rome, published by Marangoni, assign Siricius a pontificate of fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. AREV.]

20. Siricius, a most illustrious pontiff and bishop of the Roman see, wrote a decretal work addressed to Eumerius, bishop of Tarragona. In it, among other ecclesiastical regulations, he decreed that the baptism of heretics should by no means be rescinded by the Church. We have also found another letter of his sent to various bishops, in which he condemns the heretic Jovinian and Auxentius, together with their other followers. He presided at Rome for fourteen years. He died while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning.

## CHAPTER XVII

[Note: [Col. 1091D]

21. In the year 410 he was bishop of Nola. This is the Paulinus who is frequently mentioned by Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, and Gennadius. Many in our own age, following Honorius of Autun, wrongly make two Paulini: one the bishop of Nola, the other a presbyter of Milan and author of the *Life of Saint Ambrose*. Yet Paulinus himself writes in his letter to Alypius that, although he had been ordained a presbyter in Spain by Lampius, bishop of Barcelona, he nevertheless obtained through the favor of Saint Ambrose that, wherever he might live in the world, he would be called Ambrose’s presbyter.

Moreover, the Lives mentioned by Isidore—namely, those of Ambrose of Milan, Germanus of Auxerre, and Paulinus of Nola, the bishops—written by Paulinus, Constantius, and Oranius, are extant in a very ancient exemplar of the Church of Toledo and are said to have been printed by Laurentius Surius. PEREZ.

Ibid. Perez is mistaken, as are many others, in believing that the Paulinus praised by Isidore was the bishop of Nola, as Miraeus and the editor of the works of the Toledan Fathers have already noted. The latter observes that it may be doubted whether Paulinus, Saint Ambrose’s deacon, ever rose to the order of presbyter, since only that much is read in Isidore.

Zaccaria adds that Paulinus the Milanese presbyter, author of the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, must also be distinguished from Paulinus of Béziers, although Dupin confused these two Paulini. Cave and Oudinus had thought that Isidore, through carelessness, attributed to Paulinus Rufinus’s work on the same subject, mentioned above at number 8. But Paulinus’s work is different: Martianay published a fragment of it among the works associated with Jerome, and Mingarelli published the complete little book in *Anecdotes of Ancient Latin Fathers*, Bologna, 1751.

Mingarelli thinks that Isidore wrote “according to a twofold interpretation,” because that better suits the work. Zaccaria believes that Constantius, whom Isidore calls a bishop, was the presbyter celebrated by Sidonius, concerning whom Oudinus writes. This makes the comparison between the presbyters Constantius and Oranius, and Paulinus likewise a presbyter, more appropriate.

Schottus thought that Oranius was the surname of the poet Fortunatus, who, after Sulpicius Severus, composed in verse a work on Pontius Paulinus, perhaps the man who was bishop of Nola. Gallandius, in vol. VIII of the *Bibliotheca*, p. 211, published some more extensive and corrected poems of Paulinus of Nola from Mingarelli’s recension. In vol. IX, p. 23, he published three little works of Paulinus of Milan: the *Life of Saint Ambrose*, the *Little Book against Caelestius*, and another *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. In the prolegomena to that ninth volume, against Tillemont and Fontanini, and together with Fabricius and the aforementioned Mingarelli, he defends this chapter of Isidore. Among the works of Paulinus of Nola is his *Life*, written by Uranius, or Oranius. AREV.]

21. Paulinus, a presbyter, explained in a book composed with sufficiently concise brevity the blessings of the patriarchs according to a threefold interpretation. At Augustine’s request he also wrote a life of Ambrose, abounding in miracles and not unequal to the apostles in doctrine and merits. Constantius the bishop likewise composed the life of Germanus, and Oranius published the death of Paulinus.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1093A]

[Note: [Col. 1093C]

22. Proba. In the year of Christ 410; her surname was Falconia Valeria. Cento. Jerome mentions it in his letter to Paulinus. Gelasius calls it apocryphal, distinction 15. PEREZ.

Ibid. In Aguirre’s manuscript: “Proba, who is called Falconia by surname, wife,” etc. Miraeus thinks that Isidore was deceived in calling Proba the wife of Adelphius; but he himself is rather mistaken in believing that the poetess Proba was Anicia Faltonia Proba, mother, daughter, and wife of consuls, as Fontaninius observes in *On the Antiquities of Horta*, book II. On the most noble family of the Anicii, see the commentary on Prudentius, book I against Symmachus, verses 553 and following. Proba, the wife of Adelphius, belonged to the same family, although he is not found in the lists of proconsuls otherwise known to us. Instead of *in laude*, some read *in laudem*. On this cento, see the notes to Gelasius’s *Decree*, after Sedulius, number 52, pp. 425 and following. Compare also Diego Covarrubias, book IV of the *Various Resolutions*, chapter 14, in distinction 15. AREV.]

22. Proba, wife of Adelphius the proconsul, is the only woman placed among ecclesiastical men because she devoted herself to the praise of Christ, composing a cento about Christ fitted together from Virgilian verses. We do not marvel at her diligence, but we praise her ingenuity. Nevertheless, this little work is inserted among the apocryphal Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Note: [Col. 1093D]

23. John, etc. In the year 398. PEREZ.

Ibid. On Saint John Chrysostom, one may consult Montfaucon in his edition of the works of the holy Doctor, Fabricius in the *Greek Bibliotheca*, vol. VII, pp. 560 and following, and the Bollandists, vol. IV of September. Zaccaria notes, against Johann Georg Walch in the *Ecclesiastical History of the New Testament*, p. 1374, that Chrysostom’s surname had already been established in the sixth century, and before the Sixth Council, held in the year . . . 680. In the verses published by Isidore for his own library, John is also called Chrysostom, and the reason for the name is given. It is not known who the Latin translator was of the two little books that Latin speakers used in Isidore’s time. Some identify him as Anianus, or Mutianus, the scholasticus. AREV.]

23. John, most holy bishop of the see of Constantinople, surnamed Chrysostom—“Golden-Mouthed”—whose discourse conveys both the greatest compunction of heart and great sweetness of eloquence, composed many distinguished little works in Greek. Of these the Latin-speaking world uses two little books of his on the fallen, written to a certain Theodorus and filled with lamentations and exhortations, since he had fallen away from a good way of life. Because John had practiced the monastic life with him in one and the same monastery, he reminded him in those books of the life they had led there, urging him toward his former purpose and showing that no sinner or impious person need despair if he returns to repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1094C]

24. *On the Conflict*. In some copies, *On the Struggle*. See the *Isidoriana*, chapter 84, number 20, where I discussed the *Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, attributed to Isidore. Certain little works of Saint John Chrysostom have recently been published in Galland’s *Bibliotheca*, vol. VIII, p. 239, and vol. XIV, appendix, p. 136. AREV.]

24. We also read another book by him whose title is: “No One Can Be Harmed by Another, Except by Himself.” There is also an outstanding work of his addressed to a certain most noble matron, Gregoria, on the conduct of life and the formation of character, or *On the Struggle of Virtues and Vices*. There is also among the Latins another book of his, *On Compunction of Heart*. Another was written to a certain Eutropius, when, expelled from the palace, he had taken refuge at the altar.

[Note: [Col. 1094C]

25. In the thirteenth year. Perhaps the seventh year, for it is established from Marcellinus and Nicephorus of Constantinople that he occupied the see for six years. Deposed in the year of Christ 404, according to Marcellinus; he died in exile in 407, according to Paul the Deacon. “Body.” These words are added in one manuscript. PEREZ.

Ibid. From the history it must be established with certainty that Chrysostom was oppressed in the seventh year. Schottus observes that in one Toledo manuscript, instead of *our bishop*, one reads *nine bishops*. Others omit *our* and *nine*, producing a better and more accurate sense. When Chrysostom is said to have been driven into exile in Pontus, this is to be understood as meaning that he died at Comana in Pontus, while he was being transported from various other places to Pityus. From other editions I have restored *in the year from the day of his elevation*, since in Grialius’s edition the word *from* is omitted. AREV.]

25. He also composed many other varied treatises, which it would take too long to enumerate. Of the fruits of this work, although not everything, nevertheless a very great number of his streams of eloquence were translated from Greek into Latin. In the thirteenth year of his episcopate he was oppressed by the dissension of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. The bishops who supported our emperor Arcadius condemned him though he was innocent, deposed him from the episcopate, and confined him in exile in Pontus. In the thirty-fifth year from the day of his death, his body was brought back from exile to Constantinople and buried in the Church of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER XX

[Note: [Col. 1094D]

26. Sedulius. In the year 430. Three books. Gelasius praises him, distinction 15. PEREZ.

I explained his life in the prolegomena to Sedulius and discussed his works. Zaccaria’s *Literary History of Italy*, vol. IV, p. 200, may also be consulted. Miraeus attributes to the poet Sedulius the *Annotations on the Epistles of Paul*, which belong to another Sedulius; in them certain words of Pelagius, or of some Pelagian, are noted, whether inserted by others or adopted by the author. AREV.]

26. Sedulius, a presbyter, published three books composed in dactylic heroic meter. The first of them most powerfully celebrates the signs and mighty deeds of the Old Testament; the others resound with the mysteries or miracles of Christ’s deeds.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Note: [Col. 1094D]

27. Possidius. Thus in the old manuscript, not Possidonius. He was bishop of Calama in Numidia, at the Seventh Council of Carthage, in the year 418. The *Life*, etc., is extant. PEREZ.

[Col. 1095C] The notes in Grialius’s edition had been confused; I have restored them to order. John Salinas published Possidius’s index and *Life* in Rome in 1731, and defended its reliability against John Clericus, or Phereponus, in his annotations on the works of Saint Augustine. Possidius’s *Life*, written by an eyewitness, is also found among the Bollandists under May 17. AREV.]

27. Possidius, a bishop of the African province. He wrote in a careful style the life of Saint Augustine, and appended to that work an index of his writings, enumerating how much the most blessed Doctor wrote; the volumes of more than four hundred books are counted there. The number of his homilies, letters, and questions is beyond reckoning, so that scarcely anyone could write by his own effort as much of another’s work as he composed through his own labor.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Note: [Col. 1095C]

28. Primasius. In the year 553. Ibid. Fortunatus. He is called bishop of the province of Byzacena in the Fifth Council of Constantinople, collation 2. Ibid. “May he demonstrate.” His commentaries on the Apocalypse are extant. PEREZ.

Ibid. After *may he demonstrate*, some editions add: “He flourished under Justinian”; for *Justinian*, they mistakenly read *Julian*. Miraeus says that Primasius died not in the year 440, as Xystus of Siena reports, but in 503. Perez gives the year 553. AREV.]

28. Primasius, an African bishop, composed in scholarly style three books on the heresies, addressed to Bishop Fortunatus. In them he explained what blessed Augustine had once left unfinished in his book *On Heresies*, death having intervened: in the first, he showed what makes someone a heretic; in the second and third, he arranged what demonstrates that someone is a heretic.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1095B] [Note: [Col. 1095C]

29. Proterius. In the year 457. Ibid. “But this man,” etc. Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 15; Liberatus, chapter 16. PEREZ.

[Col. 1095D] Ibid. Proterius’s letter on Easter was published by Aegidius Bucherius in chapter 2 of his commentary on the canon of Victor of Aquitaine. In place of *successors*, Zaccaria conjectured *supporters*. Proterius’s death occurred in the year 457, on the fourth—or, as others prefer, the fifth—day before the Kalends of April. AREV.]

29. Proterius, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, wrote letters to Leo, bishop of the Roman see, concerning the festival of Easter. During the reign of the emperor Leo, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, with Timothy as their leader, stirred up a revolt and murdered him with extreme cruelty; they then installed Timothy as bishop of Alexandria for themselves.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Note: [Col. 1095D]

30. A letter. The letter was written in the year 445. It is extant together with Leo’s letters, vol. I of the Councils. This Paschasinus was bishop of Lilybaeum in Sicily and Leo the pope’s legate at the Council of Chalcedon in the year 451. Ibid. At the hour of baptism. It occurred in the year 417. A similar miracle occurred in Spain in the year 583, according to Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 22, and Sigebert. PEREZ.

Ibid. I have also restored to order the notes of Grialius’s edition, which were confused in this place. Paschasinus; in some copies, Paschasius. Instead of *Meltinas*, some read *Miltinas*, others *Mentina*; and instead of *discedit*, others, less correctly, *descendit*. Since Saint Gregory of Tours reports that a similar miracle occurred in Spain, Schottus says it is strange that Isidore does not record it, either here or in the books of the *Etymologies*, where he discusses the Paschal candle. John Moschus relates other similar miracles in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 214 and 215; others relate still more, as may be seen in the notes to Saint Ildefonsus’s book *On Knowledge of Baptism*, vol. II of the Toledan Fathers, chapter 105, p. 210. There the most learned author tries to show that the similar miracle mentioned by Ildefonsus is the very one Gregory of Tours attributed to Spain, although Ildefonsus did not specify the place of the miracle. Nevertheless, it must always seem strange that neither Isidore nor Ildefonsus indicated that such a miracle had occurred in Spain. Miraeus is said to date Paschasinus’s letter to the year 443. What Perez says—“It occurred in the year 417”—appears to refer to the miracle. AREV.]

30. Paschasinus, bishop of Sicily, published a paschal letter addressed to the aforementioned Pope Leo, in which he relates the miracle of the paschal mystery in these words:

> There is, he says, an estate called Meltinas, situated among lofty mountains and very dense forests. There is there a very small church, built with humble workmanship, in whose baptistery, on the most holy paschal night, at the hour appointed for baptism, although there is no channel or pipe, nor any water at all nearby, a spring fills itself from its own source. After the few who are present have been consecrated, since there is no conduit by which it might be led away, the water departs of itself, just as it had come.

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger, son of the emperor Arcadius.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Note: [Col. 1096C]]

31. Julianus. In the year 450. PEREZ.

[Col. 1096D] In the same place: Gallus. Gennadius says that he was a Moor. Therefore some mistakenly confuse Pomerius with Julianus, bishop of Toledo, who died in the year 690. PEREZ.

In the same place: This is a very ancient error, by which Julianus of Toledo is confused with Julianus Pomerius, as is clear from ancient manuscripts. Otherwise Julianus of Toledo often praises and follows Pomerius. See *Hispania sacra*, vol. V, p. 300, and the *Life of Saint Julian, Bishop of Toledo*, vol. II of the *Toledan Fathers*. It should be observed that, although Gennadius calls Pomerius a Moor by nationality, he nevertheless asserts that he was ordained a priest in Gaul. Isidore may perhaps allude to this when he calls him a Gaul; alternatively, “Gaul” should be omitted, as it is in some editions. AREV.]

31. A certain Julianus, a Gaul, surnamed Pomerius. He composed eight books on the Nature of the Soul in the form of a dialogue. The first of these contains an account of what the soul is and how it is believed to have been made in the image of God. In the second he discusses whether the soul is corporeal or incorporeal. In the third he examines the origin of the soul of the first human being. In the fourth, whether a new soul is created without sin, or whether it derives the first human being’s sin from him by original transmission.

[Col. 1096B] [Note: [Col. 1096D]]

32. Schottus suspects that the eighth book, on the things that will occur at the end of the world, is that *Prognosticon* which Boetius Epo published at Douai. But this *Prognosticon* is certainly the work of Julianus of Toledo, in which the words of Pomerius are repeatedly cited. AREV.]

32. In the fifth he describes the soul’s faculty. In the sixth he explains the source of that discord by which the spirit is opposed to the flesh and the flesh to the spirit. In the seventh he writes about the difference between lives and deaths, or about the resurrection of the flesh and the soul; that is, about the death of the flesh and its resurrection. In the eighth he speaks about the things that will occur at the end of the world, or about the questions commonly raised concerning the resurrection, and about the ends of good and evil.

33. Nevertheless, in the second book of this same work, agreeing with Tertullian’s errors, he said that the soul is corporeal, attempting to establish this by certain deceptive arguments. He also published one little book on the instruction of virgins, and three others on contemplation of the future life, on active conduct of life, and on vices and virtues.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 1097A]

[Note: [Col. 1097C]]

34. A *Life* exists in Surius. Concerning Severinus, see Gregory, book VII, letter 84; Paul the Deacon, book I, chapter 12.

Importunus was consul in the year of Christ 509. A letter of Fulgentius of Ruspe to Eugippius exists. Cassiodorus says that he saw Eugippius, book I of the *Divine Institutes*. PEREZ.

In the same place: Fabricius and others observe that the Eugippius whom Cassiodorus says he saw was another, a younger Eugippius. Loaisa and Schottus conjecture that the text should read “after the consulship of Importunus and the younger Decius.” This does not please Zaccaria, for Importunus was consul alone; and Importunus might have been called “the Younger” because of some brother of his, or of another member of a family distinguished in that age but not himself a consul; or “Junior” may perhaps have been a surname. If anything is to be changed, Zaccaria thinks that *Junioris* was placed by an incompetent copyist instead of *iterum* (“again”) or *illustris* (“illustrious”). AREV.]

34. Eugippius, abbot of the town of Lucullanum near Naples in Campania. For a certain deacon named Paschasius he composed, in a concise style, a little book on the Life of the holy monk Severinus, and sent it to him. He also wrote a rule for the monks residing in the monastery of Saint Severinus, which, when dying, he left to them as a kind of testamentary bequest. He flourished after the consulship of Importunus Junior, while Anastasius was emperor.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 1097C]]

35. Fulgentius. In the year 500. PEREZ.

[Col. 1097D] In the same place: Joannes Molanus added a learned preface to the edition of Fulgentius’s works prepared by Joannes Olinmerius and printed by the Plantin press. In Galland’s library, vol. XI, pp. 230 ff., one may read a book by Peter the Deacon and others addressed to Fulgentius and other bishops of Africa, on the Incarnation and grace of Jesus Christ, as well as a book by Fulgentius and other bishops on the same subject addressed to that same Peter the Deacon. Among the works of Fulgentius Ferrandus the Deacon listed in the same volume, pp. 329 ff., there is also a life of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, apparently composed by Ferrandus. Codex Regiovaticanus 125, p. 69, contains a sermon by Bishop Fulgentius on the Nativity of the Lord, beginning “Desiring to say something,” etc., and on p. 82 a sermon by Fulgentius, bishop of Carthage, on Saint Stephen. AREV.]

35. Fulgentius, an African and bishop of the church of Ruspe, distinguished in the confession of faith, most richly learned in the divine Scriptures, also eloquent in speech and subtle in teaching and exposition, wrote many works. Among them we read seven books of *Responses* on the grace of God and free will. In these, replying to Faustus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, who consented to Pelagian depravity, he strives to overthrow the profound cunning of his opponent.

36. We also read his book on the Holy Trinity, addressed to Felix the notary, as well as a book entitled *The Rule of True Faith* and another on the Sacrament of the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ. There are also two books of his on the Truth of Predestination, sent to bishops, in which it is demonstrated that God’s grace precedes the human will in good actions, and that God, justifying certain people by the gift of his predestination, chooses them beforehand, while by some hidden judgment he abandons others to their wicked ways.

[Note: [Col. 1097D]]

37. Trasamundus is also written *Thrasamundus*, *Transamundus*, and *Trasimundus*; a similar variation occurs in the *History of the Goths*, no. 81. AREV.]

37. There is also his book of disputation, in which the blessed Fulgentius debated the faith with King Thrasamund. He also wrote for Ferrandus, a deacon of the church of Carthage, a little book containing a set of Questions. Among these works he composed many treatises for priests to use in the churches. Numerous other monuments of his intellect are also reported. We have plucked only these few items from the precious flowers of his learning. May the Lord grant a better fortune to anyone who is able to enjoy all his books. He flourished under Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, while Anastasius was emperor.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1097D]]

38. Eucherius. In the year 430. He was bishop of Lyons, according to Gennadius and Marcellinus. “Brevity,” etc., are Cicero’s words (*Orator* addressed to Brutus). PEREZ.

[Col. 1098C] In the same place: “Bishop of Gaul”; others read “priest of Gaul,” perhaps because bishops were sometimes also called priests, and Saint John Chrysostom occasionally speaks in this way. On Eucherius, see P. de Colonia’s literary history of the city of Lyons. Fabricius, discussing the Eucherii in vol. II of the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, observes that Dionysius Faucherius quotes what appear to be words of Isidore from this work, although they are found in no ancient manuscript or edition, namely: “He wrote other commentaries on many sacred books, no less necessary than useful, especially on Genesis and the books of Kings, addressed to the brothers Salonius and Veranius, bishops—a lengthy and most learned work.” AREV.]

38. Eucherius, bishop of Gaul, elegant in his maxims and adorned in his language, published for Hilary, bishop of Arles, who had withdrawn to the desert, a brilliant little work on the Praise of that same Desert, composed in a sweet style. In this work we praise the teacher, who, although saying little, says beautiful things. “Brevity,” as someone has said, “is sometimes a praise in a particular part of discourse, but in eloquence as a whole it does not win praise.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 1098C]]

39. In the year 432. Gennadius writes about him. PEREZ.]

39. Hilary, bishop of Arles, wrote the Life of his spiritual father and predecessor, the most holy and venerable Bishop Honoratus, composed in a sweet and splendid style.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Note: [Col. 1098D]]

40. Apringius. In the year of Christ 540. A large manuscript work on the Apocalypse circulates under the name of Apringius. But when I saw the Gothic Leonese manuscript itself, written in the eighth century of the era, I noticed that the author’s name was not certain; rather, the work had been published for the benefit of a certain Etherius. Moreover, in the preface that author says that he gathered his material from the books of Victorinus, Isidore, and Apringius, so that it is manifestly not the Apringius whom Isidore mentions. PEREZ.

In the same place: Florez, vol. XIV of *Hispania sacra*, where he discusses the bishops of Badajoz, says that Apringius flourished from the year 531. He suspects that the manuscript work of which Perezius speaks is by Beatus, the man who, together with Etherius, refuted the errors of Elipandus; Bayerius confirms this from several manuscripts in his notes to Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*. This commentary of Beatus, as is believed, appeared at Madrid in 1770. Braulio mentions an earlier commentary by Apringius in letter 25, vol. XXX of *Hispania sacra*. AREV.]

40. Apringius, bishop of the church of Badajoz in Spain, eloquent in language and learned in knowledge, interpreted the Apocalypse of the apostle John with subtle understanding and distinguished speech, apparently more successfully than the ecclesiastical writers of earlier times. He also wrote certain other works, which nevertheless have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He flourished in the time of Theudis, prince of the Goths.

The Illyrian Synod, in the year 549. Justinian also condemns it in his confession of faith, which is found in volume I of the Councils. See above, the note on Theodore of Mopsuestia at chapter 4. PEREZ.

In the same place: I have explained above, no. 5, as much as is necessary concerning the affair of the Three Chapters. AREV.]

41. The Emperor Justinian published certain books on the Incarnation of the Lord, and sent them throughout the various provinces. He also composed a rescript against the Illyrian Synod and, through perverse zeal, against the African bishops who defended the Council of Chalcedon. In it he attempted to condemn the Three Chapters: namely, the writings of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; the writings, or rescripts, of Theodoret; and the letter known as that of Ibas, bishop of Edessa.

Gallandius, in vol. XI of his *Bibliotheca*, pp. 665 ff., included the twelve books of Facundus in defense of the Three Chapters, furnished with Sirmond’s notes and corrected and supplemented by Joseph Blanchinus. 42. Facundus, an African and bishop of the church of Hermiane, wrote twelve books in defense of the Three Chapters. By his argument he demonstrated that the aforementioned Three Chapters had been condemned in the prescription of the apostolic faith and in the attack on the Council of Chalcedon: namely, the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, addressed to Maris the Persian; Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia; and the writings of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus. He flourished after the consulship of Basilius, in the tenth year of the reign of the Emperor Justinian.

In the same place: This Justinian appears to be the same man who subscribed, in second place, to the Council of Valencia during the reign of Theudis and who is called Justinus by some. But from manuscripts Florez, vol. VIII of *Hispania sacra*, p. 160, restored the name Justinianus. He concludes that this man was ordained bishop in the year 531 and lived at least until the year 546. AREV.]

43. Justinianus, from Spain and bishop of the church of Valencia, one of four brothers who were bishops and were born of the same mother, wrote a book of *Responses* to a certain Rusticus on proposed Questions. The first response concerns the Holy Spirit; the second is against the Bonosians, who say that Christ is an adopted Son and not a true Son; the third response concerns Christ’s baptism, which may not be repeated; the fourth concerns the distinction between the baptism of John and that of Christ; the fifth concerns the fact that the Son, like the Father, is invisible. He flourished in Spain in the time of Theudis, prince of the Goths.

Later, instead of “because they are unknown to us,” others read “concerning whom”; since they are unknown to us, we confess that silence is preferable. III, among the miscellaneous letters, p. 119, the second letter is that of Justus, bishop of Orgellia, to Pope Sirga: “Knowing you,” etc. It ends, “May he cherish you in the Lord.” It offers a treatise, a book on the *Song of Songs*. AREV.]

44. Justus, bishop of the church of Urgell in Spain and brother of the aforementioned Justinianus, published a little book of exposition on the *Song of Songs*, examining the entire meaning very briefly and clearly by allegory. His brothers Nebridius and Elpidius are also said to have written certain works; but since they are unknown to us, we confess that silence is preferable.

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Col. 1100B] [Note: [Col. 1100C]]

45. Martinus, bishop of Dumium, was a Pannonian by nationality, as is clear from Gregory of Tours’ *History* and from the epitaph composed by Martin himself, which we possess copied from an ancient book. It begins as follows:

> Born among the Pannonians, crossing vast seas,  
> Brought by divine command into the bosom of Gallaecia.

He founded the monastery of Dumium in Gallaecia, as is said in the Tenth Council of Toledo. Accordingly, Bishop Martinus subscribed to the First Council of Braga in the year of Christ 561. He was then made archbishop of Braga and subscribed to the Second Council of Braga in the year 562. According to Gregory of Tours, in the *Chronicle* and in book I of *The Miracles of Martin of Tours*, chapter 11, and according to Almoine, book III, chapter 39, he governed these churches for thirty years. Some of his little works are reported to have been printed; we possess more that have not yet been published. PEREZ.

In the same place: Saint Martin was bishop from the year 572 to the year 580. Florez describes his Life and deeds in vol. XV of *Hispania sacra* and includes some of his works among its appendices, several of which appeared there for the first time. Gallandius, vol. XII of his *Bibliotheca*, pp. 273 ff., collected and edited seven little works of Saint Martin of Dumium, though he was unaware of the edition prepared by Florez. Instead of *in Gallaeciam*, some printed editions incorrectly read *in Gallias* (“into Gaul”). It is also written *Gallecia*. AREV.]

45. Martinus, most holy bishop of the monastery of Dumium, sailing from the regions of the East, came to Gallaecia. There he converted the Suevic peoples from Arian impiety to the Catholic faith, established for them a rule of faith and holy religion, strengthened the churches, founded monasteries, and composed abundant instructions for pious formation.

46. I myself have read his book on the Differences of the Four Virtues and another volume of Letters, in which he urges the correction of life and conduct according to the faith, perseverance in prayer, the distribution of alms, and above all the cultivation of every virtue and of piety. He flourished under Theodemir, king of the Suevi, at the time when Justinian held imperial power in the Roman state and Athanagildus held it in Spain.

[Note: [Col. 1101C]]

In the same place: The letters of Avitus existed in Sirmond, who published some of them in vol. I of the councils of Gaul. Gallandius, vol. X of his *Bibliotheca*, pp. 697 ff., collected, in addition to the poems praised by Isidore, letters, homilies, and fragments of other works. AREV.]

47. Avitus, bishop of Vienne and highly learned in secular literature, published five little books composed in heroic meter. The first is on the Origin of the World; the second, on Original Sin; the third, on the Essence of God; the fourth, on the Flood of the World; and the fifth, on the Crossing of the Red Sea. He also wrote for his sister Fuscina one book on the Praise of Virginity, composed in exceptionally beautiful verse and arranged in an elegant epigram.

In the prolegomena I discussed the author at length; I conjectured that he was a Spaniard. Whether he was a priest is unknown. AREV.]

48. Dracontius composed in heroic verse a *Hexameron* on the creation of the world, and composed and wrote it with considerable brilliance.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Col. 1101B] [Note: [Col. 1101D]]

49. I possess a manuscript *Chronicle* of Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, in which, after Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper, he continues the account of events from the eighteenth consulship of Theodosius the Younger—that is, from the year of Christ 444—up to the first year of Justin the Younger—that is, the year of Christ 567. There he laments his exile, which he seems to me to have richly deserved. For he resisted the decrees of Pope Vigilius, the Emperor Justinian, and the Council of Constantinople while stubbornly defending the Three Chapters mentioned above. In Isidore, book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 38, he is incorrectly called “of Tours”; others call him “of Tunnuna,” while Trithemius calls him “of Cumae.” But in an ancient manuscript he himself calls himself “of Tunnuna.” I think this is the town in proconsular Africa called Tunis by Polybius and Strabo, *Tunisa* by Pliny, and declined by Livy as *Tunes*, *Tunetis*. It was famous in these times because of the expedition of the Emperor Charles V. Ado of Vienne and Otto of Freising also mention this Victor, book V, chapter 4. PEREZ.

[Col. 1102C] In the same place: Grialius calls Victor “of Tunnuna” in book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 38, no. 7. Schottus, relying on the Ingolstadt manuscript, preferred *Tunmuensis*. Some invent *Tmuensis*, which is the name of an Egyptian city. Isidore also mentions this same Victor in the preface to his *Chronicle*. It should be observed that Victor, after Prosper, as Perezius says, continued the course of events and thus continued the history which Eusebius had begun from the creation of the world. Gallandius published his *Chronicle*, restored in many places and supplied with notes, in vol. XII of his *Bibliotheca*. AREV.]

49. Victor, an African bishop of the church of Tunnuna. From the beginning of the world to the first year of the reign of Justin the Younger, he published a brief history arranged by annual consuls, covering military and ecclesiastical affairs. It was highly distinguished, illuminated by praise and critical observation, and most worthy of remembrance. For defending the Three Chapters, he was expelled from his church by Augustus Justinian and transported into exile in Egypt.

50. From there he was summoned again to Constantinople. When he resisted the Emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, who were detractors of the same Three Chapters, he was again sent to be confined in a monastery of that city. Remaining, as they say, under the same condemnation, he died.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

[Col. 1101C] [Note: [Col. 1102C]]

51. He is called “the Faster” by Nicephorus of Constantinople. PEREZ.

In the same place: John the Faster is distinct from another John of Cappadocia, bishop of Constantinople, who died in the year 535; see Fabricius, vol. XI of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 1571. In Isidore’s text, “a Cappadocian by nationality” may perhaps have been added by another hand. The Greeks celebrate the memory of John the Faster on the fourth day before the Nones of September. He died in the year 595. See P. Le Quien, vol. I of *Oriens Christianus*, col. 226. AREV.]

51. John, bishop of Constantinople and of holy memory, a Cappadocian by nationality, to whom the blessed Gregory wrote the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, was a man of incomparable abstinence and so exceedingly generous in almsgiving that the Emperor Maurice, moved against him by zeal for avarice, ordered the poor to be expelled from the city.

52. In the Greek language he published a rescript on the sacrament of baptism, addressed to our lord of blessed memory and predecessor, Bishop Leander. In it he says nothing of his own, but merely repeats the opinions of the ancient Fathers concerning triple immersion. He flourished in the time of Prince Maurice and died while the same Augustus was reigning.

## CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 1102D]]

In the same place: Not only in the printed editions, as Perezius says, but also in many ancient manuscripts, the book of the *Pastoral Rule* appears to have been addressed to John of Ravenna. AREV.]

53. Gregory, pope and prelate of the apostolic Roman see, full of compunction arising from fear of God and outstanding in humanity, was endowed through the grace of the Holy Spirit with such a light of knowledge that no teacher, not merely among those of the present age but even among those of the past, was ever his equal. At the beginning of his episcopate he published the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, addressed to John, bishop of the see of Constantinople. In it he teaches how a person should come to the office of governance and how, once he has come to it, he should strive to live and to teach his subjects.

54. At the request of Bishop Leander, he also expounded the book of blessed Job in a mystical and moral sense, explaining its entire prophetic history in thirty-five volumes through a rich stream of eloquence. In these works the mysteries of the sacraments are disclosed in such abundance, the instructions directing us toward the love of eternal life are so numerous, and the ornaments of language shine with such brilliance, that no wise person could explain them, even if all his limbs were turned into tongues.

[Col. 1102C] [Note: [Col. 1102D]]

It is said,” etc. Loaisa and Fabricius observe that something is missing after “he published.” Miraeus notes that the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory nobly defend Baronius against the accusations of Melchior Cano in the notes to the *Roman Martyrology*, 23 December. 55. He also wrote certain letters to the aforementioned Leander. One of them is attached as a preface to the same books on Job; another discusses the immersion used in baptism, in which, among other things, it is written:

> It can in no way be considered reprehensible, he says, to immerse an infant in baptism either once or three times, since in the three immersions the Trinity of the Persons can be signified, and in one immersion the unity of the Divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1103C]]

56. “Of the Gospels,” etc. The Forty Homilies on the Gospels exist. He died in the year of Christ 604. PEREZ.

In the same place: “Of the Gospels,” etc. This indicates that the material concerning the homilies added at the preceding number in some editions is interpolated. AREV.]

56. It is nevertheless reported that the same most holy man wrote other moral works and expounded the entire text of the four Gospels by preaching to the people—a work unknown, naturally, to us. Yet happy, indeed exceedingly happy, is the person who was able to know all his studies. He flourished under the Emperor Maurice Augustus. He died at the very beginning of the reign of Phocas, ruler of the Romans.

## CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 1103C]]

57. “Of the province,” etc. Lucas of Tuy and others falsely add “as commander.” “From Arianism,” etc. In the Third Council of Toledo, in the year 589; Gregory, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 31; and Gregory of Tours. PEREZ.]

57. Leander, born to Severianus, of the province of Carthage, a monk by profession, and from a monk made bishop of the province of the Church of Seville in Baetica, was a man sweet in speech, outstanding in intellect, and illustrious both in life and in teaching, so that through his faith and diligence the people of the Gothic nation returned from Arian madness to the Catholic faith. During his exile abroad he composed two books against the doctrines of the heretics, exceedingly rich in knowledge of the sacred Scriptures. In them, with forceful style, he attacks and exposes the perversity of Arian impiety, showing what the Catholic Church holds against them and how far it differs from them in religion and in the mysteries of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1103C]]

58. “To Florentina,” etc. The book on virgins exists at Oviedo and has now been printed. PEREZ.

[Col. 1103D] In the same place: “In the entire Psalter,” etc. This refers to prayers for ecclesiastical offices excerpted from the Psalms according to the first and second editions of Saint Jerome, as I explained more fully in *Isidoriana*, chapter 87, nos. 20 ff. AREV.]

58. There also exists another praiseworthy little work of his against the institutions of the Arians. In it, after presenting their statements, he sets his own replies against them. Moreover, he published for his sister Florentina a little book on the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt of the World, prefaced by divisions into chapters. He also devoted considerable effort to the Ecclesiastical Offices; for in the entire Psalter he composed prayers according to a double edition, and in the sacrifice, as well as in praises and psalms, he composed many pieces in a sweet melody.

[Note: [Col. 1103D]]

59. “He flourished.” In the year of Christ 600. “The end of life.” Our historians disagree about the year in which Leander of Seville died. Therefore, for the sake of our Isidore, who was both his brother and his successor in the Church of Seville, I am pleased to establish the year of Leander’s death with certainty. I conclude from the following considerations that Leander died in the year of Christ 600. First, Isidore says that his brother died in the time of King Reccared, who is known to have died in the year of Christ 600. For Isidore states in his book on the Goths that King Liúva succeeded Reccared in the era 639, that is, in the year of Christ 601. That Leander did not die before the year 600 is clear from the fact that Pope Gregory wrote to Leander of Seville in book VII of the *Register*, letter 125, in the second indiction and the ninth year of his pontificate, namely in the year of Christ 599. Thus the total number of years of Isidore’s episcopate will be established; Isidore succeeded his brother Leander, as we have said. For, according to Saint Ildefonsus, Isidore governed his Church of Seville for almost forty years. Since it is absolutely certain that Isidore died in the year of Christ 636—a point we shall confirm shortly in the section on Isidore—anyone who reckons backward will easily find both Leander’s death and the beginning of Isidore’s episcopate, and will recognize the truth of Ildefonsus’s statement that it lasted almost forty years. PEREZ.

In the same place: “Of life.” Others read “of active life” or “of mortal life.” AREV.]

59. He also wrote many letters: one to Pope Gregory on baptism, and another to his brother, in which he warns that no one should fear death. He also issued many personal letters to other bishops—if not sufficiently splendid in language, nevertheless sharp in thought. He flourished under Reccared, a religious man and glorious prince, during whose reign he also ended his life in a remarkable death.

[Note: [Col. 1104C]]

Some of our writers recently reported that he had been transferred from Carthage to the bishopric of Valencia, without sufficiently understanding Isidore’s words. A letter of this Lucinianus to Pope Gregory was published together with the *Moralia*. In addition, I possess a manuscript of a very learned letter by this Lucinianus and his colleague Severus to the deacon Epiphanius, in which he proves that angels are incorporeal, and another letter to Vincentius—not Vincentius of Zaragoza, but the bishop of the island of Ibiza—who believed that certain letters had fallen from heaven. PEREZ.

In the same place: “He flourished.” Around the year 590. PEREZ.

In the same place: In the Vulgate one reads, “But the righteous, if he is overtaken by death, will be in refreshment.” Saint Eulogius of Córdoba, in his *Apologeticus*, under the section “For what reason,” reads it in the same way as Saint Isidore. Saint Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*, likewise has “by whatever death.” As for the letters which Bishop Vincentius of Ibiza believed had fallen from heaven, and which Perezius discusses in his note, it should also be observed that Lucas of Tuy, *Against the Albigensians*, book III, chapter 18, mentions certain letters which the Albigensians circulated, pretending that they had been written by the Son of God and transmitted to human beings by the hands of angels. 60. Lucinianus, bishop of Carthage in Spain, learned in the Scriptures. We have read many of his letters, including one on the sacrament of baptism and very many addressed to Eutropius the abbot, who later became bishop of Valencia. The rest of his diligence and labor has not come to our knowledge. He flourished in the time of the Emperor Maurice Augustus. He died at Constantinople, reportedly poisoned by his rivals; but, as it is written, “The righteous, by whatever death he is overtaken, will have his soul in refreshment.”

In the same place: “He flourished.” In the year 590. PEREZ.

“Colleague and companion,” that is, in some monastery. See Florez, vol. XII, p. 303. Severus was bishop of Málaga from approximately the year 578 to 601. There is also another little book by him on Virginity, addressed to his sister, which is called *The Ring*. We confess that we know its title but are ignorant of its contents. He flourished in the time of the aforementioned emperor and, while that emperor was reigning, ended his life.

[Note: [Col. 1105C]]

62. John, bishop of the church of Gerona, a Goth by birth, was born at Scalabis in the province of Lusitania. As a young man he went to Constantinople, where, equipped with Greek and Latin learning, he returned to Spain after seventeen years, at the very time when, at the instigation of King Leovigild, Arian madness was raging. When the aforementioned king compelled him to embrace the cruelty of that wicked heresy, and John utterly resisted, he was driven into exile and banished to Barcelona. For ten years he endured many plots and persecutions from the Arians.

[Note: [Col. 1105C]]

63. I possess a copy of the *Chronicle* of John, abbot of Biclarum, whom Isidore mentions, taken from a very ancient Gothic book. This author, as he himself says of himself, carried Victor of Tunnuna’s *Chronicle* further, from the year of Christ 566 to 590, where he follows with great learning the history of our kings Leovigild and Reccared year by year according to the reigns of the emperors. PEREZ.

In the same place: “To write.” Others read “to have written,” which should be noted; for many infer from the verb “to write” that John of Biclarum was still alive when Isidore wrote this. Pinius concludes in his dissertation on the Gothic liturgy, chapter 2, section 3, that John introduced certain rites from the Eastern Church into the Gothic liturgy. In the latter, however, *seventeenth year* may be restored. AREV.]

63. Later he founded the monastery called Biclaro, where, after gathering a community of monks, he wrote a rule beneficial to that monastery [Col. 1106A] and also quite necessary for all who fear God. He is also said to have added, in a book of Chronicles, a very useful History, written in historical and composed style, extending from the first year of Justin the Younger’s reign to the eighth year of the reign of Maurice, emperor of the Romans, and the fourth year of King Reccared; and he is said to have written many other things that have not come to our knowledge.

64. Eutropius, bishop of the Church of Valencia, while he was still living in the monastery of Servitanum and was the father of the monks, wrote to Pope Lucinianus, whom we mentioned above, a very useful letter in which he asks him why chrism, and afterward an anointing, is administered to baptized infants. He also wrote to Peter, bishop of Ircavicensem, a letter composed in salutary style concerning the discipline of monks, and very necessary for monks.
