# APPENDICES TO THE WORKS OF SAINT ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

[Col. 1107]

## APPENDIX I. THE BOOK OF SAINT ILDEFONSUS, BISHOP OF TOLEDO, ON THE WRITINGS OF ILLUSTRIOUS MEN

(To this book, for which the Roman Editor had a suitable reason for placing it here, we reserve a more appropriate place in our Library—namely, in volume LXXXV of the *Patrologia*, among the other works of Saint Ildefonsus.)

[Col. 1107]

## APPENDIX II. 178 ANCIENT ARCHBISHOPS OF TOLEDO

From the edition of Grialius and volume III of the Toledo Fathers.

[Col. 1107A] 1. Saint Eugenius (around 112), sent by Saint Dionysius and martyred at Paris. — 2. Melantius (312 and earlier), at the Council of Elvira. — 3. Pelagius (around 325). Here Saint Ildefonsus begins the enumeration, as does the catalogue of Saint Aemilianus, perhaps from the peace of Constantine. — 4. Patrunus. — 5. Turibius. — 6. Quintus. — 7. Vincentius. — 8. Paulatus. — 9. Natalis. — 10. Audentius, concerning whom Gennadius writes. See Ildefonsus, chapter 2. — 11. Asturius (400; others, 405), concerning whom Ildefonsus writes, chapter 2. — 12. Isicius. — 13. Martinus. — 14. Castinus. — 15. Campeius. — 16. Sinticio, or Sinticius. — 17. Praumatus. — 18. Peter I. Here some insert Hector, from an ancient manuscript of the Council of Tarragona. — 19. Celsus. — 20. Montanus (522–531), concerning whom Ildefonsus writes, chapter 3. — 21. Julianus. — 22. Bacauda. — 23. Peter II. — 24. Euphemius, or Euphimius (579 and following). He signed the Third Council of Toledo in 589 and was also admired among foreigners, as is clear from volume I of Schelstratius’s *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*. — 25. Exuperius. — 26. Conantius. [Col. 1107B] Others prefer Adelphius. — 27. Adelphius (597). He signed a certain Council of Toledo in the twelfth year of Reccared. — 28. Aurasius (603–615), concerning whom Ildefonsus writes, chapter 5. — 29. Saint Helladius (615–623), concerning whom Saint Ildefonsus writes, chapter 7. — 30. Justus (633), concerning whom Saint Ildefonsus writes, chapter 8. — 31. Eugenius II (636), concerning whom Ildefonsus writes, chapter 12. — 32. Eugenius III (646), concerning whom Ildefonsus writes, chapter 13. — 33. Saint Ildefonsus (657). Julianus writes about him. — 34. Quiricus (667). He signed the Eleventh Council of Toledo. [Col. 1108A] — 35. Saint Julianus (680). Felix writes about him. — 36. Sisebertus (690). He was deposed at the Sixteenth Council of Toledo. — 37. Felix (693). He signed the Sixteenth Council of Toledo. — 38. Guntericus, or Gundericus (700). — 39. Sinderedus (around 710). Fleeing to Rome during the time of the Saracens, he signed the Roman Council under Gregory II. At the same time Oppa, or Oppas, was an intruder. Urbanus likewise performed the duties of Sinderedus, who was absent.

From this point the following bishops lived under the yoke of the Saracens.

40. Urbanus (after 721), first vicar and then, as may be believed, bishop after Sinderedus’s death. — 41. Sunieredus (around 740). — 42. Concordius (around 760). — 43. Cixila (around 774). He wrote the Life of Saint Ildefonsus, and Pope Adrian wrote to him. — 44. Elipandus (around 783). His opinion was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt in 794. — 45. Gumesindus (around 820). — 46. Wistremirus (around 850), whom Saint Eulogius of Córdoba also mentions as living at this time. — 47. [Col. 1108B] Saint Eulogius of Córdoba (859), elected in 859, in which year he died a martyr. — 48. Bonitus. — 49. John (around 950). He is said to have died in the Spanish Era 994, according to the Codex of Saint Aemilianus. — 50. Paschalis (1058). He was ordained at León in 1058. He was still bishop of Toledo in 1067. See *Hispania Sacra*, vol. XXXV, p. 83. Information about the other bishops is lacking until 1086, when, after Toledo had been taken from the yoke of the Saracens, Bernard was appointed archbishop.

[Col. 1107]

## APPENDIX III. POEMS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT ISIDORE

Verses that were read in the Library of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, and others attributed to Saint Isidore. (C, S)*

[Col. 1107C] [Note: [Col. 1107C]

I. What deserves particular attention in these verses was accurately explained in *Isidoriana*, chapter 81. It need only be repeated now that they were not composed according to the exact rules of meter and Latin. In title 1, verse 1, some read *mundialia* instead of *mundalia*; verse 3, *floris* instead of *florum*; verse 5, the printed editions have *gemmae*, incorrectly, instead of *geminae*; verse 6 could be read, “here the new together with the old,” as was observed concerning similar verses of Alvarus of Córdoba in the cited chapter of *Isidoriana*, no. 9.]

### I

Here are many sacred things; here are many worldly things:

From these, if any poems please you, take them and read.

You see meadows full of thorns, and an abundance of flowers.

[Col. 1108C] If you do not wish to take thorns, take roses.

Here twin venerable volumes of the law shine,

Here the new have been placed together with the old.

[Note: [Col. 1108C]

II. Others read, “I am that Origen”; others, “That Origen am I,” or “That, then, is Origen.” In the Madrid Codex and in the Vatican Palatine, after the first verse comes:

Whom illustrious Greece first gave to the faith.

I was eminent in merits and renowned for abundance of speech,

Suddenly snatched away … Instead of *Graecia*, the Vatican has *gratia*; and instead of *clarus*, the Madrid manuscript incorrectly has *clarius*.]

### II

That Origen am I, once the truest teacher,

[Col. 1109A] Suddenly snatched away by a harmful tongue.

If you believe it, I labored to compose so many thousands of books

As the legion leads armed men sent forth to war.

No blasphemy ever touched my thoughts.

But vigilant and prudent, I was safe from the enemy.

Only the work called *Periarchon* brought me misfortune;

Because of it, impious weapons press upon me.

[Note: [Col. 1109C]

III. Perhaps:

Gaul gave me birth; Pictavis, with its thunderous voice, … Instead of *alumna*, others have *alitque*.]

### III

Gaul gave me birth; Pictavis sent me, its teacher Hilary, with thundering voice.

[Note: [Col. 1109C]

IV. *Enitet*; others, *eminet*.]

### IV

Ambrose, a teacher distinguished by miracles and hymns,

Shines here in titles; he shines in eloquence.

[Note: [Col. 1109C]

V. Florez has it corruptly, “Augustine.”

He lies who claims to have read you completely.

Instead of *an quis*, others have *aut quis*. On the matter itself, see *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 7, no. 3. In verse 4, others have *quae loquor*. Instead of *ipse*, others have *ipsi*, which does not fit the meter. Instead of *prudentia*, others have *volumina*, which may perhaps be preferable, although it conflicts with the meter.]

### V

He lies who claims to have read you completely.

Can any reader possess all your works?

For you shine, Augustine, in a thousand volumes.

Your own books testify to what I myself say.

Although the wisdom of many books may please,

If Augustine is present, he alone is sufficient for you.

[Note: [Col. 1109C]

VI. Others incorrectly read, “the whole world celebrates you.” Some printed editions [Col. 1109D] indicate that another pentameter is missing after this verse; but these seem rather to be three hexameters without any pentameter. The third verse is discussed in *Isidoriana*, at the cited place.]

### VI

Jerome, interpreter, most learned in various languages,

[Col. 1109B] Bethlehem celebrates you; the whole world resounds with your name.

Our library too proclaims you through your books.

[Note: [Col. 1109D]

VII. “Called”; others, “you are called,” or “he is called.” The Vatican Palatine Codex has *vocatus*; either this or *vocabar* must be retained. Verse 2 appears thus, incorrectly, in the Madrid manuscript:

Because our tongue brings forth your golden work.

Instead of *nostrum*, others have *nostra*. Then, in verse 5, the Madrid Codex incorrectly has:

I composed the morals of men; I called the rewards of virtues.

See Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, where he discusses Saint John Chrysostom and praises his work on the conflict between virtues and vices.]

### VII

Called by the name John Chrysostom from that circumstance,

Because our tongue makes the work shine golden.

Constantinople shines with me as its teacher,

And everywhere I am celebrated through my books.

I composed morals; I spoke of the battles of virtues,

And I taught miserable guilty people to weep over their crimes.

[Note: [Col. 1109D]

VIII. *Refulges*; others, *refulgens*.]

### VIII

Brighter than all in eloquence, Cyprian, you shine.

A teacher once, now you are present as a martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1109D]

IX. *Tedet*: thus it should be written instead of *taedet*, so that the first syllable may be short. Instead of *par erat*, others have *par eat*.]

### IX

If Maro, if Flaccus, if Naso and Persius repel you,

If Lucan and Papinius weary you,

The excellent Prudentius was their equal, sweet in speech,

He, sufficiently renowned for his varied poems.

[Col. 1110A] [Note: [Col. 1109D]

X. *Gentilibus*. Others, less well, *gentibus*. On this title, see the prolegomena to Juvencus, no. 92, and to Sedulius, no. 167. From an error in manuscript 1 of the Vatican archive, *quam in Galiope*, one might conjecture *quid tibi Calliope?* instead of *quid tibi Calliroen?* Others have *Callirrhoem*; still others, other readings.]

### X

Read through the learned Avitus’ eloquent poem;

Look, Juvencus and Sedulius are here for you.

Equal in language, both flourishing in verse,

From the evangelical spring they bring abundant cups.

Therefore cease to serve the pagan poets,

While you can possess such great blessings; what need have you of Callirhoe?

[Note: [Col. 1110C]

XI. Eusebius, Orosius, Gregory.]

### XI

Histories of events and the ages that have passed—

This chest contains them all, inscribed on parchment.

[Note: [Col. 1110C]

XII. Eusebius, Orosius, Gregory.]

### XII

As greatly as you, Hippo, shine through Augustine as teacher,

So greatly does Rome shine through its bishop Gregory.

[Note: [Col. 1110C]

XIII. “Leander the prophet.” Others, “Isidore the bishop,” as I said in *Isidoriana*, at the cited place.]

### XIII

You are not regarded as inferior to the ancient teachers,

Leander the prophet. Your words teach this.

[Note: [Col. 1110C]

XIV. Theodosius, Paul, Gaius.

The same passage. Others read, “They bear not small books,” and so forth, or “They bear very many books,” and so forth. This and the three following couplets constitute the first title of the Library issued by Lord Isidore in the Madrid manuscript; it is followed by another title: “Here are many sacred things,” and so on through “take roses,” as above in the first title. Instead of *pone*, others incorrectly have *depone*. Instead of *frater*, others have *lector*. Then:

What need have I now of so much,

As I meditate on study, with nothing of myself remaining?

Others:

What I meditate upon in study, nothing remains for me; or:

What I meditate upon in studies, nothing remains of my own.

Perhaps *nil super ecce* should be read instead of *superesse*. Then:

I have explained the histories and traversed everything in the law,

If you say these words … Others:

I have explained the histories and traversed the crimes of the law.]

### XIV

Here is contained the most extensive series of laws of jurisprudence,

Which governs the Latin forum with truthful speech.

These chests do not contain sham books.

You who desire them, look: read, if your wishes incline you.

Cast off sluggishness here; lay aside the distaste of your mind.

Believe me, brother: you return from here more learned.

[Col. 1110B] Or perhaps you say: “What need have I of these things now?”

What I might meditate upon in study does not remain for me.

I have explained the histories and traversed everything in the law;

182 Truly, if you say this, you yourself now know nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1110D]

XV. Cosmas, Damian, Hippocrates, Galen.

The same passage. *Sunt medico* is printed incorrectly as *sunt medio*. In some manuscripts, *Item* occurs before the verse *Quod debes*, and likewise before the verse *Pauperis attende*; this indicates that these are two different titles, although both were composed for a physician. Instead of *curret denuo*, others have *occurret denuo*.]

### XV

Those whom the world celebrates as famous masters of medicine—

This present image marks these men in paint.

Gifts are for the physician, so long as each person is ill.

The sick man now rises; no flask comes.

What you owe the physician, pay, sick man, lest evils again

Come upon you; no one will run to you a second time.

Let the physician attend to the means of the poor man and of the powerful:

An unequal condition must be treated in an unequal manner.

If he is rich, let there be a proper opportunity for profit;

If poor, one payment is sufficient for you.

[Col. 1111A] [Note: [Col. 1111C]

XVI. In verse 2, others have:

Whatever the wave of the Idumaean sea carries forth.

Instead of *pervehit*, perhaps *provenit*. In verse 6, others:

And an immense house overflowing with delights.

In verse 7, others:

We enjoy the humble grasses born in the meadows.

In verse 9, others:

Therefore farewell, sacred mountains and fields of the Pierides.

Thus *sacri* is excessive. In verse 11, others:

Here lie fragrant cinnamon and breathing frankincense,

Whatever the Seres sow, whatever the Sabaeans bring.

Although many kinds of ointment may be beautifully abundant,

Nothing can be more pleasing than a rose or violets.

It would be better to read *cedet et his* instead of *cedet et hic*. Instead of *Cypro*, others have *Cyprium*, and instead of *quae*, *qui*.]

### XVI

Whatever Arabia bears to its altars, whatever the Indian brings of fragrance,

Whatever the wave of the Ionian sea carries forth,

Shining cinnamon, myrrh, leaf, and cassia,

Balsam, frankincense, calamus, and Corycian saffron—

These may belong to the perfumeries of great kings,

And to a house overflowing with immense riches.

We enjoy the cheap grasses sprouting in the meadows,

Which low valleys and lofty ridges produce.

Therefore farewell, sacred mountains and fields of Hesperia.

For our gifts are potent against many cares.

Here lie fragrant things; here cinnamon and frankincense breathe,

Whatever the wealthy Arab and the Sabaean bring.

Although many kinds of ointment may be most pleasing,

Nothing, neither rose nor violet, can be more pleasing.

The Elinian will yield to them; the Amaracinian will yield to them;

[Col. 1111B] And this one from the region of Cyprus will also yield.

Here you see various ointments that Greece has sent,

And very many from the land of Hesperia.

In fragile vessels made of compacted earthly dust

We carry pigments; we give no cups.

[Note: [Col. 1111D]

XVII. *Novit*. Others, *cupit*. Everything from here to the end, “go outside,” is absent from Muratori. In verse 3, I have written *quisque*, which is commonly taken for *quisquis*. In the printed editions and manuscripts: *quisquis vagus*, or *qui vagus hic*. Perhaps these two hexameters constituted another title on the same subject.]

### XVII

Whoever knows how to compete with a dead hide by means of a pen,

183 Let him come here, if he wishes; let him wage his battles here.

Let every scribe who has been wandering about for half an hour

Be struck across the back with two whips.

[Note: [Col. 1111D]

XVIII. “To the intercessor.” Florez has, probably incorrectly, “to the more intervening person.” The sense of the first two verses is obscure. Instead of *bis*, others have *dis*. The final couplet seems to belong to another title concerning the same intercessor. [Col. 1112C]]

### XVIII

If a scribe knew better how to do what he wants done

More, twice, three times, and four times, it would be necessary, friend.

If you are wise and understand, I tell you this: be silent.

The scribe does not permit anyone to speak in his presence.

There is nothing here for you to do, chatterer; go outside.

[Note: [Col. 1112C]

XIX. I discussed these verses in *Isidoriana*, chapter 65, no. 46, and chapter 81, no. 12. I attach them to the other verses of the Library because they belong to the same class. The Madrid edition of Ulloa, in verse 2, has *egregius* instead of *egregias*, and in verse 7 omits *praecepta*, for which *simulacra* is conjectured in the note. We follow Vatican Codex 650.]

### XIX

Solomon sang this book with wondrous sweetness,

Which contains the outstanding songs of the Bridegroom and the Bride,

[Col. 1111C] Singing here and there the praises of the Church and Christ.

It recalls the faithful companions, male and female, of the bridal chamber.

These, I beg you, young man, remember to commit to your mind.

These songs are far better than the excessively false songs of Maro.

They sing to you the true precepts of everlasting life.

That poet will sound evil frivolities and falsehoods in your ears.

[Col. 1112A]

## Poem on the Eclipse of the Moon

[Note: [Col. 1112D]

VERSE 1. What should be thought about this poem can be found in *Isidoriana*, chapter 76, nos. 12 and following. We now present it corrected more carefully than before, according to the manuscript codices and editions. Instead of *in luco*, others have *in lucis*.

8. *Cum teneat*. Perhaps *cum tentet*.

12. *Pernices*. Thus correctly in Codex Regiovaticanus 255. The Pisa edition has *praeveniens*; Ulloa has *permisces*, from which the reading *pernices* is confirmed.

21. Ulloa’s edition reads corruptly:

“Or with the dew of Styx, resounding against the mother earth of the upper air.”

From this someone might be able to extract the true reading.

23. *Dispescit*: others, *dispexit* or *despexit*.

25. *Lumina*. Others, *culmina*.

26. *Detinet*. Others, *deserit*; others, *desinet*.

28. Instead of *aggerei*, others have *aggere*; others, incorrectly, *ageret*.

31. *Clueat*. Others, *luceat*.

35. *Curribus altis*. Others, *cursibus altis*.

36. *Vel desuper*. Others, *ut desuper*; others, *cum desuper*.

[Col. 1113A] 51. *Sed sudum*. Ulloa’s edition:

“Yet, approaching the clear sky, with a lofty assault against the dark places.”

Let others determine what can be extracted from this.

55. *Devia tortos*. Thus the Pisa edition, apparently from the correction of Pierre Pithou. Ulloa’s edition has *deviat ortos*.

[Col. 1113B] 56. *Colligit anfractus*. Ulloa’s edition and the Vatican manuscript: [Col. 1114A] “While he reads the winding paths.”

58. *Cur*. Others, *ubi*; others, *ibi*.

59. Ulloa’s edition places before this verse: “When between the earth …”

60. *Almi*. Thus Ulloa’s edition; others, *almae*, perhaps instead of *alma*.

[Col. 1114B] 61. See *Isidoriana*, at the cited place.]

You perhaps, languid in a grove, produce wandering songs,

And among clear waters and musical breezes

Pour liquid nectar over your Pierian mind.

But us a confused mass of affairs obscures,

[5] And iron cares press upon us with a thousand soldiers.

The law-court’s din resounds, the forums bark, trumpets disturb us.

And farther across the Ocean we are borne, all the way to where snowy

Vasco holds sway, and the dreadful Cantabrian does not spare us.

Look at those for whom you indicate that the leafy branches of Phoebus

[10] Should be girded, or that ivy should shade their hair more nobly.

Look at those whom you command to fly, aflame, through the ether.

Indeed, if you wish, the sluggish elephant will outrun swift eagles;

The tortoise, though slow, will outrun the fleet Molossian hound,

184 Before we pursue the moon flowing with dew in our song.

[15] Yet, bent beneath earthly weights and straining,

I shall explain why the circle grows pale in its weary orbit,

[Col. 1112B] And why the purple radiance fades from its snow-white face.

It is not, as the people believe, that a most dreadful woman,

Howling beneath the underworld shadows in black caves,

[20] Drags it down from its lofty, wandering mirror; nor, overcome by a spell,

Does she attack it with Styx’s dew [lacuna],

Seeking a cry that can be overcome; for through the ether,

Where the swiftest boundary divides the troubled from the clear,

It travels inviolate. Rather, the earth, with its vast body,

[25] Which occupies the middle, the lowest part of the heavens,

While it holds back the light of its brother with shadowy boundaries,

Makes the round wheel pale beneath its dense shadow, until it passes across the axis—

The swift mound of the earth’s raised mass—and, in its rosy mirror,

Allows the brother’s flames to be restored freely through the sky.

[30] But since you find it wondrous that, although the sun’s greatest power

Is eighteen times greater than that of the earthly globe,

It now surrounds the earth’s boundaries with light,

Take this established work of reason; look at Phoebus,

How high he travels through the golden vault of the world,

[35] And how he illuminates the lowly earth with lofty chariots:

[Col. 1112C] However greatly he may scatter fires from above,

Or however he may shine upon it with an oblique axis,

The rays are broken upon the earth; the sun’s remaining

Light, wherever it emerges greater with its piercing rays,

[40] Moves through the vast emptiness, unhindered by the globe,

Until the vanquished shadow completes the summit of the pyramid.

Through this, when Phoebe drives her powerful, moist team,

The lowest region sometimes, near its neighboring shadows,

Lacks her brother and fades bloodless from her empty face.

[45] [Col. 1113A] But why the moon alone should be stripped of light

Is no wonder; for, needing light, she is nourished by another’s light,

And when the nearer part of the boundary begrudges it,

She awaits the rays of her brother, unhappily darkened.

But the remaining choir of stars is not touched by shadows.

[50] Each has its own radiance, and they do not redden from the sun.

But the clear sky [lacuna]

185 Beyond the sun it is carried with the vault of heaven.

Now why does it not always grow pale in a six-monthly orbit?

[Col. 1114A] Their courses provide this through an inclined path.

[55] For when, wandering in a fixed circuit, it gathers its winding deviations,

The sun leaves the boundary at a distance,

Throws the veil of night across it, and shines upon its sister.

The same explanation accounts for why the sun’s radiant splendor

Is broken by sudden shadows, deprived of light,

[60] When, between earth and sun, the wheel of the life-giving body,

The moon, travels, blocking her brother with a direct obstruction.

[Col. 1113]

# APPENDIX IV. CHRONICLE OF THE VISIGOTHIC KINGS

[Col. 1113B] In the Spanish Era 400, Athanaric became the first king among the Goths. After him came Alaric; when he died in Italy, Athaulf was chosen. During his reign the Goths, abandoning Italy, occupied Gaul and afterward Spain. The years of the kings are recorded in the following summary.

[Note: [Col. 1113C]

APPENDIX IV, no. 1. In Saint Isidore the era is given as 407. For Athanaric’s thirteen years, the edition of the Toledo Fathers conjectures twelve years. The numbers of the Spanish Era and the years of Christ placed in parentheses are taken from Grialius’s edition, in which, after the Chronicle of the Goths, there is appended a catalogue of the Gothic kings in Spain, collected from Isidore, from the ancient councils of Spain, and from this Chronicle. See *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, nos. 9 and 10.]

1. Athanaric (Spanish Era 407; A.D. 369) reigned thirteen years.

2. Alaric (S.E. 420; A.D. 382) reigned twenty-eight years, in Italy.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

3. In the same edition, instead of six years, perhaps five years.]

3. Athaulf (S.E. 449; A.D. 411) reigned six years.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

4. Segeric. Others, Sigeric. In the same edition I would prefer to read seven days instead of seven years. Lindenbrog presents seven years; elsewhere only half a day. The matter is obscure.]

4. Segeric (S.E. 454; A.D. 416) reigned [Col. 1113C] seven years. Elsewhere, only half a day.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

5. Perhaps four years.]

5. Walia (S.E. 454; A.D. 416) reigned three years.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

6. Others, Theuderic … twenty-three years. By conjecture, thirty-two years.]

6. Theuderedus (S.E. 457; A.D. 419) reigned thirty-three years.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

7. Turismundus; others, Thurismodus. One year, not three, should be assigned to him.]

7. Turismundus (S.E. 490; A.D. 452) reigned three years. Elsewhere, one.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

8. Theudericus; others, Theudoricus. The thirteen years should be retained, not seven.]

8. Theudericus (S.E. 491; A.D. 453) reigned seven years. Elsewhere, thirteen.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

9. Fifteen years. Others, twenty years, and by conjecture eighteen. In other respects the author seems to have followed Saint Isidore in his History of the Goths.]

9. Euricus (S.E. 504; A.D. 466) reigned fifteen years. Elsewhere, seventeen.

186 10. Alaric (S.E. 521; A.D. 483) reigned twenty-three years.

[Note: [Col. 1113D]

11. Gisaleicus; others, Geselicus, Gesaleicus, or Gesaericus. After one year, Lindenbrog adds: “Elsewhere, fifteen.” The reason for this is not understood, unless perhaps his reign is joined with the reign of Theuderic, who spent eleven years in Spain. See Saint Isidore.]

11. Gisaleicus (S.E. 544; A.D. 506) reigned three years, and spent one year in hiding. Elsewhere, fifteen.

[Note: [Col. 1114C]

12. Theuderic; others, also Theudoricus. This likewise indicates that another of the same name preceded him, as below in the case of Livua and in Reccared, nos. 20 and 24. The figure forty-one years is false. He reigned fifteen years as co-ruler. [Col. 1114D] Others give eleven years, because he spent that many in Spain. Masdeu, vol. X of *History of Spain*, p. 311, describes the Chronicle of the Visigothic kings and observes that five years are assigned to Amalaric because his first four years are counted under Theuderic. For the year of Christ 523, others have 526. Instead of Amalaricus, others have Amalericus.]

12. Theuderic (S.E. 549; A.D. 511) ruled in Spain from Italy, acting as guardian of his grandson Amalaric, for eleven years according to the consular records. Elsewhere, fifteen.

Amalaric (S.E. 561; A.D. 523) reigned five years.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

13. According to Isidore, seventeen years should be counted rather than sixteen.]

13. Theudis (S.E. 569; A.D. 531) reigned six years and six months. Elsewhere, seventeen years and five months.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

14. Others have five months instead of six.]

14. Theudisclus (S.E. 586; A.D. 548) reigned one year, six months, and thirteen days.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

15. Six months. Others, three months.]

15. Agila (S.E. 587; A.D. 519) reigned five years, six months, and thirteen days.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

16. Others, thirteen years. Those who count fifteen years begin from the year in which he first rebelled.]

16. Athanagildus (S.E. 592; A.D. 554) reigned [Col. 1114C] fifteen years and six months. Elsewhere, fourteen years. The reign was vacant for five months. Elsewhere, thirteen years.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

17. Masdeu understands this as one year by himself, followed by two years with his son.]

17. Livua (S.E. 605; A.D. 567) reigned one year.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

18. Leovigildus; others, Leubegildus; others, Livigildus.]

18. Leovigildus (S.E. 606; A.D. 568) reigned eighteen years.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

19. Six months. Others, one month. The fifteen years are reckoned from the year in which he received the title.]

19. Reccaredus (S.E. 624; A.D. 586) reigned fifteen years, six months, and ten days.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

20. One year should be retained rather than two.]

20. Livua likewise (S.E. 639; A.D. 601) reigned one year. Elsewhere, two years and six months.

21. Witericus (S.E. 641; A.D. 603) reigned six years and ten months.

[Note: [Col. 1114D]

22. Fourteen days. Others, thirteen; others, nine.]

22. Gundemarus (S.E. 648; A.D. 610) reigned one year, ten months, and fourteen days.

[Col. 1115A] [Note: [Col. 1115B]

23. Sixteen days; others incorrectly have six days.]

23. Sisebutus (S.E. 650; A.D. 612) reigned eight years, eleven months, and sixteen days. Elsewhere, six months.

[Note: [Col. 1115B]

24. Three months. Others, four months. Incorrectly, three years in other witnesses.]

24. Reccaredus likewise (S.E. 659; A.D. 621) reigned three months. Elsewhere, a few days.

25. Suintila (S.E. 659; A.D. 621) reigned ten years.

[Note: [Col. 1115B]

26. Four years. Others, three years. Masdeu asserts that four years conflicts with the Toledo councils. Instead of fourteen days, Lindenbrog has sixteen days.]

26. Sisenandus (S.E. 669; A.D. 631) reigned four years, eleven months, and fourteen days.

[Note: [Col. 1115B]

27. Nine months. Others, eight months, which alone pleases Masdeu.]

27. Chintila (S.E. 674; A.D. 636) reigned three years, nine months, and nine days.

28. Tulga (S.E. 678; A.D. 640) reigned two years and four months.

187 [Note: [Col. 1115B]

29. Chindasuinthus; others, Cindasuindus or Chindisuindus. Others less correctly say that the years of his reign together with his son amount to three, with twelve days. Lindenbrog incorrectly assigns the Spanish Era 661 to him.]

29. Chindasuinthus (S.E. 680; A.D. 642) ruled alone for six years, eight months, and eleven days. Then, together with his son, King Reccesuinthus, he ruled for four years, eight months, and eleven days. He died on the day before the Kalends of October, in Spanish Era 691.

[Note: [Col. 1115C]

30. Reccesuinthus. Others, Reccesuindus. Instead of *regnavit*, others have *solus regnavit*, but *solus* must be deleted. Others have three months instead of seven; others, six; and instead of eleven days, Aguirrius has twelve days, others two days. Lindenbrog, corruptly, has thirteen years. The text’s figures must be retained throughout, including the year of the Incarnation 672, for which Lindenbrog gave 662.]

30. Reccesuinthus (S.E. 687; A.D. 649) reigned twenty-three years, seven months, and eleven days. He died on the Kalends of September, on the fourth day of the week, at the third hour, in Spanish Era 710, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 672, in the eighth year of the nineteen-year cycle, with the moon at three days. Together with his father he likewise reigned four years, eight months, and eleven days.

[Note: [Col. 1116B]

31. *Domnus*: others, “the glorious lord.” Instead of the thirteenth day, others incorrectly have the fourteenth.]

31. The lord Wamba (S.E. 710; A.D. 672) assumed the reins of government on the same day on which Reccesuinthus died, on the aforementioned Kalends of September; the solemnity of his anointing was postponed until the third day before the Kalends of October, [Col. 1116A] when the moon was twenty-one days old, in the same Spanish Era. The glorious King Wamba likewise reigned eight years, one month, and fourteen days. The aforementioned ruler also accepted penance on Sunday at the beginning of the first hour of the night, which was the day before the Ides of October, with the moon at fifteen days, in Spanish Era 718.

[Note: [Col. 1116B]

32. *Autem*. Others, *statim*. In the same place, *noster* is omitted by others. Instead of the twelfth day before the Kalends, Aguirrius incorrectly has the fourteenth. After “twenty-five days,” Masdeu supplies “until the fifth day before the Ides of November”; and he explains *altera die* as “on another day,” without its necessarily being the following day. Instead of December, Aguirrius incorrectly has September. Lindenbrog and Aguirrius end with the moon at twenty-two days, in the same Spanish Era. Maiansius and Florez added the rest.]

32. On the following day, a Monday, the glorious lord our lord Ervigius (S.E. 718; A.D. 680) assumed the royal scepter. This was the Ides of October, with the moon at sixteen days, in Spanish Era 718. The solemnity of his anointing was postponed until the following Sunday, which was the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, with the moon at twenty-two days, in the same Spanish Era. The glorious King Ervigius likewise reigned seven years and twenty-five days. On that day, while suffering from a final illness, he chose as his successor in the kingdom our glorious lord Egica; and on the following day, which was the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, a Friday, the same lord Ervigius accepted penance and absolved all the elders, so that they might proceed with the aforementioned glorious prince, our lord Egica, to the seat of his kingdom at Toledo.

33. Our lord Egica (S.E. [Col. 1116B] 725; A.D. 687) was anointed king in the church of Saints Peter and Paul at the Praetorian district on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, a Sunday, with the moon at fourteen days, in Spanish Era 725.

[Note: [Col. 1116B]

34. “On the day on which.” Perhaps *die quae*, or, as in no. 32, *die quod*. The edition of the Toledo Fathers correctly notes that Florez reads the eighteenth day before the Kalends. Masdeu maintains that one should read the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, Spanish Era 739—that is, the year 701. Others assign the year 702. In the catalogue of the Visigothic kings in Grialius’s edition, it is added that Witiza reigned ten years, Roderic one year, and, according to others, three. All these matters can be compared with the following chronology, so that they may mutually assist one another.]

34. Witiza (S.E. 739; A.D. 701) was anointed king on the day that was the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in Spanish Era 738.

# APPENDIX V

Chronology and succession of the Gothic kings from Regiovatican Codex 667.

[Col. 1115C] 188 1. Athanaric was the first to reign among the Goths, for thirteen years. He was the first through whom the Arian heresy entered, by means of the emperor Valens, among the entire Gothic people. [Col. 1115D] Under this king the Goths began to have laws and letters; and under the same king they were expelled by the Huns from their native land. The king also ended his life at Constantinople under the emperor Theodosius. (See *Isidoriana*, chapter 79, no. 11.)

2. Alaric reigned fourteen years. To avenge the Goths*, whom the Romans had killed, he moved an army and captured Rome; there he plundered Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius, together with many possessions. Later he died in Italy under the emperors Honorius and Arcadius.

3. Athaulf reigned six years. He took the aforementioned Placidia as his wife and, in the fifth year of his reign, went from Italy to Gaul. When he wished to proceed to Spain, he was killed by his own men at Barcelona under the emperors Honorius and Arcadius.

4. Sigeric reigned one year. When he wished to make peace with the Romans, he was soon killed by his own men under the aforementioned imperial rule.

5. Wallia reigned three years. He was a warrior; he made peace with the emperor Honorius and returned his sister Placidia to him. Entering Spain, he destroyed the Vandals and Silingi [others: “Vandals, Selingi”] in battle in Baetica and reduced the Alans to nothing. [Col. 1116D] He planned to cross by fleet to Africa, but the Gaditanian sea did not allow him. He returned to Gaul, where he ended his life under the rule of Honorius.

6. Teuderedus reigned thirty-three years. He destroyed the Roman commander Litorius and many thousands of Romans together with him; he killed two hundred thousand of the Huns, and was killed there in battle under the rule of Theodosius the Younger.

7. His son Turismundus reigned one year. Because he was savage and harmful, he was killed by Theuderic, Frigdarius, and his brothers, under the emperor Marcian.

8. Theudericus reigned for 13 years. When he gave Emperor Avitus assistance against the Goths, he consequently entered Hispania with the permission of that same Emperor Avitus and with a huge army. At the twelfth milestone from Asturica, by the river Urbicus, he defeated Rechiar, king of the Suebi, in battle; pursuing him, he captured and killed him at Portucale. He captured Bracta [perhaps Bracharam]; then he returned from there through Lusitania to [Col. 1117A] Gaul. There he was killed by his brother Euricus, under the emperor Leo.

9. Euricus reigned for 26 years. He ravaged Lusitania, captured Pamplona and Caesaraugusta, and gave the Goths a law. He died at Arelate under the emperor Zeno.

10. Alaric, his son, reigned for 23 years. King Clovis of the Franks killed him in battle near Pictavium. To avenge his death, his father-in-law Theudericus, king of Italy, terrified the Franks and restored the kingdom intact to the Goths, under the emperor Anastasius.

11. Gesaleicus, the son of Alaric, reigned for four years. Defeated at Narbo by Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, he fled to Barcilona. From there he went to Africa, to the Vandals, seeking assistance, but did not obtain it. Returning from there, he was killed near Barcilona by a commander of Theudericus, king of Italy, under the emperor Anastasius.

12. The aforementioned Theudericus, after killing Gisaleicus, held the kingdom of the Goths for 15 years and left it to his surviving grandson [Col. 1117B] Amalaric. He himself returned to Italy and ended his life there under the emperor Justinian.

13. Amalaric reigned for five years. Defeated by Childebert, king of the Franks, he perished at Narbo under the emperor Justinian.

14. Theudis reigned for 17 years. Although a heretic, he granted peace to the Church and gave the bishops permission to hold councils in the city of Toledo. He defeated the Frankish kings in Hispania as far as the Minius; someone pretending to be insane killed him in the palace, under the emperor Justinian.

15. Theudisclus reigned for one year. Since he dishonored the marriages of many and, in passing, devised the deaths of many others, he was soon stabbed to death with a sword at a banquet in Hispalis, under the same Justinian.

16. Agila reigned for five years. While he was fighting against the city of Corduba and, in contempt of Christ, had polluted the tomb of the holy martyr Acisclus with some act of horror, his son was killed there with a large number of men, and he lost the entire royal treasure. He fled to Emerita, where [Col. 1117C] his own men killed him, under the emperor Justinian.

17. Athanagild reigned for 14 years. He fought for a long time against the soldiers of Emperor Justinian, whom he himself had requested against Agila, and destroyed them. He died a natural death at Toledo, under the emperor Justinian.

18. Livua reigned for three years, at Narbo. He gave the administration of Hispania to his brother Leovigild; he himself governed Gaul.

19. Having obtained Gaul and Hispania, Leovigild reigned for 14 years. Being deeply devoted to the Arian heresy, he inflicted persecution on the Catholics and removed the privileges of the churches. He sent Masona, bishop of the Emeritans, into exile. He was ruinous to his own people and condemned the powerful out of greed. He defeated the Suebi and incorporated the kingdom of Gallaecia into that of the Goths. He was the first to sit upon a throne clothed in royal garments. He established a city in Celtiberia and named it Recopolis. He first revised the laws of the Goths and died a natural death at Toledo under the emperor Maurice.

[Col. 1117D] 20. Recared, his son, reigned for 15 years. At the beginning of his reign he embraced the Catholic faith, recalled the entire Gothic people to the worship of God and to the right faith, and through a synod of the bishops of Gaul and Hispania confirmed the Catholic faith. He defeated 60,000 Frankish enemies in battle in Hispania and honored the period of his reign with every virtue. He died peacefully at Toledo, under the emperor Maurice.

21. Livua, his son, reigned for two years. Wicteric killed him, though he was harmless because his right hand had been cut off, and assumed the kingdom for himself, under the emperor Maurice.

190. 22. Wicteric reigned for seven years. He was indeed a vigorous man in the art of warfare, but devoid of victory; what he did, he received in return. For he was killed by his own men during a banquet, under the emperor Phocas.

23. Gundemar reigned for two years. In a single expedition he ravaged the Basques, and died a natural death at Toledo under the rule of Heraclius.

24. Sisebut reigned for eight years. By force of authority he brought the Jews to the faith of Christ, and magnificently founded the church of Saint Leocadia at Toledo. He subdued the Asturians and Basques, who were rebelling in the mountains, and was benevolent toward his own people in every respect. Some assert that he was killed by a disease of his own; others, by an excessive draught of a potion, under the rule of Heraclius. At that time the impious Muhammad preached the wickedness of his law to foolish peoples in Africa.

25. Suintila reigned for ten years. He was great in victory and counsel. He defeated the Basques, captured two Roman patricians, governed all Hispania and Gaul energetically, and on account of his merit was called “the father of the poor.” He died a natural death at Toledo under the rule of Heraclius.

26. Sisenand reigned for four years. He held synods of bishops, was patient, and proved orthodox in accordance with the Catholic rules. He ended his life at Toledo under the rule of Heraclius.

27. Chintila reigned for three years. He held many synods at Toledo with the bishops and strengthened the subjected kingdom in the faith. He died at Toledo under the rule of Heraclius.

28. Tulga reigned for three years. He was gentle in all things.

29. Chindaswinth reigned alone for six years and with his son Recceswinth for four years. In his time Hispania enjoyed peace, and through synods he instructed the Church. He died at Toledo under the rule of Constantine the Younger.

30. Wamba reigned for nine years. In the first year of his reign, when the commander Paul was rebelling against him with a certain part of Hispania, he first subdued the fierce Basques in the region of Cantabria. Then, after capturing all the cities of Gothic and Gallic territory, he finally defeated Paul himself in the city of Nemausus and subjected him to himself in a celebrated triumph. Later he was deprived of the kingdom by Ervigius, under the rule of Constantine the Younger.

31. Ervigius reigned for six years. He held many synods at Toledo with the bishops and gave his daughter in marriage to Egica. He died at Toledo under the rule of Justinian.

32. Egica reigned for 15 years. When he received the kingdom, he subjected Ervigius’s daughter by an oath of Wamba. He appointed his son Witiza to rule with him. He died at Toledo under the rule of Leo.

33. Witiza reigned for ten years. He ended his life at Toledo under the rule of Tiberius.

34. Ruderic reigned for three years. In his time, in the era 752, the Saracens, summoned by Farmalio [the reading is uncertain], occupied Hispania and seized the kingdom of the Goths. They still stubbornly possess part of it; they wage war with the Christians by day and night and fight daily, until the divine predestination should thereafter command that they be cruelly expelled. The kings of the Goths came to an end. They were (sic) under one [rule] for 314 years. While Alaric was reigning, from the era 301, the Goths entered Italy. After this, the Gothic kings entered Gaul. 191. Seven years later, the Goths migrated to Hispania. In the era D. IX. LXV [perhaps 835], Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of Rome, reigned.

[Col. 1119]

# APPENDIX VI. EXPOSITION ON THE SONG OF SONGS OF SOLOMON (C, G, S)*

[Col. 1119A] [Note: [Col. 1119D]

**Chapter I—Note 1.** What should be thought about this Exposition I have stated in *Isidoriana*, chapter 65, note 45 and following. In interpreting the Song of Songs mystically, the Hebrews and the holy Fathers of the Church agree. Among other works, that of Ludovicus a Ponte on the Song of Songs is especially worthy of being read. Instead of *a chrisma*, one should perhaps read *a chrismate*.]

## Chapter I

1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, whom I have heard promised so often by the prophets. “For your breasts are better than wine.” The sweetness of evangelical teaching is better than legal austerity. “Fragrant with the finest ointments.” With the gifts of the Holy Spirit: from *chrisma* comes Christ, that is, “anointed,” from *unction*, because this name, together with the grace of the Holy Spirit, is poured out upon all the faithful in baptism. “Therefore the maidens loved you.” The souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism.

[Note: [Col. 1120D]

**2.** Most Fathers and more recent interpreters judge that the Bride in the Song represents the Church.]

2. “Draw me after you.” So that I may follow you as you ascend into heaven. “The king brought me into his chambers.” By faith, into the inner joys of the heavenly homeland. “We will exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts as better than wine.” In you, not in ourselves; remembering in every respect that the grace of faith is superior to the teaching of the Law. “The upright love you.” No one loves you except the upright; and no one is upright except one who loves you. “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” The voice of the Church concerning her afflictions. Black in the pressures of persecution, but beautiful in the splendor of virtues.

[Col. 1119B] 3. “Like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.” Darkened by the temptation of demons, but beautiful in putting to death carnal desires. “Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discolored me.” Do not be surprised if outwardly I am despised by human beings because of the heat of temptations. “The sons of my mother fought against me; they appointed me keeper of the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep.” The harshness of the sons of the Synagogue made me fail to guard the vineyard at Jerusalem, but made me the guardian of many vineyards, that is, of churches throughout the world. “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions.” Tell me of my shepherd, whom I love with my whole mind, and in what pastures and resting place he may be found, lest, disturbed by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him among the gatherings of his companions, that is, of heretics.

4. “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks of your flocks.” If you do not know that under such conditions of temptation you have been betrothed to me, go out from my sight and follow the various actions of those who wander astray. “And pasture your young goats beside the tents of the shepherds.” That is, nourish lost hearers, following the teachings of foolish teachers. “I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry in the chariots of Pharaoh.” Just as I freed the former people from fear of Egypt, so, my bride, if you trust in me, I will free you from empty threats.

[Note: [Col. 1120D]

**5.** *Murenula* comes from *muraena*; nevertheless, many write *murenula* without the diphthong.]

5. “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove.” I have adorned you with such a great virtue of salutary modesty that you do not corrupt the chastity of the faith promised to me through the seduction of wicked teachers. “Your neck is like necklaces; we will make you golden chains, studded with silver.” Teachers are signified by the neck. Works are expressed by necklaces, because they show by their deeds what they teach in words. In the chains, sacred Scripture is represented: inwardly it shines with the gold of spiritual meanings, and outwardly it gleams with the silver of heavenly eloquence.

6. “While the king was at his table, my spikenard gave forth its fragrance.” While Christ the King rests in the blessedness of heavenly secrecy, the virtue of the saints supplies us with the grace of great sweetness. “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will lie between my breasts.” The death of my beloved, which he endured for my salvation, will always remain in my memory. “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me in the vineyards of Engaddi.” He who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of his passion is himself a cluster of Cyprus in the sweetness of his resurrection. Myrrh brings sadness; wine brings joy. “In the vineyards of Engaddi,” because of the divine gifts that he bestowed after the resurrection upon those who share in them through baptism. Engaddi, “the fountain of the kid,” signifies baptism.

7. “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful.” Beautiful in simplicity of heart and purity of works. “Your eyes are like those of doves.” Because your perceptions are endowed with spiritual understanding.

8. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful.” You alone are beautiful by nature; I am beautiful from you. “Our couch is flourishing.” The peace of the holy Church flourishes with holy virtues and multiplies through spiritual offspring. “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress.” The beams and ceilings are the teachers in the holy Church, on account of their protection and beauty. They are cedar and cypress because of their outstanding virtues [Col. 1120B] and the fragrance of their good life.

## Chapter II

1. “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” I am the adornment of the world and the glory of the humble. “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters.” You seek rest and praise the couch; remember that you are made whiter by the barbs of tribulations, and that the fruit of preaching is greater than that of repose.

2. “As an apple among the trees of the forests, so is my beloved among the sons.” Just as an apple surpasses the trees of the forest in appearance, fragrance, and taste, so Christ surpasses all the saints, who are called sons of God by grace, whereas he alone is so by nature. “I sat down beneath his shadow, whom I had desired.” Under the protection of the one whose presence I always sought, I rest and remain secure. “And his fruit is sweet to my palate.” Because he has refreshed me with the heavenly sweetness of his grace.

[Note: [Col. 1120D]

**Chapter II—Note 3.** Cassiodorus, Anselm, Bede, and other interpreters of sacred Scripture also teach that the wine cellar signifies the Church figuratively.]

3. “He brought me into the wine cellar; he ordered charity in me.” The wine cellar should be understood as the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is customarily given and received. Its grace is designated here by the name of wine. In this cellar charity is ordered, so that a person may love God with all his heart, more than himself. “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I am sick with love.” Console me with the examples of those beginning or completing the way of salvation, while I still languish in weariness of this pilgrimage through love of the heavenly vision. “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.” The left hand of Christ signifies his temporal goods; the right, the blessedness of eternal life. Here he strengthens the mind through hope, and there glorifies it through reward.

4. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the does and the stags of the fields, that you do not stir up or awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.” I appeal to the peaceful souls of the faithful, by the virtues proper to each, which are signified by clean and ruminating animals, not to hinder the pious efforts of the brethren through any importunity; rather, let each rejoice in the progress of his neighbor as in his own.

[Col. 1120D] 5. “The voice of my beloved.” The words “this is” are understood: this is the voice of my beloved, whom I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken me while I rested in his embrace. “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.” Such leaps my beloved made. From heaven he came into the womb; from the womb into the manger; from the manger to the cross; from the cross into the tomb; from the tomb he returned to heaven. He is the one who was raised above all mountains and hills, that is, above the heights of the saints.

6. “My beloved is like a doe and a fawn of the stags.” In the assumption of flesh and the humility of the doe, Christ is compared to a doe; in the variety of virtues and the innocence of a fawn of stags—that is, of the patriarchs—Christ is compared to such a fawn. “Behold, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices.” Clothed in the wall of our mortality, he remained hidden; but, looking at us through lattices and windows, he performed miracles, so that from the miracles it might appear that he was God, who was hidden by his sufferings. “Behold, my beloved speaks to me.” He urges me to preach, saying:

7. “Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come.” Rise from the bed of repose, in which you seek to care only for yourself; hasten and come to devote yourself also to the salvation of your neighbors through diligent preaching. “For winter has already passed, the rain has gone away and departed.” The cold of unbelief and the rain of iniquity have now departed, though they covered the whole world until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. “The flowers have appeared in our land.” That is, the beginnings of faith and righteousness have blossomed in the world as the Church grew.

8. “The time of pruning has come.” That is, so that, once the shoots of empty religion have been cut off, human hearts may be prepared for the future fruit of faith. “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” That is, the voice of Christ our Savior saying: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near.” “The fig tree has brought forth its unripe figs.” The precepts of the old Law have fallen. “The flowering vines have given forth their fragrance.” That is, the evangelical people, or the flowering vines of holy conduct, have spread the fragrance of their life far and wide.

9. “Arise, hasten, my friend, my beautiful one, and come; my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall.” O bride and friend, to whom I have offered such great blessings, arise and come; gird yourself for the contest, from which you will receive eternal rest. “My dove,” through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. “In the clefts of the rock,” that is, in the wounds which the bridegroom received for the salvation of the bride. “In the hollow of the wall,” that is, in the guardianship of the heavenly virtues. “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.” The voice, namely, of praise or preaching. “For your voice is sweet, and your face is beautiful.” That person’s voice is sweet to the Lord to whom it is sweet either to announce the word of the Lord or to sing praises to the Lord himself. And that faith is beautiful which, adorned with works, does not fear to endure adversity.

10. “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” That is, conquer heretics and schismatics: those who are perverse in faith and deceitful in speech, who habitually tear the inexperienced minds of the faithful with the tooth of wicked teaching. “For our vineyard has blossomed.” That is, the peoples of the elect are sprouting everywhere.

11. “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” That is, he alone is my beloved and my sole helper. And I alone am beloved by him, because no one else rightly loves Christ except the one Church, and no other does he love. “He pastures among the lilies.” That is, among the purity of faith and the brightness of virtues. “Until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” Until the eternal light of the age to come arises and the shadows—that is, the errors of the present life—pass away. “Return; be like a doe and a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of Bether.” I beseech you, my beloved, to return to me more often through the sweetness of your visitation—you who, in the flesh that you took from the lineage of the patriarchs, ascended above all the heights of the heavenly mountains, so that you might relieve the labor of my pilgrimage through the contemplation of the eternal homeland.

## Chapter III

1. “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him.” “For a long time,” she says, “I sought the Lord with great devotion; but because I was still subject to the allurements of my flesh and blinded by the darkness of ignorance, I did not find the light of truth,” that is, the Lord. “I will rise and go around the city; through the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him.” I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, travel through lands and seas, and hear the teachings of philosophers; but even so I did not find him.

2. “The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The watchmen who guard the Church are the apostles and teachers, who discovered paganism through diligent investigation of the truth. “A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.” When I entrusted myself to their teaching, I immediately found the light of truth that I had sought. “I held him and will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” I hold him with firm faith, until at the end of the age, through the ministry of preaching, I bring him into the house and chamber of the Synagogue, which gave birth to me in the Lord, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

3. “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem,” and so forth. The bridegroom repeats this verse so that no one might think he was less concerned for the Church gathered from the Gentiles than for that gathered from the Jews, but so that from both there might be one bride, and that bride most beloved.

4. “Who is this who rises through the desert?” The Synagogue marvels at how the people of the Gentiles, purified by no mystery of circumcision and instructed by no admonition of the prophets, could suddenly rise from the lowest pleasures, through the desert of idolatry and paganism, to the lofty summits of virtue and the embrace of the bridegroom. “Like a column of smoke from aromatic spices.” Kindled by the fire of love, she strives toward heavenly things with every effort of virtue.

5. “Of myrrh, frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer.” From the mortification of carnal pleasures, the purity of prayers, and the fragrance of every virtue. “Behold, Solomon’s couch; sixty strong men surround it, from the strongest of Israel.” Solomon’s couch is the conduct of the saints; the sixty strong men are holy preachers and the most valiant warriors, who are worthy to see the Lord with a pure heart.

6. “All holding swords and most skilled in warfare.” They hold the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; what they teach with their mouths, they fulfill in their deeds. “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night.” The terrors of the night are hidden fears on the day of temptation. The preacher’s sword is vigilant discipline, restraining the desires of the flesh lest the impurity of life stain the word of preaching.

7. “King Solomon made a litter for himself from the wood of Lebanon.” Solomon’s litter is the holy Church, which carries believers to the banquet of eternal blessedness and is constructed from the strong in spirit, as from incorruptible woods. “He made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold.” The silver columns are teachers shining with the light of eloquence. The golden backrest is the hope of perpetual rest promised to the faithful.

8. “Its ascent is purple.” What is the purple ascent except the blood of the martyrs and the passion of our Redeemer? For one does not ascend to the banquet of life except through the mystery of Christ’s passion. “He paved its interior with love, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.” Everyone who has love of God and neighbor will joyfully arrive at this rest and at this banquet. Christ provided all these ornaments of the Church because of the exceedingly great love with which he loved us and gave himself for us.

9. “Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon.” Go forth in mind and deed from the turbulent conduct of the world, so that you may be able to see the King of peace. “In the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” See the Lord Christ in the humanity that he assumed from his virgin mother and placed at the right hand of the Father’s majesty. “On the day of his betrothal.” That is, at the time of his incarnation, when he came forth from the virgin womb to join the Church to himself as his bride. “On the day of the joy of his heart.” That is, the redemption of the human race, which was Christ’s day of joy.

[Col. 1123A] 196. ## Chapter IV

1. “How beautiful you are, my friend; how beautiful you are!” He calls the Church beautiful and repeats that she is beautiful because he saw her as praiseworthy both in action and in preaching. “Your eyes are like those of doves.” Your perceptions are excellent and venerable through the contemplation of spiritual things. “Apart from what lies hidden within.” The glory of an outward work is great, but far more incomparable is the glory of eternal recompense, which cannot yet be seen.

2. “Your hair is like flocks of goats.” In the hair the faithful people may be understood, who by their great number provide the Church with its greatest adornment. “Which have come up from Mount Gilead.” Gilead is interpreted as “heap of witness,” which fittingly applies to the united multitude of the saints. “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.” Those who are more fragile are designated by the hair, while those more perfect and suited to govern the Church are designated by the teeth.

3. “Which have come up from the washing.” That is, from the font of holy baptism. They have been shorn and washed—that is, stripped by renouncing the world and cleansed by the washing of life. “All with twin offspring, and none is barren among them.” There is no one among them who does not produce the offspring of a good work. “Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet.” The scarlet thread signifies the teaching of truth. The bride’s lips are compared with scarlet because the Church never ceases to proclaim the price of the Lord’s blood by which she was redeemed, or because holy preaching blazes with the ardor of charity.

4. “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate.” In the cheeks modesty is expressed; in the pomegranate, the passion of Christ. Thus the bride possesses the redness of the pomegranate in her cheeks when she confesses the mystery of the Lord’s cross in words and proves it by deeds. “Your neck is like the tower of David.” The tower is the Church; the neck, the preachers, whose faith and constancy are firm in that same city and everywhere impregnable. “It was built with battlements.” The battlements of that city are the defenses of the holy Scriptures, or of the preceding Fathers.

5. “A thousand shields hang upon it.” For as many precepts as there are in the divine books, so many are the defenses of our breast, by which we are protected against every ambush. “Every armor of the strong.” Every preparation, whether of action or of heavenly teaching, through which we not only escape but also overcome. “Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a doe, feeding among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline.” The two breasts are the two peoples who come from circumcision and from the Gentiles. Through humility they understand themselves to be small and sinful, but running in love they pass through all the obstacles of the world. They feed among the lilies—that is, upon the most radiant examples of the holy Fathers—until, when the eternal day breathes, we pass beyond the shadows of our present mortality.

6. “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.” In myrrh the mortification of the flesh is expressed; in frankincense, devotion in prayer. It is as though the bridegroom said: “I will frequent and glorify with a gracious and holy illumination those whom I perceive to be exalted in the virtue of suffering or of prayer.”

[Col. 1123D] 7. “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon.” Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness,” that is, a soul made white by good works, whom the bridegroom urges three times to come. First, while living in the flesh through good works; second, when freed from the flesh to receive blessed life; third, when, having received the body, she enjoys perfect joys after the resurrection.

8. “You will be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” Lions signify the evil spirits because of their pride; leopards, because of their cruelty. The mountains of Amana signify the proud hearts of unbelievers, where unclean spirits have their dwelling. When holy preachers convert such people to the way of salvation, they are crowned from the head and summit of the mountains, that is, from the leaders of the proud, because the crown of glory grows from the labor of the contest.

9. “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.” In the wounding of the heart, the greatness of Christ’s love for the Church is understood. “With one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” In the holy unity of the teachers, that is, of the eyes, and in the holy unity of the people, that is, of the hair. “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride.” Again, by the name of breasts the holy teachers are designated, because of their consolation of the weak and their support of the little ones, which is expressed by milk. “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.” The sweetness of grace is more beautiful than the austerity of the Law. “And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” The most delightful fame of the faith spread throughout the whole world is broader than that of the old Law and of the fathers within it, which was confined to Judea alone.

10. “Your lips, O bride, are a dripping honeycomb.” A honeycomb is honey in wax. Honey in wax is the spiritual meaning of divine things in the letter, dripping honey because nearly every sentence has multiple meanings. The lips are the spirit of the teachers, who reveal that sacred writings contain manifold meanings. “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” Milk signifies the instruction of little ones; honey, the more perfect teaching of the mature; “under your tongue,” that is, in the meditation of the heart.

11. “And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” The Church’s garments are her works, which are compared with the fragrance of frankincense because everything holy that the Church does for the Lord returns the favor of prayers for her. “A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.” The enclosed garden is the Church because she produces varied shoots of spiritual works; she is a fountain because she overflows with saving doctrine; enclosed because she remains fortified by the Lord’s protection; sealed by the word of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1123D]

**Chapter IV—Note 12.** Calmet, on chapter I, verse 13, describes *cyprus* as follows: “A shrub the height of a pomegranate tree, with leaves resembling those of the olive, a white and fragrant flower, and fruit hanging like a cluster, with a very sweet fragrance.” For other fragrant trees, see Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapters 7 and 8.]

12. “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of orchards.” Through the irrigation of holy baptism, the holy Church has sent forth from herself a paradise of pomegranates [Col. 1124C], that is, of holy martyrs, with the fruits of orchards, that is, with the fruit of holy virtues. “Cyprus with spikenard, spikenard and saffron.” Cyprus is an aromatic tree and signifies the blessing of heavenly grace. Spikenard represents the type of the Lord’s passion; saffron expresses the fervor of charity. Cyprus is joined to spikenard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer for Christ. Likewise, spikenard is joined to saffron when we willingly accept death out of love for Christ.

13. “Cinnamon and cinnamon bark, with all the trees of Lebanon.” *Fistula*, also called cassia, is an aromatic tree, but a small one, and therefore signifies those humble in spirit. Likewise, cinnamon signifies those who despise themselves. It too is a short tree, but fragrant and sweet. Humility, however, has great praise and sweetness before the Lord. “With all the trees of Lebanon.” Just as fistula and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, the trees of Lebanon demonstrate their exalted actions. Myrrh and aloe are aromatic trees [Col. 1124D] that express continence of the flesh.

14. “With all the finest ointments.” That is, with the more excellent gifts of the virtues. There is a beautiful joining of these trees, because when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the spirit. “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon.” The Church is both: a fountain of gardens because she produces spiritual fruits, and a well of living waters that flow forcefully from Lebanon because of the hidden mysteries disclosed to the saints alone through the revelation of the Holy Spirit; living waters because of the divine utterances that proceed from the invisible treasuries of divine grace; from Lebanon, that is, from the Church herself, which is both white through the purity of faith and lofty through the virtue of glory.

15. “Rise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden.” In the north wind the adversities of the world are signified, and in the south wind its blandishments; by this twofold assault the Church is tested. “Rise together” is the voice of one permitting, not commanding. “And let its spices flow.” That is, let it spread abroad the constancy of its virtues with marvelous fragrance.

## Chapter V

1. “Let my beloved come into his garden.” Let the Lord come into his Church, so that he himself may preserve it undefiled everywhere and make it fruitful with the harvest of faith. “And let him eat the fruit of his trees.” Let him willingly receive and graciously regard the works of his servants.

2. “I came into my garden, my sister, my bride.” “I come,” he says, “very often into my Church, and I come to correct, assist, and strengthen.” “I gathered my myrrh with my spices.” Through myrrh, passion or mortification is expressed; through spices, all the virtues. He gathers myrrh with spices when he brings the martyrs, together with the other elect, to the maturity of their rewards.

3. “I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk.” In the honeycomb and wine, preachers are understood; in the honey and milk, hearers. The inner judge approves and rewards both. “Eat, friends, and drink, and become intoxicated, beloved ones.” Friends, by doing what I command, I beseech you: fill your hearts with the deeds of the saints as with choice banquets.

4. “I sleep.” By God’s gracious gift, I honor him in the peace of the present life. “And my heart is awake.” The more peacefully I rest under external assaults, the more deeply I see within how good God is. “The voice of my beloved knocking.” The Lord knocks at the door of the heart when he arouses us to progress in virtue. “Open to me,” that is, open your heart to me, my sister. “My friend,” because you are aware of my secrets. “My dove,” because you have been enlightened by the gift of my Spirit. “My undefiled one,” because you alone are worthy of my gaze.

[Col. 1125C] [Note: [Col. 1125]

**5.** “Charity growing cold,” and so forth. Saint Augustine says much the same in *Tractate 57 on John*, as do other Fathers and interpreters of sacred Scripture concerning this passage.]

5. “For my head is full of dew, and my locks with the drops of the nights.” The head of Christ is God. The locks are the gatherings of the faithful. In the dew and the drops of the nights, the cold charity shown by many is indicated—the charity they ought to have toward the Lord and their neighbors. Therefore the Lord necessarily arouses each of the faithful to the work of preaching, and the Church, provoked to the labor of teaching, responds.

6. “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” As if she were openly saying: “For your sake I have abandoned worldly affairs; how shall I resume them?” “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” I have now washed earthly thoughts with the tears of secret repentance; how shall I again be polluted by the filth of the world? For the ministry of preaching can scarcely exist without worldly occupations.

7. **My beloved put his hand through the opening.** The beloved put his hand through the opening when the Lord invisibly kindles us, through hidden compunction, to the work of the virtues; and he recalls to our memory how, and how greatly, descending from the bosom of the Father, he suffered for us. **And my inward being trembled at his touch.** Recalling these things, the bride’s inmost conscience is utterly afraid; and, accusing herself of the slothfulness of repose, she hastens to the labor of preaching. Hence it follows:

8. **I arose to open to my beloved.** That is, to preach the word of the Lord. **My hands dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh.** For “hands” signify works, and “fingers” discernment. In myrrh are signified continence and sufferings, which are then of the choicest kind when either continence is practiced or sufferings are endured solely for the love of God and neighbor.

9. **I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved.** He opens the bolt to the beloved who has made the temple of his breast worthy of divine visitation and indwelling. **He had turned aside and passed on.** Since no one in this life is granted the full vision of God as it is granted in the future, the beloved is therefore said to pass on—that is, he shows himself as one to be seen and enjoyed more fully in the future.

10. **My soul melted when my beloved spoke.** “The more sweetly,” she says, “I received the voice and nearness of my beloved, the more sublimely whatever was cold in me was warmed by love, and whatever was rigid was melted.” **I sought him, but did not find him.** Since the gift of compunction and inward sweetness does not lie in the power of the one who wills, but in the mercy of the giver, they do not always possess him equally; for God does not offer himself in the same way to those laboring in exile as to those reigning in their homeland.

11. **The watchmen who go about the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my cloak.** The keepers of the city—that is, of the Church—are the holy teachers. By diligent preaching they go about the hearts of individuals, wound them with the darts of heavenly love, and, so that they may burn more intensely, set them aflame; they also remove from them the protection of their former way of life.

12. **I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, tell him that I am faint with love.** The bride rightly grows faint when, struck by the sword of God’s word, she strips off her earthly garment; and she adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls worthy of God—to report to the Lord the greatness of her love, and to ask heavenly assistance for herself, that she may behold his glory.

13. **What is your beloved more than another beloved, O fairest among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?** “I beg you,” she says, “since you have so adjured me that, through the love by which you say you are languishing, you may also make me burn through the word of preaching, and show me what your beloved is like in that respect in which he can be loved rather than feared, because perfect love casts out fear.”

14. **My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands.** White because he is without sin; ruddy with the blood of his passion: Christ, who alone is the mediator between God and human beings. **His head is the finest gold.** The head of Christ is God, who alone is good and supremely good. **His locks are like clusters of palms, black as a raven.** The locks are the companies of the saints who cling to God in faithful service. They are “lofty,” or “chosen,” palms because of Christ the head; they are black because of afflictions.

15. **His eyes are like doves beside streams of water.** His eyes are the teachers through whom the Church sees what is right. They are rightly compared to doves because of their simplicity, and to streams of water because of the divine charisms. **Washed in milk and resting beside abundant waters.** He says that they are washed in milk—that is, cleansed by divine and most sweet grace—and that they rest beside abundant waters—that is, amid the abundance of all spiritual gifts. The streams may signify instruction in the old Law, and the abundant waters the perfection of evangelical teaching, since holy preachers bring forth from their treasures things new and old.

[Col. 1126D] 16. **His cheeks are like plots of spices planted by perfumers; his lips are lilies dripping first-rate myrrh.** In the cheeks of our Savior both modest piety and severity are expressed. The plots of spices signify virtues, sweetness, and renown. They were planted by the prophets and apostles: the former recounting the mysteries of his future incarnation, the latter the things he accomplished. His lips are the words of his teaching. They are lilies because they promise the splendor of the heavenly kingdom. They drip first-rate myrrh because they preach that, through contempt for present pleasures, one must arrive at this kingdom.

17. **His hands are turned work, of gold, full of hyacinths.** “Hands,” that is, works, because he fulfilled by deeds what he taught in words. They are “turned work” because they contain in themselves the whole rule of justice. Hence he says: “I must fulfill all righteousness.” They are also hands of gold because everything he did as a human being perfected the riches of glory. They are full of hyacinths because they stir us to hope for heavenly things and to love them, since the hyacinth is a gem of golden color.

18. **His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires.** The belly of the beloved signifies the fragility of his humanity; ivory signifies the beauty of chastity. Sapphire is the sublimity of heavenly virtues. It is adorned with sapphires because in him human fragility is understood partly through hunger, temptation, weariness, and death, and divine exaltation partly through miracles, resurrection, and the glory of ascension.

19. **His legs are marble columns founded upon golden bases.** By “legs” the journeys of Christ’s incarnation are suggested; they are compared to marble columns because of their firmness and uprightness. They are founded upon golden bases because everything done concerning him or through him was arranged, in accordance with the counsel of divine providence, before the ages of the world.
