20. **His appearance is like Lebanon; he is chosen like the cedars.** As Lebanon surpasses other mountains in the height and beauty of its trees, so the Lord Christ surpasses all the saints in the height of their merits and the beauty of their virtues. **Chosen like the cedars.** Just as the cedars surpass in dignity the other trees that grow in Lebanon, so Christ transcends in his glory all who are born within the Church unto life.

21. **His throat is most sweet.** In his throat the inward sweetness of his words is remembered; whoever tastes it does not hunger. **And he is altogether desirable.** What more do you seek? He is altogether desirable because he is wholly God and wholly human, and into him the angels long to look. God in the majesty of the Father, human in the virginity of his mother: in him, the creator; in her, the Savior.

22. **Such is my beloved, and he is my friend.** The more devotedly someone loves the Lord, the more familiarly he possesses the Lord as a friend. You must understand him in this way if you wish to have him as a friend. **Where has your beloved gone, O fairest among women?** This is the voice of the Synagogue; for the speakers’ roles are varied for the sake of poetic beauty. But only the Church of Christ, since it is represented under the title of bride, is designated “fairest among women.” The individual churches of the saints are beautiful, but the whole of the holy Church throughout the world is fairest. **Where has your beloved turned aside, and we shall seek him with you?** He who once lived on earth in bodily form—tell us where he has turned aside, so that we may follow him with you.

## CHAPTER VI

1. **My beloved went down to his garden, to the plot of spices.** It is as though he had said: “He went down there, into the garden—that is, his Church—in order to irrigate it with the fountain of his glory, as though it were a plot of spices, so that it might sprout with the flowers of the virtues.” **To pasture in the gardens and gather lilies.** I prepare within myself a place of dwelling for my beloved, and he prepares one for me with himself, where he is always nourished among the holy desires of pure minds. Thus far the voice of the holy Church has been seeking and praising; now what the one who was sought answers is added.

2. **You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely, like Jerusalem.** He calls his holy Church “friend” because the desire of her life is already likened to the vision of inward peace. **Terrible as an army arrayed for battle.** That is, united and compact through love, so that no opening may be given to the enemy through the evil of discord; for we are terrible to the enemy only in the unity of peace.

3. **Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away.** That is: Do not seek to know me perfectly with the eyes of your mind along the road of your pilgrimage, because this is impossible. The more intently you seek to understand me, the more certainly you will recognize me as incomprehensible; and do not seek on the way the reward reserved for the homeland. **Your hair is like flocks of goats,** and so forth. These verses were set forth earlier, but repetition is an indication of firmness. In the hair, the people; in the teeth, the teachers; and in the paired offspring, the commandments of love are understood.

4. **As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, apart from what is hidden within you.** The cheeks of the holy Church are the spiritual Fathers, wondrous in virtues, venerable in conduct, and not ashamed to glory in the cross of Christ. These things that are seen in her are very great, but those that are unseen and reserved for the future are much greater.

5. **There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number.** The queens are those who, through preaching the truth and the font of sacred baptism, beget spiritual offspring for the eternal King, moved by love of the bridegroom and hope of the heavenly reward. The concubines are those who teach Christ by preaching or baptizing solely for carnal advantage. Therefore the former are signified by the perfection of the number six multiplied by ten, on account of the Decalogue. The maidens are souls recently reborn to Christ, whose total, because of the multitude of the heavenly citizens, exceeds all reckoning.

6. **One is my dove, my perfect one.** Namely, the holy and universal Church throughout the whole world. **She is one to her mother, chosen by her who bore her.** “To her mother,” that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all. From her the grace of the Holy Spirit descends upon us, through which we are born to God. **The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed.** Those whom he previously called maidens he now calls daughters; all the ancients praise the catholic Church.

7. **Who is this who comes forth like the dawn, rising?** The Church comes forth like the dawn because, after the darkness of long ignorance, the rising of the true light is now shown to the world. **Beautiful as the moon.** Because, illumined by the sun of justice, she lights up the night of the world. **Chosen as the sun.** Because she bears the image of her creator in all justice, holiness, and truth. **Terrible as an army arrayed for battle.** She is terrible to the powers of the air through the unity of love, faith, and hope.

8. **I went down to the garden of nut trees, to see the fruits of the valleys.** The garden of nut trees is the present Church, where we do not yet see one another’s consciences; but when the shell of the body is broken, the fruit of inward sweetness will appear. The fruits of the valleys are the fruits of humility. The holy Church descends through holy teachers to those who are advancing toward good fruits and to those who still need the irrigation of instruction. **And I looked to see whether the vine had blossomed and whether the pomegranates had budded.** I looked to see whether the pursuit of the virtues had blossomed and whether any who were prepared in imitation of the Lord’s passion were ready to pour out their blood.

[Note: [Col. 1127D]

**CHAPTER VI, no. 9.** Although the older manuscript codices, most of the ancient editions, and the Church in its office read *Sunamitis*, it is nevertheless more probable that *Sulamitis* should be read, with our Vulgate; Calmet shows this from the Hebrew.]

9. **I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab.** I did not recognize the gifts of spiritual grace in you, bride; but my soul troubled me because of the arrival of the evangelical chariot by which Aminadab—that is, Christ, whose name is interpreted “spontaneous one of my people”—is carried throughout the world. To this the Church immediately responds by way of consolation:

**Return, return, O Sulamite; return, return, that we may look upon you.** Do not be troubled, but return to the knowledge of your Redeemer, who was promised to you so many times in the prophets and in the Law. Return in the purity of faith; return in the perfection of works, O Sulamite—that is, captive one. Having now returned from the bonds of unbelief, return to your Redeemer, so that you may be saved.

## CHAPTER VII

1. **What will you see in the Sulamite, except the choirs of armies?** You grieve over the hardened Synagogue; the time is near when in her you will see choirs of those fighting against evil spirits and praising the Lord. **How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of a prince!** Now the praises of the Church are spoken by the bridegroom himself. First, her steadfastness in works and the mortification of pleasures are praised, because she is the daughter of a prince—that is, of Christ—through the grace of baptism.

2. **The joints of your thighs are like necklaces fashioned by the hand of an artisan.** The concord of the two peoples, fruitful in spiritual offspring, is signified in the joining of the thighs; for just as a necklace is fashioned by the hand of an artisan, so this concord has been firmly established by the ineffable generosity of our creator. Good works are expressed in the necklace.

3. **Your navel is a turned-work bowl, never lacking drink.** The navel—that is, the fragility of our weakness—is a bowl when, reminded of our mortality and weakness in conscience, we strive with ready minds to offer the cup of saving doctrine to our neighbors. **Your belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies,** and so forth. It is a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies when an abundance of good works is gathered solely in hope of perpetual light. In the belly, memory is expressed; in the wheat, the multiplication of good works; in the lilies, chastity. Likewise, in the wheat, bread is expressed, and in the bowl, drink—things given to the poor.

4. **Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.** The two breasts have been discussed above. The two breasts are the teachers of both peoples. In the twins are the two Testaments; they are twins because of their single harmony. **Your neck is like an ivory tower.** Here too the teachers are signified by the neck; they are compared to an ivory tower because of their firmness and beauty. They provide both strength and adornment to the city of God.

5. **Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude.** Here too the eyes of the Church are the teachers, because of the nourishment they provide. They are rightly compared to pools because they do not cease to offer the streams of doctrine to their hearers. Heshbon is interpreted as “belt of mourning,” because the saints restrain themselves with the belt of abstinence instead of the vain joy of the flesh; and rightly it is said to be by the gate of the multitude, on account of the abundance of peoples entering the Church through the gate of faith.

6. **Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which faces Damascus.** Here too, in the nose, the ministers of the word of God are designated on account of discernment. It is a tower because it occupies the most eminent place in the Church. It faces Damascus—that is, the bloodthirsty and impious one, since Damascus is interpreted as “drinking blood.” It signifies the carnal and cruel, against whom the holy teachers continually keep watch in the tower of Lebanon—that is, in the firmness of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1129D]

**CHAPTER VII, no. 7.** In the Vulgate the reading is *bound with channels*. In the manuscripts, *bound* and *joined* are often confused. Some think that *Carmel* is used for purple, from the Hebrew *carmel*, or *carmil*, from which perhaps the Spanish *carmin* and *carmesí* derive.]

7. **Your head is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like royal purple joined with channels.** In the head the mind is signified, and in the hair, thoughts. Just as the limbs are governed by the head, so thoughts are governed by the mind. They are occupied in Carmel—that is, in lofty things—and in the passion of Christ, which is expressed under the name of purple. The channels are the inner affections of the saints, in which such thoughts are bound.

8. **How beautiful and how lovely you are, most beloved, in delights.** Beautiful in faith and lovely in works, most beloved in delights—that is, in spiritual virtues. **Your stature is like a palm tree.** That is, the uprightness of good action always tends toward victory. **And your breasts are like clusters of grapes.** The breasts are compared to the teachers of the Church because of the milk of their first instruction, and they are likened to clusters because of the exceedingly sweet mysteries of eternity.

9. **I said, “I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruits, and your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.”** The most victorious cross is aptly compared to a palm tree. When Christ climbed it, he grasped its fruits—that is, the gifts he bestowed upon the holy Church. From that time she produced clusters of the vine: holy teachers who abound in greater knowledge and grace because of the Savior’s cross and resurrection.

10. **The fragrance of your mouth is like apples, and your throat like the finest wine.** In the throat, the voice of present doctrine is shown; in the fragrance, the reputation of one who is absent. Thus the former is compared to wine because of the fragrance of the virtues, and the latter to apples because of the sweetness of the reputation of the absent one.

11. **Worthy of my beloved to drink, and of his lips and teeth to taste.** The bride seized the word from the bridegroom’s mouth, because he compared her to the finest wine and added: **Worthy of my beloved**, that is, the evangelical preaching is of such sublimity that the beloved himself, appearing first through it in the flesh, opened the heavenly way to the world. **And of his lips and teeth**, that is, he gave it to the apostles and the greatest preachers for meditation.

12. **I belong to my beloved.** And not to another, since I devote all my care to his service and love. **And his turning is toward me.** He loves and helps me alone, lest I fail on the way. **Let us go out into the field; let us stay in the villages; let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed, whether the flowers are producing fruit, whether the pomegranates have blossomed.** For the Church is in no way sufficient either to go forth to good works, or to remain in the exercise of good works, or at least to rise to the purpose of doing good, or to discern how much the minds of her hearers have advanced, unless she is assisted by the grace of God, who said: “Behold, I am with you,” and so forth. Likewise, in the field the Christians are signified; in the vineyards, the Churches; in the flowers, faith; in the fruits, virtues; and in the pomegranates, martyrdom. In each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.

13. **There I will give you my breasts.** That is, the instructors of my little ones, because holy teachers advance in all these things. **The mandrakes gave forth their fragrance in our gardens.** Because of its many kinds of medicinal properties, the mandrake is compared to the virtues of the saints. The holy teachers are the gates of the Church. In such gates the mandrakes gave forth their fragrance when each spiritual person spreads the reputation of his virtues far and wide. **All new and old fruits, my beloved, I have kept for you.** The new and old fruits are the commandments or promises of the New and Old Testaments, because the Church refers them all to his grace.

[Note: [Col. 1130D]

**CHAPTER VIII, no. 1.** In place of *And I will find you*, it seems that *So that I may find you* should be read.]

## CHAPTER VIII

1. **Who will grant you to me as my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside?** This is the voice of the ancient righteous, longing for the coming of Christ in the flesh. **Nursing at the breasts of my mother**, that is, being born and nourished in the Synagogue according to the nature of the human condition. **And I may find you outside.** The beloved was within when “in the beginning was the Word”; outside, when the Word became flesh.

2. **There I will kiss you.** That is, I will see you face to face, and speak mouth to mouth. **And now no one will despise me.** Before the coming of Christ, the Church existed only within the narrow confines of Judea; after the Ascension, she was expanded throughout the world and became venerable. **I will take hold of you.** That is, I will receive you as you come with ready and faithful devotion.

3. **And I will lead you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of my mother; there you will teach me.** When the dispensation of the flesh had been completed, I would lead you, returning, into the house of my mother with joyful eyes. Into the house of my mother, where the heavenly Jerusalem is our mother. There you will teach me to hope for greater gifts than I had possessed under the Law. **And I will give you a cup of spiced wine.** That is, fervent love adorned with various spices of the virtues. **And the must of my pomegranates.** That is, the glorious triumph of the holy martyrs, who endure the flames with the most fervent love and do not hesitate to pass through them to you.

4. **His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me.** The left hand signifies the gifts of Christ’s flesh, and the right hand expresses the future joys of the saints with Christ. **Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?** This is the voice of the Synagogue, wondering how the Gentiles had suddenly ascended from the desert into the embrace of the bridegroom. **Overflowing with delights**, that is, with the beauty of all good things. **Leaning upon her beloved**, referring everything she possesses to the grace of the beloved. **Her own**, whom I thought was to be sent to me alone.

5. **Under the apple tree I awakened you.** Under the tree of the cross I recalled you from eternal death, as I did the apostles and the other elect from among the Jews. **There your mother was corrupted; there your mother was violated.** That is, the greater part of the people was rejected by denying Christ and choosing Barabbas. **Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm.** Just as we bind some sign on a finger in memory of anything, so the heart signifies thought and the arm signifies action. If you wish to have me as your bridegroom, let there be within an unfaked love of faith, and outwardly a devoted practice.

6. **For love is strong as death, jealousy is hard as hell.** My love for you, O Synagogue, is strong even unto death; but your jealousy against me was hard as hell. Turn your jealousy into love, and you will become a bride to me, your bridegroom. **Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame.** The lamps of love are the hearts of the faithful; they are fire because of the fervor of the heart, and flames because of the effectiveness of action.

[Note: [Col. 1131C]

**7.** In the Vulgate: *Many waters could not.*]

7. **Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.** By “many waters” and “rivers” he means the assaults of temptations, which never cease to attack the souls of the faithful, visibly or invisibly, but to which love does not yield. **If a man were to give all the substance of his house for love, he would utterly despise it as nothing.** The saints truly despised as nothing the substance of their entire house for the greatness of love.

8. **Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.** This signifies the earliest times of the Church’s birth among the Gentiles, when she was still small in number and less capable of preaching the word of God. It is as though the bridegroom of the Synagogue had said of her: **What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be addressed?** As though he plainly said: “The Church of the Gentiles is indeed small in number, and is not yet sufficient to undertake the ministry of the word. What, then, do you think should be done with our sister, O Synagogue, when she is to be addressed—that is, led into faith through the ministry of the word?” While the Synagogue remains silent, the bridegroom himself answers what should be done.

9. **If she is a wall, let us build silver battlements upon her.** As though he said: “If she has within her some who are strong in faith, distinguished in intellect, or trained in philosophy, let us add to them silver battlements—that is, knowledge of the divine Scriptures—so that they may more easily protect the weak and unlearned. If she is a door, let us panel her with cedar boards. If they are simple, yet eagerly desirous of being taught, let us set before them the examples of the righteous of former times, so that they may fulfill the work of teaching with greater certainty and effectiveness.” The cedars signify the virtues of the saints, and the boards the breadth of love. To these things the Church herself responds.

10. **I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.** From the time when I was made before him as one finding peace, I have been joined together from living stones, united by the cement of love, and built upon an immovable foundation. The breasts—that is, the strongest teachers—are like a tower: they know how to nourish the little ones and to drive out every evil thing. This happened to me from the time when Christ reconciled me and, through him, I found peace.

11. **My peaceful one had a vineyard in her who possesses peoples.** The vineyard—that is, the Catholic Church, abundant in the fruit of faith—belonged to the peaceful one, namely Christ, because he made peace in heaven and on earth, in that congregation which possesses many peoples from the whole world, not Judea alone. It is entrusted to keepers: prophets, apostles, or angelic powers and dignities.

12. **A man, however, for its fruit.** That is, for the eternal reward of this vineyard. **He brings a thousand silver pieces.** That is, for the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom, which is the fruit of the vineyard, he has abandoned everything belonging to the world. The number one thousand signifies perfection—that is, the one who abandoned everything. Silver pieces are understood as all money. **My vineyard is before me.** This is the bridegroom’s voice. “Nevertheless, even if I commend you to other keepers, I always keep you in my presence, seeing and rewarding your devotion in labor in all things.” **A thousand are yours, O peaceful one.** “A thousand of yours,” with “silver pieces” understood. As though he had said: “The one who abandons all that is his for love of me will be in peace, because he loses his entire substance, signified by the thousand, for the love of God.”

13. **And two hundred for those who keep its fruit.** These are the holy teachers, who abandon everything belonging to the world and do not cease to labor in preaching the word. They are given a twofold reward with me, signified by the number two hundred. **You who dwell in the gardens, the friends listen.** Since our speech must now end, hear this final farewell from me: Dwell always in the gardens of the virtues, and know that the friends—that is, the angelic spirits and the souls of the saints—always observe you and rejoice in your appearance. **Let me hear your voice.** That is, while you live, let the voice of your preaching always be heard by me.

14. **Flee, my beloved.** As though she plainly said: “Since, appearing in the flesh, you deigned to confer upon me the commandments and gifts of heavenly life, now that these things have been accomplished, return to the bosom of the Father, O my beloved. Be like a gazelle and a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices.” Let this also be my consolation: Since I cannot behold you in continual vision, remember to console me with frequent visitation.

[Col. 1131]

# APPENDIX VII. ON THE CONFLICT BETWEEN VICES AND VIRTUES (G, S)*

[Col. 1131D] [Note: [Col. 1131D]

**No. 1.** In the *Isidoriana*, chapter 84, nos. 20 and following, I discussed this book, which some ascribe to Saint John Chrysostom, others to Saint Augustine, others to Saint Ambrose, others to Saint Isidore, others to Saint Leo the Great, and others to Ambrosius Autpertus. I transcribed Cajetan’s admonition concerning this book and reviewed the editions and manuscript codices. For Grialius’s edition, Cyprian Suarez corrected the work, but added no notes or variant readings. The Maurists placed this little book among the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine, noting variant readings in some places. Concerning the title of the book, see our commentaries on Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*, an excellent poem of the same subject and title.]

1. The apostolic voice cries out throughout the world, and tells those stationed in the battle line of faith not to grow sluggish through security: **“All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution”** (2 Tim. 3:12). And behold: although Christianity is now religious and faithful even in its rulers, the bonds, beatings, scourges, prisons, racks, crosses, and whatever other kinds of torture there may be are absent from those living devoutly in Christ Jesus. How, then, will what sounded forth through the Apostle be true—that all who live devoutly will suffer persecution? Perhaps no one wishes to live devoutly in Christ Jesus in a time of peace, and for that reason these things are absent? Who, even if foolish, would say this?

[Col. 1133A] 208 [Note: [Col. 1133D]

**2.** *Mortal*; others read *material*.]

2. In this statement of the Apostle, therefore, not the persecution of certain individuals in particular but the general persecution of all must be understood. Indeed, there are many within the bosom of Mother Church who, while living devoutly in Christ, are subjected to insults, reproaches, injuries, and mockery. Is this truly the general persecution that the Apostle described as suffered by all who live devoutly in Christ? I would not readily say so, since there are certain religious people whom no wicked person dares openly to disparage. Another kind, therefore, must be understood: one more savage and more harmful, which is not inflicted by mortal severity but is produced by the hostility of vices.

[Note: [Col. 1133D]

**3.** *Opposing*; others read *attacking*.]

3. For when pride fights against humility, pretense against true religion, contempt against submission, vainglory against fear of the Lord, envy against fraternal rejoicing, hatred against love, detraction against the freedom of just correction, anger against patience, insolence against gentleness, swelling arrogance against satisfaction, worldly sadness against spiritual joy, sluggishness or laziness against the practice of virtue, loose wandering against firm stability, despair against confidence in hope, greed against contempt of the world, hardness against mercy, fraud or theft against innocence, deceit and falsehood against truth, gluttony of the belly against moderation in food, foolish merriment against measured sorrow, excessive talk against prudent silence, impurity and lust against bodily integrity, spiritual fornication against purity of heart, and desire for the present world against love of the heavenly homeland, thrusting itself into the midst—what else is this than the cruel persecution of those living devoutly, raging against the massed ranks of the virtues?

[Note: [Col. 1133D]

**4.** *Drove out*; others read *destroyed*; others *threatened*. In place of *collisa*, others read *consilia*.]

4. O how dreadful, O how bitter is the assault of pride! It cast angels from heaven and drove human beings from paradise. Its army and the clash of its weapons are the vices that we have briefly summarized. But let us see how the camps of heaven and hell fight, and how the weapons of Christ and the devil clash in battle.

5. **(Pride:)** Certainly you are better than many, indeed almost everyone, in speech, knowledge, wealth, honors, and all the gifts, whether carnal or spiritual, that are available. Therefore despise everyone and show yourself superior to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1133D]

**6.** *Through a certain wise man.* The same expression occurs below. The Maurists consider this phrase characteristic of Ambrosius Autpertus.]

6. **(Humility:)** Remember that you are dust (Gen. 3:19), that you are ashes, that you are decay and a worm; and even if you are something, unless you humble yourself in proportion to your greatness, you will utterly lose what you are. Are you higher than the first angel? Are you more splendid on earth than Lucifer in heaven (Eccl. 3:20)? If he fell from such sublimity through pride, how will you, proud as you are, ascend from lowliness to heavenly height, when, as long as you live here, you are held under that condition? Of this condition it is said by a certain wise man: **“The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks on many things”** (Wis. 9:15).

7. How dense, we may suppose, are the earthly darknesses of pride in which our clay is wrapped, if in heaven the star that was rising in the morning could lose the globes of its light (Isa. 14:12). Hear, then, rather, the light of truth saying: **“Whoever follows me,”** he says, **“does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life”** (John 8:12). Elsewhere he warned in what way he himself should be followed, saying: **“Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls”** (Matt. 11:29).

[Col. 1134A] 8. Hear, swelling pride; hear the teacher of humility saying to this: **“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted”** (Matt. 23:12). And this: **“Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?”** (Isa. 66:2). Hear also what the Apostle says about the one who invites you to pursue humility. For he says: **“Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross”** (Phil. 2:6–7). If divine majesty thus lowers itself in such great humility, how should human weakness be proud of anything?

9. **(Vainglory:)** Do whatever good you can; show everyone the good you do, so that you may be called good, so that all may proclaim you holy and venerable, so that you may be known as one chosen by God, so that no one may despise or look down upon you, but that everyone may pay you the honor due to you.

10. **(Fear of the Lord; right intention:)** If you ever do anything good, do it not for passing honors but for eternal ones. Hide what you do as far as you can. If you cannot hide it completely, let the desire to conceal it be in your heart; then there will be no rashness of ostentation, nor will it be a crime ever to make known what you always wish to keep concealed. In this way you will seem to fulfill two sayings of the Redeemer that appear almost contrary to one another: **“When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, but let your alms be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you”** (Matt. 6:3); and: **“Let people see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”** (Matt. 5:16).

[Note: [Col. 1134D]

11. “May it befit you”; alternatively, “may it befit you.” And shortly afterward: “their reward from the people—the praises that they loved.” “Pay attention,” etc. Below, after “the crown of exultation,” some add other material from the same passage of Ecclesiasticus, which many omit.]

### 11. Beware entirely lest that saying apply to you which is spoken of hypocrites:

“They perform all their works so that they may be praised by people; truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew VI).

Pay attention to yourself in everything you do, lest, struck by the pride of vainglory, you hear, together with those who also gloried in signs of miracles:

“I was watching Satan, like lightning, falling from heaven” (Luke X, 18).

But be afraid, for it is written:

“The fear of the Lord is glory, exaltation, gladness, and a crown of rejoicing” (Ecclesiasticus I, 11, 17).

“The fear of the Lord delights the heart, and gives gladness, joy, and length of days. It will go well with the one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed.” And below:

“The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and its branches are length of days.”

### 12. (Dissimulation:)

Since you do nothing good in secret, lest you be hated when known by everyone, pretend outwardly to be what inwardly you do not wish to be.

### 13. (True religion:)

Do not do that at all; rather, strive to become good, though you are not. For what else is showing people that you are not other than condemnation? Remember, therefore, what is said:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of rapacity and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Matthew XXIII, 25).

14. And likewise that saying repeatedly impressed upon us in the Gospel:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful outwardly to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity. So you also outwardly appear righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (ibid., 26–28);

and also that other passage written concerning such people:

“They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matthew VII, 15).

[Note: [Col. 1135D]

15. In the margin: “Pride objects”; alternatively, “disobedience says.”]

### 15. (Self-exaltation:)

“What sort of person are you, that you should obey those who are worse and serve those who are inferior? You, rather than they, ought to command, since they cannot equal you in intelligence, diligence, or strength.”

Obey, therefore, God’s command, and have no further concern for anyone.

[Note: [Col. 1135D]

16. “Ordained by God”; alternatively, with the Vulgate, Romans XIII, 1: “ordained by God.”]

### 16. (Blessed submission:)

If God’s command must be obeyed, it is necessary to submit to human authority; for he himself says:

“Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

“So it ought to be,” you say, “but if the one who commands were such a person—yet he is not such a one through whom God commands.”

But the Apostle says the opposite:

“There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance.”

What sort of people those who command ought to be is not for subjects to investigate.

17. Indeed, to the first shepherds of the Church the Lord says:

“You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority among them are called benefactors. It shall not be so among you; rather, whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the servant of all, just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life for many” (Matthew XX, 25).

Nevertheless, because he foresaw that not all such rulers would be, taking the persons of all subjects into account through the disciples, he warned them, saying:

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat. Therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matthew XXIII, 2).

### 18. (Envy:)

“In what respect are you inferior to him or to them? Why, then, are you not equal or superior to them? What abilities do you possess that they do not? They therefore ought not to be superior—or even equal—to you.”

### 19. (Fraternal rejoicing:)

If you surpass others in virtues, you preserve yourself more safely in a lowly place than in a lofty one; for a fall is often worse from a height. But if, as you claim, certain people are superior or equal to you, what harm does that do you? What damage does it cause you?

Take great care lest, while you begrudge others the place of eminence, you imitate the one concerning whom you retain this written:

“Through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom II, 24).

[Note: [Col. 1135D]

21. “Through Solomon and the apostles”; alternatively, “through Solomon the apostle.”]

### 20. (Hatred:)

“Far be it from you to love the one whom you find opposed to you in everything—who disparages you, insults you, exasperates you with matters proved against you, reproaches you with your sins, and always hastens to precede you in words, deeds, and honors. For unless he envied you, he would certainly not put himself before you in this way.”

### 21. (Love:)

“Is it therefore the case that, because these qualities you describe are to be hated in a person, God’s image in that person is not to be loved?” So Christ, when placed upon the cross, loved his enemies and, before the torment of the cross, warned them, saying:

“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 44).

And through Solomon and the apostles it is said:

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Proverbs XXV, 21).

22. To this saying the Apostle added from his own teaching:

“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans XII, 20, 21).

Conversely, concerning those known to hate their brothers, John says:

“Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (I John III, 15).

And again:

“Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and is in darkness even now, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II, 11).

[Note: [Col. 1136D]

23. “The outstanding preacher.” The Maurists recognize this also as Ambrosius Autpertus’s own. Some manuscripts, contrary to this, add “Paul.”]

### 23.

“But,” you say, “it is enough for me that I love those who love me.”

But the Lord says the opposite:

“If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” (Matthew V, 46).

What can you object to this? Certainly this:

“Whoever hates his brother remains in death, and whoever loves remains in God, and God in him.”

Therefore vomit out all the bitterness of gall, and in whatever way you can, take up the sweetness of charity; for nothing is sweeter, nothing happier, than it. “God,” John says, “is love” (I John IV, 10); and the outstanding preacher says:

“The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans V, 5).

Thus charity is not without reason said to cover the deeds of sins, as it is written:

“Charity covers all offenses” (Proverbs X, 12).

### 24. (Detraction:)

“Who could endure, who could cover in silence, how much evil this person or that person commits, unless perhaps he is consenting?”

### 25. (The freedom of proper correction:)

The evils of one’s neighbor must neither be concealed nor approved, but one’s neighbor must be rebuked openly with fraternal charity, not secretly slandered.

If someone objects, “For this reason I do not wish to rebuke my brother before his eyes: lest, becoming irritated, he fail to advance through correction and instead take scandal from the correction,” divine Scripture responds and, in turn, declares this to be the greater scandal, saying:

“While sitting, you slandered your brother and placed a stumbling block before the son of your mother” (Psalm XLIX, 20, 21).

### 26. (Discreet correction:)

The one who understands that someone is slandering him suffers a greater scandal than the one who endures a rebuke. And because the faults of wrongdoers must sometimes be covered in silence for a time, so that they may be corrected at a more suitable moment, the passage continues:

“You did these things, and I kept silent.”

But lest detractors flatter themselves because of this discreet silence—those who, while always preferring to disparage secretly, never advance to open rebuke—the text further adds:

“You thought wickedly that I would be like you.”

As if it said: “It is wicked to think that I should appear like a detractor because, by remaining silent for a time and not disparaging, I await an opportunity for open correction.” Hence it immediately adds:

“I will rebuke you and set you before your face.”

That is, not secretly, as is your custom, but openly, as my concern requires, I will await a suitable time for correction, rebuke the sinner, and set his offenses before his face.

### 27.

“But,” you say, “I do not hate him; I love the one whom I judge and rebuke in secret.”

No; you hate him more, and do not love him. That is why you slander him and do not correct him.

How detestable the slander of one’s neighbor is, divine Scripture testifies in many places. Thus we read:

“The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Psalm C, 5);

and:

“Whoever slanders his brother slanders the law” (James IV, 11);

and:

“The one who slanders his brother will be uprooted”;

and also the words of the Apostle Paul:

“See that you do not bite and devour one another” (Galatians V, 15).

### 28. (Anger:)

“I cannot bear with equanimity what is done against you. Indeed, it is a sin to tolerate it patiently, because if these people are not resisted with great indignation, they will thereafter heap things against you without measure.”

[Note: [Col. 1136D]

29. “For he,” etc. Thus Autpertus, Book I on the Apocalypse, chapter 7, as the Maurists observed.]

### 29. (Patience:)

If the suffering of the Redeemer is brought to mind, nothing is so harsh that it cannot be endured with an even temper. For Christ, as Peter says, “suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Peter II, 21).

He himself says:

“If they called the master of the household Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household” (Matthew X, 25);

and:

“If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20, 23).

But how great are the things we suffer in comparison with his sufferings? He endured insults, mockeries, affronts, slaps, spittle, scourging, a crown of thorns, and the cross; while we wretches are wearied and cast down, to our own shame, by a single speech or a single word.

[Note: [Col. 1137D]

30. “Is found”; alternatively, “is indicated.”]

### 30.

And what are we to do about what is said:

“If we do not suffer with him, neither shall we reign with him” (II Timothy II, 12)?

Therefore the goads of anger must be blunted, and its condemnation feared. Hence we read:

“Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

Yet a remedy is found in what follows:

“If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first and be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew V, 22, 23).

[Col. 1137B] [Note: [Col. 1137D]

31. “From your hearts”; some omit this.]

### 31.

As if it were plainly said:

“Do not pour forth even a silent prayer in your heart unless you first lead your offended neighbor, by making satisfaction, to a gentle and peaceful disposition.”

For our gift is our prayer, and our altar is our heart. Whoever diligently does this whenever anger has been aroused without cause between two people will by no means incur the threatened condemnation.

But there are many who do not forgive the offenses of those who ask them for pardon. Against them comes that saying of the Lord:

“If you do not forgive people their sins from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI, 14).

### 32.

“But,” you say, “he has committed many offenses and has often injured me.”

To this I do not respond; the Lord does. When Peter said to him:

“How often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Up to seven times?”

he said to him:

“I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matthew XVIII, 22).

How many there are who slowly release their own injuries, but forgive God’s more quickly! It sometimes happens that, under the pretext of avenging the Lord’s injuries, angry people avenge their own.

### 33.

What else should be said about those who, blinded by fury, go so far as to utter words of cursing, except what the Apostle says:

“Nor will the revilers possess the kingdom of God” (I Corinthians VI, 10)?

James, detesting this vice with emphasis, says:

“No human being can tame the tongue, an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless God and the Father, and with it we curse human beings, who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing” (James III, 8).

“My brothers, this ought not to be so. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?”

For this reason it is also said elsewhere:

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs XVIII, 21).

### 34. (Insolence:)

“Should gentle words, and not rather the harshest words—as befit such people—be directed at fools, senseless persons, and brute animals when they do wrong?”

### 35. (Gentleness:)

You must follow not your own persuasion in these matters but the Apostle’s command. Concerning this very issue he admonishes his beloved disciple, saying:

“Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity” (I Timothy V, 1, 2).

And again:

“The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth” (II Timothy II, 24, 25).

[Note: [Col. 1137D]

36. “And he will love you.” In Saint Ambrose, some material is added here.]

### 36.

And again:

“Rebuke, appeal, exhort, with all patience and teaching” (II Timothy IV, 2).

The evil of insolence harms subjects even more than superiors; for it often happens that they reject a rebuke delivered gently and with the sweetness of charity, and in response to words of humility launch darts of contempt. Hence it is written:

“Whoever rebukes a scoffer brings insult upon himself” (Proverbs IX, 7, 8).

Conversely, concerning the one who advances through rebuke, it is said:

“Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you.”

### 37. (Swelling:)

You have God in heaven as your witness. Do not concern yourself with what people on earth suspect about you.

[Note: [Col. 1137D]

38. “Those designated by the Christian name”; in Saint Augustine, “those professing the Christian faith,” and the Maurists supply “that an idol is nothing.” This is not satisfactory. Others: “those agreeing with the Christian faith”; in Saint Leo, “those professing the Christian faith.”]

### 38. (Humble satisfaction:)

One must not provide an occasion for slander or a pretext for whispering; but if there are matters requiring correction, they must be made known. Or, if such matters are absent, they must certainly be denied through a humble declaration, since the Apostle also warns us not to give the devil any occasion for reproach (I Timothy V, 14).

He also detested this in those who, bearing the Christian name, reclined in an idol shrine to eat. Although they regarded the idol as nothing and consumed the sacrificed food as though it were harmless, by this action they nevertheless led the weak consciences of their brothers toward the detestable rites of idols (I Corinthians VIII, 4).

### 39. (Sorrow:)

“What do you have from which to rejoice, when you bear such great evils concerning your neighbors? Consider with what sorrow you must look upon all those who are involved in so much bitter hostility against you.”

[Note: [Col. 1138D]

40. “Perhaps there is a place for sorrow.”]

### 40. (Spiritual joy:)

I know that there are two kinds of sorrow—indeed, I know that there are two sorrows: one that produces salvation, and another that produces ruin; one that leads to repentance, and another that leads to destruction.

You are recognized as belonging to one of these, but plainly to the one that produces death. Therefore one should not grieve over the things you recommend, but rather rejoice in those that you do not yet understand, since the giver of everlasting joy also said:

“When people persecute you and speak every evil against you falsely because of my name, rejoice on that day and exult; for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Matthew V, 11).

Remember the heights of our religion: “The apostles went forth rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V, 41).

Therefore there should be no place for sorrow where such great joy follows.

### 41. (Torpor and idleness:)

If you devote yourself constantly to reading with unbroken zeal, you will suffer dimness of the eyes; if you shed tears without ceasing, you will lose even your eyes themselves; if you pay the full psalmody of prolonged vigils for your own sake, you will acquire madness of the head. If you wear yourself out through daily labor, when will you rise for spiritual work?

[Note: [Col. 1138D]

42. In Saint Augustine: “Shake off the body’s sluggishness … the violent, and those who use force.” The Maurists conjecture *excute* (‘shake off’) for *discute*.]

### 42. (Practice of the virtues:)

Why do you still promise yourself such long stretches of time yet to come? Do you know whether you will live tomorrow? Or even whether you will spend a single hour in this life?

Perhaps you have forgotten what the Savior says in the Gospel:

“Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matthew XXV, 13).

Therefore shake off the inertness of torpor, and always remember that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the lukewarm, the soft, or the idle, but by the violent and fervent.

### 43. (Dissipated wandering:)

If you believe that God is everywhere, why do you guard one particular place in which so many evils are committed, instead of moving elsewhere?

### 44. (Firm stability:)

If it is as you claim—that you confess God to be everywhere—then this place which you desire to flee must not be abandoned, because God is in it as well.

“But,” you say, “I seek a better place, and I find one.”

I respond: Will you find one better—or even one like the place in which you know that the devil and the human being were lost?

Remember, therefore, that the first angel fell from heaven, and the first human being was expelled from paradise and came to the distress of this world (Genesis III, 23).

Consider that Lot, tested among the Sodomites by the ordeal of evils, was holy; but on the mountain, growing careless through security, he became drunk with his daughters and sinned (Genesis XIX).

This weariness of wandering also produces another form of the same evil: while withdrawing certain people from spiritual concerns even though they remain in one place, it strives either to entangle them in earthly business or to occupy them with the most worthless matters, acting contrary to the Apostle’s words:

“No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Timothy II, 4).

And again:

“Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thessalonians V, 16).

[Note: [Col. 1139D]

45. “To attain.” Thus also some read it passively.]

### 45. (Despair:)

“What and how many things have you committed? How serious are your crimes? How countless your sins? And yet you have not changed your life for the better, nor corrected your manner of life profitably.

For behold, as you see, you remain bound by an evil habit; you strive to rise, but, weighed down by the burden of sins, you fall back.

What, then, is to be done, when certain condemnation threatens because of the past, and no amendment comes to mind concerning the present? Nothing except to admit the pleasures of temporal things, since you cannot attain the delights of the age to come.”

[Note: [Col. 1139D]

46. “By the filth of sins”; alternatively, “by the filth of fornications.”]

### 46. (Confidence in hope:)

If the matter concerns crimes and sins, behold David, guilty both of adultery and murder, is described as freed from the jaws of hell by the Lord’s mercy (II Samuel XI).

Behold Manasseh, the most abominable, impure, filthy, and pleasure-loving of all sinners; nevertheless, through repentance he returned from death to life (II Chronicles XXXIII, 12).

Behold Mary Magdalene, defiled by countless filthinesses of sin, anxiously running to the fountain of mercy, watering the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiping them with her hair, kissing and licking them, and anointing them with ointment; she was deemed worthy to be cleansed (Luke VII, 37).

### 47.

Behold Peter, bound by the chains of his denial, loosened the knots of his faithlessness with the bitterest tears (Luke XXII, 62).

Behold the thief, guilty both of sedition and of shedding his brother’s blood, passed in a single hour and with one word of confession from the cross into paradise (Luke XXIII, 42).

Behold Saul, persecuting the Church of God and killing many for the name of Christ, and, so to speak, staining himself entirely with the blood of martyrs, was made an apostle and transformed into a vessel of election (Acts IX, 1).

[Note: [Col. 1139D]

48. “Give way.” In Ambrose, “let them not give way.” The Maurists observe that *dent* is used in the sense of *cedant* (‘give way’). For the words “On whatever day,” etc., Ezekiel XVIII, 21, and XXXIII, 11 are cited. See the note on chapter 14 of *On the Order of Creatures*, no. 12.]

### 48.

Where, then, so many and such great examples precede, let the evil counsels of despair give way, since it is also written:

“On whatever day the sinner is converted and groans, he will be saved” (Ezekiel XVIII, 21).

And again:

“I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord” (Ezekiel XXXIII, 11).

What else should I answer concerning a manner of life not yet changed for the better, except that what each person did not do yesterday, he should do today, while he is still permitted to live, and that he should not delay from day to day (Ecclesiasticus V, 8), since he does not know whether he will have even one day for correction?

Always resisting the evil habit according to the strength granted from above, let him say morning and evening:

“Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm LXXVI, 11).

### 49. (Greed:)

You are entirely without blame when you desire to possess certain things, because you do not seek to increase your possessions but fear to be in need; and what another holds badly, you yourself spend more usefully.

### 50. (Contempt of the world:)

These things are not obtained without danger or offense even among worldly people, because the more anyone begins to possess, the more he desires to possess. Thus it happens that he has no limit in desiring, while he hastens to serve the countless cares of this world.

For as Scripture says:

“The greedy person will not be satisfied with money” (Ecclesiastes V, 9).

Paul indicates how detestable this is when he says:

“Greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians III, 5).

Explaining how harmful it is, he says:

“Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil, and into many harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and ruin” (I Timothy VI, 9).

A certain wise man declares how detestable it is when he says:

“Nothing is more wicked than a greedy person” (Ecclesiasticus X, 9).

James reveals how harmful it is, saying:

“Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted; your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire” (James V, 1).

### 51.

Nor did our Redeemer wish to pass over how harmful the evil of greed is. He says:

“How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God” (Matthew XIX, 23).

And again:

“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for the rich to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark X, 25).

If, then, the pursuit of greed is so dangerous for worldly people, how much more dangerous is it for those who have already ceased to be worldly in habit and manner of life, who have devoted everything they are to God?

To them especially apply the Redeemer’s words, by which the disease of avarice may be destroyed:

“Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear. The nations seek all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew VI, 31).

### 52.

O how blessed, how secure, how worthy of embrace is this saying! No one in this life is as secure as the one who desires to possess nothing except Christ; under this promise he is proved to have everything necessary, just as Paul, a very rich poor man, said:

“As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Corinthians VI, 10).

Thus let us have not everything superfluous, but only what is necessary, as he himself confirms by saying:

“Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Timothy VI, 8).

### 53.

“You may say that holy and religious men ought to possess more, so that they may distribute it to Christ’s poor better than ordinary people can.”

I agree—but this applies to superiors, not to subjects, whom the example of Lot’s wife especially deters. As she left Sodom, she looked back behind her and, being changed into a pillar of salt, breathed out her spirit (Genesis XIX, 26).

Hence Christ also warns that such conduct must be avoided, saying:

“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke IX, 62).

Therefore Peter says:

“It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (II Peter II, 21, 22).

For the saying of the true proverb will happen to them:

“The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud.”

217 [Note: [Col. 1140D]

54. In Augustine: “Hear what: Naked … there; hear what,” with “they will profit” understood in both places.]

### 54.

This disease of avarice is never restrained more effectively than when the day of death is remembered without forgetfulness, and when a person considers what he will shortly be like in the grave.

This was certainly fixed in the memory of the one who said:

“Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job XXV, 6).

These thoughts had not departed from the heart of the one who said:

“In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 40).

What good, I ask, what good then will preserved riches do? Hear what Job says:

“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I, 21);

and the Apostle:

“We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it” (I Timothy VI, 7).

[Note: [Col. 1140D]

55. “Without money”; alternatively, “without want”; but the former should be retained.]

### 55. (Hardheartedness:)

“If you give what you possess to the needy, from where will you nourish your subjects without money?”

### 56. (Mercy:)

If you follow the Apostle’s rule in this matter, you will be able to accomplish both. For the same Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. It is not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but according to equality. At the present time let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, and there may be equality, as it is written: ‘The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little’” (II Corinthians VIII, 12; Exodus XVI, 18).

[Note: [Col. 1141D]

57. “In contrast.” The Maurists observe that Ambrose Autpertus often uses this manner of speaking.]

### 57.

Hence a certain righteous man admonishes his beloved child, saying:

“If you have much, give abundantly; but if you have little, share even that gladly” (Tobit IV, 9).

Hence also the incarnate Truth says:

“Nevertheless, give alms from what you have, and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke XI, 41).

Hear this, hardened hearts:

“Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy” (James II, 13).

In contrast, through the prophet the Lord admonishes us, saying:

“Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isaiah LVIII, 7).

### 58.

Remember what happened to the rich man dressed in purple. He was not condemned because he had taken away another’s possessions, but because he had not given his own to the needy poor man. Hence, when he was in hell, he came to ask for the smallest things, because here he had refused even small things (Luke XVI, 20).

Remember also what the judge of heaven will say to those placed on his left:

“Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV, 41).

And again:

“I was hungry, and you did not give me food,”

along with the other things terribly enumerated there.

### 59.

Theft and fraud, although they use different degrees of expression, nevertheless say the same thing.

### 60. (Theft:)

“If you do not take what belongs to others, you are unable to be rich or self-sufficient from your own possessions.”

### 61. (Fraud:)

“If you hand over intact everything that your superior entrusted to you for safekeeping, and do not judge that even a small amount should be kept back, you will have nothing from which either to provide for your own needs or to please your friends and comrades.”

### 62. (Innocence:)

It is better to be poor and lacking, pleasing no one through what is given, than to injure anyone by theft or fraud. For whoever unjustly seizes another’s property in any manner closes the entrance to the kingdom of heaven against himself.

Hence the outstanding preacher rebukes certain people, saying:

“There is altogether a fault among you, that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather endure fraud? But you commit injustice and fraud, and this against your brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” (I Corinthians VI, 7).

And among other things he adds:

“Neither thieves nor the greedy will possess the kingdom of God.”

[Note: [Col. 1141D]

63. “To injure”; alternatively, “to mock.”]

### 63.

Deceit and lying also say the same thing. Deceit is carried out through cleverness, whereas lying is carried out through a simple word, when someone seeks to injure another by refusing to give.

[Note: [Col. 1141D]

64. “What he has”; alternatively, “the one who has,” or “whatever he has.”]

### 64. (Deceit:)

“Why do you delay and create obstacles when I ask? I do not have anything that I can give you.”

Thus he conceals in his heart what he has—either what he keeps for himself or what, if he is willing, he might give to others.

### 65. (Lying:)

“I absolutely do not have what you ask for,”

although, unlike deceit, which operates through contrived cleverness, he frustrates the petitioner with the simple word of denial.

### 66. (Truth:)

One must deceive no one either through contrived cleverness or through a simple word, because, in whatever way a person lies, “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom I, 11), and “the lot of all liars will be in the lake of burning fire and sulfur” (Apocalypse XXI, 8).

### 67. (Gluttony of the belly:)

God created everything clean for eating. What, then, does the person who refuses to be satisfied by food do other than contradict the gift granted to him?

### 68. (Moderation in food:)

One part of what you say is true: so that human beings would not die of hunger, God created everything clean for eating. But so that they would not exceed the measure of eating, he commanded abstinence.

For among its other evils, Sodom perished especially through satiety of bread, as the Lord himself testifies when he speaks through the prophet to Jerusalem:

“This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: fullness of bread” (Ezekiel XVI, 49).

Therefore, just as a sick person should approach medicine, so everyone should approach food, seeking no pleasure in it but attending to necessity.

[Note: [Col. 1141D]

69. “More carefully prepared”; alternatively, “more sumptuous.”]

### 69.

Hence the incarnate Truth says through the Gospel:

“Take care lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34).

Against the Jews’ insatiable greed the Apostle says:

“Many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears, as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame; they set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians III, 18, 19).

And again:

“Food is for the belly, and the belly for food, but God will destroy both it and them” (I Corinthians VI, 13).

He fully overcomes this vice who, in taking food, not only maintains moderation—so that hunger always commands him to refresh himself—but also, except in the case of bodily weakness and the reception of guests, despises dishes that are more carefully prepared and more sumptuous.

### 70. (Foolish joy:)

“Why do you hide the joy of your spirit within? Go out into public rejoicing; say something publicly that will make either you or your neighbors laugh; make them happy through your happiness.”

219

### 71. (Moderate sorrow:)

“From where do you have such great joy? Have you already conquered the devil? Have you already conquered the punishments of hell? Have you already come from exile to your homeland? Have you already received assurance concerning your election?

Or perhaps you have forgotten what the Lord says:

‘The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be changed into joy’” (John XVI, 20).

72. Or perhaps you have forgotten what he says elsewhere:

“Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke VI, 25);

and what is said through Solomon:

“Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs XIV, 13);

and, conversely, what is said through the Gospel:

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew V, 5);

and again through Solomon:

“A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but everything is reserved uncertainly for the future” (Ecclesiastes IX, 1).

Therefore restrain empty joy, since you have not yet escaped the misery of punishment. Is not everyone considered insane who, shut up in the darkness of a prison, tries to rejoice?

[Note: [Col. 1141D]

73. Others: “rather, the one who is proved to speak few but evil things.”]

### 73. (Many words:)

It is not the one who speaks many things, but good things, who will be held guilty; rather, it is the one who is proved to speak few things, but evil ones.

[Note: [Col. 1142D]

74. “Things begun”; alternatively, “beginning.” The Maurists observe that this accords with the rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 6: “One must sometimes refrain even from useful words.”]

74. (Discreet Silence:) What you say is true; but although many seem to utter good things, it often happens that speech begun with good matters turns toward something perverse, as Holy Scripture itself declares: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. X, 19). And even if, amid innumerable words, criminal matters are avoided, can useless and idle words also be avoided—words for which an account will certainly have to be rendered in the future? A measure must therefore be observed in speaking, and sometimes even useful words must be restrained, just as [Col. 1143A] the blessed Psalmist is read to have done. For he says: “I was humbled, and I was silent from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII, 3).

75. (Uncleanness:) It is no great crime to be defiled without intercourse between man and woman, whether by one’s own hands or by another’s.

76. (Integrity of the Flesh:) The Apostle does not say this. What, then, does he say? “Nor will the unclean,” he says, “possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 9).

77. (Lust:) Why do you not now indulge more fully in your pleasure, when you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the time granted to you in desires, because you do not know how quickly it will pass. For if God had not wished human beings to join in the pleasure of intercourse, he would not have made male and female at the very beginning of the human race.

78. (Unblemished Chastity:) Do not pretend that you are unaware of what you will receive after this life. For if you live piously and chastely, you will rejoice without end; but if impiously and lustfully, you will be subjected to eternal fires. For this reason you ought to live the more chastely, since, as you say, you do not know how quickly the time granted to you will pass [Col. 1143B]. But when you declare that at the beginning of the human race God created male and female for this purpose, that they should join in mutual embraces, you speak entirely and most truly. Yet you do not take into account that permission to marry is granted to some—namely, to those who have not professed virginity or widow’s chastity—but is not granted to others, that is, to those who have resolved to be virgins or continent. For fornication is granted with impunity to no one.

220. [Note: [Col. 1143D] “Eternal life”; alternatively, “future life.”]

79. Do you think that what the Apostle says to the wanton is to be disregarded? “Flee fornication: every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who fornicates sins against his own body.” And if you consider this of little importance, hear what you will afterward lament and mourn forever: “Neither adulterers,” he says, “nor fornicators, nor those who lie with males, will possess the kingdom of God.” Oh, how brief is the hour of intercourse, by which eternal life is lost! What benefit, then, does it bring to the body? What profit does it grant, when it silently leads the soul to Tartarus?

[Col. 1143C] 80. (Spiritual Fornication:) Is one who consents to lust in his heart, but does not proceed to the act of lust, doing anything deserving condemnation?

[Note: [Col. 1143D]

81. Hence also through blessed Job; alternatively, “By contrast, through blessed Job,” as above, no. 57.]

81. (Purity of Heart:) One who does not preserve the chastity of the soul is altogether guilty. Hence the author of purity also says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). Hence it is also said through blessed Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from the heights?” (Job XXXI, 1–2).

82. For if the thought of a wicked consent were displeasing to our Creator, he would certainly not have said through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. I, 16); nor would he have said to the Pharisees in the Gospel: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. IX, 4). Nor would the Apostle have said: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel, through Jesus Christ” (Rom. II, 15).

[Note: [Col. 1143D]

83. “And clusters”; alternatively, “and little clusters”; alternatively, “and among good things.”]

83. (Desire for the Present World:) What is more beautiful? What more honorable? What more lovely? Or what can be more delightful than what we see daily in the present life? Oh, how wondrous is the chamber of heaven, in the pleasant air, in the light of the sun, in the waxing and waning of the moon, in the variety and course of the stars! How delightful is the earth—in the flowers of the groves, the sweetness of fruits, the loveliness of meadows and streams, the luxuriant stalks of the crops, the leaves of the vineyards and the branches full of clusters, the shade of forests and open spaces, the running of horses and dogs, the leaps of stags and does, the flights of hawks, the voices, feathers, and necks of peacocks, doves, turtledoves, and birds of every kind, the painted walls and ceilings of houses, the ringing melodies of organs and musical instruments of every sort, the lovely appearance of women, and their eyebrows, hair, eyes, cheeks, throat, lips, nose, and hands, and the necklaces adorned externally with gold and gems—finally, in the countless varieties and uses of heaven, earth, and sea, and whatever else the senses do not now recall!

84. (Love of the Heavenly Homeland:) If these things that are beneath heaven delight you, [Col. 1144B] why do the things that are above heaven not delight you more? If a prison is so beautiful, what is the homeland, the city, the dwelling? If such are the things cultivated by strangers, what are those possessed by sons? If mortals and wretched people are rewarded in this life in such a manner, how will immortals and blessed people be enriched in that life? Therefore, let love of the present world depart—a world in which no one is born without dying—and let love of the future world take its place, in which all are brought to life so that thereafter they do not die; where no adversity disturbs, no necessity constrains, no trouble disquiets, but everlasting joy reigns.

85. If you ask what exists there, where such great and such blessed happiness endures, it cannot be said otherwise than this: whatever is good is there, and whatever is evil is nowhere there. “What good is that?” you ask. Why do you question me? It has been defined by the Prophet and the Apostle: “What eye,” they say, “has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV, 4; I Cor. II, 9).

[Col. 1144C] [Note: [Col. 1143D]

86. “For what is there for me in heaven?”; alternatively, “What remains for me in heaven?” The Vulgate has “the strong and living God.”]

86. David, though surrounded by many riches of the world, yearned for this happiness when he said: “For what is there for me in heaven? And besides you, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25). Though abounding in many royal banquets, he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed; my soul thirsted for God, the living fountain. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI, 3). And again: “Woe is me, because my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. CXIX, 5). Hence Paul: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better” (Phil. I, 23).

[Note: [Col. 1143D]

87. “I showed the camp of our enemy,” etc. Alternatively: “I showed the camp of our fornicating enemy”; alternatively: “I became a great terror to our enemy, for the camp,” etc. In other copies the work does not end as it does in Isidore, in the edition of Grialius, which we follow. In some manuscripts: “Attend to what I say, and give credence to the truth that calls you and gently admonishes you.” Many additional passages are found in Saint Augustine, Saint Leo, and in some manuscripts of Saint Isidore; these have been copied from Constantine Cajetanus in the Isidorian material, chapter 84, nos. 23 and following. What I think about this epilogue may be seen in the same chapter, no. 34 and following. [Col. 1144D]]

87. Having thus gone through these matters, although I have omitted much, nevertheless, as it seems to me, I have shown the strong camp of our enemy, which never ceases to assault those who live piously in Christ Jesus. But the devil, still not content with these things, turns to other strategies: when, through certain dreams, he repeatedly speaks the truth to some, in order at some point to lead them into falsehood; when he awakens sleeping people before the proper hour or time, so that during the time appointed for wakefulness he may weigh them down with deepest sleep; when he disturbs those who are singing psalms and praying with shrill hisses, various barks, and inarticulate sounds, even throwing stones or excrement, so that by any means he may draw them away from spiritual works and render them useless. But you, man of God, attend with vigilant devotion to what I say, with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1145]

## APPENDIX VIII. EXPOSITION OF THE MASS (G, S)*

[Col. 1145A] 1. “The Lord be with you” (see *Isidoriana*, chap. 84). He greets the people and prays that the Lord may be with them. “And with your spirit.” This is the people’s response and prayer: just as the priest prayed that the Lord might be with the people, so the people pray that the Lord may be with the priest’s spirit. When the priest says, “Let us pray,” he asks everyone to pray that his prayer may be heard by the Lord. And when he says, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” the priest prays to the Lord Father that the prayer may be brought to completion through his Son, who is equally our Lord, as is the Father. When he says, “Who with you lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” he wants the people to believe and understand that the Son lives and reigns with the Father without beginning and without end, and is God just as the Father is God; and that the Holy Spirit has one power with the Father and the Son, one substance, and in all things one unity of divinity.

2. “For ever and ever.” The same Son, with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, just as he existed in divinity before all ages [Col. 1145B], so also is believed to live equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the present age and in the future age, where the just will remain with the holy angels and the unjust will be tormented with the devil, and to be bounded by no end. “Amen” is the people’s confirmation of the prayer, and in our language it may be understood as though everyone were saying: “May it happen just as the priest has prayed.” But its proper interpretation is: “Truly,” or “faithfully.”

3. “Lift up your hearts.” The priest admonishes the people to raise their hearts upward—that is, above themselves—to the Lord Almighty and to pray faithfully, so that help may come to them from above, from the heavenly Lord by whom all things were created. “We have them with the Lord.” This is the people’s response, by which they profess that, just as the priest commanded them to hold their hearts above, so they retain them there. “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” The priest gives thanks to God in accordance with the people’s profession, because they have confessed that their attention is directed toward the Lord. “It is worthy and just.” The people, together with the priest, give thanks to God, whom [Col. 1145C] it is right and worthy to thank in prayer, because we have received all good things from him, in the name of the Lord. Amen.

4. “It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary.” The priest confirms the people’s profession and says that it is truly worthy and just to give thanks to God for everything; and that it is right—that is, upright or fitting—and salutary, that is, full of salvation, to give thanks to him who gave us eternal salvation. “To give you thanks always and everywhere.” After the people’s profession, the priest turns toward the Lord and speaks as though to one present, because we are always in the presence of the Lord, and he sees our thoughts; and the priest says that he gives thanks both for himself and for the people. “Lord,” because he rules over all, and everything is under his dominion. “Holy,” because he is holy and through him all things are holy, since you created all things holy and good.
