In Greek, *pater* is said; in Latin, *genitor*, because he himself begot the Son without any [Col. 1145D] defilement or corruption.

5. In Latin, *pater* is said from *patrando*, that is, from *perpetrando*, which means completing or helping, because he made all things that have been made, and helps all things that have been helped; and he willed us to become his adopted sons through sanctification, by which he sanctified us. “Almighty,” because he can do all things; therefore he is called almighty, and no word is impossible with God. “Eternal God”—that is, the distinction among the eternal, the everlasting, and the temporal. The eternal is what has no beginning and will have no end, but always was, is, and will be. The everlasting is what began to exist but will have no end. The temporal is what had a beginning and will have an end.

[Col. 1146A] 6. And therefore he is called here “Eternal God,” because he neither began to be nor ceases to be, but always is. God is said to derive from loving, because he loves and governs all things and created them. Alternatively, God is named from divinity, because he is divine, knows all things, and apportions all things as he wills.

7. “Through Christ our Lord.” In Greek, *Christos*; in Latin, *unctus*, “anointed.” This Christ was ineffably begotten by the Father before all beginnings, as pleased him. The Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin Mary and anointed her womb with divine anointing; he was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary.

8. For in the Old Testament priests and kings were also anointed, and therefore were called *christs*, because they were anointed with a temporal anointing. This Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, is eternally Christ and is called eternal with the Father; and through him we have been redeemed, through whom we give thanks to the Father. He himself is our Lord and God, because he rules over us. [Col. 1146B] “Through whom angels praise your majesty.” Through that Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, the angels praise the Father’s majesty, because he is equal to the Father in divinity. “Majesty,” because God’s power is greater than human power. Through Christ the angels praise God’s majesty, because Christ, together with the Father, created the angels.

9. For in Greek *angelos*, in Latin *nuntius*, is interpreted as “messenger.” “Angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; those who announce are by nature spirits. “Dominions adore.” The Dominions praise and adore the majesty of God the Father through the Son. Dominions are an order of angels. There were ten orders of angels. The tenth order fell and through pride was turned into the devil. The other nine remained in their holiness. These are their names: angels, archangels, virtues, principalities, powers, thrones, dominions, cherubim, seraphim. The names of the last two are not Latin. *Cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge.” *Seraphim* is called “burning.” [Col. 1146C] The remaining names of the orders mentioned above are Latin, except for *angels* and *archangels*. Angels are named messengers; archangels, exalted messengers.

10. Pope Gregory of Rome, in his homily on the Gospel reading, “Publicans and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him,” explained these orders most fully. Let us return, however, to our subject. “The powers tremble.” This is said of the orders mentioned above. He does not say this because the orders mentioned above are bodily, but speaks according to our custom, because we usually tremble and fear before our lords. He says that they tremble so that we may understand that all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things tremble and fear before the sight of the divine Majesty.

11. “The heavens and the powers of the heavens.” The heavens themselves obey the divine vision, because they have no power to show themselves clear or cloudy. The powers of the heavens are the angelic orders mentioned above, as Gregory attests in his homily on the Gospel [Col. 1146D] reading, “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars.” And “the blessed seraphim.” The seraphim have been mentioned above. “They celebrate together with united rejoicing.” All preachers, with united rejoicing, equally celebrate the majesty of God the Father through Christ. “With whom.” This is our supplication: that the heavenly Father himself, through Christ his Son, through whom we give him thanks for everything, may deign to admit our voices and join them to the voices of the angelic orders mentioned above.

12. “Saying with humble confession.” That is, with humble acknowledgment. What is humbler than to commend ourselves to the eternal Father through the eternal Son, to presume nothing from our own conscience or goodness, and, in accordance with the angelic voices, continually to believe and proclaim him [Col. 1147A] essentially holy? “Holy, holy, holy.” The evangelist John wrote in the book of the Apocalypse that he saw before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four living creatures standing and continually saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” and so forth. It is said three times “holy” so that the Father is understood to be holy, the Son holy, and the Spirit of the Father and Son holy. Yet although “holy” is said threefold, it is not said in the plural, “holies,” but in the singular, “holy,” so that one holiness and one eternity may be understood in these three persons.

13. “Lord God of Sabaoth.” Many customarily interpret *Sabaoth* as “almighty,” but many others as “of hosts,” so that he is the Lord God himself who arranges all the hosts of angels and human beings. “Heaven and earth are full of your glory.” Thus heaven and earth are governed by his glory, and those who are in heaven and those who are on earth glorify and honor his name. “Hosanna in the highest.” Why is *Hosanna* now said corruptly? [Col. 1147B] Formerly *Osiana* was said. *Osi* is an interjection of one praising or magnifying. *Anna* means “save.” But it is said corruptly as *Hosanna*, and it may be understood as “save” or “grant salvation.” “In the highest,” that is, in the heights. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.” When Christ came to Jerusalem and descended from the Mount of Olives, the sons of Israel cried out, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” But what did that coming of Christ to Jerusalem signify except the future resurrection, when he will come to judge the living and the dead and will appear to us in the same flesh in which he suffered for us? Then, as the Apostle said, every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bend in the name of Jesus, and so forth.

14. “You therefore, most clement Father.” “You therefore”—that is, “you certainly, most clement Father.” *Clemens* is said as though from *clara mens*, “clear mind,” or from abundance; and *clementissime* means, as it were, “with the clearest mind” or “most abundantly,” because he is most clear in mind and a most merciful Father. We do not call him gentle and merciful because he is composed of bodily members, heart, or mind [Col. 1147C] as a human being is; rather, we proclaim him gentle and merciful so that we may feel and understand from him that gentleness and mercy by which we are to be saved.

225. 15. “Through Jesus Christ.” In Greek, *Iesous*; in Latin, *Salvator*, “Savior,” or *salutaris*, “salutary.” He is called Savior because he saves his people from their sins. He saves from sins because he has the power to forgive sins, as he himself said: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. IX, 6). He is called salutary because he gave us salvation, so that, if we keep his commandments, we may be able to receive eternal life. “Your Son,” namely, your only-begotten Son, because he alone is begotten from the substance of the Father, while we are adopted sons through him who is the only-begotten, proceeding from the Father and coeternal with the Father. Therefore, through him we humbly ask the Father, saying:

16. “We humbly beseech and ask you.” *Supplices*, that is [Col. 1147D], “humble.” “That you may accept and bless.” That is, “that you may receive and bless.” “These gifts, these offerings, these holy and undefiled sacrifices.” Gifts are things freely given. Offerings are things presented in exchange for some gift or reward, just as we offer to God so that our sins may be forgiven. Sacrifices are things that have already been consecrated together with prayers. “Undefiled” means the same as “unstained” and free from every taint of malice. Gifts and sacrifices are undefiled when they are offered without the stains of scandals and have been acquired through just labor. It does not mean, as many err by saying, that “undefiled” means “not dedicated.” Read the seven Conferences of the Fathers, and in the second conference, in chapter nine, you will find what “undefiled” means.

17. “In the first place, the things that we offer to you.” That is, “the things we offer to you,” for whom they are offered indicates the meaning: first of all, they ought to be offered for your holy catholic Church. In Greek, *ecclesia*; in Latin, *congregatio*, “assembly.” It is called catholic, “universal,” because all who believe in the Lord [Col. 1148A] ought to be in one assembly. “Which may you deign to pacify, protect, unite, and govern throughout the whole world.” May you deign to preserve it pacified and united throughout the whole world. “Together with your servant N.” That is, together with the one who occupies the see of the apostle Peter, because the Church in which Peter, chief of the apostles, sat is the head of all catholic Churches. This is because Christ says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock,” and the rest (Matt. XVI, 18). Because of this saying, we all ought to pray for the one who is in that same Church.

18. “And our bishop N.” That is, for the bishop; he is our shepherd and preacher. “Remember, Lord, your servants, men and women, and all who are standing around.” The priest has already prayed for the apostolic leader and for his own bishop. If a bishop celebrates Mass, he ought not to say “our bishop,” because he himself is the bishop. If a presbyter celebrates Mass, he ought to say “our bishop.” Prayer has already been made for the elders; afterward [Col. 1148B] prayer must be made for the people. When the priest says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” he beseeches the Lord Father to deign to remember all who have come to the office of the Mass, whether men or women. By “those standing around,” men and women alike are understood—whoever are standing there.

19. The priest has now prayed for all who have come to hear Mass; 226 then finally he prays for those who bring their offerings. [Perhaps: “who offer them.”] “Who offer you this sacrifice of praise.” It is called “of praise” because they offer it first for the praise of God, and afterward for themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and safety; and they return their vows to you, eternal, living, and true God. They offer because the faith of all who are standing around, whether offering or not offering, and their devotion are known and recognized by the living and true God of all. All return their vows. They are called vows because they are promised willingly, since we ought willingly and gladly to make vows. “Sharing in communion and venerating the memory, first of all, of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, but also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.”

20. “To communicate” means to participate in the commemoration [Col. 1148C]; “to venerate” means to hold honorably in memory the fact that holy Mary the Virgin became the mother of the Son of God, Jesus Christ, through the coming of the Holy Spirit; he is God and man, through whom we beseech the Father, and with whom we ought to share the faith and believe that, when the Holy Spirit came, the Son of God was born from her and her virginity was not violated. “But also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.” In our language, an apostle is called “one sent.” A martyr is called a “witness.” They are called apostles because they were sent by Christ. They are called martyrs because they are witnesses that Christ suffered for us, and they themselves suffered for Christ.

21. “Therefore, Lord, we ask you, appeased, to accept this offering of our service and also of your entire household.” The priest commends his offering and that of all [Col. 1148D] who serve God—that is, who serve the Lord—so that it may please the Lord [perhaps, “so that they may please the Lord”] and that he may be favorable to us. “And order our days in your peace, and command that we be snatched from eternal condemnation and numbered among the flock of your chosen ones, through Christ our Lord.” For the one for whom the priest offers, he ought to pray that the priest may be heard, that everyone’s days may be ordered in peace, and that we may be snatched from eternal condemnation. Concerning this, our Lord Jesus Christ will say to the impious at the end of the world: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire,” and so forth. And may we deserve to be numbered by the holy angels among the flock of his chosen ones, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV, 34), and the rest.

22. “Which offering, O God, we ask you to deign to make blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect.” The priest supplicates that the almighty Father may deign to accept as blessed [Col. 1149A] the offering that he offers for himself and for the people, and to have it enrolled—that is, assigned—so that it may please him. “Ratified,” that is, judged, so that he may judge it worthy to be offered in his sight. “Reasonable”: may he deign to make it full of right reason, because it is then acceptable to him if, believing rightly, we offer it according to right reason. It is right to ask that the almighty Father may, by sanctifying, make that offering which we offer reasonably. “So that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Son is beloved by the Father, as the Father himself testified from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth (Matt. III, 17). And we ought to love him, because he first loved us and suffered for us.

227. 23. “Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands; and, raising his eyes to heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat from this, all of you: for this is my body.’” [Col. 1149B] “In like manner, after supper had ended, he also took this noble chalice into his holy and venerable hands; likewise giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and drink from it, all of you. For this is the chalice of my blood of the new and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do these things, you will do them in remembrance of me.’”

24. What we omitted—“who, on the day before he suffered”—means “on the day before he himself suffered for us.” He wished to hand over to his disciples the mystery of his body and blood, so that they might hand it over to us. Who would ever believe that bread could be changed into flesh and wine into blood, unless the Savior himself said so—he who created bread and wine and made everything from nothing? It is easier to make something from something than to create everything from nothing. The Savior himself wished to assume a human body and unite humanity to God, so that Christ Jesus, a human being, might become the one mediator between God and human beings [Col. 1149C]. He wished us to offer bread and wine to him, for them to be consecrated divinely by him, and for the faithful people to believe that the mystery is true—the mystery that he himself handed over to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat from this, all of you.” And when he raised his eyes to heaven and gave thanks to the Father, he taught us that we ought always to beseech the Father, so that he may deign to bring so great a sacrament to completion through our hands.

25. And when he said, “Whenever you do these things, you will do them in remembrance of me,” he commanded us to remember his Passion. We ought at all times to remember how much he endured for us when we celebrate this sacrament, and to place our confidence in his mercy, not in our own goodness. Hence also we say: “Therefore, remembering, Lord, we your servants, but also your holy people, remember Christ your Son, our Lord.” We priests profess that we remember, and we testify that the people remember Christ your Son, our Lord. Therefore priests ought to remember faithfully [Col. 1149D], because they themselves celebrate Mass; for a request is foolish if the one asking does not know what he is asking. The holy people ought to remember because Christ suffered not only for priests but also for the holy people. They are called holy because they have been sanctified by receiving the faith and baptism of Christ.

26. They now indicate what they ought to remember: namely, both the blessed Passion, and also the resurrection from the dead, and also his glorious ascension into heaven. We ought to remember the Passion of Christ your Son because he deigned to suffer for us. Of his resurrection from the lower regions: through his resurrection, they were freed [perhaps, “souls were freed”]. We ought to remember his glorious ascension because he carried the human body that he had assumed, joined to divinity, into heaven by his own majesty, without anyone’s assistance. We have said “without anyone’s assistance” so that it may be understood that he ascended into heaven not by the vehicle of human beings, angels, or any creature, [Col. 1150A] but was raised by the Father of majesty, 228 concerning whom he himself said in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.”

27. “We offer to your glorious Majesty, from your gifts and bestowals, a pure offering, a holy offering, an unblemished offering, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation.” Lord, remembering all the goodness mentioned above, we offer to your Majesty a pure offering—that is, from a pure body, because your body is pure, which we believe is made from this bread. “A holy offering,” because you sanctified your body when you assumed humanity into God; and now sanctify this bread so that it may become your body. “An unblemished offering,” because you suffered for us without the stain of sin.

28. “The holy bread of eternal life,” because you are the living bread who came down from heaven, and you wished us to receive your body in this bread sanctified by you; and through the chalice of your Passion you wished us to receive your blood [Col. 1150B]. Sanctify this offering so that it may become your body and your blood for us. “Upon which may you deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance.” We beseech this: that the holy Father may deign to look upon the good things offered by us with a pious, gentle, and radiant countenance—that is, to see them and accept them. “Just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and what your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice, an unblemished offering.” The Lord accepted Abel’s gifts because he offered to the Lord whatever best thing he found; and we ought to offer just gifts to the pure God with a pure heart. Abraham did not spare his own son Isaac, but, obedient to the Lord’s command, wished to offer him.

29. Melchizedek was the first priest to offer bread and wine to the Lord, and therefore it is written in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). For just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine, so Christ in his Passion offered his body and blood to God the Father [Col. 1150C] for us; and in bread and wine he wished us to imitate the mystery of his Passion when, giving bread and the chalice to his disciples, he said: “This is my body, and this is the chalice of my blood.” We also ought to beseech God that, just as the gifts of the Fathers mentioned above were acceptable to him, so our gifts may become acceptable.

30. “We humbly beseech you, almighty God: command that these gifts be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar in the presence of your divine Majesty.” We humbly ask that the heavenly Father command our gifts, offered upon this altar that can be seen, to be carried by the hands of his holy angel to that high altar before his divine Majesty, which we cannot see with our eyes, because it is not corporeal but spiritual. And just as we cannot investigate the divine Majesty of the Father, so we ought not to investigate the things that are in his presence, but rather believe them. “So that as many of us as have received the most holy body and blood of your Son from participation in this altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.” We ought to pray to the heavenly Father that everyone who receives the body and blood of the aforementioned Son from his altar [perhaps, “all who receive from that altar”], upon which we offer to God the Father in remembrance of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, may deserve to receive every heavenly blessing, through Christ our Lord.

31. “And to us sinners, your servants, who hope in the multitude of your mercies, may you deign to grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles, martyrs, and all the saints.” All these sacrifices are offered by both priest and people so that almighty God may not reckon our sins against us but grant us a portion with his saints. “Admit us into their fellowship, we ask, not as one who measures merit, but as the giver of forgiveness.” This [Col. 1151A] is what we ask: that he himself, who said, “On whatever day the sinner turns and does penance, all his sins will be forgotten before me,” may not assess the repayment due for sins, but may himself be the giver of forgiveness, so that he may place us within the fellowship of the saints, through Christ our Lord.

32. “Through whom he created all these gifts; may he himself sanctify them, bless them, and make them profitable for us, so that through Christ, through whom they were made, and in Christ, in whom all things were made, and with whom all things were made—who is coeternal with the Father—we may always give thanks to the Father for ever and ever. Amen.” “Having been instructed by saving commandments and by the divine…” We have been admonished, commanded, and formed by Christ’s commandments, which are full of salvation because he himself is eternal salvation. We have received from Christ our Lord the same form and example, and we have dared to pray as he taught his disciples. We believe in our Father, who created us, and we say:

[Col. 1151B] **33. Our Father, who art in heaven.** Christ said after his resurrection: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father.” He called him his Father in one way and our Father in another. He is his Father because he is the proper Son of the Father, begotten from the substance of the Father before all ages and coeternal with the Father. He is our Father because he created us in time, and we are adopted sons; we ought to possess the heavenly inheritance of our heavenly Father if we fulfill [our promise] by works, since we have promised the reception of faith. “Heaven” (*caelum*) is said from *celare*, “to conceal,” because it conceals divine secrets. Alternatively, heaven is named from *celsitudo*, “height,” because it is higher than earthly things. We therefore say, “Our Father, who art in heaven,” to show that we believe in the heavenly Father; and just as sons desire to fulfill the commands of their father, so we too should desire to fulfill his commands and always strive toward heaven.

**34. Hallowed be thy name:** that is, may we be worthy to hold his holy name in our hearts, so that, just as the holy angels who are in heaven know and understand the holiness of his name, we too, who are on earth, may, with his help, deserve to know his holiness; so that his name may be hallowed on earth as it is in heaven. **Thy kingdom come:** that is, may we deserve to know his kingdom and power, and may the devil no longer reign over us because of our sins, but may his kingdom come, as it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

**35. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth:** that is, just as those who are in heaven do his will, so may we, who are on earth, do it. “Earth” (*terra*) is named from *terere*, “to wear down,” because it is worn down by feet. **Give us this day our daily bread.** Among the Greeks, *bread* (*panis*) is interpreted in our language as “everything.” We pray that the almighty Father may deign to bestow upon us at all times every means of sustenance, spiritual and bodily. **And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.** For he who demands a debt from one who owes him does nothing unjust; but if almighty God were to demand all our debts from us, no one would doubtless be found free. Therefore we must forgive the debts of our debtors, so that the Almighty may forgive ours, because he said: “If you do not forgive each one of your brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. XVIII, 35). And elsewhere: “All scandals are removed from his kingdom” (Matt. XIII, 41); and likewise, a sacrifice is not received if it is offered with an offense. Rather, one is commanded to leave it before the altar until he has been reconciled to his brother, and then to offer it with a clean heart.

**36. And lead us not into temptation.** That is, may we not enter that temptation in which the devil tempts us and consent to him; rather, may the Lord himself defend us, so that we are not led into demonic temptation. For if the Lord abandons us, we are immediately brought into the devil’s snare. Therefore we ask that he himself deliver us from evil, that is, from every demonic assault. [Col. 1152A] **Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future.** We ask that he himself deliver us from all evils, he who created us pure and good, and in whom there is no evil. Past evils are those which we committed earlier, when we were sinning, and for which we therefore endure scourges. Future evils are those which, at the devil’s prompting, may still come; and therefore we pray that we may be delivered from all of them, because before the sight of God there are neither past nor future things, but all are present.

**37. With the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and with the blessed apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew interceding for us.** We invoke for our help the Mother of God, who was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. We also invoke the blessed apostles, who handed down to us the mysteries to be celebrated, so that they may intercede for us, because we ourselves are not worthy to merit forgiveness for past and present matters, nor caution concerning future matters, unless it is granted to us through their prayer. [Col. 1152B] We have already prayed that we may be delivered from evils; now let us pray that, through the intercession of the saints mentioned above, he himself, in his mercy, may grant peace in our days—he who is powerful to deliver us from evil.

**38. Peace from the devil’s temptation, so that we may not be led into it; peace from evil people, so that we may not suffer their scourges.** **That, aided by the help of your mercy:** that is, aided by God’s help, may we always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance. This means that, having been forgiven our sins in the present age, we may not again be disturbed by sinning, nor suffer eternal disturbance on the day of judgment. **May the peace of the Lord be always with you.** Christ is the eternal peace who reconciled us to the Father through his passion, so that we would not be held in hell because of the sin of the first man. The priest prays that this peace may remain with the people and make them all harmonious, so that we may deserve to reign peacefully with Christ in heaven.

**39.** [231] And for this reason we make peace at that point, before we receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ into our bodies, because without concord we are not worthy to receive holy communion. For if we have discord with our neighbors, the gifts are not received by the Lord until we have been reconciled. Then the clergy pray by singing: **“Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”**

He is called a lamb because of his innocence, since he harms neither human beings nor beasts; and when he is led to the sacrifice, he does not injure the one killing him, but after his death restores his killer. So too Christ harmed no one, as the Apostle says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (I Pet. II, 22). Yet after his passion he restores many of his persecutors, once they have been converted, through the holy communion of his body and blood, and makes them believers. He took away the sin of the world when he granted us forgiveness of sins.

**40.** For before his passion, the righteous and sinners alike descended into hell, and in the Old Testament we nowhere read of forgiveness of sins. [Col. 1152D] But through repentance Christ promised us not only forgiveness of sins but also angelic joy, saying: “There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV, 7).

We ask Christ himself, the innocent Lamb of God who suffered for the salvation of the world, to have mercy on us, saying: **“Have mercy on us.”** For in the Old Testament a lamb was offered for the sins of the people; and in the New Testament Christ offered himself to God the Father, so that through his passion he might free the human race from sin. Therefore “Lamb of God” is sung when the body and blood of Christ are received, so that we may all believe that the body and blood of that Lamb are then taken—of the Lamb who took away the sins of the world by dying and granted us eternal life by rising again: Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

**41.** And after the Mass has ended, the deacon says: **“Go; it is the dismissal.”** *Diaconus* means “deacon” in Greek, and *minister* in Latin. He announces to the people that the prayers have ended, because no one should leave the church before the announcement has been made by the minister; and all respond: **“Thanks be to God.”**

[Col. 1153]

# APPENDIX IX, BOOK FOUR OF THE SENTENCES (S)

[Col. 1153A] **CHAPTER I. On rulers: how they ought to conduct themselves**

**1.** A ruler must always be pure in thought, so that no impurity may stain the one who has undertaken this office of wiping away the stains of pollution even from the hearts of others. It is necessary that the hand which takes care to wash away the filth of others strive to be clean, lest, if it holds mud while pursuing dirt, it soil everything it touches even worse. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Cleanse yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII, 11). For they bear the vessels of the Lord who, in the integrity of their conduct, take responsibility for leading the souls of their neighbors to the eternal sanctuaries. Let them see how much they must be purified within themselves, since they carry living vessels to the temple of eternity in the embrace of their own promise. Hence the divine voice commands that the breastpiece of judgment be fastened upon Aaron’s breast with binding cords (Exod. XXVIII, 15), so that no fickle thoughts may possess the priestly heart, but reason alone may restrain it (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, II.2; Taio, *Book II of the Sentences*, ch. 33).

**2.** Let the one appointed as an example to others think neither anything indiscreet nor anything useless; by the gravity of his life he must always show how much reason he carries in his breast. On the breastpiece of judgment, which is placed upon Aaron’s breast, it is commanded that the names of the twelve patriarchs be inscribed. To carry the written fathers always upon one’s breast means to think without interruption about the life of the ancients. A priest walks irreproachably when he continually looks upon the examples of the fathers who preceded him, when he considers without ceasing the footsteps of the saints, and suppresses unlawful thoughts, lest his foot in action extend beyond the boundary of his order. A ruler must always distinguish good from evil by careful examination, and diligently consider what is appropriate, to whom, when, and in what manner; he must seek nothing for himself, but regard his own advantages as belonging to his neighbors.

**3.** Let the ruler be distinguished in action, so that by living well he may proclaim the way of life to his subjects, and so that the flock, which follows the voice and conduct of its shepherd, may advance better through examples than through words. Through the divine law it is commanded: “The priest shall take the right shoulder for the sacrifice, and it shall be set apart” (Exod. XXIX, 22), so that his activity may be not only useful but also exceptional; and so that he may not merely do what is right among the wicked, but may also surpass his subjects who act well in the virtue of his conduct just as he surpasses them in the honor of his rank. The breast and shoulder are given to the priest for food, so that he may learn from the sacrifice which he is commanded to take what he ought to learn to offer of himself to the Creator. He must not merely think of what is right, but must also invite those who observe him to higher things by the shoulder of his works (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, II.3).

**4.** Let the ruler desire nothing and fear nothing belonging to the present life; let him despise the world’s flatteries by considering inwardly the terror of judgment. Let him also scorn terrors by considering the sweetness within. Let the ruler be near to each person through compassion, yet lifted above all through contemplation, so that through the inner organs of pity he may transfer the weakness of others into himself, and through the height of contemplation may transcend even himself by desiring invisible things. Thus, while seeking lofty things, he must not despise the lowly things [Al.: weaknesses] of his neighbors, nor, by accommodating himself to their lowliness, abandon the pursuit of lofty things. Shepherds do not merely seek upward by contemplating the holy head of the Church, namely the Lord; they also descend downward in compassion toward his members (ibid., ch. 5).

**5.** Hence Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle: the one who is caught up within in contemplation is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; outside, he carries the burdens of those subject to the flesh. The Truth itself, revealed to us through assuming our humanity, remains devoted to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles in the cities (Luke VI, 12), thereby laying before good rulers the path of imitation: even if they seek the highest things through contemplation, they must nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion.

Those who have been placed over others in pastoral government should show themselves to be such that their subjects are not ashamed to disclose their hidden matters to them; so that when the little ones endure the waves of temptation, they may run to the shepherd’s mind as to a mother’s lap. And whatever impurity they foresee themselves contracting from the dirt of pressing guilt, let them wash away through the comfort of his exhortation and the tears of his prayer.

**6.** Let the ruler not diminish care for inward matters amid outward occupations, nor abandon provision for outward matters amid concern for inward things, lest he either fall from inner things by devoting himself to external affairs, or, occupied only with inner matters, fail to provide for his neighbors what he owes them outwardly. Through the law priests are commanded to cut their hair, “shaving their heads” (Ezek. XLIV, 20), so that they may provide for temporal concerns as much as necessary, yet cut them back quickly lest they grow beyond measure. Thus, while bodily life is protected through the administration of outward provision, and is not hindered by a measured attentiveness of the heart, the hair on the priest’s head is both preserved, so that it covers the ears, and cut back, so that it does not cover the eyes (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, II.7–8).

**7.** It is necessary for the ruler to watch carefully lest the desire to please people assail him; lest, while he diligently penetrates inward matters and prudently supplies outward necessities, he seek to be loved by his subjects more than he seeks the truth; and lest, while he appears alien to the world because he is supported by good deeds, his own love make him a stranger to the Creator. He is an enemy of the Redeemer who desires to be loved by the Church for the good works he performs in the Redeemer’s place, because he is guilty of adulterous thought if the servant seeks to please the bride’s eyes through whom the Bridegroom sent his gifts. It is especially necessary for rulers to temper the care of government with such skill in moderation that, when the minds of their subjects are able to perceive certain things rightly, they may speak out with freedom of speech, yet freedom may not burst into pride. Otherwise, while perhaps excessive freedom is granted to their tongue, humility of life may be lost by them.

**8.** Good rulers ought therefore to seek to please people in such a way that, through the sweetness of their good reputation, they draw their neighbors into affection for the truth—not by desiring to be loved themselves, but by making the love shown them into a kind of road through which they may lead the hearts of their hearers into love of the Creator. It is difficult for a preacher who proclaims anything right, but is not loved, to be heard willingly.

All that we have set forth is rightly done by a ruler if, inspired by the spirit of heavenly fear and love, he diligently meditates daily on the commands of sacred speech, so that the words of divine admonition may restore in him the force of concern and the careful vigilance toward heavenly life which the practice of human society continually destroys; and so that he who is led toward old age through association with worldly people may always be renewed toward love of his spiritual homeland by the breath of compunction (ibid., ch. 11).

**9.** Since we have already shown above what a shepherd ought to be, let us now demonstrate how he ought to teach. The same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, because not everyone is bound by the same quality of character. Often things that benefit one person harm another: frequently the herbs that nourish some animals kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but incites puppies; a medicine that reduces one illness adds strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the strong kills the little ones.

The bells are appropriately described as inserted into the pontiff’s garments. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than right works, as the prophet testifies when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9)? Bells therefore cling to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim the way of life with the sound of his tongue (Gregory, preface to Part II of the *Pastoral Rule*; Taio, Book II, ch. 35).

**10.** Because we are weak human beings, when we speak to people about God we must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider in what manner of teaching we should care for our weak brothers. Let us therefore consider whether we are now what some people are whom we correct, or whether we were once such people; and if, through the operation of divine grace, we are no longer such, let us correct them with a heart so much more restrained and humble as we more truly recognize ourselves in those whom we amend.

It is written: “Do you have daughters? Keep watch over their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face” (Ecclus. VII, 26). Weak souls, devoted to the desire for the world, are sometimes better preserved by severity, so that a hardened face—that is, a face covered, through the guardianship of severity, against every hope of frivolous leniency—may terrify the unstable spirit and restrain it from the pleasure of vices by the rigor of discipline (Gregory, *Moralia*, XXIII.13, no. 25; Taio, Book II, ch. 36; Gregory I, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, 12, no. 31).

**11.** When this is done by a teacher, sweetness and humility must always be retained in the heart, so that he may love greatly and never, through arrogance, become proud against the other person; yet he must not refuse, for that person’s benefit, to reveal his love and humility. When the ruler’s spirit is moved by zeal, he must take the greatest care that the anger which is taken up as an instrument of virtue not dominate the mind, lest it advance as a mistress; rather, like a maidservant prepared for service, it must never depart from behind reason. It is then raised against vices when it serves reason as a subordinate.

He who is moved by zeal for righteousness should correct the faults of wrongdoers in such a way that he himself, the one correcting, first grows through patience; he should judge his fervor by rising above it, lest, aroused beyond measure, he wander far from righteousness through that very zeal for righteousness (Gregory, *Moralia*, V.45, no. 82).

**12.** There are many shepherds who, because they do not know how to measure themselves, desire to teach what they have not learned. They judge the burden of teaching all the lighter because they are ignorant of its greatness; and because, unlearned and headstrong, they desire to possess the art of teaching, they are driven back from the boldness of their rashness at the very doorway of speech. No art may be presumed to be taught unless it has first been learned through concentrated study. With what presumption, then, is pastoral teaching undertaken by the inexperienced, when the government of souls is the art of arts?

There are some within the holy Church who seek the glory of honor under the appearance of government; they desire to be seen as teachers, wish to rise above others, and, as the Truth testifies, seek the first couches at banquets and the first seats in assemblies (Matt. XXIII, 6–7). The more they have come to the teaching of humility through mere exaltation, the less they are able to discharge the office of pastoral care worthily. For the tongue itself is confounded in teaching when one thing is learned and another taught (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, preface; Taio, Book II, ch. 37; ibid., ch. 1).

**13.** With great restraint, the shepherds of the Church should strive either to loose or to bind. But whether a shepherd binds justly or unjustly, the shepherd’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest the subordinate, even when perhaps unjustly bound, deserve the sentence of his binding because of another fault. The holy preachers who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls and condemn or free others, though they feared being condemned themselves. The bishops in the Church now occupy their place: those who receive the rank of government take up the authority to loose and bind.

Pontifical honor is great, but the burden of that honor is great. It is difficult that one who does not know how to control his own life should become judge of another’s life. It often happens that the one who holds the place of judgment is one whose life is in no way suited to that place. He often acts either to condemn the undeserving or, himself bound, to loose others (Taio, Book II, near the end of ch. 38; Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, 26, nos. 4–5).

**14.** Often, when loosing and binding their subjects, shepherds follow the impulses of their own will [Al.: pleasure], rather than the merits of the cases. Thus the one who exercises the power of binding and loosing for his own pleasures, and not according to the merits of his subjects, deprives himself of that power. Often a shepherd is moved toward a neighbor by hatred or favor. But those who follow their own hatred or favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly. Hence the prophet rightly says: “They put to death souls that do not die, and they brought to life souls that do not live” (Ezek. XIII, 19). He puts the living to death who condemns the righteous; and he tries to bring to life one who will not live who attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment.

**15.** Some bishops habitually turn the gift of the received Spirit into an instrument of trade and bend the signs of miracles to the service of avarice. Hence Simon, desiring the miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wished to obtain the gift of the Spirit with money (Acts VIII, 18), so that he might sell more wickedly what he had acquired wickedly. Our Redeemer, making a whip from cords, drove the crowds from the temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves (John II, 15). To sell doves means to give the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, not for the merit of life but for a reward.

There are some who do not receive monetary rewards for ordination, yet bestow holy orders for human favor and seek from that same generosity only the recompense of praise. These plainly do not give freely what they received freely, because from the sacred office bestowed they seek a coin of approval (Gregory I, *Homilies on the Gospels*, 4, no. 4; Taio, II.40).

# CHAPTER II. On clerics: what they ought to be

**1.** A cleric must be admonished to live in such a way that he may provide secular people with a good example of life. If anything is rightly reproved in a cleric, the reputation of our religion itself is burdened by his fault. Clerics should learn to fulfill what their elders command them, and to submit humbly to their orders, so that neither submission may crush them nor a superior position exalt them. Clerics should learn how to order their inner selves before the eyes of the hidden Judge through humility and obedience, so that they may not be punished with the reprobate but may also receive a share of the rewards with the elect.

Clerics must be admonished to live with that much greater vigilance concerning themselves insofar as they are not entangled in the care of others. Clerics must be told not rashly to judge the life of their superiors if they perhaps see them doing something blameworthy, lest they sink into deeper things through the impulse of pride precisely where they rightly rebuke evils. Clerics must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they observe their faults; rather, they should judge their superiors’ wrongs privately in such a way that, restrained by divine fear, they still do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them. The deeds of superiors are not to be struck down with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of correction (Taio, II.44; Gregory I, *Homilies on the Gospels*, 17, no. 18; *Pastoral Rule*, III.4).

**2.** Most clerics are restrained from the vice of shamelessness only by harsh rebuke, because, since they do not know that they are doing wrong, they must be rebuked by many. Modest exhortation usually sets modest clerics in order for the better, because for their conversion it is enough that the teacher gently bring their evils back to their memory. Modest clerics make greater progress if what is reproved in them is touched obliquely, as though by the hand of a flattering tongue.

We bring fainthearted clerics back more suitably to the good path of action if we obliquely seek out some of their good qualities; while correcting and reproving other things in them, let us embrace and praise these, so that praise heard may nourish their tenderness, which rebuke of their fault chastises.

Often we make better progress with clerics if we recall their good deeds and, if they have done anything disorderly, do not rebuke it as though it had already been committed, but forbid it as though it must still not be committed. Many clerics, while fearing that they will be caught in their fault, always seek dishonest defenses, but are tormented by fearful suspicions. Nothing is safer for presenting oneself than purity, and nothing easier for speaking than truth; for when someone is compelled to defend his deceit, his heart is wearied by hard labor.

Often clerics caught in a fault, while they refuse to let their character be known, hide themselves beneath the veil of deceit and attempt to excuse what they are doing and what is already plainly visible. It often happens that the one who strives to rebuke the faults of wicked clerics, misled by clouds of falsehood spread about him, seems almost to have lost what he had already held as certain about them (Gregory, ibid., chs. 7, 11).

# CHAPTER III. On envious and insolent subjects

**1.** Often subjects placed under pastoral government, when they presume themselves to be very exalted, disdain others by reproaching them, while they judge everything they do to be uniquely important. The works of the insolent must therefore be examined carefully by the one rebuking them, so that it may be shown that what pleases them displeases the Lord. We correct the insolent more effectively when we show that the things they believe they have done well were done badly, so that useful shame may follow from the very source from which glory was believed to have been gained.

When subordinate persons recognize that they have not at all committed the vice of insolence, they come more quickly to correction if they are confounded by the reproach of a more obvious fault, one sought out obliquely, so that from what they cannot defend they may realize that they are wickedly clinging to what they defend.

When Paul saw the Corinthians insolently puffed up against one another, with one saying that he belonged to Apollo, another to Paul, another to Cephas, and another to Christ (I Cor. I, 12; III, 4), he brought into their midst the sin of incest, which had both been committed among them and remained uncorrected, saying: “It is reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (I Cor. V, 1). It is as though he openly said: “Why do you insolently say that you belong to this or that person, when through the laxity of your negligence you show that you belong to no one?”

Envious subjects must be admonished to consider how blind they are: they fail through another’s progress and waste away through another’s exaltation. They must consider how unhappy they are: they become worse through their neighbor’s improvement (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, III.8; Taio, II.43; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, III.10).

**2.** While they look upon the increase of another’s prosperity, they die inwardly, afflicted by the plague of their anxious heart. While the envious do not guard themselves from jealousy, they sink into the wickedness of the ancient and cunning enemy. For it is written of him: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). Since he himself lost heaven, he envied the human being who had been created, and, in his ruin, he increased his own condemnation by ruining others as well.

The envious must be told that, while they consume themselves inwardly with this plague, they also kill whatever other good they appear to possess. Hence it is written: “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh; envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. XIV, 30). Through the vice of jealousy, even things that seem strong to human eyes perish before the eyes of the Lord. For bones rotting through envy means that even certain strong things decay.

That subordinate is truly humble in good things who is not a defender of himself in evil things. A subordinate is then accused concerning his evils and kindled against the words of the one rebuking him when, while seeming to falter humbly concerning his good qualities, he seeks to be adorned by the language of humility rather than instructed.

# CHAPTER IV. On the life and conduct of monks

**1.** All monks, having abandoned the world, do not cease to expiate by weeping the sins they have committed. They afflict themselves with profound sorrow because, having been cast far away from the face of the Creator, they do not yet share in the joys of the eternal homeland. Of them Solomon rightly says: “The heart that knows the bitterness of its own soul will not allow a stranger to share in its joy” (Prov. XIV, 10).

The hearts of good monks know their own bitterness because they understand the misery of exile by which they have been cast out and torn apart; they perceive how peaceful are the things they have lost and how confused are the things into which they have fallen. Monks who live in bitterness of soul desire to die utterly to the world, so that, just as they desire nothing in the world, they may now be held by no obligation to the world (Gregory, *Moralia*, V.3; Taio, II.45).

**2.** It often happens that a monk no longer holds the world in his mind, yet the world still binds the monk through certain occupations: he is dead to the world, but the world is still alive to him. The world still desires him, since it strives to snatch him away while he is intent on other things. If a dead body and a living body are in one place, although the dead does not see the living, the living nevertheless sees the dead. But if both are dead, neither sees the other. Thus the monk no longer loves the world, yet he is loved by it, unwilling though he may be; although, like a dead person, he does not see the world, the world, which is not yet dead, still sees him.

But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is retained by the world’s love, then they are mutually dead to each other, because, while neither desires the other, the dead person pays no attention to the dead.

When the glory of this world is offered to sorrowful and grieving monks, they are afflicted by the penalty of a most powerful fear. For although they themselves do not hold the world, they still fear that they might be such as are held by the world; for unless they lived for it to some small degree, it would certainly not love them for its own use.

**3.** For the sea retains living bodies within itself, but immediately casts dead bodies outside itself. Sometimes monks do not reach the desires they have conceived precisely so that, through the intervening delay, they may be expanded toward those same desires with the breast of their mind opened wide. Thus what they might perhaps carry weakened once fulfilled is brought about by a great design so that, rejected, it may grow more abundantly.

Many monks desire to be mortified to the present age in such a way that, if permitted, they might already perfectly contemplate the face of their Creator. But their desire is delayed so that it may advance, and it is nourished in the breast of its delay so that it may grow.

In the *Song of Songs*, the bride, longing for the face of her bridegroom, cries out: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, and did not find him” (Song III, 1). The bridegroom hides himself when he is sought so that, when not found, he may be sought more ardently. Why is the seeking bride delayed from finding him? So that, made more receptive by the delay, she may eventually find more abundantly what she was seeking. When spiritual monks fully desire their mortification, the nearer they come to the end, the more ardent they show themselves in their work (Gregory, ibid., ch. 4, no. 6).

**4.** Therefore they do not grow weary by laboring, but rather grow through the practice of labor. Because they consider the rewards to be nearer, they sweat at their work with greater delight. Many monks, who are lulled to sleep by the works of the world not in body [Al.: not through sluggishness] but in virtue, sleep more laboriously than they could remain awake. For, in surpassing the activities of this age after abandoning them, they struggle daily against themselves in a vigorous conflict: lest the mind grow sluggish through negligence; lest, subdued by idleness and desire, it grow cold toward unclean desires; lest it burn more than is right for good desires themselves; and lest, under the appearance of discretion, it grow weak from sparing itself and fall short of perfection.

A good monk withdraws himself completely from the restless desire of this world, abandons the noise of earthly activities, and, through the pursuit of quiet, keeps his mind intent upon virtues; thus, as though awake, he sleeps.

# CHAPTER V. On the humility and work of monks

**1.** A monk must be admonished always to examine with care the reverence due to his habit—in his actions, speech, and thoughts—and to abandon perfectly the things of the world. What he displays to human eyes by his habit, he should display before the eyes of the Lord through his conduct. All monks who refuse to be scattered among external cares remain simple in thought and in the dwelling of their conscience (Taio, II.46; Gregory, *Moralia*, V.11, no. 20).

**2.** Hence it is written of Jacob: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents” (Gen. XXV, 27). The chosen monks are said to dwell in tents when transient prosperity smiles upon them, when, as though unaware of the world’s favor, they conceal it, and with a firm step inwardly trample upon that by which they are outwardly lifted up. Often monks who do good works still feel the scourges of the Father, so that they may come to the inheritance more perfect in proportion as the discipline that lovingly strikes them purifies them daily even from the smallest faults [Al.: also from the smallest faults].

# CHAPTER VI. On the lukewarmness and idleness of monks

**1.** Some monks flee the activities of the world but exercise themselves in no virtues. They sleep, plainly, through lukewarmness and not through zeal; and for this reason they look upon the earth, because they have placed their head not upon the Rock but upon the earth. [239] It often happens to monks that, the more securely they cease from external activities, the more broadly they heap up within themselves the noise of unclean thought through idleness. Hence, under the figure of Judea, the prophet mourns over a soul numb with idleness when he says: “Her enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I, 7) (Taio, II.49; Gregory, *Moralia*, V.31, no. 5).

**2.** Often, according to the commandment of the law, work is ceased from externally on the Sabbath. Enemies therefore mock the Sabbaths when they see them, whenever evil spirits drag the very leisure of inactivity toward unlawful thoughts, so that each soul, the more it is believed to serve God because it has withdrawn from external activities, the more it serves unlawful tyranny.

Through the most wise Solomon it is said: “Whoever is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to one who destroys his own works” (Prov. XVIII, 9) (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, III.34).

[Col. 1159C] 3. The hand of the strong worker does not raise begun good works to completion if the very slackness of working fights against what has been done. If what is dead within us is not kindled to life [Greek edition: “if what is dead”], then even that which is held as though it were still alive is extinguished. In this world the human soul is, as it were, like a ship ascending against the force of a river. It is permitted to stand still nowhere, because it falls back to the depths unless it strives toward the heights.

## CHAPTER VII. On the aids to be employed for the body’s necessities

1. When we attend to the necessities of our nature, often more than is fitting, and neglect the care of the mind, from the misery of our negligence and weakness we add the squalor of sin. The necessities of the present age have this especially dangerous feature: it is often not at all discernible in them what is done out of concern for usefulness and what through the fault of pleasure. To give negligence free rein in response to the weakness of our nature is nothing other than to add misery to calamity and, from that same misery, to multiply the squalor of our actions [Al.: “the weakness … through negligence … and the squalor of vices”] (Gregory, *Moralia* XX, 14, no. 28; Taio III, 12).

2. In everything they do, holy men distinguish with the most diligent intention, lest the weakness of their nature demand from them more than is owed to it, and lest, under the covering of necessity, the vice of pleasure grow within them. The elect endure one thing from weakness and another from the suggestion of temptation; and, established like perfectly just arbiters between necessity and pleasure, they restrain the former by comforting and relieving it, and the latter by pressing it down. Thus it happens that, although they endure the calamity of their weakness, they do not descend through negligence into the squalor of misery.

3. For it is itself a form of calamity to endure the necessities of nature through the weakness of corruptible flesh. He desired to escape the necessities of the present life who said: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV, 17). For he knew that the sins of pleasure often break forth on the occasion of necessities, and, lest he willingly admit anything illicit, he strove to have removed the very thing which, unwillingly, he endured at its root.

4. When most people seek clothing to cover their limbs, they desire not only what will cover them but also what will set them off; against the torpor of cold, not only what will protect them through its thickness but also what will delight them through its softness; not only what will soothe through its softness, but also what will entice the eyes through its color. Desiring, then, to be freed from such necessities, the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from my necessities.” For what is it other than to turn the cause of necessity into the use of pleasure, except to join the squalor of misery to one’s own calamity?

5. Often we fill the body with food lest, weakened, it fail; we weaken it through abstinence lest, filled, it weigh us down; we invigorate it with movement lest it decay through the inertia of stillness; but by setting it in place more quickly we bring it to rest, lest it succumb through its very activity; we cover it with this aid of clothing lest the cold destroy it. And we cast off whatever has been added [Al.: “whatever aids have been sought”], lest heat consume it. Meeting so many diverse needs, what are we doing except serving corruptibility, so that at least the multiplicity of services rendered may sustain the body which the anxiety of frail mutability burdens? (Gregory, *Moralia* IV, 34, no. 68.)

## CHAPTER VIII. On the elect who live well amid the turmoil of the reprobate

1. Most of us complain that not all who live with us are good. We do not wish to endure the evils of our neighbors. We decide that all ought already to be saints, while we do not wish to be what we must bear from our neighbors. But in this matter it is clearer than daylight that, when we refuse to bear the wicked, we show how much we ourselves still lack of goodness. For no one is perfectly good unless he is good even among the wicked. Blessed Job asserts this of himself, saying: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job XXX, 29). Hence the apostle Paul says to his disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Phil. II, 15) (Taio III, 15; Gregory I, *In Ezechielem*, hom. 9, no. 22).

2. Hence Peter, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, says: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the shameless conduct of the wicked; for that righteous man, living among those who from day to day tormented the soul of the righteous with wicked deeds, was righteous in sight and hearing” (II Peter II, 7). When we often complain about the lives of our neighbors, we desire to change our place and strive to choose as our dwelling a secluded life far away, plainly unaware that, if the Holy Spirit is absent, a place does not help. Lot, after all, was holy in Sodom, but sinned on the mountain. Since places do not fortify the mind, the first parent of the human race himself bears witness to this: he fell grievously even in paradise.

3. Yet all that we say about the earth is of less importance; for if a place could save, Satan would not have fallen from heaven. The Psalmist David, seeing that temptations exist everywhere in this world, sought a place to which he might flee, but without God he could not find a fortified place. Therefore he asked that God himself become his place, for whose sake he had sought a place, saying: “Be to me a God who protects me, and a fortified place, that you may save me” (Ps. XXX, 3). Just as it is a more serious fault not to be good among the good, so it is a matter of immense praise to be good even among the wicked.

## CHAPTER IX. On the elect’s suffering and compassion for their neighbors

1. Holy men, caught in the warfare of tribulations, at one and the same time endure those who strike them and persuade others. Against the former they raise the shield of patience; against the latter they hurl the darts of teaching. The elect rise to both modes of combat with marvelous skill in virtue, so that inwardly they teach wisely and outwardly courageously despise adversity. By teaching, they correct some; by enduring, they restrain others. The elect despise hostile assailants through patience, but have compassion on their weakened fellow citizens for their salvation. They resist the former lest they carry others away as well; they fear for the latter lest they utterly lose the life of righteousness (Taio III, 35; Gregory, *Moralia* III, 21, no. 39).

2. Let us consider how great a labor it was for the apostle Paul, at one and the same time, to endure adversity outside and protect the weak within. Outside he suffered battles, because he was torn by blows and bound in chains; within he endured fear, because he feared that his suffering might harm not himself but his disciples. In his own suffering the Apostle feared for the falls of others, lest, when the disciples saw him himself afflicted and beaten for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers. Hence he writes to them, saying: “Let no one be shaken by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (I Thess. III, 3).

3. O immense [Greek edition: “of immense”] inward compassion of the apostle Paul! He despises the sufferings he himself endures, and takes care that his disciples suffer no corrupt persuasion in their hearts. In himself he disregards wounds of the body; in others he heals wounds of the heart. When strong men stand in battle array, there they strike hostile breasts with darts; here, placing a shield behind them, they protect the weak, and thus keep watch on both sides with swift vigilance, so that they may pierce the bold before them and defend the frightened behind them from wounds.

## CHAPTER X. On discernment

1. The subtlety of discernment is a great mastery of discipline, so that every ruler may know how discreetly to spare the faults of those who offend and how piously to cut them away. Those who forgive sins in such a way that they do not correct them, or strike as though correcting in such a way that they do not forgive, do not possess the spirit of discernment. It is written in the book of Genesis: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. IV, 7, according to the Septuagint). An offering is made rightly when something is done with right intention; but it is not divided rightly if what is piously done is not also subtly discerned. To divide offerings rightly is to weigh all our good efforts through discernment. Therefore whoever neglects to do this sins even while offering rightly (Gregory II, *In Ezechielem*, hom. 9, no. 20; Taio III, 42; Gregory, *Moralia* III, 13).

2. Often, when we undertake something with good zeal but carelessly neglect to discern it, we do not know toward what end it is judged. Hence what is thought to be a cause of virtue sometimes becomes a charge of crime. We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good zeal; but we do not divide rightly if we postpone exercising discernment in a good work. He enters the narrow way who is carefully constrained in everything he does by the subtlety of discernment. For whoever expands himself with a secure mind according to his own will bars himself from access through the narrow gate. Holy Church perceives through discernment what temptations arise from individual causes and detects from above the wars of vices that are to come (Gregory I, *In Ezechielem*, hom. 2, no. 12; *Moralia* XXVIII, 11, no. 26).

## CHAPTER XI. On repentance

1. Every sinner ought to have a double groaning in repentance: namely, because he neither did the good that he ought to have done nor did he refrain from the evil that he ought not to have done. When we do not rise to good works, it is necessary that we mourn ourselves in two ways, because we have neither done what was right nor practiced what was wrong. Through blessed Moses, one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and another as a burnt offering (Lev. V, 7). A burnt offering is called something wholly consumed by fire. We therefore offer one turtledove for sin when we express our groaning over guilt; we make a burnt offering of the other when, for the good we have neglected [Al.: “neglect”], we burn with the fire of sorrow, utterly consuming ourselves (Taio III, 47; Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, 3, no. 4).

2. Blessed Job, advancing through scourges and disagreeing with himself in severe self-reproach, says: “Therefore I reproach myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job XII, 6). To do penance in dust and ashes is, after contemplating the highest Being, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ash. In sackcloth are shown the roughness and pricking of sins; in ashes, the dust of the dead. Therefore both are customarily applied to repentance, so that in the prickling of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the ash-dust consider what we have become through judgment. Let the vices that prick be considered in sackcloth. Let the just punishment of the vices that follows through the sentence of death be considered in ashes, because on account of the sin of the flesh the insults of the flesh arose.

3. Let a person see in the roughness of sackcloth what he did through pride; let him see in ashes how far he reached by sinning. The sinner is pricked, as by a kind of sackcloth, when he is broken in his mind by the sharp goads of reproaches [Al.: “rubbed raw”]. He does penance in ashes when he carefully considers what he was made through the just judgment arising from the first sin. “We turn day into darkness” (Job III, 4) when, strictly punishing ourselves, we torment through the lamentations of severe repentance the very enticements of wrongful pleasure. Therefore, we pursue with tears whatever we sinfully touch in our hearts through pleasure [Al.: “silently”]. The almighty Lord carefully considers our deeds, yet mercifully releases them to those who repent; he sees hardness in sinners, but by preceding grace softens it for repentance (Gregory, *Moralia* IV, 14, no. 26).

4. The Lord counts our faults when he turns us toward mourning each thing we have done; he mercifully releases them because, while we punish ourselves, he by no means judges them in the final examination, as Paul bears witness, saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI, 31). What we do outwardly, unless we wash it away through the intervention of repentance, is kept in the secret places of God’s judgments under a certain concealment, so that one day it may emerge from the seal [Al.: “sack”] of secrecy into the public judgment. But when we are worn down by the scourge of discipline for the evils we have done, and mourn them through repentance, it marks and heals our iniquity, because it neither leaves it here unpunished nor reserves it to be punished in the judgment (Gregory, *Moralia* XII, 17, no. 21).

5. Blessed Job, assuming the person of the human race, says: “You have sealed up my offenses as though in a sack” (Job XIV, 17). Our sins are sealed in a sack when we weigh continually, with an anxious heart, the evils we have done. For what is the human heart except the Lord’s sack, where, when we carefully consider how greatly we have sinned, we carry our sins as though sealed in the Lord’s sack? The merciful Creator releases for us the faults that we recognize by looking upon them and repenting. Rightly, after “You have sealed up my offenses as though in a sack,” it is said: “But you have healed my iniquity.” It is as though he openly said: “What you now seal, so that I may see it through repentance, you undoubtedly do in order that it may not be seen in retribution.”

## CHAPTER XII. On the confession of sins

1. It is a testimony of humility both to recognize one’s own iniquity and to disclose what has been recognized by confession in words. It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling [Greek edition: “by hiding”] and, having committed it, not to disclose it by confession but to defend it by denial, and, when convicted, to multiply it by defending it. From the fall of the first human being we derive these increases of wickedness, since from that fall we drew the very root of guilt. The first human being was summoned for this purpose: that he might erase through confession the sin he had committed by transgressing. He is asked where he was (Gen. III, 10), so that he might look upon the guilt he had perpetrated and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the face of his Creator (Taio III, 48; Gregory, *Moralia* XXII, 15, no. 30).

2. The signs of true confession are present if, when someone calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. It is written: “The righteous man is his own first accuser” (Prov. XVIII, 17). When someone confesses himself a sinner without anyone accusing him, he desires to appear not more a sinner but righteous. The truth of confession is proved when another reproves the evil we have done. If we proudly defend ourselves, it is clear that we were calling ourselves sinners falsely and from our own lips. We must take the greatest care both willingly to confess the evils we have done and not to deny them when others accuse us. It is a vice of pride that what one deigns to confess as though spontaneously, one disdains to have said about oneself by others. The confession of a sinner is a debtor’s pledge. A pledge is taken from a debtor when confession of sin has already been obtained from a sinner.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the kinds of dreams

1. We must recognize with the greatest care that dream images touch the mind in six ways. Sometimes dreams are generated by fullness of the stomach or by emptiness; sometimes by illusion; sometimes by thought together with illusion; sometimes by revelation; and sometimes by thought together with revelation. The first two we all know by experience. We find the four that follow in the pages of sacred Scripture. For if dreams were generally produced through illusion by the hidden enemy [perhaps: “were not produced”], the Wise Man would never have said: “Dreams have led many astray, and vain illusions” (Ecclus. XXXIV, 7), or certainly: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Lev. XIX, 26). By these words it is clearly shown how detestable are those things that are joined to divinations (Gregory, *Moralia* VIII, 4, no. 42; Taio IV, 7).

2. Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with illusion, Solomon would not have said: “Dreams follow upon many cares” (Eccles. V, 2). Unless dreams sometimes arose through the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen in a dream that he was destined to be preferred to his brothers (Gen. XXXVII, 7), nor would Truth have warned Mary’s husband in a dream to flee into Egypt after taking the child away (Matt. II, 13–14). Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, explaining Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would not have begun from the root of thought, saying: “You, O king, began to think in your bed what would happen after these things” (Dan. II, 29). Therefore he who reveals mysteries shows you what is to come.

3. A little later, therefore: “You saw, and behold, as it were one great statue; that statue was large and of lofty stature, standing before you,” and so forth. Thus Daniel, while reverently indicating both that the dream would be fulfilled and from what thought it arose, plainly shows that this is often generated from thought together with revelation. Since dreams vary according to so many kinds of causes, they ought to be believed with all the greater difficulty, since it is not readily clear from what impulse they come. Holy men distinguish, by a certain inner savor, among the voices or images of visions themselves, between illusions and revelations, so that they may know what they receive from a good spirit and what they suffer from an illusion [Al.: “an illusor”] (Gregory, *Dialogues* IV, 48).

4. If the mind is not cautious concerning dreams, it plunges itself into many vanities through the deceiving spirit, which sometimes customarily foretells many true things so that at the end it may be able to ensnare the soul through some single falsehood. Often the evil spirit, seeing those who are wakefully intent upon love of the present life [Al.: “intercepts”], promises prosperity even to them while they sleep; and those whom he observes to fear adversity he attacks more harshly with images of it in dreams, so that he may affect the undiscerning mind in various ways and confuse it, either lifting it up with hope or depressing it with fear (Gregory, *Moralia* VIII, 24, no. 43).

5. Often the ancient enemy also strives to affect the hearts of the saints with dreams, so that they may be diverted, at least for a time and a moment, from the purpose of firm thought, although they immediately shake their minds free from the illusions of imagination. But the ambushing enemy attacks them more severely while they sleep, since he cannot overcome them while they are awake. The heavenly dispensation kindly permits the enemy of the human race to act wickedly even through dreams, lest sleep itself should be entirely deprived of the reward of suffering in the hearts of the elect.

## CHAPTER XIV. On nocturnal illusions
