1. A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation through which something shameful is conceived in the heart by dark thought, although it is not completed by the body. The Law commands one polluted by a nocturnal dream to go outside the camp (Deut. XXIII, 10), because it is fitting that one who has been polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful, set the merit of his fault before his eyes, and despise himself in the estimation of the good (Taio IV, 8; Gregory, *Moralia* IX, 55, no. 84).

2. The Law commands one polluted by a nocturnal dream to return to the camp after sunset, having washed himself with water, because it is necessary that, when the heat of temptation has cooled, each person should again take confidence in fellowship with the good. He returns to the camp after washing with water when the sun has set who, after the lamentations of repentance, once the flame of illicit thought has cooled, is restored to partake of the benefits of the faithful [Al.: “to presume upon”]; so that he no longer considers himself far from the others, rejoicing that he has been cleansed through the death of his inward ardor.

## CHAPTER XV. On Satan’s manifold arguments

1. Through destructive arguments the ancient enemy raises up the powers of his cunning and corrupts the wavering hearts of mortals. Hence the divine voice says to blessed Job: “The sinews of his testicles are entangled” (Job XL, 12). His testicles are wicked suggestions, through which he burns in the corruption of the mind and begets the offspring of an evil deed in the defiled soul. The sinews of Behemoth’s testicles are entangled because the arguments of his suggestions are bound together with overwhelming force, so that they make many people sin in such a way that, if they perhaps seek to flee from sinning, they cannot escape without another snare of sin; they commit a fault while avoiding one, and cannot free themselves from one bond unless they consent to be bound by another (Taio IV, 9; Gregory, *Moralia* XXXII, 20, no. 35).

2. Sometimes someone abandons everything belonging to the world and seeks in every way to break his own wills, and desires to submit himself to another’s rule. But through insufficiently cautious inquiry he fails to discern whom he ought to have placed over himself in the Lord. Perhaps the person chosen without judgment, once he has begun to rule, forbids him to do what belongs to God and commands him to do what belongs to the world. The subordinate, therefore, weighing both the guilt of disobedience and the contagion of secular life, fears to obey and fears not to obey, lest by obeying he abandon God in the superior’s commands, or, by refusing to obey, despise God in the chosen superior.

3. This man, therefore, is plainly bound through the vice of his lack of discernment by the entangled sinews of Behemoth’s testicles, because whether he obeys or does not obey, he is bound in the guilt of transgression. He had been striving to break his own wills, and takes care to strengthen them even while disregarding his superior. He had resolved to abandon the world completely, and is compelled by another’s will to return to worldly cares. There is a certain argument that may usefully be employed to destroy Satan’s subtleties: when the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins, if no place or entrance for escape without sin is open at all, the lesser should always be chosen. For one who is shut in on every side by the circuit of walls so that he cannot flee throws himself into flight wherever he finds the shorter wall.

## CHAPTER XVI. On manifold vices

1. The ancient enemy attacks from every side with the wound of his temptation. Often, when gluttony is restrained so that lust may be subdued, the goad of vainglory strikes the mind. But if the body is not worn down by the affliction of abstinence, the flame of lust rises up against the mind. Often, while we strive to preserve frugality, we slip into stinginess. And often, while we give away what we possess lavishly, we are led into avarice, because we seek again to gather what we may give away. The cunning enemy suggests every sin, but by consenting to his suggestions and continually committing sins, we heap them up. Many people, while stirring up within themselves crowds of vices or carnal desires, trample their prostrate mind under the foot of miserable repetition (Taio IV, 10; Gregory, *Moralia* XIII, 16, no. 19; IV, 30, no. 57).

2. One submits himself to the rule of lust and forms before the eyes of his mind images of shameful rehearsals [Al.: “shameful perpetrations”]. Since the deed’s fulfillment is not granted, this is performed all the more frequently in the intention of thought. The perfection of pleasure is sought, and the mind, shaken beyond measure, anxious and blinded, searches here and there for an opportunity for the most wicked completion. Thus the mind suffers, as it were, a certain populace, ravaged by the insolent tumult of vices.

3. Another lays himself under the dominion of anger, and what does he enact in his heart except quarrels [Al. adds: “even”] that are not there? Such a person often does not see those who are present and contradicts those who are absent. Within himself he utters and receives insults; then he responds more harshly to those he has received; and when no opponent is present, he composes quarrels in his heart with loud shouts. He therefore endures a crowd within, pressed down by the heavy weight of inflamed thought.

[Col. 1165B] 4. Another gives himself over to the rule of avarice and, disdaining what is his own, covets what belongs to others. Often, unable to obtain what he covets, he spends his days in idleness and his nights in thought. He grows sluggish in useful work because he is wearied by illicit thought. He multiplies plans and spreads the bosom of his mind more widely through inventions of thought. Sometimes, overcome by desire for another’s property, the human mind already possesses, as it were, what it coveted and, driven by thought, brings it forward as though to a better appearance. But immediately it considers the plots of the envious and weighs what quarrel may be stirred up against it. It seeks what answer to give, and, although it holds no property at all, it is already fighting in defense of property. Therefore, although it has received nothing of what it coveted, it nevertheless already has in its heart the fruit of covetousness: the labor of quarrel. Thus it is heavily pressed as though by a crowd, ravaged by the tumult of avarice that provokes it.

5. Another is subjected to the tyranny of pride, and, while raising his wretched heart against human beings, lays it beneath the vice. He desires the insignia of lofty honors and seeks to be exalted by success; he paints for himself in his thoughts everything he desires to be. Already he presides, as it were, from a tribunal. Already he sees the services of subjects prepared for him. Already he appears to himself to tower above others. Already he inflicts evils upon some and repays others because they have inflicted them. Already, surrounded by ranks, he proceeds in his own mind into public view and sees by what services he is supported.

6. A person is subjected to vices when he wanders here and there in empty thought amid many phantasms. Some he tramples down; others he raises up. Already he satisfies hatred against those he has trampled down and receives favor from those he has raised up. What else, then, does one who impresses so many phantasms upon his heart see except, as it were, a dream while awake? While he endures all the causes of the things he invents, he plainly carries inwardly the crowds born from his desires. Often, when a person joins himself familiarly to vices, he is undoubtedly entangled in their causes; he often consents to illicit things and commits evils which he would not desire for their own sake, because of others that he has not abandoned.

## CHAPTER XVII. On certain vices that pretend to be virtues

1. Often vices pretend to be virtues. For stinginess frequently disguises itself under the name of frugality, while extravagance conceals itself under the designation of generosity. Often disordered leniency is thought to be compassion, and unbridled anger is considered the virtue of spiritual zeal. Often precipitous action is regarded as the effectiveness of speed, while slowness in acting is thought to be the counsel of gravity. It is necessary that every elect person distinguish virtues from vices with vigilant care, lest either stinginess occupy the heart and someone rejoice to appear frugal in his management, or, when something has been squandered lavishly, he boast of being generous, as though out of compassion; or, by sparing one whom he ought to have struck, he lead his subjects to eternal punishments; or, by striking savagely what has been done wrong, he himself commit a graver wrong; or, by arriving prematurely at what could have been done rightly and gravely, he cheapen it; or, by delaying the merit of a good action, he exchange it for something worse. Sometimes the unclean spirit presents the appearance of discernment to human eyes and leads them into the snares of lack of discernment. This happens when, at its prompting, we allow ourselves more food than discernment grants us on account of weakness, but indiscreetly stir up the wars of the flesh against ourselves (Taio IV, 11; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule* II, 9; *Moralia* III, 36, no. 68).

2. Sometimes the adversary of the human race displays the appearance of humility in order to remove the effect of usefulness [Al.: “the disposition of humility”]. This happens when he asserts that certain people are more weak and useless than they are in their own judgment, so that, when they consider themselves excessively unworthy, they fear to undertake works by which they could benefit their neighbors. The hand of compunction examines with great subtlety the various vices that the ancient enemy conceals under the appearance of virtues. For whoever truly grieves inwardly firmly foresees what ought to be done outwardly and what ought not to be done. If we bind ourselves with strong zeal against the incentives of vices, we even transform vices themselves into the service of virtue. Anger possesses some people, but when they subject it to reason, they turn it into the mystery of holy zeal. Pride raises up others, but when they incline their mind toward divine strength, they convert it into the voice of free authority for the defense of justice. Often, while someone is exalted by the purity of chastity, he is defiled by the filth of avarice; while he appears beautiful through the virtue of generosity, he is stained by the spots of lust; and while he is clothed in the beauty of chastity and generosity, he is darkened, as though by zeal for justice, through the savagery of cruelty.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That virtues arise from virtues and vices from vices

1. All virtues support one another before the Creator by reciprocal assistance, so that, because one virtue without another is either altogether nothing or very small, they may be upheld in turn by their union. All other good things are of no value if they are not approved in the eyes of the hidden Judge by the testimony of chastity. If humility abandons chastity, or chastity abandons humility, neither purity nor humility can benefit before the author of humility when chastity is proud or humility defiled. When we oppose the dominion of vices, we struggle against the iniquity that separates us from the Lord. When we resist habit violently, trample perverse desires, and claim for ourselves against them the right of our innate freedom, we withstand a most fierce conflict. When we strike down faults through repentance, wash away stains of filth through tears, and strongly resist vices (Taio IV, 12; Gregory, *Moralia* XXI, 3, no. 6).

## CHAPTER XIX. On harmful and harmless thoughts

1. Often from good works we learn how much purity of life we should construct in thought. Almost all good works proceed from thought, but there are certain sharp insights of thought that arise from action; for just as action is taken from the soul, so the mind is in turn instructed by action. It is very necessary that, when thought is led outside its proper use, the eye of the mind immediately be recalled to deeds already performed. Let each person weigh what he has done while subject, and he will recognize it at once. Often the merciful Lord washes away the sins of the heart more quickly because he does not permit them to pass into action; and evil conceived in thought is released more quickly the more strictly it is not bound by the completion of a deed. Through the distinguished Psalmist it is said: “I said: I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impieties of my heart” (Ps. XXXI, 5) (Taio IV, 13; Gregory, *Moralia* X, 15, no. 26; *Pastoral Rule* III, 29).

2. He who submitted the impiety of his heart indicated that he wished to declare the iniquities of his thoughts when he said: “I said, I will declare,” and immediately added: “And you forgave.” He shows how easy forgiveness is for thoughts: while he still promises himself that he will ask for something, he has obtained what he promised he would ask. Sometimes the sin is committed in thought alone, and because the fault does not reach action, repentance does not reach torment; but affliction conceived in thought cleanses the mind more quickly than iniquity merely conceived in thought pollutes it. The same Psalmist says: “My wounds stank and became corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6) (Gregory, *Moralia* IX, 55, no. 83).

3. Often what has already been erased from the Judge’s sight through the intervention of tears returns to the mind by thought. The conquered fault tries once more to creep into pleasure, and is revived in the old struggle by renewed assault, so that what it first did in the body it later turns over in the mind through importunate thought. Holy men, who are compelled by the necessity of office to serve in external ministries, always retreat diligently to the secrets of the heart, and there ascend to the summit of their innermost thought. They receive the law, as it were, on a mountain, when, setting aside the turmoil of temporal actions, they search out the sentence of the heavenly will at the summit of their contemplation. Often thoughts that arise pollute the hearts of the righteous and touch them with pleasure in temporal things. But when they are quickly driven away by the hand of sacred discernment, action is promptly taken lest the darkness of temptation cover the face of the heart, which it had already touched with illicit pleasure (Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, 20, no. 38; ibid. XVI, 42, no. 53).

4. Sometimes, during the very sacrifice of our prayer, importunate thoughts intrude and are able either to snatch away or stain what we offer to the Lord with tears within us. When the patriarch Abraham offered sacrifice at sunset, he endured birds settling upon it and diligently drove them away lest they snatch the sacrifice he had offered. So, while we offer a burnt offering to the Lord on the altar of the heart, let us guard it from unclean birds, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch what our mind hopes to offer to the Lord. When the power of divine assistance does not abandon our intention, the angel touches the sacrifice placed upon the rock as though with a staff.

5. From the rock fire comes forth, and consumes the hide and the flesh, because the Spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns our heart with such a flame of compunction that it consumes everything illicit within it, whether of action or of thought. Often the tumult of empty thoughts depresses the human mind: anger disturbs it, and when anger withdraws, foolish joy succeeds it; it is pressed by the goads of lust; through the heat of avarice it stretches far and wide to seize what belongs to the earth; sometimes pride lifts it up, but at other times disordered fear casts it down in weakness (Gregory, *Moralia* XI, 44, no. 60).

## CHAPTER XX. On pride and vainglory

1. The occasion of our destruction was the devil’s pride, while the means of our redemption was found in God’s humility. Pride has often been a seedbed of lust, because while the spirit raised people as though to a height, the flesh plunged them into the depths. Those who are first secretly lifted up through pride in the heart later fall publicly, because while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall through manifest lapses of the body. Thus the exalted deserved to be struck by a just retribution: because through pride they place themselves above human beings, through lust they sink to the likeness of beasts. We must beware, and guard the mind with every care from the swelling of pride. For our thoughts do not fly empty before the eyes of God, and no moments of time pass through the mind without a condition of retribution (Taio IV, 14; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule* III, 17; *Moralia* XXVI, 17, no. 28).

2. If a human being, through pride, despises his Creator, he rightly receives warfare even from the flesh subjected to him; hence that first disobedient one, as soon as he sinned through pride, covered his shameful parts. For because he had inflicted an insult upon God in spirit, he immediately encountered an insult from the flesh; and he who had refused to be subject to his Creator lost authority over the subjected flesh that he ruled, so that the confusion of his disobedience might rebound upon him, and, having been overcome, he might learn what he had lost by being elated. Whenever a good work is undertaken, it is necessary first to conquer its elation in the heart, lest, if it proceeds from the root of a wretched intention, it produce the bitter fruits of wickedness. When the pride of the heart [Col. 1168A] extends outward even to the body, it is first revealed through the eyes. For they, inflated with the swelling of arrogance, look down as though from a height; and the more they abase themselves, the more highly they exalt themselves (Gregory, *Moralia* XXIII, 11, no. 20).

3. The assertion of an unrestrained voice usually accompanies the proud. They speak, indeed, through the pride of elation and the foolishness of their speech, yet they believe that they speak through the freedom of uprightness. It must be considered that we often correct the proud more profitably if we mingle with their corrections certain encouragements of praise. For we must bring before them either other good qualities that are in them, or at least say what qualities they could possess if they do not have them; and then the faults that displease us should be cut away, once the good things that please them have first made their minds receptive to hearing. We first touch untamed horses with a gentle hand, so that afterward we may more fully subdue them with blows; and honey’s [Col. 1168B] sweetness is added to a bitter draught of medicines, lest the harsh bitterness of what will promote health be felt in the very act of tasting. While the taste is deceived by sweetness, the deadly liquid is emptied through bitterness (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 17).

4. In the case of certain proud people, the beginnings of an attack must be tempered with intermixed praise, so that, while they admit the favor they love, they may also receive the corrections they hate. For the proud, precisely because they desire to appear higher, become through their elation far removed from the true essence of God. They cannot stand, because they are separated from the solidity of the eternal essence; and they endure this first ruin because, through private glory, they fall within themselves. As the Psalmist says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Psalm 72:18), because inwardly they collapse in the same measure as they rise wrongly outwardly. Thus a stalk of straw is snatched upward by the breath of winds, but is quickly brought back down by its fall. The mind of the hypocrite is never free from thoughts of wickedness. Whether he seeks earthly things or praise, he envies others what [Col. 1168C] he longs to have attributed to himself, and strives to make others appear as perverse as he desires to be considered holier than everyone, so that, when others become contemptible, he himself may always appear more worthy of reverence. Hence it happens that, concerning the opinion of his neighbor, he stretches out the snares of his tongue, so that he alone may obtain the esteem of those whom he desires to please. Every proud person despises his own return, despairs of forgiveness, and exults in his guilt; yet inwardly he has fear as a witness to his wickedness. And although he may seem to act boldly outwardly in matters that appear insignificant, nevertheless he is compelled to tremble before himself concerning them (Gregory, *Moralia* XVII, 8, no. 10).

## CHAPTER XXI. On Greed

1. “Greed is the service of idols” (Ephesians 5:5), like a jar holding the mouth of the heart open in its pursuit of gain (Zechariah 5). Many are dull in understanding, but in the things they desire they are roused by the goads of greed. Those who are blind to seeing good things become watchful for carrying out evil when rewards stimulate them. The sin of greed is especially represented by lead, whose nature is heavy [Col. 1168D] in weight; for it makes the mind that it infects so heavy that it cannot in any way be lifted toward sublime things. It should be understood that Shinar is a very broad plain, in which, when the diversity of languages occurred, the tower called Babylon was built—the name referring to the very confusion of minds and languages. Nor is it without reason that the jar of greed is placed there, where Babylon—that is, confusion—is built. Since it is certain that all evils arise through greed and impiety, greed and impiety themselves are rightly said to dwell in confusion (Taio IV, 15; Gregory, *Moralia* XIV, 53, no. 63).

2. People inflamed by the heat of greed display greater works in the eyes of human beings precisely in proportion as they desire greater gifts to be offered them by human beings. Whoever is ambitious to increase his wealth neglects avoiding sin; and, caught like a bird, when he greedily desires the bait of earthly things, he does not recognize that he is being strangled by the snare of sin [Col. 1169A]. Those who hasten at the beginning to inherit [perhaps, “to make themselves heirs”] cut off their share in the final blessing, because, while they desire to multiply their possessions here through the wickedness of greed, there they become disinherited from the eternal patrimony. Desire often arises secretly in the mind, but it openly produces in action the stings of every sin. The distinguished preacher immediately points out these stings rising from this root when he says: “Some, desiring it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On Anger

1. Since anger often lashes the tranquility of the mind, it disturbs it as though torn apart and split, so that it is not in harmony with itself and loses the power of its inward likeness. Through anger wisdom is lost, so that one has no understanding at all of what should be done, or in what order. As it is written: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Ecclesiastes 7:10), because it withdraws the light of understanding when, by disturbing the mind, it throws it into confusion. Through anger life is lost, even if it seems to be preserved wisely, as it is written: “Anger [Col. 1169B] will destroy even the prudent” (Proverbs 15:1). For a confused mind does not accomplish even what it is capable of understanding wisely. Through anger justice is abandoned, as it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:20). For when the disturbed mind makes the judgment of its reason harsh, it considers everything that fury suggests to be right. Through anger the grace of social life is lost, as it is written: “Do not be a constant companion of an angry person, lest you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Proverbs 22:24–25). For one who does not restrain himself by human reason must necessarily live alone like a beast (Taio IV, 16; Gregory, *Moralia* V, 45, no. 78).

2. Through anger concord is broken, as it is written: “An impetuous man produces quarrels, and an angry man pours out sins” (Proverbs 15:18). The angry person pours out sins because he makes even bad people whom he rashly provokes to discord worse. Through anger the light of truth is lost, as it is written: “Let not the sun go down [Col. 1169C] upon your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). For when anger casts the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God conceals from it the ray of his knowledge. Through anger the splendor of the Holy Spirit is excluded, as it is written according to the old translation: “Upon whom does my spirit rest, unless upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2). When he said “humble,” he immediately added “quiet.” For if it removes the tranquility of the mind, it closes the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. When the Holy Spirit withdraws, the mind, emptied by anger, is quickly driven into open madness and is scattered outward as far as the surface from the innermost foundation of its thoughts. For the heart, inflamed by the goads of its anger, throbs; the body trembles; the tongue stammers; the face burns; the eyes become fierce; and familiar people are scarcely recognized. The mouth forms a cry, but the mind does not know what it is saying.

3. This person, therefore, is not far from those seized by madness, since he is not conscious of his own action. Sometimes a person [Col. 1169D] does not raise his hands in anger, but turns his tongue into a dart of cursing. He asks in prayer for the death of his brother and desires God to carry out what the perverse human being either fears or is ashamed to do himself; and so he commits murder by wish and voice even when he refrains from injuring his neighbor with his hands. Sometimes anger, with the mind disturbed, imposes silence as though by judgment; and what it does not express outwardly through the tongue burns more fiercely within. Thus an angry person withdraws his conversation from his neighbor and, by saying nothing, declares how estranged he is. Sometimes, however, the severity of silence is practiced as an exercise of discipline, provided that the form of discretion is carefully preserved inwardly.

It should be understood that anger kindles some people more quickly and abandons them more easily. It moves others slowly, but holds them longer. Often the fires kindled by anger, not unlike those that are heavier and harder, take hold slowly, yet, once kindled, are extinguished with greater difficulty; and because they [Col. 1170A] rouse themselves more slowly to harshness, they preserve the fire of their fury longer. Most people—and this is worse—both take in the flames of anger more quickly and lay them aside more slowly. Others are slow to take anger upon themselves and quick to lose it. In these four ways, the attentive reader will clearly recognize that, in approaching the good of tranquility, the last comes nearer than the first, while in evil the third surpasses the second.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How Anger Should Be Restrained

1. Anger, once it has taken possession of the mind, becomes unaccustomed to it in two ways. The first is that the watchful mind, before beginning any action, should set before itself all the insults it may have to endure, so that, considering the reproaches of its Redeemer, it may prepare itself for adversities. It receives these adversities coming toward it with all the greater strength the more cautiously it has armed itself through foreknowledge. Whoever is caught unprepared by adversity is found, as it were, sleeping before an enemy; and the enemy kills him more quickly because he encounters no resistance [Variant: “pierces him”]. But whoever anticipates impending evils through [Col. 1170B] vigilance and so keeps watch through the night awaits hostile attacks like someone awake in ambush; and from the very point at which he was thought to have been caught completely unaware, he girds himself powerfully for victory. The mind should carefully meditate upon all adversities before the beginning of its action, so that, always thinking of them and always protected against them by the breastplate of patience, it may wisely overcome whatever comes, and consider whatever does not come a gain. The second method of preserving gentleness is that, when we observe the excesses of others, we should think of our own sins by which we have exceeded in relation to others (Taio IV, 17; Gregory, *Moralia* V, 45, no. 81).

2. Consideration of our own weakness excuses the faults of others for us. For one patiently tolerates an injury inflicted upon him who devoutly remembers that perhaps he still has something in which he himself ought to be tolerated. As fire is extinguished by water, so fury is extinguished when, as anger rises in the mind, each person recalls his own fault; for one is ashamed not to pardon sins who remembers that he has often sinned against God or neighbor in matters requiring pardon [Col. 1170C]. It should carefully be understood that one kind of anger is aroused by impatience, and another is formed by zeal. The former arises from vice, the latter from virtue. If no anger arose from virtue, Phinehas would not have appeased the assault of divine retribution with the sword. Because Eli did not possess this anger, he aroused against himself the movement of heavenly vengeance that could not be appeased. For in proportion as he was lukewarm toward the faults of his subjects, the anger of the strict eternal Ruler burned against him. “Be angry,” says the Psalmist, “and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5).

3. Those who want us to be angry only with ourselves, and not also with neighbors who are sinning, do not understand this correctly. For we are commanded to love our neighbors in such a way that, when they err, we become angry with them as we do with our own vices. Hence Solomon says: “Anger is better than laughter” (Ecclesiastes 7:4), because the face’s sadness corrects the mind of the sinner. The same Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm 6:8). Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind. Anger arising from zeal, however, troubles it, because when someone is shaken even by an emulation [Col. 1170D] of uprightness, the contemplation that can be perceived only by a tranquil heart is disrupted. In time, this same right emulation of zeal, through gentleness, opens the eye of the mind more widely in eternal tranquility; meanwhile it closes that eye through agitation. From the very point at which the mind is troubled so that it cannot see, it advances toward seeing more truly and clearly.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Envy

1. We can envy only those whom we consider better than ourselves in some respect. Thus the person killed by envy is a little one, because he himself bears witness that he is smaller than the one whose envy torments him. The person killed by spite is a little one, because, unless he were inferior, he would not grieve over another’s good. It must be understood with the greatest care that, although poison is infused into the human heart through every vice that is committed, in this wickedness the serpent shakes all its inward parts and spews forth the pestilence of evil to be impressed upon it. Concerning this it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24). For when the corruption of spite has overcome [Col. 1171A] and corrupted the heart, the outward features themselves also reveal how severely madness goads the mind. Through envy the complexion is affected with pallor, and the eyes are cast down. The mind is inflamed, while the limbs grow cold. There is madness in the thoughts and gnashing in the teeth. And when envy, increasing, is hidden in the heart’s recesses, hatred darkens the conscience with blind pain [Variant: “pierces the conscience”]; and the wound enclosed within allows no joy in one’s own possessions. Because its own punishment satisfies the wasting mind, while another’s happiness torments it, the more the true structure of another’s work is raised on high, the more deeply the foundation of the envious mind is undermined, so that, in proportion as others prepare themselves for better things, it itself falls more disastrously. In that collapse, moreover, even what seemed to have risen through perfect accomplishment in other actions is destroyed. For when envy has wasted the mind, it consumes all the good deeds it finds (Taio IV, 18; Gregory, *Moralia* V, 46, no. 84).

2. Through the most wise Solomon it is said: “A sound heart [Col. 1171B] is the life of the flesh; envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Proverbs 14:30). For what is signified by flesh except certain weak and tender things, and what by bones except strong deeds? Often it happens that some people appear weak in certain actions while possessing genuine innocence of heart. Others already perform certain deeds that appear strong before human eyes, yet inwardly waste away through the pestilence of envy toward the good of others. It is therefore rightly said: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh,” because if innocence of mind is guarded, even outward weaknesses are eventually strengthened. And rightly it follows: “Envy is the rottenness of the bones,” because through the vice of spite even strong deeds of virtue perish before the eyes of God. For the rotting of bones means that even certain strong deeds are destroyed through envy.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Suppressing Envy

1. It is difficult for someone not to envy another what that other desires to obtain, because whatever temporal thing is possessed becomes less for individuals in proportion as it is divided among many [Col. 1171C]. Therefore spite torments the mind of the one who desires, because the thing he seeks either, by being received by another, takes it away from him entirely or reduces its quantity. Whoever desires to be completely free from the pestilence of spite should love the inheritance that the number of co-heirs does not diminish. It appears all the more abundant in proportion as the multitude of those receiving it expands. The diminution of spite is an effect arising from inward sweetness, and its complete death is the perfect love of eternity. When a person is perfectly carried away into the love of eternity, he is also completely established in love of his neighbor without any envy. For when he desires nothing earthly, there is nothing that opposes his love toward his neighbor (Taio IV, 19; Gregory, *Moralia* V, 46, no. 86).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Malice

1. In the Gospel the Truth says: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do also for them” (Matthew 7:12). Through these two commandments of the two Testaments, malice is restrained by one and kindness extended by the other, so that, by not doing what one does not wish to suffer, each person ceases from inflicting [Col. 1171D] harm. The greatest care must be taken that each person show the bold a gentleness of patience, that he display the grace of kindness toward those languishing in malice [Variant: “bestow it upon them”], that he fortify the discordant with peace, and that he equip those already in agreement for the desire of true peace. The worst heart wastes away from its own malice, not that of another. As it is written: “Jealousy has seized an uninstructed people, and now fire consumes the adversaries” (Isaiah 26:11). Just as the fire of love lifts up the mind, so the fire of malice entangles it. For the Holy Spirit lifted up the heart it filled toward love, whereas the heat of malice always bends it toward lower things. The wicked are not only tormented afterward by fire in punishment; even now they are burned by spite, because those who will later be punished by the penalty of retribution now afflict themselves with the torment of malice (Taio IV, 20; Gregory, *Moralia* X, 6, no. 46; *Homilies on Ezekiel* I, homily 2, no. 12).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Discord

1. Those who are discordant must be admonished that, however greatly they may excel in virtues, they can in no way become spiritual [Col. 1172A] if they neglect to be united with their neighbors through concord. One does not reach the single hope of the calling if one does not run toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors. Often some people, in proportion as they receive certain special gifts, lose through pride the gift of concord, which is greater. Thus, if someone perhaps subdues his flesh more than others through restraint of appetite, he may despise in abstinence those whom he surpasses, refusing to be in agreement with them. Whoever separates abstinence from concord should consider what the Psalmist admonishes. He says: “Praise him with tambourine and choir” (Psalm 149:3). In the tambourine, dry skin resounds when struck; in the choir, voices are harmonized through fellowship. Therefore whoever afflicts his body, if he abandons concord, praises God with the tambourine but does not praise him in the choir.

Often greater knowledge lifts certain people up and separates them from the fellowship of others; and the more they know, the more foolishly they depart from the virtue of concord. The better anyone knows, the worse he sins if he abandons concord [Col. 1172B]. And therefore he will deservedly receive punishment without excuse, because, had he wished, he could prudently have avoided sin. Those who disagree must be admonished to understand that they offer God no sacrifice of good work for as long as they are at variance with the love of their neighbors (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 22; Taio IV, 21).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Hatred

1. If we remain silent about the correction of people because we fear that hatred will rise against us, then without doubt we are seeking not God’s gain but our own. It is necessary for us sometimes to tolerate hateful people silently as what they are, so that by living among us they may learn what they are not. We must take the greatest care lest loquacity drag the tongue beyond measure and extend it into the wantonness of slander, lest malice arouse hatred and incline the mouth toward the dart of cursing. In the Gospel the Truth says: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do also for them” (Matthew 7:12). It is as though he were saying openly: “What you hate being done to you by another, see that you do not do to another through hatred” (Tobit 4:16). It must be carefully understood that sometimes [Col. 1172C], when wicked people are reproved, they become worse and pursue us with great hatred. Therefore we spare them, and not ourselves, if we cease reproving them out of love for them (Taio IV, 22; Gregory, *Moralia* XX, 21, no. 47).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Desire of the Eyes

1. Whoever carelessly looks outward through the windows of the body often falls into the pleasure of sin, even unwillingly, and, bound by desire, begins to want what he did not want. The rash soul, because it did not foresee beforehand lest it see what it might desire, afterward begins blindly to desire what it has seen. Hence the prophet’s mind, which had often been lifted up and present among inward mysteries, because it looked carelessly upon another woman, was afterward darkened and unlawfully united itself to her (2 Samuel 11:2). The holy man, because he presides over the senses of the body that he has received as over subordinate ministers, like a most equitable judge, sees faults before they arrive and, like one lying in wait for death [Variant: “the enemy”], closes [Col. 1172D] the windows of the body, saying: “I have made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think upon a virgin” (Job 31:1). That is, he would not first carelessly look upon what afterward he might love against his will. Once the appearance of a form has been fastened to the heart through the eyes, it is scarcely loosened by the hand of a great struggle (Taio IV, 23; Gregory, *Moralia* XXI, 2, no. 4).

2. Therefore, lest we turn over slippery things in our thoughts, we must take precautions. One ought not to look upon what one is not permitted to desire, so that the mind may be kept pure in thought. The eyes must be lowered from the wantonness of their pleasure, like robbers leading one to guilt. For Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree unless she had first looked upon it carelessly. It is written: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, and beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to look upon; she took of its fruit and ate” (Genesis 3:6). We must carefully consider with what restraint we ought to restrict our sight in relation to forbidden things, we who live under mortality, since even Eve, the mother of the living, came through her eyes to death [Col. 1173A]. In the voice of Judea, which, desiring what it saw outwardly, had lost the good things within, the prophet says: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lamentations 3:51). For by desiring visible things she lost invisible virtues. Because she lost the inward fruit through outward sight, she suffered the plunder of her heart through the eye of the body.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Desire of Gluttony

1. It must be understood that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the time of need. Sometimes it does not anticipate the proper time, but seeks more sumptuous foods. Sometimes it demands that whatever foods are to be eaten be prepared with excessive care. Sometimes it accords with both the quality of the food and the proper time, but in the very quantity consumed exceeds the measure of refreshment. Sometimes what it desires is even more humble, yet it sins more seriously through the very heat of its boundless desire. We can show the stages of these vices more clearly if we establish them through evident examples [Col. 1173B].

Jonathan incurred the sentence of death from his father’s mouth (1 Samuel 14:27), because he anticipated the appointed time for eating by tasting honey. The people led out of Egypt perished in the wilderness (Numbers 21:5), because, despising manna, they asked for meat, which they considered more sumptuous. The first fault of the sons of Eli arose (1 Samuel 2:12) because, at their demand, the priest’s servant was unwilling to receive the meat from the sacrifice cooked according to the ancient custom, but sought it raw, so that he might prepare it with greater care [the printed text reads *de isacrificio*, evidently for *de sacrificio*] (Taio IV, 24; Gregory, *Moralia* XXX, 18, no. 60).

2. When it is said to Jerusalem: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance” (Ezekiel 16:49), it is openly shown that she lost salvation for this reason: with the vice of pride, she exceeded the measure of moderate refreshment. Esau lost the glory of the firstborn because, in the great heat of desire, he coveted a cheap food, namely lentils. By preferring them to his birthright when he sold it, he showed the intensity of his longing for them. For it is not food but appetite that is at fault. Thus we often consume more sumptuous [Col. 1173C] foods without guilt, while we taste humbler foods with a guilty conscience. Esau lost his primacy by eating lentils, while Elijah preserved the strength of his body [Variant: “spirit”] in the wilderness by eating meat (1 Kings 17:6). Often the fault of the first parent is committed even when humble and cheap things are consumed. For it was not Adam alone who received the command of prohibition, that he might abstain from the forbidden fruit (Genesis 3:6). When God indicates that certain foods are contrary to our health, he recalls us from them as though by a sentence; and when, desiring them, we touch harmful things, what else are we tasting but forbidden things?

3. We should eat those things that the necessity of nature requires, not those that the appetite for eating suggests, lest, if this distinction is not observed carefully enough, one plunge oneself into the abyss of unlawful desire. If immoderate talkativeness did not carry away those devoted to gluttony, the rich man who is said to have feasted splendidly every day would not burn so grievously in his tongue. For he says: “Father Abraham [Col. 1173D], have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24). These words show that he had sinned more frequently with his tongue by feasting every day, since, burning all over, he especially desired to be cooled in his tongue.

Often gluttony leads all the way to lust, because when the belly is distended by satiety, the goads of desire are aroused. The prophet testifies that lust follows those devoted to gluttony. While narrating outward things, he announces inward ones, saying: “The prince of cooks destroyed Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 39:13, according to the Hebrew and the Septuagint). For the prince of cooks is the belly, which the cooks serve with great care so that it may be filled delectably with foods. The walls of Jerusalem are the virtues of the soul, lifted toward the desire for heavenly peace. Therefore the prince of cooks casts down the walls of Jerusalem, because when the belly is distended by gluttony, the virtues of the soul are destroyed through lust (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 19).

[Col. 1174A]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Excessive Speech

1. Those who devote themselves to excessive speech must watch carefully and see from how great a state of uprightness they decline while they slip away through their many words [perhaps, “through wordiness”]. The human mind, enclosed like water, gathers itself toward the heights, because it returns there from which it descended. When released, it is wasted because it uselessly spreads itself through low places. Whoever is scattered by superfluous words from the discipline of his silence is led outside himself through as many channels. Hence the mind is not sufficient to return inwardly to the knowledge of itself, because, scattered through excessive speech, it excludes itself from the secrecy of inward contemplation. It exposes itself completely to the wounds of the enemy lying in wait, because it does not enclose itself within any defensive guard.

It is written in Proverbs: “As a city lying open and without the circuit of walls, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Proverbs 25:28). For the city of the mind that has no wall of silence lies open to the enemy’s arrows; and when it casts itself outside itself through words, it displays itself openly to its adversary. The enemy overcomes it with as little effort as possible because the city [Col. 1174B] being conquered fights against itself through excessive speech.

Often the indolent mind is driven into a pit of downfall through certain stages. When we neglect to avoid idle words, we reach harmful ones: first it becomes pleasant to speak about others, then the life of those about whom one speaks is wounded by detraction, and finally the tongue bursts out into open insults. For whoever serves excessive speech cannot in any way maintain the uprightness of justice. The Prophet testifies to this when he says: “The talkative man shall not be established upon the earth” (Psalm 139:12). Hence Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10:19). Wicked people are as flighty in understanding as they are rash in speech; they neglect to consider and restrain what they are saying, and whatever a frivolous conscience conceives, a still more frivolous tongue immediately speaks (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 14; Taio IV, 26; Gregory, *ibid.* and *Moralia* VII, 37, nos. 57–58; V, 13, no. 30).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Taciturnity

1. The tongue must be restrained with discretion [Col. 1174C], not bound inseparably. For it is written: “The wise person will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclesiasticus 20:7), so that, when he considers the time opportune, he may set aside the discipline of silence and devote himself through speech to what is useful. Concerning the discipline of silence and speech Solomon says: “A time for keeping silence, and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). The times of alternation must be weighed with discretion, lest either, when the tongue ought to be restrained, it flow uselessly through words, or, when it can speak usefully, it restrain itself sluggishly.

Considering how useful taciturnity is, the Prophet says: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psalm 140:3). He did not ask that a wall be placed around his lips, but a door, which can be opened and closed. Therefore we too must carefully discern how a discreet mouth should open its voice at the appropriate time and, again at the appropriate time, be closed by taciturnity. Those who are excessively silent should earnestly take care to consider not only what kind of people they should show themselves outwardly, but also what kind they ought to display themselves inwardly [Col. 1174D], so that they may fear hidden judgment arising from their thoughts more than reproach from their neighbors arising from their words (Taio III, 43; Gregory, *Moralia* VII, 37, no. 61; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 14).

2. Those who are excessively silent must be informed that, while they carelessly flee certain vices, they become secretly entangled in worse ones. Often, because they restrain their tongue too immoderately, they tolerate more serious excessive speech in their heart, so that thoughts boil all the more in the mind as violent custody constricts them through indiscreet silence. Often it happens that the mind of one who is excessively silent presses down the tongue, elevates the mind, and, while giving no consideration at all to its own wickedness, accuses everyone before itself all the more freely the more secretly it does so.

Often those who are excessively silent, when they suffer some injustice, proceed into sharper pain precisely because they do not speak about what they endure. For if the tongue were calmly to express the troubles inflicted, the pain would flow out from the conscience. Closed wounds cause greater torment [Col. 1175A]; when the corruption boiling within is expelled, the pain is opened toward healing. Those who are silent beyond what is appropriate must know that, amid the troubles they endure, while they hold back their tongue, they intensify the force of their pain.

They must be admonished that, if they love their neighbors as themselves, they should by no means remain silent about matters for which they rightly rebuke them. The medicine of the voice contributes to the well-being of both: the wrongful action is restrained in the one who inflicts it, and the heat of pain is moderated through an opened wound in the one who suffers it. Those who observe the evils of their neighbors and nevertheless restrain their tongue in silence are like people who, after seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine; and they become the authors of death precisely because they refuse to cure the poison those wounds contain.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Perverse Speech

1. Just as perfect people ought not to flee from perverse neighbors, because they often draw them toward uprightness and are themselves never drawn toward perversity, so all who are weak ought to avoid the company of the wicked, lest they take pleasure [Col. 1175B] in imitating the evils they frequently see but cannot correct. Just as bad air, drawn in through constant breathing, infects the body, so perverse speech, continually increased, infects the mind of the weak, so that it wastes away in delight at wicked conduct and in the iniquity of constant conversation. Hence Paul says: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33) (Taio IV, 27; Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel* I, homily 9, no. 23).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Lust

1. The evil of lust is committed either in thought or in deed. For our cunning adversary, when driven away from the execution of an act, attempts to pollute secret thoughts. Whoever, lifted up by the successes of this world and enticed by the joy of his heart, feels himself tempted by the goads of lust should recall Joseph’s example and preserve himself in the stronghold of chastity. When slippery pleasure tempts a person amid prosperity, these very prosperities should be set against the sting of temptation, so that we may be ashamed to commit what is wrong precisely because we remember that we have received from God gratuitous and good gifts.

The prophet David suddenly fell through lust when, walking on the roof [Col. 1175C], he desired another man’s wife, took her, and killed her husband at the cost of his army (2 Samuel 11:4). He fell through a sudden catastrophe when that mind, accustomed to heavenly mysteries, was conquered by an unexpected temptation and subjected to the most monstrous disgrace. It was as though a stone had been moved from its place when the prophet’s mind, excluded from the mysteries of prophecy, turned to thinking about shameful things.

That formerly most wise Solomon, overcome by an excess of lust, through the immoderate use and constant presence of women, was led so far that he built a temple for idols. He who had previously built a temple for God, having been subjected even to faithlessness through the constant practice of lust, did not fear to build temples for idols (1 Kings 11:7). Thus it came about that, from the constant wantonness of the flesh, he reached even the faithlessness of the mind, because, as the infusion of sin gradually stole upon him, the soil of his heart slipped away toward destruction.

To lovers of the pleasures of the flesh it is said: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:5), that is, “fornication [Col. 1175D], uncleanness, lust, and evil desire” (Taio IV, 30; Gregory, *Moralia* XXI, 2, no. 30; *Pastoral Rule* III, 27; *Moralia* XXX, 10, no. 38; XII, 18, no. 23; XXVI, 17; II, 27).

2. Often the poison of lust springs from the root of pride. The flesh then conquers when the spirit secretly swells with pride, because the soul fell through the origin of sin into the wantonness of beasts when, exalting itself in the manner of birds, it flew beyond where it ought. Sometimes prolonged continence is suddenly dissolved through the vice of pride; and often virginity preserved even into old age is defiled, because humility of heart is neglected, and the righteous Judge despises bodily integrity. At times he announces through manifest evil those whom previously he tolerated as reprobate in secret. Whoever suddenly loses a good long preserved had retained another evil within himself, from which he suddenly burst forth into another. Thus he was already alienated from almighty God even when he showed himself to cling to Him through bodily purity. For the human race to be tempted by sin is itself sin. Since, as long as we live, we are never wholly free from it, the teaching of preachers could not completely expel it; nevertheless, it removed its dominion from the dwelling of our heart, so that illicit desire, even if it often secretly inserts itself into our good thoughts like a thief, may at least not rule when it enters (Gregory, *Moralia* XXI, 3).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Torpor of the Soul

1. Often the human mind is struck while asleep to the care of its own vigilance, yet feels no pain, because just as it does not foresee the impending evil, so it does not recognize it after committing it. It is dragged along and feels nothing, because it is led through the allurements of vices, yet is not aroused to guard itself. Although each person may be weighed down by the sleep of torpor, so that he fails to guard himself, he nevertheless strives to remain awake for worldly concerns, so that he may always be intoxicated by pleasures. While he sleeps with regard to what he ought to watch over attentively, he desires to watch over what he could laudably have slept through.

Through Solomon in Proverbs it is said: “And you shall be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea, and like a drowsy helmsman who has lost the rudder” (Proverbs XXIII, 34). He sleeps in the midst of the sea who, placed amid such temptations, neglects to foresee the movements of the vices rushing upon him, like heaps of waters in an impending wave; and he loses the rudder like a helmsman when the mind loses the anxious care required to govern the ship of the body. It is written: “The lizard supports itself with its hands, and dwells in kings’ palaces” (Proverbs XXX, 28). Often birds, which wings lift for flight, remain in the thorn bushes; but the lizard, which has no wings for flight, holds fast to the building of the kingdom by supporting itself with its hands. For often the ingenious, while they grow torpid through negligence, remain in wicked actions; whereas the simple, whom no wing of ingenuity assists, are lifted by the virtue of their works to obtain the walls of the eternal kingdom (Taio IV, 3; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule* III, 31).

2. “The lizard supports itself with its hands and dwells in royal palaces,” because the simple person reaches by the intention of a righteous work the place to which the ingenious person scarcely ascends. A question arises: Why is the gift of understanding sometimes granted to the negligent, while the diligent person is hindered by the slowness of his intellect? The answer is given more quickly when Solomon immediately adds: “Nothing on earth is without cause” (Job V, 6). The slothful person often receives ingenuity so that the negligent may be punished more justly, because he scorns to know what he could have attained without labor. Conversely, the diligent person is sometimes weighed down by slowness of understanding so that he may find greater rewards in recompense, in proportion as he labors more greatly in the effort of discovery. Nothing, therefore, is without cause on earth, since slowness advances the diligent toward reward, while speed increases the punishment of the slothful. When the soul’s sloth is not kindled by suitable fervor, it is secretly slaughtered by torpor, while the desire for good things grows thoroughly strong (Gregory, *Moralia* VI, 11, no. 13; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 15).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Laziness

1. The lazy must be admonished lest, by postponing good deeds that ought to be done, they lose them; and lest, while unwilling to do at the proper time what they can do, they soon afterward be unable to do it when they wish. Often, while the lazy person neglects to do what is necessary, he places certain difficulties before himself; he fears certain things without due caution; and, while he seems to find something that he may supposedly fear justly, he shows that he grows torpid in idleness as though not unjustly. Solomon says to the lazy: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow; therefore he shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him” (Proverbs XX, 4). The lazy person does not plow because of the cold when, bound by slothful torpor, he evades doing the good things he ought to do; and, while he fears small evils in opposition, he neglects to perform great ones. The following is rightly added: “He shall beg in summer, and nothing shall be given him.” Whoever does not now sweat in good works will beg in summer, when the sun of judgment appears with greater heat, asking in vain for entry into the kingdom and receiving nothing.

The same Solomon says: “I passed by the field of a lazy man, and by the vineyard of a foolish man, and behold, it was all filled with nettles; thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Proverbs XXIV, 30). To pass by the field of a lazy man and the vineyard of a foolish man is to examine the life of anyone who is negligent and to consider his works. Nettles and thorns fill them, because in the hearts of the negligent there spring up the itching desires of earthly things and the pricks of vices. When the vigor of discipline is dissolved in the hearts of the reprobate because laziness dominates, all good works are held in contempt before their eyes, and they judge that whatever they see in the virtues of the elect is worthless (Taio IV, 32; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 15; *Moralia* XX, 25, no. 54).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Murmuring

1. When a perverse mind is corrected by reproach or urged toward good by the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse through the correction; and it is inflamed with the wickedness of murmuring by the very means through which it ought to have been restrained from wickedness. Whoever is struck on account of sin, unless he resists by murmuring, begins thereby to be just, in that he does not accuse the justice of the one striking him (Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel* I, homily 9, no. 32; Taio IV, 33).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Lying

1. The path of truth is entirely level, whereas the journey of lying is arduous, as it is written: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to commit iniquity” (Jeremiah IX, 5). Whoever, abandoning the truth, deliberately lies in order to deceive the minds of his hearers—what labor it is for him carefully to ensure that his very deception cannot be detected! He places before his eyes what those who know the truth might answer him, and with great deliberation considers how, through arguments of falsehood, he may overcome the proofs of truth.

Every lie is iniquity, and every iniquity is a lie, because whatever disagrees with truth certainly differs from righteousness. Sometimes it is worse to devise a lie than to speak one. For speaking is often the result of haste, whereas devising a lie is the product of deliberate wickedness. Who does not know how greatly guilt differs according to whether someone lies through haste or through deliberation? Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although sometimes a certain kind of lie is a lesser fault, if someone lies in order to provide a benefit. It is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul. You will destroy all who speak lies” (Wisdom I, 11; Psalm V, 7) (Taio IV, 34; Gregory, *Moralia* XII, 42, no. 47).

2. Perfect men also avoid this kind of lie with the greatest care, so that neither anyone’s life may be harmed through their deception, nor their own soul be injured while they strive to benefit another’s flesh, although we believe that even this kind of lie is very readily remitted as a sin. For if any fault is customarily cleansed by a subsequent pious deed, how much more easily is this one wiped away when piety itself, the mother of the good deed, accompanies it?

In the recompense of the Egyptian midwives it is understood what punishment the fault of lying deserves. The reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid to them in eternal life, was diverted into an earthly recompense because of the fault of lying mixed with it, so that in their lifetime they might receive the good things they had done to preserve life through a lie, and might no longer possess the reward they expected for their merit. Blessed Job says to his friends, who held an incorrect opinion: “Does God need your lie, so that you may speak deceitfully for him?” (Job XIII, 7). God does not need a lie, because Truth does not seek to be supported by the aid of falsehood (Gregory, *Moralia* XI, 25, no. 37).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Ways in Which Sin Is Committed

1. Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and brought to completion in action in four ways. In the heart it is committed through suggestion, delight, consent, and the audacity of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the audacity of self-defense through pride. Often guilt, which ought to have terrified the mind, elevates it; and what ought to be cast down it raises up, yet in raising it up it causes it to fall more grievously.

Thus the ancient enemy shattered the uprightness of the first human being with these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve delighted; Adam consented; and, when questioned, he refused through audacity to confess his guilt. What happened in our first parent is known to happen daily in the human race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evil to human hearts. Eve delighted, because the carnal sense immediately subjects itself to delight at the serpent’s words. The man who had been placed over the woman gave his assent, because, while the flesh is carried away into delight, the spirit too, weakened in its uprightness, is bent down (Taio IV, 35; Gregory, *Moralia* IV, 27, no. 49).

2. Just as sin is committed in the heart in four ways—namely, by suggestion, delight, consent, and the audacity of self-defense—so sin is also brought to completion in action in four ways. First, the hidden fault is committed; afterward the guilt is openly revealed before human eyes without shame; then it is brought into habitual practice; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.

In our first parent we learned that the wickedness of every fault is committed in three ways: by suggestion, delight, and consent. The first is committed through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. The plotter suggests what is wrong; the flesh submits itself to delight; and finally the spirit, overcome by delight, consents. Through the devil’s suggestion we sometimes recognize sin; through delight we are conquered; through consent we are also bound. Hence we must cry out with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?”—so that we may hear the consolation that follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII, 24).

Very often one and the same sin is both punishment and the cause of sin. We can show this more clearly if we bring the matters themselves into view. Unrestrained gluttony of the belly stimulates the fullness of the flesh into the heat of lust. Once committed, lust is often concealed by perjury or homicide, lest it be punished by the vengeance of human laws. Blessed Job, designating the type of sinners within the Church, says: “He has struck me with wound upon wound” (Job XVI, 14). Holy Church is struck in her infirm members with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is intensified more grievously. The person whom avarice drives to robbery is led by robbery to deceit, so that the committed fault may also be defended by falsehood. What is such a person except one struck by wound upon wound? (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 29; *Moralia* XIII, 17, no. 20).

## CHAPTER XL. On the Eight Principal Vices and How to Exhort Minds Possessed by Them

1. There are eight principal vices that assail the human soul. Observing their suggestions carefully, the outstanding teacher Gregory explains the saying spoken by the Lord to blessed Job, where it says: “The exhortations of leaders and the howling of an army.” The vices that tempt us, which wage invisible warfare against us, serve the pride that reigns over them. Others follow in the manner of an army. For not all faults corrupt us by an equal approach; rather, when the greater and fewer ones anticipate the neglected mind, the lesser and innumerable ones pour upon it in a troop. When pride itself, the queen of vices, has almost captured the conquered heart, it immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as to its commanders, to be devastated. The army follows these commanders, because from them, without doubt, arise the troublesome multitudes of vices. We shall therefore show this more clearly by enumerating and setting forth, as far as we can, the commanders themselves and the army itself.

2. Pride is the root of all evil. Scripture bears witness to this when it says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” From this poisonous root its first offspring—namely, the seven principal vices—spring forth: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we had been taken captive by these seven vices of pride, He came to the spiritual battle of liberation filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

Each of these has its own army against us. From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptions of novelty. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, and rejoicing at a neighbor’s adversity, while distress arises at his prosperity. From anger proceed quarrels, homicides, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, torpor regarding the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward illicit things. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, acts of violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony are propagated foolish mirth, buffoonery, impurity, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding regarding what must be understood. From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and dread—or despair—of the future.

[Col. 1179B] 3. Since, then, the seven principal vices produce such a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they drag along with them a troop of the army that follows. Of these seven, five are spiritual and two are carnal. Each is joined to the others by such kinship that one can be produced only from another.

The first offspring of pride is vainglory. When it corrupts the oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy, because, while it desires the power of a celebrated name, it wastes away lest someone else be able to obtain it. Envy likewise generates anger, because the more deeply the soul is wounded by an inward injury, the more it loses the calmness of gentleness; and because a suffering limb seems to be touched, the mind feels the action being undertaken as though it were pressed more heavily. From anger, sadness arises, because the disturbed mind confounds itself by directing toward something else what it agitates disorderly; and when it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing remains to it except the sorrow that follows from disturbance. Sadness is also transferred into avarice, because when the confused heart has inwardly lost the good of joy within itself, it seeks outside itself something by which it may be consoled; and it desires to acquire external goods all the more because it has no joy to which it can turn inwardly.

4. Two carnal vices remain—namely, gluttony and lust—but it is clear to all that lust arises from gluttony, since, in the arrangement of the limbs, the genitals appear to be supported by the belly. Thus, when one is improperly satisfied, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts.

The commanders are rightly said to exhort, and the army to howl, because the first vices insert themselves into the deceived mind as though beneath its tail; but the innumerable vices that follow, while dragging it toward every madness, confuse it as though with a bestial cry.

Vainglory usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “You ought to seek greater things, so that by whatever power you are able to surpass many, you may also be able to benefit more people” (Compare Appendix VII above). Envy likewise usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “In what respect are you inferior to this or that person? Why, then, are you not equal or superior to them? How much are they able to do that you are not able to do? Therefore, they ought not to be either superior or even equal to you.”

Anger likewise usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “What is being done against you cannot be endured with equanimity. Indeed, to tolerate these things patiently is a sin, because if one does not resist them with great exasperation, they will thereafter be heaped up against you without measure.”

Sadness likewise usually rouses the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “Why do you have anything over which to rejoice, when you bear so many evils from your neighbors? Consider with what grief those people must be regarded who are turned against you by such a quantity of gall and bitterness.”

5. Avarice likewise usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “It is entirely without fault that you desire to possess certain things, because you do not seek to increase your wealth but fear to be in want. Therefore, what another holds badly, you spend better.”

Gluttony likewise usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “God created all things clean for eating; and whoever refuses to be satisfied with food, what else does he do but oppose the gift that has been granted?”

Lust likewise usually exhorts the conquered heart as though from reason, saying: “Why do you not now expand yourself in your pleasure, since you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the time granted to you in desires, because you do not know how quickly it will pass. For if God did not wish human beings to mingle in the pleasure of intercourse, He would not have made male and female at the beginning of the human race.”

## CHAPTER XLI. On Patience

1. Solomon indicates the height at which the virtue of patience excels when he says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities” (Proverbs XVI, 32). Victory in capturing cities is the lesser, because what is conquered lies outside oneself. Greater is what is conquered through patience, because the soul itself is overcome [the Greek edition adds “by itself”] and subjects itself to itself when, through patience, it lays itself low in humble endurance.

The good earth produces fruit through patience, because whatever good things we do are worthless if we do not also tolerate the evils of our neighbors with equanimity. It is written: “Charity is patient” (I Corinthians XIII, 4). Therefore, when it is not patient, it is not charity. Through this vice of impatience the teaching that nourishes the virtues is also scattered.

“He who is patient,” he says, “is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities.” The patient person is rightly preferred to the conqueror of cities, because in that action the victor is a victor over other human beings, whereas in the gentleness of patience the soul is victorious over itself.

Solomon says: “A man’s instruction is known through patience” (Proverbs XIX, 11). Therefore, each person appears less learned in proportion as he appears less patient. For he cannot truly impart good teaching if, in his life, he does not know how to tolerate the evils of others with equanimity. The Lord showed that patience is the guardian of our condition, because He taught us that without it we do not possess ourselves, saying: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19) (Taio III, 26; Gregory, Homily 35, book II, on the Gospels, no. 5; *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 9; Homily 6, book II, on Ezekiel, no. 7).

2. The patient must be admonished not to grieve inwardly over what they bear outwardly with patience, lest they corrupt within themselves, by the plague of malice, the sacrifice of so great a virtue that they offer whole to the outside. The patient should be told to strive to love what they necessarily must tolerate, lest, if love does not follow patience, the virtue displayed be turned into the worse fault of hatred.

It often happens to the patient that, at the very time when they suffer adversity or hear insults, they are struck by no pain, and so display patience that they do not fail to preserve the innocence of their heart. But when they later recall to mind, after a short interval, the very things they endured, they inflame themselves with the fire of pain, seek arguments for revenge, and, reconsidering the gentleness they displayed while enduring, turn it into malice.

[Col. 1180D] 3. The patient must be admonished to fortify the heart after victory, to take care that the enemy, overcome in open battle, does not lie in ambush against the walls of the mind, and to fear an illness that may creep in later, lest the crafty enemy rejoice with greater exultation in the deception in proportion as he tramples upon the previously stiff necks of those who conquered him.

In our love of neighbor we must preserve both patience and kindness, because of this same love it is now said: “Charity is patient, it is kind” (I Corinthians XIII, 4): patient, namely, so as to bear with equanimity the evils inflicted by neighbors; kind, so as to bestow its own good things desirably upon neighbors.

True patience is to endure the evils of others with equanimity and not to be gnawed by any pain against the one who inflicts the evils. For whoever bears the evils of a neighbor while nevertheless grieving silently and seeking the time for a fitting repayment does not exhibit patience but only displays it. It is written: “Will the poor be forgotten forever? The patience of the poor will not perish forever” (Psalm IX, 19). However patient we may be in adversity or humble in prosperity, let us in no way seek present goods to be repaid to us in this life. Rather, through the labor of patience, let us hope for the goods of the life to come, so that the reward of our labor may begin when all labor has already completely ceased (Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel* II, homily 9, no. 2).

## CHAPTER XLII. On Humility

1. For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our humility; for this reason the invisible One appeared not only visible but also despised; for this reason He endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of derision, and the torments of suffering: so that, being humble, God might teach human beings not to be proud. How great is the virtue of humility [another reading adds “our”], and how sublime is the height for the sake of which alone the One who is immeasurably great became small even unto suffering, in order to teach it truly (Taio III, 28)!

2. Humility is the teacher of human beings and the mother of virtues. As Truth says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI, 29); for, while the humble abase themselves, they rise to the likeness of God.

The true signs of humility are for each person to recognize his own iniquity and to disclose what he has recognized by confessing it aloud. The humble must be shown how true is the excellence they hold by hope, how eternal are the things they seek, and how transitory are the things they despise.

3. The simple must be admonished to strive never to speak falsely, but to know that sometimes they should remain silent about the truth. For just as falsehood has always harmed the one who speaks it, so truths heard on certain occasions have harmed some people. The simple must be admonished that, just as they always usefully avoid deceit, so they should always usefully speak the truth.

Nothing is happier than a simple heart: because it displays innocence toward others, it fears nothing that it may suffer from others.
