Simplicity possesses, as it were, a certain stronghold of fortitude, and it does not suspect that it will suffer what it does not remember having done (Taio III, 28).

[Col. 1181C] ## CHAPTER XLIII. On Gentleness

1. Often the gentle suffer the torpor of laziness, which is near to them and, as it were, placed beside them; and through an excessive relaxation of leniency they soften the vigor of strictness beyond what is necessary. Frequently the gentle grow torpid through weariness of this relaxation, because a vice is secretly joined to their virtue.

They must therefore be admonished to flee what lies near them and to embrace the vigilance that sharpens the negligence of excessive kindness. No one is filled with the Holy Spirit who either abandons the fervor of zeal in the tranquility of gentleness or, conversely, loses the virtue of gentleness in the ardor of zeal (Taio III, 30; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 16).

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Obedience

1. It must be known above all that sometimes obedience is nothing if it contains something of one’s own, while at other times it is of little value if it contains nothing of one’s own. When the splendors of this world are commanded, when a position of superiority is ordered, the person who obeys in order to receive these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also longs for them from his own desire. For he does not direct himself under obedience who serves the desire of his own ambition in order to obtain the advantages and prosperity of this life.

When contempt for this world is commanded, when insults and reproaches are ordered, the person diminishes the merit of his obedience if he does not desire these things of his own accord, but descends unwillingly and reluctantly to what is despised in this life (Taio III, 31; Gregory, *Moralia* XXXV, 14, no. 30).

2. Sometimes obedience is led to its detriment when, in accepting the reproaches of this world, the mind is not accompanied on its own part by its own wishes. Obedience must possess something of its own in adversity, so that, conversely, it may be more genuine in prosperity, in proportion as the glory it receives from God in the present is completely separated from the mind.

It is written in Solomon’s book: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (Ecclesiastes IV, 17). Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifice another’s flesh is slain, whereas through obedience one’s own will is slain. Therefore, each person appeases God more quickly in proportion as, with the pride of his own will restrained before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself by the sword of the commandment. Disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the greatness of the virtue of obedience may be demonstrated.

3. Its praise is therefore better shown by contrast. If resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to acquiesce like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it anyone is proved faithless, even if he appears faithful.

Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? Yet the first human being, because he held to his own will and refused to do it, departed from the joy of paradise. But the Second, coming for the redemption of human beings, showed that He did the will of the Father and not His own, and taught us to remain within through the merit of obedience.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Shame

1. Gentle and modest exhortation sometimes reforms shamefaced minds toward a better life, because often it is enough for their conversion that a teacher at least gently recalls their evils to their memory. The Apostle Paul, an outstanding preacher, reproved the faults of the shamefaced as though sympathizing with them, saying: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that at last you have revived in your concern for me, as indeed you were concerned; but you had no opportunity” (Philippians IV, 10). Thus the outstanding teacher acted to heal the faults of the shamefaced with medicinal kindness, veiling their negligence by tempering it with gentler speech.

Just as shame is praiseworthy with regard to evil, so it is blameworthy with regard to good. To blush at evil is wisdom; to blush at good is folly. Hence it is written: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty” (Luke IX, 26). A certain wise man says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclesiasticus IV, 25). Whoever, ashamed, blushes while repenting of the evils he has done does not reach the freedom of life; but whoever is not ashamed to do good does not fall from the state of uprightness and does not move toward condemnation (Taio III, 32; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 7; *Homilies on Ezekiel* I, homily 10, no. 17).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Detraction

1. Those who feed upon detraction from another’s life are undoubtedly satisfied with what belongs to others, as it is written: “Do not eat with those who provide flesh for eating.” To provide flesh for eating is, in conversation of disparagement, to recount in turn the faults of one’s neighbors.

Solomon rightly says of detractors: “For those who linger over drinking and give contributions will be consumed, and they will be clothed in rags of sleep” (Proverbs XXIII, 20). They linger over drinking who intoxicate themselves with abuse of another’s life. To give contributions means to contribute words in a conversation of detraction, just as each person customarily contributes food from his portion for eating (Gregory, *Moralia* XIV, 37, no. 61; Taio III, 44).

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Hospitality and Almsgiving

1. It is exceedingly necessary for us to love brotherly hospitality and to cherish works of charity. Therefore the outstanding preacher, commending both to us, says: “Let brotherly charity remain among you, and do not forget hospitality” (Hebrews XIII, 1). We must consider how greatly hospitality rooted in compassion for a brother is worth, and how greatly the bowels of mercy unite us to almighty God. For we approach Him who is above all things from the place where, through compassion for our neighbor, we lower ourselves even beneath ourselves (Taio III, 50; Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels* II, homily 23, no. 2).

2. For our edification, it is not enough that the Redeemer of the human race declared that at the final judgment He would say: “As long as you did it to one of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew XXV, 42). He also had to show before the judgment that this is what He had said, in order to demonstrate that whoever now displays good works to the needy bestows them especially upon the One for whose love he has displayed them. Therefore, each person receives a greater reward in himself in proportion as he does not despise even the one who appears more deserving of contempt.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Various Forms of Giving

1. Whoever provides external possessions to a needy neighbor but does not guard his own life from wickedness gives his property to God and himself to sin. He offers the Author what is lesser and preserves for iniquity what is greater. Whenever we give alms after sin, we seem to pay a price for wicked acts. Hence the Prophet says of one who does not do these things: “He will not give his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm XLVIII, 8). The price of alms frees us from faults when we mourn and renounce the sins we have committed. For whoever both wishes always to sin and, as though always, to give alms gives in vain, because he does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices (Taio III, 34; Gregory, *Moralia* XIX, 25, no. 38; XII, 51).

2. The offering of alms cannot redeem a proud rich man, since the robbery committed at the same time by him does not permit his gift to rise before the eyes of God. Hence Eliphaz says: “Let him not believe, deceived by error, that he can be redeemed for any price” (Job XV, 31).

Often proud rich people, when they give alms, give them not out of desire for eternal life but in order to extend their temporal life. They believe that they can postpone death by their gifts [variant: donations], but they can by no means obtain from what they spend the ability to escape the appointed end.

In the Gospel Truth says: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew VI, 3). That is, the glory of the present life must in no way mingle with pious stewardship; the desire for praise must remain unaware of the work of uprightness (Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 20).

3. Often people give much to the poor, not because they love those same poor people, but because, if they did not give, they fear the anger of the heavenly Judge. If they did not fear God, they would not wish to give what they possess.

Those who mercifully give their possessions must be admonished not to exalt themselves in proud thought over those to whom they distribute earthly goods, and not to consider themselves better because they see that the others restrain themselves. Let those who mercifully distribute what they possess recognize that they have been appointed by the heavenly Lord as stewards of temporal resources, and let them give with humility in proportion as they understand that what they distribute belongs to another.

Lest they rejoice immoderately in the benefactions of their generosity, let them hear what is written: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; what we were obliged to do, we have not (sic) done’” (Luke XVII, 10).

4. And lest sadness corrupt generosity, let them hear again what is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Corinthians IX, 7). Lest those who give alms seek repayment for the grace they have bestowed, let them hear what is written: “When you prepare a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or rich neighbors, lest perhaps they also invite you and repayment be made to you. But when you prepare a feast, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you” (Luke XIV, 12).

Lest distributors scatter uselessly what they possess under the pretext of generosity, let them hear what is written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand.” And lest, when much is necessary, they give little, let them hear what is written: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.”

5. Lest, when little is appropriate, those who give distribute too much and afterward, unable to endure want, break out into impatience, let them hear what is written: “Not that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you, but that, by your equality, their abundance may supply their want, so that their abundance may also be a supply for your want” (II Corinthians VIII, 13). Thus, when the mind of the giver does not know how to bear want, if he takes away from himself what is illicit [variant: much], he seeks an occasion for impatience against himself.

6. Lest distributors provide nothing at all to those to whom they ought to contribute even a little [Al.: something small], [Col. 1184A] let them hear what is written: “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke VI, 30). Therefore, lest they provide not even something to those to whom they ought to contribute nothing, let them hear what is written: “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the wicked” (Ecclus. XII, 4). Some rich people of this world, while Christ’s poor are tormented by hunger, feed actors with lavish generosity. But whoever gives his bread to a needy sinner—not because he is a sinner, but because he is a human being—clearly nourishes not a sinner but a righteous person, because in him he loves not guilt but nature.

7. Those who distribute their possessions mercifully should carefully take heed lest, while they redeem committed sins with almsgiving, they continue to commit sins still requiring redemption; lest they consider God’s justice to be for sale, if, when they take care to give money for their sins, they suppose that they can sin with impunity. Let us carefully consider that those whom we now see in poverty we shall one day see in abundance; and that we who are seen to be prosperous, if we [Col. 1184B] neglect to give generously, shall one day be poor. Whoever now gives temporal assistance to the poor, expecting to receive perpetual recompense from him afterward, cultivates, so to speak, the earth for harvest: 268 what it has received, it returns more abundantly. Honor those whom you see to be poor, and regard those whom you see despised outwardly by the world as friends of God within. Share with them what you have, so that one day they may deem themselves worthy to share with you what they have (Greg., *Moral.* XXI, 19, no. 30; *II in Evang.*, hom. 40, no. 12).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the hope and fear of the elect

1. Often the mind of a righteous person already grieves over what it remembers having done perversely. It not only abandons its evil deeds, but also punishes them with the bitterest laments. Yet, while it recalls what it has done, it is terrified by great fear of the judgment. Each of the elect has already converted himself completely, but he does not yet raise himself up to complete security, because, while he weighs how severe the final examination will be, [Col. 1184C] he trembles inwardly, anxious under this fear; for he does not know what the just Judge, when he comes, will reckon concerning his deeds, or what he will forgive. Often the mind of the penitent remembers what wrongs it has committed, but it does not know whether these offenses have been forgiven if it has wept over them worthily. It fears lest the enormity of its guilt exceed the measure of its repentance. Every holy person, even here, does not know that he has received mercy, because a person abandons his sin by correcting it and by repenting of it, yet he still fears the severe Judge’s recompense for it (Greg., *Moral.* IV, 36, no. 61; Taio III, 46).

2. There every person, safe [Al.: just], and without any fear freely sings of the Lord’s mercies throughout eternity: there uncertainty about the forgiveness of sin will no longer exist; there the memory of his guilt will no longer be added to the secure mind [Al.: will no longer enslave it]; there the spirit will not tremble under accusation, but will freely rejoice in the Judge’s indulgence. When the prophet David asked, saying, “Turn your eyes from my sins,” he added shortly before: “My sin is always before me” (Ps. L, 11); as if he were saying: “I ask you [Col. 1184D] not to look upon my sin, because I never cease to look upon it myself.” Hence, through another prophet, the Lord also says: “I will not remember your sins, but you remember them” (Isa. XLIII, 25).

Those who mourn their sins must take care to consider each offense individually; and, while they mourn over the iniquity and defilement of their error in each one, they should cleanse themselves wholly and together with their tears. It is said through Jeremiah: “When the individual sins of Judah were weighed, my eyes poured forth streams of water” (Lam. III, 48). We pour forth divided streams of water from our eyes when we offer tears apportioned to each individual sin (Greg., *Reg. past.*, p. III, c. 29).

3. For the mind does not grieve equally over everything at one and the same time. Rather, while the memory of one guilt and then another touches it more sharply, it is moved concerning all of them in each particular case and is cleansed. Those oppressed by fearful dread should be admonished to trust in the mercy they ask for, lest they perish through the force of excessive affliction. [Col. 1185A] For the merciful Lord would not place sins requiring tears before the eyes of sinners if he had wished to strike them severely by himself. It is clear that he wished to hide from his judgment those whom, in his mercy, he made judges of themselves by anticipating them. Hence it is written: “Let us come before his face in confession” (Ps. XCIV, 2). Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI, 31). It is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI, 1). We cover sins when we place good deeds over evil acts. For whatever is covered is placed underneath, and that by which it is covered is drawn over it from above (Greg., *I in Ezech.*, hom. 4).

269 4. Therefore, when we reject the evils we have done and choose the good deeds we are to perform, we draw over them a covering, as it were, because we are ashamed that they should be seen. Holy men, while they are still in this life, nevertheless have something that they ought to cover before God’s eyes, because it is altogether [Col. 1185B] impossible for them never to sin either in deed, thought, or speech. Hence blessed Job, who had said that he was perfect in every respect, when he heard God’s voice and reproved himself for that very perfect speech, said: “I will put my hand over my mouth” (Job XXXIX, 34). The hand signifies action, and the mouth signifies speech.

5. Therefore, to put one’s hand over one’s mouth is to cover sins of speech through the power of good works. The upper and lower millstones are necessarily joined to one another, so that one is useless without the other. Thus hope and fear must constantly be joined in the sinner’s heart, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice. Conversely, anyone fears justice in vain if he does not also trust in mercy. The upper millstone is forbidden to be removed as a pledge, because one who preaches to a sinner must arrange his preaching with such careful balance that he neither removes fear by abandoning hope nor leaves the sinner in fear alone by withdrawing hope (Greg., *Moral.* XXXIII, 12, no. 24).

[Col. 1185C] ## CHAPTER L. On the desire for the heavenly kingdom

1. The great cry of the saints is a great desire. For each person cries out less the less he desires, and expresses a greater voice in the ears of the boundless Spirit the more fully he pours himself into that desire. Since the mind that asks is accustomed to be moved in one way, and the mind that is asked in another, and since the souls of the saints cling to God in the bosom of the inner secret in such a way that they rest by clinging to him, how are they said to ask when it is clear that they do not differ from the inner will? How are they said to ask when it is certain that they know both God’s will and the things that are to come?

Yet, because they are placed in him, they are said to ask something from him—not because they desire anything that differs from the will of the one they behold, but because, the more ardently they cling to him in mind, the more they receive from him so that they may ask from him what they know he wishes to do (Greg., *Moral.* II, 7, no. 11; Taio, III, 37).

2. Let no one who is heard more slowly [Col. 1185D] believe that he is neglected by heavenly care. Often our desires are heard even though they are not quickly fulfilled, and what we urgently ask to be accomplished prospers better through the very delay. Often our voice is perfected by being postponed; and when the request is outwardly neglected, our desires are fulfilled more deeply at the root of our thoughts. So, too, the seeds of crops are hardened by frost, and what emerges more slowly from the surface rises more abundantly toward harvest. Our desires are extended by prolongation [perhaps: delay] so that they may advance; they advance so that they may grow strong for what they are to receive. They are exercised in the contest so that they may be increased by greater rewards in recompense. The labor of battle is prolonged so that the crown of victory may grow.

3. Therefore, when the Lord does not quickly hear his own, he continually delays what he seems to reject. The inner physician cuts away within us the contagions of sins that he rejects as deeply rooted, and removes the infection of corruption with the iron of tribulation. He therefore pretends not to hear the sick person’s cries [Col. 1186A] because he is bringing his sickness to an end. The prophet David says: “I cry by day, and you do not hear; by 270 night, and it does not lead me into foolishness” (Ps. XXI, 3). As if he were saying: “It does not benefit me toward foolishness that you do not hear me each day, though I cry out by day and by night.” For by abandoning me, as it were, in temporal tribulation and not hearing me, you educate me more deeply toward eternal wisdom.

Again the Psalmist says: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation” (Ps. IX, 10). In speaking of tribulation, he placed “opportunities” first, because we are often shaken by tribulation, yet the time is not opportune unless we are helped toward the desire for deliverance.

## CHAPTER LI. On harmony among the good

1. Charity frees people from the yoke of guilt when, through love, it makes them subject in turn to the service of others; when we believe that the good things of others are our own and offer our own possessions to others as though they were theirs. Let people know with complete certainty that, however many virtues they may possess, they cannot become spiritual [Col. 1186B] at all if they neglect to be united with their neighbors through harmony. It is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is peace, charity, joy” (Gal. V, 22). Therefore whoever does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit. Hence Paul likewise says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (I Cor. III, 3). Again he says: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Taio, III, 38; Greg., *Reg. past.*, p. III, c. 22).

## CHAPTER LII. On divine judgments

1. Since God’s judgments are very hidden—by which in this life the good are sometimes treated badly and the wicked well—they are still more hidden when the good are treated well here and the wicked badly. For when the good fare badly here and the wicked well, this can perhaps be understood: the good, if they have committed any offenses, receive their recompense here so that they may be more fully freed from eternal damnation; and the wicked find here the good things they do for this life, so that afterward they may be led to torments alone. Hence it is said to the rich man burning in hell: “Remember, son, that you received good [Col. 1186C] things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke XVI, 25) (Taio IV, 2; Greg., *Moral.* V, 1, no. 1).

2. When things go well for the good in the present age and badly for the wicked, it becomes highly uncertain whether the good receive good things so that, being stirred up, they may grow toward something better, or whether, by a safe and hidden judgment, they are receiving here the reward for their works, so that they may be emptied of the reward of the life to come; and whether adversities strike the wicked for this reason, so that, by being corrected, they may be rescued from eternal punishments—or whether their punishment begins here, so that, when completed later, it may lead them to the final torments of Gehenna.

Because the human mind is weighed down by the grave darkness of its uncertainty amid divine judgments, holy men, when they see worldly prosperity supplied to them, are disturbed by fearful suspicion. They fear that they may receive here the fruits of their labors; they fear that divine justice may see a hidden wound within them and, while heaping external gifts upon them, reject them from what is inward.

3. Hence the Psalmist says: “His eyelids [Col. 1186D] examine the children of men” (Ps. X, 5). God’s eyelids are his judgments, which close something to us and open something to us. By opening, they examine whether we are not lifted up through understanding. By closing, they examine whether we despise what we are unable to understand. Let no one seek to scrutinize divine judgments: why one person is rejected and another chosen, or why one is chosen and another rejected. For, as Paul testifies, we have learned that “his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable.” The deeds of divine judgments must always be revered without questioning, because they can never be unjust. To seek an explanation 271 of his hidden counsel is nothing other than to act proudly against his counsel (Greg., *II in Ezech.*, hom. 5, no. 6).

4. When the reason for God’s judgments is not perceived, it remains for us to be silent humbly beneath his deeds, because the perception of the flesh is wholly insufficient to penetrate the secrets of Majesty. Let the human mind [Col. 1187A] return to itself and not seek what it cannot grasp concerning divine judgments, lest, if the cause of divine anger is investigated, it provoke that anger all the more by its investigation, and lest pride inflame irretrievably what humility could have appeased. Through the apostle Paul it is said: “O man, who are you to answer God?” (Rom. IX, 20). Considering himself, a human being falls silent and fears to scrutinize divine judgments, because he recognizes himself as dust. He is shown to be unable to answer because he is called human: having been taken from the earth, he is not worthy to scrutinize heavenly judgments (Greg., *Moral.* IX, 14, no. 21).

## CHAPTER LIII. On those who are hardened by God’s judgment

1. Just as no one resisted the generosity of God who calls, so no one opposes the justice of God who punishes the delinquent. God does not harden the sinner’s heart; he is said to harden it when he does not free it from hardness. He is said to harden it through justice because he does not soften the hearts of the reprobate through grace. God’s shutting up is not opening to those who are shut, but [Col. 1187B] leaving sinners in the darkness of their own deeds.

The merciful God grants us time for repentance, but when we turn the patience of his grace into an increase of guilt, he turns this very time, which he mercifully arranged for sparing us, into a stricter occasion for striking us. When someone refuses to return from the dark paths of his error even after receiving an interval of time, he increases his guilt through the very means by which he could have washed it away, had he wished to turn back (Taio, V, 5; Greg., *Moral.* XI, 9, no. 13; *I in Ezech.*, hom. 11, no. 25).

## CHAPTER LIV. On the prosperity of the reprobate

1. Whoever is turned away from God and prospers becomes all the nearer to destruction insofar as he is found to be estranged from the zeal of discipline. Many of the reprobate, while they are bound by the chains of their sins, never return to the path of righteousness. They are like the minds of the insane, who consider the madness by which they are overcome to be strength; they do not know that what they can do more than the healthy proceeds from illness, and they suppose that they have grown in strength while they approach [Col. 1187C] the end of life through increasing sickness.

Sometimes the reprobate, like madmen who lack the use of reason, weep and laugh; and they expand in such great exultation because, being insensible, they do not know the evil they are suffering. It is written in the books of Ecclesiastes: “I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth” (Eccles. X, 7). Everyone who sins is a servant. Servants are on horses when sinners are exalted by the dignities of the present life; princes walk like servants when no honor raises up many who are filled with the dignity of virtues, but the highest adversity here presses them downward as though they were unworthy (Greg., *I in Ezech.*, hom. 12, no. 18; *Moral.* VI, 16, no. 26; Taio, V, 7; *Moral.* XXXI, 24, no. 43).

## CHAPTER LV. How those who have fallen can rise after their ruin

1. Those who have experienced sins should at least fear the sea after shipwreck and dread, now that they know them, the dangers of their destruction, lest those who have been mercifully healed after committing evil [Col. 1187D] should die by wickedly repeating it. To the sinful soul that never ceases from sin it is said: “You have the forehead of a prostitute; you did not wish to be ashamed” (Jer. III, 3). Those who have fallen should therefore be admonished to strive, since they were unwilling to preserve intact the good things of nature that they had received, at least to mend what has been torn.

What will those who have experienced sins of the flesh say if, while others stand in integrity, they do not come to their senses even after their losses? What will they 272 say if, while they carry many others away with them, they neither return themselves to the Lord who awaits here? Those who have fallen should be told to consider their past offenses and avoid those that threaten, so that they may recall their completed sins to mind and be ashamed to be defiled by accidental occasions.

Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “If a man dismisses his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return [Col. 1188A] to me, says the Lord” (Jer. III, 1) (Greg., *Reg. past.*, p. III, admon. 29).

2. Behold, an argument from justice is brought forward concerning a woman who has fornicated and been abandoned, and yet, when we return after our fall, not justice but mercy is shown to us. From this we should certainly infer: if such mercy is shown to us when we sin, with what wickedness do we sin after the offense when we return? Or what forgiveness will there be for the wicked from the one who does not cease calling after guilt?

The prophet Isaiah says: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one admonishing you behind your back” (Isa. XXX, 20). Each person recognizes God’s admonitory words as commandments as though standing before him; to stand still before his face is not yet to despise him by sinning. But when, abandoning the good of innocence, a person chooses and pursues iniquity, he now turns his back upon God’s face.

3. The almighty Lord admonishes us as though following behind us, since even after guilt he persuades us to return [Col. 1188B] to him. He recalls the one who has turned away, does not look upon the offenses committed, and opens the bosom of his mercy to the one who returns. We hear the voice of one admonishing us behind our backs if, after our sins, we return with a humble and contrite heart.

Therefore, if we wish to fear justice, we must be ashamed of the mercy of the one who calls, because he is despised with all the greater wickedness insofar as, even after being despised, he does not disdain to continue calling. Through the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “You shall come as far as Babylon; there you shall be delivered” (Mic. IV, 10). Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Often, after someone has fallen into the confusion of vices, he returns to repentance, ashamed of the evils he has committed, and raises himself from his falls by living well. What does this person do except come as far as Babylon and there receive deliverance? Sometimes, ashamed of the evils he has done, a person raises himself against himself and returns to a state of uprightness by doing good. He is therefore delivered in Babylon who, by divine grace, is shown to have been saved even from confusion.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the desire for human praise and the favor [Col. 1188C] of flatterers

1. Every person who seeks human praise for what he does seeks a witness on earth. But whoever hastens to please the almighty Lord by his deeds considers that he has a witness in heaven. When many exalt evil deeds with praise, the result is that guilt, nourished by favor, continually increases. A wound that appears worthy of rewards and praise is neglected instead of being healed.

Thus Solomon rightly says: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent” (Prov. I, 10). Sinners entice when they either introduce evils to be committed through flatteries or exalt evils already committed through favor. For what else is it to sin than to lie down dead? But because they pursue the sinner with 273 praises, they hide him, as though dead, beneath a mound of their words.

As soon as the wind touches a reed, it is carried to the other side. And what is signified by the reed except the carnal mind, which, as soon as it is touched by favor or criticism, bends in whatever direction? (Greg., *Moral.* XIII, 24, no. 28; Taio, V, 13; Greg., *Moral.* IV, 28, no. 51.)

[Col. 1188D] 2. If a breeze of favor has blown from someone’s mouth, the desire for human praise grows cheerful. The person is lifted up and bends himself entirely toward approval; but if the wind of criticism bursts forth from the same place from which the breeze of praise came, fury soon bends him in the opposite direction with violent force.

Lest flattery gradually and with impunity grow stronger, it must immediately and without delay be struck down by the sword of the mouth and utterly extinguished through zeal for justice. In the Gospel, the foolish virgins are rebuked with the words: “Go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves” (Matt. XXV, 9). The sellers of oil are flatterers, because, in whatever grace they have received, they offer the splendor of glory through their empty praises, as though they were selling oil.

The head is the ruling part of our body. For the mind that governs the body is called its head. Therefore the head is fattened by the sinner’s oil when the favor of the flatterer soothes the mind. If, when hearing the praises of others, a person returns to consideration of the heavenly judgment and fears lest he be burdened by these praises [Col. 1189A] before the hidden tribunal, he has, as it were, grown to the fullness of brightness through the fire of purification; and from the very source from which he endures the flames of trembling, he shines more brightly (Greg., *I in Evang.*, hom. 12, no. 3; *Moral.* XXVIII, 8).

## CHAPTER LVII. How Holy Scripture expresses the sentence of a curse

1. Since we certainly know that Holy Scripture forbids cursing, why do we sometimes say that something is rightly done which we know the same sacred eloquence teaches us to avoid? We must understand that Holy Scripture mentions cursing in two ways: one kind it approves, and another it condemns.

A curse is uttered in one way through the judgment of justice, and in another through the spite of vengeance. A curse through the judgment of justice was uttered when the first man sinned and heard: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Gen. III, 17). A curse is pronounced through the judgment of justice when it is said to Abraham: “I will curse those who curse you” (Gen. XII, 3).

Again, because a curse is sometimes spoken not through the judgment of justice, [Col. 1189B] but through the spite of vengeance, we are admonished by Paul’s preaching when he says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII, 14); and again: “Those who curse shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10). The almighty God is said to curse, and yet he forbids a human being to curse, because what a human being does through the malice of vengeance, God does only through the examination and power of justice (Taio, III, 3; Greg., *IV Moral.*, 6).

2. When holy men pronounce a sentence of cursing, they do not break forth into it from a desire for vengeance, but from the justice of judgment. Within themselves they perceive God’s subtle judgment, and they recognize that they ought to strike outwardly arising evils with a curse; they therefore do not sin in cursing, because they do not disagree with the inward judgment.

The apostle Peter hurled a sentence of cursing at Simon, who offered him money, saying: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts VIII, 20). By saying not “it is,” but “may it be,” he indicated that he had spoken in the optative rather than the indicative mood. Finally, Elijah said to the two commanders of fifty who came to him: “If I am a man of God [Col. 1189C], let fire come down from heaven and consume you” (IV Kings I, 12). The outcome of the matter showed with how much truth the sentence of each had been confirmed. Simon perished in destruction 274, and a flame coming down from above consumed the two commanders of fifty.

The subsequent working of power testifies with what disposition a sentence of cursing is uttered. When the innocence of the one who curses remains intact, yet the curse consumes the one who is cursed even unto death, it is gathered from the outcome on both sides that the sentence was hurled against the guilty by one and the same inner Judge.

If we carefully weigh how each blessed person in Holy Scripture expresses a sentence of cursing, we find that his curse proceeds not from the malice of the offender but from the uprightness of the judge. It proceeds not from anger stirred up, but from calm instruction. For one who has already uttered a righteous curse has not succumbed to the fault of disturbance, but has carried out the office of teaching.

## CHAPTER LVIII. What jubilation is

[Col. 1189D] 1. “Jubilation” is said to occur when the mind conceives an ineffable joy that can neither be concealed nor disclosed in words, yet is revealed through certain movements, although it cannot be expressed in any precise form. The prophet David, observing that the minds of the elect conceive such great joy that speech cannot disclose it, says: “Blessed is the people who know jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 16). For he does not say, “who speaks,” but “who knows,” because jubilation can indeed be known by the understanding but cannot be expressed in words.

Through jubilation one perceives what lies beyond perception; and when the consciousness of the one who feels scarcely suffices for contemplation, how can the tongue of the one who speaks suffice for expression? (Taio, III, 36; Greg., *Moral.* XXIV, 6, no. 10.)

## CHAPTER LIX. On the discernment of the sevenfold Spirit

1. In the minds of the faithful, the first step of ascent is fear of the Lord, the second piety, the third knowledge, the fourth fortitude, the fifth counsel, the sixth understanding, and the seventh wisdom.

The prophet Isaiah, enumerating in Christ [Col. 1190A] the steps of sevenfold grace, says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI, 2).

Thus, speaking of heavenly things, he counted the steps by descending rather than ascending: wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. Since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. IX, 10), there is no doubt that one ascends to wisdom through fear; one does not return from wisdom to fear.

Wisdom certainly possesses perfect charity, as it is written: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (I John IV, 18). Therefore Isaiah, because he was speaking from heavenly things downward, began with wisdom and descended to fear. But we, because we strive from earthly things toward heavenly things, should count the same steps by ascending, so that we may be able to reach wisdom from fear.

There is fear of the Lord in the minds of the faithful; but [Col. 1190B] what kind of fear is it if piety is not present with it? Whoever does not know how to show mercy to his neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in his tribulations, has no fear before the eyes of almighty God if he is not raised up to piety.

Yet piety often errs through disordered mercy if it spares what ought not to be spared. Sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the blows of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares temporarily, leads to eternal punishment (Greg., *II in Ezech.*, hom. 7, no. 7; Taio, III, 23).

2. To be true and ordered, piety must be raised to another step: namely, so that it may know what to punish through mercy and what to forgive through mercy. But what if someone knows what ought to be done yet lacks the strength to do it? Our knowledge must therefore grow toward fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to act through strength of mind, lest it tremble with fear and, collapsing in dread, be unable to defend the good things [Col. 1190C] it perceives.

Fortitude often falls through its own presumption if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices. It must therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify everything it is able to do courageously. Counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For whoever does not understand the evil that weighs down the person acting, how can he make firm the good that helps him?

Therefore let us ascend from counsel to understanding. If understanding is vigorous with great keenness but does not know how to govern itself through maturity, then one must ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that what keen understanding discovers may be ordered with the maturity of wisdom [Al.: maturely by wisdom].

Thus, because we rise through fear to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge we are strengthened toward fortitude, through fortitude we advance to counsel, through counsel we progress to understanding, and through understanding we arrive at the maturity of wisdom. By seven steps we ascend to the gate through which access to spiritual life is opened for us.

[Col. 1190D] ## CHAPTER LX. On the various blows of the world

1. Those who love God are commanded to rejoice and be cheerful at the end or destruction of the world, because they will soon find the one whom they love, while the one whom they have not loved passes away. Far be it from any faithful person not to desire to see God and to mourn over the blows that strike the world, when he knows that the world is brought to an end by those very blows.

To mourn over the world’s destruction belongs to those who have planted the roots of their hearts in love of it, who do not seek the life to come, and who do not even suspect that it exists. We, who know the eternal joys of that heavenly homeland, ought to hasten toward it as quickly as possible. We should desire to depart sooner and to reach that life of perpetual happiness (Taio, V, 24; Greg., *I in Evang.*, hom. 1, no. 3).

## CHAPTER LXI. On the conversion of the Jewish people near the end of the world

1. The holy Church, made fruitful in its beginnings by a multitude of nations, will scarcely receive the Jews whom it finds at the end of the world; [Col. 1191A] gathering them at the last, it will set them in place like the remnants of a harvest. Concerning these remnants of the Jewish people Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

When Elijah comes, it is promised that he will turn the hearts of the children back to their fathers, so that the teaching now taken away from the heart of the Jews may then, through the Lord’s mercy, return, when the children begin to understand concerning the Lord what their fathers preached.

The Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin at the end of the world, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI, 25). As the prophet says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, the remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X, 22).

The holy Church, while it is still placed in this life, receives double rewards for the labors it endures when, after fully receiving the Gentiles, as we have said, it also turns the hearts of the Jews to itself at the end of the world, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Taio, V, 25; Greg., *in praef. IV Moral.*, c. 4; *praef. in Job*, c. 10, no. 20).

[Col. 1191B] CAP. LXII. On the times of Antichrist

1. The ancient enemy approaches to test the world more fiercely at its end. He becomes all the more fervent in savagery the nearer he senses himself to be to punishment. 276 He considers what is close at hand: that he is about to lose the license of his most wicked freedom. And the more he is confined by the shortness of time, the more widely he expands through manifold cruelty.

Whatever the devil is wickedly capable of, he will seek more cunningly at the end of the world. Then he will raise the neck of pride higher, and through that condemned man whom he carries he will wickedly display everything that he can prevail over temporarily.

For stars to fall from heaven to earth means that some, having abandoned hope of heavenly things, under his leadership yearn for the ambition of worldly glory. Thus this dragon sent forth his tail and dragged down a third part of the stars. The dragon’s tail drags down part of the stars when, through the final persuasion of Antichrist, certain people who seem to shine are carried away (Taio, V, 26; Greg., *Moral.* XXXIV, 1, no. 1).

[Col. 1191C] 2. Some maintain that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, as it is said through the patriarch Jacob: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s hooves, so that its rider may fall backward” (Gen. XLIX, 17).

In this passage Dan is asserted both to be a serpent and to bite. Therefore, not without reason, when the Israelite people were receiving lands in the division of the camps, Dan was the first to encamp toward the north, signifying the one who had said in his heart: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13).

Concerning him the prophet also says: “From Dan the snorting of his horses has been heard” (Jer. VIII, 16). Antichrist is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. In Greek, *cerata* means “horns.” The serpent said here to be horned aptly signifies the coming of that same Antichrist, because against the life of the faithful he is armed not only with the bite of poisonous preaching but also with the horns of power (Greg., *Moral.* XXXI, 24, no. 43).

## CHAPTER LXIII. On bodily health and sickness, and the life [Col. 1191D] of the present corruption

1. For the righteous in this life, the very burden of their corruption is burdensome. Sleep is sought for what vigils have exhausted, so that the labor and anxiety of wakefulness may be moderated. Sometimes sleep itself also kills; hunger wears down the body, and food is sought to drive away its necessity. Yet often food too becomes burdensome, although it had been sought to remove the burden of weakness.

As long as we are subject to corruption, we do not at all correspond to our Creator, because, since corruption is far removed from incorruption, there is no fitting likeness for our correspondence. The human creature, by the very fact that it has been created, possesses within itself the tendency to flow downward beneath itself. Yet from his Creator the human being received the capacity both to be carried above himself through contemplation and to be held within himself in incorruption.

Those in good health should be admonished to use the health of their body to exercise the health of their mind, lest, if they turn the grace of the health they have received toward wicked use, they become worse through the gift and afterward deserve heavier punishments because they now do not fear to misuse God’s more abundant [Col. 1192A] blessings (Greg., *Moral.* XII, 13, no. 17; Taio, III, 51–52; III, 14, no. 18; *Reg. past.*, p. III, c. 12).

2. Likewise, the healthy must be admonished not to despise the opportunity of earning salvation forever. For it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2). They must be told that if, when they are able, they are unwilling to please God, then, when they are willing, they may be unable to do so—too late. When bodily health, received for the purpose of doing good, is despised, how great a gift it was is understood only after it has been lost. And what was granted at a suitable time but not used profitably is sought in vain at the end. Through the wisest Solomon it is said: “Do not give your honor to strangers, and your years to the cruel, lest perhaps strangers be filled with your resources, and your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body” (Prov. 5:9–11).

Who are those alien to us except the evil spirits, since they have been separated from the lot of the heavenly homeland? [Col. 1192B] And what is our honor except that, although placed and formed in earthly clay, we were created in the image of our Creator? Or who else is cruel except that apostate angel who, through pride, struck himself with the punishment of death and, though ruined, did not spare the human race from inflicting death upon it?

3. He gives his honor to strangers who, created in the image and likeness of God, administer the time of his life according to the wills of evil spirits. He gives his years to the cruel one who spends the time allotted for living according to the will of the wicked ruler, his adversary. Whoever, through the bodily health granted to him and the mental wisdom bestowed upon him, labors not to exercise virtues but to commit vices, multiplies not houses for himself by his own strength but dwellings for strangers—that is, for unclean spirits—acting, plainly, either in debauchery or in pride, so that by adding himself to them he may increase the number of the lost.

Often the health of the flesh that has been received is spent upon vices; but when it is suddenly withdrawn, when the flesh is worn down by afflictions, when the soul is already being pressed to depart, the health that was long possessed badly is sought, as though for living well. Then people rightly groan that they were unwilling to serve God, when by serving they can in no way recover the losses caused by their negligence. Hence it is said elsewhere: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Ps. 77:34).

## CHAPTER LXIV. On Bodily Illness

1. The sick must be admonished to recognize themselves as God’s children precisely when the scourges of discipline chastise them. For if he did not intend to give an inheritance to children after correcting them, he would not take care to educate them through afflictions. The sick must be told that, if they believe the heavenly homeland to be theirs, it is necessary for them to suffer labors in this life as in a foreign land. The stones of the divine sanctuary were hewn outside, so that they might be placed in the construction of the temple without the sound of a hammer; for evidently they are now hewn outside by scourges, so that afterward they may be arranged within God’s temple without the blows of discipline. In this way, whatever is superfluous in us may now be cut away by blows, and then only the harmony of charity may bind us together in the building.

The sick must be admonished to consider how harshly the blows of discipline chastise carnal children for the sake of receiving earthly inheritances. Why, then, is the punishment of divine correction grievous to us, through which we both receive an inheritance that can never be lost and avoid punishments that will remain forever? Let the sick consider how great a salvation for the heart is bodily affliction, which recalls the mind to knowledge of itself (Taio, III, 53; Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, III.12).

2. Therefore, since health very often casts away the memory of infirmity, it must be restored, so that the mind—which is carried outside itself into exaltation—may be reminded, through the flesh that it suffers being struck, to what condition it is subject. The sick must be admonished to consider how great a gift bodily affliction is, since it both washes away sins already committed and restrains those that might be committed. It also inflicts upon the shaken mind the wounds of repentance, received from the blows that come from outside.

In Solomon’s Proverbs it is written: “The bruise of a wound cleanses away evil, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. 20:30). The bruise of a wound cleanses away evil because the pain of scourges washes away either wickedness that has been contemplated or wickedness that has been perpetrated. When we are struck outwardly, we are silently and sorrowfully recalled to the memory of our sins, and we bring before our eyes everything that we have done badly. Through what we suffer externally, we grieve more deeply within for what we have done.

Thus, amid the open wounds of the body, the hidden wound of the belly cleanses us more thoroughly, because the hidden wound of pain heals the wickedness of evil action. The sick must be admonished to preserve the virtue of patience, so that they may constantly consider how many evils the Redeemer endured from those whom he had created. Why, then, is it thought harsh that a human being should endure scourges from God for his evils, if God endured so many evils from all for the sake of the good? Or who, possessing sound understanding, would be ungrateful for being struck, if the one who lived without sin did not depart from this life without the scourge?

[Col. 1193B] ## CHAPTER LXV. On the Brevity or Misery of the Present Life

1. What are the nations in the world except flowers in a field? Let us turn the eyes of our heart toward the breadth of this present world, and behold: it is full of almost as many flowers as there are human beings. Thus life in the flesh is a flower in the hay. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Man: his days are like grass, and like the flower of the field, so he will flourish” (Ps. 102:15). The greenness of the flesh displays us, but the dryness of dust withdraws us from sight.

We appeared like a flower, although we did not previously exist; we wither like a flower, although we appeared for a time. And because each day, moment by moment, a human being is compelled toward death, it is rightly said in the book of blessed Job: “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition” (Job 14:2). Here a human being receives the strength to live for a little while, so that he may pass into eternity, where his life will not be enclosed by an end. But during this brief span, in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what he will find in eternity—either so that he may rejoice forever or so that he may not escape the punishments he has incurred.

Everything that passes is brief, even if it appears to come to an end slowly. We walk along the path of death, from which we shall not return—not because we will not be restored to the life of the flesh by rising again, but because we shall not return again to the labors of this mortal life, as though to acquire rewards through labor (Gregory, *Morals* XI.50, n. 67; Taio, III, 5; Gregory, *Morals* XIII.27, n. 31).

2. Whoever considers what he will be in death always becomes fearful in his activity; and by the very fact that, in his own eyes, he already lives as though he did not live, he truly lives in the eyes of his Creator. He desires nothing that passes away. He contradicts all the desires of the present life, and considers himself almost dead, because he does not fail to recognize himself as destined to die.

The meditation on death is perfect life. While the righteous carefully practice it, they escape the snares of sin. Hence it is written: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Sir. 7:40). However long the time of the present life may be, it is brief precisely because it does not remain. Nor is it worthy to be judged long-lasting if it is bounded by an end. For if everything done here is carefully considered, it is punishment and misery. Even serving the corruption of the flesh in what is necessary and permitted is misery, since clothing is sought against the cold, food against hunger, and coolness against heat.

3. Bodily health is guarded with much care, but often it is lost even after being guarded; once lost, it is acquired or restored only with great labor, and even when restored it always remains uncertain. What else is this but the misery of mortal life?

We love our friends while fearing that they may be offended. We fear our enemies, yet we are not secure concerning those whom we fear. Often we speak to enemies with the confidence due to friends. Sometimes we receive the sincere words of our neighbors, who perhaps love us greatly, as though they were the words of enemies. And although we never wish either to be deceived or to deceive, through our very caution we fall more grievously into error.

The glory of the wicked, when it is often extended over many years, is judged by the minds of the weak to be long-lasting and almost stable. But when a sudden end interrupts it, it undoubtedly proves that it was brief, since the determining end makes it known that what could pass away was of little duration.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Bodily Death

1. The days appointed by God’s inward foreknowledge can neither be increased nor diminished, unless it happens that they are foreknown in such a way that they are lengthened together with excellent works or shortened together with wicked ones. Thus Hezekiah earned an increase of days through the pouring out of tears; and it is written concerning the perverse: “Death comes upon the undisciplined.”

Everything for which we labor according to the present age scarcely lasts until death. For death intervenes and cuts off the fruit of our labor. But what is done for eternal life is preserved even after death, and it begins to appear when the fruit of carnal labors has ceased to be seen. Therefore that recompense begins where this life ends.

Our Lord wished the final hour to be unknown to us so that the mind might always remain apprehensive and, since we cannot foresee it, might prepare for it without interruption. Because we do not know the time of the death that is to come, and cannot work after death, it remains for us to seize the time granted before death. Thus—yes, thus—this death is conquered when it comes, if it is feared before it comes.

Our Redeemer accepted death so that we would not fear dying. He displayed the resurrection so that we might trust that we can rise again (Gregory, *Morals* XII.52, n. 58; Taio, III, 54; Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels* II.27, n. 5; I.13, n. 16; *Morals* XV.55, n. 68).

2. For this reason he also willed that the same death should last no more than three days, so that, if the resurrection were delayed in him, hope of it might not altogether perish in us. Once the flesh has been removed, the human eye no longer sees the soul; for after death grace does not liberate the one whom, before death, it did not reform for forgiveness.

Blessed David says: “Their spirit will go forth, and he will return to his earth” (Ps. 145:4). Then the spirit is cast down to the earth through knowledge of its guilt, when the flesh—which it considers its life—is compelled to return to dust.

A human being is strengthened for a little while in the present life, because here he receives the strength to live for a short time, so that he may pass into eternity, where his life will not be enclosed by an end. But during this brief span, in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what he will find in eternity—either so that he may rejoice forever or so that he may not escape the punishments he has incurred.

Just as those who are still alive do not know where the souls of the dead are, so the dead do not know how the life in the flesh of those who live after them is ordered, because the life of the spirit is far removed from the life of the flesh. And just as corporeal and incorporeal things differ in kind, so they also differ in knowledge. This, however, must not be understood of holy souls, since it is not in any way to be believed that those who inwardly see the glory of almighty God are ignorant of anything external (Gregory, *Morals* VIII.15, n. 30; XII.19, n. 24; XII.20, n. 25).

3. The almighty Lord wished our end to remain hidden from us so that, while we are uncertain when we shall die, we may always be found prepared for death. Why, then, should one exalt himself as though secure, when his life is held under the punishment of uncertainty?

Just as a brave man, when he girds himself with weapons because battle is already near, both trembles and hastens, quakes and rages—appearing to fear through his pallor, yet being driven forward with great force by anger—so the holy man, when he sees himself drawing near to the suffering of death, is shaken by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope. He trembles at approaching death, yet rejoices that through dying he will live more truly.

No holy man can pass to the kingdom without death intervening. Therefore he is confident while, as it were, doubting, and confident as though doubting; he fears while rejoicing and rejoices while fearing, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor the thing that lies between.

When we wish to drive illness from our body, we sorrowfully drink the bitter cup of purification, yet rejoice because we are certain of the health that will follow. Since the body cannot otherwise attain health, we take pleasure even in what disgusts us in the drink. And when the mind sees that life is contained within bitterness, it grows cheerful although disturbed by sorrow (Gregory, *Morals* XXXI.33).

4. Since the time of our life is undoubtedly appointed for us by divine foreknowledge, it must be carefully considered in what sense Scripture now says that the wicked are removed from the present age before their proper time. Almighty God often changes his sentence, but never his plan. Therefore each person is removed from this life at the time at which, by divine power, he was foreknown to be removed before his time.

But it must be understood that almighty God, who creates and orders us, disposes the end of each person according to his merits: either so that an evil person may live briefly, lest he harm many who are acting well; or so that a good person may remain longer in this life, so that he may assist many in good works; or again so that an evil person may be kept alive longer, so that he may increase his wicked works, through whose temptations the righteous, having been purified, may live more truly; or so that a good person may be removed sooner, lest, if he lived here for a long time, wickedness corrupt his innocence.

Although almighty God foreknows the time of each person’s death—the time at which his life comes to an end—no one can die at any other time than the one at which he dies. For if fifteen years are said to have been added to Hezekiah’s life, the time of his life increased from the point at which he had deserved to die. The divine arrangement had then foreknown the time when it would afterward remove him from the present life.

Since this is so, what does it mean to say that the wicked were taken away before their time, except that everyone who loves the present life promises himself longer stretches of that life? But when death comes and removes them from the present life, it cuts short the span of their life, which they had been accustomed to extend in thought as though it were longer.

## Other Chapters of the *Sentences*

1. Why is holy Church feared by her enemies like a line of battle in an army? This comparison is not without profound meaning and must therefore be examined carefully.

We know, and it is certain, that a battle line is then shown to be terrifying to its enemies when it has been so compacted and massed that it appears broken at no point. For if it is arranged so that an empty space is left through which the enemy can enter, it is plainly no longer terrifying to its enemies.

Therefore, when we are placed in the line of spiritual battle against evil spirits, it is supremely necessary that we always be found united and closely bound together through charity, never broken apart by discord. For whatever good works may exist in us, if charity is absent, a place is opened in the line through the evil of discord, by which the enemy can enter to strike us.

The ancient enemy does not fear chastity in us if it is without charity, because he himself is not weighed down by the flesh and cannot be dissolved in its lust. He does not fear abstinence, because he does not use food and is not driven by bodily necessity. Nor does he fear the distribution of earthly possessions if charity is absent from that work, because he himself has no need of the support of riches (Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel* 8, n. 6).

2. But he greatly fears true charity in us—that is, the humble love that we show to one another—and he intensely envies our harmony, because we possess on earth what he lost in heaven by refusing to possess it there.

Thus it is rightly said: “Terrible as an army set in array” (Song 6:3). For evil spirits fear the multitudes of the elect insofar as they see them fortified against themselves and gathered together through the harmony of charity.

The power of harmony is shown by the fact that the other virtues are shown not to exist without it. Abstinence is indeed a great virtue; but if someone abstains from food in such a way that he judges others for eating and even condemns the foods that God created for the faithful to receive with thanksgiving, what has the virtue of abstinence become for him except a snare of guilt?

Hence the Psalmist, indicating that there is no abstinence without harmony, says: “Praise him with the tambourine and the chorus” (Ps. 150:4). In the tambourine, dry hide resounds; in the chorus, voices sing in harmony. What, then, is signified by the tambourine except abstinence, and by the chorus except the harmony of charity?

Therefore one who practices abstinence in such a way as to abandon harmony praises God with the tambourine but does not praise him in the chorus. We ought to abstain or fast in such a way that we do not subject ourselves to the necessity of fasting or abstinence, lest we perform a voluntary act no longer willingly but unwillingly.

If, for example, I refresh any visitors by interrupting my fast, I do not break the fast; rather, I fulfill the duty of charity. But if, because of abstinence, I distress spiritual brothers [possibly: “the brethren”], whom I know to take pleasure in my relaxation, my abstinence must not be called a virtue but a vice. For the continuation of abstinence, unless it is set aside when circumstances require, both inflates me and grieves my brother, whom charity ought to assist—or certainly demonstrates that I possess no fraternal charity.

3. Pride is the beginning of every sin, while desire is the punishment of sin. Therefore vicious desire cannot be conquered in any other way unless pride, its enemy, is first guarded against through the virtue of humility.

Proud will causes God’s commands to be despised; humility causes them to be kept. Pride made demons from angels; humility makes human beings like the holy angels. Pride makes rebels subject to the devil; humility joins the humble to Christ.

The proud desire to have what they do not do praised in them; the humble avoid having whatever good they perform recognized. The former excuse their own vices by distancing them from themselves through the perversity of their will, and, assigning their good works to their own powers, shamefully boast of themselves. The latter, if they have committed any sins, accuse themselves by confessing them voluntarily, and, assigning all their good works to the divine gift, continually praise God.

Therefore, if virtue does not dwell in a vicious soul, pride does not yield to the rule of humility. The mind cannot possess the kingdom of virtues unless it has first shaken off the yoke of vices. Vices then truly depart from the heart if they yield their place to virtues; otherwise, once expelled, they either lie dormant for a time or return, unless virtues succeed them in the places from which the vices were driven out (See above, chap. 20, and Isidore, *Sentences* II.38).

4. Therefore, let piety resist cruelty in us; let patience, firmly established, restrain anger; let chastity conquer lust; let tranquility remove contentiousness; let measured silence restrain loquacity; let spiritual delight diminish carnal desires; let the rigor of abstinence blunt the goads of the flesh; let spiritual study succeed curiosity; let drunkenness yield to sobriety; let savagery succumb to gentleness; let maturity rule over frivolity.

As love of God and neighbor increases, let desire for the world be consumed. Let frugality exclude gluttony’s excess. Let the virtue of diligence chastise laziness. Let true humility restrain deep boasting. Let pure simplicity drive away pride. Let artificial fickleness not impede constancy. Let those who are corrected increase discipline. Let religious clemency break savagery. And let acquired goodness uproot wickedness completely, so that, through the expulsion of vices, the glorious introduction of virtues may be celebrated.

5. It has now become clear, in any case, how we should understand what Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sir. 10:15). Here, too, let us examine what the holy Apostle says: “Desire is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

Since the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophet, also spoke through the Apostle, he cannot be inconsistent with himself. We must therefore carefully consider why the one wished to call pride the beginning of every sin, while the other called desire the root of all evils.

Or perhaps the Apostle Paul explained the prophetic statement, as he often does, since whether you say “the beginning of every sin” or “the root of all evils,” you signify one and the same thing. Desire and pride are, moreover, so much one evil that neither can pride exist without desire nor desire without pride.

Indeed, the devil—in whom pride holds the chief place—desired his own power and the destruction of the human race. The human being himself, through desire for the forbidden tree and through his aspiration to divine likeness, showed that he had been afflicted by the disease of desire.

From pride are born heresies, schisms, detraction, envy, loquacity, boasting, disputes, contentiousness, ambition, self-exaltation, presumption, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind.

6. But who would doubt that these also proceed from desire, since all who have been corrupted by all the diseases I have named are considered desirous as well? Again, since desire makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunk, greedy, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, violators, incestuous, and infamous, how could such people become so without pride, without which God’s commands cannot at all be despised—the commands that prohibit all the evils included above?

Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our contest, let us first beware of desire and pride—not two evils but one—from which all evil acts take their beginning. For without pride, what sins could even be begun, since it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin”? Or without desire, which is the root of all evils, what evils could be committed, since without a root all things are either counted as nothing or are dead?

Furthermore, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my own pleasure, which is characteristic of desire, and despise God’s commands, which is [the characteristic of pride—text corrupt or omitted], then every sin proceeds from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin.

7. The envious person, who makes another’s good his own punishment by envying it, seems to be provoked to envy by no desire but to be troubled only by the disease of pride. But if you examine subtly and deeply the pestilence of his mind, by which he is driven headlong while inflamed, you will find that he desires the destruction of the person whose ruin he wants, and that he is held by the evil of pride, through which he continually grieves that someone better than himself is preferred to the one he envies.

Who could easily express in words how great this evil is? The envious person pursues with hatred the divine gift in another human being, when that person ought instead to be loved even for the holiness of his merit.

A just punishment has as many torturers for the envious person as the envious person has had admirers. Excellence of merit makes someone envied; the punishment of sin makes someone envious. No human remedy can be applied to him whose wound is hidden (See above, chap. 24, and Isidore, *Sentences* III, chap. 25).

8. Let us now see by what signs pride can be detected, so that, just as it became clear above (See *Book III of the Sentences*, chap. 23) that no sin can be committed without it, so here its signs may become evident, by which it can be shown that pride must be avoided.

I pass over those whom even their appearance and manner of walking reveal as proud. Their raised neck, grim face, fierce eyes, and terrifying speech condemn their naked pride. Possessed by the lust to rule, they subject to themselves by force whomever they can, confuse human and divine laws, and swell with honors. They seize everything indiscriminately, rejoice in their crimes, and, corrupted by the disease of pride, do not grasp that they themselves are in its power.

I therefore pass over these people, in whom pride rules so openly that they neither deign nor are able to conceal it. I will point out those who deserve the deepest sorrow and declare that their examples must be avoided: those who, already converted and making some progress, are secretly captured by pride; those whom it throws into the depths of evils through fraudulent condemnation and continually tramples down so that they may never emerge from there.

Pride itself makes a place for the devil in the hearts of such people. It opens a fortified breast familiarly to his arrival. It receives him as he enters. It establishes for those whom it has captured the right to live destructively. It strips away all good from those whom it has once invaded. It kills whatever remains in them that might resist vices, lest it perhaps grow strong against itself.

9. Hence it is that those whom the purulent corruption of a proud mind infects do not observe the commands of their elders but judge them. When rebuked for their negligences, they either insolently rebel or murmur. They dispute about superior positions and shamelessly desire to be preferred even to better men. They foolishly magnify the simplicity of their spiritual brothers. They brazenly boast of their own opinions. They disdain services offered to them and stubbornly seek what is denied. They prefer birth to character.

Exalted, they look down upon their juniors. They do not believe that anyone can be compared with them. Disdaining equality with others in character [possibly: “with their inferiors”], they place themselves above them through the mere swelling of their minds.

They do not preserve reverence in service, modesty in speech, or discipline in conduct. They have stubbornness in their intention, hardness in their heart, and boastfulness in their conversation; deceit in humility, sharpness in speech, obstinacy in hatred, impatience with subjection, and pursuit of power. They are hateful to all good people.

They are lazy in good works, harsh in fellowship, hard in service, ready to speak about what they do not know, prepared to undermine others, and inhuman in everything by which fraternal society is sustained; rash in listening, presumptuous in teaching, loud in speaking, disdainful in hearing, shamefully unrestrained in laughter, burdensome to friends, hostile to quiet, ungrateful for benefits, inflated by services, and domineering toward their subjects.

10. These are the signs of rampant pride, by which God is offended, departs, and abandons proud hearts. The devil rejoices, nourished by these evils, and is invited to come. He enters proud minds in order to hold them; he raises them up in order to strike them down; he cherishes them in order to destroy them.

He exults inexplicably in the very captivity of the lost, so that he may possess by right his captives, whom he has subjected to himself under the authority of pride, and may exercise through them all the evils described above.

Such people are therefore rightly abandoned by the just judgment of God, secretly condemned to punishment, because they are not forcibly enslaved but willingly yield to the rule of deceptive pride. They could resist it, if they wished, by the freedom of their will—freed and strengthened through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, if even such people, divinely stirred to recover salvation, conceive hope of repentance and do not despise themselves in despair because of their sins, they can be healed by the medicine of fruitful satisfaction. By taking up firmly established humility, they can overcome the pride that, having made them swollen, had driven them away from their God, and can be released from the bonds of condemnation.

How this can happen we have already explained above, when we discussed pride itself—where it came from, where it arrived, and what it did. For it came from the devil, reached the first human being, and in him corrupted the whole human race, as a root, through the deformation of a nature that sinned willingly.

11. The order of the discussion itself seems to demand that we say a little about envy also. It flowed so greatly from the fountain of pride that the devil, who perished through pride, immediately destroyed the first human being, inflamed by the gall of envy.

Therefore, since the same devil appeared both proud and envious through his pride, pride was not the fruit of envy; rather, envy proceeded from the root of pride. And since the preceding discussion has already disclosed how greatly envy afflicts the envious, it does not seem necessary here to speak about the punishment by which they wear themselves out as they tear apart their own souls. We must show only, with the Lord’s gift, how the envious make the merits of those who live securely into sins by envying them, and how greatly envy corrupts whatever good is in them.

Whatever good they hear being done or said by holy people, they either do not believe at all or turn well-accomplished deeds into evil by interpreting them maliciously. Every evil that lying rumor spreads about them they immediately believe, as though they themselves had seen it. They savagely contradict those who try to prove that it is not true. They invent everything against their rivals and are undone by their progress.

They hide hatred within themselves and nourish it for their own torment. They envy those who are advancing, favor those who are sinning, and rejoice in the evils of the good. They grieve over progress, burn with gratuitous hostility, fear that sinners will be exposed because of their own wickedness, always bitter and never secure, friends of the devil and enemies even of themselves. Hateful to everyone, they are anxious when they ought to rejoice and joyful when they ought to grieve—perverse everywhere. They sow discord among friends. When people are already in disagreement, they attentively strengthen them in their discord if they can.
