12. They stain the reputation of good people with lies. Among spiritual people they praise carnal things, so as to persuade them that spiritual goods are lacking in those people. They feign friendship so that, by whatever art they can, they may deceive those who have entrusted themselves to them in charity. Through wicked suspicions they heap up opportunities for hatred against themselves.

They make demons, whose deeds they imitate, rejoice; they distress holy men who know them. Friends in service but enemies in mind; restrained in speech but disgraceful in action; lavish in exposing others’ secrets but tenacious in suspicion; empty of good things but full of filth; endowed with frauds; adversaries in heart of the virtues; wicked in conduct; and treacherous toward all who live simply with them.

These and similar traits show that all envious people are enemies of the good in desire or intention. They descend into these evils by savagely excluding themselves from the fellowship of all good people—persecuting those whom they ought to follow and loving those whom they ought to abhor—so that the good they persecute may rightly not be found in them.

Consider, I beg you, how their own evils will punish the envious, whom even the goods of others punish.

13. Where can those who are evil in goodness become good, or when will those who do not cease to use good things badly make good use of evil things?

The holy martyrs made good use of evil things. They were truthful witnesses to our Savior and vigorous fighters in the spiritual camps. Afflicted and tested alike by tribulations, losses, and various tortures, they exchanged earthly things for heavenly ones and, having advanced through the good use of evils, reached the joys of eternal goods.

The envious person, on the other hand, uses good things badly. Cut off from all the good things that miserable person curses, he is left to be afflicted by the punishment of his own mind. And who can help those who make themselves their own executioners through envy? Or where will the envious person prepare salvation for himself, when, by using good things badly, he draws ruin from the very material of salvation?

Nevertheless, if the envious also, like other sinners, rise through divine inspiration into hope of recovering salvation and are displeased with themselves over how they may please God, they must not imitate Cain. Blinded by the fury of ruling envy, Cain criminally took the life of his brother and, struck in his soul by the death of his brother’s body, condemned himself to the punishment of eternal death. Overwhelmed by despair of obtaining forgiveness, he said to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4:13)—that is, he said to God: “I do not ask you to forgive me, since the greatness of your forgiveness is overcome by the magnitude of my sins.”

14. Indeed, nowhere is it read that he either repented of his crime or obtained forgiveness. If, therefore, those who reject his example take themselves away from themselves and restore themselves to God, and do not cast themselves into the depths of evils by despairing of salvation, who could doubt—or rather, who could fail firmly to believe—that forgiveness of their former wickedness can be granted to them?

if, once the wound of envy has been healed, they are corrected and drive the bitterness from their breast through the sweetness of fraternal love, sincerely loving those whom they hated, they may be assisted toward the good of fraternal fellowship by the milk [possibly: “and”] peace of all good people, whose merits burden them, and by their examples.

Having thus discussed envy, I shall next explain how grave an evil vanity also entangles vain people.

### 15

So that this may more easily be avoided, let us briefly explain what corruption it contains. For vanity is a kind of inflated affection of a languishing spirit toward various pleasures, eager for the enjoyment of honor and at the same time ignorant of how to attain it. Inflated by the disease of empty distinction, hollow and diseased, turbulent, mistress of shallow minds. It is flattering toward all who are badly grounded, seductive toward those who resist being captured by it, invincible over those whom it has captured. A pretence of virtues, the soul of vices, fuel for carnal pleasures, a stain upon character, an appetite for dignities, sweet to the wretched, bitter to the perfect, dangerous to the doubtful, imperious toward subjects.

It easily captivates the susceptible, entertains those whom it has captivated, torments the ambitious, inflates the narrow-minded, and humbles the inflated. The swollen serve it; the exalted lie beneath it; those whom it finds, it finds ruined; toward it they run who are about to fall; in it those who have fallen imagine themselves to be standing.

This is vanity, which does not, as is supposed, breathe forth some virtues, but strengthens the license of vices once they have been received from the vicious. In any case, it does not penetrate minds full of virtues at all; therefore it tests those who are empty and supported by no virtues, and plunges those themselves who are inflated with the arrogant ambition of ruin into certain hidden disgraces, to be enjoyed through public [Forte, famae: perhaps “fame”] pleasure—just as a vacant ship is tossed in different directions by a storm amid swelling waves, and, while the grains of wheat remain fixed by their own weight on the threshing floor, the wind snatches away the light chaff.

But if this is so, vanity does not make them vicious; rather, it reveals them, carried about by the wind of its breath and whirled around by slippery impulses, as people who accommodate themselves to all its thrusts through the zeal of their own will; those who shamefully boast of works of which they are not conscious; those who, disgracefully, desire to be praised by everyone; those who despise holy men in comparison with themselves; those who, lifted up by the breeze of popular favor, think that they lack nothing of perfection.

They rejoice in the greetings of those who meet them, favor their flatterers, obey their wishes, and please everyone in what is disgraceful. They eagerly undertake to teach what they do not know; they want sublime things to be believed about themselves; they put what is pleasurable before what is weighty; they curse in words what they desire in their minds. They give the names of virtues to their vices, deceive themselves, and deceive those who favor them. They are swift in promising what is honorable, liars in performance, changeable in what is good, tenacious in evil, weighty in speech, disgraceful in mind, deceitful everywhere, cheerful in prosperity, fragile in adversity, inflated when serving, anxious when reproached, immoderate in their joys, accommodating in human matters, and always difficult in what is honorable.

### 16

Vanity oppresses those whom it has charmed with these and similar things, and permits them neither to recognize their illness nor to come to the physician. And what is it to come to the physician except for the sick person to acknowledge his illnesses, not to please himself, but to be ashamed of deeds that had seemed glorious to him?

Certainly, those do not do this who, inflamed by the desire to acquire a reputation, devote themselves only to those works by which human favor is purchased, and despise goodness of character. The ardor of human praise inflames them so greatly that they undertake laborious works—which the people admire and through which fame is spread—without effort, and perform them gladly.

Hence it is that they fast, abstain, keep vigils, frequent the church, or sing psalms—even though none of these things is done without labor—with pleasure, because they desire to please everyone by means of them. Not that they do not do these things, and all the things of God, but because those who strive more fervently to excel even in holy conduct are [Forte, probentur: perhaps “shown to be”] offering them more to God than to human beings.

But if someone shines outwardly, where he can be thought great, and is filthy inwardly, where God alone sees, who does not understand that all those continual labors of abstinence, vigils, and fasts—which vanity makes tolerable for us—are not ornaments of character but coverings for vices?

Therefore vigils, fasts, abstinence, almsgiving, and other things of this sort ought to increase our goodness, not to make sin effective; they must be offered to God not on account of sadness but together with righteousness. Those who are prepared to transcend the commandments through love of perfection ought to fulfill them with much greater attentiveness.

Otherwise, if they do not restrain envy, arrogance, pride, greed, and similar evils of the heart, yet wear out their bodies with fasts and the labor of even continuous abstinence, neither do those works, expended for vanity, justify them, nor do they cease to despise these vices, which they neglect to amend.

---

## APPENDIX X. EXHORTATION TO HUMILITY. FROM THE EDITION OF FLOREZ. (S)

### 1

Whoever, by God’s will, shines with the dignity of any office, and by the usefulness of prudent governance stands before other people, please receive this little exhortation of mine carefully [Al., “graciously”]. Do not look for rhetorical flourishes in it, because the virtue of humility is sought not through verbal exaltation but through purity of mind.

And if I happen to seem to speak somewhat harshly, this is the fault of the truth, not of me. For some things are hard and some are gentle; and although all people ought to speak truth to one another, I shall nevertheless speak freely, since nothing ought to be said more truthfully to anyone than to one who presides over many. Even if something harsh is sometimes offered to him from the truth, as commonly happens, it is like a kind of antidote: however bitter it may be, because it is healing, it must be drunk even if it causes bitterness (see *Isidoriana*, ch. 84, no. 19).

### 2

This, then, I urge above all: always fear those excessively pleasant flatteries of men. For in this matter one must exercise no less vigilance than in repelling those speeches which, if they weaken the firmness of the mind by a certain delight in pretence, seek access to favor not through the merit of labor but through the cleverness of flattery.

Therefore receive words that are useful rather than merely compliant; seek what is upright rather than what is agreeable and pleasant. To rejoice with a flatterer is indeed a royal vice, while to flatter is servile. But although rejoicing with a flatterer is royal, it is nevertheless a vice native and almost proper to them to follow closely the words of the powerful and to fashion their speech according to their wishes.

For if they happen to praise something and then notice that it is not gladly heard, they immediately condemn it [Al., “what they had praised earlier”]. But if they have condemned something, they praise it again if that is what pleases their patron. Thus among such people the mind of the flatterer is carried about like a ship amid various blasts of wind: because it has no way out, it is tossed to and fro.

Among these people, whose richest profit is especially to live according to the desires of others, constrain your mind with the utmost measure of discernment. When flatterers on every side insinuate nothing except what pleases, offering certain words of glory in which what is said to you is also said to God, recognize that nothing in these things is properly yours except what will remain with you, and with you after you have departed from this life.

Therefore, in all matters in which excessive flattery has exceeded even the limits appropriate to a human being [Forte, homini: perhaps “to a person”], remember that Davidic lesson in which he, avoiding the poisons of flattery, says:

> “Let the righteous strike me in mercy and reprove me, but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head.”

For the sinner’s oil is flattery, which, with a light and pleasant anointing, as though rubbing it with oil, makes radiant the head of the inner person, which is the heart. The prophet David therefore said that it was better for him to be rebuked or admonished by a righteous man than to be praised by any flatterer.

He rightly designated the flatterer by the name “sinner,” since before God his greatest and most detestable sin is to hold one thing in his heart and utter another with his mouth. Of such people he also says in another psalm:

> “His words are softer than oil, yet they are darts.”

But of the righteous person he says:

> “He speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue.”

So that no human subtlety in these matters may ever draw your mind into agreement through any title of praise, turn your attention to those evangelical deeds of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and you will find that the Lord of rulers gave us a great example of humility amid human praises.

Cultivate this, have this as your teacher, and set it up as your judge amid the allurements of praise. Do not permit yourself to hear with accommodating ears how much of what people bestow by praising you, or for how long it is yours, because it is fabricated.

### 3

Finally, this holy humility, once it has withdrawn from you the allurements of every pretence, will open heaven to you when it says in your ear: “Because you are earth.” It will bring you into that true fellowship of God’s inheritance when it admonishes you in all things: “Because you are human, and a sinner.”

And when you have examined all the accounts concerning you in the reckoning of this humility, I shall say something remarkable: you will find that people, by adding to the sum of your honor, diminish it, while this humility alone, by diminishing, adds more.

Therefore, however great you are, humble yourself to that extent (as Solomon says). For even when you have governed many, there is still no perfection if, while what is greater remains, you alone are left unable to govern yourself. You will truly go before others when you have first gone before yourself.

I speak these things not to the wicked but especially to the good. For if you look to the teaching of God, commandments were given not only to sinners but also to the holy. The word of Truth is spoken to them too—not so that they may become good, since they are good, but so that they may not become evil, which they are not.

I believe, moreover, that what is pure and sincere pleases the good more. For our God is appeased not so much by the sweet prayers of those who worship him as by innocence and simplicity. He inclines his ear more to those who offer him a sincere and pure mind than to those who bring the pleasing blandishments of prayers.

I have not seemed to have anyone else to address concerning empty glory or pride except you, whoever you are who stand before others. Even if you do not receive these things, everyone presents them to you, everyone flatters you, everyone exalts you, and none of them offers you something that is so sweet while nevertheless being far from danger.

Nor do I wonder that praising a powerful person is readily available to everyone, since it involves neither labor nor fear.

### 4

It was therefore fitting that I should extend these instruments of humility to you, and to you, who hold the rudder—even though you possess it yourself—I should add this further moderation. For the stronger the height of honor, the stronger is the wind of elation there.

I desire that you always walk before the eyes of God, to whom the abyss of human conscience lies bare, with a humble heart, because it is written:

> “Upon whom,” says the Lord, “shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and the one who trembles at my words?”

I desire that you keep all Christ’s commandments, and, when you fulfill them through good works, remember what was said to the apostles themselves. For he said to them:

> “When you have done all these things that I command you, say: ‘We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’”—

that is, not from a gift as free persons, but from an obligation as servants.

For no person, however perfect in all things, has ever anticipated the things pleasing to God so completely that, having lent him something first, he was not a debtor but a creditor. Who has anything that was not given by him? Or who, as the Apostle says, has first given to him, so that he may be repaid?

> “Because all things are from him, and through him, and in him; to him be glory forever. Amen.”

### 5

Behold, this is that true and Christian humility. In it you will govern those over whom you preside most excellently. In it you will be able to gain victory over every vice, attributing what you have conquered to God, not to yourself.

For when vices that have sometimes been overcome by patience regain their strength, believe me, this is nothing other than our failure to say to God what that warrior David said while fighting the Lord’s battles:

> “In you,” he says, “we have scattered our enemies, and in your name we have despised those who rise against us.”

And again:

> “For a man is not made strong by his own power; the Lord makes his adversary weak.”

But perhaps someone will answer me: “Then do we not give thanks to God and return praises to him?” I believe that we do give thanks—but in words only, and in secret. We give thanks privately to God, but publicly to ourselves; we give praise to God with our lips, but to ourselves both with our lips and in our hearts.

Behold, this is what repeatedly raises up the enemy who has been bent down. The sin of our arrogance is his strength.

Therefore humility of heart alone, by declaring itself weak, is able to do all things; it obtains everything that is good, always attributing it to God and not to itself. Whoever rises in this humility has nowhere from which to fall.

All other virtues may urge us toward their perfection through certain lofty and difficult heights; this one alone is on level ground. And although it may appear lower than the others, it is higher than heaven, because in its kingdom it leads a person not by ascending but by descending.

Through it the saints obtained the rewards of future blessedness, keeping that saying of the Lord:

> “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

That person is humble, namely, who is rich in spirit, abundant in a certain breath of exaltation, and inflated like a wineskin. [The text appears corrupt here.]

### 6

But now, let your charity pay attention for a little while to how this virtue itself is obtained.

First, if you wish to begin some good work, you will begin it not with the intention of acquiring praise, but with the desire to begin the practice of goodness.

Then, when that good work—whatever it may be—has been completed, you will guard your heart with every precaution, lest, yielding to human favor and judging yourself by it, you please yourself, or seek glory from any action. For the nature of glory is like that of a shadow: if you follow it, it flees; if you flee from it, it follows.

But always consider yourself the least of all, and remember: whatever good may have prospered for you throughout your life, ascribe all of it to God, who gave it, not to yourself, who received it. Convict yourself by Paul’s testimony:

> “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

Likewise, remember the apostolic saying:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.”

When you have adorned your heart with these most precious stones of holy humility as a temple for the Holy Spirit, then, praying in it and taking up the song of the prophet David, you will sing it not merely in word but also in deed:

> “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up. I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me.”

You will then be able to offer this song to God in truth, when by humbling yourself you praise him alone, to whom you too say daily, together with all the faithful:

> “Praise is fitting for you,”

glorifying him alone.

---

## APPENDIX XI. TESTIMONIES OF DIVINE SCRIPTURE AND OF THE FATHERS. (C, G, S)*

### CHAPTER ONE — On the One God

#### 1

In the Prophet:

> “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.”

In the Gospel:

> “No one is good except God alone.”

Paul to Timothy:

> “For there is one God, and an intermediary [sic] between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for us.”

#### 1

In the Epistle of John:

> “Because there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the Blood; and these three are one in Christ Jesus. And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one.”

In the Second Epistle:

> “Because many deceivers have gone out into this world, who do not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Such people are deceivers and antichrists.”

#### 1

In Solomon:

In the same book:

In the same book:

> “Flee sins as you would from the face of a serpent. If you approach them, they will seize you, like the teeth of a lion when devouring.”

#### 1

In Proverbs:

In the same book:

In the same book:

#### 1

In Exodus:

#### 1

> “Hypocrites and the crafty provoke God’s anger.”

In the Gospel:

In Proverbs:

> “If your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he is overthrown do not let yourself be exalted, lest the Lord see it and it displease him, and he turn his anger away from him.”

The Apostle Paul:

Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be: ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’ Whatever is more than this is from evil.”

### CHAPTER XVII — Also on Restraint of the Mouth
[Col. 1208C] 1. In Proverbs: “Contention arouses hatred, but friendship protects all who do not contend.” Paul to Timothy: “Avoid profane novelties of speech, for they promote impiety greatly, and their speech spreads like cancer.” In Psalm 134: “A talkative man shall not be established upon the earth.” In Proverbs: “You will not escape sin through much speaking; but he who spares his lips will be wise.” Again there: “He who uses many words injures his soul.” Again there: “By making yourself very silent [or: mute], you will appear to be wise.” Again there: “He who answers before he hears: it is folly and reproach to him.” Again there: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; but he who is self-controlled shall eat its fruit.” Again there: “He who guards his mouth and tongue preserves his soul from distress.” Again there: “If you see a man swift in words, know that the fool has greater hope than he does.” Again there: “Do not be silent with your tongue, useless and slack in your works.” Again there: “He who is a whisperer in everything, and unnecessarily so, will be hated.” [Col. 1208D] Again there: “The silent and prudent man will be honored with honor.” Again there: “In the midst of the prudent, preserve a word for the proper time; but in the midst of those who discuss matters, be assiduous.” Again there: “Do not accustom your mouth to speak without discipline, for the word of sin is there.”

## CHAPTER XVIII — Drunkenness to Be Avoided

1. In Proverbs: “Wine is insolent, and drunkenness is abusive; every fool becomes entangled in these.” Again there: “Do not be a winebibber, nor exert yourself to repair the flesh; for every drunkard and fornicator will beg, and will be clothed in torn garments, as will every sleepy person.” Again there: “For if you stain yourselves and give cups to your eyes [sic], you will walk at the end more naked than a hair.” Again there: “Let the powerful who are prone to anger not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom and be unable to judge rightly on behalf of the weak [or: the lowly].” Again there: “Thorns grow in the hands of a drunkard.”

In Ecclesiasticus: “Wine and women make the wise apostatize and reproach the sensible, and he who joins himself to fornicators will be worthless rottenness, and worms will inherit him.” [Col. 1209A] Again there: “A drunken and erring woman is great in anger and insult, and her shame is not covered.” Again there: “For a disciplined man, wine in small quantity is best; while sleeping, he will not be troubled by it, nor will he feel the pain of wakefulness.” Again there: “You who love wine, do not provoke it, for wine has destroyed many. As fire tests hard iron, so wine rebukes the hearts of the proud. Wine is an equalizer for human beings, not drunkenness. Wine was created for joy, not for drunkenness; from the beginning, wine drunk in moderation was the exultation of soul and heart. Wine drunk in excess produces irritation, anger, and many calamities for drunken minds.” [297] In Ecclesiasticus: “It is better to go into a house of mourning than into a house of drinking.”

Paul to the Ephesians: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Again to the Corinthians: “Neither drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners shall possess the kingdom of God.”

In Proverbs: [Col. 1209B] “Do not pay attention to the deceits of a prostitute-woman, who for a time fattens your throat; but at the end you will find her more bitter than gall, and she will be sharper than a sword sharpened on both sides.” Again there: “Do not be excessive with another man’s wife, nor join yourself in her embraces, since she is not yours.” Again there: “My son, do not let the desire for beauty overcome you, nor be captivated by your eyes, nor be carried away by your eyelids. What is the price of a prostitute? The price of one loaf of bread.” Again there: “As a moth destroys clothing and a worm destroys wood, so an evil woman destroys a man.” Again there: “Do not look upon a promiscuous woman, lest you fall into her snares. Do not spend your time with a dancer, nor listen to her, lest you perish through her seduction.” Again there: “Do not give a woman power over your soul, lest she proceed in your strength and you be put to shame. Do not give your soul in any way to fornicators, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance. Do not wander in the vices of the city, nor wander through its streets. Turn your face away from a dressed-up woman, and do not look upon the appearance of another’s wife. Every [Col. 1209C] prostitute is trampled like dung in the street. Many have admired the appearance of another’s wife and have been rejected. For her conversation burns like fire. Do not recline at table with another man’s wife, leaning upon your elbow, and do not quarrel with her over wine, lest your heart incline toward her and you slip through blood into destruction.”

## CHAPTER XIX — The Uninstructed Young Are to Be Corrected

1. In Proverbs: “He who spares the rod hates his son; he who loves him disciplines him diligently.” Again there: “The disgrace of an undisciplined son is not hidden.” Again there: “Do not cease correcting a child, for if you strike him with a rod, he will not die; indeed, you will strike him with a rod, but you will deliver his soul from death.” Again there: “Instruct your son, and he will gladden you and give beauty to your soul.” Again there: “A young man who is with a holy person has his way made straight; the ear hears, the eye sees, and both are the works of the Lord.”

In Ecclesiasticus: “Do you have sons? Instruct them from their childhood. Do you have daughters? Guard their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face.” [Col. 1209D] Again there: “He who loves his son continually applies the rod to him, so that he may rejoice at his end and not touch the doors of his neighbors. He who teaches his son will be praised in him and honored among his friends through him.” Again there: “He who teaches his son with zeal stirs up the enemy. The father is dead as though he were not dead, for he will leave someone like himself behind him.” Again there: “An untamed horse goes among thornbushes; an undisciplined son goes headlong. Bend his neck in his youth, and beat his sides while he is an infant, lest he grow up, become hardened, and not obey you, and become a grief to your soul.”

In Ecclesiasticus: “Be constant with a holy person, whoever you know to preserve the fear of God. According to your ability, beware of your neighbor, and associate with the wise and sensible.”

## CHAPTER XX — Just Measures and Weights

1. In Deuteronomy: “There shall not be in your house a large and a small weight; there shall not be in your house a large and a small measure. [Col. 1210A] Rather, let the weight and the measure be just for you, so that you may live many days upon the land that the Lord your God will give you as a possession, because everyone who does unjust things is an abomination to the Lord.” [298]

In Proverbs: “A dishonest balance is an abomination before the Lord, but a fair weight is acceptable to him.” Again there: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful balance is not good before him.”

## CHAPTER XXI — Concerning a Vow

1. Again there: “As soon as you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay to fulfill it. Therefore, whatever you vow, fulfill; it is better not to vow than to vow and not to pay.”

In Ecclesiastes: “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh quietly.” Again there: “Anger is better than laughter, because in the face there will be pleasure; the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.”

In Deuteronomy: “There shall not be male things upon a woman, nor shall a man put on a woman’s garment, because whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord.” [Col. 1210B] Again there: “Parents shall not die for their children, nor children for their parents; each person shall die in his own sin.”

Paul to the Ephesians: “And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger, but nourish them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”

In the prophet Hosea: “Sow righteousness for yourselves, and reap the fruit of life; seek the light of righteousness, wait for the Lord until he comes to you. Reap the fruit of his righteousness.”

In Proverbs: “Who boasts that he has a clean heart, or who dares to say that he is pure from sins?” Again there: “My son, bring forth tears for your dead, and, as though you had suffered severely, begin to weep; according to the judgment, cover his body, and do not despise his burial. Because of the report [or: the removal], weep bitterly for his mourning for one day, and console him because of his grief.”

## CHAPTER XXII — Not Defrauding, and Not Boasting

1. In Exodus: “You shall not commit theft, and you shall not lie.” [Col. 1210C]

In Proverbs: “He who shares in the affairs of a thief hates his own soul.” Paul to the Corinthians: “Neither thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor extortioners shall possess the kingdom of God.”

In Proverbs: “Be confident with all your heart in the Lord, but do not exalt yourself in your own wisdom.” Again there: “Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord and turn away from evil. Then there will be health for your body and care for your bones.” Again there: “I saw a man who considered himself wise in his own estimation; but the fool had greater hope than he did.”

In Isaiah: “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight.”

Paul to the Romans: “For while claiming to be wise, they became fools.” To the Corinthians: “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?” Again there: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I will seize the wise in their craftiness’; and again: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.’” [Col. 1210D]

In Ecclesiastes: “It is better for you to be told, ‘Come up to me,’ than to be humbled in the presence of a powerful person.”

In Exodus: “For your murmuring is not against us, but against God.”

Paul to the Thessalonians: “He who despises a human being does not despise a human being, but God.”

To the Romans: “For just as through the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one many are constituted righteous.” [299]

## CHAPTER XXIII — Not to Investigate Higher Things, Nor Listen to Heretics

1. In Proverbs: “He who trusts in falsehood feeds on winds; he himself follows flying birds. For he will abandon the way of his vineyard and wander from the furrows of his cultivated field; he walks through dry places, deserts, and land established in droughts; he gathers barrenness with his hands.” Again there: “Therefore withdraw from another’s water, and do not drink from another’s spring, so that you may live for a long [Col. 1211A] time, and years of life may be added to you.” Again there: “He who pursues vanities lacks understanding. Do not add to his commandments, lest you be reproved and become a liar.”

In Ecclesiastes: “Do not seek things higher than you, and do not investigate things stronger than you; but always consider what the Lord commands you, and do not let your heart dwell on many of his works. For suspicion turns many away and holds their understanding in vanity.”

In the Book of Wisdom: “We scarcely understand the things that are on earth, and we discover with labor the things that are before us; but who has investigated the things that are in heaven? And who knows your mind, unless you give the interpretation?”

## CHAPTER XXIV — Concerning Fasting

1. In Ecclesiasticus: “What benefit does his washing bring to one who is baptized from a dead person? So also a man who fasts in his sins and again commits the same things: what benefit does his humbling himself bring? Who will hear his prayer? A saving sacrifice is to heed the commandments and depart from all iniquity.”

In the Gospel: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, gloomy. For they disfigure [Col. 1211B] their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, so that you may not appear to people to be fasting, but to your Father who sees in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

## CHAPTER XXV — The Example of the Ant or Bee for a Person Without Sloth in Labor

1. In Proverbs: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and, observing its ways, imitate it, and become wiser than it. For although it possesses no field, has no overseer, and is not under a master, how does it prepare food in summer? Yet it makes abundant provision at harvest. Or go to the bee and learn how industrious it is, and what a holy work it produces. Its labors bring kings and common people to health; it is gracious and glorious in all things, and although weak in strength, it has been made prominent as a teacher of wisdom.”

“How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you rise?” [Col. 1211C] “You sleep a little, you sit a little. You sleep for a little while, you embrace your breast with your hands for a little while. Then poverty will come upon you like an evil traveler, and want will flee from you like a swift runner.”

Again there: “A sluggard who is rebuked is not ashamed.” Likewise, those who change wheat at harvest. Again there: “Desires kill the sluggard, for he does not apply his hands to do anything.” Again: “The sluggard seeks excuses and says, ‘There is a lion in the streets; there are murderers in the streets.’” Again there: “As a door turns on its hinge, so the sluggard turns in his bed.” Again there: “The sluggard seems wiser to himself than one who brings a message to the assembly.”

## CHAPTER XXVI — Concerning the Fool

1. A foolish man fabricates evils for himself, but stores up fire on his own lips. Faithful lips do not suit a fool, nor lying lips a just man. Again there: “Why do riches abound for a fool, when he cannot possess wisdom because he lacks understanding?” Again: [Col. 1211D] “An unwise son is anger to his father and grief to his mother.” Again there: “He does not desire wisdom who lacks understanding; rather, he is called imprudent.” Again there: “The mouth of a foolish man is his ruin, and his lips are a snare for his soul.” Again there: “A stone is heavy and sand scarcely bearable, but anger is heavier than both for a fool.” Again there: “As a dog that returns to its vomit and becomes hateful, so a fool who returns to his sins through his wickedness.”

“He who is diminished in skin [uncertain text] thinks vain thoughts, and an imprudent and erring man thinks foolish things. The heart of a fool is like a broken vessel, and no knowledge will remain in it. Wisdom is closed to the fool, but the knowledge of the sensible consists in expressible words. Shackles: the feet of fools are instruction, and their right hands are as though bound. A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man scarcely laughs quietly.” Again there: “The heart of fools is in their mouth, but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.” “He who teaches wisdom to a fool is like one who glues a potsherd.”

Again there: “It is easier to carry sand, salt, and a mass of iron than an imprudent, foolish, and impious man.” [Col. 1212A] Again there: “Do not take counsel with fools, for they will not be able to contain themselves.”

Again in the prophet Isaiah: “The fool speaks foolishly, and his heart understands vanities.”

## CHAPTER XXVII — Anger Must Be Laid Aside

1. In Proverbs: “Every simple person is a blessed soul; but an impetuous or angry man does not act honorably.” Again there: “A fool declares his anger on the same day, but a clever man conceals his insult.” Again there: “There are those who wound by speaking, like swords. An angry man acts without counsel, but a prudent man endures many things. Anger destroys even the wise, but a gentle answer turns away anger.”

Again: “An angry man prepares quarrels, but a patient man also calms future ones.” Again: “Do not befriend an impetuous man. Do not stay with an angry friend, lest you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul. The fool pours out all his anger, but the wise man apportions it gradually.” Again: “An impetuous man digs up contention, [Col. 1212B] but an angry man has swallowed sins.”

In Ecclesiasticus: “An angry man provokes a quarrel, and a sinful man troubles his friends. He introduces accusation among those who have peace.” Again there: “Jealousy and anger shorten days, and anxious thought brings old age before its time.” Again there: “Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of fools.”

Paul to the Ephesians: “Now lay aside from yourselves all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and excessive talk.”

In the Gospel: “Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment.” Again: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; but whoever says, ‘You fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Here Mixed Together

1. In Ecclesiastes: “Be gentle in hearing a word, so that you may understand, and speak your answer with wisdom.”

In Proverbs: “A prudent servant will obtain mastery over foolish masters and will divide an inheritance among brothers.” Again there: “Nothing good will come from a deceitful son, but the actions of a wise servant will [Col. 1212C] prosper.”

In Ecclesiastes: “If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul, and treat him as a brother, because you have acquired him at the cost of your own blood. If you wrong him unjustly and, becoming proud, he departs, whom will you seek, and by what road will you seek him?”

Again there, in Proverbs: “The commandment of the law is a lamp. As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so iniquity is to those who practice it.” Again there: “A man kills himself through his own wickedness.” Again there: “By the things through which a person sins, by those same things he is tormented.” Again there: “The Lord established man and left him in his own free choice. He added commandments and precepts: if you are willing to keep the commandments and make a faithful commitment, he set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before man are life and death, good and evil; whatever he chooses will be given to him.”

Again there: “As a moth harms clothing and a worm wood, so sorrow harms the heart.” Again: “A joyful heart makes for good will, but the [Col. 1212D] bones of a sorrowful man wither.”

In Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord.” Again there: “Cursed are those who trust in man, because God has made him nothing.”

In Ecclesiasticus: “Do not be absent from those who weep at the gathering, and walk with those who mourn; do not be slow to visit the sick, for through this you will be strengthened outwardly in love.”

Paul to the Romans: “I bruise my body and bring it into slavery, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified.”

In Proverbs: “The Lord will destroy the houses of the proud.” Again there: “He who makes his house high seeks its ruin.” Again there: “By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is raised; by intelligence storerooms are filled with all good and precious things.” Again there: “Do not bring just anyone into your house, for there are many snares of the deceitful.”

In the Canticles: “Beware of the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.” “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart and see nothing at all, like foxes in the desert.” [Col. 1213A]

In the Gospel: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.” Again there: “Whoever divorces his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery.” Again there: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times a day, and turns back to you seven times a day, saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him.”

Again there: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man; the field is this world. The good seed are the children of the kingdom. The weeds are the children of wickedness; the enemy who sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the completion of the age; the harvesters are angels. Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so it will be at the completion of the age.”

In Solomon: “There are six things that the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising the worst thoughts, feet swift to run [Col. 1213B] into evil, one who brings forth a lie, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.”

## CHAPTER XXIX — Testimonies of the Fathers

1. “There are four disturbances of human souls: desire, joy, fear, and sorrow.” “The mind itself is memory, and the power that is called memory.” Again there: “There are eight principal vices that afflict the human race. The first is *gastrimargia* (γαστριμαργία), that is, gluttony of the belly; the second, fornication; the third, *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία), that is, avarice or love of money; the fourth, anger; the fifth, sorrow; the sixth, *acedia* (ἀκηδία), that is, anxiety or weariness of heart; the seventh, *cenodoxia* (κενοδοξία), that is, boastfulness or vainglory; the eighth, pride.” (In the book of the *Collations*, namely, of Cassian.)

## CHAPTER XXX — Testimonies from Evagrius’s Sayings to the Brothers

1. “Just as flame burns a forest, so hunger extinguishes evil visions.” Again there: [Col. 1213C] “A sleepy monk falls into evils, but he who keeps watch will be like a sparrow.” Again there: “As fire liquefies wax, so good vigil dissolves the worst thoughts.” There: “He who loves silver will not see knowledge, and he who gathers it will be darkened.” There: “As fire tests gold and silver, so temptation tests the monk’s heart.” Again there: “Poverty with knowledge is better than riches with ignorance.” There: “Just as a raven flies away from its nest, so an unclean soul flies away from its body.” There: “As the southwest wind is upon the sea, so is fury from a man’s heart.”

Again there: “A worldly person serving a brother in sickness is better than a monk who does not pity his neighbor. A lazy monk murmurs much, and a sleepy one blames his headache. A two-tongued monk disturbs the brothers, but a faithful one brings rest. A gentle worldly person is better than an angry or impetuous monk. God loves a gentle monk, but drives a turbulent one away from himself. Humility precedes charity, and love precedes knowledge.”

[Col. 1213D] “Just as the morning star is in heaven and snow in paradise, so a pure mind is in a gentle soul. The light of one who investigates banquets is extinguished, but his soul will see darkness. Weigh your bread carefully, drink your water in measure, and the spirit of fornication will flee from you. Give wine to the elders, and bring food to the sick, because they have worn out their bodies in their youth. I saw an angry old man, exalted in his time; but a young man had greater hope than he did. He who loves the bee eats its honeycomb, and he who gathers it will be filled with honey.”

## CHAPTER XXXI — Testimonies from the Book of Saint Martin, Not That of the Bishop of Tours, but of This Father Who Was a Monk

1. “Although you praise a weak man immediately, he will become stronger. If you admire someone carrying a small weight, he collapses. If you tell a lazy man that he is swift, he will immediately fly away. Although this stain of pride generally afflicts many, it is no more to be feared by others [Col. 1214A] than by those who pursue either spiritual perfection in virtues or, carnally, an abundance of vices. The wind of elation is always stronger where the height of honor is greater.”

“We readily believe, and we become angry before we are judged; for many are driven by suspicions, interpreting worse things from another’s expression and laughter and becoming angry during the night. The curious person who investigates what has been said about him and draws out malicious speeches, even when they were spoken secretly, disturbs himself; for while he interprets them, he brings matters to the point where they appear to be true.”

“He overlooks many insults and does not receive most of them, either because he does not know them or, if he does know them, because he turns them into play and jest. If the man who inflicted the insult is good, do not return it; if he is bad, do not imitate him. Yield to the wiser person; forgive the fool.”

“Everyone has within himself the spirit of a king, wishing that permission be granted him over others but not wishing it to be granted to others over himself. It is not fitting for a sinner to correct sins. But if a wise man becomes as angry as the enormity of crimes demands, he ought not merely to be angry but to become frantic.” [Col. 1214B]

“Nothing is more glorious than to exchange anger for friendship. Is someone angry? In response, provoke him by kindness; the quarrel immediately falls away.”

“Physicians’ remedies are useful not during attacks of illness but during its remissions. Often truth retains the face of a lie. Often a lie is concealed under the appearance of truth. For just as sometimes a friend shows a serious expression and a flatterer a pleasant one, so it is colored with the appearance of truth.”

“Praise sparingly, blame more sparingly; for excessive praise is no less reprehensible than immoderate censure. A prudent person never feeds his mind on idleness; sometimes he possesses leisure, but never is he wholly unoccupied. The virtue of humility is required not in exaltation of words but in purity of mind. Abstain also from shameful words, because license in them nourishes shamelessness.”

“Make your conversations subtle [sic]. Make all people your equals. If you do not despise your inferiors through pride, you will not fear your superiors if you live rightly. Be kind to everyone, a flatterer to no one; intimate with few, yet fair to all.”

“Give without arrogance what you know to the person who asks, eager and teachable; [Col. 1214C] and ask, without concealing your ignorance, that what you do not know be imparted to you. The just person does not betray secrets: he is silent about what must be silent and speaks what must be spoken. Thus he has deep peace and secure tranquility, while through him other evils are conquered by good ones. Great-heartedness consists in fearing neither a person nor the bold.”

## CHAPTER XXXII — From the Book of Saint Ambrose

1. “Let religious devotion grow in the vine, peace in the olive, and the modesty of sacred virginity in the rose. My brother is white and red: white by merit, because he is the Father’s splendor; red because he is the offspring of a virgin. In him the color of both natures shines and glows.”

“Chastity also makes angels: whoever preserves it is an angel; whoever loses it is a devil. A virgin is one who marries God; a prostitute is one who makes gods. For this reason, following their reversed footsteps, the sons of Noah covered their nakedness. What the shameless man saw, the modest man blushed at, and the pious man covered, lest those who saw it also be offended.”

“What power [Col. 1214D] wine has, that those whom floods did not strip naked, wine should strip naked! For the one who teaches ought to excel the one who is taught. It is more tolerable to possess a virgin mind than virgin flesh.”

“Shadow for the carnal Jews, image for us, truth for those who will rise again. For we have learned that according to the law there are these three things: shadow, image, and truth—shadow in the law, image in the Gospel, truth in judgment. And therefore, through Moses, the law is through shadow, as through a human being; the figure is through the law; the truth is through Jesus.”

“What is a treasury? The consolation of the faithful, the expenditure of the poor, the rest of the needy. Sins are either forgiven, erased, or covered: forgiven by grace, erased by blood, covered by charity. When David says, ‘Deliver me from bloods,’ that is, he asks to be delivered from mortal sins.”

“Do not subject yourself to the powers of the flesh, since God wished you to be free. You have no excuse regarding the pursuit of marriage: these things belong to pleasure, not necessity. If you are kind toward the needy, you will be great before God. Since you call [Col. 1215A] God ‘Father,’ show this in your actions.”

“A good mind is the choir of God; an evil mind is the choir of demons. As many vices as the soul has, so many masters does it have. The foundation of piety is self-restraint, but the summit of piety is friendship. Do not consent to anyone persuading you to do what is not good. It is worst for sinners to come together when they are sinning.”

“Many foods hinder charity, and lack of restraint in food makes a person unclean. It is not the foods introduced through the mouth that defile a person, but the things that proceed from evil conduct. Receive from God those things that you cannot receive from a human being. It is better to throw a stone in vain than to throw a word.”

“A wise man will be brief in speech at judgment; a long narrative is a sign of ignorance. When you preside over people, remember that there is a God over you; and when you judge people, know that you yourself will also be judged by God. Honor a wise man as the image of the living God. Do not honor anyone merely because he has much money; it is difficult for a rich man to be saved.”

“You will [Col. 1215B] never be wise if you think yourself wise. God does not hear the prayer of a man who does not hear the needy. He who does not obey the wise will not obey God either. Do not take away what you did not put down; let what is yours be sufficient for you.”

“Flee drunkenness as disgraceful, because the person who is like a beast in his belly is overcome. As much as you labor for the body, if you labor so much for the soul, you will be wise. Honor a philosopher as a minister of God, after God. It is better to minister to others than to be ministered to by others.”

“It is better to die from hunger than to stain the soul through lack of restraint in the belly. Whoever speaks a word about God to those to whom it is not permitted ought to be considered a betrayer of God. It is not true that the person who harms a human being worships God. It is better to possess nothing than, while possessing much, to share it with no one. If you do not give to the needy when you can, you will not receive from God when you ask.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Testimonies from the Book of Prosper
1. If my rusticity made me incapable, I believed that I became capable through your faith, since you ordered me to be so. The treatment of necessary questions, even if it does not instruct the mind of the one who finds what he seeks, exercises the understanding of the one seeking salvation. Knowledge, just as it puffs up without the gift of God, which is love, so, if love is added to it, builds up. Thus the just are separated from the wicked forever, so that neither do those who have been rewarded ever bring their reward to an end, nor do the condemned ever bring their punishment to an end. For just as bodily satiety makes all who are full equally satisfied, although individuals have received food not equally but according to their capacity, so all the saints—even if distinguished by some diversity in their ranks—will all be perfected in one blessedness, because they will also be blessed in one perfection. On the day of judgment, not words but deeds will be required of us. Whoever has not believed, since he does not have faith, will be unable to have either righteousness of heart or salvation. The speech of a pontiff ought to be so weighty that no one, however unlearned, is excluded from understanding it. A sound mind ought to desire the fruit of obedience more fully, in an incorporeal manner, than to avoid the disgrace of unjust detraction. When truth cries out from whatever source, it must not be ascribed to human ingenuity but to God. Founded upon the virtue of obedience and patience, they do not scrutinize the ordinances of their elders, but carry them out. They now flee patiently from public appearance, while hiding the poison of anger in their hearts, ready to do harm when they find an opportunity to do so. Thus every person ought to be healed—now by teaching, now by exhorting, now by enduring, now by rebuking—so that, under Christ’s assistance, no one in this life should despair of salvation. “Reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching,” as if he were saying: reprove equals, exhort elders, rebuke the younger.

A person mildly corrected shows reverence to the one correcting him; but, offended by the harshness of excessive rebuke, he neither accepts rebuke [the text reads *nec increpatio*] nor salvation. Those who cannot bear to be rebuked for their rebuke must be carried with gentle compassion. Just as virtue is burdensome to the vicious, so vicious pleasure is bitter to the friend of virtue. For as long as someone is ignorant of his own sins—which he ought to know and mourn—he remains curious about the sins of others; but if, turning toward himself, he examines his own conduct, he does not seek what to criticize specifically in others, because he has within himself something to lament. Therefore we ought not readily to accuse our brothers, but to groan.

Those whose sins are hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor made public by others, if they are unwilling to confess or correct them, will have God, whom they have as witness, as their avenger also. He is insulting who makes a false accusation, and he makes a false accusation who commits an insult. Indeed, secure in his wickedness, the one who does not possess heavenly things vigorously supplies earthly things to those who are engaged in warfare. We ought to seek those riches which can both adorn and protect us; for this reason, those who serve God must flee earthly things. Those who wish to possess such riches with all their heart do not seek them without toil, find them without difficulty, preserve them without care, possess them without anxious delight, or lose them without pain.

Whoever enjoys idle repose, unless he has lived spiritually, lives like the beasts. No one possesses God except the one possessed by God; let him first be God’s possession, so that God may become his possession and his portion. The Creator of all things, to whom none of the things he made can be compared, does not deem it worthy to be possessed together with the things he created. Whoever wishes to possess God must renounce the world, so that God may be his blessed possession. He performs God’s work who does not abandon things consecrated to God out of any desire, but with the intention of the most faithful administration. Therefore the possessions that priests receive after being taken from the people must no longer be regarded as worldly property, but as God’s.

Adam and Eve did not blush because they were outwardly protected by a divine garment; indeed, before the sin they were naked and did not blush, because they had committed nothing against God’s will for which they should be ashamed. Thus open concupiscence would not have stirred them, fallen away from their Creator through attachment to the creature, unless hidden pride had first corrupted them. The desire of the flesh was fulfilled in them when they tasted from the forbidden tree; the desire of the eyes, when they wished to open their eyes; and worldly ambition, when they believed that they could become what God is.

Salvation becomes sweeter when pain torments, and the bitterness of illness commends the sweetness of lost health. Adam made us liable to all evils through his own fault; Christ’s coming, through grace, set us free from them. Any delicacies, if enjoyed without desire, are harmful; and coarse foods often hinder the benefit of abstinence if they are consumed greedily. Moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach; drunkenness weakens both mind and body. Those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for bodily health do nothing against abstinence; it is not pleasure that offers it to them, but illness that permits it.

If I refresh any visitors by interrupting my fast, I not only fast, but make charity an example. But if, on account of abstinence, I distress spiritual brothers whom I know by refusing, for my own relaxation, to please them, my abstinence must not be called abstinence, but vice. Just as true virtue justifies the mind that sincerely clings to it, so simulated virtue condemns it. The mind cannot possess the kingdom of virtues unless it has first shaken off the yoke of vices.

An envious person has as many torturers in his just punishment as the envied person has praisers. If excellence makes someone envied, envy will be the punishment of sin; nor can a remedy be applied to him by another whose wound is hidden. Everyone speaks of what he loves, and listens with pleasure to what he turns over in continual thought. Thought is what, if shameful, pollutes the mind, but, if honorable, purifies it. Unclean thoughts do not make the mind unclean; rather, unclean thoughts arise from an unclean mind. For obscene words die away with their sound in chaste ears and do not break into the secret place of a modest heart.

The pleasure of taste does not break into the mind through the mouth of the flesh; nor does an obscene word burst forth from the mind unless the mind has first willingly corrupted itself. Each person frequently has on his lips the names whose desires he bears in an afflicted heart; and the shamefulness that he is embarrassed to practice in deed he nevertheless holds as guilt in his mind—not by human judgment, but by divine judgment. Consider, I beg you, how the envious must be punished by their own evils, since even the good things of others punish them. What benefit is it to anyone if he shines outwardly, where he can be thought great, while inwardly, where God alone sees, he is filthy?

## CHAPTER XXXIV — On Fasting

1. Fasts, abstinence, vigils, almsgiving, and other things of this kind ought to increase the good. For not covering [the text reads: “sin”]. Nothing keeps us free from every sin so completely as fear of punishment and love of God. Those puffed up by the arrogance of vain loquacity desire their words to be praised rather than put into practice; they are concerned not with the holiness of their work but with the elegance of their elaborated speech. For a person sins from that part of himself in which he loves God less; but if we love him with all our heart, there will be nothing in us that serves the desire for sin.

As we wish to be helped, so let us help others according to our ability; or, if ability is lacking, let us retain the will to help. If I see someone sinning and not only do not rebuke him but even consent to his sin, I make myself a participant in his condemnation; and I sin in all sinners when, through a certain cruel wickedness of spirit, I do not rebuke those whom I know to have sinned. Whoever loves a friend for some temporal advantage is shown to love not the friend, but the advantage.

## CHAPTER XXXV — From the Book of Sentences

1. True innocence is that which harms neither oneself nor another; and no one sins first against another rather than against himself. People must be loved in such a way that their errors are not loved, because it is one thing to love what they have become and another to hate what they do. The confession of one who blesses is true when the sound is the same from mouth and heart; but to speak well and live badly is nothing other than condemning oneself by one’s own voice.

He has good understanding who correctly understands what ought to be done, such as [the text reads] “without fear of wisdom.” A death preceded by a good life must not be regarded as an evil death. Whatever evils the Lord inflicts upon the just through the wicked are not punishment for a crime but a testing of virtue; for the good person, even if he reigns, is a servant.

The proud devil led the proud human being to death; the humble Christ brought the obedient human being back to life. For just as the former, lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented [the text is corrupt: *jecit ob et consentientem*], so the latter, humbled, rose [the text is corrupt: *surrexit credentem*]. Perfect hatred is that which lacks neither justice nor knowledge: that is, you should neither hate people because of their vices nor love vices because of people.

Those who are in wickedness are in great poverty, possessing neither the work of justice nor the treasures of wisdom; but those who serve the Lord acquire goods that cannot perish. Confession of sin is good if healing follows. For what benefit is there in exposing a wound and not applying medicine?

The first death holds the grieving soul in the body; it is shared by both sides, so that the soul suffers from its own body what it does not wish. When you do something good, do it cheerfully; for if you do something good sadly, you become worse than the good you do. Humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good deeds. No unjust person does good, even if what he does is good, because the spirit of fear accomplishes nothing where the spirit of love is absent.

Equanimity of mind is better than health of body. For Christ is the end of the law; in him the law of righteousness, as the text reads, “is not taken up” (*non sumitur*), but is fulfilled. As the earth awaits rain and light from heaven, so a human being ought to await mercy and truth from God. The first salvation is to turn away from sin; the second is not to despair of forgiveness. For the person who does not turn to the remedy of repentance before the merciful judge perishes forever.

The virgin of the Christian faith is stirred at three times: evening, morning, and midday. In the evening, the Lord was on the cross; in the morning, in the resurrection; at midday, in the ascension. The first pertains to patience in being killed, the second to life in being raised, and the third to the glory of majesty in sitting at the Father’s right hand.

Tribulations afflict people so that the vessels of election may be emptied of wickedness and filled with grace. The unjust penitent’s sorrow is better than the unjust doer’s joy. It is good to be conquered by truth; in correction, let truth prevail over pleasure. Indeed, truth conquers even the unwilling.

Those who worship idols are like those who see empty things in dreams. But if their souls are awake, they understand when something has been made and do not worship what they themselves have made. Those who thirst for God ought to thirst with their whole substance—that is, with both soul and flesh—for God gives the soul its bread, namely, the word of truth, and God supplies the necessities of the flesh. He nourishes both because he made both.

Two loves make two cities throughout the whole world: love of God makes Jerusalem; love of the world makes Babylon. Therefore let each person question himself and discover from which city he is a citizen. There is no difficulty in lacking unless there is desire in possessing; therefore only that is rightly loved which is never rightly admitted [the text is uncertain].

In the first human being it became evident that human free choice had power for death; in the second, that God’s help had power for life. The first was human—not [that] human [the text reads *non is homo*]; the second, however, was God and human. Sin came about through abandoning God; righteousness is not achieved without God.

The Lord says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” This means: through me one comes to me; in me one arrives and remains in me. A good fragrance is a good reputation, which a person acquires through the works of a good life while following Christ’s footsteps; in a certain sense he bathes Christ’s feet in the fragrance of precious ointment.

The labor of the godly is exercise, not condemnation. The just are born from God, not from human beings, because one becomes just by being born, not by ascending; hence they are also called regenerated children of God.

It is one thing to migrate in body and another to migrate in heart. To migrate in body is for the body to change its place; to migrate in heart is for you to change the inclination of your heart. If you love one thing that you formerly loved another, you are not where you were.

## APPENDIX XII — SERMONS (C, G, S)*

## SERMON I — On Removing Meat

[Col. 1217D]

**Note:** [Col. 1217D]

**SERMON I, no. 1.** I discussed this sermon in *Isidoriana*, chapter 72, nos. 8 and following. In certain places it has been corrupted through the carelessness of scribes. In place of “on the most sacred day,” it would be preferable to read “at the most sacred time.”

1. Dearest brothers, I ask and admonish you that on this lawful and most sacred day, except on Sundays, no one should presume to eat lunch—unless perhaps he is someone whom illness does not permit to fast. For on other days fasting is either a remedy or a reward; during Lent not fasting is a sin; at another time, whoever fasts receives indulgence, but during Lent whoever is able to fast and does not will feel punishment.

**Note:** [Col. 1218D]

2. “The excused person is able to fast.” But “not” must be added. The remainder, although it requires correction, is nevertheless sufficiently intelligible. In the printed text stood *non valere* (“not to be able”), for which I have placed *non velle* (“not to wish”). I do not understand what *adlucet* means.

2. Yet even he who is not able to fast [the text reads *qui (non) jejunare praevalet*] should, more correctly, prepare for himself alone—or, if another sick person is with him, for the two of them together in his own house—what he is to receive. And they should not invite those who are able to fast to lunch, because if they do this, not only God but also human beings may understand that they are not unable to fast because of illness, but unwilling to fast because of gluttony. Let it be enough for him that he is unable to fast. And all the more, with groaning, sighing, and grief of heart, [let him do so] because, while others are fasting, he cannot abstain [the printed text is corrupt].

3. Whatever each sick person needs, let him have prepared privately, either for himself alone or with another sick person likewise, because he ought not to ask a healthy person to lunch, lest he increase his own sin through another’s gluttony. Nevertheless, because he cannot fast, he ought to give more generously to the poor, so that the sins he cannot cure by fasting he may redeem by giving alms. It is good to fast, brothers, but it is better to give alms.

**Note:** [Col. 1219D]

4. Perhaps: “It is sufficient without fasting.”

4. If someone can do both, there are two good things; but if he cannot, almsgiving is better. If there is no possibility of fasting, almsgiving is sufficient without fasting; but fasting without almsgiving is wholly insufficient. Therefore, if someone cannot fast, let him give alms. Almsgiving without fasting is good. If, then, he is able to fast together with almsgiving, it is a double good; but fasting without almsgiving is no good, unless perhaps someone is so poor that he has absolutely nothing to give. For those who have nothing from which to give, good will is sufficient, according to what is written: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

5. But who will be able to excuse himself, when the Lord has said that he will give a reward even for a cup of cold water? And why did he say “cold”? Perhaps so that some poor person might not excuse himself on account of a lack of firewood, or say that he had no vessel in which to heat water. Finally, through the blessed prophet, dearest brothers, the Lord so urges and admonishes people to give alms that scarcely any poor person can excuse himself. For he says:

“This is the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord: Break your bread for the hungry.”

He does not say that it should be given whole, lest perhaps that poor person have nothing else; rather, he says, “Break it”—that is, even if you are so poor that you have only one loaf, still break it from that loaf and give it to the poor, and bring the needy and homeless person into your house. If someone is so poor that he has no food, let him prepare a little bed for a stranger in one corner of his house.

**Note:** [Col. 1219D]

6. It would seem that one should read: “when we are ignorant … when we do not believe,” or perhaps: “with us being ignorant … with us not believing.” This expression occurs in Isidore and others. See the note on Sedulius, book IV, verse 8.

6. What will we say, brothers? What excuse will we be able to offer, when we possess large and spacious houses yet scarcely ever deign to receive a stranger? We are ignorant—or rather, we do not believe—that Christ is received in every stranger, just as he himself said: “I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me”; and: “As long as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me.”

7. Is it laborious and repugnant for us to receive Christ among the poor in our homeland? I fear that he may say to us: “Go,” and not receive us into his blessedness. Do we despise him in this world? I fear that he may despise us in heaven, according to what he himself said: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food”; and: “As long as you did not do it for one of the least of these, you did not do it for me”; and what follows afterward.

8. May God avert this from us, brothers. For afterward he adds, saying: “Depart from me, accursed ones; go into the eternal fire.” I judge no one according to this sentence. Let each person attend to his own sentence. Nevertheless, I do not accuse or rebuke you, because perhaps it has sometimes happened through negligence that garments which ought to have been given to the poor have been damaged by moths; and I fear that those very cloths may be brought forward as witnesses against you on the day of judgment, according to what James says: “Come now, you rich; weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted.”

**Note:** [Col. 1219D]

9. “Or I and my …” These passages are corrupt and cannot easily be restored without the help of manuscripts.

9. And all these things, as Christ said through his Apostle, although they terrify us greatly, must not lead us to despair of God’s mercy. Either I and my companions, if with God’s help we negligently yet willingly wish to correct ourselves when we can, should distribute more generously the alms that we have hitherto given sparingly; and what we are taught by the Lord’s mercy to do for past sins—with sorrow, groaning, and hope of rest—

**Note:** [Col. 1219D]

10. Perhaps: “but meanwhile, as for the present,” and so forth. Shortly afterward I have restored *ne in terra pereat* (“so that it may not perish on earth”), where the breviary has *ne inter pereat*.

10. Therefore, as we suggested above, dearest brothers, let the richness of almsgiving commend our fasts, because fasting without almsgiving is like a lamp without oil. For just as a lamp lit without oil can smoke but cannot shine, so fasting without almsgiving indeed torments the flesh, but does not illuminate the soul with the light of love.

Meanwhile, as for what is being done at present, let us fast in such a way, brothers, that we give our meals to the poor; let us store what we were going to eat not in our purses but in the bowels of the poor, because the hands of the poor are Christ’s treasury. Whatever it receives, so that it may not perish on earth, the hand of the poor stores in heaven; for although what the poor person receives is consumed, the reward of the good work is nevertheless stored up in heaven.

**Note:** [Col. 1220D]

11. Perhaps: “and just as nothing is taken away from your body,” and so forth.

11. For if we make a point of spending our meals at dinner on refined flavors and multiplied courses, so that delicacies are not only not withheld from our body but even doubled, and thus nothing is diminished from your body, nothing is increased in your soul. I admonish you in this, brothers, fearing it more than believing anything evil about you. For I know that, by God’s favor, many of you continually receive strangers and frequently give to the poor. Therefore may what I suggest contribute to this end. But whoever does not do so—or perhaps has done so more slowly—should make this holy and wholly pleasing work a habit.

12. Although I believe that, with God inspiring you, whenever the festivals approach, your charity always preserves chastity and love for many days even with your own wives, nevertheless—even unnecessarily, since I believe that you already do this—I admonish you concerning the love of contemplation, to preserve chastity and love throughout the whole of Lent and until the end of Easter, with God’s help. Thus, in that most holy paschal solemnity, you may be clothed with the lamp of love, whitened by almsgiving, and adorned with prayers, vigils, fasts, and various heavenly and spiritual pearls—not only with friends but also with enemies—so that, as peacemakers, approaching the Lord’s altar with a free and secure conscience, you may receive his body and blood not for judgment but for healing.

**Note:** [Col. 1220D]

13. He wished it to be done with him. So one should read, or “he wished it to be done for himself.” The breviary has “he wished it to be done to himself.” Of the other sermons about which I spoke in the cited chapter 72 of *Isidoriana*, I will append only three; for either the others are not Isidore’s, as I then said, or they are excerpts from other works of Isidore, including the homily beginning “Brief is the happiness of this world,” namely from the *Synonyms*, book II, no. 91. As for what the Madrid editor had noted regarding sermon 4, no. 11—that the words “unless you eat,” and so forth, were, as it seemed to him, incongruously applied to baptism—I judged that this should be omitted; for the author of that sermon does not apply them to baptism, but infers from them that baptism is conferred upon little children not only for glory but also so that they may possess spiritual life within themselves.

13. But when we speak of almsgiving, let cramped poverty not be troubled. For anyone can fulfill everything when he has done what he could, because the perfect will to act is counted as the deed itself. But the person fulfills this who wishes to regard the poor person as himself and to give to the poor person just as he would wish it to be done to him if he himself were in such need. Whoever acts in this way fulfills the precepts of the New and Old Testaments, fulfilling that Gospel saying: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them.” For thus the law and the prophets are fulfilled, unto the glory to which the devout Lord may lead you by his protection, through the law of true and perfect love. Amen.

By the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and dominion without end, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON II — Against the Arians

1. Come, Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, who possess equal power with the Father. Come and crush the head of the great dragon, and tell us what you are, since this Arius teaches something other than what you are. Tell us, tell us; let us hear, so that we may refute the heretics.

Hear, dearest brothers, what the Lord says: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” According to divinity, he is truth and life; according to humanity, the way. But you, heretic Arius, who wish life and truth to be lesser in divinity, it follows that you do not reach the Father.

Yet still, Lord Jesus, crush the dragon’s head and tell us what you are with the Father. Let us hear you speaking, not the heretic blaspheming; tell us what you are with the Father. “I and the Father are one.” Say more: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” Say more still: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

2. Do you now believe, heretic, such authority? Or do you refuse to accept his testimony about himself and seek other witnesses? Behold, those who will convict you are brought forward.

Speak, Paul, witness of God, organ of holy Mother Church, who went even unto blood for this testimony and laid down your life lest you succumb to false doctrine. Speak. Let the one who fears conviction hear. You say to each person: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God.”

Do you hear, heretic, “equal with God”? Do you hear “the form of God”? And do you dare to call the Son lesser than the Father?

Let another witness come, so that the equity of truth may be confirmed by two or three witnesses.
