And you, holy Peter, say what the heavenly Father—not flesh and blood—revealed to you: “You are the Son of the living God.” And in the second epistle addressed to the nations: “We make known to you the power, foreknowledge, and greatness of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Do you hear, deceiver, power? Do you hear foreknowledge? Do you also hear greatness? In what respect, then, heretic, do you say that Christ is lesser?

But let a third witness enter, so that three may speak one true testimony concerning the one Trinity and the triune divinity. And you, holy John, who reclined upon the Savior’s breast and saw the Word of God above the heavenly wonders, speak, I say, what truth you hold concerning the Son of God:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word.”

And in his epistle: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know what is true and may be in his true Son; for he is the true God and eternal life.”

3. But you, poisonous serpent, by saying that the Son who is the true God is lesser, will not have eternal life. But to refute your obstinacy, let the Father himself bear witness to the Son, so that you seek and believe nothing further. For through the prophet he says:

“With you is the beginning on the day of your power.”

The Father is beginning; the Son is beginning; therefore the Father and the Son are beginning without any beginning. “With you,” he says, “is the beginning on the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

It is as if he were saying: “You proceeded from me so that the saints might be enlightened.” Clearly, dearest ones, there was no other reason why the very names of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should appear distinct except that holy people might be instructed.

But what was said to Moses by the very substance of the Trinity? “I am who I am”; and thus you shall say: “He who is has sent me.” Therefore the Son was generated from the womb in the splendor of the saints. But lest you understand this generation as carnal or temporal, hear how he begot him. “My heart,” he says, “has uttered forth a good word.” John, the witness, says: “In the beginning was the Word.” God the Father says: “My heart has uttered forth,” he says, “a good Word.” The prophet Habakkuk says: “The Word was walking.”

You hear “the Word,” and that the Word is in the beginning with God and is God. The testimony of the Trinity cries out against you throughout the whole world. And you, worst of Arians, bark like a rabid dog against the whole world?

4. But hear further, so that you may be more fully convicted that the perfect Trinity is one true God. For it is the Father’s voice to the Son through the prophet: “In the splendor,” he says, “of the saints, from the womb I begot you.” It is likewise the voice of that same Father through the prophet concerning the Holy Spirit: “The Spirit,” he says, “proceeded from me.”

The Son’s voice in the Gospel shows that the Father is in him and he in the Father, where he says: “The Father dwelling in me himself does the works.” It is likewise the voice of the same Son concerning the Holy Spirit, showing that just as the Spirit proceeds from the Father, so also from the Son himself, where he says to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they will be forgiven.”

Hence the words of the apostle Paul: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him.” If, then, the Son is in the Father and from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is likewise both in the Son and in the Father, the Trinity is not divided where there is perfect unity. Therefore let the pestilential, labyrinthine Arian depart—that dragon. Let him depart now, I say, confounded and guilty, because the Trinity is one God.

5. But how will my words benefit your perverse heresy, since you are a deaf asp, stopping your ears lest you hear the voices of those who enchant? Nevertheless, know that you will be devoured by the serpent’s rod when that shepherd has led back to his own fold the sheep whom you hold captive, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

Therefore this shepherd of ours, dearest ones, who feeds and rules with the rod, is himself our shepherd, himself our ruler, himself our maker, himself our architect. I see you as a great shepherd, Lord Jesus, feeding the sheep, seeking the wandering one, and carrying the one you have found back to your flock upon your shoulders with joy.

For I see you as a great architect, carrying the rod and performing many miracles with that rod. Therefore I greatly fear, brothers, an exposition of the rod; but when I consider the passages of the divine Scriptures, the rod is holy Mary, the rod is Christ himself, the rod is the cross. And by this rod, how many great and marvelous things he accomplished! He made ladders by which he raised fallen humanity to the Father. By these ladders, holy people ascended—those who were continent, united, and faithful—not by the steps of their feet but by the steps of their conduct.

6. If good conduct is sought, it is found everywhere. For each sex and every age has in the conduct of the saints an example for imitation [the text reads *unitationis*]. Let old men imitate the conduct of holy Tobit, who, though blind in body, showed the way of life to his son in his heart: the son led him by the hand on earth, while he raised the son to heaven by holy admonitions.

Let young men imitate holy Joseph, handsome in body but more handsome in mind, whom chastity so possessed that the threats of an immoral mistress could not violate the body whose mind the Lord already possessed. Let holy virgins imitate blessed Mary, the mother of their Lord. Let widows imitate the devout widow Anna. Let married women also imitate chaste Susanna.

For Mary, the virgin mother of Christ, fulfilled what she knew; Anna, the widow, persevered in prayers and fasts to the end; Susanna, chaste in marriage, went even to the danger of death for her modesty. Therefore now, married women, attend to what kind of imitation of this passage is proposed by Holy Scripture. It does not praise her because she was outwardly adorned with gold, necklaces, or expensive clothing, since inwardly she was certainly adorned with the modesty of chastity.

But Christ gave life to all those whom he instructed in good conduct. For this reason he himself deigned to be born from a woman, because both sexes were to be freed from death by him.

We have said many things, brothers. You have listened most attentively and eaten the Lord’s banquet most willingly. Therefore repay your minister in kind, so that, if he does not feed you with words, he may at least feed you with your prayers.

[Explicit.]

## SERMON III — Homily

1. Brothers, we ought to fear greatly the three causes through which the whole world perished: gluttony, greed, and pride. For through these three causes the devil deceived Adam, the first human being, saying: “On whatever day you eat from this tree, your eyes will immediately be opened.”

Let us always fear these three causes, brothers, lest, like Adam, we be condemned in hell. Against gluttony let us maintain abstinence; against greed, generosity; against pride, humility. For we know that we are called Christians and that we have a guardian angel, because the Savior himself said: “Amen, I say to you, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.”

2. For we must believe with certainty that all our works, by day as well as by night, at every hour—whether good or evil, whatever we do—are reported by that angel himself in the presence of God. When the angel urges us with counsel to perform good works, we believe that we always have that angel at our right hand. But when we think of doing evil or attempt to commit sins, whether grave or minor, then we have the wicked counselor, the devil. When we think of sinning and do sin, the devil rejoices and that holy angel grieves.

When we speak idle and perverse words, this is the devil’s counsel. But when we groan and sigh and think of doing some good work, then we have that holy angel of God as our counselor.

3. For the three evil works that we mentioned above—the devil supplied them to Adam through evil counsel: gluttony, greed, and pride. These three causes generate many evils: sacrilege, homicide, adultery, theft, avarice, lust, false testimony, anger, discord, and perjury. Through those three transgressions all these things were supplied to humanity by diabolical art [perhaps: “are supplied”].

By these dangers souls are bound in hell. Therefore let us take up the weapons of God’s angel, namely the cross of Christ. Let us set humility against pride, abstinence against gluttony, generosity in almsgiving against greed, true repentance against sacrilege, love of God and neighbor against homicide, continence against fornication, goodness and kindness against theft, generosity against avarice, chastity against lust, [the text has an asterisk here] patience, good harmony and true peace against discord, and fear of the Lord and the right path against perjury, holding the firmest faith before God and human beings with justice and holiness.

4. These are the angelic weapons, the strong breastplate, the firmest shield, and the helmet of salvation. Whoever carries these weapons with him in every place will not be able to be harmed by any devil; rather, he will be saved both here and forever.

O dearest brothers, we ought to arm ourselves so greatly against the worst enemy that we may be able to overcome him, because he is prepared like a thief to steal good works; he counsels and supplies evil. Many are deceived through the adversary’s boldness and a false security, and think among themselves, saying: “I am young, and I have time to enjoy the world; when I grow old, I will do penance.”

O wretched person, you who think such things, because you do not possess even the span of one hour of your life, nor the power of a single day.

5. Brothers, let this perverse presumption of security not deceive you; rather, let us always keep the day of death before our eyes, with fear and true repentance. Say: Where are the kings? Where are the rich? Where are their riches and their ornaments? They themselves passed away like a shadow; they vanished like a dream. Their gold, silver, and all their ornaments remained in this world, while they themselves are tormented without end in hell, where their worms do not die and their fire is not extinguished. In that hell there is no voice except groaning; there is no rest there except flame. Many seek the end of death and cannot die. For it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments.”

6. O brothers, understand what the Psalmist says: “The dead will not praise you, Lord, nor all those who descend into hell.” Brothers, how can those who are always in darkness, in a dark place, name God? They are always crying out:

“Woe to this darkness of a place, to this dark pit, to this obscure cavern, to this bitter place, to this most wretched life, to this painful dwelling! From such a short life, so long a death; from such slight consolation, so long a captivity; from such brief joy, so long a sorrow; from such small profit, so great a loss; from such little honor, such prolonged pains; from such slight pleasure, such bitter tears, such immense sighs, such mournful groans, such great anger and sadness!”

There the father does not help the son, nor the son the father; there no friend is found who can redeem a friend, nor brother who can aid a brother. There repentance is loved, but it is practiced too late. Woe to that harsh dwelling, that torturous flame, those immense torments!

7. There the wretched are with the wretched, the proud with the proud, murderers with murderers, adulterers with adulterers, wicked thieves with false merchants, false monks with false girls, false priests with false bishops, and laypeople likewise with the worst laypeople. There the most wicked women are with the most unfortunate prostitutes. All will be tormented by indescribable flames, and they will have no rest except on the Lord’s day of resurrection, as blessed Augustine says:

“On the Lord’s day of resurrection, at the hour when our Lord rose from the dead in the morning, the souls of the righteous come to visit their graves and say: ‘Farewell, good companion, because you treated me well in this world; good vessel, dearest friend. You consented more to the angelic weapons than to the assault of the devil, for it is written: “I wished to fast, to do penance, to give alms, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, to come to church, to hear and keep the Holy Scriptures, and to love God’s servants.” You consented to me and honored me, because you are God’s work, while I am the inspiration of life, created by God. Rest for a little while in peace, secure; I shall return to you in the eternal dwelling, so that you may see what kind of dwelling and how great a glory God has prepared for us forever. For blessed are those who serve him, and they shall shine with him like the sun,’ as the Lord himself says: ‘The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father.’ Then they will rejoice with me without end. For although there had been two desires—of the eyes and of the mouth—you did not consent to them. The time is near when you will receive eternal reward with me, and there you will rest forever and ever.”

8. Likewise, that sinful soul speaks with the most wicked angel Satan, together with its slander and vices, saying:

“Alas, alas, wretched body! Why did you do such great evils with me? And I was with Satan and with his vices, because you did not consent to the angelic weapons against the devil’s snares. For you desired to eat, drink, indulge in luxury, kill, commit adultery, fornicate, steal, covet, lie, bear false witness, and perform the works of the devil; and you did not do penance. Rather, in wicked presumption and negligence, you took delight. You lie in the depths, while I am tormented in hell. The day of judgment is near, when I shall return to you; and you will rise on the last day to receive the evils you committed in the world with the devil, the author of death. You will be with me in the condemnation of death and will be tormented without end forever and ever.”

O man who hears these things, tremble on account of your sins and negligences. While you have time and opportunity, hurry and do penance before the door of life is closed, so that you may securely receive the rewards of glory and eternal life with the angels of God and with all the saints forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON IV.—On the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter

1. The greatness of heavenly benefits exceeds the limitations of the human mind. Therefore divine Providence ordered that what reason, overcome by the magnitude of realities, could not contain within us, devoted faith should conceive, and that firm belief should nourish the understanding. Since, then, through the first transgression by Adam we had become subject to guilt and death by our origin, the Lord, looking down from on high, repaired us according to the character of our captivity by the gift of redemption. That is, in place of the death we owed, he offered a death he did not owe, because we had no means by which to live, nor did he have any by which to die.

2. He received material from our mortality so that, immortality having been bestowed from his own being, life might die for the dead. And because he was about to remove the assumed body from our eyes and carry it up among the stars, it was necessary for him on this day to consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that what was once offered as the price might continually be honored through the mystery. Since redemption for the salvation of human beings was continually and unceasingly taking place, the offering of redemption also had to be perpetual. That enduring victim was to live in memory, so that it might always be present in grace. It is truly the one and perfect sacrifice, to be judged by faith, not by appearance; not to be evaluated by external sight, but by the inward devotion of the heart.

3. Therefore heavenly authority rightly confirms that Christ’s flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. Let every uncertainty of unbelief depart, since the one who is the author of the gift is himself also the witness to its truth. For the invisible priest, by his word and secret power, transforms [perhaps, converts] visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying:

“Take and eat; for this is my body.”

And after repeating the act of sanctification he says:

“Take and drink; this is my blood” (Matthew 26:26–27).

Therefore, just as at the command of the Lord who ordered them, the heights of the heavens, the depths of the waves, and the vast expanses of the earth suddenly came into being from nothing, so by equal power, in the spiritual sacraments, the power of the Word commands and the effect obeys.

4. Consider, then, how great and how worthy of celebration are the benefits brought about by the power of divine blessing. And so that it should not seem new or impossible to you that earthly and mortal things are changed into Christ’s substance, question yourself, who have already been reborn in Christ. A short while ago you were alien to life, a stranger to mercy, and an exile, inwardly dead, from the way of salvation. Suddenly, initiated into Christ’s laws and renewed by saving mysteries, you passed into the body of the Church—not by seeing, but by believing—and from a son of perdition you merited, through hidden purity, to become an adopted son of God.

5. Remaining within visible measure, you became greater than yourself invisibly, without any increase in quantity. Though you remained the same person, you came to be far higher through the advances of faith. Nothing was added to you outwardly, yet you were wholly changed in the inner person. Thus, the human being became a son of Christ, and Christ was formed in the human mind.

Therefore, just as without bodily sensation, laying aside your former baseness, you suddenly put on a new dignity; and just as you believe—not with your eyes, but with your inner senses—that the Lord has healed in you what was wounded, cleansed what was defiled, and wiped away what was stained: so, when you approach the revered altar to be refreshed by saving food and drink, behold in faith the sacred body and blood of your Lord, marvel with reverence, raise your mind, receive him with the hand of your heart, and take him in above all by an inward drinking.

6. If that manna of the Law, of which it is written, “He rained manna upon them, that they might eat” (Psalm 77:24), tasted to each person according to what his desires craved—so that what was taken was one thing and what was seen another, while that invisible flavor was formed in each person’s senses—then that manna of the Law, falling from heaven through manifold sweetness, exceeded the quality of its nature and kind as perceived by the senses. And when the generosity of the giver adorned his creature with varied diversity, taste supplied what sight did not know. According to the recipient’s desire, novelty and dignity arose for that food; and the honeyed gift of that rain, with the manifold service of the dry shower, refreshed each person with different and unfamiliar flavors.

7. Since this is so, let what appetite accomplished there be accomplished here by faith. Thus we read: “A man approaches the deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Psalm 64:7). Therefore, what pleasure obtained there in the throat, let blessing work here in the senses. The very power of the one who consecrates strengthens us to recognize and receive the sacrifice of the true body.

May the one who was then hidden and prefigured in the manna now be manifest to you in grace. That he was prefigured in the appearance of that manna, the Prophet also clearly shows, saying: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:25). And what is the bread of angels except Christ, who satisfies them with the food of his love and the light of his splendor?

Concerning this bread the Prophet says: “On the sixth day you will gather twice as much, but on the Sabbath you will not gather.” It was given from the first day—that is, the Lord’s day—under the Law, but was withheld on the Sabbath alone.

8. Already then Christ is shown as to be received by the Church, to which the Lord’s resurrection consecrated Sunday, and is proclaimed as to be rejected by the Synagogue, to which observance of the Sabbath belonged. For this is the seventh day, which is deprived of the heavenly bread through deceit.

Concerning this bread the ancient history relates: “Neither did the one who had gathered more have too much, nor did the one who had prepared less find too little” (Exodus 16:18). This body, when dispensed by the priest, is as much in the small portion as it is known to be in the whole. When the church of the faithful receives it, it is shown to be as complete in each individual as it is full in all together. From this understanding the apostolic statement is derived: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little” (2 Corinthians 8:15).

9. If we were to place bread before hungry people to eat, it would not reach each person in its entirety, because each would receive a portion according to his share, divided and broken into smaller pieces. But with this bread, when it is received, each person has no less than all have. One receives the whole, two receive the whole, and many receive the whole, without diminution, because the blessing of this sacrament knows how to be distributed but does not know how to be consumed by distribution.

We also find the form of this sacrament expressed in the pages of the Jews. For we read of Melchizedek in Genesis: “Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought out bread and wine, and blessed Abraham; he was priest of God Most High” (Genesis 14:18–19). In this, while the future circumcision of the uncircumcised—that is, of the Gentiles—is blessed, the glory of the Church is proclaimed, and the people acquired from the Gentiles is placed before the unbelieving synagogue.

10. This Melchizedek, whose genealogy or origin was hidden from the knowledge of that time, prefigured this sacrifice of Christ through the offering of bread and wine. Concerning him the Prophet declares: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:4).

Blessed Moses also, speaking of that mystery, signifies wine and blood under one designation, demonstrating long beforehand the Lord’s passion in the patriarch’s blessing, saying: “He will wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Genesis 49:11). Observe how clearly it is established that the creature of wine is now called the blood of Christ.

11. Whatever more you ought to inquire concerning this twofold form, recognize it with the Lord himself as witness. “Unless,” he says, “you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

This testimony is most clear and powerful against the Pelagians, who, having seized upon impiety, presume to assert that baptism is to be given to infants not for life, but for the kingdom of heaven. For under those words of the Lord in which the Evangelist declares, “you will not have life in yourselves,” every soul lacking the gift of baptism must plainly be understood not merely to be deprived of glory but also of life.

The Lord himself showed that the wine of his blood is to be mixed with water, not only by tradition but also by the very manner of his passion: from his sacred side, blood and water flowed forth when it was struck by the lance. As the Prophet had long before foretold: “He struck the rock, and waters flowed” (Psalm 78:20). And the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Corinthians 10:4). You see that whoever drinks from Christ’s grace is followed by Christ’s mercy.

12. In Solomon too we read that this was foretold concerning Christ: “Wisdom,” he says, “built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1)—that is, he assumed a human body in which the fullness of divinity dwelt. And he added: “She hewed out seven pillars,” because the blessing of the Holy Spirit filled him with sevenfold grace.

“She slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine in the mixing bowl, and prepared her table.” And afterward: “Come, eat of my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you.”

Thus we read of wine mixed with water; let us now inquire why the Lord wished both to be mixed. When, at the wedding feast of the Jews, wine—that is, faith—failed among them, wine, I say, failed because the vineyard refused its fruit. Concerning it is said: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isaiah 5:2). Hence also the crown of thorns was placed on the Redeemer’s head.

13. Therefore, when at the time of the wedding feast—that is, when the Bridegroom was to be joined to his Church in Paschal rejoicing—the Lord changed water into wine, he plainly prefigured that multitudes of the Gentiles would live through the grace of his blood. That waters signify peoples is disclosed by the sacred writings. Thus we read: “The waters that you saw are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages” (Revelation 17:15).

We see the figure of the Gentiles represented in the waters, while the blood of the Lord’s passion is shown in the wine. Thus, when wine is mixed with water in the sacraments, the faithful people is incorporated into and joined to Christ, united with him by a kind of bond of perfect love, so that it can say with the Apostle: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or persecution?” and so forth (Romans 8:35).

14. God is mixed with the human being when, through sanctification, faith, a love of justice, mercy, and devotion are poured into the human breast. In this too, the fact that we know bread is made from numerous grains of wheat clearly signifies the unity of peoples.

For just as grain, prepared through the sustained care of the purifier, is brought by the labor of the mills into a bright form and gathered by water and fire into the substance of one bread, so various peoples and different nations, coming together in one faith, form from themselves one body of Christ.

The Christian people, like countless grains of wheat, is seen to have been gathered from sacrilegious nations through faith that purifies and sifts; when it is separated, it is collected into one, as the weeds of unbelievers pass away. And when, through instruction in the Testaments, it shines like grain prepared by the twofold labor of the mills, it is changed by its natural whiteness into the dignity of its first origin; and through the water of baptism, as through the fire of the Holy Spirit, it becomes the body of that eternal bread.

15. Therefore, just as grains cannot be separated from the union of the bread once it has been made, and just as water, once mixed with wine, cannot return to its own substance, so all the faithful and wise who recognize that they have been redeemed by Christ’s blood and passion must be joined to their head as inseparable members through faith, conduct, and the most ardent devotion.

They must be joined so firmly that they cannot be separated from him by will, by necessity, by any ambition for earthly hope, or finally even by death itself.

No one should doubt that primary creatures can pass, by the command of power and the presence of majesty, into the nature of the Lord’s body, when he sees that the human being himself has been made the body of Christ through the work of heavenly mercy.

Just as anyone who comes to faith, before the words of baptism, is still bound by the chain of his former debt, but, once these words have been spoken, is immediately stripped of every stain of sin, so, when creatures to be blessed are placed upon the sacred altars by heavenly words of blessing, before they are consecrated through the invocation of the supreme name, the substance present there is bread and wine. After Christ’s words, it is the body and blood of Christ.

16. What is surprising, then, if he who was able to create by a word can change by a word what has been created? Indeed, it seems a lesser miracle if he can change for the better what he is known to have made from nothing.

Consider what can be difficult for him who easily brought forth visible and invisible things by the command of his will; for whom it was easy to fashion the human being from the material of clay and clothe him also with the image of his divinity; for whom it is easy to call him back from the underworld, restore him from destruction, raise him from dust, lift him from earth to heaven, make an angel from a human being, render the human body like the body of his glory, and exalt his creation into participation in his kingdom.

May he who assumed the body of our weakness assume us into the body of his immortality. May he deign to prepare you by devout works for that glorious resurrection, he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# APPENDIX XIII. ON ECCLESIASTICAL DOGMAS (C, S)

## CHAPTER ONE.—On Faith in the Trinity

*[Note: [Col. 1227D]*

**Chapter I.** Compare this work with the Isidoriana, chapter 83, where I added Vezzosius’s preface and Hernandez’s observations concerning Bishop Bracharus of Hispalis as the author of this same work. From Vezzosius’s notes I shall select whatever seems more appropriate. Isidore discusses the arguments of the first chapters in many places. See Book II, *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 23. Bignaeus presents the text as follows: “Therefore the Father is the beginning, the principal name of divinity, because just as…”; after *principal* he notes in the margin: “perhaps, of the whole.”]*

[Col. 1227D]

We believe that there is one God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Father, because he has the Son; the Son, because he has the Father; the Holy Spirit, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and is coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Father, therefore, is the beginning of the Godhead: just as he was never not God, so he was never not Father. From him the Son was born; from him the Holy Spirit proceeds—not born, because he is not the Son; not unbegotten, because he is not the Father; not made, because he is not from nothing, but proceeds as God from God the Father and God the Son.

The Father is eternal because he has an eternal Son, whose eternal Father he is. The Son is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father. The Holy Spirit is eternal because he is coeternal with the Father and the Son.

The Trinity is not confused into one person, as Sabellius says, nor is divinity separated or divided in nature, as Arius blasphemes. Rather, the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God in nature in the holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER II.—On the Incarnation of Christ

*[Note: [Col. 1228D]*

**Chapter II.** The Codex of Mansi reads: “so that he who was the Son in the divinity of the Father might himself become, in man, the son of man.” A little later Bignaeus reads: “who was not the Son of God by birth.” “Therefore the Son of God…” and so forth. Later, the words “it is believed … with distinct separation” are omitted by Bignaeus, as are several other passages; the Maurist editors generally agree with Bignaeus among the appendices to the works of Saint Augustine.]*

The Father did not assume flesh, nor did the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone. Thus, he who was the Son of God in the divinity of God the Father became, in humanity, the son of the human mother, so that the name “Son” would not pass to another who was not the Son by eternal birth.

Therefore the Son of God became the son of the human being: according to the truth of nature, born from God as the Son of God; and according to the truth of nature, born from a human being as the son of a human being. Thus, the truth of the one begotten possessed the name “Son” by birth, not by adoption or designation, in both births, and one Son was true God and true human being.

We therefore do not confess two Christs or two Sons, but one Son, God and human being, whom for this reason we also call the only-begotten. He remains in two substances, as the truth of his nature has established—not with the natures confused or mixed, as the followers of Timothy wish, but united in fellowship.

God assumed the human being, and the human being passed into God—not through a mutability of nature, as the Apollinarians say, but through God’s gracious condescension. Thus God was not changed into human substance by assuming the human being, nor was the human being changed into God by being glorified, because alteration or mutability of nature produces both diminution and abolition of substance.

We believe that the holy Trinity is joined without confusion and distinguished without separation.

Therefore the Son of God was born from a human being, and not through a human being—that is, not from intercourse with a man, as Ebion says—but drawing flesh from the Virgin’s body and not bringing it with him from heaven, as Marcion, Origen, and Eutyches assert.

Nor was he born in appearance—that is, without flesh—as Valentinus claims; that is, he was not merely imagined or apparent, but had a true body.

He was not merely flesh from flesh, as Marcianus says, but one Son, true God from divinity and true human being from flesh: in divinity, the Word and God of the Father; in humanity, soul and flesh.

The soul was not without sensation and reason, as Apollinaris says, nor was the flesh without a soul, as Eunomius says. Rather, he had a soul with its reason and a body with its sensations, through which he endured the true pains of his flesh in the Passion and before the Passion.

## CHAPTER III.—That the Eternal God Was Born from a Virgin

*[Note: [Col. 1229D]*

**Chapter III.** Some copies read “from a virgin,” followed by lacunae: “so that the beginning of divinity…”; “as Eunomius wishes”; “nothing equal in grace, as he wishes…”; “nothing by persuasion or stealth…”; “as the Anthropomorphites [say]”; “nothing for himself,” and so forth. Vezzosius observes that it is uncertain or false that Melito taught God to be corporeal, and that Tertullian should be excused for saying “corporeal,” whatever is opposed to nothing.]*

[Col. 1229C]

He was not born from a Virgin in such a way that the human being received the beginning of divinity by being born, as though God had not existed before he was born from the Virgin, as Artemon, Berillus, and Marcellus taught. Rather, the eternal God and human being was born from the Virgin.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the Perfect Trinity

Let us believe that there is nothing created or servile in the Trinity, as Dionysius, the source of Arius, maintains; nothing unequal, as Eunomius and Arius maintain; nothing unequal in grace, as Aetius maintains; nothing earlier or later, lesser or greater, as Arius maintains; nothing foreign or serving another, as Macedonius maintains; nothing inserted by persuasion or stealth, as Manichaeus maintains; nothing corporeal, as Melito and Tertullian maintain; nothing represented corporeally, as the Anthropomorphite and Vadianus maintain; nothing invisible to the creatures in itself, as Origen maintains; nothing visible to creatures, as Fortunatus maintains; nothing differing in character or will, as Marcion maintains; nothing drawn down from the essence of the Trinity into the nature of creatures, as Plato and Tertullian maintain; nothing singular in function or incommunicable to another, as Origen maintains; nothing confused, as Sabellius maintains.

Rather, everything is perfect, because everything is from one and one is from everything; yet it is not solitary, as Praxeas and Silvanus presume in that accursed doctrine of the Pentapolis.

## CHAPTER V.—On *Homoousios*

*[Note: [Col. 1230D]*

**Chapter V.** Vezzosius reads: “the Son and the Holy Spirit.”]*

The Son is therefore *homoousios*—that is, coessential—in divinity with the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son; and the one Son, remaining God in the human being, is *homoousios* with God and the human being.

He remains in the glory of the Father, desirable to be seen by the angels. Just as the Father and the Holy Spirit are worshiped by the angels and by every creature, so too he is worshiped—not as a human being made apart from God, nor as Christ alongside God, as Nestorius blasphemes, but as the human being in God and God in the human being.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Resurrection

*[Note: [Col. 1230D]*

**Chapter VI.** Vezzosius reads “rises in truth” rather than “will rise.”]*

There will be a resurrection of all the dead, but one resurrection, simultaneously and once for all. There will not be a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of sinners, as the fable of dreamers claims, but one resurrection of all.

If that which falls is said to rise again, then our flesh will truly rise, just as it truly falls. Nor, according to Origen, will there be a transformation of bodies—that is, another new body in place of the flesh. Rather, the same corruptible flesh that falls, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous, will rise incorruptible, able either to suffer punishment for sins or to remain in eternal glory according to its merits.

## CHAPTER VII.—The Common Resurrection of All

*[Note: [Col. 1230D]*

**Chapter VII.** Some copies read “to be changed” (*mutandos*) rather than “to be transformed” (*immutandos*); the meaning is equivalent.]*

[Col. 1230B]

There will be a resurrection of all human beings. If it will be of all, then all die, so that the death derived from Adam may rule over all his children, while that privilege remains in the Lord which is said specifically concerning him: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 16:10). His flesh did not see corruption.

We have accepted this view because the great multitude of the Fathers transmitted it. Yet there are other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that those who are to be found alive at the Lord’s coming, while their souls remain in their bodies, will be changed into incorruption and immortality; they regard this as equivalent to rising from the dead, since such people lay aside mortality through transformation rather than through death.

Whichever view one follows, one is not a heretic—unless one becomes a heretic through contentiousness. It is enough, according to the rule of the Church, to believe that the resurrection of the flesh will come from death.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the Judgment of the Living and the Dead

[Col. 1230C]

When we say in the Creed that, at the Lord’s coming, the living and the dead will be judged, we believe that this signifies not only the righteous and sinners, as Diodorus thinks, but also those who will be found alive in the flesh. Some believe that these will still die; others that they will be changed. According to the latter view, they will be raised or transformed immediately and judged together with those who died earlier.

## CHAPTER IX.—After Judgment, No Restoration Is to Be Expected

After the resurrection and judgment, let us not believe that there will be a restoration of all things, as Origen deliriously claims: that demons or wicked human beings, after their torments—as though purified by punishments—will either return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or be granted fellowship with the righteous. He holds this because it would accord with divine compassion that none of the rational creatures should perish, but all should somehow be saved.

Rather, let us believe in the judge of all and righteous retributor, who said: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46), so that they may receive the fruit of their works.

## CHAPTER X.—The Creation of the World and of the Angels

In the beginning God created heaven and earth and water from nothing. While darkness still concealed the water itself and the water hid the earth, the angels and all the heavenly powers were made, so that God’s goodness would not be idle, but would have beings in whom to display its goodness through the many ages beforehand. Thus this visible world was made and adorned from the material that God had created.

## CHAPTER XI.—God Alone Is Incorporeal

Nothing should be believed to be incorporeal and invisible by nature except God alone—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is rightly believed to be incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and encompasses all things. He is therefore also invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal.

## CHAPTER XII.—Every Creature Is Corporeal

*[Note: [Col. 1231D]*

**Chapter XII.** The author of this work appears to call everything created “corporeal.” See Book II of *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 24, and *The Differences of Things*, numbers 100 and following.]*

Every creature is corporeal: the angels and all the heavenly powers are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual creatures to be corporeal because they are circumscribed locally, as is also the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh, and the demons, who in substance belong to the angelic nature.

## CHAPTER XIII.—Intellectual Natures Are Immortal

We believe intellectual natures to be immortal because they lack flesh and have no means by which they can fall, so as to require a necessary resurrection after their ruin.

## CHAPTER XIV.—How the Human Soul Is Created

*[Note: [Col. 1231D]*

**Chapter XIV.** John of Hispalis copied this chapter, as I said in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 83, numbers 18 and following. In his text one reads, followed by lacunae: “and not at once…”; “Cyril, and many of the Latins…”; “with the consequence of nature serving.” There are other matters of this kind, which are closer to Bignaeus’s edition than to Vezzosius’s.]*

Human souls were not present from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, as Origen imagines. Nor are they sown together with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latins assert, as though they were following the continuity of nature.

Rather, we say that only the Creator of all knows the creation of the soul. Only the body is generated through the union of marriage; by God’s judgment it is coagulated in the womb, joined together, and formed. Once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being consisting of soul and body may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance.

## CHAPTER XV.—There Are Not Two Souls in a Human Being

We do not say that there are two souls in one human being, as James and other Syrians write: one animal soul, by which the body is animated and which is mixed with the blood, and another spiritual soul, which supplies reason.

Rather, we say that there is one and the same soul in the human being. Through its association it gives life to the body, and by its reason it orders itself, possessing within itself freedom of choice, so that in the thought of its own substance it may choose what it wills.

## CHAPTER XVI.—The Human Soul Is Immortal

We believe that only the human being has a substantial soul, which lives when separated from the body and actively retains its senses and faculties. It does not die with the body, as Aratus asserts, nor after a short interval, as Zeno says, because it lives substantially.

## CHAPTER XVII.—The Souls of Brute Animals

*[Note: [Col. 1231D]*

**Chapter XVII.** Some copies read “by an incitement” rather than “by incitements.”]*

The souls of animals, however, are not substantial. They are born with the flesh through the vitality of the flesh itself, and they end and die with the death of the flesh. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander think, but are driven by every impulse of nature.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—The Soul Is Infused

The human soul does not die with the flesh, because, as we said above, it is not sown with the flesh. Rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, the soul is created by God’s judgment and infused, so that the human being may live within the womb and thus emerge into the world by birth.

## CHAPTER XIX.—The Two Substances of the Human Being

*[Note: [Col. 1231D]*

**Chapter XIX.** Some copies read “flesh” rather than “body,” in both occurrences.]*

The human being consists of only two substances: soul and body. The soul has its reason, and the body its senses. Yet the body does not move these senses without the association of the soul. The soul, however, retains its reason even without the body.

## CHAPTER XX.—Soul and Spirit Are the Same

There is no third substance, spirit, in the human being, as Didymus maintains. Rather, the soul itself is called “spirit,” either because of its spiritual nature or because it breathes within the body.

The soul is called *anima* because it animates the body for living or gives it life. But the third element, which the Apostle introduces together with soul and body, should be understood as the grace of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle prays that it may remain whole in us (1 Thessalonians 5:23), lest through our fault it be diminished or driven away from us, because “the Holy Spirit will flee the deceitful person” (Wisdom 1:5).

## CHAPTER XXI.—On Free Choice

*[Note: [Col. 1231D]*

**Chapter XXI.** Some copies read “he might avoid” rather than “he might correct.” Vezzosius thinks that what is said—“that we should assent to saving inspiration is in our power”—appears to savor of Semi-Pelagianism. The words beginning “Yet not to obtain…” and the following thirty chapters are absent from the Maurist copy and from most other manuscripts; in some copies they have been inserted from Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, from the Council of Carthage against the Pelagians, and from the Second Council of Orange. Nevertheless, as Vezzosius observes, Thomasius considered these additions necessary.]*
Man was entrusted to the freedom of his own will immediately at his first creation, so that, with only the vigilance of his mind striving alongside it, he might also persevere in keeping the commandment, if he wished to remain in that condition in which he had been created. But after he fell through the serpent’s deception by means of Eve, he lost the goodness of his nature and likewise the strength of his will—not, however, his capacity for choice, lest the avoidance of sin not be his own act, and lest what he had not wiped away by his own choice be forgiven by merit. Freedom of choice therefore remains for seeking salvation—that is, rational will—but only after God has first admonished and invited him to salvation, so that he may choose, follow, or act in response to the opportunity for salvation, that is, through God’s inspiration. But that he may obtain what he chooses, follows, or undertakes in response to that opportunity, we freely confess to be God’s doing. Thus we have the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy; that we should assent to saving inspiration is within our power; that we should attain what we desire by assenting to the admonition is a divine gift; that we should not slip after attaining the gift of salvation belongs both to our diligence and likewise to heavenly assistance; that we should slip belongs to our power and our negligence. Yet it is not possible to obtain [salvation] without him who makes those who seek find, who opens to those who knock, and who gives to those who ask. Therefore, just as we believe that we possess the beginning of our salvation through God’s mercy and inspiration, so we freely confess that the choice of our nature follows divine inspiration. Accordingly, that we should not fall away from the goodness either of nature or of merit belongs both to our diligence and likewise to heavenly assistance; that we should fall belongs to our power and our negligence.

### CHAPTER XXII—Grace

[Note: [Col. 1232D]

**CHAPTER XXII.** *Ille* (“he”); another reading, *olim ille* (“formerly he”). These words, *liberum enim arbitrium*, etc., which are set off by quotation marks, are by Innocent I and are also reported by Celestine I.]

It must be believed with the utmost firmness that, through Adam’s transgression, all human beings lost their natural possibility and innocence, and that no one can rise from the depth of that ruin through free choice unless the grace of the merciful God has raised him up: “For free choice, having suffered this, while using its goods too recklessly, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression; and thereafter it found no way by which it could rise. Deceived in its freedom forever, it would have remained overwhelmed beneath the weight of this ruin, unless Christ’s coming, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised it up; for through the cleansing of new regeneration he purged every past fault by the washing of his baptism.”

### CHAPTER XXIII—No one is good of himself

No one is good by himself unless he who alone is good has granted him participation in himself.

### CHAPTER XXIV—Perseverance in good comes from God

Even one renewed by the grace of baptism is not capable of overcoming the devil’s snares and conquering the desires of the flesh unless, through God’s daily assistance, he has received perseverance in a good way of life.

### CHAPTER XXV—Free choice

[Col. 1233B]

That no one uses free choice well except through Christ, the same teacher proclaims in the letter sent to the Council of Milevis, saying: “Understand at last, O doctrine of the most perverse minds, that freedom itself so deceived the first human being that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from this unless the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored to him the condition of his former freedom.”

### CHAPTER XXVI—Merits

[Note: [Col. 1233D]

**CHAPTER XXVI.** *Placeat* (“may it please”); another reading, *placet* (“it pleases”); and *accepimus* (“we have received”), for *accipimus* (“we receive”). And below, the plural forms *retulistis*, *vidistis*, and *dixistis* (“you have reported,” “you have seen,” “you have said”).]

All the efforts, works, and merits of the saints must be referred to the glory and praise of God, because no one pleases him for any other reason than that which he himself has granted. In this opinion the authoritative rule of Pope Zosimus, of blessed memory, directs us; for, writing to the bishops of the whole world, he says: “We, however, at God’s prompting—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—reported everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops.” The African bishops venerated this statement, radiant with the light of the purest truth, with such honor that they wrote to the same man as follows: “But that which you placed in the letter you arranged to be sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Yet we acted at God’s prompting,’ etc., we understand to have been said in such a way that, as you passed swiftly by, you cut down with the sword of truth those who exalt human freedom against God’s assistance. For what did you attribute to free choice so much as the fact that you referred everything to the awareness of our humility? And yet you faithfully and wisely recognized that this had been done at God’s prompting, and you truthfully and confidently said so. For this reason, surely, because ‘the will is prepared by the Lord,’ and so that they may do something good, he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations (Proverbs 8:25, according to the Septuagint). ‘As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God’ (Romans 8:14), so that we may neither feel that our free choice is absent nor doubt that, in every good movement of the human will, his assistance is stronger.”

### CHAPTER XXVII—Whatever is good comes from God

God works in the hearts of human beings and within free choice itself in such a way that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of a good will are from God, because through him we can do something good, and without him we can do nothing.

### CHAPTER XXVIII—The power of grace

326 Whoever says that the grace of God, by which we are justified through Jesus Christ our Lord, is effective only for the remission of sins already committed, and not also as the assistance of grace so that sins may not be committed, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXIX—Understanding comes from grace

[Note: [Col. 1234D]

**CHAPTER XXIX.** *Per ipsum* (“through him”); another reading, *per ipsam* (“through her/it”).]

[Col. 1234A]

Whoever says that God’s grace through Jesus Christ helps us not to sin only because through him understanding of the commandments is revealed and opened to us, so that we know what we ought to desire and what to avoid, but that through it we are not enabled both to love doing what we have recognized must be done and to be capable of doing it, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXX—The priests’ prayers

Let us also consider the sacramental rites of priestly supplications, which, handed down by the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in every Catholic Church, so that the rule of praying may establish the rule of believing. For when the bishops of holy congregations discharge the office of an embassy entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine mercy; and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, once the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may recover through receiving the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of repentance may be granted to the fallen; and finally that, once catechumens have been brought to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them. That these things are not requested from the Lord superficially or in vain is shown by the outcome of the matters themselves, since God deigns to draw many people from every kind of error, transferring them, rescued from the power of darkness, into the kingdom of the Son of his love, and making vessels of mercy out of vessels of wrath. The whole of this is perceived to be so entirely a work of God that, whenever such people are enlightened or corrected, thanksgiving and confession of praise are always rendered to God who effects it.

### CHAPTER XXXI—Exorcism and exsufflation

We should also contemplate, with attentive consideration, that which the holy Church uniformly practices throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. When either infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the fountain of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy, so that it may then truly become evident when “the ruler of this world is cast out” (John 12:31), and how “the strong man” is first bound and afterward his goods are plundered (Mark 3:27), being transferred into the possession of the victor, who “leads captivity captive and gives gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19).

### CHAPTER XXXII—Grace and free choice

[Note: [Col. 1234D]

**CHAPTER XXXII.** “Let us confess the author,” namely, the holy Celestine. And, “let us not doubt that from his grace.”]

We confess God to be the author of all good affections and works, of all efforts, and of every virtue by which one turns toward God from the beginning of faith. Nor do we doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through whom it comes about that we begin both to will and to do something good. By this assistance and gift of God, free choice is not taken away but liberated, so that what was dark becomes bright, what was crooked becomes straight, what was weak becomes healthy, and what was imprudent becomes provident (Philippians 2:13). For God’s goodness toward all human beings is so great that he wants the merits that are his gifts to be ours, and for what he has bestowed he will bestow eternal rewards. He works within us so that we both will and do what he wills; nor does he allow the things he has given us to be inactive within us—things to be exercised, not neglected—so that we too may be co-workers with God’s grace. And if we see anything in us growing weak through our own slackness, let us diligently return to him who heals all our weaknesses, redeems our life from destruction, and to whom we say daily: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13).

### CHAPTER XXXIII—Adam was created immortal

[Col. 1235A]

Whoever says that the first human being, Adam, was made mortal, so that whether he sinned or did not sin he would die in the body—that is, depart from the body—not by the merit of sin but by the necessity of nature, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER XXXIV—On baptizing infants

Whoever denies that newborn infants should be baptized, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but derive nothing from Adam’s original sin that is cleansed by the washing of regeneration—so that it follows that in them the form of baptism “for the remission of sins” is understood to be not true but false—let him be anathema. For what the Apostle says, “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12), must be understood in no other way than the Catholic Church, spread everywhere, has always understood it. For this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sins personally, are therefore truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have acquired through generation may be cleansed in them.

### CHAPTER XXXV—We are all truly sinners

Whoever thinks that what the holy apostle John said—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”—should be understood to mean that, out of humility, we ought not to say that we have no sin, but not because this is true, let him be anathema. For the Apostle continues and adds: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Here it is sufficiently clear that this is said not merely humbly but also truthfully. For the Apostle could have said: “If we say, ‘We have no sin,’ we exalt ourselves, and humility is not in us.” But when he says, “We deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” he sufficiently shows that whoever says he has no sin is not speaking truth but falsehood.

### CHAPTER XXXVI—All must pray for the forgiveness of sins

Whoever says that the saints say “Forgive us our debts” in the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:12) for this reason: not that they say it for themselves, since this petition is no longer necessary for them, but for the other sinners who are among their people; and that therefore each of the saints does not say “Forgive me my debts” but “Forgive us our debts,” so that the just person is understood to ask this for others rather than for himself, let him be anathema. For the apostle James was holy and just when he said: “For we all offend in many ways” (James 3:2). Why else was “all” added unless this statement was meant to correspond to the psalm where we read: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2)? And in the prayer of the wisest Solomon: “There is no one who does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7:21). And in the book of holy Job: “He seals the hand of every human being, so that every person may know his weakness” (Job 37:7). Hence Daniel, also holy and just, when he said in prayer in the plural, “We have sinned; we have committed iniquity” (Daniel 9:5), together with the other things that he truthfully and humbly confesses there, lest anyone think—as some maintain—that he was speaking not of his own sins but of those of his people, afterward said: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God.” He did not say “our sins,” but mentioned both those of his people and his own, since, like a prophet, he foresaw those who would later understand this so wrongly.

### CHAPTER XXXVII—Debts are forgiven even to the saints

Whoever wishes the very words of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), to be spoken by the saints in such a way that they say this humbly but not truthfully, let him be anathema. For who could tolerate someone praying and lying not to human beings but to the Lord himself—saying with his lips that he wishes his debts to be forgiven while saying in his heart that he has no debts requiring forgiveness?

### CHAPTER XXXVIII—Adam’s fall

If anyone says that, through the offense of Adam’s transgression, the human being was not changed entirely—that is, in body and soul—for the worse, but believes that, while the soul’s freedom remained unharmed, only the body became subject to corruption, he is deceived by Pelagius’ error and contradicts the Scripture that says: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4); and: “Do you not know that to whomever you obey, and by whom anyone is overcome, he is made that one’s slave” (Romans 6:16; 2 Peter 2:19)?

### CHAPTER XXXIX—Adam’s sin in his descendants

If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression harmed Adam alone and not also his descendants, or declares that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, but not sin itself, which is the death of the soul, passed through one human being into the entire human race, he makes God unjust by contradicting the Apostle, who says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all human beings sinned” (Romans 5:18).

### CHAPTER XL—Grace

[Note: [Col. 1235D]

**CHAPTER XL.** Another version: “If anyone says that grace can be conferred in response to human invocation,” etc.]

If anyone says that God’s grace can be conferred by human invocation, but not that grace itself makes us invoke, he contradicts the prophet Isaiah—or the Apostle saying the same thing: “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I appeared openly to those who were not asking about me” (Isaiah 65:1; Romans 10:20).

### CHAPTER XLI—Good will comes from God

If anyone maintains that, in order that we may be cleansed from sin, God awaits our will, but does not confess that even our willing to be cleansed comes about in us through the infusion and working of the Holy Spirit, he resists the Holy Spirit himself, who says through Solomon: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 19:14, according to the Septuagint). He also resists the Apostle’s salutary proclamation: “It is God who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing, according to his good will” (Philippians 2:13).

### CHAPTER XLII—Grace works everything

If anyone says that not only the increase of faith but also its beginning, and the very affection of belief by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and arrive at the regeneration of holy baptism, is naturally present in us rather than coming through the gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who turns our will from unbelief to faith and from impiety to piety—he is shown to be an adversary of apostolic teaching, since the blessed Apostle Paul says: “We are confident that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6). And: “It has been granted to you on Christ’s behalf not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:28). And: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift” (Ephesians 2:8). For those who say that the faith by which we believe in God is natural thereby define all who are alien to the Church of Christ as, in some sense, believers.

### CHAPTER XLIII—Everything is owed to grace

If anyone says that divine mercy is granted to us who believe, will, desire, strive, devote ourselves, ask, seek, and knock without God’s grace, but does not confess that our believing, willing, and ability to do all these things as we ought come about in us through the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit; and if he adds the assistance of grace to human humility or obedience, but does not agree that our being obedient and humble is itself a gift of that grace, he resists the Apostle, who says: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7); and: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (ibid., 15:10).

### CHAPTER XLIV—Human beings can do nothing without God

If anyone affirms that, by the power of nature, without the illumination and inspiration of the Holy Spirit—which gives everyone sweetness in assenting and truth in believing—one can think or choose, as is necessary, anything good pertaining to the salvation of eternal life, or assent to saving—that is, evangelical—preaching, he is deceived by a heretical spirit and does not understand God’s voice in the Gospel, which says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); nor the Apostle’s words: “We are not competent of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our competence is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

### CHAPTER XLV—God alone draws the human being

[Note: [Col. 1237D]

**CHAPTER XLV.** Acts of the Council of Orange: “For he asserts the free choice of all,” etc., with *non* (“not”) omitted.]

If anyone maintains that some can come to the grace of baptism through mercy and others through free choice—which is acknowledged to have been corrupted in all who were born from the transgression of the first human being—he is proved alien to the right faith. For he does not assert that everyone’s free choice was weakened by the sin of the first human being; or at least he thinks it was injured in such a way that some are nevertheless able, by themselves and without God’s revelation, to seek out the ministry of eternal salvation. The Lord himself proves how contrary this is, for he testifies that not merely some but no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). So also he says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17); and the Apostle says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

### CHAPTER XLVI—Free choice

The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; and what was lost cannot be restored except by the one from whom it could have been given. Hence Truth says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

### CHAPTER XLVII—Grace

Even if human nature had remained in the integrity in which it was created, it could in no way preserve itself without the assistance of its Creator. Therefore, since without God’s grace it cannot preserve the salvation it received, how will it be able to restore without God’s grace what it lost?

### CHAPTER XLVIII—Whether grace is nature

Just as the Apostle says most truly to those who wish to be justified by the law and have fallen away from grace, “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is most truly said to those who think that the grace commended and received by the faith of Christ is nature: “If righteousness comes through nature, then Christ died for nothing.” For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature already existed here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: through him the law was to be fulfilled, for he said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17), and through him the nature lost through Adam was to be restored, for he said that he had come to seek and save what had perished.

### CHAPTER XLIX—Repetition of the foregoing

According to the statements of the holy Scriptures written above, and the definitions of the ancient Fathers, we ought, God being propitious, both to preach and to believe this: through the sin of the first human being the human race was so inclined that thereafter no one could love God as was fitting, believe in God, or do what is good for God’s sake unless the grace of divine mercy had first gone before him. Therefore we believe that the illustrious faith of righteous Abel, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the whole multitude of the ancient saints—which the Apostle Paul praises in their honor (Hebrews 11 and following)—was bestowed not through the goodness of nature previously given in Adam, but through God’s grace. We know and believe that, even after the Lord’s coming, this grace is conferred on all who desire to be baptized not as something possessed by free choice but as a gift of Christ, according to what has already often been said and what the Apostle Paul proclaims: “It has been granted to you on Christ’s behalf not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29); and: “God, who began a good work in you, will bring it to completion until the day of our Lord” (ibid., 1:6); and: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift” (Ephesians 2:8). And, concerning himself, the Apostle says: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25). [Col. 1238B] He did not say, “Because I was faithful,” but “so that I might be faithful.” And: “What do you have that you did not receive?” And: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). And: “No one has anything unless it has been given to him from above” (John 3:27).

### CHAPTER L—The human will after baptism

We also believe, in accordance with the Catholic faith, that after receiving the grace of baptism all the baptized, with Christ assisting and cooperating, can and ought—if they are willing to labor faithfully—to fulfill what pertains to the salvation of the soul. But we not only do not believe that some have been predestined by divine power to evil; if there are people who wish to believe so great an evil, we pronounce anathema upon them with complete abhorrence.

### CHAPTER LI—Whence merits begin

In every good work, we do not begin and then receive assistance through God’s mercy; rather, he himself, without any preceding good merits, first inspires in us both faith and love of himself, so that we may faithfully seek the sacraments of baptism and, after baptism, with his assistance, be able to fulfill what pleases him. Therefore it must be believed most clearly that the wondrous faith of the thief whom the Lord recalled to the homeland of paradise (Luke 23:43), of the centurion Cornelius to whom the Lord’s angel was sent (Acts 10:1), and of Zacchaeus, who was worthy to receive the Lord himself (Luke 19:6), was not from nature but was granted through the generosity of divine grace.

### CHAPTER LII—Who are to be regarded as baptized

[Note: [Col. 1237D]

**CHAPTER LII.** This is chapter 22 of the Maurist edition, in which, as I said, the preceding material is omitted. Instead of *Paulini*, some copies have *Paulianistae*; instead of *Montani*, *Montanitae*; and instead of *Theodosius*, *Theodorus* or *Theudotus*.]

331 There is one baptism, but it is in the Church, where there is one faith, and where it is administered in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Therefore, if some have been baptized among those heretics who baptize with confession of the Holy Trinity and come to us, they should indeed be received as baptized, so that the invocation or confession of the Holy Trinity is not annulled. But they must be fully taught and instructed in the sense in which the mystery of the Holy Trinity is held in the Church; and if they consent to believe or agree to confess it, they should, already cleansed by the integrity of faith, be confirmed by the laying on of hands. If they are infants or unintelligent persons who cannot grasp the teaching, those who present them should answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism; and thus, strengthened by the laying on of hands and chrism, they should be admitted to the mysteries of the Eucharist.

But those who were baptized among heretics without invocation of the Holy Trinity and who come to us, we declare ought to be baptized, not rebaptized. For we must not believe that those have been baptized who were not immersed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit according to the rule established by the Lord—such as the Paulinians, Proclians, Borborites, Siphori, now called Bonosians; the Photinians, Montanists, and Manichaeans; and the various offshoots of impiety, or the other plagues arising from these groups or belonging to their orders—those who introduce two unknown principles, such as Cerdon and Marcion; opposing principles, such as the Manichaeans; three barbarous principles, such as the Sethians and Theodosius; many principles, such as Valentinus; or those who hold that Christ was a human being without God, such as Cerinthus, Ebion, Artemon, and Photinus. If any of these, I say, come to us, they are not to be asked whether they have been baptized or not, but only this: whether they believe the faith of the Church; and then they are to be baptized with ecclesiastical baptism.

### CHAPTER LIII—The Eucharist

[Note: [Col. 1239D]

**CHAPTER LIII.** “Daily,” etc. Compare chapter 18 of book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, with the notes. The Maurist edition has: “provided that the mind is not inclined to sin.”]

I neither praise nor condemn receiving communion of the Eucharist daily. Nevertheless, I advise and urge that communion be received every Sunday, provided that the mind is not inclined to sin. For I say that someone who still has the will to sin is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified by it. Therefore, even if someone is troubled by sin, provided that he has no further desire to sin, let him approach the Eucharist without fear and confidently, if he makes satisfaction with tears and prayers before communicating and trusts in the Lord’s mercy, which customarily forgives sins to sincere confession. But I say this of one who is not weighed down by capital and mortal sins. As for one oppressed by mortal crimes committed after baptism, I urge him first to make satisfaction through public penance and then, reconciled by the priest’s judgment, to join the communion, if he wishes to receive the Eucharist not for his judgment and condemnation. We do not deny, however, that mortal crimes may be absolved through private satisfaction, but only after the secular manner of life has first been changed, religious devotion confessed through correction of life, and continual—indeed perpetual—mourning undertaken, with God’s mercy; and only so that he does the opposite of those things for which he repents, and receives the Eucharist every Sunday, suppliant and submissive, until death.

### CHAPTER LIV—Penance

[Col. 1239C]

True penance is not committing things for which one must repent, and mourning what has been committed. Satisfaction in penance is cutting off the causes of sins and not allowing access to their suggestions.

### CHAPTER LV—Divine promises

[Note: [Col. 1239D]

**CHAPTER LV.** “As Papias,” etc. The Maurist edition has: “As Papias, with Irenaeus as his authority, Irenaeus, Tertullian,” etc. Vezzosius concludes from Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*, the chapter on Papias, that both texts are corrupt. Bignaeus reports it as follows: “As Papias, or Cerinthus, and Tertullian, and Lactantius agree.” In the text Vezzosius has *post mille* (“after a thousand”); but in the note he more correctly gives *per mille* (“for a thousand”) with the others. He adds that Nepos was earlier than this opinion concerning a double resurrection.]

In the divine promises, let us expect nothing earthly or transient, as the Meletians hope; nor the union of marriage, as Cerinthus and Marcion rave; nor anything pertaining to food or drink, as Tertullian and Lactantius agree, following Papias on the authority of Irenaeus. Nor let us hope that Christ’s kingdom will be on earth for a thousand years after the resurrection and that the saints will reign with him in delights, as Nepos taught, inventing a first resurrection of the righteous and a second of the ungodly, and placing between these two resurrections of the dead nations ignorant of God, to be preserved in the flesh in the corners of the earth. After the thousand-year reign of the righteous on earth, these nations, instigated by the devil, are to be stirred up to battle against the righteous who reign; and, while the Lord fights for the righteous, they are to be restrained by a fiery rain, and then, having died, are to be resurrected with the others who had previously died in impiety for eternal punishments in incorruptible flesh.

### CHAPTER LVI—No one is saved except with God as author

We believe that no one comes to salvation unless invited by God; that no one who has been invited works out his salvation unless God assists; that no one merits assistance unless he prays; and that no one perishes by God’s will, but by his permission, in accordance with the choice of free will, lest the free power once attributed to human beings be forced into servile necessity.

### CHAPTER LVII—Evil is not from God

[Note: [Col. 1240D]

**CHAPTER LVII.** Another version: “Evil or wickedness was not created by God but invented by the devil, who,” etc.; the continuation is understood, in the manner of Isidore.]

Evil or wickedness was not created by God but invented by the devil, who himself was created good by God. But because, as a rational creature, he had been entrusted by God with free choice and had received the capacity for thought, he turned his knowledge of good toward evil and, by thinking many things, became the inventor of evil. He envied in others what he had lost in himself; and, not content to perish alone, he persuaded others so that he who had been the inventor of his own wickedness might become the author of theirs as well. Thus evil or wickedness spread to the other rational creatures.

### CHAPTER LVIII—Nothing except God is immutable by nature

From this we recognize that nothing is immutable by nature except God alone—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who cannot be changed from the good, because he possesses goodness by nature and cannot be anything other than good.

### CHAPTER LIX—Stability in the angels

[Note: [Col. 1240D]

**CHAPTER LIX.** The Maurist edition has *suo Domino servaverunt* (“they preserved for their Lord”), which Vezzosius rightly considers the correct reading. But perhaps *servantes* (“preserving”) should be changed to *servaverunt* (“they preserved”).]
