The angels who persevere in the blessedness in which they were created do not possess the good by nature, so that they were not changed along with the others; rather, they preserved by free choice a good will, the goodness of their condition, and faith in their Lord. For this reason they are deservedly called holy angels by the Lord himself: they retained the holiness of free choice and, by the example of their companions, did not deviate from the good.

### CHAPTER LX—Nothing by nature is evil

[Note: [Col. 1240D]

**CHAPTER LX.** This chapter and the following two are absent from the editions of Bignaeus and the Maurists.]

The true faith, which is Catholic, confesses the substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, to be good, and declares that evil has no nature, because God, the creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good. Hence the devil too would have been good if he had remained in that in which he was made. But although he misused his natural excellence and did not stand in the truth, he did not pass into an opposing substance; rather, he departed from the highest good, to which he ought to have adhered.

### CHAPTER LXI—The angels’ happiness

The angelic powers that remained fixed in divine love, while the proud angels fell, received this reward as a gift: they are no longer wounded by any rust of creeping guilt; they remain without end in the contemplation of their Creator, and, being thus created, persist in eternal stability.

### CHAPTER LXII—The angels’ free will

The angels were created in such a way that, if they wished, they could remain in the light of blessedness; but if they wished, they could also have fallen. Hence Satan fell with the legions that followed him. But after his fall the angels who persevered were so confirmed that they could not fall at all, because they received the power of immutability so that they would never again fall at all.

### CHAPTER LXIII—Marriage

Marriage is good, but for the sake of children and to restrain fornication.

### CHAPTER LXIV—Continence

Continence is better, but it is not sufficient by itself for blessedness if it is maintained solely out of love of chastity; it must also be chosen with the desire to devote oneself to the Lord. Otherwise it seems rather a divorce from marriage than a pursuit of chastity.

### CHAPTER LXV—Virginity

Virginity surpasses both goods, because it overcomes both nature and struggle: nature through bodily integrity, and struggle through the peace of chastity, which is at peace solely through love of purity.

### CHAPTER LXVI—The choice of foods

It is good to take food with thanksgiving and to eat whatever God has commanded. To abstain from certain things, not as though they were evil but as though they were unnecessary, is not evil. To moderate their use according to necessity and time is properly Christian.

### CHAPTER LXVII—Marriage and food

[Note: [Col. 1241D]

**CHAPTER LXVII.** Some copies have *vel mali causas percipientibus* (“or to those who understand them as causes of evil”); and *Encraticorum* (“of the Encratites”) instead of *Hierachitarum* (“of the Hieracites”).]

To call marriage evil, or to compare it with fornication or sexual immorality, and likewise to believe foods evil or to think that they cause wickedness in those who partake of them, is not Christian but properly characteristic of the Hieracites and Manichaeans.

### CHAPTER LXVIII—Merits and abstinence

To equate consecrated virginity with marriage, or to believe that those who abstain from wine or meat out of love for disciplining the body gain no merit, is not Christian but Jovinian’s doctrine.

### CHAPTER LXIX—The Blessed Virgin was always a virgin

It must be believed with complete faith that blessed Mary, the mother of God and of Christ, conceived as a virgin, gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin after giving birth. 334 Nor should we accept the blasphemy of Helvidius, who said: “She was a virgin before giving birth, but not a virgin after giving birth.”

### CHAPTER LXX—The elements of the world
We do not believe that the elements—that is, heaven and earth—will be destroyed by fire, but changed for the better; we believe that the form of the world, that is, its image, will pass away, but not its substance. [Col. 1241C]

### CHAPTER LXXI—On Distributing Possessions

It is good to distribute one’s possessions to the poor with prudent administration. It is better to give them all at once out of the intention of following the Lord, and, freed from anxiety, to suffer want with Christ.

### CHAPTER LXXII—Impediments to the Clerical State

[Note: [Col. 1241D]

CHAPTER LXXII. Others read *afflictione*; alternatively, *afflatione*.]

A man who, after baptism, has been the husband of two married women is not to be ordained a cleric. Nor is one who had only one woman, but a concubine rather than a married woman. Nor is one who took a widow, a divorced woman, or a prostitute in marriage. Nor is one who, overcome by some indignation or by a just or unjust fear, mutilated himself in any member of his body. Nor is one who is convicted of having accepted interest, or is known to have acted on the stage. Nor is one who publicly laments mortal sins through penance. Nor is one who at some time, having turned into a frenzy, went insane, or was tormented by the affliction of the devil. Nor is one who, through ambition, offers money in imitation of Simon Magus.

### CHAPTER LXXIII—On the Relics of the Saints

We believe that the bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed martyrs, are to be honored with the utmost sincerity as though they were the members of Christ; and that basilicas called by their names, as holy places dedicated to divine worship, are to be visited with the most devoted affection and the most faithful reverence. Whoever comes against this judgment is considered not a Christian, but an Eunomian and a Vigilantius.

### CHAPTER LXXIV—On Deceased Catechumens and Unbaptized Martyrs

[Note: [Col. 1241D]

CHAPTER LXXIV. Others read *contingitur*; alternatively, *tingitur*; and *locutorium* instead of *habitaculum*.]

[Col. 1242A]

We believe that baptism alone is the way of salvation. We believe that no catechumen, however much he may have died in good works, possesses eternal life, except through martyrdom, in which the entire sacrament of baptism is completed. The person to be baptized confesses his faith before the priest and, when questioned, responds; the martyr likewise does this before the persecutor: he confesses his faith and, when questioned, responds. After his confession, the former is either sprinkled with water or dipped in it; the latter is either sprinkled with blood or touched by fire. The former receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; the latter becomes a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks, but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in him. The former shares in the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the latter dies together with Christ himself. The former confesses that he will renounce the works of the world; the latter renounces life itself. All sins are forgiven the former; in the latter they are extinguished.

### CHAPTER LXXV—How the Eucharist Is to Be Offered

[Note: [Col. 1241D]

CHAPTER LXXV. Others read “mixed with water,” which was given after the meal; but water issuing from his side, pierced by the spear, shows wine pressed from the true [lacuna].]

[Col. 1242B]

Pure water ought not to be offered in the Eucharist, as some are deceived by an appearance of sobriety; rather, wine mixed with water, because wine too was present in the mystery of our redemption when he said, “I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine” (Matthew 26:29). It was mixed with water—not the water that was given after the meal, but that which, together with blood, issued from his side when pierced by the spear—which shows wine pressed from the true life of his flesh together with water.

### CHAPTER LXXVI—On Human Flesh

[Note: [Col. 1242D]

CHAPTER LXXVI. Others read *Florinus* instead of *Florianus*, and *in qua* instead of *in quo*.]

Our flesh is good, and very good, since it was created by the one good God; it is not evil, as the Sethian, Ophian, and Patrician maintain; nor is it the cause of evil, as Florianus taught; nor is it compounded of evil and good, as Manichaeus blasphemously asserts. Although it is good by creation, it becomes for us either good or evil through the will of the soul—not through a change of substance, but through the recompense of its actions. For it is the flesh itself that will stand before the tribunal of Christ, in which the soul will bear what is proper to its body, according as it has done either good or evil.

### CHAPTER LXXVII—The Resurrection

[Note: [Col. 1242D]

CHAPTER LXXVII. Others read: “Although deprived of sex, yet only with respect to the condition of this life.”]

In the resurrection from the dead, the form of sex will not be changed: a dead man will rise in the form of a man, and a woman in the form of a woman, though deprived of the condition of the sexes belonging to this life, not of their natural appearance. Otherwise there would not be a true resurrection, if what rises were not the same as what falls.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII—The Souls of the Saints before the Lord’s Passion

Before the Lord’s Passion, all the souls of the saints were held in hell under the debt of Adam’s transgression, until by the authority of the Lord they were freed from servile bondage through his undeserved death.

### CHAPTER LXXIX—The Souls of the Saints after the Ascension

[Col. 1242D] After the Lord’s ascension into heaven, the souls of all the saints are with Christ, and when they depart from the body they go to Christ, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with him they may likewise be changed into complete and everlasting blessedness. Likewise, the souls of sinners, placed in hell under fear, await the resurrection of their bodies, so that together with them they may be thrust into eternal punishment.

### CHAPTER LXXX—The Forgiveness of Sins

We firmly believe that sins are abolished through repentance, even if a person repents of his offenses at the final breath of life and his sins are made known through public lamentation, because God’s purpose—by which he decreed to save what had perished—remains immovable. Therefore, since his will does not change, forgiveness of sins is to be confidently hoped for from him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn from destruction through repentance and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live (Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11), whether through amendment of life when time is granted, or through confession under punishment when life is immediately ended. Whoever thinks otherwise about God’s most just mercy is not a Christian, but a Novatian.

### CHAPTER LXXXI—That the Devil Does Not Know Thoughts

We are certain that the devil does not see the soul’s inward thoughts; but we have learned by experience that he infers them from bodily movements and indications of the emotions. The secrets of the heart, however, are known by him alone to whom it is said: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (1 Kings 8:39).

### CHAPTER LXXXII—Thoughts

[Col. 1243B] Not all our evil thoughts are always stirred up by the devil’s prompting; sometimes they arise from a movement of our own will. Good thoughts, however, are always from God.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII—How Demons Possess Human Beings

We do not believe that demons, through energetic operation, enter the soul substantially; rather, they are united to it through attachment and oppression. To enter the mind is possible only for him who created it, who, subsisting incorporeally by nature, is capable of entering his own creation.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV—On Signs and Virtues

336 We have learned from God himself that even sinners can perform signs, wonders, and healings in the Lord’s name; and while they help others through this presumption, they harm themselves through their ambition for human glory, because they glory in a false gift rather than in the due reward of merit.

### CHAPTER LXXXV—That No One Is Made Holy by Signs

We rightly believe that a Christian can become renowned through signs and wonders, yet not holy if he lives with intemperate and harsh behavior. Conversely, through temperate and peaceful conduct, even without the efficacy of signs, a person can become holy, perfect, and a man of God.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI—The Saints Also Are Sinners

No saint or righteous person is without sin; yet for this reason he does not cease to be righteous or holy, since he holds fast to holiness in his devotion. We acquire holiness not through the powers of human nature, but through the assistance of our purpose by God’s grace. Therefore all the saints truly declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to lament: if not the reproach of conscience, then certainly the instability and changeability of their transgressing nature.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII—Easter

Easter, that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, cannot be celebrated before the passage of the spring equinox and the completion of the fourteenth lunar day of the moon born in that same month.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII—The Soul as the Image of God

[Note: [Col. 1243]

CHAPTER LXXXVIII. The author says above, in chapter 12, that the soul is corporeal.]

Because of the new lawgivers who say that the soul alone was created in the image of God so that, since God is rightly believed to be incorporeal, the soul too may be believed incorporeal, we freely confess that the image is found in eternity and the likeness in conduct.

[Col. 1243]

## APPENDIX XIV. STATEMENTS OF THE DISTINCTIONS BETWEEN THE ACTIVE AND CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE (S)

[Col. 1243C]

1. There are two lives through which all the elect attain eternal blessedness: the active and the contemplative. The active life pertains to love of neighbor, while the contemplative pertains to love of God. For the two are so closely joined to one another that neither can be sufficient without the other. Love of neighbor is of no benefit without love of God, nor can love of God bring anything to perfection without love of neighbor (see *Isidoriana*, chapter 85, no. 8).

2. In the meantime, many make progress in the active life, but few in the contemplative. Those are recognized as perfect who, within the Church and at the proper time, know how to rise from the active life to the contemplative and know how to descend from the contemplative to the active through fraternal compassion.

3. Active work, if rightly retained as it ought to be, acquires eternal life for its followers. The contemplative life, however, accumulates not only life but also reward.

4. Honest marriage therefore belongs to the active life, while virginity and continence belong to the contemplative. For this reason marriage is commanded; virginity and continence, however, are not commanded but recommended.

5. Such is the saying of the Apostle, where he says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice” (1 Corinthians 7:25). And the Truth says in the Gospel: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:11). And below: “Let him who can receive it receive it” (ibid., 12).

6. Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord promises eunuchs—that is, virgins—and says: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my sabbaths, choose what I have willed, and hold fast my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not perish” (Isaiah 56:4–5). For where the choice of the elect is proposed, it is undoubtedly granted.

7. The active life is appropriate to each faithful married person: to use his own wife, not desire another’s, and, while his wife lives, not divide his body among other women. The contemplative life, however, involves despising marriage, rejecting sexual intercourse, imitating a celibate life in this mortality, and begetting spiritual children not by flesh but by word and example.

8. Active work is appropriate to each faithful person within the Church: to possess his own property and administer it rationally; not to desire what belongs to another, nor seize or defraud it. The contemplative life, however, involves abandoning all one’s possessions completely and, freed from the world’s anxieties, devoting oneself to God.

9. The following belongs to the active life, which the Truth first proposed to a young man who questioned him: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” He said, “Which ones?” Jesus replied: “You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness. Honor your father and your mother, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The following, which he added, pertains to the contemplative life: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:17).

10. The following therefore belongs to the contemplative life: our same Redeemer prayed alone on the mountain at night. The following belongs to the active life: during the day he mingled with the crowds, preached to them, and healed their sick.

11. The following belongs to the contemplative life, which the Apostle Paul says of himself and the other perfect: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.” To the active belongs what he added: “Whether we are sober, it is for you. For the love of Christ urges us” (2 Corinthians 5:13–14).

12. To the contemplative life, through which each perfect person builds more excellent virtues upon the foundation of faith, belongs what the same Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, if anyone’s work which he builds upon it remains, he will receive a reward.” To the active life refers what he added: “wood, hay, stubble”—that is, earthly possessions and concern for household affairs. Concerning this he adds: “If anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss. He himself, however, will be saved, but as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:12).

13. He says “he will be saved,” but he did not say that he would receive a reward, as he did of the one who builds gold, silver, and precious stones—that is, spiritual riches—upon the foundation. The fire in this passage is to be understood as the tribulations of the present life, through which the righteous are tested.

14. Caring for the poor, feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick and those in prison, receiving strangers, consoling the sorrowful, burying the dead, not neglecting the members of one’s own flesh, serving the servants of God, justly judging the affairs of the people, assigning to each person his proper right, aiding the oppressed, rescuing the weak from the hand of the violent, protecting widows and orphans, resisting the wicked, and restraining criminals from evil acts through severity—all these belong to the active life. All these and similar things are necessary only in the present life.

15. The theoretical, that is, contemplative, life involves abandoning the present age completely and becoming a stranger to the world’s activities; setting aside in one’s mind all present things; extending one’s purpose toward heavenly things; despising all visible things as though they had already passed away; fixing the mind not on what is seen but on what is unseen; devoting oneself to reading; persisting in prayer; and keeping watch without interruption in the praises of God.

16. As was said above, the person lives vigorously who knows how, at the proper time, to rise from the active life to the contemplative and knows how to ascend from the contemplative to the active [perhaps: descend]. From this active life, that is, from simple action, if someone inclines even slightly toward lower things, he will immediately fall into vices that do not lift him upward but plunge him downward into the abyss of sins.

17. The contemplative life is signified by that inner cave in which Abraham buried his deceased wife Sarah and in which he himself rests buried; so too eternal contemplation receives all the elect after the course of the present life, which is compared to the active life.

18. The active life is indicated by the outer part of the same cave, through which one passes to the inner part. For just as the active life of the world is a monument, so contemplation is the tomb of the active life.

19. In the active life, a person dies to every sin, as the Apostle says: “Love of neighbor works no evil.” In the contemplative life, however, like one who is dead, he is buried away from every activity of worldly affairs.

20. The intention of contemplation is figuratively represented by what Jacob saw: angels of God ascending a ladder leaning up to heaven. The active life is represented by the angels descending. Concerning this ascent and descent, the Truth says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:51). By the angels of God he signifies the holy preachers; by the Son of Man, all the faithful of the Church, who are the members of Christ.

[Col. 1246A]

21. The active life, that is, simple action, is mystically signified by the six years in which the law commanded us to sow our fields and cultivate our vineyards. The higher life, that is, the contemplative, is represented by the seventh year, in which we are commanded to cease from earthly work, neither sowing the field nor pruning the vineyard.

22. This is so that we may allow the land of our possession to keep its sabbaths—to sabbatize them—that is, so that we who formerly served the world, which was made in six days, and had been occupied with its activities, may at last, having turned to the service of God and been freed from the anxiety of this age and the burdens of the world, be able to sabbatize in God, that is, to rest in mind.

23. The perseverance of the active life is represented by the living creatures that signify the holy preachers in the prophet Ezekiel’s book: they went forward and did not turn back. Their going forward and turning back pertains to the measure of the contemplative life. While someone devotes himself to it, he is thrown back by his own weakness, bends, and then, with his purpose renewed, rises again toward the things from which he had descended. This cannot happen in the active life; if anyone turns back from it even slightly, he is immediately overtaken by the indulgence of vices.

24. The wings of these same living creatures—that is, of holy men—indicate the higher life, the intellectual life, by which they are lifted to lofty things, that is, to the heavenly. The active life is represented by their hands placed beneath their wings, because contemplation rises above action, while action follows contemplation.

25. The active life is therefore mystically figured by the six cubits of the measuring reed with which the prophet Ezekiel saw the entire spiritual building measured. The contemplative life is expressed by the span, which is said to have been added above the six cubits in that same spiritual measure.

26. This is because active work has its perfection in the present life, whereas the contemplative life begins here but is perfected in the future. For this reason it reaches in the present life not a full cubit but, as it were, half of the future contemplation.

27. The active life is mystically signified by Leah, Jacob’s wife. Although she was fertile in children, she was bleary-eyed, because active work, although it begets many children through good deeds, cannot clearly perceive the things of God because of the anxiety of this age.

28. The contemplative life, however, is signified by Rachel, who is said to have been barren in children but nevertheless pure of face, because the contemplative life becomes clear in the contemplation of God to the extent that it is free from worldly activities. An energetic reader can infer the same comparison from Peninnah and Hannah, and from Mary and Martha.

29. It must be understood that everyone who turns to God must first, through the active life—that is, through simple action—drain away the former vices that oppose him on the way of God, and only then rise to contemplation. Thus purified from every filth of sin, with a pure heart and a righteous body, he may freely behold the things of God.

30. For one who is not yet fit to act well through simple action ought by no means to extend himself toward contemplation, lest, while indiscreetly attempting to begin what he cannot persevere in, he fall and fail, take up again the things he renounced, and his last state become worse than the first.

31. This is signified by what the Truth, healthfully restraining all the weak-minded from this intention, says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble”—by which the contemplative life is signified—“tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew 5:29). There are two eyes in the face: the active life and the contemplative life in the human being.

32. Whoever, therefore, taught error through contemplation should, after plucking out the eye of contemplation, preserve for himself the single sight of the active life. It is more useful for him to go to life through simple action than to be cast, through the error of contemplation, into the unquenchable Gehenna.

33. The same Lord again showed this in the case of the man whom he freed from a legion of demons. When the man wished to follow him, he forbade him, saying: “Go to your house and tell how much God has done for you” (Matthew 9:6). This mystically expresses that one who is still burdened by many vices cannot follow God through contemplation.

34. The law also commands this figuratively when it says: “If anyone has built a new house and has not dedicated it, let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man dedicate it. Who is the man who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common, so that he may eat from it? Let him go and return to his house” (Deuteronomy 20:5), and so forth.

35. That is, one who, through the simple life, does not yet know how to govern himself properly or preside over his household ought by no means to aspire to spiritual warfare, that is, to the priestly ministry, lest through sloth of mind and a rejected life he himself perish and leave an example of destruction to those who follow him.

36. The Apostle says of such men: “For if anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? Not a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:5–6).

37. It must be understood that active work, if rightly retained as it ought to be for obtaining life, is sufficient for itself without the contemplative life—that is, without the reward of things—even if one cannot renounce all that he possesses. But the contemplative life, as long as we live mortally, cannot unfold without the active.

38. No one can live in this life so perfectly suspended in the contemplation of God that it is not necessary for him, at least because of bodily weakness and fraternal compassion, to descend to earthly action.

39. Therefore the active life has its beginning and its end here; the contemplative life begins here but is received [perhaps: perfected] in the future. For this reason it cannot attain before the death of the flesh, but only after death, what it ardently loves.

[Col. 1247]

## APPENDIX XV. A RULE OF LIFE (S)

[Col. 1247B]

341 1. Act, son, as you ought; act as is fitting; act as is worthy. Resolve that you will not sin, that you will not repeat your faults, and that after falling you will not offend again. Bear good and evil as they come; endure with a free mind whatever happens. Above all, devote yourself to patience and gentleness. Overcome mockery by despising it. Break the arrows of insult with the shield of patience. Prepare the shield of patience against every appearance of hostility; offer the shield of forbearance against the sword of the tongue. By keeping silent, you will indeed conquer better (see *Isidoriana*, chapter 82).

2. Learn modesty from Christ; learn moderation as well, and attend to Christ’s forbearance, and you will not grieve over injuries. It is the greatest virtue not to harm the one by whom you have been harmed, or even, if harmed, to permit it. It is the greatest virtue to spare anyone whom you were able to injure. For when you are tortured, your sins gird you; when you threaten, your evils make their way forward. Whatever adversity happens to you happens because of your sins. Therefore temper your grief by considering justice; you will bear grief better if you attend to the reasons why it happens to you.

3. When you are disparaged, pray; when you are cursed, then bless. Oppose blessing to cursing, and strive to soothe the angry person with patience. Drive away boiling anger with kind words. Conquer wickedness by goodness of speech and malice by kindness. Calm all enemies through modesty; overcome the evils of others with your goodness. Destroy insults inflicted upon you with a tranquil mind; open your sorrows with a calm heart. A wound deep in the heart, however grave, evaporates when opened, but it devours the mind when enclosed. The more you cover it, the more you increase it. Therefore open it with a grateful spirit, and do not let it torment you.

4. If you have saddened your brother in anything, make amends to him. If you have sinned against him, do penance with him. If you have offended anyone, appease him with prayer; quickly spare him; swiftly ask pardon for your offense and reconciliation. Do not sleep unless you have turned toward peace; do not rest unless you have been reconciled with your brother. Call him back with the swiftest affection of love. Call him back to grace through humility; prostrate yourself before him in humble affection and beg pardon in a suppliant manner. If he asks you for pardon, readily grant it; and to one seeking forgiveness, grant it in a pacified spirit.

5. Embrace holy reverence and immediately receive it with kindly charity. Do not simply pardon the sinner justly, but know that judgment will come upon you; you will not receive indulgence unless you have given it. Even if he does not plead and does not humbly ask to be forgiven, and even if, through bad habit, his conscience does not recognize his sin, you nevertheless must release it from your heart and grant forgiveness of your own will. Remove fraternal offense—or resentment—from your heart, and do not serve another’s wickedness. Hatred separates a person from God, nor is it erased by the shedding of blood.

6. Love peace; cherish peace; have and preserve peace with everyone; embrace all in gentleness and charity. Prepare yourself to love more than you yourself are loved. Do not be unfaithful in peace or fickle in friendship; always retain the bond of constancy. Invite those who hate you to peace.

[Col. 1248C]

7. Judge yourself by your own judgment, not another’s; measure yourself not by another’s speech but by your own mind. No one can know better or more fully what you know than you can, since you are conscious of yourself. What benefit is it to you to be proclaimed wicked or good? Or what does human praise have to do with you if you are other than the person you are praised as being? Therefore shun pretense; shun hypocrisy. Do not counterfeit holiness beneath a darker garment. Be in your profession and appearance what you wish to be considered. Let simplicity be present in your walk and purity in your movements. Let nothing shameful, nothing wanton, nothing insolent, and nothing arrogant appear in your conduct. Bodily gestures are a sign of the mind. Do not offer yourself as a spectacle to others or give others an opportunity to disparage you.

8. Do not attach yourself to frivolous people or mingle with the vain. Shun the wicked; beware of the unjust; flee the malicious; despise the ignorant. Remove crowds of people from yourself, especially those of an age inclined toward vices. Join yourself to the good and associate inseparably with the holy. If you do this, you will be a companion of their way of life and of their virtues. It is dangerous to associate with the worst; their hatred is better than their companionship.

9. Close your ears so that you do not hear anything immodest. Empty speech quickly pollutes the mind; it is easily injured by shameful and evil things, and what is heard is readily put into practice. No one is believed to hate those whose report does not cause him distress. Let nothing proceed from your mouth by which you may become degraded or which is itself shameful. Rather, let these things burst forth from your mouth and lips which do not pollute the ears of those who hear. Empty speech is an indication of an empty conscience. The tongue reveals a person’s character, and the kind of speech displayed confirms the kind of mind. Restrain your tongue from idle speech, and do not speak empty words; idle speech will not be without judgment. Everyone will have to give an account of his words; each person's words will stand before his own face. Whoever does not restrain evil words quickly proceeds to harmful acts; and whoever does not reject small things breaks out into great ones. The fault of lesser things generates greater faults.

10. Vices grow little by little, and while we do not guard against small things, we slide into great ones. Avoid lesser things, therefore, and you will not reach greater ones. Let what you say be cultivated with gravity and instruction, and let your speech be irreproachable and useful for the expectations of those who hear. Strive always to say whatever is appropriate; distinguish what you should say from what you should keep silent. Pay attention, speak, and become skilled in speaking. Deliberate at length about what you wish to say, lest you be unable to recall what you have said. Avoid slips of the tongue, and do not leave your mouth open to the arrows of insult. With a friend, always preserve silence; observe the right time for speaking, presenting, and weighing a statement. Let moderation remain in your mouth, and let there be a balance in your speech. Cut away from your tongue the vice of detraction, and do not defile your mouth with another’s evil. Fear this in yourself which you detract from another.

11. Never desire to know what people say among themselves, nor seek anyone who will tell you. Leave aside a matter that does not concern your soul, and, without forgetting your own character, do not investigate the affairs of others. Correct your own vices with as much seriousness as you have devoted to observing those of others.

12. Flee every kind of lie with the utmost care. Do not defend anyone’s life through the zeal of talkative brothers or by any kind of deceit. No lie that departs from the truth is just; this also forbids repeated swearing, for constant perjury produces a habit of perjury. Do the good that you have promised: be not easy in words but difficult in deeds and actions. Do nothing or presume nothing without consideration. When you are able to do something, do not promise to do it. You will be greatly liable before God if you do not fulfill what you vow. But in evil promises, break faith. A promise that is fulfilled with pain is not a true promise.

13. If you wish to fulfill your virtues, do not betray them. Hide your virtues lest you become elated; conceal your good deeds lest you become arrogant. Avoid being seen as what you have deserved to be. What you could lose by revealing, preserve by silence. Reveal the vices of your heart; immediately make your evil thoughts known, for revealed sin is quickly healed, while concealed guilt grows. If a vice is exposed, what was great becomes small; if sin remains hidden, what was small becomes great. It is better to avoid a vice than to correct it, lest, once you have fallen into it, you be unable to turn back because of a very bad habit. The bonds of habit are scarcely loosed, and things long ingrained are corrected more slowly.

14. Deliberate for a long time about a decision you are beginning, and carefully investigate, test, and undertake what you wish to do for a long time. In action, nothing is better than delay rather than a hasty decision. In good things, however, let delay be removed; delay harms what is good and obstructs what is beneficial. In good things let sluggish negligence and carelessness be absent. The vices of the flesh quickly seize the inactive. Through torpor, strength and intelligence ebb away, and sloth corrupts nature. Dullness extinguishes the light of knowledge, but diligence makes it better. Intelligence becomes more ardent when joined with effort, and slower minds are sharpened by study. Industry awakens the torpor of nature, and constancy sharpens the slowness of the spirit. Vigilance perfects the spirit; through vigilance one learns more. Often it overcomes habit, and often the effect of nature arises from habit. Perseverance produces character; constant practice turns into nature. What you accomplish with difficulty, through practice you will accomplish without difficulty.

15. Learn what you do not know, lest you be found an unprofitable teacher. Teach the good that you have learned. When you share wisdom with others, you increase it for yourself; wisdom becomes greater through this. When retained, it is smaller; when shared more widely, it abounds. When your words precede the deed, what you promise with your mouth, fulfill in deed; what you teach in words, display and demonstrate in execution. Be not only a teacher but an imitator of virtues. If you teach and act, then you will be glorious. It is not enough to praise what you have said unless you mix deeds with words. In instructing yourself, keep yourself from human praise. Instruct others in such a way that you guard yourself; teach in such a way that you do not lose the grace of humility.

16. Beware lest, while raising others by teaching them, you yourself be brought low through desire for praise. When you instruct them, do not use obscurity; speak so that you may be understood, lest by speaking you displease the simple or offend the prudent. The speech of teachers should correspond to the spirit of their hearers. Instruction must begin according to their character; remedies must be applied according to the wound, for different wills require different disciplines. Each person therefore must be taught according to his profession. The usefulness of the persons must be examined, and each one must be treated accordingly in instruction. Entrust to everyone the secrets of your profession; speak openly.

17. Announce concealed matters to the few; do not be ashamed to speak what you know how to defend. What you recognize to be lacking in your knowledge, seek from others. By asking, hidden things become clear, and difficult things are opened through discussion. Let there be no curiosity in you about knowing hidden matters, nor seek knowledge beyond what is written. Do not desire to know what is not permitted. In argument, do not contradict justice or strive to empty what is right of its force. In every dispute, hold to what is right, and love listening more than speaking. At the beginning, listen; at the end, speak. In every matter, attend to the outcome and seek the final point; the last word is better than the first.

18. Revere all who are better in knowledge and life, and give each person, according to his merit in holiness, the reverence appropriate to the higher rank; do not present yourself as equal to one who is holier. Offer obedience to elders and obey their old age through service. Obey everyone in commands in such a way that, by obeying the wishes of human beings, you do not offend God. Do not become accustomed to doing evil in the sight of others, nor, even if punishments threaten, consent to anyone who sins. It is better to suffer death than to fulfill destructive evils. For not only the doer, but also one who is conscious of the sin, is held liable; nor is he free from crime who obeyed in order to do evil. Whoever obeys an evil person is like the one who does evil; bind the doer and the obedient with equal punishment.

Source preparation: Supplied textual variants, notes, verse fragments, and column references retained.

19. Strive to be venerated rather than feared by your subjects, so that they may cleave to you through the duty of affection rather than through the compulsion of opposition. Let your subordinates revere you more than they fear you; for love proceeds from reverence, whereas hatred is produced by trembling. Fear removes loyalty; affection restores it. Fear does not preserve lasting fidelity; wherever fear dares, strength follows it; wherever there is fear, boldness follows; and where there is dread, despair appears. Therefore restrain the sowing of your speech, and rule your subjects with the greatest goodness. Do not be terrifying to those under you, but govern in such a way that they take pleasure in serving you.

20. Maintain moderation at all times, so that you do nothing immoderate, neither less nor more than is proper; and even in good things you must be moderate. For all medicines are useful, and everything becomes useful in its proper time; right things are corrupted by immoderate use, [Col. 1250D] and every excess is a fault. Therefore consider what is suitable for you and for the time, and where, when, why, and for how long something ought to be done. Examine the causes and times of things, and carefully distinguish the proper discernment required by each undertaking.

21. Recognize everything that you do: why you begin something good and why you carry it through. Preserve discernment in every action, and be indiscriminate in nothing. Once you have properly discerned your task, you will find that many things have been corrupted by custom, many presumed upon through wrongful practice, and many appropriated contrary to modest conduct. Then by no means adhere to custom and law: practice must yield to authority, and law and reason must overcome wrongful practice. Do not harm anyone by your testimony, nor employ the voice of testimony to anyone’s detriment. Let your speech hinder neither anyone’s soul nor anyone’s possessions; defend no one against the truth.

22. When you judge, do not be turned aside by affection for any person. Whether the litigant is poor or rich, consider the case, not the person. Reject a gift, lest justice [Col. 1251A] be corrupted through it; for gifts always pervert the truth, and justice is quickly violated by a person. Do not seek temporal profit from a just judgment, nor ask any reward for yourself from justice while you are judging. Preserve your recompense for the future, and do not seek on earth what is owed to you in the future. Keep your hands free from every gift if you wish to dwell in heaven; and in judgment also sit without mercy. Guard the justice of discernment, and do not be more just than is fitting. For everything excessive is a fault.

23. It is an impious justice not to forgive human frailty. Therefore do not love condemning, but rather correct than punish. Maintain severity in discerning justice, but let compassion follow the investigation of judgment; let indulgence temper the severity of discipline. Be as merciful in the faults of others as in your own, and judge no one more strictly than you judge yourself. Judge others as you wish to be judged; for when you forgive the sins of others, you show mercy to yourself. The judgment that you impose on others you yourself will bear. For [Col. 1251B] in the matter in which you judge, you will be judged; with the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured back to you.

24. Decide everything you investigate with justice; never judge by the authority of suspicion. First establish the facts, then judge. For it is not the accused but the accuser who is guilty; it is dangerous to judge anything presumptuously. In doubtful matters, reserve judgment. You know what belongs to you; when you do not know, reserve it for divine judgment. Do not attempt to condemn by human judgment what God has reserved for his own examination. Let us not judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes at last, bringing hidden things into the light. For although such things are not to be believed, they should nevertheless be dismissed unless—reading the two printed *et non* clauses as corrupt—they are established by certain indications, submitted to open examination, and proved by judicial procedure.

25. Let supreme truth be of the highest honor to you. Although you possess exalted power, restrain your elevation within yourself. Let honor not puff you up, but let humility preside over the summit of your eminence. The greater your dignity, the more conspicuous you should be in humility. [Col. 1251C] Fulfill humbly the responsibilities imposed upon you, and receive with a submissive mind the ministry entrusted to you. Be obedient to the divine ordering, and do not dare to oppose its will. Exercise the rights of the power you have acquired with moderation, and arrange everything with a tranquil, not a turbulent, heart. Beware of honors that you will not be able to hold without guilt. [Col. 1252A] For the exaltation of honors is the greatness of crimes; in a higher station, without doubt, the punishment is greater.

26. If you wish to be at peace, desire nothing of the world. You will always have rest of mind if you cast the world’s care away from you, and you will always enjoy eternal quiet if you withdraw yourself from the tumult of earthly things. Cast away from you whatever might impede your good purpose, and hate with your whole soul the losses that the world loves. Whatever you possess, possess it for the sake of mercy. Let your virtue be effective in works. Do not choose whom you will pity, lest you pass over someone who deserves to receive. Give to everyone, lest the one to whom you do not give should be Christ himself; and give to the one to whom you distribute with cheerfulness. Whatever you give, give with affection. Show mercy without complaining; offer alms without weariness.

27. Let your benevolence, however, be greater than what is given. Let your favor be greater than what is expended; for your work will be such as your intention has been. What is distributed with a good affection, God receives; [Col. 1252B] but whoever gives with weariness loses his reward. Whoever extends his hand with sadness loses the fruit of recompense. There is no mercy where there is no benevolence. Give to the poor from your own just labors. Do not take away from one person in order to give to another. It is of no benefit if you refresh one person from what makes another destitute. Such pity condemns rather than reconciles. Do the good you do for the sake of mercy, not ostentation; do nothing for temporal reputation, nothing for fame, but for eternal life and the love of God. Whatever you do, do it for the future reward; let the expectation of eternal recompense hold you. Moreover, whatever you do for the sake of glory, that is the result of your deed.

28. If you give in such a way that it becomes known to people, you have bestowed it not on a human being but on your own person, and it contributes not to eternal glory but to the glory of this life [perhaps: “of this life”]. Behold, you have received a little instruction; a rule of life has been given to you. No ignorance excuses you: you are no longer ignorant of life, nor imprudent or uninformed. I have set out the law [Col. 1252C] that you ought to follow and the ordering according to which you ought to live. You possess knowledge of the commandments. You now know what it is to live rightly. Take care not to offend further; take care that what you receive by reading you do not despise in living. It is good to know; retain what you have received, and fulfill in action what you have learned through instruction. Henceforth take care not to despise the good you have received. Amen.

[Col. 1251]

## APPENDIX XVI. EXHORTATION TO REPENT, WITH CONSOLATION AND THE MERCY OF GOD, FOR A SOUL FEARFUL OF THE FUTURE JUDGMENTS

[Note: [Col. 1251D] See *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, no. 19 and following.] (C, G, S)

[Col. 1251C]

Why do you waver, soul, shaken by storms of sorrow?

How long are you troubled by manifold thoughts?

[Col. 1251D]

A mind confused by weariness, taking paths that lead astray,

Traverses the tracks of darkness, deprived of light.

[5] Do not sigh for possessions taken away, the little chambers and torches of the world;

Mourn not the falls of honor, but the ruins of the soul.

Do not grieve over these funeral destructions of the flesh;

Fear rather the torments of Tartarus that endure.

Do not drive away the sorrows of the prison, from which you will have no release;

[10] But, looking ahead to the perpetual miseries of Avernus, avoid them—

347 Which here can be redeemed by an easy and brief exchange,

If you turn the world’s affections into love of Christ,

And do not neglect to strip yourself of iniquity.

Drive away all sins, torn from your heart;

[15] Remove utterly wrongful things, and, at least when struck,

Abhor them, so that in rough sincerity, even if late, you may resist.

The world cast you off, struck you, wrote you off, and mocked you.

[Col. 1252C]

Why do you not consider what Christ requires of you?

[Col. 1252D]

Do not suppose that you suffer such things by human hand,

[20] But believe that they have come upon you by divine judgment.

You have provoked the Lord against yourself by the offense of sin;

He reproves, restrains, and afflicts you, correcting you with scourges.

At the cost of the lash he warns you to recognize your errors,

And, having recognized them, to correct, restrain, and amend them in penitence.

[25] You must understand that you are struck by the blows of an impending scourge

So that you may exist as one separated from evil and favored,

Rejecting harmful things and seeking what is harmless.

He now wishes to examine you in the furnace of contrition,

So that, having been melted, you may lose your former, fouler stains.

[30] Why, then, do you run dispersed through empty-minded thoughts?

Gather the steps of your understanding toward the end of the examination.

Examine your heart; question your mind more carefully.

Let it reveal what it retains or has done that is shameful.

[Col. 1253A]

Let it disclose what savage or harmful thing it has conceived or concealed;

[35] And while there is opportunity, hasten to condemn everything beforehand.

Behold, all that has been perpetrated stands before your eyes,

And your whole mind sets it forth in secret murmuring.

What do admitted crimes require except lamentation?

What does the wound of a deed desire except the poultices of tears?

[40] No crime is expiated in any other way than through repentance—

Indeed, through punishment, so that it may no longer be present—

It is erased. Therefore, if you are displeased that you have fallen through wicked living,

Rise honorably. By doing better, anticipate the future Judge,

Fearing him who destroys the wicked.

[45] After the crimes of the world, appease him by works of justice.

Fear the black fires of hell, which are the second death;

But in repentance punish your admitted sins, and you will live.

In this life extinguish the flames of Tartarus with tears,

[Col. 1253B]

And by killing your crimes weaken the powers of death.

[50] Death there does not reclaim those whom it loses here while they are living,

For whoever cuts himself off from sin joins himself to justice;

And, obedient to the spirit of life, he keeps the commandments,

Rejecting sins and scorning to serve death.

He will no longer die, and death will not rule over him;

[55] Nor will Tartarus receive him in death, but heaven will receive him.

348 Do not doubt this in any way, nor ever distrust it;

For the divine sayings decree this as something to be proclaimed:

They have certainly passed into the kingdom to live with Christ,

Those who are proved to have repented of the evils they committed.

[60] Let nothing make you doubtful concerning mercy.

For God is ready in kindness to spare the unworthy

And gladly to grant pardon to the penitent—

Only repent, and do not again commit what must be repented of.

[Col. 1253C]

And therefore, though called a mocker and a scoffer,

[65] Turn repentance into punishment for your peril.

It is labor without fruit and a most empty hope

To mourn sins in such a way that one does not cease to sin.

It is as though someone were to destroy what he had built and restore what had been demolished;

If he washes what he soils and stains again tomorrow,

[70] He is not considered washed, but always unclean.

Such a person does not receive pardon but provokes anger,

Since he does not wash away the deeds of his crimes but enlarges them.

Therefore, avoiding with greater care the examples of such people,

Repent that you have sinned, and cease now to sin.

[75] Disperse past faults through the work of tears.

Give alms, if you have the means; redeem your disgraces,

And reject the pursuit of the most empty things; take care to despise them.

[Col. 1253D]

Let sin now be renounced and always abominable—

Sin that tears one away from heaven and casts one into hell.

[80] It is better to seize the glory of the kingdom in splendor

Than to endure the loss of the kingdom in the horror of filth.

Turned toward the Lord after darkness, grasp the light;

Embracing life, abandon mortal deeds.

Confess to him, be pierced with remorse, mourn, and ask.

Say: “I have sinned greatly; spare me, have mercy”—proclaim it.

[85] Bend the knees of your heart, prostrate in body upon the ground.

Entreat continually, with prayers poured forth in tears,

That you may appease as a humble person the one whom you angered in pride.

[Col. 1254A]

For the humble and weeping obtain God’s clemency;

Those who laugh do not obtain it, nor do the defiant win their plea.

[90] Let you truly repent whatever you have done wrongly,

So that, hating it, you may shudder at whatever you loved improperly;

Whatever modest shame rightly rejects with a blush,

Finally seek pardon in due form through the prayer of tears.

For by these remedies the soul heals its sins,

[95] And all its wounds recover their former health.

Thus you quickly calm the divine fury;

Thus you will certainly obtain whatever you ask for while weeping;

Thus, finally, you will be able to escape whatever

Closes, binds, obstructs, afflicts, or overshadows you,

[100] 349 And in this way you will rejoice to return to the grace of God.

[Col. 1254B]

Although you are a sinful, impious, malignant, and unjust person,

Polluted by every kind and contagion of crime,

Ask God for pardon, with no hesitation in faith—

He cleanses every crime from all who repent.

[105] True repentance for sin forgives every crime,

And there is no crime that tears cannot wipe away.

Although the day of judgment may terrify you because of justice,

Now true repentance possesses mercy.

God condemns the delinquent for what is past

[110] If he is found good at the end after having been evil,

As it is said to the impious: if he abandons his impieties,

Does works of justice, and turns at the end,

All his impiety will be forgotten and removed,

And, taken away from death, he will live forever.

[115] [Col. 1254C] Thus Paul, made faithful from being unfaithful,

Is free from all the crimes he once committed impiously.

Thus Matthew came from being a tax collector to be an evangelist.

Thus Cyprian became a priest and martyr from a magician.

Thus Augustine, once a more ardent lover of the flesh,

[120] Becomes from a Manichaean an approved teacher of the world.

[Note: [Col. 1253D] See *Isidoriana*, cited above.]

Thus the Ninevites, mourning their impious, obscene, and unspeakable

Crimes, earn life through repentance.

Manasseh, who had filled God’s temple with idols

And profaned the law formerly given from heaven,

[125] Later, after losing his kingdom, was taken captive and bound

With many iron chains. Appeasing the Lord through repentance,

He was restored to his kingdom, released from chains and sins.

Thus David redeemed the guilt of adultery and murder.

And similarly Ahaz escaped the wrath hanging from heaven,

[130] Concerning which God had said that he would punish him directly.

[Col. 1254D]

Peter, having fallen through faithlessness, rises again through repentance.

Thus also the harlot of the Gospel and the tax collector

Cleanse themselves from great guilt by pouring out a few tears.

And many others, whom the Scriptures once declare,

[135] After their crimes, to have become celibate men through repentance.

So, conversely, those who possess heaven fall to Tartarus

When, desiring evil, they abandon their former good.

As it is said of the righteous: if he departs from iniquity

And becomes wicked, all his righteousness

[140] Will perish, and he himself will be condemned to death.

[Note: [Col. 1254D] Perhaps something is missing.]

Thus Judas, once suddenly made wicked,

Lost all the good that he had previously accomplished in blessedness.

[Col. 1255A]

Thus nothing good that Solomon had done before

Is counted to him, but he is condemned for his final evil.

[145] 350 In whatever disposition or deed someone is finally found,

In that he will be judged, just as the Lord himself said concerning this:

“I will judge you in whatever condition I find you.”

And, if you believe further, God loves those very people

Who strive to be more upright after their wickedness,

[150] And who afterward exercise themselves in great virtues after their vices,

More than those who are known never to have committed grave evils

And who, sluggishly, are reluctant to do good.

Just as a master embraces more warmly the servant

Who, after losses, brings back greater gains

[155] [Note: [Col. 1255B] The edition reads *damna quaedam potiora*, “some greater losses.”]

[Col. 1255B]

Than the one who lost nothing and produced no increase,

So an emperor loves more the soldier

Who, returning after flight, brings down the enemy by pursuing him

[Col. 1256A]

Than the one who never fled and never did anything bravely.

[160] So a farmer loves more the land that brings him abundant

Crops after thorns than the land that never nourished thorns

[Note: [Col. 1256B] The edition reads *quam illam, quae tribulos vel spinas*, “than that land which never bore thistles or thorns.”]

And at no time produced a fertile harvest.

Do not despair of pardon, but rather hope for salvation,

If, intending to do what is best, you decide to condemn what is worst.

[165] Correct your offense, change your conduct, renew your life,

And afterward you will not grieve at being punished by any penalty.

The person who repents of having been formerly in sin will not remain in guilt;

The person who has again become devout will not be called impious.

But let the following verses, composed as laments,

[170] Be read with sighing and sometimes sung with weeping.

For the Lord can turn mourning into joy

[Col. 1256B] And change every adversity into prosperity.

Him they glorify with eternal praises in the heaven of heavens,

And his worshipers exalt him with the highest honors throughout the world.

Amen.

[Col. 1255]

## APPENDIX XVII. A LAMENT OF REPENTANCE

[Note: [Col. 1255] See *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, no. 25 and following.] (C, S)*

[Col. 1255]

Hear, O Christ, the sorrowful weeping

And bitter song

Which the stricken and contrite

Spirit modulates.

See the streams of tears,

And listen to the sighs.

To you, greatly wounded,

I raise the voice of weeping,

[5] From the depths of my heart

I send forth deep sighs,

Asking whether, perhaps appeased,

You may wish to forgive.

Lift the burdens

Of my grievous calamity,

Which press upon me too long

And crush me wickedly,

And do not depart, so that I may recover

The breath of life.

[10] The comforter having been taken away,

Shut in by a squared stone,

351 I groan in mourning and sigh,

Crying, “Have mercy!”

I knock and ask all day,

But you always delay.

Do not hold against me, I beg,

The sin of my youth

And of my ignorance,

But mercifully determine

[15] To overlook it now

And spare one who is unworthy.

From your ancient goodness

Do not turn away, I beseech you;

For if you command me to undergo

The rigor of justice,

I am liable to a thousand punishments,

Worthy of a thousand deaths.

Look now, merciful God,

Upon the afflictions that I endure.

[20] Remove my contritions

And restrain the scourges.

Do not, I beg, in anger

Oppress and crush me.

[Col. 1255]

I have spent my years in sorrow,

My life in groans;

I have ended it, made worthless.

Spare me, I beseech you;

I can no longer endure.

Give me your right hand and rescue me.

[25] You have made the hand of the wound

Heavier upon me,

Crushing my flesh

With the dreadful scourges

Of slaughter, iron, filth, pestilence,

And the prison of darkness.

You increase the periods of distress,

You add burdens to mourning,

Delaying to give me, greatly afflicted,

Rest;

[30] Yet against this I return thanks

And do not resist with murmuring.

“You have,” I say [Note: [Col. 1255] *Abes* for *habes*, “you have.”], “the truth

That you kill the impious;

But, after discipline,

Give pardon when appeased,

For you desire not the death

But the life of the wicked.”

I accuse myself; I do not excuse myself,

Praising you because you are gentle.

In proportion to my sins

A small punishment is given;

These things, and greater things, I cry out,

I am worthy to receive.

For the remedy of evils

And for the eternal judgment,

It is better now to be struck

By a temporal scourge

Than in the future to be given

Over to everlasting torments.

[35] If it pleases you, apply still

The goads of torment,

By which the ancient

And rotten crimes may flow away.

Only let salvation, and finally life,

Follow the diseased condition.

[Col. 1256]

Apply them, but not in anger,

So that what you command me

To endure because of my crimes

May be bearable,

And so that, once corrected,

You may again be gentle after the blows.

[40] This is bitter, yet light,

Because it passes away;

But what is more bitter and heavy

Is what cannot be revoked,

Where the punishments have no end

And the sorrow has no rest.

There the burning flame scorches

The bodies of the condemned.

Beyond return there is no hope

For the one whom it has received;

At its terror I waste away

And melt with fear.

[45] When you yourself, the Judge

And impartial witness, arrive

To render a just reward

According to each person’s merits,

You will find no work

By which you may decide to save me.

Seeing the strict examination

Of judgment by God,

I lead my life in sorrow

And continual groaning,

Already terrified, I fear

That I shall see the just Judge.

[50] Then your face will be bitter

And fearful to the impious,

Because no one who has crimes

Will remain unpunished,

Except the one who, while living now,

Has wiped them away with tears.

You will never be changed

From your tranquility,

But you will appear gentle to the just

And terrifying to the impious,

Whom conscience will hold

Guilty of their fault.

[55] Swiftly separating all the just

From the wicked,

You will place the goats on the left

And the sheep on the right.

You will give these to eternal light,

But those to darkness.

Who will not be troubled

By the anger of your wrath?

It cannot be restrained

By any creature,

When you destroy the wicked

With the sword of your mouth.

[Col. 1257]

[60] Cutting off the necks of sinners

By your word, not by iron,

You will destroy in the storm

The impious who hasten toward you,

About to bestow the rewards

Of everlasting life upon the just.

“Receive,” you will say to them,

“the kingdom prepared for you

For the fruits of justice

And of mercy,

For these and the other deeds

That you performed”—you, bearing witness to all.

All souls will stand

Before your tribunal,

Each recounting whatever they have done

In the flesh [Note: [Col. 1257] The edition reads *gesserit in carne*, “whatever he has done in the flesh.”].

What answer will I, wretched,

Give for such unspeakable crimes?

A decorated assertion

Will make no one just;

[65] You will receive only the deeds

Of good acts, not words,

Seeking from each person

The talents given with interest.

When excuses have been driven away

And rejected,

Behold, only the man and his works will be spoken of;

Having examined them, he will immediately receive

What he deserves.

[70] Then you will examine

The hidden secrets

Of every conscience,

As a face is seen in a mirror.

Alas for me! How shall I appear,

Worse than every evil person?

You will not turn your gaze

Toward a person’s status, but toward merits.

You will not make one distinguished by birth

Or exalted by wisdom

Your companion,

But the one innocent in deed.

[75] Iniquity will be abominable

Before you;

For no unclean person

Will be joined to you.

How then shall I, a stinking goat,

Be joined to the clean sheep?

Before you even the justice of the just

Will not be secure

If you investigate it strictly;

And if you do not spare even the righteous man [Note: [Col. 1257] Perhaps *Etsi justus*, “Even if he is just.”],

Woe! he will be in danger.

Rebuking in truth,

You will determine judgment,

And in your equity

The just person will scarcely be saved.

Where then shall I appear,

A sinner and an impious person?

[Col. 1257]

[80] When the records have been opened,

The deeds of all human beings

Will be publicly laid bare,

As will the thoughts of the impious.

You will weigh everything

On the scales, in the balance.

When good or evil has been placed upon the scale,

That portion of the worker

Will vindicate him

Toward which the scale’s balance has inclined.

[85] What shall I do if the weight of evil

Throws me onto the left?

You will be unable in any way

To turn away from justice;

You will accept no person,

Nor anyone’s gifts,

But will repay each person

According to his works.

The wicked will look upon the just

When they have earned

The blessedness of glory

[Note: [Col. 1257] Perhaps *meruerint*, “when they have deserved it.”]

And will grieve bitterly

That they did not live so justly

That they might likewise be free.

[90] They will pass from sorrow

Into worse sorrow

When you yourself say to them:

“Depart, accursed ones,

Into the fire prepared

For you and for the devil.”

They will see themselves removed

From the rest, life,

And fellowship of the blessed,

And joined to the devil,

To be given with him

To everlasting torments.

They will raise a howl

And an immense roar,

Making a great lament,

Bitter and violent,

[95] Such as never occurred,

Was spoken, or was seen.

Nation against nation,

Man against man,

They will beat their breasts;

Tribe against tribe and kingdom

Against kingdom will strike;

Finally, the men separately

And the women separately.

Then the angels will join together

Those alike in crime,

Whom, hurling down headlong,

They will consign to the fires of hell,

So that equal punishment may always burn

Those whom equal guilt unites.

[100] Cut off from life

And deprived of joy,

They will have perpetual mourning

And enduring sorrow,

With no consolation

And no return ever.

No one will turn back

From the judgment you have pronounced,

Nor from the one whom you yourself,

In judgment, have destroyed,

Punishing all the wicked

With everlasting vengeance.

To God I send the special offerings of prayers,

Pouring out tears while I live,

Asking while I understand,

That you may not judge me condemned

According to my evils.

[Col. 1258]

[105] Harsh are the things I have done,

Bitter and grievous.

If you decide to pursue me justly

Because of them,

You will find me liable to death

[Note: [Col. 1257] Perhaps *si persequi me juste tu decreveris, Morti* [Col. 1258] *debitum*, “If you decide to pursue me justly … liable to death.”]

And punishment.

If you turn your eyes

Toward my iniquity,

You will find no one

Whom you may deem or judge worthy

[Note: [Col. 1258] The printed *Facto, poena quae condignum* is corrupt; perhaps *poenaque condignum*, “and deserving of punishment.”]

To be burned and consumed with me.

According to the measure of my sins

And the abundance of my crimes,

I scarcely believe that the punishments

Of Tartarus themselves will suffice,

Since no wicked person

Has committed such things or so many.

[110] For this I sigh anxiously,

Because I have acted impiously.

[The printed *sanctus* (“holy”) is probably corrupt:]

I am wounded by the wound

Of the worst sins—

I think it difficult

For me to be saved from such evils.

I am pressed on every side by distress,

Compressed by anguish.

My heart wavers in sorrow

And floats in tears;

There is no rest for my spirit

Amid such great fear.

[115] I will not be secure [Note: [Col. 1258] The printed *Non turbabor* means “I will not be troubled”; perhaps *non tutabor*, “I will not be protected.”] in the expanses

Of field, sky, or sea,

For even these will flow away,

Dissolved by the heat of fire.

Where shall I, wretched, hide?

Where shall I flee before you?

Is the circuit of the world

Closed by your immensity?

You creep over heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 1258] The text reads *tu reptes*, “you creep”; perhaps *tu regis*, “you rule.”],

And without you nothing exists.

If someone does not have you appeased,

Where will he flee from you when you are angry?

[120] My sick mind is driven about,

Considering various possibilities,

But nowhere does an escape

For evasion shine forth.

There is flight from you, Lord,

And return to you.

Taking up the weapons of repentance,

Sackcloth and haircloth,

I knock at the ears of your mercy

And the heart of your clemency,

Presenting words of weeping

And sorrow with tears.

Hear the prayers

That my sick mind brings forth,

And, considering its sufferings,

Apply poultices,

Because I am your handiwork

And your creation.

[125] Apply, I beg, a remedy

To my worst wounds,

Binding the flowing ulcers

Of my vices,

Restoring what is corrupt

To perpetual health.

Take me out of the mire

Of all sins.

Do not disdain to cleanse me

Before you examine me;

And then I shall not be unclean

If you now purify me.

[Col. 1259]

You receive sinners too,

But those whom you now justify.

You look upon many as you looked upon Peter,

If they repent while weeping,

And so you raise those who have fallen

Toward hell up to the heavens.

With you there is redemption

And mercy.

Unless, once appeased,

You decide to spare me,

Woe to me! For I shall precede

All the wicked to the slaughter.

[130] And therefore, miserable as I am,

I wish that I had not been born,

Because even the present light

Is already darkness to me,

As I fear [Note: [Col. 1259] The printed *Pavendo* means “by fearing”; perhaps *paveo*, “I fear.”] the destruction

Of eternal condemnation.

Having no good

To set against my evils,

My conscience, shaken by fear of punishments,

Trembles,

While it fears to undergo

Endless dangers.

Good God, I beg you, now help

One who is perishing.

Now free me both from everlasting wrath

And from death,

So that the one whom justice punishes

You may save by clemency.

[135] Kind Father, forgive

What I acknowledge and confess.

I pronounce my evil;

I do not conceal it to avenge myself.

Receive my confession

And grant indulgence.

You have bestowed the mercy of your goodness

Freely, forgiving sins

Of many who did not deserve it.

Do not withhold from one person

What you gave to very many.

You are appeased by the soothing power

Of the humble person’s confession;

You are more quickly bent toward forgiveness

By the weeping voice,

Accustomed to assist

The penitent’s tears.

[140] Your hand is not shortened

So that you cannot bestow;

You are abundant in forgiveness.

Therefore forgive, I cry out;

Have mercy, do not destroy;

Spare, do not kill.

Do not strike me, I beg,

With a double scourge.

Suspend your anger for a little;

Have patience,

For I am very wretched,

But you are more merciful.

Turned toward mercy,

Restore grace.

Do not wish to extinguish

Life together with sin.

Preserve the blessing

Of the pardon to be received.

[145] Bruise the flesh for its sin

As much as you please;

For I will willingly receive

Temporal wounds.

I beg only that in anger

You do not inflict everlasting ones.

Afflict me here with pains,

Visit me with sorrows;

[Col. 1259] Purify me now through scourges,

So that you may not punish me in the future.

Let the soul be redeemed

By the punishment of the flesh that sinned.

Decide mercifully and kindly

To seek the lost,

You who with wondrous goodness

Gather up the rejected

And turn back those who have turned away;

You correct those who wander.

[150] I mourn that I formerly went astray,

Polluted and prodigal

Through meretricious love,

Losing my fatherland’s goods.

Therefore I return to you,

Wretched, needy, and stricken.

I cry out that I am unworthy

Of the place of sons,

Because, rejecting the admonition

Of your fatherhood,

I wandered through various paths

And ran through trackless places.

I, wretched, did evil

In foolishness.

I provoked you to anger

By hard crimes,

By which, rightly terrified,

I am crushed with great mourning.

Yet I return through tears,

Confessing in penitence.

Remove your indignation,

Forgetful of my guilt,

And, in fatherly mercy,

Take in, I beg, the one who has gone astray [Note: [Col. 1259] Perhaps *errulum*, “the little wanderer,” for printed *erroneum*.].

[155] If you still judge me

With blows to be punished,

Bear with me as with those whom you love;

Chastise and rebuke me,

But mercifully, so that you may correct,

Not kill.

As my grave sins deserve,

Do not rage so fiercely;

Temper your severity;

Cease striking,

Lest, crushed by the wound,

I despair and perish.

This too I sometimes ask of you:

Do not let me be violently overwhelmed

By temptations

Through which I am repeatedly perverted.

Lest, defeated, I wretchedly succumb,

Give me help, I beg.

[160] Alas, I beg you, in the end,

Do not permit me to be deceived,

For I shall not be able

To endure the temptations of demons.

Restrain the malice

Of their desire.

Therefore, kindly God,

I earnestly beseech you,

Incline yourself to appease me,

However little,

So that here also you may forgive,

Lest, subdued by prolonged punishment,

I become utterly wretched.

Do not place my flesh

In everlasting sorrow.

Do not compel my soul

To depart cruelly.

Bring the torments to an end;

Let the spirit rest.

Take hold of my conduct, visit me—

Indeed, come and rescue me.

Rise and say to the captive:

[Col. 1260] “Come out, wretched one.”

Lift up the one thrust into prison;

Open what is now hidden.

Wash my head and remaining limbs

With clean water,

And purify inward filth

By grace,

So that you may permit all my weakness

To depart from me.

[165] I mourn, confused,

At the evils I am remembered to have done.

I pour out prayers and laments,

Sorrowful in soul.

I beg you not to deny

The pardon offered to the penitent.

Tears against sin

Are indeed not sufficient;

But what I cannot expiate

With small weeping,

I ask you to remove through pity

And wash away by clemency.

By your mercy

Make the impious just,

The dark radiant,

The hideous shining,

The unjust innocent,

The dead living.

Now, having had mercy, set aside

The offenses of my crimes,

Rescuing your creation

From the hand of the devil.

Remember your handiwork,

And be appeased.

Your hands made me;

Your fingers formed me.

In my mother’s womb

You traced my body limb by limb,

And by your power you enclosed

The soul that you created.

Do not surrender your work, Lord,

To the ruin of death

Because of a carnal sin

Which you have declared can be washed away

Through lamentation—

And—wondrous woe!

[170] You have affirmed that no one perishes,

Even if carnally polluted

By a grave crime,

If he returns in repentance

And does not hesitate in faith

That pardon can be received.

Proclaiming through yourself and your

Messengers and disciples:

“Repent; the kingdom of heaven

Has drawn near,”

And that remission of every sin

Is given in Christ.

You testify that you rejoice not so much

Over many righteous people

As over one sinner,

Most shameful in his sins.

You came to seek and save

What had been lost.

There is no guilt so great

That it has no pardon.

Repentance erases

Every crime of sin,

If someone, having rejected evils,

Carries it out in health.

There is no evil that cannot be

Erased by tears.

You have said that every sin

Is forgiven to human beings,

Except blasphemy against

[Col. 1261] The Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1261] Perhaps *In Spiritum tantum sanctum*, “only against the Holy Spirit,” for printed *Spiritus tantum sancti*.].

[175] Will the fixed purpose

Of your word be undone?

Far be it, Lord God,

That you should reject anyone

Who, recovering after evil,

Turns to you and follows you.

Set your goodness against it

And conquer wickedness.

Grant time for repentance;

Delay the time of death.

Make salvation follow,

So that destruction may not overtake me.

With complete confidence I believe

That, not wishing me to perish,

You subjected me to scourges

By which I might recover,

So that, loathing my guilt,

I might return to grace.

May it please you, Christ,

To restore the condemned,

The shipwrecked survivor,

From the error of destruction.

As you seek me, may I return,

And, from being wicked, become

A worthy servant.

I have sinned against you, I have sinned,

And I have sinned wickedly.

But do not destroy me once turned back,

And grant what I ask:

Cleanse me before death,

And redeem me while I live.

[180] Do not ask who I have been,

[Col. 1261] But who I desire to be.

Do not, I beg, count me damnable

Because of my old guilt.

See my desire to amend,

And release the debt.

Although I am confused

By the guilt of what I have done,

I know that you judge anyone

By the end, not the beginning:

Either you crown him for the good

Or judge him for the evil.

Receive, Lord Father,

Your servant who has fallen through flight.

Take away death from the penitent;

Free me as I pray to you,

And recall me to life with the chosen

In the Lamb’s book.

Do not permit me to be rejected,

Whom, because of my merits,

You have long pressed and worn down

Under immense oppression,

But whom you afflict while living,

Receive after death.

Release, Christ, the fetters of my feet,

The bonds of crimes.

Unbolt the dark threshold

Of the shadowy prison.

Return to the light

One who has been buried,

A stranger to his homeland.

Take everlasting fury

From the mind of the ruler.

With you as appeaser,

[Col. 1262] Let those whom in my miserable anger

I have long endured as hostile

Now become appeased toward me.

[185] Come, Jesus; do not delay,

Before death snatches me away.

Raise me, weary from the dust,

And reconcile me.

Wipe away continual tears;

Make the sorrowful heart glad.

Christ, rich in the diversity

Of your graces,

I beg you to grant

Fruit and merit to one who lives,

Lest, seeing me sterile,

You cut me down thereafter.

Do not permit me, I beg,
