To be wasted away after my sins.

By your gift may I have

Things to offer,

So that, lifted from the left,

I may pass to the right.

Do not join me to the devil

In death with the impious,

Nor suffer me to be overwhelmed

In the abyss of Tartarus—

You who came to redeem from death

Those who believe in you.

[190] Now, awake, I shall sing your glory,

Completing the alphabet,

To you, Father and Son,

And renowned Paraclete,

To whom praise and power shall belong

Through eternal ages. Amen.

[Col. 1261]

## APPENDIX XVIII. PRAYER FOR THE CORRECTION OF LIFE: SINS TO BE MOURNED ALWAYS

[Note: [Col. 1261B] See *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, no. 29.] (C, G, S)

[Col. 1261A] **1.** God, author of all wonders, Father of mercies and of consolation, refreshment in tribulation, by whose grace man, having been forewarned, considers, mourns, and amends his sins; by whose regard and gift he begins either to do good, avoid evil, and reject it, to pursue righteousness and turn aside from iniquity, to desire eternal things and dread those that perish, to confess your mercies and renounce his impieties—for man possesses nothing of his own, but his conversion and progress are your gift; nor can anyone be corrected by himself, but only by you—as the prophet says: “I know, Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor is it given to a man to walk and direct his steps” (Jer. X, 23); and the Apostle says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16); and you yourself say: “I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

**2.** Be present, therefore, to my supplications; attend to my prayer. And graciously accomplish what I ask, [Col. 1261B] and, being reconciled, heed it. For you have drawn me away from the snares of the world and led me out from the net of sins. You opened my mouth to confess to you when I was bound by every sin; and you made me understand how, or for what things, I should beseech you. You placed confidence in my heart to ask for what my soul needs, because—as the prophet said—“You will return, desiring mercy, and will have pity, forgetting human evils and passing over sins in your kindness” (Mic. VII, 18–19); and you yourself said: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. VII, 7).

**3.** For he who grants permission to be asked and entreated is doubtless ready to give and to open; nor is he miserly in bestowing who cries out that those without possessions should ask. Therefore the one who has neglected, while there is still time, to seek from the dispenser the remedies appropriate for himself will afterward regret his own need. For this reason I cannot remain silent, warned by the touch of the grace that has come upon me. For I confess, Lord, that your mercy came before me, unworthy as I was; and while I lay crushed in a kind of deadly sleep upon the bed of the many sins of this world, you sent your grace, amid the sound of scourges, to awaken me, who was torpid in damnable sluggishness. Thus, when I was roused with open eyes, and recognized that I possessed in myself no victorious good work, I came to you to ask for the sustenance of life, lest encroaching want should suffocate me at the very end.

**4.** Therefore, rising toward you with cries of lamentation, and striking at the hearing of your mercy with manifold prayer, I watered each letter of the alphabet that I set before you with a river of tears [possibly: “I water”]. For fear of your judgment compelled me to weep longer, [Col. 1262B] and your grace made me boldly entreat, believing that in you, my God, I would cross the wall of all my iniquities, which had surrounded me, and that, snatched away from the afflictions of my distress, I would pass over into the vast expanse of the widest joy—not, of course, that of this age, but of the age to come. For this reason I will not cease to entreat you until you have mercy on me and save my soul, which today confesses to you while situated in the valley of weeping: because you led me into it; because, not by my merit but by your gift, I reached the narrowest enclosure of repentance and entered its fountain of tears to wash away the various stains of wickedness. This repentance was bestowed on me not because I had yet sought it, but because you granted it; and, through your mercy providing it, although I had not yet sought it, I found it.

**5.** Behold, for no little time now I have been sweating in the heat of its affliction and laboring under its strict rule. Struggling with it, I am examined by daily scrutiny; its pressure draws great groans from me, compels me more and more to weep because I have sinned, and continually teaches me to give thanks to you for your great patience, by which you endured me in my wantonness for so long and preserved a time for correction in which I might turn back, abandoning transgression, lest by pursuing sin without ceasing I should perish forever with my sin. And now, mercifully instructing me with your rod, you work my salvation, withdrawing my life from corruption and my soul from destruction, so that I might learn to pass beyond evil things by choosing good.

**6.** And trusting in this, I hope that, just as you have brought upon me the tribulations of repentance, so you will also grant the mercies of forgiveness. Not only this, but I bless your holy name because you delayed the outcome of death, lest I should fall asleep in the torpor of sin into everlasting punishment; and from afar, foreseeing the remedy of my healing, you came to my aid, since you entrusted my soul, torn by a pestilential ulcer, to the medicines of this repentance to be healed. For its goading is good for me: it teaches me to flee past offenses and warns me beforehand to avoid future ones. I consider its yoke of burden light, because it removes sufferings heavier than those it inflicts; and while it presses temporarily, it redeems eternally.

**7.** Its bonds are dear to me: now they bind me for a little while so that they may make me free forever. Its outward filth is pleasing to me, because by the roughness of those same things the soul within is cleansed from its sins. Its bitterness is now sweeter to me than the sweetness of luxurious living in the past, because through the former the soul is suffocated, whereas through the latter it rises again from such a death. What that one befouled, this one washes away. What that one bloodied, this one heals and cures. For if I saw an external and harmful wound on my body, or felt some inward pain in my organs, I would run at once to a physician; I would surrender my flesh to be cut with iron amid pain, and to be burned with a glowing cautery, nor would I refuse to drink the bitterest antidotes for the sake of restoring health.

**8.** Why, then, should I bear these things unwillingly, through which the soul is restored from everlasting destruction to perpetual salvation? What shall I repay you, most merciful God, lover of human beings and gracious justifier of sinners, for what you have done for me? I will take the cup of salvation; therefore I will call upon your name with praises. You have brought my steps back to the way of life; I will not cease to give you thanks. For this is the way by which one returns from the underworld to heaven, from sin to righteousness, from offense back to your grace; and, to sum it up briefly, this is the restoration of every ruin. Finally, when the Publican prayed in the temple, this surpassed the righteousness of the Pharisee and made him more righteous; this led Lazarus through temporal scourges to eternal rest.

**9.** To you, Lord, be praise and glory, who strike and heal, wound and cure. You give passing pain, and shortly afterward refresh with eternal joy, because you are just and merciful: just, because you by no means spare the one who sins; merciful, because you do not withhold mercy from the penitent. Again, you are just and merciful because first, here, you correct a person from sins, and afterward free him from eternal punishment. For, as I have said, you do not spare the sinner, whether you strike him with a temporal scourge for purification, or leave him to be punished by eternal judgment, or the person himself punishes through repentance what he has done wrongly; and thus you are rightly said not to spare the offender. For no sin can be left unpunished, since sins deserve punishment. Either the person punishes it and you free him, or, if he postpones it, you punish him, according to what the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged.” As though he said: “If in this age we separated ourselves from sin, the future punishment of sin would not chastise us.”

**10.** It is therefore necessary for a person to punish sin, so that he does not incur eternal punishment; for repentance took its name from punishment, as though from *punitentia*, since a person, by repenting, punishes what he wrongly committed. For those who truly repent do nothing else except ensure that what they have done wrongly does not remain unpunished. In this way you spare those who do not spare themselves, for no one escapes your profound and just judgment who despises it. Repentance, however, is perfected by erasing past things and not admitting future ones. It is like a fountain, so that, if some sin should creep in through the devil’s assault, it may be cleansed by this satisfaction. Satisfaction consists in excluding the causes and suggestions of sins and not repeating sin thereafter. Repentance itself must be practiced according to the quality of the offenses: just as light sins are erased by private prayer, so grave sins are remitted before the Church through repentance and satisfaction.

**11.** Therefore, since the satisfaction of repentance is weighed by your judgment, not by human judgment, and since the mercy of your forgiveness is hidden, it is necessary to weep without interruption. Nor should the penitent ever have security concerning sin, because this is its enemy: it gives birth to negligence, and negligence often leads the careless back to past vices. Rather, he must be as ready to repent as he was inclined to sin, and must advance in humility all the more sublimely the lower he is known to have fallen through pride. He must mourn not only because he did the evil he ought not to have done, but also because he failed to do the good he ought to have done. This concern makes one exceedingly cautious; it does not justify a negligent worker. True repentance is anxiously diligent in every holy work.

**12.** It has no laughter at all; it admits no empty stories, nor is it polluted by desires or shameless deeds. It does not desire earthly things but longs for heavenly ones; it thinks about its end, constantly considers the coming judgment, and daily takes care to appear worthily before God. It serves God alone and is entangled in none of the affairs of the world. It is most frequent in vigils and prayers, disciplined in fasting, moderate in food and drink, constant in labor and reading, everlasting in charity, perpetual in chastity, utterly truthful in speech, restrained in oaths; it is kind and patient, not inflamed by envy, not overcome by anger; it avoids boastfulness, loves humility, does not repay insult, hates greed, flees empty glory, detests pride, rejects pleasures, and embraces groans, sighs, and tribulations, knowing that your mercy is not granted to the negligent or the laughing, but is given to the afflicted and contrite in heart, as you yourself say: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). And again: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Jas. IV, 9–10). And the Apostle says: “Be miserable, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning [Vulg.: ‘be turned’], and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves before the Lord [Vulg.: ‘in the sight of the Lord’], and he will exalt you.”

**13.** It is certainly true that every guilt is dissolved by weeping, if, with one’s way of life reformed, the evil of the past is not repeated. For it is not enough to turn away from evil unless doing good also follows, as it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI, 27). And elsewhere: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isa. I, 16). Thus, when the satisfaction of repentance is set against sin, and past evil is at once covered and wrapped in the goodness that follows, it perishes, and what is found to be lesser is put to death. Therefore, since through the satisfaction of weeping the fallen soul is raised again, and through such a washing it receives the dignity of its former purity, it is fitting for me to increase my weeping and make my tears abundant over my frequently repeated iniquities, which I have committed beyond number. I do not think that weeping is sufficient for me according to the abundance of my offenses. For this reason I will continually mourn my sins in bitterness, if perhaps it may please you to cleanse me completely from them. Would that the fluids of my head were turned into blood and that I poured out blood instead of tears, so that I might wash away with cruel lamentation the cruel sins with which I once wickedly wounded myself through slothful folly.

**14.** Therefore my soul is overturned, striving amid immense weariness; it has also dried up, terrified by dread of your fury. My life has been turned into the sap of wormwood; my inward parts overflow with gall and vinegar; my heart is corrupted by deep pains; sigh follows sigh, and groan rushes upon groan. Bent and humbled to the end by fear of future punishments and by the present misery of scourges, I cannot lift my head, weighed down by a manifold burden. Death stands before my eyes, and immeasurable crimes stand with it; there is no resource from which redemption might arise. For this reason, ineffably troubled, I use neither direction nor counsel; the anguish of oppression drives me to the brink of despair, and, as though standing upon a spider’s thread, the state of my mind wavers, ready to collapse. At times I fear, because of the severity of my faults, that you may be unwilling to forgive; at times I trust, because of the gentleness of your mercies, that you have determined to free me. There is no small disturbance of my heart between hope and fear: if you wish to destroy, justice urges you; but if you wish to save, mercy invites you. And although the present scourges free one who has turned from sins, my mind nevertheless trembles lest my wounds should not suffice to purge all my offenses. Yet the subtlety of your wisdom inflicts punishments outwardly just as it perceives guilt inwardly.

**15.** But who can be at peace concerning your judgment, when, under the strictness of your examination, even the righteousness of the righteous is not secure? If an account must be rendered even for an idle word, how shall I be secure, who have committed principal evils? There is no security at all in my mind from the face of your judgment, nor peace in my conscience from the sight of my sins. Therefore my contrition is great, like the sea, because my wound is dreadful. I seek a harbor of escape, and cannot find how to return from Satan’s snare of deception; it has entangled my feet, and I have no strength to prevail. I cry out, overcome by the multitude of my pains, and there is no one to rescue me. I labor, shackled in mourning and groaning, abandoned in the distress of prison, and there is no one to console me. Woe is me! Woe to me, miserable and unhappy, whom most just punishment terrifies, whom deserved retributions crush, whom scourges and reproaches rightly strike down, whom various afflictions of misery opportunely ravage, because I sinned wickedly, transgressed cruelly, erred grievously, and fell disastrously! Woe to me, who polluted myself with such evils and defiled myself with so great an evil, who did not know how to avoid drinking from the poison of the devil’s cup, which killed the soul!

**16.** And now I would not need to be brought to life again if I had guarded myself most carefully against being pierced by his spears; I would now be without a wound and would not be seeking medicine if I had understood how to flee and not be caught in his snares; I would now be free and would not be crying out for release. Unhappy man that I am, who will free me from such bonds and from the peril of this death, except your grace, almighty Father, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom you appointed as redemption for the salvation of the world? In whose righteousness and sanctification every iniquity is erased and the dominion of death is abolished; he who, as the prophet says, was “a rock, a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. CIII, 18), that is, the protection and salvation of the sinner. Of him John also says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John II, 1). In him all salvation has been established by you, as Peter says to the Jews: “There is salvation in no other; nor is there any other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved.” He holds the keys of death and the underworld; he opens the gates of the abyss and closes the entrances of darkness; he opens, and no one closes; he closes, and no one opens. To him you gave all power in heaven and on earth. At whose name every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; he [Col. 1266A] is the man of your will, in whose hand everything that is pleasing before you is accomplished. Although he is the radiance of your glory and the likeness of your substance, bearing all things by the word of his power, seated at your right hand, making purification for sins and interceding with you for sinners, he is the beginning and end of the whole creation (Acts IV, 12; Rev. I, 18; III, 7; Phil. II, 10; Heb. I, 3).

**17.** For before him no creature existed, and through him every creature began to be made; and he will be the consummation of all creation when he gives the world its end and judgment. For he is the man whom you prepared to judge the living and the dead; you yourself judge no one, but have given all judgment to him. He alone has power to destroy and to free, because it pleased you in him. You exalted him above all the heavens and above every principality, power, and dominion, giving him glory and honor, appointing him over all the works of your hands, and subjecting everything beneath his feet. Through him all things were made and established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible; from him they are sustained, and in him all things hold together. Through him you founded the earth, established the heavens, enclosed the abyss, and fortified the sea. For he himself is your wisdom, counsel, power, hand, and right hand, creating and giving life together, cooperating and vivifying together all things, and those that are in all things, through the Holy Spirit, who proceeds ineffably from you and from that same Son of yours. In him I too have faithfully believed from my earliest age; to him I confess that I have sinned, and from him, with profound humility of heart, I ask forgiveness.

**18.** Therefore, my Lord Jesus, since many mercies are in your hand and you do not permit anyone to perish, but desire all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; since you do not rejoice in death or delight in the destruction of the living, nor desire the ruin of a human being but his salvation, and for this reason humbled yourself, although you were God, so that the human being who had indeed perished might be found, you deigned to become human: I have rightly resolved that I must return to you from my transgressions. Receive me, returning into your hands with tears before you; graciously accept the prayers of my confessions and save me as I confess. Do not despise repentance, Lord. I repent that I have gone astray, and now grieve that I foolishly committed the most wicked things long ago. But do not turn your face away from me, because, if you will, you can cleanse me. For yours is the power to put to death, to give life, to free, to bind, and to loose. I gave my soul over to be bound by the bonds of various crimes, and, as you see, wounded it with the worst wickedness. Loose, Lord, loose now the bonds of my neck, by which, bound, I have long cried out to you in many ways, and in mercy apply medicine to the exposed wound.

**19.** Restore my former health, and let my soul live by your remedy. You may indeed judge my wound grievous, and I do not deny that it is grievous; nevertheless I confidently believe that you can certainly heal it, because I believe that nothing is difficult or impossible for you. For I have learned from your testimony that all things are possible with the Lord, since you expressly declare that it is easy for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. I have sinned, Lord; I have sinned greatly. For this reason, as you yourself foresee, my tribulations have been prolonged, tormenting my heart night and day. It is not because the heap of my guilt or sins is small that my groans are many and my mind is most sorrowful through the upheaval of great disturbance; rather, by considering your great and innumerable mercies, your kindness directed me, struggling gradually to rise from the stain of danger, toward hope of forgiveness, so that, hesitating in no way in faith, I might ask pardon and not die but live.

**20.** Therefore, returning to you who strike me and have power over my wounds—that is, to you, my Lord—I bend my knees before you and, with diligent prayer, confession of repentance, and the contrition of fasting, entreat you, giving glory to your name with frequent praise and blessing. For you taught me this in the solitude of my confinement. Will you not in this way restore the falls of my ruin? I firmly believe that you will. I therefore have hope in confession; firmly established in it, I neither have despaired nor will despair, but employ perfect confidence. Through it, after wickedness has been erased and abolished from my heart, may I, with my petition already offered, revive through you from every death caused by crimes and, with confession interposed, be purified from every defilement of sins; for you are faithful in your words, and you will not make void what has proceeded from your lips. Your mercies have not been brought to an end, nor has confidence in rising been cut off from those who fall in this life by whatever misfortune, since you have appointed a return from every kind of sin and preserved repentance as the sinner’s remedy: “I do not desire the death of the impious, but that he turn back and live,” you say (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). And again: “If, when I say to the impious, ‘You shall die,’ he turns from his impiety and practices repentance, does justice, walks in the commandments of life, and so forth, he shall surely live and shall not die” (ibid., 14).

**21.** And in Jeremiah: “Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot, destroy, and annihilate it. If that nation repents of its evil, concerning which I have spoken against it, then I too will repent of the evil that I thought to do to it” (Jer. XVIII, 7); and so forth. And again: “Behold, I am fashioning evil against you and devising a plan against you. Let each person turn back from his evil way, and direct your ways and your practices.” He who says, “By no means; we have despaired; we shall follow our own plans, and each of us shall carry out the perversity of his evil heart.” And to Jerusalem, while the whole people were turning after idols in every most heinous crime, you say, “retain” [the syntax and reading are uncertain]: “See your ways in the valley; know what you have done, a swift runner unfolding your ways; a wild ass accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of its soul, has drawn in the wind of its passion; no one will turn it away” (see *Isidoriana*, cited above, no. 31).

[Col. 1267C] **22.** It is commonly said: “If a man divorces his wife, and she departs from him and marries another man, will she return to him again? Will that woman not be polluted and defiled?” But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord. Lift your eyes straight ahead and see where you have been cast down. You who sat waiting for them like a robber in the wilderness, you polluted the land with your fornications and your wickedness. Therefore the drops of rain were withheld, and there was no late rain. You acquired the brow of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed. At least from now on call me, “My father,” and you are the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry forever, or will you persist to the end?

**23.** And again: “Return, rebellious Israel,” says the Lord, “and I will not turn my face from you, because I am holy, says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever. Turn back, you who are returning, because I am your husband; I will take you, if you remove your offenses from my sight, and you will not be shaken” (Jer. III, 12). Again, through Jeremiah, you say to a people persisting in crime and still unwilling [possibly: “willing”] to return, while patiently holding back: “Do not withhold the word; perhaps they will hear, and each will turn back from his evil way, and I will repent of what I thought to do to them because of the wickedness of their practices.” And in Isaiah he says: “I am the one who speaks righteousness, and I am a champion for salvation. If you return and rest, you shall be saved.” And again: “Return to me; do not forget me, and I will redeem you. I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. For I know that you will transgress grievously, and from the womb I called you a transgressor. For my name’s sake I will remove my fury far away, and by my praise I will bridle you, lest you perish.”

**24.** And again he says to sinners, so that they may be washed through repentance: “Wash yourselves; be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my sight. Cease to act perversely; learn to do good,” and so forth. “And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall become white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall become like clean wool.” And to the transgressing and delinquent people, unwilling to turn back, concerning whom you had already said that you would destroy them in the fury of your anger because of the enormity of their crimes, you say in Hosea: “My heart is turned within me; my repentance is stirred together within me. I will not act in the fury of my anger. I will not turn to destroy you, because I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst” (Hos. XI, 8). If, then, you offered such patience and such mercy to a people that had turned away and did not repent, which, having abandoned you, had subjected itself to every abomination, indecency, and idol, how much more readily can you be reconciled to one who has not turned away from you and, repenting of his sin, bends down to entreat you?

**25.** Therefore another prophet rightly cries out: “Turn back to the Lord, because he is kind and merciful, patient and of great mercy, and relenting over evil” (Joel II, 13). David says: “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Ps. CII, 8). And in Solomon: “The Lord has had mercy on the penitent” (Ecclus. XII, 3). And again: “For the Lord is kind and merciful, forgiving sins in the time of tribulation to all who seek him in truth” (Ecclus. II, 13). For this reason the Apostle also exhorts us with the testimony of the prophet, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his glory, so that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help (Heb. IV, 7). But you, Lord, cry out to those laboring in iniquity and burdened with the weight of sins: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28). And there are many other passages of this kind, which it would be lengthy to write out from all the Scriptures.

[Col. 1268C] **26.** Therefore I shall eagerly seek the Lord of such great patience and such great mercies; I shall approach him boldly, follow him gladly, embrace him firmly, hold him humbly, never let him go, and entreat him with confidence. In his compassion and mercy, the way of repentance opens for me: a return to life from death, a return to heaven from hell, an entrance into light from darkness. This, then, I ask first, Lord, and so I shall proceed to the rest: give me the most devoted intention of mind for repentance, acceptable and pleasing before you. Give me the compunction of humility, so that my mind may sigh from affection for you and groan over its wound, its hardened heart being dissolved. Awaken all the senses of my innermost being, so that they may cry out to you with the strength of an inward voice. If at any time you should hear me entreating, may the sighs of my breast be moved and a murmuring groan resound in your ears. Loosen the reins of my eyes, and let my eyelids pour forth waters in a generous stream from their fountain, so that the offenses of all my crimes may be washed away by the rush of tears [Col. 1268D], and let the channels of the veins of my head run without ceasing until every impurity of iniquity is wiped away.

**27.** Let my mouth be filled with words of utterly truthful confession, by which you may be pleased and graciously strive to spare me, and not delay to grant forgiveness. Let my repentance become fruitful for me, giving birth to joy from mourning, bringing forgiveness from need, and leading from labor to rest, so that through the narrow path of the afflictions of prison you may lead me to the entrance of life and, by the iron chain of bondage, grant me release from sins. Behold, Lord, the time of confession is at hand, and the days of remission have arrived, in which promised pardon is granted to those who ask. What more can I confess to you than that I do not deny myself to be worse than all the wicked, whom you will establish as righteous in comparison with me? For there was no sinful crime or criminal deed whose vice I did not stain myself with, whose contagion did not pollute me: hasty toward lust, shameless toward wantonness, frequent in luxury, immodest toward fornication, daily piling crime upon crime. I did not cease to add worse things to the worst: cruel in will, perverse in mind, dishonorable in conduct, polluted in heart, blasphemous on my lips, angry and abusive.

**28.** Because of this I am confounded and ashamed now to raise my eyes, judging myself unworthy to see the stars of heaven. But act for the glory of your name, my God. Place forgiveness before me as I confess to you, for salvation; grant the remedy of pardon, so that, having become gracious and reconciled, you may erase all the crimes of my sins and not seek out the iniquities committed by the slippery, inexperienced, wanton, empty, and foolish age of my youth—prone to evil, most sluggish toward good, swift toward death, slow toward life, hating the works of light and loving those of darkness, delighting to fall and neglecting to rise. Salvation is bitter to it, and destruction sweet. Loose, Lord, the guilty man bound by inexplicable knots; break apart the snares of crimes and let me depart set free, so that you may save me according to your good will and I may not perish in my wickedness or descend into hell, from which there is no ascent afterward. For your mercy is more abundant than the abundance of my sins. You are also far kinder than I am wicked. I am malicious and headlong; you are gentle and patient. I am inclined to fall and fragile; you are ready to raise up and strong. If you look back upon what has been done, you might immediately judge me doomed; but if you attend to my present will and desire, I believe you will judge me worthy of salvation, because you have directed my heart toward your desires, in which you see my mind serving you more ardently, since my soul thirsts for you, and my flesh likewise delights in you.

**29.** Redeem me, Lord my God, from all my distresses, and may it please you to rescue me from destruction. Call me back from the gate of death and lead me again onto the eternal way, so that I may run along the path of your commandments and walk in your truth. Let neither the cavern of darkness hold me nor the abyssal pit or caves shut me in; but, light of light, open for me the entrance to eternal life. Unseal the harbor, for you are the God who receives the tears of a contrite heart and accepts the humiliation of penitents. For you will not be called merciful among those who do not sin, but when you turn toward an impious person and show mercy to a sinner in his evil. I have always fallen into worse things and slipped from evils into worse evils; but you are a highly skilled craftsman, knowing how to fashion for yourself a useful vessel from what is useless. For this has been your work from the beginning: to make the righteous from the unrighteous and the worthy from the unworthy; to raise up again those who have been struck down and repair the ancient ruins of those who are falling. For, as you yourself declare, “The physician is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill” (Matt. IX, 12). This too caused you to descend into this world: to save sinners, of whom I am the chief. And if you then desired to save enemies, adversaries, those who had turned away, and the impious through the sufferings of your passion, can you now destroy friends who have turned back and repented? Far be it from you. You truly delight to forgive sinners if they turn back, since you did not refuse to undergo death for sinners. For you would certainly not ascend the cross for the unrighteous if you refused to spare the unrighteous.

**30.** For if you did not refuse an unrepentant legion of demons, without tears, the herd of pigs it desired, how much more readily will you be prepared to grant forgiveness of sins to a faithful soul beseeching you with tears? For this reason I faithfully offer you the prayers and tears of my repentance; you will save me, just as you save the others who repent that they have sinned. Or will confidence and your promise of kindness and forgiveness—which saves all the families of the earth that turn back—remain fruitless in me, or become dry and void in me alone? Will your abundant clemency, which can never be diminished by giving and is not constrained by the effect of anyone’s need, become insufficient for one penitent? Will you confine yourself to me alone, lest you grant what is asked, becoming barren of the fruit of mercy? Will you grieve against me forever because of a sin of brief duration, which, by the disposition of your providence, I now repent of, cursing and abhorring it, although I am a creature formed from corruptible earth and ashes, mortal, while you are God, the incorruptible and immortal Creator? Hardened in mercy, will you not hear one who is crushed and humbled? Or will you judge that the one confessing to you should be punished, or suppose that the one entreating you should be destroyed? I will not believe this, nor will I suspect that you will it, because that would be impious and contrary to the nature of divine mercy. Therefore, suppliant and confident, I beseech your mercy, so that in your gracious will you may fulfill my petitions.

31. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes and see my desolation. See the many afflictions and miseries that crush me like a wagon crushes straw, devour me like moths devour wool, and consume me like rotten wood [Perhaps *fire is missing*]; assuage your fury and suspend the scourge. Now have mercy on me, be appeased, and turn back; spare my soul, spare my sins. Do not forget me forever; do not remain angry with me eternally; do not abandon me utterly, nor in any way forsake me as one destined to perish. Rather, restore your grace to me and save me in the place of danger where my flesh lies stiffened by iron, struck with wounds, wearied by punishments, exhausted by illnesses, abandoned by human care, separated from society, shut in by squared stones, in a dungheap and given over to stench by just judgment, exposed to prolonged misery in darkness and deadly shadows. You yourself see all these things, you who sit above the cherubim and gaze upon the abysses.

32. My crushing and my smiting have now become ancient and worn with age, and there is no one who remembers your compassion, nor anyone who, pierced in heart, reflects and says: “Now, for the Lord’s sake, I shall have mercy on a mortal, to whom a mortal has given an everlasting prison and perpetual iron. No mercy of deliverance has been reserved for me; I have been condemned by an irrevocable judgment, since it was not said, ‘Let us return and grant pardon to one who is perishing.’” Remember, Lord, your mercies toward me, and change this grievous and exceedingly harsh sentence, because you said: “You shall not afflict your neighbor forever,” and, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.” Although I am justly dying because of my wickedness, nevertheless, because you are compassionate, kindly prepare aid for my life. Lord, in your favor, provide divine assistance where human help has withdrawn. I alone have been left to you; help me in my solitude. Do not be a stranger to me in the days of distress, nor abandon me in the time of tribulation. Do not cease protecting and guarding me, and do not stop cherishing and nourishing me.

33. Keep your eyes fixed upon me, lest I perish; watch over me and save me. Be for my soul and body alike the giver of life and life itself, and the healer and health of all my infirmities, so that I may live by the gift of your beneficence and praise you in my life before my brothers, until, appeased by your inspiration, the indignation of the one who afflicts me comes to rest. For yours is the power both here to bend the hearts of rulers so that they may be favorably inclined toward the body, and there to free the soul from future punishments. No one will say to you, “What have you done?” nor will anyone resist your judgment or oppose your will. Nor will anyone then dare to accuse a guilty person whom you have now absolved from his faults. Rather, he will be blessed without any contradiction, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Psalm 31:1–2); and the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who can be against us? God is the one who justifies; who is he that condemns?” (Romans 8:33). Test me, Lord, test me in the furnace of humiliation, in which you examine the unworthy for so long.

369 34. I ask only that you not reject the task of burning away the harmful rust of my sins; scorch the pernicious filth of my crimes, so that you may draw out pure and gleaming gold from its adulterated mixture with lead. Hasten, too, to rescue me from the temporal scourge; disclose the excesses of my faults, so that in the future you may leave nothing to punish, but only what you may bless.

Here, Lord God, cleanse me from all crimes; here wipe me clean of every pollution of vice; here release me from every bond of sin, so that, if you release me while I live, I may depart purified, or, if you decide to call me, I may be taken up thoroughly cleansed. Govern my soul while it is placed in the body; receive it when it leaves the body; and grant that it may cling to you forever, so that what has been entrusted to you, Lord God and its creator, through many tears may never perish.

But if a longer life is still preserved for me in the flesh, let it be ordered with the new beauty of good works. Strip me of the foulness of every vice and clothe me with the dignity [perhaps *with the dignified character*] of all the virtues, implanting and sowing within me the shoots of charity and kindness, humility and self-control. Cut away the rotten old growth of desire, greed, vanity, arrogance, anger, impatience, and every other wickedness; circumcise what is superfluous, cut off what is dishonorable, press down what is exalted, and prune what is harmful and fruitless, so that the bitterness of the evil tree, transformed, may produce good sap; so that after the bitterness of troubles it may bear sweet fruits for you, and what nature previously lacked may now offer as something bestowed by grace.

35. Awaken in me an occasion for fleeing from sin, and eagerness for the practice of good. Again, remove the desire to sin and exclude every carnal affection. Let there be in my soul no lust for foul pleasure; rather, let love of the fairest chastity dwell there. Let the ambition of this world be far from me, so that I may not, because of its obstruction, turn away from a right purpose. I desire that only the grace of your fear and love may always be present in me; through their fruit may I revive again from every mortal condition of vice. For through fear one withdraws from evil, and through charity a good work is accomplished. Again, fear guards through love what charity accomplishes, lest it perish through pride. Charity also hastens and joins one to God, while fear does not permit one to be separated from him. This is the holy fear that endures forever and ever.

Let harmful prosperity and the friendships of this age not approach me. Temper adversities, however, so that I may be able to endure them, for prosperity casts down, while adversity teaches; prosperity often entices the mind to sin, whereas adversity both holds it back from sin and continually urges and persuades it to hate the present life and desire the future one.

Therefore do not permit me to become further entangled in any affairs of the world. Let me belong to you alone and serve you always; let me adore you without ceasing and sing psalms to you day and night. Repel from me the seeds of evil thoughts, the dew and kindling of useless desires opposed to good intention. Against all its temptations and crafty deceptions, set up the protection of your help and defense, so that, foreseeing me firm in good perseverance, the devil may withdraw in confusion.

36. Permit me to weep over all my sins, but not to desire them. Make me hate what you hate and embrace what you love. Let my mind obey your commandments and my will agree with your will, so that nothing base, nothing unjust, nothing dishonorable, nothing indecent or impious, arising in the delight of my conscience, may cling to it. Rather, let the intention of my mind, breathing after your love, attain the work of justice and compassion.

Let my work be pure, and my prayer, as you command, in secret, so that I may not serve merely for appearance, as though I wished to please human beings. Permit me to know the admonitions of your laws and the most honorable deeds of the fathers, and grant that I may be filled with milk. Draw me back from every snare of sin and hold me back from the stain of every error. Always bind me with the restraints of your discipline, and hold me most firmly so that I do not fall again.

Draw me after you and lead me wherever you please; do not permit me in any way, turning backward, to turn my back again [perhaps *to turn away*]. Let me be watchful in your fear, perfect in love, constant in faith, and in no way doubtful in hope. Let me burn with love of my neighbor, but not be consumed by the heat of hatred or waste away through the pallor of envy.

[Col. 1272A] 37. Always inspire me to think of holy works; compel me to do them; persuade me to love them; strengthen me to hold fast to them; guard me lest I lose them. Let pride, the mother and queen of the seven chief vices, neither enter nor rest in the dwelling of my heart, nor let her offspring cling to me—that is, desire of gluttony, fornication, greed, envy, anger, sadness, and vainglory.

Instead, give me profound humility, by which the height of pride may be bent down; give me measured abstinence, by which the belly’s excessive greed may be restrained. Give me chastity and purity of heart, by which filthy lust may be put to sleep; give me a generous will for distributing alms, by which grasping greed may be rejected. Give me the love of perfect charity, by which the jealousy of envy may be extinguished. Grant the patience of endurance, through which anger, once overcome, may fail; bestow the hope of eternal joy, by which the bitterness of sadness may be sweetened. Then make me rejoice inwardly in my mind over a good work in you, so that the outward boasting of vainglory may proceed from me.

[Col. 1272B] 38. Grant me also to maintain justice, magnanimity, and self-control in all things. Make me prudent with simplicity, so that I may both live a blessed life sincerely and prudently avoid evil; and grant that I may discern and foresee the devil’s fraudulent and deceptive cunning, lest he deceive me under the appearance of good.

After this, make me gentle and benevolent, peaceful and meek, modest and bashful, reverent and fearful, fair-minded and truthful without pretence, reasonable without deceit, and in harmony with the good; constantly diligent in vigils, fasts, and prayer. Grant also that in gentleness I may keep measured speech and at times enjoy silence with a friend, so that I may speak what is fitting and be silent about what ought not to be said. Whatever you deign to bestow from the fruits of the virtues, let humility, the guardian of them, preserve after vainglory has been put to death.

39. Grant that I may preserve for you, without any error of false religion, an undefiled faith, and that in accordance with the faith I may be a worthy laborer, so that I do not pollute right faith by wrong conduct; that I do not deny by evil living the one whom I confess through right belief; and that I do not offend by negligent action the one whom I follow with vigorous faith.

Make me, as I conduct myself in a holy purpose, pursue justice, love mercy, love truth, reject falsehood, devise or speak nothing false, fear you without ceasing, revere religion, preserve peace with everyone without deceit, recall those at odds to harmony, offer sincere charity, scandalize no one, prefer myself to no one, but judge myself lower than the lowest of all. Let me resist rulers and authorities in nothing, but obey in all things; show reverence and honor to elders; offer obedience and charity to equals; display the grace of fitting affection toward the younger; bear with equanimity the burdens or dangers of brothers.

Let me revere a friend as my own soul, love a parent and neighbor as myself, and benefit everyone alike, not harm them; injure no one, oppose no one, slander no one, place an obstacle before no one, judge no one, disparage no one, condemn no one, wrong no one, criticize no one’s life, investigate no one’s straight path, and be concerned only with myself.

Let me never repay evil with evil; let me neither remember nor avenge my injuries, but overcome every wickedness with goodness; prepare a blessing for one who curses; suffer adversity rather than inflict it; love an enemy as a friend; endure the insults and abuse of those who are angry without returning them; quickly forget injury; promptly forgive one who has offended me; always be ready to grant pardon; desire nothing belonging to another, and take nothing away on any pretext. Let me mercifully distribute my own possessions to those who lack them; release a debt owed by a debtor; restore what has been unjustly seized; return a pledge to the one who lent it; and retain nothing belonging to another.

Then let me refresh the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, gather in the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick, seek out the imprisoned, console the sorrowful, sympathize with the afflicted and mourning, provide necessities to the one who has none, share food and clothing with the needy, embrace the indigent, support the members of my household, love the foreigner, redeem the captive, receive the newcomer, protect the orphan, assist the widow, help the oppressed, provide aid to the desolate, break the bonds of wickedness, set the broken free, and undo every burden—as all the precepts of your teachings declare. Let me ardently seek them out, diligently read them, prudently handle them, hastily practice them, and eagerly fulfill them.

40. Turn my eyes away, Lord, from vanity, and my transgressions from the paths of injustice. Let my ears not receive reproach against my neighbor; nor, having abandoned truth, let them itch to hear tales of vanity or words of falsehood. Let my tongue not itch to slander or curse a ruler, a priest, or any other human being whatever. Let it not be scurrilous, empty-talking, abusive, or deceitful.

Let me not deceive my neighbor by calling his way good when it may perhaps be shown to be evil. Rather, moved by humble compassion, let me speak the truth privately, so that he may turn away from error; and if he listens, his soul may be saved and, as it is written, a multitude of my sins may be covered.

Let me be quick to listen and measured in replying. Let knowledge not puff me up, nor the swelling of arrogance distend me. Rather, overflowing in speech and good work, let me always be humble, so that I may rise and not fall, be lifted up and not be brought low, ascend and not descend.

Let praises not corrupt me, nor criticisms disturb me; let flatteries not deceive me, nor lies mock me; let prosperity not exalt me, nor adversity bend me; let a favorable reputation not raise me up, nor an unfavorable one cast me down; let joy not make me changeable, nor sadness make me unlike myself. Rather, in all things let my life be even, and my countenance constant in one manner.

[Col. 1273C] 41. In health let me praise you; in illness let me give thanks; under correction let me not rebel; under the scourge let me not murmur. Let me not be lifted up by a good work, nor attribute any good deed to myself, glory in myself, or trust in myself for anything. Rather, may you yourself be the glory, hope, strength, praise, and every delight of my soul.

Let me believe in you with my heart, confess you in praises, let my voice resound with you, and let my tongue continually proclaim you. Let me please you, not myself, and make your will, not mine. Let my whole mind meditate upon you and delight in you, and let my intention follow you, so that, denying myself, I may follow you with my cross, ready to lose my life for you, in order that through you I may find it.

Thus may the furnace of repentance restore to you a new person from useless oldness, after all the thorns of vice have been burned away, and, at the end of life [perhaps *of life*], may it reform one most elaborately arrayed in perversity of conduct. Thus, having renounced errors, may the ancient enemy discover or find nothing of his own in me hereafter.

Now, therefore, Lord my God, with great exultation I glorify your holy name. You persisted in teaching my foolishness and softened my hardness through your scourgers, until, though unwilling, I heard your voices calling me for so long, and, converted, followed the one proclaiming to me according to the verse of the psalm that says: “With bit and bridle restrain the jaws of those who do not draw near to you” (Psalm 31:9).

[Col. 1274A] And I, Lord, recognized and understood the sound of your cry. Rebuking myself, I was converted and did penance before you, as this day proves. Therefore, to your praise and my consolation, I sing to you the prophetic words: “Chastise me, Lord, for I have been instructed, like an untamed young bull.”

42. For after you converted me, I did penance; and after you showed me the way, I struck my thigh, was confounded, and was ashamed, because I bore the reproach of my youth. I remembered my God and said: “I will confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 118:1). For through your mercy my soul revived and rose from the dead, because you separated me from the sins of my youth, corrected me from my youth, converted me, and I did penance before you.

Therefore I have become a man of good hope, because you preserved for me a time of conversion, in which, considering my sins, I was pierced with remorse and did penance before you. Henceforth, joyful, I shall now and always render you countless thanks, imploring you with all my inmost being and commending myself to you with complete devotion. For, so that I might be found, you sought me; so that I might return, you compelled me; so that I might be beaten, you looked upon me; so that I might confess, you acted within me; so that, recognizing myself, I might mourn, you granted it to me.

Place my tears, Lord, in your sight, and let the prayer of the publican and sinner reach you in heaven. May the confession of my mouth be pleasing to you; and in place of offerings of gifts, which I do not present with my hand, I submit to you as a sacrifice this weeping of my contrite heart. And accept this act of penance as an offering, if acceptance has been denied me, because the act itself is imposed by you, whereas acceptance is not demanded.

43. Be, Lord, my helper and protector unto salvation, and may your mercy follow me all the days of my life. Placed in joyful shades, refresh me by the shadow of your wings protecting me.

When, however, you bring in the day of my calling, behold, Lord, weeping I say: “Wretched, trembling, and fearful, I shall enter the exceedingly bitter, most obscure, unknown, and irreparable path of death, which plunges into deep darkness.” Be present, I beg you, and help me; receive the spirit commended to you into your hands, freeing my soul from the mouth of the fiercest dragon and from the hand of the most terrible hell when you have received it and taken me from the midst of the shadow of death. Rather, lead me along the wooded and brilliantly clear path of light into the region of the living.

Place me, Lord, in the safest folds of your flocks, and count me among your sheep in the shelters of the heavenly dwellings, where your saints Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, enjoying the pleasantness of light and refreshment, dwell with the entire multitude of your saints. For you are the good shepherd who leads and brings back the lost, protects and saves those who have been found, cherishes and heals the sick.

You are the merciful Lord who does not confound those who hope in you, does not abandon those who seek you, and does not despise those who return to you, but receives them with exultation and praise, rejoicing more before your angels over one penitent and converted wanderer than over the ninety-nine blessed ones. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong one Godhead, glory, strength, dominion, and power forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1273]

## APPENDIX XIX. PRAYER AGAINST THE DEVIL’S AMBUSHES

[Note: [Col. 1273D] See *Isidoriana*, chapter 81, no. 33.] (S)

[Col. 1273D] 1. You, Lord, are the true teacher and provider, creator and redeemer, giver and protector, advocate and dreadful yet merciful judge. You give sight to blind minds; you make possible for the weak what you command; you are so compassionate that you wish to be entreated continually; so generous that you permit no one to despair.

Forgive me all my sins and every error, and, in your freely given goodness, good Jesus, lead me to that desirable contemplation where I can no longer go astray. For you know through how many vices I have fallen, you who are the knower of hidden things. You know how wretched and prone my weakness is; you recognize with what an enemy I am continually afflicted and oppressed.

You, Christ God, most powerful warrior and ever most victorious conqueror, are sought for an unequal combat; you are desired by mortal weakness. For it is the glory of your majesty if the roaring lion is overcome by a weak sheep, if the most violent spirit is conquered by the weakest flesh, and if, even when by the permission of your just judgment we suffer his domination for a time, we are in no way swallowed by his insatiable jaws. Make him, lover of humankind, sorrowful at human joy—the one who rejoices at our offense.

[Col. 1275]

## APPENDIX XX. BOOK ON THE ORIGIN AND DEATH OF THE FATHERS

Concerning this, see *Isidoriana*, chapter 61, no. 48. (C, G, S)

[Col. 1275A] Concerning Saint Abraham, who was the first path of believing.

[Col. 1275B] 1. **ABRAHAM**, son of Terah, son of Nahor; brother of Haran, father of Lot; father of Ishmael and grandfather of Jacob. The eleventh from Noah and the twentieth from Adam. He believed in God with his heart and received the Trinity as guests. He speaks with God and, after victory, is blessed by Melchizedek. In his old age he was granted a son, whom, out of love for God, he offered to God. Born in Chaldea, he sojourned in Canaan; exceedingly rich, he pleased God. Full of days, he died at the age of 175 and was buried by his sons Ishmael and Isaac in the double cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite, near the city of Kiriath-arba, which is also called Hebron by another name.

2. **ISAAC**, son of Abraham, born in his parents’ old age—that is, of a ninety-year-old mother and a hundred-year-old father. He was born at Gerar, between Kadesh and Shur; named by God before he was born; circumcised on the eighth day; obedient to his father; and offered to God as a figure of Jesus Christ, who was offered to God the Father.

Isaac’s wife was Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, Abraham’s brother; she was the mother of Jacob and Esau. Isaac, full of days and an old man of 180 years, died righteous and was buried by his sons.

3. **JACOB**, son of Isaac and brother of Esau, the supplanter of his brother. Blessed by his father unwillingly; blessed by God, and by his mother as well, willingly. Born in Beersheba, he became the father of thirteen sons. While sleeping at Bethel, he saw a ladder, angels on the ladder, and God appearing in a vision; he wrestled with God and was blessed by him. God changed his name and called him Israel.

Very rich, he went to Egypt because of famine. There he died full of days, at the age of 147 years. Embalmed with spices, he was brought from there by Joseph and buried in the double cave in the land of Canaan, where Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and also Leah lie buried together.

4. **JOSEPH**, son of Jacob and Rachel, brother of Benjamin. In Mesopotamia of Syria he was hated by his brothers but loved by his father, and was a truthful dreamer. He was sold by his brothers into Egypt as a figure of Christ, who was sold for a price of silver. Sent without guilt into prison, truly through the deceit and false accusation of Potiphar’s wife, he had the Lord with him in prison.

He revealed the dreams of King Pharaoh, which no one could interpret. For this reason he was honored by the king, made prince of Egypt, and named by Pharaoh “Sara tofane,” which in Egyptian means “Savior of the world.” He nourished his brothers and his father alike during the time of dreadful and severe famine.

He lived to an advanced age for many days, 120 years. He died in Egypt, was embalmed with spices, and was placed at Bresith in Egypt. As he himself had requested, Moses carried his bones from Egypt with him in a cart; in the time of Joshua, the king’s minister, the people buried his bones at Shechem.

5. **JOB**, also called Jobab, whose father was Zara and whose mother was Bosra. Zara was the son of Raguel, son of Esau, son of Isaac, and the fifth illustrious king from Abraham in the land of Edom.

He was a simple and upright man, a servant of the Lord, rich and renowned in sons and daughters and possessions: seven thousand sheep, fifty yokes of oxen, and a large household. Tested by God and tempted by Satan, he was deprived of his property, struck with leprosy, bereaved of his children, greatly cursed, falsely consoled by false friends, and grieved in heart by their words.

He spoke with the Lord and, questioned by him, reproached himself. He did penance in dust and ashes. Freed from the affliction, he received added possessions. Blessed by the Lord, he received double blessings in life and sons by God’s favor. He lived many days—120 years—after the affliction and died old and full of days.

6. **MOSES**, son of Amram, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Jacob. The seventh from Abraham; brother of Aaron and Miriam, whose mother was Jochebed, daughter of Levi, son of Jacob.

Moses was born in Egypt and hidden for three months. Then he was placed in a basket of rushes and set down on the riverbank. There Pharaoh’s daughter found him; she named him Moses, ordered him to be nursed, and adopted him as her son.

When he became a man, he visited his brothers. After killing an Egyptian, he fled to Midian, where he became a shepherd of sheep. There he saw the Lord in the burning bush; the Lord called him from the bush and appointed him leader of his people.

Through him the Lord performed many wonders in Egypt, at sea, and in the wilderness. Moses saw the Lord face to face. At Sinai the Lord gave him the law, which the Lord himself wrote with his finger; concerning it [perhaps *and which*] he always instructed the people. He saw the promised land but did not enter it.

At God’s command he ascended the summit of Pharga, and there, dying full of days at the age of 120, he went to his fathers. His eyes were not dim, nor were his teeth changed. No one saw or knew his tomb, because the Lord himself buried him, and the people mourned him for thirty days.

7. **AARON**, son of Amram and brother of Moses, older by three years in birth but inferior in honor in many signs. Priest of God, prophet of his brother, anointed with holy oil and clothed in splendid garments, he entered the Holy Place once a year, praying for himself and for the people.

Born in Egypt, exhausted in the wilderness, he sinned through the calf. His brother prayed for him, and afterward he pleased God. He was deprived of a share in the inheritance of the promised land because he did not believe the word of truth, when the rock was struck at Kadesh-barnea with the water of contradiction.

For such guilt the Lord, angered, said to Moses: “Take Aaron and his son and lead them to Mount Hor. When you have stripped the father of his garment, clothe Eleazar his son with it by your hand.” Thus Moses did as the Lord commanded: he stripped the father and clothed the son.

Aaron died on Mount Hor before all the people in the fortieth year of the people’s departure from Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, when he was 123 years old. He was buried there and mourned by the people for thirty days; Eleazar was appointed priest in his place. His sister Miriam fell dead at Kadesh and lies buried there by the people.

376 8. **JOSHUA**, son of Nun, who was first called Auses by his parents [correct to *Hosea*], of the tribe of Ephraim, servant of the Lord and minister of Moses. Born in Egypt, strengthened in the Lord, after the death of his master he became the foremost leader of the people.

He sent spies into the city of Jericho. He spoke with the Lord and heard from the Lord: “Today I will exalt you before my people.” He crossed the streams of the Jordan with the people of God on dry feet. In the plain of Gilgal he overthrew cities, tyrants, and the kings of the nations. He commanded the sun and moon; they stood in the sky, and the laws of nature stood upon the earth.

He assigned cities and villages and distributed them by lot. He always proclaimed the law of the Lord to the people and judged Israel continually in the seat of peace. He lived to an advanced age, full of days, 110 years. He was buried at Timnath-serah, in his portion of the inheritance, on Mount Ephraim.

9. **SAMUEL**, whose name is interpreted “placed by God,” son of Elkanah, son of Jeroboam, son of Elihu. He was born on Mount Ephraim, at Ramah; a leader and prophet, a Nazirite from infancy, servant of God, and minister of the priest Eli.

His mother, who was barren and was called Hannah, prayed to the Lord in the temple and became fertile. She sang the song: “My heart rejoiced in the Lord.” Samuel lived faithfully. He placed Saul and David upon the thrones of the kingdom; he asked for rain, and rain fell from heaven. He always prayed to the Lord for his people and ruled the people for many days.

Advanced in years and old, he went to his fathers. The people of Israel mourned him, and in his own house at Ramah they buried him in the ground.

10. **DAVID**, son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz. Born from the tribe of Judah, at Ephrathah; renowned for his appearance; king and prophet. He overcame kings, sang psalms, struck down beasts, killed Goliath, always feared the Lord, and ruled vigorously.

He foretold the birth and baptism of Christ; he revealed his passion and resurrection; he prophesied his ascension and his coming at the end of the world to judge it. God’s chosen one, whom God loved, humble and gentle, he fed his father’s sheep. He reigned over Israel for forty years: seven years at Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.

He lived to an advanced age. He slept with his fathers in the city of David and was buried in Bethlehem.

11. **ELIJAH THE TISHBITE**, whose name is interpreted “The Lord,” a great prophet of God, still living, servant of the Lord, future preacher, destined to fight with Antichrist at the end of the world. He fasted for forty days.

He raised Jonah from the dead; he withheld rain for three years and six months; he brought down fire from heaven upon whomever he wished and caused water to come. The fire consumed the ox, the stones, and the water. A devouring flame killed 102 men.

The same Elijah lived in a cave while ravens ministered to him; he blessed the widow’s oil and flour. He killed all the priests of Baal. He ascended to heaven in a fiery chariot. He was born in the land of Arabon and from the tribe of Aaron.

12. **ELISHA**, whose name is interpreted “the salvation of my Lord,” prophet of the Most High, disciple of Elijah and teacher of Gehazi. He received his master’s grace. He divided the streams of the Jordan and crossed the river on dry feet. He changed bitter waters into the nature of water; he sweetened a pot boiling like gall. He called an axe-head up from the depths of the river.

He cleansed Naaman, commander of Syria, who had been struck with leprosy; he struck a greedy disciple with the affliction of leprosy; he blessed a widow’s small amount of oil. The oil blessed in the few vessels filled not a few vessels; the widow repaid her creditor’s debt, freed her sons with the oil, and lived with her sons on what remained.

Elisha raised a dead man while alive; Elisha, dead, brought a dead man to life. Elisha was born at Abel-meholah, in the land of Reuben. When his mother gave birth to him, a golden calf cried out at Gilgal with a great bellowing, so that the people in Jerusalem heard the bellowing. Then the priest who was present and heard the miracle said: “Today,” he said, “a prophet of future things is born, who destroys [the text also reads *distributes*] the images of the idols of the city.” Elisha died in Samaria and was buried there.

13. **ISAIAH**, son of Amoz, whose name is interpreted “the salvation of the Lord,” an outstanding prophet in Jerusalem and a righteous martyr, noble by birth and nobler in speech. He prophesied under four kings: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.

He contemplated the Lord seated upon a lofty throne. He heard the seraphim, with twelve wings, praising the Lord with a clear and celebrated song: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.” One of them flew to him and cleansed his lips with heavenly fire.

To the nations sitting in the darkness of death he announced salvation and light. He foretold that a child born of a Virgin would be God, human, ruler, and father of the age to come. He prophesied the rod proceeding from the root of Jesse, flowering and bearing fruit through the sevenfold Spirit, and he foretold the overthrow and devastation of Babylon.

For three years, at the Lord’s command, he walked naked and barefoot. He foretold that the highest and cornerstone stone would be placed in Zion. He announced the Savior, ruler, and most just judge reigning in Jerusalem; he declared the Lord’s cross, passion, tomb, and resurrection; and he prophesied the coming judgment and the resurrection of the dead.

He preached in Jerusalem under King Manasseh. He died after being sawn into two parts and was buried beneath the oak of Rogel, near the course of the waters that King Hezekiah had once blocked with dust.

14. **JEREMIAH**, whose name is interpreted “exalted of the Lord,” prophet and priest, whom the Lord sanctified in his mother’s womb. While still a very young boy, in Benjamin, by command of the Lord he prophesied the watching rod and saw a boiling pot from the face of the north.

He lamented the ruin of his city in a fourfold alphabet. At the Lord’s command he wore a loincloth; in the sight of the Lord he broke an earthen flask; the priest Pashhur put him in the stocks; and the Lord showed him two baskets full of figs.

He mixed for the nations and kings a cup full of the wrath of God. He wore a chain around his neck and was confined in the court of the prison. Then, released, he wanted to go to his homeland. But the city guard again seized him and handed him over to the princes. The princes, angry, had him flogged and sent him back to prison.

The king then sent for him and drew him out of prison. The princes seized him again and, wishing to kill him, lowered him by ropes into a very deep and dry cistern. But through the hands of Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, the Lord rescued Jeremiah from the cistern and from death, and he remained in the vestibule of the prison until the day on which the city was captured.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, freed Jeremiah from prison and chains. Jeremiah was born in the village of Anathoth, a small village three miles distant from Jerusalem. He was led captive into Egypt and there, at Tahpanhes, was stoned to death by the people.

He lies buried in that same place, which Pharaoh the king had inhabited, because, at his request, the serpents were driven away from that place and he made the Egyptians safe from the bite of asps. The Egyptians also venerate him there with great reverence.

### 15. EZEKIEL

Ezekiel, son of Buzi—which is interpreted as “strength of God”—was a prophet and priest of the Most High. He was led captive into Babylon with King Jehoiachin. In the thirtieth year of his life and the fifth year of the captivity, he began to prophesy and speak to the captives. The heavens were opened to him, and he saw obscure and wondrous visions of God.

The word of the Lord came to him, and the hand of the Lord was upon him in a great and marvelous vision: in wind and a shining cloud, in fire and gleaming brilliance, in glowing amber, [Col. 1278D] among which he saw four living creatures with wings, feet, and hands—man and lion, calf and eagle. He saw four wheels beside the creatures, full of eyes on every side. As they moved together with the creatures, he heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of armies and many waters. They bore upon their heads something like a firmament, and above the firmament something like a throne was set. Upon the throne he saw something resembling a human face, like shining amber in the midst of fire.

Seeing all these things, he fell upon his face. He heard a voice speaking to him and raising him to his feet. The voice showed him a book held in its hand, unrolled the scroll, and said to him: “Open your mouth and eat this book.” He immediately ate it; it tasted like honey and filled his inward parts, and he preached to the people. He saw other manifold visions, in which he proclaimed by the word of the Lord the plagues that would come upon cities, kings, nations, islands, and peoples. He saw a field full of dry bones, upon which sinews and inward parts came; and while he prophesied, the spirit of life entered all the bones. He saw a spiritual and marvelous city extending toward the south, with gates, streets, and many buildings—something that could not in any adequate bodily sense stand.

### 16. EZEKIEL

Ezekiel is interpreted as “strength of God.” He was born in the land of Sarira and, as we have said, was led captive into Chaldaea. There the people of Israel ordered him to be killed, because the same prophet reproved them for serving idols. The people therefore buried him in the field of Maurim [the text reads *auri*], in the tomb of Arphaxad.

### 17. DANIEL

Daniel, son of Abda—“judgment of God”—was born of the tribe of Judah, in Upper Beth-horon. While still a very young boy he was led captive into Babylon. He was a distinguished prophet, and the Lord was with him; for he set him as a prince over a prince. He revealed the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar: the great image and the great tree.

He himself saw great and marvelous visions. He saw four great winds of heaven [Col. 1279B] fighting upon the sea, and four terrible beasts rising from the sea. He saw thrones set in place and the Ancient of Days seated upon a fiery throne. Thousands upon thousands of angels ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. He saw the judgment set and the books opened. He saw the Son of Man coming and the Ancient of Days. He saw a great ram tossing [something] with four horns [the reading is uncertain], and a terrible and mighty he-goat fighting against the ram. He looked upon the ram that prevailed and turned his face toward the Lord his God.

In fasting, sackcloth, and ashes he worshiped the Lord. With marvelous confession and pure supplication he entreated the Lord for himself and his people. For three weeks he mourned for the people; during his fast he ate neither bread of desire, nor meat, nor wine. In all these things the archangel Gabriel strengthened Daniel and announced to him all the visions he had seen and revealed: that Christ would be born and reign, suffer and rise again. He foretold kingdoms of the world that would fight among themselves and declared that the Antichrist would come and fight against the saints.

[Col. 1279C] This Daniel showed King Belshazzar three terrible statements written upon the wall. He freed Susanna from a false accusation. He condemned the wicked elders to death. He destroyed Bel, the idol of Babylon, and killed the terrible dragon with pitch and bristles. He caused the seventy priests of Bel to perish. Habakkuk brought him a meal, having been carried in an instant by an angel from Judaea to Chaldaea. The Lord delivered him twice from the lions’ den.

While proclaiming the almighty God in Babylon, he died; and alone among all the Hebrews he was buried in the region . . . [lacuna].

### 18. HOSEA

Hosea, son of Beeri—whose name is interpreted as “Savior”—was a prophet of the Lord who proclaimed the word of the Lord under five kings. He frequently names Ephraim, Samaria, Joseph, Jezreel, and Israel, as well as a wife of fornication and daughters of fornication; and an adulterous woman shut up in a chamber, sitting as a widow for a long time beneath mourning garments and awaiting her husband’s return.

He proclaims the word of God to the people and harshly and terribly rebukes their crimes. He encourages everyone to flee to the Lord and come to him, because he heals, strikes, and cures; he puts to death and gives life; he loves mercy more than sacrifice and seeks the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. He prophesied that Christ, the Son of God, would be called out of Egypt.

This prophet Hosea was born of the tribe of Issachar, in Belemoth, and there he fell asleep in peaceful death and was buried.

### 19. JOEL

Joel, son of Pethuel—whose name is interpreted as “the Lord beginning”—describes the land of the twelve tribes as laid waste and consumed by the caterpillar, the locust, the devouring locust, and the mildew. He declares that the earth trembles and the heavens are shaken before the face of the Lord. He indicates that the sun, moon, and stars conceal their brightness. He foretold that the great and exceedingly terrible day of the Lord would come.

He affirms that the Lord God is kind and merciful, patient and compassionate, and gracious toward human wickedness. He summons the people to the church to offer sacrifice and fast. He proclaims that the elders, young men, and children, the joyful bridegrooms and brides, and the priests, the ministers of the Lord, should proclaim the Lord, spare the people, and grant peace. He promised those who served him abundance of grain, wine, and oil, together with the Lord’s peace.

He foretold that the Lord would pour out his Holy Spirit upon his male and female servants; he prophesied that the elders would dream dreams and the young men would see visions in the Lord.

The prophet Joel was born of the tribe of Reuben, in the field of Beth-horon. He died there and rests buried there.

### 20. AMOS

Amos the Tishbite is interpreted as “powerful,” or “strong,” or “one who tears the people apart.” He was a prophet, a shepherd, a rustic, and a gatherer of *mora ruborum* (“bramble-berries”); his message cannot be explained in a few words. For who could worthily express the three and four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, and Moab, and, at the seventh and eighth degree, those of Judah and Israel?

He speaks to the fat cows that are on Mount Samana and testifies that the greater and the lesser house will fall. He himself sees the maker of the locust, the Lord standing upon a plastered—or adamantine—wall, an onyx *pomerium* (boundary), and one drawing punishments upon sinners. He sees famine in the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of God.

This is the Amos whom King Amaziah had often struck. Uzziah, his son, publicly wounded the same prophet with a deadly injury, piercing him through the temples. Thus, two days after he had been brought back to his native land, this seer breathed his last and was buried there.

### 21. OBADIAH

The prophet Obadiah is interpreted as “servant of the Lord.” Thunderously speaking against Edom, Jacob’s brother and perpetual rival, he struck down the stars . . . [lacuna]. He rebukes the pride and arrogance of the proud. He proclaims that the wise and prudent of the world, the tyrants, and its strong men will perish and be struck down by the Lord.

He prophesies salvation from Mount Zion, the coming of the Savior, and the Lord’s eternal reign.

This Obadiah was born in the field of Beth-acaran and came from the land of Shechem. He was a disciple of the prophet Elijah and the third captain of fifty, sent by Ahaziah to Elijah with fifty soldiers. When he made his request, Elijah spared him, so that fire would not consume him as it had the two captains of fifty sent before him.

Obadiah then abandoned Ahaziah’s service and prophesied. He died and was buried with his fathers.

### 22. JONAH

The prophet Jonah, son of Amittai—whose name is interpreted as “dove” or “one who grieves”—was the son of the widow of Zarephath, whom Elijah raised from the dead. The Lord sent him to preach in Nineveh.

He sought a ship and fled to Joppa. God raised up a great wind upon the sea, and the sea therefore surged in a mighty tumult. The sailors struggled against the wind and sea.
