They awakened Jonah, who was drowsing and asleep. They threw their belongings into the sea, worshiped their god, and cast lots to discover whose fault had brought about this danger.

The lot immediately fell upon Jonah the Hebrew. Then they said: “Where do you come from? What have you done? From what people were you born?” He answered: “I am a servant of the God of heaven, and I am a Hebrew by birth.”

Trembling with great fear and unable to remain silent, they said: “What must we do with you, man?” The servant of God told them what they had to do: “Take me out of this ship and throw me into the sea.” Then they threw him into the sea, as he had ordered.

God sent a great fish to swallow the prophet. The fish swallowed him, as God had commanded, carried him for three days and nights, and from the fish’s belly he cried out to the Lord. The Lord heard him and at once delivered him. The fish vomited him onto the land, which he himself had not wished for; he went to the city of Nineveh and preached repentance to the king and the people.

When the king and the people heard him, they believed in God, from the least to the greatest. In sackcloth and ashes, not only the people but also the animals repented. For three days and three nights they cried out to the Lord and fasted, and God delivered them from the plague they feared.

Jonah most beautifully prefigured the Lord’s passion through his own shipwreck; he calls the world back to repentance and, under the name of Nineveh, announces salvation to the nations.

As one travels toward Tiberias, there is a small village where the tomb of the same prophet Jonah is also shown.

[Col. 1281A]

### 23. MICAH

The prophet Micah—“Who is this?” or “humility”—was born of the tribe of Ephraim, in Moresheth. His name signifies “heir.” The word of the Lord came to him in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

He calls all peoples to hear the Lord. He mourns the ruin of Judah and Jerusalem. He rebukes unjust judges, powerful wicked men, and false prophets. He announces the two thieves of the temple and Jerusalem. He announces a high mountain prepared above all mountains and hills. He indicates that all peoples and many nations will ascend that same mountain. He declares that the law of God, Zion, the word of the Lord, and Jerusalem will go forth from it.

He declares righteous judgment between peoples. He confirms that, because of the greatness of peace, swords will be fashioned into plowshares and spears into pruning hooks. He prophesies that a ruler will come forth from the city of David and reign in Israel. He foretells that the cheek of the judge of Israel will be struck.

He indicates what is good for a human being and announces what God seeks from him: to practice righteous judgment, to walk carefully with his God, and to love mercy. He did not hesitate to foretell the coming persecution: that no one should trust his own wife, that sons would persecute their fathers and daughters their mothers, that a daughter-in-law would contend against her mother-in-law, and that a man’s household enemies would become his own.

He prophesied, as far as he was able, the greatness and patience, mercy and compassion of the Lord. He affirmed that the Lord would cast the sins of the repentant into the depths of forgetfulness.

This prophet, because he repeatedly reproved the sinful Ahaz, was thrown from a very high precipice under Joram, his son, and died. He was buried in his own land near the Polyandreion, which is near Naim.

### 24. HABAKKUK

The prophet Habakkuk is interpreted as “embracing.” He was born of the tribe of Simeon, in the field of Beth-zachar. He prophesied that the Lord would come from afar and would be born.

He chastised the unbelieving. He affirmed that the righteous live by his faith. He terribly rebukes the greedy, the avaricious, murderers, drunkards, and worshipers of idols.

This same Habakkuk, a strong and stern wrestler, stands upon the fortress so that from afar he may contemplate Christ upon the cross and say:

> His glory covered the heavens,  
> and the earth is full of his praise.  
> His brightness shall be like the light;  
> horns are in his hands;  
> there his strength is hidden.

This prophet departed from life in the field of Sabarith two years before the return of the children of Israel from captivity.

[Col. 1281C]

### 25. ZEPHANIAH

The prophet Zephaniah—whose name is interpreted as “the one who hides her”—was the son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah, of the tribe of Simeon. He prophesied in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah.

He is the watcher and knower of the Lord’s secrets. He hears a cry from the Fish Gate, wailing from the Second Quarter, and destruction from the hills. He also indicates wailing for the inhabitants of Sila, because all the people of Canaan have fallen silent and all who were wrapped in silver have perished.

He is the one who prophesied that the day of the Lord would come wondrously and terribly, saying:

> The great day of the Lord is near,  
> it is near and exceedingly swift.  
> The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter;  
> there the mighty man will be troubled.  
> That day is a day of wrath,  
> a day of tribulation and distress,  
> a day of calamity and misery,  
> a day of darkness and gloom,  
> a day of cloud and whirlwind,  
> a day of trumpet and battle-cry  
> against fortified cities and lofty corners.  
> I will trouble human beings,  
> and they shall walk like the blind,  
> because they have sinned against the Lord.

Zephaniah died in the little field of Sabare (another reading: Sarabath) and lies buried in the earth.

### 26. HAGGAI

The prophet Haggai—whose name is interpreted as “solemnity”—prophesied in the second year of King Darius about the return of the people from the captivity of Babylon and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel the high priest.

He therefore promised in the word of God that God would grant every good thing to his people. He strengthened the ruler, the people, and the high priest to restore and build the temple of God with the great help of God, saying:

> Thus says the Lord of hosts:  
> Set your hearts upon your ways.  
> Go up into the mountain, bring wood,  
> and build the house;  
> then I shall accept it,  
> and I shall be glorified,  
> says the Lord.

He prophesied the barrenness of heaven and earth and that of the trees, because of human sins. He prophesied an abundance of grain, wine, and oil; an abundance of peace and health for the people, for God’s servants, and for those who serve him.

He prophesied that God the Father and his Spirit would always be among his people. He told them not to fear, saying:

> Be strong, all you people of the land,  
> says the Lord of hosts,  
> and act, because I am with you,  
> says the Lord,  
> and my Spirit shall be in your midst;  
> do not fear.

He prophesied that God himself would shake heaven, earth, sea, dry land, the nations, and the thrones of kingdoms, and that the Father’s Only-Begotten would come, saying:

> Yet a little while,  
> and I shall shake heaven and earth,  
> the sea and the dry land.  
> I shall shake all the nations  
> and the thrones of kingdoms,  
> and the one desired by all nations shall come.

Haggai came from Babylon to Jerusalem when he was very young. There he breathed his last and lies buried near the tombs of the priests.

[Col. 1282B]

### 27. ZECHARIAH

The prophet Zechariah—whose name is interpreted as “mindful of the Lord”—was the son of Berechiah. He and Haggai prophesied in one and the same year, under one and the same King Darius.

Zechariah’s prophecy is varied and mystical. Seeing diverse and obscure visions, he prophesied mystically, because the angel of the Lord spoke through him. He saw at night a man mounting a red horse and standing among myrtles in the depths, with red, dappled, and white horses behind him.

He heard an angel asking about the time of mercy for Jerusalem. He heard the Lord speaking to the angel good and consoling words concerning Jerusalem, Zion, and the cities of Judah. He saw four horns tossing Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.

He saw a man holding a measuring line in his hand and measuring Jerusalem in length and breadth, saying:

> Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall,  
> for the Lord shall be a wall of fire around her.

He saw a written stone with seven eyes, and a golden lampstand supporting seven lamps, with seven tubes hanging from the lamps; and two olive trees standing beside the lampstand, one on its right and one on its left.

He saw a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide. He saw a talent of lead being carried and a woman sitting in the middle of an amphora, who is wickedness; a mass of lead was placed in her mouth. He also saw two women with wings like the wings of a kite, lifting the amphora between heaven and earth.

He saw four chariots emerging from between two golden mountains. In the first chariot were red horses, in the second black horses, in the third white horses, and in the fourth strong, dappled horses. He saw many other obscure and mystical things.

He prophesied the return of the people and the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple. He prophesied that a poor and humble king would come, saying:

> Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion;  
> shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem.  
> Behold, your king shall come to you,  
> righteous and saving,  
> poor and riding upon a colt,  
> the foal of a donkey.

He prophesied that the same king would be handed over and sold for silver, saying in his own person:

> They weighed out my wages, thirty pieces of silver,

and what follows.

He wondrously prophesied in every respect the passion of that same king, that is, of our Savior, just as it happened. For he says:

> I will strike the shepherd,  
> and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.

And again:

> What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?  
> I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.

And again:

> They shall look upon me whom they pierced.

Concerning his death he prophesied:

> They shall mourn for him with a mourning  
> as for an only son,  
> and they shall grieve over him  
> as one grieves over an only son.

He foretold the future baptism, saying:

> On that day there shall be an open fountain  
> for the house of David  
> and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem,  
> for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman.

Concerning the death of this same prophet Zechariah, I have a faithful witness who neither deceives nor is deceived: namely, Jesus our Savior in the Gospel according to Matthew, rebuking the unbelieving Jews and saying:

> Let all the righteous blood poured out upon the earth come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar.

Zechariah, therefore, having returned from the region of the Chaldaeans to his own land at a very advanced age and, as we have said, having been killed, lies buried in Jerusalem near Haggai.

### 28. MALACHI

The prophet Malachi is interpreted as “Angel of the Lord.” He recalls mystical matters and the mysteries of God, teaching that honor must be given to parents and masters, saying:

> A son honors his father,  
> and a servant his master.

In the person of God the Father he asks all the living:

> If I am a Father, where is my honor?  
> And if I am a Lord, where is my fear?

He rebukes unworthy priests who minister to God unworthily and culpably. He praises the worthy priest and calls him an angel, saying:

> The lips of the priests should guard knowledge,  
> and instruction should be sought from his mouth,  
> because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.

But he calls the one who offers blemished gifts to his God from his possessions accursed, saying:

> Accursed is the deceitful man  
> who has a male in his flock  
> but, when making a vow, sacrifices the weak to the Lord.

He showed that there is one Father of all and that one God must be worshiped. For he says:

> Have we not all one God who created us?  
> Why then does each one despise his brother?

He foretold the coming of John, the Lord’s forerunner, saying:

> Behold, I send my angel before your face,

and what follows.

He prophesied that Elijah the prophet would come and preach before the judgment, saying:

> Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet  
> before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes;  
> and he shall turn the hearts of fathers toward sons  
> and the hearts of sons toward their fathers.

At the end of all the prophets, Malachi openly prophesied the rejection of Israel and the calling of the nations, saying:

> I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts,  
> and I shall not accept an offering from your hand.  
> From the rising of the sun to its setting,  
> my name is great among the nations,  
> and in every place sacrifice is made  
> and a pure offering is offered to my name.

After the return of the people of Israel from Babylon, Malachi was born in Supha. He died there while still very young and has a tomb among the Gibeonites; he lies buried in his own grave.

### 29. AHIJAH

Ahijah the Shilonite, from the city of Elijah, foretold to King Solomon that he would turn aside from the commandments of the Lord because of women. King Uzziah died and was buried near the oak in Shiloh.

### 30. IDDO

Iddo was born in Samaria. He warned Rehoboam when he was unlawfully offering sacrifice. As Iddo was returning to his own place, a lion strangled him on the road. He was buried at Bethel in the tomb of the prophet who had deceived him.

### 31. AZARIAH

Azariah is interpreted as “the help of the Lord.” He was born in the land of Sabatha. He died and was buried in his own field.

### 32. ZECHARIAH

Zechariah is interpreted as “mindful of the Lord.” He was the son of Jehoiada the priest. When he had lived thirty years, the people gathered in the court of the house of the Lord at the command of King Joash and killed the holy prophet by throwing stones at him. The priests immediately lifted him from there and buried him beside his father.

### 33. TOBIT

The holy prophet Tobit, servant of the Most High God, was born of the tribe and city of Naphtali. In the days of Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, he was led captive while still young into the city of Nineveh among his fellow captives, though he was old and wise in counsel and mind.

He charitably gave all the good things he possessed to his fellow captives. Though still a little boy in age, he was mature in the fear of God. He avoided vain idols and always kept the law of God. He mercifully served proselytes and strangers. He gave tithes worthy of God. He took Anna, from his own tribe, as his wife. She bore a son, and the father gave the child his own name and taught him the law and fear of God.

He always abstained from the food of the Gentiles. He guarded his soul undefiled and always remembered his Lord in his heart. The Lord granted him favor in the sight of King Shalmaneser. He did whatever he wished and went wherever he desired. He enriched the poor of his own people from the king’s gifts. To the poor Gabael, from his own people, he gave ten talents of silver under a written bond.

He fed the hungry, clothed the naked, and buried the dead. King Sennacherib, the enemy of God, wished to kill him, but the Lord guarded him with his wife and son. Afterward he would leave his dinner guests, conceal the slaughtered dead of his people, and bury them during the night.

In all these things he pleased God and displeased his neighbors, because he did everything for God’s sake. Then God tested him: he took away his possessions and wealth and struck him with beggary and poverty. He endured insults and mockery from his parents, wife, and relatives. Like Job, he suffered abuse from kings and false friends.

Yet in all these things the holy man Tobit remained steadfast in the fear of God. He always blessed God and asked for God’s mercy with groaning and tears. The Lord heard him and delivered him from all his tribulations. He sent his holy angel Raphael from heaven, who strengthened him in all his counsels.

Tobit thought Raphael was a human being and asked him to travel with his son. Thus Raphael became an angel in the manner requested by the holy father. He traveled with the son and brought him safely as far as the city of Rages in Media. He conversed with him as with a fellow servant and brother. He rescued him from the bite of a fish and caused him to take Sarah, daughter of Raguel, as his wife. Raphael restrained the demon named Asmodeus and bound him in the desert of Upper Egypt. He brought great joy to the girl’s parents, recovered the holy father’s money from Gabael, and brought Tobit back safely to his father with great possessions, his wife, and a large household.

He restored the sight of the holy old man’s eyes, and Tobit joyfully saw his son and his household. Then the angel showed them all the mysteries of his journey, of Sarah’s prayers, and of the healing. The angel Raphael told them that he was an angel of God and had been sent by God.

They were afraid, fell prostrate upon the ground, and the angel said to them:

> Do not fear. Peace be with you.  
> Bless God, praise him,  
> and tell of all his wonders.

When he had said this, he vanished from their sight. They remained prostrate upon the ground for three hours, blessing God. Then they rose and recounted all his wonders.

The old man opened his mouth, blessed God, prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem and the temple, and foretold the overthrow of the great city of Nineveh. He lived very wealthy and renowned for many years amid blessings. He was fifty-six years old when he lost the sight of his eyes. For four years he was blind and poor. At sixty he received back his sight and his wealth doubled. After he had been restored to sight, he lived forty-two years and saw the children of his grandchildren.

When he had completed 112 years, he departed in peace in the fear of God and was honorably buried in the city of Nineveh, together with his wife Anna.

### 34. JOHN THE BAPTIST

John the Baptist—whose name is interpreted as “grace of God”—was the son of the priest Zechariah, of the tribe of Levi, born in Israel. He was conceived when an angel announced it, and named by the angel before he was born. He was born in his parents’ old age.

He was the forerunner of the Savior in a marvelous manner: by being born, preaching, baptizing, dying, and descending to the underworld. He was born six months before the Savior, beheaded before the Lord’s passion, and descended to the underworld as Christ’s first herald. He was the servant of the Lord, prophet of the Most High, voice of the Word, friend of the bridegroom, witness of the Lord, herald of the Judge, lamp of the Light, soldier of the King, end of the prophets, and beginning of baptism.

His father remained mute and silent for nine months because he did not believe the angel who prophesied. The one who had been foretold deprived his father of the power of speech; when he was born, he released the function of the tongue. Before he had been delivered, he prophesied Christ and greeted him from the womb.

Among those born of women no greater than he arose. The Lord praised him, called him an angel, and named him a prophet and more than a prophet, because he pointed out with his finger the one about whom he had prophesied.

He was full of the spirit and power of Elijah. When he appeared at birth, he brought great joy to many. He recognized the Savior in the dove, revealed him in the wilderness, baptized him, and preached repentance. His clothing was camel’s wool; the wilderness was his dwelling; his food was wild honey and locusts.

When he forbade Herod to violate his brother’s marriage, Herod ordered him to be confined in the darkness of prison. Herod’s daughter, dancing, asked for his head as a reward. Drunk amid his cups, Herod gave her his severed head, which she had wickedly requested.

He was conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, born on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, and suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. He was buried in the town of Sebaste in Palestine, formerly called Samaria, which Herod, king of the Jews and son of Antipater, called Augusta in Greek in honor of Caesar Augustus.

The head of John the Baptist has been placed in a glass vessel at Emesa, in his honor, by the favor of our Lord.

### 35. JOSEPH

Joseph—whose name is interpreted as “increase”—was the son of Jacob, son of Matthan, of the tribe of Judah and the family of David. He was born in his own city of Nazareth and was a craftsman by trade. He was the brother of Clopas and the husband of Mary, by assistance rather than by carnal union.

Clopas was the father of the apostle Simon the Cananaean; Joseph was the father of James, the brother of the Lord, who is called James of Alphaeus. Mary of Clopas—that is, the wife of Clopas—was the sister of Mary, the mother and Virgin.

A sufficiently obscure question nevertheless arises concerning Joseph, Mary’s husband, in the genealogies of the Gospels, namely those according to Matthew and Luke. According to Matthew he is called the son of Jacob, in these words: “Matthan begot Jacob, Jacob begot Joseph.” According to Luke, however, he is named the son of Heli, in these words: “Joseph, who was of Heli, who was of Melchi.”

But to those who understand the Scriptures well, there is nothing contradictory in these words. Matthew affirms that he was the son of Jacob according to the flesh, whereas Luke declares him the son of Heli according to the requirement of the law.

Jacob and Heli were uterine brothers, born of one mother named Estha, but they were not born of one father. The father of Jacob was Matthan, whom Estha bore to him; the father of Heli was Melchi. After Matthan died, leaving one son named Jacob, Melchi took Estha, the mother of Jacob, and she bore him a son named Heli.

Jacob, his brother, having no children, took Heli’s wife and raised up a son for his deceased brother according to the requirement of the law, naming him Joseph; according to nature, however, he was his own son—namely Joseph himself, who is called Mary’s husband and proclaimed as Christ’s father.

### 36. MARY

Mary—whose name is interpreted as “lady,” or “illuminatrix,” or “star of the sea,” or simply “star”—was of illustrious lineage: daughter of King David, branch of Jesse, rose without a thorn, fruitful olive, golden column, dawn of the sun, queen of women, bride of the Savior, daughter of the living God, handmaid of the High Prince, enclosed garden, sealed fountain, bridal chamber of the Trinity, mother of the almighty Lord, mother of the sun and flower, mother of the lamb and lion, mother of life and vine, mother of light and peace, mother of the way and truth, mother of servant and king, mother of God and man, mother of shepherd and bread, temple of God, and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit.

Holy virgin, pregnant virgin, virgin before childbirth, [Col. 1285D] virgin in childbirth, virgin after childbirth: she believed the son she bore to be the Creator, had him as her father, and worshiped him as Lord. She received the greeting from the angel and recognized the mystery of the conception. She inquired about the manner of the birth and did not refuse the faith of obedience contrary to the law of nature.

She became the mother of a man without intercourse with a husband. She nursed the infant and remained an undefiled virgin.

Some assert that her life ended in martyrdom. For the holy Simeon, carrying Christ in his own arms, prophesied, saying:

> And a sword shall pierce your own soul also.

Yet this was prophesied not of a bodily sword but of a spiritual sword, that is, the word of God, which is more powerful and sharper than every very sharp sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit. For neither the letter nor history teaches that Mary departed this life through the suffering of bodily martyrdom.

This, however, is certain: no one knows her death or how she departed from this light, although her tomb is certainly situated in Jerusalem.

The Nativity of holy Mary, the Mother of the Lord, is celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of September. Her Assumption is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September.

### 37. JESUS CHRIST

Jesus Christ is interpreted as “anointed Savior.” Jesus is a Hebrew name, called *soter* in Greek—“savior” in Latin. Christ is Greek; in Hebrew he is called *messiah*, and in Latin “anointed.”

He is the Son of David, son of Abraham, as Holy Scripture records in the holy words of the holy evangelist and apostle Matthew, who writes and says at the beginning of his Gospel:

> The book of the generation of Jesus Christ,  
> son of David, son of Abraham.  
> Abraham begot Isaac,

and what follows, down to the place where it says:

> When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah  
> in the days of Herod the king of Judaea.

All these things affirm in what order he was announced from heaven to the Virgin through the archangel Gabriel; how he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb; in what place, at what time, under what king, [Col. 1286B] and among what people he was born; and how he was named by the angel. These matters have been briefly stated above.

No one living by nature can—not merely narrate or investigate, but even estimate—the greatness, height, depth, breadth, and obscurity of this mystery, except that one alone. Yet this mystery, as he willed, established, and consecrated it, the Holy Spirit affirms through Isaiah, saying:

> Who shall declare his generation?

And through the apostle Paul the same Holy Spirit cries out and says:

> O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!  
> How unsearchable are his judgments  
> and how inscrutable his ways!  
> For who has known the mind of the Lord,  
> or who has been his counselor?

And again he says:

> From him, and through him, and in him are all things.

For who among angels or mortal human beings could investigate, conceive, or proclaim the true God and the Only-Begotten of God—who is incomprehensible and beyond estimation, begotten before the ages without a mother—and the true human being, in flesh, soul, and nature, from a true Virgin mother without sin; conceived and born without an earthly father at the end of the ages? Or how can human frailty comprehend him?

For he is God from himself and in himself: God Most High, God in God, God with God, God in man, and man in God. He is true man by nature and humanity, and true God by power and majesty.

The Lord Jesus Christ commanded his Church to do what he did, believe what he taught, and hope for what he promised. He graciously came humbly to us and dwelt among us bodily and mercifully for thirty-three years and six months.

His conception and passion occurred at the spring equinox; his birth at the winter solstice; his circumcision on the Kalends of January; his baptism in January; his resurrection on the sixth day before the Kalends of April; and his Ascension into heaven on the third day before the Nones of May. There he reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever.

### 38. THE APOSTLES

All the apostles were disciples, but not all the disciples were apostles. For *apostles* in Greek means “sent” in Latin. *Disciples* are those who learn fully.

### 39. SIMON PETER

Simon Peter is called by three names. First by his parents Cephas, then Simon, and third Peter. God called him by these two names: Simon, which is interpreted as “obedient”; Peter, “recognizing.” Formerly a fisherman of fish, he afterward became a fisher of men. Christ held him like a fish in the net of election when he called him to come after him.

He is the recognizer of Christ, the key-bearer of the kingdom, the foundation of the Church, prince of the apostles, son of Joanna, brother of Andrew, born in the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, which is beside the lake of Gennesaret. He is third in rank according to John, first according to Matthew; the first confessor of the Son of God, a disciple who loved the Lord, and a denier.

Praised for confessing, lifted up through presumption, fallen through denial, purified by weeping, proved by shame, crowned through suffering. His name is given according to his work, and a title is imposed according to the merit of his authority. He became renowned in the world for virtues and signs [Col. 1287A]. With the tread of his feet he walked upon the raging sea. As he passed by, his shadow healed the sick; by his power he handed over the living to death; by his virtue he raised the dead to life. In his mercy he restored walking to the lame. He restored the weakened limbs of paralytics to their proper condition.

He struck down Simon Magus, the sorcerer, as he ascended into heaven, and under the emperor Claudius he founded the Church at Antioch. Under Nero, however, he governed Rome. He preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and the other neighboring provinces. It is found that he traveled about preaching only to the Jews; at last, because of Simon Magus, although by the hidden will of God, he reached Rome. There, preaching the Gospel, he held the pontificate of that city for twenty-five years.

In the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion, under the emperor Nero, he was suspended on a cross, as he had desired. His birthday is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of July. He was buried in the Vatican, three miles east of the city of Rome [perhaps west].

### 40. PAUL

The apostle Paul, who was first also called Saul. Paul is interpreted as “wonderful” or “pious”; Saul, however, is interpreted as “impious.” Thus Saul, that is, the impious man, persecuted Christians. Paul, that is, the pious man, preached Christ to the peoples (sic).

A preaching shepherd, a distinguished preacher, an excellent teacher of the nations, an advocate of the Jews. Chosen by Christ, called from heaven, happily rebuked, cast down upon the earth, he fell with sight and rose up blinded; a savage persecutor, full of charity, an elect vessel, transformed from a wolf into a sheep. Last in his calling, first in preaching; a disciple in the school of Gamaliel, a servant in the Gospel of Christ.

Born in Judea, descended from the tribe of Benjamin, laboring more than all the others, preaching much more widely than the rest, teaching the Gospel of God in a circuit from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, whose miracles shine forth brilliantly. He was caught up and ascended into the third heaven. By command he condemned the spirit of the Python. He raised a dead young man. He struck a magician with blindness and restored the proper gait to a lame man. He felt no harm from the bite of a dreadful serpent, but gave it over to the fire. By prayer he healed Publius’s father of fevers. He endured unbelievable sufferings for Christ.

He bore blows from Jews and Gentiles; misery and toil, thirst and hunger, cold and nakedness; he was beaten with rods three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, submerged in the depths of the sea for a day and a night, struck by a thousand dangers and blows, thrust into prisons, bound with chains, handed over by Jews to Gentiles. He escaped after being let down in a basket through a wall. Afflicted by punishments, he suffered the violence of beasts; bound in prison, he was released when an earthquake occurred.

In the second year after the Lord’s Passion he was baptized by Ananias at Damascus. After all these events he spent two years in custody at Rome; then, after completing eighteen years in which he fully instructed the western nations, under Nero, on the same day on which Peter was crucified, he himself was beheaded on the Ostian Way and buried there with honor.

### 41. ANDREW

Andrew, the apostle of the Lord, brother of Simon Peter, was first in birth before Peter and third in the order of the pontificate [Col. 1287D]. A Galilean by race, he was born in the city of Bethsaida. Formerly a fisherman, he afterward became Christ’s disciple. While he was dragging fish from the sea with net and boat, he himself, like a fish caught in a net, clung to the great Fisherman.

Leaving both net and boat, he followed the blessed Redeemer of the world. Following the Lord and Savior, he became both a fisher and a preacher of men. He followed Christ as far as the raising up of the cross, and he manfully held to Christ’s footsteps until the Passion of the cross.

For Andrew is interpreted as “manly” or “beautiful”: truly manly, and he acted manfully, because he preached Christ crucified to barbarian peoples, praised his cross wondrously, and believed and prayed with wonder.

He therefore evangelized beside the Caspian Sea, in Scythia, Macedonia, and Achaia, where he won many peoples for Christ. He was filled with the greatest ardor of love for Christ and for Christ’s cross; in justice, holiness, and devotion he surpassed almost everyone.

When he saw the cross prepared for him, he said, filled with indescribable [Col. 1288A] and immeasurable joy and exultation: “O good cross, O glorious cross, O precious cross, O holy cross, adorned as if with the pearls of Christ’s blood; O cross sought and desired for so long, receive me, I beg you, and restore me to my master Christ.”

He did not fear the cross as an instrument of death, but loved and embraced it with excessive affection. For he beheld his Master with incomprehensible love; therefore he did not fear the gallows, although he felt it. Then he joyfully ascended the cross, because he had obeyed his Master even unto death.

The blessed man hung upon the gallows for two days and, shining brightly with an angelic countenance, did not cease preaching to the peoples. The people both saw and heard these things wondrously and attempted with great effort to release him from the cross, but no human being born was able to touch him, because the Lord wished to lead his soldier away with himself.

Then he greeted the peoples and his brothers in Christ and joyfully departed with his Master and the angels into the rest of the kingdom. These events took place under the proconsul Aegeas in the city of Patras, on the day before the Kalends of December. Blessed Maximilla brought his little body from there with honor and placed the holy body in spices (sic). His relics—that is, his arm—were transferred to Rome in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantine and honorably placed in the church of Saint Peter, his brother [Col. 1288B].

### 42. JAMES

James, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” son of Zebedee and brother of the apostle John, was first a fisherman by trade and afterward became a follower of Christ. Leaving net and boat, he followed the Savior, leaving his father Zebedee. He obeyed almighty God.

Leaving the sea and its fish, he became a heavenly fisherman in the sea, that is, in the world. He preached to the Spaniards and the western regions and died by the sword under Herod. He was buried in Marmaric Achaia on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

### 43. JOHN

John the apostle and evangelist, whose name is interpreted as “the grace of God,” son of Zebedee and brother of James. He was the son of Saint Mary by adoption and Christ’s brother in virginity.

He was chosen and loved by the Lord to such an extent [Col. 1288C] that he reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper. John himself stood by Christ’s cross; to him alone, as he hung there, the Savior entrusted his mother Mary.

This John wished to take a wife at Cana of Galilee, when the Lord Jesus changed water into wine. But the Lord Jesus drew him toward the example of virginity, so that a virgin might assist a virgin and the mother might have her own son. For when the mother received the disciple of her master, he too was in a certain way left as another son in Christ’s place.

John, the disciple of the Lord; John, archbishop of Asia; John, full of the love of God; John, a river of oil in the mysteries of the Gospel; John, seen as the eagle in Ezekiel’s vision of the four living creatures.

While preaching Christ’s Gospel in Asia, he was bound in chains by the emperor Domitian. There he beheld the Apocalypse, that is, the Revelation, where he both spoke and wrote the mysteries of God. After Domitian was killed by the senate, John was released from exile and happily withdrew to Ephesus.

There, at the request of the bishops of Asia, he wrote the Gospel, in which he surpasses the others in speech just as he precedes the others in love. Among his other virtues, the greatness of his signs was especially remarkable.

He was truly a martyr in his will. For he was sent into a cauldron of boiling oil and escaped unharmed. He drank a cup of poison, and it harmed him not at all. He raised two men who had died from poison. He changed wild branches bearing leaves into gold, transformed stones from the shore into gems, and restored fragments of the gems to their proper nature. At the command of the people he also raised a widow, and restored the body of a certain young man who had returned from death to the condition of life. What is even more remarkable to say, he displayed Christ’s generation to the world.

After the Savior’s Passion, in the sixty-eighth year, under the emperor Trajan, worn out by the long old age of his years, when he sensed that the day of his departure was approaching, he is said to have ordered a tomb to be dug for him. After bidding farewell to the brothers, he prayed. When the prayer had been completed, he entered the tomb as he looked upon it.

From this it happened that some people assert that he is alive and insist that he lies in the tomb not dead but sleeping, especially because there the earth is said gradually to bubble up from below and rise to the surface of the tomb, as though the breath of the person resting below were boiling upward.

But Pope Leo, the apostolic man, filled with the Holy Spirit, unquestionably removed this dispute and opinion from Christian hearts. For, discussing this same John and the resurrection of the saints, he says:

“Indeed, perhaps many of those same blessed martyrs will have obtained the bodily resurrection with the Lord, or will have obtained it in due order; for we read that at the first feast of the Resurrection, when the Lord raised himself, many bodies of the saints were raised, lived, and entered the holy city.

“But perhaps someone will say: ‘The tombs are closed and monuments have been constructed; how could they have come forth from there?’ To say nothing of the fact that all things are possible for God, and that he can bring forth a spiritual body even when the inner chambers of the tombs are closed—to pass over all these matters, we have an example in an apostle whom the tomb was able to receive and enclose but was unable to keep. For it lost the body it had taken in.

“By the grace of the resurrection he was removed from the doors of the tomb, so that the burial place remained but the buried man could not be found. Finally, when the priests sought the body in order to honor it, after the entrance had been opened, the tomb could not return the one it had received.”

The birthday of this same John is therefore celebrated at Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January. Others say that his falling asleep is observed on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, when the nativity of John the Baptist is celebrated.

### 44. THOMAS

Thomas, whose name is interpreted as “abyss,” and by another name Didymus, that is, “like Christ,” for in bodily appearance he was made very similar to the Savior. Hence Judas said to the Jews, handing over his master: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.”

After his resurrection, the Lord deigned to show Thomas the wounds of his Passion. When the apostles assured him that Christ had risen, he refused to believe, saying: “Unless I see the mark of the nails in his hands and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”

Jesus came again, with the doors shut, to his disciples, and Thomas was then found among them. Then Jesus said to Thomas: “Bring your finger here and put it into the places of the nails, and put your hand into my side, and do not lose your faith.” Then Thomas feared and believed and recognized the Lord as his God, saying: “My Lord and my God.”

Thomas performed many wonders through his apostleship in the regions of India, which it would now take too long to recount to you. Those who nevertheless wish to know them can find them wonderfully recorded in his Passion (sic).

Yet, so that I may not seem to have passed over all his miracles, I shall try briefly to relate one of them. Thomas was once at a banquet of the king, where everyone had whatever all wished to eat and drink. He himself, however, refused to eat and drink, but raised the eyes of his heart and body toward heaven.

The king’s cupbearer saw this, came angrily to the apostle, struck him in the face, and said: “Why do you not eat and drink from the food and wine at the king’s banquet?” Then Thomas, answering in Hebrew, said to him: “I will not leave this banquet until a black dog places your right hand in the middle.”

No one at the banquet understood these words except a Hebrew girl who played the harp for the guests. It happened as the man of God had said: the cupbearer went outside to bring water; a lion met him on the road and strangled him to death, breaking all his bones into tiny pieces.

Dogs came from the king’s palace to the corpse and divided the cursed man’s limbs among themselves. One of the dogs brought the cupbearer’s right hand into the middle of the banquet, just as Thomas, the man of God, had foretold.

When the Hebrew girl saw this, she came to the apostle playing the harp. Standing before him and sounding the harp’s songs, she was filled with faith and the ardor of God’s love. She began to sing a spiritual song on the harp and wondrously praise the almighty God of all, saying:

“One is the God of the Hebrews, who created all things; he made heaven [Col. 1290A] and earth and founded the seas.”

When she had sung this again at the apostle’s command, she bowed at his feet with great faith and devoutly believed in Christ, the Savior of all.

When all the people saw and heard these things, they were greatly amazed and afraid, and many of them believed in Christ.

Thomas therefore preached to the Parthians and Medes and to the innermost eastern region. There he proclaimed the Gospel and suffered martyrdom. He was pierced through with a lance and died in the city of Calaminica in India. He was buried there in honor on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January.

### 45. PHILIP

Philip, whose name is interpreted as “mouth of the lamp,” was born in the city of Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. His memory is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. He was one of the seven deacons who were ordained by the apostles together with Saint Stephen. Their names are: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timothy, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte from Antioch.

This Philip had a wife and fathered four prophetesses by her [Col. 1290B], and afterward became the Lord’s apostle.

He went to Samaria filled with the power of the Lord. There he was the first to preach the word of the Lord to the Samaritans. The power of divine grace in him was so great that even Simon Magus was overcome by his preaching. At that time Simon was held in great renown among the peoples of Samaria, so that he was thought to possess the great power of God.

But when he saw the signs and miracles performed by Philip through the power of divine grace, he was astonished and terrified, withdrew, and pretended to believe in Christ, even receiving baptism.

Afterward Philip preached Christ to the Gauls. Later, in Hierapolis in the province of Phrygia, he was crucified and died by stoning. He rests there together with his daughters. His birthday is celebrated on the Kalends of May.

### 46. JAMES

James, whose name is interpreted as “supplanter,” son of Joseph Cleophas, whose memory is recorded in the Gospel. This James is recorded as the brother of the apostle Thaddaeus, who by another name is called Judas; both are said to be Christ’s brothers.

This same James was the first bishop of Jerusalem [Col. 1290C]. He was surnamed Justus and bishop of the apostles.

There were many men named James, but this same James, the son of Alphaeus, who, as we said earlier, was surnamed Justus, surpassed the other Jameses because he was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor strong drink and ate no meat. Iron never touched his head; he was not anointed with oil, was not washed in a bath, and wore no woolen garment, but was clothed only in a linen cloth.

He alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies. He alone entered the temple and lay upon his knees praying for the people’s forgiveness, so that through praying he developed calluses on his knees like those of a camel, always bending his knees and never ceasing from prayer.

Thus, because of this extraordinary self-restraint and supreme righteousness, he was called Justus and Oblias, which is interpreted as “bulwark of the people.”

While preaching Christ, the Son of God, in Jerusalem, he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the temple. The Jews struck him on the head with a fuller’s club and overwhelmed him with stones. He was buried there beside the temple. His birthday and ordination are believed to be celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

### 47. BARTHOLOMEW

The apostle Bartholomew received his name from the Syriac language and is interpreted as “son of the one who suspends waters.”

He was well formed in appearance, handsome in face and eyes, and splendid in clothing and jewels. Yet he was neither lifted up nor made proud by this. The Lord gave him such power over demons that whenever he wished, the demons in idols were silent; and whenever he wished, the demons unwillingly revealed and proclaimed their shame and misery from the idols.

It happened once that Bartholomew displayed such a miracle before the people. He ordered the people to stand before an idol and, by the power of God, commanded the demon to come out of the idol, display itself to the people in its great misery and deformity, and preach.

Then the wretched demon, unwillingly, began to speak with groaning and howling:

“O fools, see what kind of God you worshiped in me, wretched as I am! O senseless people, consider me, miserable, misshapen [Col. 1291A], and despised in every way, whom you asked to help you. O deluded people, behold what sort of lord you believed in with your most foolish and blind heart. O deceived people, pay attention: I am not God, but a most wretched demon, deceived through pride and fallen from heaven. Once I was an angel in glory; now I have become a devil under God’s wrath.

“I lost glory and angelic life in heaven and found endless punishments and countless torments in hell. I lost my glory in such a way that I can in no manner find forgiveness or God’s grace, because I have no flesh and no material for repentance.

“For if I, miserable creature that I am, could have had one finger with a claw from human flesh, I could have redeemed myself from my misery and cruelty. You senseless creatures, created along with all things and made according to the two images of God, why do you deceive and destroy yourselves? Why do you stray from the Creator, when he gave you feet for standing and walking, hands for touching and working, eyes for seeing and knowing, ears for hearing, a tongue for speaking and praising God, and a heart for believing and understanding?”

Then the apostle answered him: “How could you, wretched creature, with one clawed human finger, have redeemed yourself from your calamity?”

To him the demon answered again with howling:

“With that one finger and claw I could have cleaned one person’s nostrils, another’s ears, and a third’s eyes; I could have scratched everyone’s limbs as they wished. If I had diligently done these things, perhaps one person would have said, ‘God bless you’; another, ‘May God help you’; a third, ‘May God free you from your evil.’ Through these many and great blessings, I would have come forth free.”

After he had said all this by God’s command and without his own will, the wretched demon vanished from the sight of everyone.

When all the people saw and heard this, they were greatly afraid and amazed. Abandoning the vain [worship] of idols, they believed and blessed almighty God.

Bartholomew therefore preached in Lycaonia. At last, while still alive, he was flayed by barbarians in the greater city of Albanum in Armenia and beheaded by order of King Astyages. Thus he was buried on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

### 48. MATTHEW

The apostle and evangelist Matthew received his name from the city of Matthea, and it is interpreted as “given.” At first he was a publican, afterward the Lord’s disciple.

He sat in the tax office and controlled the treasures; he sinned publicly, inwardly darkened and blinded by worldly cares. At a certain time, when God willed it, he saw the sun of righteousness and heard the words of truth with the ear of his heart.

He followed the sun that he had seen; he believed and worshiped the truth that he had heard. Leaving the tax office, he followed the Lord of all. Leaving a perishing treasure, he followed the king who remains forever. Leaving falsehood and vanity, he followed the way and the truth. Leaving death and the world, he followed life and the kingdom. Forgetting foolish speech, he wrote and preached the Gospel.

He was called by three names: Matthew, Levi, and Publican. He was called Matthew from his city, Matthea, as we said above; Levi from the tribe of Levi, from which he descended; and he was surnamed Publican because he administered public affairs.

Matthew is interpreted as “given”; Levi, “minister”; Publican, because he sins publicly.

First, in Judea, during the reign of Gaius, king of Rome, he composed and preached the Gospel; afterward in Macedonia. He suffered in Persia on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October and rests in glory in the mountains of the Portae.

### 49. SIMON THE ZEALOT

Simon the Zealot, whose name is interpreted as “zeal.” He was first called Cananaeus from the village of Cana, which is interpreted as “possessing.” He was also called Simon by his third name, burning with zeal for God.

He was Peter’s equal in surname and his equal in honor. The Lord’s apostle and cousin; son of Cleophas and Mary. This Mary is called Mary of Cleophas in the Gospel. Cleophas, his father, and Joseph, who is called as it were his father, were brothers of Christ; and his mother, who is called Mary of Cleophas, was the sister of Mary, the mother of the Lord.

Thus, in a remarkable manner, two brothers had two sisters as wives: Cleophas in the flesh, Joseph in the spirit.

Simon therefore received authority for preaching in Egypt [Col. 1292A]. After James the Just, he is said to have held the episcopal seat of Jerusalem. After 120 years, under the emperor Hadrian, he deserved to suffer the martyrdom of the Passion by crucifixion. He lies in Bosporus. His birthday is celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

### 50. JUDAS LEBBAEUS

Judas Lebbaeus, that is, “little heart,” meaning “from the heart.” He is also Thaddaeus, and he is Judas of James, son of Joseph, brother of Cleophas. His name is interpreted as “confessor.” He preached in Mesopotamia and in the interior regions of Pontus.

He was buried in the city of Crito in Armenia. His festival is celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

### 51. MATTHIAS

Matthias, or Matthian, was one of the seventy disciples and was appointed among the twelve apostles in place of Judas Iscariot. Chosen by lot, he alone had no surname. The preaching of the Gospel in Judea was assigned to him.

### 52. THE APOSTLES

These holy apostles were Christ’s disciples, lights of the world, precious stones, friends of the Savior, preachers of the faith, attendants of the bridegroom, princes of the world [Col. 1292B], key-bearers of the kingdom, salt of the earth, branches on the true vine, sowers of righteousness, reapers in the field of the master of the household, lovers of truth, teachers of the nations, conquerors of demons and tyrants, explorers of paradise, good shepherds of Christ’s sheep, and judges of the Jews, sitting with the Judge at the great judgment upon twelve thrones.

Although they were all one, each received his own particular and definite region in the world as his lot for preaching:

Peter, Rome; Paul, from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum; Andrew, Achaia; James the son of Zebedee, Spain; John, his brother, Asia; Thomas, India; James, the brother of Judas, Jerusalem; Matthew, Macedonia; Philip, Gaul; Bartholomew, Lycaonia; Simon the Zealot, Egypt; Judas, Mesopotamia; Matthias, Judea.

### 53. ON THE APOSTLES

Concerning the apostles who undoubtedly had wives, I heard Saint Clement say the following. He was their companion and disciple and was the third pope after Peter in Rome. For he says:

“Peter and Philip indeed had wives, and they even gave them in marriage to other men. Nor is the apostle Paul ashamed, in one of his Epistles, to mention and greet his wife, whom he nevertheless says he does not take about with him so that he may be more free for preaching the Gospel.

“So also it is said of Peter. ‘They say,’ he says, ‘that blessed Peter, when he saw his wife being led to her passion, rejoiced in the grace of her election and return to her own home, and called out after her as she was being led away, addressing her by her own name: “O wife, remember the Lord.”’”

Such were the marriages of the saints; so perfect was the affection of the blessed.

### 54. MARK

Mark, whose name is interpreted as “exalted,” was God’s evangelist and Peter’s son in baptism, as well as his disciple in divine teaching.

Serving as a priest in Israel, he was a Levite according to the flesh. Converted to faith in Christ, he wrote the Gospel in Italy during the reign of Caesar Claudius.

It is said that after coming to the faith he cut off his thumb so that he would be considered unfit for the priesthood. But according to God’s dispensation and the merit of his faith and life, he afterward became a bishop [Col. 1292D].

They relate that this Mark first went to Egypt and preached there the Gospel that he himself had written. This is also called a praiseworthy theft, because what Peter had preached by word, Mark wrote secretly at the brothers’ request.

He himself first built a church at Alexandria and was the first preacher and bishop in that city. He was also called by another name, John. Some assert that he was crowned with martyrdom. Jerome, however, says that he departed to heaven in the peace of the Church.

His deposition is celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

### 55. LUKE

Luke, whose name is interpreted as “raising up” or “rising,” was the third evangelist, a Syrian by nationality and from Antioch. His praise is sung in the Gospel. By profession he was a scribe and physician, a disciple of the apostles, and afterward followed Paul until Paul’s confession, serving the Lord without blame.

For he never had either a wife or children. He was a physician of bodies and souls [Col. 1293A]. He wrote two books concerning the spiritual medicine of souls: the Gospel in the regions of Achaia during Paul’s time—which the apostle Paul calls his own Gospel, for he says, “according to my Gospel”—and another book called the Acts of the Apostles, which he composed for the holy bishop Theophilus of Antioch.

He died at the age of seventy-four in Bethany, full of the Holy Spirit. Later, in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantine, he was transferred to Constantinople together with the relics of the blessed apostle Andrew. His deposition is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November.

### 56. BARNABAS

Barnabas, also called Joseph, was a native of Cyprus, a city founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians. Together with the apostle Paul he obtained the apostolate among the Gentiles.

Later, because of John the disciple, who is also called Mark by surname, he separated from Paul. Nevertheless, as an apostle, he carried out the work of evangelical preaching entrusted to him.

### 57. TIMOTHY

Timothy, bishop of the Ephesians, was from the city of the Trienses. His father was a Greek, that is, a Gentile, while his mother was Jewish, namely Eunice [Col. 1293B]. As the apostle Paul reports, saying: “For faith lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice, and it is certain that it lives also in you.”

He was a disciple of the apostle Paul and his spiritual son. Paul the apostle took him with him as a boy. He remained chaste and a virgin. He rests with great honor near Ephesus, on the mountain called Pion.

### 58. TITUS

Titus was a disciple of the apostle Paul and his son in baptism. A Greek by nationality and the only one from the Gentiles circumcised by the apostle Paul after the Gospel, he was left by that apostle to establish the churches of Crete.

There he died in peace and rests buried.

### 59. STEPHEN

Saint Stephen, full of grace, a worthy deacon and, after Christ, the first martyr, was the nephew of Zacchaeus and the son of Simon.

Stephen was a great soldier, distinguished by birth and radiant in appearance; yet he shone more brilliantly before the world through faith and signs. He read the Gospel, understood the Gospel, preached the Gospel, fulfilled the Gospel [Col. 1293C], and proclaimed Christ perfectly to the peoples. By wisdom he overcame the synagogues and performed great signs among the people.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, he overcame the barking dogs who opposed him. He saw the heavens opened and looked upon Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God.

In Jerusalem he wisely sang the holy Scriptures and diligently taught his Jewish brothers from God’s law. With confidence he rebuked those who were hard of heart and unbelieving; filled with charity, he chastised those who did not believe with gentleness.

When God’s enemies saw these things, they gnashed their teeth at him. When God’s enemies heard these things, they sought how they might kill him. Madmen raging and filled with fury barked against the holy man like dogs. False witnesses shouted lies. Miserable men condemned Christ’s soldier to death. Stiff-necked and cruel in heart, they gathered stones and, dragging Saint Stephen outside the city, stoned him.

They stoned him; he prayed. They hurled hailstorms of stones upon him; he joyfully bent his knees to his Maker. They slaughtered him with hands full of curses; he, filled with the ardor of charity, flashed forth. Those foolish companions of Satan raged against the holy man; the holy man persistently sang praise to the supreme Savior. They, darkened by fury, gnashed their teeth; he shone with an angelic countenance and radiant face [Col. 1294A].

The executioners competed in throwing stones; he truly prayed for forgiveness for his persecutors. They cruelly shattered the holy man’s head and body with stones [Col. 1294B]; he, gazing upon the Holy One in heaven, said: “Do not hold this sin against them, Lord.”

They poured Saint Stephen’s blood upon the earth; Saint Stephen saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing. They split Saint Stephen’s sides with flints; he steadfastly gave thanks to Christ. They ran about in fury, anger, and shouting; he cried out to Christ while preaching, praying, and singing psalms. They tore the limbs of the great soldier with stones; the great soldier commended his spirit to Christ.

Thus Saint Stephen, kneeling and praying, fell asleep in Christ. As we said earlier, Saint Stephen saw the heavens opened and entered them.

His prayer made Saul a Christian for the Church and brought down the distinguished and pious preacher Paul, because if Stephen had not prayed then, the Church would not afterward have had Paul.

After this, truly God-fearing people came from the city and mourned Saint Stephen with great lamentation. They buried his body with great honor. There, by the Lord’s favor, great miracles both appear now and appeared then.

His martyrdom is honored throughout the world and is always celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of January. After some time, on the third day before the Nones of August, his body was sought and found there, where Christ is believed and worshiped by many thousands.

[Col. 1293]

## APPENDIX XXI. BOOK ON NUMBERS

Concerning this work, see *Isidorian Works*, chapter 63, sections 10 and following (C, G, S).

### 1.

With the help of our most high Lord and the gracious granting of our most merciful Savior Jesus Christ, I wish to write briefly, yet usefully, about number and its mystical mystery.

What do I and II and III signify? What do IV, V, and VI affirm? What does VII signify? What do VIII, IX, and X convey? And if we can reach as far as XXIV, we wish to say what they reveal.

### 2.

One alone therefore belongs to God, because in all things, before all things, and above all things—in his omnipotence, magnificence, and incomprehensibility—he is one, just as the divine voice spiritually affirms at the head and beginning of Sacred Scripture, saying: “Hear, Israel: the Lord God is one.”

For who in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth could be like God alone in eternity, power, trinity, unity, divinity, or humanity?

Therefore God is called one and alone, because neither before, nor afterward, nor then [nor] now is another found or read to be like him in heaven or on earth. For the one who, through pride, wished to be like him in heaven soon grew weary, fell, and perished, and deserved to become a demon, Satan, and prince of demons in hell.

Many things in God’s creatures and in the sacred Scriptures appear to exist in multiplicity, yet are called by one name as one thing: man, soul, faith, baptism, charity, hope, peace, bread, the Catholic Church, and many others, which for the sake of brevity I now pass over.

Nevertheless, concerning the things mentioned above—that is, man, soul, and the others that follow—even if not in their proper order, we shall narrate them in their respective places, as God grants.

### 3. From what was man made?

At the beginning we find that one man was made by God. From whose rib we read that one woman was made; one language, namely Hebrew, was spoken, as is attested, until the building of Nimrod’s tower. That tower was being built in the plain of Shinar.[^c0129-1] One Abraham is attested, who is also said to have been the head of faith, because from Adam up to the birth of Christ no other man named Abraham is found. Of him it is said: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Did not Abel believe, and did he not deserve to be crowned as the first martyr? Did not Enoch believe, who still lives in the body? Did not Noah, having been justified, believe—he whom the Lord delivered with the ark and all that was in it? Yet neither Abel, nor Enoch, nor Noah was called the head of faith.

Why is this so? That is, although the faith of those righteous men appeared in their time, it was nevertheless rare and always lacking. But from Abraham until now, and until the end, faith has neither failed, nor is it lacking, nor will it fail. Therefore Abraham was called the head of faith.

There was one Noah, who built the ark; and if there was another, Scripture has kept silent about it. This same Noah was the first, after the Flood, to build an altar to the Lord in the mountains of Armenia, because there, among the mountains, the floodwater left the ark.

The writings report that one woman—namely Lot’s wife—was changed into a statue of salt. That statue still stands today, so that everyone who sees it may fear God and believe him to be almighty.

One woman appeared in the world such that no other like her was ever born: she carried the sun and fire in her womb for nine months, and they did her no harm in any way.

I read that one virgin suckled a lion; I do not hesitate to believe it, and I never cease to marvel.

There is one supreme mediator between human beings and God, who on the human side truly became man. Therefore he can and could truly be called mediator, because neither did divinity harm humanity, nor was humanity opposed to divinity.

There is one city in heaven, which is the mother of all the saints, called Jerusalem and interpreted as “vision of peace.” No one who is unworthy, proud, and impure has entered, enters, or will enter that city.

Thus far we have spoken about one; now we shall speak about two.

### 4. Of how many substances does man consist?

Man consists of two substances, made in the image and likeness of God: that is, of soul alone and body. Yet within these two substances, joined together into one, many forms appear.

In the human body nine measures are unquestionably combined: four principal ones—earth, water, air, and fire—and five further kinds, namely salt, hay, flowers, stones, and clouds. To understand all these in a better way, read as follows:

Earth in man is the thickness and heaviness of the flesh. Water is sweat and saliva. Air is the moist, cold, and warm breath itself, breathed through the mouth and nostrils. Fire in man is what cooks food in the stomach and is present in the heat of the blood. Salt is in the saltness of blood, sweat, tears, and urine, since all these are salty in man. Hay is in the hair and bodily hairs. Flowers are in the variegation of the eyes. Stones are in heaviness and hardness, because bones are called the stones of the earth. Clouds are the instability of the mind and thoughts.

The body, composed of these nine measures and joined together by larger and smaller bones, consists of 365 principal joints. The number of the other, smaller ones can scarcely be found. Likewise there are 365 principal veins, while the smaller veins are countless. It is also composed of nerves and blood, flesh and skin, marrow, cartilage, the head, and three brains: the first is called memory, the second the senses, and the third movement.

There are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

There are six ages: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, and advanced old age. Infancy ends at seven years; childhood ends at fourteen; adolescence extends to twenty-eight; youth ends at fifty; old age concludes at the seventieth year; but advanced old age is not completed by any fixed period or number of years, but by labor, pain, and death.

Man has ten fashioned windows. Through the first window he utters words, receives and breathes air, takes food, and tastes it. Through two windows he sees far and near. Through two other windows he smells and breathes. Through two other lower windows he expels the body’s necessities. The tenth window, called the navel, adorns the belly.

In the heart man has understanding and thought, counsel and fear; in the spleen, laughter; in the gall, anger; in the liver, love; and also breath and lightness in running and swimming.

Naturally, by all these things, and by many others that I omit for the sake of brevity, the human body is constituted. The nature of this same body carries within itself four conditions: it hungers, thirsts, desires, and sleeps. The use of this nature is therefore fulfilled by four things: eating, drinking, begetting, and sleeping.

This is a brief account of the body. Now let the origin of the soul be discussed.

### 5. What is the soul? And if it is some thing, from what are souls made?

What is it itself? What is its name? What use does it have among created things? Does it live, or not? If it lives, what does it contribute to the affections of the universe? Does it lead a blessed life or a wretched one?

What, then, is the soul? It is not heaven, nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor God, nor the stars; nor does it come from the soul of the father or mother, as many suppose. It is not sight, hearing, smell, taste, or any of the other things whose enumeration would be lengthy, whether in heaven or on earth. None of these is the soul.

From where, then? The soul is given by God, made from nothing, and created by God, as the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “I made every breath”—that is, every soul. Likewise in the Psalm he says: “He who fashioned their hearts one by one”—that is, their souls, because human hearts are the lampstands of souls.

What the soul is must be stated briefly, since God has kept silent about it in his Scriptures. The soul is a rational and sensitive life, vivifying spiritually, invisibly, and wondrously all the inward parts and limbs of the whole body, inside and out, at the command of its Creator. In a wondrous manner it ministers to the body’s five senses: through the eyes it sees, through the ears it hears, through the nostrils it smells, through taste it distinguishes flavors, and through touch it governs all the limbs.

It subsists spiritually in a fourfold manner: through sense, wisdom, thought, and will. Sense pertains to life; wisdom to understanding; thought to counsel; will to defense.

Although the soul is one thing, it possesses many forms and adornments within itself. When it breathes, it is spirit; when it senses, it is sense; when it has taste or understanding, it is mind; when it understands, it is intellect; when it rightly distinguishes, it is reason; when it gives consent, it is will; when it remembers, it is memory; when it gives vitality to the limbs, it is soul; when it lives well, it bears the image of God; when it is well adorned and pleasing to God and the angels; when it is full of good virtues, it is the seat of the Trinity.

The soul’s adornments are these: through hearing it believes; through desire it seeks; through wisdom it finds; through prayer it asks; through grace it receives; through humility it preserves; through mercy it comes to the aid of others; through kindness it forgives; through teaching it acquires; through repentance it restores; through example it is beautiful; through knowledge it is luminous; through good zeal it is free; through gentleness it is calm; through prudence it is cautious and clear; through simplicity it is sincere; through stability it is sober; through justice it is upright; through patience it is long-suffering; through obedience it is ready; through action it is clean; through hope it is stretched toward its goal; through abstinence it is temperate; through chastity it is holy; through spiritual joy it is glad; through confession it is open; through martyrdom it is adorned; through unity it is catholic; through harmony it is peaceful; through love of neighbor it is generous; through love of God it is perfect.

These are the soul’s adornments.

The body’s necessities are these: food in hunger, drink in thirst, rest in labor, sleep in weariness, a song in pleasure and boredom, health in pain, strength in weakness, refuge in fear [uncertain reading: *tunore*], light in darkness, peace in war, and many other things that it would now be lengthy to mention for the sake of brevity.

Just as human flesh cannot live happily without these necessities, so the soul cannot remain perfectly in the body without what it needs. The soul’s food is the divine commandment; its drink, pure prayer; its bath, lawful fasting; its clothing, alms from one’s own substance; its instrument, continual praise of God; its rest, perfect poverty; its health, bodily weakness; its refuge, pure repentance; its peace, complete charity.

O man, whoever you are, constituted of these two substances, as we have said—that is, body and soul—imitate Christ and the holy Fathers who went before you. Learn humility from Christ, devotion from Peter, charity from John, obedience from Abraham, hospitality from Lot, long-suffering from Isaac, endurance from Jacob, patience from Job, chastity from Joseph, gentleness from Moses, steadfastness from Joshua, kindness from Samuel, mercy from David, abstinence from Daniel, almsgiving from Tobit, contemplation from Eli, action from Paul, tearful repentance from Mary Magdalene, pure confession from the thief, martyrdom from Stephen, and generosity from Lawrence.

### 6. On pride and envy

There is no doubt that there are two poisonous and deadly roots for all living beings. From them have arisen every iniquity, every impiety, every calamity, every cruelty, every storm, every pain, every plague, every punishment, every disease, every mortality, every tribulation, and every evil whatsoever that is found and can be felt in heaven, on earth, or in hell. One root is called pride; the other is called envy.

Who among the wise and those who understand the Scriptures does not know that pride is the root and queen of all evils, as Scripture bears witness, saying: “The beginning of every sin is pride”?

Through pride, the prince of the angels—called Lucifer at that time and appearing almost as the seal of the living God—was the first to depart from God, from the throne of the Most High, from the height of heaven, and from that great and holy city called the vision of peace, in which there are nine orders of angels. He himself, with a tenth part of the angels, went down into the Tartarus of hell.

O deed so cruel, so evil, and incredible! That most hard-hearted dragon, his own deceiver and inventor of death, found in that very expulsion of his the second root of all death, which is called envy. Thus holy Scripture says: “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world.”

In this way, then, sin first entered through envy, and through sin death took its origin—that is, it arose from the wicked suggestion of the most cruel enemy. From the wicked suggestion an evil thought burst forth within; the evil thought produced pleasure; pleasure produced consent; consent, action; action, habit; habit, necessity; necessity, an evil death; and evil death, destruction.

Through the devil’s suggestion, Eve was deceived by the serpent, and thus the first man, Adam, was deceived through Eve and transgressed the commandment of his Creator. In that transgression he found labor and death, and left them afterward to his offspring. Therefore God said to Adam in connection with that labor and death: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”; and again: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.”

Affirming this, Scripture says: “As death was given in Adam, so it will rule over all his children.”

After labor, death, misery, corruption, and the curse had been discovered and countless other things had been left to his descendants, he himself, together with his offspring, was held in darkness and torments from the day of his death, in the first age of the world, until the resurrection of Christ.

### 7. The two ways

There is no doubt that there are two ways in this world, the way of life and the way of death: one by which the saints proceed happily, and another by which sinners destroy themselves. Concerning these ways the Holy Spirit says in the first Psalm:

> “The Lord knows the way of the righteous,  
> but the way of the ungodly will perish.”

The way of the saints is the Lord himself, as he said: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” The way of sinners, however, is the darkness of death, as it is read in the Psalm:

> “Let their way”—that is, the way of sinners—“be darkness and slipperiness.”

The way of the saints is catholic faith; the way of sinners, perverse unbelief. The way of the saints is upright hope; the way of sinners, dry despair. The way of the saints is perfect charity; the way of sinners, hateful iniquity. The way of the saints is diligence of mind; the way of sinners, negligence of heart. The way of the saints is fear of God; the way of sinners, transgression of the commandment. The way of the saints is good will; the way of sinners, evil desire. The way of the saints is continual prayer; the way of sinners, evil verbosity. The way of the saints is confession of weakness; the way of sinners, excuse for iniquity. The way of the saints is pure simplicity; the way of sinners, dark obscurity. The way of the saints is steadfast patience; the way of sinners, temporal instability. The way of the saints is true humility; the way of sinners, polluted exaltation. The way of the saints is temperate abstinence; the way of sinners, uncontrolled excess. The way of the saints is holy chastity; the way of sinners, unclean lust. The way of the saints is beautiful sobriety; the way of sinners, drunken excess. The way of the saints is generosity in giving; the way of sinners, greed in hoarding. The way of the saints is silence in keeping quiet; the way of sinners, talkativeness deserving punishment [*vapulandi*, sic]. The way of the saints is remembrance of the good; the way of sinners, forgetfulness of God. The way of the saints is holy reading; the way of sinners, presumptuous murmuring [*murmuratio*, sic]. The way of the saints is justice and truth; the way of sinners, falsehood and perversity. The way of the saints is harmony of peace; the way of sinners, discord of dissension. The way of the saints is to give thanks in all things; the way of sinners, always to despise. The way of the saints is good zeal in the love of God; the way of sinners, evil zeal and love of the world. The way of the saints is good instruction; the way of sinners, evil display. The way of the saints is to store up treasure in heaven; the way of sinners, concealment in the depths. The way of the saints is the humility of Christ; the way of sinners, the pride of the devil. The way of the saints is love of the future life; the way of sinners, love of the life that will perish.

On the one way, what is loved here is taken away; on the other, what is loved is possessed forever.

### 8. The two hells

We also read in Scripture of two hells: one on earth, in which the saints are tested; the other beneath the earth, in which demons and the ungodly are condemned. Although they are called by one name, they are very far apart. In one there are labor and rest; in the other, perpetual misery without end.

In the hell of the saints there is saving compunction; in the hell of sinners, punitive torment. In the hell of the saints there is true repentance; in the hell of sinners, repentance too late. In the hell of the saints there is pious remission [the text reads *abremissio*]; in the hell of sinners, just condemnation. In the hell of the saints there is testing with consolation; in the hell of sinners, punishment without interruption. In the hell of the saints there are affliction and refreshment; in the hell of sinners, continual torment. In the hell of the saints there is hope of receiving a reward; in the hell of sinners, despair that the punishment will end. In the hell of the saints there is perpetual sweetness; in the hell of sinners, the burden of endurance. In the hell of the saints there is fear of offense; in the hell of sinners, vengeance for transgression. In the hell of the saints there are labor and rest; in the hell of sinners, an injury always involving punishment. In the hell of the saints there is visitation of the weak; in the hell of sinners, forgetfulness of visitation. In the hell of the saints there is the weeping of penitents; in the hell of sinners, tears and gnashing of teeth. In the hell of the saints there are night and day; in the hell of sinners, outer darkness. In the hell of the saints the good are tested; in the hell of sinners the wicked are punished.
