In the hell of the saints fire is seen and serves; in the hell of sinners it is possessed and torments. In the hell of the saints angels keep watch; in the hell of sinners the adversaries are tormented. In the hell of the saints there are grace, kindness, and mercy; in the hell of sinners, bitterness, anger, and indignation. In the hell of the saints the holy are helped; in the hell of sinners demons and the ungodly are condemned. In the hell of the saints there are good and evil [sic]; in the hell of sinners there is nothing good. In the hell of the wicked there is no end to evils; in the hell of the saints there is hope of the kingdom of heaven.

### 9. On drunkenness

I have found two things, and have come to know them as greatly opposed to one another in miserable human life. One is called drunkenness; the other is called sobriety. Of their opposition I shall say a little briefly.

Drunkenness is quite useless: an unworthy thing in men, immodest in women, insulting in servants, reprehensible in priests. It destroys dignity in kings, forgets truth in judges, erases mercy in the rich, stirs up evil habits, wholly disorders a person, recalls hostilities, provokes killings and disasters, prepares the murder of parents, arouses quarrels, makes the healthy insane, makes the wise foolish, renders the sober senseless, washes away memory, cuts down perception, neglects the mind, confounds understanding, excites lust, entangles speech, corrupts the blood, violates sight, hardens the ears, makes laughter noisy, disturbs the inward parts, cries out indecently, does not speak rightly, moistens [or “makes wet”] the brain, demands sleep, weakens the limbs, hinders sacred mysteries, dries the throat, scatters the marrow, makes promises in the evening and lies in the morning, stains body and soul, and destroys every form of health.

### 10. On sobriety

Sobriety, however, is useful in all things. It is good in heaven and on earth, good on the way and in the homeland. It restrains the young, honors the old, lengthens life, enriches the heir, makes offspring fruitful, and increases honor. It is dignity in men, modesty in women, favor in servants, adornment and praise in priests, glory and victory in kings. It displays truth in the judge, patience in the poor person, and generosity in the rich.

It promotes good habits, preserves the whole person, renews friendships, mitigates quarrels, reconciles those who disagree, calms the healthy, adorns the wise, teaches the foolish, guards the sober, retains memory, illuminates hearts, purifies the mind, sharpens understanding, brightens the face, restrains the expression, despises lust, overcomes vice, opens the ears, relieves the brain, is silent at the proper time, speaks rightly, cares for the veins, strengthens the blood, waters the bones, nourishes the marrow, gives strength to the limbs, enjoys sleep, opens the eyes, restrains laughter, reveals sacred mysteries through a few words, is sparing in speech and faithful in action. It cleanses body and soul together and guards every form of health.

### 11. On peace and discord

I have truly seen two other things that are very far apart from one another. If one alone had reigned and the other had not come at the proper time, no human being would have lived happily. I wish to say a little about them, since I am now hastening on to other matters.

One is called discord, and the other peace.

Discord is greatly to be feared and very seriously avoided by every Christian. It makes children of the devil from children of God, enemies from friends, and adversaries from brothers. From it come whispering, complaint, fury and anger, controversy and falsehood, oaths and perjury, injury and scandal, deceit and envy, spite and homicide.

Discord is nothing other than the separation of peace and the disruption of unity, the devil’s discipline, the way of death, the destruction of life, the breaking of commandments, the alteration of judgment, the scattering of understanding, the devil’s house, the path of hell, the expectation of punishment, the expulsion of forgiveness, the overthrow of discipline, contempt for charity, suppression of humility, disturbance of the mind, disorder of the limbs, a deadly evil, the serpent’s poison, the viper’s bite, the breath of the basilisk, the vomit of the regulus, the closing of the kingdom, the opening of hell, God’s enemy, and the devil’s friend.

### 12. On peace

Peace does not act in this way, for it brings God near to man and man near to God. Therefore true peace must be held fast and preserved by all Christians in heart and body.

Such a teacher is sweet and greatly to be loved: she performs many miracles and is wondrous in making children of God from children of the devil, friends from enemies, brothers from adversaries, relatives from strangers, and members of one household from aliens. From her come sincerity and simplicity, mitigation and gentleness, meekness and forgiveness, openness and truth, silence and justice, stability and patience, love and protection [*tutio*, sic], aid and healing.

Peace is nothing other than the house of God. For God himself said to his disciples: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.”

What else is peace but nearness to God, the grace of God, and union with God; health of judgment, sharpness of understanding, the house of God, the path of the kingdom, expectation of rewards, gathering of diligence, firmness of discipline, perfection of charity, circle of humility, shield of tranquility, restraint of authority, and serenity of the limbs?

O, if only I had been permitted to proclaim peace fully and plainly! I ought to have written many lines with my fingers, for it surpasses every understanding. Its life-giving, honey-sweet delight is the opening of the kingdom, the closing of hell, God’s friend, the devil’s enemy, happiness in the present life, and joy and gladness in everlasting life.

### 13. True repentance

True repentance is recognized in two ways. The first is to mourn and repent most devoutly and with the most abundant tears for the sins committed. The second is not to commit again those things that must be mourned and repented.

Repentance is called *paenitentia*, as though it were *punitentia*, because a person punishes himself for what he has done wrongly.

A servant of God ought to have such remembrance of sin that he always bewails with tears what he has done. Nothing is worse than to recognize guilt and not mourn it. Every sinner ought to have a twofold weeping in repentance: either because through negligence he has failed to do good, or because through presumption he has committed evil. He did not do what he ought to have done, and he did what he ought not to have done.

That person performs repentance worthily who laments his guilt with lawful satisfaction, condemning and mourning what he has done, and doing so more deeply in proportion to how inclined he was to sin.

Great indeed is the power of tears: without a voice or the sound of words they obtain the pardon they request for sins. Peter burst into tears; he asked for nothing in words. I find that he wept, but I do not find what he said. I read his tears, but I do not read his satisfaction.

Peter rightly wept, because what can be mourned can be excused; what cannot be defended can be washed away. Tears wash away a sin that one is ashamed to confess aloud. Tears therefore serve modesty in weeping and salvation; they are not ashamed when seeking pardon, and they obtain what they rightly ask for in prayer.

### 14. Tears

Tears, I say, proceed silently in a certain way; they ask for pardon and deserve it. They do not state the cause, yet they follow mercy. Tears are certainly more useful than spoken prayers, because speech may perhaps deceive in praying, whereas tears never deceive. Speech sometimes does not disclose the whole matter; tears always reveal the feeling.

O tears, how sweet, how strong, how precious, how gentle you are in the breasts of the mother repentance! Just as a loving mother supplies milk from her breast to an infant, so loving repentance offers tears from the compunction of the heart to the penitent. The mother nurses the infant so that it may grow; repentance makes the penitent weep so that he may live again. The mother wishes the infant to grow old in life; repentance wishes the penitent not to grow old in any evil. The mother does not wish life for everyone; repentance wishes salvation for everyone.

O repentance, great are your breasts, full of the wine of compunction! Through them you revive the guilty, raise up the fallen, call back those who flee, strengthen the broken, cleanse the sick, wash lepers, strengthen the weak, gladden the sad, comfort the despairing, heal the wounded, bind up the mutilated, restore the lost, and raise from the dead those who have died in sins.

O repentance! What shall I say about you? I cannot praise you as I wish, because you are more precious than refined gold. Through you death is destroyed and the devil is driven away; through you life is found and God is discovered; through you hell is closed and the kingdom is found.

That person therefore performs worthy repentance who so laments past sins that he does not commit them again in the future. A repeated wound is healed more slowly. Repetition of sin is a grave evil, like illness coming upon illness or rain upon rain. For whoever mourns a sin and then commits it again is like someone washing an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.

Let no one doubt God’s goodness; let no one despair of God’s mercy. Let him seek forgiveness with his heart, and he will receive it. Let him repent in body and mind and move God to mercy.

After his sin David sang a psalm; he did not lose the kingdom and found pardon. The impious King Manasseh wept before the Lord and obtained peace for himself and his people. Zacchaeus climbed a tree and found salvation. Mary wept and deserved pardon. Peter wept bitterly; he did not lose grace and obtained pardon. The thief entered paradise with Christ in a single utterance. Longinus opened the Savior’s side with a lance, and not only found pardon, but also deserved to possess the honor of the episcopate, the glory of martyrdom, and a crown.

### 15. Two commandments

The whole law and the prophets depend on two commandments: love of God with all the powers of body and soul, and love of neighbor as oneself.

There are two ways of believing: perfect faith and perfect action.

The cross is carried in two ways: either the body is afflicted through abstinence, or the soul is afflicted through compassion for one’s neighbor.

Divine speech is distinguished in two ways: either the Lord speaks by himself, or words are formed through an angelic creature.

### 16. Two kinds of righteous people

There are two kinds of righteous people in this life: one kind consists of those who live well but teach nothing; the other of those who live rightly and teach the same right things.

Divine striking is understood in two ways: first, in a good sense, when we are struck in the flesh so that we may be corrected in soul and mind; second, when we are wounded in conscience through charity so that we may love God more ardently.

God looks upon human beings in two ways: either for pardon or for vengeance—for pardon, as he looked upon Peter; for vengeance, as upon Sodom and Gomorrah.

### 17. Two thieves and the daughters of Lot

Two thieves were crucified with Christ: Dismas on the right and Gestas on the left. Other names for the thieves are Chacham and Chamna.

Lot, the son of Abraham’s brother, had two daughters. One was called Adah; she bore her father a son named Moab, from whom the Moabites arose. The other was called Moah; she likewise bore her father a son named Ammon, from whom the Ammonites came.

These two sons were not born without guilt, because the father had his daughters as wives; this was brought about not by intention but by drunkenness. Thus the guilt was wondrously arranged: the father had his daughters as wives, the sisters became mothers to their brothers, and the sons became brothers to their mothers, because the daughters were born from their father’s seed, and sons were again begotten from their father’s seed in the daughters.

Therefore this offspring deserved a great curse, and did not enter the Church of God until the tenth generation. Yet Ruth the Moabite was a good woman and deserved to have a share in the generation of Christ. She was the mother of David’s grandfather. For David was the son of Jesse, Jesse the son of Obed, Obed the son of Boaz, and his mother was Ruth. A grandfather is the father of one’s father.

### 18. The two sons of Isaac

Isaac had two sons: one was rejected by God, and the other was chosen. Thus Scripture says: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

This was not without cause, because both were sons of a good father and both were children of the same good mother in the womb. Yet the chosen one supplanted the rejected one in his mother’s womb and seized from him both the birthright and his father’s blessing.

But God willed this to happen because all the chosen arose from Jacob and from his seed. Yet God did not abandon the rejected one, because Job, both a servant of God and a king, arose from his line.

I have mentioned this briefly because the wicked arise from the good and the good from the wicked:

- The wicked from the good: demons from angels.
- The good from the wicked: saints from the nations.
- The wicked from the good: Ishmael from Abraham, Moab and Ammon from Lot.
- The good from the wicked: Abraham from the Chaldeans.
- The wicked from the good: Dathan and Abiram from Levi, Hophni and Phinehas from Eli.
- The good from the wicked: Ruth of Moab and Rahab of Canaan.
- The wicked from the good—something I ought to have said earlier: Cain from Adam, and Ham from Noah.
- The good from the wicked: Jonathan from Saul.
- The wicked from the good: Absalom from David.

Why should I say more? It will be so until the end: the wicked will arise from the good and the good from the wicked. But when he comes who alone is good, he will separate the good from the wicked.

### 19. Two men still living

We read that two men are still alive, but we do not know where the living and hidden ones are.

One is Enoch, the seventh from Adam; the other is Elijah, who was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot.

We have spoken briefly enough about two, because we are hurrying on to three.

### 20. The three persons of the Trinity

The three persons of the Trinity, in one power and majesty, are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Among the Hebrews these three persons are called Abba, Ben, and Ruba. Among the Greeks, however, they are called Father and Bar; how the Spirit is called in Greek I have not yet found. They nevertheless say *ageos*, which in Latin sounds as *sanctus* (“holy”).

Abba: Father. Ben: Son. Ruba: Holy Spirit.

Yet *Pater* is Greek and in Latin means “begetter.” *Bar* is Greek; “son” is Latin.

The Trinity is therefore named on account of the distinction of persons, while unity is named on account of the inseparable substance of the Godhead.

The Father is called Father because he has a Son, and every fatherhood that exists in heaven and on earth is named in him and from him. The Son is called Son because he has a Father. The Holy Spirit is so called because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

He is called God on account of power and love; Lord on account of dominion; almighty because he can do all things and nothing is impossible for him.

And if God is almighty, what is it that he cannot do? He cannot be deceived, he cannot die, and he cannot sin.

Through the Father we live, move, and exist. Through the Son we have reason, knowledge, and understanding. Through the Holy Spirit we are enlightened with every good gift.

God is called in three ways:

1. Essentially, as Paul says: “Who is blessed forever.”
2. Nominally, as the Lord says to Moses: “I have appointed you as a god to Pharaoh.”
3. Falsely, as it is said: “May the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish.”

In the beginning God created three things: angels, …, and unformed matter.

*(The rest is missing.)*

## APPENDIX XXII. GLOSSES ON HOLY SCRIPTURE

From an old codex of the Vatican Archive.

## GENESIS

### Editorial note

**GENESIS—CHAPTER I.** On these glosses, consult the *Isidoriana*, chapter 65, numbers 38 and following. The codex begins: “The Spirit of God was carried”; perhaps one should next read “providentially, how he created all things.” It was written *creasse* instead of *creasset*. The words “his word” had been punctuated. “He made morning.”

### Chapter I

**The Spirit of God was carried.** [Perhaps read:] “Foreseeing how he had created all things.”

**Let there be light.** It is the same light that afterward was diffused into the vessels of heaven, that is, the stars.

**He said.** He made it through his word.

**Morning.** The beginning of creation.

**Evening.** Its end.

**Image, likeness.** The image stands out in the spirit of man; the likeness in good works.

### Editorial note

In the Vulgate the reading is *plantaverat* (“he had planted”) instead of *patrarat*. Perhaps one should read: “one earthly … the other heavenly.” The glosses “the tree of life,” etc., could be arranged or transposed differently. The Vulgate has *bdellium*, but *bidellium* is found in medieval writers. The mention of Hevilath—or Evilat, as in the Vulgate—should come before that of bdellium.

### Chapter II

**Patrarat** (“he had completed”). He had perfected.

**Paradise.** There are two: one earthly, where Adam was; the other heavenly.

**The tree of life, the tree of knowledge.** In keeping the commandment there was knowledge of good.

**Of good and evil.** In transgressing it there was knowledge of evil.

**Bidellium.** It is collected from a tree and is a pigment.

**Evilat.** This is the proper name of the land.

### Chapter III

**Aprons.** Coverings for the thighs.

**Turning.** Vibrating.

**Versatile.** It is said of something because, when the time came, it could also be removed.

### Editorial note

In the Vulgate the reading is “you shall be cursed upon the earth,” unless these words have been transferred here from chapter III, where the Vulgate has, at verse 17: “Cursed is the earth in your work.” From verse 9 of chapter IV the word *Num* is taken, namely: “Are you a keeper…?” 

### Chapter IV

**He changed color.** He changed the color of his face.

**Sin.** If not so.

**Cursed is the earth in your works.** Here it expresses not the work of cultivation but sins.

**Num.** You say.

**Eden.** It interprets the most sacred place of paradise itself.

**Moreover.** Namely.

### Editorial note

The manuscript has *nominata* instead of *nominati*. It is not apparent to what the words “he dwelt … unstable” belong. The knot in the abbreviation of the letters is obscure. Perhaps one should immediately read *limpidatis*. On the word *tristega*, see Ducange.

### Chapter VI

**Famous.** Named by fame.

**He dwelt in the land of Haid.** In Hebrew it has “an unstable knot.”

**Smoothed.** Of clearness.

**Bitumen.** A kind of glue; some call it pitch, others resin.

**Tristega.** Three-chambered.

### Chapter VII

**Floodgates.** Windows.

**At the moment of day.** At the beginning of day.

### Editorial note

IX.

The manuscript had *vegetati*. In place of *ejecti* (“expelled”), I would prefer *geniti* (“begotten”). The glosses have been transposed: *vegetat* (“he makes fruitful”) belongs to verse 13; *dilatet* (“may he enlarge”), etc., belongs to verse 27.

---

[^c0129-1]: The Latin reads *Diram*, apparently an OCR or textual corruption; the intended place-name is materially uncertain.

IX. May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem. *Japheth* means “enlargement,” from whom the multitude of the nations arises; *Shem*, from whom the Hebrews, fewer in number, were expelled. *Vegetat*: it nourishes. *Confortat*: it strengthens.

XI. *Ur*: fire, or light.

XII. *Illustrem*: illustrious, magnificent.

[Note: [Column 1303C]

XIII. I restored *in oppidis* (“in towns”) in place of *in opis* in the manuscript. A distinction is nevertheless sometimes observed among *castrum*, “fort,” *castellum*, “castle,” and *oppidum*, “town.”]

XIII. *In oppidis*: in towns. *In castris*: in camps.

XV. *Trimam*: three-year-old. *Altrinsecus*: separately. *Abigebat*: he drove away, expelled.

XVI. *Libet*: according to your will. *Ferus*: angry, untamed.

[Note: [Column 1303C]

XVIII. In the glosses of Robert of Sorbonne: “taking a modius and a half.” Compare Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVI, chapter 26, and Du Cange.]

XVIII. *Sata*: the name of a measure; it contains a modius and a half.

[Column 1303B] [Note: [Column 1303D]

XIX. I understand the word *cubitum* to belong to chapter XIX, verse 4, concerning the two angels received as guests by Lot: “Before they went to bed”; but I do not understand what the gloss *passi duo* indicates, unless we read *pasti duo* (“two fed ones”).]

XIX. *Cubitum*: to bed. *Passi duo*: two who suffered. *Vallaverunt*: they surrounded. *Culminis*: of height. *Vim*: strength. *Intuitus*: looking attentively.

XXI. *Stirpi*: to the race, lineage. *Nemus*: an arranged stand of trees, or a wooded place.

XXII. *Pariter*: together. *Vepres*: brambles.

XXIII. *Funeris*: of the body. *Quin*: rather, or more correctly. *Siclus*: six denarii. *Antrum*: cave.

[Note: [Column 1303D]

XXIV. The author of the gloss seems to have read *distraxit* or *destraxit* in the text, changing *i* to *e*, as was customary at that time. The Vulgate has *destravit*, that is, “he put down the baggage,” from the verb *desterno*. For the gloss *interrogati* (“questioned”), I would read *interrogarunt* (“they questioned”).]

XXIV. *Destravit*: he divides, or sells. *Aio*: I say. *Suscitati*: raised up. *Interrogati*: questioned.

[Note: [Column 1303D]

XXV. *Iesca* was written. In Robert of Sorbonne, two glosses are wrongly distinguished: *Edulium, victus* (“food, sustenance”); *Esca, esus* (“food, eating”).]

XXV. *Hispidus*: hairy. *Protinus*: immediately. *Adultis*: mature. *Gnarus*: experienced. *Edulio*: food, sustenance, or eating. *Parvipendens*: regarding as nothing.

[Note: [Column 1303D]

XXVI. The Vulgate writes *accersito*. In the codex one reads *modicum aliquid* (“a little something”). The gloss *irascitur* (“he is angry”) was added by some incompetent person in place of *sevit*, which derives from *sero* (“to sow”), not from *saevio* (“to rage”). The gloss *inventum* (“found”) is likewise inept in place of *auctum* (“increased”).]

XXVI. *Arcersito*: having been summoned. *Evocato*: having been called forth. *Perspicuum*: manifest. *Coire*: to lie together, or to come together. *Quispiam*: some insignificant person. *Modicus aliquis*: some small person. *Sevit*: he sows. *Irascitur*: he is angry. *Locupletatus*: enriched, made wealthy. *Invidentes*: harboring envy. *Humo*: earth. *Olim*: formerly. *Repererunt*: they found. *Jurgium*: quarrel. *Auctum*: increased. *Inventum*: found.

[Column 1303C] [Note: [Column 1303D]

XXVII. In the old codex, *theca* or *thecam* should be read in place of *tega*. *Indomitus* (“untamed”) is perhaps an error.]

XXVII. *Pharetram*: quiver. *Theca*: a case for carrying arrows. *Dudum*: formerly. *Consternatus*: dismayed. *Indomitus*: untamed. *Orbabor*: I shall be bereaved, without children.

XXVIII. *Innixum*: leaning upon.

[Column 1304A] [Note: [Column 1304C]

XXIX. In place of *septem annis* (“seven years”), I would prefer *septenarium* (“a group of seven”).]

XXIX. *Valet*: he is well. *Hebdomadam*: seven years. *Copulae*: to the joining.

[Note: [Column 1304C]

XXX. I transferred the gloss concerning mandrakes to this location; in the old manuscript it occurs between *cubitum* and *vallaverunt*, that is, in chapter XIX. What is said about mandrakes should be compared with the *Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 9; with the biblical dictionary; and with the commentaries of Calmet and the dictionary of Valmont de Bomare. Most of it is fabulous. The word *bidulaneus* is uncommon. In the *Acts of 11 July*, volume II, *Life of Saint Ulric*: “He cut himself a staff from bidulline wood.” In the additions to Du Cange it is conjectured that *betulaneus*, or *betulaceus*, should be read, from *betula*, “birch.” The true meaning is drawn from our glosses.]

XXX. *Edente*: producing. *Mandragoras*: fruits resembling apples grow on that plant; it has two sexes, masculine and feminine, and in its root it displays a likeness. It is fertile, and it is said that whoever uproots it cannot survive. *Experimento*: knowingly through experience. *Dem*: I shall give. *Furvus*: brown. *Populeas*: poplar-colored. *Bidulaneas*: bidulline. *Serotinus*: late.

[Note: [Column 1304C]

XXXI. In the old manuscript: *Fetos, portantes* (“bearing offspring”). Shortly afterward, in place of *vastati* (“laid waste”), one should have written *vastaverunt* (“they laid waste”). But many such forms belong to the Middle Ages.]

XXXI. *Facultate*: possibility. *Inclytus*: noble. *Fetus*: bearing offspring. *Opes*: riches. *Clam*: secretly. *Abigeres*: you would drive away. *Esto*: even if you should think so, or “behold, if.” *Necetur*: let him be killed. *Nequeo*: I cannot. *Depopulati*: laid waste.

XXXIV. *Stupri*: violation of virginity. *Scorto*: prostitute.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XXXV. The Vulgate has *recedentes* (“departing”), and the gloss *obedientes* (“obeying”) does not fit. The word *cedentes* occurs in the Gothic Bibles of Toledo. See the prologue, chapter 65.]

XXXV. *Cedentes*: obeying. *Libans*: tasting.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XXXVI. In the old codex, between the glosses *funeris* and *quin* in chapter XXIII, it was written: “At the well,” and so forth.]

XXXVI. *Ad puteum juramenti*: at the well of the oath. *Ad aquam fidei*: at the water of faith.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XXXVII. The glosses have been somewhat transposed. In place of *incendium*, perhaps *incentivum* (“kindling”) should be read.]

XXXVII. *Ditioni*: to authority. *Fomitem*: kindling, fire, [Column 1304B] or beginning. *Nitebatur*: he labored. *Polymita*: embroidered work. *Stactem*: a kind of precious resin. *Acquieverunt*: they agreed.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XXXVIII. The gloss *non convertit* (“does not turn”) is not very suitable. Concerning *teristrum*, or, as the Vulgate reads, *theristrum*, compare the *Etymologies*, Book XIX, chapter 25; the glosses of Robert of Sorbonne; and Du Cange. The old codex has *instantium* in place of *instantem*.]

XXXVIII. *Divertit*: he turns aside. *Non convertit*: he does not turn. *Opilio*: shepherd of sheep. *Teristrum*: a head covering, or linen cloth.

XXXIX. *Arbitris*: judges. *Lacinia*: the edge of a garment.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XL. Others call it *buticularius*, *buttelarius*, or *bottellarius*. Consult Du Cange, under *Butta*. The old codex has *texetur*, and perhaps the author intended *texitur* (“is woven”).]

XL. *Pincerna*: cupbearer. *Butiliarius*: bottle-bearer. *Canistra*: what is woven from palm rods for carrying bread.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XLI. I restored *in culmo* (“in the stalk”) in place of *in culmine* (“at the summit”).]

XLI. *Conjectores*: estimators. *In culmo*: in the reed, in the straw. *Uredine*: a burning wind. *Demum*: afterward. *Praesagum*: foreknowing. *Conjicere*: to estimate. *Macie*: thinness of body. *Squalore*: filth. *Industrium*: diligent, pressing. *Segetes*: crops. *Semina*: seeds.

XLII. *Nutum*: providence, or power. *Machinantur*: they devise. *Molimur*: we think, or attempt.

XLIII. *Dilatio*: delay. *Admissio*: admission.

XLIV. *Augurari*: to cast lots. *Flagitii*: of sin, evil, or disgrace.

[Column 1304C] XLV. *Quantocius*: more quickly. *Solo*: earth.

[Note: [Column 1304D]

XLVII. The word *solo* does not occur in the Vulgate; it appears in the Gothic Bibles [Column 1305C] in the sense of “place of the land.” See the prolegomena, chapter 65. Perhaps the reading is *in thesaurum* (“into the treasury”). I do not know from where the word *hemina* was brought into this passage. There is a well-known controversy concerning the pound of bread and the hemina of wine in the Rule of Saint Benedict; Du Cange may be consulted on this, in his dictionary. Compare also the *Etymologies*, Book XVI, chapter 26.]

XLVII. *In aerarium*: into the treasury. *In thesaurarium*: into the treasury. *Hemina*: half a sextarius. *Serite*: sow.

XLIX. *Cerastes*: a horned serpent that harms by its breath. *Emissus*: a stag is called *emissus* when it follows a hind. [Column 1305A] *Obiit*: he died. *Aream*: arable land. *Resistere*: to flee, or contradict.

# EXODUS

[Note: [Column 1305C]

EXODUS. It appears to have been written *Ellesmoth*; [Column 1305D] in the *Etymologies*, Book VI, chapter 1, it is *Elesmoth* in this same codex of ours. Others write *Veellesemoth*.]

## Chapter I

*Ellesmoth* is Hebrew; *Exodus* is Greek; *Exitus* is Latin. *Lateris*: of bricks. They are made from earth and straw, without firing. *Mares*: males. *Ingrueret*: it might rush upon them.

[Note: [Column 1305D]

II. *Ponaer* appears to be an error for *panerium* (“basket”); it was also written *in domum navis* (“into the house of a ship”), and shortly afterward *plaustri* (“of a wagon”), or *in maris* (“in the sea”), as others [read]. Concerning *mariscus*, see Du Cange.]

II. *Elegantem*: beautiful. *Fiscellam*: little basket. *Ponaer*: in the shape of a ship. *Scirpeam*: made of rushes. *In carecto*: in a marshy place, or in a marsh; others read “channel.” *Per crepidinem*: along the top of the bank. *Alvei*: a channel in a river, or a bay of water. *Papyrione*: papyrus. *Adultum*: mature, or young man.

III. *Rubi*: a thorn bush on which a rose grows.

IV. *Instar*: likeness. *Ab heri et nudius tertius*: it signifies the whole past time. *Impeditionis* [read *impeditioris*]: more impeded, or less prepared. *Diversorio*: a lodging place. *Illico*: immediately, or soon. *In montem Dei*: to Mount Sinai. Horeb and Sinai are one [mountain]. “You are a bridegroom of blood to me”: because you were born from my blood, or because you were circumcised.

[Column 1305B] [Note: [Column 1305D]

V. It is unclear whether *cum vim* should be read in place of *vi*. The glosses at this point had been placed in reverse order. For this gloss precedes the others of chapter IV, where the Vulgate reads *sponsus sanguinum* (“bridegroom of bloods”) instead of *sanguinis* (“of blood”).]

V. *Exactoribus*: officials who exacted [labor] by force.

[Note: [Column 1305D]

VI. Perhaps *carcere* (“prison”).]

VI. *Adonai*: Lord. *Ergastulo*: private confinement, or prison. *Praesertim*: especially. *Patruelam*: the son or daughter of one’s paternal uncle.

VII. *Colubrum*: he treated the serpent and the dragon as one creature. Aaron’s staff and Moses’ staff were one. *Arcana*: secret or hidden things. *Malefici*: inventors of magical arts.

[Note: [Column 1305D]

VIII. The gloss *statuit* (“he decided”) does not seem to belong here, unless it is also an explanation of *condixerat* (“he had agreed”).]

VIII. *Abigantur*: let them be driven away. *Condixerat*: he agreed, or consented. *Statuit*: he decreed. *Aggeres*: a mound of earth. *Sciniphes*: very small flies. *Abominationes Aegyptiorum*: sheep, which they worshiped and refused to eat.

IX. *Renuis*: you refuse. *Turgentium*: swelling. *Virens*: green. *Induravit*: because he did not soften.

X. *Corrodet*: he will gnaw, tear apart. *Densae*: thick.

[Note: [Column 1305D]

XI. Here also the order of the glosses had been reversed, as often elsewhere.]

XI. *In solio*: on the throne. *Mutiet*: let him murmur softly. *Ostenta*: the signs foretold.

[Column 1305C] [Note: [Column 1305D]

XII. The old codex has *ritu observantium* (“according to the rite of observers”), and afterward *vel ibi qui* (“or there, who”).]

XII. *Coetum*: assembly. *In aedibus*: in houses, or temples. *In monumentum*: in memory. *More*: according to rite or observance. *Indigenis*: citizens, or those born there. *Dimittit*: permits. *Caeremonias*: sacrificial rites. *Dudum*: formerly, or long ago. *Religio*: holiness, goodness, piety. *Efferetis*: you shall carry away.

XIII. *Israel*. *Proficiscentis*: of one departing. *Columna*: pillar. The pillar of fire and the pillar of cloud are believed to be one, fiery on one side and cloudlike on the other.

XV. *Obriguerunt*: they stiffened. *Coturnix et perdix*: quail and partridge.

[Note: [Column 1305D]

XVI. Perhaps *sextarios* (“sextarii”). I restored *ephi* in place of *aephi*, although the Gothic Bibles of Toledo spell it *aephi*.]

XVI. *Pilo*: pestle; elsewhere, spear. *Gomor*: a measure [Column 1306A] containing twelve sextarii. *Scatere*: to boil or seethe. *Atui*: I nourished, or fed. *Ephi*: *ephi* and *batus* are the same, a measure containing three modii.

[Note: [Column 1306C]

XVII. The Vulgate reads *jurgatus* and *paululum* in place of *pauxillum*. The Gothic Bibles likewise have *pauxillum*, and perhaps also *jurgata*, for they have *lapidabii* in place of *lapidabunt*.]

XVII. *Jurgata*: having quarreled, or having suffered an injury. *Pauxillum*: a little.

XVIII. *Praestolatur*: he watches, or awaits. *Disceptatio*: dispute, contention, or debate. *Tribunus*: one who commands a thousand men. *Strenuis*: useful, or strong.

XIX. *Jaculis*: weapons, or arrows shot or hurled. *Clangere*: to sound. *Micare*: to flash, shine. *Perstrepebat*: resounded. *Paulatim*: gradually, in stages. *Prolixius*: longer. *Contestare*: to adjure.

[Note: [Column 1306C]

XX. The gloss for *zelotes* is missing; in the manuscript it is joined to the word or gloss *conjurare*. In Robert’s glosses: *zelotes*, “rival, avenger.”]

XX. *Zelotes* . . . . . *Insontem*: innocent. *Frustra*: without cause, without reason, in vain.

[Note: [Column 1306D]

XXI. Perhaps *sicut diis* (“as to the gods”) in place of *sicut do tibi* (“as I give to you”). The Vulgate has *per industriam* (“deliberately”). The Toledo Bible has *de industria* (“deliberately”).]

XXI. *Liberi*: children. *Diis*: that is, “as I give to you.” *De industria*: deliberately, with care. *Cornupeta*: a young animal that charges with its horn.

XXII. *Acervos*: heaps. *Segetes*: harvests. *Deferat*: [Column 1306B] may he carry. *Conductum*: gathered together.

[Note: [Column 1306D]

XXIII. In the Vulgate, this chapter does not have *severis*, but *seminabis* in verse 10 and *seminaveris* in verse 16, where the Gothic Bible has *serveris*. The word *furrlones* is unknown to me.]

XXIII. *Solemnitatem*: the seven weeks from Passover to Pentecost. *Severis*: you shall sow. *Crabrones*: hornets. *Furrlones*: [uncertain]. *Ultroneus*: spontaneous.

[Note: [Column 1306D]

XXV. Instead of *anteranaglypham*, perhaps *interanaglypham* should be read. Most explain *interrasile* by *anaglyphum*, “sculpted.” Consult Du Cange. In Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses, two glosses are wrongly distinguished: *interrasilem*, “ornamented”; *anaglypham*, “sculpted.” These are in fact three nouns explaining *interrasilem*. Shortly afterward, *in modum calami* (“in the form of a reed”) seems to be the correct reading, as in Robert’s glosses. There, *rotundas* is read in place of *rotundatas*, or *rotunditas*, as in our manuscript.]

XXV. *Concinnanda*: to be arranged. *Ephod*: a linen robe, or shoulder garment, or dalmatic. *Compingite*: join. *Oraculum*: the oracle and the mercy seat are one, where divine utterances were heard. *Interrasilem*: *anteranaglypham*, ornamented or sculpted. *Acetabula*: small bowls. *Acinarios*: acinarii. *Phialas*: smaller cups. *Calamos*: the form of a reed. *Scyphos*: larger cups. *Sphaerulas*: rounded in the form of a sphere.

[Note: [Column 1306D]

XXVI. I would readily read *strincas* or *fiblas*; hence the Italian *stringa*, “lace,” and *fibbia*, “buckle.” Shortly afterward comes *miscebitur* (“it shall be mixed”).]

XXVI. *Saga*: one piece of cloth in the curtains. *Fibulas*: *ilrincas*, or buckles. *A summo usque ad summum*: from end to end. *Inseretur*: it shall be placed upon, mixed in, or enclosed.

XXVII. *Fuscinulas*: three-pronged forks. *Arula*: a square bronze vessel in which coals are carried. *Caelaturis*: engravings. *Paxillos*: a kind of measure called a *palus*, “stake.” *Contusum*: crushed. *Oppansum velum*: an extended curtain, [Column 1306C] spread open on every side.

XXVIII. *Applica*: join, gather. *Fungantur*: let them use, obey. *Rationale*: a square cloth on the breast. *Cidarim*: the *cidarim*, mitre, and tiara are the same. *In marginibus*: at the edges, at the upper ends of the garments. *Malum Punicum et mala granata*: pomegranate and pomegranate fruit are the same, fruits of remarkable beauty. *Portabit iniquitates*: he who intercedes for iniquity. *Feminalia*: coverings for the thighs. *Femora*: thighs, from *femine* [as printed].

[Note: [Column 1306D]

XXIX. The Latin word is *axungia*, but perhaps in the Middle Ages it was written *exungia*, whence the Spanish *enjundia*. Compare Du Cange, under *exudia*. The explanation [Column 1307C] of the measure *hin* is obscure in the old manuscript; I restored it from other glossaries, but in the glosses of Robert of Sorbonne *8* is mistakenly read in place of *VIIII*, as in our manuscript.]

XXIX. *Ariet es immaculatos*: rams of one color, neither diseased, scabby, nor injured. *Lagana*: it is made from flour; first it is placed in water, then fried in oil. *Initiaberis*: you shall be sanctified, when, as the year returns, all things are brought to completion in the seventh month, since the Egyptians made it both the beginning and the end of the year. *Mactabis*: you shall kill. *Jecoris*: of the liver. *Arvinam*: fat, *exungia*. *Vitalia*: the inner organs. *Expiandum*: to be purified. *Jugiter*: continually. *Hin*: the larger measure contains nineteen sextarii, the smaller nine. *Libandum*: to be sacrificed.

[Note: [Column 1307C]

XXX. In place of *liba*, the Vulgate has *libamina*. The Toledo Gothic Bible, with the glosses, retains *liba*. More correctly, it will be *scrupulus semis* or *semiscrupulus*. See Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25. In place of *zmirnae*, the Vulgate has *myrrhae*; Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses have *Zmirrhae*, with an interpretation. Some claim that it is *calamus*, others that it is the resin of myrrh. *Supellectilem*: various objects.]

XXX. *Liba*: sacrifices. *Summam*: number. *Recensiti*: counted. *Nomen*: authority. *Obolus*: half a scruple. *Labrum*: basin; *labium* and *labrum* are the same—a square bronze vessel in which the priests wash. *Zmirnae*: calamus. *Casiae*: reeds or tubes.

XXXII. *Callide*: to lead cunningly, cautiously. *Quivero*: after the guilt of the offense.

XXXIII. *Papilionis*: of a tent.

[Note: [Column 1307C]

XXXIV. The old codex has *dictus et quod*; perhaps *dictus eo quod* (“so called because”). Below, *spopondi* may be read more suitably.]

XXXIV. *Deinceps*: again, or afterward. *Aras*: altars. *Lucus et nemus*: grove and woodland are the same; and it is called [a grove] because it scarcely lets light through. *Aemulator*: imitator, or envious person, or follower. *Pepigi*: I made a pact, or pledged myself. *Foedus*: perpetual peace, or friendship.

[Note: [Column 1307D]

XXXV. The Vulgate has, in verse 5, *et prono animo* (“and with a willing spirit”). The Gothic Bible has *et prompto animo* (“and with a ready spirit”). In the old book the word *praeceps* is obscure, and this passage may be mutilated. The Gothic exemplar, verse 25, has: “He offered [it] for the work of the tabernacle of the testimony.” The New Vulgate has: “They offered.” Shortly afterward, with Robert’s glosses, it would be preferable to read *rotundae sunt* (“they are round”) in place of *rotundarunt* (“they rounded”). The gloss for *polymitarii* seems to have been inserted by someone else, as though derived from *polus*. *Imaginem* (“image”) was written in the codex.]

XXXV. *Catervam*: crowd, multitude, assembly. *Prompto*: with willing speed, or headlong. “He placed the testimony in the ark”: the two tablets. *Armillas*: bracelets. *Rotundarunt*: they rounded. *Dextralia*: they are broad and are worn before the sleeves. *Abietarii*: carpenters, from the fir tree. *Polymitarii*: “for the roundness of the image”; *polus*, round.

[Note: [Column 1307D]

XXXVI. The Vulgate has *compaginem*. The Gothic Bible has *compagem*. In the old codex there is a sign of weight after twenty-one, of the sort described by Isidore, Book XVI, chapter 27; nevertheless, it differs from our sign in every respect. I have interpreted it as *cochlearia* (“spoonfuls”), since a *cyathus* is said to consist of ten drachmas and a spoon is half a drachma.]

XXXVI. *Necteretur*: it would be bound. *Compagem*: joining. *Cyathos*: twenty-one spoonfuls.

XXXVIII. *Ad plagam*: to the side. *Septentrionalem*: toward midnight. *Australem*: toward midday. *Bracteas*: very thin gold plates. *Excubabant*: they kept watch.

XL. *Sub tecto testimonii*: under the roof of the tabernacle.

# LEVITICUS

*Vagecra* is Hebrew; *Leviticus* is Greek; *Ministerialis* is Latin, because the ministries of the priests are written in it.

[Note: [Column 1307D]

LEVITICUS—CHAPTER I. The old codex has *Vagecra*, as in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1; others write *Vajicra*, others *Vaijera*.]

## Chapter I

*Crepidinem*: foundation.

[Note: [Column 1307D]

II. The old codex has *turres*. The Gothic Bibles have *torres*. The Vulgate has *torrebis*.]

II. *In clibano*: in a chimney, in an oven. *Torres*: you shall roast. *Asses*: you shall roast. *Farris*: a kind of grain.

[Note: [Column 1308C]

III. On *nebula* as food, Du Cange has more.]

III. *Ilia*: the side near the groin. *Inficians*: lying in wait. [Column 1308A] *Quodlibet*: whatever. *Collyridas*: a cake, which we call a *nebula*.

X. “I shall be sanctified in them”: I punish those who presume. *Profanum*: illicit, violated, polluted. *Lugubri*: mournful.

[Note: [Column 1308C]

XI. The names *choerogryllus* and *haliaeetus* have been supplied from the Vulgate, since they appear corrupt in the old book. Concerning *cavannus*, consult Du Cange. The codex has *avis qui*, “white bird.” Something is also missing in the explanation of *porphyrion*. Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses say: “*Porphyrion*, a bird of purple color, as the name seems to signify”; others say it is white and like a swan, others a pelican. The gloss on *stellio* was added by an interpolator. Then, in place of *calva*, I conjectured *surric*, “mole-shrew.” *Vespertilio* is mentioned above at verse 19, and perhaps the passage is mutilated as follows: “*Stellio* . . . *Vespertilio* . . . *Talpa*.” In Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses, *chytropodes*, or, as it is read there, *sertropodes*, is explained as earthenware cooking vessels with three feet. Calmet explains it otherwise in his biblical dictionary.]

XI. *Choerogryllus*: a spiny beast larger than a hedgehog. *Haliaeetum*: a bird like an eagle, but larger, though smaller than a vulture. *Larum*: a sea bird with talons like a hawk. *Bubonem*: a night heron. *Onocrotalus*: a bird that makes a sound in the water, or a pelican. *Porphyrionem*: others say a white bird like a swan. *Herodionem*: it is larger than all birds, because it seizes an eagle. *Bruchus*: like a locust, but larger. *Crocodilus*: an animal in a river, like a lizard but large. *Mygale*: like a chameleon. *Chamaeleon*: like a lizard, and it changes colors when observed. *Stellio*: a gecko. *Verpestilio*: bat. *Talpa*: mole. *Sorex*: shrew. *Chytropodes*: an earthenware vessel with feet.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

XIII. The manuscript has *inolitam* and *nominatam*; I restored *contaminatam* (“contaminated”), and in place of *appellaverit* (“has called”), *apparuerit* (“has appeared”). Perhaps in place of *effloruerit* (“has blossomed”), with the Gothic Bibles, *fuerit* should be read. The codex has *vulnus sed minor* (“a wound, but smaller”).]

XIII. *Inolita*: contaminated. *Effloruerit*: has blossomed. *Appellaverit*: has called. *Perspicuae*: manifest, clear. *Ulcus*: a wound, but [Column 1308B] smaller. *Haud dubie*: without doubt.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

XIV. The Vulgate has *valliculas* (“little valleys”).]

XIV. *Papulas*: warts that appear on lepers. *Vallicula*: hollow places.

XV. *Sagma*: saddle.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

XVI. It is possible that *vovens* (“vowing”) should be read in place of *solvens* (“releasing”).]

XVI. *Nebula eorum*: the smoke of aromatics. *Imprecans*: releasing.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

XVII. These words were corrupt in the old book: *accusatio*, or “one who listens to the bleating of sheep,” in place of *aviscapio*, and so forth, as I infer from Book X of the *Etymologies*, under *auceps*.]

XVII. *Quilibet*: whoever. *Aucupio*: catching birds, or one who listens to the songs of birds.

XVIII. *In pellicatum*: into the house of concubines.

XIX. *Praeputia*: the impurity of fruits sacrificed to idols. *Susurro*: one who murmurs secretly, or spreads injuries. *Stigmata*: figures, or marks. *Noverca*: stepmother. *Pythonicus*: an incantation, divination.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

XXI. I do not know to what the gloss *Aula, vicinus* belongs, or what may be concealed under these words.]

XXI. *Incisuras*: for mourning. *Aula*: neighbor. *Prostibulum*: a house of prostitution.

XXII. *Inquilinus*: a tenant, native servant. *Spatulas*: palm fruits before they open.

# NUMBERS

*Vaje Dabber*, that is, “number,” because the children of Israel are numbered in it.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

NUMBERS. In the manuscript the Hebrew word *Vaje Dabber*, or *Vagedaber*, is missing. It begins with *Ed est*, or *Id est* (“that is”); for *e* frequently occurs in place of *i*.]

## Chapter I

*Cuneos*: multitudes.

II. *Vexilla*: victories.

[Note: [Column 1308D]

CHAPTER III. The words “of all” are obscure, and something is missing for the sense.]

III. *Sanctificavi*: I sanctified. *Caput radet*: he shall shave his head. *De omnibus cibis pulmentum*: a stew made from all foods.

[Column 1309A] [Note: [Column 1309D]

IV. The old writing points more to “pale blue” than to “violet.” *Spaludra* was also written in place of *spatula*. Other glosses have “iron shovel.”]

IV. *Hyacinthinus*: violet-colored. *Coccineas*: red. *Batilla*: iron shovel.

V. *Zelotypiae*: of jealousy. *Toro*: bed. *Congessi*: I gathered together. *Duntaxat*: namely, certainly.

VII. *Consuleret*: he would inquire and ask.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

VIII. *Stips*, or *stipes*, is usually taken for money given to the poor; but here *stipes* means a piece of wood. The words *conscius longius* are not understood.]

VIII. *Stipes*: beggar; elsewhere, wood. *Conscius*: aware. *Longius*: farther.

X. *Dimicant*: they fight; elsewhere, they shine.

XI. *Nausea*: vomiting.

XII. *Aenigmata*: proposition, questions.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XIII. The Vulgate has *praecoquae* (“early-ripening”).]

XIII. *Praecoce*: too early. *Lustravimus*: we went around.

XIV. *Vasta*: deep. *Querelas*: accusations, or outcries. *Forent*: they would be.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XVI. The old book has *primati*, which may perhaps be retained. I readily believe that the words *expassus, duo passus* are corrupt.]

XVI. *Proceres*: nobles, or exalted persons. *Concilium*: assembly. *Parum*: small, or little. *Expassus*: two paces. *Globus*: a troop, or round object. *Coacervassent*: they had gathered together. *Desaevit*: he moderated his anger, or ceased raging.

[Column 1309B] XVII. *Cohibebo*: I shall deprive. *Querimonias*: laments.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XVIII. The gloss *pareat, obediat* (“let him obey”) seems to belong to another passage.]

XVIII. *Sceptro*: royal power. *Cedit*: it happens. *Pareat*: let him obey.

XXI. *Contagione*: pollution.

XX. *Petra*: the rock that the Lord commanded Moses to strike. *Alioquin*: otherwise, or if not.

XXI. *Puteus*: the well over which the Lord spoke. *In libro bellorum Domini*: in the book of the wars of the Lord. *Bellorum Israel*: of the wars of Israel. *Quin potius*: much rather.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XXII. In place of *inquireris*, perhaps *inquieteris* should be restored, although I do not like that reading either.]

XXII. *Ariolus*: one who casts lots, or a diviner. *Cuncteris*: you delay. *Inquireris*: you are investigated.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XXIII. I would prefer *sortilegium* (“lot-casting”) in place of *sortientes* (“those casting lots”).]

XXIII. *Rhinocerotis*: a beast with a horn on its nose. *Augurium*: augury. *Sortientes*: those casting lots.

XXIV. *Complosis*: struck together. *In trieribus*: in army ships.

XXV. *Pugionem*: dagger. *Lupanar*: place of prostitutes.

XXVII. *Replicavit*: unfolded, or rolled back.

XXVIII. *Juge*: perpetual, always continuing.

XXX. *Pollicita*: promised. *Distulerit*: he will have concealed or deferred.

[Column 1309C] [Note: [Column 1309D]

XXXI. The Vulgate has *noverunt* in place of *nerunt*, and *cognoverant* in place of *cognorunt*. I cannot determine what lies beneath the words *Cis mista ripa*.]

XXXI. *Norunt*: they know. *Jugulate*: kill, punish. *Cognorunt*: they came together. *Periscelides*: bracelets; others say ornaments for the legs. *Cis*: mixed bank.

XXXIII. *Clavi in oculis*: goads in the eyes.

[Note: [Column 1309D]

XXXV. The old codex had *impingerit* in place of *impegerit*.]

XXXV. *Impulerit*: he will have compelled, struck.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

XXXVI. The Vulgate has *promulgata est* (“has been promulgated”) in place of *promulgatur* (“is promulgated”).]

XXXVI. *Promulgatur*: it is conveyed, displayed.

# DEUTERONOMY

[Note: [Column 1310D]

DEUTERONOMY. Others have *Elle haddebarim*.]

*Helle addabarim* is Hebrew; *Deuteronomium* is Greek; *Secunda lex* is Latin.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

CHAPTER I. The Vulgate writes *Enacim* and *Emim*.]

## Chapter I

*Guaros*: knowledgeable. *Ennacherim et Enim*: they were of the race of giants. *Fanum*: temple. *Egregiam*: noble, excellent, outstanding.

IV. *Portenta*: miracles.

V. *Sequester*: one who receives a pledge. *Protelentur*: let them be prolonged, delayed.

VII. *Spurcitia*: uncleanness. *Anathema*: abomination.

[Column 1310A] [Note: [Column 1310D]

VIII. I corrected *duorum palmorum* (“two palms”) in place of *durum palmarum*, and supplied *habens* (“having”), unless one prefers to read “with a curved and venomous tail.”]

VIII. *Dipsas*: a kind of serpent, a foot and a half long and two palms thick, [having] a curved, venomous tail with which it stings. Its name means “thirst,” because a person struck by it dies of thirst.

IX. *Ingentes*: great. *Concio*: assembly of the people.

XI. *Procul*: far away.

XII. *Caprea*: wild she-goat. *Capra*: domestic she-goat.

XIV. *Sicera*: every drink apart from wine that can cause intoxication.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

XVI. “[I shall correct:] *cadunt*” [uncertain].]

XVI. *Lucum*: in this passage *lucus* is the name of a tree whose leaves do not fall.

XVIII. *Lustret*: let him illuminate by drawing [it] through fire.

XX. *Cuneos*: many crowds of peoples.

XXI. *Reatus*: guilt. *Cruore*: blood. *Caesariem*: hair of the head. *Ungues*: claws. *Contumacem*: contemptuous. *Protervum*: perverse. *Coercitus*: prohibited, contradicted. *Plectendum*: to be beheaded.

XXII. *Nefas*: crime.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

XXIII. The old book has *Mazer* in place of *Mamzer*; others write it differently.]

XXIII. *Mamzer*: son of a prostitute. *Gerens*: acting, carrying.

[Column 1310B] 416 XXIV. *Nuper*: now.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

XXVI. The manuscript codex had *paner*. Concerning *panerium*, meaning basket, Du Cange should be consulted, together with the additions.]

XXVI. *In cartallo*: in a basket. *Panerio de virgis*: in a basket of twigs. *Funebri*: mortal.

XXVII. *Laevigabis*: you shall smooth. *Impolitis*: not rounded.

XXVIII. *Rubigine*: with a corrupting wind. *Pruriginem*: itching. *In suris*: in the calves. *In poplitibus*: behind the knees. *Procacissimam*: most shameless. *Illuvie secundarum*: with the filth of the afterbirth—the unclean fluids that follow childbirth.

[Note: [Column 1310D]

XXIX. The manuscript codex has *adsumat* in place of *absumat*, and *culturam* in place of *cultura*.]

XXIX. *Classibus*: military ships. *Absumat ebria sitientem*: may the drunken woman consume the thirsty person. She who was already drunk leads the thirsty person into error through the worship of idols.

XXX. *Cardines coeli*: the east, south, west, and north. *In sobole*: in offspring. *In genere*: in the race.

XXXII. *Meracissimum*: purest. *Opitulentur*: let them help. *Recens*: at present. *Novum*: in the future.

XXXIII. *Thesaurus arenarum*: earthly wisdom.

# SAINT JEROME’S PREFACE TO JOSHUA

[Column 1310C] [Note: [Column 1310D]

PREFACE TO THE BOOK OF JOSHUA. The printed editions have *postliminio*, which means the right of recovering a lost possession from a stranger and restoring it to its former condition. Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses agree with ours.]

*Tandem*: finally, or now. *Efferunt*: they say. *Exaplois*: in exemplars. *Arcuato vulnere*: with a curved wound, because a scorpion’s tail is curved, and from it the scorpion strikes. *Editiones*: translations. *Postlimen*: after the death of the father and mother. *Flagitat*: demands, asks. *Sirenarum*: prostitutes through magical arts, or rippling waves.

# THE BOOK OF JOSHUA

## Chapter II

*Quippe*: certainly, namely, without doubt. *Fateor*: I confess. *Funiculus iste*: this cord with which she girded herself from the loins to the breast. *Coccineus*: red.

III. *Mole*: magnitude.

V. *Polenta*: very fine flour.

[Note: [Column 1311C]

THE BOOK OF JOSHUA—CHAPTER VII. Perhaps the words mean “collected into a ball.” I restored *lablelli* in place of *lablegi*, which the manuscript codex has. Du Cange discusses the word *lablellus*, or *labellus*. The Vulgate has *regulam auream* (“golden rule”); nevertheless, I retained the manuscript’s *legulam*, which is the lowest part of the ear, also called a *lamina*, as though *ligula*, unless one prefers to read *ligulam* in place of *lingula*, as some less correctly pronounce it. Compare Forcellini. Interpreters of Scripture explain *regulam auream* as a golden rod shaped like a tongue, or a golden plate; this agrees remarkably with *legula* or *ligula*.]

VII. *Per prona*: headlong, along slopes. *Conglobali*: collected into one, or gathered. *Legulam*: *lablelli*.

VIII. *Vallatus*: surrounded. *Digesserat*: he had described, arranged.

[Column 1311A] [Note: [Column 1311D]

IX. I restored *emplastris* in place of *palastris*, since Celsus uses *pittacium* for a plaster. Here it indicates a piece of any cloth or leather.]

IX. *Pittaciis*: plasters. *Decrevit*: he determined.

X. *In libro justorum*: in the annals of the Hebrews. *Praesidia*: strongholds. *Saltem*: namely.

[Note: [Column 1311D]

XI. The Vulgate has: “Hazor fire consumed.”]

XI. *Subnervabis*: you shall subjugate, or render powerless. “Only Hazor did he burn with fire”: because he alone burned it completely.

XII. *Raphaim*: giants.

XV. *A lingua maris*: from the sound of the sea. *Civitas litterarum*: “city of letters,” because learned people lived there, or letters were kept there.

XVIII. *Marcetis*: you languish. *Ignavia*: weakness. [Column 1311C] *Imbecillitate*: weakness.

XIX. *Carmelum maris*: Carmel of the sea, a proper place-name.

XXIII. *Connubia*: marriages. *Sudes*: stakes.

XXIV. *Novellis ovibus*: one-year-old sheep that have not yet given birth.

## Chapter I

*Judas ascendit*: Judah went up. *Othoniel*: from that tribe. *Arctavit*: he oppressed on every side. *Ascensu scorpionis*: “the ascent of the scorpion,” a proper place-name.

II. *Experiar*: I shall certainly know.

[Note: [Column 1311D]

III. The Vulgate has *filii Jemini*, namely, “sons of Benjamin,” who was also called Jeminus. The author, or interpolator, went astray through the word *Gemini*, which also occurs in some Bibles. Perhaps *acutum* (“sharp”) should be read, since the Vulgate has “a double-edged sword.” In place of *porticum*, *posticum* (“rear entrance”) should apparently be restored; the Vulgate indeed reads: “He went out through the rear entrance.” Nevertheless, *porticus* occurs in medieval writers for a doorway or gate. Consult Du Cange, with the additions, under *Posticium* and *Porticus*.]

III. *Satrapas*: princes of the Philistines. *Filii Gemini*: sons of the sons of Joseph, since there were two of them. *Ancipitem*: sharp on both sides. *Capulum*: hilt of a sword. *Sicam*: sword. *Alvi*: belly. *Posticam*: rear entrance. *Circiter*: approximately.

[Note: [Column 1311D]

IV. Perhaps *ferrum*, “iron,” since.]

IV. *Clavum tabernaculi*: an iron nail that he carried from the tabernacle.

[Note: [Column 1311D]

V. The Vulgate has *sibilos gregum* (“whistling of flocks”).]

V. *Barathrum*: deep place, or chasm in the earth. *Discrimini*: judgment. *Magnanimorum*: of high-minded men. *Rubenitarum*: of the Reubenites. *Sibilos regum*: the whistlings of kings. *Blandimenta*: flatteries.

[Note: [Column 1312C]

VII. The Vulgate has “and they had broken the jars”; afterward, however, the word *confodio* does not occur, but *complodere* occurs in verse 19.]

VII. *Hydrias*: earthenware jars. *Confodere*: to pierce. *Collidere*: to strike together.

[Note: [Column 1312C]

VIII. In the old codex there is *pondus* in place of *pondo*, which, when used absolutely, means a pound; but both terms are used of gold, iron, and other things. In this chapter *pondus* occurs, and in the following chapter *pondo*, for which the gloss seems to have been written. I do not know what is concealed in the gloss *fidelis* in place of *monilibus*.]

VIII. *Bullas*: seals, or belt ornaments. *Pondus* and *libra* are the same; but *pondus* is used for iron and *libra* for gold. *Monilibus*: *fidelis*, or ornaments. *Torques*: golden rings worn around the neck.

IX. *Rhamnum*: a small thorn tree. *Compulit*: compelled, or drove against. *Palantes*: wandering.

[Column 1311C] XI. *Sodalibus*: contemporaries, companions.

XII. *Jugulabant*: they killed, or destroyed.

XIV. *Problema*: proposition, question, parable. *Pronubis*: bridal attendants, or those who preside over weddings.

XV. *Faces*: torches, or flames. *Suram*: lower leg.

XVII. *Teraphim*: image.

XVIII. *Opulentam*: full of riches, or abundant. *Haud procul*: not far away.

[Column 1312A] XIX. *Belial*: name of an idol.

XX. *Diverti*: I turned aside. *Posui in locum*: I placed in a location. *Bacchati*: raging.

[Note: [Column 1312C]

XXI. The Vulgate has *ad ducendos choros* (“to lead the dances”).]

XXI. *Ducentes choros*: holding one another’s hands in a dance.
