# SAINT JEROME’S GALEATED PROLOGUE TO THE BOOKS OF KINGS

[Note: [Column [source breaks off]]

1312D]

### PROLOGUE OF SAINT JEROME, THE “HELMED” PROLOGUE.—CHAPTER 1

*Twice in the manuscript* **colones** *occurs instead of* **coloni**. *For* **Abthet** *I have restored* **Bethel**, *from* 2 Kings 17. *Immediately afterward, perhaps one should read* **apud colonos illos**.

1. **By characters. By figures.** The Samaritans also write the Pentateuch of Moses in the same number of letters. They write it in the ancient letters of the Hebrews. But how did ancient letters come to be found among them? After colonists had been sent there from Assyria and had been devoured by lions and wild beasts, they afterward informed the kings of the Persians that they could not live there. The kings of Persia sent them a priest to teach them the ordinances of the land. When he came to Bethel, he received a copy of the Law from the tribe of Judah, copied out the Pentateuch for them, and expounded the Law. After Judah and Benjamin had been taken captive by the Chaldeans, and the Law had been burned, it remained in Samaria—that is, after those colonists, a copy of the Law written in ancient letters remained there, since they had done them no harm; for they were subject to them.

> **[Note: [Col. 1312D]]**
>
> 2. In the old manuscript it read: “they interpreted,” followed by “while the Law …,” and below, “afterward only.”

2. **Ezra.** He found other letters, because he did not know the earlier ones. The name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, was written in the ancient letters. We find it written in certain Greek books—not, however, in the canon—which were translated by the translators of the Septuagint, while the Law was being burned by the Chaldeans; only after such a long interval, under the Greek kingdom, did the seventy translate it. But in their own histories, because the name of the Lord had been spread among all nations and throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, they heard many wondrous things that he had done.

> **[Note: [Col. 1312D]]**
>
> 3. Jerome here mentions five doubled letters of the Hebrews: *kaph, mem, nun, pe,* and *ṣade*. In fact, these are the only five written differently at the end of words, although certain others are enlarged into a broader form.

3. **By incisions.** By cuttings and divisions of verses. **Doubled.** Among the Hebrews five letters are doubled, because they have a double form and a double name, such as *aleph, ʿayin, ṣade, samekh,* and *sin*. For they begin differently by means of these letters. Thus among us the beginnings of words are often written with the letter *k*, as in *kalendae*, while endings are written with *c*, as in *fac*.

> **[Note: [Col. 1313D]]**
>
> 4. In the glosses of Robert of Sorbonne I found several passages from our material concerning this prologue. Instead of “*Nonjamin*, etc.,” they read as follows: **DIBRE**, “words”; **JAMIN**, “of days,” not, as is now found, **BRESITH**, “beginning,” which the Hebrews place in their books. It will be useful to read this with Robert: **gimel**, that is, “fullness,” and so forth. Instead of *ista lex*, “this Law,” I would prefer *altera lex*, “the other Law,” or *iterata lex*, “the repeated Law.”

4. **Dibre hajamim.** “Words of days”: *dibre*, “words”; *hajamim*, “of days”; *nonjamin*, “of the right hand.” **Beresith.** “In the beginning,” because the Hebrews gave their books names from their beginnings. **Exodus.** “Departure.” The Hebrews write the letter *aleph* above Genesis; it is interpreted as “teaching,” as in: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Above Exodus they write *beth*, interpreted as “house,” because of the construction of the Tabernacle. Above Leviticus they write *gimel*, because it discusses sacrifices most fully. Above Numbers they write *daleth*, because it speaks of the arrangement of the boards of the Tabernacle. Above Deuteronomy they write *he*, interpreted as “this Law,” because the Law is repeated. Job, David, and Daniel are placed among the Hagiographa—not because of contempt, but because of dignity and holiness. *Hagio*: “holy.” *Graphia*: “writing.” They begin the order of the prophets with Joshua son of Nun because all Holy Scripture deserves the designation of prophecy, since it signifies future things. Joshua, in nearly all his deeds, prophesied the future works of Christ.

> **[Note: [Col. 1313D]]**
>
> 5. Perhaps: “they provide worship.”

5. **Chronicle.** “Temporal.” **By five incisions.** He mentioned five incisions in order to satisfy those who were accustomed to assert this. **With faces prostrate.** With heads bowed. **Their crowns.** Offering their help—that is, their works—because they teach the worship of the one God through works of reverence and submission, by which one reaches crowns.

> **[Note: [Col. 1313D]]**
>
> 6. The old manuscript has *occultatur dubia*, “it is hidden, doubtful.”

6. **Standing before the four living creatures.** Since the whole prophetic Scripture was fulfilled in the Gospel. **Helmed.** Fortified or adorned. **Apocrypha.** Hidden or doubtful. **To be set aside.** To be separated; the expression is as though one said, “I place apart.” **Phrase.** An expression or interpretation.

> **[Note: [Col. 1313D]]**
>
> 7. In the old manuscript it reads *conjectionem*, “conjecture,” and it also had *interpretationem*, which the same first hand altered to *interpretatorem*, “interpreter.” It likewise read *nesciebas*, “you did not know,” instead of *nesciebam*, “I did not know”; immediately afterward one should supply, “but it is found in the Septuagint.” The glosses of this prologue are sometimes placed outside their proper location, but the words of the prologue can easily be found.

7. **Paraphrast.** A conjecturer or interpreter. **Skins.** Haircloths. **Strength and labors** in the Church, which resist temptations and persecutions well. **Song of Songs.** Because of the excellence of the poem. **Wisdom of Solomon.** It is not found among the Hebrews—something I previously did not know—but it is found in the Septuagint and in other manuscripts.

## BOOK I OF KINGS

> **[Note: [Col. 1313D]]**
>
> **BOOK I OF KINGS.—CHAPTER I.** The explanation of the word *Ramatha* is taken from Eusebius and Jerome. See Bonfrère, *Onomasticon of Biblical Cities and Sacred Places*, under “Armatha Sophim.” Calmet holds a different opinion in the *Biblical Dictionary*, under “Ramathaim Sophim.” See also Gaspar Sanctius on 1 Kings, chapter 1. In the old manuscript it reads *Diaspolim* instead of *Diospolim*, and below *Arabitinia* instead of *Acrabitena*, following Jerome at the cited place, under “Selo.” Instead of *humida es*, the manuscript has *humides*; Robert of Sorbonne has *humidas*. The Vulgate, verse 18, reads: “And her face was no longer changed.” Concerning the differing time and manner of weaning, consult Gaspar Sanctius. It is uncertain whether the scribe intended *accommodatur* or *accommodatus*.

### CHAPTER I

**Ramatha.** The city itself, called *Arimathia* in the old translation. It belonged to Elkanah and Samuel, in the region of Tamnath, near Diospolis; Joseph, who is mentioned in the Gospel as being from Arimathea, was from there. **Sophim.** A mountain in the tribe of Ephraim. **On the appointed days.** Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles. **At Shiloh.** Shiloh is in the tribe of Ephraim; the Ark of the Covenant remained there until the time of Samuel. It is eleven miles from Neapolis, in the region of Acrabitena. **One portion.** When they offered sacrifice. **Rival.** Adversarial. **She troubled her.** She tormented her. **When the time returned.** In the cycle of the year. **Intoxicated.** Wine-drinking, drunk. **Put away.** Put aside drunkenness. **You are wet.** You are moist. **Daughters of Belial.** Daughters without the yoke of the Law of the Lord. Belial is called *Bel* in Hebrew and was an idol of the Ninevites, since Bel was the father of Ninus. **Her face was no longer changed.** In another translation: “Her face did not fall again”; that is, she no longer had either sadness or alteration. **I will not go until the child is weaned.** She spoke contrary to custom; for that reason Scripture mentions it. The Hebrews assert that the time of weaning was six years; others say twelve. **That the Lord may fulfill his word.** What he promised through the mouth of Eli the priest when he said: “May God grant you your request.” **I beg you, my lord.** The implied sense is: “that you may receive him kindly.” **I have lent him to the Lord.** For as long as he shall be, he is lent to the Lord; for as long as he lives.

> **[Note: [Col. 1314D]]**
>
> **II.** In the manuscript: *formido*, “fear,” instead of *fortitudo*, “strength.” After *vetera*, “old things,” it seems to read *enim*, “for.” After *locaverunt*, “they placed,” one reads *collocabilis señ*, which is obscure. Instead of *carnes crudas in altari*, “raw meats on the altar,” it had *carnes crudae in altare*, and immediately afterward, *detrahebant homines sacrificium Domini*, “people withdrew the Lord’s sacrifice”; I have restored the wording of the Vulgate.

**II. My horn.** My height and strength. **Old things.** Reproaches and insults. **Those who had first been satisfied with loaves placed themselves.** Twenty … and they gather themselves among others by asking for bread and whatever necessities there are, although previously they seemed to lack nothing at all. This is said of Peninnah. **He brings down to the underworld.** Into dangers, as though to death. **Hinges.** Foundations. **Sons of Belial.** Sons of the devil. **Fork.** Trident. **Cauldron.** Pot. **For I will not take cooked meat from you, but raw.** It was customary always to offer raw meat on the altar. The fat was burned first; then those who carried the meat cooked it, both for the priests and for themselves. **They withdrew people from the Lord’s sacrifice.** Because people did not wish to come to sacrifice to the Lord: either because by their evil examples they separated the people from sacrifice, or because they compelled people to blaspheme during the sacrifice. **How they slept with the women who kept watch.** They were widows who devoted themselves there to prayers, yet they were not permitted to enter the Temple, as the rest of the people were. **But if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?** He shows the difficulty of the matter, so that prayer may be made for him—not that he himself should pray in priestly fashion for others. **Manhood.** An age fit for war. **Before the anointed one.** Before the king. **A round loaf.** This is to be understood as any kind of petition, so that by it he might purchase the priesthood. **That I may eat a morsel.** In the place of the Tabernacle, like the other priests.

**III. The word of the Lord.** He is speaking of prophecy. **Precious.** Rare. **There was no vision.** Prophetic. **Moreover Samuel did not yet know the Lord.** He had not acquired the custom of hearing the word of the Lord. **A second time.** Twice. **Both his ears shall tingle.** They shall sound from terror, as though something were being heard. **And it did not fall.** Into emptiness: what is irrevocably fulfilled does not fall in vain. **His words.** Samuel’s. **And the word came to pass.** It became known.

> **[Note: [Col. 1314D]]**
>
> **IV.** The scribe omitted the gloss on “yesterday and the day before yesterday.”

**IV. Aphek.** A city of Israel. **Yesterday and the day before yesterday …** She bent down and gave birth. It is the nature of women to give birth quickly when suddenly terrified.

**V. And he struck the men.** They were struck by an affliction that the Greeks call *syringion*. **Extales and anus.** These are one and the same; they made them in the likeness of intestines. **Satraps.** In the language of the Philistines, princes are called this.

**[Col. 1315A]**

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **VI.** Instead of *pecuniam*, “money,” perhaps one should read *pecunias*, “moneys”; and, with the Vulgate, *Abelmagnum* should be read instead of *Adabelnagnum*. I restored *civitatis*, “of the city,” instead of *civitatinos*, as it stands in the manuscript.

**VI. But the Levites set down the Ark of the Lord.** For some Levites were there at that time. **From the fortified city to the village.** Hence they collected money from everyone; from it they made vessels, so that it might benefit all, since one plague had affected everyone. **Adabelmagnum.** A proper name of a stone. **But he struck.** The Lord did so, because it was unlawful for anyone except the priests to see the Ark. **From the people seventy men.** Of the city of Beth-shemesh. **And fifty thousand of the common people.** The common population outside the city. **Kiriath-jearim.** Kiriath and Gibeah were cities near one another, and the Levites were there.

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **VII.** The manuscript reads *Aminadab*.

**VII. Abinadab.** He was a priest in those days. **Gibeah.** Samuel’s city. **The twentieth year.** From the time when the Ark was brought into Abinadab’s house until David transferred it to himself. Then all Israel rested in divine religion, no longer worshiping idols, and all evils ceased among them. **They drew water and poured it out before the Lord.** They did this as a testimony, so that their minds might not afterward be recalled from the Lord, just as poured-out water cannot be collected or recalled. **Below Beth-car.** Near Mizpah and Shen, two places and cities. **And they did not add any more.** This is said of a long period.

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **VIII.** The manuscript has *pareant* instead of *parent*. Properly, *focaria* is a woman who serves around the hearth. Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses at this place read: “who might prepare food,” or “dyers.” In the manuscript it was *Domini* instead of *Domino*.

**VIII. Female servants.** Those who prepare food for him, or female dyers. **The produce of the vineyards.** What can be gathered from the vine and the honey. **In the ears of the Lord.** Praying beforehand, before the Lord.

**IX. Sons of the man Jemini.** Jemini was a family belonging to the tribe of Benjamin; Saul also arose from it. **Better than he.** More worthy. **The land of Salisa.** A proper place-name, not “a salty land.” **In saddlebags.** In sacks or in a purse. **The slope.** The valley. **On the height.** They always used to place altars in a high place, though not beneath a building.

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **X.** Perhaps: “the prophets were dwelling.” Shortly afterward I restored *praedicendum*, “to prophesy,” instead of *praedicandum*, “to preach”; and *cor aliud*, “another heart,” instead of *cor David*, “the heart of David”; and *visus inter*, “seen among,” instead of *usus inter*, “used among.”

**X. A flask of oil.** A small quadrangular bronze vessel, open on one side. **Near Rachel’s tomb in the territory of Benjamin.** For the boundaries of Benjamin are near those of the tribe of Judah. **At the oak of Tabor.** Named after some man, as the oak of Mamre. **The hill of the Lord.** A proper name of the place, either because of some help from the Lord, or because there was a high place and an altar there, and prophets lived there. **A company of prophets.** Not because they were always prophesying about future things, but because they were always ready to prophesy and praise. **And before them a psaltery.** Because they held it in their hands. **You shall go down before me to Gilgal.** The implied sense is as though he said: “Whenever you need me, or some dangers threaten, go down there, so that you may have a fixed place in which to await me.” **The Lord changed his heart into another.** He confirmed him in the kingdom. **You shall wait seven days.** Do not be wearied by waiting; therefore Gilgal is mentioned, because there the people celebrated Passover with Joshua and were circumcised. For that reason the place will be honored. **As a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”** Because he had not previously been seen among them, nor had he come from a prophetic family. **And Samuel summoned the people to the Lord.** Because in the presence of the Lord he disputed with the people.

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **XI.** In the manuscript: “Jabesh-gilead, a city in Gilead of the people.”

**XI. Jabesh-gilead.** Jabesh, a city; Gilead, of the people. **Following the oxen.** It happened by chance that the oxen went before him. **The spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul.** Saul did not prophesy about the future, but praised the Lord.

**XII. And Jephthah and Samuel.** He said this about Jephthah.

> **[Note: [Col. 1315D]]**
>
> **XIII.** For the difficult passage “Saul was a son of one year,” etc., consult Gaspar Sanctius in his commentary. The fact that Saul already had a son when he began to reign, whom he placed over a thousand men, argues against our author’s first explanation. In the third explanation something may perhaps be missing. The Vulgate has “against the way of Ephra,” and afterward *stimulum* should be corrected. The Gothic Bible has “against the way of Ephrata.”

**XIII. Saul was the son of one year.** He was twenty-one years old, because the Law commanded that those twenty years old and above should be chosen for war. Thus he is said to be “of one year” because he was one year beyond twenty. Alternatively, “son of one year” may be understood as “the son of Kish, reigning for one year”; he accomplished nothing great but remained humble. In another translation: “son of one year,” meaning those born in that year, so that they might be raised for his service. **He reigned two years.** This was when his son was chosen. **Garrison.** Army. **He shouted after Saul.** He followed him, or encouraged himself to battle. **But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan.** They fled toward the eastern region. **They proceeded along the road to Ephrata.** Along the road that leads to Saul’s land, in the tribe of Benjamin, where Ephrata is. **To the road of the boundary overlooking the valley of Zeboim.** The boundary that divided the Philistines and the Jews overlooked the valley of Zeboim. **No blacksmith was found.** Because the Philistines did not permit it. **Israel went down to the Philistines.** Whenever it was necessary to sharpen their tools for some work. **Mattock.** With which the earth is dug. **Sword.** Weapon. **As far as the goad.** From the greater things down to the lesser. **Correcting.** Oxen and every kind of beast of burden.

> **[Note: [Col. 1316D]]**
>
> **XIV.** I restored *unde tumultus*, “from where the tumult arose,” instead of *videre tumultus*, which yields no sense. The Vulgate has *clamavit*, “he cried,” instead of *conclamavit*, “he cried aloud.” I do not know what is intended by *dum terra fit*, “while the earth is made.” The manuscript reads *favum*, “honeycomb,” *et collectum ab apis*, “and collected by bees,” and *examen apium*, “a swarm of bees.” The other translation reads: “Behold, there was a swarm of bees”; Sabatier does not indicate it in *Ancient Latin Versions of the Bible*. The gloss on “his eyes were enlightened” is missing from the parchment. For *moriemur*, “we shall die,” I restored *moriamur*, “let us die,” unless one prefers “and in your vengeance we shall die.” The gloss on “if a hair should fall” is obscure.

**XIV. At the far end of Gibeah.** At the far end of Gibeah. **At Magron.** A proper place-name. **In the middle of a yoke of land.** It was a stretch of ground sufficient for the corpses of twenty men. **Bring the Ark of God here.** Bring it here. **Withdraw your hand.** Wait a little longer, until we learn where the tumult comes from, although he had previously said, “Bring the Ark here.” **Saul and the people cried out**, encouraging one another to battle. **Flowing honey.** It was on the grasses and leaves of the trees, as often happens while the earth is being formed; or a honeycomb appeared in many places, collected by bees. Another translation has: “Behold, there was a swarm of bees.” **And his eyes were enlightened …** **Roll a great stone to me now.** Either so that he might build an altar as an offering for sin, or so that, according to the rite, there might be witnesses, since they prohibited the people from eating meat with blood. **Let each man bring me his ox, etc.** Do this in my presence, and do not sin. **Without delay he shall die.** He shall die without postponement. **Give holiness.** Let us know that we shall die in your vengeance. **If a hair should fall.** Not a hair fell. **The kings of Zobah.** In Syria; Zobah is a city in Syria.

> **[Note: [Col. 1316D]]**
>
> **XV.** The manuscript was corrupt: *quia degeneris uxoris mos fuerunt Cinaei*, “because the Kenites were the custom of a degenerate wife.” After *arcum volutum*, “rolled arch,” two words cannot be read with certainty; perhaps they sound like *Siccine, sic etiam*, “Is this how, so also,” from verse 32 of this chapter: “Is bitter death thus divided?”

**XV. Like lambs.** Because of obedience. **He recounted how Amalek opposed Israel.** When they came out of Egypt. **And Saul said to the Kenite.** Because the Kenites were descended from Moses’ wife. **I repent that I made Saul king.** God’s “repentance” means a change in things established by him; this succeeds according to the changing circumstances of things or according to the ordering of what is right. **At Carmel.** Carmel is called *Carmel* in Greek and Latin, and *Carme* in Hebrew. There are two mountains called by this name: one where Nabal, Abigail’s husband, lived, in the southern region; the other near Ptolemais, overlooking the sea, where the prophet Elijah obtained rain on bended knees. **A triumphal vault.** A chamber or rolled arch. **Is this so?** So also. **And Samuel did not see Saul again.** Samuel did not come to Saul or visit him afterward.

> **[Note: [Col. 1317D]]**
>
> **XVI.** The phrase *in malus erat* is obscure. The manuscript is also corrupt at *omnipotentis pietatis*, “of almighty mercy”; immediately afterward it has *naturale est mentis ipsa mentium mitigare posse*, “it is natural that the mind itself can soothe minds.” I conjectured: “It is natural that music can soothe minds themselves,” or “can transform them into admiration.”

**XVI. He sanctified Jesse and his sons.** Samuel commanded them to wash with water and abstain from their wives. **A wicked spirit from the Lord tormented Saul.** Into the land. **The evil spirit of God.** How could it be of God if it was evil? Because everything brought forth by the Lord’s authority is subject to divine dominion. Therefore the devil himself—not as he now is, but as he was when created good by the Lord and always subjected to the Lord by his omnipotent power—belonged to the Lord. **Knowing how to play the lyre.** It is natural that the mind itself can be calmed into admiration by this art.

> **[Note: [Col. 1317D]]**
>
> **XVII.** The Vulgate has *Socho* and *Azecha*. *Superius immundis* was corrupt; I wrote *spurius*, “illegitimate,” instead, just as shortly afterward I read *squamata*, “scaled,” instead of *amata* or *hamata*; *aiebat*, “he said,” instead of *agebant*, “they were saying”; and *farinae*, “of flour,” instead of *farina*, “flour.” The Vulgate has “very clear stones.” By conjecture I restored *et veris tempore torrescunt*, “and in springtime they dry up,” instead of *et certis temporeorescunt*. See *Etymologies*, book XIII, chapter 21, section 2. *Cogitatum caeterorum* is obscure.

**XVII. Socoh and Azekah.** Two places. **In the boundaries of the Lord.** The name of a city. **Illegitimate.** Unclean. **Helmet.** A helmet. **Scaled armor.** Linked armor. **On the legs.** Greaves on the shins. **Phalanxes.** Ranks, armies. **He said.** He was saying. **An ephah of meal.** This measure contained three *modii* of the finest flour. **Someone.** Anyone. **Is it not a word?** Is it not my father’s command that I should come? **Very clear.** Very pure. **From the torrent.** We call torrents streams gathered from winter waters, which dry up in springtime. **Sling.** A sling. **Assembly.** The gathering of the people. **From what stock he descended.** He asked this out of envy, as though he did not know, or in order to investigate what the others thought about him. **If I know.** I do not know.

> **[Note: [Col. 1317D]]**
>
> **XVIII.** The interpreters take *secundo* a second time to mean “again,” and different people explain the passage in different ways.

**XVIII. To the sword, bow, and javelin.** She likewise gave that. **With sistrums.** These are a kind of musical instrument. **Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousand.** In these numbers only completeness was intended, since David achieved the greater victory. **And he prophesied in the midst of his house.** He spoke like a madman. **A second time.** Successfully. **In two matters my son-in-law.** Either because he promised the greater and gave the lesser, or because he had killed Goliath and brought back the foreskins of the Philistines.

> **[Note: [Col. 1317D]]**
>
> **XIX.** The Gothic Bible has *Rama* instead of *Ramatha*, as also in the following chapter. In the gloss on “a hairy skin,” etc., certain words are corrupt: *nigrum* instead of *nigram*, and *Judaei* instead of *Davidi*, as I conjecture. The Vulgate reads “at Naioth in Ramah.” After *lictores*, “lictors,” the manuscript has an obscure word, and immediately afterward *et ligatores*, “and binders,” belongs with it.

**XIX. A thrust with a blunted wound.** With the wound deflected. **Guards.** Attendants, lictors. **A hairy goatskin.** Black, because David’s hair was black and very beautiful in appearance. **At Naioth in Ramah.** In the high place of that city. **He stripped himself of his clothing.** He did this because he was in an ecstasy of mind. **Naked.** Not that he was entirely naked.

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XX.** The Vulgate has “which is in Ramah.” The glosses on *perendie*, etc., are entangled and obscure. In the Vulgate *Ezel* is written instead of *Zohel*.

**XX. What was in Ramah.** Situated in a high place. **And David swore again.** Jonathan swore that he would not conceal from David what he heard from Saul. **The day after tomorrow.** The third day. **On which it was permitted to work.** **And to inquire of the Lord:** this was inserted by the scribe. **Vengeance.** Your sitting. You who ought to have rendered judgment are being questioned. **Zohel.** A proper name of a stone. **Within you.** On this side. **And Jonathan rose.** He rose so that Abner would not sit beside the king on the other side, in David’s seat, but so that David’s vacant seat would be evident. **Earnestly.** Attentively, submissively. **Son of a woman.** The implied meaning is: “You are not my son but the son of an adulterous mother, since you love your enemy.”

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XXI.** The word *epilenticos*, “epileptics,” is absent from the Vulgate but is also found in Robert of Sorbonne’s glosses. It may belong to verse 5: “Are there no madmen among us?” It should be read *epilepticos*, since David was pretending to have epilepsy.

**XXI. After the ephod.** Beside the ephod. **Epileptics.** Those who fall down.

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XXII.** The Vulgate has “in distress.” After the gloss “Have I only today begun,” etc., four or five lines have almost entirely faded, so that the context cannot be read.

**XXII. He appointed those in distress.** Those who had been exiles from other nations. **Burdened with debt.** With the tribute they owed to foreigners. **In the stronghold.** In the fortified place that he possessed there. **He came to the forest of Hareth.** To the woodland that is in Ramah. The wood was in the high place of the city. **Have I only today begun to inquire of God for him?** Because I know him to be your enemy.

**XXIII. And David said: “Lord God of Israel.”** So that afterward the priest might answer him: **On the shadowed mountain, on the hill of Hachilah.** There was a hill and high place in a city situated to the right of the wilderness, south of the tribe of Judah. **Ziph and Maon.** These were desert places.

**XXIV. En-gedi.** A desert place near the shore of the Dead Sea.

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XXV.** I supplied *mensurae*, “of measure,” after *genus*. The gloss on *uvae passae*, “raisins,” has been omitted.

**XXV. Samuel died.** David added this. **A seah of meal.** *Seah*: a kind of measure; *meal*: flour. **Raisins …** **Figs.** The fruit of fig trees. **In the bundle of the living.** In the congregation of the living.

**XXVI. May the sacrifice smell sweet.** May it be pleasing, like a sacrifice.

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XXVII.** Perhaps one should add “in ancient days.” The manuscript had *que gentis* instead of *quod genti*.

**XXVII. These villages were inhabited in the land from ancient times.** Ezra said this as though he were saying: “Not now, but at some time in former days.” **As they went from Shur to the land of Egypt.** Proceeding through those villages, they traveled. **Jerahmeel and the Kenites.** In the tribe of Judah; therefore he truthfully said “toward their south,” so that the king would not think that he was harming his own people.

> **[Note: [Col. 1318D]]**
>
> **XXVIII.** Perhaps this is a recapitulation. The gloss on “magicians and diviners” is missing.

**XXVIII. Now Samuel had died.** This is a recapitulation. **Magicians and diviners …** **Having a python-spirit.** Divination: *python* was the name of the serpent whom Juno sent to pursue Latona when she was pregnant and later gave birth to Apollo and Diana on the island of Delos. Latona afterward commanded Apollo to avenge himself on the python that had pursued her. Thus it happened that he killed the python on the heights of Perine [reading uncertain]; he flayed it and built a temple on the island of Delos, where he had been raised. Hence Apollo was called Delian, and he placed the serpent’s skin in the temple; it was called a *cortina*. From this the curtains of tents were also named *cortinae*. There he and his priests were accustomed always to hear—or perhaps, as the conjecture reads, “to utter”—responses, and they practiced divination in the skin of the python. Hence those who divine are called *pythons*.

**XXIX. And it is with me for many days, or years.** He said this of a long period. **In his thousands.** In his armies. **In his ten thousands.** As though he had a larger army.

**[Col. 1319A]**

**XXX. Careth, Caleb.** Cities in the territories of the Jews.

# BOOK II OF KINGS

> **[Note: [Col. 1319A]]**
>
> **BOOK II OF KINGS.—CHAPTER I.** The phrase “out of flattery” is obscure.

### CHAPTER I

**Standing over him, I killed him.** He lied about this, but reported it to the king out of flattery. **In the Book of the Upright.** They had many books that Ezra did not restore. **At the crossroads.** In the villages. **Killed by blood.** Because of bloodshed.

> **[Note: [Col. 1319A]]**
>
> **II.** The manuscript had: “They came as far as the hill of the aqueduct,” because the aqueduct was on the hill and the place was inspected at the direction of the aqueduct.

**II. And they came as far as the hill of the aqueduct.** Because the aqueduct was on that hill. **Opposite the valley.** Facing the valley. **The road of the wilderness at Gibeon.** Because the road through the wilderness leads to the city. **And they came as far as the encampment.** “Encampment” refers to the place where Jacob saw the angel.

> **[Note: [Col. 1320A]]**
>
> **III.** The conjunction before “woman” is obscure. Perhaps it means “so soft as a woman.”

**III. Dog’s head.** Since everyone hated me because of you. **Sira.** This is the name of a cistern. **Holding a spindle.** Thus: “soft” and “woman.” *(The remainder is missing.)*
