# APPENDIX XXIII  
## BOOK OF DIFFERENCES, OR ON THE PROPER USE OF EXPRESSIONS

*From the Paris Edition. (C,S)*

> **[Col. 1319B] [Note: [Col. 1319D]]**
>
> **1.** In Breul’s edition this book is called Book I of the *Differences*, while Book II is *Differences of Things*, or spiritual differences. The alphabetical book published by us in volume V was known to Breul only late and was relegated to the end of the works. Grialius added no notes to this book, perhaps because most of its material had already been explained in alphabetical order in the preceding example. After Gothofred’s *Authors of the Latin Language*, this book was published under the title: “Extracts from the Differences communicated by the distinguished man Jacques Bongars, royal envoy. It begins: On the proper use of expressions, or of things.” In Vatican Codex 624 there are also differences of this sort in another order, beginning with number 52: “Between fear,” etc.

1. The difference between **to promise solemnly** and **to promise** is that we promise when asked, but make a solemn promise voluntarily.

2. The difference between **nothing** and **no one** is that *nullus* can refer to a thing, whereas *nemo* refers to a human being; *nemo* is as though one said *ne homo*, “not a human being.”

3. The difference between **inside** and **inward** is that I go inward but am inside; I am outside but go outward.

> **[Note: [Col. 1319D]]**
>
> **4.** Vatican Codex 624 has: *lustra* with a long first syllable … *lustra* with a short first syllable, “hiding places of wild animals.” Festus teaches that the first syllable of *lustrum* is long when it signifies the purification of the people and a period of five years, as though it were written *loustrum*.

4. The difference between **lūstra**, with a long vowel, and **lŭstra**, with a short vowel, is that *lūstra* are fixed periods of time, whereas *lŭstra* are hiding places of wild animals or refuges of disgraceful people.

> **[Note: [Col. 1320D]]**
>
> **5.** Vatican Codex 624: *servitium* is the number of slaves.

5. The difference between **slavery** and **service** is that slavery is the necessity of serving, whereas service is the duty performed by servants.

> **[Note: [Col. 1320D]]**
>
> **6.** Vatican Codex 624 adds: “or of pleasure.”

6. The difference between **boundary** and **end** is that a boundary is not established without the hand; “end” may be understood of speech, of intention, or of anything whatever.

> **[Note: [Col. 1320D]]**
>
> **7.** Vatican Codex 624: “It refers to *ferox* by nature.”

7. The difference between **rough** and **fierce** is that the rough is so for a time, whereas the fierce is so from birth.

> **[Note: [Col. 1320D]]**
>
> **8.** Vatican Codex 1491, after “and when filled with snow,” adds: “in summer it burns, that is, it dries.” Vatican Codex 624 reformulates it as follows: “The difference between a river, stream, watercourse, and torrent is that *fluvius* is so called from flowing; a *rivus* is seasonal water; an *amnis* is named from its winding course, being filled in winter by rain and clouds and dried in summer.”
>
> Vatican Codex 624 also has: “and harmless … *innocuus*, one who does not possess the power to harm.”

8. The difference between **stream**, **river**, **watercourse**, and **torrent** is that *flumen* is so called from flowing; *fluvius* from seasonal water; *amnis* from pleasantness, as though it were *amoenus*, “pleasant”; and a torrent is one that swells in winter and is filled by rain and snow.

9. The difference between **innocent** and **harmless** is that “innocent” refers to holiness of conduct, whereas “harmless” refers to one who has no intention of harming.

**427** 10. The difference between **high-born** and **noble** is that the high-born is born so, while the noble becomes so through wealth.

11. The difference between **royal** and **king** is that a royal boy is regal, whereas a king is one who rules a kingdom.

12. The difference between **insane** and **deranged** is that the insane person retains part of the mind, whereas the deranged person is entirely without a mind; the former is so called as though from “a diminished part of the mind.”

13. The difference between **flocks** and **cattle** is that by *pecudes* we understand sheep alone, whereas *pecora* is a mixture of all animals.

14. The difference between **to show** and **to demonstrate** is that we show once, but demonstrate repeatedly.

15. The difference among **rich**, **respectable**, **wealthy**, **fortunate**, **well-provided**, and **opulent** is that the rich person is rich in gold and silver; the respectable person is so in character; the wealthy person is named from *pecus*, “cattle”; the fortunate person from the soul; the well-provided person from being full of purses; and the opulent person is full of all these things, as though eminent in resources.

16. The difference between **openly** and **before** is that “openly” indicates the presence of people, whereas “before” requires reference to a person.

17. The difference between **white** and **shining white** is that white is natural, whereas care makes something shining white.

18. The difference between **sense** and **understanding** is that sense is natural, whereas understanding arises from an obscure matter.

19. The difference between **lifeless** and **inanimate** is that the lifeless has been deprived of life, whereas the inanimate has never possessed a soul.

20. The difference among **shower**, **storm cloud**, and **rain** is that *imber* derives from the Greek meaning, as though it were “shadowy”; it falls with great force and descends quickly. Rain is what clouds discharge under the pressure of winds; hence *plorare*, “to weep,” is said when tears are forced out by grief. A storm cloud also bursts forth so as to occupy a smaller part of the sky and leave the greater part clear.

21. The difference among **blood**, **gore**, and **purulent matter** is that blood is so called while it is inside the body, from the idea that it makes us sound, that is, keeps us together. Gore, when spilled, is so called because it makes one fall. Purulent matter belongs to a decaying body.

22. The difference between **backs** and **hides** is that human beings have *terga*, whereas animals have *tergora*. In the singular we say a human being’s *tergum*, but an animal’s *tergus*.

23. The difference between **mi** and **mihi** is that *mi* is a simple pronoun, while *mihi* is compounded; alternatively, *mi* is an expression of emotion and always requires the vocative case.

24. The difference between **then** and **at that time** is that *tum* signifies order, whereas *tunc* signifies time.

25. The difference between **anger** and **irascibility** is that anger lasts for a time, whereas irascibility remains in the heart.

26. The difference between **by night** and **at night** is that *noctu* is formed like *interdiu*, “by day,” and signifies some part of the night; by *nocte*, “at night,” we understand the whole night.

**[Col. 1320D] 428** 27. The difference among **to speak**, **to talk**, **to converse**, and **to narrate** is that we *fari* when we say something eloquently; we *loqui* by nature; we *sermocinari* when we contend in speech with someone; and we narrate learnedly.

28. The difference among **to hold**, **to take**, and **to receive** is that we hold what is in our power; we take what has been set down; and we receive what has been given.

29. The difference among **to look at**, **to look upward**, **to inspect**, **to look ahead**, **to look down upon**, **to gaze at**, **to see**, **to watch**, and **to visit** is that we look at something by chance; we look upward toward a higher place or show reverence; we inspect when we are about to judge; we look ahead at things that are far away; we look down upon a lower or weak place; we gaze when there is a reason; we see by nature; and we visit what we have experienced.

30. The difference between **fury** and **madness** is that fury is a temporary defect, whereas madness is permanent.

31. The difference between **another** and **the other** is that *alius* is used of many, whereas *alter* is used of two.

32. The difference between **crime** and **deed** is that crime is an offense, whereas a deed may also properly be spoken of in praise. Sallust says “a good deed.”

> **[Col. 1321B] [Note: [Col. 1321D]]**
>
> **33.** Vatican Codex 624: “The difference between *gifts* and *services* is this: *gifts* are said …; *services* are the acts of service that the poor render to the rich in the place of a gift. Alternatively, gifts are given to God, while services are assigned to human beings.”

33. The difference between **gifts** and **services** is that gifts are given to God, whereas services are assigned to human beings. Services are also those duties by which human beings—that is, soldiers—perform their obligations; these are properly called *munia*.

34. The distinction between *vestis* and *vestimentum* is that women’s clothing is called *vestes*, men’s clothing *vestimenta*.

35. The distinction between *humidum* and *uvidum* is that something *humidum* is thoroughly soaked, whereas something *uvidum* is wet only halfway through.

36. The distinction between *vetus* and *vetustum* is that *vetus* is compared with what is new, whereas *vetustum* refers instead to antiquity.

37. The distinction between *terrere* and *deterrere* is that whoever frightens compels someone to fear, whereas whoever deters prevents someone from persevering.

38. The distinction among *solum*, *unum*, *solitarium*, and *unicum* is that *solus* is one who has been left by the others; *unus* serves as the beginning of many; *solitarius* is one who always lives without the others; *unicus* is regarded as alone because of the lack of others.

39. The distinction among *aphaeresis*, *syncope*, and *apocope* is that only *aphaeresis* occurs at the beginning of a word, removing letters and syllables, as in:

> *Si genus humanum, et mortalia TEMNITIS arma*,  
> “If you despise the human race and mortal weapons,”

for *contemnitis*. *Syncope* removes something from the middle, as in:

> *Apparent rari nantes*,

“the scattered swimmers appear,” for *natantes*. *Apocope* occurs at the end, as in:

> *domus luxu instruitur*,

“the house is furnished with luxury,” that is, with *luxuria*.

40. The distinction between *solecism* and *barbarism* is that solecism occurs in meaning, barbarism in expression.

41. The distinction between *relictum* and *desertum* is that we leave something willingly, but abandon it unwillingly.

42. The distinction between *misereri* and *miserari* is that we *miseremur* when, at the same time, we grieve over someone’s misfortune and assist the sufferer; *miserari* means merely to console and to remain within the emotion of grief.

[Col. 1322A] 429

[Note: [Col. 1321D]

In Vat. 624 there follows:

“The distinction between a *puteus* and a *lacuna*, that is, a *cisterna*, is that a *puteus* has—perhaps *puras putas*, ‘you consider pure’—waters flowing from a living spring; a *cisterna*, which cools, possesses its own external and imported waters.

“‘To speak *in persona*’ is one thing, and ‘to speak *ad personam*’ another: in speaking *in persona*, one does not speak to the person herself but speaks on behalf of the person to others; in speaking *ad personam*, the speaker is understood to direct the speech to her.

“The distinction between a *fornicaria* and an *adultera* is that a *fornicaria* is one who has intercourse with several men, whereas an *adultera* is one who, abandoning one husband, joins herself to another.

“The distinction between *videre* and *credere* is that we see things present, but believe things future.

“The distinction between death and hell is this: death is that by which the soul is separated from the body; hell is the place in which souls are confined, either for refreshment or for the torments of punishment, according to the quality of their merits. Death is compared with a harlot, because just as death divides the soul from the body, so a prostitute divides brothers from one another.

“The distinction between *aegritudo* and *aegrotatio* is that *aegritudo* is said of the mind, whereas *aegrotatio* is said of the body.”]

43. The distinction between *orare* and *precari* is that *orare* is so called because it is related to *oris ratio*, “the function of the mouth”; and whoever prays (*orat*) also makes petition (*precatur*), while whoever asks (*rogat*) makes entreaty (*deprecatur*). Not everyone who makes petition prays, since even the uneducated resort to petitions.

44. The distinction between *nescire* and *ignorare* is that whoever *nescit* lacks knowledge of everything, whereas whoever *ignorat* is ignorant of something.

45. The distinction between a *legatus* and an *orator* is that a *legatus* is chosen by the state for an official duty and is sacrosanct; an *orator* is sent to make a plea, so that by an address from his mouth he may set forth what he seeks.

46. The distinction among *tardus*, *piger*, *iners*, and *segnis* is that *tardus* is one who drags out time; *iners* is without skill and incapable of any duty; *piger* is in every respect like a sick person; *segnis* has been removed from warmth.

47. The distinction between *natus* and *gnatus* is that *natus* is derived specifically from the verb *nasci*, “to be born,” whereas *gnatus* means “son,” from generation.

48. The distinction between *infamis* and *famosus* is that *famosus* may be used in either a good or a bad sense, whereas *infamis* is used only in a bad sense.

49. The distinction between *juventus* and *juventa* is that *juventus* denotes a multitude of young people, while *juventa* denotes the age of one person, or even the goddess of youth.

50. The distinction between *decus* and *decor* is that *decus* refers to virtue, *decor* to the body.

51. The distinction between *supra* and *super* is that *super* is what projects above, while *supra* is what has something beneath it.

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

In Codex Vaticanus 624: “*Pavor* is a movement of the mind; hence also …”]

52. The distinction among *metus*, *timor*, and *pavor* is that *metus* looks ahead to future things, *timor* is a sudden bewilderment of the mind, while *pavor* is a movement. Hence we also speak of frightened animals.

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

Codex Vaticanus 624: “whose mention is one.”]

53. The distinction among *omnes*, *cuncti*, and *universi* is that *omnes* refers to those who have been mentioned, *cuncti* to those who are everywhere, and *universi* to those who have been turned together in one place.

54. The distinction between *unda* and *aqua* is that *unda* is abundant water, whereas *aqua* is natural water.

[Col. 1322C] 430

55. The distinction between *tacere* and *silere* is that whoever ceases to speak is silent (*silet*), while whoever has not begun to speak keeps silence (*tacet*).

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

Vat. 624: “that necessity may be given”—said because it stands ready for the occasion.]

56. The distinction among *auxilium*, *praesidium*, and *subsidium* is that assistance (*auxilium*) is sent to those in difficulty; protection (*praesidium*) is prepared; support (*subsidium*) is kept in reserve, so that it may be given when necessity demands it.

57. The distinction between *insequi* and *consequi* is that we overtake a friend who is going before us, but pursue an enemy.

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

This distinction occurs again at no. 251, where it is explained more fully.]

58. The distinction between *principium* and *initium* is that *principium* is the beginning of an entire body, while *initium* means, as it were, “first.”

59. The distinction between *simulare* and *dissimulare* is that we pretend what we do not know and deny that we do not know it; we conceal what we know.

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

One should read *simitu*, not *simitum*. *Simitu* is an ancient word, often occurring in Plautus, almost in a comic sense, for “together,” “at the same time,” or “in one.” See Nonius, chapter 2, no. 814.]

60. The distinction between *simul* and *simitum* is that *simul* means “together,” as when one thing is clearly present in conjunction with another, for example: “We read together; we write together.” *Simitum* carries the meaning of profit, as though derived from *simulitum*.

[Col. 1323A]

61. The distinction among *scelestus*, *sceleratus*, and *scelerosus* is that *sceleratus* is contaminated by his own crime or another’s; *scelestus* is a planner of crimes; *scelerosus* means, as it were, “treacherous” or “dangerous,” or entirely a day or a mind because of its difficulty.

62. The distinction between *reliqui* and *ceteri* is that we call those *reliqui* who have been left over from the whole, but those whom we do not know *ceteri*.

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

*Redibidum* is not easily found in other authors. Grammarians commonly explain the distinction between *recidivivum* and *redivivum*.]

63. The distinction between *redibidum*, with the letter *b*, and *redivivum*, with the letter *v*, is that *redibidum* is something that is born, whereas *redivivum* is something that comes back to life.

64. The distinction between *patrius* and *paternus* is that *patrius* comes from one’s homeland, while *paternus* comes from one’s father.

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

Compare below, no. 158.]

65. The distinction between *pometa* and *pomaria* is that we call plantations *pomaria* indiscriminately, as we do *olearia* and *ficaria*; *pometa* means, as it were, *maleta*, *ficeta*, and *oleta*—plantations of apple, fig, and olive trees.

66. The distinction between *aeger* and *aegrotus* is that *aeger* refers to the mind, *aegrotus* to the body.

67. The distinction between “he came first” (*prior venit*) and “he came before” (*ante venit*) is that *prior* refers to rank, while *ante* refers to time.

68. The distinction between *inficere* and *officere* is that one who harms (*officit*) does injury, whereas one who dyes (*inficit*) dyes wool or something else.

69. The distinction among *contingere*, *accidere*, and *evenire* is that good things *contingunt*, bad things *accidunt*, and both kinds *eveniunt*.

70. The distinction between *grates* and *gratias* is that we return thanks (*grates referimus*), but give thanks (*gratias agimus*).

71. The distinction between *oleae* and *olivae* is this: we call the fruit itself, from which oil is made, *olivae*; we call the trees, from which olive groves arise, *oleae*.

431

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

Another form of this distinction appears at no. 152.]

72. The distinction between *nixus* and *nisus* is that *nixus* refers to the body, while *nisus* refers to the mind, that is, to effort.

73. The distinction between *nefandus* and *nefarius* is that *nefarius* is understood from past things, whereas *nefandus* refers to an action.

74. The distinction between *nutrit* and *nutricat* is that a woman *nutrit*, “nourishes,” while a nurse or fosterer (*nutritius*) *nutricat*.

75. The distinction between *maritimus* and *marinus* is that *maritimus* means “near the sea,” whereas *marinus* comes from the sea itself.

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

In Vat. 624 there follows: “The distinction between *merum* and *meratum* is that *merum* …”]

76. The distinction among *laniat*, *lacerat*, and *lancinat* is that one *laniat* when one stretches something apart limb by limb; one *lacerat* when one deprives limbs of their parts; one *lancinat* when one tears limbs apart uselessly.

77. The distinction between *patulum* and *patens* is that something *patulum* cannot be closed or covered, whereas something *patens* can be closed again once it has been opened.

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

This distinction is presented in another way at no. 238.]

78. The distinction between *gutta* and *stilla* is that a *stilla* falls, while a *gutta* stands.

79. The distinction between *delictum* and *peccatum* is that we *delinquimus* when we fail to fulfill salutary commands, but we *peccamus* when we presume to do what has been commanded not to be done.

80. The distinction among *incola*, *accola*, and *advena* is that an *incola* cultivates his own land, in which he was born; an *accola* cultivates the land of his birth, but that land belongs to someone else; an *advena* comes from his own land into a foreign one.

81. The distinction between *hesternum* and *externum* is that *hesternum* derives from “yesterday,” whereas *externum* means “foreign” or “external.” For many uneducated people call an external day what is not admissible.

82. The distinction between *baltea* and *balteos* is that by *baltea* we mean the straps themselves; the other items we call *balteos*.

83. The distinction between *bibere* and *ebibere* is that one who drinks (*bibit*) leaves something in the cup, while one who drinks it up (*ebibit*) empties it completely.

84. Although we have briefly explained, for those who understand the matter keenly, the distinction among *geminatum*, *junctum*, and *duplicatum*, let us teach it more fully by examples. *Geminatum* is what consists of two similar things, as in Cicero: “Twin boldnesses.” *Junctum* is what consists of two equal things, as in Virgil: “Now griffins will be yoked to horses.” *Duplicatum* occurs when one thing is placed twice: “With both knees doubled toward the ground.”

[Note: [Col. 1323D]

In my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 150, I discussed the nouns *reclinis* and *reclivis*, where I suggested that Isidore’s words could be emended as follows: “The sun is *declinis*, a place *declivis* … likewise a man is *acclinis*, a place *acclivis*.” From this comes *acclivum*.]

85. The distinction between *decline* and *declive* is that the sun is *declinus*, while a place is *declivus*. The same principle should be understood for *accline* and *acclive*: a man is *acclinus*, a place *acclivus*. From this comes *acclivum*.

432

86. The distinction between *commentarii* and *commentaria* is that books are called *commentarii*, while volumes are called *commentaria*.

[Note: [Col. 1324D]

Vat. 624: “that which precedes another, the first all.”]

87. The distinction between *primus* and *prior* is that *primus* is used of one among many, *prior* of one among two. The same distinction should be observed between *postremus* and *posterior*.

88. The distinction between *disertus* and *desertus* is that an eloquent speaker is called *disertus*, while *desertus* means abandoned.

89. The distinction between *dilator* and *delator* is that a *delator* is one who reports someone for accusation, whereas a *dilator* is one who postpones something in order to bring it forward later.

90. The distinction between *adversum* and *adversus* is that one who is opposed to you is *adversum te adversarius*, whereas one who changes against you is *adversus te mutator*.

91. The distinction between *pauperies* and *paupertas* is that *pauperies* is loss, whereas *paupertas* is the condition of one who possesses nothing.

92. The distinction between *exprobrare* and *obprobrare* is that one *exprobrat* who casts a person’s own fault in his face, whereas one *obprobrat* who brings an insult against him.

93. The distinction between *accersire* and *arcessire* is that one *accersit* who summons, whereas one *arcessit* who accuses.

94. The distinction between *acervus* and *acerbus* is that an *acervus* is a heap or mass, whereas *acerbus* means unripe and harsh.

95. The distinction between *labrum* and *labium* is that the upper lip is called *labrum*, the lower lip *labium*.

[Col. 1324C]

[Note: [Col. 1324D]

The word *tuga* does not occur even in Ducange. *Tofus* is ordinarily the Latin word; in the Middle Ages it was written *tufus*. Some understand *tufa*, or *tupha*, as a certain kind of banner.]

96. The distinction among *toga*, *tuga*, *tuba*, and *tufa* is that a *toga* is a garment; a *tuga* is a channel through which water is led; a *tuba* is an instrument sounded by blowing; a *tufa* is a stone formed from coagulated water, which we call *tufum*.

97. The distinction between *comosus* and *comatus* is that *comosus* derives from the use of hair (*coma*), while *comatus* refers to nature, as in “hairy Gaul.”

98. The distinction between *certo* and *certius* is that *certo* derives from *certus*, while *certius* derives from *certe*.

99. The distinction between *caecitudo* and *caecitas* is that *caecitas* is blindness itself—followed by the corrupt or uncertain phrase *viae ceritas*—and is also called *calamitas*; *caecitudo*, however, is an affection, as *lippitudo* is called.

100. The distinction between *castimonia* and *castitas* is that *castimonia* is said almost as *caerimonia*, “ceremony,” whereas *castitas* refers only to the body.

101. The distinction between *copiae* and *copia* is that *copiae* is used in the sense of an army, while *copia* means an abundance of things.

102. The distinction among *circum*, *circa*, and *circiter* is that *circum* refers to time, *circa* to place, and *circiter* to number.

103. The distinction between *fidus* and *fidelis* is that a servant is called *fidus*, a friend *fidelis*.

104. The distinction between “like his” (*illius similis*) and “like him” (*illi similis*) is that *illius similis* refers to similarity of character, while *illi similis* refers to similarity of appearance.

433

[Note: [Col. 1324D]

For *flemma* one should apparently read *phlegma*, or *flegma*; and for *plemma* one should restore *plemina*. On this word see Festus. Nevertheless, Caper, *On Orthography*, p. 2243 in Putsch, writes: “*Flemina* are cases in which the legs abound in blood; *plemina*, when there are calloused furrows on the hands or feet.” In Vatican Manuscript 624: “The distinction between *flemina* and *plemina* is that *flemina* … *plemina* …”]

105. The distinction between *flemma* and *plemma* is that *flemma* occurs when the legs abound in blood, whereas *plemma* occurs when calloused furrows arise on the hands or feet.

106. The distinction between *mammae* and *ubera* is that the breasts of human beings are called *mammae*, while those of cattle are called *ubera*.

107. The distinction between *avena*, without aspiration, and *habena*, with aspiration, is that *avena* is a sterile shoot, whereas *habenae* are reins for animals.

108. The distinction between *donum* and *munus* is that *donum* belongs to the giver, *munus* to the recipient. The former derives from *dare*, “to give,” the latter from *munire*, “to provide or fortify.”

109. The distinction between *arguere* and *coarguere* is that *coarguere* means to restrain or check, while *arguere* means to show or disclose, as in Virgil: “Fear reveals ignoble spirits.” Hence *argumenta* are also so called because they reveal the case.

110. The distinction between *afficere* and *adficere* is that we are affected (*afficimur*) by honor, but afflicted (*adficimur*) by death or injury.

111. The distinction among *advocatus*, *invocatus*, and *evocatus* is that one is summoned as an advocate to give legal protection, invoked to provide assistance, and called out to offer service.

[Col. 1325B]

112. The distinction between *illuvies* and *ingluvies* is that *illuvies* is filth, while *ingluvies* is the belly. The former is so called from not washing, the latter from swallowing.

113. The distinction among *commonere*, *admonere*, and *monere* is that we *commonemus* things past, *admonemus* things present, and *monemus* things future.

114. The distinction between *temeritas* and *audacia* is that *temeritas* is said of action without deliberation, *audacia* of action after deliberation.

115. The distinction between *velocitas* and *celeritas* is that *velocitas* is said of feet and bodies, while *celeritas* is said of minds and actions.

116. The distinction between *vivus* and *vivens* is that *vivus* is said of one who is living, *vivens* of one who is dying.

117. The distinction between *nasci* and *enasci* is that what falls from the womb is *nascitur*, whereas what rises from earth or water *enasci­tur*.

118. The distinction among *abducere*, *perducere*, and *deducere* is that we are led away (*abducimur*) from a dishonorable matter, led forward (*perducimur*) to studies, and led down (*deducimur*) to honor.

[Note: [Col. 1325D]

Here *eluxit* appears to be derived from *eluo*, and one should read “*eluxit*, he who put away mud.” For *eluxit*, from *eluceo*, has nothing in common with mud. Moreover, *eluo* has *elui*, not *eluxi*, as its perfect. In Agraetius, from whom most of these distinctions are taken, we read: “*Eluxit*, he who puts away mourning; *illuxit*, when light appeared.” Therefore the text in Isidore should be corrected to “he who put away mourning.”]

119. The distinction between *eluxit* and *illuxit* is that *eluxit* means “he who disposed of mud,” while *illuxit* means “he who appeared with light.”

120. The distinction among *nuntiare*, *denuntiare*, *renuntiare*, and *annuntiare* is that something is *nuntiatur* from a distance, *denuntiatur* in the present, *annuntiatur* concerning the future, and *renuntiatur* in order to excuse or reject.

434

[Note: [Col. 1325D]

Agraetius also varies somewhat here.]

121. The distinction among *conscribere*, *exscribere*, *transcribere*, *inscribere*, *ascribere*, and *describere* is that *conscribere* means to write together at one time; *exscribere*, to transfer writings; *transcribere*, when our right passes to another; *inscribere*, to make an accusation; *ascribere*, to assign; *describere*, to set out in words or in order. The verb *scribere* itself is incomplete.

122. The distinction among *exstruere*, *instruere*, *astruere*, *construere*, and *struere* is that *exstruere* means to advance upward; *instruere*, to draw up a battle line or arrange an action; *astruere*, to affirm; *construere*, to join together by building; *struere*, to place the remaining things upon what has been laid beneath.

[Col. 1326A]

123. The distinction among *consuescere*, *insuescere*, and *assuescere* is that we become accustomed (*suescimus*) to good things, accustom ourselves (*insuescimus*) to bad things, and become accustomed (*assuescimus*) to both.

124. The distinction between *fungi* and *defungi* is that *fungi* means to perform, while *defungi* means to complete. Hence the dead are called *defuncti*, because they have completed the course of this life.

125. The distinction among *adolescere*, *inolescere*, and *exsolescere* is that *adolescere* means growth; *inolescere*, growth by addition; *exsolescere*, fading away.

126. The distinction among *deportare*, *apportare*, *comportare*, and *exportare* is that *deportare* and *apportare* mean to bring something; *comportare*, to collect it in one place; *exportare*, to carry it away.

127. The distinction among *temperantia*, *temperatio*, and *temperies* is that *temperantia* belongs to the mind; *temperatio* to things; *temperies* to breezes.

128. The distinction between *recipere* and *suscipere* is that we *recipimus* when asked, but *suscipimus* voluntarily.

129. The distinction between *arundo* and *hirundo* is that *arundo* is a reed, while *hirundo* is a bird that habitually clings to beams.

130. The distinction between *spirare* and *exspirare* is that *spirare* means to live, *exspirare* to die.

131. The distinction between *pertinacia* and *constantia* is that *pertinacia* is said of a bad matter, *constantia* of a good one.

132. The distinction between *consequi* and *assequi* is that we follow with our feet, but attain through effort.

133. The distinction between *laetari* and *gratulari* is that we rejoice over our own things, but congratulate our friends on their good things.

[Note: [Col. 1325D]

Goldastus, in his notes on Saint Valerian, *On Good Discipline*, p. 54, attempts to emend this passage as follows: “We call a place *herbidum* in which … is accustomed to exist … easily produces … Likewise, we rightly call a drink *aquaticum* which receives … from elsewhere … Likewise, a *merica* drink,” and so forth.]

134. The distinction between *herbosus* and *herbidus* is that we call a place *herbidum* when grass is present there, even if it is ordinarily dry; we call it *herbosum* when it readily produces grass, even if it is temporarily dry. We also correctly call a drink *aquatum* when it receives water from elsewhere. A place that pours forth water from itself is called *aquosum*; similarly, we call a drink *meracum* and wine *merosum*.

135. The distinction between *subter* and *subtus* is that *subter* refers to something pressed and trampled by another thing above it, whereas *subtus* refers to something lowered beneath another thing and not touched.

136. The distinction between *sinus* and *gremium* is that we call the receptacle of a folded garment a *sinus*, whereas the concealed part of a belted garment is a *gremium*.

137. The distinction between *largitas* and *largitio* is that *largitas* belongs to kindness, *largitio* to ambition.

[Note: [Col. 1326D]

These and several of the following distinctions belong to Agraetius.]

138. The distinction between *muliebre* and *mulierarium* is that *muliebre* is said of something made by women; *mulierarium* of something arranged by women and carried out by men.

139. The distinction between *diligere* and *deligere* is that *diligi* refers to affection, *deligi* to judgment; hence an army is ordered to be selected.

[Note: [Col. 1326D]

In Vat. 624 the following is added:

“The distinction between *comptus* and *compositus* is that *comptus* refers to care, *compositus* to nature.

“The distinction between *consequimur* and *assequimur* is that we *consequimur* with our feet, *assequimur* through effort.

“The distinction between *construere* and *exstruere* is that *construere* means to build, while *exstruere* means to spread out [perhaps *sternere*].

“The distinction among *consuere*, *suere*, and *assuere* is that *consuere* is used of clothing or books; *assuere* of leather; finally, we use *suere* when torn and opened things are sewn together.”]

140. The distinction between *commodare* and lending mutually is that we *commodamus* a friend a horse, garment, slave, or similar object for a time; but we lend money, grain, wine, or other such things mutually.

[Col. 1327A]

141. The distinction between *ligare* and *legare* is that one ties with a bond (*ligat*), but bequeaths by a will (*legat*).

142. The distinction among *loqui*, *obloqui*, *alloqui*, and *eloqui* is that *loqui* belongs to a human being; *obloqui* to a detractor who objects or opposes; *alloqui* to one who exhorts or judges; *eloqui* pertains to honor.

143. The distinction between *percussum* and *perculsum* is that we use *percussum* of the body, *perculsum* of the mind.

144. The distinction between *fremor* and *fremitus* is that *fremor* is the murmuring of human beings, *fremitus* the growling of beasts.

145. The distinction among *flavus*, *furvus*, and *fulvus* is that *flavus* means red, as in *flava caesaries*, “red-gold hair”; *furvus*, black; *fulvus*, blackish-red, as in a tawny lion.

146. The distinction between *postulare* and *poscere* is that something is *postulatur* carelessly, but *poscitur* shamelessly.

147. The distinction between *frixum* and *frictum* is that *frixum* derives from *frigus*, “cold,” while *frictum* derives from *frigere*, “to fry.”

[Col. 1327B]

148. The distinction between *diutinum* and *diuturnum* is that *diutinum* is what existed for a long time, whereas *diuturnum* is what lasted for a long time.

[Note: [Col. 1327D]

*Delitum* derives from *delino*, “to smear over”; *inlitum* from *inlino*, or *illino*. I do not know the author of the distinction offered here.]

149. The distinction between *delitum* and *inlitum* is that *delitum* is so called because it is sudden, whereas *inlitum* is something smeared over.

436

150. The distinction among *damnum*, *dispendium*, and *detrimentum* is that *damnum* is so called from something having been diminished; *dispendium* from the loss of weight; *detrimentum* from *terere*, “to wear away.”

151. The distinction between *dominium* and *dominatus* is that *dominium* refers to what belongs to private right, while *dominatus* refers to rule.

[Note: [Col. 1327D]

Compare no. 72.]

152. The distinction between *nixus* and *nisus* is that *nixus* refers to being on one’s knees, while *nisus* derives from *niti*, “to strive,” that is, “to make an effort.”

[Note: [Col. 1327D]

*Enubere* and *denubere* are customarily said of women who marry beneath their station.]

153. The distinction among *nubere*, *enubere*, and *denubere* is that a citizen woman marries a citizen (*nubit civis civi*), she marries a foreigner when she *enubit*, and she *denubit* when she comes under a husband’s authority.

154. The distinction between *noxa* and *noxia* is that *noxa* is punishment, while *noxia* is the fault itself.

[Col. 1327C]

155. The distinction between *necessitas* and *necessitudo* is that *necessitas* signifies compulsion, while *necessitudo* signifies a relationship of blood or affection.

156. The distinction between *clausum* and *obturatum* is that *clausum* derives from bolts and keys, whereas *obturatum* refers to the blocking of openings, as when ears are stopped up, not closed.

157. The distinction among *operire*, *adoperire*, and *inoperire* is that we cover something with a lid (*operimus*); we cover doors (*adoperimus*); and we cover something when we place an object over something lying down (*inoperimus*).

[Note: [Col. 1327D]

The distinction explained at no. 65 concerning these words is different, since it comes from different authors.]

158. The distinction between *pometa* and *pomeria* [perhaps *pomaria*] is that *pometa* are places where fruit grows, while *pomaria* are places in which it is stored.

159. The distinction between *palma* and *palmum* is that *palma* refers to a part of the body, while *palmum* is a measure. This measure extends from the first thumb to the little finger.

160. The distinction between *poplites* and *suffragines* is that *poplites* refers to the knees of human beings, *suffragines* to the hind knees of animals.

[Col. 1327D]

161. The distinction between *praeparare* and *apparare* is that one *praeparat* who renews a desire by preparing, whereas one *apparat* who adds something to what has already been prepared, that is, prepares an accusation.

162. The distinction among *stipulatio*, *restipulatio*, *astipulatio*, and *constipulatio* is that *stipulatio* has a fixed meaning; *restipulatio* applies when something agreed upon has been done; *astipulatio* concerns the same sum of money, so that either party may reclaim it; *constipulatio* is a linked *restipulatio*, if it has been made by fraud.

163. The distinction between *saturitas* and *satietas* is that *saturitas* is said only of food, whereas *satietas* is said of other things.

164. The distinction between *vicinia* and *vicinitas* is that *vicinia* is said of the closeness of places, *vicinitas* of persons.

165. The distinction between *fluctuo* and *fluctuor* is that I *fluctuo* in mind, as though I were making waves and flowing here and there; I *fluctuor*, “I am borne by a wave.” Thus the sea *fluctuat*, while a ship *fluctuatur*. The same distinction should be observed between *luxurio* and *luxurior*.

437

166. The distinction between *potero* and *potuero* is that *potero* expresses the certainty of one making a promise, while *potuero* expresses doubt.

167. The distinction between *Hispanus* and *Hispaniensis* is that *Hispanus* denotes nationality, whereas *Hispaniensis* is like *Massiliensis*, and similar forms.

168. The distinction among *escendere*, *ascendere*, and *conscendere* is that we *ascendimus* elevated places or a position of honor; we *escendimus* when we climb up onto something higher; we *conscendimus* when we ride on a horse.

169. The distinction between *uterque* and *utrique* is that *uterque* is used with singulars, *utrique* with plurals.

[Col. 1328B]

170. The distinction between *pignero* and *pigneror* is that one *pigneror* your mind, while I *pignero* when I take your pledge.

171. The distinction between *mereo* and *mereor* is that *mereo* is used of merit in service, while *mereor* is used of work performed for wages. The same applies to *rumino*, *ruminor*, and similar forms.

172. The distinction between *laurus* and *laurea* is that *laurus* is the tree itself, while *laurea* is a crown or branch.

173. The distinction between *caeruleum* and *caerulum* is that we say *caerulum*, like *aurum*; *caeruleum* is from *caerulum*, as though [from] *argentum*.

174. The distinction between *imum* and *infimum* is that *imus* refers to position, *infimus* to rank.

175. The distinction between *cura* and *diligentia* is that *cura* contains an anxiety that agitates, whereas *diligentia* is the management of affairs.

176. The distinction between *vires* and *virtutes* is that *vires* belong to the body, *virtutes* to the mind.

177. The distinction among *anima*, *animus*, *spiritus*, and *mens* is that the *anima* is what enables us to live; the *animus* is what governs us; the *spiritus* is what enables us to breathe; the *mens* is a quality that can refer thought toward good or evil.

178. The distinction between *grave* and *ponderosum* is that *grave* depends on the condition of the person carrying it, whereas *ponderosum* is heavy by nature.

[Note: [Col. 1328D]

Vat. 624: “The distinction between *ulcisci* and *vindicare* is …”]

179. The distinction between *ultor* and *vindex* is that we avenge an injury we have received, but take preventive action so that we do not receive one.

180. The distinction between *fallax* and *pellax* is that *fallax* means untrustworthy, whereas *pellax* refers to speech, from *appellare*, “to address,” that is, speaking for oneself.

[Note: [Col. 1328D]

The printed editions had *cum moles in caput*; I restored *mola*.]

181. The distinction between *immolare* and *mactare* is that *immolare* is said when meal is placed upon the head; *mactatum* is said when this has been done, as though it had been increased.

[Note: [Col. 1328D]

In the printed editions Ovid’s verse appeared as *Victima dextra habet*. Other scribes had omitted the remainder. The passage is *Fasti* I, 335.]

182. The distinction between *hostia* and *victima* is that a sacrifice is called a *hostia* when a commander sets out against the enemy; it is called a *victima* when he wins, as Ovid says in the *Fasti*:

> “The sacrificial animal that fell by a victorious right hand is called a *victima*.
>
> From conquered enemies the *hostia* receives its name.”

183. The distinction between *eruere* and *diruere* is that hiding places are *eruta*, “dug out,” while elevated structures are *diruta*, “demolished.”

438

184. The distinction between *nequidquam* and *nequaquam* is that *nequidquam* means “in vain,” whereas *nequaquam* means “not at all.”

185. The distinction between *iter* and *itiner* is that *iter* is the road by which we go, while *itiner* is called a pathless or trackless place.

186. The distinction between *proprium* and *propius* is that *proprium* belongs to ownership, whereas *propius* refers to place.

187. The distinction between *vereor* and *revereor* is that *vereor* refers to fear, while *revereor* refers to the resulting effect.

[Col. 1329A]

[Note: [Col. 1329D]

Vat. 624: “They can be referred to the singular.”]

188. The distinction between *liberi* and *filii* is that *filii* is masculine in gender, while *liberi* is used of either sex; and that *filii* can be used in the singular. For no one who has a son says, “I have one *liberum*.” Also, *filii* is understood indiscriminately of every condition, both freeborn and enslaved; *liberi* is used only of the freeborn.

189. The distinction between *dulce* and *suave* is that *dulce* can mean the same as *suave*, but *suave* does not necessarily mean *dulce*. We call honey *dulce*, and vinegar *suave*, although it is not sweet.

[Note: [Col. 1329D]

I do not know what author is responsible for what is said here about *avellum*. I would gladly read: “a civil *duellum*,” and so forth. Festus says: “*Duellum*, that is, war, in which two sides fight for victory.”]

190. The distinction between *bellum* and *avellum* is that war among foreign peoples is called *bellum*, while war among citizens is called *avellum*, because the people are pulled apart into two sides.

191. The distinction between *exemplum* and *similitudo* is that an *exemplum* is a historical account, while a *similitudo* is a confirmation.

192. The distinction between *divinatio* and *divinitas* is that *divinitas* refers to the power of the deity, whereas *divinatio* makes people foreknowing of future things.

[Col. 1329B]

193. The distinction between *vis* and *virtus* is that *virtus* is encouragement, while *vis* is injury or violence.

194. The distinction between *rogus* and *pyra* is that a *rogus* is prepared for the dead, a *pyra* for sacrifices.

[Note: [Col. 1329D]

The printed editions had *missibilia*, for *missilia*.]

195. The distinction among *arma*, *armamenta*, and *tela* is that *arma* are the things by which our bodies are protected in war; *armamenta* belong to ships; *tela* are missiles, such as javelins.

196. The distinction between *vir* and *masculus* is that *vir* is understood as a species, *masculus* as a genus; and that *vir* is understood in three ways: by nature, by virtue, and by marriage. *Masculus* is also distinguished from a human being, as in the case of animals.

197. The distinction among *profugus*, *exsul*, *relegatus*, and *transfuga* is that a *profugus* has apparently left voluntarily; an *exsul* is expelled after condemnation; a *relegatus* is sent away for a time; a *transfuga* is one who passes over to the enemy.

198. The distinction between *altus* and *excelsus* is that *altus* can mean either raised toward the upper region or lowered toward the depths, whereas *excelsus* refers only to what is above.

199. The distinction between *vis* and *vires* is that *vis* consists in force and injury, while *vires* refer to goodness and bodily strength. Thus *vis* produces violence, while *vires* [produce] something defective.

200. The distinction between *saevus* and *crudelis* is that *saevus* concerns words, while *crudelis* is shown by bloodshed.

201. The distinction among *bellum*, *acies*, *proelium*, and *pugna* is that the entire conflict is called *bellum*; the battle line is arranged (*acies ordinatur*); the engagement is joined (*proelium committitur*); the fight is conducted (*pugna geritur*). Moreover, *acies* applies both to iron and to the eyes.

262. The distinction between *passum* and *expertum* is that we suffer willingly, but undergo or experience something under compulsion.

203. The distinction between *genus* and *gens* is that *genus* applies both to human beings and to animals; *gens* refers to a gathering of many who descend from one head. Thus we say “the nation of the Gauls.”

204. The distinction among *terra*, *tellus*, and *humus* is that *terra* is the third part of the world; *Tellus* is a goddess; *humus* is called the place of burial, from *humare*, “to bury.”

205. The distinction between *moenia* and *aedificia* is that *moenia* are public works, while *aedificia* are private buildings.

206. The distinction between *omne* and *totum* is that *omne* consists in number, while *totum* refers to parts taken together.

207. The distinction among *ulcus*, *vulnus*, and *plaga* is that an ulcer (*ulcus*) emerges of itself, a wound (*vulnus*) is caused by iron, and a *plaga* may be a level blow. Thus an ulcer is a matter of lesser severity, a wound of greater severity; blows are also called *plagae*.

[Col. 1330A]

208. The distinction between *sic* and *ita* is that *sic* points to examples, while *ita* refers to reasoning.

209. The distinction between *duo* and *ambo* is that *duo* counts, while *ambo* gathers together.

210. The distinction between *paret* and *apparet* is that something *paret* in obedience to a command, while it *apparet* to those who see it.

211. The distinction between *pullus* and *niger* is that *pullus* is the opposite of white, while *niger* is understood in terms of color.

[Note: [Col. 1329D]

Vat. 624: “The distinction between *arbitrari* and *aestimare* is that *aestimare* belongs to our inward judgment, while *arbitrari* is to express the judgment of the mind. Elsewhere, as here, it looks toward the form of a hidden matter.”]

212. The distinction among *putat*, *aestimat*, *opinatur*, *arbitratur*, and *suspicatur* is that one *putat* who doubts; one *aestimat* who states an assessment of what has happened; one *opinatur* who trusts either his own opinion or someone else’s; one *arbitratur* who brings a doubtful matter to an end; one *suspicatur* who perceives the form of something hidden.

213. The distinction between *prohibere* and *inhibere* is that *prohibere* means not to allow something by right; *inhibere* is said of force. What we *inhibemus* by right, we *prohibemus* by command.

[Col. 1330B]

[Note: [Col. 1330D]

Vat. 624: “without a solid body it presents itself to us … it is set before the ears, a portent … it is produced in bodies … a comet, a star, and at night …”]

214. The distinction among *ostentum*, *prodigium*, and *monstrum* is that an *ostentum* is something new that shows itself without a solid body, both to the eyes and to the ears. A *prodigium*, however, is something perceived in solid bodies, such as a comet in the sky, or a star, or light at night and darkness by day. A *monstrum* is something recognized as departing from nature, such as a serpent with feet or with four wings.

[Note: [Col. 1330D]

The printed editions had *Eticuere*, which I changed to *Reticuere*, since it corresponds to *reticuit* below. Vat. 624: “The distinction among *conticuit*, *obticuit*, and *reticuit* is … he provided silence of voice everywhere … left no hope of speaking.”]

215. The distinction among *conticuere*, *ob­ticuere*, and *reticuere* is that one who *conticuit* produced silence everywhere, as the ancients say (Virgil, *Aeneid* III.718):

> “At last he fell silent, and, having brought this to an end, rested.”

One who *obticuit* left no hope of speaking; one who *reticuit* brought his replies to an end in silence.

[Note: [Col. 1330D]

Vat. 624: “A *sepulcrum* is a place in which bodies are burned; it is called *sepulcrum* from *sepelire*, ‘to bury.’”]

216. The distinction between *sepulcrum*, *tumulus*, *monumentum*, and *bustum* is this: a *sepulcrum* is a place in which bodies are buried, and is so called from *sepelire*, “to bury”; a *tumulus* is what covers ashes; a *monumentum* is what surrounds a tomb, its name deriving from fortifications; a *bustum* is the place in which bones are kept, as it were “well burned” (*bene ustum*).

217. The distinction between *astra* and *sidera* is this: *astra* can exist without a *sidus*, and the stars (*astra*) are fixed in the sky; the constellations (*sidera*) move.

218. The distinction between *deripere* and *diripere* is this: we use *deripere* when we snatch something from an upper place down to a lower one; we use *diripere* when we tear it apart and draw it into different directions.

219. The distinction between *causa* and *ratio* is this: *causa* has many species, *ratio* very few; and when something is brought about by reasoning, the cause is sought.

220. The distinction between *Italus* and *Italicus* is this: *Italus* refers to a man, *Italicus* to an arch; thus the former relates to a person, the latter to a thing.

221. The distinction between *devius*, *invius*, *avius*, and *pervius* is this: *invius* is a secluded place without a road; *devius* is a deserted place; *avius* is outside the road; *pervius* is a place through which one travels.

222. The distinction between *dexteram* and *dextram* is this: some, without justification, thought that the letter *e* was superfluous, following the ancient usage found in *reprendo* and *reprehendo*, and in *vemens* and *vehemens*; thus one says both *dextram manum* (“the right hand”) and *dexteram prosperam partem* (“the favorable right-hand side”).

223. The distinction between *leges* and *jura* is this: *jura* were discovered through honorable custom, whereas *leges* arise from what we establish among ourselves as things to be approved; *jura* are so called from the justice of each individual, *leges* because they are read.

[Col. 1331A]

224. The distinction between *invidus* and *invidiosus* is this: someone is *invidus* because he envies another; someone is *invidiosus* when he is envied.

225. The distinction between *protinus* and *protenus* is this: *protinus* means “immediately,” “at once,” and is an adverb of time; *protenus* is as though derived from *porro-tenus*, “as far onward.”

226. The distinction between *demitto* and *dimitto* is this: *demittit* is used of one who sends something down from a height; *dimitto* of one who sends something in many directions.

227. The distinction between *altaria* and *arae* is this: altars (*altaria*) are set up for God, while *arae* may also be set up for the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1331C]

228. Vaticanus 624: “A half cannot signify portions unless the complete whole is supplied. *Dimidiatum* is … as though a whole; without *hora* there cannot be a *dimidia* … but *dimidiatum*, or a half-portion, is something diminished.”]

228. The distinction between *dimidium* and *dimidiatum* is this: *dimidium* can signify a part only if one supplies the complete noun; [the transmitted text then reads uncertainly: “without *dimidiatum*, it is,”] as when one says “a full hour”: *hora* is the complete noun, as though it were the whole, and without *hora* there cannot be a *dimidia*. Therefore one says either *dimidiata hora* (“a half-hour”) or *dimidium horae* (“half of an hour”); *dimidium* is the half, whereas *dimidiatum* is a diminished portion.

229. The distinction between *fiducia* and *confidentia* is this: *confidentia* involves the fault of rashness; one has *fiducia* if one lives with honorable steadfastness.

230. The distinction between *legio* and *dilectus* is this: *legio* is so called because brave men useful for military service are selected (*leguntur*); *dilecta* refers to those whom we love most dearly, such as children or a father’s relatives.

231. The distinction between *assidue* and *quotidie* is this: *assidue* expresses diligence, whereas *quotidie* expresses perseverance.

232. The distinction between *moeret* and *meretur* is this: one who *moeret* is sad; one who *meretur* expects a return equal to his benefit, according to another’s judgment.

233. The distinction between *plenitudo* and *plenitas* is this: *plenitudo* refers to a body, *plenitas* to a thing; thus we speak of the *plenitudo* of obese people, but of the *plenitas* of any varied thing.

234. The distinction between *precor* and *deprecor* is this: we *precamur* God, but we *deprecamur* human beings.

235. The distinction between *fortuna* and *felicitas* is this: *fortuna* does not exist, whereas *felicitas* is a person’s wealth.

236. The distinction between *tueor* and *tuor* is this: *tuor* means “I guard”; *tueor*, “I see.”

237. The distinction between *ludibrium* and *ludicrum* is this: *ludibrium* involves an insult to another; *ludicrum* is something in which we take delight without injury to anyone.

[Note: [Col. 1331C]

238. For this distinction, see no. 78.]

238. The distinction between *stilla* and *gutta* is this: a *gutta* is a drop of rain; a *stilla* is a drop from a bucket or of vinegar.

239. The distinction between *fidus* and *fidelis* is this: *fidus* may also mean “a friend”; *fidelis* means “a servant.”

[Col. 1332A] [Note: [Col. 1331C]

240. Vaticanus 624: “Between *cognoscere* and *agnoscere*.”]

240. The distinction between *cognoscimus* and *agnoscimus* is this: we *agnoscimus* people whom we have known; we *cognoscimus* things we have never seen.

241. The distinction between *clypeum* and *clupeum* is this: *clypeum* is a shield; *clupeum* is the object on which images are placed.

242. The distinction between *germanus* and *frater* is this: a *germanus* is a true brother by both father and mother; a *frater* may be from a different father or mother.

243. The distinction between *morsare* and *mergere* is this: *mersare* means to immerse repeatedly, *mergere* to immerse once.

244. The distinction between *agere causam* and *dicere* is this: the advocate (*patronus*) conducts the case, the defendant (*reus*) speaks.

245. The distinction between *eminus* and *cominus* is this: *eminus* means “from a distance,” *cominus* “on foot, at close quarters.”

246. The distinction between *capere* and *decipere* is this: we *capimus* those who deserve it, but we *decipimus* the innocent; alternatively, we *capimus* by skill, but *decipimus* by treachery.

247. The distinction between *consilium* and *sententia* is this: *consilium* is a thought; *sententia* is the pronouncement of a decision.

[Note: [Col. 1331C]

248. Perhaps: “Thus Fortune willed.”]

248. The distinction between *fors* and *fortuna* is this: *fors* is chance, *fortuna* is something granted; as someone said, “Thus chance prevailed,” as though [he had said], “death.”

249. The distinction between *voluntas* and *voluptas* is this: *voluntas* belongs to the mind, *voluptas* to the body.

250. The distinction between *interea* and *interdum* is this: *interdum* is an adverb of time; *interea* indicates the cause of a matter.

251. The distinction between *initium* and *principium* is this: the *principium* of any entire work is one, as the work’s first chapter; *initium* is understood and used more frequently, as often as either the person changes, as though one passes inward into another matter. Thus *principium* occurs once, *initium* more often.

*Principium*: “Arms and the man I sing.”

*Initium*: “Muse, recount to me the causes.”

Nevertheless, beginnings are found that by their nature lack the character of *principia* but have the appearance of *initia*, such as:

“But the queen, long since wounded by grievous care.”

And:

“Thus he spoke weeping, and gave the reins to the fleet.”

252. The distinction between *meditari* and *velitari* is this: we meditate in the mind, but engage in mock combat with the body.

[Note: [Col. 1331C]

253. This distinction was expressed more briefly at no. 58. The first two verses cited occur at the beginning of Book I of the *Aeneid*; the third at the beginning of Book IV; the fifth at the beginning of Book VI. Vaticanus 624 [Col. 1332C] inserts several other distinctions, such as:

“The distinction between *armenta* and *greges* is this: *armenta* are herds of horses and cattle, whereas *greges* are herds of goats and sheep.

“The distinction between *laevis* and *levis* is this: *levis* is used in verbal forms [perhaps ‘beardless’]; *laeve* refers to anything free from hairs and roughness.

“The distinction between *pronomina* and *articuli* is this: those are considered *pronomina* which, when standing alone, fulfill the function of a noun, such as *quis*, *iste*, *ipse*, and *ille*. *Articuli*, however, are joined to pronouns or participles, such as *hic*, *huius*, *huic*, *hunc*, and *ab hoc*.”]

253. The distinction between human beings and beasts is this: beasts serve the belly, human beings reason.

[Col. 1331]

## APPENDIX XXIV

### BOOK OF GLOSSES

Collected from various glossaries circulated under the name of Isidore.

[Col. 1331]

## A

[1] [Note: [Col. 1331] 1. In the Isidorian materials, chapters 57 and following have said more than enough about this glossary. I present it here in a more corrected form, using Semler’s manuscripts, other printed editions, and some of my own observations, occasionally adding conjectures. For *spontaneus*, perhaps read *sponte*, “voluntarily,” “without force,” or “of one’s own accord.”]

*A se*, spontaneous.

[Note: [Col. 1331] 2. Immediately below, no. 5, *abaso*. Spanish *abajo*, Italian *abasso*, meaning “lower.” In the printed editions: *infima domus*.]

*Abaia*, the lowest house.

[Note: [Col. 1332] 3. Medieval lexicographers call *abadir* the stone which Saturn swallowed instead of Jupiter. See Papias, the *Breviloquum*, Solomon of Constance, and others.]

*Abadir*, a stone.

[Note: [Col. 1332] 4. Others read *Aschemon* or *abarcenon*, as though from *arceo* (“I restrain”) or *aparthenon*, from Greek. Still worse, others read *anaclaenam*, “a bucket,” or *abastenum*, “foreign to art.”]

*Abastenum*, dishonorable.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1332] 5. *Infirma*; alternatively *infima*, as at no. 2.]

*Abaso*, a weak house, which [Col. 1333] is without a base.

*Abgrego*, I separate.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 7. *Ablutes*; perhaps better *alluvies*. Instead of *coenosa*, some less suitably read *arenosa*, “sandy.”]

*Ablutes*, a washing-place, muddy locations.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 8. Perhaps *abhorrens* (“abhorrent”) or *abnormis* (“abnormal”).]

*Aborris*, scandalous.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 9. Perhaps *aurigo*, *aurugo*, *obryzum*, or *aurigeum*.]

*Abrigeum*, the splendor of gold.

[10] *Abrogans*, humble.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 11. Semler wishes to read *ablegat, abrogat*, namely, “he removes, he repeals a law.”]

*Abrogat*, he sends away, he repeals.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 12. *Absternit*; hence *sternaces*, and perhaps *sternutare*, “to sneeze,” unless one reads *aspernit* (“he rejects”) or *absterret* (“he frightens away”).]

*Absternit*, he casts away, he repels.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 13. In the Pithoean glosses, *arrepta*, a type of ship, *acatus*. *Acatium* is a ship’s sail. Cerda reads *accepta*, a kind of bird. Semler takes *accepta* as neuter, but shortly afterward preferred Cerda’s conjecture.]

*Accepta*, a kind of ship.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 14. Instead of *acclibanum*, *acclivum* or *acclivatum* seems to be the reading.]

*Acclibanum*, sloping.

[15] [Note: [Col. 1333] 15. *Accuculia*; perhaps *agagula*, “a procurer,” or *aquacula*, “a water-carrier slave of a prostitute,” so called from frequently fetching water. Others read *agagulo*, *agagula*, *accucula*, *acculia*, or *acacula*. See nos. 24 and 48.]

*Accuculia*, shrewd, skillful.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 16. *Acation*. The printed editions have *acatheon*; Janson has *archistion*.]

*Achateon*, the largest sail, in the middle of a ship.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 17. Read *axilla*, “wing.” Others read *axia*, “wing.”]

*Acia*, a wing.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 18. *Acieres*, from *acies*. The Spanish call steel *acero*.]

*Acieres*, a kind of axe.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 19. *Acinari* and *aginari* are the same word. *Aginator* means “merchant,” *aginare* “to trade,” especially in small matters.]

*Acinari*, to quibble, to linger over a small matter.

[20] [Note: [Col. 1333] 20. Perhaps *acroama*, “a performance,” from *auditio*, or *acroamatis*, “of a performance,” to indicate the genitive *acroamatis*.]

*Acroamata*, the sound of lyres or flutes.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 21. *Aculus*. Graevius thinks it derives from *caliculi*; Semler from a broken form of *vernaculus*; others read *aulicus*, *auc(u)lus*, *acubus*, or *acolathus*.]

444 *Aculus*, a household official of the royal palace.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 22. Some conjecture *acus calamistra*, “a razor,” or *calamistra casonium*; others *calamistrum*. By another name, *acus* is *acula* or *acucula*.]

*Acus*, a curling-iron case.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 23. “Lightly.” The printed editions have *leniter*. See Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 2, no. 15.]

*Acrozymus*, bread lightly fermented.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 24. See above, no. 15.]

*Acucula*, *aculus*, skillful, *agagula*.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1333] 25. *Nata*; the Pithoean reading is *natu*.]

*Adasia*, a large sheep, born [Col. 1333].

*Adfiliatio*, almost an imitation of nature.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 27. Others prefer *adfutabulum*, *acetabulum*, or *adsutabulum*. See *Futis*, no. 760.]

*Adfrutabulum*, a small vessel.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 28. Perhaps *adligula*.]

*Adlicula*, a kind of garment.

*Adluviis*, in muddy places.

[30] *Adoptarius*, a boy born through adoption.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 31. *Adorea*; Reinesius conjectures *adora*, from *ador*. Graevius reads *liba* for *libamenta*; Semler, *adorea*, “sacrifices,” “offerings.”]

*Adorea*, offerings.

*Adpectoret*, he applies to the breast.

*Adpetulantia*, with boldness.

*Adplanat*, he levels, smooths, makes equal.

[35] [Note: [Col. 1333] 35. *Adrummare*, according to Festus, means “to spread rumors,” perhaps from *rumen*. *Arumare* is “rumor,” just as *clamor* comes from *clamare*.]

*Adrummavit*, he brought rumors.

*Adsecla*, a household servant, a groom.

*Adseclae*, household attendants, followers, procurers.

[Note: [Col. 1333] 38. Some conjecture *adseda*; others *adsidella quadrijugis*, namely, “a table”; still others *adsella*, from *adsellare*, that is, “to evacuate the bowels.”]

*Adsella*, a seat for a four-horse carriage.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 39. It seems that *adsecula* should be read; that is, *adsecula*, meaning *adsecla*.]

*Adsuetula*, a groom.

[40] [Note: [Col. 1334] 40. In the Pithoean glosses, *adtaminat*, “he pollutes, uses.” Semler thinks *adtamen*, or *attamen*, derives from *tangere*, “to touch.”]

*Adtaminat*, he uses.

*Aegret*, it becomes sour.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 42. Reinesius wishes to read *aedemius*.]

*Aemidus*, swollen, inflated.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 43. “Species,” because the sense is shaded by means of images.]

*Aenigma*, a figure, or type, or form.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 44. Read *aequilanium* or *aequilibrium*.]

*Aequilatium*, equalization.

[45] [Note: [Col. 1334] 45. Semler reads *aphrodita, aphroditus*, from *hermaphrodita, hermaphroditus*.]

*Affostrata*, income.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 46. Read *agaso*, as below, no. 50.]

*Agabo*, one who conducts business.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 47. Stewart, *Analecta*, Book I, chapter 8, derives it from the German language, *a*, “one,” and *gageler*, “a mountebank.” See no. 15.]

*Agagola*, a procurer, a pantomime performer.

[Col. 1334]

*Agagula*, a procurer.

*Agaron*, an official servant.

[50] *Agaso*, an official servant.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 51. Better *aginantes*, from *agina*, or from the opening by which a balance turns. Compare Ducange and above, no. 19.]

*Agginantes*, explainers.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 52. Rutgers reads *anginae*; Semler, *aciae*, “little swords.” See no. 22.]

*Agiae*, glands.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 53. Better *agoniae*, instead of *agonei*.]

*Agonei*, victims.

*Agonia*, a sacrificial victim.

[55] [Note: [Col. 1334] 55. The *Breviloquum*: “agrarian, rustic, one who cultivates a field.”]

*Agrarius*, agrarian.

*Alacrimonia*, joy.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 57. Graevius: hazelnuts, Praenestine nuts. Cerda defends “Alban nuts.” Macrobius favors Graevius.]

*Albanae*, in the plural, ancient nuts.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 58. *Albuna*, from *albicare*, “to become white”; *Matuta*, from *mane*, “morning.”]

*Albuna*, Mother Matuta.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 59. According to Festus, *alebria* are things that nourish well.]

*Alebra*, good things by which we are nourished.

[60] [Note: [Col. 1334] 60. Read *ablegmina* or *absegmina*, from *secare*, “to cut.”]

*Alegmina*, portions of the entrails, which are called *prosegmina*.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 61. Graevius: “foreign-born, born outside”; Semler: *alica*, “born from the earth,” from Festus.]

*Alia*, carried across.

*Alibre*, nourishment.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 63. Janson: *allustrare*, from *lustrando*; Graevius: *ballistrare*, “to moisten,” with the *b* having dropped out.]

*Alistrare*, to moisten.

*Allex*, the big toe of the foot.

[65] [Note: [Col. 1334] 65. The printed editions have *alliger*; Barthius, *gallier*, “a cock,” from the German idiom. *Aliger*, “a cock,” should be read, from Sedulius, Book V, verse 8.]

*Alliger*, a cock.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 66. The scholiast on Horace, *Epodes*, Book [sic], Ode 16: “The Allobroges are red-haired Gauls.”]

*Allobroga*, a red-haired Gaul.

*Allutes* and *Allutia*, muddy places.

*Alluvium*, the collapse of banks through water.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 69. Among the Britons and ancient Gauls, the name of the alder is *vernum* or *verna*.]

*Alnum*, wood, that is, alder.

[70] [Note: [Col. 1334] 70. *Stricturae*; perhaps *trichorreae*, that is, “a flow of hair.”]

*Alopecia*, an ailment of hair loss.

[Col. 1335] [Note: [Col. 1334] 71. More correctly, *alapus*.]

*Alopus*, one who receives slaps for payment.

*Altar*, an altar.

[Note: [Col. 1334] 73. Prudentius, in the hymn to Saint Eulalia, p. 675 of my edition.]

*Altar*; Prudentius: “An altar, and what has been placed upon it.”

[Note: [Col. 1334] 74. *Altilis*. The word was also known to the ancient Latins.]

*Altilis*, a paste, from *alere*, “to nourish.”

[75] [Note: [Col. 1335] 75. In other glosses, *amanet*, “he remains outside.”]

*Amansit*, he waited.

[Note: [Col. 1335] 76. Barthius: *amesco*, “I desire to be loved.”]

*Amasco*, I desire to love.

[Note: [Col. 1335] 77. See the commentary on Prudentius, p. 524.]

*Ambro*, a devourer, consumer of inheritances, bankrupt, luxurious, extravagant.

[Note: [Col. 1335] 88. It is also written *anciromagus*, *aniliromacus*, *angromagus*, *anguiromacus*, and *anguiromagus*. In *Etymologies*, Book XIX, chapter 1, no. 16, it seems to be derived from *ago*, “I drive.”]

*Ansile*, the inner boss of a shield, which is held from within.
