Corugio: a boy; it is a game in which proverbs are recited. Elsewhere, therefore: *coragium* is a part of games in which proverbs are recited.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 481. Better *vibrans*; or “winter vibrates,” “flashes.”]

Coruscatio: winter flashes.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 482. Below, *cracerat*.]

Cracat: *cracerat*.

Cracentes: slender.

Cracerat: *cracat*.

[485]

Crea: dung, filth; hence we say *excreare*, “to expel filth.”

Creagras: three-pronged forks.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 487. Festus: “*Porcae* are called the rare furrows, for the more closely spaced furrows are called *limi*.” Hence Semler thinks the gloss *crebro*, etc., was fabricated.]

Crebro: *nis*, a ridge of earth standing out between two furrows.

Creditaria: chambermaid.

Creditarius.

[490]

Crematum: *collybum*, a small coin.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 491. *Cremutium*. *Crematium* or *crematum*. Martinius reads *hypocaustum* instead of *holocaustum*.]

Cremutium: burnt offering.

Creporem ferri: the sound of a chain.

Crepundiis: beginnings.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 494. Above, *clitellae*.]

Cretellae: *clitellae* (small baskets).

[495]

Cristatus: honorable, proper.

Cruminat: ruminates.

458

Crustaria: a shop named from vessels with a crusted surface.

Cubio: male.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 499. *Cucier*. Replace it with *curio*.]

Cucier: a Pontic priest.

[500]

Cutina: a privy, a place of retreat.

Culit: struck violently.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 502. See the commentary on Prudentius, p. 1016, and Lebrun’s note on Lactantius, book III, chapter 4.]

Culleus: a tunic made of rush in the form of a purse, which the people coated with pitch and bitumen. Parricides were shut inside it together with a monkey, a snake, and a rooster; it was sewn up and thrown into the sea. As the animals struggled with one another, the man was subjected to greater punishments.

Culpa piabunt: they will atone for sin.

[Note: [Col. 1345] 504. *Cuma*. Read *corna*.]

Cuma: wild fruits.

[505]

[Note: [Col. 1346] 505. Others read *camerus*, “curved”; others *comis*, “urbane.” Semler, from Festus, reads *cumerus*, “winnowing basket.”]

Cumerus: urbane.

Cuppes: fastidious, greedy.

Curagulus, that is, curious; *curaculus*, curious.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 508. See below, *oppilago*, *curcilla*.]

Curcilla: obstruction.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 509. *Curio*; rather, *cruor*.]

Curio: blood.

[510]

[Note: [Col. 1346] 510. In the excerpts, *coruscus*. Cerda reads *grossus*, or *crassus*. Others read *ceruses*. Others, from Festus, *cerus*, “hand.”]

Curustus: great.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 511. *Cusire*. The Italians use this form today. Others would prefer *cusuere* or *cossuere*, instead of *cusire*.]

Cusire: to sew.

## D

[Note: [Col. 1346] 512. Graevius reads *dalmatica*.]

Dalmata: a white priestly garment with purple bands.

Dalum: the smallest sail of a ship.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 514. Graevius reads *damnatitius, dedititius*, “surrendered, assigned to a moneylender.” *Datitius* is not Latin, etc. Semler reads *damus*—[correct to *danista*]—“moneylender.” *Datitius*: surrendered.]

Damnatitius: surrendered, assigned.

[515]

[Note: [Col. 1346] 515. Graevius reads *damnatitius, dedititius*, “surrendered, assigned to a moneylender.” *Datitius* is not Latin, etc. Semler reads *damus*—[correct to *danista*]—“moneylender.” *Datitius*: surrendered.]

Damus: moneylender.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 516. Graevius reads *damnatitius, dedititius*, “surrendered, assigned to a moneylender.” *Datitius* is not Latin, etc. Semler reads *damus*—[correct to *danista*]—“moneylender.” *Datitius*: surrendered.]

Datitius is not Latin, but *dedititius* is: if a barbarian surrenders himself to the Romans, he is *dedititius*.

Dativa: gifts.

Decalco: I whiten.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 519. Better *dicentarius*, from *dicere*, “to speak.”]

Decentarius: prompt, ready, ingenious.

[520]

[Note: [Col. 1346] 520. Restore *deglubere*, “to strip,” *decoriare*, “to flay.”]

Decluere: to be adorned.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 521. Graevius reads *distentio*, “extension, occupation.” Semler reads *decurio*, “officer.”]

Decardo: occupation.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 522. Becmann thinks *delticum litteratum*, “a learned doctor,” comes from the Hebrew *daleth*, “tablet, page of a book.”]

Delticus: a learned doctor.

Demundinat: makes known to everyone.

Depalata: made manifest.

[525]

Depanare: to tear apart.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 526. *Deplicare*. With the opposite meaning, “to apply.” Semler thinks the interpretation is missing after *deplicare*, and that another gloss begins with *decedere, devitare*, “to withdraw, to avoid,” or “to depart from life.” Thus *devitare, decedere* would be better.]

Deplicare: to withdraw, to avoid.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 527. Festus: “one who is prevented from becoming mature by bristles.” Breviloquus: as if “downward from the bristles.”]

Depubis: a suckling pig q . . . from the bristles.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 528. *Derarat*. Semler thinks this was placed wherever a rare word was found; or read *derorat*, “dew falls, it grows cold.”]

[459]

Derarat: is numb, is cold.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 529. Read *piger* instead of *impiger*; or *deassiduus*, “active, diligent, tireless.”]

Desiduus: lazy, tireless.

530

[Note: [Col. 1346] 530. *Subsolano*. More correctly, *subsolanus*.]

Desolanus: eastern.

[Note: [Col. 1346] 531. I would prefer *destitutio*, “desertion.” Others read *destitudo*, “destruction.”]

Destitudo: destruction.

[Col. 1347]

[Note: [Col. 1347] 532. Below, *distrigare*. Both derive from *extrico*.]

Destricare: to finish.

Detectus: the matter is now being handled; that is, the testing of recruits is taking place.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 534. *Devibiae* must be changed to *decubiae*. What follows *vigiliae* belongs elsewhere.]

Devibiae: watches; commonly, a woman’s straw.

[535]

Devirginat: corrupts.

Devoratores: gluttons.

Devoto: I accuse.

Dextralia: armlets.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 539. Others read *dialabis*, *dialepsis*, or *dialabe*. Semler reads *didia*, “twice.” *Diathecae*: imperial decrees.]

Dialapis: an imperial decree.

[540]

Diale: daily, midday.

Ex diametro: a year taken not from the beginning of the zodiacal sign but from the middle.

Diaria: a day’s food.

Diaria: daily wages.

Diatim: from day to day.

[545]

Dictatorius: belonging to a dictator.

Didatim: separately.

Diditum: spread abroad, publicized.

Diennium: a period of two years.

Diescit: it becomes day.

[550]

Diet: now it becomes day.

Diffarreatio: dissolution between husband and wife.

Differentior: more eminent.

Diffitiscit: is dissolved.

Dilargus: one who gives much.

[555]

Dimus: two-year-old.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 556. *Dinidor*. From *nidor*, “odor,” and the Greek *dys*, “bad.”]

Dinidor: bad smell.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 557. Others read *duplomatarius*. *Diplomatarius* is understood as one who sells and fastens together folded parchment.]

Diplomatarius: one who duplicates.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 558. *Gubernatum*; others *duplicatum*; others *quaternatum*.]

Diplomum: steered.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 559. See the prolegomena to Prudentius, pp. 565ff.]

Diptycha: tablets that we carry.

[560]

[Note: [Col. 1347] 560. *Dique*; perhaps *deinque*.]

Dique: finally.

Diribere: to count out.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 562. Graevius reads *diribitorium*, a place in the Campus Martius. Semler retains *contubernii*, “of the military building where pay or other things were distributed to soldiers.”]

Diribitorium: a barracks.

Discipulati: instructed.

[Col. 1347]

Discussor: examiner.

[565]

[Note: [Col. 1347] 565. *Disdonat*, as “he distributes,” etc. Graevius reads *dissonat*, “sounds differently.”]

Disdonat: gives different gifts.

Disgrex: separate.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 567. *Dispecatis*. From *pecus*. Printed editions read *dispeccatis*.]

Dispecatis: flayed.

Displatidus: morose.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 569. *Dona*, etc. Perhaps because one who strikes out the names of debtors entered on tablets seems to forgive the debt; or because when the name of discharged soldiers was struck out, something was given to them.]

Dispunctores: those who distribute gifts to soldiers.

[460]

[570]

[Note: [Col. 1347] 570. *Dona*, etc. Perhaps because one who strikes out the names of debtors entered on tablets seems to forgive the debt; or because when the name of discharged soldiers was struck out, something was given to them.]

Dispungere: to give.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 571. Semler says that two kinds of soldiers are noted, some *dissultores*, others *singulares*. *Dissultores* and *desultores* are the same.]

Dissultores: individual soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 572. See above, *decardo*.]

Distatio: occupation.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 573. *Distrigare*. Rather, *districare*. Above, *destricare*.]

Distrigare: to finish.

Divale: divine.

[575]

Diversiclinia: irregular forms.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 576. Others read *dimoverat*, “he had separated”; others *divomerat*, “he opens, plows,” namely, from *vomer*, “ploughshare.”]

Divomerat: he had opened.

Divus: an emperor who received the name of a god after death.

Doctitat: frequently teaches.

Dolumen: shrine.

[580]

[Note: [Col. 1347] 580. *Dorsennus*. From Horace, *Epistle* 17, where others read *Dossenus*.]

Dorsennus: a character of parasites.

Dosius, or Dosinus: a horse with ass-colored hair.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 582. Graevius reads *aramea*. See below, *framea*. Nevertheless, *framea* is missing under the letter F.]

Dramea: after *framearum*.

[Note: [Col. 1347] 583. Papias reads *draquili*. Semler: *dragmitae*, “enclosed pearls,” or *draconteae*, “envious hands.” A *dragma* is a fastening for gems.]

Draquiti: the hands of an envious person.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 584. Graevius understands the name of the emperor Drusus, from Drausus, whom he defeated. Semler prefers *durus*, “hard.”]

Drusus: enduring, rigid.

[585]

[Note: [Col. 1348] 585. *Femina*. Read *gemina*, although some think it refers to an adulterous woman.]

Dualis: a divided woman.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 586. *Duellio*. Perhaps *duellis*. Breviloquus: *duellio, duellionis*.]

Duellio: rebel.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 587. Restore *Dorica*, etc. From Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III.]

Durica castra: stations of ships.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 588. See *Etymologiae*, book VIII, chapter 11, at the end.]

Dusius: demon.

## E
[Note: [Col. 1348] 589. Perhaps “ruin.”]

**Eccitum**, danger.

[590] **Ecloga**, a part of a poem.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 591. Below, *egones*. Perhaps *aegones*, shepherds, rustics. From *pastores* someone may have made *sacerdotes*, whom Christians call “shepherds.”]

**Econes**, rustic priests.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 592. Others read *sedea*; others *edea*; others, better, *essedа*.]

**Eda**, a pack carriage.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 593. *Excludit*; others *excutit*.]

**Edentat**, it exposes the teeth.

**Edilitius**, a secretary who belongs to an aedile.

[Col. 1348] [595]

[Note: [Col. 1348] 595. Correct to *aedituus*.]

**Editius**, a custodian of a shrine.

**Eduli**, gluttons, those who gorge themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 597. *Effatui*. From *fatuus*. Instead of “without effect,” others read “or *effati*.”]

**Effatui**, empty talkers without effect.

**Efficabilis**, competent in everything.

**Effeminatorium**, a house of prostitutes.

[600]

[Note: [Col. 1348] 600. *Egeator*; rather *egetor*, from the Greek, not from the Aegean Sea. Perhaps the passage in *Etymologies*, Book XIX, chapter 2, no. 4, belongs here: “*Agea*, roads, etc.”]

**Egeator**, an encourager of a ship, from the Aegean Sea.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 601. Festus: “of the nymph Egeria,” etc. Reinesius reads *nixia*, instead of *noxia*. Barthius, col. 2048, notes that *egeriem* is called by Paulinus that which is discharged as superfluous from digested food.]

**Egeria**, harmful.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 602. Perhaps the interpretation has been lost. Semlerus thinks it is *egestio*, “needy,” from *egere*, or a corruption of *egestuosus*.]

**Egestio**, harmful.

461 **Egestuosus**, a beggar.

**Egones**, priests of rustics.

[605]

**Egrex**, distinguished, eminent.

**Egrotatitius**, one who is frequently ill.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 607. Graevius reads *elogiis*, “with eulogies, poems.” *Elogium* usually has a laudatory sense, though sometimes a bad one. Semlerus says it should properly be written *ellogium*.]

**Elegiis**, accusations, or evil poems.

**Elogium**, a narrative of one who gives an account, or an ordered list of accusations.

**Elogium**, some answer in which an explanation is given—as if someone were to say of a person, “I shall disinherit him.” “Why?” “Because he was insolent toward me.”

[610] **Elogium**, a text of evil statements, which they call a public accusation.

**Emacitas**, eagerness to buy.

**Emanceps**, a servant released from slavery.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 613. *Emedium*; others *epirhedium*; others *essedum*.]

**Emedium**, a vehicle.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 614. *Ementum*. From *eminiscor*.]

**Ementum**, an invention.

[615] **Eminiscitur**, he brings back to memory.

**Emissarius**, an executioner.

**Emissarius**, bloodthirsty.

[Note: [Col. 1348] 618. *Enica*; others *ethnica*, with the spiritual sense “adulterous”; others *meca*, instead of *moecha*.]

**Enica**, an adulteress, an adulterous woman.

**Enigma**, obscure speech.

[620]

[Note: [Col. 1348] 620. *Minus*. Graevius reads *minuive*. That is, something either enormous, or so large that nothing greater can exist, or so small that nothing smaller can exist.]

**Enormate**, to which nothing less can be added.

[Col. 1349]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 621. Read *aeneolum*, or *ahenum*. Compare *Etymologies*, Book XVI, chapter 20, no. 8: “This also is a boiler,” etc.]

**Enulum**, a boiler.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 622. Others *epibata*, in Latin “arriving from above.”]

**Ephebion**, a place where beardless boys are violated.

**Epibatae**, laymen.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 624. *Etymologies*, Book XIX, chapter 19, no. 7: “*Epigri*, etc.” Others read *epiuri*; others *epiri*.]

**Epigri**, pegs by which one piece of wood is fastened to another.

[625] **Epimenia**, gifts presented each month.

**Epulatitius**, one who devotes himself to banquets.

**Equotus**, a private person.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 628. Semlerus reads *evitatus*, “deprived of life.”]

**Ereptoria**, things to be taken away, or to be returned.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 629. *Talentum*; others *metallum*; others *tullianum*; others *latomium*. Instead of *sub*, perhaps *seu*.]

**Ergastulum**, a prison, or a place where condemned men cut marble or perform some other labor—what in Latin is called *talentum*—under private custody, where there is no darkness.

[630]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 630. *Ergat*; others *errat*; others *gyrat*; others *aerat*, “surrounds,” that is, from *aes*, “bronze.”]

**Ergat**, it goes around.

**Erranei**, wandering.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 632. “Prophecy”; perhaps “hallucination.” Or “frenzy,” instead of “error.”]

**Error**, prophecy.

**Erugat**, he makes level.

**Eruli**, masters.

[635]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 635. Restore *esculentus*, instead of *escit lentus*, and add, if desired, “fat.”]

**Escit**, sluggish.

**Esculentia**, fatness.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 637. Perhaps *ethica*, or *edica*, instead of *idica*, from the Greek.]

**Etica**, property.

**Eticon**, one’s own property.

**Evadatur**, he demands, insists upon.

[640]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 640. Semlerus conjectures *exudo*, “I oil,” or *evaporo*, “I oil.”]

**Eubo**, I oil.

462 **Eviscerat**, he eats out the entrails.

**Evitaneus**, one who lasts through the ages.

**Exadituat**, he excludes from shrines.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 644. Replace with *hexapla*, “sixfold,” or *secupla*, “tenfold.”]

**Exapla**, examples.

[645]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 645. Printed editions have *excoliatus*.]

**Excastratus**, stripped of the skin.

**Excavet**, he takes precautions.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 647. *Excellare* and *excilare*, as if “to leave a cell and a monastery.”]

**Excellare**, to be with one’s wife.

**Exceptoria**, a cistern.

**Excilare**, to be with one’s wife in freedom.

[650] **Excipulum**, a hunting spear.

[Col. 1349]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 651. “To be judged”; perhaps “to be stripped.”]

**Exdorsuandum**, to be judged.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 652. *Etymologies*, Book X, no. 83: *exornatus*, “very adorned.” *Enim* is used instead of *valde*, “very.” Hence *exenim* was fabricated.]

**Exenim**, very.

**Exfretat**, he sails.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 654. *Exibus*; others *axungia*; others *sebum*.]

**Exibus**, fatness.

[655]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 655. Cerda reads *manus*, “hand,” instead of *marinus*. Semlerus reads *exsilia*, “wanderings of the sea,” from Virgil, *Aeneid* III, beginning: “Diverse exiles.”]

**Exilta**, a maritime wanderer.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 656. Some think *exeneta* was formed from *proxeneta*, and from this the corrupted form *eximequi*.]

**Eximequi**, brokers.

**Eximietas**, sublimity.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 658. The word *rare* should be deleted, having arisen from *are* repeated: *exippito*, *as*, *are*. The etymology is uncertain.]

**Exippitare**, to yawn repeatedly.

**Exminutuare**, to make poor.

[660] **Exundat**, it flows back.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 661. “A song,” etc.; evidently at the end of a comedy.]

**Exodium**, a comic and buffoonish song in the theaters.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 662. Read *enormis*, or *exnormis*.]

**Exornis**, monstrous.

[Note: [Col. 1349] 663. “To drive away”; perhaps *alapare*, “to strike with slaps.”]

**Expalmare**, to drive away.

**Exparta**, empty after giving birth.

[665]

[Note: [Col. 1349] 665. This appears to be a repetition of the preceding corrupted gloss: *exparta*, “empty after giving birth,” “having given birth.” Graevius reads *expatata*, “open places.”]

**Expartoa**, open water.

[Col. 1350]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 666. *Experti*; rather *expertes*.]

**Experti**, outsiders, outside the sphere of knowledge.

**Expilatores**, stealers of another’s inheritance.

**Expotata**, drained.

**Exprodita**, excluded.

[670] **Expudoratus**, shameless.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 671. Semlerus leaves *expuncta* without an interpretation. Then follows a new gloss: “the entrails, the fibers of the chest.”]

**Expuncta**, the fibers of the chest.

**Exsumptuavit**, he impoverished.

**Extensio**, a region.

**Externavit**, he made foreign.

[675]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 675. Others read *extrarius*, “those who are outside”; others *extraculis*, as immediately below *extraculas*.]

**Extestinum**, foreign.

**Extispices**, haruspices.

**Extracautis**, turned outward.

**Extraculas**, turned outward.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 679. *Extromis*; rather *extrimus*.]

**Extromis**, outermost.

[680] **Extruncis**, a tree cut off at the trunk.

**Exulto**, I drive away, avoid.

**Exundantibus**, flowing back.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 683. *Prorogat*; perhaps *irrigat*, “irrigates.”]

**Exundat**, he prolongs.

# F

**Fabarii**, singers.

[Col. 1350] [685]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 685. Isidore, *On Offices*, Book II, chapter 12: “The ancients,” etc.]

**Fabarius**, a singer.

**Fabulo**, composing stories.

**Fabulones**, inventors of stories.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 688. “Like a sword.” Others read “like a bearer”; others “a man who carries,” or “a bearer.” *Phalangae*, *palangae*, and hence *falangae*—Spanish *palancas*, Italian *stanghe*—are poles by which heavy loads are carried by bearers. Semlerus wanted *falcarius*, as in the following entry.]

463 **Falangarius**, like a sword.

**Falcarius**, a gladiator carrying a sickle.

[690]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 690. “He estimates.” Added by someone.]

**Falcitat**, he thinks, cuts, estimates.

**Falcones**, those who have their big toes inside their heels.

**Falsatus sum**, I have been deceived.

**Falsosum**, surrounded, deceived.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 694. *Famis*; others *fames*; others *famix*; others *tumex* and *vibex*, instead of *faucis*.]

**Famis**, a bruise of the throat.

[695]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 695. Graevius reads *famul*, “serving the Oscans,” from Festus and Nonius. Others retain *famulosus*.]

**Famulosus**, serving.

**Fanculum**, fennel.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 697. Perhaps the words should be deleted.]

**Faria**, many words.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 698. Correct to Greek **γράστις** (*grástis*). The Spaniards say *forrage*. Varro: *farrago*, “a mixture,” from *far* cut with iron.]

[700] **Fascinat**, it burdens.

**Fasculum**, a dish.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 702. Graevius deletes *piscator*; others read *priscis*, instead of *piscator*.]

**Favitor**, a fisherman, a supporter.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 703. Breviloquus: “a light hatred,” which quickly passed and falls away like that wind.]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 704. Graevius reads *fecundispices*. Pithoeus reads “the goddesses Felices.” Semlerus reads “fertile clods, fertile earth.”]

**Fecundispices**, fertile goddesses.

[705]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 705. Others write *filiatum* and *foliatum*. Graevius reads *foliatum*, “spikenard”; Semlerus *falcatum*, “curved.”]

**Feliatum**, curved.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 706. Read *fellebrem*, “still living on milk,” from *fello*, “I suck.”]

**Fellebrem**, still living on milk.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 707. “He sucks.” Printed editions incorrectly have *fugit*, “he flees.”]

**Fellirat**, he sucks.

**Femellarius**, devoted to women, whom the ancients call *mulierarius*.

**Fensus**, angry.

[710] **Feriferus**, raging.

**Feronia**, goddess of fields.

**Fertores**, those who make offerings with a *fer-tum*.

**Ferula**, a ferule or hand-ruler; a fly-whisk.

**Festalis**, a solemn day.

[715]

[Note: [Col. 1350] 715. *Festilia*. Perhaps *festalia*.]

**Festilia**, festival days.

[Note: [Col. 1350] 716. See *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 11, at the end.]

**Ficarius**, a faun.

[Col. 1351]

**Ficatum**, what the Greeks call “fig-fed [liver]” (**συκωτὸν**, *sykōtón*).

**Ficte habet**, he quibbles.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 719. *Fictura*; others *fissura*; others *sictura*, and hence *fictura*.]

**Fictura**, a cut.

[720] **Filiaster**, a stepson who was born earlier.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 721. Others *functus*, instead of *finctus*; others *vinctus* or *cinctus*, evidently “bound with a thread.” Immediately afterward: “of the dignity called *flaminalis*.”]

**Finctus fuerit**, he attained the highest dignity, and it is called *fluminalis*.

**Fiscella forma**, a mold in which cheeses are pressed.

**Fiscellus**, a lover of soft cheese.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 724. Perhaps “large figs.” The forms *fiscos* and *siccos* are corrupt.]

464 **Fiscos**, dry large figs.

[725] **Fistulor**, I whistle.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 726. Semlerus reads *suarius* or *subarius*, instead of *flabarius*. Others read *flabarius*, a keeper of beds or corpses, because with a fan they drove flies away from beds and from exposed corpses.]

**Flabarius**, a swineherd.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 727. Three glosses appear to be involved: *flabri*, *flabulosi*, “windy.” *Fabri*, “perfect”; *fabrum*, “perfect.” For *flabrum*, Reinesius, Cerda, and Graevius read *fabrum*, whence *affabre*. Perhaps the glossators were misled by *praefectum fabrum*.]

**Flabri**, windy, full of wind, perfect.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 728. Three glosses appear to be involved: *flabri*, *flabulosi*, “windy.” *Fabri*, “perfect”; *fabrum*, “perfect.” For *flabrum*, Reinesius, Cerda, and Graevius read *fabrum*, whence *affabre*. Perhaps the glossators were misled by *praefectum fabrum*.]

**Flabrum**, perfect.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 729. Read *flameum* or *flammeum*.]

**Flamineum**, Babylonian.

[730]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 730. *Flaminor*; rather *flammor*.]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 731. Cerda: *latus clavus*, a kind of garment.]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 732. Semlerus: Phlegyas, son of Mars.]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 733. Cerda: *philonichia*, vanity.]

**Folonitia**, vanity.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 734. *Trames*; others *trama*. Symmachus, in a letter: “Between the warp and the wool-combs of girls.”]

[735]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 736. Better *forica*.]

**Foria**, a latrine, a privy.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 737. Perhaps *foro*, that is, *perforo*, “I pierce.” The printed editions have *nec eo*, instead of *noceo* or *neco*.]

**Foris facio**, I offend, I harm.

**Formastrum**, a baker’s product.

**Fractillum**, something for breaking pepper.

[740]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 740. “More difficult.” Replace with *debilior*, “weaker.”]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 741. Perhaps *fraginatio*.]

**Fragus**, the bending of the hamstring, also called *suffraginatio*.

**Fraternus**, a brother’s son.

**Fratruelis**, a maternal aunt’s son.

**Frea**, *ae*, or *mundiana*, left behind by her parent.

[Col. 1351] [745]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 745. *Fretat*. Replace with *frenat*.]

**Fretat**, he rules, restrains.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 746. Write *phrygiones*, *phrygium*; compare Nonius under *vestis Phrygia*.]

**Frigiones**, a kind of garment.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 747. Write *phrygiones*, *phrygium*; compare Nonius under *vestis Phrygia*.]

**Frigium**, a mitre.

Constantine the Emperor: “We placed the *frigium*, with its white brilliance, upon his most sacred head.”

[Note: [Col. 1351] 748. *Fritillum* is a perforated vessel used for various purposes and for dice.]

**Fritellum**, a trickle of dung into a dung heap.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 749. Read *fundibulum* or *fundibalum*. *Etymologies*, Book XIV, chapter 6, at the end, and Book XVIII, chapter 10.]

**Fudibulum**, a sling or projectile-launcher.

[750]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 750. Understand *fucinat*, from *fuco*, “I deceive.” Papias has *fascinat*. Instead of *impedit*, others have *impetit*.]

**Fuginat**, he obstructs by flattering and deceives by praising.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 751. Semlerus: “*Fulcra*, beds, are,” etc.]

**Fulcralia**, ornaments of a bed.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 752. “Rustics”; perhaps “Etruscans.”]

**Fulguratores**, rustic haruspices.

[Note: [Col. 1351] 753. Semlerus has *culina*, *culinare*, omitting the others. But *fucina* or *focina*, from *focus*, is correct. Italians call a forge *fucina*.]

**Fulina**, a kitchen.

[Col. 1352]

[Note: [Col. 1351] 754. Semlerus has *culina*, *culinare*, omitting the others. But *fucina* or *focina*, from *focus*, is correct. Italians call a forge *fucina*.]

**Fulinare**, to cook.

[755] **Fullo**, a decorator.

**Fungitur**, he pays, discharges.

465 **Funus imaginarium**, a mound without a corpse, that is, an empty tomb.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 758. Perhaps *furacula*; others *foraculum*, as in the next entry.]

**Furabula**, darkness.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 759. Others *perforaculum*, a drill.]

**Furfuraculum**, darkness.

[760]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 760. Better *futilis* or *futile*.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 761. Festus: *futare*, “to accuse,” whence *confutare*.]

**Futo**, by refutation (**ἑλέχως**, perhaps for **ἐλεγχῶς**).

# G

[Note: [Col. 1352] 762. These three glosses belong together. See Rosweydus in the *Onomasticon*. Semlerus takes *insulsus* instead of *salitus* and deletes *barbarus*. It is also written *gabbarus*, *gabbares*. In manuscript glosses: *gabator*, a joking person. Perhaps this is the source of the Italian *gabbare*, “to deceive.”]

**Gabarus**, tasteless, barbarous; hence *gabares*, the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 763. These three glosses belong together. See Rosweydus in the *Onomasticon*. Semlerus takes *insulsus* instead of *salitus* and deletes *barbarus*. It is also written *gabbarus*, *gabbares*. In manuscript glosses: *gabator*, a joking person. Perhaps this is the source of the Italian *gabbare*, “to deceive.”]

**Gaberina**, a chest.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 764. These three glosses belong together. See Rosweydus in the *Onomasticon*. Semlerus takes *insulsus* instead of *salitus* and deletes *barbarus*. It is also written *gabbarus*, *gabbares*. In manuscript glosses: *gabator*, a joking person. Perhaps this is the source of the Italian *gabbare*, “to deceive.”]

**Galbares**, embalmed bodies of the dead.

[765]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 765. Rather *galenum* or *calenum*.]

**Galenum**, a wine vessel.

The ancient Romans called *calenum* wine.

[Col. 1352]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 766. Perhaps *galea*. Italians and Spaniards call triremes *galeras*.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 767. Rosweydus reads *galeros*, “camelaucia.” Hence *camauro*. Consult Macer in the lexicon.]

**Galerum**, a shepherd’s cap made of rush.

**Galgulus**, a berry, a kernel (**πυρήν**, *pyrēn*).

[770]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 770. Graevius reads *gallulat*, “he reaches puberty.”]

**Galivit**, he will perish.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 771. Hides are tanned with gall.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 772. Write *ganea*, from *Etymologies*, Book X: *ganeo*, etc.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 773. Perhaps *galnapis*, instead of *gaunaca*, from the *Rule of the Monks*, chapter 13.]

**Gaunaca**, a shaggy woolen cloak.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 774. Correct to *janitrices*, from *Etymologies*, Book IX, final chapter, no. 17, and below, no. 844.]

[775]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 775. *Gellonem*, or *gillonem*; Spaniards call it *cangilon*. See Rosweydus. It is a kind of vessel.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 776. Perhaps “gem-encrusted bedspreads.”]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 777. *Aquigeni*; more correctly *aequigeni*.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 778. Graevius reads *gymnades*, Lacedaemonian women, in the Greek language.]

**Gemmatum**, adorned with gems.

[780] **Genialis lectus**, a bed made up for the wedding day.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 781. *Geniatus*. Hence Barthius, p. 1425, restores in Statius *moles geniata*, instead of *moles gemmata*. Others read *moles geminata*.]

**Geniatus**, genial, pleasant.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 782. Restore *genuinum*, “innermost, interior,” etc.]

**Genubium**, innermost, interior, domestic.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 783. *Gessiae*. Write *Gazae*.]

**Gestiuncula**, a small matter.

[785] **Gesum**, a spear, a javelin, a dart (**βολίς**, *bolís*).

[Note: [Col. 1352] 786. See the beginning of the *History of the Goths*.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 787. Others read *Getice garrit*, “he chatters in Gothic”; others *getat*, “he chatters.”]

**Getage**, he chatters; he speaks Gothic.

466 **Geti**, Goths.

[Note: [Col. 1352] 789. The gloss has been moved from its proper place. Graevius thinks that double baths, for men and women, are called *geminarium*; Semlerus reads *aenarium*, instead of *geminarium*.]

[790]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 790. It should be written *gyrgillus*, from *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 15, no. 2. See below, no. 818.]

[Note: [Col. 1352] 791. Graevius reads *gonia*; others have other readings, as in the next entry.]

[Col. 1353]

**Gissium**, a lip, a boundary, an ending.

[Note: [Col. 1353] 793. *Glirium*. From *glis*, “dormouse.”]

**Glaucia**, green.

**Glebo**, a rustic, a plowman.

[795] **Glirium**, sluggish, stupid.

**Glis, glitis**, sticky soil.

[Note: [Col. 1353] 798. Perhaps *gnabat*, “begot”; *generabat*, “generated”; *gnatus*, “born,” etc.]

**Gnabat**, born, generated, a son, created, or brought forth, in the Gallic language.

**Gnavat**, he carries out vigorously.

[800]

**Grassus**, bristly, hairy.

[Note: [Col. 1353] 803. *Gremia*. Read *cremia*, “dried wood.”]

**Gremia**, dried wood.

[Note: [Col. 1353] 804. *Cervicosus*. Others *conviciosus*. But *cervicosus* seems to have been taken from “a stiff neck,” which signifies pride.]

[805]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 805. Perhaps *agger*, “mound, heap,” instead of *ager*, “field, tract.”]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 807. For *gumba*, read or understand *cumba*, *catacumba*; and *crypta* instead of *cripa*. Graevius reads *cuniculus*, “tunnel,” instead of *cuneus*.]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 808. Others *guma tectorium*; others *gumba*, “a hut.”]

**Gumma**, a covering or shelter.

[810]

**Guva**, windy or flatulent.

[Note: [Col. 1353] 813. *Ventuosa*. Better *ventosa*. See *Etymologies*, Book IV, chapter 11, no. 4: “*Guva*, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 815. Write *hariolus jucundus*.]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 817. Semlerus reads either *ause*, from *audendo*, “from daring,” or *reapse*, “in reality.”]

[Note: [Col. 1353] 825. The following glosses appear to be corrupted from the preceding one.]

469 **In palam**, openly.

[Note: [Col. 1355] 890. Printed editions have *in popularis*.]

[Note: [Col. 1355] 892. Correct to *institae*, “the little cords of a bed.”]

[Note: [Col. 1356] 900. “A word.” Graevius reads *crebro*; Barthius *versum* or *verum*. From *jocista* we say *juglar* in Spanish.]

**Jocista**, one who makes a game of words.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 901. *Inguvium*. Graevius reads *jugum*; Semlerus *injugium*.]

**Inguvium**, slavery, captivity.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 902. *Hipparius* should be written.]

**Ipparius**, a charioteer.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 903. Others *illustre*, “holy”; others *hirsute*, “bristly”; others *Ister*, “Scythian.”]

**Istre**, cut.

**Jugit**, a kite when it emits a sound.

[905]

[Note: [Col. 1356] 905. *Julca*. Write *hiulca*.]

**Julca**, fissile.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 906. *Lectile*. Graevius reads *flectile*; others *juncata*, “milk.” From other lexica: *juncata*, “curdled milk.” Italians say *giuncata*.]

**Junceum**, a bed.

**Juraticus**, scholarly, learned in law.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 908. *Juris juramen*; perhaps instead of *jusjurandum*.]

**Juris**, an oath.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 909. Semlerus reads *jussa*, *jussorum*, instead of *jussorianem*; others *jussoriamen*.]

**Jussorianem**, an injunction.

[910]

[Note: [Col. 1356] 910. Here, as at no. 906, *juncea* or *juncata*, “milk-bearing.”]

**Jutia**, to suckle.

**Juvenestres**, strong men.

[Col. 1356] K

[Note: [Col. 1356] 912. Perhaps **χαῖρε** (*chaire*), from the expression “Caesar, hail!” Instead of *amicos*, “friends,” *ave*, “hail,” could be substituted.]

**Kaere Caesar**, friends.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 913. *Kai*, *kari*, or *kae* is still in use among the Belgians and Germans. Semlerus suspects that all these words beginning with *k* are writing abbreviations.]

**Kai**, railings.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 914. *Kai*, *kari*, or *kae* is still in use among the Belgians and Germans. Semlerus suspects that all these words beginning with *k* are writing abbreviations.]

**Kaii**, railings.

[915]

[Note: [Col. 1356] 915. Read *kalones* or *calones*, soldiers’ helmet-bearers.]

**Kalones**, soldiers’ helmet-bearers.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 916. Festus: “*Casnar*, an old man in the language of the Oscans.”]

**Kaniser**, an old man.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 917. It seems it should be read *capax*, “capable.”]

**Kapax**, mindful.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 918. Perhaps *chalybs*, “steel,” instead of “an iron fork.”]

**Karibs**, a punishment fork, otherwise *Kalibs*.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 919. Others *chartallum*; others *capulum*, from *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 11, no. 7. Printed editions have *afferuntur*, “are brought.” The addition “elsewhere” seems to indicate that *katulum* is written elsewhere, as in the next entry.]

**Kartulum**, with which the dead are carried elsewhere.

[920]

[Note: [Col. 1356] 920. Semlerus thinks that after *deferuntur* a Frankish-German word, *kittulus*, “garment,” etc., has dropped out.]

470 **Katulum**, in which the dead are carried, clothed, worn out, or in linen.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 921. Others *cupedinarius*.]

**Kuppedinarius**, pleasure-loving.

# L
[Note: [Col. 1356] 922. “A tool”; others read “of robbers.” *La verna* is preferable, namely the goddess of thieves, instead of *laberna*.]  
**Laberna**, a tool of robbers, or highwaymen, or thieves. **Laberna**, a gladiator.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 924. “A robber”; perhaps *lavernio*, from Festus.]  
**Laberna**, a robber, or one who seduces other men’s sons.

[925]  
[Note: [Col. 1356] 925. Restore *labina*, “causing a fall,” from Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 4.]  
**Labina**, the lower lip.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 926. Others read *lactucismus*, from *alliciendo*; others *laccus*, supposedly written in this way instead of *laqueus*.]  
**Lacatismus**, a snare, a trap.  
**Laciniosum**, ragged, tattered, torn.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 928. Others read *mactena*, from *macto*; others *mactena*, a butcher’s shop; others *lacerna*, a cloak, from Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, no. 14.]  
**Lactena**, a hammer.

[Note: [Col. 1356] 929. Barthius reads *lambrio* or *lamurio*, “lame”; others *lampiris*, “shining”; others *lambo*, “I flatter”; others *lanio*, “butcher.”]  
**Lamiro**, flattering.

[Col. 1357] [930]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 930. Others read *lampium*, from lamps; others *lectorium*.]  
**Lampium**, a pulpit, a reading desk.  
**Lancibus**, serving dishes.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 932. *Lanistra* instead of *lanista*, like *balistra*; but others read either *lanistio*, “a wool-worker,” from *lana*, or *lanista*, “a butcher,” or *laniarius*, from *laniando*. See Book X of the *Etymologies*, no. 160.]  
**Lanistra**, a wool-worker.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 933. Perhaps *larigena*, “domestic,” or *lar*, a household spirit.]  
**Largens**, domestic.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 934. Others read *larva*, “a razor,” from the German word *rasen*, “to rage”; others *larva*, “a demon”; others *lar*, *laris*, *larium*; others *larva*, “a monster”; others think that *larva*, “a razor,” or a file, was brought here from no. 966, *limula*, “a larva” (*parva*).]  
**Larna**, a razor.

[935]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 935. Barthius reads *latroconum*, from the German *con*, “a fast ship”; others *latena*; others *latrocinatorium*, or *latronium*, or *littorarium*.]  
**Latororum**, a kind of ship, but associated with piracy.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 936. Here too Semler reads “a coastal ship,” without explanation. See Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 27, *trabariae*, etc.]  
**Latos**, a ship.  
**Latrunciat**, he fights from a ship.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 938. From Festus: flour was called *lautitia* when mixed with water.]  
**Lautitia**, flour mixed with water.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 939. Formed from *laxare habenas*, “to loosen the reins.”]  
**Laxamina**, reins.

[940]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 940. Soon, at no. 945, *leno*, “a glutton.” The Italians call *leccare* “to lick,” and call a glutton *lecconem*. In German too, *ganeo* means “a glutton,” according to Barthius.]  
**Lecator**, a glutton.  
**Lecticalis**, one who makes small beds.  
**Lectistium**, a bedstead or bed-station.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 943. *Lectrum*, from *lectorium*.]  
**Lectrum**, a reading desk on which one reads.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 944. See the Book on the Order of Creatures, chapter 9, chapter 4 and following, with the note.]  
**Ledo**, the swelling of the sea.

[945]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 945. Above, no. 940. Some wish to read *locator* instead of *lecator*. Here *mediator* means a reconciler in sexual misconduct.]  
**Leno**, a glutton, a mediator.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 946. Perhaps *lenocinatur*, “he practices pimping.”]  
[Col. 1357] **Lenocinator**, he serves through disgraceful flattery.  
**Lenociniis**. Donatus: “He pronounced it pleasantly, with remarkable flatteries.”  
**Lenocinium**, gluttony.

[Col. 1357] **Lentandus**, to be bent.

[950]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 950. In Plautus, *lenullus*; in Priscian also the other diminutive, *lenunculus*.]  
**Lenulus**, a little glutton.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 951. Barthius understands a military garment, *levisatam*, from *levis actus*; others read *lacerna*; Semler reads *levidensata*, from Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22, no. 19.]  
**Levisata**, a military tunic.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 952. *Lebitonarium* is written in Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 21, no. 24.]  
**Levitonarium**, a sleeveless linen garment, a *colobarium*.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 953. Restore *lumbatorium*.]  
**Libatorium**, a hip covering.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 954. *Libitina* is ordinarily understood as a bier and as death.]  
**Libitina**, the place from which the dead are carried away.

[955]  
[Note: [Col. 1357] 955. Others read *licens oneris* or *operis*, “free from burden” or “work,” instead of *liber*; others *imicerius*, corrupted from *primicerius*; others *lucernarius*, a candlestick; others *licini*, white lamps, as below.]  
**Licerceris**, a centurion.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 956. Others read *liniani*; others *linigeri*, because Egyptian priests were clothed in linen; others *vaticinia*, prophecies.]  
**Liciani**, prophets.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 957. Barthius thinks *licini* is a German word; but Isidore should rather be compared, Book XVII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6, no. 25: “wood was called,” etc. And elsewhere.]  
**Licini**, candles, lamps, or small lamps.

[Note: [Col. 1357] 958. Perhaps the following should be arranged thus: *licitator*, gladiator; *lictor*, attendant, executioner; *licentiosus*, one to whom many things are permitted.]  
**Licitator**, a gladiator, an attendant, an executioner, one to whom many things are permitted.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 959. *Licius*; others *licitator*; others *licitarius*.]  
**Licius**, a merchant.

[960]  
[Note: [Col. 1358] 960. Barthius writes *linque*, “leave,” instead of the others, *inventui*, “for discovery.” A thing regarded as abandoned is said to be left and becomes the property of the first taker. Others read *limbo*, found elsewhere instead of *limbus*; others *limbo*, found elsewhere for purple.]  
**Limbo**, elsewhere, “he finds.”

[Note: [Col. 1358] 961. For a ship, *lembus* is written; elsewhere *limbus* has another sense.]  
**Limbus**, a pirate ship, or the purple band on royal clothing, or the clothing itself.  
**Limfaticus**, one who fears water, whom the Greeks call **ὑδροφόβος** (*hydrophobos*), “water-fearing.”

[Note: [Col. 1358] 963. Below, *linarius*.]  
**Liniarius**, a net-fighter.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 964. Graevius reads “places of the martyrs.” If *mortuorum* is retained, it must be understood of tombs, which were located outside the gates of cities along public roads. Semler conjectures “doorsteps,” without explanation. Then “places of the dead,” as though *livitina* or *libitina* had dropped out.]  
**Limina portarum**, places of the dead.

[965]  
[Note: [Col. 1358] 965. Graevius deletes *mortiferum*; Semler reads *libitinium*, or *illicium*, or *liminium*, as though separated from *limen*. Others offer conjectures from *postliminio*.]  
**Liminum**, deadly servitude, captivity.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 966. Others read *lingula parva*, “a little tongue”; others *limula*, “little”; others *lamia*, “a ghost.” See above, *larva*, “a razor.”]  
**Limula**, a ghost.  
**Linarius**, a net-fighter.

[Col. 1358]  
[Note: [Col. 1358] 968. Others read *lignicisivus*.]  
**Linguiscisinus**, an iron tool with which rods and shrubs are cut.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 969. Correct to *linguis trisulcis*, “with three-forked tongues,” from Virgil.]  
**Linguitri**, with furrows divided into three parts.

[970]  
[Note: [Col. 1358] 970. *Linivia*. Papias: *linaria*.]  
**Linivia**, nets.

**Lintres**, small boats on the Nile.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 972. Either *litiarius*, from *lis*, “lawsuit,” or *licitarius*, as above under *licitator*.]  
**Litarius**, a gladiator.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 973. From Nonius. Hence *lixivium*; in Spanish, *lexia*. Barthius, from Papias’s *lix*, “goat,” derives *lix*, “he-goat.”]  
**Lix**, ashes.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 974. From Festus: *lixabundus*, one who travels freely and expansively. Others read *luxabundus*, as though “walking in luxury.”]  
**Lixabundus**, he walks about; one who walks for pleasure.

[975]  
[Note: [Col. 1358] 975. Others read *lix*, “water.” *Lixae*, those who walk among the soldiers. The ancients called water, etc.; others read *lixae*, water-carriers, who [walk] among the soldiers, etc.; others read *lixae*, a marching column that moves among the soldiers—the ancients called this *lixum*; others read *liquis*, “a corner,” along which one walks by the boundaries—the ancients called this *lixum*. Others read *lixa*, one who carries water to the soldiers. The ancients called water *lixam*.]  
**Lixe**, water which moves among the soldiers; the ancients called it *lixum*.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 976. Breviloquus: *lixor, -oris*, a water-carrier.]  
**Lixiones**, water-carriers.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 977. Graevius: *lucar*, money collected from a sacred grove near the city of Rome; Semler: *lucar*, a grove, or [money] from sacred groves near Rome. From *lucar* comes *lucrum*, “profit.” Below, no. 980.]  
**Locar**, a place near the city of Rome.  
**Lubrica**, a rampart, or rather a ditch.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 979. Rather, the *Excerpta* omit this. Cerda: *ludicrum*, a rampart. Semler: *lubricum*, “vain”; from this the corrupted reading *vallum*, “rampart,” arose, and later *sine fossa*, “without a ditch,” was added.]  
**Lubricum**, mud together with a fall.

[980]  
**Lucar**, a tax, an expenditure made in sacred groves.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 981. Others read *lucerna*, a kind of wax or candle; others *lacerna*, a kind of hooded cloak.]  
**Lucerna**, a kind of hooded cloak.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 982. *Ludarius*, from *lutum*, “mud.” The Spanish say *lodo*, “mud,” and *lodazal*, “muddy place.” Cerda: a muddy, deceptive place; others *lubricus*; others *volutarius* instead of *ludarius*.]  
**Ludarius**, a deceptive place where one quickly slips.

[Note: [Col. 1358] 983. Barthius reads either *lustrices*, from *lustra*, “brothels,” or *lodices*, which are also called mattresses; prostitutes are also called *meretrices*. Compare Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 26, no. 2.]  
**Ludices**, prostitutes.  
**Luecula**, a small plague.

[Col. 1359] [985]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 985. Graevius: *ligues*, *ligures*; others *lugdunes*, inhabitants of Lugdunum; others *luceres*, inhabitants of Luceria.]  
**Lugues**, inhabitants of Lugdunum.

**Luitio**, a legal term.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 987. This is called *lumum*, and the feminine *luma*. Instead of *lenae*, see Book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 23, no. 3. Others read *lumae*; others *linnae*. Martinius: *lurica*, a horse’s cloak.]  
**Luma**, a square cloak.  
**Lumbare**, a loincloth.  
**Lumbones**, belts around the loins.

[990]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 990. *Lumentum*; rather, *lomentum*.]  
**Lumentum**, soda or natron.

**Luna semenstris**, the moon of mid-month.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 992. A lunar illness is indicated. Barthius wishes to read *quod fluit*, “what flows,” instead of *quod fit*, “what occurs,” so that it may be understood of women’s menstruation.]  
**Lunatica**, what occurs at the full moon.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 993. *Lupal*; others *lupar*.]  
**Lupal**, a brothel.

**Lusores**, false witnesses.

[995]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 995. “Oil.” Read *olidum* or *oletum*, “foul-smelling.”]  
**Lustramentum**, stench, foulness, oil, fetidness.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 996. “He wanders.” Correct to *vagator*, “a wanderer.”]  
**Lustro**, he wanders.  
**Lurore**, with a yellow color.

## M

[Note: [Col. 1359] 998. Semler attempts *macera*, a butcher’s shop, a place for cheating or selling.]  
**Macere fallio**, a place for cheating.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 999. It may be inferred from this that *moenia* can be taken for buildings of any kind.]  
**Maenit**, he builds, constructs.

[1000]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 1000. On *maforte* or *mavorte*, compare Rosweyd in the *Onomasticon*, and Isidore, Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25, no. 4.]  
**Mafortes**, a covering for women’s heads.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1001. *Calculo*, “I calculate,” instead of *calculator*, unless the latter should be restored. See Martial, Book X, epigram 2: “The schoolmaster,” etc.]  
**Magister ludi**, a schoolmaster; **calculo**, I calculate.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1002. *Media*; perhaps *medica*.]  
**Maia**, a midwife.

**Maialis**, a fat pig sacrificed to the goddess Maia, as to the mother of Mercury.  
**Malarium**, an orchard.

[1005]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 1005. Instead of *malce*, others read *malacus*, *malcus*, or *malcio*; others *macello*, from *macellum*, as *ganeo* comes from *ganeum*.]  
**Malce**, a tavern-goer, one who loves going to taverns.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1006. Martinius: *mandra*; Semler, better, *menda*.]  
**Manda**, deception, fraud.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1007. *Madones*, from *mandendo*, “chewing.” See Nonius.]  
**Mandones**, gluttonous busybodies and idlers.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1008. *Mandratur*; perhaps *mendatur*, from *menda*, “fault.”]  
**Mandratur**, he quibbles.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1009. *Mandus*. Also written *mantus*. See Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, no. 15.]  
**Mandus**, a maiden’s garment.

[1010]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 1010. From Festus: “shameful threats,” etc.]  
**Maniae**, images of terrifying things.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1011. *Manifex*. Rather, *manifer*.]  
**Manifex**, one who gives a warning.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1012. “One who gives help.” Semler: “one who carries a standard,” from other lexica.]  
**Manipulum**, one who gives help in war.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1013. From Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 55. Read *mannus burricus* or *buricus*.]  
**Manius**, a little donkey.  
**Mannulus**, a horse, a donkey.

[1015]  
**Mansionarius**, a doorkeeper.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1016. More correctly, *manticulari*, from Festus.]  
**Manticulare**, to defraud or deceive.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1017. Semler: *manualis*, a basket.]  
**Manucalis**, a gate.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1018. *Manuae* is better than *manua*.]  
**Manua**, bundles.  
**Manuale**, a book suitable for carrying, called an *enchiridion*, a handbook.

[1020]  
[Note: [Col. 1359] 1020. *Orarium*, instead of *sudarium*, “handkerchief.”]  
**Manuale**, a handkerchief.

[Note: [Col. 1359] 1021. Graevius: *manubiae*, plunder, booty. Semler: [Col. 1360] *manuale*, writing, a textbook; or *manuale*, repetition of instruction.]  
**Manubla**, repetition of instruction.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1022. *Manubiare*. Martinius: *manicare*. Graevius: *manere*. Perhaps they said *manubiare*, from *mane*, “morning,” instead of “to spend the night.”]  
**Manubiare**, to keep watch, to spend the night.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1023. Others read *manutus*.]  
**Manutius**, having large hands.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1024. *Expiarium*. It was also called *manupiarium*. Nevertheless, Graevius restored *sudarium*, “handkerchief.”]  
**Mappa**, a shaggy cloth, a small covering, an *expiarium*.

[1025]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1025. Others read *momarsiculus*. Others, *momar*, “a Sicilian,” that is, among the Sicilians, from Festus. Below, no. 1058: *momar*, a Sicilian.]  
**Marsiculus**, one who is quickly moved to anger. Plautus: “What do you say, marsicule, man?”

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1026. Semler: *masortia*, without interpretation, instead of *mafortia*. Then *marsupium*, without interpretation.]  
**Masortia**, a purse.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1027. Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 28, no. 8: *masticinum*, etc.]  
**Masticina**, saffron-colored.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1028. Semler: *metapontus*, a change of the sea; and he corrects it to *metaplus*, -i, instead of *metapontus*. See no. 1044.]  
**Matapontum**, the mother’s change.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1029. “Poor,” that is, reduced to the register of the poor.]  
**Marticularius**, poor, needy.

[1030]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1030. Salmasius, in his note on Vopiscus, reads *via matta* in Cicero, instead of *via aperta*, “open road,” and understands it as “damp.”]  
**Matum est**, it is moistened, softened, stained.

**Meatim**, in my manner.

[Col. 1360]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1032. “Bath attendant.” From Nonius and others.]  
**Mediastinus**, a bath attendant.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1033. Graevius: “placed in the middle of the auction”; others: “in the middle of an action”; others *mediustinus*, “in the middle of a burning.”]  
**Mediastinus**, placed in the middle of an auction.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1034. The *Excerpta* of Pithoeus: “on parchments, on hides.”]  
**Mempanis**, through sluggishness.

[1035]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1035. A tavern, namely where unmixed wine was sold.]  
**Meraria**, a tavern.

**Mercedarius**, one who pays wages for work done for him.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1037. “Sticks, saws”; Graevius, “bundles of reapers”; Martinius, “iron rods.” A *mergus* is a cormorant, and a *marculus* an iron hammer.]  
**Mercedonius**, one who pays wages.  
**Mercurius**, a heap of stones on the top of hills.  
**Mergi**, cormorants; sticks; saws.

[1040]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1040. *Mergorae*. More correctly, *mergora*.]  
**Mergorae**, buckets with which water is drawn from a well.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1041. Semler reads *meraria*, as at no. 1035. But *meritoria* is correct, meaning a brothel or a tavern for hire.]  
**Meritoria**, places of tents.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1042. Others read *mosculus*; others *mosillus*; others *musculus*, instead of *mesillus*.]  
**Mesillus**, a small custom.

**Mesopicatum**, half-pitched.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1044. *Metabulum*. Semler: *metaplus*.]  
**Metabulum**, a favorable voyage.

[1045]  
**Metaplum**.  
**Metatores**, preparers of lodgings.  
**Metreta**, half an amphora.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1048. It may be joined as *militaris opinatus*, “an experienced soldier.” He is called *opinatus* because he is approved, or because the term refers to the *opinatores* mentioned below.]  
**Militaris**, experienced, that is, a veteran soldier.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1049. *Millum*, etc., from Festus.]  
**Millum**, a dog collar.

[1050]  
[Note: [Col. 1360] 1050. *Minnarius*. Correct to *mimarius*.]  
**Minnarius**, a buffoon, a fool, a bad man.

[Note: [Col. 1360] 1051. Soon, at no. 1053, *minicus*. Graevius reads *erinacius* in both places. Semler reads *mimicus* and *histricus*, instead of *ericius*.]  
**Mincius**, a hedgehog.  
**Miniculo**, for assistance.  
**Minicus**, a hedgehog.  
**Miridicus**, saying marvelous things.

[Col. 1361] [1055]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1055. *Numeratorum*. In the *Excerpta*, *imitatores*, “imitators”; perhaps *miratores*, “admirers,” as immediately below.]  
**Miriones**, reckoners of empty fantasies.  
**Miriones**, admirers.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1057. Others read *missitius*, one who has left military service.]  
**Missilius**, one who distributes missilia (largesse thrown to a crowd).

**Momar**, a Sicilian, a fool who is quickly moved to anger. Plautus: “Why, you Sicilian Momar, man, are you so presumptuous?”

[1060]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1060. Correct to *momentana*, from Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25, no. 4.]  
**Momentanea**, consisting equally of two pans and one pointer in the middle. It is a small balance for money.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1061. Again, the pointer by which the *momentana* is moved. Graevius: “by which, when moved, the balance moves.”]  
**Momentum**, the pointer by which the balance is inclined.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1062. Better, *monocosmum*. Schefferus, *monachus*.]  
**Monacosmum**, something drawn by one beast, a type of vehicle.

**Monopolium**, a stall where one kind of thing is sold.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1064. From other lexica: *monopticus*, in a single case.]  
**Monopticus**, a mime . . .

[1065]  
**Monotonus**, rigid.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1066. *Meratores*; perhaps from lawsuits being prolonged; or *muginatores* should be read, from no. 1068, from which *causatores* was made, with “advocates” as the meaning.]  
**Moratores**, advocates.  
**Morificando**, by causing delay.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1068. From Nonius and others: *muginari*, “to mutter,” etc.]  
**Muginatur**, he makes excuses.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1069. *Mulcare* is confused with *mulctare*; others distinguish them.]  
**Mulcat**, he strikes.

[1070]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1070. Cerda: *molitiones*, a secret, secrecy, constitutions. Others: *moles Adriani*, “Hadrian’s mole,” a secret, constitutions. Others: *munitiones*, a secret archive, constitutions. For *constitutiones*, others read *constructiones*.]  
**Mullitiones**, Hadrian’s secret, or a constitutional matter.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1071. The *Excerpta*: *molossus*, a little dog.]  
**Mulosus**, a rustic little dog.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1072. Read *mussitanter*.]  
**Mulsitanter**, gently.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1073. *Muna*. Rather *munia*, as at no. 1075.]  
**Muna**, gifts given to soldiers.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1074. Perhaps “a man of worldly status.”]  
**Mundialis**, a man of worldly status.

[1075]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1075. *Salvationis*. Rather, *salutationis*, “of greeting.”]  
**Munia**, duties of salvation, or gifts.  
**Munifer**, one who carries gifts.  
**Munificentia**, a public work.

[Col. 1361]  
**Munitoria**, front belts.  
**Munitoria**, under-belts.

[1080]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1080. Chapter 7. Rather, Book VII, chapter 4. The Maurini read *minuscularius*; others *minutularius*, that is, a small and minor tax-collector.]  
**Munuscularius**. Augustine, *On the City of God*, chapter 7.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1081. *Murcinarius*, from the goddess Murcia. Likewise *murcidus* and *murcus* were said. Compare the lexica.]  
**Murcinarius**, mutilated.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1082. Semler distinguishes them: clever, a grumbler.]  
**Murgiso**, a clever grumbler.  
**Murilegus**, cunning.  
**Murrat**, he murmurs.

[1085]  
**Murrire**, to cry out, properly of mice.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1086. Perhaps *mussitantium*, “of those hesitating.” In the *Excerpta*: *mussitat*, “he hesitates, murmurs.”]  
**Musarum**, of diviners.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1087. Semler: *muscerda*, mouse droppings.]  
**Muscarde**, they are mouse droppings.

**Muscipula**, a little trap.  
**Muscipulator**, a deceiver, an advocate for another.

[1090]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1090. A small ship. Semler: a little mouse, or a small mouse. See Book XVIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11, no. 4: *musculus*, etc.]  
**Musculus**, a small ship.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1091. From *mus* comes *musio*, cat; *musiarius*, *musea*, *musia*, *musiae*, etc., as in the following entries.]  
**Musiea**, nests of shrews.  
[Col. 1361] **Musiae**, nests of shrews.  
**Mustarius**, because he searches through *musia*.

[Note: [Col. 1361] 1094. Others read *mustricula*. Above, *muscipula*.]  
**Mustricola**, a device for tightening mouse traps.

[1095]  
[Note: [Col. 1361] 1095. It is uncertain what this glossator noted here. Perhaps he indicates that *mutelus* is reddish, since what came before was *rubrum*, “red.”]  
**Mutelus**, after *Rufus*, before *Rubrum*.

## N

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1096. Perhaps *navita*, *nauta*, “sailor.”]  
**Nabita**, having obtained.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1097. Semler: *nacare* or *naccare*, from *naca*, a fuller, who seems to rock while working; or *nacare* or *nutare*, “to nod.”]  
**Nagare**, to stagger, to sway back and forth.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1098. “Without adulteration,” that is, without admixture of another substance; hence *pisticum*, “genuine” or “faithful.”]  
**Nardum pisticum**, genuine chrism without adulteration.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1099. Graevius: *Naryci*, Bruttians, because the Naryci came to the Bruttians; others *narici*, *bruci*, or *brucosi*, whose noses are always running, according to John of Genoa.]  
**Narici**, brutes.

[1100]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1100. “Mocking”; others *subsannator*, “a mocker.”]  
**Nario**, mocking.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1101. An ornament that protects the nose.]  
**Nasale**, a horse ornament.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1102. Perhaps *aginari* or *agginari*, as above, *agginantes*.]  
**Natinari**, to conduct business.

[Col. 1362]  
**Naucupes**, they have the same sharp foot.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1104. Others read *naupegus*.]  
**Nauficus**, a shipbuilder.

[1105]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1105. This gloss and the next are corruptions from *navarchus*.]  
**Nauregus**, naval.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1106. This gloss and the next are corruptions from *navarchus*.]  
**Nauricus**, a ship’s commander.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1107. Others read *damae*; others retain *Dianae*, who is depicted with a deer’s hide, from Servius and Virgil.]  
**Nebris Dianae**, Diana’s hide; she is depicted with a deer.

**Nec nocte**, neither at night nor deceptively.  
Pers . . . “Nor at night will the father weep.”

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1109. Semler: *neculatum*, half-alive; or *necoleatum*, without *coleae*; or *Nicolaum*, a pastry, because Augustus called a certain kind of cake *Nicolaus*, which pleased Nicolaus of Damascus.]  
**Necolatum**, foolish and enfeebled.

[1110]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1110. Graevius: *nefandus*, *nefarius*, “unspeakably wicked.”]  
**Nefandarius**.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1111. The other lexica agree; from *nefrendes*, pigs scarcely weaned.]  
**Nefrenditium**, an annual tribute which country people ordinarily offer to their masters, or pupils to their teachers, at a fixed time, provided only that it is something made of meat, such as a piglet.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1112. *Nervicus*; others *nerviceus*.]  
**Nervicus**, sinewy, strong.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1113. Others *netorium*, and *fusillus*, instead of *fusile*.]  
**Netorsum**, spun, capable of being spun.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1114. Correct to *nivatus*, *nivata*.]  
**Nibarus**, splendid.

[1115]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1115. Correct to *nivatus*, *nivata*.]  
**Nibita**, water made from clouds.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1116. *Nicolaus*—perhaps a little mime? See above, *Necolatum*.]  
**Nicolaum**, foolish.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1117. Augustus called the fruit of the date palm *nicolaus*.]  
**Nicolaus**, a date.

**Nictit canis**, the dog yelps sharply.  
**Nihil censi**, nothing assessed; **nihil judicati**, nothing adjudged.

[1120]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1120. *Niniticus*; perhaps *nimius*, “excessive.”]  
**Niniticus**, excessive, extraordinary, monstrous.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1121. Graevius: *naeniosus*. In Spanish, *niño* means “boy.”]  
**Niniosus**, talkative.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1122. Read *mimarius*.]  
**Ninnarius**, one whose wife commits adultery and who remains silent.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1123. Semler: *nitellae*, *nitores*, “small shiners,” a diminutive.]  
**Nitellae**, eunuchs, diminished little men.

[Note: [Col. 1362] 1124. *Nitura*; others *gnatura* or *natura*; others *nisura*.]  
**Nitura**, generation.

[1125]  
[Note: [Col. 1362] 1125. Perhaps *nexe*, “joined.”]  
**Nixe**, fortified.

[Col. 1363]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1126. In Festus, *noneolae* or *noneoleae*; perhaps *nuculae*, “little nuts.” The printed editions have *captae* instead of *caprae*.]  
**Nomicolae**, the bumps beneath a she-goat’s chin.

**Nominosus**, famous, renowned.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1128. Semler: *nassicula*, from *nassa*, “fish-trap,” or *nubecula*, “little cloud,” because Greek **νηφέλη** (*nephélē*) means “cloud,” and a net for birds.]  
**Nonnula**, a net for catching birds.

**Non putativum**, it is not doubtful.

[1130]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1130. *Norax*. Correct to *noxax* or *noxius*, “harmful.”]  
**Norax**, a sinner, a criminal.

**Notarius**, a scribe, a draftsman.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1132. *Noxilis*; perhaps *noxialis* or *noxius*. In the *Excerpta*, *noxit*, “may harm.”]  
**Noxilis**, harmful.

**Nugigerulus**, a disgraceful messenger.  
**Nugiparus**, one who produces nonsense.

[1135]  
**Nullatenus**, in no way.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1136. “One who sells”; perhaps “one who chews” or “eats,” and *ad mandendum*, “for eating,” instead of *ad vendendum*, “for selling.”]  
**Numida**, one who sells herbs, or one who raises livestock for sale.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1137. The goddess of number, who teaches children to count.]  
**Numeria**, the goddess of number.

**Nuptant**, they marry.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1139. Buildings intended for weddings were called *nymphaea* at Rome.]  
**Nuptorium**, a house and place of those marrying.

[1140]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1140. *Nutinare*. Cerda: *natura*. Semler: constitution, instead of body. Graevius: genitals, instead of generation.]  
**Nutinare**, body, character, generation.

## O

**Obfibulare**, to enclose, surround.  
**Obicula**, a little barrier.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1143. Graevius: *oblimat*, from the manuscript of Constance.]  
**Obilat**, he makes clear.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1144. *Oblogat*; others *oblegat*; others *objurgat*; others retain *oblogat*, from *logos*.]  
**Oblogat**, he rebukes.

[1145]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1145. It seems that *psillus*, *marsus* should be read. Pliny and the lexicographers discuss these two peoples. Snakes did not harm them.]  
**Obsillas**, a Marsian.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1146. Better, *obsoletatur*, as in the *Excerpta*.]  
**Obsolitatus**, polluted, defiled.

**Obtundit**, he blinds.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1148. Some write *obtunsa* instead of *obtusa*.]  
**Obtunsa**, foolish or stupid.  
**Obtunsus**, blinded.

[1150]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1150. Graevius restores *obvallatum*, “fortified.”]  
**Obvallum**, fortified on every side.

**Occa**, a harrow.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1152. *Contisio*. Martinius: *contusio*, namely of clods.]  
**Occamen**, a breaking up.

[Col. 1363]  
**Occentare**, to utter an evil omen.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1154. Cerda correctly reads *concistrio*.]  
**Occistrio**, a tavern-keeper.

[1155]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1155. *Oes*. Graevius: *aestrum*.]  
**Oes**, madness.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1156. “Are marked.” Cerda: “are tied.”]  
**Offendices**, knots by which books are marked.

**Offex**, an impediment.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1158. *Offex*, from *officiendo*, “hindering.” Others *officiens*; others *obex*, “barrier.”]  
**Officialis**, a minister of sacred rites.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1159. *Sacrorum*. Semler: *officiorum*, or *sacrorum*, because of ecclesiastical offices.]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1159. Others read *Officiperdae*.]  
**Officiperdi**, those who receive no remuneration for their labor. They are also called *Officiperdi* by Cato.

[1160]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1160. *Ogit*. Correct to *obit*.]  
**Ogit**, he dies.

**Olacitas**, stench, foulness.  
**Olax**, foul-smelling.  
**Olerare**, to plant vegetables.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1164. Martinius correctly reads “everything in one’s own hand”; likewise Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, no. 7: *holographum*, etc.]  
**Olographa**, the whole document in one’s own hand.

[1165]  
**Olovitreum**, entirely made of glass.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1166. *Mappa*. Others *membrana*. From Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 130: *omentum*, etc.]  
**Omentum**, a cloth of the belly.

**Opersolatio**, said of things shut, from *persolae*.

[Note: [Col. 1363] 1168. Cerda: *oppessulatio*, closure, from *pessuli*, “bolts.” Graevius: *operculatis*, closed, from *opercula*, “covers.” Others *oppesulatis*, closed, from *pessuli*.]  
[Note: [Col. 1363] 1168. Or “by skill.” Semler: see above, so that we may be referred to the letter M, under *militaris*.]  
**Opinatores**, estimators, or military men by skill.  
**Opinax**, manifest.

[1170]  
[Note: [Col. 1364] 1170. Perhaps *opinosa certamina*, “great contests.”]  
**Opinosa**, great contests.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1171. Above, no. 508: *curcilla*, “a blockage.” Semler, instead of *curcilla*, restores *furcilla*, namely several small pieces of wood joined together and filled or blocked with merchandise.]  
**Opillago**, a blockage.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1172. *Oppito*. Read *oppido*, “very much,” and delete *sospito*, “I greet,” or transfer it elsewhere.]  
**Oppito**, I protect; I greet very warmly.

**Orcinus**, freed by death.  
**Ordinarius miles**, a soldier who is in proper order or number.

[1175]  
[Note: [Col. 1364] 1175. Reinesius: *urge, occide*, “press on, kill,” as a battle cry of soldiers charging. Semler: *orce* or *orcus*, without interpretation; and *occidit*, likewise without interpretation.]  
**Orge**, kill.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1176. Perhaps *oritus*.]  
**Oricus**, talkative, one who has a large mouth.

**Originarii**, natives.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1178. It seems that *crypta*, “a wedge,” should be read. “Crowd of people” was added because this is another meaning of *cuneus*, “wedge.” See above, *gumba*.]  
**Oripta**, mad, a crowd of people.

[Col. 1364] [1179]  
[Note: [Col. 1364] 1179. Understand *horispex*, “observer of hours.”]  
**Orispex**, observer of the hours.

[1180]  
**Ovispex**, observer of sheep.

## P
[Note: [Col. 1364] 1181. Understand *pavo* (“peacock”).] **Pabo**, a one-wheeled vehicle, with a *b*. **Pabulator**, a shepherd who provides fodder for oxen. **Pabulator**, a father who provides fodder.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1184. Graevius reads *pactorio*, *plantatorio*. Semlerus reads *pagatio*, *plantatio*.] **Pactario**, *plantario*.

[1185] [Note: [Col. 1364] 1185. *Paculum*. Rutgerius reads *phasculum*.] **Paculum**, a little sack, a little basket (*pasceolum*).

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1186. Semlerus: *pagae*, marble statues, idols, because *pago* is the same as *figo* (“I fix” or “set up”). Or rather, [they are called] *pagani* from a grove, or from idols.] **Pagae**, memorials without idols.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1187. Others read *vir* instead of *ut*. Semlerus gives *paganitius cultus* without interpretation.] **Paganitius**, as “hidden.”

[479] **Paganitius**, as “hidden.”

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1188. Semlerus: “or he plays a lyre,” namely, verses.] **Pagit**, either “he drives a stake” or “he touches a lyre.”

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1189. Others read *repagula*, “bridles”; others *sera* instead of *frena*.] **Pagula**, bridles.

[1190] **Pagus**, a college, a curia.

**Παλαιὸς μωρὸς νέον φρόνιμον οὐ ποιεῖ** — “An old fool does not make a young man wise.”

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1192. Read *pellax*, as in the *Excerpta*.] **Palax**, deceitful, treacherous.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1193. Graevius: *pallae lugubres*; perhaps *pallae pullae*, “mourning cloaks.” From Nonius.] **Palla**, hiding-places (*latubres*).

**Palmosus**, victorious.

[1195] **Palpones**, those who lead blind people.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1196. Correct *pluteum* instead of *palteum*.] **Palteum**, a wall or a pediment.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1197. See Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24, no. 15. *Mantum*, etc.] **Paludatis**, *mantuatis*.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1198. Others: *paemenicum*; others *paemaeum*.] **Pamaeum**, a shepherd’s garment.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1199. *Excipulum*, because it receives loaves.] **Panarium**, a receptacle.

[1200] [Note: [Col. 1364] 1200. *Panchra*; below, *panera* and *panora*, corruptly. See Nonius and the lexica, under *impancrare*. Semlerus connects this with *pancarpiae coronae* in Festus.] **Panchra**, plunder.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1201. Others read *pandox*, others *pando*, others *pantex*, from Plautus, for “intestines”; hence the Spanish *panza*. Others read *pandax*.] **Pandex**, one who always opens his mouth to drink.

**Panegyricis**, praiseworthy things.

**Panegyricus**, praise delivered extemporaneously.

[Note: [Col. 1364] 1204. *Panera*; rather, *panchra*, as above, or *pancra*.] **Panera**, plunder.

[1205] **Pangitare**, to praise.

[Col. 1365] [Note: [Col. 1365] 1206. *Panora*. Read as above, *panchra*.] **Panera**, plunder.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1207. *Ambibat*. Correct to *ambulat*.] **Pansa**, one who walked with his feet turned outward.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1208. Correct *pantapola*, “druggist.”] **Pantapola**, a druggist.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1209. Others read *papas*. It also occurs in this sense in the Acts of the Martyrs.] **Pappas**, a tutor who accompanies students.

[1210] [Note: [Col. 1365] 1210. *Suffusoria*. Graevius explains this as sauce, seasoning, or side dishes. Semlerus: vessels from which broth is poured over food during dinner. Others write *paropsides*.] **Parapsides**, serving vessels for pouring sauce.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1211. Sirmondus and others read *paropsis gavata*, or “a bowl.” See Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, no. 10.] **Parapsis**, a *granata* or a bowl (*catunis*).

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1212. *Particus*; others *partiarius*; others *particularius*; others *pararius*. For *qui partes*, Graevius reads *qui per partes*. For *agomanus*, Reinesius reads *dragomanus*. Semlerus: *aginans*, or *aginator*, as above under *mercator*.] **Particus**, a merchant who sells shares or portions, called an *institor* and an *agomanus*, because he conducts business in different directions. **Partiliter**, separately, by portions, distributively.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1214. *Praeclara*. Graevius reads *aprugna*, from the Scholiast on Juvenal. Semlerus thinks the gloss corrupted from *pastophorium*, “atrium.”] **Pastam**, excellent.

[1215] **Pastoforium**, the courtyard of a temple, or a sanctuary.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1216. Read *pastoforium* or *pastophorium*, “the temple-channel,” or *safarium*. *Safarium*, “courtyard,” occurs below.] **Pastorium**, the temple-channel, or *safurium*.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1217. Festus: *patagus*, a kind of disease. So also the *Excerpta Pithoei*, where Theophrastus and Pliny are cited. Reinesius proposed *petigo*.] **Patago**, a kind of dead person.

**Patercularius**, belonging to a little father.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1219. Perhaps *propatulum* or *peribulum*, from the notes at no. 304. Salmasius suspects that it was formerly written *paetibulum*, from which *patibulum* remained in some places and *peribulum* in others; but he prefers *peribulum*.] **Patibulum**, an open or exposed object.

[1220] [Note: [Col. 1365] 1220. *Fecit*. Graevius reads *egit*.] **Patravat**, he made a father.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1221. Perhaps *pater patriae*, without interpretation.] **Patres**, of the fatherland.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1222. *Patreus*; others *patrous*, from Greek.] **Patreus**, a stepfather.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1223. *Paximatum*; others *paxamatum*; others *paximatium*. Rosweydus finds no further occurrences of this bread elsewhere in the *Onomasticon*.] **Paximatum**, bread baked beneath hot ashes.

**Pecuosus**, one who has many cattle.

[Col. 1365] [1225] [Note: [Col. 1365] 1225. *Pedalis*. Rosweydus reads *pedulis*. Others *pedalis nodus*; others *pedica*, “a noose,” instead of *pedalis novus*. Compare the lexica.] **Pendana**, *-ae*, a new foot-piece sewn onto a boot.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1226. *Pegaso*; others *petaso*, so that it would be *perna*, *petaso*; then *verna*, *petaso*, “a joker,” would be corrupt.] **Pegaso**, a humorous or joking person.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1227. Others *proluvium*; others *perluvium*; others *praeluvium*.] **Pelagus**, a foretaste (*praelubium*).

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1228. *Pelops*; perhaps *pellicator* or *pellicatus*. Or *pelops* without interpretation; then *pellex*, “a man who has a wife and a mistress.”] **Pelops**, a man who has both a wife and a mistress.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1229. Others *poenula*, “a cloak,” *lacerna*, or *stola*.] **Pencina**, a fringe or a robe.

[1230] [Note: [Col. 1365] 1230. Semlerus distinguishes it as a royal hall or palace.] **Penita**, a royal hall.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1231. It seems that *pennum*, “sharp,” should be supplied: *bipennum*, “twice sharp.”] **Pennum**, twice sharp.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1232. Semlerus thinks the glosses arose from this single one: *pertaedet*, “it greatly wearies.”] **Percartapsere**, to divide greatly.

[Note: [Col. 1365] 1233. Semlerus thinks the glosses arose from this single one: *pertaedet*, “it greatly wearies.”] **Percataprat**, to be greatly wearied.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1234. *Peripsima*; others *peripsema*; some call it a shoe, others a cloth for wiping.] **Peripsima**, the middle of the sole of the foot.

[1235] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1235. *Pero*. Better, *perones*.] **Pero**, hairy footwear.

**Persolenter**, continually, assiduously.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1237. Read *pirula*, from Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 43. Pearls are also called *pirulae* or *perulae*; Spanish *perlas*, from *pilula*, “a little ball.”] **Perula**, the tip of the nose.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1238. Martinius changes *verbosus* to *perversus*. Semlerus supplies from the gloss under the letter V: “*Verbosos*, the worst of babblers.”] **Pessimus**, verbose.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1239. Correct *pestincius* to *pertinacius*, from the *Excerpta*.] **Pestincius**, more violently.

[1240] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1240. Others *pestinuntius*.] **Pestinuntium**, one who announces a plague.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1241. Semlerus: *partiliter*, “separately,” rejecting *dimisse*.] **Pestiliter**, humbly, separately.

**Petitius**, one who frequently asks.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1243. Others *petilus*. See Festus and Nonius.] **Petulus**, a horse with white feet.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1244. Graevius: *phascola*, “a purse.” — *Perna*, *petaso*.] **Phaculla**, a ham, a shoulder of pork, or a little shoulder of pork.

[1245] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1245. Correct *phagos* instead of *phago*.] **Phago**, food; hence **φάγος ἡμερινὸς ἄρτος καὶ τυρὸς καὶ οἶνος** — “*phagos*: daily bread, cheese, and wine” — [Col. 1366] in the *Life of the Monks*.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1246. *Carmina*, that is, incantations.] [481] **Phylacteria**, charms or incantations.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1247. It is also written *pitacium*, *pittacium*, and *pyctacium*; in a later period, *petia*. Hence the Spanish *pedazo*. See Rosweydus in the *Onomasticon*.] **Pictatium**, a short and small letter. **Pictatiuncula**, a small piece of parchment.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1249. Semlerus reads *pictiores*, “those who appear to excel in painting.”] **Pictiones**, those who surpass sellers in painting.

[1250] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1250. Semlerus reads *tigella*, an *artopta* in the German language.] **Pigella**, an *artopta*, a kind of vessel.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1251. *Pilasca*; see Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6, no. 2: “*Phlascae*,” etc.] **Pilasca**, a leather wine vessel.

**Pilax**, a mouse-catcher or a cat.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1253. *Pilax*, from *pilo*, “I plunder,” *furor*, “I steal,” *expilo*, “I strip.” Spanish *pillar*, *pillo*.] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1253. *Calamaucum*; others *camelaucium*; in Italian, *camauro*. Consult Macer in the *Hierolexicon*.] **Pileum**, a *calamaucum*, a tall ecclesiastical cap.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1254. Lipsius and others discuss *pilicrepus* extensively in their notes on Seneca’s Letter 56.] **Pilicrepus**, one who plays ball.

[1255] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1255. *Polotello*; rather, *pilotello*, from *pila*, “ball.”] **Piludius**, one who plays *polotello*.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1256. *Pilliones*. Corrupt, either from *vespillones* or from *pollinctores*.] **Piliones**, bearers of the dead.

**Pilumen**, anything that is pounded in a mortar.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1258. *Pindae* should be corrected to *pennae*.] **Pindae**: *pinnae* were said to derive from *pendendo*, “hanging,” but usage prevailed so that they are called *pinnae*.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1259. Correct *sectatores* to *secutores*, and compare Book XVIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 55. Some gladiators used to wear *pinnae*, as soldiers wore them on their helmets; hence *pinnirapus*.] **Pinnirapi**, followers, gladiators, because they snatch the *pinnae*.

[1260] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1260. Of hens, *pipare*, *pipire*, and *pipiare* are used, and perhaps also *pipilare*.] **Pipilare**, to resound.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1261. A poem about the nightingale. “The hawk *pipat*.” Concerning the hawk, or *acceptor*, Isidore, Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 7, no. 55, with note.] **Pipiunculus**, a hawk.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1262. Semlerus: *pipulo*, “with abuse,” or “with weeping.”] **Pipuli**, wept for with abuse.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1263. Other lexica more correctly have *pissaigra*, from Greek.] **Pissago**, liquid pitch.

[Note: [Col. 1366] 1264. An old lexicon: *pisema*, “a mirror.” Semlerus conjectures *pissaxera*, “dried pitch,” or *pissumor*, “I smear with pitch,” or *pissacium*, “a board made from pitch.”] **Pisseima**, I observe.

[1265] [Note: [Col. 1366] 1265. There are various conjectures. In the *Excerpta*, *pitigmata*, “headdresses”; Graevius, “the Macedonians’ *causiae* caps.” Semlerus: *pitisma*, “tasting,” or *aigmata*, “branding.” Jansonius: *aigmata*, “caustic substances.”] **Pitigmata**, caps.

**Placor**, tranquillity.

[Col. 1367] [Note: [Col. 1367] 1267. Perhaps “with thinner ears.” See Festus on *plaudae* or *plautae*, dogs.] **Plautos**, with slender ears and body.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1268. *Plaria*; rather, *plana*, “level.”] **Plaria**, clear.
