[Note: [Col. 1367] 1269. *Plaustri*. It should be read *plaustrit*, from *plaustrium*, “marshy,” which is found in other lexica.] **Plaustri**, that which sounds like a wagon.

[1270] [Note: [Col. 1367] 1270. Reverse the explanation: *plebescere*, “to imitate the common people”; *plebiscitari* or *plebiscitare*, “to address the common people.”] **Plebescere**, to address the common people.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1271. Reverse the explanation: *plebescere*, “to imitate the common people”; *plebiscitari* or *plebiscitare*, “to address the common people.”] **Plebiscitari**, to imitate the common people. **Plebiscitat**, he addresses the common people.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1273. *Calusi*. Read *callosi*, and compare the distinctions among the words in the appendices, no. 105: “Between *flemma* and *plemma*,” etc.] **Plemina**, when there are calloused furrows on the hands and feet.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1274. Semlerus: *ploti* instead of *plauti*; others *plocei*, “stuffed.”] [482] **Plotei**, proper.

[1275] **Lead in the eyes**, a lead-colored spot.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1276. Semlerus: *paedarius*, a very small boy, or a gouty, infirm person, especially in the feet.] **Podiarius**, among the mimes.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1277. Restore *polyandrion*, from other lexica.] **Polingon**, a place where corpses are laid. Greek.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1278. *Polose*, *polosus* are derived from *polus*.] **Polluctare**, to consecrate.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1279. *Polose*, *polosus* are derived from *polus*.] **Polose**, high.

[1280] **Polosus**, high.

**Pomatium**, a soft and liquid food made from apples or other fruit.

**Poneprope**, near and beside.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1283. Different kinds of eating houses: *meraria* or wine shops, *crustaria*, etc.] **Popina**, a wine shop, a pastry shop.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1284. *Basum*; correct to *prasum*, from Greek.] **Porrum**, *basum* [i.e. Greek *prasum*, “leek”].

[1285] [Note: [Col. 1367] 1285. *Portemia*, or *porthmia* or *porthmium*. See Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 26, where Semlerus wishes *scythici* or *sarmatici* to be read instead of “of Syrian origin.”] **Portemia**, a little boat.

**Portitorium**, a small portico (*porticulum*), a stick of camp-followers.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1287. Abbo Cernuus uses *positorem* for “architect.”] **Positiones**, buildings.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1288. Graevius reads *pontifices*.] **Postifices**, judges.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1289. *Postilio*, *postulatio*: words of the augurs, which interpreters say, with disagreement, refer to human sacrifice.] **Postilio**, a petition (*postulatio*).

[1290] [Note: [Col. 1367] 1290. Perhaps *pomarium*, “orchard.”] **Posmurium**, something inserted.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1291. Graevius: *postridie*, “on the following day.” Semlerus says that the following had been annotated: “yesterday, the following day, today,” from which the glossator was misled. But perhaps *postpridie*, “today,” should be retained. In the Gothic Missal, one of the prayers said daily is entitled *postpridie*.] **Postpridie**, today.

**Postulatitius**, one who asks.

**Postumus**, last, latest.

**Praeclues**, very bright and renowned.

[1295] [Note: [Col. 1367] 1295. *Praedarius*. The *Excerpta* have *pedarius*. Cerda and others: *praebendarius*. Semlerus: *praediarius*, “providing a pledge,” or assistance.] **Praedarius**, one who provides assistance.

[Note: [Col. 1367] 1296. *Praeluvium* should be read.] **Praelubium**, a flood.

[Col. 1367] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1297. Distributors were called *praerogatores* according to the Scholiast on Persius, because money used to be weighed rather than counted.] **Praerogator**, a distributor.

**Praetenta**, placed before.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1299. “In a ship”; perhaps *praetoriola* was formed from *navis praetoria*.] **Praetoriola**, a little house on a ship.

[1300] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1300. Rutgersius: *prandium*, a kind of food. Do not change anything.] **Prandeum**, a kind of belt.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1301. Others *promulsidarium*.] **Pransorium**, a *promulsarium*, a dish for appetizers.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1302. Restore from the Codex Constantianus: *prima peto*, “I seek the first place,” or *primum locum*, “the first place,” or *egregia exposco*, “I demand excellent things.”] **Prima porta**, the first place, or a Greek exposition.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1303. Servius on *Aeneid* I, “and they forbid [him] to stand on the first lands,” that is, on the shore.] **Prima terra**, the shore.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1304. Cerda: *clavarius*, one who is first in military service among the *virgae*. Semlerus retains *caballarius*.] **Primivirgius**, a cavalryman, because he is first in military service among the *virgines* [text uncertain].

[1305] **Privignus**, commonly, one born earlier.

**Procapibus**, nearest.

**Procapis**, nearest.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1308. We approved it; read *provocavimus*, from Festus under *procitum*.] **Procivimus**, we approved.

**Proculprocul**, very far away.

[1310] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1310. From “Away, away, you profane ones.”] **Proculum**, an abomination.

**Proculus**, one born while his father is far away abroad, or born far from his father.

**Prodactis**, consumed.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1313. “They proceeded”; or should it be “they advanced”?] **Profecta sunt**, they advanced.

**Proficiens**, placed in front, advanced.

[1315] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1315. Write *proliquere … proliquit*.] **Prolicere**, to flow out, to stream forth. Varro: “At last, when the sweet water has flowed forth.”

**Polumum**, a place of sacred things.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1317. Others *promptuaria*, bedrooms.] **Promptria**, sleeping quarters.

**Promulare**, a wall before a wall.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1319. From *pro nefas*, “against what is permitted,” “against justice.”] **Pronefas**, before what is permitted, contrary to permission.

[1320] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1320. Or *quam*; others *vel etiam*.] **Pronefas**, more than must not be said, or than unlawful.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1321. Perhaps *prorostra*, “before the speakers’ platform.”] **Pronefas**, crime, lack of restraint.

**Pronostra**, before ours.

**Propagando**, by extending.

[Col. 1368] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1324. Write *propola*.] **Propala**, one who puts goods up for sale.

[1325] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1325. Read *praepedit*, “hinders.”] **Propedat**, he hinders, restrains.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1326. Semlerus: *praetorii*, envoys, ministers, magistrates.] **Propii**, envoys who bring gifts to their mother.

**Propolae**, shopkeepers.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1328. Others *praepos* and *praeposcit*.] **Propos**, very powerful.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1329. Others *praepos* and *praeposcit*.] **Proposcit**, he asks.

[1330] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1330. Read *pro pudor*, “O shame!”—an outcry, confusion, or interjection.] **Propudorio**, a beating together [text uncertain].

**Prosatrix**, mother.

**Protelat**, postpones, prolongs.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1333. “Running ahead”; others “managing,” omitting *et anteambulo*.] **Proxeneta**, a man who runs ahead of any business.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1334. “Running ahead”; others “managing,” omitting *et anteambulo*.] **Proxeneta**, as if an intermediary between buyer and seller, or a man who goes ahead.

[1335] **Prurientes auribus**, those who eagerly desire to hear something bad about another person.

**Pubeta**, or *pubeda*, a young man.

**Pugillones**, boxers.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1338. It may be read *pulpido*, *colyphia*, or *coliphia*.] **Pulpidinem**, *colophia*.

**Pulpitum**, a lectern, a reading stand.

[1340] [Note: [Col. 1368] 1340. *Pulvicinare*; others *pluvitare*; others omit it.] **Pulvicinare**, to rain frequently.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1341. Read *pulvinaria*, “open areas”; see above, *Ariae*.] **Pulvinceria**, a burial-ground.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1342. Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 11, no. 3: *Punicani*, etc.] **Punicani**, little beds.

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1343. It is conjectured to be *purpur*, that place outside the gate where people dressed in purple were born; or *purpura*, the part of the palace used by imperial women in childbirth.] **Purpurilla**, a place outside the gate where they wore purple clothing.

**Puteal**, the seat of the praetor.

[1345] **Puticuli**, places into which corpses are thrown.

## Q

[Note: [Col. 1368] 1346. Two small coins. From Jerome, chapter 5 on Matthew.] **Quadrans**, two small coins.

**Quaestuarius**, one who lives by earnings from his body.

**Quaestuosus**, **ποριστής** (“one who acquires or provides”).

[Col. 1369] **Quantocius**, as quickly as possible.

[1350] **Querelantem**, bringing complaints.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1351. The festival of Minerva was called *quinquatrus*, by others *quinquatria* and *quinquatriae*. The glossator perhaps took this from the Scholiast on Juvenal, according to whom Minerva was within a circuit of five courtyards or porticoes.] **Quinquatria**, a circuit of five porticoes.

## R

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1352. Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22, no. 23: *Ralla*, etc. It is believed to be a diminutive of *radula*. See also the *Rule of the Monks*, chapter 18. A garment is a shorn covering, etc.] **Rallum**, a scraping or shaving tool.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1353. *Randum*. Read *rendum*, from *reor*, “I think.”] **Randum**, something to be judged.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1354. Perhaps *ratificent*, “let them declare” or “pronounce.”] **Raricent**, they speak as patricians.

[1355] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1355. It should be written *rati sunt* instead of *ratiscunt*.] **Ratiscunt**, they estimated.

**Rator**, a judge.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1357. *Ravie*; rather, *rauce*.] **Ravit**, he speaks hoarsely.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1358. *Reburrus*; or “from *birrus*”?] **Reburrus**, bristly.

**Receptor**, an intermediary who establishes reconciliation.

[1360] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1360. *Recidua*; better *recidiva*.] **Recidua**, things regenerated from a ruin.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1361. Graevius: a recognized son whom the father acknowledged as his son.] **Recitabulum**, a place where something is recited.

**Recognatus**, a son acknowledged by his father.

**Rectitas**, justice, fairness, and truth.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1364. From Festus, Nonius, and others.] **Redandruare**, to return a favor.

[1365] **Redhibere**, to give back.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1366. Write *reduvias*, as in *exuvias*.] **Redimiae**, things bought back from robbers.

**Redimicula**, ribbons with which a mitre is tied.

**Redubias**, remnants.

**Reducta concava**, hollowed-out depressions.

[1370] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1370. Semlerus: *rogulus* instead of *redulus*.] **Redulus**, a pile of burning wood.

[Col. 1369] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1371. Semlerus: “he repels with his forehead.”] **Refrontat**, he repels from the forehead.

**Regillus**, a little king.

**Regimonium**, government.

**Remasculata**, restored with manly strength.

[1375] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1375. Restore *remiligines* from Festus.] **Remilicines**, things that delay.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1376. Festus: *remillum* is said as though from *repandum*. For *pronullo*, Graevius reads *prominulo*. Perhaps *remillo* comes from *remus*, and likewise in the following entry, *remillus*.] **Remillo**, I spread out, I project forward.

**Remillus**, spread out, projecting forward.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1378. Perhaps *remoramentum*, as in other lexica.] **Remotum**.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1379. It seems it should be read *resides*, “resting, idle.”] **Rendis**, idle rest.

[1380] **Repatriat**, he returns to his homeland.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1381. *Repelta*. Papias: *repeta*. Semlerus: *rupella* or *rupicula*.] **Repella**, a lofty stone.

**Repignerat**, he receives a pledge.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1383. See no. 682, *exundantibus*.] **Repluentibus**, overflowing.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1384. For *species*, read *vestis*, or “the appearance of a garment.”] **Replum**, the appearance of a woman.

[1385] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1385. *Retanda*. From Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, chapter 17.] **Retanda**, things to be cleansed.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1386. Martinius: *ridica*, by which wood is raised; others *redica*; others *retica*, wood by which tied wood is raised. *Retica* is a support for strengthening vines.] **Retica ligna**, wood by which wood is raised.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1387. *Revidare*; others *rebitere*; others *reviare*.] **Revidare**, to return, go back, or retrace one’s steps.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1388. Write *rheuma*.] **Rheuma**, the outflow of the sea, when, at high tide, water gathers in ditches and remains there.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1389. *Remidia*, “I tremble”; Semlerus thinks the whole entry corrupt from *repedo*.] **Rimidia**, a bank or raised edge.

[1390] [Note: [Col. 1369] 1390. Martinius: *rinas*, “nostrils,” or *nasa*, from Greek.] **Rinas**, ships, or a mass.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1391. *Roga*. Ducange supplies examples.] **Roga**, alms.

**Rogatarius**, a petitioner.

[Note: [Col. 1369] 1393. *Ructa*. Hence *ructare*. See *rumen* in the lexica. The printed editions have *ructa* or *frumen*.] **Ructa**, or *rumen* in a human being, *tumen* in an animal: the part of the throat next to the uvula.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1394. *Rues*, like *labes*, *lues*, *strues*.] **Rues**, ruin.

[Col. 1370] [1395] **Ruffatus**, stained with blood.

**Rumare**, to bring rumors.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1397. This seems corrupt from *runa*, “spear,” *runata*, “speared.”] **Runa**, battle.

**Runata**, fought.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1399. *Rupa*. Martinius: *rupta*, that is, cliffs of mountains.] **Rupa**, sharp on both sides.

[1400] [Note: [Col. 1370] 1400. *Rupina*. It occurs in Apuleius.] **Rupinas**, mountain cliffs.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1401. *Ruspantur*. From Nonius and Festus.] **Ruspantur**, they search out anxiously.

## S
[Note: [Col. 1370] 1402. *Sabarium*. Shortly afterward, *safarium*. Some restore *pastophorium*; others *sabarium*, a temple storeroom.] **Sabarium**, temple courtyard. Chaldean.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1403. Semler again here reads *sabarium*, “storeroom.” Barthius derives it from German *Saba*, “moth,” and interprets it as “full of spiders,” or “spider-infested.”] **Sabbatini**, of spiders.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1404. *Sacra*; perhaps *sarga*, from Lombardic *arga*, “useless.” Others read *sargo* or *sarco*, from *sarcire*, “to mend,” as in *sarco sutorius*, *sarco sartorius*, “a tailor who repairs,” but useless for new work. Barthius reads *scurra* for *sacra*.] **Sacra**, an unsuitable practitioner of his own craft.

[1405] **Safarium**, temple courtyard.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1406. Graevius reads *sagda*; Semler, *saga*, a woman’s name. In the *Excerpta*, the name of a spirit.] **Saga**, the name of a gem.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1407. Others read *soldarius*; others *salariarius*; others, better, *spatharius*.] **Salatarius**, a bearer of arms.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1408. Barthius reads *sambucinarius*, “one who plays the *sambuca*,” or *sambucinarius*, a kind of flute-player. Others read *canit* (“he sings”) for *dixit* (“he said”).] **Salmentum**, salted provisions.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1409. Papias: *Sambucistria*, “a woman who plays the rustic harp.”] **Sambuciarius**, the one who speaks.

[1410] [Note: [Col. 1370] 1410. Graevius reads *sambucista*; Semler, *sambucer*, “actor, dancer.”] **Sambucistria**, a woman who plays the harp. **Sambucistrio**, a dancer. **Sambucus**, a dancer.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1413. *Samelubro*. In the *Excerpta*: *saurilubro*, *saurilubre*. Barthius reads *sat elaboro*, “I work very diligently,” or *artifico*, “I manufacture.” Semler, *samia*, “earthenware vessels.”] **Samelubro**, by craftsmanship.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1414. *Samica*; rather, *samia*.] **Samica**, dust.

[1415] [Note: [Col. 1370] 1415. Reinesius reads *sicinissat*, from Greek *scinis*, a kind of dance. Cerda reads *encaenissat*, as though from *encaeniat*. Semler, *sambucissat*. Barthius, *saracenissat*, namely “triumphing over the Saracens.”] **Sancenissat**, he rejoices, he triumphs.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1416. Barthius reads *sappa*, “dregs”; Semler, *sappa*, as though “a hoe,” or *sappa*, “with which one hoes,” that is, digs; or *sarpa*, *sarculus*, “a small hoe.” Hence *sarpo*, *sarpere*.] **Sappappa**, as though “with a hoe.”

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1417. Barthius reads *subripia*; others, *subreptio*. Semler thinks this gloss arose from the preceding *sarpa*.] **Sarapia**, of robberies.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1418. *Sarcitator*; rather *sarcitector*, from Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, no. 2.] **Sarcitator**, one who repairs roofs.

[Note: [Col. 1370] 1419. *Sardius*, without interpretation. Then another gloss transferred here: *sacella*, “small shrines,” sacred places.] **Sardius**, small shrines, sacred places.

[Col. 1371] [1420] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1420. *Sarge*. See *sacra*, no. 1404. Barthius investigates a German origin in *sorge*.] **Sarge**, suitable for any craft; elsewhere *sarga*, an unsuitable practitioner of any craft. **Sario**, with a hoe.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1422. *Uxoriosum*; perhaps *luxoriosum*. See Book II of the *Differentiae*, tome V, no. 398.] **Savium**, a marital kiss.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1423. *Saures*; perhaps *saurices*.] **Saures**, shrew-mice.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1424. Distinguish *pumicea*, “pumice-like,” from *aspera*, “rough.”] **Scabra**, rough pumice.

[1425] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1425. *Scaevitas*, a word of Apuleius.] **Scaevitas**, injustice.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1426. Graevius: *scabillum*, an instrument of a musician. Semler: *scabillum symphoniaci*, without interpretation. Perhaps from *scabillum* the Spanish word *cascabel* is derived. Salmasius: *scabillum*, a musical instrument, from Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22, no. 14. Barthius reads *scamellum*, where musicians are.] **Scamellum**, of a musician. **Scammata**, arenas where athletes wrestle.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1428. Correct *scena* in place of *scana*.] **Scana**, excessive density of trees.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1429. Martinius reads *scansile* for *scansuae*.] **Scansuae**, the iron by which a horse climbs.

[1430] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1430. Others read *scapulium*.] **Scapolum**, a long staff.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1431. See Nonius, chapter 2.] **Scapus**, a fixed number of gatherings of written paper.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1432 and following. Semler: *scabies sicca*, “impetigo, itching, leprosy.” Perhaps *sarna* for *scaturrio*, *scatus*, from Book IV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 8, no. 6: “impetigo,” etc.] **Scaturrio**, leprosy. **Scatus**, impetigo, dry scabies.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1434. Read *exceptoria*, as above.] **Sceptoriae**, cisterns.

[1435] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1435. *Scillae*. From Scylla, which is sometimes hidden. Or “reefs”?] **Scillae**, rocks hidden in the sea.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1436. *Scinthiae*; perhaps *stigmatia*. Or *cymbia*, ships, small boats.] **Scinthlae**, a birthmark, a spot. **Scipio**, a staff carried before triumphators. **Scipiones**, the consuls’ staffs.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1439. Barthius: *scissiatum*, *instratum*, *lithostratum*, *lapatum*, or *lapidatum*. Reinesius: *licospadum*, or *lycospadum*, “wolf-colored”; others, *crispatum*, *jubatum*.] **Scispadum**, crested.

[1440] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1440. See Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 10, no. 5: *Funalia*, etc.] **Scolaces**, what we call rope-lights (*funalia*), because they are *scoliae*, that is, twisted; the Romans called them ropes and *funalia*.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1441. Correctly, in the *Excerpta*, *sculna*, “sponsor,” from Gellius, Book XX, chapter 10.] **Sconna**, a bridegroom.

[Col. 1371] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1442. *Scordalus*, a word of Seneca and others.] **Scordalus**, fierce.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1443 and following. Perhaps *scortiscum*.] **Scordiscum**, raw hide. **Scordiscum**, a harlot.

[1445] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1445. Perhaps *scoriones*, or *scurrae*.] **Scories**, fools, dullards, simpletons. **Scorio**, a foolish, silly man.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1447. *Screa*; hence *excreare*.] **Screa**, phlegm.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1448. *Scriba*. See above, *aedilitius*.] **Scriba aedilitius**, one who belongs to an aedile, so called from the office of aedile.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1449. *Scribula*; perhaps *schedula*.] **Scribula**, a letter.

[1450] [Note: [Col. 1371] 1450. Graevius: also *scripulatur* or *scrupulatur*, “is troubled.”] **Scripula**, a letter; also, *scripula*, “one who causes anxiety.”

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1451. The Wednesday before Easter was the day of the scrutiny, or catechetical examination.] **Scrutinium**, that in which infants are examined.

[Note: [Col. 1371] 1452. *Scrutitum*. Read *scorteum*, or *scortisca*, “leather.”] **Scrutitum**, leather.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1453. In Festus, *scrutillus*.] **Scrutulus**, a stuffed little stomach. **Scurra**, a parasite, a table-companion.

[1455] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1455. *Incopriatur*. A *scurra* was called a *coprea*. See Becmann, p. 1026.] **Scurra**, one who is covered with dung.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1456. *Sebra*. Correct, from other glossaries, *scabra*.] **Sebra**, old.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1457. Or “the seizure of property.” Graevius: *sectio*, “sale of property.” Perhaps “seller of property.”] **Sector**, an usurper, or seizure of property.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1458. *Fert*. The *Excerpta* more correctly read *facit*.] **Securicularius**, one who carries axes. **Secus**, evil.

[1460] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1460. *Semestria*; perhaps *semestris*.] **Semestria**, a book containing proceedings for six months. **Semiermis**, without weapons.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1462. Correct *semiustus*, “half-burned.”] **Semijustus**, half of a just man. **Semivecors**, “very slightly mad,” from *vecors*, “mad.”

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1464. The *Excerpta* read *semunia*, “sadness.” Martinius, *senium*, “sadness.” Semler, *semnia*, “ascetic houses.”] **Sennumia**, sadness.

[1465] **Sententia**, ἀπόφασις (*apophasis*), a judgment. **Sentes**, a firm judgment and an indisputable answer, ἐπιφώνημα (*epiphonema*), an exclamatory conclusion.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1467. Alvarus of Córdoba uses the word *sension* in the *Indiculus luminosus*, no. 25: “Let no bold presumer dare, unless a price has been paid, to presume to purchase the *sension* which inherent necessity demands, whatever the circumstance”; where *sension* seems to indicate “permission,” unless *sessio* should be restored. For the discussion concerns open places in which fairs were held, which the Muslims sold.] **Sensio**, a judgment.

[Col. 1372] **Sentitare**, to discern gradually in the mind. **Separ**, separately, on one side.

[1470] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1470. Persius, Satire 3, verse 12.] **Sepia**, ink. Persius.

**Sequela**, an example. **Servitium**, a multitude of slaves, and the service of free persons. **Sextertiarius**, one who pays out.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1474. Others read *clunaculum* for *cluniculus*, and *spathona* for *splendona*.] **Sica**, a little buttock, a sword, a *splendona*.

[1475] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1475. *Ramorum*. Read *armorum*. For *vidubii*, perhaps *venabuli*, “hunting spear,” or *sibunae*, which is a kind of hunting spear.] **Sica** is a kind of branch, similar to a *vidubium*. Those who practice brigandage among the Italians use it especially.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1476. *Silo*, a word of Plautus. It is also called *silus*.] **Silo**, with a cut-off or retracted nose.

**Simfoniaci**, musical singers.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1478. Correct *semiplagium*, from other glossaries.] **Simplagium**, a smaller net.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1479. Guests were also called *simplones*. *Simpulum* is a vessel used in sacrifices.] **Simpulator**, a friend of the bridegroom who remains constantly with him at the banquet.

[1480] **Simpulator**, a banqueter.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1481. *Simultum*. Others read *simulta*. Concerning this worm, see Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, no. 10: “The ram,” etc.] **Simultum**, a worm in a ram’s horn.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1482. Supply: “speaking in gasps,” one who speaks as though through the opening of the throat.] **Singultim**, one who speaks through the throat.

**Sinum**, a vessel in which butter is made.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1484. *Sirascula*; others *situla*; others *sitiscula*; others *siticula*; others *sitella*. In the *Catholicus*, *soriscula*. Rosweyd, in the *Onomasticon*, under *Suriscula* or *Syriscula*, affirms that many used the word for a vessel.] **Sirascula**, a water vessel.

[1485] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1485. *Stringina*. Graevius changes it to *stranguria*, against the other witnesses. The order of the letters favors *stringina*.] **Stringina**, retention of urine.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1486. From Festus, *sispes* for *sospes*.] **Sispes**, safe, healthy.

**Solerare**, that is, to make solid; from *solus*, *soleris*, that is, “solid.”

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1488. *Sonticus*. From Nonius, Festus, and others.] **Sonticus**, truthful.

[Note: [Col. 1372] 1489. Perhaps *sorbillator*, “taster.”] **Sortillator**, a glutton.

[1490] [Note: [Col. 1372] 1490. Reinesius: one who judges by lot; Semler: one who sees by lot.] **Sortinidus**, one who judges by lot.

[Col. 1373A] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1491. Horace mentions the Sosii more than once.] **Sosii**, two brothers who bought good books and later, after preparing them, made considerable profit by selling them.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1492. Martinius corrected *spargana*, “the beginnings of infancy.” Perhaps this refers to rattles.] **Spargana**, beginnings, infancy.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1493. *Spoliaria*. See Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, no. 41: *Apodyterium*, etc.] **Spoliaria**, the outer rooms of bathhouses.

**Sputarium**, spittle.

[1495] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1495. Semler conjectures *stannare*, from Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22, no. 1, “The etymology of tin,” etc., as I noted at that passage.] **Stagnare**, to separate mixed metals.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1496. *Statio*, “harbor,” seems correct. But Barthius thinks it is *stamio*, “cloth,” from *stamen*, “thread.” Hence *stamina*, Spanish *stamena*.] **Stamio**, birth.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1497. See Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25, no. 16: *Stater*, etc.] **Stater**, two didrachmas.

**Stellionatus**, a crime in which one thing is sold to two people. **Sternaces**, fearful.

[1500] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1500. It is written *stigia*, *stichia*, *striga*, *sticia*, and hence *stica*. It is Greek *stichia* or *stichium*. The following glosses derive from this.] **Stica**, a tunic. **Stigia**, a tunic. **Stigina**, royal ornaments. **Stigium**, a kind of clothing.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1504. Semler: *stliquadrum*, “square”; because *st* and *stl* were often prefixed, as in *stlocum* for *locum* and *stlitem* for *litem*.] **Stilinquadrum**, that is, square.

[1505] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1505. In Festus, *stlataria* is a kind of broad ship; hence the form with prefixed *st*, as in the preceding gloss. Here, *navis* may be read for *vestis*.] **Stlataris**, a pirate’s garment.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1506. Read *sternaces*, “fearful,” as above, from *sterno*; hence *sternaces* of horses.] **Strauaces**, greedy.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1507. Read *strio* for *histrio*, as *Spania* is used for *Hispania*.] **Strigio**, a stage mime.

**Strofarius**, deceitful, an impostor, a fraud. **Stultomalus**, a bad fool.

[1510] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1510. Graevius: *succendia*. Semler: *succensiva*; others *subcentia*. See above, *Fomenta*.] **Subcensia**, fomentations.

**Subcenturiatus** is said of one who succeeds in the former number, as though in place of his own century.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1512. *Subcisivus*. Semler: *succensivus*, or *suggestivus*. See Book X of the *Etymologies*, no. 131: *Incentor*, etc.] **Subcisivus**, a bad interpreter.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1513. *Subcus*; perhaps *subcutitus* and *intercutitus* for *intercus*.] **Subcus**, subcutaneous; **subcirratus** [uncertain]; **intercus**, between the skin; **intercutatus**, between the skins; **subtercus**, beneath the skin, subcutaneous.

[Col. 1373] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1514 and following. See Becmann, p. 1036, besides Festus and the glossaries.] **Sublestia**, weakness, sadness.

[1515] **Sublestis**, weak, sad.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1516. Write *submeies*; it is also called *submeiulus*.] **Submeles**, one who urinates in his little bed, a *meles*. **Subles**, one who sits beneath.

**Sububeres**, infants who are still at the breast.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1519. *Auribus*. Read *cruribus*. Then *subrogatus*, or rather *suffragatus*, “substituted,” etc.] **Suffraginatus**, with broken legs, or substituted in the place of one who has fallen.

[1520] [Note: [Col. 1373] 1520. *Sugrudia*; perhaps *suggrundia*, the projecting ends of a roof that keep rain away from the wall.] **Sugrudia**, foundations.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1521. *Suggrundaria* were called the graves of infants.] **Sugrundaria**, graves.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1522. Semler: *salitor*, “one who leaps,” or *sultor*, and conversely.] **Sultor**, a cultivator.

**Sumptuarius**, one who pays expenses.

[Note: [Col. 1373] 1524. Perhaps *suppetium*.] **Supedium**, refuge.

[1525] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1525. Graevius: *suppara*, a ship’s sail.] **Supera**, a ship.

**Superaria**, a garment worn over another. **Supparant**, they supply.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1528. Read *superaria*, as above.] **Suppararia**, a garment worn over another.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1529. Others read *supes*, *suppis*, that is, “beneath”; others *supes*, *suppes*, that is, “under the soles of the feet.”] **Supes**, *supumpis*, that is, with the feet turned upward.

[1530] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1530. *Suprema*, that is, “the supreme storm,” from Festus.] **Suprema**, when the sun is suppressed.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1531. Cerda: *succenset*, “he is angry”; others *surculatur*, “is born.”] **Surcetur**, he becomes angry.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1532. Graevius: *surus*, a tree shoot.] **Surus**, a muscle of the arms.

**Surus**, a tree shoot.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1534. Read *subses*, “fit for sitting beneath.”] **Susses**, one who is fit for sitting beneath.

[1535] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1535. Better *sururro*; for *senillosus*, others read *sententiosus*, others *senticosus*.] **Susurrio**, old, bilingual.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1536. More correctly *subtella*, like *postella* and *antella*.] [490] **Sutela**, a strap stretched beneath a horse’s tail.

[Col. 1374] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1537. Correct to *sutrinum*. For *species*, perhaps “garments.”] **Sutrium**, a place where certain garments are sewn.

# T

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1538. Semler: *tabani*, “flies.”] **Tabae**, gnats.

**Tabernio.**

[1540] **Tagax**, a boil.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1541. *Talax*; from the scholiast on Horace, Book I, Satire 3.] **Talax**, bandy-legged.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1542. Vulcanius: *talitrus*, a callus or a corn on the heel.] **Talitius**, a blow on the heel.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1543. Read “a gaming-piece on a board.”] **Tallus**, a gaming-piece, a board.

**Tam nefas**, such a wicked, such a detestable deed.

[1545] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1545. *Tames*; rather *tabes* or *tabus*.] **Tames**, gore, blood.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1546. It is also called *tarmes*, *termes*, or *termus*.] **Tarmus**, worms in flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1547. Others read *tartareum* or *tartarinum*.] **Tartarium**, horrible.

**Tautones**, eyelids.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1549. See below, *tugellaria*.] *(In other copies)* **Tegellaria**, a sorceress.

[1550] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1550. Better *tergora*, *tergus*.] **Tegora**, *tegus*, the hides or backsides of beasts of burden.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1551. Perhaps *telonium*. See Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, no. 45. Graevius: *telones … conductor*.] **Telonem**, as though the fiscal lease of all tolls.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1552. *Tenere*; more correctly *teneri*.] **Tenilis**, one who can hold.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1553. *Terimentum*. Semler: *intetrimentum*, from Plautus.] **Terimentum**, nourishment.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1554. Graevius: *toral* or *torale*; Semler: *talare*.] **Terrale**, a kind of garment.

[1555] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1555. Pithoeus suspects *terripiscinae*. Semler: *terricipinae* or *terricipia*, unless the word is corrupt from *terrigenae*, without interpretation, in which case the gloss was fabricated by some ignorant person.] **Terrigiponae**, things that catch earth, that is, pools, which country people also call ponds.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1556. *Testinium*. Correct to *tempestivum*.] **Testinium**, opportune, suitable.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1557. Perhaps *togae*, “the stripe of a toga,” or *tunicae*, “the stripe of a tunic.”] **Thoca**, yellow, or a garment.

[1560] [Note: [Col. 1374] 1558. Graevius: *triarii*.] **Tiaries**, divisions of standards.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1559. Perhaps the sword-belt, namely the *balteus*.] **Tinctorium**, a sword.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1560. *Rudinem*. Correct to *rudimen* or *rudimentum*.] **Tironatum**, a beginning.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1561. The *Excerpta* have *tironizare*; correct to *tirocinari*.] **Tironicare**, to serve as a soldier.

[Note: [Col. 1374] 1562. Perhaps *titinnitus*, “a clang,” etc. Graevius: *titinniens clangor*, “a ringing clang.”] **Titiensis clangor**, that is, a sound accompanied by tumult.

[Col. 1375] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1563. Semler: *tatus*. A gaming-piece was called *computus* from pebbles, because they are arranged there; for *calx* is a stone, etc.] **Tocuis**, a gaming-piece called *computus*, made from pebbles because they are arranged there. For *calx* means “stone,” and *calculus* is its diminutive.

**Togillatim**, individually.

[1565] **Togipurium**, a plain toga.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1566. *Tollerunt*. Read *tulerunt*.] **Tollerunt**, they begot.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1567. Semler corrects to *suggillatim* for *sigillatim*, because Tongilius, from whom these adverbs derive, mocked those who met him.] [491] **Tongillatim**, one by one.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1568. Semler corrects to *suggillatim* for *sigillatim*, because Tongilius, from whom these adverbs derive, mocked those who met him.] **Tongillatim loqui**, to speak with vicious words. The expression derives from Tongilius, a parasite who had discovered in this a way of provoking laughter: when greeted, he replied with an insult, and addressed the insulter with the greatest sweetness.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1569 and following. When the subject is a fishing net and dragnet, *trahum*, from *traho*, is preferable; when vegetables are meant, *tragus*.] **Tragum**, a kind of fishing net.

[1570] **Tragum**, among vegetables. **Tragum**, a dragnet.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1572. Others read *trichile* or *trichilia*, plural; others *trichila*, singular. Compare Forcellinus. Semler: *vites*; others *uvae* for *vaciae*.] **Trictilia**, where *vaciae* hang.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1573. Graevius: *trepidat*, “trembles”; *tremiscit*, “quakes”; *horret*, “shudders.” Semler: *Trivia*, Proserpina, or *trimata*, “after three years.”] **Trimitat**, afterbirth.

**Tritile**, something that can be ground.

[1575] **Trochus**, a wheel used in play.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1576. *Trocinus*; others *trochiscus* or *trocisus*. See Book IV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 9, no. 16, from which a dry kind of juice should be read here.] **Trocinus**, a kind of dry juice.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1577. Reinesius emends to *tubi*, “underground tubers.” Graevius: *tuberes* or *tubera*, “underground foods.”] **Tuber**, an underground root.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1578. The scholiast on Persius, Satire 2: *Tucetum*, seasoned beef among the Alpine Gauls. Semler gathers from other glossaries that *edulia* (“foods”) should be read for *bubula* (“beef”) and *bula*.] **Tucetum**, seasoned food among the Alpine Gauls.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1579. Read *tegularia*, “sorceresses.”] **Tugellaria**, sorceries, because they sacrifice above roof tiles.

[1580] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1580. Perhaps corrupt from *tongillatim*, “piecemeal,” that is, “individually,” concerning which see no. 1566. Others read *falcatum*, “cut”; others *titulatum*, “covered”; others *tilptalium*, “cut piece of linen.” See Ducange under *tilpatalium*.] **Tuligatum**, cut up.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1581. Semler, from the Constance manuscript, restores *meditullia*, “the middle regions of the earth.”] **Tullia**, middle, or royal.

**Tuore**, by sight.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1583. Vulcanius: *gutturilla* and *gutturi* for *turturi*, and *pani* for *panem*. Others retain *turtur illa* and read at the end “that is, of a tavern,” or “that is, of the penis.”] **Turturilla**, thus was called a place where corrupt practices took place, because there the *turtur* was served, that is, bread.

[Col. 1375] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1584. One might read *tus*, “pollen,” or *manna*.] **Tuspollem**, manna, or a kind of spice.

# V

[1585] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1585. *Vabra*: correct to *vafer*; and in the following number *vafrum* for *vabrum*.] **Vabra**, clever, artful. **Vabrum**, varied, many-formed.

**Vadatur**, he promises, pledges, gives his word.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1588. In place of *vadere*, it would be preferable to read *vadare* or *vadari*, the latter being better.] **Vadimonia**, legal proceedings, in which one may appear before a judge through a surety. **Vadimonium facit**, he provides a surety.

[1590] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1590. *Vaginatus*. Perhaps *evaginatus*, “drawn out.”] **Vaginatus**, driven away.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1591. *Vagitatur*; others *vagitat*.] **Vagitatur**, he weeps violently.

**Vagurrit**, he wanders about at leisure.

[Note: [Col. 1375] 1593. Vulcanius: “with feet projecting in opposite directions.” Semler: “with legs turned outward.”] **Valgis**, turned outward, swollen.

**Valitant**, they are strong.

[1595] [Note: [Col. 1375] 1595. Semler conjectured *vallica*, that is, *phallica*, *ithyphallica*. But the genuine reading is *vallematia*, or *ballematia*, or *ballimatia*; Ducange discusses the word under *balare* and believes it should be written *ballismatia*. See the note on Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22, no. 11.] **Vallemac pia**, indecent songs, shameful poems, and obscene jokes.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1596. *Vani parentes*; from Servius on the *Aeneid*.] **Vani parentes**, empty, deceitful, useless, deceiving parents.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1597. Read *vara vibia*, “poles,” etc. In place of *vibia*, *varam* follows; in Ausonius it is *vara vibiam*, but Scaliger prefers the reading of the gloss because *vara* is an upright pole and *vibia* a crosspiece.] **Varam tibiam janam**, two poles fastened together, which support a beam. Hence the proverb: “The *vibia* follows the *vara*.”

**Ventriloqui**, enchanters.

**Varicat**, he turns aside, he walks.

[1600] **Varicavit**, he walked.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1601. *Vascillum*. The glossator intended *vasillum*, from the cited verse, not of Macrobius but of Marbode, chapter 18, on heliotrope:

“Which is placed in water in a small vessel beneath the sun’s rays.”

Marbode lived around the year 1123; this provides some indication concerning additions to these glosses.] **Vascillum**, a small vessel.

Macrob.: “Releasing the rays, in water placed beneath in a small vessel.”

[Col. 1376] **Vatia**, with different plants.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1603. *Vefaba*: here *ve* signifies “small”; elsewhere it signifies “badly.”] **Vefaba**, a small bean.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1604. Read *vehiculorum*, or *vehiculum*, from other glossaries.] **Vehigelorum**, a kind of river boat among the Gauls.

[1605] **Veneripeta**, lustful.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1606. *Venitia*. Rather, *venilia*.] **Venitia**, the swelling of the sea that comes toward the shore. Varro: “*Venitia*, the wave that comes to the shore; *salatia*, the wave that returns to the sea.”

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1607. Read *vafer*, “clever, shrewd, changeable, deceitful.”] **Vepra**, clever, a witness, of varying appearance.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1608. Perhaps *sonticus*, “truthful.” See no. 1488.] **Verax**, truthful, reliable, faithful.

**Verbosus**, a very bad trifler.

[1610] **Verbo tenus**, for example.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1611. Semler: *verna cellarius*, one who wakes the monks on feast days. Cerda: *vernacellus* (*vernaculus*), one who makes rounds during the spring days.] **Vernacellus**, one who wakes people on feast days.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1612. As though *vespelio* came from *sepelire*, “to bury,” and *vespilo* from *spoliare* or *expilare*, “to strip or plunder.”] **Vespeliones**, gravediggers who bury the dead.

**Vespertilio**, late, evening.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1614. As though *vespelio* came from *sepelire*, “to bury,” and *vespilo* from *spoliare* or *expilare*, “to strip or plunder.”] **Vespilla**, a visitor of tombs.

[1615] [Note: [Col. 1376] 1615. Perhaps *vestis*, “garment,” or *barba*, “beard,” from Servius on Virgil:

“Golden their hair, and golden their garment.”

Or *vestibula*, “vestibules,” *valvae*, “doors.”] **Vestiae**, stammering women.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1616. *Erogatorium*, namely a place where garments are distributed.] **Vestiarium**, a place of distribution.

**Vestiplica**, a woman who folds garments.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1618. *Tonis*; Cerda reads *histrionis*, “of an actor.”] **Vestis ludiaria**, theatrical, belonging to an actor, *tonis*.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1619. Semler: “clever in circumvention.”] **Veteratricem**, that is, clever, not to be circumvented.

[1620] [493] [Note: [Col. 1376] 1620. *Vexillaia*. Semler: *vexillatio*. For *carrorum*, Graevius reads *castrorum*.] **Vexillaia**, a powerful charge of wagons.

**Victimo**, I sacrifice.

**Vidubium**, a woman who has lost two husbands.

**Viduvium**, widowhood.

[Note: [Col. 1376] 1624. Perhaps *territoria*, “territories, estates, lands,” or *villatoria* for *villaturia*.] **Villaturia**, territories.

[1625] [Note: [Col. 1376] 1625. Martinius: *viocurus*, “road-layer, carrier of a shield.” Semler: *viocarus*, without interpretation; then *virgo*, “a shield-bearing woman,” from *caestus*, that is, the belt with which a newly married woman was girded.] **Vioturus**, and immediately afterward *cestifer*, “belt-bearer.”

[Col. 1377] [Note: [Col. 1376] 1626. Others read “the membrane of the virgin in which it dwells”; others, “the member of virginity in which it dwells.” See Prudentius with commentary, p. 1214.] **Virginal**, the virgin’s members, in which it dwells.

[Note: [Col. 1377] 1627. *Virgobretus*. Among the Aedui. From Julius Caesar.] **Virgobretus**, the name of a magistrate.

[Note: [Col. 1377] 1628. Perhaps *viriae*, *viriolae*; Book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 31, no. 16.] **Viria**, a bracelet, an armlet.

[Note: [Col. 1377] 1629. Others read *virosus*; others *vultuosus*, which is preferable.] **Viriosus**, harsh.

[1630] [Note: [Col. 1377] 1630. *Virops*, from *viripos*, that is, “able to take a husband.”] **Virops**, a woman who now requires a husband.

[Col. 1377] **Visor**, those who see.

[Note: [Col. 1378] 1632. *Viticus*; rather *villicus*, from other glossaries.] **Viticus**, an administrator, a collector of a villa’s rents, a landlord of an apartment building.

[Note: [Col. 1378] 1633. *Patricus*; more correctly *patrinus*.] **Vitricus**, *patricus*, a stepfather.

**Unca manu**, with a closed hand, μυλλῆ (*mylle*).

[1635] [Note: [Col. 1378] 1635. Others call *unicuba* a woman who sleeps alone, even if married.] **Unicuba**, a wife of one husband.

[Note: [Col. 1378] 1636. *Unorum*. Graevius: *uno ore*, “with one mouth”; others *unitorum*, “of united things.”] **Unorum**, of many.

[Col. 1378] **Votificantibus**, making offerings, presenting gifts.

**Utensilia**, travel expenses.

**Vultuosus**, sad.

# Z

[1640] [Note: [Col. 1378] 1640. Acro, commenting on Horace, Book I, Satire 6, explains *zanga* as “skins.” See Ducange.] **Zanga**, a skin.

Acro: “He covered the middle of his leg with black skins.”

[Col. 1377]

## NOTICE: Concerning certain omitted materials and the indexes that follow

[Note: [Col. 1377] We have postponed those indexes to the end of volume LXXXIV. Editors.]

[494] A few small works, not even of considerable length, still remained, which I had formerly intended to place among the appendices. But since for the most part they are fragments taken from Isidore’s other works, and are repeated more than once in the *Synonyms*, in the *Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, and in the *Rule of Living*, while some are also less worthy to be listed among the appendices, it seemed better to add nothing further to what has been explained chiefly in the third part of the Isidorian works.

In the Index of Sacred Scripture, one must bear in mind that Isidore often adheres to the Vulgate version, sometimes follows the Old Latin version, occasionally expresses the sense rather than the actual words of the Bible, and at times even names one sacred writer in place of another.

Besides what is evident from the Index of Subjects, it should be observed that the canons drawn from and corrected on the basis of Isidore’s works are found in volume I, p. 206 and following; that the index of authors cited in the *Etymologies* and the books of the *Differentiae* is given in the same volume I, p. 431 and following; not to mention the Glossary that I have just presented.
